crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte at tage på udveksling ved Aix-Marseille Université, da jeg gerne ville bo i Sydfrankrig og forbedre mit franske. Aix-en-Provence er en studieby og der er derfor virkelig mange studerende i byen, og jeg tænkte derfor, at det ville være et godt sted at tage hen som udvekslingsstuderende. Universitetet er anerkendt og et af Frankrigs største universiteter.
info_ease: Alle nødvendige informationer blev sendt til mig via KU-mail, så det var nemt at finde dem.
arrival_assistance: Jeg ankom to uger før semesteret startede, hvor jeg deltog i en introduktionsuge sammen med de andre jurastuderende. I disse uger fik vi både praktiske informationer og lærte hinanden at kende. Der er en koordinator der tager sig af alle udvekslingsstuderende på jura, som er behjælpelig hvis man har nogen spørgsmål.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Der gik noget tid fra jeg var blevet nomineret fra KU til at jeg fik en mail fra Aix-Marseille Université. Alle nødvendige informationer stod i de mails jeg modtog med nogle guides til hvordan man skulle gøre.
registration_help: Hvis man havde nogen spørgsmål til processen, kunne man sende en mail til koordinatoren fra Det Juridiske Fakultet i Aix
registration_success: Jeg blev tilmeldt alle de kurser, som jeg havde skrevet mig op til.
registration_advice: Man skal være opmærksom på, at der er ret mange frister, som skal overholdes. Man skal derfor tjekke sin KU-mail ofte (også i sommerferien). Alle informationer er på fransk, og det kan derfor godt tage lidt ekstra tid at læse og udfylde alle ting korrekt. Ellers var processen ikke så svær.
course_level: Alle kurserne svarer til 6 ETCS, og de er derfor ikke så dybdegående som man er vant til på KU. Undervisningen foregår udelukkende på fransk, så på den måde bliver man stadig udfordret i forhold til indholdet.
teaching_comparison: Måden at undervise på er markant anderledes i Frankrig. Der er ingen powerpoints eller lignende til forelæsningerne og der er meget begrænset dialog. De franske studerende skriver alt hvad der bliver sagt ned, fordi det kan komme som spørgsmål til eksamen; Der er ikke nogen bøger, så pensum er hvad professoren har sagt til forelæsningerne. De franske studerende er meget søde til at dele deres noter med udvekslingsstuderende.
courses_enrolled: Droit de la propriété littéraire et artistique Droit des libertés fondamentales Droit de la presse et de l'édition numérique Droit des organisations internationales Droit international économique
recommended_courses: Jeg kan klart anbefale “droit de la presse et de l'édition numérique”. Indholdet af faget er spændende og handler meget om pressefrihed og pressens udvikling generelt. Professoren er nem at forstå og virker engageret i faget. "Droit de libertés fondamentales” minder mere om forfatningsret end om IGR, hvilket man skal være forberedt på. "Droit de la propriété littéraire et artistique” var et spændende fag, og med mange spændende diskussioner – dog havde jeg lidt svært ved at forstå professoren i dette fag.
unexpected_costs: Jeg skulle købe nogle ting til mit kollegieværelse, eftersom der hverken var tallerkener, bestik, glas, elkedel, dyne osv.
cost_comparison: Aix-en-Provence er en dyr by i Frankrig, men ikke dyrere end man er vant til i København. Generelt er det billigere at gå ud at spise, drikke et glas vin, gå i byen og tage offentlig transport. Man kan f.eks. komme til Marseille tur-retur for 2 €, hvis man er studerende.
activities_available: Aix-Marseille Université har et meget bredt udvalg af sport og andre aktiviteter, man kan melde sig til gratis. Derudover bliver der løbende arrangeret fester og andre aktiviteter for Erasmusstuderende og også for studerende på Det Juridiske Fakultet.
activities_recommended: Jeg vil anbefale at melde sig til sport gennem universitetet, da det både er sjovt og en oplagt mulighed for at møde især franske studerende på. Man kan gå til næsten alle sportsgrene gratis. Jeg gik selv til padel tennis og fitness en gang om ugen – særligt padel tennis kan jeg anbefale!
weekend_recommendations: Der er virkelig mange muligheder for at tage på endags- og weekendsture fra Aix-en-Provence. Marseille ligger ca. 30 min. væk, og vi tog derfor forholdsvis tit til Marseille. Hvis man vil bade, kan man tage til ”Les Calanques” ud fra Marseille, som har nogle virkelig gode strande. Derudover har jeg været på ture til bl.a. Montpellier, Nîmes, Arles, Avignon og Nice. Der er også gode vandremuligheder, bl.a. bjerget Sainte-Victoire, som ligger lige uden for Aix. Der er en TGV-station ved Aix-en-Provence, så man kan komme hurtigt til andre større byer i Frankrig – bl.a. Paris, som tager ca. 3 timer.
culture_adjustment: Jeg havde ikke de store problemer med at tilpasse mig fransk kultur. Jeg havde boet i Frankrig før, så på den måde var det ikke så nyt for mig. Franskmænd er generelt søde og særligt i Sydfrankrig er folk lidt mere afslappede.
socializing_tips: Man kan melde sig til sport gennem universitetet. Ellers er det nemt at møde dem hvis man er på bar eller lignende.
cultural_challenges: Jeg skulle vænne mig til at alt ikke var så planlagt, som det måske er i Danmark – f.eks. fik jeg først mine datoer for eksaminer at vide ugen før jeg skulle op.
culture_appreciated: Sydfrankrig er et dejligt sted at være på udveksling. Der er godt vejr hele semesteret og folk er søde og imødekommende. Der er virkelig mange caféer og restauranter i byen, og folk sidder stort set altid uden for med et glas rosé eller en kop kaffe. Stemningen er generelt mere afslappet i Sydfrankrig, end den er i f.eks. Paris. Jeg kan kun anbefale at tage til Aix.
top3_advice: Der er virkelig mange udvekslingsstuderende på Aix-Marseille Université, så det er nemt at få venner og møde nye mennesker. Selvom det kan være udfordrende at følge med, når alt foregår på fransk, er de generelt forstående for, at fransk ikke er dit modersmål – også til eksaminerne. Aix-en-Provence er ikke en særlig stor by, men det betyder samtidig, at man hurtigt føler sig hjemme og ofte støder på folk man kender, når man går rundt i byen.
other_useful_info: Jeg var afsted i efterårssemesteret og vi var ca. 60 Erasmusstuderende alene på jura. Universitetet har derfor rigtig mange udvekslingsstuderende hvert år og er vant til at tage hensyn til udvekslingsstuderende. Alle eksaminer for Erasmusstuderende er mundtlige. I starten af semesteret er der en introduktionsuge samt en uge med fransk undervisning, hvilket jeg vil anbefale at deltage i, hvis man kan. Jeg lærte en masse folk at kende i introugen.
most_rewarding: Jeg fik venner fra mange forskellige dele af Europa, lærte en masse fransk, fik en masse nye oplevelser og besøgte andre dele af Sydfrankrig. Jeg kan klart anbefale at tage på udveksling!
greatest_challenge: Den største udfordring var sproget. Alt undervisning og eksaminer var på fransk, og særligt i starten var det svært at følge med til forelæsningerne. Jeg havde haft fransk i gymnasiet og boet i Paris, så jeg kunne godt tale hverdagsfransk på forhånd – men jeg havde ingen erfaring med juridisk fransk. Selvom det var en udfordring, er jeg glad for, at jeg kastede mig ud i det. Jeg bestod alle mine eksaminer, selvom mit franske ikke er helt perfekt. Mit indtryk er også, at der bliver taget hensyn til, at man ikke har fransk som modersmål.

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Sometimes, it can be difficult to adapt to different systems/administrations. I had some hardships with the French administration, which is why I only give the experience a 9/10, but overall a really successful exchange year.
registration_process: The registration for the courses was quite easy for some, more complicated for others. As I attend a university where my courses must be pre-approved, it complicated the process, as I would have to get the pre-approval and then sign the online learning agreement again, since it was mandatory at Aix-Marseille University to change the learning agreement. This was complicated be the fact that the courses at the university had changed for the next 5 year period, which made it harder to get the course contents. However, both universities were swift and the process worked out.
registration_help: It was always possible to contact our coordinator at Aix university. She helped us with various problems, such as getting course contents for new classes etc.
registration_success: Completely successful.
registration_advice: Now it should be easier to get the courses, depending on your home institution it can vary how easy the process is. If you're required to do pre-approval I would suggest doing it in advance. However, you have 3 weeks upon arrival to change classes, which was enough time to rearrange your learning agreement etc. Therefore, it is likely it will work out with the classes you want to take.
academics_comments: Sometimes, it can be difficult to adapt to different systems/administrations. I had some hardships with the French administration, which is why I only give the experience a 9/10, but overall a really successful exchange year.
course_level: My classes were well suited for me. I would recommend doing most master classes, as the level might be a bit lower on the bachelor courses. I did 4/5 classes on a master level, and they were the most interesting courses. However, the bachelor classes are still difficult, as they tend to be more based on the internal legal system in France, and going in with no knowledge of this makes the bachelor classes challenging as well.
teaching_comparison: It does ressemble the lectures in the amphitheatres at UCPH, but there is a difference, which is that at UCPH you have your books and you come prepared for class for the professor to elaborate on the things in the books. At my host institution you have to come to lectures, but you don't have additional mandatory books or articles, it is solely the teachings of the professor you must know, and you must know it well. Therefore it can be challenging, since the French students go to class, open their computer, write down a dictation of everything the professor says, and then study it for the exams. As an exhange student this can be challenging in French, but I managed by listening/understanding the lecture and asking the French students for their notes, so that I could study before my exam. This went well.
courses_enrolled: Each course is 6 ects, so I took 5 classes; Droits et libertés fondementales, Histoire des relations internationales, Introduction au droit de l'environnement, Ordre juridique approfondi l'Union européenne and Criminologie.
recommended_courses: I would recommend Introduction au droit de l'environnement since it is a course that is very interesting if you're interested in green/environmental law, the French system has a lot of this in place and its very eyeopening. Furthermore, I would recommend all my classes as the professors very understandable and very welcoming towards the exchange students.
unexpected_costs: The cost of living in France is quite high, so therefore it took me a bit by surprise. There were no further costs that surprised me, as I had budgeted for insurance, transportation etc.
cost_comparison: Food in general. It is not as expensive to eat out at restaurants, but the supermarkets are quite expensive.
activities_available: There is a really great Erasmus network in Aix that arranges both social activities and cultural activities at a very reasonable price. Furthermore the host institution had various arrangements that were free and easy to access. The best part is the sports, as exchange students can participate in 2 different sports at the university free of cost, just as the French students can.
activities_recommended: Doing the sports activities. Even if you're not that sporty, it can be a great opportunity to meet French students and get a new network, and since it is free it would be a shame to miss out on this opportunity.
weekend_recommendations: Go explore the area/region. South of France is well connected with public transportation, and it is inexpensive if you make a free bus card at the station. It's 2 euros to visit most places then. There are beautiful cities, hikes and the ocean nearby, and Marseille is only a 30 min bus ride away, with museums, shops and beaches. There are also boat rides, and the Calanques which is a must visit.
culture_adjustment: Easy, since France is not that different from Denmark. The only thing is the politesse, which takes some adjustment. Saying "vous" every time you encounter someone/speak with your coordinator or professor.
socializing_tips: Do sports. There is a buddy system set up to meet French students. Furthermore, they are very nice and will help you both socially and academically, so approaching them in class is a great opportunity.
cultural_challenges: Just the language was difficult at first.
culture_appreciated: The food and the region with its incredible nature.
top3_advice: 1. You have to speak French or be prepared to learn. 2. Have an open mind and practice French with the French or other exchange students - leave your English behind for the time being. 3. Enjoy your time but make sure to attend every class as this is where you get prepared for your exams. The classes are interesting and worth your while!
other_useful_info: Don't stress it, everything works out in the end. It may feel overwhelming at first, but there are many friends to be made and your language will improve if you put in the effort.
most_rewarding: Improving my French and making international relationships with people from all over Europe, learning a new way of university with interesting subjects such as environmental law and finding out that I'm able to do what I put my mind up to.
greatest_challenge: The language, but it improved very fast and I became friends with native French speakers so it helped me a lot.

cultural_challenges: Sometimes the french can be a bit harsh, but usually theyre nice!
culture_appreciated: Food, the laissez-faire culture
top3_advice: - be open-minded - seize opportunities - help each other and be there for each other (meaning the other exchange students)
other_useful_info: If youre having challenges with the erasmus coordinator sometimes, be patient, youre not the only one. If you live in a dorm, the kitchens are not the best but think of the prize! Yes, study but also, if you start a moth before exams youll be more than fine.
most_rewarding: The self-development, getting better at french, meeting people from all over and maybe even friends for life.
greatest_challenge: The part in the beginning where I didnt have any social connections. Its weird suddently going from a place where theres always stuff to do and then having "nothing". But that changes within a week and then its great! Also doing daily life things in french, like speaking to someone in a store is also a good challenge but that just makes you better!

crucial_aspects: I did not get accepted for my first priority, but I was very pleased to be accepted on Alexandria University instead, and really enjoyed my stay there. It of course had to be a destination where I would be able to speak arabic every day outside of my studies as well, because I study Middle Eastern Languages and Societies with arabic as my chosen language.
info_ease: i would say it was easy, we were notified via email in advance.
arrival_assistance: We were offered to be picked up at the airport, and in general they encouraged us to contact them if we experienced any issues.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It went smoothly as far as I remember, as we weren't many students, and it was easy to communicate with the administrative workers at the university
registration_help: I'm not sure what is meant, but the help was sufficient if i remember correctly.
registration_success: This was no problem, as it was a mandatory stay with pretty much fixed subjects. the others from copenhagen, same semester, all took the same classes as i did for this reason so it was very easy.
registration_advice: I'm pretty sure it's easy to communicate with the Tafl center about subjects so contact them and ask what is available
course_level: it was BA level, and i had the higher level in the classes where we were divided in levels. this was a very good way.
teaching_comparison: I found the teachers very encouraging and competent, and they very well knew the struggle of learning a new language, because they're so used to work with foreigners. This was very nice and positive. Sometimes there was of course a language barrier, but it wasn't a big issue for me, I think it worked out good. From some teachers at UCPH, i've unfortunately experienced less encouragement and patience, which i don't view as a good teaching strategy. It intimidates and it worsens the gaps in level, so did really like being at Alexandria university and experiencing a different teaching style. This doesn't apply to all my teachers/professors at UCPH, but a few.
courses_enrolled: Fusha, modern standard arabic. 7,5 ects egyptian colloqial arabic. 15 ects arabic litterature. 7,5 ects
recommended_courses: It was a mandatory stay with pretty fixed subjects, so i would of course recommend these, and if you havent had these subjects before, and they match your arabic level, then it definitely makes sense to do these courses.
unexpected_costs: My phone bill back home was not able to be paused, so i had to pay that on top of my egyptian phone bill. The insurance of course cost a bit. It was super cold when we arrived, so we had to buy thick blankets (dyner) to sleep with. For instance having to buy bottled water all the time as well was not something I'd thought about beforehand. the residency card was 150 dollars on top of our regular visa of 25 dollars, so this cost a bit, but we were told in advance. because i was in egypt though, these things were not very expensive, so it was fine - it was more costly the trips we went on. But i did also try to save a lot of money and not spend so much during the trip.
cost_comparison: Most things were less expensive than anticipated, and for instance the flight tickets weren't so expensive. Some things were much cheaper than in denmark, and then other things were almost the same price as in denmark, but that would for instance be danish butter. it was mostly not expensive unless you experiences someone wanting a higher price from you because you obviously was a tourist.
activities_available: there was a singing club, a cinema club, a cooking club and a calligraphy club - and other events in the city, that teachers would let us know about
activities_recommended: i attended them all, and enjoyed it. i would especially recommend cooking club
weekend_recommendations: To see more of the city and more of egypt - and grab any opportunity that you have the energy for, to experience new areas, foods, cities, meet new people etc.
culture_adjustment: it wasn't very hard, but i've also visited the country before. people are very nice and curious and happy to answer your questions when you have any. people can also be a bit too approaching, which is annoying, but it's okay to say no, and to say you're not interested in talking
socializing_tips: i wish i had done this more, so i dont have advice. but maybe there are events you can attend, and people are so open and talkative mostly, that i would recommend to just go op to someone and ask them about themselves and introduce yourself. and to try to find the people that you really want to become friends with, because that will be such a great thing to take with you, a new friendship
cultural_challenges: that women are not as present in the streets and out and about, and they're not as approaching as men - so it's harder to find female friends than male friends in egypt. and in general there is a lot of sexism, that i've experienced, a lot of cat calling and so on, which is definitely the biggest challenge for me.
culture_appreciated: the openness and warmheartedness of people
top3_advice: not sure
other_useful_info: not sure
most_rewarding: the language improvement and the experiences and trips, and my relations to people i met during the semester.
greatest_challenge: The experience of being a woman, knowing how much different everyday would have been as a man.
other_comments: in general a very good stay though, i really have enjoyed it.

crucial_aspects: I would say that it has been a mix between academic opportunities as well as my wish to explore new cultures in the middle east, where it will also be easier for me to further advance my communicative skills in arabic, as well as seeing and experiencing the daily life, norms and traditions from up close instead of through books and movies. This exchange has also allowed me to meet a lot of different people from all-around the globe and exchange our thoughts on several topics and future ideas and hopes.
overall_comments: In the beginning it was hard to get into the daily life and get accustomed to living in a different place and culture, but I think both the staff at the university as well as my companions from DK helped me easing myself into the life and experience of it all Overall I have enjoyed my stay, some of the classes could have been better structured level-vise (the egyptian dialect), but I also think a bit more preparation from my side would have helped it.

In this class we were told about general norms and what to be careful of by the teacher and got several recommendations for restaurants and cultural experiences we could enjoy during our stay.

unexpected_costs: None that I can remember
cost_comparison: meat was more expensive than expected and vegetables were much cheaper I remember normal stuff like brooms and such costing quite a lot but it was quite confusing how some items were cheap and others more expensive than expected, but I cannot remember any specific items or prices at the moment
activities_available: We had calligraphy, cooking, cinema and singing clubs, but I know the Norwegians had some different clubs as well such as journalism
activities_recommended: I enjoyed the calligraphy and cinema clubs
weekend_recommendations: I can recommend going on small trips to the surrounding cities such as siwa, aswan, luxor, cairo and all those
culture_adjustment: I got into the local culture after around 3-4 weeks I think and after I found some local friends that I could hang out with
cultural_challenges: At the moment I can't think of any
culture_appreciated: I really enjoyed the open-mindedness of the people and how we could talk with anyone about anything and how easy it was to find partners for a discussion
top3_advice: Remember that this is also a cultural opportunity and not just a time to study Focus on developing your language Enjoy your time and don't stress about the school so that you cannot go out to enjoy the culture and history
other_useful_info: Enjoy your time and keep in contact with both the locals and other exchange students
most_rewarding: I would say it is both the advancement of my Arabic and my new cultural view on several topics and experiences I don't just know about the different traditions and norms but have experienced them and the impact that religion has on a whole society and how people can coexist
greatest_challenge: Sometimes I could get homesick and feel alone in a different part of the world, but you can always remember that the others are probably experiencing the same, and that this is a new and exciting experience

crucial_aspects: I had heard really good things about the TAFL center at Alexandria University
overall_comments: Two of my subjects worked out really good and I feel like I liked coming to the classes and learned a lot! Unfortunately I can’t say the same about the Egyptian dialect class.
info_ease: All the formal things with visa and so on was easy enough. It was a bit more tricky with how to find a place to live, maybe TAFL could help the students a bit more there, maybe reach out to them before arrival and talk with them about options
arrival_assistance: We had a PP presentation about life in Egypt and how to handle it, I think it was a little bit dramatic. We were also introduced to our studycalender and the rules at TAFL and I think that was also a bit over the top; fx that it said we would get minus points if we spoke English in class. In the end we could anytime ask a question in English and it wasn’t so strict luckily, so I think TAFL needs to relax a bit more on the first day and not scare the students like that
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Two of my subjects worked out really good and I feel like I liked coming to the classes and learned a lot! Unfortunately I can’t say the same about the Egyptian dialect class.
registration_process: We had to send some things to them before we arrived, it was pretty simple, and then we needed to get a student visa when we got down there, and we spend a few hours at TAFL + the police station in groups - it was very simple - we had a nice woman with us that told ud what to do
registration_help: Staff from TAFL
registration_success: I couldn’t choose the classes myself, but it was easy to register for them
registration_advice: Relax:)) It’s all gonna be fine
academics_comments: Two of my subjects worked out really good and I feel like I liked coming to the classes and learned a lot! Unfortunately I can’t say the same about the Egyptian dialect class.
course_level: Good level: very challenging but nice teachers and I ended up becoming really good on those 4 months - expecially in understanding and talking more freely and in longer sentences
teaching_comparison: Very different teachings of Arabic. TAFL has some amazing methods, like we basically try to only speak in Arabic in class, we don’t use the dictionary but sinply try to use our own (small) knowledge to understand a poem fx and we use the root system a lot - and I think this is where the Arabic language is genious!
courses_enrolled: MSA, Egyptian dialect and Literature 1
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Literature 1 and MSA but it was mainly because of my teachers. It is very nice to learn some Egyptian dialect but I would wish that the subject maybe took up less space/hours pr week and then was a bit more focused, more homework and smaller classes. It’s mainly a speaking class but I didn’t speak so much compared to my two other subjects. I didn’t feel like a really learned much more new knowledge after the first month or so. I think it went too fast with completing 3 books and I generally feel like the class wasn’t so good organized
unexpected_costs: Remember to do something about your Danish simcard so you don’t pay double during the semester. Eating out can be really cheap and probably also cheaper than buying and cooking yourself. Make sure to bring some money for shopping nice glass, ceramics etc and go on trips to Cairo, Marsa Matruh, Siwa etc
cost_comparison: Everything is generally extremely cheap
activities_available: 4 clubs I think: cooking, singing, caligraphy, Cinema
activities_recommended: Check out operas, events going on around the city. Fx at the French Institute, at the Library or the Anna Lindh Foundation
weekend_recommendations: Greek Club restaurant has a private Beach which is nice (cost 400 EGP I think) otherwise walk around Alex, go to the big fishmarket (that also has a lot of other things) Trips to Cairo, Marsa Matruh, Siwa, maybe Fayoum, Port Said etc
culture_adjustment: It was easy enough to follow the dressing rules and so on. But it’s generally very different than DK as you could expect so be prepared for that
socializing_tips: Consider to get a language partner, try to use some of the new words you learn in class when you go shopping or take a cab or something
cultural_challenges: People wanting to take photos, shouting at you, maybe even sexually harassing you

crucial_aspects: I had not been to the Gulf region before, and have mostly/only traveled in North Africa (Tunisia and Egypt, particularly Egypt) so it was an exciting opportunity to travel once more and travel to a part of the Middle East which I had not made acquaintance with in person before.
overall_comments: The university and trip itself was great, I was struggling with some financial issues and was surprised to find the study-visa to be more expensive than I had anticipated (more so than e.g. Egypt), which also meant I probably didn't explore as much as I could and should have, on top of that there were some challenges with getting the necessary Erasmus/Exchange-documents in order, but aside from that the university in Dubai was excellent and I met friendly and helpful people so overall a good if shorter than expected experience.
info_ease: Good question. The campus was relatively small and I had been put in contact with a student from AUD already who was very helpful in telling me about transportation system, cost of living, helping me search for accommodation, as well as being a personal connection when I had questions about the campus and such. A map of the campus would've helped though, like a digital one sent to the mail so you can see which building is which.
arrival_assistance: I suppose I covered that in the previous question but the first day I had to ask the guard where the "B"-building was, and at one point I had to ask my friend where the "C"-building was to find the administrative offices. Other than that the University was right next to the metro station so that was pretty easy.
arrival_comments: As I said, a map of the campus would be awesome. Even just a basic of "which building is which, and if you have to go see the student affairs offices - here's the main building" or something.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The university and trip itself was great, I was struggling with some financial issues and was surprised to find the study-visa to be more expensive than I had anticipated (more so than e.g. Egypt), which also meant I probably didn't explore as much as I could and should have, on top of that there were some challenges with getting the necessary Erasmus/Exchange-documents in order, but aside from that the university in Dubai was excellent and I met friendly and helpful people so overall a good if shorter than expected experience.
registration_process: I received mails fairly early on about upcoming application and enrollment, including information about things i had to do (visa, health checkups, enrollments, tuition fees - which i then didnt have to pay anyway because I was an Erasmus student - and their website application form, and later course selections). I dont remember it in detail as it started way back in march or april while I was on exchange in Cairo. But i remember the process felt confusing and it seemed like the contact persons (which also wasnt entirely clear whom i had to report to) were not always up to date on what i had sent and needed to send or action to take.
registration_help: They have a university website aud.edu with lots of information and forms, although i think it would've been cool for a section of "if you are an exchange student, click here - step by step guide on what you need to do" a bit similar to Mobility Online here, with an easy-to-overview design so you constantly know where you are in the process.
registration_success: I mean my situation was quite unique because it was a two-semester Erasmus exchange, so the classes by and large were OK for registration, but I had to renew my pre-approval application from UCPH so often that it itself became a challenge to make all ends fit. On one occasion the registration messed up however, as there were multiple classes at AUD for the same course, and the person at AUD registering me put me on the correct course but the wrong class - which collided with the timing of another course I also applied for, meaning I couldn't get in, and by the time I found out, there were no spots left on that course. But overall it was OK, their course overview (such as this: https://online.aud.edu/Campus/fall2023ug.asp ) was very well done with clear overview of courses, schedules, spots left, room numbers, and later on exam dates.
registration_advice: The undergraduate course schedule is invaluable so they should use it for the class registration, and then look up course catalogue for a deeper description of the courses (which matches the course code in the course schedule, use ctrl + F to find the desired code quickly) As for registration.. im not really sure, be sure to have a spare 10.000 DKK for the visa however, even though no tuition or course fee is paid. IF you are in doubt about whom to contact, I would suggest going directly to Sara L. Montero and either ask her, or ask whom you should contact. She's the dean of student affairs and extremely helpful, and when you do arrive you can go by her office in the C-building(the big building with the cafes and campus-kiosk and everything), unless she's off somewhere she's usually happy to have a conversation with an exchange student, even if you haven't arranged any meeting.
academics_comments: The university and trip itself was great, I was struggling with some financial issues and was surprised to find the study-visa to be more expensive than I had anticipated (more so than e.g. Egypt), which also meant I probably didn't explore as much as I could and should have, on top of that there were some challenges with getting the necessary Erasmus/Exchange-documents in order, but aside from that the university in Dubai was excellent and I met friendly and helpful people so overall a good if shorter than expected experience.
course_level: I took BA courses but i took at least one course which i THINK might be on MA level if it had been at UCPH, it was a much more advanced macroeconomics course focusing on the financial institutions and monetary system, it was fairly difficult. I also took an arabic class aimed at native arabic speakers which was naturally way above the vocabulary level I was used to, but it was really good anyway. The rest of the courses were pretty standard for what I'd expect at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Much more classroom and lecturing, the lectures are also way shorter(50 minutes per class M/W/F, and 75 minutes tuesdays and thursdays) so we usually didnt have time for in-group work except for the arabic class which sometimes incorporated it. I wouldve liked more of the UCPH style of "you work in groups within the class" whereas AUD was more top-down lecturing with input from students towards the teacher, and some courses featured heavy expectation of solving assignments particularly at home which isn't bad in itself, but it felt both more independent (as you'd have to study more on your own) and simultaneously less in-class capacity for getting the material under your skin. I would have enjoyed more pair/group-work, and maybe also feedback other than just a grade / right-wrong signs from my assignments.
courses_enrolled: Arabic Proficiency I Principles of Microeconomics / Principles of Macroeconomics (two courses) Applied Econometrics Money & Banking
recommended_courses: I mean it depends on their major and interests, if its arabic students - the arabic proficiency classes are very good to give a vocabulary challenge, I feel like Im fairly good at UCPH - except maybe for grammar - but I got very challenged as it was in an environment of arabic speaking natives, who might be on a similar level with grammar-proficiency but naturally have a much higher vocabulary even in standard arabic which isnt their "mother-tongue" (as most speak dialects) but they still have a better command of the language than me, and it was pretty clear from reading out loud to translation. Applied Econometrics is a great course for data analysis, it wasnt so heavy on the mathematics of econometrics, but still enough statistics (which is a recommended pre-requisite, that i didnt have though i do have some statistical knowledge) that if you arent from a math background you'll have to study. The micro/macroeconomics courses are as you can expect and i suppose on a similar level to UCPH, good courses in my opinion but my degree while being within the arts, is turning more towards economic-cultural bridging due to my natural interest in more "social-sciences"-aspects of the MENA region. Unfortunately I didnt try the cultural courses about MENA as i wanted, like mentioned above, due to course-registration conflicts.
unexpected_costs: Okay so its pretty important to give my personal circumstances: my apartment was probably slightly more expensive than campus-apartments, so the rent could be slightly lower. I also lived almost two hours away by bus and metro, so i paid 50 DKK a day in transportation costs. Food costs was a pretty low end for me as i was trying to save and eat cheaply, living off chicken (which was only like 18 DKK for 400g), noodles, and strawberry milk. The visa costs of 10.000 DKK was a huge surprise, which would include health insurance and such hence the high price. I ended up not paying for internet on my phone as i had wifi in the apartment, mostly to save costs. Otherwise its a few hundred DKK a month i suppose.
cost_comparison: Chicken breast was pretty cheap. I shopped at something called Shaklan in International City, only about 9 AED or 18 DKK for a 400g chicken breast. Foreign products, candy, milk and such were fairly expensive but not really worse than Denmark. Overall I maintained a similar budget to Denmark or slightly less, out of my own choice. Eggs were also not too expensive if i remember correctly. Some shops/supermarkets like Shaklan is also cheaper than Carrefour, which is otherwise my go-to supermarket chain in MENA. I didnt cook so much myself other than cooking noodles, but they do have a lot of rice and other asian-food since they have so many indians, filipinos, and other asians there. Meat / rice and likely carbs in general were pretty cheap, but its also standard in the Middle East to eat such types of food.
activities_available: They had sports teams including Badminton areas, Swimming pool, but im unsure if you can just use them or if you have to be part of their sports teams. There were often plastered advertisement on the activity-walls however about things you could apply for (including dancing), and letters were sometimes sent out with news of upcoming events - they also have an instagram page (@audstudentlife) theres also lots of benches outside to sit at, which was comfortable during the autumn and early winter as the temperatures were temperate (around 20-25C). People were also friendly but i didnt find it as easy being social as in Egypt, but thats probably more to do with me having difficulty being social in general. - oh and before i forget, they DO arrange tours to the deserts and such, which would be a fantastic opportunity.
activities_recommended: Go on sightseeing trips arranged by the University or someone affiliated with it. If you're a little more social adept than me it might also be possible to go out and enjoy some cafes with friends from the university, but i didnt really manage to do that myself so i dont have a lot of advice. You could try and ask the offices in the C-buildings though or Sara Montero if she has ideas, she's ready to do her part to integrate and give students a good time. Also ask already before arriving! I was given an exchange student that was supposed (but couldnt get visa) to go to Denmark to study at UCPH and she was a great pen-pal for me. Try and ask AUD if they can make it a practice to offer their students to sign up to be "contact-friends" for incoming exchange students from abroad.
weekend_recommendations: Try and see Palm Jumeira or some of the exciting places in Dubai, I was very constrained financially so mostly I met up with two friends (one saudi and one algerian) coming from abroad, with the former visiting.. I think Hilton Hotel or something around the Jumeira area, it was really cool to visit that place honestly but I didnt have the most luxurious experience due to financial shortage myself.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. I mean the Emirates is obviously culturally different especially with regards to the natives (who wear their traditional clothing, you aren't in doubt). But there are a lot of foreigners, and the UAE is accustomed to being more accommodating of westerners, particularly americans, so honestly i didnt feel much of a difference except i didnt have many "close" people to talk to.
socializing_tips: I never really find a good technique, though they often made contact with me to hear where I am from etc and greeted me in the halls so they were pretty friendly, but arguably it was easier for me to socialise in Egypt as they are naturally more "aggressive" in making friends. But honestly, just try and talk with the guy or girl next to you, i felt they were very friendly even the Emiratis though the girls can be a little more reserved. My biggest tip though: Get their whatsapp numbers in class, we used it a lot anyway to communicate and coordinate.
cultural_challenges: Indians (relevant on the metro) have a different concept of personal space than most people in the west. Egyptians also, but i found the indians to be worse. Other than that, my own biggest challenge has been the socialising part. Egypt like i said was easier because they mostly come to you, but the Gulf is more reserved as a far as socialising goes - and "hanging out" with mixed genders is even more difficult. I did make a good female friend there, but we only really talked deeper on a personal level towards the end of the semester, despite talking often on whatsapp throughout the semester since she often had questions regarding economics and such.
culture_appreciated: I felt people are very friendly and helpful, in fact I felt a bit sorry for the exchange student who was supposed to come here - because the visa authorities in Denmark were everything but helpful, even though she did everything on time, whereas I was met with a lot of accommodation despite messing up deadlines and such. Unfortunately she didnt get it in time and wasn't able to come, I met her once or twice at AUD in Dubai to say hi. But definitely the friendliness and respect, I always feel like MENA gives some "white privilege" to westerners, which is heartwarming.
top3_advice: 1. Make sure your finances are in order. I left with around 24.000 DKK (having faced some hardship due to having to lend money to family members the year prior) and it was not enough. Flight, apartment, and rent before you get SU, 1500-3000 DKK for food as well as Visa adds up very quickly. If you can make sure you have at least 40.000. 2. Pretty niche, but i bought books for the courses equivalent to what i was going to study abroad (actually i had bought them the year prior because i knew id be taking those courses anyway at UCPH), buy them at UCPH's library then you can study the courses beforehand. I had chewed through my economics textbook within the first three weeks of the semester, which meant i was pretty well prepared for the course material. Personally i like it that way if i can be well prepared for the course so i can relax more during the semester, this is maybe more related to economics where you already sort of know what you will be studying. 3. My phone broke during my stay and i wasnt able to fix it until i came home because the new phone i had was unable to scan my passport and the local municipality cant issue you a new activation code online/through webcam meeting, so i was effectively locked out of my UCPH mail, Bank access (except for physical card), everything requiring MitID to access.
other_useful_info: hmm.. i wish i had more to say on this but i cant think of any.
most_rewarding: For me, definitely seeing the UAE. I didnt get to see all i wanted, which again the moral of the story is "dont be poor" haha but yeah.. i feel like my trip has been good to sort of getting me acquainted with the area, so if i go again it would be easier to find my way around and go enjoy places sometime later in life. A huge part of it was to simply see the country as I had never been there, and I guess mission complete on that part.
greatest_challenge: think i said it more than enough but my skinny bank account. It really put a strain on everything.
other_comments: A VPN is useful as the UAE blocks some websites (also most voicechat), and IF you happen to be in a very unfortunate situation where you have to make an online payment and its getting blocked, its likely because of this - use a VPN to get around it. Its not illegal to use, only if you use it for something that actually is illegal. Also, UAE speaks english for the most part. *rarely* have i had to use arabic to communicate, as most are international and speak english just fine, so dont worry about that. Other than that, enjoy it.

weekend_recommendations: Nature in Greece: especially the Islands Thassos and Skopelos, the mountains in Northern Greece, and the beaches of Halkidiki. culture_adjustment: The first month I was really frustrated about the inefficient university system. But when the registration were done, it was actually not hard adapting to the culture. Ps. you almost always get free desser after a dinner :)
socializing_tips: Engage in the events at the beginning. Even if you don't really like the event in it self, it's a great way to meet other students, and as many students find their main friend groups in the first weeks, it's a great idea to attend in the beginning.
cultural_challenges: All systems work poorly and you need to print almost everything
culture_appreciated: The open and warm people, the no-stress culture, eating for hours at the tavernas,
top3_advice: Make an effort to find a nice apartment with a fair landlord/landlady, and likeminded roommates.
other_useful_info: Though it's annoying that the university system is inefficient and slow, it means that you don't need to stress either
most_rewarding: Going on beautiful trips with nice people, especially spending the weekends on the beaches of Halkidiki, visiting islands and the bordering countries. Also the good weather (especially April - June) was amazing to live in
greatest_challenge: Registration / receiving Academic ID card, living with roommates for the first time, and being surrounded by younger, more energetic, party people for such a long time. Most students were at the age of 20-24 where I was 27/28 and one of the absolute oldest.

crucial_aspects: Visiting Australia was always something that excited me, so I chose the country and then the university after.
overall_comments: My exchange was amazing! I met so many amazing people, made a ton of friends, had exciting courses and got to travel around the coutry. My only regret is that I could only go for one semester and that I had to leave all my friends behind.
info_ease: It was quite a challenge. Because Australia is so far away there was significant time delays every time I contacted the university. Also, the way ANU does things are totally different from KU so there was a lot of adjustment. Australia is also quite hard to get into, so having all papers, vaccines etc. prepared was a massive task that took hugh amounts of my time.
arrival_assistance: The university hosted a series of information and social events. The friends I made at the student hall were also helpful.
arrival_comments: Going on exchange is a MASSIVE undertaking! Do not underestimate the amount of time you will spend preparing. Sometimes it seems like it won't be worth it, but it definetly will!
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My exchange was amazing! I met so many amazing people, made a ton of friends, had exciting courses and got to travel around the coutry. My only regret is that I could only go for one semester and that I had to leave all my friends behind.
registration_process: I cannot remember everything anymore, but there was a lot of deadlines and things to fill out before. Also, ANU uses many different websites which makes it all very confusing. The time difference also meant that I had to get up in the middle of the night sometimes to do odd jobs.
registration_help: ANU has a support mail, but it was very slow and the time difference did not help.
registration_success: I was succesful, only problem was they cancelled all my courses. It is also a very slow process, and ANU can be a bit hard to convince that you fulfill the pre-requisites.
registration_advice: Take it slow! Start early! And write down everything! Make "to-do lists", write notes contact ANU do everything to make it as easy as possible for yourself and make sureyou don't forget something or have to go through hundreds of documents again to find what you are looking for.
academics_comments: My exchange was amazing! I met so many amazing people, made a ton of friends, had exciting courses and got to travel around the coutry. My only regret is that I could only go for one semester and that I had to leave all my friends behind.
course_level: The level was very fitting (maybe a bit easy sometimes compared to KU). However, ANU does very poorely in describing the course-content. I signed up for what I though was introduction to Game Theory but turned out to be introduction to Advance Game Theory, because ANU does a lot of Game Theory during their micro courses. Also, the lecturer was a math graduate from MIT, so the course was extremely math-heavy, went fast and had lots of assumed knowledge.
teaching_comparison: Less scheduled classes and lectures (i.e. you have to study more at home). People don't show up for the lectures, so be prepared for the lecturers to directly ask those who show up. Once you've gotten used to this though it is nice since they learn your name and take a direct interest in your learning. Also the tutorials are just going through the answers to questions, so you have to prepare everything beforehand.
courses_enrolled: - The World Economy since 1800 - Development, Poverty and Famine - Behavioural Economics - Game Theory
recommended_courses: Behavioural Economics was super interesting and professor Simon Grant was really engaging (many found him a bit heavy on notation though). Also, Development Economics is super relevant and professor Martine Mariotti did super well in relating course material to the real world and assign interesting articles for the course. I would highly recommend these two courses!
unexpected_costs: There were many events and social activities that cost money - though I highly recommend going. Also, you want to experience Australia and everyone flies everywhere, but with rising petrol costs it is VERY expensive. Most national parks also cost money to go to.
cost_comparison: Food is more expensive in Australia. Mobile phones are really expensive as well. I spent less on transport than expected, but probably because I lived in Canberra and bought a bike early on.
activities_available: Every kind of sport, board game societies, cultural societies, academic clubs - they had everything.
activities_recommended: Board game nights were really fun and a great way to meet people. Also sign up for some student hall sporting events or become a coach (I coached badminton), since you will also meet a lot of people this way.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Tasmania! So beautiful! Tidbinbilla nature park is nice, War Memorial in Canberra is interesting and the parliament building is very impressive. I also recommend getting a bike and exploring Canberra and especially biking around lake burley griffin.
culture_adjustment: It took a while to make friends, but Australians are very friendly and outgoing, so it wasn't a big problem.
socializing_tips: Join a student hall and just talk to people. Also participate in many O-week events, even if it seems scary.
cultural_challenges: Australians go out clubbing a lot, which I don't really like. But I found friends who didn't go out too often, so that suited me very well.
culture_appreciated: The people and the rich history of the indigenous people. I highly recommend attending a "welcome-to-country"-ceremony
top3_advice: - Be open to everything. - Join a student hall. - Prepare yourself to cry when you leave and have to say goodbye to your friends.
other_useful_info: Engage with your lecturers. They really appriciate someone talking to them about things other than marks or extensions for assignments and they give back what you give them. Also say yes to everything in the beginning. It can be exhausting but you will make a lot of friends and the you can relax a bit later on in the semester.
most_rewarding: The friends I made.
greatest_challenge: Saying goodbye to my friends and Australia - it is such an amazing country.
other_comments: Go on exhange! But know that it is a LOT of work.

crucial_aspects: Jeg søgte ANU, da universitetet rangerer som en af de bedste i verden inden for international politik og antropologi. Derudover synes jeg, at det var spændende at komme længere væk end Europa og springe over den danske vinter.
info_ease: Der var lidt bøvl med at vigtige e-mails blev sendt til forskellige mailadresser. Nogle blev sendt til min private, mens andre blev sendt til min ANU e-mail. Jeg mistede derfor et obligatorisk arrangement den første uge. I semester 1 (det der svarer til forårssemester i DK) bliver der afholdt O-Week, hvor der er en del studiearrangementer arrangeret af universitetet. Sideløbende med disse arrangementer holder de forskellige "on-campus houses" også aktiviteter, som er væsentligt mere relevante.
arrival_assistance: Jeg modtog ikke ligefrem assistance, men jeg ankom også meget sent om aftenen. Der kører vist shuttlebusser fra lufthavnen i introugen, men ellers er det nemmest og billigst at komme til Canberra med en greyhound fra Sydney, da busstationen er tæt på. Der blev afholdt et par arrangementer for udvekslingsstuderende under orientation week (O-week), som fungerede meget godt. Her blev man introduceret til australsk kultur, mad, normer mm., og hvor man også kunne møde de andre udvekslingsstuderende.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Man tilføjer kurser på platformen ISIS. Man skal dog først have søgt om godkendelse til faget. Hvis du er kandidatstuderende skal du uploade dit optagelsesbrev/indskrivelsesbekræftelse (helst underskrevet af en studievejleder). Jeg kom til at uploade mit bachelorbevis, hvilket gjorde, at de kun ville give mig bachelorkurser. Det gav en del bøvl under O-Week, hvor jeg brugte lang tid på at tilmelde mig fag i stedet for at deltage i sociale aktiviteter. Jeg fattede ikke, at man også skulle tilmelde sig på MyTimetable (det som svarer til holdundervisning). Husk på, at det er muligt at skifte fag de første par uger, så vær ikke bange for at skrive til administrationen, hvis du ikke er vild med det fag du er på. Derudover er det en god ide at sikre sig, at kurserne ikke ligger oveni hinanden, det kan man nogle gange se gennem TimeTableViewever. Jeg havde to fag som lå på samme tid, hvilket betød, at jeg så det ene fag gennem optagelser og var til det andet fysisk. Disse programmer bruger du kun den første og sidste uge. Derefter er det Wattle som svarer til Absalon og din e-mail som du skal tjekke.
registration_help: Studievejledningen findes ved Kambri, hvor man også får sit studiekort. Her er hele tiden åbent under O-week, hvor man kan stille alle sine dumme spørgsmål. Derudover kan man skrive til Global Programs som arrangerer hjælp til udvekslingsstuderende, men de har ofte ret travlt under O-Week, så prøv at ring eller møde op på kontoret, hvis de ikke svarer på e-mails.
registration_success: Jeg fik alle kurser jeg ønskede. Der er virkelig mange kurser på ANU, og det er sjældent, at de bliver fyldt helt op. Derudover er holdene ofte mindre end på mit studie, hvilket gjorde at dialogen mellem underviser og studerende var langt bedre.
registration_advice: Se om du kan enrolle i dine kurser før du ankommer, så du kan fokusere på at være social i O-week.
course_level: Kandidatfag
teaching_comparison: Jeg har mest været vant til, at en professor underviser i en forelæsningssal med 300 mennesker, hvorefter at en instruktor (ofte en kandidatstuderende) diskuterer med de studerende. At man rent faktisk blev undervist af en professor eller ekspert var en kæmpe forskel. Derudover skal du forberede dig på, at der langt mere skriftligt arbejde end på KU - men mindre læsning (i hvertfald i forhold til statskundskab). Man har ikke en final-exam, der bliver din endelige karakter. I stedet har man en lang række assesments i løbet af semestret som så bliver til din endelige karakter.
courses_enrolled: Pacific Studies in a Globalising World Strategic Studies Global Security Foreign Policy Analysis
recommended_courses: Jeg ville anbefale alle samfundsvidenskabere at tage mindst et antropologisk fag og/eller et om Asia-Pacific. Det er deres specialeområde, og selve universitet blev grundlagt med henblik på at forstå kultur, politik og sprog i området omkring Australien. Jeg tog Pacific Studies in a Globalising World, hvilket blev undervist af Katerina Teiawa, som vandt prisen for bedste underviser i Australien i 2022. Det var et meget anderledes fag, hvor man f.eks. kunne vælge at lave et kreativt produkt eller performance som sit afsluttende projekt. Det var overraskende nok det fag som tog mest af min tid, da der var en hel del undervisning og forberedelse. Jeg var lidt skuffet over Strategic Studies, som mest bare var folk fra militæret som ville lære om, hvordan man bedst lagde militære strategier. Global Security var også virkelig spændende og ret let - visse dele er repetition fra IP3 på statskundskab f.eks. sikkerhedsteori. Foreign Policy Analysis var også meget spændende og semi-let, hvor man lærte om forskellige variabler, der har betydning for udenrigspolitiske outcomes.
unexpected_costs: Det var en ret øv udgift at skulle betale husleje en hel ekstra måned efter jeg var taget afsted. Har hørt om enkelte, der slap ud af deres lejekontrakt før tid, men stort set alle blev afvist - også folk som havde lægeerklæringer på at skulle hjem. Derudover var der et ret stort depositum på 1000 dollars, en residential fee på 300 dollars og to ugers forudbetalt husleje på 670 dollars som skulle betales med kontrakten. Sørg for at få markeret fejl i værelset, når du ankommer, så UniLodge ikke tager røven på dig, når du flytter ud. Dertil kom en cleaning fee på ca. 100 dollars, når man flyttede ud.
cost_comparison: Jeg har ingen idé om, hvor meget jeg brugte på mad, personlige ting mm.. Priserne på fødevarer er de samme som i DK. Alkohol og tobak er væsentligt dyrere (dog ikke vin, som er billigere - længe leve Goon). Barista kaffe er billigere end i DK ofte kun 15-20 kr., men der er sjældent filterkaffe. Fly rundt i Australien er også semi-dyrt ift. Europa. Jeg plejede at rejse med Greyhound til Melbourne og Sydney, og med Murrays når man skulle en weekendtur til stranden.
activities_available: Der var stort set mulighed for at dyrke hvilken som helst sport - men det deltog jeg ikke i. Nogle highlights var Mounteneering klubben som tager sporadiske ture til bjergområderne. Der blev også arrangeret, at udvekslingstuderende kunne komme ind på stadion og se en australsk fodboldkamp (footie, som er en mærkelig blanding af rugby og fodbold). Der blev også arrangeret en weekend surfertur, som jeg dog ikke var med til.
activities_recommended: Hvis man har dykkercertifikat kan man tage afsted med dykkerklubben, som tager op til Great Barrier Reef til en brøkdel af den normale pris. Hvis jeg havde vist det ville jeg nok have taget certifikat førhen f.eks. i Indonesien, hvor det er billigt. Jeg tog et pitstop både på vej hen til Australien og på vej tilbage. Jeg rejste alene i Bali i to uger, og rejste med nogle venner i Vietnam på vejen tilbage til DK. Det var en virkelig god beslutning, man fik taget den lange rejse i nogle bidder, fik rejst rundt omkring og derudover blev flyrejsen til Australien også billigere.
weekend_recommendations: Hvis du gerne vil rejse rundt i Australien skal du helst gøre det i den første halvdel af semestret. For i den anden del bliver der rimelig presset med afleveringer. Jeg tog korte ture rundt i Australien med andre studerende hver weekend i den første halvdel af semestret f.eks. Blue Mountains, Jervis Bay, Sydney, Mount Kouziousko, Batemans Bay, Hyams Beach og Broulee. Man har en lang ferie i midten af semestret, hvor vi fløj til Cairns og lejede en van, hvor vi kørte ned til Byron Bay. I anden halvdel var der så mange opgaver, at jeg kun nåede en kort weekendtur til Melbourne. Jeg nåede ikke til Western Australia, Darwin, Uluru eller Tasmania. Flybilletterne var for dyre, da jeg først ledte i sidste øjeblik.
culture_adjustment: Super let. Australiere er nemme at omgåes med og virkelig velkomne over for tilflyttere (særligt europæere, som de jo synes er meget spændende). Og min oplevelse var, at det var endnu lettere at være ny på ANU campus, da stort set alle er tilflyttere og står uden et social netværk. De fleste kommer fra Sydney, Brisbane eller Melbourne.
socializing_tips: Vær ikke bange for at snakke med australiere. Det er langt mere socialt accepteret at snakke med folk på gaden eller på en cafe end det er i Danmark. Australiere er ret spontane, så det er ikke ualmindeligt at lave store aftaler i sidste øjeblik.
cultural_challenges: At de kører i venstre side er sygt mærkeligt. Lige indtil at man vænner sig til det i de sidste uger af opholdet, hvorefter det føles sygt mærkeligt at køre i højre side i DK. Det kan i nogle tilfælde være svært at forstå enkelte australiere, men mit indtryk er, at de ændrer deres accent og brug af udtryk, når de snakker med internationale.
culture_appreciated: Spontanitet, åbenhed og humor
top3_advice: 1) Få søgt en masse legater. Jeg havde held med at få 10.000 kr fra Nordea Fonden og 13.000 fra Knud Højgaard. Det er dyrt i Australien. Men husk at det også er en investering i din fremtid, så cut dig selv noget slack og tag et SU-lån. 2) Få rejst i starten af semestret for det er hurtigt slut. Mit råd er at omgive sig med nogle andre studerende som er lige så friske på at rejse. 3) Bo på campus for Canberra er røv, og alle de sociale ting foregår her. Jeg kendte to fyre som fik en stor lejlighed, hvor de kunne invitere folk over til fest - men med mindre det er tilfældet så hold dig til campus.
other_useful_info: Wifi og internet er lort i Australien.
most_rewarding: Alt. Både de gode og de mere udfordrende oplevelser. Udveksling udvider din faglige horisont og opbygger utrolig meget akademisk og personlig selvtillid. Udveksling kan ikke måles som en cost-benefit - se at komme afsted.
greatest_challenge: At jeg søgte standby plads og skulle ordne et helt års forberedelse med legater, visum, ansøgninger på en 1,5 måned imens jeg havde bachelor, fritid og arbejde. Derudover var der virkelig mange skriftlige afleveringer ift. KU, og jeg havde endda valgt fag som havde en relativt lidt. Jeg var lidt presset af, at jeg arbejdede 15 timer om ugen på ambassaden i Canberra, hvilket også betød, at der var visse ting jeg gav afkald på.
other_comments: Fuck UniLodge. Og når ja, se om du kan vælge fag som ligger de samme dage. Så du f.eks. kun har undervisning mandag, tirsdag og onsdag, så man kan rejse på en forlænget weekend.

crucial_aspects: The academic opportunities but also places where I could travel.
info_ease: It was actually pretty easy to get the information from UCPH before arriving in Australia. Søren, the exchange coordinator, was so helpful and made it easier.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any from UCPH, as it was not required. We had an incident on campus during the semester, where UCPH contacted me to secure if I was okay.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You apply for courses through ISIS (there website), but you get answers of registration a week before study start. This makes it hard to know your schedule.
registration_help: Student central and every college have their own student help desk
registration_success: I got 4/4 courses but ended up switching one course
registration_advice: Choose the courses they find interesting, then show up in the first week and figure out whether you want to continue on the course. Otherwise, you have two weeks to change the course
course_level: The level was okay. I took three of the toughest courses within the College of Business and Economics. But the level of courses in general varies within the different colleges
teaching_comparison: I think that UCPH is more theoretical in addition to many other universities. ANU was more applied, which was also tough, since you are not used to think in the same directions.
courses_enrolled: Applied Valuation Applied Corporate Finance Portfolio Construction Trading & Markets
recommended_courses: All of them. Trading & Markets is one of the best courses that I have ever had. They had readings for every week and pre-recorded lectures, then you show up to an in-person lecture to discuss what the pre-recorded lecture was about. In the tutorials they built a trading platform, where you used the theory in practice.
unexpected_costs: Cleaning fees, buying equipment for the room. Basically, everything that had to do with housing
cost_comparison: Beer, was expensive. Meat also expensive. The coffee is great everywhere in Australia, and only 5 dollars (approx. 25 DKK)
activities_available: Everything. Every Village on campus played against each other in different types of sports. There were also the Sports club for the University. A lot of parties, and different creative clubs were available.
activities_recommended: Sports. They gave you the opportunity to be social.
weekend_recommendations: I went to Tasmania, Melbourne and Sydney. Sydney is only 3 hours in a bus away. Fly Jetstar, as this is cheap. Many took the bus from Canberra to Melbourne, which is 8 hours. But the flight takes 50 minutes and is only 20 dollars more expensive.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. As the Australian and danish culture is more or less the same.
socializing_tips: Live on campus. I chose Yukeembruk Village. Even though it was expensive I had a lovely time there. You felt welcome from day one and they host social get togethers every Thursday.
cultural_challenges: Australian people are so kind
culture_appreciated: I appreciated the kindness.
top3_advice: 1) Enjoy ANU. Canberra is not known to anyone, but it is a great city. I loved every bit of it. ANU is one of the best universities in Australia. I met a lot of Australians, and they told me that people on exchange want to study in Sydney or Melbourne, because they are large city, but the students in Australia actually want to study at ANU. 2) Socialise. The time in Canberra will be so much better with friends. 3) Travel around. Canberra is close to the east-coast. Visit some cities, go on surf camp and enjoy that you do not have the same winter down under as we have here 4) Remember sun-screen. The sun is dangerous.
other_useful_info: Do not be afraid to ask questions. The employees in the student central are nice.
most_rewarding: The academics and making friends worldwide.
greatest_challenge: Going far away from home

crucial_aspects: High academic level, English speaking country, and potential outdoor experiences.
overall_comments: Great experience all around!
info_ease: Their website had a lot of information, the student accommodation that you end up at will contact you and send you packing lists etc. Only thing that was never mentioned in time was that the week before the orientation week is an additional and also optional orientation week.
arrival_assistance: We had a student senior resident at the student accomodation whose job it was to assist us. The international student office at the university was also really helpful and timely.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Great experience all around!
registration_process: You register on their registratoin website with a reserved spot (because you are on exchange) and then you sign up for the lectures and lab sesions that fit you in a first-come-first-served basis.
registration_help: Your senior resident, as well as other assigned help you can find at the student services or your residence.
registration_success: I got all of the classes i wanted.
registration_advice: Sign up for you exercise sessions asap, the good time slots gets filled up pretty quickly.
academics_comments: Great experience all around!
course_level: A lot of master courses are essentially just bachelor courses you can do as a masters student without it begin much different from taking it as a bachelor student.
teaching_comparison: Here all courses give you a score from 0-100 with total transparency of what points you need to get a certain grade. This also means that all assignments and exams just give you points that counts towards the 100 and everything becomes very quantitative.
courses_enrolled: Computational networks in Computing Analysis 2: Lebesgue Integration and Hilbert Spaces Statistical Machine Learning Computer vision
recommended_courses: Computational networks in Computing was a really interesting course that we don't currently have at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: To apply for a student visa you have to pay a somewhat substantial fee.
cost_comparison: Meat is cheaper but greens is more expensive, otherwise it is pretty comparable to Denmark.
activities_available: Every kind of student club you can think of is available.
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend the Caving club if you want to try something really different on your stay abroad.
weekend_recommendations: Take weekend trips to the larger cities when not spending it around Canberra.
culture_adjustment: Somewhat easy, Australia is a really western culture like Denmark.
socializing_tips: Get into an on-campus residence, then the rest is easy.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: The language was really fun to experience first hand and in a day-to-day setting.
top3_advice: 1. Remember to enjoy other cities than Canberra. 2. Join some student clubs. 3. Go to the big events like Big Night Out that take place on campus
other_useful_info: Remember that the week just before the orientation week is also an orientation week that focuses on your residences.
most_rewarding: Getting to experience such a great part of the world, both the nature and the people.
greatest_challenge: Having time to see it all and do all of the stuff. Australia is such a big and rich country you could spend a lifetime being a tourist there.
other_comments: If you go to Australia, definitely go see what the inland areas and the outback are like.

crucial_aspects: First of all, I wanted to go abroad an experience other cultures. It was important to me to go to a place, where English is the first language. I considered both Washington, Edinburgh, Sydney, and Canberra as possible destinations. I also considered Tokyo, but that was with different expectations of my stay than if I went to ANU in Canberra. I chose ANU in Canberra as my first priority also because it is a part of IARU, which is why it was possible for me to apply for a large grand from The Novo Nordisk Foundation. Without this grant, it was not financially possible for me to go on exchange. Tokyo is also a part of this, which is why I considered this as well. Secondly, my girlfriend has lived in Australia and has a close connection to the place. I wanted to get to know the culture that she had lived in, so this was also a part of my choice. I also have heard from several people that Australians are, like Danes, laid back and humorous, which is also important to me. I went on exchange to get friends, not a cultural chock. Of course, looking back, there was some cultural chock, but at the same time, the locals around me have been very open and easy going.
overall_comments: I have been feeling quite lonely for some of my stay and have struggled with my mental health for a long time before I went on exchange. It has been very challenging be alone on the other side of the Earth. I'm looking forward to being with my friends and family again. The academic experience was mixed as well, where I have several times seen lectures state things that are wrong or misleading. Also, during the semester I had either almost nothing to do or I had several assignments stacked upon each other or exams right around the corner. The semester felt very "back-loaded", meaning that almost all the work I did during the semester was in the last 4 weeks of it, where I personally handed in assignments worth around 60% of my final grades in total in the last 4 weeks of the semester as well as doing three exams worth 55%, 55%, and 50% each for each course in a span of 5 days, with only one week of studying before-hand, even though the exam period spans two weeks. Maybe I was just unlucky, but it felt unnecessarily hard. Also, the exam formats were not of good quality, and two out of three written exams had mistakes in them, which had to be corrected during the exam. The academic level was not as high as at University of Copenhagen, but the exams were very challenging, especially because of their formats, in my opinion.
info_ease: ANU themselves handed out a lot of information, and I was feeling very overwhelmed and missed some important stuff, because we got so many emails. My hall was helpful, but they were not very quick to answer. I had a lot of problems with my visa, but that had nothing to do with the university. Going to Australia is easy AFTER you've received your visa. I think that ANU was very slow, as they were only handing out acceptance letters in December/January. I got mine in the beginning/middle of January, meaning I had under a month to get my visa in place (I was flying out of Denmark the 5th of February). I got my visa 5 hours before my flight, even though I applied in mid January. For me, I had wished that they were quicker, as I needed only the acceptance letter to get several grant and visa applications going. I was ready for this already in the beginning of November, if I remember correctly. ANU did fail to - in time - tell international students when to arrive to campus. This information was given out only a few weeks in advance of the start of my stay, and I had bought tickets several months before this based on a more rough calender, stating that the semester started the 15th of February, where as the orientation and social weeks went on the two weeks prior to this. This was not known to me before after buying my flight ticket, which I did not buy excessively early.
arrival_assistance: I received a lot of help, when I arrived with small practicalities as well as general orientations. I wished I had gotten more social help, but that is more the responsibility of Bruce Hall, where I lived. ANU Global Programs has been extremely helpful throughout the whole process, both before and during my stay. They were very invested in my well-being and were available every workday of the week.

They do not offer topics courses to exchange students, which I think is a weird rule that doesn't make a lot of sense to me.
registration_help: Global Programs were available and also had a presentation on how to do this.
registration_success: Semi-successful. I got many of the courses I wanted, but I did not get Special Topics in Statistics, which was something I wanted to do.

course_level: The level of the courses I took were of a good standard. There were some discrepancy between exam difficulty and course difficulty in some courses, but I expect that that is pretty normal, and something course convenors always have to adjust. For a university of this size, I would have expected higher quality of lectures. The lectures were all recorded. Some of the TA sessions were good, but it mostly depended on the TA themselves.
teaching_comparison: It was more applied than at UCPH. Statistics and Computer Science at UCPH is also very theoretical. This made many of the courses easier to do, but on the other hand, when you are used to be taught with a bottoms-up approach, it can feel weird to be taught with a more top-down approach. Not all courses were like this, though. The exams only counted for around 50-60% of the exams, and the rest of the grades were based on assignments.
courses_enrolled: Statistical Machine Learning Applied Time Series Analysis Survival Models Computer Vision
recommended_courses: I would recommend Statistical Machine Learning and Applied Time Series Analysis. They were good courses. The first is very theoretical compared to the other. The other two were not very interesting.
unexpected_costs: The visa was costly, I payed around 5000 DKK because I had to get a medical examination as well.
cost_comparison: Pricing in Canberra is close to Copenhagen in general. I do not currently have a good overview of my monthly fees though.
activities_available: Many kinds of sports, hiking clubs, cave diving, social clubs of all kinds etc.
activities_recommended: Depends on what you like.

culture_adjustment: Very easy, Danes and Australians are very alike
socializing_tips: Just be open and approach.

culture_appreciated: The openness and laid back vibes.
top3_advice: Go to a social hall (BnG) Save money for trips See as many people as possible
other_useful_info: Go. To. A. Social. Hall.
