crucial_aspects: I chose to study in Beijing because it was important to me to be in mainland China. I wanted to experience what it’s really like to live in China and to immerse myself in its culture and history.
overall_comments: Overall, my experience was highly positive in terms of the academic quality of the program, the friendships I formed, and the meaningful personal and cultural memories I gained during my time there. However, the poor organization and the lack of clear responsibility between Bisu and KU created ongoing challenges. Communication issues between the two institutions often caused confusion around administrative matters, which led to unnecessary stress and sometimes took away from the overall experience
info_ease: BISU did not provide much clarity or take clear responsibility. Information was often hard to find, and it was difficult to communicate with them when questions came up. When I did receive answers, they were sometimes inconsistent, which caused confusion and added stress.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival at BISU a few days before registration day, we received several emails with important information. However, the emails were overwhelming and unnecessarily complicated, which caused stress given the limited amount of time we had to read through and follow all the rules and required documents. After arriving at BISU, most information was shared through a WeChat group that included new students and teachers. This group became the main way to receive updates and ask questions. The first few days were very practical and focused on completing many administrative tasks, such as document submission, registration, student card collection, health checks, class division, and other requirements for new students.
arrival_comments: There was little direct guidance from teachers, and students were generally expected to manage these processes independently. However, it was possible to ask questions in the group or contact teachers privately if needed. There was very little assistance, along with a clear lack of responsibility and communication. It often felt as though the different teachers and staff members in charge were not communicating with each other. As a result, information was inconsistent, and students were frequently given unclear or conflicting instructions, which made the process more stressful and confusing than necessary
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall, my experience was highly positive in terms of the academic quality of the program, the friendships I formed, and the meaningful personal and cultural memories I gained during my time there. However, the poor organization and the lack of clear responsibility between Bisu and KU created ongoing challenges. Communication issues between the two institutions often caused confusion around administrative matters, which led to unnecessary stress and sometimes took away from the overall experience
registration_process: You had to go to different buildings on campus to complete the registration, which made a lot of walking and was a bit tiring, but the process itself was not very difficult.
registration_help: You can ask the teachers for help, if they don't know they usually are willing to guide you for further help
registration_success: We were divided into classes based on the oral and online tests we completed, and I was very satisfied with the class I was placed in. If the level felt too difficult, students also had the option to switch classes.
registration_advice: Don’t stress too much, even though there are times when strict deadlines can feel overwhelming. I noticed that many people didn’t complete everything on time, and it usually wasn’t a big issue. Going through the registration process with friends definitely helps, or finding people to complete it with, since it can be confusing—especially in a foreign country. Supporting each other makes the whole experience much easier.
academics_comments: Overall, my experience was highly positive in terms of the academic quality of the program, the friendships I formed, and the meaningful personal and cultural memories I gained during my time there. However, the poor organization and the lack of clear responsibility between Bisu and KU created ongoing challenges. Communication issues between the two institutions often caused confusion around administrative matters, which led to unnecessary stress and sometimes took away from the overall experience
course_level: The level of the courses was well matched to my language abilities, which made the learning process both manageable and effective. Being placed in a class based on my actual level allowed the teaching to be more focused and structured, and I felt that the pace was appropriate without being overwhelming. This made it easier to follow the material, participate in class, and see clear progress in my language skills compared to my previous studies.
teaching_comparison: You get divided in class based on your level. For me my level was bit higher than my other danish classmates. The language courses were divided into six different subjects, and I was placed in 中级三班, which was slightly more challenging than some of the other classes. I could clearly feel a difference compared to my classes in Denmark. In China, most lessons were teacher-led, with students listening, practicing, and completing exercises under the teacher’s guidance. In Denmark, the classes felt more focused on group work and independent student activities. I personally preferred the course structure in China, as it felt more effective, more challenging, and, most importantly, faster-paced, which helped me make progress more quickly.

recommended_courses: The language course
unexpected_costs: We had to get health check around 300dkk and student insurance even though I had one already from denmark. The one In china was around 300dkk.
cost_comparison: Food and transport very cheap, housing expenses was a bit expensive since I decided to live off campus
activities_available: The music club. The school organized New Year event performances that students could attend or take part in. In October and November, the school also held a cultural day for international students, which was very fun and interesting.
activities_recommended: The cultural day was very fun and interesting to visit different booths from different countries
weekend_recommendations: You can visit the city or if you wanna go to other city like Tianjin which was very close to Beijing I would recommend.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy since im from a Chinese household, and I've been to china many times before. But if your Chinese is very limited I would say it's quite hard to begin with because the teachers, staff and everything is in Chinese. Housing as well is very hard to to do when you don't speak Chinese.
socializing_tips: I actually didn't interact with local students, most of the time was international.
cultural_challenges: Not challenging but you just have to get used to the social norms in public etc.
culture_appreciated: The locals were very nice and helpful, which made adjusting to life in a new country much easier. Whether I needed directions, advice, or help with everyday tasks, people were generally friendly and willing to assist.
top3_advice: To be aware of the lack of responsibility from both BISU and UCPH. I faced many problems related to my passport, and there was very little communication or coordination between the two schools when I needed help. I had expected KU to take a more active role when issues arose, but as an individual, I ended up having to handle most of the problems on my own. The UCPH coordinator was not very helpful, which caused a lot of stress. UCPH provided very little information beforehand, so when I arrived at BISU, I was surprised by many things that I hadn’t been informed about. Get your Chinese apps and vpn ready, do research so you don't get too lost when you arrive.
other_useful_info: Honestly, the best way to get accurate information is to contact students who have already studied abroad. Asking the coordinators, UCPH, or BISU often doesn’t provide the real answers or the detailed information you need. Try to gather as much information as possible before you go to avoid being overwhelmed and to reduce unnecessary stress.
most_rewarding: The memories I made are unforgettable. I met so many amazing people whom I will cherish forever. Despite the poor organization between the schools and BISU, the friendships and experiences I gained made the entire experience truly worthwhile.
greatest_challenge: There are a lot of practical things you have to take care of when you are in China. The country is quite strict about rules, and your passport is required for many processes. Almost everything is digital—transport cards, paying for meals, ordering food, and receiving packages—which makes life very convenient and easy. However, the process can be frustrating if something doesn’t work, and it’s often unclear who to ask for help. That’s why having friends in China is so important and helpful.
other_comments: Enjoy it, this has been one of the best experiences of my life. There were many ups and downs, but for me personally, it was completely worth it. I met amazing people, made lifelong friendships, and learned so much—not just academically, but also about myself and the world. Living in China was incredible: it was convenient, full of delicious food, and had so many fun places to explore. The challenges I faced only made the experience more meaningful and helped me grow. Overall, studying in China was unforgettable and something I will always treasure.

registration_success: Some of them ended up not existing when I arrived. Then there are some that I wanted to join but couldn't because only students from that specific department could. Also, a big and important part of the process is to write emails to the professors and ask to be enrolled in their classes. This was very new to me, but you have to kind of beg to be enrolled, explain why the course is important to you, etc.

But I ultimately went on exchange for academic opportunities, which was fulfilled.
course_level: As the BA in Denmark is 3 years and the BA in Turkey is 4 years, it can be a bit difficult to find out which courses are adequate for your level. Both my easiest and hardest courses were 3rd year courses, so you really have no idea, but looking at the syllabuses thoroughly can give a good hint.
teaching_comparison: Very different, at least to the sociology department at UCPH. In Copenhagen I only have big lectures with 60+ students in auditoriums. At Bogazici most of the courses are in smaller classes with between 15-40 students. Also attendance and active participation is mandatory and will affect your grade. It is thus more comparable to the danish "gymnasium". But personally I learned way quicker and I appreciated the more personal relationship you get to the professor, where they actually know your name, compared to the danish system.
courses_enrolled: - Sociology of religion - World Environmental History - Politics and society in The Middle East - Social Anthropology - History of social and political thought - Pilates
recommended_courses: Although being very challenging, I recommend the course Sociology of Religion, as it is a rare chance of having this type of course, a "seminar". Here we sat around a big table with the professor and together discussed and analyzed the weekly texts. I felt very privileged to have such an interesting course. Also, I strongly recommend the course "World environmental history" if you have the opportunity to be taught by professor Faisal Husain.
unexpected_costs: There are quite a lot of costs associated with attaining the residence permit. You have to pay for a 1-year turkish insurance + to get your rental contract notarized and translated + pay for getting professional ID pictures taken + pay for registering as a tax payer (even though you are not going to pay taxes). I don't know excatly how much I used in total on the residence permit application, but at least 2500 DKK. .
cost_comparison: Prices are getting insane in Istanbul, so don't expect it to be inexpensive. But the schools cafeteria which serves 3 meals a day is VERY cheap. It costs around 6 DKK for a meal. I highly recommend saving some money by eating here.
activities_available: They have an abundance of clubs: sports, knitting, dancing, political, cooking, climbing!
activities_recommended: I really recommend that you join the clubs, it's here you will meet people and also through the clubs that parties at the universities are thrown.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going on at least two trips. I went to Fethiye with the Bogazici Erasmus club and to cappadocia with ESI (Erasmus sports istanbul). I recommend that you follow ESI on instagram, they have many activities every week.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy.
socializing_tips: Join the clubs and go out and drink tea with them on the breaks in class.
cultural_challenges: I am not sure how much I can express here, but the political climate is obviously very different than in Denmark. It's both way more present in your daily life, while at the same time not being something that people talk openly about. I would not advise against going to Turkey because of this, but I wish I had had a deeper understanding of how it affects university students. I advice, that if you're choosing Turkey as your destination of exchange, then talk to students who have done the same, to learn about the lived experiences of the politcal climate.
culture_appreciated: Many parts, but especially the street animals everywhere, also in classrooms! (Probably not the place for you if you're allergic) and of course the food! I highly recommend trying the dessert "Künefe".
top3_advice: The campus is beautiful, you will spend excessive time on public transport, and don't stress too much about grades. The professors go easy on exchange students.
other_useful_info: Yes, try to plan your schedule so you have some lunch breaks at campus. It's where a lot of the social interaction takes place.
most_rewarding: That I grew academically a lot and got to go beyond the euro-centric perspectives I've learned at UCPH.
greatest_challenge: To have time to socialize and go on adventures - I had a hard time with the required attendance and weekly assignments after being used to the way university is in Denmark.

crucial_aspects: I chose Boston because of the language, because I like the city, and because Boston is home to some of the best universities in the world. I was recommended Boston College by a fellow KU student who had been there the previous year.
overall_comments: Being on exchange in Boston was really great. However, the whole process upon studying in the US was very extensive as well as very expensive. It's a lot of work and money for just 4 months abroad.
info_ease: I think it was fairly easy to find information about preparation for studying in the US because KU's international team held meetings with us and provided us with an informative powerpoint. It was difficult to find specific information about Boston College though.
arrival_assistance: The international team at Boston College was very helpful. They had arranged orientation/introduction days for all the exchange student, and I knew where to find them if I had any questions.
arrival_comments: There were a lot of repetition but it was still helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Being on exchange in Boston was really great. However, the whole process upon studying in the US was very extensive as well as very expensive. It's a lot of work and money for just 4 months abroad.
registration_process: In January, when you create your formal application for Boston College, they ask you to list ten courses you're interested in. They have an online catalogue. You only have to take 4-5 courses but they cannot guarantee that you will get all of your top choices. Make sure that the courses you want the most do not overlap. In the spring, when you become accepted to the university and get your student account, you can see what courses they have put you in. You will still be able to make adjustments. Either you can write them an email, and they can switch you to another course if the class have any spots left. Or you can wait to the add & drop period which is the first one or two weeks of classes. Here you can try out different courses and make adjustments to your schedule. Sometimes the professors can overrule the initial student availability in their class. I ended up getting all the courses I wanted to, even though it was quite a hassle during the first two weeks.
registration_help: The international team explained to us how the registration worked, and the professors are responsive and helpful as well, if you want to take their class.
registration_success: Some of the classes, I wanted to take, overlapped which was a shame. However, the four classes I ended up wanting (that did not overlap) I managed to get all of them.
registration_advice: Make sure the courses do not overlap. If you are statskundskaber on 5th semester - I was able to take DAK3 but they did not have EP. Instead I took Microeconomics which I had pushed from 3rd semester. They have lots of electives to choose from, and those were easy to get accepted by KU.
academics_comments: Being on exchange in Boston was really great. However, the whole process upon studying in the US was very extensive as well as very expensive. It's a lot of work and money for just 4 months abroad.
course_level: I think the academic level of my courses were pretty similar to my courses at KU. In my experience, the BC classes were less critical and more practical than KU. We did not really talk about ontology and epistemology much.
teaching_comparison: The BC style of teaching was more similar to Danish gymnasium. Closer professor-student relations and more running assignments and feedback. The amount of classes and readings were about the same.
courses_enrolled: Microeconomic Theory (Økonomi 1) Political Parties, Voters and Party Systems in Comparative Perspective (DAK3) Globalization (valgfag) United States Foreign Policy 1945 to Present (valgfag)
recommended_courses: United States Foreign Policy 1945 to Present (valgfag) was really interesting. It was sort of a history class where we learned about and discussed US foreign policy since WWII. We discussed the strategics of different paradigms and events and different presidents. The professor was great and I feel like I learned quite a lot about American foreign policy.
unexpected_costs: We had to pay a Campus Infirmary Fee on $303 when we came, in addition to the Health care. Gym membership on campus was $180. Athletic Gold Pass (to watch all the BC sports games) was $150.
cost_comparison: Dorm room and meal plan was more expensive than I had expected. I should have known this earlier had I made better research. Living off-campus in an apartment was typically just as expensive - if not more. Of course they would have the opportunity to cook for themselves, but even groceries in Boston are quite expensive. In general, it's an expensive city to live in.
activities_available: There were all the sports and clubs that one could dream of. They had a fair in the beginning of the semester where one could talk to members of all the clubs. This could be cooking club, music clubs, film clubs, acapella clubs, various volunteering clubs, academic clubs, networking clubs. Basically everything. The recreational center (the gym) was amazing. They had everything - tennis courts, basketball courts, squash, swimming pool, indoor running track, climbing wall, as well as all kinds of machines and gears. They also had many different sports teams. It was hard to qualify for the competing teams, but they also had intramural teams where you could form your own team and compete against other amateur BC teams in volleyball, soccer, basketball etc.
activities_recommended: Definitely get a gym membership. If you are interested in politics, I can recommend Model of United Nations. We had the chance to go to conferences at Boston University and Georgetown in Washington D.C. They participate in different conferences every semester. The music listeners society was fun too.
weekend_recommendations: In the fall break, we rented cars and drove to Arcadia National Park in Maine. We stayed in an Airbnb for 3 nights. The nature and hikes were absolutely amazing. New York City - 4.5 hours away by bus. So much to see and do!! In late November there's Thanksgiving break. I had classes off from Wednesday to Friday (and the weekend ofc). Some had the whole week off. This is a great chance to go on a trip. I went to Charleston, SC to spend Thanksgiving with some American friends. Other exchange students went on trips to NY, Nashville, DC, Puerto Rico, Cali etc. I also recommend to get the most out of Boston. - Watch a Celtics (basketball), Bruins (ice hockey) or Red Sox (baseball) game. - Kayak or SUB at Charles River Esplanada in the summer or just to for a walk there all year round. - Check out galleries, markets and vintage shops in SoWa. - Walk around Beacon Hill during halloween. They'll even let you trick and treat lol. - Go line dancing or sing live band karaoke at Nashville bar (on Thursdays). - Go visit cute shops and cafes or the old movie theater in Coolidge Corner. - Have a drink at a speakeasy bar or rooftop bar. (maybe Yovenne's or Lookout) - Shop and eat at Newbury Street! - Check out Harvard and the botanic garden in Cambridge - Go to Revere Beach (summer time) - Eat great food and listen to jazz or blues at Beehive in South End. - Downtown: visit Public Garden, Boston Public Library, Brattle Bookshop and Isabell Gardener museum
culture_adjustment: I think it was very easy to adjust. We know so much about American culture and college life from movies and medias so there's hardly much of a culture shock. College students in the US are very young (18-21) compared to Danes. There were grad students too but I didn't see them much.
socializing_tips: You will be introduced to the other exchange students immediately. If you live on-campus you will most likely also live in the same buildings. It's a very easy and natural group to get acquainted with. If you want to socialize with American students you have to make a little more effort. Joining clubs and societies is definitely a good way to do it. Also don't be hesitant to talk to students in your class. A lot of BC students go on exchange themselves and will most likely be quite eager to talk to you. You can also sign up for the buddy program and get a local student body who has been on exchange themselves. I also talked to many Americans who were a bit older (23-30) when I went out to the city. On bars or even just on the train ride.
cultural_challenges: - That they try to make money off of you any chance they get - Paying tips - People saying "how are you" instead of just "hi" when they pass you, not expecting to engage in conversation - American youth (especially girls) being a bit superficial: telling you they love you without really knowing you. Making plans with you but never showing up or canceling last minute. (this ofc does not happen all the time but I had quite a few of these encounters).
culture_appreciated: The hospitality! Americans can be extremely welcoming, warm and generous when they want to. If you would like to try and celebrate Thanksgiving with Americans for instance, you could easily get invited by fellow students or even faculty.
top3_advice: - Be aware it's gonna be very expensive. - Live on campus! (unless you really can't stand the thought of having a roommate) - Participate in sports games, clubs and societies and all of the events, the student organizations arrange. Boston College has such a rich and vibrant campus culture that you'll never experience in DK!
other_useful_info: Boston College is in the suburbs - not in the city. It takes about 20-25 minutes to reach downtown Boston by car. There're plenty Uber and Lyft cars. They also have fairly good public transportation (in American standards) and there is a T-stop near campus. However, the T is very slow, and It can take almost an hour reaching the city. Also they stop running after 1 AM or so, which means you'll have to get an Uber home if you stay out later on a night out. Everything closes at 2 AM anyways,
most_rewarding: Feeling like I was at højskole but on university level in the US. Living on-campus really feels like living on a højskole in many ways. Not having to worry about anything outside the BC bubble. It was very un-stressful. It was also very rewarding to finally feel like a good student. At home I had a tendency to skip a lot of classes and readings, but there I felt much more motivated to participate in class.
greatest_challenge: I don't tend to get home sick but of course you'll miss friends and family and your way of living at home. I honestly think my greatest challenge was everything being so expensive.

crucial_aspects: I chose Boston because I have long been fascinated by the United States as both a cultural and political space. Studying in the US is normally associated with extremely high tuition fees, making it inaccessible for most international students. This exchange opportunity therefore represented a unique chance to experience an American university environment without the otherwise prohibitive financial burden. Furthermore, Boston is one of the leading academic hubs on the East Coast and is widely recognized as a center of knowledge, research, and intellectual innovation. With its concentration of world-class universities and a vibrant academic community, the city offers an exceptional environment for learning and personal development. For me, this made Boston the ideal destination.
overall_comments: I would rate my overall experience a 10 out of 10. During my stay, I had the opportunity to travel extensively, which allowed me to explore different parts of the United States and gain a much deeper understanding of the country’s cultural and regional diversity. I also rented a house together with four other girls from around the world, and this international living environment became one of the highlights of my stay. We formed close friendships, and I truly feel that I have gained friends for life. Academically, the level and structure differed from what I am used to at home, and in general the academic demands were somewhat lower. However, I was aware of this before going, and therefore it did not negatively influence my overall experience. Instead, it allowed me to focus more on cultural immersion, personal development, and building an international network.
info_ease: Finding the information I needed prior to and upon arrival was very easy. The university was highly responsive and provided clear guidance throughout the entire process, which made it straightforward to prepare for my stay. Their communication was quick, and they offered extensive orientation materials that helped me understand both administrative procedures and practical aspects of student life. I did experience some challenges related to the visa process, but this seemed to be a common issue for many international students. Despite this, the overall availability and clarity of information from the university significantly eased the transition.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival, I received extensive assistance from the university. Their exchange team is truly excellent (its a really rich college :)) and ensured that international students felt supported from the very beginning. They provided clear guidance during orientation, helped with practical matters, and made themselves available for any questions or concerns. This level of support created a smooth transition into both academic life and everyday living in Boston.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_process: Before the semester began, I received extensive information by email, guiding me to the university’s online platform, which functions similarly to Canvas/Absalon. Through this system, I created my initial course “table,” selecting the classes I planned to take. It is important to be aware of several rules when registering: exchange students may take a maximum of 16 credits, courses are not allowed to overlap in schedule, and it is not permitted to take all four courses within the same department. Although the initial registration requires attention to these details, the table can be easily adjusted once you arrive on campus. Advisors are helpful, and the system is flexible, ensuring that students can finalise their schedules without unnecessary stress.
registration_help: Mailing them and reading the instructions send out.
registration_success: Overall, I was partially successful in registering for the classes I had planned. I was able to secure a course that fulfilled the requirement for DAK3, which was my primary academic priority. However, the university removed the course on European Politics shortly before the semester started, which created a significant challenge. I attempted to find an equivalent replacement, but the University of Copenhagen was not willing to approve any of the alternative courses offered in Boston. As a result, I ended up taking three electives along with DAK3, while completing the European Politics course online from home. Although this solution worked in practice, it was somewhat stressful to coordinate and required additional planning.
registration_advice: My main advice to future exchange students is to stay open-minded when it comes to course selection. The academic structure and teaching style differ significantly from what we are used to at the University of Copenhagen, so it is helpful to approach the process with flexibility. Courses may change, be removed, or require additional documentation, and it is likely that you will need to reprioritise or revise your initial plans. It is important not to let these adjustments overshadow the overall experience. With proper planning and a willingness to adapt, the registration process becomes much more manageable, and students can still create an academically valuable and personally enriching study programme.
academics_comments: I would rate my overall experience a 10 out of 10. During my stay, I had the opportunity to travel extensively, which allowed me to explore different parts of the United States and gain a much deeper understanding of the country’s cultural and regional diversity. I also rented a house together with four other girls from around the world, and this international living environment became one of the highlights of my stay. We formed close friendships, and I truly feel that I have gained friends for life. Academically, the level and structure differed from what I am used to at home, and in general the academic demands were somewhat lower. However, I was aware of this before going, and therefore it did not negatively influence my overall experience. Instead, it allowed me to focus more on cultural immersion, personal development, and building an international network.
course_level: One of the most striking differences in the academic level was the pedagogical approach. The system places a stronger emphasis on memorisation, personal political opinions, and active participation rather than on developing an objective, theoretically grounded academic understanding. Discussions often encouraged students to express their viewpoints, but not necessarily to anchor them in broader theoretical frameworks or methodological rigor. As a result, it sometimes felt as though the classes remained on the lower steps of the theoretical “ladder.” While students engaged actively, the courses rarely moved into deeper conceptual analysis or advanced theoretical synthesis of the kind typically expected at KU. This difference does not make the courses less valuable; rather, it highlights a distinct academic culture where engagement and opinion formation are prioritised over theoretical abstraction. To me its wild paying that much and the recieve that little in terms of academic development.
teaching_comparison: Like gymnasiet
courses_enrolled: Immigration in Contemporary Europe, ENVS 3345-01 Environment and Public Health, PHIL-1070 Philosophy of the Person I, Political Parties, Voters and Party Systems in Comparative Perspective (Thibaud Marcesses course)
recommended_courses: Try different things. Having the migration in Europe course was fun (mostly to hear the american perspective - they were wrong most of the time).
unexpected_costs: Visa (was expensive), going to the doctor - Boston is really expensive in general
cost_comparison: Travelling was less expensive than I thought.
activities_available: Sport, language clubs etc.
activities_recommended: I would highly recommend that future exchange students consider joining the rugby team (I did not play rugby before going), as this was one of the most enjoyable and welcoming environments I experienced. The team was down-to-earth, inclusive, and provided a great opportunity to meet students outside the typical exchange circles. The university’s outdoor club is also an excellent option. Through this group, I was able to go on hikes with local students in various states, which offered a unique chance to explore the natural landscapes of the East Coast while also building meaningful connections. Additionally, I participated in a prison education programme, where students visited correctional facilities to teach. This was an extraordinarily enriching and eye-opening experience—both academically and personally. It offered a rare opportunity to engage with social issues in a direct and impactful way, and I would strongly recommend it to anyone interested in community engagement or criminal justice.
weekend_recommendations: I would strongly encourage future exchange students to take advantage of the many travel opportunities available on the East Coast. During my stay, I visited New York, Canada, and Puerto Rico — and all three trips were truly fantastic experiences. Each destination offered something completely different: the cultural and architectural intensity of New York, the natural beauty and welcoming atmosphere in Canada, and the unique Caribbean culture and climate in Puerto Rico. Travelling during the semester provided valuable breaks from academic life and allowed me to experience the broader cultural diversity of the region, which greatly enriched my exchange experience.
culture_adjustment: For me, adjusting to the local culture was relatively easy. I quickly found a large group of wonderful people and ended up forming what felt like a small European “bubble” within the US, which made the transition smooth and enjoyable. However, it became clear that experiences varied significantly among exchange students. Some students from Spain, France, and other countries found it more challenging to adapt. Several struggled with the academic structure, which differs markedly from many European systems, while others found the cost of living overwhelming or encountered difficulties with on-campus housing. Overall, while the adjustment process depends heavily on personal expectations and circumstances, my own experience was positive due to the strong social network I built early on. - Boston is really save and kinda European, so its very nice.
socializing_tips: Join club and put an effort into it, then im sure they will let you in.
cultural_challenges: I really hated Tailgating, the football and the fratparties - which a lot of the exchange people wanna join, so i had to stand that out a couple of times :)
culture_appreciated: What I appreciated most about the culture in the United States was its complexity and diversity. The country is full of contrasts—socially, politically, and culturally—which makes it an incredibly dynamic place to experience. The U.S. offers countless opportunities, but it also contains tensions and challenges that are important to witness firsthand. Experiencing these dynamics up close gave me a much deeper understanding of American society than I could have gained from a distance. Being on exchange provided a unique opportunity to explore this multifaceted culture in an immersive way, and it confirmed for me how valuable international study experiences can be in broadening one’s perspective.
top3_advice: 1. Consider what kind of cultural experience you want. If your goal is to make American friends and truly challenge your worldview, I would recommend considering an exchange in the Midwest. Although I loved Boston, I sometimes wished I had chosen a location where it might have been easier to integrate more deeply into American everyday life. 2. Save up before you go. Boston is an expensive city (and the college is a college for some of the richest kids in MA), and having some financial flexibility makes a significant difference. Saving up beforehand allows you to fully enjoy the experience — whether that means travelling, joining activities, or simply participating in social events without stress. 3. Say yes to everything. The exchange experience goes by incredibly fast, so take every opportunity that comes your way. Even the less successful or challenging moments become valuable experiences in hindsight. Be proactive, invite others to join, and travel whenever you can — most people are happy to come along if someone takes the initiative.
other_useful_info: Get vaccinated in advanced, it complicates thing if you do it last minute like me ;) Bring warm clothing - it gets cold.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the personal development it brought. Living abroad gave me a renewed sense of gratitude for my life at home, while also pushing me to grow in ways that would not have been possible otherwise. I met an incredible number of new people from all over the world, each contributing to broadening my perspective and challenging me socially, academically, and personally. Being placed in new environments and situations forced me to adapt, reflect, and step outside my comfort zone. These experiences — from forming deep friendships to navigating unfamiliar systems — collectively made the exchange one of the most meaningful and transformative periods of my life. The US is an amazing country.
greatest_challenge: Balancing my social battery and academic work.
other_comments: GO GO GO - you wont regret it. Find people to live with in a house - It gives a better foundation for deep friendship and you want ever feel lonely or homesick

crucial_aspects: I wanted to be in the center of biotechnology, therefore I choose to study in Boston. Also, it was important for me that it was an English speaking country
overall_comments: I feel that I got the full college experience, but there is I few things that I would have done differently
info_ease: It was very easy, the most important information was sent to you in email before arrival, and Sage the coordinator was very helpful.
arrival_assistance: I didn't really receive assistance. I would have liked a specific welcome program for the exchange students before classes started. There were a couple of events but else you were let to yourself.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I feel that I got the full college experience, but there is I few things that I would have done differently
registration_process: In April you could start register for classes and change and add classes until October. The website was kind of old, but easy to navigate.
registration_help: The professors who taught the courses were very helpful about registration.
registration_success: Many of the courses I wanted was already closed when I could register, but it was nice too add and drop courses until October.
registration_advice: Look at the recommendations from other students before deciding. And, just choose the courses you find most interesting you can always drop them. Choose more than you should in case one of them is bad
academics_comments: I feel that I got the full college experience, but there is I few things that I would have done differently
course_level: The level of the courses was lower than KU, but the workload was bigger.
teaching_comparison: You get points for your participation, which can be challenging sometimes, but the teachers were very helpful. The lectures were very much the same
courses_enrolled: Developmental Biology Introduction to Neuroscience General Microbiology
recommended_courses: I liked all my classes, especially Developmental Biology. The professor, Cynthia learned all of our names and was so passionate and smart. Even though it was the class with the heaviest material it was the lectures I enyojed the most. In Introduction Neuroscience, there is a lot of freshmen, but our guest lectures were very interesting. General Microbiology you have lab for two hours, twice a week. The workload for this course is big, but the material is straight forward, The work in the lab was sometimes a bit boring.
unexpected_costs: The mandatory health insurance is pretty expensive. I was surprised about how expensive the US is, restaurants, groceries... Don't buy the metro card to the T (the metro). cost_comparison: The food! You have to tip 15-20 % each time you eat out which often will make it more expensive than eating out in Copenhagen.
activities_available: The limit does not exist. Over 200 different clubs.
activities_recommended: I joined the running club, where I met a lot of sweet Americans. Get to know Boston and visit Harvard and MIT. Look for local activities and explore the national holidays. Befriend an American and explore the culture.
weekend_recommendations: Public transportation is cheap! take the train to New York for a long weekend. Also make sure that your insurance cover renting a car and driving to New Hampshire, Maine, or Cape Cod for hiking. The Amtrak train can also take you to nice neighboring cities like Providence.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy! Americans are very friendly! But it takes some work to get close to them.
socializing_tips: Join the clubs! And talk to your classmates! Many of them don't know one either. Always say yes for social events outside class.
cultural_challenges: The Americans are very good at first impression but it takes some work to really befriend them. I found it easier to get friends with the other exchange students.
culture_appreciated: Very friendly and easy to talk to. The people were more open.
top3_advice: Focus on the social in the start, this is where you find your friends. Join some clubs. And be open-minded.
other_useful_info: Don't stress over the classes, most often you will have three exams spread over the semester which enables you to keep track of how it goes.
most_rewarding: To get to make unique friendships with people all over the world.
greatest_challenge: To find "your people". You have to do a great effort to find your friends, and get out of your comfort zone.
other_comments: Try to get some scholarships before arrival

crucial_aspects: I had always wanted to try and live in the US, and I had heard a lot of good things about Boston, because it is such a big university city. I did a lot of research and decided that Boston was one of the destinations I was most interested in.
info_ease: It was quite easy. I wrote a lot to Sage Suorsa, the exchange coordinator from BU, and she was usually very fast at answering. But from Copenhagen University it was a little more difficult, the coordinator wasn't very helpful. There was a zoom meeting for exchange students a few weeks before the semester started, and there they made a whatsapp group with everybody. Then there was a lot of events in the first week, though they were mostly for freshmen, but we went to them to meet new people. I had met the other danish exchanges students from KU and also from CBS in the week before school started.
arrival_assistance: I received all the information about school start, covid, all the events and activities, orientation, moving-in etc.
arrival_comments: I wish they would have had a specific event just for international students, because we were older than the freshmen so the events weren't always so fun.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: On StudentLink you click register and choose the class you want. You can look up the classes on BUs website before and find the code.
registration_help: I tried to write to my professors if there wasn't a spot available, but they couldn't do anything because of covid rules, they weren't very flexible about letting extra people join.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. Game Theory: wasn't my favorite professor. But interesting courses. Behavioral Economics with Prof. Fisman was very good! International Economics I was a "prioriteret valgfag", which was very interesting, but it was evening school and only 4 people on the course, which I didn't know before getting there.
registration_advice: Just keep checking all the time if there is a class which is full, even after the semester has started, because a lot of people drop out.
course_level: I took two 300 classes and one 400 class.
teaching_comparison: Very different - there are midterms, sometimes several, which forces you to study the material early on in the course, which I liked. I also almost didn't have any assignments, which is very different from my courses at KU. Instead there were pop up quizzes and attendance/participation was 5/10% of your grade.
courses_enrolled: Game Theory Behavioral Economics International Economics I
recommended_courses: I would recommend Behavioral Economics, it was definitely my favorite courses.
unexpected_costs: Ubers and going out. It can be quite expensive to go out in Boston, and the public transportation doesn't work after 1, so we always had to take ubers home. But they aren't too expensive when shared.
cost_comparison: Transport card (CharlieCard) - don't buy it! It costs $300 and I definitely didn't use it enough. Instead you can get a bluebike subscription.
activities_available: There are over 400 clubs, and there is a free gym which was very good. Hockey games are fun too.
activities_recommended: You should join sports classes at Fitrec and join clubs at Splash. I can really recommend going to a Tailgate at Boston College and then seeing the football match. Also baseball at Fenway, and going on trips to NYC, Cape Cod.
weekend_recommendations: I went to NYC twice, it costs only 300kr roundtrip with Flixbus and it was very fun. Cape Cod is very beautiful too.
culture_adjustment: Very easy! Boston is a very international city. It was fun to experience the things I had seen in movies and TV in real life.
socializing_tips: It was kind of hard to get to know local students, but if your classes has group projects that is a good way! Or at the clubs too. I was mostly with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Nothing
culture_appreciated: The openness and friendliness of the American people.
top3_advice: Summer clothes!! It was so much hotter than I thought it would be. Raincoat. A danish "stikdåse" - so you can use your regular chargers, but just put an adapter on the stikdåse.
most_rewarding: Meeting my new friends and challenging myself by leaving everything behind and traveling by myself so far away, especially during covid where it wasn't easy to travel back and forth.
greatest_challenge: Definitely the first week in Boston by myself before I met any people.
other_comments: no

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to study in an English speaking country, since all research are made in English. I then wanted a city or country I would feel safe in, and believed would be a good fit. So I wanted to go to Canada, but I did not have the grades. My brothers girlfriend told me about her visit to Boston and I thought that Boston sounded like a great city, so I applied.
overall_comments: I have experienced SO much, but it did not meet my expectations. The US was not a great fit for me. I had a lot of trouble adjusting to the American way, and I was lonely a lot of the time. It was very difficult to find friends, since they dont make friends the same way as we do in Europe. I am grateful for all the amazing experiences I have had, but if I had to chose again, I would go somewhere else.
info_ease: It was fine. You had a contact person, who was a big help if you did not understand or could not find the information you needed. Once you had your BU account, it was okay to navigate the systems. They are a lot like the systems at KU. Also you had to take some online courses that explained the systems, and how the american education system works.
arrival_assistance: None really. You were pretty much left all by your self. When I checked in to my dorm, the resident assistant helped me understand how the building worked, and said I could always ask for help if I needed it.
arrival_comments: I thought it was very helpful all the online classes I could take from home, so I wasn't blindsided when I arrived. Though I am very disappointed that no one showed us (exchange students) around, or made any get togethers for all of the exchange students. You just arrived, and then you had to find everything on your own, even someone to talk to.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I have experienced SO much, but it did not meet my expectations. The US was not a great fit for me. I had a lot of trouble adjusting to the American way, and I was lonely a lot of the time. It was very difficult to find friends, since they dont make friends the same way as we do in Europe. I am grateful for all the amazing experiences I have had, but if I had to chose again, I would go somewhere else.
registration_process: You had to find the classes you thought sounded interesting in the BU course catalog. Then you registered for the classes on student link (their website for students). You could always change your registration until the add/drop period ended.
registration_help: You could write to your contact person.
registration_success: At first I did not get any of the classes I wanted, but then later I got two of the classes, just by writing checking student link often, but also by being on the waitlist. It was actually really great that I did not get the classes I wanted to begin with, because it got me to expand my search, and I found a course I ended up really loving. It was the best course I had.
registration_advice: Spend time before registration begins on finding all the classes you might be interested in. The more the better, and then register the minute you can. Keep checking student link if you did not get a spot the first time, because many are making changes to their schedule right before classes starts.
academics_comments: I have experienced SO much, but it did not meet my expectations. The US was not a great fit for me. I had a lot of trouble adjusting to the American way, and I was lonely a lot of the time. It was very difficult to find friends, since they dont make friends the same way as we do in Europe. I am grateful for all the amazing experiences I have had, but if I had to chose again, I would go somewhere else.
course_level: As an undergrad you can take up till 500 level courses, and please do. They are not too hard, and they have smaller classes, so it is easier to meet people and get to know your professor. I had two 500 level courses and one 300 level course. The biggest different was that you got more help in the 300 level course. It wasn't easier per say, but it felt like you had training wheels and the professor held your hand more. It actually made the work load bigger because you couldn't manage your own time as much.
teaching_comparison: In my 500 level courses it was like gymnasium. Class learning instead if big lectures. In my 300 level course it was big lectures and lab. There was no class discussions or task solving classes. The professor who was in charge of the course chose what type of teaching they wanted to teach. They have more creative freedom than the professors at KU.
courses_enrolled: CAS BI 513 - Genetics Lab CAS BI 572 - Advanced Genetics CAS BI 311 - General Microbiology
recommended_courses: All of them! I really loved Advanced genetics. We learned about different model organisms and how they are used in research, so you really got to think about experiments and how you got the results you wanted and which methods to use. I also really loved General Microbiology, because it provided me with a greater knowledge on how the world works. Microbes are so important for the world and for us humans. I feel it is important to know the basics about microbes in order to fully understand diseases and research of diseases.
unexpected_costs: None really. But I did end up using a lot of money on food. Also trains are expensive, so if you plan on going away much, you have to order the tickets in great time.
cost_comparison: Housing, dining plan and US insurance was VERY expensive. 60.000kr for 4 months. Also eating out isn't as cheap as it used to be. But cloth and stuff for your room was cheap enough. Amazon is AMAZING!!!
activities_available: So so many. They have a big meeting on the football field in the begining of the semester, where you can meet all the clubs and join if you want.
activities_recommended: I had two PDP classes, yoga and Hiphop. They where held in fitrec, which was free for BU students. FitRec is HUGE. They have everything you want for every sport you may play.
weekend_recommendations: Just see Boston! It is an amazing city. Walk the freedom trail and see the public garden. See Quincy market and little italy. If you have the time, then hike the blue mountains.
culture_adjustment: Not really. They have very strict alcohol laws, so you cannot drink in public and all events are without alcohol, which was very strange to me. Also most people you meet are under the age of 21, so they cannot drink, which makes them feel more immature then 18-19 years old do in Denmark. Also everything is sweet, and they do no care about quality of the food they eat.
socializing_tips: Yes, join a club. any club. They is the only way you meet people. Also try reaching out to the other exchange students. You have to be very open and "agressive" in order to meet people. You ask people you meet for a cup of coffee or if they want to eat lunch. It is very strange to that open and straight forward, but you have to if you want to meet people. Also try to meet with the other danes back home before going over there, so you are not totally alone.
cultural_challenges: Their alcohol culture as explained. Also their healthcare system.
culture_appreciated: You can customize everything which i really like. Also they care a lot about sports, so I went to see many ice hockey games, basketball games and so on. That culture is really fun. supporting your own university and spend every weekend with seeing some sport, mostly ice hockey.
top3_advice: Be prepared for how expensive it is! BU makes nothing social for the exchange student, so you have to be very straight forward and open if you want any friends. Take every opportunity you get. See the sports games, go the the festival or whatever happens that week. Read BU today that is sent to your email for inspiration on what to do that weekend.
other_useful_info: Go to every class, even though your grades do not matter. If you are behind from the beginning, then it is hard to relax in the end. Also check out Boston Collage before you decide. BU is right next to the city, so it is easy to experience Boston, but campus is so boring and long. Boston collage is smaller and prettier, however it is further out. But there are trains and Uber/Lyft. Also you spend so much time on campus, so you have to make sure it is a place you actually like. I was very disappointed when I first saw BU campus, because it is not like Harvard. It is a city campus, and looks like it. Also BU has its own pub, called BU pub. It is very cozy, so make sure to check it out. also it is a great way to meet people your own age.
most_rewarding: Seeing Boston, New York and New England in general. I have always wanted to see the east coast. Also I feel like you have a certain view of USA here in Europe, but it is different to experience first hand how the country is. I have a new understanding of USA.
greatest_challenge: Finding friends! I felt lonely most of the time, because I had so much free time. crucial_aspects: I knew I wanted to go to the US since I've visited before and liked it a lot. The reputation of the university and which schools I had heard of beforehand definitely had its influence on which universities I ended up applying for as well. The US have a lot of schools with a good reputation within my field of study which also contributed to me applying for BU. For me, sports and school spirit also had a certain say when deciding between the universities available in the US. I wanted to experience the atmosphere when going to American football games or other sports games - although Boston University does not have a football team, they still have a lot of other sports teams where you can get this experience, especially ice hockey is popular. Also, I did not realize this before going to Boston, but the city has a lot of other colleges that have, for example, football teams, and you can buy tickets for their games so it ended up working out very well in the end! What courses the universities offered was also an aspect I was very aware of. When trying to decide which universities I wanted to apply for I also read reports from other UCPH students who went there previously and noted down pros and cons. Things such as a Boston being mentioned as a great city, BU having a cohesive campus, people being friendly and welcoming, there being a lot of different clubs, and great dining halls weighed in a very positive direction.
overall_comments: What made me rate my overall study experience an 8 instead of 10 was the fact that Boston University did not really seem to do anything to introduce exchange students to each other. It would have been great if some events for exchange students had been held so that we could get to know other people. Other Danish students from UCPH and CBS very quickly became my social circle which was great, but it would have been good to get to know other exchange students. I am not sure if COVID and not being able to gather a lot of people at the same time and place had something to do with it, but if that was the case, then it would have been great if something like the UCPH SCIENCE Buddy Programme had been put in place such that we had had the opportunity to get to know just a small group of other exchange students as well as have some BU students to turn to with any questions we might have had.

They had a pre-departure website with a lot of important and useful information about course registration, housing, dining plans, visa, and what to bring or buy in Boston. If I had any questions that I could not seem to find the answer for, the BU program coordinator was very helpful!
arrival_assistance: We did not really receive any assistance when arriving. It should be mentioned that my friend and I went to New York for a week before going to Boston, but we did not get any information about any assistance that we could have gotten. On the pre-departure page, we were informed how to get from, for instance, the airport to the BU campus and what to do when arriving at the campus for check-in at the dorm.

registration_process: The registration process was a little confusing in the beginning but as you take the time to roam around on StudentLink, BU's "KUnet", it gets easier. The pre-departure page has the process drawn out, so when the time comes if you follow the information there you are good to go! When you are looking on the course catalog website, or looking at courses on the different colleges websites, make sure that the course is available during the semester you attend. Some courses are only offered during the Fall or Spring semester. I would it somewhat difficult to find this information up until shortly before registration, so have an open mind when it comes to courses you'd like to take. If you have your BU login before registration starts, you are able to search the courses you want and add them to your planner. This way, you are able to make your own schedule, and can use the "Graph" option to show your schedule. If you've added all your desired classes to your planner, you can then choose the register for all the classes added to your planner when registration opens! You can also simply search for a specific class and register for it. NB: for some classes you have to send in a registration form to the BU program coordinator. Also, some classes might be full when you get to register. Sometimes you can find information on how to get on a waitlist on StudentLink. If you cannot seem to find this, try to email the BU program coordinator and ask, if she knows the procedure.
registration_help: Mainly the pre-departure page, but if I had any questions that I could not find the answer for, the BU program coordinator was more than happy to answer my questions through email.
registration_success: I was very successful. I had one class I really wanted to take but it was full when our registration started. I got on the waitlist but unfortunately never got off of it. This class, however, had lectures simultaneously with another class I also wanted which I ended up getting into, so I decided to go with the one I got into. Thus, in general, I'd say my registration was easy and successful.
registration_advice: 1. If you have your BU login, register as soon as possible, or get on waitlist for the class as soon as possible. Classes tend to fill up quick, in my experience. 2. Make sure you have registered for all the required class sections.

course_level: I took a 300- and two 500-level classes. The 300-level courses are described as Advanced undergraduate, and the 500-level courses are described as Advanced undergraduate and/or graduate courses. Personally, I think these course levels, and the combination I ended up with, was fitting for me. The courses definitely required a fair amount of work on my part, but I also tend to spend a lot of time on the different aspects of the classes, so the fact that I spent a lot of time should not steer you way from taking classes on these levels. A fair amount of the concepts that were presented in the two genetics classes has been presented in previous courses at UCPH, however, I do think I learned a lot - many new concepts and new knowledge about different model organisms, and the concepts we had heard of before were developed further.
teaching_comparison: It was/is very different. Your final grade consists of a lot of different components - not just a final exam as many of the courses we have encountered. Participation, written assignments, and approximately two midterms/exams and a final exam are things taken into consideration for the final grade. If you are between two grades, the professor might bump you up if you've attended the classes in-person (we were able to follow two of my classes online if you got COVID, or didn't feel comfortable coming in for lectures), had attended office hours during the semester, or in other ways expressed curiosity for the course topics.
courses_enrolled: CAS BI 311. General Microbiology, CAS BI 513. Genetics Laboratory, and BI572. Advanced Genetics.
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the courses I took for future exchange students. If you find viruses interesting, then the last part of the General Microbiology course is definitely for you. I found that section especially interesting. Additionally, I just started my bachelor's project, and a couple of things presented in the lab section of General Microbiology have already been mentioned. I think the time I spent on the course will turn out to be well spent since I learned a lot of basic information about microbiological organisms which can be used in the future. Advanced Genetics is a really good course if you want to learn about genetics in other organisms as well as in humans. We have a pretty good grasp on the human section of the cause because of Medical Genetics, however, Drosophila and C. elegans genetics are also presented which I think will be very helpful when reading scientific literature in the future and to know in general. A very thorough run-down of knock-outs in mice, as well as deciding what methods to use to investigate specific things is also one of the aspects in the class that I found very useful! Genetics Laboratory was a great course to get some hands-on experience (especially since we unfortunately had our Protein chemistry and Enzymology II course online and not in-person). We also got to do a lot of PCR preparation and sequence analysis on mutations in the two designated genes we worked with. In general, I think this course was very giving, although it was a little unstructured.
unexpected_costs: If you want to go to sports games you either have to buy a SportsPass (130 USD, lasts the entire year), or you have to buy tickets for every game you attend (approx. 20 USD every time). I decided to purchase the Sports Pass since I wanted to go to a lot of ice hockey games - but it should be mentioned that I got a free hockey jersey since I went to 8 Men's Ice Hockey home games.
cost_comparison: Printing was less expensive - we got the first approx. 100 black and white pages for free (i.e., you got 8 USD to print for, and a double sided black and white printed piece of paper was very cheap). My phone plan was also less expensive than expected. I ended up getting a World Plan through CBB where I could send texts and call people in Denmark and the US for free, and I could use the data included. I was told I would only be able to use the plan for 2-3 months before I would be contacted somehow and told to "change my behavior", i.e., "go back to Denmark". I never got a text or email telling me to change anything and just kept using it. No additional charges came either. I even spent some time after my semester ended with some family in the US and did not arrive back in Denmark until January, and my plan still worked. So I definitely saved a little bit of money since I know my friend got a T Mobile plan in the US where she paid 40 USD each month (plus a 10 USD fee when she registered and got her number).
activities_available: In regard to cultural activities, besides the cultural clubs you might be able to join, BU also planned events such as Pumpkin Decoration around Halloween, and probably a lot more that I just don't remember. In relation to athletic activities, you were able to join different sports teams. Some of the competitive teams have try-outs, whereas others you can pretty much just join. They also have intramural sports clubs where you play others - students or faculty - within BU. The school also has FitRec - the Fitness and Recreation Center - where you can use the gym and swimming pools for free. Different social activities were also available. Before the semester started, they had a lot of different events as part of "Weeks of Welcome", and different social and/or cultural events also took place throughout the semester.
activities_recommended: Join a club or sports team - whether it is associated to BU or not. I found it really nice to be able to stay physically active through practices with my handball team, and you get to meet a lot of people and make new friends and acquaintances. It is also a great way to get a more diverse way of living such that school isn't the only thing. Sometimes you also get to travel the country or the nearby states or cities with your team or club which is really cool!
weekend_recommendations: Of course, experience Boston. Walk the Freedom Trail, go to museums, walk up and down Newbury Street, go to Boston Common and the Public Garden. Definitely have a study day at Boston Public Library, and go hiking in Blue Hills if you enjoy that. Visit Harvard University and MIT, experience Cambridge, watch a movie at Regal Fenway movie theater. You should also try to go to a Red Sox game at Fenway Park, watch some american football at some of the other universities in Boston (e.g., MIT, Harvard, or Boston College), and catch a BU Men's hockey game. You can also take the T to Providence or Salem, maybe rent a car to go to Cape Cod, or take the train to New York City for a couple of days. Boston and the surrounding area has a lot to offer so you won't find yourself bored!
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy for me, I would say. I've been to the US a couple of times before, although that was in the South, but I had a pretty good understanding of the American culture.
socializing_tips: Try to join a club or team at BU. If you are in a smaller class or lab, try to hit up a conversation with some of the other students there.
cultural_challenges: I didn't really find any cultural differences challenging - mostly interesting and funny (such as the fact that they call what I would say is a Chicken Burger a Chicken Sandwich).
culture_appreciated: I really appreciate the open-mindedness of talking to strangers out in public - although, people in Boston are more reserved compared to people in the South. One of my first days at BU, I was done getting the required vaccine shots. I was waiting for the T, and it started raining a little. Two girls, each with an umbrella walked by, but then one of them ended up asking if I wanted to share hers. We then started talking a little, and ended up chatting on the T until they got of.
top3_advice: 1. Try to take initiative to talk to people - other international/exchange students, and Americans. From what I've experienced, BU does not really seem to initiate any social gatherings between any of the international students (one of the exchange students had to suggest making a WhatsApp group for all the exchange students at BU). 2. Be prepared for a very different way of "doing school" - there will most likely be a couple of assignments, and at least two midterms/exams and one final exam. 3. Don't be stressed about wanting to see all of Boston in the beginning - although time passes by fast, you have plenty of time and weekends to see and experience what you want!
other_useful_info: 1. If you have the time and energy, try to apply for some scholarships from private companies and foundations. It is very expensive to attend BU - mostly because of the housing cost. 2. Make sure to start your visa application right when you receive the documents from BU. You can even start before getting them - you don't really need the information from BU until the last part of the DS-160 form (the first form you have to complete, if I remember correctly). It was really difficult for me and other Danish exchange students to get our visas because of the COVID situation, but I have heard it is somewhat difficult to get appointments at the US Embassy even when things are normal. 3. I would recommend taking the TOEFL test in person, if possible. I did it at home, and it was kind of a hassle since you had to clear your entire desk, you had to show the proctor your entire room, and sudden movements can be interpreted as cheating even if you are not. In general, there were just a lot of preparation to do besides just preparing for the test itself.
most_rewarding: Getting to experience the culture of Boston and the East cost of the US. Meeting other Danish exchange students, people from all around the world, and making great connections.
greatest_challenge: Before the exchange, it was getting our visa. However, during my exchange, it was getting to know exchange students from other countries. I ended up socializing primarily with other Danish exchange students at BU, a couple of American students from my classes, and my handball teammates, but meeting other exchange students would have made my experience even better than it already is.

crucial_aspects: I have previously studied in the United States and because this had been such a great experience, I was eager to do this again. The last time, I was in the South so this time it made sense to study in a northern state. When choosing the specific area in which I wanted to study, then the academic reputation of Boston was obviously an important factor. Also, Boston made sense to me because I have relatives living close to the city. So overall it seemed like a great match.
overall_comments: Overall, perhaps I overestimated how great living and studying in Boston would be because of my previous experiences with studying in the United States. Looking back on it, perhaps I should have chosen a completely different destination. This being said, I was still very disappointed with how Boston University uses its students for additional profits. It is a sad development how Universities, such as Boston Univesity, care more about making profits than academic integrity.
info_ease: Getting to the University and getting checked into the room I had been assigned was not too difficult. The international students' office had done a great job at preparing all the information that was needed so that we had a checklist of things to be completed upon arrival in Boston.
arrival_assistance: I hardly did not need any assistance when I arrived in Boston. Within the first couple of weeks, I had a few questions regarding the courses that I had chosen and a few technicalities, but they were very well handled by Sage Suorsa who was the program manager for the exchange students at Boston University.
arrival_comments: Boston University had a lot of online orientation and mandatory online introductory courses that seemed so unnecessary for anyone who is a normal grown up. It seems like such a waste of money for the University to have these courses but I guess it all looks good on paper however unnecessary it may seem for the students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
