registration_process: Registering for new courses was easy and any student used to the system at the University of Copenhagen should not have any difficulties figuring this out. One can rather easily find general information about the courses and then add the courses to a list of courses prior to the start of the registration process. Then actually registering for courses after the registration opens can be done in a matter of seconds.
registration_help: The university provided a great description of how one should complete the registration process and should any exchange students have any difficulties then the coordinator for the exchange students was very helpful.
registration_success: I did not at first encounter any difficulties in registering for the classes I wanted, however about a week into the classes I was still missing one of the required immunizations. This meant that I was restricted from registering for any new courses and effectively meant that I could not change courses. When I found out that one of my courses was perhaps a bit irrelevant/too easy then this became somewhat of a problem. Morale of this story: Make sure to stay compliant with any requirements from the University, so that they do not restrict your course registration.
registration_advice: One should familiarize themselves with the system used in the United States for measuring the difficulty of the available courses and one should be aware that the general difficulty of most courses is below the difficulty of similar courses at the University of Copenhagen.
academics_comments: Overall, perhaps I overestimated how great living and studying in Boston would be because of my previous experiences with studying in the United States. Looking back on it, perhaps I should have chosen a completely different destination. This being said, I was still very disappointed with how Boston University uses its students for additional profits. It is a sad development how Universities, such as Boston Univesity, care more about making profits than academic integrity.
course_level: The level of the courses at Boston University was in general below that at the University of Copenhagen. I had registered for one course that I had expected was below the level I was at but it proved to be even less difficult. When concerning mathematics, Americans in my experience have a tendency of focusing on the essentials necessary for understanding theory and applying it in the workplace. It is not really my impression that they care all that much about the details in the theory which is unfortunate because essential theoretical understanding is lost. In my opinion too much emphasis is on the application of theory instead of understanding the underlying more challenging reasoning.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was in some of my classes more like being back in high school in the sense that one had homework for every class, and this had to be handed in. It has been my experience at the University of Copenhagen that students are expected to follow the course material for their own benefit and if one does not keep up with exercises then one will not be prepared for the finals. At Boston University however, since the final grade also depends on your overall participation in the course, then it is also important for professors to have physical evidence of how you perform every week during the course. This results in a lot of dull mandatory exercises were one sometimes waste time on making it presentable instead of being able to focus on the actual theory.
courses_enrolled: CAS HI151 - The Emerging United States to 1865 CAS MA226 - Differential Equations MET AT751 - Individual Insurance Applications of Actuarial Principles MET AT762 - Mathematical Finance for Actuarial Science PDP FT140 - Marathon Training
recommended_courses: Even though the mathematics involved with the course was not at all challenging, I think I would recommend “Individual Insurance Applications of Actuarial Principles” to any student with mathematics who wants to familiarize themselves with life insurance in the United States. This course covers many details about the construction of insurance contracts and aspects of how insurance companies determine reserves. On a more personal note, I really enjoyed learning about American History prior to 1865 with the philosophy that if one is interested in American history, where better to learn about it than in Boston from American professors?
unexpected_costs: I was assigned to a different type of housing than I had preferred, and this was more expensive than I had estimated at first in my budget. Any potential exchange student should make themselves aware of how Boston University might assign housing different from what students have requested and one can thereby encounter unexpected extra charges.
cost_comparison: I was surprised by how expensive food is in Boston in general. Massachusetts overall has a relatively high sales tax and combined with living expenses just being higher in the city, then general everyday grocery shopping was surprisingly expensive. Also, as I have already mentioned a couple of times, housing was ridiculously expensive, and one would not be able to look closer at this without realizing how Boston University is exploiting that international students do not have that many alternatives when moving to Boston. Boston University has one purpose and one purpose alone, and this is sadly to maximize its profit.
activities_available: Boston University had a wide range of activities available for students. During the first week or so they even had an event planned where one could explore all the different clubs at the University. This was a very overwhelming experience but also a great way of getting involved with organizations appropriate for one's interest.
activities_recommended: I chose to join the running club which I would recommend other exchange students to consider. Physical training is important for ones physical as well as mental wellbeing, but it is also a great way to make new friends.
weekend_recommendations: Any exchange student in Boston studying there during the fall should explore some of the nature outside of the city when the leaves start to change color. New England in general has a reputation of being gorgeous during the fall. I spent a weekend in New York with some of the other exchange students. Although it is expensive to be in New York it is an obvious place to visit. But overall, I would just recommend potential future students to be open to any social event or weekend they may be invited to by fellow students. It is wonderful to interact with local students and one will most likely learn how most of us are not really as different as we sometimes have a tendency to believe that we are.
culture_adjustment: I had previously studied in the United States and so, I pretty much knew what to expect and how it would feel to be speaking one's second language all the time. However, I would note to new students that the overall culture in Boston is in my experience more European than many other places in the United States and so one should not really expect something radically different from when living in Denmark.
socializing_tips: Chat with your fellow classmates and be open for invitations to social events. Also, join a club of your interest! (…Or possibly a fraternity if you are under 21 and have the time for it)
cultural_challenges: Boston is very European in many ways and so I did not find that many challenging cultural differences. However, one might find that Americans have a slightly different sense of humor in some ways and at times I found that they seemed more immature than I would have expected from my peers back in Denmark. One very surprising cultural difference I encountered in Boston was that most of my classes mostly consisted of Chinese students. This is especially the case in courses within mathematics.
culture_appreciated: One quality that I think we could learn from in Denmark is how Americans reward and celebrate the great achievements. Danes have a tendency of thinking that we should all be the same and therefore nobody is allowed to be recognized as being better at something than others. Americans view the great performance as something to be inspired by and they recognize the great performance without any hint of bitterness.
top3_advice: - Be aware that it is expensive living and studying in Boston so include some extra room in your budget for unexpected expenses. - Boston University does not in my experience care much for stimulating the social life at the dorms, so be advised that one should find their own social groups. A good way to do this would be to join one of the many clubs at Boston University. - Follow your classes and keep up with the homework but remember to take the time to explore Boston and make great friendships. In the end, these are the things you most likely will remember.
other_useful_info: Personally I would recommend exchange students to communicate a lot throughout their stay and invite each other for different social events. It may be great to make some local friendships in Boston, but it may be even more rewarding to make friendships all around the globe.
most_rewarding: Find a goal that you want to achieve and do your best to succeed. For me it was running a Marathon and I accomplished this after many practices in the running club and having joined a marathon running class.
greatest_challenge: I found it challenging to accept how Boston University as an institution did not care for its students but only for maximizing profits. Luckily, I managed to set this somewhat aside and enjoy the time I had in Boston. I had some interesting classes with great professors and also made some great experiences and friendships.
other_comments: Do not live on campus. Find housing off campus with the other exchange students!

crucial_aspects: The exchange at Boston University allowed me to take courses in different fields such as sociology, literature, genders and sexualities and critical race theory. Taking these courses broadened by academic horizons and made me more aware of power structures and relations that dominate not only academia, but also the wider world. I feel this exchange has given me more empathy and understanding for other people, cultures and a will to change the world for the better through my academic pursuits.

registration_process: It is important to know that only some courses are open for registration during the course registration period. Most courses (especially upper-level and graduate courses) require permission from either the course coordinator or the faculty. This process is INCREDIBLY slow. All the courses that I wanted to register for required pre-approval. I had to collect transcripts from both my bachelor's and master's degrees, write motivational letters, and get letters of recommendation of people who could vouch for me. I tried desperately to get everything sorted before arriving at BU, but in the end, that was not possible. Therefore, I registered for the only film courses that were open to exchange students and then changed them in the two-week add/drop period that starts at the beginning of the semester. So my advice: make a list of the courses that you wanna take that need pre-approval, and go talk to professors during the first two weeks of class. They will tell you what they need in order for you to take the class.
registration_help: This is very faculty dependent. At my faculty (Department of Communication), there was an incredibly sweet lady called Rachel who helped me register for everything. I only found her after being transferred 5 times from person to person.
registration_success: It was a struggle but in the end, I registered for all the courses that I wanted.
registration_advice: - Just register for the courses that are open to exchange students - Make a list of the courses you actually wanna register for. - Gather all the documents that state that you meet the prerequisites for that course (for example, I wanted to register for a course that required you to have done a course in Film Studies, so I had a course from my BA that was quite similar and attached its syllabus to my application) - Email Sage this material, but don't expect to get admitted to the courses while being in Denmark - Once you're at BU, talk to the professors and ask what you need to do to get admitted to these courses.
academics_comments: I had an amazing time at Boston University. The VISA application was a nightmare, so some extra help would have been much appreciated in that regard. The host university also did not organize a nice orientation week, so that was quite disappointing.

teaching_comparison: - The classes were smaller - More exams and papers throughout the semester, not one big exam at the end of the semester - Your grade is made up of several assignments - It's quite easy to get high grades - Most students need to follow 4 courses, but KU students only need 3. So our workload is lower compared to other students

recommended_courses: COM FT508 Line producing for undergrads: incredibly useful if you want to work in the film industry since they teach you how to work with MovieMagic Budgeting and Scheduling. These two programs are used throughout the entire industry, so it's very good to put on your resume and for it to be a part of your skillset.

activities_recommended: Was not part of any
weekend_recommendations: - Go to Salem during Halloween - Definitely go to NYC (Flix Bus has student discounted tickets if you log in via Student Beans or UniDays) - Visit New Haven (Yale) and Providence (Brown University)

top3_advice: - Make sure you have all your vaccinations. BU requires students to have certain vaccinations that you don't automatically get vaccinated for (such as Hepatitis B and some others), so make sure in advance that you have all the required vaccines. There is also a form that needs to be signed by a doctor, so make sure that you also take care of that in advance. When I saw that we needed vaccinations as students, I assumed it was the COVID-19 vaccines, but there are a bunch of other ones. - As part of your application, you need to have at least $10,000 in your account or have someone (like a parent) stand as a guarantee for you. So it is important to be aware of this before you apply. - Check out Mint Mobile, Red Pocket, or Tello for an eSim. You can keep your Danish phone number, and pay for an American eSim which is super convenient. Share your referral code with a friend who's also studying in the States, and you'll both get a discount!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to try and study in an English-speaking country, and Boston seemed like a great university city due to the many universities located in the city. Also, I liked the fact that NYC is only a couple of hours away by train/bus and I had heard that New England should be very beautiful in the fall.
overall_comments: I can highly recommend Boston and Boston University. I had a great semester there and enjoyed exploring the city as well as traveling and doing day trips on the weekends and during holidays. Boston is more European than many other cities in the US which made it easy to adapt, and it is historically a really interesting city. Boston University is a great university, and I especially appreciated all the facilities and benefits they offer to its students. The campus itself is located on a big road and is not the most charming one though. The good thing about it is the balance between being in the university campus bobble and still being in the middle of the city, which I think is one of the features that make Boston University special.
info_ease: You are very early on in the process assigned to a coordinator from Boston University who is reachable by e-mail and can answer all of your questions. This made the process upon arrival very manageable. Besides that, the university provides you with many resources on its website to help you figure everything out. You get the impression that they are very used to international/exchange students and have solutions for everything.
arrival_assistance: When you arrive, there are three days of orientation before classes start, where you will get a lot of information and you will be able to ask all the questions you may have in terms of courses, visa, expenses, etc. You will also meet other students.
arrival_comments: In terms of information and assistance, the orientation was very good. You get a lot of information, and they will cover everything you need to know and do. You will also meet the international coordinator whom you have been in contact with before arrival, and she will either be able to answer questions you have or put you in contact with a person who can. Regarding the social aspect, I was not completely satisfied with the orientation program. You are assigned to a group of freshmen/international students/exchange students with whom you spend the days, and I was lucky to be in a very good group where I met some really good friends, but there are not many social activities and therefore you need to reach out yourself and take initiative. Also, the orientation was both for freshmen and for exchange/international students meaning the other students you meet here are very young (freshmen are 17-18 years old), and a lot of the information you get and activities you do are not relevant for you. Overall, I was happy that there were these orientation days though because it was a good way to get familiar with the university and meet some other students before classes started.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_process: The course registration opens pretty early (in spring if you are doing a fall exchange). Course registration opens later for exchange students than for regular BU students, meaning some courses were already full when registration opened for us. I found this really annoying and also a bit unfair, but you can check regularly if somebody has dropped the course. You are able to add and drop courses during the first two weeks of the semester which I really enjoyed and took advantage of because you then are able to attend the first class to see whether you like the course and/or the professor or not (just remember to update your forhåndsgodkendelse from KU). It is also possible to write the professor if the class is full and ask if you can be enrolled anyway. I had success with this in one course, because I was very eager and wrote him before as well as showing up on the first day of class.
registration_help: You can always write Sage, the coordinator who is in charge of exchange students if you have any problems, or otherwise talk/write to professors.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure to register for courses when registration opens. Check regularly to see if a spot opens if a course you want is full. Add all the courses you are considering, if you can, on your forhåndsgodkendelse from KU so you have the freedom to add and drop in the first two weeks of the semester if you realize that a course isn't what you expected. If a course you want is full, I can recommend the page buninja.com. Here you can list which course you want to get into, and then you'll get a sms/e-mail when a spot opens up (you'll need an American phone number to sign up though, so I only used it after arriving in Boston).
academics_comments: I can highly recommend Boston and Boston University. I had a great semester there and enjoyed exploring the city as well as traveling and doing day trips on the weekends and during holidays. Boston is more European than many other cities in the US which made it easy to adapt, and it is historically a really interesting city. Boston University is a great university, and I especially appreciated all the facilities and benefits they offer to its students. The campus itself is located on a big road and is not the most charming one though. The good thing about it is the balance between being in the university campus bobble and still being in the middle of the city, which I think is one of the features that make Boston University special.
course_level: I was overall happy about the levels of my courses because I didn't want to be too busy studying. I wanted to have time to travel, socialize and explore Boston, and therefore I tried not to pick too challenging courses. I had one 200-level course which was pretty easy, but I still found it very interesting because it was taught from an American perspective, which was new to me. I had two 500-courses, one of them was specifically for international students and was very easy too, while the criminology course was the only course, I felt matched my academic level. I didn't mind that the courses were maybe a bit too easy for me, because I still found much of the course material and discussions in class interesting since it was based on an American perspective and entailed discussions and topics that were new to me.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching differed a lot from what I am used to at KU. Your grade is not only based on one final exam as is the case on KU but on several assignments and participation. My classes were way smaller than at KU and it reminded me a lot of high school, where the professor knows the students' names, expects the students to participate and takes attendance (it affects your grade if you don't show up for class). In general, I found the workload during the semester higher than I am used to because you have quite a lot of quizzes, papers, presentations, etc. but the level of difficulty was lower, which made it manageable. Also, I really enjoyed that my grades didn't only depend on one final paper, which meant that the workload was spread out more evenly over the entire semester.
courses_enrolled: MET CJ 570 - Criminology and Crime Policy (4 credits) MET MG 545 - American Institutions and Culture (4 credits) CAS SO 242 - Globalization and World Poverty (4 credits)
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the course Criminology and Crime Policy. I thought it was super interesting and professor Cadigan is very sweet and helpful.
unexpected_costs: I had to reschedule my flight home and in general, I didn't expect Boston to be as expensive as it is
cost_comparison: Phone plans can be quite expensive, but I can recommend phone carriers such as Mint Mobile and Red Pocket which are pretty cheap and more like Danish prices
activities_available: There are more than 400 clubs at BU with all sorts of profiles. I joined the Unicef club, which was a great way of meeting American students and feeling more like a part of BU
activities_recommended: Join a club, a sports team or volunteer
weekend_recommendations: In Boston: take advantage of the free access for BU students at museums in Boston, enjoy the view of Boston from Washington Tower in Mount Auburn Cemetery, check out bars in Allston, go to BU ice hockey, basketball, and soccer games (even though you are not normally into sports) Outside of Boston: Visit Cape Cod while the weather is still nice, visit Salem during Halloween, go to Providence during the WaterFire event, visit New Haven (Yale University is really beautiful), go to other states in New England for fall foliage (I can recommend New Hampshire and Maine), rent a car, do the Ocean Drive in Newport, Rhode Island, and enjoy the scenic view
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. Boston is one of the most European cities in the States, and you can get around by foot or bike. Americans are generally very open compared to Danes and are more likely to approach strangers, which can be really nice when you are new and want to meet people.
socializing_tips: Get to know your roommates or floormates (and try to accept the potential age difference), join a club or a sports team, talk to students from your classes
cultural_challenges: Bars and clubs are very strict when it comes to ID, so always bring your passport when you are going out. The T is really slow and makes you appreciate the metro in Copenhagen. Always tip 15-20% even though it seems like a lot, and get used to always being asked "How are you?"
culture_appreciated: The helpfulness and openness I experienced from Americans
top3_advice: 1. Don't panic if it takes a couple of weeks to adapt and unwind. I thought it was very exhausting at the beginning with all the small talk and new people and impressions, but you will find friends and have a great time. 2. Make sure to enjoy your time in Boston, go on trips, and do fun stuff. The semester is over before you know it, and then it's nice to have a lot of memories to look back at. 3. It is expensive to go on exchange, especially in Boston, and if you signed up to live on campus be aware that you will need to pay the full amount of rent + meal plan for your entire stay at the beginning of the semester.
other_useful_info: Remember that KU transfers grades as pass/fail, so don't stress too much about them.
most_rewarding: All the amazing people I have met, trips and experiences I had, the improvement of my English skills, one of my classes in which I learned a lot
greatest_challenge: Money matters, finding a place to live, being away from your people back home

arrival_assistance: On the first day of the intro-days, they hosted a meeting for students from abroad, providing me with any information i needed and gave me the possibility to ask any question i wanted to.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You are given access to a portal where you can register for classes and are allowed to take (almost) any classes you want - if you live up to the requirements and there is space left in the class.
registration_help: The exchange coordinator is very helpfull and will try to get you into the classes you want to attend
registration_success: I was able to register for 5/6 classes I wanted to attend.
registration_advice: Even if you are not qualified for a class you want to take, talk to the professor and ask if they will allow you into a class anyways. Sometimes you have another course from your UCPH that will qualify you even though you didn't take the qualifying course at BU. The exchange coordinator will also gladly help with this.
course_level: Some of the classes had a very demanding workload. I took an extra class for enjoyment, and I would not necessarily recommend this - at least if you only attend graduate-level courses as I did. As far as I heard, there is a big difference in the workload of graduate and undergraduate courses, so if you want to attend more classes than required, mixing in some undergraduate classes might be a good idea.
teaching_comparison: The processors at BU strive to create a relationship with the students and have open office hours that the student widely uses - in addition, many of the classes (in particular graduate classes) was smaller than the ones at UCPH. Furthermore, the courses had a lot of assignments throughout the semester, making up the final grade. Thus, it was very different than at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Political Risk Analysis Intelligence Issues Political Campaigns Digital Diplomacy
recommended_courses: I recommend Political Risk Analysis. Professor Oates is very vibrant and seems like he enjoys teaching. Furthermore, his course is oriented toward the real world, not just academia
unexpected_costs: There is (almost) no way around paying approximately 1200 for insurance at BU.
cost_comparison: I was shocked by how expensive everything is - grocery shopping was almost double the price compared to Denmark.
activities_available: They have unbelievably many clubs. BU has a club for anything you can think of.
activities_recommended: If you want to do volunteer work, sports, theater, language, journalism, or anything else, attend the Splash event, where all clubs are in attendance. Furthermore, I recommend that students take advantage of the facilities, such as the SportsCenter, which also has a pool. My nr. 1 recommendation would be to get sports-pass and attend games. In particular, hockey games are a lot of fun since BU has one of the grates hockey teams in all of America - some games are even played at TD Garden.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going to a basket game with the Celtics at TD Garden and a hockey game with the Boston Bruins. It is expensive but worth it.
culture_adjustment: Very easy - not that different compared to Denmark.
socializing_tips: Attend sports games and other social gatherings. You can also join a club and meet people interested in the same thing as you.
cultural_challenges: Not really anything to be honest
culture_appreciated: The sports-culture
top3_advice: It will be expensive, but worth it. Do yourself a favor and apply for grants - many of them are available for US students. Do attend the games - it is so much fun.
other_useful_info: Be aware that the winters in Boston are freezing! Even colder than you think.
most_rewarding: The professors are fascinating, and almost all of them have had a career outside academia, making the lecture incredibly interesting.
greatest_challenge: I took four graduate-level courses, and I think that is was a big work-load. If I had a redo, I would have mixed in an undergraduate class or stuck to the recommended three courses.

activities_recommended: Meld jer ind i nogle klubber i starten! Man kan altid lade være med at komme hvis man ikke gider mere
weekend_recommendations: Jeg var meget i New York.

cultural_challenges: ved ikke.

other_useful_info: No.

crucial_aspects: As a vibrant student city, Boston is home to numerous prestigious universities. Further, Boston University is especially known for its welcoming environment for international students. The city's European feel eases the transition from Denmark, reducing culture shock. Additionally, Boston is bike- and walk-friendly, making it convenient to navigate and explore. Lastly, I had never been to the east coast of United States before.
info_ease: It was relatively easy to find the information I needed upon arrival. Boston University was very helpful in providing the necessary resources and guidance for a smooth transition.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival, we received assistance from staff who helped us check into our housing accommodation. Additionally, there were two orientation days—one general and one specifically for exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We could register a few months before from Denmark. It was just through StudentLink and it was kind of easy. Further, everyone has the option to change courses in the first two weeks - called "shopping week".
registration_help: You could read about the different courses online - that was it concerning the course content. However, we got a good introduction about how to register at StudentLink from our exchange administrator.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. However, exchange students gets to choose courses after regular students - so a good amount of courses were already full when I got the chance to regsister.
registration_advice: Be flexible and don't panic if you don't get the courses you want straight away. Often, American students overload the first week and then drop courses they don't want - so just keep an eye on StudentLink in the first week and you will be good.
course_level: On average, the course levels were similar to Denmark.
teaching_comparison: We were fewer students so you really had to participate. In this way, you will also probably get a closer relation to the professors compared to in Denmark.
courses_enrolled: History of Neoliberalism w/Quinn Slobodian Political Analysis w/Jacob Brown GLobal Policy Methods w/Mahesh Karra
recommended_courses: I would recommend any of these three or other similar courses from the same professor.
unexpected_costs: A lot of more expensive travel days than I expected, but that was entirely my decision (haha),
cost_comparison: Everything was kind of expensive in Boston.
activities_available: A lot of clubs. I joined a soccer club and we started a running club in the exchange group, but BU also has an official running club which I joined one time. Also, Fitrec has a lot of offers - also outdoor hikes etc.
activities_recommended: FitTreks - join some of Fitrec's outdoor activities!
weekend_recommendations: Outside Boston: Within a relatively short distance to Boston, I went to NYC, Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Washington D.C. Further, I went on a FitTreks hike to New Hampshire. In Boston: Go to a sports game or the parks in the center.
culture_adjustment: Boston is known as a "European" city so there is no real culture shock.
socializing_tips: Join the university clubs or talk to your classmates (even though they are not always so talkative in class).
cultural_challenges: The frat parties were overwhelming and not for me (haha).
culture_appreciated: The university sports culture was great!
top3_advice: Firstly, be excited—Boston is a fantastic place for your exchange experience. Secondly, be outgoing and join clubs and activities to make the most of your time and meet new people. Lastly, explore other places on the East Coast; there's a lot to see and do beyond Boston.
other_useful_info: Don't buy the local transportation semester card. Buy the Charliecard when you are there - you will figure out how it works. Also, you can subscribe to Bluebikes to rent bikes - it's easy and cheap.
most_rewarding: Meeting new friends.
greatest_challenge: Classes are smaller than in DK, so I had to participate a lot while my English was not that good.

crucial_aspects: My major has a lot of mandatory courses which means I had to choose a school based on the availability of certain courses and other than that I wanted to go to an English speaking country as I know that would make it easier to find friends and participate in class, etc.
info_ease: BU provides a full website with everything you need to know from the moment you apply through finding housing, registering courses, getting your visa, and arriving in the US
arrival_assistance: There was a 2-day orientation after we arrived
arrival_comments: Some of the orientation is done with freshmen students which means there is also a lot of information which does not pertain to you as an international student
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Exchange students get access to registration as the last ones so you should make a list of first picks for your courses as well as backups in case there is not enough seats in the course. If you go on the website there is a planner where you can put in the courses you intend to take and see if they fit into a schedule together. That way you can add all your courses in one go when registration opens but beware there is a max amount of credits!
registration_help: There is a step-by-step guide available but I would recommend you take a look around the website as it is not that intuitive
registration_success: Yes but not on the first try. I had to email one of my professors about enrolling in his course which he fortunately allowed so if you're really desperate I would recommend reaching out to hear if they can overenroll the class or put you on a waitlist
registration_advice: Don't panic if you don't get all your classes at first. Many students drop in and out of classes all the way until the semester starts and then you have two weeks where you can "shop" by going to different classes and feeling them out before your schedule is locked
course_level: The academic level of undergraduate courses are not as high as in UCPH
teaching_comparison: There is a lot more participation in class which often counts as part of your grade. If you don't feel comfortable speaking in class there is also the option of going to the professor's office hours and talking to them there. Even though the academic level isn't that high there is a lot of work throughout the semester like smaller assignments, quizzes, presentations and midterms so it's important to stay on top of your work
courses_enrolled: PS241 Developmetal Psychology PS471 Special Topics in Psychopathology PH248 Existentialism MB102 Ashtanga Yoga
recommended_courses: I loved PH248 with Dr. Sheeley and would recommend anyone to check out the courses from the Philosophy Department. I would also recommend checking out the PDP classes where you can try out different sports for free!
unexpected_costs: You take a lot more Ubers in Boston because even though there is public transportation it isn't always running at night
cost_comparison: Housing and food is the same price or more expensive than Copenhagen
activities_available: There are 200+ clubs at BU e.g. knitting club, running club, nordic countries club, etc. You can check them out at the club fair called Splash in the beginning of the semester
activities_recommended: FitTrek offer hiking trips, whale watching, skiing and kayaking throughout the semester for a reasonable price - the tickets are limited so get them sooner rather than later. Sign up for the student fitness center which has a swimming pool, hot tub, weight room, running track, basketball and volleyball courts, climbing wall and more.
weekend_recommendations: Check out the different neighborhoods and all the cool museums in time, go outside the city to Cape Cod, Cape Ann, Salem, etc., check out sports games with the Celtics/Bruins/Red Sox, take a weekend trip to New York or DC
culture_adjustment: I have been on exchange in the US before so it was super easy
socializing_tips: It can be harder to strike up conversation with classmates as most Americans don't hang around after class so I would recommend signing up for clubs, sports or trips and trying to make friends who you can then invite out for coffee or a similar activity
cultural_challenges: It can be hard to move past small talk to an actual friendship with some Americans but don't be discouraged and keep trying until you meet someone who puts in effort to you as well
culture_appreciated: Friendliness and helpfulness! If you reach out there is almost no limit to what you can do
top3_advice: 1. Take advantage of the many cheap and free events in town like discounted prices at Red Sox games and the Symphony Hall and free entry to most museums in Boston if you show your BU student ID 2. Don't miss out on career fairs and your professor's office hours if you're looking for academic and professional opportunities like internships or research positions 3. Check out the different dining halls and find your favorite (mine was Fenway), be aware that the food is more processed and can take some time getting used to
other_useful_info: Look out for grants and scholarships as Boston is quite expensive and other than that be open and say yes to things! Even if it doesn't seem that interesting to you, you might meet some cool people and make new memories.
most_rewarding: To be honest it was the community with the other international students which made the experience super special, I learned about all different kinds of cultures and have friends all over the world now
greatest_challenge: Balancing my studies and having fun - there are so many things to do in and around Boston so it was hard to stay on top of work at times which is also an important reason why I went on exchange
other_comments: I loved Boston as a city and would definitely recommend studying here!

weekend_recommendations: Visit New york, walk around Boston, there is so much to see but stay in the safe areas please. I recommend following Instagram accounts that showcase the "best Boston cafes, museums" etc., you could find some hidden gems
culture_adjustment: The american culture is very easy going and outgoing. However, really close do you rarely get to american students. They might party a lot and might be loud etc. but it is not a very personal culture. I would recommend getting to know the other exchange students since you are all in the same boat.
socializing_tips: It is quite easy to get into conversations with americans, they are mostly loud and outgoing.
cultural_challenges: I found it very challenging that american students are this loud and non discrete. I bounded mostly with other exchange students and even the Professors who were rather discrete and calm.
culture_appreciated: The openness, the students were mostly interested and kind, although I did not like that they seemed loud and "rough".
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy the experience at an american university, everything is different, from the very first day on: loud music, big colorful screens and screams to welcome the new students 2. Since everything is so different, try not to get too overwhelmed, but keep contact to your family and friends back home, it will help you "survive" in the loud messy american system 3. Enjoy the privilege that us exchange students do not have to pay the annnual 90k$ tuition fees and be aware of the fact that you will be surrounded by american students either coming from rich families or students that have the best grades and have already been to Harvard University, Cambridge University and whatever before. It is a different environment than at KU, definitely.
other_useful_info: Just to repeat myself: book housing on campus, no matter how disgusting the housing is (in case the other students dont help in the cleaning process), you safe lots of time and nerves living on campus and having a meal plan. The full meal plan is also much cheaper and saves time than having to buy groceries and cook every day. Almost every exchange student that I got to know had a meal plan and all students were living on campus.
most_rewarding: Experiencing the incredible reasearch facilities at one of the best american universities (which has a lot of money)
greatest_challenge: To keep up with daily life activities (cooking food, contacting people from my home country) since I was busy studying 24/7 and sometimes had days from 6.30am-8pm doing research on research vessels, in the lab etc. The american working culture is a hustle culture and the complete opposite from the danish working culture.
other_comments: The american system is very different. Since there are lots of opportunities and offers you might feel overwhelmed and get burned out easily. The experience in the end however is worth it.

crucial_aspects: These are my general reflections upon my stay in Boston. Graduate courses in the US are typically specialized and at a high level, and I wanted to try that. BU has an impressive array of courses available to me as a student of English. Generally, BU is strong when it comes to the humanities; they do not deprioritize it in any way. I have found that at KU, the courses offered have often not been so tangibly useful or CV-oriented. The courses I took at BU are future-oriented; I did media writing, copyediting, and marketing communications. I have not been able to find that at KU. I should stress that the workload over here (including assignments and testing) throughout the semester is intense, but you get used to it. And given the hands-on nature of the courses, I get to really finetune my writing skills by producing my own original copy, receiving loads of feedback from instructors (they have SO much time for their students), editing my own texts, and editing other peoples' texts. I have one professor over here who keeps mentioning how her previous students have gotten jobs because of their endorsed copyediting skills that they got in her copyediting class. I also wanted to experience the romance of the New England foliage which definitely lived up to my expectations; never have I seen brighter red, orange, and yellow leaves light up a city than during these past months. I also want to stress what it means to be with people who come from backgrounds that are different from my own. I find it refreshing to have the Danish common denominator removed in social interactions; when the layer of pre-agreed opinions is not there, conversations move in a way that allows more people to be comfortable and partake freely. I want to work with producing communication. You cannot write a good text if you don't know to whom you are writing. This fall, I have gotten to cooperate and spend my time with people from Italy, Switzerland, Taiwan, India, the US, Britain, Pakistan, France, Brazil, China, etc. The multinational dynamic I have experienced feels healthy, and it has been highly rewarding both academically, professionally, and personally.
info_ease: Pretty easy. There was loads of information but also people and resources available to help me.
arrival_assistance: Not really any assistance other than attending introductory meetings etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

You can also go on the waitlist if the class is full.
registration_help: Plenty of helpful resources are presented to incoming exchange students at BU.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted to take.
course_level: I don't think the academic level was super high. However, the immense workload makes up for that. I learned SO much because I had to be super active in class and between classes.
teaching_comparison: At BU, I had lots of class presentations, minor assignments, homework to be handed in, and occasional quizzes. At KU, I am more so used to one big exam by the end of the semester.
courses_enrolled: Basic Media Writing Copyediting Fundamentals Marketing Communication
recommended_courses: I would recommend all three courses I took to any student who wants to improve their communication skills. I have worked in depth with so many aspects and layers of text and other modes of communication.
unexpected_costs: Boston is an expensive city. I did not really have unexpected costs. However, the price levels were higher than I could have imagined.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to go to the US, and I heard that Boston was great place to study abroad. Boston is a city with many different and well renowned universities which motivated me to choose Boston University as my first priority. Moreover, the city is very European in some aspects which also was one of the main reasons why I chose this university compared to others in the US. Furthermore, there is many people in Boston who come from different cultures all over the world which further enhanced my dedication in choosing this university among others.
overall_comments: If you have the time and the money, I would highly recommend to study abroad. I have developed a lot as a person and met many interesting people from all over the world (eg. US, India, Colombia ect.). The professors are also enthusiastic and are alway there to help if you are having difficulty with something. I stayed in a hotel for the entire exchange, which meant that our room was nicely decorated and always clean (I didn't pay more for this, as the university provided this).
info_ease: It was fairly easy to some point. We had some meetings with exchange manager at Boston University, and they also had a website that listed everything we needed to do and know before arrival. You will get an email where you will receive all important information regarding the exchange. Note, that they are a bit slow to respond to emails which was quite annoying.
arrival_assistance: We got an introduction to the university the first three days of the exchange. Here we met with others who were on exchange and learned a little about the university and their inclusion.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: If you have the time and the money, I would highly recommend to study abroad. I have developed a lot as a person and met many interesting people from all over the world (eg. US, India, Colombia ect.). The professors are also enthusiastic and are alway there to help if you are having difficulty with something. I stayed in a hotel for the entire exchange, which meant that our room was nicely decorated and always clean (I didn't pay more for this, as the university provided this).
registration_process: More or less the same as UCPH. You sign into your BU account and get a list of different courses you can choose from. It says if they are full or available. If they are full, you can get on the waiting list [If it is not full], and if it is available you can enroll right away. Some courses may have prerequisites, but they often don't ask if you have had these courses. However, I would not recommend you choosing something totally new.
registration_help: The exchange student manager [Sage] was helpful with the process and if you encountered any problems you were always welcome to send her an email.
registration_success: Pretty successful with the process. There was only one course that I didn't get, but that was alright. I was on the waiting list for two of the courses I wanted, but I only got a place on one course [Game Theory].
registration_advice: Even though you are on the waiting list at the very start of the semester, I would highly recommend not to remove yourself from the waiting list. I was number 13 or something in July for Game Theory and was quite anxious if I got that but two weeks before the semester started I eventually got enrolled in the courses. Moreover, you can always talk to the professors. They may be more susceptible to let exchange students enroll in courses that are full.
academics_comments: If you have the time and the money, I would highly recommend to study abroad. I have developed a lot as a person and met many interesting people from all over the world (eg. US, India, Colombia ect.). The professors are also enthusiastic and are alway there to help if you are having difficulty with something. I stayed in a hotel for the entire exchange, which meant that our room was nicely decorated and always clean (I didn't pay more for this, as the university provided this).
course_level: Some courses were easier than others. Undergraduate courses (Level 400 and below) was easier than undergraduate courses at UCPH. On the other hand, graduate courses are somewhat more difficult than the undergraduate. I would say they are more like the level we have at UCHP or even harder. I had one [EC531] which was quite hard.
teaching_comparison: Undergraduate courses are easier while graduate courses are similar or even harder.
courses_enrolled: Urban & Regional Economics [CASEC 328] Game Theory [CASEC 403] Market Structure & Industrial Organization [CASEC 531]
recommended_courses: Would recommend Urban & Regional Economics if you want something with less math but that works with some exciting topics. Game Theory was also pretty good and the professor was good. I took it as a substitute to Micro III. If you like theory and math (Like Micro I), I would recommend Market Structure & Industrial Organization.
unexpected_costs: The is some vaccines you have to get, but you can get them for free though the insurance. I would highly recommend doing that and save the money [I paid around 3,000 DKK for the vaccines].
cost_comparison: Prices were as expected. Boston is an expensive city, so if you want to grab a drink or eat out, you can expect the same prices as Copenhagen.
activities_available: There were many different kind of cultural, athletic and social activities available for the students at the university. Trivia nights, bingo and so on. You can also sign up for different sports activities such as long distance running, sailing, rugby, volleyball, football [soccer] and so on. They have a huge gym where there are plenty of opportunities to do all kinds of sports (Swimming, climbing, weightlifting).
activities_recommended: If you like to run, I would recommend joining the long distance running club. It is a great way to start your day, but it is also a great opportunity to meet new people. If you want to meet new people in general, join one of the many student activities.
weekend_recommendations: Many people traveled to New York City for a weekend trip. If you have never seen it and it is on your bucket list, I would highly suggest going, as it is only a 3-4 hour drive from Boston. During Thanksgiving, I and 9 other exchange students and fellow friends from Denmark traveled to Maine (Further north than Boston). If you want to go out of town and see some beautiful nature, I would endorse Maine and see Acadia National Park. [Note that we rented cars through Turo with was the easiest]. While you're in Boston, you should also walk the Freedom Trail and see some of their museums, especially Isabella Stewart Gardner.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy to say the least. It will take maybe two weeks or so to get used to it completely. Economics at UCPH only lectures only in courses in Danish, why it takes some time to get used to it. However, most master courses are in fact lectured in English, why study abroad ultimately helps you in your future studies.
socializing_tips: Students are very sweet and open and in some courses there are group projects where you will get a study group. I would also recommend to share a dorm with others as this is a great opportunity to get to know others. As mentioned above, you can also join one of the many fitness clubs.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find anything particular challenging. You just had to get used to the currency, language, and their tipping culture. The tipping was probably the hardest, as we are never used to do it in Denmark. But you will figure it out while you are there.
culture_appreciated: People's openness. They are so nice in the US and comments if they like your shoes and what not. You will never hear a Dane say this. Moreover, the professors at BU comes from all over the world and the same is true for the students. I really appreciated this as I gained insight into new cultures in relation to my own.
top3_advice: If you want to try something new in relation to UCPH, where you can improve yourself as a person, meet new people and get to know new cultures, and at the same time get an experience of a lifetime, I would definitely recommend you go. It's worth it.
other_useful_info: I would recommend you at least try Fenway dining hall once for dinner. It won't disappoint you. I would also recommend buying a power outlet, as it is quite useful. If I were you I would get the dining plan
most_rewarding: The friends and the personal development. As I have already pointed out, this is an experience of a lifetime.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was probably leaving Denmark and say goodbye to friends and family. It was nerve-racking and I was afraid of being lonely and not meet anyone. But once I arrived and met my roommate, this nervousness was already gone. You have to know that everyone is in the same boat.

crucial_aspects: I had long been certain that I wanted to study in an English-speaking country, as this would eliminate any language barriers and ensure that all instruction was in a language I fully understood. I applied to several universities in both the United States and the United Kingdom, but ultimately chose Boston as my first priority for several reasons. First, I wanted to experience life in the United States firsthand. Second, I had heard that Boston is an exceptional city to live in, particularly for students. Finally, I found many of the courses offered there to be especially interesting and well aligned with my academic interests.
overall_comments: I truly valued my study abroad experience. While certain aspects—particularly the social side—were more challenging than I had initially anticipated, this is why I have not rated the experience a full ten. Nevertheless, I gained a great deal from the experience, both academically and in terms of personal growth. I would strongly recommend that anyone who is even considering studying abroad take the opportunity, as it is without a doubt a highly rewarding and worthwhile experience.
info_ease: The process was very straightforward. Boston University provided extensive information before the start of the semester, including an online course for all new BU students that introduced the university, available opportunities, and resources for support. In addition, there was a separate online course specifically for international students, which explained what to expect in the United States, including the grading system, how classes are structured, and even appropriate ways to address professors. The exchange program manager was also very proactive in sharing clear and helpful information both prior to the semester and during its initial weeks.
arrival_assistance: In addition to the information mentioned above, there was an introductory week for all new students at the university. During this week, international students were grouped together, which provided an opportunity to meet one another. The program included both social events and more practical sessions, such as introductions to the university and its facilities. Overall, I found the introductory week somewhat confusing and not particularly helpful, largely because it was primarily designed for students beginning their full degree at the university rather than exchange students. That said, the meeting with the exchange program manager was very helpful. I would have appreciated a more thorough campus tour and additional social time with other exchange students. However, I did not feel that I began the semester lacking any crucial information or feeling overwhelmed, which was reassuring.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I truly valued my study abroad experience. While certain aspects—particularly the social side—were more challenging than I had initially anticipated, this is why I have not rated the experience a full ten. Nevertheless, I gained a great deal from the experience, both academically and in terms of personal growth. I would strongly recommend that anyone who is even considering studying abroad take the opportunity, as it is without a doubt a highly rewarding and worthwhile experience.
registration_process: Before course registration opens, students have access to an online portal that lists all available courses, including detailed descriptions and any prerequisite requirements. The portal also includes a “schedule builder” feature, which allows students to add courses they are interested in and see how they fit together in a potential timetable. When registration opens, courses are allocated on a first-come, first-served basis. It is therefore important to register promptly, particularly as full-time degree students are given priority access, which can limit the number of available spots. If a course is full at the time of registration, it is possible to join a waitlist. Many students adjust their schedules or drop courses before or during the beginning of the semester, meaning that being on a waitlist is not without hope. I was personally on the waitlist for three courses and was ultimately admitted to all of them.
registration_help: Before registration opened, all exchange students participated in an online meeting with the exchange program manager, during which she explained the registration system very thoroughly. This included guidance on how to register, how many courses we were allowed to take, and common mistakes students often make during the registration process. She was also readily available by email to answer any questions related to registration, including on the day registration opened, when she responded within minutes.
registration_success: Many of the courses I had initially planned to take, based on my early research into the university’s offerings, were ultimately not available during that semester. In that respect, I was not successful in registering for the specific courses I had originally intended to pursue. However, once I reviewed the courses that were actually offered, I was able to register for all of the classes I selected. In that sense, the registration process was ultimately successful.
registration_advice: It is important to keep in mind that even if a course is listed as usually being offered in a specific semester, this does not guarantee that it will actually be available. I found several courses on BU’s website that were indicated as being offered in both the fall and spring semesters, but when registration opened, many of these courses were not available during the fall semester when I was there. If you have particular courses you are especially interested in, it may therefore be worthwhile to contact the university in advance to confirm their availability. Additionally, it is important to note that the U.S. system allows students to change courses at the beginning of the semester. For example, after the first week, I realized that one course was not what I had expected and was able to drop it and enroll in another instead. It is also possible to register for more courses than required initially, which allows you to explore different options before finalizing your schedule.
academics_comments: I truly valued my study abroad experience. While certain aspects—particularly the social side—were more challenging than I had initially anticipated, this is why I have not rated the experience a full ten. Nevertheless, I gained a great deal from the experience, both academically and in terms of personal growth. I would strongly recommend that anyone who is even considering studying abroad take the opportunity, as it is without a doubt a highly rewarding and worthwhile experience.
course_level: In my personal experience the courses are neither harder nor easier at Boston University than at Copenhagen University. But the teaching style, described below, is very different and that can make it feel harder, especially in the beginning. Although I initially found this teaching style intimidating, I ultimately came to appreciate it, as it fostered a highly engaged and well-prepared learning environment. However, the continuous stream of assignments, quizzes, and assessments throughout the semester, in addition to regular readings, also meant that I had significantly less free time than I had expected. For students who place a strong emphasis on achieving high grades, it is important to be prepared for a heavier and more consistent workload throughout the semester compared to KU, where the most intensive work typically takes place during the exam period.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at Boston University differs significantly from that at KU. In my experience, there is a much stronger emphasis on participation at Boston University. In all of the courses I took, the final grade was composed of multiple smaller assessments, including assignments, presentations, quizzes, class participation, and in some cases a final exam. Attendance was often factored into the overall grade, which created a clear incentive to attend classes regularly. The focus on participation also led to far more in-class discussions than I was accustomed to at KU. Rather than primarily listening to a professor lecture, classes frequently involved active dialogue, with professors posing questions and, at times, allowing discussions to take up most of the session. Because participation was graded, there was a strong motivation to prepare for class and complete the assigned readings—something most students consistently did.
courses_enrolled: Archaeology of Cites Minoan and Mycenaean Civilizations Sexuality in Ancient Greece and Rome Greek and Roman Religion
recommended_courses: I would recommend all my courses, but especially Sexuality in ancient Greece and Rome. The subject was fascinating and professor Smith was so knowledgeable and enthusiastic about the topic.
unexpected_costs: I did not really encounter any unexpected costs. I went on a lot of trips to other places in New England which is not part of the budget above.
cost_comparison: Food is a difficult category. I was not shy about going out to restaurants or ordering take out. While groceries are expensive my food budget would probably have been lower if I ate more home cooked meals. Also, my food budget is based on me living of campus. Most people living on campus don't have a kitchen and are instead required to buy a meal plan for the dining halls. I also bought a meal plan, but it was a cheaper one designed for students living off campus who just want to eat a few meals in the dining halls.
activities_available: There are over 400 clubs at Boston University, including academic clubs, sports clubs, cultural/religious clubs and clubs for different hobbies. There are clubs like the school newspaper, model UN, debate, board games, Dungeons and Dragons, rocket Science and so on.
activities_recommended: I was part of the Classics Association and the History Club. For all international students I would recommend the international dinners held weekly in the basement of Marsh Chapel, the church on Campus. It is a great place to meet other intentional students and you don't have to be religious to join (I wasn't).
weekend_recommendations: Boston is an amazing city, especially if you like American history. There are so many historic sites related to the American Revolution in Boston and the surrounding area. I would definitely recommend doing the Freedom Trail. Are you there in the fall, then I would also recommend doing a foliage tour in the White Mountains. I would also advise people to explore the rest of Massachusetts, for example Cape Cod. I went to both Plymouth and Nantucket and would recommend both places. Salem is also a must see. And go watch a Red Sox game!
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. Boston is probably the most European city in the US.
socializing_tips: It is very hard. In my experience Americans love small talk, but it is hard to get closer to them than that and actually form a real connection. It is also my experience that some American students aren't interested in getting to know exchange students because we aren't there very long. I literally had a local student tell me that it wasn't worth the effort getting to know me because I would be leaving in a few months. The easiest place to socialize with local students are at the clubs. It can be hard to find time to talk to people during class, but if you join some clubs you are sure to meet American students who share your interests. Again, my experience is based on me living off campus. It might be easier if you live near the local students. Though most international people I have talked to share my experience and I know most exchange students living on campus end up living with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Other than the social aspect explained above and the teaching style explained further above, nothing was that challenging. But remember that Boston and the US is a lot more dangerous than Denmark. There are definitely parts of Boston that you should not go to at night.
culture_appreciated: Looking back, I greatly appreciated how proud Bostonians are of their city. People take genuine pride in Boston’s history, food culture, sports teams, and its many unique quirks. While this pride might initially seem intense or even slightly nationalistic, what stood out most to me was how willingly and enthusiastically they shared their city with others. Rather than conveying a sense of exclusivity, the attitude was very much one of openness - an eagerness to welcome others and invite them to experience what makes the city special. This enthusiasm is contagious, and it does not take long before you begin to share in that pride yourself. Overall, it creates a warm and welcoming atmosphere that makes you feel truly included.
top3_advice: 1: Are you 26 or older you cannot live on campus 2: The teaching style is very different and can be hard to get used to 3: Boston is an amazing city. I fell in love with it immediately and it will always have a special place in my heart.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: The academic program and experiencing Boston.
greatest_challenge: The social aspect.

crucial_aspects: The city of Boston, academic opportunities, and experiencing the "college" life.
info_ease: Very easy. Boston University (BU) is very proactive and willing to help. We had an exchange coordinator who we could always contact if in doubt. Also, she emailed us all the relevant information before arriving.
arrival_assistance: A lot. We met with our exchange coordinator during the first week, had a guide to show us around campus, and lots more.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Be aware of the opening day for registration. Full-time BU students get to choose before exchange students, so it is important to be ready when they open for registration. With that said, I also change a course after getting here, and attended a few that I did not like. Most people end up getting all the courses that they want.
registration_help: The portal. Also, you chan reach out to the exchange coordinator. I also contacted a few professors directly and asked for a spot in the class. I successfully got spots on both. These were graduate courses, and usually they don't allow for undergraduate students to participate in graduate courses, but I got lucky. If you show prerequisites and interest in the class, they will maybe allow you to join.
registration_success: Very successful. I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Reach out to professor - they are very helpfull and want you in class if you show interest. They like exchange students as we are typically very dedicated and mature.
course_level: The level varied a bit from class to class. For me, the level was similar to KU, but I also had two graduate classes instead of choosing only undergraduate. Most find the level a bit lower compared to KU, but it really does depend a lot on the classes you take. The classes are ranked in levels (1 through 8). So all classes being between 100-199 are level 1 and so on. 100-400 is undergraduate, and above 500 is graduate.
teaching_comparison: It is actually quite different. We are use to big lecture with around 200-300 people and exercise classes at KU. At BU, most classes are around 10-40 people. It is almost a high-school teaching style, and you typically feel closer to your professor. It is also more common to ask questions in class, and most professors also care about participation. In some classes, a percentage of your grade is based on participation.
courses_enrolled: - EC365 B1 Economic Institutions in Historical Perspective (transferred as: Økonomisk Historie) - EC403 A1 Game Theory (transferred as: microeconomics III) - EC502 Macroeconomic Theory (transferred as: macroeconomics III) - EC545 Financial Economics (transferred as: prioritised elective) This class is similar to Financial Decision Making at KU.
recommended_courses: I recommend all of them. I got very lucky with getting my classes transferred to some KU classes that I would have to take back home anyway. If you are into business, I recommend considering some classes at Questroom - school of business. I were supposed to have a class there (Investment Banking), but decided to drop it as I found the others more interesting.
unexpected_costs: - $600 for housing guarantee. - Payment for visa
cost_comparison: You get $280 worth of "dining points" from your dining plan. Those can be spent at places like Panda Express, Raising Canes, Dominos etc. They can also be spend on coffee or snacks from the convenience store.
activities_available: Endless activities. There are so many clubs. You have the possibility to join all of them. I tried out for the basketball club team, and I had friends playing volleyball, tennis, dancing etc.
activities_recommended: I did not attend many, so I am not the one to ask.
weekend_recommendations: Go on extended weekend trips! I went to: - New York - White Mountains - Kennebunkport - Newport - Miami NY is a must in my opinion. Miami was good fun because we went as a big group, but this is more of a party city. The rest on my list are more relaxed and very "New England"-style.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. People are so welcoming. My main friend group was 8 Danes, but we hung out with Italians, Spanish, Japanese, Irish, British, and of course locals. Boston all in all is a very European city, so there was no big culture chok.
socializing_tips: Be ready during orientation week! People are very open to new friendships. Try to find other exchange or transfer students (BU will definitely help you with this. They put all of us in the same orientation group, so we naturally fond each other on the first day.)
cultural_challenges: Not that many. But naturally you speak English a lot.
culture_appreciated: The New England lifestyle is very nice. People are nice here.
top3_advice: You won't regret it. It is a lot of money, but it is so much worth it. You get friendships and experiences for life.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Friendships I can bring back to Copenhagen (danish friends), academic opportunities, and I feel like I found my academic focus for my bachelor thesis and masters here.
greatest_challenge: Being away from friends, family, and girlfriend for 4 months. Maybe also the time difference can be a bit annoying when wanting to connect with connections in DK.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience a different culture compared to the Danish one. I thought that Italy was a good choice based on my starting point of wanting to experience something different. They have a different culture and they have good food. I also thought it would be a good place to improve my English
info_ease: I received a lot of mails from host university, but I think a lot of the information came quite late compared to when I needed the information. I had to find a lot of the information that I needed by myself, but I got the mobility/exchange e-mail from my host university and wrote to them a lot. So the information should have been easier to find then you have to find it yourself. And the university should have send out information earlier than they did.
arrival_assistance: I did not get any physical assistance probably due to covid. But the university were good at answering emails with useful answers, but sometimes it took a little long.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: First I had to get access to the online student area of my host university. I did this by using a step-by-step guide I received by e-mail together with my student number and code The second thing I had to do was make a study plan through a function in the online student area where I add the courses from my pre-approval. To do this I also followed a step-by-step guide I received in another e-mail. The last step was to add the courses on the moodle page and get the rest of the information for the course there and in class.
registration_help: I received e-mails with information and different step-by-step guides for each step of the registration process.
registration_success: I was able to register for all of my classes with the step-by-step guides I was even able to change a course during the semester as the course changed the language from English to Italien.

course_level: I took both courses at both BA and MA levels. I would say that most of the courses were at the expected level, which I expected to be a little bit lower than at KU. But it is hard to say since I had both kinds of levels and I don't really thought about the difference in levels while I was there. I also had some courses were some of the topics of the course syllabus I had already had in courses at my home university.
teaching_comparison: I think the biggest difference between the teaching was the form of the examination. At KU most of the exams are on a computer with closed books. In Venice, the exams are written by hand, but also with closed books. The style of the teaching I think it is kind of the same as at KU. We had lectures where the professors reviewed the most relevant from the syllabus and then there was also time to do excises on our own and there were also some assignments to do during the semester.
courses_enrolled: Behavioural Economics Financial Economics Labour Economics Economics of Inequality Advanced Management of Nonprofit Organizations
recommended_courses: I would just recommend to choose courses that are on the economics department in Venice. One of the courses (corporate finance) i choose was in Treviso which is a city right next to Venice, but you would have to take the train as it is another campus and the courses changed from English to Italien as all of the other students were Italien and I think that students who attends that campus are Italiens and not exchange students.
unexpected_costs: I had hoped to visit other cities in Italy, but I didn't know how many I would have time for
cost_comparison: I had expected that food would be expensive, but eating at restaurants was more expensive than I thought. But on the other hand, the drinks were less expensive than I expected.
activities_available: There was different kind of sports activities as I received emails about football and rugby. The cultural and social activities it was mostly offered by the Erasmus organization which were trips to other cities as well as trips to some of the Vendian Islands. The university had a few aperitivo (food and drinks) nights in the end of the semester, but it was only advertised for in their own canteen
activities_recommended: To go on the trips that the Erasmus team organized. They go to a lot of nice places both in Venice, and also other cities. It is also a good way to meet other students and get new friends
weekend_recommendations: They should go see the st. Marco square and some of the many churches in Venice and just walk around the city without a GPS. They should also visit Burano, Murano, and some of the Vendian Islands.
culture_adjustment: I thought it was easy to adjust, but I also lived with another exchange student from KU so we encouraged each other to go out and so on.
socializing_tips: Go to the campus and other social activities they have. Talk with students in the classes. And get a welcome buddy which the university offers at the beginning of the semester.
cultural_challenges: Maybe they are way more open and whereas Danes are more reserved and reticent.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciate the Italians' helpfulness and openness as well as their food and social life.
top3_advice: - Go to the welcome activities and other social activities in the beginning to make friends - Be patient - in general, things are a little slower than in Denmark, both in shops and at university. The university is a little bit low to give information and answer your questions, but answers will come and they don't ignore you. - Enjoy the city and don't forget to have fun and experience Italy
other_useful_info: I think I have mentioned the most relevant
most_rewarding: All the friendships and acquaintances I made and being allowed to experience and hear about other cultures.
greatest_challenge: Not all Italians are good at English so sometimes you have to be imaginative
