Socially, there were regular student events, like themed parties, movie nights, and pub nights, where students could meet and socialize. Overall, the campus offered a vibrant social scene, but I would have appreciated a wider range of athletic activities.
activities_recommended: I would highly recommend participating in picnic events to future exchange students. These are a great way to relax, enjoy the outdoors, and meet people from different backgrounds in a casual setting. The picnics often take place in beautiful parks or on campus lawns, creating a laid-back atmosphere perfect for making new friends and experiencing local culture. It’s also an affordable and fun way to spend time with fellow students outside of class.
weekend_recommendations: I highly recommend visiting the Dolomites during weekends or holidays. The stunning mountain range offers incredible opportunities for hiking, skiing, or simply enjoying the breathtaking views. Whether you’re into outdoor adventures or just want to relax and take in the scenery, the Dolomites provide a perfect escape from the city. It’s an unforgettable experience that gives you the chance to connect with nature and explore some of the most beautiful landscapes in the region.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy to adjust to the local culture of my exchange site. The people were welcoming, and there was a strong sense of community, which made it easy to settle in. I enjoyed exploring the local traditions, food, and customs, and was able to connect with both locals and other international students. While there were a few cultural differences, they were mostly interesting to experience, and I quickly adapted to the new environment.
cultural_challenges: One cultural difference I found particularly challenging was the pace of life. In my host country, people tend to take their time with daily activities, which was a bit slower than I was used to. This meant I had to adjust to a more relaxed approach to time, whether it was during meals or social events. Another challenge was the language barrier. While many people spoke English, there were still situations where local language skills were important, especially in more informal settings. It took some time to feel comfortable navigating conversations outside of academic or tourist environments.
culture_appreciated: What I most appreciated about the local culture was the relaxing and laid-back style of life. People seemed to really value taking time to enjoy simple moments, whether it was savoring a meal, spending time with friends, or just enjoying the outdoors. This slower pace helped me to feel less stressed and more present, and it gave me the chance to appreciate the little things in life. It was a refreshing change and something I’ve come to value during my time abroad.
top3_advice: he three most important things I would tell a UCPH student going to my host institution on exchange are: Check the course offerings carefully: Make sure to look through the courses available and confirm that they align with your academic interests and requirements. Some courses may have prerequisites or specific registration dates, so it’s important to plan ahead. Double-check the exam dates: Exam schedules can sometimes differ from what you might expect, so it’s essential to verify the exam dates early on. This will help you avoid any surprises and ensure you’re prepared. Complete the Online Learning Agreement (OLA): Don’t forget to make sure your OLA is completed and approved. This is a crucial step in ensuring that your credits transfer smoothly back to UCPH, and it helps avoid any administrative issues later on.
other_useful_info: One thing I would recommend is to get familiar with the local transportation system early on. While most places are accessible by public transport, knowing the best routes, passes, and how to navigate the system can save you time and money. Additionally, take advantage of any international student networks or meetups. These groups can help you adjust to life at the host institution and offer advice on everything from housing to local customs. Lastly, be open to exploring local traditions and events – there are often festivals, markets, or community activities that provide great opportunities to immerse yourself in the culture and meet new people.
most_rewarding: he most rewarding part of my exchange experience was definitely meeting new people. I had the chance to connect with students from all over the world, learn about different cultures, and form lasting friendships. These interactions not only made my time abroad more enjoyable but also broadened my perspective and enriched my personal growth. It was inspiring to hear others' stories, share experiences, and build a sense of community with people from diverse backgrounds.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was that the subjects I took did not overlap. This made it more difficult to ensure that the courses I completed abroad would count towards my degree requirements. It required extra effort to plan my course selection carefully and make sure that I could meet all necessary academic goals. While it worked out in the end, the lack of alignment between the two institutions added some complexity to my exchange experience.

Start looking for housing early and be prepared for limited availability, especially if you wish to live on the island. 3. Take advantage of the location by exploring Venice itself and travelling to nearby cities, as this greatly enhances the overall exchange experience.
other_useful_info: The administrative system can be somewhat confusing at first. It is important to note that students do not register directly for courses, but instead enrol on Moodle to access course instructions and materials, and only need to register for exams.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was living in Venice and experiencing everyday life in a unique cultural setting, having the opportunity to travel and explore different parts of Italy, and taking courses that closely matched my academic interests.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during the exchange was the high level of tourism, which sometimes made it difficult to fully engage with local everyday life and also made it more challenging to pick up the Italian language.

arrival_assistance: They did 1,5 weeks of orientation, first international student orientation and then freshmen orientation.

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_advice: Make use of the add/drop period

courses_enrolled: The elements of quantum chemistry X-ray crystallography The formation and evolution of planetary systems Research project
recommended_courses: The formation and evolution of planetary systems was a great introductory course for planetary science. Even though I am chemist a could easily follow the course and the professor and TA are both amazing.
unexpected_costs: Maybe not so unexpected but we did a lot of trips during the weekends/thanksgiving. These added a bunch of expences
cost_comparison: The food and accommodation is expensive, but mandatory
activities_available: Almost anything you can think of.

weekend_recommendations: There are a lot of great national and state parks within driving distance of Pasadena, such as Joshua Tree and Sequoia.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy to adjust. It is not that different from Denmark, and they also have a lot of international students
socializing_tips: The incomming freshmen are pretty young so maybe just focus on getting to know the juniors/seniors
cultural_challenges: There were not a lot of huge cultural differences just smaller ones
culture_appreciated: People are very welcoming/talkative so it is pretty easy to get to know people
top3_advice: You are there for a really short time, so make sure you get the most out of it. Even though it is a really good school, remember that you are also there to enjoy some time away from UCPH and get some new experiences.
other_useful_info: The academic level might in some cases be higher than at UCPH so be smrt about the number/courses that you take
most_rewarding: All of the amazing experiences also away from campus.

crucial_aspects: As I study area-studies, it was important for me to have it be an area of significance. Prague was an interesting middle-ground between the west and the east, so it turned out to be a pretty optimal place for me to go, in order to explore the relationship between western- and Eastern Europe.
overall_comments: The only downside was the EU bureaucracy and administrational bumps on the road.
info_ease: I arrived quite early, but the people at Charles Uni have been great at providing information through e-mails et.al.
arrival_assistance: E-mails, introduction meetings via Zoom, the possibility of getting a 'local buddy' etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The only downside was the EU bureaucracy and administrational bumps on the road.
registration_process: 1. Look up courses (open to incoming students, taught language, which faculty etc.) 2. Decide, and have the courses amount to 30 ects 3. Wait until the enrollment begins 4. Pray that you can enroll in time 5. If not, enroll anyway and pray that some people de-enroll and make room for you.
registration_help: Not much apart from "just try and wait and see, maybe someone will de-enroll and then you get the spot". And that miraculously worked.
registration_success: Not very. I had to give up 5 courses and choose 4 different instead.
registration_advice: Be as quick to enroll as possible. And make sure to have a plan B and C in case your first choice courses aren't available.
academics_comments: The only downside was the EU bureaucracy and administrational bumps on the road.
course_level: I had 5 MA level courses and 1 BA level course. The BA course was relatively easy, while the MA courses resembled what I am used to at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Every professor teach differently, so I cannot compare on university to another. It's individual and also depends on the kind of class.
courses_enrolled: - Geopolitics of Great Powers: Russia - Populism and Democracy - Historical and Contemporary Geopolitical Issues in Europe - European Comparative Politics and Society - Russian Politics and Society - Symbolical Figures of Czech History
recommended_courses: My two favourite courses were Populism and Democracy as well as Russian Politics and Society. The professors, Petra Guasti and Karel Svoboda, are two of the most bright, friendly and relevant people I have ever met. And the tro courses themselves were really good too.
unexpected_costs: The cost of Covid-19 tests when you are not a Czech citizen; around 220DKK for a PCR test.
cost_comparison: Meat (especially beef) and cheese was a lot more expensive than expected. Vegetables, bread and public transportation was less expensive than expected.
activities_available: Help-Ukraine concerts and fundraisers, football / hockey games, karaoke night, pub crawls, weekend-trips around Czechia etc. They did really well.
activities_recommended: Emerge yourself in Czech culture; whether it be beer, weird food, traditional customs or other things that set Czechia apart from your own country. (And explore Prague's techno scene. It's so much fun.)
weekend_recommendations: Definitely go on some day- or weekend trips to Liberec, Plzen, Kutna Kora, Cesky Krumlov etc. Also, for the hiking/outdoor minded, Slovakia is absolutely stunning.
culture_adjustment: The language was a barrier; the Czechs usually aren't that good at English. Apart from that, the Czechs aren't very different from the Danes, so it's hard to get into a social circle at first, but once you're inside, it's really great.
socializing_tips: Be open and curious about Czechia and their culture.
culture_appreciated: The architecture as well as the weird mix of Slavic and Germanic cultural traits.
top3_advice: 1. Make sure to have a back up plan for your courses of choice. 2. Spend some weekends away from Prague; I really wish I had taken a few more weekends away than I did. 3. Be open and curious. Some of the people you meet are gonna open up so many options around Europe for you.
other_useful_info: It's definitely easier to socialize with the Czechs if you like beer!
most_rewarding: The friendships and connections, as well as the renewed perspective I now have on my own home country.
greatest_challenge: Sometimes feeling alone and/or isolated. Especially in the beginning of the semester.
other_comments: Make sure to go out there, drink a Braník and meet some people! Ná zdraví!

registration_process: I found a lot of courses that I wanted, and was ready at the exact time when they opened for enrollment. registration_help: The international Office, and they are so kind and helpfull - a great experience!
registration_success: Many of the courses I originally wanted did not exist in the end, but i managed to find other interesting ones.
registration_advice: Be ready at the exact time for enrollment! The spots disspear very fast. And expect to make a lot of changes.

The level in Anthropology of EU and Urban Anthropology was not great, the professors level in english was not great, and therefore it was not always easy to follow him. recommended_courses: Contemporary social Theory and Medical Anthropology. Great courses with participation and interesting readings! Not too much work, but enough to also process and understand the themes.
unexpected_costs: I regeral, you just end up spending a lot of money on traveling. I traveled around the country, and also to other European countries. This was a really great experience, so be ready to spend a little more than you expect!

activities_available: Some cultural workshops and sometimes some social activities from the social clubs at the faculties.
activities_recommended: Go to the social activities arranged by the social clubs. The Manifesto marked and the events there are great! They have nothing to do with the university, but all the Erasmus students go there, and you meet a lot of new people.
weekend_recommendations: Travel around the country and see Bohemian Paradise, Brno and so on. Visit other great cities close, like Budapest and Krakow. Explore the many great food places in Prague! And Manifesto marked in the beginning, to meet new people. And also, go to Dog Bar!
culture_adjustment: I did not find it difficult. Czech people can be a bit grumpy and introvert, but get used to this. A bit difficult with the language sometimes, but most often it was not a problem.
socializing_tips: Get a buddy!
cultural_challenges: The grumpyness of Czech people. Not always very service minded.
culture_appreciated: I loved trying Czech food, going to the park and going for walks in the city and the beer culture of course.
top3_advice: Get ready for a bit confusing and challenging enrollment process, where you have to make a lot of changes. Get at student transportation card and enjoy the trams. other_useful_info: The enrollment system, and also, a great idea to attend some of the classes before choosing - I should have done that
most_rewarding: The social life!
greatest_challenge: The courses, because I was a bit dissapointed in two of them. Also the communication with our landlord, which was a bit challenging.

culture_adjustment: Didn't meet local students
socializing_tips: Didn't meet local students
cultural_challenges: Didn't meet local students
culture_appreciated: Didn't meet local students

crucial_aspects: Charles University has a large selection of courses, for which diversity was the key for me. The courses average 5 ECTS, making it possible for me to choose 6 different courses, in constrast to courses at the Humanities at University of Copenhagen, where all courses are 15 ECTS. My philosophy degree has thus far been saturated with the analytical anglo-saxon school, fundamentally uninterested in art, history, literature, cinema, and culture and society in a broader more nuanced sense, so finally being able to explore these other fields in connection with philosophy was of crucial importance for me. Charles University is also a part of the 4+EU program, which made me think my enrollment would be smooth, avoiding any bureaucratic stop-blocks.
info_ease: Yes - any trouble I had was largely my own fault for not reading through all the information given or seeking help in time.
arrival_assistance: I do not quite remember, but there were several emails with information sent to me, such as a comprehensive newsletter involving sight-seeing, information about the university facilities and student organizations and activities.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I do not remember in detail. It started off with an application prioritizing the possible institutions and filling it in with courses (which probably would not be availible during the semester abroad). After the acceptance, a learning agreement had to be filled in, as well as a pre-approval of courses, both of which I had to revise and send in again, when I finally knew exactly which courses I was taking.
registration_help: I do not remember, but with the existence of the internet, help can always be found, albeit not always in the most convenient places.
registration_success: The registration process at Charles is quite atrocious with course registration opening at an exact hour at which all students register at the same time, making the site crash continously, having to refresh over and over again, until the site was availible. Luckily I was ready then, but it took me over an hour to enroll in all my courses. With regard to my host institution, University of Copenhagen, the registration simply consisted of a pre-approval of courses.
registration_advice: No concrete advice at all.
course_level: The level of courses suited me well, although the two philosophy courses I took could not balance the level of complexity in the seminars, since a lot of non-philosophy students participated as well. One of the courses was even at an MA-level, from which I expected a lot more intense engagement.
teaching_comparison: There was much more focus on discussion, and discussion which tolerated many viewpoints and a plurality of ways of expressing oneself. Philosophy at the University of Copenhagen lacks such an open and free space of vigor and critical engagement not governed by an exclusionary principle of "rationality" or a formal "reasonable" way of expression - both concepts here being very spurious and tending to counteract exactly what they try to foster; an open productively engaging discussion.
courses_enrolled: 1. Literature: on U.S. fin de siécle (turn of the 19th to 20th century) fiction, centring around a kind of decadence of bourgeoise life, where traces of the capitalism life-world and critiques of capitalism in the terms of Debord's idea of "Society of the Spectacle" and Baudrillard's notion of "Consumer Society" can be found. 2. Film: Theoretical study of post-war cinema in relation to postmodernism and countless other analyses and critiques of society and the world of the late 20th century (to today) at large, including many philosophical theoretical texts and the live-viewing of films at the Film Academy, where the discussion were immensily fruitful. 3. History: On the relationship between literature and history, dealing with a plurality of theoretical texts trying to understand the fact that history is something written, how it strives towards a "neutrality", what this neutrality is, what "narrative" is, and how the structure of narrative (most exemplary in myths) invades the writing of history, and in addition what we mean by "history" at all, and what the purpose of history even is. 4. Latin: Reading of latin texts from the golden and silver age of roman literature, focused on improving grammar skills and the ability to interpret inside a historical context. Great practice in terms of the language and beneficial for the enlargement of historical knowledge of the period itself. 5. Philosophy of Image: On what an "image" is, through the phenomenological tradition; Husserl, Heidegger, Derrida, Merleau-Ponty, Henry, Deleuze, as well as a study of the paintings of Van Gogh, Cezanne and Bacon. A critical engagement with the school of phenomenology, historically and theoretically, and fruitful free-form discussions of the approaches of the different thinkers and the role of phenomenology and philosophy as a whole. 6. Philosophy of Personhood: What is a "person", a critical engagement with the historical roots of the concept itself, from Christianity and Trinitarian theology by way of Boethius, focusing on medieaval philosophy, namely Thomas Aquinas and John Duns Scotus, comparing them to a modern thinker, Edith Stein, and her balancing of the phenomenological approach to the concept, bordering on theological and speculative thinking.
recommended_courses: All the courses I took, but especially courses offered at the Department of Anglophone Studies, where all the courses are in English. In the case of someone knowing Czech, I would recommend the many exciting philosophy courses, which I lacked the knowledge of Czech to participate in, sadly.
unexpected_costs: The kitchen at the dorms were frequently occupied and the dorms were in general not comfortable to spend time at, so I often ate out, which cost more, but I had the money for it, luckily, since the rent was so low. A lot of money was spent on beer and coffee though.
cost_comparison: Especially the transport was cheap, as well as taking the train to different parts of the Czech Republic as well as nearby countries. Almost everything was cheaper than in Copenhagen, but I ended spending a lot more money than originally planned, since I came into the habit of spending time at cafes, bars and restaurants, and even though it was cheap I frequented a bit too often, and it became costly. But it was very enjoyable living such a life, and I had the money to do it. With hindsight, I still would have controlled myself a bit more...
activities_available: I do not know, I did not look for anything of the sort.
activities_recommended: Again, I do not know any specific student activities, but since the university facilities are in the Old Town, you meet a lot of your fellow student and friends from the dorm very often, which was great! Hanging around the centre of the city on various cafes was a great pleasure. In Copenhagen, the University is a bit off to the south of the centre and feels very empty culturally and historically.
weekend_recommendations: Just walk around, the city is very "touristy", so exploring (or simply just revisiting the same places over and over) different parts of the city outside tourist season is very fulfilling. Use the train often to visit other parts of the Czech Republic!
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. I wish I had spent more time on learning Czech though. I could have reached a level, where I could steadily practice it day by day, reaching a good knowledge and practice of it by the end of the semester, but I started engaging with the language quite late into the semester (mainly because the language courses were places in the same time-slots as my other courses).
socializing_tips: Going aborad is a great practice in socializing, and at the end I feel more courageous engaging with all sorts of people.
cultural_challenges: Not anything in particular. The culture is very European, and because of my slavic background, the non-European culture mainly being slavic, I was pleasantly surprised by recognizing a lot of things.
culture_appreciated: Going to cafes and bars regularly, as well as independant music-venues.
top3_advice: 1. Do research on the housing availible and consider finding housing on your own, knowing that the housing at the dorms is very bad. 2. Take a plurality of courses in different fields if possible, and watch out for which language is course is taught in. Know that one can enroll in many courses and then un-enroll during the first couple of weeks; see what suits you best. 3. Participate in some extra courses without searching for pre-approval (knowing that you will not get points) just purely for interest - watch out though, because the intensity of the courses vary a lot!
other_useful_info: The three mentioned above are the most crucial. Also, Prague might be the best European city to study abroad in. I would only recommend something in France, Italy, Germany, Spain and Portugal, if part of your plan is to learn the language as well, but without a plan to achieve a certain degree of fluency, taking courses in the native language as well, Prague is simply the best place.
most_rewarding: Learning to socialize more and realizing how much more crucial non-academic discussions are to developing one's own way of thinking, and listening to so many points of view, which are not to be found inside academia.
greatest_challenge: The dorms were hard to get used to.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: I was very sure of the fact that I wanted to go on an exchange this semester, the destination wasn't as important for me. The most important factor for me was the possibility to try to experience studying in an international context. When I learnt that my good friend from my studies planned on going to Prague in Czechia, it was a no-brainer that we could plan on going together.
overall_comments: It was a nice experience, however there were some unexpected cultural shocks regarding the study structures.
info_ease: The student system was a little bit difficult to navigate, considering the fact that some of the teachers used another system (Moodle) and barely updated the former student system. Some had a Moodle page, but didn't update that, and some even just used google docs for information. It was however easy to find the campus and classes, even though most of the staff didn't speak English.
arrival_assistance: We were signed up for a tour around campus on our first day of school, however we couldn't find the tour guides at all, even though we were there earlier. Apparently this was due to a miscommunication error, however it was quite disappointing. However, the International Office at Charles University were very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was a nice experience, however there were some unexpected cultural shocks regarding the study structures.
registration_process: I had some issues with the course registration which were very stressful, however it all worked out in the end.
registration_help: The International Office was quick and effective when answering all of our questions, and they did so in the best way they could.
registration_success: Not very successful at all. I was only able to register for two out of five classes that I had wanted to begin with. And one of them I even had to write to the professor to be sure to get into, since I was put onto a waiting list. One class apparently wasn't available for exchange students, which seemed weird, since it was accepted by the host university. It was only more frustrating as I was actually registered the course before getting kicked out again and having to find an alternative solution. Another class had been removed from when I first looked for classes until registration. It would have been a lot easier if we were notified which courses were a part of the full time students schedules, so we could steer around those, since they were full even before we could register. The registration was such a stressful process, even though I started registrating as soon as the option opened.
registration_advice: Make sure you register for backup courses regarding the courses you need credits for in your home University.
academics_comments: It was a nice experience, however there were some unexpected cultural shocks regarding the study structures.
course_level: The level was generally quite low, which came as a surprise to me
teaching_comparison: It was just chaotic. I'm used to very structured teaching in UCPH, but it seemed like the teachers decide their own structure at Charles University, which made it confusing and all out terrible in some cases. It was also difficult having to concentrate for 80 minutes straight without a break.
courses_enrolled: EU Institutions Promoting Democracy Abroad: The US and the EU in Third Countries European Economic Integration Anthropology of the EU Comics as a Medium
recommended_courses: EU Institutions was great for getting to know the institutions in the EU, however there were a lot of anecdotes so be aware of that. Promoting Democracy Abroad: The US and the EU in Third Countries was a very nice course with a pedagogical and outspoken teacher. The teacher in European Economic Integration was very knowing and taught us a lot. I would not recommend Anthropology of the EU at all. Comics as a Medium was probably my favourite course, however it wasn't very academic.
unexpected_costs: None, it was all quite cheap. I did however order a lot of takeaway, since it was so cheap, which spiked my food budget a lot.
cost_comparison: Public transportation was crazy cheap. Around 120 dkk for three months free transportation.
activities_available: No clue, I didn't really look into it. It wasn't really advertised that blatantly however.
activities_recommended: Try to partake in the events in the introweek. It was filled to the brim, but I think you could just show up nonetheless. It seemed like it was nice.
weekend_recommendations: Go for trips around Czechia. The train tickets are exceptionally cheap, and Czechia is such a beautiful country. You could go to Cesky Krumlov and Brno for example. You could also visit the surrounding countries since the tickets are that cheap. This is what most students do.
culture_adjustment: It was easy to feel a part of the city, but Prague is also very touristy. As long as you drank beer you belonged.
socializing_tips: Partake in the events by the student organisations in the introweek, that is how I got to know local students. Other than that it seemed like an impossible task to be honest.
cultural_challenges: A lot of people didn't speak English.
culture_appreciated: The cheap beer, beautiful city and parks, cheap and very good public transport and the fact that Czech people are usually not all up in your business, which suits me well as a Dane.
top3_advice: Try to find friends outside of your classes too, since you don't get any breaks, so it's difficult to get to know them. Don't be afraid of living in the dorms, the ones I saw looked very nice (although they were quite far away), it's very cheap, and it's an easy way to get to know people. Also, you can always switch dorms if you'd like. Don't expect to be challenged academically. Use it as a well-earned easier semester.
other_useful_info: Use the International Office if you need help. They're great. A lot of the other offices in Prague are not very helpful.
most_rewarding: Getting to experience living in another country and getting to know another culture. You almost felt like a local by the end of it.
greatest_challenge: Having to figure out what you needed to fill out, how to register and the sorts. People who have been on an exchange earlier are usually very good at helping out however.
other_comments: Enjoy your exchange!

crucial_aspects: The study destination was chosen based on a place that is different from my home city. The country and especially the city is a very beautiful place and is very well suited for an Erasmus exchange. Besides, Charles University which is a very superior university, gave rise to a lot of nice courses. Also courses that I won't be able to take at home. These are the reasons for my choice of study destination.
info_ease: It was fine, however it was sometimes difficult to get in touch with the Erasmus office it you were in doubt of specific things, which were difficult to find information on the website.
arrival_assistance: Everyone was very nice, and especially the orientation day was a good way to start the semester. Both to meet the other students but also to meet other Czech students.
arrival_comments: It was much easier when you had arrived and it was possible to talk to them personally, where they were very helpful and you could get all the help you needed.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: At the orientation day you heard all the important information needed and then everyone could one at a time go to the person in charge and get registered with a signature.
registration_help: I could always contact them through email and then meet them at the Erasmus office close to campus.
registration_success: It took a long time to figure out which courses I could get, as it was not easy to find out which days at which times they were at. When I had figured that out, I could register for the courses after changing my Learning Agreement which I then had to get signed by three different people. Then it was different for each course how to register and if they were in one or the other website.
registration_advice: Know that it will take time, as it is a new system you need to learn and a lot of documents need to be signed by different people, so have patient. You will succeed.
course_level: Each course was very different. I had one practical laboratory course, which was very beginners friendly and I had already done all the things we learned there. Another course which was Cytometry was difficult as it is a difficult method but it was very nice to have. The other courses were at a good level and compatible to mine.
teaching_comparison: It was very different as most courses were only 3 credits where I am used to at least 7,5 credits per course. I had approximately one lecture per week and then some I had also practicals once a week. The lectures were 1,5 hours long and there were no breaks, whereas at UCPH we usually have a short break each 30-45 minutes. For all the courses I didn't read any books as it was optional. Slides from the lectures was used to study for the exam, which was very new for me.
courses_enrolled: Parasitology, Botany of Non-vascular Plants, Proteins of Signaling Cascades, Cytometry, Molecules of Life and Mutations, Practical Molecular Biology, Model Organisms in Developmental Biology, Czech Language course for beginners.
recommended_courses: I would recommend Proteins of Signaling Cascades, Cytometry and Molecules of Life and Mutations, as they are good to have and understand. However, Cytometry is very difficult so you should know that before choosing it.
unexpected_costs: I didn't have any unexpected costs. Prague was very nice and a cheap place to live.
cost_comparison: With my student ID I could get a lot of nice discounts which were unexpected.
activities_available: They had multiple groups of students planning trips and events for Erasmus students which was nice in the beginning to meet new people.
activities_recommended: Participate in as many events in the beginning as possible as it was nice to meet people who also were looking to meet new friends.
weekend_recommendations: Visit all the nice places in middle of Prague, like Old Town, Charles Bridge, Prague Castle and so on. Then it is very easy to go to day trips to a lot of nice cities like Kutna Hora, Cesky Krumlov and Pilsen. It is also easy to go hiking in Czech Republic where you can see the beautiful nature.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy, and then when I had learned a little bit of Czech it was nice to use in super markets and shops. A lot of old people don't speak english, but a lot of young people do.
socializing_tips: I didn't hang out with a lot of local students as I had a lot of courses with other Erasmus students. I talked a lot with the local students who organized the trips and were a part of Erasmus Club.
cultural_challenges: Sometimes the local people weren't that polite as I am used to back home. However, you would quickly get used to it, and then when someone is very polite you get very happy about that person.
culture_appreciated: I loved the nature in Czech Republic, and a quick train ride led to a beautiful little hiking trip. Prague is a very hilly city and gave rise to a lot of nice views of the city. The city is so beautiful.
top3_advice: 1. There are a lot of campuses around the city and also outside of Prague. 2. Don't expect the lecturers to be very structured. 3. Their english can vary. However, most of the teachers are very nice even though some of them can seem a little scary. Since it is a little more relaxed and the courses are so small you also get the chance to talk more with the teachers.
other_useful_info: Enjoy the small classes as you will get close to your colleagues and maybe even the teachers.
most_rewarding: It was amazing to live in such a beautiful city that Prague is and enjoy it with all the other Erasmus students that were all open and adventurous like myself.
greatest_challenge: It could be challenging with the lack of english the older people had. For example when I had to go to the foreign police and register myself in the country, they couldn't speak one word of english and it was difficult to tell them what we needed to do. Also, when I had a course outside of the city center, I had to be allowed to enter the campus and they couldn't speak english either. So sometimes they wouldn't even let me in even though I was a student. I learned in the end how to manage it.
other_comments: I really loved to live in Prague and can't wait to visit the city again in the future. I have met wonderful people that I will cherish for life. Now I can't wait to get back and have the routine of UCPH that I will cherish much more now. the structure and the teachers and so on.

crucial_aspects: It was important for me that i could choose certain courses. Charles University provide a wide range of courses, which made it easy to finds subsitutes. As Charles Univeristy is a 4EU+ partner also made it an "easier" destination. Prague is also famous and fantastic city which was also crucial for my decision. Futher Czech Republic is also a country with a low cost of living, meaning that as a student your money goes a long way, which enables students to participate and get a lot of experiences outside of the university as well.
info_ease: It was easy. The International Office at my faculty was very helpful, and provided a lot of information both before and after my arrival.
arrival_assistance: Unfortunately due to covid our introduction day was cancelled. However there was an online introduction day instead which provided us with a lot of information and we could then afterwards go to the office for extra information and questions. And I got really fast replies by email, which was nice.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I think that the proces with getting signatures from both universities and sending it back and forth by email was a struggle. Why not have a common digital platform where this takes place.
registration_help: E-mail.
registration_success: At Charles Univeristy the lecture schedule is published very late, which meant that i WASN'T ABLE TO TAKE ANY of the courses i had pre-approved. This only gave me extras stress that i had to get additional course approved and that all the work done earlier was wasted. Further many of the courses i had pre-approved was even removed....
registration_advice: Don't put too much work into your pre-approved courses. It is most likely that you will have to find many new ones when they publish the lecture schedules.
course_level: The level was high in some courses and low i othes. But this was also because i had to change my courses so much and ended up also having a first-year course.
teaching_comparison: A hybrid-form and a recording was avaibale in all my classes which was nice. There as less problem solving which i think it too bad because this is where i really learn the material.
courses_enrolled: History of Economic Thought Principles of Economics II Economics of Global Business Introductory Banking Czech as a Foreign Language I
recommended_courses: Principles of Economics II was a nice macro economics course if you need this. Economics of Global Business gave a different view on international business, organization and prolbems realted to multi-national-enterprises
unexpected_costs: I didn't encounter any unexpected costs. Everything is extremely affordable in Prague.
cost_comparison: Everything from food, transport, cinemas and experiences were all very cheap compared to Denmark.
activities_available: Due to Covid there was not much available in the start. However later i the semster there was more than evough of social activites. From dinner activities, trips to other cities, pub crawls and so on. So much that you definitely can't participate in everything at all.

crucial_aspects: I was supposed to go to Australia on exchange, but it got cancelled because of Covid-19. So instead, I had the opportunity to apply for a "left-over"-spot in Europe. Because my friend was going to Charles University in Prague, I chose the same destination.
info_ease: There are a lot of information, deadlines and documents you need to keep track of. It is a bit confusing, but it is important to follow the guidelines in Mobility-One and keep an eye on emails from UCPH.
arrival_assistance: We had two welcome meetings where we were given important documents and got introduced to the university - both the social and the professional aspects and opportunities. I also signed up for a "buddy" and therefor I was paired up with a local Czech student who helped me get to know the city and uni-life. That was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was really challenging. We had one online introduction seminar on how to get registred for courses, but it was not enough and not very helpful. The online system at Charles University is pretty old and confusing. I ended up writing all the professors to ask them if they could help me get registred at their course. The professors were very helpful.
registration_help: My buddy and the professors, that I wrote on my own initiative, were helpful. Otherwise, it was pretty difficult.
registration_success: I was pretty succesful. But the different faculties are open for registration for courses at different times and classes startet at different times according to each faculty. Therefore, I missed the first week of some of my courses. So you should be aware of this.
registration_advice: Write to the professors whose subjects you are interested in and ask them to registrer you.
course_level: I had 3 BA-level courses and 2 MA-level courses. The level of the MA-courses was ok, but the BA-courses were not that great.
teaching_comparison: The facilitation of teaching was not the greates in Prague. The teaching was often characterized by randomness, lack of structure and low standards. Professors paid little attention to how they ensured that students got the most out of their lessons. In contrast, teachers in the DK are very concerned to ensure that students benefit from the lessons and that the level and quality are high.
courses_enrolled: Gender, Men and Masculinities Ethnic conflicts in central and eastern Europe Anthropology The fight against totalitarian regimes om Czechoislovakia, 1939-1989 Academic writing
recommended_courses: The most interesting course was Gender, Men and Masculinity. The professor, Ecem, was super cool and made the teaching and course very interesting. I can definitely recommend this course!
unexpected_costs: In general, I used way more money than I thought I would. You are very active and do a lot of stuff when you are on exchange, which requires money.
cost_comparison: Wine at Vinotekas are very lovely and cheap!
activities_available: There was an organization made by local students which made a lot of activities for exchange students.
activities_recommended: Go to some events in the beginning - it is a good way to meet people.
weekend_recommendations: Go on trips outside of Prague, explore the city, go hiking and join a club or organization outside of university to meet other people!
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy.
socializing_tips: I would recommend the "buddy"-program and joining an activity or club outside of campus - a debate club, foodball club, etc.
cultural_challenges: The lack of structure.
culture_appreciated: The welcoming attitude.
top3_advice: Try to find housing in good time, so you get to know the housing market, the prices and the good apartments. Reach out to professors or coordinator by phone or email - it is way easier and they are very helpful. Check out the exams and demands of the courses so it fits your needs.
most_rewarding: Getting to know a new city, a new culture and finding new friends all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Problems with our appartment and the communication with the owner and the company.

crucial_aspects: All courses were taught in English (Master's level mathematics), and Charles University had a large number of interesting courses to choose from.

registration_help: I could always write my coordinator at UCPH or Charles University if I was in doubt about anything.
registration_success: I got 5 out of 6 courses that I wanted, which is very lucky from what I hear from others. The first three weeks, I could switch courses so the course selection process was not stressful.
registration_advice: In practice, the stuff you put in your Learning Agreement is preliminary, and it will probably change.
course_level: In general the courses had a level similar to UPCH, except for one course which was crazy difficult.
teaching_comparison: More chill vibe with the professors, and less formal and less bureaucracy. A bit more theoretical, and fewer problem sessions.

recommended_courses: Commutative Algebra was crazy difficult. Knot Theory was a bit more chill, and pretty cool. Formal Mathematics was a lot of guest lectures as well and a very easy exam. In general, I was happy with my courses.
unexpected_costs: Beer is cheap, but if you drink enough often enough, it adds up. It is super cheap in shops though.
cost_comparison: Fast food is almost Danish prices. And Irish pubs are expensive. Food on restaurants and beers in general were cheaper than expected.
activities_available: ESN Prague arranges a lot of activities for socializing in the beginning. That was very nice.
activities_recommended: Go on some trips.
weekend_recommendations: There are a lot of nice day trips, also weekend trips. It is cheap to travel inside Czech Republic. Go to Cesky Krumlov and Bohemian Switzerland. And to Vienna or Krakow or something.

socializing_tips: A lot of them were curious to talk to me, and in general they were very nice. Also, there are a lot of international students who study in Prague for longer periods of time, and they are also great.

top3_advice: If you are in doubt, always say yes. Prague has a lot of interesting areas. Try to experience as many as you can. Prioritize the social life.
other_useful_info: Find someone with the same hobbies as you.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many amazing people and spending time with them in complete freedom without having to worry about work and duties from back home.
greatest_challenge: Going home.
other_comments: Exchange was probably my best decision. It is amazing to be together with so many people in the same boat as you and having so much free time to make friendships and explore a whole new city. And explore new sides of your own personality that are hidden back home. I have grown more confident in myself and have gotten a greater motivation for meeting new people back in Copenhagen as well. If you consider going, you really should go.

overall_comments: Prague was the best city to study in. The culture, the prices and the people. There is many students living in Prague and many opportunities for Erasmus students everywhere.

crucial_aspects: I had only been to Prague once, very shortly as a child, and I found it had a lot of interesting culture.
overall_comments: Prague is a great place to be on exchange, it has a lot of student life for Erasmus students!
info_ease: Generally everything you needed to know was on their website, so pretty easy. Courses were a bit hectic to figure out though, since the schedules are published at the earliest two weeks before classes start..
arrival_assistance: I don't know that I had a lot of assistance, but I was also very prepared and didn't need much help. I had some issues with my name being registered twice in the system (one with 'o' and one with 'ø') which gave some issues with the student card and course registration, and took a lot of pushing from my side to make them figure out what the issue was.
arrival_comments: I specifically had some issues with registration, but other than that pretty straight forward. I did hear some of the students from other faculties got more assistance from their faculties than just registration day, which would have been nice.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Prague is a great place to be on exchange, it has a lot of student life for Erasmus students!
registration_process: Every faculty has a registration day, which is obligatory, and they tell you the process. It was a bit annoying however, that the regular students had already been able to register for courses before exchange students, so some courses were already full. Also at my faculty, we weren't able to get the login to register for courses until we got our student cards, so for me where the registration was double I wasn't able to register for classes until late.. And I know at some of the other faculties they got logins before their student cards, so they could register at the same time as the regular students..
registration_help: The most help you can get is if you just show up during office hours if it's kind of urgent. Your coordinator is pretty much the main person to help you, and if you're having issues it is their job to help you. Unfortunately my coordinator was a bit slow to help me with my registration problems, being persistent helps.
registration_success: Not very, I was late to be able to sign up for courses, and since at my faculty we were already late to register as Erasmus my most wanted course from pre-approval was already full. In general you can still write the professors and ask for a spot even if the class is full, and waitlist to see if someone drops it until registration ends. Another problem was that the schedules were posted so late, so I didn't know until right before registration, that pretty much all the courses I had picked didn't match in the schedule, and therefore had to change almost my entire pre-approval.
registration_advice: Don't worry too much, you'll figure your courses out somehow. But also don't have your eyes set too much on specific courses, pick out more alternative options in case your combination of courses don't fit, so you won't be disappointed if the schedule doesn't fit.
academics_comments: Prague is a great place to be on exchange, it has a lot of student life for Erasmus students!
course_level: In general course level is pretty similar to KU, but assignment workload feels like more at Matfyz at least, since you have more classes, and in my case, therefore more assignments weekly. Their method of teaching Computer Science specifically is also quite different to KU, in my experience at least. Their exams are also more of just remembering everything by heart, and to my experience always closed book.
teaching_comparison: Lectures are pretty similar in structure. Some classes don't have practicals at all, and those that do is more of being in a smaller class with often a different teacher, where you sometimes do some exercises, but that usually isn't the main focus. In some ways similar, but feels more like working individually and then asking questions individually, and maybe going through some similar problems to the homework/assignment or prompts that practices for the exam.
courses_enrolled: Programming in C# (5 ECTS), Programming in Java (5 ECTS), Introduction to Machine Learning in Python (5 ECTS), Introduction to Computer Linguistics (3 ECTS), Data Science with R I (6 ECTS), Intensive Czech Language Course for Erasmus Students (7 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I highly recommend doing the Czech language course, even if your faculty won't approve the credits! You get a chance to meet other Erasmus students, learn some basic Czech and about Czech culture, and explore Prague all before the semester starts, highly highly recommend! Also Data Science with R was probably my favourite course, I really liked the structure of having deadlines, but being able to do the course in my own pace (since lecture were pre-recorded). If you find Machine Learning interesting it is of course a super useful course. It is a lot of work, so definitely find a good group from the beginning if you consider this course, otherwise you will most likely break your neck trying to pass the assignments, or loose a lot of your social life.
unexpected_costs: Generally everything is cheaper in Prague, and there weren't that many costs I didn't consider. When staying in the EU for more than 4 months without going home you might want to consider getting another SIM card to not get charged absurd fees on data. (That is what I did) Also I spent a lot of money going out and going on a bunch of trips outside of Prague, which is definitely worth it!
cost_comparison: Public transport is so cheap! I got two three-month student travel passes for 360 CZK each (about 112 DKK). In general most anything is cheaper, except the fish options are few since Czechia is not surrounded by water like Denmark.
activities_available: There were a few options at the faculties, but mainly I just used the Erasmus organisations.
activities_recommended: Go to ESN events when you have time, it is a great place to meet other internationals, and also the organisers (usually Czechs) are usually super sweet.
weekend_recommendations: Go to at least one of the ESN trips outside of Prague, you just need to sign up, it is generally a good deal, and they have an itinerary that you maybe wouldn't have come up with yourself. Explore as much outside of Prague as well, these are places you wouldn't usually get to see on a regular vacation, and the other cities also have a lot of charm.
culture_adjustment: Easy, at times there definitely was a language barrier, but in general there was no issues as long as you're respectful.
socializing_tips: Finding local friends can be kind of difficult since you're there temporarily, so the easiest way to find local friends is through the Buddy system, or befriending the ESN organisers. Regardless you might still find some nice local friends randomly at bars or in class.
cultural_challenges: Language was the main barrier, but was not a problem most of the time. If you have patience, a smile, and google translate you will have no issues culturally, most people are super sweet.
culture_appreciated: The beer is super cheap, and a big pride of Czechia. The city is also super well kept and you will never tire of looking at the pretty buildings and finding new culture gems.
top3_advice: 1. Be aware that you most likely will have to change your courses after arrival from your pre-approval. 2. Be open-minded, down to learn some basic Czech, and enjoy your time, it is a great opportunity. 3. I cannot recommend enough exploring outside of Prague!
other_useful_info: It is always good to have some cash on you, since even though most places take card you will probably run into a few places that don't, especially at bars. You won't have a problem using cash, since unlike Denmark a lot of places actually prefer cash.
most_rewarding: The social life. Going to smaller cities, and making a bunch of international friends.
greatest_challenge: Courses, even getting to register for courses was a hassle, but I ended up struggling a lot with assignments because of my study group splitting up for Machine Learning. In my opinion, whether the course is credit + exam says more about the workload than the ECTS appointed the course. I would have liked a breakdown of how they calculate the credits for each course, since I don't think the workload is correctly taken into consideration for all the courses.
other_comments: Despite everything, if you're even considering going on exchange, I would recommend just applying! How many times do you get an opportunity like this, and everything considered it is still completely worth it!
