arrival_assistance: Charles University organized an introduction week for all the international students with both an introduction to the system of the school as well as a small city tour where they showed us how to get student ID, transportation tickets etc...
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was a little bit difficult because the system is very old, but once you get the hang of it its pretty easy. We had a 2-week add and drop period so we could test out classes before finally choosing them which was really nice. But it also ended up being a bit stressfull because courses got filled quickly.
registration_help: The university was very good at helping whenever i had questions and its always possible to ask teachers or the international office if you have questions,
registration_success: I got all the classes i wanted, so i was pretty sucessful, but it was a big puzzle trying to make all the classes fit with the 30 ECTS points required since a lot of the classes are 2,3,4,5,6 points each.
registration_advice: Try a lot of classes in the add and drop period! Some of the classes i though would be most interesting from the descriptions i ended up dropping and vice versa. And also check out classes from other faculties they have some really interesting ones! But beware of the different registration dates for the different faculties
course_level: I had some BA and some MA courses and therefore the academic level of the courses also varied a bit, but i think the overall level was alright.
teaching_comparison: I did not really have any lectures, mostly seminars which i enjoyed, but the style of teaching is more old school and attendance is mandatory in all classes.
courses_enrolled: Medical Anthropology: Illness, Medicine and the Body Body, Affect and Society Observing the city: Introduction to fieldwork in an urban environment Gender and Religion Feminism, Art & Pop Culture Iconology: Art-historical and Philosophical Aspects Of Reading The Cultural Phenomena
recommended_courses: My two favorite courses were Medical Anthropology and Observing the city. Medical Anthropology was a really interesting class with a nice syllabus and a very professional teacher. I really enjoyed this course even though it is a bit more work. Observing the city was also very interesting. We went on fieldwork in 3 different locations in Prague which was a very nice way of getting to know the city as well as Czech culture. The teacher in this course was also very nice and well prepared for each class.
unexpected_costs: I did not have a lot of unexpected costs, but i did have to pay a booking fee of approx 1300 DKK apart from the deposit on my shared apartment
cost_comparison: Food, drinks, and experiences like the cinema, bowling, museums etc was cheaper than expected. General rent prices and grocery shopping was more expensive than i had anticipated.
activities_available: In the beginning there were some social activities organized by the university, but after the first weeks the students organized things by themselves. Outside there are groups like ESN and other firms/communities organizing a lot of events and experiences for erasmus students, so it was not a problem that the university did not organize that much.
activities_recommended: There are a lot of nice, museums, monuments, parks, restaurants, bars, cafes, clubs, vintage stores and so on to explore as well as small cities in the rest of Czech republic you can visit.
weekend_recommendations: Go on weekend trips to ex Budapest, Vienna, Berlin etc with your friends! there are a lot of cheap busses and trains going from the central train or bus station.
culture_adjustment: Since its a european country it was pretty easy. One that surprised me was the fact that the service in restaurants etc is very rude and some places they refuse to speak english, but most people are nice enough. And they have a lot of special traditions which are fun to explore.
socializing_tips: Unfortunately i mostly socialized with other exchange students. The Czech students kept a lot to themselves and were a bit hard to get in contact with, maybe because of the language barrier. I think a good idea for getting to know more Czech students is getting a buddy through the system at the university.
cultural_challenges: Czech republic is a very homogenic country and they dont have many immigrants, so this was different from Copenhagen. Otherwise I did not encounter a lot of challenges.
culture_appreciated: The city is very beautiful and if you seek out the right restaurants the local food can be quite good! Czech republic has a very interesting history which is worth diving into. And they really love cheap beer.
top3_advice: Find a shared apartment with other exchange students, it is really a great way of meeting people right away when you arrive and a good way to prevent feeling lonely in a foreign country. Enjoy that eating out, going to bars and all the other stuff you can do is a lot cheaper than back home, use it to its fullest. This is also where you meet new friends and learn about the culture. Always make sure that you have some cash, even though a lot of places take cards most bars for example only take cash.
other_useful_info: The people at the university are always happy to help, so dont hesitate with asking questions. The faculty of humanities is located a bit far out from the city center, so if you want to study in the center of the city take classes from other faculties as well. And use some of the many beautiful libraries in the city.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and living with people from all over the world. Exploring the city and all the possibilities that it holds!
greatest_challenge: Probably the language barrier sometimes and figuring out what classes to take. But fortunately I did not have a lot of challenges

crucial_aspects: It was a city that was nice to live in for exchange students. Other exchange students had had good experiences here. Prague is very much an Erasmus city and you can really feel that while you are there.
info_ease: Our Erasmus coordinator wrote me already before I came there and she was very quick to get back to you if you had any questions.
arrival_assistance: I came to Prague between 2-3 before I had to start school. Therefore I had a lot of time on "my own" before I got involved with the university. But I had found a flatshare with other exchange students before I arrived. So already the day I arrived I was surrounded by exchange students and we helped each other out. Otherwise the introduction days in the university they help you with getting in touch with a doctor, student ID, transportationpasses (where to buy) etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I am not very good with the deadlines concerning registration and so on. So I am really not the right person to ask with questions like this. I don't even remember to be honest. Also because our erasmus coordinator at Charles University was so nice, so I feel like it could never go really wrong. Always help to get.
registration_help: Erasmus Coordinator Lenka. So sweet.
registration_success: There are two weeks in the beginning of the semester where you can sign up for new courses and drop other. The add/drop period. This was so nice!! I had actually expected it to be very stressful but I was so happy it was possible because I ended having completely different courses than the courses I had had preapproved with KU. For me the workload of the courses was very important since I was mostly there to have fun and have the erasmus experience. Therefore I did not want to have courses with too heavy workloads and this was possible to avoid because of the add/drop period. I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Do not stress before hand. In the add/drop period make sure you sign up/check when some of the classes you might want have available spots. In these two weeks I was checking in often to make sure I got the classes I wanted.
course_level: Wrong person to ask haha. I had some pretty easy going courses because that is what I was looking for. I could have taken higher level courses though.
teaching_comparison: Attendance is mandatory with often 2 absences allowed per class. I had to get used to this being so different from back home. More seminars and less lectures. More courses than in DK because the courses are 'worth' fewer points. In some courses mid-terms. The final grade depends on your attendance, participation, midterms or papers during the semester (sounds like a lot but it is not) and final paper. This feels more like high school in Denmark. But it was really okay even though it sounds like a lot it was not at all. I would definitely recommend checking out courses at other faculties than your own. I was in faculty of humanities but a lot of my courses were also in faculty in social sciences.
courses_enrolled: Gender and religion (6 ects) Observing the city (3 ects) World of documentary film (5 ects) Iconology: Art-historical and philosophical aspects of reading the cultural phenomena (5 ects) Cities in civilisation (3 ects) Prague as a living city (6 ects) Yoga (2 ects)
recommended_courses: Observing the city. Our teacher michal was so nice and engaged. You get to do three mini fieldworks in the city where you focus on fx appropriation of space. I liked the course, I felt like I learned something and the teacher was so nice! If you want easy courses: Both iconology and cities in civilisation only require your attendance and nothing else! You literally only have to show up: no reading or final paper. Iconology was really difficult to understand though. I think you need some philosophy / art historical background in order to understand (I did not understand a lot). But the teacher was sweet! World of documentary film: Also very nice teacher.
unexpected_costs: If I have written 0 it is because I dont know how much I spent on this specific one! I was very 'free' with my money. I did not care that much because I was like, now we are here, lets go.
cost_comparison: Public transportation is very cheap when you buy the passes and especially the student passes. Everything is just cheaper than in Denmark. Food, beer, drinks, the cinema etc. I think a cinema ticket was 40 DKK.
activities_available: Again not through the institution (maybe!!). I had yoga as a course and there were some sport courses you could get ects for.
activities_recommended: Beach volley with erasmusinprague or ohmyprague is very nice especially in the beginning when it is warmer. I only stopped going because I dislocated my shoulder. A lot of people meet outside to play something no matter what level you are.
weekend_recommendations: Vienna, Bratislava etc is not that far away. I had weekendtrips to Vienna, Budapest, Berlin, Brno it was nice to go on trips with the friends I made there. I would not recommend going to Pilsen, it was very boring. Maybe also not Brno (in good weather I think it is nicer than when I was there).
culture_adjustment: Czech people are not so welcoming people but I think they are quite funny. Even though they consider themselves to be centraleuropeans they really have that oldschool (especially the older generation) kind of harsh/closed of (sometimes rude service) but then there are also the really nice ones and then when you get good service you really appreciate it haha. Now I think I made them sound too harsh they are not. It was very easy although sometimes the language barriere can be big (not always). I felt very home in Prague in a short amount of time.
socializing_tips: To be honest I did not really do this. I think it is a lot like with erasmus students here in DK they often keep to themselves because they are there for a limited amount of time and dont know anybody and need a social circle so they are really in the same position and then it is really easy to find each other. However with that said I think you could actually quite easy socialize with czech students if you want to. I just did not seek it out.
cultural_challenges: Language barriere: you find out that in Denmark we are actually really good in english. Maybe the closed off ness I wrote about earlier. But I did not really find any of this particularly challenging.
culture_appreciated: I love how much Czech people love beer (most beer consuming country in the world). Even though the food is not that good (very much sovs og kartofler (brød dumplings) I really miss it. The food, especially in the canteen, is just gravy, pork and dumplings and it is not really good but I miss it so much!! It's part of it. I miss trams!! So good transportation system in Prague. I miss their attitude, the grey Czech cuisine, the beer, the prices (!!!!!), and that everything is so old.
top3_advice: 1. Find a flatshare with other exchange students. My flatshare has had a massive impact on my experience. 2. I have been the type to have a lot of friends in school and be around in an exchange community like the one in Prague. But this time I was very determined to find a 'few' 'right' people for me. I have 8 really close friends with me home. I did almost everything with these people. They are my whole stay. 3. Don't let the money stop you. You can always earn them back later. And it is Czech Republic so stuff is kinda cheap (not crazy cheap but cheaper than DK) which means you can actually "live" so much more here, because your money gets you further - enjoy that!
other_useful_info: Not really anything I can think of that I have not mentioned already.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange is 100 % the friends I made there. I have really gotten everything I wanted from my exchange in Prague. Originally I was going to Melbourne in Australia so suddenly it was something very different than I had expected my whole exchange experience to be like. But I would not change it for the world. I have gotten so close friends, cliche but really friends for life. We are still in contact and travelling around europe this spring/summer to visit each other. I love and miss them so much. My experience is actually that when you go on exchange inside Europe you have more international friends compared to going overseas to fx Canada or Australia here you definitely have some but most of your friend group is danish (from what I can see with my friends!). And I am so happy I have close friends in France, Netherlands, Norway etc now (even though it is hard too). And beside all of this: Prague is really a great city to live in. It is so beautiful and old, and with lots of opportunities.
greatest_challenge: To not drink too much when the beer was so cheap. No I don't really know. For me probably having a shoulder injury while abroad.
other_comments: Go to Prague!! I was not expecting a lot because I was sad for a long time about not going to Australia and I really feel like I have had the best possible experience I could have had.

crucial_aspects: Pris Kursusudbud
info_ease: Det var meget nemt. Det internationale kontor sender flere mails før ankomst. Jeg vil anbefale at deltage i orienteringsmødet på semestrets første dag.
arrival_assistance: Intromøder, guides og e-mails.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Man skal forholde sig med tålmodighed, da det først er muligt at tilmelde sig kurser lige før semestrets start. Universitet er også meget opmærksomme på, at man måske kan føle sig stresset af processen, men det er altid muligt at finde en løsning.
registration_help: Man kan enten skrive til Internationalt Kontor eller møde op.
registration_success: Jeg fik 4/5 kurser, men ændrede to af dem efter at have deltaget i første seminar. Skriv til underviseren hvis du hellere vil ind på et andet kursus.
registration_advice: Tag det roligt.
course_level: Det faglige niveau er ikke lige så højt, som det man vant til på KU. Dog kan man godt blive overrasket over arbejdsindsatsen i løbet af semestret, hvor man skal aflevere flere opgaver eller lave præsentationer.
teaching_comparison: Man har et tættere forhold til sin underviser og skal forvente, at man skal deltage aktivt i løbet af undervisningen.
courses_enrolled: Small States in the EU Grand Debates of European Integration Political Geography German European Policy Political Strategy
recommended_courses: Grand Debates of European Integration - man får mulighed for at debattere med andre studerende Political Strategy - faget er meget praktisk og er sjovt, hvis man interesserer sig lidt for politiske kampagner.
unexpected_costs: Ingen.
cost_comparison: Husleje var dyrere end forventet.
activities_available: Det er muligt at deltage i forskellige sportsaktiviteter igennem universitet. Det internationale kontor og ESN arrangerer også flere kulturelle og sociale ture/arrangementer.
activities_recommended: Tag på turene rundt i Tjekkiet med ESN.
weekend_recommendations: Udnyt billige tog- og busbilletter og rejs rundt i de omkringliggende lande.
culture_adjustment: Det var ikke et kulturchok at komme til Tjekkiet.
cultural_challenges: Det kan dog godt fremstå lidt uhøflige, men man skal ikke tage det personligt.
culture_appreciated: Den afslappede omgangsmåde.
top3_advice: Stress ikke over kursusregistering Lav en liste over de opgaver/præsentationer, du forventes at lave i løbet af semestret Tag det roligt omkring eksamenstid
other_useful_info: Hvis det ikke er tydeligt, hvilken indsats der forventes på kursus, så spørg endelig underviseren.
most_rewarding: Det er en anden form for frihed, man har på udveksling. Udnyt det mest muligt til at fordybe dig i de kurser, du finder allermest interessant. Hvis du gerne vil vide om det, så står underviserne altid til rådighed.
greatest_challenge: At indse at man ikke behøver at arbejde lige så hårdt, som man er vant til på KU.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go as east as I could. Due to the war a lot of options were cut down, and Prague was the best choice.
info_ease: Very easy - Both Copenhagen and Charles University are super helpful.
arrival_assistance: Nothing at all really - but the international office at Charles are soo sweet.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: it is a good thing to be prepared and to have researched the courses before the registration opens - at Charles the courses have limited seats.
registration_help: Use the international office if you are in doubt
registration_success: I got almost all the courses I wanted
registration_advice: be prepared beforehand
course_level: I feel like at Charles they are a bit more 'concrete' in their teaching compared to Danish Universites.
teaching_comparison: normal lectures and class disucssions - and also a lot of presentations
courses_enrolled: great powers Russia, economic transformations of post-soviet space, the modern history of the Caucasus, society and culture in central Asia, and Russian-turkish rivalry in the Balkans
recommended_courses: great powers Russia, economic transformations of post-soviet space, the modern history of the Caucasus, society and culture in central Asia, and Russian-turkish rivalry in the Balkans
unexpected_costs: well if you choose to travel in the Czech Republic and the surrounding countries during your stay - it can add up the cost
cost_comparison: housing was more expensive than expected
activities_available: all sorts, they were really good at organising pub-quizzes, cultural events, concerts, barbecues etc.
activities_recommended: I regret not finding a team sport with a fixed schedule - I think meeting some locals and doing stuff on your own is really good
weekend_recommendations: go to some of the smaller towns in the country - they are beautiful
culture_adjustment: very easy - Prague and the Czech Republic is lovely
socializing_tips: honestly no - it is hard, but I did manage to socialise with some by talking to them before/after lectures
cultural_challenges: nothing
culture_appreciated: it's easy going, humorous, and very pleaseant
top3_advice: try reading about the history - it makes to a much more interesting stay, do stuff on your own, and have fun and enjoy it - it is such a lovely city
other_useful_info: Please try and be open to how they do things instead of thinking the the KU way is the only and best way to learn
most_rewarding: the academic part - i really enjoyed my professors, by readings, the feeling of having more time than I do back home to submerge myself into it
greatest_challenge: finding a good reading spot for studying

crucial_aspects: A place where I could have a certain economic freedom and where I could get in with my grades
info_ease: Very easy. You get most things served on a silver palte for you and its very easy to find information if needed
arrival_assistance: I got mails, there were presentations and I always had people to ask about problems. The Erasmus office was always helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I just showed up at registration day, found the room, filled a piece of paper, and that was it.
registration_help: The Erasmus office was the main help
registration_success: I overslept on the day of the registration, but there's so many interesting courses that you won't be missing the ones you didn't get to start with
registration_advice: Talk with people at registration and make some friends. They're all looking for friends just like you, and something so simple as a conversation with them can ease your own, and their mind if feeling stressed about making friends
course_level: A little bit easy. I was so lucky to have few courses where we got homework so I had a lot of spare time to hang out with friends and go on trips around the country and the surrounding countries. But if I had problems, the teachers would hold office hours every week to settle doubts
teaching_comparison: Its very much the same with just the teacher speaking for the duration of the class with minimal student interaction.
courses_enrolled: Colonial propaganda in cinematography, Medieval Psychology and Empirical Science, Ancient Mysteries and the Environment: Religion and Mythology of Sacred Nature, Milestones of Older Czech History (until 19th Century), The Czechs in the Austrian Monarchy 1740 - 1848, History, Art and Archaeology of Cyprus: from the Neolithic to the Roman province
recommended_courses: Milestones of older czech history, because its 8 credits and there's no homework you need to do from week to week. Its just once a week where the teacher talks without stopping and that's it. Make sure to take notes tho
unexpected_costs: none that I can think of. Everything was a third the price of Denmark
cost_comparison: Beer was very cheap, as well as entrance to night clubs. Trains were also incredibly cheap. Flixbus to Vienna was more expensive than I thought it would be, but the best means of transportation when going to neighboring countries
activities_available: The university offered sports courses, and with my friends we played volleyball every friday in courts we could rent, as well as occasionally playing football.
activities_recommended: Go to parties and esn sporting and travel events. Its cheap and makes it easy to make friends or bond with you friends.
weekend_recommendations: Travel to the czech towns as they have some very beautiful towns, as well as going to neighboring countries as everything is pretty close by.
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: I didn't talk with a single czech student
cultural_challenges: People can be surprisingly racist. Multiple times I had to almost get into fights with or push away drunk people because they were abusing my indian friend
culture_appreciated: the beer culture made beer incredibly cheap
top3_advice: Take initiative and don't be afraid of making friends. Everyone is in the same situation as you and don't know anyone. Go to the social events and travel since you have more spare time
other_useful_info: none that I can think about that I advent mentioned
most_rewarding: Being so close to your friends. Since most of my friends lived at the same dorm, I was always only 5 minutes away, if not less, from all of my friends whom I would see on a daily basis
greatest_challenge: Keeping in contact with your friends from back at home. I kept forgetting about them as it felt like I was living another life, and I was always so busy with my friends in Prague that I completely forgot about my friends back at home. Another challenge could also be getting used to the new place and so many new people.

crucial_aspects: I am academically interested in Central and Eastern Europe, and Charles University offered courses with these topics. At the same time I had the possibility of trying to live in one of these countries.
info_ease: It was okay but could have been better.
arrival_assistance: Nothing apart from a few emails from the international office.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You had to wake up early in one of the first weeks during the stay, and be ready to register for the courses. It was a stressing process, as you had to rush a lot to get only some of the courses you wanted, as they quickly got filled up.
registration_help: Nothing. It could have been helpfull with an introduction on how to use the course registration system (sis)
registration_success: I got some of them, and some of them I did not get.
registration_advice: Check the courses upon the day of registration and save the course codes so that you can search them easily. Be ready when the registration opens, and the rest is luck.
course_level: The level was much lower than I am used to at UCPH. It was easy to pass most of the courses without putting a lot of effort.
teaching_comparison: At UK we had to make presentations in order to pass courses, which I rarely experience at UCPH. At UCPH all my exams are long written essays, and at UK it was presentations, tests and oral exams.
courses_enrolled: - Czech for advanced beginners - Everyday Life Under Socialism: Strategies and Practices - Geopolitical Importance of Central Europe - Milestones of Modern Czech History (1848–1989) - Modern History of Central Europe - Political and Cultural History of Modern Afghanistan
recommended_courses: - Czech for advanced beginners: I had two very good and sweet teachers who made a good environment for learning. - Political and Cultural History of Modern Afghanistan: very good and passionate teacher. More thematically than the rest of the courses which was only about learning specific names and years. I learned a lot.
unexpected_costs: Dentist, new screen for my phone because I broke it, paying for vacuum and laundry
cost_comparison: Public transport was more cheap than expected. I can really recommend to buy a 3 months pass to save money. Fitness was more expensive than expected.
activities_available: I do not know. I did not look it up and I did not participate in anything.
activities_recommended: I did not participate in anything at the school. I can recommend going to the pub quizzes arranged by the Erasmus student organisation.
weekend_recommendations: Take a trip to Plzen and Terezin. Very recommendable.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy as it is very similar to Denmark (culturally, religiously). It also helped that I learned some Czech.
socializing_tips: No. It do not know where to find them.
cultural_challenges: Nothing.
culture_appreciated: I felt very safe in Prague, which I appreciated a lot. The prices are so cheap compared to Denmark, which gave me a lot of freedom in how I wanted to spend my time.
top3_advice: - Stay at one of the dormitories offered. You will make a lot of great international friends there, compared to staying in an apartment and only socialising with people from your own country. And it is cheap. - Do not stress so much about deadlines and documents. Everything will be solved at the end. - Be open for learning about other cultures. You may learn something new. - Don't worry about your english level. You will adapt in a few days.
other_useful_info: - buy a 3 month pass in the "pid litacka" app for public transportation. - Enjoy your time!! - Book some trips around Europe. A lot of bus and plane tickets are cheap from Prague.
most_rewarding: To get a lot of international friends from other countries in Europe. These will be life long friendships, and they learned me a lot about myself, my own country, and theirs.
greatest_challenge: To fix formalities with the sending and hosting institution.

crucial_aspects: I knew I wanted to go on Erasmus exchange in Europe, and from there my choices were a bit random. I ended up choosing Prague for several reasons. Firstly, I liked the size of the city. Secondly, Charles University offered a large range of interesting courses. Lastly, I was interested in going to Eastern Europe, as I haven't been there much and their history is fascinating. The cost of living is also quite cheap, coming from Copenhagen, and that also played a role.
overall_comments: Going on exchange was one of the best things I've done.
info_ease: Upon arrival it was quite easy, and the office at Faculty of Arts at Charles University are very helpful.
arrival_assistance: Nothing out of the normal emails from the university.
arrival_comments: None.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Going on exchange was one of the best things I've done.
registration_process: They open up for course registration at a specific time, and then it's first come first served principle because there are a limited amount of space on each course - some bigger than others. But apart from that it's very easy to do, and you have a lot of time to change your courses around (I think it was almost a month).
registration_help: The office at your host faculty. The other exchange students.
registration_success: Mostly succesful. Some courses didn't provide a description for the course and then i couldn't get them pre-approved by my home university, and the teachers weren't great at answering emails. So I couldn't choose that course.
registration_advice: Make a list of the courses you would like to choose and make it longer than just the required amount of ects points so you're ready for the course registration. Rather register for too many courses in the beginning, as you have time in the following weeks to remove them.
academics_comments: Going on exchange was one of the best things I've done.
course_level: Quite easy compared to what I'm used to. The courses are also smaller so they take up less of your time, but then you have more of them.
teaching_comparison: Very similar. The "relationship" between teacher and students are kind of the same - they are not very authoritative or formal.
courses_enrolled: Highlights of Czech Theatre Strategy of Image in the 21st Century Women’s Rights in Modern Czech History Modernization and exploitation of the Amazon Introduction to Scandinavian film Susanne K. Langer: Aesthetics and beyond English. Exploring Art and Visual Culture
recommended_courses: Strategy of Image in the 21st Century Highlights of Czech Theatre
unexpected_costs: None, really.
cost_comparison: My apartment was an apartment for erasmus students, and compared to my friends here who rented rooms in other apartments mine was very expensive.
activities_available: In the first two weeks or so there are a whole calendar of events for exchange students like city walks, pub quiz, day trips, different parties. I didn't really go to them but I think a lot of people did.
activities_recommended: There's a lot of stuff to do in Prague! Museums, theater, cinema, events around the city. And it's quite cheap for students.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the Czech countryside for a weekend it's very beautiful! Prague is also an easy city to do weekend trips from - it's close to Germany, Austria, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and so on.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Talk to people you meet when you go out. But mostly the local students don't really interact super much with exchange students.
cultural_challenges: The cultural difference is not that big.
culture_appreciated: Very friendly and easy-going people. Very beautiful city.
top3_advice: Say yes to almost everything in the beginning, it's how you meet everyone. Walk around and get to know the city. Spend some time researching Facebook events happening. Download RA Guide. Download Pid and get the three month pass - there's a lot of public transport in the city and it's very easy to just jump on and off whenever when you have the pass.
other_useful_info: Explore the areas outside of Prague 1 - Holesovice, Vinohrady, Zizkov, Karlin. They are a lot less touristy. Don't pay too much in rent (like I did).
most_rewarding: The friends I made! I was lucky to find a really great group of people very early in my stay, and I've become very close with them.
greatest_challenge: It wasn't really that challenging. Maybe being away from your family and friends at home for a longer period of time, but then again 5 months aren't that long, and you're usually too busy with everything happening to think about it.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: The selection of courses, quality of the city and affordability of czech republic
overall_comments: I found it overall to be a great time. Lots of good people, nice city and my host university had exciting courses and not too complicated paperwork
info_ease: We recieved many informative mails about what to do

crucial_aspects: I wanted my destination to be a large city in Europe that could offer culture and social activities in the city. Furthermore, I wanted to go somewhere I had never been. Also I wanted to go to a university with a wide variety of courses taught in english. Prague fulfilled all that.
info_ease: A bit difficult and confusing. I didn't really seem like there was a routine way of doing it from Charles University which surprised me since they have been taking international students for many years. At times it seemed as it was the first time for the university as well. A bit chaotic and not very transparent in the beginning.
arrival_assistance: Some e-mails with links to different websites explaining stuff as well as a Zoom-meeting.
arrival_comments: It would be nice if it was a bit more streamlined and less chaotic. There was a lot of information from a lot of different sources which made it confusing. It would make it a whole lot easier if the information was coming from fewer sources and a bit more cut to the bone.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was done through their online system. You had to find the courses in their catalog and then apply for them. It was easy enough once you understood how the system worked. However, the system is very old and not very intuitive.
registration_help: You could go to the Erasmus office and ask for help or send them an e-mail (the response time for e-mails was very long though). Mostly I asked other students or teachers.
registration_success: I was able to register for most of the courses I wanted to.
registration_advice: Be patient and don't panic. In the end it will all be solved.
course_level: Some were on a high level some were not. That of course made some courses more interesting than others as it became a bit boring in some. In some of the courses I took, the teacher did not expect a whole lot from the students, which almost deactivated people so they only delivered the bare minimum.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. I'm used to more lectures in auditoriums and then when we do class courses at UCPH the teachers normally demand more active participation from the students.
courses_enrolled: Science Fiction for he Moment Modernism and Modernity Contemporary Poetry and Poetics American and Canadian Literature: Civil War to WWII What is an Image? Philosophical Reflections Introduction to Scandinavian Film English. Exploring Art and Visual Culture
recommended_courses: Modernism and Modernity Contemporary Poetry and Poetics These two coursed I really enjoyed and learned a lot from. They were challenging but in the end I really feel like a learned a lot. Also it was a small amount of students that attended these courses which made it possible to be very active in class.
unexpected_costs: Not really any.
cost_comparison: Buying groceries were a bit more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: Different parties and social stuff arranged by the ESN.
activities_recommended: I didn't do a lot of activities through uni. I mostly did stuff with friends outside of uni.
weekend_recommendations: Charles Bridge, The Clock Tower and all bars because the beers are so cheap. It's like Berlin but just cheaper.
culture_adjustment: It was fine. Not that different from my home country.
socializing_tips: It's a bit difficult getting to local students as they mostly stick to themselves which I understand. I don't really know just try to talk to them and be nice I guess.
cultural_challenges: The fact that people had so many different classes so you never really got to know people from your classes which is different from what I'm used to.
culture_appreciated: I think the Czech people are very direct and honest which makes it a lot easier to get to know people.
top3_advice: Try out new courses that are different from what you normally study - it's a good opportunity to try out other subjects. Try to grab coffee or lunch with the people from your classes. It's nice getting to know your fellow students which can also make boring classes more fun to attend to. Don't spend too much time stressing about the courses and make the most out of the new city you've just arrived in.
other_useful_info: Don't let the slightly chaotic beginning stress you out too much and just have a good time. All the courses and different stuff will be solved and the employees are very friendly, helpfull and flexible.
most_rewarding: Experiencing that you can go to a different city in a different country where you don't know a single person, and then in only half a year you can build up an entire life with friends and a connection to the city. That was a very motivating experience for me.
greatest_challenge: Saying goodbye to people leaving in the end. It's difficult because people are from all over the world so all of the sudden you can't see each other that often.

info_ease: It was quite easy.

For my mandatory 7.5 ects course at home (DAK3), I had to have 3 different courses here (total of 17 ects) to cover it.
registration_advice: If you have some mandatory courses at home, be aware that the course catalogue is not always the same as the year before - be ready to change plans. If everything is elective, enjoy that you can change courses in the first two weeks
course_level: 4 MA courses, total of 23 ects points, 2 BA courses total of 9 ects points and one sports course (2 ects), but the sports course did not get transfered.

At CU when discussing a text we mainly talked about it and did not have any sort of critic towards it. For some lecturers I think the communication was too bad - getting know you have a big assignment 10 days before you have to hand it in does not make sense in my head - why not tell in further advance? Some courses did not have syllabuses, because we have to do our own reseach - that would never happen in Cph.

activities_available: Many sport opportunities.
activities_recommended: If you wanna talk to locals, go for a sport.
weekend_recommendations: Go skiing, go to the mountains on a hike at the german border - there is probably also nice at the polish border area. Go watch some football, go for the techno venues, go for cheap beers
culture_adjustment: It was alright, it is different from Denmark, but not that much.
socializing_tips: Sign up for a sports course
cultural_challenges: Not really
culture_appreciated: Its hard to point out specific things to be honest.
top3_advice: Enjoy the public transport Go out of Prague a time or two Dont be afraid to talk to new people - everyone's new
other_useful_info: Some of the exams are handwritten
most_rewarding: Getting new international friends but also getting really tight with my danish roommates who Ill still be seeing back home
greatest_challenge: Feeling alone and away from friends and family back home

crucial_aspects: I thought the city was a nice combination of a different culture but not too different so that there would be many culture shocks for me. It was also student friendly meaning not too expensive to live in as a student. The city was placed in the centrum of Europe which gave a lot of opportunities to travel to other destinations.
info_ease: It was easy enough to find information but not all information was correct. For example was it stated that the semester would last until mid february however in reality it was possible to be done with the semester at before christmas.
arrival_assistance: I recieved mostly emails with information. There was also one short information meeting before the semester started.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You signed up through the universty web site after a week where you could attend all the available classes. It was a first come first served basis but it was possible to sign up for classes even if it had been filled up on the website.
registration_help: You could attend all the available classes before signing up. There were video guides explaining the process of signing up too.
registration_success: I got all the classes i wanted.

recommended_courses: Legal Reasoning: First Amendment Case Law Private Law Introduction into Central European Legal Culture

cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than expected.
activities_available: We got an e-mail about the opportunities both when we were 2 months into the semester.
activities_recommended: I did the intensive czech course before which were a good opportunity to meet people from other faculties too.
weekend_recommendations: Go on trips in Czech Republic the bus tickets are were cheap. Go travel to the cities close to Prague. Visit the national teater students get a discount.

socializing_tips: Join some classes were local students attend. Get a "buddy" that the university offers.

culture_appreciated: Much consideration was given to students, especially when it comes to prices.
top3_advice: The city is very easy to live in, the public transportation is great. if you want to travel in your semester the location is great. Do not expect the locals to understand english.
other_useful_info: Do not worry about information it will usually come last minut no matter what you do.
most_rewarding: Meeting students from other countries. Trying to live in a new city.
greatest_challenge: Not always feeling welcome in Prague
other_comments: If you consider going on an exhange do it, it is a great experience and opportunity.

crucial_aspects: - A beautiful city with significant history. - A historical faculty at the host university. - Not too expensive to live in. - Decent dorm opportunities. - The host university does not require learning a new language to study there.
info_ease: Very easy, people were extremely helpful.
arrival_assistance: There was an information meeting, and it was possible to schedule office hours with coordinators.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We went to the faculty for registration, and formed a line. It was smooth.
registration_help: Two erasmus coordinators were there to answer any questions.
registration_success: It was about being as fast as possible as soon as registration opened. I only missed out on one class that I wanted.
registration_advice: Just be patient and perhaps try to talk to your fellow students while waiting. It can be a good introduction to socialization..
course_level: They were MA courses, but for some of them, BA students could also attend.
teaching_comparison: As I previously mentioned, less emphasis on debate/discussion and more time devoted to individual presentations. For me, this discouraged the class in engaging with every text each week.
courses_enrolled: Symbolic Poem - Keats Southern Literature Writing as an Experiment British Literature of the Asian and African Diaspora Samuel Beckett: the Plays
recommended_courses: I liked all of the courses, but my personal favourites were Symbolic Poem - Keats and Samuel Beckett. The lecturers were great.
unexpected_costs: Using the washing machine in the dorm (not unexpected, but might be worth noting).
cost_comparison: Everything was cheaper than Denmark, which was nice.
activities_available: There was a bunch of opportunities, but I didn't sign up for that much, I focused on efforts organized externally by students.
activities_recommended: Keep an eye on film festivals, semester opening events, perhaps try going to an ice hockey game or some other sport events. I really enjoyed playing volleyball and football with fellow students.
weekend_recommendations: Try to also visit other towns outside Prague. I had some amazing memories in Karlovy Vary, Cesky Krumlov and Budapest. All stunning and doable for a weekend trip, or even daytrip. Other students have raved about Vienna, Warsaw, Dresden, Brno, Plzen. There are so many options in the vicinity. Take advantage of Prague's proximity to these fantastic places.
culture_adjustment: Very easy for me personally. But it all depends on personality types I believe, and it's very important to make an effort to get along with your roommate, even if just on a superficial, friendly level.
socializing_tips: Go out of your room. Sometimes just showing up to an event or in a common area will mean you make a friend for life.
cultural_challenges: In my opinion Czechs seem similar to Danes in that they are introverted to a degree, until alcohol is involved. Therefore it wasn't such a culture shock. But if you don't drink, then try to discover what events are going on that don't involve drinking.
culture_appreciated: People are always down to do things. Sometimes all it takes is asking, reaching out. People are on erasmus to make friends, just like you, so don't be too shy.
top3_advice: - Try to make a list of goals/things you would like to do before you leave, and keep those in mind while you are on exchange. Time flies fast, don't let it pass you by. - Be kind and accommodating during your stay. You are a guest in another country, you should expect having to acclimatize to the country a bit, not the other way around. If things aren't the exact way you expected, don't let it defeat you. - Enjoy it. It's one of the most exciting times you'll ever have. Don't overthink it too much, live in the moment and be present.
other_useful_info: Jana Palacha 2 is a beautiful building. That's all.
most_rewarding: Making friends from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Probably juggling academic workload/social desires. It's hard to be satisfied with both simultaneously.

crucial_aspects: I had never been there before and everyone spoke well of the city, and there were many exchange spots, and it is cheap :)
info_ease: Very easy! The faculty of humanities was very good at sharing information by email before the semester started and in the intro week.
arrival_assistance: We got 5 days of introduction about uni stuff, information about the city, the country, it's traditions, places to visit and where to go in Prague
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There was a add-and-drop period for Erasmus students which allowed you to try some courses and then drop them if you didn't like them or add new ones that you heard good things about or something. It was very useful, but also made the process harder since they had so many good courses available AND because you can choose from all faculties to some extent.
registration_help: The Erasmus coordinator was always good at helping. She would answer very fast and was so helpful!
registration_success: Very successful, I got all the classes I chose in the preregistration, but then I changed them up a bit in the add and drop. I am very happy and content with my courses!
registration_advice: Don't look too much, just make a decision and stick with it. There are so many cool courses so you can keep looking forever. But also pick some cool ones if you can! And be quick in the preregistration period and register for too many and drop out rather than too few and be in trouble later.
course_level: I took a vide variety of courses. They were all interesting and very different. Some had lectures, som had seminars. Some had a lot of readings and projects over the semester, but others only had a final exam.
teaching_comparison: It varied so much. Most of the courses had more projects throughout the semester than in UCPH and therefore less stressful final exams.
courses_enrolled: Czech language course for beginners Introduction to brain Feminism and environmental movements Gender and religion Can I hate God? Ancient mysteries and the environment Music and space/place And Yoga for fun
recommended_courses: Introduction to brain!! And the sports courses. They were not accepted in the preapproval but still fun to participate in. Also the Gender and religion course I enjoyed a lot.
unexpected_costs: Nothing I can remember
cost_comparison: Alcohol less expensive. Coffee more expensive
activities_available: You could join the sport courses and the introweek which were both very fun.
activities_recommended: Sports and introweek
weekend_recommendations: There is a lot of good techno/electronic clubs, concerts of all kinds of music, and events going on all the time. Also easy to take a bus to another city or country, and pretty cheap.
culture_adjustment: I did not get to know a lot of Czech friends except one girl that showed us around during the intro week. The courses I took had mainly Erasmus students in them, and the Czech students would mostly talk to other Czech students. Outside of school I experienced the same. Czech people didn't really talk to me that much, I met mostly international people.
socializing_tips: Talk to them before or after class I guess.
cultural_challenges: I felt like the Czechs were not very talkative and kept mostly to them selves, and I wish I had met more of local people.
culture_appreciated: Their Beer :P and their cute houses and beautiful city. I love the parks, Riegrovy Sady has the best view of Prague.
top3_advice: 1. Get social on the first day of introweek/uni!!!! People are so ready to meet and make friends and for me it was important to make use of that day. I made most of my friends on the first day of introweek. 2. Do something everyday. The time runs away so fast that even though I was tired I tried to do at least a little bit of sightseeing, go to a new cafe/bar, go to some events or something, just do something small (or big) everyday. 3. Don't worry too much about school. It will be fine.
other_useful_info: I don't remember anything right now. Just enjoy every moment.

crucial_aspects: For me the most important thing was finding a destination where I didn't have to worry about money, I could make new friends and still have courses that was relevant for my education. In all these aspects Prague was the ideal destination.
info_ease: It was very easy. Prague is used to getting exchange students and are giving you all the information that you need. Furthermore, they have an organization called Erasmus in Prague which is driven by volunteers. They are helping alot, both with accommodation, parties, trips and more.
arrival_assistance: The faculty of social science had a welcome meeting for exchange students. They gave all the information that you need in the beginning. Before you even arrive, they sent me two documents with relevant information. Furthermore, they have several different what's app groups where you can always ask for the help you need. There is one big group for all exchange studens, one with the organisation Erasmus in Prague, if you live in dorm there is a dorm group and other than this there is running grounp, techno group, football group...
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: i don't remember the exact progress, but I remember it wasn't complicated at all. they are all the time giving you information about the next thing you have to do.
registration_help: i had a koordinater on my host university who I could always contact, if I had any questions.
registration_success: you need to be ready for the registration. the registration starts on a specific day and time. when the registration start you need to be fast, because there are limited spots. if people only want 4 courses they will probably register for around 8-10 courses just to make sure. this mean that you can easily end up on the waiting list, but even though I was on the waiting list for all my courses I actually ended up getting them anyways. so don't be that nervous not to get the course right from the beginning.
registration_advice: I would recommend you to always read all emails carefully and be on top of the deadlines. it can easily seem overwhelming with all the things you need to do if you are doing them too late. this is especially incase something isn't working or if you are in doubt what to do. if you are doing things early you have the time to ask for help.
course_level: I think the level of the courses was the same as in Denmark. the school is only about 3 months so the syllabus seemed smaller than usual. however I still used quite some time on school. it was sometimes annoying, but im happy that I actually learned something on my exchange.
teaching_comparison: the style of teaching was pretty much the same, besides we didn't have small classroom practice - which im used to in copenhagen.
courses_enrolled: I took following courses 10 ects advanced macroeconomics - master course (in Denmark: makroøkonomi 3) 9 ects advanced microeconomics - master course (in Denmark: valgfrit valgfag) 8 ects international trade - bachelor course (in Denmark: valgfrit valgfag) 5 ects behavioral economics - bachelor course (in Denmark: Behavioral economics) I took courses with very high amount of ects to make sure that I only had to have 4 courses. im not sure if it really made it easier for me since the courses where demanding. they have courses that is only 3 ects.
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend advanced macroeconomics and behavioral economics. macroeconomics was a really nice and structured subject. it gave me a lot of knowledge. behavioral economics was a really exciting subject, I learned a lot and it was easy. international trade was actually a nice course considering the syllabus, but the teacher was very boring and he used a lot of time on a lot of things that didn't really matter for the course. however it was quite easy to pass - I didn't give much effort to the class but I got a C anyhow. I would NOT recommend advanced microeconomics. its kinda similar to mikroøkonomi II in Denmark, but they are for some reason only focusing on some specific subjects. it was kinda hard to pass even though its multiple choice. there might be 1 correct answer, might be 2,3 or 4. it doesn't say in the task. but if you don't choose all the correct answers in each task you will get 0 points.
unexpected_costs: no unexpected cost
cost_comparison: food and drinks are SO cheap. half a liter of really nice czech beer cost 15 DKK. The clothes is a bit cheaper but most beauty products is the same. you can easily get a meal on a restaurant for 60 DKK. as a danish person with both SU and Erasmus money (approximately 500 euro per month) you will live like a king in Prague haha. Something that is really cheap is bolt. it cost 30 dansih crowns to get 7 km in the early morning when I was on my way home from the club.
activities_available: there is an organisation called esn. the organizes day trips around czech republic where you can see other czech cities. Erasmus in Prague also organize trips, both to other countries and they organize that people can go see a sport together and sometimes even do sports together.
activities_recommended: watch ice hockey visit Karlovy vary go to popocafe try a gourmet restaurant, its cheap try escape room - cheaper than Denmark try the horror and thrill park just have a walk in the city, it is a very beautiful place.
weekend_recommendations: Prague is in Central Europe so it is pretty cheap to visit other countries. for instance I was visiting Berlin. it costed 20 euro for the bus and I paid 26 euro for 3 days in a very nice hostel.
culture_adjustment: for me there wasn't much adjustment. the weather is really similar to Denmark besides it is raining less, which is nice. furthermore -5 degrees in Prague isn't as cold as -5 degrees in Denmark, since there isn't a lot of wind in Prague. The food is kinda similar, but I don't think they have as many healthy options as in Denmark.
socializing_tips: well in general its easy mostly to socialize with other exchange students and when I think about it I have never personally spoken with an exchange student in Denmark so maybe that's just how it is. I meet a few czech people. 3 at parties and 1 in advanced macroeconomics - we were making our assignments together. I will however recommend you to find friends from other nationalities. I had contact with other danish people, but my best friends in Prague is from ukraine, germany, turkey and others. it is really interesting to learn about other cultures. for instance, while I thought Prague was really cheap, my Ukrainian friend thought it was kind of expensive.
cultural_challenges: for me I think czech people in general seem very rude. a lot of czech people do not speak English, so its hard to communicate and the get mad when you don't speak czech. if you are a girl I won't recommend you to take a bolt alone.
culture_appreciated: Prague is in general a beautiful city. I also enjoyed the prices since its so cheap so you don't have to worry about money. 3 months of public transportation is 37 danish crowns.
top3_advice: im not sure if there is 3 specific things I wanna tell. just remember that even though 5 months may seem like a long time, then its going by so fast. remember always to get out and be social instead of regretting sitting at home. the first two weeks I was almost not even home, but in those two weeks I found my best friend in Prague. People are very friendly and open since you are all in same position.
other_useful_info: im not sure what it should be.
most_rewarding: it was definitely my personal growth. I got new friends, I learned more about myself and I got so close to another city. I feel so attached too Prague and I feel like its my second home. I would personally never move from Denmark, but if I had to, it should be to Prague.
greatest_challenge: for me it was the low level og hygiene. te other students were disgusting if you ask me. in the dorm. people didn't wash their hands after the toilet. I even saw a girl going to the toilet, coming out, not washing her hands, and then she went directly to the kitchen and starting cooking her dinner. also I got a roommate from England who never cleaned her "side" of the room. even the first day we came I was surprised to see that the room was very dirty so I cleaned my own side of the room before I packed out my suitcase. my roomie on the other hand just packed out her stuff and placed it on top of the dirty desk and so on. she didn't clean her room ones. she didn't change her sheets for 3 months even though the dorm is washing them for you and you can get new ones ever 2 week. moreover she had old moulded things in the fridge including a 3 months old milk. I was probably really unlucky since I didn't here anyone experiencing anything like it, but still it was very challenging for me to live in.
other_comments: as I said, the dorm wash your sheets ev very 2 weeks, which is really nice. also there is a bar in the dorm where you can both drink alcohol, coffee, have food and more. they have som events every week, for instance karaoke. its a really nice place.

crucial_aspects: For my it was interesting to study political science in a country with such a different political history than what I'm used to and what counts for most of Western Europe. In that regards I wanted to go to one of the most different countries I could within the EU. Furthermore, it was important for me that there were some possibilities of exploring beautiful nature within a reachable distance of my exchange.
info_ease: It was very easy to get information and there was a lot of meeting beforehand including guiding documents with information on the admission process and applying for courses.
arrival_assistance: There was an introduction day with social science, but I heard there was a whole introduction week at the humanities faculty, which I really wished I had the possibility too. Especially because it gave them a better social grounding right at the beggining.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We received information beforehand. Then the registration opened at different timeslots for different faculties with a first-come-first-served process, but if you didn't get into a courses you wanted to could register for a waiting list and the professors were very flexible in terms of allowing students not on the official lists to participate in the first class. There was also a flexible period in the beginning where you could register for more courses than you needed to check them out.
registration_help: Zoom meeting, helping manuals and very fast responding Erasmus coordinators.
registration_success: Very successful. I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Have some back-up courses in case your plan A doesn't work
course_level: Augusta x x x x x x x x x All of my courses, except one, was on master level, but the generel level of the courses was surprisingly low, although I had two very good courses. My only bachelor course was on a high level.
teaching_comparison: There was a lot of focus on oral participation in the classes and an overall grade reflecting not only the exam but the performance throughout the whole semester. This differed a lot from what I'm used to.
courses_enrolled: ASZTV0068: Bouldering JEB026: European Economic Integration JPM805: Democracy - Current Challenges and Innovations JSM777: EU Comparative Politics:Tensions in Representative Democracy JTM254: Promoting democracy abroad: the US and the EU in third countries JTM382: EU Institutions
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Promoting democracy abroad: the US and the EU in third countries. The teacher is one of the best I have come across. The discussions in class was very good and interesting.
unexpected_costs: I ended up spending a lot of money on transport going back and forth because I didn't want to fly.
cost_comparison: Transport within the Czech Republic was very inexpensive. I had thought my rent would be cheaper.
activities_available: There were a lot of sport opportunities, everyone could sign up for one sports-course. There were some activities in the beginning for the faculty. There wasn't a lot of information about other clubs or "local" life on campus.
activities_recommended: Take a sports course. I met a lot of very nice Czech students there!
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going to the close other big European cities (Berlin, Budapest, Wein). I also went to Bohemian Switzerland, where Narnia was filmed and to Špindlerův Mlýn to go skiing- both things was very fun.
culture_adjustment: I have been in Prague many times before, so it was very easy. I also lived with three people that i knew from home, which also made it more easy.
socializing_tips: Go to the events (I didn't, and i regretted it) and don't be afraid to just talk to people in your class.
cultural_challenges: I didn't really find any cultural differences particularly challenging. Some people didn't speak english, but that is fair enough.
culture_appreciated: The use of parks. the Czech people loves nature, why they also use the parks a lot! You can also swim in some parts of the river and in some lakes. There were also a lot of concerts and events that were easy to find!
top3_advice: 1. Worth paying for private life 2. Go into nature and use the cheap culture options in the city 3. Go to the events in the beginning - but you don't need to go party
other_useful_info: Get the goout app!
most_rewarding: Meeting all my friends!
greatest_challenge: Feeling confident in the social aspect of exchange.

crucial_aspects: 1. That my destination was student-friendly in terms of ambience/environment and price/cost. 2. The possibility to study and experience a different country's law system in general. 3. That the city is beautiful and nice.
info_ease: It was somewhat easy. I rarely felt like I was missing certain information, and when I did, I got that information from other exchange-students who had the information.
arrival_assistance: Did not receive any assistance from Erasmus or host university when arriving.
arrival_comments: The introduction to the host university was very sparesome. We had a brief walk-around the faculty and a presentation with information, but then that was it.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There was an acceptance-registration which was quite thorough. Once accepted and at the university, the enrolling in courses was fairly easy to manage.
registration_help: Unsure what to answer.
registration_success: I'd say 80% succesful. I didn't get all the classes I had envisaged beforehand, but I got the ones most important for me, and the new ones were nice as well.
registration_advice: Students should know, that the enrollment/registration is a 'first come, first served' system, which can come as a surprise for many people. I didn't know beforehand, that you absolutely had to be ready at the specific time when registration opened to make sure you got the classes you wanted. This is crucial information for many students, as some relies on having specific classes during their exchange.
course_level: The level varied a lot from class to class. Some classes were very thorough while others were at a very low academic level. By this I mean, that some of the classes didn't require or involved any actual juridical method, it was just a matter of remembering information. Therefore keeping the level at a explanatory and not analytical level.
teaching_comparison: It was mostly lecture-based, with the teacher arriving and speaking singlehandedly for the duration of the class. At UCPH, we mostly have seminars where the focus is more on working actively with cases where our skills can be trained and enhanced. This was not the same at CU. I believe the way of teaching at UCPH is way more beneficial for the students, and would prefer this way of teaching.
courses_enrolled: - Legal Reasoning: First Amendment Case Law - Theories of Legal Personhood - Financial Law - Private Law - Natural Resource Law - Intellectual Property Law - Czech Legal History
recommended_courses: The course "Legal Reasoning: First Amendment Case Law". I would recommend this course, as it's really interesting and the teacher is phenomenal. He incites exciting and critical debates amongst the students. It was a really giving course.
unexpected_costs: No answer.
cost_comparison: Groceries. These were as some of the only things not more cheap than back home.
activities_available: Some events were arranged at my faculty which were very cool (like a night party, and a debate). I also attended a traditional Scandinavian Christmas arrangement at another faculty which was nice.
activities_recommended: There are MANY activities you can attend, so just attend what you would like to be honest.
weekend_recommendations: Visit neighbouring countries by bus. Try Escape-Rooms! Prague is very good at making them!
culture_adjustment: I felt it was very easy.
socializing_tips: I did not socialize a lot with local students. Mostly other exchange-students.
cultural_challenges: None were particularly difficult.
culture_appreciated: The easy-going, laid back vibe. No one seemed to be stressed. I liked that.
top3_advice: Prepare for the costs of Denmark in general (quite expensive for people not from Scandinavia).
other_useful_info: Get in the various WhatsApp groups that exists, as you can meet many new people there.
most_rewarding: Having fun and experiencing the city+country with other exchange students.
greatest_challenge: Social fatigue. At some point you get burned out. But you should not worry as it's totally natural and it's OK to take a breather and not attend every event that occurs.
other_comments: None.

crucial_aspects: The only thing I knew was that I wanted it to be within Europe, therefore I applied to universities in Europe I had the option of applying to.
info_ease: It was quite easy, and if we had questions there were a lot of people we could write to via e-mail and get help from them.
arrival_assistance: We had a large gathering for all exchange students at the faculty of social science where we got all the important information. And they updates us via e-mail with deadline etc. we should remember.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You needed to go onto the university system side, and then you could search for the subjects. You need all of the course codes, which can be found in the course catalogue. And then you can choose the ones you want, but there is no guarantee that youl will get a spot or that the course is provided in your semester. A tip is to search for the courses you want to attend the most first, so the spots do not get filled before you search it.
registration_help: We of course got information of how we should do on the registration day, and I believe it was recorded and uploaded to us as well. But on the day we were on our own.
registration_success: Not very succesfull, a lot of the ones I wanted was not provided in my semester. I only ended up getting two of the courses I wanted out of five.
registration_advice: The situation can be a bit stressful and disapointing (at least it was for me), but try to keep calm and contact the teachers and attend the courses you have registrated for too see which ones you like the most. But in the end I found courses that were interested and linked up with the amount of ETCS points I needed, so you most likely will too.
course_level: I had mainly BA courses, and then one MA course. For me the MA course was very good and interesting, and not to hard to follow.
teaching_comparison: In terms of lectures it was pretty much the same, just the professor lecturing and then we could ask questions during the lecture if we wanted too. In the seminars it was a bit different, where the exercises were done in plenum and at home we get to do the exercises on our own and in groups and maybe discuss them afterwards.
courses_enrolled: Contemporary crises and social-ecological transformation Principles of Economics Advanced Data Analysis in MS Excel Topics in Industrial Organization International Trade Energy Security in Israel and the Middle East
recommended_courses: I would really recommend: Contemporary crises and social-ecological transformation - as it was very interesting and we got to do a group project of our own choosing which was quite nice. Advanced Data Analysis in MS Excel - if you want to learn how to use Excel and different functions I would recommend this. I got a lot out of it. Energy Security in Israel and the Middle East - this course was also very interesting.
unexpected_costs: Not really anything unexpected.
cost_comparison: Food were less expensive, but my rent were a lot higher than I expected.
activities_available: A lot of different things were available, you enroll in different sport activities, and there were also held a lot of MSN events you could sign up to, to meet other exchange students (for example, pub quizzes, international dinners, game nights etc.)
activities_recommended: I would recommend to sign up for some of the different MSN events, depending on what you would like to attend. It was a great way to meet new exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend to just enjoy the city and explore it on the days off. In the weekends it is fun to visit other cities in Prague, for example, Karlovy Vary or Brno. Also, the national museuem was a quite nice experience. Or else just go out and have fun with the other exchange students.
culture_adjustment: It would say it was quite easy, I did not feel like there were a major difference.
socializing_tips: In my experience we did not really meet that many local students, and if we had classes with them they mostly kept to themselves. But maybe you could ask them for advice or what they would recommend as locals in the city.
cultural_challenges: The only thing was that the elderly population could not speak english, so that could be a barrier, but otherwise there wasn't really much of a difference.
culture_appreciated: The locals were always very nice to speak too. Also the city was just beautiful.
top3_advice: Be prepared with the course codes before the course registration starts. Enjoy and explore the city as much as possible. Try to get to know other people than from your own country.
other_useful_info: Don't feel stupid for asking questions to your coordinators, they are there too help you. And also it could be a good idea to get a "buddy".
most_rewarding: To experience something new, it was fun trying to live in another country and studying there.
greatest_challenge: Missing the people at home, but they will still be there when you get back.

crucial_aspects: Choosing somewhere that were different from what i knew
overall_comments: Met wonderful people and the city of Prague is beautiful.
info_ease: Most information could be found online.
arrival_assistance: I did not recieve any help right on arrival, but we did have orientation day the first day of school. I do know it is possible though to get a university "buddy" that potentially could assist you from day one.
arrival_comments: Orientation day was on the first day of school, which interfered with first day of classes, so that was a little bit annoying. But it was quite informative, and the contact person at the university was quick at answering emails if I had any further questions.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Met wonderful people and the city of Prague is beautiful.
registration_process: On the first days of classes you get your login that enables you to register for classes. Then you have three month were you have the possibility of changing your courses.
registration_help: You could write to the erasmus contact person at the university, who was fairly quick at answering emails.
registration_success: I ended up getting all the classes i wanted.
registration_advice: If you find something you really want to sign up for, then do so as fast as possible since the courses can fill up. And once you get able to login you get more information about the courses, like whether they are BA level or MA level.
academics_comments: Met wonderful people and the city of Prague is beautiful.
course_level: The level was close to the level of KU courses, at some points more difficult but that might be because it was the first time for me doing MA courses.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was close to how it is at home, with lectures and exercise classes, but teachers are allowed to do whatevere they want so it might vary.
courses_enrolled: English for mathematicians NJAZ096, Czech for beginners NJAZ098, Algebraic number theory NMAG430, Nonlinear Differential Equations NMNV406, Functional Analysis for physicist NMMO302, and Groups Representations NMAG438.
recommended_courses: I really liked my language courses, both really interesting in different ways and with very nice teachers. Algebraic number theory I would also recommend, although it was a difficult course. Nonlinear differential equations I would really recommend, as it was very nicely self contained. I would recommend not to take functional analysis and group representations, as the first one had a really confusing exam, and the second one was very difficult.
unexpected_costs: It was actually cheaper that I expected.
cost_comparison: Daily groceries were cheaper, eating out cheaper.
activities_available: Not that many hostet by the university itself, but a lot by other erasmus groups.
activities_recommended: Do events hostet by the city, like during my stay I went to Museum by night, Witch burning ceremony, concert on the river Vltava, music festival on the river islands, and more. They are fun and let you see the city in a different way.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend Krakow in Poland, and although i havent been myself i heard good things about Wien and Budapest. But there is also a lot of beautiful one day trips within Czechia like Brno, Carlovy vary, Cesky krumlov, Kutna hora and more.
culture_adjustment: Not too difficult.
socializing_tips: Like expected I ended up mostly speaking with eramus students, but the local students are a lot like danish students in that they mostly keep to themselves and for them it is business as usual, but a lot of them are also not that good at english. The ones I did speak with were very nice.
cultural_challenges: Going to the supermarket can be tough when everything is in czech or sometimes german.
culture_appreciated: Beautiful buildings with an appreciation for old architecture.
top3_advice: Try not to stress too much about courses before hand, they will fall into place once you get there. The best way to enjoy Prague is to just walk through the city. And dont worry too much about the classes, remember you are there to experience so much more than just the university.
other_useful_info: How the exams unfold can be very confusing, so just be aware of that when you get towards the end of your stay.
most_rewarding: The connections I made with other people.
greatest_challenge: All of the paperwork before the exchange itself.

registration_help: Could receive help by either mail, phone or consultants.
registration_advice: Don't bother too much with course selection

info_ease: It was fine, especially because of the Erasmus+ team, and the meeting beforehand, that helped a lot
arrival_assistance: We had a meeting in the beginning that was very informative
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We got a lot of information, so it was easy.
registration_help: Always someone to write to, and they always gave us a lot of information
registration_success: I didn't get all the ones I wanted, but it turned out great anyways.
registration_advice: Have a lot of courses ready for the course registration - and read the information they send you thoroughly.
course_level: A bit easier than my home university, but more interesting courses because they were very practical and real-life related - less theoretical than at home, which I really liked.
teaching_comparison: Hard to say

unexpected_costs: Phone bills, as I had to change my phone company every second month because of the EU rule (you can't be in another country for more than 60 days with the same phone company) or something like that
