crucial_aspects: I applied in the third round so at that time I could not take the chance of applying for a uni with only few spots. I applied for Prague because it had 75 spots, I like the city and I really just wanted to go on exchange.
info_ease: I found it quite easy. Charles University had given me an appropriate amount of information
arrival_assistance: I had received some emails with details about what to do and what not to do.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We were given a time slot to come by on the first day to get our arrival documents signed. I could get my document signed before my quite late time slot so it wasn't a problem.
registration_help: There are people who can help you at uni both people working there and other exchange students. The administrative personel is not good at English so do not expect that much help from them,
registration_success: I had to apply for all new courses because the ones that I had found were not available.... But there is a lot of courses so I did not worry
registration_advice: Expect not to get the courses you initially wanted but dont be stressed by it!
course_level: The courses differ in levels. Some are relatively low work (no obligatory readings) but others are more demanding. The courses do not have as heavy a work load as in CPH.
teaching_comparison: It was much less student interaction which was sad.
courses_enrolled: Russian politics and society War, the State and Society II Geopolitics of Great Powers: Russia Security Issues in Japan and the South East Asia Strategic Studies
recommended_courses: Geopolitics of Great Powers: Russia: Great teacher!! The most engaging and demanding that I had but loved it. Security Issues in Japan and the South East Asia: The issues are really interesting and there is quite a low work load Strategic Studies: The teacher was American and he was a true expert. It was very interesting and a lot of student activity.
unexpected_costs: Danish phone subscribtion abroad is a bit of a complex thing but I managed. Look into it before going. Data is not cheap in CZ.
cost_comparison: It was quite as expected acutally. Food was cheaper than back home but clothes and stuff like that are not.
activities_available: Erasmus in Prague - there is a lot of social stuff like tours around CZ and parties
activities_recommended: You have to go travel CZ when you are here but also neighbouring countries!
weekend_recommendations: Find friends and go drink beer new places each weekeend!
culture_adjustment: Difficult with the language but it wasn't a problem for me. Most speak good English.
socializing_tips: Seek them out yourselves! Classes wont let you socialise because there are no breaks in class were you can socialise and people are busy so they leave straight after class.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: Cheap beers and the food.
top3_advice: 1. It is not all about the studies. Go traveling and explore the country and neighbouring countries. 2. Befriend people from your classes - they are great especially other exchange students 3. Do not stress about uni and the administrative part of it. It is fairly easy to take care of.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Being away frome home so I could plan everything on my own (and my girlfriend) who was also here at the same time hehe. I really just love Prague. It is a beautiful city but not so big so you can actually manage to visit all parts of the city fairly easy.
greatest_challenge: Being to old to get student discounts.

crucial_aspects: A city that seems interesting and a pleasant place to live
overall_comments: I would recommend everyone to go study abroad
info_ease: 6/10. Everything was scattered in diffrent Emails, that weren't the best structured always, so you had to create your own "to-do" list out of what you could decipher. It would have been nice just to have been given a very structured, this is what you need to do before theese dates.
arrival_assistance: The Erasmus office was pretty helpfull
arrival_comments: The Erasmus Club students were amazing!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I would recommend everyone to go study abroad

registration_help: You could talked to the office about stuff, but mostly you were on your own. It helped that we created a messenger group with the rest of UCPH who were going to Charles so we could exchange experiences doing the process.
registration_success: I do not really get stressed easyly

academics_comments: I would recommend everyone to go study abroad

cultural_challenges: Czechs can be quite closed off
culture_appreciated: That everything seems to be taken care off in Czechia
top3_advice: 1. Go on the intro tour if you faculty has one 2. Be out there, dont be shy to ask people to do something 3. Take intiative for activites yourself
other_useful_info: If you are unsure, ask someone
most_rewarding: The freindships i made
greatest_challenge: Exam season (not too challenging though)

crucial_aspects: As I applied for exchange in the final run with very short notice, I had less optional destinations to choose from. From the ones available I prioritized the aspects of transport possibilites (train/bus/public transport connection possibilities) and thoughts about whether I would have opportunities in the future to choose this excactly destination as a place to live for a longer period of time.
overall_comments: I find the approach to the teaching in classes very different from what I have been used to, which has been interesting and inspiring, and has as well increased my rate of the overall study abroad experience, which I also found of a lower academic level than what I have been used to at my home university.
info_ease: I found it difficult to feel sure and safe about the information, that I found on the different webpages and systems, which made it crucial to me that I was able to email and communicate with administratives at both my home and host university.
arrival_assistance: I mainly received assistance to student and document registration. I also attended an online introduction meeting, which was useful to sum um basic deadlines and places to take notice of.
arrival_comments: I found that the availability to communicate with administratives and receive help and answers to questions was very accessible, but that I wouldn't have managed only through the online orientation.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I find the approach to the teaching in classes very different from what I have been used to, which has been interesting and inspiring, and has as well increased my rate of the overall study abroad experience, which I also found of a lower academic level than what I have been used to at my home university.
registration_process: The registration had multiple steps, which first had to settle the acceptance as a student of the host university, and from then on registrations on the courses.
registration_help: I was informed, that I could contact the administration of my home university and of my host university. And besides of course search for help through the webpages
registration_success: I ended up with the classes, that I wanted to register for, but I found it difficult to get an overview of the actual courses available until the very day of registration. The system in which the courses are registrered and appear is difficult to search within.
registration_advice: I would recommend to look up kinds of classes, that has an interest, but to not settle for final choices until just before the atual day of registration, as the classes may not be available at the term. I would also recommend to have gathered a list of more classes than actually needed, in case you don't get a spot in the class, as well as to be ready to apply the minute the registration day opens up, because some classes may be filled up in very short time. I also recommend to attend more classes than needed during the first few weeks, as the period of registration is interchangable within the first few weeks of the term. This I found very nice - that I was able to attend classes and cancel them afterwards, if I was not interested anyway.
academics_comments: I find the approach to the teaching in classes very different from what I have been used to, which has been interesting and inspiring, and has as well increased my rate of the overall study abroad experience, which I also found of a lower academic level than what I have been used to at my home university.
course_level: I found the level or the formalities and requirements less academicly strict, which overall gave an impression of a lower academic level
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was more in touch with the students in a way of including or depending on their presence.
courses_enrolled: Czech Modern & Contemporary Art & Architecture. Game Theory. Politics, Culture & Visuality: Czech and Slovak Film 1950 - 2000.
recommended_courses: I found all three courses very inspiring and educational from my points of interests. At the same time, specifically the czech film course and the czech art & architecture class, both had a broad focus on czech history, which I appreciated alot. I also very much recommend to attend the pre-term introduction language course, if it is available! It was a key decision for my stay an introduction to people, the culture and the city in overall.
unexpected_costs: I don't think I encountered unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: The public transport was very cheap and cheaper than expected. The generel living expenses are very cheap compared to danish costs.
activities_available: I have heard of different sports activities such as hikes and ball-sports. Many tours round the city were arranged by the esn association, as well as pubcrawl, quizzes etc.
activities_recommended: I would recommend attending the social activites arranged, if they are of interest, as it is a fine opportunity to meet other excange student at an early point. I would though also not feel pressure to attend, if not feeling like it at first. There are plenty of opportunities to meet people during the stay.
weekend_recommendations: personally I have prioritized to spend ad much time in the city, which I exchanged to, and the outskirts of it, as I wanted to realy get to know the town that I was living in. I also enjoyed a few travels out of town, but mainyl stayed in the town and used alld ifferent sites, and cultural facilities that was always tending new events in th weekends.
culture_adjustment: I found it easier than expected, as I found some suprising similarities to danish culture and behavoral aspects. at the same time I found it of great help to have attended the pre-term intensive language course - a key element to adjust to the local culture for me.
cultural_challenges: I think a difference not big but present would be regarding behaviour in public space and a certain sense of a specific politeness or rudeness, which I take notice of to be able to adjust to.
culture_appreciated: Overall I found the atmosphere of the city safe and relaxed. Of cultural experiences I appreciated the film and arts alot, there are many incredible museums and kinos to attend and visit!
top3_advice: In the proces of registration I found it usefull to keep a 'diary' with all changes/deadlines/accomplishments, to keep an overall overview of te process. In the proces choosing courses I recommend to register for and attend more courses than needed, and then to unregister from some of them again - to take use of the possibility to try courses before settling for good. I also recommend to live central enough to be able to travel by feet at least to some extend.
other_useful_info: The workload varies alot from course to course. Maybe that is a good thing to ave in mind when putting together a scheme of courses.
most_rewarding: As this was my first experience of staying abroad for a longer period of time, to me this part is definitely the most rewarding of my exchange experience.
greatest_challenge: On a practical level I think it was a challenge to settled on my final scheme as the registration system and procedure was entagling and long.
other_comments: I deeply recommend attending the pre-term language course, if it is offered.

crucial_aspects: Different architecture and nature.
info_ease: Relatively easy if you read the emails and website carefully.
arrival_assistance: Not much except the student tutors.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There's a list provided on the uni website with available ersamus courses for each faculty - however, when you go to the registration system, SIS, some look a bit different and some are just not available. It was difficult to make a realistic schedule since each course was 1-5 points which means you need a lot of courses to reach 30.
registration_help: The lady at the erasmus office was nice, but mostly advised me to write to the teachers for each course if I had questions or wasn't sure whether or not I could enroll.
registration_success: Somewhat. I didn't get half the courses I initially had approved from home since they had reached capacity, were cancelled or not available in english. But the ones I got were still (mostly) relevant and interesting.
registration_advice: Get a lot of courses pre-approved - makes it so much easier to create a schedule where the lectures don't overlap.
course_level: Mostly MA since they were in english.
teaching_comparison: Soewhat the same. More rote learning though.
courses_enrolled: Landscape Changes and Society General Ecology Forest Geography Field exercises in Botany Field Course in Restoration Ecology Ecology in landscape and urban design Arachnology
recommended_courses: Forest Geography Field exercises in Botany Field Course in Restoration Ecology Ecology in landscape and urban design The excursion courses were really fun and rewarding. Forest Geography gave a broader sense of climate and ecosystems than I had before.
unexpected_costs: You had to pay for excursions, which is not mentioned until well into the semester. Going out almost always came with expences.
cost_comparison: Housing and groceries more expensive, eating out cheaper.
activities_available: Loads of trips to other cities and countries. Pub crawls and quizzes
activities_recommended: The trips outside Prague were fun and cheap.
weekend_recommendations: Get out of Prague and see the countryside and forests. Hiking and cycling.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy, since it's pretty similar.
socializing_tips: It doesn't necessarily come naturally, so you have to actively try.
cultural_challenges: You had to be overly polite to elderly people in order to avoid getting slagged off. Had a guy ~70 repeatedly bump his supermarket cart into me in the queue since I apparantly wasn't moving fast enough. Also there's a tendency amongst the elderly part of the population the be a bit xenophobic :(
culture_appreciated: Sense of heritage. Lots of beautiful churches, streets and castles.
top3_advice: Take advantage of the cheap transport. Stay away from Duplex Go on field trips
other_useful_info: Some teachers don't have high expectations when it comes to exchange students, but some do, and it IS possible to fail an exam. (Especially since usually only the teacher is present at exams)
most_rewarding: Meeting loads of new people and seeing my studies from a different perspective.
greatest_challenge: Budgetting and keeping up with social stuff while actually studying.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial for me to an exchange in central europe, to explre the culture
info_ease: Compared to other faculties we did not get a lot of information at the science faculty before the introduction day, but after that things went smoothly.
arrival_assistance: on the social part we were invited to a bigger erasmus whatsapp group with loads of events. Study wise we got the information we had been waiting on, on the day of introduction.
arrival_comments: it was not always easy figure out the system, but luckily the coordinators were super nice and helpfull.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: we had an introduction day where everything was taken care of, but we did not get any information up until then.
registration_help: the coordinators were very helpfull, either in person or via mail.
registration_success: very. most of the classes was very easy to get into.
registration_advice: show up on the dates you have been told, and they will take care of you.
course_level: I had a lot of elective courses, and there was a large catalogue which i could choose from, both MA and BA courses were available.
teaching_comparison: At UCPH i spent a lot of time on campus, where as in Prague i only spent 1-2 hours a day and the rest we had to read from home.
courses_enrolled: - Landscape changes and society - General ecology - Ecology in landscape and urban design - Introduction to plant systematics, evolution and ecology - Forest geography
recommended_courses: - General ecology - Ecology in landscape and urban design - Introduction to plant systematics, evolution and ecology - Forest geography
unexpected_costs: you wanna explore the country while you are there which includes a lot of travel which can be a bit expensive
cost_comparison: especially going out to eat were very affordable, prices in supermarkets were a bit cheaper than in Copenhagen but more or less the same. In general Prague was a fairly cheap city.
activities_available: erasmus club arranged plenty of social events and trips, there were several sports programs at the university also but the spots were mostly taken by czech students.
activities_recommended: definitely going on weekend trips around the czech republic was very nice.
weekend_recommendations: Czech Republic has a lot of cozy small citys that are easily accessible from Pragaue. other than that there is some really nice national parks for instance Krokonose, and bohemian schwitzerland.

Some other students took the czech language course, were they got an understanding of the culture and met some nice people, i think would do that i if i had the chance.
socializing_tips: most of the classes you have are with other exchange students, but there are several of social event on the school with the local students during the stay which you can partake in.
cultural_challenges: wasent that huge differences.
culture_appreciated: first of all Prague is a very beautiful city with incredible architecture. other than that there was always markets to visit, and in general a lot of things going on in the streets.
top3_advice: Take advantage of the many social events that are being organized, its a very good place to meet new people. Go on trips around the Czech Republic and neighbor countrys. remember to go out and eat, the czech food is not that bad and really cheap.
other_useful_info: the youtube channel honest guides makes great videos on what to see in prague.
most_rewarding: Meeting people form all around europe
greatest_challenge: learning Czech words....

crucial_aspects: Many different things - the university and the classes that were available, but also the social life of the faculty.
info_ease: Yes very.
arrival_assistance: None needed.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Registration through SIS (online portal) and then going to the erasmus office afterwards to get them approved. I had no issues, but I know other people who struggled a bit...
registration_help: Erasmus office open twice a week, could also email them. Also student organization for Science Faculty at Charles could help I think.
registration_success: Succesful
registration_advice: You have a couple weeks to try out the classes you're interested in - sign up for more classes, try them out and then drop them if you want. Sometimes the workload and ETCS does not make sense... But mostly it is fine!
course_level: Some MA and some BA, a good mix. No problems following along.
teaching_comparison: Less participation, less work during the classes in general. Often you sit down and listen (or not). But I had some really passionate and good professors!
courses_enrolled: Environmental Informatics, Human Geography Research of Czechia II, Selected Chapters from Physical Geography and Geoecology, Quaternary Palaeoenvironments, Ice Sheets and Glaciers in the Warming World, Natural Hazards and Risks, R and Python in Geosciences.
recommended_courses: If you want an exchange, where the focus is not too academically challenging, so you can engage in other aspects of the exchange: - Environmental Informatics - Ice Sheets and Glaciers in the Warming World - Selected Chapters from Physical Geography and Geoecology If you want something with a more challenging exam and more coursework: - Natural Hazards and Risks (some people said the exam was the most challenging one they had had at Charles) - R and Python in Geosciences (more coursework, but easy if you're ok with coding)
unexpected_costs: - I don't think I experienced any
cost_comparison: - Eating out and going out is cheap. - Public transportation is VERY cheap. 100kr for 3 months... - Food in the grocery stores is cheaper - but some prices are similar (eggs, meat etc.) - If you want to find an apartment or room be prepared to spend money. You can be lucky, but some people end up spending 4000.00kr for a room in a shared apartmet... Also beware of scams!
activities_available: Erasmus club hosted events all the time. Easter events, quiz nights... you name it!
activities_recommended: Join karaoke, and the cultural events! Try to go to as many as you have the energy for at the start of the semester. :-)
weekend_recommendations: Go travel in surrounding countries with people from uni
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: I didn't do much of that

crucial_aspects: I chose my study destination because I believed the strong collaboration between the University of Copenhagen and Charles University would make the process easy (which turned out not to be the case). I also considered the possibility of getting my courses approved, but this proved to be more complicated than expected. Additionally, I wanted to travel sustainably, and the location in Europe was important since I was taking courses on the EU. Lastly, the short distance from Copenhagen meant that friends, my partner, and family could visit easily.
info_ease: Charles University in Prague provided the necessary information efficiently, making it easy to find what I needed upon arrival. In contrast, the University of Copenhagen was very difficult to get in touch with and collaborate with, which made the process more challenging.
arrival_assistance: Charles University organized a well-structured introduction week with numerous information meetings, which were very helpful. The support upon arrival was well-planned and made the transition much easier

registration_advice: My advice to future exchange students is to discuss with KU what to do if courses are not offered. Ultimately, it’s the student who is left in a difficult position if they haven’t had their courses approved before departure. In the long run, the current process from KU is unsustainable, and the collaboration between KU and Charles University isn’t working well
course_level: Overall, the level of courses was lower compared to KU, except for my elective courses (which were at the Master's level). These courses were more challenging, but most others did not meet the academic level I expected.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at my host institution was different from UCPH. The classes were smaller, and the professors/lecturers were generally less experienced. registration_process: You have to sign up at very specific times. The Czech students have priority for the courses, so there's a good chance you don't get a spot where you want. Then you can sign up for a waiting list (everyone were on waiting lists), and you might get a spot. You have two weeks or so, to try out the courses (you can attend more than you plan on following) and then you have to decide which to follow. This is a very useful way of choosing, since the course descriptions rarely reflect the teaching methods, level, expectations etc.
registration_help: You could always write or call the coordinator
registration_success: I got what I thought I wanted - turned out the courses were not as well-taught as I expected in some cases.
registration_advice: Register for a lot of courses that you might think are interesting, and attend the first lecture(s) before deciding what to follow.
course_level: The level can be divided into two categories; teaching and expectations. The quality of the teaching was rarely up to the standard that KU students will be used to, but luckily the level of expectations is generally not either.
teaching_comparison: Not a lot of exercises or group work. There is a lot more hierarchy between students and lecturers. In two of my courses, they tried to cover a completely unreasonable amount of topics, leading to very superficial knowledge of each topic, and they rarely made it through all of the prepared material, before the lecture was over.

overall_comments: My exchange was characterised by ups-and-downs, which I think is common, but I must admit that I have felt uneasy most of the time due to personal as well as cultural issues. As regards the personal factors, it is important to feel good with yourself before departure, i.e. be in a good mental state, and you have to come to terms with the fact that exchange can be quite lonely and depressing - especially if you have a hard time socialising, like I did. For the cultural issues, I felt that Czech people in general were a bit rude and some even unfriendly, but this does of course not apply to everyone; some people were very nice (especially the staff at Charles University that was very helpful).
info_ease: Very easy. Charles University has multiple webpages with everything you need to know, e.g. concerning registration at the Foreign Police, accommodation, selection of courses, where to study, what to do in Prague and beyond, etc. Besides, the University has a YouTube playlist with informations, including recorded Zoom-meetings from previous years, and they also held an online pre-arrival meeting, which I can definitely recommend to join, with informations on many valuable things such as getting your student card, how to register for courses, etc.
arrival_assistance: During the first day of the intro-week (orientation day), there was a presentation with things to remember doing, and they also shared information on student counseling, etc. Moreover, there was the above-mentioned Zoom-meeting. The International Office also continuously sent emails with valuable information.
arrival_comments: The International Office was very helpful, so do not hesitate to contact them if you have any (even small) inquiries, and they definitely will make you feel welcome.

registration_process: Course registration started on 6 February and ended on 23 February. This was the regular course registration, where you logged in to the intranet and registered. When you have to register for courses, the easiest way is to have the course codes ready and then copy/paste them into the system. Then you register for the courses you want, but you might not get all courses in the first instance, as there most likely will be a waiting list. I was quite surprised to find that I only succeeded to register for about 4-5 courses, and then the rest was on the waiting list, but I got some after an hour, and some a few weeks after - so do not worry. From 24 February to 2 March, only the teacher could register or deregister you from their course. From 3 to 28 March (add/drop period), if you wanted to drop a course, you could only do so by getting the teacher to sign a request form with the condition being that you have not followed the course or delivered any paperwork. From 29 March, no further changes could be made. For registration at other faculties than Social Sciences, you must be aware that other dates might apply. Check their academic calendars on their websites.
registration_help: The International Office held a Zoom-meeting on the day the registration opened, as I can recall, or maybe a few days after. They also sent a detailed registration guide to the students and informed us about course registration in a pre-arrival Zoom-meeting.
registration_success: I succeeded in getting 7 out of the 7 courses, I originally intended to take. However, I was on the waiting list for multiple of them, and I ended up switching one of the courses with another that I found more interesting.
registration_advice: Even though you might be on a high placing on the waiting list, you can always contact the course coordinator in person or via email to inquire about the possibility of getting accepted to a specific course. I managed to get accepted to a course, where I was number 10 on the waiting list, so it can definitely pay off to write them an email with your motivations for choosing the course. However, if you do not succeed in getting a specific course, look for alternatives. See the videos on course registration in the International Office's YouTube playlist and participate in the Zoom-meetings. Inform yourself about the dates for course registration at other faculties, if you intend on taking courses there.
academics_comments: My exchange was characterised by ups-and-downs, which I think is common, but I must admit that I have felt uneasy most of the time due to personal as well as cultural issues. As regards the personal factors, it is important to feel good with yourself before departure, i.e. be in a good mental state, and you have to come to terms with the fact that exchange can be quite lonely and depressing - especially if you have a hard time socialising, like I did. For the cultural issues, I felt that Czech people in general were a bit rude and some even unfriendly, but this does of course not apply to everyone; some people were very nice (especially the staff at Charles University that was very helpful).
course_level: The level of the courses really varies. Some feel like a high school class, whereas others are more demanding. For instance, some courses have quite a heavy workload, whereas others have no readings or assignments. In general, however, I will definitely say that the course level is lower than UCPH, but not bad. Besides, academic challenges comes in many forms. Whereas the academic level is not that high, courses can be demanding in other ways. For instance, I had a couple courses with student presentations, simulation exercises for the final exam, continuous written assignments, and some seminar with obligatory participation. In that sense, the teaching form is quite alike to what you might be used to in high school, but if you want to get to know other teaching forms than what UCPH is offering, Charles University will definitely be for you.
teaching_comparison: See above. Also, the most evident difference is that you are used to read during the semester at UCPH and then write an exam at the end of the semester. At Charles University, there are of course readings, but there might also be written assignments during the semester and presentations, and some courses end with an oral simulation rather than a written exam. In some courses, you are also obliged to actively participate in discussions to get the necessary points. At UCPH, courses usually ends with a 3 day take home exam or a 10-hour exam, etc., but I do not believe Charles University has any of those. Instead, in some courses you have to submit a final paper with a topic of your choice before a certain deadline, but theoretically, you can begin writing the paper whenever you like, i.e. there are for example not three days or 10 hours assigned for you to sit down and write an exam.
courses_enrolled: - History of Human Rights in International Relations (MA) - EU negotiation (MA) - Russian-Turkish Rivalry over the Balkan and Caucasus Areas (MA) - Interinstitutional Relations: European vs. Domestic Institutions (EU) (MA) - NGOs in International Relations (II) (MA) - Introduction to Animal Studies (BA) - Geopolitics of the Climate Crisis (MA)
recommended_courses: In general, all the courses were good, but these are the courses, I would definitely recommend: - Interinstitutional Relations: European vs. Domestic Institutions (EU): It gave a very interesting perspective on EU politics, focusing on dynamics between key institutions of the EU as well as between institutions of the Member States of the EU and the EU institutions, e.g. between national parliaments and the EU - Geopolitics of the Climate Crisis: It is developed by a team of climate experts within specific fields, who are also teaching the course, which I found interesting. Besides, the course ends with a simulation; I for instance participated in a COP30 negotiation, which was very fun. You also get to write a policy brief during the semester on a topic of your interest (within the course topics) and do a peer-review of another student's policy brief.
unexpected_costs: Nothing.
cost_comparison: - Food is cheaper than Denmark, but meat is more expensive. So if you plan on becoming a vegetarian/vegan, head to Prague. - It is really cheap to go to restaurants – even Michelin. - Transport is really cheap and operates smoothly. For 5 months, I only paid 186 DKK (620 CZK).
activities_available: There was a two-week intro programme, which was both packed with social and academic events. There were also some sports events during the semester, cultural evenings, and parties. Take part in whatever you like and do not feel pressured if it feels a bit overwhelming.
activities_recommended: I would recommend taking part in some of the activities during the intro programme to challenge yourself.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend experiencing Prague. There is a lot of beautiful architecture, and the old city is very interesting. There are also some parks worth visiting such as Riegrovy Sady. I also recommend going to Divorka Sarka, outside the city centre – it is a very beautiful nature park. There are also many museums in Prague, e.g. the National Museum, which is definitely worth visiting. You can also try Czech pastries such as the Kolac. I did not have the time to go to other places in or outside Czechia, which I had expected to, because the workload was quite intensive, although it obviously depends on your level of ambition. However, I intended to visit Karlovy Vary during the intro weeks with the student network, who arranges very cheap trips to cities and places in Czechia in the weekends. Unfortunately, I caught a cold, but I would definitely recommend going to one or several of these trips.
culture_adjustment: It was more difficult than I thought. Obviously, there is the language difference, and people are quite different from Denmark. However, I felt that it got better, as time went by.
socializing_tips: Take part in the intro week – and (a bit of a cliche) remember that you are all on the same page. Learn some basic Czech, if you want.
cultural_challenges: The language and people’s general behaviour.
culture_appreciated: Nothing.
top3_advice: 1) Prepare in good time before the course registration and sit ready when the course registration opens. If there is a course you prefer above everything else, register for that specific course first to decrease the risk of getting on the waiting list. 2) Choose courses at other faculties than the one you are affiliated to, to get some variation. I had courses at the Faculty of Humanities and Faculty of Arts, even though I was affiliated to the Faculty of Social Sciences. 3) Challenge yourself by choosing courses with different styles of teaching. For instance, I was a bit sceptical choosing courses with (oral) simulations as part of the final grade, where you for instance have to negotiate e.g. on behalf a country in the COPs, as I had never done anything similar at UCPH. But I found it very valuable and fun.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: - Getting to know a different learning culture and being in an international environment, and getting to know yourself better and become more independent and robust. I would also say that another rewarding thing is that you learn to really appreciate your life in Denmark.
greatest_challenge: - Being away from home and leaving the things you care about/your everyday life behind. For me it was very hard coming to terms with the fact that I could not just visit my family every now and then, but keeping in touch and reminding yourself that it is ”only” 4,5-5 months you are away, definitely helps. I guess that for people having already been on longer travels in their gap year etc., it is no problem – but I had never been away from my family for more than a month, and I am a bit of a comfort addict. - Adapting to a new city and settling in was also difficult for me, especially when you are not familiar with the culture, have never been to the country/city before, etc.
other_comments: Apply for scholarships.

crucial_aspects: Career opportunities, cultural exchange, and the opportunity to meet new people and build meaningful friendships were central to my choice of study destination. I was motivated by the possibility of gaining international experience that could strengthen my academic profile and future career prospects, while also immersing myself in a different cultural environment. Experiencing everyday life in another country, learning from new perspectives, and expanding my social network were all important factors in making the decision.
overall_comments: I found it difficult to make friends, especially with the Czech students, which made it harder to feel fully integrated into the social environment. I was also somewhat disappointed by the lack of structure and formality at Charles. Courses and activities were largely planned individually by professors, and there seemed to be limited coordination or oversight from the institution. In some cases, this created situations where student well-being and safety did not feel sufficiently considered or supported.

The emails we received from the Erasmus programme and Charles University were clear and helpful, and they provided the practical details necessary to get started. This made the transition smoother and gave a good overview of what to expect in the first weeks.
arrival_assistance: There was very limited assistance upon arrival. Most of the practical aspects had to be handled independently, and there was little direct support or guidance on site beyond the information provided beforehand.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_process: The registration process was stressful and somewhat chaotic. It followed a “first come, first served” system, which meant there was no guarantee of getting the courses you needed. This created a lot of pressure and uncertainty. I also had to take responsibility for securing some mandatory courses myself, which made the process more demanding and time-sensitive.
registration_help: The available help was quite limited. There was some general information provided, but practical guidance and direct support during the process were not very strong, which made it harder to navigate things when challenges came up, only the Erasmus office was helpfull.
registration_success: I was ultimately successful in registering for the classes I wanted, but it required a lot of effort. I was somewhat lucky, and I had to write several emails and actively request to be registered in certain courses before it finally worked out.
registration_advice: Be prepared that you may not get all the courses you initially want, as registration can be competitive and somewhat uncertain. It is important to act quickly, stay flexible, and communicate proactively with professors and coordinators if issues arise. Also be aware that professors have a great deal of autonomy, both in course planning and grading, and there is typically no external examiner involved. This makes it especially important to understand course requirements clearly and maintain good communication throughout the semester.

course_level: Overall, I found the academic level of the courses to be relatively low compared to what I am used to at the University of Copenhagen. The expectations, workload, and depth of the material were not as demanding as I had anticipated, and I was not particularly impressed from an academic standpoint.
teaching_comparison: Compared to UCPH, the teaching style felt much more unstructured in many courses. The organization and expectations often depended heavily on the individual professor, which led to a very uneven experience across classes. There was also considerable variation in English proficiency, which sometimes made communication and learning less consistent.

recommended_courses: I would recommend the International Trade course, primarily because the professor was highly engaged and delivered well-structured, well-prepared lectures. Compared to many of the other courses, the organization was clearer, expectations were communicated more transparently, and the overall teaching quality was noticeably stronger. The course also created a better learning environment, where it was easier to stay motivated and follow the material. Discussions were more focused, and the professor made an effort to explain concepts in a way that was accessible to international students. Overall, it stood out as one of the few courses where the academic experience felt consistent and rewarding.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any significant unexpected costs. Most expenses were predictable and in line with what I had planned for before arriving, so there were no major financial surprises during the stay.
cost_comparison: Most everyday expenses were cheaper than I expected compared to Copenhagen. Food, transport, and general living costs were noticeably lower, which made day-to-day life more affordable. The main exception was gyms, which were not significantly cheaper and in some cases were closer to Copenhagen price levels than I had anticipated.
activities_available: They were very limited and not strongly organized by the university. There were few structured cultural, athletic, or social activities specifically aimed at exchange students, so most initiatives had to be found independently,
activities_recommended: I would not recommend relying on university-organized activities. Instead, it is better to look for opportunities in the city on your own, such as local events, gyms, language cafés, or social groups, as these are easier to access and often more engaging.
weekend_recommendations: Take advantage of the city’s cultural life. Explore museums, historical sites, cafés, and local neighborhoods, and travel within the country or nearby regions. The cultural environment outside the university is one of the strongest aspects of the experience.
culture_adjustment: It was quite difficult to adjust at first. I did not find it easy to connect with local Czech students, and I rarely experienced that they were very open or talkative toward exchange students. This made it harder to feel integrated into everyday student life and to build local connections, especially in the beginning.
socializing_tips: I unfortunately did not have much success with this myself, as many local students tended to stay within their existing social circles. My advice would be to be proactive early on join group work, attend smaller classes, and take initiative in conversations. It may require more effort than expected, and integration does not always happen naturally.
cultural_challenges: One of the main challenges was the social distance between local and international students, as well as a more reserved communication style. It sometimes felt difficult to read social situations and know when or how to engage, which made it harder to form connections and feel fully included.
culture_appreciated: I especially appreciated the city’s cultural life, history, and everyday atmosphere. Prague offers a rich cultural environment with museums, architecture, cafés, and public spaces that make it an inspiring place to live. Even if social integration at the university was challenging, the broader cultural experience of living in the city was very rewarding.
top3_advice: 1. Be proactive with course registration and communication with professors, as the process can be uncertain and requires initiative. 2. Do not expect the same academic structure and level as at UCPH; much depends on the individual professor. 3. Focus on the cultural and personal experience of living abroad, as this may be more rewarding than the academic part.
other_useful_info: It is important to be independent and flexible. Many practical matters, from housing to course selection and daily life, require personal initiative. Starting preparations early and not relying too heavily on institutional support can make the experience smoother.
most_rewarding: Living in a new city and experiencing a different culture on a daily basis was the most rewarding part. Exploring Prague, meeting other international students, and gaining a broader perspective beyond my home university made the stay valuable despite some academic and social challenges.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge was the lack of structure academically and the difficulty of integrating socially with local students. crucial_aspects: The choice was guided by how well the destination aligned with my Political Science programme, ensuring that I could take relevant courses and receive credit transfer. Access to a grant was also an important factor in making the exchange financially sustainable. I was also motivated by the opportunity to experience a different cultural context then westeren Europe while still being based in the continent. Prague offered a balance between familiarity and newness, and its central location made it easy and affordable to travel across Europe , which I saw as an important part of the exchange experience.
info_ease: It was quite easy to find the information I needed. The university had very helpful advisors, and they organised several information sessions both before and after arrival. It felt like there was always someone to ask, and the process was clearly explained, which made settling in much easier.
arrival_assistance: I received support both online and in person. Before arriving, there was clear communication and guidance through online platforms, and once I got there, the university offered in person assistance through advisors and introduction sessions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process took place online at a specific time, where all students signed up for courses at the same time. This made it quite competitive, so it was important to be ready when registration opened. I would strongly recommend having a clear plan in advance, including backup options, so you know exactly which courses to choose. If you are not prepared, you risk not getting the courses you need for credit transfer at your home university.
registration_help: There was support available through student counselling, where you could get guidance on course selection and administrative questions. It was also possible to speak directly with professors during their seminars. If a course was full, some professors were open to letting additional students join if you asked in person.
registration_success: It took some time and a bit of flexibility, but in the end I was able to register for all the courses I needed.
registration_advice: Have a clear plan for your courses in advance, especially if your home university requires specific courses for credit transfer. It is not something you can figure out on the spot during registration, so preparation really matters. It is also a good idea to work in teams with other students in the same situation. Also, don't lose hope. If you take it seriously, you will figure it out in the end <3
course_level: The overall level of the courses felt manageable and in many ways less demanding than at my home university. The main challenge was not the academic level itself, but adapting to a different teaching style. There was a stronger emphasis on presentations and continuous participation, and the structure of courses and how literature was approached felt quite different. It also takes some time to adjust to studying and presenting in English, but there was definitely room to make mistakes and learn along the way, which made the transition easier.
teaching_comparison: Attendance was taken, and classes were smaller, which meant that participation was more visible. This also created a stronger sense that the professor was assessing you more individually, both in terms of engagement and performance throughout the course.
courses_enrolled: Democracy – Current Challenges and Innovations (5 ECTS) EU Comparative Politics: Tensions in Representative Democracy (6 ECTS) Introduction to History, Politics and Society of Russia and Eastern Europe (6 ECTS) Current Central Asia: Building Autocracy for the 21st Century (6 ECTS) Party Democracy in the EU: Crisis and Consequences (6 ECTS) EU in Practice (6 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I would recommend Democracy - Current Challenges and Innovations (5 ECTS). The course was very accessible and engaging.
unexpected_costs: Prague is generally affordable, which was great as it made it possible to eat out more often and travel around. One thing I did not expect was related to rent. My landlord required payment for the full final month, even though I only stayed for half of it. In Copenhagen it is often possible to pay only for the time you actually stay, but that was not the case here. I would recommend clarifying this in advance.
cost_comparison: Rent was more expensive than I expected, especially compared to other living costs in the city. On the other hand, things like alcohol, food, and public transport were very affordable, which made everyday life and social activities much cheaper overall.
activities_available: I did not personally take part in the Erasmus activities, but there were many options available for students. These included sports, social events and parties, organised trips, language courses, and different ways to explore the city. It seemed like there were plenty of opportunities to meet other students and get involved if you wanted to.
activities_recommended: I would strongly recommend taking the time to travel outside of Prague. The Czech Republic is incredibly beautiful and has many interesting destinations that are easy to reach, which adds a lot to the overall experience. I would also recommend exploring the cultural life in Prague itself. The city has a rich cultural scene, with history, architecture, and local traditions that are worth engaging with beyond the university.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend exploring beyond Prague, especially smaller cities, cabins, and nature areas. There are many unique places that are easy to reach and really worth seeing. At the same time, Prague itself has a very lively weekend atmosphere, with lots of great bars and a strong nightlife. Thrift shops are also surprisingly good and very cheap, with many unique finds. I would also recommend visiting the local farmers markets by the river, where you can eat well and find vintage items at very reasonable prices.
culture_adjustment: It was not always easy to build close connections with locals. However, I would strongly recommend being open to meeting people from other cultures. For me, that was a key part of having a rich exchange experience.
cultural_challenges: You can still sense the historical legacy of communism in certain everyday interactions. For example, there is generally less of a service oriented mindset, and some older people do not speak English, which can make simple situations a bit more challenging. Compared to Denmark, where friendliness towards strangers is more common, interactions can sometimes feel more distant. However, you quickly learn not to take it personally.
culture_appreciated: I especially appreciated the openness and friendliness among young people. They were genuinely kind and curious, and interactions felt relaxed and welcoming. Rather than any sense of attitude, there was a clear openness that made it easy to connect and have nice conversations.
top3_advice: Be prepared to deal with a fair amount of bureaucracy, both with UCPH and Charles University. It is manageable, but it requires lots of patience and staying on top of administrative details. Take time to really explore Prague. It is a beautiful city with a lot to offer, and some of the best experiences come from walking around and discovering it at your own pace. Finally, try not to fill your entire exchange with visits from home. It is great to share the experience with others, but it can take up a lot of time and energy. Giving yourself space to settle in and explore on your own makes the experience much more meaningful.
other_useful_info: ake the time to reflect on what this experience means to you. An exchange is something you give yourself, and there is no single right way to do it. There are many paths you can follow and it is easy to just go along with what everyone else is doing, but it is worth being a bit intentional. Be open, but also make your own choices in a way that supports your personal growth beyond the academic and social part.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was realizing that I can build a life for myself in a different country. I learned that I am able to create something for myself even without my usual network around me. At the same time, the experience gave me a new appreciation for Copenhagen. Being away made me more aware of what I value at home and helped me see my everyday life from a new perspective.
greatest_challenge: Missing home

crucial_aspects: In Europe, but still a different (academic) culture compared to Denmark.
info_ease: There is a lot of information, but it was doable. Some things just first make sense when you have arrived, so with some aspects it is just 'trust the process'.
arrival_assistance: The orientation day at the host university was helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: they have a very confusing system. It is not possible to see schedules for courses before the semester starts, so even though you try to plan what courses you want, you can end up re-doing it. The course registration can also be a bit confusing and they have like a 'trial' period, so you can try out courses before you decide - it can be both beneficial, but also confusing.
registration_help: They have an Erasmus office that can help, but they are only open a couple of hours a week, and in the beginning many students need help. The Czech students that helps Erasmus students are very helpful.
registration_success: I ended up registering for ca. 50-60% of the courses I originally planned for. Either because they didn't fit to my schedule or just because I found others interesting.
registration_advice: Just have in mind that it can be a slow, analogue and sometimes a bit frustrating/confusing process. People are there to help. Also a lot of the offered courses are quite low number of ECTS-points, so it can be a puzzle to make a decent schedule at the same time as reaching the 30 ECTS-points for a semester. My advice it to take as many courses with high numbers of ECTS-points, so you in total have as few courses as possible. Many courses are doable during the semester, but the exam period is quite harsh with 6-7 exams in a few weeks (as I had).
course_level: same level as at UCPH
teaching_comparison: Some courses really similar to UCPH, some not. Also there is quite a difference in the level of english by the professors - some more understandable than others, but you get used to it.
courses_enrolled: 1. Environmental issues, background examples and solutions 2. Exploring contemporary migration trends: Diasporas, Refugees and Environmental migration 3. Flood Risk Management 4. Fundamentals of Demography 5. High-impact Weather Phenomena 6. Hot topic of environmental sciences 7. Introduction to Polar Ecology
recommended_courses: 1. and 7. were a lot more biology than I expected, so if you are not ready for that, I would say it is doable, but quite hard. 6. is a really nice course. It is about how nature is valued, and give different perspectives on it. It is a small intimate course, where debate and talk is a part of it. Really good and nice teacher. 4. is a pure demography course. It can be a bit tough, but it is really in the depth with a topic not really covered at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: none
cost_comparison: Quite cheap to live. Our accommodation was quite expensive (we learned after getting to know other people that payed a lot less)
activities_available: The erasmus club does a lot of activities
activities_recommended: Did not really engage in them, so can't recommend any, but there is definitely something for everybody
weekend_recommendations: do day trips, either on your own or with some of the orgnizations.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, I didn't engage a lot with local people, but the city is easy to find your way around in.
socializing_tips: No
cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: There are many restaurants with different cuisines and it is quite cheap to go out
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy the city, it is beautiful. especially outside the citycenter there are really nice areas to explore. It is a city you can easily walk around in and explore. 2. Dont get frustrated during the process, everything will work out. 3. Talk to people in your classes, you will get new friends.
most_rewarding: It is nice to experience the academic differences on another university and nice to meet people from other places. Everybody is there to have a good time, so engage in them.
greatest_challenge: The language barrier can be challenging, but you will get used to it.

crucial_aspects: I chose Hong Kong due to a combination of factors. First of all because of an interest in visiting a region affected by the crossing of cultures, and because of a wish to explore a very politically exciting area. In addition to this most people are either fluent or very good English speakers, so communication and getting around in the city is straightforward. The Chinese University of Hong Kong has a very good and broad choice of anthropology courses - my main major - which spoke a lot to me as well.
overall_comments: CUHK is an excellent university: with a good study environment, many social activities to attend, and a broad choice of courses. My experience was that the level of study was a bit lower than in Denmark, but as far as I hear from students on exchange in other countries, this is very common. The courses are still both interesting and they definitely broadened my anthropological knowledge.
info_ease: There was a lot of information regarding covid-19, which was a bit difficult to navigate. The information regarding registration at the University and related things were much easier. Their website is somewhat packed with information though, so it takes some time to get into all the details. I recommend pairing up with other students going to CUHK from Denmark if you can.
arrival_assistance: A lot. They a very good at making sure we have all the information we need. They communicate mostly through email, but at their office, they were always available for us if we had questions. They inform us a lot about the selection of courses. It is possible to rechoose courses upon arrival, and even to try out some courses during the first couple of weeks, to see if it is the right fit for you. Also, they arrange tours in the city, and a lot of information on the different options of activities on campus, what kinds of apps to have, have to get around in the metro, and so on.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: CUHK is an excellent university: with a good study environment, many social activities to attend, and a broad choice of courses. My experience was that the level of study was a bit lower than in Denmark, but as far as I hear from students on exchange in other countries, this is very common. The courses are still both interesting and they definitely broadened my anthropological knowledge.
registration_process: There are a lot of documents you need to fill out and send. This takes some time, and especially in this part of the process I recommend partnering up with other students from your own university/country going to the same place - it helps a lot to have to heads to not forget anything important. It's an ongoing process from around 6-8 months before you go, so be patient and ready to put time into the things before the deadlines.
registration_help: You can always contact the international office at CUHK, both by phone and mail (be aware of the time difference though).
registration_success: Very successful. Also, I put a lot of time into applying for the ones I wanted before I went to Hong Kong, only to realize that I was able to choose again when a arrived. So no stress about applying for the right/perfect classes before you go. (except if you want to take a mandarin or Cantonese course - then you need to apply in advance. They send you information on this option by email.).
registration_advice: Start in good time, don't hesitate to ask the university for help, and don't stress about choosing the right courses before you go. Also be aware that Mandarin and Cantonese classes take a lot of time and effort - which is fine if you enjoy language learning, but can also be a bit frustrating from time to time.
academics_comments: CUHK is an excellent university: with a good study environment, many social activities to attend, and a broad choice of courses. My experience was that the level of study was a bit lower than in Denmark, but as far as I hear from students on exchange in other countries, this is very common. The courses are still both interesting and they definitely broadened my anthropological knowledge.
course_level: The level is a bit lower than what I have experienced at the University of Copenhagen, and the expectations from the teachers are as well. But they are still very interesting and on the plus side it gives you a lot of surpluses to enjoy and dive into the lectures and topics.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was similar in the way that the courses were mainly built up around a lecture and then a smaller seminar to discuss the readings. A big difference is that all your attendance and work count as a part of your final grade, meaning that you have less freedom to study as it best suits you. Also I was used to having large but few courses, and at CUHK you have to have 5 courses when you are from UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Written and spoken putonghua (mandarin) (CLCP1113 and 1123) Anthropology of Body, Love, and Emotion (anthropology) Meanings of Life (anthropology) Understanding Masculinities and Social Change (gender studies)
recommended_courses: Anthropology of Body, Love, and Emotion together with Understanding Masculinities. The teachers are very good, sharp, and strong in their fields. They definitely have the heart in them, and they also demand something back from you, want to challenge you, and are open to being in dialogue. These are definitely the courses I learned the most from, and from which I attained knowledge that I use in my other studies afterward.
unexpected_costs: Only that I quickly spend a lot on food if I didn't buy kitchen supplies to cook myself.
cost_comparison: Transportation was extremely cheap. Drinks and alcohol on bars a very expensive! Drink before entering or go out on ladies' night if you are a woman.
activities_available: Everything from dancing, tennis, swimming, fitness, kayaking, and martial arts. The university also arranges a lot of cultural activities for students to learn more about the culture of Hong Kong (food, language, art...).
activities_recommended: Using the pool - it's very cheap and nice in the warm months. But hiking is a must-do in general! So many beautiful routes and a good way for socializing or just take a break alone and away from a life with a new and intense social and study life. Keep an eye on your email - they send out a lot of interesting offers.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking. Going to a meditation day at the big buddha in the plum-village temple (look it up online - it's mainly on Sundays). Take the boats from central to Peng Chau, Cheng Chau, and Lamma Islands! Especially during the warmer months. There is a good chill hippie vibe, and it's good if you need a break from the big city. Explore the city by walking around, or taking the tram to Hong Kong Island. Visit random cafés - especially Alley Coffee! They have the best light-roasted coffee. Go to a horse race at Happy Valley.
culture_adjustment: It was easy, mainly because most people speak good English. As long as you are open, friendly, and respect the culture people are extremely helpful, nice, and interested in speaking with you. But there also exists a certain shyness, so don't hesitate to contact and show interest in the culture and people yourself.
socializing_tips: Be open, show interest, and ask questions yourself! Then most people are very interested in getting to know you.
cultural_challenges: My experience was that people don't tell you directly if they feel like you have done something wrong or stepped over a line. This can be good to pay attention to since it is easier to accidentally cross some lines when you are two people from very different cultures staying together.
culture_appreciated: The openness, politeness, and how helpful people were.
top3_advice: Bring warm closeth for when the unexpected cold comes. Bring some nice stuff for your room to make it homely. Be open and make contact with local people yourself.
other_useful_info: I was surprised by the richness of nature! I didn't expect that from Hong Kong, but really it is basically a big city with so much to experience, and it is both easy and fast to get around.
most_rewarding: The fact of making a home in Hong Kong and getting to know the city as well as I did. To get local bars to go to, coffee places, and streets you know well. Just exploring all the different corners of the area. It's an amazing concrete jungle surrounded by mountains and with so much to offer.
greatest_challenge: Fomo in the beginning. To just remember to let myself take social breaks - and also study breaks. Give yourself time to adapt and do what you need to do - not always what you feel you should.

crucial_aspects: Academic connection, your ambition, social status
info_ease: Yes, the agent from university will give you a proper guide before your arrival. And you can always contact them if you have any questions.
arrival_assistance: Registration, campus tour, application for transportation card
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: For postgraduate students, your first step will be an online pre-selection, which usually starts before other degree students, but the number and range of options are very limited. It's hard to enroll in your favorite graduate course at this stage. After the official start of semester, they will enter add/drop week, and exchange students are not allowed to choose courses through the system during this stage. You are always required to submit your application directly to the course provider by email. You need to download the application form from the website yourself, edit it and send it to the appropriate department for approval. If approved, you will receive a stamped document. You will also need to submit it by yourself to the department responsible for exchange student affairs (i.e. OAL). The process of negotiating with the course provider is very cumbersome, and it is difficult to get any guarantees up front. You need to be patient at this stage. It is important to note that if you really want to register for a course, you must maintain attendance at this stage, even if you do not have formal registration permission. Many professors will not waive your absence just because you have not yet secured a place in the class.
registration_help: OAL is always available to help, including an in-person tutorial. They will know your pre-selected courses in advance and confirm their registration status. In addition, they will find out about other courses that you are not pre-selected for, but would like to try to register for during the add/drop week. They will tell you which college or department you need to apply to. However, the final decision is in the hands of the course provider, and OAL cannot provide any guarantee.
registration_success: Pre-selection stage: I applied for six courses and five of them have been registered successfully. Add/drop phase: I dropped four of the pre-selected courses. I applied for about 12 new courses and four of them have been registered successfully.
registration_advice: Quotas for postgraduate courses are always very limited, and they usually give priority to ensuring enrollment of degree students. Once you have confirmed that you want to register for a certain course, you should apply to the course provider as soon as possible. In many cases, course registration will be on first-come, first-served basis.
course_level: If you are a postgraduate students, you should only take the 5xxx or 6xxx courses in CUHK. KU's Academic Affairs department will review your courses list in pre-approval to see if it meets the requirements for a postgraduate program. If there are any questions, you should speak with KU's academic supervisor.
teaching_comparison: CUHK courses have a faster teaching pace and more course content. The number of Assignments is also much more than that of KU. In the Hong Kong teaching environment, the academic content will be more cutting-edge. During the course, you will experience more lectures, but the professor will provide fewer opportunities for discussion. You do more face-to-face discussions with professors after class.

recommended_courses: You can choose to take Cantonese courses, some of which do not require your credit. You can ask your academic supervisor in CUHK for details
unexpected_costs: Nothing.
cost_comparison: Nothing.
activities_available: OAL regularly hosts activities for exchange students, and they provide many opportunities for foreigners to learn about Hong Kong and Chinese culture. Sports activities rely on a number of sports associations, and students can actively send applications. There are also many unofficial organizations in exchange students' social media groups that regularly organize games.
activities_recommended: I would recommend exchange students to keep an eye on their email. All extra-curricular activities will be sent via email.
weekend_recommendations: During some traditional Chinese festivals, you can also try to explore some folk activities on your own, please always pay attention to the news and social media.
culture_adjustment: For me as Chinese people, it is easy for me to adjust to the local culture. English is not always worked in any place. Always get your translator prepared.
socializing_tips: You can choose to participate in the exchange activities offered by OAL or get in touch with foreign students who have previously studied at CUHK. Whatsapp and Wechat will be the main communication tools.
cultural_challenges: Hong Kong uses more cash or a transportation card they call Octopus, which you can use in almost any restaurant or mall. In some big shopping malls, credit cards or alipay/wechat pay will also work.
