crucial_aspects: Since I major in Asian Studies with a focus on Japan it was only logical to apply for a university in Japan. Seeing as I intend to write my thesis on Japanese working cultures I thought it would be relevant to look at law and policy studies to better incorporate these academic fields.
overall_comments: The biggest obstacle I faced and lesson I learned in academic terms was that courses offered for Graduate students were dismally few in number and exclusively law classes. The acronyms "SS" and "FS" do not, in fact, stand for "Spring Semester" and "Fall Semester" but instead "Second Semester" and "First Semester", their first semester commencing in spring. All courses I had intended to take were therefore not available to me.
info_ease: All information was available on their online intranet named manaba. It was therefore easily accessible and was complimented by an orientation meeting before class start. Additional information was made available at the dormitories, but seeing as I did not obtain a room I had to forgo that.
arrival_assistance: There were several things that needed to be done, such as registering at the local city hall as a resident, getting your taxes and insurance calculated and send, registering for courses, etc. As a student making self-arranged accommodations I had to figure out most of it myself. The orientation meeting and continued assistance from their international office was a big help though.
arrival_comments: The international office was helpful and skilled English speakers. The lack of assistance in terms of registering at city hall was my own responsibility as my accommodations were self-arranged and therefore needed to take place at the corresponding city hall.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The biggest obstacle I faced and lesson I learned in academic terms was that courses offered for Graduate students were dismally few in number and exclusively law classes. The acronyms "SS" and "FS" do not, in fact, stand for "Spring Semester" and "Fall Semester" but instead "Second Semester" and "First Semester", their first semester commencing in spring. All courses I had intended to take were therefore not available to me.
registration_process: Again, there is a stark difference between course selection and admittance procedure. The admittance procedure had 3-4 deadline clusters where various documents were required. It was a bit of a mess, whereas my own university forgot to notify me that I was nominated, so the first deadlines were uncomfortably close whilst it was too late for scholarship applications, hence my self-arrangement. Dormitory applications demanded that rent was paid in full for all 5 months in advance in cash, which I simply did not have. Course selection on the other hand was relaxed, albeit slow in updating. The syllabus provided was 2 years old with the relevant syllabus uploaded after the orientation meeting.
registration_help: The dormitories provided ample assistance with registering at city hall, tours of the area, etc. Or so I have been told. Besides that, there was the orientation meeting as well as continued assistance by the international office. They were very helpful and despite having a rule written on their online page stating that students were required to apply for consultation ahead of time, I sort of forgot that and simply turned up unannounced. They always helped and never told me of the rule so I only noticed several months in.
registration_success: Very unsuccessful. As mentioned, the syllabus that I had based my planning on was very different in course selection when it finally updated, the SS/FS acronym debacle destroyed my plans a second time with an even narrower course selection as several demanded that you attended from spring. In the end, due to having no prior knowledge in psychology and engineering, I had no choice in what courses to take to fulfill the ECTS requirements from home. Japanese language courses above a certain level demanded JLPT-certification to attend with all lower-standard classes remaining uncreditted for Graduate students. All language proficiency statements from my professors were therefore superfluous. I did attend Japanese classes as an audit student but all classes were in the mornings whilst my full courseload ensured my classes ran until 5PM most days. Admittedly, I did not have the energy to keep attending on top of my commute and other classes. Finally, all classes were legal classes aside from Public Administration with a professor with less attendance throughout the year than my personal "best". It was quite impressive, really.
registration_advice: If you are a BA-student then there are a plethora of courses to take within several fields of study. If you are a Graduate student without a JLPT-certificate, then the courses are indirectly selected for you. There simply are no additional options if you wish to meet ECTS demands from home. Two classes can be chosen between as they lie in the same time slot, but aside from that I hope that you want to study law.
academics_comments: The biggest obstacle I faced and lesson I learned in academic terms was that courses offered for Graduate students were dismally few in number and exclusively law classes. The acronyms "SS" and "FS" do not, in fact, stand for "Spring Semester" and "Fall Semester" but instead "Second Semester" and "First Semester", their first semester commencing in spring. All courses I had intended to take were therefore not available to me.
course_level: The level was high and competent but from a beginner's level so that students such as myself could follow.
teaching_comparison: The classes were mainly teacher-centered lectures with required readings provided on manaba and then discussed by the professor, typically with a case study in mind. Some classes aimed at student discussions, two actually had them. There were homework that required you turn in a very small essay or made a short presentation on a topic seen from your own country's perspective. Exams were manifold but pleasantly short compared to the length typically required at home.
courses_enrolled: -Legal Systems in Major Foreign Countries (although it says 'major countries' it was exclusively based on the American Supreme Court) -Japanese Law -Law and Society (This was mainly based on student discussions in comparing differing views on these keywords from the countries of origin) -Comparative Constitutional Law (Had several teachers, not all with understandable English but an interesting class nonetheless) -Contemporary Challenges in the Law of the Sea (interesting but difficult course) -Comparative Privacy and Data Protection Law (interesting class with a relaxed and humorous professor. Exam was integral to the classes and were therefore done before the exam period. Highly recommended to ease the exam period load. He also included segments in which he recommended places to go. He did not, however, know anything about technology). -Public Administration -Advanced Public Administration (PA was taught by the same professor. Advanced was necessitated by the fact that I did not have enough classes. I was the only participant in the latter and so she never convened a class. We had collectively 6 classes she did not cancel, she did not seem to want to be present and little to no information on exams were provided. I was ultimately told that a final paper for the advanced course were needed for a grade not the credit. As the deadline was simultaenous with the other course I elected to forgo writing it. I am now 2 credits short, to which I in no way harbor bitter feelings over)
recommended_courses: -Law and Society was heavily engaging for students with both exchange students and Japanese students attending. Discussions were the driving force where law and society were viewed from the standpoints of the nationalities represented in class. -Comparative Constitutional Law were taught by the Vice Principal as well as other teachers at other points of time. As I have a personal interest in Japan's Constitutional Law and was one of the few classes I had intended to study before arriving, I was quite satisfied with the course. The English skills of the teachers varied, however, but was interesting even so. -Comparative Data and Privacy Protection Law was relaxed in atmosphere, gave students free reign in choosing what they wanted to write about within the field, the exam was an essay and presentation which were written and presented throughout the course, freeing students for other exams. It also came with a cultural segment where the professor recommended places to visit. Contemporary Challenges in the Law of the Sea was an interesting topic that dealt with current disputes addressed through UNCLOS. It dealt with many regions throughout the world and discussed challenges which are broadly relevant for all. It was, however, probably the hardest course that I took.
unexpected_costs: -I lost my laptop in Shinjuku one month before exams started. Replacing it was expensive and unpleasant. I would advice anyone getting stuck mid-city with bulky belongings once trains stop running to make use of the coin lockers located at train stations. -I wanted to acquire currency at Copenhagen Airport before departure and chose a vendor there. They promised an updated exchange rate with a small handling fee. I ended up losing 1.500 dkkr in said "low fee." Advice: If they ask you to sign a waiver before processing the transaction you are likely being scammed. ATM's can be found in all 7-11's in Japan with actual low fees. -Japanese books ran for roughly 200dkkr pr. Had I not been an audit student it would have cost a pretty penny all books combined. -Transportation is not cheap when added up. "charge" at bars and restaurants is a fee for sitting down. A manga cafe I slept at offered a fix price for 3 hours which I agreed to and paid. They did not call the room when time was over and instead called me 5 hours later. The bill was considerately high and forgetting my cell phone resulted in an additional cost to retrieve.
cost_comparison: Alcohol and dining out is wonderfully cheap compared with Denmark. Giving you the bill after you are done, however, can get expensive if you are not careful. cell phones are cheaper and I would have bought one if not for losing my laptop. Coincidentally, laptops are not cheap.
activities_available: There were several clubs of a huge variety, although it is mostly written in Japanese for those that do not read it. There was a school festival and a student-arranged welcome party in Shibuya. The party cost 200dkkr to enter and apparently the drinks were 50dkkr after that. Advice: Buy a ticket for an all-you-can-drink-party in the vicinity and alternate between the two to make it worth the money. Again, keep in mind when the last train leaves.
activities_recommended: Drinking. Japanese alcohol prices are cheap and a good way of talking with locals that get (sometimes overly) enthusiastic about talking with a foreigner if you speak even elementary Japanese. Eating. Dining out is also cheap and of high quality. Specifically Mazesoba is highly recommended. Wandering/hiking. The scenery is beautiful with many mountains surrounding the city. Besides nature, going to a random train station and simply wander around can be interesting with unusual sights befitting the largest city in the world.
weekend_recommendations: I did not go that many places as I was chronically broke. Visit Shibuya for shopping, visit Shinjuku for serious drinking, visit Kamikitadai for drinking in close proximity to where you live. Check out Asakusa, and other than that. Look around. Too many places to see for anyone to cover it all.
culture_adjustment: Seeing as it was not my first trip to Japan it was easy enough. The trains stopping at midnight, however, gets me every time.
socializing_tips: Live at a dormitory and participate in clubs. Take a course with a mix of Japanese and exchange students. Seeing as I lived outside of dormitories and am over 30 years of age I was more interested in socializing with locals outside of school. When arriving, I recommend staying at a hostel for at least a few days. It is agreat way of meeting students from other universities as well as unafilliated Japanese citizens.
cultural_challenges: Trains stopping at midnight. The times I was caught in the city until morning were 10 too many. Also, smoking areas are strictly adhered to and typically located either inside in a booth or outside with an accompanied roof, which defeats the point of avoiding toxic fumes in my opinion. Japanese hesitance to say what they are thinking in combination with my own occasional failings at picking up on subtle social cues.
culture_appreciated: Drinking with random locals as well as friends I had made there. Mazesoba. Apparently it is a Taiwanese dish and not Japanese which is why it took me 4 months to locate as Japanese people do not know what it is. Still worth the wait. Clean streets and people not being unneccessarily loud. The polite and friendly attitudes in general. Convenience stores that truly have verything from ATM's, decent prices, chargers to rent for phones, actual chargers for sale, and just about everything else, etc.
top3_advice: Get a dormitory room. Get the full and instant insurance option for your plane ticket home. Check and double check train schedules with all transit points recalculated. If google maps believe that you can change trains in Shinjuku in 5 minutes, do not trust it. That station is neverending with an unproven connection to Narnia. -Bonus advice: Do not underestimate the power-level of 'strong zero'.
other_useful_info: If you are a Graduate student I sincerely hope you are deeply interested in law. Also, get a dormitory.
most_rewarding: Meeting new friends in places I did not expect. Realizing I lived within viewing distance of mt. Fuji when randomly looking to the horizon. Gaining a deeper understanding of Japanese law through my courses and the society outside of them. Also, and I can not stress this enough, Mazesoba.
greatest_challenge: Finding mazesoba. It was truly a long and arduous journey to find a place. Also, losing my laptop and having to replace it whilst surviving on SU. Finally, having my plane ticket home cancelled on me by the airline still no refund in sight. Writing 6 exams in two weeks.
other_comments: Crime in Japan is famously low. That does not, however, mean that there is no crime. Tokyo is the largest city in the world and as such, you may potentially encounter anything, money scams being the most common.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to go to Japan as I think the country is fascinating, great food culture, nature, etc. I did not know a lot about the academic level but I had a good impression of the university.
overall_comments: It was an incredible time. I loved living in Japan. People were nice, food was great, city and nature was great. The university was a good experience as well.

arrival_assistance: As mentioned, very easy to email them. Furthermore, there was an orientation day which was fine. housing_how: I found housing on my own

The courses/study plan had to be "approved" my my academic advisor. He didn't seem to care that much so I cannot imagine they will not accept the courses you choose.
registration_help: Email service with the international office who spoke English. There was also an office in Myogadani Campus, but they did not really speak English. You can still do it with Google Translate and everyone do everything they can to help even though they do not speak English
registration_success: I got all of them. There are very few courses to take in English though. Especially in political science so I had to choose law courses
registration_advice: Use the international office for assistance if you have any questions. They help with everything - I have never received so efficient and helpful advice and assistance before, incredible! Be aware there are not that many English courses to take.
academics_comments: It was an incredible time. I loved living in Japan. People were nice, food was great, city and nature was great. The university was a good experience as well.
course_level: I took MA courses but also BA as I had to take 6 courses due to Japanese visa rules. there were really few, relevant MA courses unfortunately. The BA courses were audit courses. The level was varying, but overall fine.
teaching_comparison: More presentation, you have to be more active. Less reading. Lower level. Nice and listening teachers willing to help and also adjust the teaching after your preferences.
courses_enrolled: Human RIghts in a Globalized World Law and Society Public Governance Ethics and Humanitarian Intervention Global Tutorial
recommended_courses: I would recommend Public governance and Law and Society. Nice and capable teachers, very interesting topics.
unexpected_costs: I used the trains/metros etc. a lot which got quite expensive. The Shinkansen is also extremely expensive. There is also an obligatory Japanese insurance, but it wasn't that expensive.
cost_comparison: Food was incredible and quite cheap! I ate out every day and it wasn't that bad financially. People talk as if Tokyo is incredibly expensive but I found it very reasonable, especially compared to Copenhagen.
activities_available: Hiking, sports, dancing, manga, etc.: lots of clubs
activities_recommended: Food, Izakaya, hiking, enjoying living in TOkyo
weekend_recommendations: Several nice day trips such as going to Hakone. Hiking Mt Fuji was also a great experience. Okinawa was beautiful and fascinating. Museums are good. You can do pretty much everything in Japan :-). There are also several food, music, etc. festivals in the spring and summer.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy. Of course it was difficult not speaking Japanese as many do not speak English. But people were helpful, you always felt safe. Also, I got several Japanese friends at university who were open and nice.
socializing_tips: Talk to the Japanese students you take classes with. I experienced that many were interested and wanted to learn English and they were always kind if you say hi. Also, you can join clubs.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier.
culture_appreciated: The food, the incredible hospitality. Everyone was nice and helpful. The university staff as well.
top3_advice: Learn a few phrases of Japanes or download Google Translate (use the picture translating feature!) Read up on which courses are available as there are only few courses available Enjoy the amazing experience! It is an amazing privilege to be able to live in Tokyo and Japan and go on exchange in general.
other_useful_info: Try to engage with Japanese students you take classes with. most_rewarding: Meeting new friends, eating great food, learning about the Japanese society and getting new perspectives on my own studies. Traveling.
greatest_challenge: The language barrier.

crucial_aspects: I wanted a big culture shock. I found that Japan was perfect combination of being safe and modern while having a very different culture that i could explore during my exchange.
info_ease: Very easy. I lived in an international dorm at the university which provided info-meeting and also had local university students who could help with japanese translations.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance with registering as a temporary resident, applying for health care (which was both required) and applying for being a resident without having to pay pension. I was also provided contact information to the international office, who could help me with any issues that might arise.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We were provided an excel sheets of programs in english. All we had to do was to pick the ones that interested us and post the corresponding information in an application.
registration_help: The international office was surely available, but i mostly used the other students at the dorm and asked their help and reccomendations.
registration_success: There were no issues at all.
registration_advice: Don't be afraid to ask other students, they are often the ones with the knowledge you seek.
course_level: It was fairly easy. Really nothing compared to computer science at KU. I believe it is because many of the courses i took involved being able to express oneself clearly in english which is on average a lot easier for danish people than for Japanese students where the english proficiency, i found, was usually a lot lower.
teaching_comparison: It was more like danish high school. You sit in a classroom (i had only one course that used a lecture hall) and you get points for attendance and participation. You even fail a class if you do not attend some specified number of times.
courses_enrolled: Data Analysis Data Science International Product Development Japanese B I (2) Japanese B II (2) Japanese Management Philosophy Public Management
recommended_courses: Data Science was good introductory course for people who have no knowledge of computer science. The format and the teacher was great.
unexpected_costs: Make sure you have enough money to go travelling around in Japan. It's not expensive but it can be difficult to make a budget for before arriving, because a lot of travel plans happen spontaneously with other students.
cost_comparison: Food and clothing was much less expansive than i though (decent meal at a restaurant is 45 DKK). Tokyo has a rep for being an expensive place, but I think that must be the rent for living. Since i lived in a cheap dormitory everything seemed very cheap compared to danish standards.
activities_available: Cultural exchange programs, cooking-parties and also event-based parties were available.
activities_recommended: Go out with other exchange students and Japanese students. Do a lot of Karaoke and go to Izakayas.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking is a top recommendation. Mt. Mitake and Mt. Takao are nice spots not far with train from the University.
culture_adjustment: Since the culture is so different it took some time getting used to. But everyone was nice and helpful and my Japanese roommate explained a lot of Japanese Customs for me.
socializing_tips: Don't be shy go talk to people! The Japanese might do it first though, they are very interested in foreigners. If you are a shy person I can recommend hanging out in public areas - if you seem welcoming people will likely come talk to you.
cultural_challenges: The language is a big one. Do yourself a favor and learn some Japanese, even if you think you will never use it after your exchange. Being able to have very basic conversations with local students and people you meet on your travels makes it so much more enjoyable, to not mention the obvious practical aspect of being able to ask questions.
culture_appreciated: The helpfulness and humble attitude. It takes some time getting used to and might seem awkward at first, when you realise how crude your own behaviour might be in relation to it. But very likely you will assimilate it doing your stay and might even become more self reflective in avoidance of causing other trouble.
top3_advice: Stay at the International Dormitory Chuo (IRC). Having social activities and people available really enriches an exchange. It also means that you will live with Japanese, which makes immersing in the culture and getting help navigating Japan so much more easy.
other_useful_info: I've written it before, but I will write it again. Learn some Japanese, interacting with local people is very rewarding and being able to ask for help and read signs makes everything much easier when travelling in Japan.
most_rewarding: My roomates. I had a Korean and Japanese roomate. They gave me a lot of insights into Korean and Japanese culture and we went and did a lot of the authentic Japanese activities, which is what you come to appreciate once you've done all the touristy-stuff. You can always come back to Japan and be a tourist, but you will (usually) never again be a student in Japan. So immerse in the Japanese Student life!
greatest_challenge: It was clearly again the language barrier. Even though i studied Japanese and know the basics I still needed help for practical things like signing up for a gym, signing out as a resident when i had to leave etc. You might think google translate or DeepL can solve such problems but often they fall short when translating Japanese for some reason.

arrival_assistance: I received assistance through the University's online portal. If I had any problems, I could always contact Chuo University thorough the online portal.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: This was maybe the most "difficult" part of the process. If was difficult to find out the right course-number, and suddenly we could pre-register for some courses, which I think was quite confusing.
registration_help: Chuo University always replied fast to my e-mails. Just contact them!
registration_success: Very successful!
registration_advice: Contact Chuo University when in doubt. It can be a bit confusing.
course_level: I think all of my courses was on a quite easy level compared to our courses at Copenhagen University.
teaching_comparison: I think it was the same. Quite small classes.
courses_enrolled: Law and Society, Comparative Constitutional Law, Environmental Law and Politics and Contemporary Challenges in the Law og the Sea.
recommended_courses: I really liked all of my courses. Law and Society was very interesting to me because I got to learn a lot about the Japanese Culture in this class!
unexpected_costs: Nothing unexpected. It is quite cheap to live in Japan. However, if you want to travel around you should save up some more.
cost_comparison: Food is cheap, but transportation and housing are Danish prices.
activities_available: I know they had a lot of activities on campus, but as I did not live there, and I did not attend.
activities_recommended: Travel!
weekend_recommendations: I would travel both down to the south of Japan in cities like Fukuoka and Beppu, but also the more classic ones like Kyoto, Hakone and Hiroshima.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The Japanese people are very kind.
socializing_tips: Maybe to stay on campus. I know a lot of Japanese students lived there.
cultural_challenges: Maybe the language. All of the Japanese students were unfortunately not good at speaking English which could be a bit challenging
culture_appreciated: Politeness.
top3_advice: 1) Learn some Japanese, 2) Always have some cash, 3) Do not be afraid to try any food in Japan - everything is good.
other_useful_info: When in doubt just ask the Japanese people - they always want to help foreigners.
most_rewarding: To see how Japanese people are living and behaving - very calm (especially in public transportation). I really want to practice some here in my life in Copenhagen.
greatest_challenge: To live by my own in the largest city of the world.

crucial_aspects: The curriculum. I wanted courses that matched what I wanted to write about in my master's thesis.
overall_comments: It was great. Great teachers, great dorm, great help, great everything.
info_ease: Super easy. Chuo's website was easy to navigate and had all the information I needed. When I was still in doubt, then the international center was quick to answer my emails. 10/10.
arrival_assistance: I was a master's student so I didn't get a study helper (a Japanese student to help you acclimate to JP etc.), but it seems bachelor students do, which sounds like a great system. I had loads of help to find in the dorm manager where I lived and the international center on campus.
arrival_comments: If I ever had a question it was super easy to get answered and people were super sweet and helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was great. Great teachers, great dorm, great help, great everything.
registration_process: You had to pre-register for some courses due to congestion risk, but it was no problem and everyone who signed up got the courses they wanted. Otherwise, you just follow the online procedures, and it is very intutitive.
registration_help: International Center. An on-campus office that helped with any question you had. They were honestly great, super sweet and easy to talk to. Great English as well, so no worries communicating.
registration_success: I got all I wanted, as did everyone else.
registration_advice: Don't miss the deadlines. I was placed in a Japanese language class that conflicted with my scheduled other courses, and I was allowed to change my Japanese class to one of higher level to accomodate my schedule; the university is more flexible than you think.
academics_comments: It was great. Great teachers, great dorm, great help, great everything.
course_level: They were spot on. Not too hard not too easy.
teaching_comparison: It is a seminar style way of teaching so lots of discussions, which is about the same as TORS faculty style at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Comparative Constituional Law, Introduction to Japanese Law, Law and Business in Japan, Law and Society 2, Japanese Advanced 2.
recommended_courses: Introduction to JP law and Law and Business in JP. Super relevant hands-on knowledge about navigating the legal side of business in Japan.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay an additional National Health Insurance Policy, which is about 1000 yen pr. month; 50 kr. ca.
cost_comparison: Food was super cheap. Everything was super cheap, but that's cause the yen was weak when I went. In general eat out at restaurants and drinking is very cheap though.
activities_available: There were club circles, but I never joined those, but I believe you could. Otherwise, it was mostly events held by the residents assistants at my dorm, and the university wrote out about events that were happening in Tokyo that you could join.
activities_recommended: Make friends with the Japanese students in your dorm. They will create fun events and take you to interesting places in Tokyo.
weekend_recommendations: Look for event posters around the stations. It's a good way to see what is going on in Tokyo at the moment.
culture_adjustment: Easy. I've been to Japan 3 times before though. They speak quite good English in Tokyo though, so shouldn't be an issue.
socializing_tips: Get Line and Instagram. They are the main communication tools.
cultural_challenges: The food, if you eat out a lot, can be quite heavy. Lots of deep friend stuff.
culture_appreciated: How polite everyone was.
top3_advice: Make friends with the Japanese students, say yes to everything (a bad experience in the moment, becomes a fun story in the future,) bring clothes for summer and winter.
other_useful_info: Go in with an open mind.
most_rewarding: The people. I made some great friends and had some great experiences.
greatest_challenge: The food. If you eat out a lot, then be prepared to not eat a lot of vegetables. The food was delicious, and amazing, but after 2 months of eating out everyday (it was super cheap), then you'll begin to miss vegetables.
other_comments: It was great. I cannot recommend Chuo University enough!

crucial_aspects: Level of safety in country of destination and personal connection/interest in East Asia.
info_ease: Chuo University provided a very clear timeline for deadlines and practical information before and upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: Chuo University provided a great deal of assistance in answering any questions I had regarding arrival etc. I lived in the dorm at Tama Campus, and the Front Office was also very helpful. However, because I am a graduate student, I did not get all the orientation information that the undergrats got. I only received some of the information and not until a day prior to the particular events.
arrival_comments: The application process going there is long (like any other study abroad). I think the fact that the university is located in Japan made it even more challenging because Japan has some pretty strict immigration rules. However, once all the practicalities were done, the process was fairly easy.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It is all online, so pretty easy. They also made a template so exchange students understand how to fill out the form.
registration_help: The university was very helpful with most questions I had.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. I found it a bit challenging understanding the course fact sheet because it is separated into graduate and undergraduate, but as an exchange student you can choose both. However, it seems to make a difference which one you choose in terms of credit transfer.
registration_advice: Make sure to have thoroughly looked at all the possible courses you can choose from and figure out how many credits the courses each represent at the University of Copenhagen.
course_level: I chose a mix of BA and MA courses because of a combination of my personal interest in the courses and for credit transfer reasons.
teaching_comparison: More discussion-based classes at Chuo University with participation making up a big part of the final grade. They take attendance in class and expect you to participate actively during class, but there is less homework.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Japanese Law Competition Law & Policy in Global Context Comparative Labour and Employment Law Business and Human Rights Doing Business in Japan Advertising and Marketing Communications
recommended_courses: Competition Law & Policy in Global Context Comparative Labour and Employment Law Doing Business in Japan
unexpected_costs: You have to pay health insurance in Japan too. No matter whether you have your own or not.
cost_comparison: Public transport and groceries were more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: There was a group of Japanese students in the dorm (Resident Assistants) whose job it was to make sure that the dorm was a nice place to live. They also arranged social activities, e.g. sports day, summer festival, cooking competition between countries, and curry dinner. The university also provided a space where students could exchange culture and language.
activities_recommended: EVERYTHING! Seriously, the more you socialise the better. You never know when or where you will make new friends.
weekend_recommendations: Go outside of Tokyo. The city is great and should definitely also be experienced, but Japan is so much more than just Tokyo. There is a huge regional difference in Japan - from Okinawa all the way to Hokkaido.
culture_adjustment: Japan is very different from Denmark. I have travelled quite a lot in Asia before, so I was prepared for differences. However, there were still things I didn't expect. Some of the other exchange students from Europe found the adjustment very difficult.
socializing_tips: Live in the dorms! Especially the one at Tama Campus is amazing.
cultural_challenges: They are (in my opinion) overly polite. They bow and say "thank you" all the time, and everything takes a long time because they double check everything. It seems very inefficient from a European perspective.
culture_appreciated: The orderliness. Everything is clean and organized. People are respectful and mindful if they bump into you on the train, and they keep quiet in public which was amazing to experience considering how massive Tokyo is and how many people live there.
top3_advice: 1. The application process is tough, so prepare yourself for that and be on top of deadlines - don't wait until last minute applying for official documents etc. I know that many people get stressed by this because they do it very close to the deadline. Being on top of deadlines gives you more room to relax during the application process. 2. Consider housing thoroughly before you choose. There are pros and cons to living at Tama Campus vs. in the the city centre, so choose what is most appealing tom your needs. You have the change to be VERY social in the dorms, but if that is not for you, you might want to find some off campus housing in the city centre. 3. Mentally prepare yourself for the exchange before going - what is it gonna be like living in another country? What style of teaching do the courses have? What do you want to get out of your exchange?
other_useful_info: There is not a lot of courses in English, so check out the course catalogue before applying to make sure that you can obtain enough credits.
most_rewarding: The friends that I made and the experiences and memories I got to share with them.
greatest_challenge: Keeping up with deadlines at my home university - course registration for the new semester etc. When you are on exchange, you don't think about courses back home, and since the semster is pushed a few months in Japan, it can be hard to keep up with deadlines at the end of the semester back home.

crucial_aspects: That it was foreign and completely new for me.
info_ease: You got plenty of help from the school, and they were very accessible on mail even before the stay started. I lived in the dormitory on campus, and they were extremely helpful, both with requests regarding the dormitory, but also other issues you could need help with in Japan.
arrival_assistance: You were guided into your dormitory and got a tour of both the campus and the dorm, to show the many different facilities.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You were asked to fill out a couple questionnaires to choose how you wanted to live, seiseki (closer to centrum in Tokyo) Tama (in the Tama campus) or if you wanted to figure it out yourself. It was not difficult, but make sure to adhere to the deadlines! :)
registration_help: You could again write to the front office for the dormitory, and they were again very helpful.
registration_success: No issues.
registration_advice: It can be a bit overwhelming in the beginning, but make sure to follow the different deadlines.
course_level: It was a mixed bag, some courses were very academic, and some were not.
teaching_comparison: Similar in some courses, very different in others.
courses_enrolled: I chose a japanese language course, IT Strategy, Business Communication, Business Negotiation, Philosophy, Global Tutorial, International Product Development and Cognitive Marketing.
recommended_courses: I can recommend Cognitive Marketing and International Product Development, and if you want to learn japanese, the japanese language course.
unexpected_costs: Put some money to the side to experience stuff. You're in Japan!!
cost_comparison: The transportation prices can very quickly run up if you go to Tokyo centrum a lot. Food is however very cheap if you choose to eat in the cafeteria, or cook yourself.
activities_available: You could join a lot of different "circles". A list of these can be seen on Chuo's website.
activities_recommended: Play some sport or participate in the foreign exchange forum on campus.
weekend_recommendations: Travel to the outskirts of Tokyo or do some day trips. AND most importantly, eat some good japanese food! Good sushi, unagi, kaiseki etc.
culture_adjustment: You adjust pretty quickly. People will not get mad at you if you don't adhere to the public norms, especially in public transportation, the japanese are too polite for that, but expect some weird looks if you don't.
socializing_tips: I used the facilities in the dormitory a lot to meet the local students, and I made a lot of Japanese friends this way.
cultural_challenges: I wouldn't say that there was any particularly challenging aspects of Japanese culture. Danish culture is also very polite. Maybe the fact that you don't disturb people in the train, keep quiet or don't talk too loud.
culture_appreciated: The food and the polite nature of all Japanese interactions. And of course the vibes.
top3_advice: Be open to meet more people! Your stay will be a lot more enjoyable if you do. Be ready to experience new stuff. Enjoy your stay, it's amazing.
other_useful_info: Make sure to quickly do your pre-approval of courses.
most_rewarding: Getting to interact with so many new foreign cultures.
greatest_challenge: Finding enough energy to experience stuff all the time! Make sure to give yourself breaks.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study and experience a culture at place where I had never been before and Japan seemed like a good fit because of its modernity and vastly different culture to the European ones
info_ease: Quite easy. The university was great at communicating and if I ever had a question they answered in no time.
arrival_assistance: The front office at my dorm were quick to give me some info about the place which was nice. The university didn't really give anything until the actual studying began.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We were provided with the syllabus in advance where we could look up the contents of each course. Then you choose which courses you want and then you have a week to try and see if that course is for you - otherwise you can choose another one. I was satisfied with the ones i originally chose, but my faculty at home wouldn't let me choose the Japanese language course so i had to choose two more courses. It all worked out fine with no problems.
registration_help: There was the offices of the major programmes and student counseling but i don't think anyone used those services. It was easy to find information on the syllabus.
registration_success: Very successful, i got the ones i wanted.
registration_advice: The english level is horrible. There are very few courses that are offered in english so read that syllabus carefully. Some courses have a different name as to what is actually being taught - for example i chose Philosophy (thinking that is was, you guessed it, philosophy) but it turned out to be more directed towards market economy which i thought was a little strange.
course_level: Very easy level of academics, at least the ones i took. The things being taught were quite outdated and on the level of secondary education which stunned me. I don't know if it was because of the english level being low or the courses themselves but it was definitely different from uni back home in terms of substance, teaching-style and general level. Some theories being taught in some of my courses had flat out been disproved since many of the texts used were outdated (some books were from the 70s!) but when we confronted the teachers about it they just said that the book said so.
teaching_comparison: Somewhat similar but a bit more high-school type of teaching where the classes are small and the teacher wants the students to engage in discussions. You have to show up to the lectures. I think that the style depended a lot on how many people were in your class.
courses_enrolled: Philosophy, Hellenism and Islamo-Christian Thought, Social Issues, Social Inequality in Japan, Language and Culture E, Global Lecture, Global Tutorial
recommended_courses: The global tutorial ones were good and the teachers there were passionate and very sweet (and they actually did research on the topics they were teaching). If you want an easy one then choose Language and Culture E (it was just about Great Britain in general). Again, look at the syllabus and see if the courses sounds good to you:)
unexpected_costs: The trains were more expensive than i anticipated (also because the cost of getting into the city from Tama Center was about 40DKK each direction, so it quickly adds up). There were some small hidden fees with the housing but nothing too expensive. I would recommend having a good amount of money for trips, experiences and shopping!
cost_comparison: Food is very cheap compared to danish standards (surprise) it is cheaper to eat out than cooking yourself so have fun trying a bunch of different restaurants and Japanese cuisine!
activities_available: There were a bunch of clubs but they were not really advertised to us, you sort of had to know who to ask. Almost all of the clubs had no english speakers so it is difficult to join if you dont speak Japanese.
activities_recommended: No clue. There is a bunch of sports teams so try those ones. But again, if you dont speak Japanese then it will be difficult.
weekend_recommendations: Go explore! Go into Tokyo and experience the crazy night life, the cool cafe culture and the energy. Go to a bunch of nature spots and travel around Japan! It is such a beautiful country with so much to offer - so dont skimp out on experiences! I also went to Hong Kong and Seoul because flights were cheap and because i wanted to see more of Asia which i am so glad i did!
culture_adjustment: It was okay i think. Japan is very popular right now so i knew most of the customs before i went like bowing, receiving things with two hands and covering up tattoos (thanks to social media). The only thing i really wanted to try was a traditional onsen, but i am heavily tattooed (and that is a big no-no) so no luck there (but there are more touristy ones that allow tattoos). The train system is good and the locals are sweet to help. Plus, people can see that you are a foreginer so they don't uphold you to the same standards as they do themselves. The most difficult thing was the language barrier as not a lot of Japanese people speak english. But hand gestures and Google Translate gets you very far!
socializing_tips: Learn Japanese. Very few students spoke english to the point where you could have a meaningful conversation. They were all so so sweet but it is quite difficult to form a deeper friendship when you dont understand each other - at least in my opinion.
cultural_challenges: I had to get used to people staring a little bit. In the center of Tokyo its not bad at all, but in Tama Center I don't think that the locals are that used to seeing foreign faces. I was often stopped on the street by locals trying to say things to me (which was fun, cause they were super sweet). You can generally go very far with a smile and a positive attitude. The thing that was most challenging, apart from the language, was the lack of modernity that i am used to in Denmark. When registering to live in Tokyo everything was on paper and very old-school. It was less tech-savvy than i thought it would be.
culture_appreciated: The attention to detail and the hospitality. Everyone was so great to try to help is there was ever a small issue. I personally liked the more traditional aspect of the culture like shrines, temples the craftsmanship.
top3_advice: 1. Learn at least just a little bit Japanese before going. It will help you tremendously 2. Go on as many cool trips as possible and try to talk to people 3. Choose the easy courses and focus on being on exchange. It really is a great experience
other_useful_info: Think about what you want to get out of your exchange. Do you want to engage in the culture, meet people, travel, learn, immerse in school or something else? Bring your big wallet and apply for grants and scholarships.
most_rewarding: Meeting a bunch of new people and getting to experience a totally different culture.
greatest_challenge: Language barrier and the lack of useful academics. I think that if the housing was closer to central Tokyo it would have been a better experience in term of experiencing things. Also, the academics were pretty useless.
other_comments: Just go. It's a great adventure and the worst that can happen is that you're a little sad. But then at least you're sad in Japan.

crucial_aspects: My previous experiences with that part of the world. Language requirements and covid-restrictions also played a big part.
info_ease: I recall it as being easy. If you are in doubt email your contact person or the relevant teacher.
arrival_assistance: I arrived a few weeks late due to covid related issues. Therefore I had other exchange students helping me out.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was abit messy. First of you have to pre-select courses. I ended up getting half of those courses. The others were already filled, not offered for some reason or the course material was only partially in english. When the online registration opened up I found it hard to figure out what courses I was able to apply for.
registration_help: I cannot recall to be honest.
registration_success: About half I would say. I ended up just going for what I thought sounded interesting while being somewhat relevant.
registration_advice: It seems your best shot at getting courses is through pre-registration.
course_level: I did not find the courses difficult but there was a high work load with 5 courses at once.
teaching_comparison: More group assignments, multiple choice tests, and powerpoint presentations than I was use to. Being asked to rate the presentations of my fellow sutdents also felt abit unusual. That only happened in one course though.
courses_enrolled: Fundamentals of Persuasive Communication Fundamentals of Advertising Cognitive Psychology Media and Society Architecture and Space in Chinese Culture
recommended_courses: In hindsight I would have picked different courses. Fundamentals of Persuasive Commnication provided some insight in applied communication and arugmentation which I did apperciate. Fundamentals of Advertising touched upon a lot of the same things. Media and Society felt abit like a repetition of other courses taught at Kommmunication og IT. If you have any interest in Ancient Chinese Archtecture I would recommend that course.
unexpected_costs: Doctor and hospital fees. These were very low however ( 200-300HDK ).
cost_comparison: Many groceries are pretty expensive. Because of that most exchange stundets I talked to also did not bother cooking at home.
activities_available: There were alot of societies and clubs, but I think you need to apply for those before the semester starts. There will also be events offered via your CityU Mail such as a one day archery course.
activities_recommended: If you are interested in latin dance there is after work Sala at Rula Live every monday at 8pm. Other thant that enjoy the city life and go hiking.
weekend_recommendations: It was not possible to visit Maccao or Shenzhen due to covid, otherwise I would have. Go camping with some friends on some of Hong Kongs remote islands.
culture_adjustment: I found it fairly easy. I found it more liberal than mainland China. Just keep in mind that it is a bit city fast paced and crowded.
socializing_tips: I found it hard to get to know Hong Kong students. The best way seemed to be participating in some of the events. Joining hikes and social events is in general a great way to meet new people.
cultural_challenges: When visiting small local resturents prepare to use pictures and practice a few phrases of Cantonese. It is a part of the experience.
culture_appreciated: I like the fact that Hong Kong is a mixture of Eastern and Western in a lot of ways. I am also a big fan of the local food.
top3_advice: Bring money and more of it than you expected. Remember summer clothes for the hot days as well as clothes for the cold aircon at the library. Do not forget to have a great time!
other_useful_info: Not on top of my head.
most_rewarding: Not to sound cheesy but the friendships made along the way.
greatest_challenge: Managing my time! The day goes fast. Balancing a lot of courses, socializing and exploration can be though.
other_comments: Hong Kong is great, the place has alot of variation! Big city life, small villages, beaches and mountain tracks all with 2 hours of transport.

registration_help: Jasmine Wong.
registration_success: As explained above.

weekend_recommendations: Going to the beach, hiking, eating out (there are some local cheap restaurants e.g., dim sum). Sightseeing in the city, especially Mongkok, Central, Causeway Bay. A "hidden gem" in Hong Kong is Sai Kung were we went camping on the beach and could do hikes/go swimming at very beautiful beaches.
culture_adjustment: Most university staff (security guards, canteen staff etc.) barely spoke english, which made it quite hard to interact. Kowloon Tong (were the university is located) is very local/chinese inspired. If you live in Hong Kong island it is very western and international.
socializing_tips: Very hard to interact with the local students at the Student Residence and at the university in general.
cultural_challenges: Language barriers.
culture_appreciated: Nice food.
top3_advice: Be open-minded and curious. Share an apartment with friends in Hong Kong island instead of living in Kowloon Tong at the student residence.
other_useful_info: Although the student residence is cheap, it is very costly to eat at the university canteen facilities. Buy simple kitchen utensils at IKEA and cook meals yourself.
most_rewarding: New international friendships that will last a lifetime. My english improved a lot.
greatest_challenge: Complying with very strict covid-19 restrictions. Undergoing quarantine at a government designated hotel and taking a lot of covid tests on a weekly basis. Wearing a mask 24/7 - inside and outside.
other_comments: Do it! It might be challenging - but most of all rewarding and memories for life! Hong Kong is perfect for a 4 month duration. Best period to visit weather-wise is Semester A.

crucial_aspects: Grades under 7, so limited options.

It was a bit uncomfortable not having a fixed schedule the first week before classes, as it made it hard to meet people in a new country
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You prioritize the courses you want before arrival, but you can change courses during the first 2 weeks
registration_help: They had some pretty thorough info online
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Some classes can get filled quickly, so look into what classes you want beforehand so you can choose them quickly
course_level: Most courses were beginners courses. The academic level varied a lot between courses
teaching_comparison: It varied a lot. Many of the courses had interactive teaching style, involving the students a lot.
courses_enrolled: - Gender, culture & Diversity - Food. Science, Culture & Society - Engineering your health - Mandarin for non-chinese speakers - World Religions
recommended_courses: Gender, culture & Diversity was very intersting. The teachers were good, and it was interesting to learn about these subjects from a non-western perspective. They also had some cool guest-speakers
unexpected_costs: Not sure
cost_comparison: Food is quite expensive. Eating out is generally a little cheaper than in DK, but most groceries are more expensive.
activities_available: Most clubs were for people either playing instruments or sports at a higher level. For others, there weren't a lot of options
activities_recommended: There were some activities for exchange students once in a while arranged by students which were quite fun
weekend_recommendations: Hiking, going to the beach, going out in LKF (Lan Kwai Fong, party area), sightseeing, going to street markets around Mong Kok, visiting the surrounding islands
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, as HK is very international and welcoming to people of other cultures generally. The culture is generally more "western" than mainland China, so its not as big of a culture shock
socializing_tips: Socializing with local students was generally quite difficult. They are mostly shy and keep to themselves.
cultural_challenges: The fact that the local students are so shy. They mostly didn't participate orally in class, so it was hard to have class discussions. Also, it was a common problem that the students were talking loudly during class, and doing a lot of other stuff (playing games on the computer etc). It was the same in all my courses. It was hard to concentrate, and seemed disrespectful towards the professor.
culture_appreciated: HK culture is a very cool blend between modern and traditional. On the same street you can encounter a buddhist temple, a skyscraper, a fortune teller, a Lamborghini and a 100+ year old tram
top3_advice: - Save up enough money. Things are pretty expensive in general + a lot of students do traveling to neighboring countries, so have enough money if u don't want to miss out - Choose a social accommodation, if you choose not to live in the student dorm. It can be hard finding a social network otherwise, since CityU doesn't have the best facilities to meet other exchange students
other_useful_info: Go to China if you have the chance. Shenzhen (China) is only 45 min away in train, but its so different from HK. There is so many things to do here, food is cheaper (and better in my opinion) than HK, you can shop a lot of cheap tech in HaqiangBei street. Would definitely recommend
most_rewarding: Learning about HK culture and history.
greatest_challenge: Some cultural differences

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I'm not sure I fully remember, but we were told to meet up at an office (a little hard to find) to register and to get an ID card.
registration_help: I ask employees and students for help finding my way. Worked nicely.
registration_success: I managed at the end, but again it was a bit difficult. Most I registered in from home though.
registration_advice: Just follow the process, then you will be fine. Application is analog though, so be in good time to send it by mail. I teamed up with other danish students to split the cost of sending it.
course_level: they seemed easier than my BA classes at home.
teaching_comparison: Lectures and group work - in almost all classes there were group works, and you were expected to figure out a group yourself.
courses_enrolled: Photography, Documentary 1, Movies and psychology, Hong Kong History, culture and society & Principles of Public Relations.
recommended_courses: Definitely my photography and documentary classes - AMAZING teachers.
unexpected_costs: In general Hong Kong is an expensive city, so going out for drinks is costly - but you can find great happy hour offers in a lot of places.
cost_comparison: Drinks were more! Buying full meals at restaurants were cheaper than I thought. Food in the supermarket more expensive.
activities_available: A lot, but I didnt take part in any though.
activities_recommended: Its not related to school, but the city as amazing nature all the way around it - go on hikes, camp at beaches and rent a boat with friends for a daytime party!
weekend_recommendations: Shenzhen is wild - go clubbing but bring someone speaking chinese is you can.. I also visited Macao, definitely an experience. Would have loved to go more into China, there are so many BEAUTIFUL places nearby. In general plane tickets are really cheap from Hong Kong so plan after taking weekendtrips - Korea, Taiwan, Japan is not that far away! Safe up for this.
culture_adjustment: I found it interesting to get to know the culture, but it was diffivult to get to know locals. I had group work with some, but we stayed professional. Most of my free time was spend with other exchange students.
socializing_tips: Group work is a good starting point
cultural_challenges: I was acutally shocked how safe I felt. Hong Kong is highly surveillanced and even though some might dislike it, it was a joy as a woman travilling on your own to feel this safe walking the streets alone, even at night!
culture_appreciated: The food and the spirituality!
top3_advice: stay away from the dorms, safe up for weekend trips - and don't stress about school. All it will reflect on your papers are a pass/no pass, so enjoy your time away from home!!
other_useful_info: I think I said it all.
most_rewarding: The people I meet, the parties and the hikes!!
greatest_challenge: Eating meat (i was vegetarian before, that was not possible here)

crucial_aspects: I wanted to explore a different culture and try to live and study in a place that was very different from my home country. I also had to consider that some of my courses were mandatory and needed to be fulfilled during my exchange, and this was one of my options. Additionally, I had heard many positive things about Hong Kong from others.
overall_comments: Hong Kong is the perfect place if you want to live in the city but still be close to nature. It's location is great if you want to travel to other countries in Asia as well.
info_ease: The orientation organized by the university had limited information and most of the orientation week and further activities were designed to the exchange students living on campus.
arrival_assistance: There was a campus tour, introduction to facilities, and orientation about social clubs, when you arrive.
arrival_comments: The limited amount of orientation during the first weeks makes it very difficult to meet fellow exchange students, especially if you don't stay in the dorms. At the dorms they have their own orientation week, and people get to know each other at this time.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Hong Kong is the perfect place if you want to live in the city but still be close to nature. It's location is great if you want to travel to other countries in Asia as well.
registration_process: Before arrival you have applied for the courses you wish to take and then you can change the courses after arrival during the first two weeks. It can be a bit difficult to change the courses afterwards, so choose wisely.
registration_help: They have information online and then you have a coordinator you can contact either in person or by email. They reply quickly.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Some classes can get filled up quickly, so be prepared.
academics_comments: Hong Kong is the perfect place if you want to live in the city but still be close to nature. It's location is great if you want to travel to other countries in Asia as well.
course_level: The academic level varied a lot between the courses. Some courses were quite easy while others were very different from KU using different programmes you had to learn by yourself.
teaching_comparison: It was very creative and innovative, involving and engaging the students a lot. Our own personal thoughts and opinions were a big part of it compared to KU.
courses_enrolled: Movies and Psychology Sexuality, Culture and Diversity Language and Cognition Cognitive Psychology Designing Experiments in Psychology
recommended_courses: I found the course Sexuality, Culture and Diversity particularly interesting. It covered among others Butler and Foucault, Polygamy, Bisexuality, Transsexuality, Intersex, Pornography, sexual politics and sexual citizenship.
unexpected_costs: Travels to other countries.
cost_comparison: Food is more expensive than I thought. We would eat out everyday because our kitchen didn't work. It is the same price as in DK to eat out and groceries are also more expensive. Transportation is less expensive - especially bus and MTR.
activities_available: They had a variety of different clubs at CityU, but it seemed like most of them were for the locals.
activities_recommended: Go to the activities for exchange students which are arranged once in a while, they can be quite fun and is a great place to meat some of the other exchange students - especially if you live off campus. They are also free.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking (Dragon's back, Lion's rock, Jardines lookout, Lantau peak and spend the night in tent on the beach in Sai Kung), visit the islands (Lamma island, Cheung Chau), Big Buddha and Tai O on Lantau island, go to the beach, go out in LKF (Lan Kwai Fong) or Mr. Wong, travel around (Shenzhen, Macao, Beijing), visit the different neighborhoods in Hong Kong. Join some activities outside of uni (e.g. painting course, sports club etc.) - in this way you will meet some more locals.
culture_adjustment: Even though HK is very international I still found it to be quite the culture shock. But you adjust pretty quickly.
socializing_tips: Locals in HK can seem to be quite reserved and keep to themselve but once you talk to them they are super friendly and kind. So you just have to reach out yourself.
cultural_challenges: People would either sleep during class or talk very loudly and the locals don't take part of oral discussions.
culture_appreciated: I love how HK is a mix of old and new, city and nature.
top3_advice: Save up money and apply for grants - HK is super expensive and if you would like to travel to other countries it is expensive as well. Consider where you want to live. If you are traveling alone I would suggest living on campus even though it is far away. This is also cheaper.
other_useful_info: Many of the courses at CityU has continuous assessment meaning a lot of mandatory attendance and many assignments and presentations during the semester, but then they don't really have final exams.
most_rewarding: Get to live in a city that is so special. HK is such a special place, I don't know anywhere like it. And also all the people I met - exchange students, locals, teachers, strangers.
greatest_challenge: Making time for everything you would like to do while you are there! Time flies by and there are so many things to explore.

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte Hong Kong som udvekslingsdestination, fordi byen tilbyder et unikt akademisk miljø i krydsfeltet mellem øst og vest samt et indblik i globale, sociale og kulturelle dynamikker, der er relevante for mit studie.
info_ease: Det var relativt nemt at finde den nødvendige information, da universitetet stillede klare retningslinjer og deadlines og var hurtige til at svare på mails, hvis man havde spørgsmål.
arrival_assistance: Der var 2 korte introdage hvor vi blev vidst rundt og fik information om byen, universitetet mm.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Universitetet gav på forhånd klare trin-for-trin-instruktioner med vigtige deadlines og nødvendige dokumenter, og der var let adgang til support via mail, hvis der opstod spørgsmål.
registration_help: Man kunne enten ringe eller skrive til dem. Dog skal man være lidt opmærksom på tidsforskellen.
registration_success: Jeg fik næsten alle de fag jeg ville. Der var lidt bøvl med det, men det løste sig i sidste ende.
registration_advice: At sætte sig grundigt ind i fagene og deres krav for at bestå. Derudover er det en god idé at søge forhåndsgodkendelse til flere fag, end dem man umiddelbart ønsker, da man ikke er 100 procent sikker på at få sine førstevalg - og det derfor er vigtigt at have en plan B.
course_level: Det faglige niveau var til at overskue, hverken for svært eller for nemt.
teaching_comparison: Det afhænger af hvilke fag man vælger, men man skal være forberedt på at arbejde meget i grupper. Derudover har de fleste fag også præsentationer og løbende quiz/tests.
courses_enrolled: GE1137 Movies and Psychology GE2129 Psychology for Young Professionals GE2211 Sexuality, Culture and Diversity GE2248 Persuasion in Everyday Life PIA3544 East Asia and Globalization
recommended_courses: Dem jeg havde, var alle ret gode. De havde løbende bedømmelse, hvilket vil sige at du ikke kun bliver vurderet på en enkelt eksamen, men at test, præsentationer, fremmøde mm. tæller med i den endelige karakter.
unexpected_costs: Rejser til andre lande i Asien
cost_comparison: Ved ikke
activities_available: Der var pool og fitness på uni samt andre sportshold og klubber/fællesskaber man kunne tilmelde sig. Jeg brugte det dog ikke.
activities_recommended: Tag ud og se naturen! Hong Kong har virkelig gode Hikes og flotte strande. Besøg de små øer!.
weekend_recommendations: Tag på ture til nabolandene eller til Mainland(Kina). Tiden går virkelig hurtigt når først man er afsted så det er bare med at opleve når man har muligheden. Ellers har Hong Kong et nice byliv og virkelig gode shopping muligheder.
culture_adjustment: Det tog lige en uges tid men det afhænger nok lidt af hvem man er som person. Der er så meget som er anderledes, men det er det hele værd!.
socializing_tips: Universitetet tilbyde ofte ture man kan tilmelde sig - benyt det!.
cultural_challenges: Ved ikke.
culture_appreciated: Det hele.
top3_advice: Vær åben og opsøgende, forbered dig på en anderledes studie- og undervisningskultur, og brug udvekslingen aktivt til både faglig og kulturel læring. Derudover tag på Mr.Wong (virkelig billige øl :)) alle udvekslingsstuderende i byen samles ofte der og det er altid nemt at møde nye bekendtskaber der.
other_useful_info: Sørg for at være ude i god tid med praktiske forhold som bolig og engagér dig socialt, da det har stor betydning for at man ikke bliver føler sig alene i en kæmpe by hvor alt er fremmed til at starte med.
most_rewarding: At blive udfordret både fagligt og personligt ved at studere og bo i en helt anden kulturel kontekst end den, jeg er vant til.
greatest_challenge: At ville nå det hele: Hong Kong har enormt meget at byde på og ligger perfekt i forhold til billige rejser til andre spændende destinationer, men på kun fire måneder er det umuligt at opleve det hele - så sørg for at lave en god plan og en klar prioriteringsliste.

info_ease: I am very disapointet
arrival_assistance: I am very disappointed by the lack of information and guidance from the University of Copenhagen. My experience of Universidad Complutense de Madrid has been much more satisfying, and was very much a help in the otherwise chaotic situation.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to downloaded a registration form, fill it and get it signed over email
registration_help: On email (fast answers!) or in present at an office.
registration_success: I couldn't get all the classes I wanted, so for my exams there were some overlap problems.
registration_advice: talk with other erasmus students about it
course_level: The level was quite okay but not very high, but because it was in Spanish it was more challenging. The workload was quite high though, although there was almost no reading.
teaching_comparison: Not big lectures as at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Politica comparada Sistemas políticos de América Latina Seguridad y defensa europea Sistema de la Unión Europa Sistema Político Español
recommended_courses: Sistemas políticos de América Latina Seguridad y defensa europea
unexpected_costs: It is quite expensive to go out. Maybe not as expensive as in Denmark, but in Denmark we go to parties on campus, and in Spain you only go out in the city. So all in all it is more expensive.
cost_comparison: The metro was less expensive.
activities_available: There were some social clubs like debating etc. I didn't sign up.
activities_recommended: Maybe try the debate team, I didn't know it existed.
weekend_recommendations: Retiro - especially in the spring and summer.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, everyone is very nice and welcoming.
socializing_tips: Don't be afraid of reaching out. But also don't try too hard, it will all work out.
cultural_challenges: Spanish people are more open, and also they go out more.
culture_appreciated: The energy is amazing. People are always up for meeting new people.
top3_advice: If in doubt just write the uni, they answer quick. Choose courses based on the teacher and not the theme. Pack light, you will buy stuff.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: To improve my Spanish and get friends from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: the exams were hard, because it is difficult in another language, and because it is difficult knowing what to expect and how to study for them.

crucial_aspects: It was very important to me that the courses were good and I knew I had a lot to choose from at the Complutense which is why I chose that university. It was also very important for me that the professors were good, which they were, and I also knew I wanted to live in Madrid as I have a strong connection to that city. It also looks good on my CV that I have been at the UCM, because I know it is one of the best places to study spanish philology.
info_ease: It was quite easy to get information, because if I couldn't find it somewhere I would just write to the Erasmus office at the Complutense who were always ready to help, so I didn't have any noticable problems upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: The Erasmus office at the UCM were very good at giving information and answering emails etc. There was also a welcome session at the complutense which was nice because there I got to meet other erasmus students as well.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I went to the erasmus office and they signed my paper.
registration_help: There was a meeting for Erasmus students right at the beginnning.
registration_success: Very sucessful, it went very smoothly. I had to change several classes, however, it was very easy to make the changes.
registration_advice: In the first two weeks of the semester we got to try out all classes we wanted, which I would recommend other students to do before they confirm their final classes, because it's nice to see whether or not you like the teacher etc. before signing up for the class.
course_level: I took 5 courses and some were harder than others. Especially the literary courses were a bit difficult because the teachers kept making references to other spanish works and periods which I haven't studied. However, the teachers were always very helpful and explained things nicely to me as they knew I was an exchange student, so generally there wasn't any big problems. The level of the courses were perfect for me, of course it did take a bit longer to study as everything was in spanish, but I quickly got used to it and it was actually not a problem at all in the end. Overall I did just as well, and better, than the spanish students so I am very satisfied.
teaching_comparison: The teaching at Complutense was centrered around the professor who would talk most of the time, however there were also discussions and open questions in the classrooms. A big difference I noticed is that the spanish teachers don't give out homework, they just give a list of books which need to be read for the exam. Another difference to the UCPH is that in copenhagen I am used to more group work, however I personally prefer individual work so the style of teaching at UCM fit well for me.
courses_enrolled: Cervantes y su tiempo. Literatura del siglo XVII. Fundamentos filosóficos para el estudio de la lengua y la literatura. Retórica y crítica literaria. Introducción a la cultura y mitología clásica.
recommended_courses: I would recommend the 'Fundamentos Filosóficos para el estudio de la lengua y la literatura' because it was a subject where I as an exchange student could contribute a lot by having a different perspective than the spanish students. I had a great teacher who was very nice to engage in dialogue with me and gave me space to express my thoughts. At the same time it was a subject which combined philosophy with literature in a way that I did not expect and which was super interesting. Generally I would recommend all the courses because they were all really interesting.
unexpected_costs: I ended up buying more books than I expected, but that is also part of my hobby and it wasn't strictly necesary for the university.
cost_comparison: The housing was a bit expensive, but apart from that thing such as food and transport is really cheap.
activities_available: There were some conferences and also some sort of music festival.
activities_recommended: The ESN trips are a great oportunity both to meet knew people and to see spain.
weekend_recommendations: There are lots of things to see in Madrid and because of it's central location it is easy to travel to different parts of Spain as well. I went to Galicia and Alicante, both really nice cities.
culture_adjustment: It was really easy for me, as I have lived in Madrid before and know my way around.
socializing_tips: It's good if you can speak in spanish to them, because many students don't feel very comfortable speaking in english. It's also easy to make friends hanging out in the cafeteria at the university or going to a local taberna after studying.
cultural_challenges: The way of studying was a bit difficult in the beginning because the professors don't give homework for each day so I had to figure out a routine myself.
culture_appreciated: Living in Malasaña was really lovely and I really enjoyed being able to speak spanish all the time and also visiting the different museums in Madrid.
top3_advice: That it's good to read the texts in the beginning and during the semester, even though the teacher might not mention them in the class until the end, because at the end of the semester all exams and papers are at the same time so there isn't a lot of time to study. It is also quite important to get some spanish friends as they can help you with all the questions you might have. And lastly one must remember to enjoy it and say yes to the experience because it's over really quickly.
other_useful_info: It's always ok to write to the Erasmus office, they're really good at giving information.
most_rewarding: The academic courses I took really enriched my experience as I have learned a lot and gained more knowledge in a field that I now know I want to continue studying. I was also really rewarding to get spanish friends as I have practised my spanish a lot and become really comfortable in the language.
greatest_challenge: Studying for the exams was a bit tough, but I managed it very well in the end.

crucial_aspects: I wanted a destination where I could experience the Spanish culture and learn the Spanish language. Moreover, I chose Madrid because of the opportunity to create relations to both national and international people.
overall_comments: Many aspects of my trip were great.
info_ease: I received most of the information when I arrived. There was a lot of trouble with my application and therefore, information about courses etc. were delayed.
arrival_assistance: I got help from the international office from my faculty. Moreover, the university host many welcome sessions where they explain necessary information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Many aspects of my trip were great.
registration_process: Firstly, I had to register on their website, but since they did not receive my application in time, I had little time to do it and I did not have the necessary documents. Moreover, when you arrive you have to register again, and register to the courses again. Here you have to contact every professor and ask them if you can enroll in their classes and ask for them to sign a document. This took a lot of time, as some professors are really slow to answer, and you don't have much time to do so.
registration_help: The international office is good to help with everything.
registration_success: I successfully registered to the classes I wanted at last. However, the first classes I wanted to take were not available to Erasmus students and I, therefore, had to find new courses to take when I arrived.
