crucial_aspects: I wanted to have an authentic American college campus experience, and Cornell University was the perfect choice for that since it was located in a small town, Ithaca, where the university and its students made up the majority of residents.
overall_comments: I had an amazing experience and made friendships and connections which I still keep in touch with.
info_ease: Very easy, the coordinator for exchange students, Jess Hawkey, was very well organized and very helpful and gave us all the necessary information.
arrival_assistance: We had an orientation day for all the exchange students in August before the semester started where we recieved all the practical information as well as some useful cultural tips for our stay at Cornell.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had an amazing experience and made friendships and connections which I still keep in touch with.
registration_process: Course registration was quite conveniant. If courses required prerequisites, you could email the professor directly and enquire about whether the course would be suitable or not, and in general the professors were very willing to help and I experienced no problems in getting the courses I wanted. At Cornell, there is a 3 week period where you can basically attend lectures and if you don't find the courses interesting or relevant you can still enroll in other courses and drop out of courses without it being registered on your transcript. This also means that if a course is full and you cant pre-enroll, you may still be able to enroll in the course as some other students may drop out of it in this period. In general, it never hurts to reach out to the professor and ask if there is space on a course, as often you will get a yes.
registration_help: There was a website where you could search for courses available in the semester and see if it was compatible with your timetable, i.e. that the courses didn't overlap with each other. This was very helpful.
registration_success: I was able to get all of the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Figure out the courses you might want to take in advance and remember to pre-enroll so you are guaranteed a spot. Thereafter, if there are other courses which might seem interesting, go to a lecture or two and perhaps you might want to enroll during the drop-period.
academics_comments: I had an amazing experience and made friendships and connections which I still keep in touch with.
course_level: Two of the courses I took, were courses which were combined courses for both BA and MA students. The courses had different official names, however the lectures were the same. The only difference was that sometimes the MA students had to do slightly more challenging questions in asssignments or perhaps had more questions on the exam. Aside from that, it was the same course. Coming exchange students should be aware of this, as they may wish to consider whether to take the BA version of the course or the MA version, depending on how much they wish to challenge themselves. In terms of the academic level, it was perhaps slightly lower than what I am used to studying Mat-Øk at the Maths Institute at KU, however there was more work than at KU. In most courses, your grade was comprised of assignments, preliminary tests and a final exam, which meant you had to follow along and perform well throughout the course if you wanted to get a good grade. As opposed to at KU, where in many courses your grade is determined solely by your final exam.
teaching_comparison: It was very similar; a combination of lectures and practice lessons (labs), where older students who had already taken the course were instructors.
courses_enrolled: ORIE 4630: Operations Research Tools for Financial Engineering ORIE 3300: Optimization 1 CS 1100: Introduction to Computing: A Design and Development Perspective
recommended_courses: It is impossible for me to recommend specific courses as it totally depends on the interests of the student. While I didn't take it myself, I knew many people who took "Wine Tasting" as a course, which sounded like a lot of fun :)
unexpected_costs: We had to have a mandatory insurance which cost 1200 USD. Groceries were also more expensive than I expected. I ended up buying a meal plan (they can be quite expensive) so that I could eat on campus, since the food was actually very good and we lived quite far away from the nearest supermarket, so shopping was a bit inconveniant.
cost_comparison: You could use all of the local buses in Ithaca for free with your student ID card.
activities_available: See answer to previous question.
activities_recommended: The running club is a great way to meet new people and explore the area. You don't have to be a good runner at all, as there is always a social pace run where people chat and have fun.
weekend_recommendations: The obvious choice is to spend some time in NYC as it is only a approx 4.5 hour bus ride away from Ithaca and it is an amazing city (though expensive). Personally, me and some other exchange students rented some cars and drove to Quebec, Canada over the thanksgiving break, which was a lot of fun. There is a small local airport which flies to NYC, so some more adventurous people travelled further over the fall break. Niagara falls is also only abour 2.5 hours away, howeveer it isnt worth more than a day trip as the city itself isnt that interesting.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. People were very welcoming and open. It is a very international/diverse crowd of people who attend Cornell, so it barely feels like you are a foreigner in that environment.
socializing_tips: Join clubs, and attend any official school events. Eating at the dining halls for lunch or dinner is also a great way to meet new people.
cultural_challenges: There was nothing which I found particularly challenging.
culture_appreciated: How open-minded and easy people were to talk to, as well as how driven and intelligent many of the students were.
top3_advice: 1. If you are living off-campus, make sure to stay either near North campus (Cayuga Heights) or in Collegetown (south of campus), just dont stay in downtown Ithaca (west of campus) 2. I would recommend getting some form of meal plan, as the food in the dining halls, in particular Morrison dining hall (the newest one) is actually really good, and I have some of my fondest memories eating dinner with friends there. 3. Enjoy the nature and explore the local area.
other_useful_info: A lot of the social life also revolves around fraternitites and sororities, so it may be worthwile making some friends who are members of "greek life" if you are interested in partying etc.
most_rewarding: Making friends with so many interesting people, both Americans and other exchange students from different parts of the world.
greatest_challenge: Leaving Cornell :)

crucial_aspects: The most important aspects were location and the course catalog. I always wanted to experience the American system. Dartmouth offered a perfect combination of high academically quality, and beautiful nature close to bigger cities like Boston and New York
overall_comments: Indeed, it was an experience for life. It was exciting, educational, inspiring and fun, but it was also challenging and at times tough. People should be prepared that studying abroad takes a lot of energy, but it is definitely worth it.
info_ease: Pretty easy. Dartmouth sends out a lot of information upon arrival, and if you have any other questions you can always contact their counselor for exchange students, who is really sweet and helpful.
arrival_assistance: Arrival was a bit overwhelming, but the administrative staff were extremely helpful. I also found support in the other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Indeed, it was an experience for life. It was exciting, educational, inspiring and fun, but it was also challenging and at times tough. People should be prepared that studying abroad takes a lot of energy, but it is definitely worth it.
registration_process: You have to take a language test. The rest is just online forms. Be aware of the emails they send you, especially the one providing you with a Dartmouth email . All important informations like housing will be send to this.
registration_help: I could always email the counselor for exchange students. The replies came within a few days, often just hours.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Some of them I didn't get in the first try, but I recommend emailling the professor. In my experience they like having exchange students in there classes, and are open to help you if they can. Also, be patient. The first week is drop/add, so you can be lucky that a spot opens up.
academics_comments: Indeed, it was an experience for life. It was exciting, educational, inspiring and fun, but it was also challenging and at times tough. People should be prepared that studying abroad takes a lot of energy, but it is definitely worth it.
course_level: According to Dartmouth rules you can only take undergraduate courses tough you are a master student in Denmark. However, the level is pretty high so it doesn't really matter. They working load is extreme compared to KU. You should be prepared at spending a lot of time studying for class and finals.
teaching_comparison: A LOT of readings. Especially in the political science departement. Their quarter system makes it quite intense, since you have both midterms and finals within ten weeks. The classes are small and you will have a close relation to your professors, who also offer office hours, which is great for sparring. But they also expect a lot from you, and the amount of quizzes and assignments is a bit crazy. It is hardcore, but you will learn a lot, and their courses are great.
courses_enrolled: First term: The American Political System War and Peace in Modern Age Fall and Rise of Great Powers Second term: Political Misinformation and Conspiracy Theories Introduction to the Middle East Inequality and American Democracy (seminar)
recommended_courses: War and Peace in Modern Age Political Misinformation and Conspiracy Theories Inequality and American Democracy (seminar) I recommend taking a seminar. It is more demanding but worth it. Also I recommend courses with Brendan Nyhan who is in expert in his field, Benjamin Valentino and Herchel Nachlis. They are all great professors.
unexpected_costs: Everything from visa to language tests are quite expensive.
cost_comparison: I was surprised how expensive it is to live in the US. Going out for coffee og dinner is just as expensive as in Copenhagen
activities_available: All sorts of things. They are very sporty, but I am not sure how easy it is to join a sports team due to our limited time. But there is a free gym, free hikes offered in the weekend etc.
activities_recommended: I strongly recommend going on the trips arranged by the Outdoor club. Its free and a great way to see the area and meet new people. I also enjoyed their cinema (The Hop) and the jewelry workshop (Also at the Hop)
weekend_recommendations: I really liked Boston. But you can also take a bus to NY directly from campus. There is also a lot of nice things to see in New England, though it requires a car.
culture_adjustment: A bit challenging. They are much more introvert than I expected. And their extreme focus on school makes it a bit difficult to get to know them, but be patient. Usually there is around 8-10 exchange students and a lot of international students, who can provide you with support as well.
socializing_tips: I personally had succes in sending emails out to people from my classes who I though were nice. Join the outdoor trips.
cultural_challenges: They are younger, and less open than you might expect. They work hard, and it sometimes takes their focus from social events. But they are also extremely kind if you are patient and give them a change.
culture_appreciated: The opportunity to focus on school without any other obligations. The beautiful nature, the American politeness, and the academically connection the the professors.
top3_advice: The workload is quite extreme, so don't expect it to be a holiday The location is a bit isolated, at times boring, but it is also beautiful. Try to benefit from the many opportunities for skiing, iceskating, hikes etc. Use your professors knowledge, they will love to help you in any way
other_useful_info: Again I want you to be aware of the workload. I found it a bit overwhelming. But it is manageable once you find a rhythm.
most_rewarding: The nature and the academically part
greatest_challenge: The social scene and the workload
other_comments: Dartmouth is a great place, where you will learn a whole lot both academically, about the US and not at least yourself

most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of new friends, traveling around the US and experiencing the great courses/academics.

weekend_recommendations: Go out enjoy the night life, go on a hike or study - you will need to spend some of your weekends studying :D
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy - people are quite friendly, but it might take a little bit of time to get close to people as it is easy to make new friends but a little more difficult to make close friends.
socializing_tips: Go to the frats - that is the best place for meeting new people.
cultural_challenges: The small talk can sometimes be a little socially draining if you are not used to constantly interacting with people. culture_appreciated: the openness and how willing random people were to talk to you and invite you to random things.

other_useful_info: Enjoy it - It flys by super fast.
most_rewarding: The best part was getting to make a bunch of new friends from all over the world who were all incredibly kind.
greatest_challenge: Either getting used to the cold and darkness in winter term or Econ81

cost_comparison: The meal-plan, a dorm room and the insurance

weekend_recommendations: The surrounding nature, sports games and Fraternity parties
culture_adjustment: Quite easy as it is a small space and people are extremely welcoming and friendly
socializing_tips: Participate in the events that the school provide!
cultural_challenges: The age difference as I'm a 26 year old MA student and this was 19 year old freshmen. My stay wouldn't have been the same if it wasn't for the six other Danish exchange student. culture_appreciated: How welcoming and embracing the other students where. I got a lot of American friends and contacts while I was there
top3_advice: The fall term is only 22,5 ECTS point That housing, meal-plans and insurance are mandatory and quite expensive (but it makes it that much easier!) other_useful_info: all public transportation in Hanover is free:)
most_rewarding: Meeting all these wonderful people (both Danish and American), and experiencing a very intense, but instructive academic environment. Experiencing the election first hand and the political debate (even in the light of the very depressing results)
greatest_challenge: I had to go to the hospital and the insurance situaiton afterwards was a hard process.

crucial_aspects: I was particularly drawn to the cultural experience of living in Australia and the opportunity to study in an English-speaking environment. This combination felt both academically relevant and personally enriching.
info_ease: It was relatively easy. Deakin University has a very informative website, almost too informative at times, which meant that most of the practical questions I had were already answered online.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any specific or structured assistance upon arrival, but general support was available if needed.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The process involves some back-and-forth: even after KU allocates you a spot, you still need to complete a formal application through Deakin. Fortunately, everything went smoothly. Deakin sends all required documents and forms, and the steps are clearly outlined.
registration_help: The administrative staff were very friendly and ready to help with any questions throughout the process.
registration_success: I was able to register for all the courses I had hoped to take.
registration_advice: Pay close attention to intensive courses, as these typically take place over about a week and involve very concentrated teaching. Also make sure to check whether a course is at the bachelor’s or master’s level, depending on what you need. If in doubt, contact the administration they are very helpful.
course_level: There was a clear difference between BA and MA courses, but overall the academic level was not higher than what I have experienced at the University of Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: Some courses had a similar structure to UCPH, while others were noticeably more interactive and engaging. Class sizes also varied significantly, which influenced the teaching style.
courses_enrolled: ADS734 GEOPOLITICS AND POLITICAL ECONOMY OF DEVELOPMENT AIP347 MEDIA AND POLITICS: CAMPAIGN STRATEGIES AIR349 DIPLOMACY AND THE UNITED NATIONS ALR718 PUBLIC RELATIONS, ACTIVISM AND SOCIAL CHANGE
recommended_courses: AIR349 – Diplomacy and the United Nations Highly engaging course with a unique approach: each student represents a country in a simulated UN setting. ALR718 – Public Relations, Activism and Social Change Taught by Thaera, who is extremely engaging and brings a dynamic and thought-provoking perspective to public relations.
unexpected_costs: Used more on public transportation as Campus was placed faraway from the city and groceries.
cost_comparison: Less expensive to go out to eat but groceries where expensive.
activities_available: There were plenty of opportunities - cultural events, sports clubs, and various social gatherings. However, not all clubs were equally easy to join when staying for only one semester, as some activities require longer-term commitment.
activities_recommended: If you live on Res (on-campus housing), there are many free weekly activities that change from week to week. They are great for meeting new people and settling into the community.
weekend_recommendations: Australia offers countless beautiful places to explore, but the Great Ocean Road is an absolute must-see. It’s one of the most scenic coastal drives in the world.
culture_adjustment: The Australian culture is not very different from Danish culture - if anything, it’s more relaxed - so it was generally easy to adapt.
cultural_challenges: I lived with other international students, so I was exposed to multiple cultures beyond the Australian one. The biggest challenges were adjusting to different food habits and sleeping routines within the shared housing.
culture_appreciated: Australians are incredibly outgoing and helpful, which I really appreciated. It made everyday interactions warm and enjoyable.
top3_advice: Save up beforehand so you can travel and explore Australia as much as possible. Take time to explore the wide range of courses Deakin offers - there are many unique options. Be social from the beginning. It can be exhausting at first, but it makes a huge difference in building a network and settling in.
other_useful_info: Be aware of the location of the Deakin campus it is quite a distance from central Melbourne, so factor that into your expectations for commuting and city activities.
most_rewarding: I gained both academically and personally, but the most rewarding aspect was learning to stand on my own in a new country, new culture, and new university environment. It taught me a great deal about myself.
greatest_challenge: For me, the biggest challenge was speaking English all the time and participating actively in classes in a second language. However, it was also the aspect that taught me the most.

crucial_aspects: An institution in high regard within my field of interest as well as a tradition for international cooperation. I wanted to get a feel for the advancements and prospects in the field in order to decide if I wanted to devote my career to its pursuits. Finally I wanted a place with an interesting and different culture and an opportunity to try and find my feet in that.
overall_comments: As I was only there for 6 months, I didn't invest time in learning the native tongue prior to my stay. I hind sight this was a mistake that let to some social difficulties. The institution and administration around it was overall excellent.
info_ease: Very easy - the administration was always very helpful and easy to get in touch with
arrival_assistance: I received several e-mails with important information about what, when and how, in order to get set up in my new surroundings.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: As I was only there for 6 months, I didn't invest time in learning the native tongue prior to my stay. I hind sight this was a mistake that let to some social difficulties. The institution and administration around it was overall excellent.
registration_process: I registered for a pre-planned semester called 'a minor', which contained a selection of 7 courses of a total 30 ECTS - the registration for these happened all at once, and so I only needed to register for the exams as they came along
registration_help: The administration was always very helpful and available - both in person and per e-mail.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted and so there were no issues. I do not know however, if this generally applies outside the pre-planned 'minor'-structure.
registration_advice: Register as much in advance as possible. Additionally, for some reason students are not automatically signed up for the exams when registering for the course - they have to do that manually 6 weeks before the examination date. Remember to do that! Or ideally just do it at the first day of the courses - you might be forced to do a re-sit or take the exam on reduced time if you forget the deadline.
academics_comments: As I was only there for 6 months, I didn't invest time in learning the native tongue prior to my stay. I hind sight this was a mistake that let to some social difficulties. The institution and administration around it was overall excellent.
course_level: The university was a technical university and so I felt that the importance rested more on being able to apply, not necessarily understand - at least not in a deductive sense. Furthermore, the courses were held across faculties (physics, math, computer science, electro engineers, etc.) and so the level of theory was restricted to a 'lowest common denominator'. If one sought a deep theoretical understanding of the field, I would therefore say that the level was quite low. However, what they set out to do was the cultivate interdisciplinary cooperation and a broad understanding of the field, and that I think they succeded with quite nicely.
teaching_comparison: Much more 'Here are the general results, derived in a hand wavy manner, now go and apply them' as opposed to the approach at UCPH which I personally feel is more rooted in students understanding the 'why/how' and the capability to derive theory themselves. I think the difference rests on the institution being a technical university with close ties to the industry, which is fine, but something to keep in mind.
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled in the minor "Quantum Science and Quantum Information" of 30 ECTS total spanning over a semester. The sub-courses included: - TN3105 Mathematics for Quantum Physics - TN3126 Information and Computation - TN3166-A Semiconductor Quantum Bits - TN3166-B Superconductor Quantum Bits - TN3145 Quantum Communication and Computation - TN3156 Quantum Sensing and Measurement - TN3175 Quantum Engineering Group Project
recommended_courses: I think this package is recommendable to anyone wishing an overview of the current field of quantum computation and information - given that one is interested in the interdisciplinary more engineer-like approach of things. If you want to understand theory on a deep level (as a physicist), this is not programme for you :)
unexpected_costs: Mostly events or going on bigger trips.
cost_comparison: Food was generally cheaper than in DK - I especially noticed avocados, nuts, beer and coffee(!) To eat out on a restaurant however was kind of expensive, but where isn't it? ;)
activities_available: The university has what I would describe as a sports/crea -city next to it called 'X'. For an annual subscribtion you get access to every sport, dance form, martial arts, meditation, yoga, spinning, drawing, music -class - you name it! Additionally many of the more competitive associations in the city (swimming, rowing, sailing) are under the umbrella of X and so generally cheaper that elsewhere. Social events are arranged both by X but also volunteer student associations at or around campus. For instance they have a very serious/popular culture of sorority houses with rituals, uniforms, etc. as you picture it in american high school/college films.
activities_recommended: Definitely subscribe to X, as it opens a lot of doors to try out many different sports, activities and events - athletic as well as creative. The sororities have a reputation of being pretty rough in their rituals (cutting the hair of new-comers or making them eat live fish etc.). I personally had a blast at the association DSZ Wave, which combines swimming, cycling and running for very low cost, with the opportunity to work out every day outside the weekend if that is what you wish. They have a great community and lots of social events/activities - no pre-history in either discipline is required. This is generally true for all the above - just go there!
weekend_recommendations: I recommend to plan trips outside the home city - go see Haag, Rotterdam and Amsterdam, but also all the small cities around the country. Additionally I had great experience with using Flixbuses to visit the nearby countries (Germany, Belgium - even France) for a prolonged weekend.
culture_adjustment: Overall the culture was very easy to blend into. People are very friendly and ready to drag you along as a newcomer. However, if you want social interaction outside the community of international students, I highly recommend learning some Dutch! Not that people dont speak excellent english, but in large groups of Dutch people they quickly fall back to their native tongue (understandably), and then you quickly lose touch with the conversation. So do yourself a favor and learn at least something if you really want to get involved with the locals!
socializing_tips: Beer is a hit! As a general rule I would say: never say no to an invitation - always yes. It won't hurt you and you get to meet a lot of new people and try new stuff. Also try to be proactive yourself and invite people for lunch, coffee, movie night, whatever. The more you do this in the beginning, the better - otherwise you might quickly get into the habbit of just sticking with yourself...
cultural_challenges: Maybe the alcohol culture is a little strong, but if you're form DK it shouldn't be too much of a chok. I never experienced a situation where I felt forced to drink beyond my limits though.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and the importance of being a good host/guest (bring each other flowers and similar stuff)
top3_advice: Get out of your apartment! Seek out students and associations - the sooner the better. Sign up for X and try out something new each week! Keep up with your studies, but remember all the other things in life. You are there for a limited amount of time - make sure you make the best of it.
most_rewarding: Feeling capable - that it was in my power to take care of my self and build a life of studying, living and meeting people from scratch in a foreign country.
greatest_challenge: To manage myself when things got rough or I was feeling down - you want to have a web of people and activities to keep you up and going, or chances are you might tend to isolate yourself in your room and jsut kill time untill you can go home again.

The course catalogue of the packages was readily available online, and contained course codes which could be looked up on the universitys platform. As an exchange student, I did not have to pick any electives or apply for course, once I had been enrolled.

course_level: They strongly resembled the master's courses at my home university. The structure was almost identical, having two quarters in a semester, each quarter often consisting of a a design course, with a theory course alongside it. The theory courses would however only make up 5 ECTS points, where the Design courses took up 10 ECTS points. The expected amount and level of deliverables were higher than expected - meaning higher than I've been accustomed to at my home university. This is rather niché being a design-oriented master's programme, but it meant for some very, very busy final weeks for each and every course.
teaching_comparison: Indeed very similar. A lot of the course teaching consisted of lectures backed up by following excersizes.
courses_enrolled: AR1LA011 - Architecture and Landscape: Design Studio (10 ECTS) AR1LA021 - Architecture and Landscape: Theory, Method and Critical Thinking (5 ECTS) AR1LA051 - Dutch Landscape: Design Studio (10 ECTS) AR1LA061 - Dutch Landscape: Theory, Method and Critical Thinking (5 ECTS)
recommended_courses: The same courses - there simply are no other choices available to exchange students on the Landscape Architecture programme.
unexpected_costs: Some housing in the Netherlands do not include certain public services such as collection of refuse or maintenance of sewers and the waternet within the municipality. It is possible to receive surcharges for these by letter. I strongly suggest to check your contract, and subsequently contact the municipality in order to prepare and budget for these costs. The transportation by train can become enormous quite quickly - I recommend all students to invest in the personal OV-chipcard, with a monthly weekend-free subscription. It is equivalent to one trip to Amsterdam and back, each month, and allows for tree train service all weekend, all over the Netherlands. Some intercity trains (named Intercity Direct) require an additional ticket - it is not always apparent on the route planning apps, that you'll need one, so make sure to check the type of train as well. They aren't expensive at all, but the fine for not having one sure is.
cost_comparison: Generally, I was surprised at how similar everything was in price to Denmark. Groceries are just about the same in my experience, with take-out being somewhat cheaper - for better or for worse.
activities_available: Tonnes were arranged, however I mostly participated in private arrangements between friends from my classes.
activities_recommended: There is an introduction programme in place, which I particapted in myself. This was a great opportunity to meet new people, and become acquianted with the campus grounds and facilities.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend most design-interested students to visit the Museumpark in Rotterdam, as well as the Nieuwe Instituut right next to it. Otherwise, both Den Haag and Amsterdam are full of art museums, highlighting dutch painting history - these I found to be very fulfilling.
culture_adjustment: Rather easy, I must say. Denmark and the Netherlands seem strikingly similar.
socializing_tips: Attend as many after school activities as possible, and be yourself
cultural_challenges: I found none particularly challenging - the Dutch people I met were generally open and friendly.
culture_appreciated: The appreciation of bicycles in the Netherlands is unavoidable - and having a bike is really quite crucial for getting around. Luckily, there are several great opportunities for finding a used bike, or renthing on at a fair price.
top3_advice: - Take care of the paperwork in due time - Make sure to read the fine print - Befriend as many people as you would allow yourself
other_useful_info: Nothing in particular - it is a well structured University with tonnes of different ways of contacting them regarding any issues that may arise. Professors are also generally friendly and helpful, so don't hesitate to ask if you're unsure - even if it is regarding non-academic issues.
most_rewarding: Interacting with new and likeminded people from all over the world in my class was very fulfilling. I've made new friendships which I look forward to cherish for many years to come.
greatest_challenge: Overcoming the housing circumstances ended up being a real nuisance. Despite this, I thought the exchange was rather challenge free. The only real tasks apart from attending classes of course, are paperwork leading up to the exchange.

crucial_aspects: Duke Law School’s strong academic reputation, its high-quality academic environment, and the opportunity to gain educational and cultural experience in the United States.
info_ease: Very easy. The team at Duke provided clear guidance and made the process straightforward.
arrival_assistance: No assistance was needed.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process was very easy. Oleg and the team at Duke provided clear instructions and frequent follow-up emails, making it hard to miss any steps.
registration_help: There were presentations on some of the courses, most syllabi were available online, and it was possible to contact professors directly to discuss a specific course.
registration_success: Very successful. I had no problems registering for the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: If there are specific courses you prefer, register for them early before they fill up. This is explained clearly during orientation, and it was not a problem for me.
course_level: The exams may be slightly easier than in Denmark, but most courses require active participation and involve cold calling, which we do not have in Denmark. It is better than it sounds and encourages engagement. The difficulty of a course can vary depending on the professor, so that is worth considering. Almost all courses also have a fixed grade median of 3.5.
teaching_comparison: Teaching at Duke Law is more demanding in terms of preparation and participation. Unlike at UCPH, where it is possible to attend seminars without having prepared and catch up later, students are expected to have completed the readings in advance due to active participation and cold calling. The professors are also more engaged with students and are generally excellent teachers who really know their subject matter—often to a higher degree than what I have experienced in Denmark. They actively encourage one-on-one meetings with students, which is not common at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Business Associations Business & Economic Law Firm Practice (Credit/No Credit) Legal Analysis, Research & Writing for International Students Distinct Aspects of U.S. Law Negotiation
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of the courses I took. Business Associations with Professor Bishop is a bit tougher than the others, but it is very well taught and provides a strong learning experience.
unexpected_costs: Food and groceries were significantly more expensive than in Denmark, especially if you do not want to rely on fast food. There is also a lack of public transportation, which meant spending quite a lot on Ubers.
cost_comparison: See above.
activities_available: There was a great gym with excellent athletic facilities, as well as many social activities such as weekly bar reviews and other student-organized events.
activities_recommended: I would recommend attending the weekly bar review, as it is a great way to socialize, meet other students, and get to know the law school community.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend going on road trips, as they are a great way to explore more of the U.S. and make the most of weekends and holidays.
culture_adjustment: It was easy to adjust. Being part of an LLM cohort with other international students meant that everyone was in a similar situation, which made the transition smooth.
socializing_tips: It can be harder to socialize with local students, as many American J.D. students tend to spend most of their time with each other. However, having an open mind, being proactive, and making an effort to socialize helps, and it will be fine over time.
cultural_challenges: Americans’ tendency to engage in frequent small talk, which takes some getting used to.
culture_appreciated: The openness of people and how welcoming and friendly they were.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared for a participation-based teaching style with required readings and cold calling. 2. Register early for any courses you are particularly interested in. 3. Be social and say yes to activities—make an effort to have fun and engage with the experience.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Getting to know the other students in the LLM groups, as well as some American students, and building meaningful connections.
greatest_challenge: Initially, my English skills were a challenge when I first started at Duke, but they improved significantly over time. If English is holding you back, it should not discourage you—many international students are not fully fluent at the beginning either.

crucial_aspects: It was important that the culture was different from my home culture, and that the language spoken in the given country was a language I hadn't previously been exposed to.
info_ease: It was very difficult to find the information I needed in terms of acceptance to the host university as well as what to expect next. The incoming mobility coordinator at Eötvös Loránd University was rude and didn't seem as if she wanted to help the incoming students, however, they had a new coordinator appointed some time during the semester who does her job well. All in all, it was not easy to figure out how to access information. Moreover, we received two emails on orientation, but the second email a lot of us did not receive, which of course caused a lot of stir and stress among us, because we had missed important information.
arrival_assistance: None. We were told we would have a tutor, but the tutor never contacted me, and when I contacted her, she said she was on vacation, but that she would contact me when she returned, but she never did.
arrival_comments: The orientation barely existed, this can and should be done much better.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We would be notified of the process 1 week before we had to register. We were to contact the professors of the courses we wanted to attend. When the professor gave us permission to attend the course, we needed a signature. When all your courses had been accepted by the professors, we needed to send the signatures to the incoming mobility. However, because everything was online, we could also just send the emails from the professors to the coordinator.
registration_help: Not much help, as the previous coordinator was still the only help, and she didn't help us very much. Often times she didn't reply at all, so we were kind of left alone.
registration_success: I registered for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Be prepared that it is an absolute mess, but the coordinator is much nicer now, so she will definetly be more helpful.
course_level: The level of courses was good and fairly high in some courses, however, when term paper/exams came it was obvious that they haven't been taught how to write an academic paper, so the level of academic papers weren't too high compared to UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was very different, as you receive a mark for your participation as well, meaning that a lot more participated in the class discussions and that made it even more interesting.

recommended_courses: I recommend The History of Political History, generally any course with the professor in this course. Moreover, 21st Century Critical Theory, Gender in Contemporary Fiction, and if interested in phonology and the like choose English Varieities.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Transportation was less expensive, housing was more expensive than expected.
activities_available: There were a lot of sports courses, but I did not attend.

socializing_tips: Just talk to them, they are very interested in you and why you chose Hungary.
cultural_challenges: Not that many differences actually, rather the language.
culture_appreciated: I appreciate their welcoming spirit and their curiosity.
top3_advice: Be prepared to not know everything that is going to happen in orientation. Go to the social activities. Do not sign up for Erasmus Life Budapest, unless you love partying.
other_useful_info: If you're from the University of Copenhagen it may seem a bit much and challenging that you receive marks on everything you do, but the professors are (in general) very nice and easy-going.
most_rewarding: The social experience.
greatest_challenge: Adapting to the study culture at the university.

socializing_tips: Sadly we didn't meet many.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier.
culture_appreciated: Many had a quite good humor. We went to a lot of comedy shows.
top3_advice: I) Socialize all you can, there are hundreds of exchange students II) Travel in the weekends and holidays and see more of Eastern Europe III) Enjoy Budapest as the great city it is - it never sleeps.
other_useful_info: Before leaving I was a bit afraid that Budapest was more of a weekend get-away city. I didn't get tired of it at all though. It is a great city with a lot to do and it is also cheap, which makes it a bit more fun to be an exchange student. Even though it might be a little uncommon to go to Budapest/Hungary from Denmark, it is a very popular destination from other countries. I think we were close to a thousand exchange students that semester, even with covid and everything. I only spent time with people from other nationalities, which I think is also the point of going on exchange - and I made some very close and good friends. Furthermore, we rarely ate at home, because food and drinks are very cheap. But you still have to save up, because you spent more than you think. Regarding the university, I liked the campus and the extra activities. The academic level in the exams was not very difficult, but I still feel like I learned a lot through the semester, without being slammed with "homework". All together I felt it was a great place to be an exchange student.
most_rewarding: All the experiences and getting some new relations. It is good to get a break from your everyday life in DK.
greatest_challenge: The war in Ukraine, which made our situation a bit unsure in the beginning, since we all of a sudden were quite close. But I also think it was important to see what was happening, and how many of the locals in Budapest that did everything they could to help the refugees. You are in your own bubble on your exchange, but there is still and outside world, which we were reminded. We met quite many citizens from Ukraine, and I think it was an important experience to meet and talk with them as well. Besides from that, the city didn't change much during our stay, and a lot of turist were still visiting.

other_useful_info: Have patience and trust that it will work out and allow yourself to relax as much as you need, because the amount of pressure can be rough.
most_rewarding: Dance classes in my free time.
greatest_challenge: The whole administration process from the first application in UCPH, all the steps during the preparations before the exchange, the registration and not knowing if the international office in Denmark would approve my courses and not knowing if the Erasmus Grant would be cut in half or not.

crucial_aspects: Going to a destination with a different culture than the Danish, and in an area of Europe, where I didn't have much knowledge.
info_ease: Very easy. I received all the information needed in good time before my arrival. The professor, in charge of the Erasmus-programme at the host-university, reached out to us and gave us a digital guide with a lot of information, which provided all the help I needed.
arrival_assistance: Besides the information handed to me digitally, we had a meeting at the faculty, where we were introduced to the place. This meant information about studying at the university, living in the city and other useful information. We received contact information for different people, who we could reach out to, if we had questions/needed help regarding studying, social life or other things.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The process was divided into two phases. The first phase, where courses were distributed randomly among the students registering for the specific course. In the second phase, we could apply for new courses, if we didn't get the courses we applied for in the first phase. In this phase, the courses were distributed by the principle of first come first served.
registration_help: We could always reach out to the university if we had questions about the process, how to manage our time-table, or if we wanted to change courses after already choosing some.
registration_success: Some courses were cancelled, some were conflicting with each other's timetables, and others had a very limited amount of students able to participate, which meant that I had to reconsider and find courses did I didn't expect to participate in before leaving Denmark.
registration_advice: Be open to courses you didn't expect to participate in before leaving Denmark. Write the university if you are really dependent on a specific course or if you made a mistake in the registration process.
course_level: Every course is 5 ECTS points, which meant that the courses are quite small compared to the usual size of courses at the university in Copenhagen. The expected preparation time is way below what I have been used to, and the level is, in general, below what I have seen at Copenhagen University.
teaching_comparison: At my host university, most of the teaching was like a lecture at UCPH. This means that the style of teaching is less active for the students. Usually, the students at the host university do not have to prepare anything for the classes, which means that the preparation for classes only exists of reading the provided material.
courses_enrolled: - The Law of the Internal Market 1. - Civil Liberties in the United States - Multinational enterprises and private international law - Current challenges in international, European and Hungarian refugee law - The law of asset planning and asset management - Chapters from the History of Constitutional Adjudication
recommended_courses: The law of asset planning and asset management: - This course gives a comparative look on asset-legislation around the world. The course is a good way of touching upon a new area of law, which does not play the biggest role on the bachelor at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: I did not really encounter any unexpected costs
cost_comparison: Groceries are in general not as cheap, compared to the prices seen in Denmark, as they were just 4-5 years ago. Public transportation is really cheap as student - both inside and outside of the city.
activities_available: A lot of sports clubs organized by the university in many different types of sports. The Erasmus organisations makes a lot of social events for Erasmus-students from all over the city. This could be hikes, trips outside of the city, parties, movie-nights, museums days, visiting local restaurants etc.
activities_recommended: Participate in a sports club: Its a good way to meet people in the beginning of you stay. This makes sure that you meet people in different contexts and it is also a great way of meeting locals.
weekend_recommendations: There is a lot of good towns within a few hours of Budapest. Many of them are close to interesting nature areas, and visiting the towns are often a better way of getting a broader impression of the Hungarian people than staying inside the capital. For instance: - Eger, and the Bükk national park - Visegrad - Esztergom - The Balaton lake - The Tokaj region There is also good access to other central-european countries, such as Austria, Slovakia, Poland, Rumania and Croatia - all of these countries have interesting sights close to the Hungarian border and can often be reached easily by either train or bus.
culture_adjustment: It is really easy to adjust to the local culture. I didn't really have any practical challenges with settling and a lot of things work in a way that is similar to Denmark. Some things actually work more smoothly compared to Denmark. The introduction period was vital in adjusting to a new country, and especially finding people you like to spend time with when not at the university is important. It makes it much easier to explore the culture when you have good people by you side.
socializing_tips: Be active in classes and talk to other students before and after class. Participate in a sports club or another type of organization where locals participate. Go to parties at locations, where locals would go as well.
cultural_challenges: The Hungarian language is really different from everything else, and the locals(the professors) do often have an accent in English, which can be a bit difficult to understand at times.
culture_appreciated: Its a culture which bears marks from big historical events, and this can be seen and felt throughout the entire city. There is a lot to learn about and this often has a greater connection to Europe in general. For instance the current situation with Hungary in the EU, the communist rule in Hungary, the two world wars etc.
top3_advice: 1. Participate in as many social events as possible, especially in the beginning of your stay 2. Follow, prepare for and pay attention to the classes during the semester, in order to have a chill exam period and a good ending to your stay 3. It is really easy to settle and manage the practical stuff about moving to Budapest, so don't stress out about this. The university will also give you all the help and information you need.
other_useful_info: Make sure to make a plan for every week and make sure that you don't have to study during the weekend. It was important for me to make the most of the weekend, hence why I made sure that I didn't have to study when I was planning to go on trips etc.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from different cultures and sharing experiences and knowledge with them. Getting to live in another country, getting to know a new culture and exploring Central Europe.
greatest_challenge: Finding time for all of the things I wanted to do and see.

crucial_aspects: ELTE is a very international university with people from all sorts of countries and a lot of research going on. Budapest is a vibrant city with a rich international community and it is easy to find cheap accommodation
info_ease: Relatively easy upon arrival. The hard part was the planning before arrival.
arrival_assistance: Introduction week with all the information needed
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I just had to fill in a survey
registration_help: There is an international coordinator that i emailed a lot with before arrival. He can be very slow sometimes however
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. This wasn't clear before arrival, but apparently ERASMUS-students are highly prioritized in getting the courses they want, so even though I registered way later than everybody else and it seemed like I was on the waiting list as number 30 out of 20 on most of the courses I ended up getting all of them.
registration_advice: I don't really know. It was a huge mess the months before i arrived because KU wanted to know which courses I were to take even before ELTE knew which courses would be available.
course_level: The level of the courses was very easy
teaching_comparison: I had more practical courses than on KU and less lectures. The relation to the teachers was more like the relation you have to teachers in high school than in university in Denmark. Most of my classes were mandatory to attend and autonomy wasn't as important as it is in Denmark
courses_enrolled: Individual Differences in Cognition CBT-skills development Traumainformed individual and group interventions PTSD and Trauma-therapy The Psychology of Empathy and Assistance Altered States of Consciousness and Hypnosis Career Development Communication Training
recommended_courses: PTSD and Trauma-therapy was very nice
unexpected_costs: I had to buy some boxes in Ikea and i spend a bit more on take away the first month because of the cockroaches
cost_comparison: I was a bit surprised that super market prices in Hungary are exactly the same as in Denmark
activities_available: A lot of different sports, that you could even get credits for, and also musical ensembles, choir etc.
activities_recommended: I didn't attend any, so I don't know
weekend_recommendations: In Budapest there's both the regular ESN network, but also a private organisation called Erasmus Life Budapest. Both of them have a lot of events, so I would say it's definitely worth to take a look at their Instagram accounts. I think there's nearly an event every day
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: I got an amazing mentor via ESN, so that's definitely worth it. I think they'll tell you in the introduction days, but the app where you can apply is called Papaya
cultural_challenges: Maybe that people in the streets seem less happy than they do in Denmark. I think that affected my mood a little bit
culture_appreciated: The folk dance is really fun to take part in and they always appreciate newcomers.
top3_advice: - Have a lot of patience before going, and keep your nerves calm, because in the end it will probably work out even though it's hard - Get a mentor - If you like to party try and make sure you haven't got anything scheduled on Tuesday mornings, as Monday is the big party day for ERASMUS students in Budapest
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: To get to know a lot of people from different parts of the world. A new and very strong appreciation for the Danish system and society
greatest_challenge: To create a social network. In the beginning it can be a little lonely

crucial_aspects: Mostly going to a city and a part of Europe I had not been to before, and get the chance to really experience the place over a longer period of time.
info_ease: I found it a bt hard to find information, especially in terms of courses.
arrival_assistance: When arriving to the university we got some general information about social things and school related info
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I found it confusing and a lot of the courses from the additional list was not offered.
registration_help: There was help at the international office, but they seemed to be to few people working there, so it was hard getting help when you needed it.
registration_success: I managed in the end because I was allowed by masters teachers to join some of their courses, but I did not get all the courses I initially wanted
registration_advice: I would advice them to take a good look at the courses available, and maybe have a plan b if the courses boy planned to take are not offered, or does not match each other in the schedule
course_level: The level of the courses I did not really think matched the level at UCPH, but also the courses are smaller so it is hard to compare fully.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was usually more loose, but it was also more normal with smaller classes, which I really liked.
courses_enrolled: Wellbeing and Health Promotion at the Workplace Altered States of Consciousness and Hypnosis Culture and Psychology Culture and Society Introduction to Counseling Psychology Leadership and Organizational Studies Psychological Ethics and Legal Issues Study and Communication Skills
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the Altered States of Consciousness and Hypnosis class, and also heard a lot of good things about the Psychedelics class and Sex Education class.
