unexpected_costs: Did not really encounter any
cost_comparison: Groceries was more expensive than expected. Public transport and city bikes are really cheap.
activities_available: There is a lot of activities at all times, and you also have the opportunity to have sports as elective courses. There was a lot of different sports, a lot of city life events, and also more casual clubs.
activities_recommended: I would recommend doing some kind of sports. It is also cheaper than in Denmark to do sports in Hungary. I would also recommend going hiking.
weekend_recommendations: A lot of good hiking trips outside and inside the city, a lot of culture and architecture to see, and also fun nightlife.
culture_adjustment: I think it was not too hard, also because you share the experience with other exchange students. But of course there is small cultural differences that will be weird in the beginning, but also super interesting.
socializing_tips: I think going to local events, they use Facebook a lot for events.
cultural_challenges: In the beginning I was surprised by the temperament of the people in Hungary, because I was not used to people yelling in public, but people are also very sweet. It can also be a bit hard to get used to seeing poverty and homeless people a lot more than in Copenhagen
culture_appreciated: I really loved the cultural life with a lot of live music, folk music, folk dance, and cool authentic places where you could hang out both day and evening
top3_advice: Be a bit proactive with finding courses in the beginning and then it will probably work out Don't stress too much with the social events in the introduction week, there is plenty of chances to meet people Don't stress about the exams, even though there might be many
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of
most_rewarding: I think the social part, and also experiencing the city
greatest_challenge: Balancing spending time with new friends, doing all the things you wanted to experience, having people to visit and also getting alone time could be challenging

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience a big and exciting city in a country with cultural differences to Denmark, and which I didn't know much about.
overall_comments: I would highly recommend anyone taking a semester abroad. Budapest is an excellent city for studying as it has a rich history, diverse culture, affordable living, and a lively social scene filled with young people, including many international students. Living independently in a new country and meeting people from around the globe was an amazing experience.
info_ease: It was very easy, the university, ELTE, provides all the information you need.
arrival_assistance: Plenty of assistance, as this is also provided by ELTE by mail and in person during the first weeks of school.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I would highly recommend anyone taking a semester abroad. Budapest is an excellent city for studying as it has a rich history, diverse culture, affordable living, and a lively social scene filled with young people, including many international students. Living independently in a new country and meeting people from around the globe was an amazing experience.
registration_process: It was divided in two parts: you register for the courses you wish based on a list from the university's website, which has detailed information on the courses and their exams. They use the system, Neptun. If you don't get the ones you want you can re-register in the second round, and you can also do this if you change your mind about one or several of the courses.
registration_help: The coordinators and mentors were very available to help with the process.
registration_success: I got all the classes i wanted.
registration_advice: Check the courses beforehand, also in regard to the timetables to make sure they don't overlap. The coordinator will make it really simple for you to have an overview over this, so don't stress about it. You can probably also manage to switch courses during the first days of school.
academics_comments: I would highly recommend anyone taking a semester abroad. Budapest is an excellent city for studying as it has a rich history, diverse culture, affordable living, and a lively social scene filled with young people, including many international students. Living independently in a new country and meeting people from around the globe was an amazing experience.
course_level: The level was actually higher than I had expected, and the professors was really competent and good at teaching. However, some of the classes were a bit chaotic and less structured than what I was used to at UCPH, and because the courses are so "small" most of them will be more superficial than at UCPH. The exams was much easier, being mostly essays on self-chosen topics or short in-class written exams.
teaching_comparison: It was similar to UCPH, and varied from class to class. Most classes followed a lecture format, with teachers presenting the syllabus using PowerPoint. However, some courses emphasized in-class participation, group work, and presentations.
courses_enrolled: Consumer Protection, International Criminal Law, European Private Law, Childrens' rights in the EU law and Policy, Fundamental Rights Before Courts & EU Human Rights and Criminal Justice.
recommended_courses: International Criminal Law was very interesting and was run by passionated teachers. EU Human Rights and Criminal Justice was my favourite class, as it was 5 hours every other Friday, which gave time for in depth work on the subjects. The teacher was highly competent and good at creating in-class discussions.
unexpected_costs: My rent was much higher, as I lived alone and in a very central neighborhood. I also traveled much more than I expected, the costs of which are not included in the above. I would recommend to factor in this as you probably will travel a lot to many of the nice places close to Budapest.
cost_comparison: Supermarkets were more expensive than I thought. Transportation was extremely cheap, less than 2000 HUF for a monthly pass to travel through entire Hungary.
activities_available: There were many sports courses available as well as a free trial week for trying out any you were interested in. The Erasmus organizations also planned several social activities for any taste on a daily basis.
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend to sign up for a sports course like Volleyball, to meet other people, or pilates or spinning as exercise. It's a good way to meet people and to experience a new hobby.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend to spend weekends and holidays exploring the city or other small, but beautiful, towns of Hungary. Many amazing places is also only a train ride away like Slovenia, Prague and Vienna. But Budapest is big and very active, so you will not be bored!
culture_adjustment: It was very easy.
socializing_tips: I didn't socialize much with local students, but, as mentioned, joining a sport will guarantee you to meet locals. It was also nice to go bars that were not touristic (you will not meet them at Szimpla Kert).
cultural_challenges: The elder people speak non to very little English, which could be challenging but not a big problem. Hungary is in general a more conservative country than Denmark, and though I didn't have any negative experiences myself, it was something I was aware of. Even though the people of Budapest seemed much more open-minded, and there are many pride-friendly places, it is worth noting the Hungarian laws on homosexuality ect. before you arrive.
culture_appreciated: Budapest is a beautiful city to walk around in and the way it looks today bears the mark of a long history (such as the ruin bars and thermal baths). Today, it is very multicultural and has something for every taste.
top3_advice: First, the university is very helpful and will do a lot to make you comfortable. Second, they have a lot of interesting courses and competent teachers and the university of ELTE is in general more "open" than I would have expected from a country like Hungary. Third, it's a big city that offers many fun experiences if you are open to look for them
other_useful_info: I met only one other student from Denmark, so it might be worth knowing that Budapest is not a common exchange destination for Danish students. However, it is for many other countries, so it's not a problem to meet kind people and get friends!
most_rewarding: The people i met was the best part of the experience, but it was also really rewarding to become more independent and learn to live on your own outside of the comfort of your own familiar country.
greatest_challenge: In general it was no too challenging, but the greatest challenge was probably the practical preparation and registration process. However, it was not as difficult as I feared.

crucial_aspects: For me it was important to study in a European city, and preferably a capital or big city. Budapest was not my top priority but ended up being perfect for me. It was also a big plus, that it was a bit cheaper to live in than some of the other cities
info_ease: Before leaving for Budapest it was a bit hard to find out who to contact from the university in Budapest with questions and I did not know which courses I was going to take, when I arrived because the application process for courses opened a bit late in my opinion, and a lot of the courses I got pre-approved did not get created in the end. Therefore I had to redo almost all of the administrative work I had done before arriving and had to spend a significant amount of time getting a proper overlook and finding the information I needed.
arrival_assistance: The host univeristy in Budapest was not the best at replying to mails, before I got there. They were closed for summer-break 2 weeks in August, where everything needed to fall into place, before leaving, which stressed me out a bit. Once their break ended, it was necessary for me to call them a couple of times, and they seemed a bit stressed out and annoyed with this. This can maybe have something to do with the fact that they told the students upon arrival, that they had been understaffed. Once I got to Budapest, however, they were really nice and helpful, had gotten another staff-member for the Erasmus-students, and everything fell into place
arrival_comments: Once I got to Budapest, everything got sorted out with the assistance from the host university and also the very helpful assistance from KU. So my advice would be to, of course have all your documents, pre-approvals and applications filled out and sent to the respective parties, but most of it had to be re-done when I got there, so try not to stress too much about this stuff beforehand
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Look above in the "orientation and asistance upon arrival" field.
registration_help: It was possible to send mails to both the university, that had a mail address for incoming Erasmus students and call them, even though you have to search a bit to find the phone numbers. Once I was in Budapest I ended up having to text some of the specific professors teaching the different courses I wanted to register for, as it was up to them to decide if I could take their courses as some of these were masters-courses, and they seem a be a bit strict about only accepting master students for the master courses in the beginning. Once I e-mailed the professors however, these would most of the time let me attend the course with a few exceptions
registration_success: Mostly succesful I would say. As beforementioned some of the courses I originally got preregistered ended up not being created and it seemed like I would not be able to register for some of the ones I needed to cover for my obligatory course at home as these were masters courses, so for a while I was worried that I would not be able to take enough ECTS-credits at the host university to cover for this. But it ended up working out, and I got most of the courses I wanted and needed by texting the specific professors. Fortunately, ELTE offers many courses in the same fields, I think, so it should be possible to find something in your field
registration_advice: Be persistent in telling the respective parties about which courses you need to take. Then they will be helpful in making sure, you can get enough credits in my experience
course_level: Read above
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was noticeably different from that of UCPH and the academic level was lower. The courses are a lot less ECTS-credits, so I took courses with 2, 3 or 4 ECTS meaning that you have to take more courses than at UCPH. I did not find the content of the courses as challenging as UCPH - for me the hardest part was organising all the courses and getting an overlook of the demands and requirements of each of the courses, as some of these had exams, some did not, some you were only allowed to miss a few times, and some did not keep attendance at all, and some had assignments every week, while others did not. For me the reading burden was very low compared to UCPH, and for some of the courses it was not required to read anything. I had to do a lot of assignments through the semester though. For me, the facilities were not as great as those of UCPH in my opinion. There were no auditoriums and no real places to sit and study, which I missed.
courses_enrolled: - Human Memory across the Lifespan - Cognitive Psychology 2 - Cognitive/Affective Neuropsychology - Cognitive/Affective Neuroscience - Crisis, Crossroads, Trauma and Resilience in Films - Hungarian Culture: Narratives of Freedom and Oppression - Psychological Ethics and Legal Issues - Psychology and Crime - Psychology and Crime - Case studies
recommended_courses: I really liked the "psychology and crime - case studies" and found it very interesting. Also the "cognitive psychology 2" had some nice topics on the syllabus. The professors of the different courses I attended were mostly really nice and passionate about their subjects, which was inspiring to me
unexpected_costs: The utilities in my housing ended up being much more expensive that the price (50 euros) we payed each month beforehand. This was the case for many of the people I met there.
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than I thought - pretty much the same as in Denmark. Going out to eat and drink was cheap in my experience. Transportation was really cheap - with the student discount, you could get a monthly past for all of Hungary for only 40 dkk.
activities_available: I actually do not know. ESN (Erasmus Social Network) and ELB (Erasmus Life Budapest), which were 2 organisations for Erasmus students were however, really good at organising parties and events, and I attended a lot of these and found them really nice
activities_recommended: I would recommend attending the ELB events, because these are fun and a great opportunity to meet new people
weekend_recommendations: There are very good opportunities for going out to eat or drink, so I would recommend taking advantage of that. The historical sights were really impressive
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy
socializing_tips: Join the ELB events
cultural_challenges: The attitude of hungarian people towards foreigners was not always the nicest and some did not speak english
culture_appreciated: The city was beautiful and there were a lot of things to do
top3_advice: 1. Be patient and positive about the application and registration process - it will get sorted out in the end 2. Budapest has a lot to offer in regards to going out, the nightlife and the cultural sights - take advantage of it 3. I only met 2 other danish people in the whole semester. But it did not matter actually - my advice is to be open and take it as an opportunity to meet interesting people and learn about other countries and cultures
other_useful_info: I think I have covered all of it in the other fields
most_rewarding: The whole experience actually. It was very nice to experience how everything works at other universities, I met a lot of nice people and enjoyed living in Budapest a lot
greatest_challenge: Of course it can be tough being away at times, but it was definitely worth it

crucial_aspects: I wanted to live in a hustling and bustling city, in a country with a very different culture compared to ours in Denmark.
overall_comments: It was the time of my life, and I can't wait to go back to Hungary in one way or the other!
info_ease: The university sends you e-mails that outlines all of the information that are relevant to the exchange students.
arrival_assistance: Besides the briefings via e-mail, they hold a presentation for the new exchange students in the first weeks you're there. Moreover, they quickly respond to inquiries submitted to their e-mail.
arrival_comments: We had a bunch of tutors we were matched with, so we had ample opportunities to seek assistance when necessary.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was the time of my life, and I can't wait to go back to Hungary in one way or the other!
registration_process: You're registered manually by the faculty staff, after which you'll receive your login to the IT-system of the university.
registration_help: It was easy to get in touch with the faculty staff via e-mail, and you can also visit the Erasmus coordinator within his office hours. The professors also gladly answer any questions us students have.
registration_success: I got all of the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: To remember all of the documents that are required, including the proof of attendance - document. I almost forgot the latter!
academics_comments: It was the time of my life, and I can't wait to go back to Hungary in one way or the other!
course_level: I would say that the knowledge of the professors were the same as the knowledge of the professors back in Copenhagen. However, the exams are way more laid-back than the exams we've been through in Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: It's very similar to lectures, but fundamentally different from the seminars. I only had a minor group project once.
courses_enrolled: -European Private Law. -Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism. -Transactions in an International Environment (Mergers & Acquisitions). -Healthcare in the Internal Market. -Law of Asset Planning and Asset Management. -Mobility of Companies in the European Union.
recommended_courses: I particularly recommend the course of "Healthcare in the Internal Market". The professors in that course are generally energetic, and you gain knowledge of the free mobility of EU Citizens in-between healthcare-providers in the member states of the EU.
unexpected_costs: The sheer size of the total utility bill of almost 600 DKK per month.
cost_comparison: -Accomodation is still cheap despite the size of the utility bills! -Groceries and eating out are as expensive as in neighbouring Austria, so it's not that much cheaper than Denmark.
activities_available: I loved the pub crawls, but I know that a lot of people also join the ELTE Sports Association to play, e.g., badminton.
activities_recommended: The ESN events, because the Hungarian organizers of the events are really friendly! Moreover, you meet all kinds of awesome people from all over the world at those social gatherings!
weekend_recommendations: While many other students liked to visit the big cities in neighboring countries, I loved to venture far out into the remote areas of Hungary. I loved to hike on the puszta, i.e., the steppe, but I also liked to travel around in the mountains right outside of Budapest. Lake Velence is also a nice and chill place! My favorite town in Hungary outside of Budapest is Jászberény.
culture_adjustment: I really liked the culture, because the Hungarian people are very proud and helpful. It's important to know that it generally is a more formalistic culture compared to its Danish counterpart.
socializing_tips: Join the ESN events because the Hungarians you'll meet there are really kind! It's also cool to hang out with the Hungarian tutor that's assigned to you.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any of the cultural differences challenging, but it's important to note once again that they're a very proud people. This means that you have to be less direct in your communication than you'd be in Denmark, and show that you respect them in a clearly visible way with your choice of words and body language. Otherwise, they'll generally come across as rude if viewed from a Western vantage point, which is why a lot of tourists from abroad complain about the alleged Hungarian "rudeness", which simply tend to stem from major cultural differences between Western Europe and Eastern Europe.
culture_appreciated: I love how proud and no-nonsense the Hungarian people is! They tend to have a fighter spirit because they've been through a lot in their history. However, they're still tremendously helpful and down-to-earth which I love about them!
top3_advice: -That it's a really good idea to look at the exam type in the course description before you finally choose a course. Some exam types are more intense than others! -That it's a good idea to ask your tutor to show you where the rooms are before the classes commence. It's quite challenging to find your way around in the beginning! -That you can't miss more than three classes in the semester unless you have a doctor's certificate or some form of proven emergency. Otherwise, you can't take the exam at the end and get credits for the course!
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: To immerse myself in a very different society from its Danish counterpart, while meeting people from all over the world. A couple of whom have become really close!
greatest_challenge: The language barrier can be pretty big, because the Hungarians who grew up before the change of regime in the early 1990's didn't learn English but Russian in school. So whether or not you can communicate with the Hungarians tend to depend on which age group they belong to.
other_comments: Only that Budapest has become my favorite city alongside Copenhagen, and that I'm certain you'll fall in love with it as well! It's a truly international city where you can meet people from everywhere!

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte Budapest, fordi jeg gerne ville blive inden for Europa, og fordi jeg gerne ville til en storby, hvor jeg kunne få lidt mere for pengene end så mange andre steder. Jeg havde også hørt, at Budapest var en meget populær destination blandt Erasmus-studerende. Det var også vigtigt for mig at vælge en by, hvor det var nemt for min familie og venner at kunne besøge mig, og Budapest er både nemt at komme til med tog/fly, og så er billetterne oftest til at betale:)
overall_comments: Det bedste jeg nogensinde har gjort for mig selv! Man bliver et helt nyt, stærkt og udviklet mennesket - på den rigtig gode måde. Det eneste, der trækker ned, var det besværlige arbejde med administrationerne... Men det var det hele værd til sidst!
info_ease: ELTE’s afdeling for udvekslingsstuderende var super søde og imødekommende. Det var ikke altid lige let at finde den information, man havde brug for, men hvis man skrev en mail til dem, var de rigtig hurtige og gode til at besvare de spørgsmål, man måtte have - både i forhold til det faglige og sociale events i introduktionsugen.
arrival_assistance: Der blev afholdt en dag på fakultetet for psykologi, hvor de fortalte om, hvordan semesteret ville komme til at forløbe, og samtidig gennemgik de praktiske informationer om kursusregistrering, tilmelding og andre nødvendige deadlines for Erasmus-studerende. Man kunne også tilvælge at blive parret op med en ‘Buddy’. Jeg valgte det dog ikke, men jeg ved, at det for mange var en tryghed at have en, man kunne sparre med - især i starten.
arrival_comments: Man skal holde godt øje med hjemmesider og mails, hvis man ikke vil misse arrangementer eller vigtige datoer
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Det bedste jeg nogensinde har gjort for mig selv! Man bliver et helt nyt, stærkt og udviklet mennesket - på den rigtig gode måde. Det eneste, der trækker ned, var det besværlige arbejde med administrationerne... Men det var det hele værd til sidst!
registration_process: Denne proces var et kæmpe kaos - specielt når man som psykologistuderende har nogle obligatoriske fag at udfylde, så man ikke bare kan vælge frit. Der var meget forvirring omkring, hvilke fag man kunne tilmelde sig, og hvornår man var sikret en plads. Det fungerede på den måde, at man “tilmeldte” sig til de fag, man ville tage, og så stod man i venteposition, indtil de åbnede den endelige registreringsperiode. Når den endelige tilmelding var åbnet, blev pladserne udfyldt, og dem der ikke fik plads på kurset blev smidt af listen - herefter kunne man så eftertilmelde sig de andre fag. I og med man i første omgang ikke kunne tilmelde sig kandidatfag som bachelorstuderende, var der også en masse bøvl med denne proces.
registration_help: Igen var kontoret for Erasmusstuderende rigtig søde og hjælpsomme - et rigtig godt råd er at kontakte dem, når det hele sejler.
registration_success: Jeg fik omkring halvdelen af de fag, jeg havde ønsket, og så måtte jeg finde alternativer til resten af fagene. Jeg skulle have 15 ECTS, der skulle overføres til et obligatorisk fag, så det var helt klart sværest at finde alternativer til dette. Resten var valgfag, så det skete der ikke så meget ved.
registration_advice: Hold hovedet koldt i registreringsprocessen. Ofte er professorerne/lærerne rigtig venlige til at have en ekstra med på holdet, hvis det er vigtigt for dig at have netop det fag. Tøv ikke med at kontakte kontoret for Erasmus-studerende - de skal nok hjælpe dig! Og man må gerne skrue bissen lidt på, hvis de ikke tager det seriøst.
academics_comments: Det bedste jeg nogensinde har gjort for mig selv! Man bliver et helt nyt, stærkt og udviklet mennesket - på den rigtig gode måde. Det eneste, der trækker ned, var det besværlige arbejde med administrationerne... Men det var det hele værd til sidst!
course_level: Niveauet på de forskellige fag var meeeeeeget forskelligt, og ofte kom det an på professoren/læreren, om niveauet var højt eller lavt. Generelt var niveauet meget lavere end på KU, så det er ikke det akademiske niveau, man skal være nervøs for:)
teaching_comparison: De går ikke lige så højt op i pensum på dette universitet. Fokus er meget mere på at være aktivt deltagende i timerne og byde ind i klassediskussionerne. Der er også et par afleveringer her og der, men de fleste aktivitetskrav er i forbindelse med mundtlige præsentationer og oplæg. Derudover er kurserne også meget små i forhold til ECTS. Jeg havde kun kurser af 2-3 ECTS, så man skal være forberedt på at have rigtig mange fag, men til gengæld forventer de heller ikke lige så meget af dig i hvert fag.
courses_enrolled: Organization Development Organizational Psychology -lecture Organizational Psychology - seminar Introduction to Work and Organisational Psychology Leadership Theory Study and communication skills Psychology and crime Introduction to Counseling Psychology Introduction to Psychology Psychological Skill Training: Social Communication Skills Psychological Skill Training: Basic Clinical Interviewing Skills Psychological Skills for Personal Growth and Resilience
recommended_courses: Jeg ville generelt anbefale fagene, der er på kandidatniveau - dem får man lidt mere ud af:) Derudover var jeg meget positivt overrasket over Leadership Theory, fordi professoren var rigtig engageret og motiveret for at lære fra sig.
unexpected_costs: Ikke noget som sådan - jeg havde lavet et budget hjemmefra, så jeg var forberedt på de fleste udgifter.
cost_comparison: Jeg var meget overrasket over, at fitness/træningsabonnementer var så dyre - det er næsten dyrere end i DK. Derudover var det også meget dyrere at handle i deres supermarkeder, end jeg lige havde regnet med. Offentlig transport er rigtig billigt dog:))
activities_available: Erasmus Life Budapest (ELB) har en hel masse aktiviteter for Erasmus-studerende, som vi ofte tog til. Derudover fik man også en masse rabatter på fester, museumsbesøg, de termiske bade mm.
activities_recommended: Erasmus Monday på Morrison’s 2 er altid sjovt:) Det er en bar, hvor de fleste internationale studerende samles hver mandag til billige øl og sangria:) Og ellers er det også populært at tage til andre ELB-arrangementer.
weekend_recommendations: De fleste internationale studerende rejste rigtig meget i deres weekender - både til andre byer rundt omkring i Ungarn og andre lande i nærheden. Jeg var selv på forskellige ture til Zagreb, Krakow, Prag og Wien under mit udvekslingsophold, og det var super nemt med enten tog eller Flixbus.
culture_adjustment: Det var faktisk meget nemt. De fleste ungarer er søde og imødekommende - ikke lige så reserverede som os i DK:))
socializing_tips: Jeg mødte/snakkede kun med lokale studerende til forelæsninger - ellers havde vi ikke så meget med dem at gøre. Men her er en buddy også en god ide, hvis man vil mingle lidt med de lokale.
cultural_challenges: Der er rigtig mange hjemløse på gaden - det skal man lige vænne sig til.
culture_appreciated: Deres åbne sind og taknemmelighed. ‘Köszönöm’ (tak) er et af de første ord, man lærer, fordi de siger det hele tiden:)
top3_advice: Hav is i maven i forhold til det praktiske og forbindelsen mellem KU og ELTE - det hele skal nok gå, men de kan være tunge at danse med undervejs. Gør dig selv en tjeneste at deltage i en masse arrangementer hos ESN og ELB (især de første uger) - det er her, man virkelig finder sine nye mennesker, og folk er rigtig åbne og søde. NYD DET - tiden går alt for stærkt!
other_useful_info: Hvis du har obligatoriske fag, kan det være en god ide at være hurtigt ude i forhold til tilmelding af kurser, når registreringsperioden starter. Hvis du er BA-studerende og gerne vil have KA-kurser, skal du ikke blive skræmt af, at der står på hjemmesiden, at man ikke må blande, for det må man gerne - man skal bare have lov af professorerne, og det er meget nemt:)
most_rewarding: 100% den personlige og sociale udvikling, jeg har fået - og selvfølgelig alle de venner og bekendtskaber, jeg har taget med hjem. Du skal ikke gøre det for akademisk udvikling udelukkende :)
greatest_challenge: Det sværeste for mig var at få det hele til at gå op med KU… Fag, der skulle godkendes og dokumenter, der skulle underskrives - og administrationen, der altid er 100 år om at svare på mails:)
other_comments: Afsted med dig:))))))

crucial_aspects: There were multiple reasons for choosing Erasmus Universiteit as the destination. Academically, Erasmus Universiteit is a well-renowned university that offers an international environment with high-quality finance courses, which is what I was after. Secondly, having a Dutch father I am closely connected to Dutch culture from my childhood, but I wanted to explore it on my own by living and studying in the Netherlands. Finally, not only Erasmus Universiteit but Rotterdam itself has a huge and vibrant international environment.
overall_comments: I enjoyed my semester abroad in Rotterdam and would recommend it to others.
info_ease: It was extremely easy. First and foremost because Erasmus School of Economics has an amazing coordinator who is extremely helpful and provides all necessary information. Moreover, everyone speaks English and many websites can be found in English, so searching for information online is easy.
arrival_assistance: The exchange coordinator helped me register for courses.
arrival_comments: As mentioned, the coordinator invites you to a Facebook group and makes daily updates. Moreover, she sends on-going mails to you with the important deadlines and information and she is fairly quick to answer.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I enjoyed my semester abroad in Rotterdam and would recommend it to others.
registration_process: The coordinator sent a list of courses you could choose from. After a while, she sent out a survey from where I chose my courses from. I was not registered for one course that I had chosen in one instance, so a wrote her an email and she fixed it in no time.
registration_help: The emailing with the coordinator.
registration_success: Successful. There was no trouble for me.
registration_advice: There really is not much advice to give. Read your email from the coordinator and write her an email if you are in doubt or experience some kind of trouble.
academics_comments: I enjoyed my semester abroad in Rotterdam and would recommend it to others.
course_level: The courses are high-quality and the level is comparable to the level at UCPH. You will definitely feel a healthy challenge during the blocks and you will definitely feel like you have learned a lot after the exams. Since the courses are more niche you can dive deeper into parts of economics or finance that you otherwise wouldn't have been able to at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: One lecture a week in every course and some had classes, but they weren't like the classes at UCPH. The classes were more focused on e.g. the lecturer refreshing some needed math for the course, Q&A's, review of tests etc. So more extra activities that they wouldn't waste time with in the normal lectures. Which is in contrast to UCPH where you use classes to review problem sets. The teaching at Erasmus relied more on you doing the work yourself, reading of more papers and less class-instructor teaching.
courses_enrolled: International Finance - 4 ECTS Advanced Behavioural Finance - 4 ECTS Financial Innovations and Institutions - 4 ECTS Fixed Income Securities and Portfolio Management - 4 ECTS Economics of Innovation - 4 ECTS Industrial Organisation - 4 ECTS Advanced Money, Credit and Banking - 4 ECTS Advanced International Trade - 4 ECTS
recommended_courses: I mostly enjoyed the finance courses in the second block: "International Finance", "Advanced Behavioural Finance", "Financial Innovations and Institutions" and "Fixed Income Securities and Portfolio Management". I would recommend them all as they all have their own niche focus on different parts of finance. I enjoyed the structure and content of "Financial Innovations and Institutions" as you started by theory of different financial risks and then moved on to explaining how financial regulation continuously developed due to the types of risks and how banks changed their operations as a response to the regulations. This pattern followed and the course ended with examining the banks during COVID and whether regulations in the past decades made banks more robust to the pandemic when it hit in March. "Advanced Behavioural Finance" is also a nice course that looks at empirical evidence for deviations from standard financial theory. It is mainly structured around papers, their conclusions and how they are related to behavioural biases that deviate from financial theory.
unexpected_costs: It wasn't an unexpected cost, but get a bike. The infrastructure is fantastic and it is the easiest way to move around in the city although public transport such as the tram is well-functioning as well. Regarding the bike I recommend Swapfiets.
cost_comparison: The prices are comparable to Danish prices. Groceries such as vegetables are marginally cheaper, but bars and restaurants are equally expensive.
activities_available: A lot of people enjoyed the Erasmus Sport membership which allowed you to use the numerous amount of facilities. For example, they have a huge ice skating arena that people enjoy and many people also enjoy playing Padel Tennis or Squash. If you enjoy sports there are almost no sports you cannot exercise in Rotterdam. Social activities include trips, parties, art walks around the city and film screenings. However, all these are arranged by the student organization ESN rather than the university.
activities_recommended: Travel around in the Netherlands. Rotterdam is very different from the rest of the Netherlands, but it is easy to travel around the country and I really recommend it. Moreover, Antwerpen in Belgium is just a short train ride away and if you are up for it there is a train from Rotterdam that takes you to Paris in 3 hours if want a weekend trip with new friends. Experiencing the Dutch Bar life is always a recommendation and biking around the city.
weekend_recommendations: Go for a run around Kralingse Bos. It is a nice, scenic route for your run. Other than that I recommend biking to neighbouring cities such as Delft and Gouda, which are smaller, nice, and more Dutch-styled cities. I also went to several football matches e.g. I saw the national team play in De Kuip in Rotterdam and I can definitely recommend it.
culture_adjustment: Easy. Dutch and Danish people get a long well and share many similarities with respect to their cultures, life-style and personalities (broadly speaking).
socializing_tips: Dutch people are known to be direct, so be direct with them. However, you will most likely spend more time with other internationals. Like in Denmark where Danes usually spend time with Danes unless they are on an international programme, Dutch also tend to socialize with other Dutch.
cultural_challenges: None. I am pretty used to Dutch culture and Dutch people.
culture_appreciated: Dutch bar life with their special beers and a broad range of snacks such as bitterballen. Other than that you experience a large degree of openness and kindness and you get why people talk about Rotterdam as a young and vibrant city.
top3_advice: 1) Grants or at least savings - Don't let your activities be determined by the need to save money. If you apply in advance you have a great opportunity to receive 25.000+ DKK that you can use down here and enhance your stay. 2) Raincoat - The weather is like Danish weather and you never know when it is going to rain or when the rain is going to stop. 3) Headphones - For when you're studying at the library on campus or at a café
other_useful_info: Get a bike. Use libraries and cafés for studying if you like it as much as I do. Go for a run around Kralingse Bos - My local route everytime.
most_rewarding: Living in another country and make it your home for a semester and get a feeling of being connected to the city afterwards. Meeting people from different countries within and outside Europe. The academic level was rewarding as well. In the end many factors contributed to the exchange being a unique experience that gave me new perspectives.
greatest_challenge: I had to get used to courses being shorter, so you had to focus from the beginning and couldn't fall too far behind. On the other hand, this teaches you to be more structured. While many say the workload is heavy, I disagree. Just make sure to study continuously rather than skipping here and there. Most of the curriculum will be present in the exam, so you can't gamble with what you read and what you don't.

crucial_aspects: I have been wanting to study in the Netherlands for a long time, so I had no doubts that this was my first priority. This is partially due to the language, as the Dutch usually speak English on a high level. Other than that I had heard many positive things about their educational systems, which was also a crucial aspect for me when choosing this as my study destination.
info_ease: Luckily I had prepared a lot from home which definitely helped a lot. Also, on the university's website, they had several guidelines in order to help upon arrival which I used a lot and found to be a great help.
arrival_assistance: I signed up for a buddy programme, to have a local show me around the city. I also joined several intro-events and their "One-stop-shops" which helped students getting a chipcard, setting up a bank account etc. That was really helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to contact the coordinator and send him my requests for the different courses I would like to take, and he registered for me.
registration_help: The coordinator was definitely the greatest help and all the help I really needed. I forwarded all my questions to him.
registration_success: I would say successful. I was pretty early about sending my desired courses, so I got the ones I wanted.
registration_advice: Be prepared in good time, first of all! Also, due to covid some of the courses' timetables were changed after registration had ended - which I had some difficulties with since I experienced some overlaps between exam dates. So double-check that the timetables for your desired courses do not overlap.
course_level: I think the level of courses changed a lot from course to course. Some I was shocked about "only" having 5 ECTS given the level and the reading burden, where other courses were more doable.
teaching_comparison: There was a big difference. First of all the block structure is shorter, so there are exams every 2 months instead of twice a year as in UCPH. For me, that meant I still had to get the same amount of ECTS (30) as in my home university's semester-structure, but in shorter time. Also, at UCPH there is no mandatory attendance, nor do you get graded on participation in class. Due to this, on UCPH the style of teaching is more relaxed and made (for me) a better and safer environment to participate voluntarily in the class discussion without having to worry about saying the wrong thing and getting a bad grade thereafter. That was probably the hardest thing for me to get used to at Erasmus University in Rotterdam.
courses_enrolled: Research and Writing Skills (Arbitration skills), Corporate and White-collar crime and governance, Mediation Advocay and Legal theory and Methods.
recommended_courses: Mediation Advocay and Legal theory and Methods.
unexpected_costs: Housing was more expensive than I expected and cheap accommodations were very hard to come by.
cost_comparison: Public transportation is very expensive in the Netherlands, so I'd recommend renting a bike. For example from Swapfiets which is approx. 100 kr. pr. month.
activities_available: There were multiple sports clubs you could join as well as a fitness center on campus. Apart from that a lot of opportunities to join different social clubs as well.
activities_recommended: Join either a social club or the ESN. It is a great way to meet people.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the beach at Den Haag in the summer, check out the architecture in Utrect and do a weekend trip to Amsterdam.
culture_adjustment: I thought it was fairly easy. The Netherlands and Denmark are quite similar in many ways.
socializing_tips: Go to local clubs, parks etc., and try to learn just a few phrases in Dutch. It will take you very far and they always receive you with a positive mindset.
cultural_challenges: I did not really experience any.
culture_appreciated: Definitely the people as Dutch people are very friendly. Also, there are a lot of cultural things to discover.
top3_advice: Prepare for accommodation in very good time!! Rent a bike to save money on public transportation. Don't spend money on Erasmus' "Eureka-week" as I found it to be more for the new Dutch students and not the international students as much. I'd recommend doing the ESN intro days instead.
other_useful_info: It can be a good idea to set up a Dutch bank account as credit cards/visa are not broadly accepted everywhere.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people from different places around the world.
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to another school system.
other_comments: Sometimes it can be overwhelming but in the end its super rewarding to go on an exchange and I'd recommend it to anyone!

crucial_aspects: A destination with a high academic integrity that provides me with knowledge. Secondly the university is large with a healthy student culture which further motivated the studies. Combined with sport and leisure activities this was the perfect choice.
overall_comments: Absolutely perfect. You grow as a person and develop friendships that span countries and time.
info_ease: Super easy. Erasmus university offer plenty of guidance online and via various instagram profiles that does their best to guide you.
arrival_assistance: Budy program was introduced beforehand if I had any questions I knew where to direct them. Recieved mails from the adminstration that were were helpful. Also before the exchange began concerning housing and so forth.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Absolutely perfect. You grow as a person and develop friendships that span countries and time.
registration_process: Received a mail with all the relevant information from host university. Send a mail with requested subject and received all my requests.
registration_help: Constant online assistance was ready. Now that Corona measures are limited, it is also possible to just show up at the administration building and ask your questions.
registration_success: 100% successful. Only disadvantage was, that some of the most exiting courses were placed in block 3 and 4. I did 10 point in each. In retrospect I would do 20 point in first block and then spend more time exploring host countries in following nmonths.
registration_advice: Ask if you have questions.
academics_comments: Absolutely perfect. You grow as a person and develop friendships that span countries and time.
course_level: The courses varied in level compared to UCPH. The general course was worth 5 point compared to a danish 15 point course. I greatly appreciated receiving teaching from experienced professors in most of my classes.
teaching_comparison: It varied greatly from teacher to teacher. Same approach with discussion and a blend of lectures and seminars
courses_enrolled: Company law and restructuring Private int. law investment and trade law int. health law advanced trademark law
recommended_courses: Advanced intellectual property law. Expert professor. Unique teaching style. Company law and restructuring. Amazing professor and a great amount of skilled external lectures.
unexpected_costs: Groceries were a little more expensive. When you are on exchange, you also drink a large amount of beers and want to do as many things as possible. Therefore restaurant, travel and good times drain your wallet. But it is worth it.
cost_comparison: 10% more expensive
activities_available: Multiple events hosted by university and various student organisations.
activities_recommended: Get the fitness subscription from erasmus and do as much different sport as possible. It also includes padel board, bouldering and padel.
weekend_recommendations: Travel NL. There are way too many amazing cities close by train. And bring your swapfiets bike with you. And get the museum card for 60 € so you can visit allmost every museum in NL
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: Do events and sports
cultural_challenges: You deal with a lot of different cultures at the same time, especially from other int. student. Stuff like organising dinner was the most inconvenient. But in general everybody is on the same page.
culture_appreciated: Culture in the sun. Everybody just relaxed and enjoyed themselves.
top3_advice: Participate actively in academic work Join as many activities as possbile. Time moves fast so have as much fun as possible.
other_useful_info: make sure to join ESN Rotterdam immediately.
most_rewarding: Friendships and a deep fondness of the NL
greatest_challenge: Covid in the beginning and challenge socialising. Staying in a dark room is not good for the mental health.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial that the University had courses that I found interesting. As Erasmus University of Rotterdam is placed in Rotterdam who has the biggest harbor in Europe, the University had a wide range of courses within sea and transportation law which my home university does not teach in.
info_ease: Throughout my exchange it has been very easy to navigate in the courses as the university representatives were very fast to respond to e-mails and other questions.
arrival_assistance: I received information about the possible courses as well as information about examination, including registration for the exam. Furthermore, we were provided with e-mails about a WhatsApp group for all international students that we could sign up for.
arrival_comments: Be aware of the deadlines when it comes to registering for courses as well as examinations. It is possible to change a course during the semester
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was very easy to register for exams as well as for the courses. You are able to change the courses you chose in the beginning.
registration_help: The representative of the international students was really fast to respond and helped change my courses.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I applied for.
registration_advice: Check all the courses including the examination format and date. I would recommend to have 2 courses per block. I had three courses one block which was a bit too much.
course_level: The level of the courses is very high which I really enjoyed. Everybody participates in class and the professors often gives examples from own experience which is really interesting.
teaching_comparison: Mostly the same style where the professors went through the material and the students got to ask questions. We went through cases together. Each course is different as I also had some courses that were more interactive.
courses_enrolled: Trade Finance and Banking Law, Carriage of Goods, Charter Parties and Bills of Lading, EU Competition Law and Rule of Law in a Global Context.
recommended_courses: I can definitely recommend Trade Finance and Banking Law which is taught by Johan Vannerom and Frank Stevens. Both professors are very skilled. Frank Stevens also has the class Charter Parties and Bills of Lading which was a great course as well. This course as well as Carriage of Goods are about sea and transportation law which I actually enjoyed learning about. The first three courses works very well together.
unexpected_costs: Nothing.
cost_comparison: Groceries is a little bit more expensive than in Denmark but having a beer on a bar is half the price.
activities_available: The student organisation ESN arranges a lot of events every week, e.g. parties and sportsevents.
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend participating in some of the weekly activities from ESN as well as the introduction week that is also arranged by ESN.
weekend_recommendations: You have to experience the nearest cities. Don't just go to Amsterdam - its a great city but so is Rotterdam, Den Haag and the other nearby cities. I also visited Bruxelles which is only 1,5 hour away by train.
culture_adjustment: The culture is very similar to the danish culture so it was very easy to adapt.
socializing_tips: Don't just stay at Campus. Join a local football club or your local gym.
cultural_challenges: Not really the biggest differences besides the nightlife. In the Netherlands it is more including.
culture_appreciated: Dutch people are the sweetest! They are super helpful and everybody speaks perfect english - even the older ones.
top3_advice: Don't stress it, have fun and enjoy it while it last!
other_useful_info: Try to get out of your comfort zone from the beginning. People start socializing early on and you don't want to miss out on that.
most_rewarding: The academic level was very high and I learned something that I would not have been able to at UCPH.
greatest_challenge: Socializing when living outside of campus but it is not impossible - just takes a little bit more effort.
other_comments: As a master student at my 10th semester, I found that people were quite young. The average age was around 21. In hindsight I would probably have enjoyed it more if I was at my bachelor.

crucial_aspects: I was interested in taking communication classes. Therefore i chose Erasmus University Rotterdam. I also chose the Netherlands because i thought it would be interesting living there.
info_ease: It was easy.
arrival_assistance: The people working for the exchange office did an introduction meeting and were available to answer any question via email.
arrival_comments: I didn't have any problems, but the attendance demands for passiing the classes where really strict and some of my friends got into some problems because of that. I felt bad for them because the demands on EUR are so much stricter than at many other universities in the world. There could be better support in relation to having to adapt to another system than what you are used to.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration proces went smoothly.
registration_help: We could get help from the people in charge of exchange in our faculty.
registration_success: I got some classes i wanted and some i didn't want. I ended up caring way less about the classes than i thought i would both because the way of learning on EUR is way different than in the Danmark(it is more about learning fact than applying what you learn and you have way less academic freedom) and because the subjects just weren't that interesting to me.
registration_advice: Bear in mind that the classes you can choose from can have very different levels and very different workloads. Do also bear in mind that some classes have mandatory attendance and some don't.
course_level: The day- to- day activities in the tutorials where often too easy after i got into the habit of speaking english(i mostly took 1st year courses even though i am a 3rd year student at UCPH). I would have liked to have been challanges more. In relation to essays and exams, i did fine in all of my classes so i guess that was a good level for me.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was very different. I definetely prefer the teaching style at home but the one at EUR also had its advantages. At EUR you have to live up to very specific demands and a lot of the exams a focused on you learning things by heart. That was uninspiring to me, while i am used to a lot of academic freedom and the teaching being more focused on applying knowledgde. I did however like the fact that i had a lot of class time compared to at home. It gave me a chance to be social and work on my english. I also liked having smaller assignments than usual, because it makes your life as a student more dynamic.
courses_enrolled: Communication as a Social Force, Communication and Organizations, Consumers Perceptions of Corporate Social Responsibilities, Feeling Orange, Communication Technologies and their Impacts, Intercultural Communication.
recommended_courses: None of the above courses where so interesting to me that i would recommend them to other students.
unexpected_costs: I didn't encounter any unexpected costs. I did however spend more money than i thought i would.
cost_comparison: Being on exchange is generally expensive because you go out a lot and you don't want to miss anything. Expect to spend a lot of money on going out and on travelling. In my opinion these are money well spent.
activities_available: Parties, a fitness membership(with access to classes and other sports facilities) and trips to other cities and out of the country.
activities_recommended: Participate in as much as possible the first couple of weeks - that's when you meet your friends. Know that a lot of the social activities involves partying, so if you're not a big fan of partying or drinking being on exchange at EUR may not be for you.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going to France and Belgium because both are so accessible from Rotterdam. Especially Bruges(Belgium) is beautiful. Within the Netherlands i would really recommend going to Utrecht.
culture_adjustment: I didn't have any problems adjusting to dutch culture.
socializing_tips: I think that dutch people are a little closed off compared to internationals. I don't think socializing with dutchies where particularly hard but it also wasn't easy.
cultural_challenges: See the above answer.
culture_appreciated: I like the dutch honesty. I lived with two dutch students and i think it made communication easier that they where being frank with me during my time there.
top3_advice: 1. Know that a lot of people you meet are gonna be younger than you. This means that they might be a little less mature but might also be a lot of fun. 2. Don't go for the classes because they are better at UCPH. The culture around education is way more inspiring in Denmark. 3.You will have more class time and less individual work at EUR, which i personally think is preferable for exchange life.
other_useful_info: Know that the rules for attendance and assignments are very strict.
most_rewarding: The open social environment amongst exchange students. People are very nice and show a lot of interest in you. Meeting people from other countries also opens your mind to other ways of living and to other opportinities than those you normally consider at home.
greatest_challenge: I had to get used to having a lot of assignments. In the beginning it was stressful but i got used to it. The overall workload wasn't bigger than what i am used to - just in another form.

crucial_aspects: one of the crucial aspects was the relevance and my own interests in the courses available at my destination and further that the city i was going to was a city i wanted to live in for a while
overall_comments: it has been a really nice stay and i have gotten to know many great people across the world. I further liked the courses i ended up with
info_ease: some of the information, as for instance information about the university i was going to study at, was easy, but it was difficult to find practical information about registration and housing
arrival_assistance: i did not get any, except for the intro week at the university
arrival_comments: the students was at great help, but the exchange people were difficult to get in touch with in rotterdam
housing_how: I found housing on my own

academics_comments: it has been a really nice stay and i have gotten to know many great people across the world. I further liked the courses i ended up with

top3_advice: plan some trips to some of the other cities close by, it is worth it, they are really beautiful. take the bike or walk around so you see as much of the city as possible, because there are some really nice neighborhoods in Rotterdam and cafes too, just not in the city center. as Rotterdam got bombed during the second world war the city center is really modern and has a lack of charm, but if you just go a bit to the north or west, you will find beautiful places!

other_comments: that was it I would say

courses_enrolled: Maritime Casualties Law of the ship Marine Insurance Charter Parties & Bills of Lading Carriage of goods
recommended_courses: Carriage of goods was a good course as it introduced me to a lot of different topics in the field of transport law.

cost_comparison: Transport

crucial_aspects: Firstly, it was important for me to chose a university that offered courses within the field of my current studies and career. Furthermore, i emphasized choosing a well-respected university by virtue of an international respected and acknowledged place.
info_ease: Easy. However i had to reach out to my coordinator at the host university myself to get the final details.
arrival_assistance: I got an e-mail with most of the information needed.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was easy and flexible - however the information given beforehand about the courses and how to chose/check timetables etc. was not very informative.
registration_help: There was only one person, the coordinator at my host university, to guide all the exchange students. I did sometimes to reach other people at the university but they kept on referring to the coordinator which made it difficult when he was out of office.
registration_success: Very successful. I did not experience any problems with this.
registration_advice: Make sure to take the time needed to learn how to chose the right courses - it is your own responsibility to make sure there is no overlaps etc.
course_level: I found the level of courses similar to the ones at my home university. However, some courses which had same amount of ECTS points was disproportionate by means of assignments, preparation etc.
teaching_comparison: There was a big difference. At my host university the lectures consisted mostly of class discussions and individual participation in contrary to my home university. Furthermore, there is only final exams (100% weight) at my home university whereas grade at my host university was based on assignments, in-class participation, presentations etc. during the semester.
courses_enrolled: Research and writing skills, Mediation Advocacy, Commercial contracts and Corporate and white collar crime.
recommended_courses: I personally found commercial contracts very interesting and useful for my further studies at home.
unexpected_costs: Nothing in particular.
cost_comparison: Public transportation was more expensive than i thought.
activities_available: There was a lot of activities, but i was hard to find and thus engage in these in the beginning since there was no real introduction or information given.
activities_recommended: I did attend any why i have nothing to add.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend going to Den Haag. It is only 40 minute by train from Rotterdam, and is a very nice and beautiful city.
culture_adjustment: I found it easy since the culture in the Netherlands is quite similar to the danish culture in my opinion.
socializing_tips: I learned quickly to seek and interact with the locals in classes myself.
cultural_challenges: Nothing further to add.
culture_appreciated: I found the locals very open-minded and welcoming.
top3_advice: (1) Make sure to keep up in class. The host university does not give days off with the purpose of reading as they do at the home university. (2) Seek other people in the beginning especially, people quickly find their friends and that only happens if you interact with others yourself (3) Engage in the non-academic student activities - i only heard good things about many of their events and it is a golden opportunity to meet new people - maybe even someone from other studies.
other_useful_info: I have nothing further to add.
most_rewarding: Getting to meet a lot of new people from all around the globe.
greatest_challenge: The beginning. I expected some kind of introduction days where the exchange students would get to know each other or at least that i would get some kind of information on where to contact and find other exchange students. We had one introduction day, but it was merely formal and not as much getting-to-know-eachother as i would have hoped and expected. Because of this i did not know who to reach out to in the first couple of weeks since i did not have any names or information on the others.
other_comments: No.

registration_process: None

course_level: good, i thought the standard was a bit higher at UCPH
teaching_comparison: Very diverse types of classes, less academic tone
courses_enrolled: International and Global communication, Media Campaigns and Digital marketing.
recommended_courses: International and Global communication. You learned a lot, very interesting lectures.

cost_comparison: Food was cheap in general

activities_recommended: I've heard the party committee should be fun being a part of
weekend_recommendations: Go to Amsterdam (with flixbus, very cheap). Rotterdam has a lot of great vintage shops, local markets, parks and cafes.
culture_adjustment: easy, Dutch people are very similar to danes
socializing_tips: It is easy at EUR, as there's many exchange students compared to other host universities

culture_appreciated: biking everywhere, as in Copenhagen
top3_advice: Bring cash everywhere, find a room mate and look all contracts through twice. If the question refers to going to EUR, then look up social arrangements by the university, get coffee at campus and bike to school though tram is cheap. They often filled or late.

crucial_aspects: That it was a bigger city within Europe
info_ease: There was a good amount of information from the Erasmus University Rotterdam, could have used a bit more e.g. a follow up on the insurance rules, which never came. The administration was quick to answer whenever I had a question and was very flexible.
arrival_assistance: None, beside an e-mail to state which date and place the introduction would be held.
arrival_comments: Almost all other faculties at the university, beside law, had two full introduction days, days in the middle of exchange and at the end of exchange to catch up with the exchange students and give them an oppotunity to meet each other. However, for some reason, nothing was arranged for the law students. You were pretty much on your own after the short introduction to the university.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The administration was pretty good at to continuously inform the students about what the next steps for the registration process would be in terms of courses and so on. However the exam board and the administration was very unclear when it came to anything else than that. I did, for example, ask whether a re-sit would be possible in my homecountry. The exam board stopped answering my e-mail in the middle of the correspondance, and then randomly mailed me that I was granted the permission for a re-sit. Firstly, they didn't tell me the fact that they were processing my request and secondly, the decision they granted me in the end had nothing to do with what I originally asked for (if I was still at in the country at the time the re-sit was, I would have just signed up for that one). Thirdly, it took them two months to grant the desicion, which had the requirement that the re-sit must be held before the end of august. Since I wasn't been informed that they were processing a decision, I had no clue that I might had needed to clear my calendar for August (getting the permission granted three weeks before the end of august). That was unfortunately not a good experience.
registration_help: Call or e-mail to the university's administration for international students.
registration_success: There was no problems with the registration for classes. They were also very flexible in terms of letting people switch to other classes (even though the classes had already started or would start in only a few days)
registration_advice: To just ask the university if e.g. you want to change from one course to another, since they were very flexible with that.
course_level: You should also be aware that if you arrive in the spring semester, you will start taking courses that are in the middle of the academic year for permanent students, which can be a bit confusing.
teaching_comparison: Pretty much the same, beside the fact that the university had much more guest lectures and trips out of the university than UCPH
courses_enrolled: Maritime Casualties, Intellectual Property law, EU Competition law, International Health Law and Carriage of Goods
recommended_courses: Carriage of Goods and EU Competition law
unexpected_costs: Costs for going to other cities, especially Amsterdam, could be very expensive.
cost_comparison: Groceries was pretty expensive
activities_available: A on-campus fitness center.
activities_recommended: None arranged through the university
weekend_recommendations: Go to different cities in Holland or go to places with techno-music. Go see an art gallery or go to the lake.
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: If anyone invites you to something, go!
cultural_challenges: Nothing
culture_appreciated: Lots of different ways to experience the country
top3_advice: Be aware of the housing crisis situation, try and connect with the other exchange student (e.g. make a whatsapp group or something) on the intro-day, since it makes it easier to meet up, since there wasn't any other social events through the university.
other_useful_info: There is a lot of international students at the university (beside from exchange students), so the Unviersity also felt very international in general and people would in general speak english as default.
most_rewarding: To live a very international city, while being able to be tourists with your friends
greatest_challenge: There would be exams every other month, since the exams was divided in blocks, which could be a bit stressful.

crucial_aspects: - Academic opportunities, with relevant english speaking courses for my degree - International Community and ability to travel around, whilst on Exchange
info_ease: It was fairly easy, I had already checked my e-mail a lot and created a profile for my new University. They were very good at sending information about arrival and study start. It was somewhat more difficult to find information about the introduction activities
arrival_assistance: Guided tour across campus, a brief introduction to the different platforms we would be using and a tour around the city.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We had a deadline two weeks before arrival, where we had to submit our requests for courses. It was however first come first serve, so all research about courses and scheduling should be done before hand. It was somewhat okay to find the information, but scheduling made it difficult to choose courses
registration_help: The exchange coordinator would answer all questions and try to help with scheduling conflicts, but most of it is ones own responsibility
registration_success: Somewhat succesful, I got some classes I really wanted. Others were a last minute solution to fill up the required credits.
registration_advice: Do a lot of research before hand, and have priorities ready. Be sure to check the timetable, as most courses have attendance.
course_level: The courses had a lot of assignment, but the level was similar to that of UCPH
teaching_comparison: Smaller courses and a lot more groupwork and group discussions.
courses_enrolled: - International and Global communication - ICT's and emerging markets - Digital Marketing - Digital media and Health - Media Industries: Trends and Strategies - Feeling Orange
recommended_courses: International and global communication, was a really good course. The professor was very passionate about the subject, and it made a lot of sense to learn in a setting of mostly international students, as it gave a much broader perspective. Feeling orange is a required course for all exchange students, about dutch culture. It was nice to have classes with other exchange students we had made during the exchange, and great to know more about the historical context of the culture we are in.
unexpected_costs: Flight tickets to and from places
cost_comparison: I got a very cheap bike subscription. Going out to eat and rent was pretty expensive.
activities_available: They had a big sports facility, open for everyone with teams, classes and fitness. There were also a lot of different social activities such as parties and events for all students at the university. Most of which you did not have to be a member of the committee arranging the activities
activities_recommended: The parties are a great way to meet and see other students. The campus sports centre is also a good way to spend time with other students and exercise whilst on exchange.
weekend_recommendations: Visit all the other cities nearby, the train system is really good, so you can get really far without spending too much money. Also go exploring in the city, and get a museumspass in the beginning. It gives a lot of discounts throughout the Netherlands.
culture_adjustment: It was very similar to that of Denmark.
socializing_tips: Be open-minded and ready to get to know a lot of other people.
cultural_challenges: There weren't really any.
culture_appreciated: The fried food.
top3_advice: 1. Try a lot of different cuisines in the city it is very multi-cultural 2. The campus is a great place to study and meet people even if you don't have a lot of classes 3. Join as many intro days activities as possible, it really pays off
other_useful_info: Be prepared to spend a lot of money, so that you don't miss out on experiences.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many nice people
greatest_challenge: Being very active and therefore also very tired.

crucial_aspects: I have been to The Netherlands several times, mainly Amsterdam, and I genuinely enjoy spending time there. Therefore, I chose to go to Rotterdam to experience more of the country. Moreover, Erasmus School of Law is well recognized within the field of company/commercial law + European law.
info_ease: Easy.
arrival_assistance: No assistance, only contact with the Internal Office of Erasmus School of Law.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Very easy contact with both the International Office during the registration for the courses, moreover, with the lecturers during the courses.
registration_help: Information about the courses; registration process etc.
registration_success: Very successful.
registration_advice: Always contact the International Office when in doubt about everything; they will guide you to seek other guidance if they are not capable of guiding you.
course_level: Comparable to UCPH. Of course, considering I only followed MA-courses although I am a BA-student at UCPH, the complexity of the courses were a bit higher.
teaching_comparison: The teaching methods were completely different from what I am used to from UCPH. A lot more student-involvement, including us students collecting material for our assignments etc., was a huge part of the teaching. This both made the education feel more academic bu at the same time less structured.
courses_enrolled: Blok 1: Research & Writing Skills - Company and Commercial Law (15 ECTS). Blok 2: Mediation Advocacy - Theory and Practice (5 ECTS) and Law and Policy of European Integration (10 ECTS).
recommended_courses: All of the three mentioned. The course in Blok 1 had a very student-involving way of teaching. It consisted of a lot of assignment, where we as students had to find the material ourselves to be able to answer the assignments. The course is meant to make the student more able to conduct and write their MA-thesis in the end of the master. This makes the course very flexible and highly academic. The courses in second blok are quite similar to the way courses in law are tought at UCPH. In Law and Policy of European Integration, we had to write three assignments that counts 40 % of our final grade in the course as well.
unexpected_costs: Non.
cost_comparison: Less expensive: Food, cafés, experiences. More expensive: Public transportation.
activities_available: Plenty! Everything from parties to sport activities.
activities_recommended: Dit not use it.
weekend_recommendations: I would definitely go to cities surrounding the city you live in. I went to Amsterdam, Den Haag, Antwerp, Brussels, Delft, Eindhoven, Utrecht etc.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Approach them in the student café; go on dates; be openminded.
cultural_challenges: Actually none. As long as you act respectful towards others and ask openly about their culture heritage, then it should be fine.
culture_appreciated: The direct- and openness; not being afraid to ask questions too directly.
top3_advice: 1) Build up a professional relationship with the professors! Many of them are well-recognized academic people which can be in your favor in the long run. 2) If you have physical classes, go to as many as possible to be able to socialize with other students. Then you have someone to have a coffee with, discuss an assignment with etc. 3) Be open and ask questions - no questions are dumb questions. It can be challenging to conduct knowledge on another language than the one of your mother-tongue. The more you ask, the more effectively can you perform.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Being more self-aware of my capabilities.
greatest_challenge: Speaking English - both in a social and a legal context.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to explore destinations that could be interesting to move to in the future.

I was not able to participate in the classes I originally planned on because of poor communication and planning from the administration. i am sad that this semester has been wasted at an university that does not care for or cater towards exchange students. ultimatly is would have preferred staying at UCPH.

registration_process: registration was done via email to the exchange coordinator
registration_help: email communication
registration_success: not very successful. I only got one of the courses I initially wanted.

teaching_comparison: doing a comparison of this would be like comparing Messi to my 10 year old little brother at the school playground. it does not compare.
courses_enrolled: Wicked legal ethics, Dutch law and legal culture, European integration and policy, Legal theory and methods and Comparative constitutional law.
recommended_courses: I would recommend European integration and policy as the profferers in this course are bright, professional, dedicated and motivating. this class was above any of the courses I took at EUR. it was one of the more demanding courses and required a lot of reading and preparing compared to the other courses. however compared to the courses at UCPH it was similar in preparation
unexpected_costs: The Netherlands is a very affordable country to live in so any unexpected costs were very manageable

activities_available: there are different athletics clubs like running.
activities_recommended: joining the sports program.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend visiting the campus bar after school.

crucial_aspects: Language availability, I really wanted to go to an EU country too, for the convenience of it.
overall_comments: I loved meeting new people and becoming instantly friends. The university did not meet my expectations though. If I could give half points, I would probably give it 7.5.
