The orientation days (introduction days) were lacking and I went home feeling like I didn't really get to know anyone. The days were too short and there were too few. There weren't really any "meet other exchange students" events in the early days, which I feel, affected my overall experience.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I loved meeting new people and becoming instantly friends. The university did not meet my expectations though. If I could give half points, I would probably give it 7.5.
registration_process: Their website for course registration is fairly easy to navigate. Once all the courses for the term are available, you go to the website and pick five (I think it's five) courses that you want to take per term. They also have a calendar that is easy to navigate, so you can see if your classes will overlap.
registration_help: If you had any issues or you were assigned to classes that ended up overlapping, the exchange office is quick to help.
registration_success: Out of six classes in total, I think I might have gotten four classes that I wanted, so that's fine.
registration_advice: I don't know if I have any advice.. It makes sense and it is pretty easy to do.
academics_comments: I loved meeting new people and becoming instantly friends. The university did not meet my expectations though. If I could give half points, I would probably give it 7.5.
course_level: I don't feel like I learnt anything new this semester, and that is given I also took introductory courses. The level of education here feels very low compared to UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Their courses are structured in such a way that the students do the most of the work and prepare a lot from home, and the teachers "sum it up" at the university. Except at the actual classes you're just doing group work, group presentation, and repeat. They love group work here, and you don't really get a change to show in-class what you can do. I think I've had more group work here in one semester than I've had at UCPH in all my semesters. At UCPH we are sometimes in groups, but our education is not dependant on group work and the ability of your group members. I feel like my grade/what I learn depends on my peers here, and I am not really a fan of that. At UCPH we often prepare readings from home and go to either a lecture or a class, or sometimes both, and the teacher go through everything and elaborate. They don't do that here. You do all the work from home - I've watched full-on lectures at home as preparation for class - where the teacher would say "You've already read this" and skip through it to get to the group work.
courses_enrolled: Feeling Orange (you have to take that as an exchange student) Communication Management Technology, Media, and Identity Communication Ethics Intercultural Communication Communication Technologies and Their Impact
recommended_courses: If I had to pick one I would recommend Technology, Media, And Identity. That was the only course where I felt challenged and felt like I was learning something new - or at least was learning something that was useful and relevant.
unexpected_costs: I spend a lot of time on public transport because I live far away and the weather is often bad. I would've loved to just use my bike to get around.
cost_comparison: Eating out and grocery shopping is cheaper than Copenhagen!
activities_available: They have a sports building with fitness equipment, classes and a tennis course. There are some student activities sometimes, but nothing I looked into as I preferred to do stuff with exchange students.
activities_recommended: Go to the students bars, go on trips around the country and see other cute Dutch cities!
weekend_recommendations: Rotterdam doesn't have a lot of stuff to see, but go to Amsterdam, Delft, Den Haag, Utrecht and perhaps another country. The Netherlands is located right in the middle of everything and a trip to London or Antwerpen doesn't take that long. The smaller Dutch cities have a lot of culture and they're perfect for day-trips to see something else than Rotterdam.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. It is in many ways like Copenhagen and Denmark.
socializing_tips: Local students tend to keep to themselves, so focus on exchange students. the local student you meet often already have their friend-groups and they're friendly enough in class, but I never experienced them wanting to hang out after class.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: In many ways it reminds me of Danish culture. But I do appreciate how they party and keep the streets alive.
top3_advice: Be aware of their attendance rules (especially if you plan to do a lot of travelling). Try to find housing close to the university, as it is a nice place to meet up with friends for a beer or coffee & lunch after class or on a random Tuesday. Take a look at the work-load for the courses and how they divide it. Do you want to spend your time doing four group papers or do you want to write one individual assignment and take one exam?
most_rewarding: I met a lot of other people from all over the world and we have friendship that will last for a long time. Going on exchange is a personal journey and you get to know yourself in new ways. It is so rewarding to go on exchange and just say "yes" to everything.
greatest_challenge: Getting used to a new city and a new way of doing things. In many ways Denmark and Netherlands are alike, but sometimes I found myself missing the way things are done in Denmark/at UCPH.

crucial_aspects: It was important for me to choose a destination that was not so different from my home country that I would not be able to get comfortable there in the 5 months of exchange. I'm a bit shy, so going to a place where I for example would have to learn the language as well as adapt to a different culture WHILE studying would be overwhelming to me. So, going to the Netherlands was the perfect balance of a somewhat familiar cultural environment while still allowing me to explore a new country on my own, making international and local friends, and studying without stressing too much about the external environment.
overall_comments: Best experience of my life, hands down. I would recommend anyone considering studying abroad to do it!!!
info_ease: Very easy, lots of nice personnel and exchange mentors available to answer questions.
arrival_assistance: No assistance needed for me as we were kept very well informed about introductory activities before arriving.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Best experience of my life, hands down. I would recommend anyone considering studying abroad to do it!!!
registration_process: Super easy, you get to browse the course catalogue some time before registration opens, and then you just put in the course numbers that you want, when the registration portal opens.
registration_help: Lots of help! I asked a bunch of questions to the incoming exchange coordinator who was very kind to answer them all. But I did not need any help with the practical things around registration as the uni sent out many informative emails regarding deadlines and guidelines for registration and late registration as well.
registration_success: Not very, because the School of History, Culture and Communication did not offer any classes within the fields of history or culture that semester for international master students, so I had to take three communications classes that I initially did not really care for. They turned out very interesting though.
registration_advice: Really research the past years' course offers before you accept an offer from the host uni! Also make sure to ask your home uni about their agreement with the host uni, so you know whether you can maybe take lower or higher-level courses if the courses on offer for you own level is too small.
academics_comments: Best experience of my life, hands down. I would recommend anyone considering studying abroad to do it!!!
course_level: I found the level of the courses a bit too easy for me as a master student, but this is probably because a master's degree in NL is only one year, so the courses have to be short and remain somewhat introductory...
teaching_comparison: The professors were extremely organized which I really appreciated, and easy to contact. I however wish they would encourage more engaged class discussions, as two of my professors were too lax with the students, and just allowed them to be completely quiet behind their screens in the back of the room – or sometimes allowed students to talk amongst themselves which really disturbed the learning environment.
courses_enrolled: Strategic Mass Communication Digital Citizenship and Community Engagement Digital News Media
recommended_courses: Strategic Mass Communication with professor Étienne Auge! Still a somewhat 101-style course, but definitely my favorite of the ones I took. The professor forbids electronic during class, so notes are taken on paper, and students are much more focused and engaged due to the absence of screens. The professor is also very active and WILL ask you a question if he believes you are zoning out. So, his teaching style is not for the faint of heart who want to be left alone in the back, but it will be a huge help come exam time, when you find out that you remember so much more than when you took notes on the computer.
unexpected_costs: None that were unexpected.
cost_comparison: Taking the trains intercity trains between the bigger cities in the Netherlands can be really expensive, so look into getting an OV-card so you can discounted trips either off-peak hours on weekdays or on weekends.
activities_available: The EUR is very dedicated to promoting student well-being through social activities outside of studying, so there were lots of options! I really recommend checking out the Studium Generale organisation and signing up for events such as talks, movie screenings and art cafes. The univerisyt also arranges field trips to famous destinations in NL, such as the Koekenhof Tulip Gardens, for really good prices. Use these offers!!!
activities_recommended: I really really recommend going to the OpenHeART Cafés where students get to do arts and crafts on campus in a chill environment and no pressure to do great art, just have fun. Shout out to the ladies who put on the bead jewelry workshop. I joined the ErasmusPride club and went to some cool events with them.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Utrecht, it's so cute! Go to Amsterdam for an entire day or stay for a few if you have the time. Do not miss out on going to the beach in the Hague during the summer, it's beautiful and quite close. Explore Rotterdam Zuid which is extremely underrated.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, as I stated, it was important to me that I would be able to adjust quickly so that cultural differences would not become a stressor. Dutch people are super kind and the citizens of Rotterdam are very laid-back, so settling in was super easy, and if you learn the basic shop phrases, they'll love you for it.
cultural_challenges: Dutch food is not good, so look for foreign cuisines if you want to eat out, which you will end up doing.
culture_appreciated: I found the residents to be super open to foreign students who want to engage with the local culture. I really appreciate how much Dutch people like to have a good time and listen to live music and drink beers in the sunshine.
top3_advice: 1. Do your research to make sure that you can get courses that you'll like and that fit within you programme at UCPH. 2. You'll have to work hard to find Dutch friends, as EUR is mostly internationals. Get into local cultural events, volunteer maybe. 3. Rent a bike through Swapfiets, it'll save you so much money in the long run.
other_useful_info: Do not be discouraged if you don't score as high grades as you're used to. Apparently the professors are quite strict with their grades, and the point scale allow them to go into great detail with the grade.
most_rewarding: Studying was fun and challenging sometimes, but the best part without a doubt getting to find my feet in a completely new culture on my own, building a life there how I would like it to be, and making a bunch of great friends from all over the world!!! Getting to form your own group of likeminded people and learning about their cultures was so rewarding and lovely. I'll miss my exchange pals.
greatest_challenge: The first month was a little rough. You're still settling in, classes have started and are stressful, and you haven't really made close friends with anyone yet. So everything feels kind of up in the air, but it'll get so much better with just a few more weeks. Two months in you'll have great friends and won't miss home that much anymore.
other_comments: GO ON EXCHANGE!

crucial_aspects: The country and a university with courses relevant for my study
info_ease: Fairly easy, the host university provided sufficient information
arrival_assistance: Introduction meeting. Nothing else.
arrival_comments: The orientation was fine, but it was mostly learning by finding out
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Other than the formal through the exchange system I just had to send some proof of language skills
registration_help: There is an exchange student hotline for each faculty which worked fine.
registration_success: I registered for a premade course line (half of a one year master) and that was fairly easy.
registration_advice: Beware that you have courses of 5 ECTS so 6 courses in total and that they have 2 exam periods (one in fall and one in beginning of winter), and that it is very stressful if you choose to have 4 courses in the first part and two in the second part or vice versa. I would recommend 3 and 3 as it is best balanced.
course_level: The level of courses is neither lesser or higher than at KU, however the way of teaching resembles High School more than university (at least as a Statskunskabs/Political Science student). There are many assignments during the actual course, there are presentations and the exams are often closed book meaning they focus more on your ability to remember and recite rather than your analytical and especially critical thinking. This means that the level is probably the same however there is a different focus requiring some adjustment.
teaching_comparison: Again the everyday classes resemble the Danish a lot, but maybe even more participatory than at KU. Expect that teachers will engage students alot, so come prepared for class and also expect a lot of closed book exams and less long written assignments.
courses_enrolled: I was part of the International Public Management and Public Policy masters programme and had the following courses: Global Governance European Union Policy Making Comparative Public Policy International Organisations and Development Europe in the World International Public Management
recommended_courses: I would recommend taking the courses within one master, because all the different courses are related to each other especially the second part where the three courses draw on the previous three. This makes for a really nice cohesive experience
unexpected_costs: I have no clue how my spending was divided but excluding rent which I paid sort of 1 to 1 with my Erasmus Grant I probably spent between 8000-10.000 kroner per month.
cost_comparison: The groceries are around 25% cheaper than in Denmark. The beer is the same (tap beer) but they don't have cheap bottle beers, however their student bar is insanely cheap. Public transport is also expensive, so get an OV-chip card with a Flex subscription it will take 40% off prices outside rush hour with trains.
activities_available: They have all kinds of sport clubs and they have this exchange student social network but it is mostly (imo) for bachelor student, when you reach the age of 26 (like me) then 18 year old germans are not the most interesting company.
activities_recommended: Go to the nearby cities (Amsterdam, Delft, Den Haag, Gouda). Take the train to Beligum even! Other than that just discover all that Rotterdam has to offer, the museum card can be acquired for 20 euro giving you 1 euro access to all museums.
weekend_recommendations: I mean you can go to so many countries and cities from Rottedam by train which is such a nice way to travel.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, Dutch people resemble Danes a lot.
socializing_tips: Talk with the people in your class, it is very nice to have a social life with the people you study with, often many of the Dutch people also come from other cities so they are also looking for local friends.
cultural_challenges: Not really
culture_appreciated: Dutch people are pretty easy going
top3_advice: Prepare accommodation well in advance, the housing crisis in the Netherlands is not a joke. If you want to learn dutch you have to apply already in beginning of August, however a lot of the courses are free. Also you need a bike so if you don't plan on bringing your own you have to be very quick at Swapfiets because they sell out.
other_useful_info: Don't buy that ESN card, it is not very useful.
most_rewarding: Actually it was my classmates.
greatest_challenge: Definitely the study, it was more challenging than I anticipated and I knew it was not going to be easy like in Southern or Eastern Europe

teaching_comparison: A lot less focus on Exercises Classes, but more driven by lectures. Additionally course material were mostly research papers.
courses_enrolled: System Security, Security of Wireless Networks, Visual Computing, Design of Parallel and High Performance Computing
recommended_courses: Security of Wireless Networks was very interesting, with a good professor and nice labs.
unexpected_costs: Paying for registration and residence permit at the local office in my municipality.

activities_available: There was a free sports association with lots of various activities.
activities_recommended: Going on some of the trips arranged by the Erasmus Student Network (ESN) or your Institute's student association is a nice way to meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: Go on lots of hikes, there are many nice trails around the Zurich area.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy, Swiss people are quiet and polite.
socializing_tips: Sometimes you have to lead the conversation.
cultural_challenges: Nothing in particular.
culture_appreciated: How polite people are.
top3_advice: Only register for courses that you have a chance of passing (its pretty fast paced here) Be sure to enjoy your free time when you are not studying.
other_useful_info: The amount of work pr. credit is a lot more than it is in Copenhagen. I would say 30 credits here is ~45 credits in UCPH.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial to me that the university had courses in the subjects, I found interesting. Furthermore, new cultures (both University-culture and people-culture), level of education, and future career possibilities were a part of my motivation.
info_ease: You have to take time off to navigate in the documents you receive from both host and home university. However, the information was always there. You just had to find it.
arrival_assistance: The University was open so it was possible to go there and ask any questions. The most assistance, I got, was from fellow students in the same situation as me. This helped a lot and it was easy to find helpful friends in the beginning.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It is not that different from University of Copenhagen. You apply for courses through a webpage.
registration_help: Information emails from the university.
registration_success: I got what I wanted.
registration_advice: In the beginning, I would apply for all courses, I find interesting. It is possible to deregister later.
course_level: The level was much higher than University of Copenhagen. The workload was the double.
teaching_comparison: Lab courses was great. Semester courses were just lectures and then a lot of selfstudying before the exams.
courses_enrolled: Plant Biochemistry Phytopathology Concepts in modern genetics Molecular life of plants Cellular biochemistry Microbiology (Part I)
recommended_courses: The block courses Plant biochemistry and phytopathology. The rest was all good. However, I would not recommend to have too many exams in the end (four were too many for me).
unexpected_costs: Switxerland is expensive. Expect to use a lot of money on everything. I went hiking and skiing - this was only possible because of grants and scholarship.
cost_comparison: Everything was more expensive.
activities_available: Not much because of corona. A lot of sports were offered for free at the university.
activities_recommended: Hiking, skiing, all kinds of sports.
weekend_recommendations: Grindelwald, Zermatt (Matterhorn), skiing in Crans Montana was good and cheaper than St. Moritz/Davos.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. It is a european country and most people are good at english.
socializing_tips: Do the intensive German course in the beginning of the semester.
cultural_challenges: The work ethics and the expectations to students.
culture_appreciated: The great hiking culture.
top3_advice: 1. Avoid having too many exams. 2. Do block courses if possible for your study direction. 3. Expect a huge workload.
other_useful_info: Apply for grants.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and the nature.
greatest_challenge: The workload and the dorm, where I was living, was not as cozy as my home dorm.

crucial_aspects: Best university in the EU for my studies (when not counting UK)
info_ease: Very easy, all information was provided prior to arrival or during my first days here.
arrival_assistance: Mails and meetings regarding the housing, very nice informative student association helped out a lot
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: They guide you all the way regarding how to upload documents and how to apply for specific courses. really helpful administration
registration_help: See above
registration_success: I registered for 6, got all of them except one of them - and then applied for another one and got that one
registration_advice: Be on time. It becomes messy when u have to fill out docs after deadlines.
course_level: They were similar to the level of UCPH I'd say
teaching_comparison: I only took practical courses and project works, so I didn't really experience the lecture and theoretical exercise classes. However, the practical work was really good - a bit too pedagogical sometimes..
courses_enrolled: Intensive german language course, cell biology of the nucleus, membrane biology, insulin signaling, RNA biology, genomic and genetic methods in cell and developmental biology
recommended_courses: I'd recommend all of them actually. The language course gives you a lot of new friends that are also on an exchange. All of the others were lab-based lab courses where you are assigned to a Ph.D. or post-doc project and work on those projects for around a month. Insulin Signaling is quite intense in terms of the lab work. But the nice thing is that you try out a lot of different techniques.
unexpected_costs: I traveled a lot on the weekends and the personal spending per month listed is mainly due to the high cost of public transport traveling within Switzerland..
cost_comparison: Housing was less, food and especially transportation were more
activities_available: My student association arranged a lot of different social get-together events (dinner evenings, board game evenings etc..) and also on Campus quite some academic activities were planned. ESN network also arranges some nice activities.
activities_recommended: ASVZ for sports! Dinner evenings etc with your student association! If you want to go on a trip with other exchange students and don't have a group to go with, go on an ESN trip!
weekend_recommendations: I love mountains (mountaineering like hiking, climbing, via ferrata, skiing etc) and Switzerland is ideal for this! I went every weekend and I already miss the mountains
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it is quite similar to Danish culture on the surface, however, some swiss people can be a bit "shy" or ignorant maybe. But when you get to know the, they typically become your new best friends ;-)
socializing_tips: ASVZ! ESN! Student associations! Language courses! Parties at exchange dorm rooms and at "Langstrasse"! Get a buddy (a local student to help you out with socializing and meeting new people on bars etc)!
cultural_challenges: The language barrier sometimes. Swiss german is nothing like high german - however, most people here speak English
culture_appreciated: The very active culture in terms of sports and the high degree of citizens being international
top3_advice: ASVZ for sports (try everything out, jazz dance, ballet, kickboxing, swimming, judo whatever), do travel while being here if you like the alps, engage in academic activities outside your syllabus if you have time (they normally organize cool lecture-based and coffee events where you can learn about anything you like with fellow students of yours!)
other_useful_info: Apply for Novo Nordisk Intwrnational Talent program as this will give you money for traveling ;-) I don't regret a sec that I used all of the money on traveling even though sometimes I couldn't afford high-quality meals on every hike I went on;-)
most_rewarding: All the traveling and cultural experiences learned. ANd then also the nice network you get if you are a biology student and choose block courses (YOU SHOULD DO THIS!!!!!!) because you will get to know a lot of lab members within the different labs. This enables you to explore different fields of biology and let you to find out what you fancy more than other subjects :DD
greatest_challenge: Money for all the traveling :O
other_comments: DO reach out if you want to hear more about the experiences here, I'd be happy to help out with more details :) - I think it is super important to go on an exchange if you have eager to learn about other cultures and foreign ways of teaching etc OMG and the mountains!!! ;-)))

crucial_aspects: Interesting courses, mountains, nature
info_ease: ETH Zurich provides a lot of information. It is almost too much but I think you can almost find the answer to any question you have in the material they provide.
arrival_assistance: Almost all communication and help was online. You have to participate in study start events for Erasmus students in the beginning where you are also overloaded with information. It is still very helpful though! I know it's possible to receive help from the "erasmus office" at ETH and as far as I know, they were very helpful to other students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I had to show up at an exchange office during the first week and register. As far as I remember, it was super easy and they were helpful.
registration_help: Online communication and meetings at the exchange office. They are very busy the first couple of weeks, but I believe it is possible to receive the help you need.
registration_success: You can register for as many classes you want, try them out the first three weeks and then choose which classes you want to drop/keep. My recommendation is to register for too many classes, see what you like and choose based on your experience the first weeks of the semester.
registration_advice: Dont stress too much. Read the information they send you, go to the office and then it should be fine. Register for too many classes and drop the ones you dont like (I think you get 3 weeks to do this)
course_level: Both level and workload is a bit higher than at KU.
teaching_comparison: Similar teaching style. The professors are approachable and willing to help with any problems you may have.
courses_enrolled: 1) Computational Quantum Physics 2) Semiconductor Devices: Quantum Transport at the Nanoscale 3) Molecular and Materials Modelling 4) Ferromagnetism: From Thin Films to Spintronics 5) Electronic Transport in Nanostructures
recommended_courses: If you want a very difficult course, I can recommend computational quantum physics. I personally liked "Molecular and Materials Modelling" and "Electronic Transport in Nanostructures" the best. The teachers are good and they are interesting if you like nanoscale physics and chemistry.
unexpected_costs: If you want to travel around Switzerland in weekends and holidays (which you definitely have to do!), you will encounter very high costs of public transport. You absolutely have to get the "Half fare card" (costs around 1000kr) and gives you half price on all public transport for a year. If you dont get this, travelling will be way too expensive.
cost_comparison: Food is expensive. Restaurants and bars are also very expensive. Public transport
activities_available: Parties, different types of events on campus (cinema, beer-week, ...). Theres an infinite amount of sports classes you can go to
activities_recommended: Sports classes. Find a good group of friends to go and enjoy the mountains (hiking, camping, skiing) Swimming in the river, lake
weekend_recommendations: Swiss mountains! There are so many amazing places. You will not get tired of going to the mountains!
culture_adjustment: Not a problem. Everyone in the university environment are good at english and swiss people are similar to danes.
socializing_tips: Approach them, ask them about stuff. They will not go and talk to you if you dont approach them first. Just do it!
cultural_challenges: The local students work harder than what I'm used to.
culture_appreciated: I enjoyed nature more than culture. I had a feeling that everything just works in Switzerland which was pretty nice.
top3_advice: 1) you will receive a lot of information. Go through it slowly and make some "to do lists" to get your head around it. Dont worry if you miss a detail. You can get a lot of help once you arrive. 2) Make sure to apply for funding! Switzerland is expensive and it is very nice not having to think about money all the time. 3) Register for way too many courses (way too many ECTS) and drop the courses you dont like within the first 3 weeks of the semester. 3)
most_rewarding: Getting to know a lot of people from all over Europe and just enjoying being in a beautiful country with them.
greatest_challenge: Pressure and stress from university. I think the courses can seem very difficult but in the end it was honestly not that bad. The exams were fine and I think that if you just follow the lectures and study decently for the exams, you will be fine.

crucial_aspects: Det var meget vigtigt for mig at der var i min fritid var lækker natur, meget at opleve og på universitetet var mulighed for laboratoriearbejde og vælge flere forskellige fag, for at finde ud af, hvad jeg synes er sjovest. Det var også meget vigtigt at opholdet var på engelsk og byen var relativt stor.
overall_comments: Min udveksling har været rigtig god i forhold til de venskaber jeg har dannet mig fra hele Europa, og for min personlige udvikling ved at bo alene i et fremmed land, og selv lære at tage intiativ til alt det faglige og det sjove samtidigt! Da jeg har taget 30 ECTS har universitet fyldt mere end jeg havde regnet med, og med laboratoriearbejde, fulgte mange obligatoriske og lange dage på universitetet og gruppearbejde, der helt sikkert var en udfordring!
info_ease: Da jeg ankom fik man en masse papirer, der var lidt uoverskueligt. Jeg skulle søge om residence permit på kommunen, søge fag og være sikker på at alt var i orden, da man flere gange får at vide at en misset deadline er ens egen skyld og der ikke er noget at gøre ved det. Der var til gengæld massere af hjælp at hente og svar-tiden på emails var næsten altid under 2 dage.
arrival_assistance: Jeg fik hjælp til hvilke fag jeg burde tage, i forhold til min baggrund af universitetet. Men jeg fik mest hjælp fra de andre udvekslingselever jeg boede med på kollegie, og fik fat i et godt telefonselskab, et studiekort osv. og undgik at fare alt for meget vild.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Min udveksling har været rigtig god i forhold til de venskaber jeg har dannet mig fra hele Europa, og for min personlige udvikling ved at bo alene i et fremmed land, og selv lære at tage intiativ til alt det faglige og det sjove samtidigt! Da jeg har taget 30 ECTS har universitet fyldt mere end jeg havde regnet med, og med laboratoriearbejde, fulgte mange obligatoriske og lange dage på universitetet og gruppearbejde, der helt sikkert var en udfordring!
registration_process: Man skal møde op på campus i centrum, hvor man bliver registreret og får sit studiekort samt vigtige dokumenter og en tjekliste (Studiekortet skal medbringes til eksamen, så det er godt at holde fast i). Derefter er der en obligatorisk orientering for udvekslingselever, og man kan derefter starte sine fag. Det er vigtigt at huske at der både er en dansk mobility online og en schweizisk side. Dem skal man huske at opdatere løbende!
registration_help: Både mail, personlig hjælp og telefontider er tilgængelig
registration_success: på D-BIOL kan man melde sig til block-kurser, der er 6 ECTS laboratoriekurser på 3-4 uger af gangen. Disse skal man melde sig til tidligere. Det er ikke sikkert man får sine prioriteter, da udvekslingselever ikke har førsteret. Der er nogle kurser der er pladsbegrænsede. Disse kurser burde jeg have tilmeldt mig så snart jeg kunne - og gerne have tilmeldt mig for mange kurser. Man kan til- og afmelde kurser de første 2 uger af semesteret - men nogle fag er allerede fuldt bookede (det kan være fag med ekskursioner til bjergene eller diskussionsfag).
registration_advice: Søg en masse fag, og prøv så vidt muligt at prøve dem af: spørg professoren om man skal have nogen forudsætninger, tjek pensum hurtigt igennem og tjek hvad andre folk synes: gennem VSETH kan man finde alle fakulteters studenter-hjemmeside. Hvis man logger ind med sit ETH-brugernavn, kan man ofte se gamle eksamener, reviews og ratings. Det vidste jeg ikke - jeg startede med nogle fag, der ikke var som jeg regnede med, og måtte skifte til to andre fag i sidste øjeblik, ændre min forhåndsgodkendelse og læse 2 ugers pensum op.
academics_comments: Min udveksling har været rigtig god i forhold til de venskaber jeg har dannet mig fra hele Europa, og for min personlige udvikling ved at bo alene i et fremmed land, og selv lære at tage intiativ til alt det faglige og det sjove samtidigt! Da jeg har taget 30 ECTS har universitet fyldt mere end jeg havde regnet med, og med laboratoriearbejde, fulgte mange obligatoriske og lange dage på universitetet og gruppearbejde, der helt sikkert var en udfordring!
course_level: Det er mit overordnede indtryk at jeg og andre har lagt flere timer pr ECTS end jeg normalt ville gøre på KU. Der er nogen fag der minder meget om dem, vi har på ku, men til en del færre points. Jeg var heldig at D-BIOL er 100% på engelsk på 3. år, men jeg kender til flere der har taget kandidat-kurser for at få dem på engelsk, og synes at det var meget intenst og med ekstremt hårde eksamener.
teaching_comparison: Jeg valgte mine fag til dels ud fra underviserne også. Det var nogle rigtigt gode undervisere. Der er både fysisk undervisning, og live-streaming + Recording af denne, og det hele er tilgængeligt på deres Absalon (moodle). For de fag jeg tog, var der kun foreslåede bøger til læsning og ingen eksaminatorietimer - det gjorde det lidt mere til selvstudie, men jeg synes det gik godt til sidst.
courses_enrolled: Evolutionary Biology: Ecological Genetics (3 ECTS) + Population and Quantitative Genetigs (3 ECTS) Insulin Signaling (lab) (6 ECTS) Membrane Biology (lab) (6 ECTS) Parallels between Tissue Repair and Cancer (lab) (6 ECTS) ETH WEEK (1 uges intens kursus) (1 ECTS) Pharmaceutical Immunology (2 ECTS) Immunology I (3 ECTS)
recommended_courses: Deres immunologikurser var gode grundkurser der gav et fedt overblik (Kuby og Janeways bøger). Insulin-signalering er et fedt laboratoriekursus - det mest intense med 9-19 (1 times frokost) og artikel-læsning, dataanalyse, præsentationer og eksamen, men man lærte meget og det var fedt at arbejde med mus, lever og til sidst celler i de 3 uger vi havde kurset. Parallels between Tissue Repair and Cancer var også et fedt kursus, med mere overordnet introduktion til biokemiske laboratoriemetoder. Til sidst fulgte man en phd-studerende og fik lov til at vælge og designe et eksperiment som man skulle præsentere for hele gruppen og holdet (20-25 mennesker) - ekstremt nervepirrende, men en vild oplevelse.
unexpected_costs: Transport i Schweiz er genialt, men også dyrt. For mig, købte jeg ingen cykel, da jeg synes det var lidt uhyggeligt uden cykelstier og i en ny by - men månedlig transport omkostninger blev til gengæld mere end forventet. Jeg var også overrasket over mad-priserne.
cost_comparison: Restaurant og barer er vildt dyrt! Vegetarisk mad er en fordel at spise (kylling kan koste 40 kr for den mindste pakke, og et stykke laks kan koste 60-75) - LIDL og Aldi har bedre priser.
activities_available: Der er gratis sport på ETH. ASVZ. På deres hjemmeside kan du tjekke alle de aktiviteter ud, som de har! ETH arrangerer forskellige sociale sammenkomster, men man skal også holde øje med både Erasmus netværket og VSETH (studenterorganisationern). På Telegram kan man komme i grupper, hvor begivenheder offentligtgøres - Skiture og vandreture bliver hurtigt fyldt op!
activities_recommended: Svøm og bad langs med Zurich Søen om sommeren, opdag vandring i det tidlige efterår, besøg byerne i december med julemarkeder, og stå på ski eller tag hen for at kælke eller snow-shoeing når der falder sne i bjergene. Erasmus holder en velkomstfest og normalt er der et polybal på ETH i november (det var aflyst i år, men skulle være en fantastisk aften).
weekend_recommendations: Jeg startede med at ændre min rutine til at feste om torsdagen (gratis for studerende) og vandre om lørdagen (tidligt op med toget kl 7-7:30). Min hverdag var proppet med skole, men det var befriende at tage op over tågen og regnen med toget og vandre i solskin!
culture_adjustment: Jeg har haft det overraskende nemt, da folk er enormt søde og jeg stoler trygt på Schweizerne og dem jeg boede med. Jeg havde til gengæld svære ved at justere til deres work-life balance, som jeg oplever er meget mere intens end jeg er vant til.
socializing_tips: Find en sport på universitetet, det er nogen gange rart at mødes fast med et par, hvor det ikke handler om at arrangere så meget selv! Jeg endte med at have en (næsten) fast aftale om tirsdagen med 2 piger, hvor vi til sidst spiste sammen også!
cultural_challenges: Der er få tendenser til at nationaliteterne holder lidt sammen for sig selv, og da jeg synes at det kan være sværere at forstå hinanden helt præcis (sarkasme og humor) på tværs af lande, holdte jeg mig lidt tilbage til at starte med. Nu tror jeg ikke man skal være bange for misforståelser - alle er meget mere velkomne og søde end jeg lige havde troet til at starte med!
culture_appreciated: Det er helt genialt at man kan møde så mange fremmede mennesker fra alle mulige mærkelige steder, og finde ud af at man har de helt samme interesser og at man både kan lære fede ting om sig selv og om verden når man møder dem på udveksling!
top3_advice: Husk dit vandretøj og en god drikkedunk! Tag nogle danske opskrifter med for at imponere italienerne ;) Smile and pay - der er massere at opleve, skru ikke ned for det!
other_useful_info: ETH er en sjov udfordring! Der er massere at lave hernede, og man når at skabe nogle gode venskaber som man kan græde og grine med over læselivet!
most_rewarding: At blive introduceret til det schweiziske liv - arbejd hårdt i hverdagen - smid alt i hænderne - tag ud og vandre, ski eller oplev i weekenden og forny din energi! Der er utroligt mange mennesker lørdag morgen på hovedbanegården - nogle er på vej hjem fra fest, men størstedelen skal på eventyr med mountainbike- og skiholder i toget!
greatest_challenge: Jeg synes det var ret intimiderende at starte laboratoriefag i en lille gruppe af 3-5 elever med phd-studerende - at skulle introducere sig selv og spise frokost med en helt fremmed gruppe mennesker startede jeg med at synes var virkelig frygteligt til ret spændende - man får utroligt mange nye indtryk, som man lige skal lære at synes er blæret og sjovt, end intimiderende og farligt!
other_comments: Søg en masse legater i god tid og pak en kuffert med 1:1 aktivt tøj og normalt tøj! Det er muligt at rykke eksamener til tidligere i januar eller til distance exams - dog bliver det ofte mundtlige eksamener i stedet. Men man kan godt komme til at starte til normal tid til blok 3 i DK.

crucial_aspects: My priority was to experience being on exchange without feeling I was compromising the academic outcome of my semester.
info_ease: Quite easy. Once I arrived the information found me naturally.
arrival_assistance: There is an intro meeting which is nice and some information emails.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You can register/deregister for courses courses until two weeks into the semester. It is very common to register for more courses than you would like to complete and then use the first two weeks attending the intro lectures to decide which courses you want to keep. After the two weeks you registration is still not very binding/demanding. While you cannot deregister anymore you can simply choose to not register for the exam. Even if you register for the exam you can still afterwards deregister from the exam (in many cases up until the day before the exam) effectively on paper making it as if you never attended the course.
registration_help: We could correspond with our exchange coordinators via E-mail.
registration_success: I was able to register to all classes that I wanted but the main problem was balancing the timeslots and credits of the courses.
registration_advice: I would generally say be careful about choosing many small (few ects) courses as some of them are more work than proclaimed. Also if you are in doubt about which course to keep after the two weeks registration window just keep e.g. both of them and decide a little further down the road. While you may be taking up one more spot on a course that you will stop attending it might save you a lot of trouble.
course_level: The difficulty of my course were in general roughly the same or slightly higher than back home. The workload/credit was higher.
teaching_comparison: Very similar.
courses_enrolled: I did Big Data, Probabilistic AI, Visual Computing and Natural Language Processing. Big data has a great professor and is not too difficult considering that it is 10 ECTS. NLP and Probabilistic AI are quite demanding in terms of math and abstraction but are both great courses in their own ways (NLP had a lot of hickups in the assignments but it was the first iteration with assignments so I suspect this will have improved a lot). Probabilistic AI was probably my favorite course as it is really hard to point to anything specific they could improve in the course. NLP is conceptually very interesting but do not expect a course that is centered around deep learning and transformers. The course mainly deals with various ways to model probability distributions over language structure and then making simplifying assumptions such that normalization constants can be calculated efficiently with abstract (semirings) dynamic programming. Visual computing is very mediocre. The professors have very impressive achievements but in my opinion the teaching was quite poor. The course has a lot of content and almost none was very thoroughly explained.
recommended_courses: Probabilistic AI, Big Data, NLP in no particular order. I did not attend it but I think you learn a lot on the Deep Learning course but it is probably quite tough. Did not hear good thing about advanced machine learning. Introduction to machine learning has the same professor as Probabilistic AI and he is very good.

crucial_aspects: I chose ETH, because it offers a broad range of interesting courses. And Zurich has a really nice location close to the mountains - and in only a couple of hours of train ride you can be in Italy, France and Germany.
overall_comments: I was super happy about my overall stay at ETH.
info_ease: ETH is very well organised, so I felt like I was well prepared. If sth was not clear, I wrote to the International Office of ETH - they are super helpful and write back quickly.
arrival_assistance: There were several pre-arrival Zoom Meetings offered. And an Intro Day in the first week - which was super nice, because one gets to know a lot of fellow students.

academics_comments: I was super happy about my overall stay at ETH.
course_level: The academic level is in general higher than at KU. In Copenhagen we for instance did statistical analyses with small data sets in Excel - at ETH we were confronted with much bigger and much more complex data that was analysed in R. Also, at ETH one gets only very little ECTS points for a course, although the work load is much higher.
teaching_comparison: I liked it a lot that we had to solve problems in the lectures - so one is not just passively sitting there and listening. And I also appreciated that in some courses we could work by ourselves; at my faculty in Copenhagen there is way too much group work and one never really gets the chance to develop own ideas.

recommended_courses: I enjoyed the Landscape Planning and Ecosystem Services because it was a nice combination of theory (lecture) and practice (GIS). And the professor is always open to discuss!

cost_comparison: Groceries were even more expensive than expected.
activities_available: Sports is organised by ASVZ. Additionally, there are heaps of social events offered by the faculties.
activities_recommended: I took two language classes at UZH to get to know people outside my academic field, which was super nice. And I tried a lot of different sports classes offered by the ASVZ!
weekend_recommendations: Everything! Switzerland is a small but so diverse country - and most places are easily reached by public transport. I enjoyed hiking on the weekends a lot!

socializing_tips: Talk to the Swiss fellow students sitting next to you in your course :-)
cultural_challenges: I did find nothing in particular challenging.
culture_appreciated: Swiss people are very outdoorsy and love their mountains!
top3_advice: Hiking boots. Snow shoes. Climbing gear.
most_rewarding: I am super happy about all the things I learnt - it gave me a lot of good ideas for future projects!

socializing_tips: One should join the events hosted by the VSETH or VMP and talk with people in class.

crucial_aspects: University ranking and access to professors with international recognition for their research. Proximity to Denmark was also a small factor.
overall_comments: Also, when you spend the majority of your time at the university, it is preferable that the university has good facilities (well funded).
info_ease: Information was really easy to come by and their administration continously sends you update regarding social events for incoming students and deadlines for, e.g., course registration etc. There is a check-list that covers most of the steps that need to be done before, during and after the exchange stay. This can be found on their website.
arrival_assistance: There are events where the student association will answer question / show you around. The student exchange office is really helpfull, as well.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Also, when you spend the majority of your time at the university, it is preferable that the university has good facilities (well funded).
registration_process: The registration process, courses, exams, etc., is really straight forward. You will recieve a link from the student exchange office with guides on how and when to register. Specifically, they have a portal 'myStudies' in which everything from scheduling, registration/derigistration is handled.
registration_help: Video guides, student exchange office and written material on the requirements for obtaining credits (taking courses) at the different departments depending on your study programme.
registration_success: I had no issues registrering for the classes, although there were some classes which were specific to the full masters programme, hence not available to exchange students. Make sure to read carefully which courses you are allowed to take.
registration_advice: You can apply for more courses (credits) than you want/need to take and derigister after trying each course for 1-2 weeks. This is a really good opportunity to see if you actually like the course(s).
academics_comments: Also, when you spend the majority of your time at the university, it is preferable that the university has good facilities (well funded).
course_level: I took 3 MA courses and 1 BA course. The level of the material was not much different from KU, in my experience. However, the course material seemed more 'predictable' in that it was clear from the beginning (in all but one of my courses), what the students needed to get out of the course.
teaching_comparison: It was very similar. Lectures and exercise classes.
courses_enrolled: Large Language Models Rigorous Software Engineering Big Data for Engineers Computational Statistics
recommended_courses: Big Data for Engineers (or Big Data, same lecturer), is really good. It is very well structured.
unexpected_costs: If you live outside student housing you have to get 'vouchers' (stickers) that you put on your (official) trash bags to throw out. It costs about 15 DKK per trash bag. I also had to pay for radio license, electricity, gas, etc., seperately from the rent. In some cases you have to paint the room as well.
cost_comparison: I knew it was expensive going to Switzerland, specifically Zurich. Nevertheless, food was quite more expensive than I would've imagined. Transport also relatively expensive, especially since I lived outside of the city zone. Eating at the school cafeteria can in some cases be cheaper than cooking at home. Protein shakes from COOP are a steal, highly recommend if you plan on working out.
activities_available: The student association and adjacent association has all sorts of activities (hikes, tennis, dinners, etc.).
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend going to Bern and take a boat down the Aaare River (starting point is in Thun). Also, go to Lucerne, it's a beautiful city. Obviously, go on some hikes as they are really accessible. If you are under 25, you can get really good discounts for train tickets (look up 'Half-fare' and adjacent offers on SBB). Sign up for ASVZ and look at sports activity offers. Here you can meet a lot of local people as well who might share the same passion for a sport. Besides the academic activities, it is really about making sure you see what Switzerland and Zurich has to offer; so go on a few hikes and meet some international as well as local students that you can do different things with, e.g., play sports, swim in the lake, etc.
weekend_recommendations: Study, obviously.
culture_adjustment: Realy easy. It is similar.
socializing_tips: Use the WhatsApp group and student associations.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: People are very nice and the streets are exeptionally clean.
top3_advice: Find housing in time and start grant applications early.
other_useful_info: Note that many people go home in the study "break". That is, the exams can be as late as in August, so make sure you plan your summer accordingly with which courses/exams you take.
most_rewarding: Getting to experience a different student culture and taking course not available at KU.
greatest_challenge: Finding a good balance between studying and having free time.
