crucial_aspects: The academic quality and reputation of the ETH Zürich.
overall_comments: The university is great and the academic level lived up to expectations.
info_ease: Everything was neatly organized in a slideshow from ETH, there was no info lacking and I had virtually no need to seek additional information anywhere.
arrival_assistance: I registered at the university but did not receive any further assistance. I am sure that plenty of assistance is necessary if need be though.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The university is great and the academic level lived up to expectations.
registration_process: At ETH, the first week of courses is free-for-all, hence no course registration is binding until middle of the second week of semester. At this point you lock in your courses in a online web-portal similar to KUnet.
registration_help: I had trouble registering for one course, wrote to the exchange department who forwarded me to the math department, who asked me to get permission from the lecturer to take the course. He replied very fast and immediately got admitted. The whole process took around 30 min.
registration_success: I managed to register for all of them. Be aware that if you want to do seminars there are limited spaces and should be out in good time.
registration_advice: Be out in good time if you want to do seminars, use the first week to browse courses.
academics_comments: The university is great and the academic level lived up to expectations.
course_level: The level taught is high and fast-paced. It is per say not more difficult than UCPH, but the pacing is faster and hence more material is covered per ECTS credit. I would say that a 3-5 credit course at ETH easily corresponds to a 7.5 UCPH course. Exams are a bit ridicolous as they are often designed to be unsolvable in the allotted time due to the sheer volume of problems on the exam, which can be a bit stressful (even though the problems are not necessarily difficult).
teaching_comparison: Lectures are more or less the same. Less time is spend on formally proviing things and instead conveying intuition/covering more material. The students are however still expected to know the corresponding proofs. Contrary to at the math department at UCPH, excersise classes are utterly useless at ETH.
courses_enrolled: Numerical Solutions of Stochastic Ordinary Differential Equations Causality Markov Processes Student Seminar in MCMC sampling Stochastic Simulation Clinical Biostatistics (UZH course)
recommended_courses: Numerical Solutions of Stochastic Ordinary Differential Equations was super interesting, even though the teaching is not very good. If you can motivate yourself I would definitely recommend. I liked Markov Processes but it is a high workload for 3 credits if you want to understand the material. Causality is a must-take course if you have any interest in statistics - very interesting and well taught. I would in general also recommend doing a seminar as it is a good way to meet people and see some research. In addition there is no exam - which you will appreciate during the exam season. Stochastic Simulation was a good intro to a lot of simulation (MCMC) stuff. There are a lot of topics however, and if you want things explained in depth, this is probably not the right course to take. Clinical Biostatistics is very doable and probably practically relevant, but not very interesting from a mathematical standpoint. I only tookit to fill up some credits.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay radio and television tax (similar to old licens in Denmark) which is about 1500 DKK per household per half year.
cost_comparison: Having a mobile subscription was surprisingly expensive. Food is very expensive, especially if you eat meat/animal products.
activities_available: There is a lot of sports organized, but not anything i utilized.
activities_recommended: Go out to the mountains! The nature is extremely beautiful.
weekend_recommendations: You likely wont have time to do anything but study.
culture_adjustment: Switzerland is essentially Denmark with a bit higher cost of living. Adjusting is very easy.
socializing_tips: Seeing as I attended the autumn semester, I started the same time as a lot of new masters students. These are from all over the world, and dont know anyone either, so they are easy to socialize with if you attend the new students events in addition to the exchange student events.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: As mentioned above, the culture is very similar to Denmark so nothing particular to share here.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared to study (a lot). 2. Exams feel frustrating/unfair and you might think you have done poorly, but you have likely done better than you think. 3. People are a bit more competetive/intense at ETH, this is not necessarily because they are unfriendly.
other_useful_info: Not that I have not already mentioned.
most_rewarding: Having fun subjects that were academically challenging.
greatest_challenge: Managing taking 6 courses 5 of which corresponded to a UCPH course in curriculum covered.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: ETH Zürich is a very good educational and research institution with very interesting and advanced courses in biology, which is a big reason for why I chose ETH. Moreover, I wanted to explore Switzerland because of the amazing nature of course and the high quality of life
info_ease: Easy, you will generally get emails about everything you need to know and do
arrival_assistance: The exchange office of ETH were very helpful and provided all necessary information by email. They also held some intro events that were helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was quite straight forward, you just fill out an application and if you have already been granted an exchange spot from UCPH, this should not cause problems.
registration_help: It was easy to find answers to most questions you could have on the ETH website. The exchange coordinators from ETH were also very helpful and quick to reply to emails
registration_success: I took one course that had limited amount of spots, so I was put on a waiting list because I, as an exchange student, had the lowest priority for receiving a spot. In the end, there were available spots though. Most "normal" courses (in D-BIOL) dont have a maximum capacity, and you can register/deregister as you wish. I also took a seminar course with only 15 spots, where masters students had priority, so I had to wait until a registration deadline to know if I received a spot, which I did. I took 3 block courses, which are special to D-BIOL. For these, you dont register through the normal registration portal, but through a specific website. The registration opening date is a bit later than normal registration, and you make a priority list of which block courses you want to attend. A few weeks later, you are told for which ones you have been given a spot. In the first block, I did not get my first priority, but my third or fourth (I ended up loving this course though). The other block courses were my first priority
registration_advice: Keep your email notifications on, so that you know when the registration opens, if you want to register for any courses with a limited capacity. It is generally on a first come first serve basis. If there is no mention of a maximum capacity in the course catalogue, then you can register for the course whenever you want (even in the middle of the semester)
course_level: I took mostly bachelor's level courses, but I took one masters' seminar course. The level was high in all the courses, but I definitely did not feel like I lagged behind as a student from UCPH compared to the ETH students.
teaching_comparison: A lot of courses were lecture-only courses, where there were no problem-solving classes or something similar. I did not like this, as it was less motivating and harder to retain the knowledge from the lectures. The block courses, however, were amazing and I would highly recommend taking as many as possible if you are enrolled in D-BIOL. These were much smaller classes, where you got to know your teachers more personally and got a lot of hands-on experience and were exposed to the actual research the teachers are doing, which was super fun. It was much more collaborative and similar to classes in gymnasium, so you got to know the other (swiss) students as well
courses_enrolled: Systems Biology of Metabolism (MA) Immunology I (BA) Molecular Structure and Function: Proteins (BA) Introduction to Mass Spectrometry-Based Proteomics (BA) Insulin Signaling (BA) Parallels Between Tissue Repair and Cancer (BA)
recommended_courses: Immunology and Molecular Structure and Function were both quite interesting, but they were each only one lecture per week, so I didnt find it very engaging or motivating. I personally like immunology better, and it follows up quite nicely from Medical Cell and Tissue Biology (if you are a biomedicine student) Systems Biology of Metabolism was a super interesting seminar course, where you had to read 1-3 papers each week and discuss them in class. The two professors are super nice and talented. I did not have the right prerequisites in Systems Biology though, so I definitely felt that it was hard to follow along al lot of the time. It ended up going well in the end though, so dont be scared if you think the topic sounds interesting. I learned a lot. Introduction to Mass Spectrometry Based Proteomics and Insulin Signaling were both amazing block courses. The teachers were very nice and very good, and the content was super interesting. I learned a lot from both of them, that I could also use in my other courses. Would 10/10 recommend Parallels Between Tissue Repair and Cancer was also a block course, but it was far less organized than the two others, so the overall experience was not that good. The content was interesting though, but I think I could have learned more from other courses. We did get to work with organoids which was very fun, and you get good insight into what its like to work as a PhD or postdoc in a research group
unexpected_costs: Public transport, in particular transport outside the city, is VERY expensive. I usually went on a trip to go hiking/skiing/sightseeing every weekend, so this became very expensive
cost_comparison: Everything is expensive, even coming from Denmark. Coffee is a little cheaper than in Denmark. I did not have to buy any textbooks, so this was cheaper than expected
activities_available: As a student, you can become a member (for free!) at ASVZ, which is the student sports association. This gives you free access to gyms and a lot of different sports classes There were also big parties for the entire school a few times during the semester. I would recommend to check out the PolyBall, which is a big traditional ball. The main building is very nicely decorated and it is cool to attend. You can take ball-dancing crash courses in advance, which I did (learnt english waltz, discofox, jive and more) ESN Zurich also have many events for exchange students throughout the semester
activities_recommended: Go see the nature of Switzerland as early as possible, before it becomes too cold and snowy to go hiking (usually around november). There are so many incredible places to go.
weekend_recommendations: The alps. Both for hiking and for skiing
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, not too dissimilar from the danish
socializing_tips: I only socialized with local students because of the block courses I took, so if you have the opportunity to do this, I would recommend it.
culture_appreciated: It is quite orderly, so people generally follow rules, which means that e.g. you very rarely get your ticket checked on busses/trams, self-checkout at the supermarket is very smooth and you dont have to scan your receipt, cars ALWAYS stop for you immediately if you want to cross the road etc. Public transport is also generally on time and very reliable. It is also very clean everywhere
top3_advice: Do stuff with other exchange students when you get the opportunity, especially in the beginning. Dont be afraid to be the one to reach out and take initiative, often other people will also not know who to talk to/do stuff with, so people are very open and friendly. It is fun to get to know some of the local swiss students, but realistically, you are probably gonna get to know other exchange students better. They are in the same boat as you, and also dont know anyone and want to experience as much as possible. The swiss students already have an established network and can be harder to get to know, because they are less interested in doing stuff e.g. on the weekends. Study in the weekdays and do fun stuff on the weekends, such as daytrips to other places or anything else that sounds fun.
other_useful_info: You can get a "friends daypass for youth", which is a public transport daypass for 4 people under 25, that you can use for a whole day to take any public transport in Switzerland. Only costs 80francs, definitely the cheapest way to get around outside of Zurich You can also buy a half-fare pass, which means you get 50% off all public transport tickets you buy. If you plan to take public transport everyday to campus and live in zone 110, you can get a monthly 110 pass for 60francs, which is cheaper than buying a ticket everyday, even with the half-fare You can register for a 2-week intensive german course, that lies in the two weeks before the semester start. This is a great way to make friends in the very beginning, if you want to learn some basic german or freshen up your high-school german. You can also use the first two weeks of september to explore switzerland before the courses begin in mid-september
most_rewarding: The friends I made and the academic things I learned
greatest_challenge: Some of the courses were harder than I was used to, and I felt unsure of whether I would manage, however it worked out in the end

crucial_aspects: Academic opportunities which includes relevant courses and projects that I could do while on exchange
overall_comments: The experience itself in Switzerland is 10/10, but all the administrative stuff and having to deal with housing/payment/paperwork drags it down a bit for me
info_ease: It was very easy. ETH provides gudies for everything you need to know and when you need to do it. Just attend all the zoom meetings or physical presentations or get a friend to attend for you.
arrival_assistance: We got tons of presentations and guides for what we needed to do.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The experience itself in Switzerland is 10/10, but all the administrative stuff and having to deal with housing/payment/paperwork drags it down a bit for me
registration_process: This is very specific for pharmaceutical sciences, but since I decided to take block courses that were not electives (but mandatory courses for the master's students at ETH), I had to email the department coordinator for permission to enroll which was quite confusing. We got an email that we had to enroll by checking the box outside the course, but the courses I planned did not have that option so I had to email a few different people to get enrolled.
registration_help: The exchange coordinators were super helpful and quick to answer. In general all the administrative staff at ETH were quick and efficient so I recommend emailing them if you need any help or have questions.
registration_success: I got all the courses that I wanted
registration_advice: Take advantage of the fact that only 2/3rd of the courses have to be within your faculty. I took all of my courses within pharmaceutical sciences because that is what I found the least confusing but I wish I had spent more time researching what courses were available - for example there is a course programme called "Science in perspective" in which they (in my semester) studied gothic literature. There really is a very wide variety of courses available at ETH and it is a good opportunity to try something new that you might not do at home.
academics_comments: The experience itself in Switzerland is 10/10, but all the administrative stuff and having to deal with housing/payment/paperwork drags it down a bit for me
course_level: To be honest, most if not all the courses in pharmaceutical sciences were academically below what you would find at KU. We had 10 courses in 1 block / half a semester, which meant that every course was super small and superficial. I did not learn a lot of new material. The research project that I later did (at master's level) was equivalent to or even below a bachelor level project at KU.
teaching_comparison: Style of teaching was pretty similar - mostly a mixture of lectures, group work, and case work / discussions in class. Maybe a bit more lecture oriented than UCPH though it depends on your courses and home degree.
courses_enrolled: 511-0018-00 Clinical Development 511-0020-00 Pharmacoeconomics 511-0019-00 Pharmacovigilance 511-0014-00 Process & Project Management 511-0016-00 Quality Management and Production 511-0017-00 Regulatory Affairs 511-0010-00 Scientific Concepts and Methods 511-0015-00 Technical Drug Product Development / CMC 511-0012-00 Pharmaceutical Biostatistics 900-0015-00 15 Credit Project
recommended_courses: I do not recommend any courses that I took except my course in biostatistics.
unexpected_costs: Public transport is very very expensive, way more than I first expected. You can get the local monthly pass to go to school and travel in the central part of Zürich for about 500-600 DKK which is pretty affordable BUT if you ever decide to go outside Zürich it will cost a lot. For example, without any deals/add-ons etc., going to a nearby city Luzern (40 min by train), costs 30CHF x 2 for a single trip, which is about 500 DKK. I travelled basically every weekend and as much as possible, so I spend a lot on public transport. There are some ways to make it cheaper though: Get the half fare card as soon as you're able. It is a card in which you pay for upfront, and then you get 50% of every subsequent ticket and special day ticket deals. The pricing is different if you're under 25. If you turn 25 before going to Switzerland, I recommend buying the half-fare card beforehand online because it lasts for a year from when you buy it and is valid even after you turn 25. You can also get the night GA for 99CHF if you're under 25 years, which enables free travel all over the country after 19.00 or before 05.00. If you're under 25 years old, you can also get the Friend's Ticket which enables 4 friends under 25 yo, to buy a day ticket for 4, for 80CHF, which means you can travel the entire country for only 20CHF a day. The cheapest way to travel. So you can go from Zurich to Geneva for 20CHF per person round trip when a normal round trip ticket costs 200CHF. Even if you can’t find exactly 3 other people, it can often be worth it, even if you’re only 2 or 3 friends. Here it is an advantage to live in a dormitory, as there’s always someone who’s keen to go on a trip with you, so you can split the price. It is quite expensive to be above 25 years old when going to Switzerland. Eating at restaurants is quite expensive in Zürich (not unusual to pay 30CHF-40CHF for a meal in an average restaurant) and the food is often not that good anyways. Going to the doctor can also easily be 200CHF to 300CHF. If you're a member of the EU, you get it refunded (except for a payment of 92CHF), but you still have to pay the price upfront.
cost_comparison: Some fruits/berries and vegetables are actually cheaper than in Denmark. If you're able to shop at a Lidl or Aldi you will be able to find prices comparable to Denmark.
activities_available: Students of ETH and UZH have the sports organisation of ASVZ which enables you to join 100+ sports for free and the gym for free. It is very popular though, and you have to sign up early. Popular sports classes like spinning have a 50/50 chance of entering because you sign up through a lottery system. Though outside that ETH has surprisingly few groups that I found interesting - a lot of them were language groups, buisness/entrepeneur/start up related. Not really any creative or a lot of hobby related opportunities.
activities_recommended: I really recommend hiking since the swiss nature is just so beautiful. There are hiking routes for all levels and you do not need previous experience. ETH has some hiking groups though I did not attend any, and I just went with my friends from the dorm. I also recommend getting a KulturLegi for Zürich. It is a card that allows you to get into a lot of cultural events heavily discounted (like the cinema, museums etc). You just have to apply online and attach proof that you have recieved a scholarship from the state (the SEMP scholarship paper) ESN Zürich hosts A LOT of events which I heavily recommend. With ESN you get to go on trips you would not otherwise have gone on for super cheap. It is also a great opportunity to make new friends. Just sign up on the website and watch out for which events are running since there is often limited seats.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking and visiting all the beautiful Swiss towns.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy as I think Swiss culture is very similar to Northern European culture. The swiss are a bit closed off and it can be hard to make local friends, which is why
socializing_tips: Attend local events such as painting class. I was able to meet a few local people that way.
cultural_challenges: Not really any.
culture_appreciated: How clean and punctual everyone is. The nature is spotless and everything administrative or customer service related is extremely efficient, way more than in Denmark!
top3_advice: Apply for a lot of grant money before going, get into the Swiss nature, be open to make a lot of new friends in the beginning (so you can also travel for cheap).
other_useful_info: Take the German Intensive language course in the beginning. It is really nice to start out with a class of other exchange and foreign students that you are together with every day. The language course also makes you go out into the city and gives you information about basic stuff such as the culture and local history of the city.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many new people and being able to experience the amazing nature in Switzerland. I was not an outdoor type person before.
greatest_challenge: Adminstrative stuff associated with the exchange.

crucial_aspects: That the university was academically sound in my field of study.
info_ease: Pretty easy, the host university and UCPH combined provided all necessary information in due time.
arrival_assistance: My host institution provided a lot of options for obligatory and unobligatory events and information gatherings in a timely and non-overwhelming way.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Very easy and flexible. Could switch up untill a week into the beginning of the semester.
registration_help: Online platforms primarely.
registration_success: It took a lot of time finding a schedule that didn't overlap, which was very imortant for me. I found 30 ETCS and was ultimately very happy with the courses.
registration_advice: Talk to students at the university and look for off-uni means of checking grade-statistics and difficulty/comments from previous students.
course_level: 16 credits MA, 8 credits BA. Remaining 6 credits where non-compulsory courses that could be taken in BA/MA programs. Ultimately, the difficulty of all courses were interchangable. The BA course was just as tough as the MA courses (if not more so, actually, but it is probably very subject specific).
teaching_comparison: Very similar in lectures, but exercise sessions were very different. Less contact with TA's and likewise less academic support in genneral.
courses_enrolled: Algorithms, Probability, and Computing (8) Network Security (8) Concepts of Object Oriented Programming (8) Wireless Networking and Mobile Computing (4) Technology Entrepreneurship (2)
recommended_courses: Technology Entrepreneurship was a very nice and relexaing course while still being *very* inspiring. Easy exam Network Security is probably one of (if not *the*) best course I have ever followed. Great and satisfying content. Excellent lecturers and mostly good guest lecturers. A bit of a funky exam but easy to pass due to projects that give part of the final grade.
unexpected_costs: There is a lot of micro-transactions in Switzerland and transport is *very* efficient, but also **very** expensive so beware and by the half-tax travelcard early on - even if for half a year use.
cost_comparison: Supermarkets are very expensive but not so much more than in Denmark if care is taken.
activities_available: ESN provided some social events early on which was very nice to get to know fellow exchange students.
activities_recommended: Hikes, hikes, hikes, some of the amazing cities of Switzerland. Skiing if you are into that.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the mountains or meet with friends. Be strict with your self in how you divide work and pleasure. You need to also work on at least some weekends to survive most likely.
culture_adjustment: Very easy and similar to Denmark.
socializing_tips: Initiate the conversation. Nobody is going to talk to you explicitly. It is your responsibility to get out there.
cultural_challenges: The genneral ideology is a bit different from the danish. It is not common to drink a beer after a days work - not even on fridays unless previously established.
culture_appreciated: How efficient society is and day-to-day politeness of Swiss people. Easy to integrate as a Danish person.
top3_advice: Get out there early on and meet new people. Be very cautious of the difficulty level of the courses you choose. Download Tinder if lonely (it helped)
other_useful_info: Always remember how big a priviledge it is to be able to study and learn. Remember to hit the fitness.
most_rewarding: Being able to pass the courses and still succeeding in accomplishing my goals with my trip. You don't go to ETH for extra leasure time.
greatest_challenge: Balancing the study load with my ambitions for the exchange.
other_comments: Keep a cool head and remember that passing the course is all that is needed!

crucial_aspects: Two major motivations caused me to pick ETH Zürich. First of all, ETH is a renowned university ranking among the highest in the world. This was a one time opportunity to push myself to the limit and expand my academic knowledge and network. Secondly, Switzerland is an incredibly beautiful country. I love mountains, I love skiing, and I love hiking.
info_ease: Pretty easy. I stayed in a WOKO (student housing office) dorm. They sent a bunch of emails informing me of what to do etc. Likewise, ETH was good at informing me of various events and appointments.
arrival_assistance: Not sure about what is meant by assistance? I handled myself pretty much, I would say.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I don't remember it. It wasn't that difficult. I would say that if you are afraid of how difficult the registration process is, then ETH might be too tough for you. (joke)
registration_help: The mails I received from ETH were clear and well formulated, and the exchange office at ETH were quick at responding to emails.
registration_success: Very successful. Smooth sailing. I had spent a lot of time looking through the course catalog before I arrived, so I knew more or less which classes to enroll in
registration_advice: don't worry about it. If anything confuses you then write an email to the ETH exchange office and they will help you
course_level: Pretty difficult. I spend the last couple of my summer vacation preparing for my courses at ETH. But in general, everyone in the auditorium thinks that it is difficult, you are not alone.
teaching_comparison: Not as pedagogical. Not quite as intuitive. Not as much focus on 'regneøvelser' and working with the material yourself. Just attending the lectures is not enough to pass - you have to invest a lot of time in understanding the material. A similarity between UCPH and ETH is that the lecturers ask question to the students during the lecture. There is a bit of interaction, which is nice.
courses_enrolled: Experimental Foundations of Particle Physics ('Semester Project' - not visible in the Course Catalog) Phenomenology of Particle Physics 1 Neutrino Physics Symmetries in Physics Nuclear Energy Conversion
recommended_courses: If you are interested in experimental particle physics then: Experimental Foundations of Particle Physics ('Semester Project' - not visible in the Course Catalog) Phenomenology of Particle Physics 1 Neutrino Physics If you are interested in more theoretical physics then: Symmetries in Physics (but I also heard from others that the GR and QFT courses are good) If you are want to try some light engineering: Nuclear Energy Conversion
unexpected_costs: When you register at the registration office you have to pay some 50CHF.
cost_comparison: Zürich is a very expensive city in general. Food at restaurants/kebab joints/cafeterias etc. were way more expensive than in copenhagen. Groceries were more or less the same, however meat is more expensive.
activities_available: stated above
activities_recommended: Tanzquotient! (Dancing classes). Dancing is fun and then you are well prepared for the Polyball (enormous gala party in the old main building)
weekend_recommendations: Go to the mountains!!!! My top 3 recommendations are: 1. Oeschinensee (very crowded, but very beautiful) 2. Eggishorn (expert level hike, you feel like invincible once you've reached the top. View to Aletschgletscher, Matterhorn, and Mont Blanc) 3. Churfirsten, Chäserrug (very beautiful view over Walensee, the Churfirsten are legendary)
culture_adjustment: pretty easy. My greatest difficulty adjusting was to get used to swiss people blowing their nose very loudly in the middle of a lecture (come to think of it, i never got used to it)
socializing_tips: Swiss people are not gonna say hi to you, so you have to say hi to them. Attend some of the many social student events
cultural_challenges: Swiss people are not that different from us. But they are more formal.
culture_appreciated: The effectivity. Both when it comes to public transport and when it comes to answering emails
top3_advice: 1. enjoy the privilege it is to study at one of the world's best universities 2. enjoy the mountains 3. when life seems tough, have an Appenzeller Quöllfrisch (beer) with your friends and share your distress with them
other_useful_info: if you are unsure which courses to enroll in, then know that the first week of the semester is not binding - you can enroll in a course, and if you find out after the first lecture that is not something for you anyway, then there is always the option to drop it and enroll in some other course
most_rewarding: I learned a lot about particle physics, got some good connections in the field, and even got a reference letter from an ETH professor to apply for the CERN Summer Student programme.
greatest_challenge: Symmetries in Physics. That course nearly broke me.... but I like to tell myself that i've gained a lot from it

arrival_assistance: A quick welcome presentation.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: While it was not part of my motivation for choosing ETH, I ended up really enjoying Switzerland for its nature as well, going on a lot of hiking and ski trips.
registration_process: I got a mail saying registration was open, after which I could start registering for courses. I got this mail pretty late, however, so 2 of the courses I wanted to take had already been filled up by the time I was made aware I could register.
registration_help: idk
registration_success: I was able to get the course I was most interested in, but other than that I had to change my entire study plan due to scheduling conflicts and/or courses not having space for me.
registration_advice: Don't get too attached to your original study plan. Be ready to adapt. Lot's of good courses to choose from, so be open minded.
academics_comments: While it was not part of my motivation for choosing ETH, I ended up really enjoying Switzerland for its nature as well, going on a lot of hiking and ski trips.
course_level: I went during the 5th semester of my Bachelor and took exclusively Master's courses. The level of the courses varied greatly and was mostly a bit above what I was used to at UCPH. One course in particular had an insane, genuinely unreasonable, workload...
teaching_comparison: About the same. Lectures followed by exercise classes. Unlike at UCPH where exercise classes are usually split into groups of 20 students, exercise classes at ETH were held with the entire class and a few TAs in the same auditorium. The advantage of this approach was that most exercise classes had a quick (well-made) presentation by a TA. The disadvantage is that it can be difficult to get help from a TA. For some courses in particular, you had to wait a loong time before you could ask a question.
courses_enrolled: Network security Computer Graphics Computer Architecture Embedded Systems
recommended_courses: Network Security was great. Most well-organized course I've ever taken with great content and fun projects. Embedded Systems had an unintelligible Italian lecturer, but the exercises were good and the content was varied. Computer Graphics was a lot of work. If you are interested in the topic, I definitely recommend it, but stay away if you only have a passing interest. Computer Architecture was not great. Two 3-hour lectures every week with with way too much content. The workload was also quite large with 25 paper reviews on top of standard exercise sheets and some labs that could be pretty time consuming. While the research group does high quality, interesting research, you really have to put in a lot of time to not fall behind -- and time is limited on an exchange!
unexpected_costs: e-sim -- my 3-like-home subscription did not cover my entire stay, so had to get a data e-sim after the first month.
cost_comparison: Eating out in general is very expensive. Even cafeteria food can be a little pricey.
activities_available: I attended a crash course in ballroom dancing for 4 weeks. ESN also hosts a ton of cool events that I attended. (ski trip, visit to CERN, etc)
activities_recommended: Sign up for a ton of ESN events - especially in the first week. Great way to meet people and make friends quickly.
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes. I definitely didn't see myself as a nature person before this exchange, but I ended up doing a lot of hikes.
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: Again, attend ESN events. Living in a huge WOKO dorm with lots of people also helps.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: Swiss timeliness. Public transportation is always on time.
top3_advice: - Go on lots of hikes (you can do 1 a week) - Don't get completely lost in studying (within reason). Try to sign up for as many events as possible and meet new people. - Do not take Computer Architecture unless you *really* like the area and are prepared to spend *a lot* of time on it.

most_rewarding: Hiking and meeting lots of new people.
greatest_challenge: Balancing studying with wanting to go on trips.

crucial_aspects: All the above were considerations for going on exchange
info_ease: It was relatively easy as the host university (ETH Zürich) were good at providing information and introduction meetings. I will say however, the Canton of Zürich provide a lot of their information in German which is not the most helpful. I used google translate and that worked fine. Also asking people around me worked well.
arrival_assistance: The university had information meeting on what to do and sent out emails also. Upon registration in the Kanton of Zürich, they also provided a lot of information.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You register for courses online and can change courses in the first weeks. The process is pretty easy. Block courses have different registration process that they inform you about over email.
registration_help: They had an introduction meeting explaining it
registration_success: I got most of the classes I wanted. I was enrolled at the department of biology were they have block courses (6 ects courses that are mostly lab based). These are space limited and you rank them according to preference. Exchange students are prioritised last, but I ended up with courses relevant to my studies (all of them either my first or second choice).
registration_advice: Don't stress. But also just get it done early, and you can always change it within the first weeks. There was a german course 2 weeks before semester start. This was very worth it as I made a lot of friends from the start.
course_level: Cancer and the immune system was a master level course. Requires knowledge of immunology but otherwise alright. The block courses require a lot of time physically in the lab. But they are not that hard theoretically. The students are not used to reading papers so things like journal club are not at a very high level. If you can follow the courses for molecular biomedicine back home then it should be fine if you are taking courses at the department of biology (unless it is something that requires coding and math).
teaching_comparison: UCPH has better teaching with classroom hours. The block courses however are pretty cool. You get to try a lot of techniques and do experiments that are out of budget for UCPH.
courses_enrolled: 551-0351-00L Membrane Biology 551-1525-00L Cancer Progression: Mechanisms, Targets and Therapeutic Approaches BIO 251 Cancer and the Immune System 551-1515-00L Insulin Signaling 551-1511-00L Parallels Between Tissue Repair and Cancer 551-0317-00L Immunology I
recommended_courses: All the courses except membrane biology. Keep in mind that Immunology I also has a part II in the spring. But it should be more than enough to compensate for the lack of immunology in the course "Human fysiologi" The following block courses were nice to gain experience in tissue culture and a broad array of assays and techniques: 551-1525-00L Cancer Progression: Mechanisms, Targets and Therapeutic Approaches 551-1515-00L Insulin Signaling 551-1511-00L Parallels Between Tissue Repair and Cancer
unexpected_costs: Not really any.
cost_comparison: Transportation in Zurich is arounf 60 francs a month if you are under 25. For transportation in switzerland you can get a friends pass with up to 3 other people under 25. This costs around 640 DKK in total => 160 DKK pr. person. This gets you a full day of free transportation in Switzerland. This is ideal for going on hikes. They also have a half fare card for traveling that can be worth it for some gondola lifts up mountains if you like hiking.
activities_available: They had some parties, sports association and parts of the central campus has some art installlations (they had a picasso exhibition once).
activities_recommended: Hiking, traveling in Switzerland and in the neighbouring countries. Block courses are nice, but also remember to spend your time traveling while the weather is nice. You can do quite a lot in a weekend. In January I only had one exam to prepare for, so I bought a GA travel card for one month that let me travel anywhere in Switzerland for free. I went for a lot of hikes, skiied and went to Paris also. Highly recommended.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking and see the cities. There are endless hikes and mountains to see.
culture_adjustment: Switzerland is not that different from Denmark. So it was pretty quick
socializing_tips: I did not socialise a lot with local students as i lived with other exchange students and did most things with them. It was really nice as they also don't have many obligations and were always up to go on hikes and other trips.
cultural_challenges: The Kanton of Zürich sends letters in German which is a bit annoying
culture_appreciated: The nature and the cleanliness
top3_advice: Go for the nice university but also enjoy the nature! Things can be a bit expensive in Switzerland, so it is not a bad idea to have some money saved (but, if you cook everyday then it is not crazy). Depending on your studies the courses might be at a very different level. For biology it was not as bad as i feared. But, for some other studies like chemistry and physics I did hear that it was challenging.
other_useful_info: Enjoy your time there, and since courses are transferred as passed/failed you can chill a bit and have some fun outside of studying.
most_rewarding: The friends I made along the way. We had a lot of potlucks, parties and hikes / trips to other countries.
greatest_challenge: My course load was pretty heavy. In winter the sun sets pretty early so there were some days were i did not see the sun.
other_comments: If you are a EU national you can be exempted from paying insurance!

crucial_aspects: That it was in the EU and has great skiing options.
info_ease: Super easy. ETH provided all the necessary information that one needed upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: First of all they send a lot of emails with practical informations. And then, on the first day of the semester there was a info-lecture for exchangestudents, that told everything one needed for insurance, residence permit etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: For biology one signs up for "block courses" a month before semesterstart. Here it is important to choose a lot of courses, as there is a big chance not to get ones first priorities due to limitid places. (ETH sends an email about this). One signs up for courses at a designated webpage - myStudies - at the semester start. Normally students take way to many courses the first week, just to try them out, and decide what to spend the semester on.
registration_help: ETH send e-mails during the procces to guide one through.
registration_success: Not very succesfull. I think I got 50% of the courses I initially wanted, but all my courses turned out to be very interesting - so I'm not sad about this.
registration_advice: Try out a lot of courses, and dont be affraid to take courses from other departments. To easen the academic burden, it can also be smart to take one or two "guest courses", which are considered to be way easier than the normal ETH courses. I took the guest course "Technology Entrepeneurship", which I dont think was that intersting, but it gave me some slack to focus on some of my more challenging courses.
course_level: I took 30 ECTS of BA level courses and 6 ECTS of MA level courses
teaching_comparison: Less homework, and more time in the lab/classroom at ETH.
courses_enrolled: "Mass spec for proteomics" "Biophysics of Microtubule Cytoskeleton" "Insulin Signaling" "Parallels between Tissue Repair and Cancer" "Immunology 1" "Population and Quantitative Genetics" "Technology Entrepeneurship" Crashcourse at ETH/UZH sprachenzentrum "Deutch A1.1" LTK Module 1
recommended_courses: "Mass spec for proteomics" 9/10 - fun course with both wet and dry lab. The people teaching this course are also pioneers in the field, which was very inspirering. And it gave some nice experience with omics-analysis in R, without requirering any R knowledge. "Biophysics of Microtubule Cytoskeleton" 7/10. Very easy block course but we didnt do that much. Nice to get some more freetime to explore switzerland. "Insulin Signaling" 7/10. But I learned how to do all the basic methods (WB, qPCR, cellculture and immaging etc.). I learned a lot, but the workdays were loooong. "Parallels between Tissue Repair and Cancer". Actually a very nice course. Cool that one got to make ones own research project in the last week. "Immunology 1" 6/10 Just lectures. It was so so. "Population and Quantitative Genetics" 9/10 - this was just great! Not too difficult, but very interesting. "Technology Entrepeneurship" 4/10. Easy. Crashcourse at ETH/UZH sprachenzentrum "Deutch A1.1" 10/10. This is a must as an exchange student. You get a lot of new friends, and are able to talk german with your lab-mates later in the semester.
unexpected_costs: fees for residence permit (200 DKK or so)
cost_comparison: Prices are very similar to danish prices - just eating out seemed more expensive to me. Also, I have heard that meat is more expensive, but I dont buy that myself.
activities_available: In ASVZ you get the chance to try every sport, and attend really good classes/lessons (look it up - it's amazing!!!) and it's free for all exchange students. Besides there are a lot of social clubs at the university.
activities_recommended: ASVZ!!
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes!! There are so many beautiful places to see. You can start with: Murren, Creux de Van, Stoos and Pizol five Lakes. Use this for off-line maps: https://www.swisstopo.admin.ch/en/hiking-maps . Every kanton has a touris guide with great hikes:)
culture_adjustment: Swiss culture is very special, but in terms of social norms it is quite simillar to danish (introverted culture).
socializing_tips: Take small courses - either lab or seminar courses. ASVZ. Try to speak german with them - they like this:)
cultural_challenges: It is expected that you put more hours into your schoolwork than a lot of other places, and many students are very "locked in".
culture_appreciated: The nature appreciation, most students will go on hikes or skiing in the weekends.
top3_advice: 1. Be open and do things. Remember to go for all the experiences you can. It keeps you busy so you dont think about home to much, and will give you some amazing experiences. 2. Relax about school, and remember you are on exchange. There is possibility to take so many incredible courses, but make sure to take some that are also just easy, so you have time to do other things than studying. 3. Please try new style hustle in the ASVZ (Danni).
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: The amazing friends I got:)
greatest_challenge: LTK M1

crucial_aspects: Wanted a good university in terms of academics, but also one somewhat near Danmark, in a compatible culture. I wanted good courses that I could learn from.
info_ease: The process is not that complex, but ETH provided almost all information you need through emails, seminars and webinars. ETH was also helpful about adding/dropping and recommendations for workload, as well as recommendations of public transit rebates and such.
arrival_assistance: Asked the exchange office about distance exam. The ETH office was very helpful in this regard. KU not so much. It took 2 months even to get confirmation if it was possible. Once the request reached the examination office of KU however, it was quite nice from there, and they were very competent.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The website for registration (myStudies) is quite old, but actually very functional, and does what it needs to do. You are neither prioritised nor deprioritised, so you can take essentially all courses (depending on restrictions from host department), but you also need to be fast if you want courses with restricted seats. Understanding which courses are under which departments (based on which it is "offered in"), and finding actual courses to take could be quite hard, since you just got an unfiltered list of both MA and BSc courses to choose from, and there are a lot of courses
registration_help: You could contact student administration, but the process itself was quite easy (while finding the courses was quite had)
registration_success: I got all courses I registered/wanted for
registration_advice: Look at relevant degrees you can take at ETH (for instance comp-sci master and bachelor, robotics, computer engineering etc.). Each degree has several specialisations, which include variety of different courses. Thus you can get inspiration from those.
course_level: I did mostly MA by ECTS, but 2 of each. Generally courses are slightly harder than KU, with significantly harder (to pass and get 6.0 (top grade)). Most compsci courses are more math heavy and based on theory of computation than at KU, but they seem to have had less systems courses.
teaching_comparison: Lectures were to a larger extent seen as optional, and recording were almost always provided via their video.ethz.ch website (super nice). However, lectures were generally also seen as complementary to the reading material, so you would often have to read supplementary material to get the syllabus. However it depends on the exact course (e.g. COOP was 100% lecture slides as material).
courses_enrolled: - Compiler Design - Computational Thinking - Concepts of Object Oriented Programming (COOP) - Advanced Machine Learning (AML)
recommended_courses: COOP was super nicely taught with engaging lectures. Also very interesting material, and Prof. -NAME REDACTED- is probably the best professor i've ever had. Somewhat arbitrary exam, but also hard material to test in a classic end-of-year exam, and definitely doable. COOP's last year was my semester, but he said from 2027 there would be a new, similar course removing the object-oriented focus (since it was mostly already gone). CompThi was not meant for computer science students, but actually gave a quite nice overview of some of the theoretical aspects of computing (such as N=NP). If you've had DIS and AD, about 1/3 of the syllabus is directly repeated, and the rest is quite simple. Would recommend the course in general, as the teaching was quite good. Compiler Design was also super fun. 50% of grade was projects with a provided test suite, so getting a high project grade was quite easy. The projects were manageable and quite fun. Exam is somewhat hard in some aspects, but you could also get a lot of partial marks (and with some studying acing the exam is definitely not impossible). I can't really recommend AML. The course was very disorganised, had a weird quiz element that took way longer to study for than it should (since it was while normal teaching and assignments were happening). The course does give a good understanding of current (almost-)cutting edge ML, and a very strong mathematical foundation on those models, but it rarely teaches you the math, and the math is really all you need for the exam. Unless you have a very strong Stats/Probability and Linear Algebra background, it is essentially a math course added onto the ML course. This also means "optimising" for the exam means you won't learn any/very little of the ML.
unexpected_costs: Food and especially takeout is super expensive. Meat in particular is super expensive, and a kebab is 110+. Public transit is quite reasonable if you buy a half-fare card (1 year coverage, half price on public transit for 800kr one time). However public transit is also super good. Health insurance is covered by EU.
cost_comparison: Hiking trails and lifts for those is somewhat cheap compared to everything else in the country, but definitely worth it: the hikes are super beautiful. Beers as student bars is quite cheap, but beers out are more or less CPH level.
activities_available: ASVZ (student sport association) is free, and gives access to tons of both free courses (dance, basketball, group gym training, swimming etc.), and some paid where you pay to pay to rent equipment (like golf or fencing). It also provides free access to gyms on campus. There are tons of clubs on campus. I went to the chess and CTF club a few times and met some super cool people. Would recommend checking out if any are your interests. They also have robotics and space and stuff.
activities_recommended: Join some ASVZ activities and some relevant clubs. Its more or less the only way to meet local students, since many courses are large and with little group work.
weekend_recommendations: Go hiking during the summer/fall. It really is super beautiful. Winters can be spent going to other nearby countries, both Flixbus and train is quite cheap to e.g. France and Italy.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. It is pretty similar to Denmark
socializing_tips: You almost certainly much gotta have some common interest, like a club, or grouping up for an assignment. The master courses are very international, since many people come from both French speaking part of Switzerland and other countries, so people are generally more open and friendly in those.
cultural_challenges: They are pretty much as enclosed as Danish people.
culture_appreciated: High trust based society and really a well-functioning country.
top3_advice: Take courses that you actually find interesting, and follow through the semester. The course load is pretty large, but manageable if you spread it out, and most courses are super interesting if you actually care for the subjects. Go to some ASVZ activities and/or some clubs. Great way to meet people. Also recommend PapperlaPub in the CAB basement and Erasmus Student Network activities: super fun. Check the prerequisites of the courses you're taking: not just by name, but also by the actual contents. E.g. intro to ML or linear algebra is quite more extensive than in KU
other_useful_info: The exams are pretty hard, but remember that the people actually attending are just normal people swell, so if most pass of the local students, you probably will too (if you spend the effort), most exams are graded quite lenient.
most_rewarding: The people I met and the learning opportunities. I would also recommend trying to get a project if you can. I personally didn't, but the professors seemed very engaged in the project students, and it can be a great way to "pad" your ECTS across the year rather than all final exams.
greatest_challenge: the exams (especially at advanced machine learning).

crucial_aspects: In no particular order: 1) The opportunity to choose courses matching my interests. 2) A renowned university. 3) A country where I had the opportunity to experience a lot of things outside the campus.
info_ease: Very easy. ETH informs you, via email, every detail you need to know upon arrival - from signing up for courses to applying for a residence permit.
arrival_assistance: See the previous question.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You sign up for courses online in a similar way to how you do at UCPH. For some courses, you have to get permission from the professor. However, this is easy to obtain by simply writing them an email.
registration_help: Informative emails, online meetings by ETH, help from ETH's student administration.
registration_success: I got every course I signed up for.
registration_advice: Start your course registration process early. There are a lot of courses to choose from, which can make the registration process quite long.
course_level: The level of the courses is generally high. Having a found mathematical background helps a lot.
teaching_comparison: Lectures are held in pretty much the same way. The TA sessions are, however, thaught in a different way. Usually, it is one TA teaching the whole class in only some of the problems.
courses_enrolled: i) German intensive course B1 ii) Numerical solutions of stochastic ordinary differential equations iii) Statistical modelling iv) Machine learning in finance and insurance v) Seminar in computational finance vi) Asset management: advanced investments (A University of Zürich course) vii) Data visualisation in finance (A University of Zürich course)
recommended_courses: Numerical solutions of stochastic ordinary differential equations. A great course for learning how to carry out simulations and mathematical convergence analysis for stochastic models originating from applications such as mathematical finance. However, one should note that the workload of this course is very high, and the home assignments are difficult. Statistical modelling. After finishing this course my understanding of statistical models - linear models, non-parametric model, general linear models, etc. - has deepened a lot. In short: a good course to take if you want a solid mathematical and intuitive understanding of statistical models. Machine learning in finance and insurance. A good introduction to machine learning (ML). The lectures are theoretically orientated, ensuring you get a solid understanding of the field. On the other hand, the projects are finance/insurance orientated, showing how ML can be used in these fields.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Eating out and public transportation outside Zürich were very expensive.
activities_available: Attending ETH, you can sign up for an ASVZ membership for free. This is an organisation offering classes on +50 different sports. Moreover, you can workout in their gyms for free. The biggest ball party in Europe: Polyball.
activities_recommended: Go on hikes across Switzerland Attend ERASMUS events. Travel to France, Italy, or another nearby country. Attend parties at the dorm of Meierwiesenstrasse.
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes - Switzerland is full of beautiful hiking trails.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Switzerland is very similar to Denmark in terms of culture.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any culture differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: Nothing to add.
top3_advice: 1) Courses are in general smaller than 7.5 ECTS, but the workload of a single course can easily feel like a +7.5 ECTS course. A very high workload should therefore be expected. 2) Priorize social events. 3) Plan out your semester.
other_useful_info: Nothing to add.
most_rewarding: The people I have met and all the experiences I have added to my scrapbook. Additionally, the knowledge I have gained through my courses.
greatest_challenge: Balancing my social life and my studies.

crucial_aspects: ETH's overall academic reputation. I also insisted on high-functioning infrastructure.
overall_comments: I was majorly surprised by how many social activities and friends i made along the way. I was dissapointed by ETH, though, as the quality of the actuarial courses was lacking.
info_ease: Pretty easy. There was multiple dates where one could ask questions.
arrival_assistance: There was a lot of paperwork and regulatory stuff. One should keep a good notebook to keep a birds eye view.
arrival_comments: There were many mails and information about various mandatory things scatterd around the place. It would have been nice if it was more centralized.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I was majorly surprised by how many social activities and friends i made along the way. I was dissapointed by ETH, though, as the quality of the actuarial courses was lacking.
registration_process: One just adds courses in the MyStudies portal from a list
registration_help: Peers would definently have figured it out, even if you didn't. It's very easy, so i never looked for help.
registration_success: Yes, I was. I should have tried out more courses though, as many of them (3/5) dissapointed
registration_advice: Previous comments.
academics_comments: I was majorly surprised by how many social activities and friends i made along the way. I was dissapointed by ETH, though, as the quality of the actuarial courses was lacking.
course_level: It was kinda hard to understand what was what, since it appears in different levels on different study programs. I filtered by MA, but i ended up with some courses that were also meant for BA.
teaching_comparison: I found it much less pedagogical, and (in actuarial courses) worse. This is most likely because some of these courses were taught by practitioners, so their theoretical capabilities was notably lacking (atleast I thought so, even if my class mates didnt). The courses taught by professors, however, were very hard and expected a lot from the student in terms of academic maturity. (Good study ethic, etc.) My peers (in different fields, engineering) were very impressed though.
courses_enrolled: Mathematical finance 10 ECTS - Dylan Possamai Non-life insurance 8 ECTS - Mario wüthrich Mathematical models in life insurance 4 ECTS - Tobias Jonas Peter Smoothing and non-parametric regression 4 ECTS - Sucarita Beran-Ghosh Financial risk management in social and pension insurance 4 ECTS - Peter Blum
recommended_courses: Mathematical finance: Brutally hard course. If you are not very theoretically interested, avoid it. Poorly taught, bad structure in the course, but extremely good for you, if you put in the work. I spent 50-60% of my total study time on just this one. Very much depends on the lecturer, so if it is not dylan, it will probably be very different. Non-life insurance (20-30% of my time): Very good balance of application and theory. Every non-life acturary should know this. It is less theoretical than courses at home, but more theoretical than the application based courses. It hits the perfect sweet-spot. Alot of overlap with Skade1 though. Mathematical models in life insurance (5-10% of my time): Horrible course. There is little-to-no-math going on here. Smoothing and non-parametric regression (5-10% of my time): Pretty easy course, which was poorly taught. Big overlap with Statins from UCPH Financial risk management in social and pension insurance (5-10% of my time): Poorly taught course, with many glaring holes from the models being too simple.
unexpected_costs: I didn't expect to go skiing, but the people i meet convinced me :) Various random things cost money, such as going to the immigrations office, (which is mandatory). I also had to go to the dentist which could have been very expensive.
cost_comparison: Food and especially take-away was more expensive than anticipated. If you avoid Coop and go to lidl it is ok.
activities_available: Mostly sports. Loads of them.
activities_recommended: Previously mentioned sport activities. Polyball was supposedly very nice too.
weekend_recommendations: Hike/ski with your fellow exchange student friends. Make a cake, bathe in the river. All the things you do with friends.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Go for it. I wish i had indulged more in such relations.
cultural_challenges: I barely interacted with them.
culture_appreciated: They are strict about times, so trains come on time. They are also very friendly and harmless. Hundreds of people in the libraries just leave computer and everything for multiple hours when they go to lunch break. As far as i know, nothing was stolen. Culture is very trust-based like that
top3_advice: You should like to study, and have high study-maturity. You have to put in significant work, on your own terms.
other_useful_info: Just try courses before comitting. One can interact with the same material on very different levels, and it can be hard to gauge from a description. 3 of my 5 courses were too easy, and 1 was too hard/intenstive.
most_rewarding: Growing as a person from new expiriences - good and bad.
greatest_challenge: Mathematical finance - by far. (and i aced the 15 ECTS master course at home beforehand, plus some more finance courses)

crucial_aspects: It was important to me that I would learn about the pharmaceutical industry outside of Europe, since I wanted to know the industry beyond the European pharmacopeia, and thus choosing a country in Asia was prioritized.
info_ease: The host university was very helpful in giving guidelines upon arrival and thus the information needed was provided.
arrival_assistance: We received assistance from the international office on campus, the housing office as well as from local students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process was fairly straight forward. Once you enter the application page you just fill out all the information and provide a photo of yourself for the student ID card. The application page is letter used as a communication portal where the university will provide you with information throughout the semester. Furthermore you will also find your acceptance letter on the application page in the top right corner.
registration_help: I used the student councilor as a means of help, otherwise they are also able to contact the host university should a problem occur.
registration_success: I successfully registered to all the courses I wanted, but I only got a spot because I wrote to two of the professors and they allowed me in even after the registration period.
registration_advice: The registration process is super competitive so be really prepared. The way you can prepare is by first having more preapproved courses than what you plan to sign up for, so that in case you couldn't sign up for the courses you wanted, you can sign up for some other courses that you know your home university has approved of. Secondly, remember to write down both the course name and course code, so that when the registration starts you can quickly find your courses. If you didn't get to register to the courses you wanted you can always try again in the "add and drop" period, or you can write to the professor of the course and ask them if there are any available spots, since the professor usually expands the capacity of the course after the registration period.
course_level: Although I was a master student at KU I applied to be accepted as an undergraduate student at my host university after being allowed to do so by KU. So the courses I had was undergraduate courses however they were on a high academic level.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style is a bit different than that at KU. The lectures were mandatory and there both midterms and finals, so the workload is a bit hard but the environment of which you learn is really good, so you get motivated to study.
courses_enrolled: Functional neuroanatomy (Department of brain and cognitive sciences) Learning and memory (Department of brain and cognitive sciences) Marketing
recommended_courses: I recommend you take courses that you really are passionate about and that also fall in line with your major at KU.
unexpected_costs: There is a national health insurance that you must pay as a citizen in Korea. This must be paid every month after receiving your foreign registration card. The insurance is a little high but is mandatory so be aware to account for this in your budget.
cost_comparison: Food is really cheap, and often times it can cost less to eat out rather than buy groceries and cooking yourself as some groceries are quite expensive.
activities_available: There are all sorts of cultural, athletic and social activities and clubs at Ewha however I didn't participate in any of them.
activities_recommended: I recommed to be part of the peace-buddy program as a lot of information is shared in the group chats and there are a lot of different activities hosted by the buddies.
weekend_recommendations: Explore Seoul as much as possible. Seoul is such a lovely city and there is so much to see and do!
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy to adjust to the local culture as long as you are respectful of the differences and try not to make a big deal out of it.
socializing_tips: Be prepared to not talk to loudly in public spaces, and not to have phone calls on the train or even talk loudly on the train, as this is seen as rude.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: I appreciate how kind, social and welcoming Koreans are. There is a huge social scene in Seoul and thus even when being alone, it is really easy to socialize with strangers and make friends.
top3_advice: Enjoy your stay, don't stress too much and don't bring too much clothes as you might need the space for the clothes and things you are gonna buy in Korea.
other_useful_info: Be prepared for the cold winter in both February and March, but also be prepared to have some lighter clothes since after May the temperatures are really high (higher than in Denmark).
most_rewarding: Experiencing Seoul and making so many new friends has been the most rewarding part of my exchange experience.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge is balancing life outside of the university and also the time you spent on studying. Sometimes it is needed of you to just study all day, and it can be hard to both do that and also have time outside of the university, so remember to balance it well.

crucial_aspects: The courses offered by the host university
arrival_assistance: none. they had sent some directions from the airport to the dorms
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You log in to the platform when application period starts. You fill out the form and supply the documents needed. I got an acceptance email 2 days after i had sent my application.
registration_help: None really. KU kinda helped.
registration_success: i got 4/5 classes that I wanted and had to end up taking a class i didnt want. There is a course add and drop period the first week where you are able to change course selection.
