crucial_aspects: The universities available and the course selection is very important. I would want the university to have an attractive location, be located in an interesting city, and for the universities to offer interesting courses in English. For me personally, I choose the location due to personal reasons, as my boyfriend was living in the same city/country.
info_ease: The whole process went very smoothly. I'd already lived in the city before, so that made it easier when arriving.
arrival_assistance: I don't think I would say that I received any assistance. I was put into contact with another student from the university in case I needed help, which I fortunately didn't.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It's first come, first serve. You have to be incredibly quick when they open for registrations. Everything will be taken within seconds/minutes if it's popular. However, you have a trial period where you can drop or add classes afterwards.
registration_help: I don't remember as I didn't seek any help.
registration_success: I got all the classes I tried to register for. I was only limited by overlapping schedules.
registration_advice: Make sure to check the class schedule to be sure that the combination of classes you want don't overlap. And have backups ready in case all the spots are taken.
course_level: The levels were very chill, and most classes consisted of only lectures.
teaching_comparison: My biology classes were solely lectures. And very short classes compared to KU.
courses_enrolled: Ceramics, Beginner Korean, Animal Behaviour and Sensory and Perception.
recommended_courses: Ceramics was very chill and an easy A. Animal behavior was interesting and also very chill. Korean language class was intense but interesting and relevant.
unexpected_costs: I had to pay a korean insurance once I got my ARC.
cost_comparison: As I had been there before, the expenses were as expected. Food and transport is cheap.
activities_available: There were exchange clubs, but students couldn't join other clubs. There were a few events for exchange students but most had a limited amount of spots and were first come, first serve.
activities_recommended: I don't have any recommendations
weekend_recommendations: Travel to other cities
culture_adjustment: Easy as I had lived there before. It can be a bit difficult with the language barrier, but possible to get by.
socializing_tips: Join clubs and courses with group work. Join language exchange meet ups.
cultural_challenges: Language barrier and there view on foreginers.
culture_appreciated: food
top3_advice: To make sure to explore other parts of the country. To explore the city and have fun with friends, and to not worry about exams and grades. To not over pack as you would want to bring a lot of new stuff home
other_useful_info: Prepare insurance documents in English that states the total coverage amount. You can try and get out of paying the korean insurance by providing this.
most_rewarding: Getting to meet new people and explore a different culture
greatest_challenge: Having to show up for every class as attendance is mandatory.

crucial_aspects: My studies are Korean studies, so being in Korea seems a given. And EWHA has a good reputation in Korea, so wanted to experience it.
info_ease: Given that I've been to Korea before it was fairly easy. As for the messages from EWHA, I only look through those regarding arriving fast, but from what I could see they were fairly helpful.
arrival_assistance: None, seeing I've been there before and already know.
arrival_comments: If you've never been I recommend the 'Peace Buddy Program' Ewha offers. It's a Korean student of EWHA, and they're very helpful with anything you should need.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You do it only on ehwa's portal (school will inform you how to when it nears). Check out the website in general some days ahead, so you can navigate the page, because it is a little confusing. I had my address and Korean phone number ready in an open word so I could just copy paste, because they ask you to fill these things out before you choose courses. When that is done there is an area where you write in the course code (XXXXX-XX). And then you just press the save button (or called something like that, can't remember exactly). If you're accepted to the course, it will simply appear on the list. If there is no room a small information box will appear. And then you keep going like that till you have all the course credits you need.
registration_help: The school provides you a written guide how to, with pictures too. But actually sitting and doing it, you're on your own.
registration_success: Got all of them (PC café).
registration_advice: Listed in the box 'Please describe the registration process at your host institution'. Also, PC café.
course_level: It really depends on the professor. Some classes where challenging and wonderful, and others felt like high-school (gymnasium) level. As well as some made you use your tools and think for yourself, while other professor just want you to remember what they said, and repeat that back.
teaching_comparison: It's hard to compare when it's two very different cultures and approaches to studying.
courses_enrolled: Sex, Gender, Sexuality in Korea (835743-01), Current Issues (10596-01), Social Problems in Contemporary Global World (10905-01), K-MOOC: Identity, Agency, Equality, and Security in the Age of AI (11372-01) & Contemporary Photography (11164-01)
recommended_courses: Current Issues and K-MOOC - it's the same professor and she's wonderful and one of the professors that makes you think and not just repeat back. Contemporary Photography was wonderful as well, as it helped me see new perspective to - and history of photography.
unexpected_costs: It's always shocking how much I spend on food and experiences xD They're not expensive, I just do a lot so it adds up.
cost_comparison: Fruit is ridiculously expensive and duvet + pillows. But generally for food, use their online shopping 'coupang' if you can (amazing!), if not go for the super market E-mart and shop their label 'No brand'.
activities_available: There was a Chuseok celebration, Sports day and ending semester day. as well as some field trips.
activities_recommended: Well, of course go for all if you want to and for the company, you should :) But otherwise I recommend you do the 'field trips' on your own, if you can manage, as it won't be as expensive then.
weekend_recommendations: Oh my gosh - so much! Budget: subway/train travel to different parts of Seoul or even out of. There are free offers, or very cheap experiences (especially all of their cafés, so pretty!) but parts of the city as well have mural cities, statues, palaces (their entrance is cheap but free on chuseok, so on... Klook, Trip, and Creatrip are apps offers to foreigners in Korea, and have good deals. I especially recommend Klook's cooking courses or DMZ tour (which is otherwise so must of a hassle to figure out on your own).
culture_adjustment: Easy as I've been there before.
socializing_tips: It's hard. Either they're f bois, want very superficial friendships with foreigners because that's trending, or they're extremely sweet and genuine people but shy because they might not be to comfortable with foreign culture or confident in English. It was easier for me because I speak Korean. But try the peace buddy program, speak with those in your classes (as they usually will know enough English) and then usually they'll further introduce you to their friend group.
cultural_challenges: Not challenging, but just be aware; no talking on public transportation (considered really rude), they spit everywhere on the street (all ages and sexes), you will get starred at (not in a bad way at all, they're just very curious about you, but it can feel overwhelming at times), give and receive with two hands (sign of respect), respect personal sphere! (seriously don't hug, unless you know them well and know they're okay with it), remember to slightly bow when greeting, saying thank you or sorry. I think with those you're prepared for most.
culture_appreciated: I've gotten help or offered help from many elders. If you know a few words or cultural things they'll be so happy. So many side dishes when you just ordered one thing. The food!!! The convenience stores are open 24/7, good and cheap. Public transportation works so good and fast (just avoid rush hour (roughly 7-9 am & 5-7 pm), if you can, it's awful!!). Beautiful cultural/historical sites everywhere. Just love, love, love!
top3_advice: 1. Learn very basic words - like hello, thank you and sorry.
other_useful_info: I really varies with information shared by EWHA. Sometimes they're great and sometimes you have to find it yourself. Especially finding your way around campus can be a bit confusing at first. Seriously - peace buddy program! sign up :)
most_rewarding: All of it. Of coursed I'm biased, being a Korean Studies student, but I absolutely loved it all.
greatest_challenge: Being alone. You're so far away from home. Find friends. Buddy program, people in class, other exchange students, Facebook groups (especially recommend 'expat women living in korea' (can't remember exact wording)) - just don't be alone, have at least one person.
other_comments: I recommend Chingu mobile for Korean phone number and it's cheaper if you buy from home and set it to 'pick up'. Respect personal sphere as much as possible (no hugging people), give and take with two hands (especially with money), no talking on public transportation, free wifi basically everywhere, common to leave your stuff on tables, chairs, picnic blankets and no one will take it, get a T-money transportation card (in airport before entrance to train or convenience stores), easy to refill on subway stations or convenience stores, get 'papago' (app)!!!, absolut best translator for Korean (writing, live audio transaction, pictures...), Naver (app)!!! (google maps don't work in korea, naver is the Koreans own ''google maps''), Kakao T app (just need a Korean phone number and Kakao chat to set up, and then you can see the prices as you book a cab, choose 'pay to driver', and they can't cheat you price wise), Kakao (their texting app, little like messenger, you cannot avoid having to use it), conversion is roughly 'delete two zeroes and then half' - so 20.000 won, roughly 100 dkk, 2.500 won roughly 12,5 dkk. Cheapest bank to withdraw money - those on campus or KB ATMS (always 3.500 won). Dress however you want, of course, just know that in Korean culture, short skirt (even very, very short) is high fashion, but cleavage, collarbones, shoulders and such is a big no go. Not to scare you (honestly, Korea is very safe!!), but just watch out for the f bois (saying things like: 'are you russian'? = [if you're up for a one-night stand], are you open-minded? = one night stand, do you live alone? = availability for a room for s*x and so on....) and cults. It's especially if someone starts talking to you out of nowhere in the public (and especially Hongdae, Sinchon and Myeongdong), because it is so NOT in their culture to do that. It really doesn't happen too often (I hope I'm not scaring you), but just be aware and walk away when it does, especially with the cults (they'll usually start talking about god, or ancestors and such and maybe offer tea in a café nearby - just leave immediately). Also, Sindorim (신도림 /신도림동) is not a place you want to be, especially as a solo woman. Watch out for hidden cameras - people taking your picture (especially up skirts, is unfortunately happening a lot) and if you spot any holes in toilet stalls.

crucial_aspects: Like I mentioned I am a Korean studies student so that was crucial to me in choosing South Korea.
info_ease: I think it was rather easy. The school offers you to join a buddy program where you can get in contact and get help from a Korean student at the university, and otherwise you can go to the international office and speak with them if you need help.
arrival_assistance: I had help both from the buddy program I mentioned, the internation office and because I joined a club I could get help from a student there as well.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You start with figuring out which classes you want to take, note down the course number and then on registration day you have to be ready to log into the site. Ewha makes you input your personal info before you are able to register courses, and then you register the classes one class at a time. It is honestly a very stressful process, because registering for classes is like wanting to buy concert tickets and in my case it felt like having to buy 5 concert tickets because I was taking 5 courses.
registration_help: Like I mentioned we got a guide that explained the registration process.
registration_success: I got up a few hours early in the morning and was actually sitting on the registration site watching the countdown, and I think that might have contributed to me being so lucky that I got everything I wanted. However, at the same time I talked with a few people who weren't as lucky so I think luck also plays a part.
registration_advice: Get up early and prepare a list of the courses you want and in case you might not get them prepare back-up courses as well. I got the courses I wanted but one of them was a back-up course because another was full. I don't think you can see it before on registration day but in some courses there are a limited amount of spots for international students. My friend even went to a PC room to ensure she got the courses she wanted because the internet connection is better there, so it is worth considering.
course_level: It was quite interesting in comparison to the courses I have taken back at home in Denmark. In Denmark I have had one longer written assignment that determined my grade but in Korea it was determined by multiple tests, multiple written assignments (but they were shorter), attendance, presentations and participation in class. With that said I do think the level was similar to Copenhagen University. But I did distinctly feel a difference in workload, in Denmark I think it gets more intense near the end of the semster, while in Korea one thing was constantly replaced by another but it was less intense.
teaching_comparison: Because Korean studies has a smaller number of students we have the necessary time to talk and discuss things during class so class participation in not uncommon. However, I have never had so much class participation and groupwork as I feel I did in Korea, but that might also just have had something to do with the courses I chose.
courses_enrolled: World Women Through English K-MOOC: Identity, Agency, Equality, and Security in the Age of AI Current Issues Contemporary Photography Social Problems in Contemporary Global World
recommended_courses: K-MOOC is an online course but you learn so many things you have never heard about before, and it really broadens you understanding of the development of the technology we see today and will see in the future. I also personally liked the World Women course because I feel like your personal views might get a little challenged while you learn about certain dynamics and developments through history you haven't necesarily considered. I honestly think that all my courses were good, however just be aware that Social Problems was a little heavy.
unexpected_costs: It wasn't an unexpected cost since I also experienced it last time, but but the cost of restaurant and cafées is probably higher than people assume. The reasoning is that while food in Korean more local restaurants is not too bad it quickly adds up if you are mostly having your meals outside. In addition, the café culture is really big in Korea so you often end up in a café when you are meeting up with people and cafées are usually expensive.
cost_comparison: Entance fees to museums are very low becaue the government wants to encourage its citizens to learn about their own history and culture. Exhibitions on the other hand and specific trendy cultural places are more expensive.
activities_available: They had one club that specifically created events for international students so you could meet other international student, there was a language lounge where you could teach other students English, there were 2 different language clubs where you would be partnered up with Korean students so you could meet and do activities and if you were learning Korean you could also practice with them.
activities_recommended: I suggest joining the Buddy Program and one of the language clubs. In the Buddy Program you are paired up with one Korean student and then maybe 4-6 international student, so you can both meet a Korean student and ask them about stuff and become familiar with the culture and get help with school stuff and meet other international students that are experiencing the exact same things as you are. The language clubs offer a opportunity for maybe a more personal relationship with the Korean student in the sense that it is more 1-1 so I feel there is a greater chance at gaining a Korean friend.
weekend_recommendations: In the weekends go out and see some of the cultural and historical places. Some of the museums are even free so take advantage of that, the price for entering the palaces is low as well, and they have their traditional villages which you can enter free of charge. Also keep an eye on the events happening because there is usually always something you can do or go to. And during the holidays travel! Seoul is great but it gives such a nice and more comprehensive idea of Korea and Korean culture if you travel out plus there is so many beautiful places and fun things you can experience. I would sugget to at least go to Busan, Jeonju and Jeju.
culture_adjustment: Since it was my second time I think I had a rather easy time adjusting.
socializing_tips: Keep in mind many local students/Korean students live very busy lives and some might be a bit more apprehensive getting close since you might only be there for exchange (especially if it's only 1 semester). But befriend people in your classes, go to events and meet people through clubs.
cultural_challenges: You have to get a little used to being stared a bit at. it is not as bad in Seoul and it also depends on where in Seoul you are, but people are just very fascinated and curious. Korean society is still pretty homogeneous.
culture_appreciated: The food and the cultural mix between metropolitan and tradtional. I also find it very cool that people style-wise in clothing can almost look however they want without people flinching an eye vs. in Denmark.
top3_advice: Go with an open mind and be ready to go out of your comfort zone. The international office or your buddy in the buddy program can help you if you need it. Your courses can influence your experience so read up on what the courses require for you to pass, and be prepared and ready to register your courses.
other_useful_info: If you live off campus getting a resident card requires more documents and some of it can be a little complicated. The reason is that the university has an external firm to handle the resident cards for their students so the firm is very strict with your papers. But having said so you can always talk with the international office if you encounter any problem.
most_rewarding: Everything. All the experiences I have had, the people I have met, and the knowledge I have gained.
greatest_challenge: Figuring out how to balance the workload and making sure I fully enjoyed and experienced Korea. Like I mentioned there is a consistent level of intensity in Korea due to tests, assignments and presentations throughout the semster, so you have to remind yourself that you also need to make time to go out and see thing and experience the culture.

crucial_aspects: Culinary experiences, cultural history, financial aspects and recommendations from friends.
overall_comments: My personal experience was brilliant. However, the level of education in Korea is not as high as I expected, which made the academic part of the exchange below my expectations.
info_ease: Relatively easy. However, there is a lot of work connected to going abroad, so it required patience and dedication.
arrival_assistance: A fair amount at orientation. The most well-functioning part was, that the university had a really good program for the social lives of exchange students, which I highly advise other Ewha expats to join.
arrival_comments: Others should join the EWHA PEACE BUDDY program.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: My personal experience was brilliant. However, the level of education in Korea is not as high as I expected, which made the academic part of the exchange below my expectations.
registration_process: To be honest, it is very far back in my memory. I can sort of recall me having to find a bunch of documents from KU, having them signes by the right people etc. etc. However, EWHA's communication channel and personnel are very helpful with any and all questions.
registration_help: Again, two coordinators where constantly available, making the application experience way easier.
registration_success: I got very lucky and got all the classes I wanted. However, the process is first come - first served, making it very stressful, and I talked to many who did not get classes they wanted or needed desperately to accord to their home institutions demands.
registration_advice: Make sure to have backup classes, talk to your home institution about what courses they would approve, do a pre-approval application for various courses and educate yourself about the application process. That helped me a lot!
academics_comments: My personal experience was brilliant. However, the level of education in Korea is not as high as I expected, which made the academic part of the exchange below my expectations.
course_level: Some courses were theoretical, applied critical thinking and were super interesting. Others were way, way to easy, uninteresting and to be honest, some of them provided middle- and high school level education. The level in Korea is definitely lower than in Denmark, and at the time of writing I have received straight A's with less engagement than in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: Depends on the professor. Mostly it was lectures as in Denmark. However, I also had online classes, which was convenient as an expat, but less fruitful. Some professors were theoretical and critical, whilst others just provided random facts, not focusing on critical thinking. I found this highly problematic.
courses_enrolled: Sociology of Crime Social Psychology Politics of North Korea Child Welfare Cultural Diversity and Social Welfare
recommended_courses: Sociology of Crime - the professor is very talented, interesting and somewhat challenging (in a good way). Social Psychology - Same professor as the first course and same reasons. Politics of North Korea - I think all students going to Korea should take a similar course. Learning about political differences and culture in Korea is very rewarding and interesting.
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Public transport is super cheap, which is nice - same with taxis. NHIS (mandatory Korean health insurance) is quite expensive.
activities_available: Music hall with concerts, different conferences, PEACE BUDDY social program, sports facilities, lots of food, church and gym.
activities_recommended: Again, EWHA PEACE BUDDY program is a great way to meet people in the first weeks, and they plan stuff like sports day, movie night, a party etc. They also partner you with a Korean student who helps adjusting to life in Korea which is super nice. Also - go out to eat as much as you can. It is cheap and very good food is available everywhere. Experience the culture in museums, sport games, concerts etc. It is very cool and accesible.
weekend_recommendations: I think it is important to go outside of Seoul relatively often, so your everyday life does not become to trivial. I went to Japan, Busan, Jeju and Taipei, and all of my trips were wonderful experiences! Also it is common to visit the DMZ near the border of North Korea, also very worthy of visiting. many students also to Temple stays, which I think might be cool - I did not have the time unfortunately.
culture_adjustment: Due to the fact that I have been traveling a lot around Asia, I found it very easy to adjust to the local culture. I think it might be harder for some people, but South Korea is very developed and super easy to figure out.
socializing_tips: Join the PEACE BUDDY Program or similar social clubs promoting bond between expats and locals!
cultural_challenges: There is a language barrier, but google translate helps a lot here :) I did not find any cultural differences super challenging myself. However, there is something of a drinking culture, which can be overwhelming for some - so be aware when you go out. Also, Koreans outside the Uni rarely interacts with foreigners, so do not expect to meet a lot of Koreans randomly around bars etc.
culture_appreciated: The food, the prices, the weird stuff and most of all - Noerebang (Karaoke).
top3_advice: 1. Put a lot of effort into socializing the first few weeks of your exchange, and don't be shy. Everyone is feeling out of their comfort zone so just talk to people - it pays of! 2. Join the PEACE BUDDY program for an easy transition into life in Korea. 3. Do not expect Korean students to interact with you a lot. Many of them are shy and introverted around foreign students.
other_useful_info: Spend energy on finding courses suitable for you. If possible, find a student who went to EWHA before and ask them for tips!
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was definitely the people I met. Having friends from all over the world and experiencing a lot of different cultures is a privilige, and I recommend it to everyone!
greatest_challenge: A mix of two things I think. 1. Feelings of exclusion from one group I hung out with. However, I decided to just ditch the people I found exclusive in that group and focused on other friends, which made my stay way better! Listen to yourself and do not waste time on people you dont like - you are on exchange for you and not any other person!
other_comments: GO TO KOREA!

crucial_aspects: Seeing that I did my mandatory exchange last year in the countryside of Korea, it was crucial for me that I had an opportunity to do another exchange in the capital city. This was both because of personal reasons (I have family there) but also because of the broader knowledge and perspective I would be able to achieve because of the experience of both the countryside and the big city. Because I study Korean Studies, this aspect was extremely important to me since it contributed to my understanding and knowledge of Korea.
info_ease: I found it very easy. The host university was very good at giving all the informations needed and pin out specific deadlines, etc., at their communication channel. They were really quick at responding to emails as well, so overall, I was very satisfied with it.
arrival_assistance: Before arriving, I was connected to a buddy who was a big help. She had contacted me a week before I arrived and helped me with how to check in to the dormitory. My flight was delayed so I couldn’t arrive to the dormitory during the check-in time but my buddy helped me and so did the dormitory office. So I was still able to check in even though it was in the middle of the night.
arrival_comments: The directions to the dormitory could be a bit better.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process is always stressful since it is a first-comes-first-served system, and if you are not in Korea at the time of registration, you have to be up in the middle of the night with bad internet reception because it is a korean website. So a good advice would definitely be to have several extra courses at hand because you most likely won’t be able to register all your highest priorities. AND to check out the registration process thoroughly beforehand!
registration_help: There is no help for the first registration process. But the first week of the semester is a trial and error, so I would recommend to register for a lot of courses and then try them out during the first week. During the two first weeks some courses will suddenly have more available seats and you will be able to find out which courses you like or not, and you have the opportunity to register and leave courses during this time.
registration_success: I was very successful with my registration but I think it was because 50% of my courses were graduate courses and they are “easier” to get a seat at because there aren’t as many graduate students as undergraduate students.
registration_advice: Register for a lot of courses! Both graduate and undergraduate, if possible. You have one or two weeks in the beginning of the semester to drop some of the courses.
course_level: The undergraduate courses are very different from an undergraduate course in Denmark. The academic level is lower but the system and criteria are very different. The graduate courses are very similar to courses in Denmark, and the academic level is slightly lower but again, the system and criteria are different so it is difficult to compare. But academically, my experience was that the levels are almost the same.
teaching_comparison: It was quite the same. It wasn’t completely different or incomprehensible.
courses_enrolled: Korean Ceramics (Undergraduate and aimed at exchange students) Korean Heritage (Undergraduate and aimed at exchange student) Gender Relations in Korea (Graduate) Sexuality and Capitalism in Asia (Graduate and was about women’s studies and feminist theory)
recommended_courses: Korean Ceramics (Undergraduate and aimed at exchange students) The ceramics course was a great opportunity to meet other exchange students and learn about Korean pottery while working with clay yourself. It was a nice break from the other heavy academic courses. And the professor was really nice and kind. Korean Heritage (Undergraduate and aimed at exchange student) This course was a lecture-structured course and was about the cultural and religious heritage of Korea. Even though the topics could be a bit historical and kind of boring, the professor was very passionate and funny which made the courses much more interesting. Quite often, the professor brought some artifacts, food and/or drinks to share with the class so we could “experience” some of the heritage of Korea. Gender Relations in Korea (Graduate) This graduate course was really amazing. The professor was extremely kind, funny and helpful. The focus of the class was on women in Korea and was discussion based, and the professor facilitated this perfectly. We had many great and important discussions, and the academic level was on the same level as in Denmark. it was without a doubt my favorite course. These three courses were all amazing in their own way.
unexpected_costs: I had expected that I was going to spend a lot of money on personal spending but it is not a necessity. One could definitely go by without spending as much money on oneself.
cost_comparison: Groceries in Korea are insanely expensive. Especially fruits and vegetables. So, if you want to save money, don’t cook at home. You can find really cheap and delicious local restaurants everywhere.
activities_available: The host university did several social activities for the exchange students. Both cultural, athletic and social.
activities_recommended: There are a lot of opportunities to meet other students and be social, you just have to reach out and/or participate when these opportunities are there.
weekend_recommendations: There is a lot to see and/or experience in Korea, and, I think, it is fairly easy to be tourist/foreigner there. I would recommend that you do a bit of research beforehand and figure what you really want to try or experience, and then figure out when and where you can do it, because when you arrive and the semester begins time will fly by quickly.
culture_adjustment: It can be very difficult to adjust to the Korean culture, so I would recommend that you find your base and maybe some friends, so you aren’t all alone.
cultural_challenges: Koreans can be difficult to get to know and befriend. Mostly because of the language barrier. And some older people can be extremely rude to foreigners…
culture_appreciated: I can’t choose. A culture is a culture. Some aspects are lovely, some are not, but they are both a part of a whole culture.
top3_advice: Register for a lot of courses Be patient, and if you have further questions don’t hesitate to contact them Be respectful and understanding. You are a visitor and have chosen to be a visitor, so if things are different than what they are at home, you are not entitled to demand it to change for you.
other_useful_info: Think about why you want to go on exchange, and what you hope to achieve from it. And if possible, reach out to other students who have been on exchange at the same university so you can adjust your expectations.
most_rewarding: Everything. The whole experience in it self.
greatest_challenge: Everything. It is extremely rewarding to be on exchange but is is also extremely hard and difficult.

activities_recommended: Join the language exchange and don't be afraid to meet up with other exchange students/locals.

socializing_tips: Approach the students in class, and join the buddy group activities. Many feel uncomfortable speaking english, so try to learn a bit Korean and join language exchange.

crucial_aspects: The country needed to differ from Danish culture, while still being quite modern and a well-functioning society. That the destination was acknowledged for high qualitity education.
overall_comments: I 100% reccommend going on exchange in Seoul, one of my best and most meaningful decisions in my life.
info_ease: As I remember, the information was okay to find. The host university website can be a bit confusing to navigate. I feel like there were a lot of small things i did not know before arrving, but the most important information is easily communicated from the university and host university.

cultural_challenges: Social manners are a bit different, they don't hold the door, they don't give room at the sidewalk etc.

top3_advice: Be excited for the best experience in your life, pack light as you want to by everything, you will make friends!

crucial_aspects: I have Korean heritage, so I wanted to be closer to my family, experience living in Korea and improve my Korean language skills. Exchange is a good opportunity to experience living in a different country/city without the uncertainty and commitment that studying/working there full time would bring.
info_ease: I could find what I needed, but sometimes you had to dig far into emails or go through a series of weblinks to find what you were looking for. But generally Ewha was good at giving you the information you needed (I'd recommend saving the files somewhere or writing down important information so you don't have to spend a lot of time finding the information again)
arrival_assistance: I didn't need any assistance.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration period is after you arrive (in the dorms at least), the week right before the semester starts. They say competition is tough and a lot of people couldn't get all the courses they wanted, but I got what I wanted and didn't have any issues. You can choose more courses than you need and drop them afterwards. The week before you can access the portal without being able to register, where you can see the capacity for each course
registration_help: They sent an email outlining the process beforehand
registration_success: Very, I got all of the ones I wanted + backups
registration_advice: I'd recommend having a list of course codes ready to copy paste and make sure to check that the schedule fits and have backup courses ready in case you don't get what you wanted. And be ready at your computer when registration opens! (Also some courses are available in both English and Korea, with different course codes, so make sure you choose the right one)
course_level: I took a mix of easy and more difficult courses
teaching_comparison: They don't have anything like øvelsestimer, it's all just lectures, generally each 1:15 hrs two times a week. So anything practical like solving problems etc. aren't really part of the teaching, you have to do that yourself. Some of my courses (in computer science) had 'lab' sessions, but they would just explain some code and that was it.
courses_enrolled: Machine Learning, Graph Neural Networks, C programming and Lab, Human-Computer Interaction and Practical Korean 301
recommended_courses: I'd generally recommend taking a Korean language course if you're interested and your degree allows it (you have to go to the Korean version of the course catalogue to find them - Ewha also sends an email about it before registration opens. You can get Korean courses that are either 3 or 6 credits). If you want a chill exchange, I'd recommend taking Ceramics and generally taking courses made for exchange students because they're more lax. Anything that is a major requirement or generally has more Korean students, seem to grade on a scale whereas ones for exchange students seem to give absolute grades. I would also recommend C programming.
unexpected_costs: I can't think of any, but I will caveat my lack of insurance expenses by the fact that I still fall under my parent's insurance and I also have Korean citizenship, so I don't need to pay for Korean health insurance either. (Ewha requires that you have both a private insurance from home and that you pay for the Korean national health insurance). Also 4/5 of my classes didn't require any textbooks, but I also mainly took Computer Science classes (It was only Korean that required textbooks)
cost_comparison: Transportation is really cheap and generally you can get most things you need in walking distance, I only travel around Seoul for the sake of seeing Seoul. (And there are a lot of things to do near Ewha!)
activities_available: Fitness center, sports, clubs and cultural exchange clubs
activities_recommended: I joined Hangeul Assi, which paired you with a mentor you could practice Korean with, which was quite nice! They also have various other similar clubs. In general I would recommend to sign up immediately to things because there's often tough competition!
weekend_recommendations: It's easy to find recommendations for cultural attractions, cafes, shops and weekend trips, so if I were to recommend something else, I would recommend checking out craft workshops in Seoul, if that's something you're interested in. They have so many different types (leatherwork, mother of pearl lacquerware, bookbinding, screenprinting, ceramics, painting, tufting, you name it) and they all have one-day classes, but some also have ones that go over multiple weeks. I only did one-day classes, and near Ewha I would recommend danchoodan (traditional korean bookbinding) and neote leather craft (right in front of Ewha!). It's a good way to make a souvenir and maybe even practice your Korean! I would also recommend taking dance classes since Korea is so known for it, there's e.g. JustJerk right in front of Ewha. (I would also like to shout out the craft museum in Seoul, it's my favourite museum of the ones I've been to in Seoul)
culture_adjustment: Easy since I'm used to Korean culture
socializing_tips: It's hard because you only have lectures and no one talks to each other, I'd say clubs are the best way to go
cultural_challenges: I'm not sure
culture_appreciated: Everything is open quite late and it's so normal to eat out alone
top3_advice: 1) Make a list of things you definitely want to do when you're on exchange and make sure you make plans for them because time will fly by and you don't want to regret not getting to do the things you wanted to do! 2) It's okay if you don't make lifelong friends and it's completely okay to do things alone, don't compare yourself to other people's instagram stories! (And you don't have to go to a new country every weekend!) 3) Take easy courses if you can (Bonus: Make sure to go outside of campus and see the rest of Seoul! It can be easy to just stay on campus because you have everything you need there)
other_useful_info: I can't think of anything
most_rewarding: Being more comfortable doing things alone, honestly
greatest_challenge: My social battery was always low because I was sharing a room with someone and you have to be very proactive when it comes to making plans with people (because you don't naturally make friends in classes because they're lecture based). (Don't be afraid to reach out to people and don't be afraid to just do things alone!) Ewha was also not the best at making events etc. for meeting other exchange students, it was very do-it-yourself.

crucial_aspects: I chose Berlin mainly because of the cultural life and opportunities. I was also interested in the language, and the German universities offer excellent language courses for international students, both a "Vorkurs" before the semester begins (with a fee) and classes during the semester (for free)!
overall_comments: I had the time of my life and really encourage my fellow students to do a semester at Freie Universität Berlin (FU) if they feel like it. You won't regret it, this city has so much to offer.
info_ease: I found it quite easy. In the months leading up to my departure, I received multiple e-mails from FU with important information which I read thoroughly, so I wasn't worried about all the practical stuff upon arrival. But beware that much of the information you receive is in German. If you know a little German and have some patience though, you will be fine. I also found the international coordinators really helpful. They held an online introduction meeting for international students a few weeks before the semester began.
arrival_assistance: International students were offered an introductory tour on campus by some of the student coordinators. There you were able to ask questions and most importantly: get all the pro tips from a student who already knows how the bureaucracy, online portalts etc. work.
arrival_comments: I felt completely safe, and the erasmus/international office were super willing to help when I was in doubt of something.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had the time of my life and really encourage my fellow students to do a semester at Freie Universität Berlin (FU) if they feel like it. You won't regret it, this city has so much to offer.
registration_process: You sign up in the system called Campus Management (guides for both campus management as well as the two other online systems ZEDAT and Blackboard will be sent to you by e-mail!). The registration is opened up on a certain date a few weeks before the semester begins. You sign up for the classes that you want, and a few weeks later you find out whether you got them or not. The cool thing is that (in contrary to KU) you are allowed to try out the classes for a few weeks after signing up, and if you changed your mind, you can cancel your registration and choose another class. So convenient
registration_help: The erasmus office at FU can explain everything, reach out to them by e-mail or go to their office
registration_success: Got all of them
registration_advice: Don't stress too much about it, exchange is about so many other things, and if you fuck it up the erasmus office at FU can help you
academics_comments: I had the time of my life and really encourage my fellow students to do a semester at Freie Universität Berlin (FU) if they feel like it. You won't regret it, this city has so much to offer.
course_level: MA level
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was super inclusive, and my professors had a lot of enthusiasm. That's the most striking difference. I can't remember the last time one of my KU professors didn't seem tired of life and academia and cuts
courses_enrolled: 1: Language course, German A2-B1 2: Decolonizing Classrooms, Psychological Anthropology
recommended_courses: LANGUAGE COURSES
unexpected_costs: Ved ikke
cost_comparison: Fastfood er en del billigere, og alkohol og øl i byen er meget billigere
activities_available: Der er ikke rigtig fester som på KU, men der er til gengæld mange flere muligheder ude i byen. Der er en international klub på uni med sociale arrangementer, men har ikke udforsket den.
activities_recommended: Der er både mulighed for at deltage i universitetets tilbud, men der er også mange andre muligheder ude i byen, alt efter hvor dine interesser ligger. Jeg er engageret i politik derhjemme, så det var nemt for mig at finde et netværk hernede ved at opsøge politiske grupper. Virkelig oplagt måde at få et lokalt netværk, for ellers er det mest udvekslingsstuderende, man møder (hvilket uden tvivl også er super fedt)
weekend_recommendations: Hvis du er til musik og natteliv, så tjek events på Resident Advisor, og du vil aldrig løbe tør for noget at lave i weekenden. Når det er varmt, så tag i de udendørs sommerbade eller tag til en af strandene
culture_adjustment: Ja, meget lig DK
socializing_tips: Som nævnt, hvis du har en hobby derhjemme, så er det oplagt at dyrke den her i en lokal klub/organisation/netværk
cultural_challenges: Ikke rigtig
culture_appreciated: Åbenhed over for forskellighed
top3_advice: 1: Semesterstrukturen er anderledes end i andre europæiske lande, så det kan være en udfordring: 1. april-30. september (sommersemester) og 1. oktober-31. marts (vintersemester). Det er dog ikke umuligt at få til at gå op med studierne derhjemme, og for mig er det i hvert fald klart alt besværet værd:) 2: Det siger sig selv, at sommersemesteret er sjovere end den mørke vinter, så sørg for at søge det hvis muligt. 3: Just do it, Berlin er seriøst det fedeste sted at bo

greatest_challenge: Finde bolig
other_comments: Næ

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go abroad to learn german and to explore the german culture.

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I followed the instruction provided by the host insitution via an online meeting ahead of the semester start. To be honest i can't remeber all the details of the process.

registration_success: I got all the classes i registered for.

cost_comparison: Public transport was less expensive as i expected. I also expected i needed to buy books for the courses, but I didn't. The housing was a lot more expensive than i expected, but I also think that i was quite unlucky on that part.
activities_available: There were a lot of opportunities regarding athletics. Unfortunetly i wasn't participate in the one i registered for due to the fact that it was fully booked. But I only applied for that one.

culture_adjustment: It was easy for me to adjust, since Germany and Denmark are culturally pretty similar. But i think it is overall easy to adjust, since Berlin is a very openminded city.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The multiculturalism.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared to be independent, as you wont recieve much help from UCPH (from my experience). 2. Be prepared that it requies a lot of time and planning going on exchange, 3. But when you have arrived it is an amazing experince, and worth all the struggle.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Living in Berlin as it is an amazing city.
greatest_challenge: Lack of information and help from my home univeristy. It seems like they are ill prepared at helping students going on exchange.

crucial_aspects: It had to be a nice and affordable city with a good university and an opportunity to learn or practise a third language.
info_ease: It was alright. The Erasmus Team at Freie responds really quickly to e-mails and are very helpful.
arrival_assistance: I attended some virtual info meetings with practical information. To me it was very helpful to be in contact with former exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You sign up for courses during the first two weeks of the semester, so you can try different courses before you decide. It is super stressful and confusing, but you just have to be patient. In the end, everyone seems to get the courses they wish for.
registration_help: They do an info meeting about the registration process.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Have patience and don't stress about it. It will be fine in the end. Basically, you can just show up at the classes you find interesting and then ask the instructor if you may follow their class. I am sure they will say yes. Contact former exchange students for advice.
course_level: I would say that the level is in general quite high, although in a different way than at home. In terms of methods and research design, I think KU is quite stronger, but in terms of critical thinking and level of abstraction, Freie is very strong.
teaching_comparison: Critical engagement, active participation and open discussion plays a much bigger role which is super nice.
courses_enrolled: Global Tax Politics (7 ECTS) by Lukas Hakelberg Banks and banking in global politics (3 ECTS) by Andrea Binder Gqola, Hartman and Wynter – A South African – Afro-American -and Afro Caribbean Conversation on the Atlantic Slave (7 ECTS) by Sara Dehkordi Quantitative Methods in Autocracy Research (3 ECTS) by Alexander Libman Sociology of Conspiracy Theories (7 ECTS) by Philipp Wunderlich Needs: Philosophical Perspectives (3 ECTS) by Robin Celikates
recommended_courses: I would especially recommend courses from Lukas Hakelberg for those interested in IPE and Sara Dehkordi for those interested in postcolonial feminism. I also recommend trying a course at another faculty. I learned a lot from following Robin Celikates' philosophy course "Need: Philosophical Perspectives". I highly recommend not to follow the pre-semester German course (Vorkurs) - it was too expensive and very bad and stressful. There are many much cheaper and much better language schools which are also located in central Berlin, e.g. Speakeasy and die deutSCHule.
unexpected_costs: The pre-semester German course is way overprized (DKK 5.000) and it is not worth it.
cost_comparison: Prices in Germany are in general lower than in Denmark. However, I did not really feel that due to the inflation. When I came back to Denmark, I could really feel that prices were lower in Germany.
activities_available: I didn't participate in any.
activities_recommended: Just have fun in Berlin.
weekend_recommendations: Enjoy Berlin of course (there is not enough space in the world for me to do a list of nice things to do in Berlin) and do day trips to Potsdam and all the nice lakes around Berlin (Schlachtensee, Krumme Lanke, Liepnitzsee, Wannsee). I also highly recommend taking a weekend in Prague which is only a cheap 4-5 hours bus ride away.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
cultural_challenges: Germans have a very different perception of COVID-19. In Denmark, there were no restriction since 1 February, but in Germany we had to where masks in class during the whole semester.
culture_appreciated: Berlin clubbing culture :)
top3_advice: 1) Don't participate in the pre-semester German language course on Freie (Vorkurs). It is expensive, bad and far way. It is a good way to meet other exchange students, but there are other ways to meet them. 2) However, do use the opportunity to learn some German. The summer semester starts in April and the winter semester starts in end-October - so use February and March or September and October to go to a language school and follow an intensive German class. I can recommend Speakeasy in Friedrichshain and die deutSCHule in Neukölln. 3) Berlin is more than Kreuzberg and Neukölln - these areas are amazing and definitely where you wanna spend most of your time, but make sure to explore the rest of Berlin and its surroundings.
other_useful_info: If you are in Berlin during the spring, I recommend looking out for the annual Walter Benjamin Lectures in the end of June. This year, the guest was Nancy Fraser, and earlier guests have been Axel Honneth and Charles Taylor.
most_rewarding: Living in beautiful and magical Berlin <3 <3 <3
greatest_challenge: The fact that the semester goes from April to September/October, so I really recommend future students to get their exam papers done in August before the new semester at home begins.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to go somewhere with interesting courses available. And I also chose Berlin because I have family in Germany and wanted to practise the language more.
overall_comments: I had a really good experience overall!
info_ease: It is always quite stressful and confusing to manage communication between different institutions in different countries. The platforms and information available are helpful, but I have the feeling that there is always something that remains complicated. I met up with another student from KU on my own initiative, who had been on exchange at Freie as well and asked her a bunch of questions. This was really calming and helpful, because she gave me some insiders tips on how to cope with the German and Danish systems, and told me that everything will work out in the end.
arrival_assistance: There was a lot of assistance available from Freie's Erasmus team. Well prepared and planned.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had a really good experience overall!
registration_process: As the German semesters are very differently structured than the Danish ones, I decided to move to Berlin in February even though my courses didn't begin until mid-April. So when registration started, I had already visited Freie and picked up my studentcard and so on in my own slow pace. Otherwise, registration was just meeting up for the introduction day and the first week of courses.
registration_help: There was a lot of orientation and information available from the Erasmus team. I found it confusing that the German uni system makes it possible for you to try out different courses in the first couple of weeks of the semester, before you finally decide. This is really great, but not very easy to navigate as an Erasmus student, who has to live up to some very strict demands from your home university.
registration_success: Mostly successful, although I wasn't allowed to take a course I really wanted to join at Freie, because KU wouldn't allow me as a masters student to participate in a course with mixed bachelors and mastersstudents present...
registration_advice: Try out different courses in the first week and see what you like. Also, don't be scared to supply with courses from other universities in Berlin. I took two courses at Freie and two at Humbolt, even though I was only enrolled at Freie. In Germany you can always write directly to the professors and ask whether you are allowed to participate in their courses. This makes everything really nice and personal. Though, also gives you a lot of paper-work and deadlines to remember. But things will work out if you organize well.
academics_comments: I had a really good experience overall!
course_level: The level is high and I found most course at Freie really innovative in their approaches.
teaching_comparison: I had two seminars at Freie with around 20-30 people in each, this made it a really great room for discussions and participation. I loved to be very engaged as a student. I also had one course with two professors present at ever seminar, one from the philosophy department and one from comparative literature. This sparked some super interesting discussions and elaborations among the professors themselves.
courses_enrolled: Humanismen, Humus, Feminismen The face: an approach from many angles Fictions of Addiction Dis/entangling material futures
recommended_courses: The face: an approach from many angles was conducted by a visiting professor from NYU, she had a really interesting approach.
unexpected_costs: My bag got stolen, I did not have an insurance, and I had to replace a lot of things... Also: clubbing is expensive!
cost_comparison: Groceries and coffee at cafés are nice and affordable, compared to Copenhagen.
activities_available: The Erasmus team organized a lot of social stuff and sports activities, I never went. Found things on my own.
activities_recommended: Find some kind of hobby or sport to do in town, its a really nice way to spend time with other people and maybe get new friends.
weekend_recommendations: I went to the Bauhaus museums one day in Dessau and spent the whole day, really great. Also: take the trains out of the city and go hiking or swim in the lakes.
culture_adjustment: It was easy for me, since I have German family.
socializing_tips: Everyone takes the train to and from campus at Freie, so you quickly become friends with people from your classes when you walk to and from the train together.
cultural_challenges: Not very many. Maybe all the paperwork, because a lot of stuff still isn't digitalized in Germany.
culture_appreciated: All the ecological and vegan opportunities. Also: people in Berlin are very open and friendly.
top3_advice: 1) Remember to enjoy the city and the culture and not spend all your time studying 2) Its tough to be alone in the beginning, but things will change slowly, and you will start to feel really at home, so if you have the chance to go early or stay longer before or after the semester, do it. 3) Choose courses with professors that inspire you or whose approach you like
other_useful_info: Remember that you can take courses outside of Freie as well.
most_rewarding: Getting new friends and attending nice events!
greatest_challenge: Feeling lonely in the beginning, because the fact is: when you move to another city, no-one knows you. But slowly people will. Be open and have patience.

crucial_aspects: I was very interested in going to Berlin to experience studying theatre and performance in a place where this field of studying is broader and have a variety of possibilities to engage in, being a leading cultural metropolitan.
info_ease: I had a hard time finding the information I needed and it is very dependent on your own effort to figure out what to do.
arrival_assistance: The were some Orientation days and some emails coming out about the first week there, but then once you had to choose the courses the information was very limited.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Everything up to the point of arriving on the school and choosing courses was easy enough.
registration_help: There was Orientation days and an online orientation zoom call with all exchange students, but it was very general information and hard to adapt to your individual study plan.
registration_success: It was honestly very hard to figure out the course registration and I spend a lot of time on it. I ended up having to change my courses several times so to the lack of information about ects credits.
registration_advice: I would definitely hook up with other exchange students and help each other out and especially students who have the same requirements as you.
course_level: I think there was a huge different on the levels on the different courses, especially the exchange courses were less demanding than the seminars from my field of studying.
teaching_comparison: Since the structure is very different because you have 6-8 courses instead of 2 in one semester, so the individual courses are less demanding, but you have more information in generel to have an overview over. The teaching was more strict and attendance was mandatory, where I am used to way more flexibility and individual study time.
courses_enrolled: - Berlin city of water - Creative Writing - Places and non Places - Formwandel des Theaters im 20. JH - Neue Forschungsansätze zur Tanzmoderne - Space and spatial studies - Hybride Beziehungen
recommended_courses: The practical seminars are very Nice and social for Exchange students to engange in. And also the Places and non Places and the Creative writing class was very good and Creative approaches.
unexpected_costs: I brought my bike and had to fix that and spend 90 euros on dentist appointments
cost_comparison: Food is in general cheaper, which is great.
activities_available: There were fu-sports Club and some social events and gatherings.
activities_recommended: I would really recommend doing some sport acticity in the city like bouldering or dancing.
weekend_recommendations: Go to sorrounding nature parks in Germany and do small hikes and trips out from the city. There are a lot of events happening around Berlin as well.
culture_adjustment: Since it was a very international community it was easy within that, but harder with the local German culture if you don’t speak the language.
socializing_tips: Do activities and be open!
cultural_challenges: People where not as open as polite as I was used to.
culture_appreciated: In general are people who live in Berlin more openminded to diversity.
top3_advice: Be social and engage in activities. Ask people for help! Plan trips on the weekend with people.
other_useful_info: Plan ahead and check out the courses in good time.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from other cultures.
greatest_challenge: Being overstimulated socially and having to take breaks.

crucial_aspects: The theatre culture (relevant to my studies) and the language
info_ease: Regarding the exchange, quite dificult. The amount of bureuacracy makes the beginning of the exchange experience very confusing and exhausting.
arrival_assistance: I recieved some help from the Incoming Office at my recieving institution and from my Erasmus Coordinator.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was all in all quite confusing, but you just have to hope everything will be okay.
registration_help: You could always ask the incoming office
registration_success: I did not get into all the classes I wanted, but I ended up being very satisfied with the classes I did get.
registration_advice: Participate in the orientation meetings. There is a lot of information, you don't need, but the relevant stuff they tell you is VERY important and helpful in the registration process.
course_level: The level of courses was very variyng; some courses where at a highly academic, all most master level and some more first-semester level. The courses particular for Eramus students had a quite low level.
teaching_comparison: A much bigger part for the lessons where made up by student presentations. Otherwise it was quite similar.
courses_enrolled: Rituelle Aufführungsformen, Staging Gender, Musik als soziale Utopie und Praxis, Berliner Theater der 1920'er Jahre, Kultur und Politik der Weimarer Republik, Theaterkritik, Tanz und Mode.
recommended_courses: They were all really interesting. Some of them demanded a very high german level and were therefore difficult, but if your German is good enough, I would definitely recommend Theaterkritik, which has a much more practical aspect. I also really liked Rituelle Aufführungsformen, which was the most theoretical of my courses,
unexpected_costs: I did not know you had to pay a Semester Fee and stuff like that.
cost_comparison: Rent was all in all more expensive than I expected - the student housing was quite cheap, but also horrible (among other things there were bed bugs in my room) so I had to move out as fast as possible, and rent in Berlin in general is more expensive; also I moved around a lot, so I payed double rent for some months.
activities_available: They offer a lot of sportcourses (I took a Salsa course) and there's the Collegium Musicum with two choires, a big band and a symphonic orchestra.
activities_recommended: If you like to sing, the choir is an amazing opportunity to make friends and be a part of something so nice. Also the dance course was so much fun.
weekend_recommendations: THEATRE, museums, music ...
culture_adjustment: Easy enough
socializing_tips: Again, joining the choir really helped me make local friends.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any big challenges regarded cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: The cultural appetite for and interest in art
top3_advice: 1. Check out the non-academic activities! 2. Make sure to go to campus once in a while, also if classes are online - it's really nice place with lots of good libraries etc.. Like a 'student village' just outside the city 3. Take the Vorkurs! It's a good way to start off the exchange; learning some german and meeting some people.
other_useful_info: Find your own place to live! It's hard, but not impossible, and at least my experience with the student housing was very bad.
most_rewarding: The whole thing, but to pick just one I have to say the friends I got. I already miss them.
greatest_challenge: Starting off my exchange with bed bugs

crucial_aspects: Det var vigtigt for mig at universitet havde et godt ry, og kunne byde på andre undervisningsmetoder end KU. Derudover var det afgørende for mig, at jeg planlagde mit udvekslingsophold i et land og i en by, hvor jeg kunne se mig selv have et fantastisk halvt år på det personlige plan.
info_ease: Overordnet var der okay med informationer i forbindelse med introduktionsdagene.
arrival_assistance: Jeg modtog informationsmails mm i forbindelse med introduktionsdagene på Freie Universität.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Jeg tror processen har været ret klassisk - man ansøger, hvorefter det afgøres hvorvidt man er blevet optaget eller ej. Herefter er der en række administrative omstændigheder man skal forholde sig til. Igen er der nogle ting som ikke fungerer særlig optimalt i det tyske system, hvorfor processen kan virke langtrukken.
registration_help: Det internationale kontor på Freie Universitet har altid været søde og behjælpelig.
registration_success: Denne proces er noget af det mest besværlige og uoverskuelige jeg har skulle tage stilling til - så mit bedste råd er at kaste sig ud i det, og acceptere at meget ikke giver mening! Jeg fik de fag jeg ønskede og det er mit indtryk, at de fleste får de fag, de ønsker sig. Det er muligt også at have fag på fx filosofisk fakultet.
registration_advice: Mit råd er at man bare må kaste sig ud i det, go with the flow og acceptere at mange ting foregår på andre måder end man er vant til. Skriv til det internationale kontor og snak med professorerne, meget kan heldigvis lade sig gøre i sidste ende.
course_level: Jeg synes fagene havde et fint niveau
teaching_comparison: Undervisning på Freie Universitet er meget anerledes fra undervisningen på KU. Fagene lægger op til langt mere interaktion, hvilket forudsætter at man som studerende også er motiveret til at læse pensum til hver undervisningsgang. På den måde kan det måske virke mere krævende på FU til selve undervisningen - men det synes jeg kun er positivt.
courses_enrolled: The rise of the populist radical right, Politics of Social Inequalities, Social Structure of European Societies, Quantitative Methods in Autocracy Research
recommended_courses: Jeg vil især anbefale 'The rise of the populist radical right'. Swen Hutter der underviser er fantastisk og rigtig dygtig til at inddrage de studerende. I faget læses 4 værker som diskuteres. Det er et mindre hold så der er god mulighed for at udfolde sine argumenter og synspunkter.
unexpected_costs: Brugen af Uber. Flere U-bahn og S-bahn linjer lukker efter kl. 23. Jeg brugt også mange penge på et sprogkursus udbudt af Freie Universitet.
cost_comparison: Generelt er leveomkostningerne væsentlig mindre end i Danmark.
activities_available: Universitetet var langt mere stramme ift. corona end man på daværende tidspunkt var i Danmark. Det betød at flere arrangementer ikke blev afholdt. Der var uni-sport, men der blev ikke afholdt nogle fester.
activities_recommended: Benyt studenter-caféerne på selv uni. Der er fedt og mulighed for at møde lokale studerende. Uni-sport ville jeg ønske, at jeg selv havde benyttet mig af.
weekend_recommendations: Nyd Berlin og alt hvad byen rummer. Der er 1000ting at lave. Museer, parker, genbrugsshopping, koncerter, technoklubber etc. Hvis semesteret ender om sommeren er det et must at tage til søerne udenfor Berlin. En tur til Potsdam er også en dagstur værd.
culture_adjustment: Meget nemt. Den tyske og berlinske kultur - også på uni - er på mange måder lig den danske.
socializing_tips: Benyt studenter-cafeerne og mød folk ude i byen.
cultural_challenges: Ligesom i København har de lokale selv et liv - det kan derfor være svært at tage en exchange-student ind i sit liv, fordi vedkommende rejser efter et halvt år. Men det kender man jo også selv fra KU.
culture_appreciated: At der er så meget højere til loftet og at byen rummer så mange forskellige bydele og mennesker.
top3_advice: 1. Accepter de administrative uoverskueligheder! Ingen forstår dem, allier dig med andre fra KU, der også er på udveksling. 2. Forsøg at socialiser med dem du har undervisning med - det var jeg selv for dårlig til. Omvendt var vi en stor dansker-boble, og det er folk jeg stadig er venner med efterfølgende. Uanset hvad, så er det ene ikke mere rigtigt end det andet. 3. Berlin er verdens bedste by, og der er så meget potentiale for det bedste halve år. Mød folk og gør ting, du ikke ville gøre i Danmark.
other_useful_info: Fagene - som oftest - kan være på enten 3 ects eller 7 ects. Man bestemmer selv! 3 ects tildeles for aktiv deltagelse i undervisningen mens 7 ects gives for aktiv deltagelse + en eksamen. Et godt råd: De fleste eksaminer er skriftlige - men ofte kan man også vælge at tage dem mundtligt. Jeg vil anbefale at man tager et par af sine eksaminer mundtligt i selve Berlin lige efter afsluttet undervisning. Det gjorde jeg ikke og endte derfor med at skrive 4 eksaminer af 8 sider i august og september måned efter jeg kom hjem fra udveksling. Det var ekstremt hårdt!
most_rewarding: At blive introduceret til et universitet, der gør tingene anerledes og som til dels har et landet verdensbillede. At møde så mange skønne mennesker og at finde ud af - selvom det er en kliche - at verden er så meget større end en selv. Det var fantastisk at have undervisning med mennesker fra mange forskellige kulturer, der havde helt andre perspektiver på emner, man ellers dagligt tager for givet.
greatest_challenge: At lære for alvor at stå på egne ben i et system, der kan virke uoverskueligt, og hvor man ikke bare kan gå til en dansk studievejleder for hjælp - men det var også meget givende!
other_comments: Gør det!

activities_recommended: I don't know.

Visit the museums, the parks, the leftover of the Berlin wall, go to Friedrichshagen for a stroll on a Saturday and maybe a dip in the Müggelsee, go to a club for a full night, go see the huge Russian Monument in Treptower Park, go to Potsdam (mostly for the university there, and then you'll wish you went there instead!), get beers in a späti and walk around, to Markthalle 9 for amazing pasta, to the Saturday/Sunday market at Boxhagener or the one at Maybachufer.

Also, the people in front of the libraries, the Zedat center etc. only spoke German (but they were there to check corona-passports, which is fine, but hard when you didn't know you had to book to get in and they couldn't tell you where to book)

crucial_aspects: All of the aspects listed above were important to me! The opportunity to study on a foreign university with talented professors and students have definitely been an experience both academic and cultural. Living abroad has been amazing – and my destination was a dream coming true.
info_ease: Relatively easy, though I spent a lot of time trying to figure the foreign system out, but had good help from the local Erasmus coordinator.
arrival_assistance: Mails and personal contact with local institute Erasmus coordinator and orientation days and local students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registration for courses on my institute could be done in an online portal, but for all other courses I had to contact the respective professor and get their permission to follow the course. It's very different how many ECTS the different types of courses are worth from institute to institute so that was very difficult to get a hold on – I had to ask each professor who was sometimes also not sure. Also I was (and still is) unsure how the exams function; you can choose to write an essay (Hausarbeit) in the end of a seminar to obtain extra credits, but I found it difficult to find out if you needed to or not, because in some seminars it was mandatory, but in others you just needed active participation to get the credits. Furthermore local students have to complete modules (often 2 seminars) with one exam at the end, but it was not clear whether or not Erasmus students had to. I was told in the orientation days that this rule did not apply to Erasmus students in any institute, but in the last week of the semester I was told that I could not be credited for the one course I had followed on the institute of philosophy, because it was not in a module. I talked back and forth with my institute coordinator, my professor and the secretary on the institute of philosophy and ended up getting permission to get the ECTS if I prolonged an upcoming essay, so it would be 6 pages instead of 3. This was three days before the essay was due and in the last week of the semester, so I was also rather hung up in the other courses, but my professor accepted that I handed in the essay a few days later. It was though very stressful – and from talking to other (local) students I've now been made aware that the module rule does not apply to Erasmus students, just as I was initially told. Everything ended up fine, but I just didn't find it a very nice process. Nevertheless I found that I learned a lot from my confusion in the process – I think part of the experience abroad is also this trying to get your head around foreign rules and systems and handling this frustration and uncertainty :))
registration_help: It took me a while to get to understand the system and I got a lot of help from other exchange student, local students and my Erasmus coordinator. Though I received good help, I often felt very stupid with all my questions and that the coordinator and professors were tired of exchange students being confused about the course registration.
registration_success: I think the courses I ended up following were super good, but it took a long time to get there ;))
registration_advice: Don't stress too much about course registration. Everyone is interested in you completing the courses and having a good experience, though it sometimes seem like everyone is trying to make it more difficult. You'll get there!
course_level: Very much the same level as in Copenhagen. High quality! :-)
teaching_comparison: There was a bigger formality in the style of teaching and a bigger "status gap" between the students and the professors (eg. by the use of formal address or last name) – which I found overwhelming but also good for the environment. It was though something that both students and professors addressed from time to other as a problem. Furthermore I found that the students also were more "loyal" to what was said by the professor and didn't necessarily ask critical questions, but it was difficult from course to course. But overall I was very pleased with the teaching!
courses_enrolled: Experimentelle digitale Literatur (16441 / Hauptseminar) Literarische Mehrsprachigkeit und Übersetzung (16675/ Übung) Von der Notiz zum literarischen Text (16422 / Praxisseminar) Celan als Übersetzer (16418 / Proseminar) Introduction to Feminist Philosophy (16047 /Seminar) Literary Translation: Re-thinking Translation in Terms of Creative Writing (17423 / Übung)
recommended_courses: The courses offered changes so much from semester to semester, so I cannot recommend any particular courses!
unexpected_costs: Not any particular unexpected costs
cost_comparison: Grocery-shopping was cheaper than back home! Also food and coffee on campus.
activities_available: There were student sports and orchestras, which I didn't take part in. Also a few Erasmus student social opportunities. Mostly I took part in the campus student cafés which I enjoyed. But I found it a bit overwhelming to seek information about non-academic opportunities on campus in the beginning of the semester because I used all my energy studying and trying to understand the course systems, and then, when I was more settled, I found it was a bit too late to engage later on. So I ended up mostly using the other offers of the city. Maybe it would make sense to inform about eg. open spots at the sport opportunities throughout the semester where the Erasmus students maybe have more energy to engage?
activities_recommended: Use the cafes on campus, and talk to the local students there! They know what's nice to do and will probably offer you to join them
weekend_recommendations: Enjoy the beautiful city and all it offers! I didn't do any weekend trips as I just felt like exploring the city
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy
socializing_tips: Don't be too afraid to engage!
cultural_challenges: The way German people often correct you (a bit offensive) in the street eg. if you are in their way, don't have lights on your bike or something else they find annoying about you...
culture_appreciated: I though enjoyed the diversity of the city and the university, eg. how differently people dressed.
top3_advice: Don't stress too much about the course registration! Ask other exchange students and use all the ressources you can think of. Don't be afraid of approaching strangers, eg. other students on university. Danes are so reserved, and it doesn't make any new friendships! Don't spend too much time studying – it's also important to socialise, engage with local culture and experience a lot of things!
other_useful_info: Enjoy it as much as you can!
most_rewarding: The cultural experience and knowing that I am academically and personally capable of living and studying abroad :-)
greatest_challenge: The German bureaucratic system ...

Det giver mange ECTS (15) i forhold til de almindelige seminarer, som kun giver 3 (aktiv deltagelse) eller 7 (aktiv deltagelse + eksamen). Derudover er det små hold med meget vejledning, hvor du får lov at lave dit eget projekt. activities_recommended: Jeg prøvede ikke nogle, så det kan jeg ikke svare på.
