culture_adjustment: Det var nemt. Største forskel er, at folk rent faktisk holder fri om søndagen, og at supermarkeder derfor holder lukket. Brug tiden på at gå på alle de gode markeder om søndagen i stedet
socializing_tips: Tag fag på tysk - det er her alle de tyske studerende befinder sig! Men man kan sagtens bare nøjes med fag på engelsk. Det gjorde jeg.
cultural_challenges: Sproget - men det fleste kan engelsk, så det er ikke et problem.
culture_appreciated: Søndagsfri, genbrugskultur og Berlin by night
top3_advice: Vær opmærksom på den forskudte semester struktur, i hvert fald hvis du skal afsted i efterårssemestret. Det starter først i midten af oktober, og undervisningen slutter derfor først midt februar hvorefter eksamensperioden starter. Det betyder, at du kommer meget forskudt ind i dit næste semester. Planlag dine eksaminer efter dette. Jeg tog flest fag med aktiv deltagelse, og ét fag med en eksamen, så det var den eneste, jeg skulle færdiggøre, når jeg tog hjem i februar.
other_useful_info: Start med at finde bolig tidligt. Og så er der er sprogkursus forud for studiestart, som virker til at være rigtig givtigt. Jeg tog det ikke selv, men kender flere der gjorde. Det er også en god måde at møde nye mennesker på.
most_rewarding: At være i en ny by med en ny kultur, og skulle forholde mig til en ny hverdag.
greatest_challenge: Starten hvor jeg skulle have styr på alt det praktiske med fag og ECTS

info_ease: Easy
arrival_assistance: I received a lot of assistance from the central erasmus office at FU as well as the erasmus office at the Otto Suhr Institute for Political Science in terms of emails.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I don't really remember now
registration_help: I don't remember
registration_success: I was successful in registrering for classes in the Political Science MA, but not for classes from the other MA's at the same institute.
registration_advice: I don't know
course_level: All MA courses, some were research oriented.
teaching_comparison: A lot more interactive! At FU I did seminars, whereas I have mostly done lectures at UCPH. Also, at FU there was a requirement of active participation (through presentations and weekly reading notes/discussion points), and at UCPH you don't even have to show up.
courses_enrolled: Researching the EU, Peace Building in South Asia from IR Perspectives, The Semantics, Metaphysics and Politics of Race, Radical politics and (non)violent resistance, Democratic Backsliding? The United States in Perspective
recommended_courses: All of them! They were very interesting.
unexpected_costs: Buying inventory for my dorm room (which was supposedly furnitured, but did not have any kitchen supplies e.g.). Tickets home when I was sick for a few weeks in a row.
cost_comparison: Food is generally cheaper than in Copenhagen. The same goes for museums.
activities_available: The erasmus club at FU Berlin offered some events, e.g. going to the opera, city tours. However, I did not participate in any of them as they did not fit my schedule.
activities_recommended: I did not partake in any.
weekend_recommendations: Going to the Botanical Garden! And sightseeing, going for walks in Berlin's different neighborhoods.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: I don't know. Be open and friendly? Try to talk some German if possible maybe?
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: People at Uni were a lot kinder than I have experienced in Copenhagen. E.g. saying hello and 'Tchau' . And going to the cafeteria together.
top3_advice: Know that there is a lot of paperwork required (I think this goes for any exchange semester) Know that the course selection is limited if you only want to take English courses And be aware that the semester structure is different
other_useful_info: You can either do a Teilnahme- or Leistungscchein for each course (3 or 7 ECTS credits).
most_rewarding: I gained a lot more professional confidence through giving presentations and discussing with my peers in class (seminar style).
greatest_challenge: Being alone and very stressed with school.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: That the city had a lot to offer, to get out of my comfort zone, improving my German
overall_comments: The city, the uni, the people - everything there was amazing. But the bureaucracy, in particular all the papers that you need to sign and promise this and that - it felt like I was always under suspicion, and that I had to be able to predict the future and stick to a hypothetical plan all the time. I always felt uncomfortable getting a mail from the exchange offices or logging in here.
info_ease: FU did a good job providing the necessary information.
arrival_assistance: The exchange office (International and Erasmus) were, once again, sharp to address the most practical and relevant stuff.
arrival_comments: I got a response within 48 hours, sometimes on the same day!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The city, the uni, the people - everything there was amazing. But the bureaucracy, in particular all the papers that you need to sign and promise this and that - it felt like I was always under suspicion, and that I had to be able to predict the future and stick to a hypothetical plan all the time. I always felt uncomfortable getting a mail from the exchange offices or logging in here.
registration_process: You get some papers in a mail, you sign them and send back. If any questions, they are quick to answer.
registration_help: mail
registration_success: There was one class where basic information was not clearly communicated since the professor did not use any of the course/learning portals. So I had to skip the course last minute, because I realized quite late that I was already behind.
registration_advice: Just ask them, they are really nice.
academics_comments: The city, the uni, the people - everything there was amazing. But the bureaucracy, in particular all the papers that you need to sign and promise this and that - it felt like I was always under suspicion, and that I had to be able to predict the future and stick to a hypothetical plan all the time. I always felt uncomfortable getting a mail from the exchange offices or logging in here.
course_level: The professors I had were very involving and had a great interest in hearing our inputs.
teaching_comparison: It is more activating, the structure with 3 ECTS for participation and 7 for term paper seem to work okay - students are motivated to read syllabus and participate. The exams are free written term papers, and the professors were good at making sure we could pitch ideas, give feedback, present results and make sure we did not get stuck. So I felt like I was also getting more directly involved in the academic practice, and could take ownership of my learning.
courses_enrolled: Genderperspectives in peace- and conflict studies Politics of Trade Automatic text analysis in R International organizations in times of crisis Environmental Governance in fast-growing economies
recommended_courses: I would recommend courses by Lora Anne Viola, Bettina Engels and Sünje Paasch-Colberg.
unexpected_costs: I was good, public transportation was free when you had the student card, so I won't complain here.
cost_comparison: Clubs were more expensive. Everything else was a bliss.
activities_available: Sports activities were good, the international office was good at making trips, but we could have used a tour to see the more informal social life at uni - like the student cafés or where to look for parties.
activities_recommended: Explore the historical sites, go to the clubs, look at the museums, see some concerts and talk to some people.
weekend_recommendations: Same as above
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Nope
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: The language and easy-going-ness of the international office
top3_advice: Take some courses with group work - give yourself time to explore the city - take a language course to get to know other exchange students
other_useful_info: It is not important to go to the Bürgeramt. It has genuinely been a waste of time and resources for my part.
most_rewarding: Everything.
greatest_challenge: Again: The bureaucracy
other_comments: no

crucial_aspects: Several things. I chose Berlin primarily because I like the city and really would love to try to live there for a while. Also, Freie Universität Berlin is on of the highest ranked universities in Political Science among the available Erasmus exchange universities.
overall_comments: Many good things to say. I would however have loved to be in Berlin in the spring/summer semester. The winter in Berlin is pretty cold and grey. But it only fitted my study plan with an autumn/winter semester.
info_ease: I think it was easy.
arrival_assistance: Good information from Freie
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Many good things to say. I would however have loved to be in Berlin in the spring/summer semester. The winter in Berlin is pretty cold and grey. But it only fitted my study plan with an autumn/winter semester.
registration_process: Easy. Can't remember any trouble
registration_help: All I needed
registration_success: It was successful. However, you need to or talk manually to some professors to get specific courses. But Freie guides you in the process, so I got all the courses that I wanted.
registration_advice: Talk to other students who have visited Freie to understand the ECTS-system - it is a bit complex. But other than that, just be there to the intro days and ask the Erasmus coordinators at Freie.
academics_comments: Many good things to say. I would however have loved to be in Berlin in the spring/summer semester. The winter in Berlin is pretty cold and grey. But it only fitted my study plan with an autumn/winter semester.
course_level: Very different approach to Political Science - much more theory-based. Some courses better than others. But in general, competent and good professors and active students.
teaching_comparison: A lot af talk and discussion. However also a bit 'fluffy sometimes.
courses_enrolled: Banks and banking in global politics Theories of workplace democracies Democratic backsliding in US Economic sociology and political economy: an introduction into the classics Dynamics of protest politics The semantics and politics of race
recommended_courses: Dynamics of protest politics. Nice research focused course focusing on the causes and effects of political protests. The course was organized in collaboration with Humbolt Universität, so you had classes with HU-students as well.
unexpected_costs: Non
cost_comparison: Everything is less expensive in Berlin - especially food and dining.
activities_available: All kinds of things.
activities_recommended: I didn't do any of the non-academic activites at Freie.
weekend_recommendations: Enjoy Berlin. So many things to do and places to visit.
culture_adjustment: Easy. Very open minded city.
socializing_tips: They are open and friendly.
cultural_challenges: Non
culture_appreciated: The open minded and very liberal culture of Berlin.
top3_advice: The ECTS system is a bit wierd. But once you figure it out, its ok. Talk to fellow KU students who have been at Freie. Search for appartements among the many danes who owns holiday-appartments in Berlin. Choose a nice place to live. Don't care to much whether it is close to Freie or not. Transport in Berlin always take around 30-45 minutes no matter where you are and where you are going.
other_useful_info: The ECTS system at Freie - and also that the semester is a winter-semester from mid october to mid february.
most_rewarding: Living in interesting city and being outside DK for a while. Also see another way to teach and study political science.
greatest_challenge: That the teaching ends in mid february and that there are exams afterwards. It is a bit difficult to fit in a KU semester structure. But it is possible.

crucial_aspects: The language. The city itself. The closeness to home.
overall_comments: All the paperwork around it was a nightmare (especially with the semester being different than in Denmark) but the trip itself was great.
info_ease: It's not always easy to find the information you want on the schools website as it can be very confusing. But I found that I wanted a lot of information before hand that I didn't actually need. Everything you need to know (academically) thay will tell you upan arrival.
arrival_assistance: They did an online introduction "seminar" for incoming students. Also there are introduction days at campus where they introduce you to everything. Also they make it clear that you can always go to the Erasmus office with questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: All the paperwork around it was a nightmare (especially with the semester being different than in Denmark) but the trip itself was great.
registration_process: You basically register for a lot of different courses when the semester starts but you don't need to take all of them. So you spent the first few weeks shopping between courses attending different lectures and then you choose what you want to take. Then you go on the online course registration and sign off the courses you don't want anyways.
registration_help: Not much.
registration_success: Pretty succesfull. Even if you don't get certain classes you want (or maybe realise too late that you want other classes than the ones you signed up for) you can always talk to the professers personally and ask if you can join the class anyways. So I ended up getting all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Sometimes a class you thought was good, isn't what you thought it was going to be once you try it out, so register for a lot more classes than you think you need and try them out! That way you have backup options. You can always sign off them again.
academics_comments: All the paperwork around it was a nightmare (especially with the semester being different than in Denmark) but the trip itself was great.
course_level: I found that they were slightly easier than back home. But yuo get very little assistance with the exam writing, which is where it gets hard.
teaching_comparison: The teaching at Freie is very "class based". So most courses are seminars and not lectures. You do a lot more group work and depating in class, and the lecturers rarely do long presentations.
courses_enrolled: Migration and Integration: main teories and their empirical applications (masters level) Comparative European Politics Rechtsextremismus in Deutschland Einführung in die Bewegungs- und Protestforschung
recommended_courses: The teacher in Comparative European Politics is really good! And Rechtsextremismus in Deutschland is so interesting.
unexpected_costs: No really any.
cost_comparison: I was surprised to find that you pay a one time fee to the university and than you have "free" public transportation during the whole semester. Eating out and buying groceries is slightly less expensive than in Denmark. But the night life is a bit more expensive.
activities_available: I'm honestly not vey sure. Not many that Erasmus students were made aware of or encuraged to take part in. Erasmus arranged parties and some events.
activities_recommended: I would very much like to recommend doing the Vorkurs in German. The presemester intensive course is where I met litterally all my friends during my stay. And so many students take these, that if you arrive afterwards it's almost hard to mingle with the people who did the course. Because you become very close very fast with the people you do the course with. Would ABSOLUTELY recommend!
weekend_recommendations: Go to Potsdam. Thats very nice. During christitmas I visited christmas markets in near by cities like Dresden and Leipzig. That can be done in a single day trip. Also every weekend there are major fleemarkets around the cities, which are really good and really popular.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Danes and Germans are a lot alike.
socializing_tips: Get a tandemparter. That's pretty much the only local student i befriended.
cultural_challenges: They only ose cash for everything.
culture_appreciated: The language.
top3_advice: 1. Do the German presemester intensive course (Vorkurs) - even if you don't want to learn German! It's the best decision I've made in a long time. 2. Begin looking for housing early. Exhaust all sources! It's easier if you know somebody, who knows sombody. But also be patient. A lot of people only just post apartments very shortly before they want it rented out. 3. It's going to be such a fun semester, but be very aware of the many challenges it entails that the semester is not the same in Germany as in Denmark. It means A LOT of confusion, and paperwork and bureaucratic stuff. You have to be willing to put in some extra work.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: Mostly the people I met. But also the feel of the city and practicing the language.
greatest_challenge: All the bureaucratic stuff and the planning. It's really hard when you get home after the fall semester and the spring semster back home is already started and you have to finish up exams from you semester in Berlin along side following classes in Copenhagen.

crucial_aspects: I was already quite familiar with my study destination and knew a few people in the city. This, for me, was quite important.
info_ease: The contact to my host university was very good during the whole stay. Before, as well as during the stay, my host university regularly sent me informations via email – about course registration, student advising, credits, events, etc. I also always received a quick response via email when reaching out to my Erasmus coordinator at my host university.
arrival_assistance: The Erasmus coordinator met us in person on the first orientation day. We also got to meet with a student from our specific field of study who showed us campus and gave us their contact informations as well as recommendations for the university and for the city. That was all very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You can register online, or you can simply show up in the course on the first day and ask the professor if you can join the course.
registration_help: On the introduction day, all exchange students received informations about course registration.
registration_success: I more or less got accepted to all the courses I had wanted.
registration_advice: The first two weeks of every semester is "shopping week", meaning that you can go to as many courses you want to see how you like it. After two weeks you decide which courses you would like to do. My advice would be to use those two shopping weeks – it is a good way to get an idea of the professor and the type of class.
course_level: The level of courses were generally high.
teaching_comparison: Less people were in the courses at my host university compared to the courses I did at UCPH. This meant that I got to participate way more actively which was very nice.
courses_enrolled: Simone de Beauvoir, Introduction to Feminist Philosophy, Saidiya Hartman: Scenes of Subjection, Re-thinking Translation, Law and Literature, Introduction to Cultural Studies: Philosophy of the Bedroom.
recommended_courses: I found the courses in the philosophy department very nice.
cost_comparison: Housing.
activities_available: All kinds of sport, talks, readings, city tours.
activities_recommended: I strongly recommend participating in the social activities on the introduction days. I made most of my friends during those days.
weekend_recommendations: I can recommend going to the many lakes in and around Berlin. Krumme Lanke is only a few stations away from the university. I can also recommend getting a museum card which allows you to enter all of the Staatliche Museen. I can recommend the many markets, Mauerpark, Boxhagener, Bergmankiez, the Turkish market at Maybachufer.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Go to the social activities during the introduction days. Search for a language tandem partner.
culture_appreciated: The diversity.
top3_advice: You are not alone – you can always seek help at the university! Discover the cute and lively cafés and courtyards on campus. Enjoy your stay – FUB is great!!!
most_rewarding: Reaching the end of my second semester, I feel sincerely happy and proud that I dared throwing myself into this experience. I feel personally and academically inspired and motivated – and I believe the main reason for this is the lovely and inspiring people I have met along the way, on and off campus.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to choose something within Europe so that I wouldn't be to far away from friends and family. At the same time it was important to me that the courses at the host university were taught in English so that no matter my level of competence in the local language I would still be able to learn. Finally I thought this to be a great idea to learn a new language and I already know a little bit of German so it would be the easiest language for me to learn so I decided that I wanted to got to a German speaking country. It also had to be a pretty big city since I wanted to go to a place where a lot of different stuff was happening. Because of all these factors I ended up choosing to go to Berlin.
info_ease: I found that Frei Universität had excellent orientation with both tours of the campus and an introduction the to the IT system that they use. The people studying in the physics department even got a separate tour only for us that really showed us the physics building.
arrival_assistance: During that tour which was on one of the first days of the semester the Erasmus contact person in Berlin sat us international students down and explain how to sign up of courses and other practical stuff.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: To register for courses at Frei Universität you have to log into a system called Campus management and press that An-/Abmeldung button. Then make sure that you check the drop down menu, the system won't show all available courses as the default setting. Then it is as simple as press abmeldung. I think it's a little pencil icon, but i want quite remember.
registration_help: During the campus tour the student showing us around showed us how to do it.
registration_success: For me it wasn't a problem because non of the courses I wanted had a participant limit. But from what I heard almost everybody gets the courses that they want.
registration_advice: Make sure to check the time tables. It's not like Copenhagen where we have 3 time slots that courses can be in. At Frei Universität the course can essentially be at any time, so it is easy to sign up for classes that have overlapping classes.
course_level: The courses where about the same level of difficulty as the ones in Copenhagen. Like in Copenhagen I had courses of varying difficulty from pretty relaxed to very difficult.
teaching_comparison: The course structure was slightly different than back home and it was slightly different for the different courses. For all of them there was a bigger emphasis on participation during the semester. In all courses I had we had weekly assignments and the be able to attend the exam you had to get 50% over all the assignments. Some differences were course specific. QFT: Here the exercise class work differently than in Copenhagen. I'm use to that when you show up the the exercise class mostly you do the exercises there. In QFT at Frei Universität the only exercises were the hand-in/home/assignments. So in the exercise class instead having the possibilities of working on them and asking the TA. The TA would go through last weeks assignment and get students to go through some of the problems. Relativistic Particles in Condensed Matter: In this course the lectures and exercises were back to back so instead of having first two hours of lecture and the 2 hours of exercises the lecturer Maxim mixed them. So he would teach for 30 minutes than give us some exercises that we would do for a bit and then we would lecture for a bit again going back and forth.
courses_enrolled: A pre-semester German course (Vorkurs) Quantum Field Theory (QFT) Methods in Molecular Simulation (MMS) Relativistic Particles in Condensed Matter
recommended_courses: If future exchange students want to learn German the Vorkurs is an excellent opportunity for that. It is also where I met some of my closest friends during the exchange. Quantum Field Theory is a hard course with a high work load, but it is also very good. The professor (Felix von Oppen) is good and you learn a lot.
unexpected_costs: I didn't really have any unexpected costs. The only thing I can think of is that I had to dry clean that bed cover before I left my dorm.
cost_comparison: Things were generally cheaper. Especially if you avoid the touristy parts of the city stuff like beers, drinks and food gets significantly cheaper than in Copenhagen
activities_available: There is a whole host of sports that students can sign up for and they only cost around 40 euros per semester.
activities_recommended: I have thoroughly enjoyed exploring Berlins night life. The amount of unique and interesting bars and clubs is like no where else I've ever been. During the day one can walk around Kreuzberg and Neukölln which are some very interesting neighbourhoods. If the weather is for it there are several beaches along the lakes out west of the city that I would definitely recommend. Finally there is essential an unlimited amount of museum of every conceivable topic. One could go to a museum every weekend and you won't be close to getting through all of them.
weekend_recommendations: In the weekends I would recommend everything I have written above and also there are a lot of parks in Berlin like Tiergarten where you can just hang out and drink a beer.
culture_adjustment: The culture is very easy to a just to. The German culture is almost the same as the Danish one
socializing_tips: Not much I mostly socialized with other international students. The one German student I did regularly talk to was a guy I had courses with so approaching then in the breaks during courses would be my best advice.
cultural_challenges: There isn't anything that was challenging. The only thing that was a bit annoying is that that they are so cash reliant so you have to get used to always have cash on you.
culture_appreciated: I think the part that I appreciated the most is a Berlin specific thing, and that is the diversity of types of people that would will see walking around Berlin is like no where else.
top3_advice: 1. If you want a spot in a dorm you have to be ready and fast. 2. Take the German Vorkurs. It is a great way to make a lot of international friends that will stick through the semester. 3. Don't sign up for to much. Have some free time to just do stuff that comes up. You don't need a completely filled calendar.
other_useful_info: I don't think there's anything else that I haven't already covered in another box.
most_rewarding: Making friends from all over the world and knowing that if I ever visit their city I have a place to stay.
greatest_challenge: One of the big challenges for me was finding courses that didn't overlap and in the end I even ended up having courses that overlapped and I couldn't attend every class.

crucial_aspects: I have been to Berlin many times before, and wanted to go somewhere in Germany, so it made sense to choose what seemed somehow familiar in its newness.
overall_comments: It is one of the best experiences in my life, and I would do it again if I could.
info_ease: I had researched quite a lot before going, reading all on KUs website and been in touch with the exchange team at my institute, so I felt somewhat prepared - but of course there were surprises, confusing bureaucracy and stuff that is just impossible to know beforehand: I think the most important thing is to seek out the information, that seems important for you upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: There were introdays and also a very good and present counselor on the uni, if I had questions apart from the information everyone was given.
arrival_comments: It is very difficult to figure out the ECTS and course-granting system in berlin, as it is so different from ours and very analogue in a sense - you can always speak with the professor, make your own deals on points and exams, and they are very willing to help you out and make it work: It is just important to talk to them, ask questions and accept the initial confusion.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It is one of the best experiences in my life, and I would do it again if I could.
registration_process: I don't remember exactly, but since I had the language course before the semester, everything went a bit smoother, being already part of the system and familiar with the uni.
registration_help: The other students, a counselor and an exchange office for broader questions.
registration_success: I was very confused by the classes available and how many I wanted, so my registration process was a bit confusing I'll admit: In the end I was very happy with how it worked out, but maybe I would now prioritize classes where I didn't have to write a take home exam - at least in all of them.
registration_advice: I don't know, it depends a lot on how you want your exchange: I had very few courses, to have more time during the mobility, but that means I have to write three quite big exams. Maybe it would have been better having a class with credits just for participation. And I have heard very good about the JFK institute, though I didn't have any subjects there myself.
academics_comments: It is one of the best experiences in my life, and I would do it again if I could.
course_level: I had a mixture of BA and MA courses, but it was never a problem I think. They were very different levels and reading amounts, but I enjoyed it. I would say go for what you think sounds interesting, and maybe attend more classes than you need the first week, just to get a feeling of the professor's style and the subject before choosing.
teaching_comparison: I like it at KU with the lecture and the seminair going hand in hand, and I sometimes missed the very informed discussions that could create: My professors were very good at creating an open forum and opening up for the discussions which was very fun to try though!
courses_enrolled: Documental poetry Listening to water (and other voices) Transcreation Neue deutschsprachige Literatur (von Berlin aus) gelesen
recommended_courses: I think a lot of them are not repeated - the 'Listening to water'-course was taught by a guest professor, and I would definitely recommend applying for those (I think it's quite early, maybe the beginning of march)! My experience was that the students and the professor gave more of themselves.
unexpected_costs: Not really any, I think - I had saved some money and prepared to spend some more, being away and everything.
cost_comparison: Food, restaurants, activities and everything was in general cheaper than in Copenhagen. I paid a lot in rent, but it was a choice to invest in a safe, spacious and good base.
activities_available: There is unisport, and a lot of events for erasmus students
activities_recommended: I think some of the erasmus events were rather interesting, and I would definitely recommend the croquis if you like drawing - its a nice, non-binding opportunity to leave your head a little.
weekend_recommendations: Berlin is full of possibilities - it draws a lot more known theorists and artists than Copenhagen, so keep an eye open, cause I missed a lot due to general distræthed:)
culture_adjustment: I found it very easy actually: I arrived a month before the language course started, to get some time for myself and get to know the city and I really enjoyed having had some time, cause everything seemed so much more relaxed and familiar.
socializing_tips: I think be open and ready to talk to your classmates, and make some connections there. It is definitely easier to connect with the other exchange students, but in general I found people rather open and ready to talk.
cultural_challenges: I don't think there was any - I wish now, that I had been better at just speaking german in my everyday life and not letting the shyness stop me: that's maybe the most challenging, not to switch to english because it is easier. I think sometimes it can be difficult to ignore the pressure of partying and having the most fun all the time, but I think I just gave up on that, and tried to listen to what I wanted, and that helped me a lot, even though it might sound like a stupid advice.
culture_appreciated: I really enjoyed the diversity and the openness - I felt initially welcome in a different way, and with stuff happening all the time anyways, it seems to me more okay to just make it to the things that I found most important or interesting.
top3_advice: Have time to just get lost in the streets, be alone a bit and just walk around, landing in the new surroundings. I would always prioritize a safe and cozy home, because I need a good base to recharge and find energy. Don't worry too much about all the uni bureaucracy, it will solve itself, if you talk and ask for the help you need: It just cannot be solved beforehand or at the same time.
other_useful_info: Keep an eye out for the talks hosted by the different universities, some real stars come by sometimes! And find the counselor at your receiving institute, they are usually very helpful, when it comes to figuring out the confusing system of german uni administration.
most_rewarding: Getting to know a lot of lovely people, trying out my own boundaries and discovering another city that I found to be a home.
greatest_challenge: At some point I found it very difficult to be so far away from everything I knew, and when I had to go back to DK, I found it very difficult to leave all of that which I had just come to know.
other_comments: Just get going, I think its a great experience to get a bit outside of DK.

crucial_aspects: The reputation of the University and the course list. And that there were courses in english
info_ease: The administration and Abroad-team was very helpful at Freie, though it seems weird that they have not a generalized way of receiving students at each department of the uni. And in general, there are so many documents that need to be filled out, both from Erasmus and the uni, which makes it a lot of work to gather all information.
arrival_assistance: assistance pr mail primarily. An online info meeting as well. And of cource the introductory days, which made a lot of things clearer as all informations were difficult to find online.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Through a website called Campus Management which generally wasn't very intuitive. And the courses I have followed (fx on sociology or anthropology) I wasn't able to register for these in Campus Management and here I just need to rely on the individual professor to sign my registrations/attendance documents.
registration_help: Mail-contact with the incoming team. They were helpful.
registration_success: I was successful overall and got the classes I wanted. But this took a lot of time, and only until I showed up at the classes I knew whether I was accepted or not.
registration_advice: Being VERY patient and knowing that you are able to design your own stay to a high degree at Freie University if you are contacting each professor.
teaching_comparison: The style was in some ways different. At my host uni they expected much more participation which is both "more work" but also really nice and a better way to teach/learn. We had to read less pages at each class compared to my home uni, but this was only nice because then we were able to actually discuss the texts in dept. The teaching style reminded me a bit of high school but in a good way (more student participation - less lecture style)

crucial_aspects: My decision to go on exchange in Berlin was motivated by a number of things, and primary among them was the desire to deepen my understanding and connection to Germany through language and immersion. I had considered other smaller german cities, yet Berlin won out considering the size, number of possibilities, university offerings, cultural experiences and geographical location. In addition to this, I had always dreamed of coming to the city to stay, and even though it was enticing to visit a smaller and less known destination, the idea of actually *living* in Berlin seemed to offer something other than any mere visit could, so despite having been here many times, I chose to deepen my relation to it by going on exchange here.
overall_comments: I would probably recommend students going on exchange to think carefully and pay attention to what they actually feel their expectations and priorities are - are they based on abstract ideas of spatial belonging, academic aspirations, cultural curiosity, or something completely other? I feel that the destination of your student exchange will always be unable to live up every single thing that you have thought beforehand, yet I think you can get much closer to having a fantastic experience if you're honest with yourself about what you want, and maybe less strict about where (friends, family, societal-) expectations would want you to go.
info_ease: I found that the information was well delegated. I received a lot of emails from the school detailing practical information regarding both my citizenship status in Berlin, what regulations I needed to comply with at the school and in the public system of Germany, as well as general information regarding my stay. In addition, a lot of online resources were available for exchange students at services such as 'distributedcampus' and the homepages of Freie University.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance in a number of ways. Before arriving, I contacted a student that had been in Berlin before, and questioned them on school procedures and it really helped a lot. Secondly, I attended the orientation days at the school in the second week of October, which (although very short) gave a good introduction to how to apply to courses and stuff life that at the school. Thirdly, I have used the information services at the school, both the Erasmus+ office at the central bureau, and the one specific to my institute, and they have always been available and helpful to answer any questions I had.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I would probably recommend students going on exchange to think carefully and pay attention to what they actually feel their expectations and priorities are - are they based on abstract ideas of spatial belonging, academic aspirations, cultural curiosity, or something completely other? I feel that the destination of your student exchange will always be unable to live up every single thing that you have thought beforehand, yet I think you can get much closer to having a fantastic experience if you're honest with yourself about what you want, and maybe less strict about where (friends, family, societal-) expectations would want you to go.
registration_process: You have to find the courses in the online Course Catalog, and then register through a website called 'Campus Management'. When finding your courses on CM, you can use a step-by-step video made available on the 'distributed campus' website (just search course registration). There is a really long course registration period where you can shop around and sign up for many courses - just remember to sign off before the period ends. Also be really aware of what the requirements for obtaining credits are, and how the courses tie together with your schedule. If you want to take courses outside of your institute you cannot sign up through CM and will have to go to the first lectures and ask the professor if you can take part in the course (alternatively, shoot them an email). This has implications for how you will obtain your grades at the end of the semester, seeing as grades are issued through CM - you will have to get the information form the Erasmus+ office.
registration_help: I was helped by the Erasmus+ office on several occasions, as well as speaking to other Erasmus students. Additionally, 'distributed campus' was helpful. Do not hesitate to make use of these resources.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted - two of them were in another institute than my own, and it was ultimately quite easy to figure out. The professors are quite flexible with regards to requirements and are often very helpful if you have questions. I did not expect to get all the courses that I wanted, but even though some of the classes were "full", I was allowed to participate.
registration_advice: Ask what professors are inspiring before hand and try something outside of your academic comfort zone if you have electives. Attend the orientation days and use 'distributed campus'. Do not worry too much about getting the literature lists before hand if you need to get courses pre-approved at your home uni. - many of the professors are really bad at answering their e-mails, and they often do not finalize the course readings before the start of the semester. I spent a lot of time trying to track down course readings to apply for pre-approval of my courses at my home institution, and it ended up being a very energy demanding and draining experience. I would just wait till your courses have started to gather them up and apply.
academics_comments: I would probably recommend students going on exchange to think carefully and pay attention to what they actually feel their expectations and priorities are - are they based on abstract ideas of spatial belonging, academic aspirations, cultural curiosity, or something completely other? I feel that the destination of your student exchange will always be unable to live up every single thing that you have thought beforehand, yet I think you can get much closer to having a fantastic experience if you're honest with yourself about what you want, and maybe less strict about where (friends, family, societal-) expectations would want you to go.
course_level: I did not feel any difference between the masters and the bachelor courses in terms of difficulty. I had 4 obligatory bachelor courses and two masters courses on another institute, and it worked really well. The biggest difference between courses is the amount of work required to obtain credits, but that has nothing to do with the level, only the professors requirements.
teaching_comparison: As mentioned before, it was much less structured, with almost no lectures and ultimately mostly class based discussions of readings. Therefore, it was a big difference to UCPH, where we often have lectures with accompanying tuition sessions by student instructors. Here there almost only seems to be 1 session a week, and it seems exclusively to be class sessions with a professor, which are often dominated by student inputs. It varies slightly from class to class how this looks and how much the professor structures the debate. On the other hand, it brings out a lot of student perspectives that are interesting, but I find the style of teaching at UCPH better suited to my learning style.

recommended_courses: I would recommend Critical Political Ecology: Between Marxism and Environmentalism by Markus Kienscherf and Political Polarization in the US with Christian Lammert. These were taught at a high level and had professors that were extremely engaging.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay a fee for using the german TV and radio if you register your adress in Berlin. This amounts to about 18 eur. a month. You also have to pay a mandatory semester fee which amounts to about 286 eur. This covers your use of public transport through the whole of Berlin for the whole semester however! But it is mandatory. It can be extended to the whole of Germany for an extra fee - I would recommend checking this out if you plan on travelling inside Germany.
cost_comparison: Food and drinks are much less expensive than in Denmark, especially for restaurants and bars. Housing is more or less the same. Vintage clothes and second-hand stores are more expensive than expected.
activities_available: There are very good sports opportunities and they are also very cheap. Sign up for courses during the orientation days! Everything from dancing, curling, karate to bouldering and mountaineering are available. The student cafees at the different institutes have a lot of events - very often in german, but whispering translations are often offered - that can be really nice to try! There are some centrally organized parties as well, but to be honest they were only attended by Erasmus+ students.
activities_recommended: I took a university sports course in bouldering which was really cool. Do try to book in advance as the slots are quickly filled. In addition, as mentioned before, check out your local institutes student cafe and keep an eye out for events. The North American JFK Institute especially has a lot of english events offered regularly.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend trying out the Berlin nightlife, including music venues, clubs, and public events, as well as going to restaurants, bars, and cafes. Try to romanticize your experience and catch the pulse of the city. Berlin really has something for everyone. As mentioned before, dive into your local neighbourhoods' hidden gems and its history. Also try to get out of Berlin and visit Potsdam or some of the surrounding lakes and cities. There is a lot of beautiful nature and lovely experiences.
culture_adjustment: Very easy - there are a lot of commonalities between Copenhagen and Berlin.
socializing_tips: People often have a lot of different courses, and do not necessarily have a group that they follow, so they are maybe more open to talking to strangers than you would expect of UCPH! Try to strike up a conversation, and do it early on - people are very open. Attend events of your interests at the school as well, and I'm sure you will find friends. If you are more to the introverted side, using the sports offerings or specific events at school can help give a frame of common interest.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences particularly challenging. People are a bit more overtly political in their attitudes and behaviors here, which I think is refreshing. There are a lot of demonstrations and protests at the Uni. and in Berlin in general - I had good experiences talking to people and attending these, but it was not a challenge.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated the pluralism of Berlin a lot - as mentioned before, people are more political, and I also found that they also "inhabit" their preferences in a thorough and authentic way because there are so many sub-cultures and communities for almost every single identity or interest. This provides a very heterogenous public, and it is clearly visible in the school and the city at large.
top3_advice: 1) Think carefully about the amount of courses you choose, their credit distribution, and the workload of each course - there are many possiblities, and it can become relatively less or more overwhelming to complete the 30 ECTS requirement depending on how you mix and match. Also, try to take a course outside of your institute. 2) The FU is a relatively open and smooth functioning university, so make good use of the campus. There are many libraries, study halls and (really well priced) cafeterias to visit. 3) Talk to people early on, and do not be afraid to feel at home in using the student cafes or other places. The earlier you try this, the more time you will have to hang out with your new friends.
other_useful_info: A random list: 1) Try to ask fellow students which courses and professors they recommend. 2) You have a number of student benefits, including a 6-month free Amazon Prime subscription, and other discounts as a FU student. 3) Use the Mensa's (cantine's/cafeterias) - especially the Asian one called Mensa II has sushi and is really nice and cheap.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was the experince of living in Berlin. I did like the school and most of the courses I took did enlighten me, yet I must say the best thing was simply having each weekend in Berlin. There are so many good things to do and places to see! It was also very wholesome to meet new people here, and I found a number of really good friends through the school and Erasmus+.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge is managing your time between immersing yourself and slowing down to take time to notice, whilst also having to comply with school requirements and bureaucratic hurdles (especially UCPH requirements such as pre-approvals), all the time trying to get as much out of your experience as possible. I would say a trick to managing this is recognizing that you have limits and taking time to identify when to take breaks and when to push yourself a bit.

crucial_aspects: I love the city of Berlin and have had a dream of living here for a long time. The Erasmus program was a good opportunity to live in the city while having something meaningful to do i.e. studying. I also wanted to explore German culture, language and literature more, as it is a big part of my studies in Denmark.
info_ease: We were oriented very well per email by the earsmus team at Fu before arrival and afterwards there were several orientation meetings and days, so I will say I was well informed.
arrival_assistance: As said above there was orientation days and also information sent out by email. There is also a portal called Distributed Campus where you can find a lot of information. The erasmus team also held a meet-up on one of the first days, where we got to meet other erasmus students which was really nice.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: To be honest the registration is a mess. You can choose courses from your own specific program online and if you want courses from other programs, you have to write to the professor personally in order to get allowance. The first couple of weeks function as some kind of trial period, which is nice, but also very stressful. It is also a jungle to find out how many ECTS you can obtain from each class and if you can even be approved for it. All in all the course registration is a parade of German bureaucracy and makes little sense.
registration_help: Everyone is trying their best to help and there was a lot of emails back and forth woth professors, coordinators and so on. But after all, you have to do a lot of reseach and work yourself
registration_success: I got into all the classes I wanted, and my impression is that everyone I know had the same experience. They make it sound harder to get into a class than it is. But I wasn't that satisfied with my classes, so I wish I tried out even more different ones before deciding.
registration_advice: You can do almost whatever you want, as long as you have the professor's consent. I'm a literature student, but did most of my courses in the North American Institute (JFKI) and even one at anthropology. My advice is to show up to more classes than you are planning to follow, just to feel the vibe and see how big the workload is. I experienced a big different between classes with the same amount of ECTS. Also, most professors will allow you to get more ECTS than said on the syllabus if you do some kind of extra work. This can be very helpful if you need a specific amount for your learning agreement.
course_level: I was only allowed to take MA-level courses by my home university, so this is what I did
teaching_comparison: For most of the courses the style of teaching was way more loose and unorganized than at UCPH. The seminars are 1,5 hours and with no break. This was hard for me in the beginning. I didn't like that the discussions weren't very structured and for most of my courses there was no group work, which made it hard for me to participate in class discussions beacuse I get too nervous. But the overall level was mostly the same and the professors were nice and very knowledgable.
courses_enrolled: Political Depression and the Aesthetics of Sovereignty II Narratives of Home in North American Literatures Sites of Labor: Factory, Plantation, Office, Household Ambivalent Substances: Engaging elements in life-death worlds
recommended_courses: None of the courses I took will be offered again (I think), but I especially liked Dr. Freire de Andrade Neves as a professor at the anthropology department. I think he will be doing other courses in the future, so check that out :)
unexpected_costs: After some months you will get a message from your phone operator that you have to pay for every MB data used beacuse you spent more data outside DK than inside in the last 4 months. This made me panic and I considered getting a German number, but it turned out that it wasn't bad at all and the price was max 50kr higher a month.
cost_comparison: Eating out is so cheap! Transportation is expensive, but we get a discount through the student ticket. In general the student discounts are very good, often half price at museums etc. This was a nice surprise. Housing is pretty expensive but it is possible to find something affordable. And the entrance for clubs is expensive! Often 25 euro, around 200 dkk.
activities_available: all kinds of sports classes, different social clubs and a few student parties. I didn't really participate in any of them, but I only heard good things from others
activities_recommended: I participated in the German Vorkurs - a 6 week German course before the semester begins. This was a very nice way to meet people and ease into life in Berlin before starting the acedemic semester, so I definitely recommend that.
weekend_recommendations: Sooo much to do! Of course there is the club culture, but you probably already know about that. Every first sunday in the month, there is Museumssontag, where most museums have free entrance. On sundays there's also the fleamarkets, which is a nice activity. I recommend the one called Nowkölln at Maybachufer. Going for walks in different areas is a very nice activity in Berlin beacuse there's so much life in the streets and coffee or food stops are very affordable. I also went on a few canal tours, which was fun, and swimming in the lakes is definitely recommended! Krumme Lanke is not that far from campus, so bringing your bathing suit to class and going after is a life hack! Theater, concerts and cultural activities in general are often pretty cheap for students, so this is definitely worth checking out. Almost every piece of pavement in Berlin has a historical meaning, so there's so much to explore if you're interested in history, WW2, east/west division, art scene etc.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy as it is very similar to Denmark
socializing_tips: Honestly, it was pretty hard to socialize. I guess it is easier if you are better at German than I was
cultural_challenges: A loooot of bureaucracy makes it very frustrating to be in Germany sometimes. Luckily you can laugh about it with the Germans, they hate it too. People are a bit more closed than in DK and not as friendly, but it is not a big problem. I think the city is just bigger and I never had any bad experiences
culture_appreciated: I really appreciate the going out culture, how people hang out at cafes, bars, restaurants, small squares and patches of grass all the time. That is something missing in DK, I think. I also like that, despite the stereotype, everything is not so controlled and managed here. Buildings are left, there's more 'wild' nature in the city and more diversity in people
top3_advice: You have to bear with the bureaucracy, but people are generally good at helping and they know, that is it very hard to figure out. Don't be scared that campus is a bit far from everything. The atmosphere is nice and it is close to nature, lakes and has good libraries, outside areas etc. It is nice to know just a little bit of German before going. I started from scratch at an evening course once a week for half a year and then did the Vorkurs. This was very helpful both at campus and in general. But campus is pretty international and you can communicate perfectly fine with English
other_useful_info: The student cafe called Pi is nice! Has a rooftop terrace and cheap coffee
most_rewarding: Just living in Berlin, feeling at home here, meeting a lot of different people with different backgrounds. I loved the city before I came here and now I just love it even more. One of the best things is that beacuse everything is cheaper it is so much easier to do stuff, eat out, have another coffee etc. There's so much life here and so much to do so it just feels like a buffet of cool experiences and people
greatest_challenge: University was a bit lonely because it was hard for me to get to know people in my courses. This didn't bother me so much, though, because I had friends elsewhere and I think it is different for everyone

teaching_comparison: I had more different classes and different professors. They all do it differently: For one they check participation and will often check that you read through pre-class reflections fx - and you can only miss two classes. I didn't like this lack of trust in me as a student, and it made it a bit overwhelming to then juggle four different classes at the same time, but I am happy about the level and the amount I learned through this extra push.
courses_enrolled: 32114 Queer Art: New Critical Readings from the Americas 13501 Theories and Methods in Modern Art 17390 Ü-Literary and Cultural Theories: Reading the Past: Historicism, Presentism, Hauntology 16583 The Aesthetics and the Politics of Collapse
recommended_courses: The courses aren't repeated but I would really recommend Sabine Schülting - she's a GREAT prof!
unexpected_costs: I travelled to see my girlfriend (those are the other fees) The local transport is included in the Semester Fee you pay at the beginning and the all public is open to you. I bought a bike as well for 150EURO.
cost_comparison: I wasn't surprised: The food had gotten a little more expensive - both in the supermarket and eating out, but it is the same all over. I put my budget pretty high in order to also enjoy being in a new city and trying out what it could offer.
activities_available: I went to the uni-sport, there are also Erasmus-excursions, though I didn't get to try them.
activities_recommended: Spooorts! I went to both tango and balfolk and joined the social-dancing events as well.
weekend_recommendations: I would go to the lakes for sure, they are nice small escapes, and to Leipzig that aren't too far away. Other than that I would keep an eye on ICI, that has great talks, and the theatres. Also the clubs are worth visiting and many of the museums - fx Hamburger Bahnhof and Körnerpark Galerie.
culture_adjustment: I found it very easy, the german culture isn't too far from the danish, and in Berlin there are also many different and international people, so you'll fit right in.
socializing_tips: I would ask people in my course for a coffee, join sports and events also with Erasmus-students fx from a language course. Other than that dating and friendsdating are sweet ways to encounter new people, and you literally have almost nothing to lose, since every new person is a potential contact.
cultural_challenges: I didn't encounter any.
culture_appreciated: I really like the layed-back-ness of Berlin, the no rush and everything can take a little longer!
top3_advice: Remember that all admin will end up working out - also the ones you can't solve immediately Berlin is lovely, so go out explore, and it's a great city to hang out alone in - they all do it:-) If it all get's a little much, then Krumme Lanke can give you some breathing space, it's the end of the train ride to uni anyways.
other_useful_info: Ask the professors and don't be shy about taking courses outside your institute.
most_rewarding: Getting to find an everyday in another city and feeling like I grew an extra home.
greatest_challenge: The admin hanging a little over your head, since it can sometimes be hard to relax when everything feels a little out of control.
other_comments: No.

arrival_comments: There were a lot of guidance and explanation of the rather complicated and unique semester and course structure. I found it especially helpful to talk to the more senior students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: There were Erasmus coordinators and the professors and their teaching assistants who all helped us apply to uni.

registration_advice: Talk to your fellow students and the students who does full master programs at uni - they can help you as they know the system well.

cost_comparison: The food and groceries were way cheaper than expected. Almost half the price of groceries in Denmark.

activities_recommended: I would recommend to go to the different museums in Berlin as the city has such a diverse and fascinating history.
weekend_recommendations: Go to potsdam! Its a historical place and makes for a nice saturday trip out of Berlin.
culture_adjustment: It was rather easy as Denmark is not that different from Germany I would say.
socializing_tips: You should stay open minded and know that Berlin is a place with so many different nationalities and cultures. therefore its wise to keep and open mind and stay curious to learn more about other people.
cultural_challenges: I found the Germans to be extremely fixated on rules compared to danes who are more relaxed about it.
culture_appreciated: How open minded everyone at uni and in the city were towards me as an alien from another country.
top3_advice: Take it easy - you will get the courses you wish for. Go out, meet people and stay open minded. Also remember to take a break every once in a while!

most_rewarding: Living in a historical and multicultural metropole while getting to know so many fascinating perspectives academically.

other_comments: I would really, really recommend going to Freie Universität on exchange. The stay changed my perspectives on the world, Europe and I have made friends for life from all over Europe.

activities_recommended: Choir is a great place to meet people and get local friends.

culture_adjustment: Very easy. I've lived there before.
socializing_tips: Follow your interests - take classes in dance/sport/music/ceramics/yoga/politics/whatever your interests are. And if people from the uni-courses seem nice, ask to go 'Mensen' together

culture_appreciated: The appreciation for art and culture + the political directness
top3_advice: 1. Challenge yourself in terms of language - I think it's often easier to get help etc. if you at least try to ask in German, and some of the most interesting courses are in German. You can learn it! 2. Sign up for a unisport-course or something 3. If you can, prioritize to live in the city over living near the university. You will travel far everyday no matter what.
other_useful_info: It's okay not to attend every Erasmus-activity.
most_rewarding: Strengthening my language skills, deepening my relationship with the city and people in it, exploring a ton of art and culture
greatest_challenge: The Erasmus bureaucracy

crucial_aspects: For me personally, it was crucial to study in a German-speaking country, since I am studying German Language and Culture. Having already lived in Berlin during my gap year, and always wanting to return in an academic context, it felt like the natural choice. I was already somewhat familiar with the city, but I also felt there was so much more to explore – especially as a student.
info_ease: I found it very straightforward to access the necessary information after my arrival. Freie Universität (FU) was excellent at continuously sending out all the relevant information before, during, and after arrival via email.
arrival_assistance: The student information office helped me with guidance on how to obtain a German health insurance, which was necessary in order to be enrolled at the university. Afterwards, they also guided me through the course registration process and explained what I needed to pay attention to.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process at FU was well supported by both UCPH and Freie Universität. The only obstacle I encountered was finding a German insurance provider that could officially confirm to the university that I was properly insured as an EU citizen via the European Health Insurance Card. Eventually, however, I managed to solve this.
registration_help: The student information office, or the “incoming team” at FU, suggested German insurance companies I could contact. When these companies did not respond, FU encouraged me to visit one in person in Berlin. Once I did so, they immediately helped me sort out the missing document I needed.
registration_success: Very! I was able to register for all the courses I wanted to take – even courses outside of my host department (the Institute for German and Dutch Philology).
registration_advice: Make sure you sort out the documentation for your health insurance. Even if you are covered by the European Health Insurance Card, you will need a German insurance provider to confirm this to FU before you can complete your enrolment.
course_level: I have listed the courses I took below, along with the examination formats and how demanding I found them. Overall, I felt that courses designed specifically for exchange students were less demanding than those designed for German students. This was not only due to the language, but also because I chose courses in institutes and subject areas that I had not studied before. Nevertheless, I strongly recommend taking at least one course in German within a subject that you are genuinely interested in, since in my experience the teaching quality at FU was extremely high and enriching.
teaching_comparison: There were generally three types of teaching at FU: lectures, seminars, and classroom teaching. From my bachelor studies at UCPH, I am most familiar with seminars, where the weekly readings are discussed collectively, or classroom teaching, where new academic topics are introduced and worked with. These two forms at FU were very similar to my German courses at UCPH. Lectures resembled the fællesforelæsninger at UCPH. Overall, I found the courses to be of very high quality, sometimes demanding to keep up with, but the lecturers were generally very helpful and eager to answer any questions.
courses_enrolled: Einführung in die EU (7 ECTS): Written exam in German without aids (with the option to write in English). Weekly lecture (2 hours). Large syllabus, interesting but demanding. Designed for political science students at the Department of Political Science. Attendance fulfilled by giving a presentation. Deutschlands politische Landschaft: Institutionen und Prozesse (5 ECTS): Written exam in German, handwritten, without aids. Weekly lecture (2 hours). Minimal syllabus, introductory and very manageable. Weekly attendance required, plus a mandatory presentation. Designed for exchange students. Green Germany (5 ECTS): Written exam in English without aids. Weekly seminar (2 hours), group work and text discussions. With prior knowledge of German history and culture, the workload was moderate. Weekly attendance required. Designed for exchange students. Hannah Arendt, Vita Activa (5 ECTS): Exam: Hausarbeit (approx. 10 pages in German). We read Hannah Arendt’s Vita Activa in its entirety in German, discussing each chapter in the weekly seminar (2 hours). Exciting, highly educational, but very demanding – both to read the book within the semester and to write the exam paper. Passing required writing at least 6 discussion papers on chapters of choice and moderating one seminar in a group. Designed for German philosophy students. Language Course: Vertiefungsmodul A (5 ECTS): Weekly language course (4 hours) with both international and German students. Covered grammar and exercises. C1 level, very demanding. Passing required 4 written assignments (with resubmission if necessary) and full attendance. Although the assignments were tough, the feedback was excellent and the course structure well thought out.
recommended_courses: As mentioned, I would recommend German students to take at least one course in German on a topic they find interesting, even if it’s outside their field or seems challenging. Personally, I took the course on Hannah Arendt, a thinker I only knew by name beforehand, and although it was by far the most demanding course (in philosophy, very different from German studies), I learned a great deal both academically and personally.
unexpected_costs: Before departure, I was not aware that one has to pay a license fee, or “Rundfunkbeitrag,” when living in an apartment in Germany. After registering at the Bürgeramt, I received a letter requiring me to pay the fee, which amounted to around 1,500 DKK for 7 months.
cost_comparison: Living expenses, especially food and drinks, were cheaper than expected. Additionally, after paying the semester contribution, students receive the “Deutschlandticket,” which grants unlimited travel on all public transportation in Germany (except high-speed trains). I found this a fantastic benefit.
activities_available: There were countless opportunities for students at FU. I mainly explored the sports activities, where a catalogue offered everything from dance, yoga, pilates, kickboxing, and tennis, to much more. Many of these activities were advertised around campus, making it easy to find something that matched your interests.
activities_recommended: I found it very rewarding to take part in an activity like tennis or yoga. Beyond that, I recommend exploring the city itself: discover the places you like, set aside time for adventures, and keep at least one day a week free from studies to enjoy Berlin. Use that time either individually or with others to experience the city.
weekend_recommendations: Take a day trip to Potsdam to visit Sanssouci Palace. In summer or on warm days, Berlin’s nearby lakes are perfect for swimming – I especially liked Schlachtensee, Teufelsee, Krummelanke, and Flughafensee. Leipzig is also a great weekend destination, especially during their book fair. From Berlin, it is easy to reach many major European cities, so I highly recommend traveling if you enjoy it. Personally, however, I found Berlin itself so vast and diverse that there was always more to discover within the city.
culture_adjustment: As a German student who had previously lived in Berlin, it felt very natural for me to adjust. For those unfamiliar with Berlin, the city can feel overwhelming at first, but once you establish your own daily rhythm, meet people, and find your favorite spots, the city opens up in a very unique way that I haven’t experienced elsewhere.
socializing_tips: Take courses in German, join study groups, and get involved. For me, my first contact with local students was purely academic, but gradually this developed into friendships outside the classroom. It may feel intimidating at first, but it pays off. I also signed up for a tandem partner program at FU, where I was paired with a German student who wanted to learn Danish. This was another excellent way to meet local students.
cultural_challenges: In professional and academic settings in Germany, professors, lecturers, and staff are still addressed very formally. I didn’t find this a problem, but it does require a shift in mindset compared to Denmark. Despite the formal tone, I always felt that both lecturers and fellow students were approachable, helpful, and eager to support me.
culture_appreciated: The inclusivity. Both Berlin as a city and FU as a university embrace diversity and are welcoming to everyone, which I greatly appreciated.
top3_advice: First and foremost, I would encourage everyone to ask for help with the things that may seem incomprehensible or overwhelming, whether practical or academic matters. I had an incredible number of questions and at times along the way I doubted whether I would manage to sort everything out, but it really helped to reach out again and again – and it will work out, as long as you ask when in doubt. In the academic context, I would like to point out that you may take on a different role or study experience than the one you are used to back home. However, you should not let this intimidate you, but instead take it as part of the experience and accept that it is okay to be more quiet, reserved, etc. – but on the other hand also dare to speak up or throw yourself into something when you feel you have something to contribute. For the third point, I would simply encourage other students to immerse themselves in experiencing Berlin as a city and to make use of the many opportunities it has to offer for every taste. In doing so, you can gain a special personal connection to the city, and I believe this makes it a place you will want to return to in the future.
other_useful_info: Through the introductory language course (Vorkurs), I had the opportunity to apply for a mentor and was paired with a local student studying German literature. We met weekly to discuss assignments, questions, and all sorts of topics. This was an extremely valuable and positive experience, which I would highly recommend to others.
most_rewarding: Realizing how much I am capable of when I challenge myself academically. In addition, forming friendships with students from Berlin and from all over the world has been an incredible experience, and I look forward to keeping in touch with them in the future.
greatest_challenge: Taking courses in German at the same level as local students. It was extremely demanding, but I managed to succeed, and I am very proud of that.

registration_success: I got all of the ones I wanted.

cost_comparison: Books. I didn't spend money on books at all. The 6-week language course BEFORE the start of the semester that Freie offers costs 5800 DKK. This can also be part of your budget.
activities_available: There were multiple activities and events arranged for students. I have no complaints here.
activities_recommended: I would really recommend doing a 6 week language course before starting your studies - specifically the one that Freie offers. Even though it is a bit expensive, it is a really great way to get to know other exchange students and also improve your german.
weekend_recommendations: Hamburger Bahnhof Gropius Bau Tempelhofer Feld Körner Park!! Hang out at: Helmhlotzplatz Richardkiez and discover Schöneberg - the area close to Nollendorfplatz!
culture_adjustment: This was no problem!
socializing_tips: Be part of a class that is taught in German. This was the way I got to know local Germans. Also, find housing through WG-gesucht. I got to live with three German students and really enjoyed this!
cultural_challenges: Speaking German in front of native german speakers. This was intimidating.
culture_appreciated: The way people use bars, restaurants and green spaces in Berlin during the spring and summer period. Everyone is out on the streets, which I enjoyed a lot.
top3_advice: - Ask a lot of questions to Freie's Incoming Erasmus Team - Do a language course before hand if you want to improve your German - Live off-campus and find your own place to live
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Improving my German language skills. And meeting a lot of nice people!
greatest_challenge: Missing friends at home, and still studying when summer begins in Denmark
other_comments: I can definetely recommend spending a semester at Freie!
