registration_advice: I can recommend coming to a lot of different classes the first week and then register or deregister.
course_level: Lower level than home university.
teaching_comparison: Lot of class discussion. Not lectures. This is both positive, but I felt that sometimes people had not read the texts and then it felt a bit stupid to start discussing the text without a common understanding of the core arguments. Also it depends very much on the teacher how the style of teaching is. Some teachers were very good at structuring a discussion while some were more relaxed and didn't moderate the discussion.
courses_enrolled: 15451 Resilienz demokratischer Systeme (Resilience of democratic Systems) 32520a Lecture Series: US Foreign Policy in Turbulent Times 15461 Moderner Rechtsextremismus (Modern right-wing extremism) 15493 Deutsche Außenpolitik seit 1945 (German foreign policy since 1945) 31501a Civil Society and Mobilization 15532 Knowledge politics and economy of conflict and violence part 1 & 2
recommended_courses: I can recommend Democratic Resilience, German Foreign Policy, U.S. Foreign Policy, and Civil Society and Mobilization.
unexpected_costs: There is a semester fee at the university that covers transportation. Its the Deutschlands Ticket that gives you free transportation in Berlin and in all of Germany in all S-Bahn, Busses, U-Bahn and regional trains.
cost_comparison: Food is not as expensive as in Denmark and going out for a drink at a bar. You have to remember to give tips.
activities_available: A lot of museums are available and free if you have the student card.
activities_recommended: Museums, going to the lakes and Grunewald.
weekend_recommendations: Leipzig, Dresden, Sächsische Schweiz.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy.
socializing_tips: Take the language course. There is also a social and cultural programme to this.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find anything particular difficult or challenging.
culture_appreciated: The vibe and kiez's in Berlin
top3_advice: There is a lot of bureaucracy at Freie, but it is still nice. Go in spring - Berlin is best in spring and summer.
other_useful_info: Not really.
most_rewarding: I became better at German.
greatest_challenge: German courses.

crucial_aspects: I had visited Berlin a few times before and really liked the city. Also, I have friends who had lived in Berlin and studied at the FU, who recommended it
info_ease: It was rather easy to find information
arrival_assistance: I recieved emails with information about fx courses and there was two orientation days
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to register both at Campus Management and write to the professors if they had a spot available in their seminars.
registration_help: Information sent out from the university and information at the orientation day
registration_success: I got a spot in all the seminars that I wanted
registration_advice: At Campus Management it is not first come, first serve. However, I could not register for all the courses I wanted there, so I had to write to the professors to get a spot in their seminar - in these cases in the popular courses it´s a good idea to write as quickly as possible to the professors, because otherwise you might not get a spot. Another important thing to know is that you can reregister for courses in the first two weeks, so you are able to “shop” around between the seminars and then reregister based on which ones you find most interesting
course_level: I found the level of the courses appropriate.
teaching_comparison: At the sociology program at Freie, it´s small seminars (max 18 students) and in most seminars it is discussion based, so the professors expect you to have read the literature and participate in the discussions. Because it is active participation, you have to be present in 85% of the seminar and hand in questions every week, do presentations or something like that depending on the seminar
courses_enrolled: Emotions and Social Class (seminar) Mixed Methods Approaches to Migration and Health Inequalities (seminar) Religion and Migration (seminar) Contested Intimacies: Understanding (Non-)Monogamy (seminar) Globalization of Science: A Gender Perspective (seminar) Cultural Differences and Similarities (lecture)
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of the seminars, as I found them all interesting and you learn a lot, because you have to participate and discuss the themes. The lecture was interesting as well and the workload was quite small compared to the seminars, but I definitely feel like I learned more in the seminars
unexpected_costs: I didn´t encounter any unexpected costs
cost_comparison: The prices were what I expected, which was that it is cheaper to go out to dinner, bars, museums (almost all are free when you are a student) and so on than in Copenhagen, which made it possible to explore the city more, without being too concerned about your expenses
activities_available: All different kinds of offers such as UniSport which had all sorts of sport offers for students, FU campus run/summer party
activities_recommended: You had to be quick to sign up for some of the sports courses in UniSport, so I didn´t participate in that, but the FU campus run/summer party was nice
weekend_recommendations: Just explore the city, all the different neighborhoods, the history, go to musems, bars, flea markets, the lakes, hang out in the parks, go to Potsdam or other cities in Germany (which is free to travel to with the Semesterticket)
culture_adjustment: I found it relatively easy to adjust, as Berlin has a lot of things in common with Copenhagen
cultural_challenges: I didn´t find anything particularly challenging, other than just adjusting to living away from home
culture_appreciated: I especially appreciated that Berlin is very multicultural and has a lot of history
top3_advice: 1. Attend a German vorkurs at the language center at FU before the semester begins, both to learn the language, extend your stay and to get a social circle – the vorkurs was especially useful for the latter reason 2. Take the seminars rather than the lectures 3. Remember to not only focus on studying, but also enjoy and explore the city
other_useful_info: Nothing I can think of
most_rewarding: To study at a university in another country, living outside of Denmark and meet a lot of interesting people from all over the world
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was being away from friends and family back home, but luckily Berlin is not that far away

crucial_aspects: I have family in the area, and I could access study programs at FU we don't have at KU- It was extremely helpful in order to get more knowledge in my field of study.
overall_comments: Very nice subjects, very nice people. But I felt a little bit lost during my stay regarding the systems at FU. We got a brief introduction, but the teachers were not really aware of how to let me into the courses.
info_ease: Some of it worked well - we had a tour and heard about the options at the university. But after that: It was difficult! The first days was okay, but I had the feeling that we were a little bit on our own at the department of Theater Studies. I had a hard time picking my subjects and I was not let into the Blackboard (teaching portal) for one of my subjects. I found the communication with the professors a little difficult - I still don't know how the formalities of the exam works, but they are very good people.
arrival_assistance: I had a meeting with our coordinator.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Very nice subjects, very nice people. But I felt a little bit lost during my stay regarding the systems at FU. We got a brief introduction, but the teachers were not really aware of how to let me into the courses.
registration_process: I do not know what is meant by this. I described some of my experiences above.
registration_help: I had a coordinator.
registration_success: I was successful, but it took a lot of effort and I still need final paperwork on the courses I participated in.
registration_advice: Show up and talk to the professors if you can't sign up online!
academics_comments: Very nice subjects, very nice people. But I felt a little bit lost during my stay regarding the systems at FU. We got a brief introduction, but the teachers were not really aware of how to let me into the courses.
course_level: I took MA classes, because I found that they suited my level and my interests. Also we start the university earlier in DK, so I was more sorrounded by people my age. I learned a lot! And also - they were in English.
teaching_comparison: It was very different, more theory-oriented and a lot more focus on the texts.
courses_enrolled: * Hope, Utopia and negativity * Valeska Gert Guestprofessorship with Viktor Rubal * Researching communities of practice: Fieldwork and histor. methods * Choreographic Interventions
recommended_courses: The Guest Professorship! REALLY a big experience.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Eating out and going to the theatre!
activities_available: All sorts really!
activities_recommended: I did not attend them.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the nature parks on the border to Tjekkiet. Also - use the amazing free offers around the city. You can find good things on Rausgegangen (an app). Go do something you never did before! I went to Qigong, saw my friend dance Flamenco, went to concerts. Say YES to opportunities <3 Go to fleamarkets.
culture_adjustment: It was harder than I thought, the city can be rough, but I eventually found my way. There are so many great things to do here.
socializing_tips: It takes time, but give it time and it will blossom <3 Also - I met a girl in yoga class who is now a really good friend of mine - if you meet someone with a great energy, talk to them!
cultural_challenges: That the people I encountered in the beginning seemed very closed off - but now I have really good friends.
culture_appreciated: THE ARTSCENE!! And the possibility to eat out and have a coffee - the city is very vibrant.
top3_advice: 1. Get to know the rules of the courses/exams/registration etc. ASAP 2. Be kind with yourself if it is hard to connect with people - it will come 3. READ THE MATERIAL!
other_useful_info: Just enjoy Grunewald every once in a while.
most_rewarding: Being in a very vibrant international environment. Performing at ADK with my class. Such a cool experience.
greatest_challenge: Finding out how the practical stuff works.

crucial_aspects: As I am studying a language, it felt very natural and as a opportunity I couldn't miss, to explore the language and the culture even more trough exchange.
info_ease: It was definitely a bit difficult and stressful at times. You defiantly need to prioritize time and effort to do these things, and can expect information to come to you without searching for quite a while, that was my experience at least.

housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: Guides online and info at the introduction day
registration_success: I was succesfull
registration_advice: I used google a lot, to just search the courses i wanted, and then took it from there. And I used other Erasmus students, so we could help each other as we were all a little confused and in the same boat
course_level: I had to Erasmus courses with only international students in german, and two where I was the only exchange student in german as well. That was a good balance for me
teaching_comparison: I didnt experience the biggest difference, as my courses at UCHPH also are in german. But there was some different ways of participating that i hadn't tried before. Making a "response paper" and a "protocol" was something i hadn't tried before as examples.
courses_enrolled: - Film der Weimarer Republik - Migration und Religion - Hedwig Dohm im Kontext der Frauenbewegung - Kreuzberg als Topos und Schauplatz in der Gegenwartsliteratur
recommended_courses: For me it made a lot of sense to do courses that i could imagine being a potential theme for my bachelorprojekt. I tried to choose as many culture and literature courses, because that's where my interest is. I didn't choose anything based on social presences, but only academic interests.
unexpected_costs: A deposit for my apartment
cost_comparison: It was cheaper to live than i thought, the most expensive thing was housing
activities_available: Museums, sports-clubs, political groups
activities_recommended: I was really happy to participate in the political and activist life both on and off campus
weekend_recommendations: Enjoy all the free cultural opportunities. There are so many. Lakes, parks and other outside offers are great as well.
culture_adjustment: I found it natural and easy, but took a little time of adjustment of course
cultural_challenges: Language of course, and a general lack of interest from the german students. But among exchange students, I found everyone to be open
culture_appreciated: The culture around music, the history that is everywhere in the city, the diversity in the city
top3_advice: 1: School is important, but you can learn so much from exploring the city as well, find a balance and trust it! 2: Be brave and talk to new people (the entire stay), so many people are desperate for a friend, so you are all in the same boat. 3: Take pictures!!
other_useful_info: You can actually find a lot of information by just googling it, if the website is difficult to navigate. And use the mensa, will save you so much money
most_rewarding: The connections and friends I made has changed me fundamentally as a person
greatest_challenge: Coming home, I find it very underwhelming to come home with so many new experiences in the bag. I wish i could have stayed, but at least I know now that is could be a possibility for me to come back and live there one day

crucial_aspects: I have always wanted to try and live in Berlin as I have been there some times before and really liked the city, so an exchange semester in Berlin seemed like the perfect opportunity to do that
info_ease: I think it was quite easy to find the information you needed, I wasn't really in doubt about anything
arrival_assistance: E-mails containing information and orientation days at the university. I also had the impression that the incoming office at FU was ready to help and answer questions if you needed anything
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You register for the courses you want to sign up for through a platform called Campus Management and then you get assigned to the courses after the deadline. However, it wasn't possible for me to register for all the courses I wanted and needed through Campus Management, and in this case you have to write the lecturer of the course. It is also possible to reregister for courses during the first two weeks of the semester if you change your mind about which courses you want, as long as there are available spots in the course
registration_help: E-mails from the university with information and the orientation days, where the registration process was demonstrated and you could ask questions
registration_success: There were two courses I wanted that was filled up when I wrote the lecturer of the courses
registration_advice: I thought it was a little hard to make your schedule yourself and choose between the courses but everything worked out in the end, so my advice would be to not stress so much about it

courses_enrolled: Globalization of Science - A Gender Perspective, Religiosity of European Societies, Islamist Extremism and Radicalization, Introduction to Social and Religious Movements, Throwback: Cultural Shifts towards Regression, Nostalgia and Deceleration and Measuring Social Constructs

unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs
cost_comparison: It was as expected. Groceries, restaurants and bars are cheaper than in Copenhagen
activities_available: There were a lot of sports activities you could sign up for, but I didn't do that
activities_recommended: I didn't attend the sports activities
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city and everything it has to offer
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy to adjust
cultural_challenges: I didn't find the cultural differences challenging
culture_appreciated: The diversity
top3_advice: 1) Attend the German Vorkurs offered by FU before the semester starts - this is where I met most of the people I hung out with during my exchange. 2) Try and make a schedule where you don't go to the university every day so you also have some days "off" to enjoy and explore the city. 3) Take advantage of the opportunity to choose some courses on subjects that you wouldn't normally be introduced to
most_rewarding: To try and live in another country and to study at another university
greatest_challenge: I didn't really find anything in particular challenging, other that being away from family and friends and being "out of your comfortzone" but that is a part of being on exchange.

crucial_aspects: Money. I had to be sure, that I would not bankrupt myself on an exchange. Here the Erasmus grant was paramount. Likewise, the academics. I study Theatre and Performance, and the only University in Europe that made sense for me, was then Berlin. Especially since they offer Dance Studies, which we don't have in Denmark.
overall_comments: There has been ups and downs. I'm not good with bureaucracy, and trying to figure out all the documents to be filled out before- during-, and after the exchange was mentally super taxing for me, and gave rise to a lot of stress. I realise – and appreciate – the measures that have been taken to make it as comprehensive as possible for the student, but I still don't understand how I managed to do it all. And as I'm writing this, I am not done yet. And then there are personal matters as well: Subletting my apartment turned into chaos, which was also draining. The experiences I've gotten at my exchange destination have been life changing, however, and I've definitely grown!
info_ease: Honestly, everything is such a blur, because a lot of things happened at the same time, but I remember it being all right.
arrival_assistance: There were meet-ups (meet 'n' greet) which were super helpful, campus tours which was also nice, very fruitful. An arranged meeting with my faculty Erasmus Coordinator was worth its weight in gold.
arrival_comments: The only comment is that I wish that we were given written information about the Campus Management anmeldung, because that confused me profoundly, seeing as it is miles apart from how we do things at UCPH. I tried to take notes at the oral 'how-to' presentation, but still felt at a loss when I actually had to do it.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

The experiences I've gotten at my exchange destination have been life changing, however, and I've definitely grown!
registration_process: Well, I guess I didn't make it easy for myself, since I took part in MA courses even though I'm a BA. That means that I couldn't register on Campus Management, since those courses weren't available to me. This resulted in a lot of back and forth e-mailing with several professors. It was worth it though!! Without a doubt. Process: 1. Look at the course catalogue and figure out what courses you want to attend 2. (Only relevant for Erasmus students) Figure out how many ECTS credits the courses give you. This was unnecessarily difficult. 3. Do the ECTS credit math, and try to make it match your interests + requirements from home 4. Apply for those courses on Campus Management if they are there (as said, MA courses are not visible for BA students) 4.1 If they are not there, write the professor 4.2 If you have not gotten your immatrikulationsnummer, write the professor. Actually, during this whole process, the most common answer to my questions was, "write to the professor".
registration_help: I was super lucky to be sitting in the student café, when I did the application. The other students who knew the system were super helpful. The big auditorium presentation was also helpful to some extend. My Erasmus coordinator was also very nice with helping me build a good schedule.
registration_success: I got all of the classes I wished, so I would say quite succesful. Though I wouldn't recommend bending the structure too much, like I did. As an Erasmus student you have the option do to extra work for extra credits. I did this, in order to take some classes that interested me, but would leave me with not enough credits. Dance Studies offered a structure for the ideal MA course of study, and I should have followed that one.
registration_advice: Don't be afraid to talk to the other students!! And be in the student café(s) as much as possible. There's a lot of help to be found there. At least that was my experience.
academics_comments: There has been ups and downs. I'm not good with bureaucracy, and trying to figure out all the documents to be filled out before- during-, and after the exchange was mentally super taxing for me, and gave rise to a lot of stress. I realise – and appreciate – the measures that have been taken to make it as comprehensive as possible for the student, but I still don't understand how I managed to do it all. And as I'm writing this, I am not done yet. And then there are personal matters as well: Subletting my apartment turned into chaos, which was also draining. The experiences I've gotten at my exchange destination have been life changing, however, and I've definitely grown!
course_level: I did three on the BA level and three on the MA level
teaching_comparison: I have come to appreciate UCPH teaching quite a lot. FU's style of teaching (when it comes to classroom teaching and not Übungskurse) is very much discussion based, meaning that you show up, have a discussion, and then leave. I prefer the UCPH model where the teacher interprets the text(s) of the day, naming its most important points, why we have read it etc. and THEN we go into a discussion. I find this to provide a better starting point for meaningful discussions than "just" jumping right in. Though it's difficult to put to words, I find UCPH's teaching more structured which fits me better. However! The practical courses (Übungskurse) that FU offers, were beyond amazing. I really miss more practical work at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: "Writing Dance on Film", "Introduction to Critical Dance Studies", "Rhythm & Movement", ""The personal is political" – Micropolitics in Dance and Performance", "Listening Together" and "Erkunden/Entwerfen/Probieren"
recommended_courses: Practical courses! Without a doubt. Simply because we don't have them at UCPH. But keep the ECTS credits in mind – there's a puzzle that has to come together. And if I may, anything that Professor Lindsey Drury teaches, I would highly recommend. She is a powerhouse of an academic/artist.
unexpected_costs: I didn't realise that you had to rent cleaning supplies at the place where I stayed. I ended up renting through UniRents. And that no pillow/duvet was supplied, which I then had to buy.
cost_comparison: Food is way less expensive in Germany. The price for washing clothes was also higher than expected.
activities_available: These are Erasmus coordinated and might not count then, but we were offered a tour of the Bundestag, a boat tour of Berlin and a Festival of Lights quiz (that one I did and it was awesome)
activities_recommended: Well, as a theatre/dance student I would say explore the cultural scene. Enjoy the richness of the Berlin stage so long it lasts (they are experiencing budget cuts). Try to find some nice bars/cafés to explore different Kiez-vibes. Hochschulsport was great, I met friends there, and it's cheap.
weekend_recommendations: I haven't been good enough at taking advantage of the D-Semesterticket. Take some (day) trips to Potsdam, Görlitz and the like. And go to Flohmarkten!
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. It's not that different from Denmark, and I've been to Berlin before.
socializing_tips: Get involved in student initiatives. I choose to work at the student café, and it was wonderful.
cultural_challenges: None, really.
culture_appreciated: Berliners have a quite laid-back attitude. They're not really in a hurry.
top3_advice: 1. Prepare for way less structure than at UCPH. You have much more influence at FU. 2. Prepare for quite a lot of active participation and obligatory attendance. 3. Just when you feel that now you know the city, it'll be time for you to leave. Time flies. Therefore, - do that thing that you wanted to, talk to that person that you find cool, ask that friend that you do something together. Learn as you go.
other_useful_info: FU can seem unstructured and chaotic at first, but you will get it. Don't be afraid to do what is "expected" or follow a quite straight forward path, - it's not boring. It will (hopefully) provide you with more time and calm.
most_rewarding: Two things: The people I met, and the courses at Critical Dance Studies. I was so incredibly, unfathomably lucky with the people I got to study with, and being allowed to take MA courses and really focus on dance which is my great passion, was fantastic.
greatest_challenge: Seeking revised pre-approvals, getting new Online Learning Agreements etc. Basically the bureaucracy. I even messed up, and am still dealing with it now as I am writing this.
other_comments: No:)

crucial_aspects: Det var vigtigt for mig at vælge en destination, der var tysktalende, da jeg gerne ville forbedre mit tysk, og så ville jeg også gerne til en europæisk by, hvor der var masser af kulturelle muligheder - og det må man sige, at der er i Berlin.
info_ease: Freie Universität var gode til at sende løbende informationer via mail, og også hurtige til at svare, hvis man havde opfølgende spørgsmål. Nogle ting spurgte jeg dog andre, der også har været i Tyskland, om hjælp til - fx sundhedsforsikring mm., da Tyskland er et meget bureaukratisk og forvirrende land.
arrival_assistance: På Freie var der en introuge, hvor man den første dag var til en semi-overvældende dag med stande og boder fra diverse studenterforeninger, man kunne møde. De følgende dage var mere organiserede - her blev man inviteret til en rundtur på campus med andre Erasmus-studerende fra ens eget studie, som var guidet af en lokal studerende. Der var desuden aktiviteter uden for campus, som man kunne melde sig til - en bådrundfart, en tur i Bundesrat, en fest på Matrix og en brætspilsaften. Man fik også et oplæg af ens Erasmus-koordinator til valg og tilmelding af fag, hjælp til OLA og proof of attendance - Freie var meget hjælpsomme og venlige!
arrival_comments: Der er masser af hjælp at hente, hvis man rækker ud til Freie - de svarer hurtigt og er informative!
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Ved fag, der hørte under ens eget fakultet tilmeldte man sig gennem noget der hed Course Management (tænk ku-net). Ved fag, der ikke hørte under ens eget fakultet måtte man enten skrive en mail til den givne underviser, eller blot møde op til deres fag (begge disse informationer kunne som oftest findes i Course Catalogue. Sprogundervisning tilmeldte man sig et helt separat sted - husker det som, at det var via email. Generelt er det en god strategi at tilmelde sig flere fag, end man har brug for, og derefter framelde sig igen. Det er mere loose end på KU - man kan vist nok også godt nå at blive en del af et fag, efter det er startet, hvis man spørger underviseren pænt (for de fleste senest efter 2-3 undervisningsgange)
registration_help: Tyskland, eller i hvertfald Freie, er lidt særlig på den måde, at ECTS-point ikke er skåret i sten for undervisere, og at man (efter min oplevelse) ofte selv kunne ønske, hvilken eksamensform man gerne ville have og hvornår - så lad dig ikke skræmme, hvis noget ikke lever akkurat op til kravene på dit hjemmeuni, for hvis du spørger underviseren pænt fysisk eller via mail, er mange villige til at strække sig.
registration_success: Efter en brav kamp fik jeg de fag, som jeg gerne ville have - men det krævede også, at jeg netop sendte mange emails til diverse undervisere, og mødte op til en masse forskellige fag.
registration_advice: Send emails til undervisere, hvis du gerne vil have deres fag! Og husk også, at man på Freie ikke er bundet af sine fag, bare fordi man er tilmeldt - og at man derfor også kan nå at tilmelde sig andre fag, hvis man er der inden for de første 2-3 undervisningsgange.
course_level: Meget varieret niveau fra fag til fag - A&O var som nævnt meget teorifattigt, men meget udenadslære (man skulle kunne styrken på korrelationer fra diverse empiriske studier udenad). Niveauet på holdundervisning var ikke højt. Mit marxisme-fag på Latinamerikastudier var højt niveau på den fede måde - vi læste meget udfordrende tekster, og havde svære og interessante diskussioner om dem til holdundervisning. Diversity Management var slet ikke højt niveau - og føltes heller ikke særlig bogligt - vi skulle mest reflektere over egne privilegier i en rundkreds, tale om intersektionalitet og hvordan man kan øge og understøtte diversitet. Så et vigtigt fag, men bestemt ikke udfordrende. Tyskundervisning var lige på det niveau, som jeg selv er på - vi tog nemlig en placeringstest inden holdstart.
teaching_comparison: Det er ret så anderledes. Jeg er vant til fra KU, at man læser teoretiske tekster inden en undervisningsgang, og diskutere denne på holdet i undervisningen. Det var slet ikke formatet her - man mødte bare op, og blev stillet nogle spørgsmål om, hvordan man tror tingene hænger sammen ud fra egen viden og levede liv, og derefter kobler underviseren empiriske fund på. Det var personligt ikke et format, som jeg brød mig om. Mit fag på Latinamerikastudier var en anden sag. Der var det netop med udgangspunkt i teorien, at vi havde faglige diskussioner, hvilket endte i de fedeste debatter og perspektiveringerne til nutiden - mange af vores diskussioner der har klædt mig godt på til mit videre arbejde med kritiske teorier, herunder min bachelorskrivning.
courses_enrolled: A fundamental critique of society: Marxian thought, the Frankfurt School, and its Latin American Reception (Latinamerikastudier), Diversity Management, Arbeits-, Organisations und Wirtschaftspsychologie og Deutsch als Fremdsprache
recommended_courses: “A fundamental critique of society: Marxian thought, the Frankfurt School, and its Latin American Reception”!!! Eller et andet fag med Myriam Sauer, hvis man er glad for marxistisk teori, psykoanalyse og queer-teori. Og så var jeg selv meget glad for også at have sideløbende tyskundervisning - det gav mig mange nye sprogkundskaber, og også et safe space at øve sig intensivt i.
unexpected_costs: Jeg skulle betale et semestergebyr på 2300 kroner - var ikke lige noget jeg havde regnet med, men det betalte til gengæld al offentlig transport i løbet af semestret, hvilket var top dollar.
cost_comparison: Genbrugstøj er dyrere i Berlin, øvøv. Til gengæld er mad, kaffe og alkohol markant billigere, så det nød jeg godt af.
activities_available: Som nævnt var der sociale aktiviteter for Erasmusstuderende og lokale studerende (semesterfester, klubber, cafeer etc). Også mange gode hæng-ud-steder - kan anbefale Pi-café og Galilea ved Mensa II. Og så Uni-sport, som jeg skrev lige før.
activities_recommended: Jeg kan jo kun tale ud fra personlige præferencer, men jeg nød at spise på en masse vietnamesiske restauranter i byen, klatre ved RAW-gelände, tage i teatret, drikke kaffe, tage på diverse markeder, besøge museer, går dagsture i Grunewald og ellers bare få kortlagt alle Kieze i byen ;-)
weekend_recommendations: Husk, at nærmest alt findes i Berlin!! Så hvis du har en eller anden niche hobby, så kan du helt sikkert finde et fællesskab/sted for det i byen.
culture_adjustment: Tyskerne er jo ikke så langt fra danskerne, så ingen store kulturelle forskelligheder udover sproget - jeg følte mig ret så hjemme! Den største kulturelle overraskelse var, hvor enormt stille der er i S-Bahnen, og at nogle (særligt af de ældre generationer) er meget stirrende.
socializing_tips: Vær ikke genert ved at få talt en masse gebrokken tysk! Jeg fik primært talt med lokale til undervisning, og der havde jeg det som mål aldrig at skifte over på engelsk, om end at jeg nogle gange virkelig havde lyst. Og vær ikke bange for at spørge, hvis der er noget du ikke forstår.
cultural_challenges: Tysk bureaukrati! Man skal blandt andet lave en såkaldt "Anmeldung" ved ankomst, dvs. bestille tid ved det lokale Bürgeramt, hvor de kan melde ens ankomst i byen. Man skal også lave en "Abmeldung" via post, og det må jeg jo ærligt indrømme, at jeg aldrig har fået gjort. Inden ankomst i Berlin skal man også skrive til en tysk sundhedsforsikring, som skal godkende ens blå sygesikring, og så sende til Freie. Lettere besværligt, men værre er det heller ikke. Jeg betalte i øvrigt heller ikke Rundfunksbeitrag i den tid jeg var der, til trods for at jeg fik et brev omkring det. Jeg var så heldig ikke at være til lægen undervejs i mit ophold, men det har jeg også hørt skulle være rimelig besværligt.
culture_appreciated: Berlins mange mangfoldige muligheder og særheder! Jeg nød, at der var så mange ting at tage sig til, og synes der er en meget inklusiv kultur i byen, fordi den nok tiltrækker lidt mere alternative mennesker.
top3_advice: 1. Ræk ud til Freie og dets hvis noget volder dig besvær ift. dit studie! Selv hvis det er noget, du ikke er vant til kan løses (fx eksamensdato, mængde ects-point etc.) - for min oplevelse var, at de var meget fleksible og villige til at strække sig for en. 2. Vær hurtigt klar ved tasterne, hvis du gerne vil have en kollegieplads via Freie - og undersøg de forskellige muligheder på forhånd. 3. Spis en masse billig döner og nyd byens mange muligheder!
other_useful_info: Der var mødepligt i en del af mine fag - det var noget, jeg ikke var indstillet på inden dag. Jeg kan klart anbefale at tage afsted med flest mulige valgfag, da man så har frihed til dels at vælge hvad man vil have rent fagligt, og dels finde fag med krav, som man kan og vil leve op til.
most_rewarding: Menneskerne, jeg mødte, at få byen og dets mange områder og historier ind under huden, at blive bedre til tysk og så også mit marxisme-fag.
greatest_challenge: At tale tysk! Hvis jeg kunne gøre noget anderledes, ville jeg klart have været bedre til at få talt en hel masse fra starten af mit ophold uden frygt for at lave fejl. Og så synes jeg at det var lidt heftigt at have 30 ects-point når man er udvekslingsstuderende. Til flere af mine fag skulle man mindst møde op til 80% af undervisningen. Det var krævende for mig personligt, da jeg har en kronisk lidelse - men som nævnt er underviserne meget kompromisvillige, hvis blot man spørger.
other_comments: Berlin er formentlig ikke den 'nemmeste' destination pga. det forskudte semester, bureaukratiet og sproget - men jeg synes bestemt ikke man skal lade sig skræmme, hvis Berlin er den destination, man helst vil til. Det hele skal nok løse sig i sidste ende, og Berlin er jo en vildt fed by! :-)

crucial_aspects: I've always wanted to do an exchange, particularly in Asia, I applied to South Korea in my bachelors but this feel through due to Covid. I was ecstatic to be admitted into a university such as Fudan, a top school in a profoundly exciting country. The ability to be in one of the most populated cities learning things that are not necessarily provided within the Asian context. Academically felt very rewarding. Socially, it was nice to be able to be in a social bubble in the Fudan university campus. Being in fudan, living on the campus was just about english friendly and international enough, which was a big costernation before coming here.
info_ease: It wasn't particularly straightforward due to language barriers, both interpersonal and through accessing the websites. Things were often hard to understand in english and this could be work on more. Luckily I made friends who were familiar/could speak chinese
arrival_assistance: Had help getting to the dorm from the airport. The orientation day was useful for getting the intitial, important information.
arrival_comments: English was not a strong suit so I can't give an extremely high mark
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: After being nominated by KU, it was about 2 months of back and forth with Fudan, accomodated by forms and submiission of further files and pdfs. Still quite straightforward, the only hard part was getting everything confirmed in a timely manner. It wasn't until about 2 months before embarking on the exchange that I was certain that I could leave for China with everything set in place. This could affect price ticket's and one's planning of life, etc..
registration_help: Email contact.
registration_success: Extremely, not many options, but I wasn't rejected from any classes.
registration_advice: As mentioned above but make sure you do your research so that you know what to expect regarding language barriers, technical difficulties, try to learn some chinese for formalities at least. It is quite a different culture with different so be prepared for that. Complemented by the language barrier, It is a better destination for studying dilligently than partying I feel, which is perhaps not everyone's cup of tea for exchanges.
course_level: Master courses specifcially from the International relations sphere, different from my Msc in Social Data Science.
teaching_comparison: I preffered it to be honest, mostly small scale, lecture based, relaxed and extremely informative. Reading amount/workload was similar but teachers were more accomodating.

cultural_challenges: Introversion level,
culture_appreciated: Very smart people, extremely impressive city and culture

crucial_aspects: For at kunne opleve Kina, som jeg studerer.
info_ease: Det var ret svært at indsamle information fra forskellige steder. Man får en masse information, men ikke den vigtige information, hvordan man får internet på kollegiet eller hvordan man finder nok kurser (de er ikke alle oplyst i skemaet over engelske kurser, så man kan søge lidt rundt i kursusportalen for at finde flere)
arrival_assistance: Vi fik et kort over campus med alle kantiner og nogle få af de mange kaffebarer, supermarkeder og læsesteder, og så fik vi en lang folderguide til affaldssortering, opladning af elscootere osv. Derudover fik vi forskellig information afhængig af hvilket fakultet man var tilknyttet. Jeg var tilknyttet International Politics afdelingen, og de var gode til at give information og at være tilgængelige, når jeg havde spørgsmål.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Der er flere runder af kursusregistrering, og den sidste runde (som er den eneste, de fleste udvekslingsstuderende kan bruge) åbner første undervisningsdag, så det kan være svært at planlægge forud. De fleste kurser vil være fyldte allerede, men mange vælger at droppe kurser i den første uge, så man skal holde sig til på kursusportalen. Hvis der stadig ikke er plads, kan man spørge underviseren om en ekstra plads ved at udfylde en formular.
registration_help: Man får en guide til kursusportalen, men ellers er man lidt på egen hånd, men det er heller ikke fordi man behøver yderligere hjælp.
registration_success: Først fik jeg kun halvdelen af de point, jeg skulle bruge, men da jeg fandt ekstra kurser ved at søge i portalen, fik jeg dækket dem alle. Jeg måtte kontakte en underviser for at en plads på hendes kursus, og det gik også helt fint. Det er en lidt kaotisk process, men jeg tror næsten alle fik deres kurser i sidste ende.
registration_advice: Søg i kursusportalen efter keywords eller kurser fra tidligere lister, som ikke er på den for dit semester. Tag for mange kurser i starten og prøv dem af de første to uger, så du ved hvilke du vil beholde.
course_level: Kurserne er tidskrævende, og arbejdsbyrden er op til den enkelte underviser, så det kan variere, hvor meget der forventes til hver uge og til eksamen. Generelt var mine kurser meget overkommelige niveau-mæssigt (jeg tog primært kurser i engelsk litteratur og akademisk skrivning), men jeg brugte meget tid på afleveringer, fremlæggelser og eksaminer.
teaching_comparison: På KU er der en ret ensartet undervisningsform, og man kan søge information i studieordningen eller hos studievejledning, men på Fudan er der ikke en overordnet struktur, så hvert kursus er forskelligt i undervisningsmetode, struktur og arbejdsbyrde. De fleste af mine undervisere på Fudan var enormt søde, og gode til at engagere hver studerende, men min oplevelse er også, at de engelsksprogede kurser havde mindre hold end de kinesiske, så man havde rig mulighed for at deltage aktivt.
courses_enrolled: FORE110076.01 Selected Readings in English Short Stories FORE130362.01 Thesis Writing FORE110099.01 British and American Suspense Short Stories FORE130454.01 Style and Writing I/Multi-genre Writing (Part 1) FORE130192.01 Topics in British and American Literature PHIL110045.01 Artistic Charms of Chinese Traditional Culture
recommended_courses: Jeg vil varmt anbefale kurser i akademisk skrivning (jeg har taget Style and Writing og Thesis Writing), da de forbereder en på at skulle skrive bachelor, og underviseren hjælper en med at udarbejde sit emne.
unexpected_costs: Man betaler selv for elektricitet (og vand i de gamle bygninger) på kollegiet. Det gik ud til ca. 100 kr om måneden i alt.
cost_comparison: Mad var dyrere, end jeg havde forventet, fordi man ikke selv kan lave mad og er nødt til at spise ude hver dag. Det er billigt at spise ude i Kina, men ikke ligeså billigt som hvis man budgetterer og laver mad selv i Danmark
activities_available: Stort set alle typer sport, en del kreative klubber som fotografi, band og billedkunst, nogle teklubber, områdespecifikke klubber, klubber for traditionel kultur, militær entusiaster, skatere osv. Ret stort udvalg
activities_recommended: Teklubberne var meget populære, faktisk så populære at jeg ikke fik en plads, men de skulle have været spændende
weekend_recommendations: Forsøg at rejse så meget som muligt, og om muligt læg dit skema, så du har fri flere dage i træk og kan tage på nogle længere ture. Der er gode instagramprofiler for spændende ting, der sker i Shanghai, så hold øje med dem.
culture_adjustment: Jeg studerer selv Kinastudier, så for mig var kulturchokket ikke så stort, men jeg var overrasket over at stort set ingen taler et ord engelsk, selv i den internationale by Shanghai, men man kan komme langt med Google Translate.
socializing_tips: Meld dig ind i en fritidsklub med kinesiske studerende, det havde mange stor succes med.
cultural_challenges: Man skal forberede sig på at have sin mobil ved håndenen altid. Vi skulle bruge den til alt: at betale, tage toget, komme ind og ud af campus, ind på værelset på kollegiet. Man skal have sin powerbank med altid, og sørge for at downloade en god VPN hjemmefra (EduVPN er gratis for KU (og mange andre) studerende, og virker fint)

crucial_aspects: To get far away - both geographically and culturally. I wanted to challenge myself and really broaden my horizons. I also found China particularly interesting considering the current international political landscape
info_ease: Upon arrival it was relatively easy. All university related stuff was easy enough since it was in english, but anything outside of uni was a bit more challenging due to language barriers. A lot of locals were super helpful though, so it didn't take long to figure out - you really just have to ask for help!
arrival_assistance: Some volunteers at the university helped me get my sim card upon arrival (there's a shop on campus), and all things related to university and classes were handled as well.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I don't remember it that well - it takes some time but is duable. Just remember to have all the documents ready in time, including a recommendation from a professor, TOEFL test etc. On campus registration was similar - not the most efficient and spread out on different locations and steps, but people were helpful and it was a good way to get to know campus :')
registration_help: Not much, you had to figure it out on your own. Fudan is terrible at answering emails, but if you show up at the international students office it usually helps a bit - and they're very friendly and helpful when you show up in person.
registration_success: Very succesful, I got everything I wanted
registration_advice: Be patient and don't be afraid to ask for help - and trust that it will all work out
course_level: I took LL.M courses, which meant that all classes were for exchange students only. It was nice, since it was catered to an exchange students needs in terms of flexibility and academic demands, but it would also have been cool to have classes with local students.
teaching_comparison: Similar - seminars where the teacher presented, occasional group work and presentations.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Chinese Law China's Practice on international law Chinese Securities Law Chinese Commercial Arbitration Chinese Legal Culture Chinese Language
recommended_courses: China's Practice on international law was very interesting for political reasons - and I actually learned a great deal. The teacher was great and the topics were very interesting - especially from a western perspective. Chinese Commercial Arbitration was also a highlight - it was very internationally oriented, so if you want to learn about international arbitration, it's a good option. I learned a lot and it was my most academically challenging class - in a very good way!
unexpected_costs: Not many to be fair - my computer screen broke, but i was able to fix it for 900 kr. by getting a chinese speaking friend to help me. It is also worth noting that you pay your rent for the whole semester up front if you choose on housing campus, which was a bit of a surprise for me
cost_comparison: Food can be both very cheap and expensive - the cafeteria and small whole-in-the-wall restaurants are very cheap, but you can also get expensive meals. It's easy to end up spending a lot of money because many things are cheap and you want to have a good time
activities_available: Anything you can imagine. Martial arts, different kinds of normal art, dance, fishing, diving, soccer, sailing, music - literally everything. There's a huge fair at the beginning of the semester where you can get introduced to all the different clubs.
activities_recommended: The running club! I also heard great things about traditional painting and pottery.
weekend_recommendations: First of all, experience Shanghai! It's a huge city with so much to offer. Go to all the rooftops, visit the bund, the french concession, the marriage market in People's Park, Yu Garden, Jing an - i could go on forever! The food is amazing too - you have to experience hot pot at haidilao as well as xiao long bao, which originates from Shanghai. In terms of trips, I went to Beijing, Hangzhou Qiandao, Jiangxi/Fujian provinces round trip, Sichuan province round trip and Yunnan province round trip - and would recommend all of them. China has so much amazing nature as well as interesting cities and places to visit, and I cannot recommend enough to take advantage and explore while you're there. Shanghai is very different from the rest of China and it was incredible to experience the huge diversity in culture and landscapes throughout the country. Also, domestic flights and high speed trains are cheap and accessible so might as well!
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy, as there are many internationals on campus. However, China is very different in every single way, and it's very much a "learn as you go" experience. You get used to slurping your noodles, the loudness of everything, squat toilets everywhere, and before you know it it does not even bother you. I would really just recommend to go with the flow and not be too intimidated by the cultural differences and just go with the flow. It's interesting to experience, and makes for a lot of fun conversations - and soon enough, you're blending in with the locals. If you ever need a taste of home, Shanghai is also amazing, as it is very western compared to the rest of China. There's plenty of options for western food and vibes.
socializing_tips: Just be open. They're usually very curious and want to talk to you (and will probably approach you).
cultural_challenges: The spitting and loud phones
culture_appreciated: The food and culture of social style dining! Also, Chinese people are extremely helpful and contrary to the stereotype, not rude at all. Most of the things that gives them the perception of "rude" are cultural differences you learn to appreciate, and they're very eager to talk and help at all times.
top3_advice: Enjoy it so much - and again, trust that it all works out. You're in for an experience of a lifetime, so be open, curious and patient with yourself and everything around you.
other_useful_info: Bring extra credit cards!
most_rewarding: How much confidence I gained. Moving to China on my own, making so many friends and building a wonderful life in Shanghai really boosted my confidence and has made me resilient to any challenge that may arise
greatest_challenge: I don't remember having any great challenges - but some great advice would be to reach out to those around you and to make sure to build a good support network
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: I decided to go to China because of a personal connection to the country, as well as the unique academic opportunity to study at one of China’s top universities.
info_ease: The first days, spent navigating and organizing all the practical practicalities, were the most challenging. During this time, I relied heavily on my Mandarin-speaking friends.
arrival_assistance: During dorm registration, there were initially no English-speaking staff available, although I later realized this was likely a matter of bad timing, as I did meet English-speaking staff members on other occasions. However, very little information was provided regarding when, where, and how to complete the registration process. Much of this information I received through other exchange students, who shared their own experiences and guidance. My contact person at Fudan University also repeatedly provided incorrect information. For example, we were given the wrong dates for dormitory sign-up, directed to the wrong building on orientation day, and were not informed in advance about the requirement to purchase insurance. Despite these challenges, everything worked out in the end. Since all of the exchange law students shared the same contact person, we were equally confused, which fortunately allowed us to support one another and find comfort in the shared experience. However, I do not blame Fudan University as an institution. Some of my friends, who were also exchange students in other programs, had excellent orientation experiences. Their contact persons were highly supportive, organizing trips, social activities, and providing clear guidance throughout the process. This showed me that the overall experience largely depended on the specific faculty and coordinator rather than the university itself.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: At first, my contact person responded quite quickly, but the main issue was that she went on vacation right before the most important period—during registration, dorm applications, and the general arrival process. Many of my friends, who were also exchange law students, experienced similar problems with her communication. She provided incorrect information to several of us, which created unnecessary confusion and stress during an already challenging transition period.
registration_help: Although my contact person was not particularly helpful, I was introduced during the first or second week to local students who showed us around and helped us settle in. One of them in particular was an enormous help, and I found myself reaching out to him far more often than to my official contact person. In general, the Chinese local students were incredibly kind, welcoming, and always willing to help, which made the transition much easier and contributed greatly to a positive exchange experience
registration_success: You are generally guaranteed a place in all the classes you sign up for, which is a major advantage and makes course selection much less stressful. However, it is important to be aware that the curriculum provided during the registration process can change significantly once the semester begins. In my experience, professors have far more discretion over the course structure and assessment methods than what I am used to in Denmark. For instance, one course was initially described as having an essay-based exam, but it ultimately became a written sit-in exam instead. In other courses, additional tests and assignments were introduced that had not been mentioned in the original curriculum. When I asked my contact person about these changes, she explained that professors are free to decide such matters themselves, and that the curriculum sent out beforehand should only be considered tentative.
registration_advice: Try not to stress too much—everything usually works out in the end. One piece of advice I would definitely give is to make friends with people who speak Mandarin, especially if you do not speak the language yourself. It has been incredibly helpful for me on many occasions, both in practical situations and in making everyday life much easier.
course_level: I spent less time preparing for classes than I normally would at home. Most of my courses were coursework-based, meaning that the final assessment primarily consisted of an essay. Presentations or midterm exams were often included as well, usually accounting for around 10–30% of the final grade, while attendance and class participation made up a smaller percentage. However, the essay remained the main component in most courses. The essays were challenging because very little guidance was provided regarding expectations, structure, or grading criteria. It often felt like writing several mini bachelor’s assignments, and it was difficult to assess what academic level was required in order to achieve a good grade. However, after receiving my grades, I found that the assessments were more generous than I had expected. Despite the common perception that academic grading in China is particularly strict, my experience was that the professors were fair and, in many cases, quite lenient.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style varied greatly depending on the course. In some classes, professors would frequently cold-call students, while in others we had fixed seating arrangements so attendance could be monitored more closely. This was important because in certain courses, missing more than a specific number of classes would automatically result in a failing grade. There was little to none groupwork. At the same time, it was also my impression that many professors genuinely cared about their students. If you attended classes regularly and participated actively, they were often very kind, supportive, and understanding. For instance, I became quite sick during the exam period. Most of my professors were extremely understanding and provided me with extensions.
courses_enrolled: Chinese Environment and Resources Law = The professor cold calls, but really sweet if you participate. Chinese Legal Culture = The professor seemed to enjoy lecturing at length without much focus on student engagement or practical discussion. I would not particularly recommend this course, as it did not feel especially relevant as a law course and lacked the academic depth I had expected. Chinese Pratice on International Law = The professor was at times difficult to understand, but the overall atmosphere of the class was very relaxed. The professor was extremely easygoing and seemed to prioritize making students feel comfortable rather than creating unnecessary pressure. As a result, it felt like almost everyone received an A in the course. Chinese Civil Law = I absolutely loved this professor - highly intelligent, engaging, and clearly passionate about the subject. The class was very interesting. I strongly recommend this course. Chinese Commercial Arbitration = Very interesting if you like arbitration. Introduction to Chinese Law = I had two professors for this course—one was very stoic and reserved, while the other was much more engaging and dynamic in class. I was told that the latter also often participates in a Chinese television show, as a debater (I think(?)), which added an interesting dimension to his teaching style. I would recommend this course, as it was spread over two days, had a very relaxed structure. Chinese language I = I did not receive credits for this course, as it is not a law course. The course was taught by my absolute favorite professor during the exchange. She was incredibly engaging, kind, and genuinely enjoyable to learn from. Her teaching style made the class both fun and memorable. I strongly recommend this course!
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the courses above, with the exception of Chinese Legal Culture
unexpected_costs: Honestly, there were no major unexpected fees. However, it is important to remember that the university requires students to purchase mandatory insurance. If I remember correctly, the cost was around 800 RMB, so it is worth keeping that in mind when budgeting for the semester.
cost_comparison: One of the biggest financial advantages was how inexpensive everyday life was, especially on campus. The canteen food was incredibly cheap, even compared to the generally low food prices in China. Online shopping was also very inexpensive, and costs for travelling, hotels, and high-speed trains were surprisingly low as well. This made it much easier to enjoy both daily student life and weekend trips without constantly worrying about expenses.
activities_available: There were many activities, clubs, and student societies available on campus—almost every type of club imaginable seemed to exist at the university. This made it easy for students to get involved beyond academics and meet people with shared interests. One memorable event was a cooking competition where chefs from university canteens across the country came to showcase their skills. The university also organized various trips, tours, and social activities for exchange students, although the extent of this depended greatly on the specific faculty and program. Some faculties were much more active in creating these opportunities than others.
activities_recommended: Join a club!
weekend_recommendations: One of the most important parts of studying abroad in China is to travel as much as possible. One of my professors said during the first or second week that, in order to truly understand China and Chinese law, you need to experience the culture firsthand rather than only read about it in books. I found this to be absolutely true. For nature and landscapes, I would highly recommend Zhangjiajie, Yangshuo and Jiuzhaigou. These places offer some of the most breathtaking scenery. For city experiences, I would especially recommend Chongqing, Shenzhen, and of course Shanghai. Each city has a completely different atmosphere and gives a unique perspective on modern China. For cultural and historical experiences, Nanjing, Xian and Beijing are must-visits, offering important historical sites and a deeper understanding of China’s past and present. Other fascinating destinations include Harbin, especially during winter when it hosts the world-famous Harbin International Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival, featuring enormous illuminated ice sculptures and castles. Sanya and Yunnan are also very popular during the winter months, especially for those who prefer warmer weather and want to escape the cold.
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Be curious, ask questions, invite them to stuff with your (exchange) friends
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: Hard to say, because the real answer is everything: the people, the food, the nature, the culture, etc.
top3_advice: 1. Be open-minded. Do not go on exchange if you are not willing to challenge your own perspective and embrace something different from what you are used to. China can feel very different from Denmark in many ways, and the experience becomes much more rewarding if you approach it with curiosity rather than comparison. 2. Talk to the locals. Chinese students and local people are incredibly kind, genuine, and helpful if you make the effort to start a conversation. Even with language barriers, people are often very welcoming, and some of my best experiences came from connecting with local students rather than only staying within the international student circle. 3. Travel as much as possible within China. China is incredibly underrated and has everything—modern megacities, rich history, breathtaking nature, mountains, beaches, and unique regional cultures. Exploring the country gave me a much deeper understanding of both Chinese society and daily life, and it became one of the most valuable parts of my exchange experience.
other_useful_info: Refer to some of my earlier answers
most_rewarding: The friendships I made and the stronger sense of connection I developed with China were some of the most valuable outcomes of my exchange. Living there allowed me to gain a much deeper and more nuanced understanding of a country that is often heavily scrutinized and simplified in Western media. Experiencing daily life firsthand gave me perspectives that could never have been gained through news articles or academic reading alone, and it helped me appreciate the complexity of Chinese society, culture, and people far beyond common stereotypes.
greatest_challenge: One of the biggest challenges I faced was the language barrier when I became sick and needed to go to the hospital. Communicating medical concerns in a foreign language was stressful, especially in an unfamiliar healthcare system. Fortunately, I had Mandarin-speaking friends who came with me and helped translate, which made the situation much easier and far less overwhelming.

info_ease: Everything was well informed in the E-mail and people were on site to help you. It was really easy to follow the signs and guidance from staff.
arrival_assistance: Student helpers greeted you and helped you with filling out the lease and find your room.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was through their student portal Oasis and it was very to select and change courses.
registration_help: The International Relations Office could provide guidance or do it for you.
registration_success: Very successful. After the start I found out that I wanted some other courses and I got these as well.
registration_advice: It is super easy but be aware that you must make sure that the schedule matches afterwards and there may be some courses you can't take because they are at the same time and they only make 1 class so you can't find the same course at another time.
course_level: It was a lot of work. You have to hand in assignments during the semester in all courses with will constitute half (or less) of your grade. Therefore it is also busy during the semester and not just in the end when you have exams. You also need to attend all classes to understand and pass since there are no books in most of the courses.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style is very different. It is only professors who teach and not practitioners. Furthermore it is much more reflective content than at home. It is also not case based like back home but more general.
courses_enrolled: EU Criminal Policy, EU Competition Law, EU Banking and Capital Market Law, EU Law and ICT, European and International Biodiversity Law, Cybercrime, Technology and Surveillance.
recommended_courses: European Law and ICT, Air and Space Law, EU Economic Law
unexpected_costs: Since you are not allowed to bring laptops to the exam you have to print out all your notes which costs money.
cost_comparison: Croceries
activities_available: Every kind of sport. ESN arranged some games but you could also pay a fee to join all sorts of sports.
activities_recommended: Volley because it's an extremely popular sport there and when the weather is nice a lot of people meet to play beach volley and there you can also meet locals.
weekend_recommendations: Go to other cities close to Gent like Brugges, Leuven, Antwerpen and Brussels. It's also super cheap with either train or flixbus to go to adjacent countries like Luxembourg, France and The Netherlands.
culture_adjustment: It was very similar but way more relaxed.
socializing_tips: Use the buddy you are assigned to and sign up for sports.
cultural_challenges: Some say that Belgiums are even more reserved which seem true but it is possible to find nice Belgium friends as well.
culture_appreciated: The nightlife
top3_advice: 1. Try and get a room at the University's campus. It seemed as if the people who stayed there had a better time because they naturally met more people. 2. Go visit other cities and countries it's such a nice opportunity. 3. Be prepared for the fact that you have to hand in assignments during the semester and do them in good time so that everything doesn't clash at the same time.
other_useful_info: It came as a shock to me that exams are written in hand and that you are not allowed to bring your laptop.
most_rewarding: The friendships I made.
greatest_challenge: Having 6 exams in 20 days but it is duable

activities_recommended: Bare sig ja til alt, find energien til det i starten og så bliver det den bedste vane nogensinde.
weekend_recommendations: Tag ind til byen, spis og drik det landet byder på, rejs en lille smule rundt, men egentlig synes jeg ikke der er så mange andre byer, der er værd at besøge i Belgien - brug hellere tid på at lære Gent at kende. Synes selvfølgelig man skal besøge Bruxelles og Brugges, men lad os bare sige to gange i hver by kan gøre det. Til gengæld ligger det perfekt til at tage på ture med de andre erasmusstuderende til f.eks. Paris eller Amsterdam!
culture_adjustment: Ret nemt, udover manglende offentlige transportmuligheder om aftenen, og så er det er vildt underligt at størstedelen af alle belgier enten bor hjemme eller tager hjem hver weekend. Det betyder bare, at du skal bare ikke regne med at tage en øl med dem i weekenden - der har du heldigvis din egen Erasmus-familie at være sammen med.
socializing_tips: Man skal som altid bare være imødekommende og åben. Og så er det okay at investere tid i din "lille" erasmusfamilie (i mit tilfælde ca. 15 personer), altså dem, der har valgt samme studie som dig, så kan man altid møde alle de andre studieretninger senere i forløbet og på kryds og tværs af ens erasmusvenner. Det bare for at sige, at selvom man gerne vil møde alle flinke mennesker, der findes, så kan det betale sig at investere i måske færre relationer, fordi disse faktisk kan blive til ægte venner, man forhåbentlig kan have hele livet.
cultural_challenges: Belgier er måske ikke så "handlekraftige", på trods af at de (åbenbart) er meget utilfredse med visse ting. Det kan bare være svært at forstå.
culture_appreciated: De går super meget ud og bruger byen med dens barer og cafeer, hvilket giver det hyggeligste liv i centrum!
top3_advice: Vær åben. Husk du har stor indflydelse på, hvor meget du skal have ud af forløbet både ift. fagligt, socialt eller personligt udbytte (og det ene kan være mindst lige så vigtigt som det andet for den enkelte person). Søg legater.
other_useful_info: Det er normalt at finde bolig (alt for) tæt på arrival time. Enormt stressende, men det skal nok gå!
most_rewarding: Jeg har oplevet at starte på et hospital, hvor jeg intet forstår af sproget og arbejdsgangen, men bare må få tingene til at lykkedes - det har både været sjovt og lærerigt. Derudover er den Erasmus-familie jeg fik det fineste, jeg kunne forestille mig. Det er fantastisk at møde en gruppe mennesker, hvor stort set alle er der med samme formål og bare vildt gerne vil være venner med hinanden. Fantastiske mennesker jeg har mødt, herunder også en masse søde, sjove belgier!
greatest_challenge: At bo uden for byen. Min udlejer var enormt sød, men lokationen var virkelig ikke fed.

registration_process: The registration process at our host institution is straightforward and user-friendly. It begins with an online application where you provide your personal and academic information. Once your application is reviewed and accepted, you will receive an email with further instructions. This includes setting up your student portal, where you can register for courses, pay fees, and access important resources. Support staff are always available to assist you throughout the process, ensuring a smooth and stress-free experience.
registration_help: At our host institution, a variety of help is available to support students. Academic advisors are on hand to assist with course selection and academic planning. There are also tutoring services for additional academic support. For personal and emotional well-being, counseling services are readily accessible. The IT helpdesk provides technical assistance for any issues related to online platforms or devices. Additionally, there are numerous workshops and seminars aimed at skill development and career planning. The institution ensures comprehensive support to help you succeed.
registration_success: I was quite successful in registering for the classes I wanted. The registration system is efficient, and I found it easy to navigate. Most of the classes I aimed for had available spots, and the few that were full had clear waitlist options. The academic advisors were very helpful in suggesting alternative courses that fit well with my schedule and academic goals. Overall, I was able to secure a schedule that I’m very happy with.
registration_advice: For future exchange students, my advice would be to start the registration process early. This ensures you have the best chance of getting into your preferred classes. Utilize the resources available, such as academic advisors, who can guide you in selecting the right courses. Be flexible and have a few backup options in mind, as some classes may fill up quickly. Finally, familiarize yourself with the online registration system ahead of time to make the process smoother. Being proactive and prepared will make your registration experience much more successful and stress-free.
course_level: The level of courses at our host institution varies widely, accommodating different academic needs and backgrounds. There are introductory courses that provide a solid foundation for beginners, often with a focus on fundamental concepts and skills. Intermediate courses build on this foundation, offering more in-depth exploration of subjects and requiring some prior knowledge. Advanced courses are available for those who have a strong background in the subject, offering specialized and comprehensive study, often with a focus on critical thinking, research, and practical application. Regardless of the level, the courses are designed to be engaging, challenging, and supportive, ensuring that all students can achieve their academic goals.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at my host institution has some distinct differences compared to the University of Copenhagen (UCPH). At the host institution, there is a strong emphasis on interactive and participatory learning. Classes often involve discussions, group work, and hands-on activities, which help to engage students actively in the learning process. In contrast, UCPH tends to have a more lecture-based approach, though it also incorporates interactive elements. The host institution also offers a variety of online resources and platforms to complement in-person teaching, providing a more blended learning experience. Overall, both institutions strive to deliver high-quality education, but the host institution leans more towards an interactive, student-centered teaching style.

Personal Care Items: Toiletries and other personal care products were more expensive than I was used to. Less Expensive: Clothing: I found that clothing, especially during sales, was more affordable than I expected. Entertainment: Local events, student discounts for cultural attractions, and cinema tickets were reasonably priced. Utilities: If you live off-campus, utility costs were quite manageable compared to other living expenses. activities_recommended: There was a rich variety of cultural events, diverse athletic opportunities, and vibrant social activities available for students at my host institution. weekend_recommendations: I recommend visiting students explore the historic city center of Ghent, including Gravensteen Castle and St. Bavo's Cathedral. crucial_aspects: I had Ghent and Utrecht on my list, and chose Ghent, since this exchange was a few weeks longer. It was important for me that I knew the university held a high standard and had a high equine case-load.
overall_comments: Had an amazing time! Learned a lot and got exactly what I wanted out of my exchange! Ghent is a beautiful city and I would warmly recommend an exchange there to everyone.
info_ease: In the beginning it was a little confusing, but once you got orientated at their website, you could find most information there. The international office in Ghent was also really kind and helpful to help if you had any questions, but expect a little waiting time on the emails, and the most important information we got sent out on email!
arrival_assistance: We had a welcome day at the faculty, and got plenty of information then. We also got assigned "mentors" you could ask if you had questions.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Had an amazing time! Learned a lot and got exactly what I wanted out of my exchange! Ghent is a beautiful city and I would warmly recommend an exchange there to everyone.
registration_process: I chose the equine course in my OLA, then I registered in OASIS and received emails from Ghent when I had to proceed with something. What I can remember now, I didn't find this too difficult. I had some problems getting my OLA into OASIS, but that got solved. Be patient with the registration process, it takes some time.
registration_help: Tanya at the international office is very helpful! Also the help from UPCH was very good.
registration_success: I applied in my online learning agreement that I wanted to do the equine rotation, and got an email later on that I was assigned that.
registration_advice: Try to read up on their website as much as you can, I prepared myself as much as I could. Keep an eye out for updates on your email. Ask if needed! and again - be patient. :)
academics_comments: Had an amazing time! Learned a lot and got exactly what I wanted out of my exchange! Ghent is a beautiful city and I would warmly recommend an exchange there to everyone.
course_level: They expect you to know what a last year students there know. But we got send out a list a few months before with skills we should know, so we could practice those before arrival if needed.
teaching_comparison: I would say it's very similar. What I liked is that they do rounds in Ghent in the morning, where you learn about the patients, but also get quizzed about the diseases/clinical approach. I learned a lot through that! I experienced the case-load in the equine clinic is higher than in Copenhagen --> you will see more cases and different kinds of cases. They give you a lot of freedom under responsibility. The 3 masters are responsible for the medicines on their own, drawing bloods, taking the anamnesis and first clinical examination of new patients, keeping an eye on critical patients during nights etc etc. I learned a lot through this. We had practicals, both on internal medicine and surgery, where we got to e.g ultrasound abdomen, endoscope, castrate, distal limb ultrasound, they were great! All the vets were very kind and helpful, and liked when you asked questions.
courses_enrolled: Equine Clinical Rotation.
recommended_courses: I would say, that if you want to integrate with the Belgian students and learn more, it is easier if you do one of the full programs and not the mixed one. When doing the mixed one, you never really learn how the departments roll and get to know people, and I experienced that those Erasmus students had a harder time at the clinic because of that.
unexpected_costs: You need to rent scrubs at the clinic (20€/set), but you will get your money back once you leave.
cost_comparison: It's similar prices to Scandinavia.
activities_available: There were plenty available, also through the ESN, but I didn't do any (since clinic took a lot of time, and I explored the country on my own).
activities_recommended: N/A
weekend_recommendations: Ghent, Bruge, Brussels, Knokke, Seaside/beach, Hallebos forest etc. Do all the touristy stuff in Ghent - I loved the boat-tour!
culture_adjustment: I would say very easy. It was very smilar to the Scandinavian culture.
socializing_tips: Be open! I spent more time with local students than with Erasmus ones, and I met all of them in the clinic. Ask them questions about the course and the university, ask them about good tips in Ghent. I found all of them very welcoming and helpful.
cultural_challenges: I didn't experience any cultural differences during my exchange.
culture_appreciated: The food, the history of the country and the people! I found Belgian people very welcoming.
top3_advice: - Socialise with Belgian students and not only Erasmus students - Don't be afraid to ask them to speak in English! I doubled it a little in the beginning when they forgot, but if you keep on reminding, they will remember switch over more and more. I haven't experienced any problems with the language. - If you're doing the equine course - look into the practicals! They don't really tell you about the ones on the surgical department, but you're allowed to sign up on Ufora, I did e.g. castrate a horse "on my own".
other_useful_info: I had my car, and really enjoyed being able to explore the country a bit outside the cities. You don't need a car though, but for me it was really nice. The clinical guide you receive, wasn't really updated (at least this year). But it gives you a good baseline.
most_rewarding: I had an amazing time from start to finish!! Super happy with the academic clinical course, with the city of Ghent, the Belgian culture and all new friends I have made. The vets were really good to explain and teach, and if you want - the opportunity to learn a lot is there. The case-load was high, and that means you do have a lot to do - but I also saw cases I never thought I would see in real life and that was really cool.
greatest_challenge: Coming as a new student and not knowing where stuff is in the clinic. Be proactive and ask them to show you a lot during your first weeks, this will make you more independent.
other_comments: Go go go!! I can warmly recommend it!
