crucial_aspects: It was close the Denmark, the university had a great academic profile and offered some courses that were different from the ones I could choose at UCPH. Moreover, I had an opportunity to improve my German.
info_ease: It was fairly easy. In the beginning I had some troubles finding information about the courses, but has soon as I got familiar with the website, it was easy.
arrival_assistance: I was in contact with the global office at the university and the faculty before the study period, and they were very helpful.
arrival_comments: The was only one zoom-session, and it was right before the study-period started. I didn't learn anything new, and received any information that wasn't available on their website.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The course registration was very frustrating. In general, you do not register for the course, but only for the exam - and the deadline for the exam is very close to the actual exam date. With this procedure, you are able to try out a lot of different courses before you sign-up for it which is nice. But it is also very annoying, as you need the "pre-approval" from the back home and also need to make the learning agreement. And furthermore, a lot of courses had limited spaces. So in the end, two week after the semester started I knew which courses I was registred for.
registration_help: Information on the website and one student assistant working at the international office at the faculty.
registration_success: Luckily, I got all the courses I wanted and three of them even had limited participants.
registration_advice: Go to the first lectures before signing-up. The procedure can be quite frustrating, but just take it easy and do not stress to much about it - it will all work out in the end :)
course_level: I would say the teaching-level is quite high, at least on the same level as at UCPH. But the exams are easier. I also had seminar, which was a little complicated for me as the format was very different from the seminars that I knew from UCPH. So, I spend a lot of time studying for it but at the same time I also learned a lot.
teaching_comparison: The teaching is not as interactive between the students and teacher as in Copenhagen. And some of the courses also didn't really have any particular readings. In a lot of the courses you also have to do a presentation, which accounts for percentage of the final grade.
courses_enrolled: International Macroeconomics Monetary Theory and Policy Wealth and Income Distribution Causal Inference in Economics: Methods and Application in Empirical Political Economy Topics in Growth Theory (Seminar)
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend "causal inference in economics" and "monetary theory and policy". Both really cool courses, and I learned a lot. Especially in the first one, which was an econometric course but explained in a very practical way, which made it easy to understand. I am sure I will use a lot from the course in the future.
unexpected_costs: I paid a Semesterbeitrag, which is mandatory at most German universities. At Goethe uni, it was 376 euros for one semester. But it also covers all public transportion within Frankfurt and a large area around the city. Therefore the local transportion I have listed is only for the bike that I rented while I was there.
cost_comparison: Going out to eat, groceries and the food at campus was way less expensive than I expected. I didn't expect to spend so much on housing.
activities_available: A lot of different sports, events, a semester-party. The student-card also gave access to the botanical garden. The university definitely had an amazing campus-life, which is what I am going to miss the most.
activities_recommended: I didn't participate in any sports myself as it didn't fit my schedule, but I heard a lot of good things about it.
weekend_recommendations: I definitely recommend visiting the cities and small towns located around Frankfurt, like Wiesbaden, Heidelberg, Marburg, Cologne. I also recommend to go on some hikes, as there is some amazing nature and places close by.
culture_adjustment: I didn't find it difficult at all. The only thing I had to adjust to is that all stores and supermarkets are closed on Sundays in Germany ;)
socializing_tips: As all my courses was only offered to mainly two master-degrees, which are both very small with about 40 students per year and have a lot of other international students, I easily got to talk with the local students. But, I think I would just recommend to start a conversation yourself. I found that everyone is very open to meet new people. And, in general, Frankfurt is a very international city.
cultural_challenges: It is not so much of a cultural difference, but I found it challenging that people working in stores, restaurants and health care do not speak english very well.
culture_appreciated: I really like that Germany is such a diverse society, with influences from many different cultures. And at the same time, I also really appreciate the German culture.
top3_advice: Get a bike, use the facilities of the university (the libraries are amazing), and participate in the German course before the lecture period starts. I gives you an opportunity to meet other exchange students, get to know the University and settle before the lectures starts.
other_useful_info: Not anything I haven't mentioned before.
most_rewarding: It is all the people that I got to meet from around the world, and just all the different perspectives on the world that I learned.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge for me was that I was the only danish person among the other exchange students at the university. It would have been have nice to have someone, where you share the same references and background.

registration_comments: I really enjoyed my experience in Frankfurt. It is a city that deserves much more attention. I really liked the university campus. The facilities, the professors, and the vibrant social life on campus were truly amazing and among the main reasons why my stay was so rewarding.
registration_process: You get access to their course portal. You find the courses you are interested in and you find the document with the exam dates. Then you need to plan so you don’t have two or more exams on the same day, and also make sure classes are not at the same time. You make your own weekly schedule based on the courses that fit with each other. After finding the courses that work for you, you simply fill out a form with the courses you want, your student ID, and sign it. Send it by email and they then confirm if you got the spot. If you find out you don’t want one of the courses, you just fill out a de-registration form. You can do this up until approx. two weeks before the exam but you need to check de-registration dates before you apply so you don’t end up in a bad situation.
registration_help: They help you a lot. You can write the administration or any German ESN student and they will help you. I asked German students before applying about the courses and their experiences to get some recommendations, and it helped me a lot.
registration_success: I was succesful. You can apply for more courses than you need. I applied for 8 courses, and after 2 weeks of class I deregistered from 3 that I didn’t like as much, so I ended up with 5.
registration_advice: Apply for more than you need, but remember to deregister from the ones you don’t take. And plan carefully around exam dates.
academics_comments: I really enjoyed my experience in Frankfurt. It is a city that deserves much more attention. I really liked the university campus. The facilities, the professors, and the vibrant social life on campus were truly amazing and among the main reasons why my stay was so rewarding.
course_level: For all courses you have to read a lot. But it is okay, because there is way more of a studying life compared to at Copenhagen University, and they had space for everyone. I could always find seating around campus and they have great libraries. I had five classes, where three of them were quite demanding, not only in regards to reading but also the level of difficulty in the exercises.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at Goethe University was much more to my liking. The culture was that everyone came prepared for class, which meant professors could engage students more actively. This led to better discussions, and students asked way more questions than what I am used to at UCPH. From a practical point of view, lectures and classes were quite similar to UCPH, with professors using slides and exercises. However, some professors preferred a more traditional approach, teaching only with the blackboard and not providing any notes, so you had to make sure to write everything down yourself. What I especially liked was that the professor-student relationship was more traditional and professional. I appreciated this atmosphere of mutual respect and professionalism, and it felt more like a university with high expectations for itself and a focus on maintaining a certain standard. Another difference I noticed is that at Goethe University, the teaching stayed neutral in terms of politics.
courses_enrolled: Insurance and Finance Advanced Behavioral Finance Asset and Liability Management in Insurance Companies Advanced Management Ethics, Morality and Economics
recommended_courses: Insurance and Finance: The professor teaches in a traditional way, using only the blackboard, and I really enjoyed his lectures. With his extensive experience from the insurance sector, all the theory made sense when he illustrated it with real-world examples. The pace and structure of the course were excellent, and if you, like me, are curious about the insurance industry, this course gives you a solid understanding.
unexpected_costs: German mandatory radio bill.
cost_comparison: German radio bill was more than I expected (50 euro per quarter).
activities_available: All kinds.
activities_recommended: Try a lot of them. Personally, I really enjoyed the language café and the different sport clubs.
weekend_recommendations: Here are a few: - Explore the city’s many opportunities and areas. I really liked Westend. - The bars all over Sachsenhausen. - Watch a Frankfurt football game. - Explore the cities around Frankfurt. Because everyone has a Deutschland Ticket, every weekend there was a one-day trip to a city relatively close by. Examples: Marburg, Heidelberg, Mannheim, Würzburg, etc. - I personally also went on longer trips with other exchange students, for example to Dortmund to watch a football match, Trier, Luxembourg, Cologne, etc.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy because I already spoke German. Just be aware that it is good to be able to speak German because even though the university is very international and most speak English, your daily life in the city and at places like the supermarket or municipal offices is just easier when you speak German.
socializing_tips: Join student organisations, language cafés, and sports clubs. They are great ways to meet German students. Group projects in class are also a good opportunity to connect, so try to be active and engaged.
cultural_challenges: There wasn’t really anything that I found particularly challenging. Everything came quite naturally and the locals were super helpful. I would mention one thing, which the locals will also tell you: stay away from Hauptbahnhof.
culture_appreciated: The outgoing locals and other internationals. Because the city is very multicultural, my experience was also that you could speak with anyone.
top3_advice: 1. Study regularly during the semester. The exam period is short, intense, and more stressful than at UCPH. 2. Don’t overthink the administrative side. Most things are arranged for you, and the process is easier than it looks. They are super helpful and there is always someone to contact. 3. Enjoy it while it lasts. The semester goes by quickly, so take the opportunities that come your way.
other_useful_info: Be quick with housing applications.
most_rewarding: The friends I met and how much I enjoyed living in another country and speaking German.
greatest_challenge: The exam period. I had never been so stressed and tired at the same time, but it was manageable because I kept up with my studies during the semester - something the local students thankfully warn you about from the very beginning. And they don’t give you access to previous exams when you prepare, therefore it’s even more important to follow the lectures and do the exercises.

overall_comments: I had the best study abroad experience.

arrival_assistance: I received all the assistance that I needed when I arrived at my university. They arranged an information day, where the new exchange students where introduced to the university and the city.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had the best study abroad experience.
registration_process: Before my arrival I registered for my courses and got these confirmed during my introduction days together with my personal timetable.
registration_help: I could always reach out to my contact person at Goldsmiths if I had any questions.
registration_success: I got all the courses that I wanted, so the registering process was very successful.
registration_advice: Do it! And have patience, the process can be long, but it always works out for the best. It all becomes easier when you arrive and are able to talk to your contact person in real life and get advise and help from other students.
academics_comments: I had the best study abroad experience.

activities_available: All kinds of sports clubs and teams such as football or tennis, and many different creative and social activities where available for students that are into art, culture, movies and much more.
activities_recommended: I did not join any activities or clubs during my term abroad, but had I lived on campus I would have join the tennis club since the university had to great courts at campus.
weekend_recommendations: London is a massive city, so there is lots of great opportunities to always do something fun in the weekends or holidays. I loved to go visit new parts of the city. My favorite part of London is Hampstead (where I lived), if you need a break from the "city" life and wants to enjoy the nice little streets and the beautiful park called Hampstead Heath. Other than that it is really fun to hang out in Shoreditch or Richmond. I can also recommend taking a trip to Cotswold to see the more rural side of UK without having to travel far from London.
culture_adjustment: Really easy. The brits are very friendly and the culture is not that different from the Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Get to know your fellow classmates and maybe join some of the university clubs or activities.
cultural_challenges: There was not really any cultural differences that I found challenging, since it was not that different from Denmark.
culture_appreciated: The kindness. Everywhere you go people are extremely polite. They thank the bus driver before getting off the bus, the teachers pauses to say "bless you" if you sneeze in class and if you ever need help or look lost, you can expect people to come help you. I have had the best conversations with strangers at bus stops or at the local coffee shop.
top3_advice: 1. Have patience during the process 2. Dont be shy to join the class discussion 3. Use the help your teachers offer when planing and writing your assignments
other_useful_info: No, I think you are given all the information you need when attending Goldsmiths.

greatest_challenge: To have faith in your own academic skills.

crucial_aspects: I liked the modules offered at Goldsmiths, wanted to practice my english and wanted to live and study in London, because it is one of the most exciting cities in the world :).
overall_comments: Overall it was a wonderful experience! I would say the only drawbacks were 1) the cost of living in London and 2) administrative chaos at Goldsmiths.
info_ease: Things like housing and info on social activities were quite easy to find, but everything related to more practical info on choosing modules, finding my timetable etc. was a complete chaos. There had just been a "restructure", which meant that they had fired most of the administrative staff and pooled all the positions together in weird teams. The result was that no one was really able to answer any questions about modules etc., because no one believed it was part of an area they should cover. Everyone, and especially the study abroad students were confused about how to get info; the student hubs had hour-long queues and no one answered their emails due to "the number of emails they received". Hence, I didn't get my timetable until around a month after I arrived and was very confused about whether or not I had been accepted to the modules I had applied to, It worked out alright, it was just a really frustrating experience.
arrival_assistance: Technically there was assistance available from the study abroad team, but they were so busy with all the chaos in the first couple of weeks that you couldn't realistically get an answer. The lecturers were nice and tried to help, but they were also confused and frustrated with the administration, because everything had been restructured. Other things were easier to get info on, for example they provided assistance with things like the possibility to sign up with a GP, a campus tour etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Overall it was a wonderful experience! I would say the only drawbacks were 1) the cost of living in London and 2) administrative chaos at Goldsmiths.
registration_process: In terms of modules, we were supposed to say which modules we wanted before arriving. This form was however full of errors, where most of the modules they had listed weren't available in the term I was there. It took weeks for them to figure this out, and then we had to fill out a new form. Despite this, I was still approved for a module that wasn't offered. I ended up just emailing the study abroad department during the first two weeks of term, where you still have the possibility to change modules. This was fine for me, since none of the modules were full, but it was quite complicated for some of the other exchange students.
registration_help: You could talk to the student hub and email the study abroad department, and they would try to help you.
registration_success: I got 2 out of the 4 courses I wanted, and 2 I had not applied for initially.
registration_advice: Have patience. Don't panic if it takes them awhile to make your timetable, just show up to the classes you expect to take anyway. Use the 2 week period you have for changing modules to go to different lectures. It is okay to not like a module you initially signed up for and wish to follow another one.
academics_comments: Overall it was a wonderful experience! I would say the only drawbacks were 1) the cost of living in London and 2) administrative chaos at Goldsmiths.
course_level: It was fine, I think the teaching was a bit different from KU, but the level wasn't necessarily higher. Their reading lists are a bit different, but reading the key readings for each lecture was doable. Then you could look at the rest when writing essays etc.
teaching_comparison: It was structured a bit differently: they have a weekly 1 hour lecture followed by a 1 hour seminar for each module. So 8 hours of teaching per week, but half of it is seminars. It was nice to experience this more classroom centered teaching, although I thought the students were very quiet in most of the seminars, at least compared to Danish high school classrooms. In general, it seemed like they didn't have much experience with oral participation; we had to do a debate in one seminar and two presentations for another module, and it seemed like quite a big thing, although I found it pretty chill. I was surprised by the emphasis they put on office hours, because we don't use it much at KU. They often encouraged us to go to the office hours to discuss our essays etc., and I think that was really nice.
courses_enrolled: Confronting the climate crisis Race, racism and social theory Social change and political action Visual explorations of the social world
recommended_courses: Race, racism and social theory was really good and covered things that are not as easy to find courses on at KU. Even though it dealt with difficult themes, it was a really sympathetically taught module and I learned a lot from it. Visual explorations of the social world was also really nice, and fun because you got to do your own project and thus examine something you find interesting. Socially it was also quite nice to take this module, because there was a lot of workshops with group work etc. where you could get to know the other students a bit better. It was also one of very few methods modules, so good to take if you want to try that as well. The other two were also fine, although Social change was a little simple, probably because it was a second year module. I would advise to only choose third year modules if you have the possibility, as these are way more interesting.
unexpected_costs: I spent more money on tranport than I expected. This was due to going on a few weekend trips and also there was a lot of transport issues because train and bus drivers were striking all the time. I thus rented a bike to travel more freely, but still ended up using the tube and overground quite a lot when going further away etc.
cost_comparison: Did not have to buy any books for the modules, so that was cheaper.
activities_available: Loads of different things! Go to the welcome fest in the beginning of the term and see what it's possible to join. I joined the athletics team and the arts and crafts society, and that was fun. My friend really liked pole dancing, but I'm sure most of it is nice! I also joined a critical philosophy reading group, so i would just recommend keeping an eye out for anything you are interested in, they probably have an activity related to it :)
activities_recommended: Depends on your interests, they offer all sorts of stuff! If you stay in halls, then also try to go to some of the Loring Hall meet up things or trips if you fancy getting to know the other LH-students. And go to some of the events at the student union like the parties, trashy tuesdays, jazz evenings etc.
weekend_recommendations: Go on a few trips. I went to Oxford and Cambridge, which was fun. Also went to Charleston in Lewes, which is a pretty museum house about the bloomsbury group. Also try to check out some of the festivals and events happening in London or see if there is a concert you like etc. Most of the museums are free to visit, so maybe check out some of those. I also really liked to explore the areas around Goldsmiths like Peckham, Deptford, Greenwich.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, british culture is not that different, and London is so diverse that pretty much everyone is welcomed. If you do feel homesick or just want to speak a bit of Danish, maybe check out the sunday dinners or events at Dansk KFUK in Hampstead, where there are loads of Danes willing to chat, give advice etc.
socializing_tips: I think joining a sport or another kind of society is one of the easiest way to socialise. Also try to chat to the people in your modules, people are generally very welcoming.
cultural_challenges: Maybe British food being so bland, haha. No but on a personal level I don't think there is that much cultural difference between danes and brits. It was more political/societal things I found challenging, mostly because there were so so many strikes while I was there: train & bus strikes, royal mail strikes, uni strikes, nurses and ambulance strikes, which of course made daily life a little more difficult.
culture_appreciated: That most people in London are a lot more welcoming and easy going than in Denmark, and also the diversity and possibilities of London.
top3_advice: Try to have a flexible budget, because London is expensive. Try to save on things like food and transport rather than experiences. Make a list of what you most want to see/do in London, because once you get there you will have so many choices that it can be hard to prioritise. Enjoy your modules and the possibility of "just" being a student without also working part time, volunteering etc.
other_useful_info: Try to do some work on your essays during the term, so you don't have to starte from scratch in January. Talk to your lecturers in their office hours or email them if you are confused or just want to go over an idea with them.
most_rewarding: The friendships made, everything I was able to explore in London and what I learned in the modules.
greatest_challenge: Confusion related to administrative and practical things.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial to me that it was a place with a different climate than i was used to, a new city i hadn't lived in or explored before and that it presented lots of opportunities for traveling and personal development throughtout the semester.
info_ease: The university was great at sending all the information you needed before arrival and offered lots of assistance to those who need it.
arrival_assistance: I personally didn't use any of the assistance offered as i have gone on exchange and lived abroad a couple of times before so i felt confident doing it on my own. I also didnt go directly to the city where my host university was located when arriving in Australia, and therefore lots of the help offered wasn't necessary or available to me.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You have to have your preferred courses accepted by both the host institution and your home university. You enroll by searching for the coursecode and choosing your schedule as soon as enrollment opens in November (for trimester 1). If you find it confusing you can always wait and get help during O-Week, but you risk your classes being full.
registration_help: During O-week theres several places to get help such as the library or the international student advisory lounge. Before you arrive, however, you can e-mail the school and they will guide you. As the professors has to accept you into their class, it can sometimes take a very long time before you know if your request are denied or accepted, but you just have to be patient.
registration_success: I successfully registrered in almost all the classes i wanted. I had one class where i was denied due to not having met the prerequisites.
registration_advice: Plan your classes to be on the same days so you have long weekends every week to travel and explore. Also expect several assessments throughout the semester, whichcan seem stressful as they seem to require a bit of work, however, the expections and the quality actually expected seemed quite low and so you dont need to stress. You will be fine.
course_level: I had one BA course and three MA courses. At BA level i felt the class and teacher were much more engaged and the level of education was decent, but quite low compared to what i expected. There was a good match between what was taught and what was expected in the assessments, however the teacher kinda carries everyone through it and seems to have very little faith in what you can do as an exchange student. My MA classes were all intensive and there was much reading before every class. However i found that the reading and the actual teaching didnt match up and neither did the assessments, so you had to do most of the work yourself. Class was also much less engaged and everyone very old. However i didnt find the level to be hard at all either, as you could skip the reading for classes and just focus on the required assessments.
teaching_comparison: Very different, as all my lectures were online and then i had a workshop in person. At the workshops/tutorials on BA level they help you prepare for assessments. On MA level you only have lectures and so you can choose between watching online or in person when you want.
courses_enrolled: Media Law - BA International Negotiations - MA International Oragnisations - MA International Environmental Law - MA
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend Media law and International Organisations. I found both subjects interesting, and really liked how media law combined both a self chosen research topic on a current law reform and a case based assessment combining all the skills taught throught the class. In IO we were taught negotation skills and tricks and were placed in situations to these test out. Very different but fun.
unexpected_costs: Obligatory health insurance through host university
cost_comparison: Rent. I lucked out and got a fully furnished room for about 250aud a week (1125 DKK). This was very cheap compared to what i expected and also what most were paying.
activities_available: Lots but i didnt really participate.
activities_recommended: I dont know
weekend_recommendations: Travel travel travel all around Australia.
culture_adjustment: Very easy as i have lived in Australia before, so i knew what to expect.
socializing_tips: Talk to people in your classes.
cultural_challenges: How young people are in Uni and also that they all get up around 5am and go to bed around 20pm in the Gold Coast - also on weekends.
culture_appreciated: How laid back they are
top3_advice: Sorry, i really dont know.
other_useful_info: I dont think so.
most_rewarding: Getting a bit of a break and exploring someplace new. Also meeting a bunch of amazing people
greatest_challenge: Probably missing your friends and family back home.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a destination where the main language was english, and having been to Australia once before and falling in love with the country, i wanted to revisit, but go to a spot i had never been. At first i considered studying in Brisbane itself, but luckily, i chose to study at Griffith University Gold Coast Campus, which is the best decision i have made in a long time. I wanted to be close to nature, and close to the sea, to really experience the aussie surf culture, and one can definitely say i got to do that, as i ended up living 100 meters from the beach with a balcony view. I also prioritized that the university had subjects that would fit into my degree, as i have mandatory courses that needed to be heeded, but other than that, they offered a great array of electives. The australian structuring of years and classes permittet that i took whatever classes made sense in terms of KU, and in terms of scheduling, as long as i could live up to the prereqs put in place.
overall_comments: I got truly immersed in my experience, as i chose to seek out other internationals and australians. I definitely got out of my comfort zone and tried new things, went on roadtrips, learned to surf, caught the sunrises and built up network of international and australian friends i will have for life. Studying in Australia was surprisingly tough. It seems that psychology is one of the only majors i encountered in Oz that we at home describe as social science, but in Australia, it is mostly natural sciences. this meant way more lab reports, statistics, academical writing and literature searches than i had anticipated. I ended up collectively in 4 courses writing 5 different six-page reports of my own academic research on a given topic, and in one case also conducting a study on myself for 5 weeks in advance. furthermore, a lot of very specific knowledge was required for exams, and i spend a lot of time memorizing stuff in order to pass exams.
info_ease: very easy! the student help centre and the student guild were amazingly helpful and provided all the ressources needed for university, alas, you had to seek them out, if you didnt participate in the orientation week, which i HIGHLY recommend you do! showing up to the first activity "Mates in minutes" led me to meet the people i would spend the rest of the semester with, go on trips with, and later travel with. go to orientation week please! I definitely, unfortunately, noticed that the people who didnt go had a harder time making friends, as people all have different majors and different classes
arrival_assistance: orientation week had stalls and tours, where we got to talk to the different couselling offices, learn where all the important things were, and were handed a "manual" to what was going on on campus, outside campus in gold coast etc. I didnt need any help with scheduling or something of that sort, and i didnt live on campus (please dont if possible, its much better and cheaper to live elsewhere, closer to the beach and facilities, and you can still make friends living outside the campus village). If you lived on campus, they had a bunch of introductory events, and also welcoming officers to sho you around the campus village.
arrival_comments: it was really nice - the Griffith mates were SO eager to help, and stuck around all semester, making fun activities and providing opportunities to meet new people. Just go to as many events as possible - they may sometimes seem lame, but i promise, its worth it! The mates events and orientation week stuff is both on and off campus, giving you a chance to see the city of Gold Coast as well (Which is quite big for a small town).

course_level: i had first year, second year and third year classes
teaching_comparison: way more online, SO much online stuff to do actually. their version of Absalon/ Canvas is used so much, and youve got to keep up during the semester, because they have midterm exams in week 5, and if you dont pass, theres a high risk of your points cumulatively not making you pass your courses.
courses_enrolled: mental health, psychology and the criminal justice system (really nice and interesting small course) cognitive psychology (really heavy course) cognitive neuropsychology (really good course) positive psychology (sounds easy, is SO much work)
recommended_courses: cognitive neuropsych was definitely one of my favorites - it was really nuanced, and was the course that closest matched the way we get taught, and the mindset brought to the courses at KU. it felt like something i could actually use later in life. Mental health, psychology and the criminal justice system was a really good look into the less nice things about australian culture, and specifically the issues that are present in modern day Queensland. the teacher James Ogilvie is one of the best teachers ive had at any university, and he has worked with mental health cases in prisons, institutions, juvys, and with aboriginal and torres straight islanders.
unexpected_costs: alcohol was really really expensive - so good on ya if you can party without having a beer first. costwise, australia is just really expensive, so yeah, wasnt reallt surprised by how expensive it all was
cost_comparison: the university student guild provided free groceries every monday and thursday at 2pm - all the basics like greens, beans, pasta, bread. that really helped out my economy. Didnt eat out much, mostly at home because it was SO expensive
activities_available: all sorts! free dinner every tuesday, we did a paint n sip, a musem trip to HOTA, surf club trips, parties, and the O-week was of course also filled with activities. My friend played on the rugby team, another was on the cheerleader team, and there were a lot of options to actually get involved.
activities_recommended: surfing! hiking! just go outside and enjoy the beautiful place. the burleigh beach walk is amazing, the springbrook and tambourine mountains are filled with waterfalls you can swim in and hikes and glowworm caves. there is so much cool stuff to do outside on the coast. Uh! also go to coombabah to see real koalas living in the wild - please dont just go to currumbin wildlife sanctuary - the koalas look so sad in there.
weekend_recommendations: please please please go to byron bay and broken heads for at least a weekend trip! also go to fraser island, and from the beginning of the semester try to find a group of friends to go on a semester break roadtrip with - driving up to whitsundays, taking a 1 or 2 day cruise and driving back down, whilst also doing fraser island is the coolest thing ever. the weeks go by so fast, and by the semester break, everyone already have their small groups and their plans - going to fraser and great keppel islands and whitsundays and byron is well worth the money! also depending on you schedule, you might have a lot of days off like me - when youre not studying, these can be put into prolonging weekend trips
culture_adjustment: pretty easy - the aussies are nice, well tempered and everything is in english everywhere. the hardest thing to adjust to was walking on the left.
socializing_tips: talk to the people in your classes - you might feel annoying, but theyre actually quite curious, and love to make friends - in general it seems that a lot of aussies know people before they start uni, so they never go to O-week orientation etc. youve gotta catch them in their classes.
cultural_challenges: i was kinda baffled by the fact that the aussies go barefoot anywhere -no shoes in a mall is crazy. but! then i tried it and cant lie, theyre kinda right
culture_appreciated: how easygoing and outdoorsy people are. its more about watching sunset at burleigh hill with your friends, getting up early to surf, going on a roadtrip or hanging out in front of the tele than about glamour and going out. aussies have a strong tall poppy syndrome - jantelov if you must - they dont care who you are, as long as youre nice, and theyll give it to ya straight.
top3_advice: - please please go to O-week! even if it seems lame you make friends forever - find someone with a car to be your best friend! its SO helpful and will make your experience so much better - heck, if you have the money, buy a car! they range between 7-10.000 AUD depending on the car and how shitty it is - watch all the sunrises you can! i was skeptical at first, but waking up with the sunrise is amazing. i will carry those mornings by the water, swimming in the sunrise with me for the rest of my life.
other_useful_info: theres an on campus doctor - best thing in the world. they are so nice, and with the OSHC, they just batch bill the insurance, so you never pay out of pocket. also! speaking of OSHC, buy it yourself through Allianz (the one griffith wants you to get anyway) and send them proof. i purchased my own for 200 AUD, my friend bought hers through uni, where it cost 440 AUD.
most_rewarding: all the friends ive made, and the discovery that saying yes to something new is scary, but noones gonna laugh at me, and everything is gonna be fine.
greatest_challenge: balancing keeping in contact with the people at home, and still not alienating myself from my exchange experience. I ended up almost not writing home, because i was so immersed in what was happening in the now, at the gold coast. it was a blessing to put down the phone and just be with the people i was with, but at te same time, it meant that my relationships to the people at home suffered a bit. i wouldnt change anything, but it was a struggle
other_comments: gold coast was the perfect place to go for nature, surfing and that aussie feel - i think this exchange is the best thing ive done in my adult life, and i will honestly be forever grateful for it.

arrival_comments: Getting courses approved before the start of the trimester could be difficult, but there was assistance at the student center and they informed me, that some of the courses start a week later, so no need to stress.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was a fantastic experience and it was the right choice to do it and totally worth the time spend on the practical things before going on exchange. I will fully recommend going on exchange at Griffith University, Gold Coast, Australia.
registration_process: I made my registration for courses on their internal website. It was easy to find and easy to use. However the approval of courses took quite a long time and I got my approvals late.
registration_help: You could get help by emailing them or by going to the student center.
registration_success: I got half of my applied courses approved. I managed to find other relevant courses instead of the ones I applied for in the beginning.
registration_advice: It is an easy process, but be patient for the approval of courses. Otherwise go and ask for help at the student center. Have some extra courses ready to apply for.
academics_comments: It was a fantastic experience and it was the right choice to do it and totally worth the time spend on the practical things before going on exchange. I will fully recommend going on exchange at Griffith University, Gold Coast, Australia.
course_level: I found the level on the courses to be easier than in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: My lectures were only online which could be both good and bad. It was flexible, but also more boring to watch the lectures alone. I had a couple of labs or workshops at campus during the week, but not many hours spend on campus, except for when I choose to go to the the library and study.
courses_enrolled: Exercise sports nutrition, Motor learning and control, Physiology of exercise, Research methods and statistics.
recommended_courses: The labs were good in Physiology of exercise.
unexpected_costs: Transportation to trips, flights and housing on holiday trips
cost_comparison: Vegetables were more expensive. Food, restaurants, and housing were similar to prices in Copenhagen.
activities_available: There are a lot of clubs, both cultural, social and athletics.
activities_recommended: I would totally recommend to attend the orientation week. This is a great opportunity to meet new friends and get around campus.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going to the beaches, taking surf lessons, going to the national parks and take your swimming clothes with you, having a barbecue near the beach, doing snorkling, going on an island, having a dinner night with your friends, participate in a park run. In generel I recommend to rent a car to get around.
culture_adjustment: It was super easy. People are so kind in Australia.
socializing_tips: Attend orientation week, be part of a club or do a voluntary job at campus to get to know more people. Don't be afraid to talk to people in your classes.
cultural_challenges: Nothing.
culture_appreciated: Their friendliness and the happy and calm ambience.
top3_advice: Don't be nervous, people are very friendly and you will easily find friends if you are attending the o-week or other socializing offers. Enjoy it, don't be stressed, and try to adapt to the calming ambiance in Gold Coast. The workload is not as big as in Denmark. Go to the beaches and see the nature and animal life.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Enjoying my life with a lot of nice people in a more calm and beautiful environment, while studying.
greatest_challenge: Nothing very challenging beside from being far away from home.

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte at tage på udveksling for at udfordre mig selv personligt og professionelt. Jeg oplevede at Griffith havde et større udvalg af fag inden for mit interesse område end på KU. Derudover ønskede jeg også at udvikle mine engelsk kompetencer i profesionelle settings. Desuden var jeg nysgerrig på den australske levestil, kultur og natur.
info_ease: Griffith var rigtig gode til at sende guides og hjælpedokumenter til skrive sig ind osv. Hvis jeg var i tvivl om noget, var de også nemme at få fat i, og de svarede forholdsvis hurtigt.
arrival_assistance: Der blev afholdt en orienteringsuge, som egnetlig mere var en kalender af aktiviteter og informationsmøde. Her man selv skulle man selv planlægge sin uge. Det var på den ene side smart og fleksibelt, men også lidt overvældende og demotiverende.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Det var meganemt at skrive sig op til fag. De havde en god hjemmeside, hvor man kunne se det potentielle skema, man skulle have, imens man planlagde.
registration_help: De var igen hurtige til at svare på mail.
registration_success: Der var to fag, jeg ikke kunne få desværre, fordi den ene var på et advanced niveau og det andet på kandidat niveau.
registration_advice: Lav et word dokument, med et overblik over kursusbeskrivelserne, og brug det 'skema' som der er på hjemmesiden.
course_level: Niveauet er lidt lavere end i Danmark, og ikke nogle af fagene ikke nær så akademiske. Der er heller ikke et krav om selvvalgt pensum til opgaverne og eksaminerne.
teaching_comparison: Mine forelæsninger var kun online, mens holdundervisningen var på campus. De var lidt mere hands-on på Griffith. På trods af at lavede akademisk niveau, var der flere cases and real life eksempler, som vi arbejdede med til undervisningen.
courses_enrolled: 2506LHS Global Journalism, Media and Communication 2505LHS Ethical Communication 2006GIR Politics, Spin and the Media 1513LHS Digital Media: Portfolio Production
recommended_courses: Jeg kunne virkelig godt lide Global Journalism, Media and Communication og Digital Media: Portfolio Production, hvor underviserne var supergode og personlige
unexpected_costs: Visum kostede meget mere end jeg havde regnet med. Og så betalte jeg dobbelt husleje i nogle uger, da jeg flyttede fra on-campus til off-campus.
cost_comparison: Student Visa kostede 7.200 kr, hvilket var mere end forventet. MEns offentlig transport kun kostede 0.5$ per tur, hvilket et 2,25 kr., ligemeget hvor langt man skal i Queensland (udover lufthavnen).
activities_available: Løbeklubber, sportsklubber og noget til enhver interesse. Det var meget tydeligt hvad der var at vælge imellem til orienteringsugen.
activities_recommended: Løbeklub, uni bar
weekend_recommendations: Der er rig mulighed for nogle fede dagsture, når man bor i Gold Coast. Brisbane, Byron Bay, Springbrook. Og så er indenrigsflyvninger ret billige :)
culture_adjustment: Den australske kultur ligger ikke særligt langt væk fra den danske. De er meget venlige og snaksaglige, og så har de deres helt egen slang. De står meget tidligt op og dagen slutter også for dem før end her i Danmark.
socializing_tips: Gruppearbejde, og sociale klubber:)
cultural_challenges: Ikke særligt
culture_appreciated: Deres laid backness og at der er en dag før arbejdsdagen begynder.
top3_advice: 1) Nyd de nye venskaber. 2) Spørg, spørg, spørg, hvis du er i tvivl om noget eller du vil have anbefalinger. De lokale er SÅ søde til at hjælpe. 3) Lav en hverdag, som du er glad for, surf, hvis du vil, eller løb, du kan lave helt nye vaner.
other_useful_info: Jeg synes, Burleigh var en mega fed suburb, der gad jeg godt have boet. Det var godt nok en time væk i offentlig transport, men der er flere muligheder for at gøre de ting som jeg syntes var fede, dernede. Hvis du har mulighed, så køb en bil. Ja, offentlig transport er meget billigt, men det er også ret udueligt. Biler er ret billige dernede og lette at sælge igen. Jeg klarede den foruden, men jeg følte mig ofte begrænset.
most_rewarding: Den personlige udvikling, jeg er gået igennem, og så de ture, jeg kom på i weekenderne og ferierne.
greatest_challenge: At man ikke bliver krammet så ofte som i DK

crucial_aspects: Mainly the weather and the travel opportunities to many far away places that you rarely or never would visit
info_ease: Very easy
arrival_assistance: Didn't receive any assistance
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Very easy. I applied for all the pre-approved courses and got in easy. Griffith's system is very stress-free
registration_help: There is a 24 hour student desk. I didn't use it but I know a few who got a lot of help from them.
registration_success: 100% succesful
registration_advice: Griffith has a lot of campuses. I recommend determining whether you want to stay in Brisbane or Gold Coast beforehand. I went to Nathan (Brisbane South), which is the main campus in Brisbane but it is not in the city. The campuses that Griffith has in the city of Brisbane are very small and mainly for art and cultural students, so if you want to attend Griffith and live in Brisbane, your best bet is to register for courses at Nathan and commute (25-35 min from city center) with the cheap public transport. Sidenote: Griffith is opening a bigger campus in the city center for Economics and Law students by 2027 (I think)
course_level: The academic level is pretty low compared to KU. I do believe you can find courses with higher acamedic level if you take time to research the level of the courses beforehand.
teaching_comparison: The courses, I took, had no sit-in exam, which meant that the assessments were split out through the trimester. I didn't have any courses that required attendance but I know that a lot of courses do require that. Be prepared for group assignments and presentations as part of your assessment but also know, that not a single Australian attended any of my courses (solely international students) so the average Danish student is going to excel due to English proficiency
courses_enrolled: Global Business Strategy Accounting and Governance Economics
recommended_courses: I wouldn't only recommend these courses if you plan on not attending school and want as much free time as possible
unexpected_costs: I had to pay 150$ on a bond cleaning My computer also broke down so I had to buy a new one
cost_comparison: Public transports is very very cheap. Every bus and train fare is 50p no matter the length (except if you go to the airport). Uber is very cheap You can find excellent dining deals on EatClub meaning going out for dinner is cheap.
activities_available: Griffith has a wide range of different activities but I didn't really attend anything other than the social activities during O-week. The Orientation week, the sporting and cultural events of UQ and QUT are way better. I recommend attending these instead
activities_recommended: I think the activities during O-week is a must if you want to meet people at Griffith. However, the sporting facilities of UQ and QUT are way better and the O-week for these Universities start 1 and 2 week after Griffith's. I really recommend going to these.
weekend_recommendations: Do day trips to Gold Coast and weekend trips to Byron Bay and Noosa Heads as much as possible. Also do a 2/3 days trip to Fraser island / K'gari In general, Brisbane is a pretty boring city but the area around Brisbane is so beautiful and South-East Queensland is a travel hotspot with so much to do. Rent a car and explore
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: There are basically no local student at master's level in Australia
cultural_challenges: Not really any. The only thing is, Australia has a lot more homeless people than Denmark. Avoid engaging with them as they do get aggressive some times and they don't like foreigners.
culture_appreciated: Being outside. Australians love being outside. They love exploring nature and socialising in the sun. Enjoy that - you will miss it when you get back to the cold.
top3_advice: If you plan on staying in Brisbane, reach out to other international students beforehand to find accommodation. Griffith is NOT in Brisbane and the on-campus accommodation is bad and very far away. Engage in other Universities' activities as their social and sport clubs are way better Travel as much as possible. Brisbane is simply perfectly located for traveling
other_useful_info: Many exchange student attend Griffith because of their Gold Coast campus. Consider registering for courses there instead of Brisbane if you enjoy surfing and going to the beach.
most_rewarding: The people you meet along the way and all the travel experiences.
greatest_challenge: The first week. It's always tough to move to the other side of the world (especially if you know no one)

crucial_aspects: weather, people, language, nature
overall_comments: A lot of bureaucratic and logistics work before the exchange and stressfull finding an apartment, but completely worth!!!
info_ease: Good - BUT a lot of courses on the Griffith webpage appear applicable for everyone, but actually more courses are restricted to only domestic students - e.g. if you seek field work within marine science, some courses such as BIODISCOVERY, SCIENCE CAPSTONE is not possible to get even though they don't write it (I found out by mailing the convenor)
arrival_assistance: Go to orientation week! The people are AMAZING and incredibly helpfull and kind
arrival_comments: Go to orientation week! The people are AMAZING and incredibly helpfull and kind sign up for as much as possible
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: A lot of bureaucratic and logistics work before the exchange and stressfull finding an apartment, but completely worth!!!
registration_process: It was pretty easy to register and apply for the exchange - what took A LOT of time was applying for the expensive student visa (25 pages), applying for funding (make an overview and calendar-based plan here to make it work and do things in good time!) and all the other small things like finding housing, what courses you can take and get merit from etc.
registration_help: some coordinators at KU responsible for exchange to New Zealand and Australia were very helpfull because they answered fast Griffith uni took more time replying but were also very helpfull when answering the questions
registration_success: I was happy with my courses, and most teachers and classes at Griffith are great! BUT, as mentioned, it was frustrating that I chose the university partly based on the expectation of taking courses with fieldwork (like MARINE BIODISCOVERY 2803ENV), only to find out one month before the exchange started that some of these courses are for domestic students only — something they don’t mention on the course pages :( So definitely don’t hesitate to email the course convenors to check whether a class is open to international students as well.
registration_advice: do everything in as good time as possible, you'll be surprised how long time everything can take and different challenges can occur
academics_comments: A lot of bureaucratic and logistics work before the exchange and stressfull finding an apartment, but completely worth!!!
course_level: Neurobiology – a heavy course that requires quite a bit of time, but very interesting. Programming Principles – also more time-consuming than expected, but very relevant. Marine Mammals and Planetary Health – not too hard; interesting content! But some times very unstructured. Unfortunately our (only) dissection class was cancelled last minute. Environmental Management – not too hard except for one big assignment, but it requires engagement in voluntary work, which is really cool and a fun way to meet people - and also relevant for future career development.
teaching_comparison: more online teaching in general
courses_enrolled: Neurobiology – a heavy course that requires quite a bit of time, but very interesting. Programming Principles – also more time-consuming than expected, but very relevant. Marine Mammals and Planetary Health – not too hard; interesting content! But some times very unstructured. Unfortunately our (only) dissection class was cancelled last minute. Environmental Management – not too hard except for one big assignment, but it requires engagement in voluntary work, which is really cool and a fun way to meet people - and also relevant for future career development.
recommended_courses: those which interest you and which are not (only) online - engage in the Uni life, ask some aussies if they wanna grab lunch with you etc.!
unexpected_costs: (weekend)-Travels, food, hostels, parties, everything just runs up
cost_comparison: food were more expensive than I expected - and you go out more than expected as well Spontaneous trips cost a lot
activities_available: A LOT of activities and clubs available - they had one (wednes)day after orientation week where many clubs were presented, but they're also listed online (ask StudentGuild) I joined the uni orchestra, Harmony in Health — honestly the best decision I made. It was amazing socially, culturally, and musically. My only regret is not joining from the very beginning instead of a month into the trimester.
activities_recommended: pick up and play - sport activities try the free facilities every friday go to the cook-up (free dinner) at tuesdays etc. Trivia night Orchestra Hiking club! Diving club surfing club
weekend_recommendations: Byron bay, Noosa, Brisbane, if you have a week off then a van trip on the East coast, Fraser island, Whitsundays etc. And get a car or find some friends with one! then you can go on amazing day-trips to the forrest, Spring brook etc. You can see glowing worms! Do Mount Tamborine first during daytime (then you educate yourself (e.g. DON'T use iPhone light since it can kill the worms - only RED light!) and you'll know what to look for, really good conservation center) and then do the natural cave in Natural Bridge at evening! Such a beautiful experience not a lot of people know about
culture_adjustment: Surfers Paradise has a bit of a superficial, touristy vibe.. like a little Las Vegas.. but uni life is amazing and the system in general is pretty Western
socializing_tips: sign up for the activities and club(s), ask if people wanna grab lunch after class or coordinate this with some other exchange students, take initiative for weekend/day trips etc. e.g. Coombabah and GO TO ORIENTATION WEEK - this is where most exchange students connect
cultural_challenges: The superficial vibe of the people in some areas of Surfers paradise (Meriton particularly), found this place on Flatmates
culture_appreciated: the general openness and kindness of people that people really seek sunrises, sunsets, nature and just good vibes in general surfing culture was fun to try A lot of Asian GOOD food in Southport (Southport Library is so nice as well)! Mostly how amazing the uni was with sooo many social initiatives + they care a lot about your well-being:) LGBT+ friendly, filled with native plants, amazing facilities etc.
top3_advice: I think sorting out your apartment or housing as soon as possible is important so you can really enjoy the first part of your exchange. Also, be prepared that the first few weeks (maybe up to 1-1.5 months into the program) can be stressful (don't hold back on calling home to friends/family) - finding people you connect with might take time, and you may try different social groups. Be patient and kind to yourself, stay courageous and curious, and keep attending different social activities (like the hiking club, and don’t be afraid to ask for a lift). Eventually, you’ll find your people ❤️ And remember - it’s totally fine if you’re not into surfing! There’s so much other great stuff to do, especially with all the nature around and other social clubs at uni:)
other_useful_info: JUST DO IT:) it will be worth Gold Coast campus is the best<3
most_rewarding: Friends from all over the world, not just Europeans - Australia is the most international place I've ever been experiencing the amazing university life and being part of the Uni Orchestra the beautiful nature that is very close living by the beach
greatest_challenge: finding a nice and cheap place to live - if possible, live with people from uni (not on campus tho)
other_comments: Even though it's scary and can be very stressfull the first period, it is VERY rewarding to do and you learn a lot Remember to take breaks! Taking time for yourself is essential to actually be able to enjoy the time you have there Don't stay on social media but be present and enjoy the conversations and nature:)

crucial_aspects: The destination was chosen for us. I am studying Turkish, so of course it would be Turkey. And the University of Copenhagen has an agreement with the university in Ankara.
info_ease: Before we even got to our destination, we were had an contact person at our host university. That was very nice. And upon arrival she helped us a lot, and gave us the information that we needed.
arrival_assistance: Before we even got to our destination, we were had an contact person at our host university. That was very nice. And upon arrival she helped us a lot, and gave us the information that we needed.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: When we arrived we were told to go to the "Student Affairs Office". It is located on campus. They just needed our passport and then they could register us in the system. We then needed to make a student ID card, we got some papers and we gave them to another office, also located on campus. And then 3 days later it was ready and we could pick it up. Then we were actually registered. It was really easy and the staff at Student Affaird spoke english.
registration_help: The student affairs office helped us alot. Our contact person was always ready to answer our emails as well.
registration_success: We needed to change some of our classes upon arrival. But we were succesful with those.
registration_advice: Always just ask if you are unsure of something. They are there to help and guide you. And dont worry, everything will be done it just always takes longer in Turkey.
course_level: The level was very high, language wise. I did not feel fully prepared for the classes. My level of Turkish was not good enough for the classes. But I got the feeling that the classes wasn't actually that difficult, if you know the language well.
teaching_comparison: It was only classes where the teacher was talking from a powerpoint. And of course the students could ask questions, but it was never group work or anything. Just sit and listen (and take notes..)

unexpected_costs: I didn't have any unexpected costs.

activities_available: They had a lot of "clubs" that you could be a part of. Sport, politics, arts and so on.
activities_recommended: I dont know since I didn't participate in them.
weekend_recommendations: Ankara does not have that much to offer "tourist" wise. There is a few things that you can see, and sure go see those. Otherwise I would recommend taking a weekend trip to another city fx Istanbul.

Looking at my stay more generally, I believe I would have been able to meet, benefit and enjoy Ankara and the city's cultural and social aspect of it if the country hadn't been so severely hit by the earthquake in February.

However, the international office as well as the Erasmus+ coordinator was very helpful. Sometimes up to slow reply time can however occur.
arrival_assistance: I had been told that I would follow regular university courses, but upon arrival I learned that I in stead would be following the intensive language course aimed at non-Turkish scholarship students. To get introduced to this, I had a meeting with the former as well as current Erasmus-coordinator, and was enrolled into the former coordinator's spring class as a kind of extra thing. From there the coordinator followed me to the TÖMER department, where I was told when to come and do a placement test. They asked me to come the next day where a class was doing their mid-way exam in B1. After this I just kept coming, nothing to worry about at all. Everybody were kind and attentive.

academics_comments: I'm studying Turkish language and for this, Hacettepe Üniversitesi is a great university in many ways. Their TÖMER language course is intense and rewarding. Looking at my stay more generally, I believe I would have been able to meet, benefit and enjoy Ankara and the city's cultural and social aspect of it if the country hadn't been so severely hit by the earthquake in February.
course_level: Turkish class was way more intense at Hacettepe University than at UCPH. Only speaking Turkish, always learning new topics, gramatical constructions and relatively long days make up the intensity. I would say that you have to study outside of class to keep up, but we very rarely had homework, and in that sense you can also choose how much energy you want to put into it. You have to pass the class to continue to the next level though. The semester ends with a big exam and you get a diploma. The one "normal" academic class I followed had the title "Avrupa'da Türkçe" and I took that more out of interest and curiosity than as a course I could contribute to and exel in. The level seemed a bit lower, but it is difficult to say. The course was probably 4 ECTS and was 2 x 40 minutes weekly, not all weeks had readings.
teaching_comparison: The teachers I met were extremely pedagogical at TÖMER, I guess since they are used to having very young people at around 17-21 yrs old. Its also inherently personal to learn a language, so except for the heaviness of the learning curve, it sometimes felt more like being in kindergarten. I don't think I can say a lot about the teaching style in "Avrupa'da Türkçe" since it was zoom. It was always slide show based and we never had essays or presentations, only occational readings that you could get away with not reading if you wanted to.
courses_enrolled: ÇTL318 Avrupa'da Türkçe TÖMER
recommended_courses: I can't reallt comment on this.
unexpected_costs: Getting your student visa. - I paid around 350 TL for the special health care insurance made in Türkiye that is mandatory to apply. - Then maybe 50 TL to get biometric photos (remember to get them scanned and sent to you, otherwise the application website won't accept it - Then 1500 TL to my airbnb host to get our passports verified, the contract verified, etc etc. OBS! The economy changes quickly in TR so these prices definately don't apply anymore, it is just to give you an idea. :-) I probably spent around 100€ on visa.
cost_comparison: I was happy that you could take the comfortable train to Istanbul for like 280 TL (at that point like 70 DKK/9 EUR) each way, or to Konya or wherever.
activities_available: There is probably more that I just never had an opportunity to discover but: library, football field, stadium, tennis courts, running court, small lake, small forest, a range of cafées. There weren't really any social or cultural stuff going on while I was there.
activities_recommended: I don't know.
weekend_recommendations: Of course Ankara is worth exploring. I especially liked the old town in Ulus and the museums. It rained a lot of the late spring so I never hung out a lot in the parks. And then students should visit other cities in Turkey. Istanbul is 4,5 hrs away with train, Konya 1,5. Izmir is 10 hrs with bus. I wish I had travelled more east too, there is so much to see.
culture_adjustment: I don't find Türkiye in itself difficult to adjust to. There are a lot of prejudice surrounding the country, but you can pretty much find you group of people there, no matter wether you're into museums, bar hopping, study groups or field trips. Of course there are more socially conservative and islamic sentiment, but I doesn't really affect your everyday life, like how you dress, eat or interact. Expect to receive attention from men if you are a woman, especially travelling alone, wearing something eye catching or come across as an "open person". Learn to tell them off.
socializing_tips: Unfortunately no, not really. Going to cultural events, I would say, the few people I met I met like that. In general, the students never came to Ankara since they could attend university online instead, but that being said, young (and old) Turks are pretty chill and open to talk to.
cultural_challenges: As mentioned above: certain special treatments as a women. I've lived in TR for two years and now 5 months in Ankara and I've never had anything actually bad happen to me -- but it can still be intense. Men talking to you on the bus, on the restaurant, in a bar, stuff like that. Develop a strategy and remember that it isn't you who should be feeling bad or embarrassed.
culture_appreciated: All the other people who are super kind - being in a country where you can dive into majestic roman and islamic architecure - the fooood omg - the literature, so much cheaper there, even in translation
top3_advice: 1) Remember to explore the campus, wether to enjoy the nature or to find the art departments buzzing workshops 2) Don't postpone getting your documents ready for the visa, you will probably encounter something unexpected 3) Go to every event that attracts your attention to meet people and see new places, on or off campus, because Ankara is the local's city.
other_useful_info: Not for my host institution maybe, but for Ankara: Read books or watch movies on Türkiye, if you haven't already. I read Ahmet Hamdi Tanpinar and Elif Shafak while I was there and it really adds depth to the otherwise foreign impressions. Also, getting an insurance was really tricky for me. Every office I found on google or saw on a sign where magically non-existent when I arrived. When you find a place, stress that you need an insurance for the student visa application (ikamet) when getting an insurance. It shouldn't be more than around 15€. I almost paid 180€ because they didn't knew what I meant. If nothing else, go to TİMURLAR SİGORTA GENEL MÜDÜRLÜK by Kocatepe Camii, I got my insurance there.
most_rewarding: Learning Turkish for real.
greatest_challenge: The loneliness and extreme lifeless-ness of the city caused by the state of the country after the earthquake.

crucial_aspects: It was mandatory to go Israel, however I choose Hebrew University because its so critically acclaimed, well respected and has produced many great scholars. Academically I found it to look good both on a CV as well as for future academic performance.
overall_comments: When I first came to Israel, the experience itself was amazing! But the whole experience prior to me going was terrible, bordering on the mentally debilitating. However this was almost completely the fault of my teacher and faculty as well as some problems with the embassy, but once that got sorted and I got in contact with another teacher it became better. So there was a lot of work to be done prior to going and it was a challenge but I singlehandedly did everything (with the help of the other teacher). But this should not be a problem for future students. The experience itself in Israel was wonderful and extremely rewarding. The classes were interesting, the campus very nice and pleasant; with a good atmosphere as well as a botanical garden! The online info for each course once the semester had started was easy to navigate in and it was quite easy to get around campus as well. The housing was very good - nothing fancy, but I ended up loving my room - it had the best view of the whole city. I come from a faculty which is so SO small and I am the only Hebrew student of my year, so being with other students was better than I can describe. The international environment was great and it was easy to get to talk to a lot of people. I made a bunch of new friends, travelled with them, had dinners and parties. So if future students don't experience the same turmoil as me prior to their exchange, then their exchange will be equally as great as mine.
info_ease: The Hebrew University was quite good with helping and I had a few contacts there. I had contact with one lecturer from UCPH who was extremely helpful and I don't think I could've gone without her - however she was not supposed to help me, but because my own lecturer didn't want to help, she became my guide. But in general it was quite difficult to find the needed information. From pre-approval to how to apply for merits, to know the deadlines and so on. Everything was very confusing, poorly organized and extremely tiring - especially when there was not help from my own lecturer, despite her being the one who was supposed to help and know everything. So be in good time and reach out for help if things are confusing. In general the experience from UCPH (again, apart from the one lecturer who helped) was not very good, people were quite rude and slow and when I contacted the study guidance they also were not so helpful. Hebrew University was completely different and extremely helpful.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any specific assistance when I arrived in Israel; I was already in touch with the necessary people and had gotten the specific emails, so finding my dorm was quite easy and finding out where to have my classes and what to prepare etc was also not a big problem
arrival_comments: I came later, so I missed some of the orientation meetings and such. It didn't matter so much to me because I was just happy to be there, but it seemed like there was quite a lot of interesting things to go to in the beginning and it would've been enjoyable for me to go to those.

registration_process: I independently searched for better course descriptions and syllabus and found it online and then I contacted the person who was responsible for courses and asked a few questions to clear up. When the course registration opened I had asked the questions I wanted and was a little bit more clear in what I wanted. At Hebrew University the first week is called a "shopping week" where the students go to the courses they have chosen and find out if they are as expected. I came the week after the shopping week so I missed my chances of finding out what the courses were about and was "stuck" with what I had chosen. It ended up being extremely good courses - with only one course being slightly boring. But I missed the shopping week because of circumstances out of my control and future exchange students probably won't miss it.
registration_help: There was an advisor connected to me and a handful of other students (around 30-50 students) who wrote us with the necessary information and was easy to contact. We also had two meetings with her. The first I had on zoom, because I was still in CPH but the second was in-person. The first one was talking about which courses I wanted, if it was possible and made sense in regard to my studies in Denmark and so on. It was very helpful because it cleared up some confusion and it was just nice to talk to someone and clear my thoughts and doubts. The second was mid-way where I could evaluate all the courses that I had taken and tell her what I thought, how it could be improved and so on. The course registration and advisor connected was, if anything, probably the most successful and pleasant experience. It was easy to contact my advisor and she delivered clear information
registration_success: I got all the classes that I signed up for, so very successful.
registration_advice: Be in good time and be independent. The link that is first provided for courses only gives you the title and very little information, so I found my courses based on the title - but I had to independently search (on google) for the syllabus to see what it was about. So be independent and don't be afraid to ask lots of questions!
