course_level: The level changed depending on the course. I had one course which was not very academic and where we had complete freedom in regards to our assignments. Then I had an International Relations course which was a bit more demanding for me, because it was very theoretical with a high focus on theories that I had never been taught at UCPH - And the rest of the class had, so I had to work a bit harder. I pretty much only had sociology/political science course even though I am from humanities and that was just extremely satisfying and fascinating. And apart from the very theoretical-heavy course the others were fine. In general there is a lot more to do. Apart from my language course which I had approximately 7 hours a week I had 5 other courses. In Denmark I normally have 2. I had classes 20 hours a week and many of them had midterm assignments, multiple presentations, critical reflections for homework and all had a big final exam. I wrote approximately 5 final assignments assignments (all around 10 pages). Then the Hebrew language course had a lot of homework and assignments during the semester as well as three final exams; oral, written and listening. So even though the classes themselves weren't harder or more difficult that what I was used to at Copenhagen University the workload during the semester was much harder and the final exams in all courses were also much more demanding. Also important to note that everything is in English, so if future exchange students are not so comfortable in that - especially writing - then it is quite challenging for them - especially the exams will be difficult. I've studied at an international university before so for me it was not a problem at all, I actually thrived in it, but it is something to bear in mind.
teaching_comparison: It was better. This was partly because we were more people in the classes compared to home, but in general it was just very structured and organized , whereas my teacher at UCPH is extremely unstructured and unorganized and this impacts the teaching. But in general it was very similar to what one would expect at a danish university.
courses_enrolled: Winter Ulpan (one month prior to semester start) Hebrew Language course (Modern Hebrew) Globalization, Education and Inequality Bi-Nationalism in Israel / Palestine Theories of International Relations and Realities in the Middle East The Arab Society and Arab Education in Israel Making News: Pluralistic Journalism in New and Old Media
recommended_courses: Globalization, Education and Inequality. It was my absolutely favorite course; the teacher was excellent and so so talented, the dynamic in the classroom was good (there were mainly Israeli students and we were only 4 international students). The course was so well-organized and it all made so much sense, both during the semester as well as in the end. From beginning to end the course just worked so well! Making News: Pluralistic Journalism in New and Old Media - was also a really interesting course; it was different from what I expected but it ended up being quite interesting. It was also well-taught, the assignments made sense and the teacher was very talented as well
unexpected_costs: There were no utensils, pots or pans or bedsheets - nothing in the dorms, so we had to buy everything ourselves.
cost_comparison: It was a bit more expensive than expected - I have been in Israel many times so I knew that it would be expensive but the prices and the shekel has just gone up, so everything was a bit more expensive.
activities_available: There was a very expensive sports club connected to the University with swimming pool, tennis and a training-center. I did not sign up for it, but my roommate did and was somewhat satisfied with it. I think it was way too expensive for what it offered and I bought a yoga mat instead and a few of the girls had a running club. I also joined a Wattsapp group for university football and two of my roommates participated in university rugby. Furthermore I did a Krav Maga class. A lot of the opportunities cost money and took a lot of hours from other activities.
activities_recommended: I have a looong list! But in general just to familiarize yourself with the city. And find some other students to travel with. I traveled with either the girls from my dorm or other students and it was a good way to see the country. I had been to many of the cities before but it was great being there with people my own age and with like-minded interests.
weekend_recommendations: The rest of the country! See every city you can visit and walk around Jerusalem as much as possible. If you want something similar to Tel Aviv - with a beach, clubs/bars/shopping and easy going people go to Haifa. If you want to see an Arab city within Israel then go to Nazareth and talk to the locals. If you want total relaxation and great diving experiences go to Eilat. And then go to the West Bank and talk to people there as well.
culture_adjustment: I found it very easy, but I have been in Israel many times. In the beginning I was a bit worried about living in Jerusalem because of the tensions and all the religious people, but I found Jerusalem to be so relaxing - Especially where I lived. The dorm is up by the university and the area was very quiet and relaxing, so that helped. And then it was just really fascinating finding little corners of the city which you only find if you live there. But the mentality of - especially the Israelis are different and often difficult. They can be very rude and insensitive, so best be prepared for that. Some of my fellow students and/or roommates found it either very difficult or had controversies with people. But if you have a somewhat laissez faire mentality then it will not problem. And notice that they don't do it to be evil but that their mentality is just different from the Danish - and that is okay. You are also in a new country, so that is also part of the experience.
socializing_tips: Take a language course - Here I met many of the people that I became friends with and some of them introduced me to other people I became friends with. Live in a dorm - I lived with 8 other girls so I was automatically socializing with people. Don't stress - If there are days where you don't have anything to do or don't hang out with people, don't stress about it. I was so extremely happy to just be on exchange which impacted my mentality. Where I can sometimes stress a bit and feel like I'm the only one without plans, in Israel I was just happy to be in Jerusalem and be on exchange that even just walking to the grocery store alone became a great experience. Take initiative - I live in a dorm in Copenhagen as well so I took some of the traditions and ideas that we do here with me to Israel. I started a food club for the girls at my dorm - we only had one stove and food in Israel is expensive, so to combat that I started the food club. They were all really happy with the idea and I even organized one big food club where I cooked for 15 people outside of the dorm. So be creative and don't be afraid to take initiative. I also organized a shabbat dinner for a few people where we all brought something, so it can be both big and small initiatives. Sometimes it can be something as simple as asking someone if they are also going to the grocery store and then go together.
cultural_challenges: Again, I have been in Israel many times so not really. It was difficult seeing so many religious people and where others found it fascinating - which I of course did to some degree - I mostly found it infuriating. I realized just how amazing Denmark is but also how radical we are in our way of having religious symbols or in general being religious and how we connect through other things than religion. So it made me appreciate Denmark and I could sometimes just relax and not talk religion or politics with people, but religion is very much 'in your face' in Israel and that was a bit stressful and something which I did not like. I had one incident where I was wearing shorts in a supermarket which was mostly dominated by religious Jews and I got quite nasty looks from - mostly the Jewish women. So the religiousness of, especially Jerusalem, sort of limited my sense of freedom.
culture_appreciated: The warmth of some of the people. As annoying, insensitive and extremely rude the Israelis can be, they equally can be so so sweet and warm. The same goes for the Palestinians. In general a lot of the people were so sweet and willing to talk and take interest in you. And it was also really nice to connect with like-minded people, both in university and outside. It was nice to be with people who really wanted to be there and who also shared the same interests as me. And in general both the Israelis and Palestinians are wonderful people with fascinating (as well as tragic) stories and just being in the country for a long time was a big experience
top3_advice: Be prepared to be independent, be flexible and enjoy your time. Be independent and prepared to do a lot of work yourself. This is very rewarding in the long run, both personally but also academically! Be flexible - things might be chaotic or messy but learn to go along with it and learn from these experiences. This is also extremely rewarding personally. Enjoy your time! - Don't stress or try to force something: everyone has different exchange experiences and everyday might not be filled with instagram-worthy events, but learn to find little spots in the city (or other cities) and share them with people. Everyday is unique and it really is over before you know it.
other_useful_info: Bring lots of money and/or apply for funds. Have an open mind but be stern and a bit tough if people are rude or not helpful. Sometimes it helps to shout or write a tons of emails, so don't be afraid to "get in there". I lived with a german girl who was very shy and had a hard time that everything was not like in Germany. She had such a hard time, where as the other girls were a bit more flexible and pro-active and in general took things a little easier, so we had so much fun and great experiences. And remember, the mentality is different but no one is being rude or insensitive just to be rude - often times they don't think about it. And it's also extremely healthy to experience other cultures and mentalities and learning to take everything a little lighter can also be a rewarding experience. And remember to be flexible! You're in a new country and sometimes the Israeli way is chaotic or messy but this is equally a part of the experience and not necessarily a bad or a worse way of doing things.
most_rewarding: How independent I can be and how flexible I truly am. I've always thought I was both, but I truly learned that I am very good with adapting to new things and just going with the flow - I also learned how little stuff (clothes, gadgets etc) I can do with, which is a valuable lesson for future travels. And then how independent I can be; I truly did pretty much all of my preparations prior to my exchange on my own with no help (beside one lecturer) and even though it was not fun (at all), it has prepared me for the future. And then I learned that if I want to take a master in another country I can definitely do that. It sounds so sentimental to say that it changed me as a person, because I think a lot of the features that I take with me were already there, but now I'm more affirmed and secure in my abilities. And of course meeting the people I met and learning the things I did. The people, whether it be the girls from my dorm or the teachers or other students just contributed to this being a good experience. And the course were just amazing and really made this worthwhile. While I might not see the people more, I still have so much knowledge from my course that have taken with me home.
greatest_challenge: Everything prior to the exchange - but perhaps in someways the challenges before I could go probably also made everything very worthwhile. So even though it was extremely tiring and mentally tough, being on exchange was worth it and I miss it everyday.
other_comments: Go go go! It was simply the best experience ever and I miss Israel, Hebrew University and the people every single day.

crucial_aspects: The Israeli-Palestinian conflict
info_ease: It was relatively easy. But you have to be patient, because information comes at different times, and often a bit late.
arrival_assistance: none
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You look through the catalogue beforehand and choose the courses you find interesting, and then you have an arranged video call with one of the professors at the university that will help you sign up for the courses.
registration_success: Successful! i got all the classes i wanted
registration_advice: Rothberg Courses are easier, gives more credit, and they are shorter than the courses at the faculty (they kind of reminds of high school/gymnasie courses). But the faculty courses are more academically challenging.
course_level: Rothberg Courses are easier, gives more credit, and they are shorter than the courses at the faculty (they kind of reminds of high school/gymnasie courses). But the faculty courses are more academically challenging -> i did some MA courses that were on my level from my BA in CPH.
teaching_comparison: Rothberg is teaching based, and the Faculty is research based. So it depends on the courses you take - i would say the faculty courses feel more similar to the ones in KU.
courses_enrolled: Spring semester: Seeing Space walking contemporary Jerusalem seeing with multiple lenses Holy Ecology Environmental Aspects of Contemporary Jerusalem Smart Cities and Sustainable Mobility Ecosystems Data Project: Data for Managing the Smart City From the Dome of the Rock to the Taj Mahal (Rothberg) Geography of light pollution
recommended_courses: In general i would recommend to take courses that has field trips, they are free and you get to discover the area. I even went to Akko with a course which was really nice! Geography of light pollution if you study geography, physics or something related. It is a very unique course. The course has 2 field trips and the lectures are recorded and uploaded on youtube so you can watch it whenever you have time.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay for a TOEFL test (800 kr) before going.
cost_comparison: Israel is VERY expensive. Expect the grocery prices to be double the price as in Copenhagen and eating out is also expensive - but falafel is usually relatively cheap. Alcohol is expensive (except for happy hour). Public transportation is OK and it is relatively cheap to go outside of Jerusalem (to Tel Aviv/Jaffa, Haifa/Akko, etc.)
activities_available: They arrange day trips (dead sea, jaffa, night trip to the desert) that you have to pay for
activities_recommended: - Go to hataklit or record to drink a beer and dance at video or pergammon afterwards. - Go to Ramallah, betlehem. Palestinians are sooo nice, and these areas are amazing. And they are open during shabbat and public transportation still runs to these areas. But watch out for the news, things happens all the time with raids in the West Bank, etc. - Go hiking! Israel/palestine is a small country, so its easy to take the bus and walk in the many national parks that they have. - Explore the old city (temple mount, wailing wall, walk on the walls, eat great food, sit on the rooftop, etc.)
weekend_recommendations: Read the above. Go to Eilat, Haifa, Nazareth for a weekend trip. In Haifa the public transport runs even during shabbat! Go to Egypt and Jordan! It requires a bit of planning, but it is so worth it. I went to Cairo, Alexandria in Egypt and i went to Amman, Aqaba, Petra and Wadi Rum in Jordan. Amman and Cairo is especially nice and Petra and Wadi Rum is a MUST, some of the most beautiful sights in the world...
culture_adjustment: It was not that difficult for me personally, but for some other people it might be difficult. There are a LOT of soldiers and civilians walking around with giant weapons. It is a very diverse culture in Jerusalem with jewish, christian and arab influence. When you first arrive you feel like you are in a movie with the Haredi (jewish) people walking around with their special attire and looks...
socializing_tips: I didnt spend much time with local students. But i had classes with them and i went occasionally on tinder dates with them. They are very friendly and open - way more than Danish people. They are willing to make friends with exchange students!
cultural_challenges: If you think you know anything about the israeli-palestinian conflict.. you will be even more confused when you arrive. Palestinians will tell you one thing and Israelis will tell you another thing. That is also why it is difficult to have this conversation with the locals about this conflict. Stay open, and remember you are just a foreigner that in reality doesnt know anything.
culture_appreciated: Food!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! Falafel, hummus, sabich, dolmades.... I will miss this so much when i go back home. The weather was nice. Jerusalem is not as humid as the cities located at the coast, which is highly appreciated in the summer.
top3_advice: - Go travel. Go to palestine, that should be mandatory! You can easily take the bus to Jordan and Egypt as well - they are amazing countries! - Dont spend too much time on studying - EAT FALAFEL!
other_useful_info: !!IMPORTANT!!! When studying at HUJI, you need to have 20 credits which KU says is the same as 30 ETCS. In reality, ALL the exchange students at HUJI have 15 credits, which HUJI says is the same as 30 ETCS. So if you study at HUJI, you have to expect to study more if you want to do 30 ETCS point in total. I ended up doing 15 credits, so i only returned home with 22,5 ETCS points...
most_rewarding: Getting to know about middle eastern culture.
greatest_challenge: Reading about the awful things happening in the West Bank while i am in Jerusalem, and knowing theres nothing you can do.

crucial_aspects: That they offered courses on continental philosophy, which my home university doesn't! Also, the fact that it was in Germany as i had a wish, both academically and personally to learn German. my original plan was also to go with my, now, Ex-girlfriend and since it was an EU4+ Uni, there were enough spots in the exchange program for us both. that plan didn't materialize as we broke up, it was however a plus that there were more students from my home country as it helped me deal with bouts of longing for home.
info_ease: not that easy - not alot of information online and the systems that are in place are confusing... when however i realized that germany barely has begun its digitalization and that most things require that you show up in person or call at certain very limited office hours, it was easier to figure out if not to actually succeed with.
arrival_assistance: a great buddy program, a couple of introductory days and some great student tutors - but not a lot of helpt from the Administration...
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: i received my matrikkelnr. too late to apply to certain courses. in several of the courses you had to write directly to the professor or show up at the start of classes in order to register. also several courses utilized two different online systems at the same time - i had to apply to both... examine registartion was pretty simple though
registration_help: other students? my buddy and my tutors...
registration_success: after much struggle i succeeded for the most part - the piont system was confusing though and i ended up taking too many courses...
registration_advice: get help from the student body, they know how shit works
course_level: the level was way higher than at my sending institution but i never felt like i couldn't follow - questions and discussion was highly encouraged and the educators very helpful. overall an A+ experience
teaching_comparison: better... smaller courses, both when it came to the amount of students and the amount of points, much more specialized and in-depth. lots of seminar work, not a lot of lecturing which encouraged that students worked with the material themselves.
courses_enrolled: Jaspers&Sartre Phänomenologie und psychopathologie der Affektivität Cost of Comfort Wiederholung Introduktion to philosophy
recommended_courses: all of them! the courses change each semester though so it wont be possible... Phäno&psycho is taught by the leading researcher in psychiatric phenomenology and is great! the introduction to philosophy is a bit boring but really helpfull in order to get the terminology specific to the field in german!
unexpected_costs: some necessary insurances... the high price for internet
cost_comparison: food were cheaper - cafés, restaurants and bars as well...accommodation was pretty cheap too
activities_available: sports... a few classical concerts i guess a litterature festival
activities_recommended: go out a lot!
weekend_recommendations: go to cave54 on tuesdays for jazznight, boho for socializing on monday nights. hang on the neckarwiese when its sunny, and when really hot go to the tiergardenschwimbad. go on weekendtrips with the other Erasmus students and maybe go to bodensee or Tübingen or something
culture_adjustment: relatively easy!
socializing_tips: dont be afraid to ask if people want to drink a cup of coffee or weineschörle after class - people are more outgoing than in in denmark and the city is small enough that fresh blood from exchange students is fascinating to the local students!
cultural_challenges: the supermarkets sucked... the bike lanes were nonexisting and traffic rules confusing
culture_appreciated: the openness
top3_advice: its okay to be tired and say no! prioritizing both social, academic and recreational time is important it is easier than you think to establish a network have fun with it! everything will work out
other_useful_info: ask questions if there is something you don't understand, it'll spare both you and your professors time, and most people are very understanding! confusion is normal when you arrive at a new place but it only goes away if you ask the questions
most_rewarding: the social and cultural parts.
greatest_challenge: the language barrier

crucial_aspects: I would very much like to try to expand my German language in order to be able to use these skills in the things I wanted to do at KU. At the same time, the German language has also been a general interest of mine, and something had to be done to take it seriously. That's why I wanted to do an exchange in Heidelberg.
info_ease: Very gut. Much is done physically in Germany, so there is always an open office you can come to if you have any questions. Information on where and how has usually been sent in various emails in the past. So it's a good idea to be aware of it and get it in order before you arrive.
arrival_assistance: There are dedicated Erasmus staff available. In addition, there are introductory days where all of the relavans are reviewed. However, you are also responsible for making all the information useful in the sense that it is all unclear until you try it yourself.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You start receiving instructions about six months before. After that, a process starts in which you have to fill in various documents regularly.
registration_help: When you had questions, you could always write an email to the Erasmus staff. However, you are often redirected or it takes a long time. You have to be proactive and write the same email several times to several people.
registration_success: I just showed up and asked if I could participate. Otherwise, it is also normal to write an email directly to the teacher with the same request. It was very charming and a plus of the conservative approaches.
registration_advice: Be patient and do things at the pace they occur. Although I'm still not convinced it will all work out, enough people say it will.
course_level: I took both Hauptseminar and Vorlesungen. There is a lot of work to do. Though not as reading-heavy as I've been used to at KU, but it was also very conditional to my Professor Roland Reuß method. So hard to say anything in general, as I'm sure it depends on many things.
teaching_comparison: Much more detail-oriented. There was no hurry. Often we spent a week going through half a page. At KU, it was usually 300-400 pages you had to go through.
courses_enrolled: Hölderlin, Hyperion Tagebücher - Kafka, Musil, Doderer, Jünger Lyrik & Edition Vorlesung Wiederholung - Kierkegaard bis zum Deleuze
recommended_courses: Those you can choose bei Herr. Reuß or Herr. König
unexpected_costs: Much more expensive rent due to relocation
cost_comparison: Rent. And food too. It not like in Berlin or the northern part of Germany. It it really like Denmark in the 'south' of Germany
activities_available: Everything between heaven and earth of sport. Even rowing and more 'narrow' sports. Culturally, I was under the impression that you had to go to Mannheim. In Heidelberg there are not many opportunities. However, a theatre and a concert hall, which were fine. By the way, the theatre is free for students
activities_recommended: Be with friends and walk in the forrest.
weekend_recommendations: Be with friends and walk in the forrest.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. The people and culture are much like the one we know in Denmark.
socializing_tips: It's a difficult balance, but my impression was that it comes if you just show interest and be open minded. But it's hard to give advice on such complex issues.
cultural_challenges: The politeness and conservatism of the language you should be aware of.
culture_appreciated: The general openness and unpretentious kind of coziness that can arise in smaller towns like Heidelberg. And the language and literature. And music etc.
top3_advice: Be patient with all the formalities. There are a lot of them and you will definitely be stressed because you are so often looking for answers to all sorts of questions. Also consider that semester times are staggered, which also makes things and practicalities harder to deal with.
other_useful_info: Nothing further.
most_rewarding: To get an insight into how universities and Germany work and the opportunity to learn the language. They are very proud of all their 'Great'-Geist-personalites. And it's a pleasure to get an insight into, if you're interested
greatest_challenge: Keeping calm with all the paperwork and finding a new place to stay after arrival.

crucial_aspects: My original destination, New Zealand, was cancelled due to COVID-19. Learning the german language and learning about the german academic tradition as well as german society, culture and history. Getting international friends was important to me as well.
info_ease: Most information was easy to find, it was mainly hard to find information on the whole process of choosing courses, how to register and how many ECTS-credits they would give, they have another system in Heidelberg.
arrival_assistance: Information on what to do was provided via e-mail. I just had to print a lot of documents, get them signed and deliver them to a mail box.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Depends on the course, the professors might have different processes for their courses. This was really confusing, there was not one standardized procedure like in Copenhagen.
registration_help: Just trying to send e-mails to the administration, but the most effective help was talking to other students.
registration_success: I managed to in the end, but I was unsure until the day the classes had already started.
registration_advice: Go to Heidelberg a month before the semester starts, take the language course offered in this month. That extra time to get settled in is valuable. Join the buddy programme and ask what is the most sensible thing to do for your study area/faculty.
course_level: They were master's level
teaching_comparison: My impression is, there is a lot of focus on memorising a lot in the german academic culture. Less mandatory group work/presentations in Heidelberg compared to Copenhagen. Could also just be the courses i chose.
courses_enrolled: An introduction to machine learning Aromaten und Heteroaromaten Bioinformatics & computational biology Chemie und Biochemie der Alkaloide Pharmazeutische Biologie: Arzneipflanzen, biogene Arzneistoffe, Biotechnologie Pharmazeutische/Medizinische Chemie Programming Curse with Python for Biologists
unexpected_costs: I had to buy a lot of kitchen equipment, because I expected that to be there as I was moving into a dormitory.
cost_comparison: Public transportation was more expensive than I expected. But you can buy a "semester-ticket" for approximately 170 euro with which you can travel in the area of Heidelberg for the semester.
activities_available: A lot of Erasmus related events were available, of all kind. You can go to the theater often for free when you're a student.
activities_recommended: Take part in the language courses at Max Weber Haus. Go travel to German cities, there are a lot of interesting cities and historical sites around Heidelberg.
weekend_recommendations: Go visit the nearby cities (Mannheim, Speyer, Schwetzingen are all a visit worth) and go hiking in Odenwald and Schwarzwald (go see Freiburg as well).
culture_adjustment: It was okay, it helps to take a language course before the semester starts and meet som people. Become friends with at least one person who is german and knows the area, that is a big advantage.
socializing_tips: Be an extrovert, else its near impossible to get into a group of germans
cultural_challenges: None, it was just hard to get into an only german speaking class and socialize.
culture_appreciated: The language and history
top3_advice: Be open to learning the language and take advantage of the language courses, they are free for erasmus+. Seek to talk german from the beginning and make use of the many interesting travel destinations in southern germany. Don't worry so much about the course registration, you can just show up after they have startet
other_useful_info: Try to get a room through the "Studierendenwerk" because otherwise it can be difficult to find a room to a reasonable price.

Also trying to get into a german social group at the university was near impossible, but there is always the erasmus-group.

crucial_aspects: As I had already learned German for an exchange that were cancelled due to COVID, it was crucial that it was in Germany. Besides that, the most crucial aspect was the academic opportunities - I wanted to explore a different academic culture with another approach on a high level. Other important aspects was that it was a beautiful city and close to nature.
overall_comments: It was such an amazing experience! I have learned so much, I really gained inside into the culture of Heidelberg and got to know many locals and I made some really nice friends and also had a bit of time for travelling. I am VERY happy, that I took this opportunity, and it has definitely been a formative experience for me. When it doesn't score a perfect 10, it is because the workload at the university could be quite overwhelming and because it was sometimes quite a struggle to find my way through German bureaucracy.
info_ease: This was surely one of the most challenging aspects of the exchange. Everyone was very helpful, but the whole process is spread across many institutions, so it can be quite difficult to know who to ask for help - the history department in DK, the international department there, the history department in Heidelberg, the international department there, the city municipality in Heidelberg, the Studierendenwerk etc.
arrival_assistance: As mentioned above, people at all the abovementioned institutions were very helpful. When I came with questions they helped answering them, but I wasn't always sure what to ask were. I came a month before my exhange began for a language course, which meant that the introductory meetings that were given came at a time when I no longer needed the information.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was such an amazing experience! I have learned so much, I really gained inside into the culture of Heidelberg and got to know many locals and I made some really nice friends and also had a bit of time for travelling. I am VERY happy, that I took this opportunity, and it has definitely been a formative experience for me. When it doesn't score a perfect 10, it is because the workload at the university could be quite overwhelming and because it was sometimes quite a struggle to find my way through German bureaucracy.
registration_process: I registered from home during the summer. Then I went there in the end of August, but as the semester didn't start until 1st of October, it took some time, before I could register. I honestly cannot remember the whole process, but there were some meetings to guide us through the process, and then you fill out a few papers and give to a few persons. You also pay a fee of around 200 Euros for the semester.
registration_help: As mentioned above, there were a few meetings. You could come to both History Department and International Department with questions, but you didn't always know what to ask or where to go.
registration_success: Very! I had a lot of really great courses and I got everything I wanted. But you have to write the professor or assistant to register (google "Kommentiertes Vorlesungsverzeichnis Heidelberg Geschichte" to see the courses and who to write), and a few courses were already full at that point.
registration_advice: If you want to be sure to get the courses you want, look for subjects in good time. The course catalogue is usually published 2/3 months before the start of the semester, and you can register even before you enroll. Just write the professor of the course, most of them are super nice AND I had a prejudice about Germany being super strict and always following the rules very thoroughly. But the process of registering for courses was a lot more relaxed than in Denmark. In the start, I was panicking about deadlines coming up and still not receiving a lot of information on courses. But then I discovered, that I just needed to be more patient, as everything worked out in the end. People also register for more classes than they need and go to all in the first week to hear more, after that they decide. There is a second registration for exams later in the semester, and that is really the binding registration.
academics_comments: It was such an amazing experience! I have learned so much, I really gained inside into the culture of Heidelberg and got to know many locals and I made some really nice friends and also had a bit of time for travelling. I am VERY happy, that I took this opportunity, and it has definitely been a formative experience for me. When it doesn't score a perfect 10, it is because the workload at the university could be quite overwhelming and because it was sometimes quite a struggle to find my way through German bureaucracy.
course_level: Many people study their BA in Heidelberg and then go elsewhere (typically Berlin) for the MA. This means, that there is a somewhat limited number of MA-Students in Heidelberg, and classes often combine BA- and MA-studentes. Perhaps because of my difficulties with the language of teaching, I still found it quite challenging, it is a really high level.
teaching_comparison: You have a lot of different formats in comparison to Denmark. The Vorlesungen are like the Danish Forelæsninger with a teacher talking and students asking questions in the end. But e.g. Übungen and Kolloquien are mainly student-driven. In general, the teaching is more driven by students than in Denmark. It is harder to get by, if you haven't read beforehand, and students are asked to think somewhat more freely than in Denmark, I found (somewhat surprisingly) - for example, in several subjects I had to develop my own research design in a degree of freedom, that I only know from my BA-thesis in Denmark. You also work with more personal academic genres, like essays (a la Susan Sontag) and Blogs.
courses_enrolled: - Kunst und Kultur in der Krise in den „roaring twenties“ - 2 ECTS - Körper(um)welten (Marsiliusbrückenseminar) - „Alleinstehende Frauen“, „Freundinnen“, „Frauenliebende Frauen“ - Lesbische Lebenswelten im deutschen Südwesten (ca. 1920er-1960er Jahre) - Geschichtsphilosophie - „Auf der Suche nach der verlorenen Wahrheit.“ Begriff und Problem der Wahrheit in der Geschichtswissenschaft zwischen Historismus und Gegenwart - Multisensory Histories: Archives and Methods in South Asian Studies - Violence and Non-Violence in Colonial India
recommended_courses: If you have the possiblity, take part in a Marsilius-Brücken Seminar!! They are interdisciplinary seminars, where you develop a project on your own and then discuss it. I had one on the relationship between bodies and environments between history, ethnography, literary studies and biologies - and it was definitely one of the most interesting courses I ever had. There is a lot to choose from, but I was especially happy for Kama Maclean and Karen Nolte. Both where very helpful, when I didn't get things as a foreigner, and they both have an innovating and exciting approach to teaching and research.
unexpected_costs: The prices for internet and telephone. It is quite a lot more expensive than in Denmark and most often you are obliged to pay for at least two years, so that was really unhandy. I got someone to take over my internet as I left and I bought "taletid" at ALDI (ALDI TALK), because it is without binding. But I lost the SIM-card and got lazy, so I just used my Danish phone, even though my free roaming went away after two months and it got crazy expensive. Food, personal spending and transport can be done quite a lot cheaper, I lived the good life.
cost_comparison: Alcohol and candy are cheap, so that's nice. Housing was a lot cheaper than expected and food in the Cantina/Mensa is also quite cheap. I was surprised of the prices for phone and internet.
activities_available: BUDDY-program, where you get set up with a fulltime student from your subject, who can show you around and often make friends with. ENS (Erasmus Student Network) arranges A LOT of events for exchange students, which I used a lot in the start to make friends. They have a lot of high school sports, a choir, a student council, a philharmonic orchestra etc. I was not involved in this, but if there hadn't been a pandemic, they had a lot of fun alternative sports really cheap.
activities_recommended: Two institutions were decisive for my stay in Heidelberg. One is Clemens in the bookstore "Artes Liberales" - he is really friendly, has an amazing knowledge of literature and does a lot for the local community. He has the bookstore as well as "Universitas", another room which you can loan, where he makes weekly readings and a lot of other events. He even agreed to make a reading group for me and a few friends - every second week he would bring wine and teach us about great literature and the German language for free! His "Stammkneipe" is called Orange, and it is the most wonderful place I have ever been to. The owners Claudia and Osama are incredibly friendly. As I didn't feel so well at my home in Heidelberg, this bar really became a second home to me. I made a lot of friends there from actors and musicians at the Heidelberger Theater to the old secretary of Gadamer, who also studied by Koselleck. Through this bar I really got integrated in the local intellectual environment, in a way I did not think possible.
weekend_recommendations: Try to spend as much time as possible in Orange. Apart from that take advantage of the fact, that you are living in the middle of Europe - it is so easy and cheap to get to Alsace and Strassbourg, to Frankfurt, to Freiburg and Schwarzwald or to Basel. So travel as much as you can, I discovered this a tad late, but still had some nice travels in Germany, France and Italy. Also discover the Odenwald and go hike in the mountains as often as possible, as they will be right by your doorstep.
culture_adjustment: There was a language barrier to overcome, but after that I found it surprisingly easy - I do not think there are really large cultural differences between Germany and Denmark
socializing_tips: ORANGE!!! And try picking courses in German, I was often the only non-German in class, which meant that people took an interest in me and were really friendly. "Local" is also not a very meaningful thing in Heidelberg, as most students come from other cities to study in Heidelberg. I only met one person born in Heidelberg during my stay. As the city is 25 % students, this means that most people are really eager to get to know others, as everyone is in the same boat.
cultural_challenges: Language and academic culture. People were patient and helpful, but the course formats are quite different, as are the exams.
culture_appreciated: As an old university city, it is quite snobbish. This can be quite disgusting, as when people in Heidelberg critique the neighboring Mannheim for being more working class. But it also means, that there is a great interest in history, literature and philosophy, which you can discuss with most people. Also the Theater is free for students, meaning you have access to endless plays, concerts and dance performances. I really appreciated the opennes, people were in general a lot more friendly than expected and really made me feel at home.
top3_advice: 1. Learn German. I was in no way fluent as I arrived, and had to struggle with this for the first few months. But by learning German I had access to a lot more interesting courses as well as making friends with German students and other inhabitants in the city. I think my stay would have been quite different, if I didn't know German. 2. Balance your study - I was quite bad at this and got really stressed at times, because of the huge workload. So accept that you are going to perform mediocre and then just delve into the things you find the most interesting. 3. Travel a lot! I discovered this too late, but in the end I went somewhere every weekend. You can easily go somewhere like Karlsruhe or Bad Wimpfen to just spend the day there, and with one night in a hostel, you also have time to see Freiburg or Strassbourg.
other_useful_info: Yes, go to Orange as often as you can :)
most_rewarding: My academic gain! I really learned a lot here and feel like I grew from a student just attending classes to someone who has a clear understanding of the direction in which I want to research.
greatest_challenge: Probably the German bureaucracy. All the different phone numbers, things that cannot be done online, the running to letterboxes and being passed on to the next office. I understand why Kafka wrote "The Trial" in German. And Weber even developed his theory of Bureaucracy in Heidelberg, which makes sense to me :)
other_comments: Go there, have fun, stay in school!

housing_how: I found housing on my own

activities_available: I know you could join volleyball and I think football as well. I don't really remember what else

crucial_aspects: A german-speaking country since I wished to improve my German language skills. Also a smaller student friendly city.
info_ease: It was alright. The University was good at sending information about studentcard etc. (however a little bit confusing with insurance and documents needing to be send), and the hospital informed me well about dates and meeting points.
arrival_assistance: There was a lot of offers from the university about introduction days to the city and uni, but it wasn't relevant for me since I was primarily at the hospital for an internship and already knew the city well from being there some time.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Lots of email during the time before my exchange - but everything was pretty clear. Maybe a little confusing what was for my home university and what was for the host university, but other than that fine. I got set up with a coordinator at the hospital, where I had my internship and they were very nice at putting together a schedule according to my wishes.
registration_help: The coordinators at my home university was really a big help in the process - when I was unsure about the next step or information from my host uni, they were really good at clearing and confirming whatever I was unsure about.
registration_success: Didn't take classes, but internship at hospital. I got the three department that I asked for and also during the time period that I wanted - this was through email correspondence with the coordinator at the hospital.
registration_advice: Follow the instructions given by email - and don't stress about it. It takes some times but all the necessary informations and steps will be reach before arrival. Use your coordinator at your home university - they were super nice and very professionel.
course_level: NA
teaching_comparison: In general I find the internships in Denmark more well planned with good introductions to the department and information about your learning goals and expectations, which was not the case here. Depended a lot on the department and staff but in general the responsibility for learning is on yourself. When that said, the staff was very nice and there were lots of things to see, participate in and learn - you just have to be very outreaching.
courses_enrolled: Internship at hospital
recommended_courses: Try and visit a couple of different departments. It is nice to see something different, but also nice to stay a bit longer in one place so you get more comfortable with the people, tasks, etc.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Lived up to my expectations.
activities_available: Didn't use any, but I know that there were really good sport offers through the uni with many sports to choose from and affordable prices. There was a very nice canteen (Mensa) at the Uni, which was a really good hangout spot for students - sometimes events, flee markets etc.
activities_recommended: Many nice cafes and bars to meet after uni. There are quite a lot of outdoor ping pong tables around Heidelberg which we enjoyed a lot for playing and hanging out. There is also some outdoor pools, which were nice to go to on warm days and also a really nice boulder hall a little outside of town. Spend time exploring the different neighborhoods.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the mountains around Heidelberg, Philosophenweg, Thingstätte. Take small trips to smaller towns along the Neckar. Visit Klosterhof (a nice small brewery in the hills). Just enjoy the cafes and bars of the city and make sure to visit the different neighbourhoods of the town.
culture_adjustment: In general life it was very easy. At the hospital it was more of a challenge, since they do some things so different from Denmark - but that was also something I really enjoyed; to see and experience all the differences. It also took me some months to feel comfortable in the German language.
socializing_tips: Live with local students. I met a lot of people through the few German friends I got in the beginning - just say yes to everything people invite you to. Heidelberg is such a small town full of students, that you will meet the same people again and again, which make it very comfortable and easy to get to know people.
cultural_challenges: Mostly the language. It was also a bit difficult to navigate in the hospital - what I was allowed to do, what was expected of me etc.
culture_appreciated: I really enjoyed living in a smaller town that still had such a vibrant student life with filled cafes and bars. Also getting an insight in a different health system through the internships was interesting.
top3_advice: - Really try and speak the language even if you don't feel comfortable at first. It is really rewarding learning a new language and something I really enjoyed. Wished I had tried a little harder from the beginning. - Spend the weekends in the city and explore the place you are living instead of traveling too much around. Heidelberg is such a beautiful place to live and many things too do - Take a language course. You will meet a lot of people right away and get into the language quickly.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Getting out of my familiar settings and meeting some wonderfull new people. It was also very fun to learn a new language and experience the different culture in the hospital. Also living in such beautiful surroundings.
