crucial_aspects: I know that the physics departments in Germany are good, which led me to look at Heidelberg. Later, I discovered that there were courses in Neutrino Physics which I was really interested in taking, especially since the structure was nothing like the course structure at my home university. I spoke to a professor who turned out to have worked at an institute closely related to the university, and she encouraged me to go down and reach out to this institute, and it just so happened that a few of the professors associated with the course I was looking forward to were dual hired between the university and the institute. Going to Germany has always been a dream - there is something very different about going away from tiny Denmark, and just seeing how huge everything is down here and the possibilities that allows for, has changed something in my way of thinking about what a university has the possibility of being.
overall_comments: One thing that was slightly has to adjust to was the change in examination - Normally at my home university I do quite well, but down here I was afraid I would not pass the courses - not because of difficulty, but they relied more on memorization and not having access to any of the material used dutring the course. This I struggled with in the last few few, and I know all of my fellow Scandinavian Erasmus students struggled with as well. Not sure what can be done about that, but it was a major headache the last couple of weeks.
info_ease: I seemed to have struggled with it - I did not have access to any of the university when I arrived and showed up to get some university identification and found out I had missed my first lecture. I then spent the first week trying to figure out what courses to take, because the ones I had picked apparently where overlapping a lot - So the first week was stressful and I did not have the information on my email, as it only came to the Heidelberg University email.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance from the university about how to access the online portal of the university - however, it was other students who told me where to find all this information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: One thing that was slightly has to adjust to was the change in examination - Normally at my home university I do quite well, but down here I was afraid I would not pass the courses - not because of difficulty, but they relied more on memorization and not having access to any of the material used dutring the course. This I struggled with in the last few few, and I know all of my fellow Scandinavian Erasmus students struggled with as well. Not sure what can be done about that, but it was a major headache the last couple of weeks.
registration_process: First you register online with a code, to get a University account (and if you forget your code, you physically have to go to the it department). For physics, you can then register for courses on the LSF site for Heidelberg, although some professors want you to sign up in Moodle. However to find out what the course is about, you need to go on to Üebungen, which you only have access to as a student.
registration_help: The IT-department, and then I contacted the Erasmus department because I did not know who else to contact, but they did not get back fro several weeks.
registration_success: unsuccessful in regards to my original choices, because there was no way of knowing the schedule until April - and I only found out late in April, as I did not have a University account.
registration_advice: Write very far in advance to try to figure out if they already know that courses will be overlapping - and make sure you have a back up. I relied on my fellow students, which I should not have to - but I did not have information about who to contact.
academics_comments: One thing that was slightly has to adjust to was the change in examination - Normally at my home university I do quite well, but down here I was afraid I would not pass the courses - not because of difficulty, but they relied more on memorization and not having access to any of the material used dutring the course. This I struggled with in the last few few, and I know all of my fellow Scandinavian Erasmus students struggled with as well. Not sure what can be done about that, but it was a major headache the last couple of weeks.
course_level: The courses relied much more on the individual professor than at UCPH. The professors generally did not follow books, but rather their own set of lecture notes. This was quite frustrating when you are used to following a book, but has its own merits. For one, the courses could take any shape the professor wanted, and so the students might shape the direction of the course. However, the downside was (for hand-written notes atleast) that missing any lectures was kind of bad, as the professors are not all great at writing lecture material - whereas someone who makes a best-seller physics book might have presented the material in a better way, which could then be presented by a professor (as I am used to at UCPH). The physics level was good - the department is much larger than at UCPH, so there are many very clever people, which was catered to by the professors. Failing a course seems much more likely down here than at UCPH. Many of the full-time students I became friends with were failing their classes, but were quite intelligent. Maybe the structure is just different, or they want to create a higher threshhold.
teaching_comparison: The are many more course structures available than at UCPH SCIENCE. There are courses from 2 ECTS to 24 ECTS. in the 2-4 ECTS range the format was very rote teaching, a lecturer lecturing to a class of students falling asleep - if they turn up. From there on it gets better. 6 ECTS was a good format - it provided different types of courses which were challenging. For example I had a course which was quite standard in structure (lecture, lecture notes, problem sessions) yet you had time to go in depth with anything you found interesting during the lecture/problem sessions, because it was not as tight a schedule as others. Another 6 ECTS format was the seminar: Here the students of the class each pick a topic from a list/find a new topic to present to the other students, followed by a discussion, in which a few professors might jump in (4 were present for the seminar I had) - the overall topic is also stated, so people know what they are getting in to. Then there were 8 ECTS courses - these were much more akin to the lectures at UCPH SCIENCE. Very fast paced, big classrooms, not a lot of time to go in-depth, but you learn a lot.
courses_enrolled: Nonlinear Dynamics and Pattern Formation Condensed Matter Theory 2 Standard Model of Particle Physics Looking for the Invisible: Dark Matter and Neutrinos Modern Aspects of Nuclear Physics
recommended_courses: The Looking for the Invisible: Dark Matter and Neutrinos seminar was very good - it allowed for a lot of questions which could be asked and fruitful discussions. The Condensed Matter Theory 2 Course was also good, but very fast paced if you have not read before the lectures. The Nonlinear Dynamics and Pattern formation was very interesting, but the lecturer would trail of while writing - so very hard to follow along during the lecture, and his lecture notes were not very readable. The topic itself was quite interesting, and he was very open to questions - so a good course if you ask a lot of questions.
unexpected_costs: I was abroad quite a bit and had some trouble coming back to Germany, so a few thousands went with that.
cost_comparison: I mostly bought food - the food was slightly cheaper than in Denmark (Copenhagen), but different things cost quite different. I was also not used to cheap cafeteria food - nobody brings a packed lunch down here. Also, going to a Café is much cheaper and good for studying. I also took advantage of their university library, where you can borrow any book for 3 months. So I didnt need to buy any books - which I did not need anyway, because most of the material was covered in the lecture notes, but these were awful, so I needed supplementary material.
activities_available: Theater is free for students - but in German most likely. There were many reduced prices for students, including the local movie theater, which shows non-dubbed international films on specific week days.
activities_recommended: The movie theater was very good - very much an old school vibe. From all of my friends I also gather that the sport union is very, very good!
weekend_recommendations: Go to Königstuhl and just around the Rhine valley on a bike - or into the hills if you dare (hint: they are bigger than any hills we have in Denmark, so bring good lungs). There is good transportation opportunities to go to the big Southern and Western German cities such as Frankfurt, Stuttgart and Freiburg - all very beautiful!
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, the Germans are not that different from the Danes - although the Church bells ringing every 15 minutes takes some getting used to. Them not being very different from the Danes also means they do not go out of their way to speak to strangers - although it is a University town, so if you speak english somebody might notice and ask where you're from. Also, nearly any young person here studies, so that's an easy in.
socializing_tips: Get into the buddy programme! The Germans I got closest to down here (apart from my host family) were through the buddy programme.
cultural_challenges: Nothing in particular, except the language barrier at times. Oh and tipping. I hate tipping. Just include it in a fair wage.
culture_appreciated: Although they are not very different, their history is quite different. The relationship of our generation with older generations is therefore not the same as ours. A lot of people also just have a different drive from what I have experienced in Denmark, academically and non-academically - that I found very inspiring. Being down in the South also meant people were friendlier than in Denmark, especially if you flashed them a smile. If you are not in Heidelberg however, you might have some difficulty if you do not speka any German.
top3_advice: Take advantage of the different structure and try to unfold your creativity - since your grades do not matter it also does not hurt to 1. Ask stupid questions and get lost in course material that does not matter much for the exam, and 2. take time out of university to explore the town and definitely join the sports union! Being a university town, I highly recommend living in the actual city - it is much easier to just pop down and meet your friends, getting to class and also getting home after a night out.
other_useful_info: Remember to take time outside of University. At least for Physics there is the Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics - reach out to them and ask about any projects - they very much encourage engagement and they do a lot of very high-end work!
most_rewarding: Probably feeling stupid and asking stupid questions. It was very rewarding to let myself dumb down - I feel much more ready to tackle actual research now. The friends I made down here also made for a lot of fun and I look forward to seeing them again in the future!
greatest_challenge: Balancing all of the things you want to do while on exchange - meeting new people, studying, seeing the country, practising the language, trying new things - I only managed by choosing a subset of things which I would focus on during my actual study time at the university. Maybe it works better for some to try many different things, but spending 10 hours a week on transport I was already quite low on effective time I had for exchange things.
other_comments: Thank you for the opportunity!

crucial_aspects: I knew absolutely nothing about the host uni. I chose only based of the partner unis of ucph within countries where I partly knew the language. And then picked a smaller town than the capital, thinking it would be easier to socialize with locals in a smaller town.
overall_comments: I had a lot of fun and I learned a lot. What was still missing for me was that I didn't realise that most exchange people arrived 3-4 weeks before me, and most of the social events where already done. So I did feel like I missed out on some social events due to unclear information on semesterstart and introduction for internationals.
info_ease: It was moderately difficult. I had a lot of trouble communicating with my contact at the host uni, and the informations about courses, documents needed and housing was difficult to find and had pretty unclear information.
arrival_assistance: None.
arrival_comments: We were invited to orientation days, but then told that there would be no orientation for medical students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had a lot of fun and I learned a lot. What was still missing for me was that I didn't realise that most exchange people arrived 3-4 weeks before me, and most of the social events where already done. So I did feel like I missed out on some social events due to unclear information on semesterstart and introduction for internationals.
registration_process: as far as I remember I just had to fill out one page with infos about A4 format. And that was it
registration_help: I have no idea. I didn't experience any problems and didn't look for help
registration_success: Pretty succesful. I was informed upon arrival that one course I registered for would not be available, but was then offered an alternative course.
registration_advice: The official registration process is not the problem. The problem is arranging clinical courses with the contact person at the medical faculty. She does not always answer her mails and is generally unhelpful.
academics_comments: I had a lot of fun and I learned a lot. What was still missing for me was that I didn't realise that most exchange people arrived 3-4 weeks before me, and most of the social events where already done. So I did feel like I missed out on some social events due to unclear information on semesterstart and introduction for internationals.
course_level: I had clinical courses. I felt that they were generally at a slightly lower level than at ucph. But being a bit proactive and asking to do more brought me through at an acceptable level
teaching_comparison: We were much less independant at my host uni than at ucph. Much more classical teaching in my exchange, where we got lectures and quizzes from senior doctors. At ucph I feel we get to learn by doing more often, which I like better.
courses_enrolled: clinical course of Internal Medicine (endocrinology) clinical course of Surgery (visceral surgery) clinical course of Anesthesiology
recommended_courses: Since these are the only courses available at this semester, probably the same. I would definitely recommend visceral surgery! for internal medicine I don't think it matters that much which specialty you choose.
unexpected_costs: the semester fee of a 110 eur. I did not expect to have to pay to the uni. But I have had a lot of use of the transport benefits and the canteen that these money go to.
cost_comparison: Generally I expected to be paying more for food and housing. So there I was positively surprised
activities_available: sports and choir that I heard about. Probably also an orchestra. A lot of differents sports available
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend doing some of the sports during the semester. It is a good way to meet new people, both local and international.
weekend_recommendations: As much as possible! Definitely go to Strasbourg and see that. Go to the other historic towns in the neighbourhood. Go hiking in the amazing nature! Go to the city-festivals!
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. Coming from another northern european country I did not have a lot of difficulties fitting in. The only thing maybe being that it was difficult to get used to using cash everywhere. And that nothing in Germany is digitalised.
socializing_tips: Join a sports or choir. Take classes in german. Do not be afraid to take the initiative to talk to the local students.
cultural_challenges: the absense of digitalisation and the overall use of cash
culture_appreciated: I found the germans more open towards foreigners, than I know danes to be
top3_advice: Bring cash! Take the german course offered by uni heidelberg. take german courses and don't be afraid to approach germans.
other_useful_info: You need all your documents printed out.
most_rewarding: Seeing how much my language has improved and how my confidence has grown in speaking german.
greatest_challenge: Probably planning the exchange

crucial_aspects: The language - I speak Danish and English already, but I wanted to improve my German. And then I searched Google for the four possible German universities and I really liked how beautiful Heidelberg looked. Therefore, Heidelberg became my first priority, and Mannheim my second.
info_ease: Fairly easy in general.
arrival_assistance: They had a lot of people ready to welcome us, which was great. The bad part was that it was in Heidelberg, not in Mannheim.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I gave a copy of my passport and had filled out a paper, and submitted it to the study office. A couple of days later I got my student ID.
registration_help: People I could ask were there in person.
registration_success: Only did clinical rotations.
registration_advice: Make sure you have prepared everything for your arrival in Heidelberg, so you can walk over and registrer immediately! Especially if you live in Mannheim.
course_level: Not applicable, only did clinical rotations.
teaching_comparison: Not applicable, only did clinical rotations.
courses_enrolled: Not applicable, only did clinical rotations.
recommended_courses: Not applicable, only did clinical rotations. I would recommend the language course though.
unexpected_costs: I had to buy a month travel card, since I had a language course in the beginning before the semester technically started, so my student ID wasnt valid for me to buy a semester ticket (which costs 180 euro and was going to cover the entire semester). The month card was 100 euros.
cost_comparison: It was unexpecting that I had to pay for my room for the entire semester, but I was also to sublet it for the last two and a half months.
activities_available: Sightseeing tours, hiking, pub crawls, parties, christmas market tours and Octoberfest!
activities_recommended: All of the above, it was great! Wonderful sights in Heidelberg and the Odenwald area, trips to Strasbourg, Munich and along the Neckar.
weekend_recommendations: Experience the local area and take some trips to go somewhere farther once in a while, if possible.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy.
socializing_tips: Participate in ESN (Erasmus Student Network) activities, and make a Whatsapp Group with people you meet in the building.
cultural_challenges: All of the physical paperwork, and the need for a German bank account, since my bank didn't allow SEPA transfers.
culture_appreciated: The openness to foreign students.
top3_advice: 1) Go! It was great. Even if you are going to Mannheim, and you asked for Heidelberg, you will still have a very nice time. 2) Make sure to be open to making a lot of new friends continually. If you go to Mannheim and do the language course in Heidelberg first, you will need to get to know people once again in Mannheim, since you are in a new city now. 3) Speak German as much as possible to learn the language.
other_useful_info: Get a semesterticket when you get to Heidelberg, it makes travelling easier.
most_rewarding: The other exchange students I got to know - just hanging in the evenings in people's rooms, and drinking tea or something. Alcohol wasn't needed unlike in Danish culture.
greatest_challenge: The bureaucracy was very difficult to deal with. Other than that I had a hard time with the change from being in Heidelberg during the language course and then being in Mannheim for clinical rotations. It was socially exhausting.
other_comments: Go abroad and enjoy being abroad. And go without another Dane to get the full international experience, or at least don't hang out with the Danish friend all the time.

crucial_aspects: Location (smaller city), academic reputation, language (already fluent in German).
info_ease: I got a lot of emails, which were confusing. I would have loved to get one common one with all the needed information. There did not seem to be cooperation between my home university and the host university. It took some energy to figure out, but not more than that. The secretary from the host university was confused and did not know which departments were at her university hospital - she placed me in a non-existent one.
arrival_assistance: There were some intro-days, but no particular information for medical students like for the others.
arrival_comments: It was very difficult getting a student ID in order to get clothes at the hospital. A lot of bureaucracy...
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to submit which departments I wished for, and had to submit some vaccinations. Not that complicated. I did, however, find the online mobility and different platforms quite confusing.
registration_help: From Copenhagen University, only emails. I asked to schedule phone calls, but this was unfortunately not possible.
registration_success: I got the departments I wished for. However, infectiology did not exist as its own, even though it said to in the university folder. Instead, I was placed in gastroenterology. The secretary did not know this.
registration_advice: I can recommend taking a look at the university hospital's webpage to double check which departments actually exist.
course_level: Clinical rotations, 2. semester.
teaching_comparison: It seemed like a similar level, except for the fact that medical students in Germany have some different tasks than we do here.
courses_enrolled: Clinical rotations in anaesthesiology, internal medicine, surgery.
recommended_courses: Anaesthesiology at Kopfklinik and the department of Visceral Surgery, because of very diverse surgeries, transplantations and anaesthetic procedures. European Pancreas Center is in Heidelberg.
unexpected_costs: Immatriculation fee of about 130 euros from the host university to get a Student ID, where you get free transportation on the weekend as well as after 7 pm on weekdays.
cost_comparison: Things were generally more inexpensive than in Denmark. I can't think of anything.
activities_available: A lot of different things. Both sports, and free concerts/cinema tickets as student.
activities_recommended: Go to the castle, it is a small 10 minute hike and just enjoy the view. Bars in Untere Straße, chill at the Neckarwiese.
weekend_recommendations: Visit the whole beautiful region (Baden Württemberg) and surroundings. Take a lot of hikes. It is amazing and underappreciated.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy for me, but I knew about both cultural differences and the language from beforehand.
socializing_tips: Go to the ESN-arranged intro weeks with hikes, pub-crawls, and so on. There you will meet other Erasmus students. Be in it from the beginning, otherwise it may be difficult to 'become part of a group'. Especially if you do not participate in the German course! About German students: As we do not take courses, it is close to impossible to socialise with local students. At every hospital department there were German PJ students (who were in their last year of med school), and I personally hung out with them, went to their afternoon teachings and ate lunch with them and their friends. I can also recommend signing up for the buddy programme, as my buddy introduced me to arrangements with other local students as well.
cultural_challenges: Hierarchy in the hospital, where there for example is a Chefarzt who no one dares speak up to. It was difficult getting used to saying 'Sie' instead of 'du' to all the doctors. It is a fine balance.
culture_appreciated: Effectiveness, focus on learning.
top3_advice: Double check the departments, look for accommodation well in advance, but most of all go and enjoy it. (be prepared to take a lot of blood samples and put in iv's - those are medical student's tasks in Germany. Not necessary to be able to do it in advance, but be prepared to learn it) Also - do NOT expect that the departments know you are coming or will be waiting for you. They most likely will not know, and you have to introduce yourself and take a lot of initiative. Only the secretary knows you are coming.
other_useful_info: Yes, what I wrote above. And get your student ID as soon as possible. Expect a lot of bureaucracy from both Copenhagen University as well as Heidelberg University.
most_rewarding: Just living in the gorgeous city, visiting the region, meeting great people, making connections in the hospital, assisting and doing a lot of procedures I would not be able to here.
greatest_challenge: Bureaucracy - getting clothes, student ID, and so on. Also adapting to the culture, differences in tasks as a medical student here and there. Making sure my 'log-bog' was signed, which the students in Copenhagen do not need to.
other_comments: I can only recommend, but sad to leave before all the other students who actually take courses that last until the end of July. It would have been nice to have a full semester instead of only 3 months.

crucial_aspects: The good reputation of Heidelberg University Hospital and the opportunity to improve my German language skills and broaden my career opportunities.
info_ease: The information from the University of Copenhagen and Heidelberg University was easy to find and well coordinated but there was very little information regarding clinical rotations and the first days in the clinic were a bit chaotic.
arrival_assistance: I received little assistance, mostly information from medical students who has previously completed their rotation in Heidelberg.
arrival_comments: The communication for medical students doing clinical rotations could be improved so that the receiving departments were informed of our arrival and stay.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I was put in contact with a coordinator who arranged my clinical rotations according to my study plan and priorities.
registration_help: Both Erasmus coordinators at the University of Copenhagen and Heidelberg University were available to help.
registration_success: I was able to complete rotations in the departments I wanted.
registration_advice: Contact the coordinators early and reconfirm your stay and rotations before your arrival.
course_level: I was doing clinical rotations at the hospital, mainly in the emergency departments. This meant a high patient flow and opportunity to see and treat many different conditions. I did my internal medicine rotation in the internal medicine ER (internistische Notfallambulanz), my surgery rotations in the surgical ER (Chirurgischen Ambulanz) and anaesthesia in Kopfklinik.
teaching_comparison: Supervision and teaching varied a lot between departments and mostly depended on the doctors as there was no structured programmed for us.
courses_enrolled: Anaesthesia (ECTS 2,5) Internal medicine (ECTS 7,5) Surgery (ECTS 7,5)
recommended_courses: I can highly recommend anaesthesia in Kopfklinik. The doctors are very nice and helpful, they are great at teaching and supervising and you get lots of hands-on training in many practical skills. Internal medicine in internistische Notfallambulanz also gives you the opportunity to see many patients with a broad spectrum of internal presentations as well as practice many clinical skills. Chirurgischen Ambulanz tends to have many students and less patients which means you do not get to see many patients compared to the other places.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Organic fruit and vegetables were more expensive than expected.
activities_available: The university offers many sports activities for a very cheap price compared to other places in Heidelberg.
activities_recommended: Join a local sportsclub to meet people outside campus and get a chance to practice your German.
weekend_recommendations: There are many great one-day or weekend trips from Heidelberg including München, Nürnberg, Freiburg, Paris and Luxembourg.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, I found everyone to be helpful.
socializing_tips: Join sports activities at campus or visit bars in the city.
cultural_challenges: I did not encounter any challenging cultural differences but you have to adjust to a different hierarchy among students and doctors in the clinic compared to Denmark.
culture_appreciated: Heidelberg is a great city with a relaxed atmosphere and beautiful nature nearby.
top3_advice: 1. Make an effort to learn the language. 2. Enjoy the city and make use of the beautiful surroundings. 3. Join a local club to meet new people.
other_useful_info: Make an effort to speak the language and be active in the clinic. Often you can find a couple of doctors in your department who have time and interest in teaching clinical skills and helping you practice. Be aware of what skills you wish or need to practice and make an effort to pursue them. Sometimes you can learn a lot from showing up in the evening or weekend shifts where there are less students and therefore more work.
most_rewarding: Improving my German language skills and getting an insight into another health care system.
greatest_challenge: Getting the most out of all clinical rotations and align the purpose of my rotation and level of clinical skill as this was different from the German medical students who are either doing rotations early in their studies or as part of their final year.

crucial_aspects: The exchange would not be a burden financially or timewise to prepare.
info_ease: It was very easy. They provided it throughout. But be sure to get an overview of all the systems as soon as possible. University of Heidelberg and Heidelberg Studerenwerk are separate institutions, and the latter is the one for most intro, accommodation and student life. Check LSF regularly prior as course descriptions come continuously. Registration for courses differed, find that on LSF:
arrival_assistance: I imidatly got my key from Studerenwerk and apartment on arrival. There was a full week of introductions that informed about everything from where to get a bike, courses, student societies, sports and much more. I advise to join all of it, even though some parts may seem boring. It is nice not to miss out on information.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Some was prior. For courses it differes from course to course, so check LSF. You need to mail documents to the main building or bring them yourself. They cannot make your studentcard before that, and you depend on the studentcard for Moodle (their absalon), the library, canteen, local transport and more. So I recommend actually sending it by mail as soon as possible from home. Thay had to make so many in the first week of the semester, that it took at least a week to get it.
registration_help: You could get a lot of help at the offices. However the orientation week is the main place to get help.
registration_success: Very successful. Mainly because I really made sure to check LSF regularly and get an overview of the registration process.
registration_advice: Prioritize preprations and getting an overview. The students that had not prepared had a substantially harder time in the beginning compared to me.
course_level: The economics students level and courses are very similar to here. The MA students have a mandatory math course, where they thoroughly learn the math that we will probably have learned bit by bit in our courses. So in the beginning of the MA first semester, their math skills were a bit lower than our average, but they caught up. Their econometric skills may be slightly lower than ours, where in the seminars Diff-n-Diff, IV, and Regression Discontinuity were kinda of what was considered the "harder" parts and sufficient, whereas in my experience, the MA level here, like AME, is far beyond that.
teaching_comparison: Substantially more discussion based leaning and student engagement. The lectures had far more responsibility, freedome and flexibility for the curriculum, assignments and exam wich means that it can be based on the students interests. I did a LOT of presentations as part of my courses.
courses_enrolled: Advanced Experimental Economics Applied Methods on Environmental and Development Economics (Seminar) Politics in Contemporary India Political Ecology of Urbanization in South Asia West Punjab: Heratage, Memorilization and Ethnography International Reserach Seminar: Heritage Conservation in Postcolonial Pakistan
recommended_courses: All of them. Advanced Experimental Economics was far more practical and active that I am used to, where we mainly did the experiments with each other and had to come up with a design. For the seminar, the paper had to replicate another paper and add an element. I found that to be both slightly easier than our seminars, but also a very good starting point which meant that I actually could lean more and do better then if I did not have to base it on another paper.
unexpected_costs: It was not unexpected, but to get kitchen equipment and stuff for my felt that I did not bring, I went to the thrift store Bric & Brac and got absolutely everything I needed, which was very cheap.
cost_comparison: On the weekdays at certain hours, students have free local transportation, and you can get a cheap semester card so you can travel all the time in a more extensive area. My rent was incredibly cheap compared to the fact that it was the absolute best location you could imagine, large with a bathroom and small kitchen and my own. Getting to Heidelberg from CPH is also cheap; there is a Flixbus that goes directly during the night, and as DB is known for delays and fuck ups, it is the best option. Since it is free to go for walks, that means that the most amazing parts of Heidelberg is at no cost. As Heidelberg is a very rich city, the prices in supermarkets etc. are in the same arena as CPH, maybe a bit more.
activities_available: The main part of Heidelberg's history and beauty. It's no wonder that it is a huge tourist attraction. So beautiful during Christmas, and when I arrived in the start of October, I saw people play beach volley shirtless. You can kayak in the Necker. The Neckerwiese is incredible. Walk philosophweg. Hear about the history. Visit Germany's first prime minister's childhood home. Go to the castle. Go to Christmas markets. Go to private parties at strangers' houses, because that is the nightlife in Heidelberg. Visit Manheim for an urban vibe. Connect with the other Danish exchange students to have a safety net and have each other back.
activities_recommended: The majority of the student life is at Mensa, where you can eat but also have a beer or latte at Marstall the cafe. They also host poetry slams and shit.
weekend_recommendations: See the above. Go for walks by the Necker or the mountains. It's crazy what is does to not be in such a flat place.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Prioritize making friends in the beginning. Don't prioritize Germans, but the other internationals, they are way more open. Maybe you are one of those people that I was on my first exchange, thinking you are not there to make friends and can do without. No. It can get lonely. You need people to support you. Seek a base with the other danish students. I know you may think you did not go to hang out with danes. Sure, you should also make international and German friends. But they will probably be where you will get a meaningful and trusting relationship easiest, and that is important to have.
cultural_challenges: In stores, especially bakeries, they are not foreign-friendly. Practice the basic German terms. You need to use titles for your lectures, and there is more of a hierarchical distance between you in general, but that is mostly a formality. People go to strangers' private parties?? It was so weird initially when I was invited to a friend-of-a-friend-of-a-friends home. But that is normal because their public nightlife is very much like Gothersgade, so hated by most.
culture_appreciated: That it was easy as it is so similar. I was not there for a big cultural experience but for a nice and smooth trip. For that it was really nice to go.
top3_advice: 1) Arrive early to get settled and prioritize the orientation week. 2) Prepare from home 3) Make friends with the other Danes for a saftlyned
other_useful_info: They are obsessed with Mate.
most_rewarding: The beauty of Heidelberg and the pleasure of living a short while in a city where the uni and student life is at the core.
greatest_challenge: I don't like Mate.
other_comments: Nope.

crucial_aspects: The country (Germany) and field of study.
info_ease: It found it easy to find the information as such, but I found it complicated to get an overall view of the steps required in the process.
arrival_assistance: I was welcomed by Studierendenwerk when I picked up the key for my WG. They provided me with very useful information and a number I could call if I was in doubt about something regarding the accommodation.
arrival_comments: The people from all the departments I went to were very nice and helpful. Especially the secretaries and professors at my institute (HCCH) who guided me a lot. I was the first exchange student at the institute and was a lot in dialogue with the them as the process was also new to them. However, in the beginning, I had to wait for their reply (pr. mail) for weeks.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I don't remember it exactly, but I remember it as being only a formula.
registration_help: I didn't use any.
registration_success: I got accepted in all courses I applied for. The registration process was a bit complicated though as the university's system isn't very intuitive. I got help from a friend that had studied at the university before.
registration_advice: You can always ask your professor if you want to know more about a course. My experience is that they are only happy to talk about it.
course_level: The level was high and the courses very interesting. I come from another field of study than the one I was taught in at my host university and so many things were new to me. This might also have played a role in my experience of the level of course.
teaching_comparison: Because of the smaller courses consisting of less ECTS (e.g. 2, 5 or 8 ECTS), we were fewer people in the class rooms. It created a more intimate atmosphere during the lectures. There was a lot of interaction between professors and students - even in the Vorlesungen - and more physical presence.
courses_enrolled: Seminar „Vom Umgang mit Mumien, Moulagen und anderen Kostbarkeiten: Basiskurs Objekthandling"; Immaterielles Erbe: eine Zukunftsressource?; „Kulturelles Erbe. Eine Einführung Teil II: Immaterielles Erbe und Kulturelles Gedächtnis“; Übung: "Schreibwerkstatt zum Immaterielles Kulturerbe"; Vertiefung von Themen und Debatten in Heritage Studies, Museumswissenschaften und Denkmalpflege; Projektseminar: Komplexe Welterbestätten; and Immaterielles Erbe.
recommended_courses: "Immaterielles Erbe: eine Zukunftsressource?" because it was a lecture series featuring several prominent researchers and more. It was very exciting to get an overview of a broad range of knowledge within the field.
unexpected_costs: Duvet, duvet cover, sheets, pillowcases, towels, and storage boxes.
cost_comparison: Food in the canteen was less expensive. Use of washing machines was more expensive.
activities_available: Sports and different voluntary work/organisations.
activities_recommended: Participate in as many Erasmus events as possible. Especially the weekly event in Boho on Mondays.
weekend_recommendations: Besides the main attractions in Heidelberg, e.g. the castle, the bridge, and the Philosophenweg, visit Kunsthalle in Mannheim, Thingstätte, and all the second-hand bookshops in Heidelberg.
culture_adjustment: I found it very easy as I think German and Danish culture have many similarities.
socializing_tips: If you can, join the courses taught in German.
cultural_challenges: All the paperwork in public institutions which is digitalized in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: I personally really like the German language. And the exchange stay enabled me to speak and improve it. And the beer drinking culture :-)
top3_advice: Dont worry, everything will work out in the end, even when things may seem overwhelming at times or if you've missed a deadline. When studying at a German university, the academic calendar is often different from Danish universities. For instance, the spring semester in Germany runs from April to September. This means there are certain deadlines at the University of Copenhagen that you may need to extend. In the end, it all works out as long as you remember to contact your home university. Also, I can only recommend to reach out to a contact person or professor at the host university if you have any doubts or questions, as they are always willing to help. Professors have designated times in their schedules for student consultations (Sprechstunden). Make use of these, as it usually pays off when you need to give a presentation or take an exam, or when you're uncertain about anything. I reached out to one of my professors during my stay because my workload became quite heavy, and they accommodated it. As mentioned before, participate in Erasmus events as much as you can manage. It's nice to have some companions :-) In Heidelberg, most Erasmus-related communication happens through WhatsApp, so make sure to have it installed and join the group before you leave. This way, you'll be somewhat briefed in advance. Lastly, I highly recommend taking a language course that the university doesn't offer but promotes once you've been accepted. Not only to improve your language skills, but most of all to meet other international students before the semester starts - these courses typically take place in the month before the semester starts. For the spring semester, for example, it would be in March.
other_useful_info: I find it very important to let coming Erasmus students in Germany, or at least in Heidelberg, know that the German system differs from the Danish, meaning that it is unusual for the German students to take all 30 ECTS per semester. I had to enroll in seven courses in order to acquire 30 ECTS credits, making me the only student in my MA program for that year who had such a heavy course load. As there are many week-to-week papers, presentations, excursions, interviews, and a rule saying that you can only have two days of absence in every course (Fehlertage), I sometimes found it very stressful to keep up. Technically, you have 30 ECTS as you would have back home but due to the existing norm in Germany/Heidelberg, where students have fewer ECTS per semester, they often have more time available for each course. As a result, professors tend to expand the scope of the workload for each course, beyond what the number of ECTS would typically suggest. Therefore, a workload of 30 ECTS can be a lot more extensive than in Denmark, in my experience.
most_rewarding: Language improvement and the friends a got from both inside and outside Germany.
greatest_challenge: The university workload.

info_ease: Somewhat easy. Theres always someone you can write an email to. I did feel like I had to doublecheck everything myself tho. Every situation for every exchangestudent is unique.
arrival_assistance: Lots of informative emails. And then there’s the introweek in the first week of april, but I didn’t really participate. If you take the languagecourse in march, you’ll be able to receive a lot of the same information - also by just living there for over a month before semesterbegin.

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I registered for everything I found interesting, as I felt very lost in how hard it would be getting the courses I wanted (and also just enough). The registration is online, but some of the courses didn’t have the option of registration. Then you’ll just have to write directly to the professors to get registered (which is very normal and also makes it much more personal and charming in my opinion - but is of course a bit more work and feels more unofficial?)
registration_help: With the course registration I felt like i was more or less on my own. But as said, theres always someone ypu can write an email too or arrange a physical meeting with. Otherwise just ask the professors directly! Also if you need more information about a specific course:))
registration_success: I was way more sucessfull than I had expected. I got into every course i had regisered for except one seminar. Since I had registered for more courses than i planned to take, i just deregistered afterwards or just didn’t attend.
registration_advice: Register for everything interesting. There’s lots of flexibility, which can be difficult to adapt to/understand coming from KU.. At Heidelberg it’s very normal to shop courses in the first couple of weeks of the semester. Attendance is mandatory, but everything is very much a communication between you and the professor directly, so if you end up not attending a course anyways or want to join a week or two into the semester, it feels like everything can be arranged. The amount of credits you get is dependent on what you personally arrange with your professor at the end of the semester.
course_level: Proseminars are for ba students only. Can be a bit introductory, which I sometimes, as a ba-student on my last semester, found a bit too ‘mild’. Hauptseminars/Oberseminars are for both ba and ma students. More work, bigger exams and more ects points. I only attended proseminars, but in retrospect I would have liked to attend a Hauptseminar too:)
teaching_comparison: The seminars compares to ‘Holdundervisning’, but with more emphasis on active discussion. Way more intimate (often only around 10 students). In some seminars it is expected that every student do a presentation at some point in the semester. These student-held-presentations makes up 50% of the course, I would say. Not so much reading, more in depht engagement with a smaller amount of pensum literature. I really liked Vorlesungen even though it’s also a lot of information and passive listening. Very competent professors!! Every course (seminar or vorlesung) is 1,5 hour one day a week (unless blockseminar/excursion/something ‘out of the box’) I felt like i had to put in more work pr ects point in Heidelberg compared to at KU, but i think it’s also because both system and language was new.

Take the S-bahn to Mannheim (15 min) and visit Kunsthalle Mannheim (the museums in Heidelberg are a bit more ://) Go an lots of eveningwalks. If you’re into bouldering, it’s possible to do outside, at Riesenstein, only 15-20 min on foot from Altstadt. It’s also just a nice walk in itself
weekend_recommendations: Get a bike, bike outside Heidelberg through the countryside. When the rapseedfields bloom!! Bike to Waidsee. Get the deutschlandticket and leave Heidelberg haha (Frankfurt, Freiburg, i went all the way to Strassbourg with it).
culture_adjustment: German culture isn’t that different from danish culture, so not that hard. I think it’s more in the detail, what sets it apart, living there as a student. Heidelberg isn’t owerwhelmingly big and is also filled with students, which makes it easier to adjust.
socializing_tips: The local students are very open!! It’s (somewhat) easy to merge into friendgroups over lunch in the mensa. Just ask if someone wants to grab a coffee - oftentimes the local students themselves don’t know anyone in the specific seminars, since every student follow their own very flexible semesterplans.
cultural_challenges: The humor? I don’t know… If you get lucky and find the right people, cultural differences and awkwardness (?) can become a way to bond.
culture_appreciated: Hmm hard to sum up? The academic seriousness? The unexpected social openness? The language and it’s literature?
top3_advice: Everything is new, so stressfull feelings of uncertainty and inadequacy can become overwhelming. See it as a part of it and just take one thing at a time. Luckily you will be walking around in a fairytale city everyday, so it can never be that bad;) Learn the language!! Don’t take yourself too seriously, speak it, you’ll make mistakes (I did everyday) and it doesn’t matter. Be open<3
most_rewarding: The friends i made. And honestly learning german, maybe my biggest achievement haha, it opened up the whole experience (wasn’t at all fluent when i came, but things come quickly when you live there if you just dare and try your best).
greatest_challenge: Missing the ocean! The city can feel a bit claustrophobic at times due to it’s size, being surrounded by hills, it’s social homogeneity, being almost too idyllic.. Heidelberg is very homely and welcoming almost from day one (at least in the summersemester)

crucial_aspects: My interest in the native tongue and the location in the southern Germany, which in many ways is quite different from the northern parts.
info_ease: I needed some basic information about studying in Heidelberg. For instance that you can extend your semester by taking exams and writing seminar papers and that you in this way don't have to rush 30 ECTS in three months. But I didn't know that I needed that information, and no one told me.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation day.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You sign up online on a website or by sending emails to the professors/ lecturers. But since there are so many courses, you can never know if a course will be cancelled for not meeting the minimum requirements of five students.
registration_help: I don't know. I just contacted the professors, and they were very helpful.
registration_success: Very successful. No problems there.
registration_advice: Don't get your hopes up until the second week begins - because of possible cancellations. Don't register for classes worth 30 ECTS, but take an exam or write a Seminararbeit/ seminar paper, which will yield something like 6 ECTS on top of the ECTS for attending the course.
course_level: Nothing to elaborate. The level was appropriate.
teaching_comparison: The style differs in that you typically attend some seminars with 5-15 people. Instead of just hearing a lecture you will be expected to participate actively, and this gives you a chance to learn a lot more than usual.
courses_enrolled: Seminare: Albert Schweitzers Ethik Calvins "Unterricht in der christlichen Religion" Einführung in die Methoden neutestamentlicher Exegese Nachdenken über Jesu Opfertod: Der Hebräerbrief Neues Testament: Forschung, Quellen, Hermeneutik Übungen: Kirchengeschichte in Heidelberg Hebräisch II: Das Buch Ruth Hebräische Lektüre eksamensrelevanter Texte Vorlesungen: Überblicksvorlesung: Einführung in das Neue Testament Die Auferstehung Jesu Christi
recommended_courses: Hebräisch II: Das Buch Ruth Hebräische Lektüre eksamensrelevanter Texte You can learn a lot of Hebrew from Mr. Schwiderski! Überblicksvorlesung: Einführung in das Neue Testament Mr. Becker also has a PhD in classical philology, and therefore gives a thorough introduction into the ancient world. Kirchengeschichte in Heidelberg A very good way to get to know the city!
unexpected_costs: The apartment was practically empty when I moved in (except from a bed, a closet, office chair, a book shelf and a desk), so I for instance had to buy everything that I needed for the kitchen.
cost_comparison: Everything was generally - as expected - a bit cheaper in Heidelberg. Although getting stuff like pillows and duvets in the centre of the city is not recommended, since it's very expensive to go to Galeria as an example. Instead I would suggest going 7 kilometers south of the city centre to Jysk.
activities_available: Lots! Climbing/ bouldering, rowing in the Neckar river, volleyball and much more.
activities_recommended: Join the bouldering group! Every wednesday evening the last semester. It's fun to climb and an easy way to meet and talk to new people - especially locals.
weekend_recommendations: Take a hike to Heiligenberg (Thingstätte, Stephanus monastery, Waldschenke), get a good bike and go on a bike trip in the sorrounding area, and get a Deutschland Ticket and take the train to all of the interesting neighbouring cities: Baden-Baden, Stuttgart, Colmar, Strasbourg, Freiburg, Konstanz, Basel, and even Paris are just a short trip away.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The culture doesn't differ much from danish culture, and the people are in my experience very welcoming and nice.
cultural_challenges: None whatsoever.
culture_appreciated: The tendency that atleast some people tend to have more often in Germany and in smaller cities especially: Being heart warmingly polite and welcoming.
top3_advice: 1: Don't register for courses exclusively! Take and exam and write a seminar paper. That way you won't have a super stressed and short semester. 2: Sign up for the sports stuff that the university offers. 3: Concentrate on meeting locals and people with a different culture than that of your own. You can always go home after and meet new friends in your own city, but you only get so many chances to enrich your own life with other cultures - and THIS chance is a really fun one!
other_useful_info: Get a bike from Radhof Bergheim. You can get some decent ones, and at the end of the semester they'll buy it right back if you kept the receipt - and for a good price if you've kept it's condition.
most_rewarding: Just the experience of living in different country. Everyday is a small adventure that you can go on according to your own wishes. It's worth all the bureaucracy!
greatest_challenge: Having to take 30 ECTS credits worth of classes. My schedule was completely overbooked, and since the faculty members from University of Copenhagen chose to ignore all of my emails, I didn't have the opportunity to make a change in my study programme until it was far too late.

crucial_aspects: De afgørende elementer var dels Heidelberg Universitets meget lange teologiske tradition og dertilhørende meget høje akademiske niveau og dels for at kunne indgå i den danske teologiske tradition at rejse til Tyskland for at supplere ens danske teologiske studier.
info_ease: Informationen var meget tilgængelig.
arrival_assistance: Ikke det store, udover den administrative, der blev givet af Studierendenwerk.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Ja, grundlæggende dukkede jeg bare op med mine immatrikulationspapirer, hvorefter jeg hurtigt blev udstyret med mit studiekort.
registration_help: Både hjælp over mail og personlig.
registration_success: Meget, jeg fik adgang til alle seminarer og forelæsninger, jeg havde ønsket. Dog ikke dem, som jeg jo havde brugt i min første forhåndsgodkendelse, da disse var de udbudte fag fra efteråret, da forårssemesterets fag endnu ikke var blevet udbudt.
registration_advice: Bare opsøg informationsafdelinger, hvor man kan modtage personlig betjening. Medarbejderne ved Heidelberg Universitet er meget hjælpsomlige.
course_level: Det teologiske fakultets fag i Heidelberg er struktureret anderledes end i København, således at der ikke opdeles i bachelor og kandidatfag, hvorfor jeg har taget fag, der ville passe til de senere bachelorfag og fag tilsvarende til kandidatfag i København.
teaching_comparison: Stærkt overlegent, da men ikke har de store overbliksfag, som vi arbejder med i København, men derimod et væld af små fag til den effekt, at fagene bliver meget dybdegående og så specialiserede, at de ikke kan være andet end spændende.
courses_enrolled: Das biblische und historische Israel Auf dem Weg zum Monotheismus Das alttestamentlich-jüdische Erbe in der Diakonie Überblicksvorlesung: Ethik des Alten testaments Neuere Forschungen zum AT: Klagenlieder Der Römerbrief Dämonen und Exorzismen im Neuen Testament Neuere Forschungen zum Neuen Testament und seiner Umwelt Die Auferstehung Jesu Christi Nachdenken über Jesu Opfertod: Der Hebräerbrief
recommended_courses: Det kan jeg ikke udtale mig om, da fagene skifter fra semester til semester.
unexpected_costs: Ikke noget særpræget.
cost_comparison: Det meste, det er et væsentligt billigere land end Danmark. Men i forhold til mine overstående udgifter, skal opmærksomheden henledes på, at mange daglige udgifter indgik som en del af min husleje, så de økonomiske udgifter for f.eks. mad vil være højere for dem, der ikke er bosat på kollegier som mit, hvor måltiderne i hverdagene blev dækket af huslejen.
activities_available: Der er et stort udbud gennem Hochschulsport Heidelberg, der tilbyder en lang række sportslige aktiviteter. Fik aldrig taget del i dem selv, da der ikke var så meget der lige fangede mig eller passede i mit skema.
activities_recommended: Det var ikke noget jeg gjorde gennem universitetet, omend Hochschulsport Heidelberg udbød det da også (deltog dog ikke pga. skemaoverlap og fordi jeg på kortere ture fandt det mere underholdende at gå for mig selv i et tempo), men det er et fantastisk område at vandre i, og jeg har gjort det tit og ofte.
weekend_recommendations: Vandre og så udnyt Heidelbergs lokation; det er meget let at lave udflugter til byerne i området, der er spækket med historie og kultur - Speyer, Freiburg, Worms, Strasbourg, Basel m.m.
culture_adjustment: Ganske let, tyskerne er et meget venligt og imødekommende folkefærd.
socializing_tips: Udnyt pauserne i undervisningen til at få talt med de andre studerende.
cultural_challenges: Særligt det religiøse miljø i byen er væsentligt mere fromt end jeg som dansk teolog er vant; det er som sådan ikke en udfordring, men lige noget man skal forholde sig til, hvis man kommer i de kredse, jeg gjorde. For det er sandlig ikke, fordi min egen religiøsitet er mindre inderlig eller afgørende for mig, men det synes, at hvor den for mig er anledning til at man kan leve meget frimodigt, bliver den for flere en anledning til en stringent og selvbegrænsende adfærd.
culture_appreciated: Hvor utroligt høflige folk er. Der er en særlige ordentlighed over tyskerne, som er en fornøjelse at være omkring.
top3_advice: Hav et godt tyskniveau; jeg kom afsted med et for lavt niveau, hvilket var tilstrækkeligt til at følge med i undervisningen, men ikke højt nok til at selv effektivt at engagere mig - lignende var det også en snublesten i sociale sammenhænge. Ved teologi, hvor man stadig som udvekslingsstuderende får sine karaktere på papir, skal man være opmærksom på, at docenterne ikke altid har styr på, hvor mange ects-point, man er berettiget til. Hvis der opstår fejl, eller der er ting, der undrer en, så skal man bare altid skrive til Prüfungsamt. De har styr på det og er meget hjælpsomme. Undervurder ikke hvor meget arbejde, der ligger i al undervisning. Jeg havde 10 fag, hvilket viste sig at være noget i overkanten. Det synes bedre i stedet at skrive en opgave eller to.
other_useful_info: Ikke noget slående.
most_rewarding: Alt relateret til undervisningen; det var et fantastisk højt niveau og immervæk utroligt spændende.
greatest_challenge: Sproget, immervæk sproget.

culture_adjustment: Of course there were some differences, but i felt like the teachers were very tolerant towards Erasmus-students, which was great.
socializing_tips: Its difficult. It was easy to socialize with other international students. But with the locals, you have to do something active. It doesn´t just happen by itself.
cultural_challenges: To some extent everything seemed to be more loosely organized than in Copenhagen. The Leistungspunkte-System was very different than in Denmark, and i often felt like i would get more ECTS-points for an assignment/test in Danmark. It was hard to make it all add up, where in Copenhagen you would just write to assignments in the end of the year and get 30 ects-points.
culture_appreciated: The beauty. Heidelberg, and some of the other smaller cities (Weinheim, Ladenburg) were so pretty.
top3_advice: 1. Dont forget to enjoy it. It will soon be over. 2. Try to get a good relationship with you professors. That can help a lot in the end. 3. Try to challenge yourself academically. Dont be afraid of failing, taking a hard course.
other_useful_info: Dont drink too much. Its not nice if you spend too many days having hangover, especially when youre there for such a short time. Erasmus doesnt feel stressfull in the beginning. But in the end, when exams arrive, it suddenly goes from 0-100. Be prepared. If you can already begin to write parts of you assignments in the semester period, it might be easier for you.
most_rewarding: Travelling with friends. Going to northern Germany, France and Italy in a van. I even went to Malmø, Sweden: a city ive never been to, even know i live in Copenhagen.
greatest_challenge: The exams. The assignments which i had to write in the end, in a foreign language, which very little time. The Bureaucracy. A lot of things you figure out

crucial_aspects: Landscape, student life and the available courses, quality of life.
info_ease: It was very easy - they were accommodating and helpful
arrival_assistance: Tours and talks about their online systems, many hikes and events for international students. It was awesome.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Once you have your student ID, you have to search on the different platforms (HeiCO, Moode, Müsli) and find the courses you found in the module handbook (assuming they're taking place and not cancelled. Then you simply click register, so that's the simple part.
registration_help: I sent loads of emails to the professors and exchange coordinators, which always solved my problems.
registration_success: Not very, but it's alright as there was a good selection. I got 2/4 courses that I wanted and took some alternative ones which were satisfactory.
registration_advice: Check out the module handbooks online to make sure you like the selection of courses, then do a preliminary learning agreement with the assumption that you will have to change it. Later you might have to select different courses, but just keep that in mind.
course_level: 3/4 were easier than UCPH courses. My 30 ECTS felt like 20 ECTS I'd say
teaching_comparison: At home: more strict and precise, less handwavy, professors are better at answering questions.
courses_enrolled: MM15 - Finite Elements - 8 ECTS ICS - Computer Games - 8 ECTS IIP - Inverse Problems - 8 ECTS MScTI_HAPTICS - Haptics and Robot Human Interaction - 6 ECTS
recommended_courses: The best one of those four was Inverse problems. Not because of the teaching, but because of the content. I learned a lot of interesting things about the powers of linear algebra and it has given me a lot more confidence in my signal processing abilities. Finite Elements I learned the most in, but it's also the most intense one for a non-mathematician like me. You get to dive pretty deep into function spaces and finally understand Hilbert Spaces, which is a term that's been thrown around nonchalantly in ML during my bachelor's degree.
unexpected_costs: Rundfunkbetrag, which is around 50€ a month for the radio licence.
cost_comparison: All of it is slightly cheaper, except for cheese.
activities_available: The institution didn't really provide anything.
activities_recommended: Many biketrips! The landscape is amazing, bring 3-5 friends and go check out the local areas. I did multiple 40+km trips with my international friends, it was so awesome (I'm getting emotional writing this).
weekend_recommendations: Go to Mannheim perhaps once just to say you've been there, but it's really not that nice. Check out Schwetzingen and Ladenburg, go to Waldschwimmbad Schriesheim, go to Freiburg and Strassburg and Frankfurt.
culture_adjustment: Easy peasy.
socializing_tips: Talk to them before and after class (so show up early). Also they are super interested in you because you "chose" them, so just mention you're an international student.
cultural_challenges: Nothing.
culture_appreciated: I did not feel anything in particular. I hung out with internationals a lot. That's the real meat.
top3_advice: Get a bike. Go socialize a lot! Push yourself to try new things.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Cannot be disclosed for privacy reasons but I'll let you know it was amazing.
greatest_challenge: The friends in CPH having holiday while I'm studying for my exams.
other_comments: Go on exchange! It will change your life a lot more than staying at home could.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to Germany and it was important that the city was nice to live in as a student.
info_ease: It was not very easy, I think the information was spread out on to many different platforms
arrival_assistance: I attended the introduction week, which was helpful, but not really any "assistance" I guess.
arrival_comments: The university just had a big digitalisation of their system, which made it difficult for the "tutors" to inform us well on how to do the different things.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I don't remember it well, but I didn't find it easy.
registration_help: People at Uni was helpful, but I often had to write to several people to figure out what to do.
registration_success: Unfortunately there were about 2-3 classes that I wanted to have that I didn't get because they were full, which was quite frustrating.
registration_advice: To register before going to the classes. We were told(and informed online by former erasmus students) that you could just go to a class and then be signed up - this was not the case for me in all classes, because some lectures/teachers already had a full list of people who wanted to attend the class.
course_level: A really high level in general - I was almost only in classes that were taught in english with a lot of international students.
teaching_comparison: We had more group work, and sometimes a bit too much for me. But it made sense since it was seminars, where I'm used to more of a mix between lectures and group work. I think it was a bit annoying that there were almost no lectures in my field, so I had to choose seminars.
courses_enrolled: Debates across World Regions: Socio-Ecological Transformations in Energy and Food Food movements Humanitarianism, Charity and Volunteering Don't skip class: Advances in Research on Social Class and Adolescent Development Diversität, Differenzierung und Inklusion
recommended_courses: I liked the courses I had on Bildungswissenschaft, because I found them easier to follow(since it's my field). But I actually found all my courses interesting, the workload was just a bit overwhelming.
unexpected_costs: I moved from my student dorm to another private flat after 3 months, which costed me almost 2 months extra rent, since I couldn't quit the first contract.
cost_comparison: The canteen was cheap Experiences was expensive
activities_available: Language exchange, hochschulesport(that you have to pay for), different sport on tv in the canteen, events and a couple of festivals
activities_recommended: The fesitvals at Mensa were great Visiting the city's pools in the summer.
weekend_recommendations: Karlstor Bahnhof has some nice events, festivals and parties. Trips to the different small cities nearby, but also München, Stuttgart and so on.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy
socializing_tips: Good idea to meet with your buddy and just show up to the different uni events
cultural_challenges: That you can not always pay with credit card
culture_appreciated: In general I found people friendly and down to earth.
top3_advice: The bureaucracy is annoying, but things will work out in the end(most of the time) Show up to the ESN events in the beginning to make friends - It didn't seemed like people were socializing in class. Enjoy the surrounding landscapes with some hikes or bike rides!
other_useful_info: I can't think of more than what I have already written
most_rewarding: I made great friends, I got better in both german and english and I think Heidelberg is a nice city to live in for a semester!
greatest_challenge: To figure out which courses I could take, the workload and the bureaucracy!

culture_appreciated: Det kan jeg ikke svare på.

crucial_aspects: I've heard a lot of positive feedback from my peers in terms of their experience abroad in Heidelberg and the university itself.
info_ease: It was centered around the mobility platform, which made it more easy to grasp, although it was a bit difficult overall.
arrival_assistance: I, as well as the other international students, received a welcoming from the tutors at the university. There were a lot of different events, that you could attend to both to be informed about the faculties as well as to meet other students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We got all the information we needed from the beginning by attending the first introduction week.
registration_help: Mainly the tutors and the overall administration.
registration_success: I got in on all the classes I signed up for.
registration_advice: You can alway write an e-mail when in doubt. There are a lot of people, who work in the international department and are ready to help at all times.
course_level: I had to do a lot more reading than usual during the semester - but I found it all very exciting so I really enjoyed it, although it was challenging at times.
teaching_comparison: I found it a bit more analogue and some seminars were really discussion-based, which you had to prepare a lot for by yourself.
courses_enrolled: "P1: Einführung in die Philosophie". "Einführung in die Literaturwissenschaft". "Goethe: Die Wahlverwandtschaften". "Die Wut, die bleibt - Simone de Beauvoir im zeitgenössischen Feminismus".
recommended_courses: "Einführung in die Literaturwissenschaft". This programm is great for both beginners and for non-beginners at studying literature; you really get to apply a lot of general knowledge about literary theories and it introduces a big rage of text material - both novels, short stories, poems and plays. The class is an open space for discussions and you probably won't be the only Erasmus student attending.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: None.
activities_available: Sports, summer parties (organized by the student council) and other social events.
activities_recommended: Going to the parties and social events, where you get to meet a lot of new people and build a network.
weekend_recommendations: Going outside from the city and experience new locations.
culture_adjustment: Easy. People were really welcoming.
socializing_tips: Most people are really sweet if you just come up and say hi.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The whole atmosphere around attending university and studying.
top3_advice: 1. Try to choose courses around campus; not just at one faculty. 2. Be a tourist! The city is amazing and a must to experience. 3. Don't be afraid to talk to non-Erasmus students in class.
other_useful_info: None.
most_rewarding: Proving that I could do it for myself; live and study in a foreign city.
greatest_challenge: I had to build up some confidence at first using my language. I found that really challenging in the beginning.

crucial_aspects: Typer af kurser og dejlig by.
info_ease: Meget nemt. Man var aldrig "alene", information blev konstant "leveret"
arrival_assistance: Uni Heidelberg havde arrangeret introdage med information om uni, det specifikke institut man var på, byen, studieliv, kulturelle tilbud og generelt ryste-sammen-aktiviteter.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Man fik altid en "to-do-liste" fra Uni Heidelberg og derfor var det hele til at finde ud af. Man skulle gennem en tysk Krankenkasse vise at man har det blå EU-sygesikringskort. Man skulle ned og hente sit studiekort. Alt var skrevet ned som "to-do-liste" og hvis man var i tvivl, kunne man skrive og fik altid hurtigt svar.
registration_help: Mails. Og et kontor i Altstadt, hvor man kunne møde fysisk op.
registration_success: Fik alle de kurser, jeg ville have.
registration_advice: Hvis du bare følger to-do-listerne, skal alt gå. Ellers skriv en mail
course_level: Godt niveau, spændende kurser, engagerede og inspirerende undervisere
teaching_comparison: Jeg havde seminarer (undervisning med dialog) og to forelæsninger (ja, som en forelæsning). I Tyskland har man dog 90 minutter ad gangen og ingen pause
courses_enrolled: Grundlagen Spracherwerb, Einführung in die Fremdsprachendidaktik, Einführung in die Psycholinguistik, Einführung in Deutsch als Fremdsprache, Textkomtpetenz B, Latein für Germanisten
recommended_courses: Jeg fik rigtigt meget ud af "Textkompetenz B", som var for studerende med tysk som fremmedsprog. Kurset hjalp mig til at blive bedre til at skrive på tysk. Derudover var jeg rigtigt glad for Einführung in die Fremdsprachendidaktik, Einführung in Deutsch als Fremdsprache (fantastisk forelæser) og Grundlagen Spracherwerb.
unexpected_costs: Ikke nogen
cost_comparison: Fødevarer billigere. Øl i byen billigere. Mensa (kantine) billig (2,9 eur = 22 dkk), når man tager "Power Meal"
activities_available: Ligesom at vi har studenteridræt, tilbyder Uni Heidelberg "Hochschulsport" til rigtig gode priser. Gratis for studerende at komme i teatret (hvis der var pladser).
activities_recommended: Hochschulsport
weekend_recommendations: Skoven om Heidelberg. Heiligenberg. Næsten hver dag er der "Wochenmarkt" (udendørs) hvor man købe lidt ind (lidt dyrt), super hyggeligt
culture_adjustment: For mig var det nemt, da jeg taler tysk og kom i kontakt med tyskere - jeg kom ud af den "internationale boble".
socializing_tips: Tal med folk, når du sætter dig ind i et undervisningslokale. Sig hej og hvad du hedder og så kører det
cultural_challenges: Ingen udfordringer ift. kulturelle forskelle - man gør sig observationer og ser hvilke forskelle der er. Man er typisk Des med underviserne og på efternavn (få tilfælde dus)
culture_appreciated: Jeg kan godt lide distancen og respekten, når man er Des
top3_advice: Fed studieby og super skønt uni, glæd dig!
other_useful_info: Tag det roligt mht. tilmelding af fag. Deadlines for tilmelding er efter at forelæsningstiden er begyndt og du kan derfor gå til nogle forelæsninger/seminarer og se, hvad du kan lide, hvorefter du beslutter dig
most_rewarding: At opleve en anden universitetskultur. Og at alt var på tysk, det har virkelig gjort noget godt for mit sprog.
greatest_challenge: Nogle gange føler man sig alene og det er helt ok. Du ankommer uden din vennekreds, sandsynligvis med få genstande og i et andet land. Tag det roligt og gør det, som du synes er fedt.

crucial_aspects: Jeg tænkte Heidelberg er en hyggelig, lille studieby som man hurtig kan finde rundt i. Desuden har universitetet et godt ry.
info_ease: Jeg synes hele processen op til opholdet var ret uoverskueligt, i det man er i kontakt med mange forskellige mennesker. Jeg var altid lidt bange for at overse eller glemme noget, inden jeg tog afsted. I sidste ende fungerede det hele dog fint, selvom informationerne først kommer lidt hen ad vejen.
arrival_assistance: Ikke så meget. Men jeg var kun i praktik på sygehuset og deltog derfor ikke i kurserne. Informationerne fra afdelingerne var lidt varieret, men det fungerede ok.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Jeg kan ikke huske så meget, men skulle jo heller ikke vælge kurser osv.

registration_advice: Spørg universitetet, hvis man bliver i tvivl.
course_level: Ikke relevant, har ikke taget kurser
