Der har været afdelinger, hvor jeg kun har taget blodprøver og hjulpet i de daglige arbejdsopgaver uden at lære det store, og hvor man som studerende ikke fik særlig meget opmærksomhed. Synes også det var lidt ærgerligt at vi ikke fik adgang til computersystemerne. Som altid er det meget afhængig af afdelingerne og de læger man følges med. Mit generelle indtryk er dog, at der var lidt mere pres på og der derfor ikke var så meget overskud til læring. Man skal selv være god til at stille spørgsmål og opsøge læringen. Men jeg har alligevel lært meget om sundheds systemet og er de forskelle der er ift. Danmark
courses_enrolled: Praktik på hospitalet
recommended_courses: Ej relevant
unexpected_costs: Semester bidrag til Studierendenwerk. De har dog mange gode tilbud til de studerende (bl.a. billig mad i mensa), så synes det er pengene værd
cost_comparison: Det var overraskende billigt at købe mad i supermarkedet og alkohol i barerne er også billigere
activities_available: Jeg har ikke deltaget i tilbud fra universitetet. Men har hørt at der findes mange gode tilbud.
activities_recommended: Erasmus student network (ESN) tilbyder mange forskellige events, hvor man kan lære de andre erasmus studerende at kende
weekend_recommendations: Ligge på Neckarwiese, tag på vandreture i de omkringliggende skove, spis en masse Käsespätzle, nyd det sydeuropæiske flair i Altstadt
culture_adjustment: Jeg har selv tyske rødder og kender derfor til kulturen. Har dog været overrasket over kulturen på sygehuset.
socializing_tips: Prøv at sige ja til så mange ting som muligt. Prøv at tale til nogen på en bare eller lignene. Min oplevelse er, at de tyske studerende er mere åben end vi er i Danmark.
cultural_challenges: Kulturen på hospitalet. En mere skrap tone og tydeligere hieraki.
culture_appreciated: Jeg er hurtigt faldet i snak med en masse mennesker og føler det er ret nemt at komme i kontakt med andre.
top3_advice: 1. Nyd og prioriter din fritid. Det er det du kommer til at huske, når du tager hjem igen 2. Selve processen op til opholdet har været ret tidskrævende og bøvlet, men det er det værd 3. Prøv at komme i kontakt med andre studerende. Hvis ikke det lykkedes med de lokale studerende, så tag til ESN events, der er der en masse søde og sociale mennesker :)
other_useful_info: Den professionelle tone kan nogle gange være lidt skrap, men man skal ikke tage det personligt.
most_rewarding: At finde nye venner, som jeg forhåbentlig kommer til at ha' resten af mit liv. At få en pause fra ens travle hverdag
greatest_challenge: At føle mig lidt overset på hospitalet.

crucial_aspects: university with a good reputation in a nice city with many students. It was important to have many opportunities socially with students fx for finding new hobbies and attending social events.
info_ease: It was easy since all the necessary information was send to me per mail.
arrival_assistance: Not much, I went to the students office once to get some help and that was good.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was a bit chaotic with many deadlines starting very early in the semester before you go on Exchange. Often I didnt know what I had to do next and luckily a friend who went on Exchange with me could help me and I could help her. The whole proces took a long time, 3 months minimum.
registration_help: Mails from the Erasmus coordinators that explained what was missing in the proces and could guide one through it.
registration_success: Very, I got every intership that I wanted.
registration_advice: Be early on planning your stay, check your mails often and dont hesitate to mail/call the Erasmus coordinators.
course_level: It was okay, but didn`t fit completely to what I wanted to learn.
teaching_comparison: The classes were intersting but not very student activating like they are at UCPH. It sometimed was very old-school fx without any questions to the students and without any slides and with a lot of hierachy, which did`nt make it easy to ask.
courses_enrolled: Clinical stay at the department for anestesiology, internal medicine and surgery
recommended_courses: I learned a lot in all deparments, but mostly in anestesiology and internal medicine, because it was a nice learning environment.
unexpected_costs: cafés and shopping
cost_comparison: Alkohol was unexpectly cheap, food was cheap as well
activities_available: a lot of sports, choir, hiking trips
activities_recommended: Choir-because you meet a lot of other students and its fun sport-because you will be more motivated
weekend_recommendations: See the old town, the castle, museums, art galleries, go to techno partys/ concerts with other students, hike in the mountains especially on the "Philosophen Weg" or go for a run
culture_adjustment: The culture was simuler to mine in many ways and it was easy to adjust
socializing_tips: Ask your roomates what their plans are and join for partys or coffee dates whenever possible. Try to meet with people for your courses. You can also find many events in the Erasmus groups although that is not with local students.
cultural_challenges: The priorities were differnet and their was not a good work life balance. Apart from that many people were nice but quite introvert so its good to start Conversation in order to understand them better.
culture_appreciated: The ambition that all students had in common
top3_advice: -be good at the language or take a class before -its good to talk about your/ your host institutions expectations when you start so you don`t get disappointed or uncomfortable if they ask to much -try to do as many activities as possible to meet people form the city and other internationals
other_useful_info: Look on websites to find other sport of music groups if you dont get into the universities.
most_rewarding: Become integrated, find great friend and learn many knew skills
greatest_challenge: Get used to the different expectations to students and to the way the healthcare system workes as weel as the communication between the different groups

crucial_aspects: Det var en akademisk anerkendt institution og en smuk by.

Det er både en god mulighed for at lære folk at kende og det giver en god "booster" inden man starter klinik. Min tredje ting er, at man også kan tage dette ophold, selv det eneste tyske man umildbart har haft er fra gymnasiet. Jeg havde et godt og lærerigt ophold på trods. crucial_aspects: Heidelberg is a very beautiful city with an interesting history and buildings. Their university is also known to be very good and as I had never been to southern Germany, that was also a motivation for me to choose Heidelberg.
info_ease: It was fairly easy, although I experienced some bureaucratical/practical challenges, e.g. regarding insurance and getting documents signed.
arrival_assistance: I received a lot of assistance from Studierendenwerk (The organisation responsible for all things about your study, except the study itself). They gave us a very detailed guide to how to do different things. Also at the first in our intro week at the university we received a lot of different guides about the city and how to do things regarding our study/courses.
arrival_comments: I was pretty satisfied, but in regards to information about different courses, I did not get enough help or guidance, in which as a result, I chose one course at Master Level although I am still studying for my bachelor degree. This course was a bit harder for me, and it would have been nice to be better informed on beforehand, which courses are directed/meant for Bachelor students and which ones for Master Students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process partly took place online, where I had to send personal information to the University (Picture of myself, date of birth, my earlier studies, information about insurance) and then the responsible persons had to sign different documents, e.g. Enrollment. When I arrived in Germany, I had to fill in more information online, to be able to get my Student Card. I also had to announce that I had moved to the city at the city council.
registration_help: There is an institute that only works with helping international students. It was possible to contact them over email or physically in the central part of town. Apart from that, an employee from Studierendenwerk and two from the university had a mail correspondence with all Erasmus students, to help and inform us about things we had to do and answer questions. They were all very nice and helpful.
registration_success: I was very successful. I got accepted into all the courses for which I had applied.
registration_advice: Make sure to check your Ku Mail, as you will be reminded about steps you have to do in mobility online.
course_level: I am currently taking my bachelors degree and I were as well, when I was doing my exchange. Most of my courses except one course (that were on Masters Level) were on Bachelor level and three of my courses were specifically aimed at Erasmus students.
teaching_comparison: It was a little bit more formal than at UCPH and all exams were written in hand with no accommodations (Notes, computer porgrammes) available. That was a very different experience for me, as at UCPH exams normally take place digitally and you may bring your notes, use digital programmes etc. as help. ECTS points are also granted in a much different way. In Denmark it is very fixed from the beginning, but in Germany it was much more "flexible" - meaning that you could make an agreement with your teacher about how many ECTS you wanted/needed, and then write an assignment according to that.
courses_enrolled: Grammatik im Kontakt Grundlagen Spracherwerb Wortschatz C2 Textverstehen und Textproduktion B2 Konversation in Kleingruppen B2 Gegenwartsdramatik im Kontext des 42. Heidelberger Stückemarkts Die französischen Revolution und Napoleon in der deutschsprachigen Literatur
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the courses at IDF that are specifically aimed at Erasmus students, since it was very nice to get to know people from other countries and their culture and languages and it was very relevant topics in regards to improving my German, written as well as spoken/oral proficiency. I would also recommend the course "Grammatik im Kontakt", as we were a lot of students with mixed backgrounds and the combination with grammar/Contact between languages made the course very relevant and super interesting. The course "Gegenwartsdramatik im Kontext des 42. Heidelberger Stückemarkts" was also super interesting. It was interesting to learn about a current literary/cultural event taking place in the city and we were invited to see the theatre and hear interviews with the autors behind the plays, which was also very nice.
unexpected_costs: The Rundfunksteuer. (German tax for radio and television)
cost_comparison: Food was a little bit more expensive than I thought. Housing were way less expensive than I expected, before finding my housing.
activities_available: All kinds of different sports activities were available via Hochschulsport. They had Kayak classes, hiking, ballet etc. Apart from sport, they also offered two choices. It was free for students to visit the theatre and the prices for cinema tickets were reduced.
activities_recommended: Choir. You get to know a lot of new people and it is fun to sing. Also groups for finding friends/meeting new people in the city.
weekend_recommendations: Sail on the Neckar, visit the old castle. Go to the cinema or on museum. There is also a lot of opportunities for hiking in nature.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. germany is a lot like Denmark. The only little thing that is different, is that they are generally a bit more formal than Danes typically are.
cultural_challenges: It is normal to have a more formal relationship with your teachers, e.g. not calling them by their first name, but last name. I found that a bit difficult sometimes, as I am not so accustomed to it. Apart from that I did not find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: I like German literature and food, and the people are a lot like danish people, which makes it very easy to fit in.
top3_advice: Be aware that the university system is more unstructured than at UCPH, and that you may need to ask more questions/to ask more for help in general, to make sure that everything is at should be. It is a good idea to think about transport (If you want to buy the Germany ticket), e.g. if you have plans to visit your family during your stay or just want to visit and explore more of germany while being on Erasmus.
other_useful_info: No:))
most_rewarding: I have gotten way better at speaking German as well as understanding it by attending classes only in German and by living surrounded by people only speaking German to me, to a point where I am almost fluent in understanding the language. It feels as if I have "gained" a new language In a very short amount of time, and it is a very good skill to have acquired. I have learned a lot about the beautiful city of Heidelberg (where I was at exchange) and it feels a bit like my second home now - that is also a very rewarding part of my exchange experience. I have gotten to know a lot of new people and had classes and courses that were very interesting and where I read a lot of interesting literature and learned many interesting and useful things.
greatest_challenge: To live alone so far away from home (10 Hours by train). I have always lived in Copenhagen and I lived with my family before my exchange. Having to balance practical things, being social and preparing for university classes in a foreign country was a little challenging in the beginning and from time to time during my exchange, but I have gotten a lot more independent and learned that it is possible to manage it, even though I was sometimes a little scared.

Go maybe to Marbach to see Schillers birth place and the german museum of literature. Maybe also to Weimar. The old opera house in Frankfurt has good concerts once in a while. Theater in Heidelberg is ok, and sometime the screen good movies at Karlstor.
culture_adjustment: Yes very easy but also demanding at times. Germans can do mind their own buissiness a lot like people do in Denmark and they usually never approach you in public unless they are very drunk. There are many festivites in Heidelberg old city and therefore a lot of noise but this is also charming.
socializing_tips: Just approach people and be not afraid of exhibiting yourself and your flaws. Get their number and go for a walk go get lunch together at marstall. Enjoy solitude.
cultural_challenges: That people look into their phones so much in public. Especially in the trains. It is horrible to be among these screens all of the time. Germans love staring at their screens whenever they go outside their door. There are a lot of tourist in Heidelberg and they are very indifferent to your presence which sometimes feels a bit estranging. they constantly take photos of the bride and the castle.
culture_appreciated: I appreciate that the germans are ready for a debate about politics or history. You can always get a long discussion about opportunism for instance and they will listen to you carefully if you are polite.
top3_advice: That Heidelberg can offer you a lot of knowledge and new strategies to approach your research academic career. You can make friends there that you can have for a long time afterwards. Strong bonds are likely to form!
other_useful_info: The university usually dont offer examples of previous exams for you to practice on. So you just gotta learn everything that they present on their powerpoints or on the blackboard. Usually this means solving the tasks they give you during the course and learning how to solve them by heart, this will make you do well at the exams.
most_rewarding: To make new friends. To learn.
greatest_challenge: Having to do my exams in Heidelberg while my semester in Copenhagen had already begund in the begining of februrary. That was kind of annoying but manageable.
other_comments: I generally recomend going on exchange! Its a good idea especially if you havent lived outside Denmark before. It changes your sense of sovereignty and your life ulitmatly.

course_level: I found the level very fitting for what I am used to. I only took seminars, which made for a lot of academic discussion. However, I did find that there is a lot more mandatory work to be turned in.

crucial_aspects: One of the main reasons I chose this destination was the opportunity to improve my German.
overall_comments: My exchange semester was a very rewarding experience. I had the opportunity to develop academically, improve my German, and experience everyday life in a different culture.
info_ease: It was quite straightforward to find the information I needed upon arrival, as most practical details were available online and easy to access.
arrival_assistance: Overall, I was very satisfied with the support available. It was easy to find the information I needed, and the staff were helpful when I had questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: My exchange semester was a very rewarding experience. I had the opportunity to develop academically, improve my German, and experience everyday life in a different culture.
registration_process: One important part of the registration process was the health insurance documentation. Even though I had the European Health Insurance Card, it still had to be approved by a German health insurance provider. After this, the provider sent the confirmation directly to the university. This was a necessary administrative step before the enrolment could be completed, so it is something future students should be aware of in advance.
registration_help: The International Office in Heidelberg was very helpful whenever I needed assistance. They did not respond very often by phone, but they were reliable in replying to emails, so email was the best way to get support.
registration_success: I was very successful in registering for the courses I wanted. At my host institution, it was generally not necessary to register for the classes themselves, but only for the exams. This made the process much easier and gave me flexibility in choosing and attending courses.
registration_advice: Take the process as it comes and try not to stress too much, even if it feels bureaucratic at times. In the end, things usually work out. My advice would be to stay patient and not worry too much if the process seems slow or administrative. It can feel complicated at first, but it becomes clearer step by step. It is a good idea to be patient and prepared for some bureaucracy. Even if the process takes time, it is manageable, and the International Office can help if needed. Do not panic if the registration process feels confusing in the beginning. It involves several administrative steps, but if you follow the instructions carefully, it will work out. Be prepared for a process that can feel quite bureaucratic, and make sure to complete each step carefully. It is also helpful to communicate by email, since that was the most reliable way to get assistance. Try to stay organized and keep track of deadlines and required documents. The process can take time, but it is easier if you approach it calmly and one step at a time.
academics_comments: My exchange semester was a very rewarding experience. I had the opportunity to develop academically, improve my German, and experience everyday life in a different culture.
course_level: I found the courses quite challenging, both in terms of the academic level and the workload. The exam format was also very different from what I was used to at UCPH, so it took some time to adjust to the expectations and methods of assessment.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at my host institution involved smaller classes than at UCPH, which created a more interactive and personal learning environment.
courses_enrolled: Enviromental economics Advanced Macro behavioral public finance Development economics
recommended_courses: depends on the student
unexpected_costs: Nothing
cost_comparison: Food was generally cheaper than I had expected, especially when grocery shopping. Going out, such as eating at restaurants or meeting friends for drinks, was also more affordable than I had anticipated.
activities_available: There were a range of activities available for students, including Erasmus programmes and events, which made it easy to meet other international students. The university also offered sports programmes and other student activities that gave students opportunities to be active and social outside of their studies.
activities_recommended: I would especially recommend joining the Erasmus programmes, because they are a great way to meet new people, take part in social events, and get to know both other international students and the city more quickly.
weekend_recommendations: Nürnberg Strasbourg
culture_adjustment: It was very easy to adjust to the local culture, as life in Germany felt quite similar to life in Denmark in many ways. Because of these similarities, it was easy to settle in quickly and adapt to everyday life.
cultural_challenges: I found that the culture was somewhat more strict than what I was used to in Denmark, especially in relation to rules, structure, and formal procedures. However, since Germany and Denmark are quite similar in many ways, this was not a major challenge and was easy to adjust to over time.
culture_appreciated: I especially appreciated that the culture felt more formal, as it created a sense of structure, respect, and seriousness in both academic and everyday settings. At the same time, it was still easy to adapt because German and Danish culture are similar in many ways.
top3_advice: ry to learn some German before or during your stay, join Erasmus events to build a social network, and do not stress too much about the practical and administrative parts of the exchange, as things usually work out in the end.
other_useful_info: It is a good idea to always carry some cash with you, since not all places accept card payments. This is especially useful in everyday situations such as smaller shops, cafés, or local restaurants.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was improving my German. It was valuable to be able to practice the language in everyday life and to feel more confident using it over the course of the semester.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during the exchange was being away from home and adjusting to living independently in a different country. Even though it became easier over time, this was probably the most difficult part of the experience for me.

crucial_aspects: Recommendations from friends
overall_comments: Very different school with a lot of workload and high expectations, so most of the semester was spent at the library instead of talking and learning cultures. Not what i expected from Erasmus.
arrival_assistance: There was an introductionary day, but most of the stuff only applied to people doing their entire master's degree, and not Erasmus students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Very different school with a lot of workload and high expectations, so most of the semester was spent at the library instead of talking and learning cultures. Not what i expected from Erasmus.
registration_process: Everything has to be done physically at the school or using a VPN with two-factor authentication. It requires a login to setup 2FA, but it requires 2FA to login. Took a long time to find the way through. Then a lot of documents needs to be signed, both online and physically at different offices. Not very streamlined.
registration_help: i think it would be possible to write erasmus coordinators.
registration_success: I managed in the end. It does requires registrations on multiple platforms. Much of the information about the course is different than what is presented on the website. Especially the correct weekly schedule was only available at the first or second lecture. So it was almost impossible to plan which courses to take up until a week or two into the semester. This would not be a problem, if the courses didnt have mandatory weekly assignments. The result is that students have to attend many classes for some weeks, until a proper schedule could be made.
registration_advice: Show up in person for everything. Dont trust the system and website. Write all professors directly. Also for things like schedule, requirements etc.
academics_comments: Very different school with a lot of workload and high expectations, so most of the semester was spent at the library instead of talking and learning cultures. Not what i expected from Erasmus.
course_level: The level is not that high, but a lot of work is expected. Most of everything you do has to be handed in and graded which is very time consuming. So even if the problems are easy and you already know how to do them, you have to spent hours writing solutions and transfer it to a format that sufficient for a graded report.
teaching_comparison: The style at host institution is very old school. You have to figure things out yourself, and if you dont you will be told that you are bad and might not be able to go to exams. It feels like the teachers think students are just lazy people who needs to be forced to do everything. Example: if a lecture is bad (that is: does very confusing lectures with unreadable handwriting and countless mistakes), many students decide not to show up because time is spent better learning from other sources. The fix to this: force students to show up. Comparing with UCPH theres a lot more teaching involved. The students learns through dialogue with the tutors and sometimes the professors, and staff seems to trust that you know what you are doing. But again, the scandinavian countries are also know for a flatter hierarchical structure, that Germany is not known for.
courses_enrolled: Fundamentals of Simulations Methods Condensed Matter Theory Optimization in Machine Learning and Vision Dynamical Systems Theory in Machine Learning Introduction to GPU Programming and Architecture
recommended_courses: Optimization in Machine Learning and Vision. Generally any course that a "seminar". This is the only part where Heidelberg got it right. These courses are about reading scientific papers and presenting them to other students. Here dialogue and communication is essential, and you get a lot of presentations that are cutting-edge and more digestable than usual lectures.
unexpected_costs: Theres a lot of things you need to get when you arrive at an empty room, like duvets, sheets, clothes lamps etc. This ended up being more expensive than i though.
cost_comparison: Food can be very cheap. The canteen at uni can give you a full semi-healthy cooked meal for 2-5 euro. Going out is also very cheap (drinks and restaurants).
activities_available: Basically every sport, and a lot of smaller clubs. Its not difficult to find things to to. The difficult parts is finding free time to do them.
activities_recommended: Go to the ESN events in the beginning, although it might be scary. People are really nice and interesting.
weekend_recommendations: Heidelberg uni does not have holidays, except some days around christmas (but you get homework for this break). Weekends are mostly for catching up on courses, but most things are closed on sundays, so i would recommend exploring the nearby mountain forests.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. But again, german and danish culture is not that different.
socializing_tips: Just start talking to people in your classes/at sports. Everybody has no problem speaking english.
cultural_challenges: The work mentallity is very different. People have no problem spending their nights studying and sleeping 4 hours each day. Makes it quite difficult to keep up with their level of productivity. It also makes it hard not just to follow their path and ending up ruining yourself. University students in germany are generally quite young, and many people are very dedicated students. This means that many university students havent done that many other things than studying, which contributes to the "young" feeling. Sometimes university is comparable to 2.G and 3.G in gymnasiet in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: The germans has a lot of systems, but in the end none of them really works. This means that if you want something done you just show up and talk to people. It can be frustrating in the beginning, but in the end its much easier. No more waiting for responses and filling formulas. Just show up and they will fix your problem and sign your papers.
top3_advice: The workload is very intense, and theres not really any help to get. Would really try to take easy courses or less than 30 ECTS if possible. None of the locals do 30 ECTS semesters. Its not build for that.
other_useful_info: Interrail has an Erasmus pass, which gives you 6 travel days very cheaply. Perfect for a getting there and back, and perhaps a visit home or to neightbouring countries. Kleinanzeigen has cheap used things. The Mensa's of Heidelberg are really good and cheap for students. Dont worry about packing a lunchpack ever again.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all over the world and hearing about their backgrounds and culture.
greatest_challenge: The workload. It was very difficult to find time to do things with many weekly written reports and loads of classes. Theres tons of opportunities to meet people, experience the area and do cultural things, but most weekends is spend at the library.

activities_recommended: In the beginning I went to the ESN-events to meet other students, but this is mostly internationals. To meet "locals" I would definitely recommend joining a sport, reading club or orchestra (just anything that you find interesting).
weekend_recommendations: The city itself is lovely. Was only there for four months, but would have loved to see more of the surroundings.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy - German and Danish culture are quite similar.
socializing_tips: See above
cultural_challenges: It's not normal to be friendly/familiar with patients and as a non native speaker it's hard to remember to use the "Sie".
culture_appreciated: In comparison to Danes the Germans have a great work ethic and I find that in general people were very friendly!
top3_advice: 1) Don't go if you want a good academic output 2) Go if it's more important to explore the lovely city 3) Go if you want to develop personally and not academically
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: That I know that I can survive any clinical rotation.
greatest_challenge: Well I think my previous answers speak for themselves.

crucial_aspects: Location, Availability and Social life.
info_ease: Both Heidelberg and the ESN did a good job of making sure that every exchange student was well informed. I personally only had problems, when it came to choosing courses.
arrival_assistance: Socialising, orientation and information regarding opportunities at Heidelberg University.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I got a document from my host university with a step by step guide for registration, which made the registration process really easy and straight forward.
registration_help: Step by step guide from host university.
registration_success: Not a single course from the course list was held this years winter semester... I ended up with 0 out of 5 courses that i wanted.
registration_advice: Just take it easy, don't stress too much. Remember you can always send a mail to the erasmus coordinator and they will help you out.
course_level: I was forced to take a Masters course, since only 8 english courses were available for Computer Science students. The level was definitely high, but i'm not sure if it was the language barrier, the professors or the teaching style that made it even more difficult.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was pretty similar in terms of structure. I had both lectures and exercise classes, just like at UCPH. The biggest difference was the exams being hand written 90 minutes.
courses_enrolled: 1. Algorithms and Data Structures 2 2. Einführung in Software Engineering 3. Embedded Machine Learning 4. IT-Sicherheit 1 5. Programmierkurs
recommended_courses: I can recommend Programmierkurs and einführung in software engineering. These are both very interesting courses and they go hand in hand really well.
unexpected_costs: Rundfunkbeitrag (8 euro/month).
cost_comparison: Local transport is really expensive if you don't have the D-Ticket. Everything from the supermarket is cheap (compared to denmark) and the same goes for restaurants and bars.
activities_available: Hochschulsport provide sport groups that you can join for free or very cheap. The only problem is that the amount of people who can join these groups is very limited.
activities_recommended: Bouldering, tennis, football and calisthenics.
weekend_recommendations: Go to other close cities, visit bar streets, board game nights and sleepovers.
culture_adjustment: I have already been to germany many times (since my grandparent's live there), so I was already very used to it.
socializing_tips: Go to the ESN events (local students also come to these sometimes) and sign up for the buddy program.
cultural_challenges: Paying with cash almost everywhere and some places not accepting credit card.
culture_appreciated: Friendly, outgoing and entertaining people.
top3_advice: 1. don't go there if you are studying computer science. 2. check out private housing (if you are early you might find way better alternatives) 3. make sure you have a SEPA approved bank account (it is a lot less stressful when you don't have to worry about manual money transfers every month)
most_rewarding: Getting out of my comfort zone, meeting people from all over the world and gaining friends for life.
greatest_challenge: Navigating websites, using heico, moodle, müsli.

institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
crucial_aspects: I visited Hong Kong for a week on holiday a few years prior and decided there that at some point I wanted to live there for a few months. Given that rent is the highest in the world and they have some good universities, I figured that going on exchange and living in a dorm would be my best opportunity to do that.
overall_comments: I believe that my exchange was very unique and hard to compare with other exchanges to the same university due to the Covid restrictions.
info_ease: Quite easy, it was all explained in a single email.
arrival_assistance: I recieved an email containing information about where to be and when.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I believe that my exchange was very unique and hard to compare with other exchanges to the same university due to the Covid restrictions.
registration_process: You have to register on an old and reliable website that the whole school tries to get on at the same time. To make up for this they allow people to register at different times.
registration_help: Not much.
registration_success: Not successful. Nowhere in the information provided to us exchange students did it say that a lot of courses run out of space on the same day you are allowed to register. I starting registering for my courses 2 hours after it opened and 2 of my priority courses were already full so I had to settle for other courses.
registration_advice: Sit ready to register the second they open it up.
academics_comments: I believe that my exchange was very unique and hard to compare with other exchanges to the same university due to the Covid restrictions.
course_level: The general level was adequate but there was a very big difference from course to course. Some courses I would spend 10 hours a week to prepare for, others I would use 30 minutes max.
teaching_comparison: It focused a lot on mandatory attendance and weekly assignments, making it feel a lot more like high school than university at UCPH. That doesn't mean the workload is too much though, if you choose "exchange friendly" courses you'll be more than fine.
courses_enrolled: Topology, Game Theory, Introduction to music theory I, Design and analysis of algorithms and AI ethics.
recommended_courses: My strongest recommendation would definitely be "Negotiation". Although I didn't have the course myself, I heard from a lot of other exchange students that had that course and they all loved it. It was fun, interactive and the perfect workload to payoff ratio. Of the courses I myself had I can reccomend game theory, especially seeing as we don't have a similar one back home. It is a fun math courses that gives a very good introduction to the field while clearly showing how applicable it is.
unexpected_costs: You spend a lot more than you initially budget for on exchange. Although cantines on campus are cheap and there technically are the facilities to cook, you won't have time for that and without noticing you'll be eating out most evenings with your new friends. Bare in mind that these costs are with covid, so given that the nightlife and cultural parts of the cities will be open in the future, expect to spend even more than this.
cost_comparison: Public transport is very cheap and convinient but food is more expensive than you think once you leave campus.
activities_available: Due to covid there weren't any planned activities yet I've heard from local students that normally exchange students have plenty of acitivies they can sign up to.
activities_recommended: The campus is heaven for all sport fanatics. It's filled with plenty of sports facilities in perfect condition with a beautiful ocean view.
weekend_recommendations: There are also plenty of good hikes around campus that lead to small and cozy beaches.
culture_adjustment: Due to covid it was never truly necessary. The only true difference was the cuisine, but that was easy to adjust to.
socializing_tips: Due to covid I didn't interact a lot with local students.
cultural_challenges: Not really any. Not many non-student locals spoke english so you had to communicate with your phone quite often but that's about it.
culture_appreciated: The food.
top3_advice: 1. Get a big group of exchange students together and go to Mr.Wongs
other_useful_info: Expect to spend more than what you budget for, it always costs more than expected.
most_rewarding: Meeting all the other exchange students and having 4 months exploring a new country with them.
greatest_challenge: Balancing school work with all the social things you want to do, especially if you study something with a typically high workload.

institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

info_ease: Reasonably easy, there were many emails & I really had to keep up with sorting important vs. non-important stuff and often had to ask my colleagues for information. But in the end, it worked out.
arrival_assistance: Other students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You can choose between many courses and are relatively free in doing so. That was nice. However, the wait times are not really convenient.
registration_help: Profs & online.
registration_success: Got all the classes I wanted to take.
registration_advice: Try as many courses as you can in the course registration period, KU did accept all my proposed courses and I really could choose according to the teacher & topic and not only the title and description.
course_level: Took 2 undergrad, and 2 grad courses. Grad courses were easier and less competitive (because grades are not curved), would definitely recommend this if you're optimizing for an easy semester.
teaching_comparison: Less group work, more competitive, way more assignment work.
courses_enrolled: Applied Game Theory Public Policy & Ethics Microeconomics & Public Policy Peoples and Cultures of South East Asia
recommended_courses: Applied Game Theory, great prof Peoples and Cultures of South East Asia, because you're there and it's nice to learn something about the culture of your host country.
unexpected_costs: Groceries were way more expensive than I anticipated
cost_comparison: Everything was more expensive than expected, sports facilities on campus were free
activities_available: Everything! Very, very broad and comprehensive
activities_recommended: Everything sports, hikes, swims, etc.
weekend_recommendations: Go traveling, to Korea, Japan, Taiwan, South East Asia, and go hiking!
culture_adjustment: Good, you're still in an international bubble :)
socializing_tips: Use Tinder to connect to locals (you can just use it as "I'm looking for friends"), elevated my stay very much!
cultural_challenges: People are a bit less friendly than in Denmark, everything is extremely fast-paced.
culture_appreciated: Food, Music, Hikes, Family-based values
top3_advice: Don't judge Spend your weekends seeing things (city or nature), even the uni is stressful. You can always study but you can only be in Hong Kong once Eat Indian Food
other_useful_info: Read a lot about the culture, and ask other people who've been there what to do, talk to locals, they know better

institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
crucial_aspects: I wanted to go the far east. South Korea and Japan required too high grades. China seemed like too big of an culture shock for me - so I applied for Hong Kong and Taiwan.
info_ease: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology was extremely helpfull, very informative and quickly to respond to questions. Only thing I found miscommunicated is how expensive Hong Kong is. Supermarket prices are easily doubled compared to Denmark and if you eat anywhere else than canteens and streetfoods eating out is rather pricy as well.
arrival_assistance: As soon as I arrived to the university I got all the information I needed. You could receive further assistance through the buddy program of the school if needed.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Courses are released --> You pick what you want --> First comes first.
registration_help: You can write the professors for questions
registration_success: Classes I had expected to take before I arrived were not available anymore. So I had to choose other things.
registration_advice: Easy and simple.
course_level: The general level of the academic was lower than in Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: I loved the much more practical way used at HKUST. On UCPH you have to read hundreds of pages each semester and not using things learned before the exams. On HKUST you get small assignments every other week which is apart of your grade, forcing you to keep up to date with the stuff, which made me feel much more prepared for exams in the end and felt like I remembered much more of the things I learned.
courses_enrolled: Urban Air Pollution Mass Balance Energy Resources and Usage Atmospheric Dynamics Survey of Ocean Science
recommended_courses: Atmospheric Dynamics for the math lovers Urban Air Pollution for lot of facts
unexpected_costs: Food is EXTREMELY expensive. Especially healthy food. 7-eleven jumping for going out is a must. A beer in most clubs/bars is 80-110 DKK GLASS BOTTLE
cost_comparison: Electronics is cheap Food is expensive
activities_available: I swam every 2nd/3rd day at my stay since I had a swimming pool 100m from my room.
activities_recommended: Sign up for everything in the start.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city and do hikes.
culture_adjustment: Hong Kong is pretty similar to other big metropols, just with a chinese twist. The Hong Kong Island and campus was not that big of cultural change. Some places in the outskirts of Kowloon is very chinese though
socializing_tips: Participate in things, even though you don't always have the surplus to do so.
cultural_challenges: Some foods and the way food is served was not my exact taste. Most older people are not that humble.
culture_appreciated: I love the way people just tend to sleep wherever they want to. If you are tired you can just lay down and sleep wherever you are. I found most young people very free spirited and dressing up just as they want to not following the social norms.
top3_advice: Nice facilities! More nature than you would expect! Expensive and rather poor food :-(
other_useful_info: You will figure out yourself
most_rewarding: You just evolve as a human

institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
crucial_aspects: Due to covid the exchange options in Europe was quite limited. Another thing was that a lot of the universities in USA you had to be on the bachelor, and I was on my first year of the master. The third things was language requirements, I also looked at Paris, Munich and South America, but all had requirements for getting a certain grade on the language test. It also needed to be a university with no GPA or lower than 7 grade GPA requirement, as my GPA at the application time was 6,8... So all Japanese and Korean universities and American and Australian universities were not available for me. Lastly, I spent a lot of time looking into the courses available, and I was looking for places where I could get courses about nanomaterials etc.
info_ease: I think HKUST was quite good at sending out information about everything before hand, so it was easy arriving. They even did most of the work handling student visa.
arrival_assistance: Before hand HKUST had fixed everything according to student visa and medical insurance (it was part of the rent money). So at arrival and orientation days it was just following the signs and then you got your student-ID as well.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We arrived, checked in at our dorm rooms, we just had to show a document. At orientation day they showed us around and told us about all the important information. Later that same day we could collect our student-ID.
registration_help: They answered their emails quite fast, and you could always go to their office and talk with them.
registration_success: I got into all the classes I applied for. They had a swapping period the first two weeks, and the courses I wanted to swap is was able to.
registration_advice: Just read the emails they send and do as most as you can before leaving, then everything is going to go quite smoothly at arriving. I can really recommend staying at a hotel a few days before arriving to sleep out the jetlag.
course_level: Generally, the level is lower than I DK. The 5th year course I took, which is the highest level you could take, could very well have been a 3rd year course in DK. The hard part was mostly getting a lot of assignments, projects and presentations at the same time.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. The lectures was a teacher talking and going through slides for 80 min without a break. Some courses it was even 3 hours without a break... The practice classes was just a master or PhD student going through solution of the assignments for 50 min and not us actually having time to get help how to solve thing, also practice classes was ONLY 50 min a week. There was not really any feedback on the assignments, you just got a grade, which in my opinion is not very development oriented, but just "I have to do this and get It done" from the teachers side.
courses_enrolled: CENG5840: Nanomaterials for Chemical Engineering Applications CHEM4420: Statistical Machine Learning for Chemical Data Analysis LIFS4320: Data Science for Biology and Medicine LIFS3240: Introduction to Neurobiology PHYS3042: Structure and Properties of Crystalline Solids
recommended_courses: I would really recommend the Nanomaterials for Chemical Engineering Applications course and Statistical Machine Learning for Chemical Data Analysis course. The lectures were sweet and listening, but also the most interesting of the courses I had.
unexpected_costs: I had to get a new backpack and jacket due to mold because of the humid dorm rooms.
cost_comparison: The food at the canteens and fast food restaurants were cheaper than I expected. Also public transportation was really really cheap. The cinema was also quite cheap, and I could even get student discount (so about 50 DKK for a ticket)
activities_available: There were planned trips for the exchange students in the first month only. But we were out seeing a temple, visiting Lamma island and painting ceramics. They sometimes had opening to join sport clubs, but the places was so limited that it was impossible to get a place.
activities_recommended: I would really recommend looking into the free sport facilities. I brought my own tennis racket and balls (you could also borrow) and play twice a week. Their indoor and outdoor swimming pools was also great. Outside of the university I will recommend hiking trips and kayaking in the Sai Kung area.
weekend_recommendations: Go hiking and kayaking, a lot of HK is nature. Go visit Victoria harbor and Victoria peak, the Big Buddha, Ozone bar, Ladies market, Kowloon walled city park, go to the cinema. Take the ferry between HK island and the TST area, also take the ferries to Lamma island and Cheung Chau. You get free entrance to the science museum and other some other things with your student-ID. If you want to stay at a hotel in the city I will recommend finding a hotel in the Central area or Mongkok area, not TST.
culture_adjustment: I think it was fairly easy.
socializing_tips: You really have to be the one engaging and talking. They are quite shy and don't engage much.
cultural_challenges: The thing with not being able as much to influence the teaching (80 min without a break is mean, only getting grades and not any feedback etc.), not being able to talk with the teacher and just "accept" that the students doesn't have anything to say was frustrating.
culture_appreciated: The food was incredible! Also how helpfull the global office was at the university.
top3_advice: 1. Save up enough money so you can enjoy the time fully. HK is a bit more expensive than DK, and there are also great opportunities for traveling to the nearby countries. 2. If you go in the spring semester the weather are going to change from 13 degrees to 30-something degrees and quite humid during those 4 months. So bring some dehumidifier balls for your clothes and things. 3. Go out and experience the city when it is most alive, in the evening. The classes aren't that hard, so use your time to have fun as well
other_useful_info: Generally they are a bit more "controlling" in drinking/partying on campus and especially in the dorms (where it is forbidden). And also the dorm life is not like living a kollegium, it feels a bit more like a hostel.
most_rewarding: Getting a break from the same routine of KU. I was away on my 8th semester, so it was nice to have a change in the way of having courses and exams. And also just experiencing a new place, learning in different environments, and being able to travel around afterwards.
greatest_challenge: How the whole teaching system/hierarchy is build up.

institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
crucial_aspects: Far away as well as Hong Kong being an interesting place to me as well as being very different from Copenhagen. The University also had many interesting looking courses within my field. With this university I also had the opportunity to go with my girlfriend, which also weighted a bit. Another thing is the facilities and beautiful location of the university.
info_ease: I don't remember there being any problems.
arrival_assistance: There where introduction seminars as well as flyers and mails. I also had a very good exchange buddy.
arrival_comments: All exchange student had their orientation together. So easy to meet the other exchange students. I would have liked to have had some introduction events with my line of study to be introduced to the locals and the exchange students within my studies, although you are not really connected to a spsecific study.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It is all through their online system, but it is a bit confusing at first and it all happens a couple of days before the semester start until two weeks into the semester. I am not sure I remember it completely. In the beginning there is a period were you can add courses to a wish list. If their are any prerequisites or if it is a post-graduate course and you are undergrad you have have to apply for approval with the professor. Then their is a period were you actually sign up for the approved courses. After the semester starts you can add/drop/swap courses for two weeks. You might be pre-approved and signed up for courses you have listed in the application process.
registration_help: Online guides.
registration_success: Didn't get one course because the approval came after the course was full.. Worked fine with other courses. It seems quite a few professors are away on vacation when the course registration starts, so a few approvals came quite late.
registration_advice: Send the approval asap. They don't have to be very detailed. I suspect they don't look that closely at them. Get approved for all courses you are interested in. In the add/drop period (the first two weeks) most courses have no assignments and all lectures are purely introductory, so use it to find out which courses you want as their is quite little information available, it is easy to swap.
course_level: I had one year 3 course, three year 4 courses and a year five (post-grad). The post-grad course may have had the lowest workload. The academic level is slightly below KU.
teaching_comparison: Much more focus on lectures, which were of generally much poorer quality than KU. Mostly done on power points. The slides (lecture notes as they called them) is their most important course material even though most were not that good. Their TA session are a joke. If there is a TA session it is only 50 minutes a week. The ones I have had, has been a TA going through some computer program or method at a lecture room or walking (very fast due to the tome) through solutions to exercises. You don't get to sit down with the exercises yourself with the TA being available to help you, which is what I am used to from KU. The TA is there to tell you how do it, not help you learn it, but that is most likely a cultural thing.
courses_enrolled: CENG5840: Nanomaterials for Chemical Engineering Applications. CHEM4420: Statistical Machine Learning Methods for Chemical Data Analysis. LIFS4320: Data Science for Biology and Medicine MATH4335: Introduction to Optimization PHYS3142: Computational Methods in Physics
recommended_courses: CHEM4420: Teaching is not the best, but it is very chill and the professor is very friendly. You only have to do a project in the end. PHYS3142: If you can already program in python it will be quite easy. The workload is quite high with an assignment each week and an exam projects. The bar for passing is quite low though, the professor said he passes all that has at least tried to do all assignments. It is also decadently taught.
unexpected_costs: Had to buy a new computer.... Computers are much cheaper than in DK.
cost_comparison: Many Groceries are more expensive than DK. Restaurants are generally cheaper than DK. A meal in the canteen is 25-40 kr. Public transport it very good and cheap.
activities_available: There were some student clubs. Didn't participate
activities_recommended: Do sports and go hike in the beautiful HK nature
weekend_recommendations: Go to Macau for a day. Didn't go to mainland China as it was still difficult to get in, but it might get better. Travel South East Asia.
culture_adjustment: No too bad. There is some stuff that is difficult to get used to, fx a different socially accepted behaviors.
socializing_tips: No, it is quite difficult I think. They are very shy and often surprisingly bad at English considering everything at the university is in english.
cultural_challenges: Teaching style. Different socially accepted behaviors.
culture_appreciated: The food. I mostly appreciated experiencing the culture.
top3_advice: Don't worry too much about the relative grading. Sign up for as many exchange intro activities as possible. Explore the nature - go hiking.
other_useful_info: Apply for a student octopus card asap.
most_rewarding: Trying something completely different.
greatest_challenge: Befriending locals, adjusting to and accepted the teaching style.
other_comments: It is a cool campus with beautiful location in the mountains and down by the water. The on-campus facitlities are mostly good with many restaurants , McDonalds, super market, 7-11, sports facilities etc. The transportation to and from the city could have been easier as the metro doesn't go all the way to campus.

institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
crucial_aspects: I knew I wanted to go to Asia to experience a completely different culture and get some new perspectives. Two of my friends who had gone on exchange in Hong Kong recommended that I go there.
info_ease: It was very easy. The university contacted me and emailed me all the information that I needed. I had a contact person who I could ask for help and she always replied to me within a day or two.
arrival_assistance: My contact person invited me to an orientation meeting and I was the only MA student in the humanities department. She showed me around the whole campus, helped me get my student ID and answered all my questions. She even had some small gifts prepared for me.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: My contact person sent me an email with the description if the courses available to me and then I just had to choose five and email them back to her. Then she signed me up for the courses. This was done so that I could choose before the rest of the students and that was very helpful. The course descriptions for the available courses are published quite late around mid-August.
registration_help: I could ask my contact person any questions. She also showed me how to add/drop courses in the system if i wanted to change any of my pre-selected courses.
registration_success: I was very successful as I could sign up before the other students.
registration_advice: Just choose the courses that sound interesting to you. After you start you can always change to another course. HKUST use a "shop around" system which means that until mid-September you can go to the first classes of any course and see if you like it. Before you drop a course make sure that there are other available courses and that they aren't full.
course_level: As an MA student you are not allowed to take any BA courses, but you can join mixed courses. I had two mixed courses where the requirements for the exam were different depending on whether you were a BA or an MA student.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was very similar to UCPH, as many of the professors were educated from US universities. However, they used a lot of Chinese sources and ideas. There was a greater focus on grades than at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Politcal Culture, Fascism, History and the Future, Images of Japan, Animals and Society.
recommended_courses: In Political Culture I had a great professor who really understood how to get the best out of her students. She used new and relevant studies to teach us about how to measure culture and she was not afraid to talk about sensitive political topics even in a room filled with mainland Chinese students and local Hong Kong students. In Animals and Society I was given a new perspective on societies view on animals. It was incredibly interesting and I learned about so many new perspectives on medicine, covid-19 and global warming.
unexpected_costs: I didn't encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than I anticipated. You can get cheaper food than I did, but it will take some planning. Public transport is subsidised and you can get money back every month by using these machines at the big stations.
activities_available: They arranged barbecues, Christmas dinner, hikes and culture walks with food. You could join a kayaking class and other water sports activities.
activities_recommended: I didn't really join in any of the cultural activities, so I can't say. This was probably a side-effect of living off campus, but I did get emails about activities I could join I just didn't. Other students told me the sailing club was really fun.
weekend_recommendations: There are so many things to do in Hong Kong. Go to Sai Kung on a hike and visit the beautiful pier. Go to the many beautiful Islands. Go on a Junk boat to meet new friends, swim and party. Go to Sham Shui Po and visit the huge market! (Remember to bring cash). Go to central and take the mid-levels escalators to Tai Kwun to sit on the square of the old prison. Visit Macau's old town, eat the traditional almond = cakes, dragon beard candy and the delicious egg tarts. Bring your friends out for Yum Cha and eat traditional Dim Sum. Eat the best food in the world! There are endless things to do and see in HK.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Talk with them in between classes and in the breaks. People are very friendly but they also have their own friends, so be proactive and ask them to eat lunch together or hang out. I was approach by many people to talk and connect. Although, most people that approach you are probably exchange students themselves, some are local. The Mainland Chinese students are the most interested in you in my experience. People share their snacks and ask about your country.
cultural_challenges: I don't find any differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: The food! The friendly people and language.
top3_advice: Ebneezer's Kebab is the best for lunch There's a shuttle bus from campus to the big areas of HK - use it, it is free! The security guards will help you if you are lost
other_useful_info: Bring a sweater because it might be hot outside but inside is super cold. People wear masks when they are sick, but still come to class. The professors are very helpful so write them with any questions you have. Enjoy!
most_rewarding: Getting to discuss current topics with students that have completely different reference points and knowledge than you.

info_ease: Very easy. housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The best decision I've ever made. Met the most amazing people from all over the world and made friendships for life. Besides this, it was an incredible opportunity to get insight into other cultures.
registration_process: You log into this website and search for the course by using a course code. Then you enroll in the course. You can either be waitlisted or enrolled straight away. If you are waitlisted you are not guaranteed to get a spot, it depends on how many students are in front of you. When you get enrolled, the add/drop period starts. This is where you can try out the course and see whether you like it or not. If you don’t like it, you just drop it and add another course.

recommended_courses: Biochemistry of disease because the course teaches you the clinical manifestation and pathophysiology of common human diseases, with an emphasis on the biochemical basis underlying the development of the diseases and their treatments with drugs. Human Genetics and Personalized Medicine because the course teaches you the principles and up-to-date technologies for the discovery and analysis of human genetic variations. You learn how genetic factors can determine many variations in the human population such as hair thickness, tolerance to milk in adults, high blood cholesterol, and susceptibility to certain types of cancer. unexpected_costs: You spend way more money on transport than you expect. The campus is outside of the center and the buses/metros stop going at 1 am, therefore if you are on a night out or just having a late dinner you need to take either an Uber or taxi home back to campus.
cost_comparison: Food on campus was very cheap. Grocery shopping at the supermarket on campus was very expensive compared with the supermarkets in town.

weekend_recommendations: Spend the weekends or holidays exploring the amazing nature and culture of Hong Kong. Leave campus and go do something fun, whether it’s going out to eat, going to the beach, or going shopping. Hong Kong has it all.

socializing_tips: They are a bit shy but want to talk to you. You should just approach them and say hello. cultural_challenges: The fact that you eat rice every single day. They don’t eat many fresh vegetables or salads
culture_appreciated: The way everyone is very helpful. No matter who you ask everyone is always more than happy to help you.
top3_advice: 1) Don’t worry, you will get friends. The host institution plans a lot of activities in the first couple of days to make sure that you get to meet some of the other exchange students and make some friends. 2) Join some of the sports- or activities clubs. it’s a good way to meet new people and get to know the locals 3) If you can choose between living on campus or in the 'Jockey Club' choose on campus. most_rewarding: All of the amazing people I have met and the experiences I got to have with them. Getting to be taught by some of the best professors in the field of biochemistry.
greatest_challenge: Coming out of my comfort zone and taking the step of going. Leaving Copenhagen all by myself to go to a country on the other side of the world, knowing no one. institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
crucial_aspects: Full freedom of choice (EU universities require 2/3 of total ECTS to be within home-uni faculty), I wanted to take courses in mechanical engineering
info_ease: Quite easy, HKUST is very well organised
arrival_assistance: Not much, mostly videos and Zoom meetings _before_ the exchange. Information was however always readily available either online, or in-person at UST.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Upon arrival, I went to the dorms to register, and then (a few days later) had to go to pick up my student ID (which is necessary for dorm access, library access, printing, identification, etc. etc.) and that was that. If you miss the ID pickup date, you can still pick it up later at a different location, emails will be sent out about _EVERYTHING_.
registration_help: Administration for international students was quick to reply if necessary, as well as plenty of information being available online. Furthermore, you will get tons of e-mails about all sorts of things, ranging from general events and talks, to mandatory things for exchange students as well as general information.
registration_success: Register early, especially if you're registering for 1000-level courses, as a lot of these are "common core", meaning a lot of students will be taking them. You can (and it's a good idea to) register for too many courses (to get a good position on the wait-list) and later drop them if you don't want them, or don't get a wait-list position. Also, depending on the course and the professor, the prerequisites for the courses can be/are quite strictly enforced, be way of this.
registration_advice: Register for courses early, and if at all possible do the "pre-enrollment" which is the earliest possible. Also, during pre-enrollment it seemed that professors were more willing to ignore prerequisites. Also, during the add-drop period, you can go to any lectures and "try them out" to see if you want to attend or no.
course_level: First number denotes year, their bachelor's degrees are 4 years long (so a 4xxx course is still bachelor's level). Difficulty varies wildly, but the exams are generally quite difficult. Everything is curve-graded, so getting a passing mark is "easy" but getting a good grade (A- and above) is rather difficult.
teaching_comparison: More memorisation, otherwise a similar pace, but with 5 courses at once instead of 2 (as at the Science Campus). I'd estimate a 30-60% greater workload to UCPH depending on courses taken.
courses_enrolled: ELEC1010 (electronic and information technology)(common core business students' course) - nonsense course with easy course material and a deceptively difficult midterm and exam compared to course material MECH1910 (Foundations of mechanical and aerospace engineering) (common core engineering course) - mostly nonsense course, with decent material, but poor teaching/lectures, no midterm, exam was of appropriate difficulty compared to course material MECH1907 (Introduction to mechanical and aerospace engineering) - difficult but _very good course_ and lecturer, will be renamed and moved to 2xxx after this semester, appropriately difficult exam compared to course material MECH2310 (Thermodynamics) - difficult course, very good, but very strict/harsh professor, exam was quite difficult compared to course material COMP3311 (Database management systems) - The contents and learning goals are good, but the slides, and the teaching itself is rather poor. Exam was of appropriate difficulty compared to course material
recommended_courses: This is based on my own expecience as well as from conversations with local students as well as other exchange students (on other courses than myself): Mechanical Engineering, Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, and Computer Science (and Computer Engineering) are (considered) very, very difficult and stressful, but are also in my opinion quite fulfilling. Generally speaking, if you have coursers with a lot of tutorials and labs, you will not a have a lot of free time left over, so be mindful of that. Generally speaking, stay away from common core courses (a lot of 10xx, 11xx, 12xx courses are common core - show up to a lecture during add/drop, and if there's more than 100 people there, it's common core for sure, otherwise ask).
unexpected_costs: Air-conditioning was paid separately (other fees), but not too expensive
cost_comparison: Hong Kong does not have it's own production, so _EVERYTHING_ is imported. A lot of western products are hideously expensive, and vegetables and fruit aren't cheap either. Otherwise, eating out (e.g. canteens or smaller local or chain restaurants) is _very_ cheap relative to DK, but does add up in the long run. Hong Kong has 0% VAT (sales tax), and as such, it's a great place to shop for clothes, electronics and other non-consumables when compared with Denmark.
activities_available: Athletic activities: very easy-to-find and accurate descriptions on school website, lots of options for lots of different sports as well as an on-campus gym. Cultural activities: usually announced by e-mail, quite a few of them throughout the semester Social activities: not that many, also announced by e-mail.
activities_recommended: I personally played squash, and was met by a bunch of very nice people in charge of the squash club (as part of the HKUST Student Union [HKUSTSU])
weekend_recommendations: Go for a walk around the city, both on the north as well as south side of the harbour. Lots of hiking trails available; a group of exchange students very quickly established a hiking group on Instragram, and went on hikes several times a week.
culture_adjustment: The on-campus culture is a bit different from the day-to-day city culture. The on-campus culture feels not dissimilar to UCPH, but it took a while to get used to interacting with people, services, restaurants etc. etc. in the city.
socializing_tips: Though local students may seem (and are) rather shy, don't be afraid to say hi to whomever you happen to be sitting next to during the first few weeks in the lectures halls, and see if you can strike up a conversation. Once you get to talking, they are usually very quick to open up, and quite happy to speak with you.
cultural_challenges: None in particular - if you don't already know, at least to some degree how to use chopsticks, do spend a bit of time practicing from home, it will help a great deal, as quite a few restaurants don't provide western cutlery by default (although I assume you can always ask for it). A lot of people (especially older than, say, 30) do not speak English very well, and you can forget all about pronouncing Cantonese words correctly (even simple phrases will easily go misunderstood or be met with a look of confusion) if you haven't practiced with someone local first.
culture_appreciated: People are incredibly friendly and helpful (especially to foreigners), and are from my experience, quite eager to learn about Western culture, and a lot of them are quite interested in Denmark, specifically (happiest country and all that). Other than that, I was a great fan of the very down-to-earth way of socialising, e.g. grabbing lunch or dinner together, or having a relaxed drink at the on-campus Uni-bar, or simply going for a walk around campus.
top3_advice: No preparation period/study break (læsuge) before/during midterm exams; life simply goes on, and you might easily have both a midterm exam and other lectures during the same day - can become very busy/hectic, so be prepared! Get an Octopus Card (their Rejsekort) at the airport and top it up, other than there, it can only be topped up with cash (at 7-Eleven). Check your bank for international fees (e.g. I had 1.5% on every transaction and 3% on withdrawals), and get e.g. a Revolut account if the fees are high. Thoroughly explore your options during the add-drop period, so you get as many courses you actually want as possible. When requesting a prerequisite waiver (based on courses taken at your home institution), it might take a day or three to get the application processed, so things might not work out last-minute. If in doubt of anything, you can always, always, write the professor an e-mail, most are quick to respond.
other_useful_info: Mingle with the locals, most are a bit shy but generally very sweet (and scarily smart)! Some courses (depends on the lecturer) take attendance, which _usually_ counts towards your final grade (5-10%) If you want to have time to go to the city during weekdays, make sure to plan your courses such that your day ends early, or beings _very late_ (e.g. only one lecture at 17 or 18), since getting to the city centre (or back to UST) takes ~1 hour.
most_rewarding: Most definitely the number of new people whom I now consider friends, or even close friends, after just 4 months of stay. This is both local as well as other exchange students (I also met my now girlfriend [local] there, but I assume this is a slightly rarer occurrence ;))
greatest_challenge: Definitely the balance of academics and free time. Admittedly, I did have a very busy schedule, even by UST standards (confirmed by local students) for only taking 15 credits (30ECTS), but generally speaking, UST is not a particularly relaxing place (neither is the entirety of Hong Kong, in my opinion), but it is very rewarding.
