institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
crucial_aspects: English speaking country, A top ranking university, Close to where I have family (in Asia)
info_ease: We received a lot of information up front by the international office of HKUST. It was a lot to go through with every email, but it worked.
arrival_assistance: We had 3 days of orientation, which included a small campus tour, an organized trip to IKEA to purchase things for the dorm etc., a welcome dinner with all exchange students, and a voluntary day tour (two options) where you can explore Hong Kong (the tour had to be paid in advance).
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: During August we already had to plan out our courses that we are interested in and use a website where you see if the courses clash time-wise. Then you get a time slot from when you are able to register for courses. This differs per person. It's hectic because it usually coincides with the time when exchange students are arriving in Hong Kong so make sure to have time for that. You get waitlisted for most courses in my experience and then have two weeks (so called add/drop period) where you get to finalize your choices. Definitely already attend the classes you want to take even though you might not be enrolled yet.
registration_help: The international office and the office of academic registry send you emails and informs you of deadlines. The shopping cart tool is also helpful, as well as the timetable planner (both are from HKUST) to map out the courses you're interested in.
registration_success: I got into all of the classes I wanted, but for some of them I was on the waitlist and they had to manually add me because the class capacity was full.
registration_advice: If you approach the prof in the add/drop period and ask to let you join, it most often works. Also even if that period is open there will still be a chance to change courses if you have valid reasons for it. Ask the department that you were allocated to for help.
course_level: I had 4 courses in total - 3 were BA level and 1 was MA level. I was informed when applying that most courses I am able to take would be BA level due to HKUST regulations on that, but I was able to enroll into one MA level courses.
teaching_comparison: There are more forms of assessment throughout the semester, and the semester itself is shorter (beginning of September until mid December).
courses_enrolled: Data Visualizations, Data Mining, Cloud Computing and Big Data Systems, Fundamentals of AI
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the course Data Visualizations (COMP6411D) and would recommend taking that.
cost_comparison: Fruits and Veggies are more expensive than other food items in HK.
activities_available: There were some sports clubs like volleyball, soccer, track & field etc. and there are two small gyms. The Shaw Auditorium has a few cultural events and performances which are free for students. And there are clubs on campus that you can join for social activities, e.g. a club for arts, various sports clubs, etc.
activities_recommended: I would recommend to go travelling if you can and to explore the lesser known neighbourhoods in HK.
weekend_recommendations: A trip to Shenzen is easy and fast since it borders HK. I highly recommend going to Guangzhou for a weekend trip!
culture_adjustment: It was okay to adjust, but in my experience you will stay in your exchange bubble anyway. Of course try to interact with local people too.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier was a bit tougher than I expected. Even though all students are able to speak English too, it seems that a lot of full time local students feel more comfortable with Cantonese and already have their friend groups, so they are less open to talking to exchangers.
culture_appreciated: The food
top3_advice: 1. Share a taxi to campus with other people arriving around the same time (get in touch via Whatsapp etc beforehand). This way you already get to know people and also share the costs. 2. Get an octopus card on campus at 7eleven and top it off with cash (it only works with cash so make sure you already have that sorted). There are also ways to have it digitally. 3. Bring your own bedding if you have space for it, otherwise you can also get it second hand at the "adopt don't shop" campaign during orientation or at IKEA
other_useful_info: There are two ATM machines on campus, the right one at least doesn't have an additional fee for when I withdrew money.
most_rewarding: Being able to travel within Asia and visit friends and family of mine.
greatest_challenge: Connecting with other people on a deeper level and living with a roommate.

institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
crucial_aspects: The most crucial aspects for me were: - That the destination was international and I could easily communicate in English - A total different and new culture to my home country - That the university offered had a good reputation and interesting courses for me
info_ease: Very easy, they sent a lot of emails for the exchange students.
arrival_assistance: We had a meeting with all exchange students to explain what we need to know and we were also assigned a coordinator in each hall.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Before arriving we needed to create our email and Canvas account. Once at the campus, we needed to register at the hall were we lived and pick up our stundent ID, which was used to enter the residential halls, library, gym, etc., all the facilities in the university.
registration_help: You could either contact exchange coordinators or you assigned hall coordinator.
registration_success: I was rejected from the courses at Mater's level, as we were only allowed to take undergraduated courses. For those, for exchange students they ask for some proof that you are qualified (you have the basic knowledge) to take the course.
registration_advice: Some teachers need proof that you are legitimate to take that course, so be prepared to offer some proof.
course_level: Exchange students were not allowed to take MA courses. However, the BA courses were already quite intensive. Specially in my case, where I chose Computer Science courses, the level of programming was above mine (even being a master's student). The lectures are intensive and we also had a lot of assignments (labs) and Programming assignments to do.
teaching_comparison: It is not very different, as the lectures are completely theoretical and then we also had TA session in case we needed help with the assignments. The only difference is that in some courses we also had lab sessions that were mandatory to attend.
courses_enrolled: COMP 2012 OOP and Data Structures COMP 3021 Java Programming COMP 3211 Fundamentals of A. I. COMP 4461 Human-Computer Interaction
recommended_courses: If the student is interested in learn a programming language in more depth, I recommend COMP 2012 and COMP 3021, as they only focused on C++ and Java programming (respectively) in a very intensive way.
unexpected_costs: I had to go to the hospital, which is covered, but in case they need to open any medical material or you need drugs, you have to pay for that. If you have a travel insurance, they will cover that.
cost_comparison: Food was much less expensive than I excepted (except coffee).
activities_available: There were a lot of sport clubs (football, badmintong, sailing, martial arts, etc), cultural clubs (gaming, music, environemnt, etc).
activities_recommended: I do not know, I did not take any.
weekend_recommendations: Travelling from Hong Kong was very easy, so if you have time, visit other countries. In HK there are a lot of things to do as well. The university also prepares day tours and hiking the first days.
culture_adjustment: For me was very easy.
socializing_tips: They are very shy, so just be nice and see if they want to interact.
cultural_challenges: Cars do not stop at the crosswalks for pedestrians, and burping and farting in public is normal.
culture_appreciated: The generosity and helpfulness of the people.
top3_advice: 1. Ask for help to reach the residential hall. 2. Go everywhere with at least 10 minutes of anticipation (the campus is huge). 3. Download the Octopus for tourists app to pay at the canteens and the bus.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Meeting all the people I have met and travelling.
greatest_challenge: Some of the courses were harder than I though.

institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
crucial_aspects: Languague was important, I choose a destination with high english speaking skills. I also chose a destination with good career opportunuties and high education level. Lastly, I chose a destination with a very different culture, climate and history compared to Denmark.
info_ease: Upon arrival, there was a thorough onboarding from HKUST, so this part was good. There was some confusion between a lot of apps and sites, but not anymore than you would find at any other university.
arrival_assistance: Welcoming days to onboard new exchange students. This was several days, and otherwise there was a number and email to contact if you needed further assistance.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There was a visa application that the host university handled, then there was a lot of personal information that you had to provide to the university personally. Upon arrival, the real course registration period started. The course registration was the worst part of the process. It could have been much more clear and done much earlier before the semester start.
registration_help: There was a phone number and email to contact. I could not find a physical office for guidance, when I needed help.
registration_success: It was a difficult process, because there was a pre-registration, but at that point I didn't know if the courses were valid or not, if I had the requirements to take that course, and if it was even a course in the spring or autumn semester.
registration_advice: Try to plan your courses as precisely as possible beforehand, and research if it's held during your exchange stay, and research whether you need aan approval if you don't have prerequisite courses.
course_level: There was a mixed level, because I had courses meant for first, second, third and fourth year students. I also had courses from different subjects, so it was very mixed, but the level of education was generally very high.
teaching_comparison: It's less free, since many courses have mandatory participation. It was also a bit less interactive with professors and TAs, but this depends heavily on the specific course.
courses_enrolled: VBA programming bridging course Programming with C++ Cryptography International Trade and Investment Tech startup and entrepreneurs ecosystem: growth and innovation
recommended_courses: Tech startup and entrepreneurs ecosystem: growth and innovation, because this course had a lot of international students, and the entire atmosphere was international by nature. The professor was very interactive with students, and spoke english well. The course put high emphasis on participation, but was not stressful, since there waas not a high workload in terms of assignments and midterms. The final exam was a group presentation.
unexpected_costs: The campus is some distance from the inner city, so you take unexpectedly many ubers and taxis, especially if you need to get home late at night.
cost_comparison: I did not need to buy any books, so that was cheap. Generally, I was not surprised by anything being too expensive.
activities_available: There are societies for a lot of different hobbies. Most of them are officially sponsored by the school, and there are also some, which are still just completely student-run. There are about 20 sport societes, but since the football team was only for full- students, I joined many unofficial football groups.
activities_recommended: Join football groups where you play university staff, or the one where you play the smaller fields.
weekend_recommendations: My favourite activites were hiking, sailing, Happy Valley horse racing and the nightlife of Hong Kong. When you have several days free, I recommend you travel to Shenzhen, Macau and Guanzhou, and these are just the nearby easy options.
culture_adjustment: It was easy enough, but the biggest difference was living on-campus, compared to living privately in Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: My best tips for socializing is go out at night in the first weeks, and specifically go to Mr. Wongs and Happy Valley races, where international sutdents from all universites in Hong Kong socialize. Other tips would be to try sports societies.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find the cuture hard to adapt to.
culture_appreciated: Hong Kong is very safe, and you will not find many people looking for trouble, if any.
top3_advice: Socialize a lot early. Explore Hong Kong and perhaps also mainland China or Macau. HKUST campus can be like living in a bubble. Carefully plan your courses. Don't make it hard for yourself. I wish I took easier, less technical courses, so I could have enjoyed more time to learn about Hong Kong and travelling.
other_useful_info: Remember to find experiences outside of campus, whether in nature or in the city.
most_rewarding: Experiencing a totally different part of the world. I learned about a new culture and met new friends, both Hong Kong locals and international students.
greatest_challenge: I wish I put more emphasis on socializing in the beginning. You meet so many people, but I wish I focused on getting a close friend group early. This took some more time for me.

institution: Houston Methodist Hospital – Texas Medical Center
crucial_aspects: Getting to know another healthcare system and still be able to communicate with the patients.
info_ease: It was so difficult getting all the information and documents and little to no help from the host hospital. You were pretty much on your own trying to figure out everything.
arrival_assistance: I was met a the office and placed in a room for 3 hours to wait for someone to show me where to get scrubs. I never got a tour of place or any information on when to meet or how to contact the other doctors at the department.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Once you get the WB visa at entry in the US you get a mail with information on how to register and how to finish online courses which took me about 8 hours to completer. Apart from that youll have to complete a zoom-course about Epic. Once all of that is done, you show up at the bagde office to get your bagde and access to the hospital.
registration_help: I had a contact from the education department to help me with the registration and to contacts from the vascular department which helped me with the initial meeting.
registration_success: There arent any classes. Its only clinical rotations. A bit of a shame that there arent any lectures or so offered for the students.
registration_advice: Be patient and persistent.
course_level: Didnt take any since they didnt offered them.
teaching_comparison: I only went to one "teaching" sessions with the residents. Its was really good. You got to answer some of the questions even though you were a med student.
courses_enrolled: Vascular surgery Cardiac anesthesia Cardia/ transplant surgery
recommended_courses: The above.
unexpected_costs: Went to a conference and payed 15 USD. Supposedly the department would pay it but I wanst informed of that so I payed it myself.
cost_comparison: Food and housing was way more expensive than I thought. Public transportation is cheap (1,25 USD for 3 hours unlimited rides) but takes way longer than UBER or car.
activities_available: None.
activities_recommended: Go see the different cultures Houston has to offer and try all kind of different cuisines.
weekend_recommendations: See as much of Houston as possible. There are so many things to do outside the hospital. Go visit the NASA space center, the museum of natural sciences, museum of fine arts and so much more. Looks for festivals in your area, the original greek festival was nice. Go see some parades, the thanksgiving parade is huge and fun. Find other local activities by searching google and asking hospital staff.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: There are a lot of medical students from all around the world (Mexico, Hungary and so). Ask about medical school in their country and meet a lot of other students in the same situation as yourself. Often they are as frustrated as you are. Share your thoughts and frustration and figure out how they deal with them. Use and help each other.
cultural_challenges: Americans are extremely polite. Always remember using sir and ma'am. Remember to greet people with "how are you" and be thankful.
culture_appreciated: The openness.
top3_advice: Its going to be challenging both before and during your stay Its going to be hard to get to do anything at the hospital, but you'll see a lot of interesting operations and complex patients. Enjoy your freetime and go see all of Houston.
other_useful_info: Be persistent otherwise you will be forgotten.
most_rewarding: Being in another country all by yourself for 3 months.
greatest_challenge: Getting to do things at the hospital and being alone and by yourself.

institution: Houston Methodist Hospital – Texas Medical Center
crucial_aspects: At jeg havde hørt om det fra en medstuderende, som havde fortalt om sine oplevelser. På den måde vidste jeg, at det ikke blot var et "observations-ophold", men at man rent faktisk kunne få noget hands-on-erfaring med kirurgi. Og så at kirurgi var det store fokus for opholdet var også grunden til at jeg søgte og valgte netop dette ophold.
overall_comments: God, det var virkelig fedt og virkeligt lærerigt. Det var hårdt og det var lange dage, men det lærer man også noget af.
info_ease: Det var virkeligt svært at få styr på papirarbejdet forud for opholdet, og også lidt ved ankomst, men mest før opholdet. Det havde været rart hvis det var lidt mere transparent hvor meget de egentligt kræver man har klart på forhånd.
arrival_assistance: Jeg blev registreret til udlevering af adgangskort og så fik jeg en mail om hvordan jeg fandt op til afdelingen. Herefter var det om at koble sig på en læge indtil jeg selv lærte at finde rundt og hvordan systemet fungerede.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: God, det var virkelig fedt og virkeligt lærerigt. Det var hårdt og det var lange dage, men det lærer man også noget af.
registration_process: Først skulle jeg have en mailadresse fra KU til at kontakte Houston Methodist Hospital (HMH). Så skulle jeg via denne kontakt aftale datoerne for mit ophold og have et letter of acceptance. De svarer generelt langsomt, så start i god tid. De fremsendte mig så en Merlin-application, som jeg jeg skulle udfylde med en masse papirarbejde og blodprøver, vaccinationer, straffeattest og meget mere, så der skal man virkeligt starte i god tid. Efter den fik jeg tilsendt en masse elearning fra HMH som jeg skulle gennemføre og først herefter var jeg klar til at starte. Jeg anbefaler at man uploader MERLIN mindst 2 måneder før man rejser afsted, fordi man risikerer at de ikke godkender den (hvilket skete for mig). Desuden skal man tjekke hvad de skal have af dokumenter på deres hjemmeside allerede så snart man får den tilsendt, fordi det powerpoint de også sender dækker slet ikke alt hvad de kræver og deres svartider er langsomme.
registration_help: Jeg kunne spørge KU-exchange om hjælp. De var rigtig gode når jeg havde store problemer, men svarede langsomt, når det var mindre problemer og vidste ofte ikke hvad de skulle gøre. Ellers kunne jeg sende mails til min kontakt på HMH som også var langsom til at svare. Så igen, start i god tid. Min største hjælp var at jeg kendte hende som var afsted et halvt år før mig, så jeg kunne spørge hende om en masse ting.
registration_success: Jeg var kun på hospitalet og ikke på uni, så spørgsmålet er ikke helt relevant. Men lad mig sige det sådan: Hvis der er et speciale på HMH du gerne vil besøge og se, så spørg din supervisor pænt og gør det med uddannelse for øje, så kan det meste tit lade sig gøre. Men man skal være meget opsøgende selv.
registration_advice: Start I god tid, pres på når du har brug for noget både før og under din exchange, fordi hvis de ikke svarer, så send en rykker og det skal man nogle gange flere gange.
academics_comments: God, det var virkelig fedt og virkeligt lærerigt. Det var hårdt og det var lange dage, men det lærer man også noget af.
course_level: Det var klinikophold på hospitalet. Det var en masse kirurgisk, og ret fleksibelt hvilke funktioner i de tilddelte specialer man var med på. Jeg prøvede både at gå stuegang, observere i ambulatorie og mest af at, at være med og assistere på operationer.
teaching_comparison: Klinikophold som i Danmark, men man kan få lov til mange flere ting, hvis man er opsøgende. Men man skal virkeligt slev koble sig på og holde sig til, fordi der er ingen der tager én under armen som de gør hjemme i Danmark.
courses_enrolled: Klinikophold: 6 uger på karkirurgi, 4 uger på thorx/hjerte/transplantations kirurgi og 2 uger på anæstesi.
recommended_courses: Dem alle, det var fedt at se variationen
unexpected_costs: Transport er dyrt, fordi man ikke så godt kan tage det offentlige. Dog havde jeg en cykel, hvilket hjalp en del. Mad er overraskende dyrt også selvom man handler ind og laver mad selv.
cost_comparison: Intet
activities_available: Konferencer og journal clubs ind i mellem. Men ikke det store. Desuden en masse klaverer, som man kan blive godkendt til at spille på, hvis man kan. Men ikke det store

Man kan også tage til Galveston eller San Antonio. Desuden skal man besøge Houston Space Center. Jeg brugte også appen "meetup" til at møde mennesker. Der er masser af gratis events, hvor man kan møde mennesker, hvilket var nice.

culture_appreciated: At se et helt andet hospitalsvæsen på godt og ondt, samt venligheden og åbenheden blandt amerikanerne generelt.
top3_advice: Det er hårdt og det skal man være indstillet på. Det er lange dage. Men der er mega meget personlig og teknisk læring at hente, hvis man bare gider.
other_useful_info: Nej
most_rewarding: At blive rigtig god til at tænke som en kirurg og befærde sig sterilt, samt at lukke forskellige incisioner. Det er de rigtig gode til at lære en, hvis man spørger. Desuden at se kæmpe store operationer og deltage hvor man kan få lov i bl.a. organudtagning fra organdonorer x mange
greatest_challenge: De lange dage. Man møder kl 6.30 eller 7.00 og går hjem kl 16, hvis det er en tidlig dag, eller kl 20 hvis det er en lang dag. Men man lærer en masse udholdenhed og bliver stærkere af det.
other_comments: nej

institution: Houston Methodist Hospital – Texas Medical Center
crucial_aspects: Jeg har længe været interesseret i det amerikanske sundhedssystem og har rejst i landet mange gange. Derudover er Houston Methodist førende indenfor flere specialer.
info_ease: Det må jeg indrømme ikke var super lige til. Man får en kontaktperson på hospitalet som man er lidt i dialog med inden ankomst - men jeg viste ikke særlig meget inden jeg ankom. Generelt svært at komme i kontakt med dem, men når det først lykkes at få lidt information, var det egentlig okay.
arrival_assistance: Man får at vide over mail hvordan man får sin badge (adgangskort). Jeg fik også at vide hvor og hvornår jeg skulle møde på afdelingen. Det kan være meget svært at finde rundt, da det er et kæmpe stort område - det fik man ingen hjælp til. Så et godt råd er at tage afsted i god tid den første dag :)
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Dette var virkelig ikke særlig nemt, må jeg sige. Der gik virkelig lang tid før jeg hørte fra hospitalet - og meget lang tid imellem svarerne på mail. Dette var lidt frustrerende - og KU kunne ikke rigtig hjælpe, selvom de prøvede. Jeg kan virkelig anbefale at skrive ud på KU's Facebook-side og forhøre sig hos studerende der tidligere har været afsted - man kan godt føle sig lidt lost. Da jeg først kom igennem til dem, gik det nogenlunde, men selve visumprocessen var også svær, da man selv skulle finde ud af det hele. Det lykkedes dog til sidst :)
registration_help: Ikke rigtigt det store. Jeg stod ret alene med det - derfor skriv endelig ud i facebookgruppen, hvis der er tvivl om noget - det hjalp mig.
registration_success: Man bliver sat på forskellige afdelinger - dette kan man ikke selv vælge (karkirurgi, anæstesi og transplantationskirurgi/intensiv)
registration_advice: Det er lidt nævnt ovenfor. Jeg vil anbefale at skrive til hospitalet så tidligt som muligt og holde sig til. Derudover opsøge studerende der tidligere har været afsted. I forhold til visum bør man ansøge om et B1/B2 visum - ESTA dækker kun 90 dage.
course_level: Det var jo et klinikophold og ikke kurser som sådan. Generelt super højt fagligt niveau - man lærer meget, hvis man er opsøgende.
teaching_comparison: Der er jo generelt en anden arbejdskultur i USA - og et andet hieraki på hospitalet, end vi er vant til i Danmark. Igen, man får lov til en del, hvis man blot er meget proaktiv.
courses_enrolled: Klinikophold på tre forskellige afdelinger, samlet 12 uger.
recommended_courses: Man vælger ikke selv.
unexpected_costs: Ikke nogle
cost_comparison: Offentlig transport er meget billigt -der kører nogle sporvogne og busser i byen. Uber og Lyft kan man også benytte sig af - det er ikke ret dyrt. Vil anbefale dette hvis man er ude om aftenen eller lignende - man skal passe lidt på og ikke gå rundt om aftenen selv.
activities_available: Ikke det store - dette opsøgte jeg selv.
activities_recommended: Jeg vil anbefale at opsøge noget sport (hvis man allerede dyrker en sport, så opsøg endelig dette derovre)
weekend_recommendations: Houston er en kæmpe by, og der er meget at se. Brug endelig weekenderne på at opleve byen. Der er mange museer og rigtig god mad (China Town eksempelvis) :)
culture_adjustment: Det synes jeg gik nemt.
socializing_tips: Jeg fandt nogle ungarnske studerende, på hospitalet, som jeg var meget sammen med. Vi tog på mange weekendturer - blandt andet New Orleans og San Antonio (anbefaling herfra!)
cultural_challenges: Ikke rigtig nogle.
culture_appreciated: Amerikanerne er meget imødekomme - dette var rigtig rart, især i starten.
top3_advice: 1) Det er ikke nemt at komme i kontakt med hospitalet, men det skal nok lykkes - hold dig til. 2) Vær opsøgende under klinikopholdene 3) Oplev byen og opsøg sportsklubber eller lignende - det kan være udfordrende at være afsted alene.
other_useful_info: Spørg endelig de søde residents om at følges med dem - fang dem til morgenmødet eller lignende. De fleste er meget søde og vil gerne lære fra sig, men de har super travlt og arbejder som heste - så hiv endelig selv fat i dem.
most_rewarding: Jeg har lært rigtig meget fagligt - men måske i højere grad på et personligt plan. Det er meget givende at tage afsted selv på den måde. Det var også utrolig spændende at lære et anderledes sundhedssystem at kende.
greatest_challenge: At være afsted selv og vænne sig til de lange dage på hospitalet (nogle gange 12-timers dage) - men dette vænner man sig til, og det er meget forskelligt fra afdeling til afdeling hvor lange dage man har.

crucial_aspects: My boyfriend was doing a MBA-degree in Berlin at the time, and therefore it fitted well in to our lives.
info_ease: Not easy at all. Both the German system in general, and the administration at HU were not very accessible.
arrival_assistance: There was a 20-minute zoom-call in German for the international students at the law faculty. The host hadn't prepared any slides or like-wise, so it was hard to keep track as a non-native German speaker.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There was a lot of mistakes from the HU administration - especially in connection with the registration for courses, where I had to double check with them, whether the information in the course catalog was correct, and then they provided me with the correct information 7 out of 10 times.
registration_help: E-mail with 1-2 day responses.
registration_success: I ended up taking all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Have patience, and be prepared to use 60% of your stay on administrative issues and 40% studying.
course_level: Very basic in all courses I did. Reminded me more of high school exams.
teaching_comparison: Most of my courses were lectures, and therefore it was a lot of one-way-teaching, compared to the "seminars" we know from KU. I prefer the lectures over the seminars, so for me it was great.
courses_enrolled: Private international law Introduction to software law The English legal system: a historical introduction Verhandlungspraxis im Privaten Baurecht Internet recht Internationales Vertragsrecht Morality and Religion in the Jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights
recommended_courses: Private international law Introduction to software law The English legal system: a historical introduction Internet recht Internationales Vertragsrecht Morality and Religion in the Jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights
unexpected_costs: Language course (350 EUR)
cost_comparison: In general Berlin is a cheap city compared to Copenhagen - especially when going out for dinner and drinks.
activities_available: Many different sport activities were offered, but you have to be quick in order to get af free spot!
activities_recommended: Anything you feel for in HU activity page. Remember to sign up for their newsletter (you'll become an invitation upon registration at HU)
weekend_recommendations: The many different museum, and maybe get a city-guide, so you'll be able to find attraction suiting your interests.
culture_adjustment: Easy - it's a lot like Copenhagen - just bigger and a bit crazier
socializing_tips: Be sure to connect in the WhatsApp group for Erasmus-students. also the language course prior to the semester brought me together with some of the people I ended up talking to my whole stay.
cultural_challenges: N/A.
culture_appreciated: The open-mindedness and free culture.
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy the life in Berlin to the fullest, and don't worry too much about HU's very German way of doing things 2. Have patience 3. Be open-minded to social opportunities
other_useful_info: N/A
most_rewarding: becoming better in both German and English. Breaking my comfort-zone. Realizing how good we are treated at KU
greatest_challenge: Dealing with the international office and not knowing the expectations from the professors.

crucial_aspects: fun city, good university, chill vibe compared to at KU
info_ease: The university was helpful with a lot of info via email. However Germany is a bit behind on digitilization, so for example most contracts are still signed by hand etc so there's a lot of travelling back and forth to different offices to get the right papers signed/stamped etc, which can be slightly confusing in the beginning. What was also a bit annoying was that some important info on e.g. how to sign up for exams came via letter only, and if you didn't receive this letter (due to DHL's bad delivery service or delays with anmeldung) you had to get the sign up code at a specific office at a specific time.
arrival_assistance: Uni helped with Anmeldung, which is currently a three month wait at the official office in Berlin due to delays after Covid, so that was very helpful. Other than that a lot of good info via email. But finding apartment and other logistic stuff is up to one self.
arrival_comments: I think the uni are doing as well as they can keeping people up to speed and helping with different stuff, but bureaucracy in Germany is just on another level, which is a bit annoying. However, they should drop the "via letter only" information, as delivery service in Germany is rotten and it is very confusing how to get access to info if you haven't received the specific letters. Keep this in mind if you go on exchange to Germany, know which letters you are supposed to receive at what time
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You can attend any class you like for the first 2 weeks, then you register online for the ones you want to take.
registration_help: the exchange student's office I guess?
registration_success: I got them all but they overlapped. Seminars are very difficult to get and you need to sign up way earlier, so keep that in mind and apply for several to have a shot
registration_advice: It's literally ONLY exchange students that take 30 ECTS during a semester. I didn't meet a single Berlin student taking more than 3 courses per semester (6 ECTS per course) as the exam period is 2 days after last lecture and all exams are happening within 2 weeks. So imagine taking 5 courses lol. Take a seminar to get somewhat of a break, those are usually due 1 month after exams
course_level: Depends what you take. If the course says "Advanced", it's not as advanced as in Cph. But for only 6 ECTS it's a lot of work still
teaching_comparison: At CPH you calculate stuff in basically any course you take, that's not the case in all courses at Humboldt. If you take e.g. Public econ, competition policy, network based energy systems, you'll calculate micro stuff all day long. But e.g. Advanced International Trade introduces ~50 models which you don't need to calculate but interpret
courses_enrolled: Advanced Marketing Modeling Marketing Management Advanced International Trade Valuation European Economic History since 1914 until today
recommended_courses: European Economic History since 1914 until today ! Really interesting, really good professor as well. Same professor in Advanced international trade, which was also a good course. Advanced marketing modeling was also a favourite course, a little demanding but really nice in terms of applied econometrics in R
unexpected_costs: Gas and electricity prices are insane in Germany right now, and its only summer... we went from paying 20 each in an apartment of 4 people, to paying 54 each. Internet became more expensive all of a sudden. TV bill in the mail. In general, companies really rip off ex-paths living in Berlin, you always get a worse deal if your'e not German or speaking good German.
cost_comparison: Groceries is just as expensive in DK, that was a surprise given the wage level here. Depends where in the city you are, Mitte is 2x as pricey as Neukölln. Go to Neukölln <3
activities_available: No idea
activities_recommended: RAVES! This is one of the sole reasons I came here. There's a lot of good clubs and parties (and a lot of bad ones) were music is bouncing and people are super friendly. Very queer friendly city which is just super nice. People are more relaxed than in Copenhagen, you don't encounter the newest Asics or NB sneaks for 2000 dkk on people very often. Just more laid back in general. If your'e into art there are several interesting exhibitions as well and also good cinema
weekend_recommendations: Berghain
culture_adjustment: easy peasy lemon squeezy
socializing_tips: yes. It is 100 x easier to interact with local students at HU compared with KU. Literally any foreign student at KU I've ever met has complained about how hard it is making Danish friends. That's not the case in Berlin, I met 3 German guys my first day in class whom I hung out with every day at school. Also my partey friends in another class :* just be open and chill, people are way more chill here than in Cph so you don't need to say which bank your'e dad works for and that you got a 12 in Macro III
cultural_challenges: The exam period. Taking 5 in one shot is literally impossible. I had several exams in the days after each other. Absolutely horrible, no time to study for them properly. Usually german students take 1-2 exams in the first period, and 1-2 in the second period. As an exchange student, you try to take all 5 in the first, which is horrible. I don't even think the uni expects anyone to do that
culture_appreciated: Everything. The multicultural and queer vibe in the city
top3_advice: 1. Be aware of the process for settling in; find apartment with anmeldung, know which papers you will receive and when you should receive them 2. Take a seminar - to have 5 sit in exams is horrible. If possible, take less than 30 ects 3. Go out partying! It's not only about 'partying', but you'll meet some of the best people of berlin doing this. Its ok to go out alone in this city, youll meet so many friends this way. Otherwise hop on Bumble and see if you find compatibles who wanna go out. Check Resident Advisor if you don't know any places. Try both clubs and independent parties (raves), I prefer the latter
other_useful_info: Have fun, go to events, meet people, don't take things too seriously, you'll be fine. Just have a plan with the exams lol
most_rewarding: The people. Really some of the best friends ive ever met, after only a few months
greatest_challenge: The exams
other_comments: Have fun, go to events, meet people, don't take things too seriously, you'll be fine. Just have a plan with the exams lol

crucial_aspects: My connection to the city was important to me, and my ability to study in german was a huge plus. I have lived in Berlin before and wanted to go back, and I also wanted to try to study there, as I am considering doing my Masters degree in Berlin.
overall_comments: I had a wonderful time and enjoyed every second of it. The only minus being that the paperwork before, during and after the mobility was quite a lot, and the communication between KU, HU and me was a bit confusing.
info_ease: It was a bit difficult, as the online portals of KU and HU are quite different and everything wasn't in one place.
arrival_assistance: We had a short introduction meeting for Erasmus students at the faculty, which was really helpful and created a great overview.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had a wonderful time and enjoyed every second of it. The only minus being that the paperwork before, during and after the mobility was quite a lot, and the communication between KU, HU and me was a bit confusing.
registration_process: First of all I had to go to an office to get a PIN-code, so afterwards I could sign in to all the portals and get my student ID. For regestering for classes we actually just had to go to the first one and then decide if we wanted to take part or not.
registration_help: There were some intro-meetings via zoom before the start of the semester, where we were able to ask questions. Also we were able to contact the coordinator at the faculty if we had questions.
registration_success: I wanted to take some of the Berlin Perspectives courses, but I didn't get any of them. All the other courses were no problem at all though, I could basically just choose freely.
registration_advice: It's a good idea to just go to a bunch of courses in the first week and check out what you find interesting. You have a lot of possibilities. And maybe don't expect to get a spot in a Berlin Perspectives course.
academics_comments: I had a wonderful time and enjoyed every second of it. The only minus being that the paperwork before, during and after the mobility was quite a lot, and the communication between KU, HU and me was a bit confusing.
course_level: Most of my courses were in german, so this has to be taken into account: You need to be able to speak german well in order to take part in the discussions. Generally, the courses were on a high academic level, but I think it was about the same as KU.
teaching_comparison: There were a lot of discussion-based seminars which were quite different than what I'm used to at KU. But also classic lectures.
courses_enrolled: 532835 Feminist Urban Geography 532836 Geschichte der Astrologie 532812 Verwundbare Körper des Politischen. Vulnerability revisited 532840 Techno Culture. Geschichte und Gegenwart elektronischer Tanzmusikkultur in Berlin 532810 Behinderung – Kultur - Wissen 532811 Sadismus mit und ohne Sade
recommended_courses: The Techno Culture course was super interesting and well planned. It was a project seminar counting 15 points, so it was a lot of work but it paid off. Also Feminist Urban Geography was really interesting, and it was nice that it was planned as a block seminar with only 4 days in total.
unexpected_costs: My personal spending was higher than expected. The 120DKK extra was for renting a bike every month.
cost_comparison: Groceries were a bit more expensive than expected, probably because of increased inflation. Public transport was less expensive than expected because I didn't know about the semester ticket, but also because of the 9Euro-ticket: I will be paid back the amount that differs to what I paid for my semester ticket for three months.
activities_available: A lot of sports, language courses, and some activities for Erasmus students around the city specifically.
activities_recommended: I didn't take part in any.
weekend_recommendations: Go to bars, bike around, sit by the water, go to clubs, go to festivals, go to the lakes when the weather is good, meet people on apps, go thrifting, go to flea markets, eat at a bunch of different restaurants. Specifically with the 9-euro-ticket it's also nice to go a bit out of the city.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. I knew it already, but also it doesn't differ from Copenhagen that much, except it being more open and international.
socializing_tips: This was actually a bit hard for me, except in the course where I was part of a study group. I used my own connections outside of the university, but also apps.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: That it's a very international city with so many different people and ways of living, and it's easy to meet people. Also just the queer community there is amazing.
top3_advice: 1. If you take courses in german, you should be prepared to speak it on a high level, or you won't get a lot out of it. 2. Start looking for housing early on, as it is probably the most tricky part about moving to Berlin. 3. Take time to enjoy everything the city has to offer every day, because of course it's the best city in the world. Especially the clubs on the weekends: Here I have my best memories.
other_useful_info: None that I can think of.
most_rewarding: I really got to use my german language skills. But just meeting so many nice people and having so much fun every day and every weekend has been amazing.
greatest_challenge: I had a few stressful weeks were I had to do quite a lot of readings and assignments, so it's good to be organized from the beginning of the semester and do your assignments early, so you won't have to do them all at once.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to take classes with more of a cognitive neuropsychological focus. This was possible at department of Psychology, but also Berlin School of Mind & Brain.
overall_comments: I am very happy that I went and loved most of my classes, but I was very left alone through the entire thing. I wish I would have known that I would be the only Erasmus student in all of my classes!
info_ease: It was okay looking in Agnes for courses, but tough to figure out what my chances were for getting into the classes.
arrival_assistance: I e-mailed back and forth with the Erasmus coordinator. I was initially a bit chocked that it was only possible for me to take courses equivalent to 9 (!) ECTS points due to a lack of classes in English. I had been falsely informed that everything would be in English, but apparently there was still an adjustment period at that time. When I got very frustrated, I still could not get any meetings or phone calls with anyone, only communication on e-mail. This was highly frustrating and tedious!
arrival_comments: Only Zoom meetings, even in spring 2022. I really wish there had been some introduction in person.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I am very happy that I went and loved most of my classes, but I was very left alone through the entire thing. I wish I would have known that I would be the only Erasmus student in all of my classes!
registration_process: Could be easy if you could simply sign up on their platform (Agnes) - however, to get specific class approved, they must be grouped together in modules of 3-4-ish which made everything very complicated. I had to get special permission to join a lecture series at School of Mind & Brain to be able to take classes at department of Psychology which was easy when e-mailing a specific professor who knew some people there - but I had no chance of getting enough credits on my own.
registration_help: Erasmus coordinator on e-mail (took lots of work), direct help from professors.
registration_success: I ended up getting every class I wanted, but there was only enough in English for me to take 22,5 ECTS. Also, none of these classes were the same as the ones I got pre-approval for.
registration_advice: I hope it will be easier from this year where everything should really be in English. If you end up in problems, try contacting your teacher directly and explain your situation - they might have more power than they typically do in Denmark.
academics_comments: I am very happy that I went and loved most of my classes, but I was very left alone through the entire thing. I wish I would have known that I would be the only Erasmus student in all of my classes!
course_level: Much higher level in statistics. I took a class where the description said no specific knowledge was required, but the level among German psychology students is much higher in statistics. High level (maybe too high for most students) at the seminars at School of Mind & Brain. On the other hand, I went a few times to a clinical psychology seminar where I would say the level is much lower than at UCPH. They go about it completely differently and discuss the themes of paper intuitively without any additional theoretical perspectives.
teaching_comparison: More traditional dynamics between teachers and students.
courses_enrolled: Fundaments of the Mind and Higher Cognition Advanced Longitudinal Data Analysis Principles and challenges of 'brain reading' Memory and the Brain Scientific explanations in cognitive neuroscience Neuroimaging
recommended_courses: The longitudinal data analysis class was very interesting and new to me, but also super challenging. Scientific explanations in cognitive neuroscience was the first time I have encountered in-depth philosophy of science discussions within the natural sciences, also very cool. I also loved Memory and the Brain with very good literature and inspiring Professor (Roberto Cabeza).
unexpected_costs: I did not know you were required to buy a student local transportation card. This plus some extra (smaller) fee cost me around 2000 DKK.
cost_comparison: Food was less expensive and I did not have to buy any books.
activities_available: See above.
activities_recommended: I don't know. There was not much.
weekend_recommendations: Berlin is amazing! You definitely have to try clubbing there, otherwise the many museums, flee markets, shopping.. Also nice to go see other cities, I went to Dresden and Leipzig for weekend trips.
culture_adjustment: Harder than expected, since we are neighboring countries. Also, I was sometimes the only non-German speaker in a class, making it a bit awkward to stand my ground on the class being held in English as promised. Luckily oftentimes the students would help me with this.
socializing_tips: No - I almost didn't other than minimal small talk. I wish there had been done something from their side to make it a bit easier, but I ended up just meeting people in other ways (e.g., Bumble for friends, Erasmus meet ups, dating apps...)
cultural_challenges: Bureaucracy, less transparency in who has power over what. Using more formal language (calling teachers by last name, for example).
culture_appreciated: Berlin culture is very tolerant which I find very cool. Also a lot of internationals, making it easy to make friends outside of uni.
top3_advice: All for psychology, specifically: 1. Only go there if you are into neuro- or cognitive psychology. My impression of other disciplines is pretty bad. 2. Make sure to live close to the S-Bahn. The psychology department is in Adlershof, which is a bit far away from most popular areas. I also made sure to live on the east side of the city for the same reason. 3. Be prepared to do everything on your own with not much help. This goes for academic as well as social stuff.
other_useful_info: If I could change something, I would have signed up for the HU German classes. I didn't because it was on Zoom and a bit expensive, but I saw that other people made many friends that way.
most_rewarding: Super cool neuropsychology classes, very challenging but made it through. Also met my boyfriend hehe.
greatest_challenge: Getting enough classes. And the summer semester runs from late April with the last exams in late September, so now I am working on a big exam while also having started a new semester at home.
other_comments: Nejjj

crucial_aspects: Firstly, the language. I have always wanted to improve my German, and learning a language is a completely different challenge to studying a Master's degree in Law (in your own language). Secondly, the city. It seemed like the perfect opportunity to study German law in one of the most vibrant and diverse cities in Europe. I had visited Berlin a few times before my exchange but I wanted to be able to really get to know the city and make use of all the opportunities it has to offer. Especially the food scene and cultural experiences. Thirdly, the international recognition of Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin and the courses offered by it.
overall_comments: I had high expectations before I arrived in Berlin, but I never imagined that I would be so fortunate to experience so much and meet so many new people. I truly fell in love with the city and I plan on visiting Berlin many times in the future. I strongly recommend to go on an exchange to Berlin - you will not regret it!
info_ease: It was fairly easy once I took the time to research properly, but the Humboldt-website (Agnes) can be quite confusing in the beginning and a good German proficiency level helps a lot. But Humboldt sent all of the Information that I needed a few months prior to the beginning of the semester. The only thing that wasn't easy to find out was the expected exam dates. The law faculty at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin has a very different system when it comes to registering for exams. The exam dates needs to be cleared with each professor, so you need to write to them individually. And the exams in the courses recommended for Erasmus students at the Law Faculty are usually held before the stated exam period for the rest of the law students. During my exchange I eventually found out when I could expect the exams to be held but it was quite frustrating not knowing when the semester actually ended in order to e.g. apply for the Erasmus Grant and plan ahead in general.
arrival_assistance: Humboldt offers a "studis4studis" programme, where you get a mentor. However, I didn't register for the programme and the written information sent by Humboldt prior to the beginning of the semester and a "Zoom-Info-Meeting" was overall sufficient. Humboldt also helped with information regarding how to book an appointment at the Bürgeramt for the "Abmeldung" (a form you need to fill out in order to register your address in Berlin).
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had high expectations before I arrived in Berlin, but I never imagined that I would be so fortunate to experience so much and meet so many new people. I truly fell in love with the city and I plan on visiting Berlin many times in the future. I strongly recommend to go on an exchange to Berlin - you will not regret it!
registration_process: You can find all of the available courses at agnes.hu-berlin.de under Vorlesungsverzeichnis/Course Catalog.
registration_help: Only an overall explanation on how to register, but you need to contact the professors yourself.
registration_advice: Visit as many lectures as you can - especially in order to: 1. get an idea of the required prior knowledge about German law and 2. see if you can actually understand (most of) what the professor says during the lecture. Some of them speaks very clearly - and some of them don't. This was crucial for me since I took all of my courses in German.
academics_comments: I had high expectations before I arrived in Berlin, but I never imagined that I would be so fortunate to experience so much and meet so many new people. I truly fell in love with the city and I plan on visiting Berlin many times in the future. I strongly recommend to go on an exchange to Berlin - you will not regret it!
course_level: The level was high enough, but the most of the courses are only 5 ECTS - so definitely manageable.
teaching_comparison: Very different. The courses where mostly taught with lectures where the professors doesn't involve the students that much, but it depends on the professor. Two of my courses had quite a lot of cases and discussions in plenum. The curriculum is mainly what is said during the lecture and the professors only recommend certain literature (that usually isn't recommended to Erasmus students). I bought one recommended book and that was probably a waste of money.
courses_enrolled: - Privates Baurecht und Vertragsgestaltung (5 ECTS) - NS-Unrecht (5 ECTS) - Internationales Privatrecht (5 ECTS) - Legal Tech - Einführung in rechtliche, technische und wirtschaftlich-organisatorische Grundlagen (5 ECTS) - IT für Juristen (5 ECTS) - Einführung ind das internationale und europäische Steuerrecht (5 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I can especially recommend the following courses: 1. Privates Baurecht and Vertragsgestaltung. The professor is so nice to Erasmus students and gives a lot of examples during the lecture. This makes it way easier to stay focused, which can be quite hard when German is your second foreign language. 2. NS-Unrecht. Even though this course, during the semester, seemed extremely hard and almost impossible to pass, it was definitely manageable. The professor was so nice and the exam was very surprisingly a really good experience. The topic is so interesting and a unique opportunity to learn something about German history and how the Nazi-regime has influenced German law. But it is by far the course I had to study the most for. Less could probably have been sufficient. 3. IT für Juristen. The professor was so cool and it was so much fun to try and learn to code (which was an optional part of the lecture). The lecture itself involved cases and discussions in plenum, and there were quite a few online lectures, that we had to watch prior to each lecture. This was, however, also manageable.
unexpected_costs: I did not expect to spend so much money on food - but it was almost impossible for me to resist the temptation to try out as many as possible of the amazing restaurants that Berlin has to offer. Both the cheaper options and the more fancy ones (which btw still are way cheaper compared to restaurants offering similar standards in Copenhagen).
cost_comparison: Insurance was cheaper than expected.
activities_available: Humboldt offers a lot of sport activities (HU Hochschulsport). But make sure to register in time - a lot of them are sold out quickly.
activities_recommended: Try out a new sport through HU Hochschulsport - I tried out top rope climbing and it was so cool to meet other people through a sport activity.
weekend_recommendations: I never went outside of Berlin. The city has enough to offer.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy - but it is really hard to adjust to the language in the beginning. But it got quickly easier and my German improved greatly.
socializing_tips: Be social - you have to take initiative yourself.
cultural_challenges: Having to pay in cash all the time and having to speak and write in a formal tone to the professors.
culture_appreciated: The diversity and the food scene in Berlin. But mostly the culture to go out and use the city instead of only hosting private events or staying home. Berlin is so much more vibrant than Copenhagen and it is evident, that locals really spend most of their free time in public spaces and parks. This creates an amazing atmosphere.
top3_advice: 1. Don't be afraid of taking courses in German! 2. Take the intensive German course offered by Humboldt! The teachers are so good and I met most of the people I ended up hanging out with throughout the whole semester at my language course. 3. Apply for scholarships early. And apply for a lot of them.
other_useful_info: Berlin is fantastic during summer - so choose to go there during the summer semester!
most_rewarding: Meeting so many new people from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: The language - but it is so rewarding to see how quickly you improve if you make an effort.

crucial_aspects: That the academic level wasn't too low. That it was rather close to Copenhagen (didn't know what the state of the world with respect to COVID would be at the time of application). That the city had 'something to offer' in terms of history, culture and politics.
info_ease: It was a really tedious process. KU and HU have different semesters, so my preparations started way before HU even finished their second round of exams. It was quite frustrating since I felt I was always behind KU-wise but HU hadn't really started yet. For example, HU hadn't released the course catalog when I had to send in the preapproval. When the introduction began it was only a few weeks before the start of the lectures and questions usually arise in the process and not during the introduction lectures or when reading the (outdated) materials. I am surprised that it worked out in the end considering all the chaos.
arrival_assistance: HUGS (student organization) had some introductory lectures on zoom, the faculty held an introduction day with a presentation and a dinner, and then the international coordinator was answering e-mails if my questions was understood.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Because of the preapproval process, I knew which courses I wanted to take. The process of registration for regular courses at my faculty was quite straightforward (on paper at least). 1. Find your courses on Agnes (their kunet-ish), keep an eye on the course descriptions where they will post a link to the Moodle (their Absalon-ish) and an enrollment key, 2. enroll on Moodle within some time limit. Officially you only have to register for the exam. The exam registration opens when the exam dates are released around 1,5 months before the exam period. The process is different for seminars I believe but I don't know that process.
registration_help: An e-mail to reach the international coordinator.
registration_success: Completely successful.
registration_advice: It seems somewhat more relaxed than what I'm used to. The professors should tell you when you need to do something.
course_level: The level of the courses is somewhat similar to KU. The exam period is crazy intense (I had 5 exams in 3 weeks and lectures in 2 of those weeks) but I was surprised by how high my grades were so I believe they might compensate a little bit. I didn't meet one HU student who did all of their exams in the first round. They split their exams so they did 2 in February and 3 in April.
teaching_comparison: Somewhat similar.
courses_enrolled: Applied Migration and Development Economics, Finance Theory, Economic Growth, The Theory of Labor Markets with Search Frictions, Introduction to Advanced Macroeconomic Analysis.
recommended_courses: The Theory of Labor Markets with Search Frictions: Really interesting topic and extremely nice professor (prof. Burda). Introduction to Advanced Macroeconomic Analysis: It transfers as Business Cycles but it is really straightforward and easy points (prof. Weinke).
unexpected_costs: You have to pay Rundfunkbeitrag (German broadcasting fee). As with everything else, the registration process is in German but there exist some guides in English. I don't think the students living in dorms had to pay but if you live in private accommodation it is mandatory. It is around 18 euros per month per flat.
cost_comparison: Food is cheap. Both in supermarkets and at restaurants.
activities_available: Some kind of sports and then the student organization HUGS also offered some guided tours and such.
activities_recommended: Free guided tour! Not necessarily offered by the host university but it is definitely offered in all bigger cities in the world. Really good and interesting when moving to a new city. They offer different kinds of tours; historical, Cold war, foodies, etc. The thing is that you pay what you believe the guide deserves at the end of the tour so it is not totally free.
weekend_recommendations: Berlin is relatively close to a lot of other cities for example Vienna, Prague, or Budapest.
culture_adjustment: Easy. As long as you keep in mind that everything is a lot more formal.
socializing_tips: Everyone is on WhatsApp. That's where it happens.
cultural_challenges: I didn't really use to address the professors as 'professor [Last name]'.
culture_appreciated: It is really not that different from the Danish 'culture'.
top3_advice: Be prepared for a huge load of practicalities with both HU, KU, and the German authorities (Anmeldung/Abmeldung/Rundfunkbeitrag, etc.). I spend so much time just uploading or filling out the right documents both before and also now after. It is never-ending and it is insanely frustrating. But I think that applies for everyone going on exchange. Sadly.
other_useful_info: The exam period is crazy and since they don't release the exam dates it is close to impossible to plan ahead. The professors didn't really respect what was written in the introduction materials (lectures will end 3 weeks before the exam) so there wasn't any real exam period. My exams ended in late February so if you have to go back to start the semester at KU you have to devote some time to figure that out.
most_rewarding: That I made it considering the number of hours I put into the courses. And also some of the perspectives you get from living in a city that relatively recently was reunited after years with different regimes and wars. Since Berlin - or maybe Germany on the whole - is an attractive place for people from all around the world, I met people from both Ukraine and Kashakstan who had a terrible start of 2022. It really puts things in perspective.
greatest_challenge: There are so many things that you need to get in order and really no one to help you. The workload from everywhere was immense. And never-ending. Not only in terms of studying but also with all this practical and formal stuff that you need to do.

crucial_aspects: The unique culture of Berlin. Always wanted to stay there for a longer time than just vacation. Also Academic level was high of European (non Elite British) standards.
info_ease: The host university provided good communication from their coordinators through mail and information meetings. However the Enrolment process is very bureaucratic and non digital why there was a lot of information needed to be communicated
arrival_assistance: Mails and meetings from the Erasmus Coordinators
arrival_comments: The bureaucratic nature of the enrolment can be very confusing but I ended up not missing anything
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Can't remember it all to be honest. A lot of online stuff before you get there. Then you have to show up at campus at a special time to get a registration document so you can create your student card in two different machines at campus. (you want to do this as early as possible because you have unlimited public transport with this card and it can be expensive to buy single tickets all the time. You register for the examns (non-seminars) later but also need a special document you only can pick up at campus to do so. Just follow the emails from the coordinators and you will be fine even though it can be a bit confusing.
registration_help: Dedicated coordinator who wrote good mails and held meetings and were very friendly if you had questions
registration_success: I was not as sharp on registration for the seminars as I wanted to be. Seminars are courses with half the amount of lectures but with a term-paper instead of an exam. You have to register for these some weeks before teaching is starting in contrast to the normal cources were you do not register to attend lectures but have to register for the exam in the middle of the semester. (I got 2 seminars translated to 1 KU economics seminar which was very nice). If you do 5 courses (30 ECTS) you want maybe 2 or 3 seminars so you don't have to do 5 exams in a very short periode of time. Also the Seminars are small classes (max 20 people) so I would say the quality of the lectures is higher and topics mores specialised. However because there are only room for max 20 of each seminar, many of the interesting seminars are really popular and your chances of getting a spot very low. I didn't know that and therefore only applied for 2 seminars, thinking I would get both. I was lucky to get 1 but there had been over 4 times the amount of possible attendees who had applied in both of them. I wound therefore recommend people to register for many seminars to maximise their chances of getting a spot. There is only binding registration a couple of weeks into the seminar so if you get to0 many you can just register for your preferred ones. I ended up getting a second seminar because its deadline were later but again I was really lucky with that.
registration_advice: As written above register for many seminars since you probably won't get a spot on all of them. The deadlines for registration can be several weeks before teaching start so look into this as soon as possible.
course_level: Comparable to master courses at KU. Some of them have a big workload (2-3 papers to read every weak for 6 ECTS points) were others were more chill (look at the assignments every week). But the professors were sharp and into their subjects
teaching_comparison: Much the same for the classic courses. However some courses have exercises which basically just were second lectures with a PhD student instead of the professor. The Seminars had weakly lectures with weakly readings.
courses_enrolled: * European Economic History II * Advanced International Trade (ended up not finishing) * Public Economics (ended up not finishing) * Seminar: political economy of radicalisation * Seminar: History of statistics
recommended_courses: European Economic History II was really nice. Intersting subjects, good papers for reading, and a really good professor who have written on the subjects himself. Seminar: political economy of radicalisation was probably one of the best courses I have experienced. Really well structured with good papers on many different aspects of political economy and discussions in class so you really got to understand the papers
unexpected_costs: The semester ticket, but it gave unlimited public transport so I would probably have bought it even if it was not mandatory
cost_comparison: They have good canines were you can choose som very cheap options. Also the coffee at campus is good and cheap.
activities_available: A lot of sports to a good price. I would really recommend people to sign up to those before the semester start
activities_recommended: look above
weekend_recommendations: Seems cheesy to write but off course you have to experience the electronic music scene in Berlin. There are so many good clubs so I would definitely recommend you try a lot of different ones since they all have their specialities. In the summer it gets really warm, so spend your daytime in the Summerbads. There is a nice one next to the olympia stadium were you swim in the olympic pool.
culture_adjustment: Very easy its not that different from Danish and everyone speaks English. However the Germans off course speak German with each other and may not be as comfortable speaking in English. If you have the opportunity I would therefore definitely recommend learning German to a level were you can understand conversations.
socializing_tips: Hard to meet people on campus, easier in sports or language courses.
cultural_challenges: You still had to were the mask in classes and public transport. However it is only public transport now.
culture_appreciated: The club culture
top3_advice: 1. Find some social life as early as possible. Because I was with my girlfriend I probably did not think I needed it that much, but the hardest time away was when I missed more social life with friends. In this regard registering for sport courses is a good opportunity. Even though it is a bit expensive I would probably have registered for a language course also. Just a great way to meet people who are in the same situation as you (was for my Girlfriend) 2. Register for many seminars (if you are a Econ student) since you won't get spots on all of them. If you don't get a spot you can try to 'play the exchange student card' and get a spot anyway. 3. Use cantines for lunch and libraries for reading. There are some really nice spots around the city and you can use other universities' cantines and libraries as well.
other_useful_info: not really
most_rewarding: Experiencing Berlin clubs
greatest_challenge: Getting a good social life up and going.

crucial_aspects: The German marked is of great importance to Denmark and knowledge to the German Legal system and skills in the language is a great advantage.
info_ease: The Copenhagen University delivered a very nice overview of the requirements and the deadline. However the material from Humboldt was all written in German in a very high level which did make the process a bit complicated and confusing.
arrival_assistance: Humboldt had an exchange office where you could receive guidance.
arrival_comments: There were certain courses which were possible to apply and receive the material but where the administration apparently didn't approve that Erasmus students could attend. This was very confusing since the professors etc. would tell you that you could attend the course but then you would receive a denial from the administation several weeks after the beginning of thee course,
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: As written above all the material regarding thee course registration etc. were in German and was complicated so the registration process was a bit confusing.
registration_help: Google Translate
registration_success: Not so succesfull. As written above I was able to successfully apply for courses through the university's internet portal but then later was told by the administration that I wasn't allowed to attend to those courses.
registration_advice: Really take your time making sure that the administration approves it. It dosen't matter that you successfully have applied for the course hrough the university's internet portal or receive the professor's acceptance.
course_level: It was good.
teaching_comparison: It was more the professors talking and the students listning compared to KU.
courses_enrolled: Patent Law and the Life Sciences. Introduction to the English Law of Contract. Mergers & Acquisitions in der anwaltlichen Praxis. International Sales Law and Arbitration. Bankregulierung. I Internationales und Europäisches Investitionsrecht.
recommended_courses: All of them but there is a big difference in the teaching style from german professors and the international professors. Both of them are good and recommendable so therefore I would suggeest that you try them both.
unexpected_costs: Zero
cost_comparison: Germany introduced a summer national travel discount where you could get a ticket of the use of all public transports the whole summer for 9 euro only. That obvious saved some money.
activities_available: There were sports activities and cultural activities available.
activities_recommended: Go to Kreuzberg or Neukölln when partying and try visit the techno clubs even though you are not the typical type.
weekend_recommendations: VIsit some of the other germans cities.
culture_adjustment: Very nice. Germans in Berlin are very polite and cool.
socializing_tips: Just be open. The German (especially the youth) are very polite and cool.
cultural_challenges: None I have only positive things to say.
culture_appreciated: The subculture and techno environment in Berlin even though I'm not the stereotypical type. I know many of the others were not as well but they were all impressed. I my advise would be to drop your prejudices (if you have any) and be open minded.
top3_advice: 1) Try your best to speak and learn german. Even of you are terrible people really support you and appreciate you trying. And you will improve very fast if you just are trying. 2) Explore thee subculture of Berlin 3) Enjoy one the greatest cities in Europe
other_useful_info: I would recommend to spend the summer in Berlin. I have heard that Berlin can be a bit rough during the winter.
most_rewarding: Knowledge to german (language and professional knowledge)
greatest_challenge: Remembering to study since you are having so much fun.

crucial_aspects: The city history, as well as the motivation for learning to speak German.
info_ease: Very difficult. Communication with host University as well as Erasmus was very slow and often not very helpful.
arrival_assistance: Very little. Had to find much needed information myself, often done through other students, since information on curriculums as well as practical aspects were in many cases neither elaborate nor helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process seemed to me outdated, anarchistic and unnecessarily time consuming and stress provoking. People applied for more courses than they intended to attend, which led to chaotic classes in which teachers had no idea, how many students attended class. It seemed like no one, not even the administration had a clear idea of the course organisation, and I personally had very many problems finding out how to organise my classes.
registration_help: Not very much help was available - often there passed weeks before my mails were answered, and it seemed like the administrative staff expected Erasmus students to be comfortable with a very manual, non-digital course registration process in German, which for me not was very simple.
registration_success: Not very succesfull. When I finally had chosen courses, that were offered after I left, OLA took 6 weeks to recognise my courses, and decide, that I had chosen wrong ones. This was a very stressfull experience, to find out, that I attended wrong courses in the middle of the semester/June.
registration_advice: Rather choose not so attractive courses, than being in need of ECTS points to succeed.
course_level: Some courses seemed at extremely high level, where others, combined BA and MA courses were more basic and focused on rote learning.
teaching_comparison: The UCPH style is in general more critical and academic, which I like better, where the HU style is more focused on building knowledge by heart without being too critical towards sources.
courses_enrolled: A combination of academic courses and internship, which had good learning outcome.
recommended_courses: "Musikpraxis" was a really lovely experience. I also did a German Course which was great!
unexpected_costs: none
cost_comparison: In general, Berlin prices are a little lower than Danish, appr. 20 %.
activities_available: I played in an orchestra, which was a fantastic experience.
activities_recommended: Musik an der HU!
weekend_recommendations: Go to the opera - the Abendkasse youth tickets cost only 15 euro one hour before performance, where you receive best available seats and it is world class, esp. Staatsoper unter den Linden!
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy, since I was so keen in learning about the culture and language. The German "Ordnung muss sein"-mentality can be really annoying though.
socializing_tips: Learn German!
cultural_challenges: "Ordnung muss sein", especially with corona restrictions.Very strange to live a place where everyone wear Darth Vader looking masks and think it makes corona go away, but people still shake hands all the time while very few cares about washing their hands regularly and keeping distance which has not been a very visible part of the strategy here. I feel much more exposed to Covid through this strategy than I do in Denmark even though I don't care about the illness very much.
culture_appreciated: The cultural heritage: Architecture, literature, music, theater, history!
top3_advice: Have patience with courses. Go experience the rich culture. Learn German!
most_rewarding: Learning German, experiencing culture. Everything non-academic.
greatest_challenge: The general administration at the HU as well as mobility online huge stacks of documentation requirements, which was badly coordinated with my own university as well as OLA - very slow communication. In germany: , "Ordnung muss sein" and the very exhausting Maskenpflicht, where citizens non-critical approach and lack of logic in wearing this without doing anything else made it strenuous to be present at many public places.

greatest_challenge: Sproget.
