crucial_aspects: Det væsentligste aspekt ved valget af destination var sproget og kulturen. De akademiske muligheder ved udvekslingen bør naturligvis vægte højt, hvad de også gjorde for mit vedkommende, men det er lige så væsentligt, at man kan fungere såvel fagligt som socialt på sin udvekslingsdestination, hvorfor man ikke skal gå på kompromis med sine ønsker, uanset om de er af faglig eller social karakter.
info_ease: Man skulle selv være ret opsøgende for at finde den nødvendige information. Universiteterne må naturligvis gerne forvente, at en universitetsstuderende kan opsøge den nødvendige information selv, men det ville nu være lettere, om man evt. kunne få en 'velkomstpakke'. Dette ville være en støtte, når man ved studiestart skal have styr på så mange ting i et andet land. Informationerne er dog tilgængelige efter lidt søgning - og det er derfor ikke en egentlig kritik.
arrival_assistance: Jeg blev inviteret til et meget kort møde med en studievejleder kort før semesterstart, som opfordrede til, at vi kunne kontakte hende om nødvendigt. Hun besvarede altid mails hurtigt, og man var aldrig overladt helt til sig selv.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Humboldt sendte mails, når der skulle uploades eller sendes dokumenter til dem. Fordi det er Tyskland, er alting en lille smule omstændigt. Først sendte de en godkendelse af studieopholdet, som skulle underskrives af København. Derefter skulle man sende dem et billede af sit pas, sit EU-sundhedskort, en kopi af en e-mail fra en tysk sundhedskasse, hvori det var angivet, at man som EU-borger ikke behøver en tysk sundhedsforsikring. Når alt dette var gjort, modtog man en e-mail med endelig godkendelse af optagelsen, hvorefter man kunne printe sit studiekort og tilmelde sig kurser igennem deres system, Agnes. Tilmeldingen til kurser var nem og smertefri.
registration_help: Der var links til en række hjemmesider og nogle e-mails, man kunne skrive til, men meget var forklaret i detaljer i optagelsespapirerne, de sendte ud. Der blev holdt flere online-kurser i kursusregistrering, eksamenstilmelding mv., samt Anmeldung i Berlin, så der var bestemt hjælp at hente.
registration_success: Jeg havde ingen problemer med at tilmelde mig kurser. For mit studiums vedkommende fungerede kursustilmeldingen ved, at man dukkede op ved den første forelæsning i det givne kursus - sådan er det givetvis ikke for alle, hvorfor mine erfaringer naturligvis må tages med et vist forbehold.
registration_advice: Uanset hvor uoverskueligt, besværligt og uløseligt det ser ud, så skal det nok lykkes.
course_level: Der var et højt niveau i undervisningen. Tager man til Tyskland, skal man være opmærksom på, at det meste foregår på tysk. Dette var imidlertid en af grundene til, at jeg selv valgte Tyskland - og det var jeg meget tilfreds med. Underviserne forudsætter, at studenterne har læst til deres undervisning, og derfor bliver man som student også taget meget alvorligt. Af den årsag forventes der en del af studenterne, hvilket utvivlsomt hæver undervisningens niveau.
teaching_comparison: Den rendyrkede forelæsningsform var en sand fryd! Denne form, hvor en professor i et givent emne præsenterer sin forskning i halvanden time - uden spørgsmål, uden kommentarer fra auditoriet, - findes ikke umiddelbart på mit studium i København, men det var en virkelig stor oplevelse at få serveret så meget viden på en så komprimeret måde.
courses_enrolled: Forelæsning i Romerbrevet, seminar i jødisk-kristen apokalyptisk litteratur, seminar i sundhed og sygdom i teologisk perspektiv.
recommended_courses: Jeg vil altid anbefale, at man tager en forelæsning - for at opleve den tyske forelæsningsform, der er virkelig givende. Kurserne ændrer sig år for år, og jeg kan derfor ikke anbefale, at man tager ét kursus.
unexpected_costs: Man bliver naturligvis altid overrasket over, at man bruger flere penge, end man ville gøre derhjemme. Men det er helt normalt, når man skal se og gøre alting på næsten ingen tid.
cost_comparison: De generelle fødevareprisstigninger er naturligvis også nået til Tyskland, men det generelle billede er, at priserne generelt er lavere i Berlin end i København.
activities_available: Der var tiltag som sportsaktiviteter, fælles gudstjenesteture, guidede ture omkring i byen, fredagsbar etc.
activities_recommended: Gør det, du finder interessant. Der er masser af muligheder for at dyrke din interesse i fællesskab med andre - og derigennem finde gode kammerater.
weekend_recommendations: Berlins rige kulturliv - alt fra områder af byen til restauranter og barer.
culture_adjustment: Det var nemt.
socializing_tips: Lær at tale deres sprog. Det gør alting nemmere!
cultural_challenges: Berlins ikke-tolerante wokeness, sådan som den findes i visse miljøer.
culture_appreciated: Alt andet.

crucial_aspects: As a student of history, Berlin is an awesome place to be. The international vibes in the city helps any foreigner feel welcome, while still exploring some German culture and history. I chose Berlin because I have an affinity for Germany, but I was unsure if i would be able to speak the language well enough to function in other places in the country. I now realise that I could have done so, but Berlin is especially good for english speakers.
overall_comments: For anybody living in close proximity to Berlin, such as students in Copenhagen, it is awesome to be in a new place with a new adventure, whilst still feeling close to home.
info_ease: Humboldt Uni were supremely efficient in helping me through email correspondence. Once i arrived, our Erasmuskoordinator arranged for all Erasmus Students of history to meet, where we were given all the required information, and were able to make some new friends.
arrival_assistance: The Erasmus coordinator of Humboldt's history department arranged a meet-up, and afterwards, we could write to him or come to his office whenever needed. He was very helpful all throughout the semester, a super great, friendly and approachable guy.
arrival_comments: At the faculty of history atleast, Humboldt University has the best possible assistance to international students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: For anybody living in close proximity to Berlin, such as students in Copenhagen, it is awesome to be in a new place with a new adventure, whilst still feeling close to home.
registration_process: To register, one must first send application documents back and fourth from Humboldt, before arriving in the country. Because Germany's semesters are from october-marts and april-august, this paperwork will often not fit in with the automated time-schedules proposed in your own university's Erasmus application. Once you're accepted, and you arrive in Germany, you recieve a letter in your physical mailbox (In Germany, everything is done on paper and not online). You take this letter to the Humboldt Administration (in their very limited office hours), and they then register you, you recieve your online account, your student-ID, etc.. For classes, you must then register the ones you want on this online account that you can now access, before the semester begins.
registration_help: Basically you just follow the instructions in their emails and letters. Mostly, you ask fellow students for advice, although i'm sure you could write an email to the administration and ask for advice as well. For registering classes, links to guide-videoes were send out per email. If there was any questions, the erasmus coordinator was very helpful and knowledgeable.
registration_success: I was 100% succesful in registering for the exact classes i wanted.
registration_advice: In Germany, you have to decide if you wanna do an exam for each class yourself. These exams then give additional ECTS points. This is worth considering from the beginning, as it must be written on your online learning agreement, and the teachers of the individual courses will want to know before long.
academics_comments: For anybody living in close proximity to Berlin, such as students in Copenhagen, it is awesome to be in a new place with a new adventure, whilst still feeling close to home.
course_level: The history courses at Humboldt varies greatly in difficulty and quality. As with any university, it really depends on the individual professors. I will say, however, that taking courses in German, you really atleast have to understand the language. Most professors will have mercy on your speaking abilities, but you must be able to understand what they're saying to you.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style is mostly the same. In Vorlesungen, you sit and listen, in other courses, you debate throughout the lecture. It really is almost the same as in Denmark
courses_enrolled: DaF Deutsch Kurs (vor dem Wintersemester) - language course that prepares you for speaking and understanding German, costs a bit of money and takes a month, but i can only recommend it. History of the communist secret police in Eastern Europe - very interesting course on Stasi and other opressive police forces during the could war. Diplomatie und Spionage in der Frühen Neuzeit - super good master-level course on espionage and diplomacy between the years 1600-1900 . Bachelorseminare neuere und neueste Geschichte, Markt und Koorporation: Geschichte der Europäischen Integration - Amazing course on european integration from the end of ww2 and forwards. Dr. Alexander Nützenadel is a great professor. Deutschland und Frankreich seit dem Zweiten Weltkrieg, Konflikt und Verflechtung - very good Vorlesung for understanding the history behind the current relationship between Germany and France
recommended_courses: Definitely look into the DaF studievorbereitend language courses, which they ask you if you want to apply for very early in the application process at Humboldt. They cost some money, but you get 4 hours of German training a day for a whole month, nothing prepares you better for your time at Humboldt. And, you get to meet people in similar situations to yourself, which is a great opportunity for making friends.
unexpected_costs: There were really no unexpected costs, aside from the very good language course at Humboldt. You pay 180 euroes for a "semester fee", but this gives access to all public transport in Berlin for the entire duration of the semester, so it is well worth it.
cost_comparison: Food, drinks, and everything for living is less expensive than other places in Germany, and even Denmark. Over-expensive food or restaurants are priced like the danish ones.
activities_available: Great opportunities for fun at Humboldt, if one wishes to engage in it. For instance, you can sign up for sport classes of all kinds. Otherwise, living at a campus will give great social possibilites. Living in housing you found yourself, you will have to make friends locally and through classes and activities.
activities_recommended: Definitely go to the first activities and meet--ups hosted by the university, they are paramount for forming good bonds for the entire semester.
weekend_recommendations: Go clubbing in Berlin, but go and embrace history and culture as well. They have 3 opera houses in Berlin, all very cheap for students. Go see historic sites, and remember to take some trips outside of the city aswell.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy to adjust to the culture, because they are a lot like Danes in northern Germany.
socializing_tips: German students are hard to talk to, it is easier to speak with other international students. But, they are very kind, and if you manage to make some German friends, you will see that they are awesome.
cultural_challenges: Nothing, Berlin was very welcoming as a whole.
culture_appreciated: I appreciate the Berliners' fashion sense, because danish style is unbelieveably boring and unrecognisable. Also they have great beer.
top3_advice: 1. Don't worry, you will have an awesome time here. German bureaucracy is no joke, there is a lot of physical paperwork involved, but it is all worth it. See it as a challenge, and remember that the Germans themselves meme on it. Because the semesters are in a weird time-frame compared to Denmark, you will have a lot of bureaucracy issues with the online erasmus-application. Don't worry, just communicate it and it will be no problem. 2. Be very proactive with seeking housing, it can become a nightmare if you don't have it taken care off. Get it done, so you can enjoy the time here. 3. Don't be put off by rumors of Berlin as a city, especially if you're not very good at German, or you don't like clubbing. Berlin is very welcoming, you don't have to speak perfect German, and you don't have to center your time here around clubbing. Berlin is a cultural hub, there is a whole crowd for jazz-clubs, classical music, sports, art, etc.. whatever you're into, you'll find it here.
other_useful_info: For Humboldt University, do the studievorbereitend language courses, even if you have to save up a bit of money for them! And remember to consider which courses you wanna do exams in as well.
most_rewarding: I have found myself 10x more capable than i thought through this experience. 1. day in my apartment i locked myself out, and had to call 8 German locksmiths before one of them understood my broken German, and came to help. The Erasmus-experience is packed full of challenges, but you grow 10x as a person in comparison to a normal semester at home. And if you like foreign cultures, languages and history, an exchange trip is an absolute must. You will feel alive every day.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenges were the language barriers and struggling to keep up with people who speak the language as their first language. This, along with the bureaucracy found in Germany, made the experience difficult, but it is absolutely worth it.
other_comments: If you've had the idea to go on an exchange semester, and you kinda wanna do it but you're not really sure - stop thinking and just go! Academically, professionally and personally, this is what gives you an adventure of a lifetime, and it will set you apart. Just go!

Working alongside professionals from different scientific disciplines not only expanded my knowledge base but also enabled me to forge valuable connections and engage in cutting-edge research at the forefront of multiple fields. I had the privilege of working with esteemed scientists from different countries, which broadened my horizons and exposed me to diverse perspectives and approaches. These international collaborations not only enriched my research experience but also nurtured my cultural understanding and equipped me to address complex challenges on an international scale as a globally-minded medicinal chemist. The exceptional faculty at Humboldt University played a pivotal role in my academic and professional development. Working alongside distinguished scientists, renowned researchers, and accomplished professionals was a transformative experience. Their expertise, guidance, and support not only fostered my academic and research skills but also provided invaluable insights into the latest advancements and emerging trends in medicinal chemistry. The mentorship I received from these esteemed experts significantly shaped my educational experience and set me on a path towards success in the field. I am immensely grateful for the invaluable knowledge, skills, and connections I gained during my time at Humboldt, which will undoubtedly shape my future endeavors as a medicinal chemist.

crucial_aspects: I already lived there once and had a grab on the German language, which I wanted to make even better - both for personal reasons and because German is a crucial language inside the world of theology (which I study). Berlin (where I was) - and Germany in general - is an epicenter of theology, and I wanted to experience that from the inside. Also, I wanted to go to Berlin to experience its history, its multiculturalism, its art scene, its colors, all of the things that attracts most people to the city.
info_ease: It was all right. I was helped much by the contact person at the faculty at HU.
arrival_assistance: I received some assistance from the administration office, but because we were only three exchange students at the faculty, we had to figure out many things ourselves that were not natural for us to know. For instance when it came to collecting ECTS-point and what subjects we where supposed to choose. Never the less, there were administrative people there expecting our arrival and telling us what to do, and that was nice.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to fulfill different requirements respectively from the administrative office at Copenhagen University and the administrative office at Humboldt-Universität. It was clear that they had two different systems with two different ambitions for the students.
registration_help: It was actually quite flexible to register at Humboldt: the teachers and the administrative people were openminded and helpfull. However, during the stay, it turned out that one of the classes, I was following and Copenhagen had accepted, wouldn't be able to live up to their own requirements for ECTS-points. Very unfortunate. I also had doubts all way about which person in Copenhagen, I should contact with my questions. That was not the case at Humboldt.
registration_success: I was able to register at the classes I wanted at Humboldt. However, as mentioned above, it wasn't all of the classes that turned out to be acceptable for Copenhagen - and that made me very uncertain in the process.
registration_advice: Make sure that the two institutions are not - figuratively - speaking two different languages. Talk to a person who have been abroad were you are going, since that is often the expert - not the administration offices.
course_level: The level was very good. The teachers were very attentive, and all of the courses felt relevant and important. There was a good conversation between teacher and students, meaningful discussions, where the student's words and opinions were taken at face value.
teaching_comparison: More students were involved at HU than at CPH. It was less formal at HU than at CPH, more natural to debate with the teachers. Spaces were created that were more about learning and being curios than about how to get through an exam. Generally very little - if any - focus on exams in the classrooms.

recommended_courses: Especially the courses with Amir Engel. They were vibrant and relevant and were not dictated by form and formalities.
unexpected_costs: - I had to rent a bike, because my own broke - I lost almost all of my deposit to the apartment I was renting due to an unaccountable landlord - In general: public transportation - trains and busses that didn't arrive at time, meaning I had to pay double or triple for tickets
cost_comparison: Public transportation was more expensive. The costs for living in an apartment and not being treated fairly by the landlord was more expensive. Foods, drinks, concerts and so on were less expensive than expected.
activities_available: I went to sports every monday through Humboldt. Otherwise, I didn't experience that many social or cultural activities were available.
activities_recommended: Go to concerts, to the museum, in cinemas, go drink beers ind different areas, go to a sport and meet people there.
weekend_recommendations: See the city where you live. Bike around. Go to flea markets.
culture_adjustment: It was alright. In general, people were very friendly and open minded.
cultural_challenges: Maybe the fact that I had to say 'Herr' and 'Frau' and 'Sie' instead of 'du'. That was a challenge, because I'm not used to that.
culture_appreciated: The open-mindedness. The patience and the goodwill when it came to my German.
top3_advice: 1) Make sure that you want to learn and speak German throughout. There is almost no English during the stay. 2) Find a dormitory or another institutional place instead of renting an apartment privately. 3) Try to establish contact to a person from your home university who already went to the place were you are going abroad - that person can be a good life guard, who most likely already experienced, what you are going through.
other_useful_info: Make sure to register at a language school before the semester starts! That is a very convenient way to start to speak German and to land in the city.
most_rewarding: That I am now able to speak German.
greatest_challenge: Administrative and bureaucratic stuff.

crucial_aspects: I chose Berlin because I wanted to brush up on my German while experiencing living in a larger European city with a vibrant cultural and musical scene. The academic aspect was only partially important in my case, but I was positively surprised in some areas and less so in others. Specifically, the academic level varied across available subjects, so you can both choose 'hard' and 'easy' courses.
overall_comments: The only thing I would change is my choice of accommodation. I had not thought it important until I tried living far from the center, in a pleasant but remote area. Specifically I lived in Allee der Kosmonauten, which is a cheap and decent dorm and one of the options offered to Humboldt exchange students. It's unfortounately quite far from the center and from my faculty, the business faculty,, albeit with a tram connection, and grocery stores 15-20 min by foot away. That's not necessarily a problem; some might call it a whiny luxury problem, especially when the dorm is cheap, but I do regret not paying more to live closer to the center or just within walking distance of a U- or S-bahn. That's just a personal preference. My 'regret' probably also stems from my specific room in the dorm; the apartments are either 2- or 3-room apartments with a shared bath/kitchen. I got the smallest room in mine, while my two roommates got 1.5-size and 2x size rooms, compared to mine, both with a mini-balcony. Their rent was only marginally higher; 30-40 euro or so. Quite unlucky (and unfair, in my opinion). That, and I would have participated in the month-long intensive language course in September. I unfortunately arrived in the second half of September so couldn't participate, but I wish I had arrived earlier - don't miss out on that for language skills and social connections!
info_ease: It was a bit of a mixed bag. Information was relatively easy to get once you actually arrived, but the pre-arrival information was pretty lackluster - especially if you needed any 'seminar' courses for one reason or another, a good chunk of which already had their 'application deadlines' passed by the 1. of October. The semester officially starts on the 1. of October, but classes in reality only start two weeks later, and those are introduction classes - would have been nice to know. All of this applies to my own faculty, WiWi, to be clear. An introduction event was held a week before the start of classes; we were informed of said event by mail a day or two before it was to take place. During the event we found out that it was directed at both bachelor's and master's students (I am a master's). After the event the student council had organized a sightseeing-on-campus walking tour and a subsequent meet n greet - it was only here that I found out that the official event, and the subsequent social event, was not something specific to exchange students, of which there were few (which is not an issue!), but also for all people beginning their education at the faculty. It was fun and good from a social POV, but just a tad confusing and could have been better communicated beforehand. The seminar stuff mentioned earlier especially.

arrival_comments: Comments are mostly directed at pre-arrival, not so much upon arrival.

registration_process: The paperwork wasn't so bad in general, but you need to get a mandatory insurance exemption (given that you have travel insurance) and it's a bit confusing and not very well explained how you're supposed to do that prior to semester start. If you wish to take 'seminars' those are also both pretty confusing to get into. Some require sending an email with a motivational text for why you wish to take it, others just make you register and then if there's too many sign-ups (the registration slots are quite small/limited 30-50 or so for most) they just do a lottery. For context, you usually don't sign up to classes, you just sign up to exams in January / show up to the ones you want to take, but for seminars it's the more traditional pre-semester registration process that Danes are used to, except you don't know if you'll get a slot, you're not guaranteed a slot and some have registration deadlines before the actual introduction events, so you only find out about those once those deadlines have already passed.
registration_help: The university answered questions and helped in regards to the mandatory exemption stuff, but in regards to seminars and planning classes you were more or less left to your own bureaucratic abilities and ability to make an overview.
registration_success: I didn't get into some of the seminars that I wanted, but got into others. You're very much left to your own abilities here, so if you need seminars, you need to put in the work yourself beforehand. If you just need normal classes with lectures, you can just wing it on arrival.
registration_advice: All of the bureaucratic stuff is quite messy compared to the streamlined way KU students are likely used to and more things are required to be done by hand and then scanned/sent, such as signed documents - you can't just digitally sign them - but it's not so bad. My best advice would be to arrive in September, one month before semester start, and take the intensive language course. You can get a head-start on the paperwork required by doing so, not to mention the other benefits.

The average 'academic level' of the courses seemed lower than at KU, but this was offset by some courses being really tough and undemanding, so you can find those if you're really looking for them. If you're an Economics student, you can also take courses offered at the general Berlin School of Economics, which covers all the Berlin universities.
teaching_comparison: The exercise classes, at least those that I partially experienced, are mostly a student assistant going through solutions rather than you working through the problems yourselves - at least that's what it seemed like most of the time. The seminars can be tough and intensive, depending on the seminar, and some have pre-chosen topics to select with weekly meetings with a supervisor. The Danish seminar system is mostly a self-study / self-writing exercise; this is only true for some seminars at WiWi, as some seminars have 'normal' weekly lectures, some seminars just have weekly 'office hours' and other seminars have a weekly meeting with your supervisor and constant deadlines; the last part mostly applies to the Information Systems seminar. All of the normal/none-seminar exams at WiWi are done by hand, unfortounately, so be prepared for that. Moreover, the exams are very short, 60-120 minutes, so coming from Denmark it really becomes a question of time management like never before - at least if you write significantly slower by hand, like I do, and writing text answers on physical paper therefore becomes a huge travesty time-wise,.
courses_enrolled: Seminar Information Systems Business Analytics and Data Science Behavioral Finance and Asset Pricing Seminar Entrepreneurial Finance and Venture Capital Seminar Econometrics (uncompleted) Structural Vector Autoregression (uncompleted)
recommended_courses: For the Fall I can especially recommend the Information Systems seminar, which is really demanding and though for those not used to coding in Python / machine learning, but also really rewarding. Helmut Lütkepohl's SVAR intensive course in October is also a big recommendation, but it takes place outside of Humboldt/WiWi's usual setup and you have to manually register by email (sidenote; the last week of October you write a short self-chosen exam paper; I was unfortunately sick during that period and didn't complete the course, but it's an excellent course nonetheless, as Helmut is literally the man who wrote the textbook used by KU on the topic)
unexpected_costs: Of unexpected costs: a relatively small license fee required by the municipality; requires you actually registering with them, though. General comments: Humboldt required an up-front registration fee of roughly 200~ euro upon registration. The fee is not for tuition, but a sort of fee for the student council and includes a transportation card for the entirety of Berlin for the duration of the semester; a really good deal, all in all. Not sure if that'll still be the case in the future, but it was when I went in the autumn/winter semester of 2023/2024. I did not buy a separate travel insurance but used the insurance included in my DJØF general insurance. The travel insurance there lasts for 120 days (or something like that), but those days 'reset' if you stay in Denmark for 24 hours throughout your stay; I had to visit home for various reasons a few times during my stay in Berlin, so could basically rely on said insurance for the entirety of the stay without any top-ups. Other fees therefore covers those costs along with a cheap gym membership.
cost_comparison: Food and grocery shopping was way more expensive than I had anticipated. Some grocery items were more expensive than they would be in Denmark. Anything sugar-related was way less expensive, while some things, eg. a fruit like kiwi, was significantly more expensive than what you could often find on offer in a Danish supermarket. Coffee is way cheaper. Going out (clubbing, drinking, etc) is cheaper, but not by much. Museum entry is somewhat cheaper, but varies across museums. The opera, at least the Staatopera, is WAY cheaper and easily recommended. If you visited Berlin prior to corona and the start of the Ukraine-Russia War (of 2022), be aware that the price level is significantly higher now than it was previously - at least that was the case when I went, so don't expect to live the high life on a shoestring budget.
activities_available: My faculty's, WiWi, student council did do some social events and were cool folks, but it's not a big faculty so don't expect anything grandiose. The faculty building closes at 21.00 and the social events were mostly dozens of people going to a nearby bar after a student council meeting (which is held in German). Humboldt does offer a bunch of sports classes and a gym (I think?), which are mostly reasonably priced, but by the time you'll find out about them a lot of the interesting ones will be filled and some activities like tennis might be held very far in the outskirts of 'urban' Berlin, so the travel time alone is a huge disincentive. I just went with a cheap local 24/7 local gym instead. There was also some random Erasmus events/parties sometimes unrelated to Humboldt, but I never went and they didn't seem terribly popular among people I knew.
activities_recommended: Going clubbing in Berlin, especially during the warmer months, is a very unique experience - there's a Berlin aesthetic that is a good idea to familiarize yourself with before going, and you should probably learn a few German phrases at a minimum, but that's not strictly necessary unless you're going to somewhere like Berghain. While there's a great variety of museums, what I really recommend of purely cultural activities is visiting the Staatopera next to the main Humboldt campus. You get 50% off as a student; the cheapest seats are consequently priced at as low as 13 €, with the cheapest viewing seats at around 20 €. Compared to what you have to pay in Denmark, it's a really great deal for 3-hour live performances of classic opera. The Staatopera is often quite filled, but sometimes you can pull a fast one and move to unoccupied 'better seats' shortly after the start of the performance - being a poor student comes with /some/ privileges, sometimes! PS: If in doubt how to dress for a night out, dress in black, unless you're going to Sisyphos, where you dress colorful, or KitKat, where you dress according to that day's theme. Getting into Berghain is quite doable; if you just want to go to cross it off your bucket list, try going alone at roughly 3-4 am Saturday, i.e. 03.00 Sunday, while wearing semi-casual black or not too colorful clothing - not white sneakers! - and a backpack. The latter is to show you're a regular, even if it's empty, but having a pair of changing clothes in the backpack is not a bad idea. Be sober at the entrance, or at least appear to be. Good luck!
weekend_recommendations: Berlin has a vibrant night life and cultural life, but visitting Potsdam, especially during the Christmas market(s) period, and other scenic locations outside of Berlin is quite easy and doable using public transportation.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. The academic and bureaucratic culture took some getting used to, as described earlier, but it wasn't that bad. One thing to keep in mind - the 'Germans use fax'-thing is literally NOT a stereotype or a joke. A lot of things in Germany are less digitalized than you'd think and cash is still king in Berlin, with quite a few places only accepting cash, eg. (none-chain) eateries, bars, bakeries and coffee shops,
socializing_tips: Attend the intensive language course if you can; you'll meet lots of other Erasmus people that way. If you're going to WiWi, most of the people you'll meet there are also new to Berlin and likely took their bachelor's degree elsewhere, so hang around for the introduction event(s) and join the chat groups. While I might have had some reservations about my dorm, I also met lots of cool people there. There's every opportunity to be social and find friends, so that shouldn't be an issue; just show up to things!
cultural_challenges: The extent of the use of physical paper documentation, the exam-by-hand-on-physical-paper-thing and the amount of cash-only places. The university bureaucracy and associated systems are also quite messy compared to KU.
culture_appreciated: Berlin is really more of a European melting pot than a bastion of German culture, outside of the public bureaucracy, that is, truth be told, so if that's your thing definitely go, but if you want to be local with the local Germans then there's better destinations than Berlin. I was quite satisfied, however.
top3_advice: 1. If you need/are going to take seminars, badger the administration for information beforehand - the information you'll get prior to arrival likely won't be sufficient. 2. Attend the language course. 3. Consider what matters to you in terms of accommodation and the associated tradeoffs.
other_useful_info: Not really - you should definitely go.
most_rewarding: All of it.
greatest_challenge: The bureaucracy and physical distance to the faculty.

arrival_assistance: There were a welcoming event when they provided a lot of information
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_help: The reply on e-mail was a bit slow, but I think it was because I contacted them in september and the semester does not start until mid october
registration_success: The system is very confusing. So apparantly everyone applies for at lot of courses, and then gets rejected to most (I got rejected for all of my courses, which was a bit stressful when you dont know that it's normal procedure), and then you just physically attend the courses you want and then the professor will most likely allow you on the course.
registration_advice: Maybe to just relax a bit, cause you will probably get the courses you want, they are just very chill about the registration, you don't apply in advance, you just figure it out as the courses are starting.
course_level: I think it was fine. The system is quite different from the way the biology courses are structured at KU. So there's both a practical, lecture and seminar part, and the practical part and seminar part can be quite demanding, as the practical requires long, intense days, and the seminar can be a lot of work as you have to conduct a 30 min seminar. At least that was the structure of the courses that I attended in the biology faculty.
teaching_comparison: The structure as I mentioned above. The teacher-student relationship also required some getting used to on my part.
courses_enrolled: Biodiversity and Evolution 1 (Theory) Soil Ecosystems as Biodiversity Hot Spot Cognition, Evolution and Behaviour
recommended_courses: Biodiversity and Evolution was a fun course, and did not have a practical part actually. It involved a lot of different teachers with many different academic background which was very interesting. Soil Ecosystems as Biodiversity Hot Spot turned out to be a very interesting course even though I am not normally that interested in soil ecosystems, but it was interesting. Cognition, Evolution and Behaviour was a quite intense course with long days during the practical part. You get to get some experience with experimental animals and you conduct an animal experiment as well.
unexpected_costs: Semester fee, but then you also get a student card which gives you free transportation, so I was not sure if I should put that amount (1.980,00 DKK) in the transportation box.
cost_comparison: It is much cheaper than Denmark, but I expected it to be. You can live very cheap if you want
activities_available: There is a long list of sport activities quite cheap through the university, I also have a friend who got free instrument lessons
activities_recommended: there's a possibility to do whatever you want, so I would recommend to try out a lot of things. you can also attend classes a single time
weekend_recommendations: there is a lot of museums, museums are free on the first sunday of every month. Then there a lot of cultural activities going on every weekend and day.
culture_adjustment: It was easy as german and danish culture are similar and most germans in berlin are good at english
socializing_tips: attend the HUGS attend
cultural_challenges: sometimes the germans forget to smile :) and public transportation can be a bit chaotic
culture_appreciated: It is very relaxed, lots of opportunities, very free and non-judging atmosphere
top3_advice: do the language course on HU, I did not do that and I regret is as it was a very good social opportunity. Take your time finding a good place, consider the dorms as they are cheaper and then you'll have more money for fun stuff, and transportation takes a while no matter where you live, so it's not a problem if you dont live very central. And just dont stress to much about the way the administration works, cause they dont, it will all work out.
other_useful_info: Try to understand the course registration at your faculty, maybe contact some students who went to the same as you're going to, that will be a big stress relief I think.
most_rewarding: Experiencing a different culture and another university.
greatest_challenge: Gaining the energy for some of the more intense parts of my courses while establishing social life and navigating in a new country

socializing_tips: Patience?

socializing_tips: Just talk to them after class.
cultural_challenges: Would have loved to practice my german more before I went, but not a big problem. Culturally its not so different from DK/KBH, just more open.
culture_appreciated: Not sure, just the atmosphere.

So I didn't learn as much accademically as I hoped I would. It was very nice and interesting to see how they do stuff in Germany though. Next you have to send a lot of documents to actually enroll to the university and pay the semester fees. Then you can beginn to send emails to the departments in which you want to do your clinical rotations - some of them aqcuire a lot of documents too. When you've organized that, you have to send your plan to the coordinator. Lastly you have to get a couple of vaccines and blood samples and a signature from your general practitioner in Denmark.
registration_help: The coordinator, Nikola Lepom, has been a great help throughout the process. She also helped organize the first clinical rotation.
registration_success: The departments which I firsted emailed never answered, so I didn't get my first priority, but I figured it all out in the end. I'm just happy I managed to get clinical rotations at departments, that will be accepted in Denmark.
registration_advice: Start early, so it isn't stressful. It always takes longer time than you expect, because you have to wait for so many different people to respond to your emails.
academics_comments: Berlin is amazing and it's very easy to get to know people here. They also organize events with Erasmus students from all over Europe and I got an Erasmus-Buddy, a german medical student, who became my friend right from the beginning. On the other hand as a student you're not allowed to do as much in the hospital in Germany as you are in Denmark, so I didn't learn as much as I could have in Denmark. So I didn't learn as much accademically as I hoped I would. It was very nice and interesting to see how they do stuff in Germany though. Lastly I think it's a pitty that there is so much bureaucracy involved in a Erasmus program.
course_level: Only clinical rotations.
teaching_comparison: The hospitals are kind of different. At Charité it's way less digitalised in it is in the hospitals near Copenhagen. Also it's the doctors job to draw blood in Germany, while it's something the nurses do in Denmark, which is why I've gotten really good at drawing blood and at doing similar procedures.
courses_enrolled: Clinical rotations: - Department of Infectious Diseases at CVK - Department of musculoskeletal surgery at CCM
recommended_courses: I can indeed recommend the Department of Infectious Diseases at CVK, but I didn't really like the Department of musculoskeletal surgery at CCM.
unexpected_costs: Semester fees (the public transportation/a Deutschlandsemesterticket was included). It was 300 euros 3 months before my arrival, which I didn't expect.
cost_comparison: Doing sports and taking classes offered to students! They are very cheap and very good. I can indeed recommend. It's also a nice way to get to know other students at the university.
activities_available: Everything you can imagine!! Humboldt University is huge and they have maybe 200 or more different activities to choose from. They have everything you can think of! You just have to be quick, because the spots are quickly sold out.
activities_recommended: I did latin dance and arabic - both were very nice. I also did a presemester intensive german course, which means I got to know a lot of international students and other Erasmus students even before the semester started. I'm not that much into clubbing, but if you're you will have 50-100 Erasmus students who will happily accompany you to the clubs and party with you.
weekend_recommendations: Stay in Berlin and spend time with the people you're getting to know! The time is so short, so the faster you're getting friends the more you're going to enjoy. Also visit Christmas markets, when that time of the year comes.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Everyone is very open minded and welcoming. And also I don't feel the differences between and Denmark and Germany are huge. I keep forgetting to give tips in restaurants though, because I'm not used to it. Other than that the language has been the biggest challenge - writing admission letters in german was indeed a challenge.
socializing_tips: Do sports and activities offered by the University - that's the easiest way to get in touch with germans. Or find a "WG" with german students - I wish I would have done that. Other than that attend to Erasmus activities - a lot of german students are there too!
cultural_challenges: Giving tips at restaurants. The language. And I also lived the two from Parkistan, who didn't know how to sort waste, which was also kind of challenging haha.
culture_appreciated: That everyone is so open and welcoming, and that so many german students are organizing those Erasmus events.
top3_advice: Do the "Farma"-exam in the 7th semester and attend a presemester german course before the exchange. It was very nice and a very nice way to extend the very short exchange. Sign up for sport classes or whatever you want - as long as you're meeting new people! Attend to the Erasmix-events. They are very nice.
other_useful_info: It might be more difficult to get all the signatures you need from UCPH than it would have been in Denmark. The last year medical students in Germany are doing less than what UCPH expect Danish students to in their fourth year, which makes it difficult.
most_rewarding: Speaking to patients in German and building a connection with them in a language that's not your mothertongue. I went to Germany half a year in my gap year, which means German is NOT my mothertonuge, and that's why it feels very good everything I've succeed with something here (speaking with patients, understanding lectures or writing admission letters).
greatest_challenge: The language and learning all the medical terms in German, but that was indeed also one of the best parts of the exchange! And it feels very rewarding afterwards.
other_comments: Actually I think I would recommend to do the exchange in the 11th semester instead of the 8th as I did. At that time you're more flexible, you can choose whatever departments you want and you don't have an OSCE exam waiting for you when you get home.

crucial_aspects: I am interested in Arctic studies and I was excited to live and study in a different part of the Arctic (prior to my MSc I lived in Alaska). Nuuk also offered the opportunity to be involved in scientific research in the Arctic alongside my academic studies.
info_ease: Very easy. -NAME REDACTED-, the international student coordinator at Ilisimatusarfik, is extremely helpful. He gave me a tour of campus on my first day, introduced me to other students and was available to answer any questions I had during the term.
arrival_assistance: Because I organized a project outside course scope at Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, GINR allowed me to stay in one of their housing buildings, which was affordable and conveniently located on the same campus as both the Institute and the university.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Just had to email the international student coordinator my choices, and he registered me.
registration_help: -NAME REDACTED- was very helpful, although it wasn't super clear what the courses were about before I was registered. The course catalog gave only a cursory description, not a full syllabus.
registration_success: Successful, but see above.
registration_advice: Ilisimatusarfik is a small school, so you might not have a lot of course options, especially if you don't speak Danish or Greenlandic. Still, the experience of being in Nuuk is way bigger than just your course choices so I would not weigh that too heavily in your decision to study in Greenland.
course_level: Both courses felt appropriate for my level.
teaching_comparison: I'm used to more group project based learning at KU and we didn't really do project work in my Ilisimatusarfik courses. Courses were mostly lecture-based with individual projects at the end.
courses_enrolled: Arctic Economy Advanced Economic Methodology
recommended_courses: Arctic Economy was really interesting, especially if you are interested in learning about how the Arctic economic development, natural resources and social issues.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Flights to and from Greenland are incredibly expensive. Food is more expensive than in Copenhagen but less than I thought it would be.
activities_available: The university does a good job making sure the international students have opportunities to socialize. They organized a fishing trip for us at the start of the semester and a biweekly (every other week) kaffemik to have coffee, cake and socialize. We did not have a lot of opportunities to mix with local students but I think that has more to do with the culture of the university. Many students are also parents or have jobs in addition to their studies, so they don't stay on campus beyond class time for the most part.
activities_recommended: Most of my time was taken up by school, research and a part time job, so I didn't look into student organizations much, but I did spend a fair amount of time with my fellow international students.
weekend_recommendations: Rock climbing at the børnehave, volunteer at the animal shelter, go to the pub quiz at Daddy's on Thursday nights, attend cultural events at Katuaq, go hiking or look for northern lights, take a boat tour into the fjords or (more expensive) take the ferry to Ilulissat for a few days.
culture_adjustment: Reasonably easy. Nuuk is a bustling city and most people speak Danish. To me the culture shared similarities with both Alaska and Denmark, in terms of the language and traditions, so I didn't feel like it was hard to adjust. Certainly you're still an outsider, so I think it's best to be open, observe and ask (respectful) questions.
socializing_tips: I could have done a better job at making stronger connections with local students but I did make a point to ask other students questions during class breaks and say hi when I saw people around town. Even though most local students have their own busy lives I found everyone to be friendly and welcoming.
cultural_challenges: Not speaking Greenlandic definitely limits the level of communication and integrating you can do, but most people also speak Danish and many speak English as well.
culture_appreciated: I found people very friendly and welcoming and curious about me, so even though I was new and an outsider, I felt a lot of warmth. There are also a lot of cultural events, arts, music and theater, happening in Nuuk so it was easy to attend and learn more about Greenland's culture.
top3_advice: 1. Book flights early before prices go up. 2. Find housing early, try to look at bus routes when you choose where to live. 3. Academics are only a small part of your time in Greenland, try to experience as much as you can while you're there, get outside and out of the city if possible.
other_useful_info: n/a
most_rewarding: Getting to experience the incredible nature of Greenland with new friends who are also interested in the Arctic.
greatest_challenge: I was pretty homesick for the first couple months, as it took me awhile to feel comfortable in my new community, even with a lot of new people around to be friends with.

There were 2-4 lectures about Drug design which were very interesting. Coursework for the course was modelling in program coot with x-ray data and NMR assignment in ccpnmr. crucial_aspects: The strong academic reputation of Imperial College London, the relevance of courses to my field, and the opportunity to gain international academic and professional experience in a leading research environment were the main factors
overall_comments: The exchange was academically very rewarding, but also extremely demanding. The workload at Imperial is intense, and combined with the high cost of living in London, it sometimes felt difficult to fully enjoy the city or have much free time. However, I learned a lot, grew academically, and made close friends, especially among other exchange students. Overall, I am very grateful for the experience and the opportunities it provided

arrival_assistance: There was an orientation programme that included a campus tour and meetings where we could ask questions, which was very helpful. The orientation took place about a week before courses started, giving enough time to settle in, get familiar with the campus, and organise practical matters. I did feel that there was relatively little information earlier in the process, but the support upon arrival itself was good.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

The workload at Imperial is intense, and combined with the high cost of living in London, it sometimes felt difficult to fully enjoy the city or have much free time. However, I learned a lot, grew academically, and made close friends, especially among other exchange students. Overall, I am very grateful for the experience and the opportunities it provided
registration_process: Before the semester, students receive a link where they can rank their course preferences (e.g. three priorities per slot). The allocation process worked smoothly, and it seemed likely to receive a first or second preference. After allocation, there is an opportunity to confirm or adjust selections if needed.
registration_help: Administrative staff and course coordinators were available via email and provided guidance throughout the process. Information was communicated clearly, and it was possible to ask questions if anything was unclear.
registration_success: I was allocated my first preferences initially, but I later had to change one course because it could not be approved as a limited elective by my home university. Overall, the system allowed flexibility to adjust, which was helpful.
registration_advice: Make sure to check in advance which courses can be pre-approved by your home university, as this can affect your final choices even if you receive your preferred allocation. Rank your priorities carefully and have backup options, as some students may not receive their first choice. Planning ahead and confirming eligibility early can make the process much smoother.
academics_comments: The exchange was academically very rewarding, but also extremely demanding. The workload at Imperial is intense, and combined with the high cost of living in London, it sometimes felt difficult to fully enjoy the city or have much free time. However, I learned a lot, grew academically, and made close friends, especially among other exchange students. Overall, I am very grateful for the experience and the opportunities it provided
course_level: The courses were academically demanding and required a high degree of independence. Much of the learning relied on self-directed reading beyond lectures, and students were expected to engage deeply with the literature. For “Advanced Topics” courses in particular, having a strong foundational background is important, as the material builds quickly on advanced concepts. There was also a significant amount of group work and presentations.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was more independent and research-oriented compared to UCPH. There was less structured guidance, and students were expected to take responsibility for identifying relevant reading and deepening their understanding outside of lectures. This encouraged critical thinking but could feel demanding, especially when adjusting to the expectations.
courses_enrolled: Advanced Topics in Infection and Immunity Advanced Topics in Parasitology and Vector Biology
recommended_courses: I would recommend the Advanced Topics courses for students who are interested in research and prepared for a challenging academic environment. They offer exposure to cutting-edge topics and encourage critical engagement with scientific literature. However, students should ensure they have sufficient background knowledge and be prepared for a significant workload.
unexpected_costs: Unexpected costs included higher-than-expected transport expenses, additional mobile data and SIM costs, and one-off setup costs such as purchasing household necessities (e.g. bedding, kitchen items). I also incurred visa-related fees (ETA), flights to travel home during the stay, and found that gym memberships (ca. 1000kr pr. month??) and everyday activities were significantly more expensive than anticipated. Overall, the cost of living in London was substantially higher than expected.
cost_comparison: Housing and transport were significantly more expensive than expected, and food costs were also high. Social activities and general day-to-day expenses in London added up quickly. Items such as gym memberships and basic services were noticeably costly. Overall, most aspects of living expenses were higher than anticipated.
activities_available: There were various student societies, cultural events, sports clubs, and social activities organised through the university and student union. Regular events and opportunities to get involved were communicated via email and student platforms
activities_recommended: I would recommend exploring student societies and social events early in the semester, as they seem like good opportunities to meet people and build community. Getting involved early may help balance academic commitments with social life.
weekend_recommendations: Take advantage of being in London by exploring museums, parks, and different neighbourhoods, many of which are free to visit. I would also highly recommend exploring the food scene, as London offers a wide variety of authentic and diverse cuisines from all over the world. Trying different restaurants can be a great cultural experience, especially if your budget allows. It is also worth travelling to other parts of the UK or nearby countries, as London is very well connected.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting was relatively straightforward, as I had visited London before and was familiar with the general environment. However, living and studying there felt more intense than visiting, especially due to the fast pace and busy atmosphere of a large city. Over time I adapted, but I did miss the quieter environment of Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: Many local students already have established social groups, especially in later years, so it can require some initiative to connect. I found it helpful to engage through group work or shared academic activities, but I also formed strong friendships with other exchange students who were in a similar situation.
cultural_challenges: The pace and intensity of daily life in London, including crowded public transport and a generally fast-moving environment, felt different from Copenhagen. The academic culture also placed strong emphasis on independence, which required adjustment.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated the diversity of cultures and perspectives at the university, with many international students from different backgrounds. It was inspiring to be in such a global academic environment and to learn from leading researchers.
top3_advice: Be prepared for a very high academic workload and a strong expectation of independent study. Plan finances carefully, as living costs in London are very high. Start planning housing and course approval early to reduce stress.
other_useful_info: The exchange is academically and professionally very rewarding, especially due to the strong reputation of Imperial and exposure to world-leading research. However, students should be prepared for a demanding environment and a fast-paced city, and consider how they prefer to balance academic and social life.
most_rewarding: The opportunity to study at a world-leading institution, learn from renowned researchers, and gain valuable academic experience that will be beneficial for my future career. It was also rewarding to build friendships with other international students.
greatest_challenge: Managing the high academic expectations alongside the practical and financial challenges of living in London, as well as adapting to a very busy and demanding environment.
other_comments: Overall, the experience was academically enriching and will be valuable for my future career. While the pace and workload were demanding, the exchange provided significant personal and professional growth.

institution: Institut d'Etudes Politique de Lyon (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: The language learning opportunity, the size of the city/amount of students, closeness to other interesting cities, access to interesting courses.
info_ease: Fairly easy. The hardest part was probably to make sure that all papers and descriptions were in check both with the home University and with the receiving university
arrival_assistance: well, there were a great team of international coordinators at Science Po who must have answered a ton of emails!
arrival_comments: It's a different system with grades, evaluation form, course election etc. But overall this was communicated fairly well
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I did a START course where everyone was introduced to the school at one big welcome meeting in late August. At the same time we were granted our student cards and informed on the important days and deadlines for sports activities, cafeteria, the international student organisation at the school and of course our courses
registration_help: The International student/mobility office on 2nd floor in the Science Po building was available at a decent amount of hours.
registration_success: It's very different from home and the deadline for making the final decision on whether you want a course of not is usually mid September. registration_advice: Don't stress when it comes to figure everything out the first week or even the first month. The French system is quite laissez-faire and some course descriptions might not drop before mid term. Also, just ask your fellow students ( and the WhatsApp chat), your professors and international coordinators about anything. really!
course_level: When it came to the day to day lessons I would argue that the level was lower than what I'm used to. However the evaluation could be tough and often required more detailed knowledge and exact facts that I'm used to. I'll say it was also a part of the learning experience to observe the different culture of academia and I found the switch quite refreshing really. In the end it's like at home - you get back what you give.
teaching_comparison: Less bigger lectures. More smaller classes. More group work and presentations from week to week. You were kept engaged throughout the semester.
courses_enrolled: Discourse on Borders, walls, nation and security. The Politics of Covid. EU Nuclear Independence. The politics of European Sanctions. Global Justice: an EU Perspective. Cities and aspects of globalization (additionally, a French speaking course 2h/week)
recommended_courses: The Borders course was truly amazing! Massimiliano is a extraordinary gust professor from Torino and I loved all of the classes - he's both really passionate and professional! If you like Foucault - this one is the most post-structuralist course they offer in English at least :))
unexpected_costs: Lost my passport. That's expensive when abroad - not recommended! Buying the wrong kind of ticket at the main station the first couple of time is a classic. Getting a subscription to their city bike system 'VeloV' is such a great idea! The city is very accessible on bike - and if you are a copenhagener you have the skills to manage the traffic in Lyon
cost_comparison: Food and housing is fairly expensive. Public transport and some trains were quite cheap!
activities_available: There are many after school clubs at science po to engage in. Band, Musical, community kitchen, different Fora. Besides that, the city is very much alive with Jazz Clubs, food festivals, cinema festival, Lights festival and a new event of the big place Bellecour every weekend. You just need one insider or local to tell you all the good spots.
activities_recommended: Jazz Club ' Hot club Lyon - super authentic, intimate setting and the jazz plus wine combination is a whole mood. Go to a few close by cities for hiking - especially around Saint Etienne there are some great mountain views. Cinemas, restaurants (Lyon is a gastronomical capital of France). A weekend- or day-trip to Annecy cause the lake and the mountain view is out of this world pretty! Make a tradition with other students! We had a pub quiz at Wallace Bar every Monday and it was the best way to start off a new week!
weekend_recommendations: Annecy, Saint tropez, Paris, Perrouges, saint-malo, Bourdeaux and Toulouse
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, it's France after all. It's a really good idea to speak the language or to learn at least some basics and then use them. They will not judge you as harshly if you at least try.
socializing_tips: Again, language! Also, have lunch with them - lunch is a big deal and usually is a couple of hours event.
cultural_challenges: Though I didn't experience this much personally - there is still some sexist remarks from people on the street. If you can and it's daylight - call them out on it or let is pass. Also, saying high to people that you meet on stairs, elevators in classrooms are just the rule. It's super rude to ignore people on your way. Danes are not the best at this so we can probably learn a trick or two #bekindplease
culture_appreciated: The French frankness. It seems to me that the French in general are less shy when it comes to conflict and announcing when something is wrong/intolerable. It really is refreshing to hit these issues right on (maybe instead of raging of Social Media later) they talk about things more openly and are not so afraid of admitting that the opinion they held a couple of minutes ago might not be the only version of the truth. I really like this part!
top3_advice: Take it easy and enjoy that you probably don't get every part of the French society and university system right away. See it as an opportunity to embrace a bit of chaos and work on your feet. It's a part of the exchange to face sudden challenges and changes as long as these don't stop you from doing exciting things, you'll be glad for them in the end. Make room in your budget for pivoting, sudden changes, spontaneous trips etc. And give yourself a rest day to catch up with yourself, deadlines, the mobility platform when you loose your sense of clarity.
most_rewarding: The people! I miss them so much !
greatest_challenge: Housing, making sure I was living up the the Erasmus requirements and getting all my ECTS in check. Pre-approval can be quite tought when they don't really do course descriptions before really late in France...

overall_comments: I thought the trip overall was good, but I still consider all the documentation work and communication between universities to very overcomplicated and a lot more time inefficient than it could have been. After all, I surely can't be the first student from Copenhagen to go to a French University, but it often felt that way.
info_ease: That part was pretty easy.
arrival_assistance: I received all the information I needed, I think.

course_level: I don't think the level at Sciences Po Lyon was impressive. The courses were rarely structured in a way that made sense or included academic work that endorsed analytic thinking. Some Professors seemed unprepared, did not take the time to make a bibliography, spent way too much time giving personal opinions or anecdotes, and were almost provoked by questions from the class.
teaching_comparison: It was a lot more tailored to the individual teacher instead of resembling certain minimum standards, which is what we are used to in UCPH. In Lyon, some teachers doesn't really care if no one in the class room understands what is going on, and they use academic research or data to support their sessions. It was actually quite striking even from the beginning. If you ask a question in class that is perfectly relevant to the topic of the class, some teachers will make a sarcastic remark to you and then just ignore you instead of approaching whatever question you have in a professional way. Also, it was in several occations completely impossible to figure out what the criteria for examination was, whereas in Copenhagen the Professors want to be able to test everyone on the same terms, so they make the examination method very easy to understand and then let the academic abilities count. An example of this is to avoid short 1 hour og 2 hour tests, or presentations.

recommended_courses: I would really recommend Persecution and Toleration. Frederic is a really good professor with great attention to historic details and the underlying social movements that has great relevance nowadays.
unexpected_costs: I planned pretty well, so I don't think that there were any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: I don't really think anything is more expensive than living in Copenhagen. I paid a monthly rent for apartment that was similar to danish prices, and there were no extra costs for studying.
activities_available: There were a lot, I just didn't go. I met a lot of friends in class and we had our own fun.
activities_recommended: Go out and speak to the locals. That is the best way to learn the culture and the language.
weekend_recommendations: Chamonix, Paris, Vienne, Dijon, Prapoutel for skiing.
culture_adjustment: I am not quite sure what you mean by exchange site.
socializing_tips: No because I was not too good at that either. I think one way to go, is to attend some of their community offers, and not just the exchange communites. So if they have a debat club, maybe try that out even if it is in French.
cultural_challenges: The only thing I found challenging was the academic procedures. I surprised to see how big of a difference there were from home. Especially in the demands the institution have for their professors. If the professor do not like you, it is your problem.
culture_appreciated: I really enjoyed the extent to which they nurture and embrace their own culture. They like to celebrate cultural happenings, they like to go out to eat, they like to spent a lot of money on art and they take pride in their work even if it's administration or service jobs... and then of course the food and the wine.
top3_advice: 1. Be very patient with all the bureaucracy. If it seems illogical at times, it is completely normal. You will have to do simple things such as fill in boxes or ask for a course description over and over, but it will work out in the end, and other students experience this too. 2. Make sure you don't fall into the Erasmus-trap. That is, only talking to international students. It is uncomfortable, but you have to actively search for French friends, if you want to get a real sense of their culture. They don't come to you, obviously. 3. Do a little research on the quarters of the city before you go. They are very different and it is hard to get a sense of it before you are there. So when looking for an apartment, maybe see if you can find something in Croix-Paquet, Croix-Rousse, the old city or Part Dieu. You can easily end up in a quarter far away from the nice places or in a neighboorhood that can seem uncomfortable for some, like Guillotierre.
other_useful_info: Not really.
most_rewarding: The amazing people from all over the world I had the chance to meet. It is invaluable.
greatest_challenge: All the documentation work
other_comments: Not really.

institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: I had already lived and worked in Paris before starting my studies at KU, so the exchange semester seemed like a perfect way to go back and reconnect with old friends and once again live in Paris. Another motivation was the academic opportunities. Sciences Po Paris is a highly renowned school with really good education. I had heard many good things about the place from friends in Paris before applying. And I was definitely not disappointed!
info_ease: Finding information on host universities websites can be very difficult in general. I do however think that the Sciences Po website is quite straightforward. There is a section about exchange programme where most information was available. The course catalogue is also available on the website in good time so you can look at classes before actually deciding to apply (there can be changes in the catalogue though, so you cannot be a hundred percent sure that a specific course will be offered in the final catalogue).
arrival_assistance: There was a Zoom meeting set up with an academic adviser in charge of the exchange programme when I arrived in Paris where we got pretty much all the information we needed and contact information on who to get in touch with if we had any issues. When the semester started we could pick up our student ID card in a tent set up in the rue saint-Guillaume garden (remember to finish your administrative registration on the student platform in due time!).
arrival_comments: I did not receive so much assistance, but I am sure it was available if I had needed it.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The course registration is quite straightforward, but you have to prepare for it in advance. The registration takes place on a first-come-first basis so you have to be ready when it opens. Prepare a prioritized list of courses and alternatives for each course. Remember to verify that they do not have conflicting time schedules.
registration_help: There are written guides on the Sciences Po website as well as videos guiding you through the registration process. You can also find videos on youtube. Watch these in advance to prepare yourself.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted, except for one that was not offered in the final catalogue.
registration_advice: Watch the video material on the Sciences Po website. Prepare a prioritized list of courses and alternatives. Especially if you have specific courses that are important to you. Do not hesitate to write professors if you have questions about the content of courses or about pre-requisites.
course_level: The academic level was, in my opinion, not that high compared to what I am used to at KU. But the courses are livelier and more intensive. There are a lot of presentations/exposés that you have to prepare throughout the semester as well as smaller assignments that you hand in. There are fewer and less heavy readings, but the workload is still higher because you have to prepare a lot of things during the semester.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style is quite different from KU. The classes are often much smaller and much more active participation is expected from the student. In many classes participation is a part of the grade. I had to get used to this style of teaching at first, but I ended up really liking it. The classes become more dynamic and livelier. There are more in-class discussions, and you get a closer relation to your professor and to your fellow students. As there are not too many readings, you have more time to discuss them in-depth in class. Because the assessment take place through-out the entire semester (presentations, assignments, mid-terms, participation etc.) you are not as stressed out in the final exam period.
courses_enrolled: Behavioral Game Theory (DECO 25A02) European integration and its challenges: the euro, migration and populism (DSPO 25A02) Economic Sociology (DSOC 25A01) Big Data et sciences sociales (CSOC 25F06) Espace Mondial (ASPO 25F00)
recommended_courses: Big Data et sciences sociales was amazingly interesting. I deeply recommend the course if you are interested in quantitative methods in social science. The course is interdisciplinary (it draws on Sociology, Economics, History and Philosophy of Science) and it is taught by two young professors who are really passionate about the course. The atmosphere was really nice and relaxed and the course was filled with interesting discussions. It is taught in French, but you can write exams and participate orally in English if you would like. The EU course was also very good. The workload was quite big, but I learned so much. Espace Mondial (international relations, international economy and political sociology etc.) was also very interesting. The class is divided into a main lecture (in French) and smaller class sessions that you can take in English. All of the courses I took were really good! The professors were highly engaged and there was a very nice atmosphere in the classroom.
unexpected_costs: Covid-tests are not free if you do not have a carte vitale (French health insurance card). Antigen tests cost 25€ and can be taken at pharmacies.
cost_comparison: I bought a subscription for the city bike system (Vélib) which was really cheap. Only 2,9€ per month (although you have to commit to a full year). I would recommend this.
activities_available: I am not really sure as I did not really participate. I know that some other exchange students went to social activities such as guided city tours, Erasmus parties and social events etc.
activities_recommended: Go out and meet new people, talk to strangers at cafés and bars and enjoy parisian joie de vivre. Try to learn French - life in Paris is so much more interesting if you speak French, even if it is just a little. Sciences Po is very intensive and school can easily take up a lot of your time – remember to enjoy life in Paris as well while you are there!
weekend_recommendations: Visit all the different neighborhoods in Paris. They are all so different. Go to cafés and to restaurants to eat out a lot. It is generally a lot cheaper than in Copenhagen. If you climb, go to Fontainebleau or Viaduc des Fauvettes just outside of Paris!
culture_adjustment: Very easy, because I had already lived in Paris before. But also because the culture is not that different from in Denmark.
socializing_tips: Take a Lecture course (10 ECTS) instead of only seminar courses (5 ECTS) – local Sciences Po students are required to have Lecture courses. Do not be afraid to take classes in the evening. I had three courses taking place from 19.15 to 21.15. This was a nice occasion to go out to eat or have a drink after class with my classmates.
cultural_challenges: French bureaucracy can be a bit much and some administrative processes can seem impossible or paradoxical. But from my experience the system often turns out quite flexible when you actually talk to people. Call or write people at Sciences Po if you have any issues. I could not for example get results from my French test in due time to document my French level, but I was able to take courses in French anyway after I talked to them.
culture_appreciated: The culture of going to cafés more often and eating out at restaurants a lot. Going out in the evening for a glass of wine. I enjoyed this so much.
top3_advice: 1. Prepare yourself for course registration day. Have a list of courses ready, make a plan. Especially if you have courses that you really want to take. 2.
