institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: The fact that the destination had courses in English, which would also be able to be pre-approved by University of Copenhagen (UCPH). Since I went on exchange during the 5th semester of my bachelor, finding courses that could substitute Dansk og Komparativ Politik 3 and Europæisk politik wasn't easy. Also, I love France and the French language, so I saw this as an opportunity to improve my French language skills and get a French perspective on politics.
info_ease: The welcome program was online due to Covid so it was not too informing, but the Premiere Cycle Echange people are really good at answering any questions via email (unless they're on vacation, which they were almost all of August).
arrival_assistance: Not a lot. I had to seek information and guidance on my own most of the time.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The administration sends out the final course catalogue and a guide for the registration. The registration opens (usually at around 16h and closes some time next day). Throughout the course registration period, some students will drop courses, so if you don't get your first priorities right away, keep checking throughout the registration period because spots might open up. It was very stressful, especially because I needed to register for certain courses that would substitute the obligatory courses I was supposed to have back home at UCPH. I suggest being in touch with the Premier Cycle Echange people weeks in advance. They should send you the list of courses that they expect to offer when you're going on exchange, however, the course list can be subject to change (as late as days before the registration). This happened to me. One of my “obligatory” courses were suddenly not on the course list, so I had to find a new course and send a new pre-approval application to UCPH (who were on vacation and didn't approve it until the first week of August - and by that time Sciences Po had gone on vacation). The course registration is open for about 24 hours and I definitely suggest sitting ready when the registration opens because the courses are filling up fast. I also suggest preparing a list of at least 5 other courses, that you can choose if your first priorities are filled up.
registration_help: Again, the Premier Cycle Echange people were ready to answer any question I had about course registration. But they don't answer any questions during the registration period - during the registration, you're on your own.
registration_success: After the whole situation with the course, that suddenly wasn't on the course list, and after finding a new course to substitute that, I got all my first priority-courses. I was also ready by the computer when the registration opened, which I think is the best advice I can give anyone who is going to Sciences Po. Also, use the search function on your computer to search for your courses on the list, because there are a lot of courses.
registration_advice: Prepare a list of courses, be ready when the registration opens, prepare yourself for the possibility that you wont get all the courses you want, and finally, be prepared to send more than one pre-approval to UCPH.
course_level: The courses at Sciences Po were a lot more practical than theoretical, compared to the courses at UCPH. There was a lot more work at Sciences Po throughout the semester and the type of assignments varied a lot - I had to do presentations, research papers, essays, handwritten exams, news analysis etc. A big recommendation is to start on your assignment as early as possible because by the end of the semester there is a lot of work to do, and it can be very stressful the last couple of weeks.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching varied from course to course. In some courses the teaching style was more based on class discussion, whereas in other courses the teacher spoke for 2 hours and then the students just listened and took notes. There is really no way you can know what teaching style each teacher has until you take the course (course description doesn't say).
courses_enrolled: European Integration and its Challenges (5 ECTS) - was approved by UCPH as Europæisk Politik The Decision-Making Process of the European Union - an Insider's View (5 ECTS) - was approved by UCPH as Europæisk Politik Comparative Politics (10 ECTS) - was approved by UCPH as Dansk og Komparativ Politik 3 Citizen Politics and Democracy in Times of Crisis (5 ECTS) International Conflicts (5 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I can definitely recommend International Conflicts with Jean-Yves Haine. Even though it's mostly him that talks during the class, he is so knowledgeable about the subject and I found that the 2 hours ran by. If you like IR like me, then you will love this course.
unexpected_costs: I didn't experience any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: The coffee - a latte usually costs 4,5 or 5 euros. Most things in Paris are expensive - especially the cafés and restaurants near Sciences Po. However, it is (usually) cheaper to eat at restaurants than in Copenhagen.
activities_available: Sciences Po has a lot of athletic and cultural activities that you can even get ECTS for - I however wasn't able to join any, because I could register for max 30 ECTS, and all my ECTS had to be related to political science courses. A lot of the other exchange students from other countries participated in these activities, but they could also choose more freely from the courses.
activities_recommended: I didn't partake in any, unfortunately.
weekend_recommendations: The museums, the monuments, take a walk along the Seine - or really anywhere in Paris. Walking is the best was to see and discover new places. The Louis Vuitton Foundation had a great exhibition when I was in Paris. L'Orangerie (free if you're under 26 but you need to book a ticket in advance) and Musée d'Orsay (free if you're under 26) is also great museums and a lot smaller than Louvre (also free) , so you can see all of it in one day.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy - people are very nice and the other exchange students are also very eager to get to know you, so as long as you're open to talk to new people, you'll be fine. The international students and the “local” students at Sciences Po doesn't really socialize with each other though - there's very much “two communities”.
socializing_tips: In terms of socializing with the other international students, just strike up a conversation with the person sitting next to you in class. Don't be afraid to talk to the people in your class, because almost everyone is just like you and doesn't have any friends yet. In terms of the local students, I don't really have the answer to that, other than to take courses in French. All the courses in English are mostly filled with international exchange students, while the courses in French are mostly filled with local Sciences Po students. You can also get a “buddy” when you arrive (a buddy is a local Sciences Po student, but I haven't had one myself).
cultural_challenges: Many local French people don't speak English. Knowing a little French can get you a long way.
culture_appreciated: (Most of) the people are really nice and helpful.
top3_advice: 1. The process isn't as easy as UCPH makes it seem. The most challenging thing for me was getting my courses pre-approved and finding courses that could potentially get pre-approved. Even though the process is long, stressful and difficult, I highly recommend going. It is so worth it. Looking back, all the challenges only made me stronger. 2. Be prepared for a lot of work. It is not going to be 4 months vacation - if anything it's going to be the hardest (but best semester) of your bachelor. Start on your assignments as soon as possible, but remember to enjoy the city and your stay (you only need to pass) 3. Be open. If you have that approach, you will make friends easier, do more things out of your comfort zone and develop, both academically and socially.
other_useful_info: There is a lot of information on Sciences Po's website, but it can be a bit difficult to find. Write to Premier Cycle Echange for any questions.
most_rewarding: Meeting amazing people, exploring Paris and trying a whole new way of studying at university.
greatest_challenge: Balancing studying and free time.

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It is based on a first come first serve principle. Everyone sits ready by the computer when courses become available and quickly pick courses. A very hectic process.
registration_help: The Erasmus coordinator explains the procedure.
registration_success: I was lucky that I got courses in my top 10.
registration_advice: Prepare a long list of courses you would like as the other students get priority - exchange students gets whats left, so some may be unavailable by the time it is opened up for exchange students. Check when the course is held as some are on Saturdays.
course_level: It really depended on the course. Some were high level, while others (especially the formation commune classes) were more like a BA introductory course.
teaching_comparison: There is much more focus on participation - presentations and class discussions. Your grade also depends partially on it.

unexpected_costs: Thing for the kitchen as the student residency's kitchen was poorly equipped.

activities_recommended: I didn't take any, so I don't know.

culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: I mostly hung out with international students. Local students already have a network.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier. I was surprised by how many people didn't speak english.
culture_appreciated: The café culture, brasseries and wine.
top3_advice: Practice a bit of french beforehand, explore France and enjoy Paris.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: Meeting many interesting people from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Learning french.

It didn't hurt that it is also a reputable university. overall_comments: Overall, I have been very satisfied with my study abroad experience. Four out of five courses have been interesting, my professors have been knowledgeable and passionate about their subjects, and most of my fellow students have been prepared for class and willing to contribute to class discussions by asking relevant questions and sharing their thoughts, opinions, and insights. arrival_comments: N/A
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall, I have been very satisfied with my study abroad experience. Four out of five courses have been interesting, my professors have been knowledgeable and passionate about their subjects, and most of my fellow students have been prepared for class and willing to contribute to class discussions by asking relevant questions and sharing their thoughts, opinions, and insights. registration_process: Again, I cannot recall all the steps. I remember the process as being rather time consuming and not something that could be completed in one go.
registration_help: It was possible to contact a help desk and/or Erasmus coordinator who were able to assist with the registration process.
registration_success: Not successful at all. I had a list of about 20 courses I was interested in and ended up with just one of them. This despite being ready the moment course registration opened. It was quite frustrating at the time, but luckily I ended up being satisfied with most of my courses.
registration_advice: Look into which courses are offered well in advance and prepare a list of the ones you're interested in. Make sure there are no timetable clashes and prepare yourself for the likely possibility that you will still have to be flexible and sign up for other courses once course registration opens. Try to maintain a positive mindset. At PSIA it is possible to add/drop courses the first week of the semester.

unexpected_costs: N/A
cost_comparison: Transportation was less expensive than I expected. Food on the other hand can be quite expensive, although cheap alternatives exist as well (e.g. lunch/dinner at CROUS).
activities_available: I can't recall since I didn't attend any of them (aside from 2-3 events with guest speakers).
activities_recommended: Surely that depends on the individual. Look at the opportunities you have and give some of them a go if you feel so inclined.
weekend_recommendations: I used nearly all my weekends in Paris. There is so much to see and do (museums, concerts, the restaurant scene, the nightlife, the architecture, markets etc.) – either with new friends or visitors from back home. I would however also recommend exploring different parts of France if you have the time.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Just approach people from the get-go. Talk to other students in the break. Most are extremely friendly and open to go grab a beer or coffee after class depending on the time.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Parisians know how to spend their free time in optimal ways and the city is always buzzing with life. Make the most of it.
top3_advice: 1) Start working on your midterms and final essays early. Otherwise, you will quickly become too overwhelmed. 2) Professors encourage you to reach out with any question you might have regarding the course or your assignments. It's highly recommendable to take them up on their offer. 3) Take your studies seriously but don't forget to enjoy your free time! You're in Paris. Take advantage of that.
other_useful_info: Nothing I can think of.
most_rewarding: The whole experience. Getting to live in Paris with interesting people from all over the world and attending a great university.
greatest_challenge: I was slightly overwhelmed with the workload at the end of the semester. It was frustrating having to study all the time without being able to take advantage of my last weeks in Paris. Therefore, I cannot stress this enough: start early on your final assignments.
other_comments: N/A

institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: I found both the city and the university interesting, and both things lived up the expectations :)
info_ease: Not very easy of various reasons 1) a lot of information was in french, 2) it was difficult knowing who to contact for help, both at UCPH and SciencesPo.
arrival_assistance: When I arrived I received a lot of help from SciencesPo and the process of getting into courses were more relaxed than in Denmark; it is okay to start a course and then change during the first weeks. There were also an introduction week where people were very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Everything went fine. I did have one problem: I took a language test that cost money, and found out later that I didn't have to do it anyway because I was from Denmark - even though it said so on SciencesPo and UCPH's website. So save your money :) !
registration_help: The administrative help of both UCPH and SciencesPo have been confusing, but there wasn't a lot of problems since I arrived at the university, as it was easier just to ask the administration in person, and then they are helpful.
registration_success: It wasn't difficult to get the courses I was interested in. There is a registration process before arriving that is confusing. But after I arrived I was admitted to most of my courses by asking the teacher if it's okay if you take the course and then beeing admitted by the administration. So don't worry if you don't get the courses you wanted on the day of course registration! Lots of people change courses within the first weeks.
registration_advice: Even though it seems stressful, don't worry, there are lots of interesting courses. The course registration website is confusing, and people sit ready with a list of courses they are interested in. So I can recommend doing the same and do some research before on what courses you are interested in, and then try to register for them as fast as possible when registration begins. But if you don't succeed (I didn't) it's often possible to enroll in them at a later time after your arrival.
course_level: The level was a bit higher than UCPH. The teachers have higher expectations to the students and the workload is higher regarding reading for the classes, class participation, exams and presentations. But the other students are also very engaged and passionate, which is inspiring :)
teaching_comparison: There are smaller classes, so each student have more time with the teacher. I resembles more the teaching style of gymnasium in Denmark. It is expected to a larger degree that the student participate a lot in class with presentations eg. And they also mark if you come to classes or not, and you fail the class if you consecutively don't show up to classes without a valid reason, which is something I had to get used to! They are however helpful/understanding if you get sick.
courses_enrolled: - Sociology of Inequalities - Causal Analysis in Sociology - Quantitative Methods I - Demography: Challenges and Policy Implications - Sociology of Migration - Francais Niveau A2
recommended_courses: Sociology of Inequalities, Causal Analysis and french (or other language) classes if you can get it transferred :)
unexpected_costs: I didn't visit other french cities as train tickets were more expensive than i thought. So if you want to travel around during your breaks or weekends be sure to put some money aside, so it's possible :) !
cost_comparison: The Navigo card is 75 € which is cheap in the light that you can travel freely in all of Île de France. Groceries are a bit cheaper than in Copenhagen and so was restaurants, bars, cafés, concerts, cinemas etc.
activities_available: There were many social activities at SciencesPo and many students participate in them. There is a rich student life. There are however fewer parties and no 'fredagsbar'/alcohol on campus.
activities_recommended: I can recommend coming to the welcome week where you can meet other exchange students and also to register for sports, art classes etc. to meet people outside of your classes.
weekend_recommendations: There are many things to see in Paris, it's a very big city! I spent many days/weekends walking in the different areas, visiting museums, parks, stores etc. My experience was that the semester went by very fast and there was still lots of things to see towards the end :)
culture_adjustment: It was easy, there are small differences from Denmark, but all in all the culture is somewhat similar. The language barrier was the most difficult, many french people are not good in english, especially older people, so I can recommend practising some french before going on the exchange. Apart from that people are very open and sociable!
socializing_tips: Participate in activities hosted by SciencesPo and register for eg a sports team or art/language classes. People were generally very nice and open.
cultural_challenges: Language barriers was by far the most difficult. The administrative process were more relaxed which could be an issue when being used to the Danish way of doing it; In Denmark you register for courses the semester before and there is no way of changing it while at SciencesPo it was unclear which courses were available until just before the semester started and people were changing classes a lot.
culture_appreciated: People were very open and friendly :) The food is very good, the city is very beautiful and the weather is slightly better than in Denmark
top3_advice: Register for the introduction week, remember to socialize even though there is a lot of work during the semester and take french classes
other_useful_info: You don't need to take an english test/certificate!
most_rewarding: The classes were very interesting and i met a lot of nice people
greatest_challenge: I am not used to doing presentations in front of other students in English, so I found it challenging to do it. But it was required for me to do it multiple times through the semester, both in French and English, so I got gradually more comfortable with it, and today I am happy i did it :)

institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: I chose Paris because I like the city and I wanted to try to live in it for a longer time. I have family and friends living there, which also played an important role, and I had heard good things about Sciences Po.
overall_comments: I really enjoyed the exchange. I experienced so much in those 3,5 months and met a lot of people. Going on exchange has been something I wanted to do for a long time, and I think it gave me a lot and made me grow. The most difficult thing for me was to relax. Since the exchange was only 3,5 months, I always felt like I wanted to get the most out of it.
info_ease: It was not that difficult.
arrival_assistance: Not much, but I didn't need much assistance.
arrival_comments: I don't really know, since I didn't participate in the introduction week. I guess most of the orientation and assistance was given there.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I really enjoyed the exchange. I experienced so much in those 3,5 months and met a lot of people. Going on exchange has been something I wanted to do for a long time, and I think it gave me a lot and made me grow. The most difficult thing for me was to relax. Since the exchange was only 3,5 months, I always felt like I wanted to get the most out of it.
registration_process: As far as I remember it takes some time, but it is doable.
registration_help: I don't really remember.
registration_success: The class registration was very stressful. It works on the first come first served principle, so you need to be ready and prepared when the registration opens.
registration_advice: Before the registration, I definitely recommend writing a list of all the courses you are interested in (and 3-5 alternatives for each in case you don't get your first priorities). When the registration opens, make sure to register for your mandatory classes (if any) as the first ones, because they can be filled up in a few minutes. I didn't succeed in getting all the courses I wanted even though I was well-prepared and fast. If a course is full, you can try to refresh the website for some minutes, and if you are lucky there will be a free place later on.
academics_comments: I really enjoyed the exchange. I experienced so much in those 3,5 months and met a lot of people. Going on exchange has been something I wanted to do for a long time, and I think it gave me a lot and made me grow. The most difficult thing for me was to relax. Since the exchange was only 3,5 months, I always felt like I wanted to get the most out of it.
course_level: It depends on the specific course. In general, I think the courses at Sciences Po were less academic and theoretical and more focused on facts. In all of my courses, the teachers made sure to make a good introduction in order to give everyone the same base. During the semester you will have to prepare several presentations and do some assignments, but the amount of reading is less than at Copenhagen University, so I wouldn't say the workload was bigger at Sciences Po. At the end of the semester, there are fewer big exams than at KU, so for me, it felt more chill than at KU in general.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is very different from the one at Copenhagen University. You get more evaluated during the semester and there are fewer exams. In many of my classes, I had to do presentations and assignments during the semester and I only had a small Q&A at the end of the semester (and not a real exam). The system reminds me a bit of Danish high schools in that way. It is mandatory to attend the classes. I got the impression that there are fewer big lectures and more teaching in small classes of 20-30 people.
courses_enrolled: Comparative Politics (ASPO 25A11) European Integration and its Challenges (DSPO 25A02) Europe in the World Economy (DECO 25A03) The Age of Economists (DECO 25A05) L'économie au Défi du Genre (CECO 25F01)
recommended_courses: I can recommend L'économie au Défi du Genre (CECO 25F01). That was definitely my favorite class. The teacher (Helene Perivier) is very good: She knows a lot about the subject, is very motivated, and has done some interesting work/papers. Be aware that it is in french.
unexpected_costs: It was more expensive to go out than I thought. Especially if you want to go to nightclubs, many of them cost around 20 euros for the entrance. But you can definitely find a lot of cheaper (and less known) and great places to go out!
cost_comparison: More expensive than expected: clubs, drinks/beers at bars, public transportation, supermarkets. Less expensive than expected: books (for most of the classes, you don't need to buy any books), bike rental, the cafeteria at Sciences Po:-) If you get around by public transportation it can be worth it to buy a Navigo pass. But If you don't want to spend 80 euros per month on transportation, I would recommend registering for a Velib pass. You pay either 3,10 euros per month (for only non-electric bikes) or 8,30 euros per month (including electric bikes) for unlimited use of bikes (and there are a lot of stations all around the city). That is what I did, and I really enjoyed biking around the city, which is also often faster than taking the metro.
activities_available: There were a lot of activities available at Sciences Po. They have a lot of associations, and they also offer many sport activities for a cheap price. If you want to register for a sport activity, you need to keep updated on when the registration opens and to be ready to register when it opens, since the activities get booked very fast.
activities_recommended: I didn't register for any of the activities at Sciences Po, but I heard that many of the sports were great and also the cinema association.
weekend_recommendations: Museums! Paris has a lot of amazing museums, and if you are under 26, many of them are free! I personally like the north of Paris: the 9th, 10th, 11th, and 18th arrondissements are my favorite ones: A lot of bars and places to go out, and cheaper than the arrondissements around Sciences Po.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy. Sciences Po is a very international school with a lot of other exchange students, so you don't feel like you have to adapt to a specific french culture at school.
socializing_tips: Try to do some of the group work with french people from your class - that's how I made french friends at Sciences Po. Else, I think being part of an association or doing a sport at Sciences Po is a good way to meet local students.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find many cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: The late lifestyle. The French people I met and lived with had another rhythm than many Danes. Fx eating lunch and dinner way later than in Denmark. The food seems more important in France. People gather more for dinner or lunch, and it is easy to find good and cheap food in many places. The nightlife. First, I was a bit disappointed about the clubs (and the expensive entrance). But there are so many smaller clubs/bars that have events and concerts almost every night. Also, people, in general, seem to get less drunk than in Denmark when going out, and I appreciated getting used to going out without being completely wasted.
top3_advice: Try to find a balance between studying and exploring/enjoying the city and life in Paris. Don't stress too much about meeting people in the beginning. You can easily meet new people after the first weeks as well, so remember to take a rest sometimes. Even though it at first can seem expensive to go out, that shouldn't hold you back. You can find a lot of cheaper places if you search a bit (especially in the north of Paris).
other_useful_info: Be prepared for another way of teaching and evaluating students. In the beginning, it might be a bit overwhelming to have to do so many presentations, but remember that on the other hand, you will have fewer big exams and less reading.
most_rewarding: The people I met and the relationships I got. Also, it was the first time I lived abroad on my own, and I learned a lot about myself from this experience. I think it made me more open and confident in general.
greatest_challenge: For me, the biggest challenge was my FOMO. There were always people wanting to go out, and in Paris, there is always a nice event you can attend. Since I was only there for a short time, I felt like I didn't want to miss anything. Next time I would be more aware of taking time to relax.

institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: The most important aspect was that Sciences Po offered courses that were able to replace my mandatory courses (Dansk og komparativ politik 3 and Europæisk politik). Another crucial aspect was that Sciences Po is the third best university in the world for politics (following Harvard and Oxford).
info_ease: Very easy! The staff in the reception does not speak English but just check your email or ask other students if you need help.
arrival_assistance: Not much. You can sign up for a 'buddy' (and be paired with another Sciences Po student) but I chose not to. I also did not sign up for the introduction week because you had to pay to attend. There were some free activities (such as tours of the campus and library, presentations of student clubs/associations, etc.) but I had covid that week and did not go. Therefore, I had to just show up for my lessons the following week without knowing my way around campus but I asked random students for directions and everything worked out.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You register online about a month before the semester starts. I was in Chicago and the time difference meant that I had to get up really early, as it is first come first serve and you have to be ready when registration opens. A lot of courses filled immediately and my screen froze multiple times. I had a lot of technical issues and it was very stressful! All the error codes were written in French, and overall, it was just not a good experience at all. If this happens to you, take screen shots so you can prove that you had technical issues.
registration_help: I emailed IT multiple times. They replied quickly.
registration_success: At first I could not get the courses that I needed for Europæisk politik at home as they had all filled up in a matter of minutes. I recommend waiting around for a little while if this happens to you because eventually a spot opened up for one of the courses I needed and I quickly registered for that one. I still needed one more mandatory course, and I chose to register for a random course that had 'Europe' in the title. It had not been pre-approved by my home university so it was very risky but I did not have any other options. I immediately sent an application to KU but they spent more than the promised five or six weeks to approve the course. I called and emailed KU multiple times and had to attend my first lesson of the course without knowing whether it had been approved. Eventually, however, it worked out and they approved the course. As for my elective courses, the two that I had wanted to take and that had already been approved by KU were either full or removed from this year's course list. Therefore, I ended up choosing two random courses that seemed somewhat interesting and did not clash with my other lessons. They were eventually approved without any issues (but only after the semester had started because KU was so slooooooow).
registration_advice: Get as many courses pre approved as possible. Don't just apply for the minimum amount of courses that you need because you may not be able to register for them and in that case it is good to have some backup options.
course_level: The teaching was definitely less research based compared to KU. There were nearly no readings and I only had one lecture a week. The others were seminars where you're expected to actively participate and sometimes make presentations. Overall, Sciences Po was more practical and less theoretical compared to KU. The final exams did not draw on the readings but rather on what your teacher had told you in class.
teaching_comparison: It felt more like high school than university. There are lots of small assignments such as presentations and creative writing exercises. In some classes you are also graded based on your participation. All of these assignments weigh differently and contribute to your final grade. We also had a lot of multiple choice exams. Most exams were pen and paper and closed book. The advantage is that it is easier to predict what grade you end up with and that it is a more active learning style. The disadvantage is that it feels less academic.
courses_enrolled: Nation and nationalism: several approaches to basic concepts (5 ECTS - elective) Technology, war and politics (5 ECTS - elective - do not recommend) EU integration and its challenges (5 ECTS - Europæisk politik) Social policies in Europe (5 ECTS - Europæisk politik - highly recommend) Comparative politics (10 ECTS - Dansk og komparativ politik 3)
recommended_courses: Social policies in Europe. The professor is highly knowledgable and great at drawing comparisons between different welfare models. The course is very historical and one of the more academic ones I took.
unexpected_costs: I don't recall any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Housing was really expensive. There were no books which was unexpected so no expenses there. You can definitely spend less money on food, I just really liked going out to eat at really amazing French restaurants.
activities_available: They had some sport clubs but you needed a doctor's notice (even for yoga) so I did not participate
activities_recommended: I did not participate in any. Paris is such a great city so my activities consisted of going on long walks and visiting museums (most of them are free), bars and restaurants. I was really busy with that so I did not need to sign up for anything via Sciences Po.
weekend_recommendations: See above. Please just take advantage of the fact that you'll be living in one of the best cities in the world. There are endless things to see and do
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Some people say they don't speak English but if you're patient and creative you'll be able to communicate just fine.
socializing_tips: I exclusively hung out with other international exchange students. I really enjoyed that because I love being part of international communities.
cultural_challenges: The French are rude. There is not much you can do about it.
culture_appreciated: Food, art and wine
top3_advice: 1. The university is fine although not super academic 2. Going on exchange (anywhere) is amazing and I highly recommend doing so 3. Make sure to have a lot of potential courses pre-approved
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of
most_rewarding: My social life. I met so many wonderful people from all over the world. Everyone is very open and quite spontaneous as they do not really have many other responsibilities. Everyone is very keen on making friends and having a good experience studying abroad.
greatest_challenge: 1. Being ill. I sadly had to deal with a lot of illness which was exhausting and quite lonely (especially in the beginning). 2. Housing. Moving twice was hard

crucial_aspects: 1. "Adventure": I found Paris to be a very exciting city to live in, where I could practice my french and get to live in an iconic capital with many cultural offers like museums, restaurants, music etc. 1. "Academic opportunity": SciencesPo Paris is a great university for political science, so that also played a very important role for me when i choose my study destination
info_ease: It was very easy. I think the university send out a lot of e-mails in advance and their student website was okay easy to navigate
arrival_assistance: The university had arranged a welcome week program, which was great both as a pratical introduction (where is the campus, how does the printer work etc.), as an academic introduction (how to write assignments at SciencesPo) and as a social introduction (meet french students and exchange students)
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: A few weeks in advance we were given information on how to register. However, as an exchange student our registration opened later than registration for "normal" students, which meant we could only choose between "left over" courses/there were very few spots available, which I think was a shame. Further, it was very stressful because the registration was based on a "first come - first served" base. Personally, I think making a priority list of courses works better.
registration_help: There was a zoom presentation one could join + information on e-mail, which got send out in advance of the registration
registration_success: I didn't get any of the classes I wanted. Each time I clicked on a class to register I realized it was full, and in the mean time the other classes I wanted also got filled up.
registration_advice: Be very fast with registration and have a plan a-z, because you can't at all count on getting the classes you want
course_level: I think the level was very fitting
teaching_comparison: It was in general very similar to the style of teaching at UCPH. The classes consisted of app. 20-30 students and had an open environment for debate, while the lectures of app. 200-300 students were very similar to those of UCPH, where the communication is more top-down with the prof lecturing and less interaction. However, a difference I noticed was that the students seemed to get a bigger say in the smaller classes than they do a UCPH - e.g., in two of my classes the students had a say in the exam format, when deadlines were set etc., which I think is more set from the beginning at UCPH
courses_enrolled: 1. GENDER, SOCIETIES AND ECONOMICS 2. CHINESE POLITICAL CULTURE THROUGH HISTORY: AN ECOLOGICAL PERSPECTIVE 3. GENDER AND REVOLUTIONARY SITUATIONS IN THE MIDDLE EAST 4. DISCRIMINATION AND INEQUALITY IN COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVES: THEORIES, EVIDENCE AND POLICIES 5. THE SYRIAN CRISIS AND ITS CONSEQUENCES FOR EUROPE AND THE MIDDLE EAST (2011-2023)
recommended_courses: I really liked the course on the Syrian Crisis and its consequences. I liked it for three main reasons: 1) It was super well structured starting from the Ottoman Empire up untill today, 2) It dealt with several aspects of the crisis - e.g., the international aspect, the refugee aspect and the domestic aspect and 3) The teacher had a great deal of knowledge on the topic and was very engaged in the course.
unexpected_costs: I didn't really experience any unexpected costs
cost_comparison: I found the supermarkets to more expensive than I had expected + going out (e.g., buying beer, wine, entrance to nightclubs etc)
activities_available: There was a lot! There was so many associations that I can't even list them all, but the activities ranged from parties, wine tastings and interesting talks to going to sports like dance, tennis, soccer etc.
activities_recommended: I really enjoyed going to interesting talks with prominent politicians, academics or people working in the field (e.g., NGOs, UN institutions etc). I thought is was a super nice way to arrange an interesting night. Often I combined it with going out to dinner with friends, so it was a nice way to gather around a common interlecual interest
weekend_recommendations: There is a lot of fun stuff to do in Paris during weekends and holidays. During weekends I loved visiting museums (both the popular ones like Louvre, d'Orsay etc, but also less famous ones like l'Orangerie, Petit Palais and Rodin). Further, there is a lot of nice restaurants, open air markets etc, which is also nice to do in a weekend, and finally its wonderfull just to take a stroll in the many amazing Paris districts - my favorite is probably the 10th arrondissement! On holidays I will recommend maybe going out of the city - the TGV trains are super fast and well connected to nice cities in France. I did a hike in the Normandy from the city of Fécamp til Ètretat that I can really recommend.
culture_adjustment: I found it very easy, but I think that France and Denmark is also very much a like, so that wasn't a big problem.
socializing_tips: "Unfortunately" I mainly socialized with other exchange students living in the Cité Universitaire like me. Hence I don't have any great tips on making local friends, but it was still an amazing experience getting to know other exchange students from a wide range of countries.
cultural_challenges: I didn't really find any cultural differences challenging, but of course language was sometimes a barrier, even though I found that Parisians spoke better english than what people normally say
culture_appreciated: I just love the french food- and going out culture.
top3_advice: 1. Prepare for a big workload. You often hear that exchange is "easy" in terms of workload, but that is not at all my experience. I found the academic level very high, and had a lot of assignments during the semester, but on the postive side, I had a shorter exam period in the end, because I had handed in a lot of papers during the semester. 2. Be fast with course registration! The courses fill up quickly 3. Don't be afraid to engage in the courses. The courses a very much based on student participation, so it is very rewarding to participate actively in the classes
other_useful_info: I you want to apply for french language courses at the university be aware that the level (in my opinion) is very high. I took one class in french level B1, and found that that level was higher than what I had expected
most_rewarding: Getting to know a lot of amazing fellow exchange students and trying to live in such a wonderful city as Paris
greatest_challenge: Balancing workload+wanting to do good in school, while at the same time allowing yourself to also spend time on seeing Paris and take the time off to do that
other_comments: No

institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: It was more than crucial to find a study destination with the perfect intersection between academic opportunities and fascinating culture/city. As I already spoke a little French before arriving, I found that Paris and Sciences Po was the perfect match for me.
info_ease: I must say that I found the process very demanding and for the most of the time you're left alone as a student. However, after the formel submission and application to Sciences Po, the process went smooth.
arrival_assistance: I received the necessary information by e-mail.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had a number of opportunities available at 4 pm. When clock reached exactly 4, you had to choose your preferred courses. However, you had to prioritize your time as they did it by first come, first serve.
registration_help: Informational videos.
registration_success: I had two courses that I wasn't able to get, but I was satisfied overall.
registration_advice: Take your time to prioritize the courses before 4 pm. Make a plan for what you will choose if some courses aren't available.
course_level: The academic level at Sciences Po in itself is not higher than in UCPH. However, the work load is out of this world with assessment to be done every 3-4 days during the 4 months. I ended up having 18 assessments throughout the year.
teaching_comparison: At Sciences Po we had smaller lectures with more interaction with the teachers. That was something that reminded me of High School and it served to be very beneficial.
courses_enrolled: European Disintegration Population Aging and Pensions Middle Eastern & Northern African Politics History of Capitalism Inclusion of Migrants through Social Innovation Global Social Policies French classes
recommended_courses: Middle Eastern & Northern African Politics Global Social Policies French classes
unexpected_costs: A lot of the nights out and "soirées" are rather expensive.
cost_comparison: Coffeeshops in Paris hold the same prices in Denmark. Going out for dinner is actually a little cheaper. The food in the cantina at Sciences Po is half the price of UCPH.
activities_available: Everything from wine tasting to football.
activities_recommended: If you enjoy sports, enroll yourself in a sports class. it's such an easy way to get friends.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Canal St-Matin and have a glass of wine. The Canal is way less crowded than the Seine.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The Parisian culture is not far from the one of Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: Local Parisian students run their own show. They are faced with heavy workloads from working and studying so many of them keep themselves away from exchange students. However, most are very kind and are from my experience very kind to help with language difficulties.
cultural_challenges: A lot of homeless people in Paris. Can be difficult to deal with as a scandi. Also there was a lot of demonstrations and strikes during my stay which paralyzed the public transportation.
culture_appreciated: Wine & chill culture, meaning that people in Paris can sit outside of the bistros and drink wine all night without getting absolutely drunk. That differs a lot from the danish drinking culture, I find.
top3_advice: Do everything you can to find a studio in the city centre. They expect you to do A LOT of work, but they don't expect the same academic levels at UCPH. Try to get out of your comfort zone, and find international friends by joining the welcome programme.
other_useful_info: As I've mentioned a couple of times, don't worry about the workload. They prefer quantity over quality.
most_rewarding: Exploring new cultures and getting international friends.
greatest_challenge: As I also followed a French class (in which we can't get transferred the ECTS from to UCPH) I ended up taking 34 ECTS points. 34 ECTS points at Sciences Po is more than challenging, and as you also want your exchange experience to be a social experience, some days are tough and late.

institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: I wanted to go on exchange to a university with an academic level that ensured my learning during the exchange. I also wished to experience and learn the French culture and language as well as get to know the famous city of Paris.
overall_comments: I have enjoyed my stay, but I am dissatisfied with the circumstances that made it difficult to be able to study the language while being in Paris. Firstly, it is not possible to include language courses as a part of the programme by UoC-rules, secondly the work load of Sciences Po made it difficult to put much effort into self-studying language outside the 30-ECTS worth of courses.
info_ease: Fairly easy, great communication through the Sciences Po email system
arrival_assistance: Mostly assistance by email. I was informed of where to go and ask if I needed further information or assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I have enjoyed my stay, but I am dissatisfied with the circumstances that made it difficult to be able to study the language while being in Paris. Firstly, it is not possible to include language courses as a part of the programme by UoC-rules, secondly the work load of Sciences Po made it difficult to put much effort into self-studying language outside the 30-ECTS worth of courses.
registration_process: For the course registration, you were told to be ready at an exact time (something like 10:21 a.m.). You had to be quick to get the courses you needed/wanted. It was important to be strategic and very well prepared, having already considered 2-3 alternatives for each of the courses.
registration_help: An overview of courses, their information (about teacher, course description, examination, etc.), and time of classes.
registration_success: I managed to get most of the courses I wanted. One was quickly full and so I had to choose alternatives. Two weeks before the beginning of the semester, I received the message than one of my courses had been cancelled, and therefore I had to choose another course between the ones that still had extra spaces.
registration_advice: Be very well prepared and look into many courses! Check out the time of classes if you want to maybe structure some days off during the week. Also, if you want to "balance" the work-load, you may be able to read from the description of examination how much work is in the course and when.
academics_comments: I have enjoyed my stay, but I am dissatisfied with the circumstances that made it difficult to be able to study the language while being in Paris. Firstly, it is not possible to include language courses as a part of the programme by UoC-rules, secondly the work load of Sciences Po made it difficult to put much effort into self-studying language outside the 30-ECTS worth of courses.
course_level: The level was never too advanced to be able to follow. I had a lot of professors with interesting experience from institutions or research which made the classes very interesting most of the time.
teaching_comparison: All classes have 2-hour duration and don't include any breaks (if lucky, maybe 5 minutes halfway). For some of my classes, it was mainly teacher monologue, and student engagement was limited to weekly student presentations and sometimes debates, but never in-class group work for example.
courses_enrolled: EU Security and Foreign Policies EU Challenges (migration, climate change, populism) Comparative Politics Learning from The South (The Horn Of Africa) Planetary health and epidemics
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the course with focus on the Horn of Africa! The teacher was very interesting and invested in her field of research.
unexpected_costs: Nothing unexpected
cost_comparison: Housing was much more expensive than I had hoped Books were less expensive (only required to buy 1 book)
activities_available: There were opportunities to engage in parties, social gatherings, and sports activities related to Sciences Po, but I didn't.
activities_recommended: No comment
weekend_recommendations: Explore the amazing city. I spent all my time in Paris and never 'finished' exploring it!
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, most difficult was getting used to the 2-hour classes without breaks.
socializing_tips: I didn't succeed in this, but mainly talked to other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: No comment
culture_appreciated: No comment
top3_advice: Prepare for a work-load heavier than the average exchange semester (even though it definitely depends on the courses you pick) Expect that the housing process can be difficult unless you get a room in the Cité Universitaire or just find something else by luck :) Get a bike if you feel comfortable to do so! Swapfiets costs 21€ a month. It is a great way of getting to know the city. Most areas are safe for biking, even though you have to learn how to 'navigate' in the Parisian rules.
other_useful_info: No comment
most_rewarding: Living in Paris and learning about the city and country
greatest_challenge: In my case, the work-load. I spent many (!) hours studying, especially the last month and a half.
other_comments: No comment

institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: Learning the language (french) was a central reason to choose Paris as a destination. Also the academic opportunities at Sciences Po attracted me. Finally I really wanted to explore french culture.
info_ease: It was pretty easy, I generally experienced that the staff at Sciences Po were helpful / available via e-mail to answer questions when you contacted them
arrival_assistance: There was several offers of introductory tours, guides etc, but I did not make use of them as I did not find it neccesary
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Overall I found it fine, however be aware in the registration period to check your host institution platforms (both e-mail and other platforms) regularly so you don't miss any new added requirements and deadlines
registration_help: Online resources were available as I recall it, and also I found that you could get questions answered via e-mail if necessary.
registration_success: I was luckily a 100% succesfull, however the course registration process is very stressfull and I know of several people who did not get the classes that they had gotten pre-approved. However, I dont know of any for whom it did not work out in the end.
registration_advice: When it comes to course registration I would advice you to get as many course as possible pre-approved as course registration is very competitive and course get filled up in a matter of seconds. Also make a structured plan of what courses you need to apply to, and be ready on the clock when registration opens. Also have a list of relevant alternatives ready (even if you did not get them pre-approved yet). Finally if you did not get you courses, keep refreshing and revisiting the page over the registration period.
course_level: Generally I did not find the level of the course in terms of theory and complexity to match the level of my home university, neither did I find the academic standards for assignments very high. With that said the courses where in no way easy, a really large workload was required as well as generally a good deal of factual knowledge (even in introduction level classes) if you wanted to perform well.
teaching_comparison: The approach is way more practical than theoretical, which I enjoyed in most parts. Linked to this it was rewarding to be thought by professionals from a given field. Furthermore, the style of teaching is based on mandatory participation and several assignments, presentations etc in each course that are mandatory and part of your grade, thus I found that you did not have much autonomy to manage your own time which I did not really enjoy. Lastly, teaching was often not very closely linked to the readings. Finally, some teachers had a more "old school" way of teaching.

crucial_aspects: The city and the specific host university
info_ease: Sciences Po sent me very many emails with practical informations of various kinds, which made it somewhat easier to get the necessary upon arrival. We were also a larger group of students from KU, and we helped each other quite a lot.
arrival_assistance: There was a introductory week and a "meet the campus"-day

registration_help: You will receive a comprehensive guide on how to be an exchange student at Sciences Po, which contains all the information (and more) that you need.
registration_success: I got 4 out of 5 of the courses that I wanted, so somewhat successful.
registration_advice: Get as many courses pre-approved as possible - especially for the courses you want as substitutes for the obligatory courses at KU. And be aware that if the course says that a part of the validation is a "Final Exam" this usually means that it is a written in-hand sit-in exam.
course_level: The workload is much higher than at KU during the semester. You have to submit small essays and do presentations in all of your classes typically. However, my impression is that while it is hard get very high grades (the grade "20" is reserved for God, as some professors put it), it is not that hard to get decent grades or just pass.
teaching_comparison: The professor is much more in charge of the course. There is no external control, it seems. The quality of the courses therefore varies a lot. Generally, the teaching style is much more unstructured and messy, compared to UCPH. They also do not have the same strong focus on learning theories, as we do in UCPH. They focus more on descriptive knowledge and that your academic arguments are sound and original.

weekend_recommendations: There is a lot to do in Paris, so I will not try to list everything here. However, I can ensure you that you will not be bored.

recommended_courses: All courses by Jean-Yves Haine: ASPO 25A23 - International Wars and Conflicts, DAFF 25A65 - Europe's Foreign and Security Policies I chose all the courses this guy taught based on a previous review here and it was the best decision ever. "This guy is the best professor I've ever had. His knowledge is so thorough and his reasoning so clear. Very good at explaining very complex issues, cases and subjects and giving historical examples. Very good at connecting the dots and giving critical assessments. This course was a real eye opener for me and I was sad when it finished. I also loved the form of examination being a lot more about independent argumentation and reasoning not bound to the syllabus rather than the traditional way of remembering facts by heart and focussing on syllabus. His way I think is a lot more useful." He is brilliant at critical thinking and reasoning, explaining great details by example and also the broad strokes. His classes are just him talking in 2 hours which for most would be very boring, but not him. The way he thinks is out of the box and extraordinary. I've never been so amazed and star struck by a professor. It is not about who said what but about understanding the ways of interaction among states and their actors. Also his way of examination and assignments is: "fuck the syllabus and readings and learning by heart, what are your opinions and can you make a good and clear argument?" Unfortunately he also teaches in Rome so he is not always teaching in Paris and therefore you may not be able to choose him. Also he was the one in charge to chart the foreign policy of not just France, but the whole of the EU some years back. Check out his credentials, they are amazing. Also he is very nice and sweet and you feel very comfortable being around him. A bit like a grandfather-ish energy.
unexpected_costs: Nothing
cost_comparison: Groceries were in general more expensive than Copenhagen, but some things are cheaper. A solution is to eat as many meals as possible at CROUS restaurants where you can eat for 3,3 € for a full meal or just 1 € if you go to CROUS at Mabillion (3 Rue Mabillon, 75006 Paris) during their opening hours to get an IZLY card (meal card to pay for meals). If it is the right lady (thin, young and African decent who only speaks French) sitting there on the ground floor reception your Erasmus grant will qualify you to the 1 € meal since you'll be regarded as a "boursier". I found out by sheer luck and got the 1 € meal. But most other places don't offer this 1 € meal to Erasmus students. I ate this 1 € meal two times a day (2 times a day is the limit, the rest cost 3,3 €) every weekday and this was half of the times sufficient for me. The rest I would eat "Fromage Blanc", very cheap healthy and tasty since it is not as sour as normal Danish yoghurt. I only needed to cook for the weekends and holidays. Therefore I lived for less than 1000 DKK per month which would have been impossible in Denmark. I didn't go out to eat at all though. The food was the best and most healthy I've eaten as a student since I could pick fish at CROUS for nearly every single meal. A lot of vegetables as well and nearly no processed food, mostly home-made. You can also go to eat at CROUS without an IZLY card, but then you'll have to pay 3,3 € if you can show your student card. Also you can buy your meal take away with no extra surcharge if you say "importer". Also if you're not full yet you can grab your empty plate and go back in and say "Du Rab" to get a free refill of the starch and veggies but without the meat (only at CROUS Mabillion and not CROUS Cité Universitaire). Also there are cakes and sandwiches, all non-profit and very much state subsidised especially the 1 € meal since it is CROUS. CROUS restaurants/cafeteria is probably one of the best parts of studying in France since we don't have this in Denmark at all. The queues can be a bit long though, but hey it would have taken longer time to buy the groceries, cook and wash the dishes and a lot more expensive. Also you can get free travel insurance through a Norwegian Bank credit card which I did. Otherwise the blue EU health insurance card should be sufficient, since you pay the same going to the doctor as the French. You also don't need to buy a sim-card since roaming for 4 months is totally fine and free without any warnings or issues (I use Telmore). No book purchases are required at Sciences Po therefore 0 DKK. Also check out APL from CAF, it is like boligstøtte and you're eligible being an EU citizen albeit it takes a very long time and everything is in French and very bureaucratic. For transportation I just rented a Swapfiets bike for 21 € with student discount which was the cheapest option, but biking in Paris is a nightmare. I didn't buy anything or spent money on any tickets because most attractions such as museums are free if you're under 26 from the EU. The flight tickets to Paris are more expensive than I imagined so remember to buy them as early as possible. I had to pay around 1000 DKK one way to go to Paris with a checked in suitcase. Also the public transport is less expensive than Copenhagen. The Ile de France ticket monthly ticket for adults is around the same as the price of a ungdomskort in Copenhagen, but going to the airport without a monthly/weekly ticket is way more expensive than Copenhagen. Also there is a 1 year ticket for students for 365 € so if you're staying here for longer than 4 months it could be worth it.
activities_available: https://www.sciencespo.fr/en/life-at-sciences-po/culture-athletics-and-associations/
activities_recommended: Going to the museums/palaces for free if you're under 26. Paris is probably the city in Europe with most attractions and things to see and do. Check out the huge amount of free activities at Cité Universitaire even if you're not a resident you can join all the public stuff such as concerts, opera, theatre, book talks, dances, parkour, movie screenings etc. Baguette is always good and cheap, but remember to buy them fresh. Go to the bakery and try their pink equivalent to kanelsnegl, they are fantastic. Also French food in general is way superior to Danish food so try out: cheese such as Comté with fig jam, all their tarts, eclair, all their fruits and vegetables tastes a lot better than the ones in Denmark since they are more ripe/have had more sun, e.g. their apples actually taste good! Also appreciate the much milder and warmer weather, the longer days during the Autumn since Paris is to the west, but in the same time zone as Denmark, which extends the possibilities of doing activities outdoors. Even in December the sun first sets at 17:00.
weekend_recommendations: See above. Day trip to Versailles + Trianon & Fontainebleau all free for youth under 26.
culture_adjustment: In between I would say. Probably a lot easier than going outside of Western Europe, but still quite different from Denmark. The French love to comment and "stikke næsen i alting". And there is so many rules and documentation/bureaucracy needed everywhere and much is still written in paper and not online. Thus much less digitalised than Denmark. But the French are also more open to foreigners than Danes and it is more easy to become friends with the locals than in Denmark. Paris is very international so the local culture was not only the French, but people from all around the world especially at Sciences Po and Cité Universitaire.
socializing_tips: Just go to CROUS restaurants and talk to the people sitting next to you. This is OK in Paris even though it may feel intimidating as a Dane, since we usually keep to ourselves at home. But it is totally worth it. You'll be amazed of how diverse people you'll meet there. I got several local friends this way and even more international friends. Befriending local students at Sciences Po is way harder since they usually don't take courses in English and thus you don't get to meet them.
cultural_challenges: On top of the heavy air pollution: Smoking/vaping everywhere outside, in every courtyard, street etc. also at Sciences Po. This is Denmark 20 years ago. Nobody cares about passive smoking and none have heard about bagged nicotine you can put in your mouth and not bother others (quite popular in Denmark among the youth). I'm not a smoker and I hated this Also a lot less recycling and sorting waste.
culture_appreciated: See above. Also: The Parisian women dress so well, especially around Sciences Po. I cannot summarise it with words but they love their trench coats, pantyhose/stockings and high heeled boots. Their style and fashion is some of the best I've seen and feels so effortless and understated yet chic. It is not about bright colours and prints but well tailored pieces in uniform colours. Very inspiring. I feel they are next level compared to us Danes and we're very underdressed.
top3_advice: Cheap and healthy meals at CROUS restaurants with loads of opportunities at meeting others Fantastic academic opportunities and variety of quality courses at Sciences Po Paris with small classes and lots of money and resources to back it up. Lots to see and do in Paris most of which is free when under 26
other_useful_info: See above
most_rewarding: Being able to live by myself while managing to complete the 2x workload compared to UCPH. Trying the "Sciences Po approach" of teaching which I really liked compared to UCPH. Being able to talk to so many different people especially at CROUS restaurants. I've never met so many nationalities before, I've talked to people from all around the world and the international perspective of Paris is probably unmatched in Europe besides London.
greatest_challenge: Finding a place to live. Managing my time with the double workload and frequent deadlines compared to UCPH. Missing my partner back home in Denmark.

institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: I have been to France and Paris many times, and I love the culture. So when I had to choose a city to go on exchange to, Paris was an obvious choice, since I have long wanted to improve my French language skills. Additionally, I knew that Sciences Po had a reputation for being very ambitious and academically challenging, which I thought could be interesting to experience myself.
overall_comments: There were both positive and less favorable aspects of my exchange stay. Some of the courses I took were incredibly exciting and enriching, while others were downright dull and almost a repetition of courses I had in the first semester of political science in Copenhagen. Experiencing a different teaching culture and a high workload was interesting, but at times, it was also overwhelming and affected my mental well-being. I loved walking around and experiencing Paris with my friends – that was purely enjoyable!
info_ease: I remember Sciences Po sending a lot of emails containing the necessary information. I do not recall feeling that any information was missing.
arrival_assistance: No assistance other than information sent over email. But in my individual case, it was not necessary either.
arrival_comments: I have no additional comments.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

I loved walking around and experiencing Paris with my friends – that was purely enjoyable!
registration_process: It has been a while, so I do not remember the registration process very clearly. But I recall something about going into the portal and finding the specific courses you wanted to enroll in from the overall list of courses, then clicking on them, and finally saving them all to your user account.
registration_help: Fortunately, I got all the courses I wanted in the first round, so I did not look into what kind of help was available if something went wrong.
registration_success: Very successful. I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Read the guide document thoroughly and make sure you understand the registration process. Sit down well in advance with your computer ready. Ensure you have a good internet connection. Keep a cool head.
academics_comments: There were both positive and less favorable aspects of my exchange stay. Some of the courses I took were incredibly exciting and enriching, while others were downright dull and almost a repetition of courses I had in the first semester of political science in Copenhagen. Experiencing a different teaching culture and a high workload was interesting, but at times, it was also overwhelming and affected my mental well-being. I loved walking around and experiencing Paris with my friends – that was purely enjoyable!
course_level: All my courses were at the undergraduate level. I remember having courses with both second-year and third-year students.
teaching_comparison: In four out of five courses, the class was very small, around 20-30 students. This created a much closer relationship with the professor, which was very rewarding. Overall, the teaching style was more authoritative and hierarchical compared to Copenhagen. In most of my courses, there was a more empirical focus than in Copenhagen, where we are taught more theory. Generally, the teaching was more broad-strokes rather than delving into the details, if I can put it that way. There was significantly less required reading than in Copenhagen. Instead, there were many oral presentations and written assignments throughout the semester, which is quite intense and requires good planning and time management. Attendance was also mandatory.
courses_enrolled: 1) Comparative Politics, 2) Decision-Making Process of the European Union: an Insider's View, 3) European Integration and its Challenges: the Euro, Migration and Populism, 4) Political Identities in the Age of Discontent and 5) Democratic Theory and Democracy in Crisis.
recommended_courses: If you have an interest in political theory, then choose Political Identities in the Age of Discontent and Democratic Theory and Democracy in Crisis. The professor is an amazing teacher, and you read some very interesting texts.
unexpected_costs: I lived in a dormitory where cooking facilities were very limited, so I ended up spending quite a bit of unforeseen money on takeaway.
cost_comparison: The supermarkets were more expensive than I thought. Bars and restaurants were significantly cheaper than I had expected.
activities_available: I do not know. I did not have the energy to explore the options because the academic workload was so demanding.
activities_recommended: I do not know as I did not participate in it.
weekend_recommendations: I spent a lot of my free time just wandering around the city and getting to know the different neighborhoods. I recommend, of course, visiting the well-known museums, parks, and other attractions. And, of course, enjoying all the delicious French food!
culture_adjustment: It was relatively smooth. It is a big advantage to speak a bit of French. Many people outside the university speak very little English.
socializing_tips: I myself did not manage to do that. The French students I was studying with were a couple of years younger and kept to themselves most of the time. However, I made friends among the other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier.
culture_appreciated: The French really know how to make the most of the day. Even if you finish work or studies late in the evening, they still go out and enjoy each other's company. French people use the city and public spaces more and often sit alone, sipping coffee and reading a book. There is an atmosphere of enjoying life that you do not find in Copenhagen. They are also more passionate and assertive compared to Copenhageners, which can be very refreshing.
top3_advice: 1) Determine if you are truly willing to be challenged with a heavy workload. 2) Put effort into finding a place you actually want to live. 3) Practice your French before you go.
other_useful_info: Remember to experience and enjoy the city, even though the university is demanding.
most_rewarding: To be academically challenged without losing courage. To create a daily life I enjoyed in a foreign city without my family and friends.
greatest_challenge: The weeks when the workload was exceptionally high. The periods when I missed my life in Copenhagen.
other_comments: One learns a lot about oneself by going on exchange, both academically and personally.

institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: For me, the proximity to my home city Copenhagen was an important factor, and then obviously the cultural and historical atmosphere of Paris. The prospect of learning French was also a plus, when choosing Paris
info_ease: The university provided lots of info on the intro week and the semester. Actually, I think there may have been too much info, and that it eventually was treated more as spam messaging than useful info from Sciences Po. Concerning the city, it was easy to find your way around, and I had a generally positive experience with information sharing from public services such as transportation and stuff like that. The locals, teachers, neighbors etc. was all very helpful, and interested in providing the info necessary for settling in a new city.
arrival_assistance: There was a whole introductory week planned, which I didn't attend because it was a little too expensive for me. Additionally, there was a day, where students could meet the different communities and student organizations on campus, which gave a nice impression of the university. Furthermore, we received many mails daily on our student account on how and where to study.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It is an online course registration process, which opens in the morning and has a deadline 24 hours afterwards. You have to register manually and course by course along all other future exchange students online and then complete and close the registration file, when you are approved on the right amount of ECTS-points.
registration_help: I am not aware.
registration_success: I got all the five courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Be ready with a wishlist of courses when the registration process opens and have some second wishes ready if one of your main priorities gets full during the process. I believe it is a good idea to register when it opens and not hours afterwards, where many of the courses have been occupied.
course_level: Many of the courses did not have a syllabus and seemed more loosely structured. It sometimes reminded me of high school more than a university.
teaching_comparison: Even though Sciences Po is considered an elite university/grande ecole it seemed more like high school and very focused on attendance, class participation and echoing teachers statements. It sometimes felt like the form 'elitist' was prioritized over substance and academic depth, which stands in contrast to the University of Copenhagen, where attendance and class participation are not part of your evaluation, but much more how you reflect and consider the syllabus texts and the way you use it to make sense of your surroundings.
courses_enrolled: ASPO 25A11 Comparative Politics, DSPO 25A02 European integration and its challenges: the euro, migration and populism, DSPO 25A13 Decision-Making Process of the European Union: an insider's view (The), DAFF 25A18 Israeli Politics through Cinema, DAFF 25A89 Geopolitics and heritage dynamics in the Balkans
recommended_courses: I recommend choosing the courses you find most interesting yourself on the syllabus. None of the courses I took were bad overall, but not recommendable in particular either.
unexpected_costs: No unexpected ones
cost_comparison: I researched before arriving in Paris, so I was not surprised of the expenses. However I found supermarket prices to be more expensive overall than I thought. I believe that many groceries can be bought cheaper in specialized vendors like greengrocers, butchers, bakeries etc.
activities_available: I am not aware, because I wanted to explore the city rather than Sciences Po.
activities_recommended: Visiting museums, eating French food, exploring the city, going to libraries and so forth.
weekend_recommendations: Paris is in many senses the European capital of cultural institutions and if you are an EU citizen between 18 and 26 years many of the state owned museums and attractions are free to visit.
culture_adjustment: I think it was easy because most of the people I encountered were very helpful and kind to strangers like an exchange student as myself. I have been taught French in primary school and high school, so I was able to order in bars, cafés, restaurants and grocery stores without revealing my foreign nationality.
socializing_tips: My impression is that local students like speaking French with each other and a good way to socializing and meeting those is to learn French on a more advanced level, than I was able to. If you are able to converse in French in an informal way, it is easier to approach local Parisians and students.
cultural_challenges: The language mostly.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciate the French mentality in public spaces and their politeness towards each other. The way they use their city is quite elegant, and makes you want to participate in it.
top3_advice: The amount of work is much higher. There are a lot of class presentations, which feels like oral exams in front of other students. You are obliged to attend classes, if you are absent more than two times in a class during one semester you automatically fail the course.
other_useful_info: No, I believe most has been said :)
most_rewarding: Getting to experience another education system and analyzing, why it is built in that way. I treated all experiences as learnful ones, which I recommend future exchange students doing as well. It was also rewarding to live in Paris for such a long time, and not just to visit it as a tourist for a change.
greatest_challenge: The amount of work and the education mentality at Sciences Po.
other_comments: No

activities_recommended: Unfortunately, I didn't participate in university programs, but went to several extracurricular activities such as French and dance.

cultural_challenges: It was a bit challenging in the beginning to get used to the late courses. I went to school at 7 to 9 o'clock every monday, which was a bit hard in the beginning.
culture_appreciated: The language, the food culture and the politeness of the French.
top3_advice: You have to be aware that it is a university with a lot of school work, tests and presentations during the semester. If you are prepared and ready for it, Sciences Po will be a fantastic experience.
other_useful_info: There is an absence/attendance policy which means that you fail the course if you are absent from more than two classes. I think it is important to draw attention to this.
most_rewarding: Certainly, to get a completely unique insight into the French academic culture, which is so different from the Danish one. In addition to meeting students from all over the world, who all share an interest in learning more.
greatest_challenge: It was probably to have to get used to and learn the French method. They have a different way of doing assignments and presentations. It was a bit overwhelming at first, as it was an extra dimension that you have to navigate, on top of reading and preparing for the courses.
