course_level: As I stated earlier my fellow students has been very talented and the course readings has been interesting as well.
teaching_comparison: At Sciences Po they put way more emphasis on active participation than at UCPH. That also means that students are talking a lot more than the professor. However I don't think the active participation format is well-suited for a class of 90 people... Furthermore there is more continuous testing and presentation at Sciences Po. recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend Kevin H. O'Rourke's course "The History of the Global Economy". O'Rourke is a star and he convey the course material with such precision and nuance that you can't avoid being inspired and humbled.
unexpected_costs: I can not remember encountering any unexpected cost.

activities_recommended: I tried bouldering which is a nice way to get to know people. However it was mostly international students and not a lot of local Frenchmen - but I guess that is just how it is.
weekend_recommendations: Buy a pass the jeune at SNCF and go with fast trains to other parts of France. Visit Fontaine-Bleau! You can take the train to Bois-le-Roi (there is a cute little local market on satursdays) and go for a hike or do some bouldering (it is a mekka).
culture_adjustment: People in Paris a very nice and welcoming and not much different from the Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Enroll in some sports-/cultural activities. Have courage! Say hello to the person next to you in the lecture room. That was how I met my best buddies down here.
cultural_challenges: Paris is a massive city and takes some time to get out the city. But go to all the lovely parks to rest you ears ;)
culture_appreciated: I love going to concerts and Paris obviously offers a lot of oppurtunities for that. Download DICE and Shotgun, they gather music events. Otherwise I used Spotify a lot to discover concerts.
top3_advice: 1. Be aware that Sciences Po is a school for practioners. They are not very research oriented (at least not PSIA). That mean that they put emphasis on presentation and practical knowledge. 2. Make up with your self how much you wanna prioritize the studies and exploring Paris. There are assignment enough for you to do nothing else that studying if every single of them should be perfect... 3. Enroll in a french class. You won't talk much french if you dont attend a class. Despite the rumour Parisienne speaks perfectly English and they switch to English if they sense that you are not comfortable speaking French.
other_useful_info: Practice your handwriting ;) You gonna need it for the 3-hour essay exams.
most_rewarding: There is a lot of things which has been rewarding. I have enjoyed just exploring Paris with completely new relations who comes from all-over the world. Realizing that you can establish new habits with new people has been empowering.
greatest_challenge: I've heard from a lot of people and now experienced my self that you will encounter a valley half-way threw. For me it was the end of October and I was drowning in midterm exams and I probably also missed my friend and familiy.

crucial_aspects: The reputation of the university and the city.
info_ease: I believe that it was very easy.
arrival_assistance: Not really any assistance. I received a lot of emails from the hosting university in advance so that it was easy for me to know what to do when I arrived in my study destination.
arrival_comments: I was satisfied with this. Lots of information were available. However, it was hard to get in contact with the administration regarding specific questions, as the opening time slots were small, and many students had questions for the administration.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: it was very stressfull. On a specific timeslot in a day in July, all students at the host institution should register at the same time for the same courses online, first come, first served. If you were too late to register for a course, than just bad luck for you. Lucky for me, I got all the mandatory courses that I needed, but this was not the case for some of my fellow students. They simply were too slow (I believe it was a matter of seconds when trying to register online) to get the needed and mandatory courses, and thus they ended up missing some of these courses, as the administration could not move then around later on. I believe this is problematic when some students are going on exchange with mandatory course to take, and that they can not be sure whether they will be granted to have the courses after being granted an exchange semester at the host institution.
registration_help: I believe that too little help was available right after the registration process. It was hard to get in contact with the administration in case of specific questions.
registration_success: I ended up registering for the classes I needed, but some of my fellow students did not get the courses they needed in order to get merit from UCPH - due to the registration process of "first come, first served".
registration_advice: to make sure that your wifi connection is stable so that you can register for the courses as fast as possible.
course_level: In general, I believe that the level of the courses were lower than what I'm used to from back at my sending university.
teaching_comparison: Far less pedagogical and more hierarcichal at Sciences Po compared to UCPH. However, the classes were more cased based and more practical and empirical oriented, which I liked a lot. Also, most of the courses consisted of 5 ECTS and were solely class-based with no lectures. This created more room for two-way communication between teacher and students, and it also created greater room for discussions.
courses_enrolled: DAFF 25A36 - From Ajax Operation to the Nuclear Deal: an introduction to contemporary Iran DAFF 25A99 - Small and Micro-states in Global Politics DSPO 25A02 – European Integration and its Challenges: The Euro, Migration and Populism DAFF 25A71 – European Political Economy ASPO 25A11 - Comparative Politics
recommended_courses: I highly recommend the following four courses: (1) DAFF 25A36 - From Ajax Operation to the Nuclear Deal: an introduction to contemporary Iran (2) DAFF 25A99 - Small and Micro-states in Global Politics (3) DSPO 25A02 – European Integration and its Challenges: The Euro, Migration and Populism (4) DAFF 25A71 – European Political Economy. They were all very oriented and included interesting cases during the classes. Especially the course on European Political Economy was very instructive and interesting to follow, with good teaching as well. The fifth course, I took (ASPO 25A11 - Comparative Politics), was not as well executed as the other courses. I missed a red threat between the syllabus, the class-teachings, and the lectures.
unexpected_costs: the general cost of living in Paris are high, but they also differ a lot depending on where you are in the city. A cup of coffee or a lunch might be much cheaper in areas that are not located around the Seine.
cost_comparison: Paris is in general an expensive city. However, what was less expensive than what I expected, was the lunch program called Crous. Here, you get very cheap lunch served in big portions. Great value for money.
activities_available: many things, especially through the BDE (student services). I did not engage in any of these student activities, but I attended a yoga course through Sciences Po, which I liked. Many other sport forms were also available, such as tennis, football, MMA, running, etc.
activities_recommended: I participated the hatha yoga-class, which I can highly recommend. These classes were a good way to stress off and experience something else.
weekend_recommendations: discover the outher arrondissements of Paris, especially 10e arr and Belleville.Also, I can recommend to take a weekend trip to Marseille if possible (the French train system is amazing) - especially when the weather is still good - I went there late september, and it was amazing.
culture_adjustment: For me, it was easy. I went to Paris with some of my best friends from back in Copenhagen, so it was easy and comfortable to land in a new city.
socializing_tips: be open. Initiative is warmly welcomed. Everyone is kind of nervous and overwhelmed in the beginning of the semester, and therefore it was nice when people opened up and initiated conversations themselves.
cultural_challenges: the most challenging would be that people come from all over the world, but this would also be the most interesting part. to get to know people from other parts of the world
culture_appreciated: I liked the way that it was more laid-back compared to at home. As a student at the university there are always more pages to read, more work that could have been done, but I believe that the "culture" (if one cal call it that) was a little more laid-back, which I appreciated.
top3_advice: 1) lots of school assignments. It is an elite university, which is easy to feel with all the presentations and papers to write during the semester. 2) the level of the education is generally a bit lower than what I am used to from back in UCPH. 3) the empirical approach of Sciences Po is very interesting, kind of refreshing in contrast to the rather theoretically driven UCPH bachelor
other_useful_info: attend and engage in the class seminars. Easy points in the bag if you overcome the burden of speaking another language and engage in the discussions during the sessions. Also, participating actively makes the sessions more interesting.
most_rewarding: To experience the city of Paris and another academic environment.
greatest_challenge: to overcome the hurdle of speaking academic English, but I also learned a lot from this in the end. So, I will highly recommend to just do it.

institution: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: It is a valuable addition to my CV, and I have always wanted to live abroad, particularly in Paris.
info_ease: As I participated in the introduction programme, I received all the necessary information upon arrival in Paris and had access to contact persons during the first week of my studies who could assist with practical matters related to both living in Paris and the academic aspects of the programme.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival, I received information regarding meeting times and locations. During the introduction week, I participated in a campus tour as well as several guided tours around the city, which helped me settle in quickly and feel comfortable in my new environment.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process was conducted online and operated on a first-come, first-served basis, which made it highly competitive and time-sensitive. And honestly quite stressful.
registration_help: Information about courses was available through the course catalogue; however, it only contained courses from the previous academic year, which meant that it was not always possible to rely on course availability or schedules not overlapping. That said, Sciences Po’s website was helpful, as it provides a guide to the course registration process, which was useful given that it is not possible to test the registration system in advance and students are introduced to it for the first time when registration opens.
registration_success: I was not able to register for the courses intended to replace European Politics at my home institution, which required me to follow the course concurrently from home and complicated the course approval and Erasmus process. I strongly recommend having several pre-approved course combinations to avoid being dependent on a single registration outcome.
registration_advice: I would strongly recommend using Sciences Po’s course registration guide in advance to become familiar with the platform and the registration process. It is also important to review the course catalogue early in order to have a clear overview of possible courses and to be fully prepared on the day of registration. Finally, I advise obtaining pre-approval for several different course options to increase flexibility during registration.
course_level: I found the academic level of the courses to be largely comparable to that of my home institution, the University of Copenhagen, although in some cases slightly lower. The courses were still academically engaging and well structured, with a strong focus on applied learning, discussion, and continuous assessment rather than purely theoretical depth.
teaching_comparison: I only had one course taught in a lecture format, while the majority of my courses were conducted as small class teaching with approximately 20–30 students. This made the teaching style more interactive than at UCPH, with a greater emphasis on discussion, participation, and student presentations. Students should also be aware that tests and exams are often handwritten, which feels more old school compared to UCPH, where digital exams are more common. This places a stronger emphasis on memorization and, in some respects, results in slightly lower expectations regarding the level of detail and the amount of written work one is able to produce within the given time
courses_enrolled: Comparative Politics (10 ECTS) Agriculture, Food & Globalization (5 ECTS) Mapping Indopacific: Actors, Theories, Practices (5 ECTS) The evolution of child protection policies in the contexts of global challenges and critical transformations (5 ECTS) The Politics of Urbanism (5 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I found the course The Politics of Urbanism (5 ECTS) to be particularly interesting, both academically and in terms of its practical relevance. The knowledge gained was highly applicable and relatable, and the workload was manageable, as the final grade was primarily based on a research paper and a midterm exam. In addition, the instructor was very passionate about the subject, which further enhanced the overall learning experience.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping was generally more expensive than I had expected, particularly when it came to vegetables. Otherwise, I found prices to be fairly similar to those in Denmark. On the positive side, many museums and cultural institutions are free for EU citizens under the age of 26, which helps reduce cultural expenses. There are also affordable lunch options available through CROUS, the university canteen system. Personally, I chose to eat out quite often, as Paris offers a wide range of excellent cafés and restaurants. Overall, I believe it is largely a matter of prioritization, and it is certainly possible to live more cheaply than I did.
activities_available: While I did not participate extensively myself, there appeared to be a wide range of cultural, athletic, and social activities available through numerous student organizations. These included both academic and non-academic associations, offering many opportunities for students who wish to engage in activities outside the classroom.
activities_recommended: I would highly recommend participating in events organized by the Danish Church in Paris, as they offer a welcoming community for Danish students and provide a nice sense of familiarity while living abroad. The events are generally very cozy and well attended, and I met many good friends through these activities. Additionally, I would strongly recommend taking advantage of the free museum access for EU citizens under 26, as it allows you to explore a wide range of cultural institutions without feeling pressured to spend an entire day at each one.
weekend_recommendations: Museums and simply exploring the city on foot were how I spent most of my time. Paris is a city where you can easily spend hours wandering through different neighborhoods and discovering new places. In addition, there are endless opportunities to visit excellent cafés and restaurants, making it hard to know where to begin. Paris truly offers something for everyone.
culture_adjustment: I found it relatively easy to adjust to the local culture. I lived in the 5th arrondissement, which is central but also quite local and calm, and this made it easy to settle in and establish everyday routines, such as finding local shops, public transport, and the route to and from the university. There is some truth to the perception of a language barrier, as at times I encountered locals who were not always willing or comfortable speaking English, or not particularly patient with attempts to speak French. However, this was generally manageable and should not discourage future exchange students.
socializing_tips: Socializing with local students can take some effort, as French students are often primarily present in French-taught courses and may already have established social circles. However, the French students I interacted with were generally very friendly and willing to help, for example by offering advice or tips. I also found that there tended to be more French students in larger courses, such as Comparative Politics (10 ECTS), which provided better opportunities for interaction.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier was one of the main challenges, and I found that the general approach to service can feel more reserved compared to Denmark. Paris can also be intense and overstimulating at times, as there is constant activity and less informal interaction with strangers. In addition, there is a strong culture of queuing - whether for restaurants, museums, or other attractions - so patience is sometimes required.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the strong culture of enjoying everyday life. There is a vibrant dining culture, with people going out to eat regardless of the day of the week, and the city is constantly alive with new events and experiences. As a result, it feels like you never truly finish exploring Paris.
top3_advice: Start looking for housing early. I would strongly recommend Airbnb, as it can be a flexible and relatively straightforward option compared to many traditional rental agencies in Paris. Do not be intimidated by the academic level. I was initially concerned, as Sciences Po is often described as an elite university, but students from UCPH are generally very well prepared academically. Be aware, however, that the workload can be higher than in Denmark. Even so, make sure to experience the city—this is what you will remember in the long run, and you do not need to be perfect to pass. Prepare thoroughly for course registration. Familiarize yourself with the registration process in advance, have backup course options ready, and obtain pre-approval for multiple course combinations if possible. Extra tip: Apply for scholarships and grants! A small investment of time in this can really pay off!
other_useful_info: Teaching at the host institution is relatively traditional, with a strong emphasis on memorization and handwritten exams. Whether this suits a student’s learning style is largely a matter of personal preference, as there are both advantages and disadvantages to this approach. Additionally, attendance requirements are quite strict, as students are generally not allowed to miss more than two classes per course without documentation before failing the course. Overall, the French academic system can feel more demanding and structured than some other exchange destinations, and students should be prepared for a less flexible and more academically rigorous environment.
most_rewarding: One of the most rewarding parts of my exchange was meeting so many great people, both Danish and international students. I also really enjoyed experiencing everyday life in another country and building a routine in a new city. My biggest advice is to really enjoy it — time goes by incredibly fast. The semester is only 12 weeks, and suddenly it’s over. On a personal level, it was a huge confidence boost to complete a full semester abroad. Sciences Po has a reputation for being academically demanding and highly selective, which honestly felt a bit intimidating before I left. Going through the semester and succeeding there was therefore very rewarding and showed me that I could easily keep up in a new academic environment.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge was the workload, which at times was quite intense and required long days at the library. I also found it challenging to strike the right balance between academic responsibilities and making the most of living in Paris. At times, this came with a bit of guilt—either for studying instead of exploring the city, or for being out enjoying the city when I felt I should be studying.
other_comments: Reading back my answers, some of this may sound a bit negative or overwhelming, but that is not the overall picture I want to leave. My exchange was an incredibly rewarding experience—academically, socially, and personally. If you are in doubt about going, my advice is simply: do it. You learn so much, gain countless new experiences, and come home without really missing out on life back home. Once you return, everyday life continues as if you were never gone, and suddenly the whole exchange almost feels like a dream.

cultural_challenges: I didn’t experience any major cultural differences that were particularly challenging. Most differences were small, such as communication styles or social norms, and were easy to get used to over time.
culture_appreciated: I most appreciated the strong focus on enjoying everyday life, especially through food, cafés, and socializing. top3_advice: 1. Be prepared before the course registration 2. Look into what the requirements are for the courses - the courses can vary a lot in terms of assignments, exams, syllabus etc. 3. That everything will work out!

And also, even basic French can be helpful in everyday situations and is appreciated by locals, so making an effort to learn a few phrases goes a long way.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was living in the environment of Paris. Being surrounded by history, culture, and beautiful buildings made everyday life feel special
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was that the courses were very time consuming.

registration_help: It was easy to get into contact with help services at Sciences Po, however, their answering time varried.

institution: Institut d'Etudes Politiques de Toulouse (Sciences Po)
crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere where I could take classes in French because I wanted to learn French while abroad. Of the three French cities I could go to (Paris, Lyon, Toulouse), Toulouse was the smallest, the most charming, and seemed like the easiest place to learn French. I also wanted a very "liveable" city rather than a tourist destination.
overall_comments: It has been a very chill enjoyable experience. Lots of sweet people, and going to cafes and bars and having a good time, but nothing "wild" like a lot of travelling or partying.
info_ease: Once there, it is pretty easy to get the information. If you take the French track, you start out with a week with French classes where you get to know the other internationals on French track, and during the week they host a preparatory information meeting for all internationals. It is possible to write an email and ask question or, even easier, just drop by the international office and talk to them. The part that can be hard (if you have mandatory classes at the sending university that you have to replace) is to get the necessary information in advance.
arrival_assistance: French class, information meeting, emails with information. They send out the email with information about where to find more information, for example where to find the "welcome desk".
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It has been a very chill enjoyable experience. Lots of sweet people, and going to cafes and bars and having a good time, but nothing "wild" like a lot of travelling or partying.
registration_process: You have to send a bunch of documents, including proof of language level, but it isn't that complicated.
registration_help: You can email the international office and ask questions.
registration_success: I got exactly the classes I wanted. You start out with a one/two week period where you try out the classes before you do the final registration, which is very helpful. They are pretty flexible with which French classes internationals take. When taking “normal” classes in French with the French students, there is a formal limit of five international students, but if the teacher doesn't mind having more, they don't enforce it.
registration_advice: Definitely try out a lot of courses before deciding to get an idea of what you like.
academics_comments: It has been a very chill enjoyable experience. Lots of sweet people, and going to cafes and bars and having a good time, but nothing "wild" like a lot of travelling or partying.
course_level: In general, it is lower than in Copenhagen. Classes are way less theoretical and to a larger degree concern a specific topic. The hard part is taking French classes if it isn't your native language. But because the classes count for 5ECTS for internationals, and they are made to count 2/3ECTS for the normal students, the workload isn't too big.
teaching_comparison: Classes are way less interactive. Some of them (but definitely not all!) just consist of a teacher reading a document out loud. Instead of doing a combination of lectures + smaller classes, the classes are either or. They are more empiric and less theoretical. They are less (not at all) quantitative and more qualitative. They are more concerned about form (the French “dissertation”) and less about content.
courses_enrolled: Institutions politiques comparées, Sociologie des conflits, L'Europe du vote, Institutions européennes, Culture et civilisation françaises, Histoire de la pensée féministe.
recommended_courses: Histoire de la pensée féministe was awesome but probably won't be available next year. Sociologie des conflits is really good cause you get an insight into some of the worlds biggest conflicts (eg. Israel-Palestine, Afghanistan) and the teacher is really good. L'Europe du vote was nice cause there was a bit of interaction – presentations about texts and then a little discussion after the presentations. Culture at civilisation françaises was very patriotic but also really good to just learn in general about the history of France, and the teacher is well prepared. Avoid Institutions européennes if you can, it is just a teacher reading a boring document out loud. In general see if you can do some "seminaires" - it's smaller classes on the master which are more fun than the big lecture classes.
unexpected_costs: Nothing big.
cost_comparison: Lunch and dinner could be cheap because we often ate at the publicly funded university restaurant (Resto U' Arsenal) where you can get a filling meal for lunch/dinner for 3,30€. French veggies were surprisingly expensive. A tip for transportation if you wanna bike is (beside VeloToulouse which is a really good system) to rent a bike at Maisondevelo, where it costs 10€ per month.
activities_available: A whole bunch of associations. If you're fast you can sign up for a sport at UT Capitole. Sometimes the university hosts an event, eg. an informational election night the night of the American presidential election. But you have to be proactive and search it out.
activities_recommended: Sign up for associations to get to know french people. Go hiking in the Pyrenees, it's not that far – there are some cheap options like going with ESN or with a sports association at UT Capitole. You can also go yourself by train or BlaBlaCar. You can also go visit some of the cute smaller towns in the area, with well-preserved buildings from the Middle Ages and renaissance (like Albi, Carcassonne, Narbonne). Also in general, just use the city, there's lots of life and things to do – cafés, bars, the theater etc.
weekend_recommendations: See above answer.
culture_adjustment: It is always gonna take a little while to settle in when moving to a different country. You have to figure out how to navigate in a country with another language and find new habits for things like cooking and getting around. But for the most part it didn't take more than a couple of weeks.
socializing_tips: If you wanna speak French with them, then sign up for lots of associations. You won't get to talk a lot to them in class so really the best place to get to know them is associations. Some of them don't work out or they meet very rarely so try to go to information meetings and events with multiple to see what you like and what works out. Not all the sports associations actually worked out, but dance and football seemed good. I liked the cultural association Posculture. Follow a lot of them on Instagram to see if they post events. However they mostly speak and share information in French so it's mostly for if you wanna learn french.
cultural_challenges: Speaking french. The non-interactive teaching style. Also they eat super late, so if you live in a colocation, you might also end up eating very late.
culture_appreciated: The culture for going out and enjoying life. There's lots of just sitting in cafes, drinking your coffee, doing your work. And lots of going out for beers.
top3_advice: Take initiatives so you get to know the other exchange students, don't stress out about having to “accomplish” anything specific with the stay, and remember to just enjoy it.
other_useful_info: If you're on the french track, all your classes are gonna be with different people, making it a bit difficult to get to know people to begin with. So do some classes with the internationals so you meet up a couple times a week, and take initiative to get to know each other in the beginning.
most_rewarding: Learning that I can do something that seemed impossible : studying in a language that I didn't speak very well to begin with.
greatest_challenge: In the beginning it was tough getting used to the language, and the first two weeks it was really really hard for my head that everything was in French. Also, on the french track it can be a bit tough to not have a social "base" because all the classes are with different people, so again make sure to get to know some of the internationals in the same situation well.

info_ease: I find the application proces to be easy. The University of Lisbon send me several information e-mail before arrival so I wasn't in any doubt at any time.
arrival_assistance: I did not recieve any assistance, I just took a taxi to my place of accomondation.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We got an email about enrolment for the courses and that it would open on a certain date and time, but I was at work at the time, so when I finally - a few hours later - went to sign up for the courses I wanted, there weren't many available. On top of that, you had to check if these courses overlapped on the schedule, but I think it worked fine. There was also a lack of transparency around the fact that once you hit submit, you couldn't do it again. This stressed me out as I had chosen a course that I definitely didn't want, so I had to email the host university back and forth.
registration_help: A guide on e-mail and then just e-mail, they didn't pick up the phone at the host University.
registration_success: As I said, I was late, and it was first come, first served, so I wasn't that succesful, but everything were fine in the end.
registration_advice: Be ready when registration opens if it's first come, first served.
course_level: We were adviced by our sending University (UCPH) that we should apply for master courses because the level were often low on bachelor courses in Lisbon, so I took both. But to be honest, the level were low on all my courses, it was comparable to high school first year in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: Most classes weren't as structured and teachers would just ask students what they thought instead of teaching themselves. The lectures where the teachers were prepared, the level of what was presented was unfortunately very low.
courses_enrolled: Statistical Indicators, Field Research, Inquiry Methods Online, Contemporary Social Inequalities, Portuguese History and Culture
recommended_courses: I liked Portuguese History and Culture. Even though I am a social scientist and the subject is humanities, I thought it was perfect to learn about the country you were in, its history, people, culture, etc. It gave some great insights. And also the teacher were the best I had.
unexpected_costs: Nothing really unexpected. Just remember to save up money for travels.
cost_comparison: Housing was definitely more expensive than expected. Also because many companies want you to pay for at least 6 month, and for many people, a study exchange is about 5 months, so you need to pay for a month when you don't even live there.
activities_available: I didn't join anything, så I can't answer that question.
activities_recommended: There are some organisations that organise a lot of activities in collaboration with Erasmus. These can be good to participate in during the first weeks, there were various trips to the Belom area, Sintra, and party-related activities such as Pub Crawl and Boat Party. After the first few weeks, however, I sought out more local social activities, I went to cross fit, joined a gym and went to football training with international teams. I found these on my own. In my time I also went to many Benfica and Sporting matches. Also champions league and europe league.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend them to go to the beaches, to Sintra, to the Algarve coast, to maderia, to the Azores, to Porto. Plan some trips with other exchange students, I went there with my roomies.
culture_adjustment: It was easy, the Portuguese are very nice.
socializing_tips: It's easy to feel lonely in a foreign country at first, so I highly recommend finding shared accommodation with other exchange students. It was the best decision I made. That way I didn't have to look for other people at my school as much because there were 12 of us at home having fun together. We played padel together, went on runs, travelled, had Christmas parties, went out, etc.
cultural_challenges: It challenged my patience that it was so difficult to find the items you needed in the supermarket and that you queue a lot in Portugal. There were also quite a few men who would whistle at you or say something to you on the street, presumably because you were Nordic-looking with blonde hair. But you just have to ignore that.
culture_appreciated: The openness, the friendliness. The good restaurants and bars.
top3_advice: Remember to look for acommondation well in advance so you can find something cheaper that I did. And be realistic, you will not find anything under 700 euros. Remember good shoes for walking. The city is very hilly and there are cobblestones all over, it is very slippery when it rains. Enjoy the beaches during the summer period.
other_useful_info: The academic level is lower than UCPH, so don't choose this destination for academic reasons.
most_rewarding: The people I met, the experience from living in a foreign country, the improvement of my English language.
greatest_challenge: Not having a packed weekly calendar. I'm used to juggling sports, full-time study, part-time work and social life. And often in Lisbon, I had to find things to fill my days myself.

crucial_aspects: For me it was crucial that the exchange destination was different from what I am used to in Denmark - when it comes to for instance religion, culture, language, landscape, architecture etc. I wanted to be taken out of my comfort zone and explore new things that could feed my curiosity. Moreover i chose the destination because of my academic interest in urban sociology, and Istanbul is such an interesting city in the eyes of an urban sociologist.
info_ease: It was actually a bit difficult. It was hard to get in touch with the Istanbul Bilgi Office.
arrival_assistance: We were assisted online (1 online class), and then I got a local buddy from the same department as mine, so if I were unsure about something/ needed to use a local phone number or just couldn't find my way around I could reach out to my buddy. Additionally they had an Erasmus Office at Santral Campus where they were helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The system is very logical. The exchange students were (by default, I hope) given access to the system later than the ordinary students, so when I finally got access all of my planned courses were already full and closed for registration, but I ended up with some good alternative courses.
registration_help: You are given the contact information for a teacher in your department, whom you can contact. Moreover you have your buddy, who is more han familiar with the system
registration_success: Not succesfull at all. They were all closed for registration or had requirements that I was not aware of.
registration_advice: Be aware of the time of registration, so you can access the system as the exact time the registration starts. If your classes are "closed for registration" don't hesitate writing an email to the professor and ask for special permission - this helped me get in to several classes.
course_level: I was a BA student at Copenhagen at the time of exchange and at Bilgi University I took classes on nearly all levels (first year, second year, third year and master).
teaching_comparison: Smaller classes, less of an like "lecture" vibe. I had to pretty involved in all of the sociology classes, but since it was so interesting it was not a problem, and the environment between professors and students were very relaxed so it seemed natural to contribute, ask questions etc. Most of my exams were 2-hour hand written exams.
courses_enrolled: Change in Contemporary Turkish Society Social Inequality Art, ecology and society Basics of sociology Psychology of learning
recommended_courses: I would really recommend taking classes with Firat Genc (Social inequality & Change n Contemporary Turkish society). He is such an inspiring urban sociologist and a very good and passionate teacher. If you can only chose one, you should take the class "change in contemporary turkish society".
unexpected_costs: You have to pay for the residence permit
cost_comparison: Everything was just so, so cheap compared to Copenhagen.
activities_available: So many different activities - ranging from ceramics to ultimate
activities_recommended: Not hosted by the university, but I would definietly recommend to travel around Turkey whenever possible. It is such a diverse and beautiful country.
weekend_recommendations: Istanbul has an amazing food scene - take adavntage of the cheap prices and try some of the top restaurants (Neolokal, Aheste, Mikla etc.). Take a one-day-trip to the Princess Islands. Walk around the neighborhoods of Kadikoy and along the waterfront there is a cool park - great for relaxing. Istanbul is full of different neighborhoods, which is represents something totally different. Take one neighborhood at a time and see how the life changes, how all women wears scarfs one place (e.g. Fatih) and none another place (e.g. Moda), how you can drink alcohol at every corner in Cihangir or Moda, when you are not allowed to serve in Balat etc. Take the ferries as much as possible - especially during the golden hour. You can also take the ferry (2 hour) on a weekend trip to Bursa for hiking and seeing an old and beautiful city center. Moreover it is easy to travel around turkey by bus. I went to Sinop - Ankara - Cappadocia - Pamukkale - Kusadasi - Ephesus - Izmir - Ayvalik, and I can recommend all of these places.
culture_adjustment: I need to be extremely observant of how others were behaving, talking, dressing, but it was not uncomfortable
socializing_tips: live with them!
cultural_challenges: gender stereotypes and the political vulnerability
culture_appreciated: religion, food and everything else
top3_advice: I think that I have expressed many of the things in the above listed sections - but you shpuld really look forward to seeing the city - it's just breathtaking.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of right now
most_rewarding: Traveling around Turkey, living with a local Turkish guy and a Syrian refugee and just walking around the beautiful city each day.
greatest_challenge: Can't think of any
other_comments: no

crucial_aspects: The most crucial aspect to me choosing Istanbul as a destination was that Turkish culture is very different from Danish culture, and that I wanted to learn more about the Turkish way of life. Istanbul has a rich history, which is apparent in historical landmarks, cultural institutions and religious buildings.
overall_comments: Due to personal issues I did not have the best study abroad experience, but the destination itself was very interesting and I learned many new things I would not have, if I had not chosen to go on exchange.
info_ease: Istanbul Bilgi University sent out an information package before my arrival. This was very informative with recommendations for housing, student clubs, cultural customs and so on.
arrival_assistance: The International Student Office and the Erasmus Office at the main campus was able to assist with any questions I had about registering for courses and etc.
arrival_comments: Due to covid restrictions, the university did not have any intro days or gathering with information upon arrival. This would have been useful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Due to personal issues I did not have the best study abroad experience, but the destination itself was very interesting and I learned many new things I would not have, if I had not chosen to go on exchange.
registration_process: The university sent out a guide for registering for courses. You had to have a student ID first however, and if you did not receive this in your mail, you had to go to the Erasmus Office, where the employees were helpful. Thereafter you registre through Bilgis system.
registration_help: Help was available at the Erasmus Office.
registration_success: I was succesful in registreting for my classes, but you have to contact the professors prior to choosing the class, because not all classes were suitable for Erasmus students or taught in English even though it said so on their website with course descriptions.
registration_advice: Contact professors prior to choosing the course to make sure that it is suitable for you as an exchange student.
academics_comments: Due to personal issues I did not have the best study abroad experience, but the destination itself was very interesting and I learned many new things I would not have, if I had not chosen to go on exchange.
course_level: The level of courses was lower than expected. There were more weekly assignment and less bigger projects.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was more classroom oriented with smaller classes and more engagement between professors and students compared to UCPH. This was definitely positive and I was very satisfied with this part.
courses_enrolled: 'Issues in Cyberculture', 'Introduction to Post-Colonialism', 'History of Nationalism, Memory and Commemoration', and 'Femininity, Masculinity and Modernity'
recommended_courses: I would recommend the course 'Femininity, Masculinity and Modernity' as the professor was very engaged and the classes were interesting. I would also recommend 'History of Nationalism, Memory and Commemoration' as you learn a lot about Turkish history and their relationship with the rest of Europe.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Clothing and groceries were slightly more expensive than expected.
activities_available: Yoga and Volleyball
activities_recommended: I did not attend any non-academic activities on campus. I found a ceramics course off campus that I enjoyed.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going to the Prince Islands.
culture_adjustment: It was easy to adjust to the local culture, as Turks are very open and keen to share their culture.
socializing_tips: There was created a whats app group, where events were posted and you could arrange meet ups with other Erasmus students.
cultural_challenges: You can smoke inside a lot of places in Istanbul, which can be a bit unpleasant.
culture_appreciated: Turks are very open and easy to talk to. There are lots of cultural sights in Istanbul.
top3_advice: 1. Find housing before you leave, even if it is just temporary. Once you are there it is easier to find a place through friends you meet and to figure out which areas you like the best. 2. You have to go to the Erasmus Office a lot to get set up with your courses in the beginning. 3. Engage and meet up with other students through the whats app groups.
other_useful_info: You don't have to know everything before you leave.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding experience was meeting students from other countries, who were going through the same experience.
greatest_challenge: My greatest challenge was to make close friendships - but there are always other Erasmus students you can hang out with.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a country that was as different as my home country as possible. And I was very excited about the opportunity of going to Istanbul and explore everything that the city had to offer. Moreover, exploring Turkey was also something I had wanted to do for a long time, so it was such a good opportunity to do that.
overall_comments: During my months in Istanbul, I also realized that living in such a big and chaotic city is perhaps not ideal for me. Living in the city was with many torn feelings, as I on one hand enjoyed all the opportunities, friendships and connections I made there, while I also experienced getting very stressed of how busy the city is.
info_ease: It was so-so, but I found a lot of the information along my way and by talking to the other Erasmus-students + the ESN-network.
arrival_assistance: I mainly got assistance from the ESN-group at Istanbul University, who were very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: During my months in Istanbul, I also realized that living in such a big and chaotic city is perhaps not ideal for me. Living in the city was with many torn feelings, as I on one hand enjoyed all the opportunities, friendships and connections I made there, while I also experienced getting very stressed of how busy the city is.
registration_process: It was VERY complicated to put it the least. As an exchange student in anthropology, I was also registered at the faculty, where the department of anthropology is. However, there were no anthropological courses taught in English, and only a few ones at the faculty for political science, which is a different department. I found that the course registration was very confusing and time-consuming, as it was not the easiest to take courses in a different faculty from the one I was registered at.
registration_help: The professors were helpful in this process. The headmaster of the Department of Anthropology was also helpful, as I felt very sorry that there were no English classes in anthropology (he had not been told that 3 Erasmus exchange students in anthropology were arriving).
registration_success: I managed at the end.
registration_advice: Be patient and in the end, everything will get solved once you are there.
academics_comments: During my months in Istanbul, I also realized that living in such a big and chaotic city is perhaps not ideal for me. Living in the city was with many torn feelings, as I on one hand enjoyed all the opportunities, friendships and connections I made there, while I also experienced getting very stressed of how busy the city is.
course_level: I found that the level was relatively low for a master's class to be. It felt more like a bachelor's class, and it was sometimes lacking structure. The level of English from the professor's side in one of my classes was also lacking to my experience.
teaching_comparison: It was more just listening to the professor. It was not as engaging as what I have been used to at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: 1. Theories and Concepts in International Relations 2. Comparative Nationalism and Nation Building
recommended_courses: Theories and Concepts in International Relations was very interesting, and the professor very dedicated with interesting perspectives.
unexpected_costs: Insurance cost. They only accept insurances in Turkish, so even though I have a global health insurance from Denmark, it was not enough.
cost_comparison: Turkish food and transportation is very cheap, while international food is more expensive.
activities_available: I took part in the ESN-activities, which was a great opportunity to meet other Erasmus students and make friendships - especially in the first month.
activities_recommended: Take part in the options that arise.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the country and get out of Istanbul more than I did - it is nice with breaks from the bustling city.
culture_adjustment: It was so-so. There was first of all a massive language barrier, as the level of English is very, very low. Second of all, I would say that future exchange students should be aware of scams. If you get a Turkish friend, get your Turkish friend to arrange your SIM-card, bureaucracy and purchases that are done at markets, bazaars, etc. The prices are higher for especially Europeans.
socializing_tips: Use the app Bumble Friends and settle with the fact that there will probably be a language barrier.
cultural_challenges: The fact that so many wanted to scam me.
culture_appreciated: The energy of people and how passionate they can be.
top3_advice: - Be patient with the bureaucracy - Accept that things are less structured - Take opportunities to get out of Istanbul during weekends, holidays, etc.
other_useful_info: Embrace how spontaneous your life will be.
most_rewarding: Making all the friendships I did.
greatest_challenge: Dealing with my housing situation, as I was very unlucky with water leaks, mould and other housing challenges (e.g. a broken vacuum, a broken shower, a broken water pibe).

crucial_aspects: James Cook University, JCU, is a well renowned institution within the field of marine biology, and with its location adjacent to the Great Barrier Reef there was no doubt this was the place I wanted to go.
info_ease: Rather easy. All staff were incredibly helpful and they sent out heaps of material to prepare you for your arrival to the uni. I also participated in a pre arrival zoom meeting with the other internationals in which the international students team at JCU welcomed us and went through everything we needed to know prior to coming there.
arrival_assistance: JCU staff were incredibly helpful and inviting to the international students which made settling in very easy which was lovely. We were showed around campus and they pointed out the education central where you could get your student ID and receive help with course planning. They also offered brush up courses in the intro week, however, I only participated in the social events during this week. There were introductions to the social sports, fitness, quizzes, and speed friending events.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Keep a thorough eye on your KU mail. I got a lot of information here, and when you follow the instructions given it's very straight forward. I applied pre approvals for a number of courses at both JCU and KU and then I chose the ones that fit together timetable wise in the eStudent portal. You select the courses and then you register for classes. They tell you all about it and I also got lots of help at the education central desk on campus because I chose to change subjects at the beginning of the semester.
registration_help: You could easily get answers to your questions by email or simply by hopping down to the education central on campus. Lovely staff.
registration_success: I got all classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Just keep a close eye on your KU email, your JCU email when you get one of those, and on deadlines for subject registration as some subjects are really popular.
course_level: The courses were at an appropriate level. Assessment is spread out over the semester with grading of reports and presentations that contribute to your grade. This means that the final exams are typically no more than 30/40 % of your grade and they are typically easier than exams at KU. However, the workload is spread out over the entire semester, and the assignments took more energy than what I've experienced at KU.
teaching_comparison: Compared to the workload I was used to at KU there were way more written assignments at JCU. Although the workload was fairly small in the beginning of the semester it really peaked towards the end of the semester with at least one big report and or presentation every week. I cannot stress enough how happy you will be to have EndNote or another reference program handy. I didn't use it before coming to JCU, but the amount of reports and time spent on it just made it worth while to get EndNote. The librarians were very helpful with downloading and introducing me to it.
courses_enrolled: Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology Ecological and Conservation Genetics Coral Reef Ecology Marine Conservation Biology
recommended_courses: Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology was a super cool subject. Jan Strugnell who taught the course was an absolutely great professor. Cool practicals taking blood samples from live fish and dissecting fish as well. Marine Conservation was really cool, covering all things marine conservation, deeply rooted in current research. Geoff Jones was the course coordinator, however, he will not be next year, so I don't know how much the course will change. Ecological and Conservation genetics was an incredibly demanding and a bit stressful course. Although I now, at the other side of it, can see that I have learnt a lot, it was just a lot of pressure during the semester. The subject is built around a single report about koala genetics, and throughout the semester we used seven different kinds of software to analyse SNP data. Very directed at hands on genetics, so if you're into that I say go for it. Otherwise, I say not worth it on an exchange semester, as it was too much to deal with while taking in the rest of the experience.
unexpected_costs: I spent a lot of money on diving and weekend trips as Townsville itself is not the most inspiring city to spend all your time. I also had to pay for a lab coat for Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology (200 DKK) and a field trip with Coral Reef ecology (1700 DKK).
cost_comparison: Food was less expensive than I had anticipated. However, the on campus options for grocery shopping are quite limited. Instead there are many cafes and food stalls so to avoid spending all my money there, I did weekly shopping trips to Stockland with the bus to buy groceries which made it easier to keep my budget.
activities_available: Every Tuesday there was Café International arranged by JCU. They served free coffee and snacks and had some kind of event on. Almost all international students would show up and it was always really nice to catch up with people or have a chat with the staff. They were really looking out for the wellbeing of their students. Often times on campus there was free food somewhere so keep an eye out!
activities_recommended: Definitely go for social sports. It was really fun and a great way to mingle.
weekend_recommendations: I personally spent many weekends on Magnetic Island just a 20 minute ferry ride away from Townsville city centre. I also spent some of my weekends SCUBA diving with the JCU Dive Club on liveaboards which was absolutely incredible. Daytrip to Wallaman Falls is also a great activity. I also went to Cairns for a weekend - went over to Fitzroy Island, big recommendation! A lot of people also went to Airlie Beach for a weekend. In general just explore the options with the Greyhound bus up and down the coast if you're not getting a car. The lagoon is just a 15 min bike ride from uni which is lovely for an after uni dip in the pool on week days.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The Australian people were incredibly open, helpful, and welcoming. The only thing that was really different is they always ask you how you're doing at the beginning of any interaction which is very unlike danish people to do.
socializing_tips: I met local students at the speed friending event at the beginning of the semester and in class.
cultural_challenges: None really.
culture_appreciated: Their open-mindedness.
top3_advice: 1) You'll be writing a fair bit of reports but that's alright - just get EndNote! 2) Make the most of your weekends. 3) Join the dive club on as many of their events as possible. If you're not a diver yet, get certified as early in the semester as possible. Many of the international students there regretted not doing it. There's so much fantastic diving in Australia.
other_useful_info: If you are really into living in the middle of a big and busy city, Townsville is not the place for you. It's a rather small city and campus is located 12 km from the city centre so you'll have to take the bus or get a car. However, if you are good at making the most of your weekends, there are some amazing places close to the city to explore - and beautiful Magnetic island is always just 20 minutes away.
most_rewarding: A lot of really inspirational professors, cool practicals, and a lot of beautiful scuba diving!
greatest_challenge: Definitely the Ecological and Conservation genetics class. Quite the workload!
other_comments: Definitely a great place to go if you're into marine biology! If I were to go again I would opt for on campus accommodation to be part of the social activities at the dorms, seeing as how the city centre was quite far from uni.

crucial_aspects: I chose Australia as a travel destination I have always wanted to go to. Townsville is located right next to the great barrier reef and tropical forests.
info_ease: JCU Townsville has an excellent website, but I still don't underestimate the time required to fill out forms.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival, we had an orientation week with a lot of information, including the phone number of a 'tutor' you could text about anything.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Once accepted by KU, the process was very straightforward. You fill out a few forms and examine which subjects you find interesting. You are thoroughly guided through emails and videos, and I always get swift replies to my emails.
registration_help: Email mostly, but also beneficial videos on their website.
registration_success: Registering your classes can be a bit tricky. Coming from FRB. Campus with a straightforward structure, JCU Townsville is very different. Finding fantastic subjects was elementary, but many of these would overlap, making it difficult to make a schedule.
registration_advice: Choosing subjects that don't overlap may be tricky, but it is also okay to show up on campus and ask for help in the first weeks of your exchange. (as well as changing subjects if it wasn't the right fit etc.) So don't stress too much about it. Also, exchange is about so much more than attending university, so try not to do too many complex subjects or subjects with many prerequisites.
course_level: I did three 2. year subjects and one 3. year subject. Some I found very easy, others were complicated. I also chose topics because I lived in Australia and wanted to learn more about them. Therefore I had many subjects with very little knowledge beforehand.
teaching_comparison: We had very few on-campus lectures and subjects, with almost only online courses. Also, you hand in assignments throughout the semester that count towards your final grade. This makes the exams less intense and makes the projects more critical. However, I enjoyed this, though there was more stress throughout the semester. Also, my exams at JCU were all closed-book, which I find very challenging.
courses_enrolled: Australian terrestrial diversity Wildlife Ecology and Management Australian landscape processes and Evolution Functional biology of marine organisms
recommended_courses: I enjoyed Australian terrestrial diversity and Wildlife ecology and management. It is the same lecturer hosting these two courses, and he is just a unique and passionate person. These subjects offer a lot of freedom in online recorded lectures with a lot of fieldwork and a field trip. I would not recommend Australian landscape processes and Evolution unless you are really into geology (although this lecturer was also outstanding in teaching). Functional biology of marine organisms, I didn't find fascinating, and many down cuts in previous field trips and excellent laboratory exercises etc., have made this a weighty subject because of the amount of theory.
unexpected_costs: I travelled and went diving an unexpected amount of times:) Don't underestimate that you live in a fantastic country with much to offer and see.
cost_comparison: Food is expensive, and Townsville housing is cheaper than Copenhagen (especially off-campus).
activities_available: I played a lot of beach volley, I climbed in a centre, and every week an International cafe is hosted. Social sports, where you try various sports, are also highly recommended. Dancing lessons in the city were also a lot of fun. In the first week of orientation, a big market day is hosted, where you meet all the different societies - I highly recommend attending this. I also joined a yoga club which was also very nice. And OF COURSE, you should join the dive club. It has a fantastic community and many significant events and trips.
activities_recommended: If you plan your week right, you might be able to join free BBQs and lunches almost every day:)
weekend_recommendations: Try to travel around and see Australia. Especially by car is incredible. Also, diving is fantastic.
culture_adjustment: The heat during summertime was brutal to adjust to. But the people are very chill, and the food is American/westernised.
socializing_tips: Attend every possible International cafe and free lunches etc., on campus. Campus life at JCU is fantastic, and connecting with other exchange students is easy. If you are a very social person, I also recommend staying in on-campus accommodation, as this offers further socializing with other students
cultural_challenges: Only the heat/humidity is fierce. Otherwise relatively easy to adjust to, I would say.
culture_appreciated: Talk to the local people. They are all charming, and often you'll get invited to stuff with them.
top3_advice: 1. Accommodation: Do you want the VERY social life on-campus or the more chill off-campus? It is easy to find both, but staying off-campus means you can't find a place until you are there to sign and see the room first. 2. Save up some money. It is nice to say yes to all the possibilities that might come your way. 3. Of course, you should take university seriously, attend classes, etc. But the exchange is about so much more than that. So don't be too afraid of missing out a bit now and then if this means you get to experience something unique.
other_useful_info: Take advantage of all the significant initiatives, both on and off campus. You will meet a lot of cool people doing so.
most_rewarding: I was getting to know so many new people around the globe in a tropical country with fantastic wildlife and nature!
greatest_challenge: I struggled to balance my academic life with my social life. But everything turned out more than fine in the end. So don't go too hard on yourself.

crucial_aspects: I knew that I wanted to go to a university with high standards, and that was the impression I got when reading about the department of marine biology on James Cook University. I was also motivated by the fact that the Great Barrier Reef was within such short distance, thus allowing for a more hands-on learning, where I knew that I could go diving and actually see the ecosystems that we would be learning about through lectures.
info_ease: It was extremely easy, as James Cook University makes sure that every student knows where to seek the information they need. I was very confused, but the instructions on where to meet up the first day were very clear, and from then on, the staff were so helpful and understanding.
arrival_assistance: I was picked up in Townsville Airport by a shuttle bus arranged by the university, and that was very helpful. I just had to let them know when I would be arriving, and then they took us each to our destinations.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There was a lot of booths set up, and then there were a couple of staff members from Student Service ready to register our arrival. The whole day then focused on getting us the information we needed by presenting a slideshow that contained the most useful points.
registration_help: Student Service was open from 9-17, and they would make sure that they had resolved my issue before moving on.
registration_success: I was able to succesfully attend all the four classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: I was a bit stressed about how I was going to be able to have my classes fit together, because I did not understand the system when I was looking it at home. So my advice (which could have saved me a lot of worries) is just to have a lot of classes approved from KU, and then figuring out which subjects fit together with the help of the Student Service staff. This was way quicker and much easier then wasting time figuring it out from home.
course_level: The four courses that I took were: Marine Conservation Biology, Coral Reef Ecology, Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology and Ecological and Conservation Genetics. For the first three courses above, the level of the courses were high, but doable. I learned a lot from them, but I will say that it took a lot of Saturdays at the library to be able to do so. The workload is generally so much higher than at KU, so there is a lot of assignments and midterms compared to UCPH, and that is definitely an adjustment. For the last course, Ecological and Conservation Genetics, the level was absurd. The lectures were the same for both BA and MA (which were the case for all my subjects, actually) but this particular course had extremely high standards, and for the most part of the semester, I was afraid that I would fail the course. In addition to a lot of assignments, there was a difficult midterm- and final exam, but also a huge assignment that we as bachelor students were expected to write on the same level as master students.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching differs quite a lot. The lectures are much alike in teaching style, but the fact that we often had to do small assignements and hand them in, is very different to UCPH. At UCPH, it is expected of the students to take responsibility for our own learning, where at JCU, it seems like the teachers were looking over our work constantly, making sure that we understood the material every step of the way.
courses_enrolled: Marine Conservation Biology Coral Reef Ecology Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology Ecological and Conservation Genetics
recommended_courses: I would recommend Marine Conservation Biology, Coral Reef Ecology and Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology to future exchange students. Marine Conservation Biology builds a good overview, and the lectures were exciting and very current. Coral Reef Ecology was a nice subject to have, as it provided me with the knowledge of a lot of different corals, that I then could go snorkel or dive to see closer up. My favorite subject was Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology. The teacher, Jan Strugnell, was the most caring and motivating teacher, and there was a lot of lab work, which I also learned a lot from.
unexpected_costs: The costs of living in Australia matches that of Denmark pretty well, so I was not too surprised with any costs.
cost_comparison: Coffee was quite cheap compared to Denmark, as there is a huge coffee culture in Australia. This was certainly a plus, as I went for coffee with friends a lot of times.
activities_available: A lot of social sports: volley, soccer, kayak and so on. There were many social activities, e.g. parties, climbing trips, trips to the beach.
activities_recommended: Climbing. There is a Facebook group called "Rockclimbers Association of NQ (Townsville)" and they host a lot of trips to Mount Stewart. Even if you have never climbed before, you can still go and learn. It is cheap (200 DKK for three months membership, thus including trips), and it is an experience you do not want to miss.
weekend_recommendations: Crystal Creek (1 hour by car), Jourama Falls (1 hour and 15 minutes by car), Castle Hill (just in the center of the town), Magnetic Island (20 minute ferry ride from the town center).
culture_adjustment: It was easy, as the locals all were extremely friendly and outgoing. I can't count the times I've been called "doll", or "love" by non-creepy strangers. The fact that I would come home from school with bats flying over my head and to a wallaby sitting on my front porch was something that I was always just in awe of, so for me that was not too hard to adjust to. I found it much easier to make friends with Australians than Danish people, as there is general culture of being open and hospitable.
socializing_tips: The parties were the best for socializing.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences challening.
culture_appreciated: I particularly appreciated the opportunity to learn more about the indigenous people and their culture, as it is a big part of the Australian mentality.
top3_advice: Be prepared for an academically challenging semester - but also extremely rewarding semester. To make the most social connections, I would recommend staying on campus for accommodation. And lastly, I was warned about Townsville on the grounds of it being a town of much crime, but I at no point felt unsafe. I was aware of my behaviour at night, but I felt that I was scared more than I needed to be at the beginning, because people around me kept telling me to be aware.
other_useful_info: For some of the courses, the field trips would cost around 1500 DKK (and for some other courses more), which would need to be budgeted. I was not aware of this when I chose the subjects.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was all the friendships that I made with people from all over the world. I especially grew close with my roomate, and I know that I will have a friend for life.
greatest_challenge: I got decompression sickness during a dive in Cairns, and being in the hospital far from home was definitely a challenge. I went to the hyperbaric chamber in Townsville for treatment, but with the support from friends, I was able to recover and be able to finish the semester.
other_comments: JCU is a lovely university, and I cherished my time there. The campus is overwhelmingly stunning, with a lot of money being put towards the science department, and a lot of great places for students to study.

crucial_aspects: The classes available in Australia were so amazing and hands-on. I chose JCU because of the location close to the rainforest, outback and the Great Barrier Reef. I wanted to go to a smaller town, where you could easily feel at home. I thought it was a good opportunity to obtain an academic level of english.
info_ease: JCU were very helpful in general! They had a big market day the first week with all the school clubs, which made it easy to access information about how to become socially active at the school.
arrival_assistance: I wrote questions to the tutor that was assigned to us about safety in Townsville and what was going on in the orientation week.
arrival_comments: All the practical information was very easily accessible. I was dissapointed in the planned social events during orientation week. I chose to live off campus and there was a clear lack of events, which made it difficult to meet new friends. I would therefore recommend living in one of the dorms for social reasons.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You did your best to register for classes before arriving. JCU sent all the information on your JCU email about when to show up for intro day.
registration_help: If you had trouble registering for classes you could go to the student center. My friends who did this got everything fixed quite easily.
registration_success: I managed to register and find classes that didn't overlap. I chose the four subjects I wanted the most. I would recommend waiting to register untill they open the registration online, because then it becomes clearer which timeslots are labs, lectures and so on, so you might not have to attend all timeslots.
registration_advice: The class registration was quite confusing because sometimes you only had to attend some of the timeslots and some field trips didn't appear in the time table. JCU can help you with all of this upon arrival. They might even approve classes that overlap a bit, so I would definitely tell coming students to worry less about class registration. I highly recommend getting more classes approved from Copenhagen University than 7 classes due to the high risk of the classes overlapping. I wrote to the professors of the classes I was interested in, and they all responded sharing the outline for the semester, which was very helpful.
course_level: I chose 3 second year subjects and 1 third year subject. I did exchange on my fourth semester of my bachelors.
teaching_comparison: Much more field work - that was absolutely amazing. Many more assignments. The workload was very different from class to class. In my marine chemistry subject I had to hand in many lab reports and I had two quizzes that I had to study for during the semester. You can see this in the subject outline if you request it in an email to the professors. The professors are very down to earth and talkative. They all do very cool research and I felt more personally connected to them than the professors in Denmark. Especially because I went on 3 multi-day field trips. The classes in general didn't have the academic level of reflection that I was used to at Copenhagen University. All my second year subjects were more focused on definitions, basic terms and understanding the science. The classes are less broad and more focused, which I liked.
courses_enrolled: CH2042 Marine Chemistry BZ3740 Wildlife Ecology and Management BZ2725 Australian Terrestrial Diversity EV2401 Australian landscape processes and evolution
recommended_courses: I absolutely loved my classes with Conrad 'Wildlife ecology and management' and 'Australian terrestrial diversity'. He is amazing and down to earth. You do wildlife surveys - learning to trap animals and ID them. The Australian nature is a great experience. When conrad was guiding you it felt very safe too. The field work in the two classes is very similar though. In 'Wildlife ecology and management' we spent 4 days in the outback doing wildlife surveys. That field trip was so unique. Marine Chemistry had a big workload, but other than that I really liked the class. We went on a very cool field trip to Orpheus Island with magroves, black tipped reef sharks and stingrays, and that field trip in itself made the class worth it. I learned a lot in this class.
unexpected_costs: Field trips were quite expensive. I paid 3400 DKK for 3 multi-day field trips. Visum: 3100 DKK Students services and amenities (whatever that is): 750 DKK
cost_comparison: Transport: I bought a terrible used bike for 185 DKK. I took the bus sometimes. Student dayticket costs like $3.
activities_available: EVERYTHING! this is one of the best things about Australia - and a great way to make friends. Both sports, academic, dive club, board games. International café every tuesday with free coffee and snacks was a great and effortless way to connect with friends.
activities_recommended: Social sports - where you can choose between different sports is a great way to meet new people. Your level of experience doesn't matter. I got my Open water with the dive club on a liveaboard. This was a really good trip and I met a lot of my good friends on this trip. This way you also met people who wanted to go on dive trips later in the semester.
weekend_recommendations: I visited Melbourne, and that was absolutely fantastic - the food, the culture, the music. Go to Cairns! visit the Daintree rainforest, go diving on the GBR and see the beautiful waterfalls on the way there. Visit Airlie beach and the whitsundays - here you can drive inland and see platypusses and broken river and drive to Cape Hillsborough national park at sunrise where kangaroos visit the beach. Magnetic Island!! I was there four times.
culture_adjustment: Townsville is a bit of a redneck city where you encounter the people you imagine when you think of a real Australian with a mullet and a cowboy hat. The people in Townsville were so friendly and they want to hear about your culture.
socializing_tips: Field trips and all the clubs are a good way to meet new students.
cultural_challenges: The people who studied on the second year at uni that I had classes with were mostly 19 years old. I am 23, so that age difference sometimes made it difficult to bond. They are either very focused on drinking and think it is the best thing in the world or they don't really drink at all. Many Australians haven't left the country.
culture_appreciated: The kindness, the interest in my country, the 'ohhh nowwwws', the welcoming to join them and their friends in going to a rugby game or the waterpark, the helpfullness, their relationship to nature - a lot of them really enjoy being outdoors and finding animals
top3_advice: Be patient - friendships take time. Take advantage of the amazing nature that surrounds you. JCU campus is great - enjoy the clubs, events and free food.
other_useful_info: There are free volleyball courts at George Roberts Hall and Rotary that you should definitely take advantage off. Check in the subject outline what kind of exams the different subjects have. I ended up with four closed book exams and the workload in the exam period was immense...
most_rewarding: The adventure spirit shared by all the exchange students was my favorite thing. Everyday people would spontaneously want to play volleyball, go salsa dancing at the Heritage Exchange and watch the sunset from the pontoons at Ross River. I spent so few weekends outside the exam period actually in Townsville, because I was going on trips almost every weekend in the beautiful surrounding nature - all you need is to rent a car.
greatest_challenge: I was surprised by how difficult it was to form deep connections to people, which at times felt lonely. It was difficult both due to the cultural differences, the fact that most Australians already have a network and many friends and the age differences. But also it takes a lot of effort and reaching out to form friendships. Be patient and happy with the friends you do make quite naturally through shared experiences - it is alright to seek some safety. You are far away in Australia with a big time difference. I barely spoke to people at home.
other_comments: Just do it! I had the best time of my life.

crucial_aspects: Good courses, focus on marine biology, field work opportunities, nice weather :)
