arrival_assistance: Staff helped me with where to go on the first day of classes, and roommates as well. There was a very detailed orientation for all international students about both studies and life in Townsville
arrival_comments: None
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Australia is a great destination for a biologist, There are many opportunities for weekend trips not far from Townsville, such as Cairns, Airlie Beach, Crystal Creek etc. However the campus is located 40 min bus ride from the city, making it quite isolated, and a car is almost a necessity, although having friends with cars is also a bonus. weekend_recommendations: Whitsundays, Cairns (Uncle brians tour) Crystal Creek, Alligator Creek, Magnetic Island (i was there 10 times its so good and only a 20 min ferryride from townsville)

socializing_tips: Live at a dorm with other aussies

crucial_aspects: I chose James Cook University (JCU) due to its expertise in Marine Biology, which I’m very interested in, and then I also really wanted to travel in Australia.
info_ease: Pretty easy. However, it was a bit confusing to know whether I had done everything that I needed to do, or if I had overlooked something. Would have been nice with some sort of check list.
arrival_assistance: I emailed a bit with the inquiry email available at JCU about my courses. Other than that they gave us an online introduction meeting and a presentation of the uni at orientation week.
arrival_comments: There could have been more arranged for the international students when we arrived at the uni. E.g. more social events to help us meet new people. There was only one day that was fully planned for us, and the rest of the week it was a bit hard to figure out how to meet new people. I heard from previous students that there used to be more set up by the uni, and that would have been nice.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: When you get the confirmation from KU that you have been admitted, you'll need to wait for JCU to allow you to apply for the confirmation of enrollment (COE). This may take some time. Hereafter, you'll fill out a lot of paperwork to get the COE, and your payment for the tuition fee needs to go through. This may also take some time.
registration_help: I only emailed a bit with the enquiri email at JCU to get information about the students health care (you'll need one that is partner with JCU, and you therefore can't just use your own from e.g. your travle ensurrance.)
registration_success: I got all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: The registration process takes quite a lot of time and is a bit confusing - Don’t lose patients, because it is definitely worth it.
course_level: The level of the course wasn’t necessarily higher, but it might sometimes be assumed that you have some knowledge that you don’t have. For example, I had Coral reef ecology, and in this course, it was assumed that you knew the basic biology of a coral, which I didn’t, and I therefore had to do a bit of extra work in the beginning, but after that it was fine. In many of my classes it was also assumed that you knew basic statistics and could work in the program R. Even though I had a course in this at KU in Denmark, I had forgotten a lot of it, and I would therefore recommend doing a little brush-up on beforehand. They were however also very helpful with assisting you, and I became much more confident in using the program afterwards, so you’ll also be fine without the brush-up. I would say the level of the exams was pretty much the same as back home.
teaching_comparison: I would say the quality of education is very high at JCU - especially if you are doing courses in marine science. The style of teaching is a bit different than at KU, since you have a lot more assignments. This was a bit stressful, but also kind of nice, because then your grade isn’t just based on one exam. To begin with, it was also difficult for me to do the assignments, since most of them had to be written as scientific articles where you had to find your own literature, and I just hadn’t really had that much experience with this a my home university. So, this was definitely a challenge to begin with, but it actually ended up being a quite nice way of learning, and I really learned a lot from it.
courses_enrolled: Coral reef ecology - MB3190 Geographical Information Systems (GIS) - EV2502 Inductory marine science - MB1110 Marine conservation biology - MB3200
recommended_courses: I would in particular recommend Coral reef Ecology and Marine Conservation Biology (if you are interested in marine biology). The professors teaching these courses are extremely competent and on top of their research field. The material is also very new and relevant, which makes the content even more exciting. In Coral reef ecology you’ll also go on a field trip, where you collect your own data while diving/snorkeling, and afterward, you’ll analyze the data and write a scientific report. The trip in itself is a lot of fun. People are very friendly, and you get to go snorkeling and see coral reefs during your time studying! You’ll also just learn a lot from the entire trip, and I thought It also was very nice getting some experience with some hands-on practical work since the bachelor in biology at KU isn’t that practical. Inductory marine science was alright, but it was a 1st year subject, and it tried to cover a lot of content. However, it was all quite superficial, and therefore some of the things were kind of hard to remember, and i therefore actually found it a bit difficult to prepare for at the exams. GIS was a good course as well, and it was well structured with an easy exam in the end. I mostly chose it because it's a very good skill to learn when studying biology.
unexpected_costs: JCU requires you to be covered by a specific overseas health cover (e.g. OSHC from Allianz Care), which you’ll pay for when you pay your tuition fee when applying for the confirmation of enrolment at the host university.
cost_comparison: Vegetables and fruits were cheaper than in Denmark, so a vegetarian diet is quite cheap. Dairy products and alcohol were however quite expensive.
activities_available: There were a lot of student sports - Volleyball, soccer, basket, ultimate frisbee, ect. There were also many BBQs arranged by the university or the dorms.
activities_recommended: I think the people who joined a sport were quite happy with it. I didn’t do that however, and I still met a lot of people through my dorm.
weekend_recommendations: There are really a lot of things to see and visit when in Australia! Townsville in itself might not be the biggest tourist attraction, but if you like to explore nature, then it’s location in the northern Queensland is actually really good. There is first of all a lot of beautiful nature just around the city - e.g. Crystal Creek and Alligator Creek with beautiful waterfalls, rockpools, and streams going through the mountains, and rockslides that you can glide down from. There is also Ross river which runs through Townsville, where small freshwater crocodiles and turtles live in, and you can swim in it by the Pontoon, which is a really nice place to hang out with friends after classes. The best place near Townsville however, is Magnetic Island (!!), which is just a 20 minute ferry ride away from the city. The island is very beautiful and nice to walk around on, and you can do many things there - e.g. Do the forts walk and see koalas on the way (the island has the highest concentration of koalas in Australia), and then walk down to Florence bay where you can snorkel on the coral reefs. The visibility varies a lot and is not always great due to Ross river running through Townsville, but it is still really beautiful reefs, where you can see many different corals, fish, sharks, rays, turtles! Me and my friend also got our diving certificate there. We went to Magnetic Island 10 times when we where there, and every time was a pleasure! We also did weekend trips to the Whitsundays and Cairns. Cairns is a great place, where you can see a lot of nature - for example the Daintree rainforest, waterfall trips in the tablelands, or diving on the Great Barrier reef!! Me and my two friends did a 3-day liveaboard with the company Prodive, where we lived 3 days on a boat on the Great Barrier with 25 other people and got 11 dives at different diving sites. This was really an amazing experience, and I would definitely recommend it even though it is quite expensive. The Whitsundays is also a very beautiful place know for its white sand beaches and crystal clear water. After our semester me and a couple of friends traveled down along the east coast in campervans. This was really nice as it was a very flexible way to travle, and you get to see a lot more, than you would by just traveling with bus from city to city. We “only” traveled along the east coast, and I’m quite happy we focused just on this, as I otherwise would be afraid that the traveling would be kind of superficial.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. It’s very similar to something you already know - mix between english and american.
socializing_tips: Live in a dorm, don’t be shy to arrange a dinner/movie night/trip with someone.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Australian people are generally very friendly and helpful. This was really nice, especially when you are in a country so far away from home, where you probably don’t know anyone on beforehand.
top3_advice: 1) Keep an open mind for meeting new people and remember to make an effort and take initiative. 2) Take all the opportunities you can to travel. 3) Don't worry too much about your grades - Your subjects are only transferred as pass/fail anyway.
other_useful_info: Not anything that i haven't already mentioned.
most_rewarding: All the travelling experiences and the people I’ve met.
greatest_challenge: Being far away from family and friends, but remember that it’s only for half a year, and time will really fly by so quickly!

crucial_aspects: Choosing James Cook University in Townsville, Australia, was influenced by its academic excellence, especially in marine biology and environmental science, and its unique location near the Great Barrier Reef. The university's supportive learning environment, modern facilities, and dedicated international student services were crucial factors. Additionally, the opportunity to immerse myself in Australian culture and participate in numerous field trips to study diverse ecosystems made it an ideal study destination
info_ease: I spent a considerable amount of time finding the information I needed upon arrival, especially regarding course selection and other academic details. However, once I arrived at James Cook University, the staff were very helpful in assisting me with everything I needed
arrival_assistance: Upon arriving at my study destination, the assistance I received made the transition remarkably easy. James Cook University offered a convenient pick-up service from the airport, taking me directly to my on-campus accommodation. This support was invaluable in helping me settle in quickly and comfortably, ensuring a smooth start to my exchange program
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process at my host institution was quite frustrating and time-consuming. I was nominated for the exchange program in the spring a year before I departed, but I didn't receive an official placement until half a year later. Once accepted, navigating the course registration on their website was incredibly confusing. They had a peculiar timetable layout which made it difficult to understand when courses overlapped. Overall, this part of the process was quite challenging, and there were moments where I almost gave up
registration_help: The help available initially was limited to email correspondence due to the time difference making it impractical to call them. It wasn't until I arrived and visited their office in person that I received more effective assistance. Before arriving, there were many issues I struggled to resolve remotely and was unsure how to navigate. Fortunately, they were very helpful once I was on campus, though I wish I had known more about their support beforehand.
registration_success: Registering for classes was incredibly challenging for me. I ended up changing my courses multiple times because it was difficult to ascertain the content and prerequisites required for each. There was even a course I enrolled in that I did not have the necessary background for, despite the description indicating no prerequisites were needed. This process was frustrating and required a lot of adjustments throughout the semester.
registration_advice: My advice to future exchange students regarding registration at my host institution would be to carefully use their timetable website to check for course overlaps. It's crucial to thoroughly review the course descriptions to understand the expected prior experience or prerequisites. Additionally, I would recommend reaching out to academic advisors or student services early on for guidance and clarification, as the registration process can be confusing. Being proactive and seeking help as soon as possible upon arrival can save a lot of time and frustration later on.
course_level: As a second-year student during my exchange, I enrolled in courses that were typically designated as second and third-year level at James Cook University
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at my host institution differed from UCPH, especially regarding exams and course delivery. Exams were typically lecture-based without supplementary reading materials, which could be challenging with less effective lecturers. Some courses relied heavily on lectures with limited written resources, and there were also online lectures with physical attendance required mainly for fieldwork. This mix required adapting to different teaching methods compared to what I experienced at UCPH
courses_enrolled: - Australian terrestrial diversity - Wildlife Ecology and Management (BZ3740) - Marine Chemistry and Chemical Ecology (CH2042) - Earth Resources, Exploration and Environment (EA2510)
recommended_courses: - Australian terrestrial diversity - Wildlife Ecology and Management (BZ3740) I would highly recommend taking courses taught by Conrad Hoskin to future exchange students. His expertise and teaching style are exceptional, making the learning experience both engaging and enriching. His passion for the subject and ability to convey complex concepts clearly make these courses standout choices for anyone interested in environmental sciences or biology
unexpected_costs: They have a OSHC (Over Seas Health Care) that you have to have. It cost 103 dkk for on semester. Futhermore, various administrative fees that UCPH does not cover, was pretty expensive, such as international student fees and additional charges for certain campus services or facilities Fieldtrips! I used around 3300,- on fieldtrips
cost_comparison: More expensive.
activities_available: There were a wide variety of cultural, athletic, and social activities available for students at my host institution. From cultural festivals and art exhibitions to sports tournaments and fitness classes, there was something for everyone's interests. Socially, there were clubs and societies catering to various hobbies and causes, providing opportunities to meet new people and engage in meaningful activities. Overall, the host institution offered a vibrant campus life with numerous options for students to participate and enrich their exchange experience.
activities_recommended: Explore Australia's natural wonders like the Great Barrier Reef and national parks. Attend local cultural events and festivals to experience traditions firsthand. Engage in outdoor sports such as surfing and hiking. Take road trips to discover scenic routes and hidden gems.
weekend_recommendations: Magnetic Island is an amazing place for diving, snorkeling and seeing koalas!
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture was manageable due to Australians' friendliness and openness. Engaging in local activities and university events helped me understand and appreciate the cultural nuances better, despite occasional differences like the younger age of university students starting their studies. Overall, it was a rewarding experience with an open mind and willingness to embrace new experiences.
socializing_tips: Joining clubs and societies is a fantastic way to socialize with local students during your exchange.
cultural_challenges: One cultural difference I found particularly challenging was the younger age at which people start university in Australia. Many students begin their university studies at around 17 years old, which was quite different from what I was accustomed to. Adjusting to this age gap in social settings and classrooms initially posed a challenge for me. As a result, I naturally gravitated towards forming friendships with other Scandinavians and international students who were closer to my age and had a similar academic background. This helped me feel more comfortable and find a sense of camaraderie during my time on exchange.
culture_appreciated: What I most appreciated about the culture in Australia was the warmth and helpfulness of the people. Australians are genuinely friendly and welcoming, always ready to lend a hand or strike up a conversation.
top3_advice: 1. Explore the Underwater World: Don't miss out on diving opportunities! The Great Barrier Reef and nearby areas offer unparalleled experiences for divers of all levels. Whether it's snorkeling or deep-sea diving, take the chance to explore Australia's rich marine life and stunning coral reefs. 2. Plan Road Trips and Explore: Consider renting or sharing a car with friends who have one. Australia's vast landscapes and natural wonders are best experienced through road trips. You can visit national parks, remote beaches, and charming towns beyond the city. It's a great way to appreciate the country's diverse beauty. 3. Build a Network and Embrace the Community: Connect with local and international students. Join clubs, participate in campus events, and engage in social activities. Building friendships and connections not only enriches your exchange experience but also helps you feel more at home in a new environment
other_useful_info: Not anything I haven't written already
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the opportunity to immerse myself in a completely different academic and cultural environment. I gained a broader perspective on my field of study through interactions with professors and students who offered unique insights and approaches. Living in a new country also allowed me to explore diverse landscapes, traditions, and perspectives, enriching my personal growth and understanding of the world. Overall, the exchange experience challenged me to adapt, learn independently, and embrace new challenges, which ultimately broadened my horizons and left me with lasting memories and friendship
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during the exchange was adjusting to a different style of learning and a new academic system. Courses often required handwritten exams, which was a departure from my usual experience. Additionally, not knowing anyone initially meant I had to actively engage in social activities to make friends and integrate into the community.

crucial_aspects: I chose JCU based on the many marine subjects available and the unique opportunity to do fieldwork in northern Australia (e.g. a field trip collecting data on corals).
info_ease: Very easy. It is easy to find JCU staff in the education central who will help in the beginning and the university has many student help services.
arrival_assistance: I think the staff in the education central helped me make sure all my details and subjects were correct in the JCU system after I arrived.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You register for classes through eStudent. JCU sent emails describing the process beforehand. I registered in Denmark beforehand but it is possible to register and change classes after arriving. Some classes does, however, fill up early (e.g. Coral Reef Ecology).
registration_help: There is an email to get help. When in Australia, go to education central to get help.
registration_success: I got all the subjects I wanted.
registration_advice: Register from home and early if you want a popular subject. You can change your mind and registration until the end of the first week of the semester.
course_level: I took only level 3 BA courses. At JCU they are taught together with master students so the lectures and workshops are at MA level. The difference between the BA and MA students is in assignments and exams. MA students had more assignments and typically more difficult or higher expectations from professors.
teaching_comparison: More assignments and tests, and they count towards the final grade. The final exam only counted for 30-40% of my grade. The style of teaching was a mix of lectures and tutorials/workshops (similar to many courses at JCU). The reading material in all my classes was research papers (no books).
courses_enrolled: BC3203 Bioinformatics MB3190 Coral Reef Ecology MB3200 Marine Conservation Biology MB3270 Coastal, Estuarine and Mangrove Ecosystems
recommended_courses: Marine Conservation Biology was great and had some interesting assignments. It was my favorite course. Coral Reef Ecology was really interesting and has a field trip to Orpheus Island to collect data for an assignment about coral reef population structure. Really fun field trip and amazing to learn about corals while living so close to GBR. The bioinformatics class was great and the professor is really good at explaining everything (I had very little prior knowledge). Coastal, Estuarine and Mangrove Ecosystems had a high workload of assignments and they could be a bit confusing. There was a one day field trip connected to an assignment but it was not very well organized and we didn’t really know what data we were supposed to collect for the assignment. I would have picked another class instead. For an exchange semester it was not worth the time and effort.
unexpected_costs: No big costs that I remember
cost_comparison: Food. I am vegetarian and it was cheaper to buy groceries than I expected. Tofu is cheaper in Australia than in Denmark.
activities_available: Many student societies. Examples are Zoology Society, Marine Society, Finstitute and the dive club. I highly recommend to take part in societies. They host social events as well as workshops and talks. It is also possible to play sports through JCU student association. I took part in social sports where we played a new sport every week (very fun!!).
activities_recommended: Societies and social sports
weekend_recommendations: Trips to see the beautiful nature in Northern Queensland. Some nice spots: Magnetic Island, Crystal Creek, Daintree and Great Barrier Reef!
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: Student societies or sports would be good places to meet local students. Take part in the social events that are not just for international students.
cultural_challenges: I don’t remember anything very challenging.
culture_appreciated: People were incredibly open and very polite. You thank the bus driver before getting off a bus and small talk is way more common than in Denmark.
top3_advice: Take part in the events and find a student society that fits your interests. People are friendly and everyone wants to make friends. Explore the area during the weekends! There are so many beautiful places in North Queensland. Expect many assignments but don’t spend all your time working on them. Enjoy living in Australia, seeing things and making friends.
other_useful_info: I studied there for one semester but JCU is changing to trimesters. I don’t know what will be different with classes and opportunities for field work compared to my experience.
most_rewarding: Being part of the student community at JCU and exploring nature and seeing cool wildlife with friends.
greatest_challenge: Being so far away from family and friends. Time difference.

crucial_aspects: The location, the nature and wildlife around, interesting subjects (that KU doesn't offer) and language (English)
overall_comments: I rate my experience 10/10 - everything wasn't perfect of course, I did have some challenges - that is life, but everything else was seriously beyond amazing. James Cook university is perfect for someone who loves nature and wants to be immersed in wild life, while also having really interesting subjects and a great social community at uni. It is perfect if you want to be around a bunch of people who loves being adventurous and nerdy about nature and wildlife.
info_ease: It was fairly easy - a bit overwhelming because of the big amounts of information, but I had gotten a bunch of e-mails beforehand and key was just to ask at the student central. Most information will be given to you as long as you show up to the information events in the beginning.
arrival_assistance: Got a bunch of information at events and got picked up at the airport by uni-staff, shown around at my dorm, and Student central was ready to help with anything - also things that were not uni-related.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I rate my experience 10/10 - everything wasn't perfect of course, I did have some challenges - that is life, but everything else was seriously beyond amazing. James Cook university is perfect for someone who loves nature and wants to be immersed in wild life, while also having really interesting subjects and a great social community at uni. It is perfect if you want to be around a bunch of people who loves being adventurous and nerdy about nature and wildlife.
registration_process: First we had to enrol in the subjects and then later we had to register for classes in each subject – each subject has some options for workshops/tutorials so you can “design” your own timetable. This although also means you have to find every subject’s timetable on JCU’s website to make sure you can design a timetable without overlap between your subjects. The website was a bit difficult to navigate in that regard.
registration_help: I got some emails with instructions, I looked at JCU’s website a lot, and you can always email or call student service. When I got to JCU there is also a desk with staff ready to help – and they are really good at that.
registration_success: Got all subjects and classes I wanted.
registration_advice: My advice would be to enrol and register right away. Some subjects – like coral reef ecology, which I had – are very popular and have a student limit, so I registered as soon as it opened. You can also change classes and subjects even after classes have started – so I would rather register fast and then change later if needed, than wait until I was Australia.
academics_comments: I rate my experience 10/10 - everything wasn't perfect of course, I did have some challenges - that is life, but everything else was seriously beyond amazing. James Cook university is perfect for someone who loves nature and wants to be immersed in wild life, while also having really interesting subjects and a great social community at uni. It is perfect if you want to be around a bunch of people who loves being adventurous and nerdy about nature and wildlife.
course_level: I had three 3rd year courses, and we had these together with master students, only difference were the demands for their reports and the number of assignments. Level was although fitting – some subjects harder than others of course. I found the level of the assignments a bit higher than at KU, which I had to get used to, but I also think I learned a lot form it.
teaching_comparison: Lectures and workshops/tutorials were basically the same as at KU. We had a lot of hands-on work, there are some really cool field trips and they use a lot of guest teachers from companies, research groups and organizations, which is really cool. More assignments though, since the exam won’t count a 100% of your grade. Each assignment will be a percentage of the final grade, and therefore I think they have a bit higher expectations than what I have been used to at KU.
courses_enrolled: Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology AQ3007 Marine Conservation Biology MB3200 Coral Reef Ecology MB3190 People of Australia: Multiculturalism and indigeneity SS1010
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the subjects I took but especially these: Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology AQ3007: Really good teacher (Jan Strugnell), very well organised and lots of hands-on work in labs. I enjoyed it a lot. (Even though it is an aqua culture subject it does not revolve around aquaculture – it is just as useful for biologists for example). Coral Reef Ecology MB3190: A subject you can’t get many other places, very interesting, probably the hardest subject I had as well. Morgan Pratchett was the teacher, and he was quite ruthless but also a big shot in the field – I think he is taking a break from teaching though. We had a really cool field trip to Orpheus Island where we did field work in the coral reefs around the island, which was an amazing opportunity. People of Australia: Multiculturalism and indigeneity SS1010: This was a first-year social science subject and the work load was less than the other subjects, which was really nice, since you really have a filled schedule as an exchange student. It was really interesting to learn about the Australian society with focus on the people and especially Aboriginal people. I don’t think I would have experienced Australia in the same way without this subject – I learned a lot. Many of my friends wish they had taken this subject or something similar.
unexpected_costs: Had to pay 400 dollars for a health insurance that the university requires you to have, which I didn’t expect since I already had my own insurance. I did end up spending a lot of money on small trips and diving – a bit more than expected. Other than that, no real unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Food is bit cheaper than in Denmark and public transportation was cheap in Townsville.
activities_available: There were a bunch of clubs like finstitute, zoology society, JCU dive club, JCU Marine society, Red Frogs (Christian group), bible studies I think and much more. There was also a gym with weekly classes, and you could make a team of friends and join social sport, where different friend groups play against each other every week in different sports. The colleges on campus also had sports teams and theatre, band, choir and dance – All these groups would practice a few times a week and then compete against the other colleges in the end.
activities_recommended: I really enjoyed social sport because it is a fun way to hang out and you get to try some Australian sports like netball and touch footy. JCU dive Club was amazing – Really cool people and some of my best memories from Australia has been on the liveaboards with this club. Whe you are right by the Great Barrier Reef you have to go diving. Zoology Society – this was such a nice club, super nerdy and fun people, and everyone can be a part of it, no matter how nerdy you are yourself. They often arrange night walks, which costs no money and is such an easy way to hang out and find some cool animals. Wish I went on some more trips with these guys.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the strand, Visit Magnetic Island (go snorkelling, diving, hiking, lay on the beach, stay overnight, so much to do here), “study” at Riverway lagoon, stroll around Ross River or take a dip, go to night markets and Sunday markets in town, visit Crystal creek and Alligator Creek, take a trip to Cairns, Daintree and Mission Beach, go diving!!!, go whale watching. After our exams I went on a road trip down the east coast with friends, which I of course can also really recommend.
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: Talk to the people in your classes, on your college and in the different clubs. Not being afraid of talking to new people and taking initiative to hang out is key.
cultural_challenges: Their extreme air condition threw my body off. No real challenges though.
culture_appreciated: Love Australian slang and humor! I also enjoyed trying some Australian sports and I really appreciated how chill and kind people in Australia are.
top3_advice: The application process is slow and draining – but it is worth it, it just needs to be done, and everything will work out. My tip is just to do everything right away and check all your email accounts frequently – don’t postpone these things. Don’t worry too much about school and grades. Have fun and go on all the trips – you will be fine, trust me. Try new things! Try a sport you haven’t tried before, go on a trip with new people, join a club about something you know nothing about, try a subject you didn’t expect, talk to people you haven’t talked to before.
other_useful_info: Maybe get in contact with someone going the same place as you or someone who has been there. I found that helpful in the application process.
most_rewarding: Experiencing Australia with adventurous people passionate about biology - the friendships and all the experiences we got together.
greatest_challenge: Greatest challenge was probably adjusting to the college I lived in, because I didn’t get to live at the colleges that I initially wanted to - but I ended up really enjoying where I lived anyways!
other_comments: No matter where you end up going on exchange, it will be worth it, I think. I have never heard of anyone regretting going on exchange. And regarding choosing between the different universities – obviously it plays a big role, but in the end it is almost always the friendships and the experiences that count the most. And when you fill out this evaluation after your stay, write in a word document and then copy paste it in, because otherwise everything you have written might get deleted if you use too long…

crucial_aspects: English speaking "western" country, biologically relevant subjects, travel destination wishes, warm weather, not a very big city, close to the ocean, campus looking nice and modern
overall_comments: I loved it. A really cool experience and a competent university. I've learned a lot.
info_ease: Fairly easy. They send out lot's of emails where you can find all information otherwise, visit the student center, the webpage or call/write the university.
arrival_assistance: Free transfer from the airport to my accomodation, and a week full of introduction and social events at the university. Just make sure to visit the front desk at Student Services to registrate and they will tell you everything you need to know.
arrival_comments: Prepare your self for a shock in regards to the tropical warm and humid climate you will arrive in (if starting in january/february) and also prepare your self for very limited possibility of public transportation. The introduction events were mixing people that went there for an exchange semester and people who came to study an entire degree, which was slighly confusing.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I loved it. A really cool experience and a competent university. I've learned a lot.
registration_process: Figuring out how to log-in to the JCU online systems. Then log-in to e-student and choose your subjects. You can read about and choose all available subjects in the course handbook before. Be prepared that some subject fill up quickly so you are not guarenteed a seat.
registration_help: Online help. Or you could have a personal drop-in meeting at the uni.
registration_success: Successful but I had to change some of them because I changed my mind on which ones I wanted.
registration_advice: Read about subjects and decide on a small list of options for you before hand. Check weather there are time scheduele clashes.
academics_comments: I loved it. A really cool experience and a competent university. I've learned a lot.
course_level: The level of courses were similar to or easier than at UCPH. A bit more literature reviews and written assignments than I've been used to at UCPH. Also the way they assess you and hence your grade is very different to Denmark. It's similar to USA and Canada.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style were quite similar except we had more field work and ALL lectures could be watched online. A little bit less "being in class"-time compared to at home.
courses_enrolled: Australian Terrestrial Diversity Managing Marine Megafauna Coral Reef Geomorphology
recommended_courses: Australian Terrestrial Diversity was great cause you got to go out and catch Australian animals and identify them. Managing Marine Megafauna was more theoretic but a great teacher. Coral Reef Geomorphology was extremely intensive (2-weeks course) - too intensive in my opinion but interesting contents and a nice field trip to Orpheus Island.
unexpected_costs: Car rental and fuel, medical bills (the mandatory insurance only covers like 60 % of a normal doctors visit).
cost_comparison: Most groceries were more expensive than Denmark... But eating out at a restaurant was cheeper. Fuel is also cheeper but it's counteracted by the great distances down under.
activities_available: Sports clubs, fitness, diving club, other clubs, events, free lunch sometimes etc.
activities_recommended: I don't know.
weekend_recommendations: Magnetic Island, Billabong Sanctuary, the Strand, Castle Hill, trip to Cairns and Whitsundays, outback roadtrip, go sailing and snorkling etc
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. There's a lot of Australian accent and slang you need to get used to but people are friendly and open. Laid back culture.
socializing_tips: You'll meet them automatically in your classes otherwise, attend clubs and activities.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The happiness and openness, and the "always apreciate the outdoors attitude"
top3_advice: You need a car if you live off-campus or if you want to explore - for your own freedom and as a practicality. Pack up all your summergear and outdoor gear! - you don't need long trousers here, it's extremely warm most of the time. Don't be afraid to reach out! - you'll get information and help easier and you'll meet lots of new friends.
other_useful_info: The student visa is extremely expensive (around 7500 kr + maybe a mandatory health examination of 2000 kr) and flight tickets to Australia isn't cheep either. There's no way of getting around it. It has been a huge expense for me choosing Australia as my exchange destination. I applied for more than 30 scholarships (legater) but didn't get any funding so there's no guarentee that you will be financially supported and I've ended up paying everything out of my own pocket.
most_rewarding: Experiencing the Australian nature and animals!
greatest_challenge: Relationship difficulties...
other_comments: Just do it. It's worth it.

crucial_aspects: Exploring a new academic setting while exdperiencing living in a foreign country. The fact that I could be close to friends and family in the country was a bonus; while making new connections and friendships and bonding over a shared experience. A different take on academia was also what I was craving and the other classes offered at the location.
info_ease: Very easy, the university had a good setup with informing the incoming students of events happening. The only complaint I have is that a lot of the introduction events were very generalised, targeted towards undergraduates or targeted to specific whole degrees at the university; none of which were relevant for me.
arrival_assistance: None specifically, I just participated in the planned stuff.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I do not remember it - it was 6 months ago.
registration_help: I do not know, I think maybe there was some videos explainign it?
registration_success: On what scale? I got every class I wanted.
registration_advice: Follow the guides and it will be easy.
course_level: I took level 500 courses, which are masters levels courses.
teaching_comparison: Very different. I've learned that in DK we have much more training in oral presentation, while that is not prioritied much in other countries. At JCU there was a bigger focus on many small assignments throughout the teaching period and less on the final exam - and most of the exams were without aids at JCU as opposed to in UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Soil properties and processes Environmental Law and policy Hazards and disasters Advanced water resource system planning and management
recommended_courses: Depends on what they are interested in. I loved the water class because it is an engineering class and I got to work closely with the professor and the engineering students and got a community through that class - but I could say the same about the hazards class.
unexpected_costs: Well the public transportation system is very cheap but not very reliable or safe (I was told by people on campus to not take the bus alone at night), so I ended up renting a car, which is quite expensive - but the cost in ubers and taxis before that was running up as well.
cost_comparison: Bus was very cheap.
activities_available: None free, like at UCPH. But plenty of marine focused clubs, zoology club, scuba diving club, yoga club, a gym, a student bar etc. It was through my student housing that I got most of my cultural and athletic activities.
activities_recommended: Yoga club and living on campus as most of the activities are "college v college" where one can only participate if they live on one of the campus collages.
weekend_recommendations: Visit Maggie island, get a car and drive up to the big and little crystal creek and visit the nearby towns and beaches.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy I'd say.
cultural_challenges: Not really - language maybe? It gets fatigueing to talk to people of many different accents and understanding it.
culture_appreciated: I loved the indiginous culture bits.
top3_advice: Be prepared for the weather to be different than expected - it is a tropical destination, and I experienced both a flooding, a typhoon and an earthquake. Things work different there compared to DK, everything is slower and less developed. You might want to book your ticket to leave the day after finals ends and be out of there, but give yourself a few days after to soak the last of the experience up.
other_useful_info: Not particularly.
most_rewarding: The memories.
greatest_challenge: Learning how the university wanted assignments to be written - very different from UCPH.

crucial_aspects: The best academic opportunities within Marine Biology
info_ease: Fairly easy. I went to the student center, as I knew nothing when I arrived. They were very helpful and got me set up
arrival_assistance: At the student center they helped my with getting my student card, registering my arrival and how to apply for courses. Later on, due to their different study calendars (Block, trimester, and semesters). There were different orientations I partook in. They were all good, but at that point (a few weeks into my stay) I already knew most of it.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You have to register to each course timeslot individually. If you already have something in that timeslot you cannot register for it, even if it is mandatory. Then you have to get help at the student center. The class calendrers are not available until a few weeks prior to start of term. You can only view one calendar at a time, and only one week at a time.
registration_help: There is plenty of help available at the student center
registration_advice: Make sure you start in good time and take all the help you need. Is is an annoyingly complicated process.
course_level: I took one 1st year class and three 3rd year classes. I would say the levels matched this. All the 3rd year classes were taken together with 1st year master students. The only difference was the master students had a few more assignments and a different final exam.
teaching_comparison: All exams are pen and paper. The switch to blocks and trimesters is still new and the classes are not set up properly for it. There is also a plan for all lectures to be turned into 15 minutes online videos with no option for in-person lectures. All lectures are recorded, which is nice.
courses_enrolled: MB1110 Introductory Marine Science, 3 credit points = 7,5 ECTS MB3200 Marine Conservation Biology, 3 credit points = 7,5 ECTS MB3190 Coral Reef Ecology, 3 credit points = 7,5 ECTS BZ2480 Restoration Ecology, 3 credit points = 7,5 ECTS
recommended_courses: MB1110 Introductory Marine Science, 3 credit points = 7,5 ECTS A good introductory class if you are new to marine sciences. Otherwise, there is a lot of repetition. However, I would still recommend as it provides a nice introduction to JCU as well. MB3200 Marine Conservation Biology, 3 credit points = 7,5 ECTS MB3190 Coral Reef Ecology, 3 credit points = 7,5 ECTS Very good classes, thought by leaders in the field. Provides a unique view into the current and historical knowledge in the topics. There is some overlap between the two BZ2480 Restoration Ecology, 3 credit points = 7,5 ECTS Super fun and unique class with tons of independent fieldwork. The class was, however, very unstructured, and you were left on your own for most of it. Next to all lectures were online and hard to follow. Hopefully the structure will improve, as it is very interesting.
unexpected_costs: You have to buy your own lab coat and safety goggles if you have any lab work. I also had to buy a calculator for one of my exams as I did not bring one (didn’t think I would need it).
cost_comparison: Public transport is only 1 AUD for a day ticket.
activities_available: The university constantly host all sorts of events. Every Tuesday there was café corner, where you could go get snacks, meet people and play games. There were also larger events held throughout the semester. One included a petting zoo and a climbing wall.
activities_recommended: I liked café corner. If nothing else, it was nice to get some snacks between classes. The larger events were also always fun and often included some free stuff.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely explore as much as you can. The beach may be exiting, but for good swimming experiences visit crystal or alligator creek. Magnetic island has amazing hiking. The snorkelling is not the best dur to high sedimentation. You will get better snorkelling by booking trips out to the proper reef.
culture_adjustment: I did not experience the culture to be very different, but it definitely depend on what you partake in. I did not really go out to town much. However, I heard that you have to be very careful as there is a lot of crime and people don’t really trust the police.
socializing_tips: Be open to meet new people especially during orientations. You may have to be more persistent later on, as people settle into their groups. The more you participate the easier it is. Roommates and classmates are definitely an easier place to start off.
cultural_challenges: The fact it was not safe to go out alone, especially after dark.
culture_appreciated: The people I associated with were all very friendly and generous. I was offered rides to the supermarket by multiple people and generally people were good at sharing and helping each other.
top3_advice: Be aware that JCU is currently going through lots of changes. The change from semester to blocks and trimesters. The change to online lectures. AND the loss of many excellent professors that previously placed them as one of the best universities for marine science
other_useful_info: Townsville is known in Australia as having lots of criminal activity. People do not trust the police and Queensland in general have a lot more old fashioned people with degrading views of any non Europeans or any one in the LGBTQ+ community. (It is kind of Australia's version of Florida/Texas (not that I have ever been there))
most_rewarding: Learning about myself. Experiencing Australian wildlife and interacting with it through volunteering. I am also so happy about what I learned of restoration as well as the expanded perspective on marine biology, I learned through my classes.
greatest_challenge: I ended up enduring a mental health crisis while there, though that was due to a friend I met, not being at James Cook. James Cook University were actually very helpful in that period, as they provided free counselling. Generally, I experienced a much larger focus on metal health while in Australia compared to Denmark.

crucial_aspects: The weather - I knew I was going during the autumn semester and I didn't want to freeze.
info_ease: Not very - I had issues getting to the university and the taxi driver, while getting me to the campus, dropped me off at the wrong building. It would have been great if someone had been available to pick me up, since the University pressed me to arrive earlier than scheduled, and that is a service they provide to people who show up at the exact time they scheduled.
arrival_assistance: A student greeted me once I finally got to the correct dormitory building, and helped make sure that I understood the system and which parts of the buildings I could access.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I don't recall, sorry!
registration_help: The office for international students could provide help if any was needed, whether this just be ordinary things or if you needed help with paperwork.
registration_success: 100%, I got all of the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: No clue.
course_level: It was perfectly balanced, as all things should be. While there was a lot of homework, it balanced out and it was easy to adjust your own level of participation in most classes depending on your energy level that day.
teaching_comparison: I quite enjoyed it. It was more in the style of lectures, with a little bit of participation, for most of my classes. The language class was very hands-on and reminiscent of UCPH.
courses_enrolled: "Analyzing K-Movies in the Mass Media" (2 credits), "Introduction to Jeju Mythology" (2 credits), and "Jeju Seen from a World Perspective" (2 credits), as well as the language course.
recommended_courses: "Introduction to Jeju Mythology" - if you have even the slightest interest in folklore or mythology, this class is for you. It was by far my favourite class, and you get to dive into uncommon mythologies where English material is incredibly rare. It if it still the same professor, Hahn, then she is the one who wrote the English material on the subject, and you can ask her about a ton of things.
unexpected_costs: None, I found myself pleasently surprised that almost everything was included.
cost_comparison: The food. As someone with a lot of food allergies, I sustained myself on a diet of pre-boiled eggs from the convinience store, popcorn, instant rice & instant ramyeon. It was not healthy, and I do not recommend this location if you're unable to eat pork/beef. Not being able to eat the local cousine meant that I spent an ungodly amount on "food" every month.
activities_available: There was a sports festival (we were team exchange), as well as a various trips (for the exchange students only) during my semester. We went to a botanical garden, went mandarin picking, walked around an ancient forest, etc.
activities_recommended: Ask you buddy to arrange a hangout between a couple of the exchange students and their buddies as well. A few people's buddies did that (not mine), but from what I heard they managed to then make a friend or two at the local university. But if the university is still offering the mandarin picking trip, it's a must!
weekend_recommendations: Hear me out, "Jeju Island Teddy Bear Museum" kind of slaps. On the more physical side, climbing Hallasan should be on everyone's bucket list, as the view from the top is simply stunning (as is both the view up and down the mountain. Lastly, while it can be hard to get to, "Jeju Stone Park" on a foggy day in January is one of the craziest experiences I've ever had - it felt like a place that existed outside of our own world. If ghosts or spirits are real, that's where they live.
culture_adjustment: It was a little hard, actually, though I believe this might be because of the separation that occured between the regular students and the exchange students. Other than that, adapting felt sort of smooth, apart from the jetlag.
socializing_tips: Say yes to everything. If the debate club has an event on, go! If your buddy wants you to meet some of their friends, go! If your professor asks if you want to come to an art show along with a few other students, go!
cultural_challenges: Jeju still feels a bit backwards in regards to LGBTQ+... I didn't tell my buddy until the end of my semester, and good thing that I waited, because she ghosted me afterwards even though I owed her money. Can't win them all, I suppose. Though it would be nice if the host university included "LGBTQ+ friendly" in their buddy applications.
culture_appreciated: The craftmanship that seemed to be abundant and around every corner. They take great pride in their wares, and in being from Jeju, and it absolutely sold me on the place - I want to go back one day.
top3_advice: Consider if you have food allergies and plan accordingly, make sure to befriend your roomie, and go explore the island every weekend. A small group of us went out to different places or activities once every week, to make sure that we made the most of our time.
other_useful_info: Bring your own bedding. Yes, I'm serious. Go to Ikea, buy a cheap pillow and duvet and leave them in their vaccuum sealed bags, then pack some old covers and linens and bring them with you. It sounds crazy, but when you're going home and don't have space for your bedding, you'll be happy to not have spent an insane amount on it and can pass it on to someone else.
most_rewarding: Being able to immerse myself in the language and go exploring the island, using what I'd learned in both my language and culture classes.
greatest_challenge: Food. I'm not kidding when I say I came back home four kilos lighter and in desperate need of food that wouldn't trigger my allergies. Also, keep your meds on you - cross contamination is more likely than you think, and slowly feeling yourself being unable to breathe during language class is not an experience I would recommend.
other_comments: (The fact that this report does not automatically save, considering the absolute length of this beast. It is now my third time filling it out and I am losing my mind juuust a little. The save button won't work until you've finished the entire thing. Terrible design choice.)

greatest_challenge: Finding emotional support when your established support system is so far away, that’s also why i say it’s important to create your own little community while you’re there.

crucial_aspects: A semester abroad in Japan is a mandatory part of the University of Copenhagen's bachelor's in Japanese studies, and I specifically chose Kanazawa for three primary reasons: 1: Kanazawa is a city with a particularly rich cultural heritage. 2: It was recommended to me by others with previous experience. 3: I figured that a smaller and more quiet city like Kanazawa would personally suit me better than larger cities like Tokyo and Kyoto.
info_ease: Sufficient information was provided both on the website and through emails.
arrival_assistance: A help desk was set up on campus, which allowed me to complete paperwork there that would usually require me to visit city hall.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The course registration for the first quarter-semester only opened the day before classes started, which made registration a somewhat stressful affair. Syllabuses from past semesters were available, but they only gave an idea of what classes could be available, and you could only see the actual list once registration opened. The registration period continued through the first week of classes, allowing students to deregister from classes after attending orientation and signing up for new ones in their place. It thankfully opened a week beforehand for the second quarter-semester, though.
registration_help: An information lecture was held on the day registration opened, and I was able to contact academic advisors for help.
registration_success: It was somewhat burdensome to navigate, but I managed to successfully register for the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Try to predict what classes you would like to sign up for as well as possible before the registration period begins.
course_level: I took a mix of BA classes in the humanities and social science, and Japanese language courses at beginner-intermediate level.
teaching_comparison: I noticed a comparatively higher focus on classes than self-study. The level of digitalisation varied between classes, but it was overall less than UCPH. All of the written exams were pen and paper only.
courses_enrolled: Elementary Japanese 2 Kanji & Vocabuary 2 Cultural Anthropology Introduction to Japanese Culture & Thought International Management Introduction to Diplomacy A Critical Introduction to Modern Japanese Literature Japanese Culture E UNESCO Biospheres English Conversation Hokuriku Region Archaeology Theory of Museum Education Introduction to Modern Chinese Society Intercultural Understanding
recommended_courses: If you want to study Japanese culture and society while in Japan, then I recommend both the cultural classes and the UNESCO biospheres one. Introduction to Japanese Culture & Thought consists of student presentations on a variety of topics, ending with making a short video about your time at the university and writing a paper about a cultural topic of your choice. Japanese Culture E consists of lectures and a written exam at the end. Both courses granted me fascinating insight into many aspects of Japanese culture, society, and history.
unexpected_costs: None in particular
cost_comparison: I knew that Japan was a much cheaper country to live in than Denmark, but I was still somewhat surprised by the extent of it. Expenses such as food and rent are much lower than what I'm used to.
activities_available: Japan has a strong school club culture, and there were clubs for pretty much every common sport and hobby. The international student section also offered bus trips for visiting cultural sites and engaging in activities such as skiing.
activities_recommended: Joining a club can be a great way to befriend Japanese students, but potential linguistic and cultural barriers can cause issues. The aforementioned bus trips are fantastic ways to see parts of the country you likely wouldn't visit otherwise, and I highly recommend them.
weekend_recommendations: Kanazawa itself is a culturally rich city with many museums and sights to visit during the week. The Kenroku-en garden and the Omicho Market are personal favourites of mine. Local trains can take you to under-appreciated parts of the Hokuriku region such as the Wakuraonsen spa town, and the city is part of the Shinkansen bullet train network, which allows for easy access to other regions. Kanazawa is located between Kyoto, Osaka, and Tokyo, and I went on weekend trips to all three, which I highly recommend doing.
culture_adjustment: The biggest challenge for me was the language barrier. I had studied Japanese for about a year before coming, but I was still far from fluent. I could navigate everyday situations just fine, but more complex interactions such as dealing with bureaucracy required the use of nonverbal communication and translation tools. The actual culture wasn't that difficult to adjust to, as Denmark and Japan both value order and reservedness.
socializing_tips: The Japanese have a reputation for being reserved and difficult to get close to, but it depends on your Japanese language proficiency and social confidence. There are occasionally events to meet new people, and that's a great way to start.
cultural_challenges: I suppose the language can be called a cultural difference, and it proved a challenge, like I wrote above. I'm a somewhat socially anxious person, and I sometimes missed out on opportunities to interact with locals because I feared embarrassing myself by making mistakes while speaking Japanese. I ended up socialising with other international students more. Partially because I lived in the dormitory for international student students, which naturally made me closer to me, but also because the linguistic barriers simply weren't present.
culture_appreciated: i highly appreciated the Japanese dedication to order and efficiency. The services I needed to access were accessible and functioned well, and any communication issues I encountered were quickly resolved through the helpfulness of the people.
top3_advice: 1: Try to get a good idea of what courses you wish to take beforehand to save yourself trouble during the hectic registration period. 2: Make an effort to quickly establish social connections. Groups form quickly and can be difficult to enter if you try to join later. 3: Knowing at least basic Japanese will go a long way in your everyday life.
other_useful_info: Not particularly.
most_rewarding: To have had the opportunity to experience the society and culture in my everyday life.
greatest_challenge: Like I have described above, the language barrier proved the greatest challenge.

Community Service Vi var fire der fik lov til at være hjælpelærer i engelsk på et childrens care center, som er lidt tilsvarende en SFO, men stadig er en slags skole. Her fik vi øvet os rigtig meget i vores koreanske fordi hverken de voksne, som arbejder der, eller børnene taler engelsk. Så det var virkelig givende og en virkelig unik mulighed. Kæmpe anbefaling!

cultural_challenges: Der er virkelig mange. Jeg tror, det vigtigste er, at man ikke skal regne med, at der er noget, som er, som herhjemme. Alt er anderledes, og det skal man være forberedt på. crucial_aspects: It was an obligatory stay, arranged in connection to my study.
overall_comments: It was an overall good experience, but it might be challenging to go to KNU, if you're going alone.
info_ease: Some of it was out a little late. For example, we got the wrong dorm address, and the correct one was only updated on the day of our arrival on a platform we weren't familiar with. But the staff was super helpful and quick to reply. Orientation was adequate, but done on zoom along with the 'full time exchange students' and graduate students, so it was a little complicated to figure out what info was relevant to us, specifically.
arrival_assistance: About a week before semester-start, we had an online zoom orientation. Upon arrival, there were people who helped check us in at the dorm and provided bedsheets. A couple of days after we had a physical welcome orientation. (Before arriving, our buddies helped with course selection and such, but this was a rather complicated issue).
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was an overall good experience, but it might be challenging to go to KNU, if you're going alone.
registration_process: Were were told certain dates that we, as exchange students, could sign up on. The course registration starts at noon Korean time, so at 3am here. As some of them fill up quickly, it would be advised to try so sign up then, or get your buddy to help you. The English courses couldn't be added on the pre-date (which we hadn't been informed of), but could only be accessed when the general registration period started. Then you signed up to your courses, and the first week of classes is a trial week, so after trying the classes, you could change them or drop them if they weren't for you.
registration_help: The buddies can help a bit, but it differed how much, from buddy to buddy. They are responsible for helping you, but not doing the sign-up for you.
registration_success: I was rather lucky in getting all the courses i wanted, thanks to my buddy and being prepared with course numbers for signup.
registration_advice: Be prepared with all of your papers and course id's etc. for registration. The people at the uni are helpful, but a bit unclear at times. But contact them if you have issues. They really would love to help, and do their best to accommodate you.
academics_comments: It was an overall good experience, but it might be challenging to go to KNU, if you're going alone.
course_level: Some were very interesting and proper for uni level, but others left a bit to be desired in the academic aspects. The professors are super nice though, and as long as you show up to classes, you will do fine.
teaching_comparison: The Korean courses were a bit more strict and structured. There was marginally more oral presentations and more challenging written exams, but the courses in themselves were very informative. The English courses differed a lot. Some of them were very similar to the teaching style at KU, and others felt like a highschool course. The structure is very similar to that of college in the US.
courses_enrolled: Everyday Korean for foreigners. Pilates. Community service at an eveningschool for children age 5-8 (teaching english). Philosophy in the age of AI. Case Study of Corporate Management in Korea and Overseas.
recommended_courses: For Korean Studies Majors, I would recommend the 'Everyday Korean for foreigners' course. The course description doesn't fit, but you will learn a lot about academic Korean, how to do presentations, and write assignments. It is a challenging course, but the teacher is very good at meeting people at their level and trying to make it educational for everyone. I personally also gained a lot from partaking in Community Service. This was a great way to practice my Korean while getting to experience being in a Korean workplace. The staff don't speak English very good but are very welcoming and appreciative. And the kids are adorable and fun to teach. For the English courses, I would recommend any course with Professor Jay Park. She is very sharp and an incredibly passionate (and compassionate) teacher.
unexpected_costs: The insurance fee was higher than expected, and if you join a club you have to pay.
cost_comparison: Dorm fees were lower. Insurance was higher. Transportation was lower.
activities_available: Clubs. University festivals and events for exchange students.
activities_recommended: The festivals. Join a club, if possible. It is hard to get local friends, otherwise.
weekend_recommendations: Try do do social things. Go exploring. The nature in Chuncheon is incredible. Go hiking. Explore Korea. Go to the bars at humun. That's how you can socialize with the locals.
culture_adjustment: I already lived in South Korea for half a year before, so it wasn't personally a big issue.
socializing_tips: Join clubs and go to bars.
cultural_challenges: The caution when speaking with foreigners and using english.
culture_appreciated: The openness and kindness. If you just try to use a little korean, they are so happy.
top3_advice: Try to learn a bit of the language before you go. It is a bit far out, so not a lot of people know and are comfortable speaking English. Make sure to chick all the rules for dorm and required documents for your stay. Remember to have fun. School is of course important, but you would miss out on a really big part of your stay if you didn't engage in social activities etc. Culture is an equally big part of the stay.
other_useful_info: Beware of your absence. You are only allowed to miss the classes per course before you automatically fail. But other than that, failing is nearly impossible.
most_rewarding: The language and culture experience and the community service. By going a bit away from the main city, you truly get to experience the colours of Korea authentically.
greatest_challenge: Making local friends. They are not too eager to speak english sadly.

crucial_aspects: I chose KI both because of the university's reputation as a leading medical university in europe, their course catalogue as well as because of the many nice things I have heard of Stockholm as a city.
info_ease: Very easy both with accommodation through Karolinska as well as the contact with the Erasmus coordinator and information about courses!! All in all really nice and helpful so you can focus on being excited on going on exchange instead of stressing about these things.
arrival_assistance: I think usually there is offered a pickup by other students in the airport (a buddy system like in copenhagen) but because of COVID this was not possible. But we received a lot of guides on how to get from the airport to the accommodation on campus.
arrival_comments: I think this is due to COVID, because usually there would be a buddy system and a tour around campus, but it was no problem since the campus in Solna is easy to find and figure out where to go for lectures etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: when you get a spot through Ucph, you need to apply to Karolinska directly. I received an email with all information, links and what i needed to fill out. It was very easy and clear.
registration_help: You have the sweetest erasmus coordinator, Giulia, from Karolinska, who the danish coordinators put you in contact with and she is so nice and fast to reply and help with any question or anything you are in doubt about. I emailed her a lot both before and during my exchange and that was so nice.
registration_success: Very - I got the courses I applied to
registration_advice: Rather ask too much than too little - KI really wants to help you with any issue or question you may have
course_level: I chose 3rd year on bachelor of Biomedicine at KI, so I followed two courses on 15 ECTS each. The level was good and not too hard. I would say the level was a little lower than copenhagen, but maybe that was just because you don't get grades - only pass or fail so you can relax a little more and on my courses the level of details needed for the exam was not as high as at UCPH
teaching_comparison: There were mostly lectures, like in Copenhagen. But I missed the class room teaching a lot - like SAU or TØ. You only had lectures, but then there were also lab, maybe a few assignments and presentations which was nice to practice a little more since I haven't had that much oral presentations in UCPH. There were also a larger focus on the clinically parts of biomedicine which was interesting too.
courses_enrolled: Molecular Medicine - Oncology (15 points) Molecular Medicine - Cardiometabolic and infectious diseases (15 points)
recommended_courses: I really liked both of these courses and since they are on the same semester and year, you get to have classes with the same people throughout your stay (if you only plan to be there for 1 semester). I chose KI because of oncology which was really interesting.
unexpected_costs: Not really anything - you are covered by the EU card for health insurance (might need extra travel insurance so check that before). It seems that KI does not really use books or studying before lectures, so that was nice to not have to pay for it
cost_comparison: food is more expensive - both for going out for dinner and in the supermarkets (especially meat, chicken and fish). Alcohol is super expensive also both in systembolaget and out on bars and restaurants...
activities_available: The gym was free for students on campus, there were a few events for international students such as hikes or pub crawls you could sign up for that was nice. Also our erasmus coordinator was good to arrange dinners with all erasmus students.
activities_recommended: the KI global friends on facebook had many good events like hikes or bars etc so that was nice
weekend_recommendations: we went to uppsala one day and Sigtuna another. We also took a cruise/ferry to helsinki as well as Tallinn, where you sleep on the boat and have a whole day in the destination before returning - really cheap and a good way to see places you haven't seen - i was very positively suprised by Tallinn in Estonia!!
culture_adjustment: very easy
socializing_tips: At first the people in my class were a bit shy but after a week or two they opened up to us and that was nice! I spend most of my time with the 4 other exchange students on my courses as well as people from my housing that i met in the kitchen on the floor or through parties and other events
cultural_challenges: You can only buy alcohol in Systembolaget which closes super early in the weekend so this needs to be planned but other than that i didn't feel like there were that many differences from DK
culture_appreciated: It was nice and easy to get used to since it was so like copenhagen and denmark
top3_advice: 1) live in a housing with shared kitchen or in another way where you meet people!! crucial_aspects: I chose to go on exchange because of the academic opportunities but also very much because of the social experience. I was supposed to go to Vancouver in Canada, but due to Covid-19 I ended up applying within EU, too. I chose Stockholm as I have only heard good things about the university and the city. I also wanted to go to a place with a high academic level. Here, Karolinska ranks as the 6th best medical university in the world, and I therefore think that going there was an exciting opportunity in light of my career and to receive some of the best teaching worldwide within my field.
overall_comments: The only minus, and why I don't give a 10-mark, is because Stockholm is not that great a city for students. Karolinska moreover wasn't that a social university with a big student community, bars, and parties (maybe also in light of Covid-19). As I really was seeking the social experience on my exchange this became a small minus. Furthermore, Swedes are (like Danes) quite isolated, and it's hard to mingle with them. The educational program, I followed, was international (6 out of 60 persons were Swedish), so it was not a problem in school. The international/exchange student community was amazing, the academic level was outstanding, the housing was great, and Stockholm is beautiful and very cool, so everything else would get a 10-mark.
info_ease: The Karolinska Institute was extremely easy to be an exchange student on - both before you arrive and when you're there. Their website is super informative and intuitive, it's easy to understand their platform and find which courses they offer. Furthermore, the exchange coordinator Giulia is absolutely the sweetest and most helpfull person ever, and you can always reach out to her before, during, and after your exchange.
arrival_assistance: Not much. A girl from my educational program in Denmark, also went so we figured everything out together. Not that it is hard: you get your schedule and try to find the courses the first days, and then it becomes more and more easy. They didn't have a buddy program in autumn 2021, which could have been nice.

registration_help: KI and KU can always help you and are super sweet with a lot of support.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted. I had "Oncology" and "Cardiometabolics and Infectious diseases". Both courses was 15 ECTS.
