crucial_aspects: The reputation of the university, the course catalogue and the opportunity to explore London!
info_ease: Quite easy through KUnet and emails from the host university.
arrival_assistance: Emails with information on registration and there was an introduction week. However, it was mainly targeted at full time bachelor students and with a few events targeted at exchange students.
arrival_comments: There was no specific welcome to postgrad students at the faculty. I don't mind reaching out to people myself but I found it strange. A lot of the communications through exchange students was through informal chats and groups on WhatsApp and Instagram.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You apply for minimum 4 up to 10 courses - the earlier you apply the more likely you are to secure your dream module. It is important to note however it is good to be flexible as KCL admits you to courses regardless whether they're scheduled at the same time. Remember to check your schedule carefully for classes. I had to change a few classes after the first week as they clashed which is common.
registration_help: A small but dedicated team helping all exchange students.
registration_success: I got most of the classes I wanted. Because of a schedule clash I had to swap two classes which positively surprised me.
registration_advice: The module handbook may change between application and official registration. It is very important to flexible about courses and make sures there's more than a handful you are open too.
course_level: All MA level with full time MA students at KCL.
teaching_comparison: All classes consisted of a one hour lecture and a one hour seminar. The teaching style was focused on developing logical arguments and critical discussions, which I enjoyed. Compared to UCPH the European & International Studies Department were quite policy-oriented and in general the teachers were very engaging.
courses_enrolled: European Union & Identity, Lobbying & Policy-making in the EU, Democratic Legitimacy of International Cooperation and Russia & the European Union.
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend European Union & Identity thanks to the passionate module coordinator and with of concepts discussed.l The lobbying course requires a solid understanding of the EU but was very interesting and also included lectures with practitioners. To be honest, I would recommend all of these courses.
unexpected_costs: Transportation can be quite expensive but it is possible to get a young adult rail card to save money.
cost_comparison: I really recommend getting an E-sim and food was a bit cheaper than expected.
activities_available: A lot. There are societies for almost everything open to everyone. There is also a gym on all campuses, a swimming pool available to students, run clubs, yoga and so on. London is a great city and there's something for everyone - whether it's organized by the university or not.
activities_recommended: Free yoga if you live through uni accommodation!
weekend_recommendations: I recommend taking full use of all the discounts available to students in London! At the British Film Institute, you can go to the cinema for £4 and you can watch shows at most theaters for £10 if you're under 25. Then there's also the classics, like Big Ben, Westminster Abbey and so on. Almost all museums are free including the British Museum and the V&A. I really recommend getting a rail card if you want to travel as you get 30% travel throughout the UK. For example, Bath is a lovely city to visit in the Autumn.
culture_adjustment: Easy thanks to the language I would say!
socializing_tips: It is already a boost that everyone speaks English. As a postgrad/master's exchange student you will likely study with people who have just started their full time degrees. KCL is very international and people studying the same courses might be doing different degrees and likely confuse you with being a full time student. Roll with it and suggest going to the pub after class and don't be afraid to show up to mixers and other events which aren't necessarily targeted at exchange students.
cultural_challenges: None.

crucial_aspects: Exchange in Japan specifically was mandatory for me. I would have chosen Japan regardless though.
info_ease: The information was there but there was a lot of it. It was hard to navigate in at some times. I'm glad that me and my fellow students, who where also going to Japan, had a group thread online so we could help each other. I would recommend this to everybody who's going.
arrival_assistance: The host university had a 'buddy system'. Every exchange student got assigned to a local, Japanese student. This student helped us a lot. Most paperwork is in Japanese, so I would have felt pretty lost without her. She helped us with most practicalities: she took us to the ward office, helped us filling out papers, helped us getting the necessary health insurances and so on.
arrival_comments: The amount of information is overwhelming, but the host university did everything they could to help us.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We registered about 7-10 days *after* the semester began. This was a bit confusing because it's so different from KU, but it made sense once you understood the system. This system makes it possible to attend several lectures before you choose which ones to follow - I really liked this process. I changed my mind with a couple of courses I planned on following after attending the introduction lecture, so I think this way of doing it makes sense. Registration was done by filling out a pre-made lecture schedule in excel, and sending this to the university.
registration_help: A .pdf-guide was available.
registration_success: I successfully registered for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: The system is very different from KU. Check out the available courses before you come to Japan, and mark the ones you find interesting. Talk to your fellow students and ask them for recommendations - there are many courses so you might have overlooked some. Make a plan the first week to attend as many introduction lectures as possible. Think about if the course and lecturer matches your study style, and think about logistics (I choose classes so I had one day without lectures every week, this was really nice because of the transportation time) Also, there were few classes available in English, and more classes available in a mixture of Japanese and English. I attended introduction lectures in some of these and experienced that it was still far more Japanese than English. This was too hard for me, so I ended up only choosing classes that had lectures in English (except the Japanese language classes). The subjects of these classes weren't as relevant for my study field, but at least I had classes with Japanese students who spoke English. I learned a lot about Japanese culture this way. So I would recommend people to think about this when choosing classes. Don't force yourself to attend lectures where you won't understand majority of what's being said, just because the subject of the alternative classes don't seem relevant to your studies. In the English classes you meet Japanese students who want to practice their English, and this was where I learned the most about Japanese culture and got Japanese friends.
course_level: The level was generally lower than that at KU. In language classes it depends on what level you are placed at in the placement test.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. Most days I had to hand in homework before attending class, and you have to attend almost every class in a course to get a grade. More strict than KU.
courses_enrolled: Japanese language classes + Academic Skills + Global Justice + Global Learning Skills/Global Expat Seminar (they were both half a semester)
recommended_courses: All of them! They were all interesting, and they all had a good mixture of Japanese students and exchange students.
unexpected_costs: I was suprised how expensive commuting to university was.
cost_comparison: My rent was super cheap, and it was cheap to live as well. Going out to eat is affordable compared to Denmark and Copenhagen, and groceries are cheap as well.
activities_available: There were sports communities, cultural exchange clubs and different activities available. I attended to trips organised by the university, these were great opportunities to go on trips to see Japan, and to meeting other students.
activities_recommended: Definitely the trips. They were affordable and I got to see some places I wouldn't have seen otherwise. This is also where I met some of the people I became friends with.
weekend_recommendations: Go on those trips with other students. Almost doesn't matter to where - everything is an experience. I would recommend Nara though, not just for the deers but also for their annual Fire Mountain Festival. Also Kinosaki Onsen - an onsen paradise and a great place to try living in traditional Japanese housing. Onsens in general, also the local ones, they offer affordable and well deserved rest during a busy time.
culture_adjustment: I found it a bit hard. Everything is different, but this is also one of the reasons why the experience was so educational and interesting.
socializing_tips: Be open and ready to adapt to social norms. Participate in clubs and trips. Talk to the Japanese students in your classes.
cultural_challenges: Most of the Japanese students weren't confident in speaking English. This means that they can come of shy in for example group discussions. In my experience it's important to give them space to talk, since culturally they tend to be more reluctant to take up space. Silence doesn't mean they don't have anything to say. Ask questions instead to invite them to speak.
culture_appreciated: Were kind and helpfull people. Delicious food. Safe and organised society.
top3_advice: 1. Use the people around you, you don't have to figure out everything on your own. 2. Ask for help if you are stressed or concerned, there's always help to get. 3. Be prepared that it's both wonderful and challenging to go on exchange. And that's okay! It can be both at the same time.
other_useful_info: I can't think of anything specific.
most_rewarding: Meeting people, both Japanese and other exchange students.
greatest_challenge: To keep track of all informations and deadlines. Also in the application process.

crucial_aspects: I knew I wanted to go abroad to a country very far away to challenge myself more and preferrably a place where English wasn't very used so I would have to learn how to talk to people in another language to do even simpler things. I had a growing interest in Korea and therefore felt a slight connection as I did know a bit about what to expect being in the country and meeting the culture and people and thereby would also havr a bigger chance of having something in common with other international students. In my choosing I also thought about the general safety and access to the health care of a country, in which Korea ranked high.
info_ease: At first it was very confusing, especially as a graduate since a lot of the information I did get early on was directed at undergrad students. Finding the course list available for international grad students was hard for example. Covid 19 did make it more confusing as there was a lot more steps to every process but as we got closer to course add/drop they did end up giving out correct and detailed guides and information. We also got a welcome package/book as school began. This seemed kind of late as several of the steps in the guides had already past before we got it. Again Covid 19 kind of was to blame as well as there was no real introduction besides a short video, whereas normally you would all have met a korean buddy, gone to orientation etc. Which was all cancelled as we couldn't meet physically
arrival_assistance: Even though I arrived pretty early and in a messy situation (having to quarantine by myself for 14 days) the university already connected with me on mail and had me contact them daily and answered most questions I had. The global service center has a super quick response whenever I had questions. I did get connected to a Korean buddy before school started as well but since we couldn't meet, this wasn't as helpful as I thought it would be. Besides this we also get offered to connect with a mentor, a korean student who can help with all academic things, and a æanguage exchange buddy who will teach you korean. Most help from the school itself came through email and was ok, though a bit late with important informations making it a bit stressful.
arrival_comments: Had it not been during the pandemic, I'm sure it would have been a 5
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: As a Grad student it is a lot easier than the undergrads as Grad course selection only has one round in which it went smooth and I got all the classes I wanted after changing one halfway through add and drop. Undergrads have several rounds though and just seeing my friends go through that system and again and again not getting the courses they wanted was stressfull. Final course selection is also very late which can seem a bit stressfull (basically as the first week of classes begin you are still trying to pick your courses) For grads you basically just browse the course site to find english taught courses open for exchange students that you would like, write down the course codes and as add/drop opens you go in and add them with the codes. After the opening you have a few days to then change your courses by dropping the ones you don't want and hopefully being able to then add the one you want. Undergrads will have two free passes (which are basically extra spots in any given course) to apply for courses directly through the teacher who can add them manually if they are okay with adding an extra spot in their class. Grad students do not have these passes which did stress me out in the beginning, as relevant courses on grad level for me were kind of lacking. Thankfully I was able to still get added to a class after initial selection as I had to drop another course by simply talking to the professor directly through mail.
registration_help: I used the global service center for questions relevant to course selection. Besides this we had also gotten a digital guide and a mail about the process from our buddies.
registration_success: I ended up getting all the classes I wanted. It does seem like it is a lot easier to get into courses on grad level as there a fewer students than undergrads who have to compete for spots.
registration_advice: Inform yourself - find all the information you can and have your preferred courses prepared before add/drop. Be quick and don't be scared to just contact a professor directly to ask for a spot. The professor are all very friendly.
course_level: I took three graduate level courses all of which were in different departments and had different diffculties.
teaching_comparison: I took a contemporary art class which compared to my home studies in comparative literature was quite easy as it was mainly lecture based with one 3 hr lecture a week and very few but good readings. I also did have quite an easy time following along as I did take a contemporary art class during my undergrad studies as well and the amount of homework and classwork was very low as most knowledge was to be learned during lectures. Our midterm was also changed from a 40 minute test into a final report on the class and final exam instead which the professor let us decide as a democracy. My film theory class used so many interesting teaching styles. Each week we watched a movie, read a theoretical relevant text and wrote a short blogpost sharing our views and thoughts and then had 3 hrs of lecture mixed with debates and discussions and a student presentation on the movie. The final exam and midterm was a free choice between research paper or creative project with report - which I really appreciated. In the final weeks we had a workshop where we just had creative fun with the knowledge we had gained and then the last week was a class conference where everyone presented their final project. Lastly I took a history class in which the level felt really high. This was based on several readings a week and classes were based on 3 hrs paper presentation and discussions as each time a student was picked as discussion leader. We worked very long and focused on the final research and the teacher was very strict along the way but ended up being quite generous with her grades. All courses were graded on different aspects as professors choose themselves what to weight when grading, I had a less stressfull time during midterm as one of mine was changed and the two other's were presentation based. All courses final exams were oral based with film theories and gender history having a class conference where every student present their final to the other students, and a final paper, and my art course had a 45 minute oral presentation to the class with debate and questions after. All in all I was quite surprised at the different levels of difficulty as it varied a lot. I was also quite surprised that the oral parts of exams were all class based in front of all students. Which I was stressed about but actually ended up liking more than what I'm used to at home.
courses_enrolled: MAC638 Film Theories med Helen as professor, IMA614 Contemporary Art Theory with Raul as professor and HOK744 Study on the Political History in the Late 19th Century with Leighanne as professor.
recommended_courses: I would wholeheartedly reccommend any course you can find with Helen Sin (신 혜린) as she was by far the best teacher I have ever had in my life and her course Film theories the best course I've ever had. She created an amazing class environment for learning and I always felt excited to share my interpretations and knowledge in a way I've never felt like before. She supports and cares about all her students and their potential working for everyone to reach their full portential. If interested in art and okay with 3 hour lectures I would also reccommend Raúl Sampaio Lopés course as I did learn a lot and didn't feel too burdened. Lastly I'm not sure if I would reccommend Leighanne as a professor. Before going I saw her name mentioned positively by previous exchange students and therefore picked her class. The material and subject itself was very interesting (so interesting in fact that I decided to go further with it and do my final thesis on it) but as a teacher I did not enjoy having her at all. She was cold, rude, pressuring and unempathetic. Having her class brought on anxiety weekly as I feared her classes. You were never right and you never did well in her class. The grade she gave did not reflect how she treated me throughout the semester which makes me think this way of being is just her particular teaching style. Besides her personality I didn't particularly like the structure of the classes. Barely any lecturing and only discussions. I felt like she wanted me to know so much that she didn't even teach me since she rarely spoke. I'm sure she is super smart and knowledgable but besides picking texts for our classes and telling us when we were wrong she barely taught me anything.
unexpected_costs: They just made it mandatory for long term residents to have national health insurance on top of your own insurance from home. Which felt like a ridiculous way to double spend. Everything could be done cheaper than I did. I lived in a pretty expensive house, travelled around a lot and ate lunch and dinner/got coffee/dessert out mostly every day.
cost_comparison: Groceries. Which means I ended up mostly eating out as it was cheaper than buying and cooking for yourself.
activities_available: I am unsure as most things were shut down for health reasons
activities_recommended: Again I don't feel like I can comment on that.
weekend_recommendations: Travel around, do a few bigger trips and some smaller daytrips. Getting around is easy you just have to plan a little bit. I would reccomend Busan, Jeju, Paju, Nami Island and all parts of Seoul :)
culture_adjustment: For me it was quite easy but I was also pretty prepared and already knew about the culture
socializing_tips: Korean students - sign up for both mentor and language buddy - this will be your one way tickets to social interactions with local students. By lucl you can get good courses with local students as well.
cultural_challenges: None really
culture_appreciated: The friendliness Everyone seemed very kind, helpful and nice
top3_advice: Don't stress too much about your exams and grades ( they'll turn out just fine!), balance your time! Dont just focus on school, remember to go out and do what you want, time flies by so quickly

registration_process: You register online during the registration period. Beforehand you are able to look at classes in the system and even add them to a wish list so they will be easy to find during the registration period. Later there is a secondary registration period where you can drop classes and have a second chance and getting the ones you wanted.
registration_help: You can email the global center at the university.
registration_success: On first try I barely got any classes I wanted or were even relevant for my field of study but through the secondary registration I was able to get good classes.
registration_advice: Make a prioritised list in advance and include the course numbers so you can quickly search them during the registration period. Register right away, as soon as registration opens. It is very competitive and classes fill up within minutes.
course_level: I found the academic level in general to be similar to home with a some exceptions that were sometimes harder and sometimes easier.
teaching_comparison: Depends on the course, as it varied a lot.
courses_enrolled: Media and Gender, Theories of Media Effects, Ethics and Information Society, British and American Literature Through Film, Critical Theory.
recommended_courses: Media and Gender, and Theories of Media Effects were both good classes with good professors. Especially the latter was really engaging with lots of class discussions.
unexpected_costs: National health insurance
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive but eating out was less expensive.
activities_available: I know there were groups and activities but I didn't look much into it.
weekend_recommendations: Visit other cities like Busan or Paju, or even Jeju Island. There is lots of exciting things to do within Seoul too.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy. People were usually polite and helpful.
socializing_tips: I found that you often have to make the first step.
cultural_challenges: I thought the culture of studying to be a bit challenging. Lots of late night meetings during group projects.
culture_appreciated: Amazing food and cafe culture.
top3_advice: - Do your research on registration and have everything ready. - Make sure you enjoy the city despite your busy schedule at uni!
other_useful_info: Don't miss the university festivals!
most_rewarding: Making friends from all over the world, being on my own in a brand new place.
greatest_challenge: The heat during the summer. But you get used to it.

crucial_aspects: I am interested South Korean culture. I heard from others who stayed in Seoul that it was a great destination.
info_ease: It was okay easy. The host university was very helpful. Copenhagen University did not help me much.
arrival_assistance: Nothing.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You need to go to their website and then it is quite accessible.
registration_help: The KU GSC-Exchange/Visiting Student Team are very helpful. I asked them a lot.
registration_success: I registered for 5 out of 6 classes that I wanted. The Add/Drop period is very good if you want to change your courses.
registration_advice: It is ok.
course_level: The level in most of my courses seemed very introduction-ish. I had to drop a course because the teacher's English was so bad.
teaching_comparison: It seemed more like high school. The exams does not count as much as in Copenhagen. You have midterms, tests, presentations, and also a part of your grade is participation. Nevertheless, I liked it.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Political Science Social Network Analysis Abnormal Psychology Special Topics in Korean Studies (about religion in Korea)
recommended_courses: The course Social Network Analysis was great!
unexpected_costs: Nothing.
cost_comparison: Food is very expensive even groceries! Find cheap local small Korean places if you want to save money on food. I spent too much.
activities_available: I think a lot is available, but I am not sure since it was not operating.
activities_recommended: I don't have any recommendations.
weekend_recommendations: WHAT TO DO IN SEOUL - namsam tower - olympic park - seoul forest - insadong - bukchon hanok village - mmca - national museum - coex mall - lotte world - jogyesa temple - gyengbokgung palace - bukhansan - common ground - gwangjang market - namdaemujn market - changdeokgung palace - jongmyo shrine - national folk museum - seoul tower - deoksugung palace (mmca) - seoullo 7017 - noryangjin fish market - seoul wall trail (east side) - seoul wall trail (west side) - dongdaemun design plaza - han river - yongsan family park - sungneum gate - gangnam style statue - leeum samsung museum - cheonggyecheon stream - bongeunsa temple - hangang park - suwon - incheon - dmz - naksan park - war memorial of korea OTHER PLACES I VISITED Busan Jeju Island Seoraksan Nationalpark Yang Yang Sokcho Gangneung
culture_adjustment: I found it quite hard actually. Koreans tend to be a little bit narrow-minded. I experienced stuff as getting eggs thrown at me, yelled at in subways for talking, and denied access to restaurants and cafes. Their covid-19 rules were sometimes a bit discriminatory, and even though I was fully vaccinated I was never counted as so in their system. I know the pandemic is almost over, but it is something to consider. This was unpleasant, but I still had a great stay. The stay was just more Erasmus-oriented with a lot of Europeans compared to what I expected. Of course, I didn't attend school, so it might have been different if I had the opportunity to encounter other Korean students.
socializing_tips: No.
cultural_challenges: See the answer above.
culture_appreciated: Their historical and cultural sights. I enjoyed "sight-seeing" very much and I had many great experiences.
top3_advice: 1) Live in Simple Spaces 2) If you study social science chose the course - Social Network Analysis. It was great. 3) Be sure to exploit all the great historical and cultural options that Seoul offers.
most_rewarding: Getting new friends all over in particular Europe.
greatest_challenge: Getting to know Koreans. They are not so open-minded and the covid-19-pandemic did not help in the situation.

crucial_aspects: Det skulle være en stor by, som jeg på forhånd var fan af og betaget af. Mange muligheder og mange mennesker.
overall_comments: Bedste oplevelse i mit liv. Would recommend.
info_ease: Course registration var svært, fordi vi endnu ikke var startet fysisk på uni. Eller var alt som det skulle.
arrival_assistance: Al nødvendig assistance. Vi blev mødt af hundredvis buddies/hjælpere, som stod klar til at hjælpe med alt og få os i gang. Det er et helt program, der sikrer at alle kommer om bord, får venner og bliver tilknyttet en lokal studerende. Det er idiotsikkert. Hvis noget føles utilstrækkeligt, må man se indad, for alle de lokale gør et umådeligt flot og stort stykke arbejde. Både inden og under ankomst - og egentligt gennem hele opholdet. 10/10
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Bedste oplevelse i mit liv. Would recommend.
registration_process: Uklart spørgsmål
registration_success: The whole "do exchange here bc of these amazing courses available" spiel er bullshit. Ingen er sikrede de kurser, de får forhåndsgodkendt. Vi (dem jeg boede med - cirka 30 stk) fik maks 1-2 ud af de 5 kurser vi ville have. Jeg fik et. Course registration er et kæmpe gedemarked. Det er kaos. Det er først til mølle. Man kan være heldig eller uheldig. Alle jeg mødte var uheldige og fik ikke de det ønskede sååå. DERFOR: Vælg ikke destination baseret på et par fag du tror du kan få. Vælg på baggrund af alt andet.
registration_advice: Du er ikke garanteret en skid når det kommer til valg af kurser. Så lad være med at vælg udveklslinglokation på baggrund af et specifikt universitet med specifikke kurser du ønsker. For al sandsynlighed er at du ikke får dem i sidste ende. Vælg din by, fordi du synes den er sej og cool og altid har drømt om at bo der. Fordi folk er nice der og fordi du vil opleve den. Ikke fordi du tror du kan få et meget specifikt kursus. Please keep in mind.
academics_comments: Bedste oplevelse i mit liv. Would recommend.
course_level: Uklart spørgsmål igen. Øv.
teaching_comparison: Det er meget anderledes. En sand oplevelse. Skal ikke sammenlignes.
courses_enrolled: Writing for English Majors Language aquisition Language and media Introduction to media
recommended_courses: I would only but strongly recommend "Writing for English Majors". Hold kæft hvor jeg lærte meget - som jeg kan bruge resten af min studietid. Kurset fokuserer på academic writing og skrivestil generelt. Kurset tager dig tilbage til fundamentale byggested indenfor engelsk grammatik og skrivning de første par uger. Derefter lærte jeg bare så meget på så kort tid. Absolut det mest lærerige kursus på min bachelor. For langt til yderligere at uddybe her.
unexpected_costs: none
cost_comparison: Frugt og grøntsager er meget dyre. Tøj er meget billigt.
activities_available: all of them
activities_recommended: Just go to the club fair and see for yourself.
weekend_recommendations: You must figure that out for yourself. Cant tell you what to do or see.
culture_adjustment: Its all about your own mindset and attitude. Hvor der er vilje, er der vej. Det er ikke svært at tilpasse sig. Husk at respekter kulturen og for din egen skyld forsøg at integrere dig i den. Det er noget helt særligt. Deltag.
socializing_tips: do your research beforehand and youll know what to do and what not to.
cultural_challenges: Det ER et konservativt og traditionelt land og kultur. De er gammeldags i deres måde at tænke på og opføre sig på. På flere måde regresser de, hvilket er trist at overvære. Der er social rangorden baseret på hudfarve og etnicitet. Det er meget langt at forklare. De accepterer i høj grad heller ikke andre seksualiteter. Der er mange undtagelser, og man bemærker det ikke til hverdag. Jeg ved det, fordi jeg har haft mange gode og ærlige snakke med lokale og hørt personlige historier. Man må nogle gange sluge nogle piller. Sådan er det.
culture_appreciated: Alle er så utrolige venlige, ordenlige, velopdragen og ydmyg. Det var så utroligt behageligt at opholde sig i landet. Alle respekterer hinanden - på en måde man slet ikke oplever i Vesten. Vi kan lære så meget af dem. Ikke EN gang oplevede eller så jeg konflikt. Det er imponerende. Det har været svært at komme hjem igen, hvor folk taler grimt til hinanden, er uhøflige eller grove, slås osv. Det har jeg satme ikke savnet. Det oplevede jeg ikke i Korea.
top3_advice: Go to KU because everyone is incredibly nice there. They want to make foreign friends. Some og my best friends are from KU!
other_useful_info: Beware of the course registration period(s) - yes plural.
most_rewarding: The people! Alle the people. FOR SURE. From my classmates to my housemates to my professors to my landlord, to alle the nice ladies and gents in all the stores and restaurant to the fun people you meet on nights out. EVERYONE has been so nice and welcoming and open.
greatest_challenge: Accepting that their society and their norms and culture is different and thats okay. You are merely a guest. Make the best of it. Adapt and get the best time of your life. All the tiny negatives are LARGELY outweighed by en countless positivies! Surrender yourself and recieve the best experience of your life.
other_comments: 10/10 would recommend!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to Asia, but the countries i could visit was limited because of the partner universities, and i thought that South Korea had a lot of culture and interesting things that i could explore, and i expected a lot from their education.
overall_comments: It was the experience, the place and the people who made it a fantastic experience.
info_ease: Quite easy, you get a lot of emails from the university, however there is a lot of information. And before i was enrolled in the university it was really hard, because i had to find all the information myself, and it is a chaotic the university website.
arrival_assistance: We had an oriantation in the beginning where we got a lot of information, but it was also a bit chaotic. Furthermore there is an organiation who deals with international students, that you allways can contact if needed.
arrival_comments: We had to make a student card, that in Korea also works as a credit card, so we had to sign a paper 12 times, and everything was in Korean, so actually didn't know what we signed. It worked well with credit card, but the proces and information about it was not that well explained. Furthermore we were over a 1000 exchange students, and we were devided into 8 groups, i was the last group so waited around for at least 1 1/2 hour, it wasn't structured that well.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was the experience, the place and the people who made it a fantastic experience.
registration_process: It was long and chaotic. I got the registration quite late, first in march and i was told by Copenhagen university that i would get in within 1 month. I didn't so was really stressed about it. There was a lot of things to fill out, and i first new that i was accepted in June, which was a bit late compared to everyone else. At my host university it was easy enough.
registration_help: I could write to some from Copenhagen university, who dealt with exchange student.
registration_success: I got 2 of the courses i wanted, and the other 2 i didn't get.
registration_advice: I takes a lot of time, but don't stress about it. You will be grateful once you've been accepted.
academics_comments: It was the experience, the place and the people who made it a fantastic experience.
course_level: Quite low. I was dissapointed. One of my courses my professor could barely speak english, and he just read aloud from his power point. And sometimes he switched to korean. The other where better with english, but i didn't learn a lot of knew things. There are few homeworks, and it's mostly lectures and not many assignments or exercises.
teaching_comparison: UCPH is a lot better, because we reflect more about what we learn and discuss it, and have exercises, where in Korea it was more that you blindly trust what your professor telles you because he is a professor.
courses_enrolled: Geophysics, Environmental Geography, Urbanization and industrialization in East Asia, New Media.
recommended_courses: Environmental Geography. It was interesting. However it is a freshman course, so i didn't learn anything new, because geography is my major, but for others i think it would be interesting. New Media, was different because we watched movies and talked about them.
unexpected_costs: Changing flight ticket. And taxis sometimes, beacuse the metro stops going between 01-05
cost_comparison: Cooking home was more expencive than expected, because vegetables was a bit expensive. Eating out and drinking, and seing museums and so on, was cheap.
activities_available: They have a lot of sports, but not everything is available for foreigners, because they speak in Korean.
activities_recommended: Karaoke
weekend_recommendations: Go outside of Seoul and see more of the country. Go on hikes, there is a national park really close to Seoul. See different district in the city. Watch temples and so on. You should got to Busan and Jeju.
culture_adjustment: Difficult, mainly because of the language. Many are not good at or don't speak english.
socializing_tips: I tried really hard, but i was difficult because many are shy or don't speak well english. So i gave up a bit. But the KUBA buddies are nice and good at english, and otherwise i think it is easier to get friends that you have classes with.
cultural_challenges: There is a bit of racism in the country towards foreigners. I didn't experience anything disturbing but i know people who have, but many are also approaching you and want to speak with foreigners. A challenging things, is that you should not speak loud or barely speak in public transport. Many korean are quiet in metro and buses, and will tell you to be quiet if you are loud.
culture_appreciated: The food
top3_advice: Get out of your comfort zone and socialize a lot especially in the beginning, it's important to get friends so you don't feel lonely when you are away, it's good find a balance between being social and by yourself. Make sure to experience a lot, times fly by so don't postpone things to much. Be open to another culture.
other_useful_info: nope
most_rewarding: It an experience i will have with me for life. And i am happy that i tried it in an environment that is to different from mine, i learned a lot.
greatest_challenge: Halfway through i got homesick, and a bit tired of the culture and people in Seoul, but many experienced the same, so i just pushed through and talked with your friends and family. Furthermore there was the Itaewon crush where 162 people died, it was hard being there when something like that happen.
other_comments: It was a really great experience that i don't regret at all.

crucial_aspects: Some of the most crucial aspects of choosing my destination were the language, culture, and personal interests. My chosen country was Soth Korea, and I began involved in the culture during Covid which motivated me to learn the language and my interest to experience the country.
overall_comments: Some parts didn't work out well, but overall I had a really amazing experience.
info_ease: It was fairly easy. At first, it was a bit difficult to navigate the website of my exchange university, however, some of their services helped a lot. You have to be prepared to double-check everything, to make sure everything is in order.
arrival_assistance: At Korea University they had a Global service center which helped a lot in terms of practical information and course registration.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Some parts didn't work out well, but overall I had a really amazing experience.
registration_process: It is a long process because you have to give a lot of information and prepare a lot of documents to get accepted. Be sure to read everything twice or more to ensure you send everything the host university need to evaluate your application.
registration_help: You can always mail home the university about the process if something is unclear, however, if you just read thoroughly it all makes sense.
registration_success: At Korea University it was a bit hard to find courses that fit all the requirements of the home university and in the first registration period, you have to be prepared on the dot to get spots on the courses you want.
registration_advice: Ensure that you know the specific time of the first registration period. You may have to wake up at night or early morning for registration of courses. Have a few back up courses as well, because you may not get a spot on some of the courses.
academics_comments: Some parts didn't work out well, but overall I had a really amazing experience.
course_level: At Korea univeristy the academic level was pretty high since it is one of the top univeristies in South Korea. However, the courses were very interesting which motivated me to work hard.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style involved a lot of discussions that motivated students to participate in class. In my courses, we had research projects in groups which gave us the opportunity to get to know each better and explore and go in-depth with a specific theme.
courses_enrolled: Media and Gender, Media technologies and culture, Theories of media effects, Mass media and popular culture in Korea, and Korean society and culture
recommended_courses: I recommend choosing courses that are relevant to your field and combining Korean culture courses which can enhance knowledge about the country and its history and culture.
unexpected_costs: Did not encounter anything unexpected, however, I changed my accommodation once during the 4,5 months a spent there, which meant that my rent increased a bit.
cost_comparison: Almost everything in Korea is less expensive compared to Denmark, especially transportation. Clothes and food were affordable as well.
activities_available: They had several sports clubs like football, badminton, and dance. I don't feel like they promoted the clubs very well and for me it was hard to obtain information about the clubs available on campus.
activities_recommended: Exploring different parts of the city
weekend_recommendations: I recommend visiting other cities such as Busan and Jeju Island. There are so many diverse activities in Seoul and many cafés that offer different activities such as painting or making your own phone covers. You have to try noraebang which is karaoke!
culture_adjustment: It wasn't hard. The first few days you learn the customs and you get used to the culture.
socializing_tips: Be involved in clubs and your KUBA group which will be assigned to you at orientation!
cultural_challenges: When you are a foreigner in Korea people tend to look at you more (mostly older citizens), however, most people were very sweet.
culture_appreciated: The language and the Korean pop culture (k-pop).
top3_advice: Be sure to plan everything far in advance, work load might be higher, and be involved in your KUBA groups social activities.
other_useful_info: Be aware of all the deadlines when applying for the exchange program as well as the courses you need to enlist in.
most_rewarding: Getting new friends and experiencing all the amazing activities and spots in Seoul
greatest_challenge: I had five courses which was a bit much and a bit stressful at times, however, it is required when applying as an undergraduate student

crucial_aspects: It was relevant for my studies.
info_ease: Everything was send on email, more than once, so it was very easy to find the information as long as you made sure to read all the emails carefully, since a lot of information gets send out.
arrival_assistance: I didn't really receive any assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: All the information gets send to you via email for both undergrad and graduate courses. So I just followed the guide and saved the names and course codes for the courses, which made it easy to sign up.
registration_help: It was always possible to write the global service center and ask them for help if needed. They answered within a day.
registration_success: I registered for all the classes I wanted. And for the other classes I considered taking, it was possible to ask the professor during the introduction week if it would be possible to participate.
registration_advice: Just follow the emails and ask if you have any questions, then it will be really easy and simple.
course_level: Despite the courses feeling a little bit harder and more demanding than in Denmark, I wouldn't say the level of the courses was that much different. There was a lot more homework in terms of reading material than I'm used to and the amount of work that has to be submitted throughout the semester was also fairly larger than in DK.
teaching_comparison: Most of the courses expected the students to participate and take control of the class, so that the professor kind of worked like a meditator. There was a lot of presentations from the students and not that many lecture style classes.
courses_enrolled: I took Emerging Media, Film Theories and History and Theories of Cultural Studies all at the Graduate School of Media and Communication.
recommended_courses: I didn't take any exchange student only courses, thus I was for the most part the only exchange student in my class, however all of the professors were really helpful and very kind, so I would recommend taking any courses that you're interested in. In particular for the courses I took, Film Theories was really good and the professor was very engaging and encouraging everyone.
unexpected_costs: Nothing really.
cost_comparison: Nothing.
activities_available: They had clubs and also activities both cultural and social for exchange students through KUBA.
activities_recommended: I didn't do any, since everyone was mostly undergrad students.
weekend_recommendations: If there is time, I would definitely recommend travelling outside of Seoul.
culture_adjustment: Since I've been there many times I had zero problems adjusting.
socializing_tips: It is definitely easier if you take regular courses and not exchange students courses, if you want to talk with them.
cultural_challenges: Nothing.
culture_appreciated: Most Koreans are really friendly and helpful.
top3_advice: Read the emails carefully, since all information is send via email. Be open towards new people and new experiences.
other_useful_info: Nothing I can think of right now.
most_rewarding: Gaining a lot of new knowledge as well as some very close friends.
greatest_challenge: Finals.

housing_how: I found housing on my own

recommended_courses: Media and Gender, the teacher was great, the subject was thrilling and educational

activities_available: Dinner with tutor groups and football matches as far as I've been informed. Might have been other social activities I was not informed about

culture_appreciated: The safety, the politeness, the food, the culture
top3_advice: Make sure you get information from the university, make a group chat of people from UCPH going to the same host university for social life and help, don't get too hung up on academics and remember to enjoy and have fun
