crucial_aspects: I chose the destination South Korea, as i wanted to experience a culture and a country i didn't know. I chose it as it was an overseas destination, a non-english speaking country, and somewhere which i had never been. I also chose South Korea as the semester timewise aligns well with our semester at University of Copenhagen.
overall_comments: I loved it! Would recommend the experience!
info_ease: I think it was easy. The most complicated thing was having to register for Alien Registration Card upon arrival. But the Korea University did a good job at informing us about the application process.
arrival_assistance: We received assistance from the school itself as well as buddies. The buddies were very willing to help, if we had problems with anything also. I had some complications with borrowing books atthe library though. Here the global service center at Korea University was quick to reply but not really helpful.
arrival_comments: Mentioned above.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I loved it! Would recommend the experience!
registration_process: Courses open at a specific date and time. You better b e ready to sign up for the courses right as they open, or you can be almost sure not to get into the course. There's an add/drop period at the first week of the semester, which was a saving grace for many students who did not get the courses they wanted in the beginning.
registration_help: I got luckily got admitted to my prioritized courses in the first try, so I don't know.
registration_success: Successful (but lucky that i wanted unpopular courses). But I also got permission to attend to courses, which were originally unavailable for exchange students.
registration_advice: Be ready when registration opens. And do have a plan B, if you don't get your prioritized courses.
academics_comments: I loved it! Would recommend the experience!
course_level: It was different. One course had a really heavy work load and i very high academic level. The others were also good but a bit more easy.
teaching_comparison: One course was very similar, the two other very different. I had one course were the final was a memorization test, which is very unlikely and uncommon within humanistic disciplines (at least in Denmark).
courses_enrolled: MAC638 Film Theories IKS316 Korean Cinema In A Global Context IKS317 History Of Korean Art
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of these courses, however, the last two are normally not available for exchange students. The first one, which is available, has a very talented professor. She has a very engaging teaching style, and i learned so much during this course. But the workload is very heavy.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay for NHI (National Health Insurance) even if you have travel insurance. It's not very expensive, but it is annoying. You also have to pay for applying for Alien Registration Card (ARC). Phone plans are also quite expensive in South Korea, and you do need a Korean phone number to book an appointment for ARC. Otherwise most other things are cheaper in South Korea than in Denmark.
cost_comparison: Phone plans are more expensive. If you plan to do any free time activity (i signed up for a yoga studio for instance), these can also be pretty expensive. Food is cheap! And you can live really cheap if you're willing to live in a very small space.
activities_available: There was a lot of dinners with your KUBA group (Korea University Buddies Assistants) in the beggining. They also made a trip to a theme park. There was an international students festival also, but I didn't go.
activities_recommended: I signed up for a international yoga studio called the Flow Room. It was a it expensive but really nice. Even though there are many things to explore, it's important to make time for your usual hobbies .
weekend_recommendations: To travel around South Korea when you have time, maybe just for weekend trips. There's so many other areas that are interesting to explore besides Seoul. Almost all exchange students made sure to visit Busan and Jeju Island, so save up for these trips! I also did a templestay for christmas, which was absolutely amazing, and not very expensive!
culture_adjustment: I had a pretty easy time adjusting, but I also love exploring foreign cultures, and did research in advance, so I didn't really experience culture shock.
socializing_tips: I mostly socialized with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Mostly that many things are hard to do without a Korean Phone no. and Alien Registration Card. You will get your ARC 2-3 months into your stay. You also need to make sure your phone plan offers official authentification. You need these to pay for anything online, order food, make appointments online for clinics and doctors, reservation for sports games, cultural events etc. This is a nuisance for a foreigner who has just arrived in South Korea
culture_appreciated: I think people were very talktative and open, which was really nice! It's easy to find someone to speak to. The food is also so delicious! I would recommend to both explore th traditional as well as the more modern aspects of Seoul, there's so muvh to learn and see! There's often interesting public events such as fireworks, lightshows and markets which were so much fun to attend!
top3_advice: 1. Sign up for courses the second course registration opens. But even if you don't make it here, know that you might still be able to change it in the add/drop period. 2. Ask if your phone plan offers official authentification before buying it. 3. Visit destinations outside of Seoul such as Busan and Jeju Island.
other_useful_info: If you do off-campus housing BE CRITICAL. They're not honest when it comes to pictures and size of rooms/apartments. But remember that probably won't spend so much time in your room anyway, as you're out experiencing South Korea and Seoul. So maybe it's okay to live small, as long as it's cheap.
most_rewarding: Just to get to experience and live in a foreign culture. You are able to immerse into the experience differently than if you're just on vacation which is very rewarding.
greatest_challenge: To sign up for things and make reservations withou a Korean Phone number (with official authentification) and Alien Registration Card.
other_comments: It's not as normal to do gap years in other countries as it is in Denmark, so depending on your age stage of your studies, you might experience quite an age gap. I'm a 25 year old graduate student, and most local students and exchange students are undergraduates, who has not done any gap years. Also as most exchange are undergrads, in my experience the University sometimes "forgot" to deliver information to graduate students. For instance the course list for graduate students is difficult to find, and towards the end of the semester the Global Service Center forgot to add graduate students to the mailing list (meaning we had to ask for information regarding grading, transcripts etc. ourselves, while this information were automatically delivered to undergrads).

crucial_aspects: Explore new cultures
info_ease: Very easy
arrival_assistance: All the exchange students had a mentor who was a student at Korea University.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We got an email from our host university in which they explained the whole process.
registration_help: It was possible to contact the Exchange Student Team from our host university, if there were any problems with the registration process, or if you had any questions.
registration_success: Considering the limited amount of English courses offered for exchange students, I was very lucky.
registration_advice: Before registrating for courses at your host university, read the course syllabus and make sure that the class is relevant for you and that it is a topic that you find interesting. That will make the experience way better.
course_level: The courses were MA courses taught in English, and while the academic level was high, it was still possible to keep up with what was expected from the students.
teaching_comparison: At Korea University it was very common that the professors wanted students to be very engaged in class. Preparation before class was very common, and they typically wanted us to upload a reflection paper on different articles once a week. They also wanted us to discuss the articles in class. This teaching style is a bit different at UCPH where you're often not obliged to attend classes or expected to participate in class. I really liked Korea University's form of teaching style, as it forced students to be fully engaged and participate in discussions.
courses_enrolled: 1. Topics in cultural studies 2. Public Organizational theory 3. Image and Litterature
recommended_courses: It really depends on what topics they find interesting.
unexpected_costs: During winter, me and my roommates whom I shared housing with, had to pay for an extra gas bill which was a little expensive. So be aware of that.
cost_comparison: Clothes were more expensive than expected. Food was less expensive than expected.
activities_available: Everything.
activities_recommended: Traveling.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city and spend time with friends.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy.
socializing_tips: It can be difficult to socialize with local students at the university. However, if you participate in the different activities at school, there's a good chance that you can become friends with them.
cultural_challenges: Nothing particular.
culture_appreciated: I liked how everyone minds their own business. Also you feel very safe in the city. You can leave your belongings on a table everywhere, and it will not get stolen.
top3_advice: Participate in the activities hosted by the university - that's a great opportunity for you to make friends.
other_useful_info: If you choose to live off campus, make sure that your place is close to a subway - particularly line 6 as it takes u directly to the campus and you don't have to change lines then. I would recommend that you choose courses with different workloads, so you do not get overwhelmed.
most_rewarding: Everything.
greatest_challenge: The language barrier.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience a totally different culture, as well as new ways to experience university life.
info_ease: We received informative emails about everything we needed to know, so it was very easy to find.
arrival_assistance: We were all given a "buddy" we could contact if we had any questions about anything. A buddy is basically a korean student who will help you throughout the semester if you need anything. We also had introductory courses.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process is a first come first served process, so you need to be quick if you want specific courses. There was a period where we could choose our preferred courses and thereafter a period where we were able to pick your final ones. The first week of the semester, we could swap out courses if we needed to.
registration_help: I received a document were everything was detailed with important dates and so on.
registration_success: I was semi successful, i got a few classes i wanted but i should have chosen more, so i could try a bunch of courses and then drop the courses i didn't find interesting.
registration_advice: I would recommend researching each course your find somewhat interesting and read through the syllabus provided for the course. Then choose many courses so you have a few backups if you aren't able to get the courses you wanted.
course_level: I found the level of the courses to be quite easy, however, i had to spend a lot of time studying.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was very different compared to UCPH. I had two courses that heavily focused on discussions where the professor would act as a mediator or a discussion facilitator.
courses_enrolled: Programming for Policy Informatics Theories of Media Effects Entertainment and Strategic Communication
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Entertainment and Strategic communication as our professor was very kind and a good at creating useful discussions. I also liked getting tangible skills or tools for strategic communication.
unexpected_costs: I did not really have any unexpected costs
cost_comparison: I did not expected produce, like fruits and vegetables, to be so expensive, which is why i rarely cooked any food myself. Eating at restaurants or fast food places in general is quite cheap.
activities_available: I did not join any clubs, however, there were a lot of social activities available that i did. They had a lot of pop op events or small concerts. I do know however that there are a lot of different clubs available to join.
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend trying all the different restaurants and cafes that are available, as well visiting other cities around the country.
weekend_recommendations: Jeju Island and Busan are good destinations.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy, as the people are very friendly.
socializing_tips: I would attend a lot the social activities and events that are held during the semester, as well as just being friendly and respectful when talking to the locals.
cultural_challenges: I didn't really find any cultural differences that challengin.
culture_appreciated: How social people are. People are frequently out eating dinner, drinking together and enjoying each others company which was probably my favorite part of their culture.
top3_advice: Attend as many social activities as possible, soak in the city and don't be afraid to try new things and make mistakes or even ask your fellow student for help if you need to.
other_useful_info: Get familiar with the campus as it might be confusing to find the locations of each class.
most_rewarding: Completing my courses and feeling like a left the country with a lot valuable experiences both personally and academically.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was probably living by myself, as i have been used to living with other people my whole life. However, there are a few places that offer social living which i have heard was pretty good.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to try something new, and see psychology in a totally different part of the world :)
info_ease: Oh wow, it definitely took some help. The Global Service Center at Korea University were amazing at helping, and had orientation and always answered questions and emails within one day.
arrival_assistance: Well, the university helped a lot, by making us buddy groups (like tutors) and social help like that. Global Service center also gave us a very good guide book, with introduction and guides to both university life and also immigration etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It's kind of hard to remember now, but it was a lot of documents and a fee etc. But it all worked out, it just takes time to fill out. I was very stressed out about it, but luckily it was all online. For visa, it was annoying that I had to prove how much money I had, but I just borrowed some and sent it back, to send them the screenshot. It all worked out. It feels like a lot of back and forth, but it is all worth it in the end. Also note, that for the VISA you have to give them your passport for 3 weeks during summer! That almost fucked me up haha! But you can go talk to them if you need it anyways, they were super nice.
registration_help: Honestly, not much. Did it myself. Just takes a lot of investment and time.
registration_success: 5/6 classes, and course registration in the beginning was definitely the most stressful time.
registration_advice: I HIGHLY RECOMMEND e-mailing the professors of the classes that you want PERSONALLY WAY BEFORE COURSE REGISTRATION! Because they DO have power over who gets their class. And I DID NOT do this, which I highly regret, because other people did it before me they got the class before I did, which resulted in a ton of stress for me. It all worked out though luckily. Also, when the day of the course registration happens (it is like clicking and getting concert tickets) go to a PC Bang (like a computer gamer place) and use their high speed computers. It helped me, and also was a fun experience. Even though I didn't get even half of my courses at that time, it all sorted itself out in the end. So put ice in your stomach! Your exchange won't come crumbling down because of course registration.
course_level: It was not harder, there was just more work during the semester, which scared and surprised me at first. They also have a different respect for the professors, so I was kind of scared to talk to the professors in the beginning, but they were of course all really nice, and I wish I had asked them more questions during the semester sooner. In general the cognitive courses I took were pretty high level, but the professors also seemed to be kind of famous and knew a lot of people in the fiels? I actually don't understand that no one else has gone to Korea University before for psychology, I think they really have some cool professors and thinkers there, also for New Media psychilogy and cultural psychology classes with lots of discussion and nuance.
teaching_comparison: More assignments, more monitoring of people's learning, more obligatory participation that counts for your grade. Midterms and end exams. It reminded me more of high school, but in general I actually really learned a lot. Group work was consistently a challenge throughout the semester - my impression was that people don't want to meet up and actually do the work together, which frustrated me through zoom calls and texts etc. We had plenty group presentations and assignments in general.
courses_enrolled: Learning and Memory Cognitive Neuroscience Behavioral Economics New Media Psychology Cultural Adjustment and Exchange Popular Culture and Society
recommended_courses: Learning and Memory (was super hard in the beginning, but I ended up LOVING this class. I learned a lot about super detailed leanring and memory cognitively) Cultural Adjustment and Exchange (super cool prof, and cool texts. definitely high work load, but high pay off as well) I wanted to take Media and Gender, but couldn't fit it in the course plan...
unexpected_costs: The obligatory health insurance that you have to pay every month for Korea (NHIS), you get a letter in the mail, it is 350kr pr. month.
cost_comparison: Food was less, phone was more. transportation was less. In general, everything is less expensive than København (its really amazing, I had the best time)
activities_available: KUBA (Korea University Buddy Assistants) made basically everything available from bars and clubs to sports events restaurants, specific foods and places to go etc. Just ask them. https://www.instagram.com/koreauniv_kuba_official/?hl=da
activities_recommended: There was a great language exchange club called LECA, but most clubs were closed for foreigners.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Seoraksan for hiking. Go to Yang Yang beach for surfing. Go to Busan. I didn't go to Jeju You can use Agoda for transportation to these places. If transportation is hard to figure out, ask someone in your class! They are shy, but they will help you.
culture_adjustment: Easy! Korea University made it very easy I think! But I mean still weird and crazy in the beginning of course. But don't worry.
socializing_tips: You can do it! Go to the lanugage exchange group. Ask buddies to go to lunch and coffee with you. And class mates as well! I was nervous to sit by Korean students in the beginning, but ended up making friends with a couple by forcing myself to sit with them hahaha. And asking for how to get online books etc. And group work!
cultural_challenges: Their shyness for sure. Not being able to speak the same language.
culture_appreciated: Omg the going out to eat, karaoke rooms, the quietness in the transportation, ugh everything, I miss it so much.
top3_advice: 1. ENJOY OMG IT GOES BY SO QUICKLY - JUST DO IT!!! 2. it's okay to take down time... and relax and just be. just sit and watch, just walk around. It doesnt have to be sight seeing everyday - I ended up enjoying my everyday life the very most. 3. sign up for a hobby, like i took dance classes with some friends, do martial arts or fitness or something right away. get that everyday life going!
other_useful_info: The Haesong Law Library is the very best place to study...... Take a long walk around campus!
most_rewarding: Making friends from around the world (through KUBA and through simple spaces)
greatest_challenge: all the beurocratic stuff. I lost my wallet and had to go to the immigration office a million times because of it. So annoying. Bring an extra card from ur bank at home!!

crucial_aspects: It was important to me to do my study abroad outside of Europe and as I have lived in Asia before, but never South Korea, it was an interesting opportunity for me.
overall_comments: I struggled a lot to find a university with courses that made sense with my major so I was very limited in my choices.
info_ease: Very easy. Korea University sent a lot of information and was very helpful with the application and visa process.
arrival_assistance: Assistance was much more limited upon arrival. Study portals and course information were primarily in Korean and I had to figure a lot of things out on my own. Korea University has a buddy assistance system (KUBA) where all international students are assigned a Korean student to help them and a bigger group that arranges social events. It is great for the social part but they were little to no help when it came to the navigating Korea and the university.
arrival_comments: Korean students are super nice and want to help you but often they can't because things are different for international students and they simply don't know how things work for us.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I struggled a lot to find a university with courses that made sense with my major so I was very limited in my choices.
registration_process: The course list gets published at the beginning/mid-July and registration opens mid-August. Registration is first come, first serve so it is important to be ready right when it opens as some courses fill up in seconds (not exaggerating). Then the first week of classes is a sort of trial week after which an add-drop period starts and you can drop any class you don't want and sign up for any available ones.
registration_help: Korea University sends a lot of emails explaining and preparing you for the registration process and it's pretty straightforward.
registration_success: I initially got pre-approval for 8 courses by UCPH but only 3 of those actually ended up getting offered. After a new search, I found additional courses and ended up getting all but one course that I wanted. Only 1 of the courses I ended up taking was from my original pre-approved list.
registration_advice: Make sure you have a lot more courses pre-approved than you need to give yourself enough options.
academics_comments: I struggled a lot to find a university with courses that made sense with my major so I was very limited in my choices.
course_level: The level felt very much like the level in Copenhagen, if anything not higher.
teaching_comparison: The teaching is very much based on student participation and I had to do multiple in-class presentations for all of my courses. The only exams I had were term papers that I had all or most of the semester to write, but I think that is only typical for graduate courses.
courses_enrolled: Human rights in global and regional context, Approaches to international peace, and Family demography and health.
recommended_courses: I would recommend “Human rights in global and regional context”, or any human rights course taught by Dr. Jeongeum Choi. Her teaching style is super engaging and I got so much out of her course.
unexpected_costs: The Korean National health insurance is mandatory once you get your ARC. You do get told about it before, but it was more than double what I thought (370kr/m).
cost_comparison: Groceries and especially fruit were a lot more expensive than I thought, almost Danish prices. Convenience store food is super cheap and really good. Plane tickets to many other Asian countries can be super cheap and I ended up going on a lot more weekend trips than I had planned. In general I eat out and traveled a lot which is why I ended up spending so much. It can definitely be done cheaper
activities_available: KUBA arranges a lot of dinners and social events, and depending on your buddy they might arrange day trips and other outings in smaller groups. There are supposedly clubs and sports you can participate in, but I don't think it would be possible to know about them or sign up if you don't speak Korean.
activities_recommended: In september there are this big sports competition against Yonsei University and a huge street party afterwards. I am not into sports at all, but it was one of the greatest experiences of my entire exchange. Definitely rent a Hanbok when you go to the palaces. It is very encouraged even for foreigners and it's a super fun experience.
weekend_recommendations: Of course do a trip to the DMZ. Try to travel at least a little bit within South Korea, but if you want to go somewhere during Chuseok book it early! Also, try to go somewhere not too popular (like Jeju and Busan) as it gets super crowded with tourists. I went to Jeongju for Chuseok and it turned out to be a super interesting city.
culture_adjustment: The culture shock was a lot bigger than I thought it would be and there are a lot of unspoken rules in society I didn't know about.
socializing_tips: It is difficult if you don't speak Korean. I only had courses with other international students so I only interacted with Korean students at KUBA events.
cultural_challenges: The general level of English is a lot lower than I expected and apps/websites are almost always only in Korean.
culture_appreciated: Safety. Both being able to feel safe at night and traveling alone but also Koreans don't steal. People will just leave laptops and wallets on tables and no one ever takes it.
top3_advice: Reach out early and make connections whether it is other students from UCPH going to the same university or other international students at Korea University. It's going to make it much easier navigating Korea and the university, and to not feel lonely. Time goes by much faster than you think so don't postpone too much, get out there, and make the experiences. Don't stress too much on the academics, it's all pass/fail in the end.
other_useful_info: Try to at least learn how to read Korean before going, even if you don't speak it. A lot of Korean words are just English words spelled with Korean letters so you'll be able to read a lot of signs and menus which is super useful. If you are able to get an international credit card like WISE definitely do that because Visa/Mastercard will not always work.
most_rewarding: The people I lived with and the friendships I made with people from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Everything is app-based or requires signing up with a Korean phone number. As a non-Korean, you will run into a lot of logistical issues because you either don't have your ARC number or a Korean bank account or phone number, or because those are not properly registered with your ARC number.

crucial_aspects: Academically, I knew that Korea - and especially Korea University, as it is part of SKY (the top universities in Korea) - was well regarded, so I did not have to worry about the level of education. However, the main driving force behind choosing Korea was my interest in the country and its culture. I wanted to try living in a country that was very different from Denmark, so I looked toward Asia. I ultimately chose Korea because it felt more “Western” than many other Asian countries, which I believed would make it easier to adapt.
info_ease: It was fairly easy. Korea University was very thorough in their emails and provided a lot of information, which significantly reduced my concerns about not knowing what to do. Before arrival, they shared detailed information about both on-campus and off-campus housing to help students get started with their search. They also provided clear information about when and where to meet on orientation day before the semester started. Since I chose on-campus housing, I also received detailed instructions on how to travel from the airport to campus, which made the arrival process very straightforward.
arrival_assistance: There is an orientation day where you meet fellow exchange students as well as your buddies. Buddies are local students who are part of a program called KUBA, and their role is to help exchange students with any questions they may have. Each exchange student is assigned one buddy before orientation day and the start of the semester, and the buddies also arrange group meetings and dinners throughout the semester. If you have questions, you can either contact the Global Service Center at Korea University or reach out to your buddy.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The process initially seems very intimidating because there are many required documents and several strict deadlines. However, both Korea University and KU in Denmark are very good at providing detailed emails explaining exactly which documents are needed, what to submit, and where to send them. If you gather the documents and follow the instructions as soon as you receive the emails, the process is not overly stressful and is very manageable. Therefore, the administrative work should not discourage you from applying.
registration_help: They always provided a contact person or a department email address that you could write to if you had questions. In most cases, you would receive a response within a few working days.
registration_success: I applied for preapproval for 10 courses (5 courses = 30 ECTS) so that I would have multiple options when registering. However, 6 out of the 10 courses were not offered that semester, as the preapproval was based on the previous semester’s course list. As a result, I had to apply for new preapprovals quickly. Course registration at the host university operates on a first-come, first-served basis, and registration opens according to Korean time. This meant I had to be ready at 3 a.m. Danish time to apply. Depending on how popular the courses are, they can fill up within seconds or minutes, so it is very important to be prepared. Fortunately, I managed to get all five courses I applied for.
registration_advice: They provide clear information and detailed descriptions of the required documents and deadlines, so my advice is to complete each task as soon as you receive the email. This gives you plenty of time to handle any unforeseen delays. It is also easy to get in contact with both KU and Korea University if you have questions. Most importantly, make sure to keep all deadlines - you may lose your spot otherwise.
course_level: For the courses I took, which were mostly media-related, the academic level was quite similar to that at KU. One notable difference is that Korean universities use midterm and final exams, and the exams are often multiple-choice, true/false, or fill-in-the-blank. Therefore, this might make the examination format somewhat different, depending on your major.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was very similar. Some classes were lecture-based, where you primarily listen, while others required active participation and usually at least one presentation during the semester. All of my presentations were group-based and very similar to those at KU, so there was nothing unfamiliar.
courses_enrolled: (서울-학부)미디어데이터사이언스입문(영강)(INTRODUCTION TO MEDIA DATA SCIENCE(English))-02 (서울-학부)미디어비평(영강)(INTRODUCTION TO MEDIA CRITICISM(English))-00 (서울-학부)미디어와민주주의(영강)(MEDIA AND DEMOCRACY(English))-00 (서울-학부)미디어학입문(영강)(INTRODUCTION TO MEDIA(English))-02 (서울-학부)소셜미디어의이해(영강)(UNDERSTANDING SOCIAL MEDIA(English))-00
recommended_courses: I would recommend INTRODUCTION TO MEDIA and UNDERSTANDING SOCIAL MEDIA. Both courses were well structured, and I really liked the professors, who were very kind and engaging. Introduction to Media is a lecture-based course where the midterm and final assessments consist of two assignments rather than exams. Understanding Social Media is more interactive and discussion-based, but the professor is very welcoming, which creates a comfortable learning environment. Both courses provide valuable insights into media on a global scale and its societal impact.
unexpected_costs: It wasn't unexpected for me but a nice to know anyway. You have to pay a mandatory national health insurance which is about 77.300 KRW (364 DKK) every month. You will get more information about what it is and how to pay when you arrive.
cost_comparison: Generally everything is cheaper in Korea - food, drinks, clothes, electronics, etc. So I chose to not bring that much clothing and then buy while I was here. For food you can cook yourself, but you won’t save much, if any, compared to eating out. Of course, depending on where you eat as well - some restaurants are way cheaper than others, e.g., Korean restaurants are quite cheap where you can get a big meal for 10.000 KRW (50 DKK), other places like western, especially if also popular, can cost around 22.000 - 30.000 KRW (110 - 132 DKK). Something that surprised me a lot was that fruit is really expensive. It costs more than in Denmark, so be prepared to either spend some money on fruit or live without.
activities_available: There are all sorts of activities and we also got information about which clubs we could apply for. I do know some clubs can be difficult to enter if you don’t speak Korean. However, I know some exchange students that joined a football club and went to matches against other schools. But I didn’t apply to any.
activities_recommended: I mean it really depends on what you like. Like I said, I didn’t apply to anything so I can’t really tell how the process is. But if you like hiking, Seoul is a very good place to be - it is located next to mountains, so there are some good trails and also just walking in the city you can come across some very steep hills.
weekend_recommendations: A lot of people use the time to travel outside of Seoul to see more of Korea - mostly Busan or Jeju are really popular places to visit. Although Chuseok, which is a national holiday in Korea where you get almost 1 week off, is very popular to travel and therefore it is way more expensive than any other time. What a lot of people did was to choose courses that didn’t have class on Fridays, so they would get Friday off completely and then spend the weekends traveling.
culture_adjustment: It entirely depends on you and the mindset you bring with you. I did a lot of preparation and learned about the culture before I went, so the culture shock wasn’t that big for me - although there were still plenty of things and moments that surprised me. The most important thing is to be open-minded and respectful toward both the people and the culture. Koreans are generally very friendly, especially if you show genuine interest in the country and its culture and behave respectfully.
socializing_tips: Early on I got myself a Korean girlfriend and almost all of my friends were locals, so I did a lot of socializing with local students. Regarding getting friends, we probably wouldn’t have become friends if I hadn’t taken the initiative to approach them and encourage them to meet up. That’s not something I would normally do in Denmark, but I felt it was necessary in order to get to know people. However, I think my curious mindset and friendly, respectful approach made it less difficult for me. There is still a language barrier, and not everyone feels comfortable speaking English, which can make things a bit challenging. That said, my encounters with people happened quite naturally. The main takeaway is that you generally have to be the one who takes the initiative. Before I went, one of the things I did to learn as much as possible about the people and the culture was to download a language exchange app called Tandem. I don’t speak, write, or fully understand Korean, but I thought people might still be interested since many want to practice their English - and a lot of them were. They were eager to share information about their country and culture, and I received plenty of advice on what to do and not to do, what to see, eat, and experience in general. So, if you’re interested in immersing yourself in the culture and making it easier to connect with people, I would definitely recommend trying that app or similar ones.
cultural_challenges: As I’ve mentioned earlier, I did a lot of preparation and actively wanted to immerse myself in the culture, so there wasn’t anything specific that I found particularly challenging. Danish and Korean cultures are quite different, so what feels most challenging can vary greatly from person to person.
culture_appreciated: I really like Korean culture, so it’s hard for me to single out just one aspect. However, if I had to choose something I find particularly influential, it would be that people are generally very polite and respectful, which makes you feel welcome and comfortable being there.
top3_advice: 1. Be kind and respectful - this is highly valued in Korea. 2. Be open and proactive when meeting people, even if that’s not something you would normally do. It will ultimately make your stay more fun and enjoyable. Remember, others are often in the same situation as you and want to meet new people too. 3. Stay in the moment and enjoy the experience. Time passes very quickly, so try to be present and make the most of it while it lasts.
other_useful_info: Before you leave, you’ll probably need to have your photo taken at a photo store, as it’s required for your visa application. If possible, ask to receive a digital copy as well. When applying for your ARC (Alien Registration Card, which functions as your ID), you need to submit a digital photo. In my case, I only had physical copies, so I had to find a photo store in Korea to get my picture taken again and obtain a digital version. It’s not a big issue, but if you can take care of it in advance, you might as well do so. I applied for the ARC around the beginning of the semester.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all over the world was extremely fun. Building meaningful relationships with people who are very different from you gives you so much to learn from, and it often leads to fun and memorable moments when cultures clash. Those experiences were probably my most cherished moments, along with forming genuine and meaningful connections with others in general.
greatest_challenge: Honestly, I’m not sure. My exchange went quite smoothly, so there weren’t any major issues. The few less-than-ideal situations I encountered were easily resolved without any significant consequences.

crucial_aspects: It was far away, and a culture that i otherwise never engage with. I also didn't want a place were english was too common.
overall_comments: A memory for life.
info_ease: Korea is different of course. But generally you can find guides in english. If you do a bit of research before leaving, it will not be too scary.
arrival_assistance: Korea University has a "buddy system" which means that local korean students are assigned to different groups. You could always text your buddy if you had any questions.
arrival_comments: They know what they are doing, you are not the first exchange student to go there. The orientation was, however, extremely long and full of information, and it was 36 degrees celcius that day... They are very thorough in Korea.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: A memory for life.
registration_process: They required proof that you had a certain amount of money, or that your parents had. And then of course you had to go to the embassy to apply for your study visa. Then the University sends you a LOT of information. You have to read it thoroughly. Luckily they also outline the application process in steps, so you know what to expect.
registration_help: You could e-mail the university, but they prefer that you just read the application material thoroughly.
registration_success: Very successful. But you have to stay up until 3am in the morning to register, because it is on a first-come-first-serve basis. Some people even go to high-speed internet cafés just to have a higher chance of getting competitive classes.
registration_advice: Read the materials, and take notes, so you don't feel stressed.
academics_comments: A memory for life.
course_level: If you just study a little bit, you'll be fine. I took Korean Language I, and that was hard. Everything else was extremely easy.
teaching_comparison: Many multiple choice quizzes and basically no readings. Mid-term exams and final exams are equally important. You cannot miss classes, because that will affect your grade. Otherwise the style of teaching is very methodical and thorough, but in a way that makes it easy to grade you on wether or not you were listening to the professor. Just show up, take basic notes and you'll get an A.
courses_enrolled: Korean Language I Popular Culture Composers of Classical music The Genre of Classical Music Ancient Chinese Law and Philosophy
recommended_courses: Ancient Chinese Law and Philosophy was super interesting. Learning Korean is also amazing, and very rewarding.
unexpected_costs: NHIS - National Health Insurance. They require you to sign up to an insurance that costs about 375dkk per month.
cost_comparison: Food is not expensive, but you'll often eat out as the way to be social. Housing was cheap if you choose Gosiwon, and transportation was only 300dkk per month, and i used it every single day.
activities_available: The buddy system was great! We often went out for drinks and food with all the other exchange students and the other Korean Buddies. A lot of music festivals and other excursions are also available.
activities_recommended: So much. Go hiking. Go to Sokcho. Go to Busan. Go on a Temple stay. There is an infinite amount of delicious food. Go clubbing in the safest environment i've ever been in. Go visit Jeju Island. There are so many things to do.
weekend_recommendations: Grab drinks with koreans, and go on hikes and trips to Busan and Jeju.
culture_adjustment: Koreans can be shy, but generally very welcoming and polite. If you are respectful and kind, you will make a lot of friends.
socializing_tips: Join the KUBA events. The buddy system will help you meet many different people.
cultural_challenges: Seoul is a busy city, and you can feel that. They are more conservative in many ways when it comes to the body, yet I never felt that personally, but it is noticeable. Some few places they didn't really want foreigners, but it was very rare.
culture_appreciated: I really enjoyed the Korean culture in general. Very polite and nice all around, and i never felt unsafe anywhere i went. Just be respectful and you'll be welcomed.
top3_advice: Don't be a "Koreaboo". Just because you like K-Pop and K-Dramas, it does not mean you know what it means to be Korean. They have a tough history, and you should be respectful of the fact that it is not like you see on TV. Go and listen to undergound music! There are so many artists and cool venues. Be curious! Try to get some Korean friendships! It is so valuable and awesome to not feel like a tourist. Actually hanging out with locals that can give you advice and perspectives is amazing.
other_useful_info: You will have to get something called an Alien Registration Card! If you want the best experience, get it yourself, and not through the institution. It will go much faster, and you need it for many things.
most_rewarding: The friendships i made. For sure. The moment it felt like i actually lived in another country, was also pretty cool. Learning Korean was a part of that.
greatest_challenge: I went on a very slim budget. I had to really be careful about spending too much money. If you are smart and save up, you'll be fine.
other_comments: Korea University was a great experience. I can't recommend it enough. But don't go because you think the classes will be amazing. Go and engage yourself in the history and culture. Learn the korean writing language "Hangul" before you go. It is actually much easier than you think, and it will help you a lot.

overall_comments: I got ill halfway through.

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I got ill halfway through.
registration_process: It's all a blur. Course registration was super stressful - in the middle of the night - but plan it out carefully, and you will probably get most of the courses that you want.
registration_help: They respond to emails super fast!
registration_success: Pretty successful. I got two or three of the courses that I wanted in the first round, but two of those actually ended up being the courses that i disliked the most. My favourite course was the one that I added last, only because it was available and fit into my schedule.
registration_advice: Sign up for the courses that seem intimdating and and maybe a bit too hard - the ones that are mostly aimed towards local students. Those are more intersting and engaging, and the academic level usually isn't that high. Also, sign up for 6 course if you are in doubt, and drop the one you dislike the most during the add and drop period.
academics_comments: I got ill halfway through.

recommended_courses: My favourite courses were Cognitive Psychology, Korean Thought, and Political Science.
unexpected_costs: ARC gruppeansøgning- 100% det værd.... ting til værelset og tupperware.
cost_comparison: Vestlig mad er dyrt!
activities_available: Hanging out with your buddies - KUBA has A LOT of events. You can also join clubs, and a lot of clubs actually want more internationals, but information about clubs is scarce for exchange students. Ask your buddis for more info!
activities_recommended: Cycling/running along the streams or the hangang river, and going to cheap/free concerts at small and local venues and bars.
weekend_recommendations: Travel within the country, and go hiking! Explore the bar and cafe scene in Seoul!
culture_adjustment: Easy - also, Seoulites are used to interacting with internationals.
socializing_tips: Take initiative and be open! A lot of local students are eager to make international friends, but are sometimes a bit introverted or insecure about their english.
cultural_challenges: Hierarchical structures at university, and a lack of self-determination for students. The fixation with getting good grades, and presenting as a hard-working student. Going to a good university is more important than studying what you want, so a lot of students take courses that don't really interest them. Oftentimes, students seem disengaged and were obviously sleeping in class - the only thing that really matters, is doing well on the standardised tests.
culture_appreciated: How polite and sociable everyone were. I expected the Koreans to be more introverted and keeping to themselves, but I honestly think most Danes would seem a lot more hostile and introverted to a foreigner
top3_advice: 1) If you want to join a club, have some ideas in mind already before going, and ask specifically about clubs relating to those interests. 2) Remember to take pictures! 3) Stay somewhere outside of Anam - otherwise you'll end up staying in the same area 24/7.
other_useful_info: Talk to your professors in person! Navigating a foreign university-system can be hard and stressful; if you are stressed or struggling, talk to your professors about it, and they will certainly be ready to help guide you. I felt too intimidated to ask questions or ask for help in the beginning, but when I started talking to my professors about my struggles and worries, thay were actually very understanding and accomodating.
most_rewarding: Learning to appreciate the things that I take for granted at home!
greatest_challenge: Being away from friends and family and the lack of freedom.

crucial_aspects: I chose to go on exchange because I have always wanted to use that opportunity while I could, and COVID-19 ruined my exchange plans on my bachelor. Also, I was recommended to go on exchange as it was considered a big plus for both academic and career opportunities. I choose Leiden in The Netherlands because I have never been to The Netherlands in the first place. The next question before I choose Leiden was: where to go in The Netherlands? I picked Amsterdam as my 1. priority, Leiden as my 2. priority and Rotterdam as my 3. priority. I ended up receiving a spot at Leiden University. I choose Leiden due to my gut feeling. I have never been to The Netherlands, so I had no experience or information on to base any informed choice. During my initial research on Leiden, I just had a good feeling. I liked the courses I could pick, I liked the city as it was beautiful and the geographic location made it a perfect spot to explore the Netherlands, located just between The Hague and Amsterdam with less than 30 minutes both ways. Also, all the reports from other students spoke very highly of Leiden and I have heard good things about The Netherlands as a culture and country.
overall_comments: I can highly recommend Leiden University as your destination as it is an extremely international student-friendly city, but please bear in mind my recommendations and comments in this report as I did experience some rather frustrating difficulties.
info_ease: It was okay easy. The websites were a bit difficult to navigate, but everything was in English. Also, the local coordinators were good to remind you by e-mail if you needed to do something or forgot anything. So I never experienced the shock of missing out on any vital information.
arrival_assistance: On my way to Leiden, I was on my own. I had to find the address and all that by myself. Luckily I meet a very friendly German girl, who was going the same way as I was. Leiden University boasted that they had a stand to help with info at the airport, but I never found it. A local student organization organised what they call an OWL-week, which is an introductory week for all international students. That was extremely helpful in making new friends, getting to know the city, getting a bike, and all the necessary preparations for my stay. It was also very good fun.
arrival_comments: The Netherlands don't accept VISA or Mastercard most places, so be prepared for that. Cash or get a Maestro card. I used Revolut
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I can highly recommend Leiden University as your destination as it is an extremely international student-friendly city, but please bear in mind my recommendations and comments in this report as I did experience some rather frustrating difficulties.
registration_process: They perceive you as a humanities student due to our study being located on KUA, but all the communication and IT courses at Leiden University are on the science campus in which we are familiar or have skills in. Also, the deal between KU and Leiden, is that we request at least 15 EC points for humanities courses during our stay. If you care about your courses for academic purposes, then think twice about Leiden, as there are only two courses on the humanities faculty that make sense for our line of study. The last 15 EC points are free choice. Since they are in doubt of our academic profile, you will get rejected for all humanities courses when you seek approval. Arrange a meeting with the coordinator the first chance you get to address this problem. Also, just apply for every single humanities course when you apply, as they will most likely pick the course they think is best for you as they course based on available seats. I had no say in what humanities courses I ended up having. Very frustrating process.
registration_help: There are two coordinators on site who can help, but they are overburdened and help is slow. If you get into any trouble, then go to them physically or arrange a meeting. It speeds up the process. Patience is key.
registration_success: Not at all. I don't know if it was a lack of supervision or whatever. They ended up choosing my humanities courses for me, as my academic profile did not fit with any of the courses as most courses had some sort of required pre-acquired knowledge or earlier taken course. I choose for myself three courses that made sense for our line of study, at the science faculty, but those were tough, and only do it if you are motivated, as they will take a lot of your time.
registration_advice: Leiden's selection of courses for exchange students on a master level is vague and most don't make sense for my line of study. Ergo, Leiden is best for bachelor students looking to go on exchange. There is an approval process after you have picked your courses. Ergo, you are not guaranteed anything. So apply for as many as you can or want, to make the process easier in the end. Also, if you want to have the freest time to explore and delve into the culture. Pick three courses with 10 EC points. I choose 5 courses with fewer points, and I spend almost as much time on those as I would have had on 5 courses with 10 EC points. Also, the science courses make the most sense for our line of study, but are difficult and require a level of maths that we do not have. I you go that way, be prepared. The best advice, apply for all courses you find interesting, as you will most likely get rejected by almost all of them. Also, pay attention to the prerequisites for each course and registering process, as some courses require special registration at the master level. Also, some course descriptions are vague and you might be surprised. Again, don't be picky. Also, stay for courses at the humanities faculty if you are going on exchange for the experience and not the academia. Also, make sure that the coordinators know you need 30 EC points. Some students from other countries don't, so it is not a given.
academics_comments: I can highly recommend Leiden University as your destination as it is an extremely international student-friendly city, but please bear in mind my recommendations and comments in this report as I did experience some rather frustrating difficulties.
course_level: Science courses are difficult. Humanities less so. Most, I learned, choose humanities courses to make it easier for them. I thought that I could take it easy with some of the courses. Turns out, the grading in Leiden is way tougher than KU, and therefore slacking was not an option in order to pass.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. The grading system is different. The assignment requirements are a max number of words. Also, your total grade over the course of the semester varies in each course, as each course's grading is up to the teacher. Be aware of that.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Machine Learning Managing software evolution Computation creativity Language, culture and cognition Language documentation
recommended_courses: Pick the ones with the easiest exam or semester plan, as you most likely will have little influence over which courses you end up having. I ended up spending to much time on my studies, and therefore I did not get to do all I wanted.
unexpected_costs: I spend around 25.000 DKK each month. The level of social events and activities blew my mind and my bank account, but it was good fun. Also, they are several trips and events to go on, and they cost money. I also went on several international trips, and they were quite expensive. It is possible to spend a lot less than I did.
cost_comparison: Public transport was expensive. The food and beer were cheaper. Otherwise pretty much the same as in DK.
activities_available: They are so many activities you can take part in. The amount of those was insane. There was something for everybody. Sports, clubs, books, cooking, etc. There was everything.
activities_recommended: Do some sports and join the ESN events and parties. Also, don't be afraid to go alone to things, most others do that as well. You will not be disappointed.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the country. Go out. Go see the culture. Make trips with your new friends. There is a lot to see and do. Also, make a journal of the all things you do. Will make it much easier to explain what you did to your friends and family.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The dutch do some things differently than we do, but in general, the culture is pretty much the same as here in Denmark.
socializing_tips: Don't be afraid to say hi. Most are also looking for friends. Remember to cross boundaries and be open-minded. Go to the events!
cultural_challenges: No challenges. Leiden is lovely, and everybody is very nice! But, remember to acquire a maestro card! Most places don't accept VISA or Mastercard. Everybody speaks English.
culture_appreciated: The dutch people are very social. Expect a lot of social and cultural events. They are also very helpfull.
top3_advice: Get a maestro card! If you are a master's student in communication and IT, don't be picky with your courses and expect difficulties. If you are a bachelor, go for it. GO FOR HOUSING ASAP! I cannot stress this enough. Some were homeless and staying with friends for the first couple of weeks.
other_useful_info: The Netherlands is a crowded place. It is the same size as Denmark, but 3 times the population, which means a lot of big cities, etc. Go out of Leiden and see the country. most_rewarding: All the new friends I got, all the things I saw and did, and the experience of being alone in a new country. It was also 4 months but felt like a year. So much happened!
greatest_challenge: Entertaining myself. Finding groups for projects on my own. Finding time to do all I wanted.

crucial_aspects: I was searching for something rather similar to Denmark and danish culture, but still wished to try something different - The Netherlands was the perfect mixture
info_ease: It was not really offered, but I showed up at the front desk at the university one day and there they helped me figure out the discrepancies I expierenced in my schedule

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: finding courses and applying to them was not too difficult, but Leiden do not offer that many anthropology courses - and many of them would be too similar to the ones I have already taken in Copenhagen, why it was difficult to find enough ects within my own faculty - I ended up doing a double major in dutch standards, and even though the courses where very interesting I would not recommend that to anyone - the burden was at times too much
registration_help: The exchange coordinator was very helpful
registration_success: Not very - I ended up taking which ever courses was advised, as it got too close the start of the semester
registration_advice: Apply early, but don't expect to get the courses you think at first
course_level: the level was quite similar to that of Copenhagen, but the study load why more extensive. I found it rather challenging ro balance school and social life due to this, but am also really appreciative of the challenge
teaching_comparison: It was much more classroom oriented - rather different
courses_enrolled: Introduction to international organisations (IO) Religion in the world Economy and Ecology Digital Anthropology
recommended_courses: IO is too intensive as it takes place over only one block and is a very fundamental course for that education - it is however rather fun to take a class in the hauge, so I would recommend that. Economy and ecology was my favourite course - super interesting
unexpected_costs: Don't park your bike illegaly - the municipality will take it and you'll have to pay to get it back
cost_comparison: Housing is expensive, but groceries 20-30% cheaper than in Denmark. I did not have to buy books for school
activities_available: Different clubs for the different faculties - also something called ESN, which I know people thought was fund to participate in different activities through, such as trips to other dutch cities or parties
activities_recommended: just say yes to everything
weekend_recommendations: go to other cities - Leiden is so central! you can get to Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Harlem, Antwerp, Brussels and much more in a very short time
culture_adjustment: I really liked living in the Netherlands and Leiden is a beautiful town, but it is rather small - I don't think I was expecting to live in such a small place, so that was something I had to learn - I spend a lot of my times with friends in Amsterdam, so I got the best of both worlds
socializing_tips: I spoke to almost no dutch people. Leiden is very much an international school and I found that there is quite a divide between the internationals and the dutch, unfortunately - I would say the best way to get in contact with dutch people is on social media :)
cultural_challenges: Not really any big cultural differences, but rather surprising to find it such an international university. Also that they have both midterms and finals - a lot of exams!
culture_appreciated: I loved the cities and their architecture - dinning out culture is also great! especially in Amsterdam - a lot of places turn in to parties during the night, which is always fun
top3_advice: 1. Try and get a room through Duwo 2. Don't forget to take care of yourself and your social life during exam seasons 3. Explore Amsterdam and other cities - Leiden is cute but small
other_useful_info: If you don't feel like you have all the information or answers before arrival, go to the student help desk - it helped me a lot
most_rewarding: meeting new people and learning to study in a different way
greatest_challenge: the same as the most rewarding parts - but that's great I guess
other_comments: overall I find that the help available from UCPH coordinators pre-departure to have been lacking. I would strongly encourage more meetings or office hours - not only for those outside of europe. We felt quite lost.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere I had a connection to. Somewhere I knew someone, so a country where I would already have contacts. I also wanted to choose somewhere with good academic opportunities and where I would be able to travel easily, I.E. where I could communicate with people easily. I had been in the Netherlands before and knew I enjoyed my trip there. I have good dutch friends too.
info_ease: It was easy! There was plenty of information online about practical matters such as Dutch systems and transport. Leiden university were also very good at providing online information about what to expect upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: I stayed at a student accomodation where there were other students able to help us with general information. Additionally, the university of Leiden had planned an option "introduction week" for new students. As I participated in this we got a lot of information both about the university and the city.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: For Leiden university they let temporary exchange students pick through a separate system compared to how regular students do. You're on a much simpler platform and are able to wish between classes. You're informed through that platform if there's space for you on the course or if you need to apply for more courses. You can find available courses in their course catalogue and are guided on how to do that by university reps in online meetings before the exchange begins.
registration_help: We were able to write the exchange office if we had any questions or problems. I was in contact with them multiple times and they were always very helpful. They also plan a few online meetings and presentations for incoming exchange students to give out general information and allow people to ask questions.
registration_success: I got rejected from a few of the classes I wanted initially because of a lack in availability for those courses. However, the other ones I ended up taking were also very interesting and I enjoyed them immensely.
registration_advice: Be quick! Overall I believe that if you apply for something early then you're more likely to get it at Leiden. That goes both for classes and housing. Other than that you just have to keep yourself updated on the process so you can react if you need to reapply for something. It's also very easy to ask for help or ask questions if you're unsure of something.
course_level: I took courses primarily at year 1 and 2 levels, one third year level. Like in UCPH a bachelor is three years long normally. The quality of the courses are very high. I wouldn't say any of them were difficult to follow if you're an active student but you don't need to worry about taking 1st year courses. They're still going to be interesting for you I think.
teaching_comparison: There are multiple different variations of teaching at Leiden university. The lectures are generally less interactive than they are at UCPH. A professor might ask a few questions but some ask basically none at all. It greatly depends. "work group" or discussion group classes are very active. They're not like the work groups we're used to where you can choose to participate. It's necessary for most of them that you show up ready to participate in dialogue and should be aware of this.
courses_enrolled: Big Media Dutch Painting 1400 ¿ 1950: Introduction to the Art History of the Netherlands, Cultuurwetenschap I Cultural Memory of World War I & II Culture and Society of the Netherlands: An Inside View Course History of Modern Philosophy Art and Self in the Age of Consumerism
recommended_courses: The Dutch painting course was incredibly interesting if you want to learn more about art and dutch culture in general. It was designed to be at a level where you could participate even if you aren't an art history student and very interesting. I also really enjoyed the Big Media and History of Modern Philosophy courses. Both of them are more introductory and accessible to everyone but with very interesting material and great teachers/professors.
unexpected_costs: The housing was pretty sparse when i first moved in so there were quite a few essentials which needed to be bought. Cleaning supplies and basic interior like towels, etc. If you move into a student accommodation I think you should expect to spend at least some money on these things.
cost_comparison: Food was cheaper than i expected. Compared to Denmark the stores are slightly cheaper, but the dutch also have weekly or bi-weekly markets where you can buy groceries. These are quite a bit cheaper and the food is fresh. If you're good at shopping at the markets you can save money. Eating out is also quite a lot cheaper than in denmark.
activities_available: There are multiple clubs you can join at Leiden university even if just for a time. There's also a university sports center where you can either use the gym or attend sports.
activities_recommended: The city of Leiden have a lot of activities that happen in the city around the year. Festivals and celebrations of any kind. I would recommend exchange students participate in Dutch festivals if they hear about them.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend traveling. The Netherlands are beautiful, even the parts that people don't usually go to. Even if transport costs a bit, the trains and public transport is easy to navigate and different cities have a lot of different things to offer.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. It's similar enough to Denmark for you to adjust quickly but different enough to be interesting.
socializing_tips: Speak to people in your classes. If you can chat with the people sitting next to you, you might get to know someone new. Especially if you're taking classes mostly attended by Dutch students, make an effort to get to know people there.
cultural_challenges: You have to speak up in stores and in general. I'm a quiet person but you learn to ask for help or to claim your space. It's not about rudeness but rather about making it clear when you need help.
culture_appreciated: The Dutch people are generally very friendly and welcoming. It was really nice to see people interacting so much and getting to be part of that. The market culture and the speciality stores like grocery stores or butchers mean you go out between people more and makes life feel very active and connected.
top3_advice: Look for housing early! It's difficult to find and you want to be first on the list. Enjoy the courses you're taking and soak in what you can learn. The academic level is very high and the professors experts in their fields. Take advantage of the fact that you can study at other faculties than just your own. Go see the different buildings, libraries, and the botanical garden.
other_useful_info: Even if you don't have friends that are going there, don't worry. There's a lot of exchange and foreign students at Leiden university, so even if you're considering going alone, you will be able to make new friends there. They might just be really good friends too!
most_rewarding: Leiden university is very old, with history back to the 1500-hundreds, and it was amazing to attend a university that old and storied. Even most of the buildings are newer, you can really feel that it's an institution of academic renown and the level of education goes along with that.
greatest_challenge: I had some personal difficulties while being away. A parent undergoing a big surgery while I was in a different country. It was hard to concentrate during the time that was going on but I tried my best to enjoy the experience anyway.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to stay somewhere in Europe and to also stay at a place that I knew had a good reputation and that other students had been happy to stay at.
overall_comments: I really liked the exchange semester.
info_ease: It was very easy for the most parts
arrival_assistance: My student housing provided me with a bunch of documents that I could read. I also attended the Orientation Week, at which I could ask all of my questions and they also gave me a bunch of documents and guides to read.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I really liked the exchange semester.
registration_process: When I had been accepted by your home university, I received an email with a login, so that I could access the Leiden application form. From there on it was a step-by-step process and pretty easy to follow.
registration_help: I wrote a lot of emails to the receiving institution. I found them generally more helpful and nicer than my sending institution. They also replied pretty fast, which was nice.
registration_success: I did not have to enroll myself. The exchange coordinators at Leiden did that for us. I did however find it difficult to know which courses were available as some of them is only available every two years.
registration_advice: Really take a good look at the course selection. I was surprised that I did not have many options. I thought more courses was going to be available, but it turned out that many of them were only there every two years.
academics_comments: I really liked the exchange semester.
course_level: They had levels from 100 to 600 and only courses with a level above 300 were master level. I only did courses at 500 or more. As for the difficulty, I found the courses pretty difficult and very comparable to those at University of Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: It was very similar. I was surprised, however that they also have participation grades in some courses and that might be included in the overall exam grade.
courses_enrolled: - Biophysics and Bioengineering - Model Organisms in Cancer Drug Development - Infectious Disease Therapies - Medicinal Chemistry and Drug Discovery - Science and the Public - In-Vivo Biomolecular Interactions Underlying Diseases
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the course Biophysics and Bioengineering and Infectious Disease Therapies. Those courses had good professors that also provided us with the opportunity to see their labs. The levels was also good.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs. I also did not have to do the language test, but in case you need it, keep in mind that it is pretty expensive.
cost_comparison: Groceries, housing and public transportation were all very expensive in the Netherlands. I was surprised that I did not have to buy a single book for my semester. All the books that we needed were handed out for free.
activities_available: The University had planned an Orientation Week (OWL). I also spend some time in the University bar and at the sports center, attending different sports classes.
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend attending the OWL week. During this week you will be guided through the city and you will meet some awesome people. I met the group that I stuck with for the rest of my semester and we will definitely be friends always. I would also recommend going to sports classes at the sports center. it is a good way to move and meet new people at the same time. Lastly, I know a lot of people who became ESN members. This is an organization for international students and they plan all sort of fun activities and parties.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend seeing the museums and doing day trips to Amsterdam. I also went on a trip to Paris with my international friends and that was very fun. lastly, I would recommend always going to the city markets. Here you can meet local sellers, eat yummy food and just stroll around.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy
socializing_tips: It was pretty difficult to get to know any locals, but I did meet some at the sports center, when I attended the classes. I would also say going to the university bar is a good way to meet locals and then just to be open minded and kind during school.
cultural_challenges: I did not find anything that challenging.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the markets every Wednesday and Saturday. Those were really nice. I also liked that the Dutch people will take every opportunity to sit outside and soak up the sun. They have a lot of good terassen, which is basically outdoor cafes.
top3_advice: 1. Trust the process. Even when it does not seem like it, things will probably work out somehow. 2. Be in very good time for the student housing and be ready the second that the rooms are released. 3. Check where you are going to be studying. They also have a department in the Hague, so make sure that you have enough time to commute between the locations.
other_useful_info: 1. Some courses are not available every other or every semester. Check that beforehand 2. You can apply for rent allowance, which might be very helpful because the rent is so expensive here 3. Remember to register at the municipality 4. Sign up for the Orientation Week 5. Some exams are on paper, so always remember a pen.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding thing was meeting amazing people there. I have met some of the best people and I expect that we will keep in contact forever.
greatest_challenge: I normally enjoy having everything under control at all times. This entire process was sometimes a bit stressful and I get a lot of anxiety if I feel like I don't have everything under control. The entire exchange experience was also about letting go of some control, because sometimes you can only do so much.
other_comments: Enjoy your time and go to all of the markets and terassen in the city. And eat a lot of Stroopwaffles.
