crucial_aspects: It was important to me to be able to go to a country/university I found interesting but which also had courses I would like.
info_ease: It was quite easy, but some things were difficult because I felt some information could have been combined information instead of separate.
arrival_assistance: None, other than Residential Assistents at the place I was living.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I felt like you had to go through different websites in order to register: finding the courses on university website, apply for it in one 'back end' system, and having the actual student website (similar to Absalon) a completely third place. Again, I feel like having one system (like KUnet) for this would be much easier. Many times during the registration process (and just the application process for both UCPH and Leiden) I felt lost and confused.
registration_help: None that I was aware of.
registration_success: I was not able to do two specific courses because it would clash with my ECTS points, but I did get into the classes I wanted regardless.
registration_advice: Take your time! Don't rush the process, it can take some time to understand and find information.
course_level: My classes were on something called 500 'level', what that means I do not know. But, personally I felt very satisfied with the level of my courses.
teaching_comparison: The biggest difference was that all three of my courses were split between two professors. It did not bother me, but I do prefer having just one professor and their style of teaching.
courses_enrolled: 1) Core course 1: Critical perspectives in Art History & Musuem Studies, 2) Interculturality: Key concepts, 3) Popular Music: Pleasure, Ideology, Technology
recommended_courses: The third one, Popular Music: Pleasure, Ideology, Technology! The professors were really proficient and the syllabus was really interesting. I also find it extremely interesting to research and analyze how something as broad as music can have an impact culturally.
unexpected_costs: Fees on paying for housing. Twice I had to pay 400 DKK extra to pay my rent because I payed with my Danish bank account. I would recommend getting a local bank account, transfer from the Danish into the local one, and then pay with that one after!
cost_comparison: Less expensive. Denmark is one of the most expensive countries in the world, so for me it was cheaper to live in the Netherlands.
activities_available: I know there were quite a lot especially with ESN (Erasmus Student Network, and they had a Whatsapp group where they sent information). At the institution itself there was also things you could join, however for a price. I wanted to join an afterschool activity, but ultimately opted out because of the cost.
activities_recommended: I don't know as I didn't join any. I wanted to do drama though!
weekend_recommendations: Go to see other cities in the country! I was lucky enough to live in a town where it was easy and close to go to other cities.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, the Dutch culture is very like the Danish.
socializing_tips: Talk to the people in your class! I was also living in a place where other students were living, and I ended up socializing more with them than my classmates. So, I'm a little bummed I didn't spend more time socializing with my classmates, even though I still managed to get friends from there!
cultural_challenges: There was no cultural challenge.
culture_appreciated: That it reminded me so much of the Danish culture, it made me feel at home away from home!
top3_advice: 1) Like I mentioned before, the process for applying can be difficult to navigate in, so remember to do your deadlines within a good timeframe. 2) Do the introduction week! It makes it easy to meet new people and see what the school has to offer. 3) Remember to enjoy yourself as well as doing your academic work. To have fun and explore the culture, to me, is just as much a part of the exchange as the schooling is.
other_useful_info: Have money saved up for when/if you get housing through the university! I thought you would have to pay at a later date, but I actually had to pay what I think was around 21.000 DKK in June (first month + the last two months of rent, I think).
most_rewarding: Getting the opportunity to get away for a semester, and stand on my own two feet alone. In Denmark most of us are used to living with roomies, but by going on this exchange I was able to live alone and experience this for the first time in my life. I also had great and interesting courses that taught me new things, and of course the friends I made doing my stay!
greatest_challenge: I had some personal challenges during my exchange, but otherwise it was an amazing experience!
other_comments: Do it if it is possible for you to go!!! It is a once in a life time experience, and I am really happy I did it.

crucial_aspects: My dad is dutch and wanted to connect with that part of my heritage and family.
info_ease: Fairly easily. A lot information came my way which was overwhelming. But the host institution has a good set up to guide me through it.
arrival_assistance: Information was given to my through emails.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After I was nomianted for a spot I rememeber having to filling out some information online, not much else.
registration_help: There was an online meeting with a presentation going over all the information. But when my home university sent my over my nomantion later, this had already happened. And I remember being quite nervous about how everything was going to be filled in. It was only when I wrote to the host institution that they informed me that there had been an online meeting. It had luckly been recorded and was shared with me. So it all worked out. Just a bit odd that I had to ask for it.
registration_success: Reasonably successful. I did as recommended by the host university and applied for 35 ECTS credits, even though I only needed 30. This was done so that if one subject was rejected, you didn't have to wait any longer. And that's exactly what happened. I was rejected from one subject and only had 30 ECTS credits left. It was a bit stressful because I was afraid of doing something wrong. But I think the host university was really good at informing me about everything I needed.
registration_advice: To apply for 35 ECTS even though only 30 is needed, beacuse then you won't need to reapply if one course is rejected. Checking your email often and keeping track of things. There are many deadlines to meet. Contact the university if you have any questions, they are really good at guiding you through it all.
course_level: Similar to my home university. I was surprised by an exam that really required multiple choice answers, as it didn't really seem like it would be at a BA level when you're working with humanities and art history.
teaching_comparison: I was similar. Some course more dialog based some lectures with many students. Both I know from home.
courses_enrolled: The History of Museums Artivism Digital Media, Culture and Society Memory and Decolonization
recommended_courses: Memory and Decolonization. Great course with insigtfull points. Dialog based teaching in a way that really works. Exam reflects they way you learn in class.
unexpected_costs: activites with new friends really added up but was worth it.
cost_comparison: Public transport is very expernsive.
activities_available: Many many options. I did not parctipate that much. I did attend few social gatherings.
activities_recommended: I dont have any recomedations
weekend_recommendations: Art museums. Going and exploring other citys such as Utrecht, Rotterdam, Amsterdam, Harlem
culture_adjustment: The culture was very much like the culture at home.
socializing_tips: join the intro week!
cultural_challenges: no
culture_appreciated: to bike every where
top3_advice: Participate in the introduction week. Keep an eye out for activities happening in the city, such as the Saturday market, October 3rd, King's Day and Pride. They do it really well and the whole city participates. They have lots of nice cafes where you can study.
other_useful_info: no
most_rewarding: Learing more ducht culture and langauge, meeting many international friends. Getting to know a city so well. And most of all maybe living in a boble where all concerns were left at home.
greatest_challenge: Making friends. Learing what need to get done to pass courses, as it was differnt then what is expected at home.

arrival_assistance: The teachers/tutors were very helpful and welcoming, although I wish LJMU had planned an introduction day/week to get to know the other students and meet other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I really enjoyed my time in Liverpool with an amazing group of international friends Highly recommend it!

registration_help: I emailed the staff and they were very friendly and helpful.
registration_success: I wanted to study Graphic Design and Illustration which isn't in the screen school program, but I was allowed to attend.

crucial_aspects: Several aspects played a role in the destination I chose. LMU is a high ranked university in Europe, which definitely entered my mind when making my decision. In addition, I know a few people in the city which help make up my mind. Geographically Munich is located such that it allows for a plethora of weekend trips e.g. skiing during winter season or hiking when the weather allows it.
overall_comments: The university and support groups set up for a great exchange semester. Unfortunately, the pandemic did play quite a large role as the semester went on and in the second half of the semester all classes were online.
info_ease: All necessary information was more or less readily available online or through supplied information by email.
arrival_assistance: A welcome meeting (on zoom, however) was arranged before the semester started. This allowed for all exchange students to ask questions if necessary and to some extent meet each other. A whatass group was created and shared in the chat during the zoom meeting.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The university and support groups set up for a great exchange semester. Unfortunately, the pandemic did play quite a large role as the semester went on and in the second half of the semester all classes were online.
registration_process: The entire process is detailed through email and is fairly straight forward. Just keep an eye on your KU-mail and everything should be self-explanatory.
registration_help: If you have any questions an email-address is stated in the enrollment email.
registration_success: I was able to register for all classes/seminars I wanted to.
registration_advice: The course catalogue is not available since fairly close to the semester's starting date, so do not get your heart set on any courses that have previously been taught. You do not actually sign up for courses, rather you sign up for the exam and simply add the course to your schedule on the online platform. As such, you are able to "shop around" for courses and try a few before deciding for which courses you will attend the exam. I would recommend signing up for one or two courses with exams at the end up the first "block" of the semester, such that all your exams are not crammed together within a couple of weeks at the end of the semester.
academics_comments: The university and support groups set up for a great exchange semester. Unfortunately, the pandemic did play quite a large role as the semester went on and in the second half of the semester all classes were online.
course_level: I would argue that the academic level was fairly similar to what you would experience at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style is also very similar to UCPH. You attend the course through the semester but are simply graded on the final exam. Most courses are split into lectures and tutorials - make sure you attend the tutorials.
courses_enrolled: Managerial Economics 1 SPS "Taxation and Regulation of the Financial WiSe 2122 Sector" (Seminar) Frontiers in International Trade The Economics of Power Markets
recommended_courses: I would recommend signing up for a seminar - the writing period is 4 weeks and if scheduled correctly can take the ease off a potentially stressful exam period. Frontiers in International Trade was a particularly enjoyable course on advanced international trade - if you have any experience with international trade courses and/or want to write a thesis within the field, the two professors do a great job presenting newer research (including their own) within the field.
unexpected_costs: Enrollment at the university of €144.4
cost_comparison: Munich is a fairly expensive city by German standard - especially eating at restaurants / going out is more expensive that e.g. Berlin. Groceries, on the other hand, were cheaper than expected (compared to CPH).
activities_available: Join the ESN Mesa group - they offer lots of trips, daily activities etc. A great way to meet fellow exchange students. I assume the pandemic unfortunately played a significant role particularly w.r.t. athletic activities.
activities_recommended: As mentioned, try to participate in as many ESN Mesa activities as possible. Have beers in the beer garden, go on day-trips or even longer weekend trips to Berlin or Vienna when offered. Sign up as soon as possible for the trips, they are very sought after!
weekend_recommendations: Go skiing over the weekend if the weather allows it. There are several companies that offer day-trips including transport and ski-lift - you can even rent the skiing equipment fairly cheaply. Studenten im Schnee or Skibus München worked well for me.
culture_adjustment: German culture is not that different compared to Danish cultute - we all love a beer, they just love great beer rather than average mass-produced pilsners. Munich also offers a range of nice cocktail bars and international dining - you do not have to eat meat and potatoes every time you dine out.
socializing_tips: Join the whatsapp or Facebook groups and arrange to meet with fellow exchange students. There are lots of green areas to hang out in and obviously a lot of great places for beers both outdoor or indoor.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences particularly challenging.
culture_appreciated: The beer drinking culture at the local breweries accompanied by a hearty meal!
top3_advice: 1) The academics are not a cake-walk - prepare to be fairly challenged, in particular in the master progamme courses. 2) Cost of living is unfortunately quite expensive in Munich, so prepare to pay a sizable amount even for a shared flat. 3) Don't stay in the city every weekend. Make use of the opportunities to go travelling, enjoying the nature just an hour or two away.
other_useful_info: Get a bike - especially if you live fairly centrally! Either buy one second hand which you can then sell once your semester is over or sign up for Swapfiets.
most_rewarding: Finally "learning" how to ski
greatest_challenge: The pandemic was obsiously a challenge. All bars/clubs ended up closing and all academic activities took place form home.

crucial_aspects: The most crucial aspects for me when choosing a destination were opportunities to discover new cultures and places, to gain useful knowledge within my fields of study, and to be able to feel comfortable and eventually at home in the city.
overall_comments: Due to COVID-19, there have been some restrictions put into place for most of my time here, and these have of course prohibited some social events.
info_ease: My home university was very helpful when I needed to gather information. Therefore, it was not a problem to find the information that I needed before my arrival.
arrival_assistance: The Erasmus office here has been very helpful in providing the needed information and answering any questions that I might have had. We had an introductory meeting for all the exchange students within my study, which was very informative.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Due to COVID-19, there have been some restrictions put into place for most of my time here, and these have of course prohibited some social events.
registration_process: As far as I recall, the registration process was easy and through the host institution's website.
registration_help: Erasmus coordinators and the international office at the host university were happy to help with the registration.
registration_success: I registered for all of the classes that I wanted, and it was easily done at the website.
registration_advice: It is possible to follow as many courses as one wants and just sign up for the exams in the courses that one wants to take the exam in. Therefore, I would recommend that students follow more than the required number of classes in the beginning and continue to do so until they are sure of which classes they would like to be examined in.
academics_comments: Due to COVID-19, there have been some restrictions put into place for most of my time here, and these have of course prohibited some social events.
course_level: The level here is quite high - comparable to that at the University of Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: I would say that the style of teaching is very much the same as that of UCPH. There were lectures held by professors, and we were about 30-60 students in each class.
courses_enrolled: Frontiers in International Trade, Experimental Methods, Economic of Power Markets, The Political Economy of Income Redistribution, and Topics in Applied Econometrics.
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the courses Frontiers in International Trade, Experimental Methods, and Topics in Applied Econometrics. If students are interested in macroeconomics, performing economic experiments, or applied econometrics, I would recommend these courses.
unexpected_costs: I actually had to pay around 150 Euros to study at LMU.
cost_comparison: A gym subscription was less expensive that I had expected. The rent was higher than I expected when I applied to go on exchange in Munich.
activities_available: There was an organisation called MENSA that organised these kinds of activities for Erasmus students.
activities_recommended: I would recommend going on as many MENSA activities in the beginning of the semester as one can, because this is a great opportunity for meeting new people and getting to know the area around Munich.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend going on trips to nearby cities, go to soccer games, go to Englischer Garten, go a biergarten, or just take a long walk through the city.
culture_adjustment: As the German culture is not that different from the Danish, it was not very difficult.
socializing_tips: I would recommend joining MENSA activities and look for social groups of exchange students on Facebook.
cultural_challenges: Germans are rule-followers and very polite.
culture_appreciated: The politeness.
top3_advice: Go on as many adventures as possible while here, get a lederhosen/dirndl, and learn to drink beer.
other_useful_info: Sign up for all the classes you think seem interesting and choose your final courses later on.
most_rewarding: The experiences that I have gotten with friends, either in Munich or on adventures in nearby cities.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during the exchange has been the restrictions that COVID-19 has put on activities here, especially the social ones.

crucial_aspects: My father lives in Munich and I wanted to strengthen my relationship with him as well as my acedemic skills in German and German Law
info_ease: Easy
arrival_assistance: The Exchange office at LMU, especally Frau Haustein, was extremely helpful
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We could choose any lectures we wanted to follow, we ust had to give the professor a notice about 2 weeks before the end of the lectures (but preferablt earlier), that we were exchange students and needed an exam to proof our attendance.
registration_help: The exchange office was always available, answered very fast and wes very helpful.
registration_success: I could register for all the classes I wanted
registration_advice: Choose the courses that are a part of the LLM.Eur programme, as they give extra ECTS-credits and are tailored in a way, where you do not need any prior knowledge of German law. These classes will also always offer an Exam at the end for the LLM.Eur students, that Erasmus students can easily attend too. In general, even though the courses are almost all in German, they have an international perspective and the lecturers are aware of many international students present.
course_level: Even though I followed LLM courses as a BA student, the courses were not at all a too high level
teaching_comparison: There are lectures and seminars, similar to UCPH. The main curriculum is just following the lectures, and there is almost no additional reading, which means that the workload feels much easier than at UCPH. Some classes have cases and material online, that they expect you to have read before the lecture and recomended readings, but I did not experience having to buy any mandatory books and the expected readings were very limited.
courses_enrolled: Europarecht I, Deutsches und Europäisches Wettbewerbsrecht, Aktuelle Rechtsprechung des Bundesverfassungsgerichts, Klimaklagen, and Deutschkurs für Studierende der Rechtwissenschaften
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the courses I took expect the German language course for law students, if the Exchange student speaks a high level of german already. The German language course was too easy. The academic courses I took were all very interesting and well tailored for a foreign student, who speaks german. If the student only has a beginners level of german, the German language course might be good. There were also Englich courses and courses tailored specially for Erasmus students and taught in an easy German language, and my erasmus freinds seemed satisfied with these.
unexpected_costs: Immatriculation Fee of 144 EUR per semester
cost_comparison: Food in the supermarket is much less expensive. Going out for dinner and beer is much less expensive than Copenhagen. Wine in bars is more expensive. Public transportation is free for students in the night hours (18:00-06:00) and in weekends. If you need it every day, you can pay an extra fee to your Immatriculation Fee and use all public transportation for free the whole semester. Otherwise tickets for public transportation is quite expensive (best solution for Danes: get a bike and use it during the day and use public transportation in the evenings when going out and during week days)
activities_available: A lot of cheap sport opportunities
activities_recommended: Sport, especially mountain sports - go rock climbing, hiking and skiining in the Alps
weekend_recommendations: Beautiful lakes around Munich, beautiful parks and castles, the Alps. Use the Englischer Garten and Olympiapark in Munich. Go shopping, cafe drinking and out at night in Maxvorstandt and Glockenbachviertel/Gärtner Platz.
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Speak to them during class, they are all very open towards foreigners once you approach them (like danes)
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: Everything
top3_advice: Get a bike but be prepared for a different biking culture than in CPH (for better and for worse), take advantage of the cheap food (also the Mensa/student cafeteria has good and very cheap meals!) and beer, go to class with interest and dedication and enjoy the limited readings and workload next to class.
other_useful_info: It is wonderful, if you speak German well. If not, it might be dificult to fully enjoy the german culture and the classes, but then you will probably get a larger erasmus student friend group instead.
most_rewarding: Getting more German friends
greatest_challenge: Covid-19

crucial_aspects: I have been to Germany many times and wanted to immerse myself in the culture while also becoming fluent in the language. I chose Munich specifically, because I found it more interesting than Heidelberg, and I had already been to Berlin many times. Also, the weather is different from the Danish weather with its warmth. In addition, I checked out the courses beforehand, and they seemed interesting. This didn't matter though, as the course catalogue was wildly different from what was offered the year before, and I wasn't able to see what was offered in my semester of Summer '22 beforehand.
overall_comments: The short answer is, I was thrilled to be in Munich learning about different cultures and meeting people from all over the world. I was though very disappointed in the University for multiple reasons. Most importantly, the course information was lacking or non-existent before my semester start so my academic experience was a bit of a patchwork of making the courses work for me. The practicalities of living in Germany were also a bit of a hassle. I recommend a more digitalized or less bureaucratic country than Germany, or both. I also dealt with some personal difficulties back home, which made it hard for me to fully enjoy the exchange and influenced my overall experience. A more thorough answer will be posted in the upcoming boxes.
info_ease: LMU provided me with an amazing PDF that basically answered all my questions regarding housing, transport, registering for courses and household stuff. However, this PDF was not specifically made for mathematics, so much of the info was just "this is the default at LMU, but your faculty might do it differently". And the mathematics faculty often did...
arrival_assistance: Which leads me to my second point, personal help for whenever I had questions that were not answered in the introductory PDF. The help desk was in the main LMU building, which was very convenient, except that it was closed due to the coronavirus. This meant I had to send e-mails to the exchange help team. They did reply quickly, but it would've been much better with personal, live assistance. I can't recall specifically what they helped me with.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The short answer is, I was thrilled to be in Munich learning about different cultures and meeting people from all over the world. I was though very disappointed in the University for multiple reasons. Most importantly, the course information was lacking or non-existent before my semester start so my academic experience was a bit of a patchwork of making the courses work for me. The practicalities of living in Germany were also a bit of a hassle. I recommend a more digitalized or less bureaucratic country than Germany, or both. I also dealt with some personal difficulties back home, which made it hard for me to fully enjoy the exchange and influenced my overall experience. A more thorough answer will be posted in the upcoming boxes.
registration_process: The process is that you either: - Show up to classes and talk to the professor - E-mail them In some cases, seats were quite limited, so e-mailing the professor well beforehand was essential. This was often the "Seminar" classes, where each student would do a presentation, so you could only have x students if the semester had x lectures. Signing up was very flexible and could be done very close to the exam.
registration_help: I suppose I could've gotten help from the exchange coordinator, but I didn't need it, so I don't know whether it was provided.
registration_success: Of the 57 ECTS worth of courses I got pre-approved, only 21 ECTS were offered. Also, one of my desired courses was a Seminar, so it had too few seats when I tried to sign up for me to get one.
registration_advice: Advice: Do not expect that a course is offered just because it was offered previously. If you come to LMU for the courses, write e-mails to the professors as you are deciding which universities to apply to. That way you can get a sense of whether your desired courses will in fact be offered and hear about the curriculum.
academics_comments: The short answer is, I was thrilled to be in Munich learning about different cultures and meeting people from all over the world. I was though very disappointed in the University for multiple reasons. Most importantly, the course information was lacking or non-existent before my semester start so my academic experience was a bit of a patchwork of making the courses work for me. The practicalities of living in Germany were also a bit of a hassle. I recommend a more digitalized or less bureaucratic country than Germany, or both. I also dealt with some personal difficulties back home, which made it hard for me to fully enjoy the exchange and influenced my overall experience. A more thorough answer will be posted in the upcoming boxes.
course_level: The level of courses was, on average, similar to at UCPH. Some of it was harder and some of it was easier than at UCPH. I think Verdichtete Mathematik was mainly targeted toward PhD students, which was part of the reason I failed it.
teaching_comparison: Style of teaching: The style of teaching was very close to how it is at UCPH, but everything around the teaching was different. There was no single platform for courses and homework. I took three courses at three different professors. One used Uni2work, the other used Moodle, and the third uploaded files to his website on lmu.de.
courses_enrolled: Mathematical and Applications to Machine Learning (MAML, easier than at UCPH, maybe would have been BA level at UCPH) Halbeinfache Lie-Algebren (HELA, comparable to UCPH) Verdichtete Mathematik (VM, harder than UCPH, probably targeted toward PhD students). This course I failed. I listed the difficulty to clarify what I wrote in "level of courses".
recommended_courses: I would recommend Halbeinfache Lie-Algebren. It is a course about the classification of all finite-dimensional complex semi-simple lie algebras. The curriculum is kind of big, but you prove some amazing results, and you aren't expected to remember everything at the (oral) exam. The course was offered for the first time in '22, and we weren't that many taking it, so maybe it won't be offered again...
unexpected_costs: I thought wi-fi would be included in the rent.
cost_comparison: Beer was cheaper than I had thought 😉
activities_available: As you can see here, MESA arranges many events, and they are all free or at least fairly priced.
activities_recommended: Deutsches Museum. It is a huge museum about tech and science, both modern and historical. It takes maybe 3 full days to see everything, or 1-2 if you're not interested in literally everything. In general the Munich museums are interesting, cheap (most are cheaper on sundays) and there are many of them. But I recommend the Deutsches Museum the most. The English Garden is a wonderful place to hang out or tan or take a run or have a beer. It's huge. Olympiadorf is also great for the same things, and there is a Bierstube for students with very cheap beer and food.
weekend_recommendations: Erdinger Therme is a huge spa with everything from sauna and massage to waterslides. It is not cheap, but it is relaxing and comforting. And you can buy drinks in the pool. And go to the Alps. I went to Eibsee a few times and took the lift to Zugspitze. The lift is kind of expensive, but it is the highest point in Germany after all. And swimming in an Alp lake is wonderful and free, after you've payed for transport. Visit a brewery. It's not expensive if you go a few people, it is good fun and you get to try different kinds of freshly brewed beer on tap. I recommend Ayinger, as it is more intimate and not so heavily visited.
culture_adjustment: I honestly thought Munich would be closer to Copenhagen culturally. I somehow found Münchners more closed than Copenhageners. Germans very much appreciate peace and quiet, so living in an apartment complex with thin walls was tough. There was a note on the wall warning that legal steps would be taken if I made extensive noise after 22. This was durable for a semester, but it was not comfortable for me personally. And the bike culture is nothing like in Denmark (more information on that in the "challenging" section). I thought it was easy to get used to the party vibe though. Munich had so many big events over the course of my semester like concerts, (student) festivals, museum exhibitions, art shows, sport events and demonstrations. I wasn't bothered by how these events sometimes got in the way of traffic and my route through the city. I just thought it was cool to have so many things going on.
socializing_tips: Learn German. I think everyone's personality is more "their true selves" when they speak in their native tongue. So you can get to know local students better if you speak German with them. Try talking to people from your classes who look approachable. I didn't really get German friends, because I was too scared to talk to people in my classes. But I would've liked to do that more.
cultural_challenges: Traffic was challenging. When I was biking, I was almost run over by right-swinging cars about 10 times during my stay. Pedestrians often walk on the bike path like it's the most natural thing in the world. And many people on bikes were on the left side of the road whenever it is more convenient for them. I know this happens in Copenhagen too, but way more often in Munich in my opinion. Lastly, the bike infrastructure was messy and traffic lights were often shared with pedestrians, making it less efficient to get around. At uni, there were quite few events for the math institute compared to UCPH. More events would have allowed me to get to know more local math students which I desired, but that could be due to the coronavirus. German digitalization is behind the Danish, and their (in my opinion high level of) bureaucracy can be frustrating. This means you have to call or send letters if you want customer service. This was hard to adjust to, but luckily their postal service is faster and cheaper than the Danish/Nordic one, Post Nord. Sometimes my friends would suggest going to a restaurant where I had to eat at home because they had nothing vegan except for potatoes and salad. As a vegan, this was a bit rough.
culture_appreciated: I liked how Municians have traditions and aren't afraid of sticking to them. This sometimes caused problems like finding vegan food (as per above), but generally I liked it. I also liked that Munich have a habit of going out for drinks and food often. The sidewalk was full of life from the center of the city and pretty far out, since there was always a restaurant in sight with people talking (outside in the summer, which is extra cozy). They had many different types of world cuisines, which I enjoyed exploring. I can recommend Orange Box, Charlie's Vegan, Soy Vegan, Tahdig, Emmi's, Siggis and Schwabinger Osterwaldgarten. As I am vegan, I can't tell you much about traditional Bavarian food except Schwabinger Osterwaldgarten, which my friends and family thought had great traditional dishes.
top3_advice: -Be prepared to send a lot of e-mails to professors if you actually want to know about the content of your courses before you take the courses. -Learn German. It is useful for socializing, some courses are only offered in German, and a lot of customer service is either better in German or only offered in German. -Plan your time well. I wasted a lot of afternoons doing nothing because I had nothing planned and I was done studying for the day. There is so much to do in and around Munich, so be sure to try these things when you're not studying.
other_useful_info: The Erasmus+ grant dates, for how long your stay is going to be, are only able to be corrected to fewer days than your initial estimate, not more days. This means you might end up getting a smaller grant than you are entitled to. Therefore, when you apply for the grant be sure to write more days than you expect to be abroad. You can't know about your exam dates beforehand, so write the end date as if your last exam is very late. You can always correct it once you find out more.
most_rewarding: I am now much better at dealing with troublesome authorities, companies and institutions. By that I mean sending e-mails sooner rather than later and calling them to ask questions. I am less nervous talking about something serious in a language I don't command fully. I understand my personality and culture much better in relation to others. Many times in Munich I thought other people were weird, but that's just because they are from different countries and cultures. I thought the whole world's idea of a "normal person" was like the Danes' idea of a "normal person", but it's not. This ties in with how I learned a lot about how different our cultures are across the world. I thought biking culture sucked, an American friend of mine thought it was great! I thought the Münchners liked to dance and party a lot, a Brazilian friend thought they liked it... not so much. It was a big eye opener for me, and I look forward to travelling to different places later in life. My German improved a lot and I learned to fit into a different University system. I learned how to socialize with strangers and find things to talk about even if we had different interests.
greatest_challenge: The university of LMU was my biggest challenge during my exchange. As explained above, it was troublesome in many ways, and it removed the focus from the curriculum. This, combined with my personal difficulties in Denmark, meant that my mental health was not so good for the majority of my stay. I was conflicted between giving up and moving back home and trying to "brush it off" and just keep working and enjoying my stay. I ended up doing a mix, visiting Denmark a few times.
other_comments: I think finding a balance between studying, socializing, sightseeing, and taking care of my mental health was the biggest reason my exchange was, in my opinion, unsuccessful. This was triggered mainly by the difficulties at LMU. If you have an academic reason to go to LMU (a specific course you're crazy about or a professor you're eager to do a project with), you should definitely study at LMU. If you're going on exchange for the cultural and social aspects, I would recommend another university.

crucial_aspects: I chose Munich as my exchange destination initially because of personal connections to the city both through friends and language, but it also checked a lot of other important boxes for me such as -great university -safe, green city, good public transport -welcoming people and culture
info_ease: It was quite easy, the staff at LMU were very helpful and easy to contact via email. It might have been a little more complicated to get information if I weren't fluent in german.
arrival_assistance: Assistance via email by the exchange department, and by certain professors if I had questions regarding their courses. I also participated in a LMU Buddy program, where I was assigned an older student to help me with questions which worked very well. Else I got assistance from fellow students in my classes if needed.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: At LMU, you don't register for courses other than adding them to your curriculum online (LSF). You can change courses at any time during the semester, and the only binding registration is for exams towards the end of the semester. You also register for most of the exams online.
registration_help: It was explained during lectures/on slides, and in emails from the university.
registration_success: Successful. Be aware that some courses are only available during either the winter or summer term.
registration_advice: Try to get pre-approved a lot of different subjects before you go to Munich, as their semesters start very late and the course catalogues mostly aren't available in time for when you first apply for pre-approval. Also, then you will have flexibility and be able to easier switch courses if there are some that you don't like.
course_level: The level is pretty high for third year Bachelor courses. They expect you to be able to apply a lot of knowledge by heart from math/statistics/econometrics/micro and macro I and II in most electives. The exams are very time-pressured and all of my exams were written by hand and closed book.
teaching_comparison: Most courses on BA-level consist of lecture + tutorial, similar to UCPH. People participate more in the lectures, which is really nice in my opinion. The tutorials are mostly taught by PHD students, and they are bigger than at UCPH. Mostly, you will go through exercises together, and the TA guides you all the way through.
courses_enrolled: Game Theory (Micro III) Environmental and Resource Economics Economics of Education Geography and Technology in Economic History Modulprüfung Grundlagen der Wirtschaftspsychologie
recommended_courses: The two courses in Economic History taught by Professor Cantoni are absolutely amazing. In the summer term, the class focuses on culture and institutions, and in the winter term it is on geography and technology. I have had them both pre-approved as Economic History at UCPH. Game Theory is also good and works as Micro III but the exam is really difficult.
unexpected_costs: None come to mind
cost_comparison: Public transport is very cheap if you get the 29 euro ticket for students. Eating out is also fairly cheap even though it is more expensive than other parts in Germany. Most books are accessible through an online library from the University, so I didn't buy any books.
activities_available: There are a few bigger parties organized by students at the university, and also sports clubs etc. but I didn't use those so unfortunately can't provide as much additional information than what the exchange staff send you.
activities_recommended: I would recommend going to concerts at the Isarphilharmonie, Herkulessaal or the Opera. Swimming in the Isar in summer is also lovely, and visiting the Christkindlmarkt in December. Of course the Oktoberfest also takes place just before the winter semester starts! Going to the English garden, or museums like Haus der Kunst and Lenbachhaus. If you like surfing, check out the Eisbachwelle, where you can surf in the middle of the city.
weekend_recommendations: Going on a hike or to ski in the mountains nearby, or go to one of the bigger lakes in the area (Starnberger See, Ammersee,...). A day trip to Salzburg is also lovely, or if you have more time, even go to Vienna or Prague! MESA (the Erasmus network in Munich) organises a lot of these trips.
culture_adjustment: For me it was very easy as I am born and raised in Switzerland, so language wasn't an issue and the culture is fairly similar. I have only experienced welcoming and lovely people, although I am told that (especially the older generation) can be quite direct and maybe a little "impolite" at times, but I didn't get this impression. You might be surprised as a Scandinavian how common cash still is, and how a lot of things aren't quite as digitalized as in Denmark.
socializing_tips: I have had great experiences just starting a conversation with people from my courses etc. , they are super kind and helpful. Also bumble bff is a great way to meet friends, local and non-local.
cultural_challenges: I had to get used to bring cash with me, and that supermarkets are closed on sundays and quite a few holidays that we don't have in Denmark. Also, most close at 8pm. German people are quite busy and often work late, so finding time to see your friends might be easier if you plan a little ahead.
culture_appreciated: People are very genuine, caring and helpful, and you don't feel like you have to be a certain way to fit in with them. I love the WG-culture (living in shared apartments as students), that is even more prevalent than in Copenhagen. If possible, I really recommend you to find a room in a WG, it's a great way to find friends.
top3_advice: -Solutions to tutorial-exercises are not uploaded, so try to ask other students if you can't be present -Use the roomfinder in the online portal LSF to find your lecture/tutorial. The buildings are very big! -I would recommend to take notes with a tablet and an "Apple pencil" or similar, as they do a lot of things by hand and it will be the fastest way to do it, especially in tutorials where they write a lot of formulas by hand. And it will prepare you better for the exam form, where you will have to write everything on paper.
other_useful_info: You have to use your student card to buy food in the canteen (first, you have to put money on it on site, most places require cash). You can reserve library spots at your faculty online, and this is crucial to do if you want to secure a spot to study during exams. A lot of exams are written almost immediately after the last lecture is held, and I had 5 exams in 9 days, so try and stay up to date with the courses during the semester or catch up in the christmas holiday, which is quite long. It's also important to note that the semesters start very late and end late, so in my case I missed the first week of my new semester in Copenhagen when I got home.
most_rewarding: Feeling home in a new place, meeting new people and forming lasting friendships. Exploring a new city and getting to know it. Attending interesting lectures.
greatest_challenge: The exams are clearly very different and challenging
other_comments: I had a great experience in Munich and would recommend it to anyone who doesn't mind studying a bit while on exchange;)

cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The german politeness, actually.
top3_advice: Go in the summer. Don't be cheap, when looking for accommodation. Buy the Deutschlandticket and travel around Germany in your free time.
other_useful_info: Have patience with the german bureaucracy.
most_rewarding: Learning german and being able to speak it freely in the end.

recommended_courses: I can not say as courses are changed up each semester. I have heard that it is a poor idea to enroll in introductionary courses as they are much harder to pass compared to other courses.
unexpected_costs: Inventory for the room.
cost_comparison: Housing ended up being less expensive than expected. Usually students that end up renting private rooms pay a lot more in Munich than I did.
activities_available: There was for sure a lot of social and cultural clubs, which were available also for exchange students, but not much information was supplied. The sports club was impossible to get into because of the demand and the limited spots. Most of the time the ESN-network was the place to go if you wanted to join up on social activities
activities_recommended: In the beginning, it is definitely a good idea to join ESN-organised events as they are great opportunities to meet a lot of different people.
weekend_recommendations: Use the nature around Munich to go for hikes/walks/jogs with people you meet. A great way to get to know people.
culture_adjustment: Rather easy. I did not find decisive differences between danish and German culture when it came to everyday life. The general culture of the university is quite different though.
socializing_tips: I did not really mange to make a lot of local friends other than my roommates.
cultural_challenges: It is not so much a cultural difference as a societal one, but the bureaucratic processes in the beginning, fx applying to be a inhabitant of the city, was quite a hurdle and very confusing even with decent German proficiency. Other than that, supermarkets closing early and not being open on Sundays ended up actually being an obstacle when you had to structure your week.
culture_appreciated: The general openeness of the Bavarians. Easy to do conversation with random people. And how normal it was to spend most of your time out and about in the city,
top3_advice: Read up on what is demanded of you and be patient with the German bureaucracy . Start searching for housing quickly. Use the ESN-network if you feel lonely, especially in the beginning.
other_useful_info: It is always a good idea to introduce yourself to the professors and be on good terms with them.
most_rewarding: The social and cultural aspect of getting to know people from all around the world, and especially from all around Europe. Also having the opportunity to travel around South-Germany. Being in contact with a university system that is so different to the one I was used to has also proven to be a quite educative experience.
greatest_challenge: Without a doubt participating on equal teams with German students, when the classes were conducted in German.

crucial_aspects: I chose LMU in Munich as my destination due to its high academic standards and the many historical sights in the city.
info_ease: I think it was intended to be quite easy to get the information you need upon arrival, but at least half of the links sent out in the information emails weren’t working. The websites of LMU are quite hard to navigate, so it takes a while to find the relevant information if the links don’t work properly.
arrival_assistance: LMU sent out information emails and had information meetings.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: At the Department of Economics, course registration is different from all other departments at LMU. You can shuffle around courses and choose the ones you find interesting without registering for them in advance. Course registration only takes place when you register for exams in the middle or at the end of the lecture period.
registration_help: There was an introduction meeting that explained the process, but the international office could also be contacted for further information.
registration_success: I only got one of the classes I wanted when I applied for the exchange at LMU since the classes weren’t offered when the final course catalog was provided just before the semester started. However, registering for classes was quite easy.
registration_advice: Don't fix your mind on specific courses before the final catalog is provided, as it can change quite a bit. Be aware that exchange students can't take any courses from the quantitative economics track, as these are only available to full-time students at LMU.
course_level: The level of the courses was similar to the level at UCPH, but the exams are taken with pen and paper, which makes them a bit harder.
teaching_comparison: I didn’t really like the teaching style in most of the courses at LMU. The professor conducted both the lectures and the tutorials, and often, the material could just as easily be studied at home with the same outcome.
courses_enrolled: The courses I was enrolled in were: - Development Economics - Monetary Economics - Topics in Climate and Resource Economics - Nonparametric Econometrics - Labor Economics
recommended_courses: I would recommend Labor Economics because it consists of only one month of lectures and had good teaching. I would also recommend Nonparametric Econometrics, as the exam is based on six hand-in assignments and is very useful.
unexpected_costs: I didn’t encounter any unexpected costs, but it’s good to have some savings if you want to attend student trips.
cost_comparison: Overall, I would say that Munich is fairly cheaper than Copenhagen in terms of food, drinks, and leisure activities. However, rent can be quite high depending on what you find.
activities_available: ESN (Erasmus Student Network) organized many activities such as parties, day trips, weekend trips, pub crawls, karaoke nights, and lots of other events. They have an event calendar for the entire semester, and I would highly recommend attending as many as possible because it is an amazing place to meet people in the same situation as yourself.
activities_recommended: There are some sports clubs, but I didn’t attend any of them.
weekend_recommendations: Use the Deutschland Ticket to travel around Bavaria and join the trips hosted by ESN.
culture_adjustment: I didn’t find it too challenging.
socializing_tips: Don't be shy! Many local students come from other countries or different parts of Germany and are very friendly if you just give it a chance and put yourself out there.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find it challenging.
culture_appreciated: Beer gardens and bars are very welcoming, and if tables are full, people don’t mind making room for strangers if you just ask them."
top3_advice: Be open-minded and step out of your comfort zone. Enjoy the nature and outdoor life of the city whenever you can. Interact with the German students—they often know the answers to many of the questions you may have about studying at LMU and life in Munich.
other_useful_info: They are not very technical at LMU, so don’t get stressed out if the platforms and online information aren’t the best.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of the exchange was probably being on my own and having to build a new social network with students from different cultures and countries.
greatest_challenge: Studying for the exams was challenging. In Germany, old exam sets are not provided, so the structure of the exam is somewhat unknown, which made preparing for the exams even harder.

crucial_aspects: My best friend lives in the city i was going to exchange in. Other than that i am also fluent in German which made Munich an obvious destination to go on exchange.
info_ease: It wasnt too hard to get information regarding the univeristy, since i was assigned a 'buddy' who also spoke my native language (danish). He helped me out a ton with all the practical information regarding the university (What courses were available, How to pay semester fees, Where the different campuses are etc.)
arrival_assistance: I had received occasional emails from the university on how i should prepare for my stay in Munich. There was also an introduction seminar for exchange students before the semester began.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Online registration through the university portal.
registration_help: Most help came from my university assigned 'buddy'. But there was also an Erasmus councillor for my faculty whom i could contact if i needed adminstrative help.
registration_success: I was succesful in registering for all my classes. However, like i mentioned, some courses i wanted to take had been discontinued, despite still being on the course catalogue. In general course capacity was no problem.
registration_advice: Be aware of the rules for your faculty, they can be kind of hidden. Nowhere, except for when i first applied through mobility online, did it state that i needed to take 60% of my courses from my faculty (Physics). Im glad i remembered that fact, else i wouldnt have been able to get my transcript.
course_level: I took 15 ECTS Masters courses and 15 ECTS Bachelors courses.
teaching_comparison: I think UCPH has a higher standard for what is expected of the teachers (Organization of course and clear communication to students especially.). But at my exchange institution i felt a lot more challenged(which was pretty refreshing actually), since there was a higher expectation to the amount of work you had to hand in every week.
courses_enrolled: General Relativity, Stochastic dynamics - from Brownian motion to fluctuating fields, Game Theory, Physics of the human body: biosignals and biosensors, Introduction to Machine Learning
recommended_courses: All of the above courses were well organized and had pretty good professors. The one exception is General Relativity where i felt lost all the time. It was a terribly organized course and it was pretty much impossible to get individual help, since all the Exercise lessons were just a teacher presenting solutions to problems (which was always messy, since the tutors were usually ill prepared) My advice is: Ask around about courses from local students before choosing.
unexpected_costs: I had to pay 85eur to be enrolled at the University for the semester.
cost_comparison: Short term fitness memberships were a lot more expensive than expected. Look for local gyns with student discounts. Groceries are pretty cheap in general.
activities_available: There was a sports association at the Uni but i didnt participate.
activities_recommended: Just engage with locals. Go to bars and public events and talk to new people. Enjoy the freedom of living in a country where you dont know anyone yet.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the mountains. You can get around pretty much everywhere with the cheap 'Germany card' where you can use all German trains for a flat fee of 38 eur. Go for a hike somewhere outside the city. Or go watch a football game at a local pub.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, since my best friend lives there and i speak the language fluently. I hung out with his friend group often.
socializing_tips: Participate in language exchange events, those look pretty fun, i saw them hanging about a few times. You could also try starting at some sports at the uni sport association.
cultural_challenges: Theres a lot more emphasis on work culture in Germany. People are less outgoing and spend a lot more time on studying than i am used to. It was hard to get people to come out to the bar. German humor is also very different from Danish humor so my jokes didnt always land.
culture_appreciated: I adopted part of the german work culture and feel a lot more disciplined as a person, which i am pretty glad for.
top3_advice: be aware that it is a much more common occurence that people fail courses at my host institution. It is not atypical for a couse to have an 80% fail rate. Do your research before picking and dont become overconfident when picking; You can easily be overwhelmed.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Living in a foreign country has made me feel much more at home in my own home country. When everything is suddenly new and confusing, its easy to feel out of place, but that just makes you appreciate the ease of being home that much more.
greatest_challenge: Finding accomodation for sure. I lived with my best friend for my first month just because it was THAT hard to find a room. I recommend looking well in advance for accomodation, and dont bet on the University providing you any (Even though they say its a 50/50 chance youll receive campus accomodation it its more like 30/70).

crucial_aspects: The university profile and reputation. The language spoken in the country. The city being a decently interesting city.

It doesn't have to be anything fancy or formal. Just coordinate a meeting between the exchange student studying the same as each other and maybe sponsor a pizza or whatever. Maybe a quick showing of campus could be handy, too. Or an introduction to social events being hosted by students (also locals) within the faculty/institute.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Most of it was explained quite thoroughly in emails leading up to the stay. I had no issues just following the instructions there.
registration_help: Thorough emails
registration_success: 100% successful.
registration_advice: Following the instructions meticulously. The international office is quick to repsond if any questions are sent their way.
course_level: Courses were generally easier than in Copenhagen but still pretty good. Germans start a little earlier at university so I would recommend picking seminars for later bachelor og master semesters.
teaching_comparison: Very similar - pretty much the same.
courses_enrolled: Habermas Krieg und Gewalt in der politischen Philosophie The European Union in Complex Policy Areas Democratic Development and Stability in Germany Debates in Democracy Research
recommended_courses: The Master courses are good, but you need a special permit from the responsible professors if you're still a bachelors student. The seminars in the philosophy department that I had were really good!
unexpected_costs: Not any, really.
cost_comparison: Having lived in Germany before, everything was more or less as expected.
activities_available: As stated above, barely any. There was one Christmas party at the Institute of Political Science, but other than that none - not any that were of relevance to me at least.
activities_recommended: Go to ESN MESA. They have an incredible amount of acitivities where you can always meet someone.
weekend_recommendations: Exploit the fact that Munich is located so centrally in Europe. Go to cities in Central Europe by train. Often times it takes no longer than four hours to reach great cities. Other than that, Munich is a pretty city. Go visit some of the older parts in the city center and explore the area around the Isar - especially Glockenbach and Gärtnerplatzviertel. Join the day trips to cities and the Alps that ESN MESA organizes.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. I had some worries about the hierarchical, very formal structure of German Universities, but it turned out to be rather chill. The professors were all kind and approachable. Other than that, there are mainly minor differences between Denmark and Germany. Engage with locals and you'll learn them quickly.
socializing_tips: Take German courses and engage with the students there.
cultural_challenges: Not really any.
culture_appreciated: Politeness, openness (compared to DK), and political awareness.
top3_advice: Start looking for a place to live early. Practice your German before and during your stay. Go to ESN MESA.
other_useful_info: If you have any administrative hindrances that you'd like to overcome - for instance regarding access to a course or whatever - talk to the relevant professor. They have a lot more 'power' in deciding administrative stuff regarding their own courses than professors in Denmark have.
most_rewarding: Probably the language part - and of course, some acquaintances too.
greatest_challenge: Being quite isolated for the first three weeks or so, and having to do the work of making new social acquaintances.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a place which was as different as possible from Denmark (but within EU, due to Corona). Besides this, the opportunities for english classes and proper information in english also ended up playing a surprisingly large role in my decision. I had never been to Rome before my exchange, so the decision was also based a lot on the many nice things i had heard about the city from friends and family.
overall_comments: Rome is amazing to live in, and it has been amazing getting to know the city so well. Besides this, what mattered the most have been all the nice people i have met there. The academic level was very low, but that just meant that there was more time for all the fun things.
info_ease: Relatively easy. There are a lot of different systems, and signing up for the classes was a bit chaotic. The exchange office was however very helpfull and fast at answering e-mails.
arrival_assistance: Online information event and various emails. There are also an ESN erasmus-welcome-programme, but they do not offer any guidance on school-related things.
arrival_comments: I might have answered differently if i had been asked right at the beginning. But it all worked out in the end. I was rather frustrated with the sign-up for the classes, because you had to work accross 4 or five different systems, but we all managed.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Rome is amazing to live in, and it has been amazing getting to know the city so well. Besides this, what mattered the most have been all the nice people i have met there. The academic level was very low, but that just meant that there was more time for all the fun things.
registration_process: You have to make sure yourself, that there are not clashes with both time-schedules and exams. And the exam-dates are not published before quite a few weeks after the start of the semester. In WebSelf service you can check which group you are in, on this page https://www.luiss.edu/cattedreonline you can check the "syllabus" of the different available classes. You also sign up in WebSelf service as far as i remember. And then there is an equivalent to absalon called "luisslearn". You can change the classes for a long time, also after they have started, so do not panic if you sign up to something wrong.
registration_help: Erasmus office, with a very helpfull lady called Roberta Limone, whom answers mails very fast and precise.
registration_success: I managed. Luckily you can change it, also several weeks into the semester.
registration_advice: Take a deep breath and remember that all classes are taught twice a week, so when making your schedule, remember to put both in there, so you don't end up with clashes. Also, do not expect to end up with the classes you have picked in your pre-approval, you have to choose them at least three times more. And write an email to Roberta Limone or her equivalent in case of any doubts.
academics_comments: Rome is amazing to live in, and it has been amazing getting to know the city so well. Besides this, what mattered the most have been all the nice people i have met there. The academic level was very low, but that just meant that there was more time for all the fun things.
course_level: As mentioned it was very low. I think i might have also managed to pick some of the worst ones - some of the EU-classes might have been a bit better. But certainly do not go there for the academics. They do not use citations, and i was several times asked to not put in references. A teacher at first said that he "did not understand why we kept asking for a book" when we asked where the syllabus where. Some classes are mainly historical facts, some try with a few theories, but on a very low level.
teaching_comparison: MANY student presentations. Which are not 10-minute ones but one and a half hour. Simulation-games takes up a lot of time. One class was without power-point and without texts, so you had to write everything down (I would not recommend "international organizations and human rights" for this reason). But other than that just normal teacher-presentations.
courses_enrolled: Sociology of terrorism, international organization of human rights, diplomacy and negotiation, chinese studies and geopolitical scenarios.
recommended_courses: None of them really. Chinese studies where very easy and the teacher was very sweet, so maybe that one. Sociology of terrorism was interesting enough, but the teacher is really not very pleasent. Diplomacy and negotiation was relatively okay, but we spend around a month on simulation games. Geopolitical scenarios was just the teachers view on world history (fun fact, Brexit is the fault of the queen of England and France should just share their nuclear weapons with the rest of Europe). International organization and human rights is the most boring class i have ever had, and the teacher Elena Scico laughs at people at their exam. Maybe try the EU-courses. I had only oral exams, and they are in front of the whole class and absolut chaos. It is not as bad as it sounds, but if you are not into oral exams, maybe consider taking a few ones with a written exam. It is hard to avoid having a few orals, but they are really not that bad.
unexpected_costs: I just think i spend more money than i expected, i am not quite sure that i can explain on what. We also did quite a few trips around the country, and traveling back and forth for Christmas was also a bit expensive. But it kind of all added up with various scholarships.
cost_comparison: Supermarkets are more expensive than expected. Drinks are much cheaper some places, beers are more expensive.
activities_available: Some sports-clubs, but i do not know much about it.
activities_recommended: Join a sport-team. Participate in the intro-programme even though it is a bit silly and expensive.
weekend_recommendations: Take trips and spend time on just getting to know Rome.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy. I had some frustrations about the teaching methods and the teachers attitudes, but the other students very very nice.
socializing_tips: They are very friendly, maybe join some clubs out of class if you want to get to know some Italians.
cultural_challenges: The professors. For instance being 20 min late for an exam, being on the phone during exams and generally much more hierarchy. I had a hard time accepting to call people "professor" (especially when they are actually not professors...). Also Italians are generally really not hiding their feelings, and i got told off but random Italians quite a few times.
culture_appreciated: Very friendly and helpfull students, and the laid-back italian attitude to many things. Met a very lot of very nice italian people, they do not seem as busy as we do.
top3_advice: 1. It is an amazing experience, please do it. 2. Do not expect too much of the academic level, but try to take the differences as an experience. 3. Enjoy it, and enjoy Rome, it is a great city to be an exchange student in!
other_useful_info: The language-cause on LUISS is very bad. We hired a personal teacher, which was not very expensive.
most_rewarding: All the nice people, experiencing a different culture, experiencing Rome, seeing the different approach to many things.
greatest_challenge: There where really not many challenges. I had three oral exams in two days, that was a bit challenging. Other then that, it went quite smooth.
other_comments: By all means go on exchange and go to LUISS, it has been a really great experience and all ways. LUISS is a private business university, so the facilities are very fancy.

crucial_aspects: The main aspects have been the opportunity to choose courses in English at the university and the student life. The host city itself was also important to me, I wanted to choose a place that I wanted to explore. The handbook received in the beginning was also a good place to look for information before arriving.
info_ease: LUISS was quite good at communicating the important information to us and they were helpful and quick to answer. The website is also helpful and has the necessary description of the courses.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any assistance.
arrival_comments: We didn't receive much information about exams, midt-terms and assignments in the beginning of the courses which caused some confusion.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You have to choose courses and register for them on the Web Self Service. You have to find the courses on the website or a list provided by Luiss. It is the student's responsibility to check if there are any time overlaps between courses. As we have to choose 5 different courses, it was a bit hard to find courses that don't overlap but it is also possible to choose courses from other faculties, which helps.
registration_help: The Mobility office at Luiss was helpful and answered e-mails quickly. LUISS also provided the students with courses available. The website and time table website is also very useful.
registration_success: I got all the courses I registered for.
registration_advice: Read the descriptions carefully and check courses from other faculties as well.
course_level: The level of courses is generally lower than at the University of Copenhagen. The courses are all only 6 ECTS, but the curriculum is quite large and does not correspond with the ECTS-points.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is mostly a traditional lecture - the teacher is presenting a Powerpoint and the students are listening. The involvement of students vary from course to course, but it is possible to engage with the professors.
courses_enrolled: Regulatory Innovation, Legal issues in Marketing, Diplomacy and Negotiation, EU law before Courts and EU Private Law.
recommended_courses: I would recommend Legal Issues in Marketing. The professor is very well-structured and good at explaining lectures in a clear and understandable manner.The course is interesting.
unexpected_costs: There are some expenses related to the student association ESN (ERASMUS STUDENT NETWORK) that organizes the Welcome Week and other activities during the semester.
cost_comparison: local transportation was less expensive than excepted (35 EURO a month).
activities_available: There were some sport teams and the ESN group, that organized activities for the exchange students. The ESN group also organized a football tournament for the exchange students.
activities_recommended: I would recommend to attend the Welcome Week and the trips organized during the semester.
weekend_recommendations: The city of Civita di Bagnoregio was very beautiful and intersting - it is possible to combine it with Orvieto or other towns in Umbria. I would also recommend visiting Castel Gandolfo - 45 minutes from Rome by train. It is best to visit is early on, when the weather is still nice.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy and very interesting to experience
socializing_tips: There are always some Italian students attending the courses, so it is possible to connect to them there. There is also a student association that organizes parties for both Italian and exchange students.
cultural_challenges: It can be a bit frustrating to adjust to the less structured way of teaching.
culture_appreciated: The food, history and energy/laid back style of the Italian people.
top3_advice: 1) if you have any problems reach out to the Mobility Office, 2) there are a lot of materials uploaded on the courses sites but it is not necessary to read/study everything, 3) pay attention to the Powerpoints - those are the exam materials.
most_rewarding: The opportunity to study at an Italian university and test my academic abilities in new environment.
greatest_challenge: Adapting to studying in English and having 5 different courses at the same time.
