info_ease: It was possible to find all the necessary information and the University even sent out a handbook with information, which was very helpful. However, it could have been useful to receive this handbook earlier than we did.
arrival_assistance: On the first day the host University held an informative orientation. However, most of this information I already had upon arrival. Furthermore, a student organisation held an orientation and had made a forum where all exchange student could talk with each other. This was helpfull for the more practical stuff if people needed help with that. The host university's mobility office was also very quick in their reply.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I had to apply for the University quite early on, where you had to fill out your basic information. When it came closer I had to apply for the courses I wish to have.
registration_help: The host University sent out a handbook with useful information.
registration_success: I got all the classes I applied for. However, it was quite a pulse to make a good schedule with 5 courses as a lot of student have less courses and there where a lot of overlaps.
registration_advice: To look at the website and wait/ask for the handbook and ask the mobility office if necessary as they are quick to reply and super helpful.
course_level: I would personally say that I found the academic level lower at the host University than my home University.
teaching_comparison: It was very different as UCCPH is interactive and depend on group work, whereas the classes at LUISS primarily was a lecture from the professor. In two of my courses we had to do a presentation in class and got feedback on this, but other than that is was not rather interactive. Ofcourse you were welcome to ask a question and they would also from time to time ask one, but I would say that if you prefer a lot of interaction and group work I would reconsider whether LUISS is the right choice. Personally I liked the style of teaching as you would get the materials explained in class and got an in depth feedback on the work you did, which sometimes can lack at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: European Business Law Public Comparative Law European Criminal Law Eu Substantive Law: Internal Market And Beyond The Protection Of Human Rights In Europe
recommended_courses: I really liked The Protection Of Human Rights In Europe as the professor was very passionate and critical about the subject. He had a different focus than most professorss I have met at UCPCH regarding human rights in Europe, which of course where interesting to hear. Furthermore, both the professor and the teacher assistent gave an in depth response on a mandatory presentation, even though it was not part of the exam. The same was the case for the exam paper. I like that they spend time on proper feedback. A lot of the students also liked European Business Law.
unexpected_costs: It was sometimes difficult to get home at night if we where in the other part of the city as the metro is closed at night and the busses can be very unreliable. Luckily I lived close to most of my friends so we could share a taxi or an Uber.
cost_comparison: I would say that if you go to the right places you can find good food and drinks quite cheap, however at least me and my friends also ate out a lot more than at home so end the send it was not less expensive. As I wrote above I was surprised how often you needed a taxi to get home if you where far away and it was not possible to walk. Some people bought a subsection to the scooters, so if you like to use these this might be an option for you.
activities_available: The host institution had an ESN office, which was really to at providing social events in the beginning especially where exchange students could meet each other. They also created a group chat, which in the being was used a lot to meet new people.
activities_recommended: To participate in the events by ESN in the beginning and also ERA makes a lot of fun events though out the semester. Especially the intro week by ESN and maybe one of the trips they do. I would say that it is important to go to the events in the beginning as this is where everyone meets and are the most open. Hereafter of course you still meet and fall into talk with new people, but it is defiantly useful to meet some nice people you like at these events in the beginning.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend to take a small trip with your new friends to another city and see the country and to go out and enjoy the nice italian cuisine.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy. The local people where nice, but it was useful/necessary to learn a couple of everyday frases in italian. It actually became more difficult in the end when the turist season came, as they then started seeing me as a tourist (I am blonde) and was not as friendly.
socializing_tips: I spend most of the time with other exchange students. I think there is a language barrier, so if you truly wanna socialize with the italian students I would recommend learning italian. I met some in class and at parties, but it was difficult to keep up as there often was a language barrier.
cultural_challenges: If you are a blond girl it can be a bit annoying that they will comment on your looks and view men and women a bit different at times. They are also a lot more opinionated about what food you order and how much you eat. If you go out and not finish your plate the waiter will comment on it. Another example is when you order coffee and what kind. Theses things they have strong rules about. Time is more loose. It will happen that the classes do not start on time and that the bus will be late (if it comes at all). So be patient and do not stress about a little delay.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated the good food, coffee and wine.
top3_advice: 1) Learn a bit of italian beforehand 2) Join the ESN events 3) Be aware that the exams is different than at UCPH and can be based partly on something you have to do in class like a presentation or that there can be a difference on the type of exam you can take depending on how much you have participated at classes.
other_useful_info: As stated earlier, it is important to not stress to much about the time as the classes sometimes starts later and sometimes end later that scheduled. It can happen that they go 15-30 minutes over time or start that much later. If you have classes close to each other you will just have to list out quietly if it continues for too long (more than 10 minutes).
most_rewarding: To meet people from around the world and to get a new prospective on my academic interrests and on life in general.
greatest_challenge: There was noting that could not be fixed, but maybe COVID-19.

arrival_assistance: The ESN (Erasmus Students Network) linked to LUISS arranged a welcoming week (mostly parties)... I don't know if this counts as assistance but it was fun. Also, I participated in the buddy programme and got linked with an Italian student from LUISS. We met a couple of times and he also invited me over for a party at his place. It got cancelled because of rain unfortunately.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Very good experience. I had a lot of fun, I learned a bit and I met some nice people.
registration_process: When applying for LUISS you'll only know the courses offered in the current academic year meaning that some courses can change. This is a bit frustrating as you have to get the "forhåndsgodkendelse" of your courses before leaving. When you get to LUISS and start taking your classes, you can change your courses in the first two weeks. This is a big bonus as you will then have time to find the right courses which can be approved by UCPH within the first two weeks of the semester. My advice would be to find courses now (as you are applying for the "forhåndsgodkendelse") that somehow fit the criteria from UCPH. Then, when you get to Rome you'll receive the list of courses offered on your semester 2-3 weeks before the semester starts and you'll have time to try out different courses and change your learning agreement so that it fits to the courses you are taking in the end.

weekend_recommendations: Italy.

culture_appreciated: Aperitivo <3

other_useful_info: Participate in the welcoming week, relax, enjoy.

crucial_aspects: I had been in Italy for some months before and had learned Italian. I chose Rome because I wanted to try living in such a big city. I also chose it because the university LUISS is academically good according to international rankings.
info_ease: It was quite easy. Compared to other Italian university, Luiss provided a lot of information. The student orientation service was also quite effective and quick to respond. Besides this, there is a big volunteer organisation of local students welcoming the exchange students.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance both from the student mobility service and the Erasmus organisation.
arrival_comments: A lot of information was available very close to semesterstart or only after the semester started. But after getting used to this, it was no problem.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There are different websites you need to register on. The communication took place via university email and was pretty straightforward. Choosing courses is done online as well.
registration_help: The student mobility service and IT service were both quick to respond. Information could be found in a welcome folder given by email.
registration_success: The only problem were time overlaps, which meant I had to choose new courses. But besides this I had no problem joining courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Ask for help if you need it.
course_level: I am in the final year of my bachelor and took only courses at masters level. Academically they were okay, and not too difficult.
teaching_comparison: There is a lot more interaction during courses, and exercises encouraging debates and presentations. It was a good opportunity to practice oral skills, where UCPH focuses on written essays and exams.
courses_enrolled: "EU Institutions and Decision-making", "EU Neighbourhood Policy", "Comparative Politics", "Storia delle Istituzioni e dell'Amministrazione", "Heritage, Tourism And Sustainable Economic Development Policies"
recommended_courses: The EU oriented courses were nice because they were in-depth and they had guest lecturers from EU institutions.
unexpected_costs: I did not really encounter unexpected costs. Only thing is I went out to eat and drink a lot more than at home.
cost_comparison: Basically everything is cheaper than in Denmark as I expected.
activities_available: I took part of the LUISS Run Club. Besides this I attended events from the university's Erasmus organization that organized many parties and trips. In total I went to activities like this 2/3 times per week
activities_recommended: Attending group trips to other places, and joining sports teams to meet other people
weekend_recommendations: All of Rome including less touristy areas like Prati, Pigneto, Testaccio etc.
culture_adjustment: It was okay. It is still Europe. The difference is mainly when and how often you go out to eat and how much you stay outside.
socializing_tips: Live with Italians or be very active in searching for friends during group work etc.
cultural_challenges: Not any particularly challenges, but the tone of voice can be a bit different and people sound more angry than they are.
culture_appreciated: The food and the culture of being outside eating, drinking and socialising all day.
top3_advice: Find housing early, attend the events and be open to new people, and take the opportunities the university provides.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Meeting new people from other European countries, that I will have contact with in the future.
greatest_challenge: Socialising every day in the beginning was a bit tiring.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial for me that it was a country I would feel comfortable in. I also wanted to study at a university that I had heard good thing about beforehand.

arrival_assistance: Look at the abovementioned.

The downside of it is that there are three mid-term tests along the way, each of which counts 25% of the total grade. cost_comparison: I was very lucky to find a cheap apartment, so the cost was much lower than I expected. In addition, living in general in Rome was also cheaper than I expected - especially eating out.
activities_available: There were a lot of activities. You could sign up for different sports teams. In addition, ESN planned a lot of social things for exchange students.

crucial_aspects: Overall, I chose my study destination on the grounds of location, courses offered and earlier evaluations from other students. registration_comments: Go on an exchange, regardless of which destination will end up being available for you.
registration_process: Before leaving home, the administration of the host university will send you an e-mail explaining the registration process. They will publish an Excel-sheet with a list of all courses for the whole university for the upcoming academic year. Be aware, that this list also consists of courses on other faculties. You will be able to look up all relevant courses on a platform describing the course, the professor and the exam method. The process begins with registering yourself at (typically) five courses on 6 ECTS – this will be done shortly after your exchange spot is confirmed. It's important to check the time-schedules of the chosen courses, so no timetables overlaps! Within one month you will receive a confirmation on your registration. Unfortunately, one of my five courses got cancelled, why I only was assigned 24 ECTS to begin with. A little while after the initial confirmation, the host university will open a second registration-period, where you can find a fifth course suiting your timetable. Because of the possibility of not being confirmed on all of your initial courses, I would recommend getting a pre-approval on at least 60 ECTS from the University of Copenhagen. By doing so, you have more courses to choose in the second registration-period. When you arrive in Rome and start at the host university, they let you “course-shop” for the first two weeks, so you can try your chosen courses and – if you're not satisfied – choose some other courses to be finally determined two weeks after the start of the semester.
registration_help: The host university will send you a full guide explaining all necessary steps to be aware of. They're very good at answering on e-mails in case of any uncertainties. In addition, you're assigned an exchange-buddy from the host university who will assist you and answer any questions that may occur.
registration_success: This is explained above. In the end – after trying different courses in the first two weeks of the semester – I got assigned to all of the five courses I wanted. There was no problem at all. In some of the courses only 20 students attended – in others 60 students, so overall, I think the host university runs the greater part of the initially available courses.
registration_advice: See above about things to be aware of during the registration. Stay calm during the process – it can be a bit challenging not knowing your final courses at semester start. This is completely different compared to the University of Copenhagen, but in the end, everything will turn out in the way you want it to be.
academics_comments: Go on an exchange, regardless of which destination will end up being available for you.
course_level: The level of the courses differs a lot. Some professors were surprisingly bad at English pronunciation and, unfortunately, that had an impact on the overall outcome of the given courses. In some courses, the professors were a bit unspecific with regards to readings and assignments, and in that way, the level of the given courses were up to the students to decide – for example through own proposals of readings and such. In other courses, the professors expected a lot; that we were well-prepared, ready to answer unknown questions throughout the lectures and tuned to day-to-day changes. Overall, I would say, that the level of courses is higher at the University of Copenhagen, but with that said, you'll still have a great outcome academically.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at the host university is very different from the one at the University of Copenhagen. First, there's a completely different relationship between the students and a professor. A professor is typically very authoritarian and conversations with a professor occurs in a very formal language. Secondly, the assessment method in each course differs a lot, and you need to be aware of how you're assessed in each course. In one course, you're assessed solely based on one test or a written assessment, in another course, you're assessed 10 percent on presence, 20 percent on active participation, 20 percent on an oral presentation and 50 percent on a final exam – written or oral depending on whether you have participated or not. You need to be aware of the fact, that many of the decisions are made solely by the professor in each course and not administratively. Finally, be prepared of a relatively heavy workload, given that the courses are only 6 ECTS, and lastly - prepare yourself on being secure in speaking english. You'll use a lot in class, and if you are to have any oral exams, they will typically be held with the whole class present while being examined.
courses_enrolled: Climate Justice (M479) Data Protection Law (M389) EU Law Before Courts: Rights and Procedures (M471) European Private Law (AD4) Media Law (M469)
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend Data Protection Law. It's a very interesting course and the professor is very competent. His teaching method is very different from the one at the University of Copenhagen, and the overall workload is quite huge being a 6 ECTS-course. Nevertheless, attending the course will help you understand the legal framework around Data Protection both in the Union but also in other parts of the world, and when finishing the course, you'll the needed amount of knowledge to feel more secure in working with personal data. If you're interested in Human Rights Law, both Climate Justice and Media Law are two great courses as well. They'll introduce you to a great part of the European human rights framework, and in the courses, you'll work and deal with very contemporary topics.
unexpected_costs: Expensive monthly bills for water, heat, electricity, etc. You will end up spending money on a taxi home during night hours. Make sure you have considered that you may need to go home to Denmark for a weekend or two during the exchange-period.
cost_comparison: It's, generally speaking, very cheap to eat out at restaurants compared to buying groceries. It's also affordable both experiencing cultural sites as an EU Under 25-citizen. And using the railway for weekend trips didn't cost as much as expected.
activities_available: Both the host university, the ESN-Network and the Erasmus Roma Association arranged everything from training, sport practices and tournaments to cultural exhibitions and city tours. ESN is a network connected solely to the host university while the Erasmus Roma Association is linked to all international students on all universities in Rome. Both organizations offer discounts on everything from dinner places to museums besides organizing such things themselves. Both organizations also arrange day- and weekend-trips outside of Rome. Be aware that every EU-citizen under the age of 25 will get access to all cultural sites in Italy for only 2 Euros.
activities_recommended: Participate in whatever you're just considering. When participating in these non-academic activities, regardless of what it is, you will get to know new people, and this is a part of the whole idea behind going on an exchange.
weekend_recommendations: Italy has an amazing railway-system. All the big cities around Italy are connected to Rome with train, and a train-ticket will often be affordable, since the two major companies operates with discounts for students and “Under 25”. I would highly recommend taking weekend trips to everything from Venice and Milan in the northern part of Italy, Pisa and Lucca in Tuscany to the Amalfi coast and Naples in the south. There are also great places to visit for a day-trip – the Vesuvius Volcano, Tivoli and Lago de Bracciano. All amazing places if you like nature and hiking.
culture_adjustment: It takes time - but it will take time no matter where you're going. Italians are, first of all, very proud of their language. Many people in the elder as well as the younger generation doesn't speak english, and this can be a it challenging sometimes. Nevertheless, Italians are very easy-going and they often take things as they may come - no one really operates with a calendar and plans for the future. This is very different from Denmark, but you'll quickly fall into the Italian way of living - it's so great to start you day off by drinking a cappuccino on your own, local café around the corner and spontaneously go out for an Aperol after class.
socializing_tips: Italians may seem a bit reserved because of their difficulties with English, but they are not - at all. Be open and use Google Translate as a tool for communication - both by message and in person. With this said, Luiss is a very internationally oriented university, and many of the local students will be good at speaking english. Just say hi and ask them, if you have any questions.
cultural_challenges: Explained above.
culture_appreciated: Also explained above.
top3_advice: Be open, be patient and be excited.
other_useful_info: Download TicketAppy for public transportation and order your groceries and dinner on Deliveroo when having a day off - always offering many different things at fair prices.
most_rewarding: Cliché, but everything. Just go.
greatest_challenge: Meeting the Italian hospital system. Make sure, that you have a good insurance by choosing the company, where you have your other insurances :)
other_comments: No.

registration_process: I don't really remember it that well since I registered almost a year ago. However, I remember thinking it was a bit inconvenient.
registration_help: You could easily send them an email and they were quick to respond.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: It is possible to switch courses until a few weeks after the beginning of the semester. That way it is possible to try out different courses.
course_level: The EU Law before Courts-course was by far the most challenging and the course most similar to the courses at UCPH as regards the academic level. The other ones weren't difficult.
teaching_comparison: Attendance is mandatory. Some teachers just talked for an hour and a half, but there were also courses in which the teaching consisted of discussions. They use teaching assistants so some of the courses had a lot of different professors and teachers. I had a few multiple choice-exams and that was very different from the exams at UCPH. Not necessarily easier.
courses_enrolled: International Organization and Human Rights. EU Law before Courts: Rights and Procedures. European Private Law. International Arbitration: Law and Practice. Data Protection Law.
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend the International Arbitration course since that was my absolute favorite. If you enjoy EU Law, you should enroll in the EU Law before Courts course which was an in-depth analysis of the basic EU principles. The International Organization course was nice since it was mostly Italian students. In the other courses I had there were a lot of exchange students. Furthermore, the classes were at another, bigger campus. I did not enjoy the European Private Law course. It was unstructured and there was too much preparation for a 6 credit course. The professor in Data Protection Law was very skilled but the course itself was kind of boring.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping is very cheap and the same goes for going out for dinner.
activities_available: I did not take part in a lot of those social activities except for a few dinners and parties during the first week organized by ESN. The exchange students from UCPH were somehow a bit older than a lot of the other students, Italian as well as other exchange students.
activities_recommended: If you're going there by yourself and don't know anyone there, you should definitely join the ESN since it's a great opportunity to meet people.
weekend_recommendations: Go explore Italy with train. Flights to Morocco are also very cheap. The beach is only a 45-minutes train ride away.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Enroll in courses that are taught in English but not created especially for exchange students. Go out in the weekends.
cultural_challenges: Not particularly a cultural difference but the Italians I met were not very good (or comfortable with) speaking English.
culture_appreciated: They're all very laid back, don't rush things.
top3_advice: Search for housing as soon as possible! Be prepared for the public transportation that simply does not work as well as the public transportation in Denmark. We walked a lot. Learn some of the basic Italian phrases.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: The experience of living somewhere else.
greatest_challenge: Being away from family and friends.

crucial_aspects: LUISS has a strong reputation within the field of political science, as well as an innovative learning approach. Furthermore, the rich culture and history of Rome was a crucial variable in my choice of destination.
info_ease: Fairly easy
arrival_assistance: I needed urgent assistance regarding my courses, as unforeseen rescheduling jeopardised my exchange.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration is a first come first service system, meaning that the registration is quite stressful. Furthermore, the registration takes place over two periods as the schedule of the courses change drastically from the first to the second.
registration_help: Not much to be honest, however Italian administration processes are organised chaos.
registration_success: Fairly successful. Had to give up one course, however got the rest.
registration_advice: Make sure to have a lot of courses accepted by KU before going, as courses may not be available.
course_level: The level of the courses are in alignment with the level at KU.
teaching_comparison: The teaching is more "high-school-like" with smaller classes and more access to the professor. Furthermore, you'll do presentation, debates etc. regarding the topics studied in order to support your learning efforts.
courses_enrolled: The International Relations of the European Union Comparative Politics European Neighbourhood Policy and Migration Crisis Communication Corporate Strategy
recommended_courses: I think "The International Relations of the European Union" and "Comparative Politics" was extremely interesting, and lectured by some of the leading professors in European academia.
unexpected_costs: I didn't encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Food - particularly meat, wheat-products and vegetables - was fairly cheap, as a consequence of diversified VAT. Utilities, particularly gas, is quite expensive though. However, in the current political context I don't think that is an exclusive competence of Italy.
activities_available: There is multiple sports teams, parties, trips and political events available for students to participate in.
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend participating in "the opening week" activities arranged by ESN.
weekend_recommendations: Apart from the obvious, Colosseum, the Vatican, Trevi Fountain etc. I would recommend going to a city just out of Rome called Tivoli, which is really rich in terms of architecture and history.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy.
socializing_tips: Drink espresso, and embrace "the aperitivo".
cultural_challenges: Less organisation, and a general approach embedded in "building the plane as we fly".
culture_appreciated: The food is absolutely fantastic.
top3_advice: 1. Start organising housing early - recommend already in February as Rome is extremely hard to find accommodation in. 2. Make sure to have a lot of classes approved by KU-merit, before departure as courses are rescheduled upon until the week before lectures start demanding a certain degree of flexibility. 3. Remember to enjoy yourself. You are going to live in of the most important cities in the history of mankind. Embrace that, and make sure you enjoy the city and all the wonderful people you are going to meet on your way.
other_useful_info: Expect a little bit more chaos in terms of the administrative department at LUISS.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many new wonderful people from diverse cultures and countries.
greatest_challenge: To make sure that I got to do all the things I wanted before leaving. Time runs fast when you are having fun.

Jeg var heldig at bo med flere der læste fast på LUISS, men ikke var italienere, så det var en rigtig god vej ind.

culture_appreciated: Maden og stemningen.

greatest_challenge: At man ikke var med kæresten i så lang tid.

crucial_aspects: The culture of the country.
info_ease: It was okay. It was not very intuitive, but the mobility offices were quick to answer emails.
arrival_assistance: There was an intro day at the university, where we got some information. The university also sent us a book about the Erasmus programme before we arrived.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had to register for courses online in June and then you got your answer about three weeks later. However, it was possible to change your courses within the first week of the semester if there were available spots for the courses. Be aware that it is your own responsibility to choose courses, that do not have time clashes.
registration_help: You could write to the student mobility office at the university.
registration_success: It was a bit confusing but I ended up getting all the courses I applied for.
registration_advice: Everything is easier to fix when you get to the university. The student mobility office is very helpful.
course_level: It is the individual professor that decides how the course is runned. However the university has some rules about the grading system that all courses must live up to. The professors do not always like this, which mean nothing is streamlined. Everything is so unstructured and it is very hard to be a part of as a abroad student. Many of the professors do not use reading lists. It is mostly about remembering stuff rather than understanding the theory and processes.
teaching_comparison: There is a lot of classroom participation and midterms. They take attendance in most courses, and you can't take the exam if you don't come to class. They also do a lot of simulations and roleplayes which often counts for you final grade. Almost every test is closed book and they care more about if you can remeber the correct names rather than understanding and using the theories and models.
courses_enrolled: Industrial Policy in Europe, Sociology of Terrorism and Political Violence, History of Foreign Italian Policy, Crisis Communication, Security Law and Constitutional Protection.
recommended_courses: Industrial Policy in Europe. This was the only good course I had. It was exciting, the professors were skilled and passionate, and they spoke understandable English.
unexpected_costs: No one
cost_comparison: I spend a lot more on food than I expected. I also spend a lot more on eating out as it was a big part of the culture
activities_available: There were so many social and cultural activities available. The Erasmus group of the University had plans you could attend more days every week. It was very good and there were so many exchange students to do all the fun stuff with.
activities_recommended: The football tournament, all the fun parties that the Erasmus Team plans. I would really recommend to by the intro package through Erasmus. It is a bit expensive but totally worth it in terms of getting to know people.
weekend_recommendations: All the cultural sights in Rome. I also recommend to use the fast trains in Italy to go on weekend trips to other cities.
culture_adjustment: It took some time to get use to the new culture but it was a fun experience.
cultural_challenges: The way they act so rude in public transportation.
culture_appreciated: How they live life more slowly. There going-out culture. The streets were always filled with people enjoying a drink in the evening. There very delicious food.
top3_advice: 1)Get used to the university being very unstructured. If you can try to find some locals students, who can help you understand the system. 2) Say yes to all the social events in the beginning, it is so much fun. 3) Find housing in walking distance from Campus if possible.
other_useful_info: Remeber you can change courses the first week of the semester.
most_rewarding: The cultural and social experience.
greatest_challenge: To understand the university teaching system.

crucial_aspects: The location and the culture based on what I have heard from other students.
info_ease: I received a lot of e-mails prior to my arrival at my study destination. They were filled with all the information I needed upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: My study destination had a Student Mobility office, where we could send e-mails to or meet in person if we had any problems. There was also IT-support.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was fine. We just needed to send an application with the most important information and a photo of ourselves.
registration_help: Again, the Student Mobility Office was helpful if we needed any help
registration_success: Because you need to attend all the classes, we had to make sure we didn't have any overlapping courses. That made me drop some courses I would have liked to attend. Other than that, no problems.
registration_advice: Remember to check for overlapping courses and try to organize your schedule in such a way, that you don't have too big breaks during the day, really late classes etc.
course_level: Because all the courses had an empirical approach, the level of the courses seemed lower than UCPH. There were no theoretical perspectives.
teaching_comparison: Really different educational approach. There were no theories, all the courses had an empirical approach. The assessment was based on class presentations, tests and oral exams.
courses_enrolled: African Politics And Society; Asian Culture and Politics; Political Thought In The Mena; Culture, Policy And Society; Heritage, Tourism and Economic Development Policies; The EU External Action
recommended_courses: Most courses were business orientated courses, so look through the course catalogue for the few good ones for Political Science.
unexpected_costs: Really high gas bills
cost_comparison: Gas bills were more expensive than expected. Museum tickets were less expensive than expected, as you can get really good discounts if you are under 25.
activities_available: Upon arrival, the Erasmus Student Network have organized a whole Welcome Week for all new Erasmus students. ESN also plan many social activities throughout the semester, which you can go to if you want.
activities_recommended: Get a recommendation list from a former exchange student with all the good spots :)
weekend_recommendations: In Rome, when the weather gets really hot, go to the lake or the beach to cool down! It is only about an hour of transportation and it is really worth it! Also go to other cities in Italy, there are so many amazing places
culture_adjustment: Quite easy! Everyone are really friendly. The only thing that can be hard to adjust to, is that the busses do not come on time....
socializing_tips: If you want to meet a lot of local students, then go to the ESN activities
cultural_challenges: Hmmmm, I don't know :)
culture_appreciated: The Italian food and of course the amazing big gestures, facial expressions and mannerism
top3_advice: Live close to the university, it makes the everyday life more easy Try to take one day per week to do all kinds of cultural stuff and see the city Eat a lot of pasta!
other_useful_info: Finding accommodation through Airbnb worked well for me
most_rewarding: Really amazing new friends <33
greatest_challenge: Not being able to bike everywhere, but having to either walk or wait for busses that does not show

crucial_aspects: I was motivated by the opportunity to explore a new culture, meet new people, while expanding my knowledge of EU law
info_ease: I didn't have any problems finding the necessary information.
arrival_assistance: We received e-mails containing the necessary information and the administration answered within reasonable time if I had any questions
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We had to use a designated portal for class registration, which was a bit confusing at first, but it worked. It will always take some time to make sure the classes are not overlapping
registration_help: You could send an e-mail to the administration, but I did not use it
registration_success: It worked fine. You could always re-register after the first week of classes if you wanted to switch.
registration_advice: Register for the classes you find the most interesting and go to the first week of classes and then you can re-register if you are not satisfied
course_level: 4 of the courses I took (Data Protection, Innovation Law, Intellectual Property, European Criminal Law) the level of the lectures were at a good level and the professors were very skilled in their fields and for the most part at educating as well. However, the exams were very easy. International Economic Law in the first part of the course it was impossible to follow the lectures due to the English level of the professor and the exam was very difficult depending on who examined you.
teaching_comparison: Mostly the same, there was little to no group work and some of the classes the final grade was based on among other factors attendance.
courses_enrolled: Innovation Law & Regulation, European Criminal Law, Data Protection, Intellectual Property and International Economic Law
recommended_courses: I would recommend Intellectual Property since Professor Geiger really made the course interesting and the exam form also was mostly relaxed.
unexpected_costs: Fitness was extremely expensive in the area I lived in (Parioli) and you also needed a medical certificate for 50 EUR
cost_comparison: Going to restaurants was mostly very cheap and groceries were a bit more expensive than I had anticipated
activities_available: There was a football tournament that I participated in which was a good way to meet other people, padel tennis tournament and weekly socialising events
activities_recommended: All the sports events and I would recommend participating as much as possible in the introduction week since it is where most of the people meet their friends
weekend_recommendations: Participate in the ESN events, Porta Cortese on sunday is a great market, Sanctuary is a nice place to go on sunday for Erasmus students
culture_adjustment: Very easy, had no issues with the culture at all. Only the more relaxed relationship with time
socializing_tips: Try to talk to people in class, they are usually very welcoming
cultural_challenges: No issues
culture_appreciated: The openness of the people and the relaxed way of living and the food of course
top3_advice: Do not stress about attending all classes. Prioritize going to as many events as possible and meet new people. Try to talk to people who are not from the same country as yourself, otherwise you might just only talk to people you could also talk to back home
other_useful_info: Ask the ESN coordinators about any questions you might have, recommendations etc. They are very helpful and it is also an opportunity to get some local friends
most_rewarding: Going outside of my comfort zone, talking to as many people as I had the energy for and gaining a lot of new friends all over the world
greatest_challenge: I didn't have any big challenges but at first it could be a bit intimidating being all alone in a new country, but that went away very quickly, since everyone is in the same boat

crucial_aspects: Previous travel reports and experiences from friends. Moreover, the distance to my home country had great importance.
info_ease: The administration on my host university was very helpful with a easy to reach office for students.
arrival_assistance: The university held several introducing lessons for Erasmus student. Here they explained all necessary information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration was digitally and we were guided in the process. The university was flexible in regards to changing ones elected courses.
registration_help: Digital guides.
registration_success: I got all my preferred classes.
registration_advice: Dont stress about it.
course_level: The courses were on a very low academic level compared to my home university. I was very surprised by the English level from my fellow students. Their lack of English skills made it difficult to communicate which was disappointing for opportunity to exchange cultures. The lack of supervision from teachers made it very easy for all students to cheat during test situations.
teaching_comparison: It was very different as we had way less teaching from the teachers on the host university.
courses_enrolled: Media Law New Technologies and Labour Law Administrative law Eu Law Before Courts: Rights And Procedures
recommended_courses: I will only recommend the course "Eu Law Before Courts: Rights And Procedures" because this course had a sufficient academic level and we had guests from EU.
unexpected_costs: Deposit related to accomodation
cost_comparison: Accomodation and insurance.
activities_available: Football tournament, Padel, etc.
activities_recommended: Especially the football tournament gathered all exchanged students which was fun.
weekend_recommendations: Take the train to the nearby Lake with the Pope's residence. Take to spa in Viterbo. Go to annually wine festival.
culture_adjustment: I loved the Italian culture
socializing_tips: Use the study groups.
cultural_challenges: The meeting time and language barriere.
culture_appreciated: Their way of living and eating.
top3_advice: Prioritize spending time in the intro week. Here you'll meet people from other studies. Choose accomodation close to a metro station as you cannot rely on the buses which are delayed constantly. Dont stress about the studies and enjoy your time on exchange instead.
other_useful_info: Reach out to older exchange students as myself in order to find less expensive and good accomodation.
most_rewarding: Meeting other people and learning about the Italian judicial system.
greatest_challenge: Transportation and group work with local students who couldn't speak English.

crucial_aspects: The country had to be culturally interesting to me including the opportunities for further exploration and food culture specifically.
info_ease: Fairly easy
arrival_assistance: There was a good introprogram both by the university and the independent student organisation.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There was sufficient information.
registration_help: An orientation presentation and a pamphlet.
registration_success: I unfortunately wanted a class that was fully booked 45 min. after the registration opened. I tried everything to get registered in the class, but the professors have no control and the administration does not budge. So if you didn't get one of your courses, you either have to give up or hope that someone drops the class.
registration_advice: Be ready when registration opens and be 100% sure of your password as the website went down, so it's impossible to recover your password in the middle of the whole process.
course_level: My bachelor courses were harder than my master courses and that was my general impression from others as well.
teaching_comparison: A lot like the teaching style in Danish high schools.
courses_enrolled: Comparative politics, The integration of Europe, EU law (terrible course), Financial Statement Analysis and Introduction to Business law. The last two courses I took outside of my study program to get access to another master program.
recommended_courses: If you are interested in extending your knowledge of law, I can definitely recommend the Introduction to Business law course.
unexpected_costs: I didn't have any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Restaurants and grocery shopping were definitely more expensive than I had expected unless you are buying Italian products. Some products were even more expensive than in Denmark.
activities_available: The organisation ESN hosts a lot of fun social activities.
activities_recommended: Padel is fun
weekend_recommendations: I went on some amazing trips in Italy. I would recommend seeing the Dolomites, Sicily and Bari/Matera! I wanted to go to Florence as well but didn't have the time.
culture_adjustment: It was okay. Italians are surprisingly bad at English, so it was hard to fully connect with the culture but that was expected.
socializing_tips: They are not that open to new people but luckily other exchange students are.
cultural_challenges: The language. Italians are not that good at English and I find it to be a very important factor in bonding with the culture.
culture_appreciated: The food and going out vibe.
top3_advice: Be prepared for the bad public transport, it's part of the experience, you will get tired of pasta and pizza, travel!!
other_useful_info: Don't go there for the academics.
most_rewarding: Travelling and meeting amazing people.
greatest_challenge: Social expectations.

culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: No

culture_appreciated: Their relaxed nature

greatest_challenge: I think it all went very smoothly

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne til en varm storby i Europa og gå på et universitet, hvor jeg vidste, at mine fag højst sandsynligt ville blive godkendt.
overall_comments: Rom er en fantastisk by at studere i. Man kan bruge alt sin tid på at udforske byen og stadig finde nye perler efter fire måneder. Priserne er studievenlige, der er mange tilbud til unge, og universitetet svarer hurtigt på alle de spørgsmål, man kan have som udvekslingssuderende.
info_ease: Luiss giver alt den information, man har brug for via mail, og deres exchange office er virkelig hurtige til at svare på spørgsmål.
arrival_assistance: Jeg fik et orienteringsskema og en 'Luiss Handbook' med al relevant information om universitetet, kontaktpersoner og byen generelt. De første par dage var sat af til intro, hvor vi fik rundvisning, kunne stille spørgsmål og mødte de andre Erasmus studerende.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Rom er en fantastisk by at studere i. Man kan bruge alt sin tid på at udforske byen og stadig finde nye perler efter fire måneder. Priserne er studievenlige, der er mange tilbud til unge, og universitetet svarer hurtigt på alle de spørgsmål, man kan have som udvekslingssuderende.
registration_process: Det er forholdsvist lige til. Hold øje med din studiemail og følg alle de instruktioner, der bliver sendt - vær opmærksom på deadlines, især ift. valg af fag.
registration_help: Luiss exchange office
registration_success: Jeg fik alle de fag, jeg havde ønsket. Dog var det en meget stressende process, og man skal sidde klar sekundet tilmeldingssiden åbner
registration_advice: Vælg en masse forskellige fag og prøv dem af i løbet af den første uge. Man kan nå at framelde sig fag i løbet af den første periode, så ville anbefale at prøve lidt forskelligt. Især fordi undervisningsstil varierer meget, og det er ikke altid, at beskrivelsen af faget matcher virkeligheden.
academics_comments: Rom er en fantastisk by at studere i. Man kan bruge alt sin tid på at udforske byen og stadig finde nye perler efter fire måneder. Priserne er studievenlige, der er mange tilbud til unge, og universitetet svarer hurtigt på alle de spørgsmål, man kan have som udvekslingssuderende.
course_level: Det er meget forskelligt fra KU. Man bedømmes løbende, og der er et større fokus på aktiv deltagelse, præsentationer og tests. Niveauet varierer ekstremt meget fra fag til fag, men man skal generelt ikke være nervøs for at vælge master kurser som bachelor studerende.
teaching_comparison: Større fokus på aktiv deltagelse, præsentationer og tests. Mere udenadslære til eksamener.
courses_enrolled: "EU neighbourhood - Policies and Migration", "EU institutions and decision making", "Comparative Politics", "Topics in African History and Politics", "Analytical and Foresight techniques for International Relations"
recommended_courses: EU neighbourhood - Policies and Migration: Det her fag kan tælle som EP i kombination med et andet EU fag. Det er virkelig spændende, og underviseren Maria Giulia Amadio Viceré er sindssygt dygtig. Det er klart mere krævende end mange af de andre fag, men til gengæld lærte jeg også meget mere her. Analytical and Foresight techniques for International Relations: Underviseren Manfredi Valeriani er god til at inddrage studerende og forme undervisningen på en anderledes og mere interaktiv måde end de fleste. Derudover er faget virkelig nemt at bestå, hvis man er interesseret i at bruge sin tid på andet end skole:)
unexpected_costs: Ikke rigtig nogle.
cost_comparison: Uber/taxa var en del dyrere end forventet.
activities_available: Der var virkelig mange Erasmus aktiviteter hver uge. Derudover havde Luiss også nogle forskellige udvalg, men deltog ikke i nogle af dem.
activities_recommended: Jeg brugte dem ikke. Hvis man vil lære andre udvekslingsstuderende at kende fra start, kan det være en fordel at deltage i nogle af Erasmus aktiviterne (OBS: lad vær med at købe den store Erasmus intropakke, det er virkelig spild af penge, og der er løbende aktiviter hele semesteret)
weekend_recommendations: Besøg Napoli, Bologna og Firenze! Flixbusser er virkelig billige rundt i Italien, og der er så mange hyggelige små byer tæt på. Tag til stranden i weekenden, og ellers bare tag på udkig i Rom - især i bydelene uden for centrum!
culture_adjustment: Meget nemt, men en kæmpe fordel hvis man prioriterer at lære en lille smule italiensk.
socializing_tips: Vær imødekommende og direkte. Der er en tendens til at studerende hurtigt grupperer sig efter nationalitet.
cultural_challenges: ikke rigtigt nogle.
culture_appreciated: Madkulturen! At tage ud og spise og drikke billigt, at mødes med folk på lokale barer efter arbejde/uni til en aperitivo. Derudover er arkitekturen og parkerne virkelig smukke, så nød at gå en masse lange ture.
top3_advice: Find bolig tidligt, prøv forskellige fag af, og lad vær med at stresse over eksamener! Der skal utrolig meget til for ikke at bestå, så nyd byen i stedet
other_useful_info: ikke umiddelbart. Kontakt exchange office, de kan svare på alt
most_rewarding: Helt sikkert at lære byen at kende. Find nogle lokale hyggelige steder, besøg dem mange gange, og få nogle nye bekendtskaber.
greatest_challenge: Ikke at kunne forstå sproget - ville ønske at jeg havde brugt mere tid på at lære det.

crucial_aspects: The crucial aspects were the rich culture and of course the food.
info_ease: Very easy. We received all necessary information from the university, including an orientation meeting at the campus.
arrival_assistance: Same as above.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: They helped you well through the registration process, which you basically finished before attending university for the first time.
registration_help: The student office was very helpful.

activities_recommended: The ESN week, and to plan a lot of trips to other parts of Italy.

culture_adjustment: The romans are very kind people, so you will easily adjust to their culture
socializing_tips: You will meet them at class, where you can socialize with them
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: The spirit of the Roman people, who are all very friendly and their way of living af beautiful, chill and nonchalant life
top3_advice: Find a good place to live, in a good and lively neighborhood, trieste, Monti, San Lorenzo (Not Tufello! or Montesacro!)
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many great people, some of whom you will meet again back home.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was not to be late, because of the deeply outdated public transport, but that is part of the charm.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte primært Rom på grund af byens størrelse, det gode vejr, forholdsvis lave leveomkostninger og det store ERasmus miljø.
overall_comments: Jeg er virkelig glad for, at jeg valgte Rom! Byen er stor nok til at du kan blive ved med at udforske den, men samtidig gøre kvarterer til dine egne.
info_ease: Luiss var fine til at sende mails omkring intro aktiviteter.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Jeg er virkelig glad for, at jeg valgte Rom! Byen er stor nok til at du kan blive ved med at udforske den, men samtidig gøre kvarterer til dine egne.
registration_process: Vær obs på at der er begrænset pladser på hold, så hvis du som jeg skal have særlige forhåndsgodkendte fag for at få merit derhjemme, skal du sidde klar når registrering åbner - eller have godkendt flere fagkombinationer på forhånd. Vær desuden opmærksom på at ikke fag bliver udbudt, hvorfor et forhåndsgodkendt fag eksempelvis kan ende med ikke at blive oprettet.
registration_help: Ved ikke
registration_success: Jeg var så heldig at få de fag, jeg skulle have for at få godkendt dem som hhv. Europæisk Politik og DAK 3.
registration_advice: Få forhåndsgodkendt flere kombinationer for særligt EP, hvis du er afsted på Statskundskab på 5. semester.
academics_comments: Jeg er virkelig glad for, at jeg valgte Rom! Byen er stor nok til at du kan blive ved med at udforske den, men samtidig gøre kvarterer til dine egne.
course_level: Du kan på ingen måde regne med et ensartet niveau eller at MA-fag er sværere end BA og vice-versa. Fagene er ikke nødvendigvis svære i sig selv, men der er stor fokus på paratviden og stedprøver, ligesom der løbende evaluering hvor fremlæggelser og quiz' i løbet af semester tæller med i den endelige evaluering af dig.
teaching_comparison: Underviserne har virkelig deres EGNE fag, så drop alle forventninger om læringsmål, studieordninger eller en fast eksamensform. I et af mine fag ændrede de eksamensformen flere gange i løbet af semesteret, så pas på med at vælge fag efter eksamensformen.
courses_enrolled: EU insititutions and decisions making + European Neighborhood Policies and migration (tilsammen erstatning for Europæisk Politik) Comparative Politics (erstatning for DAK 3) Topics in African History and Politics Analytical and foresights techniques in international relations
recommended_courses: Analytical and foresights techniques in international relations er en stor anbefaling! Vi var cirka på holdet og undervisning var meget diskuterende og interaktiv med en ung og dygtig underviser. Det var et dejligt praktisk fag, hvor vi skulle lave risiko analyser på rigtige cases, spille war games (fedt!!) og præsentere business cases. Comparative Politics var kaotisk og mærkeligt, European Neighborhood Policies and migration var virkelig spændende og brugbart!!!
unexpected_costs: Selvom det er billigere at spise ude, drikke vin og gå i byen, løber det MEGET hurtigt op, når man er ude hele tiden. Jeg brugte vanvittig mange penge på mad, kaffe og alkohol, så vær obs på at det særligt de første måneder kan blive meget dyrt.
cost_comparison: Offentlig transport er billigt - €1,5 for 90 minutters transport uanset transportmiddel. Købte nogle måneder et månedskort, hvor man kan rejse frit Hvis du vil på tur i Italien (anbefaling!), er indenrigsflyvninger billige, hvis du er ude i god tid. Ellers må du tage Flixbus 11 timer for at komme til Sicilien men tilgengæld kun betale 150 kr.
activities_recommended: Fodboldtunering, tage til nogle sportsgrene gennem eSN eller ERA
weekend_recommendations: Vandretur til dolomitterne!!!!!!!! Tog flixbus derop en forlænget weekend! Og badeferie på Sicilien! Se også Pavens sommmerresidens, tag i byen i Pignito, udforsk Garbatella, find en fast kaffebar eller resturant
culture_adjustment: De italienske studerende var ikke såå interesserede i udvekslingsstuderende, så dem så jeg ikke så meget til
socializing_tips: De er meget unge og posh I forhold til hvad jeg personligt er vant til, så har desværre ikke noget gode råd.
cultural_challenges: Alt den eksamenssnyd, som finder sted! Snak under eksamen, brug af noter til closed books, undervisere som intet gør. Derudover var mundtlige eksamener foran resten af klassen lidt specielt
culture_appreciated: Mad, tempoet, aperetivo!!!
top3_advice: Find bolig hurtigst muligt, hav penge til at rejse og drikke vin, find et stamsted, tag til pignito, følg minimalt med i undervisning og drop læsningen
other_useful_info: nej
most_rewarding: venskaberne
greatest_challenge: forvent at du også kommer til at føle dig lidt ensom, men at modgiften til det er et glas rødvin på en smal brostensbelagt gade

cultural_challenges: That local students wanted to socialize with international students.

courses_enrolled: EKHA61 Ekonomisk historia: Miljöhistoria ur ett ekonomiskt perspektiv SASH59 Gastronomy: Sustainable Eating SASH92 Social AI through the Looking Glass SASH96 Introduction to the Middle East in the Modern Periode

crucial_aspects: I chose to live in Denmark but study in Lund, so it was important that it was close to Copenhagen and therefore easy to travel to. Lund is also a highly ranked university that offers excellent study opportunities.
info_ease: Lund sent many emails upon my arrival, making it easy to find all the information I needed. They also responded quickly to emails, and everything ran smoothly. This was greatly appreciated and very different from my first exchange experience.
arrival_assistance: As I didn’t live in Lund, I didn’t use their arrival assistance. However, I know that there were student ambassadors at the airport and various train stations, as well as support available upon arrival. From what I heard from other exchange students, this system worked very well.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The application was submitted through a portal, after which you had to rank the available courses in order of preference.
registration_help: Videos and guides.
registration_success: I got all my first choices.
registration_advice: As a sociology student, I was a bit surprised by how few specific sociology courses were offered to master's students during the spring semester. In my case, no sociology courses were available. While there were several interdisciplinary master's courses, the overall range of options was not very broad.
course_level: I chose the inter disciplinary master courses. I took one statistics course, which I would say was at a very high level. However, overall, I found the courses to be easier than those in Copenhagen. Although there was more required attendance, or make-up assignments if you missed a class, and more continuous work throughout the course (due to the block structure, with only one course at a time), the exams were generally easier.
teaching_comparison: Overall, the experience was very similar. The teachers were addressed by their first names, and there was generally a sense that you could always approach and talk to them.
courses_enrolled: 1. Critical Feminist Perspectives in Social Theory (15 ECTS) 2. Process Tracing (7.5 ECTS) 3. Quantitative Methods - Multivariate Analysis (7.5 ECTS)
recommended_courses: If you're interested in learning Swedish, I know that Lund offers a popular Swedish course. I didn’t enjoy the course Critical Feminist Perspectives in Social Theory as much. I found some aspects of it to be quite biased, and a significant amount of time was spent on seminars where students presented sessions that were sometimes not well planned. Additionally, I wasn’t convinced by the use of process tracing, which I didn't find to be well presented. That said, this is just my personal experience, and others may have found it more valuable.
unexpected_costs: As I was living in Copenhagen, my experience reflects that. However, the Øresund travel card was quite expensive (around 2,000 DKK per month). I used most of my Erasmus grant to cover this cost. Some Danish students who were permanently studying there were able to get an 'Ungdomskort'.
cost_comparison: Almost everything in Sweden is a bit cheaper than in Denmark.
activities_available: There are many student nations offering various activities, and I think it's a great idea to join one.
activities_recommended: Participate in the nations activities.
weekend_recommendations: Visit Malmö and explore the city and the harbor area. Also visit Kulturen in Lund.
culture_adjustment: Very easy as I'm Danish and the Swedish culture is very similiar.
cultural_challenges: Not any in particular.
culture_appreciated: I was impressed by how well-organized the university was, not only when it came to getting documents signed, but also in terms of how the Canvas platform was structured.
top3_advice: 1. Check how many courses are available within your field of study. 2. Be aware that many courses require attendance, and if you miss a class, you may need to complete make-up assignments. 3. Although there are more assignments throughout the course, the final exams are often shorter, especially take-home written exams.
other_useful_info: The above covers most.
most_rewarding: I think it's always a great experience to study at another university and see how they approach academic teaching. It really broadens your horizons.
greatest_challenge: Time passed so quickly, and suddenly my exchange was over. Since it was winter during the first months, I forgot to take the time to enjoy the city. Toward the end, I had a more demanding course, and before I knew it, my exchange was over.

The idea is basically that the students do all the work in the tutorials, so the teacher is only there for navigating the students in their discussions. Doesn't work too well for exchange students, as we have not tried the method before. However, many times I would be the only exchange student in a class. course_level: Way too high considering what I expected
teaching_comparison: I come from a university where undergraduate teaching is primarily conducted in Danish. We had one course in the third semester worth 5 ECTS credits that was taught in English, but that was the only one. The students at Maastricht University were fluent in legal English, which meant that linguistically I was far behind my fellow students. Fortunately, I gradually caught up with the language, but this only happened after four months, by which point I had already completed my courses. Both the level of language and the academic level were extremely high. Not only were we, as exchange students, expected to have the same foundational knowledge as the other ELS (European Law Students), but it was also difficult to adapt to their teaching format. Maastricht University operates a period system where teaching is divided into two periods. Each period ended with a two-hour exam. Some exams were open-book, while others were closed-book. As a Danish student, I had never taken an exam without notes before. In the second period alone, I had three closed-book exams. During each period, we were required to submit midterms that counted toward a percentage of the final exam grade. This meant that over the course of four months, I effectively had to do an exam ten times. These midterms could take the form of debates, written assignments, presentations, or a mock trial. I can understand the advantages of making teaching more dynamic in this way, but under the conditions we were placed in, it was not possible to keep up as an exchange student. In addition, the teaching method was based on “problem-based learning,” meaning that we had to prepare a case and complete readings for every class. This teaching style is quite similar to the Danish system, which I actually appreciated. However, many of my fellow exchange students found it overwhelming and unfamiliar. My main challenge within this system was the extremely high expectations for the level of the cases, on top of preparing for midterms, keeping up with the extensive reading across multiple courses, and simultaneously struggling with the language. Whenever I did not have scheduled teaching, I spent the rest of the day in the library studying The teaching structure was such that we did not really have a teacher. Instead, we had a tutor who was considered responsible for the course. One student was either appointed or volunteered to act as the “discussion leader” and manage the class. I was appointed once, which was nerve-wracking and absolutely not something I wanted, but I did it. It is an experience I can now include on my CV, but it was not something I would have chosen voluntarily during my exchange.

registration_advice: Spend time looking into the courses but don't stress too much because changing them is relatively easy.

I had weekly readings of approximately 300 pages, weekly quizzes and multiple graded assignments during the semester. However, I don't think they were very harsh on grading since it was quite easy to get good grades. I think you would be able to set the bar low if you wanted.
teaching_comparison: I think the biggest difference was that there were more graded assignments and weekly quizzes on the lectures and readings. They were very clear about what they are expecting from students. In some classes, we had more seminar-type of discussions and others were more like lectures.

recommended_courses: If you're interested in criminology and security studies/intelligence, I would recommend all of these courses. I especially loved the one in cybercrime. They have a very nice selection of courses in this field. I recommend participating in class even though they offer the possibility to study online.
unexpected_costs: Overseas healthcare does not cover all the fees, you still have to pay a bit yourself.
cost_comparison: Covid -19 self-tests and masks were more expensive than in Europe. Eating out was cheaper than I expected. Fresh vegetables were very expensive in winter. In general, I'd say that living was cheaper than in Copenhagen.
activities_available: There was a wide selection of societies that offer different activities based on nationality (i.e., Nordic society), religion (i.e., Christian groups), and other interests such as parties, music, and different sports (climbing, volleyball, dancing)
activities_recommended: I didn't really participate in the non-academic activities but probably any of them could be nice depending on what your interests are.
weekend_recommendations: Sydney is such a cool city and there is so much to do and discover! There are so many nice restaurants to eat in, Parramatta is a cool Indian district, visit the markets in Glebe and the Rocks, hang out in Manly, transport using the ferries, and go hiking in the many national parks surrounding Sydney. Also, travel a lot of course. I visited New Zealand during the two weeks mid-semester break and it was amazing! It was relatively easy to travel during the semester even when I had classes.
culture_adjustment: Australians are relatively easy-going so it wasn't too hard to adjust. Practical things like setting up a bank account and getting a sim card were very easy. They are not very big on writing contracts for jobs or housing, so you have to be careful. The weekly system was weird at first. And don't underestimate the Australian winter, it gets cold.
socializing_tips: I found it quite easy to meet people in the class, they are very international and more talkative. Joining clubs and events would be another good way to meet local students.
cultural_challenges: The weekly system, unwillingness to write contracts, and quality of housing. They don't have as many vegetarian options available as in Europe.
culture_appreciated: They are quite easy-going, they have a lot of cultural events going on in Sydney, and many museums and galleries are free. The food is amazing.
top3_advice: If you decide to live off campus, take your time with finding a room in an area you like. Bring warm clothes if you come for session 2, it was cold in July! Get mentally prepared to study, the session was intense (only 13 weeks of studying). But the campus is very nice with loads of green areas, cool study spots, and food options.
other_useful_info: Even though the quality of housing is lower you can find very nice houses to live in with a good location. If you wish to work beside your studies, it is easy to find a job in a cafe or a restaurant.
most_rewarding: I got many chances to travel in Australia and see beautiful places. I really enjoyed my units and the teaching at my host university. I feel like I found a new perspective on my studies at KU.
greatest_challenge: Don't know if I had very great challenges but the weather when I arrived really surprised me (it was cold) and I didn't have enough warm clothing. The studying was quite tough especially when I didn't have a proper break between the semesters here and at KU.
other_comments: I would 100% recommend Macquarie University to anyone wanting to go to Australia. Even though the campus is a bit far from the center, the public transportation is good and the campus is very cool.

The course registration process was a bit complex, when registering for courses at master level, because you need to apply for a special approval for each course in order to enrol in a master level course at Macquarie University. In the special approval, you need to explain/argue how you live up to the necessary requirements for taking the course, which involve uploading the syllabus for previous classes you have taken. Information about this process was quit difficult to find.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation week hosted by Macquarie University the week before classes started, where you were able to sign up for different activities. This included a welcome meeting, where all relevant information was given and you could meet all the other exchange students.
arrival_comments: Information about how to register for courses and how the special approval process worked was very limited and could be improved. The orientation week was nice.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Sydney is an amazing city to live in, and Macquarie University offers some really interesting and unique courses within security studies!
registration_process: You have to upload some different documents, including your grade transcripts, bachelor degree transcript (if you are applying for master), and proof of English proficiency. My proof of English proficiency was that my master and bachelor degree were in English. When you are accepted you receive a letter of confirmation.
registration_help: A contact email and phone number were provided, which you could write/ring to if you had any questions.
registration_success: As mentioned the class registration process was quit complicated (at least when registering for master classes). In order to register for courses, you first need to apply for a special approval for each course in order to enrol in a master level course at Macquarie University. In the special approval, you need to explain/argue how you live up to the mandatory academic requirements for taking the course, which involve uploading the syllabus for previous relevant classes you have taken. Information about this process was quit difficult to find. But you can write to the contact email provided, and they will help you, or you can do some comprehensive researching and find the information on their website.
registration_advice: Make sure to apply for the special approvals as soon as the course registration opens to ensure that the application is processed before the semester starts. It can take weeks before the application is processed. Therefore, apply for more special approvals than you need, if some of your applications are rejected.
academics_comments: Sydney is an amazing city to live in, and Macquarie University offers some really interesting and unique courses within security studies!
course_level: I had four master level courses.
teaching_comparison: Each course often consist of 1 hour of lecture, which is either in class or prerecorded so you can watch them online, and the followed by two hours of seminar. The seminars are generally quit small, around 20 people, where you are expected to participate and engage in the discussions.
courses_enrolled: POIR8430: The Middle East in Global Politics, PICT8061: Transnational Security, PICT8018: Counter Terrorism in the Global and Australian Contexts, PICT8037: Choosing Terror - Pathways into Terrorism
recommended_courses: I would in particular recommend Counter Terrorism in the Global and Australian Contexts and Transnational Security. Counter Terrorism in the Global and Australian Contexts is a very relevant course in particular in today's world, and the course touches upon many different dilemmas and ways to counter terrorism and extremism. Transnational Security is likewise a very relevant and interesting course, touching upon different transnational security threats. The professor is also very sweet and talented.
unexpected_costs: I opened an Australian bank account to avoid paying fees every time I used my credit card. I can totally recommend that BUT be aware when you transfer money from your Danish bank account to your Australian bank account, because the exchange rate is often much worse. When making an international money transfer from your Danish bank account to your Australian, make sure that it is in AUS dollar and not in Danish kroner, then the exchange rate is better. Otherwise, you can end up loosing a lot of money due to the bad exchange rate that the Australian banks have.
cost_comparison: Food in the supermarkets is generally more expensive than in Denmark. However, it is cheaper to eat at restaurants, cafes and takeaway. As a student at Macquarie University, you get a Student Opal card, which is a transport card that allows you to travel by public transport at half price! This makes public transport very cheap! The electricity bills in Sydney are also more expensive than I thought.
activities_available: The university offered a very broad range of sports and social activities. The university also has a gym and a swimming pool, where you pay a weekly fee.
activities_recommended: Join a sports team! It is a fun way to meet other students - both exchange students and local Australians.
weekend_recommendations: Explore Sydney and go on weekend trips around NSW. Sydney has so many activities to offer and day trips that you can do, such as going to Manly, Bondi and Palm Beach. I would also recommend going to Royal National Park, where you can do different hikes, and it only takes about an hour by train. Hunter Valley is also lovely for a weekend trip, visiting vineyards. In September, you have a two week Spring break, which is the perfect opportunity to explore the rest of Australia.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. The Australian culture is very similar to the Danish, and people are very nice and helpful.
socializing_tips: Join a sports team or social club at the University, and chat with people in class.
cultural_challenges: I do not really think that there were any.
culture_appreciated: Their appreciation for the beach and being outdoors.
top3_advice: 1) Find a place to live in the city rather than on-campus, 2) Remember that you have two weeks of Spring break in September, where you can travel and explore Australia 3) Join a sports team or a social club
other_useful_info: Sydney is an expensive city to live in. I would recommend to apply for grants/scholarships - you can find an overview of all of them on legatbogen.dk. But remember to start applying for grants/scholarships early, as many of them have deadline 5-6 months before your exchange semester starts.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and living in Sydney for a semester, getting to explore Sydney's many amazing places and activities that it has to offer.
greatest_challenge: Hmmm, I am not sure. Maybe registering for courses?
other_comments: Have fun! Sydney is amazing!
