crucial_aspects: I have visited Australia before, and I really wanted to go back to Sydney. Important to me was to find a place where I could feel safe, a place where I couldn't just go back to visit my friends and family for safety, and a place from where I could travel to cool destinations and enjoy the city I lived in. Sydney and Australia has so much to offer!
info_ease: The university website was really informative, and the university is really good at reaching out and giving the information you need as an exchange student.
arrival_assistance: The website of the university and emails from the university, along with a webinar before our travel and an "Exchange Orientation" meeting at arrival and other fun activities where the exchange students got to meet each other.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: To register for the units, the university had a system/website to go through. They had introduction text and videos, so it was easy to do. The only negative thing to point out is that you cannot see the time tables beforehand, so I had to choose another unit, because my classes clashed.
registration_help: The university website, the unit guide, YouTube videos, and the registrations process was also described in the introduction webinar and in introduction emails.
registration_success: Very successful. I only had to change one unit registration, because the class clashed with another unit. However, you can change your units even after classes have started which is so cool and makes it less stressful.
registration_advice: Check out the unit guide and the Macquarie web site. Take it easy and read the emails from the university. You can always ask the nice staff to help you.
course_level: The level was fine. Some units were easier than others. The "international" law units were easier because you do not need to have knowledge of the Australian common law system. I found that the unit "Remedies" was much harder than expected, as I was missing a lot of background information.
teaching_comparison: Your final grade is not your exam alone. You get grades for participation and assignments along the way. This made it easier and made the exam less stressful. We had online pre recorded lectures in most units, and then we had tutorials which was teaching in smaller groups. The teaching was good, and I learned a lot from showing up to classes. There is a lot of reading, but it is not all required, so you should be good at distinguish the important readings from the less important readings.
courses_enrolled: LAWS8015 - International Law LAWS8098 - International Commercial Law LAWS8030 - The Law of Obligations I - Contracts LAWS8027 - Law of Obligations III - Remedies
recommended_courses: I would recommend units about different types of international law. This can be useful in Denmark as well, and it is easier to follow. However, I also enjoyed contract law, and this was fairly easy to follow as well. I would not recommend Remedies, as a lot of background information about the Australian law system is required. Most important is to go with what you find interesting!
unexpected_costs: Comment about the insurance: A required Overseas Health Cover (1.600 DKK) plus my personal travel insurance which covered many things, because I also travelled Australia before and after my exchange period.
cost_comparison: It is generally really expensive to live in Sydney. Housing and alcohol is especially more expensive than in Denmark. On the other hand, good barista coffee is cheaper.
activities_available: There is a lot of clubs of every kind! You can check out the Macquarie website, where the clubs are listed.
activities_recommended: You can most definitely find activities you would enjoy. There are lots of clubs - athletic, cultural, political and social. I enjoyed the Sport and Aquatic Center at the university (where I got a free membership through my college). In general, I also just enjoyed going to the city as a tourist and traveling Australia as well.
weekend_recommendations: Enjoy the many different places in Sydney - beautiful beaches, great architecture and a lot of amazing experiences. I especially loved The Rocks (and the markets there every weekend), Circular Quay, Darling Harbour and Manly Beach. But check out all of Sydney! There is a lot of free experiences, including free entry to every museum. Enjoy the bars and restaurants as well - I spent a lot of time with friends at different locations around the city.
culture_adjustment: Very easy - it is very impacted by the "western culture". However, I loved the multicultural Sydney, where people come from all around the world, so there is a lot to learn about different cultures.
socializing_tips: Just be outgoing and be yourself. You'll come a long way being interested in other people and always being open minded. Everyone is so friendly, and it is easy to make new friends.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: People are friendly and helpful.
top3_advice: Show up to classes and participate - you will get easy marks that way and you will understand a lot more and not lose yourself in all the readings. Enjoy the university and everything it has to offer. Also remember to get out of campus and go to the city center quite often - it has so much to offer!
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Getting to know new people from around the world and figuring out how easy it is to make new friends, when you are curious about people and open minded.
greatest_challenge: Everything you need to sort out before the exchange can be exhausting, but it is all worth it, and you forget about it, when you are there and just enjoying life.

registration_process: There's almost too much to remember... registration_help: You could write to the university staff that was in charge of exchange or try and find the answer on the websites, but mostly I found help from my friends that I had met at the University and already knew the process.

registration_advice: It is a great campus and school, make sure to check the available classes first and see how many interest you and if the match your degree and are able to teach you something that your home university might not. If you are ever in doubt about something, reach out to the fellow students of the university, they give quick answers and are happy to help. I would also recommend signing up for some of the student groups/activities they provide, it is a great way to explore, and meet other people. And be sure to make it to the orientation week! academics_comments: It was especially interesting to learn the focus points of the same degree in a different culture and how they choose to teach the different topics.
course_level: I had 4 courses, each 10 points, they had a bigger focus on weekly tasks and practical learning, than my home university that focuses more on reading and exams. It was a nice switch up - but a mix of both would have been ideal for learning outcome.
teaching_comparison: More practical approach, less reading, more small written task, less bigger written papers and exams.

recommended_courses: Performance practices were amazing and so fun! You learn in e very practical and good way. Radio and podcast production is also higly recommended at it was also very fun and I learned a lot of creative tools that I can use in various ways. Both classes had great teachers.
unexpected_costs: The health insurance only covers a very little part of the doctors appointments - even just the consultation. Be very sure when going to the doctors, and have a danish travel insurance that can probably cover the rest that the OSHC doesn't cover.
cost_comparison: Food and rent were more expensive than expected...
activities_available: A lot, everyone of them is listed on their website, so you can check them in advance, and they all have booths at orientation week, so you can go and check them out.
activities_recommended: There is the exchange student club which was good and created great opportunities.
weekend_recommendations: travel a bit, if you have the time/ money - maybe not to the more exploited places of australia, but just an hour or two away from the town you're staying at and explore the small places and see the "real life".
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy - but I am also an extrovert...
socializing_tips: Sign up for the different student clubs that interest you, try and live with new people - so not people you know from home or with more than just them and reach out to people from your home country that are going to the same host country/ university, so you don't feel completely alone when you arrive and can rely on them for support when in doubt or confused about the process. And go to the intro week!
cultural_challenges: The culture here was a lot different than what I imagined about Australie, there is a huge asian influence now which is amazing and really creates a cool perspective!
culture_appreciated: The diversity!
top3_advice: Get a hostel for the first few days while you visit places you might rent, if you're not staying with the university accommodation. Don't have flight ticket home already - you might want to alter your stay. Have money saved up sp you can go on adventures and try and find a casual job as well, so you don*t have to worry too much about money + it'll give you a better insight on life here and create more friend opportunities.
other_useful_info: Just choose your classes carefully and remember to have fun!
most_rewarding: The friendships I got here! Through University, Living situations and work!
greatest_challenge: Finding a good place to live (I was unfortunate with landlords and roommates and had to move around 3 times) And also just affording to live while inflation is going on...

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go on exchange to an English-speaking city so I could be on the same wavelength as the locals and understand everyone, rather than constantly having to communicate in a language other than my mother tongue. In addition, I wanted to go to a country with great opportunities for running and long coastlines, as well as a culture where I could relatively easily fit in. Sydney turned out to be a perfect match.
overall_comments: Absolutely amazing. It has been the best seven months of my life. Huge recommendation!
info_ease: It was easy to find information when we arrived in Sydney. Macquarie University was very good at sending emails with information, introduction programs, and similar practical details. We did experience some minor issues when arranging our timetable, as we moved things around quite a bit to try to fit all our classes into one day per week. However, the university staff were very helpful at the IT desk, and we ended up with a good solution.
arrival_assistance: We signed up for Macquarie University’s introduction program during Orientation Week. We were shown around the campus and had various practical matters explained to us by older students. It was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Absolutely amazing. It has been the best seven months of my life. Huge recommendation!
registration_process: After the University of Copenhagen had approved the courses, you applied to enrol in them at Macquarie University. Some courses required filling out a waiver request, where Macquarie needed to approve that you met the prerequisites for the course. After that, you could register for the course on a day and time of your choice, based on the options offered.
registration_help: You could contact Macquarie via their IT portal from home in Denmark. It was also possible to speak with the IT desk in person at Macquarie after arrival.
registration_success: I enrolled in the courses I wanted (three mandatory courses and one elective). I had three classes back-to-back on Wednesdays and one online class on Tuesday evening. This worked really well and gave me a lot of free time outside of class.
registration_advice: Make sure to apply for a waiver at Macquarie as soon as the University of Copenhagen has approved your courses — this will give you the most options to choose from. If you wait to enrol in courses at Macquarie, you risk only having limited options, such as Tuesday evenings from 7–9 PM or Saturdays.
academics_comments: Absolutely amazing. It has been the best seven months of my life. Huge recommendation!
course_level: I took two first-year courses and two third-year courses at the BA level. The first-year courses were somewhat lower in level than in Denmark — most of the work focused on reflecting on your own role in the subject. The third-year courses were more comparable to those in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: In general, all the lectures were online (you could apparently also attend them in person, but I didn’t). The courses were very similar to a seminar at the University of Copenhagen, with a class of around 30 students where you discuss topics, give presentations, and work on projects together.
courses_enrolled: Indigenous people in Australia (elective course) Introduction to Human Resource Management (mandatory course) Managing Change in Organisations (mandatory course) Social Research Methods (mandatory course) - This course has now been discontinued and was a replacement for Avanceret forskningsdesign og videnskabsteori (7,5 ECTS)
recommended_courses: Indigenous people in Australia! It was a really interesting and rewarding course. It provided a great historical understanding of living in Australia and the country’s history. It gave a deeper insight into many of the conflicts that exist in the country and offered some valuable reflections along the way. The lecturer was skilled and very engaged.
unexpected_costs: We travelled a lot and that was expensive but very worth it.
cost_comparison: We were four danish students who bought a car for 44.000 DKK. We sold it for 26.320 DKK. We lost more money than expected on this.
activities_available: So many different things. All kinds of athletic activities. Lots of social clubs and cultural as well.
activities_recommended: I didn't attend any.
weekend_recommendations: Visit the Pacific Islands and New Zealand. I can recommend buying a car with friends. It gives opportunity for many weekend trips around NSW, camping trips etc. We loved it! Tasmania was amazing!
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Sydney is such a nice city. We lived in Bondi and you should be aware that there is an extremely strong body-conscious culture around Bondi. It might be triggering for some people, but you get used to it.
socializing_tips: Run clubs!
cultural_challenges: There is not really a night life in Sydney. It is definitely a morning city. Everyone is up and working out at 5 am. And all clubs close around midnight or 1 AM.
culture_appreciated: The morning culture was amazing, I loved it. The aussie's are so nice people, and I loved how open and social the culture is. I loved the small talk everywhere you go. The culture around the coast line is amazing with beaches and surfing vibes.
top3_advice: 1. Live closer to the beach and not on campus around Macquarie. You will spend most time around inner Sydney/eastern suburbs. 2. Try to collect the classes on one or two day and give yourself as much time as possible to enjoy Sydney 3. If you have an elective course, do the Indigenous people in Australia. It was so rewarding.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Living so close with my friends, being each other’s primary people on the other side of the world, caring so much for one another, and making sure we were all doing well — it felt very much like a family with friends. I learned a lot from moving far away from home, but the best part was that it happened with good friends.
greatest_challenge: I felt that the culture in Sydney could sometimes feel unpredictable. Everyone is very self-aware and focused on their own personal growth. It was difficult to deal with the fact that you couldn’t always rely on other people. It’s not very Danish.

Go to stuff, hang out with friends, make new friends, take trips, go sightseeing, meet locals. Interact with the culture and really experience it - talk with locals and ask them questions, visit mosques fx to see how they live their culture, eat and drink local food and drinks (try everything), try out things that represents their culture. crucial_aspects: I chose McGill because I heard good things about the university, it's academic level and progressiveness within fields of my interest. Also, Montreal seemed like a good city to live and study in, neither too expensive nor too big but still a city with a lot going on.
overall_comments: The first half of the semester with a strict covid lockdown and a very cold winter was pretty rough, which is why I chose 7.
info_ease: I found all the immigration stuff a bit confusing to be honest. But I think it was very related to having the exchange semester postponed/cancelled several times and everything related to covid-19 travel restrictions. However, McGill were generally fairly easy to reach and had some informative webinars with the essential information so everything worked out fine.
arrival_assistance: Because of covid all our new/exchange/international students activities were held online, but I think it would be different usually. Also received e-mails with information about the most important stuff.
arrival_comments: Taken the circumstances into account it was pretty good. I found it easy to get in contact with the students service at McGill whether by e-mail, phone or google teams appointments.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The first half of the semester with a strict covid lockdown and a very cold winter was pretty rough, which is why I chose 7.
registration_process: You can start by looking over the courses in the course catalogue (https://www.mcgill.ca/study/2022-2023/courses/search). I wrote down the ones I found interesting, and waited for the minerva registration portal to open around a month before the semester started. Then I started registering, but many courses were already filled because the exchange students are let in on the site later. However, people add/drop until 2 weeks into the semester, so if you check minerva regularly (a couple of times a day), you will most likely be able to get the courses you want.
registration_help: Email mcgill if you have any issues, or email the specific instructors/professors.
registration_success: There was only one out of the 4 courses I hoped for that I never managed to get, which I think is fine.
registration_advice: Don't stress, it seems a bit confusing at first but really is not. Write an email to the professor if you need specific prerequisites or if you have trouble registering for their course. Check minerva very often if there is a course you really want. In the meantime just register for some that you wouldn't mind taking. Remember to read about the courses on minerva as well, sometimes there is some additional information available which is not written in the course catalogue.
academics_comments: The first half of the semester with a strict covid lockdown and a very cold winter was pretty rough, which is why I chose 7.
course_level: I took three 400-level and one 300-level which was a good combination. Would say the 400 level were my own level, but since the workload is higher at McGill it was really nice to have one "easy" class.
teaching_comparison: Much more work during a week. Approx. same amount of reading for each course, but the number of small papers/assignments, mid terms, presentations etc. was much higher. However, I didn't find the professors to expect particularly advanced work, seemed they mostly wanted to "check" that people actually read and understood.
courses_enrolled: CANS 306: Issues in Native Studies CANS 405: Cdn Studies Seminar 5 - Black-Indigenous Politics: From Recognition to Solidarity and Decolonization ENG 444: Studies Women's Writing & Feminist Theory - Gender and African Literature GFSF 406: Trans*Feminisms
recommended_courses: I especially liked the Trans*Feminisms course, which was taught by Calev Litvack who is an amazing and engaging professor! I really enjoyed ENG 444 as well.
unexpected_costs: The health insurance at McGill is a bit expensive, and you can actually get a RamQ card for free instead! Look it up.
cost_comparison: Groceries are expensive generally. PA and Seagal are much better than Metro and Provigo though.
activities_available: Again, I don't know much about it, but think there are several clubs.
activities_recommended: Would recommend joining the McGill outdoor club they have a cool house and also try and look up the ski club if you like skiing.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Quebec city, Toronto, New York, go skiing in Quebec or in the north of US, go hiking in the national parks, take trips to the coast.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy, I think the university culture is quite similar, maybe only people are a bit younger in general.
socializing_tips: Talk to people in class. Generally I didn't find a lot of people at McGill are actually from Montreal, but other places in Canada or US or international, so try and seek out other environments as well.
cultural_challenges: Hm, I think compared to Danes, people here are less reserved but maybe more difficult to really get to know.
culture_appreciated: There are a lot of cool events and cultural activities going on Montreal, which were easy to find and access.
top3_advice: 1) Everything seems a bit confusing from home/at first, but don't worry it will be fine 2) Try to meet people through other places than just uni, seek out your interests/hobbies/communities in the city 3) Live off-campus maybe in a shared flat, it is a good way to meet (local) people.
other_useful_info: Look for courses outside your own department, as an Anthropology student I could take courses in the whole Arts faculty (both social sciences and humanities) which was a really cool opportunity.
most_rewarding: Really good courses and inspiring professors, meeting new people and enjoying the music/art/film/party scenes of Montreal.
greatest_challenge: Probably covid.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to combine a university with high academic standards with an interesting city. Montreal has been mentioned as one of the best student cities because of the vibrant and very livable city with lots of you people and good universities.
overall_comments: My exchange semester has been postponed because of covid and all the administrative procedures before going were definitely very time consuming and frustrating. But as soon as you finally get there, it is really worth all the work.
info_ease: Check ArriveCan and you should be good to go!
arrival_assistance: McGill has a service mail and they usually answer pretty quick if you need help. I was also offered a 'buddy' (a fulltime McGill student) who could help me if I had questions.
arrival_comments: I think covid has made everthing complicated, which also affected the orientation assistance at my host institution. You had to be proactive and reach out yourself if you needed information, but that wasn't really a problem.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: My exchange semester has been postponed because of covid and all the administrative procedures before going were definitely very time consuming and frustrating. But as soon as you finally get there, it is really worth all the work.
registration_process: McGill's registration system is not the most intuitive system I have ever seen, so you have to be a bit patient. Also, you should consider starting the process long time ahead of the deadline, since you need to gather a lot of documents from your home university etc.
registration_help: You could often click on small question marks if you didn't understand something and then a help tap would appear. Also, you could always contact the administration from McGill. They are very helpful.
registration_success: Not very successful. The classed I wanted were only available in the fall (where I was supposed to go if it wasn't for covid). However, I got some other very cool classes instead.
registration_advice: Don't hesitate to contact the professors directly if you have problems registering to a class (because of prerequisites). I experienced that they would often let me join their classes if I explained my motivation and qualifications by email.
academics_comments: My exchange semester has been postponed because of covid and all the administrative procedures before going were definitely very time consuming and frustrating. But as soon as you finally get there, it is really worth all the work.
course_level: There were a lot of deadlines and much more participation grates than we're used to from University of Copenhagen. The level was higher than expected (from what you often hear about going abroad). That being said, I still didn't have the feeling that it was too difficult (maybe because we only had to pass the courses)
teaching_comparison: I really like the engagement of the professors. Also, office hours seems to be a big thing compared to UCPH. The professors were always willing to arrange a one on one talk, which was super helpful if there was something I wanted to understand/discuss more.
courses_enrolled: People analytics, Oral and written French 2, Topics in International Business, Social Inquiry
recommended_courses: People analytics was a really interesting course. The professor Matisse Hollister is really engaged and we touched upon so many interesting feels concerning Artificial Intelligence and ethics in Social data science.
unexpected_costs: I ended up going quite a few one day ski trips, which was really nice but also a bit expensive. Also, grocery stores are a bit more expensive than I expected.
cost_comparison: Eating out. Coffee at cafes (more like 25 DKK compared to 40 DKK in DK)
activities_available: Running clubs, French conversation cafes, friday bars etc...
activities_recommended: During winter: go on hikes and ski trips Summer: chill in the parcs, bike around (the BIXI systems works very well), enjoy the wide range of festivals and concerts
weekend_recommendations: rent a chalet outside montreal for a weekend with a group of friends, take the night bus to NYC, visit Vancouver
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Montreal is very international, so a lot of people have the same mindset as yourself. I met a lot of good friends outside university
socializing_tips: People are really friendly and open, so just talk to people in your classes or at cafes/bars. Otherwise, there are lots of running clubs (e.g the 6am running club).
cultural_challenges: Not much really. I think Montreal in general is a very easy city to adapt to. If anything, it would be helpful to at least try to speak french (for me this was a bit challenging here because of all the Quebecois slang, but people just appreciate that you try)!
culture_appreciated: People are used to the fact that people come from all over the world, so it's not a big deal where you're from, which I really appreciated. In general I experienced that people were very open minded and you could easily end up having a good conversation with a stranger in the super market which is definitely different from DK. Furthermore, I like the french/european touch on Montreal, which you can sense in the language as well as the mindset and culture.
top3_advice: 1) enjoy the classes and the professors genuine interest to help you 2) spend more time in plateau and mile end than downtown 3) try to practice your french. That makes the experience much more fun
other_useful_info: Bring all your woolen clothes for the winters :)
most_rewarding: All the great people I've met from all over the world and the opportunity to get to know a new city.
greatest_challenge: Keeping up with all the deadlines.

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne studere i et fransktalende land. Jeg endte dog med ikke at have overskud til at træne fransk så meget, fordi jeg i stedet fokuserede på andre kurser jeg fandt mere spændende. Derudover boede jeg på et kollegie, hvor folk var også var udvekslingsstuderende, så engelsk var det talte sprog i min hverdag. Desuden foregik alt på McGill på engelsk.
info_ease: Generelt var McGill gode til at give en masse info på forhånd og de havde en del gode infosider på deres hjemmeside. Men der skulle selvfølgelig også googles en del. Det hjalp også meget at være flere som skulle samme sted hen, så vi kunne dele info med hinanden.
arrival_assistance: De første par dage var uden hjælp fra McGill, men senere var der både infomøder og forskellige arrangementer. Desuden havde vi en koordinator fra McGill, som hed Mary, og hun var meget sød og god til at svare på mails.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Efter man officielt er blevet nomineret af KU, så skulle man søge direkte til McGill via deres system. Det var en længere smøre, men generelt fint nok
registration_help: Man kunne skrive til koordinatoren på KU, men ellers snakkede jeg med andre studerende, der skulle samme sted hen
registration_success: Der var meget run på ift. at skulle være klar på et bestemt tidspunkt, når der blev åbnet for kurser. Desuden blev der åbnet senere for udvekslingstuderende end for andre studerende, så nogle kurser var allerede fyldt. Det virker som om at mange melder sig på flere kurser end de egentlig har tænkt sig at tage, så selvom der blev fyldt på nogle kurser, så kom der pladser senere på foråret eller sommeren, så jeg endte med at få alle de kurser jeg gerne ville. Jeg tog også et fransk kursus og der var tilmeldingen lidt anderledes, fordi man først skulle kontakte French Language Center på McGill og få vurderet ens sproglige niveau, før man fik adgang til deres kursustilmelding.
registration_advice: Det er godt at sidde klar på tidspunktet når der åbnes for tilmeldinger, men hvis man ikke får det kursus man gerne vil, så skal man bare tjekke i løbet af sommeren og ellers tage til kurset alligevel, fordi det er ofte 2 uger inden i semesteret at folk melder sig fra deres unødvendige kurser. Nogle kurser kræver speciel adgang fra deres institut eller fra professoren, men så må man lige skrive til dem. Hvis man har lidt til kurser i matematik eller data science, så er der generelt mange pladser på disse kurser og det er derfor nemt at få plads der.
course_level: Niveauet på kurserne og arbejdsbelastningen svinger meget fra kursus til kursus. Kurserne er inddelt i niveauer, men 500+ niveaukurser er ofte ikke så svære. Jeg vil helt sikkert anbefale kun at tage 4 kurser, fordi der er mange afleveringer og eksamener, hvilket godt kan være lidt stressende.
teaching_comparison: Der var sjældent en bog at læse, og der var aldrig opgaver som skulle løses i forbindelse med de enkelte emner. I stedet var der afleveringer og fremlæggelser som alle talte med i den samlede karakter. Så derfor var undervisningsformen en del anderledes
courses_enrolled: PHGY 488 Stem Cell Biology COMP 451 Fundamentals of Machine Learning BIOL 592 Integrated Bioinformatics FRSL 206 Elementary French
recommended_courses: Begynderfransk eller Communicating Science hvis man vil chille. Ellers at prøve kræfter med nogle matematik eller computer science kurser. Nogle aspekter af PHGY 488 Stem Cell Biology var også meget fedt. Det var ikke så svært, men kvaliteten af professorer svingede dog
unexpected_costs: Obligatorisk mealplan på 1300$ Manglende køkkenting mm. 600 kr
cost_comparison: Mad pga. mealplan
activities_available: McGill har en masse klubber og et stort sportsområde, som jeg ikke selv benyttede mig af, men som helt sikkert vil være fedt for dem der er interesserede i at joine en sportsklub
activities_recommended: Fitnesscenteret på McGill er billigt, men der var et lille men gratis fitness center på Solin Hall
weekend_recommendations: En tur op ved udkigsposten på Mont-royal er obligatorisk. Ellers er der masser af muligheder for at se forskellig naturområder og byer. Jeg var selv et smut i New York.
culture_adjustment: Efter at finde ud af en masse basic ting i starten, så var der ikke så stor forskel på Montreal og København. Folk er generelt meget flinke og imødekommende
socializing_tips: Sportsklubber og bo på McGill residence. Der var også en introuge som de kalder Frosh. Der var lidt forskellige versioner af Frosh. Jeg var på den normale, som var en sjov oplevelse, men som også bar meget præg af unge 1. års studerende (som er 17-18 år på McGill) der skulle lære at feste. Der var også mulighed for outdoor frosh som måske kan være bedre for nogen.
cultural_challenges: Gamle mennesker uden for McGill er generelt meget dårlige til engelsk. Men på McGill og alle unge mennesker snakker godt engelsk
culture_appreciated: Folk er generelt meget flinke og klar til at give en hjælpende hånd. Montreal er desuden en meget tryg by. Der er en del hjemløse, men jeg har ikke oplevet at de gør noget ubehageligt
top3_advice: 1: McGill har obligatorisk sundhedsforsikring som er ret dyr. Den er man dog undtaget for hvis man er far Danmark og bliver en del af sundhedssystemet i Quebec. Det gør man ved at søge via RAMQ (som vist er organisationen der står for det). Man får dog svar via fysisk brev og det er ikke muligt at skrive til dem, hvis man har brug for hjælp. Jeg havde held med at komme igennem via telefon, men det var ikke nemt. Sørg for at skrive en adresse, som du ved er rigtig på din ansøgning, så du rent faktisk modtager dit bekræftelsesbrev som du skal sende til McGill. Hvis du bor på Solin Hall, så er det vigtigt, at du skriver dit værelsesnummer og at du er opmærksom på at der er to forskellige adresser afhængig af hvilken bygning du ender i. Så inden du ansøger til RAMQ, så vær helt 100 på at du bruger den rigtige adresse. 2: Man kan få et billigt kort til offentlig transport som hedder et OPUS card og som svarer lidt til et ungdomskort. På McGills version af KUnet (som hedder Minerva) står der, at man ikke kan få et "reduced-fare" OPUS card (næsten halv pris), når man kun er der i efterårssemesteret. Det er dog muligt at møde op på et kontor på tæt ved metrostoppet "Berri-UQAM", hvor man skal have proof of enrollment med. Der godkender de én til et reduced-fare OPUS card alligevel. 3: Telefonabonnementer er absurd dyre i Montreal (250 kr pr måned eller mere), så overvej om du kan få noget i danmark der gælder i hele verdenen eller om du kan nøjes med at få data via et e-sim. 4: Hvis du vil have et billigere ophold, så fin en lejlighed og lad være med at bo på McGill residence. Er du lidt ligeglad og vil gerne være i nærheden af en masse internationale studerende så er det fint. 5: Fin nogle chill fag, så du ikke har for travlt 6: Hvis du vil tage et franskkursus, så skal du være opmærksom på at ALT er på fransk. Læreren snakker for det meste kun fransk. Opgavebeskrivelser og grammatikbogen er på fransk. Det kan være ret demotiverende og frustrerende. Men det kan også være et fint chill kursus hvis du tager begynderniveau. Ellers så har jeg hørt at Communicating Science-kurset skulle være meget hyggeligt og et godt chill fag.
other_useful_info: Kig ovenfor
most_rewarding: At være så langt væk fra DK i så lang tid og at lære en masse mennesker at kende som ikke snakker dansk eller har nogen fornemmelse af hvordan det er af bo i Danmark.
greatest_challenge: At balancere mellem studie og at opleve et andet land. I starten er det en ferie, men så skal man indstille sig på, at det er okay at der går hverdag i den og at det ikke føles som om man oplever så meget specielt andet end en hverdag. At have en hverdag i et fremmed land og føle sig hjemme i en by langt væk hjemmefra er også en specielt oplevelse i sig selv, selvom den ikke føles på samme måde som normale ferier eller store rejser i et sabbatår

crucial_aspects: A civilized and safe city/country.
info_ease: It was very hard before I got my login to McGill's student platform, e.g. getting in touch with them.
arrival_assistance: Got the key and the direction to my home
arrival_comments: Didn't get my address until a few days before I got there. They were kind and understanding but it would be nice to know before leaving from home.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Different formal documents, e.g. proof of English efficiency.
registration_help: Not much, it was hard to get in touch with them.
registration_success: Semi successful. You only know what courses are available for the exact term quite late, so I had to research courses several times. And it's hard to get a clear view of the classes by just reading about it, so I got a little disappointed at some point after I arrived.
registration_advice: For McGill University: Do not study math here. If you want to learn French, start registration early! It requires an interview before being able to submit and there's limited spaces. And also: check if your university makes you able to change classes within the first weeks because that makes it less stressful that you always have the opportunity to switch.
course_level: The math teaching was too loose, had one super bad lecturer (maybe I was just unlucky). I had 4th year (undergrad) and graduate courses and the level was quite low.
teaching_comparison: At McGill there was more communication between student and teacher, but it resulted in it being too easy to e.g. get an assignment postponed. In general there is also way more ongoing grading that counts towards the final grade whereas at UCPH it's usually one exam that determines your whole grade for one course.
courses_enrolled: MATH423 Applied regression, MATH682 Statistical inference, FRSL208 Near beginners French
recommended_courses: Would recommend the FRSL courses (French as a second language). They have a lot of good teachers at McGill and since the city is French speaking there's also good opportunity to practice you oral skills.
unexpected_costs: Didn't get my mobile service up and running immediately so I lost a lot of money on phone services the first couple of days. You also have to have your own pillow, bed sheets etc. so that was a whole bunch of new expenses since it didn't make sense to bring from home.
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive than expected and prices in supermarkets/restaurants in general in Canada.
activities_available: McGill has a huge gym with all sorts of fields for different sports and also their own pool. For very little money you also have access to a quite impressive fitness centre. There's even sport teams where you can join a semester long tournament on different levels. There's a few afternoons set off for specific groups to meet, e.g. exchange students, first year's etc.
activities_recommended: Join an intermural sports teem
weekend_recommendations: You can do (long) weekend trip to Toronto/Niagara Falls and Quebec City. There is also lots of great places to hike, both during summer and winter. Also try skiing only 30 min. outside the city. It's easy and not too expensive to rent a car (discount through McGill) for whatever activity you're doing.
culture_adjustment: Montreal is the most ‘Europeanized' city in Canada so it was very easy to adapt.
socializing_tips: Talk to the people in your classes
cultural_challenges: Nothing
culture_appreciated: The enormous diversity in ethnicity. There's people from all over the world and I have definitely gotten some new perspectives in meeting so many different people.
top3_advice: Go there unless you study math. Try to get a spot living on campus – it's a great opportunity to get friends. As long as you pass your courses, do not hesitate to make the most of your weekends/holidays. Most people are so open and always ready to go on a trip even though you don't know each other.
other_useful_info: I would go there in the Fall term since it's insanely cold in the winter. That way you can also enjoy the beautiful campus way more.
most_rewarding: Coming with nothing but myself and then making such good friendships and connections although we all come from very different backgrounds and don't even speak the same language. It was also a big experience being independent for so long, both study wise and just in general when trying to make an everyday life.
greatest_challenge: Figuring out formalities with how to get an insurance card, booking a doctor's appointment, figuring out the online student platform etc. But it wasn't that much of a challenge.

crucial_aspects: There were too many universities to choose from so I had to narrow it down somehow. The first restriction was to choose something outside of Europe. Secondly, I thought North America might be a cool place to study and I wasn't really attracted to the US. So Canada it was. McGill had a really nice selection of courses so that was the main reason to go there. And of course also to experience Montreal, visit nearby cities and go hiking and skiing in the surrounding nature.
info_ease: This wasn't at problem at all. As far as I remember, at least.
arrival_assistance: There were some nice orientation events in the first week with academic advice and information and information on the social clubs at McGill.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was a bit stressfull having to write the professors and departments to be allowed to register for the courses. Also, it was annoying that the course registration opened earlier for the local students then for the exchange students. This meant that some courses was full before we were allowed to register. However, in the end I still managed to get the courses I wanted. You just have to check several times a day if a seat opens.
registration_help: Just the basics on how to register. The virtual schedule builder was helpful, though.
registration_success: I managed to get all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: If you haven't been able to register for the course, just attend the first class of the semester in the add-drop period and talk with the professor. He might let you in to the course.
course_level: The level was pretty similar to back home, maybe a bit easier.
teaching_comparison: There were way more presentations, essays and small assignments than back home. However, the grading for these things were pretty chill. You could easily get away with making a mediocre essay or presentation and still get a good grade. At least in the courses I followed. I ended up with quite a stressfull November because most of my essays and presentation were due there. So maybe think about this when you choose your courses - I didn't. But then at least my September, first part og October and December were easy.
courses_enrolled: PHGY488 Stem Cell Biology PHGY524 Chronobiology BIOL544 Genetic Basis of Lifespan WCOM314 Communicating Science
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend Chronobiology and Genetic Basis of Lifespan. Both courses were taught by amazing professors. Genetic Basis of Lifespan was also very chill in terms of workload. Just one class a week, one presentation and one essay. No midterm of final exam. However, the workload in Chronobiology was pretty high - but definitely worth it. Stem Cell Biology might be the worst course I've ever had. Just an unstructured course with poor teaching. Communicating Science was not bad. It reminded me quite a lot of danish classes in high school. I'm not sure I learned that much from the course, but it was pretty chill and kind of fun from time to time.
unexpected_costs: Overall it is just way more expensive to live in Montreal than I thought.
cost_comparison: Pretty much everything was more expensive than I thought.
activities_available: Pretty much everything
activities_recommended: I joined a running club (McGill Olympic Club) that I really enjoyed. There were trainings two times a week with a coach and sometimes we also met Saturday for a longer run. All levels could join the club, so no try-out for this one.
weekend_recommendations: First of all, enjoy Montreal - just walk around the city, go to the Islands, go to Mont Royal. But also make sure to visit the surrounding nature and cities. Rent a car an go hiking - there a good places within a two hour drive. And then Toronto with the CN tower and Niagara Falls close by is a must.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Join a club. And maybe choose courses with fewer students. It's easier to socialize this way than in large lectures.
cultural_challenges: The city is build for cars, not bikes.
culture_appreciated: Montreal and McGill are just way more multicultural than Copenhagen and KU.
top3_advice: Go travel as much as you can as early as possible. The semester might hit you in the face and demand a lot of studying later on so use your freedom in the beginning. And also, lower your academic ambitions so you have time to do other things. And join a club - this was one of the best things I did and really helped me to get a wonderful daily life in Montreal.
other_useful_info: Remember you don't have the get the International Health Insurance. You can apply for the RAMQ when you arrive which is free of charge. You don't have to pay full price for the metro card. Although McGill says that you have to be enrolled for the full year to get a reduced fare metro card there are a way to get around that. La Banquise is the only place you can get an acceptable poutine. All other places it is close to disgusting.
most_rewarding: Experiencing how fast you can adapt and feel at home in a new country and a new city. Meeting people from all around the world.
greatest_challenge: How expensive it was.

crucial_aspects: I chose McGill University both for its strong science profile and general academic level. For me, it was important to visit a university that had an academic level at least as high as UCPH. I used a lot of time (before choosing the university) to look into what possible courses I would be able to follow. Furthermore, Montreal seemed like a great city to live and study in, both because of its culture and young and vibrant atmosphere.
info_ease: Surprisingly, neither visa and study permit were acquired to study in Montreal for less than 6 months - this took some time to figure out. McGill's website is not the most intuitive, but with a bit of patience all informations was possible to dig up. Several zoom meeting were available to guide us with everything associated with the arrival and course registration, which was very helpfull.
arrival_assistance: At the airport, volunteers were there to help with any questions to incoming exchange students. How to get to downtown Montreal, etc.
arrival_comments: I was in contact with the exchange student advisors at McGill a couple of times, and they were happy to help with any questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration itself was easy, however, there are so many courses that it can be kind of a jungle to search through. Expect to use som time on this. The course description is not as thorough as I'm used to at UCPH.
registration_help: A course schedule app was available to help visualize when each course had lectures, to make sure they didn't overlap. This was very helpfull.
registration_success: Since being a master student, I was looking for courses with a level above 300. It turned out that some courses were not available for exchange studentes, other not available to students at specific faculties. So I didn't find that many very interesting courses, compared to what was available at UCPH. But I got all the courses I ended up wanting to take.
registration_advice: Remember to register as soon as the registration opens to make sure to get the spots. Registration opens to different groups of students at different times.
course_level: I had one 300-level course and three 500-level courses. As a master student I think the course level were sufficient (being close to finish my degree, I wanted to take with a certain academic level), however, the work load was also quite high in the last half of the semester. As a bachelor student, I would recommend 0 or 1 course at 500, to make sure to have time also to explore Montreal and Canada.
teaching_comparison: I didn't experience any group work, but rather more ‘static teaching' (lectures). I prefer the teaching style at UCPH, but in general it was ok.
courses_enrolled: ANAT 365 - Cellular Trafficking BMDE 507 - Formulation & Delivery of Biotherapeutics PHGY 518 - Artificial Cells PHGY 520 - Ion Channels
recommended_courses: I would recommend BMDE 507. The working load was sufficient, with both lectures, presentations, and assignments. The material was interesting and very relevant (a lot of new research and drugs/products). I found PHGY 520 quite difficult because I didn't have sufficient prerequisite. PHGY 518 was chill, but I didn't learn much new stuff, mostly because it was unstructured and consisted of a lot of student presentations. ANAT 365 was ok, but the midterm and final exam was extremely difficult.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: I found fresh produce (fruit, veggies, meat) quite expensive. The plane ticket home was very expensive, because I bought it 1-2 months before leaving. So when you buy the ticket to go there, make sure also to buy the return ticket that can be changed - this is much cheaper!
activities_available: I was really surprised at how many clubs there was available (sports, cultural, etc.). And the people there are really open to new members!
activities_recommended: I joined the outdoors club (MOC). I attended very few of the events, which I regret, because they seem really nice.
weekend_recommendations: I took weekend trips to Quebec City and a roadtrip around Ottawa. Quebec City is nice to visit just for a day or two. Then I rented a caravan with a friend and went on a “roadtrip” around Ottawa in the autumn where we visited national parks - this might be the best experience on my whole exchange stay, and was really beautiful with all the fall colors on the trees. I also went on a couple on hiking trips around Montreal, and wish I would have done more since the nature is amazing.
culture_adjustment: I found the Canadians really open and welcoming. So despite the culture being half francophone, it was really easy to adapt. I found the culture very similar to the one in Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: Join a couple of clubs at the university (especially MOC) and be open to go on hiking trips etc. with people you haven't met yet.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: I went to a couple of ‘local' private house parties, and found the drinking culture less heavy, which was nice.
top3_advice: 1) Don't join the faculty Froshes! A lot of very young people join these (down to 17 years of age) and they basically just drink in one week. I joined one of the outdoor froshes (the canoeing frosh) and this was really nice + I got an unforgettable trip in a natural park. 2) If you like to hike and spend time in the nature, make sure to bring hiking boots and warm clothes so you can also enjoy the nature in the cold months. 3) Make sure to explore the city and go on weekend trips from the beginning of your stay. Soon, it will be exam period and you will have missed important experiences, which you will regret.
other_useful_info: Pack less clothes that you think. You don't need 7 knitted sweaters and 7 pairs of pants (as I brought) - leave some space in your luggage to buy stuff over there.
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of new people, trying another studying culture, and explore Canada's nature.
greatest_challenge: I found the work load of the courses extremely high during last 1,5 months of my stay (while it was very small the first couple of months). So make sure to make your assignments early in the semester.

info_ease: This was very difficult, which sometimes made the exchange more of a frustration and hassle than a positive and exciting experience.
arrival_assistance: It was impossible to come in contact with my school through mail, even though I was well ahead of time. I had to go to the school to get help, which was also very difficult, only one person was able to help and she had very limited time.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had to apply for your courses before a certain deadline. But because I was an exchange student, I was not allowed/able to apply for any courses without an acceptance from the professor of that course, which was impossible to get, because they never answered.
registration_help: Only one person were able to help with this problem, but she was not able to be reached through email.
registration_success: A lot of the courses i wanted to take, i was not able to get, because requisitions was required. But i was able to get my second choices.
registration_advice: Be in really good time. And don't stress too much if you don't come through. Just meet up at the school when you arrive, and explain your situation and they will sort it out for you.
course_level: I had both level 300, 400 and 500 courses, and I think level 300 and 400 was pretty easy, especially level 300 was under my level of knowledge.
teaching_comparison: It was pretty much the same. Mostly lectures. But better at referring what we learned to the exam, and how to use it, and practicing this.
courses_enrolled: Sport psychology Nutrition and wellness Adapted physic activity Sleep mechanisms and behaviour
recommended_courses: Sleep mechanisms and behaviour was a really interesting course, but also a difficult one. Nutrition and wellness was also a good course, but quite easy.
unexpected_costs: I went on a lot of spontanous trips, and these were very costly, but also woth it.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping is very expensive in Canada.
activities_available: There was an outdoor club, but not manny events were hold, and the ones that were hold, you didn't really hear about. I think there was quite a lot of social events in different forms, but you don't really hear about them unless you live on campus with the other students.
activities_recommended: The frosh events before the semester seems to be important to be a part of.
weekend_recommendations: Go on trips. Rent a car and take small trips. Explore the city and their cafees. Stick to fun in the weekend and schoolwork during the week - you won't regret that! (it is the fun you will remember afterwards and look back at)
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy.
socializing_tips: Become a part of a sport. Or live on campus with student housing.
cultural_challenges: That everything, especially administrative stuff, was only available in french.
culture_appreciated: The school system, especially exams, were way more functional and relevant.
top3_advice: Don't stress before arrival, it will sort itself out when you get there. Be quick to become a part of sport clubs or other trips. Don't stress about reading all of the lecture material. Most of the times, it covers more or less the same.
other_useful_info: Don't stress too much about school. There is a lot of reading material, and it is impossible to read it all, and you will do just fine anyways. I was constantly behind, because i prioritized taking trips, and did just fine. Remember to also experience the area/country. It will always work out in the end.
most_rewarding: Taking trips and experiencing the country.
greatest_challenge: To balance school, exploring and social life. It is very intense to juggle all of these things at the same time, and it is just very different than back home. But just do it. Don't be afraid to have a busy schedule, you won't regret it.
other_comments: Put on the 'yes'-hat.
