crucial_aspects: For me personally, it was crucial that the study destination i choose had English as a first language. Also, it was important for me that academically, I was not settling for something way less than what UCPH has to offer. That said, choosing a destination with a lot to offer besides the university part, was also important for me.
info_ease: Going on exchange is something you have to do yourself, meaning that it is your own responsibility to make sure you seek out all the important information. I know that McGill offers student buddies (much like the system at KU), also they provide emails, introdays, etc. so I didnt feel like i was missing important info.
arrival_assistance: They inform you on almost everything via email. I also went to an introductory session with our contact person at McGill, used the "Ask McGill" shops around campus the first couple of days, so all in all it was a good experience.
arrival_comments: It would have been nice with some specific introductory events only for exchange students, but I didn't feel lost at all. Also know that KU generally has a pretty good deal with McGill, and so does some of the other Danish universities, meaning that there is a lot of Danes in Montreal around that time. Try to make contact with them beforehand, that way you are not alone when it comes to gathering all the necessary info.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The system is rather easy, but you have to be fast. Once the course registration opens, a lot of the smaller courses are quickly filled up, so you might find yourself lacking the course you wanted. I had picked out 4 courses and only ended up getting two, luckily I had a plan A, B and C where i knew there would be no scheduling conflicts. Also know that you are only required by UCPH to take 4 courses, but you can sign up for 5. I signed up for 5, then during the add-drop period I just had to drop one, but I had a hance to go see what the course was about and meet the profs. Also know that during the add-drop period you have a pretty good chance of getting into a course that was initially filled, you just have to check the registration page a few times a day.
registration_help: Student Service at McGill are really helpful :)
registration_success: Well, I only got 2/4 of the courses I initially wanted, but the two other I got instead where just as good (one i even think might have been a better option than my originally plan)
registration_advice: Register for 5 courses, so you have one to spare if you find out during your Add-drop period that the course wasn't what you expected (The course descriptions at McGill ae pretty sparse). Be aware of your schedule, if you are smart you can give yourself a short week, which is really nice for longer trips during your exchange. Be aware of the type of course load and exams you are signing up for. I ended up with 4 in person exams in a week, which i not recommendable ;) If you can, choose at least one course where the exam is not in person, but also be aware of not ending up with 4 courses that all have weekly assignments. In total, be smart.
course_level: The level of the course kinda responds to the year you are in, meaning that level 100 courses are for first year students, 200 for second year etc. With that being said, as a bachelors student from UCPH it is manageable to have a few of your courses being level 400-500 courses, just be aware that you might need a confirmation from the prof before choosing said course. Also, don't be shy to choose a 100-200 level course if the subject is completely new to you, as the introductory courses are usually 100-200.
teaching_comparison: I only had lecture style courses, where the lectures were very much like the ones at UCPH, but without the TØ sessions, so you are a bit more on your own. A lot of the other Danes had smaller class like courses where it was more discussion based, and they seemed to enjoy it - so I guess it just depend on the course you take.
courses_enrolled: PHAR300 - Drug Action MIMM324 - Fundamental Virology COMP204 - Programming For Life Science PSYC311 - Human Cognition and the Brain
recommended_courses: COMP204 is a really nice programming course, very basic and manageable. It has weekly assignments and quizzes that count for a part of your grade, which can be a bit overwhelming during the course, but this also means that if you do well in the weekly assignments, you can pass the course whit out attending the exam. MIMM324 is also a really nice course, some of the profs are not the best, but the general structure of the course, and the topics are really interesting. During the course, there are quizzes and two assignments, but they are pretty manageable. PSYC311 is also a really nice course when it comes to the lectures and topics, there is a bit of work in getting to know all the neuroanatomy needed (it is not a lot, but still), but I was really glad i took it. PHAR300 is the only one of my courses that I can't really recommend. It seemed fine in the beginning, and some of the topics are really interesting, but the detail level of the midterm/exam is just a lot compared to what is touched during the lectures, and to top it of, no lecture slides are handed out. That being said, some of the topics were nice, it was just not what I expected.
unexpected_costs: I think i budgettet very conservatory before i left, so there wasn't really anything that took me by suprise.
cost_comparison: Some supermarket items are more expensive than in Denmark, some are less. Also the tax+tip when you are out can really be confusing in the beginning
activities_available: Just about every club imaginable, from sports to chocolate clubs.
activities_recommended: Frosh is really fun, but consider whether you are more a outdoor or faculty frosh kind of type. Also, join a club or sports so you can meet other people.
weekend_recommendations: Toronto is relatively close, also there is a thing calles MustBus that arrange busses to a number of different destinations during the semester for cheap prices. Also, all the major car rental services has (Enterprise, Avis and Hertz), so you can get cheaper rentals.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy - Montreal has a almost europe-vibe. However, I was a bit surprised at how much French is spoken, it truly is the first language in Montreal.
socializing_tips: JOIN THE CLUBS!
cultural_challenges: The amount of French spoken in Montreal can be a bit challenging, eg. when you are in a metro that stops running and they only give announcements in French, but you get over it pretty fast. Another thing is the age of the local students, they are generally a bit younger than we are because they start uni at a younger age.
culture_appreciated: Montreal is just a really nice city to live in. It is a big city, with high rise buildings and busy streets, but it is also a city that is relatively old for north American standards, and has a lot of cultural things going on.
top3_advice: Pay attention when choosing your courses. Make sure to spend some time outside Montreal, rent a car, go on hikes, have fun. Make as much use of the summer that is left for you, once it gets colder it is no fun experiencing the city.
other_useful_info: McGill is a large university, so it can be a bit overwhelming in the beginning, but you get used to the vibe pretty fast.
most_rewarding: For me, it was just doing something fun and different for a semester, and also having to prioritise my time a bit different in order to both experience Montreal/Canada while I was there, as well as attending university at the same time.
greatest_challenge: To get to meet the locals. McGill has a lot of exchange students, and a lot of the fultime students are also not from the local area, but other exchange students can be just as nice :)

crucial_aspects: I wanted to travel outside Europe, preferably North America, and Canada seemed the obvious choice. From other students I had heard a lot of great things about Montreal as a city and about McGill University. It was important to me that I lived in a city with lots to do, as opposed to living on a campus in the middle of nowhere.
overall_comments: It was an experience I will of course never forget, and I am very happy I did it. Some of my courses on McGill were however not that good, which is why I'm rating it 8/10.
info_ease: Pretty easy. As soon as you have created your McGill e-mail, you will get a lot of information.
arrival_assistance: The coordinator for SCIENCE exchange at McGill, Mary, had an introductory meeting with all exchange students at the science faculty of McGill, and she really wanted to have a private meeting with each of us, talking about the courses we got and if we needed any assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was an experience I will of course never forget, and I am very happy I did it. Some of my courses on McGill were however not that good, which is why I'm rating it 8/10.
registration_process: Course registration begins in June, and courses fill up fast, so beforehand you should make a list of the ones you want the most. Registration itself happens on Minerva (McGill Absalon). You go to the registration page and write the course registration code for up to five courses in a field, and then you press enter.
registration_help: Exchange advisor you could write to, and many emails explaining the process.
registration_success: As mentioned, I did not get two courses that I wanted, so I had to take some of my plan B courses (one of which was very bad), so it was a bit of a letdown.
registration_advice: Some of the courses I wanted to take I did not get, so the day before the course registration opens for exchange students, you should check which courses are full and act accordingly. I did however get into a course that was full by writing to the professor. Sometimes they let you in.
academics_comments: It was an experience I will of course never forget, and I am very happy I did it. Some of my courses on McGill were however not that good, which is why I'm rating it 8/10.
course_level: Third year courses at McGill (300-level) are very basic and therefore a bit boring (I had to write an assignment about what a Western blot is, which is a method we learn in our first year at KU). The fourth year courses (400 level) were much better, and much more like the ones at KU. We had lectures and then read articles related to that lecture and so on. 400 level courses are however a bit harder, with term papers and so on, so I would recommend doing two or three 400-level courses, and then take at least one easy introductory French course to have a 'relaxing' course.
teaching_comparison: At McGill there are no SAU or TØ classes, there are only lectures. In 400-levels, fewer people are registered (25-35), so the lectures function a bit as SAU and TØ. I did not like that we only had lectures, as I very much like the classroom setting.
courses_enrolled: PHAR 300 Drug Action Supposedly an introduction to pharmacology and how drugs (both 'fun' drugs and actual prescription drugs) work and effect the body. The course is however very bad, with a horrible professor. She spends most of the lecture talking about statistics for the drug use or goes on long rants about how much she hates cigarettes, alcohol, cannabis, cosmetics, essential oils, herbal medicine and Chinese traditional medicine. Then on the exam there are very specific questions about the mechanism of action of very specific drugs, some which are not mentioned in the lecture. She also does not share her slides, as she is paranoid about copyright. MIMM 324 Fundamental Virology Very fundamental course about viruses, you need to learn about a lot of irrelevant small viruses you've never heard of before and much of their replication cycle. There are also a few viruses you learn about much more in depth (HPV, hepatitis C and HIV) which is much more interesting. PHGY 488 Stem Cell Biology A course about stem cells. Very good course and it was the most KU-like course I had at McGill. You do a presentation on an article and write a paper about another article. PHGY 518 Artificial Cells An interesting course taught by the founder of the field, who is almost 90 years old. For the same reason, the course has few lectures and is mostly you doing a presentation and 10-page paper on a topic you decide yourself within the field of artificial cells. It is however very interesting.
recommended_courses: I would recommend PHGY 488 Stem Cell Biology, even if you aren't interested in stem cells (which I wasn't), as you learn a lot of relevant information and get training in presenting and writing about scientific articles. I would also recommend PHGY 518, though I doubt Thomas Chang will continue to be in the course much longer (he is very old), just be prepared that you don't learn that much, and have to do a lot of work. There is no exam though, which is nice. I would NOT recommend PHAR 300, avoid at all cost. It is draining and frustrating.
unexpected_costs: Phone service is VERY VERY expensive in Canada. 3 GB of data each month costs around 120 kr. I had an e-sim plan, which worked fine, but I has to use Whatsapp and messenger for telephoning.
cost_comparison: The Quebec Health insurance, RAMQ, is free for Danish students. Just register at RAMQ website and you get a health insurance card. You can't do it before you arrive in Canada though, and then the card itself comes after a few weeks. For the same reason, you don't have to buy the official McGill health insurance, which is quite expensive, you can just request and exemption.
activities_available: There is a gym with a rather cheap membership and a free 25 meter pool. Socially I would recommend joining the McGill outdoor club and the knitting club. There are a few introductory arrangements at McGill, namely 'Frosh', which is for their first-year students. Keep in mind that in America you start university at 17. Therefore, the official McGill frosh I registered for (and paid 1000 kr for) was not that great, as the other people were very young. Other people went on the Outdoor frosh, with activities such as camping and hiking. Here there were more exchange students and older students, which I regret I did not register for as well. A student organization called MustBus arranges cheap bus trips to other parts of Canada and the US. My roommates and I went to Toronto for a few days, a very fun experience.
activities_recommended: Rent a car and drive to the national parks surrounding Montreal, the nature is amazing, especially in the autumn! Especially Mont Tremblant and Mont Megantic. Otherwise, Parc Mont-Saint Bruno is reachable by metro and then a bus for 30 minutes. I can also recommend taking a day trip to Vermont or upstate New York.
weekend_recommendations: Natural Parks or trips to Toronto and Quebec City. I went to New York City in my Christmas break and my family came over. That was great as well. The Greyhound bus between Montreal and NYC is very nice and relatively cheap, if you can tolerate the 9 hour bus drive. In the every day life, you should check out St. Viateur Bagels, they are so delicious (only cash payment!)
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, Montreal is a very european city.
socializing_tips: I was not that succesful in this, but you should come to the McGill clubs like outdoor club and knitting club. If you live in the McGill dorms you will have much more contact with other exchange students. Many students aren't from Quebec and don't speak French.
cultural_challenges: There weren't really any, except that local students at McGill really study a lot, so they don't have a lot of free time.
culture_appreciated: That it was so French, it was very strange but very nice (plus their croissants were amazing).
top3_advice: Find housing before you arrive. Bring warm clothes. Go to Saint-Viateur bagels with lots of cash.
other_useful_info: BIXI bikes are cheap city bikes, and as Montreal is a very bike friendly city, it is a great way to get around. The cold and snow comes in end-November, but I was lucky as it was a very mild year.
most_rewarding: Experiencing Quebec and North American Culture.
greatest_challenge: Having four courses at the same time.

crucial_aspects: An English-speaking country, cultural diversity, high academic standards, nature experiences
info_ease: In general, I think it was easy to find the information needed. Remember to use your McGill Email since most information regarding course registration, health insurance, orientation, etc. is emailed.
arrival_assistance: I participated in an orientation day for international students (social event) and the Faculty of Law hosted an Information session for exchange students about course registration, course credits, deadlines, grades etc. In general, the Student Affairs Office (SAO) at the Faculty of Law was very helpful and responded quickly to my emails.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I think the registration process was unnecessarily complicated. You need to use Minerva. I found a guide and a video that described the registration process. https://www.mcgill.ca/students/courses/add/register
registration_help: The SAO. They reply quickly.
registration_success: Rather successful. But only because of the add/drop period.
registration_advice: First of all, registration opens later for exchange students meaning that many courses were already full when I registered. Moreover, it is first come first served so remember the registration date! Second, there is a course change period (add/drop period) in the first two weeks where it is possible to add/drop courses. I changed two of my courses in this period. I would suggest using "seat alert - McGill" where you receive notifications on your McGill Email if there is an available spot in a course. That way, you do not have to look in Minerva all the time. Third, it is relatively easy to get the professor's approval if you want to enroll in a graduate course. Fourthly, remember to register for a waitlist as early as possible (but you are only permitted to register for one waitlist per term).
course_level: Due to the agreement between McGill and UCPH I was considered an undergraduate student even though I am a graduate student at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style differed significantly from the UCPH. There are no lectures, and the style of teaching is more discussion and presentation based. Generally, students are expected to participate actively. Furthermore, the method of evaluation differs from course to course (midterms, participation, final exam, etc.), and there is no reading break.
courses_enrolled: Private International Air Law European Union Law(1) Canadian Legal History Immigration and Refugee Law
recommended_courses: Private International Air Law. It focuses on different sources of private air law, unification of law of liability, conflicts of law, etc. The most practical course. It is a graduate course, so you need the professor's approval.
unexpected_costs: My room was furnished, however, I had to buy everything else (pillow, pillowcase, duvet, towels, cutlery, plates, etc.) But there is an IKEA only 30 minutes from Montreal (close to the airport). Or you can try Dollarama.
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than I expected. Coffee was cheaper.
activities_available: There are a lot of things going on at McGill. I bought a membership to the McGill gym, you can sign up for different competitions (e.g., Badminton), Open Air Pub (OAP) which is a student-run music festival, barbecue, and bar in the first two weeks,
activities_recommended: Follow LSA on Instagram. They host many social activities: Coffeehouse each Thursday, Ski Trip, Movie Night, Yoga, Karaoke, Moka Monday, etc. A great way to meet other students and socialize.
weekend_recommendations: Go hiking, explore the different areas in Montreal (entirely different), eat bagels (St-Viateur Bagel or Fairmount Bagel), see an Ice hockey Game, and visit Toronto, Ottawa, Mont Tremblant, Boston, New York, or Quebec City.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. However, Montreal is located in the French-speaking part of Canada so you may encounter a language barrier. For instance, most official information (e.g., in the metro) is only in French, and some people only speak French. I do not speak French and still found it easy to adjust.
socializing_tips: People at McGill are young but also very open-minded, talkative, and friendly. Speak to the other students in your different courses.
cultural_challenges: The language (French).
culture_appreciated: People's friendliness, talkativeness, politeness, etc.
top3_advice: Participate in the different social activities in the beginning (use WhatsApp to connect with people) Do not stress about not getting the courses you want in the first round - there is a lot of mobility in the add/drop period. Enjoy your time!
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Meeting (and becoming friends) with people from around the world (and from Denmark). Exploring a new country/culture and knowing more about the locals' culture and way of life. Learning more about myself.
greatest_challenge: Living far away from family and friends.
other_comments: A once-in-a-lifetime experience! I recommend studying abroad to everyone.

crucial_aspects: Large and interesting city, English speaking university, recognized as a good university with good academic opportunities.
info_ease: Didn't have any problems, as McGill is used to getting lots of exchange students.
arrival_assistance: I didn't really need any, but there were plenty of options to receive assistance, if you needed help with anything in regards to signing up for courses, finding your way around campus etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We were able to register before we went on exchange. Registration opens to exchange students later than for all other students, so although you are signing up for courses as soon as you are able too, there is no guarantee you'll get the courses you want. The first two weeks there is an "add and drop" period, where you can change your courses if there are available spots on other courses. Most exchange students were able to get courses they were more or less satisfied with.
registration_help: As an exchange student you were offered a conversation with a student counselor during the add and drop period. I did not need it, but I think it was helpful for the people who went.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: You can not necessarily expect to get exactly the courses you want. Prepare a list of more than four courses that you would be satisfied with and try to be open minded about which courses you end up taking.
course_level: The level of the courses really depend on the professor. If you are studying economics at UCPH, I would recommend you to take either 500-level courses, honours courses, or courses within other fields as my impression is that the level is generally lower than at UCPH if you take normal ECON-courses.This is primarily based on my experience from one 400-level course, so it is not necessarily correct for all economics courses.
teaching_comparison: There were generally fewer people in each class, resulting in more interesting lectures with more interaction with the professor, which was nice. I had 3 hours of lectures (or 2 hours of lectures, 1 hour of conference) for each course (3 credit courses), which meant I had to study more independently from what I am used to at UCPH. The TAs are generally really nice and helpful - use them for all your questions regarding the courses.
courses_enrolled: ECON460: History of Thought I with Professor Green ECON546, Game Theory with Professor Dutta ECON423, International Trade with Professor Karageusian POLI231, Political Theory with Professor Roberts.
recommended_courses: Game Theory, History of Thought and Political Theory were all great courses. The professors were good and passionate about the courses, and I really learned a lot. I would especially recommend Game Theory with Professor Dutta to all economics students. However, be prepared that the workload of the courses is relatively big. International Trade was the worst course I have ever taken. I would not recommend it to anyone. Only good thing is that the course is relatively easy.
unexpected_costs: As I lived at one of McGill's student residences I had to pay 1300 dollars for a mandatory meal plan at the beginning of my stay (on top of rent). I went to Boston, Toronto and Ottawa while I was here. All of the trips were relatively expensive, so if you're planning on visiting other cities, you should definitely leave some room for this in your budget.
cost_comparison: The CAD was really expensive when I first arrived, so everything was more expensive than expected. However the exchange rate improved while I was here, meaning everything suddenly seemed much cheaper. Montreal is not a cheap city to live in, and housing prices have risen, meaning housing is generally not as cheap as former travel reports suggest (although my rent was definitely higher than average).
activities_available: Plenty of activities were available. I went on Outdoor Frosh when I arrived (I can really recommend it to all student on exchange here during the Fall Term, find "mcgilloutdoorsclub" or "mcgilloutdoorfrosh" on Instagram to read more about it). I also participated in a couple of McGill Outdoor Club's weekly meetings, which were always nice. McGill Athletics and Recreation has a nice gym (requires a cheap membership), a pool, and courts for badminton, basket, squash etc.
activities_recommended: Outdoor Frosh, the facilities at McGill Athletics.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Toronto or Boston. Sign up for trips with Concordia Outdoor Club (more expensive than McGill, but much easier to get a spot). Go on outdoor trips/hikes.
culture_adjustment: McGill is very international and great at welcoming exchange students.
socializing_tips: I primarily spoke with other exchange students, as they were most eager to socialize.
cultural_challenges: Some of the people living in Montreal are not too friendly towards you if you don't speak French. In general Quebec has some weird language protection laws and the entire atmosphere around the language question would make me feel very unwelcome, if I were to move to Montreal more permanently. But you don't really experience anything in that regard at McGill at all, so I would still very much encourage everyone to go to McGill - even if you don't speak any French (I don't).
culture_appreciated: The culture and atmosphere at McGill is very nice. There are people from lots of different countries and cultures, and I learned a lot from that.
top3_advice: McGill is a great university for exchange students - they are used to welcoming lots of exchange students every year, and they are great at making you feel welcome. You have to be a little bit proactive both in regards to finding friends, but also in regards to your courses. I was surprised by how different e.g. the exams are here. Reach out to your TAs and professors if you have questions for the courses - most of them are very helpful. Find your own housing - I would not recommend the housing offered by McGill. Also be aware that you are not the only one who is overwhelmed by having to arrange everything for your exchange. Most people who are going on exchange finds the process overwhelming at some point. Reach out to the other exchange students from Denmark going to McGill. They are probably searching for the answers of the same questions as you are. Help each other!
other_useful_info: Apply for RAMQ as soon as possible - not everyone got it in time. Bring a SIM card for your phone from Denmark (I used CBB World). It is much more expensive here. Make sure your rejseforsikring covers the entire stay or buy an additional one (e.g. Europæiske Rejseforsikring, you get a discount as a member of DJØF). Apply for scholarships before you leave DK - otherwise the chance of getting any is very low.
most_rewarding: All the nice people I have met!
greatest_challenge: I really had to get used to how different it is to study here - e.g. when everyone had midterms and was kind of stressed out in the middle of the semester.

crucial_aspects: First of all, I prioritised an English-speaking university. I have previously been in Canada and thought it would be interesting to both study there but also travel around.
info_ease: They send different informative emails and I think those were useful.
arrival_assistance: As exchange students at the science faculty, we were assigned an advisor who held an information meeting a couple of days before classes started. She explained some of the things we should be aware of when choosing or changing courses and such.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We had to obtain and upload some different documents from KU to minerva, which is their version of Kunet. A English proficiency letter, a scan of passport, transcript that were signed and nomination letter.
registration_help: I just used the instructions from the application sheet from kunet which I found to be enough.
registration_success: Some of the classes I wanted to take overlapped so I would say that I got 3/4 of the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: You get a time slot for course registration and you have to enrol at that time. Thereafter it is easy to change courses and this can be done up until two weeks after the classes begin. So if you didn't get a class it is a good idea to check Minerva regularly.
course_level: The level was similar to courses at KU. You just need to have four courses.
teaching_comparison: The main difference is that there are quizzes, midterms, presentations and assignments during the semester (in some courses) that is a part of the final grade. I had four really different courses with different styles of teaching.
courses_enrolled: PHAR300 - Drug Action PHGY488 - Stem Cel Biology COMP204 - Programming for Life Science WCOM314 - Communicating Science
recommended_courses: I think WCOM314 was really a great course because it was really different from what I'm used to at university and it gave some tools and made me reflect on how to write and talk about science to different audiences.
unexpected_costs: Not so much. I had to buy a duvet and some smaller things for the kitchen.
cost_comparison: The prices was kind of similar with things in Copenhagen. Off campus housing were cheaper than I expected.
activities_available: There were a lot of clubs available.
activities_recommended: In the beginning they have intro which is called frosh. I attended the outdoor-frosh which was a four day trip to a campsite and about half of us were exchange students. This was a great way to meet other students and also go on a trip in the nature.
weekend_recommendations: Rent a car (google "car rental McGill" to get a link through McGill for student discount) and go the many national parks in Quebec.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Attend frosh in the beginning of the semester.
cultural_challenges: They speak French in Montreal and I don't. It is good to know some basics especially when going other places in Quebec.
culture_appreciated: Very welcoming.
top3_advice: It feels like a lot of work during the semester with assignments and such, but because they count in the final grade, there is less pressure on the exams.
other_useful_info: Attend social activities and try to go to some of the club meetings.
most_rewarding: To study and live in another country is very interesting and also challenging to balance going out on trips in the weekends and also doing school. But I found it very rewarding to give myself time to relax and not to do school work in most of my weekends.
greatest_challenge: Doing assignments weekly.

crucial_aspects: It was really important to me that I would feel safe at my destination at all times, and that there would be a lot of different museums, events and other activities taking place in the city and the areas around it. Besides that it was also important for my choice that the university had a big selection of courses I found interesting. I therefore looked at the course list in advance and chose an english speaking university to allow me to choose between all the courses.
info_ease: It was quite easy. The university send a many emails with information before I arrived, and I got a person I could contact before arrival. She also hosted a meeting upon arrival and she was available throughout the entire semester if we needed help. There were also a lot of staff walking around campus the first couple of weeks who could help solve any kind of problem.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance when I arrived other than going to the science exchange student information meeting hosted by my contact person.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I received an email from my host institution upon admission with a link to a website where I had to fill in the necessary information. During this registration process I got acces to my McGill email and website called minerva. Minerva was where the course registation took place, and after deciding which courses i wanted to take I could enter their numbers on the registration page at minerva once the registration opened.
registration_help: It was possible to get help by sending an email to the contact person or the professor if a course for instance required special admission.
registration_success: I ended up getting 3 of the courses i originally wanted and the last course I was able to register for was really similar to the one i originally wanted.
registration_advice: The course registration for exchange student opens after some other students have already registered meaning that some courses are already full or nearly full. And as all exchange students are able to register at the same time it might be hard to get the courses you want in the beginning. A lot of people are however dropping their courses again both before and during the add/drop period so it is important to keep an eye out as spots might become available. The professors are often really kind as well so if you experience any kind of problem you can try to send the professor an email.
course_level: I took one 200 level course, two 300 level courses and one 500 level course
teaching_comparison: My experience were that the professors at McGill focused less on methods compared to UCPH and instead of knowing how things work and how we know this we had to learn and remember a lot of details of the different subjects. They test you through quizzes and assignments throughout the entire semester which I found a little stressfull, but i eventually got used to it, and this made the exam period much easier. I only had one course with assigned reading for every lecture, and in general i found it easier to get a good result at McGill than at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: QCST 200 - Intro to the Study of Quebec PSYC 311 - Human Cognition and the Brain MIMM 324 - Fundamental Virology PHGY 518 - Artificial Cells
recommended_courses: It was really satisfied with all my courses, but I would especially recommend QCST 200 as I found it really interesting to learn more about the area I was living in. The course covers the history, the culture and todays issues of Quebec and the professor is great. She had guest lectures coming to class for nearly all lectures and it was always really interesting and a nice way to learn if you want to try something different from you normal field.
unexpected_costs: I didn't really encounter any unexpected costs. But I only had to pay for one book which was less than I expected.
cost_comparison: I think the prices were really similar to the danish prices. The prize was distributed differently on items in the supermarket than in Denmark, but the final price on all my groceries would be quite similar to what I would pay in Denmark.
activities_available: McGill has a lot of different clubs for students to join. I were a part of the McGill outdoor club and I also attended events made by the Mafia club (they play the game called mafia or werewolf), chocolate club and the knitting club. I were also a part of a soccer intramural team, where we got to play against other McGill teams. No matter you interest it is possible to find a club, and it was a great way to get to know other people, and we often went to a bar or planned to meet another time after the meetings and events.
activities_recommended: I would especially recommend joining the outdoor club as you can join different trips throughout the semester and experience the nature around Montreal. They also have a frosh event before the semester starts where I went on a canoeing trip for three days in a national park.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend just walking around the different neighborhoods of Montreal and try all the cafes, museum and events that you find. You should also follow the website MTLblog as they post weekly updates of things to do in Montreal the following week.
culture_adjustment: The local culture isn't much different from the danish culture, so it was really easy
socializing_tips: Join some of the clubs or sport teams as this is an easier setting to socialize with local students than in classes
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences challenging. If I should mention one thing it would be the fact that Quebec is a French speaking province meaning that messages in the metro for instance is only done in French, but it never caused me any problems even though I wasn't able to understand it.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated that the Canadians are so friendly and open. It is really easy to start a conversation with them.
top3_advice: Don't be stressed by all the deadlines. They aren't that strict when marking your assignments and it is important to have freetime to experience the city. Join all the events at university that you find interesting. People are always happy to talk and it's a great way to make new friends if you show up alone. If you are going to use the metro often you can save a lot of money by showing up at the STM office at Berri UQAM
other_useful_info: McGill has an interactive map you can find on the internet to show you the easiest ways to navigate between buildings at campus
most_rewarding: I think the most rewarding part was experiencing how I was able to build an everyday life and make new friends in a foreign country.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was accepting that things take time and that it was hard to make friends, understand all the new systems and keeping up with the deadlines in the beginning.
other_comments: Montreal is an amazing city and McGill is a great university. Things can seem hard or overwhelming but it was one of the best experiences I have ever had, and everything will eventually be solved so it is important to have fun and enjoy the stay before it is time to go home as 4 months go by so fast.

crucial_aspects: Mainly wanting to go to North America and Canada is much easier (and cheaper) in terms of visa. I wanted to explore more neuroscience and McGill was a great opportunity for this.
info_ease: Pretty easy. I signed up for the buddy program and outdoor frosh and both were great ways to meet new people and get a lot of advice and being shown around campus before the semester start. You also get a contact at the university and it's always worth just emailing and asking about anything you're unsure of.
arrival_assistance: Introduction talk at first and above mentioned.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It's a really long process with lots of steps but it's so worth it! Once you get the spot at KU it's really easy to apply to McGill.
registration_help: You get a ton of emails and just have to go through them step by step. And there are steps on Minerva (their portal) to go through as well.
registration_success: Not very much at first. Since people already studying at McGill gets to choose first. Be quick at first and try to register for the course you want right when it opens. Afterwards sign up for waiting lists - I got a spot of multiple courses this way. There is also a 2 week add/drop period at the beginning of the semester and I got exactly the classes I wanted at the end.
registration_advice: Don't worry too much if you don't get into the classes you wanted at first, you have plenty of time. There is also an app called seatalert to give you notifications when a spot becomes free for the classes without a waiting list.
course_level: Pretty similar to at home. But many more weekly assignments, quizzes and midterms.
teaching_comparison: Many classes consist of just lectures which is a bit boring this is however mainly for 300 level and below classes. 400 and 500 will be of in class teaching style. 300 and below has more of a midterm - final structure and 400 and above has more bigger assignments and much less memorization.
courses_enrolled: PHGY 314 - Integrative Neuroscience COMP 204 - Computer Programming for Life Sciences BIOL 414 - Invertebrate Brain Circuits and Behaviors PSYC 311 - Human Cognition and the Brain
recommended_courses: Great combination of classes if you are interested in neuroscience. PHGY 314 and PSYC 311 have some overlap but not very much - it does help with learning the neuroanatomy though. Both are rather tough classes and mainly PHGY 314 is really interesting but also has soo much material. COMP 204 is great for python introduction. BIOL 414 is such a great class with really interesting material. You do need to know a little bit of coding before though, but it's really not much. I taught myself a bit of python for BIOL 414 which also made COMP 204 much easier so highly recommend doing that!
unexpected_costs: Data for your phone is much more expensive. Get a sim card with data in Denmark that you can use in Canada before going!
cost_comparison: Food and clothing was a little more pricy than expected. I didn't have to buy any books which saved me a lot. Save up money before going since going on weekend trips is so worth it - but also a little expensive.
activities_available: There are so many clubs at McGill. If you haven't found anything interesting before hand then go to the activities night and check out all the clubs. Also follow SSMU on instagram - they host a lot of stuff.
activities_recommended: Go to outdoor frosh!! Great way of meeting other exchange students and the leaders will be same age as you and it's totally fine to talk to them as well since you might have some of the same classes! The lettuce club is legendary as well!
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes! You can rent cars from enterprise through McGill to get a big discount. Go to other cities as well - Toronto and Niagara falls are great and you McGill has mustbus to get there for cheap!
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. McGill is very international and it's easy to fit in. Some people might speak french to each other and you have to get used to that in general. Quebec is very french!
socializing_tips: Join everything to begin with. Everyone is looking for new friends at the beginning. A great start is going to outdoor frosh and joining camping which is more chill and more people. Go to club meetings and talk for people in class as well. Meetup with other danes on exchange as well.
cultural_challenges: I don't speak any french.
culture_appreciated: How international Montreal and McGill is.
top3_advice: Go on outdoor frosh. Higher levels classes does not necessarily mean more work. Choose classes that sound interesting - if you have fun with your classes you will have much more energy for also doing other things.
other_useful_info: Don't get too much into a mindset of what your exchange should be. There are so many opportunities and the most important thing is just to be open.
most_rewarding: Learning a lot of neuroscience and meeting so many nice people.
greatest_challenge: The application proces - it's soo long but once you go it's much easier! You have a lot of exams to balance out.

course_level: The level of courses was fine.

recommended_courses: POLI 346, POLI 410, POLI 411 and POLI 445. All the professors were very invested in teaching their courses and helpful if neededd.
unexpected_costs: n.a.

activities_available: McGill gym (for a small fee) and McGill pool (free).

weekend_recommendations: Go to Mont Royal, Mont Tremblant and just explore the city of Montréal.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Be open and friendly. They will invite you in if you ask.
cultural_challenges: The one thing is that there is a more formal way of interacting with professors compared to my home university. culture_appreciated: The welcoming nature of Canadians.
top3_advice: To be aware that there will be a lot of studying at McGill compared to what I've heard of at other universities. The academic level is ambitious and high, and there are a lot of assignments. But you do learn A LOT, and both students and professors are very good at helping.
other_useful_info: n.a.
most_rewarding: Learning from the courses and getting to know local friends from uni (had classes with them).
greatest_challenge: Striking the right balance between being invested in the courses and learnings while also making time for extraordinary experiences such as weekend trips.
other_comments: n.a.

registration_help: Man skal selv opsøge hjælp hos studievejlederne udover de mails McGill sender med informationer
registration_success: Jeg fik alle de fag jeg gerne ville have
registration_advice: Sørg for at finde mange fag du godt kunne tænke dig, hvis der enten ikke er plads eller faget viser sig at være noget andet end du forestillede dig. Giv dig selv lidt løs line og vælg i hvert fald et fag som er på et lavere niveau

Der er et meget anderledes forhold til underviseren fordi eksamen ikke er anonym og man desuden bliver bedømt undervejs som en del af ens endelige karakter. Det resulterer i at der er mere gymnasie-vibe i undervisningen... Jeg havde desuden timer hvor jeg blev krydset af og det talte med i min karakter hvor mange af forelæsningerne jeg havde været til
courses_enrolled: AEHM 205 Science Literacy BREE 529 GIS for Natural Resource Management BREE 533 Water Quality Management ENVB 222 St. Lawrence Ecosystems
recommended_courses: Science literacy var et lidt krævende fag, men underviseren er virkeligt dygtig! jeg synes at jeg fik meget ud af at blive undervist i skriftlig akademisk formidling og det er et fag jeg helt klart har manglet på KU
unexpected_costs: Hvis der er ekskursioner på dine kurser skal du selv betale for det. Derudover skal man gøre op med sig selv at man nogle gange kommer til at bruge dumme penge fordi man ikke altid helt forstår systemerne og kan regne ud hvad den bedste løsning er
cost_comparison: Mobildata er sindssygt dyrt i Canada, men meget nødvendigt. Vi var mange som brugte et selskab der hedder fizz. Simkortet kan købes i automater rundtomkring eller i kiosker og så aktiverer man det og sammensætter selv sit abonnement på nettet. Det fungerer super godt!
activities_available: Der er activities night i starten af semesteret hvor man kan gå rundt og snakke med alle klubberne. Ellers prøv at holde øje på instagram, hvor klubberne lægger opslag om kommende begivenheder
activities_recommended: Sørg for at komme på ture! Det er billigt og nemt at leje biler så hvis i er en gruppe der vil afsted er det relativt nemt. De laver også andre både weekend- og dagsture som er værd at holde øje med.
weekend_recommendations: Montreal er en storby med mange kulturelle tilbud (især i sommerhalvåret). Hold øje på sociale medier eller kig på plakater rundt om i byen, som ofte reklamerer for arrangementer
culture_adjustment: Jeg synes på mange måder at Montreal mindede meget om København så jeg følte mig umiddelbart meget hjemme. Bliv gode venner med den offentlige transport. socializing_tips: Jeg syntes at det var rigtig svært at blive venner med de lokale. Jeg ved at mange andre havde succes med frosh. Men brug endelig din tid sammen med de andre danske studerende!
cultural_challenges: Der var en meget fransk tendens til at det var lidt ildeset at tale engelsk, hvilket nogen gange var lidt op ad bakke. Jeg var glad for at have et nogenlunde niveau inden.
culture_appreciated: Montreal er en meget multikulturel by, hvilket ar virkelig fedt at opleve. Jeg lagde meget mærke til på McGill at der var en høj tolerence ift. at man ikke nødvendigvis talte mega godt engelsk fordi der var så mange internationale studerende eller quebecois studerende med fransk som modersmål
top3_advice: Forbered dig på at det også er super hårdt og til tider ensomt at være på udveksling. Jeg var virkelig glad for de danske udvekslingsstuderende som jeg hurtigt blev gode venner med. Vi tog på ture sammen, holdt julefrokost etc sammen og det var virkelig skønt! Jeg havde troet på forhånd at jeg ville kunne finde venner på universitetet, men det var svært, fordi man lidt bare blev kastet ind på et hold - og det virkede ikke som om at de havde et særlig stærkt socialt liv ifm. deres studie. Desuden er det rigtig nyttigt at kunne bare lidt fransk når man skal til Montreal;)
other_useful_info: Få et studie OPUS-kort til den offentlige transport! McGill skriver at man skal være fulltime-studerende hele året for at få det, men hvis du møder op på stm's kontor (Montreals DSB) som ligger ved Berri-UQAM kan du sagtens få det lavet dér. Jeg købte en månedlig plan som kostede lige knap 300 kr./om måneden, som gav mig fri transport på hele Montreal-øen
most_rewarding: Jeg syntes at det var fedt at være 100% ansvarlig for mig selv. At finde ud af, at jeg var i stand til at løse rigtig mange situationer uden andres hjælp eller råd var virkelig fedt. Derudover oplevede jeg at have rigtig meget tid, fordi jeg ikke have arbejde, forpligtigelser som jeg normalt har derhjemme og at studiet var noget mindre krævende. Jeg syntes, at det var lidt svært at håndtere i starten, men fandt senere ud af, at det var fedt at have tid til at gøre alle mulige ting jeg normalt ikke ville få gjort.
greatest_challenge: Jeg valgte at gå ude på MacDonald campus fordi de havde flere kurser jeg gerne ville have. Fagligt var jeg glad for det, men jeg brugte rigtig meget tid derude fordi man skulle tage bussen (ca. 40 min) derud. Jeg følte mig ofte lidt afskåret fra de andre udvekslingsstuderende fordi jeg ofte var langt væk når de lige mødtes og i frokostpausen etc. Der var heldigvis en anden dansker derude, hvilket jeg var rigtig glad for! jeg vil ikke nødvendigvis fraråde at vælge Macdonald, men du skal kun vælge det fordi du synes, at fagene vejer tilstrækkeligt op

crucial_aspects: McGill has good opportunities to try new course material compared with Copenhagen University, and I was intrigued to see how their university education is different from the Danish system. Also, I found it interesting that McGill is located in one of Canada's bilingual regions, and I heard beforehand that Montreal is a very cool place to live.
overall_comments: It was a fantastic experience, and I do not regret it at all, but McGill as a University is maybe not as great as its world ranking. They do not accommodate exchange students very well. Further explained, no regards from McGill were taken to welcome one as a student, so you just have to make friends in class or clubs. But how could this have been different, and isn't that the case in all universities? No! Most universities where I know people go on exchange have welcomed them in some welcoming program, where you can find comfort in other exchange students—examples in Canada are Guelph, Concordia and probably many more. McGill does have Frosh, but it is sadly not very well organized if you go to their Macdonald Campus Frosh. But excellent news, if you go to the downtown campus as most people do, you can then participate in the outdoor frosh. Here you will indeed have a great time and avoid the 18-year-old fresh high schoolers :)
info_ease: McGill has good sources on their website on how to apply for courses, schedule planners, and when and where to arrive for lectures. So that part went smoothly. Generally, McGill has a lot of information on their website, and all the information is there; sometimes the problem is finding it, but when writing their team for assistance, they are very helpful. Disclaimer: be prepared to spend some time on the exemption from international health insurance (IHI) McGill has because, as a Danish citizen, you have the right to get RAMQ in Quebec, the same as the Danish yellow health card. Therefore, you can save hundreds of dollars by getting RAMQ, but the system is very old school and takes time to process. Also, Minerva is a bit old, but you will use it a lot, so looking at the different themes on the website is beneficial. You can find the exemption from IHI, Schedule Builder, course application, etc.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance.
arrival_comments: Again, the welcoming program could be greatly improved, especially since you pay almost 200CA$ for Frosh.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: You can always write to someone at McGill for help and emails for the specific problem is linked on McGill official website under courses.
registration_success: I got all the classes I applied for.
registration_advice: Research the courses beforehand, which you also do when you apply for the pre-approval from UCPH, and take into account that some courses have demands for what previous courses are required for the specific course.

But excellent news, if you go to the downtown campus as most people do, you can then participate in the outdoor frosh. course_level: I took the 200-300 level; the reason behind this was I was limited by a mandatory statistics course, and this was how my schedule could piece together. But 400 and 500 courses are also fine for a bachelor's student. I would not necessarily say that a 200 course is more accessible than a 400 or 500; it depends on the course and how much premature learning you have in the course field. But of course, the 400 and 500 are more specialized courses often. Sidenote: if you go to the Macdonald's campus, then be aware that the campus is small and there is a limited amount of courses.
teaching_comparison: Very different, you call the professor "professor," and lab courses are often seen as a master's student privilege, so I found that a bit peculiar since I'm in Denmark in the lab all the time. Overall, it is a learning experience to see how different a university education system can be. Be aware that the view of student responsibility is a lot different than Copenhagen University. My impression is that less is expected of you than UCPH. I like, to some degree, that they have a continuous grading system of percentages throughout the semester.
courses_enrolled: 205 Science Literacy 300 Cropping systems 333 Pollution and bioremediation 310 Statistic methods 1
recommended_courses: 207 Science Literacy is a very good course; it offers a new view of science writing and its importance. Also, it is a very good course to ace the bachelor's or master's thesis because you learn to write well in a structured and captivating manner for the reader. From my knowledge, we do not have this as a course on UPCH, which is a shame. Some of the concepts I have been presented at UPCH, but having it as a course creates time for you to master the tools. Science literacy is a 200 course, not necessarily an easy course, but if you engage, then you will pass. 300 Cropping systems - loved the professor, loved the course material 333 Pollution and bioremediation - I liked the course, and bioremediation is fascinating; also a good way of learning how different handling of wastewater and trash is in Canada.
unexpected_costs: Simcard is expensive, but I would reccomend the company Fizz.
cost_comparison: Transportation is cheap compared to Copenhagen when you are a student. Food is a bit more expensive, but this depends on your nearby supermarkets. This somewhat determines your monthly spending since there is a difference in grocery prices in the different areas of Montreal. Not a crazy difference, but maybe a few 100DKK a month.
activities_available: There were some, but in my opinion, not many. Also, sometimes overlap with lectures and, therefore, could not attend.
activities_recommended: The open-air festival was fun, and International Student Day is a big recommendation, but it is a month into the semester and the only opportunity to meet other international students
weekend_recommendations: Go to Toronto, Niagara falls, see some national parks etc.
culture_adjustment: The students are a bit hard to approach on a deeper level. I had a lot of friends in the lectures, but outside the lectures, it was hard to connect to the students in my courses. Also keep in mind that one semester (4 months) is also not a lot of time to get to know people. A lot of local social invitations from students in my courses came at the end of my stay. However, people in Montreal are in general very friendly, so even though I did not have many friends from my courses I saw privately, I did get a lot of friends, and I was very social on my exchange. Sometimes, it is not what you expected but just as great, and that is definitely a take-home from my exchange.
socializing_tips: Join a club and try to find some international students who can relate to your situation. Also, just be friendly and start up a casual conversation. Just take every chance you get to bond with a new person.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any differences challenging despite their French being very different than European french. French is not a problem at the university because everyone can speak English, and typically, people are very including if you do not speak French. The French challenging part is more in your life interacting with locals outside the university.
culture_appreciated: Montreal is the most included city I have ever been in regarding gender. I have enjoyed learning what we can do differently in Denmark on this topic. Generally, if you are inclusive you get included.
top3_advice: - Your exchange success depends on how much effort you put into it - Be open-minded when meeting new people
other_useful_info: The bars, clubs, karaoke bars and cafes are great, and use them greatly!
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and getting my worldview expanded. Having a break from the Danish rush hour, we do stress too much.
greatest_challenge: Having to move mid-stay, otherwise, just remember that everything on exchange is just temporary and enjoy it while it last, also on the shitty days.

crucial_aspects: McGill is an old and prestigious university in North America with a great reputation. I had already been on exchange to Paris, so I wanted to go somewhere outside of Europe this time. I had visited the US approximately ten times but I had never been to Canada, so I thought it would be fun to explore. In comparison, Canada is much safer than the US, and Montreal is an old city with a fascinating colonial history. I also saw my exchange as an opportunity to be more outdoorsy (I have hiked and skied a lot this past semester) and to learn a bit of French.
info_ease: Easy. They had some webinars for new students that I watched before coming here. They also write everything on their intranet and they will send you lots and lots of emails.
arrival_assistance: Nearly none. They offered almost no orientation as I arrived for the Winter semester (starting Jan 4th). They only invited new exchange students to one pizza night on the second day of school – which was overwhelming and unstructured – and a brunch on the Sunday of week 1. No follow ups or future events. No facebook or WhatsApp groups. So it was sort of difficult to meet new people - especially because non-exchange students were quite young and already had their established friend groups. Sadly this meant that I mostly hung out with other Danish students and with my roommate and her friends.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I don't remember it well. But I think we just had to send a personal statement and give them some official documents such as passport copies and the like. It was easy, just follow their instructions.
registration_help: I did not need any help so I do not know.
registration_success: I got all the ones I wanted. I also took French, which does not count towards my KU courses, I just wanted to learn a new language for free and I would recommend other to do the same. You do not need to pass the course, just have fun with it.
registration_advice: Just play around with the schedule builder on Minerva so your classes do not clash. There is also an add and drop period at the start of the semester so your classes are in no way set in stone. Just try different ones. I would also recommend to avoid classes on Fridays and or Mondays as this allows you to travel over the weekends. Just be aware that the workload at McGill is very intense. I took five subjects including French so I had 13 lessons (1,5 hours each) a week plus homework - which means that the days that you do have class become very long. In my case, I had about 3 or more lessons a day Monday to Thursday.
course_level: As a master student taking bachelor level courses, I thought that a lot of them were really easy. Also see above^
teaching_comparison: McGill has more of an anglo-saxon teaching tradition, which I really liked. Classes were usually more engaging and less lecture like than at home.
courses_enrolled: ANTH 338 Indigenous Studies of Anthropology POLI 434 History of Political/Social Theory POLI 342 Canadian Foreign Policy POLI 380 Contemporary Chinese Politics FRSL 103 Near Beginner's French
recommended_courses: I really really enjoyed ANTH 338 Indigenous Studies of Anthropology. The professor shared a lot of wisdom and I learned a lot about an important aspect of Canada. As a poli sci student it was also interesting to know more about the discipline of anthropology.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive. I think Canada has to import a lot of food during winter so the quality was low and the prices high. They also don't show the real price at the super market as they add the taxes (approximately 15 percent) at the end. If you go out to eat you also pay tips (again approximately 15 percent) so everything is 30 percent more expensive than you think. Domestic and regional plane tickets are also really expensive.
activities_available: So so many. Basically anything you can think of they would have a club for. There's a fair - activity's night - at the beginning of the semester where you can meet all the clubs
activities_recommended: Skiing! Mustbus is great for day and weekend trips around Canada and north-eastern USA.
weekend_recommendations: New York city, Toronto, Chicago, Boston, Ottawa, Quebec City Skiing Hiking I spent a month after the semester travelling around Canada. I went to Banff and Jasper (national parks) and Vancouver with my friends. Then I went east to Quebec City and Tadoussac with my mom. I highly recommend
culture_adjustment: So easy. McGill and Montreal are very international.
socializing_tips: Just start chatting to the people you sit next to on your first day. Canadian are very friendly and sociable. Just say "hey how are you, is this the right class-room, I'm new... where are you from" etc. and it will be easy
cultural_challenges: Quebecois French is very different to French French
culture_appreciated: The restaurant and bar culture ! So many great places in Montreal and they're packed every weekend
top3_advice: 1) Bring warm clothes 2) Stay on top of deadlines 3) Plan trips to visit new places while you're here
other_useful_info: Don't let academics consume you. The semester is very condensed and intense so try to have fun as well !
most_rewarding: Travelling. Canada is STUNNNNING
greatest_challenge: The cold weather. I though it could be difficult to go out and socialise in January when it was -15 and dark. But just do it. Put on warm clothes and it will be fun. Also, the winter ends and summer in Montreal is gorgeous. Try to stay past the semester if you can. Today (June 3rd) it is 30 degrees and the city is green and lively, there are lots of festivals and I am starting to love the city more.

crucial_aspects: I did not have the opportunity to go travelling during my gap year, so it was really important for me to use this opportunity to travel. I chose Canada because i wanted to explore a country outside of Europe, but still be familiar with the culture and language. I had heard a lot of good things about McGill university and Montréal from older students, and i loved the fact that it was a medium size city.
overall_comments: I absolutely loved everything about it!
info_ease: I was very lucky to have a friend who went to McGill and Montreal the year before me, who told me a lot. But you get a lot of emails from the university and McGill are hosting several online seminars that you can sign up for, to get information on course registration, health insurance, etc.
arrival_assistance: When I arrived at McGill, all exchange students at the SCIENCE faculty were invited to an information meeting where we got information on course registration, and everyone was encouraged to get a 1 to 1 conversation with the international student secretary - overall i think the information was pretty clear.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I absolutely loved everything about it!
registration_process: All courses will have a 4 letter and 3 digit code (ex. PSYC 311). When you know what courses you want (the full course calendar will be available a few weeks before registration), you have to be ready for when the registration opens. The registrations opens a bit later for exchange students so you need to be fast. You enter the course code and then sign up. If all the spots are full you may be able to join a waitlist, but don't worry - during the first three weeks a lot of people change/drop courses, so if you don't get a spot on your first try, just keep looking for free spots and sign up after the courses have started.
registration_help: A lot of online videos and seminars were available and did have good instructions on how to sign up for classes.
registration_success: I got all the classes i wanted - however i needed to sign up for another time schedule for my FRSL 101 class, because i didn't have time to walk across campus within my 15 minute break :)
registration_advice: Use the visual schedule builder application (website) - you can pan your schedule with the classes you are considering and see how the classes match and add up. Also be aware of the campus and location of the class - you have to run very fast to go from one side of campus to the other in a 10 minute break.
academics_comments: I absolutely loved everything about it!
course_level: The levels of courses range from 100-600 (or more...) where 100 is the easiest. I had one 100 course, one 300 course, one 400 course and one 500 course. Even though the 100 course was supposed to be the easiest, it was probably one of the classes that i spend more time on - however the academic level was higher on the 500 course. I would recommend only having one 500 course and the some 300 or 400 classes. Then the academic level is fine but you still have the time to go explore.
teaching_comparison: I had some big classes (more than 300 students) and small classes (15 students). In the big class (PSYC 311) the teaching mostly consisted of weekly lectures and 5 quizzes during the semester with a multiple choice midterm and exam. The smaller classes consisted of more lectures and seminars, where you had to write a term paper and do a presentation about a research article for the whole class. This teaching more resembles the teaching at UCPH. I had one french class where the teaching was mostly seminars where we had to prepare weekly homework for each seminar. We also had to do some written and oral assignments and then a 5 minute oral exam.
courses_enrolled: PSYC 311 - Human cognition and the brain PHGY 488 - Stem cell biology PHGY 518 - Artifical cells FRSL 101 - Beginners French 1
recommended_courses: I would recommend all my courses. PSYC 311 because its more anatomically related. It is a nice break from all the small courses where you go into much detail on the molecular biology. However, there is a lot to remember and the exam is a little tricky with attention to a lot of details. The teacher is really good, and you also look into the clinical use of neuroanatomy and neurophysiology. PHGY 488 is a much smaller class with only 15 students. The teaching is very much the same as in Denmark, and the teachers are really good. In the seminars you prepare two research articles pr seminar and present one paper during the semester. You also have to write a term paper on 5 pages about a recent important research article within the field of stem cell biology. The exam consists of essay questions. PHGY 518 is tough by a very old man, Professor Chang, who developed the field of artificial cells. It was a topic that i had never heard about before, and to be tough by the man himself was a really nice experience. However, because of his age, the structure of the class is not that great. The PowerPoints are not posted, and the communication between professor and students aren't the greatest. You have to prepare a 10 min presentation and a 10 pages term paper, but there is no exam :) FRSL 101 was a really nice break from all the science. Montreal is in the french speaking part of Canada, so it was really nice to learn the basics of the french language. The teachers are really good and its nice with the fellow students because they usually are international students or 1st year students. Be prepared for weekly homework, 4 tests during the semester, oral assignments and a 5 minute interview in the end - but i thought it was really worth it.
unexpected_costs: I did not experience any unexpected costs. You pay 7 CAD = 35 DKK for a travel authorization pass which is mandatory.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than expected. Especially vegetables and diary products. However, eating out was cheaper than expected.
activities_available: There is a fitness / gym at the university that arranges several sports to try. You can sign up for yoga classes, squash, badminton, spinning or just a monthly membership at the gym. Also there are so many cultural clubs to join and they do sisal parties where you mostly can just show up. Also the outdoor club is a great opportunity to go on some great trips with other international students. You can also arrange a trip yourself and ask other from the group to join.
activities_recommended: During the first week of uni, there is a 4 day even called FROSH. It is an introduction / orientation event arranged by the different faculties and McGill outdoors club (MOC). Join the MOC FROSH. You can sign up for 4 different trips usually: camping, climbing, hiking and canoeing. The people joining this FROSH are usually older and international students and you get to go on a nice trip and explore the nature around Montreal. When paying for the trip, you are also automatically a member of the MOC. I found some of my best international friends on this trip - we still keep in touch today!
weekend_recommendations: Go explore the nature and other cities around Montreal. There are so many beautiful national parks where you could rent a car (MgCill student discount through enterprise) and go for a nice hike. I would also recommend going to Quebec City for a day or two - especially during christmas because they have the cutest christmas markets. I also really enjoyed my trips to Toronto, the Eastern Townships and Vermont. McGill has a club called MustBus that arranges cheap bus rides to some of the big cities during the semester and in the fall-break. Some of the trips are one day and some are with stays. Also just explore Montreal - there are so many things to see and do during all the seasons, so don't feel the need to go on a trip every weekend. Also you have to go watch an ice hockey game with the Montreal team and the McGill team.
culture_adjustment: Montreal is a very international city with people from all over the world, so it is easy to fit in. You fell the mix of the canadian and the french culture. In some parts of the city, they speak mostly french while other places they speak mostly English. The city have something for everyone - all the seasons, good food, beautiful nature, nice nightlife and bars and very good people.
socializing_tips: Don't be shy. Go to some social events arranged by the university, and don't be scared to go alone. A lot of people are coming to Montreal without knowing anyone, so everyone is really friendly and openminded. However, be prepared to fell that it is easier to socialize with other international students-
cultural_challenges: If you dont speak any french, it can be a challenge sometimes. In specific parts of the city they primarily speaks french, so its good to know some basic words for the grocery shopping ;)
culture_appreciated: The diverisity of the city - the city has a completely different vibe in all the different parts. I basically felt like i had four cities in one. And all the people are so friendly.
top3_advice: 1) Remember an adapter, passport, yourself and your computer 2) Remember to have fun and not concentrate too much on your studies 3) Don't be afraid to spend money - you will probably regret it when you come home
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Learning to navigate in a whole other country and culture without your family or best friends to support you. Even though it sounds terrifying, i learned a lot about my self and what i could handle on my own. I really learned to appreciate time with myself and remembered how good it feels to get to know new people, who doesn't necesarrily come from the same culture as myself.
