crucial_aspects: Affordability, vibrant city, opportunities to improve language abilities
info_ease: My host university had quite a few workshops/meetings for international students in the beginning.
arrival_assistance: There was an international students coordinator we could contact. I had a zoom-meting with them, they were helpful with information about rules and courses.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We could sign up for a lot of courses and attend them during an initial period. Then at some point you had to discard the courses you did not want. However the course would start from the beginning, so if you jumped on a course just before the deadline you might be behind.
registration_help: the international students coordinator was helpful, but I sorted it out by myself mostly.
registration_success: Quite. There was a very long waitlist for one particular course I wanted, but I wrote directly to the department and after applying in some roundabout way two times I got in. You have to take contact a lot of times and not just rely on the numbers on the screen. Oftentimes there is a way in.
registration_advice: To look at the syllabus online if you can find it, and ask former exchange students from your degree what their experience was with a particular course. You also want to think about whether you want a course with a high workload or low, a final exam or not, and so on. All can be found in the syllabus.
course_level: Before I got there I had heard that 300 level courses were easier than what they would be at my home university. I found this to be somewhat true intellectually, but the workload and memorization was correspondingly higher. So in the end, the toughest courses/the ones I spent the most time and energy on where actually my 300 courses, while my 400 course was more of a breeze.
teaching_comparison: The lectures were similar, but there were almost no workshops/regnetimer where you would work with the material in groups or anything similar; only lectures. So you had to spend a lot of time working and reading on your own if you did not have a study group. There were also a lot of quizzes that counted towards your final grade; this would force you to keep up with the material in a way that UCPH does not.
courses_enrolled: FRSL 211 Oral and Written French MIMM 324 Fundamental Virology PHGY 488 Stem Cell Biology PSYC 311 Human Cognition and the Brain
recommended_courses: PSYC 311 Human Cognition and the Brain was very interesting and full of "aha" moments, but had a big memorization load. However I found the memorization to be easier because it was interesting, and you could relate things to your own body and the cases introduced. PHGY 488 Stem Cell Biology is nice because they don't require you to do neither quizzes nor midterm, but you must follow the lectures since they are rarely recorded. It is small course, so you have better opportunities to ask questions and engage.
unexpected_costs: The frosh (introductory days with acitvities) cost almost 1000kr for a ticket no matter which type of frosh you choose. I would recommend going on the MOC (McGill Outdoor Club) frosh, as it costs the same as the faculty frosh, but you get to go out into nature and do some adventurous stuff compared to the faculty frosh that is centered around drinking (and where people are two or three years young than you).
cost_comparison: Groceries are expensive in Canada. Cheese especially, tofu less so. Going and eating out and going to cafés is maybe 10-20% cheaper than in Denmark.
activities_available: A big recreational center with gym, teamsports, yoga, squash, you name it. All for a fee, but not a crazy one. Several clubs (cultural clubs, charity clubs, music, obscure sports, games, quizzes). A mini-festival (open-air pub) in september.
activities_recommended: I would say to do some sports and to maybe join the McGill Outdoor Club if you like that sort of stuff and even if you don't. They do hikes, canoe-trips, camping, skiing, climbing, biking, apple-picking and foraging and it's all student-led.
weekend_recommendations: Do some roadtrips to the country-side, maybe rent a cottage with some friends and visit maple-sirup makers, microbreweries, ice-cream factories, go hiking. You can cross the border and visit Vermont and New York State easily. In Montréal there are good opportunities to drink a beer with friends, go to concerts or go clubbing, however everything closes at 3:00. Visit the botanical garden, the biodome or the artificial islands.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Join clubs, talk to people in your class. Best advice if you really want to get local friends is to live at a residence or share an apartment with local students. I lived with Danes so I hardly got any local friends.
cultural_challenges: You might need to speak some French some places. Usually you can get service in English, but some people are not very good at it and some even dislike English-speakers, however, if they can tell that you are not Canadian, they will give you a pass.
culture_appreciated: People really like going out in the summer; there's always people out and about.
top3_advice: - don't slack that much, if you do well on the quizzes you can have an easier time in the finals period. - try to get out there and meet new people - visit the surrounding areas (rest of Quebec, the US)
other_useful_info: Keep an eye on deadlines for registrations and so on.
most_rewarding: To live in another country, to feel independent, to meet new people and get new friends, to be away from my usual life. To learn things I might not have learned at UCPH (although some things were not interesting).
greatest_challenge: How tough the finals and midterm period can be

crucial_aspects: It was important for me that the courses at the university sounded interesting and that it was a country I hadn’t visited before.
overall_comments: I really only had good experiences with McGill University and Montreal in general. It's quite different from Copenhagen but not too overwhelming at the same time. The city is just amazing.
info_ease: Before starting classes I had a walk around campus to find my class rooms since campus is quite big. I know they also provide guided tours for new students, but I did not sign up. A lot of the needed information is also easily found on the McGill website and through E-mail.
arrival_assistance: I don't recall getting any assistance upon arrival. A week before the Semester starts the student advisor of the science faculty had arranged a meet-up for all international exchange student and she also advised every exchange student to to set up a private meeting with her. I found this very helpfull as she made sure the courses I was signed up for matched my background at UCPH. She is also very willing to answer any questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I really only had good experiences with McGill University and Montreal in general. It's quite different from Copenhagen but not too overwhelming at the same time. The city is just amazing.
registration_process: I found the whole process very stressful. Firstly, I found it difficult to find a list with all the courses available in the fall semester. Secondly, the registration for courses opens later for exchange students, which meant that many of the courses I originally wanted where already full. For some of the courses you can get waitlisted, but not for all courses. At the end i managed to get into all the courses I originally wanted. In the beginning of the semester they have a add/drop period where many people change courses, so if you can't register at first just wait till the add/drop period. I also wanted to join a course that had pre-requisites. Here I had to E-mail the professor until I could register.
registration_help: The visual schedule builder found on Minerva was a very big help in seeing how many spots that are available in the different courses and to make a schedule with no overlaps.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Stay calm if the course you want is full. Know that all the courses you look up beforehand might not be available.
academics_comments: I really only had good experiences with McGill University and Montreal in general. It's quite different from Copenhagen but not too overwhelming at the same time. The city is just amazing.
course_level: I took courses in physiology, biology and french. FRSL 302 Listening Comp & Oral Exp 1 (french): This is the easiest course I had at McGill. I really don't think you can fail the course. I did most of my homework and all assignments with moderate/low effort and still managed to get an A. BIOL 575 Human Biochemical Genetics: Compared to KU and considering this is a master course, this was also a very easy class. You get most of you grade points through presentations and everyone got a 100%/A. I had passed the course before even taking my final exam. PHGY 314 Integrative neuroscience: This class was definitely the hardest course I had at McGill. The curriculum is very big and the exam is a multiple choice closed-book exam. Still though I would say that the level was maybe a bit lower than at UCPH. PHGY 488 Stem cell biology: This course was very similar to the level at UCPH in terms of content.
teaching_comparison: In my physiology and my biology courses the teaching style was very similar with lectures. In most of my courses there was no reading material except of the lecture slides which was very nice. In my french course we had a lot of oral assignments and discussions and a lot of homework which was different.
courses_enrolled: FRSL 302 Listening Comp & Oral Exp 1 (french) BIOL 575 Human Biochemical Genetics PHGY 314 Integrative neuroscience PHGY 488 Stem cell biology
recommended_courses: French: I would recommend taking a french course if you'd like to be able to speak a bit with the Quebec people. It was a fun class and many exchange students take it, so it's a good way of making friends. Many first year students take it, so people were a bit young. Depending on your french skills you get placed on a course matching your level which is very nice. I was in FRSL 302. If you are interested in stem cells I cannot recommend PHGY 488 Stem cell biology enough. This was the best course I had at McGill. You meet people from the field, not many universities provide stem cell courses, and the professors were very nice.
unexpected_costs: Not any that I can think of.
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than anticipated but dining out is cheaper than in Copenhagen.
activities_available: There are student clubs for everything at McGill. They also have sport events like football and basket. They honestly have everything.
activities_recommended: I would recommend McGill Book Club, Knitting club, Nordic culture club, seeing a football game, joining an a capella group (or going to a capella concert) or McGill Choir society.
weekend_recommendations: Visit the Insectarium (small museum about insects), Biodome, The Montreal science center, Redpath museum on campus
culture_adjustment: It is very easy. People are more open and talkative than in Copenhagen which makes it very easy to make friends.
socializing_tips: I found this quite hard since most of the students aren't local. Like finding actual Canadian people was not easy haha. But I would say by joining a club or a sports team it's easy to make friends. At my stay we also had a big whatsapp group with all the exchange students where we planned different activities. In some of my classes people were also willing to socialize.
cultural_challenges: I once went to the doctor and he only spoke french which was a bit of a challenge but it worked out in the end.
culture_appreciated: How open and welcoming the people of Montreal are. People are just very kind and nice.
top3_advice: Don't be scared if a course with a high number (like 500-level courses) are going to be too hard - they are not Join a club, it is fun DON'T join frosh if it is offered to you, it was a waste of money and time
other_useful_info: Enjoy, it is going to be so much fun
most_rewarding: Making new friends was the most rewarding part and getting to live in another country was really a good experience
greatest_challenge: The workload is a bit more intense throughout the course at McGill compared to UCPH where you only have a final exam.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to attend a university where English is the main language – preferably at a destination that I wouldn't otherwise visit on vacation.
overall_comments: The school system (grading, midterms, assignments, attendace) is quite dfferent from the Danish school system. It demands more continuous engagement, which drages the score a bit down. As a Molecular Biomedicine student, I was only used to attending 1-2 courses per. block. At McGill you would have to attend four different courses at once – each having more continuous school work to be done, compared to the structure in Denmark (or at least at Molecular Biomedicine).
info_ease: I had some issues accessing my McGill mail before arrival at he University. I therefore missed some information fra the University that I should have reacted to – but it all worked out fine. I think McGill's portals are easier to navigate compared to UCPH. I think it would have been to know upon arrival, that McGill charges a (fairly high) mandetory cost of International Health Care – and that to avoid paying this as a Danish Student, you need to apply for extension before receiving RAMQ (that can't be applied for before arriving in Canada).
arrival_assistance: IT-support.
arrival_comments: I didn't attend the introduction week. But the university is overall fairly helpfull.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The school system (grading, midterms, assignments, attendace) is quite dfferent from the Danish school system. It demands more continuous engagement, which drages the score a bit down. As a Molecular Biomedicine student, I was only used to attending 1-2 courses per. block. At McGill you would have to attend four different courses at once – each having more continuous school work to be done, compared to the structure in Denmark (or at least at Molecular Biomedicine).
registration_process: I don't remember the process in great detail, but I remember that there where a lot of documents that I needed to obtain and send alongside my application. But there was a guide to do so, so it wasn't too hard. Registration for courses was on the other hand not a too positive experience to be honest. Upon registration I used their visual schedule builder that helped me choose courses that aligned with each other. What they don't tell you is that the McGill students (non exchange) gets to register before the exchange students do. One of the courses i wanted to attend was therefore fully before I could registere – sometimes if you write directly to the professor they can admit you in the course anyways. The schedule builder or website also don't show if you aren't able to take a course as an exchange student – which was the case for the course I wanted to attend the most. The course still has available seats but I wasn't allowed to registre even after consulting the course professor.
registration_help: A step-by-step guide was provided and schedule builder.
registration_success: I had five courses that I wanted to attend – where I would drop the one i liked the least within the two week drop-periode. I 'only' got three out of the five, with one of the ones I didn't get being the course I wanted the most. I would therefore give it a 5/10.
registration_advice: Look into if you as an exchange student are able to attend a given course – or email the course professor before registration. Sometimes it will say that the course is only for a specific major, but that is not always the case. Also, have backups in case the course you want gets full!
academics_comments: The school system (grading, midterms, assignments, attendace) is quite dfferent from the Danish school system. It demands more continuous engagement, which drages the score a bit down. As a Molecular Biomedicine student, I was only used to attending 1-2 courses per. block. At McGill you would have to attend four different courses at once – each having more continuous school work to be done, compared to the structure in Denmark (or at least at Molecular Biomedicine).
course_level: Some of my courses was entry level (level 200) while I also had 300- and 500-level courses. I don't think it necessarily is the level of the course that determines the difficulty. I had a 250 and 575 course that was equally challenging – and my least challenging courses. My 300-course was a entry to med-school course (which I didn't know upon regestration) which made it more difficult.
teaching_comparison: For most of my courses there is only lectures and no to very little course literature. A three credit course has three hours of lectures per week – either as three one-hour lectures, two one-and-half-hour lectures or one three-hour lecture. By default they don't do breaks in the lectures – not even the three-hours ones which is very different from UCPH. The humanities courses often also have conferences which is a participation class-lecture as we know it from High School. Conferences often consists of 20-30 students and a TA where you get a grade for participation and sometimes also presentations.
courses_enrolled: BIOL 575 – Human Biochemical Genetics ANAT 365 – Cellular Trafficking COMP 204 – Computer Programming for Life Sciences GSFS 250 – Sexual and Gender Diversity Studies
recommended_courses: Basically all of them but for different reasons. BIOL 575 is an 'easy' course as a Molecular Biomedicine student. More of the curriculum aligns with former courses and the topics are very relevant and interesting. ANAT 365 was most definitely my hardest course that aquired a lot of attention – mostly due to the exam forms and research project. The curriculum was on the other hand very interesting. COMP 204 is nice if you want intro to python! It does take a lot of weakly work since there's both weekly assignments, quizzes and videos to watch. But you learn a lot! GSFS 250 is nice since it's non science so you get to do something completely different. Also the curriculum is very good and should be something every body knew!
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Groceries are more expensive in Canada! Eating out on the other hand is a bit cheaper than in Denmark – we therefore, and because it's cozy, ate out a lot:)
activities_available: Basically everything! There's a activity's night in the beginning of the semester where you can meet all the different clubs. On the unis website you can also sign up for different types of sports.
activities_recommended: I attended the Nordic Culture Club and the Knitting Club – both really nice! I was also a part of the McGill Choral Society which consists of people of all ages – also really nice! We did a huge church concert in the end of the semester. I know some of the others attended tennis-classes. There is free access to the uni pool and it's cheap to sign into the uni gym.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Banff!!!! It's a national park i Alberta that for me is a must visit if you're into nature and hiking. It's the most beautiful place I've been so far. We also went to NYC – the school arranges busses to different locations in the reading break, which I really recommend. Otherwise we went a trip to Vermont and on hiking day-trips in the 'local' area. If you're up for a longer trip, then Toronto is also a nice visit! Ideally you can drive up to Ottowa (The Capital of Canada) on the way:) It's fairly easy and cheap to rent a car – you can get student discounts through the university.
culture_adjustment: The culture is somewhat european but also very northern american. It really helps if you know some French (I didn't) but as long as you stay in the cities people speak English.
socializing_tips: Join the clubs! Also don't be afraid to talk to people in your classes! It's true that Canadians are (overly) friendly:)
cultural_challenges: The amount of homeless people was for me the biggest cultural difference for me. That and the amount of French that are spoken on the street/in shops/cafés.
culture_appreciated: How friendly people are!
top3_advice: Be open to new things, go on trips and enjoy the canadian culture, and remember that money will come back but your exchange stay won't:)
other_useful_info: Nope.
most_rewarding: The friends I made! A lot of them also being Danish, that I get to hang out with post-exchange as well! And the rest has promised to visit me in Copenhagen – and also gives me a good reason to return to the city in the future:)
greatest_challenge: The amount of school-work! But I ended up doing more than just fine, so try not to stress too much about it.

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte Montreal, fordi jeg var interesseret i byens multikulturelle kultur. Som en fransk talende provins i et engelsktalende land, ser man en masse spændende politiske stridspunkter og kulturelle særpræg i både byen og provinsen Quebec. Ud over at være en fransktalende by, så er Montreal også fuld af mennesker fra hele verden. Det er et enormt multikulturelt miljø, som vi simpelthen ikke har hjemme i Danmark. Det har været virkelig spændende at, være en del af.
info_ease: Det var relativt nemt
arrival_assistance: Jeg modtog noget assistance, men det var ikke meget. Der er et kontor for udvekslingsstuderende, som man kan besøge, men man skal selv være opsøgende. Generelt set synes jeg ikke, at universitet gør specielt meget for udvekslingsstuderende. For mig var det helt fint, men for andre kan det måske være en udfordring.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Der var ikke en super lang proces. Brug deres online portal Minerva og tilmeld dig kurser derinde. Det er også gennem denne portal, at du får dit studiekort/adgangskort og et billiger rejsekort.
registration_help: Der er et kontor for udvekslingsstuderende og et kontor for alle studerende. Der kan man få en masse hjælp. Jeg vil mene, at de er en del mere behjælpelige end administrationen på KU, så jeg synes at det hele gik ret nemt.
registration_success: Jeg fik alle de kurser, som jeg ønskede
registration_advice: Hold øje med deadlines og sørg for, at du søger kurser, når de bliver offentligt tilgængelige. Husk også, at hvis der står, at et kursus har nogle forhåndskrav, så kan du altid skrive til den givne professor, og bede dem om at sige god for dig. Underviserne har en del mere magt herover, så hvis du overbeviser en professor om, at har kvalifikationerne til at følge kurset, så kan du får det.
course_level: Jeg tog højniveau bachelorfag indenfor indenfor international politisk økonomi og så tog jeg masterfag indenfor komparativ politik.
teaching_comparison: Undervisning var meget lig den i Danmark. Man tog til forelæsninger og læste stoffed. Jeg manglede lidt nogle holdtimer, da det kan være lidt kedeligt og til tider svært at få undervisningsmaterialet gennemarbejde, når undervisningen ikke lægger op til diskussion eleverne imellem.
courses_enrolled: 1. IPE: Monetary Relations 2. Democracy and the Market 3. The Contentious Politics of Energy Transitions 4. Globalization & dis/content
recommended_courses: Hvis man interesserer sig for grøn omstilling eller energipoltik, så vil jeg klart anbefale faget The Contentious Politics of Energy Transitions. Det er et af de mest spændende kurser, jeg har taget på universitetet.
unexpected_costs: Jeg skulle ikke betale for noget, som jeg ikke havde forventet.
cost_comparison: grøntsager er ret dyre i Canada, så hvis man gerne vil spise sundt, så skal man være klar på at bruge lidt flere penge på mad.
activities_available: Der er stort set klubber for alt, hvad man gerne vil være en del af.
activities_recommended: Tag på en skitur og sørg bliv medlem af en sportsklub, så kommer du til at møde en masse mennesker.
weekend_recommendations: Tag til Toronto, New York, Quebec City og en skitur. hvis du har pengene, så besøg vestkysten, hvor du får natur for alle pengene.
culture_adjustment: Det er super nemt at blive en del af den lokale kultur. Det er en fordel at kunne tale fransk, men det er slet ikke et krav. Derudover minder Montreal meget om Europa i kraft af forholdet til Frankrig, så kulturchokket er slet ikke så stort, som man skulle tro.
socializing_tips: Gå op til dem og sig hej. De er langt mere åbne end dansker. Derudover vil jeg anbefale, at du melder dig ind i nogle af universitets studenterdrevne klubber. Det er den bedste måde at møde andre studerende, da undervisningen er mere forelæsningsdrevet og har mindre elevdeltagelse.
cultural_challenges: Man kan til tider møde folk, som er lidt snobbet omkring fransk vs. engelsk. Det betyder, at man ikke får ligeså god betjening, hvis man ikke taler fransk. Det er dog min erfaring, at det er sjældent, at man kommer ud for det. På McGill taler alle engelsk, der oplever man det slet ikke.
culture_appreciated: Musikscenen i Montreal er meget levende. Der er enormt mange små spilledesteder med lokale bands, og det er virkelig dejligt, at opleve et så levende vækstlag.
top3_advice: 1. Niveauet på universitet er lavere, men der kræves en del arbejde fra de studerende, da der skal afleveres en del afleveringer. 2. Undersøg de sociale klubber og grupper, som de studerende på universitet er en del af. Det er den bedste måde at få venner på McGill, og det er kilde til masser af gode oplevelser. 3. Vær strategisk med hvor din undervisning ligger. Undervisningen går klokken 08:00 om morgenen til klokken 18:00 om aftenen, så sørg for, at du får lavet et skema, der giver dig mulighed for at opleve byen.
other_useful_info: Nej
most_rewarding: At opleve at være en del af et meget mere internationalt studiemiljø. McGill får studerende fra hele verden, som giver undervisningen et langt større perspektiv og et større rum for diskussion. Det er virkelig noget andet end på KU, hvor de studerende hovedsageligt er født og opvokset i Danmark og derigennem tilgår verden fra samme perspektiv og med samme informationskilder. Jeg nydt meget, at få perspektiver fra hele verden i klassediskussionerne.
greatest_challenge: Alderen på de studerende i Nordamerika er en del lavere i forhold til i Danmark. Det kan derfor været lidt svært at finde venner til undervisningen og på campus. Jeg fandt derfor venner gennem andre steder og fritidsbeskæftigelser. Man skal også være klar på, at hvis man kommer til Montreal i efterårssemesteret, så varer vinteren helt indtil midt/slut April. Det kan derfor være lidt svært at udforske byen, da den er i vinterhi meget af semesteret. Jeg vil derfor anbefale, at man sætter noget tid af til at opleve Montreal, når semesteret er færdigt, da byen ændre fuldstændig karakter. På den måde er det meget ligesom i Danmark.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a medium-size city, outside of the EU, and preferably somewhere they spoke English, French or Spanish, giving me an opportunity to practice my language skills.
info_ease: McGill sends out a lot of information about orientation events for first-year students as well as exchange students, so it was easy to sign-up for events and know when and where things were happening! They give you a virtual brochure, highlighting the most important information and describing the different neighbourhoods which was quite useful.
arrival_assistance: There was some initial orientation events before classes started, which was nice to get an overview of the semester, key academic dates, requirements etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I think registration opened in early June (but I'm not 100% sure), but I only registered for courses in mid/end July. McGill has a "Drag and Drop" period in the first two weeks after classes start, which means in this period a lot of students drop some classes and sign up for others – so don't worry if you are not able to register for all the classes you want from the beginning, chances are you will probably get in during this period. For the classes with waitlists, definitely sign up for the waitlist! You can always drop it in the first two weeks.
registration_help: I don't remember exactly what help (if any) I used, but I know that on McGill's website they have a bunch of guides for incoming students, which are quite useful!
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted after the "Drag and Drop" period!
registration_advice: Look through the course catalogue and get a good idea of which courses you want to take! Note that some are only offered during winter, so if you are going abroad in the fall semester disregard these. Sign up as early as you can, but if you can't register for some of the courses you want, don't worry – chances are you'll probably get it once classes start and people decide to switch. Importantly, if you are in doubt which courses you want to take, attend as many as you want/can during the first two weeks, to get a better idea and then decide afterwards!
course_level: The courses for undergraduate students (us) go from level 100 to 500. The 100 courses are often very introductory, and the 500 courses are supposed to be the most difficult. I took one 200-level course, two 300-level and one 400-level course. In the end it was the 200 level course that required the most of my attention, since it had weekly quizzes and assignments, whereas the 400 level course was more chill and similar to the courses we have at KU, where the student can decide how to structure time and workload.
teaching_comparison: I think the teaching style was similar to the one at UCPH. My 400-level course was in a small classroom setting, whereas the other three courses were in big auditoriums with 70+ students. I would say the material and level of the courses are also similar to the level at UCPH, but note that the semester at McGill is shorter than at UCPH, so you need to learn and study the material in a shorter amount of time – hence, it can feel like more work than we are used to from home.
courses_enrolled: COMP 204 – Computer Programming for Life Sciences PHGY 314 - Integrative Neuroscience ANAT 321 – Circuitry of the Human Brain PHGY 488 – Stem Cell Biology
recommended_courses: I cannot recommend the course ANAT 321 – Circuitry of the Human Brain enough! It was the best course I have had in my education thus far. The instructor is absolutely amazing and every lecture feels like a Ted Talk! Even if you don't find neuroscience interesting, I would still recommend taking this course. It was also the course with the lowest workload and the best/easiest exams! COMP204 had the highest workload but it gives a good basis idea of programming, especially if you have zero coding experience (like me). PHGY 314 had a lot of similar content to ANAT 321 but on a higher and more detailed level – I would recommend it if you find neuroscience interesting. PHGY 488 was an ok course, the material is somewhat similar to what we have learned in Molecular Biology. There is no midterm, which was nice.
unexpected_costs: I don't think there we any unexpected costs – we did a lot of travelling to nearby cities, which obviously makes the journey more expensive than if you stay in Montreal the entire semester. I did not include the costs for travels etc. in the information above.
cost_comparison: Groceries were quite expensive, but I believe that was mostly because the only supermarket near our apartment was quite fancy – I imagine the prices were similar to buying groceries in Meny in Copenhagen. Other than that, the majority of things were cheaper than in Copenhagen. A good cup of coffee cost around 25 DKK for reference.
activities_available: I did a yoga class and a barre class through McGill, which is cheaper than doing them in a studio, and a good option. They sell out fast so buy them early on! There are endless options of sports you can do through McGill, where you pay for the entire semester. I paid 75 CAD total for the entire term, but the price depends on which class you choose. There are also a huge amount of clubs for many different interests that you can engage in at McGill, like knitting club, wine club, salsa club etc.
activities_recommended: Whatever your interests, find a club that matches them! It is a great way to meet new people. I liked my yoga and pilates class, so would definitely recommend them if it interests you:)
weekend_recommendations: Go on trips! We went to Toronto, New York, Québec and Banff throughout the semester, which are all great destinations! Pro tip: You don't need more than a day to see Québec, and I'd recommend going in December to see the Christmas market.
culture_adjustment: I think it was pretty easy, Canadians are very open and welcoming! Everyone in the city speak both French and English, so it is easy to get by even if you don't speak French:)
socializing_tips: Join clubs or sports!
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any cultural differences challenging!
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and openness of the Canadians! It makes it very easy to feel included and make friends.
top3_advice: Since we don't get Erasmus for studying in Canada, I would recommend applying for scholarships and/or save money before going, so you don't need to worry too much about costs etc while you're abroad:) Make use of the holidays, or the fact that most lectures are recorded, to go on trips! Explore the city early on in the semester! We ended up saving many touristy things for last, thinking we would have plenty of time – we did not. Once midterms begin, time goes really fast and you will have more work to do.
other_useful_info: One of the things that will probably come up as an option in the beginning is FROSH. It is a few days of many introductory events and activities before classes start, but it is primarily for the students starting their first semester at McGill. We thought there might be other exchange students, but it was mostly 17 and 18-year olds students. It is quite expensive to participate, so I don't think it is worth the time and price. Instead, I would check out the events for exchange students, which are very fun and a good way to get to know the city.
most_rewarding: Getting to live in a new city;)
greatest_challenge: I don't think there was any!
other_comments: Go on exchange!!

course_level: Level very similar to UCPH (For biology) I was a third year student and mostly took third year classes and the level was good. Not too hard and not too easy. But i think it varies a lot in depending on the field.
teaching_comparison: Very similar. But for many of the courses i took it was only lectures for in person classes. No session for assignments or something. but it was fine.
courses_enrolled: COMP 204 Programming for life sciences MIMM 324 Fundamental Virology BIOL 352 Dinosaur biology (Is being changed into something about comparative anatomy so no more dinosaurs :(( ) BIOL 300 - Molecular Biology of the gene
recommended_courses: Pretty much all of them. They were very well organised and i learned a lot! BIOL 300 was a very dry course. -NAME REDACTED- doesnt speak english too well and it was only lectures, Midterm and FInal. No assignments or quizzes to get grade points like there was in the others.
unexpected_costs: Trips, events, parties and hikes and such. Nothing surprising.
cost_comparison: Housing was a little more expensive than i thought but other than that it was normal.
activities_available: There were clubs and sports for almost anything at McGill so tons of opportunity to meet new people with the same interests.
activities_recommended: Hiking and going on trips outside of the city. Especially in the fall! Tons of pretty nature to go explore a little outside of Montreal. Mont Tremblant was a very beautigul hike to the top! highly recommend. Or renting a shed somewhere in a forest with friends is also highly recommended. And other than that just go out and explore all the differents parts of the city.
weekend_recommendations: See my answer above.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. People are sooo nice there! But try to meet with some locals also to really understand ;) Go on some dates or however you want to meet new people :)
socializing_tips: I didnt attend any clubs myself but i think they are a great way to meet people!! And also try to make some friends in class if you can. It can be hard when it is mostly lectures, but try your best ;) People are very nice and typically want to hang out outside if school also. Going on dates from dating apps (hinge for me) was also super nice. Very good way to learn about people living there and meeting amazing people you can hangout with (if all goes well of course hehe) throguhout your stay. I met the sweetest girl who i hung out with througout my stay.
cultural_challenges: None really. Very few people dont speak english so that wasnt a problem.
culture_appreciated: That everyone is so friendly. And also the fact that each part of the city is so different and has their own style and vibe. Fun to explore them all.
top3_advice: Make an effort to find people you can explore the city with and have fun with. It can be very hard to find people, but talking to people on facebook groups from UCPH and meeting them in Montreal is a great way to start!! Go outside of the city also for the pretty nature! And just enjoy and experience as much as you can while you are there! You will regret not doing enough during your stay :)
other_useful_info: Can't think of something.
most_rewarding: Getting a core friend group (we were 4 people from Denmark) and experiencing the city and all it has to offer together!
greatest_challenge: Probably just studying for finals after some hard midterms. And for my courses there were always weekly assignments and quizzes that counted towards the grade which made it so that i was a little bit on edge and stressed about school after the first two months.

crucial_aspects: I mainly chose my study destination because it is a city filled with young students and a lively atmosphere. I was also excited to experience a university that is very well respected there. Additionally, it is an English-speaking country while also being in the French-speaking part of Canada, which felt a bit more European. And of course, Canada’s nature is absolutely amazing.
info_ease: It was easy. The university is clearly experienced in receiving a large number of exchange students, which was evident throughout the process.
arrival_assistance: I received a lot of helpful emails with important information, including key deadlines, details about the first week of classes, and activities beyond studying.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process at the host institution was relatively easy and straightforward through their online platform. We were given access to the registration system at the beginning of June, and the steps were clear and simple to follow.
registration_help: Clear and helpful university website and easy access to administrative support
registration_success: Unfortunately, I was not very successful in registering for the classes I initially wanted. Although I had received prior approval for several courses before arrival, many of them were already full. Local students are given access to course registration approximately two weeks before international students, which meant that many courses were fully booked by the time I was able to register.
registration_advice: I would recommend getting approval for lots of courses early. That way, if a course isn’t offered or is full, you can quickly switch to something else.
course_level: I took economics courses at the 400 level. Overall, I experienced that the level was somewhat lower than at KU. Several of the topics had already been covered during my first and second year in Denmark. However, I think the teaching style and course content were different enough that it is difficult to make a direct comparison. I was challenged in a different way than I would have been at home.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style varied between my courses. One felt similar to UCPH with lectures and written exams. Another included participation, assignments, and quizzes, which I wasn’t used to. Both courses had midterms during the semester, which I liked because it eased the pressure on the final exam.
courses_enrolled: ECON 420 Topics in Economic Theory ECON 440 Health Economics ECON 408 Public Sector Economics 1
recommended_courses: I would recommend ECON 440 Health Economics. It was not very technical and focused more on discussion. The assignments were policy briefs, and the readings were interesting research articles rather than heavy theory.
unexpected_costs: I don’t think I encountered any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping was generally a bit more expensive than in Denmark, but overall prices were similar. Public transport was cheaper than expected. You could rent unlimited bikes for just over 100 DKK per month, and a student metro pass was about 250 DKK per month. We also joined the university gym, which cost only around 300 DKK for the entire semester.
activities_available: There were lots of activities for students. They had a gym and weekly sports like ice skating, yoga, and tennis. They also did fun city tours (like a “bagel tour”). I went on a trip with the McGill Outdoors Club too. One thing I wouldn’t recommend is the first camping trip - mostly very new and much younger students signed up.
activities_recommended: Weekly sports, watch a hockey match
weekend_recommendations: Ottawa, Toronto, Québec City (recommend going in December during Christmas). During fall break I went to the Rocky Mountains for about 10 days which I would really recommend.
culture_adjustment: It was easy to adjust to the local culture. Many students in the classes didn’t know each other very well, so people were friendly and open to talking.
socializing_tips: Talk to people during classes and participate in events. Joining weekly sports activities is also a good way to meet local students.
cultural_challenges: You don’t need to speak fluent French, but sometimes, for example in supermarkets, you would meet people who couldn’t speak English. That could be challenging at times.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated how friendly and welcoming Canadians are.
top3_advice: Be flexible with course registration, join activities early to meet people and take advantage of add/drop period during the first two weeks.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Discovering a new way of studying and living, and getting to know a different culture while making friends from all over.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was getting the courses I wanted. The registration itself was easy, but I had limited flexibility in getting certain courses approved, which made it more difficult to secure the classes I really wanted.

crucial_aspects: McGill Law was an obvious choice due to its strong international reputation and its unique transsystemic approach, which offered exposure to both civil law and common law traditions. The Faculty’s particular strengths in international law, human rights, and trade law closely aligned with my academic focus and complemented my legal training at the University of Copenhagen. In addition, studying in Montreal provided an intellectually vibrant, bilingual environment that encouraged comparative and interdisciplinary thinking, which was a key motivation for choosing my study destination.
info_ease: Overall, it was relatively easy to find the necessary information upon arrival. McGill provided clear pre-arrival guidance, and key practical information regarding registration, course selection, and academic expectations was well structured and accessible online. Any remaining questions were easily resolved through orientation activities and responsive support from administrative staff, which made the transition smooth.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival, I received structured support through orientation activities and introductory sessions organized by the university and the Faculty of Law. These provided practical guidance on academic procedures, course registration, and campus resources. In addition, administrative staff were accessible and helpful in addressing individual questions, which ensured a smooth start to the exchange period.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process at the host institution was well organized and largely straightforward. Course selection and enrollment were conducted online prior to the semester, with clear guidance provided by the Faculty of Law. Any adjustments after arrival were handled efficiently, and support from academic advisors and administrative staff made it easy to resolve scheduling or enrollment issues.
registration_help: Support was available through orientation sessions, academic advising, and responsive administrative staff at the Faculty of Law. In addition, central student services provided assistance with practical matters such as registration, housing guidance, and access to campus resources, which made it easy to obtain help when needed.
registration_success: I got all my courses.
registration_advice: Future exchange students should familiarize themselves with the online registration system well in advance and carefully review course descriptions and prerequisites before enrolling. It is advisable to have a prioritized list of alternative courses, as popular classes can fill up quickly. Making use of the add/drop period and staying in contact with academic advisors can help resolve any scheduling issues efficiently.
course_level: The level of the courses was demanding and appropriate for advanced law students. Classes required a high degree of preparation, including extensive reading and active participation, and assessments emphasized analytical skills rather than memorization. Overall, the academic level was comparable to upper-level Master’s courses and provided a strong intellectual challenge.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at the host institution was more interactive and discussion-based than at UCPH. Classes placed greater emphasis on student participation, case analysis, and continuous engagement throughout the semester, whereas teaching at UCPH is generally more lecture-oriented and exam-focused. This difference encouraged more active preparation and ongoing reflection, and it complemented my academic experience well.
courses_enrolled: International environmental law International human rights law International trade law Jurisprudence
recommended_courses: The ones I took!
unexpected_costs: Some unexpected costs included higher-than-anticipated expenses related to housing deposits, winter-related clothing and utilities, and course materials. In addition, everyday costs such as groceries and public transportation were slightly higher than expected, particularly over the winter months. Overall, these costs were manageable but worth budgeting for in advance. ALSO: TIPS everywhere!
cost_comparison: Food is expensive. Coffee is cheap. Books are cheap.
activities_available: Everything literally.
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining non-academic activities such as swimming, a book club, and a choir. These activities provide a good balance to academic work, offer structured breaks from studying, and make it easy to meet people outside the law faculty. They also help create a sense of routine and community, which greatly enhances the overall exchange experience.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the Rocky mountains. Explore the rest of Quebec: Go see blue whales in Tadoussac and go on hikes with random people. Go to the MOC house. Maybe a weekend in Boston or New York. But dont support the US unnecessarily. Go to concerts. Go to sport events. Go the the cinema. Enjoy your life. Spend some time on the mountain as well. Talk to people.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture was relatively easy. Montreal is an open and internationally oriented city, and the bilingual environment made it welcoming for exchange students. Cultural differences were present but easy to navigate, and the inclusive academic and social atmosphere at the university facilitated a smooth adjustment.
socializing_tips: NO. Do it in you own way and in your own tempo.
cultural_challenges: There were no major cultural differences that were particularly challenging. However, adapting to a more informal classroom culture with higher expectations of continuous participation required some adjustment. Additionally, the bilingual context occasionally created minor practical challenges, but overall these differences were easy to navigate.
culture_appreciated: I particularly appreciated the openness and inclusivity of the local culture, as well as the strong emphasis on community and dialogue both inside and outside the classroom. The bilingual and international environment encouraged curiosity and exchange of perspectives, and the city’s vibrant cultural life made it easy to feel engaged beyond academics. Whatsoever, I did not like when Montreal became to American.
top3_advice: Plan your courses early. Familiarize yourself with the registration system and have backup options, as popular courses fill up quickly. Be prepared for active participation. Classes are discussion-based and require continuous engagement and thorough preparation. Embrace life off campus. Living off campus and joining non-academic activities is a great way to integrate into local life and get the most out of the exchange experience.
other_useful_info: Future exchange students may benefit from knowing that the academic workload is continuous rather than concentrated around a final exam, so steady preparation is important. It is also useful to plan housing and administrative matters early, as timelines and procedures may differ from those at UCPH. Finally, taking advantage of orientation activities and student organizations can greatly enhance both the academic and social aspects of the exchange.
most_rewarding: It was the break I needed from Denmark. Also, you get some perspectives on your life at home that are essentail for your further movement. I am not a whole new person. But close.
greatest_challenge: All the time on my own with my own thoughts and all my freetime without substantial stuff to do. Either you will find out that it is not that bad. Otherwise you will go insane.

crucial_aspects: I chose to study at McGill in Montreal, Canada for several reasons: I wanted to explore Canada and Canadian culture, I wanted to improve my French and English (the two primary languages spoken in Montreal), and I wanted to attend a good university.
info_ease: Very easy. McGill's website is very user friendly, and you can find all the information you need there: on how to apply to McGill, how to register for courses, what orientation events they offer etc. They also had a series of webinars on how to find housing and other practical stuff outside of the university.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any, because I didn't look for assistance. But I know McGill offers a lot of different services such as International Students Services, mental health services etc.
arrival_comments: Unfortunately, I missed the orientation week, but I've heard it's a good opportunity to meet other students. There are also opportunities throughout the semester to meet other students. For example, I went on a hiking trip which I found through McGill's B2 Gym.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There are some different documents you need to upload such as letter of nomination, proof of English proficiency, university transcript etc. But it was manageable to get those documents, and I didn't even need to write a motivational letter.
registration_help: I am not sure, I did not receive any help.
registration_success: Not very succesful. I was unable to register for a lot of the classes I had planned because the spots were already filled by the time I was able to register (and I tried to register as soon as it was possible for exchange students). However, I still ended up with very interesting courses, and there is also an add/drop period during the first two weeks of the semester, where a spot might open for you in the classes you wanted (but you can't be sure of it)
registration_advice: Make a long list of courses you find interesting, and look into which of those courses fit together in a week/which courses don't overlap. You can for example use McGill's Visual Schedule Builder. It's nice to note down a few different course combinations, as all courses probably won't be available to you (e.g. if the class is already full when you try to register).
course_level: I only took 300-level courses - none of them were really challenging, but I still learned a lot.
teaching_comparison: I mostly took classes with a lot of students (+100), so it was mostly lectures where the professor talked most of the time, but students were also encouraged to ask questions.
courses_enrolled: ANTH 338 Indigenous Studies of Anthropology; FRSL 212 Oral and Written French 1; GSFS 304 Postcolonial Feminist Theories; SOCI 333 Social Stratification; SOCI 370 Gender and Development.
recommended_courses: Definitely ANTH 338 and a French class (if it's in your interest to learn French). ANTH 338 was about Indigeneity and Indigenous peoples, and focused a lot on settler colonialism as well as Indigenous ways of thinking and being in the world (it was almost a bit philosophical). The professor did not allow computers in class, but I thought it was really nice, and there were only assignments in the class (no in person exams), so you did not have to remember everything said in class. I also took a French course just for fun (I couldn't get it transferred to KU). It was a very effective way to learn French (but expect a lot of homework that you have to hand in for every class!)
unexpected_costs: My flight tickets were cancelled due to a strike, and I did not receive any refund. I had to buy new plane tickets that were very expensive at the time (about 8,500 DKK for a one way ticket).
cost_comparison: In general, I think grocery shopping is a bit cheaper than in Denmark (but only a little). Go to Dollarama where you can get inexpensive dry goods.
activities_available: I know they have different communities (religious, LGBTQ+ etc). There is also McGill's B2 Gym that offers a great variety of sports classes. At the beginning of the semester, they have orientation week where you can meet other students.
activities_recommended: I went on a hiking trip I found through the B2 gym - that was a fun way to meet other students!
weekend_recommendations: Travel around Canada - there is so much beautiful nature to explore! I really enjoyed my trip to Banff and Jasper National Park (which is very far from Montreal, but really worth the travel), and I also enjoyed visiting Quebec City during Christmas.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy - as long as you're open to meet new people, it should be no problem.
cultural_challenges: They speak more French than I expected in Montreal (which is a good thing, if you, like me, are trying to learn French) - though their French is quite different from European French, so it can be quite difficult to understand.
culture_appreciated: Their oppenness. Sometimes (especially at university) you have to approach people yourself, but my experience was that if you did so, they were very friendly and willing to talk.
top3_advice: 1) Try to approach people - many people want to connect, but won't always initiate themselves, 2) Pack for all different kinds of weather (it rains and snows/gets really cold, but is also warm in the summertime), 3) Once you've found some people you like, invite them out for coffee or to explore the city together (take initiative).
other_useful_info: McGill has so many opportunities to meet other students - explore them before you go, and sign up for events in advance.
most_rewarding: The people who became my friends during my stay - it was really nice to be able to connect with strangers, and in a very short time become close to them.
greatest_challenge: Figuring out how to prioritize school vs socializing and exploring the city/country. I did spend more time studying than expected, but I also found the classes really interesting!!

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte at tage afsted til McGill i Canada af flere grunde. Jeg synes at Canada er et spændende land med god mulighed for at komme ud i naturen. Jeg havde også hørt godt om Montreal som en livlig, men tryg by hvilket jeg virkelig synes den levede op til. Det var også vigtigt for mig at komme afsted til et universitet med relevante kurser.
info_ease: Inden jeg ankom og lige da jeg var ankommet fik jeg en masse mails fra McGill, hvoraf noget af det var brugbart. Men der var visse ting jeg skulle finde ud af selv, f.eks. blev jeg ikke introduceret til MyCourses hjemmesiden (McGills udgave a Absalon) eller hvordan add-drop perioden i starten af semesteret fungerede. Det var dog nemt nok at finde hjælp på skolen (Student Services Desk), og jeg oplevede alle underviserne og andre ansatte på universitetet som meget hjælpsomme.
arrival_assistance: Jeg modtog ingen hjælp, men behøvede det heller ikke
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Jeg startede med at bruge Visual Schedule Builder på Minerva for at finde ud af hvilke fag jeg kunne tage sammen uden at de overlappede. Det fungerede ret nemt, så jeg skrev kursus koderne ned og sad klar da kursus registreringen åbnede. Kursus registrering åbner senere for udvekslingsstuderende end for de almindelige McGill studerende, så der var nogle af de kurser jeg ville have der allerede var fyldt fra starten af. Desuden havde jeg problemer med at jeg ikke kunne tilmelde mig nogle af kurserne, fordi de krævede specifikke prerequisites. Selvom jeg mødte kravene med kurser hjemmefra, kunne McGills system ikke godtage det. Jeg blev derfor nødt til at skrive til McGill og blev kastet lidt rundt mellem nogle forskellige mennesker i administrationen før de fandt en løsning. Men det lykkedes til sidst!
registration_help: Det var lidt svært at finde ud af hvem jeg skulle skrive til med problemer med kursus registrering, men alle jeg fik fat i ville gerne hjælpe.
registration_success: Ret succesfuld. Der er heldigvis også en add-drop periode der er ca. de første to uger af semesteret. Her kan man prøve kurserne af, afmelde sig hvis man ikke synes det var noget for én, og tilmelde sig nye i stedet. Det gjorde jeg brug af, og det virkede helt fint. Det gjorde også at der kom plads på nogle af de kurser der ellers var fyldt op fra start. Man kan skrive til sig venteliste på kurser i add-drop perioden.
registration_advice: Hav en liste af kursus-sammensætninger du kunne tænke dig, og sid klar til tilmelding når den åbner. Hvis ikke du får alle dine drømmekurser fra start af, skal det nok lykkedes at få nogle gode kurser alligevel, da meget kan ændre sig i add-drop perioden
course_level: Jeg var blevet rådet til at tage kurser der var lidt nemmer end jeg ville herhjemme, fordi niveauet skulle være meget højt. Det var ikke helt det jeg oplevede. Jeg endte med at tage en del 100-lvl kurser, hvilket var fint, men jeg kunne godt have brugt lidt mere udfordring. Som 3. års studerende på BA kan man sagtens tage 300-lvl kurser, man skal bare være klar over at der er mere arbejde i dem end i 100-lvl kurserne.
teaching_comparison: Det var meget det samme - en blanding af forelæsninger, øvelsestimer og afleveringer. Det der er mest anderledes er den måde de bedømmer eleverne. I stedet for at hele ens karakter afhænger af den endelige eksamen, tæller afleveringer, midterm-exam og (i nogle kurser) deltagelse i undervisningen også med i ens karakter.
courses_enrolled: EPSC 340 - Earth and Planetary Inference EPSC 185 - Natural Disasters ATOC 181 - Introduction to Atmospheric Science. PHYS 182 - Our Evolving Universe
recommended_courses: Jeg var egentlig glad for alle mine kurser, men særligt Our Evolving Universe, fordi professoren (Prof. Matt Dobbs) var meget inspirerende. Det var lidt nemt kursus, men det var meget givende at være til undervisning. Så hvis du har et frit valgfag og er lidt interesseret i fysik, men ikke ved så meget på forhånd er det et rigtig godt kursus. Jeg var også glad for Earth and Planetary Inference, mest fordi det var det kursus jeg havde der var mest relevant i forhold til min uddannelse. Igen var professoren meget dygtig, men der var meget arbejde i det. Vælg kun dette kursus hvis du har lidt erfaring med Matlab eller Python, og er klar på ugentlige afleveringer. Det var helt sikkert det kursus jeg fik allermest ud af, men også det mest tidskrævende.
unexpected_costs: Ingen, andet end at jeg havde problemer med flyselvskabet da jeg skulle derover, så blev nødt til at købe flybillet to gange.
cost_comparison: Nogle madprodukter er lidt dyrere end i Danmark, men for det meste er det det samme hvis ikke lidt billigere. Kaffe og cafebesøg er billigere end i Danmark;) Jeg endte med at købe en cykel i starten af semesteret, hvilket betalte sig så jeg ikke behøvede at køre med offentlig transport medmindre jeg skulle noget ekstraordinært. Dog vil jeg anbefale at man bare lejer cykler igennem BIXI når man er der (det er billigt og meget convenient).
activities_available: Man kan billigt melde sig til deres B2 gym og igennem McGill Recreation kan man gå til mange forskellige sport sammen med andre studerende. De har også enkelte endags-ture. Der er også mange andre klubber på skolen, som McGill Outdoor Club (hvor man også kan leje billigt outdoor udstyr), og forskellige madklubber osv. Der er også fester på skolen i løbet af semesteret, som også er meget grineren. Svømmehallen på skolen er gratis at benytte, men tidspunkterne den er åben er lidt skæve nogle gange. Så tjek lige op på det inden du tager afsted:)
activities_recommended: Meld dig til noget sport igennem McGill Recreation!
weekend_recommendations: Der er mange smukke områder at gå rundt i, og nabolagene er ret forskellige fra hinanden. Så gå eller cykel en tur rundt i områderne. Kan også anbefale at se de typiske turist ting (F1 banen, Notre Dame kirke, den gamle bydel, OL-stadium, Atwater Market) men særligt parken Mont Royal er smuk. I sommerhalvåret er der Tam Tams om søndagen og om vinteren kan man skøjte og kælk deroppe. Det er også bare en smuk park og udsigt. I ferier og forlængede weekender lejede jeg bil og besøgte Quebec City (meget smuk, særligt til jul!), Ottawa og Kingston. Man kan også tage tog eller bus hvis det er! Jeg synes særligt Quebec City og Ottawa er besøg værd. Jeg var også forbi Toronto, hvis man har tid kan det også være sjovt at se. I efterårsferien fløj jeg til Calgary og var på tur i bjergene Canadian Rockies (her ligger Banff National Park). Det er det smukkeste natur jeg nogensinde har set, så selvom det er langt væk fra Montreal kan jeg virkelig anbefale at tage afsted hvis man har muligheden (Det var dog ret dyrt)
culture_adjustment: Nemt, canadierne lever op til deres ry om at være søde og imødekommende.
socializing_tips: Jeg oplevede at nogle studerende trak sig lidt når de hørte at man var udvekslingsstuderende, så vær lidt klar på måske mest at snakke med andre udvekslingsstuderende. Men canadierne er også super søde, og man kan sagtens lære dem at kende hvis man dukker op til sociale ting på skolen eller tager initiativ til at læse sammen med sine medstuderende.
cultural_challenges: Jeg kan slet ikke snakke fransk, og det kom bag på mig hvor meget de taler fransk i Quebec. Man mødte en gang i mellem nogen der ikke kunne engelsk, men det var ikke en stor udfordring. Alt på skolen foregår på engelsk, så man kan sagtens tage afsted selvom man ikke taler fransk.
culture_appreciated: Hvor imødekommende canadierne er.
top3_advice: 1) Prøv at se om du kan bo med roomies. Om det er lokale eller andre udvekslingsstuderende, så tror jeg det er meget givende at bo med andre. 2) Duk op til tingene på skolen! Både undervisning og de sociale arrangementer. 3) Vejret kommer til at variere meget i løbet af semesteret, så pak både sommer og vintertøj.
other_useful_info: Ansøg om RamQ hvis du kan (quebec sygeforsikring), for så kan du slippe for at betale forsikring igennem McGill.
most_rewarding: De venner jeg har fået på udveksling:) Jeg er også vokset meget personligt, når man står helt på egene ben i et fremmed land.
greatest_challenge: Det kan godt være svært at være så langt hjemmefra når der sker store ting derhjemme. Så jeg fik nogle gange lidt fomo og lidt hjemve. Men det hjalp at snakke med mine venner i Montreal om det.

arrival_assistance: They assisted me in person!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We had to sign up online.

weekend_recommendations: Live like a local!

socializing_tips: Sign up for a sports club.

crucial_aspects: As a french-speaking person I was looking to study abroad far away (from europe) in a french-speaking city as Montreal. As McGill is the biggest university i didn't hesitate much.
info_ease: It can be overwhleming with all the information in the beginning because there is different website you need to see but they assist you well.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to leave Europe (going to another continent), I wanted to go to an English-speaking country (to perfect my English). And I felt like that America gets all attention, so I wanted to see what Canada is like. Also because this country has such a good reputation throughout the world.
overall_comments: It was simply fantastic, even though there was a lockdown in Ontario the 1st month of my exchange. But from mid-February and to the end of the exchange everything was just amazing.
info_ease: The process of going on exchange is extensive, long and thorough. Especially catalyzed by covid. Once you are enrolled in McMaster, there is still amounts of bureaucracy to do. But the good thing, though, is that the people from the university are very helpful, quick-responding on mail and seem to sincerely wanting to help you.
arrival_assistance: Not really anything. You get a mail and access-link to their platform 'Mosaic' that can be said to correspond to KUnet. And then you have 'Avenue2learn' that corresponds to Absalon. I found it pretty easy to navigate around. Simplistic design with all the needed information and courses etc easily accessible. It can be convient to check out this before arriving though, so that you're familiar with the portals already.
arrival_comments: I think this was pretty sufficient. And I think in circumstances without covid dominating every bureaucratic procedure, then the process of getting settled into McMaster should not be too bad actually.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was simply fantastic, even though there was a lockdown in Ontario the 1st month of my exchange. But from mid-February and to the end of the exchange everything was just amazing.
registration_process: There is one major obstacle here. To be approved into the courses you want to pick at McMaster, you have to provide some sort of proof that you meet their prerequisites (i.e., certain courses to be passed to enroll in other courses). So basically you have to check course requirements in course outlines from McMaster (this information is easily accessible though), and then send a mail to the course-responsible at McMaster providing proof that you fulfill the requirements, so they will allow you to enroll in the courses you want in their portal. Here it is a good idea to be proactive and get this done not too late so that you make sure the courses are not full before you are able to enroll. (... but no matter what there should be plenty of courses available even until course enrollment deadline.
registration_help: McMaster course platform is decent. And the coordinators were responding quickly, so there were no issues here.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted. :) They even helped me with one of them that was actually full
registration_advice: As aforementioned it can be beneficial to start this process early on. Helps relieving the stress getting as much stuff done as early possible.
academics_comments: It was simply fantastic, even though there was a lockdown in Ontario the 1st month of my exchange. But from mid-February and to the end of the exchange everything was just amazing.
course_level: A took a POLSCI course that was significantly easier than all the ECON-courses I've had back in CPH. Economics of Labour Market Issues was also significantly easier than what you would expect at CPH. These two course were Level 2 The level 3 courses Economic Development and Game Theory were harder.
teaching_comparison: Here is midterms through all semester. This implies you have to study all semester as these tests have a significant impact on your grade. They counted up to 30% for me. But if you study for these and do relatively well you end up having not too much pressure regarding the final exams. You have more time, the questions are easier (can be just describing economic terminology) than what is the case in CPH, so I've tried leaving more than 1hr early in these tests and still be getting good grades.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Game Theory Economic Development Economics of Labor-Market Issues Globalization and the State
recommended_courses: Game Theory corresponds to Mikro III at KU so if you want to get this one done just having to pass, then pick it here. Economic Development was more challenging and similar to the courses at KU. If you do not want academical challenges then you should pick as many level 2 courses as possible. My intention of going to Canada was for traveling and experiences and not really academically purposes, so I did not care about getting academically challenged.
unexpected_costs: Food is surprisingly expensive in Canada. And also the quality is not good (in my opinion!). Unhealthy food is cheap, good food expensive. Traveling inside Canada is also expensive. If you check airlines like Swoop, Flair, and Westjet you can get some pretty cheap tickets to Montreal, Vancouver etc. Public transport outside big cities is non-existent!
cost_comparison: I did not buy any of the books... Through McMaster you get free access to the bus system in Hamilton, which is decent, and this saves a lot of money.
activities_available: I did a trip with the outdoor club to a nationalpark 4hrs north of Toronto. This was expensive but such a fantastic experience and a nice opportunity to talk to some Canadian people.
activities_recommended: Try to join some stuff if you are on exchange with the intention of meeting new people. This is by far the best approach. I enjoyed it very much and if you can manage to get some relations in the start of the exchange this will potentially give you the possibility to have so incredibly much fun.
weekend_recommendations: Hangout in Hamilton. Plenty of places, go to Toronto. Travel around Canada. Even America is easily accessible. Take advantage of the fact that you are in North America, living here! Do all the stuff that you are not able to do at home :-) Because 4 months is actually a short time and you will have to go back to DK quicker than you realise. And then you do not want to regret that you said no to opportunities over in Canada!
culture_adjustment: No problems here. You can easily sense that Canada and Denmark are both some of the very best countries in the world. It is not hard at all acclimatizing.
socializing_tips: Go to social clubs, say yes to stuff, be open to hangout. Try to not only sticking to hanging out with the other Danish people.
cultural_challenges: Canadians do not really go out to the bars for parties. Bars close at 1am in weekends already and lots of clubs close at 2am. So instead they do homeparties in their 'frat-houses' so social life here depends a lot of having a network through which you are invited to parties. Here I prefer Denmark where people go out for the fun stuff and in evenings.
culture_appreciated: It is true that Canadians are kind. (sometimes even a bit too much, haha...) Everything is in order in this country. You have such close access to Toronto, so go and see NHL, NBA, MLB!
top3_advice: 1. Exchange is expensive. That is the way it is. There is no way around! Everyone spends more than they intend to. But the day you are going back to Cph you would not give away any of these memories you create for a bunch of money. I guarantee that! 2. Be open-minded. Talk to other people! Not only other Danes. (Because you can do that at home all the time...) You have such interesting conversations and you get sooo much perspective 3. Take advantage of the fact your grades don't matter. It does not matter if you get A+ or D-. The only person it matters for is yourself. So this is a great opportunity to relax a bit regarding school and have fun instead, especially as you do not have a job in Canada as well.
other_useful_info: Send mails to people from McMaster and KU if you have doubts about anything. They are helpful And the first month abroad can feel a bit weird because it is so new. But as the first month passes by you get used to it. It is a pretty cool feeling to realize that you are able to cope on your own. You really develop personally in a way you would not be able to back home at a regular semester in Copenhagen.
most_rewarding: Everything. It is not possible to point out a single thing. Though all the relations you create are such blessings.
greatest_challenge: To balance travel, fun, parties, school properly. You want to do everything, but you only have 24 hours in a day ;-) But do not be sad about what you did not do and rather appreciate what you have done.
other_comments: Make up your mind regarding what you ambition of this exchange is. I knew I was here for the North American experience, the fun and traveling. I even designed my schedule such that I was free every Friday. And I do not regret it the least!
