crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere outside of Europe and I had never been to Canada before. I didn't necessarily have any specific criteria, but I applied to different places in countries I wanted to visit/ live in.
info_ease: It was fairly easy, however, the application process beforehand is quite extensive and difficult to navigate.
arrival_assistance: There were multiple people to contact if you have questions and the respond time is fairly quick.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: When you apply to the university, after having been submitted an exchange spot, you will be electing courses from the old course catalog. You need to be aware that you have to re-elect courses during the summer from the new catalog, any (in my case) many of the courses were not available for the semester I was there. When you do find course you would like, you will be asked to send a list of multiple courses to your academic advisor before a certain deadline, where you'll get some of them approved. You then need to register for the courses during a certain time period, where you can also choose a course schedule - I really recommend trying to plan your schedule so you can have some days off - especially Friday, it makes it easier to go on trips with others during a longer weekend.
registration_help: There are multiple contact options available, but I would say it was still a pretty confusing process overall.
registration_success: I ended up with most courses that i wanted, however - as I described - some courses you initially want might not be available for the fall term, and even if you get several courses approved by your academic advisor, some may be already full, reserved to specific students or not available for exchange students. And, as I described previously, it is possible to change your courses again after the term has begun.
registration_advice: Take time to look at the courses and select a couple - and some back ups. Register for a couple courses that you think might be a little easier for you to follow, and be prepared to maybe not get every course you want and even if you do, it might not be what you thought, but still okay.
course_level: It is recommended that BA exchange students take level 3 courses. However, me and many of the others had courses on 1,2,3,4, level, which was not a problem.
teaching_comparison: I would say that the teaching style mostly differ from UCPH. You might be able to have courses approved for 7,5 ECTS points and if you can, I would recommend to do that so you can have 4 courses. Otherwise, you will have 5 courses in total during the semester, and there is a heavy workload - especially if you're in social sciences or humanities. I had around 4 written assignments per week, which put me under a lot of pressure - however, what's important to remember (and that i realized a little late) is that the academic level is different to the assignments you do on UCPH - it is a lot more direct and it is not expected that you do a lot of analyzing and research yourself - and if you need to, it is pretty easily done. You do, however, learn to just write and move on to the next thing, so that process in itself is a great quality. I would definetly also recommend that you consider taking some courses on different levels, and even taking some courses that you think may be a little easier for you to follow along in, because you will have a lot of work to do either way. You're professors are only doing lectures, the classes are held by Teaching Assistants (TA's), which themselves are either Master or Ph.D. students at the university. The classes (as I experienced), where mostly recapping what was said in lecture. However, they do take attendance at every class, and you need to be aware that attendance (as well as assignments, participation, quizzes, midterms and exams) holds different percentages of your final grade. You could, in a way, compare the system a bit more to high school in Denmark. There is around a weeks period in the beginning of the term, where you can change courses if you need to. However the deadline for this might be placed so you won't have had all of your courses, so it is a bit of a strange proces, but doable.
courses_enrolled: CMST3HC3 --> History of Communication SOCIOL2WW3 --> Media and Power PEACJUST2XX3 --> Social and Structural Determinants of Health PHILOS2G03 --> Social and Political Issues POLSCI 1AA3 --> Government, Politics, and Power
recommended_courses: There are no specific course I believe are recommendable - it all depends on your interests and if you want to try some different subjects. I had no subjects related to my original BA back home, which obviously made keeping up a bit harder, but I though it was interesting to try different subjects in other fields of study.
unexpected_costs: Trips, having to buy basic necessities for housing, souvenirs.
cost_comparison: Books, is not per month, but how much in total i spent on the books I needed to buy for my courses and they were fairly expensive. I lived on campus, where the expenses are payed all at once - including the payment for your mealcard, so that is the amount I've put.
activities_available: There are several events for international and exhange students. Some exchange students joined some of the sports teams. I recommend looking into the different events, and attending many of them - this is where you'll meet most people.
activities_recommended: I would definetly recommend going on the MOOSE Exchange trip, that Mac Outdoor Club plans - this is where I met most people I hung out with for the rest of the exchange. It is a great way to bond with others when you first arrive in Canada. Also, the club offers multiple other trips and events during the semester, and I really recommend going on those. Me and a couple of my friends joined the Algonquin Canoe trip, which was great, and really beautiful - really a great opportunity to see some more of Canadian nature.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend exploring the city a bit - I never really did, and I did not have a great experience of the city. Otherwise, I actually mostly recommend going to sportsgames in Toronto, or going on trips to Montreal, Ottawa, or other bigger cities in the province. We were a couple of students that planned a trip during the reading week, where we went to western Canada, and roadtripped around Vancouver, Banff, Jasper, Whistler and other absolutely beautiful places - I absolutely recommend doing this.
culture_adjustment: It was easy. There are not big cultural differences, maybe other than saying thank you to the bus driver when leaving the bus, the school system and the general attitude towards talking to strangers - people are a lot more open to talk to others than they are in Denmark.
socializing_tips: There are not really any activities that bonds you with local students - some might be on some of the trips (if you go on those), so the only possibility you might have is in your classes. But mostly you'll hang out with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: It was interesting to experiences a more American culture, but there weren't any big differences, so I'm not sure.
top3_advice: Be ready to talk to a lot of new people, be open and try to have the mentality of not saying no to anything, and remember that it is also okay to be overwhelmed (because you will be) and to stay home when you don't feel like going out or socializing.
other_useful_info: Basically everyone is there to meet new people and have new experiences, talk to all the people you want and you'll eventually figure out who you naturally hang out with more, but don't exclude people from the beginning.
most_rewarding: The people I've met and the memories I have made, both on trips and on fun nights on and off campus.
greatest_challenge: The school work load.
other_comments: Hamilton is not really a great place.. There are a lot of drug addicts and homeless people and it is overall a boring city, so the people you are with are important to your general experience. Also, if you're only there for one semester, do not apply for a study visa - you do not need one, and it takes a long time to do.

crucial_aspects: I always knew I wanted to go on an exchange, hopefully outside of Europe. I dreamed about going to Australia, New Zealand or Canada and ended up choosing Canada because it looks amazing in pictures and the people should be some of the kindest - so I really wanted to experience that!
overall_comments: McMaster University is located in Hamilton, and Hamilton is not that interesting at all... Besides Hamilton, the campus of McMaster University is full of life and so is the lovely small town, Westdale, just nearby. I spend all my time with my friends on campus and in Westdale at the local bar or one of the cafes. And the time spent with them either at the campus, in Westdale or travelling around Canada makes my overall study abroad experience almost perfect - the only downside for me is the city of Hamilton.
info_ease: It's a long process to go on exchange, no matter where you have to go! You will have to do some things more than twice and you will be tempted to give up - but please don't. Eventually, everything will work out fine, because most people really want to help exchange students. Upon arrival, it can be tricky tho. I used the fact sheet from the University of Copenhagen a lot to see what I had to do and when. And by the help of the Mobility Online system, everything is quite easy to follow. But information such as courses, where to stay in Canada, visa and so on, was quite tricky. It was possible to attend some summer webinars about visas and the city of Hamilton and so on, which I found very useful but it wasn't really proclaimed anywhere (as far as I can remember), but if you surf around on the website of the university for long enough - then you will eventually end up with something useful. Besides this, we got several emails from the university with different deadlines and links to different sites that might be good to know - and they mentioned an app (iCent), which was also quite informative in some ways. Look for 'International Student Services' and 'Mac incoming'
arrival_assistance: I attended the so-called MOOSE trip right before the semester began. It is a tour for international- and exchange students organized by the McMaster Outdoor club (highly recommended to keep an eye out on their trips!). On this tour, I met a lot of new international and exchange students and some of the students from McMaster University, who helped answer a lot of questions about everything (mostly non-academical stuff). Besides this trip, the international student services held an event where they went through some of the more practical stuff about the courses (how much you need to pass a course), the university clubs, insurance, safety and so on.
arrival_comments: The only thing is, that you might have to be persistent and send multiple emails to get ahold of the right person to answer your question.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: McMaster University is located in Hamilton, and Hamilton is not that interesting at all... Besides Hamilton, the campus of McMaster University is full of life and so is the lovely small town, Westdale, just nearby. I spend all my time with my friends on campus and in Westdale at the local bar or one of the cafes. And the time spent with them either at the campus, in Westdale or travelling around Canada makes my overall study abroad experience almost perfect - the only downside for me is the city of Hamilton.
registration_process: To be registered at McMaster University was not that difficult. After I send the application through KU and it got approved there was some information from ucphabroad at KU. After that, I had to wait for a while before I got an email from the host institution. Within this email, there was a link to another portal (just like Mobility Online), where I had to do the application at McMaster University. After a little while, this also got approved and then I was registered at the host institution. According to the courses, it was a confusing process. Because I was going during Fall 2022, the only course catalogue available at the time we had to request the courses we wanted was from Fall 2021, so some courses might have been removed or changed or even added by the time we were gonna be at campus. Finding courses that sounded interesting took a very long time and I looked through a lot of course descriptions (4-5 lines about the course content). When I had requested the 8 courses that were mandatory to request, time went by and then I got an email from the Science department with some information about whom to contact regarding course approvals. It is necessary to get the courses approved by the academic advisor of your faculty before you can enroll in them (which was a whole process alone). After final enrollment in the courses you are ready to begin the studies at McMaster University - but only a week or so, after the beginning of the term, the 'add-and-drop' period ends, which makes the first period of time really stressful if you are not satisfied with the courses you have chosen before you came. So pro tip: for your own sake, get a lot of courses approved by the University of Copenhagen, before you go and make sure to reach out to your academic advisor at McMaster as soon as you know, that you wanna switch to a new course.
registration_help: You get an email with information about your academic advisor which is very helpful in the whole course registration process. Besides that Google; "McMaster University courses" --> "Programs, Future Students" is where I found most of the things I needed to know.
registration_success: Because we had to look at an outdated course catalogue, two of my courses were not available by the time I attended McMaster University. But in the end, I ended up with four useful courses - some better than others. I would have preferred to change one of my courses, but unfortunately, that wasn't a possibility in combination with the other three courses.
registration_advice: Be patient in the registration process and begin to look at courses as soon as possible so you have an idea of a plan B or plan C if you end up in that situation. And send as many emails with questions to your academic advisor as you feel like - they are there to help and it can be really tricky to figure out their system, so take all the help you can!
academics_comments: McMaster University is located in Hamilton, and Hamilton is not that interesting at all... Besides Hamilton, the campus of McMaster University is full of life and so is the lovely small town, Westdale, just nearby. I spend all my time with my friends on campus and in Westdale at the local bar or one of the cafes. And the time spent with them either at the campus, in Westdale or travelling around Canada makes my overall study abroad experience almost perfect - the only downside for me is the city of Hamilton.
course_level: All four courses I had was level 3 courses, which means that the academic level is supposed to be around the level of our courses at this time in our BA. One of my courses was an introductory course, which was seen at the academic level. It was way easier and less technical to follow this course compared to the other three. Even tho the academic level was lower, I still learned a lot and I really liked the professor and the TA of this course.
teaching_comparison: The biggest difference is the midterms which are minor exams that test you on the stuff you have been learning up until this point (around half the course). In some of the courses, there are also a few assignments and/or presentations (either individually or in groups). Altogether, the presence of midterms, the smaller assignments, presentations and quizzes during the courses, meant that you have to keep up a bit more during the term since the midterms counted 25-35% of your final grade, but also that the final exam wasn't all-or-nothing. Overall, the academic level was lower than here in Denmark - they don't expect equally as much of you - but there are more "tests" along the way, but that just means that you can pass a lot of the course before the final exam and then you don't have to study for two weeks before the final exam to pass the course.
courses_enrolled: HTHSCI 3K03 - Principles of Virology (elective) LIFESCI 3G03 - Introduction to Epidemiology (elective) LIFESCI 3BB3 - Neurobiology of Disease (limited elective) MOLBIOL 3O03 - Microbial Genetics (limited elective)
recommended_courses: I personally liked the Epidemiology course because it's something different from what you can get back here in Denmark. It wasn't a challenging course at all which meant that I had time to do other things as well (win-win). Principles of Virology was great because of the professor (Dr. Caitlin E. Mullarkey Dphil). Her enthusiasm for the subject and her knowledge made it all way more interesting than I think I would have found it otherwise. Neurobiology of Disease was a great course if you like to get invested in the local community. The professor in this course made it a part of the course to do a 'community engagement group project' on one of three different subjects presented in class - overall a really great idea and a lovely way to get connected with other students, but if you get together with other international- or exchange students it might be a bit difficult to engage yourself fully (which was the case for me). And personally, I regretted every moment of Microbial genetics because I didn't find it interesting - but once again the professor here was a really enthusiastic young woman who loved to teach with made it durable.
unexpected_costs: Mobile deals were more expensive than I anticipated and so was meat - but overall is Canada quite expensive, so everything was pricy.
cost_comparison: It is recommendable to spend a day or two to go on a bigger shopping trip at Walmart (which will be more expensive than you anticipate), but also worth it. You can get home with pots and pans, wardrobes, pyjamas and lots of food and snacks. When travelling around Canada, I found that hostels were cheaper than I expected. And otherwise my "other fees" includes trips with McOutdoor club and a self-planned trip to the Rookie Mountains and so on.
activities_available: There were all kinds of non-academic opportunities. Go to the 'club fair' at the beginning of the term to see what kinds of clubs McMaster University has to offer. There is something for everyone! And if you don't want to join anything that's also completely fine. Just keep your eyes and ears open and then you will find something that sounds fun.
activities_recommended: Together with other international and exchange students we created a team and joined the Intramurals soccer tournament and played a match every once a week for a month or so - that was one of the best decisions I made! Besides the athletic aspect McOutdoor was amazing. I joined both the MOOSE trip and the trip to Algonquin park and both of them are worth paying for (even tho they are expensive) - so if you like nature, canoeing, and getting to know your friends while freezing in a tent or complaining over the wind while canoeing then go go go! Otherwise attending dinners for international students is also recommendable.
weekend_recommendations: I would definitely recommend you to go to Montreal on a weekend trip and go to 'The Big West' (the Rookie Mountains) around Vancouver and the national parks Banff, Jasper and Whistler when going to Canada!
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy to adjust to the local culture of Canada. Everyone is super sweet, helpful and lovely. And after the MOOSE trip, the likelihood of you getting some new friends, that might even be danish, is pretty big - and these are gonna be your safety blanket for the first couple of weeks when everything is still new.
socializing_tips: I personally socialized with local students between classes when I discovered that there were a few people that I had more than one course with. Otherwise, attend the stadium on game day, sit around campus or just by sitting at cafes in Westdale. If you want to socialize with local students, there are a lot of opportunities.
cultural_challenges: The main cultural difference was that the Canadian people are very polite and even a stranger on the bus will compliment your shoes if they like them. Besides this, they say thank you when they leave the bus, which was kinda weird at the beginning. And then you have to be aware of the tipping culture - you tip everyone, everywhere, always..
culture_appreciated: The politeness and helpfulness of the Candian people.
top3_advice: Travel to Canada before the beginning of the semester to search for accommodation, if you want to live off-campus! Go on the MOOSE trip, which is also before the semester begins. This is an expensive trip and things could be better, but this is a great way to get to know other people who are gonna be there for the next 4-12 months as well. You will not regret going when you look back and see that the friendships made on that trip are the ones you enjoyed for the whole semester. Be sure to explore other parts of Canada as well and then just enjoy a beer or two with your people at the local bar (Snooty Fox) whenever the time is there.
other_useful_info: Be aware that the courses you are choosing from are from an old catalogue so make sure you have a long list of courses to choose from and get them all pre-approved from KU before you go, so you are ready to change your course within the limited add-and-drop period - the courses have to be approved by the host institution as well, so if you have to wait for approval from KU and then from McMaster, you are possibly not gonna make it in time before the deadline. Look at places you wanna go in Hamilton, Ontario or Canada in general before you go, so you can get together with some friends quite early and try to plan different trips.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was definitely the self-planned roadtrip with 6 friends around 'The Big West' of Canada - amazing nature and a lovely way to spend time with your friends. Besides that, it was all the small things like meeting up with friends between classes, sitting at the campus the whole day because of the different schedules we all had and then ending up going to Phoenix (a restaurant on campus) to eat and grab a beer or two or even attend the trivia night every Tuesday. Going to a party at some of the other exchange students' houses was also a huge part of the unforgettable exchange period I had.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge for me was definitely finding a place to live off-campus. It took time, a lot of effort and disappointments and I could have never imagined that I ended up in the situation I did. It had its pros and cons but overall I got lucky. And you will need a bit of luck and a lot of hard work to find the "perfect place" to stay when going on exchange.
other_comments: I am truly grateful for the opportunity to go on exchange and I would do it again in a heartbeat if it was possible. So even tho it can seem scary and like a lot of hard work (because it is), then it is all worth it when you get back home, so go go go!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an English speaking country to improve my English, and I have visited Canada in the past and loved it, so I wanted to have the opportunity to see even more of Canada this time.
info_ease: Fairly easy. We were a lot of students from KU, so we helped each other finding information.
arrival_assistance: I don't remember receiving any assistance, but I didn't feel that it was necessary.
arrival_comments: The university was very good if you needed help. I was in contact with my academic advisor in the beginning, as I needed help with enrolling in some of my courses, and that all worked very well.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I think we had to go to the university and grab a student card and had some introduction day as well where they told all things that were important to know.
registration_help: Your academic advisor, the administration, other students and such.
registration_success: Very succesful, I got the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Just read the mails that they send, it explains most that you need to know in the process.
course_level: I took courses with 2nd year and 3rd year economics students. If I wanted to be challenged more I should probably had chosen 3rd and 4th year courses. You can see on the course code what year it is meant for.

Also there are midterms, and a lot more test, such that in the end, the final exam only counts for e.g. 30% of the grade. It depends on the course, but in a lot of the courses we had, the final exams that did not count for a lot.
courses_enrolled: Monetary Economics, Public policy toward business, International Trade, Analysis of Economic data.
recommended_courses: Monetary Economics was very very good. The professor was very good at uploading information about the course, you could see it online or in person, she was very thorough and the material that was covered was very interesting for me.
unexpected_costs: I had read on this site before I left for exchange, so all the cost that I encountered were cost I was somewhat aware of.
cost_comparison: Phone bill, alcohol, grocery shopping and such were more expensive. Eating out was cheaper than in Copenhagen, but you always had to add a tip and tax to the bill on top of the food, so in total just a bit cheaper.
activities_available: There were all kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students, almost everything that you could imagine, so they were very good in that department.
activities_recommended: Squash was fun. There also very a lot of trips to different parks and stuff, that was fun.
weekend_recommendations: Algonquin park was amazing! Not far from Hamilton. We rented a car and drove to that a weekend, very fun. Do it in late summer/fall where the leaves turn red, very beautiful. Other than that Montreal was nice, very european. Banff and Jasper in Alberta was amazing, we rented a car and drove through the Rocky Mountains. Vancouver is also nice. In general, very nice to go travelling in Canada, but get an international driving license, and rent a car, it gives a lot of freedom when travelling. Also because the trains and busses are not working as well as in Denmark.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy, Canadians are really friendly.
socializing_tips: Attend the events that the university hosts.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: I don't know.
top3_advice: It costs more than you think, go travel a lot, and make sure to attend the events in the beginning an get to know other students (there is a trip in the beginning of the semester called MOOSE that is very good for getting to know a lot of other peers).
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Travelling around, meeting a lot of other students from different countries.

crucial_aspects: I did not have a lot of specific requests considering the destination, but I found that McMaster had a lot of interesting elective courses that the University of Copenhagen doesn't offer. I also thought that Canada was an interesting destination to explore so this was a plus for me.
overall_comments: Hamilton is not the most charming city in Canada. It is close to Toronto, which made it easy to go on day trips and to travel around in Canada, but Hamilton city itself does not have a lot to offer. McMaster University has a very big campus, with a lot of activities going on all the time, which was fun to experience.
info_ease: I found that McMaster had a lot of information and considering that it is a very big University I found that it worked pretty well. The first orientation however was a lot of practical information, and it needed more activities where we got to interact with the other exchange students.
arrival_assistance: I had a correspondence with an academic advisor from McMaster, which worked well. However I struggled with gaining access to a mandatory course, which was quite stressful and I found that this issue could have been solved very quickly (because it seemed like it was only a technical issue that prevented me from taking the course)
arrival_comments: McMaster has something called student success center, where most of the practical information can be found. They even have a medical practice on campus (which is included in the health insurance that is mandatory).
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Hamilton is not the most charming city in Canada. It is close to Toronto, which made it easy to go on day trips and to travel around in Canada, but Hamilton city itself does not have a lot to offer. McMaster University has a very big campus, with a lot of activities going on all the time, which was fun to experience.
registration_process: I first had to submit my prerequisites for the courses that I was planning on taking at McMaster. These had to be approved before I was allowed to enroll in any courses. The system for selecting courses worked quite well, because you had an opportunity to see all of the possible schedules and select the ones that were most convenient for you. The first week of school is meant for you to try out different courses and make your final selection, but the courses gets filled up so make sure that you enroll in the ones you are most interested in, because you have a lot of time to drop the courses again.
registration_help: I mostly contacted my academic advisor whenever I had issues with the courses.
registration_success: I managed to get the courses I wanted, even after some issues with the enrollment in one of my mandatory courses.
registration_advice: When I had an issue with one of my courses I scheduled a meeting with my academic advisor and she was able to fix it - so seek all of the help that you need, and try to not stress too much about it.
academics_comments: Hamilton is not the most charming city in Canada. It is close to Toronto, which made it easy to go on day trips and to travel around in Canada, but Hamilton city itself does not have a lot to offer. McMaster University has a very big campus, with a lot of activities going on all the time, which was fun to experience.
course_level: The academic level at McMaster is quite low compared to KU and they use a lot of multiple choice exams.
teaching_comparison: Some of the courses had tutorials, but most of my courses were only had lectures. I found that people were very open, so even if a course did not have a tutorial, there was still an opportunity to work with other students in the courses that only had lectures.
courses_enrolled: HLTHAGE 1CC3: Introduction to Mental Health and Illness ANTHROP 1AB3:Introduction to Anthropology: Race, Religion, and Social Justice PSYCH 2AP3: Abnormal Psychology: Fundamentals and Major Disorders GENDRST 2AA3: Feminist Thought
recommended_courses: HLTHAGE 1CC3: Introduction to Mental Health and Illness - I took this course because I needed to to cover "klinisk psykologi" at KU. It turned out to be a really good course, because I found that the professor is very good and he has a quite critical approach to the subject of mental health which I thought was interesting. This course focuses on writing skills rather than memorizing multiple choice questions - but it is a first-year course, so the requirements are not very strict for these compared to KU. ANTHROP 1AB3:Introduction to Anthropology: Race, Religion, and Social Justice - This was one of my electives and I was really happy about this course as well. It is also a first-year course so in the beginning there was a lot of basic stuff that I found to be a bit tiresome, but once the introductory part was over I really enjoyed the perspectives that this course gave me. The instructor is really good and I like the fact that he also empathizes the fact that memorizing small details does not make sense - but gaining an overall understanding of the course is much more important. PSYCH 2AP3: Abnormal Psychology: Fundamentals and Major Disorders - I also had to take this course to cover the other part of "klinisk". This course was a disappointments, because it consisted of memorizing a lot of information to be tested on 3 multiple choice exams in total. It had a very narrow-minded approach to the subject of mental health, so I can only recommend taking this course if it's absolutely necessary (which it might be if you're a psychology student, because KU was really strict with approving my courses for klinisk) GENDRST 2AA3: Feminist Thought - This course was an elective and I really enjoyed it. Throughout the semester I had to write journal entries about the course content which made me engage with the material in another way than I otherwise would have. I also had to so a creative assignment and write a feminist manifest which I found to be a really nice experience (to get to submit assignments that are different from what I'm normally used to). I also think that this course had a big impact on the way I see the world, so it had a personal impact for me as well. The professor in this course is very good as well, so if you're interested in learning more about feminism I can really recommend this course!
unexpected_costs: It was mandatory to pay for health insurance through the university.
cost_comparison: The phone subscription in Canada was more expensive than I expected (I used Freedom mobile and had one of their cheapest subscriptions with 10 GB per month - this only worked in Ontario and I even experienced that when I travelled inside Ontario, this was quite unreliable still). There are some food items that are more expensive compared to Denmark (meat, cheese and some vegetables) - however other food items are cheaper (such as eggs and other kinds of vegetables), so it evens out. It is quite expensive to travel inside Canada, and I did a lot of small trips, which is why I put approximately 5000 DKK for other fees (this is hostel/airbnb, transport and food). I spent more money on having dinner at restaurants than I usually do at home, but this is because prices are cheaper for this in Canada (this can be done for about 85-140 DKK for a whole meal + water is free everywhere you eat out) A plus was that fact that buses in Hamilton were free if you're a student.
activities_available: There are so many clubs available for everything - you can probably find a list of the one currently available if you search for it, but otherwise they had 2 days where all of the clubs came to promote themselves where you could join if you were interested.
activities_recommended: McMaster has an outdoor club which organises trips throughout the semester - I joined a canoe trip to Algonquin park and I can really recommend doing this! It's a nice way to mingle with other students, both exchange and canadian students, and if you're there during the fall terms, the autumn colors are so beautiful at this time.
weekend_recommendations: I took weekend trips to Quebec, New York, Bruce Peninsula park and Vancouver during the semester and I found that this was totally manageable because the academic level was not very overwhelming. Also taking day trips to Toronto from Hamilton with the go bus is a nice idea. I also travelled before my semester started and I can recommend visiting Ottawa and Montreal .
culture_adjustment: This was quite easy since Canadians are very welcoming in general.
socializing_tips: Don't be afraid to approach people at lectures, most people are very friendly and don't find it odd. Also, join some clubs to get to know the locals
cultural_challenges: They use cars for everything, so sometimes this limited the opportunities to travel different places.
culture_appreciated: Canadians are so friendly and easy to approach and this made me appreciate Canada even more.
top3_advice: Don't be afraid to socialize with people - both other exchange students and locals. Make sure to check out all of the courses that McMaster offers, because they have so many unique and special courses that I don't think you'll be able to try out (as electives) back home. Go on some of the outdoor trips!
other_useful_info: The fall semester ends in december (the latest exams are held on the 22), so this gives a good opportunity to travel a bit before going back to DK (I went to Mexico for 3 weeks after my final exams).
most_rewarding: Getting to travel and experience a lot of things that I wouldn't otherwise would do during a semester. Also trying out some courses that were very different from what I normally would study was very rewarding.
greatest_challenge: I was quite stressed when I arrived because my courses did not seem to work out, so it was a bit of a rough start having to communicate both with McMaster and KU trying to figure it out.
other_comments: I was on exchange during my 5. semester, so I tried to find courses that corresponded with "klinisk psykologi", "psykiatri" and "videnskabsteori og forskningsdesign". In line with the challenge of getting my courses to work out, I found that I had very limited options when I tried to get my courses to approved from KU - I ended up only having two options for courses that KU would approve as "klinisk" (1 course at McMaster correlates with 7,5 ects), which meant that I really had to make sure to get these courses. I was also not able to take "psykiatri "(so I ended up being enrolled in the KU course during the semester and taking the re-exam once I got back) and furthermore I could not get approval for any courses corresponding to "videnskabsteori og forskningsdesign" which is why I ended up using my electives during the exchange.

crucial_aspects: First, I wanted to go as far away as possible to a destination that I would like to visit for the culture, the sights and the nature, but was difficult to visit due to the distance and price. Secondly, I wanted to go to an English-speaking country in order to practice my own English skills and be able to understand the lecturers most efficiently. A third aspect was that I wanted to go a high ranked university with courses that I find interesting, in order to get the most out of the courses. Especially within neuroscience.
overall_comments: My study abroad experience was really good. Canada is an amazing country; the people are kind, and the nature is extraordinary as well as some of the bigger cities. There was a lot to experience around in Canada, however Hamilton, the city where the university is located is quite boring. There is not much to do in the city except studying so you will have to travel away during weekends and reading week in order to get the most out of the study abroad experience. The study program and social life was good as well. So, after all I was happy to go abroad. However, i would have wished that the city was a bit more interesting with more things to do in the city. I compensated from that from travelling a lot, which was a bit expensive.
info_ease: That was really easy. McMaster provided me with several mails and an app that that explained everything you need to know
arrival_assistance: I got the mails describing what to do. In addition to that there was an introductory meeting explaining all relevant things as well. And the people working at the university was happy to show me around and helping me out. In addition to that we had a whole day where our exchange buddies showed us around campus and answered all our questions.

registration_comments: My study abroad experience was really good. Canada is an amazing country; the people are kind, and the nature is extraordinary as well as some of the bigger cities. There was a lot to experience around in Canada, however Hamilton, the city where the university is located is quite boring. There is not much to do in the city except studying so you will have to travel away during weekends and reading week in order to get the most out of the study abroad experience. The study program and social life was good as well. So, after all I was happy to go abroad. However, i would have wished that the city was a bit more interesting with more things to do in the city. I compensated from that from travelling a lot, which was a bit expensive.
registration_process: The registration process itself was easy. You got a mail with a link to an application to fill out and they you got another mail later with acceptance and a step by step guide for what to do know. However when enrolling in courses, there was some issues. There platform made it easy to see which courses to choose or if any overlapped. But when trying to enroll, it said that you did not meet the prerequisites, since we did not pass any of the McMaster courses required, so I had to text the academic advisor to get approval, so some of the courses was filled up before I was able to enroll.
registration_help: I got several mails informing me what to do. You could also get help by writing to the academic advisor, but she answered a bit slow. I ended up just showing up to a course I wanted and told her to help me register for the course, so I was enrolled the day after.
registration_success: Many of the courses I wanted overlapped, but I ended up having my 1., 2., 3. and 18th priority
registration_advice: Apply for the courses as soon as registration opens. The courses will be available to look at 3 days prior to the day registration opens. You might already look at the courses at that point and write to academic advisor immediately to get confirmation of prerequisites, since it may take a while and courses fill up quickly.

There was a lot to experience around in Canada, however Hamilton, the city where the university is located is quite boring. There is not much to do in the city except studying so you will have to travel away during weekends and reading week in order to get the most out of the study abroad experience. The study program and social life was good as well. So, after all I was happy to go abroad. However, i would have wished that the city was a bit more interesting with more things to do in the city. I compensated from that from travelling a lot, which was a bit expensive.
course_level: The level of the courses was pretty much like the level at University of Copenhagen. However, it was much more easier to receive good grades and the expectations was much more lower than was we are used to. In addition to that, there was no books or articles to read. The syllabus was only what was told during lectures and what appeared on the slides.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching varied a bit compared to UCPH. The lectures were pretty much what we are used to. However, the only thing we did during tutorials were presentations, so we didn't learn to use the knowledge we acquired during lectures. Also, they had some quizzes, assignments and presentations which all was part of our final grade together with participation points and midterms. Despite it sounds like a lot, it was fairly easy to get done in no time and it was nice to already having completed most of the final grade before the final exams. Most exams was already passed before even going to the exam, due to all of the other components. All the exams I had was for 2 hours written exams with a combination of multiple choice and short answer questions.
courses_enrolled: LIFESCI 3BB3 Neurobiology of Disease BIOCHEM 4E03 Gene Regulation in Stem Cells and Development HTHSCI 3K03 Principles of virology MOLBIOL 3O03 Microbial Genetics
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend Principles of Virology. By far the best course in my opinion. The professor was really really good, the topics was really interesting and her way of quizzing and examination was really fair. Instead of a midterm, we had 3 quizzes covering 5-7 lectures each, so really manageable to prepare for. I would also recommend Neurobiology of Disease. I am really interested in neuroscience, so I found this course really interesting. The professor is good and 40% of the grade is a community engagement project where you have to work on an assignment/scientific article and creative media to explain a disease which one of the university community partners is associated with (Epilepsy, addiction or Autism). Gene regulation in stem cells and development was a exciting course as well, despite the first lectures was rather unimportant. The professor was really good at explaining the concepts, however he was a bit arrogant and frustrating and it seemed like he didn't really want to do the lectures. This course was the only one we had which were online for some reason and there were no tutorials at all. Microbial genetics I would not recommend. The lecture concepts didn't really interest me at all and her way of testing was really unfair. It was much about applying the knowledge we received during lectures, however we didn't learn to apply it since tutorials were all about presenting scientific papers. However the professor her self was good at explaining the concepts during lectures, but wasn't really the things we were taught that we were examined in. Also I started out having Neuroscience of learning and memory, however I had to switch course since the professor had a thick accent which were impossible to understand and there was to much group work to be done, which I tried to avoid since we spend most weekends travelling.
unexpected_costs: All the prices that you see everywhere is without tax, so you have to multiply the amount with 13% in order to get the real price and even more if the product contains sugar. You also have to pay 15%-22% tips everywhere, both at the hairdresser, bar and every restaurants, otherwise you might be yelled at…
cost_comparison: The prices are much like the danish prices, except for the fact that you have to pay tax and tips, so it becomes more expensive. Fast food is really expensive as well. Soda is much more cheaper than we are used. And domestic flights and flights to the USA is really cheap as well. Skiing however is really expensive.
activities_available: There was a lot of clubs that you could be part of. There was a gym, swimming pool, squash courts and table tennis tables free of charge. You could also create your own sports team in almost every sport you can think of and play against other teams at the university. McMaster also have a Canadian football team that was free to watch play every Sunday. The university also showed all the world cup soccer games and held bonfires and barbeques occasionally. They also planned several trips out of the city to national parks, Ikea and other things.
activities_recommended: Create a sports team together with the other exchange students, show up to club fest if you want to be part of club and go on the moose trip for exchange students before the start of semester. That is where you will get most of your friendships started.
weekend_recommendations: My biggest recommendation is to go to Banff and Jasper National Park either before the start of the semester or during reading week for the midterms. That is the most beautiful place i have ever seen. However, look out for when lake Moraine and the Maligne lake cruise closes for the season, since these two places are must see together with lake Louise. These national parks are also exceptional for wildlife spotting (moose, elk and bears) and for stargazing since it is a night sky reserve. You can eventually combine this trip with a trip to Vancouver (amazing city as well as Vancouver Island) and then rent a car and go to whistler (for bungee jumping and trekking). You should go to Toronto to see the city and some of the typical Canadian/American sports eg. ice hockey and basketball. I also went to see baseball and soccer as well. McMaster has a Canadian football team as well playing every Sunday with free admission to the stands. I also recommend going to Montreal for the weekend to see the city. Niagara Falls is a must see as well. We also rented a car and drove to Algonquin park for the weekend, which was pretty nice, especially during fall to see the Indian summer (google when to go!). Flights to New york was also pretty cheap and so was flights to Boston, Washington or Miami. I also went skiing in Whistler after the exams, which were a bucket list thing for me to do. It was nice, but not worth the cost of it in my opinion (it cost 10.000 dkk for 4 days of skiing without food and flights). Also make sure you are home for homecoming. +10.000 people meet up in the street for partying all day
culture_adjustment: That was really easy. However most Canadian at the university was pretty young and we didn't get to talk that much with locals. We almost only spoke with the other exchange students.
socializing_tips: It is difficult to get to socialize with the local students. It seems like they don't do much except studying. However you could apply for a sports team as a free agent, you could try to group up with locals when doing group work or go to house parties.
cultural_challenges: I did not really find anything challenging when it comes to the cultural differences. except for the thing with their way of paying tips for almost everything
culture_appreciated: Their culture is much like ours, so it is easy to adapt. Also the Canadians in general are really friendly and they are committed to the university sport teams which is nice and most people walk around in university merch.
top3_advice: Go on the Moose trip before start of the semester, this is the best way to get friends. Plan going out of the city in the weekends. Hamilton is a boring city, however Canada has a lot of amazing places that you must see. Especially the West coast - Banff and Jasper. Try to do good on your quizzes, presentations and assignment, that way you dont have a lot of pressure in the end and have more time to explore Canada, since you already might have passed your courses.
other_useful_info: Apparently the east coast of Canada is not that cold. We had +20 degrees in november, however the week after it was snowing, so pack clothes for all weathers. Also Canada is more expensive that you might think, so save up or apply for legacies.
most_rewarding: Definatly the friendships and the travelling to amazing cities and nature around in Canada.
greatest_challenge: Finding housing was a bit anoying, since i started living in hotels and airBNBs for the first 1,5 week for 1000 DKK a night.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial for me that the location had courses that lined up (in terms of relevance) with what I’m doing back home and that it felt like I wasn’t just wasting ects points. It was also important to me that it was a predominantly English speaking country, as I think it would have been too overwhelming to both have 4 full courses and have to learn a new language to complete those courses. Another personal reason for my choice of Canada, was that it both feels somewhat similar but also very different to us culturally. This meant that I had a lot of new aspects to explore of the culture, but I didn’t struggle to find people to relate to either. It was nice to be able to blend in a bit once in a while. The access to both nature and bigger cities is also great here, which was something I was looking for too.
overall_comments: I feel that the stress of wanting to do well was a little overwhelming at times and sadly took my focus of off just enjoying the experience to the fullest. This was mainly due to the fact that there are no options for re-examination and I didn’t feel very informed about what would happen in case of a failed exam or course. It takes some time to feel secure academically in a new system even if you do well, because you have to align yourself to new standards and expectations. Besides from this though it has been a huge learning experience and I’ve met lots of wonderful people throughout my stay. So I have no regrets of going!
info_ease: It was very easy! McMaster did a wonderful job of assisting exchange students both online and in person, beforehand and during. They for example had exchange buddies you could reach out to, and people from the university waiting at the airport to help you figure out how to get to your place and/or campus with the transport systems they have. They also did a exchange orientation which provided good opportunity for asking questions and meeting a lot of the other exchange students. Their websites could be a little confusing at times, but you could always reach out to representatives on phone or email if you were unsure about any of the information needed.
arrival_assistance: As mentioned in the previous question there was the exchange orientation. Here we could sign up for different things like getting help with speaking and/or writing in English, or different clubs that would do events throughout the term etc. We also got some general information about where to get medical assistance if needed and much more. Generally they provided us with all the tools necessary for thriving. The only thing I might have wished for was a map of the different buildings on campus, but that was possible to find online if you looked up the specific buildings and the university’s name.

registration_process: First there was the application for the university in which you had to do a letter explaining why you wanted to apply to McMaster and also attach your university’s confirmation of your exchange and a transcript of your grades. When this had been accepted you had to remember to accept the offer from McMaster. Then you had to fill out a bunch of personal information, like home address and phone numbers for both yourself and emergency contacts. You also had to submit a photo for your student card. Remembering to update this information when you move to Canada and possibly change to a Canadian phone number is important. At this point you would already have received an email and password which had to be changed for security reasons, which would gain you access to an outlook email, mosaic and avenue2learn, which are their main student portals. Then you would have to make sure that you’re signed up for their healthcare program UHIP and enroll in the courses. The course enrolling happens in the summer, so be sure what courses you want to sign up for and have the pre-acceptance of them from UCPH before enrolling to make the process less stressful for yourself. It should be possible to change and drop courses at McMaster later if necessary, but you can’t be guaranteed a course if it’s already filled etc. McMaster will update you through the email you first used for contact through UCPH, but will switch to your assigned email address from them later on, so keep an eye on both during the registration period.
registration_help: Keeping close contact with both their exchange coordinators and the ones from UCPH, along with the contact person from your faculty at McMaster was helpful. They were the people I found myself needing to contact the most. Also read the guides they send you thoroughly! These guides have a lot of the information you need, like how to contact them and when different deadlines are.
registration_success: Very successful I’d say. Sadly some of the courses I initially wanted were for the wrong semester and a few of the ones I found interesting were overlapping. But I ended up finding more than enough that I found interesting to create a schedule for and register in.
registration_advice: Make yourself a list of deadlines and set yourself goals and reminders for when to have specific parts of the process done, so you don’t get stressed out and have to do things last minute in case of problems. Make use of the contact information, but remember that there’s a time difference and that answers can take a couple of days at times.
academics_comments: I feel that the stress of wanting to do well was a little overwhelming at times and sadly took my focus of off just enjoying the experience to the fullest. This was mainly due to the fact that there are no options for re-examination and I didn’t feel very informed about what would happen in case of a failed exam or course. It takes some time to feel secure academically in a new system even if you do well, because you have to align yourself to new standards and expectations. Besides from this though it has been a huge learning experience and I’ve met lots of wonderful people throughout my stay. So I have no regrets of going!
course_level: I was in my second year of my BA back home doing my exchange when I had my electives. I took three third year courses and one first year course. This seemed very fitting to my level, but that is also because I had chosen courses that were relevant and therefore extensions on my previous knowledge from home. The first year course was surprisingly the most tedious in my opinion, as they take into account that a lot of people are fresh out of high school in Canada when doing their first year. This meant that it was a much bigger class and they were a lot less lenient in the way they did assignments, tests and exams in terms of style compared to the third year courses. So third year classes is generally what I would recommend, just like they do. That being said, the first year course did come in handy as it provided very thorough guides on academic guidelines, and served as a prerequisite for some of my third year classes. I would say it is important to make sure your feel confident not just in speaking English, but in writing it as well, as that makes up a large chunk of your grade in many courses.
teaching_comparison: It was structured quite differently. Mainly because it had shorter lectures and then one tutorial for each course per week. Attendance is obviously important back at UCPH, but it is a part of your grade here and you need to actively participate to get full marks for attendance. They will (or at least should! ) make you aware of these expectations in the start of the course though. Generally the way they do final grades is very different as they grade you on your efforts throughout the semester, which means you don’t just get your exam grade like you would in a lot of courses at UCPH. So that is something to be prepared for.

recommended_courses: I would recommend all of these courses, as I felt like they were all developing different skills of great interest to me. I do recommend the 3rd year courses more though, as I preferred the smaller class and the way they were taught in general.
unexpected_costs: Kitchenware and a few other things from IKEA like a drying rack etc. as the place I rented didn’t have a sharing system in the kitchen and the dryers were the industrial kind which is no good for delicate fabrics. (I put 0.00kr in personal spendings and other fees as it is very hard to make up a consistent number per month and it doesn’t feel like it would it necessarily be very representative of the general experience.)
cost_comparison: Groceries, if choosing to buy organic some specific wares will be VERY expensive compared to back home. Yoghurt for example is almost the doubled price for organic compared to back home. School textbooks are pretty expensive too, I had four and payed around 1600kr total, which doesn’t sound like much, but the two textbooks make up 1400kr of that total. Something that was surprisingly cheap though was bus transport which I heavily relied on. I payed nothing for it within Hamilton as McMaster provided a transit pass for free.
activities_available: An art gallery, a gym, sport events like basketball and volleyball etc., an end of the semester fair, club events like board game nights, quiz nights etc., and a lot of events specifically targeted towards exchange students and international students with ice skating, free dinners, hikes and much more. They even did an IKEA trip and such for the exchange students. They even had a planetarium and a small nuclear reactor that you could visit on campus.
activities_recommended: Definitely go to the free dinners for exchange students! It’s a wonderful way to meet the other exchange students and try some different kinds of food. I would also recommend just going to whatever you get the chance to go to, sports events were for example really fun to both watch and participate in, which is not something I would normally do much at home.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city! If you live in Hamilton specifically, it might seem like a bit of a dull city, but find some friends and go see the natural areas around, visit board game cafes, go to the local cinema (Westdale cinema is cute in particular!), explore and you will surely find something for your taste. Visit Toronto for sure! Maybe go to Niagara Falls if you get the chance. Even if you don’t want to spend a lot of money you can find many hidden gems. At the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto you can for example get a free year pass if your under 25. So yeah, just explore opportunities and ask other students (both local and other exchange and international students) for tips and company on your trips!
culture_adjustment: Quite easy I’d say. People are very friendly, they even thank the bus driver on the busses in Hamilton. As long as you make the effort to be approachable and friendly, people return it happily and are super helpful. One thing that has been harder to adjust to is the amount of homeless people in Hamilton and Toronto. It can feel a little scary in the downtown areas at night as a lot of them are on hardcore drugs and can be very loud yelling at people and act quite weird at times in the streets. I haven’t personally experienced any problems with them though, despite living close to an area where a lot of them are settled. So it’s more so because it’s shocking how big of a problem it is there. Also the cities are extremely car oriented, so going on bike or foot can sometimes be challenging or a little daunting in some areas as it’s not always super pedestrian friendly. But there are still areas that are more suitable for walking and biking as well!
socializing_tips: It might seem awkward or challenging to initiate contact, but from my experience people are very excited to talk! Try and be open to opportunities, be the first to say hi and introduce yourself to people you sit next to in class. Don’t be afraid to ask for people’s social media or phone numbers when having talked, especially if you’ve mentioned that your an exchange student people will be very happy to help you with things and show you places in the city!
cultural_challenges: There weren’t really any cultural differences I found challenging to be honest. I actually found that people were easier to get to know here than back home to some degree! People are very open and friendly if you try your best to be so.
culture_appreciated: Again, the friendly people! I for example got invited to a girls family Easter dinner because she knew I obvious didn’t have my own family to celebrate it with here. So people really do their best to make sure you feel welcome and accepted.
top3_advice: 1. Prepare as much as you can from home to reduce any stress, through being thorough in your planning and reading all of the guides that they provide. 2. Do your best to participate in activities on campus and outside of campus, it makes for really fun experiences even if it’s not something you’d normally do. So be curious and seek things out! 3. Don’t beat yourself up when things don’t go as expected or if you feel stressed out about schoolwork, it’s okay as it’s an learning experience and you just have to do the best you can! At times it can feel tough, but it’ll be worth it for all the good experiences you get along the way.
other_useful_info: There can be unexpected fees and it is always good to have some savings to rely on. Familiarise yourself with the different contacts and student portals as early as possible to make life easier for yourself. And don’t be afraid to ask for help!
most_rewarding: The experiences I have had with other people and the knowledge that I can handle things very well on my own even when it feels very challenging. I feel like it has made me much more independent and resourceful, and it has reassured me that being outgoing and open can get you a long way.
greatest_challenge: All the administrative stuff both before and during the stay. Especially before as there are a lot of things that need to be planned ahead of time and a lot of uncertainties which can be scary. Also balancing doing schoolwork, having fun and relaxing can be hard if you get stressed out by schoolwork.

Canada har også et forholdsvist velfungerende (i hvert fald mere udviklet) sundhedssystem ligesom herhjemme, så jeg tænkte det ville være mere relevant for mig. Canada var den bedst at de virkelig dårlige muligheder der var for udveksling på mit studie. Jeg ville gerne opleve en anden natur og en anden kultur og det tilbyder Canada rigtig meget, da tilgangen til skole, til verden og til mange ting var meget anderledes.

arrival_comments: Generelt var det godt. Der var events for udvekslingsstuderende så vi alle kunne møde hinanden, men selve welcome week arrangementet var ikke noget at råbe hurra for. housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Det er en god skole, men måske husk at minde folk om hvor unge de studerende er på den anden sider af Atlanterhavet. Kunne godt være jeg lige havde genovervejet destination hvis jeg havde vidst det.

registration_help: Mail og eller var der Student Succes Centre som man kunne gå, det var meget behjælpeligt.

academics_comments: Det er en god skole, men måske husk at minde folk om hvor unge de studerende er på den anden sider af Atlanterhavet. Kunne godt være jeg lige havde genovervejet destination hvis jeg havde vidst det.
course_level: Havde 3 fag der var 3 års fag og 1 fag der var 1 års fag, men kunne ærlig talt ikke rigtig kende forskel på niveauet i dem. Jeg kan stadig bedst lide KU's undervisning, da den måde skaber med selvdisciplin, hvorimod på mac der når man ikke engang at overveje om det overhovedet er noget man synes er fedt, fordi du skal bare lave så mange ting hele tiden uden kvalitet i stedet for mindre med mere kvalitet. Kvantitet over Kvalitet på McMaster.
courses_enrolled: Health Ventures Demystifying Medicine Health Systems and Health Policy Innovate
recommended_courses: Health Ventures er nok det fedeste af de fag jeg havde, det er nok der hvor jeg følte det gav mig mest. Specielt underviseren, meget dygtig og behagelig.
unexpected_costs: Oplevede ikke noget jeg ikke havde regnet med. Har ikke brugt penge på noget jeg ikke havde tænkt jeg skulle bruge penge på.
cost_comparison: Madvare er dyrere end jeg regnede med, det var nok den eneste ting ellers var det meste generelt billigere end herhjemme.

activities_recommended: Prøv udendørsklubben, den er meget fed.

cultural_challenges: Buskulturen, skolekulturen. Alt var meget anderledes. Ikke på en dårlig måde man skal bare lige vænne sig til det. Venligheden er meget overfladisk og der er ikke rigtig nogen der går op i hvordan du rigtig har det.
culture_appreciated: Mere amerikansk end jeg tænkte det ville være.
top3_advice: Tag på ture i weekenden, og brug byen mere end den byder op til. Der findes mange hyggelige steder man kan side, og naturområder der er skønne.
other_useful_info: Hamilton er ikke den mest livlige by, så man skal søge det, og når man søger det bliver det også grebet.
most_rewarding: Min egen udvikling, man bliver mere selvstændig og sætter mere pris på det man allerede har.
greatest_challenge: Nok workload, det var helt ekstremt meget og skaber en unødvendig stress.

crucial_aspects: I thought about choosing a country that had a unique nature to explore. Canada is large country that has a lot of variation in terms of landscape and animals, and I thought it would be cool to see how it was to live in a country that had all that. Other than that, I thought it would be nice to get the experience of going to an American university as each university has its own sports facility, and it was something I wanted to see.
overall_comments: Overall, I think I was a really good idea to go on exchange. I got to know people from all around the world and I got to experience things I would never be able to in Denmark. This included going to ice hockey- and basketball matches as well as meeting new people from different countries. I was satisfied with what I got to explore but there were some elements in living in Hamilton which I didn't really like and was tired of which for example was trash lying around where I lived and just not the cleanest environment. Another thing is that I didn't get to see my family and friends as much as I am used to, so some of the weekends were maybe not as fun as in my home country. When that is said, I still think it's good to see how it is living aboard and I think I got to appreciate the things I didn't have there more.

culture_adjustment: I don't think it was hard to adjust to the local culture. The thing that annoyed me was that there is not as clean of an environment in Canada as there is at home. Other than that, I think I had an easy time adjusting to the local culture.
socializing_tips: In Canada people are very open minded and it is not difficult to speak to them. Plenty of students actually approached me, so there are many of them that want to talk. Having this in mind, I had an easier time speaking to other students
cultural_challenges: I don't think there were any to be honest.
culture_appreciated: I think going to different places and see what the nature looked like was a thing I appreciated as well as observing how they held events on stadiums. I thought it was good to experience the things Americans do and to see what they have in general.
top3_advice: Having a good beginning is the most important thing. Get to know as many people as possible from the start so you have a bunch of people you are connected to. It is better to have people writing to you and you declining the invitation, rather than having nobody writing to you or you having nobody around to write to, when you want to go out.
other_useful_info: The other important thing would be attending the welcome week. It is a good place to meet other exchange students and a nice beginning. Remember that other exchange students are in the same boat as you, and they would like to get some new friends too.
most_rewarding: I think the most rewarding thing was getting to know I had an easy time living in a foreign country without the people I am used to having around. One thing is to be sure you can do it, but another thing is actually doing it. I think I had satisfied feeling after my exchange ended.
greatest_challenge: I think the greatest challenge was the thing that made it the most rewarding experience, exactly not having my friends and family around. It was most challenging in the weekends as I would usually see either of them in my home country.
other_comments: Enjoy your time on exchange, it is not an opportunity everybody gets!

crucial_aspects: The most determining factor for choosing McMaster was the prospects of enrolling in Virology courses and learning more about Immunology. The second key factor was the nature that aligned with my ambitions of travelling in Canada. Another important influence was my colleague at CBMR who recommended that I chose a destination far away from Denmark to gain a new and diverse perspective on academics, which was different from the Danish approach.
info_ease: Prior to my arrival I had arranged an airport pick-up by my landlord. I know other students who used the campus shuttlebus going directly to campus. Offers like these was sent out pr email in advance, so all the exchange students where informed. McMaster also arranged tutors in the airport as a welcome. McMaster succeded in sending out all these improtant informationsn through multiple media channels, most arrival information was sent out pr. Email and the same infromation was likewise posted on the schools social media channels. Arrival was also a theme in the webinar series.
arrival_assistance: Welcome orientations on campus during the first weeks of the semester. These orientations was tailored to the exchange students providing us with a lot of relevant information about the city of Hamilton, and the University history and academic structure. The unaswered questions from these orientations was easialy answered by the respective offices pr. Email. I remember asking further into course selection. Besides the academic questions the university also provides helpful ressources regarding housing, phone bills, and banking specific questions and scholarships. My situation was different since, I moved in with a lanldord, who provided me with a lot of information regarding SIM cards, bank accounts, and rental payment in Canada.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Enrolling in courses is done through the Mosaic platform online by searching for the specific course code. McMaster operates with the rule, that the majority of courses a student is enrolled in must be from within the faculty, the student is assigned to. This rule can be bend, allowing you to enroll in more courses from a different faculty ie. Health Sciences instead of Science. In my situation I enrolled in two HTHSCI courses while bieng assigned to the Science Faculty. Once the specific course is identified the course is added to the basket on mosaic. From here its now a question of clicking enroll. If all prerequisites are met and seats are available you will be enrolled in the course. If the prerequisites does not match, you can always email the professor or the office of registry at the specific faculty. Mosaic in general has a user friendly interface where you can add and drop courses as you like, during the regristration period and the ”add&drop” window in the beginning of the semester.
registration_help: Reminders sent out pr email, by the exchange coordinator at McMaster. In the months before depature to Canada, the exchange office will host a webinar on course regristration and answer questions reagarding elligibilltiy and prerequisites. Also the iCent app is very usefull in navigating your questions. Sometimes you'll find answers to course registration or at least the people you should email with the questions.
registration_success: I followed the recommendations and signed up for my courses early in the registration period. This helped me secure my seat in the classes I had prioritised the most.
registration_advice: You do not have to enroll in 5 courses as a KU student - 4 is enough. There is some discrepencies in what constitutes a fulltime student at McMaster, sometimes 3 courses is considered full course load, in other cases student must enroll in 5 courses. Use Reddit Course title + course code. And in most cases you'll find a review of course content, group work, grading and the professor and TA (teaching assistants).
course_level: Level 3 courses are overall a bit easier compared to 8 weeks of course material at KU. Where as the level 4 courses is more similar to the KU level.
teaching_comparison: Huge difference, group work played a larger role in my Immunology and Epidemiology courses. Whereas my course in Biochemical Pharmacology is more similar to a KU, with most of the content being covered in lectures.
courses_enrolled: Principles of Virology, Introductory Immunology, Introduction to Epidemiology and Biochemical Pharmacology.
recommended_courses: Principles of Virology is my first recommendation, to anyon with the ambition of pursuing virology later on in their studies. Dr. Muularcky is a highly passionate professor with many great skills in teaching. The other course I highly reccomend is the Immunology course, where Dr. Koeing uses many great analogies and real worl examples to explian the complicated concepts in immunology. The last course I reccommend is the Epidemiology, where Dr. Pritchard gives a very detailed introduction to the field of epidemiology and the tools used in this field of research.
unexpected_costs: Prevent your computer from crashing while being abroad, by investing in one while being in Denmark. One of my friends was cutting it very close with her computer. I did experience an unexpected transfer fee, when I moved my Canadian telephone number between to phone companies. This was neccessary inorder to have the abilltiy to call my danish bank.
cost_comparison: Eggs, sliced cheese where more expensive Coffee and snacks at a caffee was less expensive.
activities_available: A broad selection of societies and clubs were available to exchange students at McMaster. A few examples would be the book club, the Outdoor Club, the Taylor Swift Society, Black Student Society, Astronomy society, The Climbing club.
activities_recommended: The outdoor club, the trips they arrange takes you to some pretty impressive and beutiful destinations, such as Alqonquin National Park.
weekend_recommendations: Short trips, waterfall hike around the Niagra Escarpment near Hamilton. Visit Niagra Falls and the town Niagra On the Lake Longer Trips, visit Toronto, Montreal, Ottowa
culture_adjustment: The canadian culturen is very similar to the western culture in Denmark, so in large parts adjusting was not that difficult. They do how ever emphasize the Indiginous population by saying a land acknowledgement. These are more prominent in the webinars and the beginning of the term.
socializing_tips: Use the opportunity through gruop work to socialize with Canadian students, it takes some effort to arrange something but it is worth it.
cultural_challenges: The entire campus has different programs spanning from humanities to engeneering and to STEM. Everyone is on the same campus, so you're likely to meet someone outside of your own program.
culture_appreciated: The overall welcomming spirit on campus. I would say Canadian univerosties is quiet similar in terms of inclusion and openess towards new cultures.
top3_advice: Bring a danish extension cord – that is a life saver, Excpect the course load to be easier on a weekly basis, however a bit challenging over the full semester. Maximize the time you spend travelling and explore Canada while you're over there.
other_useful_info: The on campus food is reasonably priced. In general professors and local students find it vluable to have an exchange student in the class room.
most_rewarding: Networking woth people in Canada. Such that I have contacts I can reach out to, the next time I am travelling. Getting to know other students from abroad in a similar situation as myself.
greatest_challenge: Balancing the academic work and the travelling with friends.
other_comments: If you have any doubts regarding the decision of going/not going. I highly recommend going abroad! I am grateful for the friendships and people I got know along the way, during my semester at McMaster University.

other_comments: Selvom du læser denne her travel report, og tvivler på om du skal tage på udveksling. Gør det! Jeg villle ikke bytte det for noget andet, til trods for ovenstående kommentarer om sociale udfordringer og ensomhed. Men uanset hvad, så handler det om hvad du gør det til, og hvad du vil have ud af det. Så selvom frygten lurer, så spring ud i det. Det er nu chancen er der.
