crucial_aspects: I wanted a place which i spoke the language was my big thing, so I only looked at english or scandinavian countries. And I wanted some places with cool natures, like huge trees, national parks, mountains ect. since I really enjoy hiking and camping. And I also chose Canada specifically cause i traveled there before and really enjoyed the people and country overall.
info_ease: I was actually positively surprised by how helpful the university was, they were quick at answering, very helpful, send out a ton of information before, and had online seminars before with everything from helping with the ETA (Canadian visa) to getting to know the different clubs on the university. The only thing you were not sure to get help with was housing, but even then they really tried hard.
arrival_assistance: A lot of the same, there was a couple people assigned to help us and they were super sweet and helpful and always keen to talk and give recommendations also during the year, with making different activities. But the first days you had to find them, cause the orientations the first couple days was very aimed at first years, who are 17-18 years old... so makes you feel very much like the odd one out. But if you power through till friday, it starts monday. Then it is very helpful and so nice cause they have an entire day only for exchange students and here it was so helpful to make a big whats app group with everyone.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I think it was pretty easy to get it assigned since you just need to write a letter. It is a bit harder with the exchange university mostly because they use other platforms.
registration_help: I did not think the home university helped a lot. They were hard to get a hold of and came with half answers. But the exchange university was very helpful and you never felt like your questions were stupid so that was very nice.
registration_success: I got most of the classes I wanted, i got 3/4. I only had to take 4 courses, and since 2 of mine needed to partly elective, it was nice to get your first priorities. One course I didn't get I ended up spamming the faculty leader until I got a spot, for the leader I wouldn't recommened it but very effective still. Plus using the exchange card is helpful, cause you are seen as exotic when you are an exchange students, which is a nice card to pull.
registration_advice: Be ready, some courses are very popular and are gonna be ripped away, so be fast and if you don't get a course try contacting the proffersor, cause they are usually very helpful. And do check the tutorial times, I found out to late that there was multiple to choose between so I just got the one suggested for me.
course_level: Genreally the level is lower, which is nice if you are visiting for the country and culture cause leaves more time to travel. But the professors are better at teaching than back home so the lectures are really interesting and easy to follow. It is also easier to pass cause the grade is split up between multiple things but it also does require more work throughout the year.
teaching_comparison: I think it is a lot of the same. With lectures and tutorials, I had on course which was different but mostly the same. You can just feel the proffeseurs are more teaching aimed and not research aimed over there.
courses_enrolled: Principles of virologi Introductory Immunology The Big Questions Science of Fictional Characters
recommended_courses: Principles of virologi - truly my favorite course, the proffesur, Doctor Mullarkey, is truly fantastic it is crazy. Science of Fictional Characters - this was a really fun course about how you use research, and trying to take risk in science in a different way, would highly recommed it. The Big Questions - fun course about astronomy, very easy to learn which is nice if you know nothing about it, but very much a fun course.
unexpected_costs: You do go on trips and eat out a lot and the price for housing is typically more expensive another place.
cost_comparison: transport was less than expected which was nice. Buying food in grocery stores was more, which sucked.
activities_available: THE GYM WAS FREE, it was so nice and the gym was huge. You could also for pretty cheap prizes sign up for different training I did kick boxing. I know there was also other things like knitting club and the exchange commitee hosted a lot of events. But i mostly did a lot of training also joined the outdoor club for going on trips.
activities_recommended: If you like training, do that it is so accesible. And something that strengthen the exchange group and made my friend group was the boys made an intermural soccer team, and played games on sunday where everyone came out and rooted for them and after we went to get beer, this was really good for friendships.
weekend_recommendations: Yes I recommened going on trips, but I would say wait and makes friends to go with you. But go to Montreal and Quebec really nice city. When it is still warm I would also recommened going to Halifax a city on the east cost. Closer I would recommened national parks like Pennisula and Algonquin park which are so pretty. And of course going to the west coast to see Banff, Whistler, Vancouver. I know some people went to New York since it is close but due to Americas situation I personally didn't wanna go.
culture_adjustment: I would say okay easy, the people are way more polite and talkative like in the bus, supermarket and so on, which is very kind but coming from Denmark a big change from how the culture is here.
socializing_tips: Talk to them, they are sooooooooooo talkative, and actually want to talk so just start yapping with people.
cultural_challenges: Not really, I think the culture is so mitch match because of the colonisation and because they are a generally a nice and open people it is really easy to adjust to the people.
culture_appreciated: The kindness, it makes it very easy to feel welcome in the country and that is super nice, cause they would just go up and talk to you and complient you which gives a good feeling.
top3_advice: 1. Be open minded and say yes, it makes it easier to get friends quicker when people remember you 2. Travel around, save money up before so it is possible and not an issue, cause it is really a beautiful country which is worthwhile to visit. 3. Make friends with the other exchange group, even if it feels silly to go to another country to talk to people not from that country. But you are in the same boat as the other exchange students and the are generally more open and want to go out and explore than the canadians.
other_useful_info: Make a big exchange group quickly on whats app or a likewise app. And then just go to everything, even if you are a bit tired especially in the start, it really helps later cause you build up so many friendships and connections.
most_rewarding: My friends i made, i mostly made exchange friends, but i got truly close with a lot of people which i cherish more than anything else i got on this exchange. And i actually enjoyed not knowing anyone before i left, cause i was forced in another way to make friends which was very nice.
greatest_challenge: Saying goodbye... I think before you got there cause there is so many uncertainities both housing and with being in another country. But since i got there after the first week when you don't know anybody it is only great.

courses_enrolled: ECON 3HH3 International Trade ECON 2B03 Analysis of Economic Data ECON 3E03 Applied Econometrics ECON 3BE3 Behavioural Economics
recommended_courses: I liked ECON 3BE3 Behavioural Economics, it was new to me and very interesting. Learned a lot, but no homework and only one assignment.
unexpected_costs: That transportation in that city was free for exchange students
cost_comparison: Milk and cheese was more expensive. Cafe coffee a bit cheaper. But confusing that they dont include taxes in the price, and the taxes was different for each thing
activities_available: Very very many. Almost everything.
activities_recommended: I did pilates Classes and the gym. I did pilates with another exchange student. I think it was a nice way to see each other.
weekend_recommendations: Visit the other big citys around. And join the exchange activity.
culture_adjustment: It was easy
cultural_challenges: I dont know
culture_appreciated: Everyone say "Thank you" when they leave the bus, I think that was cute
top3_advice: 1. Find out why you are doing exchange, and choose things that supports that. Because there will be SO many thinks to do. 2. Reach out, and the first 3 weeks is very important to socialize 3. The best coffee on campus is the Grind Cafe
other_useful_info: I dont know
most_rewarding: I think it was very nice to start an everyday in a new place. I got more comfortable speaking English. The last weeks I wanted to get the last joy out of the experience, studying together, partying and so, it felled so fulfilling.
greatest_challenge: The transportation to school took one hour, even though it was only 9 km away...

crucial_aspects: 1) language: As the language barrier plays a huge role when doing clinical rotations/ interacting with patients, I was only looking for exchange to Scandinavian, English- or German-speaking countries. 2) clinical rotations: I wanted to see as many different departments as possible during my exchange 3) personal experience: I wanted to try living in a smaller city surrounded by mountains
info_ease: Not very easy. I found it very confusing to be communicating with many different people: Monika Schlager from International Office, D. Mulser from KPJ-Anmeldung (responsible for all clinical stays), and the secretaries from the different departments. I didn't have enough insight in their organisation and therefore didn't know who to ask/ who would be responsible.
arrival_assistance: Little assistance. I knew which departments I had been assigned to during the three months. I also knew where and when to show up the first day, but the whole procedure with picking up the staff card, clothes, log-in etc. was very confusing and poorly planned/communicated. I didn't recieve any up-front information about what to expect of the first day of the clinical stay or in general the whole clincal stay. No information about working hours, holidays, no general information about the departments I would be placed at, a map of the hospital etc.
arrival_comments: The arrival and first days of my clinical stay were a disaster and made me reconsider my choice. This is not a critique of personal matter, as M. Schlager and especially D. Mulser from KPJ-Anmeldung were very helpful, I just would have wished for a better organised introduction. A student buddy would also have made a great difference: someone to show you around on campus, where to get the clothes, how the canteen works etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I would have wished for a better overview of all the steps needed. As written above, I found it very confusing to be communicating with a lot of different people. Other than that, I don't remember the registration process as complicated, also because my course "clinical stay in foreign country" was relatively fixed
registration_help: communication with M. Schlager from International office and Anne Fledelius from the Int. office from my home university, UCPH
registration_success: though there were only few options available for my clinical rotations, I was satisfied with the three departments that I got: gynecology, infectious medicine, orthopedic surgery
registration_advice: it might seem a lot of work, but get it done as fast as possible so you can start to get excited for your exchange!
course_level: clinical stay with different levels of supervision from the department's physicians
teaching_comparison: the clinical stays at my host institution (Innsbruck) seemed more disorganised and the organisation and teaching heavily depends on each department, far more than I was used to from home. There are no teaching classes apart from "fortbildungen"/"forlæsninger", which is not discussion-based. There was very little time or interest from the doctors, to discuss cases or treatments etc.
courses_enrolled: clinical stay in foreign country, 20 ECTS
unexpected_costs: fee for getting enrolled at the University of Innsbruck, around 22 EUR
cost_comparison: food and rent was more expensive than expected
activities_available: due to corona, I didn't have the impression of a lot of activities going on
activities_recommended: - sport courses at USI - Whatsapp/Telegram interest groups (table tennis, skiing, hiking, beachvolley, chess, spike ball etc..)
weekend_recommendations: explore the nature around Innsbruck! Weekend trip to Munich, Salzburg, Northern Italy
culture_adjustment: It was not a very big adjustment for me as I already knew the German culture. I still got surprised by how relatively conservative Austria still is
socializing_tips: as written above: engage in different sports, maybe even create your own group and share your interests
culture_appreciated: how everyone appreciates being out in the nature in their free time, great food and beautiful architecture
top3_advice: 1) arrive two or three weeks prior to your clinical exchange, so you can settle down and meet people, maybe even make connections with someone who can show you around on the campus 2) don't plan too much beforehand on what you want to see or do while you're on exchange 3) start looking for housing minimum 2 months before and prioritize finding a place that you can rent for the whole period
most_rewarding: completing the exchange, although I thought about quitting several times in the beginning
greatest_challenge: social challenges: not feeling welcome at a deparment, feeling "stuck" because you are assigned at a specific department and going somewhere else is not impossible but complicated, feeling left alone and not seen as a ressource (I was the only student in the department during the first month).

crucial_aspects: As a Japanese Studies student, it was crucial that my destination was in Japan, and with my hopes of constructing lasting relationships with not only locals and international students, but also with companies and individuals with connections within a professional area, a central location near Tokyo was preferred, and was one of the reasons for picking this destination. Aside from this, I knew that Meiji had a faint connection with the Nordics, and this fit with my previous exchange destinations within Japan. Finally, I felt that the courses and level of education that the selected university was capable of delivering was satisfactory to my needs, and in most cases, this proved to be true.
info_ease: I had no issues upon arrival, even despite arriving earlier than most other exchange students, as well as living in my own, seperately arranged accomodation. Mails were sent to aid us in what documents, etc. was required, and aside from this, the staff at Nakano Ward Office were extremely helpful in guiding me. It should be mentioned that I am fluent in Japanese, and had already exchanged once, so I was aware of the move-in procedures as well as the documents required for this.
arrival_assistance: Because I was able to travel over one month before the start of classes, I didn't have much in the way of guidance for the first weeks. There was no physical contact with any staff of the university until after the start of classes.
arrival_comments: I had no issues with the level of assistance at this university, although I did feel their presence was relatively small. I did not live in the dormitories like the majority of the students did, so I am unsure of the process from their side.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After a week of being able to trial classes, we could decide on our classes through an online system. Despite missing a class in this first week, it was still possible to follow it, and also to change classes last-minute. I had no issues.
registration_help: Plenty of introductory sessions helped prepare for selecting classes, and any professor was helpful in giving advice.
registration_success: A few of the classes were lottery-classes with limited numbers for international students. I was picked for all my first-priority classes, so I never paid it any mind.
registration_advice: Try as many classes as you can, and don't plan any events in the first weeks. There are some online classes which can't be trialled, and I would seriously consider leaving those behind if I was to exchange again.
course_level: Courses were BA-level, and half of my credits were for elective classes, while another half was dedicated to Realia B.
teaching_comparison: Generally, online and on-demand courses were more prevalent at Meiji University, and I think this ties in with the general style of teaching at Japanese universities. There were fewer long assignments, and professors instead focused on having you submit a small pages worth of notes from each lesson. For the final submissions, which were the only large submission for most classes, a proper page requirement was usually set, although it felt at times like the contents of this paper were largely irrelevant to the final mark. Particularly sources and source creditation seemed to be of less importance, perhaps due to the diverse background of the students present - some had not learned the conventions at the time of exchange, while others had. In any case, a higher level of strictness and adherence to rules was generally displayed by foreign professors, while local, Japanese professors seemed less inclined to care.
courses_enrolled: Animation Culture Manga Culture Japan and technology Japanese Social Systems Journalism Studies Media Studies Production Management
recommended_courses: While the Manga and Anime Culture classes may seem like free-time fun at a glance, the professor is not only extremely knowledgeable and a good presenter, but also seems to care about the products and opinions of each student. I recommend these classes. For anyone with an interest in Japan and Japanese society, Japanese Social Systems gave a good rundown of modern Japanese political and economical issues, and allowed time and space to ponder these. I don't recommend Journalism Studies and Media Studies - these were online courses, were eerily similar, and didn't have a particularly deep level of engagement. The Journalism Course was non-timed and entirely on-demand, which meant I could complete it in the month of exam preparation and in-between classes. The Production Management and Japan and Technology classes were average, with some interesting and useful points, and other somewhat redundant points.
unexpected_costs: It may come as a surprise to some, that health insurance is required despite paying from home. A monthly payment of around 1.700 JPY is required for the Japanese Government, while a one-time payment for Meiji University is required for other insurance coverages.
cost_comparison: Inflation has hit hard in Japan, so living costs, but particularly foods, are more expensive now than they were last time I was there. When I attemped to live frugally, it was not an issue, but my spending habits during the first couple of months did provide some surprises and wide-eyed looks at my bank statements. Also, Meiji allows exchange students to qualify for student discounts on things like Shinkansen-tickets, so make sure to take advantage of this while away. This should also be explained in the introduction.
activities_available: Halloween events, cultural exchange events and a Christmas party was arranged. Most actual events were paid, while I think the clubs were free. There was an indoor ball-games court at my campus in Nakano, which was apparently free to use. I never did.
activities_recommended: I liked the Christmas party, but mostly, I would recommend making some friends at the dorm and asking them to be invited over every now and then.
weekend_recommendations: There's plenty to do in Tokyo, but I often found myself just making a nice dinner at home. Raw ingredients are cheaper and different compared to Denmark, especially fish, so I recommend trying as much as you can. Tokyo is central enough that you can pretty much travel anywhere easily by Shinkansen - if not, most domestic flights leave from Haneda, which is super close to both the dorms and the university. I recommend Tohoku in winter.
culture_adjustment: I think Danish and Japanese people have a similar respect for public order and quiet, although it is more enforced in Japan, so be aware of things like talking on the phone in the train, getting drunk and rowdy with your friends, or the like.
socializing_tips: This was my biggest issue with Meiji University - there were few points where you could naturally talk to local students. There's a Study Cafe in the bottom floor of the Nakano Campus, though, and the local students that come here are usually talkative and extroverted.
cultural_challenges: Many describe Japanese as being part-time friends, with meeting once a month or so being enough. This was difficult, because as an exchange student, you only have 6 months at max. I recommend keeping a mix of international and local friends to avoid getting left alone.
culture_appreciated: Definitely the order. Later in my exchange, I was able to visit Shanghai and Wuhu in China, and the chaos there reminded me just how calm and ordered Japan is. Just be aware that this can also backfire, when you're trying to go around the rules.
top3_advice: 1: Get a dorm. An apartment is not worth it. 2: Don't waste your time just in Tokyo. Spend some cash and go see Japan. 3: In a good way, don't take your classes to seriously. You'll stress to keep up with it all, and won't have time to enjoy the local culture.
other_useful_info: You're not required to pay towards your national pension when you're just an exchange student making no money. If you ever receive the payment slips in the mail (they're alot more expensive than the health insurance, so you'll know), don't pay them, and take them, along with your student card, to the Ward Office. They'll sort it out for you.
most_rewarding: I have an interest in cars, and getting to meet and engage with people from Nissan and Toyota was a very rewarding experience.
greatest_challenge: Fighting enourmous cockroaches in the middle of the night in my cheapo apartment in Tokyo. Don't do it.

crucial_aspects: Since the exchange was only for half a year, I wanted to go somewhere where I knew I could communicate with the locals. Thus, it was important for me to go to an English speaking country. As I have already lived in North America for 4 years, Oceania was an obvious option for me. Furthermore, I have always dreamed of going to Australia and saw this as the perfect opportunity. The choice of city that I wished for in Australia depended on what each university had to offer. In the preparation process, I spent a lot of time looking at what classes each university offered. Here I found that Melbourne, and in particular Monash University, had the best options for my interests.
overall_comments: I have really enjoyed my exchange semester in Melbourne and I would encourage everyone, who has the opportunity to go on exchange, to do so. You grow a lot as a person by living in a foreign country.
info_ease: It was very easy. Monash University offers a pick up service at the airport which I had signed up for. Thus, upon arrival I just called the driver, and he took me to where I was staying the first few days.
arrival_assistance: Before the semester began, all exchange students had to attend an orientation day at Monash where they explained us a bit about Australian culture, Monash as an institution and how and where we could seek help if we needed any. Furthermore, they had a bunch of activities for all Monash students where you could learn more about Australia, do fun activities with other students, or learn about the different clubs an societies that Monash University offered.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I have really enjoyed my exchange semester in Melbourne and I would encourage everyone, who has the opportunity to go on exchange, to do so. You grow a lot as a person by living in a foreign country.
registration_process: The registration process was super easy. A few days after arriving, I just went to Monash Connect (the student service center), got my student id and then that was it. It took around 10-15 minutes in total.
registration_help: The employee at Monash Connect was very friendly and helpful. After making my id, he helped me understand how to read my schedule and unfortunately also gave me the news that 3/4 of my classes were online. At first I was very sad about it, but as soon as the semester started, I became quite happy with it because it gave me a lot more flexibility that I would've otherwise had. Additionally, it did not at all affect my chances of making new friends as I was initially worried about.
registration_success: I was fortunate to get into all 4 classes that I wanted to. After arriving at Monash, I wanted to change one of my classes to another one (one that I had also gotten a pre-approval for from KU) and this process was also very smooth. The employee at Monash Connect helped me apply for the other class, and a few days later, I was registered for that one instead.
registration_advice: Ask for help if there is anything you are not sure about. The people at Monash Connect are really friendly and they are there to help you. It can be a bit overwhelming coming to a new university and figuring out all the processes and terminology, so just asking about the things you don't understand is really my best advice.
academics_comments: I have really enjoyed my exchange semester in Melbourne and I would encourage everyone, who has the opportunity to go on exchange, to do so. You grow a lot as a person by living in a foreign country.
course_level: The level of the courses varied quite a bit. I took one course on the Australian economy and one on the Chinese economy, and these two courses were essentially the same except from the fact that they focused on two different economies. However, their structure and evaluation processes were very similar. They required quite a lot of reading but they were not difficult courses. For both courses, the teachers also explained to us that they were not meant to be difficult but rather to bring new perspectives and help students understand how each economy works. I really enjoyed both classes and even though it was a lot of readings, I did not mind it as it was very interesting. Then I also took an accounting class called Business Analytics and the level in this class was really low. Even though I've only taken one other accounting class in my entire life, I was able to easily pass this class without spending much time on it throughout the semester. Thus, it was really not demanding and I would not say I learned a lot from it, but it was nice to have one easy class when my other three classes were so demanding. Lastly, I took an introduction to programming in Java class and this was by far the most difficult class for me. I probably spent around 60% of my study time on this class. As an economics student it was also a bit optimistic to take a class in software development. Nonetheless, I absolutely loved this class. I learned so much from this class. My teacher was super good and our three TAs were so helpful. Without them, I am not sure I would've gotten through this class. The level was very high and on average 20% of the students in the class fail. But if you put an effort into it, you get 10x back from taking this class.
teaching_comparison: There are a lot more evaluations throughout the semester in Australia. For example, your assignments will count towards your final grade, you will have a midterm, sometimes weekly quizzes as well as a final exam. Your grade for the class will then be affected by all of those evaluations. I think this is very different from KU where your exam is everything. The way it is structured in Australia makes it more demanding as you cannot slack throughout the semester if you want a good grade. On the other hand, your grade will not be depending on one thing and on you being on your best on the certain day of the exam.
courses_enrolled: At Monash, I took the following classes: - ACF5320: Business Analytics - ECX5631: The Australian Economy - ECX5630: Chinese economy and global business - FIT9131: Programming foundations in Java
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend The Australian Economy and Chinese Economy and Global Business. I really enjoyed those classes and you cannot find anything similar at KU. Furthermore, they are not too difficult to pass. I think the level is very good when you're an exchange student - you learn a lot but you still have time to explore the city as well.
unexpected_costs: If you go on exchange in Melbourne as a master student, beware that you cannot get a discount on the local transportation as bachelor students can. This means that local transportation can quickly become very expensive. Student organisations have fought for discounts to grad students for more than 20 years but still without luck. Note that this is only for cities in the state of Victoria. All other states in Australia have discounts for grad students as well.
cost_comparison: Flight tickets were a lot more expensive than I expected. Food was also more expensive than I expected but this might have been due to the inflation as a result of the pandemic which many countries have experienced.
activities_available: There were a lot of different clubs available. I cannot remember all of them but I know they had an association for grad students where they sometimes organised events. They also offered different sports clubs i.e. tennis, swimming etc., outdoor clubs, a club for Australians as well as foreigners who are interested in exchanges and many others.
activities_recommended: I lived quite far from the campus and therefore I did not take part in any clubs. You can certainly still take part in clubs even if you decide to live far from campus, but for me I just had so many other things to do. The unfortunate thing about Monash is that their campus (at least Clayton campus which is the big one) is about an hour from downtown. Thus, many exchange students chose to stay closer to the city instead. It was not a problem at all as the public transportation system in Melbourne is quite good.
weekend_recommendations: I would definitely recommend that you do the Great Ocean Road. Furthermore, Wilson's Promontory is also very beautiful and worth a weekend trip. There are also a lot of activities going on in Melbourne and you can easily find several activities to fill up your weekend with in the city. There are several accounts on instagram that you can follow to get tips on what's going on in the city and surrounding areas such as "whatsonmelb" and "nathsway".
culture_adjustment: It was extremely easy for me. I did not have the slightest feeling of culture shock but I have also lived in North America for 4 years and Denmark the rest of my live. Australia is a good mixture of North America and Europe, so it felt like home for me.
socializing_tips: Don't be afraid to talk to students in your class. It can be hard to make friends with the locals because they already have friends, family and maybe a job they need to pay attention to. But Australians are very friendly and they'd be happy to talk to you.
cultural_challenges: None just all the insects and animals haha.
culture_appreciated: Australians are nice and friendly and the coffee is absolutely amazing. Seriously, at least in Melbourne, you find excellent coffee on every street corner - and enjoy the coffee while you're there because you won't find the same quality when you get back home. The best coffee I've ever had was from Studio Beans in St Kilda.
top3_advice: Go with an open mind and a positive attitude and I promise you it will be an amazing experience. The two weeks before the semester starts are extremely important as this is where you have a chance to meet other students. Take advantage of this and make sure you attend as many events as possible. Do not be afraid to approach people and ask them where they are from. There are a lot of exchange students from Denmark, the Netherlands and Germany in Australia, so you will find many people who come from a similar culture as you.
other_useful_info: Choose your classes wisely. Decide what you want to get out of your exchange semester: whether you want to take challenging classes where you will learn a lot or if you would rather take easier classes that allows you to have more time for other things. Do your research well and beware that at Monash there are quite a lot of courses that do not have a final exam. If you are smart, you can choose only courses with no final exam.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was to get to live in Australia and learn about the Australian culture. It was really amazing. Sharing the experience with so many other exchange students was also really nice as well as taking classes that taught me things I could've not taken back home.
greatest_challenge: In the beginning I found it very hard to find my group of people. I wanted to have some people that were as close as my friends back home but that takes time. Some of the others did find friends that they became extremely close to but I did not. Nonetheless, I accepted that that was also ok. I have two large groups of people that I could always reach out to to do fun activities with. I came to accept that for the time I was in Australia, it was very ok to not have any very close friends but having many that I got along with well and could have a good time with was also amazing.
other_comments: Go go go! I can only give my best recommendations to go on exchange and in particular go to Australia. It was amazing.

crucial_aspects: Unique opportunity: It’s not every day that you get the chance to go all the way to Australia. The opportunity to study in such a distant and unique country was a once-in-a-lifetime experience that I couldn’t miss. It was also important for me to go to an English-speaking country to further improve my English skills but also benefit my academic and professional pursuits. Academic reputation: The host university is Australia’s biggest university and is renowned for its strong academic programs, particularly in my field of study. I was excited about the opportunity to enhance my academic knowledge and skills, especially by undertaking units that the University of Copenhagen do not offer. The university offered a wide range of units to choose from, providing me with the flexibility to tailor my studies according to my interests and career goals, which was a crucial aspect of my decision. Cultural experience: Particularly, I wanted to learn about the unique cultural aspects of the destination. I believe that understanding diverse cultures is crucial for personal growth and global awareness, especially because we do not learn much about the importance of culture, which has a significant influence on public health. Geographical location: The destination’s location was ideal for exploring other parts of Australia by being situated in a central location with good transportation links. The opportunity to travel around and explore the rest of Australia was highly appealing, and the country's diverse landscapes and unique wildlife were significant attractions for me.
overall_comments: Overall, my study abroad experience was very positive and unforgettable. While the academic level at the university was somewhat lower than I had expected, I believe this was partly due to the specific units I chose, some of which were at the undergraduate level. However, this allowed me to have more free time to travel, meet new people, and explore the country, which was a significant part of the exchange experience. Socially, there were fewer organized events and the introduction to the university and fellow students was different from what I had anticipated, and it was easier to meet people outside of the university as many lectures were conducted online. This balance of academics and social life contributed to a highly rewarding overall experience.
info_ease: It was quite easy. You were well-guided both by your home university and the host university. I also feel that the most work was before the exchange, and once you were there, it was mostly about getting settled with the new university’s programs and finding your way with the units.
arrival_assistance: None.
arrival_comments: The orientation and introduction were different from what I expected, with fewer organized social events and a different approach to getting to know fellow students. The assistance was good, if needed. Overall, I was still very satisfied with my host institution.

registration_help: Detailed guides and personal assistance
registration_success: Pretty successful. I corresponded with someone from Monash’s exchange office who helped me sign up for the units I wanted. There was a mention of a policy about how many undergraduate courses I could take, but they couldn’t provide details on it. I also pointed out that the main concern was whether my home university would accept the credits. After that, they updated my registration to include the units I wanted, which were approved by the University of Copenhagen.
registration_advice: Make sure to thoroughly review all the information sent by both your home and host universities - they provide detailed guides and are ready to help if you run into any issues.

However, this allowed me to have more free time to travel, meet new people, and explore the country, which was a significant part of the exchange experience. Socially, there were fewer organized events and the introduction to the university and fellow students was different from what I had anticipated, and it was easier to meet people outside of the university as many lectures were conducted online. This balance of academics and social life contributed to a highly rewarding overall experience.
course_level: As mentioned earlier, the level of the units was somewhat lower than what I was used to from the University of Copenhagen. However, I didn’t see this as a disadvantage. It meant less stress and allowed more time for other important aspects of the exchange experience. It was nice not to worry too much about passing. There were two undergraduate courses that were a bit too easy, almost to the point of being demotivating. Despite this, I still learned a lot, even though the support was more hands-on. One of the courses was very easy for the instructors, which was a bit disappointing because a lot of the content was relevant, but the course design felt a bit lazy. Additionally, the assignment requirements were quite strict, and often didn’t provide enough space or word count to include all the examples and details they asked for. This made the requirements somewhat superficial, as the format didn’t allow for a thorough exploration of the topics.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at my host institution was quite different from UCPH. There was more online teaching, including lectures, which was a shift from what I was used to. On the plus side, all relevant materials were available online, and I didn’t have to spend money on textbooks. In terms of support, I felt much more guided and supported compared to UCPH. At UCPH, there’s generally more responsibility placed on students, and you’re expected to be more self-reliant. At the host institution, the approach was more hands-on and supportive, which made the experience a bit easier. That said, I also took some units that are typically taken by students early in their studies at the host university, which might have influenced my experience and perception of the teaching style. Further there was a higher emphasis on assignments during the semester rather than just one big exam at the end, meaning the work-load was a bit more distributed.
courses_enrolled: PBH2003 - Culture, society and health ATS1297 - Academic writing PG5136 - Mindfulness for workplace wellbeing and productivity APG5367 - Campaigns, advocacy and change
recommended_courses: I recommend all the units I took, but if I had to choose differently, I might have picked HSC2200 - Health across the Lifespan instead of Academic Writing. The units I took were all well-executed, interesting, and complemented my public health studies at UCPH very well. • Academic Writing was good, but it didn’t have much engagement from other students, and most of the activities were led by the lecturer. The content was also quite introductory, which might not be as beneficial for someone who has already been studying for a while. While I did learn a lot about written English, I might have found Health across the Lifespan more enriching in terms of relevant theory for Public Health. • PBH2003 - Culture, Society, and Health: This course provided valuable insights into Aboriginals and Torres Strait Islanders and gave a broader understanding of the Australian health and healthcare system. • PG5136 - Mindfulness for Workplace Wellbeing and Productivity: This was a fantastic course with evidence-based techniques that I can use in my future job, studies, and personal life. • APG5367 - Campaigns, Advocacy, and Change: I learned a lot about communication and advocacy, which I find applicable in various contexts when communication with the public and other institutions.
unexpected_costs: I encountered a few unexpected costs. I hadn’t initially budgeted for items such as towels, dishcloths, and cleaning cloths. Additionally, I needed to buy lunchbox wrapping, tupperwares, duvets, and pillows, as well as various kitchen essentials like pots and cups. These expenses added up more than I had anticipated. Furher as it felt like a big vacation you spend alot more than you would at home, especially since Australia is almost as expensive as Denmark.
cost_comparison: I had a fairly clear idea of what things would cost in Australia beforehand. Most items, including food, are about 10% cheaper than in Denmark, but they’re still on the pricier side. Coffee, however, is significantly cheaper - about half the price compared to Denmark. For home essentials, you can find many affordable items at Kmart and IKEA. On the other hand, most local experiences, for example boat trips to the Great Barrier Reef, turned out to be quite expensive. These activities can cost between 200-400 AUD per person, which was higher than I anticipated.
activities_available: There were a wide variety of activities available, though most were centered at Clayton Campus, which wasn’t where I spent most of my time. While there were many opportunities to get involved, I didn’t actively participate in any of these campus-based events. Instead, I focused on the free events, festivals, and activities that took place frequently in and around Melbourne. These events were a great way to meet other exchange students, local students, and residents, and they contributed to a rich and enjoyable experience.
activities_recommended: The free events, festivals, and activities that took place frequently in and around Melbourne CBD.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend taking advantage of the many free events happening in and around Melbourne. You can find a good overview of these on the WhatsOn website, which lists festivals, markets, and more. Explore the beautiful hiking trails in the various mountain ranges and national parks around Melbourne, such as The Grampians, Werribee Gorge, Cathedral Ranges, and Wilsons Promontory National Park. Be sure to visit the beaches south of Melbourne, especially Half Moon Bay Beach and Brighton Beach. A trip to Phillip Island is also worth it. For a broader Australian adventure, consider traveling around the country in a campervan, particularly along the East Coast to see the Great Barrier Reef, through the Outback, and to Tasmania during the summer. Don’t miss driving the Great Ocean Road and visiting the many parks and lookouts in and around Melbourne, like Point Ormond. These activities offer a fantastic way to experience the natural beauty and diverse attractions Australia has to offer.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture in Melbourne was relatively smooth. The city’s multicultural environment and the openness of Australians made it easy to adapt and feel welcome. While there were some challenges, like understanding local customs and navigating different social dynamics, these were manageable and part of the learning experience. Overall, the friendly and inclusive atmosphere helped me integrate and enjoy my time in Melbourne.
socializing_tips: To make the most of your social experience and connect with local students, start by engaging with those in student accommodations or visiting their places to meet new people. Take advantage of the many events and festivals happening in and around Melbourne - these gatherings are perfect for meeting both locals and fellow exchange students. Joining campus activities, such as clubs and sports, can also be a great way to meet people with similar interests. Make sure to participate in orientation programs and university events, as these are designed to help you integrate and meet new friends. Being open and proactive is key. Attend gatherings and activities organized by others, and don’t hesitate to take the initiative to join or organize hiking tours and other group trips that are frequently set up on Facebook. Lastly, maintaining a friendly and approachable attitude will help you connect with others and build meaningful relationships.
cultural_challenges: One cultural difference that I found challenging was interacting with Indigenous people. Their historical background and strong sense of territory can make these interactions feel delicate, and there’s a concern about inadvertently offending or doing something wrong. Although there were relatively few Indigenous people on the streets, and most are not likely to cause harm, the presence of homeless people and those struggling with substance abuse in the evenings made me prefer not to walk around alone after dark. Despite this, I generally felt safe on the streets overall.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the multiculturalism in Melbourne and the friendliness and openness of Australians and other residents. It was impressive how easy it was to strike up conversations with people everywhere, which made the experience feel welcoming and inclusive. Additionally, it was easy to build relationships and meet new people, contributing to a very positive and engaging experience.
top3_advice: Firstly, choose your campus wisely depending on whether you want to be close to Melbourne CBD or prefer more on-campus activities. Caulfield Campus is great for city access, while Clayton Campus offers more campus-based social options. Secondly, be prepared for potential housing challenges if you opt for private (off-campus) accommodation; secure your place early and have a backup plan in case your initial arrangements fall through. Lastly, actively engage in Melbourne’s local scene by attending events, joining clubs, and networking through social groups. Being proactive will significantly enhance your exchange experience.
other_useful_info: If you prefer to be close to Melbourne CBD, where most of the events and activities take place, Caulfield Campus is a great choice. It offers convenient access to the city and minimizes travel time. On the other hand, Clayton Campus provides more on-campus social activities and accommodation options, but it may involve longer travel time to the city. Many students at Clayton found themselves having to leave events early or split an Uber, as public transport options are limited in the evenings. Consider what suits your lifestyle and interests best when choosing between the campuses. If you value proximity to the city and a more manageable travel time, Caulfield might be the better option. If you’re interested in a vibrant on-campus social scene and don’t mind the extra travel, Clayton could be ideal.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was everything about it - I would gladly do it all over again. The chance to immerse myself in a new culture, meet diverse people, study at a different university, and experience a different academic environment, along with exploring Melbourne and beyond as well as other parts of Australia, made the experience truly unforgettable.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was dealing with housing issues. Initially, the living situation with my first roommates didn’t work out, which led to the stress of finding new accommodation midway through my exchange. This added a layer of difficulty to my experience, as I had to balance the search for a new place with my studies and other activities. Despite this challenge, I managed to find another suitable place and continue enjoying my time abroad.
other_comments: Go for it and make the most of your time abroad—you will never regret it! Melbourne is the perfect place for an exchange in Australia.

crucial_aspects: The choice of Monash University as my study destination was based on its strong academic standing in Economics, Econometrics and Finance, offering tailored elective courses that aligned with my academic goals. The university's diverse campus environment and the appeal of experiencing Australias unique culture were key factors influencing my decision.
info_ease: Upon arriving late at Monash University, I found the institution to be exceptionally helpful with the onboarding process. Despite my delayed arrival, the university's well-organized support systems, orientation sessions, and online resources efficiently assisted me in accessing essential information about academics, campus facilities, accommodation, and student services.
arrival_assistance: Upon my arrival at Monash University, I received assistance through an onboarding session tailored for new students. I also had the chance to take a campus tour, which helped me get acquainted with the university facilities and layout.
arrival_comments: None
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Firstly, for an Australian visa, an online university registration is required, so it's essential to complete this promptly. At Monash University, the registration process involves orientation sessions on university policies, academic requirements, and available resources. Subsequently, students utilize an online portal to select their courses.
registration_help: Monash University has a specialized department that offers support to incoming foreign students. They provide guidance on visas, accommodations, course registration, and orientation.
registration_success: Registering for the classes I wanted went smoothly without any issues.
registration_advice: Plan early
course_level: I took courses which were MA or Ph.d.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at my host institution differed notably from UCPH. Monash University's courses were more applied compared to what I was accustomed to at Copenhagen University. For instance, while assignments throughout the semester focused on applied econometrics, the end-of-term exams primarily tested theoretical knowledge.
courses_enrolled: International Economics Bank Lending Macroeconometrics Applied Derivatives
recommended_courses: I highly recommend the course "Applied Derivatives" to future exchange students. Despite its challenging nature, this course was incredibly rewarding, providing the most learning and enjoyment during my exchange. The practical application of derivatives in this course offered a valuable learning experience, making it both intellectually stimulating and enjoyable.
unexpected_costs: I encountered no noteworthy unexpected costs during my time abroad.
cost_comparison: In Australia, regular food shopping has become more expensive compared to just a year ago. Housing costs were also higher than anticipated. However, eating out and enjoying coffee at cafes is relatively cheaper compared to Denmark.
activities_available: At Monash University, students had access to diverse cultural events, athletic facilities with sports activities and fitness classes. The university hosted social gatherings, movie nights, and networking events. Additionally, volunteering and community service opportunities were available.
activities_recommended: I didn't attend any non-academic activities during my exchange :)
weekend_recommendations: I recommend visiting students to explore both the city of Melbourne and its beautiful natural surroundings during weekends or holidays. Melbourne offers a vibrant cultural scene, including museums, art galleries, diverse cuisine, and bustling markets to explore. Additionally, the natural landscapes surrounding Melbourne, such as the Great Ocean Road, Yarra Valley wineries, and nearby national parks, offer stunning scenery and outdoor activities for a refreshing break from city life. Consider using services like Turo or Uber Car Share to easily hire cars for trips outside the city.
culture_adjustment: Adapting to the local culture at my exchange site was very easy. Australia being an English-speaking country with cultural similarities to Europe in general facilitated a smooth adjustment for me.
socializing_tips: I mainly socialized with Danish students abroad, so no. But international student are usually very willing to meet new people.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any cultural differences particularly challenging during my time in Australia. Australians are quite similar to urban Danes, although I noticed that they tended to be more outgoing and initiate conversations more frequently.
culture_appreciated: The aspect of the culture that I most appreciated was the friendly and non-judgmental attitude of the people. I found that individuals generally behaved kindly and were open-minded, creating a welcoming and accepting atmosphere.
top3_advice: Take time to explore not only the university but also the city of Melbourne and its surrounding areas. Venture out to experience the vibrant city life, beautiful natural landscapes, and diverse cultural offerings that the region has to offer. AND LIVE OUTSIDE CAMPUS!
other_useful_info: None that i havent already mentioned.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding aspects of my exchange experience were the valuable learning opportunities and the overall experience of living abroad. Both aspects enriched my perspective, allowed personal growth, and provided memorable experiences that I cherish.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was finding housing. Initially, I stayed at an Airbnb for the first two weeks until I secured accommodation. I highly recommend starting the search for private housing months in advance. Personally, I started my search only a month before arriving in Melbourne, which proved to be insufficient time. Starting the housing search early can alleviate the stress of finding accommodation upon arrival.
other_comments: I hope you get the chance of going to Melbourne on exchange :)!

crucial_aspects: Different culture, nature and architecture to Denmark. I wanted to choose a study destination which was known for good weather and that was a safe travel destination.
info_ease: It wasn't that easy. Even though I got help from the host institution, a lot of information was (both for good and bad) left unexplained to find out for one self. Overall, I was able to finde the information I needed without too much strain and effort.
arrival_assistance: I was welcomed by the host instituion and their abroad group. They were very helpful in a lot of ways. However, I didn't need most of the information that they provided.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I had to formally apply and choose the courses I wanted from a list I had already made. Then, I had to set up a user for their website and other platforms (which was pretty easy). All in all, the process is easy to follow and doesn't take long.
registration_help: There were people to talk to, chat bots and phone numbers you could call to get help.
registration_success: I was successful with all courses.
registration_advice: Understand that this instituion (by deafult) relies on a good reputation and therefore demand a lot from their students. Meaning, there's many assignments during semester (which often aren't coordinated well with other units, especially for exchange students), teachers would like students to be active and do their pre-reading before class. However, it's not as bad as it sounds. Exams are often off-campus and without supervision, meaning you can sit at home and not have to feel like you're being watched whilst doing your exams. Most lectures are done via Zoom and recorded so you don't have to be there every time.
course_level: I chose three courses for third year bachelor's and one for second year. The one's that were for third year were, of course, more hard than the one for second year.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. There's many assignments during the semester which also count towards the final grade. In-person classes are very active and often have some sort of experimental case or topic of debate around it. Lectures were recorded and could be watched at home.
courses_enrolled: BIO2040 - Conservation Biology, BIO3132 - Biology of Australian Vertebrates, BIO3070 - Advanced Ecology and Evolution, BIO3052 - Animal Behavior.
recommended_courses: "BIO3052 - Animal Behavior" was an excellent course which is well-praised for its excellent teaching method with weekly meetings with a mentor for a project and a seminar afterwards (the seminars are even recorded and can be seen at home). The project you're doing is very interesting and fun, and you get to meet new people and try and make your own experiment. Your mentors are very good at making sure everyone is doing their job and not leaving anyone behind. The exam is off-campus and is very short. If you listen in on the seminars and note down the important stuff from them, you're pretty much guaranteed to pass. "BIO3132 - Biology of Australian Vertebrates" was amazing by having multiple field studies and case studies where the student is forced to think for themself and be more independent. There's a lot of work during the semester, but it's so worth it. Many of the assignments are even based on forms and reports that many students that graduate will do in the future. You also learn all about the amazing fauna of Australia and some of its history. The exam is also off-campus and short. And it only counts for 30% of the final grade. So, if you get good grades on your assignments, you won't even have to pass nor attend the exam technically.
unexpected_costs: Food can be very expensive (unless you make it yourself, then it's mostly cheaper than DK prices). Travelling is very expensive. Transportation is expensive in the long run.
cost_comparison: Transportation, processed foods, housing.
activities_available: There were many different groups and classes to attend in your spare time. They had a whole sports centre for people interested in sports. There were also many oppurtunities to speak with christian mentors and other religious people.
activities_recommended: I very much enjoyed badminton as I did in my youth. Many people from Australia, specifically in Melbourne, are from Asia. They're very good and super friendly.
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes around Melbourne. The hills and mountains around the city are sublime, absolutely astonishing. The Great Ocean Road is definitely a must see. Go visit at least one sanctuary in the city, and visit the Melbourne Zoo and Sea Life. Also, there's an 11h ferry to Tasmania from Melbourne which is delightful. Another must see is the east coast. Even if you don't like beaches or sunbathing, the east coast is so big and diverse that you're bound to find something that's to your liking.
culture_adjustment: It took some time, but I pretty much adjusted to it after 2 weeks.
socializing_tips: Go to different social clubs, attend classes at uni, go out and party, message people in the city on Facebook or Whats-app to plan travelling with other people.
cultural_challenges: Some people in classes stick to a clique and don't really let anyone else in. This can be hard as an exchange student. Most people need to have a full-time job to afford rent and living expenses so it can be hard to plan with Aussies.
culture_appreciated: They're very friendly by saying hello and waving when walking by or shopping/going on a reastaurant. Many non-Aussies are welcomed with open arms. Australia is indeed a multicultural country.
top3_advice: 1. Work load is hard and a lot more than DK 2. Socialising can be hard, especially as an exchange student. Make sure you attend some social club or other do some other form of socialization at least once or twice per week. 3. Don't let the size of Australia scare you. Start small, explore your own city first and then venture out to see the beauty that is Australia.
other_useful_info: Money are expendable, don't hog on money and spend as little as possible every day (unless you're broke). Studying abroad is a once in a lifetime oppurtunity that should be expensive, but also filled with memories, adventures, friends and fun. You can always earn more money when you're back, or you can extend your stay and work there.
most_rewarding: Travelling. Going out and exploring and taking in some of the breath taking scenic views of Autralia is so worth it. Even going a few hours to another city provides you with such a different experience than the last one. Australia is so big that there's something for everyone. You can even go skiing in the "cold" winter months.
greatest_challenge: Dealing with being on your own and not having your family around or anyone else can be very stressful and hard to deal with. It makes you tough and more independent. It provides you with valuable experiences that forces you to get out of your comfort zone and get out of bed. For me, this is the greatest challenge, but also a neccesity which many people lack in this modern world.

crucial_aspects: As a student of Food Innovation and Health, it was important to me that the destination where I would spend one semester had a broad range of cultures represented. This is because I seek to explore new cuisines, new ways of operating a food service or just to grasp how other cultures perceive food and interact with their local environment providing it. I had already gained insight into the food culture of Melbourne from friends, and in this I was assured that I wouldn't be disappointed in regards to what the city has to offer.
info_ease: It was quite easy as the abroad office on-campus was very helpful. However, arriving and adjusting to a new system and interface(s), definitely needed time.
arrival_assistance: The study abroad team were good a organizing study start events. The university did a great job at offering various services such as pick up from the airport and offering help and guidance for particular challenges one might face during ones studies.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was a very tough process. I didn't realize how different it would be from what I was used to in my home country, where you automatically are assigned courses and they do not clash. Having a schedule with four courses that did not clash and cause schedule issues by the start of the semester, was quite stressful and time consuming.
registration_help: Staff that specialized in helping with allocating courses and making schedules that fit.
registration_success: Not overly successful, as some of my preferencial courses clashed and I had to find new ones.
registration_advice: Pick AT LEAST eight viable courses that you find interesting, consider carefully that you live up to the requirements and get pre-approval for all of them, so that if you are faced with course issues in the beginning, you're more flexible to move around courses.
course_level: Depending on the course and my own prerequisites to follow them, I found some of the courses to be beyond my capabilities and experience, and other courses were just about right in terms of level and work load.
teaching_comparison: Again, depending on the course, some courses are very interactive, where you have weekly mandatory assignments and participation activites (smaller ones), which I found to be quite demanding in the beginning, but eventually adapted to and liked. Overall I found the workload to be more individualistic rather than based on group work, although there also is group work most of the time.
courses_enrolled: Intergrated Marketing Communication Food, Nutrition and Health Food Chemistry Startup Fundamentals: From setting up to securing investment
recommended_courses: Food Chemistry - If you love chemistry and food, this is definitely the course for you. However, the course is very intensive with a high workload. There are 5 laboratory exercises with individual reports that need to be done throughout the semester, with mandatory weekly quizzes, a mid-semester exam, a group oral presentation and a final exam. Integrated Marketing Communication - A very interactive course that has a good mixture of lectures, assignments, in-class discussions and weekly assignments (smaller ones). The feedback given throughout the course makes for a good learning outcome and it is overall digestible. Startup Fundamentals - A much different approach to learning, with various group oriented task and formats that are a welcoming change to traditional types of learning activities.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Some food items were cheaper than back home, some were remarkably more expensive.
activities_available: Yoga, swimming, fitness, dancing etc.
activities_recommended: I would recommend to go as much out and explore nature. It is simply just beautiful.
weekend_recommendations: Visit the various food markets around, explore a new neighborhood by bike every week.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, although the one negative is the car culture. They love their cars, but they do have the best infrastructure for public transport in Australia (apparently), although it could become much better.
socializing_tips: Be curious, open minded and have a chat!
cultural_challenges: Their car culture and infrastructure. If only they knew how much more liveable a pedestrian/cyclist/public transport city is, Melbourne could become the best city to live in the world.
culture_appreciated: Friendliness and very multi-cultural.
top3_advice: Do not get on campus accommodation near/on Clayton if you like to explore the city and be immersed in the culture. Find at least 8 viable courses and have them all pre-approved before you arrive to Melbourne. Buy a bike and explore the city freely.
other_useful_info: Compared to UCHP, I overall fond the assessment criteria to be based on individual work. At UCPH I've mostly done group work (reports or presentation) and then prepared for an individual oral or written exam. At Monash, although there are still group assignments and presentations, I found that the university really emphasises its students to become self dependent and manage their on work individually.
most_rewarding: Gaining a fruitful insight into how a slightly different education system works and how becoming better at being independent and managing work alone.
greatest_challenge: Having my courses allocated and finding new viable courses that I also needed to get pre-approved

crucial_aspects: Ville gerne til Australien og helst Melbourne.

Det skal man lige være obs på. Men Monash er gode med kursuslister og svare flinkt på alle ens mails med spørgsmål.

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Det var en virkelig god oplevelse. Melbourne er en nice by, australiere er hyggelige og rejsemulighederne mens man er dernede er virkelig gode. Oplev en masse natur og hyg er mit bedste råd, mens man er dernede.
registration_process: Man ansøger om de kurser man ønsker, tror man ønsker 6-8 i prioriterede rækkefølge. Efter får man at vide hvilke fire kurser man har fået. Derefter skal man registrere hvilket hold man ønsker at tage. Vær obs på at man kan tage mange kurser udelukkende online, man skal derfor være opmærksom på at tilvælge kursushold med fysisk fremmøde, så man ikke skal bruge et helt semester på zoom.
registration_help: Skriv til monash på mail hvis man er i tvivl.
registration_success: Jeg fik de fire kurser jeg ville. Men man skal være hurtig til at få tilmeldt sig kursushold med de gode tidspunkter. Da kurser bliver udbudt med mange hold med hvert sit tidspunkt skal man lige være opmærksom på at få en af de gode pladser
registration_advice: Skulle nogle af ens kurser komme til at overlappe, så kontakt monash. Det er meget fleksibelt at skifte kurser de første to uger, og der opstår altid plads på et hold der er fyldt ud til at starte med, fordi mange skifter hold.
academics_comments: Det var en virkelig god oplevelse. Melbourne er en nice by, australiere er hyggelige og rejsemulighederne mens man er dernede er virkelig gode. Oplev en masse natur og hyg er mit bedste råd, mens man er dernede.
course_level: Niveauet er skræmmende lavt til tider. Jeg kunne skrive en lang smøre, men pretty much er niveauet til tider virkelig lavt fordi mange asiatiske studerende tager til australien for at læse på uni, men de besidder virkelig ringe engelskkundskaber hvilket trækker niveauet af undervisningen gevaldigt ned. Dertil er det akademiske niveau på masteren bare langt under KU. Men altså, så er der tid til så meget andet. Dog er underviserne meget vidende og der er rig mulighed for at bidrage til undervisningen. Undervisningsformen og karakterer er dog baseret på et vægtet gennemsnit af mange opgaver gennem semesteret. F.eks. tæller fremlæggelser en del. Men bekymringer omkring sit eget niveauet skal man ikke have. Man kan sagtens følge med.
teaching_comparison: Jamen undervisningsformen er anderledens. Bl.a. med mødepligt til minimum 80% af undervisningen, fremlæggelser osv. Dertil er de skriftlige opgaver relativ nemme. Der er ikke så store krav til metode og sådan, det er meget mere bare at skrive en sammenhængende og velargumenterede essay med akademiske referencer. Det er forholdsvis overskuelige 30 ECTS point at få.
courses_enrolled: International political economy; Understadning Development; Poverty, inequality and opportunity; International institutions and organisations
recommended_courses: Poverty, inequality and opportunity - god og vidende professor, og jeg lærte faktisk en del grundet min egen interesse for kurset, trods størstedelen af klassen kun kunne fremføre et middelmådigt engelsk.
unexpected_costs: Det australske visum - det er godt nok dyrt. Skal du til Monash kan du nøjes med et working holiday visum. Det er halv pris af et studievisum. Monash fraråder det, men det kan man se bort fra. Det vil jeg klart anbefale at tage.
cost_comparison: Øl, virkelig dyrt. Fødevarer også til den dyre ende, bliv gode venner med Aldi det bliver din pengepung glad for.
activities_available: Jamen alt muligt. Uni er virkelig stort, og mange muligheder for at finde noget til enhver smag.
activities_recommended: Rejs ud i Australien. Tasmanien er et must, en virkelig skønt sted Dronning Mary kommer fra. Ellers lej en bil eller tag offentlig og kom lidt ud af byen til tider. Virkelig meget natur at se.
weekend_recommendations: Rejs, tag på stranden og surf eller læg i solen eller hyg med de andre danskere. Der er så meget at se/gøre.
culture_adjustment: Relativt nemt, mange kulturer i Melbourne.
socializing_tips: Det er lidt svært at komme ind på livet af australiere til tider, men man møder altid nogle søde på sin vej.
cultural_challenges: Ikke noget særligt.
culture_appreciated: Australierne, de er sgu så søde
top3_advice: Nyd din tid. Det går stærkt. Tag nogle lidt sjove fag, hvis du kan få dem forhåndsgodkendt. Så man får oplevet lidt nyt.
other_useful_info: Hvis du er i tvivl, tag afsted. Selvom det koster lidt.
most_rewarding: Opleve australien
greatest_challenge: Andre undervisningsformer, men det er også sjovt at prøve.

housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_advice: I would advice you to go to the orientation week.
course_level: The level of the courses was good. I found it easier to get high grades in Australia than in Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: I had way more online teaching than I have at UCPH. All my lectures were online, so I only had to be at the university physically when I had tutorials.
courses_enrolled: Organisational Behaviour Sustainable Human Resource Management Men, masculinity and society Gender and sexuality in film and television
recommended_courses: I would recommend the course "Men, masculinity and society" if you are interested in learning about masculinity/different forms of masculinity, the gender hierarchy, and much more.

cost_comparison: Grocery shopping is a bit more expensive than in Denmark, I would say.

cultural_challenges: It is a good idea to learn some Australian slang words since they use slang a lot.
culture_appreciated: The nature and the people. The nature is incredibly beautiful and the people are very sociable and kind.
top3_advice: I would tell you to find accommodation in Melbourne city since the campus is a bit far away. Since a lot of the teaching was online, it was more fun to stay close to the city because you didn't go to campus every day. It is easy to go with public transportation to Caulfield and Clayton campus from the city, it just takes a bit more time, but it is worth it to stay in the city. I would also tell you to socialize with the other exchange students, I met so many great people. And get the app where you can see the campus if you are going to the Clayton campus, since it is huge. Be there in good time before class.

most_rewarding: The people I met.
greatest_challenge: I found it a bit difficult to write the first research paper in English, also because they write a bit differently from what I am used to. But it worked out fine.

academics_comments: This mark is shaped by my partner traveling with me (very positive).
course_level: This was the last semester of my Master's degree and the first MA semester for many of the people in my classes. There is a participation-expectation in class discussions during the tutorials. I found this easy enough because I kept up with the readings. This is similar to UCPH, however, many of my international student friends expressed that it was hard to do in-class discussions because it was not expected of them during their BA.
teaching_comparison: It is more handheld in the sense that rubrics are given for assignments that you have to follow (cookie-cutter in this way). I liked that there were many different assignments with different grade weights compared to the final paper and final grade system at UCPH (humanities). Because of how big the university is, we had an online lecture and then there were many (so many!) workshops with a tutor and us students (20 or so). This was much different than my small UCPH classes.
courses_enrolled: Photography Understanding Media Audiences Principles of Global Media and Communication Cultural Policy
recommended_courses: Since we ran focus groups every week in Understanding Media Audiences, this was a great chance to properly get to know fellow students. The same goes for photography where we took portraits in groups. I formed great friendships in these classes.
unexpected_costs: Nothing comes to mind. All the utilities were included where we were staying.
cost_comparison: Beer was pricey. Eating out was cheaper than in Denmark, as expected.
activities_available: The clubs my friends (see above) were part of were career-oriented communications clubs. There were also some creative ones, but I do not remember those well. I was not interested in joining clubs while on my MA exchange because I had the impression that they were mainly directed to MA students. While on my BA exchange in another Anglophone country, I did participate in many clubs and found it very fun and a good way to meet people.
activities_recommended: I think that there were some hiking ones, which would be fun, especially if you are coming here on your own.
weekend_recommendations: I loved all the museums from galleries in CBD to more niche ones like the Tram Museum in Hawthorn. I would recommend spending time in different neighbourhoods for their distinct atmospheres (Brunswick, the Docks, Prahran etc.). I would also recommend going outside of the city (public transportation) for hikes (e.g. Dandenong).
culture_adjustment: Being part Anglo myself, there was nothing entirely shocking about the local culture. It was what I expected.
socializing_tips: My biggest tip is to get people's socials and not be shy to write to them and ask to grab a coffee or something.
cultural_challenges: My tutorials consisted 98% of Chinese international students, so that was a much different culture than I was expecting (more Australian) when I entered the classrooms. During class, they seemed a little intimidated by the setting and language, and often spoke Chinese amongst themselves. It was a little challenging to get to know them at first but as soon as I saw them outside of class they were super warm and friendly, somehow remembered my name, and made me feel included in their conversations. What I want to illustrate is that settings, such as classroom culture, may change people, and that it can be challenging at times to understand someone from one particular setting.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated my friendships with the Chinese international students because they were all so kind and we genuinely wanted to understand each other. I also really appreciated how gregarious Australians are (generalization, but I found that being talkative is a large part of the culture).
top3_advice: 1. It is over before you know it so enjoy it while it lasts. 2. Keeping up with the readings makes it easier in the long run. 3. Explore the city and surrounding areas as much as possible.
other_useful_info: I have said what I wanted to say.
most_rewarding: My friendships with people from different cultures than mine.
greatest_challenge: Honestly, the time and effort it takes to fly halfway across the globe.
