crucial_aspects: Several aspects were crucial in choosing my study destination. First and foremost, I wanted to study in an English-speaking country with a strong academic reputation in law. Monash University stood out due to its international outlook and the opportunity to take practice-oriented courses such as Law Chambers. I was also drawn to the cultural and geographical diversity of Australia, as well as the chance to experience a completely different legal system. Finally, the possibility of engaging in student life outside the classroom including sports, travel, and social activities played an important role in my decision.
info_ease: Most of the practical information I needed upon arrival was easy to find and well-communicated in advance by Monash University. The university provided helpful orientation materials and clear instructions through emails and the student portal. The international student welcome sessions were also very informative and covered everything from academic expectations to public transport and health services
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival, I received helpful assistance from Monash University through their international orientation program.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Before the semester started, I received detailed instructions by email on how to enroll in courses through the Monash online portal.
registration_help: During orientation week, there were support sessions available to help with enrolment issues, timetable clashes, or credit concerns.
registration_success: I was largely successful in registering for the classes I wanted. Monash University opened course registration on a specific date, and I made sure to register as early as possible, which helped secure a spot in my preferred units. While one of the practice-based courses was initially full, I was later able to enroll after contacting the faculty and being placed on a waitlist.
registration_advice: My main advice is to be well-prepared and proactive.
course_level: The level of courses at Monash University was academically solid and comparable to what I had experienced at my home university. Most law units required a strong understanding of legal principles, critical thinking, and independent analysis.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at Monash University was somewhat different from what I was used to at UCPH. While both universities emphasize critical thinking and academic rigor, Monash placed more focus on continuous assessment throughout the semester, including participation, group work, and written assignments. Lectures were often complemented by tutorials, which were smaller, discussion-based classes where students were expected to actively engage with the material.
courses_enrolled: Intellectual Property Law Environmental Law Australian legal system Migration and human righst
recommended_courses: The course I would most strongly recommend is Migration Law. The unit provided a comprehensive overview of Australia’s migration framework, including refugee and asylum law, with a strong focus on human rights and international obligations.
unexpected_costs: One of the main unexpected costs I encountered was the high price of groceries - Fresh produce and basic food items were noticeably more expensive than I had anticipated.
cost_comparison: many social and cultural activities offered student discounts or were free, which helped balance the overall cost of living.
activities_available: Monash University offered a wide range of cultural, athletic, and social activities for students. There were numerous student clubs and societies, including faculty-based groups, cultural associations, and hobby-based clubs. On the athletic side, Monash had excellent sports facilities, and students could join gym classes, sports teams, or casual competitions in sports like soccer, netball, basketball, and tennis. There were also outdoor trips like hiking and surfing excursions organized by student groups.
activities_recommended: I would highly recommend joining a student club or society, especially one outside your academic field. It’s a great way to meet local and international students and feel more connected to campus life. Clubs related to sports, hiking, or cultural exchange are particularly popular and often organize affordable weekend trips and social events.
weekend_recommendations: I highly recommend using weekends and holidays to explore the incredible diversity of Australia. From Melbourne, you can easily plan weekend trips to The Great Ocean Road. A must-see coastal drive with stunning beaches, cliffs, and the Twelve Apostles.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture in Melbourne was relatively easy. Australians are generally very friendly, open, and informal, which made it easy to feel welcome.
cultural_challenges: Overall, I didn’t find the cultural differences too challenging, but there were a few small things that required adjustment.
culture_appreciated: What I appreciated most about Australian culture was the laid-back and welcoming attitude. People were generally open, friendly, and easy to talk to, which made everyday interactions feel relaxed and enjoyable.
top3_advice: Be proactive with course registration and credit approval Start your housing search early Say yes to social opportunities and weekend trips
other_useful_info: One piece of advice I’d give is to arrive a bit early if possible — it gives you time to settle in, find housing (if you haven’t already), and get familiar with the campus and city before classes start.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the opportunity to step out of my comfort zone and grow both academically and personally.
greatest_challenge: Lastly, being far from home and in a very different time zone could occasionally feel isolating but staying connected with friends and being open to new social opportunities helped a lot.

crucial_aspects: I chose to go on exchange to Monash University in Melbourne because it has a strong reputation for law and offers a different perspective on legal studies. I wanted to learn more about how the legal system works in Australia and compare it to what I’ve studied at home. Melbourne is also a diverse and exciting city, which made it a great place to experience a new culture while continuing my studies. Monash has a welcoming environment for international students, and I knew I would gain both academic knowledge and personal growth from the experience
info_ease: The orientation at Monash University was well-organized and really helpful. It was easy to find the information I needed when I arrived. The staff and student volunteers were friendly and gave clear guidance on things like enrolling in classes, using campus facilities, and settling into life in Melbourne. The welcome sessions and tours made it easier to understand how everything worked, and there were plenty of resources available online as well. Overall, the support made the transition smooth and stress-free.
arrival_assistance: When I arrived at Monash University, I received helpful assistance through their orientation program. Staff and student volunteers were available to answer questions, help with directions, and explain how to set up things like student accounts, transport cards, and class registration. There were also welcome events and tours that made it easier to meet people and get familiar with the campus. Overall, the support made settling in much easier.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process at Monash University started before arrival, with emails explaining how to set up my student account and choose classes online. Once I arrived, the orientation week helped guide me through the final steps. I attended welcome sessions, confirmed my enrolment, and received my student ID. Staff and student volunteers were available to help with any issues, and most tasks could be done online through the Monash student portal. The process was smooth and well-organized.
registration_help: Monash University offered a lot of help for exchange students. During orientation, there were staff and student volunteers available to answer questions and guide us through things like enrolment, using campus facilities, and public transport. There were also information sessions, campus tours, and help desks. If you needed more support, you could book appointments with student services or ask for help at the international student office. Everyone was friendly and willing to help, which made settling in much easier.
registration_success: Registering for the classes I wanted was a bit challenging. It was difficult to organize my schedule so that the classes didn’t overlap, and the process was a little confusing at times. The course system and timetable were different from what I was used to, which made it harder to plan. However, with some patience and help from the staff, I was able to finalize my schedule in the end.
registration_advice: My advice for future exchange students is to start planning your classes early and double-check your timetable to avoid overlapping. Don’t be afraid to ask for help from staff if you’re confused—they’re there to support you. Take your time to understand the system, and be flexible with your choices.
course_level: The level of the courses at Monash University was adequate for my studies. They were challenging enough to help me learn and grow, but not too difficult to manage. The content matched what I expected and fit well with my background in law. Overall, the courses provided a good balance between theory and practical skills.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at Monash University was much more interactive compared to UCPH. There was a stronger focus on class discussions, group work, and practical examples, which made learning more engaging. At Monash, students were encouraged to actively participate and share their opinions, which was different from the more lecture-based approach I’m used to at UCPH.

recommended_courses: I would recommend the course Australian Legal Process and Research to future exchange students. It provides a great introduction to how the Australian legal system works and teaches important research skills that are useful for studying law anywhere. The course is practical and helps you understand the differences between legal systems, which is really valuable for anyone interested in comparative law.
unexpected_costs: Some unexpected costs I encountered included public transport fares, which added up more than I expected. I also had extra expenses for social activities and food when eating out. It’s a good idea to budget a bit extra for these kinds of costs
cost_comparison: Eating out in Melbourne was a bit more expensive than I expected. Compared to my home country, meals at cafes and restaurants cost more, especially in popular areas near campus. However, groceries and public transport were about what I expected. It’s a good idea to cook at home often to save money.
activities_available: Monash University offered a wide range of cultural, athletic, and social activities for students. There were clubs and societies for different interests, including cultural groups where you could meet people from around the world. The university also had sports teams and fitness classes for staying active. Social events like welcome parties, movie nights, and workshops helped exchange students connect and make friends. Overall, there were plenty of opportunities to get involved and enjoy campus life.
activities_recommended: I recommend future exchange students join clubs or groups to meet new people and learn about different cultures. Doing sports or exercise is also good to stay healthy and have fun. Plus, exploring Melbourne by going to festivals, markets, or parks is a great way to enjoy your time here. These activities help you make friends and have a better experience.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend visiting students explore some of Melbourne’s famous spots like Federation Square, the Royal Botanic Gardens, and St Kilda Beach. Taking a trip along the Great Ocean Road to see the Twelve Apostles is also amazing if you have more time. On weekends, checking out local markets, cafes, and live music events is a fun way to experience the city’s culture. These activities help you enjoy Melbourne and make the most of your free time.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture in Melbourne was easy. People were friendly and welcoming, and I quickly got used to the lifestyle and customs. Being in a diverse city with many international students also made it easier to feel at home. Overall, I felt comfortable adapting to the new environment.
socializing_tips: I don’t have any specific tips for socializing with local students, but I found that being open and friendly helps a lot. Joining campus activities or clubs can also be a good way to meet people naturally.
cultural_challenges: One cultural difference I found challenging was getting used to the big city environment and seeing a lot of homeless people around. It was different from what I was used to, and it took some time to understand and accept this part of life in Melbourne.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated how friendly and open people in Melbourne are. The city is very multicultural, so it was great to meet people from all over the world and learn about different cultures. I also liked the relaxed lifestyle and the strong focus on work-life balance.
top3_advice: Book temporary accommodation like an Airbnb before you arrive, so you have a place to stay while you look for longer-term housing. Start planning your course registration early and ask for help if you find the process confusing. Get involved in clubs and social activities to meet new people and make the most of your time in Melbourne.
other_useful_info: I don’t have any other information to add, but I’m happy to share more if needed.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was getting to learn about a new legal system and culture while meeting people from all over the world. It helped me grow both academically and personally, and gave me memories and skills that I will carry with me for life
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was adjusting to the different teaching style and managing my class schedule without overlaps. It was a bit confusing at first, but with time and help from staff, I was able to handle it.

crucial_aspects: Australia has long been a destination I aspired to study in. I chose Monash University in particular because of its outstanding actuarial program - the only one in Australia with multiple accreditations, and notably, Monash holds three.
info_ease: Finding the necessary information upon arrival was very easy. The orientation days for exchange students were well structured and informative, and the friendliness and kindness of both staff and students made settling in much easier.
arrival_assistance: I received general guidance upon arrival, but I did not seek out any further assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Timetables for different units were not accessible until a few weeks before the start of classes. However, there was flexibility to change units up until the third teaching week, which was helpful.
registration_help: Assistance was available both via email and in person during the orientation week.
registration_success: I was successful in registering for the units I initially wanted, though I later changed two units to achieve a better timetable.
registration_advice: Don’t stress too much about the registration process. You can always change units after a few weeks once you have a better sense of the courses and timetable.
course_level: The courses were easier than those at UCPH, but that was likely because I had already covered much of the material earlier. The manageable workload gave me the chance to explore Australia alongside my studies. While some other Danish students felt the units were too easy and sometimes boring, I personally was quite happy with the level. I also chose courses based on interest rather than how easy they were to pass :)
teaching_comparison: The teaching style involved far more assignments and continuous assessment, rather than a single final exam counting for 100% of the grade, as is common at UCPH. It also felt more modern, with full access to online materials and recorded lectures, and some classes being offered exclusively online.
courses_enrolled: ETC5256 (Statistical modelling for actuarial studies), ETC5342 (Applied insurance methods), ETC5521 (Diving deeply into data exploration), ETC5523 (Communicating with data).
recommended_courses: ETC5523 (Communicating with Data): I would highly recommend this course due to the excellent lecturer, who has a strong mathematical background and delivered some of the most entertaining lectures I’ve had. While the course is not particularly actuarial, it significantly improves communication skills and teaches how to build a Shiny app. ETC5342 (Applied Insurance Methods): This course covers material similar to Skade 1, StatIns, and QRM. It was interesting to see how actuarial subjects are taught in another country. However, the lecturer was less clear, as the teaching was somewhat unstructured and the heavy accent made it difficult to follow at times. ETC5256 (Statistical modelling for actuarial studies): This was a relatively easy course, but the lecturer was excellent (although it was his final semester teaching at Monash). The course includes Bayesian estimation.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Food and eating out were generally less expensive than expected, especially coffee. Alcohol (apart from wine) was more expensive. Travel to and from the airport was also expensive, as there is no good public transport connection
activities_available: There was a wide range of cultural, athletic, and social activities—essentially everything you could think of. Clayton Campus in particular has a strong “campus vibe,” which I really enjoyed.
activities_recommended: I’d recommend taking advantage of the free Monday dinners from the MSA. The swimming pools are also great for a relaxing break between classes. Most importantly, just join a club you find interesting - it’s an easy way to meet people and make friends.
weekend_recommendations: Weekends: Great Ocean Road Grampains National Park Sightseeing around Melbourne Surfcamp Holidays: Anywhere in Australia is amazing!!
culture_adjustment: Very easy, as the cultural values are quite similar to those in Europe.
socializing_tips: Don’t be afraid to start conversations - people are very friendly. Try to join or take initiative in social activities early on then it's way more fun in class.
cultural_challenges: Being mindful of how to correctly address and refer to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and openness of people.
top3_advice: Be mindful when choosing your units: Among all the Danes I met at Monash (maybe 30) we were only two students that were content with the academic level. But at the same time, we were the only ones that chose units we found interesting and not because they were easy to pass. The actuarial program is outstanding: Monash offers an exceptional actuarial program and is the only university in Australia with three professional accreditations, making it particularly strong for actuarial students. Take advantage of the overall exchange experience: The workload is generally manageable, which gives you a great opportunity to explore Australia, travel, and engage in social and campus life - something that really adds to the exchange experience.
other_useful_info: It is a long train ride to the campus - try to find some friends to do the trip with.
most_rewarding: All the new friendships and experiencing studying in another country.
greatest_challenge: Trying to do as much as possible in one semester.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to explore the american culture and way of life. Having been there a couple times already, I wanted to go somewhere "authentic". Not many tourists venture to Montana, and I thought it'd be a great opportunity to experience the "real" The States. I also wanted to go somewhere where I could live a different life than the city life in Copenhagen, and I knew that Bozeman was a significantly smaller city surrounded by beautiful nature.
overall_comments: I loved living in Bozeman ! The only downsides were the expenses - rent in the States is super expensive - and not having my own room as I had to share my room with another student.
info_ease: MSU was very good at giving us all the information needed and gave us lists to follow to make sure we completed all the paperwork that was required.
arrival_assistance: I found the move in to be very easy and well organized. There were students and coordinators making sure that moving in to the dorms went as smooth as possible. There was also an orientation meeting and a bbq for the exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I loved living in Bozeman ! The only downsides were the expenses - rent in the States is super expensive - and not having my own room as I had to share my room with another student.
registration_process: I only figured out which courses were offered in the fall semester quite late, as I found the system to be very difficult to navigate. Many of the classes that I wanted to join were therefore already full, and I therefore ended up having to write quite a few professors asking them if I could join their class. As it was right before semester starts, some of the professors were too busy to respond and I therefore ended up having to go to some of their classes asking in person if I could join.
registration_help: I used the MSU website to figure out what professor taught the courses and their emails, but sometimes it was difficult figuring out. The exchange student coordinator sometimes helped me establish contact with professors, when I couldn't figure out what professor to contact.
registration_success: Luckily, many professors are inclined to let you in their class even though it's full, if you let them know that you're an exchange student. I was therefore in the end quite succesfull at registrering for the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure to begin the registration as soon as it is possible, as many of the courses fill up quickly. Also, don't hesitate to reach out for help with your coordinator. I would also recommend registrering for more classes than you can take, as it is possible to drop classes the first week or so. In this way, you get to try the courses before having to commit to them.
academics_comments: I loved living in Bozeman ! The only downsides were the expenses - rent in the States is super expensive - and not having my own room as I had to share my room with another student.
course_level: One of the courses that I did was a horticulture course, and I found this course to have a significantly lower level than the other courses I did. The remaining courses were in the environmental science department, and the level of the courses were quite high, equal to the level at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching in the States is similar to gymnasiet in Denmark, as the style of teaching relies on a lot of homework, tests and many smaller assignments. Likewise, the exams don't count for your whole grade as it does at UCPH, as assignments and participation in class also influences your grades.
courses_enrolled: Restoration Ecology Landscape Pedology Elementary Japanese Vegetable Production Intermediate Yoga
recommended_courses: I loved Landscape Pedology! The level was very high, so I was very challenged and learnt a lot. The professor is awesome. We went on field trips every week and I really liked both seeing the surrounding landscape as well as having the hands-on experience with the theory we'd been taught in class.
unexpected_costs: The unexpected costs include VISA, which costs around 3.000kr in total, and flights which were around 6.000kr. I also travelled for about 5 weeks in total and ended up spending around 20.000kr.
cost_comparison: As mentioned, housing is very expensive, and food likewise. The quality and selection of the food in the dining hall was quite high and very varied though. Groceries in the States are much more expensive than they are in Denmark, so I imagine food expenses would've been around the same, if I'd lived off campus.
activities_available: There are so many clubs that you can join and the majority of them are free! Sports, art, political and cultural clubs, you name it. At the beginning of the semester (at least in the fall) they have the katapalooza, a kind of festival on campus where all the clubs and almost all other organisations in town are present and you can talk to them, hear what they're about, and sign up.
activities_recommended: I joined the ultimate team which was a lot of fun and also an opportunity to make friends with a lot of americans ;-) Experiencing the American sports culture was also an experience, as I found it to be very different than the Danish sports culture. I would also recommend doing some of the acitivty courses. I did intermediate yoga twice a week and it was really good!
weekend_recommendations: I recommend doing as much hiking as possible on the weekends, before the snow falls (around october) if you're into that kind of stuff. Otherwise, there's plenty of opportunity of doing mountain biking, climbing, there are plenty of all those outdoor activities surrounding Bozeman. If you're going in the spring semester, be sure to bring your skiing gear and get the season pass for the bridgers (the closest skiing area. the snow is the best, I've ever skied). Make sure to visit surrounding national parks such as glacier, the tetons, yellowstone. Go to the hotsprings (especially the Norris hotsprings are amazing)! Rent a car in the holidays (much cheaper, if you're over 25 yrs) and go on rd trips! Make sure to acquire a national parks pass, that way you have unlimited access to all national parks in the states for a year for about $80. Bring a tent and sleeping bag with you, that way you won't have to rent it and it's much cheaper than staying in motels in the summer. Make sure to go to Zion Nt Park in Utah and Glacier Nt Park in Montana, they're some of the most beautiful places I've ever seen!
culture_adjustment: I found it was very easy to adjust to the local culture, as the american is very similar to the Danish in many ways, and in that we're quite exposed to American culture in Europe. Americans are generally more outgoing than Danish people which can both prove to be a little overwhelming but also makes it a lot easier to meet people.
socializing_tips: Join a club. Say yes, if someone invites you to something :-)
cultural_challenges: People are way more religious than what is the norm in Denmark. Be careful about openly criticizing religion. Also, Montana is a republican state, so don't assume that everyone shares the same opinions as you do ;-) Furthermore, the alcohol policy is way stricter than it is in Europe. You can't get into bars if you're under 21, you can't drink alcohol in the streets, all the bars close at 2 am.
culture_appreciated: My favourite part about the american culture is how easy it is to talk to people, as they're far more inclined to approach you than people are in Denmark. I also loved that everyone is so polite, holding the door for you, saying sorry and how are you and thank you whenever they get the chance. Make sure to do the same!
top3_advice: Getting around without a car is quite challenging, so be sure to either buy a car or make friends with americans who have a car. If you're looking to make money while abroad, it's very easy to get a job on campus and they're usually quite well payed (and taxes are way lower than they are in Denmark). Make sure to bring gear for hiking, and get a national parks pass (you can buy it in information centers in the majority of national parks)!
other_useful_info: If you're thinking about going on exchange, just be aware that it's A LOT of paperwork. I was quite taken aback by this, as nobody tells you how much work it is. Also, keep in mind that going on exchange is not the same as travelling, there will be weekends where you won't be able to go exploring, simply because you have too much studying to do (depending on what courses you're doing ofc, but generally in the states there's a lot of homework). So don't expect your exchange to be one long holiday, it's not always just fun. However, it is fun and rewarding the majority of the time, so I'd say it's totally worth it, and you'll learn more about yourself and your field than if you're just staying in Denmark.
most_rewarding: Knowing about myself that I'm able to go to another country and study and thrive there. If I can do that, I can do a lot of things :-) And ofc seeing so much beautiful nature (the states really has it all!), and having gotten an understanding of how diverse, beautiful and conflicted a country the states is.
greatest_challenge: The paperwork maybe was the greatest challenge haha. Living in the dorms also for me was a challenge, because I realised how important having my own space is for me. Not being able to leave campus whenever I wanted, as I did not have a car.

crucial_aspects: My main concern was going somewhere that had mountains and outdoor activities which Bozeman definitely fulfills. Besides that, I also wanted to go somewhere with interesting culture and getting away from the coasts in the US, you get that. Finally, I also wanted to make sure I was able to take some classes that would benefit me academically and some just for fun.
overall_comments: I might be a little biased, especially since I've traveled a lot in the States before and swung by Bozeman but I really enjoyed myself.
info_ease: Pretty easy, most if not all was given to you in advance and if not, the office of incoming exchange students was really fast with replying to emails, within a day.
arrival_assistance: I went to a few orientation events. Didn't need the airport pickup though that was avaiable.
arrival_comments: You could definitely get more assistance than I got if you needed it or simply wanted it, very helpful and involved staff.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I might be a little biased, especially since I've traveled a lot in the States before and swung by Bozeman but I really enjoyed myself.
registration_process: You can read about the different courses on the MSU website and for the actual registration, you do it through an online portal which generates a schedule for you so you can see if any courses clash with each other. Not too difficult to register.
registration_help: Again, the office of incoming students was pretty fast with replying to emails.
registration_success: I got into all the classes I wanted, including two graduate courses (even though I'm an undergrad) and a class which was filled up but after writing the professor, I got in anyway.
registration_advice: WRITE the professor if you want a spot in a filled class, they might say no but most likely they'll say yes if you argue your case.
academics_comments: I might be a little biased, especially since I've traveled a lot in the States before and swung by Bozeman but I really enjoyed myself.
course_level: I kinda went on both sides of the spectrum: I took two second-year courses (Creative Writing and Great Books) open for everyone which were pretty easy to pass as long as you did the homework which in these courses weren't too excessive, a little time-consuming certain times but never hard to complete. On the other hand, I took two physics graduate courses (I'm a physics student) which were very difficult, weekly assignments to turn in as part of your final great and decently high level. Genereally, I would say the level depend a lot on the specific course though maybe a senior course (400-code) would fit for most fifth-semester bachelor students from KU.
teaching_comparison: Less classes and readings and more homework and due assignments. Only lectures in my physics classes, no time specificly to solve problems so you're kinda alone with your assignments. You can (and are supposed to) go to your professor's office hours and ask questions but that still wasn't optimal, I definitely struggled with my physics courses and missed the way we do it at KU. My liberal arts classes were not as bad and the creative writing class was actually a workshop resulting in more varied classes.
courses_enrolled: PHYS 501 Advanced Classical Mechanics PHYS 544 Condensed Matter Physics I LIT 203IH Great Books CRWR 240RA Introduction to Creative Writing
recommended_courses: Advanced Classical Mechanics for physics students, intense but level not too difficult as a third-year. Creative writing for everyone (Molly Damm as instructor for poetry-workshop). It was such a fun, creative, comforting and safe space, only 20 people in the class, many of whom said that the course were the highlight of their week (I felt that too). Great Books was also really fun, kinda like a big bookclub and the professor was really charismatic, smart and fun, highly recommend.
unexpected_costs: The dollar was pretty high when I had to pay for accommodation (7.5 DKK = 1 USD). Bozeman in general is pretty expensive, grocery-wise and eating out.
cost_comparison: Busses were free, splitting gas with friends is cheap. Coffee is pretty cheap.
activities_available: So many different things to do! Mostly outdoorsy adventure stuff but also debate, frisbee, bowling, choir, music, and much more.
activities_recommended: I really enjoyed various outdoor clubs for outdoor activities. Backcountry squatters (if you're a girl or non-binary) and the outdoor club (everyone).
weekend_recommendations: On weekends, everyone leaves campus to go hiking or backpacking in the mountains which I highly recommend, so much nature nearby and national parks not too far away. For longer holidays, renting a car and going on a small roadtrip is a lot of fun.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, no language barrier and the culture is not too foreign.
socializing_tips: The drinking culture is less emphasized (though still exist) than in Denmark so doing stuff that doesn't involve drinking is pretty common. Joining clubs is a great way to make friends, more common than meeting people in class probably.
cultural_challenges: Some people are more conservative and religious which you just have to remember sometimes before making a joke. Politics could be a more sensitive topic than in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: Americans are just some of the kindest and most helpful people I've ever met. Some of the small talk might seem superficial but if you make it through that, many times it can lead to actual friendships or help.
top3_advice: 1. Keep your weekends sacred for going on adventures. 2. Take fun, random classes if you have the electives to do so! 3. Smuggle food out of the dining halls during the week if you have the 5-day meal plan. That way you'll have some food for the weekends and save on groceries.
other_useful_info: Having a car available in some way was pretty essential for doing stuff on the weekends. My friends and I didn't buy one because even used cars had gotten quite expensive so we made friends with people who had cars instead.
most_rewarding: It might be cliche but the amazing people I met: internationals from Europe and elsewhere, nationals from other states and local Montanans. And I really loved being that close to the mountains with so many outdoor activities easily available.
greatest_challenge: Taking graduate courses while wanting to have fun and enjoy my time as an exchange student.
other_comments: Remember to have fun!

crucial_aspects: Since I was going to go on exchange no matter what, I thought I might as well go all in and go to a place I always wanted to have time to explore.
info_ease: It was a bit difficult, but there was a lot of people I could ask for help.
arrival_assistance: There was students helping us fill out some of the paperwork and there was an assembly giving out all the information we needed. There was also offices and I was assigned a tutor.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We had to email every individual professor we wanted to take classes from and get their permission. Then we had to register the courses to a website, print out a paper, get the signature from one of the instructors in charge of exchange students and the professor we were assigned. Then we had to hand over that paper to a particular office.
registration_help: It was difficult to find the email addresses for all the professors, even though there was email support where we could ask for help with that.
registration_success: I managed to register for all but two of the classes I originally wanted to take, but found two other classes instead.
registration_advice: If you're a graduate student, make sure to register all your graduate courses with a [G] on the website, or you will have to redo it.

New perspectives on modern Japanese Literature was also very insightful and interesting, even if the expectations for the students were also a big high.
unexpected_costs: The extra cost of withdrawing money from ATMs. I would suggest that anyone starts with at least 300,000 yen in cash that they withdrew from their private bank to avoid some the expenses involved with money withdrawal.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: There were clubs and sports, but I didn't go to any of those, because I was too busy studying. There was also parties and social events to get to know local students, and the school festival.
activities_recommended: I would recommend going to the social events because you get to make friends there, which is hard otherwise.
weekend_recommendations: There's a lot of places to see in Nagoya and the nearby cities. I would also suggest a one day trip to Kobe, especially if you want a Danish hotdog. There's a place for that in Suma, Kobe.
culture_adjustment: There was some challenges, but I made it through.
socializing_tips: Again, go to the social events and install Line on your phone.
cultural_challenges: The study culture was very different and hard to get accustomed to.
culture_appreciated: That people are generally friendly and polite.
top3_advice: Decide if you're going to take a Japanese class or not, even if you won't get any credits or ECTS points for it. When you go to the Ward Office to register your address and sign up for health insurance, either go with a group or someone who knows Japanese. Make a large cash withdrawal in yen from your bank of at least 300,000 yen.
other_useful_info: Make sure you look nice in the picture you submit to the host institution as it will be used for a lot of things.
most_rewarding: Whenever I managed to have a conversation in Japanese.
greatest_challenge: Grocery shopping and midterms.

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte min destination på grund af, at den var langt væk fra Danmark, og derfor meget anderledes. Det gav mig mulighed for at udforske et land jeg måske ellers aldrig ville have besøgt, og samtidig møde folk jeg ellers aldrig ville have mødt. Jeg valgte også min destination på grund af at universitetet havde gode engelske kurser i de fag jeg var interesseret i. Jeg valgte også et land hvis kultur jeg personligt var interesseret i, hvilket hænger sammen med at jeg gerne ville bruge muligheden til at udforske landet.
info_ease: Det var meget nemt, der var mange introduktionsmøder til et hav af diverse ting, og man kunne altid spørge folk om hjælp hvis man ikke vidste noget. Alle var meget hjælpsomme.
arrival_assistance: Vi fik mange papirer, og skulle lytte til mange orientationer der detaljerede procedurerne vi skulle gennemføre. Vi fik også en tutor og en academic advisor der begge hjalp med introduktionen.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Man bruger en online portal, hvor man blot skriver informationen på kurset. De matematikkurser og fysikkurser jeg tog skulle jeg manuelt skrive ind, mit japanskkursus var der dog allerede og jeg skulle blot vælge det over en liste af tilgængelige kurser. Efter man har lavet registrationen skal man også kontakte professorerne knyttet til kurserne, evt. inden man udfylder den online portal, og efter alt er gjort får man ens academic advisor + en anden person til at underskrive og så er man færdig.
registration_help: Man kunne spørge ind til ethvert led i processen. Der vil være mindst 3 forskelllige folk man kan spørge.
registration_success: Jeg registrerede for alle kurserne jeg var interesseret i.
registration_advice: Ikke tænk for meget over at vide præcis hvilke kurser du vil tage på forhånd, det kan du finde ud af når du er der. Mange kurser er også "gemt væk", så det er værd at spørge rundt. Richard, Serge laver nogle gode matematikkurser på diverse specialiserede emner, og Wojdylo, John laver nogle 3. års kurser på statistisk fysik og kvantemekanik der går mere i dybden med teorien end kurserne på KU gør. Hvis du er teoretisk interesseret anbefaler jeg at tage dem, da han virkelig går i detalje med mange ting jeg selv havde undret mig over. Hans statistisk fysik kursus især er meget godt.
course_level: De kurser jeg tog var et fint niveau, på trods af at jeg allerede havde haft lignende kurser på KU så lærte jeg mange nye ting, og blev tvunget til at lave MANGE opgaver, så man virkelig skulle forstå stoffet.
teaching_comparison: Forelæsningerne var meget ens, men der var ikke rigtig nogle regnetimer. Det skulle man gøre i fritiden, og så "præsentere" ens løsninger i regnetimen.
courses_enrolled: Japanese NP1, Statistical Physics II, Quantum Mechanics II, Special Mathematics Lecture (Group Theory)
recommended_courses: As before written, I recommend Richard Serge's Special Mathematics Lectures and Statistical Physics + Quantum Mechanics for the theoretically oriented. Specielt Statistical Physics II var et dejligt fag, siden det meste af faget egentlig bare er Termodynamik, men tilgangen er meget anderledes end jeg nogensinde før har set. Han bygger teorien op geometrisk, og man får virkelig at se hvordan matematiske krav til entropi/energifunktionen udspiller sig i relationer mellem materielle egenskaber. Derimod kan niveauet måske være lidt lavt, på trods af at arbejdsbyrden er høj nok til at afbalancere det. Hvis du har mulighed for at tage SPIII og QMIII ville de nok give mere "ny" info.
unexpected_costs: Der var ret mange forsikringer man skulle købe, og et national health service man også skulle blive en del af, der begge kostede nogle penge. Udover det, så alle de seje ting man finder som man har lyst til at købe kan nemt ende med at koste meget.
cost_comparison: At spise ude er langt billigere end i Danmark, smør og ost er tilgengæld ret dyrt.
activities_available: Der er mange forskellige arrangementer der bliver afholdt af alle mulige forskellige intitutioner, jeg kan umuligt nævne dem alle. Bare tjek dine mails og jeres gruppechat for emner, samt spørg rundt. Der er massere af muligheder.
activities_recommended: Der er et festival om efteråret er der virkelig sjovt.
weekend_recommendations: Der er mange flotte bjerge i nærheden. Jeg anbefaler Yoro Mountain og Kiso Valley specielt. Selvfølgelig bør man besøge Kyoto, Tokyo, og alle mulige andre store locations, men husk også at Aichi har mange mindre ting der måske kunne være interessante. Scan bare over det med google maps eller spørg din advisor om ting, de ved sikkert en ting eller to der passer til dine interesser.
culture_adjustment: Ret nemt faktisk, men man kommer nok til at føle kulturchok den første måned eller deromkring.
socializing_tips: Ikke rigtig, jeg havde selv svært ved det. Mit største tip er at kunne japansk, og så bare snakke til dem. Hvis du ikke kan japansk er det ret svært.
cultural_challenges: De går på venstre side af vejen, og mange lofte er ret lave så man er nødt til at dukke under dem. Det sværeste er dog klart at finde en skraldespand, man skulle næsten tro de ikke eksisterede. Og så kan nogle japanere være ret indirekte i deres sprog, hvilket kan lede til misforståelser begge veje (De tror du mener noget andet end du siger, du tror de mener hvad de siger).
culture_appreciated: Alle man møder er hjælpsomme, og folk tager hensyn til en hvor end man er. Man føler sig sikker om natten, og folk larmer næsten aldrig. Gaderne er altid rene, og der er toiletter overalt.
top3_advice: 1. Don't stress about course registration before the orientation at the university. Before that point, any vague, even wrong, idea about the courses you want to take is fine. 2. Talk to lots of people and make travel friends. They will make your stay a lot less lonely. 3. It's fine to be sad at any point of your stay. You are going to feel overwhelmed, and that's fine. You'll still make it.
other_useful_info: The main library has many floors, and you can take out keys on the "ground floor" for private rooms on the upper floors. Try it out!
most_rewarding: For mig var det at lave venner, og så tage på ture med dem.
greatest_challenge: Alle de nye ting, og stresset fra studiet samt turene var ret meget. Man ender med at blive virkelig træt, og det er svært at komme sig over.

crucial_aspects: Choosing a culture i didnt know in a place that is less touristy.
overall_comments: Super fun experience that i would recommend everyone!
info_ease: They send you information beforehand thats pretty comprehensive. After arrival at the dormitory (thats the first destination) they will kind of hold your hand through the rest of the process.
arrival_assistance: They help you out the first day with getting settled at the dormitory. Afterwards there are a lot of introductory orientations the first 2 weeks
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Super fun experience that i would recommend everyone!
registration_process: You find the courses you want on the syllabi, write down the codes, and submit them to a website given to you in the orientations. You are also allocated an academic advisor that just has to sign your choice of courses. Afterwards its done! I had a hard time finding a syllabi that felt up to date, so below are attached 2 links to the syllabi from my autumn semester. First link is for NUPACE courses (culture related and languages), and the second is for the G30 program courses (Courses in your major taught in english, taken together with the G30 students who are doing their whole degree at NU)
registration_help: Nupace office are always available, and the huge amount of orientations should cover all you'd need.
registration_success: Got all the courses i wanted!
registration_advice: Take a japanese class if you can. I didnt because i was unsure if i would get the credits transferred if i did. But if you can check that beforehand, i'd highly recommend it. Seemed very useful and fun.
academics_comments: Super fun experience that i would recommend everyone!
course_level: NUPACE courses and language courses are supposedly super easy and not challenging at all. The G30 courses on the other hand are notoriously hard. Be prepared! Its not just a vacation, you got to put in actual work.
teaching_comparison: UCPH is much more in depth and theoretical than NU. Here it is more about covering as big a curriculum as possible by only scraping the surface, and talking about how it can be applied. I by far prefer UCPH but to each their own. Also know that, if you're doing courses in science, you will have to use things from the curriculum (like specific equations) in the exam that you will not have used beforehand in assignments and tutorials.
courses_enrolled: Biochemistry I Particle physics Condensed matter physics I Physics tutorial 1a (tutorial for analytical mechanics) Chemical physics Intercultural competence Physical chemistry I Analytical mechanics I Earth and planetary sciences
recommended_courses: Analytical mechanics I is super good if you havent done it at KU. Physical chemistry is also super interesting in how it applied thermodynamics to more specific chemical systems. Chemical physics is more of a hardcore indepth look on thermodynamics which i enjoyed a lot But most of all, do a japanese course if you can! It's 5 credits (10 ECTS) and super useful. I regret not doing it due to missing out on so much fun with the other exchange students. If you are a physics student, i would personally strongly advice against doing classes with John Wojdylo. While he is a nice guy, his 2 credit courses would be the equivalent to 15 ECTS in workload, it is absolutely ludicrous. So only do them if you're ready to study for his class every single day of the week for multiple hours.
unexpected_costs: They dont use books here for courses, so that cost is out of the way.
cost_comparison: Food and rent is dirt cheap here, so dont worry too much about a scholarship; its easily manageable without one. Public transport is the same price as in Copenhagen, so be warned. Otherwise japan is super cheap!
activities_available: Sports clubs were everywhere, especially Judo club was popular (they pay for the dinner afterwards). Lots of advertisements all the time for cultural activities and such, so you wont miss out.
activities_recommended: Go traveling! Super beautiful country that is not worth missing out on.
weekend_recommendations: Go traveling the countryside! I'm not a big fan of Kyoto, Osaka and Tokyo due to the overtourism. So going to some random place is amazing. I'd recommend Noto peninsula and Kyuushuu!
culture_adjustment: Just be polite and try not to be loud. The japanese people are very reserved and introverted by nature, so try and respect their boundaries.
socializing_tips: Learn japanese, preferably get to N3 level if you want to actually have japanese friends. The japanese people know next to no english, so if you want to socialize with them its kind of a must. Also enroll in the tutoring system! The tutors are somewhat proficient in english and can be a gateway to meeting other japanese.
cultural_challenges: Everything is paid in cash. be prepared to pay your rent physically using cash at the convenience store every month.
culture_appreciated: How nice the japanese are! Especially if you try and speak japanese to them, they appreciate it a lot.
top3_advice: Nagoya is a wonderful city that you'd probably never heard of. I chose it for that exact reason. Going here in contrast to tokyo or kyoto will give you a much more authenic experience of what living japan is really like. You'll feel like a local and not a tourist Nagoya uni campus is very pleasant and centralized, so theres not that far between your classes. And the G30 students are super nice, try and socialize with them Nagoya is also placed in the middle of Japan, making weekend trips and travels so much more manageable. Cant recommend it enough
other_useful_info: Plugin-lab is this place underneath the northern canteen where you can study and get FREE coffee, tea, cocoa, Soda and more! I spent like 80% of my week days there.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from other nationalities, not just the japanese. Everyones kind of on their own, so its like you're setting your life at home on a pause and starting a new one here with the other exchange students!
greatest_challenge: Language. Learn it beforehand if you can. And if you cant, try and enroll in the japanese classes.
other_comments: Have fun here! Nagoya is a wonderful city with wonderful people.

crucial_aspects: The culture and the possibility to study in a country, with completely different ways.
info_ease: Fairly easy. The university sent mails with all the information I needed.
arrival_assistance: We had som orientation meetings.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We had a course list, and the we had two weeks to chose the courses we wanted.
registration_help: There was an office for the exchange students.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I applied for, but I missed some classes because they were at the same time of the day.
registration_advice: Be aware that you are having around eight courses at the same time, because most courses are 2 credits and 15 credits is needed to pass a semester.
course_level: Some courses seemed to be easier than what I'm used to from my own university.
teaching_comparison: I almost only had lectures. No classes had exercises in the class, only as homework.
courses_enrolled: Biochemistry 1 Organic chemistry 3 Organic chemistry 5 Inorganic chemistry 2 Cell biology 2 Analytical chemistry Polymer chemistry Academic writing
recommended_courses: Organic chemistry 3: A good teacher, not a lot of students so there is time for questions.
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Food were cheaper than I expected
activities_available: Not a lot of social events from the university.
activities_recommended: Go on weekend trips away from nagoya. (Osaka, Kyoto, Kanazawa, Tokyo, etc.)
weekend_recommendations: Kanazawa is a very interesting town. Especially in the autumn.
culture_adjustment: Nagoya is known to be worse at English than the larger cities (Tokyo), so if you can't speak Japanese it's more difficult.
socializing_tips: No, because I didn't get in touch with a single local student while I was there.
cultural_challenges: The language. Some places didn't accept English only speakers.
culture_appreciated: I loved how clean everything was. The food was very good.
top3_advice: Be aware that there is very strict rules at the housing and at the university. In some of my courses I only had classes with three other students in the same course. I did not have classes with people that I knew from the exchange program. Be aware that you will probably spend a lot of time on homework and assignments.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: To be able to live in and experience a part of the world that is totally different.
greatest_challenge: The time management of having 8 assignments almost every week.

crucial_aspects: I would like to know more about the culture and lifestyle in a new country, as well as the study pattern
info_ease: Everything provided by the university was clear with detailed instructions; you can get all the information by carefully following the email.
arrival_assistance: The international department in our university can help you through the entire process.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Course registration is rather flexible, where you can basically choose all the classes you want, with not much of a limitation on major(at least one class from your major). Students should check the deadline for the registration period and submit the form to professors, but 2 weeks of pre-registration period is granted for students to try the classes and finally decide which one they want to take.
registration_help: Each student is assigned one supervisor from their department. There are also tutors assigned for students whom you can ask for help from.
registration_success: To fulfill the requirements for one semester(30ECTS=15credits), the classes you should take will be around 5-6. The time conflict was a bit hard to manage if you want to choose the Japanese class(but I highly recommend it), but I still managed to fulfill the requirement.
registration_advice: Check the schedule for classes carefully. If you plan to take the Japanese class, which takes up every morning from Monday to Friday, you need to avoid the time conflict. Participation and attendence are rather important here, so it is better not to skip a lot of classes and plan well. Apart from this, the registration is rather simple and smooth, and hope you can get all the classes you want!
course_level: MA students are mostly restricted to only Master classes based on the difficulty of the courses. Still, the workload is not that heavy as you will mostly have one lecture per week. It should be easy to handle multiple classes at the same time.
teaching_comparison: The workload is indeed heavier than in UCPH. Teachers are more strict with class participation, and the style of teaching varies a lot among professors and departments. Still, the instructors are very nice and there to help, and if you follow the lectures carefully, the materials are rather easy and it won't be hard to pass all the classes.
courses_enrolled: Research Skills b [G]; Japanese Culture and Society in Tourism Context [G]; Theme Studies (Statistics for Economics and Business） [G]; Special lecture on Data Science 1 [G]; Special lecture on Data Science 2 [G]; Sustainable Materials Science [G]; NUPACE Japanese 1b
recommended_courses: The NUPACE Japanese! The teachers are all super nice, and you can actually learn the language and culture throughout the semester. The class is kind of intensive as it is held almost every day (for basic levels), but you can see yourself actually improving day by day with all your friends. It would be a fun experience:)
unexpected_costs: If you plan on travelling every weekend, the cost will rise more as little things can add up to quite a lot of spending:) In-store shopping is also enjoyable and irresistible here, so I ended up spending too much...
cost_comparison: Fruits are really expensive in Japan! Transportation is cheaper than in Denmark, but still rather high, as you may travel a lot (no available monthly tickets for exchange students). Otherwise, everything is within an affordable range.
activities_available: There are many cultural and social activities held by clubs, international student clubs, and even dorms. You will have a lot of chances to meet new friends and experience the culture as much as you want!
activities_recommended: Activities held by the dorm (Yamate North) were really fun. We had the chance to enjoy the Japanese firework festival, beach party, cooking event, etc. Also, the weekly gathering by Ace was a good opportunity to make Japanese friends and practice your language.
weekend_recommendations: I really love the onsen and sauna in Japan. There are many cheap and wonderful saunas or public baths in Nagoya or nearby cities. It is such a pleasurable experience for relaxation.
culture_adjustment: Japanese culture is rather different from Western culture. It is always good to keep good manners and stay quiet in public without bothering others too much. Japanese people are generally very nice and easy-going. It won't take long to fit in, but it will take some time.
socializing_tips: Join the student clubs
cultural_challenges: People care about behaviors in public a lot. So keeping good manners and trying to avoid bothering others is important but could be hard to follow.
culture_appreciated: Respect and politeness are something I truly appreciate from Japanese people. I experienced the most during travel.
top3_advice: 1. travel more whilst you have time, experience the culture by yourself is the best 2. participate more in university activities and make more friends 3. plan your budget well: )
other_useful_info: Reach out to professors if you are interested into any research in the school. It would be interesting to join in the lab and work with fellows in the uni.
most_rewarding: The many friends I made and the whole experience of Japanese culture
greatest_challenge: Try to travel as much as possible while keep up with all the classes:) But at the end it worked and paid off.

crucial_aspects: That the university I chose had not only relevant courses at my academic level in English, but also had pre-planned living spaces for their students.
overall_comments: I was blindsided by the fact that the agreement between Copenhagen University and Nagoya University stipulated 8 credits worth of courses being equivalent to 30 ECTS, while Nagoya University insisted I take 16 of their credits to recieve my certificate of completion. I was asked by UCPH to follow Nagoya University's plan, which resulted in a very large amount of coursework (especially considering UCPH did not approve Japanese language courses as appropriate, since they were not at Master's level). I would have liked more information about the agreement in advance - perhaps a revision of the briefings about the agreement is in order.
info_ease: Nagoya University had a lot of informative orientations and documents to consult for both important and niche information, including stuff like how to register for bike-parking, how to deal with culture shock, and where to purchase certain items at reasonable prices (pillows, cutlery, cooking supplies, groceries).
arrival_assistance: Nagoya University had a lot of informative orientations and documents to consult for both important and niche information, including stuff like how to register for bike-parking, how to deal with culture shock, and where to purchase certain items at reasonable prices (pillows, cutlery, cooking supplies, groceries).
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I was blindsided by the fact that the agreement between Copenhagen University and Nagoya University stipulated 8 credits worth of courses being equivalent to 30 ECTS, while Nagoya University insisted I take 16 of their credits to recieve my certificate of completion. I was asked by UCPH to follow Nagoya University's plan, which resulted in a very large amount of coursework (especially considering UCPH did not approve Japanese language courses as appropriate, since they were not at Master's level). I would have liked more information about the agreement in advance - perhaps a revision of the briefings about the agreement is in order.
registration_process: Nagoya University dedicated a whole day to course registration, and provided spreadsheets and overviews of teachers, periods and other course information. They also provided help in the form of documentation and workshops to help complete course registration. Registration was done both online and in person, with a starting period where you were able try out courses to see whether you wanted to stick with them or not.
registration_help: A large scale orientation, workshops, fliers and documents detailing course registration.
registration_success: I was able to join every class that I wanted to.
registration_advice: If at all possible, you should join the Japanese classes provided by the partnered institution at Nagoya University. It provides a common space for international students across schools, and a lot of friendships were created that way. Japanese may be difficult, but it is a lot of fun to learn.
academics_comments: I was blindsided by the fact that the agreement between Copenhagen University and Nagoya University stipulated 8 credits worth of courses being equivalent to 30 ECTS, while Nagoya University insisted I take 16 of their credits to recieve my certificate of completion. I was asked by UCPH to follow Nagoya University's plan, which resulted in a very large amount of coursework (especially considering UCPH did not approve Japanese language courses as appropriate, since they were not at Master's level). I would have liked more information about the agreement in advance - perhaps a revision of the briefings about the agreement is in order.
course_level: The level of difficulty varied wildly. Some introductory courses within my field had professors with an uninspiring teaching style, namely Professor -NAME REDACTED-. Others were within fields I had never before studied. Most courses provided me with a challenging but incredibly insightful look into fields of the Humanities that I had no experience with. I recommend especially Professor -NAME REDACTED- litterature courses.
teaching_comparison: My courses at UCPH have had a common throughline in not only theme, but also teaching style. The classes at NU varied a lot, according to what professor was teaching. Some professors required a lot of reading, and focused on discussion in the classroom. Others ran the classes mostly as seminars, where participation wasn't really required (neither in the form of reading or discussion).
courses_enrolled: Japanese Media and Popular Culture [G] Language and Society II [G] Philosophy of Mind and Language [G] Second Language Acquisition II [G] Seminar on Language and Culture in English-speaking Countries IIb [G] Theoretical Linguistics I [G] Theoretical Linguistics II [G] Transnational and Minority Literatures [G]
recommended_courses: I especially enjoyed the course 'Seminar on Language and Culture in English-speaking Countries IIb' by Professor -NAME REDACTED-. It was informally called 'Comparative Culture', and was about the depiction of foreign cultures from ancient Greece to modern day. It focused on discussion, and each reading for the class was thoughtprovoking and placed within its historical context. Big thumbs up. I also enjoyed Second Language Acquisition II a lot. It is very much a linguistics class for research students at the end of their education, but the high level of skill from each student meant it was a very inspiring class.
unexpected_costs: Though the Shinkansen rail system is very convenient, it became by far the largest contributor to unexpected costs. Each trip took about 11000 JPY (550 DKK). Having to purchase cooking supplies was also unexpected.
cost_comparison: Fruit and greens are very expensive in Japan, as is cheese, bread and butter. Making food for yourself may be a bit more expensive than expected, if you want to eat similarly to back home.
activities_available: There are more than a hundred clubs available, so I will not list them all. They are avaiable on the NU website. Keep in mind that many clubs/circles are all centered around being competitive (whether sports, music or something else), and people without Japanese skills will therefore have a hard time learning stuff they don't already know. The leaders of the clubs seldom have the time, ressources or English skills to instruct new members.
activities_recommended: There are several clubs centered around cultural exchange. All of these are good places to become friends with Japanese students and practice Japanese.
weekend_recommendations: If going to Tokyo, I especially enjoyed Shimokitazawa and Asakusa. You can find practically any hobby in Tokyo, provided you set aside the time to travel to that location (which may take longer than expected due to the chaotic subway system of Tokyo). Aoshima is an island in the southern part of Japan, and one of the most interesting places I have ever been. It has beautiful museums and sculptures made by a large collective of Japanese artists.
culture_adjustment: It can take a lot of time for some, but if you calm yourself, and make friends with some international students, you can adjust at your own pace.
socializing_tips: Join one of the cultural exchange clubs, and you will be sure to meet some Japanese students. Practice your Japanese often, they will be worse at English than you might expect. Nagoya University has a tutoring service that is free, and gives you a Japanese student as a kind of local guide, and to help with your studies. You should take them up on that offer!
cultural_challenges: It was really hard to ride my bike anywhere. The cities aren't really designed for it.
culture_appreciated: The Japanese have a culture of eating out, which means restaurant prices are very reasonable. I really liked going to izakaya and karaoke with my Japanese friends as well.
top3_advice: Make your room feel like home! Bring stuff that makes you feel safe and reminds you that you are not alone (pictures of your family, decorations, etc.) Try out stuff you wouldn't normally do! I had a fun time exploring activities that I had never tried - Onsen, karaoke, darts bars, jazz festivals. Take some of your international student friends with you! Plan tourist trips in advance! It may be difficult to book hotels in certain periods in Japan, especially around Golden Week and other holidays. Make a list of the places you would like to go, and when you think you will be able to go there. The academic calendar is very similar year to year, and can be found online.
other_useful_info: Courier services that transfer you luggage to and from the airport are very convenient, and commonly used. They cost about 3000 yen per suitcase (150 kr), but will save you a lot of trouble when you arrive jetlagged and dead tired in the blazing heat of summer.
most_rewarding: Getting to know the other students, and recieving recognition for my accomplishments in my studies back home.
greatest_challenge: The amount of coursework. I had little time for tourism due to the weird communication with UCPH about how many credits I was supposed to take.

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

teaching_comparison: More tests and all the Japanese courses are of course in Japanese. Everything counted towards the final grade, so all from homework, test to attendance.
courses_enrolled: Intensive Japanese 2, Japanese Religion A and Japanese Culture and Art A
recommended_courses: Japanese culture and art A was really good! The teacher is super chill and we look at art and historical buldings and other things from Japan. It was a really nice course and really chill.
unexpected_costs: Had to get a national insurence, even though I was covered with my insurance from Denmark.
cost_comparison: Food (unless you buy a lot of veggies and fruit) and clothing is a lot less expensive, transportation too.
activities_available: I don't know.. I was not a part of it.
activities_recommended: Don't know.

institution: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
crucial_aspects: The good weather in Athens even during winter, the Greek culture, and to have the experience to live and study in Athens.
overall_comments: Great experience. I can only recommend to go to Athens on exchange.
info_ease: It was easy.
arrival_assistance: Found out most of the things on my own. But, there were some Erasmus student organisations who could help with many things. Regarding the changes in the courses at the university and how the courses would be held, the university did not give very much information. However, it worked well in the end. Just take it easy - so do the Greeks.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Great experience. I can only recommend to go to Athens on exchange.
registration_process: It took some time before everything fell into place. But in the end, it worked.
registration_help: You could just text your Erasmus coordinator at the faculty.
registration_success: Some of the courses I had chosen from home were not offered when I arrived so I made some changes in my learning agreement and chose some other courses.
registration_advice: Just take it easy. It will all manage in the end.
academics_comments: Great experience. I can only recommend to go to Athens on exchange.
course_level: It was not the most difficult in the world, but still very fine for an Erasmus programme. I did not only go to Greece to study, and there was time to explore Athens, some beatiful Greek islands, some other Greek cities etc. So overall, the level was fine.
teaching_comparison: The professors most of the time just held their lectures by speaking for an hour or two. Some of them asked questions, some did not. In the classrooms at the law faculty there were no wi-fi and no opportunity to charge your computer. Therefore, it was sometimes easier just to write notes in hand.
courses_enrolled: Maritime Law Intellecutel Property Law Criminal Procedure and Special Issues in Substantive Criminal Law International Telecommunications Law Individual Labour Law
recommended_courses: I think everyone should choose the courses he/she thinks sound interesting. But I can strongly recommend Maritime Law. The lectures were very interesting and the teacher was very good. I can also recommend International Telecommunications Law as the exam in the course was to write a longer essay. It was very flexible that you could just write your essay when you had the time during the semester. Join the Greek Laguage Classes even though the University of Copenhagen does not recommend the course. It is nice to learn Greek and to be able to talk with the locals.
unexpected_costs: Nothing.
cost_comparison: Food at restaurants was cheaper than in Denmark, so I ate at restaurants often. At the restaurants, buy the local house wine - it is very cheap. Supermarkets were not that cheap as inflation also had reached Grecce. A bit cheaper than in Denmark, but not much. If you want to buy fruits and greens, then go to the weekly local farmers market in your area - it is cheaper than the supermarket, and everything is completely fresh. The public transportation was cheap as you as a student can buy a special student card that lasts for three or six months.
activities_available: The university had some sport facilities at the sports department, but I did not use them.
activities_recommended: Go to musems, archeological sites etc. Climb some of the hills there are in Athens - The view is amazing. Spend some days just walking around the center of Athens. Go out and eat at a local taverna, drink some wine, ouzo, and raki, and have a good time with your new friends - even on a Monday. Just enjoy your life and the spirit of Greece.
weekend_recommendations: Arrange some weekend trips to other parts of Greece. Some Erasmus organisations also arrange some trips. A part of the experience is to experience Greek culture, and there are plenty of time to do that.
culture_adjustment: It was easy.
socializing_tips: Go out and drink some coffee or a beer with the people you meet. Go to the things arranged by the student organisations in the first weeks.
cultural_challenges: There can be a lot of demonstrations and strikes in Athens - not only peaceful demonstrations. The police are massivively present in some parts of Athens - especially in Exarcheia as there are tensions between the state and the locals. You have to get used to that and that you see the police almost everywhere. The alphabet is not the latin one - so learn to read Greek.
culture_appreciated: The Greek way of living and enjoying life.
top3_advice: Do not be stressed if something does not go after your first plan. Go out and eat at the tavernas and drink coffee at the cafés - Do not spend too much time at home. Use the libraries when you want to study.
other_useful_info: There are some student restaurants offering free food to the students.
most_rewarding: To experience Greek culture and to make some new friendships with people from around all of Europe.
greatest_challenge: To live in another country.
other_comments: If you are in doubt if you want to go on an exchange, then just do it. And go to Athens!

Also the facilities are a lot different and there is graffiti and political posters all over the school.

activities_recommended: Mykonos and Santorini trip
weekend_recommendations: Island hopping Smut club

institution: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
crucial_aspects: To enjoy my Erasmus stay, culture, food, weather. A break from everyday life.
info_ease: Fairly easy. University of Copenhagen does a great job assisting and providing information
arrival_assistance: Not as much information about practical things, courses etc. as I am used to from my home university. It seems like the approach in Greece is more laissez faire. However, there was never a reason to stress about anything as eventually everything worked out.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There really was no formal registration process. Every course is 'open' and you can show up and take the exam if you like. For me, it was important that I passed at least 30 ECTS for my home university, which was not a problem.
registration_help: Most of the professors were really helpful in asking questions.
registration_success: Very succesful since I could freely select the classes I wanted. I ended up changing my Learning Agreement once, because I wanted some courses that were taught on the same days.
registration_advice: Don't stress too much about it. I believe you have 4 weeks to change your Learning Agreement from the first day of class, and if you have any questions, the professors are helpful in answering questions.
course_level: The difficulty of the subjects varied greatly. Most were somewhat easier than I am used to. The exams are not that demanding, but it is necessary to study to pass. All in all, I think it's balanced considering it's Erasmus courses.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching also varied greatly. Some professors used powerpoints, others didn't. Some professors included the students a lot, while others didn't. I'm more used to interaction between the students and the professors at my home university, which was not used that much at the host university, where it was primarily the professor who talked for 1-2 hours.
courses_enrolled: Labor Law, Maritime Law, Intellectual Property Law, Introduction to Greek Civil Law and International Telecommunications Law. 5 courses in total
recommended_courses: Definitely Labor Law, Intellectual Property Law and Maritime Law. I believe these are the most interesting. However, Intellectual Property Law was more demanding than the other courses, but I thought it was worth it for the academic benefits.
unexpected_costs: Not any unexpected costs
cost_comparison: Groceries in the supermarket are not as cheap as expected.
activities_available: There was a university gym, but it was located about an hour from the Law School, hence no students were really using it. A lot of activities are arranged by Erasmus Student Network (ESN), which can definitely be recommended to look out for.
activities_recommended: Go to the islands, go on hikes around Athens. Go to the beach of course. Also, go to Istanbul if you haven't been - flights are very cheap from Athens.
weekend_recommendations: Same as above. Also, just go out and enjoy the good food and culture. Athens is very big and every neighborhood is different
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. All courses are completely full of Erasmus students, so most of the time you'll be around people from all kinds of places.
socializing_tips: Yes, definitely check out the ESN instagram page (ESN Kapa Athens) and attend some activities.
cultural_challenges: Public transport is not the best compared to Copenhagen, where I'm from. Can be quite frustrating if you're in a hurry.
culture_appreciated: Greeks are very social, and there is not a lot of stress around you.
top3_advice: Enjoy yourself and have fun. Don't go to Athens if you're focusing on improving academically, but only if you want a calm semester where you can experience a lot. Don't cook at home too often - go out and eat instead. It's very cheap and there's a lot of good restaurants to pick from.
other_useful_info: What I did was picking courses so I only had to attend school three days a week, which was great since I had long weekends every week and therefore also the freedom to go on trips etc.
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of new people and having the freedom to do fun stuff
greatest_challenge: I don't think I faced any great challenges on my exchange other than the frustration of public transport - especially busses that never arrive on time and are always packed with people.
