crucial_aspects: Improving my Spanish speaking abilities and visiting and exploring a country and a culture that was previously quite unfamiliar to me. I chose Mexico partly because it is one of the countries where i had the easiest time understanding the Spanish spoken there, and because what i had seen of Mexican culture before going seemed very interesting to me.
info_ease: The people at the school were very helpful, but i did often have to go to the different faculties, which takes a lot of time since Mexico City is so large that taking a 1,5 to 2 hour trip just to sign some papers or getting some basic information seems excessive, additionally the information provided by UNAM is generally only in Spanish, which was fine but it would have been nice to get in English as well so could be sure that i didn't misunderstand anything due to lacking Spanish skills
arrival_assistance: I met with the administrator of the carrera who helped me get an overview of the provided classes, and was also put into contact with another student from the carrera through their Unamigo program which was very helpful with questions that weren't centered on practical school information
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I went to the faculty and talked to the administrator of the carrera and told her which classes i was thinking of taking, and got a short introduction to them, then i had to come back two days later to get sign the registration.
registration_help: In terms of registration there wasn't a lot of help besides the people who worked at the school, but i didn't feel like i needed much more than that.
registration_success: I got all the classes i wanted, i don't think the classes they offer really change from semester to semester, they have some electoral classes that might, but i couldn't sign up for those.
registration_advice: At least at the carrera i studied at, the syllabus is not really used in the actual classes or teaching, so don't make your decision based on the syllabus, but look at a description of the class and what the goals of the class is instead
course_level: The level of courses at my carrera were very low, the carrera is called English Teaching, and i knew that the level of english is generally lower in Mexico compared to Denmark, but the classes were closer to highschool level than university in my opinion. In most classes no readings are assigned for the entire semester, and when teachers did assign readings nobody did them, and then the following classes were spent explaining and summarizing what was in the readings instead of actually working with the materials
teaching_comparison: It is much more focused on classroom teaching, there is a 80% mandatory attendance, and they generally don't assign readings, they might assign homework for a class, but generally the homework is done fairly quickly and easily. The teaching is more focused on practical aspects, which makes sense since it is English teaching and not just English, as in Denmark, they did not work with theory in any of the subjects, but did a lot of group work and stuff like it in the classroom.
courses_enrolled: English VI, Investigation into Applied Linguistics, Literature in English II, Psycholinguistics, Translation
recommended_courses: The only course i took that i would recommend is translation, I don't feel that i learned much about translation since we the class didn't include any theory and i have already done two semesters of translation before going, but it was a really good way to improve my Spanish, if you are already fluent in Spanish and English, you may not get that much out of it.
unexpected_costs: Most of the unexpected costs were related to renting out my apartment in Denmark while abroad, other than that i don't think there was much, if there were it was not an large amount
cost_comparison: There are a lot of imported items in supermarkets, either from Europe or the US, these are very expensive, fx. you can get mexican brand pasta for about 7-10 dkk but if you get the imported pasta it will cost about 50dkk, and sometimes the labels are not great in the supermarkets. Other than that, wine is very expensive compared to europe and tequila is very cheap.
activities_available: There were sports teams and equipment available, additionally there was a language center where you can take language classes, and do other cultural activities.
activities_recommended: If you need help with Spanish, or another language, university language classes are a good way to improve while building a social circle at university, and they are usually free or very cheap for students. Outside of school, i think the best is dance, usually in mexico salsa and bachata classes, there are a lot of different people, both young and older.
weekend_recommendations: Coyoacan is a very nice part of town with a lot of markets where you can buy local food specialties, souvenirs, and other things, Puebla takes one or two hours to get to but is very nice to stay at for one or two nights. Chapultepec and the castle which is near the anthropological museum, which is nice, but very large so i don't recommend trying to see it all in one go, especially since UNAM students get into almost all museums free.
culture_adjustment: A little difficult, though i think it was more due being so far away from friends and family and suddenly losing all routines i had in my life, it helps that people are very talkative here, and since there wasn't many exchange students at my faculty people are very eager to talk to someone not from mexico and hear why they chose to come here.
socializing_tips: People will likely invite you to a lot of things, especially in the beginning when you are getting adjusted to everything and are more tired than usual, they tend to understand if you explain why you can't/dont want to go, but try to say yes sometimes even if you dont have a lot of energy, since doing since outside of the school framework helps you getting friends faster
cultural_challenges: Compared to in Denmark it feels like it is more important what you say than what you do, especially with being polite, It is very important to greet people and saying thank you and please and goodbye, but unlike in Denmark, it is not really considered rude to be late, or to invite someone to something and then cancel last minute, which can be frustrating if you aren't expecting it.
culture_appreciated: The openness and helpfulness, sometimes when asking people for help i would feel bad because they would go so far out of their way to help me that i felt i was impeding what they had to do, but i think the culture is just more helpful in general.
top3_advice: - If you are unsure of anything or need help, talk to your teacher, they are a lot closer to the students than in Denmark since they have more classes and will likely be very accommodating to whatever you might need, especially when you are on exchange. - join a whatsapp group for exchange students, i was in two called CDMX, events parties and trips & Exchange CDMX, its a good way to meet other exchange students and go on trips outside the city that you might not feel comfortable doing alone. - The culture at mexican universities is very different from danish universities, it is seen as a bit weird to be alone on campus and people might approach you and ask you about it if you walk around, eat, read alone on campus, but they mean it in a friendly way, usually.
other_useful_info: Go visit the other faculties, especially Ciudad Universitaria has a lot of fun things, like small shops and museums
most_rewarding: Getting outside of my comfort zone, improving my spanish speaking abilities very rapidly, and meeting some of my roommates who were also on exchange.
greatest_challenge: Getting used to the daily life, stuff like stuff not working properly in my apartment, having to spend more than 3 hours every day going back and forth from university to my apartment.

cultural_challenges: Loads... But I easily overcame them? A lot of bugs everywhere, indoors too... Ants, cockroaches, flying ones too... It's all a bit much in the beginning, but it gives you something to bond over with the other internationals

crucial_aspects: I did not choose Taiwan, it was a mandatory stay
info_ease: Pretty difficult, there was loads of miscommunication between KU and NTNU. The teachers had very different expectations for us based on what KU told them, which made the entire process very mentally taxing because we weren't prepared.
arrival_assistance: None really, we had to pressure KU to set up a zoom meeting so we could air out all of our concerns, one of them being the lack of help.
arrival_comments: KU gave us false information that we had to get our hands on a health statement. This was extremely constly and time consuming, as we had to schedule doctors appointments and get unneccesary X-rays done. We only found out at the visa office that it was not neccessary.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We were automatically enrolled in courses.
registration_help: We were automatically enrolled so there was no need for help.
registration_success: We did not have a choice in the classes that we took.
registration_advice: There really isn't any when it comes to mandatory stays.
course_level: The levels were okay, not any more challenging than back home, except for the amount of mandatory homework assigned every single day, which was quite overwhelming.
teaching_comparison: There really wasn't any understanding for bad days, you were expected to perform every single day like your life depended on it.
courses_enrolled: It was intensive Chinese language course.
recommended_courses: Intensive will get you good very quickly because you're forced to speak in class.
unexpected_costs: None really, our phone bill was paid in full, so that was quite expensive one time payment, but besides that not really.
cost_comparison: The food and drinks are ridiculously cheap in Taiwan. We had food delivery every single day due to the lack of kitchen and it was super cheap.
activities_available: There were a couple of clubs, but majority tailored to local students and some had even refused to take in a foreigner. They're conducted in Chinese so if you don't speak it, you wouldn't be able to participate.
activities_recommended: See other places in Taiwan, Taichung is lively and the people are kind, the same can be said for Tainan. Tainan is amazing if you're a history nerd, it had so many beautiful spots. Its easy getting high speed rail tickets to go someplace else, visit some of the small isles as well for beautiful beaches.
weekend_recommendations: Go and see some museums in Taipei, visit historical sites in Tainan, go and shop in Taichung. Go to Shilin night market, it has everything you need. My favorite place in Taipei was Ximen, best place to buy kpop albums, and anime merch. Go and experience a traditional tea ceremony as well, it's worth it. The Taipei zoo is massive as well and you can spend an entire day in there.
culture_adjustment: Initially hard because of the lack of english proficiency among the locals, i was forced to speak Chinese which worked out for the best in the end.
socializing_tips: I didn't have any communication with local students as my university department was strictly for foreigners coming to learn Chinese.
cultural_challenges: Getting used to the garbage trucks blasting the same song over and over again is something you'll have to do. The busses also have no regard for your wellbeing, so expect to be thrown around and pretend as if you're in a fast & furious franchise. It's a cash based society, so you have to get comfortable with planning a budget and paying cash everywhere you go.
culture_appreciated: The people are genuinely kind when they hear your feeble attempts to communicate in Chinese, they appreciate it, so don't be scared. They're also very polite, people move quickly because Taipei is a big city.
top3_advice: 1. Do not take everything the teachers say to heart. Sometimes they can say genuinely mean spirited things (flashbacks to my teacher telling me that i didn't deserve to be there) just treat them as a military recruiter. 2. Wave down the busses when you want them stop for you, otherwise they won't. 3. Please bring a jacket, once the weather cools down you will be freezing, even though it's technically 15 degrees which would be tshirt weather for us. We adapt to the temperature.
other_useful_info: Not really
most_rewarding: Being able to conversate in Chinese with my uber driver on my way to the airport, i wasn't even nervous. Oh and also being able to speak in Chinese on the phone to my delivery drivers, that was a big pat on the back moment for me.
greatest_challenge: Being homesick, living in a room without a window (please don't make the same mistake thinking it'll be okay, i promise sunlight does so much for us).

crucial_aspects: Exchange was mandatory as part of the curriculum on my education. Due to the covid-pandemic between 2020-2023, UCPH has not able to send student on obligatory exchange with previously partnered universities in China, and had established a pilot program with a university in Taipei, Taiwan, for my class.
overall_comments: My class was told shortly after enrollment (fall 2021), that the previous class had not been able to do the mandatory exchange with partnered universities due to at the time ongoing covid-pandemic. This resulted in the previous class being forced to follow the protocol curriculum of having comparable lectures at UCPH. Due to the evolving circumstances in relation to the covid-pandemic, we were told to prepare for the same treatment. Shortly after my class' 2. semester had begun, we were invited to a breifing from the UCPH Outgoing Exchange Office, who had initiated a pilot exchange program with new universities. The briefing was inchoate, but provided the bare necessary information and application deadlines for the obligatory exchange to be succesful. The following months were filled with chaotic messages and misunderstandings between my class and the Outgoing Exchange Office, as the Outgoing Exchange Office had failed to communicate sufficient information from the Taiwanese Trade Office, who had supreme authority on the matter (possible/impossible). The misunderstandings were solved by the students, and the pilot exchange was still afloat, provided that students were in direct contact with the Taiwanese Trade Office. Due to the circumstances of the covid-pandemic, the pilot exchange was always subject to potential changes, and put a lot of mental stress on students, ranging from uncertain housing situations to unclear transactional possibilities. No instruments for solving these issues were introduced to students by the UCPH Outgoing Exchange Office, who were solely responsible for matters related to the exchange spot on the host university. The majority of the class' students were able to overcome these issues, me included. The duration and quality of the stay good, provided that the students themselves had taken measures to ensure this. No follow-up was initiated by the UCPH Outgoing Exchange Office for at least a month into the stay. The follow-up had no substantial information to provide. All communication with the host university was done more or less by students, which involved everything from credit transfers to whether the class was following the correct studyprogram. Credit transfer became an issue upon return, as the Credit Transfers Office under the UCPH Education and Student Office was unable to confirm the credit papers from the host university. The UCPH Outgoing Exchange Office did not provide any help on the issue.
info_ease: Bad, read the above comment under General Evaluation.

crucial_aspects: Going to a country with a different culture to explore, in order to expand both my academic and personal view on studying.
info_ease: It was fairly easy.
arrival_assistance: Contact with a guidance counsellor at the university.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process for courses at NTU is done through an online course selector. It was pretty easy and fairly intuitive once you learn what is up and down. However, help for the course selector is also possible through the guidance counsellors.
registration_help: Guidance counsellors and fellow classmates.
registration_success: Very succesful, only one of my courses did not begin as the number of students registered for the course was too low.
registration_advice: Do it in good time, and ask fellow students to help you if you're unsure.
course_level: The level of courses varied a lot, depending on what you are interested in. As a BA it is also possible to do some MA courses if it is something you are interested in.
teaching_comparison: Some of the courses were very similar with a few reports having to be handed in during the semester, and with class presentations. Other courses had weekly quizzes and attendance counting for the final grade, alongside with reports and presentations.
courses_enrolled: Chinese Enhancing Course International Companions for Learning Climate and Ocean: From Past to Future Exploring Taiwan: natural environment and resources Renewable Energy and Bioresource Recycling Technologies General Chinese Language Course
recommended_courses: Chinese Enhancing Course & General Chinese Language Course: I would definitely recommend taking at least one Chinese Language course, as it is always fun to learn the language of the country you are living in. Furthermore, it can help in your day-to-day life. The courses offered at NTU is very well done, and you are able to learn a surprisingly lot of Mandarin in just one semester. International Companions for Learning: A program that is not really a course, but more of a cultural exchange with local students from elementary schools around Taiwan. It is a weekly online meeting with a class of young students, and you also have a local student from the university as your partner. During this program you also get to go on a schooltrip to the school of your students, a trip that is fully paid by NTU. It is a great way to explore the country and dive in to the local and rural culture of Taiwan. Exploring Taiwan: natural environment and resources & Exploring Taiwan: Natural Resources Conservation and Management: Any course with the title "Exploring Taiwan" is a course mostly dedicated to exchange students. It is a great way to learn about the country on many different aspects. Seminar on China and Global Climate Governance: A course dedicated to investigate the behaviour of China in regards to how climate politics are conducted and governed. Super interesting and relevant. The professor is amazing and he is very helpful and knowledgeable.
unexpected_costs: A lot of things are fairly cheap in Taiwan compared to Denmark. Many times it is better and cheaper to go out and buy food from a nightmarket, rather than cooking at home. The public transportation runs very well, i did have to spend quite a lot of money on it monthly because i lived quite far away from my university. But in general there was not really any unexpected costs, except for government documents if that is needed. But that depends a lot on how long you are staying and what you need to do while you're in Taiwan.
cost_comparison: More expensive: Public transportation (Still very cheap, just thought it was even cheaper). Less expensive: Pretty much everything.
activities_available: Any kind of club, sport and hobbies was available to the students through the university. Very well done!
activities_recommended: Travel around the island as much as possible. It is not very big, but there is still so much to see, and the landscape and topography is so diverse.
weekend_recommendations: Travel to Alishan, Yangmingshan, go to some of the smaller islands, visit Kaohsiung & Kenting.
culture_adjustment: The culture was very different, however studying with other exchange students made it very easy to adjust, while also getting to know local students helped a lot. Taiwanese people are VERY friendly and hospitable.
socializing_tips: Give them time as some students are not too comfortable with their english, even though it is at a good level. Try to learn some Mandarin to talk with them. Join the International Companions for Learning programme.
cultural_challenges: The paperwork and bureaucracy in Taiwan is horrible.
culture_appreciated: The people, the food, the architecture and landscapes and the academic life.
top3_advice: Learn a bit of Mandarin. Be open-minded to a different culture. Focus on the life outside of school the most.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Getting to live in another country and enjoying a life that is so different from the one that is known back in Denmark.
greatest_challenge: Prolonging the stay for a second semester. If you have thoughts about this make sure that you inform KU and NTU a long time in advance so they can make sure everything is in order.
other_comments: Enjoy your trip!

overall_comments: The randomness of the course selection system created a lot of problems for me.
info_ease: Difficult, I kept calling concerning course selection problems and could not get assistance.
arrival_assistance: I received a lot of assistance concerning covid rules and procedures.
arrival_comments: There was not sufficient information and guidance concerning course selections and the selection system.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The randomness of the course selection system created a lot of problems for me.
registration_process: I did not have enough courses but could only register through emailing the professors and they did not answer.
registration_help: No help for registration process.
registration_success: Not successful. The professors did not answer and I had to register for classes where it was not necessary to email professors in the last minute but these classes were not related to my studies and even though the course description said that no prerequisites were required to attend the course that was not true at all and the courses were quite demanding. Because I was registered late I missed the deadline to cancel the courses and was force to attend and fail one course.
registration_advice: You have to register for at least five times the amount of courses that you need from the beginning. If not, you will not be accepted to enough courses and will end up having to find courses during a casino like period where you can almost only add courses through contacting professors that don't answer (with few exceptions) and in the end will end up chosing those that do not require this option which are mostly science courses.
academics_comments: The randomness of the course selection system created a lot of problems for me.
course_level: The levels of the courses were fine but the workload big.
teaching_comparison: Every course was different according to the style of the professors.

recommended_courses: Chinese Historical stories for those who want to improve their Chinese.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay your electricity, you have to but your own mattress and pillow
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than I expected
activities_available: Introduction to calligraphy, Chinese painting, mahjong, baking food - on an introductory level for an evening of fun. There were clubs, but I mostly got invitations to a Buddhist club that wanted to recruit people to Buddhism and becoming vegetarian.
activities_recommended: Personally, I invested time in outside campus activities such as martial arts and archery. The campus had taekwondo but I am more interested in kungfu.
weekend_recommendations: National museum of art, the temples, Sun Moon Lake, Hualien, the south.
culture_adjustment: People are kind but many don't appreciate when you speak loudly.
socializing_tips: Attend the cultural activities.
cultural_challenges: Some Taiwanese speak with extremely low tone and it can be hard to practice Chinese in those cases.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and calmness.
top3_advice: Register for a lot of courses beforehand, don't bring nice quality clothing because the humidity can destroy it and the cleaners don't know how to treat it. Bring an empty suit case because you will find a lot of souvenirs.
other_useful_info: If you have a very good umbrella bring it, it rains a lot.
most_rewarding: Getting to know the culture and Chinese language.
greatest_challenge: The dialect.
other_comments: The streets are not safe, I sprained a foot badly by stepping down into a hole next to the dormitory. Also, the scooter drivers are dangerous.

crucial_aspects: I chose Taiwan because I've always wanted to visit the Chinese speaking world, without actually going to China. I heard some rumours that trips to China could be at best cumbersome as a non-Mandarin speaking foreigner, and heard much nicer things about travelling to Hong Kong or Taiwan, and ended up choosing Taiwan. I did not end up regretting this choice at all.
overall_comments: The trip as a whole was wonderful. There were many moments of hair-pulling frustration, boxing with cumbersome bureaucracy, and a delayed full-scale pandemic response, but all of it paled in comparison to how stunning the nature was, how amazing it was to learn history and experience a completely different culture, and how incredibly friendly the people there were. I didn't speak any Mandarin, but the locals all tried (and mostly failed) to learn English, so there was an understanding that really afforded you quite a bit of leeway to practice your charades. Taiwan is pretty excluded from the itenerarys of surrounding Asia backpackers, so all local tourist facilities are designed primarily for internal tourism. Outside of Taipei especially, you may be the first foreigner to stop by in a long while. It'll be great, I promise.
info_ease: It was pretty bad. It was definitely, DEFINITELY made worse by covid (keep in mind that this review is written in start 2023), but don't expect the consulates (de facto embassies) to go easy on you just because the regulation was loosened. Most students were given ultra-short 3-5 day deadlines to stamp maybe 5 different papers. The papers they send you on mail will probably not be the right ones. The ones they send you on mail will definitely not be sufficient. Many of the procedures can only be done in Mandarin, so make some Mandarin speaking friend before you leave, immediately upon arrival, or get very good at guessing what papers can safely be ignored and what are official papers that need immediate attention and probably a couple of stamps.
arrival_assistance: Very little. Most locals are culturally inclined to be incredibly helpful by nature, but dealing with bureacracy seems to be the one exception. Expect people to be annoyed with you for asking how to fill out a certain form. Expect people to be annoyed with you for not knowing where things are. Expect people to be annoyed with you for not knowing your chinese name. Expect registration to be minimum (1) full 40-work week, and plan that it may be twice that. I met people who were still dealing with their registration well 3-4 months into their stay.

This system supposedly alleviates the problems of the course website, but essentially entails that its near impossible for you to discern going into the period what classes you'll actually end up doing. My only recommendation is sign up for as many classes as possible, and then drop aggresively the bad ones, so you end up with a tolerable mix of classes.
registration_help: Technically you could probably ask the office of international affairs, but I've found them to be not very helpful people on the whole. You're mostly on your own.

Try to see what rumours that you can pick up on the 2 week window, as rumours tend to be a much better instruction than the website / what the instructors may tell you.
registration_advice: Sign yourself up for as much as possible, and drop quickly. Its ok to drop halfway into the semester. Plan for the fact that many things may go wrong. Most host instutitions that I heard of were alright with you not doing a full 30 ECTS block, although it in some cases had implications for funding for scholarships (e.g. Danish SU).

Outside of Taipei especially, you may be the first foreigner to stop by in a long while. It'll be great, I promise.
course_level: It was alright. I can't speak to the quality of the teaching in Mandarin, but most the English speaking classes went out of their way to be as inclusive to non-majors within their department as possible, as each department tended to only offer few actual English classes. This means that many of the classes couldn't actually require much background knowledge, and hence you will probably end up doing quite a few "introduction to ..."-type classes. Most of the professors for the English classes had an American Ivy League Ma/PhD, so the actual quality wasn't low, the problem was mainly just the target audience was very broad. There's also a HUGE gap in intensity between classes, where in some classes you may end up only studying 1-2 days for the entire semester, and some 2-3 weeks. Plan according to the trip that you want to have.
teaching_comparison: Most classes consisted entirely of lectures and a little bit of homework, i.e. there were no practice classes. You don't understand how much you miss practice classes until you don't have them. The lack of practice classes went hand-in-hand with a style of teaching where you're expected to remember the contents of the lectures verbatim, with many questions to homework/exams literally, number-for-number, having been presented as a .PPTX on the board a couple of weeks earlier. This style of teaching will be comfortable for some, and really grate others the wrong way.
courses_enrolled: 1. "Financial Market and Derivatives" 3 credits 2. "Trade Theory" 3 credits 3. "Python Programming Foundation" 3 credits 4. "Causal Inference and Prediction in Econometrics" 2 credits
recommended_courses: Causal Inference and Prediction in Econometrics has a really wonderful instructor if you're into econometric proofs. Note that you should feel more-than-confident in your multivariate optimization, i.e. the cross between linear algebra and calculus III, otherwise you're in for a rude awakening in the second half of the course. Trade Theory is almost mandatory for econ majors, as the instructor is really sweet, and it really is an easy A, thats pretty interesting along the way. Financial Market and Deriatives is the hardest course here, and has a notorious instructor, that experienced quite a bit of personal turmoil alongside the semester which translated into quite a bit of abuse at the student body, so its a little hard to recommend. The python programming courses tend to be very fun and free-spirited, and can only recommend them.
unexpected_costs: You'll notice that Taiwan is heavily tariffed by the surrounding world, likely owing to the political situation with China. Therefore, especially food will in general be much more expensive than you think. Additionally, your accomodation is very unlikely to come with a kitchen of any use, so you'll likely be eating out for 3 meals of the day. This will add up. The trains for travelling inside the country are additionally more expensive than you think, and you will want to take them, because Taiwan is wonderful to travel in. You may also want to put money aside for picking up a (cheap) airplane-ticket to Vietnam/Thailand/Philippines/Japan when your exchange ends.
cost_comparison: Most international brands (UNIQLO/IKEA/Sony) will probably be the same price as at home, maybe 5-10% cheaper at best. Local brands tend to be 40-50% cheaper than west Europe. Food adds up because of the kitchen situation.
activities_available: Literally everything was available, although only some will be in English. Go to club day, around the start of the semester, and you'll find literally hundreds of activities. Keep in mind that most of it will be in Mandarin, but if you bring a mandarin speaking friend, or just go to a pretty foreigner-friendly club in general, then you should have a great time. Met several people who did skateboarding, baking, photography, sports, travelling and so on. Reputedly, especially the "hiking groups", of which there should be several, tend to be very good places to meet new friends and experience Taiwan.
activities_recommended: I'm personally a little useless for club-activities, but I went to go see close to a million temples and museums. Often just taking a friend into the mountains to go see a temple is a wonderful way to spend an afternoon. Afterwards, try to pick up on what's happening in Taipei: There's many festivals, concerts, street parties, pop-up nightmarkets, 2 EUR michelin-star food stands and novel activities in general always available, and seemingly never that far from where you are.
weekend_recommendations: Taiwan really shines outside of its cities. Go to the hot spring, go on the hikes, rent a scooter on the islands, make new friends, anything is possible, and everything is pretty affordable. The weather is likely to be highly unpredictable, and may rain for several weeks in a row, so when the weather allows, be sure to grab the oppurtunity to leave Taipei, because you may not know when that chance appears again.
culture_adjustment: It will take a while. The initial bit of your trip may feel downright hostile while you're adjusting, but that feeling subsides after a couple of weeks. Afterwards, you'll find yourself wishing many of the conveniences of Taipei were availble at home, like the almost completely ubiqutous presence of cheap convenience stores and ridicolously cheap rental bikes.
socializing_tips: Its much easier if you have an activity. The hiking clubs will have the lowest barrier for entry, although the sports clubs also tend to be very approachable. The foreigner bars (namely Another Brick & Revolver, and to some extent most of Ximen) will also be a good entry point.
cultural_challenges: Expect Taiwenese people to be very polite, and have some difficulty to speak up if they're dissatisfied with something. You may at times be commiting a massive social faux pas, although you may not realize it, because no-one will as much as acknowledge it. The language barrier is also REAL. People may, in 1-on-1 speak to you in perfect english, but may in a group setting, or after one beer, completely lose this ability. Plan accordingly.
culture_appreciated: The politeness is real. Especially outside of Taipei, people will be so polite that you may not even realize what's happening before someone invited you into their house and fed you a full dinner and drinks. Taiwan in general is also just very safe. I lived in comfortably the dodgiest part of Taipei, and still did I not even once feel unsafe walking the streets alone at night, even when exploring dark unlit alleyways. There was a in one of my classes who got in a minor scooter-tuffle with a local, and it made national news and there was an interview and everything. It was really very minor. Taiwan is really very safe.
top3_advice: - Bring patience for the first part of the trip. The bureacracy/registration will be a nightmare, and you're just gonna have to deal with with it. - Travel as much as you can when you get the oppurtunity. Taiwan truly shines outside of its cities. You will love it, I promise. Its all the best and most interesting parts of Asia smashed together in a package where crime seemingly just does not exist. - Bring more money than you think. Taiwan is cheaper than western Europe, but not eastern europe. Budget accordingly.
other_useful_info: You don't have to do Mandarin if you don't want to, but if you're staying here for 2 semesters, I think its a wonderful oppurtunity to learn a solid introduction to a very different language pretty comfortably. If you're only staying here for a semester, and you're starting from scratch, it may be limited how much you in practice may pick up, so plan accordingly.
most_rewarding: The people and the culture that I met along the way. Even though I really did just hang out with a lot of Germans for most of the trip, it was so wonderful to be away for so long and completely submerge myself in something that's so different from home, but still really so very, very nice.
greatest_challenge: I was pretty scared of the political situation, and I freaked out a little every time my roomie burned her rice and set off the fire alarm. Additionally, you will be very far from home, so holding onto family/friends/romantic relationships will be difficult across time-zones. Most manage to do it, but you will need to put some effort into it.
other_comments: I probably wouldn't go for the academics, and I definitely wouldn't go for the registration process, but if you want to experience one of the nicest parts of Asia, a little pearl of history, cross-cultural influences and burgeoning national identity, I can't recommend Taiwan enough.

info_ease: I think it was okay. There is a website where you do the application. It's stated what kind of documents you need to upload. The only thing that was a bit difficult to find out was how to do the health report check in TW, but i figured it out. They sent a lot of emails, so it can be a bit confusing to remember everything, better write it down in your calendar. I was also assigned a local student buddy i could ask questions to. She sent me an email and then i could message her if i had any questions.
arrival_assistance: We had a campus tour where the local students showed is around the campus. We also had some kind of "information day" where people from the international office gave us information about how stuff works at NTU.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: the destination was amazing, the only reason i did not give 10 marks is because i feel like the teaching at National Taiwan University (NTU) was not that good
registration_process: You first upload the relevant documents online. Then there is a big registration date where every student gets assigned a time to show up. You need to bring documents with you, and then you go through some stations to get the documents checked. If everything is okay, you receive your student ID card.
registration_help: The international office could be contacted if there was anything.
registration_success: I needed at least 12 credits. After applying for courses ended i only got 6 credits. I remember there are two rounds where you list the courses you want. After this the add/drop period starts. Student can drop courses, and then other people can add them. courses that are full might still have spaces for students if you go to the professor and ask for a code to join the courses. Therefore i went to two classes at their first lecture to ask the professor for a code. An email also works. On the course website, you will be able to see what to do in order to get the course, some might be completely full though.
registration_advice: During course registration in the first two rounds the strategy is to apply for everything, and then drop the courses you don't want. The courses you do not get but want to have, go ask the professor for an add code. So don't get worried if you end up with too few courses in the two rounds, it all changes again in the add/drop period
academics_comments: the destination was amazing, the only reason i did not give 10 marks is because i feel like the teaching at National Taiwan University (NTU) was not that good
course_level: 2 of the courses i had was really difficult and i had a hard time keeping up. One of them i understood almost everything so no problem there. The last one the professor was really bad at teaching, so i did not go to class that much.
teaching_comparison: I had one class where the professor would cold call students to answer questions, that is rare in UCPH. Other that than it reminds of UCPH, a professor uses some slides to go through the lecture. As i had mentioned before i had no exercise classes. The grading depends on the class. It can be a mix of quizzes, presentations, attendance, final exam, midterm and etc. For my classes i was a mix between presentations, assignment and maybe a final exam. For example presentation could be 25%, final exam 50% and assignments 25%. This kind of grading system causes the workload to be higher, because you need to make sure your assignments are good. At UCPH we normally our final grade is just the final exam.
courses_enrolled: Computational methods in econometrics: Very difficult course, would not recommend because you need to spend a lot of time on it. Also you only learn the theory, but the assignments are about coding. So you essentially need to learn the coding yourself. Market & strategy. Can recommend. The professor cold calls, but his teaching is really good. I learned a lot from this course. The "final exam" is a research proposal which was actually quite fun to make. Advanced applied econometrics and international trade: Can not recommend. The professor is really bad at teaching. Also the professor is not good at giving information out and changes plans a lot. The final exam felt more like a memory test rather than an exam. Spatial economics: Mixed feelings. The course is really interesting but also very difficult. So it depends on how much you want to spent on studying while on exchange. If you're willing to spend time studying i would say go for it. I also had chinese for fun, i can recommend it. I was placed in intermediate 1A after the placement test. The teacher was really good and it's also a good way to make new friends :D
recommended_courses: I did this above
unexpected_costs: Comments to above: I walked to school so did not spend money on that, tbh i have no idea how much i spent riding public transport each month. Also the phone plan i do not remember. You can get a deal at Chunghwa telecom in the airport where you buy get a student discount with unlimited data. You pay for everything at once. Internet was included in my rent. Personal spending i also just typed something in. Unexpected costs: I did much more travel than i expected to do. But it's worth it, Taiwan is so beautiful so make sure to travel around and see stuff!!
cost_comparison: Actually the food was a bit more expensive than i expected. Travelling was really cheap. The cheapest way to get around is probably by bus. Hostels in Taiwan are super good quality. All of the hostels i stayed at provided soap, and a lot of them provide slippers.
activities_available: NTU campus is amazing. There's a lot of clubs you can join, and there are sport facilities such as baseball. football, swimming, tennis, volleyball and probably more if you are into that.
activities_recommended: There's a list of clubs. If you find anything interested go for it. Would be a good way also to meet local students.
weekend_recommendations: Travel around Taiwan. As said before it's cheap and there is so much stuff to see in Taiwan. It's really ideal to travel Taiwan because it's so small and public transport is good. I personally enjoyed hiking. Coming from Denmark which is a flat country, hiking mountains was really fun. If you plan ahead there are some mountains that requires permits. So if you wanna climb for example Jade mountain plan ahead and apply for the permit. There's also a lot of stuff to do in Taipei, i visited parks, historical landmarks, went to museums, went hiking. National palace museum is a must visit! I would recommend getting a international driver's licence before going, it will make it easier to get a scooter which is essential when going to the small islands.
culture_adjustment: I have chinese background, i also lived in Beijing for 6 months in my gap year and have been a lot of times to China to visit my family. Since Taiwanese culture and Chinese culture have some overlap, it was easier for me to adapt. For me therefore it was not that difficult, but hearing from my international friends it seems like it was not that difficult to adapt.
socializing_tips: Language exchange is a good opportunity to meet locals, surprisingly i found someone who wanted to learn Danish. Go join a club on campus, use apps.
cultural_challenges: When ordering food, seems like you just walk up and talk without the worker asking you first. Normally in Denmark i always wait for the worker to say Hi or something, otherwise it feels rude. But other than that i did not experience any problems, and this is a minor one because when ordering at restaurants, you normally just get a paper menu and cross of what you want to eat. Otherwise not really much problems, but as said before i had been to China a lot of times.
culture_appreciated: People are really friendly in Taiwan. Also Taiwan is very safe
top3_advice: Get ready for the bureaucracy, a lot of stuff needs to be done before you go, and also when you arrive in Taiwan. In Taiwan cash is still king. So you need to bring cash with you. It would be a good idea to do research into which banks offer the cheapest ATM fee. I personally only used Bank of Taiwan. Some places take linepay where you can connect your debit/credit card. Here i used revolut so there would be no exchange fee when paying in the weekdays. Travel and enjoy the experience. You will miss Taiwan a lot when getting home, remember that school is not everything. It's in my opinion just as important to travel and meet new people.
other_useful_info: There's a taiwanese like reddit called PTT. Here you can read Taiwanese students write reports about courses they took. It's of course in Chinese but google translate is fine. You prob have to do the search in chinese also. For example to look up report for market and strategy i could type "ptt 市場與策略" which is market and strategy in chinese. It probably also works if you type in the course number. The first result is this : https://www.ptt.cc/bbs/NTUcourse/M.1498144948.A.B8F.html
most_rewarding: The friendship you made when on exchange. You make friends with people all over the world! Being able to practise my mandarin was also nice. Travelling around Taiwan with friends and also alone was amazing. There's a lot of different food to try also.
greatest_challenge: Definitely the language. My chinese is probably like kindergarten level so i would have difficulty talking and understanding. A lot of menus are in Chinese only, so you would have to use your phone to translate the stuff. It was also difficult balancing school and travelling. The workload is higher at NTU than at UCPH. You're still a student so you still need to study, but at the same time you of course want to experience stuff. I personally felt like i had to turn down too many stuff in order to get my assignments done. The final month was also very stressful, with a mix of presentations, paper reports, final exam.
other_comments: It can get really hot in Taiwan in the summer. I was travelling in end of june, and i had to go into 7-11 to get some AC from time to time. The scallion pancake (蔥抓餅) close to campus gongguan（公館) is super good, it's on the michelin bib gourmand list. Enjoy it!!! I miss it a lot

activities_available: I think that would be too many to list here (and definitely too many for me to look up).
activities_recommended: There's a bunch of activities for exchange students but I would recommend also joining some local clubs. This is a good opportunity to get to know local people and they are very friendly towards foreigners.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the Islands. Take the High speed rail down south. Go hiking.
culture_adjustment: I did not have any big problems but of course the customs are very different. However, I would say that you mostly end up hanging out with the other exchange students anyways.
socializing_tips: Join a club. Learn Chinese.
cultural_challenges: Locals can be a bit shy and seem cold until you approach them.
culture_appreciated: People are very friendly towards foreigners.
top3_advice: Don't have too many expectations about how the semester is supposed to be. It won't be like that.
other_useful_info: Every other exchange student is in the exact same position as you and all local students think you are pretty interesting. Don't be afraid to engage.
most_rewarding: Gaining now friends, new academic experiences and perspectives on issues, learning a new language.

crucial_aspects: That I could get into the country. China was still closed down so Taiwan was the next best thing.
info_ease: It is always a bit stressful to go to another country, but I think they made it easier with the information sheet they made.
arrival_assistance: We did get a buddy from the university we could write with and could help us, but I never heard from mine so that was quite unlucky. Also there was a assistant that should had helped exchange students but that person changed 3 times while we were there and you never got a response back if you wrote an email.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: So you were told before coming to the country about the registration and what documents you should have with you. On the day, you bring all of them and then you go around to the tables were you one after one, give the document you need. At the last table you will get your student ID. Pretty easy.
registration_help: As I told before there was one person, but she changed 3 times, so not very helpful.
registration_success: So this was an interesting process. You had the first two weeks to try out the classes you were interested in. I was lucky to get the classes that I wanted and that is not always the case.
registration_advice: Be fast to get the registration code for the classes you really want.
course_level: You could choose between 1, 2, and 3 credit courses. The 3 credit courses were the most workload. I had most of my courses 2 credit and 1 that were 3 credit.
teaching_comparison: It was quite good. Most of the professors were good and sweet.
courses_enrolled: Exploring Taiwan: Women and Taiwanese Society, General Chinese, Enhancing Chinese, Seminar on Asian Democratization, Exploring Taiwan: Natural Environment and resources, What really bugs you.
recommended_courses: Chinese if you want to order and talk with locals. Women and Taiwanese Society were fascinating also.
unexpected_costs: Books, i did not really think about that i had to buy that. Electricity for your room, that is not in your housing free every month.
cost_comparison: Electricity cost.
activities_available: You can get into everything, a basketball club, Chinese club, handcraft club, cooking club, etc.
activities_recommended: Chinese club is very interesting. You go and trips and can try calligraphy.
weekend_recommendations: Try to get local friends and go with them to celebrate the holidays with they family.
culture_adjustment: For be it was fine, because I had already been to china before.
socializing_tips: Go to the clubs, be open and be patient.
cultural_challenges: How long they study for. They study to so late of night and still get up early in the morning for they classes.
culture_appreciated: how friendly and open they are to help you.
top3_advice: Remember to have fun and make friends even though the university workload can be challenging sometimes.
other_useful_info: Make a group with other exchange students because it was very helpful to have other that is in the same both as you.
most_rewarding: The friendships I made all over the world.
greatest_challenge: The workload from the school. But it it also the best school in Taiwan
other_comments: Enjoy it! Its the best thing I ever did.

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: in general it was good, but the forms and registration process was very confusing and stressing
registration_process: there was two days were you should registere to ass many courses possible, and then the seats would be assigned randomely, so sometime you would have too many credits and some times tou would have two few. the first two weeks you would then be able to attend as many classes as possible also those you did not get registered to, and then you had to ask the professor if there was room in their class and if you could get a code for that class. you also had to deregister classes here.
registration_help: you could ask a student voulenteer for help, and there was an online vidoe. but still confusing.
