crucial_aspects: That it was a mandarin-speaking country.
overall_comments: It was really amazing!!
info_ease: It was fairly easy to find on the website, and if it was troublesome, you could always write an email or call the international contact at NTU.
arrival_assistance: Unfortunately my assigned student volunteer did not contact me, but my danish classmates from KU who also came to NTU had a very good student volunteer we could ask for help. And fortunately I had a Taiwanese friend who was a NTU student, which I asked for help.
arrival_comments: It was a nice orientation that provided a lot of information in an engaging way.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was really amazing!!
registration_process: Stressfull and long. So many emails. But you will get through it. Use your KU classmates for help and support. They make it seem more urgent and strict than it really is.
registration_help: The international contact at NTU, but mostly I used my classmates and the local NTU student that I new. Hopefully you can use your student volunteer.
registration_success: I was fairly succesfull! But I think I was lucky, and I applied for a lot of courses (around 18 courses I think).
registration_advice: Talk with your classmates about courses, because NTU have a huge amount of courses and it's hard to choose. Talk with other internationals during and before orientation to get inspired. Don't hold back trying new courses. Don't be too quick to settle.
academics_comments: It was really amazing!!
course_level: I had taken mandarin courses and marketing courses. The marketing courses was very introductory, so they were fairly easy and manageable. The mandarin courses were definitely the most demanding, so I don't recommend the mandarin courses if your motive for going abroad is to relax and have fun.
teaching_comparison: I didn't find that big of a difference in teaching style, however the grading system is very different.
courses_enrolled: Enhancing Chinese, general Chinese, ICL International Companions for Learning, Engaging Consumers and Social Media Marketing, Global Marketing and Negotiations Skills, Green Marketing, Exploring Taiwan: Women and Taiwanese Society.
recommended_courses: If you want to learn Mandarin or improve your mandarin, I recommend the mandarin courses. The marketing courses were very introductory so if you already have knowledge within this area I would not recommend it, unless you just want to relax. I especially enjoyed Engaging Consumers and Social Media Marketing, because the teacher was very nice and engaging.
unexpected_costs: Even though taxa is very cheap compared to Denmark, it can quickly add up, because public transport closes around midnight. So if possible, use the UBike, if you want to save money. Going to cafe almost everyday also adds up. Alcohol is surprisingly expensive.
cost_comparison: Taxa was cheap and food was very cheap. Public transport was very cheap. Alcohol and phone subscription were surprisingly expensive.
activities_available: There was a lot of activities available, I recommend going to the club fair in the beginning of the semester!
activities_recommended: Join a club if you want to meet local students!
weekend_recommendations: Travel around Taiwan, there are wonderful nature and cities to explore! Taipei is also amazing and have a ton of things to see and do, both nature stuff and city stuff!
culture_adjustment: It was easy, but I am also used to asian culture. Everyone are very nice and friendly.
socializing_tips: Join a club!
cultural_challenges: The garbage truck! But that is only a problem if you don't live at a dorm.
culture_appreciated: The amazing food, nature and people!
top3_advice: Use your KU classmates during the registration period before arriving. Join a club at NTU. Try and enjoy and relax, everything works out in the end.
other_useful_info: Don't hold back to ask for help if needed! Enjoy and have fun!
most_rewarding: To experience living in another country.
greatest_challenge: To make local friends, because internationals and your fellow KU students are so much easier to talk to.

crucial_aspects: The combination of exploring new cultures and attending academically relevant courses.
info_ease: I received most of the information upon arrival, but some information was missing.
arrival_assistance: During the orientation days most information was provided and repeated to ensure that we knew what to do when, however, course registration was still a bit confusing and unclear.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You can register courses online a week or so before the semester starts. If you do not get all the courses you apply for there is a second and third round where you have to write to the professor or TA on the course for a specific code that you need to register in the online system. There is also a drop period, so you are able to drop and add courses during the first couple of weeks.
registration_help: There was an email and office for exchange students and an assigned "buddy" (local student).
registration_success: I got all except for one course during the first registration period, and after the second registration period I had all the classes I needed.
registration_advice: I was really lucky that I got almost all my courses in the first round, most didn't. I think its a good plan to seek pre-approval for more courses than you intend to take and if you don't receive the courses you want in the beginning write to the professors right away to get the code for the next round of registration. My experience was that they were quick to reply.
course_level: The courses were interesting and diverse but the level is not as high in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: There was more memorization learning and student presentations.
courses_enrolled: Health and Human Rights. Behavioral Foundations of Health and Health Care. Globalization and Social Determinants of Health. Food security in a Changing Climate. International Environmental and Occupational Health. Gender and Politics. Health Technology Assessment. ICL.
recommended_courses: Health and Human Rights - interesting topic and course content and passionate professor Food security in a Changing Climate - interesting topic and course content and professor who is passionate about the topic ICL - culture/language exchange course where you get teamed up with a local student and have weakly online sessions with a local elementary
unexpected_costs: The dorms don't even have a madness or a soap dispenser etc. so I used around 2000dkk in the beginning on basic necessities for my dorm room.
cost_comparison: Transportation and food is really cheap. I went on a lot of weekend trips and transport is generally really cheap. Food is also really cheap, but coffee was more expensive than I anticipated. You can get a really good lunch for 15 Dkk, but coffee cost 35dkk
activities_available: There are over 100 student associations that you can attend including arts, music, culture, food, sport, calligraphy etc., a lot of sports activities you can sign up for and other social opportunities like trips, cooking etc.
activities_recommended: I joined one of the sport classes which was a nice break from the academic and an opportunity to meet more Taiwanese students.
weekend_recommendations: Going hiking around Taipei and in the mountains further south, going south to the islands where you can snorkel with turtles etc, visiting both of the costs and the maybe visit Tainan for cultural experiences.
culture_adjustment: After the first two weeks of culture and heat shock it was fairly easy to adjust.
socializing_tips: Generally, all the local students I encountered were really nice, helpfull, curious and outgoing. My advice would be to just approach them, they can be a bit shy and uncertain of their English skills, but most of them wants to practice their English and are curious about other cultures.
cultural_challenges: It's socially acceptable to chew loudly and burb in class and in public.
culture_appreciated: People were really nice and polite, and I also appreciated all the good food.
top3_advice: The campus is nice with a lot of facilities, the country has amazing nature with beautiful beaches, mountains and jungle, and the staff and students at the university are nice and helpfull.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Getting to know new people from Taiwan and around the world, and being able to explore so much beautiful nature.
greatest_challenge: Time went by too fast.

crucial_aspects: Since I'm studying an area studies, I wanted to choose a location about that area as well as a location where I was able to practice the language I'm studying for my degree.
info_ease: We received many emails about different activities and registration and it was a bit overwhelming. But I think we had the information we needed through these.
arrival_assistance: We all got assigned a student volunteer. She helped me with information even before I arrived and was also very kind to help me with all my questions when I arrived as well. She always was quick to reply and had very elaborated answers.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The course selection system at NTU is quite different from the one at UCPH. It takes place in several stages where the portal is open for you to sign up. After each stage you can check your results for a limited time. If you didn't get the course you wanted at first, you can try signing up again. In the end, if you're still unsuccesful, you can either message the teacher or showing up in person on the first day of class and ask if it's possible to join. I found that it often is. However, if the class is really popular, it might not be.
registration_help: There were some information online but I used my student volunteer a lot.
registration_success: At first, I was not and I found this very stressful. I managed to join to other courses, I iniatially didn't get by either messaging the professor or showing up in class. As I thought it would be very difficult to join, I was quite suprised that I managed to join that easily.
registration_advice: I think I'd say you shouldn't stress too much even if you don't get the courses at first as it is often possible to join after, even if it says online that the course is full. Often the teacher is willing to let you join, at least in my experience. Also, I'd recommend to test out more classes in the first week and decide afterwards which one's to join or not. I perhaps chose my classes a bit too quickly since I was scared that I wouldn't have enough credits. I wished I'd taken more time to consider the different classes more.
course_level: I took courses only for MA students and also courses that were open for both BA and MA students together.
teaching_comparison: I didn't find the teaching style that different but since your grade is not only based on a final exam but also often both class participation, midterms as well as presentations, the focus might be a bit different in class.
courses_enrolled: Seminar on East Asia News Enhancing Chinese General Chinese Introduction to Translation Studies Academic Chinese Writing Sociology of Gender
recommended_courses: Even if you're major is not about Chinese, I'd still recommend you to enroll in the Chinese language courses if possible. I think the courses were very well taught and I learned a lot.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: I think I had a good idea of the price levels already so I was not really surprised.
activities_available: Through my scholarship we got to participate in events where we were matched with local families with whom we did activities with. I also was invited to dinner and trips with these families later on. I also participated in a cultural exchange program (ICL) in which I was matched with a local student and a school class in a city in Taiwan. Each week we had a skype session where I shared Danish culture and traditions with them and they shared Taiwanese culture and traditions with me. I also got to visit them one time.
activities_recommended: I think the ones I mentioned above were great. I think they were some great opportunities to get to meet local people and experience local culture. Although I myself did not have time for clubs or assocations, I knew some fellow students who participated in these and they liked it very much. This is also a way to meet other people and to connect with local students.
weekend_recommendations: I think Taiwan has a lot of nice nature spots, and I'd recommend to go visit these. Besides, Taiwan is not very big so it's quite easy and fast to go to other cities for a short visit during the weekend.
culture_adjustment: Since I've been on exchange before in East Asia as well, I found the adjustment quite easy and to happen quite quickly.
socializing_tips: I think joining events, clubs or associations are good options to meet local students.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: I found the local people to be very helpful and friendly. I liked that a lot. Also, there is a lot of trust and I never felt unsafe. I also left my stuff at cafes when I went to the toilet and I never feared that my stuff would get stolen.
top3_advice: Firstly, in the beginning it can seem quite overwelming with all the things needed to be done. But don't worry, it'll all work out after some time. During this I think it's important to consult wiht fellow students who are also going or with your student volunteer. This perhaps can lessen your worry. Secondly, try to move outside your comfort zone. I think it’s easy just to make friends with fellow Danes or other Europeans. I did that myself to an extent. But I think it’s also important to try and make friends with local people or people from very different cultures than your own. I think this was very giving and a way to widen your horizon and learn more about different cultures and people. Lastly, make sure to enjoy it. A semester goes by very quickly, much quicker than you might expect. I think I myself spent too much time worriying about the academic part and didn’t have time to do other stuff. I realized in the end that I could’ve prioritized a bit differently without it affecting my grades.
other_useful_info: The course selection system can seem quite intimidating at first and caused me a lot of stress. I think a elaborated guide for this would have been very nice as it in the end turned out to not be that complicated or difficult as I first found it to be.
most_rewarding: I met at lot of different people and got to share my own culture as well as learning about others. I also got to improve and use my Chinese language skills a lot.
greatest_challenge: I think balancing studying, being social and also experience the country you were in was the most challenging. I often felt like I was missing out on either of them if I prioritized the others.

crucial_aspects: The most crucial was the chance to study political science in Taiwan due to its geopolitical relations to China. I hoped to gain a better understanding of Taiwan during my exchange. Also I had to visit a place where I could receive Chinese lessons, so Taiwan was a good choice for this as well.
info_ease: It was super easy, we got plenty of mails beforehand preparing us for the introductionary days at NTU.
arrival_assistance: I had been given a student volunteer contact which gave me a great introduction and explanation of how things worked in Taiwan as well as on the university itself.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: At NTU there are two main rounds of course selections. The first round you pick as many courses as you can. Once you get the results of which of these courses you have been enrolled in, you can decide on which of these courses you actually want to settle with. This second election ends a few weeks into the semester, which gives you a chance to test out different courses before making your final decision.
registration_help: Classmates, teacher PA's and the student volunteers could help out.
registration_success: I got pretty much all the classes I wanted, except for one, since it overlapped with another class.
registration_advice: My advice is to select as many courses as possible in the first round. If you have just the slightest interest in the course, apply for it. You can always remove course you don't need or want afterwards. Also be aware, since there are many hidden requirements for courses which means you can select them, but you will be declined afterwards, so if you don't select a lot, you will end up lacking enough courses to get enough credits.
course_level: The bachelor-level courses were dissapointing in terms of the academic level. The graduate-level courses, however, were very interesting and had great teachers.
teaching_comparison: The biggest difference is the amount of classes. I'm used to having 3-4 different courses per semester at UCPH, whereas at NTU I had 8, which means I had way more hours at the university sitting in class than at UCPH. Also, the grading system is very different, where at UCPH it's usually just the final exam that accounts for the total grade, at NTU it is a mix of attendance, mid-terms, homework, final exam, etc. that makes up the total grade. This gave less opportunity for me to decide on which classes I had to attend, since I had to attend every class in order to not lose scoring. I definitely prefer the UCPH style of course and grade structuring. The teaching style varied greatly, with some professors having a very hands-on approach and not letting students have a lot of freedom, where other professors gave zero instructions at all and gave students pretty much full control of how to write assignments and do projects.
courses_enrolled: 1. General Chinese (Intermediate 1) 2. Enhancing Chinese (Intermediate 1) 3. Seminar on Political Economy of East Asia 4. Seminar on Asian Democratization 5. Public Administration 6. Seminar on China's Political and Economic Reform after Deng Xiaoping 7. Technological Developments, Politics and Society of China 8. Mini-Course: European Union and State Transformation
recommended_courses: The course "Seminar on China's Political and Economic Reform after Deng Xiaoping" was amazing. The professor was great and the subjects we went through were very interesting. If you have interest in Chinese politics, this course will enhance your knowledge greatly. The same goes for "Technological Developments, Politics and Society of China", which also touched upon political developments in China, but with a focus on the effects that technology has had on China.
unexpected_costs: None really.
cost_comparison: Food was super cheap, but since there was no kitchen in my studio apartment I had to buy everything on the streets, which ended up costing more than I expected initially.
activities_available: There were courses offered which focused on exploring Taiwan, these courses were made to let students see Taiwan and engage in the culture. There were plenty of clubs for everything from football to archery to calligraphy. Everything had a club you could join. I personally tried rugby and handball.
activities_recommended: Join a sports-club, it's a great way to meet the locals. In the handball club/team I was the only foreigner which gave me plenty of chances to practice Chinese and understand local culture. Taiwan is also great for hiking if you're into that.
weekend_recommendations: Travel around Taiwan, explore Taipei, go to bars, travel abroad to Korea, Japan, Vietnam, etc.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, be respectful, don't be too loud, make an effort to understand the norms of Taiwan and you will find it is amazing.
socializing_tips: Take the initiative, they are quite introverted
cultural_challenges: Mostly the language barrier, Taiwanese are generally not that great at English, so if you don't speak that much Chinese it can be challenging to communicate. The social culture is also different in my opinion, but it's about letting go of your own way of doing things and instead embrace the local customs if you want to make friends.
culture_appreciated: The respect for elderly and simply how nice everyone were. At the beginning it felt fake, but as you become accustomed it just feels natural and you start to replicate it.
top3_advice: Bring summer clothes, an umbrella and a wallet that handles bills and coins!
other_useful_info: Regardless of your level of Chinese, it is worth to take the language courses. They are a great way to meet new people from class and also gives you tools to use when in Taiwan.
most_rewarding: The friends I've made from every part of the world.
greatest_challenge: The hardest was getting used to having so many classes, since it was so different from my experience at UCPH

crucial_aspects: The location was crucial - I wanted to go to to a place in East Asia.
info_ease: It was a little difficult to find information online and in English. The counsellor also did not reply to my emails that I sent which made it difficult to ask for help because she was the only contact we had.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation and tour.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There were several rounds of applying for courses over a span of a few weeks so there was a possibility of trying out a class before dropping it or applying for it. If you couldn't get into a class you wanted, you had to find out where the class was held and attend the lecture to ask the teacher if you could join the class, otherwise find an email.
registration_help: There weren't many resources or guides - it was mostly other students that knew the system more and we talked about it amongst ourselves.
registration_success: I was successful in arranging for the classes I wanted that fit my schedule.
registration_advice: If you hang on to credits just in case you don't get into the class you want, the system will not prioritise you for the next rounds if you want to change class.
course_level: The courses are quite rigorous, especially if it is math involved. Otherwise there is usually a lot of reading for social sciences and the teachers expect you to participate or do assignments to show that you have done the reading and this counts as part of the grade.
teaching_comparison: The teachers had a lot of power to change the course - there were several instances of the teacher just changing the syllabus or grading system during the course. They also take attendance and participation as part of the grade. It is wholly up to the teacher to set the rubrics and your grade as they want and it was difficult at times to know exactly what they are looking for as some teachers are quite strict in class but lenient with the grading.
courses_enrolled: Political Communication in the Internet Age Machine Learning Political Economy of Welfare and Gender Inequality Sociology of Gender Mini-course: European Union and State Transformation Food Security in a Changing Climate
recommended_courses: Political Communication in the Internet Age
unexpected_costs: A lot of things for the dorm.
cost_comparison: With the food prices being relatively low, drinks at a cafe can get pricey.
activities_available: There were many many options - such as volleyball, golf, archery, martial arts, art, calligraphy, hiking, etc., but it could be hard to be part of the club community if you didn't speak Mandarin and most things are conducted in Chinese.
activities_recommended: Hiking could be a good one for exploration.
weekend_recommendations: It is quite easy to travel along the places on the high speed rail so that's very doable for the weekend.
culture_adjustment: It was not so difficult because I also come from an Asian culture.
socializing_tips: A lot of students are quite shy so you would probably have to take initiative and approach them to make plans first. Otherwise, everyone is quite friendly. There could be a language barrier though because some people are not comfortable with speaking English all the time.
cultural_challenges: It can be difficult with the assumptions people make based on the way you dress or look. Also, no food or drink on the metro.
culture_appreciated: I appreciate how friendly people were and are willing to help.
top3_advice: 1. Don't worry too much about grades, the teachers may seem strict with the grading in class but most are understanding and don't grade you harshly. 2. Try different foods, Taiwan has a lot to offer and lots of street food as well. 3. You will mostly be in classes with other internationals - so if you want more of the local experience you have to work harder for it.
other_useful_info: I wanted a multiple entry visa and paid 660 to get it and only ended up with 90 days. Some others got 90 day single entry or 180. It really depends on the person giving it to you. A 90 visa is fine, you can extend it there and it won't affect your entry in the country - I always explained that I will extend and ended up travelling multiple times out of the country anyway, which extended it because I got 90 days visa exempt (but you have to tell the stamp person that you want visa exempt and not part of multiple entry to get the 90 days extended).
most_rewarding: It was rewarding to experience living and studying in another country - making friends there was also a great experience. I took a violin class and ended up getting the chance to do a short performance as well. I would say take the chances that come to you with doing what you like.
greatest_challenge: It was challenging finding information about all the processes and the documents and information also came quite late to do the applications. Also, you only knew if you were getting a dorm in July if you applied for it so I was also looking for housing just in case I couldn't get a dorm - a lot of extra work if you did end up getting a dorm.

crucial_aspects: I had heard very good about Taiwan as a destination and thought it sounded very exciting
info_ease: Medium-easy: the host university is very helpful and has very good information they will send beforehand, but sometimes there are some stuff that can be a bit confusing. But in that case I just asked the university and they were quick to assist and guide
arrival_assistance: Before I arrived, I was assigned a local student who was going to be my contact person and helper. He was so nice and helped with all the questions and troubles I had with courses, living accommodation and life in general in Taiwan. He even picked me up at the airport. We ended up becoming good friends also, went out with him and his friends a few times. But I don't all local students are that involved, other people I talked to had barely heard from their local student
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: This is my one main complaint about my stay. The course registration was very chaotic and stressful to me. Before you arrive, you can sign up for courses. You will most likely not get enough to satisfy the credit requirement, so in the first week you have to go to the classes you want and ask the professor if you can sign up for their class. If the class isn't full, they will say yes, but you don't really know which classes are available otherwise.
registration_help: Got help from the university and my local student
registration_success: Got them all.
registration_advice: The first week of class is a trial-week, where you can go to all the classes you are considering. If you want the class you ask the professor for a code to sign up. I went to all the classes I could to acquire codes, so I had as many classes to choose from as possible. It is kind of a puzzle calender-wise to make it all fit, so good to have all the options open. socializing_tips: Join the groupchats on social media pre-arrival and see. I can also recommend living in a social place. My faculty had a mingling event where we get to meet and talk with each other as well. My dorm also had a welcome party with activities. Bars and clubs also had welcome parties. There are many opportunities to socialise so I wouldn't worry:)
cultural_challenges: The food and people staring were the toughest. As mentioned above, thankfully there are many different food options in Taiwan and when it comes to the staring... you get used it.
culture_appreciated: The nature and trips were my favourite part. I also did ICL so I got to go on two trips which was definitely a cultural experience.
top3_advice: 1. Look for accomodation well in advance; many people were in between places as the semester started. 2. When applying for pre-approval, include a lot of courses just in case. Get an MRT (metro) card on your first day and ensure you always have NTD cash.
other_useful_info: The most useful was what was written above. Download the Uber app, enroll in Chinese and ICL, have google translate in case. Have a couple of different payment cards in case one has issues.
most_rewarding: For me, it was definitely the friends I made. It's been over a month since I left and I still talk daily with my friends and we will be visiting each other. My exchange experience wouldn't have been as fulfilling if it wasn't for them.
greatest_challenge: The food and constantly eating out. If you stay in the NTU dorm, unless you get assigned a suite where there is a shared kitchen, you basically have to eat out and groceries arent super cheap in Taiwan. It's definitely cheaper to eat out but it gets tiring at some point.

overall_comments: NTU is an amazing campus to stay at. However, there can sometimes be a language barrier that can make it hard to understand where you can find help or the social activities you are looking for. But you can always contact the OIA, they are always very friendly and willing to help you further. Taiwan is really a beautiful and amazing country and it has been a privilege to be able to stay here and to learn more about its culture and history.

I got the health check on a hospital upon arrival in Taiwan, because I did not have enough time to get an x-ray in Denmark. I went to get the health check at Taipei City Hospital Renai Branch, but I would recommend getting it done when you are in Denmark. Then you dont have to stress about it when you arrive.

Here you can also filter the courses that are taught in english language.

teaching_comparison: The teaching at NTU is more focused on learning things by heart in stead of discussing the material. This were reflected in the multiple choice exams, which I found to be not the best way to learn about some material.

recommended_courses: I will recommend all of the courses I took. They were all very informative and had very engaged and friendly professors.

cost_comparison: Restaurants are quite cheap, while buying groceries can be quite expensive (similar prices to Denmark often)
activities_available: There is a big student gym, running field and swimming pool at the campus. I did not use any of these, but many of my friends were using them several times a week.
activities_recommended: Going hiking, night markets, restaurants and cafes.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going hiking around Taipei (there are many amazing trails around Taipei - do it before it becomes 35+ degrees and 80% humidity though), going to trips to smaller cities in the north and south. Visit Kaohsiung and Tainan. Visit the islands (xiao liuqiu is very pretty). Go to night markets and experience street food snacks.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Attend the clubs at the university.
cultural_challenges: the language barrier.
culture_appreciated: People go out to eat at restaurants with their friends a lot.
top3_advice: Enjoy the resources, delicious food and beautiful scenery around NTU campus, dont stress too much about getting the right courses at first - you can usually fix this later (I got all the courses I wanted in the end), participate in the social life around campus (I wish I did this more!).
other_useful_info: NTU is quite bureaucratic in its system - but nothing too hard or difficult about it - it can just feel a bit heavy sometimes. most_rewarding: Getting to know more about the history and culture of Taiwan - it is really an amazing country! I will recommend anyone to visit, and going there for a few months has been a huge experience and privilege I will never forget!
greatest_challenge: The language barrier can be quite tough sometimes.

courses_enrolled: IPCS5063 Citizen Science: Multiple Perspectives on Participation Geo1008 Introduction to Field Geology (Ⅱ) MDR7910 Impact of Climate Change on Geological Carbon and Water Cycle Phy1039 International Companions for Learning Forest 5035 Exploring Taiwan: natural environment and resources Geo4017 Observaing the Marine Environment Geo4018 Field and Lab for Observing the Marine Environment

crucial_aspects: The price of Taiwan, the history, how accessible it is as a foreigner, the gorgeous nature, tasty food as well as it's interesting political landscape
info_ease: We were assigned a student buddy, some were really helpful, others not so much, but it was nice to have someone to direct the questions to. other than that, the international office at NTU was very helpful, all be it, a little slow.
arrival_assistance: Student buddy, orientation, a few helpful emails regarding course signup, and for a select few (maybe half) access to the dormitories.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The online preregistration is super easy. When in TW for the final registration: You get a designated time to appear at the academic office to stand in line. You are probably not gonna get in at that time, but better safe than sorry. You are then slowly moving through having people check that you have all your papers. In the end you get your student card and you are fully registered. You need to have done your health check and have a phone number before then. They need you to fill out an online form with emergency contascts that are IN Taiwan! Go to 7/11 for all your printing needs. It is super easy and quite cheap. Regarding the class registration: There are 3 rounds, the two first rounds of preregistration, where you can pick all the courses you want and then put them in a prioritized list. If you get number 1 on your list it then blocks that time period of your schedule for all other classes you apply for, so you need to be a little tactical about it. After the first round of preregistration you get told which classes you got into, you can then choose to drop some of them and/or repeat the process to try and add more courses. I recommend signing up to any and all you find interesting since the third period is a little stressful. In the third period you can show up to the first class in the first week, or send an email to the professor, to hopefully get a registration code so you can sign up for the class. This also extends into the second week of the semester, so if you didn't get enough credits the first week fear not. During these two weeks one can also just as well drop courses that seem to intensive or that aren't to your liking. Note that one can also sign up for Badminton, volleyball lessons and so on, as credits. It is in Mandarin, but is definitely feasible as a fun and cheap activity that fosters meeting local students outside the very competitive academic subjects.
registration_help: There was a short guide online, otherwise, one can always ask one's student buddy or send an email to the office of international affairs.
registration_success: I was very successfull, I registered for some classes I ended up disliking, so I dropped them in the first and second week, which meant I was under the 30 ECTS for a few days until I recieved some codes for some other classes.
registration_advice: Sign up for as many classes as possible. Check NTU rating for some of the courses, not all are available.
course_level: Some were quite difficult, partly because I picked courses outside of my subject of maths, and partly because they just teach in a different way in some courses. I think the level of the courses I took was in general quite at my level.
teaching_comparison: Some courses really try to be very interactive, but some of the local students are quite shy. In most courses there's given points for everything, from attendance and participation to big assignments or presentations. Some felt very much like studying at UCPH, others very much not so.
courses_enrolled: Combinatorics (I) General Chinese Beginners I Programming Language: Functional Programming International Companions for Learning Algorithms Design and Analysis Machine Learning (4 credits)
recommended_courses: Studying Chinese/Mandarin is incredibly fun and interesting. The teachers are very good and one can actually learn quite a lot in one semester. The functional programming course wasn't to intensive, while being really fun and interesting. The ICL program is so fun! You are having a weekly hour online with some local kids, where you are sharing about your local country, while they, hopefully, share about Taiwan and themself. A part of the program is a free trip to your school as well as neighboring schools in the area. I'd also recommend taking either an intensive course which allows for less study hours the rest of the semester or a physical course since they seem very fun and interesting. I did neither. Do not take the python courses if you have any experience programming, unless there's no attendance. Otherwise, you'll be bored out of your mind.
unexpected_costs: Not much, maybe how much I used the public transportation? But it isn't very expensive. The bikes are free the first half hour, and afterwards costing 2,2 DKK per half hour, and the metro in Taipei costs between 4,4-5,5 DKK per trip. More if you are travelling further outside Taipei. Maybe the most unexpected expense was getting a mattress, pillow and duvet/blanket. Just go to IKEA.
cost_comparison: Alcohol is a little more expensive than I expected. Beer can often be the same price as in Denmark. Out in the night life you can sometimes get very good happy hour deals. Food is so very inexpensive.
activities_available: So many! There's a bunch of cultural clubs and athletic clubs as well as international clubs for Europe and so on. There aren't a bunch of activities for the whole school, like KU Festival, but there are some smaller ones, arranged by the clubs. The clubs that demand more talking, and doesn't have a clear international focus are probably only in Mandarin.
activities_recommended: Go hike. It is gorgeous and very accessible. If you are going on more demanding hikes, less traveled ones, or in bad weather, then make sure to prepare for this with a flashlight, food, rain protection and so on. Nature can actually be scary in Taiwan. Also just travel around Taiwan, the public transport system is very good, especially in the west, where the high speed rail allows one to get from the south to the north in just 1,5H. Alishan is beautiful, Tainan is so cool and friendly. The east is very interesting. The Hualien night market is great! A lot of indigenous food as well. Also just meet with as many other students as possible. People are so nice and just want to do stuff with other cool people.
weekend_recommendations: If it's a Taiwanese holiday I would either stay in Taipei, go abroad or plan well in advance since a lot of Taiwanese are traveling in Taiwan during these holidays. Otherwise, explore Taipei, go have a nice dinner with friends, go hike, go to another city in Taiwan, get a permit for Jade Mountain/Yushan, go out singing karaoke, enjoy the skyline with Taipei 101. Go do a tea ceremony/do Kung Fu style tea.
culture_adjustment: It isn't terribly difficult. The most difficult part is their bike lines which aren't one-way and most are a part of the sidewalks with people walking on them or you end up biking on the road. In general Taiwanese are very friendly and helpful.
socializing_tips: Join ICL, through that you get a partner. Try and talk them up in class, they probably really want to talk to you but are too shy. Join a club.
cultural_challenges: Nothing I can recall. Maybe, the lack of trash cans or their huge focus on performing well in their studies.
culture_appreciated: They are very friendly and nice. Especially, if you are outside Taipei. In the capital people mostly mind their own business. I really enjoy the communal eating.
top3_advice: Participate and do a bunch of activities with the other exchange students in the beginning. Pick your courses wisely depending on the amount of work you are willing to do. Some courses are very demanding and require a lot of work. Especially around the time of midterms or finals. Taiwan is amazing!
other_useful_info: NTU is mostly at the one campus, so if off campus you'd be advised to not live to far away from campus. You do not need to travel or have big plans every weekend. It seems like every one else does, but that isn't necessarily true. Staying in Taipei and living life there is also really valuable. Become a local and find the most amazing local spots!
most_rewarding: Experiencing a very different culture, the breathtaking views and mouthwatering food. Getting to meet lovely people from all over the world and making some very good friends through this. Being able to emerge myself and live in a different country for half a year.
greatest_challenge: Not having any close friends to lean on when the new friendships are still blooming. Being able to do all the plans and activities in just a semester. Balancing school, experiences and friends.
other_comments: If you pick NTU, you will not regret it. It's a undiscovered pearl!

crucial_aspects: NUS has a reputation for being a good uni, and their philosophy department is analytic, which was important to me. Furthermore, I wanted to go somewhere really different to Denmark. Since I don't speak a third language, though, it had to be somewhere with undergrad courses in English. Singapore perfectly fit the bill!
info_ease: Pretty easy. The Singaporean system is quite bureaucratic, but there are a lot of people ready to help, and in my experience you can often send a question to an administrative body and receive a reply the next day at the latest. That is really a huge help when trying to navigate the jungle of visas, accommodation, course enrollment etc.
arrival_assistance: I got fairly elaborate guides via email about where I had to go and when, and was quite lucky with all of the practical and logistical stuff regarding my arrival. However, perhaps my batch of exchangers were bigger than usual - it seemed NUS struggled with too few resources to guide us all properly in the beginning. I know for example that many couldn't get an appointment to finish their student visa because NUS simply had too few slots. And many didn't get student accommonation, which forced them out to the expensive and competitive private housing market. I sensed that these things made arrival quite stressful for the unlucky ones.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Again, I was very lucky: I got all of my top-priority courses right off the bat because I'm in humanities where courses are less competed for. For me, registration was totally painless. But my friends in computer science and economics didn't secure the required amount of modules in the first round, so it was unclear if they could go at all, and because they had to wait for second round of course registration, they missed the deadline for on-campus housing applications. This was super stressful for them and not very well-organized by NUS, I think.
registration_help: You can email the international office or whichever office is in charge of the area you need help with, and they will be very helpful in guiding you through the formal processes.
registration_success: Succesful. I got four of top five priorities - the last course I wanted wasn't offered this semester.
registration_advice: I really don't know how to make the process easier. I know I had a very much easier time because I applied for courses without that much competition (third year philosophy courses, a decision theory module and a module in global health). But I'm not sure strategizing helps too much, because it's hard to predict which courses are very sought after. Check out the opportunities on nusmods.com and see what strikes your interest. Oh yeah, and check out the professor online if you can before you choose. In my experience, having a good professor is (here as anywhere else) almost as important to your final learning outcome than the course content itself.
course_level: It varied a lot. My philosophy modules (level 3000) were extremely good - small classes of 6-10 people, very competent professors and motivated students. I have had some of the best teaching I have ever experienced here. And the level was high, significantly higher than in UCPH, I'd say. Readings were harder and the profs expected more of us. However, I have also had an introductory course meant for PPE students (level 3000) which was very poor. The professor was a bad teacher, students were unmotivated. This course was fairly easy.
teaching_comparison: In one module, introduction to global health, we had a lot of guest lectures from people working in different subfields. That was extremely nice. However, the assignments were hard for me to understand, simply because I had trouble getting the different format. We were asked to write 'reflections', and I never quite understood what the prof wanted for us. This module also had more group work than I'm used to. In philosophy, the style was pretty much the same as I'm used to: Prof at the whiteboard going over the assigned papers for the day and class discussion about any unclarities.
courses_enrolled: SPH2401 Introduction to global health, PE3101P Decision and social choice, PH3250 Quantification and modality, PH3245 Language and thought
recommended_courses: If you are interested in philosophy, I recommend Language and Thought very much! It's a niche topic, but the professor I had (fall 2022) made it so engaging and fun.
unexpected_costs: Well, I ended up spending a good amount traveling! Other than that, I don't think I've encountered any
cost_comparison: Public transport is very affordable! So are taxis (use Grab) if you carpool with someone. And so is food, at least when you eat in hawker centers, which I absolutely recommend. My housing (residential college on campus) was fairly affordable as well, considering it included 12 meals a week. And getting a prepaid sim card (e.g. Singtel) is a very easy and cheap solution for getting your phone online. Groceries are expensive, though! More so than in Denmark. I have not been cooking at all since I got here, so of course eating out is an expense. And note that if you don't get student housing, the private housing market is tough.
activities_available: A lot of clubs and societies. Board game club, film club, music, dancing. Definitely something for everyone! The sports facilities here are great - olympic sized pool, climbing wall, gym etc. Sports clubs as well, which are quite high-level competitive from what I've heard.
activities_recommended: The film club! A screening of a lovely international masterpiece every Friday evening with discussion afterwards! Lovely space. I think the sports clubs are a good opportunity for people at a more advanced level - not really beginner-friendly, I think. But whatever you like, search it out here. It's really valuable to get to know local students and I think this is a good way to do so.
weekend_recommendations: Exchange students here travel like crazy! To Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, even Japan, Taiwan and South Korea! This is fun, but I think it is also valuable to stay in Singapore and build a more solid foundation here. A lot of museums are free, because exchangers count as 'local resident' when we have our student pass. Go to Little India and Chinatown and explore the cities within the citites. Go to Pulau Ubin and see the hornbills, and to Sungei Buloh and see the alligators.
culture_adjustment: Easy. Honestly, Singapore is just very westernized, and I was surprised by how little of a culture shock-factor it was. Everyone speaks English, infrastructure is super efficient, everything is available online.
socializing_tips: Join clubs and sports and just be open. Be that awkward person who asks people to lunch even though you don't know them well enough for that by Danish standards. It pays off!
cultural_challenges: It can be a bit difficult to get close to Singaporean students. I guess they share some of the closed off-ness that we Scandinavians have, plus maybe some. So you don't necessarily get to know people very well through group work and the like, and it can take some stamina to get accepted into social circles, I think.
culture_appreciated: The international melting pot-vibe of Singapore. You can find foods from all regions, people from all places and backgrounds, and that's really nice. And I did find some local students who were very welcoming, invited me home to meet their parents and so on, which was so nice.
top3_advice: Don't let yourself be scared off by the bureaucracy. Once you're here and have gotten the formalities fixed, it's really quite easy to navigate the systems, figure out exam schedules and so on and so forth. Be prepared to work hard academically. I've heard many different things from exchangers - some say it's easier than at their home uni, but in my experience, demands are quite high, and profs here expect you to take responsibility for your own understanding. And then - know that it'll take some work to make friends. Any exchange takes some getting out of your comfort zone, I suppose, and this is no exception. Don't expect to necessarily meet the love of your life (though I know some have!) or make friends that'll last a lifetime. After all, 4 months is a short time to get to know people. But you can count on plenty of fun encounters and lovely people to spend time with while it lasts!
other_useful_info: A few quick things: Getting around campus is super easy with the free shuttle bus. Don't underestimate the heat: I applied for a room without AC because I generally like warmer weather and thought surely I could handle it. I wasn't prepared for the tropical humid heat and definitely would have slept a lot worse if I hadn't gotten a room with AC! There is a midterm recess week with no classes which is a good opportunity to travel. Singapore itself is a strange place: Lovely and green while at the same time filled with sky scrapers. But it's also very clean and orderly, it's illegal to demonstrate, chewing gum is banned because it makes a mess on the streets and public transport doesn't run after around 11pm to disencourage people to go out drinking. In that sense, it's an interesting place to be! And it's easy to settle in, not too much of a culture shock while being still very different from Denmark. All in all, I definitely recommend NUS.
most_rewarding: Experiencing a completely different culture in Asia and meeting people here from all over the world. Also, the teaching has really been great. I have learned much more than I could've hoped for.
greatest_challenge: Honestly, it's been surprisingly easy. One thing I have struggled with is the exchanger FOMO. Everyone travels everywhere and it seems there is this expectation that you see all of Asia while you're here. I've spent a lot of time (too much time) making travel plans just because I felt I should, and that's a shame. I wish I could've found a better balance between traveling some and also just exploring Singapore, discovering what the local communities have to offer.

culture_adjustment: Easy. Singapore is very easy in that domain.
socializing_tips: You can not categorize humans in my opinion. Its all individual. You have open people or more closed ones. My experience is everyone is friendly and respectfull. I made the most strong connections with locals outside of uni. Sometimes things just happen.
cultural_challenges: You will be fine.
culture_appreciated: Everyone is respectfull!
top3_advice: -If CS students, decide for yourself what you want out of your stay and plan courses accordingly. Keep in my CS courses are hard and overrun. - Just go on exchange. Dont be afraid of all the rules, it will be fine. - Read all the material carefully.

other_comments: Meet people! Be open! And just do it! I enjoyed the circumstances which forced me to have a light academic weight during my exchange. It made rooms for many other beautiful things.

culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. Singapore is different in many ways but also very similar.
socializing_tips: Join sports or other cultural events. Else join a hall.
cultural_challenges: Locals in Singapore study more than in Denmark, but as an exchange student I spend most of my time with other exchange students and we had a lot of time to have fun.
culture_appreciated: Be social and join sports or other cultural events. Then also walk around the city with locals or other exchange students.
top3_advice: Go into it open-mindedly. In Singapore, you will spend a lot of time with other exchange students in the same position as you so you have to socialize. Be prepared with documents. Singapore is very warm and humid so only bring summer clothes with a few hoodies and pants for the very cooled air-conditioned lecture halls.
other_useful_info: Talk with UCPH about if there are other exchange students going from KU because it helps a lot talking with others about all the practical things.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from around the world and making long-lasting friendships.
greatest_challenge: Getting everything practical ready when arriving in Singapore.
other_comments: Have fun! You will have the greatest time of your life. Be patient with all of the practical things because it will all be worth it!

crucial_aspects: A safe country to stay, high quality education and interesting modules with great academic outcomes, cultural diversity.
overall_comments: Overall, it was an excellent experience with unforgettable memories! The modules I took were very interesting and instructive! However, it was a bit challenging to prepare for the exams as examples of exam questions from previous years were not provided.
info_ease: Easy, the staff at the university were helpful.
arrival_assistance: Check-in procedures at my accommodation on-campus.
arrival_comments: There was no orientation week this semester but it could have been useful! Instead, all information were sent to our emails and we could also help each other in the exchange groupchat on WhatsApp.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Overall, it was an excellent experience with unforgettable memories! The modules I took were very interesting and instructive! However, it was a bit challenging to prepare for the exams as examples of exam questions from previous years were not provided.
registration_process: Firstly, you submit module requests for these modules preapproved by UCPH. You should attach your transcript to show that you meet the prerequisites (if needed). If you don't get all of the modules that you wanted, it is possible to request for other modules in the following rounds. If you find out later that you don't like the modules allocated to you, there is an add/drop period.
registration_help: The module registration student guide and Registrar's Office.
registration_success: I managed to get all the modules I requested. However, I switched one of the modules allocated to me.
registration_advice: Check the vacancy report provided by the university when selecting modules. If you really want to read a module but there is no vacancy, you should contact the course coordinator directly as he/she might allow you to take the module anyway!
academics_comments: Overall, it was an excellent experience with unforgettable memories! The modules I took were very interesting and instructive! However, it was a bit challenging to prepare for the exams as examples of exam questions from previous years were not provided.
course_level: As I was a master student, UCPH allowed me to read modules of at least level 4000 which were considered as undergraduate modules at NUS.
teaching_comparison: Majority of the modules at NUS had continuous assessments, therefore midterms, assignments and presentation throughout the semester. Both continuous assessments and final exams accounted for the total grades. Compared to UCPH, the reading materials were less at NUS but the workload was still high.
courses_enrolled: LSM4213 Systems Neurobiology LSM4214 Cancer Pharmacology LSM4221 Drug Discovery and Clinical Trials LSM4226 Infection and Immunity
recommended_courses: Cancer Pharmacology and Drug Discovery and Clinical Trials. Personally, I think both modules were very interesting and relevant to pharmacy, and the professors were great!
unexpected_costs: Consultation fee at a clinic and medications.
cost_comparison: Foods at Science Canteen on campus were very cheap! Generally alcohol is very expensive in Singapore!
activities_available: A wide range of activities such as tennis, soccer, dancing, cheerleading and bands.
activities_recommended: You should try to join different clubs/organisations for all NUS students based on your personal interests! If you stay in a residential college, I highly recommend to join some of the interest groups as it is a good opportunity to make new friends!
weekend_recommendations: Try Singaporean local foods at Hawker Centres! Visit Gardens by the Bay, Cloud Forrest and Art Science Museum. Travel to other countries nearby, such as Indonesia and Malaysia.
culture_adjustment: Easy. Singapore is a very multicultural country with different ethnic groups. It has a good combination of Asian and European culture. There are many rules in Singapore, but in general, if you just use common sense everything should be fine!
socializing_tips: Stay on-campus and join the social activities! Although majority of local students are competitive, they are very friendly!
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The cultural diversity. Furthermore, Singapore is an extremely clean and safe city!
top3_advice: 1. Have a positive mind as the workload can be high and it might be difficult to adapt to a whole new enviroment. 2. Use your free time to explore the city and the many options of delicious foods. 3. Socialize with both local students and exchangers.
other_useful_info: For majority of the modules at NUS, continuous assessments are very common so you should study throughout the whole semester and not only during the reading weeks. But you would still have time to do social activities!
most_rewarding: I learned to have a positive mindset even in the critical situations. I met many people with different backgrounds and I made good new friends from both Singapore and other countries.
greatest_challenge: To be far away from home in Denmark and to study in a whole new environment.
other_comments: Go on exchange in Singapore! It is a wonderful experience and you wouldn't regret it!

I found this quite disappointing because I was under the impression that NUS was quite good at and had a lot of experience with welcoming exchange students. I think this could have made a huge difference to my university experience. They did try to implement a buddy system so you were teamed up with a local student but as a lot of the buddies were first year students they were busy to get used to uni life and therefore didn't have much time to meet up and help in the beginning.
