crucial_aspects: the academic quality of NUS as the leading university in Asia and in the global top, alongside the deeply international setting in which NUS operates (both regarding Singapore as a global hub and the make-up of the institution itself), is what drew me to choosing my study destination.
info_ease: Fairly easy; given how overwhelming it is to suddenly find yourself in a new setting as an exchange student, it was still manageable to figure out which steps needed to be taken. NUS was prompt and quick to issue out thorough step-by-step guides and other informational e-mails prior to arrival in the host country.
arrival_assistance: Everything was pretty much pre-arranged by us students ourselves before arrival, as a lot of the orientation to life at NUS was done online prior to school start or needed you to book a timeslot (i.e. their initial course 'Consent and Respect Culture' with accompanying workshop).
arrival_comments: not really applicable, as 90% happened online before arrival. But they were quick to respond to questions etc. by mail.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration at NUS was two-tiered, as it required a part one and part two, simultaneously coinciding with the authorities' requirement of a Student Pass. The first part you had to start your registration online, including uploading a photo, paying the miscellaneous administrative and health security fees, and accepting your offer. From there, the actual course registration commenced, which entailed you registrering to eligible courses. The second part of registration happened after arrival, and consisted of collection and activation of our student card.
registration_help: I found that I could both use e-mail and telephone to their Registrar's office or academic activities office if I had any questions.
registration_success: not very succesful. At first I was unable to secure the credits I needed and I thus had to apply for courses again - but now from a significantly narrowed down selection.
registration_advice: set out time and really invest in getting into the registration process, as all the steps required make it very overwhelming and time-consuming. It is not difficult, but just requires time.
course_level: The courses were of very high quality. The teachers were deeply ingrained in the subject matter, having dedicated their life to their specific field of law - which made for very inspiring and knowledgeable teaching. Furthermore, the style of teaching which included, i.a., that class participation was a part of the students' assessment, entailed a very engaging classroom; prompting for lengthy debates or elaborations in class.
teaching_comparison: It was fundamentally different. At NUS, class attendance, class participation, mid-terms and other assignments all form part of your final assessment alongside the actual exam. This meant that you were constantly being evaluated academically by your professor and that preparation and school work took on a whole different meaning than at UCPH. At UCPH it is more geared towards the students' own independence and sense of responsibility regarding their approach to studying, whereas NUS did not follow the same idea of "with freedom comes responsibility."
courses_enrolled: Multinational Enterprises and International Law International Environmental Law Law and the Humanities Digital Technologies and Human Rights Maritime Law
recommended_courses: All courses at NUS have a pretty broad international focus, which I liked, but out of the courses I chose I would probably recommend 'Multinational Enterprises and International Law,' as it showcased the actual approach by corporations and enterprises working in a global setting and how they function in cross-border instances - where different rules, jurisdictions and legal thinking operates. It really showed how you utilize and work with law in international settings, in "the real world."
unexpected_costs: none I can recall
cost_comparison: I think coming from Denmark is always an advantage when it comes to the prices of food and beverages, as our average prices of such things are quite high compared to the rest of the world - this means we can't really be shocked by the prices abroad. Therefore, I actually found food were less expensive than expected - generally, the concept of a hawker centre makes it possible to live rather cheap in Singapore. Other than those places, food and drink (both in restaurants and grocery and convenience stores) were priced like in Denmark / Copenhagen and above.
activities_available: as people live on campus, and campus is a city in and of itself, a wide array of activities were available. both regular things, like various sports clubs, and pop-ups, like open-air cinema, were planned by the school and its associations (open for registration for all).
activities_recommended: the pop-ups were always quite inventive - like they did an open-air cinema in the botanical gardens and a tour of the old districts of Singapore. I also think a sports club would be a great way to socialize with the locals, but I don't play any sport so I didn't do it myself.
weekend_recommendations: Singapore is at the center of SE Asia, which means that you can, relatively easy and affordable, travel to the neighboring countries. Other than that, Singapore actually have a lot to offer in itself - from the more touristy activities like go-kart, boulders, cinema, amusement parks etc., located in downtown and Sentosa, to actual jungles and local nature where you can hike - MacRitchie Reservoir for example!
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. Singapore is a multicultural country and with strong international traction - which means that the city caters to everybody.
socializing_tips: I found the local students to be very hardworking and use a lot of their time on their studies (as is expected with Singaporean work culture). However, they were open and very friendly, which made talking very easy - Singaporeans have a global mindset and are used to expats and exchange students, which means that they are also interested in hearing about you, and where you are coming from.
cultural_challenges: Singapore is very fast-paced, and in the beginning I found it overwhelming that everything is quite transactional and straight-to-business when you're out and about. Especially coming from Copenhagen/Denmark, where we're used to acknowledging each other with eye contact etc. as a form of polite gesture. But I think that their notion of respect might be different from ours, whereas in Singapore it is more of a respectful distance to each other and their time, than in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: that the deeply multicultural setting made it possible to experience so many different people and their cultures, which is totally different from homogenous Denmark.
top3_advice: 1. Prepare to study hard, as it is one of Asia's leading universities for a reason. 2. In a place where so many cultures and their distinct foods/activities/goods are within arm's length, remember to step out of your comfort zone and try them! 3. It is very safe and clean to walk around in Singapore - but for a reason. There are a lot of rules that we're not used to in Denmark.
other_useful_info: To enjoy the stay and that everyone has a different experience of going on exchange; comparing your stay to others makes no sense as this is about you and your own development - personally and academically.
most_rewarding: I really felt that exchange provided a chance to self-reflect on a lot of things that one forget or put on autopilot when in your usual settings. It reminded me of the love of learning that drove me to university (which can kind of disappear in the everyday schoollife and grade anxiety), and I consider my exchange stay a huge gift and privilege. To be able to experience so much and also the many different impressions you get along the way really left an impact, as you learn to see your own life (back home) and what you want to keep or change - as the chance of crafting a new, temporary life on exchange enable you to form a comparative basis for assessing your own existence.
greatest_challenge: I think the greatest challenge was probably also the most rewarding part of the exchange: having to stand on your own two feet in a foreign country, having to ultimately take into your own hands the responsibility of shaping how your exchange semester is gonna look like, is really overwhelming and frightening. But in the end, it is also the most rewarding - as you successfully did it on your own.

crucial_aspects: NUS has a very good academic reputation and an amazing selection of law courses in English. English being the offical language in makes everything easier. I had also heard good things about Singapore and had colleagues living there who told me it was very safe and easy to get around. I was also keen to see more of Asia, where I had not travelled much previously.
overall_comments: I absolutely fell in love with Singapore! It is so clean, well-planned and safe (and surprisigly green and pretty) and there is so much cultural diversity and incredible food! Everything works and people are kind and polite. My university courses were all very interesting and taught by incredibly knowledgable and enthusiastic professors who genuinely wanted to also hear the students' thoughts.
info_ease: NUS sent a lot of material with all the details you needed, but you did need to take the time to really read it through and make sure you could find it again, becuase there was a lot of admin!
arrival_assistance: Teachers and other students were quite helpful if you had questions about the course or Singapore. I was paired up with a local student buddy both by the university-wide global student association and the law international student association, both of those individuals were very kind to offer help with finding my way around and making me feel welcome. There were also some welcome events, but some of them took place before the semester start. Apart from that, you are mostly on your own.
arrival_comments: I think NUS could do something more systematic to help visiting students settle in. In particular, there was very little information on exams and formalities, because they assumed everyone already knew.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I absolutely fell in love with Singapore! It is so clean, well-planned and safe (and surprisigly green and pretty) and there is so much cultural diversity and incredible food! Everything works and people are kind and polite. My university courses were all very interesting and taught by incredibly knowledgable and enthusiastic professors who genuinely wanted to also hear the students' thoughts.
registration_process: There was a remote registration followed by a second registration in person. For courses, you apply for courses when you send NUS your application (in September for me) and then you can apply for more courses and / or drop courses right before the semester starts and again right after the semester start.
registration_help: NUS sends you all the information you need and you can find information on the various websites. If you need actual help beyond that, they're not very good at responding to emails, you're probably better off asking a professor or fellow student for help. The exchange students' Whatsapp group is also good.
registration_success: I was very lucky in getting three of the courses I wanted through my initial application and getting a 4th course that I genuinely wanted right before the semester start.
registration_advice: Use NUSMods to check courses and timetables and remember the deadlines.
academics_comments: I absolutely fell in love with Singapore! It is so clean, well-planned and safe (and surprisigly green and pretty) and there is so much cultural diversity and incredible food! Everything works and people are kind and polite. My university courses were all very interesting and taught by incredibly knowledgable and enthusiastic professors who genuinely wanted to also hear the students' thoughts.
course_level: Law exchange students take courses that are available to both local 4th year BA students and MA students. The different levels are graded separately (we get lumped in with the 4th year BA students).
teaching_comparison: It is a very different culture. All my classes were taught as seminars, but unlike back home they give you a grade for attendance and participation, which typically counts for 10 or 20% of your final grade in that subject. You can easly pass this if you show up to most classes and make the occassional intelligent comment in class. However, professors do expect you to turn up prepared and genuinely want to hear your thoughts on a subject. You also have graded assignments during the semester in most subjects, as well as an exam. The tone in class is more formal and they are more hierarchical (you call your teacher "professor", not by their first name). You are technically not allowed to eat in class, but I found most of my professors were fairly relaxed on this.
courses_enrolled: World trade law, Aviation law and policy, International regulation of shipping and The law and economics of competition policy
recommended_courses: Aviation law and policy was really fun, especially with Singapore being an aviation hub, and professor Tan is the national expert in the subject! It was really interesting to discuss international, policy-related issues from a South-East Asia centered perspective. Similarly, International regulation of shipping, because Sinagpore is a major shipping hub and it is a huge part of the country, and the professor is invites the students to conferences and such. World trade law was also a super interesting subject, but the professor said we were his last class, so I don't know what will happen to the course.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Groceries were much more expensive than I's exected. However, I spent less on public transport than I'd planned, but I also lived within walking distance of the law faculty. I was surpised to find I didn't need to buy any books, but all the readings were provided electronically.
activities_available: Lots of different groups for sports, music, dance, interests and cultural identities, but you have to look for it yourself
activities_recommended: I tried a hiking group and some dance classes and would recommend it if interested. It is a good way to meet people other than classmates, especially when living off campus.
weekend_recommendations: See the city! There is lots of history and atmospheric neighbourhoods. Go out and try all the foods you can't get back in Denmark - Singapore is famous for its food scene for a reason! I would really recommend the Botanic gardens when you need to find a bit of peace - it is a UNESCO world heritage site, very imperssive and very peaceful. There are also several nature reserves worth a visit. Also, take time to visit some of the neighbouring countries. Singapre is super well connected with budget fligths to the rest of Asia.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy. The culture is more introverted, but people are very polite and friendly once you get talking to them. Be polite and respect the local rules and norms and you will be fine.
socializing_tips: Make the first move and ask them for reccommendations or advice. They were usually very nice once you got talking to them, but often a bit shy. The culture is more introverted. The same goes for the Chinese exchange students.
cultural_challenges: You need to make a bit more effort to get to know the locals.
culture_appreciated: I loved the food and the mix of cultures. I really appreciated how genuinely considerate people are. On the few occassions I found myself in any way in difficulty, someoone immediately jumped in to offer help. They are also proud of their country and their culture, so if you ask for recommendations or information, they will be genuinely happy to provide this.
top3_advice: Don't get too hung up on reading everything for your courses. Remember to enjoy yourself and explore. Be proactive at the beginning of your stay to find people you can hang out with.
other_useful_info: Bring and umbrella, some ligthweight plastic shoes and a solid jumper (or be prepared to buy them) - it's hot, rains a lot and the aircon inside can be quite agressive.
most_rewarding: Getting to live in an Asian city and experience the a very different culture
greatest_challenge: Homesickness - it sneaks up on you.
other_comments: I highly recommend going to NUS and living in Sinagpore!

crucial_aspects: That the official language of the country was English. That the climate was different from the danish. That it was outside of Europe. That the location made traveling possible.
overall_comments: Had a very good experience.
info_ease: I found it to be pretty structured in terms of what steps to do at specific times. But there was still a lot to remember and if you missed a step the process was quite long.
arrival_assistance: Most assistance was online.
arrival_comments: They have a loot of different websites and apps that can be hard to manage.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Had a very good experience.
registration_process: There is different rounds of course registration. The first one is from home and then there is a period when you arrive where it is possible to change courses that is based on your priorities. They do not allow overlaps in the course schedule so it was a bit of a puzzle.
registration_help: It was quite easy to contact the administration for help.
registration_success: Pretty successful, but I was not able to secure all the courses I wanted because of availability and schedule overlap.
registration_advice: Just relax if it doesn't work out as you want in the first place and make a long list with all the courses you are interested in because you will not be able to secure exactly what you want.
academics_comments: Had a very good experience.
course_level: The level compared to the level at University of Copenhagen, but they are quite generous with final grade.
teaching_comparison: There is a lot more deadlines throughout the semester and the grades is based on a lot of different things and not just your final exam.
courses_enrolled: Metabolism and Regulation Synthetic Biology RNA biology and technology Introduction to bioinformatics
recommended_courses: I enjoyed all of my courses. Metabolism and regulation has a high workload but is interesting if you are interested in metabolic diseases. Synthetic Biology was more easy and they were generous with the grades, a lot of exchange students as well. RNA biology and technology was very interesting and not too hard to pass either but did contain a lot of details. Introduction to bioinformatics was not that interesting but not hard to pass either.
unexpected_costs: Supplies for the room
cost_comparison: going out and eating at restaurants is expensive in Singapore. The public transport is cheap but doesn't leave at night so you needed to pay taxi. I spend most money on traveling, the everyday life in Singapore was not expensive.
activities_available: There was a lot of different sports to participate in. It is not made for exchange students but more for the local students that gain participation points when joining different clubs. This means that it is not a chill drop-in and out vibe, but you have to commit if you join anything.
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining one club either a certain sport you enjoy or something more creative.
weekend_recommendations: To go traveling to the neighboring countries. You can go by bus and ferry to Malaysia and indonesia. Also make sure to go to the different areas of Singapore in the beginning as you start to get more busy throughout the semester and there is a lot of good things to experience.
culture_adjustment: It was a bit of a culture shock at first with all the different noises, smells and climate. And as an asian country it is very different from Denmark.
socializing_tips: Join a club and live on campus it is hard to socialize at uni.
cultural_challenges: The food.
culture_appreciated: The all year summer.
top3_advice: Be open and enjoy it, it is a very unique time. And be prepared that it is hard at some points to be so far away from home.
other_useful_info: Consider having an international bank account, you will end up using cash a lot. Pack some personal things from home to place in your room and remember that you need less clothes than you think.
most_rewarding: All the people I met and became friends with. And all the travel experiences.
greatest_challenge: It was hard to socialize at the some of the courses and everyone has different schedules so you will be alone quite a lot in your everyday life.
other_comments: Go on exchange! you will not regret it

registration_advice: Make sure to register as early as possible as you have to wait some time for NUS to process your registration before you are registered formally, and this is important to be before housing applications.
course_level: I took both BA and MA courses, and the difficulty is similar to UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Teaching was similar.

greatest_challenge: Missing friends and family due to the time difference and long distance.

crucial_aspects: The level of education at the university, the location and the different culture
overall_comments: Go on exchange!
info_ease: A little difficult. NUS uses a lot of different websites for everything, so do keep track of them and the deadlines.
arrival_assistance: Not much assistance, unless you seek for help yourself.
arrival_comments: Not the best introduction and orientation, but they do host different events you can participate in.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Go on exchange!
registration_process: You have a few rounds to secure your courses. Don't expect to get all your wished courses necessarily.
registration_help: You can email them for help, they usually answer pretty quick. I did not need to seek other help.
registration_success: I did not get all the courses I wanted at first, but I found some good courses anyway.
registration_advice: Don't panic if you don't secure the best or all of your courses in the start, you have 2-3 rounds to secure the courses you want. Do apply for more courses than you need and then you can drop some of the courses you don't want later.
academics_comments: Go on exchange!
course_level: The level was pretty similar to KU, if you go for the courses fitting to the year of your study.
teaching_comparison: Less interactive than UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Immunology RNA Biology and Technology Introductory Bioinformatics Discover South Asia
recommended_courses: Immunology was a great course - the lectures had a good flow and professors were good at teaching the material. The course also included some practicals in the laboratory. RNA Biology and technology I also found interesting, but a bit more on the heavy side (not time wise, but content wise).
unexpected_costs: The student fees and visa application fees, but not a lot overall. I travelled quite a bit during the semester, which is the reason for the high personal spending.
cost_comparison: Going out to eat, groceries and alcohol was more expensive than I expected, but food in hawker centers was cheaper than I expected.
activities_available: All sorts of clubs, sports teams and social events.
activities_recommended: Go to the orientation and join a club/team if you want.
weekend_recommendations: Explore Singapore (Gardens by the Bay, Tree top walk, National Museum and so on) and travel! It is easy to travel around Asia from Singapore - especially Malaysia.
culture_adjustment: The culture is very different in Singapore - very Chinese and Malaysian, but it is also very strict and well behaved country. So I would say it was fine to adjust to the culture.
socializing_tips: Living in a hall with many local students made it easier, but also joining a sports team is a good way I think.
cultural_challenges: The very serious approach to uni
culture_appreciated: I always felt safe in Singapore!
top3_advice: The application process might be a bit overwhelming, but hold tight everything is much easier when you arrive. Join all social events in the start and meet new people - every exchange student is very open and nice. Enjoy your exchange - time flies.
other_useful_info: Write down information along the way - your NUS ID, FIN number, deadlines and so on. Use NUSMODS to put together your schedule. Pack a sweater to use in the lecture halls - they use a lot of air-condition!
most_rewarding: All the new experiences, the people and the self-development.
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to the heat and humidity. I had a room without aircon, which could be pretty hot.
other_comments: Go on exchange! It is a great experience.

crucial_aspects: To find a place where I could learn something new and explore a different part of the world with a different worldview.
info_ease: Moderately easily. The university is quite organised but some parts were really hard to figure out.
arrival_assistance: Not much. I had to do everything myself and find out information on my own.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Had to stand in a line for three hours to get a card. Then the same again the week after to the the visa.
registration_help: Other students that knew more about the university.
registration_success: Not very. had to go though three rounds to get enough classes.
registration_advice: Go to the registration with some friends so you dont get bored.
course_level: Some where on a good level where others where unnecessarily difficult, ny jamming three courses into one and putting way too much content in little time. Not enjoyable.
teaching_comparison: Very strict. No amount of freedom to think and act in your own way. You have to learn the way they want or you will loose points. And their way was certainly not the most efficient at times. At UCPH we have the freedom to learn the way we learn best and to explore.
courses_enrolled: EC3322 Industrial Organisation CS2100 Computer Organisation ST3236 Stochastic Processes EC3333 Financial Economics
recommended_courses: Industrial Organisation was really good. The professor didn't put as much pressure and he was reasonable and very nice. The others were kind of awful.
unexpected_costs: Hospital Trip. This is extremely expensive, especially if going to private hospital. Get insurance!
cost_comparison: Food can be really cheap. Especially on campus and hawker centres. Food in supermarket is insanely expensive, especially western foods and fruits and vegetables.
activities_available: All kinds of activities. Try out stuff, it is fun.
activities_recommended: Scuba Diving. Golfing. Just walking around and experiencing the country.
weekend_recommendations: Go to different places in singapore and definitely visit Malaysia. Especially Tioman Island for scuba diving if you are into that.
culture_adjustment: Easy. They are all very nice and speak good English. So it is easy to get into contact with people.
socializing_tips: I arrived earlier than all the other exchangers, so I had no choice but to talk to the locals. That was very cool to experience.
cultural_challenges: The strictness. I like freedom to do whatever I want whenever I want. But they are just very strict there.
top3_advice: It is very competitive and hard to perform well here. It is very hot outside so be prepared. You will get thousands of mosquito bites.
other_useful_info: If you want a chill and relaxing exchange. Either this place is not for you or take the easy entry level course. Dont take courses for your level ie. 3000 and 4000. They are extremely difficult and time consuming.
most_rewarding: Being done with exam and going on vacation.
greatest_challenge: Being away from family and friends and not going insane with the workload and pressure they put on students.
other_comments: While I am grateful to have been given the opportunity to go to NUS and stay in the country. I simply cannot lie and say it was the greatest experience of my life. There were of course some good moments. But the majority of the time was spent wanting it to end. There were many things in the university which just did not go well with the way I want to live. The pressure on students, is huge and multiple students committed suicide throughout just my stay. We heard news about it multiple times.

crucial_aspects: I chose Singapore because of the nice weather, travel opportunities, and the high academic level at NUS.
info_ease: Very easy – NUS provided detailed guides for every step of the process.
arrival_assistance: I didn’t seek much assistance upon arrival. They have a well-organized system for new students. If I was ever in doubt, I just talked to the other exchange students.
arrival_comments: NUS was very helpful – they responded quickly to any inquiries. I didn’t attend much of the orientation as I came a bit late to Singapore. I can highly recommend coming at least one week before school starts. It takes time to settle in, meet the other students + it is nice to get to know the city a bit before school starts.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process for courses consisted of several rounds. You begin the first registration round, before you come to Singapore. If you don’t get all the courses, you can apply again in the next round. The last round of registration is after the semester has begun. So you can even try out some courses, and then drop it again, if you don’t like it. Actually, I liked the system much more than the registration system at UCPH.
registration_help: You could always contact the school if any doubt. They responded quickly.
registration_success: I missed the deadline for the first round, but it didn’t matter. I still got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: My advice would be to try to keep up with the deadlines. But don’t stress out if you make a mistake. There is a lot of deadlines for everything, but in the end everyone just wants you to have a good exchange experience. There will always be help to find.
course_level: The academic level was very similar to what I know from UCPH, which was nice.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was mostly lecture style in classes of around 30 people. However, you get assessed on your participation. Therefore, it will also be interactive. That is different from UCPH. But don’t let it scare you. My experience was that the participation assessment was an opportunity for the students to drag their grades up. But it doesn’t affect your grade in a negative direction.
courses_enrolled: International Criminal Law, International Environmental Law, Multinational Enterprises and International Law, International Space Law
recommended_courses: I can recommend all of my courses except the latter. Probably just because I didn’t find it interesting. However, I will recommend taking three 5-units courses and one intensive 4-unit course. With this combination you will have the workload spread out throughout the semester.
unexpected_costs: The room is very minimalistic. You have to buy hangers, pillow, and utensils for the kitchen.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping was more expensive than I thought. Therefore, you will mostly buy your food in food courts, which is cheap. It is manageable not spending enormous amounts of money on food, if you choose to go to the cheap places. The food courts are placed all around campus, so it is pretty easy.
activities_available: The place, PGPR, where I lived arranged some activities – for instance a bike tour around the city during the night and yoga classes. The Law Faculty also hosted some lunches.
activities_recommended: I can recommend signing up for sports activities. I regret missing the deadlines in the beginning of the semester. It’s a great way to meet people and especially also the local students.
weekend_recommendations: I will highly recommend exploring Singapore, as it is the city you now live in. Go to the tourist attractions and museums, do the Tree Top Hike and all the other stuff. But of course you also have a great opportunity to travel around Asia during the weekends and holidays.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy to adjust to the local culture, as it is a very well-functioning country. They have a lot of rules (also some weird ones), but it also makes it easy living there and safe.
socializing_tips: Join clubs and don’t be afraid to talk to them. They might seem shy, but all of the locals I talked to, was really interested when we first started talking - even though there are so many exchangers each semester.
cultural_challenges: You have to accept that there will be more rules than you are used to. Especially, if you live on-campus, there will be rules about alcohol, visitors etc. But it is really not a problem.
culture_appreciated: I found the culture a bit non-existing at times, because Singapore is one big mix of cultures. But that also made quite an interesting culture. I think especially their culture being affected by so many rules was what made it easy and safe living there.
top3_advice: 1. Don’t stress out about the administrative work. Everything works out even though you make mistakes. Everyone wants to help you. 2. Use the other exchange students from UCPH. They are probably doubting the same thing as you are. Or they are struggling with something similar, that they would like you help with. 3. Don’t spend too much time studying. You will pass no matter what. Being on exchange is so unique. And there is so much more to do than studying.
other_useful_info: Have fun !!
most_rewarding: Experiencing that you can make a home and an everyday life for yourself in another country. Meeting great people from all around the world. And of course, all the travelling! Also, enjoying the time without job, family and friends. It made room for doing new things
greatest_challenge: That it went by so fast :-) No major challenges.
other_comments: No matter if you do a semester of exchange in Singapore or another place – just go! It might seem overwhelming, but the outcome makes it 100% worth it.

crucial_aspects: Being in a convenient location in SE Asia with easy access to neighbouring countries for travel as well as being a highly ranked university, so i expected a high quality education. Singapore is also a very unique country as it has prospered under a rule which we might consider autocratic in Denmark, which is interesting to explore as an economist.
info_ease: Mails are being sent frequently to keep you in the loop. Going on exchange to a non-EU country is pretty troublesome no matter where you go, so expect a pretty large amount of paperwork. Download whatsapp/telegram as thats what people use over there for social as well as academic matters.
arrival_assistance: I had a question about check-in which i posed in the NUS-Exchangers whatsapp group, and another exchanger helped me out. Other than that the documents i was sent by email were sufficient.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You get emails about the registration dates. I got all 4 of my first priority courses in the first round, but 1 of them got cancelled for some reason. I got the next best course in the second round.
registration_help: You can email the uni about course registration and have assistance if you need that.
registration_success: Got all i wanted with no issues.
registration_advice: Theres a period of 3-4 weeks iirc at the start of the semester where you can freely drop courses. So just sign up for too many courses and go to 1-2 lectures/classes and sort it out from there.
course_level: The level of the courses are generally low. In Money and Banking and Financial Economics half the course was about Time Value of Money, which was covered in the first semester at KU. They also didn't want us to do lagrange for optimization problems in one course, as "that might be too advanced for the exchange students"?? Game Theory was taught by an Oxford professor and was more like the level of KU. Urban economics is very conceptually interesting, it is however not very difficult either, which can also be seen as an upside of course.
teaching_comparison: Lectures are like at home. However tutorials are a complete sham. Each course had 1 hour each week for tutorial, which had the following program: Students solve weekly tutorial sheet at home, students volunteer or a picked to present a question at the whiteboard, the class sits in silence for 7 minutes while the students at the whiteboard painstakingly write every step of the derivations as they are graded on their tutorial contribution, they quickly talk through their work. Rinse and repeat for next questions, class dismissed. Grading is not based on 1 exam like it is at home. Final exam is 40-60% of your grade, and most courses have midterms which are 15-30%. Rest are canvas quizzes (literally free grade since you can take them multiple times) and tutorial participation and attendance. Attendance is mandatory, but you can skip a few times during the semester without any repercussions. I cannot overstate enough how lenient the grading is too. Passing is basically expected no matter what you do, and with minimal effort you can get a comfortable B.
courses_enrolled: Urban Economics, Money and Banking, Financial Economics, Game Theory and Applications to Economics.
recommended_courses: Game Theory and Applications to Economics to get Mikro 3 merit, Urban Economics because it's unlike anything we have at KU and super interesting imo, by far my favorite course there. Financial Economics gives merit as a "prioriteret valgfag" so that might also be important to you. Money and Banking was easy and not my field of interest, ymmv.
unexpected_costs: Alcohol is very expensive, eating out is very inexpensive. I traveled a lot (went to 8 countries during and after the exchange), so naturally there was quite a bit of "personal spending". Housing was cheaper than my apartment at home.
activities_available: They've got loads of sports and halls with all kinds of activities going on. Big olympic pool and squash courts etc.
activities_recommended: Go to the arrangements and outings people do in the Whatsapp group, easy to make some friends that way, everybody got 0 friends at first. Your housing place most likely has an orientation week as well, go to those events and get to know the people in your building, you'll be seeing them every day!
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city, travel around asia. I selected my courses and tutorial times so they were all on mon/tue so i had 5 day weekend each week. NUSMods has a tool that allows you to import the course and make your schedule that way. Also go to China, they made it visa-free for Danes in November 2024, and it's so fun to go there and speak to local and get a feel for the country by yourself. Ask about the political and economic situation if you befriend a local, they arent all as shy as we think.
culture_adjustment: I was in a bit of an exchanger bubble, but Singapore is very orderly and distinctly different from the rest of SE Asia. It's not hard to adjust at all. Most people speak english too.
socializing_tips: Theres a buddy programme you can sign up for before the exchange starts, many exchangers did so and had good experiences. Talking to people in your classes is good too, you've already got a shared interest! (or disinterest).
cultural_challenges: Understanding what the mandarin speaking ladies at some of the food stands were yelling at me.
culture_appreciated: They do a lot of "raising" the society to have proper manners, lots of campaign ads to not harass the bus driver and to give your seat to old people and pregnant woman etc. They are also way ahead of their time in many urban policies, such as having a congestion tax since the 1980's, which is now slowly being introduced in western and chinese large cities. Their research and knowledge in urban policy in general is very advanced, go to NUS Cities events if that sort of thing interests you.
top3_advice: DO NOT GET SINGTEL AS YOUR TELECOM PROVIDER 3x. Get an E-sim from someone else if you can, or something like the 200GB local data and 7GB roaming abroad from Simba (60dkk/month). Have fun :)
other_useful_info: I think i covered most of it in the previous sections.
most_rewarding: Finding interests in new economic fields, forging strong bonds, expanding my worldview to different forms of government and having a lot of fun while doing it.
greatest_challenge: There's a lot of work to do before going, by keeping up with the whole process, seeking forhåndsgodkendelse and selecting courses and housing, seeking grants (legater), subletting your accomodation in Denmark and so on.
other_comments: NUS is an amazing place to go, and you can have an unforgettable semester there. I think that's the case in most places though, so wherever you end up going, being curious and social is the key to making your exchange the best it can be.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go far away from home and experience a high level university.
info_ease: It was fine, I also knew a few people who had been on exchange in Singapore who were able to provide some information.
arrival_assistance: There was a student office and they were also easy to get in touch with via email.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was quite a long process with many documents to send and fill out etc. But worth it!
registration_help: I could ask both KU and the host university.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Dont stress about the classes - it's possible to swap them once you are there.
course_level: I took classes that where the level 4000.
teaching_comparison: It's more of a lecture style and not as much with participation from the students.
courses_enrolled: International Commercial Arbitration, Trade Finance Law, Multinational Enterprises and International Law, Environmental Law
recommended_courses: It's a good idea to take one intensive course (the 4 units ones), because the classes are done after three weeks so you have more time in the end of the semester. I really loved the course International Commercial Arbitration - however, it involved an oral moot exercise as part of the grade (40%) and it is quite demanding in terms of work load. But I loved it. Can also recommend Environmental Law - I chose one topic for my exam essay and just wrote about this.
unexpected_costs: Bying stuff for my room - the AC, pillow, sheets, etc.
cost_comparison: The AC was a little expensive. Public transportation and food was less expensive than expected. And also the on campus housing, very cheap. Budget wise cannot recommend living off campus - it's super expensive.
activities_available: All sorts of sports, concerts, film club etc.
activities_recommended: Attend the events for exchange students (there will be one big whatsapp group), and you will get a lot of friends.
weekend_recommendations: Travel. Flight tickets are cheap and there are endless destinations to explore in South East Asia.
culture_adjustment: Not to difficult - although it is Asia, it is also a quite Western and modern country.
cultural_challenges: There' s a lot of silly rules to get used to, but it's nothing serious.
culture_appreciated: The people, so kind. And the food.
top3_advice: Get on campus accommodation, attend the activities you find interesting, and prepare yourself for the humidity.
other_useful_info: Enjoy!
most_rewarding: Getting new friends, being on my own, taking high level classes.
greatest_challenge: Being far away from home and getting settled and start a new everyday life.

crucial_aspects: NUS is a leading and well-known university and I wanted to spend my exchange challenging myself both academically and personally. Singapore itself intrigued me as a place to live, as it is highly culturally diverse and as a city is fundamentally different from many other places in the world with its architecture, fast pace and futuristic vibe.
info_ease: When you receive the application material from NUS (for me, it was around June/July, and I was attending the spring semester), the university sends several PDFs that include step-by-step guides on how to apply to the university, choose courses, apply for a visa, student accommodation, etc. After you’ve been officially enrolled, they also host a webinar where they go through many of the details. There was a lot of material from NUS, but it was easy to understand and navigate. Before I received anything from NUS (which happens gradually over a few months, depending on the steps), I found it really difficult to get information through KU, so you have to be patient and wait for NUS to contact you directly.
arrival_assistance: Most of the assistance I received was through the documents sent by NUS. They send a lot of emails and reminders about where, when, and how to complete the various administrative steps when you arrive, such as getting your student card, sorting out your visa, and knowing which documents to bring. These procedures take place in a gym on campus. I stayed in one of the residence halls, and the staff there were also very helpful. NUS also has several of their own apps, for example, uNivUS, which serves as your school calendar and contains a lot of information in one place. Since you receive so much information, I recommend reading it carefully because they expect you to know the details, deadlines, and other important information stated in the documents.
arrival_comments: I was very satisfied with all the information I received from NUS, but it was also stressful because there was a lot of administrative work to do both before and after my arrival in Singapore, with little support to help ensure you complete everything before the deadlines.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: NUS sends you a step-by-step guide on how to apply for courses. The application is done through their own system and takes place at the same time as enrollment. The process is very easy, you just have to prioritize 7-10 different courses. I recommend using NUSMods to get an overview of the schedule. After classes begin, you have the chance to change courses during weeks 1-3, and that process is also quite easy. So if you attend a class and realize it’s not the right fit, you can apply for a different course.
registration_help: There was no help from KU and only limited help from NUS beyond the guides provided in their documents. I talked a lot with others who were also going to Singapore during the application process.
registration_success: I almost got all of the classes I applied for.
registration_advice: Be sure to meet NUS's deadlines. They are quite strict, and if you miss them, you risk not getting the courses you want, as you'll have to wait for later application rounds.
course_level: You attend classes with a mix of bachelor’s, master’s, and LLM students, so the level among students varies quite a bit, but you won’t be evaluated the same way as, for example, LLM students.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style is very different from KU. At NUS you are required and expected to attend and participate in class as a part of your grade (between 10-30% comes from class participation). However, the professors are very welcoming and eager to hear the students’ input and the learning environment is quite good. The approach is also more theoretical. NUS focuses more on discussing the theory and reasoning behind the rules, judgments, and articles, rather than simply learning how to apply them as you do at KU.
courses_enrolled: World Trade Law (5 units), Global Data Protection Law (5 units), Foundations of IP Law (5 units), Intellectual Property and Human Rights (4 units).
recommended_courses: I would recommend World Trade Law and Global Data Privacy Law. There’s a LOT of reading in World Trade Law throughout the semester, but it’s very up-to-date with the current situation between the US and China, and you’ll gain a solid understanding of the legal instruments related to trade. Global Data Privacy Law is a very interesting course where you study UK, US, and EU privacy laws from a comparative perspective. There’s a lot of class discussion, for example, on the clash between privacy and new technologies. It’s a great course to take at NUS because the students come from all over the world, which makes the discussions even more interesting. Plus, the professor is brilliant.
unexpected_costs: Transportation is important to consider since the campus is a bit outside Singapore’s city center. Public transport is very cheap, but using Grab is often easier and faster—especially at night when public transportation doesn’t run after midnight. However, Grab can be more expensive during those hours.
cost_comparison: Food was less expensive than I expected. It’s very cheap to eat at the hawker centres both in and outside the city center, as well as in the canteens on campus.
activities_available: NUS hosts many events throughout the semester for exchange students. There are also plenty of sports clubs you can join. I recommend applying for the NUS Buddy Programme. I had a Singaporean buddy who also studied law, and he was a huge help. He answered all my questions about NUS, gave me great insider tips about Singapore, and we went on hikes and did other activities together.
activities_recommended: Spend the days and weekends to experience Singapore. Some of the best places are: the Botanical Garden, Gardens by the Bay and the lightshow, the two domes in Gardens by the Bay, Chinatown and Outram, Merlion, Sentosa, hike at Henderson Waves, Southern Ridges and Macritchie Reservoir, Ce La Vie (Nightclub, ladies night every Wednesday, free entrance), La Pau Sat (Hawkercenter in the city center), Boat Quay (good place for beers in the evenings), Haji Lane, Art Science Museum, Singapore Sling at Raffles Hotel.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Johor Bahru and Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia and travel around Asia if you have the time. Or experience Singapore.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy to adjust as everything is in English. Even though the culture differs a bit from what I'm used to, it was easy to settle into because Singapore is so diverse and people are used to meeting people from all over the world. The whole infrastructure is also designed for international purposes.
socializing_tips: Apply for a local buddy because that is the easiest way to get to know the local students. Apply for on-campus housing on because almost all of the local students live on campus so that's a great way to meet them. Also, try to be social in the breaks during class because in my experience the locals are very interested in getting to know exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Singapore has a lot of rules you need to be aware of to avoid getting fined. For example, you’re not allowed to drink water on public transportation, and you have to wave to signal the bus to stop for you.
culture_appreciated: Singapore has so many great qualities. The people are respectful and welcoming, everything is well-organized and efficient, it’s clean, easy to get around, and there’s a lot to experience, both culturally, city and nightlife and in terms of nature. The weather is also quite nice. You can also get food from all over Asia in the Hawker Centers for no money, and some of them are on the Michelin Guide. I can really recommend trying that.
top3_advice: 1) Don’t get too intimidated or stressed by how formal and strict NUS may seem in writing. It feels much more relaxed once you’re actually in Singapore. 2) Don’t worry too much about the participation requirement. As long as you attend most classes and contribute a few times during the semester, you’ll be fine. 3) Make sure to experience Singapore itself. Not just use it as a base for traveling. There's so much to explore locally.
other_useful_info: Make sure to read all the material you receive from NUS before going and make sure to meet their deadlines.
most_rewarding: I grew a lot both academically and personally during my time in Singapore. NUS is truly an excellent university. The professors, courses, reading materials, and fellow students are all fantastic. Although there’s quite a bit of administrative work involved in preparing to go to Singapore, it’s definitely worth it once you arrive. I can’t recommend it enough.
greatest_challenge: To keep up with all of the readings while prioritizing social activities throughout the semester. Live at a dorm without AC.

other_useful_info: It provides you with so many great opportunities to experience and learn about other cultures, even though you are not taking classes about this topic. You are living in a multi cultural hub.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere with a vastly different study and living culture compared to Denmark, further I also wanted to go to a university that was academically challenging.
info_ease: It was a bit confusing as you are sent a lot of mails and it can be hard to find out which are actually important.
arrival_assistance: None except written instructions and guides.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There is 3 rounds of applications together with an appeal period. In each round you list what courses you would like to get, after which you will be given some or all of them, for the appeal you can try to change to different courses if there is one or more you are unhappy with.
registration_help: There is a website called NUSMods that lists all the courses, descriptions, reviews as well as prerequisites. Note that not all the courses on the website will be available to you as an exchange student and you will be sent lists with the courses you can actually take.
registration_success: Mostly successful.
registration_advice: Make a long lists of courses that you would like, I personally applied for around 10-12 in total. Further do not stress if you do not get all your courses right away or have issues and the administration is very helpful.
course_level: I took bachelor courses ranging from 2k - 4k with most of them being 3k courses meaning they are meant for people on their 3rd year of their bachelor. Overall, I think they were around the high-end in terms of difficulty compared to the courses I have had at UCPH however, not much more difficuly.
teaching_comparison: The lectures were very similar to those at UCPH however, the tutorials / exercises classes were very different. Rather than solving the questions in class with a TA you would solve them at home and then just have the TA or professor go over the answer either giving it to you directly or making different students present their answer.
courses_enrolled: Non-Linear Programming (MA3236), Introduction to Artificial Intelligence (CS3243), Computer Graphics (CS3241), Optimisation Algorithms (CS4234), Greek Philosophy (PH2222)
recommended_courses: I really likes CS3243 as it had a very good blend of theory and practical use, further CS4234 and MA3236 were also very interesting and challenging courses.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: None
activities_available: There is a club for basically anything you can imagine.
activities_recommended: Anything they are interested in, it is a great way to make local friends.
weekend_recommendations: Travel, there is definitely things to see and do in SG: lots of amazing hawker centers, large malls, bar strips and other tourist like activities. However, you quickly run out and with SG located where it is it is super cheap to travel to all the other countries in south-east Asia.
culture_adjustment: It takes a little bit as the people are very traditional.
socializing_tips: The local students can be a bit shy and weary of exchange students so it is very hard to get to know them unless in participate in clubs or other activities with them.
cultural_challenges: They have very different attitudes to going out and the way in which they hang out.
culture_appreciated: They can be quite straight forward.
top3_advice: Try to get your sing pass and permanent Singapore number early, having Revolut makes it a lot easier to split bills with other exchange students, some locals have it as well. Try to keep organized and get all the administrative matters done early.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Traveling with other exchange students.
greatest_challenge: Getting used to the way they study.

crucial_aspects: First and foremost it was important to me, that all the courses I wanted to take were taught in English, and that the university I went to, was of a great quality.
overall_comments: The quality of the courses varied greatly, while some where very challenging, others were almost non-academic (at least after my understanding) I did however gain other skills outside of the curriculum, such as video editing and using new software for my assignments, which we don't use at my home university.
info_ease: If anything NUS almost overloads us with information. The paperwork and the practical stuff was easily managed.
arrival_assistance: Even though I was signed up for a buddy program, I never actually met my buddy (who herself was a 1st year, so probably didn't know much more about the facilities than I.
arrival_comments: All information via email. The physical meetings were primarily social mixers.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The quality of the courses varied greatly, while some where very challenging, others were almost non-academic (at least after my understanding) I did however gain other skills outside of the curriculum, such as video editing and using new software for my assignments, which we don't use at my home university.
registration_process: Most of the registration I did from home, which was described in detail by KU Abroad. The registrations in Singapore were primarily about getting your Student Pass (the card that proves you are studying in Singapore and gives you rights as a resident for about a year (I think)
registration_help: We received a bunch of emails with instructions. Part of the student pass registration was set up on campus, which was very convenient.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted
registration_advice: Check your email every day in the first time in Singapore! You don't want to miss a deadline.
academics_comments: The quality of the courses varied greatly, while some where very challenging, others were almost non-academic (at least after my understanding) I did however gain other skills outside of the curriculum, such as video editing and using new software for my assignments, which we don't use at my home university.
course_level: MUT1201 was quite challenging (and taught at the YSTCM) most assignments were clear, but with some, the intentions were not clear. SE2224 was only focused on the practical part of the course. Very little focus on theory, and with unclear instructions for assignments. TS2233 Was a very experimenting class, where we in the first part did some very rudimentary exercises, in the second half we were rushed through a creative process, which we were in charge of ourselves. TS3243 resembled a night class. No academic texts, but we were expected to know theory, even though it was not stated as a pre-requisite to have taken other film-classes, and no reading recommendations were listed or given. The professor's analyses were the correct ones, and challenging her view was not welcome. It ended with a group project, but with no other group exercises during the semester, I ended up in a group with total strangers, or student who don't show up to class.
teaching_comparison: There was no specific style of teaching at NUS, but rather the teaching method varied depending on the professors. They each had their own methods and levels of commitment. I could write an essay about each professor.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Classical Music Composition Unmasked! An introduction to Dance in SEA Making Contemporary Performances Stage and Screen
recommended_courses: Introduction to Classical Music Composition: The professor knew her stuff, the exercises and examples stretched beyond the Classical and she had suggestions for independent exercises and was very flexible when it came to consultation times if we were unable to attend in the allotted time slots. Unmasked! An Introduction to Dance in SEA: Because there is a field trip to Bali (a bit expensive though) and you get to perform a big show. It is a physically challenging class, but also very fun.
unexpected_costs: You need money for visiting all the amazing countries surrounding Singapore :)
cost_comparison: Foods with vegetables is expensive! And so is alcohol... Taking the MRT or the bus is very cheap (compared to Danish costs)
activities_available: Almost everything - from fencing to mountaineering and martial arts to sailing. There are more than a hundred student clubs I think. The halls (accommodations) also have their own activities.
activities_recommended: Take advantage of their amazing sports facilities and use this opportunity to develop new skills! I took a sailing course for 250 SGD and can now sail a dinghy :)
weekend_recommendations: Singapore is the Dubai of Asia. There are some amazing malls, but the cultural experiences are limited.
culture_adjustment: Not very difficult. Show up on time (no academic 15 minutes) and make sure to look up! Singaporeans look into their phones when they walk haha
socializing_tips: Strike up a conversation in the mid class break. Start out with talking about the class. Or join the open meetings in the student clubs
cultural_challenges: Singaporeans mostly keep to themselves - like most Danes do. Touching and even eye contact is considered somewhat intimate. I bought a stuffed animal at the Oceanarium to cuddle haha. Beware of the climate. it is hot and humid!
culture_appreciated: The "You can do it!" attitude during exams. Our dining hall was turned into a study area late at night during exam period - where they turned on the airconditioning and we were given a goody bag with snacks. Snacks is the love language here! And stickers!
top3_advice: Focus on LEARNING! Our grades are not transferred, only pass/fail status. Focus on gaining new skills and experiencing the culture. I wish I had spent more time exploring, even though I have been to many places and done many things - there was room for more! And when making friends, don't wait for others to make the first move. Be bold, and sit next to someone you don't know and introduce yourself - but maybe wait for them to open a conversation. And find a method to remember names!
other_useful_info: There are free buses driving around on campus. Use them - walking is not worth it, you will get to class all sweaty
most_rewarding: All the extra skills I have learned and some of the connections I have made - especially with other exchange students from other countries.
greatest_challenge: You will sometimes feel a bit isolated. And the heat
other_comments: Time passes quickly! Suddenly it's time to go home and you missed out on things. Always say yes!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study far away from Denmark and experience a completely different part of the world. Asia felt exciting because it offered new cultures, opportunities to travel, and many countries nearby to explore. Singapore was especially attractive because English is the main language, which makes studying and daily life much easier. In addition, NUS has a very strong academic reputation.
info_ease: We got a lot of information from the university and it could be quite hard getting an overview because there was so much but generally we got all the info we needed in good time and there was many easy ways to access it.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any but it was possible to get a buddy from the university if you apply for it.
arrival_comments: It was pretty straight forward.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration starts early but it is a very reasonable system. You prioritise your top-10 classes and the you can see which classes you got. There are multiple rounds so it is possible to get into a class even though you did not get in the class in round 1.
registration_help: There is a lot of info online and the answer quickly if you send and email to NUS.
registration_success: I was quite succesfull and got the classes I wanted pretty much.
registration_advice: Remember there is multiple round to get the courses. You have to sign up for which tutorial you want to go to in each course in the beginning of the stay. Use NUSmods to check for times and schedule. They give a lot of information out and if you check your mail everyday you probably won't miss anything. Also use NUSmods to see info on different courses such as: Reviews, prerequisites, schedule etc.
course_level: It is more or less same level as in University of Copehagen
teaching_comparison: It is a different style of learning on NUS. You have tutorials (which reminds a bit of "øvelsestimer"), which are usually 1 hour where you have to prepare and present solutions to questions in front of the class. It is mandatory to show up to these. Some of the exams (not all) you have to remember more than understanding the formulas because you have to be very fast in the exam.
courses_enrolled: EC3333 Financial Economics EC3343 International Finance GEX1010 Thinking Like An Economist GESS1005 South Asia In Singapore
recommended_courses: EC3333 Financial Economics and EC3343 International Finance: For Econ students these courses are a good introduction to finance I think. You learn a lot of basic stuff.
unexpected_costs: There were some extra fees such as mandatory insurance, MSF etc.
cost_comparison: You can eat very cheap if you want to. Economically, it does not make sense to cook your own food since the supermarkets are quite expensive.
activities_available: They have a lot of sports and you have many opportunities and time to try it out.
activities_recommended: There are a lot of events and sports club. Show up to the events, sports club etc. It is very fun and you get to meet a lot of new people. Both exchangers and locals.
weekend_recommendations: I will recommend to go travel with friends you meet in Singapore. People are very nice and open to travel. Remember to get it done because time flies on exchange :)) Malaysia and Indonesia are super close and you can do tons of nice things there.
culture_adjustment: There is definitely a culture shock with the food, social interactions, weather etc. But I would say because everybody talks English it makes much easier to adapt.
socializing_tips: I did not socialise that much with the local student and they can be a bit shy. But I'm sure if you are very interested in talking and socialising with local students they are very nice and polite.
cultural_challenges: To get use to the food and the weather (with no seasons as we know from Denmark) was a bit challenging. But generally people are very nice and open to every culture which makes it easier to adapt.
culture_appreciated: Kind of also the same. The food was super good and you can find some very nice places very cheap if you go out to eat in the Hawker centres (Big recommendation).
top3_advice: 1. Go out to travel with new people. It is super fun and very convenient from Singapore 2. Try a 1000-1999 course not from your area of study. It is a good opportunity to learn something new and everyone can join those courses. 3. Explore the city and go often out to eat in different hawker centres. It is super fun.
other_useful_info: Keep yourself updated on the mail through the whole semester. You get a lot of information which is important and a lot of information which is not important at all. Make sure to check your mail everyday not to miss deadlines.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding for me was both to experience a school like NUS but also to meet new people and have some good experiences with them as well.
greatest_challenge: I think to find the balance between school, travel and socialising. Because you have to a lor of hours to study and they way of studying here is a bit different from Denmark.

crucial_aspects: I had never been in Asia, NUS is a very good university that offers a wide range of courses and I wanted to travel far from home.
overall_comments: Hard to find anything i would want different

arrival_assistance: I had assistance making sure I could secure the classes I needed, that they didn't overlap and was helped to switch a class despite missing the deadline for the first round (which turned out not to be a problem at all)
arrival_comments: As mentioned, sometimes there was so much information it felt difficult to keep track of everything
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Hard to find anything i would want different

registration_help: They have guides for everything, almost too many. It is hard to come across anything that NUS does not have a guide for.
registration_success: Very succesfull, be prepared that not all classes are available for exchange students.
registration_advice: Just read through the guides carefully and do not stres too much about it. Try to get in contact with other exchange students from KU, we all helped each other.
academics_comments: Hard to find anything i would want different
course_level: The level depends on the type pf class. It is possible to choose what level course you would like before hand: 1000, 2000, 3000 etc. I recommend choosing different levels, as it in my opinion was nice with some harder and some more simple.
teaching_comparison: NUS requires much more participation during the semester, most classes have attendance and assignments throughout the semester which also counts towards the grades.
courses_enrolled: SPH2203 Food Environments, Nutrition & Health: Understanding Key Drivers, Actors and Solutions MS3216 Gender and Islam SPH2004 Lifestyle, Behaviour and Public Health GESS1005 South Asia in Singapore
recommended_courses: I actually loved all my courses, but regards interests I found GESS1005 South Asia in Singapore very nice in terms of gaining knowledge about Singapore and South asian culture when visiting.
unexpected_costs: Not so much unexpected, but spend some on travlling as I had room in my budget for it.
cost_comparison: Food was very cheap in both food halls and hawker kitchens (street kitchens) - I barely ate anywhere else.
activities_available: NUS is a large university offering almost anything you can think of
activities_recommended: I loved using the facilities such as tennis courts, pools and gyms
weekend_recommendations: Taiwan if possible. Otherwise it is easy to travel to Malaysia and some Indonesian islands
culture_adjustment: Easy, everyone was very welcoming.
socializing_tips: If you want to socialize, try to get accommodation in a house. They have lots of activities almost every week.
cultural_challenges: Adjusting to the climate in the beginning.
culture_appreciated: In the end the climate, but also the people and how it is very safe everywhere. I was never worried walking alone at night, even as a female.
top3_advice: Try to get in contact with the other students going, plan some trips during the semester and be open to meet new people.
other_useful_info: Not very specific, but I absolutely loved my exchange semester and I couldn’t think of any better place than Singapore and NUS. I would change a thing about it, and I am very grateful I ended up going.
most_rewarding: My new friends and my insights in Asian culture
greatest_challenge: Being very far from home on bad days, but I could just as well have bad days in Denmark.

info_ease: There was a long pdf file with all the information send from NUS
arrival_assistance: A sign up for getting a NUS buddy, a local friend who could show me around. And possibility to buy bed sheets so they where there when I arrived in the middle of the night. And there where tours of the campus and the area you could sign up for arranged by local students.

registration_advice: Get in contact with some of the people you are travelling with!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to try living in a place that wasn't european or north american. Singapore has a lot of similarities to the west, but is still a non-western country, which made it ideal for me. I could also travel a lot during my studies (I only had mandatory classes on monday and tuesdays) and the reputation and quality of NUS is also very good.
info_ease: Very easy. Everything is easily accessible in English.
arrival_assistance: Had a few questions. Usually got an answer within a day - they are very effective!
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You sign up for courses back home and when you get there you have I think 3 more rounds to secure courses, so don't sweat it if you don't get what you want when applying online.
registration_help: E-mail them. They're friendly, professional and helpful.
