registration_advice: Don't really have any... Have good grades, so the professor (who chooses which students are able to get his class) wants to have you in?
course_level: Game Theory was decently hard, but not more than I was expecting. Urban Economics was relatively easy if you're comfortable with microeconomics (Mikro I og Mikro II on polit). International Political Economy was relatively easy (there were no pre-requisites), so everyone can take this class, so if you know a bit about macro, such as exchange-rate stuff, then you'll be more than fine. Public Finance was way harder than expected... It didn't have a lot of math but the conceptual stuff (drawing diagrams) and intuition got quite advanced, which made it a bit hard to track. The lectures contained a lot of material, which made it a bit hard to keep up if you didn't understand the last slide. Chan Kok Hoe whom was our lecturer also likes to make the exams different from the tutorial questions, so you've to extrapolate what you've learned to different situations. The median score in the midterm was 13 out of 30 and you needed 15 to pass...
teaching_comparison: Lectures were similar. You prepare your tutorial questions from home and then present them in class (you don't get time to answer them in class). There is mandatory participation in tutorials, so you can't be travelling all the time unless you stack tutorials on the same days (I only had classes monday and tuesday).
courses_enrolled: 1. Game Theory & Applications to Economics (Micro III on polit), 2. Public Finance (Public Economics on polit), 3. Urban Economics (elective), 4. International Political Economy (political science course)
recommended_courses: Public Finance was interesting but clearly the hardest class I took Game Theory can go as Micro III but the lecturers english is not the best, so sometimes hard to keep up with the math, when you don't really understand what is said International Political Economy is very interesting and also quite easy if you don't want to overload yourself. Urban Economics is also relatively easy: the tutorials are discussions moderated by the prof in groups of 10-12 people, where you discuss chapters in a book called "Triumph of the City", which I found as quite a fun way of teaching compared to standard economics teaching. Furthermore, there is a mandatory field trip: we went to Geylang, which is Singapores red light district, where an MP from the government (he is also a Social Entrepeneur from Geylang) showed us around and told stories of the migrant workers, sex workers and singaporeans who lived there. Really interesting and kind of like "Gadens Stemmer" in Denmark, where you get to see the "dark side" of Singapore and get to understand the daily life of migrant workers and also see a side of singapore, that suprisingly has a lot of drugs...
unexpected_costs: I travelled a lot (as do many other exchange students): I was in Malaysia 3 times (Melaka, Kuala Lumpur, Penang), Lombok in Indonesia, Hong Kong, Taiwan, South Korea. This costs quite a lot of money, so my personal spending would most likely be lower if I didn't travel as much, but almost all exchange students here utilize Singapore's very connected airport to travel ALL over asia.
cost_comparison: Food can be found pretty cheaply at hawker centers or food courts, but sometimes (in my opinion) the quality isn't the best, so I gravitated towards a bit more expensive places to eat, which made my spending on food go up quite a lot. If you like asian food, then Singapore is great: you can find cuisines from all over Asia here (even the world). If you have the money, there are also quite expensive restaurants that serve world class food.
activities_available: Volleyball, Football, Climbing, Food-related, Swimming, Rowing, Running, different crafts: there is a club for everyone I suppose, so if you're interested you'll probably find one that fits.
activities_recommended: Idk I didn't really participate in many
weekend_recommendations: Go to Melaka in Malaysia if you're interested in the history of the Malacca Strait and colonial stuff. Hong Kong was a top destination for me: kinda wish I'd gone there on exchange. I climbed Mt. Rinjani on Lombok with some friends, which was a really fun hike (though also a bit strenous). Taiwan is soooo peaceful and beautiful: if you want a slower pace of life than in Singapore/HK, then go here. Also remember to spend time exploring the different areas of Singapore: Fort Silosa for WW2 stuff, The National Gallery is good (had a monet exhibition), Sands Theatre had Les Miserables from West End which was really good, Marine Parade is a nice part of the city in my opinion and do the tourist stuff: Lau Pa Sat, Sentosa, MBS, Chinatown etc. Everyone travels so much that the country itself gets kind of neglected...
culture_adjustment: You don't clap after lectures - I don't make that mistake again... Singapore is international so not too hard, but locals can be quite introverted (I guess in many ways similar to us scandinavians).
socializing_tips: Join a club. I mostly made friends with other exchangers, which was nice, but I'd also have liked to have made more local friends.
cultural_challenges: Clapping after lectures is replaced by pure silence... People reserve tables by leaving their umbrella/water bottle/tissues and then go order food. It's very international and everything works efficiently in Singapore and is in English, so you'll be fine.
culture_appreciated: The food.
top3_advice: Go here if you want: 1. The credentials of one of the best universities in the world, 2. The possibility to travel around SE asia like it was your gap year, 3. not having to pay extreme amounts of money in rent compared to north america If you're more "creative" you'll probably find Singapore quite boring, as the local cultural scene is quite dead compared to other asian countries. Almost all students here want to work in finance/tech/business, so if that's ur thing then you'll fit right in. If you want a similar, but more exiciting city, then choose Hong Kong. Oh, and prepare to be sweaty: it's very humid.
other_useful_info: Nope
most_rewarding: Travelling and trying new food
greatest_challenge: Passing Public Finance and juggling travelling over the weekend with coming prepared to class

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience a living in a culture and climate that was very different from Denmark. It was also important to me that the country is really safe and that English is the main language.

registration_advice: Make a little calendar with the different registration deadlines and don't overthink it too much.
course_level: I had the option of choosing courses on level 1000, 2000 and 3000. I found it nice to also have some lower level classes because it gave me more free time.
teaching_comparison: The style reminded me a bit of gymnasiet, as there was a lot of active participation throughout the semester compared to what I'm used to back home. All of my classes had tutorials, which I actually ended up really liking, because the different discussions I got to have with the local students were very interesting.
courses_enrolled: GES1034 - We the citizens: understanding Singapore's politics, SC1101E - Making sense of society, SC2220 - Gender studies, SC3206 - Urban sociology
recommended_courses: Urban sociology was really interesting. A part of the final project was to do observations in different parts of the city which was fun. I also enjoyed having gender studies and getting insights into how gender is viewed in Southeast Asia.
unexpected_costs: Traveling.
cost_comparison: Eating out and public transportation were cheaper than I expected. Buying food in grocery stores was a bit expensive, but I never cooked myself anyways.
activities_available: There were a lot of different clubs, but I didn't really participate in any.
activities_recommended: I went to a couple of events at my dorm and it was pretty fun.
weekend_recommendations: Exploring different parts of the city like Chinatown, Little India and Kampong Glam. Going out at Boat Quay and participating in the different festivals/holidays. Singapore is really well connected for traveling to other countries like Malaysia and Indonesia, and a lot of the 'exchange culture' is centered around traveling.
culture_adjustment: I generally found it easy as most of the locals speak English and the multicultural nature of the country makes it feel pretty open to outsiders.
socializing_tips: Living in campus housing gave me great opportunities to connect with local students because I was the only foreign student in my dorm cluster. Participating in the clubs would probably also have been helpful.
cultural_challenges: I found the strict laws and amount of surveillance a bit challenging at first, but I got used to it pretty quickly. The dorm also had strict rules in some areas (no alcohol or any overnight visitors) which was a bit of a culture shock. The local dialect (Singlish) could sometimes be a bit difficult to understand but it wasn't really an issue.
culture_appreciated: The food culture is amazing, I already miss the hawker centers. I also really appreciated how multicultural and safe Singapore is.
top3_advice: Spend as much time as you can exploring, don't worry to much about school (the grades are non transferable) and try to live on campus.
other_useful_info: Join the NUS exchange WhatsApp group. Even though the amount of messages was a bit overwhelming, there was a lot of people exchanging useful information and arranging meetups. Be prepared for really hot and humid weather. Having a bit of cash on you is useful, as some stalls don't take credit cards. Going out is a bit expensive, but if you go out on Wednesdays (ladies night) or use the Aentry app you can save some money.
most_rewarding: Making friends with people from a bunch of different countries and gaining new perspectives on life and the world. And getting to live in a tropical country for a whole semester :)
greatest_challenge: I got really sick during the exchange and had to navigate a foreign healthcare system. The NUS health center was pretty helpful though.

crucial_aspects: The most important aspects for me were the university's ranking and its location.
info_ease: I received all relevant information before my arrival. NYU's website has a lot of information in relation to anything you may need to know for the start of your semester like registering for courses, finding accommodation etc.
arrival_assistance: I stayed at the university's residence halls which have a 24/7 reception desk. They were very helpful upon my arrival. The first 2 weeks at university, I attended a summer course “Introduction to U.S. Law and Practice” before the start of the Fall semester. It was very insightful because, in addition to the substantive material on U.S. law, it contained a lot of practical information on studying in the U.S. such as how to find and read U.S. cases, how to use the relevant legal databases etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There is a bidding system for courses. It is hard to say exactly how much you should bid on any particular course. It is most likely that a course that has been historically popular will continue to be popular. Some courses have a very limited number of places available, e.g., 20 so I would suggest bidding most of your points on them. There are courses which are very large and everyone who is interested, gets them, so there is no need to bid on them. If you cannot get a course that you really want, you can always try to e-mail the professor and ask directly if you can sign up. It is possible for them to make an exception (cannot rely on it though).
registration_help: NYU has a very helpful webpage with tutorial videos on the bidding process. In addition, you can always e-mail NYU to ask if you have any specific questions. I would also suggest joining the LLM WhatsApp groups because people often discuss it and it is a nice way to keep up with the process, deadlines etc.
registration_success: I got all of the courses I wanted except one (which was a very small course for only 8 people). I changed my preferences a few times and did not experience any problems with dropping/re-registering for courses, so overall it was easy to get the courses I want.
registration_advice: Bid most, if not all of your points, on the course that is the hardest to get in. For example, I bid all 1000 points on the Antitrust Law and Economics Seminar which was very popular and had limited number of spaces. The rest of my courses had a big intake to I got them “for free” without having to use any of my points for them. Another advice is to join the LLM WhatsApp group as the discussions there can be helpful in relation to determining your strategy for bidding and being on top of all daily bidding deadlines.
course_level: In my experience, the level is higher than the courses at UCPH. There is no “maximum” pages of assigned readings, as it is the case at UCPH. So, for some of the courses you may have more than 200 pages of reading per week. The exams are normally more time pressured than the exams at UCPH. The exam questions are also much harder. However, this should not discourage you because the lowest grade that seems to be given to exchange students is a B or worst case, B-. So even you find a course very challenging, this is unlikely to be reflected in your grades.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style is more interactive compared to UCPH. A lot of the courses include practical exercises such as practicing drafting or negotiating, which can be very fun and insightful. In general, most courses are aimed at making you a better lawyer in a certain field, so they are not focused purely on the theoretical aspects but also aim to give you insights into the real world and enhance your interpersonal skills. In addition, in the U.S. you are expected to prepare and participate in every class. A lot of professors apply the “Socratic” method of teaching where they call on people to answer questions in class. You are not “penalized” in any way if you are not prepared and cannot answer the question. However, it you are well-prepared and participate in classes, professors will normally bump up your grade. For example, if you receive B+ on the exam, if you have been participating in class, the professor is likely to give you A- as a final grade for the course.
courses_enrolled: Corporations, Corporate Finance, Cross-border M&A, Antitrust Law and Economics.
recommended_courses: I enjoyed and would recommend all of my courses. In general, I would recommend choosing courses relevant to the area of law that you would like to practice in your future career. It is very interesting to get the U.S. perspective and I think it can really advance your career if you want to work for international clients.
unexpected_costs: I did not have any unexpected costs, but some things were more expensive than I anticipated (see the answer below).
cost_comparison: The compulsory health insurance is way more expensive (around $2,000 per semester). Mobile phone plan + data was more expensive (around $30 per month). Rent is way more expensive than in Copenhagen. Groceries (if you shop at Trader Joe's) are cheaper than in Denmark.
activities_available: There is a free gym and sport center, discounted tickets for movie theaters and Broadway shows. At university, there are a lot of very interesting lectures and academic events with famous guest speakers.
activities_recommended: I did not participate in any non-academic activities because I wanted to use my free time exploring the city. However, you can find an overview of the different opportunities on the NYU website. For example, see https://www.law.nyu.edu/graduateaffairs/academics/cocurricular, https://www.law.nyu.edu/studentgroups
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend exploring the city and everything it has to offer such as museums, art galleries, Broadway shows, comedy shows, restaurants etc.
culture_adjustment: People are very friendly and open, which makes it easy to adjust to the local culture.
socializing_tips: The best way to meet local students is in class but in general most international students stick together and it is easier to make friends within the international group. In general, American students were very friendly and open so you shouldn't hesitate to approach them and introduce yourself if you're interested in getting to know someone. There is a large international community with people from all around the world if you struggle making friends with the locals.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated American people's openness and friendliness. It was very easy to make friends and build a network which I found very rewarding.
top3_advice: 1. If you are used to being one of the best students in your class, this won't be the case when you go abroad, especially at NYU. The earlier you realize and embrace it, the more enjoyable your academic experience will be. It is not worth being stressed out and overworking yourself to try to catch up and compete with the others. Most people there will have better understanding of common law and how to do well at a U.S. university. In addition, most people come with a few years of working experience before starting their law degree. So, try to learn from them and accept that probably you will be one of the least experienced people in class. 2. The best way to study and prepare for exams is by using outlines from previous students. They are shared in WhatsApp groups and some of them can be found on the university's website. If you can't find any, just ask the other students. The outlines are normally very comprehensive, so it is a waste of time making your own notes from scratch. 3. You should not worry too much about exams and grades whilst you are on exchange. The most important thing is to get to know and experience another culture and a different way of living. You will make memories for life, so you don't want to spend most of your time in the library.
other_useful_info: Getting a Revolut bank account is a good way to exchange money and save on bank fees whilst you are abroad.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all around the world and making new friends in addition to experiencing American culture and living in NYC as a local.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was managing my time between studying/preparing for classes and social activities outside campus as NYC has so much to offer.

crucial_aspects: The academic level was crucial to me. I wanted to be able to combine the social and adventure-like experience of an exchange semester with great learning possibilities. NYU offers both a very high level and diverse range of courses.
overall_comments: I really enjoyed my semester abroad. Both the school, the people and the city is amazing and very different from CPH. It definitely went above my expectations in all aspects.

registration_process: Students are given 1000 points each that can then be distributed across the courses that you choose to prioritize. This also means that you can bid more on the courses that are important to you.
registration_help: I recommend taking a look at the link below which shows the historical clearing prices for the courses. This makes it possible to be a bit tactical in the bidding by relying on the historical data. You dont want to "waste" bidding points on courses that almost always are very cheap for example. I hope it helps.
registration_success: I got all classes that I wanted (however not immediately - the last one I got in one of the last cycles by bidding all my leftover points).
registration_advice: Learn the system, and take time to read about the courses. I would also recommend reading about the class professor before choosing a course. Many professors at NYU are world-class and the professor is of course very important in how good a course actually proves to be.
academics_comments: I really enjoyed my semester abroad. Both the school, the people and the city is amazing and very different from CPH. It definitely went above my expectations in all aspects.
course_level: I think the level is very different depending on the course. I had a 3 courses, and all of them were very different in level ranging from clearly above KU-master-course-level to equal to that. This goes both for work-load and complexity of material. The teachers have higher expectations than at KU, and expect more independent thinking from the students than at KU.
teaching_comparison: Teaching style is different. There are some cold calling (3 out of 4 classes for me) but not too bad. One positive from the cold calling is that almost all students are very well prepared for the classes, creating a very good and dynamic class-room environment with interesting discussions. Furthermore, you are only taught by the professor in the course.
courses_enrolled: 1) Contracts, 4 credits 2) Corporate Finance, 3 credits 3) Antitrust Law, 4 credits 4) Graduate Lawyering, 1 credits
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the courses I took except GL. Graduate Lawyering is just a small skills course, but not necessary. Contracts was by far the "easiest" course I took, and was very important in creating a balance where I had a realistic chance of actually being prepared for other classes, while still experiencing the city. The professor Kieth Sharfman is both competent, very nice and understanding. It is an LLM course, so the other students are also international (LLM students and exchange students). Corporate Finance was extremely interesting and really furthered my understanding of the various themes within the finance world. It is not exactly a law course, but that shouldn't scare one away. The professor in CF is probably the best professor I had (Anjolein Schmeits). The final is very calculation-heavy and only a financial calculator is allowed, but the professor has sessions where you can practice for the exam issues outside regular hours. Lastly I took Antitrust Law. The professor Scott Hemphill was extremely competent, and brought in very interesting people to discuss different areas of Antitrust law. This course was by far the one that required the most reading and preparation, but was also very rewarding and interesting.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: It wasn't exactly unexpected, but living in Manhattan is very expensive. This goes for both food, housing, eating out, getting drinks etc. I was surprised that takeaway was also relatively expensive except the 1 dollar slices of course.Everything was more expensive.
activities_available: There are all sorts of activities. All of them are available in the material that NYU provides both before and after arrival.
activities_recommended: COVID did have an impact on many of the non-academic activities. However, you should make use of the free gyms, and read your emails that often contain interesting activities.
weekend_recommendations: I went to Cold Spring, which is an hour away from NYC and quite a popular hiking spot. It's a beautiful getaway and break from the busy city life!
culture_adjustment: I had no issues with this. People are very welcoming, and the environment is very international.
socializing_tips: Join clubs, join sports teams and attend events.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: People are not afraid to stand out and be who they are. It's very refreshing to see how people dress and act exactly as they would like to.
top3_advice: 1) once again it's very expensive, remember to adjust for that in scholarship applications 2) don't stress out that other students are reading more than you, follow your usual routine that works 3) remember to explore the city and take part in social activities, there is room for exam preparation later on.
other_useful_info: Ask others, especially the local students for pre-made outlines from former students and use it as a basis for note taking. Saves time and allows for listening instead of constant typing.
most_rewarding: Living in Manhattan, making friends and the inspiring academic environment
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to the higher workload, especially at the start where the english legal terminology is new and slows the reading down a bit. Balancing studying with social activities and exploring the city.
other_comments: None.

crucial_aspects: Location: I always wanted to live in NYC. University: New York University is a prestige university, hereby positioning myself better in my future career, where I hope to work international to some extent.
info_ease: I arrived half a month before study start. Which I consider to have been a huge advantage. It was nice to have time exploring the city and getting to know the different NYU buildings. In that way I also had time to meet with people at the Student Link Center, who could inform me on practical matters.
arrival_assistance: NYU has an amazing exchange staff, that assists in everything from VISA-application to social events. And they basically informed, and guided me the whole way. Upon arrival I went to the Student Link center to get my NYU card, there I also went later in the month to meet the other exchange students. That meeting was facilitated by the exchange staff at NYU.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I registered through the exchange system at the University of Copenhagen. It was fairly easy, and people in the exchange team at KU, was very helpful and easy to contact.
registration_help: Guidance in terms of mailing. Information meetings and an overall introduction lecture to exchange abroad.
registration_success: Very succesfull, I got all the classes I wanted at NYU.
registration_advice: Register as fast as possible!
course_level: I took all undergraduate courses, and they were fairly manageable. I had no problems keeping up with the level at all!
teaching_comparison: The students pr. lecture and class were less, meaning that you got to know the professor better. It was a nice format, where you got more personal with everyone involved: student as well as professor and TA
courses_enrolled: Human Rights and Culture, Climate and Society, Language, Power and Identity.
recommended_courses: Climate and Society - It was super exciting to enter environmental studies, and I learned a lot.
unexpected_costs: Crazy housing prices, and also the food: it is very expensive!
cost_comparison: Everything was more expensive than I expected. I did not encounter any "less expensive" items.
activities_available: Sports activities, social events, gym and swimming hall, lectures etc.
activities_recommended: I did a lot outside the University, hanging out with other danish people who were interns at the UN or the danish embassy. But I would recommend joining the Yoga sessions, as well as using the gym.
weekend_recommendations: Go Upstate for hiking! Take the boat to Queens and New Jersey. And go rooftop partying.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. It is a very international environment which is reflected in a diversity of cultures - made it easy to navigate.
socializing_tips: People are very open, so I think you will have no problems with that.
cultural_challenges: There was an extreme consumer behaviour, which I personally found a bit frustrating.
culture_appreciated: The kindness and openness.
top3_advice: Relax, Take a student loan and go have the best half year! It is worth every penny!
other_useful_info: There are a lot of poverty in New York, and you should therefore always be mindfull what areas you go to.
most_rewarding: Meeting new amazing people and living in New York.
greatest_challenge: The high prices.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: I chose NYU mainly because I heard that the courses were on a very high level and that you could learn a lot from some very skilled professors. I also chose this location because I'm very interested i New York City with its opportunities and diverse cultures.
overall_comments: It was hard to get to know people at first, I think NYU could have done more in the beginning to make sure exchange students get to know each other. When you have a network of people it's much easier live and study there. I really liked the courses, and the teachers. They all seems interested in their students and very competent in their field.
info_ease: It was easy enough to find information about courses. It wasn't that easy to find information about social events, NYU could have made that more accessible.
arrival_assistance: We had a mandatory intro day (which I wish their were more of), we also had some guidance counselors who we could write emails to or meet in person, which worked really well.
arrival_comments: It was easy enough to find information about courses. It wasn't that easy to find information about social events, NYU could have made that more accessible.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was hard to get to know people at first, I think NYU could have done more in the beginning to make sure exchange students get to know each other. When you have a network of people it's much easier live and study there. I really liked the courses, and the teachers. They all seems interested in their students and very competent in their field.
registration_process: I got lots of emails describing how to set up an online account, and I went to the office to get my ID-card.
registration_help: Guidance counselors and specific offices.
registration_success: Very successful, I also managed to swap two course after I tried one course and found out it wasn't for me.
registration_advice: Write an email to a guidance counselors if you're in doubt of something.
academics_comments: It was hard to get to know people at first, I think NYU could have done more in the beginning to make sure exchange students get to know each other. When you have a network of people it's much easier live and study there. I really liked the courses, and the teachers. They all seems interested in their students and very competent in their field.
course_level: All courses were undergrad level courses. Some were very beginner level other were more advanced.
teaching_comparison: In the US your verbal participation in class can affect your grade. This means that a lot of student say something in class, which can lead to some interesting discussions but it also leads to a lot of noise - students just saying something because they know they have to. You can always talk to your teachers about this and what they expect of you in class.
courses_enrolled: Fundamentals of Filmmaking I Acting for the camera Transgender Youth Intro to Psychology
recommended_courses: Acting for the camera - the course is great whether you want to work in front or behind the camera or if you just want to try something completely different to your other courses.
unexpected_costs: Food is very expensive because of inflation, housing is too, clothes and visiting famous landmarks is as well - actually everything is expensive in New York :) The NYU insurance was insanely expensive. I later found out that you can get it cheaper elsewhere.
cost_comparison: Food, housing and clothes is more expensive. You can get a reduced price at certain sights and museums with student discounts.
activities_available: A lot
activities_recommended: You can read about all of them and figure out what's interesting for you
weekend_recommendations: Visit the famous landmarks, try out different restaurants and fastfood places
culture_adjustment: It was harder than I thought. New York is a very loud city with lots of yelling and there's a certain over-politeness that can seem kind of fake from a scandinavian point of view.
socializing_tips: Sadly most local students are not that interested in a deep relationship with exchange students since they know they won't be there for long. You can get lucky though and meet some American students who are interested, but mostly you'll hang out with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: One thing that was very particularly hard to adjust to was the inequality. There's a lot of poor people living on the street and the problem has only grown bigger since covid. It can be pretty heartbreaking to witness. Other than that there's the loudness, lots of people yell all the time, also during normal conversations. People often get very mad at each other but I've never witnessed violence, people just let out a lot of steam. It's very hard to get close to locals, but it makes sense in a city were people quickly jump from one thing to the next.
culture_appreciated: The magnitude of everything, the buildings, the sights and also the mixture of different cultures you can experience.
top3_advice: Find a place close to a metro and affordable supermarkets. Find a community of people you like and trust otherwise New York City can feel quite lonely. Make you to explore the city and play turist once in a while, then you're living in a city and are busy studying or working sometimes you might forget how great it is.
other_useful_info: If you're having trouble finding a community I can recommend trying to find some other danish people living in New York on Facebook groups. Even if your initial idea was not to hang out with other danish it actually helps a lot to share your weird New York experience (both the good and the bad) with someone from back home who are experiencing the same as you.
most_rewarding: Showing my films in class and getting people's reactions.
greatest_challenge: Finding an affordable place to stay (moved 3 times)

crucial_aspects: The choice of destination was based on the academic opportunities of the university, both with regard to the academic level of the courses offered, the professors teaching the courses, the availability of courses of interest to me, as well as the overall academic level of the university and its students. I therefore chose to go to New York University School of Law.
info_ease: Somewhat difficult. NYU Law only takes in a handful of exchange students every semester, and their main focus is on the LLM-students and JD-students. While this is very reasonable, it does make it more difficult for an exchange student to find the necessary information that does not already apply to LLM-students.
arrival_assistance: NYU Law has a great administration handling everything relating to international students; both exchange students and LLM-students. Once the semester started (a few weeks after arrival and upon completion of the introduction course), the people of the exchange office were both very helpful and very nice.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: At NYU Law, you make bids for every course that you would like to have. Each student is awarded 1000 points, and over a certain period of time the initial bids have to be made. Then, in the first few weeks after the courses have started, students are able to drop courses and join other courses that have not already been filled up. One of the upsides of this system is that if the individual student is really eager to be enrolled in a certain course, that student can choose to make a high bid for that course, thereby overbidding the other bidders. Each student is able to make its own determination with regard to the courses that the student would like, and taking into account the available information on previous years' bidding cycles, the students are well equipped to make proper bids for the courses.
registration_help: A guide before entering the initial bids. Once we got to NYU Law, the people of the course registration office were of great help.
registration_success: I was quite successful, getting most of the courses I wanted. I was able to rearrange my entire course registration in the later bidding cycle.
registration_advice: For every semester, students are asked to review their classes, both with regard to overall experience, course work load and the professors teaching styles. I did not know of this information before registrating for classes, but it would have been of great help for me to understand the individual course better.
course_level: I took law school courses offered to 2Ls and LLM-students. Naturally, they were all graduate/MA level courses.
teaching_comparison: Much more interaction with the students, and the professors were very well prepared. The course work load was fine, much like in UCPH. But the students were better prepared for the individual class, and the law school had mandatory attendance.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to US Law. Investment Treaty Arbitration International Commercial Arbitration Contracts (for LLM students) International Arbitration and the CISG Cross-Border Mergers and Acquisitions.
recommended_courses: All of them. For each course, the professor was very well prepared, skilled, friendly and passionate. I would like to also note that taking courses specifically on US law is very interesting as an exchange student.
unexpected_costs: Registration fees incurred doing the formal process of getting accepted at NYU Law.
cost_comparison: Housing is more expensive than I thought, and every day expenses (coffee, lunch, etc.) is also very expensive as you have to include a 20 % tip.
activities_available: We had boat parties, social gatherings, LLM/Exchange student events, sport activities, tickets to broadway and so much more.
activities_recommended: Go for a run in Central Park, alongside the Hudson, and in Prospect Park. Also, take the subway to a random location and walk through the neighborhood. NYC has so much to offer, and it would be a shame to spend all of it in the library or in your apartment. Go for the sunday bottomless brunch, go to that flea market with some fellow students, arrange a movie night at Dumbo Park and have the NYC Skyline as a magnificent backdrop. You will not regret doing all of those things instead of studying your semester away. You have time for both - and then some.
weekend_recommendations: Visit Philadelphia, go do a weekend hike upstate. Go to the food market in Queens, go to Washington and Boston. With public transportation, these places are max. 3 hours away.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. NYC is an international metropolitan, and so it is easy to mix in with the "locals".
cultural_challenges: Talking to strangers and tipping.
culture_appreciated: The openness of New Yorkers. People are much more eager to talk to each other than we are in Copenhagen.
top3_advice: Be open to make friends with the LLM-students. They are just as new in the city as you are, and even though they are often older and more experienced, they also came to have a great time. Get a sense of your neighborhood, and explore the city! It is so diverse that you will never get bored of it. Be active in class. It is much more normal than back home at UCPH, and it is a great experience when you get familiar with the course topics, your class mates and professors.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Both the social and the academic experience.
greatest_challenge: Being active in class / getting called on. Bot you quickly get used to it.

crucial_aspects: I chose my study destination based on the appeal of the NYU campus which lies centrally in NYC. I had also heard that the university has good professors. I also wanted to go somewhere where the main language was English.
info_ease: Difficult and confusing. However, once I was there it became a lot easier.
arrival_assistance: Online seminar with information and an in person introduction to visa guidelines.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: They have an application portal where you fill out your details.
registration_help: You could email the offices of global services.
registration_success: I got the classes that I wanted, however, I was not able to see which courses I could take until quite late. I think they have made the courses publicly available through the Albert Portal.
registration_advice: I would recommend that you look into what courses you can take well in advance and also what prerequisites they require and what days the courses are offered.
course_level: The courses were about the same level as UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Some of the mid-terms and exams were multiple choise or short answer quizzess and in person essays. Generally, there is a higher level of monitorization with attendence for courses and weekly assignments about the readings.
courses_enrolled: The Social Challenges of Climate Change American Capitalism in Theory and Practice Social Networks
recommended_courses: Both The Social Challenges of Climate Change and Social Networks. The professors were sweet and engaging. And the course material was interesting.
unexpected_costs: Everything is more expensive in NYC.
cost_comparison: For instance, groceries are expensive. Insurance was also expensive. I would look into finding different insurance than the one NYU offers. You should do this before the end of September when you get there if you are going in the fall semester.
activities_available: Sports, good gym facilities.
activities_recommended: Explore NYC, the city has a lot to offer.
weekend_recommendations: Stay in NYC, there are always more areas to explore. I went to Montreal over the Thanksgiving break to visit a friend, this was also a good trip.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy.
socializing_tips: Talk to people in your courses. I made a few friends this way and they are willing to talk.
cultural_challenges: Adjusting to the language, both in lectures and the polite phrases used in other situations.
culture_appreciated: The diversity of the city. I was able to seek out a community that I am normally not able to find as easily in Copenhagen.
top3_advice: Apply for your visa well in advance! You need a bank statement amongst other things when you are applying. Check out courses in advance too. And everything will be fine and a lot easier practically once you get there.
other_useful_info: Check out the courses on Albert.
most_rewarding: Making friends with other exchange students and students from NYU.
greatest_challenge: There is 6-hour time difference between Copenhagen and NYC, this was a bit challenging if you needed to talk to somebody at home. It was also difficult not being able to go home for a short amount of time.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: I chose to study in NYC because of its vibrant energy and dynamic atmosphere. Having previously visited the city, I was eager to experience living there. Additionally, I was drawn to New York University due to its strong reputation for academic excellence and its welcoming, supportive community.
info_ease: NYU is a large institution with extensive experience hosting exchange students, making it easy to access the information I needed and get in touch with their staff. Additionally, KU provided detailed guides, ensuring I had no trouble obtaining the necessary information from their end as well.
arrival_assistance: I had some questions regarding housing at NYU and I received an answer to these via email.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: They have a bidding system that you have to get used to but it is actually not that difficult. You can see how much students had to offer previous years to get the course. This made sure you had an idea how popular the courses were, and thus how much you should offer on the courses.
registration_help: There were video guides as well as written guides. Furthermore, you can ask for assistance at the office of graduate affairs if need be.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. I had to bid a lot of points for one of the courses that I wanted but I also ended up getting it.
registration_advice: Spend some time on the bidding system to make sure you understand how it works. Some courses have room for everyone and do therefore not require for you to bid any points.
course_level: None of the courses I took were particularly easy, unlike what some exchange students might experience in other destinations. That said, I didn’t find the courses overly challenging either, and I was able to achieve good grades without too much effort.
teaching_comparison: Cold calling is allowed and some professors like to cold call a lot. I had to get used to this, but I felt that the professors were kind when asking the questions, and I could also see some benefits from the cold calling. Apart from that, I would not say that the style of teaching was vastly different from the one at UCPH although students generally participate a little more in the classes at NYU.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to U.S. Law (mandatory introduction course) Antitrust law Contracts for LLM students Negotiating corporate transactions.
recommended_courses: Negotiating corporate transactions might have been one of the best courses I have ever taken. I felt like I developed my skills on a professional level as well as on a personal level. It was fun to practice mock cases each time.
unexpected_costs: Health insurance was quite expensive even compared to the U.S. Moreover, New York in general is quite expensive
cost_comparison: I did not have to spend much money in books as these were provided by the university.
activities_available: There are tons of options when it comes to activities at NYU. I was part of the run club and the European Law society. Moreover I joined a lot of other events that were provided for free.
activities_recommended: The boat ride in the fall as well as the fall ball and the trips to broadway were great fun.
weekend_recommendations: I enjoyed visiting Washington D.C. on an extended weekend trip. I also went to Cancun, Mexico which was great fun too and not too pricey
culture_adjustment: I lived on campus, and while the area around Washington Square Park is lively and vibrant, it is also quite noisy and busy, which took some time to get used to. Aside from that, I found it easy to adapt to New York, as it is such an inclusive city with people from all over the world.
socializing_tips: Spend time with the LLM's. They are also international and thus new to the city and to the language just like you. They are super friendly and are eager to make new friends too.
cultural_challenges: Many of the JD students focus heavily on their studies and have little time or interest in socializing. While I enjoyed spending time with the other exchange students and the LLMs, it would have been nice to spend more time with the American students as well.
culture_appreciated: New Yorkers and Americans tend to be friendlier and more talkative than Danes. I really appreciated this, as it made it easier to start new conversations and meet new people.
top3_advice: Enjoy all of it and take some classes that you find interesting. Spend time eating out and go for long walks in the city.
other_useful_info: I transferred credits for the Introduction Course, reducing my semester workload to 10 credits instead of the usual 12. This gave me greater flexibility and more time to concentrate on the courses I was taking.
most_rewarding: Getting to know the city by heart and to have that feeling of a second home. In the beginning everything is new and exciting, but I enjoyed the last couple of months particularly much, because by then I had established routines and a social network allowing myself to relax and enjoy it a bit more.
greatest_challenge: Finding a balance between studying and socializing was important to me. I wanted to focus on my studies, but I also wanted to have time to explore the city and spend time with others.

crucial_aspects: Valget faldt på New York fordi det er en fantastisk by med mange muligheder, samtidig med at New York University School of Law er et særdeles anerkendt universitet med dygtige professorer fra hele verden. Derudover er NYU kendt for at have fag med en interdisciplinær tilgang, hvormed man som studerende får en bredere tilgang til juraen, som ikke alene er begrænset til det strengt juridiske. Hvis man ønsker at studere i et internationalt læringsmiljø med nogle af de mest dedikerede jurastuderende fra alle verdens hjørner og samtidig gerne vil bo i en pulserende storby med alverdens kulturelle tilbud og oplevelser lige uden for døren, er et udvekslingsophold ved NYU det helt rette valg.
info_ease: Det var relativt nemt at finde relevant information forud for opholdet. Så snart jeg havde modtaget mit endelige optagelsesbrev fra NYU, fik jeg adgang til deres pendant til KU-net, hvor man kan finde guides til stort set alt. Derudover modtager man også en masse via e-mail undervejs. NYU's exchange-ansvarlige medarbejder var også hurtig til at række ud, og jeg var således ikke i tvivl om, hvem fra administrationen jeg skulle kontakte ved spørgsmål.
arrival_assistance: I løbet af de første to uger deltog jeg i kurserne "Introduction to U.S. Law" og "Introduction to U.S. Legal Practice", som er obligatoriske for LL.M.-studerende. Disse 14 dage fungerede således som introuger, hvor der efter undervisningen var sat tid af til infomøder, hvor vi fik en masse information om bl.a. Visa-reglerne, hvordan man skulle forholde sig, hvis man ville rejse ud af landet under opholdet, hvem fra administrationen, der skulle kontaktes ved hvilke spørgmål mv. Min oplevelse var derfor, at jeg vidste, hvem jeg skulle kontakte, hvis jeg fik brug for hjælp til noget, og jeg synes i dén grad, at jeg fik den information, jeg havde brug for. Derudover arrangerede NYU's exchange-ansvarlige en frokost for udvekslingsstuderende hhv. i starten og slutningen af opholdet, hvor vi kunne stille spørgsmål og lære hinanden at kende.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Processen med at ansøge om optagelse ved universitetet var relativt ligetil. Man skal tage en TOEFL-sprogtest, og derudover skal KU indsende en underskreven version af éns karakterblad. Resten foregår via NYU's ansøgningsportal, og man modtager en mail med link til portalen samt guidelines.
registration_help: Der var masser af information tilgængelig på NYU's hjemmeside, og derudover var jeg løbende i kontakt med diverse personer fra administrationen, herunder NYU Law School's exchange-ansvarlige.
registration_success: Valg af courses foregår via en bidding-portal, hvor man har 1000 point pr. semester, man kan byde på fag med. Instrukser fremsendes via éns NYU-mail i maj, og jeg kan varmt anbefale at "byde" på fag allerede i første runde, da det er her, der er størst chance for at få de fag, man gerne vil have (i hvert fald de mest populære af dem). Derudover kan man på NYU's hjemmeside fremsøge en såkaldt "clearing list", hvoraf det fremgår, hvor mange point den højest bydende studerende fra forrige semester bød, for at få en plads på kurset. Det giver en idé om, hvilke kurser der er mest populære, og hvilke, der vi være nemmere at få. Kurser, der ikke fremgår af listen, er ikke blevet fyldt op på forrige semester, og man kan derfor tænke lidt strategisk og undlade at bruge for mange point på disse kurser. Derudover er mit indtryk, at det er relativt nemt at bytte fag i de første par uger efter semesteret er startet. Jeg fik ikke selv behov for at bytte nogle af mine, men det gøres gennem samme portal som dén, man bruger til at søge i første omgang. Et trick, hvis man gerne vil have plads på et kursus, hvor alle pladser er taget, er at dukke op til første eller anden time og tale med professoren. De har typisk en eller to "chance-pladser", de kan give til studerende, der ikke fik plads i første omgang.
registration_advice: Jeg vil klart anbefale at læse course evaluations fra studerende, der tidligere har taget de udbudte fag. Disse findes på hjemmesiden (man skal bruge login). Det giver et enormt godt indtryk af, om pensum er passende, hvordan professorens undervisningsstil er mv. Husk at tjekke, at professoren stadig er den samme. Derudover vil jeg anbefale at tage færre fag med flere credits frem for flere fag med få credits. Der er ikke som sådan nogen begrænsning på, hvor meget materiale professorerne kan udvælge som en del af pensum, og derfor kan læsemængden for fag til 2 credits sagtens være næsten ligeså tung, som på et fag til 4 credits. Man skal have 12 credits for at få overført 30 ECTS-point. Jeg valgte at få meritoverført kurset "Introduction to U.S. Law", som giver to credits. Kurset undervises i sommerferien (de sidste 14 dage af august), og er som tidligere beskrevet obligatorisk for LL.M.-studerende. Det gav en enormt god indflyvning i det amerikanske retssystem, og jeg ville ikke have været det foruden. Det er desværre kun muligt at tage faget, hvis man er på udveksling i efterårssemesteret. Eftersom jeg allerede havde bestået et fag til 2 credits før det egentlige semester startede, behøvede jeg kun at følge fag til sammenlagt 10 credits i løbet af semesteret, hvilket frigav en masse tid til at opleve byen, tage på ture rundt i landet mv.
course_level: Mine professorer var alle sammen eksperter inden for deres respektive områder, og derfor var kvaliteten af undervisningen også ualmindeligt høj. Læringsmiljøet var således særdeles motiverende men også mere udfordrende end på KU. Den samlede læsemængde var også større end på KU, men jeg valgte kun at læse dybdegående til det ene fag og skimme/læse outlines til de andre fag. På karakterstatistikkerne fra de tidligere år kan man se, at der stort set aldrig bliver givet lavere karakterer end B-, og det er derfor tæt på umuligt at dumpe et fag, hvis man har været til undervisningen og dukker op til eksamen. Derfor skal man ikke lade sig skræmme af, at niveauet føles højt undervejs, og at eksamensopgaverne også er markant sværere og mere tidspressede, end man er vant til derhjemme.
teaching_comparison: Undervisningsstilen er anderledes i dén forstand, at professorerne i høj grad forventer, at de studerende møder velforberedte op og har læst samt skrevet noter til pensum. Endvidere benyttes "cold calling"-metoden af nogle professorer, hvormed tilfældige studerende udpeges til eksempelvis at forklare udvalgte dele af pensum eller redegøre for en dom foran hele klassen. Min oplevelse var dog, at de var forstående, hvis folk ikke havde læst eller valgte at sige nej til at svare. I starten var det klart noget, jeg skulle vænne mig til, men det endte med at være en rigtig god udfordring, og jeg kunne virkelig mærke, at jeg udviklede mig fagligt. Man vil typisk kunne se på tidligere course evaluations, om de forskellige professorer cold caller eller ej.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to U.S. Law (2 credits) Introduction to U.S. Legal Practice (1 credit - ikke meritoverført) Antitrust Law w. Professor Daniel Francis (4 credits) Contracts w. Professor Keith Sharfman (4 credits) International Commercial Arbitration w. Professor John Fellas (2 credits)
recommended_courses: Alle de kurser, jeg tog, er anbefalelsesværdige. Professorerne var dygtige og havde en enorm erfaring inden for deres felter. Prof. Fellas har arbejdet med voldgift i mange år og har en baggrund som partner i ét af de største advokathuse i New York. Han ved derfor, hvad der er vigtigt i praksis, og han fortæller mange spændende anekdoter i undervisningen. Han cold caller ikke, men opfordrer meget til deltagelse. Daniel Francis har en baggrund fra FTC (Federal Trade Commission) og er en kæmpe Antitrust-nørd med specialiseret viden om digitale platforme. Hans cold calling er intens, men han er nok den bedste underviser, jeg nogensinde har haft. Jeg tog bl.a. til office hours hos ham, hvor der var mulighed for at stille spørgsmål til de dele af pensum, jeg fandt særligt vanskelige. Contracts var spændende, men underviseren var en smule ustruktureret og meget præget af case-fremlæggelser af de studerende, hvilket jeg personligt ikke fandt så givende. Faget var dog stadig brugbart, hvis man gerne vil have et overblik over amerikansk kontrakts- og obligationsret samt kendskab til de vigtigste landmark-cases på området.
unexpected_costs: Bøger var dyrere, end jeg troede. Men tal eventuelt med dine medstuderende og hør, om nogen har onlineadgang, eller lån dem på biblioteket og scan de relevante sider. Og så er det naturligvis dyrt at gå ud og spise, handle ind mv. Trader Joes kan anbefales til basic indkøb.
cost_comparison: Det kan klart anbefales at waive NYU's egen sundhedsforsikring. Jeg købte én fra ISO insurance I stedet og sparede tæt på 10.000 kr. på det. Jeg fik dog aldrig brug for den, så jeg ved ikke, om det havde voldt mig problemer, hvis jeg var blevet indlagt eller lignende. I henhold til visumreglerne gælder der dog visse minimumskrav til, hvad forsikringen skal dække, og dette skulle godkendes af NYU, førend jeg kunne waive deres egen sundhedsforsikring. Derfor gætter jeg ikke på, at det havde været et problem.
activities_available: Jeg meldte mig ind i NYU's run club, hvilket var en fantastisk mulighed for at møde andre NYU-studerende - også folk, der ikke læste jura. Endvidere fik jeg gratis adgang til races i løbet af semesteret og endte bl.a. med at løbe et halvmarathon i Central Park i december. Som studerende får man også gratis adgang til forskellige fitnesscentre, hvor man blot checker ind med sit NYU ID-kort.
activities_recommended: NYU Run Club
weekend_recommendations: Man får gratis adgang til en række af museer, som virkelig er værd at besøge. Det gælder fx MoMa, the MET og Whitney. Derudover kan man tage et par timer upstate med toget, hvis man gerne vil hike. I Beacon ligger et smukt kunstmuseum, som hedder Dia. Vi var også en forlænget weekend i Washington D.C., hvilket kan anbefales. Gennem NYU får man også rabat på biografbilletter.
culture_adjustment: Det var nemt at falde til, fordi folk generelt var virkelig åbne og indstillede på at møde nye mennesker. New York er en svingdørsby, hvor der bor mennesker fra hele verden, og folk er derfor vant til at socialisere meget. Derudover er fællesskabet blandt danskere generelt stærkt, og det kan eksempelvis være værd at tjekke diverse Facebook-grupper ud. Sømandskirken i Brooklyn holder endvidere et årligt julemarked og andre events.
socializing_tips: Deltag i diverse sociale foreninger afhængig af personlige interesser. For mit vedkommende var det løbeklubben.
cultural_challenges: Jeg skulle vænne mig til, at amerikanere er så åbne og snakkesalige i forhold til danskere. Men det er jo kun skønt, når man kommer til en ny by og gerne vil møde nye mennesker. Derudover var det hårdt at blive konfronteret med byens mange hjemløse og fattige mennesker. Den sociale ulighed er enorm, og på dén front er det en virkelig kontrastfyldt by, fordi der på den ene side ligger nogle af verdens dyreste ejendomme, samtidig med at mange mennesker ikke har midler til de mest basale fornødenheder. I starten var det hårdt at vænne sig til, at man ikke kan gøre noget for at hjælpe, og at man bare må passere folk uden at kigge for meget på alle de skøre mennesker.
culture_appreciated: At folk generelt var virkelig åbne og gæstfri.
top3_advice: Fokusér på at få nogle venner for livet frem for at boge den for meget - det er begrænset, hvad amerikansk ret kan bruges til derhjemme, og det vigtigste, du kan tage med rent fagligt, er øgede sprogkundskaber. Deltag aktivt i introugerne i august, hvis du skal afsted i efterårssemesteret. Alle de nye LL.M.-studerende er der med samme formål som dig, og folk er meget åbne for at få nye venner. Gør brug af alle de tilbud og hjælpefunktioner, NYU har, hvis du er i tvivl om noget
other_useful_info: N/A
most_rewarding: Alle de fantastiske mennesker, jeg har mødt, og at få lov til at bo i verdens mest ikoniske storby!
greatest_challenge: Det var en smule vanskeligt at falde til de første 14 dage, fordi der foregik så meget både fagligt og socialt. Men disse uger lægger også grundstenene for resten af opholdet, fordi du møder de mennesker, du kommer til at bruge de næste fire måneder med, så det er klart værd at investere i, selvom éns sociale batterier bliver brugt op.

crucial_aspects: I knew I did not want to go on exchange if it meant great compromises to my academic furthering. I chose to study abroad at NYU because this would let me see and live in the great city of New York while studying at a university with high academic standards when it came to mathematics.
info_ease: As a private university, NYU was great at providing personal assistance when one did not know what to do and where to find the necessary information.
arrival_assistance: As mentioned above, NYU was great at providing personal assistance. They almost always returned calls and e-mails immediately.
arrival_comments: This is not to say that it was easy to sign up for courses or knowing exactly what to do when if you had trouble understanding the VISA process, but the service provided by NYU in connection hereto was on another level.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was ofcourse quite complicated to apply for a visa, get the right vaccinations (or documents saying that you did not need them) and so on. No amount of help changes this.
registration_help: NYU was really helpful and personalized help was almost always available.
registration_success: I took all the courses that I wanted to take.
registration_advice: Write your professors! This is apparently common practice in the US.
course_level: The general level seemed to be lower at NYU (i.e. the easy courses were really easy), but one was able to take courses as difficult or even more difficult than at UCPH. I also did a research project at NYU, and I think that my supervisor allocated more time to helping me with this than would be expected in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: The reading was more extensive. Even in the easy courses, the material was greater than in Denmark. It took a little while to get used to reading more and learning less.
courses_enrolled: Probability Theory II Machine Learning Independent Study
recommended_courses: Do a research project/independent study if you can! Also, the one course I took at the Data Science master (Machine Learning) was not quite at the standards expected at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: None I think.
cost_comparison: Food is super expensive in New York. Shop at local food stands if available.
activities_available: I'm not sure. I don't think many master's students pursued many non-academic opportunities at NYU.
activities_recommended: Go see New York I guess.
weekend_recommendations: Aside from all the things to see in New York, I highly recommend taking a trip to Washington D.C.
culture_adjustment: This was not that difficult. Americans are very friendly and open-minded.
cultural_challenges: To be honest, it is way easier to be a stranger in the U.S. compared to Denmark. People a friendly and helpful.
culture_appreciated: The fact that Americans are so open-minded.
top3_advice: Start the process well in advance (most important are the language tests and the visa application). Apply for housing through Bikubenfonden (at the Academic Guest House in New York). Write your professors.
other_useful_info: If you are under 26, you can book quite nice tickets to New York through the SAS Young program.
most_rewarding: Learning new mathematics.
greatest_challenge: Learning new mathematics.

crucial_aspects: I wanted a place that had the same level of education as UCPH but that also had a very different culture that I could explore.
info_ease: The really necessary information is very available, but some other information that is nice to know is not that easy find and which you will have to discover yourself.
arrival_assistance: Very little. You pretty much have to get situated yourself. There are some mails that will tell you what you need to do, but even they can be a bit vague at times.
arrival_comments: The orientation is good for meeting other exchange students but the local students that are showing you around don't always know what they are supposed to do or might just leave halfway through. You, therefore, don't get a lot of useful information through the orientation.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You need to get waivers for the pre requisites for courses. You do this by filling out a form that they send you and then they will get back to you if they believe you to have the needed background knowledge for the courses you want to take. There are three rounds of this that you can do and only one of them is before registration starts. It is therefore good to try to do that one as well as possible so that you don't risk some of your courses filling up.
registration_help: Very little. They give you the general approach but then it is up to you and you having to be good at pursuing them, because they can be tremendously slow at getting back to you. So don't be afraid of writing them to push them to get through the forms.
registration_success: One of the classes I wanted got cancelled, but I was able to register for all the other ones.
registration_advice: Start preparing early so you are ready for the first round of forms to get waivers so that your classes don't fill up.
course_level: The Bachelor's courses are slightly easier than what you would expect at UCPH while the Master's courses would fit as fairly difficult third year Bachelor's courses.
teaching_comparison: It is quite different. The classes are much smaller and I never spent any time in a lecture hall. Recitations are also just more lectures in a sense. Also pretty much everything counts towards your final grade and there are know practice problems that you will get that are just meant to help you improve.
courses_enrolled: Computational Physics General Relativity Classical and Quantum Mechanics
recommended_courses: I especially recommend GR and CQM they had very good teachers and I learned a lot. Though if you don't study physics or something related they are probably not for you.
unexpected_costs: Groceries are very expensive as is the meal plan that they require you to get if you live in university housing. Housing is also incredibly expensive though I did end up getting offered one of the more expensive packages. Also things like housing and the meal plan have to be paid all at once before the semester or in installments throughout the semester, but if you do it in installements then there is added interest.
cost_comparison: Consumer goods are much cheaper in America, however, pretty much everything you need in your daily life is more expensive here. Especially food and housing.
activities_available: Pretty much anything you could want. Look at NYU Engage for a list of all of the clubs.
activities_recommended: The NYU Run Club is very good. It is both very social and you get to do some activities with them if you want.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city. There is much to do and many cool places if you just go looking for them. There are also many great museums like the Met or MoMA.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. NYU is very strict with there rules and some of the rules are very vague. This is the thing to be most on the lookout for since you can easily find yourself in a situation where you have broken a rule completely unaware that you are doing so.
socializing_tips: That is easy to do in New York. Americans are very open to talking so if you just talk back then it's no problem. The clubs are also a great opportunity to meet new local students.
cultural_challenges: Again the very strict rule following. There is very little sense of looking at people like individuals and taking into account that they are from a different country and culture. It can therefore sometimes feel like an unwelcoming place because they can be very accusatory at times for the slightest violation of a rule that is not communicated.
culture_appreciated: How much is going on in the city. There is always something to do or see if you just go looking for it. And there are almost always someone to go do it or see it with.
top3_advice: Join a club. It is a great way of socializing and meeting new friends especially among local students. Say yes to everything. Try to do as much as possible. Especially in the beginning so that you will meet new people and see new things at a time where you don't know anyone in the city. Don't only focus on academics. Give yourself some space to also enjoy that you are in New York and that you are able to go see the Met or walk by the Hudson anytime you want.
other_useful_info: Practically it's all about being prepared and early so that everything goes a smoothly as possible. The American systems can be difficult at times so it helps if you are prepared. Socially you've just got to say yes to as many new experiences as possible. These are the things that you will really appreciate about your trip when you are done.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people. It has been very rewarding meeting both exchange and local students. Delving into different cultures and seeing how life goes on in another country by talking with people from that country is extremely interesting and rewarding.
greatest_challenge: The first month can feel very long. It takes a while getting settled in. Also because UCPH sends so few people to NYU you will most likely not know anyone here. It therefore take a bit before you get yourself some new friends that you can properly do things with. However, after that first month things really heat up and you start getting the most out of your stay.
