crucial_aspects: I had already gone on exchange in my 5th semester and I originally wanted to go to Australia. Due to Corona it was not possible so I chose to go to England instead with my friend. We chose Newcastle because it was not a common place for people from KU to go to and we wanted a local experience.
overall_comments: Considering I already went on exchange once, I did not have expectations other than doing a different semester in the UK and to travel around. If I had been alone or this had been my first exchange, it would not have met my expectations at all.
info_ease: It was definitely a challenge. Since Newcastle had not exchanged any students with Copenhagen since 2017 every piece of information we could find were outdated. Furthermore, Newcastle was not set up for the online mobility platform that KU was, so it was quite difficult to gather the documents needed to apply.
arrival_assistance: We hardly did not receive any information. As Newcastle does quite a lot of exchange with Chinese and american students, they had had a information week a couple of weeks before we got there. Since we came right before school started everything had already happened. The staff at the school were very helpful, although we had to seek all the information out we needed ourselves.
arrival_comments: In contrast to the institution I visited my 5th semester, Newcastle had not planned anything that was of help to me and my friend.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Considering I already went on exchange once, I did not have expectations other than doing a different semester in the UK and to travel around. If I had been alone or this had been my first exchange, it would not have met my expectations at all.
registration_process: It was quite easy and online.
registration_help: We had to look at the student web page for exam information. We chose in terms of what exams were the easiest to pass.
registration_success: 100% succesfull.
registration_advice: Choose modules that have the easier exams, such as essays etc. This will make the exchange so much better so that you do not have to sit in the library your last month to memorize the entire class.
academics_comments: Considering I already went on exchange once, I did not have expectations other than doing a different semester in the UK and to travel around. If I had been alone or this had been my first exchange, it would not have met my expectations at all.
course_level: We had both a masters class (4th year) and a freshers class (1st year). The levels of difficulties were different to the british students but to us it was almost the same, because out awareness of the British legal system was less of that of the British students. It was a good academic level overall.
teaching_comparison: Much more listening and taking notes, which I quite like. Hardly any presentations or assignments during the semester. We only had one or two things we needed to attend and do doing the semester which made traveling and free planning a lot easier.
courses_enrolled: Legal Institutions and Methods, Law and Literature and Foundations of Business and Commercial law.
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of the above classes. I would recommend Legal institutions and Methods because of the introduction to the British legal system overall. I learned a lot of the country that I was doing an exchange in. The two other courses were also good and did not require a lot of work doing the semester. Furthermore the examination in the two latter courses were 100% essay which made the semester easier to pass.
unexpected_costs: It was quite expensive to travel with train which we did a lot to see the country and area we lived in.
cost_comparison: Cost of living is cheaper than in CPH.
activities_available: Clubs, sport clubs and academic opportunities.
activities_recommended: Since we had already had one exchange experience where we attended much of the School activities this exchange for us was more about traveling and going out on the weekends.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely go about and see the areas around Newcastle. Travel to Scotland and drive around. Go to football games in St. James park.
culture_adjustment: Easy. The Geordies are friendly people, although the are quite different from Danish people in regards to how the dress.
socializing_tips: Go out and talk to people at bars and clubs. It is very easy to meet people in Newcastle.
cultural_challenges: The English are not cold when they go out which means that the do not wear jackets to the club. This means that there is not wardrobe at the clubs and we were running freezing most of the time we went out.
culture_appreciated: The nightlife and the football life of Newcastle.
top3_advice: Do not go unless you are doing an exchange with a friend. I would not recommend going to Newcastle if it is your first exchange because you are on your own in regards to socializing etc.
other_useful_info: We got our acceptance letter so late that we almost cancelled the exchange. You got to have a lot of patience if you want to go to Newcastle.
most_rewarding: Traveling around the UK and meeting a lot of locals that you would not meet in cities such as London.
greatest_challenge: That we were on our own in terms of what we wanted to do with the exchange. It was challenging at first but turned out that the freedom of not getting much information and help meant that we could go about as we wanted to in terms of planning our weeks in Newcastle.
other_comments: Overall it was a great experience, but I would not recommend it unless you have already previously done and exchange or if you don't know anyone at the institution.

crucial_aspects: That I could get classes taught in English
info_ease: It was easy. My receiving university had a informative homepage and people
arrival_assistance: Information about the university and classes that helped me to know my way around and which modules to choose
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: They have their own online homepage for exchange students where it is listed the steps you have to go through to apply. I had to fill out personal information and upload the acceptance letter to go abroad from University of Copenhagen. Thereafter I had to write an essay about why I wanted to go on exchange and why I wanted to go to Newcastle. When they approved me I had to read some information and check that I had read and understood/accepted the things and then i received information on how to proper registrate at their university and make my own account to be in their system. Everything was quite simple and easy to do and it did not take to long.
registration_help: The homepage had help in itself and I could e-mail several different people depending on what I needed help with and if it was the wrong one they would forward the e-mail. It was also possible to call them if urgent, but I didn´t have the need to do that
registration_success: Very successful. It was an easy process
registration_advice: Just follow the steps shown and do it within the timeframe
course_level: It is hard to compare excactly since it was a different law system and a different way to learn law, but in general the level was more or less the same though it took some time to get used to the way the classes are tought but the content wasn´t to complicated.
teaching_comparison: There was a lot more lectures than seminars so a lot more one-way learning rather than the seminars we are used to. Also there was no group work to prepare, you did most of the preparing by your self and talked about at the seminars. There was also some selfstudying to do. You had to read some texts but you could often chose what to read yourself since it is more based on theories and cases so you just need to find something that covers all of it and the teachers do give you a reading list to chose from. Every class was also only one hour so I did not have as many classes as at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Employment Law Law and Literature Law and Gender
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed employment law and find it very interesting especially because it gives a good perspective on the employment laws in the UK and I was able to compare it to what I knew from back home and see how different it is. Law and gender was a very interesting and different module to have that gave several tools and perspectives on this area. Law and literature was a subject I would recommend but it can be a bit bored if you don´t have anyone you know who takes the same module. It is a bit more fun if you have someone to take it with.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: The train tickets varied a lot in price and could be a bit expensive at times
activities_available: Everything and if you really couldn´t find anything in your interest you could start a new society/club
activities_recommended: I did zumba with a few people I had meet which was really fun and a fun workout along with some socials
weekend_recommendations: Walk around in the city and get to know it or travel to bigger cities. Newcastle is pretty nice centered so it is possible to take the train to a lot of places like Edinburgh, London, York and so on and be there within two/two and half hours
culture_adjustment: Easy, the local culture is quite similar though there are differences that are interesting to try and hear about
socializing_tips: Say yes to everything you can in the beginning and sign up for a society or two, and don´t be scarred to walk over and say hi to new people. The changes are that they are just as interested in meeting you and other new people as you yourself are
cultural_challenges: I did not really find any cultural differences challenging
culture_appreciated: I loved how open and kind everyone was, They were always ready to help
top3_advice: Look and apply for accomodation in good time before you leave for exchange, join a society or a club and keep an open mind and remember to have fun
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: That I was able to live on my own in another country and the people I met
greatest_challenge: To fully understand how the city and country worked in the beginning and to adjust to the teaching methods

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to experience university life in England, since it's kind of similar to USA. There's a lot more focus on the activities outside of just school which I really liked. It gave you a good opportunity as an exchange student to meet a lot of new people in different settings.
overall_comments: I loved everything about the exchange, the only detractors are actually before I left Denmark because the time up until was quite stressful. There were a lot of deadlines all the time and it was also really hard to find accommodation in Newcastle.
info_ease: Newcastle University made it quite easy, but it just takes a lot of time to research it all because there are a lot of things you need to remember before you leave from home.
arrival_assistance: Newcastle University was so helpful and I felt so comfortable with them from the beginning. They made it very clear that if I had any issues or questions they were always available, so I really appreciated that. My contact person for the exchange, Emilia, was so helpful and welcoming. I was also given a mentor from year 3 and a buddy group with other international students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I loved everything about the exchange, the only detractors are actually before I left Denmark because the time up until was quite stressful. There were a lot of deadlines all the time and it was also really hard to find accommodation in Newcastle.
registration_process: I registered for courses online when I applied for Newcastle University, but when I arrived at my host institution there were a lot more choices available to me, which was a really nice surprise. You just had to send an email to the office confirming your choice of courses.
registration_help: My contact person Emilia gave us some good advice on which courses she would recommend and then we had 2 weeks to change our minds again if we wanted to.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wished for.
registration_advice: Don't worry if none of the courses you have chosen the first time seem interesting to you. A lot more will probably become available when you arrive at the university.
academics_comments: I loved everything about the exchange, the only detractors are actually before I left Denmark because the time up until was quite stressful. There were a lot of deadlines all the time and it was also really hard to find accommodation in Newcastle.
course_level: One of my courses was with the stage 2 students and the rest were with stage 3 students. But I didn't really feel any difference in the complexity of the courses.
teaching_comparison: I felt like I learned a lot more even though I had less classes. Probably because it was so intense and compact when you were in class, but then you also knew it would be over quickly so it was easier to focus completely throughout the lectures and seminars.
courses_enrolled: Criminal Law Law and Gender Law and Literature
unexpected_costs: Its expensive if you want to take the train to another city like Edinburgh or London, so book ahead of time to get the best prize.
cost_comparison: In general I would say that eating out was less expensive than in Denmark.
activities_available: Every activity you could dream of was available through the host institution. In the beginning of the semester they have a social fare were many of the activities have a booth so you can get a feel of the many possibilities.
activities_recommended: I was a part of the 20 minutes society. It was really fun and different because once a week you would get a text at some point saying that you have 20 minutes to get to a random address which could be anything from a bar to an activity.
weekend_recommendations: ESN has many great tours during the weekends, so sign up for some of them so you get to know more people and explore the country.
culture_adjustment: I feel like it was quite easy since their wasn't a huge culture difference between England and Denmark. Also the English people from the north are known to be very welcoming and friendly which I really feel like they lived up to.
socializing_tips: I think its easier to socialize with local students on an exchange in an English speaking country because there is no language barrier. My advice would be to sign up for some of the activities so you have something in common to start the conversation. Or just try to sit next to someone in class and introduce yourself, the rest will follow.
cultural_challenges: Nothing that comes to mind.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness.
top3_advice: Be open and put yourself out there. The first few days are hard, but it will get easier once you have established some friendships. Time flies faster than you think, so get the most out of every weekend.
other_useful_info: Make sure to sign up for the ESN Facebook group and WhatsApp group chat so you don't miss out on any of the events from the beginning. They usually host a welcome party for all international students which is a great way to meet new people.
most_rewarding: I feel like I learned a lot about myself and have become more confident in myself and when I meet new people.
greatest_challenge: Definitely the first welcome meeting because you feel so alone and haven't met anyone yet. But my advice would be to just find someone in the crowd and go up and sit next to them and start a conversation. When you have overcome that the first time it will be much easier the second time.

Also be aware that they have a ton of sports and creative courses, even though you can't get ETCS points for these, look into them and register for them at the same time as the rest of your classes, as most of these are very popular and will fill up quickly and before you come to campus. crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an English-speaking country, and I've never been in the United States, so it seemed like the obvious destination. US culture has a big impact and is generally the leader in many aspects of our world. Additionally, as an economics student US economy is interesting since it's the biggest economy in the world. Lastly, I wanted to go to a state/city where I could get the real college experience and be close to some of the “must see” cities since I wanted to travel. NC State/Raleigh is indeed such place.
overall_comments: It was unbelievable! NC State's facilities are very good. The university literally offers everything in terms of clubs, trips etc. The weather is very good. The southern hospitably is indeed a thing and something you must experience. It's impossible to list everything but the experience overall contained everything. Travelling, new friends, day trips, frat parties, sports games (football, soccer, basketball, volleyball, wrestling etc.) and much more. And of course, classes! My classes were interesting, but the academic level isn't a high as back at University of Copenhagen.
info_ease: Very easy. The university is very good a sending e-mail's upon arrival and making check-list for you. They are also good at answering questions through e-mail's if you have any. There is generally a lot of information on NC State's website in terms of what to do upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: Because of Covid-19 we had online intro days where they welcomed all the students and assisted with what to do. This was very useful even though it probably would be better if it was physical and under normal circumstances.
arrival_comments: The assistance and orientation upon arrival was very good and easy to understand and follow. The orientation after I arrived was good given the circumstance. But not matter what, an online format is just not as good. But NC State did a good job and that's why I give it 5/5.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was unbelievable! NC State's facilities are very good. The university literally offers everything in terms of clubs, trips etc. The weather is very good. The southern hospitably is indeed a thing and something you must experience. It's impossible to list everything but the experience overall contained everything. Travelling, new friends, day trips, frat parties, sports games (football, soccer, basketball, volleyball, wrestling etc.) and much more. And of course, classes! My classes were interesting, but the academic level isn't a high as back at University of Copenhagen.
registration_process: You basically find the courses you want in the course catalogue and then you make a prioritized list. You then later find out whether you got a spot in the class.
registration_help: You can e-mail and ask all the questions you may have. You can also e-mail the professor/instructor if you have any course specific questions.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I registered for. If you don't, then don't worry. The first two weeks or so you can add and drop classes (very normal in US). If the class you want is full, you can always talk to the professor, and they will most likely give you a spot (what I heard from other exchange students). The most important part is that you can get preapproval (“forhåndsgodkendelse”) for the classes you attend abroad.
registration_advice: Make sure to get preapproval from UCPH. Don't worry too much if you don't get a class. Everybody is basically adding and dropping classes the first weeks so you will find out when you arrive.
academics_comments: It was unbelievable! NC State's facilities are very good. The university literally offers everything in terms of clubs, trips etc. The weather is very good. The southern hospitably is indeed a thing and something you must experience. It's impossible to list everything but the experience overall contained everything. Travelling, new friends, day trips, frat parties, sports games (football, soccer, basketball, volleyball, wrestling etc.) and much more. And of course, classes! My classes were interesting, but the academic level isn't a high as back at University of Copenhagen.
course_level: I'm a master student at UCPH but took only BA courses at NC State. This obviously made the workload and academic level lower since the graduate courses are more specialized and thus the workload is bigger. However, this suited me fine since my choice of going on exchange was more about speaking English, experiencing another culture, traveling etc. This was for me more important than the academics.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at NC State is more like gymnasium in Denmark. The classes are small, more interaction between the professor and students, more exams, homework and more. I liked that because the teaching style at UCPH can sometimes be monotonous since there is not a lot of interaction and the economics exams at UCPH are (mostly) one shot. In US you have midterms, homework, and final exams. This make it less stressful, and the workload is spread out through the whole semester.
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled in: EC 431 Labor Economics EC 449 International Finance ARE 336 Introduction to Resource and Environmental Economics BUS 320 Financial Management
recommended_courses: I would recommend EC 431 Labor Economics. Professor Melinda Morrill is very good and engaged. She makes sure to interact with the students and was very welcoming. The class was also very interesting and is a huge field within economics. The course EC 449 International Finance was also interesting and specially to have an American view on the world economy. The teacher was good at explaining and had a clear structure.
unexpected_costs: I didn't have any unexpected costs but there are costs when getting your VISA that I didn't expect. But overall, the costs, that I had, was expected. Because of Covid-19 local transportation in Raleigh was free.
cost_comparison: Communication is expensive in US. I would recommend Mint Mobile. You can get 3 months for 45 dollars, and you get 4 GB data + unlimited talk and text. That's the cheapest option that I knew of, and I would say that it was enough for my needs since you can get Wi-Fi most places if you need more data. Vegetables are expensive compared to Denmark.
activities_available: The gym offers a lot of different classes. And offers day trips and activities that you can sign up to.
activities_recommended: I would recommend the yoga classes. The instructors were very good, and you just signed up through their app. Go bouldering in the gym. You can rent shoes in the gym. I would also recommend the social activities through the gym. I standup paddled and went to the day trip at Stone Mountain. This was a good way to meet other Americans and see some of the beautiful nature in US. In general – use the facilities in the gym. You can go swimming, spinning, sauna, table tennis, squash, weightlifting and much more. You can rent almost anything you need through the gym – rackets, towels, t-shirts, basketball, football etc.
weekend_recommendations: Go see the big cities on the east coast - New York City, Boston, Philadelphia, Washington DC, and Miami. Raleigh has a good airport and train station. Rent a car and go for a road trip with other exchange students. Museums are free in Raleigh - go see them. Run the City of Oaks Marathon. Reedy Creek Trail is very good for a run/walk. Go see Carolina Hurricanes. Go see Durham Bulls. Go downtown and have a beer or two. Go to a pub and see real football (Americans somehow call it soccer).
culture_adjustment: Very easy. US is not that different to Denmark. Americans are also very hospital, so you quickly feel welcome. Just be openminded and then you will adjust to the local culture quickly.
socializing_tips: Staying at Alexander Hall made it easier for me since I socialized with my roommate and his brother a lot. But joining an intramural team and/or club will make it easier. Again, Americans are easy to talk with once you open and basically just talk.
cultural_challenges: Not anything particularly. Everything is bigger!
culture_appreciated: Hospitality! Believe me. Once you been North and then go back to the South you will understand. In the South it's rude to not hold the door for someone. And once you get used to it you will also start finding it very rude when other people don't do it.
top3_advice: 1. It will be the time of your life! It will go fast so enjoy it as much as possible. You will be nervous and excited which is a part of it. But once you get there and everything is sorted out you will have a very good time. Don't be too serious about the academics. 2. Be openminded and just talk. That's the way to socialize, meet other people, and become better at English. 3. Make sure to talk and socialize with locals. It can be very easy to just hang out and talk with exchange students. But try to talk and socialize with Americans as well.
other_useful_info: Remember to bring an adapter and an extension cord. Flip flops for the shower. Googles for swimming. Backpack for weekend trips. Get your insurance from Denmark (much cheaper than the one the university offers). Be patient with all the paperwork – it's worth it in the end!
most_rewarding: Becoming more comfortable speaking English and experiencing another culture. You expand your horizon and experience an unbelievable country in terms of the nature, people, history, and culture.
greatest_challenge: For me it was being away from my girlfriend during the whole stay (because of Covid-19 she couldn't come visit me) and family and friends.
other_comments: Just do it! You may have questions, doubts and so on but once you go you will have the time of your life. I can highly recommend NC State. Very welcoming atmosphere, real college experience, unbelievable physical and educational facilities, Southern state, good weather, close to beautiful nature, close to mayor cities and much more. Go WolfPack!

arrival_assistance: They greeted me and drove me to my accommodation. The day after there was a ice-cream day, where you could say "hello" to the fellow exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You apply with your grades. The grades is the decider on wether you get a spot or not. After you receive a spot there is some work to do with the application process, but UCPH have a intuitive formula you use.
registration_help: You get a study abroad coordinator you can write to if you are in doubt about anything. Other than that there will be a meeting I would recommend to attend where most of the stuff about pre arrival is explained.
registration_success: I didn't get all my classes I applied for.
registration_advice: I would recommend to apply for credits to multiply courses (more than you want to take) at your home University so there is something you can choose between in case of you don't get the classes you want. (I didn't do it and got sorted it out anyway, but it is good to have applied for more classes than you intend to take.)
course_level: The level was easier than expected. The amount of math was unveiling compared to UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The style was more interactive oral discussion with the students and professor.
courses_enrolled: Marketing Methods International Financial Management Money, Financial Markets, and the Economy Introduction to Resource and Environmental Economics
recommended_courses: I would recommend the course International Financial Management which build upon financial decision making but with a more international approach, and the professor was really fun and good.
unexpected_costs: - I had to apply and pay for Canadian visum even though I only had lay-over in Toronto for 2 hours. - Sheets - Blanket
cost_comparison: Groceries was more expensive than expected.
activities_available: There was plenty of clubs available. From football, Rugby, Soccer, Golf, Disc Golf, Bee-club, Computer gaming etc...
activities_recommended: I would recommend to excess the opportunity to play sports you don't play as much in Europe. (Wall-climbing, Pickelball, Basketball, American Football)
weekend_recommendations: Rent a car and see the country-side. Outer banks is also magnificent. I did spent my Spring Break in Miami which was early cheap to fly to, but also an expensive city to life in.
culture_adjustment: It was easy. People are so welcome and out-spoken in the US.
socializing_tips: Go to local bar - Mitches Tavern. Sign up for sports or other clubs of your interest. Speak with your classmates. They will probably try to speak with you :)
culture_appreciated: The open-minded and welcoming attitude I liked a lot. Every time you got off the bus at night the bus driver yelled "Please, stay safe my son".
top3_advice: Sheets Money Money
other_useful_info: Get pay-pall and watch app installed before hand.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding thing was the friendships I got and the experience of have discussion about the subjects with the professor.
greatest_challenge: Missing my friends and family.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to the us.
overall_comments: Without doubt one of the best experiences of my life.
info_ease: NC State were very helpful and easy to get in touch with about any questions - both over phone, mail and whatsapp. There are quite a few online portals to navigate, but it's alright and they don't expect you to understand it anyways, so not a problem.
arrival_assistance: We had orientation with all exchange students for the spring semester the first days, and they we were set free. They helped me find the way to my on campus accommodation after arriving, which was great.
arrival_comments: We could have had some 'follow-up' orientation, also to keep meeting all the exchange students, but it wasn't needed necessarily.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Without doubt one of the best experiences of my life.
registration_process: There a course catalog, with all options available, from where you pick your courses. There's an online portal for applying for courses, but I believe we were sent a google form to fill out and the Study Abroad Office took care of everything for us.
registration_help: The Study Abroad Office are great!
registration_success: I got all my classes.
registration_advice: Take time to look through the available classes, cause there a lot!
academics_comments: Without doubt one of the best experiences of my life.
course_level: I took 9 credit hours, which is the minimum, and it was good. A bit more work than I expected actually, but about the same as home.
teaching_comparison: I think the style of teaching is somewhere between high school and uni back home in DK, and it depends a lot on the professor. Some professors just do lectures, which I prefer, but others like to ask a lot of questions for the students to discuss and answer - so there's a bit of everything. There's not really any way to know the style of the professor besides writing them and asking, so I didn't know anything before.
courses_enrolled: CSC 414 Foundations of Cryptography, CSC 515 Software Security, CSC 574 Computer and Network Security.
recommended_courses: I especially liked the CSC 574 because of the professor Brad Reeves. CSC 414 were very interesting as well, but quite heavy on proofs and math.
unexpected_costs: No big surprises.
cost_comparison: The university health insurance is insanely expensive, so get a good travel insurance from DK - it's way cheaper and then you can get the university insurance waived. On the other hand all public transportation, which is not a lot tbh, is free.
activities_available: I was part of their Sailing Race team, which was awesome! Also I was somewhat part of their Hacking club and I did different Intermural Sports - like beach volley and soccer.
activities_recommended: If you enjoy sailing definitely reach out to the Sailpack! They have practice multiple times a week, you get to travel around and compete against other universities, and you even have access to their boats whenever you want and they're not used. Also, the team has a great energy, the coach is awesome and it's a great way to meet some cool Americans.
weekend_recommendations: Honestly, there's not a lot of touristy stuff to see in Raleigh, but it's not too long of a drive to National Parks, big Cities, the Ocean, the Mountains etc. I actually think Raleigh is very well placed for being on exchange and getting around the east coast.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, it's not that different from DK. However, there's a lot of small differences. The us, and especially the southern states, are very car dependent you'll find. The food is fine, but also very american.
socializing_tips: Reach out to the other exchange students as much as possible! Everyone is there alone and want to make friends, so it's a great way to build a social network. For meeting americans I'd recommend joining clubs and organizations.
cultural_challenges: It's definitely frustrating that the us is so dependent on having a car, but the americans are often nice and drive you around, or you find alternatives with the other exchange students.
culture_appreciated: I love how many resources are put into the clubs and organizations, and how engaged the students are. It creates an awesome campus environment and opens up for a lot of great opportunities and meeting people.
top3_advice: Reach out to the other exchange students as much as possible. Don't do too many credit hours/courses, so you'll have free time. Get a travel insurance from DK instead of the university one.
other_useful_info: The visa applications process is a bit of a headache, but it's alright. Just make sure you don't start too late getting the papers in order.
most_rewarding: I have met some amazing people, both from Europe and USA, that I hope to keep in touch with. It's such a privilege getting the opportunity to go on exchange and it'll change you as a person. You learn new parts of yourself and get a completely new perspective of the world.
greatest_challenge: The feeling of being alone in another country in the beginning is something else that I'd ever experienced before. But reach out and you'll find everyone feels the same.
other_comments: Even though there's a lot of (paper)work going on exchange, especially outside Europe, it's so worth it. Look forward to the time of your life, and I wish you a great stay!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to improve my oral english skills and thus wanted to go to a place where people talk enligsh on a daily basis. Given that my aim was to explore new cultures and try different ways of learning, North Carolina seemed like a good place to go to.
overall_comments: I got to travel a lot. I gained new academic skills and was so lucky to become close friends with my roomie. On the other hand, I would have preferred to go on an exchange sooner, especially given the High School Musical environment that you experience at NC State. I unfortunately did not have the opportunity to go earlier because of Covid-19.
info_ease: It was very easy to find the information. The international office at NC State is very helpfull and answers quickly. They held introductory meetings on Zoom where they provided us with relevant information about what to do before arriving i.e. housing, visa, insurance etc.
arrival_assistance: We had an introductory session where they welcomed us and gave important information. You could always go to them for help.
arrival_comments: Welcoming and helpfull.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I got to travel a lot. I gained new academic skills and was so lucky to become close friends with my roomie. On the other hand, I would have preferred to go on an exchange sooner, especially given the High School Musical environment that you experience at NC State. I unfortunately did not have the opportunity to go earlier because of Covid-19.
registration_process: I filled out a file with the courses that I wanted and then they handled it from there. If you wanted to change or drop a course (which is very common) you just told them to help you or deleted them yourself.
registration_help: I got help from the Poole College of Management on campus.
registration_success: Very successfull. I got the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Reach out for help is you are in doubt. They are more than willing to help.
academics_comments: I got to travel a lot. I gained new academic skills and was so lucky to become close friends with my roomie. On the other hand, I would have preferred to go on an exchange sooner, especially given the High School Musical environment that you experience at NC State. I unfortunately did not have the opportunity to go earlier because of Covid-19.
course_level: I took two doctoral-courses and one graduate course. The levels of the courses are as follows: 100-400 are undergraduate courses, 500-600 are graduate, and 700-899 are doctoral courses. The level of the courses are lower than the level at UCPH. However, the doctoral classes require a bit more time than the graduate courses.
teaching_comparison: There are more class debate, presentations and homeworks compared with UCPH. The courses that I took only had 10-13 people in them so it is a different environment to be in. The style of teaching made it feel more like being back in High School.
courses_enrolled: ECG 590 Special Economic Topics: Health Economics & Policy ECG 707 Topics in Industrial Organization ECG 715 Environmental and Resource Economics
recommended_courses: ECG 590 is a good course in the sense that you learn about the US Health Care System and the subjects in this course are relevant and interesting. It is however only descriptive and not theoretical nor empirical with the exception that you learn a bit about natural experiments / quasi-experimental design through reading the research articles. ECG 707 is a good course with a passionated lecturer! You learn a lot in this course and the papers are interesting to read. The assignments can be a bit tough but you can get help from the professor if you ever get stuck. However, be prepared to do a lot of empirical tasks in different programs (STATA, Python, Matlab etc.) It is a learning-by-doing course as you are not teached how to code. ECG 715 is a heavy theoretical course with no slides and in my opinion they teached us in some of the more boring subjects within the field. I would not recommend this course.
unexpected_costs: Vaccination costs.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than I thought.
activities_available: They have everything.
activities_recommended: Go to the free fitness! It is huge and you can participate in fitness classes etc.
weekend_recommendations: Travel, travel, travel if you have the capacity! The east coast is interesting because the states are so different. Otherwise join the frat parties or invite people to go to the cinemax, get something to eat, grab a beer at Mitchs Tavern on Hillsborough Street or play some volleyball on campus!
culture_adjustment: It was easy, but it was a culture shock. You could not get far without a car, and I really missed cooking. However, the Americans are nice and welcoming!
socializing_tips: Engage in a club, go on dates if you are single, ask to get a lift, ask for help on homeworks, get an American roomie and ask if they wanna hang out.
cultural_challenges: I found it very hard to not be able to come around easily. The Americans do love their cars and I understand why, because they are their only form of transportation and the whole infrastructure is made for driving.
culture_appreciated: They are so welcoming and kind towards you.
top3_advice: 1. Figure out what you want to achieve with the exchange 2. Put on your yes-hat because you only have a limited number of opportunities to experience this 3. Enjoy it and do not stress about school
other_useful_info: Do not be afraid to reach out for help, and try your best in engaging with locals and the other exchange students. Go to the sports events including the tailgates! It is crazy and fun! Also you have to go to the State Fair (A food festival with the weirdest food) It was an experience.
most_rewarding: To travel on the east coast! I am so happy that I got to experience so many states. I would recommend you to go to: - Charleston, SC because of its history and how it looks like today - Blue Ridge Mountains in mid-october because of its beautifull colors and the black bears walking around! - Boston, MA because of its architecture and good food - New York, NY if you have not been there - Washington D.C. if you are into history
greatest_challenge: To not have a car.

crucial_aspects: I was very curious to learn more about the US and the people
info_ease: Most of it was pretty easy, however, some information went a little lost when you got so many emails from NCSU. For example, there was not very clear communication about when to come and when to go home again
arrival_assistance: There were information meetings which were very useful
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You get a login to their page where it is very easy to follow the steps you need to do and you do not have to do everything at once
registration_help: You could write an email to school (or call) and they replied quickly
registration_success: It was difficult to find syllabus but other than that, no problems
registration_advice: Get it done, so you don't stress about it last minute
course_level: Most classes were not very challenging, very outward learning
teaching_comparison: More classroom teaching (not lectures), which I actually really liked
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Resource and Environmental Economics (ARE 336) Financial Management (BUS 320) Personal finance (BUS 225) Game Theory (EC 468) International finance (EC 449)
recommended_courses: Game theory, you can get merit for micro 3, and the teacher (Thayer Morrill) was really good
cost_comparison: Uber was very cheap and I used it a lot
activities_available: you could go to school sports events, which was really fun. The gym was really big and nice, but also very crowded
activities_recommended: The sport events, I preferred tailgates and basket ball games
weekend_recommendations: take some trips and explore e.g. Outer Banks (NC), Washington DC, Charleston etc
culture_adjustment: pretty easy, Americans are very open and chatty
socializing_tips: Join some clubs og stay at the dorms, people are very social there
cultural_challenges: They really like small talking and I was not always in the mood for that

crucial_aspects: A place and a culture I had never experienced before. I have been to USA before, but only north and wanted to try something more southern. It was also crucial to be able to have the classes that interested me and aligned with my studies.
overall_comments: Absolutely loved my stay and would recommend it to anyone. I did not have a bad week and the atmosphere was awesome.
info_ease: Could have been better. Ended up being there before the intro days for exchange students as I wanted to settle in correctly (came Tuesday and intro was Thursday). Because of this "early arrival" I had to pay an additional fee of $50 - nothing that ruins the budget, but could have been avoided with better information. Be aware that school does not start until a week later and do not stress about being there early as American students do not move in until the weekend.
arrival_assistance: Had help from the counter, who showed me my room and were always helpful with whatever info I needed. This includes busses to center of campus etc.
arrival_comments: A lot of different intro dates from different e-mails. I did miss a orientation meeting as I got lost in all the mails. Nothing too serious and was easy to recover the information :)
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Absolutely loved my stay and would recommend it to anyone. I did not have a bad week and the atmosphere was awesome.
registration_process: Wished for some classes I had picked out beforehand. When registration opened I found out I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_help: Good communication with one of the corresponders.
registration_success: Was perfect.
registration_advice: Just make sure you have access to the classes you need for your studies. There are some classes only provided during spring semester and same way around for the fall semester.
academics_comments: Absolutely loved my stay and would recommend it to anyone. I did not have a bad week and the atmosphere was awesome.
course_level: I had three 400 classes, which means last year of their undergrad. One 300 and one 200 online class. I had a finance class, where I did not quite have all the prerequisites for, but was by far my favorite class - I recommend taking classes you just find interesting.
teaching_comparison: At UCPH we are used to having a lecture and in class. At NCSU we only had one in class, which were combinations of lectures and activities.
courses_enrolled: Ressource and environmental economics Game Theory Financial management of corporations Personal finance International finance
recommended_courses: Financial management of corporations was my favorite course. Professor was nice and I really enjoyed the overall material in the class.
unexpected_costs: Extra housing fees, extra payment fees (credit card fees). Early check in fee, because miscommunication. Student Visa and especially fees applying for this. Immunizations record and fees within this - I did not encounter having to get extra vaccinations, but this occurred to multiple of my friend. Health insurance can become expensive, I was fortunate enough it was not for me.
cost_comparison: Housing fees and visa was more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: A lot of clubs and so on was available - you could even start your own if you wanted to. We were presented to a website with all of them upon arrival.
activities_recommended: Join a sports team to socialize with Americans, as this can be a little harder to do otherwise.
weekend_recommendations: Mountains and beach areas. Renting a car it is beneficial to know someone 25 y/o or more, as it is cheaper.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy.
socializing_tips: Just don't be shy and join the conversation.
cultural_challenges: Adjusting to the everyday food takes some time. Healthy food can be a bit more expensive/not accessible.
culture_appreciated: The kindness of Americans.
top3_advice: 1) Move to a dorm 2) Join as many social events as possible 3) Make friends in all of your classes
other_useful_info: Don't be shy to use the facilities as these are open to everyone.
most_rewarding: Friends and academics. Still talk to multiple other exchange students from different countries, and even visited each other.
greatest_challenge: Adapting to cultural differences.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience the American collage life. Honestly to see, if it was like the movies (it was!).
info_ease: NCSU had a great website for incoming exchange studens. But you still have to research a lot of things yourself before arrival - such as the Visa process. I would also recommend reading all of the information on the website and in e-mails as early as possible. A lot of stuff before arrival, for instance housing application, has due dates.
arrival_assistance: There was a couple of days with orientation, where we got a lot of information. You could also always talk to a study abroad coordinator - they were very helpful. In general NCSU has a ton of different organizations and offices who are there to help you in any given situation.
arrival_comments: It was a lot of information in just 2 days while also meeting all of the other exchange studens. Even though it was overwhelming, I recommend you to talk to as many of the other studens as possible and get some contact informations. The 2 days of orientation was the only time, where all of the exchange studens were together (mandatory).
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was contained personal questions (contact informations etc.), class requests, and financial statement.
registration_help: At the application proces you could reach out the KU.
registration_success: For me this process was long and messy. You have to take half of your credits within one field for visa purposes. Therefore it was a puzzle to find classes that did not overlap and also could be accepted by KU. However, the study abroad office at NCSU was very helpful. I was also waitlisted on a couple of classes, but ended up getting most of them.
registration_advice: Look at classes and send a request (forhåndsgodkendelse) to KU as soon as possible. Be open to other classes - you might not get all the classes you wanted.
course_level: I took some 200-400 level classes within my mayor. The 400 level classes were of course harder, but it was alright. I also took a 100 level class in biology, which was too easy.
teaching_comparison: The final exam did not count a lot towards the final grade. Instead you get grated on a lot of assignments, smaller exams, tests, and participation throughout the semester.
courses_enrolled: BIT 473 (protein interactions). BIO 240 + BIO 242 (human anatomy and physiology + lab). BIO 105 + BIO 106 (Modern biology + lab). HESA 215 (advanced beginning swimming).
recommended_courses: BIT 473 (protein interactions) was a really interesting course. It was a very small class. The professor was great but also hard. I learned a lot in the class, but it was also time consuming. I would say it was a good course for biochem students. BIO 240 + BIO 242 (human anatomy and physiology + lab) was also a really great course. The professor was so sweet and explained things very well.
unexpected_costs: Groceries were more expensive than I expected. If you want to travel during Thanksgiving, I recommend booking flights as early as possible, since they become quite expensive.
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than I expected. Lyft and Uber was less expensive in Raleigh compared to many other cities in the US (usually $10-30).
activities_available: There are 100s of clubs. If you are interested just reach out to the club. You can always just try it.
activities_recommended: I was in a hiking club, which was very fun and a great way to see other places outside of Raleigh. However, I did not use the clubs that much. Instead I went to a lot of different events the university was hosting. NCSU has a bunch of different instagram account that post about different events. It was a great way to do something fun in between classes (and there are almost always free stuff :)). I also went to a lot of fitness classes at the gym - they have all from cycling and straight training to dance and yoga.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely go to sport events. The atmosphere is so good, and it is really fun to experience university sports. To be honest the city of Raleigh is not that exiting. However, they have a lot of cute events (especially in December), so I would recommend that you look fore those events on social media. Raleigh also have some interesting museums that are all free. I would also recommend seeing Duke's botanical garden.
culture_adjustment: I knew a lot about american culture before hand, so it was not that big of a culture shock for me. American people are very nice and helpfull, so if you have problems adjusting, you can always talk to someone.
socializing_tips: I lived with 3 americans which was a great opportunity. I also only talked to americans in my classes. They are mostly very open and welcoming. I would recommend to just go talk to people in you classes even though it might seem intimidating. Clubs are also a great way to meat local students, but I didn't use that as much.
cultural_challenges: You have to be more carefull walking around by night. I never experienced anything uncomfortable, but it is highly recommended that you are more aware and don't walk alone especially when dark outside.
culture_appreciated: The hospitality of American people. They are so sweet and welcoming, and if you are open and interested about their life, they will for sure also be nice to you. The school system is quite different from what I was used to at KU. However I liked, that the work was more spread out trough out the semester. That what finals week were less stressful.
top3_advice: - Be ready to socialize with a lot of new people in the beginning. This is where you meet all of the other exchange students. - Focus on having fun and say YES: ask other exchange students is they want to go to an event (they mostly does, because they are here for the same reason as you). Say yes, when people ask you (to a certain extent of cause). - Use NSCU many facilities. The gym and libraries are great! They also have a lot of facilities if you need help with something or need to talk to someone.
other_useful_info: NA
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of sweet people - both other exchange students and americans.
greatest_challenge: Understanding the rules in American football :)

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne have en klassiske amerikansk college-oplevelse, som man kender det fra film. Samtidig skulle jeg kunne få fag nok, så det gav mening at tage afsted.
info_ease: Det kunne godt have været bedre. De første par dage på NC state fungerede som introdage, hvor udveklsingskoordinatorerne forklarede om alt det praktiske på skolen og generelt. Jeg synes dog, at information om bolig var lidt sparsom. Jeg skrev meget frem og tilbage, for at finde hvornår jeg kunne flytte ind osv.
arrival_assistance: Første aften blev der afholdt et is-arrangement for alle udvekslingsstuderende, hvor der blev forklaret hvad der skulle foregå i introdagene.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Før man ankommer, kan man skrive frem og tilbage til NC state's udvekslingsudvalg om tilmelding til fag/hold osv. Når man så er ankommet, kan man tilmelde sig til fag via mypack. Min oplevelse er, at det er nemmere at få fag som udvekslingsstuderende.
registration_help: Jeg skrev frem og tilbage med udvekslingsudvalget på NC State
registration_success: Jeg fik alle fag jeg ønskede
registration_advice: Selvom man er bachelorstuderende, kan man også godt søge graduate fag (500+ level). Det vidste jeg ikke. Det åbner op for, at man kan tage lidt flere (måske også federe) fag end dem på undergrad niveau. På undergrad, kan du få godkendt game theory for mikro III, og professoren er virkelig god. Desuden kan man få Resource and Enviromental Economics og Labor economics godkendt som prioriterede valgfag.
course_level: Mine fag var: Game theory, Labor economics, Resource and enviromental economics, Econometrics II og International finance. Alle var EC-fag og på 400-(4. år) niveau undtagen Envi Econ som var ARE og på 300 niveau.
teaching_comparison: Det fungerer ligesom i gymnasiet med klasseundervisning, hvor professoren underviser fra tavlen og man kan stille spørgsmål. Jeg kan faktisk meget godt lide dette ift. almindelige forelæsninger, som man kender det fra KU. Holdene er også en del mindre.
recommended_courses: Som minimum game theory, der tæller for mikro III. Man kan også vælge introduction to python, som kan tælle som et økonomisk valgfag. Jeg vil dog anbefale, at overveje at tage fag på graduate niveau.
unexpected_costs: Vacciner og visum var ret dyrt. Køb forsikring hjemmefra!
cost_comparison: forvent at brug mange penge på uber/lyft. Det er ret billigt per tur, men det løber op.
activities_available: Der er også et kæmpe fitness center (Carmichael gym) med svømmehal, tennisbaner, golfsimulator osv. osv. osv.
activities_recommended: Tag til så mange NC State football games som muligt. Det er gratis hvis man får biletter gennem lodtrækning, hvilket man for det meste gør. Det er ofte tailgates inden kampene der er mest sjove. Her har alle fraternities sat tælte op med fest, musik og masser af alkohol, på en kæmpe plads ved siden af stadion.
weekend_recommendations: Tag rundtomkring i USA og North Carolina. Bylivet i Raleigh er faktisk ret godt torsdag, fredag og lørdag.
culture_adjustment: Meget nemt. Amerikanere er pisse flinke og imødekommende.
socializing_tips: Sørg for at snakke med dem fra dine classes og dine naboer på campus. På alexander hall holdte vi ofte opvarmning inden vi tog i byen, hvor vi inviterede både amerikanere og de andre udvekslingsstuderende.
culture_appreciated: At folk er så venlige og imødekommende.
top3_advice: 1) Bo på campus 2) Få venner på tværs 3) Oplev så meget af den amerikanske college kultur som muligt.
other_useful_info: Der er masser af ressourcer tilgængelig på NC State man kan benytte sig af.
most_rewarding: Helt klart de venner jeg fik. Vi var en mega god danskergruppe fra KU, CBS og DTU, der lavede en masse ting sammen, som f.eks. at rejse rundt. Det er jeg meget taknemmelig for.
greatest_challenge: At finde ud af alt det der med visum og fag. Generelt bare hele processen var planlægsmæssig hård, især fordi jeg ikke følte vi fik meget information fra KU.
other_comments: Varm anbefaling herfra.

crucial_aspects: I chose the US as I wanted to have a completely new cultural experience. The whole college life is so different from studying in Copenhagen. Of course, it would have still been fun to do an exchange in another European city, but I wouldn’t be that different from the school system I’m already used to. I really liked the idea of living on campus and having a large amount of school engagement.
overall_comments: Some of the most fun I have had in a long time. I met a lot of incredible people right from the beginning and stayed friends with them till the end. Even went traveling multiple times to Miami, New York, New Orleans and Nashville with the other exchange students throughout the semester and at the end of our stay.
info_ease: They send out a lot of information beforehand and the study aboard office was always available to help with any questions. It definitely was confusing, but you always had someone to ask, either employees from the university or fellow students.
arrival_assistance: The school held a two day orientation and social event on the first day, that covert most of the important information, plus it gave you a network of other exchange students so you weren’t alone in figuring out the practical details. The questions I had, I just asked them physically during the orientation.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Some of the most fun I have had in a long time. I met a lot of incredible people right from the beginning and stayed friends with them till the end. Even went traveling multiple times to Miami, New York, New Orleans and Nashville with the other exchange students throughout the semester and at the end of our stay.
registration_process: I was a little hard to figure out their system. They had a very complex university system with lots of different sites and forms. It is the kind of thing that made a lot of sense when you got to know it, but the process till there was frustrating for sure. The study aboard office were very good at sending out emails about what forms you had to submit and where, so as long as you check your email often and trust that it is all going to work it self out they you’ll be fine.
registration_help: The study abord office was very fast to respond on email, so do not hesitate to just ask, that’s what they are there for.
registration_success: You had to register for a lot of options for classes, so you will get some of those. I was a little hard finding classes that were not too beginner level as my danish major did not exist in their school, so I didn’t have the right prequal for some of the classes. One thing I learnt when I got there is that even though you are waitlisted for a class you want you always have the option to just show up to the fist class and ask if you can join, a lot of people will change classes in the first week so there is a big change of you getting the classes you want. I did this for one of my classes where my professor actually just texted the school to put me in the class because she thought it was interesting to have an exchange student with a different perspective.
registration_advice: Read all the emails and trust the process, everyone is trying to help you. And trust me it takes a long time and fustration.
academics_comments: Some of the most fun I have had in a long time. I met a lot of incredible people right from the beginning and stayed friends with them till the end. Even went traveling multiple times to Miami, New York, New Orleans and Nashville with the other exchange students throughout the semester and at the end of our stay.
course_level: I think I had some very interesting classes, and your exchange is a good opportunity to try something different. That being said it is not a very high level compared to the danish university, a lot of the work just consist of remembering the material.
teaching_comparison: The classes have homework, exams during the semester and take attendance so you’ll need to stay engaged throughout the semester. But that also mean that the final exam does not count for everything, and you’ll manage your grade throughout the semester, so it’s not very stressful exam period which is really nice when you are on exchange and have a lot of other things you are doing.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to biological anthropology Introduction to cultural anthropology Introduction to persuasion theory Relational communication
recommended_courses: Relational communication is the best class I have ever taken. It is basically dating 101, but at university. The teacher was the nicest person, and would bake cookie for the class and would use my perspective for a lot of the class discussions.
unexpected_costs: You will spend a lot of money on traveling, so be prepared for that. Of course this is not necessary, but so worth it to see some other places while you are there.
cost_comparison: Meal plans on campus were quite expensive
activities_available: They had all kinds of club and events all the time, you just had to look around, then you would be able to find whatever. The biggest event was football games, where you would meet a couple of hours before outside the stadium and do tailgating, which is basically just drinking in the parking lot. I don’t even like football but everyone went so it was a lot of fun (only in the fall semester)
activities_recommended: They had a free gym on campus 1 min from my housing. The nicest gym I have ever been to. It was so big and had literally everything. Of course, all the normal gym stuff, but then you could also play badminton, tennis, racquet ball, go bouldering, or swimming. Additionally, they had a lot of fitness classes for free, so you could do Pilates, yoga, spinning etc. All the exchange students used to the gym so much as a hang out spot, me and my friends took so many classes, just to try different things and as a fun activity. My favorite was the line dancing class we took ones a week, seriously the most fun.
weekend_recommendations: I went on a lot of trips with my exchange student friends. We went on a round trip to the mountain and Nashville, a weekend trip to New Orleans, fall break in New York, and ended my semester by going with a friend to Miami and Key West in Florida. A lot of people also went to the coast like Outer Banks and Charlston, which looked so nice, but I didn’t have time. It is a bit hard traveling around the places nearby actually because you need a car, so you either have to rent one or get some good American friends. New Orleans was my favorite trip, such a recommendation. Good food, fun nightlife and lots of alligators in the swamp. Stay at Hi Hostel if you want to meet other people.
culture_adjustment: I was pretty easy for me. But I’ve traveled a lot and been on high school exchange in Argentina before, so I’m used to adjusting to new cultures. But the American people are pretty open, so any doubts you can just ask.
socializing_tips: I was somewhat hard to make good American friends for me, as the people in my class were a bit younger than I was. But Americans really like socializing so if you meet someone, don’t be afraid to ask them if they want to hang out and introduce you to some of their friends. Not sure this is the best advice, but I started dating an American ended up spending a lot of time with his friend group as well. So basically, just take the opportunities you have to meet new people. I know a lot of exchange students got American friends if they were involved in clubs or if they had American roommates.
cultural_challenges: I think I’m used to the danish culture of being more nonchalant, so you have to get used to the American way of being overly excited about everything or always be very polite.
culture_appreciated: They are very open, they really do want to talk to you, and think it’s interesting that you are an exchange student
top3_advice: Engage yourself in the experience. Try all the things available while you are there, you can always chill and watch Netflix when you get back home. So whatever people invite you for just say yes. And don’t spend too much time talking to people at home, trust me they will still be your friends when you get back, it is honestly a waste of time, and distances you from the experience you are having.
other_useful_info: Live on-campus and spend time on campus. And save money to travel.
most_rewarding: You gain such a good network very quickly. I met the people I ended up hanging out with everyday during the orientation, and then we just hung out ever since. No one has a local network so everyone is down to just hang out all the time, and even go traveling together with people that you have known for a couple of weeks.
greatest_challenge: Honestly, I was chilling. The only challenging part was the whole process before with visa, housing and registration. Ones you’re there it’s just cool.
other_comments: Go alone! don't go with a friend. The idea is nice, but you are making it much harder for yourself to make good friends, and you’ll be stuck with them for the whole semester. All the people who did not go with anyone they new beforehand got a closer friend group a lot quicker, and became better friends with the people.

info_ease: Very easy - all the information was available on the NMBU website, even though it could be a bit tricky to find the right web pages in the beginning.
arrival_assistance: I had received all the information necessary prior to arrival.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I don't remember it very well, but we got a lot of help - there was a presentation and walk-through of the process, and the staff was available for guidance afterwards.
registration_help: see above
registration_success: I didn't get all the courses I wanted - NMBU is very strict when it comes to prerequisites, and there is also some courses that are only possible to apply for if you are registered in a master's or bachelor's programme (not exchange student). But even though you don't get the courses you originally wanted, you should definitely apply for exchange at NMBU anyways!
registration_advice: If you have any questions don't hesitate to call or write an email to the university!
course_level: The courses I followed were at a bit lower level than I am used to.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style varies a lot depending on the course, but I was a bit unlucky: a lot of the teaching was solely one-way communication from the professor. I missed that the professor actively engaged the students by asking questions or making discussion groups, etc. I didn't have a lot of group work either.
courses_enrolled: MVI310 Macronutrients, Their Structure and Functionality MVI393 Chemical Food Safety FMI312 Environmental Exposures and Human Health MTH300 E-learning Course: Planning and Scientific Writing of a Master's Thesis in Natural Sciences
recommended_courses: I was particularly happy with the MTH300 E-learning Course: Planning and Scientific Writing of a Master's Thesis in Natural Sciences. I got a lot of tools and useful information for my future master's thesis. I can also recommend MVI310 Macronutrients, Their Structure and Functionality if you like food chemistry. But expect group work with people from other countries and cultures, which might create some challenges. However, I think meeting and working with people from other cultures is an important part of exchange!
unexpected_costs: Membership in the gym and in some student organisations, concerts at the Students' house (Samfunnet).
cost_comparison: Local transportation - I went to Oslo 1-2 times per week, and a oneway ticket to Oslo costs approx. 47 DKK.
activities_available: There were an endless number of student organisations! Many different sports clubs, choirs, dancing associations and music associations. Also many political organisations, outdoor groups, gaming groups, botanics,climbing, etc. Every second year NMBU students arrange a festival called UKA, which lasts throughout October. There are a lot of concerts and other events such as revy / sketch show.
activities_recommended: Be part of an organisation! Doesn't matter which one - it is just a really good and easy way of getting to know people who share common interests with you. I was part of two associations, which ended up being my primary social groups: an association dancing nordic folk dance (Leikarringen Frøy), and an association playing folk music (Flatlusa). Bring your instrument and your best dance moves! ;)
weekend_recommendations: Become a member of the outdoor life association - they arrange many trips in the weekends. Generally, the different student associations have a lot of activities in the weekends, so don't be afraid to get bored, it's not going to happen.
culture_adjustment: Luckily, Norwegians understand Danish quite well, so it is not too difficult to become friends with the local people. The culture is also somewhat similar to the Danish culture, but Norwegians can seem a bit "cold" or difficult to get to know. Don't let that scare you! But don't expect them to seek your company - you have to do the hard work in the beginning :)
socializing_tips: see above
cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: That many Norwegians enjoy outdoor life!
top3_advice: Be part of a student assocaition! Learn to bake your own ryebread! Norwegian rugbrød is not really rugbrød... If you drink alcohol you should bring some from Denmark - it is really expensive in Norway.

socializing_tips: Join the events on campus and join a student organisation.
cultural_challenges: The language could sometimes be a challenge as some has difficulty understanding danish especially in bigger or louder groups.

most_rewarding: Meeting other international students and being a part of that amazing community! And the nature experiences in Norway was also magnificent.
greatest_challenge: Starting a new everyday life somewhere new could be challenging, but as soon as I got close with my roommates, it became much easier.
other_comments: I would definitely recommend going on exchange on NMBU!

There is nowhere where you can see which courses are available to exchange students.
registration_advice: Don't stress about having it figured out before you arrive, because you can register and unregister as you want for the first 3 weeks or so. So you can try the courses before deciding.

unexpected_costs: due to a delay because of weather, we had to pay extra, to get a new ticket, obviously.
cost_comparison: food was more expensive than expected.
activities_available: many different sports and trips.
activities_recommended: trips with NTNUi.
weekend_recommendations: There are many trips and NTNUi cabins nearby, which is nice to visit.

socializing_tips: If you want to socialize with other internationals, it is a good ide to join "samfundet" or become a worker/ volunteer at "uka". Also NTNUi teams is a good way to do this.
cultural_challenges: the party culture and the food culture is veri different. Many Norwegian students do not cook much themselves, and are not used to this.
culture_appreciated: The bouldering community.

other_useful_info: Don't be afraid to take initiative.
most_rewarding: Getting to know nice people, and learning to just accept the weird situations you'll be in. To find out, that you can actually do it.
greatest_challenge: To establish an everyday-life and get a proper routine, and then, after a couple of moths, having to stop it all again.

institution: Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)
crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a place with beautiful nature, possibilites to do a lot of sports and a country which isn't too far away since it's nice to be able to visit it again easily.
info_ease: The website of the university was very helpful, and it was possible to contact them if needed. Other students which were on exchange from KU could also help.
arrival_assistance: Orientation week where we got to know the campus, different student organisations and how to access all host university platforms.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: NTNU will send you mails with your account and information about how to register for courses when it's time. You get an account at studentweb.no (if your host university is NTNU), and then you can register for courses in the website under "active courses".
registration_help: NTNUs website is really helpful and it's possible to contact their international office for help.
registration_success: I registered for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: NTNU has a lot of international students and receive a lot of mails every day, so I would suggest looking at their website or asking other students how to do things before writing them an e-mail as the response time can be quite long before the exchange.
course_level: I had both bachelor and master level courses. The master level (second degree level course) (Immunology) was very good, and it was not a problem to follow along.
teaching_comparison: It depends on how much you're used to self studying. I didn't have any laboratory work, so only lectures and group exercises which meant that there was a lot of self studying as well, which I found nice since it's very flexible.
courses_enrolled: Condensced introduction to Neuroscience (15 ECTS) Immunology (7,5 ECTS) Introduction to Norway (7,5 ECTS points)
recommended_courses: Introduction to Norway was quite a nice course because it was all exchange students and you get an insight into Norwegian culture, society and history. Otherwise I loved Immunology since it was very nice lecturers and the topic is really interesting.
unexpected_costs: I needed more Outdoor equipment than I thought since I wanted to do many activities. A good tip is that you can rent equipment through NTNUI boomerang or BUA for free, just make sure to do it in time as it is very popular. Or ask fellow students/friends if they have equipment to borrow.
cost_comparison: Since the norwegian crone was low this year, everything was less expensive than expected. Especially groceries and going out to eat was less expensive. Outdoor equipment is less expensive than in Denmark, the monthly bus card was less expensive than thought (you could survive without depending on where you live/where you want to go during the week) Alcohol was pretty expensive.
activities_available: All kinds of sports at NTNUI, student choirs, outdoor groups, winterbathing+sauna groups.
activities_recommended: Trondheim really is a student city, they have so many student organisations, choirs, outdoor group etc. I recommend partaking in these, as it is such a nice student milieu. In the year I was there, they had UKA which is a Festival in October which is organized by students. I would recommend to join the volunteer work as you meet so many nice people and get to take part in the volunteer work which is really big in Trondheim.
weekend_recommendations: Go on hiking trips, either alone or with student organisations such as "NTNUI ski og fjell sport". Use the NTNU koiene (cabins) for overnight stays. In winter you should go skiing, both cross country and alpine and use the frozen lakes for ice skating. And if you have time/money, it's really worth it to see some of the other citites in Norway as well.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, since the culture is very similar to Denmark.
socializing_tips: Be a part of all the student organisations, it's very popular to join these and you'll meet a lot of other students. Studentersamfundet is definetely a place where you can get a lot of friends and fun memories, but the other organisations such as NTNUI or ESN are also worth being a part of.
cultural_challenges: Since Norwegian isn't that far from danish, you can learn to understand it pretty fast. But norwegians tend to talk Norwegian to each other and forget to speak english if there's exchange students, therefore it is important to remember to be including when there's english spearkes, and not speak norwegian/danish even though you understand what the norwegians are saying.
culture_appreciated: That everyone is nice and welcoming, and if you need any help don't hesitate to ask for it. I also really like that outdoor life and being active is a part of the culture. Furthermore, a lot of students do volunteer work which I liked a lot, without it there would not be half as many student organisations.
top3_advice: Take part in the sports and student organisations. Take advantage of the beautiful nature and nice places you can visit in Norway. Remember to enjoy it while you're there, time flies so fast.
other_useful_info: Remember to bring warm clothing and don't underestimate the weather in winter when going on a hike. Buy equipment in Norway if you don't have any, they have really good equipment stores.
most_rewarding: To get to know a lot of people, enjoying the nature and trying to live somewhere else than Denmark.
greatest_challenge: Having to say goodbye to everyone in the end.
other_comments: I had a lot of friends and family visiting from home, which was nice, but if I could have changed it I might have wanted some more weekends free to go on hiking trips (or asked my friends to join me instead of showing the city).
