overall_comments: 7-tallet er pga det lave akademiske niveau. Undervisningen var stort set uakademisk, og jeg mødte ikke særlig mange udfordringer. Ikke engang den undervisning, som jeg skulle have, i japansk sprog levede op til forventningerne. Min score på sprogtesten før og efter opholdet var stort set den samme da sprogundervisningen var så dårlig (jeg var placeret på det rigtige niveau).
info_ease: Ochanomizu var gode til at hjælpe os med det praktiske.
arrival_assistance: Vi havde en ansvarlig for udvekslingsstuderende, som man kunne spørge, og hver uge havde vi en time, hvor vi fik praktiske informationer osv.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: 7-tallet er pga det lave akademiske niveau. Undervisningen var stort set uakademisk, og jeg mødte ikke særlig mange udfordringer. Ikke engang den undervisning, som jeg skulle have, i japansk sprog levede op til forventningerne. Min score på sprogtesten før og efter opholdet var stort set den samme da sprogundervisningen var så dårlig (jeg var placeret på det rigtige niveau).
registration_process: Det er over 2 år siden, men så vidt jeg husker skulle vi udfylde en lang formular da vi ansøgte, og da vi kom tættere på fik vi tilsendt lejekontrakt for kollegieværelset osv.
registration_help: Der var guides på engelsk medsendt til de dokumenter, der var på japansk, og udvekslingskontoret svarede på e-mails hurtigt.
registration_success: Det fungerede helt fint. Vi fik meget hjælp til det.
registration_advice: Der er mange tilbud om hjælp, så brug de muligheder. Blandt andet tog nogle ansatte fra udvekslingskontoret os med ned til kommunekontoret for at blive registreret.
academics_comments: 7-tallet er pga det lave akademiske niveau. Undervisningen var stort set uakademisk, og jeg mødte ikke særlig mange udfordringer. Ikke engang den undervisning, som jeg skulle have, i japansk sprog levede op til forventningerne. Min score på sprogtesten før og efter opholdet var stort set den samme da sprogundervisningen var så dårlig (jeg var placeret på det rigtige niveau).
course_level: Jeg havde mest sprogundervisning. De kurser jeg havde på lavere intermediate niveau var fine nok, men dem på højere intermediate niveau var ret dårlige. Det var meget op til den enkelte underviser hvordan kurset var udformet, så jeg endte med en grammatiklærer, der slet ikke lærte os noget grammatik, men bare ville have at vi skulle tale om kulturforskelle, hvilket var noget vi gjorde UTROLIGT meget. I stort set alle kurserne skulle vi på et eller andet tidspunkt lave en fremlæggelse om kulturforskelle. Generelt meget uakademisk, og i visse tilfælde næsten useriøst.
teaching_comparison: Det var ret anderledes. Vi skulle have 8 små kurser. Underviserne var søde, men det var lidt underligt for mig at de helt selv planlagde kurset, så det virkelig var op til hvad de lige havde lyst til at lave. Især i mit grammatikkursus var det en ulempe. Derudover var undervisningen som før nævnt ret uakademisk. Vi læste ikke akademisk litteratur, og det var ikke forventet at vi skulle inkludere kilder i vores fremlæggelser. Jeg havde et kursus der ikke var for kun uvekslingsstuderende, og selv der var der ret lave forventninger. Dog var det en del mere akademisk.
courses_enrolled: Research in Second Language Teaching II, Seminar: Japanese IIB, Seminar: Japanese IIIB, Seminar: Japanese Culture IB. Class for Exchange Students, Intermediate Japanese Language B Conversation, Intermediate Japanese Language B Grammar, Intermediate Japanese Language B Kanji
recommended_courses: Seminarene var ok
unexpected_costs: Man skulle bruge mange penge på ting til sit værelse, da det var helt bart. Ting som dyne,pude og sengebetræk kunne lejes på kollegiet. Man skulle købe service, gryder osv hvis man ville lave mad i tekøkkenet på værelset.
cost_comparison: Det var billigt at spise ude, mens det var ret dyrt at lave mad selv, så jeg endte med at spise ude de fleste dage, da det endte med at koste det samme som at lave mad derhjemme.
activities_available: Der var klubber for næsten alt, tror jeg.
activities_recommended: Det er en god ide at blive en del af en klub, hvis man vil have chancen for at få japanske venner. Det er lidt svært at møde dem ellers, med mindre man tager normale kurser på japansk.
weekend_recommendations: Tokyo er en spændende by, og der er altid noget at lave. Nogle af højdepunkterne var Halloween in Shibuya og områderne Asakusa og Shimokitasawa. Derudover er Yokohama også virkelig fint. Til udflugter kan jeg anbefale at tage et par dage til Nikko eller Hakone. Bjergene er virkelig smukke om vinteren.
culture_adjustment: Jeg har boet i Tokyo i en længere periode før, så jeg kendte allerede til byen og Japansk kultur. Personligt har jeg aldrig følt noget kulturchok i Japan. Japanere minder lidt om danskere, da de også er introverte og ikke snakker med fremmede. Til gengæld er de meget høflige og gæstfri. En ting jeg synes var svært var at få japanske venner, og jeg endte med mest at være sammen med andre udvekslingstuderende. Det har nok også noget at gøre med at Tokyo er en STOR by og folk derfor ikke er så interesserede i fremmede. Det er ikke ligefrem sådan at folk kommer op til en og starter en samtale. Men hvis man er den mere ekstroverte type, er det måske ikke så stort et problem.
socializing_tips: Som sagt ikke rigtigt. Men jeg tror det er en god ide at blive medlem af en klub.
cultural_challenges: Jeg synes ikke der var nogle særligt store kulturforskelle. Det var mest sproget der skabte problemer, da de fleste japanere ikke er så gode til engelsk, og jeg ikke er flydende i japansk (det kan man dog hurtigt blive bedre til hvis man snakker med folk :) )
culture_appreciated: Japan er et dejligt land med meget historie. Menneskerne er meget gæstfri og hjælpsomme.
top3_advice: Vær sikker på at du vælger gode kurser. Evt. spørg nogle udvekslingsstuderende, som har været der i noget tid, hvilke undervisere er gode, da indholdet afhænger meget af dem.
most_rewarding: Jeg har fået nogle utroligt gode venner fra hele verden, og jeg har oplevet en masse spændende ting i Japan.

crucial_aspects: I am studying Japanese Studies. And I chose Ochanomizu Uni. for several reasons, including the central location in Tokyo, inexpensive on-campus housing with a private room and its own bathroom and kitchenette, as well as the university's great focus on women's progress in academia and business.
info_ease: 1. I received a lot of information about orientation and arrival by mail in the weeks and days prior to my departure from DK. There were also regular Zoom meetings with the Home Room teacher and the international students (both one-on-one and altogether). 2. If I had questions, I would either ask at these meetings or contact the International Office at Ochanomizu Uni. 3. However, the only downside to the process was that Ochanomizu Uni. was quite late in announcing the move-in date. They encouraged the international students to arrive at the end of September to be sure, and so we only had a very short time to move-in before the semester started. (We could move-in on September 30, there was campus-orientation on September 31, and the semester began on October 1).
arrival_assistance: 1. I had received many documents from Ochanomizu Uni., which should prepare me for the arrival and the first days on campus. Including instructions on how to get from the airport to campus. 2. There are a few mandatory orientation meetings on the day of arrival and the following days (about the housing, campus and the surrounding area). 3. There are regular meetings once a week with all international students in a class called "Home Room". The Home Room teacher and the international students discuss things such as important deadlines, guidelines, rules, events and more.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process is a bit complicated. You have to create a trial/ first version course registration sheet to submit to your home room teacher. Afterwards, you will discuss this sheet and you might have to make changes to accommodate both Ochanomizu Uni., UCPH and yourself. Then you will have a chance to try courses in the first week of the semester, and make new changes to your sheet. You need to get your registration sheet confirmed and stamped by your academic supervisor before it's valid for a final course registration submission. Lastly, you have a short period in which you still have the option of dropping some courses, but you can't add anymore courses. So, the process is both online and on printed paper, and multiple people have to approve of the courses.
registration_help: 1. There was information in the many documents received by mail. 2. There were also multiple meetings about the process in the "Home Room"- class. 3. The International Office on campus at Ochanomizu Uni. 4. 2nd semester international students who knew of the process.
registration_success: Some courses were suddenly cancelled at the beginning of the semester, which is something that can happen, so I had to change my priorities. However, I was a 100% successful in the end.
registration_advice: Don't feel discouraged if you find anything challenging or difficult to understand - it's better to ask and get clarity as the registration process is very different to how it is at UCPH.
course_level: Some students who had been at Ochanomizu University for 2 semesters said that the Japanese courses in the Spring semester seemed more difficult than the ones in the Autumn/Fall semester. You take an online Japanese language comprehension test before your exchange, and the home room teacher will discuss the results with you and guide you on the level of the courses. However, you have a chance to try out different levels during the first week of the semester, before you have to make the final course registration. There are few courses in English, but they are interesting and the level is easy.
teaching_comparison: UCPH has a ton of reading and preparation for each class (non-Japanese language class), whereas Ochanomizu University doesn't. It's more about participating in the class discussions following the professor's lecture - as there is a ton of group work and a lot of presentations. The teaching style of the Japanese language classes is somewhat more or less the same, but with more assignments, oral presentations and practically no use of English in class or learning documents. Sometimes there are tests more often throughout the semester, while some classes have a test each week.
courses_enrolled: 23A2415 Technology and Gender 23N0093 Facilitation 23G0202 Seminar: Japanese Culture IB 23B2045 Globalization and Labor I 23B8510 Cultural Transformations I 23B2026 Cultural and Human Relations I I also had Special Japanese Classes (Japanese language classes) besides the above mentioned courses. (Home Room is a mandatory class for international students, but not something to obtain credits from).
recommended_courses: I'm not sure which courses I would recommend, but: 1. "文化変動論"/ "Cultural Transformations" was an informative and easily comprehensive course about gender, migration and cultural transformation through time. We watched about 2-3 movies, which was a great way to further discussion and understanding. 2. "テクノロジーとジェンダー"/ "Technology & Gender" had multiple class excursions to museums, although the professor could be difficult to understand at times. 3. "Seminar: Japanese Culture IB" was a culture course with the nicest professor. She was very passionate about cultural exchange and her classes were interesting and down to earth - you also learned a lot about the cultures of your classmates.
unexpected_costs: Nothing I can think of.
cost_comparison: 1. Eating out was less expensive. 2. If you live on campus, you don't have to pay for daily use of public transportation, which is a big plus. I put 70 DKK as the cost of local transportation because I used it often to go explore in my spare time. 3. Rent and gas are charged/billed and paid for seperatly - gas was less expensive than I expected. 4. Well, most items were less expensive than I expected.
activities_available: 1. There were multiple mandatory cultural exchange events with the participation of all international students and some Japanese students arranged by the university. 2. There were various university clubs such as a tea ceremony club (with a real tea house on campus for that purpose). 3. Ochanomizu University School Festival. 4. There were multiple opportunities to participate in cultural and social activities through courses and events presented in mails from the university. These were free of charge and were only available for a limited number of participants, so you had to be quick to respond. Fx. ikebana class, kimono class, cooking class, kaligraphy class etc. 5. There was a kind of fitness/yoga room available for booking in the dormitory. (With mirrors, not with fitness gear). It seemed like there might have been a regular dance/fitness club that booked the room sometime during the week. 6. There was a Japanese café and an English café, established by the international students for language exchange once a week.
activities_recommended: Well, all of the above. I didn't get to participate in the ikebana class because of my schedule, but the ones who did really enjoyed it. It's something you don't normally experience, and it's a dying activity in schools in Japan. These small cultural courses were casual and non-academic, with mostly Japanese instructors and international students. They weren't Japanese language classes or something to obtain credits from, so you can let loose, have fun and experience something new.
weekend_recommendations: 1. Locally, definitely explore the area outside campus - just take a walk in the surrounding neighbourhood. It's quite interestingly something that many forget to do, because you live there for a longer amount of time and establish a routine. 2. Locally, visit some of the nearby parks, gardens, temples and museums - you can reach many on foot. 3. Walk from campus to nearby places like Ikebukuro or Shin-ōtsuka (lots and lots to do - fx. Sunshine City Mall in Ikebukuro). 4. Visit Ochanomizu Station - you can take the metro. 5. Attend festivals or markets depending on the time of your exchange and the season.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. The environment on campus as well as in the dormitory was welcoming. And the local culture in Bunkyō-ku, Tokyo, where Ochanomizu University is located, is quite down to earth. There are parks, temples and other cultural sights nearby - and the area is bustling with life at all times, especially at rush hour and on the weekends. The campus is very close to a metro station with a quick connection to the rest of central Tokyo.
socializing_tips: You can try to contact and befriend your assigned tutor, who will be a Japanese student. Otherwise, there are multiple university clubs (such as a tea ceremony club).
cultural_challenges: I sometimes found the indirect, read between the lines/not spoken, communication challenging. If possible, it might prove easier to receive a clearer answer by writing an email. For example, in regards to a professor or alike.
culture_appreciated: Funnily enough, I really appreciated the queue culture. As well as the various opportunities to entertain yourself in different ways - you always experience something new. And how nature is such a big part of the culture.
top3_advice: 1. Please feel free to contact and communicate with Ochanomizu University - both online and in person. They are super welcoming, quick to reply and wish you the best possible exchange experience. (It is better to ask once too much than once too little.) 2. There are some social and cultural events that are mandatory to participate in, but there are also other events with voluntary participation arranged by the university and the university clubs. These are chances to meet other students in a more casual and fun setting - although it might seem daunting at first, please try it out. 3. You will also be assigned a tutor, who is a Japanese student, to assist you throughout the semester. It's an interesting concept, where you can help each other with Japanese and English, and you can meet up and go on trips together.
other_useful_info: 1. You will be introduced to a service called Give-and-Take, which is unique to Ochanomizu University. It's a website where former students and dormitory residents give away stuff for the new students and residents to take/make a reservation for. It's free of charge, you just put the stuff back on the website before your own departure. Please make use of it, it's quite nice. 2. It's useful to know of a nearby medical clinic with English speaking personnel in case you get sick and need help/assistance/guidance. There is a very small medical clinic on campus, but you always have to make a booking in advance. The booking system is a bit complicated, the times are few and far between, and there is a lot they can't help with - so if you need help quickly, please seek out another option.
most_rewarding: I was lucky to meet some amazing people from Japan and around the world during my exchange - all of which lived in the same dormitory on campus as I did (the on-campus dormitory houses both international and Japanese students). So, sharing the exchange experience with my new friends was the most rewarding part. However, having the possibility of actually living in Japan for 4-5 months and experiencing different social and cultural contexts firsthand, have also put my education, interests and future into perspective.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was all of the official paperwork, which seemed endless at times. There is a lot of paperwork before going abroad, but it's another level in Japan. You have to fill out a lot of documents on the day of moving into the dormitory, as well as going to the local Civic Center multiple times for other documents - there are even times, when everyone seems confused. This is on repeat throughout the semester, even in the very last days before departure. But: it's easier if you find someone and do it together.
other_comments: I think my semester abroad in Tokyo, Japan - particularly at Ochanomizu University - has truly been an unforgettable and unparalleled experience. There can be difficult and challenging times, but you can find a way to approach and overcome these - remember to also enjoy your time and have fun exploring daily life in Japan.

crucial_aspects: Visiting Japan has always been a big dream of mine since I love the culture and nature there, so this was an amazing opportunity to really discover the country.
overall_comments: I highly recommend studying abroad, especially in Japan (just don't pick an intense academic program here!)
info_ease: Very easy, there were a lot of people hired to help us out, and there were multiple information meetings.
arrival_assistance: Information meetings once I arrived at the dorm.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I highly recommend studying abroad, especially in Japan (just don't pick an intense academic program here!)
registration_process: Course registration was fairly easy, but all of the bureaucratic paperwork with the bank, housing, City Hall etc. was a real pain.
registration_help: There is very helpful English-speaking staff at Global Village that can help you with all of the paperwork, which is why I recommend staying here for the first 2 months.
registration_success: Very successful, but I know other students were surprised at the limited amount of classes we were allowed to choose, so make sure to familiarize yourself with the OUSSEP curriculum first. Also, a lot of the normal classes that say they are taught in English are actually taught in Japanese, so be careful.
registration_advice: Talk to the other international students or get help from the staff at Global Village or at the IC hall on campus.
academics_comments: I highly recommend studying abroad, especially in Japan (just don't pick an intense academic program here!)
course_level: Most OUSSEP courses are very easy, especially if you choose a topic that you are already familiar with.
teaching_comparison: You actually need to show up for class, which was different.
courses_enrolled: Polymers in Daily Life and Science, Psychology of Perception and Cognition, JA100, Introduction to Scientific English, Independent Study, UC Frontier Science
recommended_courses: Psychology of Perception and Cognition: Very interesting course with a good professor. JA100: I highly recommend studying Japanese since it will make your stay way more enjoyable. But it's a commitment, since it's 3 times a week. Independent Study: Very different course that allows you to study a topic of your own choosing and get insight into Japanese research and work ethic, as well as talk to the locals.
unexpected_costs: In total, I think I spent around 100,000 DKK, but I did travel and eat out a lot, and I bought a lot of things. I would suggest having a lot more money than you think you might need, unless you're okay with having to save on a lot of things.
cost_comparison: Almost everything was more expensive than I expected. Eating out is affordable compared to Denmark, but cooking your own food is expensive, so you end up eating out 1-2 times a day which means you spend A LOT of money on food (if you want to eat decently well at least). Also, transportation is so expensive. Don't expect European flight prices if you want to travel around the country, and taking the train is just as expensive. Transportation to and from campus is ~30 DKK per day, so it adds up.
activities_available: There are Japanese clubs that you can join, but I would recommend knowing some Japanese if you want to join those. Otherwise, there are language events and international mingling events as well as some events at the dorm.
activities_recommended: I volunteered as an IELTS English tutor for a Japanese student, which I recommend if you get the chance. It was nice to talk to at least one Japanese person since it gives you a lot of insight into the culture, and you might make a new friend.
weekend_recommendations: Travel as much as you can. Japan is an incredible country to travel around, and there are endless things to see and discover. Go to the arcade. Go sing karaoke. Try all of the interesting food. Pray at the temples. Go soak in the onsens. Go have fun in Tokyo. Japan is a giant playground, so make sure to experience as much as you possibly can.
culture_adjustment: You just have to always make sure to be very polite to the locals, and they will be very kind to you. I mostly interacted with the international students, so adjusting was easy for me. I think it's difficult if you really have to mingle with the Japanese, since they are usually pretty reserved and not eager to speak English. But most of them are super nice, so it's worth the effort.
socializing_tips: Learn Japanese! It's okay if you're not good at it, they will be very happy to see you try, and it might make them more open to speaking English with you. Invite them out to eat, or have a takoyaki party with them.
cultural_challenges: The Japanese love for bureaucracy and paperwork was exhausting. And towards the end, I was pretty fed up with the politeness since, at times, it becomes almost robotic and not very human. You could also feel that a lot of Japanese people are not very happy with foreigners, especially the older generations.
culture_appreciated: Funnily enough, also the politeness. Everyone is so kind and helpful and smiling. And everyone takes their time, they're more calm and not in a rush like I'm used to in Denmark. I also loved to spend time at the onsens where you got to see a different side to the locals. Also, Japan is just such a fun place to be, there are endless opportunities for entertainment, so you will never be bored. I also really got to appreciate all of the temples and shrines and the serenity and sacredness of these places. It's a very special atmosphere. I could go on and on about the things I love about Japan, and the positive definitely outweighs the negative.
top3_advice: Travel as much as you can. Don't be afraid to speak Japanese to the locals. Have fun!
other_useful_info: Can't think of any.
most_rewarding: Becoming friends with the other international students and travelling with them.
greatest_challenge: I got admitted to a Japanese hospital for 6 days, and no one could speak English there. Another reason why it is so important that you go through all of the paperwork and make sure that you are properly insured. And make friends with someone who speaks Japanese well because you might end up needing them.

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_help: Der var en guide
registration_success: Meget
registration_advice: Bare følg instrukserne
course_level: Lidt nemmere end KU.

other_useful_info: Lad vær med spørg for meget om råd - gå på opdagelse og find selv ud af det, det er meget sjovere.

crucial_aspects: Personal interest in Japan and its culture. I wanted to combine the academic life of a student with exploring its culture, building bridges between the two.
overall_comments: In short, I'd recommend anyone with the courage and interest to use the opportunity to study abroad.
info_ease: Japan is very bureaucratic and very analog with a lot of paperwork compared to Denmark. Thus, systems were in place for almost everything even though clear information in English were often lacking. Communication with other students and dorm mates helped out a lot.
arrival_assistance: I was assisted by especially the management of my dorm for translation and instructions of needed registration, insurance, pension at the city hall.
arrival_comments: The host institution were always helpful in assisting, although I mainly got assisted by my dormitory's management (affiliated to the university) out of the convenience of them being close by.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: In short, I'd recommend anyone with the courage and interest to use the opportunity to study abroad.
registration_process: I found the registration process a little hard but doable with the help of others who had to register as well. I feel like we were given a lot of information, but everything you needed for registration was there.
registration_help: I was but helped by flat mates, the management of my dormitory and by mail by my host university.
registration_success: Having prior course approval (forhåndsgodkendelse) made getting an overview of possible courses for me to take a lot easier. I picked from my list, trying to make a realistic schedule where the courses lined up and where days were at the same campus. I found it easy to register with the information I was given.
registration_advice: Make sure to, not only pick courses that you have preapproval for, but make sure the schedule that you're putting together is realistic so you don't have to commute from different campuses on the same day.
academics_comments: In short, I'd recommend anyone with the courage and interest to use the opportunity to study abroad.
course_level: Although a master student, I was given permission take also take BA-courses since the length of a bachelor in Japan is 4 years. Academic level of BA-courses varied a lot and were noticably lower level than the MA-courses I took.
teaching_comparison: More lectures and less discussion. I recommend seminar courses for more in-class discussion that I believe we are more used to in Denmark.
courses_enrolled: Sociological Theory, Introduction to International Understanding, Multicultural Coexistance, Social Innovation and Social Design, Approaches to Understanding Cultures, Japanese JA200.
recommended_courses: I especially enjoyed learning Japanese in a "real" Japanese language class. Probably not for everyone, but if you have the interest and motivation I highly recommend it.
unexpected_costs: Apart from travel insurance from home, international students in Japan are required to pay obligatory insurance and pension monthly.
cost_comparison: Investing in a second hand bike for transportation to campus is ideal to save money on especially the monorail. Bike can be resold upon returning to Dennmark. Food is affordable if you decided to cook a lot on your own - with the exception of fruit and some vegetables. Eating out is cheap compared to Denmark.
activities_available: Many social events were hold by my dormitory, often introducing Japanese culture and seasonal events. It was easy to apply and a convenient way of meeting people from other units within the dorm.
activities_recommended: Depening on the budget, I would recommend travelling around Japan as much as possible.
weekend_recommendations: Travelling, eating out, exploring the city in which you life.
culture_adjustment: On the same time, easy and difficult. Japanese people speak very little English, often making it hard to communicate. Easy as Japanese culture is organized and convenient, e.g. transportation with no delays.
socializing_tips: Don't be afraid to ask question if you are uncertain about anything. Other students is in the exact same position as you.
cultural_challenges: Language barrier.
culture_appreciated: Most aspects, but especially food culture.
top3_advice: 1. Make sure to make a rough budget for your coming stay. Get your main expenses down to get a rough idea of how much you can/want to travel. 2. Prepare as much as possible in terms of orientating and getting yourself familiar with course list, the credit transfer to ECTS. and so on. 3. ASK QUESTIONS, everyone is ready to help you in Japan, both host institution, dorm mates and random stranges if you get lost or need help.
other_useful_info: Take your time to get an overview and apply for scholarships and funds. Many people are too lazy to do this, but applying to a lot will most likely result in you getting some kind of financial support for your stay.
most_rewarding: To explore and to immerse into another culture with likeminded peers/students. An unforgettable experience and a unique opportunity to live in another country if that is on your bucket list.
greatest_challenge: To adjust to the culture and bureaucracy of Japan, having to do everything in person when registering as a foreigner/student.

crucial_aspects: I had studied and lived here before so I knew it was exactly here I wanted to go. That it was it in city and thus had access to a lot of leisure activities and opportunities.
overall_comments: While I met great people and had unique experiences, the university itself did lack in providing assistance and guidance to us exchange students, if we wanted to get involved with anything or meet other students it was mostly up to us to do so. It did feel empthy from the university´s side.
info_ease: A lot of written information such as guide leaflets and complete folders were provided, thus it was fairly easy to get the practical things done.
arrival_assistance: The staff at the dormitory were very helpful and explained a lot upon arrival. They were very helpful through the whole stay.
arrival_comments: The orientation was lackluster, it was poorly prepared and it felt like 5 minutes worth of information followed by questions and information about small insignificant things. The orientation speech should provide a lot more information as the students arrive in a completely different environment with usually no prior knowledge or experience.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: While I met great people and had unique experiences, the university itself did lack in providing assistance and guidance to us exchange students, if we wanted to get involved with anything or meet other students it was mostly up to us to do so. It did feel empthy from the university´s side.
registration_process: Multiple rounds of documents and applications that had to be sent by set deadlines. A lot of paper work to be filled out and sent. A guide for application got provided so we knew what we had to get, but there were many steps in the whole process.
registration_help: It was possible to contact both our home universtiy, and the host university did also provide assistance through email.
registration_success: It was very smooth and easy, I got all the classes I wanted and I believe everyone did too. Since most of the courses are close to the previous semester, we get a clear idea of what courses will be provided.
registration_advice: Be prepared to both provide our home university as well as the host university with seperate applications and documents, prepare documents early.
academics_comments: While I met great people and had unique experiences, the university itself did lack in providing assistance and guidance to us exchange students, if we wanted to get involved with anything or meet other students it was mostly up to us to do so. It did feel empthy from the university´s side.
course_level: The courses were about the same and provided us with a great about of knowledge. More smaller written assignments instead of a big one.
teaching_comparison: It was a mix depending on the teacher. Some Americans and Canadians were very positive and inviting with a great deal of participation from the class, they provided a safe and open classroom where we were not affraid of failing which gave us confidence in experimenting. Other teachers were more of the formal teacher speaker - student listen kind of style. They were always open and encouraging to questions and provided a ton of information with visual aids such as slideshows and videos etc. I really liked that we had weekly small written assignments instead of one big one we have at out home university. I could experiement with small assignements and dared to try something new. It improved my writing as we did it very often but in bite sized amounts, It also helped me to get an assignment started quicker as we got more practice in doing so.
courses_enrolled: Global Studies in English (Fall Winter) Special lecture Topics in Comparative Contract and Torts Law (Fall Winter) Private Law in Japan (Fall Winter) Introduction to Common Law (Fall Winter) Multivariate Statistical Science (Fall Winter) Introduction of Mechanical Materials and Manufacturing Science (Fall Winter) Law and Society in the Middle East (Fall Winter)
recommended_courses: Global Studies in English (Fall Winter) Special lecture Topics in Comparative Contract and Torts Law (Fall Winter) Introduction of Mechanical Materials and Manufacturing Science (Fall Winter) Introduction to Common Law (Fall Winter)
unexpected_costs: Higher cost of transportation between cities.
cost_comparison: Fruit and meat was more expensive. Eating out was cheaper than expected.
activities_available: All kind of sports clubs such as swimming and archery and cultural clubs such as dance and music.
activities_recommended: Depends on your hobbies and personality, but seeking out a school club in an area you are interested in could be a great way to meet the local students.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city both with people but also alone. Nearby cities are also worth visiting. Take your time and really enjoy it when doing things insead of rushing.
culture_adjustment: The local culture is very different, probably even more different than one can image, so be prepared to be very open minded and positive.
socializing_tips: Activities and cubs are great but local roommates should also be living there.
cultural_challenges: Reading the air and following social cues. It is important to pay attention to small gestures and how people say things. People are not as direct or confrontational as Danes.
culture_appreciated: The respect of other people and their surroundings, this makes for pleasant, quiet and safe living.
top3_advice: Study up on the culture as in how people interact and their mindsets, this will help you avoid bad or awkward situations, I have seen many people do this. Be prepared to seek out things yourself, this can be scary but very rewarding The campus provide a great deal of facilities and opportunities.
other_useful_info: The host university had tree campuses, so have this in mind when choosing classes as they will be spread out and it takes up to an hour to travel between them. Try therefore to group classes on the same campus together.
most_rewarding: Meeting great housemates and going out to drink and eat with them. Learning more about myself as I can mirror myself in other people and how they are. Having classes with a very different style than our home university, I really appriciated experiencing other approaches.
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to everything being foreign and different, while it is great, it can be a shock initially.
other_comments: It is definitely worth it. There are so many great things to experience and see and people to meet. The different classroom styles and teachers give you a different perspective and thus you become a better student. Be prepared for a shock or hardship in the beginning but do not give up, you will adjust way quicker than you think and you will have the time of your life before you know it.

crucial_aspects: I'm currently studying a bachelor's degree in Japan Studies, and so it only made sense to go on exchange in Japan. I felt it was very crucial for my degree to be able to experience living in Japan.
info_ease: It was fairly easy since my host university provided a folder with basically all the information you needed.
arrival_assistance: I received a lot of information, but, unfortunately, a lot of this information was a little difficult to understand at first. It helped a lot to talk with other exchange student's about how they interpreted the information.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process at the host university was fairly easy. You were given a folder at one of the campuses with all the information needed for registration. There was a lot of information though, which was a little overwhelming.
registration_help: There was a lot of help, but the language barrier proved a big problem sometimes. I'm so fortunate that I speak Japanese and it was therefore fairly easy for me to understand, but even then I still sometimes struggled to understand what exactly I was supposed to do, and a lot of times it was difficult for the teacher's or staff to understand what I needed help with. It seemed that there was not a lot of communication between teacher's and staff and others.
registration_success: Very successful, I got all of the courses that I wanted.
registration_advice: Registration is quite simple, and there are teacher's to help.
course_level: The level of courses was very, very low compared to Copenhagen University.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at Osaka University was very low quality compared to UCPH, unfortunately. I don't really know why, I'm thinking maybe it was because they had to design a programme for a bunch of exchange student's who came from all over the world, and Osaka University had no idea what level of English student's spoke or what kind of teaching they were used to back home. Personally, I was very bored most of the time. The reading material was more interesting than going to actual classes. I did have one class that was particularly interesting, and I really enjoyed attending that class in person.
courses_enrolled: 1) Internship course, 2) Literature & Language of Japan and China, 3) Language policies & Multilingual societies in Japan, 4) Japanese Literature, Modern & Contemporary, 5) Approaches to Understanding Culture and 6) Introduction to Japanese Social Sciences.
recommended_courses: Introduction to Japanese Social Sciences. The teacher was just absolutely wonderful and very enthusiastic about the course.
unexpected_costs: I didn't really encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: None.
activities_available: I personally didn't join any clubs, but I know that there was a lot of opportunities for all kinds of clubs.
activities_recommended: None, since I don't have experience with this.
weekend_recommendations: Travelling.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. But I also study Japan Studies and have been to Japan many times, so I'm very familiar with the culture.
socializing_tips: Just talk to people.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Japanese people are incredibly considerate.
top3_advice: Literally, learn Japanese. Take a Japanese language course, preferably a whole year in advance. And read some books by Japanese authors.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: I've gained a much, much deeper understanding of the Japanese way of life, and I'm so thankful that I've been able to experience this. I'm so much more in love with my degree after this exchange semester, and I can't wait to get back to Japan. Actually living in Japan gives you a whole new perspective on Japanese culture, tradition and history. My language skills have gotten much, much better, and I've gained a whole new confidence in my studies.
greatest_challenge: Completely changing my way of life. I needed to adapt to a whole new way of life and routine, and it was only after 3 months that I felt like I had settled in. One semester was far too little time.
other_comments: I learned that a lot of other European universities won't sent exchange students to Japan unless they agree to do a whole year, simply because they don't believe that 1 semester is enough. I really think UCPH should take this into consideration as well.

crucial_aspects: High academic level and an available research project to gain more practical experience in my field. Also experiencing a different culture and different approach to my field
info_ease: The university gave quite detailed instructions on what to upon arrival, however due to the amount it was a bit difficult to keep track of what should be done.
arrival_assistance: There was an entire division to help international exchange students available, to answer questions or help with procedures.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After being contacted I had to make a huge application with: medical history, relevant classes, grades, future aspirations, fields of interest, an application itself, language score (TOEFL)
registration_help: It was pretty self-explanatory and it was easy to get help because of an available chat with the exchange division.
registration_success: I registered to FrontierLab which means that I only had to find a laboratory i wanted to do my project in. I didn't get my first priority but a laboratory based on my field of interest.
registration_advice: They offer Japanese courses, which are very fast-paced and require a lot of time and dedication. If you want to focus on the lab I would advise against registereing to japanese classes.
course_level: I only took the FrontierLab course which does not have a formal level.
teaching_comparison: I didn't recieve any lectures or classes since laboratory experience was was more in focus. I think learning to work in a laboratory is very similar across different universities.
courses_enrolled: Full-time FrontierLab
recommended_courses: I would recommend only choosing frontierlab as to have more free-time and depth in your study.
unexpected_costs: There are a lot of insurances required which ends up costing a bit. Also the english test score that is required was very expensive!
cost_comparison: Going out to eat is very cheap compared to Denmark
activities_available: Where I was not really anything. I was located at Suita campus which is less student oriented and there was also Covid
activities_recommended: There is a professor from another university (Ogura-sensei) that often invites international exchange students to do outdoor activities and is very cheap (~2000 JPY) though you have to be quick to registrate on Facebook. The group is called "Outdoor Adventure Team OGURA"
weekend_recommendations: Best ramen place in Osaka is called Menya Aozora. Osaka is located in the center of a lot of interesting places. I would recommend going to see Kyoto, Nara and Kobe as it only takes 1 hour to get there and there are more than enough places to visit.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. There are some important things to remember in Japan (Calling by surnames, adding proper suffix when adressing people) but people know you are from abroad an knows you probably struggle with it in the beginning.
socializing_tips: Be open and show you want to participate
cultural_challenges: Most students have very poor english skills. So communication on more complicated topics can be difficult. Usually they are better on writing than talking.
culture_appreciated: The people are very proper and nice.
top3_advice: Even if it seems that there are a lot of rules and deadlines you can in many cases talk to them to find an arrangement.
other_useful_info: Get your TOEFL score a good amount of time prior to the application!!! If you are not set on a particular laboratory write an email to the professor and ask them if they usually have exchange students - this makes getting into a lab with other exchange students more easy. You will also need a CESR-document for the visa application which also will take some time to arrive apply for this as soon as you can as to avoid stress regarding the visa.
most_rewarding: Just enjoying another culture and learning something everyday. Also finishing your own supervised project is rewarding in its own right.
greatest_challenge: Communication with the other students. And managing time properly.

crucial_aspects: I've always been interested in Japan and Japanese culture, and the FrontierLab program at Osaka University allows you to use your ECTS on a scientific project in one of the university's laboratories, which I was very excited about.
info_ease: The dormitory and university staff provide guidance with all the stuff you need to take care of upon arrival, so even though everything was a bit overwhelming at first (as would be expected in a completely foreing country) it was not difficult to get the necessary things done.
arrival_assistance: See previous answer.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Since I was a FrontierLab student, my supervisor took care of the registration process, so communicate with your supervisor. If you are not FrontierLab I'm sure the staff at the Center for International Education and Exchange (CIEE) are happy to help.
registration_help: See previous answer.
registration_success: Successful.
registration_advice: See previous answer.
course_level: I only took an elective Japanese language course apart from the laboratory project, so I can't comment on the level of courses related to my field of study.
teaching_comparison: In my case the lab supervision was pretty similar to what I have previously experienced in Denmark, apart from some cultural differences. I've heard from other students that this and the workload varies among laboratories though.
courses_enrolled: FrontierLab D (30 ECTS), Elective Japanese Language Course (0 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I definitely recommend FrontierLab and if you want to also learn some Japanese I suggest to take the creditless elective course so you don't have to worry about passing it.
unexpected_costs: None that I can think of.
cost_comparison: Fruit and vegetables are quite expensive. Eating out can be quite a bit cheaper than cooking your own food (depending on where you go).
activities_available: There's a lot of clubs for many different activities at Toyonaka campus, and some student associations organize social gatherings at least once a month. Also Global Village will occasionally organize social events.
activities_recommended: Definitely attend dormitory and university welcome parties to get to know people.
weekend_recommendations: There's so much to see in Japan, even just around the Kansai area. You can easily get to Kyoto, Kobe, and Nara from Osaka.
culture_adjustment: I would say you get used to it pretty fast, even though in the beginning the manners can seem a bit weird.
cultural_challenges: Sometimes it can be difficult to get a direct answer from Japanese people, for the sake of politeness.
culture_appreciated: The orderliness and organization.
top3_advice: 1. It would help to learn as much Japanese as possible before your exchange (I didn't learn much) 2. Do the FrontierLab program if you're in science, and contact a potential supervisor in advance 3. Use your free time to see as much of Japan as possible, it's a really beautiful country
other_useful_info: Can't think of anything else.
most_rewarding: The people I met, both Japanese and international students.
greatest_challenge: The language barrier with the locals.

crucial_aspects: Opportunities to do experimental work in my field and wanting to visit my friends in Japan.
info_ease: When you arrive at the university you are given a envelope full of brochures, guides, important passwords and documents that need to be filled out before various deadlines - which was practical, but a bit overwhelming.
arrival_assistance: A japanese student from my lab helped me go to the ward office to register my address and fill out insurance forms etc. And as mentioned above, I was given an envelope with all the important paper work I needed to do.
arrival_comments: Staff and students are very happy to help you out when you don't understand the paperwork or can't read the kanji - just reach out!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You need a ton of stuff like a health certificate from a doctor, relevant classes, grades, future aspirations, letter of recommendation, fields of interest, the actual application, language score (TOEFL or JLPT) etc. The process of acquiring these things is pretty time consuming - so start as early as you can!
registration_help: You're given a very detailed guide for how to apply and what documents you will need. And you can always email the Osaka Univ. Student Exchange for help or clarification if you need it - they usually answer within a day!
registration_success: Since I registered to FrontierLab I only had to find a laboratory I wanted to do research in - which I managed.
registration_advice: The laboratory work is very time consuming. So although they also offer Japanese courses, I would advise against taking these if you want to focus on your project.
course_level: I took the FrontierLab program which does not have a formal level.
teaching_comparison: Learning to work in a laboratory is probably very similar across universities. Although I wouldn't know what it's like to learn that at UCPH since corona cancelled all of my lab exercises :(
courses_enrolled: FrontierLab (D)
recommended_courses: FrontierLab! And no additional courses unless you want to stress yourself out.
unexpected_costs: Insurances! Even though you have a travel insurance from Denmark, you are still required to buy a lot of insurances in Japan.
cost_comparison: Eating out is very cheap!
activities_available: There are some different organizations that plan monthly events especially for international students at Osaka University. Information about these is included in the envelope with documents you get when you arrive.
activities_recommended: There's a facebook group called "Outdoor Adventure Team OGURA" which you should definitely try to join if you like hiking and nature! I think you can only join by being invited by an existing member, but most indian and indonesian students are members, so just talk to one of them! It's run by a professor (Ogura) who apparently has too much money, because he often pays for large parts of the trips out of his own pocket - which means you can go on really spectacular trips all across Japan for super cheap (like 1000 yen). I went on one day trips to Ise, Mt. Seppiko and Soni Kogen and on a 3-day snow hike in Shirakawago. Highly recommend!
weekend_recommendations: Visit Nara and Kyoto!
culture_adjustment: I speak japanese and have lived in Japan before, so for me it was very easy.
socializing_tips: Join events and activities! That's where you'll meet the other international students. And if you speak japanese I don't need to give you any tips - japanese people will love talking to you. Oh, and participate in all the nomikai in your lab even if you don't speak japanese.
cultural_challenges: The hardest part to adjust to was the japanese work culture - I usually went to the lab from 9-18 and I was often the last to be there and the first to go home...
culture_appreciated: The food!!! And having a bath tub even though I lived in a dorm room.
top3_advice: 1) If all the deadlines and rules seem impossible remember that people are people and you can usually talk to someone to figure it out 2) Join Prof. Oguras outdoor adventure club 3) Eat lots of ramen
other_useful_info: Bring a bicycle helmet! Bikes are easy to rent or buy in Japan, but helmets are not.
most_rewarding: Learning to work in a lab and getting to know new people.
greatest_challenge: The application process and the paperwork after you arrive.
other_comments: Have fun!!!

crucial_aspects: Language spoken at the host institution, prestige related to the institution, courses offered
overall_comments: I was not happy with the educational level at Osaka University. Many of the English based courses were taught by teachers who barely spoke English. Furthermore, most of the academic courses were not on par with the difficulty of courses offered in Denmark. The Japanese language class was amazing and everything I needed it to be, but most of the academic courses were not “academic”.
info_ease: It was easy. Osaka university is very good at helping their incoming students
arrival_assistance: Nothing
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I was not happy with the educational level at Osaka University. Many of the English based courses were taught by teachers who barely spoke English. Furthermore, most of the academic courses were not on par with the difficulty of courses offered in Denmark. The Japanese language class was amazing and everything I needed it to be, but most of the academic courses were not “academic”.
registration_process: I had to send an email with an excel document stating what courses I wanted
registration_help: You could email the exchange office for help
registration_advice: Try to pick classes with foreign professors if you want to learn anything
academics_comments: I was not happy with the educational level at Osaka University. Many of the English based courses were taught by teachers who barely spoke English. Furthermore, most of the academic courses were not on par with the difficulty of courses offered in Denmark. The Japanese language class was amazing and everything I needed it to be, but most of the academic courses were not “academic”.
course_level: As an example of how lacklustre the level of education is at Osaka University, I had a professor who twice told us fake news because she hadn’t researched it further herself. I had another professor who ended almost every class early because he “isn’t good at English” (it was an English mediated course).
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is more aligned with high school or folkeskole in Denmark - there’s not a lot of critical thinking done by the student, but we were instead just fed information
courses_enrolled: JA400 Internationalisation of higher education in Japan Gender studies Introduction to global studies Japan: society and ideology Second language learning with online resources
recommended_courses: JA400 Introduction to global studies
unexpected_costs: The price of public transportation is high, as Osaka university does not allow their exchange students to get a student pass for public transportation. This is something other Japanese universities offer, so that was very disappointing
cost_comparison: Food is very cheap in Osaka and you can definitely use less than I did if you want to. We didn’t have to buy ANY books
activities_available: We were free to join any club at the university if said club allowed exchange students (most do). I joined the cheerleading club. Furthermore, the exchange office and institutions supported by the exchange office offers plenty of cultural events
activities_recommended: Join a club! It’s a good way to speak to native students. I also liked “project help” which is a tutor project where the exchange students help a native student with preparing for the IELTS exam
weekend_recommendations: Osaka is in the middle of the Kansai area so please use that! You can travel to Kyoto, Nara, and Wakayama easily, meaning you can see so much or Japan very easily
culture_adjustment: Easy, but I also study Japanese so I had an easier time
socializing_tips: It’s difficult if you don’t speak Japanese as most Japanese students do not speak English
cultural_challenges: Language barrier. Even if you speak Japanese, Osaka Japanese is very different and difficult to understand
culture_appreciated: Personally I just liked experiencing every day life. There wasn’t one specific thing I appreciated the most, it was the entire experience that was worthwhile
top3_advice: Do not pick academic classes based on your interests if those classes are on a Friday or Monday. It’s better to have a longer weekend, because the class will most likely disappoint you. Join a club or project help! Osaka is known for its food and lively nightlife. Please explore that aspect of the city!
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Bettering my Japanese and joining a club. I made many fond memories
greatest_challenge: The language barrier

crucial_aspects: Academic nuance and new ways of learning from new aspects, that the destination had a university with subjects I wanted to take, that it would contribute to my professional profile, that I found the country and its culture interesting and wanted to explore that.
info_ease: The information was all there, but it was spread across so many different sources and hand-outs, that it was difficult to keep track of. Furthermore, the university sent wrong or outdated information a couple of times, which was okay, but confused the information-processing a bit.
arrival_assistance: I received a lot the first days of university, and then I received a lot, when I learned where to ask for help.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Signed up for wished courses, and then again for which courses you would actually like when the registration opened. Then you got some assigned and some not, which led to a new process. It was all done through excel-sheets and email.
registration_help: OUSSEP has officies at the campus, which was very helpful!
registration_success: 50/50. I got half of the ones I initially wanted, so if you really want them all, the chances are not that great. Make sure to scout out some more you would like.
registration_advice: Do it! Very interesting and fun. Some classes were not that interesting and the learnings low, but others were super interesting, challenging and I learned a lot.
course_level: The level was super confusing! Some classes were very, very easy, to the point where it felt like a waste of time. Other classes were super hard, and demanded a lot(!) of preparation. I was very confused by the level being so different from course to course! A lot of reading for all of the classes, which was a little hard to manage since I had 8 different courses. The exam period was very hectic, but also taught me quite a lot.
teaching_comparison: Differed depending on the teacher. Some taught a lot like at UCPH, but others in a more seminar kind of manner, and others in a more discussion-forum kind of way.
courses_enrolled: "Japan: Society and Ideology", "Peace and conflict Studies", "Sociological Analysis of Nihonjin-ron", "Food, Culture and Society", "Globalization Studies", "Ethics and criminology", "Issues in Gerontology" and "Seminar in Studies of Multicultural Societies"
recommended_courses: "Globalization Studies" and "Ethics and criminology" (Both with the same teacher, who was an AMAZING teacher. I learned a lot and was a great classroom for discussion and reflection), "Peace and conflict Studies" (A REALLY interesting and important class where I learned a lot. However, the teacher was very strict, or mean, did make several students cry and the work load was very heavy), "Seminar in Studies of Multicultural Societies" (Sweet teacher, interesting subjects), "Sociological Analysis of Nihonjin-ron" (nice way to learn about non-western theories and methods in academia)
unexpected_costs: I had e-sim troubles, which made som unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Pre-made food and eating out was way less expensive than home cooking. Fresh fruit and vegetables was more expensive than expected.
activities_available: Really whatever you could dream about, all kinds of interests were represented.
activities_recommended: Traveling to nearby cities. Visiting temples and shrines. Going to local culture festivals. Experiencing nightlife. Eating out a lot. Singing karaoke with friend-groups (a must do). Saying Yes to things.
weekend_recommendations: Go on weekend-trips to other cities or go to Osaka to experience all it has to offer.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy.
socializing_tips: It was very difficult. It was made easier by living at a dormitory with local students, however many were uncomfortable with speaking english, so it was easier to do "stuff" together, instead of talking.
cultural_challenges: Humor, speaking English, cleaning-standards, and when its socially acceptable to make noise - it wasn't uncommon for my roomates to wash clothing or use the vacuum-cleaner in the middle of the night.
culture_appreciated: Food, nature, spirituality (as a non-spiritual person), art and architecture, culture-meetings, and so much more.
top3_advice: Its SUPER overwhelming (especially if you don't speak japanese), but it was also SUPER worth it!!
other_useful_info: Everything is done through Line and prepare for a lot of paperwork!
most_rewarding: Learning a lot of new things from totally different perspectives.
greatest_challenge: Being away from my home, friends and family with so much time difference.
other_comments: Thank you for the help and the possibility.

info_ease: It was Okay, but not easy
arrival_assistance: There was some help from the university and also the dorm where i stayed

activities_available: a trip to Hirishima
activities_recommended: Go see some of the cultural festivals in japan, they are very interesting
weekend_recommendations: Go se the area, and visit farway places, like Aso

socializing_tips: Do the shared activities when possible

crucial_aspects: My major is Japanese studies, so exchanging to Japan seemed obvious.
info_ease: I had received handouts prior to my arrival, so it was very easy.
arrival_assistance: Various introductions. Like the dorm, or the campus.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You "pick" courses 3 times in total, which I think is superfluous, but the process is easy enough.
registration_help: The OUSSEP office was reachable via email, and you could ask staff at the dorm for help, if needed.
registration_success: I was able to take all my classes except for one.
registration_advice: There are some deadlines they want you to honor, but if you suddenly find out you want a different class, or drop a class, they will usually help you out, from what I heard from friends.
course_level: Some have a high work-load, others a very light one. The level itself is not that high, because you're taking 7+ courses. This is regarding the OUSSEP exchange courses. I can't speak for the regular classes at OU which I assume are on a higher level.
teaching_comparison: More lecture-style classes at OU. UCPH has more seminar-style classes.
courses_enrolled: Health Service and Medical Care in Japan Osaka in Modern Japanese Literature Japan: Society and Ideology Introduction to Japanese Law Digital Culture: Literature and Art, Ethics and Aesthetics Critical Thinking in a Global Context: Navigating the Challenges Ahead Cultural Psychological Experiment
recommended_courses: Osaka in Modern Literate is really interesting and has an amazing teacher. Highly recommend. Health Service and Medical Care in Japan is good if you want a laid back course.
unexpected_costs: The move-in date the dorm wants you to arrive by is not mandatory what-so-ever. They advise the last month of march, but unless you REALLY want to go as soon as possible, I'd wait till the 1st of April, as they will charge you a full month of rent and rental fees for those 1-7 days.
cost_comparison: More or less as I expected. Food is cheap, except fruit.
activities_available: Literally hundreds of clubs and circles to join. Something for everyone.
activities_recommended: I'm sure anything is fine, but I joined the English Conversation club (takakomi) to socialize with Japanese people.
weekend_recommendations: It's Japan, I'm sure you can think of something, but I recommend going to Kyoto. Endless amounts of temples and cool places to see. Koyasan in Wakayama is also really cool, and maybe my favorite cultural site.
culture_adjustment: It was my second exchange in Japan, so I acclimated fairly easily.
socializing_tips: Join the clubs/circles.
cultural_challenges: The bureaucracy is tiresome, but you can sort of everything the first week and last week of your stay, so it's not too bad.
culture_appreciated: The safety. The kindness.
top3_advice: - Keep the deadlines that OU ask of you. You'll be less stressed. - Get a Japanese speaking person to go with you to the City Hall, as it will speed up the process, and you avoid mishaps (though you'll be fine even without one). - At the immigration booth at the airport, be sure to ask about your Certificate of Eligibility (you will have received one from OU ELECTRONICALLY). They will ask for the physical original, but you won't receive it. Be adamant about it, because this is where you get your residence card.
other_useful_info: I think I covered it all.
most_rewarding: Getting to use my Japanese, and making friends.
greatest_challenge: The summer. Spring is awesome, but the summer is rough.
other_comments: Go to Karaoke! Other than the traditional cultural stuff, karaoke was my favorite activity in Japan.

crucial_aspects: Wanted to explore other cultures
info_ease: Very easy
arrival_assistance: Yes, they where very helpful
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Well, if you chose to do your study abroad in Japan, you must prepare yourself to do a lot of paperwork. I was frustrated at times, but when I think back on it now, it was only really frustrating in the moment. We are lucky, that we live in 2025 and that google translate exist (a translator app was often a must when doing paper-stuff at the City Hall)
registration_help: A lot - specially the staff at the dorm (Global Village)
registration_success: Very succesfull! I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Enjoy it!
course_level: The level of the courses was much lower than the level at KU. Although the level was lover, the workload was higher - so it reminded me a lot of being in high school.
teaching_comparison: I did not attend any lecture while studying in Japan. The teaching-style varies a lot, and it depends a lot on which course you are taking. Mostly the teaching-style consisted of the teacher doing a lacture-talk in class, but much more relaxed than a lecture at KU.
courses_enrolled: Globalization Studies Japan: Society and Ideology Self-formation throughout life Ethics and Criminology Critical Thinking in A Global Context: Navigating the Challenges Ahead (SS) Ethical and Regenerative Cities Japanese Law
recommended_courses: I would really recommend the course 'Ethical and Regenerative Cities'. The teacher was so nice and really had some cool and exciting guest-lectures to come join the class as well. For at true Japanese experience, I would recommend 'Japan: Society and Ideology'. The teacher is from Japan himself, and it is a true experience to get his perspective on a lot of things.
unexpected_costs: You have to bear in mind, that it is mandatory to sing up for the national pension and national health insurance in Japan. You would get a discount, because you are a student with no income, but you are automatically signed up - and there is no way around that.
cost_comparison: Food is so cheap, but fruit and vegetables are more on the expensive side. A lot of the times it was actually cheaper to eat out than cooking yourself.
activities_available: A lot of student activities were offered - there is a club/circle for literally anything at the uni that you can join I did not though.
activities_recommended: Travel as much as you can.
weekend_recommendations: Travel to the north of Japan, and the south of Japan. Also, Kyoto is only a 1 h train ride from Osaka.
culture_adjustment: The Japanese people are so polite, so after af few weeks you catch yourself bowing and saying thank you at the supermarket as well.
cultural_challenges: Be quiet in the train!
culture_appreciated: The politeness for sure! But also the food culture.
top3_advice: Be prepared for paperwork :) But do no hesitate, this exchange was one of the best things I have ever done!
other_useful_info: Hmm, no I do not think so. If any, the uni gives you too much information about everything.
most_rewarding: The people I met.
greatest_challenge: The people from DK that I missed greatly.

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne både opleve en anden måde at gå på universitetet og samtidig have muligheden for at være i en helt anden kultur.
overall_comments: Jeg har haft en utroligt god oplevelse med at være i Japan og på Osaka Universitet. Det har været en helt unik mulighed, at kunne tage afsted på denne her måde. Dog har det faglige niveau generelt været ret lavt... Min afslutning på fagene var også ret så hektisk, hvor der ikke var nogen eksaminer, men til gengæld 13 opgaver eller oplæg der skulle færdiggøre mine fag... Det var en ret hektisk måde at slutte opholdet. Også fordi at disse opgaver er dem, der udgør grundlaget for om man består de forskellige fag.
info_ease: Relativt let, Japan er et information overload.
arrival_assistance: Jeg mødte de andre udvekslingsstuderende fra KU inden jeg tog afsted, og de var simpelthen en kæmpe hjælp! Universitetet var også meget behjælpelige, men deres engelske kundskaber kneb lidt, og derudover er der bare sindssygt meget bureaukrati, så man skal pakke den lange tålmodighed med sig, hver gang der er brug for nogen som helst slags hjælp.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Jeg har haft en utroligt god oplevelse med at være i Japan og på Osaka Universitet. Det har været en helt unik mulighed, at kunne tage afsted på denne her måde. Dog har det faglige niveau generelt været ret lavt... Min afslutning på fagene var også ret så hektisk, hvor der ikke var nogen eksaminer, men til gengæld 13 opgaver eller oplæg der skulle færdiggøre mine fag... Det var en ret hektisk måde at slutte opholdet. Også fordi at disse opgaver er dem, der udgør grundlaget for om man består de forskellige fag.
registration_process: Man starter med at søge fag inden man tager afsted, så søger man igen når man kommer til universitetet, så igen når man starter og så skal det endegyldigt bekræftes efter en måned.
registration_help: En masse mails
registration_success: Jeg fik de fleste af de fag jeg søgte, beskrivelsen af fagenes faglige indhold lød dog mere ambitiøst end fagene egentlig var.
registration_advice: Vælg fag du synes lyder sjove, men forvent ikke for højt niveau. Overvej måske at vælg fag der ikke er en del af din uddannelse derhjemme.
academics_comments: Jeg har haft en utroligt god oplevelse med at være i Japan og på Osaka Universitet. Det har været en helt unik mulighed, at kunne tage afsted på denne her måde. Dog har det faglige niveau generelt været ret lavt... Det var en ret hektisk måde at slutte opholdet. Også fordi at disse opgaver er dem, der udgør grundlaget for om man består de forskellige fag.
