teaching_comparison: Der var mange forskellige undervisningstyper, både online, forelæsninger og seminarer.
courses_enrolled: Sociological Theory (spændende) East asian politics (spændende) Law and society in the middle east Japanese culture through stories (utroligt dårligt tilrettelagt) Chinese and Japanese language and literature (meget skiftende niveau) Global issues in education Modern and contemporary Japanese language and literature
recommended_courses: East asian politics
unexpected_costs: gebyrer på at hæve penge?
cost_comparison: Det er virkelig billigt at spise ude, men dyrt at handle ind. Derudover er der bare langt mellem mange ting, så offentlig transport løber op hurtigt.
activities_available: ved ikke
weekend_recommendations: Jeg synes helt sikkert man skal benytte sig af de mange fede ting der er at se og gøre i Kansai regionen (og selvfølgelig også tage rundt i Japan altså)
culture_adjustment: Der er en masse, som snakker om de forskellige sociale normer og regler i Japan. Man skal vide, at mange japanere grundlæggende er ligeglade med turisters gøren, så længe man ikke er i vejen. Der er lige så mange søde Japanere, som der er irriterede japanere. Det mest udfordrende er faktisk at få hjælp til ting på engelsk.
socializing_tips: Min oplevelse er, at det tager lang tid for de japanske studerende at varme op, og at de typisk er ret usikre i engelsk. Men hvis man kan japansk, eller deltager i nogle af klubberne (hvilket nogen at mine venner gjorde), så kan det godt lade sig gøre at få en japansk bekendt.
cultural_challenges: Sproget og det japanske bureaukrati.
culture_appreciated: Templerne, priserne og izakaya.
top3_advice: 1. Ikke lad dig blive slået ud af det Japanske bureaukrati 2. Tag på en masse ture ind til byen, Osaka er totalt undervurderet! 3. Vælg nogle fag der lyder spændende, og som kan udvide dit perspektiv på verden.
other_useful_info: Søg et legat fra Sasakawa foundation
most_rewarding: At ændre min omstændighed fuldstændig. Det er simpelthen så sejt at være på de anden side af jorden, og kunne tage i totalt gakkede butikker og omkring i en helt anden kultur. Og så føles det bare så sejt at kunne finde rundt i japanske metroer uden at få koldsved ned af ryggen.
greatest_challenge: Det japanske bureaukrati, den japanske undergrund og sprogbarrierer.

crucial_aspects: Det vigtigste var relevante fag i forhold til min uddannelse og muligheden for at opleve en ny kultur. Derudover havde beliggenhed, leveomkostninger og anbefalinger fra andre studerende også betydning.
overall_comments: Jeg havde en rigtig god oplevelse under mit semester i Japan. Det var spændende at opleve en anderledes kultur i hverdagen, og jeg lærte meget både fagligt og personligt. Jeg mødte mange nye mennesker fra hele verden og fik nye perspektiver. Jeg vil klart anbefale at tage på udveksling, især til Japan, hvis man er interesseret i en unik kulturel oplevelse.
info_ease: Det var generelt nemt at finde den nødvendige information. Universitetet stiller meget materiale til rådighed om både ansøgningsprocessen, forberedelse inden afrejse, fagvalg og kursustilmelding. Dog er der meget information, og det hele er beskrevet meget detaljeret, så det kan tage tid at sætte sig ind i. Det kan virke lidt overvældende i starten, men det bliver mere overskueligt, når man først er i gang.
arrival_assistance: Ved ankomst var der en rundvisning på universitetet efterfulgt af en introduktion, hvor vi fik udleveret og gennemgået en række dokumenter i forhold til oprettelse af systemer til undervisning og hvor man finder relevant information.
arrival_comments: Alt i alt var jeg tilfreds med den støtte, der blev tilbudt. Selvom mængden af information kan virke overvældende i starten, er det godt struktureret og hjælper en med at være godt forberedt.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Jeg havde en rigtig god oplevelse under mit semester i Japan. Det var spændende at opleve en anderledes kultur i hverdagen, og jeg lærte meget både fagligt og personligt. Jeg mødte mange nye mennesker fra hele verden og fik nye perspektiver. Jeg vil klart anbefale at tage på udveksling, især til Japan, hvis man er interesseret i en unik kulturel oplevelse.
registration_process: Det var generelt nemt at gennemføre kursustilmeldingen. Dog føles det i starten lidt som et puslespil, da man skal få fagene til at passe sammen i forhold til både tidspunkter og hvilke campus de foregår på. Det betyder, at man nogle gange er nødt til at fravælge fag, man ellers gerne ville have haft. For eksempel er det ikke muligt at have to fag lige efter hinanden på forskellige campusser, da transporttiden gør det urealistisk at nå frem. Det fungerer dog fint, hvis der er lidt tid mellem undervisningen.
registration_help: Der var vejledning fra universitetet samt adgang til information og materialer, som gjorde det muligt at planlægge sin kursustilmelding. Hvis man var i tvivl, kunne man også få hjælp fra administrative medarbejdere ved at skrive.
registration_success: Efter den første kursustilmelding viste det sig, at nogle fag ikke var tilgængelige alligevel, og vi skulle derfor vælge igen. Det gjorde, at man i nogle tilfælde endte med et eller to fag, som man ikke var helt tilfreds med. Det er dog svært at undgå, især når man skal have relativt mange fag (fx 7), og samtidig få skema og transport til at gå op. Men fik ellers alle fag jeg søgte. Et par enkelte fag ved jeg der kun er et vist antal pladser, så det er lotteri.
registration_advice: Det kan være en god idé at prioritere de fag, du helst vil have, men samtidig være forberedt på, at du måske ikke får alle dine førstevalg. Vær fleksibel i dit valg af fag og hav gerne nogle alternativer klar fra start.
academics_comments: Jeg havde en rigtig god oplevelse under mit semester i Japan. Det var spændende at opleve en anderledes kultur i hverdagen, og jeg lærte meget både fagligt og personligt. Jeg mødte mange nye mennesker fra hele verden og fik nye perspektiver. Jeg vil klart anbefale at tage på udveksling, især til Japan, hvis man er interesseret i en unik kulturel oplevelse.
course_level: Der var tydelig forskel på fagene. Nogle var relativt nemme, mens andre krævede en del arbejde. Generelt var det muligt at følge med. Ved at hvis man skal have Japansk dernede er det vidst også ret krævende.
teaching_comparison: Undervisningsstilen var generelt mere struktureret og mindre selvstændig end på KU. Der var ofte mere fokus på fremmøde, løbende opgaver og deltagelse i timerne, mens undervisningen i Danmark i højere grad er baseret på selvstudie. Det krævede lidt tilvænning. Meget lytte-undervisning dog også med lidt gruppearbejde, igen varierende fra fag til fag.
courses_enrolled: Media and Communications in Japan Social Innovation and Social Design Introduction to Intercultural Communication Diversity in Aging Society Planetary Health Japanese Culture through Stories Introduction to Human-Centered Design
recommended_courses: Human-Centered Design synes jeg var meget givende, og havde et godt niveau.
unexpected_costs: Man skal have både sundheds- og ulykkesforsikring for at kunne bo i Japan. Jeg havde allerede betalt for en forsikring hjemmefra, men skulle også betale for en i Japan, hvilket var en ekstra udgift. Det var lidt frustrerende, men jeg var stadig glad for min danske forsikring, da jeg fik brug for den. Jeg vil derfor stadig anbefale at have en god forsikring hjemmefra, især hvis man planlægger aktiviteter som fx skiture.
cost_comparison: Mad, transport og generelle leveomkostninger kunne faktisk være billigere end forventet, hvis man planlægger lidt. Jeg valgte dog at bruge en del penge på oplevelser, rejser og mad, da det var en prioritet for mig. Så det meste ud over huslejen kunne nok halveres.
activities_available: Der var mange forskellige aktiviteter, både kulturelle, sociale og sportslige. Dog kræver det, at man selv er opsøgende for at blive en del af dem, da de ikke altid bliver præsenteret tydeligt for udvekslingsstuderende.
activities_recommended: Jeg vil især anbefale at deltage i aktiviteter gennem dormitory, da det er en nem måde at møde andre studerende på. Der blev arrangeret flere sociale events, som var sjove og gjorde det let at blive en del af fællesskabet.
weekend_recommendations: Osaka er en rigtig god base, da der er kort afstand til mange spændende steder. Det tager ca. 30-40 minutter til Kyoto, omkring 30 minutter til Kobe, 1 time til Nara Park og nogle få timer til Kumano Kodo, som er en populær vandrerute. Der er rigtig meget at opleve inden for rimelig afstand. Jeg vil anbefale at prioritere fag, så man fx har fri fredag eller mandag, da forlængede weekender giver gode muligheder for at rejse rundt.
culture_adjustment: Det var relativt nemt at vænne sig til, men der er selvfølgelig mange kulturelle forskelle, som man skal have respekt for. Det er en del af oplevelsen og også en af grundene til at vælge Japan. Hvis man ønsker noget mere velkendt, er Europa et nemmere valg :).
socializing_tips: Jeg vil anbefale at bo i dormitory eller fx Global Village, da der ofte bliver lavet fælles grupper og chats. Det gør det nemt hurtigt at lære andre at kende og lave aftaler, fx weekendture eller sociale aktiviteter.
cultural_challenges: Bureaukratiet og mængden af papirarbejde kan være udfordrende, især fordi mange ting ikke er lige så digitaliserede som i Danmark.
culture_appreciated: Jeg satte især pris på den respekt, der er mellem mennesker, samt kulturen omkring mad og det at spise ude.
top3_advice: Vær fleksibel i dit valg af fag, da kursustilmeldingen kan ændre sig, og ikke alle fag er tilgængelige. Prioritér din tid, så du har mulighed for at rejse og opleve landet, fx ved at have en fridag op til weekenden. Vælg bolig gennem universitetet eller dormitory, da det gør det nemt både praktisk og socialt at falde til.
other_useful_info: Vær forberedt på, at der er en del praktiske ting og papirarbejde, især i starten. Det kan virke lidt uoverskueligt, men det hele bliver lettere, når man først er kommet i gang.
most_rewarding: Den mest givende del var at opleve en helt anderledes kultur i hverdagen og møde mennesker fra hele verden. Det har givet mig nye perspektiver både fagligt og personligt. Og mange nye venner verden over.
greatest_challenge: Den største udfordring var at navigere i bureaukratiet og de mange praktiske ting, især fordi meget ikke er digitaliseret som i Danmark. Du vil også modtage meget information som også står på Japansk som man må sidde og oversætte.
other_comments: Alt i alt var det en virkelig god oplevelse, som jeg klart vil anbefale. Japan er et spændende land med mange muligheder, og man får meget ud af at være åben og opsøgende under sit ophold. Jeg vil også anbefale at søge legater og ikke spare for meget, da det er en unik oplevelse, man kun får én gang :). Held og Lykke.

institution: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences
crucial_aspects: For me, it was important to choose a destination that was somewhat foreign to me, so that I could spend my time exploring a new culture while being on exchange. It was also important that the academic classes i could follow gave me new perspectives on my study program, than i could have had back home. Lastly I wanted to choose a destination which I new would be accomodating to exchange students, and where there would be a lot of opportunities to meet other exchange student and explore the country.
info_ease: The beginning of my exchange was a bit confusing. For me, I really like being able to plan ahead, and coming to a new country I wanted to know everything about how my semester was going to be like. But we didn't get all the information (like schedule and proffessors, what to do and where to go) right when arriving, as things were still being figured out. So we had to wait a bit for all of that.
arrival_assistance: When I arrived, I was called in for a "registration day" at the Erasmus office at the university, where I was shortly introduced to the Erasmus coordinator. The week after that she held a "welcome day" on zoom where she answered a lot of our questions about the semester. The Erasmus coordinator was also very nice at helping through mail if there was any questions during the semester.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: When arriving in Athens, a registration day is scheduled, where you basically go to the Erasmus office to sign some contract. Then after the Erasmus coordinator has a welcome day, the schedule of the courses available for Erasmus students are send out. (It is also possible to follow courses in greek, but in these you don't go to the classes, but plan an individual study program with the professor from the course). When you have the schedule you can start attending classes to figure out which ones you want to register for. You then have to register for them on the uniersity's online platform where you can write with the professors and see the assignments for the class. After some time you have to oficially register for the course, by sending a registration form to the erasmus office, which they sign.
registration_help: The Erasmus coordinator and the professors helps you through the process, though its your own responsibility to manage which classes to take/which requirements there are for the courses etc.
registration_success: I managed to register for the courses I wanted. As I chose only courses from Social Anthropology which was the department I was registered in, I was "first in line" in the courses where there was a limited space.
registration_advice: Don't stress about it too much. Even though it's done in a different pace than back home, most people manage to get the courses they want. And just ask your professors or the Erasmus office if you have questions, they are there to help, and they all know that its overwhelming to be an exchange student.
course_level: The level was about the same as back home I believe. The professors expected you to have some prior knowledge to the subjects, though people in class were from different study programs, so we had different skills.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching were very different from back home. In 3/4 of my classes we were only 8-10 students in a class. And we all sat around a table and discussed the lectures with the professor. So is was very engaging and you had to participate a lot compared to a lecture back home. The exams were pretty much the same as back home, same lenght and difficulty, though one of my exams had to be written in class by hand, which was a bit different.
courses_enrolled: History of the Balkan people Ethnography of non-western states Digital anthropology Anthropology and critical discourse studies
recommended_courses: I was really surprised about the ethnography of non-western states course, as the professor Makris was very engaging and the subject were very interesting. I also really enjoyed the digital anthropology course.
unexpected_costs: When I first arrived I just wanted to have my public transportation handled for the rest of the semester, so i bought an Ath.ena card for 6 months (which was very cheap for students). But i didn't consider that I would be going to the airport a lot to pick up guests from home, so I didn't include this in my card, which meant I had to pay extra every time I wanted to go to the airport. I would recommend just buying the Ath.ena card for one month at a time, so that you can include the airport in the months where you know you will use that.
cost_comparison: Public transport was very cheap! Food was maybe a bit more expensive, especially in the touristy areas.
activities_available: There are a lot of opportunities. There are gyms, sports days, greek language course, trips within Athens and outside of Athens, events like speed friending, beer pong, parties and the list goes on. I believe that you can fill almost every day with non-academic activities if you wanted.
activities_recommended: I would definitly recommend going on the weekend trips arranged by ESN and ELA. Almost every sunday there is one or more trip you can go on, and sometimes there are longer trips. I think this is a great way to meet new people, and to explore the country.
weekend_recommendations: Again I would recommend using the opportunites that ELA and ESN provide, especially in the beginning where you also want to make new friends. I would definitely see both the main land as well as the islands, as Greece has so much different things and places to experience.
culture_adjustment: People were very welcoming and friendly. The language is very difficult, but most people a pretty good at speaking english.
socializing_tips: I didn't socialize that much with the local students, mostly with other international students, but i would recommend talking to the people who arrange the trips and events for Erasmus students, as they are mostly local students, but are very open and easy to talk to.
cultural_challenges: The mentality is very different and more relaxed than in Denmark, so that takes a bit of time getting used to, but its definitly something you get used to, and end up admiring!
culture_appreciated: The kindness of the people. Everyone I met was very open and friendly.
top3_advice: Make sure to go on a lot of trips and try to experience as much of Greece as possible, you will not regret it! Make an effort in the beginning to meet people, go to events and on trips with other exchange students, even though you might not have anyone to go there with. You will definitly meet a lot of nice people there you can talk to! Find your local farmers market! Here you can get a lot of fresh and delicious greens and veggies to a much cheaper price than in the super market.
other_useful_info: Just definitly use all the opportunities you are given as an exchange student, do some research beforehand about things you want to experience in and around Athens and don't wait until the end to do them all.
most_rewarding: Makingfriends with people from different cultural backgrounds than yourself.
greatest_challenge: Learning to be more spontanious and managing to navigate in a pretty unorganized country as a Dane who plans everything ahead.

institution: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences
crucial_aspects: That my financial situation allowed it and that it was in southern Europe.
info_ease: Extremely hard. The educational system in Panteion and the structure was very different from Copenhagen. It was more or less within the first two weeks of my stay that I even had the opportunity to know the courses.
arrival_assistance: I was assisted by Erasmus+ student team.
arrival_comments: Except from physical visits at the erasmus office, it has been extremely hard to keep in contact with the Panteion. Often mails would go unanswered or maybe take 2-3 weeks to get answered.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Before the first week we had to come to the erasmus office to fill out some papers. Then a few days later there was some digital introduction on zoom.
registration_help: The erasmus office and the erasmus student team
registration_success: Not succesfull. Only one of the antrhoplogy courses on the webside ended up being created, so I had to pick very random courses from the other departments. And apply for it around 5 times in Copenhagen.
registration_advice: Trust the proces, and know that probably something will be different from your initial wished, but it's gonna work out and people are only interested in getting you through the system.
course_level: I would say that it is impossible to elaborate on the level, because the teaching style was so different from the danish one. It was more of a "gymnasium" style teaching, with a class and a teacher creating group work.
teaching_comparison: Very different. Not as much reading or structure.
courses_enrolled: Sociology of the internet (media and communication department) English language for media and communication (media and communication department) Key issues in psychology 1 (psychology department) Systems theory & social media (psychology department) History of psychology (psychology department) Critical ethnographies of precariousness, precarity and care (anthropology department)
recommended_courses: Sociology of the internet was definately the most structued one, but the professors on the department of anthropology also had some really exciting researches.
unexpected_costs: None really, most stuff was super affordable.
cost_comparison: I knew that Greece would be cheap because of the financial crisis, but I was actually surprised about the supermarket prices and how similar they were to Denmark.
activities_available: Sports clubs of different kinds. But I ended up joining an expat sport center for free called "Yoga and sports in athens".
activities_recommended: I would recommend doing volunteer word. Great opportunity to meet other expat and give something back to the city - I did volunteering in "Khora" which worked with food distribution to homeless people.
weekend_recommendations: Do usual turist stuff - museums, go for a run in the national garden, sit in a coffe shop with a book, take your flatmates out to eat, go to the market on saturdays.
culture_adjustment: Easy I would say. I had been on vacation a lot of times in greece and I love the more "village" vibe atmosphere and relaxed attitude.
socializing_tips: It can be hard to encounter locals in the erasmus enviroment, but maybe try and not sit together with your international friends but force yourself to sit with some locals.
cultural_challenges: Not really anything, but the lack of structure in the univeristy system.
culture_appreciated: The relaxed attitude and the village atmosphere, where most people in the local neighbourhood noticed you and asked where you came from
top3_advice: 1. Everything is gonna work out and you're gonna get your degree, even if the system is completely different. They only wan't you go get through. 2. Take things one day at a time, you're gonna encounter different phases of homesickness and joy, but everything will pass. 3. Try not to call your friends too much, it can interrupt the experience and make you more homesick.
other_useful_info: Use the erasmus office! They are extremely helpfull and much more easy to get a hold on physically then digitally.
most_rewarding: Knowing that I can be on my own in a totally strange place.
greatest_challenge: Maintaining a relationship longdistance
other_comments: No

institution: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences
crucial_aspects: A destination quite far from Denmark in terms of climate and culture, and that it was a big city with many cultural opportunities while being close to nature. It was also important for me that it was a affordable destination. Athens is great because you can easily take a ferry to the islands or rent a car to go to the mountains, while still being a big city with many opportunities. And the food is amazing!! and cheap!!
overall_comments: Athens is very vibrant and many events are taking place! from film festivals to concerts and political events
info_ease: It was quite easy finding accomondation in Athens, the university forwarded me some websites they recommended for renting. On the other hand was it hard to find information about the courses available at Panteion. My advice is to not spend to much time on searching for courses beforehand, everything will be way easier when you are there:)
arrival_assistance: I recieved assisteance from the ersamus office and from the people involved in the ESN (erasmus student netwotk). In genral if you need assistence, the erasmus coordinator at Panteion is responding quit fast by email or you can always visit the office at university
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Athens is very vibrant and many events are taking place! from film festivals to concerts and political events
registration_process: you get a schedule of the courses the week you start at the university. Then you can try out different courses and after almost two month you officially register for the courses you want.
registration_help: the erasmus office was always open for assistence
registration_success: I got all the courses i wanted
registration_advice: again dont stress about it, and maybe try to choose some courses that dont have to big essays to write in the end. I ended up only having courses where I had to write essays for my exams, and I therefore spended a lot of time in the library. And some courses without any form of eaxams and that was nice because I had so many assignments to write.
academics_comments: Athens is very vibrant and many events are taking place! from film festivals to concerts and political events
course_level: The level is not that high.
teaching_comparison: I bit similar just with way less resources.
courses_enrolled: Critical Theories and Ethnographies of Precarity, Precariousness and Care Anthropology of Dance Key issues in Psychology – Erasmus Environment, Infrastructures, Development: Anhropological Perspectives Managing diversity in different life domains
recommended_courses: I would recommend the course, Environment, Infrastructures, Development: Anhropological Perspectives, I think it was the only course where I had a big outpout from. The professor is interesting and you read interesting texts. Also, Managing diversity in different life domains, beacuse the professor is so funny in a weird way and you just have to attend the coruse to pass.
unexpected_costs: I just spended a lot of money on travelling, but that is well spended money! also etaling and drinking a lot out! even though it is cheap, it becomes expensive if ypu do it every day....
cost_comparison: the prizes in the supermarkets are quite similar to Denmark which really surprised me. Always buy your vegetables at the local market
activities_available: all kinds of sports
activities_recommended: there are plenty of cultural events taking place in athens. You can look at kinomatorama.net for activities, it is a left oriented websites that has a calender for events taking place in Athens. Especially political events
weekend_recommendations: go to the islands! but also the mainland is so so beautifull! especially peleponies and the mountains in the north
culture_adjustment: It was easy. But athens is way more chaotic than copenhagen. I like that but can also be exhausting
socializing_tips: I almost only had erasmus friends... but i took classes at a local dancing studio and there i found some friends. So engage yourself with some kind of sport outside of university or do som volunteer work in som of the citys many squatted places

institution: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences
crucial_aspects: As a dramatic as possible culture change - and the weather!
overall_comments: The Greek school-system can be a bit heavy, especially when you are used to clear information e.g. about deadlines and other important information from the Danish system. It flows a bit more casual.
info_ease: Very easy! Once the semester started - before that, just forget about it. Don't waste time on too much research beforehand, it will just complicate things. The Erasmus Office at Panteion was VERY helpful and always available!
arrival_assistance: I had a lot of questions, especially in the cource-selection period. I send A LOT of emails with Evie, the contact for Erasmus, and she was ALWAYS kind and helpful - I also dropped by her office some times.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The Greek school-system can be a bit heavy, especially when you are used to clear information e.g. about deadlines and other important information from the Danish system. It flows a bit more casual.
registration_process: Very easy, they have a Welcome day with a presentation, and then you just book an appointment online. You have to print out in advance the form from Mobility Online, but this is also very easy - there are copy-shops all over Athens, and it is very, very cheap to print.
registration_help: The Erasmus coordinator was always available to answer my email, usually within a few days.
registration_success: Oh this took a while.... I think other people has a more smooth experience than me. I wanted to make good use of my free selection of courses, so I chose a lot of different courses, but getting confirmation from the professors did not always happen so fast. Almost the whole first month the process is that you can try out courses, and then lock them in later. I locked down my final courses only in December, which was very late, but I cleared it with the Erasmus office at Panteion. The problem was that I needed to hit between 30 and 32 ECTS due to my university in DK, and the courses in Panteion was often very small, so I ended up with 6 courses.
registration_advice: Don't do too much research before the semester starts!! You never know what subjects from last year will be available to Erasmus. But apply for your Erasmus grant as early as possible, so you don't go without money, if the registration process drags out. Use the Erasmus course selection (different from the one available to Greek students - find it through the Panteion's Erasmus webpage), to apply for the grant. Then forget about the courses, and just wait for the new course-catalog. It will be published pretty late, when the semester starts - but this is okay! Because you have the whole first month to try out and select courses. Be aware that there is often no link between the number of ECTS and the exam that you have to perform - some 3 ECTS courses have giant exams, and some bigger have smaller. Just try to get that information, because you will start making your exams almost immediatly.
academics_comments: The Greek school-system can be a bit heavy, especially when you are used to clear information e.g. about deadlines and other important information from the Danish system. It flows a bit more casual.
course_level: I took a lot of courses outside of my normal field - so I don't really know.
teaching_comparison: It is a lot of smaller classes, especially for Erasmus, because there is a lot of courses which is only for Erasmus, and not for Greek students. I took a lot of courses as reading courses. From the descriptions I thought I would be provided with bibliography that I would have to self-study - in most instances however, I was just provided with an exam description, and I had to find my own information, and basically just start writing my exam.
courses_enrolled: Key Issues in Psychology I Language and Communication in Digital Media Criminological approaches to Criminal Law and the Institutions of Criminal Justice Ι Anthropology of Dance Behavioural Analysis Statistics II
recommended_courses: Key Issues in Psychology I is an introduction course - the exam is just compulsory attendance. They introduce the other psychology courses that are available for Erasmus, I found it exiting and that is how I found Behavioural Analysis, which was exiting, and consisted of a good book that I was provided, and a handwritten exam. Statistics II was also good, provided material and multiple choice exam. I also liked Anthropology of Dance, but it was also a bit strange introduction-like course.
unexpected_costs: Not really any.
cost_comparison: Food is cheap compared to DK - I spend more than I would in DK, but that was because I never cooked meals myself. Panteion has a canteen where Erasmus students can collect three meals per day also. Transport is super cheap for students, unlimited for 13 euro per month with Athena card, and even without transport is 1,20 euros for 90 minutes in the whole Athens area just by scanning your bank card. Computer and electronic repair is suuuuper cheap! My computer died COMPLETELY, and I had it fixed for 40 euros around Omonia.
activities_available: Erasmus student network have a lot of events, trips, parties, local events. I didn't attend.
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining a local volunteer organisation! It is a good way to connect outside of University. I worked with street cats. The organisations Nine Lives and The Adespota Exarchia. They always need help with fostering or feeding cats. Had a beautiful feeding route one day a week in Zappeion garden. There are thousands of street-cats in Athens.
weekend_recommendations: Voula is the best beaches, 1,5 hours from Athens! The Islands are of course also amazing. I stayed in Athens a lot - it is a city of endless things to do. Lycabettus Hill has the best view inside the city, and it is easy to walk, with a cafe on top. Try to catch a show at the Odeon of Herodes Atticus! It is ancient an a cool experience - both opera and dance-shows. The Eleonas market on Saturdays and Sundays, they sell every used item you can imagine. Also the 1-5 euro used clothes shops, mainly located in Omonia on Pattisia, called things like Italy Outlet. Local farmers markets on Saturdays on different streets.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, time is MUCH more relaxed in Athens - and I love it. Remember to tip service providers and restaurants! A lot of people know English, even though they say they don't.
socializing_tips: I found it difficult, because the classes are so separate. I mostly socialized outside of the University.
cultural_challenges: Also the time understanding - especially when dealing with deadlines at my own university. But it ended up not really being a problem at all.
culture_appreciated: The relaxed time, the social life on the streets - Greeks are outside at cafes and bars every evening, every day of the week at all seasons. It is wonderfully vibrant!
top3_advice: Calm down <3 It may seem to move slow, but it is suppose to - lean into it, nothing bad will happen!
other_useful_info: Hmmm, I think I covered it in the previous sections.
most_rewarding: Helping the local girls with the cats!
greatest_challenge: I arrived early, and it took me a bit of time to meet people.

crucial_aspects: As a student of Asia Studies with specialization it is crucial to master the Chinese language. The best place to do that is in China.
overall_comments: The language program at Peking University greatly enhanced my Chinese language skills.
info_ease: It was easy to find information on general logistics. The language course information would not be available until about 7-9 days into the stay. That was no problem for my stay, the only problem was that my university requested information about these courses much earlier and I could not provide it before this time. The main problem was the fact that there are no available course catalogues for graduate students. Undergraduates a provided with a webside through which they can access information about all undergraduate courses and through which they can register to courses. Information about graduate courses can only be provided by personal request to each faculty to provide information on which courses they offer on the relevant semester. Furthermore the registration procedure is in person and requires a back and forth between the faculty and the office for exchange students to fill out a document and get necessary stamples. The information about this procedure is not informed anywhere. It was through several vigorous requests in person at the office for exchange students that I was finally informed about this procedure for registering for a master level course.
arrival_assistance: I was informed to register at the office for exchange student where I could ask for assistance. I was also instructed by email to join a wechatgroup for exchange students where the staff of the office for exchange students responded to inquiries. Inquiries concerning master courses were not responded to, but all other inquiries were.
arrival_comments: I was very satisfied except this one problem. Graduate students are offered no information as to how to access information on and register for courses. It took a lot of insistance on my side, and I was rather shocked when the responsible person for exchange students advised me to take undergraduate courses instead of graduate courses. Of course I informed her that I was a masters student, and that my university would only give merit to graduate courses. Still she assured me that the undergraduate courses at Peking University are on a very high academic level and questioned whether it was me personally or my home university that would not accept me taking undergraduate courses instead of graduate courses. I think that it would be productive if this misunderstanding was dealt with between the University of Copenhagen and Peking University. It seems as if the University provides undergraduate students access to registering for undergraduate courses with a certain guarantee that they can attend courses with that aberdabei that it is a lottery whether they get a spot. When it comes to graduate courses exchange students need to get permission from the department and the professor of a given course personally. This procedure is so different from the procedure in Denmark that I think students should be informed beforehand about this procedure, specially since there is no information about the procedure on arrival and since it is only provided after a lot of inquiry.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The language program at Peking University greatly enhanced my Chinese language skills.
registration_process: I went to the Xintaiyang Student Center and registered myself, bringing the required documents.
registration_help: Alle answers to qustions were provided on the wechat group.
registration_success: I was extremely successful but it took a lot of time and effort to register for my graduate course and I was lucky to make it in time. There is no standard procedure and not much help regards registering for graduate courses. Acquiring course information required biking from faculty to faculty to ask which courses the given faculty provided for the semester. Some would print out course information, some would allow you to take a picture of the courses you were interested in from a print out. Then you had to contact the professor of a course you were interested in and ask if you could attend his course. You would have to find the professors contact details yourself since they were not provided. The official faculty webside in English would not necessarily have the information.
registration_advice: If you are a graduate student: be ready to walk from faculty to faculty OR hurry and find a Chinese graduate student friend and have him help you access his system. Then you can see which courses are provided and you won't have to visit as many faculties.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere where I knew there would be a big Erasmus network. The prospect of being part of a large and diverse community through Erasmus was appealing as it meant I would have the opportunity to meet people from various cultural backgrounds. This, I believed, would not only enhance my social experience but also contribute to a broader and more global perspective in my studies. Of course, the availability and quality of programs were also important factor for my study destination. Additionally, I considered the cost of living, aiming for affordability. Lastly, having a warm climate was a welcomed bonus for me in choosing a study destination.
info_ease: Initially, it felt like a jungle. Navigating through a different website and figuring out how the foreign university structures its courses and follows its academic calendar posed challenges. However, once the system's ways were understood, it became relatively manageable to comprehend.
arrival_assistance: I received all information on mail which worked well. There was also a dedicated mobility office for exchange students where one could drop in and ask questions. They arranged two types of introduction/orientation meetings. One for all exchange students collectively and one for your specific faculty in which you were enrolled.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: They had a link for course information and a link for course schedules which was useful to finding information. However, these links had to be accessed through the website; you couldn't copy and save them for future reference because they would become invalid after some time. And finding the links on the website in the first place could be a little bit difficult and hard to remember for subsequent use. The registration process for courses operated on a specific timeframe, utilising a first-come, first-served basis. This created a stressful experience, with the website crashing multiple times during the initial registration window. Fortunately, after 15 minutes, the system stabilised, allowing me to successfully register for my courses using the guidance provided in the PDF document sent to students before the registration period.
registration_help: I could contact them via email or phone, and they were helpful in assisting me and redirecting my call to the appropriate person when I reached out.
registration_success: Fortunately, after the system remained stable beyond the initial 15 minutes, I was able to successfully enrol in the courses of my choice. I recall only one course being already full, but luckily, my backup option proved effective. Upon arrival and completion of the first week of school, there was the option to add/drop courses, providing convenience. However, it also introduced a bit of chaos as, within such a short timeframe (one week), it was challenging to gauge the courses accurately. Nevertheless, they opened a new window for adding and dropping courses in the subsequent weeks, which was a positive aspect. Moreover, UPF followed a trimester system, whereas you may be accustomed to semesters at your home institution. Consequently, you were required to complete 30 ECTS credits at a university that typically operates with 20 ECTS credits per trimester. This translated to a substantial workload for me, involving the study of six courses as opposed to the three or four courses that others at the university undertook.
registration_advice: I would strongly find a way to not have 30 ECTS credits workload at a university that operates with less per semester/trimester.
course_level: The difficulty level was acceptable, slightly easier than what I was accustomed to at my home institution. However, the trade-off was a significantly heavier workload. Attendance was mandatory, and in most courses, there were multiple assignments to submit. This workload compensated for the comparatively lighter course content.
teaching_comparison: A notable difference was evident in the approach to class engagement and participation. The host institution placed a stronger emphasis on interactive learning methods, encompassing obligatory class discussions, group projects, and presentations. Thus, UPF demanded a more intensive commitment, with a requirement for regular class attendance and active involvement in various academic activities. However, the readings were not as extensive and weighty as those at UCPH but being able to structure your own time and way of learning as you can at home, is not so much of an option at UPF. To say it shortly, it is like doing high school all over again
courses_enrolled: Global Cities Human Resources Marketing Social Psychology of Organisations Contemporary Thought
recommended_courses: They have several faculties and campuses and you can enrol at all of them (even despite the fact that the specific agreement between UCPH and UPF is with the Humanities faculty) as long as you can make it fit in your calendar and there's are spots free of course. My courses were good and I can recommend them. Finding courses that matches your liking should not be too difficult.
unexpected_costs: I didn't encounter many unforeseen expenses. I prioritised experiences such as traveling and exploring different places, which, naturally, can be quite costly. However, it's worth noting that pickpocketing is prevalent in Barcelona. I know of a lot of people who had their phones and belongings stolen, so it's crucial to be cautious as this could result in unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: I thought groceries would be cheaper than in DK but it was almost the same. Going out for dinner er was also cheaper in general than in DK but not a lot cheaper.
activities_available: I didn't join any clubs etc. so I am not the right one to ask but I think there were different possibilities of joining different things but I am not too sure.
activities_recommended: I didn't join any clubs etc. so I am not the right one to ask but I think there were different possibilities of joining different things but I am not too sure.
weekend_recommendations: Absolutely, make sure to explore the Gaudi buildings, Montjuic mountain, and wander through the streets of Eixample and Passeig de Gracia, among others. I also took the opportunity to travel to Marrakech, leveraging the proximity to other new destinations compared to being in Denmark. Additionally, I explored Costa Brava (coast region a small drive north from BCN) and Sitges (a cute small city an hr drive from BCN) during my time in Spain. I also saw El Clásico in Barcelona and took a trip to Madrid as well.
culture_adjustment: Considering the challenges of relocating from familiar surroundings, friends, and family, the process of settling in Barcelona was fairly smoothly. While the culture and overall environment weren't drastically different from home, there were still numerous opportunities to learn and experience new things.
socializing_tips: Join the Erasmus network to socialise with other students. UPF has one of the best Erasmus initiatives and activities from trips, parties and learning Spanish/Catalan (from own experience and from what I have heard from other students studying at other universities in BCN).
cultural_challenges: The way they structured the school was definitely the hardest thing for me to adapt to. Many of the locals did not speak English which can also be a bit challenging but you always find a way!
culture_appreciated: In Spain, punctuality and adherence to meeting times are not as strict, which can create a more laid-back atmosphere once you get accustomed to the rhythm. The tapas culture, characterized by the practice of sharing, is also a pleasant and distinct experience compared to Denmark, where individuals typically order one dish per person.
top3_advice: Workload is a lot and schedule is full if you take 30 ECTS. Barcelona offers the convenience of having everything nearby! Make the most of it. The city boasts the sea, mountains within the city and other stunning landscapes just a few hours' (even just 1 hr) drive away. If you don't know anyone going to Barcelona, join their Erasmus network.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Being independent and overcoming obstacles coming out stronger on the other side every time is so rewarding in the end – because you do face challenges when you go on exchange but everyone else is facing their own challenges and often times the same as you about going on exchange. Meeting a lot of different people. I had a group project in every course I took (just a single or two in each) which meant I was in different groups learning to work with different people and adapting to different work ethics. This experience was actually quite educational and enriching.
greatest_challenge: Feeling lonely at times and figuring out how to handle 30 ECTS credits load.

overall_comments: My exchange experience was significantly affected by serious administrative and structural issues related to the ECTS requirements. In practice, the host university normally only allowed exchange students to enrol in up to 20 ECTS, which directly conflicted with the home university’s and Erasmus programme’s requirement of 30 ECTS for a full-time semester. This issue was not identified in advance but only became apparent when I personally raised the concern with my home university. This created major uncertainty about whether I would even be able to go on exchange at all and caused considerable stress during the planning process. Despite later attempts to allow some flexibility, it proved extremely difficult in practice to combine courses amounting to 30 ECTS without timetable overlaps or the risk of courses being removed. As a result, beside countless hours of emailing, stress and a big workload I am now missing 7 ECTS, despite having studied more than full-time during my exchange. I see this as a problem in establishing an exchange agreement that does not realistically allow students to meet the formal academic requirements in practice. Overall, the responsibility for identifying was on me, and there this lead to a lot of diffculties since noone could tell med how they would affect my stay , which to me is highly problematic. I strongly recommend that exchange agreements are reviewed more thoroughly in advance to ensure they are actually possible and do not place students in such vulnerable academic and financial positions.

institution: Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro
crucial_aspects: I chose Brazil because I had visited before and loved it there. What made the experience even more appealing was the opportunity to learn a new language alongside my studies.
info_ease: PUC provided clear and helpful information upon arrival, and their guidance was generally very good. However, some parts of the process took place quite late, which caused a certain level of stress, although everything ultimately worked out. On the other hand, the information from KU was less clear, and the partnership agreement was finalized just before the application deadline. As a result, I had to pay a higher tuition fee.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival, a bus picked me up at the airport, and the following day there was an introduction session at PUC. Overall, the assistance provided was very good and made the transition smooth.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process took place relatively late and you have to be fast to get the subjects that you want. I would strongly recommend being quick during registration and deciding on alternative subjects in advance in case your first choices are unavailable.
registration_help: PUC was very helpful and provided support when needed, including assisting students with enrollment in classes when necessary.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted but had more classes than recommended since my mandatory Portuguese lessons where not part of ECTS in Denmark.
registration_advice: I would advise future exchange students to be prepared for a late registration process and to act quickly once registration opens. It is important to have alternative courses in mind in case your preferred subjects are full, and to stay in contact with the host institution, as they are generally helpful with enrollment issues.
course_level: PUC does not offer many master’s-level courses, as the bachelor’s programs are significantly longer than in Denmark. However, this worked out well, and I was able to take several interesting bachelor-level courses, all of which were approved by my home institution.
teaching_comparison: Compared to UCPH, the teaching style involved more sitting and listening, with less student engagement during classes. However, several courses included field tours, which added a practical dimension to the learning experience. The academic level was generally good, and some exams were handwritten and conducted in class.
courses_enrolled: Brazilian Foreign Policy I INT AREA STUDIES III - Art & Resistance in Latin America ADVANCED STUDIES IN IR V - Extremism in the Americas DEMOCRACY HUMAN RIGHTS IN BRAZIL INEQUALITY AND DIVERSITY URBAN CONTEXTS Portuguese Level 1
recommended_courses: I would recommend Brazilian Foreign Policy I, as it provides valuable insight into Brazil’s role in international realtions and their shifting policies. I would also highly recommend INT Area Studies III - Art & Resistance in Latin America, which offers a unique interdisciplinary perspective on Latin American history, culture, and political resistance through art
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Way more expensive than expected. Luckily I received a lot of scholarships.
activities_available: A variety of cultural, athletic, and social activities were available, including different sports and many social events for students. However, I did not participate extensively, so my knowledge of the specific activities offered is somewhat limited.
activities_recommended: I would recommend taking part in social events and activities organized for exchange students, as they are a great way to meet people and become part of the student community. I would also encourage students to explore the city and Brazilian culture outside of campus, as this is a big part of the exchange experience.
weekend_recommendations: I’d recommend visiting São Paulo and Ilha Grande, but honestly there’s already so much to see and do in Rio de Janeiro that you can easily spend most weekends just exploring the city.
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy to adjust to the local culture. People were very welcoming, and spending time in the city helped me feel comfortable quickly, even though some cultural differences took a bit of time to get used to.
socializing_tips: I would recommend being open and proactive, as local students are generally very welcoming. Joining group activities, talking to people in class, and making an effort to learn and use Portuguese all helped a lot.
cultural_challenges: Safety was the most challenging cultural difference for me, particularly the need to be more cautious and avoid walking alone at night.
culture_appreciated: I really loved the culture. The samba, the overall vibe, and the energy of the city made living there an amazing experience.
top3_advice: First, don’t be too scared, it is just a big city. Second, be flexible and open-minded, especially with courses and housing. Third, take advantage of the experience outside of academics by exploring the city and engaging with the local culture.
other_useful_info: Things may feel a bit unstructured at times, especially in the beginning, but it usually works out. Patience and flexibility are important. Learning some basic Portuguese before arriving is very helpful.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the friendships I made, the experiences I had, gaining a deeper understanding of South America, and learning a new language.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was the process of starting over in a new place, which could be both mentally and emotionally draining at times.

crucial_aspects: The most important factor for me was that the language of the destination was English. Furthermore, it was crucial to go to a big city which normally have more cultural diversity than other city and normally also more exchange students.
info_ease: It was easy to find information provided by University of Copenhagen but I found it a bit more difficult to find information provided by Queen Mary University. However, I think the reason for this is that I'm used to navigating the website and system of University of Copenhagen.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance in finding my way around campus and assistance at the law reception regarding classes and exams.
arrival_comments: Queen Mary University was really good at creating a welcome programme with a lot of activities and opportunities to meet other students. The Law School also arranged their own welcome events for law students which I found really cool.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I was a bit confused as to if the registration for exchange students happened on a frist come, first served basis or not. I later found out that it did not.
registration_help: I was always possible to contact the Law reception where I received an answer really quick.
registration_success: I got all the four classes I wanted.
registration_advice: My advice is to contact the host institution to be sure how the process of registration is before the registration opens.
course_level: Three of the classes I took were at level 6 which is the level for either second or third year of the undergraduate. The last class (contract law) was at level 4 which is the first year of the undergraduate. It was easy to feel the difference between the two levels. Overall, I think the level of courses are more of less the same as UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was more of less the same as UCPH. The structure of each class was also lectures and smaller classes where we solved cases and went through the material from the lecture. Due to Covid all the lectures were online and put on the website after or pre-recorded.
courses_enrolled: United Kingdom Human Rights Law, Competition Law, Comparative Constitutional Law and Contract Law I: Formation and Vitiation.
recommended_courses: I would recommend Competition Law as it is interesting and the EU-based. I would also recommend Contract Law as it is really interesting to see how a Common Law jurisdiction deals with contract law.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: The local transportation was more expensive than expected. Groceries were less expensive. Restaurants, pubs, bars were the same as expected. Most museums have free entrance making it less expensive than expected.
activities_available: A lot of different sports club and different societies based on education, religion, belief, country, interests. It was also possible to join academic activities. I was happily surprised with how many activities there were.
activities_recommended: The Erasmus Student Network, a sports club to really connect with the British Students and different societies related to your field of study.
weekend_recommendations: London has everything. Experience as much of it as possible - restaurants, clubs, pubs, bars, museums, walks around the city, markets, shows, concerts, comedy shows, football matches etc. I also really recommend going on a day trip to Brighton or Oxford.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. I find that the British culture is very similar to the Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Go to ALL the welcome events in the beginning, join clubs and societies and go to their events.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any part of the British culture challenging.
culture_appreciated: How multicultural it is. I liked that you can walk down a fancy street, turn a corner and suddenly it is more young vibrant area.
top3_advice: 1) try to get a recommendation on campus 2) explore the city 3) engage in societies, clubs etc on campus
other_useful_info: Queen Mary University of London is a real campus university which is really nice.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange was by far that I had to build a whole new social network which led me to become friends with people around the world.
greatest_challenge: At first it was really difficult to become close friends with people because I'm not used to making jokes and fun side comments etc in English.
other_comments: GO to Queen Mary University of London!!! It was the most amazing experience.

crucial_aspects: I chose London of several reasons. First, It was my wish to study in an english-speaking country, I have always wanted to live in London and I have friends who live there.

unexpected_costs: I don't think I had unexpected cost, but the high cost of housing was very unexpected, but something I new before I went.

socializing_tips: The people there are really friendly and open - everyone was very interested in chatting and making new connections.
cultural_challenges: Did not find any challenging.
culture_appreciated: The pub culture!
top3_advice: Explore London as much as you can - three months is not long, so enjoy it while you are there! Socialize - People are very interested to make new friends It is going to be more expensive than you think, so apply for extra grants if you need it.
other_useful_info: Use the two-week introduction week and switch module if you don't enjoy the seminars - it is awful to be stuck with a module.
most_rewarding: For me the most rewarding part was to live in London and explore it with my new friends, but of course also to study at another university and to study in english - I really enjoyed that!
greatest_challenge: I think my greatest challenge in the beginning was to get over my fear of speaking in class, but in one of my modules you had to, so that helped a lot. And to afford all the things you wanna see while you are on exchange.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an english-speaking country and thought that would also be a good opportunity to further my legal english vocabulary.
overall_comments: Not a 10, because some of the information from our host university was not consistent with what we were told when we arrived at our exchange university.
info_ease: Fairly easy, but as mentioned, some of the information we got from QMUL was not consistent with what we were told back at our host-university or what was stated in the information pamphlet.
arrival_assistance: We were given the opportunity to speak with the Global Opportunities office during orientation week, which was nice.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Not a 10, because some of the information from our host university was not consistent with what we were told when we arrived at our exchange university.
registration_process: It was fairly easy as we got a link from our home institution and just had to fill out the information. After that we received a registration number which we used when registering for classes and so on.
registration_help: We could ask our home institution if anything was unclear, and we had also received an email-address for the contact person at our host university.
registration_success: I got almost all the classes I initially registered for. One of them was not created so I was given one of the alternatives I listed.
registration_advice: The options available for exchange students are quite slim, so be prepared to take classes you don't necessarily find super interesting.
academics_comments: Not a 10, because some of the information from our host university was not consistent with what we were told when we arrived at our exchange university.
course_level: The levels of the courses were quite different. I had one first year (level 4) course, while others were level 6 and intended for second year students. The courses were very different in nature so the level of them are not very comparable.
teaching_comparison: Similar in some ways and very different in others. At Queen Mary the tutorials and seminars were much more discussion based, while the style of teaching at UCPH is more of a run-through of the curriculum with time for questions and discussions if anything is unclear.
courses_enrolled: Contract Law - Competition Law - Democracy and Justice - Law, Knowledge, Power
recommended_courses: Competition Law was very informative and useful for out further studies at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: Transportation was a bit more expensive than expected.
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than expected, but it was not surprising with the general rise in prices.
activities_available: Various sorts of sports; football, swimming, running, climbing etc. The clubs organised social gatherings with the members.
activities_recommended: The sports clubs are nice if you want to try a new sport or have a interest in one already, but I didn't do any clubs so I wouldn't know what to recommend.
weekend_recommendations: There are many opportunities to do day trips or weekend trips to, for example, Bath, Oxford or Cambridge. The different markets in London are also very fun to visit on weekends.
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy as England is not that different from what we're used to and I had visited London many times before, but it did take some time to adjust to the different style of teaching and university experience in general.
socializing_tips: Everyone I talked to was very friendly and willing to help answer any question you might have about the university or school. I'd recommend just talking to people in class or at the campus cafés, everybody's really friendly.
cultural_challenges: The difference I found the most difficult was more academic as it took me a bit of time to adjust to learning about law in a common law system as opposed to a civil law system.
culture_appreciated: People are much more likely to come up and talk to you in class, restaurants and bars, which I only thought was a fun thing.
top3_advice: 1) Search for housing in good time, 2) be prepared for a limited choice of classes, 3) the teachers expect a lot more participation through discussions in seminar-based classes.
other_useful_info: The coffee at the Grond Cafe is better than at the small Starbucks at The Curve ;)
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and getting out of my comfort zone having to adjust to a whole new everyday life in a new city.
greatest_challenge: Not seeing my family and friends for such a long period of time.
other_comments: Exchange is nerve-racking, but it's an experience of a life time. If you are considering it, go for it.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an English speaking country.
info_ease: Very easy. The University of Copenhagen and Queen Mary University of London were both very helpful.
arrival_assistance: A Queen Mary counsellor helped me adding and dropping classes.
arrival_comments: The staff is really trying to help but unfortunately they gave us wrong information quite a few times. We did not know all of our exam dates before two weeks before the exam. Moreover, we were told that all exams would be done by December 16th which is incorrect because we also have exams in January.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You make an application to get KU's nomination which is quite easy and fast. After getting the nomination you must apply for Queen Mary University which is also quite easy.
registration_help: Both Queen Mary and KU are very helpful if you have any questions. The Queen Mary staff replies very fast.
registration_success: You cannot count on the module description on the website of Queen Mary. They will send you a separate document with the modules you are allowed to take. I was told that I could take classes from level 4, 5 and 6 but that is not true. You get to choose between 10 classes and most of them are about philosophy and how philosophers look at law and justice.
registration_advice: Go to London if you want to experience the city. I can recommend doing family law and competition law.
course_level: The classes are very boring and the teachers are having 2 hours monologues where they ask max. 2 questions. Most teachers do not give us breaks and if they do we get 2 min so we can't even make it to the toilets. The tutorials are good because we actually get to participate.
teaching_comparison: They do not include students very much and no breaks. The teacher will talk nonstop for 2 hours. They have very low expectations to the students. They have seminars, lectures and tutorials. I did like the tutorials a lot because students are involved. The tutorials are quite similar to the way they teach at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Family law, competition law, climate justice anf democracy and justice
recommended_courses: Family law and competition law because you learn something in those classes and they are quite interesting. You also meet British students in these classes.
unexpected_costs: I lived with family so my rent was very low compared to other places in London.
cost_comparison: I spent a lot more on food than expected. Also alcohol is more expensive than in Denmark.
activities_available: There are so many societies that I can't even say a society that is not created.
activities_recommended: It is good to join a society of any kind if you want to meet British students. Your classes will mainly consist of exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: Go out to eat. Covent Garden is really nice. If you want to go out, I liked Soho the most. Shoreditch is also good if you want to go to a bar. Many parts of the Tube closes at night so download the Uber app so you can get home.
culture_adjustment: It is not that different from Denmark so it was not that difficult.
socializing_tips: Join a society.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any particularly challenging.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study politics from a more comparative perspective - i.e. how migration is managed in the UK compared to other European countries. Furthermore, I wished to study more closely the political, sociological and economic drivers behind the UK's relationship with the EU. At Queen Mary I had the opportunity to do so.
overall_comments: I really recommend going abroad for just a term or two. It has been a great experience both academically and personally
info_ease: I think it was quite easy. The information letters/email from the Study Abroad services at the University of Copenhagen and Queen Mary provided the essential information I needed. As a student you must read these emails as a manual - following every step.
arrival_assistance: The information letters/email from the Study Abroad services at Queen Mary provided the essential information I needed. As a student you must read these emails as a manual - following every step. Once every two week, I received a mail describing how to enroll, select courses, what to do in the area, how write an academic assignment in the UK educational system etc.
arrival_comments: It was very good. I am very satisfied. The "study abroad team" answered all my questions quickly and kindly. The orientation in the first week was thorough assisting students academically and in relation to our general well-being. They were aware of the transition needed in order to live and study in a new country.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I really recommend going abroad for just a term or two. It has been a great experience both academically and personally
registration_process: Before arriving the host institution have a "pre-registration periode". In this periode you apply for the classes you want to take. After the two-week registration periode, the responsible academic department then decides whether or not you get the class. In the first two-weeks of the term you can then apply for changes to your courses - and many students attend one lecture in the first weeks in order to figure out whether they like the course. After the two first weeks of term the registration to classes are final.
registration_help: The study abroad team was very helpfull - both in person and writing (mail).
registration_success: In the pre-registration periode both of my desired classes was approved. But just before the first lecture, one of my classes was canceled. I then used the first week of the term to find another class. I found one I liked, applied and got registered successfully.
registration_advice: Take your time when readying the informative emails from the host institution - and do not be afraid to reach out and ask the administration questions. I have been writing to both lectures, study abroad officers and administrative personal and they have all been keen to help me.
academics_comments: I really recommend going abroad for just a term or two. It has been a great experience both academically and personally
course_level: The courses I could take was on the highest level available at the masters programme of Queen Mary. In general the academic level of the lectures was equivalent to that of a "elective course" at my home university. Some of the required readings was less heavy and more factual (e.g. reports from NGO's and podcasts) than I have been used to at home. So I think an average Danish exchange student would find the level comfortable and not too challenging.
teaching_comparison: It was very much alike. The weekly two-hour classes consisted of approximately one hour lecture followed by an hour of student-led seminars with either presentations or discussions in groups.
courses_enrolled: 1) International Migration and Public Policy 2) From Blitz to Brexit: Britain and the EU
recommended_courses: I can recommend both. I would especially recommend the course "From Blitz to Brexit: Britain and the EU" if you are interested in British Politics and Brexit. The course is structured chronologically, so every week you study the UK-EU relationship from a new decade under a new Prime Minister. You get an in-depth understanding of UK's European politics during Wilson, Thatcher, Major, Blair, Brown, Cameron, and others.
unexpected_costs: Council Tax if you do not get an exemption. I also needed to pay for a language course before enrolling.
cost_comparison: If you use the tube then transportation is more expensive than expected. The bus is less expensive than expected. Food prices are roughly the same as in Denmark.
activities_available: All kinds of sport (badminton, football, running, swimming etc.), creative classes, bingo, pub quiz, guided tours in the neighbourhood, museum tours etc. There a plenty of opportunities.
activities_recommended: Going with the locals on pubs. You need not to drink alcohol - but attending pub quiz or watching a football match is fun at a pub.
weekend_recommendations: Try to walk around in different neighbourhoods (Shoreditch, Sloane Square, Hampstead, Richmond). Every place has its own style and vibe. London is much more than the West End (Big Ben, Westminister and Soho). Even though London is not a cheap city - you can visit lots of places on a tight budget by taking the buses, walking and visiting free parks and museums.
culture_adjustment: London is a multicultural city. You will probably meet as many foreigners as Brits in London so the "local" culture is not as visible in the city. In general people are nice, polite and used to foreigners like yourself.
socializing_tips: Attend the social events on campus and do not be shy to ask the British students about British culture. Ask them about Sunday Roast and say you enjoy British food (then you will get friends).
cultural_challenges: Generally no challenging cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: The humour. It is sarcastic and very much like the Danish humour. I also appreciate the fact that you can communicate with everyone (unlike other places in Europe where language is a barrier).
top3_advice: 1. Reach out to the Study Abroad Team at the host university if you have any questions - they are kind. 2. Take a course where you learn something about Britain 3. Take the buses to get around
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Meeting local students and other associate students. I found it very rewarding to talk with other students with a different academic background than my own. It brings a new dynamic to studying.
greatest_challenge: Getting wifi and Council Tax exemption. You might need to get a British bank account in order to do so.

socializing_tips: Vær åben, og spørg ind til dem.
cultural_challenges: Ikke noget særligt.

Sig ja til tilbudene man får - tag med til de sociale arrangementer - det er ikke meget, man får set sine medstuderende i skolen, derfor er det en god ide at tage med ud i starten af semestret. 3. Tag det roligt, og lad være med at læse alle bøgerne på pensumlisterne - mange af bøgerne har kapitler om de samme ting, blot skrevet af en anden forfatter.
