crucial_aspects: I wanted to go on exchange for many reasons. The main one would have to be the opportunity to better my academic English, more precisely legal English. I ultimately wanted to study abroad in an English speaking country which is why I chose England. Furthermore, I have been to London multiple times prior to my stay and have a lot of family that reside in London, it just seemed like the optimal place for me.
info_ease: You get A LOT of e-mails prior to arriving in London with tons of details about the whole process. They cover most of the details, however there were a few times I had to reach out to their administration, especially when it came to my course registration.
arrival_assistance: They have a whole Global Opportunities team that is available for any inquiries. The first week at QMUL was an orientation week, where the Global Opportunities team provided a lot of information about the exchange stay and opportunities to meet other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You will get some e-mails regarding course registration, but keep in mind that Law exchange students follow a separate course registration process. The way it happened to me was I received an e-mail of the available courses for me to choose from (around 12 different courses), where I had to fill out a google form of my priorities and they would grant you them based on how they would fit into your timetable.
registration_help: You could e-mail the administration, Global Opportunities team and Law faculty staff regarding any questions.
registration_success: I got all my 4 first priorities. The first month or so there is an add/drop period where you have the chance to drop or add courses. I did not utilise this, but from what I heard from others, it was difficult to do. You can also request to change to a different team within your course if you want to take a class at a different time, which I did a few times successfully. You have to give good reason to have your request granted, which for me was that I lived an hour away from campus. This was very helpful, whereby I only had classes 2-3 times a week.
registration_advice: Be patient and ask all the questions. Not everything is in the available information so keep in mind that you may have to reach out to administration yourself.
course_level: I had four courses, all worth 15 credits each (7.5 ECTS). I had 2 first year courses and 2 third year courses.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching varied from course to course. My first year courses had a mix of online and physical lectures and 1hour seminars/tutorials, while my third year courses were only 1 2hour seminar a week. Teaching comprised approximately 8 hours per week, and therefore less than at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Contract Law I: Formation and Vitiation, Law in Context, Cultural Diversity and the Law, Equality and the Law. The first 2 are first year courses, and the latter are third year courses.
recommended_courses: I would recommend the course Contract Law I, that gives you a great insight to the principles of English contract law. Equality and the Law was also very enjoyable because it focused a lot on conducting research which was nice difference to what I had been used to at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: I do not recall any unexpected costs
cost_comparison: London is very expensive. Transportation, eating out and social things are getting increasingly expensive so bear this in mind. I did not have to pay for books because I borrowed from the library. The library has every book you need for your courses and you can borrow them up to 52 weeks (given that no one else reserves them).
activities_available: There were a lot of cultural clubs for a lot of various nationalities. There were a lot of sportsteams for pretty much every sport you can think of. There were also a lot of social activities on campus, including fresher events. Fresher events are primarily for first year students, so the age group of most of the students attending is 17/18.
activities_recommended: Attend all the things you can, most people had wonderful experiences.
weekend_recommendations: See the city! London is huge and full of different people so you can never really be bored. There is a lot to do. Furthermore, take the opportunity to experience other cities in the UK. I visited Brighton and Edinburgh while I was there.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. I have been to London a lot of times before and it is very similar to Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: Be open. People are all on the same boat and eager to find friends. Don't be afraid to reach out to people, they are super nice.
cultural_challenges: Not so much a cultural difference but there is a lot of people in London which can be very overwhelming.
culture_appreciated: London is truly a melting pot of cultures. There is people from all walks of life from all over the world which is nice to live among.
top3_advice: 1) Make sure to save up a lot in advance. Due to Brexit, the erasmus scholarship is no longer available for exchange students going to the UK. London is expensive, so you are better off saving up as much money in advance. 2) Research housing thoroughly and 3) Be open to get to know people
other_useful_info: I have covered everything above.
most_rewarding: Getting to know people and making friends from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Everything is very overwhelming in the beginning, so taking time to adjust to all the changes was a bit challenging.

crucial_aspects: I chose my study destination based on the opportunity to freely select courses taught in English, which aligned perfectly with my academic interests. Additionally, London appealed to me as a vibrant metropolis, far larger than Copenhagen, offering a unique blend of diverse cultures and perspectives. The city's dynamic environment and international character made it an ideal place for both academic and personal growth.
info_ease: It was relatively easy to find the information I needed upon arrival, thanks to the detailed emails that served as reminders and guides. KU was particularly good at providing clear information beforehand. However, I did encounter a challenge when one of my mandatory courses was unexpectedly not offered at the host university. This highlighted a lack of communication between KU and the host university. It would have been helpful if KU required the host university to have their course schedule finalized by a set deadline to avoid such issues arising after arrival.
arrival_assistance: The host university had an incredibly competent exchange team that was 100% helpful and always available. Their presence and support made the arrival process seamless, and I have nothing but praise for how well everything was handled.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I don’t recall many details about the registration process, which likely means it was smooth and straightforward. Everything seemed to fall into place without any significant challenges or complications.
registration_help: All the help I needed.
registration_success: One of my mandatory courses was no longer offered when I arrived. This was a significant issue, as it disrupted my planned course schedule. Improved communication between the host university and the home university about course availability would have been helpful to avoid such situations.
registration_advice: Don’t stress too much about registration. Both the host university and KU are there to support you, and things will work out one way or another, even if the process doesn’t go exactly as you expected. Be flexible and open to adjustments, and don’t hesitate to reach out for help if you encounter any issues.
course_level: The level of courses is somewhat easier compared to what we are used to at KU, particularly in terms of teaching methods and exams. While the material is engaging and educational, the teaching style often feels more like a high school environment. Classes tend to focus on open discussions and subjective opinions. However, I found this method beneficial as an exchange student, as the emphasis on oral participation helped me improve my English skills through frequent verbal practice.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at my host institution was quite different from what I am used to at KU. At the host university, classes were more interactive, with a strong emphasis on open discussions and subjective opinions, creating a high school-like atmosphere. In contrast, KU places more focus on independent study and academic rigor. While the host university's approach felt less academically demanding, it was beneficial for me as an exchange student, as it allowed me to practice my English extensively through verbal participation and classroom dialogue.
courses_enrolled: British Politics Comparative Politics International Relations of the Middle East
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend International Relations of the Middle East, which I took as an elective. The course was incredibly interesting, offering a deep dive into the history of the Middle East—a topic I knew very little about beforehand. The discussions in class were particularly enriching, as many students had personal connections to the region and brought fascinating and diverse perspectives. The course is structured around key themes and actors in the region, providing a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of its dynamics. Another great course was British Politics, also an elective. It was fascinating to study the British political system and compare it to Denmark’s. The differences between the two systems are significant and highlight unique aspects of each society. However, the course was challenging at times, as much of the background knowledge about British society was considered common knowledge by the other students, which I didn’t always share. Despite this, it was a highly rewarding course.
unexpected_costs: Nothing
cost_comparison: Groceries in supermarkets are much cheaper compared to Denmark, so if you have access to a kitchen, you can save a lot by cooking at home and bringing your own lunch to university. On the other hand, gyms in London are very expensive. However, Queen Mary has a fairly decent gym, and as a student, you can get a membership at a price similar to what you’d expect in Denmark, making it a good option for staying active.
activities_available: There were an incredible number of student societies covering everything from sports to hobbies and special interests, ensuring there was something for everyone. The university also had its own gym, which was a great facility for staying active. Additionally, there were plenty of social events, including many parties specifically organized for exchange students, making it easy to meet new people and feel part of the community.
activities_recommended: I highly recommend taking some time to travel around the UK. A visit to the Cotswolds, with its beautiful countryside and charming villages, offers a peaceful escape from city life. If you have more time, traveling to Scotland is an unforgettable experience, with stunning landscapes and a rich cultural heritage. Exploring these areas gives you a deeper appreciation of the UK beyond London and allows you to experience the country's incredible diversity.
weekend_recommendations: I highly recommend taking some time to travel around the UK.
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: No
cultural_challenges: Nothing.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the cultural and ethnic diversity in London. It’s incredible to experience such a vibrant mix of traditions, perspectives, and communities all in one place. It also made me reflect on how culturally homogeneous Denmark can feel by comparison, which was an eye-opening and valuable perspective to gain.
top3_advice: Just enjoy your stay and be as active s you can. The time runs up before you know it.
other_useful_info: Nothing.
most_rewarding: To be a part of the vibrant city
greatest_challenge: London as a city felt a bit overwhelming at first.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: One of the main reasons I chose to study in London was the opportunity to experience education in a different academic setting than Denmark. London is home to some of the world's most respected universities, including Queen Mary University of London, where I studied. The university’s strong reputation, combined with its diverse range of courses, made it an attractive choice. I was particularly interested in studying my courses from a British perspective, as this allowed me to gain new insights into political science, especially regarding European politics and the UK's relationship with the EU. Additionally, Queen Mary offered elective courses that I would not have had the opportunity to take at the University of Copenhagen, allowing me to broaden my academic horizon. Beyond academics, London itself was a key factor in my decision. As a global city with a rich history and vibrant cultural life, it provided a unique and inspiring environment to live and study in. Lastly, having an exchange semester at a well-known London university is also a valuable addition to my resume, as it demonstrates adaptability, international experience, and academic engagement in a different setting.
overall_comments: I had a great experience studying abroad. It was exciting to live in London, explore a new environment, and meet people from different backgrounds. The city itself offers endless opportunities, both academically and socially, making it a fantastic place to study. One of the highlights of my time at Queen Mary University of London was the opportunity to join university sports teams, which added a great social and physical aspect to my exchange experience. Academically, the courses were interesting, and the teaching style provided a different perspective compared to my home university. However, I found that the academic level, while high, was not as challenging as at the University of Copenhagen. As a result, some aspects of my courses were less challenging than expected. Nonetheless, studying in London was an incredibly rewarding experience, and I would highly recommend it to others.
info_ease: Overall, it was fairly easy to find the necessary information upon arrival. However, I found that Queen Mary’s website, particularly regarding course details, was not always as comprehensive or informative as I had hoped. Some aspects of course selection and academic expectations could have been explained more clearly, which would have made the transition smoother.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival at the university, we had a welcome day where we received important information about various aspects of student life. This included practical guidance on living on campus, using the library, connecting with other students, joining sports clubs, accessing IT services, and getting involved in student organizations. We were also given details about our exams and how to contact professors, which was helpful in understanding the academic structure at Queen Mary. The welcome session provided a good introduction to university life.
arrival_comments: While Queen Mary University of London provided a well-structured general orientation covering student life, campus resources, and administrative procedures, I was extremely dissatisfied with the handling of academic matters, particularly course selection and availability. Before my arrival, I had engaged in extensive communication with both Queen Mary and the University of Copenhagen, to ensure that my courses were properly pre-approved. A key reason for choosing Queen Mary was the opportunity to take The UK and the EU, which was essential for fulfilling my academic requirements. I had gone through a rigorous process of gathering course descriptions, securing approval from my home university, and confirming my eligibility to enroll. At no point during this process was I informed that the course would not be running in the fall semester. Upon arriving in London, I was unexpectedly informed that The UK and the EU had been cancelled for the semester, despite it still being listed on Queen Mary’s website as available. This immediately put me in a difficult position, as there were no equivalent EU-related courses offered that could be transferred for credit. Had I been made aware of this beforehand, I could have planned accordingly and taken European Politics at my home university instead of being forced to scramble for a solution after my exchange had already begun. Attempts to find an alternative course were met with slow responses and a lack of viable options. Queen Mary’s academic office was unable to offer any real assistance beyond suggesting unrelated courses, which were not applicable to my degree requirements. Their response largely placed the responsibility on me to resolve the situation, despite the fact that this issue arose due to their own administrative shortcomings. After extensive back-and-forth communication between Queen Mary, my home university, and multiple faculty members, it became clear that there was no suitable replacement course available. As a result, I was ultimately forced to take European Politics remotely and sit for the exam at the University of Copenhagen upon my return. This situation was entirely avoidable and created unnecessary stress, logistical complications, and additional academic pressure during my exchange semester. Overall, my experience with Queen Mary’s academic support was highly disappointing. The lack of transparency, poor communication, and inflexible course enrollment process made what should have been a straightforward study abroad experience unnecessarily difficult. Given these challenges, I cannot recommend that political science students apply for an exchange at Queen Mary in their fifth semester, as the uncertainty surrounding course availability poses a serious risk to academic progression. While the university offered good general support for non-academic matters, the way this issue was handled left a lasting negative impression and significantly impacted my exchange experience.

registration_process: The registration process at Queen Mary University of London was relatively straightforward in the beginning. I was contacted in May and asked to confirm my enrollment, which was easy to complete. Once I was officially in their system, I started receiving regular updates specifically for associate (exchange) students, which helped guide the next steps. In June, Queen Mary opened pre-registration for course selection, allowing exchange students to indicate their preferred modules. However, final course confirmation only happened in September, when we had to re-confirm our choices and make any necessary adjustments. Overall, the initial setup was smooth, but the two-step course registration process required some patience, as module availability wasn’t always guaranteed.
registration_help: Queen Mary University had a dedicated Global Opportunities Office with a team of around ten staff members responsible for assisting exchange students before, during, and after their time abroad. In general, they were quite responsive, and it was relatively easy to get help when needed.
registration_success: The course registration process at Queen Mary University of London turned out to be more complicated than expected. While I was able to register for some of my preferred electives, the overall experience was frustrating due to a lack of transparency regarding course availability. One major challenge was that even after pre-registering in June, there was no guarantee that courses would actually be available in September when final registration took place. This created a lot of uncertainty, as students had to wait until the semester started to confirm their schedules. The process was also highly competitive, with some courses filling up quickly and limited flexibility in swapping modules. Communication from the university was inconsistent, making it difficult to get clear answers about which courses would run. Even though I had gone through the proper channels to secure my choices, I ultimately had to make unexpected adjustments that affected my academic plans.
registration_advice: For future students, I would recommend having backup options for all courses and double-checking availability directly with both Queen Mary and the University of Copenhagen well in advance to avoid last-minute issues.

course_level: The academic level at Queen Mary University of London was generally lower than what I am used to at the University of Copenhagen. While the courses were interesting and covered relevant topics, they were often less demanding in terms of workload, critical engagement, and depth of analysis compared to similar courses at KU. Assignments tended to be more structured, with clear guidelines that left less room for independent analytical thinking. The expectations for student performance also seemed lower, with fewer required readings and a more guided approach to coursework. While this made the semester more manageable, it also meant that some courses felt less academically challenging.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at Queen Mary University of London was very similar to that of the bachelor's program in Political Science at the University of Copenhagen. Each course typically consisted of one lecture per week, followed by a smaller seminar-style class (which they refer to as "seminars"). One key difference was the strict attendance policy for seminars. Attendance was mandatory, and absences were recorded, whereas at UCPH, participation is more flexible and your own responsible. However, class participation did not contribute to final grades, so while students were expected to attend, there was no formal assessment of engagement in discussions.
courses_enrolled: Comparative Politics British Politics Populism - A Global Perspective
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend British Politics (POL243A) to future exchange students, especially given the current political landscape in the UK. The course provides a solid intermediate-level grounding in contemporary British politics and government, covering key topics such as the UK’s political constitution, sovereign parliament, electoral politics, and cabinet government. Given the political developments in recent years—including Brexit, shifts in party dynamics, and ongoing constitutional debates—studying British politics from within the country added a unique and highly relevant perspective. Additionally, the course is 100% coursework-based, which can be beneficial for those who prefer assessments over high-stakes final exams. The combination of theoretical knowledge and practical political analysis makes this a highly engaging and valuable course for anyone interested in UK and comparative politics.
unexpected_costs: One of the biggest unexpected costs was transport. While I knew London’s public transport was expensive, the daily expenses of using the Tube and buses added up quickly, even with an Oyster card. Additionally, some student discounts were not as significant as I had expected.
cost_comparison: Transport and eating out.
activities_available: Queen Mary University of London offered a wide range of clubs and societies, covering everything from sports and cultural groups to academic and special interest societies. Early in the semester, the university hosted a Welcome Fair, where students had the opportunity to explore different clubs, meet members, and sign up for activities or trials for sports teams. I personally had a great experience playing football at the university, which became a major part of my exchange. Queen Mary has five football teams, and through training sessions and matches, I built strong friendships with teammates. The football club became my main social circle, and I spent several hours each week both on and off the field with them. For students looking to get involved socially and stay active, the variety of sports clubs, student societies, and social events at Queen Mary makes it easy to find a community and connect with others.
activities_recommended: I would highly recommend joining a sports club. Whether or not you play at a high level, getting involved in university sports is a great way to meet people, stay active, and have a structured social outlet throughout the semester. The football club was an incredible experience for me, but there are many other sports available for students at different skill levels. Another recommendation is to join a cultural or nationality-based society. I was a member of the Queen Mary Scandinavian Society, which was a fantastic way to meet other Nordic students and build friendships with people who had similar backgrounds and experiences. These societies often host social gatherings, events, and networking opportunities, making them a great way to feel at home while studying abroad. For any exchange student, getting involved in both a sports club and a social society can make a huge difference in building friendships and making the most of the experienc
weekend_recommendations: There’s no shortage of things to do in and around London, but I highly recommend a mix of classic British experiences, exploring the city’s green spaces, and taking short trips outside of London. First and foremost, going to pubs is a must. London has a fantastic pub culture, and spending an afternoon or evening in a traditional pub is one of the best ways to experience local life, whether it’s for a Guinness, a Sunday roast, or even a pub quiz night. Another great way to spend weekends is by visiting the many parks across the city. Hyde Park, Regent’s Park, and Hampstead Heath are perfect for running. London’s parks offer a great escape and are worth exploring in different seasons. For longer weekends or holidays, I strongly recommend taking day trips to other major British cities. Oxford and Cambridge are both stunning university towns with a lot of history and charm, while Brighton offers a great coastal escape. Manchester, Liverpool, and Edinburgh are also fantastic destinations if you want to experience different parts of the UK.
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: The best way to socialize with local students is to join a sports club or student society. Sports teams, in particular, offer a great way to meet people, as training and matches create a strong sense of community. Additionally, going to pubs, attending university events, and engaging in group activities through clubs or societies make it easier to connect with both local and international students.
cultural_challenges: I didn’t experience any significant cultural differences that were particularly challenging.
culture_appreciated: One of the things I appreciated most about British culture was the football culture. Football is a huge part of everyday life—everyone talks about it constantly, whether it’s Premier League matches, local teams, or just casual debates about the latest results. Going to football matches at stadiums was an incredible experience. The atmosphere, the passion of the fans, and the sense of community around the sport made it unforgettable. Whether you're a big football fan or just interested in experiencing a key part of British culture, attending a match in London is something I highly recommend.
top3_advice: Be prepared for course registration challenges – Some courses may not be available even if they were listed beforehand, so have backup options and confirm availability as early as possible. Budget carefully – Rent, transport, and everyday expenses in London add up quickly. Get an Oyster card for zones 1 & 2 early on and be mindful of housing costs. Join a sports club or society – It’s the best way to meet people and build a social circle. Football was a great experience for me, but there are many clubs to choose from.
other_useful_info: Not besides all the information, tips, and advice I've given on previous questions
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was truly immersing myself in British culture.
greatest_challenge: Not really any.

Furthermore, knowing that the level of academics was at a decent level was also important.
overall_comments: It's been the perfect experience both on a social and academic level. I have gotten so many new perspectives on law, but also on life in general. The way you live in London will always be a part of me and something that will inspire me going forward.
info_ease: I would say it was relatively easy, but bear in mind that you are arriving at a completely new institution, so it feels like starting over again. So, the first few days was a bit confusing navigating between the different systems at Queen Mary.

registration_process: 1. Pre-registration (where you get to choose modules - choose them the same day they become available to make sure you get the ones you want). 2. Module registration (this is where you get notified if you got your modules). 3. Add / drop period (typically in September at intro week and the couple of weeks following, where you have the chance to add or drop modules if you are not satisfied).
registration_help: The Queen Mary study abroad team is ready to assist here, and I emailed them a couple of times about modules, and they replied within a couple of hours to a day.
registration_success: I was very successful I got all the modules I wanted, I think the key is to apply right when the registration opens as some modules have limited space for exchange students.
registration_advice: 1. Be aware of the deadlines. 2. Make sure to choose modules ASAP. 3. You can always try to get new or drop modules in the add / drop period in the beginning (so no stress).
academics_comments: It's been the perfect experience both on a social and academic level. I have gotten so many new perspectives on law, but also on life in general. The way you live in London will always be a part of me and something that will inspire me going forward.
course_level: At Queen Mary module courses are divided into level 4 (equivalent to first year),5 (second year) or 6 (third year) for bachelor students. Some of my courses were challenging me, mostly the level 6 course I chose. The other courses I had on level 4 and 5 were interesting, but quite easy and manageable academically. So if you appreciate a "high level" might be the best to only choose level 6 (or 5) courses if possible.
teaching_comparison: Definitely quite similar. The tutors are informal and easy to approach. The seminars are called tutorials and only last one hour so that feels a bit short, and lectures are often two hours. Books are available online via. LawTrove, so no need for those expenses, which is quite nice.
courses_enrolled: 1. Competition Law (Level 6) 2. Internet Law (level 5) 3. Business Law (level 5) 4. Contract Law (Level 4)
recommended_courses: Internet Law - a very passionate and interesting tutor on this module. The lectures are great with good and exam friendly slides. The module engages with various different issues regarding the internet and law e.g. Data protection, Criminal Law on hacking, intellectual property & AI etc. Competition Law - an interesting module if you appreciate EU law and is interested in competition between companies in general. Can be quite heavy on reading and case law, but this also makes it academically challenging, which I appreciated. Only one hour of teaching a week, so this makes your schedule more free, but also requires you to self-study a bit more. The exam is not too difficult. Business Law - hands down the best tutor on Queen Mary, super passionate and is very good at delivering lectures in an interesting and different way. He engages with students in his teaching, is friendly and much well-connected in the area between law and business. However, the module is a bit general and "high-flying" on legal subjects, but it provides a basic view into the legal English system and common law.
unexpected_costs: Nothing really most of my costs were accounted for in the budget.
cost_comparison: Food - this can be very expensive. However, I lived at KFUK where you get 10 free meals a month which helped on the budget. Drinking - It is quite expensive to go out in London, probably similar to Copenhagen and sometimes even more expensive. Transportation - As a Queen Mary student you are very dependent on the tube (metro) and this turned out to be a lot more expensive than expected. I can recommend getting a Student Oyster Card (apply right when you arrive!) for a fixed fee, so this will not worry you all the time. Books at Uni - These are "free" as all the books that are a part of the curriculum for the module is available on LawTrove.
activities_available: Many sports clubs (football, basketball, american football, tennis, karate etc.) Legal clubs (enter into competitions, network opportunities etc.) Nationality societies (Caribbean, Turkish, Pakistani, Nordic etc.) Debating societies AND many more.
activities_recommended: I was a part of the tennis society which was very good. You can join in at every level (beginner, intermediate or competitive). They have practice two times a week on outdoor courts. They offer fun socials too where you get the opportunity to network with other students. The tennis society provided me with many friends (also ones that are not exchange students). I was also a part of the Nordic Society which offers good chances of pub quizzing, club nights etc. This is a chance for you to connect with other nordic students (Swedish, Finnish, Icelandic etc.) studying at Queen Mary, but sometimes bigger events include students from LSE, Kings College, Royal Holloway etc.
weekend_recommendations: At Queen Mary there is reading week, which is a full week where you don't have studies at all (a part from the reading you do one your own), so this is a great opportunity to go on a longer trip. I myself went to Edinburgh in Scotland which was a fun experience. I also went to Cornwall which is south in England (probably go early on your trip, so start / mid September). Cornwall offers beaches, cliffs, beautiful oceans, local pubs and in general beautiful nature. I visited the cities Newquay (surfers hotspot) and Padstow (cute little city with a lot of good seafood). Otherwise fun day trips could be Oxford or Cambridge which is quite close to London. I went to Oxford which was so cool as the city is impressive and aesthetic especially the University.
culture_adjustment: I found this quite easy, English culture is not too far away from Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Join societies! This is almost the only way or be very open in the beginning of your modules to find mates within your classes.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really.
culture_appreciated: Pub culture! There are so many in London and they offer great ways of socialising. The creative scene! Many museums are free or you can join on student memberships. I also watched shows at the Royal Ballet and Opera House which was nice. London is also a hotspot for music with many interesting artists coming by. Sports! Watch your favorite premier league team or see NBA / NFL in London.
top3_advice: 1. Socialize in the beginning. Friends are not easily made at Queen Mary and initiatives from the university are not the best other than the voluntary intro week. So, be proactive and make your connections. 2. Plan your time - this is in general a good idea, but Queen Mary has a very sharp deadline for exams, all assignments need to be submitted by 12 th of December, and some of your exam questions will be available from start December. So, this is really a busy period, so be focused on planning your time here. Otherwise, the other parts of the semester is pretty chill at Queen Mary. 3. Timetables - in the beginning when you get your timetable for modules you might have clashes. This can be frustrating and Queen Mary is not always the best to solve this, but take it chill and follow the guidance provided.
other_useful_info: Queen Mary itself with the Mile End Campus is not the prettiest. However, it is functional and the campus has everything you need.
most_rewarding: In general, just being in a different country and getting new perspectives on life and academics.
greatest_challenge: In the beginning reading in English as the legal academic books can be a bit of a challenge. Socialising - don't think too much just connect with others all are there to make friends. I was maybe a bit slow at the start.
other_comments: GO ON THE EXCHANGE! You will not regret it (even if you don't choose Queen Mary).

The other law student and I got a spot at Queen's University Belfast and we travelled together.
overall_comments: It was a really fun exchange experience and I loved it. There is a lot of history in Belfast as the Northern Irish "capital" and the divide between Ireland and UK is very interesting. It is a smaller city and you therefore get to know the city rather quickly. People are so nice and the accent is not that hard to understand. The whole exchange process was easy and manageable, you only had to make sure to fill out all the paperwork in time. I was very happy that I chose Belfast, because it was such an interesting city that I probably would not have travelled to otherwise.
info_ease: Very easy. I would receive emails from the university's exchange office and they answered any questions I had quickly. Other than that their website was good, however, it was a little bit difficult to find the page with the modules.
arrival_assistance: They had a welcome zoom meeting with a lot of information about visas and airport transport a little before we all had to start, so if we had questions we would get the answers before travelling. When arriving, there was first a welcome week for the international students and the next week it was the welcome week for the UK students. In the welcome week we were invited to tea parties with our faculties and induction meetings with a Law professor responsible for the international students. From there we knew who to email regarding questions about our modules and assignments and so on.
arrival_comments: There was a little miscommunication with the arriving date regarding airport transport. We were informed that the earliest day to arrive to accommodation was the 13th of September, however, the University only provided airport transport for a few days before the 13th and after the 13th, but not on the 13th. At this point a lot of the international students (including us) had already bought our tickets on the 13th. This was not a big issue at all and we just called a taxi when arriving at the airport. The students who had not already bought their tickets, just bought them to match with a day with airport transport.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_process: Queens University makes the application process really easy. They send you all the documents they need and after you submit them, you receive an acceptance letter. They also accept the language documentation from KU, based on your English grade from high school.
registration_help: the hos university was really helpful and would answer all questions within a few days.
registration_success: I chose my modules by looking at the course catalogue. However, when I arrived two of my modules was changed to fully online and I therefore changed my modules when arriving. I had made sure to get a lot of modules accepted beforehand (forhåndsgodkendt), so that i could change without having to go through the process again. But one of the new modules had to be accepted while i was in Belfast, but it was not more complicated than sending a few mails to University of Copenhagen and submitting some documents.
registration_advice: I would advise you to just follow the instructions from both Universities, they have made it very easy.

There is a lot of history in Belfast as the Northern Irish "capital" and the divide between Ireland and UK is very interesting. It is a smaller city and you therefore get to know the city rather quickly. People are so nice and the accent is not that hard to understand. The whole exchange process was easy and manageable, you only had to make sure to fill out all the paperwork in time. I was very happy that I chose Belfast, because it was such an interesting city that I probably would not have travelled to otherwise.
course_level: I had 'Gender and the Law', 'International Criminal and Transitional Justice' and 'Public International Law' and they were so interesting modules. They are taught law in a different way in this University as they focus more on the legal studies and critical thinking regarding laws. So there is not the same focus on the actual laws and articles as we are used to in Denmark. I really enjoyed all three modules but if I had to recommend one it would be Public International Law because the lecturer Dr. Yassin Brunger was such a good lecturer. She creating interesting debates and it was always important to have read to material for her classes. I loved every one of her classes. We had to hand in essays in all the modules and all three deadlines were in December.
teaching_comparison: As mentioned, law is taught differently as they focus more on the critical thinking and the aim of the law rather than the use of the actual law and articles within it. But I enjoyed the switch and seeing law from a different angle.
courses_enrolled: 'Gender and the Law', 'International Criminal and Transitional Justice' and 'Public International Law'.
recommended_courses: I would recommend all three. Gender and the law focused on feminism and the view on women and how that view is visible through laws and the legal system. International Criminal and Transitional Justice was about the large sized humanitarian crimes such as genocide and how you achieve transitional justice through different mechanisms. Public international law is the same module as International Law in University of Copenhagen, just with focus on the critical thinking rather than the different international laws.
unexpected_costs: all the small things that you need.Towels, soap, cleaning supplies. But everything is cheaper in Belfast compared to Copenhagen.
cost_comparison: Things are in general cheaper and with the grant from Erasmus + SU from Denmark (and some personal savings, everything should be great.
activities_available: A lot of activities at the Treehouse in BT9 too that you should attend. Its a cafe with free tea and coffee and games to play, a great place to make new friends.
activities_recommended: make friends with the other international students too as you all can explore the city together.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely take a weekend trip to Dublin with the bus. I also booked a flight to London for a weekend (very short flight). It is a bigger city and has places to go too. In Belfast, there is so much nature and I really enjoyed Whitehead, Cavehill and Giant's causeway. I also loved the St. George's Market that is also opened in the weekends.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. It is a smaller city and people are very helpful and kind. You get to know the city really quick and it was good walking to the city, around 30 min walk to the city centre from BT9.
socializing_tips: Do a lot of things in the beginning especially as that's the best time to make new friends. Time flies and after a while you fall into a routine with the people you know. Not the say you can't make new friends, but its definitely easier though the activities provided by the accommodation.
cultural_challenges: Not that big of a culture difference.
culture_appreciated: Very very friendly and talkative people, which was so nice.
top3_advice: (1) raincoat and umbrella (rains a lot and you will walk a lot) (2) nice slippers or "home" shoes (for when you walk around the kitchen or to the Treehouse to wash clothes and so on (3) Not to worry about clothing (they are way more relaxed with clothing than in Copenhagen)
other_useful_info: Really interesting history in Belfast, make sure to explore it and find out more about the "Troubles". You can book a walking tour where you will be guided through historical events and areas of Belfast. Take the hop-on-hop-off bus and explore the peace wall.
most_rewarding: Improving my English skills by attending classes, reading material and writing essays. Getting to know both the northern irish culture and all the other international cultures. Living in a small village of students and becoming friends with people from all around the world.
greatest_challenge: I will warn you that the mattress is not that comfortable and there was a lot of issues with the shower head in the showers. Furthermore, the walls are rather thin so you can hear if people are coming back from a night out, but you kind of get used to it after a while. But the maintenance issues were definitely the biggest challenge. Everything else was great.
other_comments: I hope you choose Belfast, it is a great city with so much history! Not to big of a city so you feel at home quickly and can get around the city by walking.

crucial_aspects: The beautiful nature of Northern Ireland, the English language, the courses avaliable at the university, the student accommodation, all the facilities the university offered, and the opportunity to discover the Northern Irish culture
info_ease: It was easy. There was a reception at the accommodation site.
arrival_assistance: I talked to someone at the reception close to my accommodation and was able to ask questions, receive my key, buy a kitchen pack etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You had to fill out some information, have your picture taken, and receive a Student ID with which you could enter the library etc.
registration_help: The reception at my accommodation was almost always open and ready to help
registration_success: The website of the university had by mistake not been updated so I only got one out of three of my requested classes
registration_advice: To make sure you know what is needed regarding your Visa. And ask other students or any avaliable student support facility if you are in doubt about anything.
course_level: It seemed a lot easier than in Copenhagen
teaching_comparison: There was a lot more contact and support offered to the students
courses_enrolled: Gender and the law International criminal and transitional justice European constiutional law
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of my courses as I found all of them very refreshing and interesting
unexpected_costs: Mostly just all the souvenirs I wanted to buy :-)
cost_comparison: Most items - like food, transportation, beauty and health products - were all less expensive than expected
activities_available: There was plenty of these opportunities: many with Irish food tasting, afternoon tea, pizza nights, Irish music, baking, painting… It was very impressive!
activities_recommended: I would recommend all of them. Particularly the ones going on field trips, seeing the beautiful nature of Northern Ireland, food events where you can chat with others, and the more creative ones.
weekend_recommendations: I especially recommend seeing Giant’s Causeway, Rathlin Island, Derry, Portrush, Dunluce Castle, and Glenariff Waterfall Park.
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: The creative or active events will probably especially makes this easier as you can comment on what you are doing and bond over something
cultural_challenges: Mostly that the Northern Irish men were very direct and forward when approaching you and flirting with you
culture_appreciated: The music, the appreciation of nature, the Irish fairytales and litterature
top3_advice: Don’t hold back! Be yourself and join as many events as possible. If you still haven’t found your best friend, don’t give up, and don’t be scared to start conversations as you are only away for such a short time. A more practical advice would be to get a card for the public transport, get the Value Cab app, and stay safe in the nightlife - never leave your drink unattended.
other_useful_info: If you also come to a dorm-like accommodation with other student, I’d recommend making a plan to share everything that you all need - spices, salt, pepper, cleaning supplies, oil, sauces… it makes everything a lot easier and reduces waste!
most_rewarding: The beautiful nature, the feeling of independence and finding my way, the academic enrichment, and most of all the incredible people that I met and hope to hold onto for life
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was getting over some unpleasant nights out where my boundaries were crossed

crucial_aspects: I have always wanted to study in the UK, so i took the chance when i was offered an exchange stay in Belfast.
info_ease: It was very easy; the university offered a webinar in july, where i got all the information i needed. The university staff were very helpful whenever i had any questions, and replied quickly.
arrival_assistance: I did not need any special assistance. But if you need any assistance, they are quick to help.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There were not that many courses to choose between. We found out after we arrived, which courses we had to change. This was stressful, since we had to do this while finding everything else out. However, we had a window of two-three weeks where we could switch courses.
registration_help: It was very easy to contact the staff. They were always very helpful and always replied quickly.
registration_success: I got 2 out of the three courses i wanted.
registration_advice: Be prepared to the possibility of having to change most of the courses you selected. Add more courses to your learning agreement, so that you won't have to stress about it while you're there.
course_level: The classes i took were all for last-year undergraduate students in law.
teaching_comparison: The courses are very descriptive, and have you deal with theory and ideas around the law, rather than problem cases. There are very few classes, and you have to study a lot yourself.
courses_enrolled: Contract Law, International Trade Law, and Law and Technology.
recommended_courses: I enjoyed Contract Law, since that course dealt more with the application of the law in problem cases, rather than just theory.
unexpected_costs: The apartments and kitchen were almost completely empty, when we arrived. So i had to buy a duvet and pillow, and a lot of pans, pots, cultery, etc. in the first few days.
cost_comparison: They were less expensive than i expected.
activities_available: There are a lot of different clubs, events, and associations available to the students. The university has a sports centre with a gym. If you're on exchange, you get a free off-peak membership.
activities_recommended: The clubs are a great way to meet different people. I would recommend the sailing club, because of it's social events. I also joined the archery and snooker club.
weekend_recommendations: The giant's causeway and Titanic museum are a must. The city centre is very charming, with a lot of pubs, cafes and restaurants. Belfast has a lot of history and culture to explore, like f.eks. the peace walls, different museums, and so on. I would recommend visiting nearby towns, like Londonderry/Derry for the history and culture. You can take a 2-hour bus to Dublin, which is a nice trip. It's also easy and cheap to fly to other cities in the UK mainland, so i would also recommend going there for a weekend.
culture_adjustment: For me, it was very easy to adjust. You share a floor with other exchange students, so everyone is in the same boat. The locals are very friendly and helpful, and it's very easy to get to know them.
socializing_tips: Just be very open and curious. Don't be afraid of not being too good at english.
cultural_challenges: The accent was a bit difficult in the beginning, but i got used to it very fast.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and politeness of the locals. They are also very open and talkative, so it was easy to become friends with them. It's not for everyone, but i really enjoyed the humour/banter over there.
top3_advice: 1) Rain clothes and an umbrella - the weather is bad. 2) Public transport isn't the best - just be ready for it. 3) Do as much as you can in regards to trips, experiences, events, meeting new people.
other_useful_info: There are no direct flights to Belfast from Copenhagen. Fly to Dublin and take the express bus from the airport to Belfast. I flew transit and had too many problems with it.
most_rewarding: Coming in contact with different people, cultures, ways of living and thinking, etc. The experience really broadened my horizon and understanding of people and the world. I am also now friends with people from different countries.
greatest_challenge: Adapting to a different way of school and teaching. I am very used to the way things are done in UPCH, and navigating a completely different schoolsystem was really stressing and rewarding.

crucial_aspects: I’ve always dreamed of studying abroad, so the key aspects for me were the chance to access better academic and career opportunities and to immerse myself in a completely new culture. I wanted a destination where I could grow both personally and professionally while experiencing life from a different perspective.
info_ease: yes
arrival_assistance: I mainly received assistance with practical tasks such as where to complete my course registration and other basic administrative steps.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process wasn’t the easiest, as some of the steps were unclear at first. However, with guidance from staff, I was able to complete it.
registration_help: The main support available was through email. Each time I reached out, the staff replied and provided clear guidance.
registration_success: I wasn’t very successful in registering for the classes I originally wanted. While applying from Denmark, Competition Law was my first priority, but when I arrived at QUB I was told that it was no longer offered for undergraduates. I was disappointed because I had really looked forward to taking it.
registration_advice: I would advise future exchange students to double-check course availability before arriving, as some classes may change or be removed without clear notice. It’s also helpful to have backup course options and to contact the university early if you have questions, since they usually respond quickly by email.
course_level: I took BA-level courses, including International Trade Law, Law and Technology, and Commercial Law. The classes were undergraduate level and generally manageable, though each required consistent reading and engagement with the material.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at Queen’s University Belfast was quite different from UCPH. At QUB, the classes were more lecture-based with a stronger focus on structured teaching, whereas UCPH typically encourages more independent learning and student participation.
courses_enrolled: International Trade Law (BA-level) Law and Technology (BA-level) Commercial Law (BA-level)
recommended_courses: Commercial Law: This course was very useful and well-structured, providing practical insights and a solid understanding of key commercial law concepts.
unexpected_costs: Some unexpected costs I encountered included the residential/housing fee, course materials or textbooks, transportation, and occasional administrative fees. It’s helpful to budget a little extra for such expenses.
cost_comparison: their food was less expensive and public transport was less expensive
activities_available: At my host institution, there were a variety of cultural, athletic, and social activities for students. Cultural activities included events, workshops. Socially, there were student societies, clubs, and informal gatherings that made it easy to meet other students.
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining the student societies. They are a great way to meet new people, make friends quickly, and get involved in social and cultural events on campus. Participating in societies really helps you feel part of the university community.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend that visiting students use their weekends and holidays to explore both Belfast and other cities in Northern Ireland and beyond. Sightseeing, visiting historical landmarks, and exploring local culture are all great ways to make the most of your time. Traveling to nearby cities also gives you a broader perspective on the country and its culture.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture at my exchange site was fairly easy. Most people were extremely friendly and welcoming, and I found it easy to adapt to daily life and social norms. Of course, there were small differences compared to home, but overall the transition was smooth.
socializing_tips: My main tip would be to get involved in student societies and campus events, as these are great places to meet local students. Being open, approachable, and willing to join group activities really helps in building connections.
cultural_challenges: Most cultural differences were easy to adapt to, but one thing I found a bit challenging was the different communication style. Overall, it was a good learning experience.
culture_appreciated: I most appreciated how welcoming and helpful people were. From staff to everyone, everyone was approachable and willing to assist, which made settling in much easier and more enjoyable.
top3_advice: Check course availability in advance: Some courses may no longer be offered, so have backup options ready. Get involved in student societies: They’re a great way to meet people, make friends, and experience campus life. Be open and flexible: Adapting to cultural differences and new ways of learning will make your experience more enjoyable.
other_useful_info: I’d advise future students to explore beyond academics, join societies, attend events, and travel a bit to get the full experience. Keep in mind that some courses may change, so have backup options. Planning ahead, being open to new experiences, and asking for help when needed will make settling in much easier.
most_rewarding: For me, the most rewarding part was the opportunity to grow both personally and academically. Engaging with students from different backgrounds, discovering new perspectives, and adapting to a different way of learning helped me gain confidence and independence.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was managing finances. Living abroad can be expensive, but with careful planning, I was able to manage it successfully.

crucial_aspects: The language was important, made it easy to connect with the locals. It was very far away and had so much nature that I most likely wouldn't have the chance to see otherwise.
info_ease: It was very easy to get information about all the essentials, either just by looking it up online or asking the school staff.
arrival_assistance: I used the QUT help desk on campus to find questions about the enrollment process and asked my Airbnb host for questions about the city
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I arrived in Brisbane with my pre approved list of courses from UCPH, I then enrolled in 4 of the courses that I wanted the most. After the enrollment had been approved I planned my timetable and then I was set for the semester.
registration_help: QUT has a help desk on campus which was very helpful and answered all my questions about the registration process and made it very easy to learn about the school online systems.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted and it was a very smooth process.
registration_advice: Just go to the help desk if you're confused about anything, it helps with all the uncertainty and stress with getting started on the semester.
course_level: The courses were in general easier than courses offered on UCPH, where most of the challenges came from managing group work and projects in 4 different courses.
teaching_comparison: More practical sessions during the week and a lot more big group assignments, less theoretical in general.
courses_enrolled: I took Networks, Advanced Visualization Science, Information Security, and Cryptography.
recommended_courses: I would recommend Cryptography if you like more of the theoretical subject, it was interesting and not overbearing with assignments. Advanced Visualization Science was probably my favorite course and I would highly recommend it, a lot of personal freedom in the choice of project you wanna do, and the professor and practicals were very good. I wouldn't recommend the other two courses, as they were mostly memorization of slides and very stale teaching.
unexpected_costs: You have to put down a certain amount of weeks of rent as a bond, which you don't get back until the end of the exchange trip, this was quite a lot of money to have locked away during the trip and should be considered as well (roughly one month of rent as a deposit). Some daily items from the supermarket were also very expensive for danish standarts, but there are really big discounts on some items so i would recommend looking for that.
cost_comparison: Public transport was pretty cheap and students can receive 50% if you get a goCard.
activities_available: Most sports clubs you can think of were there, including surfing and climbing. There were a lot of different cultural clubs for asian countries and quite a few societies, but I didn't really look much into them.
activities_recommended: I personally joined the climbing club and it was really nice, they had weekly climbing on an outdoor cliff in the city and in the weekends they would take you on trips to some of the nature/national parks around the city, great way to the bush. The surfclub was also very popular and organized trips to byron bay, also a very good option.
weekend_recommendations: There is a lot to see around Brisbane, I'll list some of the best day trips that you can do. Lone Pine Koala Sanctuary (must see!), Moreton Island, Stadbroke Island, Gold Coast, Sunshine Coast, Mt Coot-tha. For long trips or holidays you can go to Byron Bay, Noosa Heads and you can also fly pretty easily to Bali, New Zealand or Fiji.
culture_adjustment: It wasn't too bad since it's mostly just england with a lot more Asian influence. Since everyone spoke english it wasn't really any difficulty adjusting and also plenty of exchange students around if the locals scare you:).
socializing_tips: Join clubs, they are super friendly to hang out with and it gives you a way into the daily life of the locals and can give you a lot of insight and ideas as to what you might wanna spend your time with during the semester.
cultural_challenges: The supermarket is, to no surprise, very different to what we have in Denmark, and it took some time to adjust to that.
culture_appreciated: Their outgoing nature and outdoor spirit made it easy to make friends and find cool things to do on weekends.
top3_advice: Don't take a first year course, they will be extremely boring. Join clubs and meet some locals, they will give you very valuable information on good places to go and you can also join them for trips sometimes. Lastly, don't book long time accommodation before you arrive, stay in a temporary accommodation for a week or two and have a look around your options in the city, it really helps to see it.
other_useful_info: There are a lot of exchange students from Norway, Germany and also Denmark/Sweden. Just be prepared to meet a lot of familiar people if you join the exchange events.
most_rewarding: Seeing the nature and animals, truly amazing landscapes and so many places to go. Meeting people there was also very fun
greatest_challenge: I had 4 roommates and they were very different from me. So getting into clubs and meeting other people through school was really important to me and allowed me to still make great connections with people even if I was unlucky with my roomies.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience a new culture and a new learning environment
info_ease: QUT was really good at providing information
arrival_assistance: No assistance
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Initially you enroll into a unit, whereupon you register into a certain class. For the class registration you might need to be quick in order to get your preferred schedule.
registration_help: QUT could be contacted in case help was wanted
registration_success: I did successfully register for all the units I wanted, however for one of the units I did not get my preferred class, but as semester started I just asked a teacher and they let me change into a different class
registration_advice: Be sure to register for your classes as soon as you can, to ensure you get the schedule.
course_level: Theoretically the courses were much easier than at UCPH, however the practical part was demanding.
teaching_comparison: A lot more focus on the practical part (more time in the lab) than compared to UCPH.
courses_enrolled: LQB490 Cytogenetic and Molecular Pathology LQB494 Viruses and Viral Pathogenesis LQB601 Cancer Biology LQB693 Immunological Approaches for Infection and Immunity
recommended_courses: I would recommend LQB601 Cancer Biology, if you are a tiny bit intersted in cancer. The unit coordinator is simply outstanding, and the work you get to do in the lab is just exciting.
unexpected_costs: I did not really encounter any unexpected costs, however I did not really take into account how expensive insurance, visa etc. is
cost_comparison: In general, everything is just really expensive in Australia
activities_available: There are a wide range of clubs - everything from surfing and climbing to a weekly meet-up with dogs.
activities_recommended: QUT surfers is a really good opportunity to make new friends and go on different surftrips during the semester
weekend_recommendations: There are a lot of national parks a couple of hours outside Brisbane, so I would definitely recommend renting a car (or buying one) a just drive to different national parks.
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Make an effort to get to know them
cultural_challenges: I did not encounter any cultural differences in particular
culture_appreciated: The Australian people are the most welcoming and helping people
top3_advice: Remember that if your units have practical, they are most likely compulsory to attend. Attend the events in the orientation week - it is a really good way to meet other international students. Start researching for housing early.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: I travelled to Australia alone, so the hole thing about being able to establish a new life alone in another country was very rewarding to me
greatest_challenge: Adapting to a new life in another country
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: A country that speaks fluent English so I can speak with everyone while simultaneously improving my English. Additionally, I wanted an amazing experience traveling across the world and experiencing a new culture, which would also give me opportunities to travel, which there are plenty of.
info_ease: It was not easy at all. Previous reports you might have read stated that it was extremely easy to find accommodation, but that is not the case anymore at least. Probably changed due to Covid. So I would recommend if you want to find a stay you need to come early.
arrival_assistance: I did not. They cannot help with a longer stay. You can contact Student One if you really need to find a place to stay.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You get your info in e-mails. You receive passwords etc. and then you can always contact the student administration for international students if needed (they were very helpful and respond fast).
registration_help: Student international administration. Find their e-mail online if you have not received it yet.
registration_success: Very successful. You do it online. They give you a deadline and you can easily register for your classes online.
registration_advice: Make sure you read the information they send over in PDF-files. It will answer a lot of your questions otherwise just contact them. They are extremely helpful.
course_level: They were Bachelor level. Extremely easy to pass, and since you have no incentive to get a higher grade just enjoy your stay instead.
teaching_comparison: It was very similar. Lectures and tutorials. However, most of the tutorials are shorter and also just go over the answers in the problem set given for that week.
courses_enrolled: Market Structure and Regulation Applied Econometrics Fundamentals of Finance Corporate Finance
recommended_courses: Fundamentals of Finance and Corporate Finance, if you are interested in Finance. However, you have learned some of the curricula already.
unexpected_costs: Alcohol and cigarettes are extremely expensive. Generally, it is more expensive to just live the same life in Australia as it is in Denmark. Everything is a bit more expensive.
cost_comparison: Alcohol and cigarettes. Fitness is also more expensive Coffee is however very affordable and cheaper than in Denmark.
activities_available: The surf club is great since they host some trips to Byron Bay. They sell out fast when they come online, however, so be ready. It is for beginners and everyone just has a good time there. A bit expensive, but worth it. There are so many clubs to choose from. You can just google it. There have to be at least 50 clubs, and probably more. I would recommend that you find some of these clubs and attend at least in the beginning as you will meet a lot of people that way.
activities_recommended: As stated above, just join some of these clubs you are interested in for social interactions and to expand your network. A lot of exchange students also join these clubs, and they are in the same boat as you so don't be shy. Just go out with a positive attitude, and you will meet some great people. Additionally, Australians are a lot easier to befriend than your average Dane.
weekend_recommendations: I loved going on road trips. It is quite easy to rent a car and just drive. Important remember to get an international license from your local municipality institution otherwise you will not be allowed to drive and rent cars. I did a lot of hiking, going to beaches up north or to the gold coast. You can always chill at the fake beach in South Bank aswell. Also, go out a lot to the party, Get drunk on goon (card box wine) instead as drinking a lot of beer or hard liquor will ruin your finances.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Their culture is similar to ours, however they are a bit more laid back.
socializing_tips: Be extremely social for at least the first month. If you are hungover and don't feel like going out, do it anyways. Social bonding at the start of your exchange is important and will help you meet even more people. Obviously, be there the first week of orientation. You get to meet a lot of people there. And probably a lot of Danes as well. Stay in hostels in the beginning. Join a lot of clubs. Get a group chat going, and meet with the people from your universities down there as it might help you make other friends as well.
cultural_challenges: They love to swear. It is all good. They are a lot more open and friendly.
culture_appreciated: Laid back and chill just gives you good vibes on an exchange, which is more geared towards having great experiences.
top3_advice: There are a lot of Danes and Norwegians there, but make sure you also get some local friends and other exchange students as friends. Open up your comfort zone. Don't worry too much about the money. It will be expensive, and you will go out to eat, drink more, and have other experiences. It will be worth it.
other_useful_info: A lot can be done online or at other times. They have some assignments that count toward your grade. Make sure you make a good effort on them so your final exam is more manageable if you have not studied as much for that.

crucial_aspects: I have visited Australia once before and completely fell in love with its people and culture. Since my initial visit in 2019, the desire to return has been strong. Consequently, there was no doubt in my mind that I had to combine my dream of studying abroad with my love for the country. My choice of Brisbane was based on my familiarity with the city, my fondness for it, and the warmer weather (compared to places like Melbourne) was certainly a significant advantage. Moreover, the courses offered by Brisbane's University of Technology (QUT) aligned perfectly with my field of interest.
info_ease: Very easy!
arrival_assistance: QUT were very accommodating in assisting with all our needs. The first week at the university was entirely dedicated to orientation, providing an opportunity to meet fellow exchange students, engage with student associations, and learn about the university's facilities and support services.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After securing the exchange spot through KU, I thoroughly examined the QUT course catalogue (available through their website). I systematically reviewed all master's programs and their prerequisites. Subsequently, I began the process of narrowing down the available courses and cross-referencing them with my prior academic qualifications to ensure I met the prerequisites. This is a very time-consuming process, so it's crucial to allocate sufficient time for it. I compiled all the relevant course descriptions that I considered important for demonstrating that I indeed met the prerequisites into a PDF file. I then submitted this file along with my course registration. Despite the fact that a full-time student typically enrolls in only four courses per semester, I opted to apply for six courses. This decision proved beneficial, as I was ultimately approved for four out of the six courses.
registration_help: There was limited assistance available during the initial course registration process.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Contrary to popular belief claiming that it's nearly impossible for master's students to enroll in master's courses in Australia, the reality is quite different. You simply need to invest time in finding relevant courses and provide effective reasonings for your qualification.
course_level: The academic standards were notably lower compared to Danish norms. Each time we submitted an assignment, there was a considerable focus on revisiting fundamental academic structures, including APA references. This emphasis on basic skills is something Danish universities presume students to have mastered at the Master's level.
teaching_comparison: It was a stark contrast. In my home institution, I am accustomed to actively participating in lectures. We frequently engage in shared discussions about a text or a specific topic. However, at my host institution, the expectation was to sit down and listen. Active involvement was reserved solely for the tutorial sessions.
courses_enrolled: 1. PUN453: Disaster Response and Recovery 2. AMN436: Developing Cultural Intelligence 3. AMN400: Consumer Insights for Marketing Success 4. AMN420: Manage Advertising
recommended_courses: 1. PUN453: Disaster Response and Recovery 2. AMN436: Developing Cultural Intelligence Although these courses may not be directly linked to my field of interest, I really enjoyed them.
unexpected_costs: I was surprised by the considerable amount of money allocated to "Personal Spending." Naturally, this varies based on the frequency of trips, social outings, etc. Furthermore, setting up the apartment incurs significant expenses, including additional kitchen equipment, bedding, pillows, duvets, and more.
cost_comparison: Food and alcohol is very expensive.
activities_available: There are many student clubs on QUT. I became a part of QUT Surfers and QUT Sport. Through these two clubs I was able to go on surf trips, and use the on campus gym facilities. In the first couple of months there were many parties as well.
activities_recommended: QUT surfers is so much fun, however they are very popular. So be ready to sign up for the trips as soon as they are available - it is a great way to meet other students.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the Gold Coast, visit Byron Bay and Noosa. Go to Sydney, go to Melbourne. Drive up the coast to Cairns. Travel as much as possible, but keep the first couple of months free so you have time to explore Brisbane.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, similar to Denmark.
socializing_tips: Go to the social events.
cultural_challenges: I did not encounter any cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: The people in Australia are exceptionally kind and warm-hearted. Explore the local pubs, attend indie music shows, and catch an Australian stand-up performance. Their charm and hospitality are truly welcoming.
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy it as much as you can, time will simply fly by. 2. Go to all the social events you can. It might be overwhelming, but it will be worth it. 3. Save up as much money as possible so you don't have to stress about it while being on exchange. It will be expensive.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Meeting so many amazing people, some of whom I am luck enough to now call my best friends.
greatest_challenge: The initial weeks can be challenging as you find yourself alone in a foreign country away from your family. However, as you start making friends and explore the local scene, it transforms into the time of your life.

I met so many sweet people on my surf trip, but unfortunately they get sold out pretty fast and can be a bit expensive, but still nice to just go on one, so you can try to surf and meet new people!

socializing_tips: I only had classes with local students, so for me it was easy to meet them. But I still got some friends in each class, you just have to be the first to approach
cultural_challenges: Mostly the group work, since they don't really do it as much here as back in UCPH. The group work mostly consisted in delegating the different parts to every group member and then meet up once or twice before you had to hand it in/do the presentation....

other_useful_info: people in the HiQ center is always helpfull and can answer most of your questions

greatest_challenge: Not celebrating Christmas with my family
