crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to Spain because I already spoke a little spanish, which I wanted to improve.
overall_comments: Living in Barcelona is amazing and I can only recommend it! The weather is almost always nice and Barcelona has everything from mountains to beaches, clubs to museums and lots of nice restaurants and bars.
info_ease: It was quite difficult. Due to IT-problems our schedules had not been published so most of us didn't know which courses we had been accepted to or when they took place. We had an online meeting the day classes began but the meeting was mostly about covid restrictions and presnetation of the school - not about the exchange program. At the meeting the administration was informed about the issue with the schedules.
arrival_assistance: After the above mentioned online meeting, the administration decided to do the enrollment manually and scheduled a 15 minute meeting for all the exchange students during the following 2 weeks. The woman who helped me didn't speak english.
arrival_comments: The first 2 weeks were very confusing because of the issue with the enrollment system.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Living in Barcelona is amazing and I can only recommend it! The weather is almost always nice and Barcelona has everything from mountains to beaches, clubs to museums and lots of nice restaurants and bars.
registration_process: In july we got an excel sheet with the time schedule of the courses and access to course descriptions for most of the courses. From this material we should find courses that didn't overlap and register online. The first 2 weeks after arrival, it was possible to add and drop courses.
registration_help: It was possible to email the program manager but she was not good at replying.
registration_success: I got all the courses that I wanted but due to the IT-issue when we arrived, the people sceduled for the last individual meeting were not succesfull in getting all the courses they wanted because the courses had been filled already.
registration_advice: Breath and be patient. The pre approval from KU can be changed so don't stress about which courses you choose. I wish I had used the first 2 weeks trying out different courses and created a schedule without too long breaks and without evening classes. The master courses began later in september and continued for longer time so I would try to avoid them - also because the workload is bigger compared to the low amount of ECTS you get.
academics_comments: Living in Barcelona is amazing and I can only recommend it! The weather is almost always nice and Barcelona has everything from mountains to beaches, clubs to museums and lots of nice restaurants and bars.
course_level: Due to the fact that the courses are only 3-6 ECTS, you only get an introduction to the course. Thus, the level seems much lower than on KU.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was very much like "seminarundervisning" on KU. Classes are mandatory and participation is included in the final grade. The exams were mostly closed book and handwritten which is far from what we're used to at KU but the questions were not that difficult and sometimes only multiple choice
courses_enrolled: 3 ECTS Investment arbitration 3 ECTS Contract techniques 3 ECTS Competition Law 3 ECTS Intellectual Proporty, Patents and Trademark 4 ECTS International Human Rights Protection 5 ECTS Comparative Law 5 ECTS World Trade Law 5 ECTS International Sales Law
recommended_courses: I think comparative law was really interesting because I got to see how different legal systems work. Intellectual proporty, patents and trademark was really an interesting course as well if you haven't had intellectual proporty before.
unexpected_costs: I don't think I had any. I knew that I didn't want to think about money when I was on exchange so I went on trips, to FC Barcelona matches, to the cinema and to restaurants.
cost_comparison: Coffee and beer were extremely cheap. Going to restaurants was in generel a bit cheaper than Denmark but not cheap cheap. Taxis were also more affordable. Apartments/rooms were more or less the same price as Copenhagen.
activities_available: As mentioned above the international student organization organized different events. Moreover ESADE has a volleyballteam, which you can find on instagram and here you find information about try-outs - it's in the beginning of the semester, so I was too late.
activities_recommended: I would recomment to explore the city. Everything is possible! I went bouldering, to beachvolley and social dancing. It's also possible to join a fitness or train at the beach in an outdoor "gym". There is an app called "meetup" where you can find gatherings with other expats.
weekend_recommendations: Go on Erasmus trips! Find Erasmus on instagram where they have a link to their website and here you can join day trips out of Barcelona ex. Montserrat, Andorra, Mont Rebei, Valencia, Costa Brava, Girona etc.
culture_adjustment: It wasn't that difficult. It was fun to observe how different it was from Denmark but not difficult.
socializing_tips: There are more local students in the master courses but in generel the exchange students didn't socialize with the local students.
cultural_challenges: The laid back culture was a bit difficult to adjust to. We often said "well it's Barcelona" when the bus didn't come, when the 5 minute break was 15 minutes and when the power in the apartment went off. In the beginning I always forgot that shops and supermarkets were closed on sundays and holidays but in the end I didn't notice.
culture_appreciated: I really liked how multicultural Barcelina was both regarding food and people. And I also liked that the day often didn't start until 10 am.
top3_advice: Be patient and openminded. Everything will work out in the end so stressing out about courses and exam dates is wasted energy. Students going on exchange are people who want to meet people, so no worries about finding friends - they will be there. Join Erasmus groups on Facebook to get information about Erasmus events where you can meet other Erasmus students. It's okay not to do something everyday because you're not on vacation, you're living in Barcelona. A day in bed can be wisely spent.
other_useful_info: Be attentive and ask when you're in doubt because you are not getting the information from other sources. If you speak spanish it's a huge advantage but it's possible to go to Barcelona without.
most_rewarding: I meet so many different people from different cultures which expanded my view of the world.
greatest_challenge: ESADE administration gave me grey hair. The whole situation in the beginning with the courses really challenged my patience. The dates for the exams were also constantly changing until mid November so it was difficult to book a flight home for christmas.
other_comments: It was worth all the challenges.

registration_process: Students make a prioritized list of 10 subjects (all between 3-6 ECTS) in a web-page which only allows for certain overlaps. After the selection period is over, students are automatically assigned between 27 and 33 ECTS points worth of courses - no matter the requirement of the sending university(!) The system regularly assigned courses not on the prioritized list and even assigned business courses to law students... Students were made to attempt to rectify these errors themselves during a change period, but because all classes were technically "full", changes could usually not be made by students. In the end, every student with wrong courses (a large portion of the students) had to book a physical meeting with the EASDE exchange program manager to have their courses fixed. Overall a bad process.

registration_success: Relatively successful. After recieving 5 courses from my prioritized list and 2 courses not on my prioritized list (one of which being a business course in geoeconomics), I only had to exchange one course in order to reach 30 ECTS worth of law courses.

teaching_comparison: There was no pre-defined curriculum. Rather, the students just had to pay attention in class, read the professor's PowerPoint slides and a handful of articles.

crucial_aspects: The main reasons for choosing my study destination were the chance to experience a new culture, meet new people, and benefit from the academic opportunities. Culturally, it was interesting to live in a different place and see how things are done there. Experiencing local traditions, food, and daily life made the experience more engaging. Meeting new people was also important. Studying somewhere new meant getting to know students from different backgrounds, which made both the social and academic environment more dynamic. Academically, the quality of education and available courses played a big role. The program offered relevant subjects and good learning opportunities, making it a solid choice. Overall, it was a mix of personal and academic benefits that made the destination appealing.
info_ease: It was relatively easy to find the information needed upon arrival. Most details were available online beforehand, and there were resources like university guides, orientation programs, and local support services to help with practical matters. However, some smaller details, like navigating public transport or understanding certain local procedures, required asking around or figuring things out along the way.

registration_advice: Look at their website for information about which classes and how to bid. I also recommend to look often during the bidding periode, since people drop classes, so there are sometimes new available classes.

Further, you do not receive any books, so it is important to attend the classes in order to be able to pass the exam. There was also a lot of presentations which formed a part of your grade.

culture_adjustment: I think it was okay. You primarily have classes with exchange students, and therefore spend most time with them. This of course meant many different cultures, but I found it very interesting to see how people are doing around the world.
cultural_challenges: One cultural difference that was particularly challenging was adjusting to different social norms and communication styles. For example, people might have a different approach to personal space, directness in conversation, or daily routines. Additionally, understanding local customs, such as dining habits or expectations in social settings, took some time. While these differences weren’t major obstacles, they required some adaptation to feel completely comfortable.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the social atmosphere and the emphasis on enjoying life. People seemed to prioritize spending time together, whether through long meals, gatherings, or casual conversations. The local food and dining culture were also highlights, offering a great way to connect with others. Additionally, the balance between work and leisure was something I found refreshing, as it encouraged a more relaxed and enjoyable daily life.
top3_advice: Find housing in good time, apply for additional grants, find housing in the center, instead og close to school.
other_useful_info: Future exchange students might find it useful to familiarize themselves with basic local customs and daily routines before arriving. Understanding how public transport works, typical meal times, can make the transition smoother. It’s also helpful to connect with current or former exchange students for practical tips and insights. Lastly, making an effort to engage with both local and international students can enhance the experience socially and academically.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people.The most rewarding part of the exchange experience was the opportunity to step out of my comfort zone and adapt to a new environment. Meeting people from different backgrounds, experiencing a new culture firsthand, and gaining a fresh perspective on academics made the experience both personally and professionally enriching. The connections made and the skills developed—such as independence, adaptability, and cross-cultural communication—were especially valuable.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during the exchange was adjusting to the differences in academic expectations and workload. The pace and structure of courses were sometimes different from what I was used to, requiring me to adapt quickly. Additionally, balancing academics with the social aspects of the exchange was sometimes tricky, as I wanted to make the most of both my studies and the cultural experiences.

overall_comments: It has been a valuable experience in some respects, but many of the courses have not been useful, and the level of instruction was not based on legislation or legal principles, but rather on theory and personal opinions. I am not sure whether this was because I simply chose the wrong subjects. In general, the school itself was not well-structured. The mandatory attendance requirements create significant pressure, and absences require a medical certificate. All exams are handwritten and without any aids, which makes little sense to me. Moreover, the teaching was often disorganised and unclear, making it difficult to understand what the lecturers were saying or expecting. We were frequently informed only a few days in advance that we had to prepare presentations, and at times we were assigned more than 30 pages of reading to complete within less than two days. The most concerning issue is that we may not receive our grades until 17 January, which poses a serious problem, as I am scheduled to start as a junior associate on 1 January.

crucial_aspects: I have several important aspects when I choose my study destination: - The academic courses - The city and the country; especially the nature - A country not too far away from Denmark - but still with a new culture and a lot of possibilities.
overall_comments: Overall a very nice experience - I would really recommend Iceland and Reykjavik University.
info_ease: Reykjavík University send a lots of useful information upon arrival. Furthermore, you could send them an e-mail with additional questions. Iceland is a very loose society with the motto 'þetta reddast' - so be aware that some information might show up last minute and exam dates etc can change during the exchange!
arrival_assistance: When I arrived at Reykjavik University, we had orientation days with a mixture of social and informal stuff. Furthermore it was always possible to reach out to the international team from the beginning to the end of the semester.
arrival_comments: The international team is very friendly and helpful!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall a very nice experience - I would really recommend Iceland and Reykjavik University.
registration_process: The application/registration was through Mobility Online which is similar to the exchange application through UCPH.
registration_help: The guides sent from the university was very helpful for me and made the proces easy. Furthermore it was possible to send them an e-mail with additional questions.
registration_success: I did not get one of the classes I wanted, since the law department at Reykjavik University is quite small and not enough people applied for the course.
registration_advice: Remember that the law department at Reykjavik University is quite small, and do not offer a lot of courses. As mentioned above there is a chance that not enough people apply for the course resulting in a cancellation. With that said, they are flexible with running courses etc. even with few students. Be aware that the Icelandic mindset and motto is 'þetta reddast' which means that sometimes you receive last minute information or dates of exams etc might change during the semester from the dates they told you in the beginning of the semester.
academics_comments: Overall a very nice experience - I would really recommend Iceland and Reykjavik University.
course_level: In my opinion the overall level of the courses were a bit easier compared to UCPH - the reason therefore might be the fact that the courses were either 7.5 or 3.75 ECTS.
teaching_comparison: Overall the teaching style was similar to UCPH; we had lectures in classrooms with a teacher presentation and some plenum discussions as well. The most different thing from UCPH was the continious exams and grades. During the semester we had assignments and exams that was a part of the final grading. Furthermore in some courses you get a participation grade.
courses_enrolled: US Litigation The US Legal System: Sources and Structure European Convention on Human Rights International Criminal Law Climate Law
recommended_courses: I really liked the courses: US Litigation The US Legal System: Sources and Structure It was interesting to obtain a general knowledge about the legal system in the US, and the teacher was very good as well.
unexpected_costs: In general a lot of things were more expensive than calculated - but the thing that surprised me the most was the expensive student housing/accommodation. The costs hereof was more expensive than stated at the calculated costs at the webpage of Reykjavik University.
cost_comparison: More expensive than expected: A lot of groceries, such as meat, vegetables etc. and as mentioned before accommodation Less expensive than expected: Sweets and candy
activities_available: Reykjavík University did not offer a lot of sports opportunities. All departments had an association with activities such as visiting companies, parties etc. There was a cost of being a part of the association. Most of it was only offered in Icelandic - but besides that it was nice to participate in. Some exchange students did on their own plan soccer, bouldering etc.
activities_recommended: If you are in Iceland please do yourself the favor and enjoy the beautiful Icelandic nature. Everyone in Iceland will give you this tip: visit the local swimmingpools - that is a very social thing to do in Iceland!
weekend_recommendations: Experience the lovely and beautiful country of Iceland as much as you can. Even visiting the same places several times during the different seasons is nice!
culture_adjustment: In general easy! Sometimes the information is given in Icelandic - but google translate helps a lot!
socializing_tips: At the law department it was a bit difficult to socialize with the local students - if that is the case, then go to social events arranged by other (local) students, such as Erasmus networks, international committees etc.
cultural_challenges: I did not really find it culturally challenging - since Iceland and Denmark is not too far away from each other. The Icelandic mindset is a bit more chill than the danish - they have the 'þetta reddast' motto, which translates to 'everything will work out'.
culture_appreciated: I really enjoyed the more chill 'þetta reddast' mindset. Furthermore the Icelandic people is very friendly and helpful!
top3_advice: Three most important things: - Apply for accommodation as fast as possible - It is nice to participate in social events - it makes the academic part more fun as well - Enjoy the nature and Iceland as much as possible
other_useful_info: Everything is expensive - but do yourself the favor and experience as much as possible during weekends ect. Rent a car with some of your new friends and enjoy waterfalls, glaciers, lava tunnels, puffins (when it is puffin-season) etc.
most_rewarding: - I improved my legal academic English skills - I challenged myself - I really enjoyed slowing a bit down and enjoying the Icelandic nature - Furthermore I got a lot of good friends
greatest_challenge: For me the greatest challenge was to live in another country with other cultures etc. Furthermore it was a challenge to balance social and academic life.
other_comments: Overall, I would really recommend Reykjavík University and Iceland!

crucial_aspects: The possibilities to go out and explore the nature.
info_ease: Very easy - Reykjavik University has a lot of information for exchange students on their webside and an international office, which you can e-mail and ask questions and they usually reply very fast.
arrival_assistance: The university had arranged a couple of orientation days, where we got a lot of practical information and got attached to tutors, who we could also ask questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I found my courses in the university's course calender and applied for them in Reykjavik University's Mobility Online.
registration_help: I could always e-mail the international office at the host university.
registration_success: Very succesful.
registration_advice: Just make sure to keep the deadlines and don't be afraid to ask questions to the international office.
course_level: It was very much the same level as of UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was very much the same as UCPH. However, we had to prepare presentations and write essays, which would count in our final grade, during the semester instead of just being graded on one final exam at the end of the semester.
courses_enrolled: Law and Economics US litigation US legal system: Sources and Structure European Convention of Human Rights Principles of Energy Law
recommended_courses: All of them - the teaching was good and the workload was managable.
unexpected_costs: Public transportation out of the city was very expensive and limited, why we had to rent a car and pay for fuel + parking everytime we wanted to go on a trip. Also some groceries was more expensive than I thought.
cost_comparison: Cheese, meat and some vegetables was more expensive than I thought. Joining a gym was also crazy expensive, so that I didn't prioritize.
activities_available: There was a handfull of academic student associations, but you had to pay to join.
activities_recommended: I really enjoyed the citypools, it's where the locals go and it's a nice and cheap thing to do with your friends or just by yourself. There is also a park called Klambratún, where you can meet up and play ball or disc golf.
weekend_recommendations: To rent a car and get out of the city to do some hikes in the spectacular nature.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Just talk to the ones in your class or join a student association.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The fascination and respect the locals had for the nature and the environment.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared to spend money. It's just an expensive country. 2. Don't worry about making friends, everyone is eager to meet new people and there will be a lot of events arranged by other students. Just be approachable and say yes. 3. Don't be afraid to take initiative yourself if there is something you want to do and be inviting.
other_useful_info: It can be helpfull to have researched a bit in advance what you would like to see or do, so you can prioritize your money on that. But you can also decide on that when you have arrived and maybe talked to some of the other exchange students.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people from different countries with different backgrounds and to explore the crazy Icelandic nature together with them.
greatest_challenge: To accept that everything was so expensive and having to prioritize my money.
other_comments: I really enjoyed not bringing my work, as it meant that I was more free and not stressed.

crucial_aspects: Seeing something new, cheap location, easy access to accommodation
info_ease: Very easy. The coordinator was really good at telling us what to expect prior to arrival. I also found it very helpful that the university suggested accommodation in Riga.
arrival_assistance: We had introduction days when we arrived. This helped us get close together in the Erasmus group.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Writing an e-mail to the administration.
registration_help: The administration was very helpful and always answered quickly.
registration_success: Always succesful.
registration_advice: It is easy and just ask the administration!
course_level: I had mostly BA courses but also one MA. The academic level was ok, but the local students were not very good. It is easy to be an exchange student from the university, but I do not think it is easy to be an exchange student from the university. I liked that it was not only the exam that counted but also the participation. It made sure that I showed up to class and was an active part of the class.
teaching_comparison: More informal. It was like being in high school and the teachers always knew your name.
courses_enrolled: Economic diplomacy, law of state responsibility, environmental law, political negotiations, tactics and style, global approaches to public diplomacy, International Human Rights Institutions, Procedures and Mechanisms, International Humanitarian law, Legal Aspects of the External Relations of EU, Geo-economics: the Geopolitics of Energy, International Law.
recommended_courses: Global approaches and Geo-economics! The teachers are amazing. Political negotiation is really fun if you like debating.
unexpected_costs: travels with my new friends. In general I spend a lot of money on having fun with friends, so it is possible to live cheaper than me in Riga.
cost_comparison: Everything was very cheap.
activities_available: There were fun parties in the school. There were other opportunities, but the local students were acting very young and it felt a bit like high school, so personally I did not go.
activities_recommended: The parties.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Estonia, Poland and Lithuania. It is all easily accessible from Riga. A day trip to Sigulda or Gauja national park is also fun.
culture_adjustment: Yes and no. The exchange community is strong, but the Latvians are not very social.
socializing_tips: Give it time. They will eventually work with you when they see that you do good academically.
cultural_challenges: The lack of spontaneity and need for structure. The Latvians we met often had a hard time adjusting to new things. They were sweet when you got them to talk, but if you did anything they weren't uses to they would get mad. The roads were very slippery and the city did nothing. Also the emergency room was closed on the weekends.
culture_appreciated: The karaoke bar was fun. Everything was cheap and that was also nice.
top3_advice: 1. The local students are academically not very good unfortunately. 2. It is easy to get good grades. 3. You have to be active in class.
other_useful_info: Focus on the friends you meet in school.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people from all over Europe. Learning new things about cultures and sharing my own.
greatest_challenge: The slippery roads of Riga and my home university not responding and "losing" my e-mail. My host university was good at responding me, but I felt like I never got any real help from my home uni.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a country that was completely different from my own or what I was used to so far. Japan was definitely the right choice, especially Kyoto instead of Tokyo. Kyoto is more traditional and smaller, but has everything you need. I believe I would have felt too overwhelmed in Tokyo. The cultural shock was positive, especially because everyone (from the university international center to the dorm management staff) was super helpful with everything, even the smaller stuff. I would recommend staying in a dorm, since living on your own here can be quite expensive (and boring). Taishogun International House has been perfect for me: not only you're surrounded by amazing people, but all the furniture etc is in good condition. As for the University, classes have been incredibly interesting and made me able to understand the Japanese culture on a deeper level. I also attended a Japanese course which unfortunately doesn't provide you with any ECTS, but it was worth it, as now I'm already at a good conversational level, after only 4 months. Overall, I would 100% recommend this exchange, especially to students who are attracted by what's different.
info_ease: It was way easier than I thought, both the International Center and the Dorm's staff provided me with all the necessary pieces of information and deadlines.
arrival_assistance: They even came with me to different places (e.g. the bank, the immigration office), to help me set up all the documents I needed, since I didn't understand Japanese when I arrived. They have brochures available, and they are extremely helpful even by e-mail.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It all goes through the Manaba+R website, but here again, the international center is VERY helpful. They send you an incredibly detailed brochure with all the necessary information, and they're available anytime by email in case you need any help. You look for the courses from a list they send you, and then register the code of the course. After a week it gets approved and when classes start, you have one week to decide whether you like the course or not, and eventually deregister.
registration_help: Brochures, e-mail, website orientation.
registration_success: I registered for all the classes I wanted to join, I felt like it was pretty easy to do so.
registration_advice: Choose the courses that fit easily in your schedule and that you feel are more interesting. I'd recommend choosing courses from the graduate school only, and not undergraduate, as they are more pertinent to what we study.
course_level: The courses were on an adequate level for an MA in International Relations, and they were all focused on Japan or Asia in general, which I found helpful as in Europe we don't pay as much attention to it. I believe it was the perfect amount of study/classes, which I could balance well with my life outside class.
teaching_comparison: I felt like the teaching styles and methods were really similar. They both relied on papers of the same length and difficulty, and group projects/presentations were very common as well. I didn't feel any discomfort or difficulty in studying here,
courses_enrolled: Globalization and Gender Issues — This course explores contemporary gender issues in relation to globalization, through case studies and multidisciplinary readings. It helps students identify and deconstruct the role of stereotypes in shaping policies, government interventions and social movements. • Non-Traditional Security — The aim of this course is to learn about the changing paradigm of security studies in the 21st Century, in order to highlight major security challenges in the age of globalism. • South Asian Studies — This program aims to build a locally-contextualized understanding of the regional history and present politico-economic and societal reality of South Asia. • Liberal Arts Seminar — This course is designed to learn about western writers' preoccupations with Japanese culture and its customs.
recommended_courses: I would totally recommend Liberal Arts Seminar, with Chris Summerville. He has been an amazing professor, and helped us dig deeper on the Japanese culture.
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Transport was way more expensive than I thought, and local insurances (which are mandatory) were expensive as well.
activities_available: I joined the University's gym and pottery club, although they had around 150 different clubs that you could choose from. They were all of different kinds, from sports activities to art, to professional work, to the cinema, etc. There is one club for anything you would like to do! Even NGOs etc.
activities_recommended: Definitely the pottery club! It's an interesting way of relaxing from all the academic stress, and you learn the Japanese way to work with clay!
weekend_recommendations: Even if it is expensive, travel around as much as you can! Kansai area is beautiful and definitely worth a visit. Take a train and go to Hiroshima, Miyajima, Okayama, Tokyo, etc. You won't probably have another chance of living in Japan for so long!
culture_adjustment: It was way easier than I thought, but then again, everybody was super helpful if you had any minor/major inconvenience. The language barrier was hard at first, but with the Japanese language course now I am able to communicate with anyone.
cultural_challenges: Japanese people don't speak much English, and that was really hard at first. However, after a couple of weeks you start to understand how they think and act, and you can work on it.
culture_appreciated: The food!!! Everything is delicious and affordable.
top3_advice: 1. Don't be afraid, it will be the best 6 months of your life! 2. Travel around as much as you can while you're here, have as many experiences as you can, try different foods, go to temples, and go hiking on a random mountain. You will be able to appreciate the small things in life. 3. Learn the language while you're here, even if you don't want to work or come back here in the future. It will be helpful for you anyway.
other_useful_info: Definitely read a guide about Japan before you come, and maybe learn some Japanese before coming here as well!
most_rewarding: Being able to experience a different culture, and being able to speak some Japanese only after 4 months.
greatest_challenge: The language barrier at first, but it is an obstacle that you can easily overcome after a while.

crucial_aspects: A well-functioning but a different country in terms of culture, nature etc. Moreover, a country with a different approach to academia.
info_ease: The staff at Ritsumeikan is excellent at providing the students with relevant information. Almost to an extreme degree. They make checklists for exchange students to adapt to the Japanese bureaucracy regarding residence status, bank account, health insurance etc. They also provide information about housing opportunities and general matters regarding the academic life, important deadlines and courses of action as an exchange student.
arrival_assistance: The SKP staff provided help and assistance with almost every matter. My landlord was also a great help and took me to the bank and helped my to understand and fill out important paperwork in Japanese.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You could apply for courses after the second application round. Upon arrival the registration results got published and it was possible to make changes though a second application round.
registration_help: You can visit the SKP staff if you have questions about the application process.
registration_success: I got all the courses I applied for, even though I had to do a second application because I had to make changes to my registration as the meritkontor, didn't accept some of my courses. If you have to make changes you can always go to the SKP staff, they will tell you what courses a still available.
registration_advice: If you study at SAMF - language courses will not be accepted by the meritkontor. I had to make changes to my course registration because of this. Apply for as many courses as possible, this makes your prior approval (forhåndsgodkendelse) way easier, as you don't have to apply through KU's slow bureaucracy once again. You can always cancel your registration at Ritsumeikan within a reasonable time. The credit conversion is a bit confusing so make sure to get a lower credit threshold from the meritkontor, so you can stay above that.
course_level: Below average compared to KU. In Japan attendance is a part of the grading. Attendance (as in being there physically) weighs quite high on your grading. Most of the courses are introductory to the subject and do not go in-depth as much as I desired (the courses are only 2 credits = 4 ects). You will be able to follow along with ease as long as you show up and contribute to the class.
teaching_comparison: Around the same style as on KU. Some of the courses were more old school, that is an old Japanese professor talking for 1,5 hours straight. However, most of my courses had group work and small seminars.
courses_enrolled: Policy Case Reading 1 Public Diplomacy Global Political History Global Peace Studies South-East Asian Studies Qualitative Research Methodology European Studies Japanese Ⅰ-1(Comprehensive)
recommended_courses: I can recommend Public Diplomacy and Global Peace Studies. The professors were engaging and had a good academic approach. I can also recommend Japanese Ⅰ-1(Comprehensive). It was fun to learn a new language it is also helpful if you want to function in the Japanese society.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay for some different campus-related insurances and the mandatory student Co-op. You also have to pay for national health insurance, this is mandatory for all persons in Japan with residence status.
cost_comparison: Food, beverages etc. are in general less expensive, and the local bus is as well. The Shinkansen and other JR-operated trains are quite expensive. And you can not get the tourist discount with your residence status.
activities_available: Hiking, Pottery, Archery, Rugby, Rudo, Karate, Goshuin club you name it.
activities_recommended: The pottery club is awesome and the members are really friendly. Club activities are in general the best place to meet Japanese students as you will be taking your courses with "the English speakers".
weekend_recommendations: Kyoto has a lot of nearby attractions. Mount Hiei and other mountain shrines are great to visit. You can take one-day trips to Osaka, Kobe, Himeji and Nara and weekend trips to Tokyo, Hiroshima etc.
culture_adjustment: The Japanese culture is really different and a lot of European norms are frowned upon (being loud in public, eye contact with strangers etc.). However, the Japanese understand that Westerners are different and is willing to help you in almost every situation.
socializing_tips: The campus clubs.
cultural_challenges: THe language barrier. If you don't understand Japanese some things can be difficult (the ward office etc). Google translate can get you a long way. No cultural difference was challenging to an extent that something became impossible.
culture_appreciated: The openness and willingness to help.
top3_advice: Be open-minded to the differences; experience Japan and remember to enjoy it while you can.
other_useful_info: It is worth the paperwork. Don't stress too much about academic matters. And regarding the finals. Most courses have written exams and you will not get days off for writing them.
most_rewarding: Being able to cement yourself in a completely different setting.
greatest_challenge: The finals. Working on seven different written exams in 1,5 months was quite a challenge.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial that the destination would be somewhere related to my major and therefore be benefitting in my studies.
info_ease: Everything was quite the process and most things were in Japanese. There were so much paperwork.
arrival_assistance: Some of the students in my dorm went with me to the ward office to fill out some paperwork, that was helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was very stressful, there were a lot of paperwork. It was also a bit expensive.
registration_help: There was one advisor, but again, the registration was in the holidays so the reply time was very slow.
registration_success: It was quite a hassle, at first I didn´t get into half of the courses I registered for and did therefore not have enough credits. Then I was allowed to apply for more courses as an exception, but when I finally had enough credits, one of my courses got cancelled because of lack of participants. Luckily they made another exception for me to apply for other courses. In the end they found out they had miscalculated the IJL course line, so instead of 9 credits, it was 8 credits. Then everyone in my class was allowed to apply for additional courses if needed.
registration_advice: The documents written and signed by the professors can be send after the deadline, as it is out of your control that the registration period is in their vacations.
course_level: The Japanese courses were around the N2 level. My lecture for humanity courses were each 2 credits but had the same workload as the 15 credit courses at KU, the only difference is that their expectations for you are lower.
teaching_comparison: I quite liked that you were evaluated the whole way through the semester, and not just with a final exam at the end of the semester. Therefore if you do bad on your final exam, it wont be a whole semester wasted. It was also motivating to do well the whole semester through.
courses_enrolled: 3 lecture for humanity courses, 1 special lecture course, Japanese listening and speaking, Japanese comprehensive, Japanese writing.
recommended_courses: 11616:Lecture for Humanities (LR) - We learned about the art of translation. I was very interesting, but it was favorite course because it was the course I felt the most comfortable in. Each class we would sit in a circle and discuss the translation of different work. One could speak freely, so it was a very pleasant experience. I don´t think I´ve ever spoken that much in any other class before. It did have some of the bigger presentations and exams, but even doing them and discussing them afterwards in the class was a good learning experience.
unexpected_costs: There´s a surprising amount of insurances you have to pay each month
cost_comparison: Most books are cheaper here than in Denmark.
activities_available: There was almost every kind of sport, art and even a club where you could go around and feed the school cats
activities_recommended: I went to the art club once, there was a very relaxing atmosphere.
weekend_recommendations: Visit the shrines and temples in Kyoto. Kinkaku-ji is located very close to the school.
culture_adjustment: It took about a week to adjust, so I think it was quite easy.
socializing_tips: Eat together in the canteen, go to a café close by the school, get a language partner, study in the BBP (a lot of Japanese students go there to study English), join a club, register for courses with both local students and exchange students, live in one of the dorms.
cultural_challenges: Most people don´t speak English here. It is still mandatory to wear masks here. Everything is done through paperwork here, you cannot do things fully online, like in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: The food is so good. Everyone is polite. I do not have to worry about randomly getting yelled at by a stranger or hostility from security guards and police.
top3_advice: Get used to studying and doing your homework every single day, the dorm kitchen is the best place for you to make friends, speak up in class - it´s the best way to learn something.
other_useful_info: Bring everything you need from home so you don´t have to spend all your money buying basic necessities here. There´s school everyday, even on national holidays, and if school or class is cancelled, you will have a makeup class in the weekends instead.
most_rewarding: My Japanese has improved a lot.
greatest_challenge: Most of my classes were completely in Japanese, so it was hard to follow along the first month or two.

crucial_aspects: I am studying Japanese Studies and exchange was a crucial part of my bachelor's degree. I wanted to dive into the language and culture of the field I was studying, so for this reason going to a Japanese University seemed obvious. Ristumeikan University was attractive due to its profile as internationally oriented and its location in the cultural hub of Kyoto.
info_ease: Ritsumeikan University takes very good care of its exchange students and furthermore, I was helped out by people at my dormitory.
arrival_assistance: I was assisted by Resident Managers at my dorm in opening a bank account, signing up for Japanese insurance etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The course registration process took place online. There were course descriptions available that where very easy to comprehend.
registration_help: I was guided by Resident Managers at my dorm.
registration_success: I was in a way over-successful. The university had warned the students that it was not likely that all of our priorities would be met, so I signed up for more classes than I needed. In the end, this turned out to be a mistake on my part as I was granted a spot in all the classes I wanted and needed.
registration_advice: Make sure to create a schedule that is not too intense and maybe I would not recommend more than three different classes in a day.
course_level: In my experience, the Japanese language courses had a very appropriate level, while my additional courses were rather easy and sometimes slightly superficial.
teaching_comparison: The teaching at Ritsumeikan University is much more focused on attendance, writing assignments and making presentations than what I am used to from the University of Copenhagen. However, I never felt that much was expected from us in class discussions, and sometimes I found that the teachings were slightly superficial.
courses_enrolled: Japanese V (Comprehensive) Japanese V (Writing) Japanese V (Listening&Speaking) Japanese Politics International Migration Cross-cultural Studies Special Lectures in Human Welfare
recommended_courses: I highly recommend the course Cross-cultural Studies. It allowed me to discuss topics with Japanese students and make many good friends.
unexpected_costs: It is necessary to pay for Japanese insurance even if you bring your own insurance.
cost_comparison: In general, most things are cheaper compared to Denmark.
activities_available: All sorts of clubs and gatherings. Sports, culture, music etc.
activities_recommended: I did not have much time to participate in club activities due to the large amount of credits required by the University of Copenhagen.
weekend_recommendations: Kyoto offers lots of beautiful temples and shrines. I also recommend people try traditional Japanese sweets, wagashi, which Kyoto is famous for. There are also many amazing hiking routes close to the city.
culture_adjustment: It was surprisingly easy. I was very grateful to the community of the dorm for making the transition simple.
socializing_tips: Take courses that are open to both Japanese and foreign students. And use BBP (Beyond Borders Plaza), which is an open space for people to socialize.
cultural_challenges: Initially, I struggled a bit with the levels of formality that are connected to the Japanese language.
culture_appreciated: I absolutely adore the city of Kyoto. It has an amazing atmosphere, cuisine and surroundings.
top3_advice: Get out of your comfort zone, explore the city as much as possible and remember to take time off on the weekends to recharge. Exchange can be very overwhelming.
other_useful_info: If you are a student of Japanese Studies like myself, I would advise you to put most of your energy into the language classes provided at Ritsumeikan University. The University of Copenhagen requires students to take quite a lot of courses and it is difficult to give it your all in all of them.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange is how drastically my language abilities have improved.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge for me was time. I needed to dedicate so much time to my additional courses that it was hard to find the time for socializing and enjoying the surroundings to the fullest.
other_comments: No other comments.

registration_success: I registered for the classes that I wanted.

teaching_comparison: Similar style, but a bit more seminar style generally.
courses_enrolled: Lecture for Humanities (Japanese Early Poetry, and Japanese traditional culture) Race and Ethnicity in the Modern World Japanese Society

weekend_recommendations: Travel, there is so much to see!

top3_advice: Be prepared for a lot of bureaucracy and procedures in the beginning and end, more homework and attendance requirements than in DK, but also a fascinating country, culture, food and kind people
other_useful_info: No that I can think of

greatest_challenge: The language barrier -- most people don't speak English

crucial_aspects: I chose Kyoto because of the rich culture and deep history that the city embodies. Furthermore, I chose it with the hopes of getting to improve my Japanese language skills, because of the amount of Japanese to foreign people that live in the city.
overall_comments: I absolutely loved being on exchange at Ritsumeikan, and I would go back in a heartbeat. One thing that needs to change to make the academic part be less stressful is to decrease the amount of necessary credits for courses. The amount of lectures and exams were very stressful and I had almost no free time because of the 15 credit requirement. I had classes 18 hrs a week, which was simply too much. After speaking with the International center at Ritsumeikan, they would recommend 12 credits total as a maximum for attended classes, which I agree with.
info_ease: It was made easier because of the wonderful RM’s at my dorm and the flyers the international center gave out. The people at my dorm were very helpful in helping me find information.
arrival_assistance: Again, the RM’s at my dorm and the people living there were so helpful, both helping me going to the ward office and helping me fill out all the necessary documents.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I absolutely loved being on exchange at Ritsumeikan, and I would go back in a heartbeat. One thing that needs to change to make the academic part be less stressful is to decrease the amount of necessary credits for courses. The amount of lectures and exams were very stressful and I had almost no free time because of the 15 credit requirement. I had classes 18 hrs a week, which was simply too much. After speaking with the International center at Ritsumeikan, they would recommend 12 credits total as a maximum for attended classes, which I agree with.
registration_process: We had to register for many things. These included the national health care insurance, a pension service, a CO-OP service for getting books and meals at campus, and aside from that we needed to open a bank account at the post office, which was a difficult task to begin with.
registration_help: The RM’s at my dorm were very helpful during every step of the way, and they certainly made the amount of bureaucracy and paperwork easier to handle.
registration_success: I was given a list of available classes aside from the Japanese language course, that I could register for. I got the ones that I chose there, no issue, but they did not match my wishes from back home exactly.
registration_advice: Rely on your RM’s and ask the international center for help when you need it! They are very helpful and want to aid you.
academics_comments: I absolutely loved being on exchange at Ritsumeikan, and I would go back in a heartbeat. One thing that needs to change to make the academic part be less stressful is to decrease the amount of necessary credits for courses. The amount of lectures and exams were very stressful and I had almost no free time because of the 15 credit requirement. I had classes 18 hrs a week, which was simply too much. After speaking with the International center at Ritsumeikan, they would recommend 12 credits total as a maximum for attended classes, which I agree with.
course_level: I was beyond satisfied with the Japanese language courses, the quality of classes there were amazing and I would recommend the IJL courses to anyone interested in learning Japanese academically. Otherwise, the level of quality was mixed. Some of the courses were very superficial, and rarely dug deep into the material we were studying, which I thought was a shame.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. We were generally speaking more students than in my Japan studies courses, and the Japanese language courses were only in Japanese and were way more conversation and listening focused than back at home.
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled in the IJL level 4 courses in listening and speaking, comprehension and writing, furthermore I was enrolled in the RCE (courses in english) courses Cross Cultural Encounters 1, Japanese Poetry, Japanese Culture and Field research and a Calligraphy class.
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend all the courses apart from the Cross Cultural Encounters class, on the count of it unfortunately being a bit too superficial academically for my taste.
unexpected_costs: I was shocked by the amount of things we had to pay for in terms of required services, and we had to pay three different deposits, which was surprising to me.
cost_comparison: Bear in mind that the personal expenses were based on my shopping and leisure
activities_available: There was a wide variety, everything from a cycling club to a theatre club and manga club.
activities_recommended: I would recommend to go bouldering in the gym Adsummum in the Shinkyogoku shopping street Teramachi, go karaokeing and hiking in the nearby forests and mountains.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the many museums, shrines, temples, restaurants, bars and go hang out near the Kamogawa river.
culture_adjustment: It was a bit daunting at first, but I eventually adjusted well and I miss it a lot. It was harder to adjust to coming home again.
socializing_tips: Talk to people, go to social events at the Borders Beyond Plaza (BBP) and practice your Japanese language skills!
cultural_challenges: I have a tattoo, and I did meet some prejudice there, not being let in to fitness gyms and onsens regularly.
culture_appreciated: So many things. I got to experience the many festivals/matsuri in Kyoto, which was fantastic.
top3_advice: I would say that it is a good idea to get the Randen pass if you live in the Tokiwa dorm, join the BBP events and to not only focus on classes, but go explore Japan a bit while you are there.
other_useful_info: Pick a maximum of 12 credits worth of classes, more WILL be stressful and leave you with minimal time for anything but classes.
most_rewarding: I have gotten some friends that I cherish a lot and experienced things that I will treasure for the rest of my life. Furthermore, I really improved my Japanese language skills, which I am very satisfied with.
greatest_challenge: It was definitely living in the Japanese summer heat. The temperatures exceed 40 degrees sometimes, so prepare for heatwaves if you go during the summer.

crucial_aspects: It just had to be in Japan. You can't really know what it's like before you go...
info_ease: Quite easy. Ritsumeikan gave us a detailed pre-arrival guide.
arrival_assistance: A briefing a ritsumeikan university and a pamphlet that contained info on different arrival procedures.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You register through an excel sheet. They explain it at the briefing as well as hand out papers that explain it.
registration_help: You can contact the international center if in doubt.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Try a CSC (Campus specific course) course or two. They are quite fun, and the work load is not too bad. Just keep in mind that they cost money and make sure you can get pre-approva (CSC is artsy stuff such as calligraphy, ikebana etc).
course_level: IJL (Intensive Japanese Language Track) was quite intensive funnily enough, but nothing crazy. Just make sure not to register for English language classes that require a lot of preparation. That is why I suggest taking a CSC course or 2.
teaching_comparison: The IJL course has a lot more classes every week.
courses_enrolled: IJL lvl 5 = Comphrehensive Japanese 5x a week Listening and Speaking 2x a week Writing 1x a week. English Language courses: 12977:Introduction to Vernacular Culture (L) 11775:Lecture for Humanities (LC) § 11776:Selected Problems in Human CSC courses: 16598:Japanese Traditional Arts II (KF) - calligraphy
recommended_courses: Calligraphy was fun to try and the work load is not too bad. Same goes for Introduction to Vernacular Culture. And the subjects are quite interesting too. IJL is quite hard, but you get to practice Japanese language every day. In addition I recommend going to BBP, where you can meet a lot of other exchange studetns as well as Japanese people. Here you can both practice Japanese as well as make new friends.
unexpected_costs: None. I've been to Japan before :) For people who haven't been before - you need to pay for national health insurance in Japan no matter what, so reconsider if you need your own travel insurance (I reckon you can do without).
cost_comparison: Housing was quite cheap in Freepia 1&2
activities_available: BBP hosts a lot of activites such as language exchanges events, social events etc.
activities_recommended: Anything in BBP. its a good place to meet people and hang out. Also Kyoto is a beautiful city, so take some time to explore it and see some of the temples /nature.
weekend_recommendations: Go see some temples, go on a hike, go to a football game - something cultural :)
culture_adjustment: Quite easy
socializing_tips: BBP. Join a circle if you have a certain interest in sports, boardgames, dancing, whatever it might be, you can probably find likeminded people there.
cultural_challenges: Sometimes Japanese people can be a bit hard to get close to. Also the traffic can be a bit tricky sometimes, as the bikes ride on the sidewalk... and don't use a bell. Don't expect cars to stop for you.
culture_appreciated: People are generally really nice.
top3_advice: Throw yourself out there (don't listen too much to advice, just do your own thing). Even though you don't speak the language, don't let that hold you back too much. Most people are nice and accomodating. Go out and explore and see for yourself.
other_useful_info: x
most_rewarding: Finishing an intensive language track and meeting new people.
greatest_challenge: The studies.

crucial_aspects: Japan offered a completely new perspective on academic life and the future career opportunities. Meanwhile, the culture itself had many depths to delve into and experience. Something that is only possible by extensive cultural contact.
info_ease: The SKP-staff and university personel in general were impeccable in providing information - perhaps to a fault. Be ware of the risk of information overload and use your peers to navigate the sometimes Kafkaesque bureaucratic systems of Japan.
arrival_assistance: The orientation day along with study guide sent out beforehand had ample information to get through the first days of arrival.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Online with parallel processes. Make sure to apply for language courses before arriving and getting positive confirmation, once you're there its too late to apply for these.
registration_help: Kind support via email or open office hours.
registration_success: I had a great deal of luck securing the classes i applied for, but they were not entirely the ones I had thought about before applying for exchange. The courses will change depending on many factors. Don't be too set in your expectations.
registration_advice: Be prepared to not get all your prioty courses and perhaps even not at the campus nearest you.
course_level: The English proficiency of not only the students but the lecturers leaned more towards BA-level.
teaching_comparison: More focus on individual performance and experiences, almost no group work, and many classes had attendance. Meaning, the trust between students and teachers were not as high.
courses_enrolled: 72143 International Research Project 71388 Globalization and Gender Issues 71576 East Asian Studies 16457 Japanese Economy 71718 Non-Traditional Security 16846 Japanese Society
recommended_courses: Just make sure to have a variety of evaluation goals - check the course descriptions - most have a final paper and these have to be handed in the same week of the semester. Try to spread it out.
unexpected_costs: Not many. Some deposits and bureaucratic stuff. Mostly you get it back at the end of the semester.
cost_comparison: Since the JPY was historically low, most things were pretty cheap. Although, fresh produce - fruits and veggies - are expensive.
activities_available: They have whole program for clubs and circles that you can join without having to speak much Japanese, just beware that you will have to dedicate yourself and your time to them, so you will have to choose.
activities_recommended: I didn't join any.
weekend_recommendations: Just go take the train somewhere - there are too many places to visit and the months will quickly pass. Even just taking the bike or the bus to a famous temple or nice ramen place a day after class will make for time well spent.
culture_adjustment: Difficult. Japanese people have little time for socialising. So ask the people with knowledge on the subject. They are also used to large-scale tourism and foreigners being "baka" (stupid), so don't worry too much. But be nice and humble and they will respect you - to an extent.
cultural_challenges: The individualism hidden behind the extremely considerate facade. Loneliness and heavy workloads everywhere - people sleeping in public transport and libraries.
culture_appreciated: Overall friendliness and accomodating atmosphere.
top3_advice: Learn the language. Every experience is better shared. Look for adventure, but remember to consider your inner balance.
other_useful_info: The course lottery system!
most_rewarding: Finding friends and relationships beyond cultures and even languages.
greatest_challenge: Striking a balance between solitude and social activities.

crucial_aspects: I study Japan Studies, and thus never really considered going anywhere else than Japan. I chose Ritsumeikan University primarily because i wanted to study in Kyoto, which is famous for its cultural and historical significance as well as being a place where one can experience a mix of both traditional and contemporary Japanese culture. Furthermore i had earlier heard a lot of positive things about Ritsumeikan University.
info_ease: It was pretty easy. At the dormitory i lived at, we had assigned mentors who helped us with doing all the procedures upon arrival, as well as making sure that we were comfortable.
arrival_assistance: As described above, the mentors at the dormitory helped us fill out paperwork as well as taking us to the local ward office to make sure all was done correctly.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: As described earlier i applied through the application process and it was very easy to do.
registration_help: The administration at Ritsumeikan was very quick at responding to the few problems i had during the application process.
registration_success: I felt that some of the syllabus descriptions of the RCE (Regular Courses in English) courses were somewhat not corresponding to the actual contents, but in the end i was quite satisfied, though i didnt think that there were enough different options to choose from.
registration_advice: Remember to apply for scholarships, which is also done through the application process. A lot of my friends from my exchange were very sad that they didnt apply, as it is very easy.
course_level: I took the IJL (Intensive Japanese Language) track and as such the primary focus was on Japanese language classes. These took up the VAST majority of my time as they are very time-intensive courses, and takes much more work per credit compared to other courses. I was very glad i took the japanese courses as they improved my language skill considerably, but as it is required to take at least 14 credits to correspond to 30 ECTS, i had quite a bit more work than anyone else on the dormitory, and Ritsumeikan themselves doesnt recommend taking courses besides the IJL courses if you take those (IJL takes up 8 ECTS).
teaching_comparison: I was very happy with my Japanese courses. As they were conducted entirely in Japanese they took a lot of work, but at the same time forced me and my class-mates into speaking more Japanese which i really liked. The RCE courses i attended was in general a bit disappointing, compared to UCPH. Though each course had its pros and cons, they were either very easy or not taught in a very engaging way. Though i liked a lot of the contents of all my RCE courses and learned a lot, there were still problems.
courses_enrolled: IJL Level 4 Introduction to Vernacular Culture Selected Problems in Humanities South East Asian Area Studies.
recommended_courses: IJL courses. They were by far the most giving to me, even though they were very work-intensive, i still think it was a huge gift to have taken these courses.
unexpected_costs: There are quite a bit of extra insurance and stuff you have to pay either to the government or to the COOP center at campus.
cost_comparison: Shinkansen is very expensive, and sometimes it is worth it to go by plane instead. General living cost is pretty cheap compared to Denmark.
activities_available: Ritsumeikan has a lot of club activities with everything from martial arts to a cat-feeding club. They also host a lot of other events, often organized by the student clubs.
activities_recommended: Attend the school festival, and if you want to learn Japanese, there are a lot fo good options to meet Japanese students at the student-clubs.
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes. There is so much beautiful nature close to Kyoto and many hikes of varying difficulty. I went to Ise-ken, which was a very good experience, both with beautiful nature and a lot of exciting history. I would also recommend to just explore Kyoto, the city has so much to offer (especially if you like visiting shrines or temples).
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy i would say. Though there are a lot of differences between Denmark and Japan (such a the biking culture or the fact that there are no bins anywhere), i would still say that it was a good experience. The Japanese people i met were for the most part very friendly, and pretty much everyone you meet will wants to help you if you need anything.
socializing_tips: As described, sign up for student clubs. Furthermore, there is an international community area called Beyond Borders Plaza (BBP) where both Japanese and international students meet up for either language exchange or just to hang out.
cultural_challenges: I think the most challenging part about Japan is the language. If you dont know any Japanese it can often be a bit difficult to communicate as many people only know a litte, if any, english.
culture_appreciated: The food, the hospitality, the shrines and temples.
top3_advice: Make sure you think about what kind of housing you want. I would definitely recommend to live in a dormitory as it helped me out tremendously both with doing paperwork, as well as meeting new friends from around the world. Make sure that you choose your courses carefully and choose something that you are sure will get approved by UCPH, as it can otherwise be quite a mess to change courses. If you dont know any Japanese, study basics on Duolingo or the like, it will improve you experience considerably.
other_useful_info: If you live in a dorm, make sure to use your mentors and ask them about anything.
most_rewarding: I made friends from all over the world, which i am very glad i did. I also improved my Japanese language capabilities so much.
greatest_challenge: For me, it was missing home and the family, friends and my girlfriend who i have here. But practically i think it was that i had so many classes compared to many other students that i had to spend a bit more time studying than others.

crucial_aspects: I prioritized an exicting culture and interesting society when choosing my study destination.
info_ease: It was quite easy but my experience is also that Japanese guidance in general are very lengthy and thorough. So it can also be quite overwhelming with all the information presented.
arrival_assistance: There was both a information meeting at the dormitory and at the university. The university also had an exchange coordinator, who was very easy communicating with.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

Some courses was limited and would result in a lottery if enough wanted to take these courses. Furthermore, it was only possible to withdraw from courses afterwards and not sign up for new courses.
registration_help: A guide was provided and a link to a courses-database.
registration_success: I was unlucky in the sense that some of my desired courses had lectures simultaneously. Otherwise, I was able to get all the courses I applied for.
registration_advice: I don't really have any.
course_level: BA courses are not worth it and honestly reminded me more of high school. Some of my courses was also discussion or group based, but the general English level was quite low and thus negatively influenced the level of these courses. I wouldn't recommend this university for the academics.
teaching_comparison: I don't think I took similar courses to the ones I'm used to in UCPH. But I would say in general they prioritized quantity in terms of numbers of topics in a course over depth the selected topcis.
courses_enrolled: - 34333 Cross-cultural Seminar - 36460 Language in Politics - 34321 Cross-cultural Encounters 2 - 81507 Advanced Topics in Computational Intelligence in Games - 33154 Databases - 53432 Liberal Arts Seminar * - 81487 e-Society
recommended_courses: Only e-Society was both an interesting and well executed courses. Very interesting and knowledgeable professor (Uwe Serdült), who organised many interesting guest lectures.
unexpected_costs: Quite many mandatory insurances in Japan. But not that expensive.
cost_comparison: It is in general quite cheap in Japan. I was expecting to pay more in rent.
activities_available: There was a guidebook with clubs and general activities. In general it seemed that many clubs existed.
activities_recommended: I couldn't use any.
weekend_recommendations: Just travel around in Japan. I had the most fun in the more rural parts of Japan, since they were less touristed compared to many sights in Kyoto.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, since it was cleary communication what was expected of you in terms of university. Difficult in terms of clubs and socializing with local students.
socializing_tips: In general it was quite difficult and many seemed quite introverted.
cultural_challenges: I would say that the most challenging part was the lacking english skills and something I didn't expect in english-taught courses at university level.
culture_appreciated: Looking beyond the university, the culture in Japan was just in so many was fascinating and interesting. Also an interesting society, so can recommend finding a good news source (I used The Japan Times).
top3_advice: My impression of the level was quite low, so don't do it for the academics. Further, use that there is so many interesting things to explore in the kanto region.
other_useful_info: I think that the guides provided is quite thorough, so I think everything can be found there.
most_rewarding: Being able to explore Japan. I don't think I have mentioned it so far, but there is also some amazing nature.
greatest_challenge: Accepting that my courses was quite different than expected and the level lower.

crucial_aspects: I wanted my study destination to offer a city with a rich history, as well as a cultural environment that felt completely foreign to me
overall_comments: I rate my study abroad experience a 9/10. Being in Kyoto itself, as well as the relationships I was able to forge with others, was an 11/10. I rate the study abroad experience itself a 9/10 because the curriculum felt a bit ineffective at times.
