arrival_assistance: I missed my orientation, so most assistance was 1:1 to help me catch up. Assistance from Mr. Murakami, the landlord of the Freepia apartments, was definitely present. He offered food, maps, and 1:1 guidance. He was a very helpful resource throughout my entire time in Kyoto.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I rate my study abroad experience a 9/10. Being in Kyoto itself, as well as the relationships I was able to forge with others, was an 11/10. I rate the study abroad experience itself a 9/10 because the curriculum felt a bit ineffective at times.
registration_process: Pretty standard registration process. The only thing that is a bit of a bummer (if you are going on exchange as a master's student, like me) is that the minimum credits needed from KU do not match the minimum credits needed from RU. So, I had to take 3 extra classes - that didn't count for KU credit - in order to be considered a full-time student at RU (which was needed to participate in the exchange). I ended up enrolling in beginner japanese language classes, and it was actually enjoyable (most of the time) to be able to learn about the content without being too worried about the grades (since the credit didn't count toward my home institution). It did represent an additional time commitment though.
registration_help: SKP staff are always very helpful, and they have walk-in hours every day on campus
registration_success: Successful
registration_advice: N/a
academics_comments: I rate my study abroad experience a 9/10. Being in Kyoto itself, as well as the relationships I was able to forge with others, was an 11/10. I rate the study abroad experience itself a 9/10 because the curriculum felt a bit ineffective at times.
course_level: The classes were interesting, for the most part, but I found the processes to be a bit on the lazy and micro-managing side. For example, attendance was taken and daily homework was sometimes given. Additionally, many of the class formats (again, at the master's level) would be the students giving a presentation to the other students while the professor listened. Sometimes we'd have "discussion" afterwards. Some teachers really did not do a whole lot of teaching. I found this unfortunate because I came to be taught by the professor, not by other international students who barely know the subject
teaching_comparison: described above
courses_enrolled: Japanese language, migration studies, public diplomacy, local and regional development, global peace studies
recommended_courses: I would recommend global peace studies as well as public diplomacy. Peace studies is taught by professor Kimijima, who is passionate about his work, and includes a field trip to the on-campus Kyoto Museum for World Peace, which I highly, highly enjoyed. The homework is extremely minimal (only 2 essays for the entire semester) and it's easy to just sit back and listen to Prof Kimijima lecture. Public Diplomacy was equally interesting, and was taught by an American professor named Nathaniel Smith. A trained anthropologist and very knowledgable person, it was a pleasure to be part of his class. The workload was a bit on the heavier side though, with weekly discussion posts stemming from the readings of numerous academic articles in international relations. It was do-able though
unexpected_costs: Gas and electric were not included in my rent, but this didn't come back too expensive, it was just a task to go pay the bills in-person every month (though made easier by the fact that you can do it at any convenience store)
cost_comparison: Food and rent is incredibly inexpensive, especially compared to Copenhagen. This was amazing. Transporation was a bit expensive, considering the cost of other things, but that's why ended up primarily using a bike (also I just prefer to)
activities_available: pottery club, horseback riding, hiking were a few that interested me. there is a very long list of other clubs that are available though
activities_recommended: Go out to eat by yourself in Kyoto; go to music events; become a regular at your neighborhood market or grocery store or cafe. Creating relationships with Japanese people, deepening my understanding of the culture and history through its food and its crafts, was one of the most rewarding and wonderful experiences
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend you go wwoofing (volunteering on a farm) before you go back home. Super cool way to check out rural Japan. During weekends in Kyoto, do yourself a favor and check out any of the numerous craft markets. You can check the online calendar "what's up in kyoto" Tokyo and Osaka are cool and all, but there are many riches to be found in less conventional destinations.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy given that it was not my first time living in a foreign culture
socializing_tips: Join clubs, do things on your own (allowing people to approach you), invite people out to get coffee
cultural_challenges: The bureaucracy of the outdated processes, the indirect communication
culture_appreciated: THE FOOD, the generosity, the thoughtful service, the safety, the cleanliness, the attachment to animistic spiritual traditions, the old temples and shrines on every corner
top3_advice: consider living in the freepia apartments, don't only socialize with other westerners, be active in your search for events to participate in and attend. oh, and get a bike.
other_useful_info: listed above
most_rewarding: building friendships with locals
greatest_challenge: my long-distance relationship (tmi?)

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte Ritsumeikan Osaka Campus, da jeg var interesseret i at undersøge mere om Japans business område.
info_ease: Ritsumeikan er vant til at have udekslingstuderende, så der er en fornemmelse af styr på tingene og de er meget hjælpsomme. Dog hver opmærksom på meget korte og strenge deadlines for forskellige til man skal tilmelde sig. Følg deres plan, så går det hele nemt og fint.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Course registration var stressende, da vi havde en enormt kort deadline og ingen mulighed for at undersøge hvad de forskellige kurser handlede om. Det eneste der var, var en meget kort beskrivelse af kurset med få bulletpoints og overskrifter. Jeg synes ikke, at deres Syllable matchede overens med de undervisning vi fik. Derudover fik vi ikke skema eller noget information om opstart før en eller to dage før. De første lektioner bestod af et overview af hvad man kunne forvente, men det handlede primært om hvordan man bestod - altså at man skulle have active participation, test, presentations og reports, og hvor meget det hver især talte i ens karakter. Ikke særlig informerende om selve kursets indhold. Alt i alt stressende med de korte deadlines for at tilmelde sig og også senere at få informationer om ændriger eller andet under kurset, for lidt information om kursets indhold og for meget fokus på at bestå. Til sidst vil jeg nævne til dem der ønsker at læse japansk som nybegynder. Dette års hold var enormt lille, selvom de har plads til en masse studerende. Man skal vælge inden man ankommer til Japan at man ønsker at starte på begynder japansk holdet, ellers kan man ikke få en plads. Også selvom holdet nærmest var tomt, kunne man ikke få lov. Det var mange skuffede over, så vær opmærksom på dette. Til aller aller sidst Mange kurser som ikke handler om business, altså kurser mere relateret til Japan, finder du ikke på Osaka campus. Der er mulighed for at søge om plads på kurserne på Kyoto Campus som har de Japan-relateret kurser. Der tilbydes dog ingen hjælp til transport og der er vist ret langt mellem de tog campus. Jeg hørte kun godt om de kurser på det campus dog.
registration_success: Hvis man har forkundskaber til japansk skal man gennemgå en test hjemme samt til samtale for at finde det niveau man passer til. Man kan godt ændre sit niveau efter man har prøvet en af timerne, hvis man ikke føler det er passende. Der gik det fint, og jeg fik mit ønskede niveau. Derudover ift til engelsk kurserne. Du kan kun vælge de kurser der bliver tilsendt til dig, når du er ankommet, i en excel fil. Der er begrænset plads på mange af dem, plus mange af dem ligger mellem tirsdag og onsdag, så jeg fik kun 3 af mine ønskede fag. Det var meget skuffende.
registration_advice: Hver opmærksom på deadlines og at der er begrænset plads på kurserne.
course_level: Jeg tog Japansk Intermediate 2 niveau. Der kan man forvente, at al ens tid skal bruges på dette kursus. Det indebar - 4 lektioner af japansk undervisning (en lektioner varer 90 minutter) - grammatik test (1 gang hver 2.uge) og grammtik hjemmeopgave (hver uge) - kanji/vocabulary test (2 gange hver 2.uge) - kanji challenge (2 gange på semesteret) - hjemmelæsning og tilhørende opgaver (2 gange hver 2. uge) - præsentationer (4 i alt) - essay (hver uge) - lytte og besvare lytte spørgsmål (hver uge) med mere. Det var enormt omfattende. Eksamen bliver ikke forklaret og du ved ikke hvad du kan forvente. Mundtlig eksamen bliver kun forklaret aftenen inden på Manaba. Jeg ved selvfølgelig ikke, hvordan det var på de andre niveauer, men forvent at meget af din tid og arbejdsbyrde går på at følge med i de her. Jeg kan ikke anbefale det i hvert fald. De er meget strenge og uforstående. Jeg spurgte på et tidspunkt om hvordan jeg kunne få hjælp til at huske alle de kanji og vocab (det er omkring 50 stk til hver test), og jeg fik bare at vide, at hvis niveauet var for svært kunne jeg jo bare rykke et niveau lavere ned :(. En anden gang, hvor jeg havde misforstået lektierne, og dermed glemt en side, blev jeg udskammet foran klassen ved at jeg skulle besvare alle spørgsmålene, og da jeg ikke kunne svare, fik jeg at vide, at der er hvad der sker når man glemmer sine lektier. De laver et anonym spørgeskema man skal udfylde og bedømme de andre elever i klassen, når man skal lave præsentationer. Folk er ikke særlig søde kan jeg hilse og sige. Alt i alt var min oplevelse at studere japansk unødvendigt hård. Jeg kan ikke forstå nødvendigheden af sådanne strenge deadlines og krav til eleverne. Lidt mere information og et klasserum hvor der er plads til at fejle eller man kan få lov at spørge om hjælp kunne være rart.
teaching_comparison: Jeg er heller ikke imporneret over de engelske kurser. Enormt skuffende. Jeg kommer ikke fra en business baggrund, derfor havde jeg forståelse for, at nogle af kurserne ville være lidt mere nye og svære for mig. Men jeg havde ikke forventet at det skulle være så dårligt. Undervisningen føles ustruktureret, og der manglede lidt en klar oversigt over det de ønskede vi skulle lære. Men især som studerende med en baggrund i kulturstudier har jeg oplevet, at professorerne var meget dårlige til at håndtere kulturelle forskelle og bias i deres lektioner. Dette er særligt problematisk, da vi både lærer om business i Japan og derfor bør vise respekt for japansk kultur, samtidig med at vi befinder os i et multikulturelt klasserum, hvor disse problematikker bør adresseres ordentligt i en akademisk kontekst. Et af de mest ubehagelige eksempler var en japansk professor (ja han var selv japaner), der gentagne gange udpegede de japanske studerende og kritiserede dem for at være for generte til at tale i undervisningen eller for langsomme til at læse engelske tekster. Han opfordrede dem direkte til at opføre sig mere som de internationale studerende for at få succes i erhvervslivet. Dette føltes både nedladende og respektløst over for de japanske studerende og skabte en ubehagelig atmosfære, synes jeg. Et andet eksempel var en gæsteforelæser, der talte om sit arbejde i Indien. I stedet for at fokusere på de udfordringer og dynamikker mellem mænd og kvinder på arbejdspladsen, kom han med den fuldstændig upassende kommentar: "I had to stop them from having sex multiple places in the factory, they are like animals." Det er utroligt, at en sådan udtalelse blev fremsat i et akademisk miljø? Der var også andre eksempler på andet mærkeligt og egentlig upassende opførsel, men de har var de mest overdrevne. Derudover var undervisningsformatet meget præsentationsbaseret. Størstedelen af undervisningen bestod af studenterpræsentationer, hvilket betød, at vi sad og lyttede til oplæg. I en tid med ChatGPT var det tydeligt, at mange præsentationer bare var oplæsninger af genererede tekster, hvilket gjorde undervisningen både uinspirerende og faktisk bare spild af tid. Det er selvfølgelig ikke kun universitetets skyld, men på grund af at undervisningen var så fokuseret på at overholde kravene for at få credits fremfor at lære os noget. Der var enkelte undtagelser med spændende og brugbar viden, men generelt set var niveauet lavt, og undervisernes engagement i undervisningen var skuffende. Alt i alt har jeg mistet tilliden til professorerne og deres evne, desværre. Synes det er vildt at sige, men jeg har ikke oplevet noget lignende. Det føltes som at gå i high school. Det var langt fra den standard, jeg havde forventet af et universitet som Ritsumeikan.

unexpected_costs: Other fees er gas og strøm det var ikke så dyrt.
cost_comparison: Man får en COOP kort, man skal betale depositum 5000, man får det dog tilbage igen. Deraf er bøger og mad 20% billigere på skolen.
activities_available: Åh der var rigtig mange forskellige klubber. Derudover var vores tutorere gode til at hjælpe og arrangere arrangmenter for udvekslingstuderende
culture_adjustment: Det er altid svært at på i et andet land, men det kan især være svært med japan på grund af sprog barriere og kultur forskelle. Vær forberedt på at ingenting er på engelsk, men folk er altid klar til at hjælpe dig.
top3_advice: Jeg ville vælge et andet campus in Osaka campus. Selvom location er lidt dårlig med Kyoto Campus, virker det til at deres undervisning og overordnet vibe var bedre. Det er bare min personlige mening, men jeg ville ikke tage til Osaka campus igen.
other_useful_info: Der er styr på tingene og de er vant til udvekslingsstuderende. Man kan nemt for pratisk hjælp. Det er dyrt at bo her, og undervisningen var enormt skuffende. Der er ikke så mange positive ting at sige desværre.

info_ease: Very easy.

crucial_aspects: There's only one reason for picking Kyoto: Culture galore! And people don't lie: Even without counting the tourist-favourites like Kinkakuji, Touji, Fushimi Inari, etc., there are so many temples and shrines that I'd wager it's impossible to stand in one single place and not see one. I also have a few friends that live in the Kansai area, so it seemed like a natural decision to experience the west of Japan on a longer-term scale.
info_ease: I had no issues. I arrived with a night bus from Tokyo on the day of the orientation, and despite being sleep-deprived and homeless (for one night), it was not a difficult meeting. We even received everything in writing and print, so we could review it when we found a home. Score!
arrival_assistance: There was some general things, such as how to register for classes, how to register for insurances, and how to register for commuter cards. There were many minus-points, such as some, rather far away dormitories not being able to register for commuter cards, and many of the insurances being split-up. Compared to Meiji University or Tokai University, which I have previously exchanged to, there was a lot more to do here. Also, we were warned with slightly odd choice of words of how to prioritise our time on exchange. One of the international guides even said, "you're here to study, not to have fun," and while the first part may be true, it should be the job of the international coordinators to ensure that the second part doesn't become true. In any case, the introduction also introduced some poorly-enforced rules of travel: You're not to leave the prefecture during the week, and you're not to leave the country during the active part of a semester. This was an issue for me, who had already arranged a trip to China midway through the semester, and I notified the staff of this immediately. No answer ever arrived, and no trouble ever came of the trip. I'm trying to say that, despite some very relevant and important information being present in the introductory assistance, it also seems to scare some students away from having a much better exchange than they end up actually having.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Similar to most other institutions I've been to. One week of trial classes, with a subsequent online registration sheet. Some of the professors did seem to game this system, however, and one even provided an entirely different exam from the one advertised on the class sheets. She presented this after the selection period had ended.
registration_help: Each class had their own syllabus sheet, and aside from this, professors seemed helpful.
registration_success: There were also lottery classes in this case, but I was succesful in getting all the classes I wanted, at the time when I wanted them.
registration_advice: Ask your professors about the exam type. Most were assignments, which is nicer for an exchange student, but not all.
course_level: BA-level courses that were meant to replace the elective classes offered at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: I'll be honest and say that I was disappointed at the level of the classes that were taken. Some classes, particularly the ones aimed at International Relations-students, were higher level, but most were conversation classes that presented top-level insight in a range of subjects. That said, some, particularly the ones about the Pacific, were relevant to my field of study.
courses_enrolled: Arts and Crafts Dynamism of the Pacific Language Acquisition Language Education Media and Society Japanese Culture through Field Trips Security Studies
recommended_courses: The professors at Language Acquisition and Education were friendly and extremely knowledgeable, and it seemed like the level of the class was artificially adjusted down to help the local students keep up. The Arts and Crafts class was rather difficult to follow, with seemingly no connection between each topic of the class, although the professor was perhaps the most serious of the lot. Security Studies seemed odd to me, and the professor was very convinced of her own ways. She was the one who decided to use a physical, pen-and-paper essay-style exam with a problem question and 3 hours to write an answer on a large A3 sheet of paper. She also often quoted "someone" in her slides, and spoke in disconnected ways that made the class difficult to follow. I'm sure I'd have respect for her academics if I read her articles, but I couldn't respect her style of teaching.
unexpected_costs: Mostly, I got surprised at the abhorrent fees that my Share House company charged me. Of the 5000 DKK deposit, I only received 250 kr. in return, despite leaving the room in pristine condition (no money was charged on account of improper maintenance, an arbitrary cleaning fee and 50% of my deposit was accounted for in the contract). Aside from this, the rental company charged me a late-fee for disclosing my check-out date within a two-month limit - despite having told the company of my length of stay from the beginning.
cost_comparison: Transport costs were almost none, since the city is small enough that everyday destinations can be reached by foot. Conversely, the train network is small and not particularly useful, so buses that run irregularly and are often full is the only alternative. I therefore ended up using the rental e-bike service, Luup, more than expected, which drove up my non-regular travel expenses.
activities_available: I don't care much for sports, so I didn't use the university gym, which was free to use. There was a sort of Buddy-system, that did see some of us international students meet with some locals, but this was not often.
activities_recommended: I recommend the BBP - Beyond Borders Plaza - for anyone who want to make some local friends. I already knew people there, and I was able to meet even more people there, and even some with whom I was able to meet on their exchange to Denmark. There is a language exchange program as well, and since Denmark is a surprisingly popular country in Japan, I was able to teach some Danish as well. I wholly recommend engaging in this environment, since it allows a very unfiltered look into the lives of normal university students, who come from all over Japan to study at Ritsumeikan University.
weekend_recommendations: The mountains to the north of Kyoto are extremely pretty, and renting car with my flatmates and exploring the tight roads and amazing views of these is a fond memory I shan't soon forget. I took a drivers license for motorcycle while I was away, and since I was able to convert my Danish drivers license to a Japanese one earlier, it was relatively quick and cheap to upgrade it to include motorcycles. The motorcycle industry has been a large part of the post-war economic miracle in Japan, and a motorcycle culture seems deeply imbedded whereever you go, particularly in Kansai, for some reason. There's even a bike temple (Hontakiji) with a friendly Harley-priest. If you meet him, tell him I said hi!
culture_adjustment: Not particularly difficult, although it is said that Kyoto has a certain irony and unwillingness to point out when you're being rude - so I'm not sure I'll ever know if I was too rude.
socializing_tips: Visit the areas where people are willing to themselves engage with foreigners. Some Japanese, not unlike Danes and indeed most other people, don't want to brave language barriers and endure cultural differences just to talk to a person who will leave the country soon, anyways. Some do, however, and finding those is much more worthwhile than converting the non-believers.
cultural_challenges: Hanging out with friends, who invites and when it's appropriate to invite again is difficult.
culture_appreciated: Quiet and order. And also the drinking culture, being less oriented around clubs and dancing, and more oriented on bars, dinners and singing your heart out at a karaoke.
top3_advice: 1: Don't listen to them: Have fun, but also study. 2: Live at the dorm. It seems awesome. 3: If you do live on your own, don't go with Share 180.
other_useful_info: A random tip is to not miss out on becoming part of Coop. It gives you so many discounts on lunches at the university, and it allows you to use the convenience store on campus after-hours. If you don't live in the dorms, there's no explicit reason to sign up, but if you don't do it early, it'll feel like a waste of money by the end. So do it early.
most_rewarding: Using the Japanese that I have learned throughout my Japanese study to accomplish the same things that a Japanese person can, and through this, unlock an entirely different side to the conversations I can have with locals. Taking a driving license in the local language, talking to a priest in the local language and getting the feeling that I am not inconvenienced by any language barrier anymore is a freeing feeling - even if there's still a lot of studying to go.
greatest_challenge: The fight with my Share House company, which was done in 100% Japanese through emails, since their office is in Nagoya, and they don't bother sending people all the way to Kyoto for petty things like a broken lock, cold showers and disabled wifi (that we're paying for). Or perhaps it was finally facing the employee that I had been mailing with for weeks, and realising that he is just a normal person, just as he realised that I am just a normal person.

crucial_aspects: That I would have the opportunity to live in an environment different from anything I’d experienced before.
info_ease: The host institution was very helpfull with orientation and sending material. But there are so many bureaucratic steps that even though they are very helpfull, it is quite overwhelming. I chose to live in a dorm, so I also had local students why could help translate, which was extremely helpfull. Although there’s a lot of paperwork to complete before and after arrival, it’s definitely manageable with a bit of patience and optimism.
arrival_assistance: The university had a helpful administration (International Center). Furthermore, each student is assigned a "student buddy" who can assist with translation. If you put yourself out there even a little, it’s easy to make local friends who are incredibly helpful with administrative matters!
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You’re only allowed to take courses intended for international students, but most of these are language courses or ones I wasn’t able to get pre-approval for. You also don’t really know which courses will be offered until right before the semester begins. Furthermore, there are laws in Japan requiring international students to take a certain number of class hours per semester, which you need to take into account. It can be a bit of a puzzle, but it’s really about “the art of the possible.” Again, it was stressful during the course registration period, but the host university’s administration was quite helpful and understanding. Unfortunately, Japan is a country where exceptions are rarely made and rules are meant to be followed. In the end, though, everything worked out — and I think nine times out of ten, it will for others as well.
registration_help: I had a very kind contact person at the University of Copenhagen’s Merit Office, for whom I was very thankful.
registration_success: I had checked which courses were offered in previous semesters, but I ended up choosing completely different ones when I arrived. This was either because the courses weren’t offered or because I learned from other students who had taken them before that they weren’t worth recommending — either due to the professor or the expected workload. I wanted to take courses that allowed me to study something interesting but, more importantly, to enjoy my time abroad. You can study almost any subject anywhere in the world, but you can only truly experience life as an exchange student under these circumstances once or twice in your lifetime. Therefore, it was much more important for me to have time to enjoy myself than to be overwhelmed with academic work.
registration_advice: Keep your head up, and don’t let bureaucratic struggles ruin your experience. Studying abroad is a unique opportunity to do so much more than just study. Take courses you enjoy or that fit well with your schedule, but when choosing them, do so with the intention of giving yourself as much freedom as possible. There’s so much to explore outside the university. And take a language course, even if you don’t get credit for it. Being able to communicate in the local language opens so many more doors!
course_level: The BA courses were more comparable to first-year courses at KU or even to high school level, while the master’s courses were held to a higher standard. The Japanese language course was perhaps the best class — with the best teacher — I’ve ever had throughout high school, my bachelor’s, and my master’s studies. I learned so much in just four months, and these classes were easily the most enjoyable part of going to university. 10/10 — highly recommended! Even though I didn’t receive any credits for them, they were absolutely worth it. When will you ever have the chance to study a language for free in another country again?
teaching_comparison: Classes were much more discussion-based and required active participation rather than one-way lectures. Overall, this format was OK, but the academic discussions were usually based more on personal experiences and interpretations rather than being anchored in academic reflection.
courses_enrolled: Globalization and Gender Issues (MA), Lecture for Humanities (BA), Japanese Society (BA), Non-traditional Security (MA), Middel Eastern studies (MA), Japanese Ⅰ-1(Comprehensive)
recommended_courses: Japanese Society (BA): Was a fun course for getting insight into Japan and some of the historical and cultural developments Japanese I-1 (Comprehensive): As mentioned, this was perhaps the best class I’ve ever taken — with some of the best professors I’ve had.
unexpected_costs: You’re required to pay for national health insurance and, generally, a bunch of other insurances through the university — but they’re quite cheap, in my opinion.
cost_comparison: Food, drinks, and experiences are so much cheaper than in Denmark. Go out and enjoy world-class food, drinks, and culture every day — all for a fraction of the price you’d pay back home.
activities_available: I was a member of the pottery club and the language exchange group — two great ways to meet local students and make local friends. It’s really a myth that you can’t make local friends; you just need to be open-minded :)
activities_recommended: Just join any club or society related to something you’re interested in learning about or already passionate about, and you’ll meet like-minded people. Join a language exchange event and meet students who are interested in learning your language while teaching you Japanese.
weekend_recommendations: Travel as much as you can — with friends and on your own. Japan is such an easily accessible country with kind people everywhere. Wherever you go, you’ll meet someone who wants to talk with you, have a drink with you, or show you around. Especially in smaller cities, people are often very excited to meet foreigners. Make the most of this privilege, and stay open-minded!
culture_adjustment: There are a lot of local norms and unspoken rules. You aren’t expected to master them all or follow every single rule a Japanese person does, but you are expected to do the bare minimum. Learn a few words and customs, and you’ll get a long way very quickly. Be respectful and open-minded, and it won’t be difficult for you.
socializing_tips: Just show up and be open-minded. It doesn’t really require more than that.
cultural_challenges: Many places only have information in Japanese, or the locals only speak Japanese. But that only makes it even more fun to try and communicate with local people — that’s why you’re going abroad anyway, right?
culture_appreciated: The kind-heartedness of the locals - people from Kyoto (Kansai) are really unique
top3_advice: There’s so much more out there than the usual academic rush of studying in Copenhagen. Explore new cultures, eat amazing food, and meet incredible people. Travel as much and as far as you can.
other_useful_info: Don’t let immediate obstacles distract you from all the amazing experiences waiting for you. There are enough bureaucratic and academic challenges to keep you busy, but don’t let them overshadow what studying abroad is truly about. Do your assignments, fill out the forms, and finish your finals on time — then spend the rest enjoying life.
most_rewarding: Making friends for life — it’s such a unique experience being abroad, with both other international students and local friends.
greatest_challenge: Going home again

crucial_aspects: I had planned to go outside Europe for my exchange, but the corona situation made it difficult. Then I heard about Royal Holloway, and since it was one of the last possibilities to go to UK as part of Erasmus, I thought it made sense to go. I also thought that the university looked very beautiful and I liked the idea of trying to live at campus.
info_ease: The communication with Royal Holloway staff was not at all easy. I had to call them several times and it took a long time before they replied to my emails, if at all. Once I got there they were incredibly helpful, but leading up to the arrival and during the application process, it was quite frustrating.
arrival_assistance: The staff were very good at welcoming us and make sure all was good. There were good possibilities to meet up with support staff physically to help with Learning Agreements and module selections. There is also a Welcome Week the first week of term (where there are no classes) which is a really nice "buffer" to have the time to sort out all the practicalities.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: When you apply you write what modules you want. Then the uni writes and tells you if you can get the courses. Once you arrive you probably have to make some adjustments, since there might be timetable clashes, a module isn't running or because it is a course that runs the entire year.
registration_help: There were several helpdesks, so it all worked out. But a bit frustrating when you don't know what modules you are doing a week before you have to start.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: The academic approach is quite different in my opinion, so as a comparative literature student, I felt like I could do well in most modules somewhat related to the humanities. Don't do the CEDAS courses (courses meant for exchange students to improve their english level and knowledge of uk) since the level is not very high and as a Danish student you will probably be bored. Also the workload in CEDAS courses seemed high compared to the courses I was doing. So I would reccommend just going for the courses you think sound interesting. There are 3 "levels" of courses, level 1, 2 and 3 (for first, second and third years). I think most Danish students would find level 1 courses too unacademic. I had 3 level 2 and 1 level 3 course, which I thought was a nice combination.
course_level: As said, the level was lower than in Denmark, but on the other hand I really enjoyed the opportunity to explore the things/art/literature/movies I found interesting. They don't expect you to be super prepared for the classes.
teaching_comparison: I had a mix of lectures and seminars. There was a lot less group work at Royal Holloway and more open class discussion. The teacher would often pose a question or ask what we thought, and then you just had to speak your opinion. I didn't always love the style of teaching since it became a bit of a monologue from the teacher and a bit repetitive. But individual teacher were very great.
courses_enrolled: Queer Histories Horror Cinema in the Hispanic World Gender and Clothing in the 20th Century Literature and Culture International Film: Readings and Representations
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Horror Cinema in the Hispanic World with professor Dr. Camilo Chiappe Bejar. It was really fun to watch different horror movies and talk about what was scary and how they functioned. My other courses were also very nice and interesting, but the Horror Cinema was my favourite.
unexpected_costs: I had to pay for an expensive corona test upon arrival (the uk system is really bad with entry tests, can be very expensive, so watch out). I also had to get a student visa because of Brexit.
cost_comparison: Food was a bit more expensive than I thought. It quickly adds up when you don't have the possibility to ever cook yourself and have to buy everything.
activities_available: Like I said, so much! I joined the Dance Society and the Craft Society. Also considered the Harry Potter society or Tennis, but you have to be selective because you don't have time for all of them.
activities_recommended: Join the trips to other UK cities that the Student Union hosts. They generally make a lot of events that you should definitely join, especially in the first few weeks where you will likely meet the most of your friends. I mostly hung out with other exchange students and it was very nice to go to eg. Brighton with them. There are also a lot of parties. But probably join a sports society! I really liked the Dance Society
weekend_recommendations: Of course go to London when you can, it's very nice to be so close to it. But I would also recommend visiting Windsor, which is very close by.
culture_adjustment: Once you get used to talking English all the time, it is very nice. People are very friendly and talkative, especially in the beginning of term. A lot of the students at UK universities are a bit younger than in the DK (a lot are around 19) so you might struggle a bit with feeling a bit old and having to socialize with people who just moved out from their parents. But hang out with the exchange students who are often a little older and you will be fine. Everyone just wants to get new friends and be sociable so just throw yourself into it and you'll find friends easily.
socializing_tips: In the first week of term there is the Welcome Week. It's basically an entire week only meant for socializing. Go to as much as you can, because this is the time where you can meet people. Go to the events for international/exchange students to meet them, and go to the different "taster" sessions for the societies. In general just spend the first weeks socialising and making connections and don't worry too much about the classes.
cultural_challenges: British people are very polite and good at small talk in my experience, so it was a bit challenging to have so many "how are you" conversations in the beginning. But I found that once I just let go and tried to relax in it I really enjoyed it.
culture_appreciated: I liked that it's so easy and normal to go to the pub with a few friends after class, just for a beer or a cider. I also think that there is a lot more room for differences compared to Copenhagen. A lot of people experimented with their hair and appearances, and there was a large focus on making sure that there was a space for LGBT people and people of color and making campus inclusive, which I found very comforting and welcoming.
top3_advice: Dont' expect to have your exchange in London - it's not. You will live in Egham and your experience will be more like living (if at Founder's) on a castle (a bit like Hogwarts) with people a bit younger than you. So don't go because you want the metropolitan London-vibe, but because you want to have a fun time and try out the British university experience living on campus. Also, the term is shorter than the Danish semester, so it's a bit short the exchange (2,5 months). It's a bit short, but for me it was nice since you get a great experience but don't have to be there for 6 months.
other_useful_info: No I think I covered it all.
most_rewarding: I loved living at the castle and campus. It is a very beautiful area. I also really enjoyed just having the time to focus on the things that interested me personally and academically and meeting people from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Not having your own kitchen and not really having a relaxing social space that is not your bedroom. I missed having a living room where I could hang out with friends etc. You are very "out there" all the time and have to interact with people you run into at campus all the time. It was nice at times but also a little exhausting in the long run.
other_comments: All in all, I really enjoyed my time at Royal Holloway. I thought I was going for an urban experience and living in London exploring the city, but it was more living on a micro-verse on campus and living very close with your friends. It was not what I had expected but I ended up being so happy that I tried this experience with all the societies and the university community that is just SO different from the university community at KU.

unexpected_costs: none
cost_comparison: Food is cheaper than Denmark but it definitely racks up if you go out every day. Taking a weekend-trip to another prefecture is not as cheap as I thought. You will spend more money than you think. Save up a lot more than you initially planned. Probably double that.
activities_available: there's several cultural exchange social activities at the campus.
activities_recommended: Get a language partner, go to cultural exchange events
weekend_recommendations: Go explore other prefectures, go to flea markets and visit temples/shrines. Also walk everywhere, you'll find unique places and those are definitely some of my best memories.
culture_adjustment: Without realising it, you'll quickly get used to the local culture and language. Took me about 2 weeks to fully adjust. Don't be worried if you can't understand what they're saying, you'll get used to it after some time.
socializing_tips: It's like talking with a shy wall but it's not impossible. You have to take initiative and go for it.
cultural_challenges: Their timidness and reluctance to approach one or take initiative in social settings
culture_appreciated: The order and cleanliness, also how everyone is quiet. You feel safe wherever you go, even more so than in Denmark. Japan is aesthetically very beautiful.
top3_advice: Save up a lot of money, go explore at any chance you get, take initiative and try new things.
other_useful_info: None
most_rewarding: Immersing myself in the language and culture. It was a valuable experience that can't be replaced with anything else.
greatest_challenge: Homesickness. It felt excruciatingly long and at the same time very short.

crucial_aspects: Opportunity to live in a dorm close to my campus as well as a station to make it easier to travel by public transportation. That the study destination/city I chose would not be as crowded as Tokyo.
overall_comments: There was lots of paperwork to fill out while in Japan.
info_ease: Easy enough. We got sent lots of information over e-mail.
arrival_assistance: We got some papers with information when we got our dorm room.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: There was lots of paperwork to fill out while in Japan.
registration_process: We had to download excel-sheets and cross off the courses we'd like to register for, and then upload said sheet. It was rather easy.
registration_help: There is a website where you can look up the syllabus for each class. You could ask R-Globe.
registration_success: I got into all the classes I applied for. I was however adjusted down from JEP-3 to JEP-2, as the teachers assessed I wasn't academically fit for the higher level.
registration_advice: Read each syllabus
academics_comments: There was lots of paperwork to fill out while in Japan.
course_level: The Japanese classes were level-appropriate but very oral-oriented. We'd often do short presentations and sit and talk in groups. Japanese Pop Culture was kind of interesting, but the workload was slightly heavy. Lots of readings each weak with questions to answer. Two presentations and a final paper. Our professor in Japanese Media and arts made the course very interesting even with all the weekly readings/watchings and questions. A final paper and a presentation. We didn't have any homework in Japanese Religions B. We went on a few trips and did a presentation on our final paper. It wasn't as demanding as the other courses.
teaching_comparison: The loads of presentations and conversations in the Japanese classes were rather challenging as we haven't practiced that much conversation at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Japanese language 'package' (taught in Japanese): JEP-2 Core, Listening, Reading, Homeroom Electives taught in English: Japanese Pop Culture, Japanese Religions B, Japanese Media and Arts
recommended_courses: Japanese Media and Arts. It was really interesting.
unexpected_costs: I don't think I had any
cost_comparison: Transportation was so much cheaper than in Denmark. I probably spent around 50dkk monthly because of class trips, but in my free time I spent more. It was still very cheap.
activities_available: I once saw a poster at our dorm that advertised free karate lessons.
activities_recommended: Our dorm went on a one-day trip to Amanohashidate and a temple. We went by bus and only paid 1000yen. I think it was a nice experience.
weekend_recommendations: Go to shrines, temples or museums. Go on walks and enjoy the nature in Japan.
culture_adjustment: Easy enough. There wasn't much to adjust to I think
cultural_challenges: I don't remember any.
culture_appreciated: I don't know.
top3_advice: Before the semester started, R-Globe helped (those of us who wanted) requesting special aid. I struggle with presentations, especially in front of large groups, so I asked to instead do them only in front of the teacher or smaller groups. We spent 1 hour+ writing the request, yet nothing happened. I wasn't even told it got outright rejected. However most of my course professors were understanding and accommodating, so I recommend you just talk directly with your professors rather than spend time with R-Globe and Karen on something that's really just for formality's sake.
other_useful_info: I don't know.
most_rewarding: Experiencing living in Japan. Seeing its beautiful nature, especially lots of mountains.
greatest_challenge: Courses with lots of presentations and all the paperwork to fill out.

crucial_aspects: The city that I chose was very appealing to me and felt like a good place to broaden my knowledge of Japanese culture.
overall_comments: The workload and academic expectations on us as exchange students was overwhelming and accommodations were disgusting and sub par in every way. I wish I had known more about the host uni and been able to make a better informed decision when applying to study abroad.
info_ease: Dorm supporters were helpful when it came to bureaucratic procedures. The first classes at uni were extremely information heavy with no translations for us non-japanese speakers.
arrival_assistance: As a neurodivergent student I was asked to come in for an hour long interview before classes started. I was asked questions about my challenges and then made to fill out an application stating that attendance can be difficult for me at times, and then sign it. I have no idea what happened after that as I received no further help.
arrival_comments: Ridiculously overwhelming and inconsiderate of our emotional state.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The workload and academic expectations on us as exchange students was overwhelming and accommodations were disgusting and sub par in every way. I wish I had known more about the host uni and been able to make a better informed decision when applying to study abroad.
registration_process: We had to go and register at the ward office and bring several forms and papers and then had to fill out and sign a bunch more papers at the ward office. We were also required to set up Japanese bank accounts in order to pay our dorm rent, but only for our last two months. Before then, we paid with bills that we brought to the convenience store and paid in cash. When the automatic bank transfer was supposed to happen in December, it didn't work and a man had to come from the bank and collect our rent in cash. Then we had to close our accounts at the bank before we left. We also had to visit the ward office again to pay our National Health Insurance. Extremely energy consuming.
registration_help: Dorm supporters.
registration_success: I got the electives that I wanted and I was very happy with each one.
registration_advice: The online process for the electives is quite easy. The Japanese classes are different as there seems to be no clear or understandable process for how they place you. Me and my fellow students from Copenhagen were initially placed in JEP 3, but after two or three classes (which we did ok in and were able to keep up), we received an email at night that we had been moved down to JEP 2 and would not be able to complain. It felt underhanded and uncomfortable. We were treated like children and had no say in our own programme structure. In the few classes that we did have in JEP 3, we were clearly targeted and constantly tested.
academics_comments: The workload and academic expectations on us as exchange students was overwhelming and accommodations were disgusting and sub par in every way. I wish I had known more about the host uni and been able to make a better informed decision when applying to study abroad.
course_level: Japanese class was level appropriate, but far too work heavy and stressful. I gave up half way through the semester. Japanese Technology was very easy and interesting. Media and arts and Pop Culture were more challenging, but also very interesting and rewarding. I learned a lot in those classes.
teaching_comparison: Polar opposites. Much less empathy and understanding of burn out and students such as myself with special needs. The coordinator who made me send the application for extra support was very passive aggressive, unhelpful and blamed my stress and mental anguish on me, rather than being understanding and trying to help me.
courses_enrolled: Japanese language (including core, listening through videos, reading comprehension and homeroom) and Japanese Technology, Japanese Pop Culture and Japanese Media and Arts.
recommended_courses: Japanese Technology because its online and you dont need any previous knowledge on the subject, you just have to be active in class and interested. Japanese Media and Arts was fantastic and Danielly is an incredibly intelligent and empathetic instructor who taught us so much. Japanese Pop Culture was also a good course, but its popular, so the class is very big and it can be difficult to concentrate with so many people in the room.
unexpected_costs: Way too much money on food. There is also a need to carry cash everywhere.
cost_comparison: The national health insurance.
activities_available: Not sure but there were lots of things posted in the dorm.
activities_recommended: Sushiro. Shabu Shabu.
weekend_recommendations: Get a color analysis if you have time. I wish I had the energy to take more trips around Japan. I only saw Kyoto and Tokyo.
culture_adjustment: The local people are kind and polite.
socializing_tips: No.
cultural_challenges: Probably adjusting to refined carbs and the fact that everything is sweet.
culture_appreciated: The people are so kind. A woman chased me down the street to give me a bandaid for my blister.
top3_advice: 1. Be superhumanly motivated and energetic. 2. Be ok with gross living quarters. 3. Remember to take care of yourself, even if you feel guilty for missing class etc.
other_useful_info: Don't go to Ryukoku. You will have no time and energy for anything but school. Especially don't go if you are neurodivergent as you will receive zero help and support from R-Globe.
most_rewarding: Sushiro.
greatest_challenge: Everything school and dorm related.
other_comments: Do your research before picking a host uni. Don't just choose based on what city you would like to live in.

crucial_aspects: I chose Kyoto and not Tokyo. I didn't want to live in the capital where it's busy 24/7 but in a rather smaller city. Best believe, Kyoto was big enough. Where we lived was quiet, but in no time with public transportation were we in city centre.
overall_comments: One thing I/we need to remember is that we were there for studying. It was very tough regarding homework, assignments, etc. My hours also doubled at the university from the semester before to the semester in Japan. It wasn't my first time in Japan and I didn't have the urge to travel the whole country since I've seen most of the most touristy spots before. But all my energy went to studying, which is a bit sad to think about. I made friends in class and the dorm, which I'm happy about. The times where I relaxed and enjoyed myself were also good and fun, with or without friends.
info_ease: I would say it was easy, but then again, not when everything is so different. We got a lot of help from our dormitory supporters, and without them we would probably be behind in all the papers we needed to fill out. There is a lot of paperwork to be done.
arrival_assistance: The most assistance was from our dormitory supporters. If we were unsure or had any questions, we could always ask them. They were the real lifesavers over there. I'm very grateful to them.
arrival_comments: The R-Globe office and our dormitory supporters worked together and their welcoming with news and all the stuff we needed to do helped us alot.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

I also observed that they have a preference for questionnaires, which is acceptable; however, how many of these are necessary? My number is 2 on the scale right before, mainly because it's time-consuming. It is a lot and can be confusing. But it was done in the end
registration_help: In all their papers or forms they say you can write to them; I don't think I did that except once. The response time was late.
registration_success: I attended the classes I chose and was successful in that.
registration_advice: Our home university requires a level of Japanese that most of us can't be on when leaving for Japan. We tried that level and after six days the teachers put us down to a lower level saying we were not good enough. Compared to the other students in that higher level class, even if we wanted to, we were not on their level. In my understanding, if that doesn't change, a way to maybe save it and avoid the "reeksamen" is for you to chose "special kanji" class as an course. The ways they teach in Denmark and in Japan are so different, that may be why we were not good enough, or we simply put just weren't good enough.

It wasn't my first time in Japan and I didn't have the urge to travel the whole country since I've seen most of the most touristy spots before. But all my energy went to studying, which is a bit sad to think about. I made friends in class and the dorm, which I'm happy about. The times where I relaxed and enjoyed myself were also good and fun, with or without friends.
course_level: The level of my BA courses were good and on par with the courses at our home university.
teaching_comparison: In the Japanese classes it was very different; they spoke only Japanese, which was difficult at first, but at the end we understood, and it helped us a lot. Our teachers were very nice. The other courses were in English and fascinating. The level was appropriate, and teachers were good.
courses_enrolled: mandatory Japanese classes, Japanese Society, Japanese Media and Arts, and Post-Colonialism.
recommended_courses: Post-Colonialism was very interesting and I would recommend it if you like history/international relations. Japanese Media and Arts for those who like manga and anime.
unexpected_costs: National Health insurance and pension. We didn't need to pay the pension since we were only there for 1 month. But the NHI we had to pay.
cost_comparison: Compared to Denmark, it is very cheap to live in Japan
activities_available: A lot of them I think.
activities_recommended: Can't say anything about it.
weekend_recommendations: If you have time, go out to eat or explore other cities or tourist places.
culture_adjustment: I think it was easy.
socializing_tips: The Japanese students in your dormitory and in your classes may be a breeze to talk to. It can be easy to find new friends/connections. The R-globe office also has some events, and also a lot of other organisations will be introduced to you.
cultural_challenges: In the beginning, it can be difficult to remember all rules, but it will come to you right away.
culture_appreciated: maybe the part where eating or shopping or doing stuff alone is normal. A small detail that is quite nice.
top3_advice: 1. remember you're there to study! It is tough! 2. Travel if you can 3. Don't hesitate to ask for help
other_useful_info: There are a lot of small details or information I can think of; I would gladly help them with the application and paperwork
most_rewarding: My level of understanding Japanese. Without me knowing, I suddenly understood a lot.
greatest_challenge: I would say the paperworks sometimes. But you can overcome it.
other_comments: For the future students, I would gladly lend my help. A lot of work has to be done before going, and a lot of small details can be mentioned before going.

info_ease: easy
arrival_assistance: Japanese students from the dorm come and pick you up upon arrival and help you with the whole process of moving in. To make sure you get introduced to the community they update the dorm´s instagram page to announce your arrival including self introductions and fun facts about your country
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: you show up to orientation and they tell you everything you need to know
registration_help: you get assigned a Japanese student from the dorm who will help you with registering your new address and go with you to any appointments you might have or when you need translation help
registration_success: successful
registration_advice: they help you with everything but remembering to get a suica card is great for smooth transportation
course_level: high level and good quality with scientifically backed study methods (for the class with the highest language level) and passionate teachers!
teaching_comparison: very similar (upper language class)
courses_enrolled: language program (upper language class) and tandem (which depending on the teacher can be great with lots of group work with Japanese students)

unexpected_costs: if you choose to open a Japanese bank account it will come with a fee when opening and closing it
cost_comparison: the train is cheap but the bus is expensive
activities_available: many events like summer fireworks at the beach, takoyaki making, Halloween party etc.
activities_recommended: going to the joint events between the dorms can be great for making new friends
weekend_recommendations: the nearby Momochihama beach, Fukuoka tower, Shopping area in Tenjin
culture_adjustment: really easy since everyone was so welcoming and interested in hearing about the outside world
cultural_challenges: nothing in particular, whenever there would be a misunderstanding due to the language barrier etc. everyone around us were super nice and would always explain everything
culture_appreciated: that it is often expected that you will do your best and so you get better at a lot of things
top3_advice: 1. the part of the administration responsible for exchange students have some of the kindest people I have ever met, so if you´re unsure about something, they are great to ask for advice! 2. don't be shy to talk to local students or join the festivals at school 3. the women's dorm has the onsen, but the mixed dorms have the most pizza parties, both are great!

crucial_aspects: Since I am studying Japanese studies it is mandatory to go on exchange in Japan, But i chose to study in the city of Fukuoka since it seemed like a nice city with lots of culture.
overall_comments: I really enjoyed my study abroad it gave me a lot of amazing experiences and oppurtunites.
info_ease: Seinan Gakuin University was very helpful in setting you up in Japan, they had a lot of systems in place that would help you get comfortable in both your dorm and the University.
arrival_assistance: Different systems like "buddy-system" and they had tutors/managers at the dorms that would help you. Via the buddy system you would be contacted by a japanese student before arrival and they would answer any questions you had about Japan and life at Seinan. The managers and tutors were Japanese students living at the dorms that would help with going to the ward office and such.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I really enjoyed my study abroad it gave me a lot of amazing experiences and oppurtunites.
registration_process: I signed up for classes before arriving in Japan and was told whether i got them or not when i arrived in Japan. The process was pretty easy.
registration_help: On campus there was and international department that would help exchange students with everything they needed from paperwork to classes, which made it easy to solve your problems.
registration_success: I got into all the classes i wanted so i faced no trouble at all.
registration_advice: Make sure you have a backup course in mind if you dont get all the ones you wanted originally.
academics_comments: I really enjoyed my study abroad it gave me a lot of amazing experiences and oppurtunites.
course_level: I think the level of the couses might be a little lower than that of UCPH, but there was a bunch of interesting courses which definitely are worth taking and are fun.
teaching_comparison: In Japan and on Seinan the focus is more on classroom teaching and attendance then that of UCPH. You need to show up to your classes
courses_enrolled: - Comprehensive Japanese III - Japanese reading III - Japanese Writing III - Japanese society and culture through manga and Anime A - Cultural exchange between Japan and the West A - Tandem learning II
recommended_courses: I highly recommend taking the Japanese society through manga and Anime if you have interest i manga or anime, since it is a super good way to learn about culture through media you already enjoy. I would also highly recommend that you take Tandem Learning. Tandem learning is a class where you are mixed with japanese student at make presentation based on activities you in class and out of class. It forces you to practice you japanese more which is good and its a great way to make friends with the japanese students at Seinan. Even though this class might be a little scary or intimidating at first its a class that will push your japanese ability.
unexpected_costs: I didn't really encounter any hidden fees or anything like that.
cost_comparison: Food is super cheap, though fruits are not, so if you are into fruits that will be a little more expensive.
activities_available: There was a bunch of different clubs you could join a lot of sports and traditional sports clubs, buty also stuff like boardgames and music clubs.
activities_recommended: The university will probalby be hosting parties and events that i would recommend you join in on.
weekend_recommendations: When on kyushu i recommend grabbing a couple of friends (hopefully on of you has a drivers license) and rent a car and drive to different cities in kyushu. Rentic a car with a couple of people is cheaper than the trains and you can see a lot more "hidden stuff" like stuff you cant easily take a train to. Some locations i recommend is Oita and and theres a lot of temples in south fukuoka. Go hiking, this was an activity i really enjoyed. Japan has lots of mountains and the views are great and the people that go hiking are typically super nice. Its also a great way to see the nature of Japan and if you are going to Fukuoka I personally recommend Aburayama mountain and Mt. Iimori (飯盛山).
culture_adjustment: I felt i was pretty easy after a week or two, i felt comfortable in Fukuoka and at Seinan
socializing_tips: Take tandem learning, Hang out at your dorm, and go to the Seinan events
cultural_challenges: I didn't find anything too challenging as much as it is just adjusting a bit.
culture_appreciated: I appreciate the general kindness of Japanese culture and how mindful they are of other people.
top3_advice: Come with an open mind. Dont spend all your time studying, go explore the local culture and nature. Pack more of the stuff you consider essential because you might not be able to buy it easily in Japan. Especially painkillers, please bring your own painkillers as they are not just over the counter medicine in Japan.
other_useful_info: You might wanna pack more deodorant from home since the Japanese ones are quite weak (this might sound weird, but trust me). Bring souvenirs (it can be small), the japanese really appreciate it.
most_rewarding: I think i really got a good grasp of the culture and i developed my japanese skills, and now being able to interact with more parts of the culture is very rewarding.
greatest_challenge: It was my first time living "alone", of course i was living at a dorm with people around me all the time, but there was a lot of stuff for me to learn but it was worth it.
other_comments: Please enjoy your stay abroad. For me it has become an unforgettable experience and i really enjoyed it. Some people might not like it as much but I think that is also ok, now you at least know that living abroad isn't for you.

crucial_aspects: It was mandatory for me to go to Japan, but I chose Seinan University because I wanted to try living in a city most people might not get the opportunity to live in.
info_ease: Very easy, the staff at the university and the dorm were very helpful.
arrival_assistance: I was told all about how the dorm functions, bills to pay and how to do it, how my class schedule was and so on.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We were presented with all the different courses we could pick and then just had to submit our priorities.
registration_help: The staff were always available to help incase you needed to change courses etc.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Nothing in particular, it was very easy and straightforward.

teaching_comparison: Quite different, but as far as I understand the way courses are done in Japan in general is different from here in Denmark.

unexpected_costs: None.

activities_recommended: Join a club.
weekend_recommendations: Travel locally, there are many amazing places on Kyushu, you don't need to go far to see something different.

cultural_challenges: Nothing I can remember right now.

top3_advice: Explore the city. Join a club. Visit a restaurant called "Fujiya" that is located close to campus.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: The Japanese lessons and the friends I was able to make while being there.
greatest_challenge: Getting used to being on the other side of the planet far away from family and friends.

Visit temples and the mountains, go for long strolls, do some shopping. Second hand stores are great in Japan.

crucial_aspects: Seinan Gakuin University had many interesting courses on offer, including joint courses with the Japanese students. The courses on offer and overall course system were changed shortly after our referrals, however, to emphasize said joint courses more. Another determining factor for me was the possibility for special academic support, and at a smaller academic institution, due to my disabilities. The English version of their website was also highly informative and easy to navigate compared to those of others, and held detailed information on all the practicalities. Lastly, my former Japanese teacher highly recommended both the university and Fukuoka, citing their own positive experiences there.
overall_comments: I was very happy with my host university and exchange stay overall. The university staff at Seinan and my professors were patient, helpful and accomodating, and I enjoyed the courses a lot - but I do know of some who had less fortunate experiences with their professors. Fukuoka was highly livable, and the dorms being right by our campus provided a convenient home base without any need for public transport to and from classes or nearby stores. However, due to events in my personal life leading to a lacking social network while abroad, the stay itself became difficult to manage. Namely due to my relatively low Japanese proficiency level. Similarly, I also felt woefully underprepared in terms of the language level, as all of our language classes were held in Japanese. By comparison, our Japanese classes at the University of Copenhagen (UCPH) were largely held in Danish compared to the language classes of other area studies, such as Korea Studies.
info_ease: The university staff were very thorough in mailing us guides and timely information both before and upon arrival. Much of the information was already available on the university's website as well, and the Center for International Education (CIE) was open for drop-ins during opening hours.
arrival_assistance: A week-long joint orientation was held for all international students, followed by meeting our assigned student helpers of the local Japanese student body to show us around and answer questions. Said assigned helpers also assisted us with the necessary procedures at the local ward office. Furthermore, as we were to move into our respective dormitories 1-2 days before the orientation, we were given a thorough rundown of the different rules of our dormitory upon arrival, such as quiet hour after 22:00 (23:00 on weekends), no smoking or consuming alcohol inside the dorms, cleaning duty, safety precautions, special rules for bicycles, et cetera. The Japanese dorm managers and student RAs kindly helped us settle in and move our luggage to our respective rooms.
arrival_comments: The orientation was very in-depth and included plenty of help with setting up our intranet user profiles, necessary paperwork for the ward office procedures (signing up for a Japanese bank account was not required), et cetera. The orientation also included a fun field trip to local sights for all international students. I was also immensely grateful for the special academic support I was able to receive even before arriving in Japan, and the opportunity to meet and get to know the Japanese students in a cooperative way was greatly appreciated. That being said, as we were seemingly assigned student helpers based on our Japanese proficiency level test scores, and my scores were for reasons unknown far above my actual level, I unfortunately struggled immensely with communicating despite my assigned helper's always kind and patient efforts to bridge the language gap. To avoid burdening them with too much extra work, I often went to the CIE for assistance instead.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
