The university staff at Seinan and my professors were patient, helpful and accomodating, and I enjoyed the courses a lot - but I do know of some who had less fortunate experiences with their professors. Fukuoka was highly livable, and the dorms being right by our campus provided a convenient home base without any need for public transport to and from classes or nearby stores. However, due to events in my personal life leading to a lacking social network while abroad, the stay itself became difficult to manage. Namely due to my relatively low Japanese proficiency level. Similarly, I also felt woefully underprepared in terms of the language level, as all of our language classes were held in Japanese. By comparison, our Japanese classes at the University of Copenhagen (UCPH) were largely held in Danish compared to the language classes of other area studies, such as Korea Studies.
registration_process: The Japanese language courses were registered according to individual Japanese placement test results and history of Japanese language study. The placement test itself was based on the TTBJ test. No interview or the like was required. Furthermore, it was possible to be moved to a higher or lower level after the initial assessment during the first week. The elective courses were split into two groups: mandatory GLA joint courses alongside the Japanese students, and regular elective courses within the international division plus special topic courses offered in the regular department. The registration process was done via two separate online forms requiring one's name, e-mail address, curriculum plan (A or B), and one's courses of choice from the given list. First was the GLA courses, then the second group of electives. In case of exceeded capacity, the spots were distributed by lottery. Re-registration was similarly done via an online form. Dropping courses was done by crossing out the course(s) in question on the printed handout and handing it in at the CIE before the given deadline.
registration_help: Detailed information about the course contents for each course was available on university's official website. The CIE were also very helpful with any and all questions I had regarding the course registration, options in case of overlapping courses, the possibility of self-studying courses that were moved form the Fall semester to the Spring semester, et cetera.
registration_success: Given my misunderstanding of the wording on the course registration form, I ended up with too many courses as I managed to get into every course I applied for - including two undroppable GLA joint courses. In this sense, I was successful in registering for every class I wanted. However, many of the courses I was originally interested in were moved from the Fall semester to the Spring semester due to the recent introduction of the GLA courses. Hence, I also had to make do with the courses that remained.
registration_advice: Be sure to check the most up-to-date course catalogue on the website, and be mindful of which courses are Fall semester courses and which are Spring. Also be mindful that it is only mandatory to take one GLA course and that registering for more in case of not getting a spot may backfire, as they could not be dropped. For the electives, I recommend going for what sounds most interesting or relevant to you or your desired specialization. Despite being a smaller, private institution, Seinan offers a wide variety of subjects from arts, history, culture and religion, to sociology, business, politics and law, national sports, the natural world of Japan, and even manga and anime-focused communications- and societal studies. I also recommend checking out the special topic courses - many were in English as well. Seinan also offered tandem learning with Japanese students on agreed-upon subjects, as well as independent study.
academics_comments: I was very happy with my host university and exchange stay overall. The university staff at Seinan and my professors were patient, helpful and accomodating, and I enjoyed the courses a lot - but I do know of some who had less fortunate experiences with their professors. Fukuoka was highly livable, and the dorms being right by our campus provided a convenient home base without any need for public transport to and from classes or nearby stores. However, due to events in my personal life leading to a lacking social network while abroad, the stay itself became difficult to manage. Namely due to my relatively low Japanese proficiency level. Similarly, I also felt woefully underprepared in terms of the language level, as all of our language classes were held in Japanese. By comparison, our Japanese classes at the University of Copenhagen (UCPH) were largely held in Danish compared to the language classes of other area studies, such as Korea Studies.
course_level: The elective courses seemed appropriately difficult while also being mindful of the different levels of English among both professors and students, particularly professors who had no prior experience of teaching entire courses in English. Note, however, that the Japanese level IV courses were of pre-intermediate level, i.e. N4-N3, rather than level III. The GLA courses were less demanding in order to accomodate the Japanese students, as said courses were held entirely in English. Another important reason for any seemingly lower level is that the university years for Japanese students are mainly spent job hunting, meaning less time for classes and thus a different approach to university-level education as a whole.
teaching_comparison: I found the style of teaching at Seinan more pedagogical than what I have experienced at the UCPH thus far. Mainly due to the emphasis on summarizing each class at the end of class, setting aside time for taking notes, practical application of what was gained from each class in shorter assignments or presentations, and more. However, each class was also 100 minutes long and usually without breaks. This allows for more time for discussions, spreading out and summarizing information, et cetera - but it can also be quite tough to remain focused for so long. Japanese levels II and above had two classes in the mornings four days a week, i.e. 200 minutes in total in a day - add to that the weekly elective courses.
courses_enrolled: Aside from Japanese level IV language courses, I was enrolled in GLA Psychology, GLA Culture, Japanese Business Culture, and Special Topic: English for Specific Purposes (a social linguistics course). Despite a few changes to the course contents, I was happy with all of them. Although, I was sad to drop Japanese History due to unexpected course overlap.
recommended_courses: I recommend every elective course I took. Our Japanese Business Culture professor made the course very engaging by drawing lively comparisons different business cultures and including the students in discussions of the class material throughout - the final project involved adapting a Japanese product or service to one's domestic market or vice versa. Psychology taught me a lot about the differences between our idea of concepts such as health, happiness, learning, orientation, habits, et cetera versus Japanese views, as well as how much of our modern psychology is increasingly similar to East Asian philosophies. Culture provided many insights into not only Japanese culture and history from a Japanese perspective, but also those of other cultures through comparative group discussions and short presentations. Finally, English for Specific Purposes gave a great view into what language is in relation to culture and society, and what linguistic differences reflect and affect in terms of how we view and communicate our world and experiences. That being said, in hindsight I wish I had taken GLA Politics and Law to fill the gap in my knowledge on both topics.
unexpected_costs: I did a lot of research into insurance and eSim costs, rental fees, curricular materials, et cetera before traveling and thus did not end up encountering any unexpected costs. Seinan also has estimates for basic living expenses listed on their website. Books were 240 DKK in total, mandatory insurance in Japan 420 DKK in total, and eSim with voice and data enough for tethering 350 DKK a month. I did pay around 6.300 DKK for 4 months of travel insurance via Gouda only to find it did not cover one of my disabilities - the mandatory National Health Insurance in Japan may offer you better coverage as it covers 70 percent of medical expenses. Also, remember to always carry an amount of cash in case of an emergency, credit cards not working, et cetera.
cost_comparison: Keep in mind that the cost of living in Japan is considerably lower than in Denmark - even the notorious fruit comes with plenty of affordable options. Despite my research prior to traveling, the low cost of living still shocked me, especially considering that many Japanese find it difficult to make ends meet - it truly put things into perspective as a student reliant on SU. Many things may be cheaper to buy in Japan than to bring along. I also bought far too many snacks for this reason, hence my high spending on food. Still, be aware that if you plan on traveling during your stay, long shinkansen trips may be expensive and low-cost alternatives such as overnight buses worth looking into. My handful of shinkansen trips account by far for most of my listed travel expenses - meanwhile, gifts for family and friends back home account for most of my personal spending. Other fees were mainly medicine, medical masks, cleaning products, gift wrapping, package mailing fees at the post office, and the like.
activities_available: Despite being a smaller, private institution, Seinan offered a considerable amount of all kinds of non-academic opportunities. These range from sports (rugby, badminton, basketball, track and field, lacrosse, boating, and many more), martial arts (kyudo, kendo, shorinji-kenpo, and more), arts (painting, photography, calligraphy, tea ceremony), music, and social clubs, to events and parties arranged by local student groups. We were even invited to the university baseball team's games to cheer them on.
activities_recommended: Seinan mails out information about events and clubs that are open to new members and international students. If any of them catch your interest, I recommend giving it a go, even if you may feel your language skills are not up to par. When engaging in something you are genuinely interested in, learning becomes much easier and more organic - while also providing an opportunity to hone your skills and meet new people along the way.
weekend_recommendations: Do not be fooled by Kyushu's distance from places like Tokyo or Kyoto, as the island still has plenty to offer. The local area has everything from beautiful parks and beaches to mountains and caves, to lively shopping centers with 11-story department stores, famous temples and shrines, cozy rural areas, and even significant historical and archaeological sites relating to Japan's Yayoi period, the battles against the Mongols, and the eras of cultural exchange and uprisings against the shogun. Additionally, Japan's infrastructure is solid and trains do run on time, so even a day trip or weekend trip from Fukuoka can take you quite far. For those more interested in shopping, Fukuoka has lots of options, from alt fashion and niche stores to international brands, to entire stationary stores and manga and anime shops - even within the same department stores. Lastly, Fukuoka is in many ways famous for food, namely its yatai food stands, and has countless options for different cuisines. To name a few recommendations within Fukuoka, the genkoborui defensive wall at Iki-no-Matsubara beach, Nokonoshima island flower park, Dazaifu Tenmangu shrine dedicated students and learning, or one of the few one-to-one scale Gundam statues at Lalaport. For day trips, places like the two active volcanoes of Mt. Aso and Sakurajima, Keya no Oto cliff, Yoshinogari Historical Park, or the giant statues at Daihonzan Naritasan Kurume temple or Nanzo-in temple are definitely worth a visit. Okawachiyama and Kami-Arita's porcelain shrine in Saga are well worth a visit for anyone interested in porcelain, and Huis Ten Bosch in Nagasaki has a spectacular fireworks show in November. You could also make weekend trips to places further away, such as Okinawa, the Shimanami Kaido, or even other East Asian countries (if permitted by your visa).
culture_adjustment: After many years of interest in Japan, it was not too difficult to adjust to the local culture. Many things are not too different from behavioral norms in Denmark. Although Fukuoka is said to be more 'conservative' in terms of clothing, plenty wore alt fashion. Furthermore, Fukuoka has plenty of signage in English everywhere due to high tourism, and even stores are open until fairly late - one local supermarket was open 24 hours. Learning the basics of how to behave in public, on public transport, and during meals makes a good foundation. Though, mistakes are likely to happen when you inadvertently become flustered in an unfamiliar environment. If you ever feel unsure how to navigate a situation, there is no shame in asking. Alternatively, there are plenty of helpful guides online - and if all else fails, just remember that you are not expected to know every rule as an 'outsider'. And that translation software can be a lifesaver.
socializing_tips: As previously mentioned, Seinan offers many academic and non-academic opportunities to break the ice with local students, as many are curious but too shy to approach due to the language barrier. Just do your best, keep an open mind, and try not to pay too much mind to any mistakes - asking for recommendations often works too. You may even be invited to them.
cultural_challenges: I did not find the cultural differences difficult to navigate, but here are a few things to be mindful of aside from the language barrier. Talking on the phone or loudly among yourselves on public transport is frowned upon, though you will certainly find Japanese who do this as well. Jaywalking happens but is illegal, and people do wait in line and for traffic lights to turn green. Many international students also complained about all the necessary paperwork. Picking up on the subtle social cues may be challenging for those used to more open communication, and direct eye contact is still generally a social faux pas. For social, outgoing students, the fact that people tend to keep to themselves may also prove a challenge - for more introverted students, it may be challenging to feel that you always stand out, even when you try not to, and the high level of efficiency may make you feel like you are being a bother if you take too long. Lastly, while not a challenge relating to culture, the heat and high humidity was almost unbearable even in September when we arrived. We were told that this was uncommon, however, do be careful.
culture_appreciated: Personally, I appreciate the cultural emphasis on cleanliness, orderliness, and efficiency, and that it is socially acceptable to keep to yourself or go on solo trips. I also greatly appreciate the emphasis on how things are cared for and presented, especially food. That places like the ward office, post offices, and healthcare clinics had translation software or interpretation services available was a great help. And despite recent stories in the media about discontent with foreigners, I did not experience any unpleasantness myself - quite the opposite.
top3_advice: 1. All deadlines are strict, and there are quite a lot of them initially and before returning home. The staff at Seinan were very generous with sending out reminders and thorough guides, but it may help to set reminders and divide each step into categories of urgent or not. 2. Do spend some time looking into not only the campus, dormitory options, and courses on offer, but also the area and what to pack depending on your plans. Especially in terms of dressing for the weather in both September and December. 3. Everyone I met at Seinan were very kind and accomodating, so do not be afraid to reach out if you need help. You are not alone.
other_useful_info: Bear in mind that Seinan Gakuin University is a Christian university. That being said, while Christianity is still a core part of the university's background, Christian beliefs are by no means part of the curriculum, nor is there any dress code or punishment for alt fashion or the like, and religious freedom is of course in place.
most_rewarding: The fact that I was able to complete a semester-long exchange far from home, despite my disabilities and the hurdles, felt immensely rewarding - particularly after many talks with the student counselors at UCPH about the possibility of not going. The kind of place that Fukuoka is, as well as the degree of accomodation at Seinan, certainly contributed to this.
greatest_challenge: Although I had studied Japanese for a year before enrolling in Japan Studies at the UCPH, the language barrier made me painfully aware of just how lacking my Japanese abilities are. It also kept me from doing many things, including eating out more.
other_comments: Remember to look after yourself too. The Fall semester was tough, as classes had to be crammed into four months instead of five due to the structural changes. It is true that you are primarily going on an exchange to study - but (guilt-free!) breaks are also important to create an environment that is actually conducive to learning. 'Gakusei' should not be literal. So remember to be kind to yourself and that it is okay if there are things that cannot be done to a T. Don't be shy or ashamed if you have questions, the CIE, your student helper, and the dormitory managers and RAs are there to help. Seinan also has an English-speaking counselor if need be. There is no 'right' way - so just do what you can.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere with a very different culture and daily life than in Denmark which is why I was interested in going to Asia. Besides, I knew that Korea is a very safe country and it has such an interesting history and unique culture so I thought it would be a safe, interesting and fun place to go.
info_ease: It was do-able but not easy. SNU's website often changes automatically to Korean so it was a constant hassle to get information in English. Their systems for applying for classes is very different and the exchange students could have used more guidance on that in advance.
arrival_assistance: We recieved a very long pdf file with info about everything at SNU.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was so complicated. First, there was a test-round where you could practice registering for courses. However, SNU forgot to tell the exchange students that the date for the test round had changed (they told os a few hours before it was supposed to start, meaning it was in the middle of the night) so we all missed it. Afterwards, there was a pre-registratiuon round where you coiuld put courses in your "shopping basket" and if the class then was not too popular, you would be registered automatically. Then after that, there was the real registration round where you could register for courses in yhour basket which was stressfull and on a first-come-first-serve basis. After that, there was a new round where you could apply for courses that were not yet full after the pre-registration round. So many exchange students had issues with getting even just one class that they wanted because the system was so different and stressfull. A while that, there were other registration rounds where you could apply for classes that were already full. By that time, I was already in Korea as it was only a week or so before classes started.
registration_help: None. Everyone got an e-mail from the international department at SNU explaining the proces very briefly, but from then on, it was your own problem.
registration_success: Somewhat succesfull. It worked out in the end, but it took a lot of waking up in the middle of the night to see if some classes had gotten extra spots available and so.
registration_advice: You have to be very fast. If you log on one minute after the registration starts, classes will be full. Besides, have a list of alternative classes ready because you are most likely not to get all the classes you want (if any in the first place).
course_level: The academic level was lower but the work load was heavier. I had presentations almost every week and often had small assignments to hand in and so. So there was more to do but the things you had to do were easier than at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: You are much more in contact with your professors than at UCPH. Classes are smaller and people are more involved and actively participating. In my classes, students took turns of presenting every week, so the students play a much bigger role than at UCPH. You could just lean back and do nothing in class, let alone not show up for classes regularly.
courses_enrolled: 1) Economic Development and Leadership in Asia, 2) Geopolitics and Political Economy of Space, 3) Public Policy and Community Wellbeing
recommended_courses: I really liked the geopolitics course. The professor was very motivating and there was a really good atmosphere and learning environment in that class. The course about economic development in Asia was very easy and we never had mandatory readings, however we got to go on a really good study trip with all expenses paid, so that was really nice.
unexpected_costs: The ARC (alien registration card), mandatory health insurance
cost_comparison: Groceries, especially fruit and vegetables, were very expensive. It was more expensive to cook a meal than to buy take out or go to a restaurant. Hence I rarely cooked. On the other hand, going out and eating out was very cheap. So was public transport and housing when traveling/going on weekend trips.
activities_available: SNU had lots of clubs, however most of them were in Korean. For the exchange students, there was "SNU Buddy" which was really good. They arranged activities every week.
activities_recommended: SNU Buddy. It was great for meeting lots of other exchange students as well as the Korean buddies. Every exchange student also got a personal Korean buddy from SNU buddy who could help you if you had any problems.
weekend_recommendations: Go to as many different parts of Korea as you can. I especially enjoyed visiting the east coast (Gangneung for example) and the south west (e.g. the tea plantations in Boseong were really cool). Besides, nature in Korea is amazing so go climb a mountain, visit a bamboo forest, and go see the tea fields in the south. There are so many things to do in Korea, it is great.
culture_adjustment: It was a bigger culture shock than I had expected. In the beginning, it was a challenge that almost no one spoke or understood English, but you get used to it pretty fast. There are cultural differences that you do not understand (e.g. that women have to cover their shoulders even when it's really hot in the summer), but you get used to it. It also suprised me how it feels standing out. As a Westerner, many people look at you and you sometimes feel like you do not fit in. But again, you get used to it. And you learn so much from being in a culture that is SO different from Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: Again, join SNU Buddy. The Koreans who join that program are really interested in getting to know foreigners, so that is the easiest way to meet Koreans. Besides, just talk to people in your classes. The Koreans are often quite reserved but once you talk to them, they open up and are really nice people.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier.
culture_appreciated: The going-out culture was really nice. People love going out for a meal and a drink (many drinks) together as often as possible.
top3_advice: 1) Don't worry too much about the money, just enjoy being there while you can, 2) Join SNU Buddy and go to as many social activities as possible, 3) Live in an area not too far from campus
other_useful_info: Download Naver Maps (it is like Google Maps but for Korea) and Papago (an app that will safe you as it translates everything for you, even menu cards, the words on your washing machine etc)
most_rewarding: Meeting so many cool people. You meet people from all over the world with so many different experiences in life, and it completely changes your view on so many issues in the world.
greatest_challenge: Missing people at home. Some days, you just really wish you were at that party that all your friends at home are at, or that you could give your boyfriend a hug.
other_comments: Going on exchange to Seoul has been an amaxing experience for me and I highly recommend it. Don't worry too much about things, just go and it will all work out.

crucial_aspects: Quality of the institution
info_ease: It was difficult, because Seoul National University was not helpful at all for exchange students, and you were left mostly to your own devices.
arrival_assistance: SNU did plan an orientation for exchange students, but the number of students allowed was minimal, and it was sold out within 24 hours, and we did not receive further help, other than emails before our stay.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: SNU has a very confusing registration process for the classes, but it ultimately allows for a lot of time to register, however classes in English are very limited, so therefore understanding the process to begin with is important.
registration_help: E-mails with guidance
registration_success: I was not very successful, due to the confusion of the class registration, however I did manage to find good classes.
registration_advice: Read the e-mail through well, and also talk with other students.
course_level: The professors had a lot of freedom to create their courses, and the Korean professors in my case were absolutely amazing professors, and I was very happy with the academic level. However one single professor was not that good, so perhaps it is also about luck.
teaching_comparison: The professors obviously had a lot more freedom to change and shape their courses to their own liking.
courses_enrolled: Queer Literature Religion and identity in East Asia Korean Literature and Korean society
recommended_courses: Queer Literature had an amazing professor, who I absolutely would recommend. The professor of Korean Literature and Korean Society was also good, however his style may not fit everyone.
unexpected_costs: The Korean Healthcare system had increased their prices.
activities_available: The club activities at SNU are more limited, and their festival budget is not as big as other universities, however SNU is known for this, and I recommend going to SNU for their academic level, if that is where your priorities are.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the other cities. Especially Busan and Jeju.
socializing_tips: Joining Korean classes if possible, if not then speak with the Koreans in your classes. Besides this, bars and clubs are the only other options I know of.
culture_appreciated: The fashion and general aesthetics are amazing.
top3_advice: You should go to SNU for their high academic level. They don't provide much for exchange students besides this.
most_rewarding: The classes.
greatest_challenge: Attending classes in Korean.

crucial_aspects: Over the past 4-5 years I have developed a personal and academic interest in Korean history, language and culture. Knowing that my master's thesis would be related to Korean history in some way was a serious academic motivator to choose South Korea. Just as importantly, though, I also wanted to experience the culture and society myself before fully settling on a direction for my thesis. I also wanted to go far away from home now that I had the chance to do so with the backing of UCPH and for an extended period of time. I wanted to push myself out of my comfort zone.
info_ease: That depends on the kind of information. Generally, the information I received was very, very good until I arrived. After that, I didn't receive a lot and usually pretty late from both the university and immigration. Orientation was cancelled, instead we received a PDF with relevant information, which was pretty useful even though I think a physical orientation would have been better. I got most of my information from the chat for international students in the SNU Buddy Programme.
arrival_assistance: I joined the SNU Buddy Programme and was assigned a personal buddy to help me when needed. I didn't reach out for help, but I know that others did and was very happy with it. I didn't personally reach out to the International Admissions Office either, but heard from others that due to a change in staff the level of help had dropped pretty significantly.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There are multiple stages of class registration at SNU. In the first stage you choose the courses that you find interesting and put them in you basket. You can then see a time table of a week of these classes so you can plan them without overlaps, their number of credits and a syllabus. I think I could choose up to 9 courses of interest and you can see how many other students have placed it in their basket to get a feel of there popularity. A few days later in the next stage you will choose the courses you register for. This is first come, first serve, and once the amount of students allowed has been reached it closes for registration. If you didn't get to register for a course that you wanted you would have the option of contacting the professor teaching the course directly and ask for permission to register as an additional student.
registration_help: There was a trial run of the stages a week before the real thing and a guide was sent to us. It was a bit difficult to figure out and seemed to assume that you had a bit of previous experience or inside knowledge, but it made a lot more sense once I got access to the website.
registration_success: I got the courses that I wanted.
registration_advice: I have a couple pieces of advice: First, make sure to try the trial run before the actual registration if you have any doubts on the process. I misunderstood the dates and didn't join the trial run in time, so I had to figure it out in the actual registration. It worked out well, but I would have liked to have tried it out first. Second, you have a bit of flexibility in the amount of credits you're allowed to take each semester. You can register for more courses than you actually need and drop one that you might not like within the first month of the semester. I joined a course that ended up being very, very different from the course description, so some of them have to be tried out before you really know what they're about.
course_level: I had three courses. One was a basic history course providing a presentation of modern Korean history. It was very simple since it was probably meant as an introduction for international students to Korean society. My two other courses were more "real" in the sense that they had a more even split between international and local students. The level was high, but not very different from at home in Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: Pretty similar to what I'm used to at UCPH. Most classes started with a lecture from the teacher/professor which was followed up by a student presentation and a class discussion.
courses_enrolled: Modern Korean History and Society Case Studies on Transnational Issues and International Cooperation European Integration
recommended_courses: Modern Korean History and Society seems to be a course that is provided most if not all semesters and it gives you a good introduction to the history of Korea since the late 1800s and the fall of the Joseon Dynasty in early 1900s and until recent time. I don't know if the other courses will be provided again, but the teacher of Transnational Issues and International Cooperation (dr. Lee JaeWon) was very, very good and is going to continue teaching as an external lecturer at SNU.
unexpected_costs: My plane ticket home was cancelled and I had to buy a new one that was almost twice as expensive as first planned
cost_comparison: Certain groceries such as dairy products and vegetables/fruits were more expensive than expected. Insurance ended up being more expensive than I had expected. The cost of rent at the dorms was much lower than what I ended up paying at my sharehouse.
activities_available: Apparently there were quite a lot, but since I lived far away from campus I didn't participate in any. I was a member of the SNU Buddy programme, but I had very mixed experiences with it.
activities_recommended: I heard positive things about the taekwondo club. If you know you'll want and be able to participate, the SNU Buddy programme will be very good.
weekend_recommendations: Just experience the city. I had planned a lot of the typical sight seeing-things, but I didn't get to do most of them. The café culture in South Korea is absolutely insane and I got to see a lot of the city by finding cafés all around to try. I lived in the area of the city called Seongsu and this neighborhood has been an up-and-coming place for a while now and was very, very popular. It's known for cafés and pop up-stores. People interested in history would probably want to see at least on of the palaces or keep an eye out for news on parades. There are constantly festivals to join. Fans of K-pop should keep an eye out for exhibitions for there favorite groups and I think most should try to go a concert to experience it. I also think it's very important to go outside of Seoul at least once. I went to the South Jeolla Province and it was great to experience a different part of Korea both in terms of nature and culture. It's very easy to be overwhelmed by the stress of Seoul, but other cities are much more calm. I didn't get to go myself, but if I could go again, I would go to Busan for a few days.
culture_adjustment: Sometimes it was easy, sometimes it was difficult. I think I know enough about Korean culture to be able to navigate in most situations, but I don't think I adjusted in the time that I was there. Being very obviously non-Korean, it's difficult to go anywhere without drawing some kind of attention. You have to get used to being stared at on the train and strangers asking you where you're from. Most of the time it's fine and people are very nice.
socializing_tips: At SNU specifically, the local students are overall pretty good at English, so there's not much of a language barrier. There is also a requirement that all students must take at least one course in English, so exchange students will probably have classes with a lot of local students. If you're comfortable socializing it should be pretty simple to make connections with the local Korean students. The SNU Buddy programme also provided a lot of contact with local students.
cultural_challenges: I don't think it was anything on the side of the Korean locals, but I personally felt hyperaware of Danish people's reputation of being very informal. I think I maybe overcompensated by becoming too polite and reserved at times. Also, when you're out in shops (supermarkets, clothing stores, make up stores, etc.) the staff will follow you around in case you need help. Sometimes they'll be silent, sometimes they'll make suggestions. It made me feel very uncomfortable and avoid shops altogether for a little while. If you don't look Korean, you will be stared at and potentially commented on. Sometimes people will come up to you and ask where you're from or random questions.
culture_appreciated: Something is always happening. You'll run into a filming set and crew, a celebrity event, a pop-up store, a temporary exhibition and/or a festival pretty much everywhere you go all the time. The mix between the extremely modern and the very traditional and historic is pretty amazing. It's definitely a culture of contrasts. You'll see a Porsche drive past a row of run down buildings, people dressed their absolute best and people in hoodies and curlers in their bangs, quick convenience store food and themed, over-the-top cafés. People are (generally) very expressive and enthusiastic which is really great to see. The food is amazing and I was never disappointed in anything I got.
top3_advice: SNU is the most prestigious university in South Korea. Everyone you tell that you are a student there will respond with "Korea number 1!" or "You must be very smart!". It's easy to expect the academic level and expectations to be impossibly high, but really it's all very reasonable. A level of politeness and formality is of course expected, but it's not extreme. Communication from the university is not great. The language course is apparently very good, but I think this is true especially if you have no previous experience with the language and need help to learn it while you're in Seoul. I had learned a bit before going and didn't take the language course and I pretty quickly learned to order at cafés and restaurants in Korean. Also, people in service jobs are generally able to speak English in Seoul. But download the app Papago, it's the best translator and I used it daily. The SNU campus in on a mountain side. Be prepared to walk on hills a lot.
other_useful_info: I can't think of more.
most_rewarding: I've confirmed my interest in Korea and its language, culture and history, and I've learned a lot about myself, what I want to do in the future and become a lot stronger from the experience.
greatest_challenge: Even when I was with people or called home I would feel very alone. The other students that I spoke to said they felt the same thing. People back home keep living their own lives and even if you become really close with the people you meet, they still only know you in the context of exchange. It's a very overwhelming experience that is mainly understood by other people who have gone through something similar. In terms of practical difficulties, getting the registration number and card is definitely a process and I wasn't prepared for it, so I think students going to South Korea should be aware of it and the process before arriving.
other_comments: South Korea is a great place to go and not just for people with a prior interest in the country or culture.

crucial_aspects: A very foreign place with good living conditions and high academic level
info_ease: Compared to my study abroad in Switzerland, everything was non-trivial. Not easy to navigate the information -- and you will need a lot of Papago/Google Translate, even for university pages.
arrival_assistance: Contacts are available for assistance
arrival_comments: No orientation was held for a majority of the exchange students. Some departments held their own welcomes -- but weeks into the semester. I suspect this might be covid-related, but do not expect a lot of assistance if you do not ask for it.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Be aware of the registration opening time. Use time.is to be ready to register to your courses. You will likely have to compete with the local students while you still are in Denmark. If you miss a course, contact the prof -- it's very often possible to get in the course anyway (if you make contact right away)
registration_help: Not much, but a lot of pdfs are provided.
registration_success: None of the classes I originally wanted were held this year (they were held the previous year), but I succesfully registered for the four new courses I wanted. Note that many people often miss the registration on popular courses since relatively few spots are available.
registration_advice: Be quick, sign up for more courses than you want and drop them later (although they cannot have any time overlap), consider the order in which you register for them.
course_level: Very varying difficulty since they group together MSc and PhD level courses. They are however very transparent about the difficulties, and the first week is for making sure you're aware of the contents.
teaching_comparison: Similar, but much less feedback and interaction with TAs. Exams are almost exclusively written. They have midterms and often grade based on many things, e.g. how often you meet up. Only one of my teachers kept track of this, however, so don't be too scared.
courses_enrolled: Natural Language Processing Financial Development of the World Geometric Methods for High-Dimensional Data Analysis Korean Language Class
recommended_courses: I recommend taking a unique course like Geometric Methods to build your academic profile. I further recommend taking either the language class SNU offers or the one at their language institute.
unexpected_costs: Nothing concretely comes to mind, perhaps because there were too many
cost_comparison: Many deposits are quite high, e.g. between 5 and 15 times monthly rent for apt. Also, 330 000 krw deposit for credit card (Woori) Fruit and yoghurt is relatively expensive Eating out is really cheap, so do that a lot!
activities_available: Crazy amount of things
activities_recommended: SNU buddy -- and go with these people for various random things
weekend_recommendations: dates
culture_adjustment: As long as you get your basic worries in place quickly for the whole period (bank, sim, accommodation, figuring out how to get around, practical registration + immigration things), you will be able to adjust more stress-free. It wasn't too difficult for me to get used to the culture -- try to act a bit like they do
socializing_tips: Ask them anything, they are so helpful
cultural_challenges: Biking difficulties. Non-students are pretty bad at English, so use translation apps a lot.
culture_appreciated: The Korean friendliness to foreigners -- just say gamsahamnida (thank you) and they will be so happy.
top3_advice: Use Korean greetings. Always! be respectful :) Take part in the SNU buddy events Try lots of crazy food (sannakji!)
other_useful_info: Open a bank account at Woori or Shinhan before the semester starts Use Coupang (or gmarket) for cheap everything Buy the Chingu mobile pre-paid plan You will likely receive your ARC very late Make use of the short semester to travel a bit around before you have to go back :) Japan and especially Taiwan were super nice.
most_rewarding: Seeing another world
greatest_challenge: Doing well academically with so many available distractions
other_comments: I already miss Korea

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience a city and country that I knew very little about. Also it was important for me to choose a very big city so there would be plenty to explore in my free-time! Also, my host university had a lot of interesting and relevant courses to choose from.
overall_comments: My study abroad experience went far over my own expectations. It was an amazing semester and all the hard work before the stay was worth it.
info_ease: At times, it was a bit confusing to navigate between all the different sources (KU-net, UCPH abroad, Host university and their coordinators). But it was never more confusing than just sending an email with questions to either my coordinator at my home or host university.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival, all exchange students were invited to a welcoming orientation where courses, maps, social programmes etc. were explained. Further communication with the coordinator at SNU (Office of International Affairs (OIA)) was through informational e-mails. The coordinator responded very quickly to e-mails.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: My study abroad experience went far over my own expectations. It was an amazing semester and all the hard work before the stay was worth it.
registration_process: After nomination, you will receive an email from Office of International Affairs where they explain the further process. Then you will need to apply officially, submitting a list of documents (bank statement, letter of approval, list of passed subjects (with stamps), statement of purpose, a photo and passport scan). A couple of months after, you will receive the official letter of approval from SNU and then you can apply for the visa at the embassy in Denmark.
registration_help: It was possible to ask questions through email to the OIA coordinator and she answered very quickly always!
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted. The course registration was a bit confusing to understand at first. It is split up in different tasks during 6 days. The first couple of days are "course cart shopping" and then it moves on to first-come-first-served. After that you can sign up for the courses that are not full. If you didnt get the course you wanted, you can send an application to the professor teaching the course, and they will decide if there is room for you as well. OIA has a youtube channel where they explain the course registration process! Check that out a few days before at least, to be sure that you know what is going down. Because some courses are really popular and will "sell out" in a matter of seconds. Luckily my classes werent as popular, but some of my friends didnt get all the courses they wanted during the first registration and had to ask the professor to get a spot. I will recommend that you make a prioritized list of the courses you want and plan out exactly which ones to apply to first. During the "course-cart-shopping"-days you can also get a hint of how popular the course is - for example if there are 25 spots and 80 people signed up, then you should try to get that course as the first thing you do, when the registration opens!:) And think of a plan-B as well!
registration_advice: There is a lot of information at once. Dont stress about it - just notice the deadlines and read the emails carefully and maybe several times!:)
academics_comments: My study abroad experience went far over my own expectations. It was an amazing semester and all the hard work before the stay was worth it.
course_level: I think the academic level were a bit lower than at univ. of Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: The courses are taught very differently from my experiences at Univ. of Copenhagen. There is a lot of focus on tests during the semester and memorizing terms. The work-load was similar to my home univ. but sometimes felt heavier, because on the focus on tests in stead of the final exam, as I know it from back home. So in my experience the semester was quite busy but not as busy closer to end of semester.
courses_enrolled: Globalizing Korea (Dep. of Anthropology) Korean Language and Literature (Liberal studies) Korean Musical Culture (Liberal Studies)
recommended_courses: All of the courses I was enrolled in were really exciting and taught me a lot about different aspects of Korean Culture and I recommend all the courses. If you can, I will definitely recommend taking a course with Professor Charles La Shure, if you can. He was an excellent professor - very humorous and good at making a great teaching environment for the class.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Flight tickets were really expensive. Restaurants are cheap but cooking yourself can be pretty expensive if your are not careful! Some grocery stores are cheaper than others and some "western" products can be really expensive as well.
activities_available: There is a buddy-program at SNU you can sign up for and I will recommend every exchange student coming to SNU to sign up for it! It was absolutely wonderful and the korean buddies were super engaged! There is weekly dinners and events during the semester that you can sign up for. It was through the buddy program that I found my friends that I ended up spending a lot of time with and going traveling with as well.
activities_recommended: At the beginning of the semester, there is a club-festival, where all the clubs at campus will sit in a tent and play games, talk to other students or present what they do in that particular club. I will recommend that you go to this festival to check out which clubs are possible to sign up for - some of them dont accept exchange students that only are at SNU for one semester so ask about that as well! I initially signed up for the hiking-club but ended up not going to any of the trips because of lack of time! But they seemed really nice and active in that club:)
weekend_recommendations: Travel as much around the country as you possibly can! It is really easy and accessible to get around and the country has so many beautiful and interesting places to visit on the weekend or on day trips. If you like hiking, there are sooo many beautiful hikes around Seoul - even at campus:')
culture_adjustment: I think it was quite easy to adjust to the everyday-life in Seoul! The hardest thing for me was figuring out how to adjust my food habits, shopping in grocery stores and the restaurant culture. I am a vegetarian and meat is a big part of the Korean cuisine, so that was a bit challenging at times! But most restaurants have at least one vegetarian option, so it always worked out.
socializing_tips: Sign up for the buddy program or the clubs at campus!
cultural_challenges: No talking in public transportation!:) Its always really quiet in public transportation and people will definitely give you the side-eye if you talk loudly with your friends!
culture_appreciated: The restaurant-culture is really cool! People usually eat out a lot to socialize with their friends or collegues and it was really fun, experiencing that part of korean culture, both with my international and korean friends! Also, people are extremely helpful if you ask for directions or help to transportation, so dont hesitate to ask if you are confused!
top3_advice: 1) Get started with planning, getting the documents for the applications, searching for housing and saving up as soon as you possibly can! Some of the documents can take some time to get. 2) Check your email often and read the emails from OIA several times so you dont miss any deadlines. 3) Sign up for the buddy-program! It is really the best way of meeting people.
other_useful_info: Dont be afraid to reach out to your peer exchange students for help! In stead of spending hours on searching for the answer to your question on your own, another exchange student might just have been through the same frustrating process just before you! It could save you a lot of time. And this is more a recommendation for Korea in general: But get started on learning reading and writing hangul, before you go. It is very accessible and quick to learn and it has helped me out A LOT in being able to navigate in course material, traveling around the country and just in life in general in Seoul! Duolingo was perfectly enough but there are plenty of other accessible resources - like "Talk to me in Korean".
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all over the world through the Buddy-program! I cannot stress enough how much I recommend signing up for that.
greatest_challenge: The months before the exchange were actually more difficult and challenging for me than the actual exchange. The application process, searching for housing and all the other things you have to get in order before departure, were extremely stressful! BUT in the end, it all worked out and once I got there, all the work was 10 times worth it. There really is a lot of things to fix when you go on exchange and it can feel like an overload of information at some times. But just do it bit by bit and once it is all done, you can enjoy your semester and focus on your studies!:)

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience a culture I was not familiar with in the slightest, that's the reason why an Asian country seemed like a good option.
info_ease: Upon arrival, I was quite confused and overwhelmed but once classes started I found most of the information I needed through talking with fellow students.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance once I arrived in South Korea, which perhaps made the first couple of weeks more complicated, but I managed to find all the information I needed by myself and through other exchange students.
arrival_comments: It was satisfactory but maybe not as thorough as what I was expecting.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Course registration is done on a website where you can pick courses you are interested in, add them to your cart and then eventually select them. The only downside is that it's a first-come first-served basis.
registration_help: Online resources showed every step of the process in ample detail.
registration_success: I was more or less successful in registering for the classes I wanted. The only issue was that a class I wanted to take was offered at a different campus so I had to replace it with another one.
registration_advice: Make sure not to miss the deadlines!
course_level: I took two BA level courses and two MA level courses.
teaching_comparison: I was taking four courses simultaneously which all ran for the entire semester, something that differed quite a bit from the block system I got used to back at UCPH. courses_enrolled: - Artificial Intelligence for New Drug Development and Clinical Application - Theory and Practice in Computational Sciences 2 - Seminar in Oceanography - Korean History
recommended_courses: I don't think I have any courses I would recommend.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than what I expected, especially fruits and dairy products. Eating out and public transportation were cheaper than what I was expecting.
activities_available: Social activities for students are frequent if you are part of the SNU buddy programme but I was not. For cultural, athletic and social activities, I did not rely on anything organised by my host university.
activities_recommended: Jogging and hiking are easy ways to exercise as an exchange student because they don't require joining any club or association. For cultural activities, Seoul has a lot to offer in terms of museums and exhibitions.
weekend_recommendations: Seoul is the perfect city to go out and that is how I spent a lot of weekends. There's also a lot of nice destinations to go on weekend trips like Seoraksan national park, Jeju island and more.
culture_adjustment: I did not find it too hard to adjust to the local culture.
socializing_tips: Socialising with local students is very difficult, the best way to do so is to speak Korean.
cultural_challenges: I starting missing European food after the first few months in Korea and it's been a bit of a challenge sometimes. But nothing too serious.
culture_appreciated: I really liked how full of life Seoul is and how Koreans are always willing to have fun, eat good food and socialise.
top3_advice: 1. Consider joining the SNU buddy programme (I didn't and missed out on a lot of social events). 2. Learn Hangul (the Korean alphabet) and join a Korean class. 3. Take some time off whenever you can to travel around Korea or to neighbouring countries.
other_useful_info: Don't expect to find housing on campus.
most_rewarding: Learning the basics of Korean, making friends from all over the world, feeling at home in a city that used to feel so far away and different.
greatest_challenge: Loneliness was sometimes hard to deal with.

arrival_assistance: there was an orientation for exchange students
arrival_comments: no
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

I remember it was extremely difficult to decide for which specific institute to apply for, because while the content of all courses offered was translated into english, it was completely unclear, which of them were actually held in English and not in Korean. Because of that, at first I applied for the International Relation institute, for which I later found out, that they only offered one course in English this semester. crucial_aspects: I chose for personal reasons mainly. I had been to Korea before and wanted to go back. Also I am considering doing my graduate fieldwork in the region.
overall_comments: The whole experience was amazing. The only reason I am not choosing 10/10, is because of the lack of guidance mainly from KU.
info_ease: Easy enough. I thought SNU were quite thorough with their explanations.
arrival_assistance: There were plenty of mails to read, and they had a few introductory events for all incoming students. I received a lot of help from the SNU buddy program as well.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The whole experience was amazing. The only reason I am not choosing 10/10, is because of the lack of guidance mainly from KU.
registration_process: A little confusing at first, but reading through it a few times made it a lot more clear. I did not have a stressful time getting my courses as most of them were not that popular.
registration_help: We were given a guide and shown a video on how to do it.
registration_success: I got everything I wanted. Most of them in the first round and two in the second round.
registration_advice: Decide on the courses beforehand, add them to your 'wishlist', have plan B's and just click fast honestly.
academics_comments: The whole experience was amazing. The only reason I am not choosing 10/10, is because of the lack of guidance mainly from KU.
course_level: The courses were generally very easy, lower level than what I was used to. Only one course I took, which was a graduate course, was really on par with the academic level at KU. The other courses were not within my field, but I had no problem following them. I did not mind the level, as it gave me time to do other things.
teaching_comparison: Two of my courses had very little participation. It seemed like the professors didn't expect you to answer any questions at all. Three of my courses had a high level of participation though. Especially one of them was great, as it was more of a round-table discussion, which I thought very productive.
courses_enrolled: Studies in Korean Culture, Understanding Modern Culture, Two Koreas, Introduction to Film Art and 20th- and 21st- Century Fiction.
recommended_courses: Studies in Korean Culture was great, but do not take it unless you are an anthropology or sociology student. Also I loved Understanding Modern Culture and Two Koreas, the latter being modern Korean history. The professors were both very engaging.
unexpected_costs: Mandatory health insurance. You can get an exemption, but it was not easy, so I ended up just paying it.
cost_comparison: I already knew the prices, but food and coffee is very cheap.
activities_available: Lots of clubs. I didn't participate much, I did not feel like I had the time. Also some of the clubs were 'unofficially' not open to foreigners, as they did not want to speak English.
activities_recommended: SNU buddy program! If you put time into it, you will not regret it. I had an amazing group and it made all the difference.
weekend_recommendations: Get out and explore the city! There's so much to do and see. Definitely go hiking no matter if you've done it before or not. Go to Jeju in May or September.
culture_adjustment: I have stayed in Korea for 3 months before, so it was no problem for me.
socializing_tips: Again I would say SNU buddy and clubs. Or talk to some in class.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really, but I might not be the best judge of that.
culture_appreciated: Smart solutions for everything and how people generally are mindful of other people. I would say compared to Copenhagen people are a lot less loud (except when drunk), don't take up a lot of space and just are generally polite.
top3_advice: Get involved with SNU buddy, be present in class even if the level is different from what you are used to (I learned a lot from hearing the perspectives of my classmates), also don't spend all your time with other Danes or travelling with friends or family from home (you can do that another time).
other_useful_info: Get a climate card if you are staying off campus.
most_rewarding: My classes, the SNU buddy program and travelling with the friends I made through both.
greatest_challenge: Having to go home haha

crucial_aspects: I have been interested in korean music and film industry for around 5 years and have since then wanted to experience korean culture myself. Thus, I knew I wanted to go on exchange to Korea since I started university
overall_comments: It is difficult to give an overall rating of my exchange to Korea. On one hand it was fun to live out a dream and learn a lot of independence skills I would have never gotten staying in a secure setting in Denmark. On the other hand there was a lot more challenges than i had anticipated. I do not regret going on exchange, but it was not as grand and amazing as I know others say it is. However, for me personally it was still better than staying in Denmark, as I believe the growth you have during the new and challenging times alone in a foreign country are super valuable in the long run, even though they are not always as fun in the moment. During my exchange it was not the best, but what I have gotten with me of personal growth back home are undeniably worth the hardships.
info_ease: SNU OIA is a great site for information. I found it a little difficult to really feel prepared for my exchange and the logistics. I spend hours and days searching everything I could, but a lot of things you cannot figure out until you land and experience it for yourself in Korea. The university is not so great at sending information, so do not expect to feel like you are prepared and confident in what, where, when and how of basically anything related to school. When arriving at Incheon airport you need to go through a immigration check which I recommend reading up on before going to korea. Also SIM-cards in korea and transport from the airport to Seoul was a challenge to manage with the jetlag so maybe prepare is from home if possible.
arrival_assistance: I arrived a little over a week before semester start so I had a bit of time to explore the northern parts of Seoul before going to SNU. The weekend before semester start there was an introduction for exchange students. The usual conference room was however under reconstruction and the new room did not have room for everyone. Instead you had to apply based on first come first served(you will learn that they love first come first served) Also, the courses I had gave zero information before semester start. Nothing about books, what to read, what to expect anything. The only thing you get is the little description of the course and if you are lucky an overview of what each week focus on(but they do not necessarily follow their own schedule) The Alien Registration Card you need in korea is managed by the school, but the process takes super long(it was okay for me as I didn't need it for anything). The deadlines and process is not so strict. When applying you need documentation for a living-space in Korea. It says you need proof of at least 60 days of staying there, but it can be shorter. Also if you move to another place, it is easy to change, so there is no reason to worry too much about it.
arrival_comments: If you love and thrive in structured and well informed environments I cannot recommend SNU. It is possible to manage okay when you are there, but I always felt that I was under-informed and confused about why there was no information/information very late.

In hindsight I would have probably liked to try a MA class to see if they were better? Other students I knew who took master classes(and bachelor) said the master classes were really difficult, but also not so difficult. You just have to show up to class and turn in assignments and then you will pass(though it won't be the best grade, but it does not matter, as the grade is not transferred to CPH)
teaching_comparison: I much prefer the teaching at UCPH. If you are unlucky you might get a teacher who speaks korean when they feel like it.
courses_enrolled: 1. Biochemistry 2 2. Introduction to Chemical biology 3. Animal immunology 4. Interdisciplinary seminar in natural sciences 5. Plant cell biology
recommended_courses: Honestly none of them. Biochemistry 2: Consisted of going through "lehninger principles of biochemistry" from chapter 13-22 Introduction to Chemical biology: Was way too difficult as I am so bad at chemistry. If you like hardcore chemistry it might be okay?? Animal immunology: Just no. The teacher was so unorganized, read off of slides, and often wasn't even there so it was over video instead + he did not give feedback on assignments or midterms Interdisciplinary seminar in natural sciences: It was the least bad out of all the courses Plant cell biology: Pretty easy but boring. Recommend it if you want to get easy through a course
unexpected_costs: All in all I spend 50.000KR for my total exchange(inclusive plane ticket to and from, and everything that had to do with the exchange ex. Vaccination) + I ended up staying at a hotel 4 different times during my stay in korea.
cost_comparison: Nothing (Food was more expensive than anticipated, but I also ate out at every meal)
activities_available: I am unsure. Heard some people joined fencing clubs. The buddy program is nice. Planned lunch and dinner every to every other week and a lot of activities during the months
activities_recommended: Obviously the buddy program. Though I didn't use it much there were good times like hiking, water parks and other group activities.
weekend_recommendations: Go see the nature. That is the best part of Korea. They have beautiful mountains and excellent walking routes both crazy scary ones and beautiful relaxing ones. I liked the war memorial museum, olympic park and Seoul Trail.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy
socializing_tips: I didn't socialize much. Probably try to attend as many activities as you can. If you are extroverted and talkative they will open up. I you don't talk you will not befriend anyone.
cultural_challenges: People can insist on talking korean to you even when you don't understand, and random people might approach you and insist on following you around. The air in Korea is really polluted. If you have asthma be aware and I also had so much trouble with my eyes because of the air. They became red and hurt like crazy after days with high pollution which is almost everyday in summer and early fall.
culture_appreciated: Love that many restaurants have screens to order from and that it is not uncommon to be by yourself at cafes, restaurants ect.
top3_advice: Do not expect to learn anything school related on exchange(and I recommend to do minimal school work, attending classes is obligatory but otherwise don't focus on it, see the city instead) Do what you really like doing. Don't go to the events if you want to explore something by yourself. And don't sit on your hands waiting for something to happen. Reach out and try new things if you want to. This exchange is for yourself, so do what you want with it. Really be happy about and cherish the good parts. It is only four months. This also counts for when it is going bad, it is only four months and the bad things will eventually become great for personal growth
other_useful_info: The exchange coordinator is bad at replying to your questions. I advice to make a group chat with the people going to the same university and get to know each other and help each other along the way.
most_rewarding: I have really come to appreciate Denmark and UCPH. Nothing makes you miss and love home as going far away.
greatest_challenge: Feeling lost in my studies. I have never felt less happy or unmotivated about studying in my life My Living situation. No heat, difficult landlord A lot of alone time, and times where you question everything, you might feel lost and alone(but it's natural and come and pass from time to time everywhere you go.

course_level: I took 6 courses, which was a lot—48 ECTS in total. This included 3 undergraduate courses and 3 graduate courses. Fluid Dynamics: The teaching was mediocre, but there was a textbook available for self-study. The tests were poorly designed, and the workload was massive. Hypersonic Vehicle Design: Honestly, this didn’t feel like a real course. The professor would talk for 1.5 hours straight about PowerPoint slides with pictures of "hypersonic vehicles," but there was no homework or any other material to learn from. There was one midterm, but we never got the results—I suspect everyone did so poorly that the professor just ignored it. For the final, I drew what I thought looked like a fast vehicle, talked about it for five minutes, and got the equivalent of a 10 for that. I learned literally nothing. Ocean Wave Propagation Theory: This was by far the best course. I actually learned something, likely because there were only three students in the class, and I was the only English-speaking one in this "English" course. As a result, the professor tailored the education to me. Power System Economics: I don’t think the professor even knew what he wanted to teach in this course. He had a midlife crisis during the semester, declaring he wouldn’t be teaching in this field anymore because “nothing in life matters” and “the whole industry is a scam.” Numerical Analysis: This was actually a challenging course, especially since the teaching style was just 1.5 hours of continuous lecturing. I ended up relying heavily on the textbook connected to the course, which helped me scrape through the tests. Keep in mind that the average test score here was around 25–30%, meaning you could theoretically score 30% on all tests and still get an A+. It felt like there was no system at all—professors just did whatever they wanted. Atomic Physics: This was the only real physics course I could choose, so I was pretty excited about it. Unfortunately, I didn’t really learn anything. One-third of the lectures were pre-recorded MP4 files, one-third were in-person, and the remaining third didn’t happen because the professor’s iPad broke, and he couldn’t record the videos. He scheduled the exam at the same time as one of my other exams, so he arranged a special oral exam just for me. His teaching consisted of writing down everything he said on the blackboard for 1.5 hours without including any formulas or calculations throughout the course.
teaching_comparison: I like KU a lot better, it really killed me that there were no exercise classes.

registration_help: The university sent out a guide on how the course application process works, and there is also a test run so you can see how many are interested in different courses.
