crucial_aspects: One thing was the academic institution and opportunities, which I did factor into my decision, but I would say that the biggest reason of them all was that I wanted to experience a new place and culture. I also thought that if I would go on exchange I would want to go far away and to a place I've never been and would want to visit.
overall_comments: I was really happy that I chose to go, and I had an amazing time, the reason i didn't give a 10/10 was because the process to get to go and registering and everything was pretty stressful and tedious.
info_ease: I think I managed pretty well. Course registration was a bit hard to figure out, but doing the test round helped a lot for me. You'll need a lot of documents and when you arrive you should apply for an ARC, but the korean sites are pretty hard to navigate. I know some exchange students did their ARC application and so on through HireVisa, so they did group applications. But I found that I got my ARC before the group one.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientiation but not everyone could attend because of limited space. But mostly you will also figure out a lot of the stuff from other exchange students. The most confusing part for me was how attendance worked, since it differed from class to class
arrival_comments: They did help out, but a lot of it you still need to figure out yourself how it works even though they give you the apps that help a lot. I signed up with the Buddy program and I was really happy I did that and if I were to go again I would 100% apply for it again. There you can also ask some of the local students how stuff works if you are unsure.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I was really happy that I chose to go, and I had an amazing time, the reason i didn't give a 10/10 was because the process to get to go and registering and everything was pretty stressful and tedious.
registration_process: Well all classes for the semester isn't released until july, then you can but them in a wishlist or liked, so you can see how popular the course is. You will also be able to see how many spots there are in the course. Then first they have a pre-registration period, which is just a trail registration so nothing you register for during this period counts. Like a trail run. Then later comes the real period. Apply for the most popular courses first! and look out for restrictions. Then later comes the add and drop period, where you can drop courses you have and add new ones. in this period it might be possible for you to add a popular course you maybe couldn't get because the quota was met. So if someone drops it you can add it if you are fast. If you still don't get a course you want because of quota or anything else, you can email the professor to ask them to add you and send an exceeding quato registration request, when that opens.
registration_help: some guides on their webpage and they sent out emails with information about it.
registration_success: I got almost all the courses I wanted except for one, because of restrictions, but I didn't end up having many courses related to my major since I lot of them were either not within my prerequisites or courses I had already completed at home.
registration_advice: Just try to get the hang of the system a bit before and you will be fine, no need to panic too much. I used the course list from the years before to get an idea of which courses might be there for the semester i went.
academics_comments: I was really happy that I chose to go, and I had an amazing time, the reason i didn't give a 10/10 was because the process to get to go and registering and everything was pretty stressful and tedious.
course_level: As mentioned in my comment it was weird. They also do not do exercise classes and basically all of it is just powerpoints or notes from the teacher every week. I did not use or have to acquire a single book.
teaching_comparison: I think I like the style of teaching more at UCPH since I find it more structured. Overall it was just a weird experience with course levels at SNU.
courses_enrolled: Topics in Mathematics 2, Extraterrestrial Planets and Life, Korean History and 13 week Korean Language Program at LEI.
recommended_courses: I found Extraterrestrial Planets and Life to be a really fun and interesting course. Not a super high level so It's pretty nice and easy to follow, even if it has nothing to do with your major. It was also interesting to take Korean History especially while living in Korea, and the language program for me I found fun and also helpful to take while being in Korea.
unexpected_costs: It wasn't really unexpected since I knew about it already but it cost more than I thought and the process to apply to not pay it was a lot of work. But once your get your ARC and are registered you will start recieving NHIS bills, which is sthe National Health Insurance in Korea, but I already had payed and insurance from back home, i used Europæiske Erv, which was around 1800 dkk for 5-6 months. So my insurance bill is pretty high since I basically payed for doubble insurance. Also you have to pay around 30.000 krw for your ARC application, and every month i payed very little for electricity.
cost_comparison: Eating out is suuuper cheap, and also you can get lunch on campus (and dinner) for as little as 4.5 dkk at one of the cafeterias. Fruit and vegetable are expensive and it basically makes no sense to cook at home. I wanna point out that I tried to overestimate a lot of the costs above.
activities_available: I went hiking and played basket like two times with my buddy group, one of the basket practices I more or less organized though, but hiking is also really fun! Also tons of board game cafes and I went to karaoke a lot. But most of it was done privatly and not through the host insitution. With the Buddy program there is a thurday pub every thurday where you can go hang out. One thing is also the SNU festival were there was music and food stalls it was worth it in my opinion to go. It's free entry and all you do is show your student card. Also it's fun to check out the club fair when they are there.
activities_recommended: The SNU festival as I said before, and The Buddy program was the best decision. Also maybe I should add that you do need to pay a bit to enter the program. They do a lot of social activities so usually you'll be able to go to stuff through that, and alsio meet people!
weekend_recommendations: I went to Busan and it was super nice. I didn't manage to but I also really wanted to go see Danyang, I'll totally plan a trip to go there if I ever visit again. After the semester ended in December I went to Japan, and it was also really cool. I would also recommend to go Hiking, if you are there during autumn you should go when all the leaves turn red and yellow, it's crazy beautiful! It's like Korea was made for Autumn to exist. Also check out some of the fancy and special cafes.
culture_adjustment: Not too hard, it was not that different from back home in regards to how people interact, and almost all koreans I spoke with were so nice! Queue culture is a bit weird sometimes they are great at it and other times really bad. But it's pretty easy to adjust to. First you need to get used to people (mostly elderly) staring.
socializing_tips: Join the Buddy Program. Local students don't really often speak to you and it can be hard to break the ice.
cultural_challenges: People walk really really slow... It was just really annoying, but nothing was particularly really challenging in my opinion.
culture_appreciated: how friendly people are and how convenient everything is.
top3_advice: I would take part in the Buddy Program, research how some of the processes in terms of registering yourself and everything works beforehand just to give yourself a sense of calmness maybe take passport photos in Denmark, since they like to use filters a lot in Korea. Lastly maybe try some of the things that you don't see in Denmark, and try going to see a lot of the different areas also other university Campuses, and just keep a lookout on you KUmail a lot up until you start university there.
other_useful_info: I think I've mentioned the most important things. I can't think of a lot more right now
most_rewarding: The people I got to meet, and trying to experience living abroad. I feel I grew a lot as a person having to navigate everything and do so many things on my own, and kind of trying to integrate a bit into another country and society.
greatest_challenge: Maybe when you miss home sometimes, also at the start before the semester started and I had met people, I had a hard time getting myself to eat, because the getting used to everything was so overwhelming. But the second you start being around people and everything it all became so much easier.
other_comments: not really

crucial_aspects: A mix of cultural differences and good academic institutions, particularly for computer science. I wanted to learn more about AI while experiencing a place that had its own very distinct character and to be culture shocked in a good way. Another good thing is that young Koreans are decent at English while Korea remains culturally very Korean.
overall_comments: I am super happy with my courses, and their program SNU buddy which was great socially. Downsides were the amount of paper work to navigate particularly around on campus accommodation that required some medical documentation.
info_ease: There was a lot of paperwork, regarding ARC visa and accomodation as well as course selection. Most of it was before arrival but generally you receive a lot of infomration, and long instructions. So you can find a lot of information but navigating it takes some time.
arrival_assistance: They have a good center for foreign students with people you can mail. They are used to handling foreign students and have a lot of foreign students at the school. You can get help if you need it.
arrival_comments: While they are super helpful they can also be quite rigid in their systems which can be quite complex or specific.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I am super happy with my courses, and their program SNU buddy which was great socially. Downsides were the amount of paper work to navigate particularly around on campus accommodation that required some medical documentation.
registration_process: Generally their systems are difficult. I first applied to CSE, the computer science department. This is very difficult to get into however. I was rejected. I then applied to Departement of Liberal Studies and got in, this is much easier. For tecnically you can apply to courses across departments, but for undergrad a lot of them are restricted to only students at their departement, keep in mind you are only selected amongst English courses with is a subset in the first place. My solution was to only take grad courses, they have less restrictions and more English courses. SNU recommends 5 undergrad courses for one semester or 3 grad so keep in mind that the conversion to ECTS may depend on this. I think i used 1 grad course to 10 ECTS and one undergrad course to 6 ECTS, but you will have to check this individually with KU. The course registration itself is a multi stage process. It has several "first come first served" type steps, for which you need to be awake in the middle of the night, clicking a button in their system as fast as you can. I recommend checking their system server time using time.navyism. If you dont get your desired courses the first time there is a decent chanse to change once you are there as well, through a course change period when other people change courses spots open up and you can apply. I ended up getting a great schedule but there is lots of uncertainty in the process and lots of planning. You should go into it knowing you may not get to study what you want, but you will most likely get some of what you want.
registration_help: You can email them, they send out lots of info and long pdfs as well.
registration_success: I got a great schedule but there was no guarantees for it.
registration_advice: Be open minded in terms of what courses you get, and really try to switch if you are unhappy once you get there, there is a decent chance a spot opens up.
academics_comments: I am super happy with my courses, and their program SNU buddy which was great socially. Downsides were the amount of paper work to navigate particularly around on campus accommodation that required some medical documentation.
course_level: I had: Deep Learning, Advanced Deep Learning, Topics in Micro Economics, Topics in Operations Management. Some courses were academically very difficult, but the expectation in terms of evaluation were not that difficult to meet.
teaching_comparison: No past tests to practise on, no exercise classes with TA like DIKU, some homework. Generally more surface level but more different topics. More paper presentations and academic discussions. But then also keep in mind i am BA at DIKU and did MA courses at SNU
courses_enrolled: Deep Learning, Advanced Deep Learning, Topics In Micro Economics, Topics In Operations Management
recommended_courses: Deep Learning, is great to get overview of all kinds of deep learning methods. I heard RL is too easy and I also took Adv Deep Learning, its mostly paper presentations and a project. Its great if you want to try something applied in AI but it feels PHD level. Topics In operations management is great MBA style teaching not too difficult teacher is great. Topics in Micro was way too mathematical, also feels PHD level, class was almost empty, don't recommend unless you're really interested in the mathematics of game theory. It is not taught very pedagogically.
unexpected_costs: Medical documentation in DK, You will most likely eat out, most of the time. Its cheap for what you get but still adds up, You will want to travel around and do stuff, with SNU buddy and for yourself. I had a goshiwon contract the first month as well as my student housing, because I was accepted late, so double rent.
cost_comparison: Eating out is cheap, student housing is cheap, flight was cheaper than expected.
activities_available: There is a lot, I joined swimming but only had time to go two times because its on a Saturday and you want to do other things then. But they show a lot of clubs in the semester start at the front lawn near building 63.
activities_recommended: Swimming, tennis, SNU buddy, go out to Ittaewon, dinners Korean BBQ etc, see other Korean cities.
weekend_recommendations: Travel around Asia, I went to Japan twice, wish I had time to see China and Taiwan as well.
culture_adjustment: Young people generally speak english which helps a lot. Everything is different but you learn fast.
socializing_tips: SNU buddy
cultural_challenges: Not sure, they are super polite and also quite social.
culture_appreciated: That there is a different way of doing everything we do here that also works. Good perspective. Love the food and that locals are out eating and enjoying the city also super safe.
top3_advice: Join SNU buddy, remember its pass fail, so take cool/difficult courses if you want, also might be smart to take some easier course so you have time to see things and enjoy. See Japan as well.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Getting to know new people through classes and exchange program.
greatest_challenge: Paper work ARC visa, phone number, bank card, medical documentation, course registration.
other_comments: What I did: Flight, etihad airways, quite cheap, free hotel stopover in Abudabi on my way back, book home trip separate as you may find out you want to travel more. Phone nr, bought on campus sim card in building 63. Bank Shinhan on campus you can open account before ARC and set up auto transfer as required by student housing, then get card once you get ARC. Otherwise Hire visa (you apply for ARC with them) also had an option to get bank account while application was pending. Get a good photo, with white background that works with ARC demands so you can use it not only for visa but for ARC. Transportation, buy t-money at airport in vending machine. If you have a period when you want to travel a lot, buy climate card for a month or a a week which is unlimited travel in Seoul. If you dont get campus housing, start with a cheap goshiwon near SNU station and figure it out as you go. If you have money to spend there are also great share houses in that area I know friends that loved that.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to try living somewhere where the culture and academic environment were markedly different from those in Denmark. At the same time, I wanted to live in a place that made sense in relation to my studies and that I personally found exciting.
overall_comments: none

arrival_assistance: There is an orientation evening that goes through the most important information. I was not in Seoul at the time, so I did not attend that evening, and I managed just fine anyway. The first week is mainly spent being introduced to your courses, for example if you want to drop a course and apply for a different one.
arrival_comments: It will always be exciting to start in a new place where you are unfamiliar with the location, the systems, and the teaching structure. I found that many things work intuitively, and they use a system that is very similar to Absalon, which they call ETL. This is where everything is uploaded, including assignments, the syllabus, and preparatory materials.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: none
registration_process: Read above
registration_help: You will receive a guide along with all the other documents from the university. Read it carefully, and everything should be fine.
registration_success: I got 2 out of 5 courses that were my first priorities.
registration_advice: Overall, I had three courses that I was very satisfied with, and two where I felt the quality was weaker. This largely depends on which professor you get and how they structure their teaching. I also took two graduate-level courses, which are at a completely different level than undergraduate courses and therefore involved a heavier workload. Compared to the University of Copenhagen, the teaching structure felt somewhat more like a high-school system. Attendance is monitored, and class participation is recorded and counts toward your final grade.
academics_comments: none
course_level: Read above

courses_enrolled: Graduate courses: Smart City, Science, technology, Innovation and International Development Smart City and Digital Transformation Undergraduate courses: Critical Communication Studies in big data and AI Holistic view of innovation Art and Science

I find it especially engaging when the material can be linked to real-world examples. Art and science: I have a strong passion for art and have always been curious about it, so I thought it was a great way to explore another interest by taking a course on the subject. I learned a lot from it.
unexpected_costs: Grocery shopping is very expensive compared to Denmark, so you end up eating out a lot. For example, five apples cost around 50 DKK, and a bag of oats cost about 40 DKK.
cost_comparison: Read above
activities_available: A lot put i didnt payed attention to it.
activities_recommended: SNU buddy programme
weekend_recommendations: Jeju island, Busan, Sokcho, Bukasan, Road trip thorugh south korea!! Hannamdong, Seongsu, Yennamdong, Yennam Hui, Mullae, Haebaechong, Seochon Village, Hannok Village, Gangnam, Hongdae
culture_adjustment: You can clearly feel the cultural differences between Denmark and South Korea, both in the way people communicate and in their body language. Many people are not very confident in English, so you often rely on gestures or translation apps. While I felt that Seoul became a home for me, I did not feel like part of the local population, as the cultural differences are quite significant
socializing_tips: SNU buddy programme
cultural_challenges: The language
culture_appreciated: The food, efficentcy, the city, museums, nature
top3_advice: I recommend applying for the ARC card outside the university, so make sure to print all the required documents in advance and submit them directly at the immigration office. Buy an eSIM—I got mine through the MobileMatter app. Also, get a Climate Card (their public transport card), which you can purchase at a convenience store. Finally, get a Revolut credit card. I recommend carrying two credit cards, as many places do not accept Apple Pay.
other_useful_info: Remember to explore Seoul out from the university!!! The city is amazing.
most_rewarding: Living far away from home and learning to integrate yourself into an opposite culture.
greatest_challenge: Socializing with strangers and doing group work in different ways.
other_comments: none

recommended_courses: 18th centrury british literature because the professor is extremely talented and enlightened.

cost_comparison: grocerys at the food store is very expensive, also fruit and vegetables are extremely expensive, so I didnt really eat much of that while I was there.

crucial_aspects: When searching for a study destination I wanted it to be in Asia, preferably South Korea, Japan or Singapore, as I wanted to know more about the Asian culture.
info_ease: It was fairly easy to find information upon arrival as most of the information had been sent by mail.
arrival_assistance: I found out by myself. There was an orientation for exchange students, but the spots were limited and overlapped the course registration period, thus I didn't attend it.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There were set times where you could register for courses. Since the course registration opens for everyone at the same time,, you have to be fast to get your courses. Roughly a week before the semester started there was an after registration period, where you could drop courses. For full courses you could hope that an open spot would open up. Therefore at least in my case I had to refresh the course registration website about every 15 minutes to get my courses.
registration_help: We received a mail with a detailed explanation of how it worked. You could also write a mail to the professors, departments and the Office of International Affairs for help.
registration_success: I got most of the classes I wanted to get. The only class I didn't get was restricted, so I couldn't get it anyways.
registration_advice: Be sure to be on time for the course registration, as it will be hard to get all your courses if you don't apply for them immediately.
course_level: Most of the courses were fairly easy with exception of my math course "Topics in Mathematics 2." This was an undergraduate course, but the contents were close to if not at PhD level, hence most of the other students who took the course were PhD students. Luckily the requirement to pass the course were low, but the contents of the course were far harder than one would expect from reading the course description and attending the first week of lectures (while we could still drop it and register for other courses.)
teaching_comparison: There was a lot of learning by heart. Most of the exams were about how much you could remember and less about problem solving problems.
courses_enrolled: "Basic Computing: First Adventures in Computing," "Korean History," "Survey in Vietnamese History," "Topics in Mathematics 2" and "Understanding Asian Philosophy."
recommended_courses: I would recommend "Understanding Asian Philosophy" and "Korean History" as they are courses that don't require too much work, while also learning a lot about the culture and history of Korea.
unexpected_costs: There is a mandatory health insurance in South Korea which is roughly 300 dkk a month
cost_comparison: Basically everything is cheaper than in Denmark. Especially eating out is pretty cheap here.
activities_available: The SNU Buddy group was very fun for exchange students as they held a lot of events for exchange students. They also had a few clubs, but as an exchange student I didn't really have time for them.
activities_recommended: Definitely the SNU Buddies.
weekend_recommendations: Just explore Seoul as it is a big city by itself. In the Holidays you should try to go to Busan or Jeju.
culture_adjustment: To me it was fairly easy. Most people just mind their own business on the street.
cultural_challenges: None really.
culture_appreciated: The locals are nice when you actually talk to them. Even when they don't speak English they try their best to communicate with you.
top3_advice: Don't take courses that require too much work as you want to experience life in Seoul instead of studying all day. Use the shuttle bus if you live close by SNU Station, as it is free. And if you travel a lot get a climate card.
other_useful_info: If you can you should get a Korean bank account. Also if you go to SNU then you will be offered to get your ARC through HireVisa, which you should totally do as it makes the process much easier and stress free.
most_rewarding: The many new friends I made and also the experience of living in a completely different setting than what you are used to.
greatest_challenge: My one math course.

crucial_aspects: I was drawn towards the city of Vienna due to its history and always its impact on my subject field, Psychology. Furthermore the academic profile of the host university appealed to me - prioritizing perspectives of psychoanalysis and social science. It was always crucial to not travel too far from my home country Denmark.
overall_comments: The academic experience of the host university was very poor, and i felt understimulated compared to university of Copenhagen. I will elaborate further on this below. Besides this, the opportunity to travel abroad - with funding - and have time to experience the culture and history of the city has been very meaningful to me.
info_ease: I am unsure of which information is reffered to. I had beforehand found accomodation indenpendently of the university, and did not require specific assistent in regards to arriving in the city. Besides this, the university was helpful to send out in information about study start, course enrollment and so on.
arrival_assistance: We got a orientation letter from the host university, explaining the basic logistics of arriving in the city. The information was very helpful in regards to transportation, visa and so on.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The academic experience of the host university was very poor, and i felt understimulated compared to university of Copenhagen. I will elaborate further on this below. Besides this, the opportunity to travel abroad - with funding - and have time to experience the culture and history of the city has been very meaningful to me.
registration_process: There was overall confusion in regards to the course registratin. Eventually it worked out fine though. But i wanted to attend courses from different faculties, and i was told that it would be possible. But because of administration issues the course catalogue of the Psychotherapy Faculty was not complete until the third week of the semester.
registration_help: There was a study service center, and they where very helpful to assist me.
registration_success: Eventually i was succesful and everything worked out fine in regards to course registration.
registration_advice: Dont expect to have a complete schedule on the first day of the semester. There will most likely be overlaps and cancellation of courses, which will cause you to "re-plan" your studies a little bit. Trust that this will work out eventually. The issue of "getting the course first" didnt seem to be a problem at SFU, as it seems at other universities. I got all the courses, that where mandatory for me (from KU), which where the most important.
academics_comments: The academic experience of the host university was very poor, and i felt understimulated compared to university of Copenhagen. I will elaborate further on this below. Besides this, the opportunity to travel abroad - with funding - and have time to experience the culture and history of the city has been very meaningful to me.
course_level: The academic level overall, was surprisingly low. Unclear if this was due to teaching or student environment, but probably both. In most classes (not all) there existed a culture of discussing with personal anecdotes and opinions without connecting it to scientific litterature. It was my experience that most of the teachers often where unable to make these connections. In Psychological Diagnostics a youtube video from a influencer psychologist was presented in order to show how a therapy session should start and end. No scientific discussion followed. Claims about the scientific value of many psychological paradigms (eg psychoanalysis) where often dismissed as unscientific, without proper argumentation. Many teachers presented subject matter without references. In clinical psychology it was obvious that the lecture slides was AI generated. Here the teacher highly encouraged the students to "share" what diagnoses they had. I found it unethical and unscientific.
teaching_comparison: Different. Lectures and seminar classes where often "integrated" meaning that the same teacher stood in front of the class for 3-4 hours. It was often unclear when we should work with texts ourselves and when the "lecture part" was going on. It was very unstructurered, and combined with VERY strict attending requirements, i felt this had a bad effect on student participation and thriving. Coming from UCPH it was a culture chok. I would not recommend other students to go on exchange at SFU.
courses_enrolled: Psychological Diagnostics 1 (Very poor) Bachelor Preparation Introduction to Philosophy of Social Science Clinical Psychology (Very Poor) Communication Research and Linguistics Fundamental principles of neuroscience History and Theoretical development of the psychotherapy schools
recommended_courses: Communication Research and Linguistics Introduction to Philosophy of Social Science Both taught by Alexander Wendt, who i think is a good teacher. Communication Research and Linguistics is rare in a Psychology department
unexpected_costs: Grocery prices where pretty high. Also, now Vienna has taken away the "semester" ticket for public transportation, so expect to pay a little more. Also when you go through the "meldephlicht", you have to pay 20-50 euro to "register" in the city.
cost_comparison: Prices of groceries where high. The rent of living was low, at least compared to my home town of Copenhagen.
activities_available: There was probably some, but i did not find them. In the beginning of the semester i asked to join the universities football team, but they did not have any. I instead found a team through the main university of Vienna.
activities_recommended: I am sorry but i cannot be helpful here, because i did not attend anything. I am aware of the "SFU-ball" in the winter, which might be fun. Besidses this the university hosts guests and talks regularly, but most where in German, so i did not go.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the sorounding capital cities, they are close by. There is wonderfull nature around the city of Wien, go on hikes or swim in the Donau. You can also take the train to the alps, and hike for the weekend. Make use of the many cultural offers in the city, it is really remarkable.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy, as i experienced the viennese simularly to the copenhagen people i am used to. Dont eat or talk on the phone in public transportation. The locals dont appreciate it.
socializing_tips: Make use of the "USI" which is the sports catalogue for students in Vienna. Here you can attend everything from football to salsa to thaiboxing. It is a GREAT way to meet other people/students.
cultural_challenges: Soimetimes the viennese can come across as unpolite. You have to get use to this. Most are happy to talk, but can seem unfriendly in the beginning. This is similar to Copenhagen, so i found it not so difficult.
culture_appreciated: Vienna is a culture city, and there is really always something to experience. I bought both the NONSTOP abonnoment that gives unlimited access to all cinema showings in Wien for 22euro/month. Wien has beautifull cinemas and often niche themes and showings. Besides this i bought the bundeskart that gives access to all the major museums for 99euro/year, i found this very nice, as a single entrance ticket often amounts to 14/15 euros. If you like museums, then this offer is very good.
top3_advice: Dont expect a buzzing student environment. SFU is a small university. There is close to non common areas, which makes it difficult to "enter" into the student environment. The student unions or communities, if there are any, are not visible. Also expect the attendance requirement culture to be very different from UCPH. At SFU, everything besides lectures, has an 80% attendance, and you need a doctors note. There is no reading hall at the university, so if you appreciate this, then find it in the city: there is plenty. TU at Karlsplatz, Kunstakademi Schillerplatz and the uni Wien at Spitalgasse.
other_useful_info: Make use of the study service center as much as you can. Also, if you come from UCPH, expect a different exam period. At SFU you will have maybe 8-10 courses to reach 30 ECTS points. For me, i had to go to an exam in all of my courses. I had 9 exams/papers in a span of 3 weeks. Most of the students at SFU postpone exams to a "second try" a month later, but because i was going home i couldnt. Also, all of the written exams are with pen and paper.
most_rewarding: The city of Vienna, with its culture and nature. Getting to know local people and other students from around the world. Getting away from my known sorroundings and out of my comfort zone.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge of my exchange stay was the academic frustration i experienced at SFU, as described above. Besides this, i found the city very liveable and with a lot of offers to socialize and experience culture and history. I would very much reccomend going abroad to Vienna!
other_comments: The above mentioned critique of SFU, might sound a little rough, but i was geniunly taken aback by the poor state of the university. The administration was overworked, and people where quiting there jobs (including our Erasmus coordinator and the main person at the Study Service Center), the academic level seemed (to me) to be equivalent to a high school level. The environment in class was characterized by talkin loudly and playing games, not paying respect to the teacher. But the teachers often didnt feel competent enough to communicate the academics in an appropriate way that corresponded to the level of the students.

crucial_aspects: To me, it was important to choose a well-recommended university. I knew that other public health students had great experiences at SFU. I was told that SFU offered both great academic opportunities and was very helpful during the whole process. Also, live somewhere with beautiful nature and opportunities to travel.
overall_comments: I would rate my stay at SFU 10/10. However, the overall rate was 8/10. The reason why is that it was stressful and difficult to plan during the COVID-pandemic (I was going just then the Omnicron-variant spread across the world). I was from time to time unsure of whenever I would be able to go. It takes a lot of time to plan everything – and I found it sometimes difficult to get the needed help from KU. But I would never choose to stay home just because there is a lot of planning. It is worth it all and you will forget all of it once you arrive!
info_ease: Simon Fraser University was very helpfull and sends out a lot of emails with all the information needed. Whenever in doubt, I send an email and got an answere the same day.
arrival_assistance: The introduction to exchange students was online due to COVID. Also, I received a lot of emails with information about travel, housing, immigration, arrival, registration of courses, social gatherings for exchange students, online “get-ready”-seminars etc. Also, I callled them if I had a quick question before going. Once I arrived, I just went to the front desk.
arrival_comments: My overall experience was that they were very helpful! My home university was also helpful – but it was at times VERY difficult to get in contact with KU.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I would rate my stay at SFU 10/10. However, the overall rate was 8/10. The reason why is that it was stressful and difficult to plan during the COVID-pandemic (I was going just then the Omnicron-variant spread across the world). I was from time to time unsure of whenever I would be able to go. It takes a lot of time to plan everything – and I found it sometimes difficult to get the needed help from KU. But I would never choose to stay home just because there is a lot of planning. It is worth it all and you will forget all of it once you arrive!
registration_process: You will receive an email with information about applying for SFU. Here you will be asked to list 8 courses that you would like to take. I would recommend applying for housing when you do this. Later, my application was accepted, and I received my ‘Letter of Admission'. SFU rewelded which of the 8 courses I was able to attend. I would then apply for those courses and SFU would enroll all exchange students based on this. I had to change some courses before going because I could not get all of them approved by KU. SFU was very helpful doing so. I just send an email and the problem solved within a day.
registration_help: Webpage, emails from the international exchange department at SFU, online seminars, etc.
registration_success: 3 of 8 courses that I applied for at SFU was not created. I decided to apply for prior credit for 4 of the remaining courses from KU. KU approved only three of these, which is why I had to choose a new one.
registration_advice: Apply for courses that you find interesting at SFU. You can always change courses once you get there.
academics_comments: I would rate my stay at SFU 10/10. However, the overall rate was 8/10. The reason why is that it was stressful and difficult to plan during the COVID-pandemic (I was going just then the Omnicron-variant spread across the world). I was from time to time unsure of whenever I would be able to go. It takes a lot of time to plan everything – and I found it sometimes difficult to get the needed help from KU. But I would never choose to stay home just because there is a lot of planning. It is worth it all and you will forget all of it once you arrive!
course_level: The academic level was somewhat the same or easier - depending on the specific course. But the workload was much higher. You have to do a lot more through out the semester. On the other hand, the final exame does not count as much as in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: There is a lot more focus on participation. I had to do mandatory weekly quizzes - don't worry they were very easy. Also, I had to write papers in all courses before midterm and final exams. They focus a lot on this too.
courses_enrolled: HSCI 120 - Introduction to Human Sexuality and Sexual Behavior HSCI 206 - Health Economics HSCI 305 - The Canadian Health Care System HSCI 408 - Plagues, Poverty, and Pollutants - The Origins and Evolution of Public Health.
recommended_courses: I would defently recommend HSCI 120, HSCI 206 and HSCI 408. All the professors are great and the courses are interesting. Also, the workload, papers, midterms and final exams are manageable. HSCI 305 is interesting from a public health perspective but it is only and the workload is really heavy.
unexpected_costs: It is more expensive to live in Canada than I expected. I don't recall any unexpected costs from SFU. But I was supprised of how expensive it was to travel, shop, etc. Remember to apply for scholarships!
cost_comparison: It was less expensive to live on campus than expected.
activities_available: Fitness center, swimming pool, track, etc. They host a lot of social gatherings among students in the Convocation Mall. Also, there are plenty of studentclubs to join.
activities_recommended: Take advantage of the U-Pass (transportation card that you buy through SFU) and go around Vancouver. Go to Whistler and ski. If you like skiing and plan on doing it a lot: Buy a season pass to Whistler before going. They are sold out quickly in the late fall/early winter. Do not wait until upon arrival. Get some local friends and get their recommendations for traveling.
weekend_recommendations: Go watch NHL and explore nature. I went on a whale-watching tour in mid-April and saw orcas. It was so cool! Go to Lynn Canyon and hike. Eat at Granville. Take the ferry to Bowen Island and hike. Go to Vancouver Island.
culture_adjustment: It was easy. Canadians are really welcoming and helpful
socializing_tips: Live on campus and make friends with those you live with.
cultural_challenges: The local students are usually younger than exchange students. It was not a challenge but just a difference that I experienced.
culture_appreciated: Their welcoming, warm and helpful attitude.
top3_advice: 1) apply for housing on campus, 2) if possible: choose courses that give you Friday off (nice if you want to go on trips on the weekends), 3) apply for scholarships, 4) ENJOY!
other_useful_info: Don't be afraid of just sending an email or calling them when in doubt.
most_rewarding: Got to know a lot of kind and sweet people, while traveling in Canada and had an overall successful stay.
greatest_challenge: The planning before going - but don't be scared: It is all worth it!
other_comments: If you consider going on exchange - do it!

I wanted to study Indigenous literature and gain a further understanding of the relationship between Canadian settlers and the Indigenous peoples.
info_ease: it was fairly easy to find the information on the SFU canvas course called exchange 101. However, it was a lot of work and stress that due to the overlapping semesters was very stress-full.
arrival_assistance: Nothing really, everything was electronic due to the pandemic. The residence and housing staff mostly helped me.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You choose 8 courses that you want and then they check if you are eligible to take these classes. May classes has perquisites that makes it impossible to gain access to them if you are not a student at SFU. It was difficult to understand. Most of the course I applied for was not possible for me. However the staff was very helpful and suggested courses that matched my interests and it all worked out in the end.
registration_help: The SFU study aboard team lead by Eshani was available for correspondence via email
registration_success: 2 out of the three classes i took were on my initial list of classes that i applied for and the last one was suggested to me by a study aboard employee and i ended up being very happy with it.
registration_advice: Keep and open mind and don't be discouraged if the courses you want are not available to you. You can often find several courses that cover the same kind of topic. Be clear and firm in your correspondence if you need help in finding another course.
course_level: I was on the last semester of my BA and I took level 200 and 300 courses. The course material , workload and lectures seemed to be on the same level as I experience in my home-institution however my own academic level seemed to be a bit higher than most of my peers.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was very similar, however SFU had a bigger emphasis on providing and encouraging a creative approach to assignments. Their way grading and monitoring attendance is different from UCPH and created a quite stress-full studying environment.
courses_enrolled: ENGL360 Indigenous Literature ENGL355 Black Canadian Literature GSWS 230 'The Angry Woman' in Contemporary Media
recommended_courses: All of the above. Studying Indigenous literature provide an extensive knowledge about the the complicated and horrific history of the stolen and exploited indigenous land that we know as Canada. It furthermore is a class in which you can feel and learn about this conflict by interacting with your peers. Sophy McCall is a very good professor. Studying Black Canadian Literature with David Chiriandy has been an absolute privilege and I would recommended it to anyone who is even slightly interested in Black literature, diaspora and the transatlantic experience. In my gender studies class i learned feminist theory that is applicable in my everyday relations. We furthermore looked deeply on the intersectionality of feminism.
unexpected_costs: You spend a lot of money and exploring and being a tourist as well as a student.
cost_comparison: tourist experiences
activities_available: I don't know
activities_recommended: skiing, hiking, sailing.
weekend_recommendations: Vancouver island, ski resorts, Lynn creek valley, whale-tours ect
culture_adjustment: Quite easy when living on campus
socializing_tips: Smile at them and don't be scared to ask people if they want to hang. Canadians are quite welcoming.
cultural_challenges: The drinking and frat culture
culture_appreciated: The nature!!!!
top3_advice: Its is going to be so much more expensive that you think save up and enjoy!! You will be academically on a higher level that what you are at home, so do not stress. Soak it up it goes by so fast!
other_useful_info: if possible do 2 semesters ! one was too little for me. Right when you are settled in and you feel at home, it over...

crucial_aspects: It was important for me that I came to a country in which people would speak English as their first language. I chose Canada for this exact reason, and I have definitely benefited from being around native English speakers every day.
overall_comments: I honestly don't know how my exchange year could have been better. I have had the time of my life, met great people and have had classes with engaging professors and interesting topics. Overall, my study abroad experience has been fantastic and very insightful.
info_ease: It was fairly easy. The exchange office at SFU has been very helpful, so I haven't been in a situation where I couldn't find the information that I needed. People around me have also been very helpful. Secondly, we were added to a group on Canvas called SFU Exchange 101, wherein we could find plenty of information about being and exchange student at SFU and about the university in general.
arrival_assistance: Well, as I have written above, the exchange office has been a great source of help. And then because I lived in residence, the Residence and Housing office helped a lot as well.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I honestly don't know how my exchange year could have been better. I have had the time of my life, met great people and have had classes with engaging professors and interesting topics. Overall, my study abroad experience has been fantastic and very insightful.
registration_process: We had to enroll in courses in early July (for reference our semester started in early September), and then once we started here we had a period of 2 weeks in which we could drop and select courses if any spots were available. If spots were available, we could enroll in those courses we wanted.
registration_help: The exchange office did all the work for us. They enrolled us in the different courses and helped us drop and select new ones.
registration_success: Because I study something very specific in Denmark, I had none of the prerequisites to get more advanced courses. For example, I could only get psychology 100, even though I have had educational psychology back home. This wasn't enough for me to be able to get any courses in psychology that weren't either 100 or 102. That being said, the course has been very interesting and not too easy. I had made a list of 4 courses I wanted that were approved by KU, but when I came here, the courses were either full or I was not able to register for them, because I didn't meet the prerequisites. I ended up having 3 other courses than the ones I had been approved for, but the overall process has been quite easy.
registration_advice: Don't stress too much about courses beforehand. Get over here and see how the courses are, and then you can drop and enroll in new courses. If you don't meet the prerequisites, send an email to the professor and explain why you would like to be in that specific class, and maybe they will let you in the class anyways. I know some of my friends did this and it worked for them.
academics_comments: I honestly don't know how my exchange year could have been better. I have had the time of my life, met great people and have had classes with engaging professors and interesting topics. Overall, my study abroad experience has been fantastic and very insightful.
course_level: I have only had level 100 courses, but they haven't been a walk in the park at all, even though it has primarily been first-year courses. It has been a good mix of easy and more difficult content.
teaching_comparison: I have almost only had lectures, meaning I have been sitting in class and listening. I have enjoyed being able to sit in class and listen to professors who are very good at what they do and have a lot of knowledge in their respective areas. Furthermore, we have had weekly quizzes and assignments that we sometimes have done in class, so for me, it has been like going to a Danish high school actually. I have enjoyed this method of teaching a lot more than the one I am used to back home in Denmark.
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled in PSYC100 (Psychology), CMNS110 (Communication), HSCI160 (Global Health) and LING160 (Linguistics). It has been four very different courses, but of course, they are all part of "social science", which is why I have been able to take them. It was very insightful to have courses that have been so different because I feel like I've learned a lot in different areas.
recommended_courses: Take courses that you find interesting and make sure the workload is spread out. I only have one course with a final exam, and instead, I have been doing assignments throughout the semester, which have taken a lot of the pressure off.
unexpected_costs: I have gone out way more than I do back home, so alcohol has been an unexpected cost for me.
cost_comparison: The prices are very similar to the ones in Denmark when you add taxes (remember that, I always forget)
activities_available: We have access to the gym and some of the facilities like soccer fields. We have been to hockey games and American football games at school. Secondly, they have drop-in sports, which means you can come and join a volleyball game, or futsal or badminton etc. They have a schedule in which you can see what kinds of drop-in sports are available throughout the week.
activities_recommended: Go to the official games that the host university has! It's a fun thing to experience. Remember loads of clothes if you go to an American football game in the winter (it's so cold). Remember to take academic breaks, and do fun things throughout the week, so you don't get caught up in school so much.
weekend_recommendations: GO ON HIKES! There are so many amazing hikes in British Columbia, so when the weather allows it, go out and explore the nature! When it's raining, go out and do fun activities in Vancouver, they have a lot of indoor things to do like mini golfing, escape rooms etc. I have also gone on longer trips, like weekend trips to Toronto or Banff. I have really enjoyed that as well since the prices for flights aren't too expensive when you fly domestically.
culture_adjustment: Canadian culture isn't that different from the Danish, or at least Western culture, so I don't feel like it has been a big adjustment in that case. Canadians are very welcoming, so it hasn't been hard to talk with people. The toughest thing for me has definitely been the age difference! Most of the people from my dorm are 18 years, and I turned 24 throughout my stay. 6 years really does a lot, which also meant I have spent a lot of time with other exchange students because we were more alike in terms of age, and because we all had the same mindset toward our stay at SFU.
socializing_tips: Be friendly and open and speak English all the time, even though you hang out with people that speak Danish too. We have gotten many friends from speaking English in public spaces because people approach you because they understand you. You can quickly become a tight-knitted group if you speak your native language, so I would really recommend speaking English all the time (even though it might be a bit weird in the beginning)
cultural_challenges: As I wrote, the age has been a huge difference and then sarcasm. I am used to being ironic or sarcastic in Danish, but I haven't been that as much here. I find it difficult to be so when I speak a foreign language. Sometimes, I have also had trouble getting if someone else was being sarcastic because I can't detect it as well in English as I can in Danish. But it's a small thing that is quite easy to adapt to.
culture_appreciated: Canadians are so nice and polite. They are very friendly and talk with many different people without really knowing them. Many people have shown great interest in hearing about Danish culture and how we do things back home.
top3_advice: Bring hiking shoes Speak English all the time Say yes to all activities that are arranged
other_useful_info: Save up money! You spent a lot of money on trips etc., and you don't wish to sit them out because you can't afford them.
most_rewarding: All the amazing friendships I have gotten. I have met many people from different parts of the world, which is super beneficial in future situations.
greatest_challenge: If you are an introvert and prefer to have some time alone, it can be hard and challenging because you hang out with people all the time. And you don't want to say no to stuff, so you keep pushing yourself a bit more, which can make you super tired some days.

crucial_aspects: I choose Vancouver because of its easy access to nature and the fact that it is still a big city. Simon Fraser University takes good care of their exchange students, and due to its small size (compared to UBC and UofT) everyone knows each other which makes the exchange feel even better.
overall_comments: Had the best time of my live and met friends from all over the world. Hiked the entire fall with a lot of overnight hikes since the weather in Vancouver was super this fall, 20+ degrees until late October, and the we skiied in November and December.
info_ease: It was easy. The university has international student service which are very helpful and answers mails quick and you can also call them anytime.
arrival_assistance: I received a lot of information from SFU beforehand and also had a zoom call that SFU facilitated. Also the website and Instagram has a lot of information as well.
arrival_comments: I got my keys and found my room, very easy and a lot of staff there to help you. The first day is busy and can be overwhelming, but be open since it is easy to make friends.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Had the best time of my live and met friends from all over the world. Hiked the entire fall with a lot of overnight hikes since the weather in Vancouver was super this fall, 20+ degrees until late October, and the we skiied in November and December.
registration_process: First you list 10 courses, then you get verified to take them based on the courses you have taken at UCPH (pre-requsites), then you have to make your own schedule in terms of how many courses you are taking and overlaps, and then finally you have your final schedule.
registration_help: International Student Services are very helpful.
registration_success: I got all of the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Try to only take classes on tuesday, wednesday and thursday - then you have a long weekend every weekend, and you can easily go on trip. Personally I only had classes on wednesday and thursday and it was the best! Also avoid Surrey and take some course downtown and explore the city.
academics_comments: Had the best time of my live and met friends from all over the world. Hiked the entire fall with a lot of overnight hikes since the weather in Vancouver was super this fall, 20+ degrees until late October, and the we skiied in November and December.
course_level: I don't think the level was higher at all, but it was so different so I still learned a lot.
teaching_comparison: Much more like High School than Uni.
courses_enrolled: CMNS 452 - E100 Race and the Media CMNS 425 - Applied Communication for Social Issues CMNS 443 - D100 Comparative Asian Media Systems
recommended_courses: Race and Media was one of the best courses I have ever had, super interesting and great teachers (Dr. Nawal) Also Professor Laba in 425 was also great! Also check how your exams are, you can choose courses with only written exams and have a stress free exams period!
unexpected_costs: Do not buy a Sim Card over here!! too expensive. It is easier to get a Danish card with international data (I got mine from CBB), soooo much cheaper.
cost_comparison: Food for sure..
activities_available: Pools, soccer, dance, yoga, hikes, skiing - everything you can think about.
activities_recommended: I played a little soccer which was fun - but for sure go hiking! British Columbia is beautiful and you need to take advantage of that. Everyone wants to hike, so it is easier to find other likeminded people to hike with!
weekend_recommendations: Go to Joffery Lakes, Wedgemount lake, Whistler (both hikes and skiing), St. Marks Summit, Vancouver Island, Toronto - Canada has so much to offer.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it is not that far from Denmark - however they have a lot of homeless people which is very different from DK. However, they are mostly very nice and do no harm. Also saying thank you whenever you leave a bus.
socializing_tips: Be open and even though it may be hard in the beginning, you will find friends! Push yourself to be social and say yes to everything.
cultural_challenges: No not really, I love Canada after this exchange!
culture_appreciated: The nature and the nice people
top3_advice: Hiking Boots Backpack for day/overnight hikes Positive mindset and a winter jacket if you can fit it haha!
other_useful_info: SFU is great, and even though it is much smaller than UBC I have had the best real life college experience, where all of the exchange student know each other! E.g. my friend group with Danes, Austrialians, Sweedes, Norweigan and Dutch people met up with lots of others all the time fx to go ski in Whistler.
most_rewarding: The friendships and change of academic structure - and also the nature.
greatest_challenge: The first weeks meeting so many new people
other_comments: Enjoy! Vancouver is the best if you love nature and being outdoors and also SFU takes good care of their exchange students, so don't worry too much!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere I normally would not have the opportunity to go to, and I chose the west coast of Canada to experience the nature, especially skiing. I also wanted to go to an english speaking country, as I figured it would be easier to create relations. The ranking of the university was not as important to me as the kind of courses I could take.
info_ease: They had signs and volunteers to guide you, all you had to do was look confused
arrival_assistance: I got shown to the place where I could get my student card by one of the volunteers, and another volunteer told me how the canteen worked. You just have to ask the questions and they will help.
arrival_comments: I could have joined more welcome events than I did, but some of them seemed more directed at first years students rather than exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_help: The website is very thorough.
registration_success: I initially accidentally signed up for classes in the summer term instead of the fall term, but the team that mails with exchange students helped me a lot even though I exceeded a deadline because of that.

teaching_comparison: They don't really do oral exams. Whenever we had presentations in class, people read out loud from a script almost, which surprised me a lot. They do much more quizzes/assignments during the courses which count a certain percentage of your final grade.
courses_enrolled: Radiochemistry (nuclear science) Materials chemistry Special topics in analytical chemistry Cell signalling in development and diseases
recommended_courses: Special topics in analytical chemistry - more discussion based, current tendencies, you choose your own topic for presentation Cell signalling in development and diseases - really good teacher, very educational
unexpected_costs: Medical expenses, but most where covered by insurance

crucial_aspects: This was my first time back in Vancouver since I moved to Denmark when I was almost three years old. I had been dreaming about an opportunity to go back like this one for as long as I can remember. I didn't know anybody over there, which helped taking it like a "fresh start" and making my own connections.
info_ease: They have great exchange coordinators that are easily available, quick and very helpful. Once you get to campus, there are signs everywhere to find the main buildings like the front desk for housing or the dining commons, as well as flyers for upcoming activities during the introductory week.
arrival_assistance: Again, the exchange coordinators were a great help. There are a lot of volunteers scattered around that are there to help with anything. Worst case, just ask anyone, people are very open and easy to approach, so don't be scared.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The process is a little tedious in terms of gathering documents. But everything is well described during the exchange meeting at UCPH and on the mobility website. Once you are approved for the exchange, you get into contact with the exchange coordinators at SFU who will help guide you through their systems and give you all the information you need.
registration_help: The exchange coordinators at SFU are readily available by e-mail, just mind the time difference if you need a quick answer.
registration_success: I got most of the courses I wanted. I had to compromise a little because of some schedule conflicts and some prerequisites I didn't have, but other than that I was pretty satisfied.
registration_advice: There isn't much to worry about since as an exchange student, you are on the priority list for course enrollment. Having said that, I wouldn't wait too long to give them a list of the courses you're interested in taking. If there any problems or requirements you missed, the coordinators will let you know and ask for additional information if needed, so you don't have to worry much about all details.
course_level: I only had 300 level courses, so third year courses for students doing their Bsc.
teaching_comparison: They are very similar overall. The classes were a bit smaller, which helps making it a bit more personal between the students and professors.
courses_enrolled: MATH 340 Algebra II: Rings and Fields MATH 322 Complex Variables (or Introduction to Complex Analysis as the professor liked to call it) PHYS 384 Methods of Theoretical Physics I NUSC 341 Introduction to Radiochemistry
recommended_courses: I enjoyed Complex Variables, as it was a nice continuation to Analysis 0 and 1 I took at UCPH. It was definitely an "introduction" to complex analysis, as it wasn't as hard as An0 and An1.
unexpected_costs: You could say the trips I went on could be a part of that category. I put 1500 DKK in other fees as an average per month on trips I participated in over the course of my exchange. Hawaii was not that cheap, but I would take it into account for that average.
cost_comparison: I feel like the cost of living in Vancouver is a little bit cheaper that it is in Copenhagen, or that the prices were pretty much the same.
activities_available: They have pretty much anything you could think of, from hiking to DnD to volunteering.
activities_recommended: I would recommend the hiking club, which is an easy way to meet new people and to go on hikes (since apparently that's what people look forward to the most going to Vancouver). I got to play basketball, squash, tennis, badminton, and even got to boulder.
weekend_recommendations: Do most of the hikes early in the semester for the best weather possible. There are a bunch of recommended places all over the internet, I would suggest them all honestly. Go to Whistler at least once, on or off skiing season. Visit Gas Town, Stanley Park, Granville Island, Kitsilano etc. Now, you won't get a whole week of holidays like at UCPH, but some days off for like Thanksgiving for example. That's where you should plan big trips like Vancouver Island or Whistler. But nothing stops you from going a bit crazier stuff like Banff, Yellowknife, San Francisco, Hawaii for more than a few days, like a week (but you didn't hear that from me).
culture_adjustment: There is nothing culturally that stands out of the ordinary coming from a European. Just be ready for some small talk with anyone, and thank the bus driver.
socializing_tips: I'll be honest, it is easier to make friends with other exchange students that it is with local students. Local students will mostly be studying, because that is what they're there to do. I'm not saying it is impossible and that they're terrible people, just that they will be less open to spontaneity compared to other students on exchange, because they need to study, and they most likely don't have the money anyway. Locals are very nice and helpful, you can always find them in common areas, the library or in the dining commons.
cultural_challenges: It's a small adjustment but tipping and taxes would throw me off more often than not. If you want a culturally rich experience during your exchange, make friends with other exchange students. My most eye-opening cultural exchange was when I went to Yellowknife with some new friends from East-Asia.
culture_appreciated: Canadians live up to the kind stereotype. They are very open and well-intended people.
top3_advice: I wouldn't consider myself as an outgoing and talkative person, I am more of the awkward type. But I am barely exaggerating when I say that I greeted everybody I crossed paths with while I was in Vancouver. There is a very freeing sentiment when you first arrive in a new place all on your own, which helps kind of reinventing yourself (not in a bad way). I would embrace that feeling, because I'm sure everyone there thinks the same. This might come off as bad advice but, I would put studying to the side a little, and try to experience as much as possible. Say yes to every opportunity that arises (which most likely will come from the dining commons). I must have spent a maximum of 3 weekends staying on campus, which goes to show that there is a lot of stuff to do and that will pop up out of the blue.
other_useful_info: I would just recommend you do your research in due time before applying for SFU, and if do go there, before every trip that you plan on doing.
most_rewarding: It's cliché but making friends. I was headed into that exchange with the mindset of a student that was going to focus during lectures and on getting good grades. But right off the bat I met some interesting and exciting people and that mindset just disappeared. I was definitely not planning on meeting as many people as I have and go on as many trips as I did, but now I can say I went to Hawaii with lifelong friends from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: I don't think there was anything particularly challenging during my exchange. Ironically maybe just getting myself to study at least a little bit for the exams.
other_comments: I wholeheartedly encourage anyone to go on exchange, because this was wiiild to say the least. If you're at least considering it I wouldn't think twice just go !

crucial_aspects: I chose a place that would be most beneficial for me in regards to my study. Keeping my studies in mind, I thought about what I wanted to gain from my exchange, would it be work-wise, language-wise, or other aspects, and then choose accordingly.
overall_comments: I would rate the overall study abroad experience between 8-9. I learned a lot from my stay, but due to covid-19 implications, some opportunities were limited such as campus life. Other than that I am happy I studied abroad.
info_ease: Depending on what you need to know, the information is easy to find. The embassy of the desired country typically has a checklist for important notices to know before leaving, and in my case, our host university sent an email with further instructions. I would advise always double-checking before leaving, so nothing comes as a shock.
arrival_assistance: I got assistance from the host university's OIA (Office of International Affairs) and they helped me with any trouble during my whole stay. I also received assistance from the airport when leaving the airport and departing from it.
arrival_comments: The host University did a satisfactory job with the orientation and assistance for students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I would rate the overall study abroad experience between 8-9. I learned a lot from my stay, but due to covid-19 implications, some opportunities were limited such as campus life. Other than that I am happy I studied abroad.
registration_process: You receive an email from the OIA about when the online course registration will be held. In this time period, you are able to register for courses on a first-come-first-served basis, so it is best to start as soon as possible if you want specific courses. The course registration in itself was easy, you follow the link sent to you in the mail, and you press select the desired course on the course list then you are all settled. If the course is full you cannot select it. The registration process was held two times, the second wave was for those who missed the time period, but the courses available would be limited. You can also contact the professor of the desired course if you can join, but you would get approval from the OIA at first.
registration_help: It is possible to contact the OIA for questions.
registration_success: I got what I wanted.
registration_advice: Be sure to check out the course descriptions before the registration process, so you know what courses you want. As the registration is on a first-come-first-served basis, it will be wise for you to add courses as early as the registration period begins. Additionally, be sure to check the timezone, so you don't mix up the time.
academics_comments: I would rate the overall study abroad experience between 8-9. I learned a lot from my stay, but due to covid-19 implications, some opportunities were limited such as campus life. Other than that I am happy I studied abroad.
course_level: My language program was fitted to accommodate my level, so I would improve. You take the placement test, and you strive to surpass it so you can study next level when you're done. The academic courses at the university were also great, it was reflective and fit the expectations.
teaching_comparison: Language program was very different and it was difficult at first to adapt, but once you get used to it, it was a good style flow. It was intense, but you improve a lot. The other course was similar to that of UCPH with a professor teaching and students taking notes and studying at home. As it was online, the teaching style was that of UCPH with zoom and PowerPoint with active debates or questions.
courses_enrolled: PSYCHOLOGY OF RELIGION and Korean Language for Academic Purposes (KAP200)
recommended_courses: I would recommend Psychology of Religion and KAP200 for future exchange students as they're very giving courses for academic purposes and insight. Psychology of Religion requires a philosophical approach, but it is available for all levels, and you don't need to be a psychology or religion major to follow it. The course highlights comprehensive thinking and debunking the fundamental problem with academic research focuses. The KAP200 is a very giving course if you want to improve your language skills with intense study. The course itself is intense and time-consuming, but time flies really fast and you get surprised with how much you've accomplished on a little time.
unexpected_costs: I did not realise I had nothing at the room upon arrival, so I had to buy blankets, pillows etc. Furthermore, as I had trouble with my SIMCARD not being able to call Denmark, I had to use my own SIMCARD and pay a lot. I would advise to get a simcard before leaving or make sure to get one on the day of arrival.
cost_comparison: Books were very cheap. One school-book was almost the same as two at home. Eating out were also on the cheaper side as you most times get side dishes for free, so I ate out a lot. Getting a transportation card were convenient, and compared to Denmark way cheaper.
activities_available: Buddy-group. You can sign up to get a buddy, and you can experience things together while language exchanging. HUG (another buddy organisation) prepare for social activities if you sign up for the facebook group.
activities_recommended: Going hiking or experiencing temples! It is refreshing and beautiful to experience nature and culture on another level than reading it. I would recommend going to the less famous ones and visiting small coffee shops as the locals are very welcoming.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend visiting the war museum, which has a lot of history and stories to tell. The entrance is free and you walk through a time-period from the first wars in Korea to the Korean War etc. At the museum they have different 'departments' with themes, so it is worth a visit.
culture_adjustment: At first a bit challenging, but once you get used to it, it is alright. The food is delicious and if you find it difficult to communicate, you can use body language or just point with your fingers on the menu etc. You pick up on the local culture fast and you don't have to be afraid to make mistakes, as they will help you.
socializing_tips: Be open and straightforward. A lot of people are shy to talk, but if you ask them for help or guidance, they will do a lot to help you. People often sat together outside the campus' convenience store, so that is a good place to start if you are shy.
cultural_challenges: When eating out, you often have to call for the waiter to come instead of waiting as we do at home. In a lot of places you call out 'here' or 'excuse me' to let them know you are prepared to order, want more etc. as the waiters will help attend other customers or kitchen instead of waiting for you.
culture_appreciated: If they see you struggle with something, they try to help you. I experienced a lot of kindness and strangers were curious and wanted to talk with me if the context allowed them to. I found it nice to talk with strangers and ask them for tips or recommendations.
top3_advice: Remember to take breaks, avoid talking in your native language or English even if its difficult, and join activities made by the university or its students. It is easy to be tempted to switch to english when you are out with new friends or when ordering etc, but you learn a lot from experience. If you cannot remember a word, try to describe it (with body language even) or guess it, the locals will either ask you or try to help you. As the study process is different from home and can feel heavy, it is important to take breaks and enjoy your time. Maybe try to study with some fellow classmates.
other_useful_info: I don't think so.
most_rewarding: Experiencing the culture and trying new things while learning. I tried not to let my (sometimes) limited language stop me from being curious and tried to keep talking, asking questions, and expressing what I felt, which meant I got to talk to a lot of different people with different purposes.
greatest_challenge: Not preparing enough. I was very late in regards to making plans, buying SIMCARDS, etc. so it was a hectic first month for me to find out what I needed in a new country I had never been in before.
other_comments: Going on an exchange does not only benefit you academically but also physically and socially. You learn a lot about culture and experience the language, culture, people, and student life on another level than what you read about. As cliche as it sounds, you grow a lot in character as you have to adapt to another lifestyle than the one you are used to. I would recommend studying abroad to improve a lot and to see the world from another perspective than from home.

crucial_aspects: Opportunities for Korean language learning
info_ease: Sogang provided a lot of info, and it was easy to prepare most information from home before arriving
arrival_assistance: No specific assistance other than information via email
arrival_comments: It was clear who to contact in different instances and the orientation days were helpful
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: They sent information beforehand and your login information that you need to register
registration_help: Emails beforehand
registration_success: I got the class I wanted :) but you have to be super fast
registration_advice: Consider the time difference if you do the registration from Denmark. It might be in the night like 4 am. And check the course catalogues from the year before to prepare for which classes you want. If you're going in Fall semester I would recommend checking the last Fall semester for classes, not Spring semester as Spring and Fall classes often differ. When you do the registration, its quick to type in the class course CODE instead of the title of the class.
course_level: I only took one course apart from the Language Program so I only have one reference of the academic level but it was a bit easier than I thought. But I think I feared a very high level so I thought it was appropriate!
