cultural_challenges: The school was really not supposed to be a fun place to be. No couches to sit on, no bars.
culture_appreciated: The professionalism of the teachers, the ambition of some of the courses.
top3_advice: Practice your speaking and listening skills as much as you, do not worry about reading and writing. Make a chat group with the international students, you can help each other. Be careful with choosing courses in the 3rd year since they can be difficult, but do it if you really want to learn something, the courses in the 1st year are ridiculously easy, and prepare yourself well for the exams.
other_useful_info: You can ask the other students for notes, they are often very willing to give them to international students.
most_rewarding: The experience of being in a French school was super interesting.
greatest_challenge: Understanding and speaking in French. You do not have to say anything in classes, you can easily escape it, but it is very important to sit in front row and listen well, not all teachers speak clearly.

crucial_aspects: Several. First of all I wanted to try going abroad in order to try a different way of studying than what we do in Copenhagen. I wanted to learn a third language, and already had some proficiency in french, and I then chose Paris, and Sorbonne in particular, because of its strong philosophical (especially phenomenological) tradition.
info_ease: Not too bad, but not easy. I had received a specific date and time where I had to show up at the international relations office in Sorbonne, which was not easy to find, as the place is a maze.
arrival_assistance: The arrival consisted of finding the international relations office to get my proof of attendance stamped, and I didn't receive too much information regarding the studies or the exchange in general.
arrival_comments: One thing that I think was missing that would have made everything easier was an Erasmus introductary week or day or something, so that you could meet the other students from your field. There was one organization, Parismus, that organized parties and events, but I missed meeting the Erasmus students from philosophy as it would have made everything easier regarding information and organization. Luckily I had inscribed in a two weeks language course where I met two people who took some philosophy courses, with whom I could vent the confusion that arose once in a while.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had beforehand decided on a number of courses when I made my learning agreement.In the first week of courses it's possible to go to different lectures as it's possible to change your inscription after a week. In order to properly inscribe in the courses at the philosophy institute I went to the office of the secretary and confirmed the courses I wanted to take.
registration_help: The secretariat was helpful when you went there physically, but France is generally very bureaucratic, and not very digitalized, so a lot of times you have to go somewhere physically to talk with somebody and then they might tell you that you have to talk with somebody else, but it always works out in the end.
registration_advice: Try some different courses before making the final choice. Once you inscribe for good after the first week or two, you cannot change your inscriptions and exams. Go talk with the secretary if in doubt.
course_level: The courses where difficult for several reasons. I was not fluent in french when I got there, and it took some time to get used to having courses in french, in the beginning I definetely didn't understand everything, which made it a lot harder. But it seemed to me that the level was also higher than in Copenhagen, maybe because the style of philosophy was a bit different, but also because the things discussed were sometimes hard to grasp.
teaching_comparison: I think it is safe to say that everything about Sorbonne is just more traditional, including the lectures. There is not so much focus on the pedagogical side of lecturing, and the lectures were more 1-way communication than in Copenhagen, also because there was often 100+ people at lectures. They do however also have TD (Travail dirigé) which is more like the seminars we have at UCPH, where the idea is that everyone should work with the topic in smaller groups. This didn't work so well, as it often became a lecture with fewer people present. That said I think there was something very positive about this more traditional lecture style. The professors seemed to be very engaged in what they were talking about, as it was always something they themselves found very interesting and were working on at the time. Another huge difference from Copenhagen was the fact that they don't have a proper syllabus, only recommended readings which are always books, and more classical books usually. What was recommended to read for a specific course usually span the whole history of philosophy (unless it was a specific history course), and the teachers also included a lot of different authors for the same topic. For example I had a course in metaphysics called 'être et amour' which was mostly about love, where the CM (lecture) professor was mainly going through Plato and Plotin, but also Hegel and Stein, whereas the TD with another professor only went through more recent phenomenological litterature, Husserl, Levinas, and Jean-Luc Marion. The main advantage of this style of teaching was that you could read what you found interesting, and always had the privilege to be reading proper books, and no research papers, which was nice for a change.
courses_enrolled: Histoire de la philosophie moderne - La certitude comme essence de la vérité Métaphysique - être et amour Philosophie de l'art - Arts et pouvoirs Option - La nature Histoire de la philosophie moderne - Critique de la raison pure Expression écrite - C1 Philosophie générale - L'idée du monde
recommended_courses: I would definetely recommend the metaphysics course, it was super interesting and really broad in it's scope (being and love) while also being really detailed as the teacher in the CM used 5 weeks to describe love as descibed in Plato. And you also get to read some phenomenology if you take the TD with M. Fournier (there are several seminars with different teachers and different readings). I also found philosophy of art very interesting, especially because we don't have anything like it in Copenhagen, but at Sorbonne they even have a masters just for philosophy of art. The modern philsophy course I had was very focused on Descartes, which was interesting but also maybe a bit too much Descartes, so unless you really love Descartes, I might recommend to steer out of it, but I personally liked it at times. The professor (M. Carraud) is a super old guy which made his lectures a bit slow, and quite boring, as he would often just quote things in latin or german for 5 min and then use 10 min on translating them and talking about some very niche things. But he's also head of the Descartes research center at Sorbonne, so if you want to learn about Descartes, he's definetely interesting.
unexpected_costs: I had some problems with the phone companies there. I thought I could just use my danish number as it's free in the EU, but it turned out that it was only free for 4 months, so I had to get a french number for the last two. So a good idea is to check whether the same applies for you, or just get a subscription that you can cancel anytime, my mistake was to buy prepaid SIM-cards and try to fill them up which didn't work.
cost_comparison: Supermarket prices are around the same, but it's cheaper to go to farmer's markets in weekends than going to the supermarket. The bakeries are super cheap (baguette/tradition = 1,2 eur). It's more expensive to drink beer (but not wine) and to eat kebab (but the libanese ones are delicious). Most museums are free if you're a student and/or under 26!
activities_available: There was a sports programme, but I wasn't enrolled. I don't believe that there was a lot of other things happening, they usually don't do so much at the university, but go out to other places and do stuff.
activities_recommended: Museums, cafés. Also I did a language course in the beginning of the semester (offered by Sorbonne) which was where I got some friends, except from the ones from my house.
weekend_recommendations: Museums, reading, go to Bois de Vincennes (I never made it, but heard it was nice). Paris is such a big city, just go to different arrondissements.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. I was a bit confused as to what to eat in the beginning, as they don't have all the same things in the supermarkets, but that was a minor adjustment.
socializing_tips: Good luck, I found it hard, but if you're really good at talking with people, or find someone who wants to speak english then go for it. My conversations with other students where limited to asking about administrative things like how the exams work, or how to write assignments.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: Food especially farmer's markets. The art museums of Paris. The cafés and second hand book stores.
top3_advice: Practice french beforehand - the better you are at french the easier it will be to understand the professors, administration, official emails and so on. Don't stress too much about the administrative things, but be vigilant as they also do make mistakes (had a friend who weren't on the mailing list of the adminstration, so I had to forward all the mail to her. She even asked to be put on but never got...) Get housing in advance.
other_useful_info: I think I mentioned quite a lot about the differences in administrating the courses, but I think it's important to remember that the learning agreement isn't set in stone, it can be changed when you get there and find out that you would have liked some other courses. Bachelor is called 'licence' in french, and if you're going on exchange on the licence, it is possible to get master courses (even though it may say on a website that it's not), but it might depend on the coordinator in Cophenhagen whether you're allowed to take them or not. The master courses might be a little more chill from what I heard. In general the courses are quite tough and I was honestly scared that I wouldn't pass all of them. The grading system is very different, it goes from 0-20 and you need at least a 10 to pass. The level of work needed to get a 10 is definetely higher that what I would say you would need to get 02 in DK. So expect to get "low" grades. That said, they are more lax with Erasmus students, and don't judge you too hard for making grammar mistakes in the assignments, or for using too simple language. The assignments you make during the year also count towards the final grade, in general I think 50% of the final grade is the exam and 50% is the work you make during the year, so it's definetely better not to slack on those assignments.
most_rewarding: Noticing how I got better at understanding the teachers and the books I were reading each week. And in the end being able to write 4-hour exams in hand that weren't that bad. It was also very rewarding to get a new perspective on philosophy and teaching by studying in Paris. It also gave me a renewed confidence in philosophy, as philosophy in Paris is a quite prestigious study, and the professors at the university believe in it 100%, whereas there is a tendency in DK that we need learn how to justify the fact that we study philosophy. Overall it was a boost to my philosophy studies.
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to a very different lifestyle without my usual friends and connections. Being content with living a bit more solitary. Writing assignments in french always took me 6-8 hours for a 2-3 pages assignment, as I struggled a lot with using the right expressions. It's a good idea to find someone better at french that can give you some feedback on writing !
other_comments: Good luck and have fun ! (In french they always make a space between a sentence and the exclamation or question mark ! Super weird right ?) You're welcome to contact me if you decide to go and have questions !

crucial_aspects: My grandmother was French, a student of Sorbonne and lived in Paris. Thus, I had the opportunity to come and visit her in Paris throughout my childhood every summer. However, after her death in 2012 I felt as if I had lost the strong connection, I had to my grandmother's city which is why I was so thrilled to have the opportunity to go back and study at the very same faculty that my grandmother studied English at many years ago. Besides I was very motivated to improve my French, and I knew my grandmother wanted me to be able to speak it well. Therefore, an Erasmus exchange at Sorbonne was the perfect choice for me.
info_ease: Very difficult The communication between KU Sorbonne seemed to be very poor as Sorbonne was sure that I and my fellow KU students at Sorbonne did not belong to the Erasmus programme since we were part of the 4EU+. Maybe this could explain that we were not fully inscribed before after the semester had started.
arrival_assistance: Quite poor assistance
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: First you do the régistration administrative" (general registration) "registration pédagogique" (inscription to the specific courses). The first is done at a meeting which you are invited to attend through email. The latter is a most difficult process where you have to write to all the specific professors and ask to then if they will inscribe you to their classes. It is very difficult to get an overview of the different classes as they are in many different folders and documents.
registration_help: Very little thorugh email or phone. It is not possible to get in touch with the administration between july and september because they will be on vacation.
registration_success: Not successful. I had hoped I could have taken classes at Panthéon Sorbonne since I am a student of political science in Denmark however for some reason I was inscribed to Faculté des Lettres which is more humanistic. I tried to contact Sorbonne to see if I could take classes at Panthéon even though I was inscribed to a different faculty, but I could not get through before it was too late because the administration was on vacation.
registration_advice: Find other students from KU and work together. It will be difficult so be prepared for that.
course_level: they vere on a very high level though they often lacked any visual presentation or itneractivity
teaching_comparison: The dissemination was certainly much poorer at Sorbonne than at KU however the classes were on a much higher level as I spent considerably more time with professors at Sorbonne than at KU.
courses_enrolled: Philosophie de la Politique. Programmation du Python. Linguistique et phonétique Française. Sociologie des inégalités. Sociologie des migrations. Sociologie du droit. Sociologie du science et environnement.
recommended_courses: I would like to recommend the very exiting course: Sociologie des inégalites. The teacher used PowerPoint. Also I would like to recommend philosophie de la politque. The classes were on a very high level though the dissemination were poor. The lectures by the famous professor Tavoillot where excellent and they had visual presentations.
cost_comparison: Books. Students of Sorbonne are in general not required to purchase any books much unlike KU where students are forced to use large amounts on books each semester.
activities_available: Man y kinds of students clubs.
activities_recommended: Parismus and students clubs
weekend_recommendations: Musée du Quai Branly - a breath-taking collection of aboriginal arts from around the world.
culture_adjustment: medium
socializing_tips: Join Parismus or other student clubs
cultural_challenges: The beurocracy and the relation between techer and students
culture_appreciated: the language, the food, arts as well as the intellectual culture.
top3_advice: Find other studetns from KU who are going to Sorbonne. Seek out students who have already done. Be prepared that it is going to be very difficult.
other_useful_info: You can get free food as a student at: https://mie.paris.fr/aide-alimentaire/
most_rewarding: The academic and linguistic abilities I acquired as well as the people I met.
greatest_challenge: The inscription and administration. Both Ku and Sorbonne where difficult to work with.

crucial_aspects: 1. That it was a French speaking country as i really want to be more fluent in the language. 2. That it was located in EU: partially due to corona (it was easier to get home and in general to travel back and forth) but also because I wanted to have friends and family from Denmark visiting.
overall_comments: All the administration in France is really bad and a therefore a bit stressfull - which is why i only gave it 9 starts.
info_ease: Not easy at all! I tried 6 months before i came to check everything and get everything fixed. But i ended up having none of the courses i wanted and when i asked my Erasmus coordinater at my home university, she was not even sure what kind of courses i was allowed to take.
arrival_assistance: I got a welcome bag with very nice stuff! and i really appreciate that. But everything else i had to figure out. I came to Paris 3 weeks before the courses started because i couldn't find informations anywhere! and the courses i had found in advance started the first week of Jan. Since i didn't get an answer regardin which courses i was allowed to i didn't get information regarding where any of the lectures took place.
arrival_comments: The administration is not so good in France
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: All the administration in France is really bad and a therefore a bit stressfull - which is why i only gave it 9 starts.
registration_process: i had to write to my Erasmus coordinator - who did not always reply. sometimes 2 months past!
registration_help: only the Erasmus coordinator.
registration_success: not Successfull - i didn't get any of the courses i wanted and I only got 12 ECTS out of 30 which was relevant for my education.
registration_advice: Be aware, that you will need to take courses in French if you are a master student on the 1 st year or under. else the courses are very very limited (or almost non-exsisting)
academics_comments: All the administration in France is really bad and a therefore a bit stressfull - which is why i only gave it 9 starts.
course_level: In France, the master is devided into 2 parts (M1 and M2). The M1 is a bit under the level in Denmark (at least at the university i took courses (paris physics master)). for me it was good, as i didn't study physics at my bachelor. Other students might find it too easy. Maybe the courses at Sorbonne is a bit more advanced (but they are in French).
teaching_comparison: Some of the teachers were very good and especially my supervisors in my internship! It's the same style as in Denmark - you have a lecture - then you have some reading material and then you have some exercises.
courses_enrolled: Advanced Quantum Mechanics 2 (3 ECTS), Atomic and molecular physics (6 ECTS), Localized spins in solids (3ECTS), French course (3ECTS), Condensed matter physics (6ECTS), Internship (9ECTS)
recommended_courses: almost all the masters in France have an internship in the 2. semester - so that is mandatory if your home University requires at least 30 ECTS. then i would recommend Advanced quantum mechanics 2 as the teacher was fantastic - you learn about group theory and the dirac equation. Condensed matter physics was also okay, but it does not really cover magnetism which i would have loved.
unexpected_costs: Sometimes it cost money to get a bank account - there are a lot of banks - some of them even give you money to be in the bank. However, transfering all your money to your french bank account is around 350 dkk. I would recommend you to use Revolut or something similar.
cost_comparison: The food is less expensive in restaurants in France compared to denmark. Buying food in the supermarkets are more expensive than buying food in the streetmarkets. There is a canteen for students called (Crous) - it's located all around Paris - where you get 3 courses for 3.3 Euro. It's much less than if you should make your own food.
activities_available: All kinds! - Badminton, yoga, swimming etc. and also language course is free at Sorbonne if you are a student.
activities_recommended: sport-activities in order to get native french-speaking friends.
weekend_recommendations: Go to other cities than Paris - Normandie (étretat), fontainebleau etc.
culture_adjustment: very easy
socializing_tips: go to sport activities! there are only french people
cultural_challenges: Many french people (even young people) do not speak french!
culture_appreciated: The food and the beautiful architecture
top3_advice: Take all the courses in French. - the courses in english are not so good.
other_useful_info: You can be very good at French without people understand what you are saying. French people are a bit picky with how you pronounce the things. The administration is not so good, but hang in! you will figure it out in the end even though it takes many many hours!
most_rewarding: To get a lot of new friends from all around the world. To be able to listen to french and understand very well.
greatest_challenge: The language!

crucial_aspects: I always wanted to study in France, since I learned French in my gap year. I had a better chance to be accepted in Sorbonne, since there were more people who could go there from UCPH. I also wanted to challenge myself and speak/live and study in French. Sorbonne University also had a great reputation in France, so looking for a job in France in the future, it would look good on my CV. A lot of my professors have written acknowledged books/papers and writes articles in the French press, which was reassuring, that I made the right choice with the academic standards the history program has to offer.
overall_comments: Some students occupied the university in April, so some weeks were on Zoom. This worked well, just a bit of a shame to not have the 'full' experience there. In total, I had two professors during the semester, who only did Zoom university. I think the experience is what you make it - they had Erasmus-parties, but people who study their bachelor (license) in France are mostly 18-21 years old. They had other activities and trips you could choose as well as an international student (catered to first comers in Paris)
info_ease: The information was there - it just came late and it was hard to find. Search for 'Coordinateurs/ Coordinatrices pédagogiques' and there will be a pdf-file and other documents to read. When choosing courses, you need to have at least 50% of your courses at your UFR (department). So, you can't study philosophy, art, history, literature, etc at the same time. What I would advice you to do is to choose 1 UFR to limit the administrative problems that you WILL fase. I had 6 courses (30 ECTS) in the History department (must have at least 2 different time-periodes).
arrival_assistance: I got an email saying where I should go to sign the arrival paper. There was an Erasmus-student welcoming team to greet us and tell us about their activities too. I also got helps from other international students.
arrival_comments: Never expect to get an answer for an email. Always try to find a place where you can meet the actual people. In the first few weeks, there was 1 weekly time slot to have a face to face conversation about your issue. I got the email for where I should go in January. No information before that.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Some students occupied the university in April, so some weeks were on Zoom. This worked well, just a bit of a shame to not have the 'full' experience there. In total, I had two professors during the semester, who only did Zoom university. I think the experience is what you make it - they had Erasmus-parties, but people who study their bachelor (license) in France are mostly 18-21 years old. They had other activities and trips you could choose as well as an international student (catered to first comers in Paris)
registration_process: You go to the Erasmus-office and get signed 'proof of arrival' or at least just to get your student card. Then you sign a paper within the first week or two of all the courses you have chosen. You chose the courses WHEN you are there mostly. You need to talk to the teacher and often write your name on a list to be sure that you have registered for the class. For some courses, there are too many students, and Erasmus-students can't reserve them online (like the French). When you have chosen them, you need to write them with the course number, ECTS points, name of the teachers and then get a signature from the head of the UFR (again - you can either arrange a meeting or show up on the 1 time a week they are open for students). Then you are set. The most important thing is to get your name on the list of the classes called the TD, which is the 'practical' class.
registration_help: There was a pdf file on the site of the UFR.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I wanted - but I also knew I could only choose once I was there, so I didn't set my self up for anything specific.
registration_advice: Be patience. You might need to hand in a new OLA and a new 'forhåndgodkendelse' - it will take time, but you will succeed if you are persistent. Please note you will not receive your Erasmus-scholarship before this is settled.
academics_comments: Some students occupied the university in April, so some weeks were on Zoom. This worked well, just a bit of a shame to not have the 'full' experience there. In total, I had two professors during the semester, who only did Zoom university. I think the experience is what you make it - they had Erasmus-parties, but people who study their bachelor (license) in France are mostly 18-21 years old. They had other activities and trips you could choose as well as an international student (catered to first comers in Paris)
course_level: I did not find it to be too hard or too easy, yet I found the level of French to be hard in some classes. You will succeed if you take notes and prepare for the classes and mostly just focus on your own presentation or assignment.
teaching_comparison: There was no individual research projects, I only had 2 group projects. You work mostly by yourself. You sit and write notes and it's not the same 'relax' atmosphere as at UCPH. You can ask to tape the teacher so that you can listen to it again. Most other students would also happily send you notes, since it's pretty hard to listen (and understand) and write proper notes. There are many deadlines (presentations, assignments, group assignment). At University of Copenhagen you mostly need to do 1-2 deadlines pr. semester, where I had 12 different in the span of 3 months. This can be 20-30 minute PP or 8-10 pages papers. Every course also have a Devoir Sur table (DST) - which is a 2-hour test you must do at the university. Some teachers know your level of French isn't the same, so they won't count it in your final note (Controle Continue). They also check if you are present at the University. You can only be absent 3 times (pr. class) without any reasoning - you need a medical note afterwards.
courses_enrolled: 1. Histoire des mondes germaniques: L'Allemagne à l'heure des empires 1806-1989 2. Histoire de la construction européenne 3. 1914-1918 et sa mémoire. Approche sociale et culturelle 4. La consommation de masse au XXe siècle 5. Histoire de l'extrême droite en France 6. Histoire de la démographie et de la famille en France
recommended_courses: Histoire de la démographie et de la famille en France - really interesting perspective on French family construction. The teacher was also very nice and welcoming.
unexpected_costs: I have no idea how much money I spend on food and personal belongings. This is very much up to the individual. You can find hot student-meals for 3-4€ at Crous, you can cook at home, but you can also expect to use 15-50€ when you go to a restaurant.
cost_comparison: I don't think there is a major difference in the life at Copenhagen and Paris - if you need to find student bars/offers you will, but if you want to go somewhere trendy/hipster then it cost more. It's a personal choice. The housing insurance was inexpensive - use the ADH - assurances etudiants . I paid the same amount for 6 months as I do for 1 month in CPH.
activities_available: They did some tours around the city, they had Erasmus-parties and they had some trips you could pay for. There are also other organisations outside of Sorbonne that does this.
activities_recommended: It's great to at least go to the Erasmus-parties once to see if you like the atmosphere. I would recommend the friday bar at Frederikskirken, where they have different activities - often with beers and food. There are many other young Danes that go there to find a network in Paris.
weekend_recommendations: Use your student ID to go for free at the museum. Do picnics in the parks and enjoy the city slow paced. Also try to get the SNCF Carte Avantage Jeune so that you can buy train tickets with a big discount and explore more of France. With the Paris metro card, you can still explore a lot of the smaller villages around Paris for free. Flixbus is also recommended.
culture_adjustment: It was frustrating at first with the administration, but once you have just realized that it's inefficient, you will take it more casual - this goes for housing, university etc. You also need to be very formal with the teachers or strangers you meet.
socializing_tips: Again - they are much younger than the students from UCPH, so it's up to you if you feel like it. They are nice and helpful. Many of them are very motivated and you could get a lot of inspiration from their career steps, since French students are very much into internships and being proactive with their career moves even at a young age. Also, go to student events outside of Sorbonne, there you will find international or French students as well.
cultural_challenges: Administration. The formal tone. The fact that you cannot discuss with your teacher or co-students. There is no individual research in the 'real world', it's very much just sources in books etc.
culture_appreciated: I really enjoyed that you could talk French, sit at bars, visit museums and enjoy the Parisian life as a local student - much easier to meet people when you feel confident in French. I love the fact that you could explore multiple neighborhoods and actually have time to see more than the Louvre, Eiffel Tower and Montmartre.
top3_advice: 1. Be patience - it will be worth it - but the administration is a nightmare and you just have to do it. 2. Be prepared for many deadlines - it's going to be intense. 3. Never expect to get an answer on email, always go directly to meet them.
other_useful_info: Talk to other exchange students to find help, you are all in it together. I would also recommend to stay with one UFR.
most_rewarding: It was very rewarding to study at one of the top universities (in humanities) in France and in French. Your French level will improve. I also found it to be such a unique experience to have the possibility to live in Paris 'with a purpose' and can put it on your CV. You will meet many other international students and have so many new memories with your friends in Paris.
greatest_challenge: The language in some of my courses. It was tough, but you just have to tape it or do some extra research on the topic.
other_comments: It's not easy to go on exchange, there is a lot of paperwork, but it has been one of the best parts of my bachelor despite that. Paris is what you make it - go out and make friends in the city, and you will feel a quicker connection to the city. If you have the possibility - save up a lot of money before going - Paris is much more fun, when you can afford to live there.

crucial_aspects: Personally knowing the language, and being personally interested in the culture.
info_ease: Quite easy. Sorbonne university were particularly good at giving information on where to find all administrative facilities like getting student ID, place of exchange and social activities for students. You had a personal contact whom you could ask questions in case there were issues.
arrival_assistance: I received no assistance upon arrival.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: All registrations for courses were planned directly with our contact at the university. The process was quite smooth.
registration_help: Help is through direct dialogue with your contact at the university, and my contact was very helpful in explaining which courses were available and how many I needed to fulfill my ECTS point goals.
registration_success: Since I applied quite late, few courses were left. But I got the courses and internships I wanted since the selection is quite large.
registration_advice: As long as you're studying Medicine at KU, prioritize on picking courses you're interested in rather than taking courses and internships you're interested in since the language barrier makes Also, take with your contact person if you're in doubt, they're very helpful.
course_level: 20 ECTS point exchange with 12 weeks of internship with morning classes at the hospital.
teaching_comparison: A lot more paternalistic and less freeform than in Copenhagen. Classes are longer and studying is situated in the classroom, compared to in Denmark where there are relatively few classes but more time for studying at home.
courses_enrolled: 12 weeks of internship at Pitié Salpêtrière with classes in the morning at the hospital.
recommended_courses: Diabetology at Pitié Salpêtrière was excellent.
unexpected_costs: Unexpected costs were mostly personal spending since the cultural and travel opportunities are so great. Plan how much you want to spend in advance, and try to put some extra aside, as you'll find things like theatres, concerts, and travel opportunities while down here.
cost_comparison: Travelling internally in France is very cheap, with high-speed trains (the TGV) going for below 30-40€
activities_available: The Cité Universitaire Sports club is very affordable (20€ per month) and provides access to >30 activities including tennis, swimming, volleyball etc. You'll definitely find something you like.
activities_recommended: Travel to other major French cities like Lyon, Bordeaux and Marseille. Hike in the French alps, visit Vinyards, sail on a boat, wander in forests. France is more than just Paris.
weekend_recommendations: Book train tickets 4-6 weeks in advance and go on weekend trips to other major French cities.
culture_adjustment: Since I was quite well prepared, the language and culture were quite easy to adjust to. Speaking to patients, writing notes and letters was doable, and after 1 month became second nature. But in case you haven't studied French since High-school, expect to spend a lot of time studying the language.
socializing_tips: Sorbonne Université has a lot of great social activities, as well as the Cité Universitaire. Sign up and go meet new people.
cultural_challenges: The way of studying and practicing medicine is very different compared to the Danish model. Clinical internships end at 6 pm, so you're usually quite tired at the end of the day. The tasks you're given are also different, where in Denmark you're more involved in panning treatments for patients and ordering blood samples, tests and ordering medications practically by yourself, in France you're more a support to the doctors, where you write their notes, write letters and contact other departments and physicians regarding second opinions.
culture_appreciated: I really admire the French systematic approach to diagnosing patients and treatment. There's a lot more continuity where it's the same doctors at each department for several weeks in a row, instead of in Denmark where each physician is at a department for a few days before rotating to the next post.
top3_advice: Learn French in advance so you can focus on your studies and enjoying the culture and city once you're in Paris.
other_useful_info: I personally thought I'd have time to work on a research project from back home in Denmark during my exchange, but postponed this, to focus on studies and cultural activities. If possible, don't bring to many work-tasks from Denmark with you, and just enjoy your stay in Paris.
most_rewarding: Meeting other french students and working alongside the french doctors.
greatest_challenge: Learning to practice medicine in a new environment. Not because the language was different, but because the way you write notes, order diagnostic tests and administer treatment are quite different from the way it is done in Denmark.

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte at tage til Paris, da jeg altid har været meget interesseret i det franske sprog, kulturen og jeg synes Paris er en fantastisk by. Jeg synes, at udveksling med et klinikophold var en god mulighed for at bo her og få en hverdag. Samtidig med at der er rig mulighed for at udforske alle de små kroge, caféer, parker, musik osv. i Paris. Hverdagen på hospitalet minder på mange måder om et klinikophold i Danmark, så det er en genkendelig og tryg setting, hvor man har god mulighed for at lære et andet system at kende (og forbedre sit (mediciner)franske, hvis man ikke taler det flydende). Samtidig oplever man de små forskelle og måder, hvor lægerne gør tingene anderledes, og det er sjovt at få lidt perspektiv på, at der ikke kun er én måde at være læge på og gøre tingene på.
info_ease: Min tutorlæge/professor besvarede ikke min mail, da jeg ankom. Så jeg vidste ikke hvad tid eller hvor præcis jeg skulle møde henne første dag. Men en hurtig Google-søgning hjalp mig til at finde afdelingen. Jeg kom kl. 8 første dag, hvor den egentlige mødetid først var 9.30. Så jeg måtte vente noget tid på de andre medicinstuderende, men sygeplejerskerne var søde til at vise mig et sted, jeg kunne sidde og drikke en kop kaffe, mens jeg ventede. Den første dag var der en grundig introduktion, og efter dét, var det nemt at finde ud af hvad tid og hvorhenne, jeg skulle møde. Det var ikke så nemt at få mit ID til hospitalet (numéro APH, ækvivalent til BAM-ID). Først havde jeg ikke fået det udstedt, så jeg var nødt til fysisk at møde op på kontoret på et andet hospital for at få ID'et. Derefter virkede koden ikke i de første 2 uger, hvor jeg var nødt til at låne de andre studerendes login. Efter jeg havde kontaktet en sekretær på hospitalet flere gange, begyndte koden at virke efter de første to ugers ophold. Derudover var de franske medicinstuderende meget hjælpsomme, hvis der var noget, jeg var i tvivl om.
arrival_assistance: Der var en Erasmus-koordinator, man kan skrive til, hvis man har spørgsmål. Men i det store hele, må man også spørge sig lidt frem for at finde ud af tingene. Derudover var der en tutorlæge, man kunne spørge om hjælp, når fx ens ID-nummer ikke virkede. Der var mange andre Erasmusstuderende i klinik samme sted som mig, som var i samme situation, så vi kunne hjælpe hinanden igennem de første opstartsvanskeligheder.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Når KU har godkendt én til udveksling, får man en mail fra Erasmus-koordinatoren på Sorbonne, og derefter skal man prioritere/ønske de klinikophold, man vil have, og sende dokumentation for klinikforsikring og vacciner. Derefter får man tildelt sit klinikophold.
registration_help: Man kan skrive mails til Erasmuskoordinatoren, hvis man har spørgsmål. Hun svarer relativt hurtigt og præcist.
registration_success: Jeg fik min førsteprioritet til klinikønske i 3 mdr.
registration_advice: Man behøver ikke at have sin egen praktiserende læge til at underskrive ens vaccinationsbeviser. Man kan bare vedhæfte sine vacciner fra sin "gule vaccinationsbog"/internettet.
course_level: Jeg tog 3 mdr. klinikophold på 11. semesters udvekslingsperspektiv.
teaching_comparison: Der var nogle undervisningstimer på hospitalet om morgenen. Noget "Raisonnement/diagnostic pédagogique..." hver tirsdag morgen, hvor man gennemgår den kliniske tankegang/anamnese/udredning, som fører én frem til en diagnose. Derudover var der nogle kliniske cases, som blev fremlagt af de franske medicinstuderende hver onsdag morgen, og "Apprentisage du Raisonnement Clinique (ARC)" hver torsdag/fredag morgen. Det var lærerigt, og mindede meget om klinikundervisningen i Danmark. I starten var det lidt svært at følge med i pga. mine (lidt rustne) franske sprogkundskaber
courses_enrolled: Udvekslingsperspektiv - 11. semester (5. semester, kandidat)
recommended_courses: Klinikophold
unexpected_costs: Hvis man inden for en periode af 3 mdr. forbruger mere data i udlandet end i Danmark, skal man betale ekstra i sit abonnement, selv hvis data i EU normalt er gratis/inkluderet i ens danske abonnement. Derfor skulle jeg købe et fransk SIM-kort/abonnement hernede.
cost_comparison: Det er ikke særlig meget billigere at handle dagligvarer ind desværre. Museer er kun gratis, hvis man ikke er fyldt 26 år endnu. Til gengæld er der rig mulighed for at mæske sig i kaffe til 1-3 euro og croissanter til samme pris! Ellers er der også supermarkeds-vin til 3 euro, og virkelig gode restauranter, som er en hel del billigere end i DK. De fleste togbilletter er også meget billigere end i DK, og man kan meget hurtigt komme ud af byen med hurtigtog (TGV) og se noget andet.
activities_available: Ved ikke
activities_recommended: Gå i operaen og se ballet. Gå ud med dine venner, og spis lækker mad og find en hyggelig bistro. Gå turen: La coulée verte på et nedlagt jernbanespor. Tag et tog ud af Paris og tag på cykeltur på din lånte Swapfiet/eller vandretur. Tag på en masse museer.
weekend_recommendations: Normandiet, Mont Saint Michel, Versailles, Bordeaux
culture_adjustment: Nemt nok. Der er lidt mere hierarki her, og det er svært at finde ud af "vous" vs. "tu" for en dansker. Her er også en del bureaukrati. Men mere vanskeligt er det heller ikke.
socializing_tips: Bo i Cité Universitaire. Tag et klinikophold på en stor afdeling, hvor der er andre Erasmusstuderende, og bliv add'et til deres WhatsApp-grupper.
cultural_challenges: Ikke noget specielt
culture_appreciated: Mad, koncerter, museer, arkitektur, litteratur. Søde mennesker
top3_advice: Bare afsted og gør det! Du kommer ikke til at fortryde det. Det bliver en fantastisk oplevelse! Det er helt okay, hvis dit franske ikke er helt top. Det er hårdt i starten, men du kommer lynhurtigt efter det. Husk at nyde det, og hæng ud med dine nye venner/bekendtskaber. Tiden går stærkt
other_useful_info: Nej.
most_rewarding: At opleve at få en helt ny hverdag i en ny by, og blive overvældet af hvor smuk byen er, og hvor søde og imødekommende andre unge studerende er. At ens sprogkundskaber udvikler sig virkelig hurtigt, når man er "tvunget ud i" at tale hver dag. At komme ud og tage på tur med ens nye venner, og opleve en by og et land fra en lokals perspektiv, som har boet her længere end én selv, og kan vise én steder, man ikke lige selv ville have opdaget.
greatest_challenge: Sproget. Jeg talte ikke særlig godt fransk, da jeg ankom. Det var enormt trættende den første uge, og stadigvæk en del de første ca. 3 uger. Men når man bliver udsat for det hver dag i klinik, og rundt om i byen, udvikler man sig vildt hurtigt, og man lærer hurtigt at forstå og kommunikere de vigtigste ting.

crucial_aspects: Learning French. Good university.
info_ease: It was a bit difficult to figure out how the course registration worked. I was very dependent on getting help from the administration.
arrival_assistance: I had a meeting with my academic coordinator who helped me with the course registration.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Meeting with coordinator and she helped me get inscribed at the courses at the faculty of science. However, I also had to follow courses at faculté des lettres, and this made the proces a bit more complicated.
registration_help: The coordinator, but we didn't have the best communication.
registration_success: Quite succesful.
registration_advice: Look at which courses you would like on Sorbonnes webpage. It is a bit difficult to find however.
course_level: For me it was especially challenging that everything was in French, but that got better over time. Otherwise the level was good.
teaching_comparison: Less discussion in class. More knowing by heart. Less (almost none) use of books.
courses_enrolled: Bioethics Philosophie of science Metaphysics Big data in public health Neurobiologi Biochemistry French Immunology
recommended_courses: Summercourse in marine flora at the marine station in Roscoff.
unexpected_costs: I got my bag stolen...
cost_comparison: Crous (university canteen) less expensive than expected (3.5 euro for a meal)
activities_available: A lot, but I didn't attend it.
activities_recommended: Explore Paris :)
weekend_recommendations: Explore Paris :)
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Join Erasmus groups if you want to meet other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Culture for administration.
culture_appreciated: Most parts of French culture.
top3_advice: Patience is needed. By insisting when you need help. Try to get courses in French to learn it.
other_useful_info: The university is not really the place where you meet people easily, so do an effort to join other social things.
most_rewarding: Finally being able to understand the courses.
greatest_challenge: Getting inscribed properly at the courses and arranging so they didn't overlap and then the exam period with 8 exams.

crucial_aspects: Being able to practice french, as well as the high hopes for the academic level.
info_ease: The information at the "Reunion Erasmus" was quite informing. But all the small things that was "nice to know", or just basic information was usually quite hard to come by.
arrival_assistance: As mentioned above, the "Reunion Erasmus" was the main source of information upon arrival.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: For someone not being native to Sorbonne, all the neccessary information seemed scattered all over the place and very disorganized. Therefore a lot of the information concering registration was a bit confusing. We had to meet up physically at the UFR to get the paper needed to enroll for classes. After that, there was a given interval where you could give back the paper, with the desired courses.
registration_help: You are very much on your own at Sorbonne, if you don't know anybody there. The people in the administration surely are not very keen on helping, unless they forced to do so.
registration_success: It was easy getting the right CM, but getting the right seminars(TD) connected to the CM, was a bit of a puzzle. Especially because the Erasmus students had to enroll after all the normal students. This meant that a lot of the TD's were already full, which can make quite a mess, because you have to make your own schedule.
registration_advice: Don't be intimidated by the administration, and don't be afraid to seek out other Erasmus students. They are probably just as confused as you are, but it makes the confusion less stressfull.
course_level: The level compared to UCPH wasn't that different. Of course, the courses being in french, certainly introduced a new problem of understanding, which is not present in UCPH. But all in all, the level seems to match.
teaching_comparison: For a non-native french speaker, the fact that the professors only talked, and didn't use any forms of visual presentations certainly increased the difficulty. A normal lecture would normally consist of the professor entering the room, opening a book, and talking for the whole duration. No to little interaction, which really differs from UCPH. Therefore there are not many ways in which the style of teaching compares.
courses_enrolled: 1. Philosophie Politique 2. Philosophie Comparée 3. Historie de Philosophie 4. Métaphysique 5. Logique 6. Philosophie de la connasaince 7. Competances transversales
recommended_courses: Every course with M. Pascal Ludwig was very nice. A very intelligent professor with more modern ways of teaching.
unexpected_costs: There didn't appear any
cost_comparison: A lot of the texts were given by the professors, or available on Moodle. Therefore little to no money was spent on books-
activities_available: I didn't look too much into that. But compared to UCPH, the student life was not really present at Sorbonne. I know that there were some sports clubs, but i dont have any other information.
activities_recommended: Don't have any recommendations.
weekend_recommendations: Literally just walk around Paris. Paris is an amazing city, and even being here for 6 months wasn't enough to explore every part of the city.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. The only difference is having to speak french everywhere you go, but that is something that settles in fast.
socializing_tips: It doesn't even seem that the local student socialize a lot with each other. There aren't a lot of opportunities to do so.
cultural_challenges: Not anything in particular.
culture_appreciated: The quality of the food and wine I must admit. A lot of the gastronomical experiences were just amazing.
top3_advice: 1. Have a lot of patience 2. Practice your writing-hand (and hand-writing) before arrival 3. Don't lose hope, even though it is quite easy to do
other_useful_info: Don't be scared to ask the professors for information. They are usually always happy to help.
most_rewarding: Probably the improvement of french.
greatest_challenge: The whole system of Sorbonne can be very unorganized, which really decreases the morale. The way of exams were very different compared to UCPH. A lot of the exams were physical and relied entirely on memory.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study at Sorbonne because my main interest is French literature from the middle ages and the renaissance, and Sorbonne was just the right place for that. I also wanted to improve my French and follow courses in French, even though it could be difficult from time to time.
info_ease: I think that it was not so easy because the French administration does not work well. For example we cannot choose courses online, we have to write them down in a paper and give it to the Erasmus-coordinator. We were told that we had to present ourselves to each teacher, so that they know we are Erasmus-students. The introduction days were a bit chaotic but when the semester began, I really started to enjoy it.
arrival_assistance: We did get information about studying at Sorbonne and how to choose courses.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: As I said, you have to write the courses you wish to follow with pen and paper. Then you will have to be a bit patient. I was not registered when the semester began and we had to wait for several weeks in order to be registered. Many students were complaining about it and I started to worry about it in the beginning as well.
registration_help: The was an introduction day and that was it. We did not get much help, but maybe we did not need more help.
registration_success: I was very successful. I wanted to study French medieval and renaissance literature and French classicissm, so I chose my course from these periods. It was very interesting.
registration_advice: Be patient. It takes time to be registered, but it will happen.
course_level: The level was very high.
teaching_comparison: At the Sorbonne, it was mostly a teacher that spoke, and I only experienced group work a single time. I was satisfied because I just wanted to listen to the teacher's French and take notes.
courses_enrolled: La scène du Graal : entre poétique sérielle et pensée medievale Naître, se marier, mourir à la Renaissance La "poétique" du Printemps d'Agrippa d'Aubigné Cultures féminines du Grand siècle Le théatre de Samuel Chappuzeau Victor Hugo, Odes et poésies diverses
recommended_courses: I may be one of the few students who enjoy ancient French literature. But if you love French literature, you are very lucky. Sorbonne has about 50 courses about French literature, so you can choose exactly what you like.
unexpected_costs: If you take the train to visit another French city, then it is very expensive...
cost_comparison: In general, it is not so expensive in France. In Denmark, it is more expensive.
activities_available: There were sometimes concerts at the Sorbonne and also many sport opportunities, but I did not try it myself because I had already much to do in Paris.
activities_recommended: Visit museums! It is free for students under 26, and there are so many museums in Paris.
weekend_recommendations: Visit the chateau de Versailles. Visit other cities in France with the train.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. I already felt part of the culture the first days.
socializing_tips: Go to events, and there are many in Paris, and especially in the Cité Universitaire.
cultural_challenges: It was not challenging, but in France, you have to say "monsieur" and "madame" to your teachers, also when you write an e-mail: "Chère Madame". And also say "vous" instead of "tu". Politeness is a part of French culture.
culture_appreciated: The food. ;-)
top3_advice: You should strive to socialize and go to many events. It makes the experence abroad so much better. You are here to learn and you should just enjoy it. When you are in another city, you should also exlore it and not just study.
other_useful_info: The French administration is horrible, and all students agree on that. Just be patient.
most_rewarding: That I have developed as a human being.
greatest_challenge: One of the exam forms was especially challenging: when you have a 2-hour-exam where you write in French with a pen and paper.

crucial_aspects: It was important for me that the courses suggested were adapted to my study program and in line with what I already have had at KU.
info_ease: It was very easy. Of course, it helped that I have a connexion to France and know people there.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any kind of assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process is very simple. It happened through an online plateform and the mobility coordinator is very good at helping, answering emails and give your the necessary advice. At arrival, I had to fill out a "certificate of arrival paper". That's it.
registration_help: Any help needed was provided by the staff present on the first day.
registration_success: My program included only compulsory courses (no elective courses), so the registration was automatic.
registration_advice: No comments here.
course_level: In my opinion, the level of the courses is approximately the same as at my home university. However, I had a total of 10 courses at the same time, whereas at KU, I used to have 2 at the same time. More structure and organisation was needed from my side to adapt to this new rhythm.
teaching_comparison: I was part of an extensive project, so we had a lot of group work. Compared to UCPH, we had less practical work (laboratory, in my case). Another important aspect to mention is that, in France, you typically have small exams every week and not one big exam at the end of the semester.
courses_enrolled: Entreprise et Entreprenariat (English, Economics and Entrepreneurship), Gestion de projet industriel (Industrial project, Computer science), Qualité environnementale (Sustainability and food storage), Formulation (Nutrition, enzymes and formulation)
recommended_courses: Gestion de projet industriel (Industrial project) was my favourite course. Note : If you choose the same exchange program as me, you will get those courses and cannot choose others.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Food is less expensive in France compared to Denmark. Housing was very expensive. Museums are free for all under 26 in Paris. Personal expenses such as hairdresser and so, are less expensive in France as well.
activities_available: Weekly sport classes, after-class parties, ski trips, Erasmus parties, tourism and sightseeing.
activities_recommended: The tourism and sightseeing together with other Erasmus students are a great way to discover the city and get to know other students.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city. It has a lot to offer and a lot of small hidden gems.

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process at Sorbonne is a bit oldschool and a bit confusing I would say. They have a portal for registration with many documents to upload, documents that are not necesarely available to us. You have to be good at reaching out to find answers.
registration_help: There is an office that takes care of exchange students to Sorbonne, which functions well (or they answer you pretty quickly).
registration_success: I got my first priority.
registration_advice: Don't panic with the confusing system, it will work out.
course_level: I found the level very high, and we had a lot of extra lessons at the hospital. I felt that it was very important to them to include the students in the working rutines and they wanted to teach us things.
teaching_comparison: I found it more "hardcore", and more demanding, which was a bit tough as an exchange student. But I also think that I learned a lot more from this style of teaching.

recommended_courses: I would recommend the one course I took.
unexpected_costs: Not any special.
cost_comparison: It is not cheap to go out in Paris, but it is worth to prioritize in your budget.

activities_recommended: The sports subscription!

culture_adjustment: It was very easy, since I have french roots. I think that it could be more difficult if you are not used to the culture, and there is not at lot of mercy for the students.
socializing_tips: I didn't socialize with local students because I had so much social life in my house. But I would say that they are very interested in you, and if you want to interact with them, they would love to!
cultural_challenges: I would say that it was rather easy, but getting used to the "no-mercy"-part is probably the hardest. Not taking it personal.

crucial_aspects: I was looking for a place with a strong academic profile in the French language and culture, and Paris allowed me to also study and live in one of the largest cultural centers and most well-connected cities in Europe.
info_ease: It did require some work. The information system is not too centralized - in fact the information software was not consistent between courses and a lot of information is available solely through email or given solely in person. I was not prompted with the necessary information and I had to reach out myself to a lot of different people and talk to other students to gain the information I needed to follow the courses. I did however feel that most things were easily sorted along the way.
arrival_assistance: I had an international mobility coordinator, who was helpful mostly with the administrative ERASMUS-stuff, student cards and likewise. For the rest, all assistance regarding information and orientation was obtained directly from the professors, and sometimes local students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process was very manual, I had to register by email to the administration, and for me it was disjoint, so different courses had different administrative personnel responsible for registration. I found the process a bit unclear, the steps are not clearly outlined, and it was tough to get confirmation of registration. However, in the end I found that I could always talk directly to the professor and things would work out.
registration_help: I had instructions from the international mobility coordinator, there was the administrative personnel, and the professors were very (the most) helpful.
registration_success: I was registered for all the courses I wanted, so I was completely successful.
registration_advice: Be on time, be patient and in the end, I felt most things were possible.
course_level: At my host institution the Master's programme is split into two: first year of Master's (M1) and second year of Master's (M2). In my experience, M2 courses were significantly more advanced and research focused than M1 courses. Whereas M1 courses perhaps had less prerequisites than corresponding courses at my home institution (UCPH), the level was quite similar with perhaps a slightly higher pace, while the M2 courses were quite a bit more difficult in my experience than the courses I have taken in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: You had to learn a lot more of the material by heart, the focus was more theoretical and we did very little in terms of applications and implementations. There was also very little groupwork and very little creative work.
courses_enrolled: Stochastic calculus and stochastic control, Stochastic geometry and random graphs (subtitles: Scaling limits; Graphons; Random graphs), Concentration of measure and mixing times (subtitle: Concentration inequalities), Introduction to Riemann surfaces, Algebraic topology.
recommended_courses: In my experience, you have a lot of options and so you have a lot of freedom to choose according to your personal academic interests. Based on my own interests (all math and statistics), I was very happy with Stochastic geometry and random graphs and Introduction to Riemann surfaces because they offered introductions to topics that were unavailable to me at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: I ended up spending more on food than anticipated, but besides that I do not recall encountering any unexpected costs. There are some costs involved with buying kitchen equipment, practical stuff when moving in and then the odd fee for access to nice libraries etc here and there. Beware that you also have to pay a fee to visit the doctor in France.
cost_comparison: Grocery items were slightly more expensive than expected, prices were as high and sometimes even a lot higher than prices in Denmark. Services (restaurants, hairdressers etc) were generally less expensive.
activities_available: There were quite a lot of activities available. For example, there was a choir, there were sporting clubs ranging from standard such as running to more exotic such as fencing, and there were multiple social clubs organizing parties and open air movie nights. I ended up doing most of my extracurricular activities in the community where I lived (Cité Universitaire), since it was more practical for me.
activities_recommended: I don't know, for me there are so many options in Paris, and so it is hard to give any general recommendations besides discovering the city, the museums and the parks. From sporting clubs, where you can pick up new sports and do sports with other students, to cultural events such as gastronomical, fashion and music festivals, live concerts or independent cinemas showing a curated set of classic and foreign films. You also have very good options to go outside Paris and get to experience France. But I can recommend using the options at the host institution for activities where you get to practice your French and make French friends.
weekend_recommendations: Just experience the city, there is so much to do, even on a budget (most museums, parks and a lot of concerts are free). There are also really great libraries with a great selection of books if you are there to study.
culture_adjustment: It was not too difficult, of course you have to get used to everything being organized in French and that the administrative process is disorganized so that most communication and practicalities are sorted directly with the professor. Then there are small things, for instance you are expected to make very thorough handwritten notes, and often no supplementary material is presented if you do not make it to class or if you miss something in class. A final small thing, for instance that there is a very strong culture for eating lunch in the university restaurants (Resto U, CROUS), and so there are very few other spots to hang out inside on campus (and you are not allowed to eat in other indoor spaces).
socializing_tips: Sign up for the activities at campus, speak French fluently.
cultural_challenges: The most difficult thing to get used to was the French administration, it was at times quite disorganized and hard to figure out, but luckily it is not the main component of the experience. Another thing is that the tone is very different, you need to show a lot of respect and formality for authorities and elderly, and if you break formal conduct, you can expect to be told so and corrected quite abruptly at times. Your ability to speak French is also scrutinized in some environments.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated getting to experience the French mentality; I sometimes find that in Denmark we focus on process, whereas in France I felt a focus on just being, and even though that distinction is admittedly vague and hard to describe, I found that reflected in a lot of places - from restaurants (or brasseries) where there is little pressure to leave to activism to public transport to the abundance of parks and outdoor public spaces.
top3_advice: 1. Make sure to apply for grants, Paris can be quite an expensive city to live in and there are grants available. 2. Unless you are very very good at French, I would advise signing up for a language course before/as soon as you start, because it is a good way to help you get used to using French all the time - especially for the courses. 3. Don't worry, it is going to be a great experience, and even if it can be tough to get everything organized, as long as you have housing (try to get into Cité Universitaire!!) and an Erasmus+ contract, the rest will get solved along the way.
other_useful_info: Keep an eye on your email, a lot of courses are entirely organized by email. Make sure to go to the welcome event - you get otherwise hard to get practical information and meet the other exchange students with whom you share the experience.
most_rewarding: I think the totality of it, when I got settled and everything was in full flow - that feeling of being able to make it in a new country, a new culture with new people while still having the wonder of discovering all the quirks and the marvels that you meet along the way. You can almost feel your horizon widening, your capabilities improving and your foundation getting stronger with more experiences. A specific academic thing I found rewarding was passing a very difficult oral exam in French, since that was one of the academic aims of going abroad to this destination.
greatest_challenge: The language barrier, but that was also one of my main motivations for going to France, and I enjoyed this challenge very much, since French is so integral to the French experience.

crucial_aspects: I chose Sorbonne, as it has a reputation for being one of the best french schools for humanities, and as I have a personal relation to Paris, where I've been living before. Besides this I wanted to improve my french, which is perfect at Sorbonne as most of the classes and all communication is conducted in french.
overall_comments: I've loved being abroad, learning about the ways university as an institution works in other countries. Though I've come to realize that the education, and the way our system works in Denmark, is much more suitable for the way I learn.
info_ease: This was pretty difficult, as Sorbonne doesn't really inform their exchange students that much. You are very much left to figure out things for yourself. On an additional note, it is therefore crucial to speak and understand french on a somewhat good level !
arrival_assistance: We had an assembly with all the exchange students enrolled at the humanities departement in the beginning of the autumn semester.
arrival_comments: There weren't really any orientation available besides the assembly, which didn't focus that much on the things you actually need to know as an exchange student. If possible before going to Paris, try to engage yourself with knowledge of how the french educational system works, so you won't be too unprepared.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I've loved being abroad, learning about the ways university as an institution works in other countries. Though I've come to realize that the education, and the way our system works in Denmark, is much more suitable for the way I learn.
registration_process: You have to fill out a format with the classes and the hours you want, both for travaux dirigées and cours magistral (seminars and lectures). These you send to the person in charge of handling the registrations. As you're an exchange student, you are not officially in their system, therefore everything is handled in hand.
registration_help: Not that much to be quite honest. I've spoken with other students in order to understand the system, but don't worry, it's not that difficult.
registration_success: I've got pretty much all the classes I wanted. Though the courses are way less ECTS points in France, so you'll probably end up having more courses that you're used to in Denmark. Therefore some of the classes tend to overlap.
registration_advice: Please take the time out to do your research on which teachers, classes and hours are best suiting for you before you actually have to registrer, as it will make it much easier for you in the end.
academics_comments: I've loved being abroad, learning about the ways university as an institution works in other countries. Though I've come to realize that the education, and the way our system works in Denmark, is much more suitable for the way I learn.
course_level: To me some of the courses seemed to be not to be on an educational level that high, as you are mostly just commanded to remember and repeat, and not expected that much to think for yourself. This depends a lot on the teacher though! I would recommend choosing some of the younger teachers, as they are often more up to the beat on how to teach in a more progressive way.
teaching_comparison: The way french people learn is emphasized on learning and repeating whatever the teacher says, and not to work in a reflecting way yourself. Therefore the teaching style could seem rather dull most of the time, and you are taught not to think outside of the box, which for me was pretty sad and didn't develop my skills in any way. Besides they are still pretty oldschool, so you'll write exams in hand, you'll have a lot of test and in some classes it's even mandatory to present (in french) in front of 50 people.
courses_enrolled: Littératures européennes (L5LM31FR), Littérature, idées, arts (L5LIZ03A), Littérature et société (L5LIZ05A), Littérature française des XIXe et XXe siècles (L5LM84FR), Anglais : Langue, littérature et culture anglophone (L5LI98AN).
recommended_courses: Each term they offer a comparative literature course, where you have to read (or translate) in an original language (this often being german, english and spanish). These courses are the best I've had each term, as they are not as focused on France and the french cultural heritage. I really loved Études comparatistes (L6LI39FR), which dealt with gender and gender representation in the novel from the 20th century (also one of the only classes, where female writers were on the curriculum..)
unexpected_costs: I'm not really sure I've really encountered any. I've experience mould in my previous appartement, where cleaning supplies costed a bit extra.
cost_comparison: Paris is a really expensive city, which I knew beforehand, as I've lived here before. But one advice I could give, is to live in some of the less expensive neighbourhoods, as it's not only the rent that's cheaper, but also the super markets, cafes and so on.
activities_available: I think they do something called "parismus", which is like a social thing for erasmus students, where they can meet and engage with other fellow exchange students. I never attended, so I can't say that much about it.
activities_recommended: I don't have any thing to recommend regarding what the school offers, but it's a good way to engage with the local community to sign up for anything really, yoga, tennis, drawing classes, whatever you like, to actually meet some french people.
weekend_recommendations: Paris has so much to offer, that you sometimes forget how central in Europe you are. It's easy to go on day trips in ile-de-france (the region, where Paris is located), go to the beach in normandy, or even take the train to Amsterdam. With the TGV (fast trains) you can move around in France (and Europe) pretty quickly. Personally I would recommend going to Marseille! It's an amazing city only 3,5 hours from Paris with the TGV.
culture_adjustment: As I study French language and culture and have lived in Paris before, I would say I'm pretty understanding of the french culture, but I could imagine it being quite a culture clash for some. It's very different from Denmark in a lot of ways. Everything from how poverty is much more evident in Paris to how the french people are actually very conservative in some ways, could be a shock for some.
socializing_tips: It's difficult, as french people in some ways are as shy to outsiders as danish people are. But I would say you just have to engage, speak with people in classe, try your best to get out there ! And learn french. French people are sometimes very insecure about their english, and on contrary beliefs, they are not arrogant, but really nice and welcoming !
cultural_challenges: Mostly their way of doing exactly what the teachers wants them to do and their lack of trying to think for themselves in class. This was difficult in doing presentations with french people.
culture_appreciated: I love the french "joie de vivre". Paris is an intoxicating city, where you have endless possibilities of culture and living. To grab a glass of wine after classes, going to museums during the day, reading in parks and just enjoying what the city has to offer.
top3_advice: Know and understand french, even though they tell you it's not crucial, it is. Don't expect it to be like it is in Denmark, neither your home, classes or even the people you meet. You're are not in Denmark, so of course things are different from what you are used to. Don't do too many classes, try to chose the ones with the high score of ECTS. Often a 4 ECTS point course has at least as heavy a workload as a 8 ECTS point course.
other_useful_info: If you do your classes in the literature department, you often don't have to do the exams, you're only controlled by the "controle continu", which is controls during the term.
most_rewarding: Living in Paris, all the cultural possibilities (cheap museums, cheap books etc.), meeting so many great people from all over the world, and really emerging in the language and the culture. Being at Sorbonne is really like being at an oldschool, beautiful campus (as long as you chose courses from the 3rd year of the bachelor).
greatest_challenge: Understanding their means of teaching and evaluating you. You really have to work in order not to flunk your classes. It's normal in France to flunk people, which we are not used to in the same extent in Denmark.

crucial_aspects: Since I study French at the university in Copenhagen, for me France was the best option, and I always had a dream about studying at the Sorbonne University, all though it disappointed me a lot.
overall_comments: I really didn't find my experience at the Sorbonne University good. First of all, there was an enormous lack of communication, lack of understanding, lack of help, etc. The main problem this semester, was not having access to the school system "moodle". There is no it-support office, so we to multiple office(s), people, teachers, administration, wrote so many mails regarding this problem, but no replies. So no-one tried to help, therefore our coordinator from Denmark had to get involved, and suddenly, there was help to get. We got access to moodle after 10 weeks, the semester is 13 weeks. Due to not being able to enter moodle, also means, you dont have access to the documents, homework, powerpoints, overview of the semester, exams, all of the important stuff. Furthermore during my periode, my personal life was a mess, during the exam-period, I was apartment scammed, my boyfriend and I broke up, due to unfaithfulness, we had a death in my family, but I was told, I had to do the exams, and there was nothing to do, even though I didn't feel well with my mental health. During our exams, we could only bring a French-french dictionary. which is a very high demand, when you are only an exchange student. Plus the level of French was beyond B2, and if I remember correctly, we discovered the UFR (bachelor) they assigned us, was on a C1 level, which didn't match the requirements, we were suppose to fulfil. There was in general much confusing among the Erasmus students, and we where told different information, and didn't feel like, there was anyone to bring our concerns to. I also tried to ask one of my teachers regarding an exam, because we didn't know what to do, and he never even responded. Some of the courses expected that the reading materiel was read before the semester, how should we have a clue about that? This school is beyond inattentive regarding exchange students. The don't care. Furthermore, the wifi is non-existing and during winter it is super cold, since the school is old, and always charge your laptop at home, because they don't have plugs in all rooms.

crucial_aspects: The history of the city and the university. I wanted to be challenged academically, and get a perspective on the academic level and academic culture on one of the oldest universities in the world.
info_ease: It was very difficult to get any information about the course plan. It is not possible to obtain these informations through any platform, all information is given directly from the coordiateur pédagogique. I didn't hear from Sorbonne for a long time, so i was unsure of how the procedure was up to my stay.
arrival_assistance: I did meet with my coordinateur before my courses started, and she offered to help with whatever questions i might have. I didn't have any specific questions, i was just doubted that i had inscribed everything correctly. She told me that everything was in order. Two months after we realised that i wasn't inscribed to Sorbonne correctly.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There was an inscription day, but sadly i wasn't informed about this day proporly. I felt very lost for the first period at Sorbonne. The process of me getting a student card was very long and tiresome. I send multiple emails to the office for ERASMUS students, and finally it was clear that i wasn't inscribed properly.
