crucial_aspects: The Sorbonne is one the most well-renowned universities in Europe, notably within the discipline of philosophy where its historical and academic influence cannot be underrated. As such, I saw an Erasmus stay at the university as a rare opportunity to go and immerse myself in a philosophically prestigious environment where I would be able to experience first hand the world famous philosophical tradition, which has shaped so much of wester thought since the enlightenment.
info_ease: Not too easy. Fortunately I had a friend who had done an exchange semester at La Sorbonne the previous semester. He shared the course descriptions with me and helped me understand the procedures of enrollment which, to me, were not at all easy to comprehend otherwise.
arrival_assistance: There were e-mails sent containing information, as well as an information meeting before the start of the semester. Much, however, was left to be guessed at. One thing that made it especially hard to make sure I was on the right track, was that I had to be in touch both with office of international relations, the office at the department of philosophy, as well as other departments in which I took elective courses. A centralization of course-finding at enrollment would, I think, make the whole process much more easy and safe.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: One was to find the courses within the course description file for each year of each discipline. These were not easy to come by, but I managed, with some luck, to find them at the university webpage after endless clicking and some help from a friend who had previously been to the Sorbonne.
registration_help: Not much, to my knowledge. I tried contacting the secretary at the philosophy Department, but she was not interested in helping me and simply referred me to the aforementioned files, without any guidance on how to find them.
registration_success: I managed, after some emailing back and forth to get exactly the courses I had hoped for. I was, however, uncertain about whether I had really gotten them until long after the semester had started — there was no confirmation of registration or anything the like.
registration_advice: To not loose hope and to know that everything usually works out in the end. I cannot say how many times I was certain that the administrative part of my stay had been messed up. This was never the case; there is just a really slow flow of information.
course_level: The style of teaching is quite different to what I was used to from the University of Copenhagen. At the Sorbonne the teaching is more rigid and conservative than that of many other European universities. Many students transcribe the lectures word-for-word which, to me, exemplifies quite well the lack of independence in the studies. Students seem to be expected to know — or, remember — just what they are taught in class, and not much else. There is, thus, not much energy devoted to developing skills in critical thinking, independent reading of texts, or of free philosophical discussion. On Swiss Erasmus student told me, she felt as if she was back in high school. I should say, in all fairness, that the courses being all in French, a third language to me, also inhibited slightly my ability to participate actively in classes. A higher level of French would have made it possible to shape the teaching experience to the better. The above mentioned shortcomings of the classes seemed however to apply to the local students as well.
teaching_comparison: Se above.
courses_enrolled: Français générale C1 FOU : Écrits universitaires – Présentiel Dieu, L'homme, Le Monde – Figures De La Transcendance Sciences et Valeurs Arts et Pouvoirs Travail personnel Theory of Translation
recommended_courses: I would recommend to take courses at the SIAL (department of foreign language learning), which offer French courses at an academic level. It is nice to be in a class with other exchange students who are there on the same premise as yourself. Further, the academic requirements are somewhat lower, which can be a very welcome relief from the very demanding courses in philosophy, and, I presume, in the other departments as well.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Rent is generally higher than in Copenhagen. I was lucky to find a small studio at 720€/Month excluding heat an electricity, which was about 60-60€/Month in additional costs. I know of Erasmus students who pay even higher rents.
activities_available: I did not participate in any, but there were options on offer to do sports and film clubs etc..
weekend_recommendations: There is so much to do in Paris! I especially recommend taking advantage of the many museums and galleries.
culture_adjustment: Easy! The Parisian life style is much of what makes an exchange stay at la Sorbonne worth while. If you are into great and not too expensive food, wine, coffee and cake, massive bookstores, and museums, it should be easy to get into the rhythm.
socializing_tips: I found that the local students in my classes were very closed and unwelcoming. I spoke to many other exchange students who had the same experience. Luckily it is not too hard to find company, as there a many students from abroad at the university. At bars and restaurants as well, it is easy to chat to people and make connections that way.
top3_advice: i/ Make connections with other students and people in general. It can be quite lonely going to the Sorbonne, and even if it seems that you do not have the time to socialize because the workload from the university is to great — I would say it pays off to take that time. ii/ Practice your French as much as possible. Many people think that if they can just achieve a B2 level which is the admission requirements, they will be all right. This is true to some extend, but you will safe yourself so much headache by really practicing hard — preferably with a tandem partner in Copenhagen. The better your French the better your whole experience! iii/ Build knowledge of the specific academic writing genres, 'la dissertation', 'l'explication d'un texte,' and 'le commentaire composé'. These are not intuitive and require to be studied before you can complete the exams.
most_rewarding: It was very rewarding to actually complete what at times seemed an insurmountable challenge. I really struggled during my semester, so it was nice to be able to complete it. I was proud of that, and happy to see my level of French greatly improved — especially in writing and reading.
greatest_challenge: Definitely getting in to the French academic tradition, which is quite different to the Danish. To be honest, I found that it was more demanding, but somehow still less rewarding. I am happy to have acquired a level of French that permits me to now work with French texts in my further studies, but the actual academic outcome from the courses was not very giving, and thus a challenge to keep following.

crucial_aspects: First and most important was the host university. I had heard a lot about Sorbonne Université and the high ranking of the university. I wanted to try a new way of studying at a university which is considered quite good internationally. The country's culture and language and the atmosphere in the city where I was going to live were also important factors in my choosing of Paris. Furthermore it was important for me to go somewhere with good opportunities to meet new people and be able to experience a lot of cultural places as these elements were important for me to explore my curiosity and have fun while studying.
overall_comments: The manner in which the studies at Sorbonne Université proceeded were very different from how it is at my home univeristy, University of Copenhagen. First of all, I had 8 courses during my semester at Sorbonne which I wasn't used to have at all as we only have one to two courses at a time in Copenhagen. Many of the courses weighted 3 ECTS points but didn't accord to the big amount of work required in the subjects. At Sorbonne Université we didn't have any academic books to study in if we didn't understand the lectures totally and we didn't get much information about the lectures before coming to it. Furthermore we had a lot of classes with physical attendance around 30 hours a week which was a lot compared to the balance between work at home and university we are used to in Denmark. The information from the professors to the students wasn't the best either, although some teachers were really good. In general, the dates of the exams were in many cases announced very late which gave little opportunity for the students to prepare for them. I experienced having three heavy exams in one day and I was therefore not able to focus on each one efficiency as it was an impossible task. I also experienced that one exam was not announced even though it could only take place a maximum of 10 days from the day I realized the missing exam date. I then sent an email to my professor asking for the date of the exam where as he then sent an email out to everyone that it would take place three days from that current day. This exam date was additionally the day after the day of the three exams. Aside from this, in most of the courses it was very difficult to know how to prepare for the exams as we didn't have exam samples from earlier years or similar documents to practice on. All these things made it very difficult for me to do my best and get good results and I didn't feel as if the university made sure that I, as an exchange student, from a university with structure, could follow properly. Other that all these factors, it has been fun to try to study at Sorbonne and experience the the everyday study life of a french student in university. Also I love the city of Paris and it has been one of the best experiences in my life to live the parisian life for a semester.

crucial_aspects: My interest in the culture and how it is to live there and improving my French
overall_comments: An amazing experience, but definitely tough at times
info_ease: Relatively easy, as I had a contact person at Sorbonne whom I could email, and everything was handled in person or by email so I wasn't expected to search for any information on any websites.
arrival_assistance: After my arrival, I emailed my academic Erasmus contact person at Sorbonne, who organised a meeting with two other academic administrative people where they helped me choose my courses in person. She also set up my Sorbonne email and Moodle (intranet) account. There was also an Erasmus welcome meeting for all the exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: An amazing experience, but definitely tough at times
registration_process: There was an online application process that included several short motivated letters, but most of it was just formalities. After I had arrived in Paris, my Erasmus contact person at Sorbonne arranged a relaxed meeting with two other academic administrative people where they helped me choose my courses. They were teachers in some of the courses themselves or researchers at the university, so I could ask them questions about the courses. They took care of signing me up for the courses I had chosen and setting up my email and intranet account.
registration_help: The administrative people present at the meeting were happy to answer questions and make suggestions about which courses I should take, and the whole meeting was about me choosing my courses.
registration_success: I ended up with courses in areas I was interested in, but most of the courses I had chosen from home were only offered in the spring semester, so I couldn't take them.
registration_advice: Notice which semester the courses are offered in. Make a longer list of courses you could be interested in, in case there are schedule conflicts or canceled courses. Be well prepared for any meetings, as you might have to decide on the spot.
academics_comments: An amazing experience, but definitely tough at times
course_level: The neuroscience courses were very challenging and definitely at a high enough level for a 3rd year Mol. Bio. student, and they were especially ambitious with creating context for the neuroscience and connecting it to things I hadn't learnt about before, e.g. congnitive/behavioural science and philosophy. As the education at Sorbonne is general Biology, the other students hadn't had as much molecular biology/ protein science, so in a subject such as Microbiologie, the level didn't feel so high, and they didn't go into as much depth with molecular cell biology or lab methods as I might have wished. But everything was challenging due to the language (all courses were in French, including exams, and we were treated no different from the French students).
teaching_comparison: The courses at Sorbonne are either 6 ECTS or 3 ECTS, which means that you have 7 or 8 courses at the same time for the semester. This meant that the courses didn't go into as much depth as they do at KU, but there was still a lot of material covered in each course. Overall, the focus was more on learning a lot of information by heart than on learning a few key concepts in depth (with the exception of the math course I took at Sorbonne). At the Sorbonne biology institute there is also a somewhat extreme amount of teaching; I could have up to 36 hours of teaching a week, but usually had around 26, which meant at least one to two 8-18 days each week and school every day. The teachers had more power to decide, and they didn't always explain why we were learning something or tell us beforehand what the lecture would be about, which felt chaotic at times. However the lectures were often more inspiring and on more untraditional subjects or with a certain angle, because the teachers had more freedom in structuring their lectures, e.g. a fascinating lecture on neurophilosophy in a neuro course. There were no books or reading material, so what the teachers said during the classes was the curriculum, and you were expected to absorb most things during lectures or TD (classroom teaching/exercises, which was repetition of the material from the lectures). But it was more acceptable/expected to ask questions during lectures, and sometimes the lecturer would start a discussion with a student and the lecture would even end up in that direction. Overall I thought it was a positive experience to be so immersed in university life and see this more oral/dialogue-based approach to teaching.
courses_enrolled: Neurophysiologie et physiologie des grandes fonctions (6 ECTS) Microbiologie (3 ECTS) Biochimie: métabolisme (3 ECTS) Mathématiques et statistiques pour la biologie (3 ECTS) Francais langue étrangère (3 ECTS) Physiopathologies humaines et stratégies de recherche (6 ECTS) Cerveau et comportement (6 ECTS)
recommended_courses: Cerveau et comportement: fascinating lectures on subjects in neuroscience, e.g. emotions, addiction, philosophy of the brain, consciousness - by very competent lecturers. Physiopathologies humaines et stratégies de recherche: interesting/useful course for mol. bio., as each lecture was on a different illness that was treated as a case and that we learnt about in depth, including the social background of the illness and the progress of research. The classroom teaching was practice reading and presenting papers about each illness. Microbiologie: a well-organised and interesting and inspiring course, even though it didn't go into as much depth as I might have wished.
unexpected_costs: Having to buy single train tickets after having lost my monthly train card When in very touristy areas, watch out for people trying to trick you into giving them a lot of money, e.g. the tourist rickshaws.
cost_comparison: Some things in the supermarkets could be randomly priced, so you had to watch out. Baguettes were very cheap :) Sports/gyms are expensive Most museums are free if you're under 26.
activities_available: Sorbonne offered relatively many sports classes at campus that seemed reasonably priced, but I didn't use any of them as I used the sports offered in Cité Universitaire. Parismus, a student organisation whose aim is to connect foreign students and French students, organised many events, from walks to parties and picnics and museum visits. E.g. Apérismus, which was a popular Wednesday bar (instead of a Friday bar) every second Wednesday. There were many other student organisations, e.g. a philosophy club that organised philosophy film viewings with discussions afterwards.
activities_recommended: Anything that Parismus organises, as it is an easy way to meet French students interested in meeting exchange students, or to meet other exchange students. There is so much going on in Paris and so many students and cultural institutions etc., so find whatever interests you! French cinemas, cafés, (book)shopping, just exploring and enjoying Paris !
weekend_recommendations: Don't be afraid to do all the touristy things. The nightlife in Paris should be experienced
culture_adjustment: Sometimes difficult, especially in the beginning, but with an open mind it was fine.
socializing_tips: Speak French :o) Just go for it, most people are very willing to talk to people they don't know and help each other with notes etc.
cultural_challenges: Chaos, over-complicated ways of dealing with some things and general dysfunctioning of e.g. the metro. The subtleties of French culture can be different from the Danish and can be difficult to get into straight away, but you can't expect to become French from living there for 5 months, sometimes you are just the clueless Erasmus student. People, e.g. university staff can sometimes seem agressive and volatile, and conflicts are more common and less serious. Spontaneity and the French way of being polite which sometimes requires a lot of alertness and quick thinking in the most unlikely situations.
culture_appreciated: Spontaneity and how you can do so many things without planning beforehand, and talk to so many people, the love of discussions. The more lively student life. The inexhaustible energy French/Parisian people seem to have
top3_advice: Take what happens at university with a pinch of salt, and focus on what you want to get out of the university experience instead of what the professors expect or the general atmosphere of stress around tests and presentations. Be patient with learning the language and speak/make mistakes. Be brave and do whatever you want to while on exchange!
other_useful_info: no
most_rewarding: Improving my French so much Meeting so many new people Creating a life in Paris
greatest_challenge: Balancing school work with social life at the student accommodation and exploring Paris and looking after myself.
other_comments: no

crucial_aspects: France, and Paris in particular, has a strong history in mathematics, and Sorbonne Université offers some fairly specialized courses, more so than Copenhagen, in the fields I am most interested in. I certainly also liked the idea of living in Paris, having visited a few times before, and thought it would be great to improve my French.
info_ease: Generally speaking, information from Sorbonne was not easy to find, lots of rules are not described anywhere in writing and will not be supplied to you unless you ask, so it is necessary to talk to secretaries, professors, etc.
arrival_assistance: There was a brief introductory session for all exchange students at the faculty, and the mathematics institute hosted an aperitif where there was also some time to clear up practical matters.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process depends strongly on the specific program, even for the math master's programs there are different systems. For the M1 courses, registration is done through an online portal (for the first time ever this year, I was told!) and for the M2 in pure mathematics (Math fonda), it is done through a google form. In both cases, exchange students are asked for an extra document which is to be signed by the person responsible for exchange students at the institute and handed in physically to the secretary.
registration_help: You will not be offered any help unless you ask for it. The professor responsible for exchange students was very helpful with everything, the secretaries not so much.
registration_success: I managed to register for all the courses I was planning on.
registration_advice: Keep asking if you are not given the information you need.
course_level: The level of courses in the M1 (first year of the master's) was generally quite low, comparable with some exceptions to the more advanced bachelor's courses in Copenhagen. There is a big jump to the M2 courses which are of similar difficulty to the harder Master's courses in Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: In math, teaching was done in more or less the same way I was used to with the exception that students were usually not expected to work on problems ahead of exercise classes. Instead, we would work on them in class. Also, lectures are 2 hours without any breaks which takes some getting used to.
courses_enrolled: Géometrie Differentielle (M1), Surfaces de Riemann (M2), Schémas I (M2).
recommended_courses: My favorite course was probably M2 Riemann Surfaces. The courses depend strongly on who is teaching them, I really enjoyed those taught by Benoît Stroh and François Loeser.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than I expected (probably in part due to inflation). Otherwise, expect similar prices to Copenhagen except that eating out is cheaper.
activities_available: I did not look into it much
activities_recommended: I did not participate in any in connection with the university.
weekend_recommendations: Paris is a huge city, surely you will be able to find something that fits your interests.
culture_adjustment: It was not a problem
socializing_tips: French students are not always very good at English, so it helps to be conversational in French.
cultural_challenges: Nothing in particular
culture_appreciated: I have no comments on this
top3_advice: Keep asking if you are not getting the information you need Make sure that your French level is good enough. In math, people students are generally allowed to do exams in English but this is absolutely not the case for every other program. Attend your classes. While it's generally not compulsory at Sorbonne (unlike many other French universities), there is typically not as much information on lecture plans, syllabus, practicalities, etc. available online as you'll be used to from Copenhagen.
other_useful_info: Apply for housing at Fondation Danoise. It's a nice place to live, the social life is great, and there are plenty of opportunities do to sports or other activities in Cité Universitaire.
most_rewarding: It's hard to pinpoint anything in particular, I learned a lot of math, made a lot of friends and generally had a good time.
greatest_challenge: Exams for the M2 courses in pure math can be very hard, so don't expect to just breeze through even if you are used to that back home. I ended up having failing one and having to go to a re-exam despite working harder on the course than for many 12s I've got in Copenhagen.

crucial_aspects: Practicing and studying in French and living in a unique city which is relevant to the field I study.
info_ease: Fairly easy, we received an email of when to meet up for a big welcome day for exchange students, where we met the other students arriving from DK, got the student card, and got some general information.
arrival_assistance: On the first week there was a meeting with the Erasmus coordinator in person, who was very helpful in answering our questions, also later on. This was reassuring as prior to arrival, communication with the general study administration was not the best with several unanswered mails and calls.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I filled out a paper during the first meeting with the Erasmus coordinator. The course catalogue for the semester however was not published until the last week of August, meaning my pre-approval application with KU was based on the outdated list of courses. So I had to redo the pre-approval application, which required some extra time and effort. However it all turned out fine in the end. The good thing about course registration is that it was possible to change/de-register from courses at Sorbonne for the first few weeks.
registration_help: The previous years' course catalogue was on the uni's website which helped to make the pre-approval application. The Erasmus coordinator managed the process on Sorbonne's end and answered questions.
registration_success: This went smoothly.
registration_advice: It's a very different system from KU and it can seem confusing, but don't stress over it - it's all gonna work out when you get there in person. If you want to take courses in other disciplines than your own, dedicate time to exploring this option during the first week.
course_level: All the art history courses tackled very specific topics and were quite detailed and advanced. All courses were taught in French.
teaching_comparison: Totally different. The classes consisted predominantly of lectures with no or very little discussion following up. Instead of reading and independent work, emphasis is put on very thorough note taking of what the professor says in class (and memorising it for most evaluations). Most courses gave a very 'factual' presentation of the studied topic going into the smallest details, but often with no critical examination following up on what we heard. Certain aspects of some courses were poorly organised; sometimes classes would be cancelled without notifying students; or it would be unclear how Erasmus students will be evaluated until quite late in the semester, or slides were not shared. That being said I still enjoyed some courses. In my perception, the syllabus for art history is more 'up to date' at KU but Sorbonne is good at providing a very solid ground of knowledge in specific topics, so in a way they complete each other. While I gained a lot of new knowledge, I found the top-down teaching style challenging, and I left questioning the value of this type of encyclopedic knowledge today.
courses_enrolled: Patrimoine : histoire, théorie, législation, institutions, collections ; Archéologie romaine ; Art contemporain 1 ; Art contemporain XXe-XXIe s. ; Art moderne 1 ; Spécifique d'art contemporain ; Projet professionnel: entretien avec des professionnels
recommended_courses: I would recommend 'Art contemporain XXe-XXIe s.' and 'Spécifique d'art contemporain' as they were the most clearly structured courses, taught by engaged professors who also aimed at sparking discussions in the classroom.
cost_comparison: Groceries were slightly more affordable than in DK
activities_available: There were French language classes for foreign students, as well as sports clubs and public lectures, film club... There is a student organization in charge of almost weekly social gatherings for Erasmus students.
activities_recommended: Attending social events for Erasmus students is an easy way to meet people.
weekend_recommendations: It's Paris, there is always something exciting to do! There is also quite a few castles with parks in the proximity of Paris, which can be interesting as there is not a lot of nature inside the city.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy as I already spoke the language quite well.
socializing_tips: That can be difficult. There were not really any social spaces in the art history institute, so my best advice is to just start talking to the people you sit next to before or after classes - people were quite curious to meet foreign students.
cultural_challenges: The hierarchies when addressing any ‘superior' (teacher, senior people) can be challenging when coming from DK - a lot of formal politeness is expected in these situations. I also found bureaucracy unnecessarily complicated.
culture_appreciated: The food culture, the city, the unique arts & culture scene of Paris
top3_advice: 1. Explore the option of taking courses outside your discipline 2. Be prepared that the teaching style is very different from KU 3. Use your time in Paris well - you can actually go and see a lot of the material you learn about if in art history or a related field, the city is a massive resource
other_useful_info: More about living in Paris: there is a great and cheap public bike system which I was happy to use. Also with your student card you can get a warm meal at the CROUS canteens for 4 EUR.
most_rewarding: Getting to know a unique city, making new friendships and polishing my French language skills.
greatest_challenge: Navigating the different teaching style.

It was also important for me to go to one of the universities that are a part of the Erasmus-exhange with UCPH, as I did not want to bother with more bureaucratic papers than necessary, hence why I chose Sorbonne Université.
info_ease: Very difficult. We had no idea when we would have our first introduction meeting or when the first day of school was. arrival_assistance: We had introduction meetings with general information.

registration_process: In short: be patient. Expect to get all information at the last minute. The registration process was to be honest fairly easy. But be prepared that even though you may have picked some courses from the catalog beforehand, not all of them will be available for Erasmus students. You also have to put time aside to figure out what classes you want at what time, as you create your own schedule.
registration_help: I did not need help, but I am sure there are coordinated people assigned to help.
registration_success: The first 2-3 weeks are "open", which means you can attend all courses and change your courses if you'd rather have something else. I ended up changing 2 things (one concerning my time and schedule, and the other the teacher). Which was fairly easy.
registration_advice: The faculties are divided in different places. I only had courses from the French bachelor from the first semester, and they are all at the Malesherbes campus. The third year is at the City Center Sorbonne (close to Panthéon), as well as the masters. So just keep in mind what semester, what faculty and what campus your course is held at.
course_level: I only had BA-courses from the first semester of the French language bachelor.
teaching_comparison: In short: it's more 'old-shool' (and not in a good way). All courses are divided in two: one seminar style class (CM: cours magistral) and then a more intimate (up to 30ish people) class (TD: travaux dirigés). All the CM's are just a big amphitheater with a teacher speaking however she/he prefers. It can be with or without powerpoints/notes/etc. Sometimes you can ask questions, other times not. The TD's vary a lot depending on the teacher. There is a different more visible hierarchy in the French culture, and the teachers words are therefore sometimes seen as the only words acceptable. It is not very critical thinking oriented and you do not always get the chance to develop your own ideas or ways of thinking. Exams: everything is done in hand at the table with no notes. And you will have a lot of exams.

registration_process: 1. There was a meeting for ERASMUS students in the UFR Langue Francaise and UFR Littérature. I was in the 3rd year in the UFR Langue Francaise. Here they gave us some info, as well as some official paper on which we could write the courses we wanted. There was one paper for each UFR (at this meeting only the Langue Francaise and Littérature). 2. Go home and fill out the papers. You had to find course info (like days, times and location) yourself online. You had to make sure yourself, that the classes didn't clash. You had to fill out a paper from each UFR where you were taking classes. Since I took one class in UFR Lit and the rest in UFR LF, I had to fill out two papers. You had to write all your info (name, student number, etc.) and then the class names, class code as well as which days you wanted (for some classes there were multiple to choose from. Be aware that each class has a CM part and a TD part. You have to choose one of each. 3. Get an e-mail with a date and time to show up on campus and hand in your papers. For me it was the 26th of January, and classes started the 29th, so I was getting kinda stressed out. I had to show up to Sorbonne Mère (the on near Panthéon) and find two offices, where the student coordinator would take and check the papers. This took a looong time, and there was a long line, so be patient. 4. Done! I luckily didn't have any problems afterwards. I had written a list of all my classes, so I knew where to go and when. Bonus: Make sure you classes don't clash. Make sure they're all in the same location, or if not, that you have time to travel to another campus between classes. It's not uncommon that a class changes classroom a few weeks into the semester, so make sure you check the Sorbonne e-mail often. You can make it automatically forward to your normal e-mail, which makes it much easier to check it.
registration_help: There was the meeting, but I didn't really feel like there was a lot of new information tbh.

registration_advice: Don't stress too much. It felt very late for me, but it was luckily all fine in the end. If in doubt, send an e-mail to your student coordinator, or ask other exchange students.
course_level: Some courses were too easy, some were perfect, and some were wayy too hard. It was a little hard to find the balance. Some of the courses, I felt like I already knew the subject, as I had had similar courses on my second or third semester. Another courses was almost impossible, if you weren't a native French speaker, which was really frustrating.
teaching_comparison: Kinda the same. I'm not used to having classes in big auditioriums, but that's mostly what I had in Paris. Some of the teachers kept forgetting to use the microphone, which was really annoying, so make sure you sit close to the front of the class.

info_ease: A bit difficult after the semester started, alright before then.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any "extra" assistance if any more than the French students. Little information was given by professors or other staff on how exams were conducted and in general how their education was set up.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We were instructed to show up to the main Sorbonne Campus in the 5th and get out student ID's and other info there on how the semester would go. Another day we came to register for classes which was not the best process. We had to wait in a long queue in the heat for a couple hours and then register by paper for classes, and some were filled up so we were told to quickly pick another instead. All in all, what you might expect from an older university but not very effective and smart process in my opinion.
registration_help: Assistance from the inscription professors.
registration_success: I had to change a couple of them to different classes so I ended up with two classes I didn't want to have 30 ECTS in total, and they also proved to be much harder than the others.
registration_advice: To research as much as they can from home about various subjects and maybe prepare a plan A, B and C just in case so they are well prepared.
course_level: The level of courses were varied, some were well-organized and well tought with good professors while others were very confusing with quite honestly a bad quality of teaching. Especially my ancient studies and literature classes were confusing and professors were often berating students for innocuous things and etc.
teaching_comparison: It was generally much better at UCPH, but I think this is because many of my values and what I'm used to is in line with danish education and therefore not the French. In France I experienced a sort of implicite hierarchy in their society and education where I didn't always feel the young students were respected. For example I experienced professors and staff speak and behave rudely to students many times. At UCPH everyone is treated like equal adults and there is no disrespect. Further, the style of teaching was mostly composed of the teacher explaining concepts by the blackboard for however long the class lasted and there was much less student interaction.
courses_enrolled: I'm not sure of all their equivalent titles in English so I will list them in French: 1. Grammaire et histoire de la langue 2. Ecrire et penser la fiction 3. Linguistique, sémiotique, communication 4. Sociolinguistique et psycholinguistique 5. Histoire du cinéma 6. Histoire de la culture occidentale pour Lettres Modernes
recommended_courses: That depends on their chosen bachelor and what courses they've already taken but above all I would say to choose classes you are very interested in and relative to your proficiency level in the given language you are taking them in. It would be best to find a comprise between the two, so you don't end up struggling with a class that's simply too hard either because of the subject matter or the level of language difficulty it's being taught in. I would therefore recommend a good balance of relevant classes for your bachelor but also some that are just for interest reasons and to balance out your course load.
unexpected_costs: Transportation, housing, extra things for apartment etc
cost_comparison: transportation - a navigo card for students was more expensive than I thought.
activities_available: Many options such as riding, swimming, running, cinemaclub etc
activities_recommended: The parismus events and maybe joining their trips around France if there's time because several of my friends said it was a lot of fun and they met a lot of people
weekend_recommendations: Explore as many of the arrondissements as possible, for example a weekend trip to somewhere outside Paris, trip to Disney, concerts etc
culture_adjustment: Quite easy as I have vacationed many times before in France and there are many similarities in general
socializing_tips: Just approach them and ask if they want to hangout at a cafe or go to a concert - I met some very nice French girls because I was going to a concert alone but ended up going with them and got to know them after. Just go for it! All the local students/people I met were all very nice and welcoming.
cultural_challenges: The hierarchal layers of society for one, as I'm not used to addressing people formally in Denmark. Adjusting to living in a much bigger city - account for more time to arrive to school in the mornings as sometimes it was almost impossible to get on the metro due to overcrowding. Sometimes processes were quite slow and ineffective compared to Scandinavia in general.
culture_appreciated: Almost everywhere I went in the city everyone was seemingly happy and very easy to talk to, there are endless opportunities of things to do in the city, amazing architecture, they value their culture life very highly - often going to museums, concerts and parks and conserving this.
top3_advice: 1. Have multiple suggestions for what courses you'd like to take as they are not always all available 2. Find good housing ahead of time to avoid stress 3. Create a good and realistic budget
other_useful_info: Manage expectations: are you going on exchange for academic reasons or to meet new people and try living in another country? Often the latter will be the more giving reason I found. For social purposes: to try and "announce" you'll go to Paris through social media if you'd like to meet new people and don't be afraid to grab a coffee and explore the city with them. Often people would post on Facebook, TikTok or Instagram just asking if they wanted to meet up. Lastly: remember to experience as much as you can and enjoy it! Especially if you're only on exchange for 1 semester, it passes by very fast.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people definitely. They are now some of my best friends and we shared some of my favorite memories together.
greatest_challenge: Housing and trying to keep up with all the classes and exams, as we had "exams" the DST's almost once every 2 weeks and many more in December - so a very different format than at UCPH.

activities_recommended: I would recommend - especially for those living in the CIUP (Cité Universitaire) to go to the trips that are often organized by the different houses. Many are way younger than typical Danish students abroad and the themes and trips can seem somewhat generic but it is a good way to make connections
weekend_recommendations: What I just mentioned above, if not, go out and eat and dance in Paris
culture_adjustment: The French are different and pretty oriented towards themselves, a bit like Danes, so it is mostly necessary to know the Language and being very active in seeking the company/ attention from others.
socializing_tips: Go ask anyone from your classes if they wanna hang out. It is not organized in anyway, so a good way to learn how to become very active in searching for new connections
cultural_challenges: The language mostly and very much the hierarchies between student and teacher.
culture_appreciated: The food and the wine.
top3_advice: Don't kid yourself, learn French if you want to study at Sorbonne unless you specifically know that you are going to take English (or whatever other language you might know) classes. Don't assume that you will as a natural consequence get new and close connections. Be active and force yourself to be outgoing. Be cautious and attentive about the requirements, deadlines etc. academically and administratively. Then everything mostly is solved as the instituion is more flexible than it might seem at a first glance.
other_useful_info: Buy a student train card.
most_rewarding: The language and the anthropological side of getting acquainted with a completely different way of teaching and interacting - very interesting.
greatest_challenge: Social connections and building a network in less then 6 months. It is interesting, funny etc. but also tough and at times quite disappointing. However, this is somewhat also the most rewarding thing about the stay, that you can actually stay up even though you do not have your usual social base.

crucial_aspects: I had already lived in Paris for a year, and completed an internship at the Danish embassy in Paris as a part of my education. I wanted to continue to live here and combine it with studies, and therefore I applied to Sorbonne.
info_ease: To be honest, it was not easy at all and I don't think the different systems communicate well. It is difficult both to find information at your home university, at the host university and from Erasmus. And there is no overall "guide" to how you proceed - you are very much on your own.
arrival_assistance: Actually, almost nothing. The administration at Sorbonne functions very poorly, and it is very difficult to receive assistance from the regarding anything. It seems like they are not used to the processes around exchange students. First of all knowing who to contact was difficult to find out, and when you found them, the assistance they provided were very slow and not very helpful. Again, you are very much on your own. There is an introduction day for exchange students at the beginning, but this is much more about being an Erasmus student in a new city, how to take the subway, social events etc. It doesn't provide you with the necessary information about how you choose courses, which courses are available to you, when the courses begin, examination, etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process is honestly a mess! It is super difficult to navigate in, you are provided with little to no information, it is difficult to know who to reach out to, and it doesn't appear as they know it either. I took me more than a month from when school started in September until I was properly registered, which was very stressful and frustrating.
registration_help: There is different offices (UFRs) connected to the different Masters at Sorbonne's Faculty des Lettres, but they communicate bad with each other, the systems are poor, and it doesn't seem as if the people who work there are sure of the processes either. So very little help - you have to consult with other students, write many many e-mails to the administration etc.
registration_success: After a month I succeeded, but it was the most difficult, complicated, and confusing process. The teachers don't communicate with the administration, and no one has any information about which and how many courses are available to Erasmus students in relation to their home university.
registration_advice: Start the process very very early and be consistent and stubborn in writing to the administration regarding the information you need. If they don't reply, you have to go there physically and ask the questions about the registration and maybe even see them register you on their own computer, so you are sure it is completed.
course_level: The level of courses is fine I think - I studied philosophy which I don't do at home so for me it was of course difficult because it was new to me. What is very different from my home university is the large amount of courses you have to take at Sorbonne to get it to add up to the mandatory 30 ECTS points. This means that there are a lot to manage, a lot of information to take in and learn and especially a lot of exams. So even though the level of the courses is appropriate the large amount of courses and exams are too overwhelming, I think.
teaching_comparison: It is much more old school and they don't practice active style of teaching as we are used to. It is a lecture; the professor lectures and the students listen.
courses_enrolled: Histoire de la philosophie moderne Introduction à l'éthique économique et sociale Philosophie penale Philosophie des relations internationales Philosophie politique Philosophie morale Textes contemporains Philosophie politique
recommended_courses: If you study political science - as I do - I think these are the best alternatives within the Master in Political philosophy. The only one not super relevant to our field is philosophie morale, as it is more a course in ethics and moral philosophy.
unexpected_costs: Public transportation is expensive in Paris. The rent is high if you want to find housing off campus. It is not unexpected but there are a lot of costs combined with living as a student in Paris.
cost_comparison: Eating out is less expensive than I expected, and people do it a lot!
activities_available: I think quite a few, but I never participated in it, so I don't know.
activities_recommended: I never tried them, so I can't recommend any.
weekend_recommendations: It depends on what you want to get out of the stay and how well you know the city. For me, I had already lived here for a long time, so I just "continued with my life". If you are only here for the exchange I recommend you get the most out of the city; experience museums, nice restaurants, walk around to see the city.
culture_adjustment: I was already familiar with the French culture, so for me it was easy. If you are not used to this, I think a French university can be very tough. It is much more formal and oldschool than I imagine it is in a lot of other countries.
socializing_tips: Unfortunately, no. I was already settled with a group of friends.
cultural_challenges: Being Danish you have to watch out for the frequent use of irony and sarcasm, as it doesn't always fit into the French culture and way of socializing.
culture_appreciated: I love the culture around restaurants and bars; the social life in Paris in all age groups I think is amazing.
top3_advice: - Start researching and planning as early as possible! Look in the course catalogues, reach out to the administration, find housing etc. - Be aware of the language barrier! Even if you passed the French language test (B2) be aware that EVERYTHING is in French, the professors are often bad at English, and the French teaching level is high - Reach out to our professors in the beginning of the semester stating that you are an Erasmus student so they are aware - my teachers were very nice in regard to this because I had told them from the beginning
other_useful_info: Be aware that a lot of exams are completed in hand writing at the university as a table top exercise, which we are not used to in Copenhagen. Thus, practice writing and taking notes in handwriting from the beginning.
most_rewarding: To complete so many courses in French within a field I have never studied before.
greatest_challenge: The language and the administration

crucial_aspects: The rich culture and history of the city (Paris)
info_ease: The french system was a little complicated to navigate in, but i found out and people there were friendly and wanted to help me.
arrival_assistance: Assistance concerning how to subscribe to courses.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I had to show up fysically and fill a paper with the classes i wanted to follow. After that a woman from Sorbonne looked at the paper to see if it was possible and then approved.
registration_help: Help via email and help via going to the office.
registration_success: I got the classes that i wanted without problems.
registration_advice: Be prepared, there is a day (friday before the semester starts) where you can sign up for classes but its a good idea to have chosen beforehand classes beforehand in order to make the process faster. Also there is a meeting earlier in that week where you get informations about subscribing for classes and other practical informations. Its a good idea attending that meeting.
course_level: It was a little too difficult for me in the beginning but later it got better. You should be realistic about your own level of french and academic level in general since it seems that the level is very high at Sorbonne.
teaching_comparison: At Sorbonne it was more "old school" with the teacher speaking and sometimes uses the blackboard. At University of Copenhagen its more normal to use powerpoints and to upload files on the intranet, which for me is a very good thing. At Sorbonne it was more difficult to understand everything the teacher told us because there were not so many documents and files on the intranet (Moodle)
courses_enrolled: Histoire de la langue et sentiment de la langue Rhétorique et stylistique Poétique et rhétorique aux siècles classiques Ecriture des savoirs et culture médiévale Le francais de la renaissance
recommended_courses: Histoire de la langue et sentiment de la langue because it gave me an idea about the developpement of the french language during time. Le francais de la renaissance was good because it gave me an understanding of the renaissance in french, we read some of the famous author and got an idea about how humans at that time understood nature, other unknown cultures and the human nature.
unexpected_costs: Not really any:)
cost_comparison: The food, beer and wine are less expensive than expected. Same with the transport, i recommend to rent a bike from Swapfiets, its about 14 euros pr month and then you have it all the time. I rented it for 5 months and then delivred it back. Museums are also quite cheap, If you are younger than 26 the many things are free,for example museums.
activities_available: There is a group called Parismus Sorbonne, which is an organisation for Erasmus Students. They have a whatsapp and an Instagram account and have some different activities.
activities_recommended: Parties, day-trips or weekends trips to other cities. (watch the website called Erasmusplace.com for these trips).
weekend_recommendations: Normandy and Brittany, for example Honfleur Deauville, Saint Malo and Mont Saint Michel. Giverny is also nice and the same with Reims. They also have trips to South of France, for example Bordeaux which is a beautiful city.
culture_adjustment: A little difficult because i didnt lived among local people (only two of the people from my floor are parisians).
socializing_tips: Talk to people from your class at Sorbonne. You can also get a language buddy via the app called Tandem (language exchange)
cultural_challenges: Parisians are a little reserved and not so open to foreigners.
culture_appreciated: The food, the appreciation of art and beauty, the archtecture and the café culture.
top3_advice: Live in Cité Universitaire Go explore Paris, there are some many things to discover Say yes to things and be aware of all the differents whatsapp groups that organise events and parties.
other_useful_info: Take some classes at Sorbonne that you are interested in, otherwise its gonna be tough. Start early on the exam-assignments of the classes.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and expanding my horizon. Getting to know a lot of amazing spots and places in Paris.
greatest_challenge: To follow the classes in the beginning since it was some difficult subjects for me and it seems that the level of Sorbonne is quite high.

crucial_aspects: I just really like Paris.
info_ease: It was challenging to find the right information from Sorbonne especially concerning the inscription process.
arrival_assistance: There was a information meeting in the beginning.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The inscription process was quite confusing and stressing. The course inscription in my UFR (institute) was done with pen on paper the week before the start of the courses but if you had to take courses at the other UFR's the inscription was online and it was difficult for the administrative people to coordinate the two.
registration_help: There wasn't much help - my coordinator got very annoyed when I wrote and asked her questions.
registration_success: I ended up getting all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Accept that it is stressful and chaotic - everything is going to work out in the end even though it might not seem like it. And ask the other exchange students for help.
course_level: I think the academic level of the courses was a lot lower than at UCPH - we did not read theoretic or secondary literature only literary works (I study comparative literature). The courses I had in English were especially "easy", they had the level of Danish high school courses.
teaching_comparison: It was a lot different. The purpose of the courses seemed to be to memorize what the teacher said so that you could repeat it in your exam. All exams were pen on paper.
courses_enrolled: Littérature francaise du XIX et XX siecles Etudes comparatistes American fiction British history from 1914-2010 American history in the first half of the 20th century
recommended_courses: I think the courses change each semester. If you study literature then I recommend you look at what books you have to read for the courses before you choose - then you can choose based on what books you would like to read.
unexpected_costs: Not really anything.
cost_comparison: Books are very cheap, public transportation is quite expensive. You can eat super cheap at Crous which is a student's cantine.
activities_available: A lot of activities were available at Sorbonne but I didn't use any. At CIUP I joined the sports programme.
activities_recommended: I don't know.
weekend_recommendations: It is cheap and easy to visit other french cities by train. The trains are very fast so you can get to fx Bordeaux in two hours. There are also lots of fun things to do in Paris of course. Most museums are free if you're under 26.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy - not that far from Danish culture.
socializing_tips: It is very difficult. It seems like the French students are not interested in becoming friends with exchange students and since there is no group work in the classes it is difficult to meet people. If you are single then I think dating is the easiest way to meet french people.
cultural_challenges: Parisians can be quite rude and angry, you have to get used to that and remember that it is not personal.
culture_appreciated: The food and architecture - and that people engage with strangers much more than in Denmark.
top3_advice: Embrace the administrative chaos - it is going to work out in the end. Take courses in French even if you don't speak it perfectly (if you want to improve) - the teachers are kind to exchange students when grading. Find friends who are also exchange students - otherwise you will be lonely.
other_useful_info: I don't know.
most_rewarding: Getting new friends and improving my French.
greatest_challenge: The pen on paper exams in French. I was very nervous but it went just fine.

activities_recommended: n/a

crucial_aspects: The culture, the language and the academic heritage.

arrival_assistance: Good assistance everyone was nice to answer my emails.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

Then write another email to an administrativ worker, who would write me on the list. For the other course i had to show up physically at a specific location, so that an administrativ worker could write some things on his computer and print a piece of paper that he handed to me.
registration_help: The co-ordinators were nice to answer all my emails.
registration_success: I succeeded.
registration_advice: It's chaos, but don't worry, it's the same for everybody. The approach is more loose than in Denmark, so you figure things out along the way.
course_level: Low academic level. There was not much involvement of academic papers. The presentations of the professors were unstructured and superficial.
teaching_comparison: Very different. Some courses it was a two hour monologue from a professor without a plan or anything visual. They are way more concerned with historical facts and not as much with methodology or theory.
courses_enrolled: New Perspectives in Religious Studies The Story of Brexit - From Entry to th 2016 Referendum Contemporary British Drama: What is political theatre? Histoire de relations internationales - L'OTAN Depuis le Guerre Froide
recommended_courses: The Story of Brexit - From Entry to th 2016 Referendum Histoire de relations internationales - L'OTAN Depuis le Guerre Froide The professors were nice and the subject interesting. Teaching methods and academic level however were limited.
unexpected_costs: Food was more expensive than expected.
cost_comparison: Rent of a bike was cheap as well as public transport.
activities_available: I think a lot, but because i was enrolled at the Cité Universitaire, i used the activities there.
activities_recommended: Football. It is just an international language that breaks down barriers and offers you to meet new people in an informal way.
weekend_recommendations: Hang out with friends, go to sports events, visit other towns in the area, and maybe to go a market by some nice food and cook a big meal together on Sundays.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy, the place i lived was also very international. However, had to get used to living in a city that big (Paris).
socializing_tips: Not really. Didn't interact much with them, but maybe ask them out. Go watch a football match together or somethin like that.
cultural_challenges: People ignore each other a lot in Paris, which i had to get used to. Starting the day later and eating later was also hard for me to adapt to.
culture_appreciated: The aesthetic aspirations, and the romantic lifestyle that still thrives in the country.
top3_advice: Don't worry too much. Things are more loose and you will figure things out along the way.
other_useful_info: Write emails that is your best weapon. Talk to the other students to make calm yourself.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people from all around the world that was an amazing experience. Really gaining new perspectives on the world and myself through discussions with other people.
greatest_challenge: Adapting to a different mindset. Accepting that you cannot control what is going on. The uncertainty about demands, rules and norms, that was difficult to cope with.
