crucial_aspects: The academic level at the University of Copenhagen is already quite high, so I didn't decide to go to abroad for those reasons. Instead I hoped that having completed an exchange semester in another country, would provide me with a more international profil.
overall_comments: It was amazing!
info_ease: It's quite hard to find everything and there is a lot of information. Especially at Sorbonne where it's mostly in French.
arrival_assistance: We received an introduction on the first day in one of the halls. Other than that, we continuously received some information online.
arrival_comments: It was difficult to receive information and Sorbonne is a difficult place. Luckily one is away with other Danes, so you pretty quickly figure it all out by relying on each other.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was amazing!
registration_process: Just did above.
registration_help: Other Danes! Other than that, you figure it out, you can contact the administration and they sort of explain it
registration_success: It took a little while, but I ended up in all the classes I wanted to.
registration_advice: Pray to the French Gods and be calm, know it eventually all works out.
academics_comments: It was amazing!
course_level: The level at the University of Copenhagen imo was generally higher. Sorbonne's history and English department is more like how you imagine universities were in the 19th century. Some professors like to be the only one to talk, and others want a lot of discussions. Some of these discussions are more interesting than others. We had one professor, very disorganized, who asked questions like "What is democracy?" When questions are this open, the class discussion becomes unproductive.
teaching_comparison: Answered that above.
courses_enrolled: Brexit Relation International Satire de Byron et Swift New Perspectives in American Religion
recommended_courses: Brexit was amazing. Madame Charlotte, Professor of British Civilisation is a fantastic teacher.
unexpected_costs: Paris is expensive. Make sure you apply for funding.
cost_comparison: Food! Food was expensive, Especially if you wanted to (you want to) eat out once in a while.
activities_available: Football, chess, all kinds of sports, board game nights etc.
activities_recommended: Take a language course through Sorobnne.
weekend_recommendations: It's Paris, a million things to do. Jazz clubs, running in the local parks, see a movie, go to the fantastic bookstores in the 5th arrondissement.
culture_adjustment: Easy because I lived in the Cite Universitiare with other international young students
socializing_tips: Speak with them from the beginning, do not care about it being awkward. Ask them questions, and just keep going. Rather be that annoying Erasmus person who talks too much but gain 3 friends, than be silent and gain none.
cultural_challenges: I had been to France a few times before so I didn't really notice that many differences. But Paris is a big city, way bigger than Copenhagen. So be prepared for living in a big city.
culture_appreciated: Their love of books. In Denmark books are expensive and always new. Hard to find old ones. In Paris it's everywhere especially archive books. The Food is great. And the University offers more of a personal connection to students (at least in the English department) You can talk more with Professors and develop more than in Copenhagen.
top3_advice: 1. Never speak English with people in Paris when you are out. If they speak English with you, just tell them you don't speak English. They won't believe you, but they will at least keep speaking French so you can practise. 2. Sign up for social clubs and activities at Sorbonne right away. Spots get taken up fast. 3. Decide if you want to live in Cite Universitaire or not. There are positives and negatives to both. Cité gives you instant friends and parties. But you are not truly immersed in Parisian culture. The opposite is true for living outside Cite-.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Speaking French with friends. Presenting in French. Meeting new people who are all incredibly talented. it's crazy in the city. people are either Phd students, singers, or able to speak a million languages. You will feel stupid compared to them, but that's great too.
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to life in Paris, its a huge city after all
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go on exchange in a country where I could practice my French while studying.
info_ease: Not very easy. I did not feel like I had any information until I showed up physically at my Erasmus coordinators office. When I did his response was: "There you are! I've been waiting you", even though he hadn't ask me to come.
arrival_assistance: I quickly learned that sending my coordinators emails was like talking to a wall whereas showing up physically always helped a lot. When in the room the coordinators were actually very nice and helpfull.
arrival_comments: I assume 1 is worst and 5 is best.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I received around 10 - 15 almost unreadable time tables with small coloured course schedules all in abbreviations I did not know. So I had to go to the university's web page to see the courses they had and then guess which abbreviations were which courses. The next problem was that the time tables changed on a weakly basis for all courses making it impossible to build my own study plan. The final problem was communicating the courses I ended up choosing to my course coordinator. I had to show up at his office the day before the courses started because I still hadn't been added to the courses despite my many emails.
registration_help: Help on person, at my coordinators office.
registration_success: As described it was a long and stressful experience but it ended up working out the day before the courses started.
registration_advice: Trust the proces. This was what I was told by a student I talked to who had done the same exchange program before me and it ended up being the best advice I got. My experience with France is that nothing ever goes as planned but that everything always end up well in time anyways. As a metaphor you could say that the busses never follow their time tables but just as you are about to give up, an unknown bus always shows up and gets you to the destination in time.
course_level: I only took bachelor level courses, following the mandatory curriculum with the local students that were in the fifth semester of their BA as well as me.
teaching_comparison: Almost scarily similar. Maybe there was slightly more passion in the teaching but I think that might also just be due to the differences in the Danish and French mentality and expressiveness.
courses_enrolled: Astrophysique, Physique des milieux continus, Physique quantique 1, Optique et électromagnétisme, and Méthodes mathématiques.
recommended_courses: The ones I took if you are on exchange in your 5th semester.
unexpected_costs: The costs of getting a french guarantor (mandatory for everyone renting accommodation in France).
cost_comparison: I ended up spending much more money on social things like café's and restaurants than I had expected. I guess that could have been prevented in principle, but in practice that is very very difficult in a city like Paris.
activities_available: A broad variety of sports and art classes and social events.
activities_recommended: I didn't really use any.
weekend_recommendations: I don't think I know a city with more museums, monuments and nice restaurants than Paris. The opportunities seem endless and in France most museums are free for everyone under the age of 26.
culture_adjustment: It took some weeks but I think that was mostly due to the fact that I was a new place. I don't think the cultural adjustment by itself was a big thing.
socializing_tips: Maybe just take some chances. Because they are most likely not going to interact if you don't take the initiative.
cultural_challenges: Something as small and silly as the different selection in the grocery stores. So as I said, the cultural differences weren't overwhelming.
culture_appreciated: The culture of eating out and eating late.
top3_advice: - Trust the proces. Things often seem stressful and impossible but usually help will turn up when you expect it the least. Just keep calm and don't panic. - Show up aphysically when you have important questions. The academic structures can be complicated and non-logical but the people in the system are nice and ready to help. - Reach out to other students! Especially other exchange students.
other_useful_info: You might hear a couple of times that the administration at Sorbonne is difficult to work with but don't get it wrong: It is definitely worth it and I think I have learned a lot from it.
most_rewarding: Experiencing that everything is gonna work out if you work for it.
greatest_challenge: For me it was studying in French. My level was probably around B2 (some things a bit under, some a bit over) but my experience was that you learn quickly when you hear it every day. And understanding the teachers is a lot easier than understanding your fellow students!

crucial_aspects: I learned French in school and has visited France multiple times. I wanted to improve my language skills while experiencing a new culture and a different health care system
info_ease: The Erasmus coordinator was very nice, and helpful throughout the stay. It was difficult with the hospital in the beginning. Not much information from the department, I had my clinical rotation at. Luckily I started with other Erasmus and local students. I would highly recommend following the rotation dates of the local students, since you will be able to join the planning of their stay and their courses at the hospital.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any assistance. I had to figure out a lot on my own. But people were very happy to help, when asked.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I needed to apply for Sorbonne Université through their own site and also register for a clinical rotation at the hospital department. Many steps an documents needed (including CV, cover letter etc.), but otherwise quite smooth process. Be prepared, they can be quite slow in sending the necessary documents and information. I only received information about when and where my rotation would take place 1,5 month before I was to begin.
registration_help: The Erasmus coordinators from both the University of Copenhagen and Sorbonne Université are available to help via mail.
registration_success: I did not have any classes. I had to prioritize which department I wanted to do my clinical rotation at. I got my number one priority.
registration_advice: Be patient. In the end everything works out.
course_level: I did not take any courses
teaching_comparison: At the hospital many things are more old fashioned than I was used to. Rounds were done in a big group with several doctors and nurses. Many things were still on paper (the patients were expected to keep all their own documents from previous lab work and hospitalizations). The students were expected to have obligatory 24h shifts, and 8-18 shifts. All other days were 8-12, since the local students have theoretical classes at the university in the afternoon.
courses_enrolled: Not enrolled in any courses. I had my clinical rotation at a department of gynaecology and obstetrics.
recommended_courses: Be aware that English friendly department does not mean that everyone speaks English. They will expect you to speak French.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Depending on what foods you want some are cheaper and some are more expensive than in Denmark
activities_available: The Erasmus students who were also enrolled in courses could participate in trips and events by the university.
activities_recommended: Explore the city. Paris has good lunch deals at most restaurants. There are markets almost every weekend (can be found at brocabrac.fr).
weekend_recommendations: Go to the smaller cities around Paris. Disneyland is a great theme park (albeit an expensive one)
culture_adjustment: The initial learning curve for me was very steep. My French improved a lot and fast during the stay.
socializing_tips: Start your rotation at the same time as them!
cultural_challenges: There can be a lot of paperwork and necessary steps in order to get things done. They can take time, but in the end it usually works out.
culture_appreciated: The locals take their time to enjoy things. Not everything has to be fast paced.
top3_advice: Go for it! The Erasmus coordinators are very nice (and speak English) and want to help. Be prepared for an immersive language experience - they talk fast, but don't be afraid to tell them that you don't understand.
other_useful_info: Be prepared for long processes and early deadlines (both for the university and for grants).
most_rewarding: Feeling that my French improved to a point where the locals would stop changing to English. Being able to enjoy the food and culture of the city at a much slower pace than is usually feasible on shorter trips.
greatest_challenge: In the beginning not understanding the language as well and feeling very stupid, when having to ask people to repeat multiple times.

crucial_aspects: The philosophy programme offered at Sorbonne University, and the possibility to improve my french, and lastly also because of the parisian culture.
info_ease: Sorbonne University had sent e-mails that were quite detailed, but they always came a bit late, so it was hard not to be a little anxious if something had gone wrong.
arrival_assistance: There were two different erasmus meetings, one general and one that was philosophy-specific which was quite detailed and thorough. Also it helped me a lot, that I have already studied there one semester during my BA-studies, so I knew my way around their particularities.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I was sent a link to a google sheets document where I had to write which courses I wanted to take.
registration_help: You can go to the philosophy office and ask the people there.
registration_success: I got the ones I wanted.
registration_advice: Go to the erasmus meetings, and stay in contact with others who are going on exchange in that department, as Sorbonne sometimes mix up mail addresses. One of my friends did for example not receive all the official mails for some reason.
course_level: I found the level on most courses to be sufficiently high, while not too difficult to follow if you spend a normal time on studying.
teaching_comparison: It is quite different in a lot of positive ways. It is more "old-school", meaning that professors usually have prepared a lecture that they give which is quite like a manuscript that they have prepared, that is usually complicated, which means that if you are well prepared you can get a lot out of it, and if you are less prepared you still learn something. What I'm getting at is that it seems that they don't focus so much on pedagogics or making sure that everyone is on the same page, but give an interesting lecture that draws on a lot of different material in order to make points about the given topic. As such the courses are usually way more topic-oriented where the professor is trying to give their own take or reading of a topic through incorporation of a lot of different sources. For me that makes the lectures more interesting because they take you through a line of thought which is similar to philosophical work, which is a bit different from the lectures that are usually given at UCPH where the focus is more that we should understand a specific text or idea for each lecture, which gives the lectures more of introductory feel. That said this more "old-school" approach has its downsides in that it is not clear what the students are supposed to read, but once you get used to this way of studying where you can more freely choose which texts you want to read, it is quite motivational. Another thing that I like which is different is that professors often encourage you to read books, rather than just academic papers, which I find more engaging as this gives you incitement to get deeper into the philosophers that are discussed in the specific course.
courses_enrolled: Philosophy of Physics Temporalities of works of art What is phenomenological in Hegel's 'Phenomenology of Spirit' 'Phenomenology of Perception' by Merleau-Ponty System and history in german idealism - methodology of history of philosophy Lastly I also took a french language course on C1 level.
recommended_courses: I especially can recommend the more history-oriented philosophy courses (Phenomenology of Perception, and System and History), but also the metaphysics course about Hegel's Phenomenoogy of spirit. Lastly I can recommend to try a course on the philosophy of art, to try to make amends for the fact that aesthetics are not on the study programme in UCPH.
unexpected_costs: Electricity bill from my apartment was way higher than expected due to electric heating and bad insulation.
cost_comparison: Books are very cheap. Food and drinks outside are generally cheaper than DK, while groceries are about the same. Transportation is not too bad if you are willing to bike on the public bike service.
activities_available: I didn't enroll in any but I know that there are some free sport activites you can join which I heard are quite nice actually. Most museums and the like are free in Paris if you are under 26 and a student.
activities_recommended: I can't tell as I didn't participate in any at the university.
weekend_recommendations: Museums, because they might be free if you are young enough and there are so many good ones. Also going to vernissages for the galleries as there are usually some free drinks and you get to see what new or upcoming artists are working on. Visiting all the well-equipped and weird antiquity stores as well as second-hand book shops. In general enjoying a cheap coffee or wine on the cafés.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy
socializing_tips: Don't be shy, although I didn't really socialize that much with the local students.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier.
culture_appreciated: The lively streets and cafés.
top3_advice: Be careful with following the procedures that you receive in e-mail from Sorbonne, but also don't hesitate to write them an e-mail if you are suspecting that they forgot to send you some important information. Don't take too many courses, as it can be hard to make a good schedule and have time to read as well, or supply with a french course as they have a lighter work-load per ECTS point. Practice your hand-writing.
other_useful_info: Get accustomed to writing by hand by taking notes by hand as well, most exams in the philosophy department are written in hand.
most_rewarding: Finishing the exams and feeling that I did a good job. And making friends with other exchange students.
greatest_challenge: Exams.

crucial_aspects: Going to a big city with plenty of opportunities, subcultures and exploring the capital and the lifestyle here.
overall_comments: What made my stay was the people I've met and the things if been doing in my freetime more than my experience with the university.
info_ease: It was difficult, I spent many many hours on trying to figure out the website of Sorbonne, trying to find which courses were available to me etc. I had to be in close contact with my councelors in order to solve administrative challenges and the host university was impossible to reach.
arrival_assistance: I was still in contact with the studyabroad councelors from Denmark online, but I didn't receive any assistance in Paris.
arrival_comments: It was very complicated to figure out who to contact for various problems, and the administrators from Sorbonne kept telling me to contact someone else, as if no one knew who was actually supposed to help.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: What made my stay was the people I've met and the things if been doing in my freetime more than my experience with the university.
registration_process: There were a lot of steps and deadlines, so you have to check your ku-mail often. Some of the steps take a long time and are quite frustrating, especially the pre-approval that is difficult to make and feels meaningless since you'll most likely get completely different courses when you arrive. We had a nice introduction to everything and the councelors were always helpfull and fast at answering.
registration_help: The UCPHabroad councelors, the student councelors and studienævnet.
registration_success: Pretty succesfull, but it was all a gamble and I was lucky with showing up in good time and having professors that accepted me even though there weren't officially more spots in the classes.
registration_advice: The registration process is chaotic, tou show up and write what classes you want on a paper - and then you get a spot if there are still available spots, if not you have to find another class. I recommend already making the puzzle with plan B's before the day where you sign up and showing up in good time so the popular spots aren't already filled.
academics_comments: What made my stay was the people I've met and the things if been doing in my freetime more than my experience with the university.
course_level: I took two courses on the 3rd year, and they were the most interesting but very difficult! The courses on 1st and 2nd year were easier but felt a lot like high school classes.
teaching_comparison: Very authoritorian. The teachers were mostly talking and always presented the right answer. Even if they facilitated a dialogue with the students they would present their own "right" interpretation afterwards. The teachers would be direct with interrupting the students and letting them know if they didn't agree with their answers.

recommended_courses: Littératures francophones if you have a good level of French - same with litteraturen européenes. I would also recommend the SIAL/FLE course.
unexpected_costs: Very expensive metro tickets before getting my carte navigo (because of the olympics). Extra insurance costs.
cost_comparison: Food is expensive + public transportation. Cultural offers are not very expensive.
activities_available: Almost everything you can imagine.
activities_recommended: Try some of the sport offers.
weekend_recommendations: Travel around France if you have the time. Go to the south with the train network! Enjoy the many museums of Paris if you enjoy that. Go to koncerts and events. Engage in local politics and activism. Markets, independant cinemas, cycle around the city, go to the forest and see the different suburbs.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. I was engaged in a very local group of French people that were extremely open and introduced me to their friends and lives. Of course it was difficult not speaking French fluently and not knowing anyone before, but they were very welcoming and people I'm staying in contact with!
socializing_tips: I actually didn't really socialize with the local students since I had such a big network connected to the people I lived with. But I do recommend socializing through dating apps, also if it's just to find friends. In that way you can find people you align with and whom are also interested in new connections.
cultural_challenges: Discussing and complaining a lot. I found it difficult to participate in those kinds of conversations.
culture_appreciated: The way of welcoming me, bringing me with them and introducing me to their friends and social groups. The way of having a home that was always open for and curious towards guests and how they tried to include me in their conversations even with my level of French.
top3_advice: Live with other people, it will open up tour world and give you connections to the city that you can keep afterwards. Come some time before and/or stay after, so you have time to explore the city and travel. Reach out to other erasmus students and to the local students to get through the courses.
other_useful_info: Don't let it tear you down that you're not doing well in the classes. Be curious and ask questions. Find other erasmus students in your classes and help each other. Focus on the formalia of the exams, it counts a lot, even more than the content.
most_rewarding: Getting to know all of these people and improving my French. Getting to know a new city and having connections here now, that I can come back to. Learning more about French culture and politics. Experiencing the French school system even though I don't see myself thriving in it.
greatest_challenge: Passing the exams and cracking the code of how to write them. Even just understanding and following the courses.
other_comments: The university will be tough, so try to put yourself in to other constelations that bring you joy while you're here - and that will make it more than worth it!

info_ease: It was not entirely simple. Generally speaking, i found the website of Sorbonne University hard to navigate, and I had to send several emails to completely understand the process of choosing courses etc. The people responsible were helpful, but i think it was hard for them to understand to what point the country's education system is different from ours and therefore to what extent the administrative approached where hard to understand.
arrival_assistance: There was a meeting where the proceedings where presented, and that was pretty much it.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_success: Very successful. Unfortunately some things weren't possible because of timetable conflicts, but the university was definitely not at fault.

teaching_comparison: Generally very different. Less pedagogical.

crucial_aspects: I knew that Sorbonne University was a university that was well known around the world. I also liked that I could develop my French language skills while being there.
info_ease: It took a lot of emails back and forward to get the information that I needed. The catalogue with their courses is hard to find and they don't offer a lot of English courses. I was allowed to be part of a master program where they spoke English but as I understand it it is not everyone that is allowed to take part of their master courses. When I was first registered as a part of Sorbonne I got all the emails from a coordinator at Sorbonne and that worked very well.
arrival_assistance: There is an exchange office at Sorbonne that provided me with a lot of help. There is also a coordinator that helped me a lot through email.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to fill out a learning agreement and send it to my coordinator. It took a few tries to get it signed but after it was signed it was very easy. My coordinator just enrolled me in all of the courses.
registration_help: I would say so yes. It was hard to actually figure out which courses I was allowed to take but after that I didn't have to do anything.
registration_success: I wished for some master second year courses (M2) that I wasn't allowed to take. I ended up getting a full semester of classes that followed the first semester of the master "from fundamental molecular biosciences to biotherapies" which I can recommend.
registration_advice: If you are good at French then take the bachelor classes because they are easier to get. If you don't want classes in French the master I went to was very nice.
course_level: I took master courses but I didn't find them harder than a bachelor course at University of Copenhagen. The level was fine. I also had a lab course where I would say it was a bit easy because a lot of the other students didn't have a lot of lab experience.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching didn't really suit me. There is a lot of courses that only consists of 2 hour lectures and that is it. 2 hours was a long time for me and I had a hard time concentrating. I also didn't feel like I got the information in because there wasn't any reinforcements.

unexpected_costs: Most people get their danish phone plan cancelled after 3 months abroad and had to get a French one but that didn't happen to me.
cost_comparison: The food was a bit more expensive than I thought but otherwise it was good.
activities_available: There was a lot of sports both at the university and where I lived and it was very cheap and easy to register.
activities_recommended: Every first sunday of the month Kapela Marna teaches a house dance class, first beginner and then advanced, at club djoon. It is called soulful sunday and it is amazing. such great vibes.
weekend_recommendations: I would definetely recommend going to Bretagne and Normandy
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy.
socializing_tips: In general it is a little hard to get contact to French students but if you can find some to live with that is a good way.
cultural_challenges: The French people are a bit more reserved because there is more hierarchy.
culture_appreciated: The fashion. A lot of people were hats, the fashion it definitely more bold.
top3_advice: It is important to call your teachers with madam and monsieur and not by their first name. It is considered rude. There is a lot of late hours. There is a lot of sports opportunities.

crucial_aspects: The most crucial aspects were my love for French culture, especially literature, film, café culture, manner of life, and their worldview. The French love beauty and have a very different approach to life then my countrymen of my native Denmark, an attitude which I found appealing. Furthermore, I wanted to make sure that I had a decent level of competence in spoken French when finishing my bachelor in French culture and language.
info_ease: Relatively easy. As long as I knew the basics of asking questions, such as directions, I encountered no significant problems. The team at UCPHabroad were also a great help.
arrival_assistance: None in particular that I recall, but it was relatively easy to find my university, classes, and such, since I had received a fair amount of instructions before arrival.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to register at a certain office, have my date of arrival at the institution signed, and sign up for a student card. Fairly easy, simply had to meet up at the time and location which was described in the documents I received.
registration_help: Most likely, but since none was necessary I did not check.
registration_success: Very much so; it was a bit difficult to understand the way to do it, but the faculty was always very helpful and patient.
registration_advice: Read the documents you receive carefully some time before the date of registration.
course_level: Some were more difficult than others; I mostly took first and third year classes. The ones that were too difficult I changed and there was a great deal of leeway, since one could change classes until the Easter vacation.
teaching_comparison: Less focused on dialogue, more on listening to lecturs and writing notes, sometimes verbatim. I prefered it frankly.

recommended_courses: Depending on your level of French mostly first and second year classes. There are also options to take classes in English which I would recommend, simply to not stress out too much about the language barrier, and to give the mind a break.
unexpected_costs: None than I can recall except for frequent visits to the boulangeries.
cost_comparison: I come from Denmark so just about everything was less expensive than I expected.
activities_available: Various, but I did not pay them any mind.
activities_recommended: Frequent walks through Paris and reading the newspaper for French practice at cafés.
weekend_recommendations: Besides the basic tourist traps? The cathedrals of Chartres, Amiens, and Reims.
culture_adjustment: It took me some months before I recovered from the slight culture shock, but I came to feel home at ease in Paris after about 2-3 months.
socializing_tips: Not many, most French seem a bit more isolated than expected. They are however kind and friendly, so I would not worry about talking to them - it's the befriending aspect that is a bit more difficult, getting them to really open up.
cultural_challenges: The French sense of humor is rather different from Danish and a Anglo-American humor. It's something that's difficult to really explain, but there is a definite difference which can be difficult to understand at first.
culture_appreciated: Just about everything! Contrary to what I have been told, the French are some of the most polite people I have ever meet. Perhaps not the always the warmest, I appreciated the norms of greeting before and after leaving a store or place, even if you're strangers. Besides that, the ease of enjoyment, simple pleasures such as taking a walk, sitting down around Paris or in a café, the food and bakeries, the weather in the warmer months, hearing the language on the streets, and so on.
top3_advice: Master the basics of greeting when entering a store or place and saying goodbye - politeness is vital for good interaction with most French people. Learn how to relax and enjoy the city, not to necessarily go to Versailles or Louvre all the time, but to just take a walk throughout the city. I do not think there is a city I have just spontaneously explored than Paris. Visit and buy from actual shops that sell meat, fish, cheese, bakeries, and please do not just buy everything at a supermarket.
other_useful_info: Keep calm and accept that there is a lot of bureaucracy and be ready to ask questions if you have the slightest doubt whether via mail or in person.
most_rewarding: The totality of French culture. It's really wonderful if you try not to force it into a box of romanticised expectations.
greatest_challenge: Definitely the language: I feel that there are sadly many things I have missed because I have not mastered the language.

crucial_aspects: I am very fond of the French language and culture, which were two important factors for me. I wanted to study in a French speaking country to improve my language skills. This was the most important factor, since I knew that choosing a French bachelor probably would come with its difficulties, so the academic/career oportunities were not too important for me.
overall_comments: The study program was very hard since it was in French but I loved living in Paris. So living in Paris made up for the tough study.
info_ease: It was quite difficult. Sorbonne Université, at least the science faculty, is very disorganized and there wasn't a lot of information about anything. If there is something that is not clear or information is missing you have to take contact to your coordinator at Sorbonne. I had a very nice coordinator who helped a lot with course registration and other practical things such as a new learning platform (Moodle) and mail, etc.
arrival_assistance: My coordinator at Sorbonne was a big help. She was helpful, but I had to reach out to her to get any information, so the information doesn't come by itself. The best way to get in contact is definitely showing up at the office in person, since an email correspondance can take a few days.
arrival_comments: There was little to no information about the program and the faculty so you had to find all the information yourself. Everyone is pretty kind and helpful when you ask them.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The study program was very hard since it was in French but I loved living in Paris. So living in Paris made up for the tough study.
registration_process: You had to fill out different information about yourself, uploading passport, picture for a student card, etc. You could also sign up for housing. It was pretty straightforward as I remember it.
registration_help: My Erasmus-coordinator was helpful if information was missing or something wasn't clear. He could take a few days to respond, and in the middle of registration he went on vacation for 2 weeks. But, it will all work out, they seem to be very large and understanding if anything goes wrong.
registration_success: This was the most difficult process. First of all, I had to learn the course codes and I ended up registering for courses on the 6th semester instead of the 5th semester the first time (L3 is year 3 and the number after 'SV' (5) is the semester - at least on the bachelor). There were multiple classes I wanted to take, but the bachelor has a very strict structure so it is not easy to compose your own schedule. I had to follow the obligatory courses like the rest of the students, since these are on monday-tuesday-wednesday (UE tronc-commun) and then all the optional courses (UE complémentaire) were thursday-friday. I had by accident chosen an UE complémentaire that hadn't been accepted as a limited-optional (begrænset-valgfri) course at KU and had to change it to another course the week before courses started. It was luckily possible to change, just show up at the coordinators office.
registration_advice: Ask your coordinator for the course schedules to see what time and days the different courses are. There are many courses that overlap and it does not say anything about it in the course catalogue. So to figure out what courses are actually available and possible to take, the course schedule is the most important thing. Look at the proposed schedule on the Sorbonne website for your study. This helps to see what options there are.
academics_comments: The study program was very hard since it was in French but I loved living in Paris. So living in Paris made up for the tough study.
course_level: I don't think the level of the courses were more difficult than they would have been at KU, but since it was in French it was way harder.
teaching_comparison: It is very different to KU. There are no books, the days are much longer because there are more classes and lectures in a day to make up for the lack of books and self-study. The lectures (CM) and TD's are each 2 hours without a break and most days were from 8:30h to 18h. There are many midterms, papers and presentations to do during the semester. I took 7 courses, compared to max. 2 at a time at KU (block structure), which made the work load a bit overwhelming at times. The amount of ECTS for most courses are 3 or 6. The workload of the 3 ECTS courses are, in my opinion, way to big for the amount of credits given.
courses_enrolled: LU3SV515 - Neurophysiologie et Physiologie des grandes fonctions LU3SV517 - Biologie du développement des Plantes LU3SV518 - Microbiologie LU3SV524 - Les microorganismes pathogènes LU3SV541 - Cerveau et comportement LU3FLE01 - French course FLE (science faculty) SIAL-FLE - online french grammar course from faculté des Lettres
recommended_courses: I recommend all of them. They are all very interesting and I don't think it is something we are taught at KU. There are more teaching in specific diseases, bacteria, functions which can be difficult to remember because the information is not that broad. LU3SV515 is a pretty difficult course with an extremely large curriculum. LU3SV541 was very interesting with topics such as conscience, emotions, addiction and different experimental methods to study the brain.
unexpected_costs: I don't think there were any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: The monthly transport pass (navigo) was more expensive than I imagined. Restaurants were a bit cheaper than Copenhagen.
activities_available: I don't know about cultural or social activities. There are many different sports like rock climbing, fenching, yoga and swimming.
activities_recommended: The Parismus events like walks around Paris, trips and parties.
weekend_recommendations: There are many things to see in Paris but also many cities/countries that are easy and close by (Luxembourg and Belgium). Museums are free for students under 26 years old. Train tickets from SNCF can be pretty cheap sometimes. Walking around in Paris is nice.
culture_adjustment: It was easy. Paris is not so different from other european cities. Most things are in french and most people only speak french, even the students, but if you speak french it is not difficult to adjust.
socializing_tips: I did not end up socializing with any of the french students, only the international students. The french students seem very closed off and didn't make an effort to speak to me just like I didn't try either. There is almost no group work and no one (not even the french students) talk to each other during class. L3 in biology is huge, with around 400 students, so there are no social events either inside the study.
cultural_challenges: The french students are not very likely to small talk, but I guess it is kind of the same in Copenhagen.
culture_appreciated: The amount of museums and other cultural things around Paris. Parisians seem to go more out for dinner during the week, which is a nice way to make a weekday fun.
top3_advice: Better to speak french at a C1 level. I spoke B2 when I arrived, it was manageable but very hard. Show up to every class, it helps with exams and other information. Trust that everything will fall into place. It is possible to change courses the week before the fall semester, the year structure is first out during the summer and I wasn't aware of the startday of any of my courses except for a few days before.
other_useful_info: It is important to write formal emails and adress the professors as M. or Mme. Definetly use the whatsapp groups and google drive for studying and reviewing.
most_rewarding: Getting friends from all over the world and living in Paris.
greatest_challenge: Studying in french.
other_comments: Even though the study was difficult, the experience of living in Paris and being abroad made up for it all.

socializing_tips: Just talk to them. They might seem aloof or distant, but when you talk to them, they are nice and open. I think the atmosphere in the classes I was in was less friendly than at the UCPH. The french students seem less friendly with eachother too.
cultural_challenges: In Paris there is a different attitude towards personal space. The city is crowded or even congested. I lived in the cité universitaire, which was nice, but I shared a kitchen with 30-40 people (which is part of the reason why I would have prefered private housing). The metro is crammed especially during rush hours. You are literally rubbing shoulders with multiple people. In the classes at the Sorbonne, there was not always enough seats and some students had to sit on the floor, even during tests/exams. The french have different approach to being ill and there is an obligation to attend classes. Therefore people often show up ill. I have tried sitting next to someone who was blowing their nose continually for three hours. This happened several times. The Sorbonne bulding is very old and there is a lot of noise outside the building. Therefore the staff rarely want to open the windows, which means that the air in the classrooms is for the most part very bad. Some of the rooms are even filled with mold. I had to change a class because of mold.
culture_appreciated: The language.
top3_advice: Live privately if you can afford it. Choose courses at master level even if you are doing your bachelor, since they seem to be more interesting. If you want a more easy stay, consider taking some courses in english. I took all my courses in french, except a french language C1 course. It meant I had a lot of studying to do, but regarding learning their specific ways of structuring papers, the different courses supported eachother, since the forms of writing were similar between the courses.
other_useful_info: It is not necessary to attend the lectures to pass or even excel at the exams. Halfway during my stay, I started mainly attending the seminars and skipping many of the lectures. There are many more classes to attend than at the UCPH, and this gave me a bit more breathing space. Attendance is only obligatory for the seminars. Often the relation between the seminars and the lectures is very vague, and the teachers are not the same.
most_rewarding: There was one teacher who insisted on evaluating all students the same. Therefore all the exchange students did not pass the mid semester exam. For the end of semester exam I studied very intensely, and I got a top grade, which was so high that it made up for the points my first exam lacked. Therefore my average was high enough for me to pass the course. This was very satisfying, also so I do not have to take another course or write a paper to make up for it at th UCPH. Most exhange students did not pass the course. It was littératures européennes. I do not recommend taking that course, also since the teacher of the seminars is not very good and communicating.
greatest_challenge: See above. The exams. The difficulty of corresponding with relevant faculty.

crucial_aspects: Academic opportunity was the biggest aspect, having worked with French thinkers and writers throughout my degree. The language aspect, then, was probably the most important of all. overall_comments: In true French grading fashion, there is always room for improvement.
info_ease: Sorbonne certainly doesn't make it easy if you want to be well ahead of time. But upon arrival the faculty had distributed pamphlets by email, clearly explaining the process, when to arrive for the orientations and how to choose courses.
arrival_assistance: Introductory orientations, as well as the possibility of meeting with an Erasmus coordinator specific to my study area within her office hours.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: In true French grading fashion, there is always room for improvement.
registration_process: Sorbonne is old school, and you register by crosschecking course lists and timetables. These documents are difficult to find if you don't know where to look. A link was distributed, but much later than expected. It is understandable, there is a lot of organising to fit all the courses in at logical times. At the beginning of the year you meet in person, having prepared your courses, and fill them in on a piece of paper, which is then handed to your coordinator. (S)he handles the rest.
registration_help: The Erasmus orientation pamphlet distributed by mail and the coordinator. Ask people who have been on an exchange before!
registration_success: More or less successful, all in all.
registration_advice: Don't stress too much about it. Keep a level head, it's gonna work itself out.
academics_comments: In true French grading fashion, there is always room for improvement.
course_level: The level was high. Studying literature in French on master level at the Sorbonne is no walk in the park. There is loads to read. Having said that, some of the students at the Sorbonne are very young, and do not necessarily have the same base of knowledge. I was surprised by the very introductory nature of one of my courses, it being a master seminar.
teaching_comparison: The teaching at UCPH is a lot more interactive, the students taking part in discussions, sometimes even in shaping the curriculum. At the Sorbonne, with few exceptions, you show up, listen to a lecture for two hours, then exit. There is always the possibility of posing questions, but the style is a lot more conservative generally. But the academic level is high all around.

activities_available: There are some clubs and sports associations. The opportunity is there, it seems. Again, I am not the right person to answer this.
activities_recommended: Do sports to compensate for all the cerebral work! And visit as many museums as you can. There are loads. If the city feels too crowded, take the train to the Fontainebleau forest.
weekend_recommendations: Take a trip to the rest of France as well, like Bretagne, Normandie, Provence …
culture_adjustment: It suits me well, they are generally outgoing, polite and forthcoming.
socializing_tips: Talk to them! They are friendly!
cultural_challenges: The French are very polite, and might seem impersonal at first, but if you talk to them they are (mostly) very approachable and ready for a chat.
culture_appreciated: The talkativeness, and the fact that people spend a lot of time on the streets. It makes the city very lively and welcoming. Within a week I was on a friendly basis with the staff at the restaurant on the corner of my building.
top3_advice: Keep calm. It's stressful, but it will work itself out. Find something to do, an activity, outside of the University. That way you'll meet more and different people. crucial_aspects: Paris has always been a city of dreams for me — not only because of its undeniable beauty and cultural richness, but also because it is the cradle of the French language. As a student of French at Københavns Universitet, immersing myself in everyday life in Paris was the best way to deepen my linguistic skills and cultural understanding. I was drawn to the academic prestige of Sorbonne Université, known for its strong humanities faculty, and the opportunity to study French in its natural habitat — cafés, bouquinistes, ballet studios, and buzzing classrooms. Beyond academics, I was inspired by the city’s rhythm — the art, fashion, and café culture — all of which shaped my experience both inside and outside the classroom.
info_ease: It was quite difficult to find the information I needed. Sorbonne’s website was very outdated and confusing to navigate, especially when trying to access course listings and timetables. Important details were often missing or scattered across different platforms. I had to rely on other exchange students and forums to piece together essential information.
arrival_assistance: I received minimal assistance upon arrival. There was, though, a formal orientation or welcome event for international students – but in French, and very short. Most of the administrative help came through email correspondence, which was often delayed or unclear. It took a long time to get clarity on course selection, and there was little to no support in helping students settle in.
arrival_comments: Despite the administrative struggles, once classes started, the academic experience was rewarding. However, I would strongly recommend Sorbonne to improve its communication and support for international students, especially during the crucial first weeks of arrival.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Most French courses had to be registered for manually by visiting the administration office and requesting your paper file, which you would physically update if you added, changed, or dropped a class. This made things unnecessarily complicated and time-consuming. For English courses, it was handled through email, but responses were often delayed or unclear. There was no central online portal where you could manage your choices or see your complete schedule.
registration_help: One aspect I really appreciated was the support I received for my mental health. I disclosed that I had a psychiatric condition, and the university was very understanding. I was granted accommodations, such as extended exam time, shorter written assignments, and the freedom to leave the classroom during exams if needed. This made a big difference for me and allowed me to focus more on learning rather than managing stress.
registration_success: I didn’t end up getting any of the classes I originally planned to take, which felt disappointing at first. But in hindsight, it turned out to be a blessing — there were so many incredible courses to choose from, and the ones I eventually got were absolutely perfect for me. They challenged me, inspired me, and I ended up doing really well academically. I truly wouldn’t change a thing.
registration_advice: Be prepared for last-minute changes and expect a certain level of disorganisation — but don’t panic. Things might not go according to your plan, but that doesn’t mean they won’t work out beautifully. Stay flexible, ask other exchange students for advice, and trust that you’ll end up in classes that suit you, even if they weren’t your first choice.
course_level: I took BA-level courses during my exchange, and overall, the academic level felt more demanding than what I was used to at UCPH. The structure was more rigid, and there was a greater emphasis on individual study and memorisation. However, as an international student with a documented disability, I was met with great understanding. My professors were incredibly kind and accommodating, which helped balance out the intensity of the academic expectations.
teaching_comparison: To be honest, the teaching style at Sorbonne wasn’t all that different from what I’m used to at UCPH. It was a mix of lectures and some student interaction, depending on the professor. The main difference was the structure around registration and course management — not the actual teaching. I also really appreciated how understanding and flexible my professors were when it came to my disabilities. They made sure I felt comfortable and supported, which created a safe and encouraging learning environment.

recommended_courses: I would highly recommend the course Études théâtrales – Contemporary British Drama: Ethics and Aesthetics. As someone who is very creative, I found it incredibly inspiring — the discussions were rich, and it gave me a lot of freedom to interpret and express ideas. I also really appreciated the distance-learning course in French. It was well-structured and gave me the flexibility to manage my own time and workload, which was especially helpful during stressful weeks. Both courses challenged me in the best way and helped me grow academically and personally.
unexpected_costs: I had to visit both a doctor and a hospital during my stay, and unfortunately, I had to pay for everything out of pocket. My private insurance didn’t cover it, and the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) was of no help at all in my case. It came as quite a shock, especially since I had expected most healthcare to be covered. I recommend other students look very carefully into their insurance coverage before going abroad — especially when it comes to specialist visits and emergencies.
cost_comparison: Surprisingly, groceries were less expensive than I had expected — especially the basics I needed for simple meals. I was able to find affordable options at local supermarkets like Franprix, Carrefour, and Monoprix. That really helped me keep my daily costs down. On the other hand, cafés and eating out could be quite pricey, so I mostly stuck to cooking at home or grabbing coffee and small snacks instead of full meals.
activities_available: N/A
activities_recommended: N/A
weekend_recommendations: Skip the packed museums and the long tourist lines — the real magic of Paris is in the streets. I recommend simply getting lost in the city. Walk for hours with no destination. Let yourself wander into hidden courtyards, small boulangeries, and charming squares. Sit down at a café, order a coffee or a noisette, and strike up a conversation with someone nearby. The soul of Paris reveals itself slowly, in moments of spontaneity and softness. Trust it — and trust yourself.
culture_adjustment: Paris is magical, but it can also be intimidating at first. People might seem distant, and the bureaucracy can be overwhelming. But once I found my rhythm — my walking routes, my favorite café, my safe places — I adjusted beautifully. The key is to observe, adapt, and embrace the small rituals of daily Parisian life. It didn’t take long before it truly felt like home.
socializing_tips: French students can seem reserved, but they’re often warm and curious once you break the ice. I recommend joining specific seminars or smaller classes where it’s easier to talk. Don’t be afraid to ask for help or offer to study together — it’s a great way to connect. Also, showing genuine interest in French culture (even if you make mistakes!) always goes a long way.
cultural_challenges: The administrative system was the biggest cultural shock — it was slow, confusing, and deeply paper-based. I also found that personal space and direct communication were handled differently than in Denmark. But with time, I learned to navigate it all with patience, a bit of charm, and a deep breath. It taught me resilience in a very French way.
culture_appreciated: I truly appreciated how open and friendly people actually were — despite the stereotypes, I found it easy to start conversations, especially at cafés. The café culture itself was something I fell in love with: sitting for hours with one drink, watching life pass by, and connecting with strangers who often became friends. There’s also a romantic quietness to how Parisians go about their day — slow mornings, beauty in small details, and a deep respect for art, language, and presence.
top3_advice: 1. Don’t trust the stereotype — Parisians are actually very kind if you approach them openly and speak a bit of French. 2. Be prepared for a chaotic registration process and old-school administration — stay patient and flexible. 3. Explore everything outside the classroom: take walks, talk to strangers, sit at cafés, and let the city shape you.
other_useful_info: If you plan to take extracurriculars like ballet or sports, be aware that the cultural tone can be very different. I took ballet classes in Paris and the teacher was quite harsh and body-focused — something that’s still considered normal in traditional French ballet culture. It was challenging, but also eye-opening. Also: bring copies of every single document you might need — printed, signed, and in multiple versions. It sounds silly until you’re standing in a Sorbonne hallway begging someone to accept your form…
most_rewarding: Finding out that I could build a life from scratch — in a new city, a new system, with a new rhythm. I formed friendships with strangers, walked miles through Paris every day, learned how to survive chaotic bureaucracy, and still managed to thrive. I grew more confident, more independent, and more in love with the world. The quiet moments — a solo coffee, a successful conversation in French, a walk in the golden light — were the most rewarding of all.
greatest_challenge: Navigating the French bureaucracy and the disorganised university system was incredibly frustrating at times. From course registration to medical care, I often felt like I was left to figure things out alone. It tested my patience and resilience. But I also struggled with maintaining mental health in a high-pressure environment far from home. Fortunately, I reached out and found support — and that made all the difference.
other_comments: Paris wasn’t always easy, but it was unforgettable. I left with more than just academic credits — I left with stories, lessons, friendships, and a stronger sense of self. I’d do it all again in a heartbeat. And to anyone going: say yes more often. Speak French even when you’re scared. Wear what makes you feel beautiful. Walk everywhere. Sit in the sun. Live it slowly.

The most tricky part was that I didn´t understand that there were certain combinations of courses I couldn´t take within Geography. They had written me an email about it, but it was very technical and I didn´t understand it. The professor who wrote be the email was not to be found in an office, and the administration I talked to didn´t know about her rules, so they allowed be to registrer for the courses I took even though I wasn´t allowed according to the professor who send me the email. It was partly my fault since I didn´t understand everything in the email. However my critique of the administration is that they gave me different information because they didn´t know of the same rules.
registration_help: As mentioned, the Erasmus-coordinator was almost impossible to reach. He didn´t reply for over a month and wasn´t in his office in his office hours. (He only had one office hour per week, and he wasn´t there two weeks in a row when I searched for him).
registration_success: In the end I managed to find some courses that were approved by my home university as well - thanks to my many free elective courses in my study program. But I had to give up on the courses in Geography that I had originally planed to take.
registration_advice: Be patient. Read the emails carefully. Don´t expect much help.
course_level: I took courses from first year of bachelor to master-level courses. They were all great. I found a couple of courses in english on master level in the program Philosophy of Science. The master courses were of course much more difficult than the ones in the bachelor.
teaching_comparison: In general the courses consisted mostly of lectures. Very little, if any group work. Often no power points. Closed book, hand written exams.
courses_enrolled: Chimie et Société, Philosophie des Sciences, Bioéthique, Francais B2, Démocratie et Écologie, Darwinism and Metaphysics, Philosophy of Medicine, Travaille Personnelle.
recommended_courses: Chimie et Société if you want the possibility to take the course online and in your own speed, there is a lot of work though. Philosophie des Sciences on first year of bachelor if you want and easy course (although it can also be time consuming) with power point. Démocratie et Écologie, Darwinism and Metaphysics and Philosophy of Medicine were all really interesting with very competent teachers. Bioéthique is difficult to understand in french because there is no power point, but the exam is not too hard.
unexpected_costs: Non. It is overall an expensive city and most of the social life takes place in the cafés, bars and restaurants.
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than expected.
activities_available: Different kind of sport.
activities_recommended: Museums and parcs.
weekend_recommendations: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont and canal St Martin - follow it all the way up north.
culture_adjustment: It is a nice culture with a lively atmosphere outside especially in the springtime and summer.
socializing_tips: Take a language course. If you have time, then do an intensive language course before the semester begins. It is a good way to meet international people. I found it difficult to become friends with french people.
cultural_challenges: The language, it is difficult to meet and become friends with french people. And there isn´t any long breaks during the courses to chat with the other students.
culture_appreciated: Also the language. Even though it makes it more difficult to meet locals, it is a lovely language and a good way to become better at french is to do a semester at Sorbonne. And then I loved the lively culture of the cafés.
top3_advice: Be patient with the administration. Take a french course and mingle with the internationals. Go to events by the university if you hear of anything - I heard about it through the students on the third year of the bachelor - there are whatsapp groups for the different programs - try to find students to add you to that and tell you about events.
other_useful_info: You have quite a long time after the semester has started to attend different courses and registrer for the ones you like the most. You don´t have to decide it all in advance.
most_rewarding: That I became much better at french and that I had some very interesting courses with good professors.
greatest_challenge: The amount of exams. You have to take a lot of courses and there are often more exams in one course.

crucial_aspects: I chose Sorbonne because I wanted to go on exchange to a university with a high academic level, and I wanted to go to an interesting country with the opportunity to learn a new language.
overall_comments: The academic level at Sorbonne was sometimes high and sometimes not so much.
info_ease: Very difficult. None of the information is sent out, and often there was not a person or office you could go to to figure things out. Extremely frustrating experience. Moreover, there is a lot of things which you dont know that you dont know, and noone is helping you with it.
arrival_assistance: None. A welcome event was held 1 or 2 weeks after the start of the semester. Ironically, half of the event was held in french. Registering for courses is not centralized, so you have to the one person in the whole university responsible for signing people up for the given course. Meaning if you take 5 courses, which is normal, you have to find the 5 individuals that can sign you up for each course. How do you find them? Luck, guess, and asking around, the information often doesnt exist in writing.
arrival_comments: I had a great semester abroad, but it was all in spite of the universitys best efforts, because as an exchange student, especially if you are not fluent in french, feels deliberately impossible.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The academic level at Sorbonne was sometimes high and sometimes not so much.
registration_process: Courses are described on different websites which are sometimes linked to by the sorbonne website. When you decide to take a course, you must physically find the person responsible for signing people up for the specific course. At my campus their offices were in corridors that were locked away from student access.
registration_help: None. The international/student help office specifically tell you in their emails and in person they can not help with this.
registration_success: Somewhat. I managed to register for some of the courses I wanted. But I was never added to the mailing list with eg. exam information, meaning I didn't know the exam format, and just had to show up and hope for the best. Stuff like that is to be expected no matter how hard you try.
registration_advice: Studying at Sorbonne takes an extreme amount of will-power, not for the academics, but for the administration. You will be misinformed, sent in circles, not answered, meat deadends and everything in between simply because you wish to sign up for courses. When I answered the universitys inqueries about which courses I wished to attend, before I left for the exchange, I was personally phoned by an administrator, laughed at and ridiculed for picking "the wrong courses" and for not speaking french. I am not making this up, and I am not mad at the university, because afterall, I had a lovely exchange, I am mentioning it to warn future exchange students that you need to be able to handle a lot and not give up to power through the administrative procedures for studying at Sorbonne.
academics_comments: The academic level at Sorbonne was sometimes high and sometimes not so much.
course_level: Some courses were very difficult, some more at a KU level.
teaching_comparison: More high-school like. Not a single book or pdf was to be read for my whole semester. Everything is based on showing up to the lectures, and writing down what the professor says.
courses_enrolled: Cloud computing Statistics in Bioinformatics and Sequence Algorithms Programming in C++ French as a foreign language
recommended_courses: All of them, I think they were all interesting. All students found Cloud Computing extremely difficult, with a lot of them spending several days every week on the labs, but it was a very interesting course. French as a foreign language was really nice for learning french, but beware of some of the teachers, some of them are very "old school" and will ridicule students who find the language hard. Lucky for me I wasnt among the worst, so I wasnt bullied by any of the teachers, but the same could not be said for all students.
unexpected_costs: I cant think of any.
cost_comparison: Public transport was more expensive. Eating at the university was less expensive at 3.3 euroes per meal.
activities_available: All kinds of sport, if you managed to find out about it.
activities_recommended: I participated in the universitys brazilian jiu-jitsu class. It was awesome, 1,5 hour sports class in the middle of the day, great facility, the vibes could not have been better.
weekend_recommendations: I dont know, go on trips, see the museums in Paris, hang out in the parisian bars.
culture_adjustment: More difficult than I thought, many frenchmen will treat you like trash if you are nice to them but dont speak french. Be polite, but dont be too nice/smiling.
socializing_tips: The only local students who were open to talking with me were in my sports class. Otherwise, they are, understandably so, pretty set in their social circles.
cultural_challenges: The arrogance. French stereotypes hold up 100% with their arrogance and displeasantries. I learned to handle this by being polite but stern, this way they dont "smell blood" and will treat you like a frenchman.
culture_appreciated: The always going out culture is amazing.
top3_advice: The administrative procedures are not for the faint of heart. Paris is amazing and full of fun. You can learn a lot of french through the universitys free french courses, but remember to participate actively.
other_useful_info: Participate in the socializing events in the beginning, they are great for getting a social circle.
most_rewarding: How much my french improved, and how well I suddenly got along with the frenchmen.
greatest_challenge: The administrative procedures of Sorbonne.

crucial_aspects: A high academic level and a city with a tangible presence of philosophical thinking embedded in the Parisian culture.
info_ease: Very difficult – Sorbonne Université is not very digitalized compared to UCPH and all the bureaucratic stuff takes a lot of time and energi.
arrival_assistance: There is a Erasmus orientation meeting and a meeting with the Erasmus coordinator of the exchange students on philosophy. crucial_aspects: Language, philosophical tradition and the history of the university.
info_ease: Fairly complicated and not very transparent. We found our way but it required a lot of time and grit. And oftentimes emails or meetings back and forth between students and administrators.
arrival_assistance: There was a very general introductory meeting with the administration and student initiatives for international students. Other than that our more specific coordinator within each our respective disciplines were available for meetings or mail correspondances.
arrival_comments: The system around finding and gaining acces to course could be much more transparent and less rigid. Also in terms of informing the students of what they can possibly do and not do. As it is now it an unecessarily timeconsuming affair for everyone involved.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: A lot of different brochures with no timetables attached to them, which you then needed to cross check with all your chosen interesting courses, making a huge puzzle. Even there, you couldn't be certain that you were allowed to choose these courses, why you needed to prepare several scenarios and possibilities. Other than that, there was a lot of confusion over the form and timing of exam, which made planning and prioritization of energy and focus very difficult for at least half of the duration of the semester.
registration_help: Brochures. After the start of the semester, the coordinator only answered emails sporadically and some not at all.
registration_success: Partially.
registration_advice: Prepare as well as you can. Read everything relevant in all of the available and relevant brochures and most importantly: be patient with the administration and the process related. It is not your fault and you should not let yourself be too occupied with tardiness and lack of organisation and cooperation. Once you are through with it, the courses in themselves, the content, the teaching and the engagement of the students is awesome.
course_level: Especially the courses at the Philosophy of Art and Political Philosophy programmes were of a very high level academically. The frame of reference and the demands of historical and contemporary knowledge was quite high and a prerequisite for keeping up and being able to think with the content, questions and thoughts of the course and the lecturer. Incredibly inspiring, inticing and stimulating.
teaching_comparison: More strictly lectures. Not a lot of debate between students and lecturer. There was some, but not a lot. Also there were no breaks every 15 minutes. Lectures are one-and-a-half to two hours straight.
courses_enrolled: 1) Les figures de la répétition (Philosophie de l'art) 2) Esthétique environnementale (Philosophie de l'art) 3) Séminaire Centre Victor Basch (Philosophie de l'art) 4) Démocratie et écologie (Philosophie politique) 5) Éthique environnmentale (Philosophie politique) 6) Philosophy of Biology (Philosophie de sciences)
recommended_courses: 1) Les figures de la répétition (Philosophie de l'art) -- Inspiring teacher and continental philosophy readings. 2) Esthétique environnementale (Philosophie de l'art) -- Interesting history of the coming into existence of "paysage", both understood as the landscape itself and the painting of same form/representation 4) Démocratie et écologie (Philosophie politique) -- Provocative, radical and progressive course, where we were allowed to doubt, critize and suggest ameliorations liberal representative democraties in the light of climate, biodiversity and environmental crises. & 6) Philosophy of Biology (Philosophie de sciences) -- Interesting to dwell upon the assimilation of the phenomenon of life into the sciences and discover, that we do not have a clear way of distinguishing neither life itself, nor organisms, nor species. We are living in a fragmental science fiction!
unexpected_costs: New battery and charger for my computer.
cost_comparison: Food was less expensive, rent was a bit more expensive.
activities_available: Sports, movie clubs, talking cafés in French and others.
activities_recommended: The movie club.
weekend_recommendations: The old cinemas in Saint Germain des Prés. All the musuems that might interest you (there are too many for one semester, so get going!). Both traditional and modern French cuisines.
culture_adjustment: I have lived there before, seven years ago, so I found fairly easy.
socializing_tips: Be kind and try striking up conversation in their mother tongue.
cultural_challenges: The competitiveness.
culture_appreciated: Le savoir-vivre.
top3_advice: 1) Learn French as well as you can before going. 2) Be prepared to work, read, write and do it all in a new way/tradition/method. 3) Surrender yourself to the culture and ways of doing things at the university and take it as a learning and an experience.
other_useful_info: Try to find stable housing in the Eastern part of Paris. You will not regret it.
most_rewarding: Producing the assignments and oral presentations through out the semester as well as exploring the city, culture and traditions within.
greatest_challenge: Finding my way through course selection and administration issues.

registration_advice: The workload is quite heavy, so think carefully when choosing your classes. I took both bachelor’s- and graduate-level courses (L3 and M1), and there is a significant difference in difficulty between the two. As a bachelor’s student, I probably wouldn’t recommend taking M1 courses, especially if you’re not very confident in your French. The lectures are very fast-paced and last two hours with no breaks. Same with the exercise classes.
academics_comments: I wish there had been a little more guidance when choosing courses. Also in regards to how much work was required, since I'm used to another system of education.
course_level: The bachelor’s courses are quite similar in level to those in Copenhagen, except that you are expected to memorize everything. All exams are closed-book and include a large number of questions. There isn’t much time for reflection—when you see an exercise, you need to know almost immediately how to solve it. The M1 courses are much more intense and difficult, so you should be genuinely interested in the subject if you decide to take them. Make sure you have the necessary prerequisites: even if the recommended courses have names similar to ones you have taken at UCPH, it is not guaranteed that the content will be the same. There is very little time to catch up, so you need to study consistently, as most courses include multiple tests throughout the semester.
teaching_comparison: It’s more intense. Lectures and exercise classes last two hours with no breaks. There isn’t much time to work on problems on your own, and the instructor goes through them quite quickly, so you really need to take time afterward to review them yourself. I didn’t have any assignments to hand in, but each class had two tests—a midterm and a final exam—so it gets quite intense. You have to stay on top of your classes at all times.

recommended_courses: Base d'analyse fonctionnelle. The professor is really good, same with the teachers in charge of the exercise classes. You learn a lot.

cost_comparison: It's cheaper to go out and eat/drink here than in Copenhagen.

weekend_recommendations: Paris is a great city, filled with museums, clubs, and bars. There are also many excellent smaller concert venues.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy.
socializing_tips: Ask if they want to go to the library or study together. Most students are very academically focused, so socializing isn’t always easy—everyone is stressed.
cultural_challenges: French bureaucracy.
culture_appreciated: The directness in communication.
top3_advice: The educational system is quite different, so be prepared to work a lot, or be very mindful when choosing courses. Paris is a great city, so try to find a balance between academics and enjoying yourself. It’s easy to get caught up in the demands of classes, but make sure to take time to take advantage of everything else the city has to offer. It’s quite normal to feel overwhelmed.
