crucial_aspects: As a Human Geographer at UCPH, I am often engaged with issues from the Global South. In order to complement theoretical knowledge with practical experience, I considered it as crucial to gain a deeper understanding of the context by going abroad. South Africa, a country faced with many crises and opportunities, provided an excellent destination.
info_ease: Stellenbosch University shared information only upon arrival. It would be easier and more convenient to be able to access online platforms prior to the arrival in order to check classroom locations, class sizes, learning materials, etc.
arrival_assistance: The study abroad team assisted generously with everything a student needed help in (technical, cultural, academic, ... issues). There was an orientation week where international students engaged with each other and the institution, which was very helpful to settle in.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Incoming international students have to send a list with courses they'd like to choose. It's often quite convenient when you are choosing generic courses, but the more specialized your UCPH program is, the more difficult it is to enquiry about courses. It is always good to contact the facilitator of the program, if you have any questions about the course content and can't find anything online.
registration_help: Some more generic guides, but the more specific your program at home, the more likely it is that you have to seek assistance in order to enquire about courses. It helps to contact the International office, or the facilitator of the course. They can mostly help best with any questions regarding topics covered, requirements, etc.
registration_success: Generally, if UCPH approves your course selection, you don't have any issues of getting accepted to the classes you'd like to register for.
registration_advice: Rather look for more 'hidden' courses that align more with your academic and personal interests, than just going the 'easy' way and register for courses that are sent to you by the International office. Those are often courses that are specifically designed for Exchange students (and if they're interesting to you, then choose them!), but they are not really academically beneficial and you don't meet any locals.
course_level: The course level in my department (the Centre for Sustainability Transitions) was quite high, sometimes even more challenging and demanding than the courses at UCPH. The workload generally is quite high, regardless of your program and in which department / faculty you end up. Stellenbosch University is a fairly demanding institution, and you are often required to attend courses, do a lot of group work, and there are both mid-term exams and final exams.
teaching_comparison: My department, the Centre for Sustainability Transitions, has a very unique way of teaching and learning. It is very progressive and focuses on immersive learning experiences, which are very different to more traditional forms of learning and teaching at home. That said, the CST is internationally recognized as a world-class teaching and research hub, so it's not necessarily bad - I would even say it challenges your engrained ways of thinking and opens up your mind in forms you would have never expected. On the other hand, the CST is zero representative of the (often) ultra-conservative patterns within Afrikaans-dominated Stellenbosch University, so if you are studying anything else than some Sustainability-related programs, expect very traditional forms of teaching.
courses_enrolled: - Leading Transitions and Socio-Ecological Ethics - Sustainable Economic Policy Options - Capita Selecta: Indigenous Knowledges and Sustainable Development - Development Planning and Environmental Analysis
recommended_courses: The program has changed its courses after I left, so there might be other courses now. If you are studying something Sustainability-related, definitely choose courses at the CST. Otherwise, I can't really help.
unexpected_costs: In South Africa, you really have to be aware of your stuff. Don't be careless, otherwise your valuables (phone, wallet, bags) is in great risk of being stolen. This can cost you a new iPad, laptop, phone, wallet - everything happened within the International cohort.
cost_comparison: The supermarket is not much cheaper, sometimes even more expensive, than at home. This is quite surprising considering the general very low cost of living in SA. Cooking yourself is still the cheapest in the long-term, but you can go out for lunch for around 30kr - and have a nice lunch even.
activities_available: There are so many societies - from wine society to scuba diving - that you can easily join one of your preference, if you would like to. You have to pay some fees though.
activities_recommended: One simple advice: Go out and explore South Africa, and Southern Africa! Cape Town, Kruger, Botswana, Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Mozambique, etc.
weekend_recommendations: Go out and explore! Around Stellenbosch, there are plenty of things to do, from wine tasting to swimming, to hiking.
culture_adjustment: Stellenbosch University has nothing to do with the rest of South Africa, or Africa for that matter. It feels like a mixture of Australia and USA, with African influences. Outside of Stellenbosch, things are quite different - more diverse, more chaotic, more friendly. It's generally easy to adjust to these new contexts I would say, but that maybe also depends a lot on the subjective experiences.
socializing_tips: Choose courses that are not specifically designed for incoming internationals and connect with locals at parties.
cultural_challenges: The widespread poverty (people living in inhumane conditions in townships), the racial segregation, the inherent racism in the South African system.
culture_appreciated: The friendly and welcoming nature of people, the diversity, and positivity.
top3_advice: 1. Put life first, university second. 2. Go out and explore, connect with other people and especially locals. Go beyond the international bubble! 3. Don't be careless, but don't be scared either. A healthy balance makes your trip safe and full of great experiences. Leave your (hopefully very implicit) forms of "White Western hegemony" behind.
other_useful_info: Rent a car (with housemates or friends). It makes things so much easier, and it's not really expensive. You can go on roadtrips all the time, go surfing, hiking, swimming, etc. Stellenbosch is quite small and you miss all the beautiful things that are outside of Stellies.
most_rewarding: For me personally the academic experience at CST, but this is very subjective given my focus of studies and unfortunately not everyone has the privilege of studying there given their academic orientation. So, I guess, besides that, it is the natural and cultural beauty of Africa.
greatest_challenge: To cope with the issues of security, racism, and poverty.

recommended_courses: If possible I would recommend taking courses relating to South Africa, as it helps you understand the country you are staying in. I enjoyed contemporary south african politics although it was at times challenging as it was a master-level course for polisci students with a lot of prior knowledge of south african politics, but I learnt a lot!
unexpected_costs: During my stay no unexpected costs, however the visa application cost more than I thought so good to keep that in mind.
cost_comparison: Everything is quite cheap which makes it easy to live as a student, for example uber and eating out is very affordable.
activities_available: A lot of clubs and sports! For example wine tasting society / scuba diving / running etc. basically anything you could imagine you could join.
activities_recommended: I did volounteering through the university which I really enjoyed. There was plenty of different volounteering opportunites and they all got presented to us and then we could easily join whichever we wanted.
weekend_recommendations: There is so much to explore! If you enjoy hiking there is a lot of trails in and around Stellenbosch. There is also so many vineyards and a weekend activity was often going for a wine tasting (for less than 100DKK) at one of them! Cape Town is also only around 45mins way and is such an amazing city with lots to do! There are also a lot of opportunities for longer travel/holidays and I went to the Krueger park for safari which was really nice! There are also a lot of music events and festivals if that is your thing.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy I would say! South Africans are super nice and welcoming people and that made it really easy to adjust. Just be open minded and you will have no issues.
socializing_tips: I was lucky to live with a South African and have a lot of neighbors that were South Africans which made it easy for me to get to know them, but there is also often a mix of exchange students and south africans in the classes which makes it very easy to get to know them! South Africans are really nice people and probably one of the easiest nationalities to befriend :)
cultural_challenges: Not really a cultural difference but South Africa is a country with huge wealth inequalities and that is something you will see more than you are used to, which can be really hard. For example in Stellenbosch you will see quite a few homeless people and there is a township not to far away. Especially coming from Denmark this might be quite difficult to see. One less serious thing is that you will be forced to adapt to a slower pace of life, in South Africa there is very rarely a sense of urgency for anything, and I would recommend adapting to this pace or risk getting a bit annoyed over it, see it as an opportunity to slow down!
culture_appreciated: South Africans are really happy people (in general) and it is not uncommon to see people dancing or singing in the middle of the day for no reason.
top3_advice: Going into the exchange I was quite nervous about the satefy-aspect as it was something I had heard a lot about. Of course, you need to be much more vigilant than back home (not walk on our own at night, be careful with your phone etc especially in crowded places) but you get used to this quite quickly and I was never in a situation where I felt geniuenly unsafe! One big perk is that uber is extremely cheap and safe (also on your own) which makes it really easy to avoid unsafe situations such as walking alone at night.
other_useful_info: Not really, South Africa is an amazing country and Stellenbosch is a lovely town and university!
most_rewarding: Being able to create a life for yourself across the world is really cool, and probably the most rewarding part of the whole experience. Of course, it was hard at times but it was truly one of the coolest experiences of my life!
greatest_challenge: Of course it can be challenging to be far away in a different country, but I would just say to embrace the experience!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a place in Europe where I could more or less speak the language with the possibility of also studying in that language.
overall_comments: On a personal level I have had a really good time, but the university didn't make it so.
info_ease: Stockholm University offers some information but on many different webpages - it can be a bit of a jungle to find the correct information and your possibilities as a new international student. There wasn't a lot of introductions to the university itself - and the few possible introduction activities were at the same time as my classes. As a master's student I felt that I was pretty much on my own - perhaps it is different at BA-level.
arrival_assistance: Nothing really. I looked into Studentkåren and tried participating in some of their activities the first few weeks.
arrival_comments: I have heard from other Swedes that have studied at other Swedish universities, that they focus a lot on introduction programmes each semester - even for the international students. I thought the information was messy and at times unclear. I did however have a kind international coordinator at my "home department" (department of swedish and bilingualism) that sent me my personal study information before the semester started.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: On a personal level I have had a really good time, but the university didn't make it so.
registration_process: I received an e-mail from the coordinator at UCPH only a couple of days before the registration deadline saying something along the lines of "sorry for the short deadline". I had already looked into the courses I was interested in beforehand and I would recommend you do the same in case you are given as short a deadline as I was. Although I had prepared myself the short deadline was stressful as I had questions about the academic requirements stated in the course catalogue on SU.se and that left me very little time to get information from the guidance counsellors at SU.
registration_help: The guidance counsellors at SU were helpful although it was a little difficult to find the correct people to contact.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Prepare yourself by looking at the available courses as you might not have a lot of time between receiving the registration information and the registration deadline. I was only allowed to choose courses from max. two different departments, so make sure you are aware of where the courses are being offered. The courses run in different "periods" - I had 2 x 7,5 ECTS in periode1 and 2 x 7,5 ECTS in periode2.
academics_comments: On a personal level I have had a really good time, but the university didn't make it so.
course_level: The level was doable, but the amount of work in the different courses changed a lot!
teaching_comparison: I prefer UCPH with bigger courses throughout the whole semester. Having the "block structure" meant that I never really got to know my classmates before we were moving on to the next courses. The online courses were only every second week, which meant that I had 3 hours of class one week and 5 hours the next; 3 hours every week at the university and 2 hours on a screen at home.
courses_enrolled: - Gender and post- colonialism in Latin America - Sociolingvistik 1- allmän del - Intercultural pragmatics - Advanced Studies in Sociolinguistic Approaches to Bi- and multilingualism
recommended_courses: The course in intercultural pragmatics and sociolinguistic approaches were very interesting, but the workload was pretty big. Unfortunately Intercultural Pragmatics was online. I would not recommend the course Gender and Post-colonialism in Latin America unless you have extensive knowledge on the Latin American countries as the course was very descriptive about the places and their political statuses rather than theoretical.
unexpected_costs: Not necessarily an unexpected cost, but make sure to look into your phone subscription beforehand as you cannot register for a Swedish subscription unless you're registered at Skatteverket (folkeregister/adress). You can however get a SIM-card and credit at local shops, but you will have to put money on it once a month.
cost_comparison: Food (especially dairy and eggs) and alcohol is expensive. You also have to pay entry fees in all museums although some have student discounts.
activities_available: If you buy a membership (it's cheap) you can participate in lots of different activities. You can buy several memberships so you can participate in the different faculty clubs' activities - I bought a membership to both the humanities and the social sciences.
activities_recommended: The Thursday bar at Café Bojan was fun sometimes
weekend_recommendations: Explore Södermalm and find your favourite local hangout spots. Find your local sunkpub to save money!
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy as Danes and Swedes are very similar - be prepared for the fact that a lot of Swedish people do not understand a lot of Danish!
socializing_tips: I didn't get a lot of social possibilities out of my classes but I participated in some of the Studentkår-activities - I would say you have to throw yourself into it a couple of times even though it may be exhausting. I did however not really meet any local students - most are internationals.
cultural_challenges: That you have to buy alcohol at Systembolaget and that the metro doesn't run in the night on week days. Not really a cultural thing but the winter is cold and the snow can be annoying. Swedish bread is always a tiny little bit sweet, which I find weird.
culture_appreciated: Again not really cultural but how Stockholm is similar to a lot of places (including CPH) but still its own in the best way. I appreciate the concepts of fika and lillördag.
top3_advice: 1. Make sure you read up on your course possibilities and housing early on 2. Have proper winter clothes and good winter boots - preferably ones that can grip into the snow/ice 3. If you like me don't come to feel a real connection to the university, try to make peace with it and make your trip into a personal experience - do what you enjoy and remember that grades aren't everything (and won't even be transferred to UCPH). Better get what you can out of the experience rather than being frustrated that the university maybe isn't what you expected.
other_useful_info: Make sure you have some money saved up as you may not receive your grant in time for the start of your exchange.
most_rewarding: Becoming familiar with the city and experiencing the seasons change from winter to spring to summer. Meeting new people and gaining life long memories.
greatest_challenge: Being on your own, feeling the stress of having to find friends, coming to terms with the university not being as I had hoped, the extreme price of butter and eggs.

crucial_aspects: Jeg har besøgt Stockholm et par gange før og synes godt om byen, og jeg tænkte derfor at udveksling ville være en god mulighed for at prøve at bo her og lære byen bedre at kende. Derudover synes jeg Stockholms Universitet havde rigtig mange spændende valgfag - og anderledes fag end hvad KU udbyder derhjemme.
overall_comments: Jeg har simpelthen været så glad for både at læse på universitetet her - alt er super organiseret, og det er rigitg dygtige undervisere og spændende fag. Og derudover er Stockholm en virkelig dejligt by at bo i.
info_ease: Ja - alt kontakt med Stockholms Universitet har været meget tjekket. De har været nemme og komme i kontakt med, og super hjælpsomme til at svare på de spørgsmål der er opstået undervejs.
arrival_assistance: Jeg fik ingen speciel assistance, men de introforløb som var planlagt af Stockholms Universitet har været super gode og informative.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Jeg har simpelthen været så glad for både at læse på universitetet her - alt er super organiseret, og det er rigitg dygtige undervisere og spændende fag. Og derudover er Stockholm en virkelig dejligt by at bo i.
registration_process: Jeg mener at jeg blev indstillet til en plads på SU af KU, og så skulle jeg efterfølgende melde mig officielt til på SU. Men SU's international office var super gode til at sende meget informative mails med alt det praktiske, og derudover var de meget nemme at få fat på. Det samme gjorde sig gældende da jeg senere skulle tilmelde mig fag. Fagtilmeldingen var dog først til mølle, hvilket jeg synes var lidt underligt, det virkede som lidt unødvendigt stress.
registration_help: Det var muligt at kontankte SU's international office, og de var super hjælpsomme og hurtige til at svare på mails.
registration_success: Jeg fik begge mine førsteprioriteter - og jeg har faktisk ikke hørt om nogen udvekslingsstuderende som ikke har fået opfyldt deres første prioriteter.
registration_advice: Bare vær obs på din mail, og endelig spørg hvis der er noget du er i tvivl om, jeg synes det hele gik meget nemt.
academics_comments: Jeg har simpelthen været så glad for både at læse på universitetet her - alt er super organiseret, og det er rigitg dygtige undervisere og spændende fag. Og derudover er Stockholm en virkelig dejligt by at bo i.
course_level: Jeg synes generelt niveauet var højt - nok ca det samme som i København. Men dygtige undervisere og spændende materiale. Jeg synes dog det har været langt nemmere at få gode karakterer her sammenlignet med i København.
teaching_comparison: Undervisningsformen her er meget anderledes end i København, det er nok noget af det der har overrasket mig mest. For det første er alt undervisning organiseret i blokstruktur, så man har kun et enkelt fag ad gangen. Derudover er eksamensformen meget anderledes - jeg er vant til at der er én eksamen til sidst i semesteret (typisk en 4-timers skriftlig) som afgør hele ens karakter. Men her er karakteren fordelt på mange flere forskellige ting - typisk f.eks. et skriftligt essay, en skriftlig eksamen, at man kommer til undervisningen osv. - det kan umiddelbart lyde som meget, men jeg synes det har været SÅ rart, og taget en stor del af det pres som jeg tit oplever derhjemme. Det gør også at man ikke har samme meget intense eksamensperiode.
courses_enrolled: 1. Family Law Across Borders 2. The Global Labour Market and International Labour Law
recommended_courses: Jeg var meget glad for det første fag jeg havde (Family Law Across Borders) - super spændende og veltilrettelagt, og en virkelig dygtig underviser (+ mange dygtige gæsteundervisere) Jeg var ikke helt så glad for mit andet fag (The Global Labour Market and International Labour Law) - jeg synes emnet var rigtig spændende, men tilrettelæggelsen af undervisningen var lidt rodet.
unexpected_costs: Jeg synes ikke at jeg har haft nogle udgifter som har været uforudsete
cost_comparison: Den svenske krone har været meget lav mens jeg har været her, så det meste har faktisk været billigere end jeg havde forventet - både at købe ind i supermarked, at gå ud og spise osv.
activities_available: Jeg ved at der er forskellige sports- og fitnesstilbud, men derudover ved jeg faktisk ikke hvilke tilgængelige aktiviteter der er.
activities_recommended: Der er rigitg mange fine musseer - jeg har været glad for at besøge f.eks. Moderna og Liljenvalchs. Derudover vil jeg anbefale at man benytter at Stockholm ligger så tæt på så meget natur, både inde i byen, hvor det f.eks. er dejligt at gå eller cykle en tur på Djurgården, men man kan også nemt tage lidt uden for byen og ud til Skærgården. Jeg tog f.eks på kajak-tur ved Vaxholm (ca 1 time uden for Stockholm).
weekend_recommendations: Tag til Sodermalm - særligt i området omkring Skånegatan og Nytorget er der rigtig mange hyggelige barer og restauranter. Derudover er det et godt sted at genbrugsshoppe - særligt i området omkring Hornsgatan. Tag ud til Djurgarden - der er både mange fine musseer og fin natur.
culture_adjustment: Det har været virkelig sjovt at være på udveksling et sted hvor man kan forstå sproget - det tror jeg helt sikkert også har gjort det lettere at tilpasse sig. Og selvom dansk og svensk kultur på mange måder er meget ens, så er der også mange forskelle som har været sjove at opleve.
socializing_tips: Jeg tror mit bedste tip bare er at være åben, og så deltage i så mange arrangementer i starten som man kan overskue. Men jeg synes generelt det har været nemt at blive venner med andre udvekslingsstuderende, fordi alle er i samme båd og interesserede i at få venner. Det har derimod været lidt mere vanskeligt at få svenske venner, men der tror jeg dog også det er en fordel at være dansk fordi der er så mange sproglige og kulturelle ligheder.
cultural_challenges: Jeg synes ikke at jeg har oplevet nogle kulturelle forskelle som har været svære
culture_appreciated: Jeg synes generelt bare det har været sjovt at lære en anden kultur bedre at kende - på en måde som man ikke kommer til når man bare besøger et andet land/by på en ferie.
top3_advice: 1. Begynd at søg housing i bedre tid, og indstil dig på at du selv skal finde noget uden om uni. 2. I forlængelse heraf - undersøg om der er mulighed for at komme til at fremleje et værelse på KTH (Kungliga Tekniska Høgskolan - det tekniske universitet (som svarer til DTU)) - det ligger perfekt inde i byen, og har samtidig en hyggelig campus-stemning 3. Ikke stress over det praksiske med fag, tilmelding osv - det løser sig! Og hvis der er noget som du er i tvivl om så endelig skriv til SU.
other_useful_info: Hvis du kommer til at bo inde i byen og ikke gider tage helt ud til SU for at læse - så vil jeg virkelig anbefale biblioteket på KTH (Kungliga Tekniska Högskolan) Det er et virkelig flot gammelt bibliotek og et helt perfekti sted at studerede - og så ligger det virkelig dejligt.
most_rewarding: Alle de gode nye venner jeg har fået fra hele verden
greatest_challenge: For mig var den største udfordring at få styr på alt det praksiske inden jeg tog afsted - særlig bolisituationen synes jeg var lidt stressende at få på plads. Men siden jeg er kommet herop synes jeg alt ting er gået super.

housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: Other students and administrative employees from the university. And during the courses you could always receive help from teachers.

cost_comparison: Grocery shopping became more and more expensive during my stay due to the inflation.

culture_adjustment: Quite easy, but probably because I stayed with Scandinavia.
socializing_tips: It is hard. Participating in group work after class and on-campus activities is a good start. Otherwise going to sports off campus helped me a lot.
cultural_challenges: The swedes tend to be a bit closed at first, but when you get to know them, they are very lovely people.
culture_appreciated: There is a huge appreciation of coffee breaks and nature in Sweden, that I really enjoyed.
top3_advice: Everything is hard in the beginning, but you will find your way and the people you need. And just show up for things, participate. Maybe only once, but then you'll find out if it is you thing or not to do.
other_useful_info: The university is a bit small, use the city libraries to study.
most_rewarding: Living abroad, the experience itself of being away from home, knowing that I able to settle on my own.
greatest_challenge: The most rewarding and the most challenging part for me was living abroad.

crucial_aspects: Jeg fandt det vigtigt at lære, hvordan nordisk – herunder særligt svensk – ret fungerer, da de nordiske retssystemer i vidt omfang ligner hinanden. I lærebøger henvises der ofte til nordiske domme, som kan fungere som et relevant fortolkningsbidrag, hvis der opstår fortolkningstvivl i dansk ret.
info_ease: Relativt nemt - SU's hjemmeside er generelt informativt og overskueligt.
arrival_assistance: SU tilbyder en arrival service, hvor man bl.a. bliver hentet i lufthavnen sammen med andre studerende. Bussen kører til SU ved Campus Frescati, hvor der serveres sandwich, og hvor man eventuelt får udleveret et SIM-kort (meget praktisk, da man dermed undgår selv at skulle købe et, f.eks. i Pressbyrån, 7-Eleven eller andre kiosker – og det er gratis). Derudover giver arrangementet et overblik over indkøbsmuligheder samt information om SUS (studenterorganisationen), hvor et studiekort bl.a. giver adgang til studierabatter, herunder studierabat til offentlig transport (SL). For at gøre processen nemmere anbefales det at udfylde relevante oplysninger hjemmefra, så studierabat til SL kan opnås med det samme. Endvidere giver arrangementet mulighed for at møde andre nyankommet studerende som er en god måde at starte udvekslingsopholdet.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Samme ovenover - du ansøger og får evt. ja eller nej. Vær opmærksom på forhåndsgodkendelse fra KU - Dog sagde KU egentlig ja til alle fag.
registration_help: Samme ovenover, skriv evt. til administrationen
registration_success: Jeg kom ind på alle de fag, jeg søgte. Swedish Law in Context kan klart anbefales og er et godt grundlæggende fag om svensk ret. Faget dækker bl.a. strafferet, aftaleret m.v. og giver et bredt overblik, dog uden at gå i dybden. EU Competition Law er derimod et meget krævende fag med en stor pensumbog og et meget omfattende læsestof, som kan virke uoverskueligt. Hvis man har planer om at arbejde inden for konkurrenceretten, er jeg dog overbevist om, at faget gør én mere attraktiv på arbejdsmarkedet. Selvom det var hårdt, oplevede jeg faget som meget givende. Man kommer desuden på besøg hos flere advokatvirksomheder, hvilket er en klar fordel, da denne mulighed ikke i samme grad findes på andre fag.
registration_advice: Søg egentlig så hurtigst muligt - kan godt være, de siger det ikke er første til mølle-princip, men det er det som sådan altid - Dog bør man ikke være bange for ikke, at få sine fag.
course_level: Som nævnt ovenfor er der en tydelig forskel mellem Swedish Law in Context og EU Competition Law. Læsemængden er markant større, og det faglige niveau er højere på EU Competition Law. Jeg vil dog til enhver tid anbefale begge fag. Jeg fik eksempelvis min primære vennegruppe (17+ personer) gennem Swedish Law in Context, da faget udelukkende består af udvekslingsstuderende. Her skal det forstås som, fordi folk er udvekslingsstuderende er de mere tilbøjeligt at være mere åben og venlig til at snakke med én sammenlignet med EU-Competition law. EU Competition Law har derimod en blandet sammensætning af udvekslingsstuderende, LLM-studerende og svenske studerende. Her kunne man tydeligt mærke, at mange allerede kendte hinanden, men jeg oplevede ikke problemer med at komme i kontakt med hverken LLM- eller svenske studerende. Dog skal man selv gøre noget, hvilket jo er klart.
teaching_comparison: Vær forberedt på, at der er mødepligt til seminarundervisning og i nogle fag også til forelæsninger. Der må som udgangspunkt højst være 20 % fravær i hvert fag. Overskrides denne grænse, dumper man faget, medmindre der foreligger en gyldig og saglig grund. Selvom mødepligt kan opleves som træls, var jeg faktisk glad for det, da det sikrede, at man mødte andre studerende og blev en del af studiemiljøet.
courses_enrolled: Swedish law in Context EU-Competition Law
recommended_courses: Begge - læs ovenover. Swedish Law in context, kan man kort sige, at det minder om juridisk metode og et relativt nemt fag, fordi retssytemet minder om Danmark, men har sine forskelle. Kan klart anbefales.
unexpected_costs: Hvis du tager en tur til Lapland (kan klart anbefales) Hvis du tager til galla-aften (anbefales, var nød til at købe et nyt jakkesæt - billigere end i DK) Hvis du tager til forskellige events som hockey, bandy og andre sociale ting (klart anbefales)
cost_comparison: generelt er sverige herunder stockholm billigere i DK - tøj, medicin osv. Dog vær opmærksom på, at kød-priserne er dyrere end i DK (nogle gange meget dyrere) Derudover, så kræver mange supermarkeder, man er medlem for at få rabatter, hvilket er træls - her skal du bruge et svensk-personnummer, typisk kan man godt oprette sig uden, men ret besværligt.
activities_available: SUS har mange aktiviteter ESN Stockholm holder også mange aktiviteter - fester, pub-crawl, film-aftner, sport-aftner osv. Dog er det ret uorganiseret og kaotisk, når det angår festerne - prøv det med dine venner, da mange udvekslingsstuderende tager til det.
activities_recommended: Hockey, bandy, hiking og lapland
weekend_recommendations: Lapland Hiking herunder Vaxholmen og nationalparkerne rundt omkring Djurgården - super hyggeligt sted med meget grønt. Her er der mange museumer i området og Gröna Lund (pendant til Tivoli) Ærligt, tag rundt i Stockholm - flot by
culture_adjustment: Relativt nemt, fordi det mindede om Danmark - dog vil jeg sige, folk virker til at være mere åben især, når man er dansk. Vær dog forberedt på at man godt kan blive mobbet (på den gode måde).
socializing_tips: Tage til så mange events som muligt - jeg lærte rigtig mange mennesker ved at gøre det. Det er dog vigtigt, at du er selv meget åben og tør at gå over til folk at snakke. Sørg for at have fokus på networking - det gavnede mig rigtigt meget, hvilket endte med, at jeg vandt året MVP ved Sitting (svensk tradition, hvor man samles og spiser mad samt synger - det bør man tage til).
cultural_challenges: Personnummer: Svenskere er generelt mere åbne omkring brugen af personnummer, som er offentligt tilgængeligt. I Danmark er man derimod mere påpasselig og betragter denne type oplysninger som mere sensitive. Uden et svensk personnummer er man relativt begrænset i, hvad man kan foretage sig administrativt. Drukkultur: Svenskerne har en markant strengere alkoholkultur, særligt når man går i byen. Man skal altid medbringe fysisk billed-ID, ellers bliver man ikke lukket ind. Dørvagter kan desuden afvise adgang, hvis de vurderer, at man ser beruset ud – også selvom man reelt ikke er det. Samlet set er reglerne stramme. Systembolaget: Hvis man planlægger at drikke alkohol, f.eks. i forbindelse med forfest, kræver det planlægning. Alkohol kan kun købes i Systembolaget, som har begrænsede åbningstider, og der kræves gyldigt billed-ID ved køb.
culture_appreciated: Fika
top3_advice: Sørg for at have et networking-mindset. Det lyder måske klichéagtigt, men det er reelt vigtigt. Det handler om at være åben og villig til at møde nye mennesker samt om at turde udfordre sin komfortzone. Sørg for at planlægge og have et overblik på, hvad du gerne vil - derudover sørg for at skabe en rutine i starten, selvom det er hårdt Tage det stille og roligt, du skal nok få nye venner.
other_useful_info: Vær opmærksom på, at svenskerne har væsentlig flere helligdage end i DK - Det betyder bl.a. at biblioteker og universitet er lukket, hvilket er træls, hvis man kan lide at læse ude. Derudover har biblioteker og universitet også forskellige åbningstider i hverdagene og weekenderne - desværre ikke ligesom i DK, hvor det stortset er åbent 24/7.
most_rewarding: De mennesker jeg har mødt - wow. Jeg var faktisk ret glad for at være den eneste jurastuderende fra KU, da jeg kun ville møde andre udvekslingsstuderende. Dog mødte jeg en anden dansker fra SDU, som også var en del af vennegruppen (vi snakkede primært kun engelsk).
greatest_challenge: EU-Competition law - lol, meget af læse, meget arbejde.
other_comments: Tage på Carmen

crucial_aspects: Some of the most important factors in choosing my location for exchange were that it should be affordable and place where I could learn a new culture. As I already visited Seoul 2 years ago for 2 weeks, I had feeling of the place and I really loved what I saw and experienced. There seemed to be an amazing and social environment for exchange students as well.
overall_comments: My exchange to Seoul turned out to be the best exchange I have ever been on, despite corona restrictions, I met so many wondeful people and Seoul truly has so much to offer. The city has endless oportunities and concepts to explore, there would always be something to do or see, and it is affordable to have a really nice lifestyle there as a student.
info_ease: Sungkyunkwan university was very helpful and informative upon arrival, which specifically was nice do to the corona situations and rules. We had a contact person we could contact from a exchange group which made it feel like that you always had somewhere to go for questions, even if it could sometimes be a little hard to get a direct answer. But overall it was very good.
arrival_assistance: we got a welcome package with all the information of how to apply for courses and who to contact for questions and so on. It even had some little imporant fact regarding accomodation, transportation and culture, which was super nice.
arrival_comments: Overall information was available and good, however the language barriers could sometimes make things a little bit tricky, but google translate or the app Papago is a lifesaver to help translating documents.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: My exchange to Seoul turned out to be the best exchange I have ever been on, despite corona restrictions, I met so many wondeful people and Seoul truly has so much to offer. The city has endless oportunities and concepts to explore, there would always be something to do or see, and it is affordable to have a really nice lifestyle there as a student.
registration_process: The registration process was good but a little complicated. For me it was online registration and you have to know what courses you want to apply for in advance, because you only have limited time to apply and remember to check that the courses you apply for are in English, especially if you are on the masters, as courses in english on the master degrees can be quite limited.
registration_help: We had a contact person we could contact through the app Kakaotalk, which is kind of a Korean version of messenger.
registration_success: I got all the 3 courses that I wanted, but I was also ready at my computer at the very moment the course registraion opened.
registration_advice: Be ready at the time the online registration opens and remember to check what language the courses are taught in.

The city has endless oportunities and concepts to explore, there would always be something to do or see, and it is affordable to have a really nice lifestyle there as a student.
course_level: For me the courses were good and easier than the ones I use to take in Denmark, however I also did alot of Korean culture courses and I knew some people who studied courses in business and mathematics who had a harder time.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was high level and there is alot respect for the profesors. It was alot of powerpoints which was helpful if the English sometimes could be a bit hard to understand. But overall the teaching style was very good and similar to the one I use to have at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Understanding Asien Culture, Contemporary Korean Culture and Society and Politics and Economy in Korea,
recommended_courses: I recommend taking the cultural courses as they are very well suited for exchange students, especially if you are on your masters.
unexpected_costs: There wasen't any specific unexpected costs, and if there were it would be little random things which were still affordable. Make sure you always have cash on you as it isn't all places that takes foreign credit cards, also they still use cash alot many places.
cost_comparison: Food and drinks are super cheap also acommodation if you choose the right areas. Clothes and transportation are also very affordable and cheap.
activities_available: The university had alot of clubs and opportunities for exchange students to join, more specifically sports.
activities_recommended: As I did'nt get to join any clubs do to covid, I reccomend people to explore Seoul and the activities the city has to offer.
weekend_recommendations: We were a group of friends that went down the southern part of South Korea called Busan. It was amazing, a place with beaches and culture to explore as well. Busan was a wondeful little getaway. We also went to Jeju Island which had the most beautiful nature and hikes. I reccomend going there when the weather is hot, people also did surfing at Jeju. Also the nature in South Korea is extremely beautiful, and I reccomend going on hikes in the mountains Buraksan and Gwanaksan. Also the national park Seoraksan was one of the most amazing places I have ever been, I reccomend going there mid/end october as the colors and leaves in the fall are stunning.
culture_adjustment: The culture is very different and very respectful. Not many speak english but people are still very helpful and sweet. I mostly spend time with other exchange students or a few Korean friends that spoke english.
socializing_tips: Move to the places with a lot of other exchange students. I lived in the Hongdae and Sinchon area where we were alot of students. We had our own little community, as we couldnt meet people at the campus due to covid, people would meet at bars alot, hostels or social media. I recommend being openminded and sign up for as many things as possible, especially in the beginning. I got some of the best friends for life there which I didn't expect, so be brave and open.
cultural_challenges: the language barrier was the toughest, get some good translation apps it will make your life so much easier.
culture_appreciated: All of it, the food and the vibe
top3_advice: Be open and respectful, download the apps: Papago and google translate, also they don't have google maps in Korea so use the app: Naver map or Kakao map. Also explore as much as you can!
other_useful_info: If you have to do quarantine in Seoul due to covid, book an airbnb (if possible with a balcony) and make sure that they allow quarintining, the government quarantine is more expensive. If you do the quarantining in your own airbnb make sure to get a SIM card before your arrival so you can order food online, you have to have a Korean sim card to use their delivery services. You can get the Sim card send to your address in Denmark through the website: Tracy.com (it takes around 5 days to recieve it). Also remember a thermometer in case they still have the app symptom tracking system. Most importaintly make sure to stay in the areas that has the food delivery services, I had no problems doing quarintine in Hongdae, but I had some friends that had issues getting food delivered in other areas, And just don't get covid before departure.
most_rewarding: The Amazing friends I made, the people were just wondeful. Also that Seoul has so much to see and offer, even though I stayed 5 months there was still alot to explore and im definetly coming back one day. As long as you are openminded and willing to explore it will be so rewarding. Check out the hikes in Seoul, the cafés and resturants. Also the little trips you can go on outside Seoul.
greatest_challenge: The language and covid rules. And of course having to go home again....
other_comments: Go to Seoul if you want to have that Asien culture experience with a little hint of Western vibes. Seoul is super modern and traditional at the same time. If you are a food lover this is the place for you, also the culture, K-pop and fashion is amazing. For me my time in Seoul was the perfect little dream world with wondeful people and so much to explore.

registration_process: It's first come first serve, so you have to be quick to sign up for the classes you want. The university didn't send me my login information in time, so I got none of the classes I initially wanted. But there is another registration period afterwards where you can ask for a place in a class or sign up for exchange-specific classes. So I still got some interesting classes regardless.
registration_help: There was a (slightly) confusing guide on how to register, and then you had the option of mailing the university staff, though they were very overworked.
registration_success: As mentioned I got none of those I initially wanted. But it was super easy to register for exchange-only classes, and I got into another class fairly easy by asking the professor.
registration_advice: Have a prepared list of classes beforehand. Also, be prepared to send kind emails to professors asking for a place in their classes in case you don't get them initially.
academics_comments: It is quite possibly the best experience of my university history. I am deducting one point for the slight COVID-annoyances and troubles with paperwork, but despite these I never once regretted studying abroad or choosing my university.
course_level: I took courses which allowed both BA and MA students, so the academic level felt lower than what I am used to.
teaching_comparison: Much more lecture style, where the professor talks and you write notes. For one of my classes there were no student discussions at all, which also was in part due to COVID-restrictions and us having the class entirely online and through pre-recorded sessions.
courses_enrolled: IEC4008: Understanding Asian Cultures. IEC4009: Contemporary Korean Society and Culture. SOC4010: Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights
recommended_courses: SOC4010: Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights. It was definitely the most engaging of my courses with loads of discussions on how AI impacts society. It also had a mix of students from both social science and computer science, which I believe made the discussions more diverse and interesting.
unexpected_costs: Not necessarily unexpected, but you have to pay national health insurance (NHIS) once you get your ARC (alien registration card). And the bill turned out to be more than expected.
cost_comparison: I was told food is less expensive than at home, and that is absolutely correct! Public transportation is also super cheap.
activities_available: Same answer as above.
activities_recommended: They did arrange a hike for exchange students in smaller groups to comply with restrictions. I didn't go personally, but heard about it from other people, and it seemed like a great way to get to meet other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: If you can, get out of the city and explore the rest of the country. It is incredibly diverse in nature and cityscapes. I can absolutely recommend Busan and Jeju Island, which are some of the biggest destinations.
culture_adjustment: I had tried to prepare myself mentally before leaving home, and because I had already had a slight introduction to the culture, it did not seem like too drastic a shift. That being said, it was very different.
socializing_tips: Take advantage of your university assigned guide. And engage with those in your classes. Koreans are super nice but somewhat shy.
cultural_challenges: For me it was mainly the food. More specifically the bread.
culture_appreciated: They are very big on coffee and cafes. Eating out, especially if you're eating Korean food, is a very social thing.
top3_advice: 1) Double-check all of you documents. 2) Connect with other UCPH students before going, so you have someone to compare/ask advice. 3) Visit the Suwon campus, even if you're studying at the Seoul campus. Also, bonus: try and get some coffee at the university library - there's a robot serving it!
other_useful_info: The university had a KakaoTalk group chat, which was super helpful since not only university staff could respond, but also other students, which was sometimes a lot quicker than sending the university an email.
most_rewarding: Experiencing and living in a different culture, and especially experiencing it with other people who also were new to the country.
greatest_challenge: I would say COVID restrictions, but also the bread situation. Bread as a meal or culinary concept is very different in South Korea compared to Denmark and majority of Europe.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience a completely different culture, far away from home.
overall_comments: The whole experience was amazing, but i had so many issues with courses and course registration that i overall will rate my exchange 9/10.
info_ease: Quite easy.
arrival_assistance: I didn't recieve much information on arrival, but if i had any question, the administration was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The whole experience was amazing, but i had so many issues with courses and course registration that i overall will rate my exchange 9/10.
registration_process: When registration was possible, i then found out that they had two phases of registration. There was online registration and offline registration. If i remember correctly, online registration was were you signed up for courses online, were i found out that you could only sign up for courses within your major, which i wasn't aware of beforehand. As the only courses within my major was either in Korean or undergraduate courses, i couldn't apply for any courses in the online registration. In the offline registration, however, i was apply to sign up for some courses that was relevant for my study back home, but it was a very limited amount of courses. I needed to have 3 courses during my study abroad, and i could only find 4 courses that were relevant for my study back home. In the offline registration, it was then required that i asked every single professor for permission to take their course, which was also a challenge. One of the professors said i probably wasn't qualified, but that i could take the course if i wanted to(which meant that most likely wouldn't pass the course). This meant that i now only had 3 courses left that i wanted to take, and i had to get permission for all 3 courses, or i wouldn't be able to complete my exchange abroad. I sent an email to the professors asking for permission to take the course. Only one of them replied, which meant that i had to find the other two professors on campus to ask for their permission. I did manage to find them, and get their permission, but it was indeed a very stressful experience. Once i was registrered in the 3 courses, i then already missed the first week of the course(because it was through offline registration), but that wasn't the big issue. The big issue was the fact that when i turned up to one of my courses, i could see that there was no other exchange students in the entire class, and they all spoke Korean. As the class was about to start, the professor came up to me, and said that i was probably in the wrong class. We then found out that i was signed up for the wrong class, as there was two courses with the same name. One would think i then should able to move to the different course(the one in English), but because it was outside of registration period, i couldn't change course, which was a big problem for me. The professor let me participate in the correct course, and i was able to join the online forum as well, but on paper i was still taking the other class. The administration said that while i couldn't change course, i could take the other course(the one in English), as an auditing student, which meant that my final grades would show that i failed the course i was signed up for(the one in Korean), but that i instead passed another course(the one in English). The administration said that i need permission from my home university in order to do that, which i tried to get. My home university never replied to my mail regarding permission to take a class as an auditing student, which meant that i spend my entire study abroad, not knowing if i would pass 3 courses to complete my exchange, which meant that i was taking a course, that i wasn't signed up for, and i had know idea whether or not i was wasting my time taking this course.
registration_help: The administration told me what was possible, and what wasn't possible. While i didn't feel like they were very effective in helping me getting the correct courses, i think it was more or less due to the system and the rules used at the university, which wouldn't allow them to help me any further. I would however like to point out that in the end i passed all 3 courses, and without having to take the course as an auditing student. So while it didn't seem to be possible, it seems like i passed the course without any issues, and it doesn't show that i failed any courses. So one way or another, either the administration or the professor(or maybe both), let me pass the course i signed up for, and i am very grateful to whoever helped with that.
registration_success: While it was a very stressful and tedious process, and i didn't know until the end of my echange if i succesfully signed up for all 3 courses, i did manage to get the courses i wanted, which was lucky as i needed these specific courses in order to complete my exchange.
registration_advice: Make sure to find out which courses are available to you when you choose university, and maybe consider applying for another major when on exchange, so that you can sign up for those courses in online registration.
academics_comments: The whole experience was amazing, but i had so many issues with courses and course registration that i overall will rate my exchange 9/10.
course_level: I had 3 courses, in which two of them was within the "Interaction science" major, and the last one was a business major course. The business major course was "Management information systems", and it was nothing like i expected it to be. The course revolved around the students choosing a research question to work with, and you would then have to work with that research question for the rest of the semester. It was good for me, as i could work with my thesis research question, which helped me find a good research question to write my thesis on, but i didn't really learn anything about management information systems(if i say so myself). The courses in interaction science was nothing like i expected either. The courses were named "Human-AI interaction" and "Service marketing and AI", and i definitely thought i would learn about AI, which wasn't the case. "Service marketing AI" was simply the process of defining a problem, and trying to find solve that problem by developing an app. The solution didn't even have to include AI at all, so that was a bit of a let down. The last course "Human-AI interaction" involved no teaching by the professor himself, which was very weird. Every single week, and selected group of students have to present some kind of AI or system for analyzing data, which was relevant to the AI part of the course, but it was very weird that the course was just presentations during the entire semester.
teaching_comparison: While presentations and group projects are very common in the courses i've had at UCPH, i was quite surprised by how each course was very dedicated to one specific kind of teaching. One course was only presentations, another course was only working on a group project, and the last course was me and 4 other students sitting in the professors own office, being targeted to answer questions on the reading material. Overall, i would say the big difference was the lack of teaching by the teachers themselves, as compared to Denmark, you usually get lectures by the professors during class on the reading material. While one course was quite heavy on reading, the other courses involved very limited amount of reading though, which is quite different from my courses at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: - Management information systems - Service marketing AI - Human-AI interaction
recommended_courses: The courses within the "Interaction science" major were quite chill, which was nice so that i didn't have to stress that much about school work while on exchange. The course "Management information systems" was however very demanding and tough, but it helped me a lot with preparing for my thesis, so while it was tough, it was definitely the course that i learned the most from.
unexpected_costs: Not any to be honest
cost_comparison: Transportation was so very cheap, and buying food at restaurants was also very cheap compared to Denmark. Fruit was however quite expensive, as well as groceries, which is why i never cooked a meal my entire stay in South Korea. When traveling around South Korea, i was surprised how cheap the hotels were, while traveling with flight or bullet train was quite expensive. This is quite different from Europe where housing is expensive, while it's cheap to travel around. Soju was also very cheap, as you could buy an entire bootle of soju for only 11 kr. in a grocery store, which was a very cheap way to get drunk.
activities_available: I played at the football club at the university, and that was a lot of fun, and they were very welcoming to us foreigners.
activities_recommended: Just as i played football on the team, and had a lot of fun with that, i know a lot of exchange students took judo classes, and they really seemed to enjoy that. Doing sports at university was a great way to engage with other koreans, that didn't involve drinking and partying.
weekend_recommendations: I travelled to Jeju island and Busan, and i would definitely recommend going there. If you go to Jeju, it's best to go there as close to the summer as possible, as it is even better to be there when the weather is great. Going to the Bamboo forest in Busan was definitely cool, and seeing different temples all over South Korea have indeed become memories that i will cherish for the rest of my life.
culture_adjustment: If you are just somewhat respectful towards their culture and customs, then it is very easy to adjust to the local culture in South Korea.
socializing_tips: While Koreans are very friendly and helpful, they become way more open and talkative when they are drinking, so that is very good way to socialize with the locals.
cultural_challenges: Not talking in public transportation was definitely an issue for most exchange students, as people in South Korea will shush you, if you speak too loud(or sometimes if you just speak at all).
culture_appreciated: They are very respectul and kind towards each other, which really helped me enjoy my stay in South Korea. While they didn't have trash cans in the street(which was anoying), the streets were very clean, with just shows how well behaved the locals are. Even as a guy, i also really enjoyed how safe i felt while in South Korea, as there wasn't a single time were i was afraid to get mugged or anything like that. All the female friends i got in South Korea also said that they have never felt as safe walking around alone at night, as they did in South Korea, which is exactly how it should be.
top3_advice: - Prepare for course registration as much as possible, as it might save you a lot of trouble down the road(only problem i encountered while in South Korea) - Learn some Korean phrases, as it can both be very helpful to know when you live in Korea, and Koreans become quite happy and friendly when you speak a little korean. - While it is of course important to fulfill your academic responsibilities, it's not a bad idea to take some easy courses while on exchange. Remember to experience as much of the culture as possible, while also engaging in as many social gatherings and activities as possible, as these will become memories that you will remember for the rest of your life.
other_useful_info: While the fall is pretty warm, it becomes very cold in the winter, so either bring a winterjacket, or buy one when at the university. You also get the possiblity of buying a university baseball jacket, which is both incredibly cool, and hands down the best item i bought while in Korea, but it is also surprisingly warm, and i've been using it during the entire winter period back home in Denmark.
most_rewarding: I learned some Korean phrases when i was still in Denmark, and seeing the Koreans being so happy when you try and speak their language was very rewarding. Even though my Korean was incredibly limited, i could still say some stuff, which was fun.
greatest_challenge: Course registration.
other_comments: I would definitely recommend going on exchange to South Korea, as it has been an incredible experience. I've created memories that i will cherish forever, and i have created friendships that will spand across the globe, which is very exciting. I'm already meeting friends from all over Europe just 2 months after the exchange has ended, so studying abroad is indeed a great way to get friends from all over the globe.

crucial_aspects: It was a place that I had been before, so I knew I would love it. My friend had studied at the same university previously and she played a big part in making me consider South Korea.
info_ease: Since I already had experience with the country it was quite easy to to figure things out. But I also have to add that Korea in general makes it easy to navigate the country and Seoul in general.
arrival_assistance: They have many different apps that help foreigners and locals alike, and if that doesn't work the locals are always there to lend a helping hand. When it comes to the school, they made it quite easy for exchange students to figure everything out by providing guides and tutorials through emails (like course sign up, payment etc.). Beforehand they also made sure to create a groupchat for all the exchange students so that students can ask questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: SKKU made it easy for us to register for courses, by providing guides on how to do it. Before registering, the website allows you to add your courses in a basket and then when its time for signing up you just have to click register.
registration_help: Tutorials, guides, email assistance.
registration_success: I was able to get all the courses I wanted in the first round, but one course ended up being cancelled and so I had to sign up for a new course in the 2nd round of sign ups. Even though many courses are full it is possible to contact the professor and ask if you can join, and most of the times they say yes.
registration_advice: Make sure to sign up for course AS SOON AS IT OPENS. My friend made the mistake of waiting a few hours and almost all courses were full.
course_level: the level was easier but this might have been due to the amount of credit of the courses. I usually have two courses each semester but this time i had 5, which means the amount of credit for each course is significantly smaller.
teaching_comparison: I enjoyed it a lot. Especially one course had a good balance of lectures mixed with student discussions where we could apply theory in praksis.
courses_enrolled: *Convergence Media and Popular Culture *Understanding Computational Media *Political & Economic Development in Korea *Economics in Global Environments *Popular Culture and Digital Media
recommended_courses: Understanding computational media Popular culture and digital media. Both professors in these courses were amazing and it was clear to see how much they enjoyed teaching.
unexpected_costs: Communication. I bought an esim at the airport and it was much more expensive than any other place. Other people used Chingu mobile.
cost_comparison: Food, clothes and smaller appliances (from daiso) can be found very cheap. At some places they are more expensive, but its usually around the same price. The reason why food expenses is the highest is because i ate out everyday and never cooked. Transportation is very cheap, since the price is the same no matter where and how far you go. If you need to find things for your house, go to daiso.
activities_available: SKKU offered many different clubs and most of them were also available to exchange students. The HI-club also hosts different events for exchange students so people can meet eachother. The university also has several festivals, such as movie night and koncerts where you can see famous singers like PSY (make sure to go).
activities_recommended: I joined the dance club Ggun and it was probably the best decision of my whole stay. I met so many different people and made a lot of friends and memories. And there is no need for dancing experience beforehand.
weekend_recommendations: Go to nearby cities such as incheaon, nami island or even busan or jeju.
culture_adjustment: There were a lot of small cultural differences but they were quite easy to adapt to. Like not talking/eating/drinking in the subway. They also have a lot of self-service at restaurants where you have to set your own table, bring side dishes and go up to the counter to pay when leaving.
socializing_tips: Make sure to take some major courses where there are Koreans! The korean friends I made were very welcoming and friendly but they might be a little shy in the beginning. Joining clubs also helps with meeting locals.
cultural_challenges: At times people might ignore you if you speak english to them since some locals are bit uncomfortable with speaking english.
culture_appreciated: Despite the previous statement, many people are very helpful even though there is a clear language barrier. Knowing a few korean words goes a long way.
top3_advice: Join some clubs, become more extroverted if you can, and don't worry too much about grades - instead focus on enjoying your time.
other_useful_info: Be prepared to walk up a hill everyday. Make sure to go to ESKARA and get some souvenirs. Try the robot coffee at the library.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all around the world and becoming friends with so many different people that I still wish to keep in contact with. I started out as an introvert but I knew that the best way to enjoy my stay would be to become more extroverted.
greatest_challenge: Accommodation since I had to move three times.
other_comments: Download KakaoTalk, Kakaomap, Naver, and buy a transportation card as soon as possible.

teaching_comparison: It was pretty different in the different classes. Two of my four professors weren't Koreans. But the culture were still similar to each other. The teacher were more 'the boss' or someone who is always right, than in Denmark. You would never call them by their first name. It was a lot of the professors talking in most of the classes, and we had at least one presentation, alone or in groups, in each course.
courses_enrolled: French cinema and cultural contents Workshop for Experimental Film and Video Contemporary Korean Society and Culture Comparative Thought and Culture: Horizons East and West Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights
recommended_courses: Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights was pretty interesting with a decent teacher. It was the heaviest of my courses, as the exam was pretty big. But still, easy compared to DK, so you can easily manage it. Contemporary Korean Society and Culture was also pretty interesting, with the nicest korean lady as our professor. She really cared about us having a good time, and not being too caught up in school and homework. This was really nice, and so easy!
unexpected_costs: Costs for Alien Registration Card, which is kind of like a license to be there. And just in general wa shopping groceries a lot more expansive than I thought, and the area I lived in was also pretty expensive.
cost_comparison: Fruits, some vegetables, rice, meat is also crazy expensive Kimbap, noodles and small korean restaurant are really cheap and so nice.
activities_available: A lot of different classes. Sports, poetry, math, chess
activities_recommended: I don't know, I didn't try anything
weekend_recommendations: Go to other places in Korea! but also really explore everything you want to do in Seoul. I ended up only taking three trips somewhere else, because there were so many places, areas, sights I wanted to see in Seoul. But go to different new areas you hear about, that may be 1-1,5 hour away, because it takes a long time to go everywhere in Seoul.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, not that I ever really got into it. But most people are used to 'tourists' and also because I was with other exchange students all the time, that helped me out to feel at home more quickly I think. But if you are somewhere where there are only older people, or really local, you cannot help but feel like a complete outcast and that you don't belong there.
socializing_tips: Mhh, it's probably easiest in school. But even then, it can be a challenge. Most Koreans are terrified of speaking English, so they will probably just shake their head and look or walk away, if you try to encounter them. However one of my friends, who is really outgoing, got two different korean friends. But they started talking to her first as well, and then you know they are comfortable speaking English.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier - 100%. Also they party differently, not as much if they take their study seriously, and they have a lot more inhibitions. They won't really dance and stuff like that. But most people are really nice and helpful if they know how to.
culture_appreciated: The temples, the food, the sharing-feeling and the feeling of community they have with each other. It's very different than in Denmark
top3_advice: Go into it with an open mind You really don't need to know anything or be a k-pop fan to be going. I didn't have any of these interests and knew nothing, and don't worry - there are a lot of people like you, you are not only surrounded by k-pop lovers. Don't plan to many visits from back home, sometimes it can be nice, but it also pull you out from the exchange bubble, which can be annoying, when you really want to be in that, and enjoy as long as it lasts. And!! don't be scared by the crazy different culture and language, it doesn't feel as alien, because you will be together with people who are in the same place as you, and who is really good at English.
other_useful_info: If there are food you are going to miss which can be difficult or really expensive to get - bring it. Also deodorants, sun lotion (without whitening in it) can be difficult and/or expensive Maybe learn hangeul - it will make your life a little easier.
most_rewarding: To get to live in another country and really feel at home there. Have a complete network, regular places, a university and favorite areas and restaurants. That is really special.
greatest_challenge: I actually was really fortunate, I really didn't have a lot of challenges. I was so surprised of how not alone and homesick I felt. Though one thing, in one of my courses the language barriers were almost impossible to work with. That got me really frustrated, and I felt alone because I didn't know anyone in the course.
other_comments: Please go!! It is an opportunity and experience that you will never get again.

crucial_aspects: Taekwon-do
info_ease: Fairly easy. I think in the moment that I thought that everything was very overwhelming... Remember, everyone wants to help you the best they can so everything will be alright if you do your best to follow along. Make sure that you attend the orientation and have read up on things and have found accommodation.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation day and SKKU has a international office that I went to with some questions about courses and general everyday things about student life in Korea.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Fairly straight forward. Filled out the forms - transcripts, bank statements, passport and then they send you a participation agreement. I didn't think it was too difficult, but they are a bit slow to send it. I felt like everyone else who attended different universities in South Korea got there acceptance and forms before us...
registration_help: They have an email... Be patient though.
registration_success: Very successful. I got up at 3 am to apply for the ones I wanted so I got them all. One of the professors asked us to drop one class because they didn't have enough space for their Korean students which kind of sucked. But I found another one when I got to SKKU.
registration_advice: Be sure to search through all the different campus' and degrees. It wasn't completely intituitive which classes I could take and some classes don't allow international student. Use the "language in international language" as a guide. However, many of the classes are still partially in Korean even though it is marked as "international language"...
course_level: I couldn't find enough relevant master courses so I took bachelor's courses. I had some trouble with a long waiting time for my pre-approval of courses because I was a masters student taking only bachelor's courses. However it worked out. Remember that it is UCPH's responsibility that you can take the courses that makes most sense for your education. Even if it takes a long time, if you have good reasons to take only bachelor's courses or a specific course, then write to Studenter service.
teaching_comparison: In SKKU, for natural sciences courses the style is way different than UCPH. It is basically, "here is a 1,5 hour presentation, remember everything." No practical exercises, no repetition other than if you do some yourself. Took me a bit of time to find a good way of studying and even then I was not as satisfied as at UCPH. However, don't stress too much about how well you are doing. The professors know that the life of an exchange student is different than native Koreans so probably they pull some punches. Just be sure to do your best and show up for the majority of the classes.
courses_enrolled: Biodatamining (GBE3071-41) Genetics (IBT2003-41) Trends in Computational Biology (IBB3017-41) Intensive Korean (IKP)
recommended_courses: Trends in Computational Biology (IBB3017-41), Balachandran is really nice and a good teacher. The only course where we got to do group work, which I missed in the other courses.
unexpected_costs: To get your visa there is a 420 dkk price tag and to get the ARC (alien registration card) after you have arrived there were some costs for taking a decent photograph. They also have a compulsory national health insurance (NHS) - if you have travel insurance at home (I made one with IDA) then you can get exempt. Do that.
cost_comparison: Food is really cheap, transportation as well. Groceries are really expensive basically like in DK but the quality is worse. Just eat out or at the convenience stores.
activities_available: A lot of different clubs and activities. I didn't really attend any, but I heard that they were great fun.
activities_recommended: Join a club. I did taekwon-do outside of university, but joining any club is the best way to get in contact with locals.
weekend_recommendations: Go out of Seoul. There are some really nice sights in South Korea. Do trips to Busan, Jeju Island and other smaller cities. Also visiting other countries in East/South-east Asia is really convenient when you are in South Korea already.
culture_adjustment: Very difficult at first, however after the first month everything was running smoothly.
socializing_tips: JOIN A CLUB!!
cultural_challenges: No talk Korea bus
culture_appreciated: They are very polite. I didn't feel gawked at or like I didn't belong. Most Koreans won't treat you that different.
top3_advice: Get accommodation. Research which courses are available. Have patience and be ready to check your email everyday and to communicate if something needs to be clarified.
other_useful_info: Be patient. Everything will work out.
most_rewarding: Having Korean language class and doing taekwon-do on a higher level than at home.
greatest_challenge: Being away from my girlfriend, family and friends for such a long time...
other_comments: You got this. Everything is going to be alright
