info_ease: SKKU (Sungkyunkwan University) is very used to getting exchange students and therefore sends out all the information needed and explains everything very thouroghly. It is all send in an acceptance package and it is also possible to google SKKU semester fact sheet to find some of the information already now. I had no problem trying to get into one of their dorms and registering for courses online since the information documents explained everything I needed to know.
arrival_assistance: The university has a social club called hi-club which are local students who help exchange students on their semester abroad. In the beginning the explain all of the university's different systems and they also create events to meet other exchange students. I did not need that much help from the university upon arrival since I had figured everything out before the exchange with the help of their information documents. The few smaller questions I had during the exchange the university also helped me with without any problems.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: They send a document throughly explaining the proces of signing up for courses, so I did not find it difficult to sign up for the courses. The website where you can look at the different courses is a little difficult to understand, but the websites for signing up for courses are much easier to understand - especially with help from the information documents. There are courses meant for exchange students only and then courses where the local students also attend. The courses where the local students attend there might be a certain amount of spaces for exchange students - keep an eye on that since the courses might fill up quickly in the registration period.
registration_help: they had the information documents, where they explained how to sign up for registration in great detail. The first week of the semester is an add-drop period, where it is possible to switch courses or get more courses. In this week the university personnel are ready to help you + it will also be described in the registration information documents.
registration_success: I got all the course I wanted since I was ready as the registration opened.
registration_advice: I would recommend looking into all the courses you want to get and learning their registration system before the registration period. If you want to register for a course with few spaces for exchange students then I recommend being ready as the registration opens as to be sure to get the courses you want.
course_level: The level was in general lower that the courses I have taken at KU.
teaching_comparison: At SKKU it is mostly lectures without exercises thorughout the classes and only few assignments. That also means that I did not have that much time at the school compared to KU. I prefer the teaching style at KU, but also found it interesting experiencing another way of teaching.
courses_enrolled: International Trade, Advanced Macroeconomic Theory, Labor Economics, Health Economics, Causal Inference for Economists.
recommended_courses: I would recommend: Advanced Macroeconomic Theory: It can be transfered as Macroeconomics III at KU and the lecturer in that course was the best I had on exchange. Causal Inference for Economists: It is more intuition behind econometrics, which we do not get as much at KU. Labor Econ and Health Econ are not that difficult courses - they are nice to see Microeconomics applied to different fields. I would not recommend International Trade since it is a 3 hour long lecture, where I do not like the teaching style of the professor.
unexpected_costs: There is a National Health Insurance that you have to pay even if you are insured from home. It is payed each month roughly and is around 350 dkr, I think.
cost_comparison: Housing through the school was relatively inexpensive. Eating out every day was also relatively inexpensive.
activities_available: There was a club called Hi-club with the purpose of helping exchange students and holding parties and events for the exchange students. In the first week it is possible to sign up for different types of clubs - some being social clubs where exchange students have a chance of meeting and becoming friends with korean students. I regret not signing up in time for these clubs since they seem like a good chance for getting more friends in the beginning - I also got a lot of friends through the hi-club events and my dorm.
activities_recommended: I would recommend the events and activities created by the hi-club and also participating in the ESKARA festival, which is a festival created by the university.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend travelling within the country to places like: Busan, Jeju, Gyeongju, Sokcho, Gangneung, Jeonju, Gwangju, Nami Island and Suwon. I went to all these places during weekends and holidays and felt like I got to see many sides of South Korea there.
culture_adjustment: It is pretty easy to adjust to the local culture since it is not that different from the scandinavian culture. For an example, they eat relatively early and therfore the restaurants close pretty early too. The biggest difference is probably that there is so many people all the time wherever you are and that Seoul is a massive city.
socializing_tips: I would recommend participating in the social clubs or the like, if you want to become friends with the korean students.
cultural_challenges: I did not find anything particularly difficult.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated how much they wanted to share their culture with strangers and eventhough we might not have spoken the same language then they still try to communicate the best they can.
top3_advice: The three most important things I would tell is: have fun, travel the country and make good friends with the othe exchange students.
other_useful_info: I would say that it is pretty tedious and long proces to sign up for exchange, but as soon as you get to go on the exchange then it is really easy and it is so much fun to explore South Korea and see all the different sides of the country. Specifically for SKKU they are very good at helping quickly and efficiently with any problem you might have.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange was getting to experience living and having a day-to-day in a country pretty different from Denmark.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during exchange was getting used to the different teaching style at SKKU compared to at KU.

crucial_aspects: At the time the exchange was a mandatory, and the destination was already determined seeing as I was a Korean studies undergrad.
info_ease: To be honest I arrived before time, and due to that it was hard to find information. National health insurance and arc/residence card are things your host university tell you about at the orientation they give.
arrival_assistance: You could apply to get a buddy.
arrival_comments: I think they should have been a little more transparent about which courses we are restricted from taking as exchange students and also based on our major.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I cannot really remember the steps to register.
registration_help: We ended up going to the International Office that helped us register for the last classes we needed.
registration_success: We definitely had some challenges and were rejected twice from two different classes. For one of the classes we were told that the professor noticed that we did not have the right major to apply, but we were not made aware of the restriction and it wasn't written anywhere on the website when we registered for the course.
registration_advice: Take a really good look at the guide for registering because the courses disappear quickly.
course_level: "Korean Language School, Regular Course" and "International Relations of East Asia" were very intense. The former was the mandatory language school we had to attend, and we regularly had written and oral tests each week. And the workload was a lot. "International Relations of East Asia" was a political course, and the professor actually told us that it was better if we were political science majors. It was very heavy and for a lot of words and concepts we had to do our own research. The workload was heavy and especially leading up to the midterms and finals.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style is quite different at Sungshin from that of UCPH. I think it is more free at our university vs. that of Sungshin. Everything seemed a bit rigid. In addtion, it was also more passive or at least that was true for our poltical course where we were mostly listening.
courses_enrolled: Korean Language School, Regular Course International Seminar: Korean and Global Affairs (001) International Relations of East Asia
recommended_courses: As the language course is mandatory I won't comment on that. So I would say the "International Seminar: Korean and Global Affairs (001)" was a really nice course. The workload was lesser than the other two but it was a course where you got to know the other students learn about their cultures and way of thinking. In addition, we also learned about Korean culture and society.
unexpected_costs: The university had their own mandatory insurance. On top of the national health insurance, the university required you to pay for their insurance as well.
cost_comparison: If you cook at home groceries can be a little expensive.
activities_available: I'm not sure. The festival had been pushed due to covid restrictions so I experienced it but usually it would be during summer I think. As for other events I'm unsure.
activities_recommended: If you go to Sungshin I think it's better to join the buddy program, because the people with buddies were more aware of any events at the school.
weekend_recommendations: Keep an eye out for any exciting events in Seoul on social media and go out and do the classic stuff. Go to famous spots in Seoul, amusement parks, exhibitions, foodmarkets etc. Make sure to make the most of it while you are there, and if you have the energy for it do some trips during the weekends or holidays and go outside of Seoul.
culture_adjustment: It was quite okay but I probably found it easier due to my major.
socializing_tips: I don't really have a tip but the easiest is probably to try and socialize with them through class or clubs. And if those aren't an option then the buddy program.
cultural_challenges: Intially the staring. People stare a lot, and in the beginning it's hard to get used to. There is typically no malicious intent behind it, they are just curious. And one funny thing is how they mix sweet and savory. I experienced getting syrup in my blt sandwich, syrup with my pizza and I heard about people getting garlic bread with sugar on top.
culture_appreciated: Food culture. I liked going to Korean restaurants and having a variety of side dishes and in general I really liked the food. Sometimes they might get a little too experimental with their food but they are often spot on.
top3_advice: It is a smaller university so they are more inclined to help you at the international office. However, don't expect to be able to take any courses you want. Definitely, participate in the buddy program or actively find something else social.
other_useful_info: The university is located on top of a hill...
most_rewarding: Getting the language course certificate! You put in so much work and it so intense through the semester, so getting the certificate was really rewarding.
greatest_challenge: The intensity of the language course.

crucial_aspects: To study in an internationally recognised university, with an interesting program and new topics and courses; To have a cheap and easy to find accomodation.
overall_comments: Uppsala is a great place to study, with students and university buildings all around the town. I think it would have been nice to know beforehand that SLU is a bit outside of the city. It means that you have to choose to have a room either close to the city or close to SLU. However, it's great to bike around and most of the way is flat and pretty. In Uppsala center, there are a lot of student groups and activities, which is very unique to Uppsala and makes it super easy to meet new people and start new hobbies.
info_ease: SLU has an agreement with several housing buildings around Uppsala, which made it super easy to arrive and move in directly. The only thing is that you need to arrive during a working day and not in the evening. The course information were sent to me both trough my regular email and on canvas. You need to set up your SLU email beforehand but you just need to video call someone from the IT department and then you can access it very easily.
arrival_assistance: I could drop by the building office to get my key and drop my suitcases directly after my arrival in Uppsala. We also had a meeting with Ulf, who is the responsible for the EnvEuro students, a bit later after we all arrived. It was nice to meet all the students and then we could keep in touch and meet eachothers.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Uppsala is a great place to study, with students and university buildings all around the town. I think it would have been nice to know beforehand that SLU is a bit outside of the city. It means that you have to choose to have a room either close to the city or close to SLU. In Uppsala center, there are a lot of student groups and activities, which is very unique to Uppsala and makes it super easy to meet new people and start new hobbies.
registration_process: You will receive a student number by email called the "T number". Then on "Ladok" you need to register for the courses you chose. I think you register for the whole semester at once. It is a bit tricky to understand because you have to register for your second choices as well, in case you are not accepted in the courses you want. In case you are interested for the internship, then you have to notify the international team by email because the "course" does not appear on Ladok.
registration_help: They were very reactive by email and super ready to help in case you have any question.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted. If not, you automatically get your second choices.
registration_advice: Ask questions by email if you are lost. Everyone is very helpful. Make sure your total number of ETCS is correct.
academics_comments: Uppsala is a great place to study, with students and university buildings all around the town. I think it would have been nice to know beforehand that SLU is a bit outside of the city. It means that you have to choose to have a room either close to the city or close to SLU. However, it's great to bike around and most of the way is flat and pretty. In Uppsala center, there are a lot of student groups and activities, which is very unique to Uppsala and makes it super easy to meet new people and start new hobbies.
course_level: The courses I chose started back to basics witch made it super nice to follow because everyone was on the same level and could understand the rest of the course super easily. However, for people who are super advanced in some topics, they might get a bit bored because most of the courses don't go too deep into one particular topic. It depends on which course you choose for sure, but for 7.5 or 15 ECTS I would have expected more work and more interesting things.
teaching_comparison: It is quite similar. The teachers are available to answer your questions. They start back from the start with most of the topics and they were usually very good at teaching.
courses_enrolled: Soil water processes in agroecosystems - MV0216 Land use and watershed management to reduce eutrophication - MV0217 Geographic information systems for environmental and natural science studies - TE0017
recommended_courses: "Soil water processes in agroecosystems" was a nice course to learn the basics of working with a soil/water model. The teacher is super nice and helpful. We had a few theoric courses and then mostly "labs" where we met in a computer room and had exercises with "Stella" the model used. We usually finished earlier than scheduled. "Land use and watershed management to reduce eutrophication" is a course about water in agriculture and we had a few field trips. However, the course is in November so the weather was already super cold and it's not the best time to stay outside. The teacher is a great woman but she had a bit too much expectations with the course as it used to be a 15 ECTS course and it has been reduced to 7.5. There is quite a lot of work and courses. "GIS for environmental and natural science studies" was a beginners' course on GIS, that was given fully online even without covid restriction in Sweden. It was nice beacuse we could schedule our work as we wanted, as the courses were prerecorded and the exercises you could do whenever you wanted. The course was super usefull! You even get a certificate in the end, with your level in GIS. The teacher is however hard to understand, especiallyy because the GIS theory is quite hard to get.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay around 150 DKK each time you use the train to and from the airport! Plus the train price. That makes it super expensive! You can take a bus but it takes longer and is still quite expensive. Transportation is expensive in Sweden but you can buy a second hand bike easily and bike around in Uppsala.
cost_comparison: Food is more or less as expensive as in Denmark. Transportation is expensive so sometimes renting a car for the weekend is the cheapest option. You also have GoMore to rent people's car.
activities_available: I think there were sports and student commities at SLU but I don't know about it.
activities_recommended: Uppsala is full of student nations, which used to be "home" for students all around Sweden. There is Stockholm nation, Gotland nation, Kalmar nation etc. Each nation has a pub that serves food and drinks. They also have specific activities such as sports, flea markets, yoga, boardgames and a lot of other things. You have to pay around 220 DKK as a membership, and then you are allowed to enter any nation.
weekend_recommendations: There are plenty of nature reserve around. Download the app "Natuurkartan" and check on which walks you can do around Uppsala. This app works for all Sweden and shows where you can ice skate on lakes in winter, where you have mountain bike tracks, walking path, fire places (usually with chopped wood available), free access huts to spend the night in, etc. Great if you want to spend time outside and in the nature. Otherwise I would recommend to go in some of the national parks around Sweden. Abikso is great for a few days but has no network. Stockholm is also nice to go to before Christmas. Sigtuna has a great Christmas Market too.

overall_comments: My experience was near to perfect. The quality of courses and teaching were great! Everyone spoke really good english. All practicalities considering the exchange worked out well.
info_ease: It was really easy, we got information through email but also a lot of important information could be found from school's webpage.

registration_process: Registration could be done in Ladok one week before the course started or on the first day in class (if I remember correctly).
registration_help: If I had questions, the course leaders and the Mobility Team were responding to emails in short notice.
registration_success: It was actually very successful. First I did not got in my first priority course. I was asking help from the Mobility Team and they quided me to ask from the course leader after the first day if anyone had cancelled their registration. So I did and ended up getting a place from the course I wanted! So that was really great. Also I wanted to change my second course as well, and that was not an issue.
registration_advice: Registration process is not hard. If you don't get your first priority course and you really want it, be brave to ask if there is any possibility to get in if someone cancelles. Also, if you notice during the exchange that you might want to change the second period course, that was not a hard process if you have a pre-approval for it.
academics_comments: My experience was near to perfect. The quality of courses and teaching were great! Everyone spoke really good english. All practicalities considering the exchange worked out well.
course_level: The level of courses was very fine. I think it was a great balance of learning but not over doing or burning out. Some of people might find the level too easy, but I think it was fine.
teaching_comparison: Since I'm not danish and I come from a northern country, I'm maybe more used to the style in Sweden compared to UCPH. And I do prefer that a lot more compared to UCPH. I have never done an oral exam before coming to Denmark, so the examinations can be really challenging or even awfull situations. Also, I think the teaching is more distant and hierarcical in UCPH than in SLU. Teachers in UCPH might "target" you and pressure a lot more than in SLU. So if you want softer way of teaching, then Sweden might be a good choise.
courses_enrolled: 1) Forest History - Human utilisation and vegetation dynamics 2) Forest Ecosystem Ecology

cost_comparison: Movie tickets and some of the groceries.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere where I could study in English but still learn a language that I did not know already. I wanted to go to a good university with many interesting Computer Science courses. Lastly, I wanted to go somewhere with mountains as I love to hike and be outside.
info_ease: I got a lot of information from the coordinators at TUM both from the university overall and from the Informatics Department. I could access TUMonline (like KUnet) as a guest early to browse courses.
arrival_assistance: Mandatory welcome meeting. MINGA mentor program where you get assigned a mentor who also studies Informatics at TUM - I would really recommend to sign up for this. My mentor was a huge help for me and we ended up becoming good friends.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registration is done through TUMonline (like KUnet). In my opinion, it's really easy and effective. Most lectures do not have a limit on the number of students - I took a lecture with almost 2,000 students. A really nice thing is that you can sign up for more courses than you need and then deregister later in the semester (often until 1st of July). Exam registration is done separately later.
registration_help: I asked my mentor for advice on the courses and the professors. The advisors, Anna-Lisa and Martina, from the Informatics Department were also very helpful.
registration_success: Very successful. I got all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Apply for Praktikums and Seminars (deadline is early, in February for the summer semester). Take a German language course if you can - you learn German, get to know other international students and it helps balance the workload of 30 ECTS which is a lot at TUM (most people take 20-25 ECTS per semester). Join more courses than you need to and spend the first week attending all of them and figuring out which ones you want to keep.
course_level: I found the level comparable to DIKU but it really depends on the courses that you take. Ask your mentor or have a look at the Chair's (forskningssektion) website beforehand to get an impression of what they do and which courses they offer.
teaching_comparison: Quite similar except for Praktikum and Seminar courses. There are not as many TA sessions, usually only once a week. Covid was very much still a thing so all classes were also streamed/recorded.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Deep Learning (I2DL), Master-Praktikum: Machine Learning for Crowd Modeling and Simulation, Seminar - Selected Topics in Machine Learning, German B1.1, Spanish B1.2
recommended_courses: Take a Praktikum and/or a Seminar. You will get more information about those from the Department but they are really interesting, with fewer students and then you also avoid having 6 or more exams at the end of the semester.
unexpected_costs: None but I was surprised by how expensive housing was.
cost_comparison: Groceries are less expensive. Housing is expensive (comparable to Copenhagen or even more expensive).
activities_available: ZHS - like KSI/USG at KU. They offer almost any sport and also trips for kayaking, hiking, climbing etc. A really nice way to get to know German students. The classes are mostly taught in German. Weekly language cafés. MINGA mentoring events and day trips. ESNA, the Erasmus network, also arranges events, day trips and weekend trips throughout the semester and during the semester break (before the semester starts).
activities_recommended: ZHS, MINGA mentoring
weekend_recommendations: Hiking in the Alps - there are so many opportunities 1-2 hours from Munich. The lakes - Tegernsee, Ammersee, Eibsee, Königsee etc. Take the train to Zürich, Vienna, Salzburg, Verona (and further down in Italy), Prague and other German cities such as Rothenburg, Regensburg, Augsburg, Würzburg etc.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. I found the Germans funny, active, polite and helpful.
socializing_tips: Sign up for sports classes at ZHS. Go to beer gardens and festivals.
cultural_challenges: Very bureaucratic system, most things have to be done physically and on paper. Some people in Bayern are very traditional and conservative from a Danish perspective.
culture_appreciated: Being outside a lot, hiking, outdoor activities, swimming in the Isar, the chill vibe, Englischer Garten, beer gardens, the proximity to many other nice European cities. So many restaurants and bars.
top3_advice: Spread the workload by taking different kinds of courses - maybe a Seminar, a Praktikum, one or two lectures and a language course. Learn German. Join the MINGA and ESNA events to explore Munich and its surroundings.
other_useful_info: WG-Gesucht for finding apartments/rooms. Some people live in Garching (where the Informatics Department is) but I was really glad that I lived in Munich and just commuted to Garching three times a week for classes. Consider buying a Deutsche Bahn BahnCard if you plan to travel a lot by train. Use the Bayern-ticket when traveling within Bayern. Consider going a month before and taking an intensive German course (either at TUM or at LMU, the other large university).
most_rewarding: Getting to know a new city, spending so much time outside and in nature, learning German.
greatest_challenge: Finding time for everything.

I especially found it challenging with the course registration, as the system at TUM is more complex and old-school than most.
arrival_comments: In the future, it would be ideal to be offered an online meeting before arrival, where the course registration protocol is introduced and general support is given. Additionally, some TUM professors and/or course responsible were very late uploading course information, resulting in several of my planned courses not being offered as expected. This forced me to take some managerial courses outside of scope and campus to obtain my required credits in time. Hence, I did not satisfy my initial academic requirements for the study abroad.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Munich is excellent, and the University is definitely of a higher academic level. However, I did find a lack of communication with the host University and the semester dates started much later than the ones at UCPH. This has forced me to postpone the following block in Denmark.
registration_process: Online registration for courses opens shortly before arrival. However, bear in mind that not all of the courses are uploaded or visible at this point. Therefore you can "risk the chance" of getting a pre-approval for courses being given in prior years but not offered at this semester or year in particular (which happened to me). And note that there is a difference between courses & modules!
registration_help: You receive a PDF with an "introduction to course registration," which is helpful. But additional online contact or service would have been excellent to smoothen the process.
registration_success: As stated above, I was forced to choose courses outside my faculty. This was due to: 1) my initial and pre-approved courses not being offered this year as expected, 2) an overlap of course schedule/teaching hours, and 3) limited spots.
registration_advice: Aim to have as many "non-limited" courses with you to make registration more flexible. And have a plan B, if you courses are not offered as expected or you are not offered a spot.
academics_comments: Munich is excellent, and the University is definitely of a higher academic level. However, I did find a lack of communication with the host University and the semester dates started much later than the ones at UCPH. This has forced me to postpone the following block in Denmark.
course_level: The level of courses was in general high and required you to do your homework and follow the lectures during the semester.
teaching_comparison: Some courses were similar (in-class teaching, group work, case study), and others were different from what I've had at SCIENCE back in Copenhagen (e.g., Seminars).
courses_enrolled: As mentioned earlier, I was forced to choose courses outside my faculty to meet the required 30 ECTS points. Therefore I will list the courses separately. School of Life Science: Consumer Behavior, Food Economics, and Food Design and Food Industry. Outside: Key Issues in Businesses Today, Organizational Behavior, and Strategic and International Management.
recommended_courses: If you study food science or find the industry fascinating, I strongly recommend you to take the course in Freising by Mr. Pearson called 'Food Design and Food Industry.' Additionally, I enjoyed the course in Consumer Behavior which offers a broad insight into the psychological reasons for consuming products specifically related to the Food industry.

cost_comparison: "Cost of living" er generelt en smule billigere end I DK. Jeg sparede derfor penge på at handle ind (endda nogle gange billigere at smutte ned til den lokale og spise en Döner til 5€).
activities_available: De har vidst en ordning som tilbyder diverse typer af træning rundet omkring München. Tror bestemt det er værd at kigge på, hvis du allerede nu har en drøm om at dyrke noget specifikt under dit ophold (havde jeg ikke).
activities_recommended: Museer om søndagen til 1-2€! Afprøv nogle forskellige klubber (jeg trænede fx med EBF, EisbachFit, som er en udendørs trænings community. Dette gjorde det nemt at møde lokale og lære byen at kende på en anden måde).
weekend_recommendations: Sørg for at tage ud af byen med tog. Dette kan f.eks. være en dagstur til Tegernsee eller Walchensee, som begge tilbyder 10/10 hikes, bavariske spisesteder og smukkeste natur!
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Be open and smiling :)
cultural_challenges: Germans can be a bit reserved at some points (though mostly the older generation, who also LOVE to speak German and not English..).
culture_appreciated: Younger German generations are most friendly and open - and love Danes! I enjoy how they, particularly, enjoy the "everyday pleasures" such as dining out and drinking beer during the week.
top3_advice: Be aware of the course registration and have a Plan B. Start looking for housing a good deal in advance (especially if you want something in Munich). Pack your active gear - cause the city is surrounded by incredible nature and the ALPS!!!

other_comments: GO TO MUNICH IF YOU CAN :) The most unique and beautiful city I have ever experienced in Germany, and SO worth it!

crucial_aspects: 1) Being able to receive the Erasmus scholarship. 2) A good university with interesting courses. 3) A large variety of courses taught in English - this turned out to be surprisingly limited in the EU.
info_ease: TUM is great at keeping incoming students updated and informed on how they run their university, e.g. deadlines, how to navigate in student platform, etc. Overall it was very well done and I felt confident and unworried about administrative things all the time there.
arrival_assistance: All the assistance I needed was provided without me needing to ask for it. Information meetings, intro days with other students at TUM, general walkthrough of the exam system and how to "normally" attend courses. Even before arriving, TUM offered much service as to what courses to choose, how and when this should be done, etc. The only assistance I reached out for has been for signatures and stamps on official documents for Erasmus and credit transfer to my home university. I think it helps a lot that TUM is such a big university.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Having received and accepted the nomination from my sending institution, I simply had to transfer a fee TUM processed my application documents. I soon received an e-mail with the decision that I had been accepted. Then, I had to complete the enrollment steps for TUM that included transferring a fee of 152,2 euros and a proof of health insurance. It was enough to have my European health insurance card (det blå sygesikringskort) verified by a German health insurance provider - please do this in good time!
registration_help: I was sent many thorough guides explaining how to complete each steps and several reminders. This was a great help to me and I never had to reach out to get additional information. TUM has 1-2 persons that are responsible for incoming Erasmus students that you are always able to reach out to, if needed.
registration_success: TUM Informatics has some different types of classes: 1) Praktikum: practical courses where you apply theoretical knowledge to a concrete problem. Very popular and small capacity for each course. 2) Seminar: theoretical courses where you explore latest developments within a field and present your findings. Also very popular and small capacity for each course. 3) Lecture: classic style course where you attend lectures (and sometimes a few practical classes). Popular but rarely have capacity limits. Then I also took language courses at main campus. 1), 2) and language courses are very popular, making it difficult to get a spot. I managed to get a spot on my 4th priority of praktikum and 2/3rd priority for seminar. I got all the lecture courses I applied for.
registration_advice: If there is a course you would very much like to attend, please reach out to the course responsible person. They want engaged and excited students, so they might be able to get you a spot, even if you did not get one through the system. Perhaps even showing up to the first classes also gets you a spot, which happened to someone at my German class since some registered people did not show up for the first class, leaving an empty spot.
course_level: I think the level was appropriate. Praktikums and Seminars are very popular partly because lectures can be difficult to pass, since the exams often are very short and demanding when Praktikums and Seminars typically are graded based on a final report and presentation. I do not think I would have passed all credits if I had only taken lecture courses. However, in general teaching was great. The professors are very skilled and generally good educators.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at DIKU is very set in stone. It is not often that courses are taught in different ways, and when they are it is as a blow of fresh air. Usually we have lectures, classes and weekly/bi-weekly handins in all courses. It was great to experience something else to switch it up.
courses_enrolled: Requirements Engineering, Security Engineering, Master-Praktikum - Machine Learning in Crowd Modeling & Simulation, Advanced Seminar Blockchain Technologies, German as a Foreign Language A1.1, English - Academic Presentation Skills C1 - C2
recommended_courses: 1) Language courses! It is always fun to learn a new language and you meet a lot of other people that you can make friends with. 2) Advanced Seminar Blockchain Technologies. A great course for diving more into the new developments within blockchain technology, even making your own implementation if that's what you are interested in. 3) English - Academic Presentation Skills C1 - C2. I become very nervous when presenting but this course helped me deal with it a little better.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Eating out is cheaper, but generally Munich is as costly as Copenhagen in most regards except public transportation that became very cheap when the Deutschland ticket was introduced. Also, the TUM student card allows you to travel for free in weekdays 18-06 and all day in weekends.
activities_available: Unfortunately the sports club was in all German and the spots were sold out within limits. Generally, it was one of the few things that there was not a lot of information about. This was in great contrast to the social and cultural events that were many and varied, thanks to TUMi and MENSA! TUMi and MENSA arranged hiking trips, dance lessons, parties, city rallies, and many other things.
activities_recommended: Please go to all the TUMi and MENSA events that you can muster. You meet so many great people there and uncover hidden gems only otherwise known to locals.
weekend_recommendations: Also, here are so many great spots to visit in the region and they are all worth a visit. Such as Königssee, Zugspitze, Eibsee, Salzburg, Landshut, Nürnberg, Regensburg - and many more! Trips are arranged by the student societies MENSA and TUMi, but once you get to know people it is also very easy to just tag along or finding others to go with with the Deutschland ticket, which makes it very cheap to explore the region.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. Germany is not that different from Denmark. Munich specifically even focuses on introducing more biking culture, making it feel even more like Copenhagen. I will miss hanging out with my friends in the bier gartens.
socializing_tips: You can meet and socialize with local students: 1) when doing group work in seminars and praktikums 2) joining the sports clubs (which I had no luck doing) 3) moving into a dorm
cultural_challenges: In all honesty, none. Munich is a little more conservative, but it was not something that I really noticed.
culture_appreciated: I loved that people often went hiking in the weekend. In this region there are many beautiful mountains, forests and lakes. Particularly for the mountains there is the whole Austrian-like culture with small huts and eating kaiserschmarrn after a long hike.
top3_advice: 1) It will most likely be stressful to sort out housing, but always remember it will work out in the end! 2) Be up front if you want to go for a specific course, do not hold yourself back. Go talk to the professor and see if you can get a spot! Registration for exams is very late so it is possible to change courses late. 3) Go take a swim in the Eisbach and chill with a beer and bretzen. It is an absolute iconic experience when going to Munich. 4) Go to all the TUMi and MENSA events you can muster.
other_useful_info: The academic level of courses is less tough as compared to DIKU, so please allow yourself to spend some time enjoying life, the people you are there with and all the experiences that are offered to you when there. But please make sure you study well for the lecture, closed books exams!
most_rewarding: I really enjoyed attending courses that were different in both teaching style and content as compared to DIKU. It also made me appreciate my academic background as I felt very well prepared to participate in the teachings, group work and exams.
greatest_challenge: There really were no challenges out of the ordinary. Of course you can struggle a bit with course material sometimes, wish you went on that hike to that beautiful, that you studied better for an exam or did not drink that extra beer yesterday, but I can't say that I was really challenged. Word of caution: the smallest beer from tap is half a liter and not .33.

crucial_aspects: The variety and quality of courses in the Informatics department, the proximity to the mountains, being able to learn a new language
info_ease: Very easy. I got a lot of information from TUM via email prior to arrival and also received a letter to my German address with some information and my student card.
arrival_assistance: There was a welcome meeting for all incoming exchange students. I also signed up for the Minga mentor program which I would highly recommend.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Quite straight-forward. You sign up for courses in TUMonline (like KUnet). It is a lot more flexible than at KU in the way that you can register for as many courses as you like and then deregister (or just not register for the exam - that is a separate process but TUM will remind you of that and help you) for those that you do not want to take. For seminars and practical courses, you have to submit an application some months before the semester begins - you will receive information and guidance about this from TUM. Language courses also have their own registration process but are really nice.
registration_help: The people working in the administration are willing to help but also quite busy during peak periods. I asked my mentor about a lot of things i.e. recommendations for courses.
registration_success: Very successful - I got all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Register for more courses than you need to take, check them out during the first week or two and then decide which ones you want to keep. 30 ECTS in Informatics can be a lot at TUM so try to balance it with some language courses or courses from other departments.
course_level: High level, professors and PhD students are generally very committed and available, writing papers (and potentially trying to publish them) is quite common so ask your professor if you are interested in that. I really enjoy attending a seminar and a practical course as opposed to only taking "regular" courses (lectures + exercises).
teaching_comparison: Lectures were quite similar. Some of them were partly taught by PhD students and it actually worked really well because they lectured about their current research. In the courses that I took, there were less assignments than I am used to at DIKU and more self-studying, reading, and doing project work (with supervision from PhDs). crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a German speaking country, as I saw the study exchange as an ideal opportunity for improving my language skills. I didn't have a lot choice: Zürich or Munich. I chose Munich mostly because of my gut feelings, and I didn't regret it.
overall_comments: The Technical University of Munich is a very good university in my opinion. It however has a very misleading name, as not all of it schools are locate in Munich. I was at the School of Life Sciences, which is located 30 min north of Munich in a little town called Freising. This shouldn't nevertheless hold you from applying to the school. The campus is amazing: very green, cute and everyone knows each other. You therefore quickly become a part of the student life at campus. Freising is also very nice. It is mainly inhabited by students and is far from dead and boring. So many events all the time! Bierfest, Nacht der Musik, and many other celebrations. You'll get the true bavarian experience by living in Freising. Most exchange students lived in Freising itself and not Munich, which I would really recommend.
info_ease: It was honestly a very stressful application process, which made me regret the destination choice big time before my departure. The administration at TUM was clearly understaffed and directly asked us not to send to emails. Moreover, my contact person didn't anser me for several months despite my many mails concerning very important steps in the application process.
arrival_assistance: We had one introduction lecture at our campus. Apart from that, we were very much alone as exchange students, but we help and support each other, and it turned out to be great.

You have no chance what so ever to know whether the courses will be offered, and neither has the university. My contact person didn't want to sign my Online Learning Agreement before I had a list of courses that will be offered. I therefore personally had to write to five professors to ask them whether their courses will be offered. When I finally arrived on campus, no authorities could help me with registrering for the courses. It turned out, that the students normally just register to plenty of courses, try them out, and just don't register for the exams, if they don't like the course. However, I have the impression that the profeessor are pretty tolerant, and would let you join if you wrote to them.

The most difficult part was to make a schedule that made sense with no overlaps between the six classes. It took me many evenings. I would recommend to choose some courses that have the exams during the semester. Otherwise you'll end up with having six exams on few weeks.
registration_advice: The Technical University Munich seems very disorganised compare to UCPH, because the organisation is decentralised. The professors are doing their things, and the adminisatrion has no control over it. This is annoying when you are in Denmark trying to understand he structure, but as soon as you are there, it is much easier to ask for help or get influence on the course and even the exam date. courses_enrolled: - Modern topics in Evolutionary Biology (5 ECTS) - Nutrition and Microbe-Host Interactions (5 ECTS) - Applied Microbiology (ECTS) - German as foreign language (8 ECTS) - Hot Topics: Recent Advances in Immunology and Infectious Diseases (3ECTS) - Transgenic and Stem Cell Biotechnology (5 ECTS)
recommended_courses: - Modern topics in Evolutionary Biology (5 ECTS) almost philosophical. You learn to read research papers about evolution written by biologist in cooperation with philosophers. It requires a lot of work though, and the exam is a three hour essay where you have to answer a complex question based on several research papers that you read in advance. - Nutrition and Microbe-Host Interactions (5 ECTS) Held by Dirk Haller, that has been working with the gut microbiome for 25 years! He's very cool. You can choose a lab or bioinformatic track. I took the bioinformatic track where we had to analyse sequencing data from our own stool samples. Also very cool. - Applied Microbiology (ECTS) I was struggling here. I didn't have a lot of basics for understanding and there was a lot of biochemistry. crucial_aspects: Honestly, the biggest reason was Munich itself. It's one of the top tech hubs in Europe, with companies like BMW, Siemens, Google, and Apple all nearby. I wanted to be in a place where I could not only study but also get close to cutting-edge technology and explore internship opportunities alongside my studies.
info_ease: Pretty easy. TUM's website covered most of what I needed before arriving, and the rest was filled in through orientation sessions once I got there.
arrival_assistance: TUM had dedicated events and guidance for exchange students, which were announced both on their website and during in-person welcome meetings. There was a general orientation, departmental intros, and some social activities to help us settle in and meet other students. It made the first few weeks a lot less overwhelming.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: TUM offers three main types of courses: lectures, practical courses, and seminars. Lectures use a regular registration process and usually don't have strict deadlines — you can just sign up when the time comes. Practical courses and seminars, however, work through a matching platform where you have to register much earlier, since spots are limited. The good news is the school sends out emails about it, so as long as you keep an eye on your inbox, you won't miss the deadline.
registration_help: The course registration website has detailed instructions, and there are also in-person orientation sessions where everything gets explained step by step. Between the two, it's easy to figure out what you need to do.
registration_success: Pretty successful overall. Once I understood the timing for the matching platform, I was able to get into the practical courses and seminars I was interested in, and the lectures were straightforward to sign up for.
registration_advice: Definitely look into the practical courses and seminars — they're small-class and often cover cutting-edge topics, which is a great experience you don't always get from regular lectures. Just remember they require early registration through a matching platform, so check your TUM emails carefully and don't miss the deadlines. For lectures, you can relax a bit since registration is more flexible.
course_level: The overall difficulty was reasonable — slightly more challenging than courses at KU, but very manageable. Lectures felt similar in workload, while practical courses and seminars tended to be a bit more demanding because they involve hands-on group work over the whole semester.
teaching_comparison: Lectures are pretty similar in format to KU. The main difference is the practical courses and seminars — they're essentially like KU projects, but pre-defined by the professors and done in groups. You don't propose your own topic; instead you join a structured project alongside other students, which makes the collaboration aspect much more central.
courses_enrolled: Responsible AI (IN45142) — 5 ECTS Artificial Intelligence in Medicine (IN2403) — 5 ECTS Campus Munich: Principles of Economics (WI001056M) — 6 ECTS Master Lab Course – Applications in Natural Language Processing (NLP) (IN4249) — 10 ECTS Cantonese A1.1 (SZ0222) — 3 ECTS Innovative Entrepreneurs – Leadership of High-Tech Organizations (WI000285) — 3 ECTS
recommended_courses: Honestly, I'd recommend any of the practical courses and seminars TUM offers — they're small-class, hands-on, and a great chance to work on cutting-edge topics together with other students. From my own experience, I particularly recommend the Master Lab Course – Applications in NLP and Responsible AI. Both gave me solid exposure to current research directions and were a nice mix of theory and practical work. If you want to make the most of your exchange academically, these kinds of courses are where you'll get the most out of TUM.
unexpected_costs: The biggest one was housing. Affordable places near the city center were extremely rare, and very few landlords offered six-month contracts, so I ended up living further out than I'd planned. Even then, rent took up a much bigger share of my budget than I expected.
cost_comparison: Public transport was much cheaper than I thought, especially with the student/Deutschlandticket options — getting around Munich and even traveling around Germany was very affordable. Groceries and food prices were roughly similar to what I was used to in Copenhagen, so no big surprises there. Housing, on the other hand, was the one category that was noticeably more expensive than expected.
activities_available: TUM offers a pretty wide range of student activities, including university sports (ZHS), student clubs, and various cultural and social events organized for international students. Honestly, since I'm not originally from Denmark either, most things in Germany already felt new and interesting to me, so I didn't seek out specific "cultural" activities — just exploring daily life in Munich was enough.
activities_recommended: To be honest, I didn't really get involved in the sports or club side of things, so I don't have much to recommend there. What I'd suggest instead is going to the welcome events and exchange student meetups early on — that's where you'll naturally meet people and form your initial circle of friends.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely make full use of the Deutschlandticket — it's one of the best deals you'll find as a student in Germany. For a low monthly price, you can take regional trains and public transport across the entire country, which makes weekend trips super easy. I'd recommend visiting places like Berlin, Hamburg, the Black Forest, Neuschwanstein Castle, and the Bavarian Alps. Munich itself is also a great base for day trips to Salzburg or smaller Bavarian towns. Honestly, the travel opportunities are one of the best parts of doing an exchange in Germany.
culture_adjustment: Honestly, I spent most of my time focused on my internship, so my exposure to local culture was fairly limited. From what I did experience, daily life in Munich felt easy enough to adapt to — things are well-organized and most people speak some English.
socializing_tips: I don't have a lot of advice here, since my own social life was mostly tied to work rather than student circles. That said, joining the welcome events and exchange student activities early on is probably the easiest entry point.
cultural_challenges: Nothing major stood out to me. The language barrier was occasionally a small inconvenience in everyday situations, but otherwise I didn't run into any cultural differences that were hard to deal with.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated how organized and efficient everyday life is in Germany — public transport, services, and general infrastructure all just work. Munich also has a nice balance between city life and easy access to nature, which I really liked.
top3_advice: - Start looking for housing as early as possible. Munich's rental market is extremely competitive and expensive, especially around the start of the semester, and most listings require a one-year contract. Don't underestimate this — it was by far the hardest part of my exchange. - Don't miss the early course registration deadlines. Practical courses and seminars at TUM use a matching platform that opens well before the semester starts. Keep an eye on your TUM emails so you don't miss out — these courses are some of the best things TUM has to offer. - Get the Deutschlandticket. It's cheap, lets you travel across all of Germany on regional transport, and turns every weekend into a potential adventure.
other_useful_info: Munich is a fantastic base if you're interested in tech and engineering — there are tons of internship opportunities at companies like BMW, Siemens, Google, and Apple, so it's worth looking into combining your exchange with a part-time internship. Also, while many people in Munich speak English, knowing even a little German makes daily life noticeably smoother, especially when dealing with housing and administrative tasks.
most_rewarding: Definitely the academic and professional exposure. The practical courses and seminars at TUM gave me hands-on experience with cutting-edge topics, and being in Munich opened up internship opportunities I wouldn't have had access to otherwise. Getting to combine high-quality coursework with real industry experience was exactly what I'd hoped for going into the exchange.
greatest_challenge: Finding housing, without question. As someone who doesn't speak German and only needed a place for one semester, the rental market was a real struggle — high prices, long-term contract requirements, and arriving during peak season made it incredibly difficult. It would help a lot if the host institution could offer more support or guaranteed housing for short-term exchange students.

crucial_aspects: The country of Japan was a natural pick for my mandatory exchange in Japanese Studies – there’s no other country with Japanese as its national language, and indeed, there is an abundance of people able to teach the language expertly. The choice of Tokai was due to its geographical proximity to Tokyo, while still remaining solidly in what most locals would call the “Inaka”.
info_ease: Most of the info I needed to travel was clearly sent beforehand, and the small bits of doubt that were left were able to be dealt with by the very responsive Study Abroad team at the destination.
arrival_assistance: At the male dormitory, there weren’t any Japanese people, but foreign students from the previous semesters assisted the workers tasked with keeping the dormitory in introducing students with limited Japanese capability. There were a number of events targeted exchange students, and these were clearly introduced during Japanese class. I suspect you’d be more hard-pressed to find info on these if you’re not taking Japanese lessons at Tokai, although posters do hang throughout campus.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: University-wise it consists of filling out a sheet of questions, but the Japanese government requires you register your address on your Zairyu card, given to you upon immigration. This is a pretty simple process, although it entails a lot of waiting at the City office (Shiyakusho) and should be done from early morning to avoid having to take the trip twice.
registration_help: Previously enrolled students agreed to go, and if everything is terrible, you could ask one of the Resident Advisors to accompany you. In my exchange, there were only RAs present in the female dorm.
registration_success: I got my wanted classes without lottery, and was even able to change classes midway through. A simple system is used, and it’s rather flexible.
registration_advice: Not much, just make sure you go with some friends to the City office to make it more fun.
course_level: I was taking Japanese courses for propedeutics and a few supplying classes for Realia 1 in Japanese Studies.
teaching_comparison: There were more online classes, and many were based on a small summary assignment to prove attendance. There’s also a midterm, which isn’t always customary at KU.
courses_enrolled: Japanese Intensive Course, upper intermediate. International Tourism. International Relations. International Economics.
recommended_courses: The Japanese courses are phenomenal and the teachers allow each student to expand their abilities immensely. Even if you’re not required to take it, i recommend the language classes.
unexpected_costs: I didn’t expect the train to Tokyo to be as expensive as it was. The price itself isn’t bad, and Odakyu is among the cheaper rail companies, but it’s a long trip, and you’ll end up taking it a lot. Budget extra for transport, despite practically living on campus.
cost_comparison: Food is surprisingly cheap, and rent is super cheap. I couldn’t believe that we got away with living that cheap, but there aren’t many hidden fees, if any. The supermarket near the station, Gourmet City, is surprisingly expensive, the cheaper ones are a fair distance by foot away.
activities_available: Students could, principally, join any circle they pleased. There was also an abundance of events, such as the Glocal Fes and the Kengakusai.
activities_recommended: Glocal Fes was fun.
weekend_recommendations: Go enjoy the local area. Definitely Kamakura, Enoshima, Hakone, etc., but also local places like Ooyama or the local summer festivals.
culture_adjustment: I found it relatively easy, since many of the foreign concepts had been introduced in class. There are obviously many hidden and unsaid mannerism in Japan, but I didn’t feel as much stress from this as I had expected.
socializing_tips: Join the activities, and arrange day trips and hangouts with them. There’s a whole International College, as well as a Scandinavian Studies residing at the campus, so I also recommend joining these activities and taking these as chances to socialize.
cultural_challenges: I thought carrying cash around was a concept I had trouble getting used to. I was also troubled by the curfew and the general attitude towards university students that they are not yet adults.
culture_appreciated: It’s with every ounce of seriousness that I applaud the Japanese drinking culture. I have had many fun evenings at the local bars, talking to the locals and making friends.
top3_advice: Make sure to join in on the activities and spend time making local friends. Any city is far away, and if you don’t have something to do in your proximity, you will feel lonely. That said, I also recommend travelling. There’s a Shinkansen station close by in Odawara, and Japan changes a lot depending on the prefecture.
other_useful_info: No, I have written everything I think is important in the other boxes.
most_rewarding: Making local friends and being able to expand my language ability exponentially by talking to them.
greatest_challenge: The rules of the dormitory.

crucial_aspects: It was very important for me to experience a completely different healthcare system and also how the relationship between the patient and doctor is in another country than Denmark. The japanese society is characterized by its conservative roots and since this is a very big difference between Denmark and Japan it is very intersting to see what kind of role it plays ind the relationship between the patient and the doctor. There is no doubt that there is many difference between these to countries which is why Japan is an ideal choice.
info_ease: It was very easy. Some members of the administrative department helped me and gave me a lot of information. It was easy to always ask them if I had any questions and if they didn't have the answer they always got back to me.
arrival_assistance: As mentioned above, some members from the administrative department welcomed me when I arrived. They showed me around campus, helped me to my dormitory and helped to go to the city hall to complete some documents in order to make me citizen of Isehara which apparently was necessary.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I applied for the exchange program through my own university, UCPH and then I was accepted as their candidate. A few months later I received an email from the host university with some documents that I needed to fill out in order to register as a student at their university. I received my letter of acceptance rather late - 3 months prior to my exchange program was suppose to begin. I could contact the members of administration at the host university in order to get some help with filling out the documents they asked me to.
registration_help: I could contact the members of the administrative department at Tokai University and could help me if I had some questions. Otherwise it was more or less a feeling of I should just "trust the process".
registration_success: Since I study medicine I can only apply for a clinical clerkship at a host university that my own university corporate with. This means I don't have any choice to apply for different classes. But I was succesful with being accepted into the program I registered for.
registration_advice: That you have to be patient. The process takes a long time. It is not difficult, but the different steps in the process takes quite a long time. So again you just have to trust the process.
course_level: Again I was attending a clinical clerkship at a hospital and not specific classes so I don't really know about the level of the courses or classes. But I would say that from what I experience in my clinical clerkship that the level is more or less the same as in Denmark. I felt that I was well prepared.
teaching_comparison: In the clinical clerkship the style of teaching was very similar to UCHP. The doctors told us about the patients and the procedures and always asked if we had any questions. Futhermore we also sometimes had a 1 hour class where the teacher / doctor would cover a subject - this is also very similar to UCHP.
courses_enrolled: My courses was my clinical clerkship where I visited 6 departments during my 12 weeks of stay. The departments were as following; neurosurgery, neurology, urology, cardiology, ENT and anesthesiology. I stayed at every department for 2 weeks.
recommended_courses: If the student can choose I would recommend to visit the department of anesthesiology, ENT, urology and neurosurgery. My favorite department to visit was anesthesiology, since most the doctors spoke english, were very kind and the explained a lot and the also activated me a lot. The program was very structured, not too long days and I feel like I learned a lot.
unexpected_costs: I had to pay local insurance. This I was not told about. Luckily it was not a big amount - around 200-300 DKK, but I was a bit surprised.
cost_comparison: Food was generally cheaper than I expected. It was quite affordable to get a lunchbox at the hospital, around 20 DKK.
activities_available: I don't know, I was not informed about them. I know that the local students had some sports clubs they could attend, but since I was the only exchange student I am not sure that the university thought about offering me to join any kind of club.
activities_recommended: As described above I cannot really recommend any since I had no experience attending any non-academic activities at the university.
weekend_recommendations: In general I would recommend the future exchange students to travel and visit different part of Japan - as much as possible in the weekends. Of course, Kyoto, Osaka, Tokyo. I personally really loved visiting Kanazawa and Ito. Ito is in Shizuoka and this prefecture is a really nice place and very accesbile from Isehara - I would really recommend some weekends in this prefecture for relaxing and just experiencing nice atmosphere.
culture_adjustment: It took some time for me, but I think this because I was the only exchange student at this campus. There was no other student in my situation which was a bit difficult to deal with since the english abilities of the japanese students also is limited which I knew before beginning my program. But after sometime I adjusted more and found some japanese students who spoke more english and I could socialize with.
socializing_tips: Have patience with them since a lot of them are shy but they really want to talk to you even though their english abilities might be a bit challenged. And if you feel like it just ask if you can have lunch together at the hospital - they are always up for it! Or even ask if you can hang out when you are finished at the hospital - maybe go out for dinner. Because they want to, they are just a bit shy to ask sometimes.
cultural_challenges: I don't think there was any cultural difference I found particularly challenging. I wanted to hang more out with the local students but they studied a lot everyday when the program of the day finished, which I respected but it unfortunately made it difficult to hang out of the hospital sometimes.
culture_appreciated: They showed a very sincere kindness and respect towards me. I really appreciated how I always felt that the local students wanted to help me and hang out with me. Even though their english abilities some times were challenged I particularly appreciated that they always tried to make contact to me anyway and talk to me. This made me feel very recognized!
top3_advice: 1. Try to make some contact to the local students! 2. Try to prepare yourself for the possibility that you might be the only exchange student at the campus 3. You will 99% of the time only observe when you are at the hospital, not much of actual training (as in Denmark) 4. Explore a bit of the local area and prefectures nearby Kanagawa (not only the touristy places in Japan)
other_useful_info: I actually I would have liked to know if there would be other exchange student from other countries - because I thought there would be, but I knew there was no other exchange student from Denmark besides me. I learned during my stay at Tokai University that in the autumn (which is when I was on exchange) the student from Denmark will be there alone. But in the spring there will be a total of 10 exchange students and one of the is from Denmark.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was to make true contact and friendships with some of the local students. I didn't expect this before attending. It made my experience so special and I am very grateful that I met so kind and thoughtful students who helped me to adjust to the hospital (and the rules) and get more comfortable during my stay. I am very grateful for the friendships I made with the local students and I could never have imagined that something like that would have happened.
greatest_challenge: For me it was being on my own in a different country. Since there was no other exchange students I could not make plans to travel to other areas in Japan with others in my situation. I had a lot of time on my own - more that I expected, because I really expected that I would met other exchange students that I could have made plans with. But I really learned to do so much stuff alone during my stay which as been an absolutely amazing experience for me as a person.

crucial_aspects: Even though I had this university/destination as my 4th priority, it should've been way higher if I had known what I was getting into. TSE (Toulouse School of Economics), a part-independent institution under Université Toulouse Capitole, ranks among the top 10 of the world's best universities in economics. The level is similar to that of the University of Copenhagen, but they have many exciting courses - one in Environmental economics, which I took. Toulouse, the fourth biggest city in France, is beautiful and situated in the very centre of the south of France. It looks like it's a huge city on Google Maps, but it's very easy to get around the city by bike (Swap-fiets or rental), metro or bus. The city is full of students from all over the world and has many nice restaurants (low prices), bars and nightclubs.
info_ease: It wasn't easy sometimes. The University of Toulouse is huge and has several buildings situated apart from each other, resulting in some problems when first arriving since you have no idea what the place is called and where each room or auditory is. I got a map from the information desk at Arsénal, which helped a lot! Furthermore, whenever in doubt, I wrote e-mails to the exchange coordinator at the University of Toulouse. I would send too many e-mails than too few. There can go a couple of days before you get your student-card and the deadline of when to apply for courses which can be stressful - but again: Write to the exchange coordinator if you're in doubt about anything!
arrival_assistance: You get an invitation e-mail from the university to attend a welcoming meeting with all the other ERASMUS students. At that meeting, you'll be provided with 90% of the information needed throughout your stay regarding the school and social events hosted by ERASMUS.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You go to the invitational meeting, where you get the info. If in doubt about the information given, then write an e-mail to the exchange coordinator.
registration_help: In person regarding the university. ANY questions.
registration_success: When you apply for the location first, you type in the courses you want to take; however, it is not certain that you will get the course once the registration opens. Registration opens once you're in Toulouse. You must get their course list for exchange students for courses in M1 and M2 (master 1&2) since these can differ greatly in level and type.
registration_advice: The first two weeks at the university, you can try out a lot of different courses - thus, attend a bunch of lectures in different courses that are open for Erasmus students and choose once the registration opens.
course_level: The level of the courses can vary a lot. But the mean level is approximately the same as that of UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Very similar. However, depending on the course, you use your computer way less, whereas everything is written in hand. Also, note that I had to write all exams by hand. Some lecturers use chalk and board teaching some use PP slides.
courses_enrolled: Valuing the Environment Fundamentals and Policies for a Greener Economy Sustainable Development Macroeconomics Causal Inference Market Power and Regulation
recommended_courses: All of the courses I wrote above are very nice. Since these courses are quite rare, I would especially recommend the environmental courses: Valuing the Environment, Sustainable development and Fundamentals and Policies for a Greener Economy. And the professors are very skilled.
unexpected_costs: I broke my foot at Futsal, so I had my foot in a cast for 1,5 months - so a lot of hospital bills however, these are covered by insurance.
cost_comparison: Grocery stores are way more expensive than I thought. Restaurants and red wine are very cheap. A cheap bar is Café Populaire, where some nights they have a happy day offer where you can get 13 drinks for 13 euros. That was quite nice :)
activities_available: The university has ALL the sports you can imagine from indoor climbing to fencing to football to Krav Maga. Though you have to remember to buy the sport-gear yourself. For social activities, ERASMUS host 1-2 parties a week, BDE (Toulouse School of Economics parties) host monthly parties and ERASMUS hosts a trip outside of Toulouse every other week.
activities_recommended: I played on the universities football and futsal team - until I broke by foot. People are not very good at outdoor football, but the futsal was quite a high level.
weekend_recommendations: Go on the ERASMUS trips, go partying with the other students, take a walk around Toulouse, try the metro, go out to eat at a restaurant, go bowling (very fun). Eat a lot of cheese, duck and wine. You're not on exchange to lose weight.
culture_adjustment: The French are quite arrogant and don't speak very great English. So expect to spend your time with the other ERASMUS students. If you want to learn french, there are plenty of french-language schools, and you can speak to french people. You can meet french people through sports activities, Tinder and in the nightlife.
socializing_tips: Be kind. Smile a lot and try to speak french. You can try to move in at a co-location with local students.
cultural_challenges: Not differences you haven't seen before - we're all human.
culture_appreciated: The French cuisine.
top3_advice: Have fun Go out Meet a lot of new people
other_useful_info: It is very hot in the summer and can be zero degrees in the winter - so bring a diverse wardrobe.
most_rewarding: You get a lot better at english and the school is very good.
greatest_challenge: The information before and during the exchange was awful. You are acting as a middle-man between the two universities, which I thought was very stressful. One didn't even go on exchange because of the information overload. Some e-mails don't matter, while some are very important with strict deadlines. Be calm and call the universities if you're in doubt about anything.
