This excludes several popular destinations such as Paris, Rome, Barcelona etc. Secondly, I also chose destination based on academic opportunities - and the Toulouse School of Economics ranks really well it its field (Economics of course).
overall_comments: The experience was great. Toulouse is a perfectly sized city to be in as a student, somewhere in between Århus and København. I of course made sure to buy a bike as early as possible, making almost everything accessible within 15 minutes. Also, the city is pretty flat, which is good in this regard.
info_ease: Horrible before arrival, as the faculty was on holidays almost all of august. But after arriving, it was definitely easier, and the mobility team are pretty helpful.
arrival_assistance: There was a presentation meeting which went through most of the formalities. I recommend writing down all the relevent contact info given at this meeting, and making sure you can find the Erasmus offices in the Arsenal building (right above the cafeteria).
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The experience was great. Toulouse is a perfectly sized city to be in as a student, somewhere in between Århus and København. I of course made sure to buy a bike as early as possible, making almost everything accessible within 15 minutes. Also, the city is pretty flat, which is good in this regard.
registration_process: Honestly nothing about it was really "hard", but the French.... They LOVE paperwork, and you are required to show up for several things before being properly registered. Furthermore, I waited a long time to actually receive my student card - which I got even after I had my first midterm exam.
registration_help: There was an office for Erasmus students (right above the cafeteria inside the Arsenal building, room 100-something) where you could show up and ask questions. But the receptionist didn't know that much, and the more knowing staff (such as Lucie Jando) are usually a bit busy. But they are always able to help. If you are at Toulouse School of Economics specifically, Genevieve Duomeng is also extremely kind and helpful. She is in the TSE building, through the door to the left of the reception and down a long hallway.
registration_success: I got almost none of the classes I applied for from home, but the staff at TSE was very accomodating, and let me choose some pretty cool Master 2 courses not usually available for Erasmus students. Although you have to convince them that you are ready for the more advanced stuff. Talk to Genevieve (TSE) as soon as possible to open these options - maybe even before arrival.
registration_advice: Get it done as soon as you arrive, otherwise you will spent too much time worrying about it. Talk to Lucie Jando about anything registration related, and Genevieve Duomeng with anything specific to Economics courses.
academics_comments: The experience was great. Toulouse is a perfectly sized city to be in as a student, somewhere in between Århus and København. I of course made sure to buy a bike as early as possible, making almost everything accessible within 15 minutes. Also, the city is pretty flat, which is good in this regard.
course_level: I think the levels are pretty appropriate at the masters courses, with the exception of the Macro course. This is roughly equivalent to Macro II at UCPH, and thus not that challenging if you already nailed that one. BUT with that said, keep up with classes - or the midterm exam of that course will overwhelm you (as it seems designed to do so) and it affects your final score. Generally the 2 ECTS courses seemed easier, but dont underestimate them. Study during the semester, as your exams will be really close (I had 4 exams in 1 week)
teaching_comparison: Generally they require you to study more yourself, and participate actively in classes. Some of my M2 courses, we even got partially graded on whether we asked questions and participated in class discussions during the year.
courses_enrolled: Macroeconomics (M1) Market Power and Regulations (M1) Understanding Real World Organizations (M1) Causal Inference with observational data (M2) Fundamentals and Policies for a Greener Economy (M2) Sustainable Development (M2) Valuing the Environment (M2)
recommended_courses: - As mentioned, the macro course is basically a recap of Macro II at UCPH. - Market Power was a great brief introduction course to the issues of regulation of international monopolies and such, and a very relevant topic today. The professor is really nice as well. - Understanding Real World Organizations is very is in the Economics sense, but a very interesting course about how different organizations work - from firms, to platforms (Uber etc.) and and terrorist organizations. Really great British professor (who also teaches second half of Causal Inference) - Causal is a great course if you like applied Econometrics. It can be very technical, so keep calm and stick to the stuff. Second half was taught by my favorite professor. - Fundamentals was basically a micro course which includes fundamentals for green economies. This includes green taxes, subsidies, and such. Professor was OK. - Sustainable was the macro equivalent of the above, which went through several macro models with sustainability included. The teaching is very mathmatical, but the exam is not so much. So dont spent time writing all the math, just listen to the intutition when the professor takes a break from the math. The professor was this insanely knowledgeable old guy, and I really enjoyed his classes - when I learned to not focus on the math. Score was split between a written exam (which was mostly intutition heavy) and a presentation of a topic you can freely choose yourself. It does not need to include any of the specific course syllabus - as long as it has something to do with the course in general. I really liked that - Valuing is a practical course about how to conduct research designs to value non-market goods such as a good environment etc. The course is taught by a Swedish professor with a lot of research background, and part of the course was to conduct a Stated Preference study with actual respondents. Really cool experience. (BUT remember to participate in class and keep deadlines - he is very strict with that)
unexpected_costs: Not really anything. I bought a bike on facebook marketplace for 50 Euros, which I had to fix a little during the mobility. Around 20 euros in maintenance. My housemates used the bike rental service, I dont remember the name at the moment. The one with blue front tires on their bikes, also present here in Copenhagen
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than expected But eating out was cheaper. And the wine..... You can get reeeeally good wine for amazing prices. I recommend Midi Minuit, Buvette, Le Volcan and La Bonne Combine for this. There are several other places, but those I used the most.
activities_available: Several, but I did not participate. Not much of a sports guy. But Toulouse has several great restaurants and bars, which I used frequently. And go watch soccer or rugby games at the stadium, it has a great atmosphere (even for a non-sports-person such as me)
activities_recommended: - Buvette (nice beers and wine bottles. Wines by glass was a bit boring) - Midi Minuit (great family style servings, and excellent wine selection) - Ginette (close to the house I lived in. Amazing local bar with all types present. Not very student like, more local) - Le Petit Voisin (cheap beers and drinks, very popular with younger people. Best watering hole close to center) - Le Concorde (Really great old bar, very nice staff and great drinks. Drink a negroni for me!) - Le Volcan (this place is so special. Really small room with an old guy selling wine at amazing prices. Smoking inside!) - Cafe Populaire (Cheapest beers in the city, great place if you are a large group looking to get drunk. Also, just walking distance from some of the great clubs (limelight etc.) - La Fiancée (one of the only places in the city with proper filter coffee (non-espresso), pour-over and aeropress. Best staff in town as well. Miss those guys) - Nasdrovia (Great high end cocktails, but you will pay extra for it!) - The boat with the nightclub in it. (dont remember the name of the place, but it is located in the small canal some 100's of meters west of Manufacture de Tabacs. Only place I found where they play non-pop electronic music) - Titanium (If you are looking to get piercings!) - Restaurant sans nom (best place I ate - but there are really many good places I never tried) - The Hopscotch (local brewed beers, scottish style. The bartender is really cool, even though he looks a bit like Ed Kemper) - Syrabite Vintage (for vintage shoppoing) - 43 Original Barber shop (for haircuts) - Mak Food or Boui Boui (for the best Kebabs) Cant remember much else. Ask the staff for recommendations every time you go to a place you like! Oh yeah eat a Cassoulet! Best local dish they offer in town (and STAY AWAY FROM THE VEAL LIVER DISH!) Oh ye
weekend_recommendations: Keep and eye on cheap tickets for Flixbus. And french train tickets are sometimes on 1€ offers! The Erasmus Network WhatsApp channels are great for keeping up with this. Also, get the app getaround if you want to rent a car. Prices are really great, and the app works well. But register beforehand, as they have to approve your drivers licence manually before you can drive! Go to Biarritz, Bordeaux Lyon and Carcassonne, and maybe even Barcelona. My personal favorite trip was renting a car, and driving to the Pyrenees for hiking. The area is amazing. Check the internet for hiking routes beforehand, so you know how tough they are, and how long they will take.
culture_adjustment: Rather easy. France is still Europe. Language is really hard though, and they are not the best at English.
socializing_tips: This is tough, as you will mostly meet exchange students. If you enroll in M2 courses like me, you will be closer to the local students - especially if the course has group work. Use this! Invite them for beers, and have talks with them.
cultural_challenges: The French are generally not great at English, but most young people speak it. The hardest adjustment is how late they eat dinner, and that many stores close for a couple of hours each day. But if you ever vacationed anywhere in southern Europe, you already know this. Other than that, mostly the obsession with paperwork amazed me. And the weird kebabs they make (nan-bread with melted cheese? Tortillas with chicken and french fries? Thats not a taco!) With that said, eat the local kebab. Those guys always speak english as well.
culture_appreciated: The food and wine, definitely. Eat lots of local food, and buy wines by the bottle when you eat out!
top3_advice: - Be patient with the university staff. They are slow and like their paperworks, but was generally really understanding. - Keep up with classes during the semester, otherwise you will die in the exam period - Have tons of fun. Check my recommendations list above.
other_useful_info: See above
most_rewarding: Having all the enviromental courses was great and very academically rewarding Going out with other Erasmus students was very socially rewarding. And also, remember to invite friends/girlfriends from home to visit you! Its really fun to show them around a city like a "local".
greatest_challenge: The... God... Damn... Paperwork!
other_comments: Not really - just have fun, drink lots of local wine, and get a bike!

crucial_aspects: I dreamed of living in an other European country.
overall_comments: It was the most challenging semester I have ever tried, both academic and social. That being said, I learned a whole lot about myself and got to have an experience I will never forget.
info_ease: I got most of the information I needed in the introduction week.
arrival_assistance: Not much, but I wasn't expecting it, although I know some people had help finding housing.
arrival_comments: Make sure to be there for the introduction week - a lot of crucial information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was the most challenging semester I have ever tried, both academic and social. That being said, I learned a whole lot about myself and got to have an experience I will never forget.
registration_process: You need an adresse to register, but besides that it was quite easy. We did not have acces to the intra web for some time but it all worked out.
registration_help: They were in general really kind at the international office.
registration_success: I got all the classes I signed up for, although I had to change my LA after arrival because some courses were removed and others added.
registration_advice: Have an adresse in Toulouse, and make sure that University of Copenhagen know about you changes.
academics_comments: It was the most challenging semester I have ever tried, both academic and social. That being said, I learned a whole lot about myself and got to have an experience I will never forget.
course_level: If you want to make it a little bit easier for yourself, take courses at BA level or at TSM. They tend to be a bit easier. I took only MA courses at TSE and it was way more work than I had anticipated. Can recommend Project Management.
teaching_comparison: Quite similar, but weird with the TP's since it was madetory to be there.

recommended_courses: Markets and Incentives : historical-critical perspective was a really interesting course. Political Economy was nice as well but the work burden was big. I can also recommend experimental economics if you are into that field.
unexpected_costs: Could not end my subscription at my phone company. Avoid for all cost the company "Free".
cost_comparison: Eating and drinkring out.
activities_available: Lots of sports activities. I did unfortunately not participate, but I would recommend doing it! Besides that, a lot of the social activities were in French, so a bit difficult to be a part of if you don't speak French.
activities_recommended: I would definitely do sports as it is a great way to learn meet French people. I would also check out the community/jazz house "Maison Blanche" - A really cool place! Can also recommend to go to the Cafe des Langues if you want to meet some other Erasmus people. A nice way getting to know other people than those from economics.
weekend_recommendations: I went hiking a lot in the Pyrenees! You can take a train from Toulouse all the way to the height of 2.500m. Go to the station Andorra L'Hopital. Plenty of good routes there. Can also highly recommend going to Albi and Bordeaux, some great places to check out!
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. The most difficult part was of course the language, but besides that it was a lot like Denmark, even though the work ethics is quite different.
socializing_tips: Sports! And go to the BDE things if you'd like to get to know some people. The best thing you can do is to learn French! Even a little French gets you a far way, so can highly recommend to do some French courses before you go abroad.
cultural_challenges: People have no respect for queues, so you have to get used to that.
culture_appreciated: The food and the relaxed atmosphere of the city. You can really feel that you're close to the Mediterranean ocean, so everything is a little more loose than in Paris.
top3_advice: Don't panic. Find a place to stay before you arrive. Make sure that your courses are compatible with those of university of Copenhagen.
other_useful_info: You will have to work hard through out the whole semester if you want to pass the final exams. The work burden is insane at TSE, so it is not possible to study for all the exams in the exam season.
most_rewarding: Learning a new language, people and getting through the semester.
greatest_challenge: The 12 different courses I had at the same time. Had some breakdowns throughout my exchange.
other_comments: Rememeber to have fun!

arrival_assistance: There was an introduction week where we were given some information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was a very challenging semester academically with a lot of lectures and classes. Other than that I had a good time.
registration_process: Fairly confusing. Some courses were "limited seats" meaning that they were firstly allocated to the people that "needed" to take the course and thereafter based on your grades. It wasn't really clear whether you were registered for a course until later during the semester, so you'd just show up anyway which wasn't a problem.
registration_help: You could send an email to the Toulouse School of Economics "Mobility and International Relations Officer" Geneviève Doumeng or show up at her office in person to ask her questions.

course_level: I had to take a lot of courses (10) to get 30 ECTS and in some of the courses the workload was quite big relative to the amount of ECTS the course was worth. I spent more time on studying than I do at KU.
teaching_comparison: More lectures and classes than at KU. You don't get to solve a lot of problems in class, instead the TA goes through the problem set and you can try to solve it on your own either before or after class.
courses_enrolled: 5 point courses: Macroeconomics Game Theory Intermediate Econometrics 2,5 point courses: Theory of Incentives R programming 2 point courses: Understanding real world organisations Evolution of economic behaviour Project management Markov chains and applications Probability modelling
recommended_courses: I would recommend Project management, Understanding real world organisations and Evolution of economic behaviour simply because the workload was less than the other courses. I would also recommend to stay away from Intermediate Econometrics unless you're already very good at econometrics. It's in my opinion the most difficult course I have ever taken.
unexpected_costs: None I think
cost_comparison: Transportation was very cheap. I almost exclusively got around by using the vélôToulouse bikes which has an annual subscription fee for 20 euros. Public transportation is also very cheap.
activities_available: Lots of different sports (if your timetable allows for it) and parties organised by the TSE student organisation called BDE.
activities_recommended: Go to a BDE party I guess. Drinking at la Garonne is obligatory as an Erasmus student.
weekend_recommendations: Take a day trip to one of the cities near Toulouse, or to the Pyrenees perhaps.
culture_adjustment: Didn't notice any major culture differences that I needed to adjust to.
cultural_challenges: Biggest problem was a language barrier since my French isn't great and not everyone speaks English.
culture_appreciated: Sitting down for a coffee and a pastry most days
top3_advice: Avoid Intermediate Econometrics, try to take courses at TSM and finally ask yourself if you're up for the challenge or perhaps should consider going on exchange at a different university to have a more relaxed semester
other_useful_info: I think Toulouse is a great city to go on exchange in, however TSE is an academically tough institution in my opinion. Therefore I would say there are pros and cons to going on exchange in Toulouse as an economics student.
most_rewarding: Making friends with other exchange students
greatest_challenge: Passing all my courses, specifically Intermediate Econometrics (I didn't)

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne til en storby i Europa, fordi så kunne jeg få Erasmus legat og havde mulighed for at lære et fremmedsprog mere. Jeg søgte derfor primært i Italien, Spanien, Frankrig og Portugal. Jeg havde Toulouse på 4. prioritet i anden ansøgningsrunde.
info_ease: På Toulouse hjemmeside kunne man se en del information omkring fag, at finde bolig osv., men der er ikke noget der bliver foræret, så man skal lave sin egen research på forhånd. Dog skal man vide at tingene løser sig, når man er der, selvom det til tider kan virke håbløst.
arrival_assistance: Ikke det store. Vi havde selv fundet bolig, så universitetet hjalp ikke med ret meget i starten.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Udvalget af fag er ikke ret stort på TSE, så det endte med at man næsten skal have alle fagene, som de udbyder på engelsk. Der var nogle fag, hvor der var begrænsede antal pladser, så de blev tildelt tilfældigt ud fra dem som gerne ville have disse fag.
registration_help: På en af de første dage i studiestarten fik vi hjælp fra en administrativ medarbejder mht. at få vores ECTS til at gå op og de var meget fleksible ift. at give en de fag, som var nødvendige.
registration_success: Jeg fik stort set alle de fag jeg ønskede, dog blev jeg valgt fra på et enkelt af dem. Jeg tror det var baseret på karakterer, at de valgte hvem der skulle have de fag.
registration_advice: Jeg vil klart anbefale, at tage nogle fag på TSM, da niveauet og mængden af fag du skal have på TSE er absurd. De siger som udgangspunkt at du ikke kan tage fag på TSM, men vi fandt senere ud af at det godt kunne lade sig gøre, når først man er dernede.
course_level: Det er uden tvivl det mest krævende semester jeg har haft på min uddannelse. Selv deres 2 points kurser er krævende og deres 5 points kurser svarer til et 7,5 points kursus på polit. Det kræver meget tid og sværhedsgraden er høj.
teaching_comparison: Alle undervisningstimer er 1,5 time i træk uden pause, hvilket klart er noget man skal vænne sig til. Derudover er der mange flere timers undervisning, når man har 10 fag. 2 points kurserne er der kun forelæsning i, hvorimod 5 points kurserne også har holdundervisning ligesom på KU.
courses_enrolled: R programming, Markov Chains and Applications, Project management, Understand real world organizations, Evolution of economis behavior, Markets and incentives, Macroeconomics, Game theory, Intermediate econometrics og Theory of incentives
recommended_courses: R programming og understanding real world organizations var to spændene og relevante fag. Derudover vil jeg klart undersøge fag på TSM.
unexpected_costs: Ikke rigtig noget.
cost_comparison: Der var bycykler i byen, som var meget billige og var en udmærket løsning. Genrelt var det rimelige priser.
activities_available: Der var alverdens arrangementer du kunne deltage i. Hver eneste dag var der en forening, som arrangerede en form for event og der var Whats up grupper til forskellige typer af aktiviteter. Alt fra sport til fest til bogklub.
activities_recommended: Jeg vil anbefale dig, at deltage i det du har lyst til og bruge det som en mulighed til at prøve noget nyt. Det er en god mulighed til at udvikle sig, da alle står i den samme situation som du gør.
weekend_recommendations: Jeg vil anbefale at rejse til nogen af de omkringliggende byer, hvor du kan få togbilletter til 1 euro den første weekend i hver måned. Derudover var jeg selv i Bilbao og San Sebastian, hvilket jeg også vil anbefale.
culture_adjustment: Det tog lidt tid for mig at vænne mig til at bo et nyt sted, hvor alt i starten vil være nyt og spændene, dog også til tider overvældende. Man skal acceptere at det tager lidt tid, men jeg synes generelt franskmændene og de andre udvekslingsstuderende var meget åbne og imødekommende, hvilket hjalp på det hele.
cultural_challenges: Der er kulturforskelle til andre lande, hvilket gjorde at det blev mest naturligt for mig at være sammen med andre udvekslingsstuderende fra norden. Der var lidt sprogbarrierer, synes jeg.
culture_appreciated: Jeg satte stor pris på den franske livsstil med at gå på Cafe og spise mange croissanter. Derudover kan jeg godt lide at det er multikulturelt land med meget forskelligt at byde på indenfor natur, mad, kultur og kunst.
top3_advice: 1. Lad vær med at stresse for meget hjemmefra, da tingene falder på plads når du er afsted. Dog brug noget tid på bolig. 2. Forsøg at tage fag på TSM for at give dig selv mere luft på skolefronten, fordi det bliver meget krævende ellers. 3. Husk at nyde det, selvom det til tider bliver hårdt. Det er en enestående oplevelse, hvor du måske tager nye venner og minder med hjem.
other_useful_info: Jeg ville have meldt mig på noget af det sport, som skolen udbyder, hvis jeg kunne gøre noget om - også selvom at det kollidere med din anden undervisning.
most_rewarding: At jeg er blevet klogere på mig selv og at jeg har udviklet mig af det.
greatest_challenge: Skolen fyldte en hel del, så det må være det.

crucial_aspects: - The curriculum and reputation of the Economics department at this university: whether courses offered match with my interest of study - Position (a place not too close to my home university so that I could experience new cultures) and living expenses (should not be a metropolitan area, so that I could afford to live there)
info_ease: The communication was very clear and direct. We had an orientation and had the chance to ask the head of department everything we need about the program. In addition, we had a faculty member who took responsibilities about our problems, who we can go directly to the office and asked for her help.
arrival_assistance: -Orientation day -Supervisor -Lots of information in their website
arrival_comments: However, I still have no idea why I got rejected by CROUS to stay in one of their dorms while 99% of exchange students in my course got it. Finding an apartment to live in just a short time is not an easy task and though I managed to do so, it still does not make sense to me why I needed to go through that.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: For required courses, it was very easy. Students will get in no matter what. For elective courses, it is limited to only some students based on their current transcripts. For some special courses, in my case, I want to take some M2 courses, it is important to get permission from head of department as well as professor of that courses. But they were all very nice to let me in.
registration_help: I have a supervisor who helps with all the registration so I was very smooth.
registration_success: I sucessfully got in everything.
registration_advice: It was very easy so no need to be worried about that. However, elective courses are limited so it is important to keep a suffieciently high GPA to get in.
course_level: 6 courses in M1 and 4 courses in M2. I think M1 is too easy for a Master's level, while I am more interested in M2 courses because they are more focused on econometric methods.
teaching_comparison: They are quite compatible, although the classes are much smaller. In all my M2 courses, we have only 3 students.
courses_enrolled: Game theory, Environmental economics, Markov chains and applications, Probability modeling, Experimental economics, Market power and regulation, Programming in Python, Empirical industrial organization, Nonparametric Econometric Method, Econometric method for Empirical Economics.
recommended_courses: I like all M2 courses that I took, especially Empirical Industrial Organization, Nonparametric Econometric Method, Econometric method for Empirical Economics, because they taught lots of new econometric methods with practical projects to implement them. However, it depends on your interest, because there are also several M2 courses based on your field.
unexpected_costs: Nothing.
cost_comparison: Public transportation fee, I was living near the university, so it did not take much.
activities_available: They have a lot of parties for exchange students, which I saw through their Instagram page. However, I am not quite interested in them. Besides, I do not speak French, so taking part in activities I want seems impossible, like the Economics magazine or the research club.
activities_recommended: I have no idea about that.
weekend_recommendations: Travel. Toulouse is close to a lot of lovely cities, like Albi, Montpellier, or even further Barcelona etc. SNCF also have offers for 1 euro trip in first week of the month so take advanatge of them to the fullest.
culture_adjustment: I have no problems with cultural differences. People here are all very nice, although I do not speak any French.
cultural_challenges: No at all.
culture_appreciated: They are all very welcoming, even to a stranger. They smiled and said hi to me anytime they saw me in my apartment, and outside, people always noticed and helped me if I had any problems. I love the atmosphere here in Toulouse.
top3_advice: - Do not hesitate to ask for permission to take an M2 course, professors here are all very nice. - Live near the school and try to search for housing as soon as possible. - Got a scooter or bicycle because the cycling route here is very complete.
other_useful_info: No I dont think so
most_rewarding: I learned lots of things from my M2 courses. In addition, the winter weather there is much more bearable than in Copenhagen (sorry...). I also loved all the trips in Southern Europe.
greatest_challenge: In the first month of my exchange, I have to fill in the new OLA after registration. However, it took to0 much time for my OLA to get accepted from UCPH. I need to call student service and then send an email to prove it is very urgent because it is close to mid-term, and after that, I can not change my courses anymore if I get rejected for any courses. Luckily, I did it just in time.

crucial_aspects: Ireland was always my dream destination to do my exchange and to me it was crucial that it was an English speaking country so that I could focus on my studies and improve my academic English. It was also important to me that I chose a country which was not too far from Denmark – so I would have an easy opportunity to go back and visit afterwards. Furthermore, I had only heard good things about Ireland as a country and the Irish people
overall_comments: I had the most wonderful time during my exchange semester and would highly recommend it to anyone considering it. Ireland and Trinity College Dublin was a great choice of destination and besides gaining new friends and experiences, I also gained new knowledge, language skills and perspectives
info_ease: Orientation happened online and while I acknowledge the difficult times we've been though, I would have wished it was in person. The orientation consisted of a few zoom presentations about the university, living in Dublin and IT. I never got the chance to meet the other exchange students or officially tour the campus before I started classes. That said, the orientation covered most of my questions and the ones I had afterwards were answered quickly
arrival_assistance: I didn't need much assistance upon my arrival. Only small things related to my university e-mail account, student travel card and other miscellaneous stuff. Everything else related to my stay I figured out on my own without involving Trinity
arrival_comments: Trinity has lots of societies and while I was introduced to a few during orientation, most of them I had to look up or research myself. It would have been nice if an introduction to the societies were part of the general orientation, but I assume that that's just part of doing the exchange during the second semester. I found it easy to get my questions answered before my arrival to Dublin. I had a contact person within the law school in Trinity and she was easy to reach and answered my questions quickly, e.g. regarding course registration and orientation
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had the most wonderful time during my exchange semester and would highly recommend it to anyone considering it. Ireland and Trinity College Dublin was a great choice of destination and besides gaining new friends and experiences, I also gained new knowledge, language skills and perspectives
registration_process: I registered via a Google Docs that was send to me by my Erasmus coordinator after having received a time table that showed the different classes and when they were taught. We weren't allowed to take clashing classes. The different times weren't available until the week before, so make sure you get more classes preapproved than you need – that way you'll have options if your preferred classes clash
registration_help: I had an Erasmus coordinator at the law school in Trinity who was easy to reach and helped with all my questions regarding classes, time tables and course registration
registration_success: Very successful. I got the classes I had wished for and while the whole process happened much later than what I'm used to at UCPH, the process was also quite quick and efficient
registration_advice: Make sure you get more modules preapproved than you need. Just in case your chosen ones clash. Look at the exam form of each module. Trinity has a lot more exams consisting of essays, response papers or presentations compared to UCHP. It's a great way to try out something new and I quickly learned that if you have different exam forms, it's more likely that the exams are spread out throughout the semester instead of happening all at ones during one week. I had three modules and ended up having deadline dates/exam dates in March, mid-April, end of April and mid-May – very manageable
academics_comments: I had the most wonderful time during my exchange semester and would highly recommend it to anyone considering it. Ireland and Trinity College Dublin was a great choice of destination and besides gaining new friends and experiences, I also gained new knowledge, language skills and perspectives
course_level: We only had a small selection of modules we could take as visiting students. I ended up choosing one 1st and 2nd year module and two 3rd and 4th year modules. There was definitely a difference between the levels of the two, but I was happy to experience both. I had the feeling that when you're visiting as a masters student, you'll always find the level a bit easier than what you are used to, but I guess that is made up for by the difference in teaching style and language
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at Trinity was quite different from the one I was used to at UCPH. I had almost only lectures consisting of the professor making a presentation of the subject for 50 minutes. This was done in a big auditorium. Questions were very welcomed, but there was no group work or discussions involved. In one of my classes I had 4 seminars throughout the semester. These were 50-minute classes with only 12 people where we were given a set of questions beforehand and talked through them in class. They didn't provided a lot of new knowledge as most of the things were covered during the lectures, but it was a good diversion in the teaching style. As long as you're prepared that most teaching will happen as lectures you'll be fine and I honestly found it quite relaxing to have a semester where I mostly listened
courses_enrolled: Conflict of Laws, Employment Law and Criminal Law
recommended_courses: I had such a great time taking Conflict of Laws. It was a very interesting and relevant class – especially if you have taken Civilproces at UCPH. The professor, David Kenny, was very smart, interesting and had a great approach to teaching. If you have an interest in employment law, then I would also highly recommend taking the Employment Law class. Criminal Law was a year 1 and 2 module, so everyone was quite young and new to law. However, it was quite interesting to get a look at the criminal law from an Irish and common law perspective
unexpected_costs: It wasn't unexpected, but housing took up most of my budget. Other than that I felt like I was fairly prepared for the costs
cost_comparison: Buying groceries were definitely less expensive than in Denmark. I only got one book for the semester (which ended up not being necessary), so that was also less expensive. Transportation became cheaper while I was there and with the Student Leap Card (travel card) you're able to get the bus or tram for only 1 €. Traveling around Ireland wasn't too expensive either, but I guess I ended up travelling a bit more than I had anticipated so that added up. In general I found that I was spending more during the last couple of months of my exchange – I went out more, travelled more, met friends for food or coffee more. Just a side note when making or preparing a budget
activities_available: Trinity has a ton of different societies and sports clubs. There is something for everyone. I ended up signing up for the yoga society, the knitting society, the international students society and the hiking society. I didn't necessarily attend a lot of the events but the ones I did I really enjoyed. Go to the events/meet-ups as early as possible – everyone is new and this is the opportunity to meet new friends. I met a great group of other exchange students in the international students society on a hike during my first month and they ended up being some of my best friends. In general, the societies are a great way to meet a bunch of new people who don't necessarily study the same as you – something we could learn from at UCPH and in Denmark
activities_recommended: Join the societies and Erasmus-WhatsApp/Facebook groups – this is a great way to meet other students and visiting students to do all the fun things with. Maybe try and have a weekly thing that you do. I really wanted to take Irish language classes (but had trouble finding a place) and a few of my friends did dance classes or drawing classes. I also found Instagram (Dublin accounts) to be a great way of knowing what went on in the city and which places to go to
weekend_recommendations: Please, go and explore what Ireland has to offer. I loved Dublin and everything that the city has to offer, but Ireland is so much more. Try to do this throughout the semester. I saved most of my travels for May (where I didn't have classes), but wished that I had done many more weekend trips to the different cities and counties in Ireland. When staying in and around Dublin, go on daytrips to Howth (most beautiful place), Bray and Glendalough. Visit the parks and museums in Dublin (The little museum of Dublin is a must), go on walks, drink at all the pubs, visit some of the whiskey distilleries, go see plays and in general just have fun while you're there. Dublin is a fairly small city and everything is reachable within walking distance. Ireland really has so much to offer
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. The Irish culture is very like the Danish one. People like to have fun, go for a pint or coffee and just talk. However, Irish people are much more open towards visitors and tourists. I've only met kind people who were interested in my culture and talking/explaining about their own. Dublin also has a lot of non-Irish people living in the city so the culture is very diverse and you'll find almost every other country represented in the food available or small communities around the city
socializing_tips: If you want to meet Irish students then my best tip would have to be to join the societies. Here you'll find both local and international students and you won't necessarily share the same studies, but you'll share the same interest whether that's hiking, knitting, dancing or planting flowers. Otherwise, go to a pub, get a pint and start talking to the people at the table next to you. I can almost guarantee it's gonna be the most interesting conversation of your life
cultural_challenges: If I had to pick something, it would probably be the approach to time. I'm very used being punctual about being somewhere at the right time and Irish people are a bit more relaxed when it comes to that. It wasn't a big problem though and as soon as you realise the difference you'll adapt quite quickly
culture_appreciated: I learned to highly appreciate the pub culture. Even if you are not a big drinker, the pub isn't necessarily about going out for five pints each night and get drunk. It's a place people meet up like a café and have a pint and a great conversation. Dublin is booming with pubs, so try out a bunch a find the one you like. I also just really appreciated the friendly approach to new people and visitors. It's a very easy culture to be a foreigner in
top3_advice: Start building a network as soon as possible. It can be daunting (at least it was for me), but it's so rewarding to have friends to talk to and do things with. So go to the pub, join the society and say yes whenever possible. Explore everything Dublin and Ireland has to offer. It's so easy (and fairly cheap) to travel around so make it a priority to be cultural and visit all the places around you. And lastly, I would recommend to take part in the Trinity culture. Go to the classes, join the societies, take part in the events that are happening and make use of all the facilities. It'll be over before you know it
other_useful_info: Do some research before arriving at Trinity. Find out what Trinity has to offer (events, student discounts, tours, language classes etc.) and make use of it. Also, Trinity has a lot of great places to study in and the campus is situated right in the centre of the city, so there are lots of great coffee places and cafes around to study in
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was probably all the new people I met and befriended. Both Irish and international people. I now have great connections in a lot of different places. In general, I just found it very rewarding to now have a place so close by to call home. I really made it a priority to get to know Dublin very well and feel at home in the city and I feel like I succeeded with that
greatest_challenge: I never really experienced any great challenges. The closest thing was being unsure of how to make friends when I first arrived. I chose to arrive a few weeks before classes started and I do remember being anxious about not meeting very many people. But as soon as classes and societies started, that problem solved itself fairly quickly. It was like a rolling snowball – once you meet a few people, you'll meet a bunch soon afterwards
other_comments: Going on exchange is such a unique opportunity. Do it because you want to want to know a new culture, make friends from around the world and have great experiences. Improving your academic studies and resume should be a factor in your decision, but not the only one. Make sure you go because you are curious about life and others. Go to Ireland. It has so much to offer and you'll be able to come back easily and relive the best semester of your life

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study in an English-speaking country. However, countries outside of the EU were not an option, due to Covid. Further, I wanted to study in a larger city, yet small enough to get to know in four months.
info_ease: It was quite easy since the information is provided through email from my Erasmus coordinator. However, be patient, since the information was provided quite late.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance from my Erasmus coordinator, e.g., on how to register, etc. Further, the academic registry and the IT-help disk were easy to reach through the phone.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process was through email to my Erasmus coordinator. The process was a bit confusing since it was very late. E.g., the courses we could register for were made available in September, and following this, I went to classes without knowing if I was registered with the course or not.
registration_help: I could always reach my Erasmus coordinator if needed.
registration_success: I was very successful since I registered for the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Be patient! Everything will fall into place eventually.
course_level: The level of most of my courses was quite easy. However, I also studied for one course (IP law) more than expected.
teaching_comparison: It was very different! The lecturer gave a 45-minute presentation, only interrupted by a few (if any) questions by students. We had no cases to prepare or no group work.
courses_enrolled: IP Law, Medical Law and Ethics and Food Law.
recommended_courses: Medical Law and Ethics and Food Law. The subjects were interesting and the exams (assignments during the semester) were manageable and gave a lot of flexibility during the semester.
unexpected_costs: I didn't have any unexpected costs... Maybe buying a new raincoat because of the heavy rain in Ireland at times.
cost_comparison: The housing is super expensive in Dublin!
activities_available: There are many different student associations/societies, which is nice! E.g., hiking society, food and drinks society, yoga society.
activities_recommended: I didn't really join any, because of Covid (it was really difficult to join the activities since we could not gather in larger groups).
weekend_recommendations: Go to Cliffs of Moher and Galway! And go to North Ireland for a weekend trip with some friends. Walk around Dublin as much as possible, and get to know the city well - you will not regret it! Go to a pub on Camden Street - it's more local than the pubs at Temple Bar.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy since Irish people are very easygoing, friendly, outgoing and have a lot of great humor!
socializing_tips: Just say hi after your classes - Irish people are very outgoing and easy to talk to!
cultural_challenges: Not any, really...
culture_appreciated: The pub culture - of course!
top3_advice: Find a room in a student accommodation, register with courses with essay exams, and be patient with the academic registry.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: The personal growth for sure! It's an amazing experience to share with your self :)
greatest_challenge: Covid - without a doubt, for self-explanatory reasons!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an English speaking country in Europe and due to Brexit my choice became Dublin. Also because of former recommendations.
overall_comments: It was a great stay overall. Due to corona there were some optical meeting new people in the begining and we had to to a lot out self to meet people. Trinity weren't very helpfull with that due to corona.
info_ease: It was alright. The staff was really friendly and helpfull, though a bit slow due to a more old fashioned way of doing things.
arrival_assistance: We received our login to TCD and through there waited for more information on classes, studentcard and so on. Not all of us student received the information at the same time.
arrival_comments: It was not the best. It wasn't really a welcomst. There were no social things planned for the Eramus students, only Freshers, who were probably priotized because of corona. You had to "book" a spot for all the activities, even getting a tour on campus, but you needed a promo code which we did not receive.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was a great stay overall. Due to corona there were some optical meeting new people in the begining and we had to to a lot out self to meet people. Trinity weren't very helpfull with that due to corona.
registration_process: You will get contacted for which steps you need to take. The order for registration is a bit random which is a bit frustrating. However, they are always very helpfull towards you.
registration_help: The Academic Registry had a hotline for help which is where I got most of my help/information.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted and there is a thinking period before the classes a finale, which gives to time and options to switch which was really helpfull for me.
registration_advice: Just be patience, read everything they send you carefully.
academics_comments: It was a great stay overall. Due to corona there were some optical meeting new people in the begining and we had to to a lot out self to meet people. Trinity weren't very helpfull with that due to corona.
course_level: They were easier than Danish classes. An entirely way of learning, discussing, talking, writing and so on. Rather interesting and I learned a lot by trying this.
teaching_comparison: Mainly big lectures where the professor would talk. Some lectures there would be discussion but otherwise no group work.
courses_enrolled: Food law, Medical law and Ethics, European Human Rights law.
recommended_courses: i recommend them all. They are all essay based which I liked. However, I had to write six essays in around the two lasts months which ended being a lot of stress. However, very good and passionated professors, who were also very friendly towards Eramus students and understanding of our different situation. Medical law was a lot more fun and different than expected, however it is common law about Ireland, so maybe not entirely useful.
unexpected_costs: I travelled a lot and did a lot of social activities which took most of my budget.
cost_comparison: Food in general were cheap. Itmens like wine were expensive. Normal stuff like shampoo and so on was cheap. The only thing really surprisingly was the really expensive rent.
activities_available: All kind of sports, language, food, acting, nature and so on. More than 200 clubs so almost everything you possible can think of.
activities_recommended: I would recommend the hiking club. Otherwise the cancer society has a good cause. and the food society gives discounts of foods.
weekend_recommendations: Dublin and ireland is full of possibility. Great hikes both close and far from Dublin. A great range of cosy pubs. Great and free museums.
culture_adjustment: It was only difficult the first few days. Ireland is a lot more different from Denmark than first expected. But it felt like home really quick and I felt comftobel in the environment.
socializing_tips: WhatsApp groups for social stuff are great. Live in a dorm room and enjoy that and try to meet people there through social activities. Try to just talk to people you meet in classes, clubs, events, housing and so on. Difficult at first but people are very friendly and open minded.

crucial_aspects: I knew I wanted to go somewhere where English was the primary language and that I wanted to go to a university that was widely known and respected. And also, I had been to Dublin before and I knew I loved the culture.
info_ease: A little diffictult, Trinity's Erasmus department is not the most informative and you often have to reach out to them in order to attain information.
arrival_assistance: There was a bus pick up service at the airports provided by Trinity which I used and I was dropped off at my accommodation. But other than that the assistance was limited, which I found to be fine though.

registration_help: You can email your department or Academic Registry and they are normally pretty fast to respond.
registration_success: I got all the modules I wanted. It does not seem like the classes can fill up in the same way they do at KU, so in my experience you can expect to get all the classes you want (as long as the classes are available to you as an Erasmus student).
registration_advice: Be ultra-patient and a little proactive, Trinity is not super good at informative when it comes to registration up until the time you need to register. But for me it all worked out even though the process was a little frustrating. So just be patient.
course_level: All my modules were BA-level. I would say the level was similar to courses at KU or a little lower. Similar amount of reading but the exams were so much less time consuming. Three of my exams consisted of take home essays and one of them was an online "exam" where I had to answer three questions in two hours (open book). But you can just choose to sign up to modules that have an exam form you feel comfortable with. Looking back I probably wish I had only chosen modules with take home exams so I would have been done with my exams earlier.
teaching_comparison: Pretty different, but in a nice way. At Trinity I had a 45 min lecture and a 45 min tutorial with a professor and a small amount of people from the class every week. So a lot more time to talk and discuss with the professor than at KU.
courses_enrolled: Globalisation and Development Poverty and Policy in a Global Context Labour Markets, Gender and Insitutions Conflict Studies
recommended_courses: I liked all of my classes, but I especially enjoyed Globalisation and Development. Also Conflict Studies was a great way to learn about Northern Ireland and the troubles.
unexpected_costs: Non.
cost_comparison: The price of food, going out to eat and going to drink at pubs is much lower in Dublin.
activities_available: They have every single club/society and sport available you could imagine.
activities_recommended: Definitely join a society, there are so many to choose from and they all offer fun activities.
weekend_recommendations: Howth is great a very close to the city. But just go to as many pubs as possible with your friends, those were some of my favorite moments of my exchange.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Irish people are so kind and welcoming. The social barrier is small because their drinking culture is pretty similar to the Danish.
socializing_tips: Live in private accommodation/uni accommodation instead of living in an apartment with other exchange students. Sign up for societies.
cultural_challenges: None, really.
culture_appreciated: The pub culture. It is just amazing and unique to Ireland.
top3_advice: - Book you accommodation as early as possible. - Be patient with the module registration, it will work out even though it can seem slow. - In my experience it was not that difficult to get good grades, so remember you only need to pass the classes and enjoy your time going to pubs and being with friends instead of studying all day long. The exchange is over so soon so enjoy every moment you can.
other_useful_info: Explore the campus, it is beautiful and historic.
most_rewarding: Becoming very trustful of my academic skills and knowing the level taught at KU is very high.
greatest_challenge: Perhaps knowing how much time I had to put into studying because it was hard to know what level the professors expected since it was my first time taking classes there. But I was positively surprised at how low the expectations were.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a European English-speaking country, where there would be an option to study EU law in different aspects. Moreover, the possibility to enhance my English made me choose Dublin as my first priority. Also, I had never been to Ireland before, so I saw it as a good opportunity to visit the country and explore its beautiful nature more in-depth.
overall_comments: It was overall the best semester of my education. So much fun living in a new city, meeting new people and getting friends for a lifetime, and also Dublin is great, and so are Ireland and the Irish people.
info_ease: It was alright. It just takes some time in general. You need to be prepared for using some time to look into different stuff. Mostly accommodation, which neither Københavns Universitet nor Trinity College can help with. However, you should not be scared away by this, because once you have been appointed a university the university's contact persons are very helpful and a lot of information will be given in due time. For me, I wanted to know everything as soon as possible, but it comes along as time goes.
arrival_assistance: I got some assistance from my accommodation and also from Trinity College and our contact person. However, the orientation week was a bit disappointing. It seemed very unprepared and the students were not that great at preparing you for the semester, so for a long time, I was a bit unsure about how Trinity worked. Also, the introduction week was not very filled up, so two or three days there was only something scheduled for an hour, which makes the rest of the day available. When starting a new place, not knowing anybody, it could have been nice if something more had been prepared.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was overall the best semester of my education. So much fun living in a new city, meeting new people and getting friends for a lifetime, and also Dublin is great, and so are Ireland and the Irish people.
registration_process: You are sent a link where you sign up for the courses you want. It is divided into categories regarding timetables, so you have no time clashes. However, it is possible to switch class if you change your mind when you arrive.
registration_help: The Erasmus contact person was helpful. Otherwise, I used these travel reports for help.
registration_success: Very. I got my first priorities. I studied Environmental Law, Intellectual Property Law, and Eu Competition Law. However, I do not recommend EU Competition law, the professor is not that good. He cancelled most of our classes and the way he taught was ridiculous. He just read from a book. No PowerPoint, or interaction.
registration_advice: Choose what interests you and what kind of exams there are. It can be an advantage to take those classes where there are essays as exam type. All exams are usually in one week in December, so you can have two exams in one day (one of the Swedish Erasmus students experienced this, with only 1-hour break between the two). Therefore those courses with essays make that week easier. Also for the first and second-year courses, the exams are usually in an exam hall with thousands of other students and you have to write your exam in hand. I did not experience this, but some of the other Danes did, and it did not sound nice. All my courses were third and fourth-year courses, and the school burden was not overwhelming so you shouldn't be discouraged by that.
academics_comments: It was overall the best semester of my education. So much fun living in a new city, meeting new people and getting friends for a lifetime, and also Dublin is great, and so are Ireland and the Irish people.
course_level: I had third and fourth-year level courses, and found them to be pretty easy. It is mostly difficult to find the right level on studying. In environmental law it was not expected that you read that much, but then it was a good idea to come to classes and pay attention. In Intellectual Property law there was a book, which I recommend reading (in part). There will be a new teacher in that module for next year, but the last one expected us to read for class. In Eu Competition Law there wasn't that much expectations, but the teacher was sooo bad, so hopefully they replace him.
teaching_comparison: A monologue from the teachers. No presentations or group/casework. There was a group exam in Environmental law, but that was optional and could be made individually. I choose to stay in a group, it felt a little bit safer having an Irish student to help with the general stuff.
courses_enrolled: EU Competition law Environmental law Intellectual Property Law
recommended_courses: There will be made some changes due to new teachers. Especially Intellectual property law, where there will come a new teacher. But this class is interesting. Also Environmental law, where the teacher is very ambitious and you learn a lot. However, the international community is very big at Trinity also among the teachers and two of my teachers were not from Ireland, but from India and Italy, so there were some thick accents to comprehend.
unexpected_costs: I spent a lot more on eating out and going to pubs. We did that a lot. Also travelling across Ireland was quite expensive in total, not much individually. Therefore the monthly budget for food is quite high.
cost_comparison: Food and drinks are less expensive, but you just go out more, so it kinda equals up.
activities_available: Basket ball club, running club, knitting club, german club, irish club etc. There are over 120 clubs.
activities_recommended: Join a club! Maybe one and then do that more intensely if you want to expand your friend group. Otherwise, join a lot of different and go with your friends. The numbers of tickets for the different events are limited, so be ready to buy when tickets are made available!
weekend_recommendations: Explore Ireland! There is so much to see and do, and it is so beautiful! I recommend taking a longer bus trip to see more. I visited Galway and Cliffs of Moher, Connemara, Ring of Kerry, Cork, Belfast and Giants Causeway (a 1-day bus trip from Belfast), Kilkenny etc. There are pretty good connections with bus and train around the country.
culture_adjustment: Yes pretty easy.
socializing_tips: Join and attend a lot in the beginning. A lot of your connections throughout the semester are made in the beginning. We were 4 Danes at Trinity and we became a very close group and hung out with a big group of Swedish but also a mixed group of German and French students. The most thing I would have wanted more was to have gotten more in contact with the Irish students, but somehow it seemed a bit difficult. But there are also so many international students (I think 24 % of Trinity students are international students). I got an Irish buddy (who can help with different stuff) and that was nice. We hung out sometimes and in groups with other Irish and Erasmus students as well.
cultural_challenges: The more laid back it was at Trinity. Otherwise, I didn't find that bid a cultural change.
culture_appreciated: The pubculture and the outgoing way Irish people in general are. They are welcoming.
top3_advice: Save money for accommodation, prepare yourself for exploring Ireland and Dublin (visit the Cathedral, Guinness Storehouse, Christ Church, Teeling distillery etc. there is so much to see and do) and be patient with Trinity College.
other_useful_info: I arrived a week before school started to explore Ireland. I had booked a three day trip around Ireland by bus with a guide, and I can really recommend that. You get to see so much before school starts and therefore get the opportunity to travel a bit further away than what would be possible over the weekend. However, It is also possible to travel during the weekdays if you don't have school or can skip a lecture, or else there is the reading week in October, where I took a trip to Cork with some of the other Erasmus students.
most_rewarding: The friends I made and the experiences I had when visiting places in Ireland.
greatest_challenge: To maintain in contact with friends at home, because there was so much happening in Dublin with you friends there.

crucial_aspects: it was crucial for me to have a renowned university as my destination, since I did not want to comprimise the quality of my overall education that I would have otherwise received at UCHP. Furthermore, the country was important. One the one hand, southern Europe was appealing. on the other hand, the top quality universities in Germany, Schwitzerland, England and Ireland was very lucrative in the perspective of future career opportunities.
overall_comments: The overall quality was 8/10. now, please read the following carefully, please: Firstly, when traveling to Ireland and studying in Dublin, you must accept that finding accommodation is REALLY challenging! I would recommend that you start at least 6 months in advance (considering you also have something to attend to in DK, of course. THe reason being that the Irish students will know whether they have been accepted into the universities during the spring/early summer, and they are thus quick to apply for accommodation. the accommodation struggle is famous in Ireland and almost everybody is effected by it. Some advice regarding accommodation: 1) look outside the center of Dublin. Public transport in Dublin is cheap (appx. 20-30 euro/month), and it is usable for the majority of the time. 2) I personally stayed in the northern part of Dublin (Northwood in Ballymun called "hazelwood"), which was sufficient but only just. I would - in line with the Irish students in general - advice against living in the most nothern parts of Dublin, since this is a troubled area. However, if you live in a gated community, you will be fine (as I did). Other accommodation in the northern part is "Aspen". Accommodation can also be found in the center, however the prices of the accommodation will reflect the lucrative location. Personally I paid roughly half as much as those who lived in the center of Dublin. However, you will have to deal with quite a lot of public transport.
info_ease: Really difficult. We only managed to acquire the information needed by communicating with other students. Do not expect Trinity to engage in anything that they are not obliged to, i.e. housing etc. Do not expect Trinity to have sorted out what modules you are enroled in, before you arrive (we did not have ours fully confirmed until 3 weeks into the semester). Most of the time you will have to be VERY patient and creative.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any. Trinity was almost completely silent up until the moment when they had to engage with us.
arrival_comments: It was an absolute joke. Nothing was prepared, everything was chaos, i.e.: - modules that you applied for and wanted to be enroled in was not taken care of. - The classrooms had not been assigned, so neither the professors nor the students knew where to meet for the lectures, - the quality of some of the professors and their ability to plan the semester out for the students. - the tutors, who were assigned by trinity to act as guidance for the excange students, had not visited the university itself until the very day they met the students that they were supposed to show around (because of COVID).
