culture_appreciated: the pub part of the culture.
top3_advice: Drink Guiness and see the pubs join a society and do a lot of travelling early on in your stay. look for housing and accommodation at least 6 months prior to your stay.
other_useful_info: join the facebook groups for housing in dublin and "danskere i Dublin". they are great.
most_rewarding: living in another country on my own.
greatest_challenge: the accommodation. by far.

crucial_aspects: Den irske kultur har altid virket særlig dragende på mig, og så skader det heller ikke at Trinity College Dublin er et verdensanerkendt universitet med en masse muligheder både på den faglige front og den studenter-sociale.
info_ease: Super easy. My coordinator at Trinity was super helpful and almost always responded immediatly if there was something I needed to have clarified. The webportal as a new incoming student was also easy to navigate and I got sent notifications each time there was something I was to be aware of.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation week before classes officially started that served as a perfect introduction to everything I would need to know during my stay, and they set up an anonymous option where people could send in all sorts of questions that they would then answer on the spot, which I thought was a really good idea.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: it took 5 minutes ish, and I got sent the registration form to my inbox at my.tcd.ie.
registration_help: We could contact our erasmus coordinator on mail, visit them in person if we had arrived or there was also a chatbot ish thing on my.tcd.ie that you could ask directly. I never used it though as the registration process was fairly straightforward.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted, which I had to fill out in a Google questionaire made for that specific purpose. It seems that at least the law schools process for registrering classes is very transparent and easy to manage.
registration_advice: Advice isn't really needed.
course_level: I would say the courses that I took (International Human Rights Law, Equality Law and Refugee Law) when comparing to the courses I have so far had at UCPH were slightly "easier" level wise. Trinity had a very good academic programme and I did feel that the level was high at certain times, but I would say that all in all I could relax more during my courses than I would be able to back home.
teaching_comparison: I prefered the style of teaching at Trinity as the teachers were more laidback in a sense, while at the same time being able to be a bit more inspiring when talking in their respective fields. They also went out of their way to incorporate and invite relevant people to have a chat during seminars with the students were we could go more in depth with the subject and engage with it in more than in just a theoretical sense.
courses_enrolled: International Human Rights Law, Equality Law and Refugee Law.
recommended_courses: The courses that I had...
unexpected_costs: Travels and day trips added up in the end, but it was all well worth it.
cost_comparison: De fleste varer er lidt dyre i Dublin, men nok nogenlunde på niveau med København.
activities_available: Der var nærmest et society for ALT hvad man kan tænke sig til, lige fra film, strikkeklub, circus society, diverse sportsgrene, musik, revy osv. Det virkede til at der oprigtigt er noget for alle.
activities_recommended: Jeg kastede mig ud i Touch Rugby hvilket var en virkelig fed oplevelse. Det er en mindre agressiv version af klassisk rugby og en god måde at få lidt motion og et fællesskab på - og så var det også mere af en social sport så selvom vi trænede teknikker og spillede kampe var det ikke alt for seriøst og der var altid et socialt arrangement efter. Derudover kan jeg anbefale circus society som var lidt syret (jeg prøvede at lære at cykle på en-hjulet, men det lykkedes aldrig...) og film society.
weekend_recommendations: PUBS. Der er ikke så overraskende en kæmpe pub kultur i Dublin og i sær dem der ligger lige ved campus er yndet besøg af studerende. Live music på en klassisk irsk pub kan noget helt magisk, og man behøver heldigvis heller ikke at drikke Guinness for at nyde det. Jeg tog tid ud af kalenderen til at rejse lidt rundt efter endt undervisning og det kan jeg også kun kraftigt anbefale. Irland er egentlig ikke så stor en ø så man kan nå en masse. Et par weekendudflugter undervejs i semesteret vil jeg også anbefale, eksempelvis en dags tur til Howth eller Bray som kun ligger 40-ish minutter fra Dublin i tog, men leder til fantastiske vandremuligheder.
culture_adjustment: Meget nemt. Jeg faldt i fælden med at primært omgås andre udvekslingsstuderende hvilket ikke er så underligt da det er netop det miljø man dumper ned i. Det lykkedes dog også i gennem at være aktiv i diverse foreninger og generelt at være åben, at møde nogle lokale irer som jeg i dag betragter som gode venner.
socializing_tips: Nej, jeg var selv rigtig elendig til at falde i snak om i hvert fald de studerende jeg havde undervisning med. Det var meget at dukke op til forelæsning, sidde der og så tage væk igen. Der hvor jeg fik interageret med de lokale studerende var helt klart mest i de forskellige societies jeg deltog i, så jeg vil helt klart anbefale at melde sig ind i 2-4 man synes rammer ens interesser eller bare lyder spændende.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Afslappetheden, det var meget nemt at snakke med folk og folk tog sjældent dem selv så seriøst hvilket var dejligt. Dublin og craic går hånd i hånd.
top3_advice: Find housing asap, socialize from day 1 and while you should take your courses seriously don't drown in coursework and remember to enjoy your experience besides the studying part.
other_useful_info: Undgå Temple Bar området, det er dyrt for absolut ingen grund.
most_rewarding: Uden tvivl de mennesker jeg mødte, og som jeg allerede har planer om at besøge så snart min bankkonto er kommet sig ovenpå første tur. Dublin er virkelig en fantastisk by, med en masse fantastiske mennesker og man keder sig aldrig da der altid sker noget, selv om søndagen.
greatest_challenge: Funding was a little tight at times haha, but I managed.

crucial_aspects: It was important for me that it was an english speakning destination because it made it a lot eaiser for me to get local friends and to get to know the culture. It was also important that there was a lot of focus on the social aspect of the college life.
info_ease: There was a person at Trinity who were avalible for the Erasmus law-students at anytime. She was therefore a really big help because it could be difficult to find the information online.
arrival_assistance: There was introduction meetings and oppertunities to ask qustions. However everything was very confusing in the beginning and I could have used a bit more guidance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Most of it was through email and the contact person was really nice and answered quick.
registration_help: A contact person.
registration_success: Pretty successful the only problem was that one of the classes that I wanted was removed to the spring semester.
registration_advice: start early so it will not be too stressful and write to the contact person if you have questions. They are really helpfull.
course_level: I really like my courses but I would say that some of it was a bit eaiser than at KU. However it is ofcoruse a bit for difficult to study in another language and some of the exams was in hand, without any books or dictionary. In general it was very much up to yourself how much time you wanted to spend on the ready etc. but it was of coruse eaiser to pas the exam if you read more than the minimum.
teaching_comparison: It was a bit more up to the student to choose what to read. Personally I liked it, but I guess it depends on what you prefer.
courses_enrolled: Medical law and ethics International Public Law European Human Rights Law
recommended_courses: European Human Rights Law. There was a really good teacher whit a lot of personal experience at the coruse, and the style of teaching was really great. I Learned a lot of new things eventhough I have had a smillar subject at KU.
unexpected_costs: I used a lot of money on traveling around the country.
cost_comparison: I was really luckey with housing but you should expect to use around 7000-8000 DKK pr. month on housing.
activities_available: There is 120 different societies at Trinity so you can do basic everything from sport to star-watching
activities_recommended: Join a sport team and the sport center at Trinity. The sport center is cheap and you can do a lot of great things. Also join some of the other societies, it is a really good way to get to know the local students.
weekend_recommendations: Everything. Ireland have so much great nature so it is perfect to go away for hicking in the weekends.
culture_adjustment: It was Pretty easy because you could understand the language.
socializing_tips: Join societies and get ready for a great pub culture.
cultural_challenges: I did not find anything really challenging.
culture_appreciated: How open Irish people is to other cultures and meeting new people.
top3_advice: Join societies. Ask your teachers if you have questions. Be openminded.
other_useful_info: To start the registration process early.
most_rewarding: The social life at Trinity.
greatest_challenge: Housing.

crucial_aspects: At der var mange kurser at vælge imellem, da undervisningssproget var engelsk, samt at det var muligt at få Erasmus+ legatet, da Irland er et EU-land modsat f.eks. Storbritannien.
overall_comments: Min positive bedømmelse handler som sådan ikke om universitet, som jeg ikke var vildt imponeret af, men mere min oplevelse i det hele.
info_ease: De havde en side, som blev opdateret undervejs, men ellers var der ikke andet hjælp f.eks. kunne et informationsmøde havde været godt.
arrival_assistance: Der var ikke nogen hjælp ved ankomst.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Min positive bedømmelse handler som sådan ikke om universitet, som jeg ikke var vildt imponeret af, men mere min oplevelse i det hele.
registration_process: Det var nemt med at registrere for Erasmus, men at tilmelde sig fag var vanskeligt, da Trinity havde lavet det sådan, at man kan prøve kurser af i to uger og så tilmelde sig endelig derefter. Dog gav det nogle vanskeligheder ift., at nogle oplevede at der lige pludselig ikke var plads på de kurser, som de troede, at de kunne tage. Dette var heldigvis ikke tilfældet for mig. Desuden havde sociologi glemt at opdatere deres liste over kurser til Erasmus-studerende, så der manglede beskrivelser af flere af kurserne. Desuden havde jeg et fag, hvor de havde glemt at opdatere modulbeskrivelsen, så i stedet for at handle om konflikter mellem lande, handlede det nu om klima.
registration_help: De har et Academic Registry, hvor man kan møde op/ringe/skrive.
registration_success: Jeg fik alle de kurser, som jeg ville.
registration_advice: Ansøg om flere kurser hjemmefra end du umiddelbart tænker at tage.
academics_comments: Min positive bedømmelse handler som sådan ikke om universitet, som jeg ikke var vildt imponeret af, men mere min oplevelse i det hele.
course_level: Trinity er nemmere end Danmark både ift. læsemængde, og hvad der forventes til eksamen. Med det sagt er der mere fælles diskussion i undervisningen og fremlæggelser, som man ikke er vant til på KU. Desuden kan man ikke regne med at ECTS-pointene er svarende ift. arbejdsmængden, da det meget kommer an på den enkelte underviser. F.eks. kan et 5 ECTS fag kræve en fremlæggelse, et essay på 2500 ord samt en masse læsning, hvor et 10 ECTS fag kan kræve præcis det samme af en.
teaching_comparison: Der var forelæsninger af 45 min og øvelsestimer af 45 min, som underviseren også selv stod for (bortset fra i statistik, hvor en øvelseslærer var på). Man blev mere inddraget som studerende i diskussioner i øvelsestimerne end man gør på KU. Desuden havde jeg en oplevelse af, at underviserne var mere subjektive end på KU, hvor deres egne meninger i højere grad kom til udtryk.
courses_enrolled: Conflict Studies 10 (Roderick Condon), Social Networks and Digital Lives 10 (Ann Holohan), Researching Society 5 (Yekaterina Chzhen), Comparative Sociology of Europe 5 (Camilla Devitt)
recommended_courses: Jeg var glad for Conflict Studies - selvom jeg blev overrasket over, at det var et fag om klimaet (og ikke konflikter mellem lande, som det først fremgik af i modulbeskrivelsen), så var underviseren engageret og meget opmærksom på de studerende. Researching Society var godt som en opfriskning af nogle statistiske begreber, men de brugte STATA som statistikprogram, så det skulle man selvfølgelig være klar på. Desuden var det det eneste fag uden en fremlæggelse, hvilket også var meget rart.
unexpected_costs: Den høje husleje.
cost_comparison: Offentlig transport er billigt. Hvis man får et youth leap-card koster det kun 1 € pr. tur i op til 90 minutter. Man kan ikke regne med den offentlige transport, men sammenlignet med Danmark, er det langt billigere.
activities_available: De har over 100 klubber på Trinity så alt fra yoga til fotografering.
activities_recommended: Vælg den klub, som interesserer dig. Jeg kender flere som fandt venner gennem disse.
weekend_recommendations: Galway, Cork og Belfast, men også alle byerne syd fra Dublin f.eks. Bray, Killiney og Dún Laoghaire, hvor man kan tage en virkelig flot togtur derned langs kysten.
culture_adjustment: Rimelig nemt, da jeg havde været i Storbritannien flere gange og mange ting minder om. Universitet gav også en kort introduktion til den lokale kultur.
socializing_tips: Ikke gør dig afhængig af Trinity. I introugen blev de overrasket over, at vi forventede social aktiviteter, så de få der blev afholdt, kom alle til og det blev vildt uoverskueligt. I stedet så tag til sportsevents i starten, tal med andre du tilfældigt møder og spørg om de vil have en kaffe/øl senere. Lige pludselig kender man virkelig mange, fordi 'nogle kender nogle'.
cultural_challenges: Ikke rigtig nogen.
culture_appreciated: Pub-kulturen, hvor det ikke nødvendigvis handlede om at blive fuld, men også bare være et oplagt sted at mødes til en god snak (man kan altid få sodvand og alkoholfri øl).
top3_advice: Vær opmærksom på boligkrisen, tag det sociale i egen hånd og oplev andre smukke byer og områder i Irland.
other_useful_info: Nyd det.
most_rewarding: Helt klart det sociale, jeg har fået ud af det. Efter opholdet har jeg nu venner i hele Europa, og jeg kan desuden mærke, at jeg både er blevet endnu mere social og endnu mere selvstændig.
greatest_challenge: At finde et sted at bo ...

crucial_aspects: Inside EU English Speaking High academic standard Variety and interesting module choice
info_ease: It was difficult to find written down information on a lot of stuff. I either had to write emails or ask in person.
arrival_assistance: I could attend a welcome presentation with general knowledge and a zoom call with more tailored knowledge for my department
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: A surveymonkey is sent out with all available modules where you can rank preferences. You then have to wait for email confirmation which might take a day or two. Your list often have scheduling conflicts so you need to redo them. It is frustrating that schedule information is very hard to find which makes the registration hard since you have to just try until you have no schedule conflicts. Meanwhile time is limited, because room on the modules are filling up, so you might not end up with your preferred modules.
registration_help: Emails or showing up at the desk on available days.
registration_success: I got none of my preferences first time around but then changed all of my preferences to something else and then I succeeded in getting those.
registration_advice: Be quick at the start of registration and try to seek out schedules for the modules you want to avoid issues.
course_level: Adequate level
teaching_comparison: Similar style where questions are encouraged and a more relaxed attitude between student and lecturer. Lecturers often attend tutorial classes as well which is an advantage over UCPH
courses_enrolled: Comparative Sociology of Europe Race, ethnicity and identity European Union Politics A Globalisation and development The Psychology of the Climate Crisis Histories and Futures of Climate Change
recommended_courses: Globalisation and development and The Psychology of the Climate Crisis are both very good
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs
cost_comparison: Groceries are cheaper than Copenhagen. Dairy products especially.
activities_available: There is a ton of societies to join both political, sports and hobbies
activities_recommended: There is a lot of very good hiking spots around Dublin
weekend_recommendations: hiking, the leprechaun museum, Board game cafés
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy. People are very nice and polite. Sometimes it is hard to engage with local students because they are often very busy with reading or friends. I recommend seeking out other erasmus students.
cultural_challenges: The politics are somewhat different and some students are more culturally conservative than what I was used to. Try not to assume someone's politics if you want to avoid offending.
culture_appreciated: The Irish like jokes and pranks and are all in all often very entertaining to be around.
top3_advice: Join a few societies and go to an event atleast once. Find other erasmus students and ask if they want to eat lunch together If you have a lot of modules, find out what the learning goals and what the assessments are early and prepare to not get overwhelmed later.
other_useful_info: The gym is not free for exchange students
most_rewarding: Being able to face and keep up in a foreign environment in a second language
greatest_challenge: Getting to know local Irish students. Much easier to find other erasmus students to hang out with.

crucial_aspects: Language, culture, history and academic opportunities.
info_ease: It was quite tough to figure out which modules I could enroll in. Otherwise, the necessary information was available.
arrival_assistance: There was a week of orientation.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: During the orientation week there was an online meeting on the sociological modules I could enroll in. As it turned out I did not get any courses with more than 5 ECTS points meaning I had to take courses in Philosophy, Theology an elective and 6 courses in total.
registration_help: Sorry, but the coordinator was not of much help. My fellow studen from Copenhagen and I figured it out together.
registration_success: I got 2 of the 4 modules I had read about and knew I wanted to get into.
registration_advice: Do not expect to be enrolled in the modules you read about from home.
course_level: It is a little bit easier than in Copenhagen, but any language barrier might make up for it. A few of the classes I took had a bit of repetition from the classes I have taken in Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: I do not think the style of teaching was that different from that of UCPH. There are more presentations in Trinity in the exercise classes.
courses_enrolled: HISTORY OF WESTERN PHILOSOPHY I A ETHICS MATTERS: GLOBAL QUESTIONS, ETHICAL RESPONSES RACE, ETHNICITY AND IDENTITY 1 COMPARATIVE SOCIOLOGY OF EUROPE GLOBALISATION AND DEVELOPMENT 1 DISPLACEMENT: EXPLORING THE HUMAN EXPERIENCE OF FORCED MIGRATION
recommended_courses: RACE, ETHNICITY AND IDENTITY 1, GLOBALISATION AND DEVELOPMENT 1 and DISPLACEMENT: EXPLORING THE HUMAN EXPERIENCE OF FORCED MIGRATION due to the subject matter and my interests.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Groceries are quite cheap. Rent is too damn high... in most places.
activities_available: All sorts of social clubs, sports clubs and debate clubs
activities_recommended: I do not partake in many non-academic activities at UCPH either so I am not the right respondent on this matter. My advice is to go on plenty of long walks around the city. Go hear some music at the Cobblestone and grab a pint. Read about the rich history of Dublin and go out and see it for yourself. Attend some comedy shows or a concert at 3arena. Find some random people in a pub and talk to them. I generally just went out on my own and was rarely bored.
weekend_recommendations: My advice is to go on plenty of long walks around the city. Go hear some music at the Cobblestone and grab a pint. Read about the rich history of Dublin and go out and see it for yourself. Attend some comedy shows or a concert at 3arena. Find some random people in a pub and talk to them. I generally just went out on my own and was rarely bored. Of course the academic stuff is important, but you have to go experience Dublin and its culture.
culture_adjustment: Real easy
socializing_tips: I did not really do that outside of the classes.
cultural_challenges: You should just be aware that religion and history is no joke in Ireland. People have strong feelings about catholics/protestants, the Irish/the Northern Irish, the British, poverty and immigration and these subjects are no joking matter... most of the time.
culture_appreciated: I found it all very interesting. Historywise, I delved into the Easter Rising and James Connolly. I also went to Belfast during 'Reading Week' and learned a lot about the troubles and the current state of Belfast.
top3_advice: 1. You cannot expect to enroll in the modules you read about from home. 2. Unless you have connections you can expect modest housing 3. Read up on Irish history. It is really worth it.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of right now, no.
most_rewarding: Just to experience the culture. I'm glad to be home amongst friends and family, but I truly miss the streets of Dublin.
greatest_challenge: To be away from my girlfriend and having to share a room.

crucial_aspects: English-speaking country, cultural opportunities
info_ease: Pretty easy after you find out how to navigate on Trinity's website
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any.
arrival_comments: The orientation week was very short but when the lectures started, you quickly found your way around.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The university sent e-mails when you had to choose your courses
registration_help: You could write them e-mails if you had problems with the registration
registration_success: I got all the courses I applied for
registration_advice: Look at the exam forms if that's important to you. I had two assignments and three exams.
course_level: I had one 1st year module, 1 3rd year module and one 4th year module. The balance was very good.
teaching_comparison: Almost only lectures and no group work or seminars but that depends on with classes you choose.
courses_enrolled: Torts; Public Interest Law; Intellectual Property Law
recommended_courses: All of them! They each were very interesting and especially in torts the lecturers were very good.
unexpected_costs: I had to buy kitchen supplies and stuff for my bedroom.
cost_comparison: Groceries and public transport was less expensive.
activities_available: There were a lot of different societies you could join for 3 EUR each. In the first weeks they had a society fair so you could talk to all of them.
activities_recommended: Choose something you're interested in but also something completely new. I started boxing and it was super fun.
weekend_recommendations: Take the bus or train to the coast and see the cliffs and nature of Ireland. Many cities like Cork, Limerick or Kilkenny are perfect for a day trip.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it was similar to Denmark.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: Their openness and politeness.
top3_advice: Look for accommodation long time in advance. Be open and just talk to people, that's how you will experience the most. Travel there a week or a couple of days before the school starts so you have time to settle in.
other_useful_info: Remember to order your student card online.
most_rewarding: The people I met.
greatest_challenge: Being on my own in a new country and having to navigate in a new city.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go on exchange to an English-speaking country and to a country where I knew there was a strong focus on a good academic and social study environment.
info_ease: There was very good support both at the University of Copenhagen and at Trinity College. My academic advisor at the University of Copenhagen has been extremely helpful and quick to respond to questions.
arrival_assistance: We had a full introduction week with many orientation sessions and social events at the university. We were assigned a tutor whom we could contact with questions. In addition, we were offered a buddy who was a student at Trinity College. My buddy gave me a tour and was always happy to answer any questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We received some information by email from Trinity College, and apart from that, the process was very straightforward. They have developed videos that you can follow, which makes the process very easy and accessible.
registration_help: They had made videos that we could watch, provided information on their website, and were easy to get in contact with.
registration_success: I got all the classes i wished/registered for.
registration_advice: I found the process to be straightforward, but it is a good idea to have the university’s email contact information ready in case you need to get in touch with them if any issues arise.
course_level: The level of difficulty varied from course to course, and the exam format is quite different from what we are used to at the University of Copenhagen. Several of the courses did not have a final exam at all, but instead relied on assignments and tests throughout the semester, which together made up the final grade.
teaching_comparison: The teaching consisted exclusively of lectures, with no seminar-based teaching. I missed having seminars, as I learn best when I am actively participating in the classes.
courses_enrolled: European Human Rights Food Law Medical Law and Ethics
recommended_courses: Food Law and Medical Law and Ethics were to really interesting courses.
unexpected_costs: nothing.
cost_comparison: The housing was quite expensive. However, this was also because I paid for a longer period than I actually stayed. It is probably possible to find something cheaper or more flexible if you rent private accommodation.
activities_available: I signed up for pottery classes, arts classes, fitness, the running club, and the hiking club. However, there are over 100 clubs available.
activities_recommended: The pottery-class was very fun.
weekend_recommendations: I went on several train trips to places including Galway and Belfast. They were really lovely cities, and the trips were very enjoyable. In addition, all the museums are free, which also made for some great experiences.
culture_adjustment: I found it very easy. I didn’t experience any culture shock and felt that I fit in well in the city and with the other students.
socializing_tips: Join the clubs; it made it easy to find a community and meet other students. Also, sign up to have a buddy; that way you’re guaranteed to have a local friend from the start
cultural_challenges: I don’t think I experienced any cultural challenges.
culture_appreciated: The nature is really beautiful. I enjoy running a lot, and the city is great for that as well.
top3_advice: Be open-minded, push some of your boundaries from home, and embrace all the experiences you can get. And most importantly, enjoy it—time flies, and it’s truly a special period in your life.
other_useful_info: Be aware that the teaching is somewhat different, and I personally found this a bit challenging, as I was unsure whether I was studying “correctly.”
most_rewarding: Meeting people from other cultures and learning a lot about myself.
greatest_challenge: Living with people from other cultures. It was challenging to live with others who had very different habits regarding cleanliness, cooking, and so on. However, it might simply have been new to me, as I had never lived with anyone other than my partner or alone before.
other_comments: It has been an amazing experience—look forward to it!

crucial_aspects: I chose my study destination based on that the destination were (i) within the European Union and (ii) english speaking.
info_ease: It was really easy to find the information upon arrival, and there were several introduction modules.
arrival_assistance: No assistance in particular other than a lot of information by email about collection of student card etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I registered in advance at home and everything was in order when I arrived.
registration_help: An e-mail was sent out to students who had to register for courses. You could get help from Academic Registry, which is a student service.
registration_success: I was successful. There were limited courses that I could take, so not a lot of choices.
registration_advice: Find courses beforehand on the website of TCD, and make sure which courses you can participate in.
course_level: I could only take bachelor level courses. The level was easier at the host institution, and limited preparation for class was required. I chose modules where I had to write an essay as the exam method, which made it less important to attend all the lectures.
teaching_comparison: It was the same style of teaching with a professor and smaller classes of approximately 20-30 students. The professors had prepared powerpoints and reading lists for each class.
courses_enrolled: I enrolled in Food Law, Intellectual Property Law, Commercial Law and Corporate Governance.
recommended_courses: I can really recommend Food Law because of the professor and the importance of food law within the European Union. If you like EU law this is a great course.
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: The housing was so expensive.
activities_available: A lot of activities were available for students such as social clubs, a gym and other athletic activities.
activities_recommended: A membership at the gym located on campus was cheap and you can go there in between classes.
weekend_recommendations: I did hiking trips in the weekend, and also trips to the UK. I can recommend to rent a car and drive along the coastline or take the train to the bigger cities in Ireland.
culture_adjustment: It was easy to adjust to the local culture, and the local people is friendly and easy to talk to.
socializing_tips: Talk to local students from your class or attend the social activities at campus. The local students are friendly, so just say hi and introduce you.
cultural_challenges: You have to get used to random people wanting to talk to you etc. in the bus or at pubs.
culture_appreciated: The local pubs were so nice and cosy.
top3_advice: Find accommodation as close to the city center as possible, be social during the week and explore ireland in the weekends, and participate in the introduction week.
other_useful_info: Get a student leap card (travel card) to use the bus and train system.
most_rewarding: Meeting local students, international students and other Erasmus students.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was adjusting to living in another country and at a place with new people.

crucial_aspects: English speaking country and rich culture

arrival_assistance: The office responsible for incoming mail at Trinity was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You have to get an offer signed which you get by sending some info. then you have to sign up for classes online. Which is done through a portal, which opens up at a certain time. I cant remember when, but I remember feeling well informed.
registration_help: The mail incoming erasmus students was very helpful
registration_advice: Make sure the classes are in the right semester. And take classes that are worth 10 ects points (most are worth 5) the level didn't feel too high nor the workload, and i was very happy with the subjects

teaching_comparison: Less classes and more self-studying
courses_enrolled: SOU4401 CONFLICT STUDIES SOU4405 LABOUR MARKETS, GENDER & INSTITUTIONS 1 SOU44071 Advanced Methods of Sociological Data Science
recommended_courses: Conflict Studies. It focused on environmental sociology and was very in-depth. It also made me realise how little attention environmental sociology receives at UPCH, which is quite ridiculous considering how important the topic is for society and how many social problems it encompasses.
unexpected_costs: Beer and electricity lol
cost_comparison: Housing was suuuuper expensive
activities_available: a lot of societies (theater, food, language ect.)
activities_recommended: Going outside the city - it was super beautiful and i regret i didn't do it more
weekend_recommendations: belfast, cork, widlow mountains
culture_adjustment: Quite easy
socializing_tips: The Irish are quite curious and friendly, but also a little reserved at first. Once you get to know them, though, they’re very warm and easy to talk to
cultural_challenges: People were very polite and used a lot of expressions like “thanks, love” and things like that. Apart from that, I didn’t really notice anything big
culture_appreciated: Chatty and pub culture
top3_advice: Find accommodation early, take 10 ects point subjects and make friends with the other erasmus students from ur classes. I did want to make more local friends, but realisticlly the other exchange students will likely be ur friends since they are also looking for friends and the also have a lot of time to do stuff
other_useful_info: The busses are very cheap for students and people under 25. But you have to order online. You refill the "leap cards" and the spars.
most_rewarding: The friends I made and the classes, were i had a lot of time to study in depth
greatest_challenge: Accommodation

crucial_aspects: The culture of Ireland, Trinity's good reputation the good reviews from students at UCPH
info_ease: Very easy, Trinity are very good at taking care of their visiting students
arrival_assistance: I had to swap courses, and they were very good at explaining how it was done and making it easy for me
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You fill out a form online before coming stating which courses you would like. Once you arrive you have a week to try out courses and make changes if needed/wanted. If you choose any of the courses that the first year students have (like torts of constitutional law) you do not get to try them before having to decide if you want to switch courses. It is very easy to switch courses and Trinity are very good at informing the students about the process and important deadlines.
registration_help: Trinity has a school of law and an Erasmus office, both of which are very good at helping with any questions.
registration_success: I got all the classes i had wanted before i went, and I got to switch one of the courses with another course i wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure to read about the exam information and amount of course work before choosing your course.
course_level: At Trinity only undergraduate (BA) courses are offered to visiting students.
teaching_comparison: Very similar, but the students are much more on their own. The readings for each class are a lot less organized but still somewhat manageable. The teaching is almost 100% the lecturer talking in front of a powerpoint to 35-70 students. There is only class discussion if the lecturer wants it, which was about 50/50.
courses_enrolled: Food Law, Commercial Law and Medical Law and Ethics
recommended_courses: Medical Law and Ethics - very interesting deep dive into Irish medical law, with good exams and decent lecturers. Food Law - EU focused course so UCPH students already know some of the information, very engaging and skilled lecturer, very good exams.
unexpected_costs: Enrolling in student societies costs money, ranging from 2 Euro to 25 Euro. It was almost always worth it paying the enrollment fee. The sports center on campus (gym, swimming pool, etc) costs 78 Euro for the whole semester.
cost_comparison: Rent was more expensive than i thought The bus was cheaper than i thought
activities_available: Trinity has a huge amount of sports clubs and social societies, ranging from boxing, kayaking, hiking, shooting and climbing, to movie club, nordic club, philosophic club and jazz club
activities_recommended: The Phil (philosophic society) - They have a lot of cool events and do debate training The Law Society - Also very cool events and parties The boxing club - Very friendly, good training 3 times a week, has space for people who are brand new and experienced
weekend_recommendations: Hiking in Howth The pubs around Dublin Galway and Cliffs of Moher Glendalough
culture_adjustment: Very easy
cultural_challenges: The Irish people are very friendly and outgoing, so had to get used to strangers talking to me more than in Denmark
culture_appreciated: The Irish people are very friendly and great to be around.
top3_advice: Take part in the very active student environment, join clubs, join societies, go to the parties. Go out and see the country outside Dublin, it is very beautiful. Choose your exams wisely, having more essays means having more freedom to plan your stay however you choose.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Getting to try out so many new things through the societies and clubs at Trinity
greatest_challenge: Having started my exam prep too late

crucial_aspects: The culture of Ireland and trinity as a historic university
info_ease: It was alright, there was not a lot information to get, but the most important was easy to find.
arrival_assistance: I changed my modules and that was very easy and the administration are helpful
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Trinity send out forms beforehand, where you have to choose the modules you want. Then you will know which you get upon arrival. Otherwise trinity sent out emails with different information (how to get your student card, how to register at their platform, etc.). You just have to follow the steps, and none of it is important that you have fully completed berfore arrival.
registration_help: There is an erasmus office at campus, and the school of law administration is also very helpful.
registration_success: Very succesful. I got everuthing I wanted and could even change for something else.
registration_advice: I would read about the type of exam for the different modules and the work load. Some of the modules are for freshman year and requires a bit more work.
course_level: The courses are easier than at UCPH
teaching_comparison: They only do lectures (the freshman year modules also have seminars) for 3 hours a week and then you just have to study on your own. They do more essay exams.
courses_enrolled: Public International Law, Medical Law and Ethics, Commercial Law
recommended_courses: I would recommend the modules with essay exams (commercial law and medical law).
unexpected_costs: The sports center was 79 euros, but for the whole semester. On the other hand you do not have to buy books, since you can rent them at the library.
cost_comparison: Food is a bit less expensive than expected, and the public transport is very cheap. But drinking and eating out was more expensive than expected. And then the housing was very expensive.
activities_available: I joined the swimming team, which was really fun and a good way to meet others and more Irish people. They have a lot of different sports, so there should be something for everyone.
activities_recommended: I would recommend to join a lot of societies. You pay 2-3 euros to join a society, but then you can get offers for different trips around Ireland and fun nights with pubcrawl etc.
weekend_recommendations: Travel. Dublin is a great city, but the whole country is so beautiful. Some areas and towns are easy to get to with train, but is also not expensive to rent a car, which is very recommended.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The Irish are very open at pubs.
socializing_tips: Join the sports teams, meet them at the pubs or trinity's bar, go on dates
culture_appreciated: The relaxed vibe that Ireland and Dublin has. There is no rush, and they always have time for a beer at the pub. Very friendly and kind people.
top3_advice: Choose modules with essay exams. Join the intro week! and then join sports teams and societies. Travel around Ireland.
most_rewarding: To live in another country, meet new people from around the world, enjoy the irish culture and scenery.
greatest_challenge: Finding accommodation and neglecting my exams.

crucial_aspects: I would like to explore the opportinuty to work in China after my education.

Some sports teams are also closed off. I have had the honor to join the schools skiing team as one of the only exchange students, but that was the exception, not the rule. arrival_assistance: Orientation and arrival assitance mostly, where they will tell you about you dorm, the rules, the cantines etc.
arrival_comments: Most of the useful information is given verbally through students, that is why getting to know people, especially the locals asap is very important. I would perhaps even say skipping the orientation for some club activities is preferable.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I would say the THU is a great place to be, IF you are extremely open minded and proactive. Some clubs such as the marching band, piano clubs etc are not open to exchange students. Some sports teams are also closed off. I have had the honor to join the schools skiing team as one of the only exchange students, but that was the exception, not the rule. In general, talking to people, even on the streets, is extremely rewarding and is recommended from my part to get to know people.
registration_process: It is kinda the same as in UCPH, where you register courses online through a portal. There are multiple periods of registration, and you can also drop courses after they have begun.
registration_help: Teachers are extremely helpful to exchange students, get in contact with the teach asap.
registration_success: This is where the problem comes in. Most of the courses provided on the excel sheet you receive prior to the stay is NOT available to exchange students.
registration_advice: 1. Ask for the final list of courses available for exchange students. 2. Ask the course professor if he/she could add you in as an extra if you did not get your relevant course.

Some clubs such as the marching band, piano clubs etc are not open to exchange students. Some sports teams are also closed off. I have had the honor to join the schools skiing team as one of the only exchange students, but that was the exception, not the rule. The teaching method is vastly different, as you are required to meetup. It is hard to explain, but expect a lot more "discussion" type courses then pure math, which is what I am enrolled into.

recommended_courses: To be fair, none in particular, unless it is something your are interested in and have not had something similar before.

cost_comparison: Hobby activities such as skiing, rowing etc.

Some clubs, as said before, are a bit more closed off, and you would either need to be extremely good or extremely lucky in order to get in.

weekend_recommendations: Join the club excursions, that is where you will get to know people.

socializing_tips: Just talk to them, they are very friendly in general. Some of my best friends obtained here was through talking to them on the streets or on the soccer field, while playing sports.
cultural_challenges: None in particular.
culture_appreciated: The helpfulness and "team" sense.
top3_advice: Be proactive x3. This is the single most important thing. As in China, nothing will come to you if you are not proactive.
other_useful_info: Come a bit earlier, so that you can get you bank, phone etc in order.
most_rewarding: The clubs hands down. You get a sense of belonging there. The friends I made are the most rewarding part of the exchange.
greatest_challenge: Nothing in particular.

crucial_aspects: My heritage as I went to Beijing and my parents are Chinese, and I speak the language. Also because the university is highly ranked.
overall_comments: I had such a nice experience overall. If you are curious and willing to put the effort, its a great opportunity to be familiar with a different culture.
info_ease: Not easy
arrival_assistance: From a exchange coordinator
arrival_comments: Some courses were not accessible
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had such a nice experience overall. If you are curious and willing to put the effort, its a great opportunity to be familiar with a different culture.
registration_process: There are different rounds. First round you sign up for courses within your department. The popular courses get filled out fast. Second round you sign up for courses out of your department. You can drop courses until some weeks later.
registration_help: Exchange coordinators etc. Not that much help which was a bit frustrating. No introduction really to the system.
registration_success: No as some courses were not offered to exchange students and some were not offered in English, even though it seem that way from the course catalogue. No consistency really with the catalogue and the courses in the portal, which is stressful as they get filled up quickly. However, for the existing courses that were open for exchange students, the coordinators were in most cases able to open up extra spots for the students.
registration_advice: Don't worry about finding the courses beforehand too much as they deviate from what is really offered.
academics_comments: I had such a nice experience overall. If you are curious and willing to put the effort, its a great opportunity to be familiar with a different culture.
course_level: Different levels. Some were harder as Corporate Finance. Some were easier, as they only graded on a book report, homework and a presentation.

weekend_recommendations: Clubs, go out for dinner, travel to different cities via. high-speed train or plane.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy.
cultural_challenges: The local students are really different, as chinese students tend to make their life more about school.
culture_appreciated: The food.

other_useful_info: Its a nice university.
most_rewarding: The people I met on exchange. All are very ambitious as it is a highly ranked university. Also curious about China, which I believe is great.
greatest_challenge: That its difficult to adapt to the pratical processes as payments etc. and people are not familiar with english. However, if you're interested of a different culture, I think its a part of the experience!
other_comments: I loved the experience as a whole!

crucial_aspects: Firstly i wanted to go to China and Beijing, both to visit people there, but also practice the language and experiencing a culture very different from danish culture, in a way that would be hard to achieve by other means.
info_ease: The university had prepared some documents, which had the most important information. The medical checkup was a bit confusing, i ended up doing it in Beijing, which seemed to be a safe option, since otherwise you cannot be sure they would approve it. If you do it in Denmark, make sure the doctor fills out everything, as otherwise they might say it is invalid
arrival_assistance: On the two scheduled arrival dates, there were arrangements and volunteers helping you with paperwork and settling down. They also helped you get added into wechat groups, which are very important for finding information and learning of events on campus. Still i would recommend getting to know as many people early as possible and making wechat groups together to share information, as otherwise it can be quite overwhelming figuring everything out yourself.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process worked fine in some ways, but also a bit chaotic. The information about how the online system works was fine. The people i talked to when i arrived was often worried whether or not they could get the courses they needed to fulfill the requirements back home, while also fulfilling the requirements of Tsinghua, based on the courses listed online. It is my impression that it worked out for almost everyone after they talked with the administration, who often could bend rules such as having to take a certain amount of credit in your faculty. Personally i wanted to take courses in the second math department Qiuzhen College, which was not listed in the online system. This worked out after contacting the administration, and the relevant lectures for permision, and then making a special request. The Chinese courses all got filled out very quickly, so if you didn't sign up within 2 minutes of release they were likely gone. So make sure to be ready when courses release. Note that courses taught in English is limited, as it is throughout most of Mainland China.
registration_help: The administration was in my impression helpful, you could either call them or go to Building nr. 23 to get assistance. Often it seem both in course registration and in general, that the rules there quite strict, but in practice were less important. This included how many credits you could take outside your faculty, health reports and other things.
registration_success: I luckily got all the courses i wanted. I ended up signing up from one course taught in English, since the lecturer was nice enough to let my come by his office hour and talk with him about the material, and the course notes was in English.
registration_advice: I would recommend the Chinese language courses a lot, and make sure to sign up immediately when the system opens, as space fills up quickly (at least this year). Secondly, if you have problems with the rules, or cannot find a course online, ask the administration and they will help you out. If you want courses from a special faculty such as Qiuzhen College, they might not be listed online, so instead contact the college or the administration.
course_level: I would say the courses targeted at exchange students where similar to danish courses or could be easier almost. Courses targeted Tsinghua students where harder. It seemed where were generally a bit more homework than a usual danish course.
teaching_comparison: Instead of exercise session where was office hours. I would in general say, that professors in Tsinghua where more popular science and more entertainers, compared to danish professors who mostly stick to the material. the teaching style is a bit similar to my impression of American universities, based on movies and tv.
courses_enrolled: Algebraic Number Theory II Algebraic Curves Topics in Algebraic Geometry Combinatorics and Algorithms Basic Chinese B
recommended_courses: My impression was that some courses where intended for exchange students, most courses taught in English, and was easier than the regular courses, while the courses intended for chinese students could be very time demanding. So if you are taking a 15 credit course load, I would try and make sure the courses are not too demanding so you can also have time to travel and experience the city. Chinese language learning courses was good in my experience and highly recommended.
unexpected_costs: Medical Checkup in the city.
cost_comparison: Food in the campus cantines was very cheap and good, while prices outside campus could vary a lot sometimes very cheap, and other times same as Denmark. Delivery and cabs are very cheap. Taking trains can cost up to 600 (fx Beijing-Shanghai) but prices in smaller cities are a lot lower, so travelling can be fairly cheap. A lot of tourist sights have very low entry fees.
activities_available: There was so many clubs. All sports had a club, many language clubs, film, singing, bands, art, chess, and the list goes on. There is also a Wechat group for european students, with useful information. There was also a lot of social events organized in the campus, both gallas and smaller things. Also there was clubs holding events close to campus, organized by Tsinghua Student clubs.
activities_recommended: I would recommend doing a lot of activities in the start to make friends and get to know people. Joining a sports club or other club would be a good way to meet some Chinese people which can be hard otherwise, as you can end up in a exchange bubble. I joined the climbing club, which was welcoming, but also had a strict attendance requirement. Would recommend to people who have climbed before, and is willing to dedicate to train 2-3 times per week. Other clubs were less strict about attendance.
weekend_recommendations: Try and travel as much as possible, trains are convenient so you can make a lot out of 3 days. There is only one holiday very early on in the fall semester, so i would recommend traveling there, as otherwise you only have weekends. Also try and plan your courses, so you either have Monday or Friday free so you are more free to travel.
culture_adjustment: As someone who only speaks basic Chinese, it can be hard to navigate outside campus as almost nobody speaks English. Learn useful phrases, and do not be afraid to use Google translate/ Baidu translate. In campus you get used to life pretty quickly, and since it has most things you need, it is a nice base to have between exploring. Most chinese people are very friendly, and are usually patient if you try your best to speak chinese.
socializing_tips: It can be hard talking to local students if you do not speak Chinese, as most students are not comfortable in speaking English. I would recommend joining clubs, and find some friends who speak both English and Chinese.
cultural_challenges: I did not find too many challenges except getting to know Chinese people well, because of the language barrier.
culture_appreciated: The hospitality and how nice everyone is. Chinese people who speaks English would sometime see me struggling to communicate, and help me out, or otherwise be patient to try and understand me. Chinese culture in general is so rich and vast, and a lot of cultural sites are well preserved.
top3_advice: 1) Prepare as much as possible: make sure you get a proper working VPN (most popular VPN does not work well, even though they say do) get Astrill, Letsvpn or ask native people what they use, and get it before you go to China. Learn how to use and pay with Wechat and Alipay. Try and make some contacts beforehand if possible. 2) Learn Chinese: The more Chinese you speak, the more you can interact with locals and do things independently, so you get most out of your trip if you are also learning Chinese there. The first steps in learning Chinese, can be done from home equally well as in China (learning tones, sounds and pinyin) as well as basic structure of language, so get these fundamentals down. the more you learn after that, the better. 3. Use your time well: China is huge and you will not be able to do and see all the things you want to, so try and plan and do as much as possible. Try and make sure not all your courses have too much homework, so you don't spend all your time doing homework.
other_useful_info: There is wechat groups for buying and selling used stuff, quite active around new semester, ask around so you can get basic furniture cheaply.
most_rewarding: The people i met, and how exciting it is to live in China
greatest_challenge: It is a lot of administrative work and planning (application, housing, visa, moving, courses sign up, heavy workload in courses). I ended up being quite stressed in some periods as I also needed to prepare my master thesis. So I would recommend to stay organized and go in a time, where you do not have anything else going on

crucial_aspects: That it was in China.
info_ease: Hard because Tsinghua doesn't send out a lot of information until about a month or two before the exchange starts
arrival_assistance: The check-in process was long but well executed.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You just go to building 23 and there are students there to help you through the process.
registration_help: Students were there to register you and the staff at the buildings were also helpful.
registration_success: Not too successful. There are multiple course lists that you can look at but they won't reflect the actual list of courses you can choose. So some courses I was interested in weren't there. I had to register classes the day after I arrived, and there wasn't much help with figuring out the school website. It was bugging for me for some time because you need the school's VPN to enter the domain, and it wouldn't always connect. So on the class registration start it's first come first. And there are limited spots on the classes and also limited classes offered in English. But it works out because the first week of classes is like a "trial" (even the teacher's treat it like that), and you can drop/register classes the week after or something. And sometimes the teachers open up more spaces in a class so more people can register (if you ask them or write to them).
registration_advice: Look at the course lists before/in good time and plan the courses you think you'll take (plan more in case some aren't available). Make some friends on the first day of arriving so you can sit together when you register classes. You'll be in some Wechat groups. In my case someone took the initiative to go out on the first night and get to know each other. If you live in a double room, you could register with your roommate.
course_level: Most of my classes were Master's level. A lot of my friends were BA students and they said they could tell the level was higher. But in my opinion it's manageable.
teaching_comparison: It has much more of a classroom feel, like in high school. So participation in a lot of the classes gives extra points towards your final grade.
courses_enrolled: Natural language processing, web information retrieval, fundamentals of computer graphics, management of technological innovation, leadership and communication, elementary chinese A.
recommended_courses: Depends on what you're studying, but for compsci I liked fundamentals of computer graphics and web IR, they were fun and you get to do some fun projects. Of other courses I recommend leadership and communication since the classes were interesting and I formed a tight group (you had to do a lot of group work in the same group).
unexpected_costs: You had to pay a student insurance (i think it was 600rmb). Also I didn't fill out the expenses for local transportation and personal spending, because technically you can stay within Tsinghua and not pay for local transportation. Subway and busses are super cheap, like a few RMB for a trip. Taxis (didi) are also fairly cheap so I used that a lot. Personal spendings is up to you and your own budget. I spend a lot on shopping (especially on taobao). And travelling is very doable during the semester.
cost_comparison: Eating at restaurants (that arent like a local stall) was a bit more expensive than I thought. I can be like eating out in Denmark (like 100-200)
activities_available: There are many sports facilities and opportunities to join that. It's a thing at Tsinghua to work out too so they're big on it. Social activities is something planned by students. There was something called "pyro tuesday" where every tuesday there would be a party at a pizza spot that would turn into a bar that day.
activities_recommended: Travelling! China is so big and has so much to offer. After all the travelling I did around China, I definitely felt that Beijing was somewhat boring at the end compared to other cities.
weekend_recommendations: Travel. But don't forget to also explore Beijing. Or go to parties or clubs with friends.
culture_adjustment: I don't think you adjust much to the local culture since I feel like the culture at Tsinghua/at any university during an exchange will differ from "authentic" local culture a bit. You're surrounded by other exchange students so it feels more international in a way.
socializing_tips: It's a bit hard because there's kind of a division between local and international students where each group keeps to themselves. It's just easier to connect with other international students because a lot of local students aren't the best at English.
cultural_challenges: Not really
culture_appreciated: The culture inside Tsinghua was very open, as everyone is open to meet new people. Outside Tsinghua, Chinese people are also open/welcoming. You'll see that it's very common to be social outside like at a park where you can play board games with random people or workout/dance in public (not that I joined it but it was nice to see people connecting in public since it's so different from Denmark).
top3_advice: Do as much preparation as you can beforehand (figure out what apps you need to have set up to pay, to get around etc.). Meet as many as you can/want but also settle into friend groups if that makes sense (for me going up to new people and trying to make new friends was out of my comfort zone, so just in general get out of your comfort zone) Travel, and prepare yourself for where you want to go.
other_useful_info: Maybe that Tsinghua is a closed area (big though!!) and you can't just enter if you're not a student/working there. So if you're bringing someone with you inside you need to give them visitation rights. If the person you're bringing is a local, the approval can be quick (like a few minutes) but if the person is international, it can take up to a few days. In my case I didn't know so I showed up on the first day with an uncle (who's a local) and my boyfriend (who was going to study at another university in Beijing) and I was only able to get my uncle in that day, but we were stopped in the process and it took a bit of time to get my uncle in. If I knew beforehand I could've set it up so both could get in with me smoothly. They're very strict at the gates!!
most_rewarding: The friends I made.
greatest_challenge: Don't think there was one.

In addition, many things remained unclear specifically with respect to course registration, even after classes had begun, however the staff responsible for integrating exchange students were very helpful and easy to reach.
arrival_assistance: We received many pamphlets of information and had persons of contact that would help us figure out things.
arrival_comments: Course information was difficult to get a hold of, and course registration was in particular very frustrating as agreed by almost all international exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Course information was scarcely available in advance, and based entirely on previous courses offered, some of which were cancelled or unavailable. Since full-degree students get priority and prior access to the course registration system, many courses are furthermore fully booked before even being accessible for registration by exchange students. In addition, particular courses were not listed in the portal while no information as to why was provided, and required interested students to seek out departments and professors on our own initiative. From when the system opened to exchange-students, less than a week before start of classes, and a few weeks into classes, most if not all exchange students were still uncertain about their options.
registration_help: Aside from information passed out in advance and during orientation, there was dedicated staff to answering questions and helping students with the procedures.
registration_success: In the end, I am very happy with the courses I was able to enroll in - they were all relevant to my academic interests and English-taught.
registration_advice: I would advice students, to be prepared and accepting of the fact that there is a lot of uncertainty with regards to courses available on arrival; however, with a little persistence and patience, it should work out.
course_level: Excellent, challenging and interesting for the most part.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was quite different; often a lot less participation and dialogue with the class, compared to what I am used to.

socializing_tips: There was a lot of community at the international dorms, and many chinese students interested in friendship.
cultural_challenges: While I welcomed it, and had tried to prepare for it by learning some chinese in advance, the level of english speaking skills outside the university, and even to some extent on campus, was more lacking than I expected.
culture_appreciated: So many things.
top3_advice: Try to learn Chinese, embrace local culture, have fun!
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: Relationships, personal growth, academic advancement.
greatest_challenge: So many things going on, it was overwhelming at times.
