crucial_aspects: Tsinghua University is widely regarded as the leading university in China. My choice was driven by a combination of strong academic opportunities, exposure to a top-tier institution, future career prospects, and the opportunity to explore a new cultural environment.
overall_comments: Whether in terms of culture, academic environment, personal discovery, encounters, or landscapes, China is truly surprising and fascinating. The career opportunities are remarkable: during the exchange, I had the chance to meet and interact with high-level professionals, including executives from multinational companies, experts from the Club of Rome, professors from top universities (Harvard, MIT, Stanford), and professionals from international institutions such as the World Bank, AIIB, and the United Nations.
info_ease: Beijing is generally well adapted to international students. Although most people do not speak English, it is still easy to navigate the city. Upon arrival at the airport, information is widely available in English, notably for public transportation like the subway. Regarding administrative procedures, I strongly recommend contacting and meeting your international coordinator as early as possible, as they provide essential guidance for all required steps. Starting early ensures that everything runs smoothly.
arrival_assistance: I arrived one week early to ensure that all administrative matters were in order, although most students arrive one or two days before the start of classes. Upon arrival, students are required to complete an online registration process and then report in person to Zijing Building 23, where on-site assistance is provided for administrative and enrollment procedures.
arrival_comments: A large amount of information is provided upon arrival, which can feel overwhelming at first. I strongly recommend writing a clear to-do list to help organize the different steps. Key tasks include completing the mandatory health check at the international hospital (it is generally easier to complete it in China, as requirements are very strict), registering online with the university, and completing the dormitory registration, among others.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Whether in terms of culture, academic environment, personal discovery, encounters, or landscapes, China is truly surprising and fascinating. The career opportunities are remarkable: during the exchange, I had the chance to meet and interact with high-level professionals, including executives from multinational companies, experts from the Club of Rome, professors from top universities (Harvard, MIT, Stanford), and professionals from international institutions such as the World Bank, AIIB, and the United Nations.
registration_process: The registration process at Tsinghua University for international exchange students involves several phases. Upon arrival, students must bring their admission letter and required documents to No. 23 Zijing Building (International Student and Scholar Centre) to complete on-site registration and collect their student ID card. Course selection is divided into different periods: first for courses in the host department, then for courses in other departments, and finally an online application for special reasons. Course slots are limited and assigned on a first-come, first-served basis, so it is important to act quickly. There are also three phases for dropping or withdrawing from courses, each with strict deadlines. Exchange students can normally take up to 20 credits per semester, with a maximum of 8 credits from other departments. However, this limit can be increased to 15 credits by requesting approval from the international coordinator, which is important if there are not enough courses (and thus credits) available in your own department or school. Keep in mind that 1 Chinese credit equals 2 ECTS credits, so 15 Chinese credits are needed to fulfill the 30 ECTS requirement for a semester.
registration_help: In this regard, the international coordinator was extremely helpful. Always attentive and supportive, Ms. (NAME REDACTED) (for the 2025–2026 academic year) strives to find solutions to any issues. Don’t hesitate to contact her if you have any doubts or questions, as she can provide guidance on administrative procedures, course registration, and other practical matters.
registration_success: I was able to register for almost all the classes I was interested in. The system operates on a first-come, first-served basis. You select courses in your own department first, and then you can access courses from other departments. This means that if there are not enough courses in your department, you may need to take courses elsewhere. Overall, you should be able to secure most of the courses you want.
registration_advice: I strongly recommend contacting the professors of the courses you are interested in. You can find this information in Tsinghua’s course listing (excel) and then search online to find the professor’s contact details or office. Explain your situation to them, some professors may open additional spots if they see that you are motivated. Since course selection occurs in multiple phases, patience is key. It is normal not to have all your courses finalized in the first week. Attend as many classes as possible during the first week to explore your options and decide which courses truly interest you. In the final phase, there is a special online application allowing professors to accept students into their courses, which is why contacting them early makes the process easier. A more practical tip: being in China is an incredible opportunity to explore the country and travel. Don’t overload yourself with difficult courses that have heavy workloads. Check the curriculum in advance and try to choose courses that are relevant to your field while also leaving time for sports, student organizations, and weekend trips to discover this wonderful country.
academics_comments: Whether in terms of culture, academic environment, personal discovery, encounters, or landscapes, China is truly surprising and fascinating. The career opportunities are remarkable: during the exchange, I had the chance to meet and interact with high-level professionals, including executives from multinational companies, experts from the Club of Rome, professors from top universities (Harvard, MIT, Stanford), and professionals from international institutions such as the World Bank, AIIB, and the United Nations.
course_level: Overall, the courses in China are of a reasonable level of difficulty, assuming a normal academic background. As a French student, I found that bachelor-level courses in France are heavier, while the master’s program in Denmark tends to be somewhat lighter. Of course, this depends on your field of study. In political science, environmental studies, and economics, most grades were based on assignments or projects, making it easier to pass if you stay consistent. According to my classmates at Tsinghua, courses in mathematics, physics, and computer science can be more demanding. However, with steady effort, there is no reason to worry. If you are considering an exchange abroad, it means you are ambitious and capable of succeeding.
teaching_comparison: The University of Copenhagen and other Scandinavian universities are fantastic, with a teaching style often based on projects and strong student–professor interaction within a flat hierarchy. At Tsinghua, the approach is more traditional: professors mainly lecture while students listen and ask questions. However, several of my courses included projects that offered a great deal of freedom, similar to the Danish style, which I found very valuable and enjoyable.
courses_enrolled: 1. Financial Institutions and Markets (2 credits) 2. Sustainable Development (3 credits) 3. International Organisations and Global Governance (3 credits) 4. Environmental Field Trip (1 credits) 5. China Studies: Industry Society and Culture (3 Credits) 6. Research Design and Thesis Writing (3 credits) NB: 1 chinese credit = 2 ECTS
recommended_courses: I would recommend Financial Institutions and Markets, which provides a comprehensive overview of the finance world and was very informative. China Studies is a good backup if you need credits, offering insights into Chinese ways of thinking and including a multi-day field trip to Shandong province, which was an incredible experience. The Sustainable Development course was also excellent, with a highly knowledgeable professor and guest speakers from organizations such as the Club of Rome and the World Bank.
unexpected_costs: China is generally very inexpensive compared to Denmark. Most of my additional expenses came from train travel outside of Beijing on weekends, as I took the opportunity to explore different regions of the country.
cost_comparison: Food on campus is very inexpensive. At the canteens, you can have a complete meal for around 1–2€, which is much cheaper than I expected.
activities_available: Literally anything you can imagine is available, and every student can find something that interests them. There are clubs and activities for all kinds of passions like marathons on the Great Wall of China, cooking classes, tea or wine appreciation clubs, robotics competitions, coding groups, sports teams, galas, and much more. The variety is incredible, and the opportunities to meet fellow students from around the world through these activities are endless.
activities_recommended: “No sport, no Tsinghua” is the university’s motto. I highly recommend participating in sports, as it is one of the best ways to meet people and unwind. Traveling is also essential. There is so much to discover in China, and it’s up to you to explore and make the most of this incredible world we live in.
weekend_recommendations: There are many great cities close to Beijing that are worth visiting on weekends, such as Tianjin, Chengde, Datong, and Qingdao, all easily reachable by train. For slightly longer trips, cities like Chengdu, Xi’an, Chongqing, and Harbin offer very different experiences. Harbin is especially worth visiting during the Ice and Snow Festival in winter. China’s National Day “Golden Week” holiday runs roughly from October 1 to October 7, which is one of the busiest travel periods of the year and a fantastic time to explore the country, though you should expect crowds and book transport early. This holiday period is ideal for discovering iconic landscapes such as Inner Mongolia in the north or the dramatic karst scenery of Guilin and Zhangjiajie (the “Avatar mountains”), and it’s a unique opportunity to see how diverse China is. Even outside official holidays, China has so much to offer that it’s worth using weekends and longer breaks to make the most of your time here.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to a new culture is never completely easy, but that is also what makes the experience exciting and rewarding. Life on campus is very comfortable, with many services available to support students, which makes adapting to the local culture much smoother.
socializing_tips: All international students are looking to make friends, so it is easy to connect with them, especially through sports or clubs. As for Chinese students, most are curious and happy to engage in conversation. Ask them where they are from, whether they have traveled, or what their hobbies are. Making friends starts with showing genuine interest in the other person, and often these simple conversations can lead to the most meaningful and lasting friendships.
cultural_challenges: Food. Chinese cuisine is often very different from what we used to, quite spicy, oily, and fried. However, there are plenty of alternatives, including vegetarian options, in the campus canteens. With over 16 canteens offering more than 1,000 dishes, the variety is truly extraordinary and makes it easy to find meals that suit your taste.
culture_appreciated: I greatly appreciated the long-term vision that is prevalent in Chinese culture. China builds with a century-long perspective, particularly in areas like energy and urban planning. Regarding climate change, although it is the world’s largest emitter (partly due to global trade) it is actively working to decarbonize and is exemplary in deploying new energy technologies and innovations.
top3_advice: One of the biggest adjustments is China’s internet ecosystem. Most Western apps are blocked, so it is essential to plan ahead and use a reliable VPN like LetsVPN (since NordVPN is not working) to stay in touch with family and friends via WhatsApp. It takes some time to get used to the local system, but it becomes manageable quickly. Make sure to download the following apps in advance: - WeChat (messaging and payments), - Alipay (metro and payments), - Amap (chinese google maps), - Meituan (food delivery and free campus bikes), - 12306 (China Railway), - Bank of China (banking). On finance, everything is digital, and most payments are done via QR codes with WeChat and Alipay. I recommend having a local Chinese bank account to avoid international fees (like Bank of China, on campus at the C building). For example, you can withdraw money with an online bank card like Revolut at the Bank of China ATM, then deposit it back into your Chinese account, this avoids unnecessary fees. On a practical note, since most apps rely heavily on internet and run constantly in the background, having a solid phone and a good power bank is essential for daily use.
other_useful_info: I would advise starting the visa and other administrative procedures as early as possible, as they can take some time to process. Don’t hesitate to ask questions and gather information in advance to ensure a smooth start to your exchange.
most_rewarding: The friendships I made and the unforgettable experiences I shared. I had the chance to travel to breathtaking landscapes, share countless laughs, and create memories that will stay with me forever. I am deeply grateful to all the people I met, as they made this experience truly unforgettable.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge for me was the language barrier. I speak English well and am used to communicating easily. It was the first time I truly felt the difference compared to my bilingual friends in Chinese. Language is not strictly necessary, you can get by with effort and technology. Nevertheless, learning even a few simple words can bring a smile to the Chinese people you meet and make interactions much more enjoyable ;)
other_comments: Have a lovely day!

info_ease: We had an orientation session with all the information we needed
arrival_assistance: Orientation session, contact with the International Office
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_help: The International Office at TU Wien was quick to answer questions and provide us with all the information we needed
registration_success: Some of the classes I initially selected when applying for the exchange were not offered this semester, but I was able to register to some new courses offered for the first time

weekend_recommendations: There is a lot to see in Vienna and around Vienna. I recommend hiking trips when the weather is good and museums otherwise. Most museums offer student discounts. cultural_challenges: I don't think cultural differences are that big

other_useful_info: These questions are very similar, I don't know what else to say

crucial_aspects: I wanted to achieve the perfect balance between academic challenges and having time to explore the culture surrounding my destination. It was very important for me that my exchange wouldn't only be about strengthening my academic abilities, but that I'd also have time to have fun, explore new things and gain other experiences.
overall_comments: It was an amazing experience overall. My only reason for not rating 10 is because of the general safety concerns surrounding New Orleans, which put a (small) dent in my overall experience. However, I think it is something everyone considering studying abroad in the US must take into account; the country is generally much less safe than Denmark.
info_ease: It was fairly easy. The university was very good at communicating what they needed from us, what we needed to do before arriving etc., and it also sent us reminders if some actions of crucial matter needed to be taken. However, the Tulane website is a bit difficult to navigate, but as an exchange student, we received all necessary information via e-mail from Tulane's international office. It was therefore not crucial to know the website in order to get information.
arrival_assistance: No assistance
arrival_comments: The introduction program ("Intro to US Law") offered during the fall semester is amazing. It gave us all the information we needed to enjoy our exchange stay, and prepared us for the semester. We learned basic matters regarding studying law in the US, how to do case reads, basic foundations in different legal areas and generally how to navigate Tulane etc. Furthermore, we also got to do different "touristy" things, which was really nice to do as a group. I'd strongly recommend to take the introduction program, even though it means leaving Denmark earlier. Because of this program, all of us internationals also grew closer and became friends, which was a relief as the start of the official semester could seem overwhelming.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was an amazing experience overall. My only reason for not rating 10 is because of the general safety concerns surrounding New Orleans, which put a (small) dent in my overall experience. However, I think it is something everyone considering studying abroad in the US must take into account; the country is generally much less safe than Denmark.
registration_process: When registering for classes, their system is a lot better than the one at UCPH. You basically create your own schedule, and can sign up for waiting lists if the classes are full. The system will tell you if your classes conflict (i.e., because of overlap etc.), and you can see how many students have registered for the class so far. The registration system is a bit difficult to navigate at first, because you have to learn how it works, but as soon as you've figured it out, it makes perfect sense and is super user-friendly. You don't "apply" for classes with priorities as you do at UCPH, instead you choose classes which have spots and register for up to 15 credits. You can add/drop classes up until 2 weeks after classes have started, which is really nice if you find out that there's a class you don't want to take, after you've had the introduction. Just beware of registering early for classes with few spots, as the waiting lists for popular classes can grow long. This is especially the case for seminars. Also beware of which type of exam the class will offer - if you're in doubt, contact Academic Services, they'll be happy to answer your questions.
registration_help: You could always e-mail either the international office or Academic Services with questions, and both were very quick to respond.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted, except for one seminar which I registered for too late.
registration_advice: Register as soon as the slot opens - make sure you've completed the immunization form before registration opens, otherwise you won't be able to register. Register for 15 credits, even though you only need 12, because you can always drop the remaining credits when you've gotten a better overview on which classes you want. Be aware of registering early for classes with few spots.
academics_comments: It was an amazing experience overall. My only reason for not rating 10 is because of the general safety concerns surrounding New Orleans, which put a (small) dent in my overall experience. However, I think it is something everyone considering studying abroad in the US must take into account; the country is generally much less safe than Denmark.
course_level: You can choose levels from 1L to 4L. I only had 4L which made it a lot more difficult, especially because I solely chose courses with legal areas I had no prior experience with. But that was my own choice. My friends who chose 1L courses had an easier schedule and workload.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is based off of the socratic method, meaning students are actively involved by using cold calling. However, the cold calling is used much more in 1L classes than higher class electives. The professors expect you to have read the cases, and be ready to present them and answer questions if you get called upon in class. Nonetheless, they're generally much nicer to exchange students, and will rarely cold call internationals unless half the class consists of internationals. I was only cold called a few times during my semester, and it was not done in a malicious way. I also had to present a case, but the professor told me beforehand, so I had plenty of time to prepare.
courses_enrolled: - Antitrust - International Commercial Arbitration - Criminal Ethics Advocacy Seminar - Insurance Law
recommended_courses: Professor Gabriel Feldman in Antitrust is a legend and made the course super fun and interesting! I'd also recommend doing a seminar, even though the workload gets heavy in the end because you have to do a paper of minimum 20 pages.
unexpected_costs: I didn't experience this, but some of the fellow internationals received expensive medical bills just by getting checked at the doctor's, even though they had insurance. If you choose the cheaper insurance (GeoBlue), regular visits to the doctor etc. will not necessarily be covered.
cost_comparison: Books were much more expensive than expected, even if you chose the "used rental"-option.
activities_available: There were a lot of different activities provided by Tulane, way too many to mention here. But download the app "Corq" and make sure to keep checking for events happening at the LBC, Rily Center etc., because there is so much stuff to do all the time. I remember the Global Café, Yoga & S'mores, free camping trips, rock climbing, workout classes at Rily, law bar reviews, free comedy nights, football games etc., just to mention a few. If you make sure to keep yourself updated, you can find something fun to do everyday.
activities_recommended: Do the law bar reviews, because they're fun. Sign up for some activities with the Rily Center, because you can access a lot of fun stuff for free that you wouldn't get the opportunity to do otherwise. If you have the time, sign up to a law society, such as the international law society.
weekend_recommendations: Travel, travel, travel! Take advantage of being in the US, and travel around as much as possible. I went to New York, Las Vegas, San Diego, Gulf Shores in Alabama and Florida, and I loved all of it.
culture_adjustment: It wasn't as difficult as I'd expected it to be, but the hardest thing was getting used to the safety repercussions. Coming from Denmark, it took a while to achieve a common sense on how to behave safely - either I acted too carefully, restricting myself more than necessary, or I acted too naïvely, thinking I could do the same things as back in Denmark.
socializing_tips: Yes, just be outgoing and seek them out, either during social events or classes. I befriended a few Americans because I sat next to them in my classes, but most of my friends were other international students. Most of the American students are very friendly and curious about where you're from etc.
cultural_challenges: Danish social culture is much more reserved in my opinion, which made it difficult to adjust to the outgoing, "in-your-face"-American social culture. It could feel intimidating and exhausting sometimes, coming from Denmark, but it didn't take much time to get used to, especially because everyone in New Orleans is very friendly. I ended up loving the smalltalk-culture, where people aren't afraid of talking to strangers in the supermarket etc. The hardest difference to get used to, was definitely the problem with safety etc., as I've explained further up in my report.
culture_appreciated: The fact that many people in New Orleans are extremely friendly and will help you out if you need it. They're also very direct, and if they find you annoying, you'll quickly sense it, which was kind of a relief because you didn't have to spend energy decoding social ques etc. In general, I loved how easy it was to talk to people and make friends, if you just pushed yourself out there and took the initiative.
top3_advice: 1) Be open! Even if there are things you don't think make sense, try to take it as a new experience. Don't be judgmental until you've tried something, and speak to people to find out where they come from regarding their point of views etc. In my opinion, the internationals who struggled the most during the semester, were the ones who refused to go outside their comfort zone and only befriended other Europeans, people from their own country etc. Try to say yes to as much as possible, even if you find it mentally exhausting. 2) Plan your travels early on, so you have an overview on when you'll be gone during the semester. Buy the flight tickets early, because the prices will rise faster than you think. In general, if you have a tight budget, try to spread it out evenly during your stay; you don't want to make yourself go into debt, but you'll also regret it if you say no to many experiences, because you wanted to save money. 3) Ask yourself how you want your semester to be (workload-wise) and choose classes based off of the answer. I loved my classes, but they were all upperlevel electives, which increased my workload substantially compared to some of my fellow students' workload.
other_useful_info: 1) Do not take the cheapest option regarding health insurance - take T-SHIP as it will cover you a lot better than GeoBlue. 2) Use your professor's office hours to talk to them about their course, especially if you're struggling. Most of them are happy to help you out and they generally encourage you to seek them out. 3) Many of the other internationals struggled with living with American roommates, because they're often younger and sometimes immature. In my experience, the people who lived with other internationals had a better experience than the ones who lived with Americans; problems such as what the AC should be set to, cleaning and noise habits often occured to those who lived with Americans. Many of the Americans studying at Tulane come from very (VERY!) wealthy families, and may therefore look at money, ressources etc. in a different way than yourself, which can be challenging.
most_rewarding: Everything, to be honest. I loved meeting other cultures and learning about how law works in other parts of the world, I loved learning about the American legal system, especially because it is pure common law and I especially loved the weather in New Orleans. In total, I think I had about 2,5 weeks where the temperature dropped below 20 degrees celcius - the rest of the time, it was warm with blue skies and sunshine, which I absolutely loved. Finally, I loved the friends I made, especially because we are now able to visit each other in different parts of the world.
greatest_challenge: Getting used to the difference in safety and academic levels. The safety issue has already been elaborated in the report, but regarding the academic levels, I would often feel a bit stupid during classes, if I didn't understand what was going on. However, you just need to accept the fact that you're new to the American system and it takes a while to adjust, which is ok. Again, the professors will gladly help you out, just make sure you go to them.
other_comments: If you're struggling with befriending people etc., please use the university's ressources. The university has A LOT of options which can help you out, and it's better to seek them out earlier than later. Remember, that the university is very wealthy, and you're not a burden if you use the ressources provided to you. If in doubt on who to contact, just contact the international office and they'll forward you to the relevant department.

crucial_aspects: Studying in an English speaking country, the placement in a culturally rich city, the courses offered by the school, the academic level at the school and the warm weather.
overall_comments: It was an amazing experience and I would definitely do it all over again. The area around the uptown campus where we lived was safe, but you had to be aware of safety measures when it was dark or when leaving the area surrounding the uptown campus. The university did inform us of this and taught us how to live in New Orleans. I didn't experience any crimes and neither did anyone i knew.
info_ease: We were sent several documents regarding the exchange. The university was always very quick at answering any questions. The documents necessary for applying for the visa came a bit late, so I had to apply as soon as they came.
arrival_assistance: I was enrolled in their intro course for exchange and LLM students, which started a month before the fall term. We received a lot of different assistance, such as practical measures (a tour of the campus, etc.), cultural experiences (a guided tour of the city, a field trip to the art museum, food, etc.) and information about the courses (setting up their exam software, how to get books, etc.).
arrival_comments: The orientation was very good and generally thorough. It was very clear that the university had a lot of resources, as it's a private university. I do wish that they had explained what the health care insurances covered.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was an amazing experience and I would definitely do it all over again. The area around the uptown campus where we lived was safe, but you had to be aware of safety measures when it was dark or when leaving the area surrounding the uptown campus. The university did inform us of this and taught us how to live in New Orleans. I didn't experience any crimes and neither did anyone i knew.
registration_process: The actual courses that were offered was not clear until getting access to Gibson. It was possible to read the course catalogue prior to that, but it consisted of courses that were only offered offered at certain times (e.g. only spring term, every third year, etc.), which was not clear. The system is different than at UCPH. Firstly, because securing a spot on a course can depend on how quick you are at registering. If you do not make it on the list while there are open spots you can apply to be on the waitlist. A lot of people change their courses, so it's very likely to get a course even when you're on the waitlist - unless it's a seminar, as they have fewer spots available. Secondly, there is an "add and drop period" in the first couple of weeks where you can try your courses and change them if you don't like them. This was nice, as you could get to learn the professors teaching method, the exam form, etc. It was not possible to find the exam form before the courses started. We were told early on that as a main rule international students get an extra 20 min for every hour of an exam, unless it's a 24 hour take home exam or a paper.
registration_help: The university was very accommodating. They were always quick to answer any questions. I know that at least two courses added spots, as there was students that couldn't get the course, but there was some instances where it was not possible to add spots (e.g. seminars).
registration_success: Two of the courses that I initially wanted were not available in the fall term. One of them were only available in the spring term and the other was only available every third year. There were a lot of other courses that I liked, so in the end I was very happy with my courses. The courses that i signed up for had a lot of available spots, so there was no issues with securing a spot.
registration_advice: Register as soon as you get access to Gibson. You can only register for a specific amount of credits, so prioritize to register for the courses that you really want or the ones with fewer available spots (e.g. seminars).
academics_comments: It was an amazing experience and I would definitely do it all over again. The area around the uptown campus where we lived was safe, but you had to be aware of safety measures when it was dark or when leaving the area surrounding the uptown campus. The university did inform us of this and taught us how to live in New Orleans. I didn't experience any crimes and neither did anyone i knew.
course_level: The level was much higher than I expected, but it was not as hard as at UCPH. The 1L courses generally seemed to be easier than the other courses. There was not as much pressure, as you only have to pass and it's generally easy to pass at the law school. They are not as harsh when grading as in UCPH, so the results are actually generally good. They generally try to give the exchange students as many points as possible.
teaching_comparison: The professors in the 1L courses used the Socratic method, where they would pick a random student in the beginning of the class and then only ask them questions during the rest of the class. No exchange students were called on in my 1L class, but I did hear that it happened in other classes. It can be a bit uncomfortable, but in the end it doesn't have any impact on your grade. In my other classes each student had to present a case throughout the term. The professors were very kind to the exchange students.
courses_enrolled: Intro to law of the US (2 credits) International commercial arbitration (3 credits) Admiralty I (3 credits) Torts (4 credits)
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed taking Intro to law of the US, as I got to know the other international students, had time to adjust the life in the US, got a very basic overview of US common law and got some cultural experiences. I could have fewer courses during the term, which I was really happy about. Although the course was a bit tiring, as we had class almost every day, class lasted for a lot of hours, we didn't get that many breaks and we got assigned readings every day. I took International commercial arbitration, as I wanted a course that was relevant to my future career. The course was somewhat difficult, as the class had a hard time following professor Force's teaching. I took Admiralty I, as Tulane is world renowned for their admiralty & maritime law program. It was a very difficult course and I would say that the level matches a course at UCPH. The course was very interesting and super rewarding when (finally) understanding it. I really enjoyed Professor Davies' teaching. Overall I'm really glad I took it, as it's made me aware of another field of law that is relevant in Denmark. Torts is a very interesting course, especially if you like Danish tort law. Professor Gajda was really good and she made class very entertaining. She's an expert in privacy and therefore had a privacy angle on torts, which was very interesting and refreshing. The class did not have as many readings as my other classes, but it was important to attend the classes. Overall I would recommend all of my courses.
unexpected_costs: I did not expect rental books from the university to be that expensive. I would recommend to buy or rent books from Amazon. You had to choose to get one of two health insurances through the university and it was not possible to waive either of these. It was very hard to understand what they actually covered, so I bought another Danish insurance which was a safe choice, and I'm glad I did it as the health insurance I chose didn't seem to cover much.
cost_comparison: The US Dollar was historically strong while I was there and inflation also became high at the same time, so everything was more expensive.
activities_available: There was a wide range of clubs and a lot of events. The law school had several events and a lot of resources. I really enjoyed the bar reviews, where the school rented out a bar a couple of times during the term, where you got drinks and food. There is a gym that is mandatory to pay for, but that entails the option of doing a lot of different group exercises. Something that stood out was homecoming week, where there was an event every day and a very fun football game at the end. There was also great events at Halloween.
activities_recommended: You should definitely go see one of the parades downtown. They are very unique and super fun. If you're there in the fall term, you should see "Krewe of Boo". If in the spring, then of course "Mardi Gras". But there are other parades! I would recommend watching some of the basketball and football games - both at the university and downtown. I really liked Frenchmen St, which had the most famous jazz bars and an art market during weekend evenings. In general I would recommend exploring as much of the culture as possible. I was there during August, where both "Red Dress Run" and "White Linen Night" took place downtown. That was two very unique and fun events, which were definitely some of the best evenings I had. I also recommend going on a weekend road trip to Pensacola, Florida or Gulf Shores, Alabama. It was very nice to be at the beach and you really see another part of the south.
weekend_recommendations: Watch a sports game. Go to Frenchmen St. Do a swamp tour. Take a walk in Audubon park and watch the sunset at the Fly on a Friday. Eat a Po' Boy and Beignets.
culture_adjustment: I experienced culture shock in the first couple of weeks, which I did not expect so it hit me very hard. It wore off after a bit of time, but it would have been easier to overcome if I had been prepared. I began focusing on the positive things, which there was a lot of. I thought about the negative things and tried to get a new understanding and perspective on the US system.
socializing_tips: Participate in the events that the school offers. The first year law students are generally more interested in talking with the internationals than the other years.
cultural_challenges: It was clear that there was some big differences between the university and the rest of New Orleans. The university has a lot of resources, which the rest of the city does not necessarily have.
culture_appreciated: The people were very open and friendly. It took some getting used to that people genuinely want to talk without having any ulterior motives.
top3_advice: Explore as much of New Orleans culture as possible, prioritize to plan trips and activities even when you get comfortable in a routine, and be safe.
other_useful_info: It was very warm outside almost all of the time, but the Americans love their AC so it was very cold inside. I would therefore recommend to bring light clothes and a sweater to wear inside. It's very cheap to buy a jacket at Goodwill if you need one. They don't have the best public transportation, but it's cheap. You can buy tickets through the app "RTA Le Pass". The bus is a bit shadier, but it's faster than the street car. The university also provides for some transportation. In the end i used Uber and Lyft a lot. I bought a bike in the beginning of the term and sold it at the end for almost the same price. I was very careful and only biked uptown, but it was nice to bike when doing grocery shopping.
most_rewarding: It's hard to choose: New Orleans culture, campus life, new good friends, exploring a new law system and travelling.
greatest_challenge: The US system when coming from the Danish system.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to study in the States and also try a destination i knew had a great culture life, a professional faculty and an environment different from what we have in Denmark.
overall_comments: My experience was amazing! The only reason it is a 9 instead of 10 is the cost of living in the States. Even though New Orleans is more affordable than NYC, San Fransisco etc., it is incredibly expensive to live in the States.
info_ease: The staff at Tulane University is extremely helpful and they provide a lot of helpful resources both before and after you arrive in New Orleans. Even though it is a good idea to start researching housing on your own (for example on Facebook groups), they will give you plenty of information about your entire stay.
arrival_assistance: They offer an introduction to US law, where they provide a lot of information other than only law lectures. I would highly recommend attending this introduction as you both get practical information, free trips around New Orleans and get to know a lot of other international students from all over the world studying law.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: My experience was amazing! The only reason it is a 9 instead of 10 is the cost of living in the States. Even though New Orleans is more affordable than NYC, San Fransisco etc., it is incredibly expensive to live in the States.
registration_process: Pretty accessible registration with helpful link provided from the host university.
registration_help: The university reaches out to the students and therefor you automatically get a person to contact. They are extremely fast at replying (when you consider the 7 hour time difference).
registration_success: I got all the courses I registered for.
registration_advice: Register for courses as soon as possible, especially if you want to register yourself on some of their popular seminars. Choose whatever courses seem interesting to you and try some of the courses that arent provided in copenhagen! I can highly recommend legal research and writing.
academics_comments: My experience was amazing! The only reason it is a 9 instead of 10 is the cost of living in the States. Even though New Orleans is more affordable than NYC, San Fransisco etc., it is incredibly expensive to live in the States.
course_level: The courses I took were either the same level of what we have at Copenhagen University or easier. You have more courses, I had 5, but each course is only around 2.5, 5 or 7.5 ECTS.
teaching_comparison: The course depends on the professor. For example, even though several are three torts classes, every class can differ because of the professor. Even how the exam is (open book/closed book) can differ. In general 2L or 3L courses have a more "laid back" vibe, where the professors dont cold call the students as much.
courses_enrolled: Intro to Law of the US – 2 credits International Human Rights Law – 3 credits Constitutional Criminal Procedure: Investigation – 3 credits Space Law: International Treaties and Jurisdiction – 1 credits Legal Reasoning, Research and Writing for LLM Students – 3 credits
recommended_courses: Intro to Law of the US: Again, I HIGHLY recommend every exchange student to take this course. Time consuming for around 3-4 weeks, but you learn all the basics of the US system. Legal Reasoning, Research and Writing for LLM Students: a time consuming course at times, but a course that teach you how to research US Law. A very valuable course! Space Law: International Treaties and Jurisdiction: Super interesting area of law! Tulane University wish to be a front runner in this area in the future.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Fresh produce and food in super markets in general. The cost was around double of what i pay in copenhagen when i go to the supermarket.
activities_available: A lot of cultural, athletic and social activities available. More than you would ever be able to attend to during your stay. There is always something to do, both on and off campus at Tulane University! You will get a Tulane mail, where they will inform you about a lot of the events.
activities_recommended: I can highly recommend attending to the sports events or any event involved with New Orleans culinary.
weekend_recommendations: Go downtown to explore the city during the weekend in the day time, and Bourbon street in the night time. Get food and go for shopping at Magazine St. Try the steam boat. See the cementaries. Go explore the city by the tram. Attend every carnival if possible! If you have the time, fly to areas in the States with their famous national parks. Zion national park and Grand Canyon are amazing!
culture_adjustment: You will adjust in no time. I have never in my life met such sweet and loving people. Southern state sweetness is definitely a thing!
socializing_tips: Try find housing with American students if you wish to socialize with other than international students.
cultural_challenges: Americans are very sweet and outgoing. But talking about politics is not a go to if you do not know the person. In Denmark this is usually not too sensitive, but it can be in the States.
culture_appreciated: How sweet and caring people from New Orleans are. They truley care for you and they are so very proud people are visiting!
top3_advice: Plan out what you want from your stay. Do you really wanna put a lot oof effort into every class and experience how the library vibes are? Do you wanna deep dive into the New Orleans culture and visit all of the famous and hidden gems? Doo you want to network and attend every social event? It can be difficult to check off everything you want to do at your stay, so I would recommend future exchange students to be intentional about what they wish to get from their stay.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: To get an insight into the American legal system and to experience how it is to study and have an everyday life in the States. Also, I have met incredible people along the way!
greatest_challenge: To relax and not stress about everything i wanted with my stay. You have either 4 or 5 months, you will have time to do what you want to do.

crucial_aspects: That it was an English speaking country.
info_ease: The university supplied us with a lot of information. It was actually almost too much information because it some times made it more confusing and stressfull to navigate in all the information and different deadlines.
arrival_assistance: The university took very good care of us when we arrived. The communication was good - it was easy to get in touch with the orientation staff, and they were very helpful and accommodating.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was a very old system, and you had to complete an immunization form and get the university's approval of the form before you could register for courses. This process put you in risk of not getting the courses you wanted/get waitlisted.
registration_help: A very long course material.
registration_success: I did not get the approval of immunization before the registration opened, so I got waitlisted on almost all the courses that I wanted. But in the end I did get most of the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure you have the approval of the immunization form (if required) before the registration opens.
course_level: I did take both first year courses and three year courses. The level was moderate to difficult, but I think it depends on what courses you take - especially whether it is a completely new course for you or if you have taken a similar course in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: The lectures are similar, but the professors cold call the students a lot more at the host institution.
courses_enrolled: Torts, Corporate Finance and Legal Profession
recommended_courses: I liked Torts - I had a good professor that made the classes fun and interesting. It was also interesting to compare the US tort system with the Danish.
unexpected_costs: Transportation costs. If you don't have a car you will use Uber/Lyft a lot.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: Everything you could imagine - fitness center, swimming activities, pool, volleyball, basketball, american football, outdoor adventures, etc.
activities_recommended: Go cheer on the university's sports teams - it is a fun and authentic american collage experience.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city you live in and travel around the states.
culture_adjustment: It was fine, but there are a lot of cultural differences that you have to meet with an open mind.
socializing_tips: If you want to socialize with local students you must be the one taking the initiative.
cultural_challenges: That it isn't safe to walk around in the evening/night because of high crime rates and gun policies in the US.
culture_appreciated: That people are fun and straightforward to strangers - that is very different from how it is in Denmark.
top3_advice: 1) take advantage of the Professors and the staff - they are much more likely to help you than the KU staff. 2) meet the culture with an open mind. 3) make a list of all the deadlines to make sure you don't miss any of them.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: The academic experience.
greatest_challenge: Definitely to adapt into the new culture both socially and privately, but it has been an interesting challenge, and I have acquired a lot of personal experience.

crucial_aspects: Most crucial to me was the cultural aspect. I've always wanted to experience what it is like to go to college in America and I really wanted to explore the southern part of the country which was where I spent my time abroad.
overall_comments: Getting the full American college experience was maybe one of the best decisions I've ever made. Everything from football, frat parties, college bars and basically living on campus was so much fun. Highly recommend.
info_ease: It was very easy to find the information I needed to know before arrival. My host institution was incredibly helpful and sent out formulas that needed to be filled out and other information by email so us international students were kept informed. If I had questions or other inquiries we could email the correct department at the host institution which also was really helpful.
arrival_assistance: I didn't get any assistance when I arrived since everything was handled before arriving.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Getting the full American college experience was maybe one of the best decisions I've ever made. Everything from football, frat parties, college bars and basically living on campus was so much fun. Highly recommend.
registration_process: The host institution emailed us when it was time to register at the university. The whole registration was very easy since you basically just have to provide them with information you already are in possession of. The whole registration at the host institution took maybe 5 minutes.
registration_help: You could email the international department if you had any questions. They answered quite quickly and gave helpful advice.
registration_success: I got every class I signed up for. Be sure to register for classes as soon as class registration opens up in order not to be waitlisted an possible miss out on a class.
registration_advice: Nothing really - it is quite self explanatory and easy to do once you have been granted a place at the host institution by UCPH.
academics_comments: Getting the full American college experience was maybe one of the best decisions I've ever made. Everything from football, frat parties, college bars and basically living on campus was so much fun. Highly recommend.
course_level: The general level seemed to be a bit easier than the one at UCPH. The level of the courses were also incredibly dependent on the individual professor with some being more chill and others being more uptight. However, they all expected that students come prepared for class but it was very different how many questions and the level of questions they would ask. But all classes were very doable by following along in class and reading the material for each class.
teaching_comparison: They used cold calling which is quite a difference from UCPH. Again, the professors would have a different approach to cold calling with some requiring each student to answer at least one question in class and others only picking on volunteers. The teaching style was also way more dependent on student interaction and discussion. Classes were way more engaging if people volunteered and the teaching style was based on student discussion on both cases and hypotheticals.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to the Law of the US, Intellectual Property, Business Enterprises, and Trusts and Estates.
recommended_courses: Business Enterprises with professor Batlan was incredibly insightful in regards to US business law. The class covered the different types of companies and also drew upon law from torts. Even as internationals, many of the principles we have learned in a non-common law country was useful so you wouldn't feel lost if you haven't taken common law classes before. The class was primarily based on cases which would be discussed in class. Come prepared to class - otherwise you will not have a good time when being cold called since she was very concerned about the factual circumstances of the cases.
unexpected_costs: The insurance provided by the school. It is not mandatory but highly encouraged. However, it was very expensive and it is better to be safe than sorry.
cost_comparison: Course books were incredibly expensive with some being around $300. Also, food on campus was quite expensive if you were to buy from the shops. You could buy cheaper food other places on campus but it wouldn't be as good.
activities_available: My host institution is known for being a big party school so there was many frat parties and general parties going on in the weekends. However, you must know somebody in order to get into the frat parties. The university also have a football team which is doing pretty good so going to games on weekends is a must and part of the whole college experience (10/10 fun). The university had a fully equipped gym with basketball courts, swimming pool, weight lifting room, crossfit rooms, squash courts, and everything else a proper gym needs to have which is free to all students. The university would also arrange different "festivals" or get togethers during the semester. You could also join things like the soccer team if you wanted to.
activities_recommended: Definitely the college football games. Stand in the student section (which is almost always full) and enjoy the atmosphere and cheap drinks. Pre-game at a day-party at a frat and hit The Boot or Palms after the game = full college experience.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend going out on the weekends and talk to the other American students and other internationals. On holidays (and weekends) I would recommend going on a roadtrip to either Texas or Miami since it is a rather short drive. Otherwise, fly to other places and see other parts of the country while there.
culture_adjustment: Incredibly easy. The environment is very international-friendly and many of the American students come from other states which makes everybody non-native to the local culture. The local culture was also very easy to adapt to since it is a very friendly place if you don't go the wrong places.
socializing_tips: Embrace being international. They love talking to Europeans and many of them have been to Europe themselves on either holiday or exchange. It is a nice ice-breaker and then you can go on from there.
cultural_challenges: That you need a car to basically do anything. Luckily, the off campus housing available is very close to campus (10 minute walk for most) but a car is almost need for everything outside of the campus area (except going downtown with the streetcar). Heavily dependent on Ubers.
culture_appreciated: How open the locals were. It is very easy making conversation with randoms both when you are on a night out but also just in a restaurant or grocery shopping.
top3_advice: 1: Be prepared to be social. You will have a way more fun time if you make decent connections in the first weeks which can lead to other relationships with Americans who can show you the "real" way of going to college. 2: Make an experience of everything. Whether you go to a football game, a rodeo, drinking downtown, or staying on campus, then see the whole thing as an experience. It is so different from Denmark and a major change of scenery which makes you appreciate being in another country and culture way more. Everything is basically entertainment, so be sure to enjoy it. 3: Be aware of your surroundings. It is not as safe as Denmark which the university also emphasizes when there. However, I never saw anything super unsettling or heard anything happen around campus, but it is recommended to stay more alert than back home in Europe.
other_useful_info: Pack clothes for every season. It can be super hot and humid but also quite cold during winter. Other than that just use your common sense and you'll be more than fine.
most_rewarding: Knowing that I can move to a different country, culture, school system and make it work out. Now I know that I'm able to go somewhere I've never been and make incredible memories, meet friends from all over the world, and have the time of my life while also doing a bit of studying.
greatest_challenge: Feeling like I had to do something every weekend in order to get the most out of my time abroad. I had to remind myself that taking a weekend off to chill by myself was cool which was a little hard if you suffer from FOMO and have many connections with both the Americans and other internationals. However, taking time off was crucial since the whole experience can be somewhat overwhelming if you feel like you have to be out and about during the weekdays and the weekend.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study in USA and especially California. I wanted to study a place with warmer weather.
info_ease: In general, it was easy. There was some difficulties with signing up for courses and waitlists on courses, but it worked out and the university helped us.
arrival_assistance: Assistance regarding visa rules, safety, the university facilities.
arrival_comments: They could have given us more social orientation. We only had one day, which was very packed with a lot of information. They could have given us more time to just get to know the other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Exchange students were the very last to sign up for courses after the LLM students and JD students. This meant that almost all courses had waitlists when we could sign up which was stressful. I had to apply for pre approval for more courses just to be sure. Students could sign up for way more credits than needed, so I had the impression that maybe people had a lot of back up plans, which just made a lot of waitlists. But it ended up being fine.
registration_help: The university was very helpful both when we arrived and when I had questions regarding the courses for my pre approval. We had a one on one meeting where we looked at our schedule. It was also possible for the university to make an extra spot for en exchange if the class was full.
registration_success: See above regarding the waitlists. But I ended up getting 3 out of 4 of the courses I had looked at, and the last I had to find after I arrived and get a new pre approval for.
registration_advice: We talked with the university about the waitlist situation, so maybe they will change it. But otherwise let the future exchange student know about the waitlist, so it is not as stressful for them.
course_level: It took two classes with first year students, and two classes with second and third years. The level was easy in all classes. Especially with the first years, they took it from scratch because it was the students' first year of law school.
teaching_comparison: First, attendance is required in all courses. Second, participation is required in most classes. They use cold calling, where the professor just pick a random from the class to answer or explain a case.
courses_enrolled: Contracts, torts, international human rights, and real estate transactions.
recommended_courses: It would recommend all of them. Contracts and torts are basic and general American law, and it gives a good perspective on the American law. I enjoyed comparing it to what I have learned from my danish courses. International human rights is relevant because it mostly is also applicable for Denmark, and it is relatable. Regarding real estate transaction, it was good to learn the concepts of real estate and the measurements (more economic also), but a big part of it was regarding what company should be chosen for different structures and tax law, which is not that important and relevant for an exchange student to know. But the professor in the class was very nice.
unexpected_costs: Be aware that there is fees on everything. There is a very high tipping culture of 15-20 %. I had my Danish insurance approved. But if they had not approved it, I would have had to pay 16.000 DKK for the American insurance.
cost_comparison: Eating out was way more expensive than I expected. Even before the taxes and tips, it was more expensive that in Denmark. I did not find grocery shopping as expensive as I expected. I knew that housing was very expensive.
activities_available: It was mostly associations either regarding a specific legal area or regarding your ethnicity.
activities_recommended: Every second Thursday, there was beers and pizza in the quad. I would recommend going to that.
weekend_recommendations: San Francisco has a lot of different neighborhoods to explore. There is a lot to do just in the city. It is a city with shopping, cafes, restaurants, but it also has beautiful nature and the sea. Some weekends we also visited other parts of California. I have been to Lake Tahoe, Yosemite, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Santa Barbara and other coastal cities.
culture_adjustment: In general, it was fine.
socializing_tips: It was a bit difficult to socialize with local students. I socialized the most with the local students in the class where I was the only exchange student. I think it would have been easier if I had lived on campus.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: People are very friendly and out going.
top3_advice: It is very expensive, especially housing. We were only 7 exchange students, which in the beginning was a bit disappointing, but we found out there was around 30 LLM students from other countries, who were in our age also. San Francisco has a reputation for being a bit dangerous city. The university is in the worst area with a lot homeless people and drugs. This is relevant when considering living on campus. I lived off campus in a very nice neighborhood, and I had no problems with the area the university was in, but I would not walk in the area after dark.
other_useful_info: When looking for housing off campus, use airbnb (and maybe get a deal outside airbnb), Craigslist and use the facebook groups.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of the exchange is meeting a lot of new friends from different parts of especially Europe. Since we were not that many exchange students, we really got to know each other and spent a lot of time together.
greatest_challenge: Finding housing off campus.
other_comments: It was a very great semester abroad, and I really recommend going! San Francisco is a very nice city to stay in, and there is a lot of other things to experience in other parts on California. The weather is very nice especially in the fall.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere where the society was different from what I was used to at home in Denmark, and which also offered good educational and career opportunities. San Francisco in the US seemed to be the perfect place to pursue these goals.
overall_comments: San Francisco was everything I had dreamed of. However, be aware that since the society is so different from what you're used to back home, it may require a period of adjustment before you feel comfortable in it.
info_ease: It was very easy. The University of Copenhagen as well as the university in San Francisco, UC Law SF, had good guides and if I had any questions, I could contact them.
arrival_assistance: We had an introduction day before the semester started, where we were presented with everything we needed and were given contact information for all the relevant people.
arrival_comments: Initially, we were given a lot of information and it seemed like we could easily contact them and get further information. However, it was relatively difficult to get answers to questions from them afterwards. I experienced several times that I was ignored.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: San Francisco was everything I had dreamed of. However, be aware that since the society is so different from what you're used to back home, it may require a period of adjustment before you feel comfortable in it.
registration_process: You must first send a motivated application. If this is accepted (in all likelihood it will be, as it is only formal that you have to send a motivated application), then you need to apply for a visa. In the visa process, you must first prove to the university that you have sufficient funds to complete your stay. When I went on exchange, the amount was 130,000 DKK. If you can prove this, the university will give you an application form to apply for a visa. (The visa process is long). If you get the visa, then you need to get ready to be a student at the university, where you need to send a picture for your student card, fill out some information, and pay for student fees.
registration_help: Guides and the possibility to contact the university.
registration_success: I went in the spring. Around November it was possible to choose courses. They have an online portal where you can see how many places are available and sign up for the course if you want to. So you don't send an application about which courses you want and wait for a response. You have the option to change courses right up until the 2nd week of the semester. In the first week of the semester, you can try out the courses you've chosen and see if it's for you, and if not, switch to another class.
registration_advice: Take it easy. You'll get in and do well. Everyone else has done it, so you can too. As for the courses, you will most likely end up getting the courses you want, so just wait for someone to unsubscribe from the course you want.
academics_comments: San Francisco was everything I had dreamed of. However, be aware that since the society is so different from what you're used to back home, it may require a period of adjustment before you feel comfortable in it.
course_level: The level is neither lower nor higher than in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: It's a lot of dialog rather than monologue. The teachers expect you to be much more prepared for the classes than in Denmark, so that you can participate actively, possibly by forcing you, as they cold-call you - it's not as bad as it may sound.
courses_enrolled: I had Criminal Law, Negotiation, Entertainment Law, and Statutory: Intellectual Property.
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend the courses that I have taken. I don't know much about the other courses, so I can't comment on them.
unexpected_costs: Although it's free to study at the school, you will have to pay 5000 DKK in tuition fees. In addition, the university requires you to use their insurance, which costs 25,000 DKK. You can apply to use your own insurance instead. You'll most likely be rejected the first few times, after which you can contact the university (and not the insurance company) and ask them to help you. I just used Gouda.
cost_comparison: Everything is much more expensive in the US. Even when you just go to the supermarket, a packet of butter costs at least 3-4 times the price in Denmark.
activities_available: No sporting activities... They had a lot of clubs for people who come from certain places or follow certain beliefs, for example, a club for people from the Middle East, a club for Asians. On top of that, they had associations for people with similar interests, for example, an association for people who like gaming.
activities_recommended: I would recommend finding a club that's right for you. There is no one club that all people like. You need to find the club that you can reflect yourself in. Clubs are great for meeting new people.
weekend_recommendations: In San Francisco I would recommend seeing the Golden Gate Bridge, Alcatraz, Exploratorium, China Town, Golden Gate Park, see a baseball game, see a basketball game. Hit the club on Monroe or Westwood and have a beer at Vesuvio Cafe. Relax in Golden Gate Park or Salesforce park. Go shopping on Haight Street. Mexican food in the Mission District. Sushi in Japan Town. Play tennis at Lafayette Park. Close to San Francisco I would recommend going to Big Sur (great nature), Yosemite National Park (great nature), Monterey (small cozy town), Santa Cruz (cool surfer town). Silicon Valley and see the headquarters of some of the world's biggest companies such as Apple and Google, or experience NASA or Stanford university. I wouldn't recommend Oakland (lots of crime) (but go if you want to see Berkeley University, which is relatively close to Oakland) and Sacramento (boring city with no life). Places you can travel to I would recommend Los Angeles, Las Vegas (flights are only $100 round trip!!!) and Hawaii. If you have a little more money to spend, I'd recommend heading to the East Coast, specifically Miami (especially on Spring Break)
culture_adjustment: The culture was different, but since it was the same language and Americans are sweet people, it was relatively easy.
socializing_tips: Join some university clubs. Sign up for some sport. Go out to a club or bar. Go to Sjømannskirken, which is a Norwegian church but is a meeting point for all Scandinavians.
cultural_challenges: They don't party until 5 am. All clubs and bars close at 2 am.
culture_appreciated: How open and welcoming Americans are.
top3_advice: Try to get out of your comfort zone and talk to people who are not from Denmark (if there are any), have fun, spend money like there is no tomorrow
other_useful_info: I think I've said everything I needed to say.
