unexpected_costs: Nothing
cost_comparison: Produce was very expensive, the rest very similar to copenhagen
activities_available: There is TSI, the student sport organiaztion where you can try a lot of different sports like sea-kayaking or cross country skiing. The uni has a lot of social clubs like board game club and the city in general is very catered towards students and stiudent-friendly activities.
activities_recommended: There are polar night morining cafes with free cofee and UV lamps which is really helpful to keep to your routine in the dark months.
weekend_recommendations: There are a lot of outdoor activities that you can do like hiking, kayaking, cross-country skiing. A lot of hiking is accessible per public transport. You can get a memebership to sleep in outdoor cabins which is super nice for weekend trips. And there is Turbo/BUA, where you can rent outdoor equipment for free and you only need to get a norwegian number
culture_adjustment: Easy, very similiar to Denmark.
socializing_tips: The sports clubs and activities are a good opportunity to meet local students.
cultural_challenges: Nothing
culture_appreciated: The fun in outdoor activities and learning about sámi culture
top3_advice: Be sure to have a good routine during polar night and use the few hours of light to be outside, I did not have a lot of lectures but rather a lot of individual readings so find a good study group, do a lot of hiking or other outdoor activities
other_useful_info: Definetlely call the student housing organisation to have a better chance. I think it is always easier in the spring semester but in the winter semester it can be really tough.

greatest_challenge: The short days and exams during polar night

institution: UiT The Arctic University of Norway
crucial_aspects: Given that I had already been on an exchange in Europe (Milan) on my Bachelor's, and that my first choice of going to Asia was rejected, I wanted something new, different, and "exotic." This is where I saw a great match with the Arctic
overall_comments: The place I lived in and the roomies I had played a crucial role in making the experience great! I was not impressed by the university level
info_ease: Relatively easy - Yet, the I was unimpressed by the help I got from a specific contact person from UiT (Mustta). I heard from several other students that this person had not cooperated very well and not answered the questions we forwarded. Ultimately, this led to me feeling limited in my choice of courses, because this person made it sound like I could not choose other courses - which was not true.
arrival_assistance: ESN intro days
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The place I lived in and the roomies I had played a crucial role in making the experience great! I was not impressed by the university level
registration_process: I don't recall the details...You're first accepted by the host university. Then you choose the courses you would like to attend. This is where I had many problems, and got very little help from Mussta, which made the whole registration process a mess. This ultimately led to not change my OLA, as I knew that it would be another round of mess, if I had to change it. Finally, once courses are apporved and OLA is signed, you are good.
registration_help: ESN coordinator via email - very bad.
registration_success: Not very good. To UiT's defence, the university in Tromsø is not ideal for an economist student - on the other hand, you get the opportunity to enroll in classes you normally wouldn't have, giving you new perspectives, which can benefit you as an economist.
registration_advice: Be open to other classes than specifically those related to your studies. I ended up having three courses on Arctic Norway, stretching from culture, to history, to politics. Although I was not impressed by the workload or level, I still learned surprisingly much in each.
academics_comments: The place I lived in and the roomies I had played a crucial role in making the experience great! I was not impressed by the university level
course_level: Arctic Norway - Aspects of (1) Culture, (2) History, (3) Politics, international relations and governance. These were the three courses I had, all BA level. Not impressed by the level nor the structure, yet I still managed to gain knowledge I didn't have before.
teaching_comparison: Unstructured, very limited workload, no one answer but more reflective answers allowed.
courses_enrolled: Arctic Norway - Aspects of (1) Culture, (2) History, (3) Politics, international relations and governance
recommended_courses: If you are interested in the Arctic, I can recommend the history and politics course. But I would also look into other courses that may cover the Arctic in more depth at a higher level.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: First times shopping in the supermarket, you are surprised by the prices...but you gradually adjust your purchasing behaviour and look for discounts. I was told that alcohol is expensive, but was still surprised to experience it myself. Beware that supermarkets stop selling "light" alcohol after 18:00 in the evening on weekdays and 17:00 on saturdays, and I think it's the same for strong alcohol in Vinmonopolet (Norwegian liquor stores). Supermarkets are closed on Sundays.
activities_available: A lot of different activities - football, diving, paddling, ...
activities_recommended: Kayaking + football
weekend_recommendations: Nature is veeery accessible near Tromsø - you can literally take a bus to the spot you are hiking or skitouring/randonee from. Most of the peaks you see and are interested in summitting, you can access. Of course, always check with locals, maps, etc. before for your own and others' safety. If you are up for cabin trips, you should get hold of a DNT key. This is the "master key" to all nearby DNT cabins in the nature. Remember to clean up after yourself and pay for your stay - it is all about trust. Other activities include going to Tromsø Badet, Pust sauna, Telegrafbukta to swim during summer (or winter if you dare), and Tromsø city.
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Participate in the first ESN activities and trips, participate in sports, etc.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: Trust society
top3_advice: 1) Go for the adventure 2) Take advantage of free waffles on Fridays 3) Beware of the darkness that will hit you in November if you go in the autumn semester
other_useful_info: To cope with the darkness, you can borrow artificial sunlight lamps that will do the trick to keep you energised
most_rewarding: Access to nature and roommates - I was able to combine the two, by accessing nature on skis with my roommates, experiencing northern lights as we ascended a peak...magical
greatest_challenge: I had very little uni during my stay, therefore it was actually the hardest to accept that I didn't have much to do, and be creative with my time in the High North.

institution: UiT The Arctic University of Norway
crucial_aspects: A new place which motitaves my studies within an Arctic envoriement.
info_ease: Yes, at UiT in Tromsø they had a very well-prepared welcome for the students and all our questions.
arrival_assistance: I had to talk with the 'Studies of Fisheries' which is the Faculty for Biotechnology, regarding what coueses i could chose. They were very helpfull!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Very simple: we gathered in a line at orientation, organized after first letter of first name, and then sorted by different demands by our home universities (fx. i needed a 'stamp' to register my exchange)
registration_help: lots of helt and guides.
registration_success: Unfortuneatly i was not able to register to the Master-courses i wished before my exchange. The have rules that no Bachelors can take Master-courses.
registration_advice: Dont plan on getting into any master courses at Uit! (haha) But they are super helpfull to find other courses for you.
course_level: The level was OK - a bit lower than what i am used to in DK.
teaching_comparison: Overall same style - but a lot more 'freetime' and not as high demands
recommended_courses: BIO-2606 and KJE-2004 makes perfect sense for a Biotech student. the Last one can be based on interests.
unexpected_costs: Lots of trips!
cost_comparison: Basic groceries in Northern Norway are quite expensive...
activities_available: Lots of clubs and cozy times! i took part in the student choire, the knitting club and there was a training facility as well.
activities_recommended: All the ones i tried.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Lofoten, Senja, Sommeroye and all the other amazing mountains you can see in Troms:)
culture_adjustment: Easy - the norwegians reminds of us in many ways. Maybe they are a bit more shy, so dont be afraid to speak first.
socializing_tips: Go for it! Try Norwgian and be prepared to switch in between Danish and English in the beginning
cultural_challenges: They take things a bit more relaxed and enjoy simple things like baking and going on trips - join thair lifestyle:)
culture_appreciated: The 'taking things as they come' - helps a lot when you might be a bit stressed from home
top3_advice: Take all the possibilities you can. Dont stress too much on getting freinds - everyone are equally stressed but just join the events and find your people.
other_useful_info: Denmark is also super expensive: maybe having a job during exhange could be a good idea
most_rewarding: the trips - i went to the mountains most of my free weekends and it was amazing.
greatest_challenge: I had to go to the hospital. they were super helpfull, and the general experience was good. But it impacted my exchange a bit unfortuneatly.

institution: UiT The Arctic University of Norway
crucial_aspects: Academically I am specifically interested in The Nordic and Arctic region in terms of security. Thus, UiT The Arctic University of Norway was a perfect choice.
overall_comments: Socially and regionally found it to be very giving and exciting. The academic level felt a bit lower than what I am used to at home,.
info_ease: It was a bit of a long process, but I assume that is to be expected. Both UiT and KU were fairly helpful in sharing information and assisting in confusion.
arrival_assistance: None really. Apart from introduction meetings about the university in general. I had already found housing when I arrived and had been in contact with my study advisor about various communal activities for my partner, who came along with me and our baby.
arrival_comments: The orientation itself could have been more informative, but it did not affect my situation a lot since I had researched and figured out a lot of things at home prior to arrival. Apart from this, there was not a lot of social erasmus gatherings at the university either. We were several students who talked about this - there were events for erasmus students held other places both in public and in private, but not very many gatherings AT the university.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Socially and regionally found it to be very giving and exciting. The academic level felt a bit lower than what I am used to at home,.
registration_process: At first, it took some time understanding the concept of choosing a "package" of courses. But once I figured it out, it was an easy process and it was quickly accepted, since all timetables for the courses were already planned out in advance. I simply followed an already-set semester structure.
registration_help: Online webinars and emails prior to the arrival. There was no phone number to call which - at one point in the process - was frustrating, because the responding time on emails was long at times.
registration_success: Successful, since I was quickly accepted for the package semester deal, I applied for.
registration_advice: Take your time to carefully choose and consider if they overlap in exam periods. If possible in any way, I would definitely consider choosing a package semester deal, since it makes it easier for you work and time wise. Another benefit of this is also, that you follow the same group of people for the whole semester, which is really nice socially.
academics_comments: Socially and regionally found it to be very giving and exciting. The academic level felt a bit lower than what I am used to at home,.
course_level: I had two courses in total. One big 20-ects course and one smaller 10-ects class. The big one was a bit dissappointing in its academic level. We had constant changes in teachers and thus teaching methods. Although this can also have benefits, it also contributed to a lot of confusion for the students. Many of the teachers' learning outcomes did not correspond. The subjects and themes interested me a whole lot, but the teaching methods and the teachers made it difficult. Some teachers' (low) level of english pronounciation also made it difficult to follow along at times.

unexpected_costs: Expensive groceries and expensive tourist bookings. I don't know if this was unexpected, but it is important to keep in mind. Especially groceries is important to budget.

activities_recommended: Since I did not join a sports team, I can't recommend that. But my partner played at the ice hockey team, and had a great experience with that. On the other hand I can really recommend joining the choir, if one is into singing.

socializing_tips: Trying to learn just a few basic sentences in Norwegian and being curious. Another thing is to join a local sports team, since this can give you the opportunity to get to know locals.
cultural_challenges: None really. There were indeed small differences in culture than from what I am used to - but none that I found challenging as a Dane.
culture_appreciated: Friendlyness and the open-minded attitude. We met so many nice local people, who gave us recommendations and tips for living in the cold.
top3_advice: Be into outdoor activities Bring suitable clothes for the weather Engage with the local community

crucial_aspects: The subjects offered by the university and the career path I have chosen as of now match.
overall_comments: Culturally very different academic wise which was interesting but also hard to adjust to. All of the exams were closed book exams, which meant no notes or any means of help. It is very much focused on memory and not so much logically applying law as in KU. It made sense for the subjects like Contemporary history, not so much for international private/public law.
info_ease: 5/10, it was quite a journey to find the correct information and all of us were very confused. Their introduction was a waste of time, as it was only meant for the Spanish students and did not once mention anything about exchange students. Also it was in spanish so only like 2 of the exchange students understood anything (which was irrelevant anyways as it was all directed towards the spanish students).
arrival_assistance: The assistant teacher joined our whatsapp group and helped with most information which was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Culturally very different academic wise which was interesting but also hard to adjust to. All of the exams were closed book exams, which meant no notes or any means of help. It is very much focused on memory and not so much logically applying law as in KU. It made sense for the subjects like Contemporary history, not so much for international private/public law.
registration_process: Oh my, it is a gruelling process. You first have to navigate through their website which by the way is a maze. Once you reach the folder offering academic courses, half of them are not available. 25% of them are in Spanish only and considering you have to make your own schedule with 5 subjects of 6 ECTS each, it is near impossible to figure out as you also have to beware of overlapping classes. I ended up after over 20 hours of struggling with matching a schedule. It was one where I had to go to class at 8-10 am and then again at 1-3 pm every day. They have placed every class taught in english between 1 and 7 pm which makes it even tougher.
registration_help: We were able to enter Excellencia classes because of the impossibility of making a schedule otherwise.
registration_success: I did not get every class I wished for but in the end, I was successful registering for 5 classes with no overlaps.
registration_advice: Be prepared to spend a lot of time creating a schedule with classes you may have regrets about. Fortunately it is possible for the first 2 weeks to try out different classes to see which ones you enjoy. The unfortunate part is that you miss 2 weeks of classes in the end for the ones you choose as you won't have time for all of them and miss the introductions/first lectures.
academics_comments: Culturally very different academic wise which was interesting but also hard to adjust to. All of the exams were closed book exams, which meant no notes or any means of help. It is very much focused on memory and not so much logically applying law as in KU. It made sense for the subjects like Contemporary history, not so much for international private/public law.
course_level: The requirements to pass are definitely lower standard than UCPH. It does not take that much effort to pass the course as long as you follow the classes. The classes are the syllabus, you do not get any books and the professors make the exams.
teaching_comparison: I liked some of the classes' way of teaching, especially international public law and keys to contemporary history. It takes some time getting used to the teachers' Spanglish decyphering what they say at times. It felt a lot like highschool with mandatory attendance and the way of grading was different. The grade is divided from 100% into sections where a group project counts for 10%, activity in class for 10%, partial exams for 20%, essays/assignments for 10% and the final exam for 50%. I did enjoy the fact that the grade is a pass/fail and does not account for whether you get 100% or 50%, as long as you are above 50%, you pass.
courses_enrolled: Keys to contemporary history, Roman law, Private international law, Public international law, UN and other international organizations.
recommended_courses: Keys to contemporary history was easy, as it is litterally just history dating from the declaration of independence in the US to the Cold war. Public international law was great because of Allan's teaching style, which i truly enjoyed a lot. If a subject is taught by Allan Tatham, you can rest assured that it'll be fun.
unexpected_costs: I enjoyed using Freenow (Taxi service) quite a bit as it is pretty cheap. It is important to remember to get a personal travelcard which you pay 20 euro for per month to use the metro/bus/etc. This can be done through CityLife online or in a person in Madrid.
cost_comparison: Pretty much everything is cheaper than in Denmark.
activities_available: No idea.
activities_recommended: Definitely going out and being a part of the culture and make friends. Try using one of the whatsapp/facebook groups for activities. Or you could try something completely different, personally I started learning Bachata Sensual which was a great experience and I enjoyed it a lot and met many people.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely explore other cities such as Barcelona for the tourist attractions and the gothic architecture. I would recommend the walking tours. You could visit Málaga for the beach vibe. Valencia was great as it is the origin city of Paella, so that is a must (also try Horchata in the Santa Catalina Horchataria).
culture_adjustment: It is a pretty relaxed culture where nobody is in a hurry. It is normal to be late which is quite difficult to adjust to as a Dane.
socializing_tips: Definitely make an effort and ask if they are down to do anything or go out. Most of the spanish students just interact with eachother and it can be tough if you are not an extrovert.
cultural_challenges: The Spaniards being late to everything. I just cannot.
culture_appreciated: The people were super friendly and it is a very collectivistic culture in contrast to the danish individualistic one. An example is that people strike up a conversation in public transport and sit next to you with no problem, which is a big nono in Denmark. At the gym, a random guy asked if I wanted to join him in his workout and that is now a great friend of mine.
top3_advice: LEARN SPANISH - even if it is just a few basic words and continue with it. I regret not getting making a greater effort. Nobody speaks English so keep your google translate open because you will need it. Explore not just Madrid but also the adjacent cities. I used the speedtrain (Renfe) a lot, as it only took 2 hours to Valencia/Barcelona and i preferred paying a bit more to avoid an 8 hour busride with Alsa. My motto was "why not" to practically anything. New experiences in particular whether it was food, going out to a club, trying a dickwaffle in Chueca (the gay neighbourhood). I met a girl in a club during a pubcrawl and we instantly become friends and the next day we went to Valencia together because why not? And she is now one of my closest friends. Academic wise I would say - stay above 75% attendance and definitely make sure you do your work as it will make the final exam count less towards your final grade. Classes are your books and everything the professor says can be on your exam, so take notes because not all courses are recorded. Also definitely ask someone for notes if you miss a class.
other_useful_info: Don't be afraid of trying new things.
most_rewarding: The friends I made, my spanish improved very much and I don't need google translate anymore. The experience of travelling abroad which also helps the CV.
greatest_challenge: Definitely an experience you would not regret. It is an emotional rollercoaster with ups and downs and was nervewrecking. Being alone in a country, knowing nobody, and not speaking the language can be difficult. But once you get over the initial stage and start exploring and making friends, it becomes easy and fun. The courses were a pain to get going as well so that was probably the greatest challenge.

crucial_aspects: I had never been to Spain, so I wanted to try to go to Madrid. I heard the university was good, and the city as well.
info_ease: Really easy, everything could be looked up in documents.
arrival_assistance: I got help from citylife madrid.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You have to be registered within two weeks.
registration_help: You could mail the university or go to the office.
registration_success: The amount of courses is not the best, but it was okay. I had the classes I wanted, so that was successful.
registration_advice: Try your best to attend class and be part of the students.
course_level: The level is medium, not really high or low. If you study throughout the semester, you should be fine to the exams.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was really different. You have to attend class, do presentations and assignments etc., compared to UCPH where you have so much more responsibility with studying.
courses_enrolled: THEORY AND HISTORY OF INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS SINGLE EUROPEAN MARKET INTERNATIONAL PRIVATE LAW CORPORATE LAW EUROPEAN AND INTERNATIONAL PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS
recommended_courses: International private law was really interesting and the teachers were nice as well.
unexpected_costs: When booking a room or apartment, you pay an agency fee that you dont get back!! My fee was 510 euros.
cost_comparison: Madrid is not as cheap as Barcelona, but still cheaper than Denmark.
activities_available: There was nothing but maybe beacuse of covid.
activities_recommended: Going to meet other exchange students as well.
weekend_recommendations: I did go on a lot of weekends trip!!
culture_adjustment: It was really easy, you get used to the new culture and language within the first week.
socializing_tips: Talk to the local students at school.
cultural_challenges: In Spain they wake up and go to bed super late. They eat late as well.
culture_appreciated: The culture is really fun and outgoing, Spanish people enjoy to go out every day of the week.
top3_advice: Enjoy your time. Dont spend to much time studying, there is other things than school. Try to meet as many people as possible.
other_useful_info: Get some international friends, so you dont just go to class all by yourself.
most_rewarding: My improvements in English and I have become more outgoing and easygoing with strangers.
greatest_challenge: To be all my yourself in a different country with a different culture.

crucial_aspects: that the language would be the only one spoken in the region and not too different from standard Spanish. That it would not be a bigger city with many tourists and where other languages would be an option, nor that there would be too many Erasmus students.
info_ease: I made it happen, but some of it could have been easier or just wasn´t obvious.
arrival_assistance: Due to covid, I missed the opportunity to join the intro day, but beside that, I got some brochures, contacted by and intro from ESN, relatively consistent updates from the local counselor. Also, it was relatively easy to get in contact with and help from the people there.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: As I remember, I had to send my OLA and fill out a matriculation form. If those didn´t coincide, I had to change my OLA. They have too many platforms so getting access to all of them was dragging a bit out.
registration_help: I was able to always write an email or ask for help, but not always getting a helpful answer. I had signed up for their tutor-buddy program but never heard from anybody.
registration_success: the scheduling of the classes does not make any sense. So unless you want to take classes from all of the same semester in the same grado, it will be very difficult to put together a schedule where the classes don´t coincide. I had to take classes in the master and another faculty as well, and drop some of the classes I had really wanted.
registration_advice: Wait to make up your mind about the classes completely, until they have posted the final schedule for the semester so you know for sure that you are able to get them. If not, you will have to change your OLA lots of times.
course_level: As we do know when going, it is a lot of memorization and not so much showing what you can do. Some of the courses seemed to have a very low level and I had to question myself whether I was taking a university level class. But others were good.
teaching_comparison: Come to the classes, listen, write notes exactly as the professor says it, memorize it, show it in the exam. For some reason, their plan docente is very important for them, but not many actually follows it or get through what we are supposed to. Some classes do have group work or things you have to do for the next class, but in general, you don´t have homework or projects/group work. Only at the end you probably will have to work on one or two final works in each class.
courses_enrolled: La variación lingüística en español Historia, Memoria y medios de comunicación Análisis pragmático del inglés Sociología de las Relaciones de Género y de la Familia Pragmática y Lingüística del Texto
recommended_courses: Análisis pragmático del inglés: The professor is very good at teaching. He makes it interesting, interactive, and is one of the only classes where I would say I learned something.
unexpected_costs: Ikke rigtig noget. Jeg fik stjålet min mobil på en rejse, så måtte investere i en ny indtil jeg modtog penge fra forsikringen. Jeg brugte penge rejser/ture, men det var forventet, dog mere spontant.
cost_comparison: Bøger! alkohol. Og tingene er generelt en del billigere end i Danmark og Madrid/Barcelona.
activities_available: Der var nogle arrangementer, og ESN lavede nogle events og ture en gang i mellem, men ikke så meget noget jeg deltog i, da jeg og de venner jeg havde fundet, mest arrangerede vores egne ting.
activities_recommended: Det ved jeg ikke.
weekend_recommendations: Der er en hel masse smuk natur omkring i Extremadura. Spørg en hvilken som helst lokal og de kan give dig en lang liste over must visits. Til en lang weekend, er det så dejligt med mange byer tæt på, kan bl.a. anbefale: Salamanca, Sevilla, Trujillo, Mérida, Cadiz.
culture_adjustment: Jeg vil ikke sige at der var nogen forskelle der gjorde det svært for mig at være der eller leve der. Men selvfølgelig er der nogle småting, men det synes jeg også er en del af det sjove.
socializing_tips: Generelt virker de ikke så interesserede i at få udlandske venner. Men vær åben og på, og giv dit nummer ud/accepter det, drik en øl i byen, eller en kaffe i kantinen.
cultural_challenges: måden at studere på og udføre eksamener. Desuden maden, spisetidspunkt og at jeg ikke bare kunne købe ind på en søndag glemte jeg utroligt nok helt op til den sidste søndag.
culture_appreciated: Op indtil to uger før eksamenerne er der intet stress og alt handler om at nyde det gode liv, få et glas tinto de verano og mødes med venner. Også hvor mange små festivaler og events der hele tiden er. Der sker hele tiden noget.
top3_advice: 1)Gør det ikke for det intellektuelle udbytte af undervisningen. 2)Selvom ingen gør det eller siger man skal, så sæt tid af til at starte med til at skrive/øve noter, så man kan huske det og ikke skal til at lære et helt semester udenad på et par dage. 3) Udover udvekslingsstuderende, kan du næsten ikke finde et menneske der kan et ord på engelsk. For mig var det en god ting, da jeg fik presset mig selv til at tale spansk og de generelt er tålmodige og venlige når man prøver.
other_useful_info: De har nogle uofficielle helligdage, som ikke står i nogen kalender eller bliver påmindet om. Men for de lokale er det helt naturligt at man ikke møder i skole de dage, og nogle gange dagene op til eller efter, og det samme for underviserne. Så spørg en lokal om de dage så du ikke møder op som den eneste.
most_rewarding: Spanske sprogegenskaber, venskaber for livet, fantastiske oplevelser/ture.
greatest_challenge: At forholde mig til min ufærdigbehandlet sygdom alene i Spanien.

crucial_aspects: Small city authentic city not big city few foreigners
info_ease: Pretty easy. I just went and asked at the university
arrival_assistance: Plenty thhe host university did a good job at helping me. They could speak spanish as well as english.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Too much bureaucracy. So much useless information. Give me a paper to fill and let me go on exchange.
registration_help: There was help available, and thanks for that. The office though at Ucph was lackluster at times, since they never fully responded to your questions.
registration_success: I was succesful
registration_advice: When you seek help at the erasmus exchange office, explain EVERYTHING inyour emails to them otherwise they won't understand.
course_level: They were fine. Good level
teaching_comparison: It was very different in that the style in Spain seems much more rigid. That is, it seems like they put more en emphasis on a sort of copy paste style of teaching where the students basically notes down everything going on in the class for then later being requiered to being able to answer those questions from memory. A style which is very different from the one in Denmark where it seems that the teachers try and create room for a discussion to be held in class. In short: Spain more rigid, more focus on copy paste style of teaching, few discussions and little involvement from the class Denmark is more dynamic, more focus on critical thinking, discussions in class so forth
courses_enrolled: Metodología de la enseñanza del español como lengua extranjera Lengua Española Historia moderna universal
recommended_courses: Lengua española and Historia moderna universal - both had great teachers that spoke clearly and tried to iinvovle the erasmus students in the teachings my teacher in Metodología spoke waaaaaay to fast and i didn't like her style of teaching. I would avoid
unexpected_costs: The cost for withdrawing money
cost_comparison: Food in general is less expensive accomodation is incredibly cheap compared to Copenhagen - some had housing as low as 130 euro a month
activities_available: ESN again, There was a gym at the university where you could train for 1.6 euro for each session
activities_recommended: go to the ESN meetings, don't be afraid to engage in conversation with the locals, find yourself a gym or a sportscenter and start training, meeting the locals to learn spanish better
weekend_recommendations: There is honestly plenty of places to visit in Extremadura, just ask the locals. They are very friendly and will often give you recommenddations for places to visit or see.
culture_adjustment: Incredibly easy, but i have been to Spain several times
socializing_tips: Just don't be afraid of engaging in conversation with the locals. They are very friendly and will help you. Have a positive attitude
cultural_challenges: Obviously not everyone speaks english here so sometimes there can be a language barrier between you and the locals, which is for the better. Then you are forced to speak spanish
culture_appreciated: Things seems less stressful here, people are more open and willing to connect with you if you will let them. I have several times been invited out for beer with the locals because we just started talking at the gym or whatever.
top3_advice: Come a little before the beginning of your stay so you can get to know the cty a little and find a place to live. I came a week earlier. Make sure you have your MOnline sorted out relax and have a good time
other_useful_info: Sort out the bureaucratic stuff as early as possible so there is less stress
most_rewarding: Being able to live with my roommates and experiencing the city and what the local people are like here.
greatest_challenge: The rigid educational system of the universities and my correspondance with the office for exchange students in Cph

crucial_aspects: The language and the culture. Also the general safety level in the country and distance from home country (= price). The specific place was my second priority so I hadn't looked too much into it beforehand (at all).
info_ease: There was no list with all the things we had to do, which I don't understand, as it must be the same for most exchange students, semester after semester. That being said, it was very easy to get in touch with coordinators that could answer my questions (what to do next, which order, where and how do I do that), and they were quick to respond, so there was never any stress or feeling of being lost or abandoned.
arrival_assistance: There was a welcome day, and good and quick communication with the relevant office.
arrival_comments: 5 would be that they would have just send out the relevant information, instead of having to ask for it, but once I asked, the response time was quick and accurate and I could always just come to the office (vicedecano de relaciones internacionales) and ask.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I just remember doing it step by step, asking at the office of the Vicedecano de relaciones internacionales and following his instructions, then asking him 'and now what?'. He could've spared himself at least five mails and five physical appearances at his office from me, had he send me the info proactively (eg. how to get registered at the Campus Virtual, etc.), but as he was quick to respond so I don't have much to complain about.
registration_help: The Vicedecano de relaciones internacionales was very responsive.
registration_success: As I had chosen classes from different years and even different grades (filología hispánica and filología inglesa) there were a lot of classes overlapping. In the end, I had three of the five classes I had chosen beforehand, and had to change the last two.
registration_advice: I would say it's pretty chill, it's not like there are any deadlines, the only problem is if you have overlapping classes and have to change some of them, but that's more on the home university to accept your changes. The only thing, really, is if you need access to the campus virtual for some reason before you have it, but then you can ask a classmate to send whatever it is you need, or talk to the teacher.
course_level: There was no public semester plan so you never knew what was gonna happen a given day. There was also no homework although that could have spared tons of time in class. Generally, the teachers didn't upload the slides before the end of the 'tema', so many students would spent the whole class desperately trying to copy down the slides. In some subject the teacher would write something on the blackboard, and then all the students would copy it, and twenty or maybe thirty minutes would pass like that, instead of the teacher just writing it on a computer and uploading to the campus virtual. Soo much of the time spent in the class room could have been given as homework, and then we could've spend the time in class going into depth with it, discussing it, or working actively with it - instead, the classes were mostly about being told something, but there was never time for applying the theory hands on (doing exercises).
teaching_comparison: No homework and very little teacher-student interaction. In variación lingüística, for example, the teacher would analyze one or several texts every class, but we never analyzed one ourselves before it came up in the exam. At UCPH, the students would have to do the analysis (often in groups), the teacher would guide the ones who need it, and then in the end you would discuss it between all and the teacher might give her/his take. During my semester, I can only think of one or two examples of group work.
courses_enrolled: Lengua española Traducción I (español-inglés-español) Traducción II (español-inglés-español) Análisis del discurso La variación lingüística en español
recommended_courses: La variación lingüística was very interesting and the teacher always helpful and friendly. Lengua española was sometimes interesting, and sometimes it seemed like nonsense. The exams are spread out throughout the semester which is nice. The translation classes were easy but the teacherm was really unpleasant. I would definitely recommend choosing the global evaluation in the translation classes so you don't have to do a presentation. The exam was super straight forward, just translating two texts, and one theoretical question that weighed very little in the evaluation.
unexpected_costs: The registration process at the uni costed 5€.
cost_comparison: Everything in general; flat, food etc. The monthly bus card was 14,50€/month and then you could use all busses freely. There's a thing called an 'abono' which you can get with the train (renfe) and bus (alsa), you pay an amount (20-50€) and then you can travel freely between two set destinations (eg. caceres-madrid with train, or caceres-seville with bus).
activities_available: football, paddle, volleyball and tennis etc. pitches, a library, a gym that costs €2 euros to use (but it's small and after one time I never came back, one of the two treadmills moved when you used it, for instance). Erasmus activities, parties and trips.
activities_recommended: Go to the stuff in the intro week, you'll get to know a lot of people.
weekend_recommendations: Barruecos is a nice natural resort with a lot of cows 15 minutes in bus from Caceres where they've shot a GOT dragon-scene. Lissabon (Sintra) is five hours away, Madrid is three hours away in train, Seville three hours in bus (not a big fan of Seville BUT from there you can go to Málaga, GRANADA(!) and Córdoba - do go watch a flamenco-show!!)
culture_adjustment: It was tough adjusting to the eating schedules, tough with the heat from April and forward, tough that people don't go to the discotecas before 1 or 2 in the morning, but the most difficult thing must be the complete absence of punctuality - when volleyball is scheduled for 5 it maaybe starts at 6:30...
socializing_tips: Talk to the people you sit next to, introduce yourself, I would say the Spanish people I met were easy to talk to and very open, but obviously it might be necessary to take the first step.
cultural_challenges: The punctuality-thing is difficult to handle for everyone involved.. ("pedimos puntualidad", "vengan yaa", "those of you who have written you name on the event, are you gonna come at all?" etc.)
culture_appreciated: There are tons of small bars everywhere and people sitting out on the streets from winter to summer, it's very nice and lively. The prices of drinks, cinema etc. makes it very easy to meet up with people.
top3_advice: Ask the teachers or co-students whenever you're uncertain about something. Check other subjects before arrival so you're somewhat ready if (when) you have overlapping classes. I would say I learned a lot from having Spanish (speaking) roommates.
other_useful_info: The abonos (renfe and alsa). The abono mensual (monthly bus card - bring passport photos).
most_rewarding: Living in the Spanish culture for several month, experiencing it first hand, talking a lot of Spanish, getting to know people from all over the spanish-speaking world. Visiting the amazing places you can reach from Cáceres; el Alhambra (buy entrance weeks before), Lissabon, Madrid, Córdoba, Málaga, and with two trains you can reach Barcelona which was a huge experience.
greatest_challenge: Finding peace with the structure of the educational system, with so much time wasted every day.

crucial_aspects: For me, it was very important to choose a country that was far away from Denmark, to try something completely new. I also wanted to go somewhere where the main language is Spanish.
overall_comments: It was the best experience of my life.
info_ease: It was very easy to find information. However, everything was going a bit slow. When you contact UDLAP, it takes some days for them to answer - if not some weeks...
arrival_assistance: When you arrive at Cholula, you will immediately get in contact with old students from UDLAP, who will help you through the whole process. They make a Whatsapp group for all the international students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was the best experience of my life.
registration_process: I think it was very easy. They have a catalog where you can see which classes you can take in the semester you are going. However, the catalog is only coming some weeks before the semester starts, which can be a little bit stressful.
registration_help: You can write to the teachers if you have any doubts.
registration_advice: Don't stress too much. The system is not so strict.
academics_comments: It was the best experience of my life.
course_level: I had five courses - i don't remember the level.
teaching_comparison: It's very different since the class is only for one hour and then you switch to another class. You only have two hours each week for each class. And there are a lot of presentations and exams. However, they are all very easy.
courses_enrolled: Organizational Psychology Leadership and negotiation Leadership and teamwork Food and life Human rights
recommended_courses: I LOVED human rights! Best class at UDLAP, and the professor, Samuel Stone, is amazing! Best professor I have had in my life. Also Gabriela Diaz is an excellent teacher, she is very kind and always ready to help you!
unexpected_costs: Nothing... Everything was so cheap!
cost_comparison: Wine :-)
activities_available: I don't really know.
activities_recommended: Again, hard to say when the campus was closed.
weekend_recommendations: I loved Chiapas, Oaxaca, Atlixco, Guanajuato, Sayulita!
culture_adjustment: I think it was easy enough! You should however get used to the Latin-American time. If someone tells you, that they will be there in 5 minutes, never believe them. It will be a least 30 minutes. Never be there in time. You will wait and look like a fool. Another thing, you will get friends after 10 minutes everywhere you go. People are so friendly, they always want to talk and get to know you. Don't be shy! Just enjoy.
socializing_tips: Go out.
cultural_challenges: Nothing.
culture_appreciated: The people! I love Mexicans. They are so friendly and warm. You are never alone in Mexico. When I arrived to Mexico, it was two days before New Year's Eve, and I had nowhere to go. A girl i only had been in contact with on Whatsapp (one of the old students of UDLAP) invited me to her house with her family to spend the evening with them! This will rarely happen in Denmark, but here it will occur at least 10 times during your stay. Mexican people are great.
top3_advice: Read all the reviews on this website - it really helps you to get an idea of everything! Everything is gonna be cool! Cholula, the city of UDLAP, is amazing! Best city in Mexico.
other_useful_info: Enjoy every moment, time flies! And bring warm clothes, it gets very cold at night.
most_rewarding: To get to know another culture. You get a new perspective on life. Be ready to visit a place that is completely different from your own daily life. Churches every 20 meters, noises every night from dogs, churches, or fireworks. A lot of fireworks, and no, not the ones that are pretty. Only a big noise... And in the first two weeks, you think someone is getting shot every time. However, it is just churches felicitating something, and that is EVERY day. Get used to it. You are not going to sleep the first weeks, so party instead! In addition, it's also a poor country, with kids on the street selling bubble gums, old people of the age of 100 still working in the markets to support their families, and people working 70 hours each week for no money. However, they still smile and keep having hope. They are grateful for living. They are not complaining about it, at least not the ones I have spoken to. Maybe Denmark is one of the happiest countries, but I don't really know how it is possible. We are always stressed or depressed. Here in Mexico, they just live. Even though life sucks. I want to have the same life perspective as them.
greatest_challenge: To not be scared. To have trust in people. To walk in the street alone, without being nervous. However, you get used to it. And you understand the norms. In the day, yes. In the night. maybe not. Mexico is not dangerous if you take care. Just don't be stupid.
other_comments: ENJOY.

crucial_aspects: At det skulle være et spansktalende land
info_ease: Så længe man selv gør en aktiv indsats og opsøger den information man har brug for, så er det relativt nemt
arrival_assistance: Der skulle have været afholdt en introuge, men dette var aflyst pga corona og politiske problemer med campus. Derfor ingen.
arrival_comments: Universitet var længe om at melde noget information ud, hvilket var stressende når KU også har nogle deadlines man skal overholde.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Da kursuskataloget blev offentliggjort, havde vi samtidig fået en tilmeldingsblanket hvor man bare skulle udfylde hvilke kurser man ville have. Meget nemt. Dog kom kursuskataloget MEGET sent ud, under en uge før deadline for tilmelding, og det var umuligt at navigere i og finde kurserne. Jeg er meget glad for de kurser jeg har haft, men jeg tror også at jeg har overset nogle spændende kurser pga. det forvirrende og fuldstændig uoverskuelige katalog
registration_help: Man kunne skrive til universitetet, ellers intet.
registration_success: Jeg fik alle mine fem ønskede kurser
registration_advice: Lad være med selv at lede efter kurserne. De kurser du kan finde på UDLAPs hjemmeside er forældede og bliver ikke udbudt. Du bliver nødt til at vente på at UDLAP sender dig en mail med det aktuelle kursuskatalog.
course_level: Det kræver en del deltagelse og engagement fra din egen side af for at følge med, men det er ikke svært at følge med og score gode karakterer. Underviserne er meget gavmilde med karakterer
teaching_comparison: Der var virkelig mange lektier, opgaver, deleksaminer og præsentationer undervejs. På KU handler det mest bare om at læse sine tekster og møde op til undervisningen og skrive noter, på UDLAP er man meget mere aktiv og en del af undervisningen
courses_enrolled: Arte y cultura de las Américas Estudio de la Traducción Sociolingüística Textos de la Conquista Comunicación y globalización
recommended_courses: Arte y cultura de las Américas: hvis man vil lære om kulturhistorie i Amerika Sociolingüística: Et kursus, hvor man både lærer meget om lingvistik i Mexico, men også et kursus hvor man virkelig får reflekteret over en masse ting ift. sprog. Comunicación y globalización: Mega relevant, interessant og udfordrende kursus. Meget aktuelt for vores tidsalder
unexpected_costs: Det er ikke mange penge, men man skal hele tiden købe vand og altid give drikkepenge på cafeer/restauranter! Drikkepenge er 10-20% af prisen
cost_comparison: Mad og transport er absurd billigt.
activities_available: Der har ikke været mange tilbud åbne på campus pga. covid
activities_recommended: Forskellige organisationer organiserer fester, udflugter, salsa timer, spanskundervisning osv. Deltag i så meget du har lyst til og orker. FOMO slår til nogle gange, men det er vigtigt at mærke efter og lytte til din krop.
weekend_recommendations: Rejs rundt så meget som muligt!!
culture_adjustment: Det er en meget anderledes kultur end vi kender fra Danmark og Europa, så det kan måske godt være lidt svært at tilpasse sig i starten.
socializing_tips: Vær åben, det er de lokale! De er altid klar på en fest, kaffe, vise dig rundt, tage dig med hjem til deres familie osv.
cultural_challenges: Pas
culture_appreciated: Mad :)
top3_advice: 1. Husk at komme ud af studierne og ud af huset og oplev landet 2. Hav tålmodighed med de forskellige processer du går igennem. Det tager tid, men alt løser sig altid 3. Tænk ikke så meget over penge! Dette er the time of your life. Få så mange oplevelser ud af det som muligt. Penge kan du altid tjene senere. Oplevelser får du ikke igen
other_useful_info: Sørg for at blive venner med de lokale og få lært / øvet noget spansk!! Mexicanere er super søde og tålmodige
most_rewarding: Klar forbedring af mit spanske og en bred kulturforståelse for Mexico og latinamerikansk kultur
greatest_challenge: At få fuldført alle afleveringer, præsentation osv, samtidig med at have tid til oplevelser!

crucial_aspects: As this was my last semester of Native American Culture and Languages I found it important to see the remaining culture in Mexico as it was one of your focuses.
info_ease: It was all given to us by mail and later by an orientation program.
arrival_assistance: An orientation program.
arrival_comments: sometimes they were slow at answering emails
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: they will give you information to fill out, insurance and you need a doctors approval for the trip. some of the information wasn't filled in by some and they still got in.
registration_help: online consultation by video and mail
registration_success: mostly but it was hard to find corsos and what they were about

crucial_aspects: I wanted a destination where they spoke Spanish, and preferably in Central America. I also did not want to live in a big city.
overall_comments: My time in Mexico was varied, but overall I would say good, and I really enjoyed it and got exactly what I needed out of it. Most of the experiences I hear about exchange is that it was completely amazing, an unforgettable, life-changing experience, with friends for life, and I unfortunately did not have that. I was a lot older than most of the exchange students (28 vs. 22-ish), and I do not drink or take drugs or party. That limited me a lot in making friends, and so I didn't really have any the entire time I was there. I found everything to really be centered around partying, so like the trips that were organized are a little bit of culture, and a little bit of partying, you can't really take the partying part away (I asked). A lot of people live together, and I lived alone, which also made it hard to make friends. I have a lot of food allergies, so I found it really hard to find places to eat, and I couldn't go around and sample all the cuisine. I don't regret my exchange, but It just wasn't as good as I could've hoped. However, towards the end, I decided to go to the Yucatan peninsula and be near the sea and that was a lot better. It was amazing to just be in Mexico, and be finished with school, without the pressure of forced interaction. It was here that I felt my Spanish improved the most, because I had to use my Spanish a lot getting around. Between the exchange students, we mostly spoke English.
info_ease: It was fine. The International Office is extremely easy to get in touch with, they are available practically every day, all day, and you can even get a virtual appointment with them if needed.
arrival_assistance: I went to the International Office in person a couple of times to arrange my courses, that was pretty straightforward and easy. The Amigos Internacionales were also pretty helpful, we had a Whatsapp group with everyone (arranged at the online orientation, so don't miss that) and it was easy to ask questions in that group and get answers. There's also an in-person orientation once you arrive, and then you get a personal appointment with someone from the office to arrange everything, and they make sure everything is fine with your entry forms, student card, courses etc., so that was great. You get this time at the in-person orientation, so don't miss orientation!
arrival_comments: Although the International Office is easy to get in touch with, to get them to actually do something is a little more difficult. They often promise they will do things, or send things, or contact people, but then don't do it, or don't get back to you. You have to follow up with them multiple times, but I think that might be part of the culture, and part of the whole experience :). It didn't bother me that much, the whole orientation process is extremely straightforward and they explain it to you multiple times.

registration_process: 1) they send you an old course catalogue during the summer, it's like an excel sheet with hundreds of courses.
registration_help: Well the International Office at UDLAP can help you, but I got most help from the whatsapp group. Tbh, I didn't actually find the International Office to be that helpful regarding this process, maybe because they're so used to this system, it's hard for them to understand that it's actually kind of complicated. They're helpful about adding and dropping courses though, like in person, even though you're technically supposed to do it with the form.
registration_success: Well. I was extremely unlucky in that out of the 50 (!!) courses I could be interested in, only about 7 were available after all. Out of those 7, about 5 overlapped each other with time, and you're not allowed to have overlapping classes, as attendance is mandatory. So. I spent an inordinate amount of time trying to figure everything out, but once I did, I got 4/5 of the courses I wanted. They didn't give me the last course because it was a marketing course and they said I didn't have any prior experience and so I wasn't allowed. So, try to pick courses you have some prior experience in, so this doesn't happen. There's unfortunately no way to know if they require previous experience though unless you email the teachers, and even then it might be difficult. I got written permission from the marketing course professor that I was allowed to take the course, and the International Office still didn't allow me to take it.
registration_advice: If you're a Master's student, apply as a bachelor's. Apply normally to KU, but once you're nominated by KU, when you have to apply to UDLAP, check the box that says you want to take bachelor/undergraduate courses. KU will approve them as master's courses, if they're 4th year courses. That way, you have a MUCH bigger variety of courses to choose from, as the courses for Master's are extremely limited. Furthermore, courses that say they're in English may actually be in Spanish. Some professors are kind and say you can just speak English, especially if it's like a language class, but some expect you to only speak Spanish, even if it was supposed to be a course in English. Once again, there's really no way to tell, unless maybe you email the professor beforehand.

I thought it was extremely fine, and very academically sound.
teaching_comparison: They put a lot of emphasis on participating/speaking in class. I think for all of my classes, a percentage of the grade actually depends on it. I had one professor that would specifically ask every single person in the class for opinions on the text, so there's no way out.
courses_enrolled: Literaturas Prehispánicas Etnología Histórica Anthropological Studies of Conflicts Literatura Mexicana Moderna Temas Selectos 2
recommended_courses: I recommend Literaturas Prehispánicas, and Etnología Histórica because they were super interesting and gave me insight into Mexico, both pre-hispanic and contemporary or modern. Literaturas Prehispánicas is a must if you're interested in ancient cultures, like Mayan, Incan, Aztec, Olmec etc., and Etnología Histórica had the most amazing teacher Laura Romano, anything by her I recommend. She's so knowledgeable and talked about the construct of race, gender, etc. although, if you already know a lot about these topics, maybe it's not so interesting, as I felt like the things she said were interesting, but pretty “beginner”. I recommend Literatura Mexicana Moderna if you're interested in the Mexican revolution or war in general, but be prepared for a lot of reading (although it comes in cycles, like “read this book – let's discuss it for 2 weeks” aka, for those two weeks of discussion, you don't have any homework since you've already read the book). Martin Larsson is Swedish, very organized, and a good teacher.
unexpected_costs: An extra statement from your doctor in Denmark before departure. They give you a form to fill out during the application process, that you need your doctor to sign, but then you also need an actual lægeerklæring in addition to that.
cost_comparison: Some food was way more expensive than I expected. I can't eat gluten, so I was ofc happy to find gluten free pasta at all, but it cost more than x3 as much than in Denmark. I bought a lot of organic groceries, which I knew would be expensive, but it was still more expensive than I thought. I ordered food a lot, so it got expensive, but for me, it was 100% worth it.
activities_available: There's both like extracurricular sports or classes like painting, photography, dance, music/singing lessons, personal defense classes, etc. which you have to pay for (talleres), and then there are also like academic “clubs” (organizaciones estudiantiles) which are free, which are more like “chess club”, “lgbtqia+ club”, “environmental club”, “science club” etc. but some of them were also like “flag football club”. I didn't want to pay so I didn't join the paid ones, plus I found it hard to reconcile them with my schedule, but I joined a couple of the free academic clubs, and I really recommend that, especially to meet other Mexicans. You can drop it after a few times, but if you go the first few, you can be in the whatsapp group, get invited to events, and possibly make friends that you can obviously keep, even if you stop coming to the meetings.
activities_recommended: I recommend “International Forum”, it's a space where Mexicans go to meet internationals, and internationals go to meet Mexicans. For some reason, most international students are not interested, so it ends up being a bunch of Mexican students and a few internationals. I liked this a lot, as there's no real structure, and the few times I was there, I just talked to other Mexicans and asked questions about food, culture, whatever I wanted to basically. They were also really eager to share. I also got in the Whatsapp group, and one time I needed a charger for example, so I asked in the group if anyone was at campus and ended up spending the afternoon with two Mexican students, while I used their charger to charge my phone. That was great, without the club/whatsapp group I would've never met them. The club kinda got boring after a while though, I think the organizers were afraid of not having structured activities, so they made us play games a lot, whereas I would have rather just had time to talk, so I stopped coming, but I ofc stayed in the Whatsapp group, and met other people through there as well. Any other club you feel would be interesting to you as well, join! If you don't like it, you're not obligated to continue. Paid activities --> (https://talleres.udlap.mx/). Academic clubs --> (https://www.udlap.mx/web/vidaestudiantil/organizacionesestudiantiles.aspx) scroll down to find the clubs, or visit their facebook page (https://www.facebook.com/organizaciones.estudiantilesudlap)
weekend_recommendations: Mexico City, Teotihuacán, Cholula pyramid ofc, Puebla City, MUSEUMS!!! Go to all the museums you can, there's one next to the pyramid in Cholula and it was amazing! Botanical gardens in Cholula. visiting small cafés in Cholula.
culture_adjustment: pretty easy
socializing_tips: hmm no, as this was pretty hard for me as well. well, join international forum. maybe join more clubs and stuff? try to meet up with the amigos internacionales?
cultural_challenges: The service-minded attitude. It seemed like in “service” situations, people were focused on giving me everything I wanted, and weren't concerned about their own needs, which I didn't appreciate. For example, when touring apartments to live in, landlords would often ask me when I would want to come and see it, and my response would always be “when does it fit you? What time is best for you? Is there something that you would you prefer?” because of course, I had all the time in the world, and I thought they would perhaps be busy, or have some preference, like maybe they're touring the same apartment at 1, so it would make sense for me to come directly before or after. But they seemed very annoyed at this attitude, and finally just ordered me to tell them what time I would come. It was the same with the cleaning lady or handymen, sometimes they would ask what time I would want them to come, and I would just say oh whenever suits you best, I'm home all day, because ofc they are busy and have their own lives etc. but that just seemed to confuse them, and make them upset so I had to learn to be kind of bossy, and be like “I want you to come here and clean/fix it at 2pm” or like “I am coming at 1 to tour the apartment”, even though I really didn't like it and never really got the hang of it to be honest. Also tipping! I consistently forgot to tip and often went back the next day to give them their tip. I always tipped 20%, unless they really didn't do anything at all, then 15%.
culture_appreciated: Everybody embraces lateness! That was so wonderful, I could take my time with everything, and know people weren't going to get annoyed or angry if I was late, and if I wasn't ready for someone to come over, I knew it didn't matter, because they were likely to come later anyways. So much less stress!
top3_advice: 1) Cholula is extremely loud. Be prepared to experience gunshot-like noises (like fireworks, but much louder) pretty regularly, as well as what sounds like small explosions. 2) Get Revolut. I don't know exactly how much I saved using Revolut, but given the exorbitant fees I know some other students were paying, like when withdrawing or transferring, I'm 100% satisfied. 3) Don't use the water for cooking. I think most people know not to drink it, but a lot of exchange students were making pasta or rice or beans with the water. They thought it would be okay because they boiled it, but Mexicans told us this is EXTREMELY discouraged by everyone, and they would never do that. (I don't know if anybody got sick from doing that, but if Mexicans don't do it themselves, and warn us straight out not to do it, I'm not going to do it).
other_useful_info: Yes, if you want, maybe visit the campus before your classes start. The campus is huge, and if I hadn't gone there beforehand to figure out where all my classes were, I would've been extremely late to every single one because I would've been lost. They do give you a tour at orientation, but I got much more out of figuring it out myself, than from that. I still found the orientation tour useful though, as you could ask questions, and see things I wouldn't have known to look for myself. The guards are super nice, just tell them you're a new exchange student and have your student number ready to give them. I personally benefitted from coming 1.5 weeks before classes started and I wish I had had more time, like at least two weeks. Then I could've spent one week just acclimatizing and finding housing, and then one week of like “vacation” and rest before school started. They recommend you to come august 1st and even sometimes offer the amigos internacionales in the airport to help you get to Puebla, but that's just a waste of time. It's super easy to find the bus to Puebla, it's literally in the airport (or like, just outside, attached to it), and you can't really go wrong. You're looking for the bus to Paseo Destino, and then you just take an Uber or Didi to Cholula, super easy. I stayed in an Airbnb while looking for housing, 10/10 recommend.
most_rewarding: improving my spanish, the blissful warmth and sunshine during the so called “cold” months, meeting wonderful people (sadly none of them were students, but what can you do!), and the group tour i booked to Teotihuacan! simply amazing. I used https://pueblatours.mx/tour-puebla-teotihuacan.html, highly recommend, see if you can get Daniel Lima, and remember to tip!
greatest_challenge: Finding food I could eat. For some reason, a lot of the food I bought at the small tiendas or market went bad/mouldy within 2 – 3 days and that was really unappetizing to me. I had a really hard time finding fresh food at all actually, most small tiendas/kiosks don't have fresh food. But maybe that was just in San Pedro, as I noticed San Andrés had more. and eventually I figured out to take a didi to the supermarket, and that worked much better for me. I guess the greatest challenge was starting all over again. I had to figure out where to buy food (especially food I could eat!), where and how to buy water (and how to get it delivered), where to buy a pump for that water jug, how and where to find housing, how to pay my rent, how to get pesos, i could go on, just everything from scratch 'cause everything is new. But I learned, and had a great time! I enjoy being challenged, I think it makes you grow and that was one of my goals for this exchange which I am happy to say I achieved. I also unfortunately struggled with my mental health, and it was hard to find resources to help me, especially in English.
other_comments: Yes, I think my experience and the struggles that I had are very particular to me, and not very applicable to the “typical” exchange student. I think most people are only happy to go to bars or clubs to meet up with people, and happy to go partying, and happy to live with other people, and therefore it will be very easy to make friends. Nevertheless, even though I only made two friends near the end of my trip (who weren't even students or Mexican), I still had a good time, and I definitely recommend it. As a side note, I also felt kind of obligated to see other parts of Mexico, and due to my mental health struggles I didn't get to see much outside of Puebla while I was in Cholula. For that reason, I went to Playa del Carmen for a few weeks, once school was over, just to see something else and get beach time in. But for me personally, this was a mistake, because all the challenges I just listed above, I had given myself again. I once again had to re-establish myself somewhere, and a few weeks just wasn't enough time. I'm sure for some people it works to backpack around or however they choose to travel, I just want to share an alternative opinion, that if I could have changed what I did, I would have 100% stayed in Cholula, and been there for 6 full months, instead of only 4.5 months. All my exams were over by December 10th.

crucial_aspects: The opportunity to live in a different culture in contrast to ours, exploring their perspective on the world. Furthermore I wanted to improve my Spanish.
overall_comments: 9 out 10, because the educational level is pretty low, but the experience is wild.
info_ease: KU is not helping you that much, so you need to put a good amount of time in finding out things on you own. You can try to write to the university’s international office, but they are also a bit slow. But in the end is not so bad, it just take some time.
arrival_assistance: Udlap have a well functioning International office, which have a lot of things planned for you in the beginning. Tours in the campus and of the area. They help you with all the practical stuff. You will experience that the local students are really welcoming, so you can always just ask them for help. People are so friendly and easy to talk to.
arrival_comments: A lot of information, but they are a bit slow to answer.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: 9 out 10, because the educational level is pretty low, but the experience is wild.
registration_process: Can’t really remember, sry. But UDLAP will send you a guide to what to do.
registration_help: You could contact the international office and the professors, but it’s kind of slow.
registration_success: Fivtyfivty
registration_advice: My advice would be just choose some courses who seem interesting before leaving. Then in the first couple of weeks of the semester is possible to shuffle courses, and resend a pre approval to KU. A smart trick is to try laying all your courses on two days, because the you have the possibility of traveling or party longer in the weekends whiteout being absence from uni.
academics_comments: 9 out 10, because the educational level is pretty low, but the experience is wild.
course_level: It varies a lot. Most of the English courses were relatively easy.
teaching_comparison: There is a Gymnasie wibe, with small classroom and the teacher standing at the board. A classroom is typically max. 30 people.
courses_enrolled: Geopolitics and strategic analysis, great teacher named Guy. Choose some courses with him, if you can. International Relations Theory, with Guy Political and Social Theory, with Dolores. Not that good, but fine enough. Zoology, with Paul. Great teacher, but a random course I took for fun. Econometrics and another political course, which I chose to drop in the begging.
recommended_courses: The courses with Guy and Paul. Furthermore I heard about some nice courses in statistics and environmental governance.
unexpected_costs: Only to the guy who is organizing the housing. You sign a contact in the beginning, which say you have to pay for min. 5 months. I only livet there for 4 months. If you choose him, try to ask him in the beginning why you have to pay for it. He is interested in renting out, so you could easily pressure him a bit. I bought a bike and sold it again after the semester. Really with it, instead of taking Ubers to things far away.
cost_comparison: Buying food to cook yourself was a bit expensive relatively to what Mexicans are paid in average.
activities_available: Language, music and different sports. They made some trips outside also.
activities_recommended: They’re sports facilities. Also go watch their university team in American Football, it’s for free and a good atmosphere. I had a great Spanish teacher, Karla. WhatsApp number +52 222 461 4010. She also studies at the uni.
weekend_recommendations: Important. Remember to chill and explore Cholula, so you don't get stressed of going on weekend trips all the time. I needed to have a bit of daily life, which is also really cool to try out, because the mood and the people are just different compared to at home. But when that is said. Smaller weekend trips in the “close” area could be walking around in Puebla and Mexico City, which are beutiful cities. In Mexico City I really enjoyed going the area Roma Norte and Condeasa, but just go around and get a bit lost. So many nice places. Climbing Malinche and Izta if you are real mountaineer. There is also a really good hike around the National center between the active volcano Popo and the mountain Izta. Malinche and the hike between Izta you can do whiteout a guide, but going on top of Izta you need a guide. Go to the local football stadium in Puebla. Really nice, when they play against Club America. Bike around Cholula and up in the hills. Some good mountain biking. A cool cactus park and so rounding mountains called Jardín Zapotitlan. We camped in the park in a tent for two days. Really nice waking up surrounded by cactus and mountains. Eat your way through their amazing food. Trips longer away, which was really nice: Baja California, El Cheppe (tourist train) and the cities on the tracks (especially Barrancas de Cobre is breathtaking), Oxaca (Puerto Escondido), Ciapas and Yucatán. But here you need a week or more, which is possible during the semester. The professors are sweet and know you are an exchange student. If you are there in the autum semester you have Dia de Muertos, which is really nice in Oxaca and Michoacán. In the winter there should be a nature phenomenon with butterflies, Mariposas Monarca.
culture_adjustment: Culture shock is the way they are thinking about time, which can be annoying, but also really stress free and more chilled. The weather in Cholula gets cold during winter. It’s on a mountain range so the temperature differs a lot during the day. Cold in the morning, the warm and cold again during the night. A bit like Denmark, just bigger differences in heat because of the mountains. Rains season means a lot of water every day, but only for a couple of hours, then it get sunny. Don’t drink the water.
socializing_tips: They will come to you. They are really open and welcoming to exchange students. Otherwise join a sports team at the uni.
cultural_challenges: The idea of time.
culture_appreciated: The wibe is really good. Warm, happy and festive people.
top3_advice: Remember to chill in the city, don’t always go on weekend trips. Be open to meet the locals and your costudents. Buy a bike Remember warm cloth and a rain jacket. When you fly you can always have one check in bag, a hand luggage and a personal item, which could be a backpack. You can always store some of your luggage, with some sweet people in Cholula, when you go traveling after the semester. Ofc. if you want to leave from Mexico. Choose one of the housing organizations.
other_useful_info: Enjoy it, it’s gonna be really nice even though it can seem a bit scary in the beginning.
most_rewarding: Meeting the people and their vibe and perspective on the world. Having a break from uni at home and learning a new language.
greatest_challenge: During all the recruitments and pre approval for the universities.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to explore the Mexican culture both for academic and personal reasons. I felt that the culture would be a great counter point to the Danish mentality, maybe teaching me important life lessons about enjoying life and being a bit more present and taking things a bit more calmly. At the same time, I wanted to explore a completely different culture, and thought that choosing a country in the Latin America countries, a region that soon the EU will colaborate a lot with, could be helpful for my future career.
overall_comments: Mexico really is an absolutely amazing country! So incredibly rich in culture.. The food, the beautiful colored buildings, walking around in a pastel heaven sipping on a fresh juice smoothie. Mexico is amazing. Understanding the diversity of this country has been one of most rewarding experiences of my stay. At the end of the stay, you will most likely have visited way more places in Mexico than the average Mexican - most Mexicans don't even get to visit another state in their life. In this way, it is very priviliged to get a chance to have 5 months to explore this hugely rich cultural place.
info_ease: UDLAP sends a lot of infomation and the exchange office are super helpful - Eduardo is a darling!
arrival_assistance: Some long PDFs explaining how to get to the airport, what to bring, what not to bring. It was all very helpful.
arrival_comments: I arrived late, so when I came I didn't even know how to log in on the students portal blackboard to see my homework. But maybe I should have been more conscious of that and have asked for help - it was just hard knowing what to ask for without having been given any information. If you arrive late, I would advice you to simply pop by the international office and ask them to help you understand the system - especially if you, like me, don't speak Spanish!
