activities_recommended: Find local people to hang out with. Especially if you would like to learn the language. In that sense i would actually abstain from going to erasmus events and rather i would mingle with the locals. But that is just my recommendation.
weekend_recommendations: There is a beautiful mountain range just south of Salamanca which is beautiful for walking and seing small towns. Garganta la olla is one.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy if you find some local friends.
socializing_tips: Yea, go to outdoor traning sites. Create a community and go from there. That's what i did. I made a ton of local friends (only spaniards and latin americans) with whom i could practice my spanish. Perfect.
cultural_challenges: Not that many actually, other than what i already described with the difference to academic processes.
culture_appreciated: The warmth of the spanish people is second to none. They invite you straight into their hearts and become your friend easily. Likewise with many latin americans
top3_advice: Only go if you truly want to go. DO NOT, like i did, choose hard courses, for the love of god. Don't choose philosophy if you already havn't finished a bachelors in philosophy. Otherwise you will not only get frustrated by the high level of spanish, which is inevitable - your level is going to be far lower than that of the natives obviously, but also by the fact that you have no experience with philosophy and so everything is going to feel overwhelming and you won't be able to understand anything going on.
other_useful_info: Information about accomodation in Salamanca would be useful information and also if the student is an L2 student studying languages how difficult it is to accostum to philosophy.
most_rewarding: Getting to know a lot of amazing people. And also, even though it wasn't the best experience, getting to know more about philosophy in general
greatest_challenge: Being a L2 student of spanish combined with studying master level philosophy being a novice myself in the subject.

crucial_aspects: Warmer than Denmark.
info_ease: It was very easy. The student coordinator helped a lot.
arrival_assistance: I received an email from Catolicas student coordinator, who informed me about the first day and so on.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was pretty easy, although it did take a while to fill out the different application forms etc.
registration_help: The student coordinator was very helpful.
registration_success: To be honest it was pretty difficult. The classes are almost randomly spread out throughout the semester, so there is really no coherent structure in it. But you will just need to adapt, and get the most of it.
registration_advice: Take the classes that sounds the most strange. For instance, I had a class called introduction to Islamic legal Thought which was very interesting. A class in that category would never be taught in Denmark. So take everything that sounds almost weird to you. Especially if you are a law student and are used to just going through paragraphs and paraphrasing old professors.
course_level: The courses vary a lot in their levels. Overall I want to say that the amount of reading and preparation for each class is A LOT lower than at the University of Copenhagen. However, that english level at which many of the classes are taught are pretty high, and if you are willing to engage in the discussions you will find that the level is quite a lot higher than one might expect.
teaching_comparison: Well I went to UCPH during covid, so some of the classes were online. However the biggest difference was the preparation for each class was much less at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Federalism and the European Union. International Law of the Sea. Human Rights. Introduction to Islamic Legal Thought. Introduction to Law in a digital Economy. Law in the age of climate change. EU Energy and Environmental Law.
recommended_courses: Introduction to Islamic Legal Thought. Very interesting and different course. Should definitely be taught in more countries as far as I'm concerned.
unexpected_costs: None really.
cost_comparison: Everything was cheaper. Especially beer!
activities_available: Don't remember.
activities_recommended: I regret not going on more trips perhaps. So do just about everything you can.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Porto.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy.
socializing_tips: Have an open mind. You didn't travel all the way for nothing, so go meet new people and strike up a conversation with someone whom you perhaps never would've talked to on your home country.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: Outgoing party vibe
top3_advice: 1. Mingle with the other students, not just the ones from your country, or the Erasmus program in general. 2. Eat everything strange that you can get your hands on. 3. Don't get lost in Bairro Alto when you are drunk. That place is a maze.
other_useful_info: Enjoy and have fun with it. School is only so much of the experience.
most_rewarding: weather, food, drinks, friends, the charme of the city
greatest_challenge: That I didn't have more time

crucial_aspects: - that I could follow relevant courses (in regards to my field of study as well as personal interests) - that the courses were taught in English - the destination/city
overall_comments: It has been an unforgettable and important experience - both in terms of personal and academic growth
info_ease: The receiving institution gave good and clear instructions. Easy to ask for help if needed.
arrival_assistance: A well organized introduction day with general instructions
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It has been an unforgettable and important experience - both in terms of personal and academic growth
registration_process: The registration process was easy. The administrative part was clear to follow. Only problem was delay in getting certain papers signed but it was easy to get in touch with the host institution with any kind of problems.
registration_help: Available contact person (help via mail)
registration_success: Very successful
registration_advice: To limit delays as much as possible - make sure your papers are in order from the beginning!
academics_comments: It has been an unforgettable and important experience - both in terms of personal and academic growth
course_level: The level of the courses was high
teaching_comparison: It varied from class to class. Each professor had a very unique style of teaching - more or less similar to those of UCPH. The level of teaching was high (as at UCPH) but the readings for the classes where (in general) less demanding. Since I followed 6 different courses at my host institution the professors had varying (personal) professional careers outside of the university - which was very inspiring but It also ment that they had very different expectations for the students
courses_enrolled: - Great Books - Investigative Journalism - Portuguese Contemporary History - Cultural and Creative Industries - International Relations - Culture and Globalization
recommended_courses: International Relations: educating, well taught, super interesting and relevant course! Portuguese Contemporary History: I would definitely recommend taking a history course to get knowledge about the host country
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive than expected
activities_available: I am not aware
activities_recommended: Socializing with the people you live with! Going on museum trips! Exploring the city!
weekend_recommendations: Going for random walks in the different neighborhoods of the city. Using the opportunity to see more of the country (the Azores are a must!!!!)
culture_adjustment: Very easy - people where welcoming and nice
socializing_tips: To go live in a housing that doesn't only have international students (usually the accommodation found through your host university will be accommodating more local people). Talking with local students in your class.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Every part. The language! The people! The country! The Azores!
top3_advice: 1: notice that you will be most likely following multiple courses of different levels/ with different professors/ in different fields - this can lead to some confusion at the beginning. 2: your fellow students are your friends!! if you feel like you have academic and/or personal problems they probably have them too - help each other out! 3: use the help available - both from the administration and the professors. They are generally glad to help.
other_useful_info: They check level of attendance meaning that you cannot miss more than 9 classes pr. course - this might be stresfull at the beginning but is totally manageable.
most_rewarding: The experiences of living in a country rich in culture and history - and getting to know it besides people from all over the world
greatest_challenge: Staying focused on University work
other_comments: I would recommend going on an exchange to EVERYONE. It is a roller-coaster worth every high and low.

crucial_aspects: Explore a new culture, which is different from the Danish one and try to have an everyday life in a new country. Moreover, it could be exciting to try university life in another country and improve my English skills.
info_ease: It was really difficult to understand what courses the university offered in English and at what level. Required a lot of correspondence back and forth with the university coordinator to get information on this and response times were long. Also, the university didn't help at all with finding accommodation, so that was also a problem. It was difficult to know where to look for accommodation and what quality the accommodation was.
arrival_assistance: We got information about the semester, the exams etc. The university staff was nice to answer questions about life in Lisbon in general.
arrival_comments: The university did not take much initiative to inform, but if you asked the staff, they were nice to give a full answer.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The university mailed an admission form to be filled out. We got it back and the university took care of the rest. Then we got a form where we had to choose subjects and then send it back. The whole process went pretty smoothly.
registration_help: One could ask questions to the university was during the whole process
registration_success: The university did not offer many courses in English, but I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Just follow the instructions you get in emails from the university and you'll be fine. Otherwise, ask questions to the staff, they are nice to help and answer, even if the response time is sometimes a bit long.
course_level: The university only offered English courses at undergraduate level or LLM, so I took undergratuate courses, so the level was obviously somewhat lower than at the bachelor at KU.
teaching_comparison: We had electives of 2-3 weeks and then exams in the last class or an assignment to take home. Much blackboard teaching with student involvement via handouts.
courses_enrolled: - EU energy and environmental law - EU Governance - EU Internal Market - Federalism and the EU - EU competition law - Property - Regulation of technology - Restorative Justice
recommended_courses: All the courses were interesting.
unexpected_costs: Higher rent than expected.
cost_comparison: Rent was more expensive, and grocery shopping was the same price as in Denmark. Eating at restaurants is cheaper. No books from the university - only pdf documents for reading.
activities_available: The university had 4-5 free excursions during the semester that you could sign up for.
activities_recommended: Explore Portugal's many different cities and landscapes, it's a beautiful country and the people are super hospitable!
weekend_recommendations: Surf all you can. Enjoy the outdoors. Go out for cheap and good food and drinks. Go to Porto, Ericera, Madeira etc.
culture_adjustment: Yes, it was. The pace in Portugal is slower than in Denmark, but you soon get used to the fact that you can't do anything about it and just relax in it. Most younger people know English, so you can get around without knowing the language.
socializing_tips: All exchange students are there to make new friends and go on trips with other young people. So it comes naturally and everyone is good at taking initiative.
cultural_challenges: None was particularly challenging.
culture_appreciated: The openness and warmth. Portugal is such a wonderful country and you can learn a lot from it.
top3_advice: Be patient. If you're proactive and meet deadlines, things will work out, even if they sometimes work a bit slowly at university.
other_useful_info: If you go on your Master's at KU, don't expect big academic challenges, but go anyway because exchange is so much more than academic.
most_rewarding: All the good friendships and experiences. It's so cool to try living in another country, like jumping out of everyday life in Denmark. The culture in Portugal is great and there are a lot of cool experiences waiting for you. Don't be afraid to go. You will automatically get in touch with other exchange students who are there for the same reasons.
greatest_challenge: Be without boyfriend, friends and family for so long. Luckily, Lisbon is no further away than you can visit.

crucial_aspects: One of the most important aspects was that it had to be a city that I could see myself live in for a longer amount of time. I focused on a city with a lot of culture, nature close by and nice weather - Lisbon gave me all of that. Another aspect was the university. I wanted to study at a university which offered courses that I was interested in.
info_ease: You get a lot of emails with all the informations needed, and if you are in doubt the International Relations Coordinator of Católica is there to help you.
arrival_assistance: Didn't really need any assistance since all the information you needed was in the emails you got before arrival.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You got an email with all the courses offered, and then you just checked of which ones you would like to attend. It was also possible to change later on, even after you already attended some of the classes.
registration_help: The International Relations Coordinator, Maria Ines, was very helpful if you had any questions.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted - so very successful.
registration_advice: The courses end at different dates, and some at a late date. So if it is a priority for you to end your studies early then you should look for courses that offers that. However, you can always change your courses later on.
course_level: As a student from UCPH then I think we will find the level at most other universities as lower compared to what we are used to. For me the most challenging was to be taught in English and learn all the legal terms in English. Therefore it was actually pretty nice with not such a high academic level, but I was also a master student attending undergraduate courses, so I think it was easier for me, then what undergraduate students will find it.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was pretty much the same - mostly the professors just teaching and a bit of group discussions. However the exams was very different. There were a lot of essays or questions where you had to give your opinion on a topic.
courses_enrolled: EU Governance Introduction to EU Internal Market The Regulation of Technology Innovation EU Energy and Environmental Law Federalism and the EU Property Introduction to EU Competition Law International Law of the Sea
recommended_courses: Definitely Property. The professor was so good and really got you interested in the course. It regards US law, so it is also an opportunity to learn about another law system.
unexpected_costs: I didn't encounter any unexpected costs. I spend a lot of money on food and personal spendings, because I traveled a lot and just really wanted to have all the experiences. You can definitely live in Lisbon for a lot less.
cost_comparison: Housing was way more expensive than what I expected, the housing market in Lisbon has really gone wild in the last few years. I also chose a more expensive option, you can definitely live for a lot less. Also it is not that cheap to buy groceries, but on the bright side it is pretty cheap (compared to Copenhagen) to eat out.
activities_available: Some sport teams.
activities_recommended: I didn't attend any.
weekend_recommendations: Portugal is really easy and cheap to travel around. I can recommend going to Ericeira for a surf camp (but there is also a lot of options to surf at a one of the many beaches in Lisbon), go watch the huge waves in Nazaré, take a trip to Porto and then you should definitely go to Madeira or the Azores. Lisbon itself is also such a nice city with so much to do. I spend a lot of weekends at the beaches, just chilled in the city or went to Cascais or Sintra.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: I unfortunately only socialized with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Everything goes so slow. Nobody is in a hurry.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the slow living.
top3_advice: Everything goes really slow, you might as well just adjust to it as soon as possible. Hereby meaning also all the administrative things, that we are used to going fast at UCPH. All courses have mandatory attendance. It is hard to get the highest grades, but almost nobody fails any of the courses.
other_useful_info: I would attend the welcome sessions since it gives you a great opportunity to meet the other students quickly.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many students from other countries. My English has really improved and it is so nice to have friends in so many countries.
greatest_challenge: Finding housing. We looked way too late and therefore also ended up with speeding way too much. I would therefore recommend looking as early as possible. We thought it would be possible to see some of the flats, but that was not an option in any of the ones we looked at, so you might as well just book from home.

crucial_aspects: Interesting human rights-oriented electives at the host university.
overall_comments: My overall experience at Universidade Catolica Portuguesa was very good. I had some interesting electives, met exchange students from all of the world, and the campus of the university was nice.
info_ease: The information provided by the host university was very limited upon arrival as the plan of electives and courses was not final before the beginning of the semester. It meant that I could not fill out the OLA, have my electives accepted at Københavns Universitet upon arrival and apply for my Erasmus Grant before the start of the semester.
arrival_assistance: The host university held a welcome session for all exchange students at the beginning of the semester. At the welcome session we finally got all the information about courses that we needed to apply for our Erasmus grant.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: My overall experience at Universidade Catolica Portuguesa was very good. I had some interesting electives, met exchange students from all of the world, and the campus of the university was nice.
registration_process: We got an email from the international office of the host university with information and a guide to register. It was easy to follow.
registration_help: It was possible to write an email to the international office of the host university, and if they knew the answer, they would reply really quick. Unfortunately, information about the available courses came very late, so they were not able to provide much information about that upon arrival.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted to have.
registration_advice: It is easy, and if you have any question, the international office at the university is very helpful.
academics_comments: My overall experience at Universidade Catolica Portuguesa was very good. I had some interesting electives, met exchange students from all of the world, and the campus of the university was nice.
course_level: It was different from course to course depending on the teacher.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. The level of participation was very important for one's final grade, and most of the exams were handwritten exams of 2 hours.
courses_enrolled: EU Asylum and Migration Law, International Criminal Law, The Law of the WTO, We the Peoples - the UN as a Legal Forum, The Law of Fighting Poverty, Introduction to International Legal Theory, Introduction to Global Law, Right to Fair Trial.
recommended_courses: I would recommend The Law of the WTO and We the Peoples - the UN as a Legal Forum. The Law of WTO is taught by a guest teacher from New York University (NYU), and he is very inspiring and made the topic surprisingly interesting. The teacher of We the Peoples - the UN as a Legal Forum is a member of the ILC and head of the legal department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Portugal, and she both has a deep academic knowledge of the topic and a practical view on the functioning of the UN.
unexpected_costs: The housing prices were higher than expected.
cost_comparison: Housing.
activities_available: I did not hear of any clubs or sports activities on campus.
activities_recommended: I did not hear about any available on campus.
weekend_recommendations: Go surfing, go on trips outside of Lisbon (Sintra, Caparica, Cascais), and visit some of all the good museums in Lisbon.
culture_adjustment: It was easy, and I like really like the Portuguese culture.
cultural_challenges: The most challenging part was that many things are decided last minute. For example, the semester plan was final the first week of the semester, and I was supposed to get the courses accepted at KU in advance.
culture_appreciated: The Portuguese people are very social, they meet outside at night, eat well and in the whole month of June, there is a huge street festival in Lisbon with community dining, barbecuing and music.
top3_advice: You will get most information when the semester has already started but things will be sorted out eventually.
other_useful_info: The host university provides "seminars" and "courses". "Seminars" are electives with classes of 1-2 weeks ending with the final exam during the semester, while "courses" have 1-2 classes every week all semester with the final exam in the exam period, around a month after the last week of classes.
most_rewarding: Meeting all the other exchange students from all of the world.
greatest_challenge: In some weeks, I had 3-4 seminars at the same time which meant that I had classes from 08:00-20:00 at the university, ending with 4 exams in only 2 days.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study in a vibrant city which was big enough to feel like a big city but still small enough so you get to know it properly during your exchange. It was also crucial to me that it was a destination I hadn't visited before, so it would be a fresh start. It was also a very big plus that Lisbon has such nice weather, so you want to be outside for all the months of your exchange.
info_ease: I think the university was pretty informative. The planning of the courses was not final, so a lot of the courses that I chose ended up being on the 2nd and 3rd trimester, so I had to switch. It was no big deal though.
arrival_assistance: There was two orientation days where they gave us the most important information. In general the people responsible for exchange were super open and helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The process of registering at the university was fine. But signing up to courses was via emails, and I had to switch courses later on. There is no platform to see in which courses you are enrolled which is a bit confusing.
registration_help: The international office
registration_success: The dates of the courses were not in place until the week before the semester started. Therefore I had to switch courses and the selection of courses available was therefore way smaller than what I first thought.
registration_advice: Take it chill. Don't stress about them not giving out information in good time, cause it will often come pretty late.
course_level: I took courses on the LLM
teaching_comparison: It varied a lot. Some professors were very interactive and others were just lecturing on their own. Also, a lot of the exams were write at home-essays, which I was not used to.
courses_enrolled: Global Financial Regulation Comparative Corporate Law Startup Law Competition Law Data Science for Lawyers The law of European Integration Legal Research European Football Law Legal Writing Generative AI for Lawyers
recommended_courses: Comparative Corporate Law - very interesting professor. The law of European Integration - very good if you want to get a better understanding of how the European Union functions in real life.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Food was a bit cheaper than expected
activities_available: Social activities were a bit limited, but plenty of opportunities through Erasmus or private events.
activities_recommended: Didn't participate in any
weekend_recommendations: Plenty of good trips to do: Maderia, Marrakech, Azores, Porto and Algarve Coast.
culture_adjustment: As I'm also European it was not too difficult.
socializing_tips: Be smiling and outgoing when meeting people in classes. Especially during the first few weeks when no friend groups are really 'settled', it is pretty easy to just talk to the people sitting next to you in class.
cultural_challenges: The slow approach to everything. Going to supermarkets og anything administered by the government will take time.
culture_appreciated: Openness and the food.
top3_advice: Make use of the good weather while you're there, do many weekend trips don't be afraid to try new things.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Meeting so many great people of different culture. It was so amazing to explore new friendships in a new city
greatest_challenge: Leaving

crucial_aspects: The weather and being close to the sea. I wanted to surf.
overall_comments: The best thing I have done for myself in relation to my studies.
info_ease: Not that easy. But it worked out. I just needed to be patient.
arrival_assistance: There was a welcome session on the first day of school.
arrival_comments: The woman in charge of the exchange students was unfortunately not easy to get in touch with - it wasn't until later that we were told she was sick.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The best thing I have done for myself in relation to my studies.
registration_process: I recieved an e-mail about where and when I was supposed to show up at school. We recieved a student card at the first day.
registration_help: Did not need it.
registration_success: The courses available for my semester were not quite the same as those I had chosen for my pre-approval. I feel like everyone had to change something at least once. I was lucky and got enrolled in all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Do not stress. It is the southern of Europe so they are very chill. It will take some time but it will work out.
academics_comments: The best thing I have done for myself in relation to my studies.
course_level: The courses are small (between 3-6 ECTS), so there was not a lot to study.
teaching_comparison: It was different. I had to participate more than at UCPH. Also, most of the teachers took attendance. But it varies from the professors.
courses_enrolled: International Criminal Law EU Asylum and Migration Law European Fundamental and Human Rights Law International Arbitration International Law of the Sea Introduction to EU Competition Law Introduction to EU Internal Market Introduction to Islamic Legal Thought
recommended_courses: EU Asylum and Migration Law - the teacher was nice, the course was relevant, and the exam was easy/doable. European Fundamental and Human Rights Law - a passionate teacher, which made it more fun - the exam was a mood court. International Arbitration - very intelligent teacher and the exam was easy:) Introduction to Islamic Legal Thought - very nice teacher, interesting subject - no one ever failed this course.
unexpected_costs: Transportation is free in Lisbon if you are under 24 y/o. I paid 40 Euros for my navegante card each month.
cost_comparison: The rent is quite high. Food is cheap.
activities_available: Women volleyball Male football
activities_recommended: Try the samba. Go to the Erasmus events at least once - then you have tried it.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Nazare and see the waves. Go surfing in Costa de Caparica. Go watch a football match. A five days trip to Madeira!
culture_adjustment: Haven't met that many Portuguese but a lot of international students which waas fun.
socializing_tips: Join the other students when they are doing something.
cultural_challenges: The Italians have a different approach to what it means to arrive on time - they are often late. The language barrier can be challenging, but I think you'll just have to get used to that.
culture_appreciated: The slow life. Don't stress too much about everything. It will all work out in the end.
top3_advice: 1. Be patient; they will probably not reply as fast as you want them to. 2. Choose the courses that start early in the semester. We all became friends because we met within the first weeks - I know other people who did not have those courses found it harder to make friends at school. 3. Be open-minded. They do it differently from UCPH, but it is a nice perspective.
other_useful_info: You don't use books. So leave the highlighters, pencils and your reading stand at home :)
most_rewarding: The friendships I made.
greatest_challenge: Establishing a new life in a new country.
other_comments: If you are in doubt, you should just do it. You will learn so much. And if you don't like it, you are not that far from home, and the semester will end at some point.

crucial_aspects: Good weather, international environment, and strong academic reputation.
overall_comments: Amazing experience with great weather, many international friends, and big improvement in my English.
info_ease: Quite easy. Most information was shared by email before arrival, but keep in mind that Católica answers slowly, so you need to be patient and pro-active.
arrival_assistance: Introduction meetings, campus tour, and help from international coordinators.
arrival_comments: Staff were friendly and helpful (but slow)!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Amazing experience with great weather, many international friends, and big improvement in my English.
registration_process: Registration was done online before the semester started, but you could edit your choices once you arrived.
registration_help: Help by email from the international office.
registration_success: I had to change most of my initially preferred courses after arrival.
registration_advice: Register as early as possible and don’t get frustrated. The university is not always certain which courses will run in your semester when you have to register, so you will most likely need to change your choices once you arrive.
academics_comments: Amazing experience with great weather, many international friends, and big improvement in my English.
course_level: Challenging but manageable.
teaching_comparison: More interactive and discussion-based.
courses_enrolled: International Commercial Arbitration and Investment Dispute Resolution Comparative Judicial Decision-Making Trademark Law Comparative Corporate Law Transnational Migration and Refugee Law Data Science for Lawyers Data Protection Law Law and Automation Generative AI for Lawyers
recommended_courses: I would recommend International Commercial Arbitration and Investment Dispute Resolution and Data Protection Law because they are practical, well-taught and very relevant for an international legal career. The tech courses like Data Science for Lawyers and Law and Automation are also interesting and different from typical law courses at UCPH. Be aware that you need to take many more courses than in a normal semester at UCPH, because several courses are quite small (often 2 or 4 ECTS). This means more classes and more exams during the semester.
unexpected_costs: Higher rent than expected, and eating out a lot (cheaper than in Denmark, but it still adds up in the end)
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive, but food, public transport and eating out were cheaper than expected.
activities_available: Sports activities, surfing, and weekend trips around Portugal.
activities_recommended: Surfing and weekend trips, because they are fun and a great way to get to know other international students.
weekend_recommendations: Explore Lisbon, visit the beaches, go to Sintra and Cascais, and travel to Porto and the Algarve.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, people are open and friendly.
socializing_tips: Talk to people in class and group work.
cultural_challenges: Administrative processes can be slow and less structured.
culture_appreciated: The relaxed lifestyle, the weather and the social atmosphere.
top3_advice: Start looking for housing early, be patient with the administration, and say yes to social activities.
other_useful_info: If you take courses from the international one-year LLM programme, which I did as a master’s (MA) exchange student, most of your classmates are full-year students who study together for the entire year. I was there in the autumn semester and started at the same time as them, which made it easier to socialize. If you arrive in the spring semester, many of them will already know each other, which can make it a bit harder to integrate socially. recommended_courses: Visual culture ! Very interesting and I likes the teacher Paula a lot. Also, History of the US (colonial to 1900) was interesting. And Contemporary Drama was nice because it was different from what I am used to, and the teacher had a very good energy and not as conservative as the other teachers.
unexpected_costs: I had to move, and did not get my deposit back.
cost_comparison: Eating out is cheap, Alcohol is cheap. uber is very cheap and I would recommend using It in the evenings especially.
activities_available: Sports and clubs
activities_recommended: Surf school. Hiking trails (there are a lot in 1-hour distance from Lisbon). Roadtrip down south or to Eirica - a lot of nice beaches and cute small cities. Also go and watch a football game, It is a big experience watching Portugal play.
weekend_recommendations: Nazare, erica, sintra (for hiking. take the train in the morning and hike up to the castles). Go to the beach or chill in all the cute parks in Lisbon.
culture_adjustment: Easy as the culture is not that different from Denmark.
socializing_tips: Be open and ask questions. Also, try to do something active with them as hiking or surfing.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier, not all Portuguese people speak English, so try to learn a few Portuguese words to make it easier to communicate. But I would say that most people are good at speaking English.
culture_appreciated: The food (fresh fish and the culture around eating out and going out also in weekdays) and the amazing nature! Also, I appreciated how the people are very direct and not shy or introvert as Danes might be to strangers.
top3_advice: 1. Don't take the course Study of culture, as the teacher is very bad and not nice. 2. Come to the intro-day as it helps a lot to meet the other students and get to see the school before your first day. 3. You can buy food and coffee in the cantina or in the cafe, and there is student cafe where you can sit and work.
other_useful_info: It is very old school in terms of technology and classroom communication, so bring cold water for the warm days and make sure that you have power on your devices when going to class.
most_rewarding: To meet a lot of new friends, experiencing the beautiful nature and eating amazing food everyday.
greatest_challenge: That I had to move apartment after two weeks because of the bad housing. But it was worth it, and I ended up living with two other danish girls in a very nice apartment in Anjos.

crucial_aspects: Mostly culture, nature and language
info_ease: It was okay to find information before arrival. We got information always quite late, but the information we then got was good and informative. The international office at ULisboa was helpful over mail if you needed, but with most things you just had to be patient.
arrival_assistance: The school organised a welcome week with activites where we got important information, as well as the opportunity to meet other exchangestudents.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You get a fenix account where you follow all the steps, and then you have to fill out a learning agreement with your chosen courses that has to be approved by both your host institution and your sending institution. The different steps in the fenix portal is clear and well-structured, but it was a bit hard to understand where they communicate with you back if there`s any issues.
registration_help: The available courses in english was available online, even though they were the ones from the year before. We got the available classes for the upcoming year later, and there was some differences. Therefore I couldn`t do some of the classes that I wanted to do as they were not on the list relevant to me.
registration_success: I had to change two of my classes on my learning agreement as the classes was full.
registration_advice: Start early and be patient. It will work out in the end, they just work at a different speed down there:)
course_level: In general the level was a bit lower than at UCPH. Majority of my classes was quite easy, and there was not a lot of readings to do.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style resembled a bit more like high school were you have multible tests and presentations during the semester that all contribute to your overall grade. You also get graded on showing up to lectures and participation in class. We had handwritten exams, and more focus on remembering facts than academic practice.
courses_enrolled: Analising of the dramatic text, C2 English in the world of the arts, C2 English Creative Writing, Philosophy of art, North American Cinema
recommended_courses: Philosophy of art and North American cinema were both very cool!
unexpected_costs: Nothing really.
cost_comparison: Food, groceries and public transport were all cheaper than I thought it would be
activities_available: They had a great sport facility, as well as multible clubs you could join. Most of the clubs were operating in portugese so it wasn`t so normal for exchangestudents to join, but it`s definitely doable.
activities_recommended: I would recommend getting involved in all the erasmus events happening through organisations like ESN Lisboa and Erasmus Life Lisboa. Such an easy way to meet people, and they arrange events almost every day!
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend taking advantage of the great weather and nature by going surfing or going for hikes. Lisboa is also a great city for cultural events, and there`s lots of concerts and cultural events to attend during the weekend. It`s also a great country to travel in, so I would definitely recommend going travelling in some of the weekends.
culture_adjustment: It was okay. Sometimes a bit tricky when you don`t know the language, but not too bad.
socializing_tips: Approach them in class and make the first move
cultural_challenges: It a bit of an old fashioned and sometimes conservative culture, and sometimes the systems are a bit analog.
culture_appreciated: Very open and warm culture, also very alive and lively.
top3_advice: Be patient and don`t stress about the paperwork, it`s going to be okay. Attend the welcome week, that`s the best place to meet other exchangestudents when you first arrive! Also, enjoy it and make the most of it.
other_useful_info: I would recommend doing the portugese course offered by the school.
most_rewarding: Getting to meet all the amazing people and all the amazing places I got to see
greatest_challenge: Dealing with the cultural differences in the education system

institution: Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro
crucial_aspects: I was in Brazil traveling a bit around 5 years ago and just loved the way people approached me. But the country is so complex that I knew I was only scraping a surface and got curious to get to know Brazil with all of its joys and problems.
overall_comments: I give it a 10 now, not in the sense that I was happy all the time but in the sense that I really got challenged personally and learned a lot. Rio is lovely and I'm really happy that I went.
info_ease: From KU's side it was quite organized and even though there are some things you need to keep check of when traveling outside of Europe travel wise where you're more on your own, I was emailed about all deadlines regarding university stuff and also got informed on the essential visa things. Information flow from Brazil was quite slow but I got to learn when I got there that they're equally flexible and it's about keeping a cool mind
arrival_assistance: We got some emails from an intro group for exchange students with meet up dates and stuff. Unfortunately I was misinformed by more official sites of UFRJ about the semester start which made the beginning very chaotic because, in addition to it all being in portuguese, I started my courses 3 lectures late and it therefore took some extra time to get into what the courses were all about. But when I found out that something was wrong, a random professor who just happened to be nearby took an hour out of his day just to help me without me even asking.
arrival_comments: The international office was really not very helpful but everybody else was just amazing to help me fix my situation.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I give it a 10 now, not in the sense that I was happy all the time but in the sense that I really got challenged personally and learned a lot. Rio is lovely and I'm really happy that I went.
registration_process: Well as mentioned, I was misinformed about the date of the university start. Long story short, the bachelor degree's semester start was delayed due to political issues and I was informed by the international office of UFRJ that mine was too, although it wasn't the case for the master's degree. So I came to the office mildly panicing about if it was even possible to be registered 2 weeks late. But I just had to ask the professors if I could join, and if they were cool with it, there was no issue.
registration_help: The master's degree administration office were quite helpful.
registration_success: Very unsuccesful haha, the 2 classes I signed up for at home were not offered so I had to sign up for some others. But it all worked out.
registration_advice: Don't think too much about the courses in advance because they do change some things that's impossible to figure out online and it all works out as you get there. And arrive early and go to the campus administration office to get some information before semester start because things work quite differently. And most importantly, know some Portuguese before you arrive, I would've been really stressed if I had been a complete beginner. The more you can communicate, the softer you'll land cause most of them really do not speak English at all.
academics_comments: I give it a 10 now, not in the sense that I was happy all the time but in the sense that I really got challenged personally and learned a lot. Rio is lovely and I'm really happy that I went.
course_level: It was quite difficult to follow the lectures in the beginning due to the language barrier. I was about intermediate when I started but daily Portuguese and academic Portuguese are quite different so it takes a little time to get into it. But had it been my first language I think I'd have been just fine.
teaching_comparison: It was smaller classes and a mix of lecture and class discussion all in one. They're not so clear on when class starts and ends and when we have breaks and stuff so I could sometimes miss the degree of structure from at home but my professors were quite enthusiastic about their classes and their academic views are really different from some of the mainstream opinions at home so I learned a lot from having contested some views I just took for granted.
courses_enrolled: EPI701 Economia Política Internacional I (taught by Mauricio Metri) EPI738 Economia Política do Desenvolvimento da China (taught by Isabela Nogueira)
recommended_courses: I'd recommend both. The courses are part of a course series and wouldn't necessarily be exactly the same but I really liked the professors and learned a lot from the content because they have a completely different discourse on both geopolitics and China. I mention the professors as an important factor because not all professors at the university are equally good and with the flexible teaching style that matters even more than in DK.
unexpected_costs: I was warned that I'd end up taking the Uber a lot but it was more true than I'd expected. I didn't feel comfortable taking the metro after 8-9pm on weekdays so if I wanted to go somewhere, I'd very often go with an Uber. It's really cheap but it adds up.
cost_comparison: Housing was cheaper than I expected. I lived quite well in a big place in a somewhat safe neighborhood for less money than I'd pay at home. It's worth the extra 500 reais a month to live in Zona Sul.
activities_available: The university itself has some social offers (dance classes and other fun classes, as well as sports teams that are quite competitive) that I didn't take part in because it was at the main campus in the north part of town and I was at the social sciences campus in the south, almost an hour away. But Rio just has so much to offer and people are so open, so if you have a hobby, go find somewhere to do it and you'll most certainly meet people if you're open too.
activities_recommended: Show up for the intro days for the exchange students!!! I wanted to try mostly being with brazilians but it's just so nice to still have a network of people who also want to go explore. And Interpoli (the exchange welcoming program) has a lot of Brazilians so often we would end up being 50/50 brazilians/foreigners when we met up and still speak mostly Portuguese. Hobby wise, I didn't do anything that had to do with uni but danced a lot of forró and went hiking every week. Rio has a lot of mountains and they're really easy to get to when you're over the firste time's hurdles, and I really enjoyed that. And everything goes on by Instagram, I'd have liked to know that earlier. E.g. if you wanna find places to dance, sites like "forronorio" tell you exactly where you can go do that every single day.
weekend_recommendations: Every single mountain top of Rio itself :) E.g. Bico do Papagayo, Morro dos Dois Irmãos and Pedra da Gavea are really nice. If you have a lot of time off at some point, Salvador and Chapada Diamantina in Bahia are lovely.
culture_adjustment: It was not my first time in Brazil so I had an idea of what I was getting myself into. And people are just so nice that it was easy most of the time. There were culture shocks along the way but I'd have been disappointed if it had all been easy.
socializing_tips: Be open and start some conversations. And patient. I only figured out I had a lot in common with a few of my classmates about a month into the course.
cultural_challenges: Their very high tolerance to noise, e.g. loud music in the living room and such. And those mini cultural codes where I had no chance of knowing that I was being unintentionally strange or impolite in their eyes until someone luckily told me. And that people didn't trust each other and some therefore also didn't make an effort to be trustable. It is true that you have to be a bit less naive on the streets of Rio than in Cph.
culture_appreciated: Their openness, their friendliness and curiosity, especially to foreigners, how easy it was to get to know people, how some would spend their time helping a stranger out without having to at all, and their latin american charm :)
top3_advice: 1) I hope you'll love it as much as I did 2) I'll highly advise you to prioritize learning Portuguese in advance, it'll mean a lot to how easily you'll get into the culture and how fast you'll start making Brazilian friends 3) Don't forget to research on and exploit all the city has to offer. Cause it really is a lot.
other_useful_info: I got stressed about the practicalities before going because I only had the last information needed for e.g. my visa quite last minute. But somehow they always make it all work out. Get a hang of the visa application process and also start quite well in advance cause you'll have to go to the embassy a few times.
most_rewarding: I did have a great time in Rio, but the most rewarding part of it all was actually all the bumps on the way. And the new friends who made me get through it, and getting fluent in a new language as a direct product of all the bumps on the way :)
greatest_challenge: I arrived well before study start which was great to get a hang of the language. But being a month on "vacation" in a new city where you don't know anyone, nor where to go to get to know new people, can be quite lonely. So the first month was a bit long.
other_comments: It's all much less scary as soon as you get there :)

crucial_aspects: Explore new cultures and new country, sunny city, nice reputation of university. And I have heard so much great about Lisbon, I knew so many that recommended the university.
overall_comments: One of the best decisions I have my made in my life. It was an absolutely amazing and perfect experience despite covid. I met so many nice people and I explored most of Portugal. Lisbon has such a nice vibe, it is a capital but still kind of small and charming.
info_ease: Very easy, both the guidance office of Copenhagen and Nova School of Business and Economics were very helpful. The answered all my questions. KU also invited me to a webinar about studying abroad.
arrival_assistance: A lot of mails, a lot of webinars and a lot of orientation and introductions at school.
arrival_comments: The mobility office at Nova SBE would reply in a couple of hours - so helpful!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: One of the best decisions I have my made in my life. It was an absolutely amazing and perfect experience despite covid. I met so many nice people and I explored most of Portugal. Lisbon has such a nice vibe, it is a capital but still kind of small and charming.
registration_process: As mentioned before, on a website.
registration_help: For me, it was not necessary to ask for help regarding the registration, it was really easy.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted! So very successful!
registration_advice: Check all your emails! You can find all the information there. But if you still have trouble, just send an email to the mobility team.
academics_comments: One of the best decisions I have my made in my life. It was an absolutely amazing and perfect experience despite covid. I met so many nice people and I explored most of Portugal. Lisbon has such a nice vibe, it is a capital but still kind of small and charming.
course_level: The level was not that high, a lot of information and not much math as in Copenhagen. Though, introduction to programming was difficult but it was easy to pass the course, because the grade was mostly based on hand-in-assignments. But courses like business history and development economics were kind of easy.
teaching_comparison: Very different from University of Copenhagen! A lot of group work, a lot of presentations and a lot of assignments. More workloade during the semester, but in the end the final exam was easier to pass. Also some of the courses had attendance and participation. For example, in development economics 50% of the grade were based on the final exam, 15% of the grade were based on a presentation, 30% were based on an assignment and lastly, 5% were based on participation.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Programming Development Economics Business History Advanced Microeconomics
recommended_courses: Development economics was really interesting. Business history was relevant but a bit boring. Introduction to Programming was difficult but really fun! I only chose advanced microeconomics because it was a mandatory course at University of Copenhagen.
unexpected_costs: I traveled a lot - for instance to the Azores, and that was of course an unexpected course but worth it! Then I just spent a lot of money on food, clothes, surf trips etc. But of course everything was cheap, but when you buy a lot of everything it just costs a lot of money.
cost_comparison: Food and drinks are cheap! You can get two beers and one shot for 2 euros! Sports were also cheap, I had private tennis lessons 4 times a month for only 35 euros (really cheap compared to Denmark). Housing was cheap as well (if you do not get scammed, as I have heard from other).
activities_available: A lot of sunset events where you drink beer and enjoy each others company. I guess if it was not for covid, more events would occur. I joined some surf trips with the school.
activities_recommended: Surf club, NovAfrica. But again, I did not join any but they seemed cool!
weekend_recommendations: See some of Portugal, visit Algarve, Porto etc. Go to Bairro Alto, go to K-Urban-Beach Club (bonus info: Portugeuse people go to clubs at 3 am to 7 am....). Go to some Erasmus events. Do not spend all your time reading books about microeconomics, spend your time with friends!
culture_adjustment: Portuguese people are really good at English, so language barrier was not a problem. Also, the local people are so nice and chill, maybe too chill.. You need to know about Portuguese time, the locals always show up late. You need to learn how to get patient.
socializing_tips: If you go to a bar or club, you will always end up talking to some locals. But at school, it is a bit difficult to interact with the locals. You spend most of the time with other internationals. Maybe if you join some clubs or the student union you could get to know the locals. When I was on some surf trips with the student union, I got to know some Portuguese students.
cultural_challenges: The Portuguese time... Everything is just slow. And they are not as remote as in Denmark. Even to get the transportation card, you need to fill in thousand of things on paper and wait hours in a queue to collect you transportation card.
culture_appreciated: The locals are so nice and openhearted. The people just enjoy life and they do not seem stressed at all compared to danish people. I felt safe all the time in the city, even though I lived in the city center, I never felt unsafe.
top3_advice: 1. Do not hold back, do all the things you want and do not pay all your attention to school. 2. Get as many friends as you can, so you always have people around you. 3. Live in the city center of Lisbon and not Carcavelos.
other_useful_info: It is summer until late october/beginning of november. I mean 25-30 degrees in late october. The sea water is really cold all year around! It will get cold in the night, so bring a warmer jacket for november and december. But still it can be around 23 degrees in november as well. Do not bring high heels, the streets of Lisbon is awful. Buy a "Erasmus Life Lisboa" card, so you can get discount and join events. Bring pencil, paper, calculator etc. Most of the exams are going to be on paper. Bring swimsuits!!
most_rewarding: Having so many amazing friends! When no one knows each other, it creates a perfect possibility to get friends from across the world. But most of all, I just had so much fun this semester.
greatest_challenge: Maybe all the team work and presentations at school, but it was manageable. Though, the best part about exchange is the social life, the greatest challenge could also be the social life. I did not have many days off where I just spend time alone. You were constantly doing something or seeing someone. That takes a lot of energy, though I do not regret all the things I did. But remember to takes some days off, if you are just too exhausted of all the new impressions.

crucial_aspects: Personally, I wanted to experience the Southern European way of life, especially of the Iberean peninsula. Also, experiencing how different universities across Europe compares to that of KU.
overall_comments: Whilst Lisbon is an amazing city and Portugal is a lovely country with so many things to see and do, the university does leave a lot to be desired. Housing quality is not that good, and if you live in Lisbon, the time spent on getting to the university can be quite high. A more personal complaint is, that both the university and Lisbon itself are very dominated by tourism, digital nomads and other international students. So you will probably not get the authentic Portuguese experience and you are quite unlikely to make any Portuguese friends. In Lisbon you are just another foreigner.
info_ease: Whilst you do get sent some information by the administration, you do have to find a lot of the information yourself. Some information can be a bit difficult to find, and I found myself often being unsure if I had found the right place.

registration_process: For master students there is a bidding system, where you are allocated a number of points that you can spend on the courses that you want. The courses are then allocated to those who have spent the largest number of point on a given course. Courses that you may want, can have overlapping schedules either for classes or the examns. This makes planning for what courses to bid on very tedious and it is quite likely that you have to make compromises, to make them fit into the schedule. Another point of bother was that the bidding only started two weeks ahead of the beginninig of classes, which again was a cause of uncertainty.
registration_help: Very limited. During a presentation by some of the staff, one of them mentioned, that exchange students tend to find the system confusing and/or annoying, but that they nevertheless insisted it is a good system. Likewise, local students also think the system is stupid.
registration_success: I got all the courses that I planned on getting, and it is usually not a problem that people get denied for their courses after the bidding.
registration_advice: Don't think too hard about it! Most courses are not of that high a level, so it is not like you are going to be missing out on that much either way.

teaching_comparison: In most courses you only have lectures by the professor and only 3 hours a week. The final grade usually only consists of 50% from the exam. Where the rest can be divided into class participation, class presentations, quizzes in class and assignments.

crucial_aspects: I found that Portugal was a country that I did not know that much about, even though it has been a country with big historical impact, both in an European and international context. However, since Portugal is in the EU I found it to be much easier to go on exchange here, compared to going outside of EU.
overall_comments: I had an excellent stay, and found people to very welcoming. In addition to this, it was very easy to meet people to hang out with, since there were so many other exchange students.
info_ease: There was many informations regarding social Erasmus activities. However it should be noted, that it said on the internet that you had to reserve a spot for all of the activities weeks in advance, when in practice, you could sign up for many activities the day before. This could have saved me for some money, since I ended up not attending some of the social activities since they often overlapped.
arrival_assistance: The university did not provide that many informations. It's important to come to the first orientation at NOVA, but also to discuss things with the other students if there's anything you're in doubt about.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had an excellent stay, and found people to very welcoming. In addition to this, it was very easy to meet people to hang out with, since there were so many other exchange students.
registration_process: Their system is set up like a betting system. You have 100 virtual coins, and then you bet the amount on each course that you want to attend. If you bid higher than others, you get on the course. There are multiple betting rounds though, so if you don't get your first priority you can bet on something else. You can also change your mind, and drop a course and get your coins back to bet on something else. Be aware that you can't have overlapping classes, since class participation is part of the grade.
registration_help: Satisfactory level of help. There was explanation on the intro day, but there was also a pdf explanation when going on to the side to bet on courses. It's a quick navigation tour but it's sufficient.
registration_success: I only took 14 ECTS, since that was all I had left of my studies besides my thesis. I unfortunately only got one of my first priorities (the courses are 7 or 3.5 ECTS for master students), but then I got my second and third priorities. I took courses that some of my friend I meet in the intro week also took, so that we could arrange group work together. I can recommend doing that. Otherwise there is also primarily foreign students at master level, so it's relatively easy to meet someone at class to talk to as well.
registration_advice: Be quick to sign up for classes. Bet high on your most important courses. Sometimes the courses are filled up, however that won't be stated, since people can sign off courses as well. I would advise betting high in the first round, and if you then don't get a spot on a course, you need to go after something else. If it's an attractive course there is a high probability that there is no more spots left.
academics_comments: I had an excellent stay, and found people to very welcoming. In addition to this, it was very easy to meet people to hang out with, since there were so many other exchange students.
course_level: I took two courses. One of the courses had a level comparable to UCPH, however the other course had much lower level.
teaching_comparison: It's quite different. Class participation is part of the grade, so people will participate much more that what I was used to. In addition to this, there is also midterms in many courses. The teachers wanted to learn students names.
courses_enrolled: Banking and Data Analytics for Finance
recommended_courses: Data Analytics for Finance was a relatively tough course where you could potentially learn a lot. However, there was an assignment every second week, a midterm as well as a final project, so it will take a lot of work. Banking was a very easy course, however not very interesting in my opinion. However, it can be registered as a seminar, which is a much much easier way to do it, compared to doing a seminar at UCPH. My workload was 80/20 between the two courses.
unexpected_costs: I ended up eating out a lot more than expected. However, it's a good way to be together with other Erasmus students, since most students don't have a place where they can invite people over. You have to get the yellow, monthly transportation card, it saves many headaches and is also very cheap compared to how far you can get on it.
cost_comparison: Food was also more expensive that expected, cheaper than Copenhagen, but not by that much. However if you go to some bars at Bairro Alto, it's a lot cheaper than in Copenhagen.
activities_available: NOVA has a football club you can sign up for. There is also many activities regarding surfing. There is also a monthly friday party.
activities_recommended: Try to sign up for surfing. It's challenging and demanding, but very fun, and very cheap compared to what you would expect.
weekend_recommendations: If you get the yellow travel card, you can go very way. Sintra is a very popular travel goal. However I would also go south and visit Sesimbra and Setúbal
culture_adjustment: People are generally quite good at English, and people are used to foreigners. I found it easy to adjust. People from the southern part of Portugal is very friendly but also more reserved than in the north, where they are more like spanish or Italian people.
socializing_tips: It's difficult to meet Portuguese people. But be open and be sure to get people you meets WhatsApp number, so you can keep in touch if you meet someone nice.
cultural_challenges: I found it quite easy to adjust. One thing however, is that the tempo is very slow. Often there is long lines since people take their time, and you can expect to wait a lot longer than expected on the bus or tram.
culture_appreciated: People are very friendly. They are also where down to earth, and are not afraid to celebrate.
top3_advice: Go on day trips and explore cities around Lisboa. Get the monthly train card as quickly as possible. However, the wait time is very long. It's at Marques du Pombal train station. Get help from someone that speaks Portuguese/spanish or use google translate Live in Lisbon, not Carcavelos.
other_useful_info: The clubs are for free for NOVA students at Thursdays.
most_rewarding: The city is very beautiful. It's run down but very charming. People are very nice. It was a great experience to go abroad where I had no expectations or obligations, I could just explore and be impulsive.
greatest_challenge: Finding accommodation, I stayed the first 4 weeks in a hostel

crucial_aspects: Location and culture of the host country and city as well as the chance to study at a well-respected, international university.
info_ease: It was a bit confusing as the university has multiple platforms with different information, however the international office was very good at communicating through Teams and SharePoint.
arrival_assistance: Information regarding the welcome day, but not much additional information. However, most was told during the introduction day.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was very easy, just had to sign some papers through email.
registration_help: In general the help was very good and useful, as the registration can be confusing.
registration_success: Registering for classes at Nova is through a bidding auction, which is very bad and can be very confusing at first. I did not get many of the classes I tried to register for, which resulted in me getting classes I didnt really find that interesting as they had to ba aligned with scheduels etc.
registration_advice: Definitely make sure you have plenty of time before the bidding process begins to asses all class schedules as well as exam schedules as they tend to overlap a lot as the exam period is very short.
course_level: Most courses are only 3,5 ECTS, which means the content is very limited and thus not that difficult. Furthermore, a lot of the courses are management and finance, which, from my experience, is generally a bit easier than other courses, but it is possible to choose courses that are more identical to the ones distributed at University of Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. At Nova, the focus is primarily on group work, presentations in class and class participation, and the exam grade is only 40-60% of the grade. However, from my experience, the other students are very dedicated and good students, so the group work part is nothing to worry about, and the presentations are fine as well, although a bit waste of time.
courses_enrolled: Financial Statements Analysis Energy Finance Strategic Costing Sports Careers Seminar Series Global Energy Markets Operations Strategy Financial Crises in History Corporate Social Responsibility
recommended_courses: Global Energy Markets Operations Strategy Financial Crises in History Corporate Social Responsibility Are the ones I would recommend. Definitely stay away from Financial Statement Analysis as the work load is very heavy and the exam is very difficult. Most students at Nova do not recommend it, and it was definitely a mistake that I attended the course. However, if you are very interested in balance sheet, income statements and forecasts you will learn a lot from the course.
unexpected_costs: There were no unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Alcohol and going to restaurants are very cheap compared to what I expected. Grocery shopping is a bit cheaper than in Denmark in general, but still more expensive than anticipated.
activities_available: The Nova Student Union arranged many different events and trips that students could attend. E.g. trips to the Azore Islands, surf trips to the best surf places in the world etc.
activities_recommended: I attended a weekend surf trip for 200 Euros with everything paid for which I could definitely recommend. It is mostly other exchange students and then the student union so everyone is open and are there for the same reasons. The various trips in general to different places I could recommend, especially for meeting new people and I recommend doing it at the start of the semester to meet as many people as possible.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the city of Sintra (when it's not tourist season) - very beautiful place with big castles and palaces. However, there are too many tourists during high peak season and everything costs money to see. Go to the Algarve coast for a weekend - I would recommend renting a house by the beach or in the city of Lagos or Albufeira. Go to Porto, a bit like Lisbon but smaller and less touristy. Go to Madeira or the Azore Islands - pretty cheap flights and they look like Hawaii. Try surfing - at Lisbon Surf Camp in Carcavelos, Nova students get 12 surf opportunities (wet suit and surf board) a month for about 50 euros with 4 lessons from professionals.
culture_adjustment: The Portugese are generally very slow and relaxed, therefore it can be a bit frustrating for as it seems sort of incompetent sometimes. However, the people of Portugal are very open and friendly and generally very good at English, so you will feel very welcome by everyone, and they all want to talk and learn.
socializing_tips: Talk with the ones assigned to your group in class and attend Nova Student Union events.
cultural_challenges: Portugal seems very inefficient, which took some time to get used to as everything was very slow. Get used to everything starting 30-60 minutes after the scheduled time.
culture_appreciated: Very welcoming and open culture, which was very appreciated coming from an exchange student from Denmark. They are very friendly.
top3_advice: Look for apartments early and use the app idealista. Look for apartments in either Bairro Alto (the party area) or Chiado (the best food and drinks and very beautiful - also right next to Bairro Alto). Both areas are close to the train station and metro. I do not recommend living in a place where you a dependant on taking the bus as they are very inconvenient. However, the metro is very good. Get the monthly metro card for 40 euros each month through Nova, also works for trains and bus. You need to take the train from the station Cais do Sodre to get to Nova. Be very engaged in events with other exchange students and students in general. Will make your stay more enjoyable and will get many experiences.
other_useful_info: There are many nice areas to live in in Lisbon, but make sure to choose an area that is close to the metro. There is a gym on campus that also has gyms in Lisbon and you can acces them all. Try to pool your classes together so you don't have them spread out on all days of the week, as they are usually only 1,5-2 hours long, and you spend a total of about 1,5 hours of transportation each day.
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of new people from different countries was definitely one of the best things about my experience as well as living in a different culture and country that is so open and friendly towards foreigners.
greatest_challenge: Not having the same network of friends and people you know, especially at university where you can ask for help on choosing courses, where to find previous exams, getting notes etc. You are very much on your own unless you get to know someone.
