course_level: Helt generelt på tværs af mine kurser, så er der ingen forventning om at man læser bøger. Der kan være tilknyttet nogle bøger til ethvert kursus, men tit og ofte, så bliver de ikke læst af de franske studerende, hvorfor at man godt kan nøjes med kun at tage til forelæsningerne. Efter min mening gør det niveauet lavere, og de udbudte opgaver i løbet af semestret og eksamerne er også på et lavere niveau end hvad jeg har været vant til på KU.
teaching_comparison: Udelukkende forelæsninger, hvor underviseren udlægger et emne med inddragelse af nogle tekstpassager, der citeres. Normen i det franske uddannelsessystem er at man nedskriver hvert eneste ord, som underviseren siger - komplet unødvendig og spild af tid efter min mening. Koblet med at det ikke forventes at man læser op, så bliver det derfor vigtigere at man tager noter i undervisningen.
courses_enrolled: Littérature comparée 4 Philosophie contemporaine Philosophie générale 10 Philosophie générale 11 Philosophie méthodologie
recommended_courses: Kurser, der specialiserer sig i én filosof eller en periode. Jeg var rigtig glad for "Philosophie contemporaine", der handlede om Arthur Schopenhauer og hans hovedværk: Verden som vilje og forestilling. Ligeledes havde jeg kurset "Philosophie générale 11", der omhandlede tysk idealisme, så vi specialiserede os i Kant, Fichte, Schelling og Hegel.
unexpected_costs: Ingen - til gengæld var det uventet, at jeg ikke behøvede at tegne et franske telefonabonnement
cost_comparison: Dagligvare er er en smule dyrere end i Danmark. Bøger er kriminelt billige, men kvaliteten følger derefter. Alt der ligger tæt på promenaden og i den gamle by er dyrere, men det pga. turisme.
activities_available: Der var nogle mindre koncerter og sociale aktivteter på universitetet. Hver torsdag ville der også være en sprogudvekslingsaften på en bar, som jeg kun kan anbefale at man tager til. Hver måned ville der også være en udflugt til et sted uden for Nice, som mange jeg snakkede med også var glade for.
activities_recommended: Torsdagsbar, selvom at du har kurser om fredagen, og udflugter hver måned, og ellers de oplevelser som byen Nice tilbyder
weekend_recommendations: Enten gå en tur i de parker Nice har at tilbyde eller smut i vandet nede på stranden. Man kan også tage på vandretur i oplandet rundt om Nice, og så er det også nemt at tage toget til Cannes, Antibes, Monaco, Menton eller de andre byer, der ligger på Azur-kysten
culture_adjustment: Relativt nemt. Hvis man har været i Frankrig, og kan en smule fransk vil det ikke komme som det store chok.
socializing_tips: Lad vær. Min erfaring med franske studerende er at de unge og umodne, og hvis dit franske ikke er på konversationsniveau, så bliver det svært for de fleste franske studerende, at holde en samtale kørende på engelsk. Mange af mine udenlandske venner hvis fransk var rigtig godt brugte heller ikke forfærdelig meget tid sammen med franske studerende. Bliv venner med andre udvekslingsstuderende: De er mere åbne og sociale og mere spændende.
cultural_challenges: Primært sprog, men også nogle skikke og normer. Bl.a. at man spiser senere i Frankrig, tid er en relativ størrelse, og at date kan også være en udfordring.
culture_appreciated: Al den gode mad og vin man kan få relativt billigt dernede, og rabat på samtlige kulturtilbud for studerende.
top3_advice: Hav tålmodighed med skolen Fjern det pres der ligger i at du skal forbedre dit franske Find dig nogle gode venner
other_useful_info: Spis frokost på en af de tre Armand-bagerier, som ligger i byen.
most_rewarding: At sidde på en café midt inde i centrum, og se folk gå forbi, mens man drikker kaffe, øl, vin og snakker om filosofi i flere timer med sin gode ven fra Østrig.
greatest_challenge: At studere på et fransk universitet, når ens sproglige niveau ikke er helt på universitetsniveau
other_comments: Ingen yderligere kommentarer - jeg synes efterhånden, at jeg har skrevet så meget

activities_available: different talent shows some culture festivals a lot of sport if you are into that, travels to iles du salut or marais de kaw.
activities_recommended: the sport at uni is cool, some marathons are held during the year in kourou and cayenne. Go out in nature and do some sentier at night, maybe get to know some other young people working in nature associations, they do a lot of outings in nature to see animals.
weekend_recommendations: Iles du salut, marais de kaw, saint laurent du maronie and go with a pirog to grand santi and fly home, saül, do some sentier, go to ilet la mere or iles du grand connetable, go to brazil in Oyapock, go see cacao d'amazonie, go take a beer with friends at ole la terre, fifties or cocosoda (le food truck peruvien in Montabo), go enjoy a beer and see Jeune Gueule brewery, go to Kourou. culture_appreciated: The difference is so huge, it's so diverse and you learn a lot about so many different cultures. it's very interesting. Guyana is so diverse culturally and in the languages. other_useful_info: You must go in nature here, even if you are not a nature guy or girl, try to go in the rainforest because it's 97 % of the territory.
most_rewarding: It's hard to choose one, Iles du salut, Marais de Kaw, the anthropology course was very interesting. The friends i met here. The kindness of Pedro and Maelle working at the BRI.
greatest_challenge: It was to walk in the rainforest and not to be scared of snakes. But by doing it and watching others do it you actually realise how normal it is and how it's not dangerous at all.
other_comments: no

crucial_aspects: I had heard good things about the city, Brussels, and I wanted to experience living somewhere else more "long-term". I also wanted to learn some French.
info_ease: It was o.k., but very confusing in the beginning. The info meeting was almost entirely in French, and the general information given by e-mail vs the info meeting did not entirely match, which led to confusion. I and my friends had a stressful time trying to sort everything out upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: A contact person (per e-mail) and she was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had to fill in a green form (personal information) and a pink form (final choice of courses). Some had to do a "google form". The first two weeks were open to "shuffle around" in courses to try them out before choosing them. For some it may have been nice, but I think I would have liked more certainty.
registration_help: The erasmus contact person.
registration_success: If I could have has more than one MA course, that would have been more suitable for me, but the choice of courses ended up ok.
registration_advice: There is a lot of information in the beginning, and it is stressed (a lot!) how important it is to respect the deadlines, otherwise there is nothing they can do - this did not seem to be true, though, and I think it would have been nice to know that despite the impression of the process being very strict, it is possible to arrange something else with the contact person.
course_level: It did not feel too different from KU.
teaching_comparison: I only had lectures and no seminars, which made it difficult to meet other students from university.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to political science Introduction to EU politics Cultural tourism issues
recommended_courses: Cultural tourism issues. Very interesting.
unexpected_costs: It is expensive to meet a lot of new people, because you would mostly meet up in public places (cafés, bars etc.).
cost_comparison: Transportation. As a student you can pay 17 euros for a transportation card that lasts a year (can be used in the city).
activities_available: Several sports activities through the university (ULB Sports).
activities_recommended: Unfortunately I can't say.
weekend_recommendations: Travel to other European cities closeby.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Be able to speak French - my level of French made it difficult, but I had a lot of tandems (language exchange partners).
cultural_challenges: The study period for the exams is different and more demanding for students, was my impression, but I took only 15 ects.
culture_appreciated: The waffles from the waffle wagons, they are the best ones.
top3_advice: I'm not sure, but in general I would recommend not being afraid to let yourself fall into the erasmus community (at least if you're not strong in French). In the end, the best friends I made were not from Belgium.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: The friends I made.
greatest_challenge: Loneliness in the beginning.

crucial_aspects: I choose ULB and Brussels as my destination to get wiser on the EU because I want to use it later in my career. I did not think- and still do not believe - that there is a better place in the world to gain more knowledge about the EU than at the Heart of the Union. As mentioned in my application I wished to improve my French by living in a country with French as official language and furthermore take courses in French. Since I am dreaming of working with European politics, where French is the key word for communication, this part was an important motivation for my exchange due to career opportunities in the future. Mastering the French language with its sophisticated and difficult nuances requires an everyday life with the language, where it fills in everything from teaching to shopping trips, but also in relationships to new acquaintances. A stay in Brussels will and have allowed me to live the life of a true European citizen.
overall_comments: Great stay. But - many bureaucratic barriers from both host university and home university. It takes a bit of the joy out of the whole process. Everything else was fine - and ULB is excellent at European politics.
info_ease: It has not exactly been easy. You are on your own and have to figure everything yourself. ULB has been good at sending out joint e-mails for all exchange students, but from the beginning I have been on my own. ULB has definitely been doing a better job than my home university (University of Copenhagen).
arrival_assistance: We got 3 joint e-mails to all exchange students with informations and instructions. Furthermore, ULB hosted a meeting on how to apply for courses.
arrival_comments: No.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Great stay. But - many bureaucratic barriers from both host university and home university. It takes a bit of the joy out of the whole process. Everything else was fine - and ULB is excellent at European politics.
registration_process: You needed to apply for courses in Google Docs followed by a pink form and later it became available online. Registration was handled through UCPH which was fine.
registration_help: You can e-mail the coordinator or use office hours.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted after the course catalogue was updated 2 weeks before the semester started. I think that was a little too late, since I already submitted my Learning Agreement at that time.
registration_advice: Be patient. Things are going slowly in Belgium.
academics_comments: Great stay. But - many bureaucratic barriers from both host university and home university. It takes a bit of the joy out of the whole process. Everything else was fine - and ULB is excellent at European politics.
course_level: I had a few MA-courses that I found very appropriate in level. The rest were BA-courses, which I think were a bit boring and banal.
teaching_comparison: It was a lot of rote learning and lacked a little reflection and larger lines compared to what I am used to in Copenhagen. However, I think the MA-courses were really good at translating theory into practice with simulation games and assignments.

recommended_courses: - Institutions and political representation: Gilles Piotters is a great teacher! - European Integration and Public Policy: Mrs. Crepsy takes the theory and place it into reality. unexpected_costs: Food was significantly more expensive than expected. You also eat out a lot.
cost_comparison: Food = more expensive Flights Denmark-Brussels = less expensive
activities_available: Sport, club for exchange students, trips etc.
activities_recommended: The exchange student club was great.
weekend_recommendations: Take trips around Belgium (get out of Brussels); Gent, Brugge, The Ardennes etc.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy, however, things are somewhat less formal and tend to be a bit messy.
socializing_tips: Meet both international students and the Danish interns
cultural_challenges: The garbage system and half solutions: Things are rarely followed to the door in Belgium if you do not push very hard.
culture_appreciated: Enjoying the weekend in peace and quiet. The shops, museums and so on are closed on Sundays, so Belgians get along with friends to relax and enjoy life
top3_advice: 1. Make use of the Danish network, but make sure not to stay in the closed Danish bubble alone. 2. Be sure to take EU-courses at ULB. They are extremely good at it. 3. Speak French - take advantage of the fact that you are in a country where you can improve your French.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: To learn about the European Union up close and have courses in French. It showed rapid progress.
greatest_challenge: Patience. Both with fellow students, professors and Belgians in general. There is a completely different pace and a more relaxed approach to things - regardless of their importance. As a Dane, it is a great contrast to experience.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: That I had the possibility to learn French, and that I could follow a lot of EU law-related courses.
overall_comments: The only downside is that it can be an administrative hell. It is very stressfull before and after you leave, and you have to fill out a lot of documents and coordinate them between the two universities. It can be difficult to attain all the information you need, and sometimes things will only get solved at the very last minute. But if you can be calm about that, the experience is really worth it!
info_ease: Very difficult! I wasn't really contacted much by ULB until a couple of days before my classes started. I also came to Brussels early to follow a French course provided by ULB, but in the end I couldn't follow the course, as it was impossible to attain information about it or contact anyone. I also ended up attending a lot of introductory lectures and events, that were only meant for full-time students, which were very confusing and not relevant to me at all, because I did not receive any information about which introductory events I could attend as an Erasmus student. In fact, there weren't really any introductory events for Erasmus students, apart from a single lunch-break meeting halfway into the semester. But on the other side, the ULB administration is very helpful and flexible (once you get a hold on them), so they can solve almost any inconvenience resulting from a lack of information on their side.
arrival_assistance: I could stop by the Erasmus coordinators office and receive a goodie bag with some ULB merchandise and a few letters of information. As far as I remember, I also received a couple of emails, but mostly I had to find information on my own on the ULB website and by asking around.
arrival_comments: No
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The only downside is that it can be an administrative hell. It is very stressfull before and after you leave, and you have to fill out a lot of documents and coordinate them between the two universities. It can be difficult to attain all the information you need, and sometimes things will only get solved at the very last minute. But if you can be calm about that, the experience is really worth it!
registration_process: First, you have to send a list of the courses you intend to follow (the OLA), which will be available to both KU and ULB. Then, you have to go to the first class of every course and ask the professor for permission to follow the course, as some professors do not want international students on their courses. Most professors were very open, but a few said no, which meant that I had to change my learning agreement last minute. However, KU were very fast at changing my "forhåndsgodkendelse", so it was not a problem. You had the opportunity to try out courses for two weeks before having to finally choose which ones to follow, which was very nice. Also, the exam dates for each course will not be available until late November. This meant that I had two exams at the same time. But luckily the ULB administration and the professors were very flexible in solving this, so they just arranged an oral exam for me instead. So if you have a problem like this, just ask the professor - they will usually be very willing to find another solution, and the system is not as strict as in Copenhagen.
registration_help: Not much! I had to find most information on the website.
registration_success: I was mostly successful. Only one or two professors had closed classes, but easily found other courses to substitute them.
registration_advice: Just keep calm, and remember that you are on exchange to learn how they do things in other countries! Few countries have a bureaucracy as organized as Denmark's, and sometimes you will not be able to get the information you need until the very last minute. But trust that it will all get sorted out in the end.
academics_comments: The only downside is that it can be an administrative hell. It is very stressfull before and after you leave, and you have to fill out a lot of documents and coordinate them between the two universities. It can be difficult to attain all the information you need, and sometimes things will only get solved at the very last minute. But if you can be calm about that, the experience is really worth it!
course_level: They were pretty similar to the level at UCPH, if not a bit easier.
teaching_comparison: Very different. There were only lectures, and in most classes oral participation at lectures counted towards our final grade. You can also choose to follow "Travaux Pratiques" (TP) for most courses, which are similar to seminar classes in Denmark. These are optional (for most courses), and are an opportunity to go more in depth with the syllabus. I only followed TP for one course, where it was mandatory. It was very time consuming, so I would not recommend it if it is optional. But it helped me a lot towards the final exam, and I also obtained a few points that counted in my final grade.
courses_enrolled: Public International Law (10 ects) Decision-making in the EU (5 ects) EU Criminal Law (5 ects) Internal Market with a focus on the Free Movement of Goods (5 ects) Terrorism and International Law (5 ects)
recommended_courses: I would really recommend Terrorism and International Law. The professor is very charismatic, and the exam is a paper that you can write after you return to Denmark. This is a relief, as the exams at ULB are mostly hand-written, closed book-exams, which is very different than what we are used to in Denmark.
unexpected_costs: I went out to eat and drink a lot, as I made some very good friends at my dorm. This was not "unexpected", but I did end up spending a lot more money on food and drinks than I'm used to. We also went on a lot of trips, which were a bit expensive, but really worth it.
cost_comparison: I was surprised that the cost of living was very similar to what it is in Denmark. Going out to eat and shopping at the supermarket was quite expensive. But coffee to go was very cheap, and books for university were as well!
activities_available: I didn't have time to join myself, but I heard many good things about ULB Sport, where you can follow all sorts of fitness classes very cheap. There were also a huge number of student organizations, that we were welcome to join (but you would need to speak French).
activities_recommended: Go on trips with your friends! You can go to Paris by train in 1,5 hour. Also, explore Belgium outside of Brussels - go hiking in the Ardennes, and visit Ghent, Brugge and Leuven.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Grand Place, visit the Africa museum, eat frites and waffles. Go on a day trip to Ghent. Go to cosy cafes such as Chyl, Cafe de la Presse (close to ULB) and Bisou. Try the "beer-o-meter" at Delirium, where you can try a selection of 10 Belgian beers.
culture_adjustment: Very easy! Much more similar to Copenhagen than I expected, but also with everything that I love about the more southern parts of Europe - farmers markets with fresh fruits and vegetables, a "going out-culture", where people meet with their friends for a glass of wine after work, and warmer weather with more sunlight over the winter.
socializing_tips: Join a student organization or attend the ESN-parties.
cultural_challenges: There were not that many cultural differences. If I have to mention one thing, it is the administration which was much slower and less effective than in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: The more extroverted culture, where people chat you up at a lecture or a bar.
top3_advice: 1. Keep calm and trust that the administrative things will all fall into place in due time, even though they will test your patience. 2. Remember to go out and relax - take a break from studying law in Denmark, where you are buried in books all semester. You don't need to do that here! 3. Be present, and don't go back to Denmark too often. Also, say no to getting too many visits from back home - you'll need the weekends to get to know your new friends.
other_useful_info: Everything is usually easier if you show up in person and ask, instead of sending emails and calling. ULB can find a solution for almost any problem you have, you just need to ask.
most_rewarding: Regaining my passion for studying law, as it had kind of died after a few years of hard studying. Here, I could focus on just studying subjects I found interesting, without having to focus on anything else such as work.
greatest_challenge: Just attaining all the correct information.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study law in French and I didn't want to go to France. I chose the university with the most EU law courses.
info_ease: We got a lot of information by e-mail over the summer (also in English), but as soon as we entered August, all information was available only in French, and the Erasmus-coordinator was only really approachable in French. We pieced our information together from the e-mails, what she told us, and (basically) rumors from other Erasmus students. It worked out in the end.
arrival_assistance: The e-mails, some office hours where we could go pick up our student card and some very basic info about the university. The Erasmus-coordinator was also available at other times, I went to see her in her office, but she didn't have hours, so you had to be lucky.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The term's (quadrimestre 1) courses were posted at the faculty's website. Through TimeEdit we could see when the classes took place. For the first 2-3 weeks we could go to any classes we wanted to, and by a deadline we had to let the Erasmus-coordinator know which courses we wanted to enroll in. It was very hard to make a schedule fit, and in the process we also discovered that not all professors accept Erasmus students. I ended up asking each professor ahead of the first class if I could join, and everyone accepted except one professor (Vaios Koutrolis for the courses in the Master de spécialisation droit international). I then wrote in the e-mail that I had gotten approval from all the professors, and I was enrolled in all the courses I wanted. For Public International Law, TP (travaux personnel, exercises) was mandatory, and enrollment into the groups/classes was done online, which was advertised as something very stressful we'd have to be very fast to get a spot in, but it wasn't a problem at all, in the end.
registration_help: Not a lot, I went to the office of the Erasmus-coordinator a few times, but she couldn't do much, and then we went to some intro lectures for new bachelor students, but mostly we just figured it out on our own.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. There were other courses I would have rather taken, but I couldn't make the schedule fit.
registration_advice: The first 3 weeks will be super stressful, but it will work out in the end. Get pre-approval for all the courses given at the faculty, so you don't have to worry about changing your pre-approval. I had to have mine changed but it was no problem.
course_level: The level was lower than I had anticipated for most, but it was nice for settling in and understanding the style of teaching and adapting to the expectations – let alone get used to the language! The workload was bigger than at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Much more sit-down-and-listen-style teaching at ULB. Most of it was lectures, where the professor half-heartedly said they wanted interaction, but the format wasn't right for it at all. In the seminar (TP) of Public International Law, we got grades for participation, so everyone was falling over each other trying to say something, which was a bad experience. In spite of the lively discussion, there was no room for being critical towards the curriculum, which I thought was a shame. In one class, Protection juridictionnelle dans l'Union européenne, the professor was very nice and actually encouraged participation. I participated the most in this class, in spite of my French not being perfect, and he was very supportive.
courses_enrolled: Protection juridictionnelle dans l'Union européenne (5 ECTS); Approches juridiques des discriminations (5 ECTS); EU Competition Law (5 ECTS); Droit de l'environnement (5 ECTS); Public International Law (10 ECTS)
recommended_courses: Protection juridictionnelle dans l'Union européenne. It was a great course, I didn't learn a lot that I didn't know already from EU constitutional law or International dispute resolution and international courts (BA elective), but it was great for learning new perspectives and especially for learning the French vocabulary. The professor, Paul Dermine, was incredible, by far one of the best I've had all my years at university. He was patient and very encouraging of my French, and he spoke relatively slow and very clearly, so it wasn't too hard to follow. Bring your Uddrag af EU-retten book!
unexpected_costs: I went to the doctor at the Services Medicales at the university, which I expected to be free, but the consultation (no add-ons) was 24 euros.
cost_comparison: Groceries were expensive, but I guess they were also at home (inflation). I think you could definitely live for less money than I did, I just didn't want to think about expenses much. I rented a bike through Swapfiets which was the best spent money the whole time I was there. Eating out and take-away was less expensive.
activities_available: Many! I was a part of ULB Sports, which cost 35 euros for the semester I think. I took some classes, it was very enjoyable.
activities_recommended: ULB Sports.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the nearby cities! You can get to Paris by direct train in about an hour and a half. I also went to Bruges. Some friends of mine also went to the mountains and to Amsterdam.
culture_adjustment: Easy because I had a good grasp of the language, but the culture itself was more difficult than I had expected. The level of politeness and the distance between professor and student made a much bigger impression on me than I had thought it would.
socializing_tips: Take classes in French, especially from the Master de spécialisation droit européen. People were super nice, and the class was about half Belgian, quarter French, and the rest international, but most spoke English as well. I had luck with jumping into conversations with people complaining about the work, the programme, the professors or the university in general. Asking questions about the same things or admin/exam things that were foreign to me also worked. People were generally quite open and nice once you just initiated contact.
cultural_challenges: Knowing how polite to be and when to address someone by "vous" or "tu". In all my classes we had to address the professor by the formal you, but they in turn also addressed us the same, and as "madame", "monsieur" or "your colleague". In e-mails, I found out teachers want to be addressed by their title, e.g., Professor Dermine or Monsieur Professor Dermine. But they also know that you are not used to this, so you get the benefit of the doubt.
culture_appreciated: All the Belgians I met were very open and helpful. The humor was quite similar to Danish, and I liked the culture of complaining. The food was also great.
top3_advice: It will be stressful but it will work out and be worth it in the end. Have patience, the administration is *much* more messy than at UCPH. Try and spend less time stressing about academic work and grades, and go enjoy the time with your classmates.
other_useful_info: There's an intensive French course for 3 weeks in August, that helped me a lot.
most_rewarding: I gained a lot more confidence from my stay. There were so many practical hurdles, but I overcame all of them. Also academically I feel more confident now. It was also an incredible full-circle moment to use the French I've spent the past 11 years learning, and I got more confident in speaking even though I'm still not fluent.
greatest_challenge: Adapting to the different teaching style and environment, all the practical issues, and homesickness.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to discover a culture and academic difference then my own.
info_ease: I was very difficult. I felt like I didn't get any information from the university about anything. They only send some flyers out by email that was outdated.
arrival_assistance: As mention, it was acutely quite bad. They gave us half an hour where we could ask questions, but it was only academic questions. they didn't do introduction week to meet other people. they didn't really prepare us before academically either, as we found out that there were some classes we weren't allowed to take. In general, it was really difficult to get any information, so as eramus student you really tried to get any information from everyone, but the hardest part was that you didn't know any other Erasmus student.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had mostly problems with my own university, because they were 6 weeks for them respond, and the host institution had not there classes ready before the semester actually started. This meant that I almost gave up on my eramus exchange in the beginning, because I couldn't get my Erasmus "scholarship". ULB has two weeks were you can try classes, before you can even sign up for them. This does not work with the Erasmus application and the deadlines at all. When I finally got the classes at ULB that I wanted (after a lot of convincing of me wanting English speaking classes), I had to wait 6 weeks for Copenhagen University to respond. Here I had a deadline at ULB at 2 weeks, and also had a eramus deadline. This lead into that I blinded had to trust that Copenhagen would approve, and I didn't have a Learning Agreement in the begning. This stressed me out so much!
registration_help: I wouldn't say that they help. it was more me trying to convince them that I was qualified enough to have masterclasses, even though I'm a bachelor student. It took a lot of convincing, but they eventually agreed because I was a third year bachelor student, and I spoke good English.
registration_success: I eventually got all the classes that I need for getting a Learning Agreement. It wasn't all the classes I wanted - especially because it would make so much more sense that only had masterclasses, but they wouldn't let me at political science. I do know, however, that the law faculty allowed bachelor student to only taking law classes.
registration_advice: You can only English classes, you just have to persistent. Write to your own university first, and make a plan A; B; C; D; etc. Because you really have to fight for it. But I would say that ULB is trying to be helpful as possible.
course_level: I think, because im a third year bachelor student from Copenhagen - most of the bachelor classes had elements that I had have before. It was mostly challenging to understand how I was supposed to study for the exam, because ULB mostly have Multiple choice exam. My most challenging Classe was a law class, because I don't study law.
teaching_comparison: It depends on the teacher. Most classes was only lectures that looks like Copenhagens. One teacher made us make presentations the whole semester. And we weren't allowed to take any seminars. One of my teacher taught both in Introduction to EU politics and Decision making in the EU. One is bachelor class, and one is master class. However, it was the same syllabus and classes.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to political science Introduction to political communication Introduction to EU politics Decision making in the EU European Integration through law
recommended_courses: European Integration through law Introduction to political communication Introduction to EU politics
unexpected_costs: Food was so expensive, and that you payed a lot of uber, because when going out the trams stop going, and you don't want to walk alone home.
cost_comparison: more expensive.
activities_available: a lot of sport was available.
activities_recommended: I didn't take any, because I was too afraid with the French.
weekend_recommendations: I visited a lot of other cities nearby, and I would recommend that. Bruxelles is more a food kind of city - so they have good food, and few sighting seeing. they do, however, have tons of museums!
culture_adjustment: I think that was okay, I would say. Kind of what you could expect. Bruxelles is also a city full of other countries cultures, so its pretty easy to adapt to whatever you like.
socializing_tips: Go the ESN events, and follow them on instagram, and really try to just go up to people and ask if they are Erasmus student, and ask if they know anything. You really have to fight to get to know anyone.
cultural_challenges: I don't think I found any cultural difference difficult. to me it was nice to se how Belgians do it. It is very French in Bruxelles to be honest.
culture_appreciated: That were so many different cultures in one city, and you could get anything from all over the world in just one city.
top3_advice: be persistent. discover other cities. And ask ULB whenever you have a problem with deadlines, they are more flexible. And you can find classes in English and get them.
other_useful_info: The exam is by hand and with a ball pen "kuglepen" which nobody had told before it sat at the exam.
most_rewarding: The experience of seeing how a university (French speaking) in Belgium teach and learn.
greatest_challenge: The whole learning agreement procedure, and finding Erasmus students.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to live in a city where french was the main language spoken, and also a bigger city.
info_ease: It was alright. ULB has a website that is good for orientation, however, it works best in French.
arrival_assistance: I received a welcome pdf from ULB and then we had an introduction seminar the week before classes started.
arrival_comments: It was a bit hard to figure out what the schedule for the courses was a long time in advance, but it was available the week before classes started.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The course registration happens through a Word document, which is sent to the academic coordinator three weeks after the semester begins. Written exams are registered for automatically.
registration_help: There is an online website (TE viewer) available a week before the semester starts where it is possible to see if there are any conflicts in the schedule.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted in the end. However, some of the ones I originally wanted had overlapping schedules.
registration_advice: Don't stress about the course registration, and that it isn't available until a week before the semester starts. The academic coordinator at ULB is super nice, and wants help solve any issue you have with the courses/schedules. Note that bachelor's students are only allowed to take two masters courses per semester. However, the academic coordinator game me permission to take three due to challenges with my schedule. It is possible to get by without being fluent in French at ULB. Although, many bachelor's programs are only in French, but many masters are in English. The university buildings in itself are not that pretty, but the overall teaching is at a good level.
course_level: I took three master's courses and three bachelor's courses, even though bachelor exchange students normally are only allowed to take two master's courses. However, after emailing back and forth with the academic coordinator at ULB, I got permission. The overall level was similar to what I'm used to at UCPH. Exams are often closed book, handwritten and multiple-choice. I found that exams for the bachelor's courses were harder to pass than the ones at the master's courses.
teaching_comparison: For my bachelor's courses, I had lectures and for my master's courses, I had smaller seminars (like holdtimer), which is also what I'm used to at UCPH. In general, there was less student participation during class than what I'm used to, but for the master's courses it was a bit more participatory.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Political Science (BA), Institutions and Political Representation (MA), Introduction to European Politics (BA), European Integration and Public Policy (MA), Gender and Social Movements (MA), Introduction to Political Communication (BA).
recommended_courses: I liked the professor at Institutions and Political Representation (MA) a lot, and the class was often open for discussion. Also, the Gender and Social Movements (MA) class had a nice professor, and the topics covered were interesting as well was the readings.
unexpected_costs: Getting home in the night can require taking an Uber/Bolt, since the public transportation in Brussels often ends at 2am/3am, even in the weekends.
cost_comparison: Public transport is only 12€ for students under 25, which is very cheap. Food pricing is approx. the same as in Copenhagen. Coffee and beer are cheaper :)) The Royal Library is not free to study at, but costs 15€ for a year subscription. I didn't have to buy any books for my classes at ULB. Traveling with Flixbus to other big cities (Paris, Antwerp, Amsterdam) can be quite cheap if booked time in advance.
activities_available: ULB has a sports card for 36€ per semester, where a lot of different sports are included: Team sports (rugby, basketball), individual sports (badminton, fencing), music classes (zumba, salsa, Body Sculpt), and much more (cheerleading, tai chi, etc.). There are also some student associations called Cercles, but those are more for local students and have some interesting - and a bit outdated - traditions/activities. For the exchange students, ULB has an Erasmus Student Network (ESN) that hosts a lot of activities throughout the semester like Bowling, museum visits, pub crawls, running clubs, parties and more (follow their Instagram @esnulbbrussels for more info).
activities_recommended: The sports I can personally recommend are zumba, stretching, and salsa. The St V Day (November 20th) is really fun. Also, the CPS Cercle hosted a big barbeque party in the beginning of the semester, which was fun. The ESN things are fun to attend as well and a good way to meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: Things to do in Brussels: - Museums: Magritte museum, Migrant museum, Africa museum - Cafes: Le Pain Quotidien, Belga & Co., Living room - Food: Yummy bowl, Maison Antoine (fries), Le botaniste - Markets: Jeu de balle (all days), Flagey (only weekends) Other places to go: Antwerp, Lille, Paris, Gent.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy. In general, everything starts later timewise; eating times, courses, etc.
socializing_tips: Go to the containers behind the canteen in the evenings to get cheap beer and talk to local students. Also, go to Place de Luxembourg on Thursday afternoons/evenings to talk to locals and international workers in Brussels in general.
cultural_challenges: There is way less structure in Brussels in general compared to Copenhagen. This is in regard to being on time (both with friends and for classes), course registration, public transportation, etc.
culture_appreciated: The city is so diverse, which I found very refreshing. In general, it is easy being a foreigner in Brussels, as there are so many of them.
top3_advice: Be open-minded and curious. Most people are going to be friendly, and the bus driver will always wait for you if you run <3
other_useful_info: Brussels can be a bit dangerous, and there are many homeless people at the metro stations and on the streets. As a woman, the city can feel a bit does feel a bit unsafe, especially at night. So I would always recommend being aware of one's surroundings when going home at night, texting friends when arriving at home, and taking an Uber if one is going home from a sketchy neighborhood.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many fun and interesting people from all over the world. I have learned so much about other cultures, both European and outside of Europe (especially Middle Eastern, African, and South American). Brussels, being the most culturally diverse city in Europe, is the perfect place to meet and connect with people from all over the world. Also, people are so nice if you don't speak perfect French since there are so many foreigners in the city.
greatest_challenge: The weather can be a bit depressing (it rains A LOT). Making friends abroad always takes some effort, but I didn't find it that hard in Brussels.
other_comments: The city might be a bit of a mess aesthetically, but being a cultural melting pot is what makes it interesting to live in.

crucial_aspects: I country where I could improve my french language skills.
overall_comments: It was an amazing experience and I would have love to stay even longer if it was possible.
info_ease: It was quite easy . However, it was at times a bit of an information overload and I got help from my fellow student to get sure that I didn't overlook anything important.
arrival_assistance: We got a mail with 'guides' from the hosting university on what to do before, under and after the mobility. The administration did also invite to a welcome meeting where we could ask questions and where we received our studentcards.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was an amazing experience and I would have love to stay even longer if it was possible.
registration_process: 1) Fill out a temporary learning agreement 2) The first two weeks, the host institution encouraged us to participate to all the courses we found interesting. 3) after two weeks (or so) we had to choose the most interesting courses (and fitting level-wise) and fill out in a final OLA and the 'Pink form' which was a form that signed us up to the written exams at the host institution.
registration_help: We were assigned a 'course coordinator', who was a professor at the faculty. She could answer questions and was quick to respond.
registration_success: I got all the courses I registered for.
registration_advice: Take your time the first weeks to explore all the courses as possible (see if it is the right level, if the professor is interesting, to find out what is expected from you as a student in terms of reading, assignments, etc.). In the beginning, I had written one class in my OLA, which sounded interesting in the course catalogue. When I turned up to the class I did not enjoy the way the professor was teaching. Luckily, I then had some other courses I could choose instead.
academics_comments: It was an amazing experience and I would have love to stay even longer if it was possible.
course_level: Some of my classes were not that challenging, with a small curriculum. Others where really challenging, where I had to read a lot and write a long paper in the end. I took most of my classes in french which i can recommend even though you don't have the highest academic level (I'm b2). However, all my teachers allowed my to write my exams in english in the end if you want to do the same thing, it is a good idea to ask your professor if you can write your exam in english).
teaching_comparison: In Bruxelles it was mostly the professor speaking in a big auditoire with or without a powerpoint presentation. The students role were mostly to take notes and sometimes to ask question. However, I got the impression that most of the support to the courses comes from former students notes and exam papers. In Copenhagen we also have our courses in auditoires, but it gets supplementet by classroom teaching, where academic assistents are facilitating the classes. Here we get to ask questions about the lectures and dive into the readings with our fellow students.
courses_enrolled: GEOG-F414 - Analyse des espaces urbains (Master) LANGB9071 - 60-HOURS-FRENCH SOCA-D4996 - Anthropologie de l'environnement (Master) POLID323 - Introduction to EU Politics CRIMC201 - Introduction à la criminologie générale SOCAD473 - Anthropologie de la religion
recommended_courses: Can recommend the 60-HOURS-FRENCH course, where you get to practice you're oral language skills more. Here you also get to meet other exchange students. I also really liked the courses: GEOG-F414 - Analyse des espaces urbains (Master) SOCA-D4996 - Anthropologie de l'environnement (Master), where I experienced the classes as more interactive between the students and the professor.
unexpected_costs: It was not directly unexpected, but Brussels is situated really nicely next to other big cities (Paris, Amsterdam, Rotterdam, etc.), so I went on a lot of trips during the weekends (maybe more than I expected)
cost_comparison: Transport was way less expensive than expected. It is only 12€ for a 12 months transportcard if you're a student younger than 26 years old.
activities_available: The ULB has a lot of offers: a really cheap sportscard, where you can apply to as many sports as you want each week. The students are really engage aswell in all kinds of clubs ('circles'). I for instant participated in their film club, feminist club, their club for anthropology and sociology students and their small vegestable garden. There is also a lot of comedy shows and concerts at the university cafe 'coin culture'.
activities_recommended: Participating in their small vegestable garden is definitely an activity i can recommend. It is a multigenerational project between student and elder people. You get to meet locals while learning a lot about vegestables and managing a compost. They also have a social event for all students once a semester called "disco soup" - it is a must!
weekend_recommendations: Ghent, Bruges, Antwerpen, Paris, Amsterdam, Rotterdam, if you want to experience some of the cities nearby Brussels. Their is a really nice flea market in Marolles everyday at Place Jeu de Balles and of course a lot of bars with nice local beers;)
culture_adjustment: Brussels is a really multicultural city - so it went quite quick.
socializing_tips: Participate in local clubs and find a place to live with locals.
cultural_challenges: Sometimes a language barrier was hard, but is was also because I insisted in speaking french.
culture_appreciated: I find the Belgians really open, curious and interested - that made it easy to participate at activities at the university.
top3_advice: 1) participate in some of all the student clubs 2) Try out as many courses as possible in the beginning of the semester 3) Take courses in french if you have an ok level (It is a really nice way to learn french and it is often possible to write your exam in english - so its a win-win)
other_useful_info: In the beginning of the semester, some ULB folklore clubs are 'baptising' the new students, which can be a bit overwhelming to experience, since it's 1,5 month of 'humiliating' activities trying to learn the new students to become independent individuals. (the general opinion on this is very mixed).
most_rewarding: It is really hard to tell, since I experience so many rewarding things; Living with only locals, participating i local student clubs and just to meet a lot of exchange students from all over the world. I has broaden my perspective on how it is being a student in many EU countries (and have lucky we are in Denmark to get our studies financed).
greatest_challenge: The first month where I was still new to the city and all a knew was new relationships - Then I missed my friends and my apartment back home a little bit.

crucial_aspects: Brussels is the center of the European Union which was very interesting for me. I have been particularly interested in European Affairs while Brussels seemed the right choice. At the same time it offered a perfect mean to learn French. Both because my subjects were in French and ULB offers many different language courses and offers which helped me a lot.
info_ease: It was fine to find all the information I needed. My host university held some introduction events in the beginning that guided us well through the first days.
arrival_assistance: Welcoming events and very detailed information from my host university that explained very well what to do and what was expected from me.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We had to go there first and get our documents signed. The university had some well functioning systems with different forms which worked fine.
registration_help: You could always text the international office at ULB that almost replied vey quickly and was very good at giving advice needed.
registration_success: Worked perfectly. The first two weeks were try out weeks which was a very nice experience because you could try out a lot of different subjects and verify whether it fitted your level. That was a very nice way of organizing the first weeks!
registration_advice: Don't stress too much. I tried to always be ahead on the applications. Most things gets much easier when you arrive to uni. So only do what's asked in the beginning and then deal with the rest at uni. Everything is much clearer once you arrived.
course_level: Very engaged and talented teachers largely speaking. I learned a lot. However 5 ECTS is very little for a subject which also meant I had to take 6 different subjects to reach 30 ECTS points. This meant that sometimes the subjects didn't have the time or curriculum to go totally in depth. On the other hand I got a good introduction to a very large scale of subjects which was also nice!
teaching_comparison: Teaching style is quite similar in the teaching room. My classes was mostly structured around a teacher or guest lecturer presenting a subjects and with good oppurtunities for students to ask questions. The difference is tho the level of reading. In Copenhagen there's much more to read and the exam are mostly based on the readings. At ULB the word of the teacher carries as much weight as the very few readings at the uni.
courses_enrolled: ECON-S-467 Law and Economics of the Environment POLI-D-403 L'Europe et la nation (Europe and the nation) POLI-D-436 Identités, communautés et espaces publics en Europe (Identities, communities and public spaces in Europe) POLI-D-538 Armement et désarmement en politique internationale (Armament and Disarmament in International Politics) POLI-D-547 Le Brésil : puissance émergente (Brazil: emerging power) POLI-D-556 Régimes politiques d’Europe centrale et orientale
recommended_courses: POLI-D-436 Identités, communautés et espaces publics en Europe Wonderful course with very interesting guests. A course that really benefits and uses the fact that ULB is in Brussels by inviting very interesting people from the policy world into ULB. ECON-S-467 Law and Economics of the Environment A course by two very talented and gifted lecturers that manages to merge to complicated areas into one course that is accessible also for political science students. It is a subject with quite a lot of hands on experience in the fact that the exam takes form in a report and presentation in front of the class. This allowed to apply the theory learned and to get deep into the subject.
unexpected_costs: I didn't really. Was however surprised that the beers were not more expensive! - Very pleasant surprise ;)
cost_comparison: Beers: Less expensive Housing: less expensive Transport: More expensive
activities_available: Quite a lot of student groups that organized super nice and relevant events. A bit hard to join them and to find info as an Erasmus student but very easy to join and participate in the planned events.
activities_recommended: Come to events and really prioritize to participate in the Erasmus events in the beginning. Those are super cool and you get to meet a lot of friends that stays around for the rest of the stay.
weekend_recommendations: Enjoy the fact that Brussels is so much in the middle of Western Europe. You got trains to Amsterdam, Paris, Cologne, Frankfurt, London, Marseille etc. directly from the train stations in Brussels. That is a very cool add on.
culture_adjustment: Easy for a dane I would say! A beerdrinking warm people that is chill and welcoming. But definitely (!!) a plus to know the basics in French. Easiest way into the culture.
socializing_tips: Hmmm. Try in your classes to talk with co-students - cause that's the place with the most local students to talk to. I went to Badminton through ULB sports every Tuesday night - That was were I met the most locals.
cultural_challenges: Language for sure! I spoke some french when I started and that helped me a lot. However to really engage it was first towards the end that I got a level high enough to really participate.
culture_appreciated: The warmth and the excitement of Erasmus students was super nice. Everyone was there to explore and have fun - that creates a super great mood!
top3_advice: - Get a very basic French (definitely possible without but huge plus to have) - Participate in the first Erasmus events - Don't be shy and reach out to people you've only met once (they usually really want to meet up)
other_useful_info: Not other than the ones mentioned.
most_rewarding: - Meeting other Europeans - was so much fun to share traditions, language and cultures with each other
greatest_challenge: The IMMENSE amount of small talk haha! But was also very given but sometimes you craved a deeper talk with some people that you didn't just meet one month before.

crucial_aspects: I have previously lived here with my family, and I was interested in getting better at French as well as I was interested in EU-law.
info_ease: It was a bit different from UCPH, since you don't need to sign up for classes before arrvial because you spend the first two weeks trying out the classes, that you might like. I feel like a lot of information was accessible on the website of ULB but the website was a bit difficult to navigate in the beginning.
arrival_assistance: We received e-mails before arriving and had information sessions when we arrived. I feel like the level of information was sufficient, but you need to have faith in the fact that everything will work out and don't stress it too much.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Once you has decided on the classes to follow, you had to change the OLA and get it signed from the responsible person. This was the wat of registerering for coureses, and even though it took some time it went quite smooth.
registration_help: The responsible person from the law faculty was available if you needed help.
registration_success: I was very succesfull. It seemed like there were no limitations regarding the number of students for each class, so there were not stress and I got all of the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Take it easy, try out the different courses, talk to the other students, Erasmus as well as locals regarding their experiences with the different courses. Don't worry too much about registration, there is room for everyone. I chose my courses based on interests, but you have to "make" your own schedule, so have a look at the platform from ULB, Timeedit, and make sure that the courses fit in your schedule and daily life.
course_level: I took one bachelor course and four master courses. The level were quite okay to follow. I took two courses in french, which was possible even though I am only in the beginning of B2. I did not praticipate in any of the travaux practique since it were not mandatory to exchange students in my courses. This made the work load quite easy compared to Copenhagen. The bachelor course I took were very explanatory and not so elaborative, so I am glad I didn't only sign up for bachelor courses since the level of these were quite low.
teaching_comparison: It is very much lecture-style with little participation. I took a lot of courses from the LLM in European Law, where more participation was expected. Furthermore, there are not any books, only PowerPoints and certain documents issued by the EU-insitutions were part of the curriculum in my experience. Therefore, it usually made more sense to study after a session than before. All exams are handwritten and mostly closed book, but with the treaties or other legislation/documents issued by institutions. I was more worried about this than needed, but it is nice to know and to be prepared for.
courses_enrolled: Droit de l'Union européenne DROIC-3003 10 ECTS, bachelor level Law of aremd conflicts DROIC-5149 - 5 ECTS EU competition law, DROIC687 - 5 ECTS Protection juridictionelle dans l'Union européenne, DROIO500 - 5 ECTS Internal market with a focus on Free Movement of Goods - DROIO627 - 5 ECTS
recommended_courses: I think that all of the courses I took were quite interesting. The most challenging, but also interesting was Protection jurdictionelle since this gave me a new perspective on EU and the legal certainty.
unexpected_costs: Not anything really, transportation is 18 euros for a card with unlimited transport for a year, and you can get access to the gym at ULB for 36 euros for a semester. Groceries are quite the same as in Copenhagen, so is eating in restaurant. Beers and coffees are quite cheap. So is fries.
cost_comparison: See the section above
activities_available: The Erasmus-organisation arranged a lot of different things, which I went to a few of. I did however spend a lot of timw with my housemates, and did not go as much as other people.
activities_recommended: Do the sports, go to Plux on THursdays and just have a great time. Enjoy the vivid life in Bruxelles, and to the cafés since there are so many nice ones.
weekend_recommendations: Visit cities in Bruxelles. Bruxelles is very centrally placed in Europe, and people often go to Paris, Amsterdam etc. I think that Ghent, Brugge, Antwerpen etc all are quite nice and cosy cities so try to visit if you have time.
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy. The Belgian culture is a lot like the danish one, exempt for the fact that people go out to eat/drink a lot more. I would recommend to implemt this habit!!
socializing_tips: If you have more than one cours with some students then try talking to them, get into the Whatsapp groups and such. People are friendly, but in my experience you usually need to be the one to approach. Thias can be difficult, but once you have done it is very nice and helpful to have someone to asks regarding exam, french things you don't understand and such.
cultural_challenges: I did not find anything that challenging. Maybe the language sometimes, but ULB also offers classes which was helpful
culture_appreciated: The vivid life and people using the city so much.
top3_advice: Enjoy the city, don't underestimate it. Try the fries with a polycrouc, it is very delicious, find a great crowd and don't be afraid to intiate things. Everyone is there to make friends.
other_useful_info: I don't think so, generally ULB was quite heplful. Trust the proces, even though it is different fromm UCPH.
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of new lovely people, getting a new perspective on EU-law and improving my french.
greatest_challenge: It was actually a lot less challenging than expected. I missed people from back home, but had visits, which was great. Generally it has been really lovely!!

crucial_aspects: I was both motivated by personal connections but also by the vast career opportunities that are in Brussels as a political science student
info_ease: The information meeting in the stat of the semester helped a lot, however, it lacked social activities.
arrival_assistance: Purely informational as there were 1-2 days og information introduction by the coordinators.
arrival_comments: I wish it took a more social nature so that you could get to know your peers.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: When you arrivie you have 2 additional weeks to choose your final courses. In that time you may take any course you'd like to try out, which is great. After that you have to fill in a form with your final choices.
registration_help: both email with 1-2 day responds time from coordinators and also physical meetings were possible
registration_success: I was able to register for all the classes I wanted
registration_advice: Explore the different courses when you get there and then make your decision.
course_level: The levels of the course strongly depend on the professor, therefore it is a good idea to attend in the fisrt weeks to get a feeling about their strictness. Generally, I found the level of master courses alright, and some were very easy.
teaching_comparison: It is more important to make sure to attend as many classes as possible as you may be tested in the contents of class discussions, however, the exams are fairly easy - presentations, multiple choice, open questions, oral exams. But it is good to know that most exams are written in hand.
courses_enrolled: Globalization Studies Migration and Gender Gender and Social Movements Terrorism and International Law International Environmental Politics Democratisation and Autocratisation additional: French course
recommended_courses: Migration anf Gender, Gender and Social Movements both had fairly easy exams while also presenting interesting content and active participation as part of the grade.
unexpected_costs: As I was in brussels for a year i registered at the commune and an ID costs around 50 euro
cost_comparison: It is less expensive than copenhagen - I recommend shopping in Lidl or Colruyt
activities_available: Broad sports club, hanging out at campus in cafees
activities_recommended: There are a lot of cultural and fun things happening all the time in Brussels, look at facebook/instagram pages and visitbrussels. there are a lot of flee markets as well in the spring/early fall.
weekend_recommendations: If you drink there is a lot of beers and bars, the best fries, traveling around the country is also nice; Brugge, Ghent, Antwerpen, Knokke
culture_adjustment: I already knew people in Brussels so fairly easy, but also if you do not know anyone, most people are super open and there are lot of international people looking for community in the city. It is a more caotic city than Copenhagen so be ready for that
socializing_tips: A lot of them mainly speak french so if you could learn a little it would be good. Otherwise just try to approach people in your class.
cultural_challenges: I dont mind it too much, but it is def. a more 'southern' mentality of seeing where things go and going with the flow than in Denmark.It is also more chaotic and administrative things may take some time, however, at uni the admin is pretty fast.
culture_appreciated: More social culture of going out and doing different things also great food from all over the world
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy it!! there are a lot of amazing people and other exchange students to hang out with 2. Attend class more - but there is less reading 2. Make sure you really explore the city
other_useful_info: Not really, just that the coordinators are super fast and helpful so do not be scared to reach out to them. Also it is important to address your teachers as professor and/or madame/monsieur [last name]
most_rewarding: Meeting my amazing erasmus friends
greatest_challenge: getting registered in brussels - but you won't have to do that for one semester;)

cultural_challenges: The culture is quite french - things will start when they start and people are often late:)
culture_appreciated: The food and city life. Markets and people sitting outside drinking wine very late on all days of the week
top3_advice: Things might seem chaotic, but the ULB staff are really nice and good at helping you - it will work out. Buy or bring a bike, I loved to have mine there. I found the academic level to be very similar to Denmark, but the exams a closed book and in hand, so I struggled a bit with them.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Being a part of a local football club with Belgians and expats - I had a lot of my social life there.
greatest_challenge: It was a bummer not speaking french - if my level was better initially I could have learned a lot more:):):)
other_comments: Brussels is such a nice city!

crucial_aspects: I was at an online event for economics students where there was a lot of information about the different destinations. I learned that Pantheon Sorbonne in Paris was a good place to go, no matter what field of economics that interests you. Besides that, I thought it would be fun to live in Paris, even though I have no connection to the place.
info_ease: It's France.. Everything was a bit messy, but I figured it out along the way.
arrival_assistance: There where some very general introductory meetings. But the people working in the administration were quite responsive, so you could always figure it out, if you were unsure about something.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Well the course registration online page crashed, so we had to sign up manually in person instead. But I did end up getting all the courses I wanted, so can't really complain.
registration_help: In person help.
registration_success: 10/10. There was a waiting list for some of the courses I wanted, but they signed me up anyways when I showed up in person.
registration_advice: Be patient, do not worry too much, it's very french and you always find a solution (and show up in person and talk to them). Don't stress too much about deadlines, they don't.
course_level: I did MA courses. The level was fine, a little less math-heavy compared to KU.
teaching_comparison: Only lectures and no small classes. Less slides. But the style of the teaching depended a lot on the specific course.
courses_enrolled: Political economy, environmental economics, epistemology and history of economic thought, development economics, industrial economics
recommended_courses: Can recommend epistemology and history of economic thought if you want to try a very french way of teaching. Otherwise I really enjoyed development economics, the level is high, the slides are great, and if you like economic history, you will definitely enjoy this.
unexpected_costs: Be prepared to spend A LOT of money if you want to have fun in Paris (it is worth it though).
cost_comparison: It turned out to be both more and less expensive to go out and eat, since it is a little less expensive than Copenhagen, but you do it way more so..
activities_available: Not at the institution itself, but made use of sports at the cite universitaire.
activities_recommended: Tennis.
weekend_recommendations: Go outside of Paris and see the area around. But just have fun and experience as much of Paris as you can.
culture_adjustment: People are more rude, but they are really just being honest instead of pleasing you, which you get used to pretty fast. Not knowing french is not that big of a deal, just do your best.
socializing_tips: Talk to people after lectures. Become part of all the whatsapp groups.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The appreciation of life, the culture of going out for dinner on a tuesday for no particular reason.
top3_advice: Do not stress. Enjoy it as much as you can while you're there. Be prepared to spend a lot of money.
other_useful_info: Email them or talk to them in person, their online systems are terrible.
most_rewarding: Making a lot of new friends. Trying a different style of teaching and examination.
greatest_challenge: Having enough money.
other_comments: no.

crucial_aspects: My exchange plans were cancelled twice due to covid. I therefor had to apply for remaining places of which Sorbonne in Paris was the best option. Furthermore due to my language skills and previous experience in France I knew that I wanted to improve my French and experience studying in France.
overall_comments: The process of applying for and going on exchange was horrible. The collaboration between KU, the host university and Erasmus was very bad especially due to lack of communication and the intersections between the three administrations - which can definitely be improved as all the problems effect the students. However while I was in France the experience was great and I would recommend everyone to go on exchange.
info_ease: Very difficult and cryptic information available to the students who are going on exchange in Europe. When I was going to Sydney more information was available to the students. I found the process very stressful and irritating due to the lack of information with regards to courses available, dates, documents needed etc. I would recommend that the travel reports from the previous erasmus students are published for the new students applying for exchange.
arrival_assistance: Almost no assistance. We got information very late in the process, and I had a lot of questions which were difficult to get answers to without forcing the administration to respond by mail or by phone. We only limited information about the introduction week and it was impossible to figure out which courses were available to erasmus students. Furthermore, there were no counselling for Erasmus students nor any mentors in charge of showing us around etc. However the Erasmus organisation hosted really nice events for the students in generel, and I loved living in Paris, meeting new people and studying in another country, which is why I would still recommend going despite all the problems with the process and administration.
arrival_comments: The French system in general is very bad with horrible digitalisation and lack of information. This was also reflected at the host university. However I still had a great experience in France.
