However while I was in France the experience was great and I would recommend everyone to go on exchange.
course_level: The French courses are at a higher level than the English courses - having taken both, I found that the English courses where there in order for the French students to learn English rather than to learn the actual content of the course. Please note that the French courses are solely in French, also the exams, however they are much more advanced and interesting than the English courses.
teaching_comparison: Since we were only allowed to take courses with lectures and no small classes, the teaching was very different to the courses on UCPH. Furthermore, the university doesnt have much control with the professors, which means that some professors are really motivated, engaged and keen to create the best course (eg. politique etrangere and introduction to post-socialist europe), while some professors seem like they dont really want to be there and dont really care if we learn anything. However, as a result I think some of my courses were brilliant and some were absolutely horrible.
courses_enrolled: Comparative European Politics, International Finance, Politique Etrangere, Politique, Religion et Radicalization, Introduction to Post-socialist Europe, Critical Approaches.
recommended_courses: Politique Etrangere, Politique, Religion et Radicalization, Introduction to Post-socialist Europe
unexpected_costs: none
cost_comparison: groceries were more expensive than expected.
activities_available: sports - however most social activities were hosted by Erasmus which were great!
activities_recommended: Going on excursions to see more of France.
weekend_recommendations: travel around France, and go to all the great museums in Paris.
culture_adjustment: Very easy - however you realise how bad the french system is compared to the danish.
socializing_tips: They didnt really seem to be interested in getting to know exchange students - therefor I made a lot of friends from other countries that I had classes with and that I met in the first week. Furthermore I met a lot of Danish people at Cité Universitaire.
cultural_challenges: the lazyness and the administrative burdens haha
culture_appreciated: the life in Paris, all the nice places, the vibe, the experience, the vibrant culture, the way of living! Couldnt recommend it enough!
top3_advice: Have patience, enjoy it and live life to the fullest - the academics are not worth stressing about!
other_useful_info: The exams are VERY different from the Danish exams at political science. They are all "closed book" sit-in exams written by hand (a pen) and some of them are oral exams, in which you have no guidance. I had 6 exams in 8 days and they are very short and weirdly structured.
most_rewarding: Meeting different people, making friends for life, and experiencing the real, local Paris with all its ups and downs. I definetely want to come back to Paris!
greatest_challenge: The system and the administration. An example: in order to cancel my phone operator called "Free" I had to call a phone number, where they gave me a physical postal address to which I had to send a physical letter stating that I wanted to cancel my subscription. An other example: In order to apply for the courses I wanted I had go to the same office three times, send 10 emails, and call three different people before the deadline.
other_comments: Please go on exchange, you will regret it if you dont! It is a once in a life time experience.

crucial_aspects: For me, it was important to improve language skills/have some pre-existing knowledge of the language being spoken in the host country, and due to having studied French in school but never having had the opportunity to use it, I chose France. It was equally important to me to study in a place that was international, cosmopolitan and offered many opportunities academically.
info_ease: Once I had received my Login data for the student portal and email of the host university, this was very easy, as all information was provided by email.
arrival_assistance: The first week in the study destination I participated in an introduction week and there was introduction event for all exchange students as well. I did not receive any direct assistance, but always felt that I could ask questions at these events when needed.
arrival_comments: One day of the introduction course as well as an introduction cocktail didn't take place as planned due to the strikes happening in France at that time (the cocktail was later moved to another date, where I unfortunately could not make it). But it feels unfair to include these "force majeure" events in the overall judgement.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Once I had a signed Learning Agreement, I had to upload this and other documents in a portal the details of which I don't remember, but it was quite easy. A few weeks later, in late November, I was emailed the first login data to use to activate my student account and email.
registration_help: I mailed a few questions and my concerns about the lack of course information in August to the Erasmus responsible; I didn't receive a reply, which makes sense now that I know that universities are basically on holiday in August in France. I did receive answers from several professors, and also had the email addresses of both the university's and my department's international contacts.
registration_success: Since my first learning agreement was based on which courses I had information on and could pre-approve, I had to make changes to my learning agreement once I had information on the courses I wanted to attend. I was succesful in this and luckily my home university sped up the pre-approval process for me since I was already abroad. The only frustration arose when the Erasmus responsible at the host university seemed to be unacquainted with the PDF format of the online learning agreement that my home university used and contacted me thinking I had signed up for non-existing courses. I needed to tell her to scroll down in the document to actually see the changes I made to the learning agreement in a second table that was attached, which she apparently hadn't done and which was a little frustrating after all the work and time I had spend on the whole process.
registration_advice: Course information and literature is often not available until shortly before the semester starts. However, many of the professors are very friendly responsive and courses repeat, so reaching out to them asking about course content / descriptions from previous semesters is definitely worth it and a good way to establish "first contact".
course_level: The courses were challenging and the teachers were very competent. I often felt challenged in a good way and learned a lot.
teaching_comparison: The French way of teaching, as is also known about French school in general, is very much more authoritarian and less lax than in Denmark. In one of my first courses, the teacher would scold every student that was late and even pretended to hit one on the head with a roll of paper, which felt like a return to school. On the upside of this more "frontal" way of teaching was that the teachers would often start talking about a topic, without any notes, and make a brilliant explanation of a certain topic. Since another big difference was the lack of powerpoints or detailed notes about every session (only some teachers did limited versions of this which do not compare to the amount of material usually uploaded by teachers in Denmark), to get something out of the course, it was required to take notes fast while the teachers were talking. This could get quite stressful in combination with the courses being three hours long with only a short break in the middle. This also meant, though, that every attendance led to thousands of words of useful notes.
courses_enrolled: - Interventions internationales de gestion des crises - Migrations, diasporas et réfugiés - Décider dans un monde incertain - Administrations européennes - Fabrique de l'autorité politique
recommended_courses: Personally I got the most out of the courses Interventions internationales de gestion des crises, administrations européennes and Fabrique de l'autorité. The teachers were very competent and added to this, these courses were only attended by students from one to two master programmes and were thus real courses in course room were you were able to contribute, as opposed to big lectures.
unexpected_costs: A lot of museums are free for students and/or people up to 25 years of age (or everyone, such as Carnevalet). However, this doesn't apply to temporary exhibitions, which can cost around 13€. Other than that, I did not encounter any unexpected costs so much as costs due to the spontaneous nature of Erasmus life including a lot of going out, concerts, et cetera.
cost_comparison: The cost of living due to inflation was quite high. Eating and drinking when going out I had expected to be cheaper than in Copenhagen, and they were, but not as much as I had thought. Paris is still an expensive city. However, the Crous canteen was a life saviour. There is one at CIUP, but also in other places (I heard there is one on a boat on the Seine though I haven't been there myself), and a meal including a salad, fruit and/or yoghurt cost 3,30€. The vegetarian option was almost always tasty. I knew a lot of people who would eat lunch and/or dinner there every day. Coffee and cake the other hours of the day are also cheap and there is a reduced price option for students.
activities_available: It was possible to book a sports course through the university, which you had to attend throughout the semester and got graded on. I did not expect that there would be a requirement of attendance and several obligatory tests, but it was still fun. There were always events happening at the university, though not that many clubs as I had expected (or they were hard to find as an international student / less active due to the strikes). There was also a volunteer organisation offering events for exchange students and a WhatsApp group, though unfortunately most events took place in the start of the semester and then it died down completely, which I assume might be due to a lack of volunteers.
activities_recommended: I booked a sports membership at CIUP where I lived, which cost only 80€ for a whole semester. I attended many different events - in Paris, there is always something happening, and there are always other exchange students planning something or events for exchange students. I wish I had attended more cultural offers at the university itself, but the talk and cinema events I did attend were great. As stated above, I can imagine that there is quite a bit more activity from student clubs in other semesters where there isn't a national strike going on almost every week.
weekend_recommendations: Paris offers so many great museums and experiences it is dazzling. Since I regret not doing this more, I recommend taking weekends and free days to take trips out of the city, since these are the places that you are less likely to go to when you are back in Paris and have limited time. I went, for example, to Étretat in Normandy, Versailles, Givergny including Claude Monet's garden, and Fontainebleau, and they were all great experiences.
culture_adjustment: The main difference was the hectic pace of Paris as a big world city with millions of people, compared to Copenhagen which is a lot smaller and more quiet. The teaching style as stated above also took some getting used to, but there were always other international students to make courses less daunting and to talk to about these experiences. So it didn't take long for me to adjust.
socializing_tips: Socialising with local students was borderline impossible given how busy they were due to the mixed pressure of the courses I also attended and the important mémoire coming up. So I don't have any tips in that direction, unfortunately.
cultural_challenges: The more authoritarian teaching style as mentioned above was probably one of the most challenging things since it could be intimidating. Other than that, I had heard many horror stories about rude Parisians, but actually had many extremely friendly interactions with French strangers. I found that people often were more open and easier to talk to than Danes, who can be quite closed off and shy despite being friendly.
culture_appreciated: All the clichéd ideas about Paris are true; there is a wonderful joie de vivre in the city, it is full of culture, good food and drink, and secret places to discover. I loved doing things spontaneously, going out, and enjoying the energy of the city. It is truly a great place to live for half a year.
top3_advice: That the course selection process can be quite frustrating and that patience is required (and contacting professors if necessary), that the Master's level courses are very rewarding especially if you select the ones that are attended by a smaller number of students, and that there are always a handful of other Erasmus students attending the same courses, at least in my experience, so you normally aren't alone.
other_useful_info: The phase before applying to the host university (getting the Learning Agreement signed, courses pre-approved and so on) can be extremely stressful, but once that is done, everything is much easier.
most_rewarding: For me it was being able to study in the old Sorbonne building in the middle of the inner city and truly feeling challenged by the courses. Also making a lot of friends and establishing international contacts.
greatest_challenge: During the exchange, it was probably the abrupt changes being caused by the strikes, and not knowing whether a building might be closed, whether a course would take place at uni, online or not at all, et cetera. Since many courses were repeated, it wasn't the academic consequences so much as the insecurity about what was going to happen that could be stressful. Of course, this was ultimately out of anyone's control.

crucial_aspects: It was mainly a connection of two things. Firstly, I choose Paris because I'm very interested in art and art history and I've always loved painting and drawing. Paris is in many ways the capital of art, with its numerous museums and rich history, why I saw it as a great way to explore my interest. Secondly, the living situation in Paris was a big plus. I had heard about the cite internationale universitaire Paris, which is sort of a campus for exchange students. This made it both much easier and cheaper to find a place to live in an otherwise very expensive city.
info_ease: It was a bit difficult. We got a mail about where to show up for the introduction week and for the welcome meetings, but other than that there were not much information. It was very step-by-step in the sense that we got more information as we needed it, but it would have been nice to have a bit more information up front as we all had many questions about course registration and other practical stuff beforehand.
arrival_assistance: We had two welcome meetings. The first one was a welcome to the entire school regardless of the department. The meeting was an introduction to Sorbonne, how the school works and the different social offers. However, the entire meeting was in French and sadly, I don't speak a lot of French so I didn't understand much of it. The second meeting was a welcome for the economics department, where we got a general introduction to the school and the registration process. After the presentation, we could ask specific questions
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I got a link to the registration webside, where I needed to input a bunch of different information about myself. It was fairly straight forward, as most of the information was standard identification or easy to find. I needed a few documents like a certificate for my language level and a signed online learning agreement. This online learning agreement caused a bit of trouble. I needed a course description to get the courses, I planned to take, approved, but as I was not enrolled into my host university yet, I could not access this description. I ended up having to talk to my home university so I could make a temporary online learning agreement, which was a bit of a hasle. After I was enrolled, I got another email so I could get an account for the host university webside.
registration_help: I got help from my home university, which was really great and very quick. I also asked some of the former exchange students what they did and that helped a lot too. I also got help from the incoming student officer, when I arrived with registering to courses.
registration_success: Registering for classes was done on a webside at a specific timeslot. As everybody tried to register at the same time, the webside became faulty and I could only register for half of the courses I wanted. The day after I went to the Incoming student officer, who enrolled me manually to the rest of my courses. I only had to change one course as the one I wanted was full, but other than that I got all the courses I had planned to take.
registration_advice: I would try to make my online-learning agreement as soon as possible, so seek pre-approval as soon as you can as it can take some time. I ended up finding some course descriptions by going trough the university webside very carefully also looking at the pages only in french. When there were no description I looked if the course had been pre-approved before.
course_level: The courses were both easier and harder than at UCPH, but this was more due to the teaching style than due to the level. In general the level was a bit lower than at UCPH, as the courses were less focus on the specific mathematics of the models and more on a general understanding of the concepts instead. Furthermore, some of the courses were also intended for non-economics master students, why some basic economic theory needed to be covered and some of the models were simplified.
teaching_comparison: All the courses consisted of 3-hour lectures with class discussions. The focus was very different from UCPH, as there were little to no formal calculations and only graphical representation of the models. Instead there were a great focus on concepts and being able to relate the models to each-other and real-life problems. As an example the exams was primarily essays and open-ended questions, which could make the courses harder if this is not your strong suit.
courses_enrolled: I enrolled in 1) Labor Economics, 2) Industrial Economics, 3) Political Economy, 4) Development Macroeconomics and 5) European Integration.
recommended_courses: I would recommend Labor Economics, Industrial Economics and European Integration. All of these courses were nicely structured, the lecturer was super clear and all the learning material was readily available. I also found them really interesting. The other two were less structured and it was hard to find the course material, so I didn't get as much out of them.
unexpected_costs: I did not account any unexpected costs besides some things being more or less expensive, as I had asked some of the former exchange students about their costs.
cost_comparison: My host university didn't use books much and if they did they provided the material so that was free. Grocery shopping is slightly more expensive than DK, where I expected it to be cheaper. The metrocard is a bit more expensive than I expected, but it is still a good deal if you want to explore the city.
activities_available: As part of the introduction week you could sign up for a 5-day french course (4 hours each day). At the welcome meeting they presented a bunch of different the non-academic opportunities, including sport clubs and social activities. They presented it in french however, so it was a little difficult to figure out what all the extra curricular were. Furthermore, all the exchange students had a WhatsApp group, where social events were posted including parties, dinners, karaoke etc.
activities_recommended: I did not really participate in anything offered by the university. I mostly partook in events from Fondation Danoise.
weekend_recommendations: Use the city. There is so much fun to do! For instance: the channels are super lovely in the sun in the 10 arrondissement, all the museums are free if you are below 26 or walk along the highline in Paris.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy, since I had been to France before and kind of new what to expect. Also France is a european country why we share a lot of the same culture and values.
socializing_tips: Meet other people in the Cite. Go to parties and to you friends houses. It is the best way to meet people if you are open to meeting them.
cultural_challenges: Strikes. The french really like to strike. During my stay there were a change in the retirement age, which was a big debate and caused a lot of strikes affecting the transportation system and garbage disposal.
culture_appreciated: Going out. The French love to go out even on a regular week day and it makes the city very vibrant and alive.
top3_advice: 1)Be prepared for the registration process. It can be very tedious at times and 2) remember to ask for help! 3) Apply for the city it is a great place to live even if you live at another house than the danish one.
other_useful_info: The exam dates are released two weeks before the actual exam period starts. Don't stress about it. All the exams are by hand so practice your handwriting :)
most_rewarding: The social life at the Cite and the danish house.
greatest_challenge: The registration process.

crucial_aspects: I have learned a bit of french in school, and I wanted to live in the city of lights. I have always dreamed of going to Paris and Pantheon-Sorbonne, so this was the perfect opportunity.
info_ease: In general information was okay to find. However, there were some difficulties with the preapproval of courses upon arrival. Further I experienced, that the deadlines for signatures provided by KU were not the same as the once provided by Pantheon Sorbonne. This caused some unnescessary stress before the semester abroad actually started.
arrival_assistance: We had an integration week with language courses and a welcome meeting (all in french). Further one person connected to the economics department could help with the enrollment of courses.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The economics department held a welcome meeting for all ERASMUS students, where they explained the enrollment, how to get the student ID (you needed to pick it up physically in the main building, not in the city center), and how to enroll in courses online. However something was wrong with the website, when we needed to enroll for courses (half of them were missing in the overview) and we could not reach the economics department. But we solved it, and our contactperson enrolled us manually to not courses not seen on the website. Further, the learning agreement could not be signed online, but only in pdf by the economics department.
registration_help: We had a contact person from the economics department - she was really sweet and helpfull. In the first couple of weeks she got a lot of emails and calls, so the response time was quite long. but throughout the semester I had a good experience with her. She was very helpfull, when I needed to change my learning agreement.
registration_success: I was enrolled in all the classes I wanted, so that was very successfull
registration_advice: Be patient and be pro-active. The french system is not a digital and efficient as the danish - but remember, everything will work out in the end.
course_level: As the courses were master level and I am only in my bachelor I found some courses a bit difficult. But not too much, and I found them super interesting as well. My fellow students were also very happy to help.
teaching_comparison: I only had lectures (no TD's / holdundervisning) and they were each 3 hours. It is a bit longer than KU's lectures, and i found it a bit too long. Further, we only had a few exercises in the lectures and one or two old exams, so there were not much material for studying to the exam in the end.
courses_enrolled: - Topics in Environmental Economics - International Finance - Development Macroeconomics - European Integration - Industrial Economics
recommended_courses: I really liked the European Integration course. It was a bit though but very interesting. The professor is super smart, and she did small quizzes throughout the semester, which also counted in the final score. It was a nice way to always make sure, we understood what was going on. I also think, that this course had a very nice way of mixing and applying trade, micro and macro theory into some practicalities within the creation of the European Union. I also enjoyed the first half of Industrial Economics a lot. He provided us small exercises and I learned a lot about markets, mergers and collusion in theory.
unexpected_costs: I general I was a bit surprised that Paris has almost the same price level as Copenhagen. But I did not come across any big unexpected costs
cost_comparison: Food is just as expensive as in Copenhagen (not coffee and croissants), and in Paris there is a different culture of going out an eating a lot. Of course, you dont have to, but I did, and it was a bit expensive. But museums are free for EU citizens under 26 years, which was super nice.
activities_available: There were a lot of different sports you could apply for through the university. I played football with a french teams, and that was super fun. Also the university offered free french classes which I also participated in. Our french teacher took us to different museums, and she was very sweet.
activities_recommended: I would for sure recommend everyone to sign up for language courses. I did not get the ETCS for the course, so for me it was just as much a social thing, which was very fun. Also I would recommend to join a sports class, as this is one of the few ways to get in contact with the french people. But be aware, that most of the sports and cultural classes are in french.
weekend_recommendations: Enjoy Paris - there is so much to see! Many museums, parks, cafes and restaurants. I went out of the city two times to travel around in France (Lyon and île d'Yeu), which was super nice, but not a must. Also we went to see PSG play football at Parc de Prince and we saw a Rugby game as well. Also the night life in Paris is great!
culture_adjustment: I did not have any problems fitting in to the local culture, I find most french people super nice an welcoming.
socializing_tips: Join a sports team!
cultural_challenges: The french people are a bit more laid back and inefficient. It took some time to adjust to, but I learned to appreciate it.
culture_appreciated: The food and wine culture, and how the local use the outdoor areas of the city.
top3_advice: - Join the integration week and the language course. Here you will meet other exchange students and this was were I meet the people I ended up hanging with the most. - Be patient with the administration, they are not as efficient as in Denmark, but everything will work out in the end. - Start looking for housing as soon as possible
other_useful_info: Eventhough the french speaking can be a bit overwhelming in the beginning, it will get better throughout the semester.
most_rewarding: I learned a lot in my courses and a lot about cultural differences within Europe from the other exchange students.
greatest_challenge: The courses were a bit more challenging than expected, but that is probably because it was master courses, and I am in my bachelor. I found the balance between school and social life a bit challenging in the beginning as well. But in the end the exams actually went great and I have meet some amazing people and had some outstanding experiences.

crucial_aspects: I mainly chose the university because I wanted to go to Paris. This was the only agreement in Paris at my master's degree. I also choose it because the agreement is made with the Sorbonne School of Economics, and I wanted to take courses in economics.
info_ease: It was a bit mixed. The administrative aspects were fairly easy, we received information on where to register and everything. When it comes to information about courses, information was a bit more sparse. I recommend just writing professors directly, if some information about a given course is missing in the course catalogue. Especially with one course that I took at another university (at Paris School of Economics - the course was part of a shared master's programme with Paris 1), there was no information available, and they could not really help me at the host university. I missed the first class because I had not been informed about it.
arrival_assistance: After arrival there was an info meeting in the first week, where they explained how to select courses and everything. The selection process itself was easy and I got all the courses I wanted (almost, but only because some schedules were overlapping).
arrival_comments: They had said up untill the info meeting that we could choose courses also from other departments than Economics, but then at the meeting they discouraged it because they said they would have no info on exam dates up untill last minute, and if exams where overlapping they would not be able to do anything. Meaning that we would have to come back in the summer (6 months after our Erasmus stay had finished) to take the re-exams. This was a bit annoying, as I would have liked to take some courses at other departments, but did not do it because of this.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The course registration happens really late - in september, so after I had arrived in Paris, during the intro week. Up untill that point we had to do our learning agreements and information about courses was not very complete. This was a bit annoying, but perhaps mainly because it stressed me a bit out that we had received no information before the summer started about when and how the registration would take place. It ended up being fine though. A thing that I found a bit annoying was that the course descriptions were not there for a lot of courses. And for some of the ones where it was, the description was not complete enough. It was difficult to choose courses with the appropriate level and content that suited my academic interests, because of this.
registration_help: There was an info meeting and you could always ask the Erasmus coordinator questions. The help was sufficient when it comes to the administrative part of the registration - but not sufficient when it comes to the content and level of the courses.
registration_success: I got pretty much all the courses I wanted. The only reason why I did not get all, was because some where overlapping.
registration_advice: For future students I would recommend just trying to go with the flow - they do not do things as well in advance at Paris 1 as I was used to, but in the end everything worked out. I also recommend being very proactive in gathering information about the courses. If you find the course descriptions lacking, just write the professors about any questions you might have. I did this towards the end of the process and it was really helpful - I should have done it earlier! If you are taking Economic History at the PSE, then find information on your own about when it starts - don't wait for Paris 1 to give it to you. Find information on PSE's own website or Thomas Piketty's website.
course_level: The level was very different at the different courses (which were at different master's programmes). I took 4 master level courses and 1 bachelor level course.
teaching_comparison: It was generally a bit more old school. For example, I had a course where there was generally no slides or much written materials, you just had to listen and write everything down the professors said. The exams are also written in hand. This made sense of course for the more mathematically oriented exams, but there was also 3-hour exams where you had to make a "problématique" (problemformulering) and answer it with a structured argument essay (this was a bit challenging for me, because it had been a long time since I written that kind of texts in hand). In general, a lot more memorizing stuff than I was used to at KU. Also some cultural differences: the professor-student relationship is more formal than at KU (en général, il faut toujours vouvoyer les profs, par exemple).
courses_enrolled: Economic History (at PSE, with Thomas Piketty) Macroeconomics: Growth (Licence d'économie L3 course) Techniques quantitatives (at the Sciences économiques et sociales master) Économétrie appliquée (at the Économie du developpement master and Économie internationale master) Questions économiques contemporaines (at the Sciences économiques et sociales master)
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend the Economic History course to anyone interested in economic and social inequality (and the interplay with ideology and justification) in a historical perspective. It was probably the best course I have ever had. Économétrie appliquée was a really good course to get a hold of some causal inference econometrics techniques (not that advanced, but interesting course). Questions économiques contemporaines was also quite interesting with different researchers presenting their topics. It was however very old school (and very French). You French level has to be quite high to follow and to succeed in the exams, I would say. Techniques quantitatives was a bit too easy - take it only if you want a basic statistics course. A lot of focus on logistic regression and interpretations. I mainly took it to focus on learning to talk about quant. methods in French.
unexpected_costs: I had some medical expenses because I had problems with my eyes. I had to pay directly at the ophtamologist, but hopefully I will get some of it reimbursed.
cost_comparison: Groceries are bit more expensive than I expected/remembered. Restaurants are relatively cheap.
activities_available: A lot of sports and language courses were available.
activities_recommended: If you have time, signing up for a sport is probably fun and a great way to meet local students. In general, i found that local students were really nice and up for talking to us erasmus students. Also when it comes to doing things after class, like eating or having some drinks.
weekend_recommendations: So many things to see and do! Museums in Paris are generally free if you are under 26 (and a EU citizen).
culture_adjustment: I had lived in Paris before and speak French, so it was quite easy for me.
socializing_tips: Talk to people after class or during the breaks. Local students were really nice to include me and invite me to stuff!
cultural_challenges: Mainly that the teaching style was a bit different. More old school, and especially the exams were quite intense (and there were a lot of them).
culture_appreciated: Life at the cafés and the fact that people talk to each other more in the public space. The culture makes the city feel more vibrant because there is always life everywhere.
top3_advice: My general impression was that the experience is a lot nicer if your French level is already quite high. There are not that many courses in English to choose from. I met some other erasmus students who struggled quite a bit with the courses in French. Before the stay: Go with the flow and don't stress out about registration for courses. It does not happen as well in advance as you might be used to/prefer. But they are very flexible when the semester starts, and you can change courses the first 3 weeks of the semester. Enjoy living in Paris! Try not to let the courses and exams stress you out too much.
other_useful_info: Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne and Sorbonne Université are not the same university. But they share some campus buildings.

crucial_aspects: First and foremost i went to follow courses in French. Secondly was career opportunities and to meet new people
info_ease: Extremely difficult. The administration was all over the place, gave unclear guidance and seemed unfamiliar with their own rules. I'll give you two examples. 1) When examining the courses at Panthéon-Sorbonne i needed to find the course catalogues. On their website i could only find the names of the courses for Master students. There was a supposed link to the catalogues but when i clicked the link nothing happened. I made the administration aware of the issue but they did nothing to fix it. Their 'solution' was that they asked me what course descriptions i wanted and then they contacted each professor responsible for the respective courses. It was an extremely inefficient was to organize it which became clear in that it took them 3-4 weeks to gather the descriptions i demanded. 2) On their website exchange students, it was stated very clearly that ERASMUS students on Political Science could only follow 25 ECTS corresponding to 5 courses in the Department of Political Science. As i was obliged by KU to take 30 ECTS/6 courses i asked the administration if this rule was valid. They said yes and told me to take the 6th course in the department of either Law or Economics. After searching and searching i found a Law course and ended up registering for that. After my first lecture it was clear that it was extremely difficult and not in any way relevant to me. Therefore I asked the administration if it was in any way possible for me to take swtich the law course to a Political Science courses despite the aforementioned rule. They replied "of course". As i referred to the rule they had no idea what I was talking about. 2) 25 ECTS
arrival_assistance: An orientation meeting where a lot of the professors were wuite late.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: See the above comments.
registration_help: See the above comments.

crucial_aspects: Paris is the city of all cities. With its unique architecture, culture, language and cuisine, Paris is the place to be in your 20's. And getting the possibility to experience Paris, for not just a week of vacation, but for half a year was something I couldn't pass up on. Further, Sorbonne is a unique institution deeply integrated into the Parisian and French history and getting the chance to study in the iconic buildings on Place de la Sorbonne and Rue du Panthéon is truly a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Also, the courses looked really interesting.
info_ease: Not that easy unfortunately. One important thing when going to Sorbonne (and other french universities, I could imagine) is that you need to have a lot of patience. And the information I got about the courses available turned out to be different from the final courses offered, meaning I had to change my learning agreement and chosen courses at the last minute. I would recommend to email IRO.EES@univ-paris1.fr if you have any questions and as quickly as possible, Chloe has been the most helpful in the process.
arrival_assistance: I was offered a one-week French course at Sorbonne in the introduction week, this was really helpful to connect with other students. There was also a an introduction meeting for all exchange students but this was held in French meaning many students were excluded from the information despite the invitation to the meeting being in English.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: This process was maybe the worst thing about my stay in Paris. Three days prior to the courses starting, it had not been possible to sign up for any courses and we had no information on how to do so either. Finally, the economic department called us in to give us the information two days before the courses beginning. Upon registering for the courses, the available courses had changed so I had to make up a new course list on the spot while also being in a hurry due to the courses being first come first served. Also... when I showed up to the first class of one of my courses, we sat in crowded auditorium with nearly 100 students for one hour with no teacher, suddenly we received and email explaining that the course had been cancelled for the whole semester, they just forgot to tell us. Total scandal, I had to choose yet another course. But ultimately, it all worked out and the student councillors were helpful with changing courses.
registration_help: Very little help, mainly one student councillor called Chloe Hubbard, IRO.EES@univ-paris1.fr.
registration_success: Not very succesful. I ended up taking 5 courses with only 2 being the ones I originally planned on taking.
registration_advice: Be very patient. In the end it will all work out. Even though you will be frustrated, at least you're frustrated in Paris.
course_level: I ended up taking 2 master courses and 3 bachelor courses.
teaching_comparison: The biggest difference between Sorbonne and UCPH is the mandatory attendance. You have to present for all teaching exercises at Sorbonne. Also another thing is the grading, while at UCPH your grade consists 100% of your final test score, at Sorbonne in many courses the grade is divided into many parts. FX in one course 50% was the final grade, 20% was midterm 1, 20% was midterm 2 and 10% was attendance and participation.
courses_enrolled: International Monetary Economics Macroeconomics: Growth Game Theory Resources and Climate Change Comparative Politics
recommended_courses: I would recommend International Monetary Economics, it gives you a very cool deep dive into the monetary side of economics that we sometimes lack at UCPH. I would also recommend Resources and Climate Change if you're into climate economics. I would recommend against taking Game Theory as despite the course being presented as being in English, the teacher prefers speaking french...
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Good wine is way cheaper than in Denmark, take advantage of this. Also get a bike, Swapfiets has worked for me.
activities_available: Sport activities were available to students but often colliding with school activities. Sorbonne didn't really arrange anything social compared to other universities. Every activity between students was arranged by ourselves.
activities_recommended: Just enjoy the city.
weekend_recommendations: Just take advantage of being in Paris. Try and avoid the most touristy areas, instead go spend time where the Parisians spend time. Go to Belleville, go to Rue du Faubourg Saint-Denis, go to jazz clubs, go to canal st martin. Try and explore the 10th, 11th, 19th and 20th as much as possible.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy. Most importantly, learn some French. Remember to say bonjour, merci, s'il vous plait. Embrace the culture you're living in and try to be a part of it. And go to as many boulangeries as possible and find the best croissant, pain au chocolat and sandwich. Also read A Moveable Feast by Hemingway.
socializing_tips: This is the hardest part, try and be active in the teaching exercises or go to Rue Mouffetard in the weekends or after class, here you will often find a lot of students from Sorbonne.
cultural_challenges: The language and tonality.
culture_appreciated: The joy of life and slow tempo of life.
top3_advice: 1. Be open to new people and new experiences 2. Don't hold back 3. Live the parisian life you've always dreamt of
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Meeting so many amazing people and sharing amazing memories together.
greatest_challenge: Leaving home but also leaving Paris.

crucial_aspects: Metropolics. It's so convenient and diverse. School itself, I chose Paris 1 University because it shares a campus with the Sorbonne University, and the school is too beautiful. The project itself. I've always been curious about finance and economics.
info_ease: It was pretty easy and I think there's not much needed to be known.
arrival_assistance: Two strangers helped me to carry my luggage.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was incredibly difficult; everyone was complaining so much that I don't want to recount the process. The credit hours and course schedules provided by the host institution were severely inconsistent with reality, and course capacity was extremely limited. They basically did nothing for two weeks, sending no emails or information, and then suddenly one evening they'd notify you to register for classes the next day. If you missed the email, you were on your own. Then, if you wanted to change courses, or if you absolutely had to (I had to change courses because one professor didn't want to speak English), it was practically impossible. The person in charge was almost never in the office, and it took a very long time to reply.
registration_help: Church, so you can go and pray. After this I understand why there's security check at the entrance of the university, students could be very mad.
registration_success: I successfully registered for about a third of the courses I wanted. The courses available for exchange students were extremely limited; excluding French courses and overlapping time slots, there were almost no options. The person in charge kept emphasizing that if I chose courses from other departments, he wouldn't be responsible for any related exam overlaps or other issues, so I was scared off choosing courses from other departments.
registration_advice: Make sure you check your email frequently and register as early as possible, ideally at the first minute, as it's first-come, first-served.
course_level: It was very difficult. Because I had never studied economics, and although the course was called economics, the teaching method was very traditional, with a lot of math.
teaching_comparison: Teachers frequently write on the blackboard by hand; almost everyone does. And compared to Copenhagen, the teachers' spoken English is generally not very good. Many teachers don't allow photos of their PowerPoint presentations because they use those materials for exam questions, and they often don't reply to emails. Many classes don't have teaching assistants, so almost everything is self-taught.
courses_enrolled: urban economics/ micro finance/ economics of education/ microeconomics: uncertainty and information/ resource and climate change/ economics of banking
recommended_courses: I recommend Microfinance, Banking Economics, and Microeconomics: Uncertainty and Information. The first two are FMBA courses, packed with information and very engaging. The last one is an undergraduate course that provides a lot of foundational knowledge about economics.
unexpected_costs: The electricity bill is more expensive than I expected.
cost_comparison: The dentist. Compared to Copenhagen, it's practically free; even without insurance, it's fully reimbursed if you have student assistance insurance.
activities_available: There was a cocktail party on the first day of school, and the desserts were delicious. There was also a buddy system where you could find a buddy, but it wasn't very useful.
activities_recommended: There's so much to do in Paris. I didn't participate much in the school's activities because I'm not particularly talkative. But I had a lot of great time on my own with friends. Paris has many cinemas, and movie tickets are very cheap. Museums and art galleries are almost all free for students. Paris has so many delicious foods! There's a fusion tapas place called Otto near Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne University; their lunch sets are a great deal, highly recommended. Paris also has many bars, and the cocktails are fantastic. The cafes are also excellent; their Korean and Japanese coffees are superb. It might sound strange, but getting a haircut in Paris is very affordable and there are plenty of options. Paris' parks are beautiful and perfect for sunbathing. Paris is a great city for walking; it's not windy, everything has a historical atmosphere, and it's beautiful—take lots of photos. Paris is a perfect city for romance. I highly recommend walking hand-in-hand with your partner along the Seine, strolling through the Marais district, and buying vintage clothing—Paris has a huge selection of vintage items.
weekend_recommendations: You could take a day trip to Versailles Palace, or attend the Montmartre Wine Festival. Keep an eye on social media for events. Or just chill: get a good sleep, have a long brunch, read or study in a beautiful library, stroll around the city, soak up the sun, enjoy a nice meal, meet friends, or watch a movie. There's so much to do in Paris. On weekends, you could also take the train to Nice or a bus to Belgium. Yes, Flixbus isn't just going to Germany anymore, haha.
culture_adjustment: It's easy. Paris is a very inclusive city. I don't think people need to adjust because Paris has almost everything, and Parisians are almost used to everything. You can always find a sense of belonging. Paris has enough space and freedom for you to be yourself.
socializing_tips: To be honest, no, because I met a lot of Chinese students, and I felt that the French didn't speak English very much, and their English wasn't very good either.
cultural_challenges: The school's administration is so chaotic, if that's what you call a cultural difference.
culture_appreciated: People know how to relax, they don't love working, they don't have age anxiety, they are very inclusive, you can find almost any food or culture here, and strangers are friendly and will help with luggage. Ladies always go first. Everyone is well-dressed and very elegant.
top3_advice: Beware of thieves and pickpockets. Don't talk to strangers; that's how my phone was stolen. Don't rely on the police in Paris. Finding accommodation in advance will give you many options. Study hard. The academic workload in Paris is heavy, and all exams are closed-book, making it quite difficult and rigorous. The teachers will not make any exceptions for exchange students.
other_useful_info: It's best to learn French in advance.
most_rewarding: I would say that this exchange program has given me more confidence, even though I did terribly academically. However, I made many new friends, solved my own moving and housing problems, and learned new subjects. I feel I've grown a lot. And I've always wanted to live in Paris for a while, and that wish has come true.
greatest_challenge: I would say the difficulties were loneliness, anxiety, and uncertainty. It was hard to make friends in a new country, and my classmates weren't very talkative. Studying was tough. Many things didn't go as planned because of the chaotic school management; sometimes I felt powerless. And I experienced racial discrimination and phone theft at the subway station; I felt traumatized, but I'm much better now.

crucial_aspects: Culturally, Paris interested me as a city with its rich history, numerous cultural offers and shere size. Academically, the exchange - as part of the electives - gave me the possibility to explore a new subject/area of research.
info_ease: I expected much worse given the complaints of previous exchange students. I think especially in the beginning it is important to let go of your need for control at least a little bit and trust that everything is going to work out - in the end, the partner university, too, is interested in making a good impression on their exchange students.
arrival_assistance: There was a one-week language course as well as a formal introductory meeting and a more informal welcoming cocktail event.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The course registration was honestly chaotic. Of course, the initial learning agreement did not work out due to overlaps and limited admission. Students are responsible themselves for checking the compatibility of courses. The course registration took place online and was based on "first-come, first-serve".
registration_help: Panthéon-Sorbonne has a dedicated coordinator who serves as guidance to the exchange students. He is generally happy to help but possibly had to many issues to resolve and was thus not always quick to reply.
registration_success: In the end, I am happy with the course selection but it definitely warrants a certain flexibility from the students' side.
registration_advice: To stay relaxed. In case you do not get admitted to a course, you can possibly ask personally whether they can make for an additional spot.
course_level: 3rd year Bachelor courses, Master 1 courses.

I found it irritating sometimes that the professors insisted on their authority and treated some students badly and not as equal discussion partners (if ever they let a discussion happen to begin with).

unexpected_costs: nA

activities_recommended: I will always recommend sport courses - also as a way to actually speak applied French with other students.
weekend_recommendations: Lots of museums, parks, concerts, restaurants and bars leave, in my opinion, no time for boredom.

socializing_tips: Sport courses, coffee breaks during the lectures.

culture_appreciated: Affordable restaurants, buzzing streets and very clean parks.

Second, to bring some flexibility and trust that the administration will help you eventually. Third, to prepare for the exam period in early January in good time - otherwise it gets very stressful during and after the Christmas holidays.

crucial_aspects: Apart from the general appeal of going on an exchange in the form of trying something new, I specifically chose Paris/France because I wanted to improve my French. I have also travelled a lot in Paris previously, and quite like the city. To be honest, the academic aspect was somewhat secondary, and I would recommend someone going on exchange for exclusively academic reasons to apply for this university
overall_comments: Overall, I had an amazing experience and greatly enjoyed my time in the city. The reason I am not doing a 10/10 is due to a few issues with the host university, administrative ones in particular.
info_ease: Before arrival, I had set up an account on the university intranet (ENT) where info was communicated, but still things felt somewhat messy. A lot of info was sent to my personal mail in the first month
arrival_assistance: Assistance mostly occurred by visiting the “Tolbiac” center, and presenting myself. There I received my study card, as well as some further information
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall, I had an amazing experience and greatly enjoyed my time in the city. The reason I am not doing a 10/10 is due to a few issues with the host university, administrative ones in particular.
registration_process: When I arrived in Paris, I already had my learning agreement approved from Copenhagen, as sending an approved learning agreement was part of the requirements for online registration. However, during the intro week, we were send course schedules which A: weren't finished and B: showed that some of the courses from my original learning agreement took place at the same time. Due to this, I had to scramble in order to find a replacement course, reaching out to professors to send course descriptions (that were never available in the first place). Eventually, once I had found a new course package, I was told to send the learning agreement to the international coordinator of the faculty to receive a signature, to then send the signed document to the Erasmus coordinator.
registration_help: Communication was very loose, and I felt very much left to my own. Fortunately, communication with UCPH was much easier, and quite understanding of the messy situation
registration_success: I eventually managed to get everything aligned and get the courses I wanted, but the whole process was incredibly messy, and could have been so much easier if the university shared course descriptions and planned the schedule sometime earlier than the week before courses start
registration_advice: Take a deep breath, and prepare for the worst. Make sure to keep in contact with UCPH and start trying to get the info you need from Sorbonne as early as possible. Expect things to go wrong and lots of frustration, but also know that if you pay attention and keep working to solve things, eventually everything should be okay.
academics_comments: Overall, I had an amazing experience and greatly enjoyed my time in the city. The reason I am not doing a 10/10 is due to a few issues with the host university, administrative ones in particular.
course_level: Somewhat below the level I am used to at KU. Notably, courses in English felt quite a bit easier than those in French. Some of this may be due to me being much more at ease with English, but it also seems the academic ambition of the English courses has been lowered in order to allow for a more comfortable environment for the French students to practice their, often lackluster, English.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style varied a lot from course to course, but overall felt less participatory than that of UCPH. Not all professors used slideshows, and not all who did shared them after classes
courses_enrolled: Médias et compétitions politiques Issues of Climate change Dimensions numériques du politique Opinion et élections France and the EU Politiques économiques européennes
recommended_courses: I would recommend "Médias et compétitions politiques", mainly due to Mr. Simon who taught the course being a very engaging lecturer - you could clearly feel he cared about the subject. I would also recommend "France and the EU", as it was fun to get a distinct French perspective on the EU, and quite approachable due to being in English
unexpected_costs: Not any really
cost_comparison: Groceries were surprisingly manageable, but perhaps anything will seem fine when you're used to Copenhagen
activities_available: An intensive French course was offered for the intro week. It was really useful, enjoyable, and I ended up making many friendships here. Different social activities were also available, but communication was somewhat poor, and I didn't really make use of them
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend the intro week French course, great way to meet other exchange students and improve your French
weekend_recommendations: Just enjoy the city, it's Paris, there's something for everyone
culture_adjustment: I guess it depends on what you consider culture to be. If we're talking administrative systems, I never adjusted, but everything else felt quite easy to get used to.
socializing_tips: I know it may seem obvious, but speaking French. A lot of the locals are not that great at English, and will find it much easier to socialize with you if you do it in French. But also, you have plenty of opportunities to socialize with other exchange students in English
cultural_challenges: ADMINISTRATION/BUREAUCRACY
culture_appreciated: I just really loved being immersed in the language, and getting to improve myself.
top3_advice: 1. Prepare for hell in terms of administration/bureaucracy 2. Make sure to go to the intro week French courses and make connections 3. Enjoy the city, you are in one of the most exciting places in the world
other_useful_info: Most courses are graded using 2-3 different tests in the form of hand ins, presentations, multiple choice tests, etc. This allows a quite comfortable process, where you have a general sense of whether you will pass or not and can adjust your effort accordingly. But the course "Dimensions numériques du politique" had a professor who chose to ignore the general guidelines, and do the entire grade through one single written essay, taking place over two hours, in hand, in French. If you feel like that would be too challenging, avoid this particular course.
most_rewarding: Making new connections with people from all around the world and feeling how my French improved
greatest_challenge: Repeating myself here, but the uni admin was horrible, prepare for the worst.

crucial_aspects: Personal connection because of both heritage and friends, as well as academic opportunities in having the privilege in attending a university of both high historic and academic status. Another aspect was the concrete possibility of housing in a university city where cultures and nationalities meet in one single campus-like town, where safety and comfort, as well as engagement with and discovery of new environments by virtue of one's abilities and willingness to socialize are greatly prioritized. Going abroad to practice language skills was equally central to the choosing, not to mention the sheer personal and administrative growth in approaching a new opportunity with care and responsibility.
info_ease: I wasn't afraid to ask whenever I was confused or lacked support in areas, but if one isn't necessarily accustomed to doing that, maybe by it being too intimidating, then I'd assume one would have a hard time finding all the right information. There were times where I felt like I was in the unknown and approaching a situation completely unaware of what would await me, in a sense.
arrival_assistance: I managed to "book" a physical appointment with a person in charge, which she suggested as she might've sensed my unknowing and wanted to cram every little question I had - which amounted to a continuous email correspondence - into one single sit-down where I could see and hear the person in front of me as well as the university itself. There were also welcoming days - one amphi seminar-like class, where students would be "welcomed" and receive information, although much of this was vague information and much of it of social relevance than academic which I struggled with in the beginning. I ended up asking my new classmates - when I in fact enrolled in the courses - for information because it was much more helpful and comfortable.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to be selected and approved for even applying to the host institution. Between that and actually applying, the procedure was a little demanding and at times confusing, because a lot had to be done of bureaucratic measures, but once all was filled out, it was pretty smooth. I had to fill out the application online which was long and within a network system that seemed outdated, although it worked fine. It was primarily ticking off boxes, so no motivational letter was necessary, but I had to attach files with evidence of both language skills, learning agreement (if I remember correctly), passport and former grades.
registration_help: There was provided several step-by-step guides to work and navigate the system, which was helpful.
registration_success: I had to work around timing and planning issues, but I received help in person from a person in charge after meeting with her physically, and eventually I got the classes I wanted, somewhat. The procedure in getting an Online Learning Agreement and a pre-approval was tricky, and felt isolating at times.
registration_advice: Talk to people! Ask questions, no matter how small or big.
course_level: I managed to get both L1, L2 and L3, meaning first year, second year and third year courses in a total of five courses.
teaching_comparison: It differed in pace and treating of curriculum. It seemed that there wasn't any mandatory reading, and courses depended on mouth to ear from teacher to student. Very by-heart learning as in one would listen to a teacher and take notes. Not much engaging which is completely different from my home university.
courses_enrolled: 1. Histoire de la Photographie 2. Archéologie et Arts de l'Afrique 3. Art et Mondialisation 4. Art du XXè siècle 5. Histoire de la Mode
recommended_courses: Art et Mondialisation by virtue of the teacher, Lotte Arndt, and the building/planning of the course with its treated subjects and themes. Histoire de la Photographie I would recommend for first year students.
unexpected_costs: Some home furnishing like pillows, pillowcases and a tray to carry things to and from communal kitchen. As for academic context, the French system requires pens and paper etc. as computers aren't used for any tests and/or exams.
cost_comparison: Can't think of any, but you can find cheaper alternatives to many things of same quality.
activities_available: Sports mainly. Also political protests and rallies, as well as exhibitions, lectures, events and student trips that were encouraged and broad to attention (although mainly by mail and/or flyers available in the halls etc.)
activities_recommended: Being social in any way shape or form, to the ability and extent that one is capable of. Being social can be intimidating, but is very much what can hold everything together and make the stay worth it in the long run. Don't be afraid to put yourself out there. There are sports, but also engaging in group chats to plan get-togethers and activities such as museum going, bar hopping (can be done alcohol-free), game nights and karaokes etc. Taking walks around the city is also a major must, as you get movement, cognitive recognition of surroundings, especially when paying attention, learning several neighborhoods. Grocery shopping and meal prepping together is also fulfilling and a fun way to do everyday things. Cinema, as in going to the movies, either alone or with someone is also great. One shouldn't be afraid of solidarity either.
weekend_recommendations: Museums, parks, monuments and taking non-planned walks, seeing the nooks and crannies of the city.
culture_adjustment: Very. Stay open and curious. Know your boundaries but don't take everything personal. Engage with people, not machines, make it a habit of asking people for help.
socializing_tips: Be honest and daring enough to get out of your shell, as long as you don't hurt yourself or push yourself too hard, beyond personal boundaries etc. Find one or two people, or a small group to be around and be comfortable with.
cultural_challenges: Not challenging, only uplifting and teaching me new ways of approaching situations, especially academic.
culture_appreciated: Food and the particular culture of enjoyment in life. Also the city's life in general, bustling both day and night. I appreciate Paris' cultural offers and the multicultural side(s) of the city. Language also, of course.
top3_advice: It can be tough, but social network will help, and trusting oneself, preferably without having too high standards or expectations towards oneself. Making mistakes and not understanding everything is normal and to be expected. The only thing you have to do is show up, both for yourself and physically in being present. Don't isolate yourself, and remember that you're for the most part on exchange to learn and experience, not to perform and perfect.
other_useful_info: Write mails or show up and ask questions. Don't be late for classes, in fact, in the beginning when you're still getting the hang of things, be a little early. Don't stress and remember to take notes, however manageable. Have access to a printer and several libraries.
most_rewarding: The language development, learning that I was able to complete this semester academically and the housing in the Cité Universitaire.
greatest_challenge: Doing oral presentations in each course, in French, when I havn't been much accustomed to that kind at home, much less in another language. The bureaucratic procedures, with three individual institutional procedures to navigate, Erasmus+ and the amount of steps to take in relation to that is on that list as well. I had a hard time joggling both exchange, housing, academic procedures and responsibilities all while being on actual exchange and going to school, being social etc.. The different elements took time away from the other elements, and my stay in general. But this is a mental issue, mostly.

crucial_aspects: I have always been fascinated by the French language, culture etc. This interest was sparked many years ago on family holidays, and when the opportunity of travelling to and studying in France was presented to me via the general information from the University of Copenhagen, I couldn't resist the temptation. The crucial aspects of choosing France – and not an English speaking country like many of my fellow students do – was the language. I simply wanted to enhance my French skills as well as trying to understand the Parisian lifestyle and French culture.
info_ease: It was fairly easy. But to many students it was very confusing to receive a bunch of information only in French. It did not seem very pedagogical and helpful. Also, to not receive the information need directly via email was frustrating. All information was provided through the University's website, and to navigate on this was not easy.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any direct and personal assistance but only general information. I quickly teamed up with other students in order to be able to find out what to do when and how.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: 1. Find the interesting courses online. 2. Show up to the courses in person in the 2 week trial period. 3. Book a meeting with the course administrator. 4. Select the courses with the course administrator and become frustrated when the timetables for the courses do not add up because of the collided schedules. 5. Quickly choose a different course from the one you wanted in first place. 6. Receive a printout of your selected courses (this seemed to me very outdated since receiving emails is a far more superior system...)
registration_help: Only the course administrator (her name was Marion Bonnefond).
registration_success: Fairly succesful. I wanted two courses I couldn't have because of the colliding timetables. This meant I followed two courses I didn't want.
registration_advice: Be prepared! There is not much help to receive and the system of choosing the courses is not transparent. Be patient and relaxed and hope for the best. There isn't much else to do...
course_level: The level of the courses was high. The professors were very well-prepared. There really isn't much else to elaborate on here.
teaching_comparison: Not at all. In Paris everything is taught in an old school fashion. There is not group work (except for in one class), there is no specific curriculum (it is only the material the teacher provides that is the curriculum), and there is no self-study (this meaning attendance at classes was mandatory in order to follow the courses). To me it seemed as if the students were not free to arrange their lives for themselves – they were simply to attached to the classes etc. Also the classes were held at outrages hours compared to at UCPH (some classses began as early as 7:45 in the morning, whereas others ended as late as 22:00 in the evening). Also the written exams I had were multiple choice which is not a type of exam provided at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Droit civil Relations internationales Philosophy of Law European Law History of the European Legal System
recommended_courses: It depends on the student's interests and desires. I believe international understand is important, and therefore courses in European Law and International Relations are important. These courses broaden the scope of understanding which in the future will be crucial.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs during my stay.
cost_comparison: Books were way less expensive than I thought, simply because buying books wasn't required to follow the courses. Food and general living costs are expensive in Paris, but not more expensive than I anticipated.
activities_available: All different kinds of sports, social soirées, job fairs etc. I found the university to always be full of life an activity.
activities_recommended: Sports! When you are new to a university getting to know other students is crucial. It can sometimes be difficult to befriend others in class, especially if there's a language barrier. But when playing sports it's way easier to talk to other students and to get to know them in a more comfortable atmosphere.
weekend_recommendations: During holidays and weekends it is really easy to take the TGV (high speed train) to other cultural sites or citys). I visited Bordeaux, Toulouse, Biarrtiz, Marseille, Geneva, Milan, Joyeuse as well as Giverny. France is a big country with many beautiful and interesting places, so the possibilities are endless.
culture_adjustment: It was neither easy nor difficult. I have been to Paris many times before and knew the city quite well. The language barrier was probably the most difficult part, but just like anything else you quickly adapt.
socializing_tips: Go to all the social acitivities available. Get to know your neighbourhood – once you know the owner of the local café just a little bit, it seems way more welcoming to sit down for a cup of coffee during weekends.
cultural_challenges: The French have no logic and love bureaucracy. Everything is done in a much more complicated manner than necessary. Nothing too extreme, but very frustrating and challenging when trying to adapt to new surroundings. There are plenty of cultural differences, and most of them are subtle.
culture_appreciated: The food, the importance of cultural heritage and the architecture.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared and begin your application for exchange more than one semester before actually going abroad. There are many deadlines, forms, grants to be applied for etc. 2. Be well aware of what your reasons are for going on exhange. Is it to enhance your resumé or is it because you actually have specific reasons for going to the desired place. I believe most people enjoy their semester abroad, but don't go if you feel a certain academic pressure – go because you want to. 3. If you wish to study French law you need to speak French on a proper level. There is no mercy from professors or other students – so be prepared to be in classes, where it's everyone to himself.
other_useful_info: If you have a girlfriend, very close family connections or friends that are close to you, be prepared for a very challenging experience. It is rewarding to go abroad but also difficult to keep the ties to the before mentioned people close and warm.
most_rewarding: The cultural understanding as well as my enhancement in French have been the two most rewarding parts of my exchange experience.
greatest_challenge: To miss friends and family.
