crucial_aspects: The deciding aspect for me was the language and culture. I have long wanted to improve my French and thought of this as an excellent possibility to do so. At the same time, I had always dreamed of living in Paris, so it was a great way of combining the two. Panthéon-Assas is at the same time the best university for Law in Paris and possibly France, why I at the same time could get a prime university experience in the centre of Paris. The university had recently also added a number of courses in English, which made it possible for me to combine courses in both French and English to ease the language difficulty.
info_ease: The university has quite a good website for incoming students with information about costs, courses, and introduction. It should however be noted that the information does not necessarily arrive in good enough time, thus it can be necessary to rely on information from previous semesters.
arrival_assistance: The university organises an intro week for law students in the beginning of both semesters, where the first day is reserved for administration and information about the university, while the remaining 4 days are an intro to French law method, which can be really helpful if you take TD classes. An advice is to go in person to the International office for incoming student as soon as possible when you arrive to make sure all the administration is in order. This could be for the student number, the creation of your ENT profile (student website), etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process is a bit different as it is very manual in its process. Once the courses are made available on their website, you can make yourself an overview of the courses you can take. Two things to keep in mind are the rather small courses, as normal CM courses (lectures only give 4 ECTS, which then requires a lot of courses to fill the min. 30 ECTS required), but you have the option of adding a TD (seminars) to the courses, which then gives 9 ECTS in total (only possible for courses in French). The second thing to mind is the scheduling of the courses, which I found to be quite limiting as some courses within the same interest field are overlapping, making it difficult to follow (not impossible). At some point the university will send you a form to fill in with the courses you want. This is quite easy, and you just send it back via email. Once the semester start, the first 2 weeks are “trial weeks” in the sense that it is still possible to change courses in that period, so you have the option of going to all the courses you want and find those you want to take. In the end, it is just important to register and confirm with the International Office, which courses you end up taking.
registration_help: The International office at the university is super helpful, I would strongly recommend to go in person when you need them instead of email (or do both).
registration_success: Very successful. Apart from limited spots in TD classes, there are almost unlimited spots in CM courses, why you can take any course you want (within the limits of you pre-approval from KU).
registration_advice: Go to the International office in person when you need and otherwise use the first two weeks to look at as many courses as you can, because the professor and the teaching method various extremely much from course to course.
course_level: Very mixed. Master 1 courses are quite challenging, but it is mainly due to the teaching method rather than the curriculum. I took only International and European law courses, hence no courses in French law, which may be more difficult to follow and understand. I would say the level is slightly lower than at KU courses in Danish.
teaching_comparison: Very different! It is the professor who has complete control and the style of teaching various very much from course to course. The most challenging part is however that there almost in all courses are no books or power points to assist with the learning, hence what you need to learn is what the professor says in the lectures. This is very different from KU and very challenging as you rely very much on notetaking or notes from others.
courses_enrolled: European Law European International Relations International Investment Law Economic Law History of European Legal Systems Philosophy of Law Droit Européen des Affaires (European Business Law) Droit du Contentieux International (International Litigation Law)
recommended_courses: European Law - Professor is really good Economic Law - Interesting economic approach to law
unexpected_costs: I had a very expensive Airbnb the first month but was then able to move to Cité Universitaire that only costs 500€ a month which is very cheap for Paris
cost_comparison: Paris is an expensive city, but so is Copenhagen, so not many surprises there.
activities_available: Sports, clubs and events are organised by the university, so there are many options to participate in.
activities_recommended: Any sports that you like or want to try. I did fencing for the first time in my life and found it super interesting and fun.
weekend_recommendations: See Paris! It is such an amazing city with so much to offer. So unless you really feel you need to see the rest of Europe, I would recommend staying in Paris and just learn and enjoy the city.
culture_adjustment: I felt it was quite easy. The city is not too different from Copenhagen and though the French culture is very different, you will spend a lot of time with other exchange students who is in the same position.
socializing_tips: Participate in as much as you can and especially the introduction week at the university is a good opportunity, because once the day is done, you can go grab a drink or similar with the others. So go to the introduction week.
cultural_challenges: The way you speak and refer to others at the university or in public. You need to be very formal and respectful when addressing them and not by first name, which is very different from at home.
culture_appreciated: The more relaxed and try to enjoy life lifestyle that the French have. They just take longer with things, which can both be frustrating and nice.
top3_advice: 1. Go to the introduction week and go in person to the international office if needed 2. Participate in as many activities as you can with the other or friends 3. Enjoy Paris as much as you can!
other_useful_info: Administration can be very difficult and annoying, so brace yourself with patience.
most_rewarding: Living in Paris and experiencing the city, as well as all the friends I got along the way.
greatest_challenge: Leaving!

info_ease: There were introductory events set up to disseminate the information, but it was quite difficult to get in touch with the coordinators for international students and to know which offices to report to.

registration_process: First there was inscription administrative, for which I waited in line for a long time in front of an office before being told that the office for inscription administrative didn't do international students. I was then sent to the direction des affaires internationales, which was exceptionally closed twice both times I came despite the office door saying it would be open on the previous day. I had hustled over from a different campus because the only opening time which suited the intro week schedule for international students left little time to make it over, so a sweaty and desperate appearance got me in the second time, where I was quickly helped. Then came the inscription pédagogique, which consisted of the choice of subjects. Was supposed to work online; didnt; I got it fixed at the direction des affaires internationales.
registration_help: The local students were most helpful! The administration was quite helpful when I succeeded in getting through to them. There was helpful information from the administration in the intro week.
registration_success: Very! I enrolled in all the courses that I wanted.
registration_advice: Have patience, don't stress too much, and know that you can argue your case with the administration. Rules aren't necessarily hard rules as such: you can oftentimes talk or charm your way around them.
academics_comments: I had a great time but was perhaps a little overly ambitious in only choosing courses in the local language.
course_level: One of my courses was Ba, the other four were Masters. Us international students had fewer courses than the local students, which was offset by the fact that the courses were rendered somewhat more difficult by being in French.
teaching_comparison: Very different. Less interactive, more of a reading with many of the professors. There were usually no accompanying visual aids (e.g. PP slides) or textbook readings.

cultural_challenges: the whole no toilet seats situation took a bit of getting used to
culture_appreciated: The value placed in food
top3_advice: join a club, befriend locals from your courses to get good notes, check out the cultural activities at la cité internationale. Also the restaurant le quartier rouge is great, they have jazz jam sessions every Sunday.
other_useful_info: The vélib bikes are a pretty great way to get around. Also get the navigo liberté card for public transport which just charges your transits to your card at the end of the month.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and speaking lots of french!
greatest_challenge: The struggle with the administration
other_comments: Enjoy the city!

crucial_aspects: For me, it was definitely Paris as a city and France in general that was the principal reason for my exchange and not the university. I didn't know much about Panthéon-Assas.
info_ease: Not very easy and often you needed to contact the administration to get your needed information. As there were some problems they would answer quite slowly.
arrival_assistance: We had an intro meeting and then you could contact the administration.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had to send the course description, ECTS, exam description etc. several times through different formulas.
registration_help: Contacting my administration, contacting the Paris administration and some guides.
registration_success: There were many courses that I wasn't allowed to get - I think I was refused 50 % as they weren't strictly discussing typical law courses. I didn't get this, as it is possible to get courses on other facultiies in Denmark and a lot of courses on law are different from traditional law courses when you choose optional courses - but very important that they are good old conservative law courses when you're on exchange!
registration_advice: Nothing really - just expect that you'll have to choose law courses and that you will probably get a couple of french courses.
course_level: The level wasn't toon high compared to the level we're used to in Copenhagen but the teaching and studying method is so different in Paris so that it will challenge you a lot.
teaching_comparison: Very conservative and primarily big amphithéatre (audiotorium) courses where they speak for 2-3 hours and you don't interact with the teacher.
courses_enrolled: History of European Legal Systems History of the European Legal Systems European Law Introduction au droit de la communication Philosophy of Law Droit de l'union européenne 2 Philosophie du droit et de la justice International investment Law I also had french courses but I wasn't allowed the ECTS that I received for them in Paris (4,5 ECTS).
recommended_courses: Take all the english ones as they are easier and more suited for Erasmsus (they are less harsh on you as they don't expect an expert in the french method. Check the exam if it's released (wasn't the case when I went). Otherwise just take the courses that you find intereseting but not too difficult and not master courses (no extra exam try if you fail)
unexpected_costs: Nothing in particular
cost_comparison: Groceries more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: If you're under 26 years old almost all museums are free and a lot of student prices.
activities_recommended: Whatever you like as Paris has most activities!
weekend_recommendations: Again, as you like. However, if you like visiting other cities then reserve a ticket for the TGV (fast train) some weeks before doing a trip and you'll quickly and very comfortably. I went to Marseille and loved it.
culture_adjustment: It was alright - the Parisians are a lot like people from Copenhagen - difficult to engage with, but if you live in the cité universitaire you'll have a social basis there and then you try to meet some real parisians and hang out with the Erasmus people if it clicks.
socializing_tips: Nothing other than what you've learned from home.
cultural_challenges: People are more direct in the trains and they are more loud and sometimes annoying - you'll get used to it. Also, you have to be more formal when talking to teachers and authorities etc. VERY IMPORTANT to say "bonjour/bonsoir" when you enter in cafés, shops, bars and clubs or they'll be annoyed with you - and I guess it's fair enough.
culture_appreciated: Outgoing and laissez-faire culture. Some much life in the city concerning culture, cafés and bars everyday outside and inside - so nice!
top3_advice: 1) Do you want to go to Paris because it's a nice city? Consider whether it's worth it as they are more harsh in Paris towards Erasmus students. If you love Paris or just wanna experience the culture badly then it's definetly worth it. If you're in between two then choose the other. 2) You gain a lot by studying french before coming! However don't stress about it it'll be alright.
other_useful_info: Idk.
most_rewarding: The people I met and the cultural experience.
greatest_challenge: Being a new place with so little help and support. Also, being confronted with the language barrier even though I had a pretty good level of French.

crucial_aspects: That I wanted to get a familiar relationsship to an European city, and I love Paris.
info_ease: There were scheduled about two meetings which were okay but not super informative. Moreover, most of it was in French, and many students in the room didn't speak not understand French.
arrival_assistance: Stated above.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You wait to choose your courses until the very last minute which makes no sense. The time tables are also only available right before the classes begin, and many of the courses you want will often clash. This proces was very frustrating.
registration_help: We went to the international office many times as well as every other exchange student. But they had too little staff to keep up, so we often waited for hours.
registration_success: Not succesful at all. I wanted English classes only, which was a possibility that the university wrote about on their website. But as soon as I saw the time tables, I realized that this would not be possible. After about two months of dealing with the issue, I gave up and ended up only achieving 26 ECTS points, since there were not enough courses.
registration_advice: Don't go to this university if you want English taught classes only and want to achieve 30 ECTS points.
course_level: All of the English classes were at BA-level. The courses were also small (4 ECTS points each) which made the course quite superficial. Also, when being on your masters, you have an advantage of having some knowledge of the different fields from finishing you bachelor.
teaching_comparison: Very different. Mostly big lectures, writing down everything the teacher says, and no books.
courses_enrolled: French Constitutional Law, French Business Law, History of Codifications, Introduction to Crossborder Litigation, Law and Economics of the Firm, French Law of Obligations.
recommended_courses: French Constitutional Law because the teacher was really cool. French Law of Obligations because it felt somewhat relevant to get to know some of these general terms in English.
unexpected_costs: Nothing I can recall.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping was just as expensive as in Denmark. Eating out is generally cheaper than in Denmark.
activities_available: Some sport activities (I didn't look into these) and very few social activities.
activities_recommended: I didn't go to any activities planned by the universities. Only events I looked up for myself.
weekend_recommendations: Don't stress about visiting other cities! Paris is huge, and there're so many things to do.
culture_adjustment: It took me some time to adjust the French way of dealing with administrative issues. They stick to the same rules always even if these rules makes no sense and/or are super ineffective.
cultural_challenges: The one stated above.
culture_appreciated: That it felt like everyone was out every night. All restaurants, cafes and bars were full on both week nights and in the weekend. It creating a very unique ambience.
top3_advice: 1) Be prepared of the administrative chaos, 2) go out to eat as much as you can (!) but be aware of the very well-known, touristy places (these are good, but way more expensive than the local, authentic restaurants), and 3) be active in the search of other exchange students - the university was not helpful in this regard.
other_useful_info: Nothing I can recall.
most_rewarding: Getting Paris as a second home.
greatest_challenge: Dealing with the host university.

crucial_aspects: Language and the character of the destination (the city).
info_ease: It was okay - there was a "folder", but the administration process was complicated and getting signed up for courses etc. did include some problems.
arrival_assistance: There was an introductory meeting which clarified a lot of questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We had to go through a link sent by e-mail and tick off boxes. It was a bit complicated in the way that you need to be well aware of the schedules of each course, and course discriptions could be hard to find. However, with a trial period of a week or two it was possible to try different subjects before choosing definitively.
registration_help: Trial period mainly. Administrative problems could be resolved by going to the exchange office.
registration_success: I signed up for the classes which I preferred, with one exception due to schedule overlap.
registration_advice: Be well aware of schedule before choosing. Also, pay attention to the type of class/type of exam as well as the language spoken when making your choice.
course_level: In general, the courses were fairly easy (also because the exams were easy/not that demanding). I only took lectures - no classroom courses, and the lectures, in general, are not that extensive and the exams reflect this too. That being said, the content of the subjects were fairly high level (especially the class on MA level) and of solid depth. The professors showed great insigt, but in the end the exams were reasonable.
teaching_comparison: I only had lectures which are very much like the ones we have at UCPH. However, there are no books in the lectures at Assas, and hence the professor's words not only are important in terms of understanding the subject, they actually constitute the curriculum of the course. For this reason, paying close attention and taking notes during the lectures is paramount.
courses_enrolled: 1) Droit de l'Union européenne, 2) Droit de la concurrence (européen et interne), 3) Philosophie du droit, 4) Introduction to cross-boarder litigation, 5) French constitutional law, 6) French law of obligations.
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed competition law and philosophy of law. These courses are in French with oral exams and thus require a solid French language. The content of both courses was high level and the professors were highly competent. For non-French speakers, I recommend only doing English courses. This will include signing up for all the French courses there are in order to obtain a full semester's credits (ECTS).
unexpected_costs: Personal spending is high in Paris - everything is a bit expensive. That being said, I did not encounter unexspected costs.
cost_comparison: I was aware of the prices on different items. Groceries are around as expensive as they are in Denmark.
activities_available: It was possible to join a large variety of student associations. Furthermore, there were tours arranged to i.e. the Senate and the Cité Universitaire.
activities_recommended: Pub crawl, the Senate and the Cité universitaire (the trips planned by the faculty) are recommendable.
weekend_recommendations: Some leave the city for the weekend from time to time, which can be nice. I did not however, since I prioritized getting to know the city with long walks in different areas and benefitting from the extensive and incredible cultural opportunities, that Paris has to offer.
culture_adjustment: Adapting to the French system can be a bit difficult, mainly encoutering the administrative procedures which are heavy and slow. Culturally, the country is european, the city is very international and for these reasons, getting settled in Paris is not difficult (even though the adapting to the French attitude, manners and slight more formal social manouvering can take a bit of time).
cultural_challenges: In general, people from the northern countries are less formal, and this means that it is possible to come off as inpolite towards a French person. There are small/subtile gestures that show a bit of cultural differences (for example it's important to say hello/bonjour before ordering anything). It is something to adapt to, but I would not define it is a challenging.
culture_appreciated: The cultural openness, the culture of reading (books everywhere!!), the general appreciation of art and knowledge and - of course - the food culture.
top3_advice: If you speak French/can improve it - do so! If you cannot, don't give up right away. While not without complications, speaking English and not French is possible (also in terms of ECTS). Have patience (namely with the administration) Be persistent (namely with the administration).
other_useful_info: Travaux dirigés (classroom courses) have a reputation of being very difficult and require a lot of work, and the exam is much harder. Therefore, think twice before picking this type of course. Many lectures are "podcasted" and can be found online. Before giving up a course due to schedule overlap, think about this and check if podcast can be an option. Only taking English courses is possible, but obtatning 30 ECTS might be complicated (i.e. due to schedule overlap).
most_rewarding: Facing new and personally developing challenges as well as improvement of language skills (French).
greatest_challenge: Courses in French and living with lectures being the only teaching form (which I chose), since this entails less social life on campus.

crucial_aspects: I had never been to Paris before, and I was very curious to try and live there. I also heard good things about the university.
info_ease: It was a bit difficult to make contact with the university, and the website is confusing to navigate.
arrival_assistance: We received assistance from responsables of exchange/mobility of the university. It was however still difficult to clarify questions and issues.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: A long time went by without knowing anything about the registration process, and when it finally came, we had very little time to choose. But it worked fine as soon as I was able to apply.
registration_help: There was assistance, but I would not always get replies.
registration_success: It was succesful, I got the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Be aware of how many English courses they offer, as they inform that it is possible to do only English courses, but it is not guaranteed that you can get English courses worth 30 ECTS.
course_level: The level of the courses varied significantly. Though the courses were very small (4 ECTS), the amount of stuff you had to learn was big in some of the courses. But the overall level was appropriate, I will say.
teaching_comparison: It is very different. No books to study, only relying on powerpoints which sometimes had very little info.
courses_enrolled: European International Relations International Investment Law Law and Economics Philosophy of Law European Law History and Principles of French Intellectual Property Law History of the European Legal System I also had a compulsory French language class
recommended_courses: European International Relations - very interesting International Investment Law - very interesting and high level Law and Economics - very interesting for a law student, because you get a different approach (economic approach)
unexpected_costs: It was very expensive to do laundry which was unexpected. Other than that nothing really.
cost_comparison: Bakeries, groceries, restaurants had fair prices, a little less expensive than DK. Public transport was a lot more expensive than I thought.
activities_available: Activities such as wine and cheese tastings and trip to the Senate
activities_recommended: I would recommend all of them
weekend_recommendations: Go to Versailles, go to the parks and chill in the weekends, see museums, walk along the Seine. Just explore the streets of Paris.
culture_adjustment: A bit difficult because I didn't speak much French.
socializing_tips: Speaking French to some level is a big advantage. The students were very nice, but a bit longer.
cultural_challenges: Again, that they are not used to speaking English to the same extent as Danish people.
culture_appreciated: Very kind people.
top3_advice: The administrative process can be a bit challenging, but it is not too unusual when going on exchange, I heard. It's a very big advantage to speak some French. I will recommend to look for accommodation at CIUP.
other_useful_info: Paris is an amazing city to live in overall.
most_rewarding: The cultural exchange, the people you meet and also what you learn at university and about yourself on the journey.
greatest_challenge: Learning to speak French and be friends with the locals.

crucial_aspects: Major European city, with good university of law and further improvement of french language.
info_ease: I had a few difficulties in the beginning, however the mandatory briefing/meeting from the host university solved it.
arrival_assistance: A mandatory introduction meeting from the host university.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The initial registration of courses were relatively simple and easy to apply since it was online, however changes required to physically go to the registration office at certain times.
registration_help: It was possible to get help at the registration office.
registration_success: Overall successful, however there was one class that I was not allowed to take.
registration_advice: Do not hesitate to transfer to a different class if you have picked wrong. In most situations the host university provides help to find a solution even though the system seems strict.
course_level: I had 4 classes on BA level and 2 classes on MA level.
teaching_comparison: Very different since all teaching was lectures and it was just the professor speaking with only a few questions to the students here and there.
courses_enrolled: History of the European Legal Systems, History and Principles of French Intellectual Property Law, European Law, Droit de l'union européenne 2, Droit de la convention européenne des droits de l'homme and Droit européen des affaires.
recommended_courses: History and Principles of French Intellectual Property Law, European Law and Droit européen des affaires.
unexpected_costs: No specific.
cost_comparison: Food/groceries.
activities_available: Different events for exchange students like wine and cheese tasting, guided tour around the city and visit to the French Senate.
activities_recommended: The wine tasting at the university was cozy, and find a running club/social runs around the city.
weekend_recommendations: To visit Paris's many museums. A lot of them are free for european citizens under 26.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Be open and try to speak in french.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The openness and kindness.
top3_advice: 1) If possible, try to improve your french before going, 2) Find courses that do not overlap each other, and 3) Be prepared for academic challenges.
other_useful_info: Everything seems very confusing at first but it will work out, be patient.
most_rewarding: New academic challenges and legal perspectives, improving my french language and making new friends.
greatest_challenge: To take law courses in french.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to France and speak French
overall_comments: The place was really nice, the Uni not as nice.
info_ease: It was really hard to know where to choose courses and we got our schedule very late, like after three weeks. I think that the system could've been exlplained better.
arrival_assistance: There was some infodays in the beginning, but most of it was school and related to how to have the courses in French. The background on French law and the information days overlapped, which was unfortunate.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The place was really nice, the Uni not as nice.
registration_process: Registration should happen from a platform, and it took a long time to fill in. I received two forms, one of which I didn't even have to fill out. So that was kind of annoying. Also we first got our student cards a month into uni, which was problematic, because we had to get them to enter. The OLA has also been a burden and hard to get signed.
registration_help: Not much, it could be translated to a bad English. Otherwise there was help when choosing the courses definitively.
registration_success: Very successful, some of the courses overlapped, but I got to choose from all three years of the licenses and first year of master.
registration_advice: Know what courses you would like to get and talk to other students about what the exam might be.
academics_comments: The place was really nice, the Uni not as nice.
course_level: In my opinion the level was good. In philosophie du droit it was kind of anticipated that you had some more background knowledge.
teaching_comparison: It is very different. They don't have books and the preparation for the exam is looking up your own notes.
courses_enrolled: Philosophie du droit (sans TD), Droit de l'Union européenne (avec TD), Introduction au droit historique (sans TD). French law of obligations, French constitutionnel law.
recommended_courses: Droit de l'Union Europenne was great, because I had some background knowledge, I think the English courses were good as well.
unexpected_costs: I had to get a French phone number in order to not pay way to much on my danish phone bill, but after I had done that, there was no problem.
cost_comparison: I thought I would have to buy books. Food is expensive en Paris, but it is kind of similar to Copenhagen.
activities_available: There was different kind of sports opportunities, I didn't sign up for any.
activities_recommended: I think the sports could've been fun, I just had better opportunities where I stayed.
weekend_recommendations: I went partying a lot with the people I stayed with. I think that taking time out to see Paris is very good, also I went to Giverny which was amazing.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it takes a few days to adjust and move in, but I feel like when the school started it was very easy to fit in.
socializing_tips: Hmm the school doesn't help with that, the best way is to ask them if they can help with anything, or to try to be as openminded as possible. I feel like it is easier to connect with other Erasmus students than Parisians.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier, and it would be nice if the school did something to connect the foreign students and the local ones. It is okay that they didn't I did meet a few, and I also had my main social circle in the Cité Universitaire, so I didn't really search for new ones.
culture_appreciated: I did appreciate the fact that whenever I was in stores and spoke French they would slow down and answer in French.
top3_advice: 1. Get to know what the exams are before signing up for a course. 2. Choose a course which juridical content you have some idea of in danish/know, then it'll get easier if it is in French. 3. Start the semester by asking one of the peers for help, that'll make the semester a lot easier.
other_useful_info: I think that it is very important to state that it is a law school and it is one of the top law schools (if not the one) in France, and you have to keep that in mind when being an Erasmus there. Also have patience with the administration office - they are VERY slow, however they will fix things.
most_rewarding: I got to meet so many new people and I grew so much as a person. I think that having a break from the "commercial" part of law school in UCPH is very good, and getting some other types of challenges.
greatest_challenge: Having courses in French, going to an oral exam in French and just learning the contents of the courses. In the beginning it was very hard just to be away from home, then I took one weekend in Copenhagen and after I returned everything was much easier.
other_comments: I can so recommend going on Erasmus

crucial_aspects: I have always wanted to live in Paris, because I love the city. I also wanted to improve my French.
info_ease: It was not always easy, because some information wasn't available online beforehand or at least difficult to find.
arrival_assistance: I received information by e-mail from my host university. There was also an introduction week, where some questions were clarified. However, the administration would often not reply to e-mails, if you asked them questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You chose your courses online about a week before the semester starts. A long time went by without knowing how to apply. The schedule for the different courses could undergo changes even after the semester had started. Therefore, all exchange students initially had to choose courses worth of more than 30 ECTS points in case some of the lectures would undergo time changes and overlap. We then later had to go to the office at the university and have the incoming coordinator remove the extra courses manually (so we only had 30 points). This was a little complicated and time consuming, since the waiting lines in front of the office were very long.
registration_help: You could e-mail the incoming coordinator, but they wouldn't always answer. You could also show up at their office during opening hours.
registration_success: Very successful, I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Have patience and know that the schedule can undergo changes.
course_level: The level was appropriate. I only had lectures, so no assigned reading. Even though the classes were only 4 or 6 ECTS points, you learned a lot and the teachers went in depth with the subject. This meant that sometimes the courses would feel like they were worth more than 4 or 6 ECTS points.
teaching_comparison: I only chose CM courses which meant that there were no books, but only lectures (a lot of the times without powerpoint). During the lectures, you had to write down everything the professors said, since this was the curriculum and the only information available. This was very different from what I'm used to at UCPH. However, it did give me a lot of free time during the semester, since there was no assigned reading or assignments, which was nice.
courses_enrolled: Droit de l'Union Européenne, Droit international public, Philosophie du droit, Legal Cultures, Philosophy of Law and Crossborder Litigation.
recommended_courses: I would recommend the courses in English, if your French Level is below B2. Crossborder Litigation was very interesting. If you have a French level of B2 or above, I would recommend the French courses, but without travaux dirigés.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than what I excepted. However, at Cité Universitaire, you can get a warm meal for around 3 euros which was very nice.
activities_available: Student associations and trips to for exemple the Senate or l'Assemblée Nationale.
activities_recommended: I didn't attend any so I don't know. I mainly socialized with other students during breaks between lectures and at Cité Universitaire, where I lived. There were a lot of social activities and opportunities.
weekend_recommendations: Explore Paris and visit the different neighborhoods. There are so many things to do in the city and museums are also free for EU-citizens under 26 years old. For trips outside of Paris, I recommend Versailles and other French cities, that you can reach by train, such as Bordeaux.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. It's not too different from Denmark, but there are of course some difference. I would say that speaking French is an advantage, but it's not crucial.
socializing_tips: The French students are very nice, helpful and welcoming.
cultural_challenges: The French school system is very different from the Danish one. For the exams, you have to learn everything by heart, since no documents are allowed. This was something I wasn't used to, since we can usually bring books and notes to the exams at UCPH. Administrative procedures in France are very slow and long.
culture_appreciated: The food, the people and the art. Paris has amazing culture in general.
top3_advice: Speaking French is an advantage, but not crucial, have patience with the administration, but be persistent and don't be afraid to ask the French students for help.
other_useful_info: Apply for Cité Universitaire (inexpensive, great social life and a very nice place to live as a student). CM courses (cours magistraux) are a lot less demanding than courses with travaux dirigés. I would therefore recommend cours magistraux.
most_rewarding: Getting to experience living in Paris and improving my French a lot.
greatest_challenge: The administration and the exam period, since I had 6 exams in 2 weeks where I had to learn everything by heart and 3 of the exams were in French.

crucial_aspects: The language and city - I have lived in Paris (where I went on exchange) during two years (gap years after high school) where I tried to learn better French, developing high school-level French. By going on exchange, the most important factor was for me to improve mig French-skills also in an academic way.
overall_comments: Overall, a very positive experience. Only element of complaint was the bureaucratic inconveniences (but I guess it was expected to a certain extent)
info_ease: It came along the way, but I would not say easy. It was easy in the sense that most e-mails were sent with relevant information, however, the system is not very transparent, so you don't get an overview from the beginning, why knowing what you need to do can be a but difficult. Following the information in the e-mails is fairly simple, but knowing it what you have done is sufficient / if you need to do anything else / why you are doing it (what the purpose is and therefore if you are doing it right) is kind of hard to know at first. Key is to be patient and trust the proces I guess.
arrival_assistance: Not much. You need to seek out the assistance your self. I don't know if it applies everywhere, but as Denmark is fairly developed IT-wise, I think in most other countries the experience is that you have to be present much more in order to find information. In Paris I had to show up everywhere, it was not given that you'd hear back whenever sending an e-mail and calling usually didn't work, as the offices did not speak with one another. However, after showing up they could usually help and they were eager to also, which was nice. (so do yourself a favor and arrive a bit early in order to get stuff cleared out a week before the school starts)
arrival_comments: We got the information, however pretty late. Also the system of choosing classes/courses was not very well-developed, but I guess it is a part of the cultural exchange to experiences that. In the end it all worked out, just be prepared to adjust to other (less efficient) ways to do things - which of course can be frustrating when you're not exactly sure of how things work. Check your e-mails and seek information by asking on your own - either the offices or other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall, a very positive experience. Only element of complaint was the bureaucratic inconveniences (but I guess it was expected to a certain extent)
registration_process: 1. Course catalogue published the weekend before school started 2. Choosing classes online (all the ones you wished, meaning more than 30 ECTS) 3. The school 'creating' the classes that could be filled out amount-of-student-wise 4. Looking at the final class-proposition and choosing the specific ones you wanted (in relation to this, re-making your Online Learning Agreement, and getting the new classes pre-approved at KU if necessary) 5. E-mailing the host university (and showing up) to let them know, what classes you wished to keep, and which ones of the originally chosen they could delete from your schedule. Now you choose so you only have 30 ECTS and you will be able to participate in the exams. 6. Getting your schedule on your online-profile (like a KU-user but for PA) and following your classes
registration_help: Not much - information from the university, but at first hard to 'understand' their system. Advice is to go with the flow, read your e-mails twice, talk to others, and be patient.
registration_success: Succesful. I got the ones I wanted and my schedule was great. Good options class-wise and time table-wise.
registration_advice: Choose classes that are CM (cours magistraux) not TD (travaux dirigé) - if you are taking French classes. The difference is that CM classes are smaller (6 ECTS instead of 10) so you end up having more classes, however, you only have one exam in the end. The TD classes demand more participation throughout the year, mid term test, and presentations. My personal opinion is, that you learn enough French as it is and that the quality of the education is not as good at KU anyway, so no need to be more stressed out through the semester anyway:)
academics_comments: Overall, a very positive experience. Only element of complaint was the bureaucratic inconveniences (but I guess it was expected to a certain extent)
course_level: The level is in general easier I'd say. However, I took French classes as my main goal was to improve my French in an academic way - this made it harder, why I think it was 'lucky' that the content of the classes was not as nuanced as we are used to. (I guess the content is nuanced but as the exams are not pratical cases but more 'apprendre par coeur' (memorizing) the substance/things you need to focus on tends to be less complex)
teaching_comparison: Very different. As mentioned above the exams focusses more on memorizing than applying rules. However, the CM classes are only lectures which also made it very different. If you take TD it is also education in classroom like we are used to, so I guess then it'd be more similar.
courses_enrolled: FRENCH: Droit de l'Union Européenne (CM, license, 6 ects) Droit International Public (CM, license, 6 ects) Philosophie du Droit (CM, lisence, 6 ects) ENGLISH: Cross-border litigation (master, 4 ECTS) Legal cultures (bachelor, 4 ECTS) Philosophy of law (bachelor, 4 ECTS)
recommended_courses: It really depends on what your 'goal' is with your exchange. I was glad that I had mixed French and English classes, but the exams will be difficult if you don't know a bit of French already... However, my French is not perfect (based on B-niveau in high school and living abroad for some time)
unexpected_costs: Regarding food and personal spendings, it really depends on who you are. I have no idea, as it also changed a lot each month. In general, it's nice to have put a little bit of money on the side (obviously) so you don't feel limited when wanting to experience life - I feel like going out in Paris to eat is a bif part of experiencing their culture, however, it can be done very cheap (compared to CPH) but also very expensive. Really depends.
cost_comparison: Basic stuff in the grocery stores can be expensive but at the same time, other things that are expensive at home, can be cheaper (baguette, croissant, fromage - very much what you'd think)
activities_available: I bunch I think.
activities_recommended: I don't know as I did not participate in any. I know they had a cross country team (running) which one of my French friends did, and I had a Swedish friend who had enrolled in a hiking group - they made trips and everything.
weekend_recommendations: Depends on what you like. Do some research or just walk around in the streets and look around:)
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: No - talk to others if you'd like (people are in general very outgoing)
cultural_challenges: Non. Pretty much the same as in Denmark. Remember to be more polite towards the teachers when addressing them.
culture_appreciated: Many aspects - the food, the characteristics of the French people, difficult to pin point
top3_advice: Be patient, seek information physically (show up), enjoy:)
other_useful_info: No, I think I've written everything useful.
most_rewarding: New experiences
greatest_challenge: Studying in French during the exams - in the end I was a bit exhausted, but you'll have energy for it, as the semester itself is not very challenging (depending on how you structure it ofc)

crucial_aspects: I chose to study at the University of Paris for many reasons. One being the amazing cultural experiences Paris has to offer, another being it's central location in the middle of northern Europe and a third is the french language. You will need to speak the native language of your exchange city and be able to attend classes in this language, and as i already spoke a bit of french, it seemed like an obvious and enriching choice.
overall_comments: I really enjoyed my semester in Paris for many reasons but the scholastic part of the exchange was not one of them. Maybe i have been especially unlucky, but as far as i can tell from the testimonies of former students, it might be a shared experience. I have run into every problem under the sun. I was prepared for the large amount of bureaucratic hoops i might had to jump through, but this was on a whole other level. I realize there have been problems, both with the dispersement of the Erasmus grant this year, and also with the international department at the University of Paris, but this semester has felt a lot like yelling into the void. That being said, Paris is an amazing city and i have been very lucky to meet some great people and friends outside of the University, which made the experience a lot better.
info_ease: This was definitely not easy. I started the application process in february of 2021 as i was set to attend the fall semester of 2021. The international department at the University of Paris stopped responding in april of 2021. In my letter of acceptance i was told that my classes would start on the 1st of september, so i arrived in Paris accordingly, a few days before. I then received absolutely no information for the next few weeks, and was told that because of COVID, students without student ID's or no set appointments were not allowed to go to campus. Fearing i'd miss classes i wrote to every single contact i could find within the administration of the Humanities Faculty. All i was told is that i wasn't supposed to start before the 18th of september. I googled which campus i belonged to and went there, with no information, and 30 minutes before my first lesson i received my first email from an administrative person, telling med they'd forgot about me, that half my classes were unavailable, either moved to next semester, at this point already filled up, or were being held at the same time. I was sent a map and a good luck. I soon figured out that half of my professors didn't have me signed up for my classes, and after multiple tries, and almost two weeks passing, it was discovered that the university had accidentally inscribed me as a masters student instead of a bachelor student. All the information and help i was supposed to have acces to was supposed to be via the international department, who never answered and instead sent out a set email explaining that they were very busy, and could not answer emails. This went on from april until december.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any help, and had to almost beg for someone to look at my files and not just pass me along to another email chain with no response. I did have the fortune of encountering some very sweet and helpful people, working in the administrative hallway, and even though they didn't have the ability to access the systems to properly help me, they did go above and beyond to try and take me by the hand and help me out. I ended up changing almost all of my courses. Thankfully the individual professors who taught these other courses were very helpful, in trying to help me catch up on the weeks of missed classes, creating dropboxes for me and sending me instructions, as i did not gain access to the online portal of the school until the beginning of december, more than three months into four month exchange.
arrival_comments: This was extremely frustrating. I am in my mid twenties and have been lucky to travel quite a bit, which luckily prepared me for this, but i felt completely stranded. The amount of bureaucracy i have encountered and the multiple, multiple systems you have to coordinate with is astounding. I have had a very lovely councilor at home at KU, who tried to help me as best as she could, but there is only so much you can do from a different country. I realize that this semester might have been different because of COVID, but none of the systems that were supposed to be in place, were available. The "buddy" system, which is offered, i never heard back from, LANSAD, the french course available to exchange students, never in four months answered, even though i spoke to them in person and the recreational activities, study groups and international events never happened.

registration_process: I had already registered for classes before the exchange began, but was more than prepared to find new classes upon arrival as i heard this was the norm. However i was not inscriped at the university at all, and in the process of figuring out why, and how it would be possible for me to achieve just the right amount of ECTS-points, without having to attend two classes at the same time, i did miss a few weeks of classes, which i had to make up for.
registration_help: I don't know what kind of help was available. I asked a security guard for an administrative floor, handed in my passport in return for a guest pass, as i did not receive a student ID, and simply knocked on every single door i could find.
registration_success: I was somewhat succesfull. By the time i was supposed to enroll in new classes, as it was discovered that the classes i had signed up for weren't available, the semester had already started and i more or less had to pick whichever classes would fit into my scheme and had the room for extra students.
registration_advice: I would definitely recommend to print out every single document pertaining to your exchange before you leave Denmark and bring it around with you everywhere. This was my only saving grace, as i had the proof that i had been accepted and was supposed to be enrolled, when they could not locate me in their systems. Otherwise id recommend to not quit. I called everyone, emailed everyone and eventually just showed up and knocked on the office doors. Ofcourse, being respectful, tactful and appreciative of the administrative staff's hard work and following up with them is very helpful as well!

That being said, Paris is an amazing city and i have been very lucky to meet some great people and friends outside of the University, which made the experience a lot better.
course_level: It is very difficult to compare the level of courses as it is very different from the courses at KU. There is definitely less reading material at home, but also more in class hours. To obtain 30 ECTS for a semester, it would mean that i attended classes five days a week for three hours a day.
teaching_comparison: I found that this varied greatly from professor to professor. I would say that in general, it closer resembles the style of classes at a gymnasium in Denmark, where you are taught a subject, maybe listen to a podcast in class, and then fill out a sheet of paper with questions pertaining to the lecture. All of my courses were classroom-courses and not in a lecture hall.
courses_enrolled: British history: Public History and Popular history. American Renaissance: Literary transmutations from 17th century England to 19th century America. Literature: Language Games. Visual Arts: The Body on Screen
recommended_courses: I think i would recommend most of my courses. I especially enjoyed British History, as it gave a thorough look at the perception of public history and memory from the 1850's-present time. All of my professors were very kind and helpfull and tought fascinating subjects.
unexpected_costs: Personally i rented a bike for my entire stay, through Swapfiets, which was very affordable public transportation. I encountered unexpected costs pertaining to my phone company. I have unlimited usage in Europe, which was supposed to work exactly like at home, but apparently that is only up until a certain amount of months have been spend abroad, so i had to buy a sim card with a french number for the last week of my stay. Grocery shopping can be surprisingly easy depending on the supermarket. Overall, not many unexpected costs, though it in general is a very expensive city for a student.
cost_comparison: Grocery is very cheap if you visit Carrefour or Lidl! Public transport can be extremely expensive, if you plan on signing for a metro card. I would not recommend this, but i generally also just walked or bought single use tickets (which are good for over an hour!) or i biked. You can take out a 0€ a month velib card, which in turn costs 1€ per first half an hour and 2€ for an hour. This is very practical when moving around the city, as all metros close at night! I did not have to buy any books, as the university provided the need excerpts online. Eating out is also very expensive in general, so look around the city for cheap eateries! Also, if you're a student, or a european union resident under 26, almost all museums (although not all galleries) are free!
activities_available: I am not aware, as i didn't use these.
activities_recommended: Despite all my administrative problems, Paris is an amazing city! I would highly recommend going to museums and visiting all the cultural institutions that are situated around the city. Also, i would recommend walking around as much as you can! Visit the green areas situated around Paris, engage in social opportunities you can find online for exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend getting away from the very touristy areas such as Marais or Montmartre. Generally everything is more affordable when you leave the first 10 arrondissements. I'd also recommend Les Puces, europes largest antique market situated at Port de Clignangourt in the 18th arrondissement.
culture_adjustment: It was somehow easy. Although i will say that there is a prevailing culture in Paris, at least when you live there, that you are expected to speak fluent french. I've run into many logistic situations in supermarkets, postoffices, office depots, where i've been waved away, because they found my french insufficient. Other than that, it is very similar to the culture in Copenhagen. Although, beware of moving around in traffic. I had all the arrogance of someone who has biked in Copenhagen all of my life, but you NEED insurance, as the rules of the road are non existent and confusing.
socializing_tips: I had very little socialisation with students at my institution. I had nice encounters with other students when working in groups, but i think the 6-7 year age gap, definitely played a part. Also the social gatherings, which were advertised ahead of time, weren't really existing. I went to a "welcome-day" for erasmus students at the end of october, over halfway through my stay and met some very nice Erasmus students from all over the world.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences particularly challengin.
culture_appreciated: I greatly appreciated the social culture pertaining to social outings. Going out to eat or for a drink, people are very open and inviting and easy to talk to.
top3_advice: 1. Really consider if you want it. You have to work hard for it both before, during and after. 2. Have patience and persistence. You simply cannot automatically assume that you will get the information that you need, as is the case at KU. It is your responsibility if you want to get any information and get the classes you want. 3. Socialize! Try and attend all the social gatherings you can. I think i counted on some inclusion into some sort of social relation with other exchange students or some university orchestrated gatherings for students, which was not the case. Try and meet people outside the host university.
other_useful_info: The Unviersity of Paris have recently merged all their different departments into one large university with different campuses and branches. According to both faculty and students i met at the university, this has resulted in a massive hole in communication, and none of the branches are able to communicate within themselves, or have direct access to the many systems that are in place. This means that the staff at the Campus of humanities have no way of reaching the international department or other departments. You will need to physically go to the different campuses and offices and appeal to the different coordinators.
most_rewarding: Living in Paris. Just experiencing the culture of a major european capital. It is extremely hectic, with so much noise, so many smells, an incredible amount of people and a thousand new tastes. It was very rewarding to be able to experience all of this first hand, and in spite of all the bureaucratic troubles, i feel very privileged to have been able to experience this cultural journey.
greatest_challenge: The administrative problems greatly soured the experience. I constantly felt i had to catch up on all my courses. The economical aspect was also very troublesome. I understand that there have been some problems with the dispersement of the Erasmus grant due to some troubles in the European commision, but this meant that i had the first installment of my Erasmus grant (70%) dispersed at the beginning of december. Less than three weeks before my classes ended and i was due to travel home for the holidays, and after more than three months spend in Paris. As many european cities, Paris is very expensive and my rent alone took up almost of my SU. This was very problematic and left me stranded, high and dry, with no means of providing for myself on my exchange.
other_comments: Overall, i have enjoyed my experience abroad. But that is also something im able to enjoy in hindsight. I spend many days in hysterics, calling the international department at KU, trying to get some help, both with my new pre-approval, having my courses approved, trying to make sure everything pertaining to my Erasmus Grant would be accepted. I am very privileged and have been able to borrow money for the first three months, where the grant was not dispersed, but to someone else, who might not have these privileges, you would essentially been stranded, or would have to put yourself into debt. The saving grace of all of this have been the amazing city in itself, it's countless cultural offers, and the very helpfull professors at the faculty of humanities, who went above and beyond to help send me files, information and courseplans, when i did not have access to them otherwise.
