registration_process: They have a portal exclusively for Visiting Students so that nothing can go wrong. The application process in itself and selection of courses was so easy, but the approval took a long time to get. I was rejected from one class but I emailed my professor and got in anyway, so they're really flexible.
registration_help: The International Office, the Administrative Office and your lecturers and professors.
registration_success: I got everything I wanted in the end
registration_advice: All courses are pretty small and superficial, the largest ECTS they had was 10 credits, which means you have between 3-6 courses total (most are 5 ECTS). There was barely any reading (except for my literature course, understandably), most of it was recommended which took me some time to adjust to, and they announce clearly (through canvas) when texts are required for class. At KU I have 2 x 15 ECTS courses. At UCC I had a total of 4 courses, which was perfect! They never went that deep into the subjects because their are weighted so lightly, so I took that as a chance to try out something different from the usual English department (music theory, film history, coding) and I think that was a good choice because they weren't that hard bc courses are so small and superficial. But during exam season some student with 5-6 courses were so overwhelmed, and I was glad I'd prioritized courses with portfolio or even an oral exam at the end, so I only had to write 2 essays of 1500 and 3000 words. So easy! Their essay length is so short even during exams that it wasn't that bad, having more work throughout the year compared to KU's 16-20 pages final assignments.
academics_comments: UCC did wonderful in making my Erasmus stay as smooth and easy as possible, although I do think that their claim to "assist with housing" is false. They do not provide housing or any guarantee of housing, they provide *help* with *finding* housing, which I found to be very different. I think mainly the unexpected housing crisis in Ireland might have something to do with this, and it definitely influenced my stay and experience in general, because I ended up in a shitty room with shared bathroom and kitchen, paying double what I'd do in Copenhagen for my own studio apartment, fully renovated, complete bath and kitchen.
course_level: I wanted a year of rest and relaxation and lots of pints, and the academic term as UCC allowed that :) not to be mean but they didn't really go into any depth, and because the assignments are so limited in length you're barely able to quote from secondary sources without running out of space. Also, thier grading is kind of weird, as in, they rarely grade above 75 or below 60 (as far as I understood) so you can't really flunk, I guess. I turned in some rather shallow analyses but still got 75. I even heard that in some of the first year courses professors would ask the class to do 500 word assignments on "what does 'baroque' mean to you" or something lmao
teaching_comparison: The professors would ask the class questions and students would answer but it would never really be a class discussion, it was more so an interactive lecture I suppose. Not that I minded but it was a little unstimulating and most questions and their answers were so surface-level lol, the discourse around texts and class material was really based in "I feel like" and "I think this". Lots of opinions backed by no critical approach and that pissed me off lol but at least it was easy and approachable, I learnt quickly to not be intimidated by the Irish students and how to assess the level of the class etc.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Irish Literature (10 ECTS) Music Theory and Aural Skills (5 ECTS) Case Studies in European Cinema (5 ECTS) American Cinema 1953-73 (10 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I was satisfied with all of them! The best was European Cinema, the movies were great and there weren't too many, the following classes on them were super interesting and engaging and easy to follow while still containing lots of information. And the exam was a 20-minute oral exam where, I gotta say, I've never had to fight harder to get a word in and to raise the taxonimical level lmao they really just asked "what did you think of this one, did you like it, do you think it is relevant today" etc. But easy and that's how I like it >:) Intro to Irish was really good and the professor was great at engaging the class so I didn't even mind the 17-18 lecture on a Thursday (and when I did, I didn't show up, and he uploaded the lectures to canvas the day after) American Cinema was also really good but there were far more movies to watch which would get a little stressful, and some of them I thought we could have skipped because the material and discussion overlapped. But Gwenda Young was an amazing and very knowledgable professor, I loved listening to her takes and general approach to film, she was great. Music Theory and Aural Skills was basic music theory and sightsinging, BUT if you don't play and instrument or can't read sheet music or have never done formal education in music I'd say it was too hard, simply because the teacher would assume we all understood the material because most students had Music as their majors and therefore knew everything beforehand. The stuff was rather easy but she'd just skip explaining everything and it would go by really fast. But other than that, it was the easiest 5 ECTS of my life.
unexpected_costs: I bought a bike and made a deal with the seller that he'd buy it back at the end of the term. I thought he said "30-40% off of the original price" so that I'd be getting 70% back after 4 months use, but he really said "30-40% *of* the original price" so that was a shock to me, that after four months I had basically rented a crappy bike that was barely my size for what you could buy a new ladies city bike complete with everything back home. That sucked. But in the end I'm glad I had it since the buses barely showed up and the ones I knew who lived out of town or didn't own a bike basically spent the same or more on taxis to get around.
cost_comparison: A pint was 6€???? A normal, standard, low-priced pint was 6€!! so the first 10 days I was there I'd spent 500 DKK on beer alone lol that was excessive and I was very surprised that beer of all things in Ireland was going to be so expensive. Barista coffee, however, a flat white or cappucino was around 3-4€ so I ended up drinking less beer and more coffee, completely opposite to what I'd predicted about going to Ireland
activities_available: I loved the English Lit society, they did Twilight screenings and book speeddating and those were the best society events in my opinion, great ways to meet likeminded people who are very different from you.
activities_recommended: We rented an airbnb in the mountains of Kerry and that was hands down the peak of my Erasmus semester even if it was only for a weekend. Stunning nature, stunning views, small roads and lots of sheep, exactly what I'd expected to see in Ireland (something that the city of Cork, unfortunately, did not deliver)
weekend_recommendations: Drink beer, go to the movies, visit cafés, go on walks, go to concerts or shows, Crane Lane Theatre, the café at 107 Barrack Street owned by an old couple who sell vintage items and fun little knicknacks
culture_adjustment: Ireland is very much like Denmark in its general behavior, but I will say the lack of infrastructural development was staggering. The roads were so badly kept, the house facades even at the center of town were rundown and deteriorating, they still had satellite TV everywhere and the phonelines were a mess attached to wooden poles along the sidewalk. And the public transportation! It sucked! It barely existed!
socializing_tips: I'd say go out on Thursdays, that's when all the students go out because they go home to their parents' on the weekends, surely you'll meet someone there. Also, don't be afraid to talk to someone after class, pretend you have a question lol they're so naturally talkative, I found everyone really easy going (if a little young — third years are like 20)
cultural_challenges: Everyone goes clubbing lmao thank God for the older friends I made that were way past that phase otherwise I don't think I'd go out as much as I did
culture_appreciated: The openminded friendlyness, Ireland I think has a natural interest towards people from other countries (at least towards mine lol) so they'd be really eager to ask what language we were speaking if we were in a group of Danes and that would start the conversation.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared to pay double if not triple your usual rent 2. for the love of God get accommodation with walking distance to campus and to town — you cannot rely on public transit 3. Drink Beamish
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of
most_rewarding: Getting to know people — I coordinated my semester with two others Danish people I met because we were all going to Cork and being able to share the experience (ups as well as downs) with someone *and* being able to bring those friendships back with me, I think, is the best part. A lot of people expect to get close to locals or to other exchange students, but I will say, don't hesitate to invest in the Danish people, too, even if it is rather stigmatized to go to a foreign country and just hang out with your own locals. Ignore that thought, lower your expectation of hanging out with mainly Irish people because it's not gonna happen and you'll be fine.
greatest_challenge: Finding housing that filled my needs but also was affordable and also had good location was difficult especially because I did not want to bet on finding something when I arrived. The entire administrative process pre-arrival also wasn't easy and demanded a lot of my own attention and independent research as info wasn't given out by KU for some reason, so a lot of emails and a lot of person-to-person communication rather than filling out forms with available information.
other_comments: None

crucial_aspects: Cork er en mindre studieby hvor der samtidig er mange begivenheder på universitetet og i byen. Det var vigtigt for mig at vælge et sted hvor der skete noget både inden og uden for universitet, men i en mindre by så jeg kunne lære folk at kende.
info_ease: UCC koordinatorer er gode til at give informationer over mail og svarede hurtigt når jeg skrev til dem med spørgsmål. Derudover har de en god hjemmeside med indviduelle sider til udvekslingsstuderende som svarer på mange spørgsmål.
arrival_assistance: Der er introdage hvor meget bliver gennemgået på en god måde for at hjælpe os igang. Når man ankommer har man ikke fået godkendt sine fag og kan nå at ændre dem i en periode. De var rigtig gode til at give informationer om hvornår man kunne forvente at ens fag blev godkendte af fakultetet. Jeg skulle selv skifte et fag og der skrev jeg bare en mail og resten blev klaret for mig.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: På det juridiske fakultet er indmelding til fag anderledes end resten af campus. Det er mindre teknologisk idet man skulle udfylde et skema med ens ønsker til fag og sende retur over mail. Det fungerede fint idet man kunne kontakte kontaktpersonen direkte ved tvivl omkring processen.
registration_help: Da vi ansøgte fag fik vi tilsendt en god beskrivelse af hvad der skulle udfyldes og derudover svarede vores kontaktperson hurtigt. Jeg fik ikke tilsendt mailen der muliggjorde tilmedling i første omgang og de løste det hurtigt samme aften.
registration_success: Jeg fik de fag som jeg gerne vill have bortset fra et enkelt som var blevet fyldt op da jeg ansøgte. Det blev hurtigt kommunikeret til mig så jeg kunne ansøge om et nyt og de tog sig af registreringen for mig så snart jeg havde meldt mit nye ønske tilbage.
registration_advice: Der er gode beskrivelser i de mails som de skriver så man skal bare notere sig datoen og følge med i hvad de skriver. Hvis man er i tvivl om noget skal man ikke være nervøs for at skrive til dem.
course_level: Som kandidatstuderende kan man både tage bachelor og kandidat fag. Niveauet svarer til det som er derhjemme ift. bachelor fagene. Kandidatfagene kan kræve mere idet UCC ikke har en generel kandidat i jura men specialiserer sig inden for et område. Man sidder derfor med studerende der kun har fag inden for et enkelt område. Man læser også flere juridiske artikler i stedet for lærebøger hvilket kræver en tilvænning.
teaching_comparison: Det minder meget om UCPH, da der både er forelæsninger og seminarer, men der er en større overvægt af forelæsninger på UCC. På de fag med færre studerende bliver forelægningerne ligesom seminarer med diskussioner. Det var ikke alle fag der havde et pensum som var delt før semesteret begyndelse og ville som reelt blive offentliggjort efter forrige undervisningsgang.
courses_enrolled: International Children's Rights 10 ECTS Constitutional and Institutional EU Law 5 ECTS Environmental Law in Practice 10 ECTS European Convention of Human Rights 5 ECTS
recommended_courses: Alle fag havde undervisere som var ansat ved fakultetet og var meget dygtige inden for deres felt. Jeg var selv positivt overrasket over International Children's Rights som har en virkelig dygtig underviser og gjorde meget ud af at gøre os så velforberedt til eksamen som muligt.
unexpected_costs: Jeg mødte ikke nogle uforudsete udgifter.
cost_comparison: Bolig i en god størrelse og stand kan godt være dyrt. Priserne på dagligvarer er til gengæld meget billigere end i Danmark. Der er ikke behov for at købe pensum, da meget er online eller på biblioteket.
activities_available: Der er rigtig mange klubber og foreninger på UCC og man kan deltage i alle uanset studieretning. Nogle har forestillinger, opvisninger, turneringer mv. som de deltager i men nybegyndere er velkommen til de fleste arrangementer.
activities_recommended: Deres mountaneering klub er en god måde at møde nye personer på og samtidig se irsk natur. Derudover har de mange unikke muligheder for at prøve f.eks. klartring eller bueskydning.
weekend_recommendations: Der er en del festivaller i byen f.eks. film og musik som ofte foregår i weekenden. Derudover er der en del busruter til omkringliggende byer som jeg ville anbefale at se for naturen og deres museer. Cork har også en del museer at se hvis man vil blive i byen.
culture_adjustment: Den danske og irske kultur minder en del om hinanden så det var nemt at finde sig til rette. Man skal dog være klar på at de er meget venlige og snakker gerne med folk de ikke kender i køen eller på gaden.
socializing_tips: Mit bedste råd er at tage det første skridt og snakke med dem. De er meget åbne og venlige når man først får gang i samtalen, men er ligesom så mange andre studerende også generte overfor nye.
cultural_challenges: Ingen, de er utroligt søde.
culture_appreciated: Deres villighed til at hjælpe var meget overraskende. Jeg oplevede flere gange at jeg spurgte om hjælp og de gjorde ekstra meget for at sørge for at de havde hjulpet mig.
top3_advice: 1. Meld dig til foreninger eller klubber - uanset om det er for at prøve en gang eller følge hele semesteret 2. Brug så meget tid som muligt på campus 3. Nogle eksamener skal skrives i hånden
other_useful_info: De fleste eksamener i eksamensugen skal skrives i hånden, hvilket vi ikke fik fortalt før slutningen af semesteret. På UCPH er vi vant til at alt er på computeren hvorimod her skriver mange i hånden og eksamenerne skrives i hånden. Der er ofte heller ikke tilladt nogle former for hjælpemidler.
most_rewarding: Underviserne på UCC er virkelig fantastiske og man kan altid spørge dem om hjælp. De er alle eksperter inden for deres felt og forsker i det som de underviser i, hvilket i min mening gav nogle af de bedste seminarer og forelæsninger.
greatest_challenge: Eksamensformen efterlader meget valg til den enkelte studerende hvilket godt kan være svært til at starte med, da man skal lære hvordan man skriver en eksamen på deres måde og derefter finde sin egen vinkel og kilder til opgaven.

crucial_aspects: A native English speaking country and not to far away from home.
info_ease: I got most of the information needed before or just after I arrived through email. It was easy to understand and follow.
arrival_assistance: Two introduction days the week before classes started at UCC which answered the most pressing questions about the academic aspect. Furthermore a group for international students in Cork was available. They arranged meetups and trips during the whole semester.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Before you arrive (1-2 weeks) you get a link through email and you need to choose your modules. For many of them the timetable is not available yet so you choose blindly. Then when you arrive you start getting accepted or rejected from modules based on timetable conflict, full classes etc. It is then possible to change modules if you get rejected and now most timetables are available. This process is first done 2-3 weeks into the start of the semester when classes has begun.
registration_help: You could write to the international office and get some guidance.
registration_success: I got rejected to 3 classes, mostly due to timetable conflict, and ended up choosing some outside my department because non of the other fit
registration_advice: to be patience and not panic or stress to much when you get rejected and how long it takes before everything is approved. And have a lot of modules to choose from because most get rejected from at least one.
course_level: I was in my last year of my BA (biochemistry) and took 3rd and 4th year modules within my subject and some 1st year modules in history
teaching_comparison: At UCC there are mostly lectures where there at UCPH also is theoretical excises. Also the syllabus is not firm at UCC. You can choose your own book(s) and you need to find the right chapters and pages that fits the lecture on your own. It is more optional to read and everything is covered in the lectures. What is really nice is that most books are avaliable for free at the library or as e-boks through the library. On the other hand, at UCPH, specific pages and chapters are connected to each lecture and they are more overview style. In connection to assessment at UCC most modules have some part of continues assesement and some don't have a closing exam but only continues assesement. Also most exams are written and only 1.5 hour long.
courses_enrolled: HI1115: Modern Irish History for international students. BC3004: cell signalling. MB3022: virology. PT3001: introduction to pharmacology. PT4005: neuropharmacology CC1110: Celts: the origins.
recommended_courses: The two pharmacology classes were really interesting and I learned a lot but also hard. There was so much stuff to learn, far above what is normally included in a 5 ECTS module. I would recommend taking both of them if you haven't taken any prior pharmacology classes since neuropharmacology builds on top of introduction to pharmacology. Also CC1110 was really fun and I enjoyed learning something completely outside my expertise. The exam was also low effort which was nice to have because some of the others required a lot of work.
unexpected_costs: I went out a lot more than usual. Both for dinner with friends, to pubs, clubs and on trips around Ireland
cost_comparison: It was in general less expensive to buy groceries but most things (e.g., eating out) was the same as in Denmark. The rent was very expensive compared to DK but I was warned beforehand so it wasn't unexpected.
activities_available: There is a lot of sport clubs (climbing, Gaelic football etc.) and societies (academic, Harry Potter etc.) available. Most of them have beginner classes at the beginning of the semester. Also a big sports centre where there is classes (e.g., spinning, yoga etc.) for free or train in the gym. There is also a big group (watchapp) for international students in Cork across the different univeristies that arrange trips and other events.
activities_recommended: The mountaineering club plan beginner hiking trips to beautiful locations that are difficult to get to without a car. If you want to try a new activity (sport) it is a good place to do it because it's free to try and there are a lot of beginners classes. But if you are already good at something there are also advanced teams. It is also a good way to meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: There is not really any holidays but it is nice to do trips to different cities in the weekends. Kinsale and Cobh are nice coast cities. Also a trip to Galway or around Kerry. You can do it yourself if you rent a car or the international group plans weekend trips. There is also a lot of events/places in and near the city: iceskating, escape room, cinema, Blarney Castle etc.
culture_adjustment: The culture is in most ways very similar to Denmark. What was most different was the going out culture. The Irish students went out during the week and home in the weekends. Also the pubs and clubs closed kind of early (at the latest 2 am) every day. Also everything that is not academic is late: when it says the party starts at 10 it will probably first begin at 11.
socializing_tips: Be open and friendly. The Irish people are very nice but if you take classes above 1st year they already know each other and has formed groups so it's difficult to get to know them properly. If you have labs that's a good way to get started or via clubs and sociaties
cultural_challenges: The public transportation was late and very unreliable. Minimum 10-15 min late and at the most I experienced 40 min (during the day). Also how everything is late. For example with module acceptance and exam dates (end of november).
culture_appreciated: The going out culture was really nice. There was always a place with live music and a lot of different pubs, bars and clubs with different atmospheres after your mood.
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy it and try to get outside you comfort zone. It is going to fly by so fast. 2. Go to as many events and trips as you want. Remember it is okay to take a break from everything once in a while. It isn't dangerouse to miss out on one or two things. 3. It is worth it even though there is a lot of work before and after.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Meeting people and making friends from all over the world and getting to know them and learning about their counties and cultures.
greatest_challenge: To remember to study. It all kind of accumulated at the end so the last weeks were filled with a lot of studying and stress.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial for me that there was beautiful nature around, and that it was a cute city, not necessarily a big one.
info_ease: It was fairly easy, and if I was in doubt I knew who to write an email to. Once you get there you will be familiar with the international office.
arrival_assistance: There was an introduction day for international students where we got a lot of useful information. And we got a lot of emails from them as well. Students of UCC also gave us a tour of the campus.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was a bit difficult to get registered at UCC. There was a lot of steps. But they sent tutorials, videos and clear instructions on how to do it.
registration_help: Tutorials, videos and clear instructions sent by the international office. Fear not, there is help.
registration_success: Most of courses I looked at from home was not the ones I ended up taking. Either because UCC didn't have them anymore or I found others more interesting. But the ones I wanted and registered for, I ended up getting.
registration_advice: Don't get too set on the courses you choose at home. There will probably be changes in the program.
course_level: The levels are different from course to course and from field to field. Generally it isn't a high level. The classes are not as analytical as the ones at University of Copenhagen. And there is not as much reading. But there is more assignments to do. The first year classes are really easy, and generally the music classes I took was a pretty low level. My film courses however were really good and challenging.
teaching_comparison: Most of the time it is lectures where the teacher talks and then prompts the students to discuss about something in class.
courses_enrolled: Singers and Songs in Irish tradition Case studies in European Cinema American Cinema: Hollywood and beyond 1953-1973 Western Music, Culture and Media Music in Culture and Society
recommended_courses: Case studies in European Cinema American Cinema: Hollywood and beyond 1953-1973 These were my favourite classes and the teachers at the film study faculty are so nice and knowledgable.
unexpected_costs: I bought a bike there which was pretty pricey. I wouldn't recommend it. Cork is small enough to walk around in.
cost_comparison: Beer is actually more expensive than I anticipated. I thought the beer in Ireland would be cheap, but it's the same prices as in Copenhagen. A normal pint is around 4-6 euro.
activities_available: There is a loooot of clubs and societies to be a part of. The list is long. I never had the time to join any but if I could do my semester again I would prioritise doing it!
activities_recommended: The mountaineering club. They make a lot of cheap hiking trips around Ireland. It's the perfect way to get out and see the beautiful nature.
weekend_recommendations: Ballycotton Cliff Hike. Dingle. Dublin. Killarney National Park.
culture_adjustment: People are very nice so it was easy to adjust. Ireland has a very friendly culture in general. The students are a bit different from students in Copenhagen. They all look the same, wear a lot of make up, sports clothes at uni and then very dolled up when they go out. All the boys wear jogging pants.
socializing_tips: Talk to them in class they are very friendly. Go to bars in the city on Thursdays, that's when all the local students go out before they go home to their families in the weekend.
cultural_challenges: The way they dress up, which also tells something about their view on gender roles and norms. It's very gendered. The girls are very pretty, dolled up and has to care a lot about their appearance. The same isn't expected about the boys.
culture_appreciated: The drinking culture and the banter/friendliness.
top3_advice: 1. Pack good rain clothes 2. and sturdy hiking boots if you wanna hike. They should be rain proof 3. You are gonna spend more money on beer and going out than you anticipate
other_useful_info: Bring an extension cord.
most_rewarding: When me and my friends rented a cabin in the mountains<3
greatest_challenge: Feeling burnt out in the beginning after doing so much and getting to know so many new people. Remember to take time for yourself and go explore on your own<3

Also, I chose a university which seemed used to handling visiting students which made the whole experience much simpler as information was easy to come by and help was only an email away.The housing was a great deal more expensive than anticipated, but living with other students was a great way to meet new people.
info_ease: Very easy. We had orientation and a third party had made a WhatsApp group, so you could ask questions there as well
arrival_assistance: We had orientation, but a lot was just learning as you go by speaking with other visiting students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We received different emails before arriving describing everything we needed to do and how (including screenshots) and which days the different things had to be done.

registration_success: I picked my courses from home, but after arriving changed one of them. Afterwards, I wished I had changed one other course but other than that I was really happy about the courses.

This meant that I had several "holes" in my time table which I used to study or chat with friends. Also, the only reading material I had was lecture slides

top3_advice: Cork International Students organize a lot of stuff for international students so join their Facebook/WhatsApp group. Join clubs and societies that interest you and meet new people. Pick courses you like, and change them quickly if you are not sure

crucial_aspects: Ireland was not my first choice. Originally I'd been accepted to New Zealand, but had to cancel that trip as it wasn't possible to go on exchange in NZ in the fall of 2022. When re-applying I was then left with choosing countries within Europe. I opted for a place that I hadn't seen before and that primarily spoke English and thus ended with choosing UCC in Ireland. Originally I looked very much into what courses were available but when applying the second time it was more about finding a place that seemed to have a novel study atmosphere and would offer exciting experiences outside of academia. UCC luckily offers some very interesting courses in biology and zoology that I couldn't have taken back home, but this wasn't my main priority when choosing it.
info_ease: It was relatively easy. UCC does a good job of giving introductory lectures and making groups on social media for providing information, however I was introduced to most of it only when arriving, not before, and mainly by my roommates who'd been there a few days longer than me. It's a little chaotic, but overall you quickly get into the flow of thing and luckily UCC in general is very good at sharing and providing necessary information.
arrival_assistance: The international office offered a number of orientation lectures as well as tours of the campus and even the city. The student union also hosted some outreach programs to assist international students and getting them acquainted with the workings of UCC. You could also contact anyone you needed though it could be difficult to get a reply by email in those first couple of weeks
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Working out the timetables for the modules is a nightmare! Unless you specifically apply for modules that are of the same year and within the same course there's a good chance you'll have modules that overlap and clash in your final timetable, which you'll then have to figure out all over again. Initially the timetables weren't even available so I just applied for the courses I found most interesting. It was only a few weeks before the semester started that the timetables were released and then I learned that several of my modules clashed. Besides there was a few courses that should have been open to international students which then suddenly wasn't. Several classes also needed department confirmation which didn't come until three weeks or so into the semester, so for quite a long time I was taking classes that I hadn't officially been accepted into yet. Figuring out how to get all my required classes to get the total amount of ECTS needed for the semester was quite an effort and I received little to no help from UCC as they do not create timetables for students. The best I can say of the registration progress is that the book of modules for visiting students is quite user friendly and it was pretty easy to get a good grasp of what modules within the different courses were available and what they were about.
registration_help: Very little. I had to figure most of my planning out myself, and the international office couldn't tell me what classes were open for internationals and which wasn't.
registration_success: I got the two main ones that I'd wanted but only because I prioritized them when figuring out how to make my timetable work, and this was at the cost of other classes that I had chosen back home. Of the six courses I'd originally applied for I had to change out three of them.
registration_advice: It's hard to predict what courses might clash with others. Prepare yourself for the risk that you propaply can't take all the ones you'd initially wanted and that you will have to spend quite some time after arriving figuring out how to get a full class calendar that works. If you want to make life easier for yourself the apply for modules of the same course and year (course is the initial two letters like ZY for zoology, and year is the first cipher so 2000, 2001, 2002 etc. for second year classes).
course_level: The Courses were very interesting and the teachers were usually great, though there is a general discourse among Irish students where they don't participate much in the classes which obviously makes it a struggle for the lectures to really engage with them. Besides I got the general feeling that expectations to student performance were lower even though the workload was higher. Generally though the level of the courses seemed on par with what I've experienced at my home university, especially if you make an effort to participate and engage with the lecturers.
teaching_comparison: It was mostly similar though they have a lot more continuous assessment than we do at my home university, which means that I had to spend a lot more time writing essays and working on assignments than I'm used to. The biggest problem is that these aren't very well spread out as most teachers want to put the assignments only a few weeks before exams, so in the final weeks of the semester everyone is typically swarmed with assignments and personally I had about 80% of my assignments due in those last two weeks, with several of the details of several of them not having been released until just a week or two earlier. On the other hand the final exams were much much easier than anything I've tried back home.
courses_enrolled: ZY3020: Animal behaviour ZY3019: Adaptations to Extreme Environments BL3004: Research Skills in Biology PH3046: Philosophy of Biology MB3005: The role and ecology of microbes in the environment CC2250: Ancient Ireland
recommended_courses: Adaptations to extreme environments is very interesting and the final assignment is a big literature review that serves well to prepare for the bachelor thesis. Ancient Ireland is a great class if one is interested in learning a bit about medieval Irish history and Celtic culture. I was pleasantly surprised by Research skills in biology and would recommend it for any biology student.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Alcohol and beer in the grocers are relatively expensive compared to Denmark. Travelling around the country is worth some research as especially between Cork and Dublin there is a variety of options that vary quite a bit in price. UCC offers free access to Mardyke Arena, a giant gym that has three gyms, a swimming pool, a climbing gym and many other facilities so no money has to be spend on such.
activities_available: There are a ton of clubs and societies to join at UCC, all of which has a calendar packed with activities and usually no obligations upon joining. I joined quite a few, but ended up mainly participating in one as that alone had so many activities that I was kept plenty busy in my free time.
activities_recommended: The mountaneering club. They offer climbing sessions with instruction at Mardyke twice a week as well as a discount to the larger climbing gym in town once a week. They also do quite a few social events so you really can get to know them and everyone else in the club. I made more friends in this club than in my classes or through my accommodation. They also do weekly hiking trips every week which is a great and very cheap way to get to see a lot of Irelands nature (though pack hiking boots if you wish to join these). A lot of international students are in this club as well so there's a good chance of making both Irish and international friends.
weekend_recommendations: The hikes with the mountaneering club. Also join one or two of the longer trips that are arranged for international students, that visits some of Irelands most beautiful cities and sights such as the Ring of Kerry, Killarney, The Aran Islands, Galway and Belfast.
culture_adjustment: The culture is not too different from Danish culture so quite easy. The accent can be hard to interpret at times though
socializing_tips: Join and particitate in a club or society
cultural_challenges: The different aspect to studying, how Irish people generally seem to take it a lot less serious than I'm used to, which could be mildly frustrating.
culture_appreciated: The countryside, the history and the general welcoming hospitality of the people (though often with a bit of sarcasm and snark)
top3_advice: Look for accomodation early and keep in mind where it is located, because living near campus or center is simply just very convenient. Be prepared that arranging you classes can and probably will be difficult Make sure to join a club or society, they are a lot of fun and a great way to meet people, and there is something for everyone. It's also a good chance to learn something new.
other_useful_info: It rains more or less every day in Ireland. Bring waterproof clothes.
most_rewarding: The many trips around the country, and interacting with the teachers who apparently are used to teaching very un-engaged student and got very excited whenever I would answer or ask a question
greatest_challenge: Figuring out all the details in advance as I struggled to get all the paperwork both from my home-university and UCC

crucial_aspects: I wanted somewhere with a rich culture, and a university who offered courses which I found interesting and useful for me, something which could expand my legal knowledge and tools. Going to a common law country surely fit that description.
info_ease: Semi easy. University of Copenhagen unfortunately was of poor help, but UCC was great and fast with replies.
arrival_assistance: We had welcome days and several emails with information of our stay. We were also provided with information of how to get further settled and help if needed.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: They will provide you with emails of what to do. Regarding the courses, do not stress. The Irish are very laid back, and chances are that your courses aren't even approved before you start attending them, but that's alright. It's also very easy to switch courses in the beginning of the semester, the biggest hurdle here is getting approval from University of Copenhagen.
registration_help: FAQs, articles on the UCC website as well as email-adresses for the people in charge of the international students.
registration_success: I got all of those I wanted. Unfortunately some of the courses I originally wanted got moved from first semester to second for this year, so I wasn't able to register for those.
registration_advice: Don't worry, it'll all plan itself out. UCC are very flexible and laid back, just go with the flow.
course_level: Primarily attended post-graduate classes, and that was fine. Mostly you are in charge of your readings and what you should be learning, as most is recommended readings and my exams mostly were a written assignment on a topic I chose.
teaching_comparison: The teaching at UCC was more focused on learning about why the law is as it is, how the law works and critically assessing this, instead of learning what the law is, legislations, jurisprudence etc. At University of Copenhagen mostly the teaching is case-based so that you learn how to apply the law, at UCC you mainly discuss the law. This could be because of their system as a common law country.
courses_enrolled: 1. Penology 2. International Security 3. International Environmental Law 4. Fintech: Law and regulation 5. Alternative Dispute Resolution: Processes and Practice
recommended_courses: 1. Penology was such a great course with a wonderful professor. Yet there isn't much law to learn here, it mainly provides a sociology and psychology aspect, which I really enjoyed. It is discussion based, and very interesting. 2. International Security was such an informative course, however very basic concerning political science and International relations. The professor Andrew Cottey will discuss current events and dilemmas, which is very interesting. 3. International Environmental Law, was fine. I though we'd get more into the law and legal issues, but the course is modeled to suit non-law students as well, why it was a bit slow, especially if you've had International Law prior. 4. Fintech, I would've loved to have some knowledge about IT, tech etc. before starting. With that said, the course was very slow in the beginning and the professor not very entertaining, why I found the readings more informative. 5. ADR was such a great course for me to do! Very interesting and very practical, will definitely use the skills I have learned here. There is a lot of preparation for this course, because it is based very much of off simulations and cases which you would have to prepare for.
unexpected_costs: Bedding, lights, toiletries etc. for my room.
cost_comparison: Groceries are so much cheaper than in DK, going out for a beer or coffee was much cheaper, and the public transport when using a LeapCard was also so much cheaper.
activities_available: So much. You could do Irish Dance, Gaelic football, Hurling, Irish Traditional Music, and even learn to speak gaelic.
activities_recommended: Whatever you want to, just get involved, it creates a great network.
weekend_recommendations: Get around the country, there is plenty to do and see! Join the mountaineering club and go hiking on Sundays.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Join the different events, there are plenty, and everyone is friendly.
cultural_challenges: The Irish do not raise their hands in class, they will just yell out their answers. They are very polite and will talk to strangers to help them, if given the change. They are also very apologetic, and will say sorry if they suspect that they walked past you too close or such.
culture_appreciated: The kind and friendly people. Everyone was so nice and chatty. I also really enjoyed how there is alway live music playing everywhere on the streets and in bars.
top3_advice: Don't stress, take it as it comes. They are very friendly and it will all work itself out.
most_rewarding: Getting to meet new people, experience new culture, and have a very laid back experience with attending university.
greatest_challenge: Learning to relax.
other_comments: Make sure that you have a credit/debit card which does not charge a currency through your bank.

info_ease: Easy enough, if I needed some information, I could just message the international office at UCC and they were good at helping.
arrival_assistance: The international office at UCC were really helpful and they replied quickly. There was orientation the first few days I arrived, and that was also helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: They have an international office, and they are very sweet and helpful.
registration_success: Very successful, I got all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Check your e-mails, do what they tell you to do and then you will be fine.
course_level: The level is almost the same as it is in Denmark
teaching_comparison: Some of my classes was just small classes were we sat around a table and listened to the teacher making a powerpoint presentation, and sometimes we would have a discussion going. Some of my other classes would just be normal seminar classes.
courses_enrolled: Mental Health Law Mental Capacity Law Social Work and the Law (Child Law) Juvenile Justice Consumer Rights: Law and Policy
recommended_courses: Do not choose Social Work and the Law (Child Law) because it is a master course for social workers, and the level was not very high and the teacher was very bad. Everyone was social workers students, and I was the only law student. I did not receive any information when the classes were cancelled and the social workers follow the same courses, so they know each other and get the same information. However, I will recommend the other 4 courses.
unexpected_costs: I did spend a lot of money during things in the weekends, and I will recommend to explore as much of Ireland as possible.

crucial_aspects: The fact that there was no restriction on which courses I could choose in UUC (University College Cork). It was also crucial to me that they spoke english, and therefore I did not need a proof of language-level prior to my exchange
info_ease: It was easy. The sites and groups presented at the orientation was useful, and so was the emails I received during my stay. I never had any problem finding information. The UCC site was likewise accessible
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration to UCC was fairly easy, and straight forward. However, the approvals for courses (these must be approved by the professor teaching the course) came in quite late, and I had to make several changes. This gave som stressfull first weeks, where I had to attend courses where I didn't know whether I was accepted or not, and didn't had acces to the online learning material. It all sorted out in the end, and the international office is very mindful of the problems that it may cause, but I wish that I knew that this was standard practice before I was there.
registration_help: The international office is open during office hours, and was always helpful.
registration_success: I had to change more than half of my courses. Not because of my academic level, but because of limited number of students in each course. But the courses that I did end up having was good, and I don't feel like I have missed out on anything
registration_advice: Have patience!! It will all sort out at the end, but it might not happen as quickly as everyone wants. And also don't spam the international office - they are doing the best they can
course_level: I deliberately chose courses where I had heard about the main topics before. For me, it was a great strategy because I could focus on understanding the knew ways of teaching and understand the irish professors. But because of this I have a feeling of the courses being "easy" and not as challenging as I would have experienced at KU
teaching_comparison: It is very different. I though that differences would be minor, but that was not the case. At UCPH we are used to learning through class discussions and having many online tools available to us. At UCC the focus is quite different - here they have a lot of multiple choice quizzes and the teaching is therefore also with a different focus. It is different but that is also part of the experience
courses_enrolled: BC3004 - Cell signalling BC6001 - Cell and molecular biology MB3007 - Molecular genetics and genomics MB3012 - Transmission and epidemiology of infectious diseases MB4030 - Advanced medical microbiology and immunology NT2013 - Fundamentals of Nutrition (part 1)
recommended_courses: I really liked my cell biology course, and would recommend this. The lectures are good and understandable and we had laboratory work as well. Also, the course on Molecular genetics and genomics were very interesting and well delivered by the professors on the course Cell and molecular biology was a challenge, but we worked a lot in groups and it was a great way to get to know the irish students and their costumes.
unexpected_costs: I don't think that I found any unexpected expenses. Just be mindful that living (housing + food) is not cheaper in Ireland compared to Denmark
cost_comparison: I think that I expected that food was a bit cheaper than it was. However, snacks and crisps are extremely cheap ;)
activities_available: As a visiting student at UCC you have access to all clubs (which has teams in all sports ever imagined) and societies (which is non-sport group activities). All these are great and welcoming to visiting students
activities_recommended: I loved traveling across Ireland. It gave such a great look into irish culture and differences.
weekend_recommendations: Dublin, Blarney castle, Cobh, Kinsale, Galway, Cliffs of Moher. Buy a guidebook and cross of all the sights ;)
culture_adjustment: It think it was fairly easy, however it is wrong to enter an exchange semester with the idea that adapting to another culture (no matter the similarity) is no problem at all - it takes some adjustment and reflections within one self
socializing_tips: Most of the irish students are quite chatty. A simple "how are you" will bring you a long way
cultural_challenges: I don't think there are any
culture_appreciated: The irish are straight forward. If they finde something unacceptable they will tell you. It is freeing and nice
top3_advice: 1) English with the Cork accent is hard to understand (really hard), but you will get there. Don't get discouraged if you understand anything the first weeks 2) If possible, choose courses where you find the topic easy. You have enough on your plate as a visiting student in a new country, as it is - leave brain space to all other important things 3) Engage in UCC activities. It is only you that is accountable for entering clubs/societies or other things put on by the collage. Do it!!!
most_rewarding: Being able to understand different teaching methods/focuses, and what that means for my learning. I have loved my time at UCC, but I have also found that the understanding of topics that I get through UCPH is great and top-level
greatest_challenge: Definitely understanding Cork-english

socializing_tips: Speak to your classmates and join a sport! Otherwise I recommend going to bars :)

top3_advice: - Be aware that Cork is a (very) small town compared to Copenhagen - Don't be afraid to chat to the Irish; they are very openminded and easy to be around - Prepare for bad weather...
other_useful_info: Not really
most_rewarding: Getting away from home for a while made me remeber how lucky I am to have what I have back home, but also made me realize that I can live a happy life in other places than Copenhagen.

crucial_aspects: I chose to go abroad both for academic opportunities and to explore new cultures. I wanted to stay within Europe and go to an English-speaking country for it to be easier to interact with local people and take part in local social life. Furthermore Ireland I believe that Ireland has a lively and significant culture.
overall_comments: I got to experience other cultures and try out new and different courses which was great. Also exploring Ireland was great. I had hoped that cork would be a more historically beautiful city and I had a tough time missing friends and family.
info_ease: You can always contact the international office with questions either in person or by email. In general information about courses and so is given very late in Ireland, so be patient. I chose my courses very late and I couldn't access the timetables prior to this. Be sure to have looked at plenty of interesting courses at UCC before you apply to as you only very late will see which might overlap.
arrival_assistance: Again the international office was open and there were also several welcome meetings for all international students. The international office also hosts a swap shop with items donated by the prior international students where you pay a small fee and can grab whatever you need.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I got to experience other cultures and try out new and different courses which was great. Also exploring Ireland was great. I had hoped that cork would be a more historically beautiful city and I had a tough time missing friends and family.
registration_process: You choose your courses in a program online and you can put different courses into a timetable to see if anything overlaps.
registration_help: You get a very detailed mail with a description of the process which helped a lot! You could always email the international office for help.
registration_success: I was lucky that my courses actually fit into a schedule without any overlaps. On the other hand I had several overlapping exams in the end, but you won't know about this until November so don't worry about this. Many international students have overlapping exams and there is a special procedure for this.
registration_advice: Stay calm and follow the detailed guide you are given. Check your mail often during this period.
academics_comments: I got to experience other cultures and try out new and different courses which was great. Also exploring Ireland was great. I had hoped that cork would be a more historically beautiful city and I had a tough time missing friends and family.
course_level: I think it really depends on what courses you take. I had a course in “Developmental Genetics” in which I found out (a little too late) that I didn't really have enough prior knowledge and this made the course very tough. On the other hand, I had an “introduction to pharmacology “course where we went through some of the things I knew from KU, but we build new knowledge upon that afterward which was really nice. For me, the course “Introduction to “Modern Irish History for Visiting Students” was a bit too advanced for students who don't have any prior knowledge of Irish history. You should note that in Ireland a bachelor's degree takes 4 years and a master only 1 year. So 1xxx, 2xxx, 3xxx and 4xxx courses are bachelor leven and 5xxx is master level.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was again very different from course to course, but in general, I feel like KU is a highly structured institution compared to UCC. In “Virology” I ended up being so confused after each lecture because no lecture had a specific theme and we had no plan for the semester. On the other hand, I had great teachers in my pharmacology courses and here there was a more structured approach, which I personally thrive in. I believe you call your professors by their last name, but I feel like the professor/student relationship is very chill, and the professors are very happy to answer questions. My courses consisted mainly of lectures and there were no scheduled smaller classes like SAU or TØ to go through the material, which I missed from KU.
courses_enrolled: HI1115: Introduction to Modern Irish History for Visiting Students 5 ECTS MB3022: Virology 5 ECTS PT3001: Introduction to Pharmacology 5 ECTS PT4005: Neuropharmacology 5 ECTS BC4011: Cell and molecular Basis of Neurodegenerative disease 5 ECTS GN4001: Developmental Genetics 5 ECTS
recommended_courses: I would really recommend Introduction to Pharmacology and Neuropharmacology which were both great courses with great professors. Both courses build upon the knowledge I had and sparked my interest in pharmacology and the development of drugs. Both courses go through specific diseases, what the problem is, and how this is (tried) solved with drugs. This made it very “reality close” and specific which I enjoyed. On the other hand, you should be prepared to practice drug names which can be tough haha. Cell and molecular Basis of Neurodegenerative disease was also a great course about Alzheimer's and Parkinsons'. The structure of the course is a little messier, but the professor is very engaged in her research and the field which made the course great.
unexpected_costs: The accommodation was very expensive.
cost_comparison: Accommodation is very expensive, but groceries are a little cheaper than in Denmark. A big gym with fitness classes is included in your enrollment at UCC which is great. Also clubs and societies are free to join.
activities_available: There are many clubs (for sports) and societies (for interests) at UCC so there is plenty of new stuff to try out and it is possible to find a community with people who have the same interests as you. These are all free to attend. Clubs include boxing, swimming, canoeing, mountaineering, and much more. Examples of societies are the environmental society, the yoga and meditation society, the photography and film society, and the foodie society.
activities_recommended: It can be difficult to get a spot at one of the club training as the university is quite big and has a lot of students. This means that you sometimes have to be ready to book a spot at the training in the portal. The mountaineering club is a great way to go on hikes in the Irish landscape but they are quite tough! Wear hiking boots even though they say that trainers are okay for beginner hikes. You should definitely just try out different clubs and societies! It's free and if you don't enjoy it you don't have to keep going to the trainings and meetings. It's also a nice way to meet new friends. ´
weekend_recommendations: A local group of people called Cork International Students arrange some free actitvities and priced weekend trips for international students in Cork. I went on one of these trips to Kerry and visited the Killarney national park, which was a great experience. Getting around Ireland can be difficult as the infrastructure is quite bad, but you can go on guided day trips by bus to several locations. I went to Slea Head and Gougane Barra which were both beautiful places.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy - they are quite similar to us in many ways.
socializing_tips: Be brave and start a conversation. Ask questions. Attend clubs and societies as there are many local students here.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: I appreciated the trad music at pubs, when the locals called me “love” and hearing about the Irish history. I also got to drink the Irish Guinness and the local equivalent Beamish.
top3_advice: Be patient in regards to information - it will come but much closer to semester start than in Denmark. Engage in clubs and societies to meet new both international and Irish friends. It is also a great. Start looking for accommodation early on as it might be difficult to find later.
most_rewarding: I really enjoyed the possibility to try out different courses within my field of interest and some of these really sparked my interest in drug development. It was cool getting to see the wild nature of Ireland and to meet young people from all over the world and learn about their culture and how it was different from mine.
greatest_challenge: It was tough for me to be away from my friends and family and I go quite homesick at times. I think you should talk to other international students about this as it is quite common.
other_comments: I had the idea that this was supposed to be the travel/trip of my life which kinda puts pressure on everything to be amazing and great. You have lots of time to travel to other places later in life so don't put so much pressure on this trip. It's okay if not everything is amazing and that it sometimes can be tough.

crucial_aspects: For me, it was very important that the university had courses that were interesting and also maybe had some courses that we are not able to take at KU. I also wanted to be in an English speaking country, so I chose based country based on that.
info_ease: It was not the easiest to find information before arrival. They did not start to send out emails about orientation and such until very close to the start of the semester, which was a bit confusing when you are moving to a different country. Also, there were some problems with the coordinater and her emails not being sent to everyone but only some people got them.
arrival_assistance: We had both social and academic orientation, which was really great and informing!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You have to log into a portal, that takes you through the process. You have to upload different documents and such.
registration_help: You could write to the international office for help.
registration_success: Because you have to take about 6 courses at UCC, it can be pretty hard to get all the courses you want since they are not allowed to overlap with their schedules. I ended up with interesting courses, but some were not my first choice. With many of the classes, you have to get approved by the department to be allowed to take the classes, and this can unfortunately take a while, which is annoying cause if you get rejected for a class, you have to register for another and also wait for approving here. The decision from the department is final and it is often not stated what the decision is based on, which can be frustration. I find this system really strange and it adds stress in the beginning of the semester which is very unnecessary and avoidable if courses were chosen earlier.
registration_advice: Don't be afraid to write to the international office for help, since the process can be really confusing.
course_level: I found the level of my courses to the a little lower than what I am used to.
teaching_comparison: At UCC there was mostly just lectures and no classes for working with the lecture material and such, which we have at UCPH in most of my courses. Generally they also went into less details in the courses, but this was probably because the courses were only 5ECTS points each.

unexpected_costs: Alcohol can be more expensive than in Denmark.

activities_available: In the beginning, the international office arranged different events so we could meet other students. There are also arranged trips to different parts of ireland. I also really enjoyed watching the school rugby team play games every Saturday.
activities_recommended: Use the free gym and go to pubs like a true irish person
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes with the Mountaineering club, they go every sunday to a new place! It's a great way to meet other international students.
culture_adjustment: I thought it was pretty easy to adjust to the culture. It is not too different to Denmark, you just have to get used to everything being in English.
socializing_tips: Join clubs/sports and talk to the people in your courses.
cultural_challenges: Really no differences stood out to me.
culture_appreciated: That the irish people are some of the nicest ever, and they are great to just bring you to places or just include you in their friend group!
top3_advice: Be prepared to not get your first priority of courses. Be patient with the registration and international office, everything will work out in the end. Start looking for housing early!
other_useful_info: Befriend someone local, so they can keep you up to date with the unwritten "party" days like freshers week, college Christmas Day and such
most_rewarding: I loved living with 4 irish girls and it really made my experience better by being brought into their world and friend group.
greatest_challenge: The lack of structure in the courses.
other_comments: Go to Cork for the people and the nature of ireland, not for the academics

crucial_aspects: I wanted to live in an English-speaking country within Europe. I did some reseach on culture, cities and nature. I also researched the university's courses and clubs/societies to make sure I would be satisfied with both the academic and social outcomes together with the need to experience new things during my exchange.
info_ease: I found most of the needed information online prior to arrival. I had a contact number to the person responsible for letting me in at the accommodation.
arrival_assistance: There was an introduction day with information on courses, websites and contact persons. Irish students were responsible for short tours on Main campus. When I picked up my student ID, I also recieved a map over campus.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I received an e-mail with instructions on how to use their online platforms on wich I had to create a log-in and enter some personal information. When I had done my part of the work, I receied an official admission letter.
registration_help: You could always contact the employees by writing an e-mail. Often they replied within the same day or the following day(s).
registration_success: Before my exchange only the course descriptions (and what semester they would be tought) from the year before were available. Not long before my exchange the correct course describtions were published and some of the courses I had considered were now not available in the autumn semester. I changed my expectations on the courses but after arriving in Cork I had to change courses again because there were changed made to the time tables of some courses. The courses I in the end registrered for were therefore somewhat different from my original plan.
registration_advice: You have to be really flexible and make sure to have a handful of courses that sound interesting in case the courses yoou want the most overlapping timetables (the timetables were published shortly before semester start). The earlier you apply for admission at University College Cork, the earlier it is possible for you to sign up for their accommodation list. This is sent to you as an online survey together with your admission letter, and they distribute accommodation on first-come-first basis.
course_level: I chose courses from first, secound, third and fourth year. The first year couse was an introductory course in a field outside my normal studies. The third and fouth year courses were academically appropriate levels.
teaching_comparison: At UCPH we usually have TØ/classes where we, as students, are supposed to say a lot. I know that some courses related to eg sociology, politics and language have seminars but for me (a science-student) there were no such thing. A few of my courses had some practicals/lab-exercises but otherwise than that, the courses consisted of lectures.
courses_enrolled: Introductory Programming in Python Introduction to Pharmacology Neuropharmacology Cell and Molecular Basis of Neurodegenerative disease Fundamentals of Nutrition Part I Aspects of Irish Folklore
recommended_courses: Cell and Molecular Basis of Neurodegenerative disease: Great teachers and good insight on Alzheimer's Disease and Parkinson's Disease. Note that a lot they say is new research and a lot of different theories are mentioned. Neuropharmacology: Topics are fun to learn and the lecturers are good. There are a lot of drugs to memorize but the overall learning outcome is good. Aspects of Irish Folklore: A couse made specifically for exchange students. The lecturer is good at telling and making the story the center of the lecture (and not the powerpoint presentation). Even if you miss a lecture or two, it is not a problem. The final grade is based on an essay on a topic you choose yourself from a list. Introductory programming in python: a good course if you do not know any programming beforehand. The lectures can sometimes be a little slow in pace but the lab-exercises are directly related to the lectures and you learn a lot from doing the programming yourself.
unexpected_costs: none
cost_comparison: Generally, the prices are similar to the the Danish market. Coffee is a little bit more affordable, but transportation and clothing as about the same.
activities_available: There are a lot of clubs and societies. Most of them are free to participate in (but if you go in trips with the moutaineering club or surfing club, it will not be free). It is also free to use the Mardyke Arena because you can enter with your student ID. They have a swimming pool, an outdoor athleticks track, gyms with varying training fascilities and studios for dancing. There were also societies for creative people and societies for people who want to talk to people like themselves. Examples are the knitting society, the scribble society, neurodivergent society and many more.
activities_recommended: Go to the club/society fair in the beginning of the semester and choose some to show up to. It is good fun and you are not obligated to return just because you were there once. It is just a good opportunity to try a lot of different sports of societies.
weekend_recommendations: Plan some weekend to go in trips to other towns or out in nature.
culture_adjustment: You notice small differences in culture, but overall the way of living is similar to the Danish.
cultural_challenges: Nothing was that challenging
culture_appreciated: The Irish are talkative when you start a conversation with them. Also the many pubs, often with live music.
top3_advice: - Cork is a small and safe city but to get the full impression of Ireland, take time and visit other cities/towns (bigger and smaller) - and if you enjoy hiking, it is definitely an experience to go hiking in the wetlands. - Start seaching for accommodation as early as possible and be willing to just pay whatever it costs. - Ypu have to be flexible and tolerant when it comes to UCC. They are often giving information last minute compared to UCPH (e.g. when it comes to course timetables and final exam dates)
other_useful_info: Transportation is cheaper with a student leap card. You have to order it online.
most_rewarding: Generally just experiencing so much and meeting so many new people. Of couse you have to study, but there are plenty of time so go on adventures with your friends or show up to a club/society by yourself.
greatest_challenge: Generally to find yourself in a completely new situation: no friends or family around, a new educational system and a city you do not know. But if you are determined to meet people and dare to show up to different social event, it quickly turns into new routines with new friends.

crucial_aspects: Ireland and Cork were my second priority after Edinburgh and Scotland. I chose Cork as my second priority because of a previous study trip to Dublin, where I had really good experiences with the country and its friendly population. Additionally, I wanted to go to an English-speaking country to enhance my language skills. Lastly, because I am fascinated by the Irish scenery, especially the coastlines.
info_ease: It was a bit of both. I think their office for international students did a good job, but there are many things and documents to keep track of, so it can seem overwhelming at times. My advice is to stay organized and not stress too much. The most important thing to be on top of is accommodation.
arrival_assistance: I had a question or two, which I got answered via email from the office for exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was a bit challenging because you had to be approved by the departments to take certain courses. This process could take some time, to the point where the courses had already started before receiving a response. But it worked out - I barely remember it now.
registration_help: The Office for International Students offered help via email and phone.
registration_success: Getting only 2 out of the 6 courses is a bit disappointing, but it sounds like you didn't choose Cork primarily for the courses.
registration_advice: Have a lot of backups in mind. Due to timetables, it's a bit challenging.
course_level: I had 3 third-year courses, 2 second-year courses, and a language course for exchange students.
teaching_comparison: As mentioned above, I find courses with 2 hours of instruction (lecture) to be insufficient, and it became too superficial for me.
courses_enrolled: EC316: Environmental Economics: The Problem of Climate Change, 5 ECTS-point GG3009 Environmental Geographies, 5 ECTS-point GG2048 Political Geography, 5 ECTS-point GG3056 Climate Change and Historical Climatology, 5 ECTS-point LC1002 English for Academic Study (B2+ level = Upper- Intermediate Plus), 5 ECTS-point GV3216 Contemporary Ecological and Anti-Capitalist Politics, 5 ECTS-point
recommended_courses: Maybe this one (GV3216 Contemporary Ecological and Anti-Capitalist Politics) because of the lecturer. However, it was very specific and narrow. It was heavily linked to reading novels about utopias.
unexpected_costs: There were no unexpected expenses in my budget. However, expect the cost of living to be almost the same as in Denmark, maybe just 10% cheaper. So, it's an expensive place to be on exchange, as my expenses increased significantly during this period compared to in Denmark (I went out more for drinks, on more trips/excursions, ate out more, etc.).
cost_comparison: Housing is expensive! Additionally, eating and drinking out are also almost the same as back home. Groceries might be slightly cheaper. Public transport is cheap (bus/train) with their Leap Card.
activities_available: Everything from rugby to step dancing on the sports front, and on the association front, everything from the Harry Potter Society to the Socialist Society. There was a lot, and it takes up a significant portion of the campus. I was pleasantly surprised by that.
activities_recommended: UCC Mountaineering is great for getting out and exploring Irish nature on full-day hikes every Sunday for around 10 euros. You get to visit some places that are challenging to reach without a car. UCC Soccer was fantastic for me as a football player, especially because it provided social interaction with some Irish guys.
weekend_recommendations: My advice is to go on weekend trips as much as possible - this is some of my best memories. And take advantage of the opportunity to rent a car. It just makes things easier! I would recommend Killarney, Kerry Peninsula, the Dingle Peninsula, and, in general, their national parks. Additionally, a trip to Dublin is a must.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy - it's not far from Denmark, and the Irish are sweet and friendly. Additionally, the pub culture was fantastic.
socializing_tips: Clubs and Societies are probably the best way. Otherwise, hope to find a place where you have Irish roommates. People don't talk much in class. Otherwise, it's at the pubs.
cultural_challenges: Irish students start university early (18-19 years old), so they are quite young. This could be noticeable at times.
culture_appreciated: The pub culture and the Irish friendliness, hospitality, and sociability.
top3_advice: About the city: Cork is small, not particularly picturesque, and not grandiose. However, I found it cozy, and I think it represents the authentic Ireland (more than Dublin). Additionally, UCC has a significant presence in the city, contributing to a good vibe. I never felt unsafe in the city. About the Irish: They are sweet, talkative, and friendly. It's a bit harder to connect with young Irish people, but it's definitely possible. About UCC: Cozy and beautiful campus, the academic level is below UCPH (University of Copenhagen) but still fine.
other_useful_info: Don't stress about the exchange - everything will work out, even though the paperwork may seem overwhelming. Try to have a structured approach, and it will be fine. When you're there, go on as many trips and visit as many pubs as possible. That's where my best memories come from. Try to say yes to as much as possible and be proactive on your own.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all over the world - and meeting the Irish. Additionally, the fantastic trips into the beautiful Irish nature and the enjoyable moments at the Irish pubs.
greatest_challenge: Experiencing more solitude than I'm used to - but it was also cool to try.

crucial_aspects: It was incredibly important for me to choose a host university that had plenty of opportunities for international students to participate in social activities. But I also really wanted to go somewhere where I was interested in learning more about the culture and history.
overall_comments: I really loved going on exchange and I cannot recommend it enough to anyone!
info_ease: It was fairly easy, everything was sent to us by email.
arrival_assistance: The first few days were dedicated to orientation, and the international office sent out thorough emails detailing all the important information
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I really loved going on exchange and I cannot recommend it enough to anyone!
registration_process: The international office sent out step by step guides via email, detailing everything you needed to know, as well as which websites you were to use and how to go about the whole thing - very easy, if a bit complicated.
registration_help: There was an email you could contact, a phone number, and the international office was open most days of the week - they were so sweet and helpful with everything.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.

academics_comments: I really loved going on exchange and I cannot recommend it enough to anyone!
course_level: The courses were incredibly interesting, taught by passionate professors who made it all the more enticing. I will say that most of the classes I took were easier than what I'm used to at UCPH, but that was perfect for a semester abroad.
teaching_comparison: It was mostly the same, although at UCC I only had lectures, but it was fairly easy to get into.
courses_enrolled: FL2012 Exploring the Otherworld: Popular Belief and Symbols EN3015 Of Monsters and Men: Old & Early English Literature GA2033 Language & Culture in an Irish-Speaking Area EN3005 Introduction to Irish Literature FL3015 Indigenous Knowledge: Herbs and Healing in Irish Folklore

Otherwise the folklore classes are also incredibly interesting and utterly unique - the professors are really lovely too, although I cannot recommend FL3015.
unexpected_costs: Laundry! I had to pay €5 every time I washed or dryed a load, on top of an already pretty steep rent...
cost_comparison: Groceries were a little on the expensive side, but the pubs and restaurants were a little cheaper.
activities_available: Almost everything you could imagine, from sports clubs to tea societies - there was so much to choose from
activities_recommended: I didn't have much time for clubs or societies, but definitely try to make time for it! I regret not prioritising this!
weekend_recommendations: Go to Galway or Dublin for a weekendtrip, go hiking in Killarney and spend time exploring the beauty that is Co. Cork - there is so much to see! Cobh and Kinsale are both lovely towns 30 minutes away from Cork by easily accessed public transport.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, the Irish are lovely people! There were so many other international students in the same boat, which was so nice.
cultural_challenges: Nothing in particular, it was a fairly similar culture.
culture_appreciated: The pub culture was particularly amazing, everyone was so friendly and there was a lot of traditional Irish music many places.
top3_advice: Make sure you travel around Ireland, it is far lovelier than you'd think. Try out different courses, there are so many to choose from! Go on the Language and Culture trip, you'll meet so many international students, and I've made friends for life in those 5 days.
other_useful_info: Try to find some sort of accommodation with other students, it makes socialising so much easier! And as close to the town centre as possible, there's so much to experience.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many other international students, it's definitely helped me grow both personally and academically.
greatest_challenge: That I couldn't stay longer! Although there were also quite a few written assignments, but this was hardly anything to complain about.
