crucial_aspects: I study law, so going to an EU country was important to me. That English is a first language was a plus, as I have found it very easy to engage with local culture. Gaining knowledge of a common law system was very appealing.
info_ease: Pretty ease. The process up to arriving I found that the coordinators in Cork were not always very helpful and would sometimes wave off your questions but once I got here the introduction and the help were all very accessible.
arrival_assistance: There was a whole introduction week for visiting students with an introduction to how the system worked, how to finalize classes, and everything Erasmus related which was really nice.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There was a registration online before arrival and a confirmation at the physical office once you arrived and then you registered for classes. Registering for classes was a long process the classes started before you were approved for them and many courses weren't available even though they were when you originally chose.
registration_help: For registering general you could email the coordinator. For help with registering for classes it was a bit harder as the coordinators did not have all the information and you mostly just had to wait until classes had been going for a few weeks before getting approved.
registration_success: There were two out of five classes that I didn't get and had to find new ones and one was solely online.
registration_advice: Try and be okay with not getting all the classes you hoped for. It will be fine and they are very helpful even though the system is slow.
course_level: Mixed courses, some graduate courses as there where limited options available for law, some post graduate and some offered as legal LLM's and some non-legal LLM courses.
teaching_comparison: Very different. Very lecture based. It was not expected that you had read for class and the text where not discussed but mainly seemed to be for the essays. Almost no discussion or questions but only passive listening. Many lecturers didn't engage but simply did a talk with a break some not even really using the slides they made available.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to International Law of the Sea, Public Law, Economic Law of the European Union, Sources and Foundations of Environmental Law, International Environmental Law
recommended_courses: Economic Law of the European Union was very interesting for me and the lecturer was passionate about it and kept a decent structure of the class. Public Law was a great way to get a basic introduction to the Irish system, legal and political, and common law.
unexpected_costs: I had to buy all kitchen appliences (knives, forks, cutting board, pan, pot etc). Further all room and bathroom supplies, like bins and toilet brush etc. Which was very expensive. Came to a total of around 2000DKK
cost_comparison: Kitchen appliences.
activities_available: Free access to the sports arena including yoga classes and other sports and a climbing wall. Also a mountaineering club and many other clubs were great.
activities_recommended: Mountaineering club is a great way to get to hikes and places that are hard to reach by public transport or if you are unsure of venturing into the hills
weekend_recommendations: Try visiting as many smaller towns as possible either for day trips of weekend. It is often duable by bus or train even it takes awhile and is totally worth it.
culture_adjustment: Like the culture, people are friendly and good at small talk but definitely easier to make friends with other exchange students.
socializing_tips: Try joining clubs or societies and going to their socials.
cultural_challenges: The language and dialect at first was pretty tricky but you get the hang of it.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness of strangers and general helpfulness and interest in what you were doing there.Very easy to go out to a pub and meet new people and smalltalk
top3_advice: Join clubs even if it's just one. So you have somewhere to go in the beginning if you don't click with your roommates. Say yes to coming along if people invite you even if you're a bit tired it's pretty important in the first month or so and the level will calm down.
other_useful_info: There is such a thing as Irish time. Everything may not get done right away and the bus may not always show but there is always the next one and people really don't mind if you ask them for help
most_rewarding: Making new friends with other students and experiencing the small towns of Ireland and going on small walks and bigger hikes. It's beautiful
greatest_challenge: Making Irish friends and finances are a bit tough with the rent.

crucial_aspects: Exploring a new country in Europe and especially a country with many beautiful natural areas.
overall_comments: It was such an amazing experience and I am really thankful for the opportunity to go abroad. Cork is a lovely city and I would definetely recommend everyone going to Ireland to explore the country's (especially the western part) natural areas (Killarney mountains, Dingle Peninsula, Burren national park, Inish islands)!
info_ease: It was fine - the international office in Cork was super helpful. And the exchange office from KU was also super helpful. It is just quite stressful and confusing before going on exchange as there is a lot to figure out (housing, course registration etc.) but just remember that it will work out in the end! I barely remember all the stress before going on exchange.
arrival_assistance: The accommodation-office from University College Cork helped me find a student-accommodation.
arrival_comments: They were helpful however, I do think they could have emphasised how critical the housing-crisis is in Cork (and Ireland in general) because I found out quite late compared to the scale of the crisis.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was such an amazing experience and I am really thankful for the opportunity to go abroad. Cork is a lovely city and I would definetely recommend everyone going to Ireland to explore the country's (especially the western part) natural areas (Killarney mountains, Dingle Peninsula, Burren national park, Inish islands)!
registration_process: It is important to search for modules (kurser) in their 'book of modules for visiting students' since not all of their modules are for visiting students. And just be prepared for changes in modules short before the actual exchange since the timetables appear very late in the process (about a week before start). I had to change some modules because of a timetable-conflict.
registration_help: The international office from University College Cork was there to help and otherwise it was fine to figure it out by myself.
registration_success: I had to change some classes just before start so sadly I did not get all of the classes I hoped for but it was okay.
registration_advice: Just be prepared to change some modules just before start hehe.
academics_comments: It was such an amazing experience and I am really thankful for the opportunity to go abroad. Cork is a lovely city and I would definetely recommend everyone going to Ireland to explore the country's (especially the western part) natural areas (Killarney mountains, Dingle Peninsula, Burren national park, Inish islands)!
course_level: I chose 3rd and 4th year bachelor-level classes and the level was not difficult compared to that I was a 3rd year bachelor-student when on exchange.
teaching_comparison: The style was quite the same with lectures and student participation however, as I noted before, some of the classes were very superficial and not that specific.
courses_enrolled: - Contemporary Ecological and Anti-Capitalist Politics - Co-operatives, Food and Rural Sustainability - Environmental Economics: The Problem of Climate Change - Environmental Geographies - Sustainable cities and communities - Introduction to French: Complete Beginners
recommended_courses: I would most of all definitely recommend 'Contemporary Ecological and Anti-Capitalist Politics'! I loved this class and its content was super interesting, thorough and radical. Laurence Davis, the lecturer, was super dedicated and and an excellent lecturer. If you're interested in anti-capitalism and radical ecologism then this course is definitely for you! :) I also really like the content of 'Co-operatives, Food and Rural Sustainability'. However, the classes were sadly not that exciting to be honest. The lecturer was super sweet but the lectures were not that revitalizing to be honest. I still liked the course and its themes.
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs just more costs than when living in Copenhagen. Not because Cork is more expensive - I think overall Cork is a bit cheaper than Copenhagen. I just spend more money because I went more on excursions and trips (which I would recommend!).
cost_comparison: Groceries etc is cheaper however, coffee and drinks (luxury goods) are almost the same. Public transport is way cheaper than in Denmark so that was reealy lovely. But as mentioned a couple of times now, the housing crisis is critical and therefore it is really difficult to find cheap housing.
activities_available: Many different options. Everything from sports to cultural activities. I joined the socialist party-society, the squash club (for a bit) and the mountaneering clubm which was really cool!
activities_recommended: The mountaneering club was really lovely since I got to see some beautiful mountains when going on hikes with them. I also liked to join the socialist society (I was there for a bit), they were very sweet people.
weekend_recommendations: Go see the country's amazing nature! The mountains in the western part are stunning and so beautiful! I would definitely recommend people to go on hikes and weekend-trips. I also really liked Glengariff. It is quite turisty in the main season but i went there with friends on November and there it was super quiet which was lovely. There is a beautiful forest and coast-line. The Dingle-peninsula is gorgeous! Go there for some days! I also really loved Killarney national park. Go se the nature in the national park (not the actual town itself) - it is beautiful and very close to Cork. There are many lovely and cozy pubs in Cork: Sin É, the Friary, Roundy's and the Abbey Tavern.
culture_adjustment: Very easy - the culture is in some ways not far from the danish. However, Irish culture is way more welcoming and including (in my opinion)! I had the super heartwarming experience of feeling so welcome and having many spontaneous and lovely talks with strangers (which sometimes seems impossible on Copenhagen God knows why!!) In classes there is maybe not that much chitchat with other students - it happens most at clubs, societies and especially in pubs!
socializing_tips: Explore the clubs, societies and pubs! :)
cultural_challenges: Sometimes it was a bit difficult to connect with Irish people in my age - but that is something one would also know from Denmark.

recommended_courses: Negotiation and Mediation was very interesting, as I had not yet had any courses on means of alternative dispute resolution before. cost_comparison: Food was generally a bit more affordable while housing was more expensive than in Copenhagen.

socializing_tips: Definitely to go to events of societies or clubs, including the organized trips.

crucial_aspects: That the subjects offered were along the lines of zoology as these type of courses are not available for bachelor students at KU.
info_ease: It was fairly easy, the exchange student team here were really nice and very quick at answering emails and getting back to you.
arrival_assistance: There was orientation, which wasn't super intense but gave you a brief idea and understanding of the layout of the campus.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I rated the registration process a bit lower only because this university had a weird process of choosing courses but then afterwards you had to make your own timetable of those courses and figure out yourself if there was any overlap. There often was and this meant it was a weird puzzle of trying to take courses that I still found interesting but also didn't overlap. I think in the end I had to rearrange and drop courses up to 5 times.
registration_help: The team was very kind in helping you find courses that didn't overlap but it was just a very stressful time especially since classes also started and if you didn't have a course by that time you weren't sure if you were possibly missing class.
registration_success: I was overall quite successful. I was able to get 4/6 of the courses I wanted. One of them was listed as an option for semester 1 courses when I signed up in the spring but when I got here they had moved it to a semester 2 course which meant I had to choose something else. The other one was full and I had to choose a different but quite similar course. Overall I was happy with my classes.
registration_advice: I would advise to double check the courses, when they are available (semester 1 or 2) and double checking the timetable for any overlap. Also making sure that you have any prerequisites that might be mandatory.
course_level: The level of courses ranged from 1st year to 3rd year, which meant that sometimes I was in a class with students that had not studied for as long as I had. This meant that some of the courses were simpler, but it didn't matter to me because it served as a refresher course for myself and also put less pressure on knowing everything or learning everything for the first time.
teaching_comparison: I felt there was much less work somehow. Lectures didn't feel as long either. Maybe it is because I prefer English as my academic language, that I just felt I was learning better in this environment than I do at UCPH but that is my own issue. The second thing that I found here was they were much more focused on writing essays, which I feel is something UCPH is lacking. It is important for us students to also learn how to write scientific essays and the bachelor's project shouldn't be the first time people are learning how to write like that.
courses_enrolled: Forensic Psychology, Applied Cognition, French for Beginners, Adaptations to Extreme Environments, Practical Invertebrate Skills, Ecology and Zoology Literature Review
recommended_courses: The literature review class that I did was very good because it taught me how to write scientifically and do research properly. I chose the class on purpose to better prepare myself for the bachelor project, and I really feel like it has aided me in that sense.
unexpected_costs: NA
cost_comparison: At this university they have a collaboration with a sports arena where students have free access to swimming pools, football fields, squash courts, inside courts, gym, etc. They also have free access to sign up for classes such as yoga, spin, etc. I was really happy to have this and was not expecting all of that to be free so I would say that sports and gym memberships was a lot less expensive than expected.
activities_available: At this university they have a collaboration with a sports arena where students have free access to swimming pools, football fields, squash courts, inside courts, gym, etc. They also have free access to sign up for classes such as yoga, spin, etc. I was really happy to have this and was not expecting all of that to be free so I would say that sports and gym memberships was a lot less expensive than expected. There were also plenty of societies to join and there were so many it was hard to decide between what to choose!
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining some societies or clubs cause it really makes your social circle bigger and gives you an opportunity to meet more people that not only have the same interests as you but also are not living in the same place as you or in your classes, which means you have more variety in where you can meet people.
weekend_recommendations: There were many trips arranged by the international students society, these cost money but were so worth it because they take you out to experience more of the country. It was quite hard to get around in this host country especially if you didn't own a car as public transportation wasn't as common so this meant that being driven around in a big bus was a great option. Exploring the city center and the pubs and restaurants and cafes the city has to offer is also a great idea.
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy. I've moved around a lot so doesn't take me long to get settled into a new country. Also because this was in Europe where we still see a lot of similarities.
socializing_tips: It was definitely most difficult to do this but I'd say joining those clubs or societies is where you are most guaranteed to meet them.
cultural_challenges: NA
culture_appreciated: The love of tea
top3_advice: Don't mind the weather. Enjoy walking around because public transportation is horrible. Join the many clubs and societies that they have to offer.
other_useful_info: NA
most_rewarding: Being able to meet new people, learn to live on my own in a different country and try new things.
greatest_challenge: Leaving, because saying goodbye is truly heartbreaking.
other_comments: NA

info_ease: It was okay. There is a lot of paper work, and it can be a bit annoying sometimes as it differs from student to student depending on the destination or field of study. But it’s totally worth it!!!
arrival_assistance: Orientation the first days and there is an international office where you can go if you have any questions. I didn't need assistance but I heard they are very nice and helpful if you have issues with overlapping courses and stuff.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: Again, the international office
registration_success: I was refused one class, which wasn’t the most important for me, but the frustrating part was finding another class that fit into the timetable and then waiting 2 more weeks for a final response.
registration_advice: Just be patient, even if it can be a bit stressfull, I didn’t hear anyone for whom it didn’t work out for in the end. crucial_aspects: That I could learn about another language and that I could learn about myths, where Ireland was ideal, as it has a rich history, and they still try to keep the Irish language alive. I also wanted to go to a place, where there was a lot of focus on the international students with a lot of activities and opportunities to meet other people.
info_ease: I received a folder with a lot of information from UCC, and they also had a guide on their website, so I found it very helpful
arrival_assistance: I was informed that there would be three days of orientation, but it was only two days and each lasted two hours each, which I found very disappointing, as I think it could have been more helpful if there was also focus on the social part and getting to know other people. There was also a lot of information during the orientation, which of course was necessary, but it was a lot and a bit confusing, as parts of it weren't relevant for me.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I think the registration proces was very easy, although it was a bit stressful for me, as I am use to choosing my subjects very early, and here you had access two weeks before school starts, and you might not even get your subjects approved before the course starts. They had tried a new system, where you logged in and then you could choose your subjects through the portal. You could see through the portal whether or not your subjects had been approved by UCC, so you could navigate in it yourself. I did however find it very confusing at first that UCC has divided their subjects into visiting students and non-visiting students. My biggest problem with registration was actually my own home university, as they would only accept classes for master, and it was my job to proof it, but UCC didn't offer any information about this. That was extremely stressful and luckily they accepted the subjects in the end
registration_help: You could stop by the international office, there was orientation, where they guided us through the proces very thoroughly and you had access to the module book
registration_success: I was very succesful, as I luckily got all the classes I wanted
registration_advice: Don't get stressed out about the very late proces. They also allow students to change subjects within the first two weeks, if it didn't fit you, and you shouldn't be scared to do it. I didn't do it, because I had had so much trouble with my own university that I didn't want to go through that again, but I think it would have been worth it.
course_level: I only had one MA class, the rest were BA classes. The level of the MA class was too difficult, while almost all the others were a fitting level.
teaching_comparison: The exams were by hand without notes, so the exams weren't as extensive as at UCPH, as we couldn't truly investigate subjects for the exams, as the focus was on remembering. However, I did also like having this focus, as it made me look at the subjects in a different way, since I really had to know the stories in order to remember them for the exam, and not "just" analyze them. So I think it was useful to try having that focus on the exam, but I do however like at UCPH that focus is on learning the deeper meaning
courses_enrolled: MA class: Livy, BA classes: Greek Mythology, Early Irish I, Celtic Saints, Mabinogi: Legends of Medieval Wales and The Roots of the Arthurian Legend
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend Early Irish I, Mabinogi: Legends of Medieval Wales and the Roots of the Arthurian Legend, as they teachers were very good communicators, and they helped you truly understand. Early Irish: I would recommend this subject, as Irish is a beautiful and unique language, and this course lets you learn the overall aspects of Irish without going into too many confusing details. Mabinogi: I had never heard about the collection of stories before, but it was incredible. The Mabinogi draws on earlier legends, both Irish and Welsh and from a common origin, and with this course you get to understand how the myths are intertwined and understand which parts can determine if it is a loan or inherited Arthur: I didn't know Arthur had Welsh origin before I took this class, and this class very thoroughly goes through all the parts that can be traced back, and why we can see that it is traced back, and how the story has changed into the story we know today
unexpected_costs: I didn't really experience any unexpected costs. UCC helps you understand the potential expenses beforehand, and I can't think of anything that I suddenly had to spend my money on unexpectedly
cost_comparison: I was surprised how cheap groceries were compared to Danish prices. The housing prices were absolutely more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: They had almost everything I would say. And the great thing here is that you can just show up for the events that the societies have, and every week on Instagram they would post all the events that were happening. One critique is that as an exchange student for only one semester you couldn't engage further than that, and I think it would have helped me get to know more local people, if I could interact with them through for example planning an event or helping set up
activities_recommended: I would recommend Book Club with the Literature Society, as it was a very cozy and chill event and an easy way to interact with others, as you have a focus point, I would also recommend performances in the hall at UCC, as they were really fun (fx seeing an ABBA cover band), and I would also recommend booking tours (either through the international office or by the international group), as it was a great way to get to see Ireland
weekend_recommendations: Experience the nature of Ireland or go see the castles, and book a lot of tours in the beginning of the semester, before you get too busy withy exams. I went to West Cork and Northern Ireland, but I would have loved to see even more nature.
culture_adjustment: I think it was easy. People are very friendly, and I think you can learn a lot from just walking around the city and experiencing how people are behaving. UCC has a lot of international students, and that makes it a bit more difficult adjusting to the local culture, as you need to get away from the university in order to actually experience the culture.
socializing_tips: I unfortunately don't, as I didn't socialize with that many local students. I did chat with some at the society events, so I think my tip would be to go to the society events
cultural_challenges: I didn't really find any parts particularly challenging, as I found the people of Cork so friendly. Sometimes the accent was a bit challenging, but I didn't meet a lot of people with a heavy accent
culture_appreciated: I appreciate the friendliness like thanking the bus driver when you leave the bus, everyone saying thank you to almost anything, for example when you leave a store you thank the store owner.
top3_advice: Get a leap card (a bus card), as it gives you discount on bus drives - and use it to go see the nature An advice I could have used is relax, as I am use to at UCPH that we have to things done quickly with deadlines, and it stressed me out a lot that the subjects were maybe approved when school started, but it is the same for everyone, so really relax Look into housing as early as possible. I think I started looking in the middle of March, and it was way too late
other_useful_info: That both UCC international office and UCC societies uses Instagram a lot for information, so go in and follow them. And I wasn't aware until late that there was a WhatsApp group with a lot of helpful information, so be on the lookout for the link too
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of the exchange experience was diving completely into another culture. I think it is amazing how much you learn by actually living in another country and not just visiting. I think some of the most rewarding aspects have been just walking around in the city, going to the local pubs and just embracing the culture and noticing the small things that people do differently.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was not overcoming the part of me that was scared of socializing and scared of not making any friends. It really helped that I made myself go to so many events in September, so it quickly became easier, and I did make some great friends. But that is the good thing about interacting with the other international students, as they are all in the same boat.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to go to a European and English-speaking country - preferably in the EU. That excluded pretty much everything but Ireland. Furthermore, Ireland is just such a nice country with really friendly people:) I'd heard that Cork was a really great student city so it just seemed perfect.
overall_comments: A bit difficult to get the courses/modules I wanted but apart from the administrative part of it, it was AMAZING.
info_ease: Fairly easy, the International Office at UCC hosts webinars prior to arrivals, and are good at emailing information.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive anything (personally) apart from the offer to have a meeting with the International Office in addition to the orientations that they host. I also didn't need anything but was aware that assistance would be given upon request.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: A bit difficult to get the courses/modules I wanted but apart from the administrative part of it, it was AMAZING.
registration_process: I don't really remember, so it must have been fairly easy:) Just make sure to check your UCPH e-mail and your UCC e-mail regularly.
registration_help: The International Office at both UCPH and UCC.
registration_success: Not very successful. I ended up getting some fine classes but had to redo my registration multiple times as some classes weren't available. This is made more difficult as you have to make your entire timetable work by yourself and can have no overlaps. There is a website that is made available for this a couple of weeks before the semester starts but prepare to redo it when you are rejected from specific classes.
registration_advice: Have a plan A, B, C, D and E about the classes you want as they can be quite difficult to get a spot in.
academics_comments: A bit difficult to get the courses/modules I wanted but apart from the administrative part of it, it was AMAZING.
course_level: I'd generally recommend doing 4th year courses rather than 3rd year (even if you're just a 3rd year) as this level is more suitable. Some classes were easier than others and the general level was a bit lower than at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: At UCC: more memorization, more lectures rather than group work and handwritten exams. But it worked fairly well and the lecturers are really good.
courses_enrolled: MB4019: Computational Biology BC4001: Advanced Cell Biology BC3021: Cell Signalling in Health and Disease MB3007: Molecular Genetics and Genomics NT2013: Fundamentals of Nutrition HI1115: Modern Irish History for Visiting Students
recommended_courses: I'd recommend MB4019 as an introduction to bioinformatics. It is nice background knowledge to have. The lecturer in BC4001 is really good but the material is similar to what I had had at UCPH. I cannot recommend NT2013 as the course is not well-structured... HI1115 was quite interesting:)
unexpected_costs: Housing is really expensive (1000 euros is not unusual for student housing), so I was very lucky but was very surprised at the general housing prices.
cost_comparison: Eating out was more expensive than expected. Public transport was less expensive that expected (please get the Student Leap Card!!!)
activities_available: Everything. More than 200 clubs/societies with all types of activities/sports.
activities_recommended: Fáilte Refugees Society is a really cool charity society. The boxing club is really good.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the nature of Ireland! Grab a pint at the local pub and listen to some traditional music:)
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Irish people are very friendly.
socializing_tips: Join clubs/societies and don't be afraid to speak!
cultural_challenges: As mentioned, I really enjoy the company of Irish people:) I was really confused about how they drive on the left side of the road though.
culture_appreciated: Their "easygoingness."
top3_advice: 1. Join clubs 2. Beware of your timetable 3. Don't be scared if your housing seems expensive (it's probably just normal...)
other_useful_info: Join the Erasmus Network and the International Students group chats as quickly as possible as they do cool activities all throughout the semester.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people
greatest_challenge: Getting all the administrative stuff done

crucial_aspects: English-speaking country
info_ease: Easy- it was all provided via zoom presentations and e-mails.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Quite easy- they sent some emails with links I think and how-tos. I don't actually remember the specifics but this means it must have been easy enough.
registration_help: There were some zoom meetings where some of the registration was discussed I think, so great to watch those. There were two main people from my host institution that were supposed to be able to answer any questions/emails- I didn't personally use this help and heard that it could take several weeks to get an answer, but that help is there. A WhatsApp group for Erasmus students was set up during one of the zoom meetings in the chat, and that was very helpful to join and hear what kinds of issues others were having and how to resolve them.
registration_success: Mostly successful- there were issues as the timetable isn't released until right before the start of the semester, so last minute I had to switch out some classes so that there wouldn't be several at the same time.
registration_advice: The registration is a little funky at UCC, so you can change classes a while after the semester already has begun- this is very helpful, so try out a few classes and don't be afraid to drop it and chose another.
course_level: My classes were all designed for 2nd or 3rd year students in their undergrad (3 classes for 2nd year and 3 classes for 3rd year).
teaching_comparison: I had almost all lecture-style classes as opposed to seminar-style or lab-style (even my lab-style class was taught as a lecture basically).
courses_enrolled: AY2008 The biology of being human; EV2003 Practical data analysis and research skills; GG2014 Geography of tourism; GG3037 Geography of heritage; GG3041 Environmental remote sensing; GG3058 Environmental geography
recommended_courses: AY2008 The biology of being human: super nice professor, fun/interesting class, other kind students during my semester.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Coffee/tea at UCC was more expensive than KU; food wasn't as expensive as I expected (but still expensive); bus-fares are a set price (I just avoided using it in general because 1.9 euro pr short ride adds up); sending postcards was expensive (but I love to do it!)
activities_available: Clubs (sports) and societies (clubs for people with similar hobbies or interests). There are a lot of different clubs and societies available and a whole fair around campus to talk to representatives from them to see if it's something for you.
activities_recommended: Join all the clubs and societies that remotely interest you and then just stick to the ones you like best! A really great way to meet people- everyone who goes is interested in talking about your shared interest and making friends.
weekend_recommendations: Take the train to a nearby city (Cobh is super cute!). I had the privilege of having great flat mates and we did a road trip to Killarney and Dingle and this was really great (in the off season no less and this was fun to explore with no other tourists around). A tour bus is also an option- I did one to the Cliffs of Moher (avoid if you get car sick though!). Cork has a load to offer though- make sure you consistently do things so you don't have a huge to-do list of museums and sites to see right before going home.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy
socializing_tips: Join clubs and societies. Say hi to the person next to you in class.
cultural_challenges: Nothing that stood out to me- perhaps brash jokes but you get used to it quickly.
culture_appreciated: Pretty laid-back people in general, even the professors.
top3_advice: 1. Join societies/clubs, make friends with your flatmates, say hi to the people sitting next to you in class 2. Do something every weekend: go to a museum, wander around Cork, take the train to Cobh, etc. 3. You have up to 6 classes at the same time, presumably with exams/essays due around the same times- start working on essays early even if you haven't necessarily covered all the topics of the class yet.
other_useful_info: Don't be afraid to do things alone- I went to societies/clubs alone and met people there, that is normal and what they're there for. Do sightseeing alone, don't wait for others. I met my best Cork friend later in the semester, so don't stop trying to make friends through the exchange.
most_rewarding: Just being able to say I did it- I went and lived somewhere where I didn't know anyone beforehand and made some great memories.
greatest_challenge: Getting out of my comfort zone, having to do university from scratch and not knowing anyone.

crucial_aspects: I was interested in Irish film and Irish history.
info_ease: UCC is pretty good at giving information regarding arrival and uni.

arrival_comments: It was a little unorganized. I would have liked to know more about their system such as library system, but overall good.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was done online. You must provide personal details.
registration_help: They send you a guide along with the registration websites. You can also email International Office if you need help.
registration_success: Pretty successful. During the first 1-2 weeks they have a trial period in which you can try out different kinds of subjects, so you can drop them if you don't want to take them anyway.
registration_advice: Try out subjects that are not necessarily directly related to your degree. UCC offers Intro to Irish culture/language/history/and more!
course_level: I had three BA courses and one MA course. The level of academia was pretty much the same as in Copenhagen, sometimes lower. I had a few written essays I had to hand it, and they were very short/small compared to the kind of essays I'm used to writing at home. I also did 3 creative video essays which was very challenging as I have never done that before.

recommended_courses: I really liked Irish Cinema - nice teachers and the assignments were at an appropriate level. It's an MA course. Gender and Contemporary Cinema was also interesting but the workload was almost too much compared to my other courses.

cost_comparison: Cost of living is less expensive than in Copenhagen. Housing is very expensive.
activities_available: You can join both clubs (sports) and societies. UCC also organizes trips around Ireland and I went on 2 of those.
activities_recommended: Join the trips and parties organized by UCC. Join a club or a society.
weekend_recommendations: Other cities in the country. Train and bus tickets are very cheap! I went to Galway, Limerick, and Dublin, as well as smaller villages in Cork County.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy.
cultural_challenges: Mainly just the dialect which was difficult at first. Other than that, people are very nice and helpful.
culture_appreciated: People are very social and want to talk.
top3_advice: Get out and do something during the first weeks as people are quick to find friends. Go on trips to other parts of Ireland. Don't stress too much about uni.
other_useful_info: Talk to people if you're in doubt about something.

greatest_challenge: Getting over the initial homesickness I experienced in the beginning.

course_level: Bachelorfagene er meget grundlæggende og fokuserer på irsk og/eller common law-ret, hvorfor jeg valgte masters-fag. Jeg bestod alle fag med en fin margin ned til dumpezonen og studerede slet ikke så hårdt, som jeg gør på KU

Udover turene i whatsapp-gruppen kan tage offentlig transport til Cobh, Ballycotton eller Kinsale, som er tre mindre byer, eller tage bussen til Blarney castle

socializing_tips: De fleste irske studerende ved godt, at du er her forbigående, og de holder sig som regel sammen med andre irere. Jeg blev kun gode venner med én irer, og det var fordi jeg opsøgte de aktivt, så det kræver nok, at du tager initiativet enten ved at spørge i klassen eller socialisere på en pub
cultural_challenges: Ikke rigtig noget, men du bor sammen med nogle fra en anden kultur, hvilket jeg oplevede, at andre til tider kunne finde anstrengende.
culture_appreciated: Irere er bare nice og atmosfæren er generelt god. Jeg synes, irsk natur og irske byer er charmerende
top3_advice: Socialisér i starten, der er hundredvis af internationale studerende, som alle vil ud og møde nye mennesker, og du kan virkelig finde nogle venner Man kan også med fordel tage kontakt til de andre fra KU, der skal afsted. Det gjorde vi, og især i starten var det dejligt at have den trykhed, at man kunne spørge om hjælp, følges til introduktionsmødet osv. Vi endte alle på forskellige kollegier og blev venner med hinandens roomies, så vi fik opbygget en stor gruppe af internationale studerende, som hyggede, festede og studerede sammen Tag ud og se den irske natur
other_useful_info: Den offentlige transport er generelt dårlig, så hvis du vil bo uden for Cork, kan det være svært at nå i skole til tiden. Spar også lidt penge op, for det ender bare med at blive dyrere, end man regner med, når man hygger med venner
most_rewarding: Venskaberne, jeg var meget heldig at ende i en god gruppe, men det kom også af, at vi KU-studerende tog kontakt til hinanden inden da.
greatest_challenge: De, der havde det svært, var ofte dem, der begyndte at savne sine gamle venner i deres hjemland. Det må man naturligvis gerne, men man skal passe på ikke at holde sig for meget for sig selv. Når det er sagt, behøver man ikke være ubetinget udadvendt for at tage afsted, det er jeg heller ikke selv.

crucial_aspects: - I wanted to study outside Scandinavia but stay in Europe. - What the country could offer, such as their culture and the opportunities at the university.
info_ease: It was easy, since I was informed per email about most things.
arrival_assistance: I had accommodation on campus, so I took a bus from the airport to UCD on my first day (Aircoach 700). When I arrived at UCD, I was welcomed by staff that helped me to find the reception, in which I would get my room key and student card.
arrival_comments: The first week was orientation week. I spent it to check out campus, the area, get to learn my roommates, get a bus card, go to IKEA etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: My studies started in January. I filled out an application for UCPH in March the year before my exchange and was offered the exchange at the end of March. After that I had to apply for admission at UCD in October with information about the modules I wanted to attend. If you are doing your bachelor thesis there, you also need to read about the different research areas they have, be clear on what you find more interesting and which supervisor you want to work with. Two weeks after the deadline I was accepted at UCD. After that you need to fill out an Online Learning Agreement, confirm your modules, and apply for the Erasmus grant (and I applied for an additional grant). The modules can be changed until a week or two after you begin the module if you don't think the module is suitable for you.
registration_help: I was offered help from my Erasmus coordinator.
registration_success: I was enrolled in the modules I applied for.
registration_advice: Don't be afraid to ask your Erasmus coordinator for help if you are unsure about your choice of modules. There are many different options on different levels. As a pharmacy student on third year, I enjoyed taking the PHAR300xx modules.
course_level: I had three modules for third year students, and my bachelor thesis was for fourth year students. In Ireland their bachelor takes four years, so they write their thesis on fourth year. The Irish students usually don't have other modules on the same time as they do their bachelor thesis, so my workload was adjusted accordingly to that. I would say that my modules and my project was on an appropiate level for a third year student.
teaching_comparison: I was spending more time on writing reports at UCD than at UCPH. Every report had to have an introduction, methods, results, discussion and conclusion. The report was graded, and you get feedback so you can improve your writing skills. You work in pairs in the lab sessions, but you write the report alone. Your grades over the semester from reports, presentations, groups work etc. counts % of your final grade. Thus, the final exam at UCD is different from that of UCPH, since at UCD the it doesn't count 100%. Depending on your module, the final exam may count e.g. 50% or 70% of your final grade. Additionally, all my final exams were closed book and with pen and paper. My schedule was fixed, so I knew what time of the week I had lectures and lab sessions in my three modules. I did not have a schedule for my research project because we had to adapt to the data we obtained and my teams availability, so we planned the lab sessions once a week. The paper I wrote was shorter than it would be at UCPH. This is because you write alone as an Erasmus student, and you have electives simultaneously.
courses_enrolled: PHAR30040: Advanced pharmacology of the nervous system PHAR30030: Toxicology PHAR30020: Endocrine, renal and reproductive pharmacology BMOL40330: Biomolecular Science Research Project
recommended_courses: Advanced central nervous system pharmacology: If you find the brain and mental health interesting, I would recommend this course. You learn about drug addiction, the gut-brain axis, ocular pharmacology and neural developmeny. Drug action in body systems II (Endocrine, renal and reproductive pharmacology): I liked this course because I got an in-dept understanding of all the drugs and mechanisms affecting kidneys, pancreas, adrenal glands, liver, endocrine cancers etc. You will know a lot about diabetes, hypertension, hormone cancer etc. after this course. This module has less group work than other modules but the final exam counts more. My project was very interesting and I learned so much about neuropharmacology and treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. The research team included me in their research, so it felt very meaningful to be contributing to that.
unexpected_costs: I had to buy kitchen equipment and bed sheets in IKEA which was around 100 Euro. Had to throw out/donate everything when I left.
cost_comparison: Bringing or buying books wasn't necessary. You can borrow so many different books from the library for free. Most of the time we read scientific articles.
activities_available: There are lots of different sports clubs you can sign up for such as football, canoe, rugby, hurling, handball, tennis etc. They have several gyms and a large swimming pool and spa. There is an international society that arranges weekend trips, so you can discover Ireland with other international students.
activities_recommended: The gym and swimming facilities were great.
weekend_recommendations: Cliffs of Moher Giants Causeway Visit a sheep farm Wicklow mountains / Glendalough Belfast weekendtrip Bray head hike Powerscourt Gardens The nightlife in Dublin St. Stephens Green and much more
culture_adjustment: I found it easy to adjust to the local culture.
socializing_tips: Getting rommates helped me to meet other people as well. Don't be afraid to talk to your Irish fellow students at school. They are very friendly and helpful. Go on weekend trips with the International Society from UCD. Consider living on campus despite the high costs. You will live close to so many other international students. Most of my friends also lived there.
cultural_challenges: I found no major cultural differences
culture_appreciated: The Irish people are friendly and have good humour. I love their nature, particularly their beautiful coastlines and mountains. And I like their talented live musicians.
top3_advice: 1. Live with roomies and close to the school 2. Apply for other grants than only Erasmus grant if needed 3. Go on lots of trips while you are there, and do it before the exam period
other_useful_info: Practice the topics of the modules early and try to memorize it. Most final exams are closed book. Bring an extra credit card and a copy of your passport in case you lose it.
most_rewarding: All the things I learned. Studying at a different university gave me valuable knowledge, since I have obtained an understanding on how things can be done differently. Additionally, I have learned about different cultures through meeting other nationalities from around the world. It was very rewarding to meet lots of new people. Some of them became good friends.
greatest_challenge: The exam period. It is spread over just two weeks, so you are busy in the exam period. Additionally, the type of exam at UCD is different than at UCPH.
other_comments: I really enjoyed my exchange trip, and I have gained personal, cultural and educational experience and created good memories.

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The university welcoming and organization along with the housing prices detract from the overall experience.

registration_help: Writing different UCD erasmus offices, via email, which often took days to answer.
registration_success: Not very succesful.

recommended_courses: I would not recommend any of the ones I had.

cost_comparison: Housing was much more expensive than expected, so was food.
activities_available: Every kind imaginable, too many to list.

culture_adjustment: It was very easy, I think Irish people in general are more straightforward and warm than Danes.
socializing_tips: I would really recommend two things: Joining different societies and engaging with them. Regularly going to the pub with a group of people, as this is the primary socialising spot in irish life.
cultural_challenges: I found it very challenging that irish people can be honest to the point of rudeness sometimes.
culture_appreciated: I very much appreciated the warmth inherent in the irish culture, everyone was always willing to talk to you and I found that strangers would often strike up conversation.
top3_advice: Housing is expensive, seriously. Engage in societies and clubs. UCD bureaucracy is very decentralized and disorganised.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: The people I met, enganging with irish culture, exploring a new country.
greatest_challenge: Definitely the academic workload and the price of housing.
other_comments: Not that I can think of.

registration_help: There was advisers available who would help you with any questions you had.
registration_success: I got all the modules I wished for.
registration_advice: Remember to check when the modules are offered, to avoid any clashes, and remember to check how much outside of class work there is for the module.
course_level: In the later years the modules are very specified, so there is a good opportunity to really learn the materiale
teaching_comparison: Most of the teaching was the same as UCPH, with lab work and lectures. There wasn't as many tutorials as there are at UCPH. However, there is more in-class tests, which counts towards the finale grade.
courses_enrolled: CCIV10040 - Vikings in the Celtic World CHEM20080 - Basis of Physical Chemistry CHEM30090 - Chemistry of Materials CHEM30110 - Instrumental Analysis CHEM30200 - Carbonyl Chemistry & Synthesis CHEM30220 - Mechanism and Stereochemistry
recommended_courses: CHEM30110 - Instrumental Analysis and CHEM30220 - Mechanism and Stereochemistry were really good courses. Instrumental Analysis is really useful if you wish to work in any chemistry lab or if you need to work with instruments, as you get a good knowledge of how the instruments works. Mechanism and Stereochemistry were a good module for getting a good understanding of mechanisms. I would also recommend taking a module in a lower level, for getting an easier one, maybe with not to much work, so you have time to explore the country and make friends.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Busses and other public transport was less expensive than expected
activities_available: There are 50 sport clubs and over 70 societies available. There are both national and internation sports, and societies for everything.
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining a sport club or societies, doesn't matter if you have ever played that sport before, as it is a good way to meet people and make friends.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend for people to take either a one day trip or weekend trip to explore the country. Cliffs of Moher is a good one day trip, but to go to Northern Ireland, is also a good weekend or day trip. A good day trip is also to go see Glendalough, where there is some hiking trips and two lakes, but also some beautiful old ruins from a monastery. If you like to hike, then there is some amazing hike tours starting and ending in the city Howth.
culture_adjustment: It is not very hard to adjust to the local culture.
socializing_tips: I would recommend to join a club, it is very cheap and you get to meet new people. Also if you feel comfortable just say hi to somebody in you class, everybody was very welcoming.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: Don't know
top3_advice: Take modules you think sounds fun, even if they don't match your degree. You have a good opportunity to take modules which they don't offer any other places int he world. Join a club or a society. It is a very cheap and a great way to meet people and make friends. Don't be afraid to join if you are only there for a semester, they are used to that and are just happy to get some members and friends. Don't forget to enjoy it. It is easy to stress about assignments and schoolwork, but remember you are there to meet know people and learn about a different culture than your own.
other_useful_info: Remember to bring some warm clothes, as there can be very cold on campus and during lectures.
most_rewarding: To know that it was possible for me to go to a new culture and live and study there
greatest_challenge: The amount of work for some of modules were pretty high, and covid. There was a lot of corona cases in Ireland during finals, which added a layer of stress about the finals and if it was possible for me to get home

crucial_aspects: Ireland is the only EU country where everything is in English. University College Dublin allowed me to choose a wide range of modules rather than sticking to a single course, which was very appealing to me as a nanoscience student. Dublin is a nice city with loads of pubs, and Ireland is a beautiful country with infinitely many hikes and sheep!
info_ease: UCD offered a reception open 24-7 for enquiries about accommodation etc. A lot of information had been sent out per email, so information was generally well distributed, and the local Erasmus office was very responsive at the beginning of my stay.
arrival_assistance: Check-in to my on-campus accommodation, a few info meetings on zoom which were, however, not very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You have to manually look up the random time-slots for every module you consider taking and make sure there are no timetable clashes. The registration is done manually by sending an email with all your desired module names. You are able to change your modules during the first three weeks of lectures, which is awesome!
registration_help: Email interaction with a coordinator.
registration_success: I ended up registering for 5/6 modules I was interested in. For my final class I had to register for a module with classes in the evening to avoid timetable clashes. The module was bad, but I met a couple of nice people there, so i guess it was worth it.
registration_advice: If you are not following a specific course (e.g. chemistry, physics or whatever they have) it can be very difficult to make the timetable work. I made several draft-timetables in excel by plugging in the times from their course catalogue, but I still had to compromise on my desired modules.
course_level: I generally had one third good modules, one third easy modules and one third poorly taught modules. For me, the easy modules freed time to have fun and travel, while the poorly taught ones offered an opportunity to dive into the topics when doing the big assignments by myself, and the good modules kept me afloat when I was about to lose motivation.
teaching_comparison: There was no hands-on lab experiences, only in the form of data treatment and computer work. Other than that the style was very comparable but he execution often left much to be desired.
courses_enrolled: English for Academic Writing 5, Data Science in Python, Nanomaterials Chemistry, Chem Proc Sust & Ren Energy, Advanced Characterisation Tech, Advanced Topics in Computational Science
recommended_courses: Advanced Topics in Computational Science: The lecturer is very enthusiastic and competent, and you get to code up some cool models without a lot of prior experience. All around good craic! (Data Science in Python): A good introduction to working in python if you, like me, could not find that at UCPH. The module is not very inspiring but I think I learned a lot of useful skills.
unexpected_costs: Nothing major, but going to bars, weekend trips etc. turned out to be essential and expensive in the long run.
cost_comparison: Buying food (not cooking) was expensive. Accommodation was expensive. Public transport for students was cheap.
activities_available: All sports you can mention as well as other societies including ones for different cultures (german, indian, french etc.), food, games, you name it.
activities_recommended: The mountaineering club do climbing classes twice a week, a hiking trip every Sunday, and occasionally longer trips, check it out! The "res-life" (people living on-campus) arrange football every week as wel as events such as dating shows, talents shows, super bowl nights etc, it's nice. The Clubhouse (the student bar) have four events a week including pub quiz, music quiz and karaoke.
weekend_recommendations: Go to everywhere in Ireland. All of the five biggest cities are well worth a trip, and I'm sure plenty of the smaller ones are too! Train tickets across the country are crazy cheap (~100DKK), but you have to be 25 to rent a car (or check out GoCar, getting very specific). There are beautiful hikes in all kinds of terrains where ever you go, even the smallest village has at least one cozy pub and around Easter there are lambs everywhere, it's wild!
culture_adjustment: The Irish culture is not too different from the Danish one in a lot of ways, although they like them their rules, so they might throw your friends out of your apartment at 11pm on a Saturday or fine you €50 if your phone makes a sound during the exam. But don't we all love and respect authorities anyway?
socializing_tips: Nope, I found it very difficult to make Irish friends. I guess don't be afraid to go talk to people and do it every time you see them, because they will probably not seek you out actively.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really
culture_appreciated: The open mindedness of people. Even though I found it hard to make real friends with the Irish, people are generally very welcoming and will chat you up in the pub or where ever you go.
top3_advice: The on-campus accommodation is very expensive, but not that much more expensive than the rest of Dublin. If you can afford it, it is nice to live close to all the other exchange students in the everyday. It is probably difficult to get exactly the modules you want to register for. However, my favorite modules ended up being completely different from what I thought, so don't worry too much about it. There is a lot of continuous assessment rather than final exams. I ended up having one essay and one exam in the exam week even though I followed six modules.
other_useful_info: There is a pub close by called the Goat. It is located in Goatstown, has several bronze goat statues AND a couple of real goats living outside. Go here.
most_rewarding: Meeting new friends from all over the world so I know where to travel the next 10 years :))
greatest_challenge: All the preparation: Filling in paperwork, applying foundations for money, registering for modules, registering for accommodation, finishing exams before leaving etc. But it was all worth it in the end!

crucial_aspects: Good University, close to city, country I wanted to visit
info_ease: Quite easy. The university had a website that was easy to navigate.
arrival_assistance: The RAs helped me find my university accommodation and answered questions I had about the area – closest supermarket, bus routes, etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was quite intuitive – there was a form on the university website, and it was easy to find the information I needed.
registration_help: I suppose I could have emailed the person responsible for exchange students at the university – they seemed happy to help.
registration_success: Quite, although some classes were on one form/website and others were on another, which in some cases made me take other classes than I'd originally planned so that I just had to use one form. But I was satisfied with the classes I ended up taking.
registration_advice: Most of the classes are worth few ECTS, which allows you to take classes that are a bit outside your field. My advice would be to take a class that teaches you something about the country/city of your university.
course_level: The courses were ranked from 1-5 depending on level, and as a BA student I was allowed to take level 1-3 courses as far as I remember. A number of the courses were recommended especially for exchange students.
teaching_comparison: At UCPH my classes are usually longer, and you are urged to actively participate and be part of the discussion. At UCD most of my classes were one hour twice a week, and they were lectures with little to no active student participation. Some of my classes were more in the style of those I have at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: AH20280 Queer Art Histories ENG10020 Children's Literature ENG20440 Reading the story of Ireland: Irish Literature in English ENG32510 Writing Dublin HIS20780 History of Science IR10050 Irish for Beginners/Gaeilge do Thosaitheoirí
recommended_courses: I enjoyed all my classes. The Irish for Beginners gaelic language course taught me a bit about Irish history and culture and I would recommend that to students from all fields.
unexpected_costs: I don't think there was anything unexpected, except price levels
cost_comparison: The price of accommodation was a surprise, but it would have been difficult to find accommodation myself, and probably also expensive so I am still glad I chose university housing. Public transport was quite cheap when I was in Dublin – 1 euro for up to 1,5 hours of transport for students/young adults.
activities_available: sports, religious, language, field specific, literature and movies, politics, food, etc.
activities_recommended: Choosing a club is about personal preference, but I'd definitely recommend looking into them. I like the movie club, as it allowed you to meet people and watch movies in the campus cinema at a very low cost – I think just 2 euro for the whole semester, which was the price level for most clubs.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend going to other cities in Ireland – Belfast, Galway of Cork for example – to see other places in Ireland. There is also a coastline train track that leads you to coastal towns close to Dublin where you can go hiking or just visit a beautiful place outside the city. Also, I would recommend visiting some of the beautiful, old pubs in Dublin.
culture_adjustment: Quite – it is not so different from Denmark. I liked Dublin, as it was easy to navigate and very charming. People were more talkative than in Denmark, but that was quite nice!
socializing_tips: I mainly socialised with other exchange students, but join a club or talk to someone in class would bemy advice for socialising with any student at the university.
cultural_challenges: The food options are more so processed or unhealthy food than in Denmark, if you want to buy something on the go or something pre-cooked that you just need to heat up at home. Also, organic produce is not as common, but can usually be found on a shelf in the supermarket.
culture_appreciated: The music, literature, friendliness to strangers, and the pub culture.
top3_advice: 1. Make sure to find accommodation a little while before you leave. It is not easy to find, and a good idea would maybe be to find university housing or to rent near the university. 2. Join some clubs or attend social events – a large part of the exchange experience is meeting new people! 3. Try to see some of the other parts of Ireland as well! It is a beautiful country.
most_rewarding: Living in a different country, the friendships and taking interesting classes that are not available at my home university.
greatest_challenge: When I had just arrived and was the only person at my accommodation and did not know anyone, or where anything was. It got a lot easier when the others arrived and we could figure things out together.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go on exchange in a country where English was the official language.
overall_comments: My exchange was amazing! the only con is the expensive accomodation.
info_ease: It was easy enough and I could just email KU or UCD if I had any questions.
arrival_assistance: at the orientation week we met the student organization that would help us throughout our exchange as well as the UCD global team.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: My exchange was amazing! the only con is the expensive accomodation.
registration_process: UCD sends out a registration form, where you write the modules you want to register + a back-up module. UCD will email you with the modules that they registered for, if any of the modules were full they will ask you to select other modules (unless you get in contact with the administration).
registration_help: The office at the science department helped me register for all my modules.
registration_success: The school administration contacted the module coordinator to register me for the modules that I did not get, The email I got previously informed me, that some of the modules were full capacity, so I ended up getting all my modules as the module coordinator agreed to let me register in their module.
registration_advice: I would advise future students to contact the school administration in the science department if they have any problems with module registration.
academics_comments: My exchange was amazing! the only con is the expensive accomodation.
course_level: The level is easier at UCD than in Copenhagen. The lectures are helpful, and the lab practicals give a better understanding of the subject in practise.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is the same. I would say that at UCPH the lectures help understand the chapters we study in the books, whereas the lectures at UCD is more of an "Everything you need to know" of the topics.
courses_enrolled: I enrolled in Toxicology, Molecular basis of disease and molecular pharmacology
recommended_courses: Toxicology was nice since there is no exam, so there is enough time to study the other subjects. I also found molecular pharmacology very interesting and helpful with regard to my bachelor project. Molecular basis of disease was also a good course.
unexpected_costs: My phone subscription ran out of EU data (Oister), so the data of my last 20 day was taxed and is very expensive.
cost_comparison: Local transportation is very cheap, and some specific groceries are much cheaper compared to Copenhagen.
activities_available: There are everything you can think of really. Information of all the clubs and activities can be seen at UCD website.
activities_recommended: Definitely the hiking club as you will get a unique opportunity t explore Ireland with other students, and they rent a bus to take you to the destination and back to UCD again, a bonus since public transport takes a long time.
weekend_recommendations: Hike in Bray, Howth, ring of Kerry in Killarney and Wicklow national park. The view is spectacular!
culture_adjustment: the population in Dublin is very international, so it is easy to blend in.
socializing_tips: Local students love pubs. There is also a pub at UCD where you can meet alot of both local and international students and get a cheap beer.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really, they are very easy-going.
culture_appreciated: Most people were really nice and went out of their way to help you with directions etc.
top3_advice: 1. Make sure data will be covered during your exchange in those 4 months. 2. Find accommodation and select courses at UCPH in case you do not find accommodation, and if you do, you can cancel the courses at UCPH. 3. Explore Ireland :-D
other_useful_info: Make sure to check your email, as the email for on-campus accommodation will be sent out a day before you can apply, and due to housing crisis on-campus accommodation is in high demand.
most_rewarding: The friends I gained during my semester
greatest_challenge: Finding accomodation.

arrival_assistance: Der er en reception som er åben 24-7, som var gode til at guide en hvis man havde spørgsmål og så kunne man også skrive til det kontor de har der hedder UCD global.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Der er rigtig mange dokumenter, som man skal holde styr på, men sådan er det generelt når man skal på udveksling tænker jeg.
registration_help: Mange muligheder for hjælp. registration_success: Jeg fik alle de kurser som jeg søgte.
registration_advice: Skriv hellere en mail for meget, end slet ikke at få svar på de mange spørgsmål der er, når man skal på udveksling. Vær inde over alle dine mails fra start.

cost_comparison: Huslejen er dyr og så er det dyrt at købe ind.

weekend_recommendations: Det hele kan anbefales - det er vigtigt at du er så social som mulig i starten.

cultural_challenges: Der er ikke stor forskel mellem Dublin og København.
culture_appreciated: De er meget høflige og hjælpsomme - de siger for eksempel tak hver gang de står af bussen.
top3_advice: Vær opmærksom på alle mails, tage en dyb indånding, glæd dig til det sociale (vær så social du kan i starten, men selvfølgelig efter hvad der er muligt for dig).

crucial_aspects: I knew I wanted to go on exchange due to personal growth in a new envoirement, which was my main reason for choosing to attend UCD. overall_comments: Even though I arrived after orientations, due to exams at my home university, the journey of going on exchange with all the people and academics could not have been more perfect.
info_ease: Not quite since I missed orientation, but UCD were very accomendating with any questions I had, which helped.
arrival_assistance: I got a contact person, a cara, which whoom I met up with and got an introduction to the university and he answeared all my questions. Otherwise non were given.
arrival_comments: There were some webinairs before arrival, which were very helpful as well with what we needed to do before arriving on campus etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Even though I arrived after orientations, due to exams at my home university, the journey of going on exchange with all the people and academics could not have been more perfect.
registration_process: We had to pick a top 3 housing types, where after it was dealt out amongst the students.
registration_help: There was a webinair, which was very helpful and you could look on the residence portal for help.
registration_success: I got my first priority.
registration_advice: That it is a university that you can always seek help from, with their 24 hour reception being open.
academics_comments: Even though I arrived after orientations, due to exams at my home university, the journey of going on exchange with all the people and academics could not have been more perfect.

courses_enrolled: PHAR30110-Cardiovascular & Renal Disease-2023/24 Spring BMOL30100-Lead Teams in Sci Enterprise-2023/24 Spring BIOC40220-Hot topics in Biochemistry-2023/24 Spring BMOL40330-Biomol. Sci. Research Project-2023/24 Spring

cultural_challenges: There is a difference in food which I had to get used to. The drinking culture on clubs and pubs were also very different. Both for good and for worse. Clothing were also very different.
culture_appreciated: I loved how friendly and open the Irish people were. I also loved that the pubs were open all day and you would find people in Dublin enjoying each others company. My favorite were Sct. Patricks day I would have to say :)
top3_advice: Amazing social life, Loads of travel opporitunities and loads of craigh (fun in Irish)!

most_rewarding: All the people I met on my stay. When staying on campus and having roomates, who are from all over the world, it got very easy to meet more and more people. That made my whole stay worth so much.
greatest_challenge: I think it was meeting people when arriving after orientation. But it took a couple weeks and I ended up being so comfortable with my friends, so it all worked out.

crucial_aspects: Any destination was crucial to me, since I really did not want to to my BSc in a gruop, and by studying abroad I could write it up solo.

registration_help: We could contact the people in charge if we needed help.

courses_enrolled: Leading teams in the scientific enterprise Drug action II Hot Topics BSc project
