unexpected_costs: Im not sure. We went on 'spontaneous' trips and hikes, but I expected this.
cost_comparison: Definitly food in supermarkets. E.g. 1kg of greek yoghurt was 1.69 euros, 12 DKK, whereas 1kg in Denmark is 32 DKK Alcohol was the same and so was dining out.
activities_available: Endless activities. UCD is a big campus and they do a lot of activities
activities_recommended: Res-Life.
weekend_recommendations: You should totally visit Dun Laoghaire, Bray, Belfast, Galway, Cliffs of Moher.... the list goes on
culture_adjustment: Very easy, th Irish are super helpful
socializing_tips: I dont, I wish i socialized more with local students
cultural_challenges: the way they work in Ireland is more 'layed back' and not that structured, at least where I worked...
culture_appreciated: The irish people<3 and the beautiful nature
top3_advice: Enjoy, it is going to be amazing. Choose easy courses to you will have more free time
other_useful_info: bring a rain coat/wind breaker, it literally rains every day and it is very windy.
most_rewarding: The people I met. They are wonderful
greatest_challenge: Doing my exam in the RDS exam hall. Over 1000 students take their exam in the same hall. It was giving Hunger Games vibes.

crucial_aspects: We did not have many universities to choose from, but choosing a university that is part of the EU has definitely made the process much easier.
info_ease: Although the university was very large, there was good information and the university was very helpful with everything. Already in advance, there were several Zoom meetings with relevant information, and they were good at responding to emails
arrival_assistance: Normally there would be people waiting in the airport at campus. But due to a later arrival this was not the situation for me. But they had a 24-hours welcome desk and everyone was wery helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: After being approved by KU, you need to secure a place at UCD. You will receive all the information you need.
registration_help: Someone contacted me regarding course selection and another person contacted me regarding my bachelor's project. She became my contact person and was very helpful with all questions.
registration_success: I got my 1st and 2nd choices and my 4th choice instead of my 3rd choice. I got the bachelor's project I applied for.
registration_advice: Talk to former students who have been there. Even if you read a course description, it can be very difficult to assess how demanding the different courses are.
course_level: The approach to learning is very different and can therefore seem more difficult. However, the knowledge you have from KU is sufficient to follow their courses.
teaching_comparison: They don't use textbooks in the same way but encourage you to find scientific articles to reference. Similarly, their lab reports are also structured that way.
courses_enrolled: BMOL40330 Biomol. Sci. Research Project (Bachelor project) BIOC40220 Hot topics in Biochemistry & Molecular Biology PHAR30030 Toxicology PHAR30040 Development and advanced pharmacology of the nervous system
recommended_courses: BIOC40220 Hot topics in Biochemistry & Molecular Biology This course had a very light workload and no exam. If you haven't done many presentations before, it can be good practice before presenting your bachelor's project. The entire course has a very relaxed approach.
unexpected_costs: Loss of travel card, ekstra trips
cost_comparison: Public transport was very cheap. Bars were very expensive.
activities_available: The university have a lot of sport clubs and societies. Everything you can think of.
activities_recommended: There is so much pretty nature close to Dublin that can be reach by public transport.
weekend_recommendations: Go around Ireland! Galway, Ring of Kerry, (Belfast), Cork
culture_adjustment: The irish people were very friendly and it is easy to adapt.
socializing_tips: A good way to socialize with local students would be trough the clubs and societies.
cultural_challenges: Nothing in particular
culture_appreciated: The international friendships
top3_advice: 1. Eventhough it is close to Copenhagen the university is very different 2. keep an open mind 3. Try and keep up to date with everything that is going on
other_useful_info: Housing can be very tricky, so if you get offered something by the campus - take it.
most_rewarding: It was something very special to be able to work with a real research group. Additionally, a lot of international friendships
greatest_challenge: To live with people that maybe haven't tried to live out before (but no major challenge)

crucial_aspects: the courses, the place, my friends
info_ease: very easy
arrival_assistance: ESN was super helpful to guide me in my experience in Dublin
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I don't remember super well, but we registered with the OLA and got a confirmation email through SISweb and thereafter had to pick up our UCD cards at the Village
registration_help: the Village workers, the exchange coordinators and the administrators in the International Building
registration_success: it would have been nice to have more English L3 and creative writing courses. Exchange students were only allowed to pick one
registration_advice: make sure you know what classes you want and register fast before all the spots are taken
course_level: I had 3 L1 courses, 1 L2 course and 1 L3 course
teaching_comparison: More courses per semester and a confusing amount of differing citation rules. All of the subjects asked for different Academic writing styles
courses_enrolled: Dublin: its museums; Language Acquisition and Disruption; Children's Literature; Girlhood in 21st Century YA literature; Race and Racism
recommended_courses: Race and Racism: Taught me a lot about what it is to be a minority of colour and what to do to help Girlhood: excellent for students interested in literature, but want to analyse more than just the classics
unexpected_costs: adapter plug for the wall, pharmacy/doctor trips,
cost_comparison: tuna was more than expected
activities_available: lots of varying societies. I was part of the LGBTQ+ society, the Spanish society, the Nordic society and ESN
activities_recommended: the societies and ESN. Great way to meet people with the same interests as you or who feel as displaced as you
weekend_recommendations: visit the inner city with someone who knows it. Go on museum trips, trips to the ocean, park trips.
culture_adjustment: Not the easiest, it felt a bit alienating at times.
socializing_tips: Don't be afraid to ask questions at the expense of sounding stupid, they probably have similar questions about your culture
cultural_challenges: The reserve some people have and their preference for people from their own country
culture_appreciated: the sense of humour.
top3_advice: Manage your expectations. Your exchange will end up wildly different than you expect. Bring extra sweaters, blankets and fluffy socks. IT IS COLD EVEN INSIDE! Don't be afraid to go explore on your own. Go visit the city by yourself, there is plenty to see/do.
other_useful_info: Your friends at home will still be there when you come back, don't hold yourself back on your exchange for fear of missing out back home.
most_rewarding: The friends I made on my exchange.
greatest_challenge: Homesickness and loneliness. Having to go through tough moments with little to no physical support because my support system was so far away.

crucial_aspects: The student language was English

arrival_assistance: I didn't need any assistance
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_help: There were both the Erasmus team and the local science study abroad team helping with registration

registration_advice: Ask for help at the different student support teams to get to know which classes are available for exchange students
course_level: It was either master level or 4th year of bachelor level courses
teaching_comparison: Only lectures and a few of the courses also had written assignments during the semester

weekend_recommendations: Travel around Ireland. It is such a beautiful country
culture_adjustment: It was easy
socializing_tips: No because I mostly socialized with other exchange students
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: The kindness and open mind of the Irish people
top3_advice: 1 Don't forget to have fun. It is not only about studying but also getting to meet new people and experience another country 2 Take a break when needed. Socializing with only new people can be tiring and it okay to take a break 3 Enjoy!
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: All the good people I met

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere where I knew I would feel home quickly. I enjoy a rainy day, and I knew the people would be kind.
info_ease: It was quite easy, although I had to change modules because of some missing information.
arrival_assistance: There was a dedicated introduction week for exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to reply an email with my module wishes, and then the host university did the rest.
registration_help: They made a webinar about it, and provided all the information on a padlet.
registration_success: Very successful, I got all my wishes.
registration_advice: Don’t expect that you can take modules that overlap, I made that mistake and had to change my OLA and everything.
course_level: I had some introduction modules outside of my subject, which were great. I had one level 4 module which I never got the hang off, since I had some exams colliding with the first few lectures followed by being sick for two weeks twice during the semester. I would therefore recommend not doing too high levels, especially if outside the main subject.
teaching_comparison: The semester is much shorter. Some mandatory tutorials. More assignments. Mid-semester exams. First I was very overwhelmed and a bit stressed about it, it felt more competitive than I was used to. But I ended up liking the structure a lot.
courses_enrolled: Oscillations and Waves, Logic, Why Trust Science, Numerical Methods for PDE’s, Methods for Physicists, Programming with Big Data
recommended_courses: Oscillations and Waves, because it’s more fun than it sounds. Logic, because it’s interesting and relevant to everyone. Why Trust Science, because it’s not a common module. It’s a mix of different subjects and the structure is very different too. Methods for Physicists, it’s great if you like solving physics problems by hand.
unexpected_costs: None as far as I remember.
cost_comparison: Housing prices were much higher than expected, including student accommodation. No books were required to purchase as all mandatory reading were available online.
activities_available: Free cultural trips were available. Free fitness membership. We all had a contact person, one of the students from the host university. They hosted a a couple of parties, not free entry though.
activities_recommended: Definitely the free trips, although they are published very late and can therefore collide with other plans. Thus I didn’t attend any, but my friends said they were great
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend staying in Ireland and travelling around the beautiful country instead of going abroad. There are so many great hikes! And surfing is a lot of fun too.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, so many kind people. Truly a lovely country.
socializing_tips: Just be yourself, because you are great. Then everything will work out.
cultural_challenges: The night life closes very early.
culture_appreciated: Everyone is super friendly and polite.
top3_advice: Find a place to stay before arriving. Do some “social” modules, where you will be talking a lot during classes. That will help you make lots of different friends. Don’t stress about participating in all of the social activities during the introduction week, because it can be exhausting.
other_useful_info: Buy a bike cheep on Adverts (second hand), it’s great to have.
most_rewarding: It gave me an academic boost, a social boost and a motivational boost for my studies and life in general.
greatest_challenge: Finding the balance between socialising and charging my social battery.

crucial_aspects: That it was an English-speaking country, for the sake of improving my English. I also wanted to stay within EU, and I think Dublin and Ireland in general has a great range of important literature and history which I am very interested in.
info_ease: It was very easy. The university was very helpful and very easy to get in touch with. They also provided us with loads of information that we could find on their website and on a Padlet.
arrival_assistance: When I arrived at my accomodation on campus they helped me moving my stuff to my room, and I got a tour around campus which was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was easy.
registration_help: Any. Phone and e-mail.
registration_success: Very succesful, however you had to be quick in order to get the classes you want the most. But it was very easy, and I also changed my class at some point without any problem.
registration_advice: Look at what classes the university offers before the registration date to make sure you get what you like.
course_level: High level on all of them, with a great learning output.
teaching_comparison: More or less the same as back home, but every teacher I had was absolutely incredible.
courses_enrolled: Syntax 2, Whiteness, Ethnicity and US film, Literature and Crisis, Exploring Ireland.
recommended_courses: Exploring Ireland as it provides you with significant history of Ireland and its literature which was very interesting for an exchange student, as you are very curious about learning these about the country you live in for that amount of time.
unexpected_costs: Nothing, I was quite prepared.
cost_comparison: Nothing, I was quite prepared.
activities_available: Library, societies, gym, cinema residence life activities, trips to places in Ireland.
activities_recommended: The gym and the cinema is very nice.
weekend_recommendations: Go around in Ireland, but also just enjoy Dublin for its lovely pubs and good vibes.
culture_adjustment: Easy, as it's similar to Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Join stuff and talk to your neighbors on campus.
cultural_challenges: Nothing, really.
culture_appreciated: The Irish people's openness to new people. I felt like it was easy to ask for help and also falling into conversation with people you met on the pubs or just outside.
top3_advice: be aware of the rent prices due to the housing crisis, it is difficult to find an apartment if you don't get on-campus accomodation and to just enjoy and take one day at a time.
other_useful_info: Do not be afraid to talk to new people! The flights are cheap to Britain, so in the weekends one can take advantage of it or in the breaks!
most_rewarding: The people I met on exchange and created strong bonds with, and also a new academic experience.
greatest_challenge: To find other stuff to do than go to pubs in the weekends, but maybe I did not explore enough.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial that the host university had interesting courses and a good study environment.
info_ease: I found it very easy, seeing that the UCD Erasmus office and UCD in general provide good resources for informing the students of things and dates to be aware of.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance in form of guidance from the Erasmus team.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: By following UCD's padlet for exchange students, it was very easy registrating for courses and subsequently getting access to the university's online platform where an email account was set up for us, where we would recieve further information.
registration_help: There are many helpful resources at UCD, such as, health care services, academic writing workshops, the student desk, the Erasmus office etc.
registration_success: I found the process of registrating for courses easy and if a course had already allocated all its spots, then it was easy finding a similar course to registrer for instead.
registration_advice: For future exchange students, I would recommend to have a few other courses in mind other than the main courses you wish to get, since it can be a reality that some of the courses get filled very quickly and then you need to apply for other courses.
course_level: I took 6 courses on level 1-3 and found the workload with test, assignments, mid-terms and the exams to be accomplishable while still having a social life and time for other things besides studying.
teaching_comparison: The teaching is quite similar between UCPH and UCD, since they both operate with lectures and tutorials/seminars.
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled in the courses called: Sociology of Crime and Deviance, Critical Thinking, Introduction to Ethics, Introduction to Irish studies, Lost Cities & Writing Dublin.
recommended_courses: I would especially recommend future students to take the course Critical Thinking as it requires you to think differently and more thoroughly with an aim to develop a better analytical way of reasoning.
unexpected_costs: I would say that the most unexpected cost before beginning my exchange period was the cost of housing as this is very expensive in general in Dublin. Otherwise, I did not really encouter an unexpected cost during my stay.
cost_comparison: The public transport is very cheap and especially being a student it only costs 1 euro per bus ride.
activities_available: There is a large variety of societies and clubs for students at UCD. All from draw society, international student society, mature society, film society, athletics club etc.
activities_recommended: I think most people would appreciate film society, since it is a nice way to unwind after being in academic settings throughout the day.
weekend_recommendations: I think exchange students should go to the city centre as it is a bus ride on 15-20 minutes away from UCD, and here plenty of free admission museums are available for people to visit. Moreover, UCD plans several trips throughout the semester for students to go to other locations in Ireland with beautiful nature sites and historical sites.
culture_adjustment: I think the Erasmus team did a great job doing a lot of activities and events for exchange students to get to know each other. And in general the students at the university are very friendly and helpful.
socializing_tips: The best way to socialise with local students would be to join societies and clubs or to talk to students in tutotials or before and after lectures.
cultural_challenges: I think the Irish culture is a very open and accepting culture which results in a great diversity both on campus but also in the city centre. Therefore, I did not find it difficult to enjoy the culture and speak with the Irish people around me.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciate how visible the Irish history is in their land- and cityscape with their many churces and beautiful ancient architecture. Furthermore, their music, food, pubs and sports are all great cultural things to engage in as well.
top3_advice: 1. Search for accomodation early in the process, since it can be very difficult to find affordable accomodation in Dublin. 2. Ask for help if you need help with anything, since the teachers and the Erasmus team are all very helpful and happy to help you out. 3. Push yourself to talk to people in your courses even though it might seem a little intimidating to begin with, because it is great having people to talk to about course related stuff but also for the benefit of social plans in non-academic settings.
other_useful_info: It might also be useful to remeber that it is a very big university. So, if you need to study and if you want to preferably sit in a librabry, there are a couple to choose from. The James Joyce library is great, but it can get a little packed there, so remeber to investigate the rest of campus and the other buildings where good study spots are located as well.
most_rewarding: It was very rewarding having a great dialogue with the teachers and having good tutorials where you could see your own progress. It was also great getting to know so many very nice students on campus.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was finding affordable accommodation.

crucial_aspects: Because of Covid, I had to choose a location in Europe, and London is a very international and academic city to live in. The language wasn't a turning point for me, but of course, made it all a lot easier and expanded my English language skills. UCL is a great university so this was also an important factor.
overall_comments: Everything school-related was amazing, and some amazing people but the living situation is a mess!! UCL is also a great university. Remember a full term is only 2,5 months in London, so you will only be on exchange from around late September to mid/late december. You are totally free all of September and January. All exams are written exams (essays), so no exams at school.
info_ease: It was very difficult to get information from UCL, and the connection between KU and UCL is not great. The system is confusing because the university is so big. You will receive information when you come, but the communication by email or phone is really not good.
arrival_assistance: When we were properly enrolled we got a lot of emails with introduction information. Remember to read ALL emails, as there is deadlines.
arrival_comments: They tried to inform, but if something wasn't in an email, it was hard to find the correct person to ask.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Everything school-related was amazing, and some amazing people but the living situation is a mess!! UCL is also a great university. Remember a full term is only 2,5 months in London, so you will only be on exchange from around late September to mid/late december. You are totally free all of September and January. All exams are written exams (essays), so no exams at school.
registration_process: You choose your courses by yourself. 50% has to be from the faculty, and the rest is toyally free. You have to make your own shedule, and therefore no overlaps between courses. This can be quite hard. When registered, with help by a student affiliate officer, you had to write to each professor from each class (4 classes of 7,5 ECTS each) why you would fit the class. Then they had to accept, of they would tell you if it was full. If full you had to look at other courses and make it fit. It took about one week (intro week) and was quite stressfull.
registration_help: The affiliate teacher helped a lot. All the professors are very helpful, it just takes time because everyone is busy.
registration_success: I got 3/4 of the classes I wanted, and the fourth the professor was really nice in trying to find a class similar to the one I wanted.
registration_advice: I would look into the classes you want already before you arrive in London, and make sure they fit in the schedule. And take contact with an affiliate teacher/advisor beforehand and say to them you want to register early to make sure classes are not filled. They will also tell you how to find the email of the professors, to get their approval. You can register when you are enrolled
academics_comments: Everything school-related was amazing, and some amazing people but the living situation is a mess!! UCL is also a great university. Remember a full term is only 2,5 months in London, so you will only be on exchange from around late September to mid/late december. You are totally free all of September and January. All exams are written exams (essays), so no exams at school.
course_level: The course level is lower at UCL than KU, simply because there is no physical exams. The education is very academic and profesional, but it is definetly easier as an affiliate because we don't have exams, only essays. You only need 40% to pass, which is not a lot. The papers are often topics you choose your own.
teaching_comparison: No SAU, only lectures. So a lot of self study, but it works fine with the essay writing part.
courses_enrolled: Cellular Pathology Introduction to Coding for Bioscience - Python Biology of ageing Applied Nutrition
recommended_courses: If you just have a small interest in coding, the Python course was amazing. The teacher is so amazing, and the course was great fun. Cellular Pathology has a great teacher as well, and lecturers that present their own publised reseach. And the exam is 'just' one essay.
unexpected_costs: Food I don't know. You can use a lot less if you eat from home, but in London you eat out a lot at social occasions. Housing is very expensive for not a lot. TIP: go a bit north/east from UCL and there is cheaper options, but the ALWAYS look at the metro line. You want to live around max 30 min from UCL with total commute (very normal).
cost_comparison: Groceries are cheap. And eating out is not the expensive either.
activities_available: Nordic Society, Introduction week, sightseeing with friends
activities_recommended: Go to a lot of intro week things, and join the intro events at the societies and clubs during the introduction week.
weekend_recommendations: We went to Edinburgh and Oxford. You can go to many places by train and bus from London.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Usually, you end up meeting the international student, but there are 50% international students at UCL which is great!
cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: The pub culture and the many societies and clubs!
top3_advice: Meet up with a lot of people!! Get out there! It scary in the beginning, but so worth it :-) Don't think about the grade too much, it will all work out. Just call, email or ask questions if you are confused. Many want to help!
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Getting new friendships and going to another university
greatest_challenge: Trying to get new friends!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a big and interesting city, and I wanted the university to have a great reputation. For me UCL was perfect in both aspects.
info_ease: Quite difficult. I wish I had known had hard and frustating it would be. However, it was all worth it when I arrived and figured it all out.
arrival_assistance: There was "Welcome-days" and opportunities to ask for help for anything like enrolment and choosing classes.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There were plenty of information about the classes available, but the system was very stupid. The have a program for you to write in classes and see it there are any clashes, however it is very amnual and took so long. You just have to try out so many combinations until you find something. Then you had to write to your coordinator that you wanted a certain class, and to the module organizer, asking if you could take that module, and they both had to accept that. And then you do that for four modules, ad if there is a problem, you start over with a new class and see if it clashes. Very annoying.
registration_help: Your coordinators will do a lot to help you, you just write whatever questions you have by email.
registration_success: I got the classes I wanted, even though all of them weren't exactly what I had hoped.
registration_advice: Don't worry to much about choosing from home, you will have to change everything when you get there.
course_level: I thought the classes was a bit easier than at KU, at least a lot less preparations and readings to do before lectures
teaching_comparison: Smaller classes, less formal (even though you call everyone "Dr." or "professor"), I liked it a lot.
courses_enrolled: Infection Receptor Mechanisms Introduction to Coding for Bioscience Research (python) Social Neurosciende of Model Animals
recommended_courses: I loved my coding class and infection (even though infection was 100% online). I would recommend both a lot!
unexpected_costs: We ate out and went out more than I had thought, but it was worth it.
cost_comparison: Eating out is cheaper than in Denmark, underground was expensive however necessary
activities_available: They had more than 300 different clubs to join, everything for "boba-lovers" and movie societies over culture or nationality societies to innovation or economy clubs. And societies just about any sport
activities_recommended: I liked the nordic society, the food market every thursday and the welcome-activities for international students, which is where I met most of my friends.
weekend_recommendations: Sky garden The street food markets of London, like Camden food market, borough market, international food market on brick lane, the food market in hackney every weekend, Seven Dials market Go to columbia street flower market!! Protobello road market, they have street food as well Try as many restaurants as you can, that is how the locals live Walking in regents park, that was my favourite Walk around Covent garden Se the view from Hampstead Heath Visit the fampus museums, they are free. Try Tate Modern, natural history and british museum Try afternoon tea!
culture_adjustment: Very easy Get a pret membership, then you fit right in
socializing_tips: Talk to then in class, people take different classes and often don't already know each other. Your not the only new face and they are not all friends already
cultural_challenges: Nothing in particular
culture_appreciated: Eating out
top3_advice: Prepare yourself for a difficult beginning, the communication with UCL is awful and finding housing is stressful (but all worth it after the first week when everything is in order) Go to the "welcome-events" the few days and talk to people in your classes Enjoy yourself, the culture is very similar and it doesn't take that much work to get used to it. So just relax and enjoy being in a great city that has something new to offer everyday
other_useful_info: Don't stress to much before arriving, you'll get it sorted out there
most_rewarding: Figuring out the difficult situation with housing myself. Meeting new friends and people from all over the world. Improving my english. Getting to know and love London, actually that is number one, it was the best.
greatest_challenge: finding housing and everything before I arrived

crucial_aspects: It was important for me that my destination was in an English speaking country.
info_ease: It was really difficult for me to get enrolled at UCL. I had to call them many times to get them to send an acceptance letter. I almost gave up in the end. It is really difficult to get in contact with someone at UCL who can help you and their response time is awfull.
arrival_assistance: I got a tutor/contact person when I arrived at UCL
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was quite difficult since you have 4 modules at UCL running at the same time. So you need to make sure that none of the 4 modules has timetables that clashes. Furthermore they expect you to contact each module leader to get accepted so it is not enough to register online like it is done at KU.
registration_help: We got a handbook with modules and there is a webpage where you can check for clashes in timetables.
registration_success: I got 1 out of the 4 modules I registered for in Denmark. Upon arrival, I had to change three of the modules because of clashes and some modules were not available anymore.
registration_advice: Check for clashes in timetables and email every module leader from the beginning to get acceptance and to see if you have the pre-requisites
course_level: The level in my modules was a bit lower than at KU. Since exchange students are not there for exams you need to hand in essays at the end of term. This makes the lectures less important since you often get to pick a topic for the essays yourself.
teaching_comparison: It is quite similar but mostly lectures and fewer seminars. Furthermore, I had 3 tutorials and an oral presentation during my modules where I got graded for my contribution. I am not used to getting grades during my modules and not from contribution to discussions so this was different for me.
courses_enrolled: Genes and neurodegenerative diseases Infection Cellular pathology Biology of ageing
recommended_courses: I really liked genes and neurodegenerative diseases since this was completely different from my previous modules and it had a good journal club, Infection was also a good module and the module leader is amazing, the workload is also quite small compared to my other modules. Biology of ageing was interesting and gave a new perspective but the workload was a bit higher than my other modules with 3 tutorials and two essays to hand in.
unexpected_costs: London is a city where people eat out all the time, so you will end up spending a lot of money buying lunch every day and meeting with friends at restaurants for dinner. This was a bit surprising for me, I ended up spending most of my money on food, the food in London is great though. You can however make it cheaper if you make food yourself but people rarely do this.
cost_comparison: I spend more money on food than expected Travel pass for underground is also quite expensive but really nice to have to get around
activities_available: They have all kinds of sports clubs and food clubs, almost anything you can imagine. They even have a nordic society.
activities_recommended: I went to the nordic society once which was fun
weekend_recommendations: I took weekend trips to Edinburgh, Bath, Bristol and Oxford. It is really easy to get around in the south of England by train. Some of my friends also took the train from London to Paris.
culture_adjustment: Really easy. The culture in London is almost the same in Copenhagen. However, the city is huge so it will take some time to learn to get around and learn some of the local nice places without all the turists.
socializing_tips: I mostly spoke to exchange students. However, if you choose modules with tutorials or group presentations it is a nice may to speak to som elocals.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: I loved that London is such a huge city. You will never get bored in London since something new is going on all the time.
top3_advice: If you do not get student housing, go to London and stay at a hotel/hostel and find something while you are there so you can see the places, there are a lot of scammers in London. Since there are no exams at UCL for exchange students you will have a lot of spare time to enjoy and you can manage your own time easily to make rooms for trips. The stay is quite short since the term is only 2,5 months so it is a bit harder to make a lot of friendships but I enjoyed having a few really good friends.
other_useful_info: The weather in London was a lot better than expected. Better than in Denmark during my stay.
most_rewarding: Improving my English, getting international friends, and getting the opportunity to live in London for a couple of months.
greatest_challenge: Finding a place to live and to get enrolled. So mostly challenges getting settled in London. You also need to be aware that London is an expensive place to live in.

housing_how: I found housing on my own

cost_comparison: The cost is more or less the same as in Denmark. It is cheeper to go out though and coffee dosen't cost as much.
activities_available: None.

weekend_recommendations: To go see other places when they are in Italy, because it's cheaper then traveling there form the home country.

socializing_tips: Go out and try to talk to people at bars, maybe.
cultural_challenges: To communicate about bureaucracy in italian was difficult.
culture_appreciated: The food, the language and the people.

other_useful_info: You will have to take a lot of the same courses just in order to gain points, which in my opinion seems quite useless, but if you don't do it, you won't gain all of your ECTS points.
most_rewarding: Learning italian so well as I did, and also to have met so many lovely people from different cultures.
greatest_challenge: To learn the language. Italian has so many different times of all kinds, which can be very challenging.

registration_success: Very. I got all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: It is a very straightforward process, so don't worry about it.

teaching_comparison: It was quite similar.
courses_enrolled: EL2512 - The Tragedy of Knowledge, DR152C - Magic, Mystery, Spells and Potions in the Ancient World and AT1502 - Introduction to Anthropology 2: Questions of Diversity.
recommended_courses: I particularly enjoyed my anthropology course, as it is something that I have always wanted to study and it was very nice to finally have that opportunity.
unexpected_costs: I don't think I encountered any.
cost_comparison: Eating out for dinner or going to the movie theatre was less expensive than I had expected.
activities_available: All kinds. They have so many "societies" or clubs that it doesn't matter what you like, there is a club for you, as well.
activities_recommended: Taking trips, whether overnight or day trips. It is a great way to learn more about the culture.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely the Loch Ness and Isle of Skye. But more locally the Bullards of Buchen was breathtaking, and Duffie Park in central Aberdeen is a lovely place to spend an afternoon.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, I didn't feel that big of a difference.
socializing_tips: The Scots are very friendly and always easy to talk to. However, they might feel as though they don't want to go exploring the country with you (same as you typically don't explore the country that you live in very much).
cultural_challenges: It took a while to get used to the fact that they drive on the other side of the road, so I missed some busses because I was standing on the wrong side of the road and was very scared of getting hit by cars at first.
culture_appreciated: Their friendliness and how easy-going they are.
top3_advice: Try new things every chance you get, talk to as many people as you can and enjoy it. It will be over before you know it.
other_useful_info: The Doric accent can be hard to understand, but they are very nice and will slow their speech for you.
most_rewarding: Meeting and bonding with people from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Being so far away from all of my friends and family.
other_comments: If you have the change to go on exchange, take it.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to experience the Australian lifestyle and culture. Australia is also interesting in terms of my field of study so it was really interesting to see how they do things
info_ease: It was very easy and the uni staff are very helpful
arrival_assistance: There were two different orientations. One for all international students which was not that useful and another for just exchange students and that was very helpful and gave you all the info you needed
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to get accepted to the courses and then I could choose which tutorials I wanted to go to
registration_help: It was very easy, they have a system where you can put different tutorials in and see how the schedule turns out.
registration_success: One of the courses I wanted was full but I got one very similar to it. All the other courses I got into no problem
registration_advice: Be early so you can get the courses you want and make the best schedule
course_level: Overall the level is pretty much the same however it is a lot easier to pass as assignements and participation counts toward your grade
teaching_comparison: It was very similar. They record the lectures so most people watch from home and only come to the tutorials, so that makes the lectures a bit less interactive
courses_enrolled: Game Theory Public Economics International Trade and Investment Policy Business Valuation
recommended_courses: Depends on what you're after. I thought Game Theory was a lot harder than the other courses but it was also by far the one where i learned the most. I would recommend that if you're willing to put in the work. International Trade was also a nice course.
unexpected_costs: Getting the visa has a surprisingly high fee, otherwise it was mostly as I had expected
cost_comparison: Some things are cheaper and other more expensive. Housing is a bit more expensive as the student accomodations are privately run and cater mostly to international students. So it is more focused on making money than a "kollegie" in Denmark. Some food types are cheaper than expected. There are a lot of places doing take away sushi were you can get it relatively cheaply. Alcohol is a lot more expensive
activities_available: Many things, like sports, sailing, rockclimbing, waterskiing etc. Just make sure to check them out early so you get your worth from the membership fee
activities_recommended: I would recommend some of the outdoor activities. There are also some parties put on through the uni, but they are a bit hit and miss with some being really fun and others not being.
weekend_recommendations: Far North Queensland is the best place i've ever been. Uluru is also very nice. Do yourself the favour of staying outdoors in a swag if you go. Don't be scared of snakes and spiders. There are some really nice sport down the Flereau peninsula and Kangaroo Island(Ferry is expensive tho). A wine trip to the Mclaren Vale is a must. In general the Adelaide Hills have a lot of nice spots, go and see some koalas
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Aussies are very welcoming and friendly. Them speaking English also makes it a lot easier to get to know people.
socializing_tips: Just try and talk to people. I ended up becoming good friends with some guys from my class just because we randomly sat down at the same table on the first day and started talking. So just start talking to people
cultural_challenges: They are not as punctual which can be a bit difficult when you are from Denmark
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and laid back vibe. Everyone is just so friendly and easy to talk to. I got a lot more integrated in the local culture than I think people do in other exchange destinations.
top3_advice: Find out early what clubs you want to join so you can make the most of it. Try to talk to local aussies not just other internationals. Go out and explore the area in your free time, you can get to a lot of nice places by bus or train
other_useful_info: Uni Adelaide and UniSA are merging right now so make sure the info you have is up to date
most_rewarding: Meeting the people and integrating myself in the culture. I have met some wonderful people and had the experience of living on the other side of the globe
greatest_challenge: For me it was that all the friends I made down there are pretty hard to see in person now. It is a bit harder saying goodbye than if you were just staying in a country 3 hours away.
other_comments: I had a great semester in Adelaide and would highly recommend it

crucial_aspects: The language and the possibility to follow courses relevant to my degree at home. I wanted to practice my english in both speaking and writing. Doing a semester abroad allowed me to work with law in depth in english both in terms of everyday language as well as professional.
info_ease: I think it was quite easy getting information upon arrival. The introduction held by the University was good, but I do with they would have made a group for getting in touch with the other exchange students as it would have made it easier getting in touch with people doing the same courses as you as well as exchanging practical information.
arrival_assistance: They did two different welcomes. One of them was for all international students, which was not that good. The other was only for the people doing exchange. This was good, I wished we'd have a bit more like that. We also did a tour of campus
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I needed to fill out a lot of boxes and questions and apply for the different courses in three different programs and websites. I had then got my courses approved manually of by the university as we couldn't put in the requisites for the courses. After approval and the start of the semester they wrote back to me that I could in fact not take those courses together so I had to go through the process again and they had to manually confirm again, and by then a lot of the courses where not available anymore
registration_help: They had a "hotline" for help at the university and an email you could write to
registration_success: It took some attemps as answered above
registration_advice: I would make sure to apply for the courses early on and check with the university that you're allowed to follow chosen courses at the same time
course_level: I took some courses that were more introductory as the law system is completely different to ours. Further I took some classes of criminology as the theories can be applied better to the danish law system.
teaching_comparison: It was very similar to the way of teaching of UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Explaining Crime and Deviance Policing and Crime Control Introduction to Law Environmental Law
recommended_courses: I really liked Explaining Crime and Deviance and Policing and Crime Control as the theories can be used internationally. Further, Introduction to Law teaches you a lot by the Australian common law system as well as the history and society of Australia, which I think is a very important part of exchange.
unexpected_costs: I had to extend my visa because I stayed an extra month. This costs 2.500,00 kr. as well as you'd be applying from Australia
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive. Other than that I think in general the prices are pretty much what you'd spend in Denmark, going out to eat and experiences costs about the same as in Denmark
activities_available: A lot of different clubs were available both cultural and sports and more. I joind the sailing club for a bit. A lot of others did painting and soccer and more.
activities_recommended: There's a few activities planned for exchange students only, which I would recommend going to.
weekend_recommendations: I think the nature around Adelaide is amazing. Explore the beaches and the hills, go to Hahndorf, visit the wineries, loads of good restaurants and walks to do in the area. If you go to the national parks you'll most definitely see both koalas and kangaroos
culture_adjustment: The local culture is very laidback and very easy. It's very western so adjusting was easy. Only thing is that Australia is very much a morning country and everything closes quite early, which you need to get used to.
socializing_tips: Join the clubs!
cultural_challenges: There's a lot of international students from Asia. I lived with two very sweet girls from Sri Lanka, but heard a lot of stories from other exchange students who lived with others who had a very different culture from them, which could be a bit challenging when sharing a space.
culture_appreciated: The laid back and friendliness of the people. Everyone is so open and welcoming.
top3_advice: Most importantly to look forward and enjoy the experience. But to make sure that the courses are confirmed in their combination as well and to join a university club
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: The memories and friendships I've made
greatest_challenge: Being aware from home was sometimes difficult. But the university is good at wording that this is completely normal and have made arrangements that are easily in reach if you need someone to talk to

crucial_aspects: That they had a theatre-program, so that I would study something that I thought I could use in my career. That they spoke a language that I already knew, so that I wouldn't have a disadvantage socially with my new classmates.
info_ease: Fairly easy. The University of Agder have a lot of exchange students, so they have a lot of detailed information on their website.
arrival_assistance: A lot. The university made groups for the exchange students that were guided by local students. That way we had a secure base before we found new friends. I also had a meeting with a teater from the art-faculty, who introduced me and the other exchange students at this faculty to our building and teachers.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: As soon as I was accepted to the university it was easier. When we arrived we got a lot of help with signing up for classes, getting our student ID etc. It was a lot easier, when we were physically there.
registration_help: They have a global-lounge with people always ready to assist you. That is the fastest way to get help – the office can be a bit slow in replying to your e-mails.
registration_success: I ended up with the classes I wanted, which was great. They did though make a mistake in my acceptance (said I wasn't qualified to take a theatre course). It took some time to fix the mistake, which was unfortunate and made it very stressful.
registration_advice: Make sure you are qualified for the courses that you apply for – they say that they "recommend" some qualifications, but what they really mean is that you need them to be accepted.
course_level: The levels were fine. Some things were easier and some were more challenging.
teaching_comparison: A lot more practical. A bit less structured.
courses_enrolled: Physical Theatre and Theatre Space + Communication, Media and Planning.
recommended_courses: Anything in the art-department!
unexpected_costs: I already knew that Norway is an expensive country, so nothing really came as a surprise. Maybe the price of alcohol – especially at restaurants.
cost_comparison: Books for classes were a bit more expensive than I thought. I was prepared for everything to be a bit more expensive though.
activities_available: Outdoor activities, traditional sports, choir, student pub, quiz-night etc.
activities_recommended: Quiz-night! So fun. Also ESN trips – we went to Preikestolen, which was an amazing experience even though it rained a lot.
weekend_recommendations: Oslo, Bergen and Preikestolen. Some of the other exchange students also went further north in Norway, which was supposed to be really nice. Kristiansand also have some amazing escape-rooms, which are definitely worth a visit, and a cinema-club called "Cinemateket". For concerts go to Vaktbua, for theatre go to Kilden.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. There were small differences, but Norway and Denmark is very similar.
socializing_tips: Invite them over to your place. Say yes, to everything you're invited to.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find anything challenging.
culture_appreciated: The outdoor activities because of the country's nature and their traditions during Christmas time.
top3_advice: 1) To have a class or a regular social activity with the locals, makes it easier to make norwegian friends. I was lucky to be the only exchange student in my class. 2) This is a semester of "yes" – Say yes to every offer you get, be open to new impressions and experiences. 3) Prioritise activities with new friends instead of big group-tours.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: Becoming friends with both locals and other exchange students.
greatest_challenge: Getting to experience as much of the country and the culture as possible while also prioritizing school.

So she let me know it weren't possibel for them to share courses and that I could chooses either, then she would forward me.

I also recived help in relation to extrendet time for the exames cause I'm dyslectic, and it were so easy I just sended my documentation to their admistrative office, and they ensured that it were sat up in all my exames.

But after the beginign you have 2 weeks to change courses, and/or try out other coruses. it is better to sign up to courses and then later drop out before the exames than having to few courses. The professors keep on going with their cours the first two weeks even though new peopel are joining. Some courses are really intense in the beginning of the semester and ends fast and others begin later in the semester.
registration_help: And the exchange coordinators are very sweet at helping you registering with to the right once, or help you find a course closer to one of the canceld once. You can choose both graduate and undergraduate.

courses_enrolled: The undergraguate courses: VKS1206140 Project Management INJFU06030 Icelandic nature ÞMN0276110 Peoples and Cultures of the Circumpolar North FSÁ0176110 Social Psychology The Mastercourse: GNR1076210 Governance of Natural Resources at the Poles
recommended_courses: The course Icelandic nature were a really good introduction to Iceland, which were really nice when traveling around, also for understanding some of the processes going on in the landscape. and to get familar with the animals. I also really recomend the course "Peoples and Cultures of the Circumpolar North" cause it gives a good perspective on the north and indigenous nordic development, which is often forgotten.
unexpected_costs: I brought a youth (15-25) year seasonal pass for the local swimminpool, which is really recommended, it costed 1055 DKK. I also brought a seasonal skiing pass for 1600DKK Which I also were really happy for.
cost_comparison: The alcohol were really expensive, same with some vegstabels. You relly have to look oiut for some items are crasy expensive and others can exchange thoughse so just keep an eye out for that. i lived without missing anyhthing, and were eating out some times, this is reflected in my personal spendings. So it is perfectly possibel to live cheeper than I did.
activities_available: The universty had a GYM which were open if you get a smartkey from the university. This were really used by a lot of the exchange students and really a nice add. So you could study all day at there luxurious libary and then take a gym break. They also have a student union, which were having some activities. Where you as exchange student sign up to the union fitting your studies the best.
activities_recommended: I really rocomend the swimminpool, as a meetup place, either just for chilling, fun or swimming exercises. It is a local oasis even in the wintertimes. I also recommend practise some skiing, I were happy to learn how to snowboard on there hill, by borrowing a snowboard and shoes, or you can by some cheep used once in hartex or facebook marketplace. Otherrwise I know a lot from our exchange team signed up for local sports teams like volleyball or boxing, which they where happy for.
weekend_recommendations: i really recomend renting a car and going on roadtrips around the country, there is great natural diffrences allwoer the island, and to have so long time there, is a uniq possibility to experience all it's sites. My personal favorites are the arctic henges in the north east and a puffin island in the east corner "Borgarfjarðarhöfn". you can also go on skiing adventures if you befriend the peopel at the ski renting place.
culture_adjustment: Peopel living in Iceland are quite simmilar to Danes, they might just be a littel more afraid of breaking codex. crucial_aspects: Going outside of Europe.
info_ease: Easy. The University sends a lot of e-mails before arriving, and there are services on campus that help new international students with arrival, accommodation, studying in Canada etc.
arrival_assistance: You receive a lot of assistance. Mostly through e-mail. Going to the international services at campus in-person is also a great help, they will tell you where to go, what to do, and how to get started with studying in Canada.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You register via the university's own portal (BearTracks).
registration_help: You receive e-mails prior to registration that explain how to register with videos showing the process / what to do. There is a lot of information on the University of Alberta website, and you can see course descriptions prior to registering. The course descriptions are not always very good though.
registration_success: Successful. As an exchange student, you do not have first priority. This goes to the domestic students. However, a lot of students drop courses, so spots become available at the beginning of the term, and you can easily get the courses you want after this period. I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Save the courses you want and pay attention to your e-mail. It will say if someone drops the course, and then you can register if you are fast enough. Plan your courses so you don't have a heavy workload throughout the semester.
course_level: You take undergraduate (BA) courses, even as a master's student. The level is not very different from Denmark. Same amount of reading. There are midterms, which is not common in Danish programs or law courses. Exams are shorter. Depending on the course, the exams can be very similar to Danish law exams (fact-patterns) or very different (multiple choice). A lot of work throughout the semester with assignments that count towards your grade. Participation also matters in some courses so your grade is not only based on a final exam. It can be hard to get used to the common-law system at first.
teaching_comparison: The courses are much more seminar based. Less group work or discussion, but this differs from every course. The professor will usually spend most of class presenting with no breaks.
courses_enrolled: Public International Law, Administrative Law, Environmental Law, Canadian Human Rights Law, Professionalism & Ethics
recommended_courses: Public International Law and Canadian Human Rights Law! Both are very good courses with great professors.
unexpected_costs: Mandatory health care from the University (200 CAD).
cost_comparison: Housing is expensive. Eating out is cheaper compared to Denmark.
activities_available: Several clubs to join. Most of them promote themselves during the first week of the term. A lot of sports clubs. Gym is free and very good. All of the university's sports games are free to attend as a student (hockey, basketball etc.)
activities_recommended: Go to a hockey game. Go skiing. Explore campus and the city.
weekend_recommendations: Go out. A lot of students go to downtown in the weekends. See the nature. Visit the big cities like Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, etc. All are very good.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. Meet other international students, they all want to make friends. Canadians are very friendly and enjoy talking.
socializing_tips: Be social. Just talk to people. In residence, at class, and around campus. It is not hard to make friends as long as you try.
cultural_challenges: There is a homeless crisis in Canada. You will see more homeless people on the streets than you do in Denmark. They are mostly harmless, but it is something you have to get used to.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness. Canadians are very open, talkative, and nice people. They enjoy smalltalk.
top3_advice: Live on campus - this is the best way to meet people and have a good experience. Be social and outgoing. Join clubs. Do sports. Travel if you can and explore Canada.
other_useful_info: Dress well. It gets cold.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all over the world. Traveling.
greatest_challenge: Getting used to the common law system.

Also, Almería is the sunniest city in Andalucía, however, that was not the case upon arrival (but the locals said it was odd too that the weather had changed so drastically)
overall_comments: Overall, I've had a good experience studying abroad. The teachers usually have been helpful and understanding towards the Erasmus students - some more than others. It has been quite difficult interacting with the local students as many of them did not seem to want to engage with the foreign students - many Erasmus students held on tightly to one another. I was fortunate to meet locals outside of the university, which was a great advantage regarding further developing language skills.

arrival_assistance: As previously stated, the personnel of the host university were helpful. I had to change some courses, and one of the ladies at the office was really helpful and provided a step-by-step guideline for me to follow as I was going to change my courses.
arrival_comments: I did not have any issues with the orientation nor the assistance at the host institution.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

It has been quite difficult interacting with the local students as many of them did not seem to want to engage with the foreign students - many Erasmus students held on tightly to one another. I was fortunate to meet locals outside of the university, which was a great advantage regarding further developing language skills.
registration_process: I got to the office and had to draw a number in order to enter the office (you also booked your appointment online prior to arriving at the university). I entered the office when it was my turn, and the person responsible for my registration asked me whether I wanted to it in English or Spanish. As I had done all the work prior to arriving, the process only lasted 5 minutes. He gave me some information about the university, the campus site, where to find a doctor and so on.
registration_help: The person responsible gave me a map of the campus site and numbers and names of the hospitals and doctors of Almería in case I needed it.
registration_success: I was successful in registering for the classes I wanted - HOWEVER, what the university fails to tell the incoming students is that a lot of the courses overlap (it is quite a common problem, and one of the issues they fix the most). So, in order to avoid that you need to look CAREFUL on the horario provided on their website - there are both theoretical and practical lessons, and these tend to overlap but usually that is NOT a problem (ask the professor of course - most of them knows that it is a recurrent problem)
registration_advice: Please fill out all of the information prior to arriving, it will make the process a whole lot easier AND less stressful.
academics_comments: Overall, I've had a good experience studying abroad. The teachers usually have been helpful and understanding towards the Erasmus students - some more than others. It has been quite difficult interacting with the local students as many of them did not seem to want to engage with the foreign students - many Erasmus students held on tightly to one another. I was fortunate to meet locals outside of the university, which was a great advantage regarding further developing language skills.
course_level: Some of the classes had a quite low level compared to that of Danish universities. I would say some of the courses could compare to the level of Danish high schools.
teaching_comparison: In Spain, you do not read as much as you do in Denmark - typically, you would just take notes from what the teacher is saying. Sometimes, there are a few exercises - but that is rarely the case. It seems more indoctrinating than in Denmark as the teacher speaks and the students take notes in the way that it is often not that interactive.
courses_enrolled: 1) Latin American Literature II 2) Business communication in a foreign language: English 3) History and culture of Hispanic countries 4) Critical analysis of discourse in Spanish 5) Specialized use of Spanish
recommended_courses: I can highly recommend the course: Latin American Literature. The professor is absolutely amazing, and really takes the Erasmus students into account as the local students at times speak a little too fast and too low to hear - also, took great pride into knowing where everyone was from (we also had a poetry event in different languages). Also, the Critical analysis course has been great as well - the professors teaching the courses have been really welcoming and friendly.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: The food in Andalucía typically is a bit less expensive than that of the capital, Madrid. Also, in generally, housing and such is cheaper.
activities_available: There has been plenty of clubs to attend (I did not) - these were also shown at the introduction day.
activities_recommended: If you want to broaden your network, while studying abroad, go on the trips that the ESN office provides. It makes your stay less lonely, and you'll make new friends, or acquaintances, that way.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the nearby cities on the weekends; Granada, Córdoba, Cádiz, Sevilla. There is PLENTY to see. Also, in the region of Almería itself. Semana Santa (Easter) was a real treat to experience in Almería as it is something that the locals prepare for almost a year. It is worth staying in town during that period.
culture_adjustment: I would say it was quite easy, also given that I befriended Spanish people as well. Although, the siesta is still not my thing.
socializing_tips: Instead of sitting with all of the Erasmus students all the time, try to sit close to the local students. Also, attend the events they go to at uni (in my case: poetry event) - it helped me speaking more with some of my fellow students. Importantly, a simple 'buenos días' or 'hola' in the morning or just in general when someone enters the classroom goes a long way.
cultural_challenges: I did find the siesta really challenging, also that the local kiosks are closed during those hours. Furthermore, that Sunday indeed is a holy day in Spain - shops and everything alike are closed, bear that in mind.
culture_appreciated: I love that they are really welcoming and always say 'hi' or 'goodbye', or in the Almerian case 'hasta luego'/'see you later' although you might not see them later or ever again for that matter.
top3_advice: 1) Get yourself involved with other Erasmus students (but bear in mind many do not speak Spanish) 2) Go on the trips, which are organized by the ESN office, or by the Sports Department 3) Have fun while studying there - it is not supposed to kill your joy for studying
other_useful_info: It will be difficult in the beginning - adjusting to the language, the surroundings, and the people. But it'll be all worth it in the end.
most_rewarding: I guess that would be my Literature teacher - she was really the main reason that I had a great stay at UAL. She truly made a difference for me - I always looked forward to her classes.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge must have been when I wanted to change my courses as they overlapped. That was chaotic, but it all turned out well in the end.
other_comments: I do not recommend anyone to take the course 'Usos Especializados del Español' - this course was truly confusing and not very intellectually simulating. The local students did not understand the concept or idea of the course very well either. Also, the teacher was nice, however, she did not take Erasmus students into account so it was difficult to attend her classes.
