crucial_aspects: For me it was first and foremost Spain because of the language, but I chose the city because of the size (a mix between a big and a small city) and the area and the nature around.
info_ease: It was relatively easy to access. But the information comes from a lot of sources (UCPH, the host university, Erasmus etc) and you have to fill in information and upload documents on different websites (campus virtual and aula virtual from the University of Almería, and also mobility online). This can be quite confusing both in the proces of applying and before arrival.
arrival_assistance: I went to the international office a couple of times to get some help with choosing subjects at the university. They were nice and helpful and I ended up choosing subjects that fit my schedule.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You choose the subjects before arriving, but you don't know the timetables. If you choose subjects from different semesters, you risk them overlapping and will have to change some of them. It was a bit confusing because you won't know the updated timetables for the subjects before you arrive, and the proces of changing was a bit unclear - in my experience, it wasn't clear if you had to talk to the teacher of the subject you wanted to change to before changing (and then some teachers said that they didn't know how many available spots they had in their class), or if you could just change it in your OLA. If you need to change subjects, you will most likely have a period of time where you don't have access to the subjects you want to change to in your aula virtual, which means you cannot see the homework, messages from the teacher etc. So you have to ask the students in the class to be added to WhatsApp group to know about changes in schedule etc.
registration_help: You can go to the international office at the university, but you have to make an appointment online, and the proces for doing that is very unclear on the host university's website. I had to make an appointment a couple of times because I needed to change some subjects, and every time I had to spend so much time just finding the link for making the appointment.
registration_success: I ended up registering for 5 classes that didn't overlap, but it was a bit difficult to find classes during the day that fit with each other. One of the classes I changed to ended up being very difficult if you're not a native Spanish speaker, which I would have liked to know in the beginning before choosing it and not being able to change. I just passed the subject because I did all the assignments and presentations during the semester, but the exam in itself is really, really hard. It's called Fundamentos para el Análisis y el Uso de la Lengua Española and I wouldn't recommend it to any erasmus student unless you're a native spanish speaker.
registration_advice: If possible, check the timetables for the subjects before choosing in the first place. It is possible to change (and maybe you'll have to anyway because you don't like the subject when you try it) but I think it would have spared me a lot of time and stress in the beginning (when everything is a bit confusing already) if I hadn't had to change because of the schedule.
course_level: In my experience as a Danish student, the work load in most of my subjects was much bigger than the work load in Denmark. Also, you don't know what the expectations are or how much you have to do to pass a subject or get a specific grade, so you would rather do everything than to risk not passing, and this ends up taking a lot of time. I had 5 subjects of 6 ECTS each, but some of them had a bigger workload than subjects I've had at UCPH of 15 ECTS. It's very different from subject to subject though. Furthermore, all my courses are in Spanish, and it's very different how much the teachers expect from you if you're not a native Spanish speaker. I talked to erasmus students that were able to do all their assignments in English, didn't have to do presentations, didn't have to take the same exams etc. so it's very different.
teaching_comparison: In a lot of subjects, it's the teacher speaking to the students without dialogue. It's basically about listening to what the teacher tells you and writing it down, so you can study it for the exams. You cannot bring anything to help you to the exams, not even your notes (some teachers allowed me to take a dictionary because of the language barrier, but others didn't), so you have to remember a lot of stuff by heart which is very different from the way they teach at UCPH. I was very scared of this beforehand but I'd say it's definitely doable if you go to the classes and then do some intense studying before the exams.
courses_enrolled: Introducción a la Literatura Fundamentos para el Análisis y el Uso de la Lengua Española Historia de la Lingüística Análisis Crítico del Discurso en Español Literatura Hispanoamericana II
recommended_courses: If you're interested in literature, I would very highly recommend taking Literatura Hispanoamericana II with the teacher Isabel. She's so kind to erasmus students (and all her students in general) and very passionate about her teaching. I love her approach to learning, which is more about actually being curious and getting to know and read a lot of amazing literature than learning a whole semester's curriculum. She does the exam at the end of the semester because she has to. You also have to read a novel in Spanish and do an oral exam about it in the middle of the semester, but if you know some Spanish it's definitely doable, and Isabel won't be to hard on the erasmus students. Isabel also teaches the subject Introducción a la Literatura which is a more general introduction to literature, but it's a good subject to take because the work load is not bad at all (and it's first year). I wouldn't recommend taking Fundamentos para el Análisis y el Uso de la Lengua Española if you're not a native Spanish speaker. The teacher Yolanda expects the exact same from the erasmus students as from the native Spanish students, so her subject's quite difficult to pass. If you do choose it, it's important to go to class because she takes 'asistencia'. I took Historia de la Lingüística and Análisis Crítico del Discurso en Español because they corresponded with a subject I would have had to take in Denmark (Kommunikation og formidling, 10 ECTS). Historia de la Lingüística is a good subject to take because the teacher Antonio Daniel Fuentes González is very nice with erasmus students and gives good grades if you do all of the assignments (in groups) during the semester. I did 3 out of 4 of the prácticas during the semester, and the final work (which counts as the 'exam' because the subject doesn't have a written exam of 2-3 hours in the university), and that was enough for getting a good grade. It's also important going to class. At first, Análisis Crítico del Discurso en Español was a bit hard because the teacher Rosario Lisciandro seemed unfriendly and to be honest a bit scary. Also apparently there was another subject in the semester before that was 'necessary' to follow this subject, so we were asked to read a whole theory book of 200-something pages from the past semester when we arrived. I ended up not finishing the book and it was fine, so don't stress too much about that. The subject is in 4th year, and therefore there are no more classes after the Easter holidays. Another pro of the subject is that there is no exam, 'only' a bunch of written assignments during the semester (but these had to be quite long and the tasks were sometimes complicated). Going to class counts quite a lot. I wouldn't recommend the subject because of the specific teacher, but it seemed like he doesn't usually teach this subject so maybe it will be someone else next year. He also talked about changing the 'exam' to an oral one, so maybe that will change too. It may be hard to avoid taking this subject if you're going on exchange on 4th semester and need 2 subjects that correspond with Kommunikation og Formidling.
unexpected_costs: I bought a bicycle which got stolen, so I had to buy another one. But later my insurance covered that. Don't place your bicycle on the street (especially not by the beach over night), even if it's locked with a strong lock. Apart from that nothing.
cost_comparison: Food is definetely way cheaper than expected, both in the supermarket and when going out to eat. They have free tapas every time you order a beer at a bar or a restaurant, so you could have 3 beers and 3 tapas for 8 euros. Also housing is way cheaper than in Copenhagen. I paid 3000 DKKK (around 400 euro) for half an apartment in the Zapillo with a view over the sea and 20 meters walk from the beach, which was amazing. I know a lot of people that paid less, 200 euro-300 euro for a room for example.
activities_available: The UAL have sports facilities which I know a lot of people used very often, I didn't myself but you can buy a very cheap sports card for the whole semester and then go swimming, to the fitness center etc. ESN Almería (the erasmus student organisation) also organizes a lot of activities all the time, so you have a lot of opportunities to meet new people.
activities_recommended: Just try and participate in the activities that the ESN organizes, especially in the beginning, even if it doesn't seem like your favourite activity. You meet a lot of nice people through that and then you can start organizing things on your own with them. A lot of erasmus students go to the beach a lot so you can always meet someone there.
weekend_recommendations: Almería is a cute city with some cultural stuff going on. Visit the Alcazaba, the art museums, go to the theater, to Classijazz for concerts or poetry, to La Guajira for concerts, language exchange events and flamenco nights. Go out a lot to have tapas in all of the different tapas bars in the city center, especially Casa Puga, El Quinto Toro and Bar Calle de Las Tiendas, or in the Zapillo, La Cala or Café Paris. There are some nice morrocan restaurants too. Go to the beautiful natural park Cabo de Gata (either by car or take the bus to San Jose and hike back to the lighthouse in Cabo de Gata). Bicycle to Aguadulce. Go out and enjoy the nightlife, Almería has a bunch of clubs in the city center (a lot with reggaeton but also some that plays techno - check out Palo Santo for that, or keep an eye out for events in Complejo Chaman/Chain Club which is located a bit outside the city). For bars I'd recommend Kutre, which is a fun place. In general, keep an eye out for festivals (Solazo fest in spring/summer) and concerts taking place in and outside the city. You also have the possibility to go outside the city for weekend trips - to Malaga, Granada (but book tickets for Alhambra some weeks in advance) and Sevilla. There are buses that connect the cities but a lot of times it's much easier and faster to go with blablacar.
culture_adjustment: I found it very easy. It's different to Denmark but more in a way that revolves around the weather and dinner times, so I didn't find it hard to adjust.
socializing_tips: It's difficult if you don't know Spanish. If you do, you can definitely talk to them after class or sit down next to someone in class. In some subjects you have to do group work with them which is a good opportunity to get to talk. In general, they're were sweet and willing to talk if you start the conversation. But a lot of them have had their friends and their class for years and might not be too interested in getting to know new people.
cultural_challenges: The challenges were definitely more about the ways of teaching in the uni and the bigger workload than differences in culture.
culture_appreciated: I think the whole vibe is more chill and relaxing. The locals are not as busy (or maybe they are, they're just not acting as busy) as the people that live in Copenhagen. This was a big plus for me. People are really sweet and welcoming and not afraid to talk to strangers.
top3_advice: 1) Just do it honestly. It's an amazing opportunity to go somewhere completely new and exciting to just study and make new friends (and the erasmus grant is a big economic support). It's going to be scary and confusing at first but it WILL get better and easier and in the end you'll be so happy you did it. 2) If you're there to learn the language, it doesn't come by itself just because you're staying in Spain. It definitely helps listening to Spanish all the time, going to class etc., but you also have to speak to native Spanish speakers. It can be really scary but the more you do it, the less scary it will be. Just remember that people don't see you as stupid if you make mistakes - they see it as amazing that you're able to say and understand someting in their language. 3) Enjoy all the things outside of uni as much as possible. Even if you have a lot of stuff to do for uni, try to make time to have fun. I was surprised about the good grades most of my teachers gave in the end - don't worry too much about not passing. If you're in doubt, ask some of your class mates in the beginning (preferably before changing to the subject for good) about the level of the different subjects you're about to choose. Some of them have taken the subjects before or know someone that has, and they can give you an idea of the expectations.
other_useful_info: - Go on idealista to find accommodation (and face time with your land lord before if possible) and - Ask the teacher about the chances of passing the subject as an erasmus student before choosing their subject - Ask your teacher about bringing a dictionary to the exams - Choose classes that are scheduled during the day - Try to go to class as much as possible, the exams will be so much easier in the end. And it's nice to have an everyday life with classes during the day and to be off during the afternoon/nights. - Take notes in class, just write everything (that you possibly can) that the teacher says. Ask your class mates for notes and use the website wuolah when studying for the exams - Ask your class mates to add you in the whatsapp group in every subject. Every subjects has their own chat group in which changes in timetable, homework etc. will be written - Go to the emergency room in the public hospital if you get sick. It's free with the blue health card
most_rewarding: Getting better at the language, meeting a bunch of amazing people that I would like to visit in their home countries and in general just living in a place where the sun (almost) always shines (when it's not crazy windy which it is sometimes in Almería) and where you can always go to the beach or out for dinner or tapas without paying a lot.
greatest_challenge: Overall, it all went really well. If I were to change something, I would have pushed myself more to talk with native Spanish speakers. It can be hard in the beginning if you don't feel like your level is that good (but it will get better though no matter what).

I never experienced a classroom to be such a welcoming and safe space, where you get acknowledged of bringing your whole person–your feelings, thoughts and what affects you in this moment of time. Tess is almost not a teacher, but more like a moderator, and the course was really enlightening in many aspects.
unexpected_costs: Food is more expensive than what I assumed. More or less like Danish prices. Maybe a bit cheaper eating out, which I did a lot as my kitchen was so small.
cost_comparison: I bought a bike, which was cheap and almost never used public transportation. The city is quite small and it's easy to get around.
activities_available: I used CREA, which is a cultural organisation offering creative courses to affordable prices for students. There's also one for sports, but I don't know the name. I also started a knitting club at my student housing.
activities_recommended: I took a course called Visual Inventions at CREA. We painted the east tunnel in the Centraal Station, which was really fun and a nice way to meet new people!
weekend_recommendations: Go to the sea, buy a museumskaart (then you can visit almost every museum in the NL as many times as you like), visit the markets and explore the city. Maybe do some day trips to nearby cities, but also cool to just chill in the city. Remember to relax and recharge.
culture_adjustment: Easy, the culture is really similar to Denmark.
socializing_tips: It's hard to get local friends, so don't count on it. I actually mostly socialized with local students at the CREA course.
cultural_challenges: I can't think of any... maybe that you don't really have to learn their language to get by? You can easily stay in the NL for a semester without learning much Dutch, which some people would find a pity.
culture_appreciated: Everyone's so good at talking English, so language barrier is not really a problem. I really appreciated how openminded and easygoing people in Amsterdam are like, sometimes they sing openly on the street, they never use curtains even though they have enormous windows facing right to the canals and they also want to help you.
top3_advice: Enjoy the extra free time and explore the city's many offers, especially the arts and cultures, but remember to do things in your own pace and find time to relax too. It's okay not to socialize all the time. Also, remember you don't need to be perfect, instead be brave, try new things and practice whatever you can get better at – this is such a nice opportunity to do so.
other_useful_info: Ask another exchange students if you have any doubts or troubles. Everyone is more or less in the same situation as you and can relate and probably also help you.
most_rewarding: Practicing my oral skills and feeling an improvement – it gradually gets easier. Of course, also meeting new people and nourishing new friendships.
greatest_challenge: Working with my performance anxiety and having a traumatic experience with one teacher. But I found a good way to get on top of it.

crucial_aspects: Most crucial of all for me was the ranking of the university. I chose the University of Amsterdam because of its well-renowned Anthropology faculty. Because of its high ranking, it opens up more opportunities for me with regards to where i want to take my Master's degree.
overall_comments: In terms of social aspects, i had an incredible experience. The university provided a much more multicultural student environment, and a lot more engaging teaching methods, as students were typically expected to take over the class for at least one of the modules. The student accommodation was great. Although quite expensive (around 600 Euros per month), it didn't bother me too much, as the quality was good - plus the price would be similar in Copenhagen anyway. A significant drawback for me, however, was the fact that one of my lecturers had to go on sick leave in the middle of a course - which is fair enough of course. But the university left us in the dark for around 2 months, with no updates regarding the course, although they expressed that we would be allowed to finish it anyway. After these 2 months, the course was taken up by 4 different lecturers who - albeit understandably - lacked knowledge of the curriculum. More transparency from the university's administration, and more communication between the different teachers would've been appreciated.
info_ease: Incredibly easy. A lot of practical information was provided by our landlords (DeKey), and the student help-desks at the university helped me a lot. My fellow students in my accommodation were also quick to let people know about practical matters.
arrival_assistance: We were given a tour of the university, taking us through the different departments, showing us where to get coffee or how to work the printers. We had several zoom meetings with general information in the beginning as well. I knew most of this just from reading the university's website, which is quite easy to navigate as well.

You have to be quick to get it sorted, because if you're not registered, you won't be able to apply for housing through the university - which makes things a lot easier in terms of finding accommodation. You had to upload a passport photo, transcript of records, general info about your studies, etc.
registration_help: There were several help-desks you could call or write e-mails to. And the website was very helpful as well.
registration_success: Although i logged in immediately once registration opened, most of the classes i wanted was taken. However, there was still many interesting things to register for. I put myself on the waiting list for some courses, which soon opened up as it seemed people had 'over-registrated' (picked several more courses than allowed). I ended up with some really interesting courses despite all of this.
registration_advice: Be quick. Have an online atomic clock ready in another window, so you can click on the link the second it opens. I was 6 seconds late, and far behind in the queue. Although i presume many are already familiar with this sort of thing from buying concert or festival tickets online.
academics_comments: In terms of social aspects, i had an incredible experience. The university provided a much more multicultural student environment, and a lot more engaging teaching methods, as students were typically expected to take over the class for at least one of the modules. The student accommodation was great. Although quite expensive (around 600 Euros per month), it didn't bother me too much, as the quality was good - plus the price would be similar in Copenhagen anyway. A significant drawback for me, however, was the fact that one of my lecturers had to go on sick leave in the middle of a course - which is fair enough of course. But the university left us in the dark for around 2 months, with no updates regarding the course, although they expressed that we would be allowed to finish it anyway. After these 2 months, the course was taken up by 4 different lecturers who - albeit understandably - lacked knowledge of the curriculum. More transparency from the university's administration, and more communication between the different teachers would've been appreciated.
course_level: Some were very challenging. Especially as i haven't written academically in English before. One course was especially difficult, which made sense, as it was for third-years only and 12 ECTS instead of the usual 6 for elective courses. The university values critical thinking and active engagement, so the expectations of the student participation in classes are much higher than in Copenhagen. However, I enjoyed this very much, and i learnt a lot, both within and outside the classroom during my stay.
teaching_comparison: It was a lot more engaging. At times the student-teacher hierarchy dissipated completely, especially during presentations, because students were expected to facilitate discussions afterwards, which often involved the teacher in a 'student' role. This created a much more equitable class environment.
courses_enrolled: Brazil: Democracy, Citizenship, and Culture Political Anthropology: The Norm, Violence, and Resistance Anthropology of the Middle East Education & International Development
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of the above to be honest. Political Anthropology has one of the most interesting curriculums i've ever come across. It teaches students how to engage politically with their field of study, and to not be afraid of taking a stance as an anthropologist. The freedom to choose your own subject for the final essay was great aswell. It challenged me to be more independent in my research process. Anthropology of the Middle East is a short course, that doesn't do justice to the scope of study it encapsulates. However, i would recommend this to everyone who has been subjected to the narrative of a 'War on Terror'. An eye-opening course, which invites the student to critically reflect on their Western gaze, without portraying cultural difference as something insurmountable. The Brazil course was especially interesting due to its political relevancy, and we engaged with Bolsonaro quite a bit throughout the course. However, there was also plenty of time to focus on the indigenous peoples of Brazil, and the teaching-team was perfectly composed to facilitate both of these perspectives. Educaton & International Development was the shortest course i took (lasting 3-4 weeks), however, it was very interesting as it introduces students to alternative pedagogies and draws them in as co-creators of the course. The empirical subject changes every year, so the course remains ever-relevant as well.
unexpected_costs: I spent a lot of money on food delivery during the exam periods. In terms of the nightlife of Amsterdam it's very expensive as well. Not just the drinks, but the tickets - it seemed the whole city was on a ticketing system at times. Price ranges vary a lot, so you can find some on the cheap - they ranged from 5 to 40 Euros in my experience.
cost_comparison: Transport is very, very cheap if you get a bike. You can also rent one quite cheaply through Swapfiets. A bike will get you anywhere in town in 40 minutes tops, and the infrastructure is suprisingly superior to Copenhagen in terms of cycling. You are much safer as a cyclist, as there is always some form of barriers protecting you from traffic. It is also much better designed for long-distance cycling, as you never really have to stop at a red light.
activities_available: We had a student bar - CREA - with cheap prices. The building was also used for band practice, dance lessons, theater, etc. And i believe it is quite easy to sign up.
activities_recommended: They have the largest flea market in Europe up in Amsterdam Noord every saturday. Many interesting artists are exhibited in the city's museums (Hieronymus Bosch recommended). Rokin Subway Station has an exhibition of all the things they dug up during its construction lined up in a huge glass box along its escalators. The city has many parks with excellent facilities for recreational sports.
weekend_recommendations: See above.
culture_adjustment: Extremely easy. Locals oftentimes told me that Amsterdam is not really the Netherlands, in the sense that everyone speaks English, and is from outside the country. The place is so multicultural that you can never really feel out of place - at least i never did. Besides, being from Copenhagen it's easy to adjust to the mode of transportation - cycling - and the prices - seemingly extortionary just like home.
socializing_tips: Leave your own culture behind. Don't try to impose your own values on others. Don't expect everything to work as intended. Don't be too nice - it can come across as boring. In terms of the Dutch locals, they are somewhat more reserved, and therefore harder to get to know, but we are used to that back home i guess.
cultural_challenges: Language - I found Dutch discernible when reading, but absolutely alien when they were speaking. A very phlegmy language.
culture_appreciated: The vibrancy, outspokenness, visual aesthetics, and the fact that it was never really singular but multifaceted as a culture.
top3_advice: Again, don't be too nice, don't be afraid to step outside of your comfort zone, and be sure to structure your time to meet the deadlines - at the end of the day, you're there to study, and if you engage with your responsibilities as a student you will have a very fruitful learning experience.
other_useful_info: Be careful not to get sucked into 'monocultural social groups'. There were two huge social groups of English and Latin American students respectively, who very rarely engaged with people outside of their groups. I got to know people from both sections, and although they were more comfortable in the beginning, i felt sorry for them in the end - as they seemed to miss out on the most vital part of exchange for me--engaging with other cultures.
most_rewarding: The social life - i met people from all over - From Japan to South Africa, Canada, Australia, Argentina - even someone from Monaco and Luxembourg.
greatest_challenge: Structuring the time and meeting deadlines.

crucial_aspects: It was my second exchange and I wanted to focus more on it being a good university and having some interesting courses than being able to do a lot of exploring, which was the case for University of Amsterdam. I've been to Amsterdam before and I like the city.
overall_comments: I enjoyed my exchange, but during the whole semester we had restrictions due to covid, which made it more difficult to meet up with people.

registration_success: Got the things I wanted.

academics_comments: I enjoyed my exchange, but during the whole semester we had restrictions due to covid, which made it more difficult to meet up with people.
course_level: I would say the level is a lot like UCPH. One semester consists of 3 blocks, the first 2 are 8 weeks (7 of classes and 1 exam week) and the last is 4 weeks (3 of classes and 1 exam week). Be aware that there are no breaks between the blocks.
teaching_comparison: I would say it was a lot like UPCH in the way of teaching, except you have to work more for the ECTS. Plus they have less tutorials.
courses_enrolled: Block 1: Condensed Matter 2 : 6 ECTS Condensed Matter Theory 1 : 3 ECTS General Relativity : 6 ECTS Block 2: Condensed Matter Theory 2 : 3 ECTS Quantum Optics : 6 ECTS Block 3: Condensed Matter Theory 3 : 3 ECTS Programming c++ : 3 ETCS
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Condensed Matter Theory 1+2+3, because we had a very good teacher. But it was a lot of work for 3 ECTS.
unexpected_costs: I bought the museumcard, which gives access to a lot of museums in The Netherlands. I spent money on going on day trips to other cities in The Netherlands, but I also took a trip to Belgium and Munich. I went to cafe and restaurants quite often.
cost_comparison: Local transport is quite expensive, so I rented a Swapfiets bike.
activities_available: The ESN have a lot of social events during the semester, both day trips, weekends trips, a social event at uni and so on. Other than that, you can register at Universum (fitness center) or some of the different sport clubs.
activities_recommended: I really enjoyed visiting a lot of the museums, so if you are interested in that I can recommend the museumcard (but be aware not all museums/art gallaries are included).
weekend_recommendations: I enjoyed going on some day trips to see other cities in The Netherlands. I can also recommend meeting up with a friend and go for a walk around the city or go to a cafe (they have lots of them).
culture_adjustment: I would say it is very similar to the Danish culture in a lot of ways, so I didn't encounter any clashes.
socializing_tips: Most of the people I spent a lot of time with (that I didn't live with) I met through the ESN introduction week, so I would definitely recommend signing up for that.
cultural_challenges: I don't know. I would say living in Amsterdam is not that different from living in Copenhagen.
culture_appreciated: The Dutch have a very strong freedom feeling, which is really interesting in a lot of ways. It was in some ways clashing a bit with the covid restrictions. I was a bit surprised about a lot of peoples resistance to the restrictions.
top3_advice: Get or rent a bike! Bring a good rain jacket and umbrella. Try some dutch traditional food like Stroopwafles and some dutch traditions.
other_useful_info: I don't think so.
most_rewarding: I met some really nice people and learnt a lot academically.
greatest_challenge: There was most female exchange students in Amsterdam and as a physics student, it was weird being in such a shifted gender distribution.

unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs per say. However, prepare for spending a lot on fun, activities, cafes, restaurants, trips etc., as Amsterdam and The Netherlands have a lot to offer.
cost_comparison: Food and restaurants are a bit cheaper than Denmark. Besides that, the prices a roughly the same, tilting to the "a bit cheaper" side.
activities_available: ESN is a club for international student, and they also host an intro week. If you want to meet other internationals from across study-programs, i recommend signing up.
activities_recommended: Go on trips in the Netherlands and the rest of Europe. Train-tickets (if booked in advance) are significantly cheaper than Denmark, and Amsterdam is well-connected to other cities.
weekend_recommendations: Go on trips, see it all.
culture_adjustment: easy, the Dutch culture is very similar to Danish culture.
socializing_tips: The Dutch students are, sadly, quite reserved. It is hard to become friends with them outside the classroom.
cultural_challenges: they do not refrigerate their eggs in the supermarket.
culture_appreciated: Borrels (meaning beer with friends in the afternoon).
top3_advice: Prepare well in advance. As soon as you know you want to go, write down all deadlines. Treat finding housing like you would treat booking a ticket for Roskilde Festival. if you want the good/cheap/downtown housing you have to be fast! Prepare for twice the reading amount you are used to!
other_useful_info: See above.
most_rewarding: The friends i made, and the city I got to live in.
greatest_challenge: getting accustomed to the "dutch way" of teaching, doing exams.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to explore a different culture without going too far from home (Denmark). In the netherlands, and especially Amsterdam, they have a very different approach to rules and norms. Also, I heard that the dutch people were very friendly and open. The University of Amsterdam also had a great reputation when it comes to media science, which was appealing to me. Last but not least, I had been to Amsterdam before and found the city to be so beautiful.
overall_comments: Amsterdam has become my second home, and I have grown so much as a person from being here.
info_ease: I found it quite easy when I understood UvA's homepage and I also got a lot of help from Online Mobility's "to do list". Of course there will always be some difficulties moving to a new country, but they were not overwhelming.
arrival_assistance: I used the ESN programme and UvA's communication science department to get to know the city and the university.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Amsterdam has become my second home, and I have grown so much as a person from being here.
registration_process: I had to register for courses through a website called Glass, where it was chosen randomly who would get a spot on the different courses. The website was quite new, and the staff could barely help me when I wrote them and asked questions. Also, it took me a long time to figure out which courses I was allowed to take, and there was very few courses to choose from. So it was a bit stressful when I didn't get two out of five courses and I had to find some more to apply to. In the end it all worked out though.
registration_help: The UvA staff could help with most questions, but as I mentioned before, they didn't really know anything about Glass which was frustrating.
registration_success: I got 3/5 of the ones I wished for, and ended up with 2 I didn't really care about.
registration_advice: Begin to look into the courses as early as possible, and dont panic if you can't figure out Glass immediately.
academics_comments: Amsterdam has become my second home, and I have grown so much as a person from being here.
course_level: The courses didn't really seem to hard. But then at the exam, the level was so high with really difficult questions. Normally my grades are pretty good, but here I barely passed some of my courses. I guess it is nice to be challenged, but it was a bit stressful at times.
teaching_comparison: There were way more people at each course which made it a bit less personal. In some courses I had really great teachers, and in some I had really bad ones. It varied a lot. It was also more important to read the curriculum at UvA to understand the lectures and to pass the course. Also, we had more small assignments at UvA than UCPH.
courses_enrolled: "Education and Work" (Sociology), "Topic What does it mean to be literate? Social and policy consequences of 21st century literacies", "Topic Content Marketing", "Topic Algorithmic Persuasion in the Digital Society" & "Topic Health Communication: From Theory to Practice".
recommended_courses: I would recommend "Topic Algorithmic Persuasion in the Digital Society" because the teachers were great and it was super interesting to learn about algorithms and their imprint on society.
unexpected_costs: I did a lot of trips outside of Amsterdam, and the train tickets were quite expensive.
cost_comparison: Beer is cheaper than in Denmark. The food in the supermarket costs about the same. If you rent a Swapfiets for about 190 kr a month, you will save a lot of money on transportation.
activities_available: I followed the ESN introduction week which really helped me to meet new friends. They had lots of events (mostly parties) some were organised too well, but it was still fun. I went on this party boat on Kings day with ESN, and the boat was really not as nice as they had said.
activities_recommended: Do the ESN introduction week. I basically met all my friends there. If you are on exchange in the spring, go and celebrate Kings day! And go out for coffee and beers as much as you can, go for long walks in the outer skirts of Amsterdam and enjoy their parks!
weekend_recommendations: Go to Utrecht, Leiden, Rotterdam and the coast. They have a lot of nice cities that are fun to visit for one day. Also, in tulip season, go to Keukenhof! I will also recommend Anne Franks house, Van Gogh museum and NXT museum.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. It is a lot like Denmark. It is more scary to bike in Amsterdam though, as people don't seem to follow rules as much.
socializing_tips: The only time I really got to talk with local students was during class. So maybe try that.
cultural_challenges: The biking and the fact that the dutch people are very straight forwards and tells you exaclty what they think. In the beginning I could be a bit offended by my roomate when he made fun of danish food or language, but in the end I was about to just laugh about it.
culture_appreciated: The open minded people. You could always find someone to talk to at a bar or club. (And bitterballen).
top3_advice: Be open minded to people who might not look like your typical friends. Be prepared to read a lot (do it in a nice cafe!). Be a part of ESN, even though it sometimes feels a bit forced.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: To meet new people from all over the world, who had a different way of viewing the world. It really put things into perspective, and you learn so much about yourself through this.
greatest_challenge: To be away from family, friends and boyfriend and to follow what the people back home are doing on social media.
other_comments: Enjoy your stay :-)

crucial_aspects: Their course catelouge was the easiest to navigate of the universities i checked, which made it a lot easier to see if there were any courses i would be interested in taking (there was). I had never been to Amsterdam/the netherlands before, so it was guarenteed to be a new experience. But the culure is also somewhat similar to at home, one of the main benefits for me being that i could still travel by bike around the city, which i'm used to doing at home.
overall_comments: I had a great experience, but i will say that for me what shaped my good experience the most was not the place or the university. It was the people i've met and spent my time with, that really shaped my experience abroad to what it was.
info_ease: Overall pretty ok, the university was fairly good at sending out information of what we needed to do, like registering at the municipality. More course specific information was harder to find and was a bit of a challenge.
arrival_assistance: There were some intro days you could sign up for organised by ESN, there were some information but it was mostly just experiencing the city and meeting other exchange students. Then I also had a intro meeting at science, where they gave a bit of information in general about living in amsterdam, but most helpfully study related information like how to navigate the building and where to find your schedule.
arrival_comments: Overall good, i was missing a bit more course specific information and i've had a bit of a hard time knowing where to go or who to talk to when i have specific questions.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had a great experience, but i will say that for me what shaped my good experience the most was not the place or the university. It was the people i've met and spent my time with, that really shaped my experience abroad to what it was.
registration_process: It's mostly one step, you have to apply, which involves sending your transcript of records, id, courses you are currently taking and informing them of which courses you want to take. After that i got accepted, they checked if i qualified to take the courses and then they signed me up for the courses.
registration_help: They have an email for exchange science at the university, where you can ask if you have any problems or questions (which i did very much end up using)
registration_success: I got registered for the classes i had indicated i wanted on my application.
registration_advice: I was not aware of this when i applied, but if you are a bachelor student, you are only allowed to take bachelor course, which there is a fairly small selection of in english (at least that was the case at science). Also they need the official transcript of records which i couldn't figure out how to get, but it's aquired through student service.
academics_comments: I had a great experience, but i will say that for me what shaped my good experience the most was not the place or the university. It was the people i've met and spent my time with, that really shaped my experience abroad to what it was.
course_level: Similar to UCPH i didn't think the level of the material was much diffrent than UCPH, but it does seem to me like the requirements for getting a passing grade are higher than i'm used to.
teaching_comparison: I struggled with it. I encountered more presentation and more researching scientific articles than i'm used to from UCPH, which personally was a challenge just cause i wasn't used to it. On the other hand i encountered fewer excercises and less assigned reading than a UCPH, which i personally missed, but that of course depends on preferences.
courses_enrolled: Functional materials, Organometalic chemistry, Green and industrial chemistry, Artificial Photosynthesis and Solar Fuels and Literature research project
recommended_courses: There were both good and bad things about all of the courses i took, my personal favourites were Organometalic chemistry and literature research project though. Organometalic chemistry is exactly what it sounds like, also had a teaching style that more closely resembles UCPH in my opinion which i liked. Literature research project is somewhat more independent course, the goal is to write a project related to a scientific paper (you have a say about the topic), but my favourite thing about the course were the lectures on academic english, it's not a lot of hours, but it's really helpful to pinpoint some of the common mistakes in academic english and how to fix them and i think these classes are really something i am going to bring forward with me and use for all my papers in english from now on. Main downside is that a lot of the course information is in dutch, but i believe that's something they planning on fixing in the future.
unexpected_costs: I had some taxes that weren't covered by the student housing (because some students may be eligible to not pay those taxes, but that wasn't the case for me). Also needed to by things like pots, apns and plates, and a used bike to get around.
cost_comparison: I think food was overall slightly less expensive than at home. Nothing was particularly surprising to me though pricewise.
activities_available: There's a fitness center type building that offers a bunch of classes, but you can also just come on your own. The ESN organises some trips, and cultural events and a lot of meet-ups at a bar. The chemistry student association, organised some chemistry related trips, a few parties and then there was like a weekly meet-up/hang-out/drinking situation. CREA also offers some creative classes (unclear on how closely related they are to the university)
activities_recommended: I mostly just hung out with friends and didn't really use the options, so i have no recommendations.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city, it's a very nice place to just walk around in.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, amsterdam is similar to copenhagen. My main struggle was being punctual enough. When the schedule says class from 9-10, it's means the lacturer started talking at 9 and you should have been there by now.
socializing_tips: I had a hard time with this, most of the other students have known each other for a while and prefer to speak dutch. My main recommendation is to go to the student association events or meet-ups, that's where i interacted most with the local students.
cultural_challenges: Mostly the being on time thing.
culture_appreciated: Biking, i liked that a lot. I have also had a good time trying different dutch foods.
top3_advice: Get a bike it's the easiest way to get around. Mastercard or visa doesn't always work, so either get a dutch bank account or make sure to carry cash around just in case. Other international students are the easiest to befriend.
other_useful_info: Be on time for classes.
most_rewarding: For me it's been the trying new things and making new friends. I think being in a new place where you know no one really encourages you to just do stuff and try thing.
greatest_challenge: Finding the information i needed about my courses, and adjusting to the different structure of how they do things with courses. For me it felt a little bit like being a confused first year student at university again, except no one else was as confused as me this time.

crucial_aspects: I knew that Amsterdam and The Netherlands in general were recognized for their media studies, and then Amsterdam attracted me, because the city is very similar to Copenhagen and the danish culture.
info_ease: As soon as I had all of the contact information on my host university and knew how their website was designed, I found it quite easy to find the information I needed.
arrival_assistance: The International Office from University of Amsterdam reached out to us through e-mail as everything at this point still was online.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: First, you had to kind of wish for the courses you wanted to have, and this was done through two different systems, which made it kind of difficult and confusing at times. Then you had to wait for some time to learn if you got the wished courses or not. If you didn't get the courses that you wished for, you had to apply through a second round.
registration_help: We could write to the International Offices e-mail.
registration_success: I was lucky and got the courses I wanted, but I know that wasn't the case for many students.
registration_advice: Even though you don't get the courses that you wished for there is always a solution, and the International Offices are really helpful.
course_level: The level was super high and challenging, higher than expected. Exchange students were also placed in the same courses as regular Dutch students, which also made the academic level higher, because we as exchange students had to catch up with what the regular students were taught. Nevertheless, the courses were super interesting and I really learned a lot!
teaching_comparison: Because the sizes of our courses were so high, we had a lot of lectures, where the teacher talked for two hours, and then the rest of the course was self-study. Though, I also had one sociology course, where we also had one weekly tutorial group, where we discussed the texts more in depth, which was nice.
courses_enrolled: Sociological Theory 2: Power, Culture, Identity Topic The Role of Emotions in Political Communication Topic Algorithmic Persuasion in Digital Society Topic Content Marketing Topic Health Communication: From Theory to Practice
recommended_courses: I really liked Sociological Theory 2: Power, Culture, Identity and Topic Algorithmic Persuasion in Digital Society. I really liked the sociological theory course, because it really challenged my way of thinking, and the Algorithmic Persuasion was just really interesting and relevant for today's society.
unexpected_costs: I don't think I experienced any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Public Transportation was more expensive than I thought, why you really need to get a bike in Amsterdam. Food wasn't cheap either. Coffee and beer was cheaper than in Copenhagen.
activities_available: You could take different kinds of drawing, painting and dancing classes. I think they also had a lot of sports activities.
activities_recommended: I really didn't really use any of the non-academic activities.
weekend_recommendations: Amsterdam has a lot of nice museums, so I would definitely but their Museumkaart to save some money on entrance. Furthermore, I would visit some of the other Dutch cities like Rotterdam, The Hague, Leiden and Utrecht. I also took a trip to Paris doing my stay, which is only three hours away with train.
culture_adjustment: Very easy as Dutch people are very similar to Danish people, and in general are very open and helpful. I also lived with three Dutch girls, which really helped me adjust to the Dutch culture.
socializing_tips: Be open and don't be afraid of starting a conversation. The good thing about Dutch people is that they are very international and speaking English for them is very natural, so there is nothing to be scared off.
cultural_challenges: Biking in the city! I thought I was used to biking coming from Copenhagen, but the Dutch people bike in a completely different way, which wasn't always that logical.
culture_appreciated: The openness and their helpfulness, it is rare to find people, who are so helpful.
top3_advice: Be aware of the high academic level Try to find some friends, who are taking the same courses as you, as you can study and support each other Remember to explore and enjoy the amazing city
other_useful_info: Everything can seem super confusing at first, but UvA always has a solution, so you don't need to stress about anything.
most_rewarding: The social aspect and living in a different country, where you have to adapt to a completely new lifestyle.
greatest_challenge: The academic level and the workload, and of course also being away from your friends and family.

crucial_aspects: Described experiences of the different study environment, my girlfriend living there, the much more hands-on approach to teaching.
info_ease: Somewhat easy, the people from the International Office at UvA were very nice and even held a personal call with me to make sure I knew what to do on my first days. Information about Erasmus and the general framework of the program and the conditions on the other hand was very hard to find. I would have wished to be informed about things like minimal requirements beforehand.
arrival_assistance: The people from the International Office at UvA were very nice and even held a personal call with me to make sure I knew what to do on my first days. They also regularly sent me emails for important matters to make sure I knew what to do.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I got sent a link where I had to fill in my personal details and the uni did the rest for me. They even handled all my immigration matters for me.
registration_help: I could always contact the international student office.
registration_success: Very unsuccessful. To be frank, registering for courses was a bit of a disaster. Since my degree (Computer Science) is a joint degree between the two universities in Amsterdam, Vrije Universiteit and the Universiteit van Amsterdam, half of the courses are from the different uni. I was told that as an exchange student you are not allowed to take any courses from the other university, which barred me from four of my five selected courses already. There were also capacity restraints which barred me from taking further courses. This left me with basically a predetermined choice of courses I could take. I also later found out that other exchange students were in fact allowed to take courses from the other university, so I am not sure what is the deciding factor there...
registration_advice: Do it as soon as possible. In basically anything the dutch have a policy of first-come-first-serve.
course_level: Some courses were on an adequate level compared to UCPH courses, some were adequate had they correctly assessed the required previous knowledge. Because they didn't I took courses that I lacked quite a lot of prerequisite knowledge for.
teaching_comparison: Teaching is much more personal and practical. Courses are rarely bigger than 50 people and I had courses as small as 13 people. The content of the courses is also much more focused on immediately applying learned knowledge rather than theoretical practice.
courses_enrolled: Programming Multi- and Many Core Systems (PMMS), DevOps and Cloud-based Software, Type Theory, Computational Biology, Climate Change
recommended_courses: PMMS is great, it is very hands-on and the professors are very enthusiastic. Unfortunately the communication for the final exam was basically nonexistent, leading almost my entire assignment group to fail the exam because they prepared for other things than were asked for in the exam. DevOps is also very fun and the professors are very enthusiastic. The course is basically a project. Computational Biology and Type Theory seem like decent courses, but I lacked a lot of prerequisite knowledge, making it hard for me to follow the courses or judge on their quality. Climate Change was the single best course I have ever had at a university. The professor is incredibly enthusiastic and passionate both about the subject and teaching the content to the students. Unfortunately, this was the last time the course was held, though, as the professor is now going into retirement.
unexpected_costs: The city of Amsterdam will charge you ~260€ (~2000DKK) for garbage disposal fees for an entire year.
cost_comparison: Transportation was cheaper than expected, with a bike you have basically zero transportation costs and bikes are incredibly cheap.
activities_available: Cannot really say as I did not use any of it, but the UvA has a massive sports offering for students.
activities_recommended: Go around town on Kings Day, the entire city turns into a festival. There are some amazing bouldering gyms in Amsterdam as well.
weekend_recommendations: De Grote Veluwe is a national park in the center of the netherlands, it's super beautiful and has an art museum at the center. The entire park can (in classic dutch fashion) be travelled by bikes which are free at the entrance. Zandvoort is a lovely town at the coast. It is also worthwhile to visit the rest of the big cities in the Netherlands at least once, like Den Haag and Rotterdam.
culture_adjustment: Super easy. Dutch people are very friendly.
socializing_tips: Find something outside of university to bond with Dutch people. Dutch students usually stick to Dutch students at uni, so it is easier to make contact with them outside of university.
cultural_challenges: None, really.
culture_appreciated: The hate for bureaucracy most dutch people have is a blessing since it simplifies a lot of things to not have to follow much bureaucracy. This also leads to some funny situations, though, where for example there is no official process to deregister from an exam, you just talk to the professor about it.
top3_advice: 1) Find housing through the Uni, housing in Amsterdam is worse than in Copenhagen. 2) Make sure the courses you choose actually fit your skills 3) Enjoy yourself!
other_useful_info: You can apply for housing support with the dutch government. It is called "Huurtoeslag" in dutch.
most_rewarding: Meeting many different people, living in another country and learning the language
greatest_challenge: Managing my courses and following courses with too little previous knowledge

But it was a intuitive process when signing up for classes at the Faculty of Humanities - more difficult to sign up at another faculty, but I did contact my host university through mail to get the help I needed. They have a block system, so you'll have to figure out how you want to spread the different classes between the 2-3 blocks. I took 3 subjects during the first block, 1 during the second block, and 1 during the third block. Three classes in one block is harder but manageable.
registration_help: I did contact my host university and they helped me. However, there was no number I could call, so all contact happened through e-mail which was slow and a bit frustrating.
registration_success: I only got 2 subjects I really wanted (out of 5). One subject was very popular and I wasn't fast enough to register. The other two subjects I wanted were at another faculty, and unfortunately, I couldn't apply for more than two, even though those subjects were the most relevant to me.
registration_advice: Check in advance which subjects you want and whether they are offered through the faculty that you'll go to or if there are offered through another faculty. And be fast when you have to register for courses - some of them get full very quickly.
academics_comments: I could take so many experiences with me home. New knowledge, friendships, insights, and experiences.
course_level: I was intimidated by their grade scale: 1-10, as I had to have a grade above 5.5 to pass the subjects which seemed high to me. But if you read all texts, go to the lectures, and study for the exam, you will be fine.
teaching_comparison: They were very familiar with each other. There were more hybrid teaching (zoom meetings and physical lectures), but that was mostly as a result of Corona. The teachers were very great and competent. I think the academic level was similar to DK, but I was unfamiliar with the multiple-choice exam that they use quite a lot. But again, if you do your readings, you will be fine.
courses_enrolled: (1) Topic The Role of Emotions in Political Communication (2) Topic Health Communication: From Theory to Practice (3) Making Media: Production, Practices, and Profession (4) Media, Culture, and Sport (5) The Five Senses of Cinema 1 = most interesting 5 = least interesting
recommended_courses: "Topic The Role of Emotions in Political Communication" was my favorite course. It used many different contexts (e.g. the pandemic) as a way to affect people's emotions by framing messages in a specific way regarding political communication. Very interesting.
unexpected_costs: I got a bill after having contacted the hospital over the phone regarding an injury. However, as I am European citizen I did have my European Health Insurance card which meant, that I didn't have to pay but instead send documentation of this.
cost_comparison: I think the transportation was a bit expensive, but mostly all prices were similar to Denmark.
activities_available: ESN organized so many activities: parties, sports events, park chillout, bowling, Galla, dinner, etc. There was for sure something for everyone, which I really appreciated.
activities_recommended: I got a mail asking if I wanted to sign up for "a local buddy" and I almost declined as I didn't know what it meant. However, I did say yes - because why not? And I'm glad I did. My local buddy ended up being a nice guy from the Netherlands who also studied at UvA and I became part of his group where I met other international students who ended up being some of my best friends at my exchange. With a "Buddy Group" you can ask your local buddy whatever questions you might have and during the stay and a few events will be created for the group to meet up and bond.
weekend_recommendations: To the beach, Zandvoort. Utrecht. Haarlem. The tulip fields or Keukenhof (if in season).
culture_adjustment: As Amsterdam is a very intercultural city and familiar to DK, there were no big adjustments.
socializing_tips: The local students I socialized with were mainly through events organized by the ESN, so I'd recommend go to the events that interest you.
cultural_challenges: The Dutch people believe that their biking culture and infrastructure are better than ours in Denmark, which made it challenging not to start a discussion.
culture_appreciated: Every Saturday many neighborhoods in Amsterdam host large street markets, where local vendors gather together and sell goods ranging from organic produce grown in the Netherlands to second-hand clothing, antiques, and souvenirs. That part I really appreciated about their culture.
top3_advice: 1. Everyone living in the Netherlands must have a citizen service number, often referred to as a BSN (burgerservicenummer) and you'll need to apply for that quite fast (and deregister when you leave). 2. Everyone is very nice - make sure to take a chance, sign up for the events, and meet people - especially in the beginning before everyone has found their own "group of people". 3. Sign up for a local buddy
other_useful_info: The healthcare system in the Netherlands is a bit difficult to figure out on your own if you need to see a doctor. In case you do need to see a doctor, you should go to the nearest General Practitioners (GP) from where you live. Normally, people register with a "huisarts" when they arrive in the Netherlands. I didn't do it and I don't know any exchange students who did, but it might be a good idea to make some research just so you'll know where to go, in case you need to see a doctor. You can always knock on their door and say that you live nearby and ask if you should register - I did when I got an injury. They told me, that I didn't need any medical help and that I didn't have to register as I had only 2 months left. However, they did tell me to come back if something else should happen to me, which was nice to know.
most_rewarding: The social experiences and the friends I made. It always seem a bit more "dangourous" when it's hard to anticipate how the exchange will be, but as soon as you have arrived it is not that difficult to figure it all out and you'll meet a lot of great people.
greatest_challenge: Mostly the practical things: to register, get different kinds of approval, and constantly be in contact with my home and host university to figure out formalities.
other_comments: Exchange is different for everyone. For me, I didn't feel lonely at any point. It all felt natural and I appreciated every second of it.

cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: That people are open-minded

most_rewarding: My amazing friends.

crucial_aspects: Primarily, I wanted a destination, where I could find enough courses in English. Furthermore, due to COVID restrictions at the time of my application, I wanted to stay within Europe. Additionally, Amsterdam's departement of logic is really good so I also wanted to experience that.
info_ease: Some were easy. Other were hard. So it depends on what aspect of the arrival I needed information about. UvA were not that good in getting information out such that you had a lot of time to respond to it. However, this were due to personal issues for the coordinator. We were informed of this. They were really good at helping if some information were lost after the arrival.
arrival_assistance: We had two international coordinators, which helped with the practicalities and if at any time during the stay we needed to talk to someone then we could contact them. Then we also had the UvA homepage.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: To get accepted you needed to send proof of enrolment at UCPH. Then after you were enrolled, you needed to make sure that you could login through SIS and mail. Then you needed to go through an application formula, which involved a copy of your passport, language test, course selection ect. You were overall guided well through that part.
registration_help: Primarily the UvA homepage, but you could also get in contact with the international coordinator. However due to personal circumstances, she were not present for the last part of June and the beginning of August.
registration_success: Overall quite successful. I only had issues with one course.
registration_advice: Take your time, research the courses well and read up on the limitations on UvA's homepage.
course_level: Some courses were very hard. Others were easier. However, in general I will say that the level corresponds to the level in Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: They were more or less identical. You had lectures and in-class sessions with other students. However, sometimes there were sometimes, where you had classes with the professer themselves.
courses_enrolled: Graph Theory and Algorithms, Numerical Linear Algebra, Dynamic and Distributed Programming, Introduction to Quantum Computing and Bayesian Statistics for Machine Learning
recommended_courses: Graph Theory and Algorithms and Introduction to Quantum Computing as I found them the most fun and interesting. Additionally, I think they will be the courses, I use the most afterwards.
unexpected_costs: The cost of travelling and moving there. Especially for Christmas, where I wanted to go home.
cost_comparison: Food were a bit cheaper. Otherwise the prices are more or less the same as in Copenhagen.
activities_available: ESN facilitated a lot of experiences, get together, outings ect., which were amazing. Furthermore, at science park there were a gym, where you had options for student memberships ect.
activities_recommended: Be a part of ESN and volunteer there. For me it gave an amazing network of people, that I still talk to. Especially also in the beginning, where you do not know anyone.
weekend_recommendations: Visit The Haag and Zaandam to see the windmills.
culture_adjustment: I had to get used to how direct and 'impolite' many Dutch people are. Other than that the culture were not that different from Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: Make it your goal to talk to them at every class and do the in-class session's assignments in groups. For me it felt very uncomfortable at first, but slowly they warmed up to me. So more or less keep trying. It takes time.
cultural_challenges: Other than how direct they say things, they are also quite reserved like Danes. This can be hard when you need to find a group for uni ect.
culture_appreciated: I really came to like the directness. You could get to your points quicker and less misunderstandings occured.
top3_advice: 1. Be aware that in the beginning you may feel very much alone and on your own. Enjoy the little things and take it one day at a time. 2. Get a museum card and be curios. They are really starting to reflect on their past and that is really interesting. 3. Insist on talking to the locals. You will learn a lot about yourself and your own culture.
other_useful_info: Be aware that you need to figure out a lot on your own, but don't be too afraid to send an email to the coordinator.
most_rewarding: The personal growth. I have gained a huge insight into myself and my own values. It is like I could see my own culture through someone else. Additionally, I have become much more confident in myself and my own abilities.
greatest_challenge: Feeling lonely. Especially in the beginning.

crucial_aspects: Amsterdam is a cool place to live and study. It was both important for me to live in a nice city with a lot of opportunities to go out and meet new people and also to study at a university where the courses sounded interesting and relevant.
info_ease: It was relatively easy. I do not recall any trouble in this regard.
arrival_assistance: I received e-mails and there was a student desk where you could ask questions at the university.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The course registration was online. You could pick more courses than you needed and then afterwards, it was possible to de-register from courses if you had too many or if some overlapped. There was also a second round of registration if you did not get the courses you needed/hoped to get.
registration_help: I did not need help and therefore, do not know this.
registration_success: Very successful. I had to have five courses of 6 ECTS points each and got five courses that I was happy with.
registration_advice: Register for all courses you want and check if they overlap.
course_level: The courses were in general of a high academic level. I had three courses in the first block and two courses in the second block. The first block was challenging since three courses are a lot of reading. I heard from other students that most people only have two in a block but as an exchange student you need to have five all together to get 30 ECTS points in total.
teaching_comparison: There was either just a weekly lecture or a combination of a lecture and a workgroup. The workgroup is familiar to the seminar classes at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: 1. EU Company Law (block 1) 2. EU Migration Law, forced and unforced migration (block 1) 3. EU Regulated Markets (block 1) 4. Advanced EU Competition Law (block 2) 5. Finance, Insolvency, and Security (block 2)
recommended_courses: This of course depends on what your interests are. I liked EU Company Law and Finance, Insolvency, and Security the best. These two courses were the only ones of the five I took that had both a weekly lecture and a workgroup. I think the workgroups were very good since that allowed for interaction and I learned a lot from this. The teachers in both of these courses were also the best I had in my entire stay. Very skilled in their areas of the law and very good at teaching difficult materials. Company Law was a bit more theoretical and less practical than what I have experienced before, this provided good perspective on company laws in general. Finance was probably the most difficult course I had, but at the same time my favourite.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: I spent almost nothing on books since most of the materials are made available online.
activities_available: There were a lot of social activities through Erasmus. There was also the possibility to join a student gym which I think would be cheaper than regular gyms.
activities_recommended: The night life in Amsterdam is very good. There are a lot of techno festivals, clubs etc. if you like that. The restaurants and cafés were also very good.
weekend_recommendations: This depends on where you come from. A lot of students from America, Australia or other places far away did a lot of trips around Europe to see more European cities when to take advantage of the close distance. I did not do trips to other countries, but I would recommend trips to other Dutch cities. It is cheap and easy to get around the Netherlands by train.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: I did not socialize a lot with the Dutch students, but my experience is that most people are very helpful and wants to talk to you.
cultural_challenges: I did not find anything particularly challenging.
culture_appreciated: I love the bike culture. I appreciated that I was not dependent on public transportation. I also felt very safe in the city to go out.
top3_advice: First, keep up in your courses. There is no real exam prep period so if you are far behind, this will be very difficult to catch up on. Second, get a bike as soon as you arrive. Third, go out and enjoy the city. There are a lot of fun places!
other_useful_info: It rains a lot in Amsterdam. The first months were really terrible weather, but summer is amazing.
most_rewarding: I have gotten some very good friends from my exchange. I also learned a lot from the courses.

crucial_aspects: I was mainly drawn by the large number of courses relevant to my studies taught in English. Furthermore, I have long wished to visit and explore the destination.
info_ease: Both my host university, and the local authorities, was of great assistance with information about my destination, studies, and local regulations.
arrival_assistance: My host university instructed me in registration with the local authorities and preparations for my studies.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Course registration is handled through a self-service online platform by the university and was fairly intuitive to me. However, I discovered that some courses (courses related to archaeology and ancient studies) are handled manually by university staff and require correspondence with these. This made the process more lengthy and confusing.
registration_help: Staff were available through messaging to answer questions and guide students through registration.
registration_success: I was able to get into most of the courses I was interested in, and since the university offered a wide selection of elective courses, I had no problem choosing more than was necessary.
registration_advice: Be in good time and ask for help in case of any confusion.
course_level: My courses were varied, but were all interesting and challenging. I thought they were all suitable for my level.
teaching_comparison: Some courses were more heavy on lectures in large groups than I am used to. Other courses followed a largely class-based discussion style as is more used at UCPH. I was surprised at the amount of obligatory written assignments during each course, which differed greatly from my prior experiences. The final gradings of the courses were also typically dependent on the outcome of different assignments handed in during the course as well as a final exam at the end of the course, which is very different to the style at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Archaeology and Society, Ancient Philosophy, Spain: Mediterranean Microcosm of Europe, Nation building and nation branding in postcolonial states, and Classical Mythology
recommended_courses: I especially enjoyed the following courses. Spain: Mediterranean Microcosm of Europe, Nation building and nation branding in postcolonial states, and Classical Mythology. I would not recommend Archaeology and Society to anybody else than archaeologists. As a historian, the course was unfortunately not as relevant to me, as I had hoped.
unexpected_costs: I choose to rent a bike for ca. 200 kr. a month instead of using mostly public transportation. On the other hand, internet and utilities were included in my rent. However, laundry and food was on the more expensive side.
cost_comparison: Laundry and food was on the more expensive side, as is public transport if you choose to exclusively use that. As a Dane, I suggest buying or renting a bike while in Amsterdam.
activities_available: There were many parties, social activities such as film nights, visits to museums, breweries etc. and the like arranged by student groups (like the Erasmus Student Network) outside of the university.
activities_recommended: Try to participate in the Erasmus Student Network's activities at the beginning of the semester, this is an opportunity to meet many other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city, Amsterdam has much to offer in terms of culture and experiences. I liked their museums, parks and walks through the city.
culture_adjustment: The Netherlands is in many ways much like Copenhagen in terms of culture and geography. Therefore, I found it quite manageable.
socializing_tips: Everyone speaks English, and I found many local students as well as exchange students in my classes. I regularly spoke with a few local students when in class, but otherwise not so much.
cultural_challenges: None in particular.
culture_appreciated: Everyone was lovely and kind to me, and I experienced a very understanding and loose culture, where everyone wanted to see you succeed.
top3_advice: The university's staff is extremely helpful with any problems you might encounter, so do not hesitate with contacting them for help. I strongly recommend getting a bike for transportation; it is both cheeper, more environmentally friendly, good for you, and gives you the greatest freedom to experience the city. The metro is excellent as well, but it is difficult to really see and feel the city, when you are mostly in a tube underground. Try to meet some people and make some friends in the beginning of your stay, as it gets harder once the academic year really picks up.
other_useful_info: University housing is only available to around 50% of all exchange students, and renting privately can be difficult, time-consuming and expensive. Be proactive and willing to spend some money when it comes to securing university housing, as short-term renting in Amsterdam can be a challenge.
most_rewarding: I learned so much! Both academically and personally. I especially appreciate the opportunity to branch out in many different elective courses with different styles of teaching.
greatest_challenge: Homesickness. I missed my friends and family at home, but Amsterdam is not much more than an hour away by plane, and visits from home as well as frequent calls was a massive advantage for me.

crucial_aspects: The courses available to me at the host university and its academic reputation
info_ease: Quite easy. The university website had a detailed checklist of things to do prior to and upon arrival. And the international office was helpful with answering questions I had regarding course registration.
arrival_assistance: There was an introductory meeting for echange students at the faculty of humanities by the international office.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The course registration is done through an online portal on a first come, first served principle. Different faculties and different courses have different registration periods and different portals, which is slightly confusing. The university sends an email with the information when the registration periods approach. The semester is divided in three blocks, and it's possible to change courses for the second and third block during the first block (if there are still free spots left.)
registration_help: The international office was very helpful in answering my questions both by phone and email. During the semester one of my professors helped me switch a course that was not available to me in the original registration process.
registration_success: I successfully registered to all the courses I wanted except one.
registration_advice: Register to one or two extra courses as you might not get a spot on the ones you want or you might be waitlisted.
