course_level: It was a very high academic level. The workload is intense, but the academic outcome was very rewarding.
teaching_comparison: There was a similar mix of lectures and student involved teaching, though more student presentations than I am used to. The preparation for class was a lot more work heavy as there were regular assignments and different kinds of running assessment that counted towards the final grade. I had approx. an assignment a week on top of the readings for class. There was also more group work than I am used to from UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Language in Use: Variation and Acquisition How Literature Shapes Society Sign Linguistics 1 Contact, Conflict and the Media Term Paper Linguistics
recommended_courses: I highly recommend Sign Linguistics 1. It was very interesting to see language and concepts about language from a different perspective. unexpected_costs: I paid a monthly subscription of around 20 euro at swapfiets to rent a bike. I think it's possible to buy a used bike for cheaper, but with swapfiets you get a good bike that you can get repaired for free and don't have the hassle of reselling it afterwards.
cost_comparison: Public transportation was expensive.

If you register at the municipality upon arrival and get a BSN number, you can get a museumkaart for 65 euro that gives free acces to most museums for a year. I especially enjoyed the canal museum (Grachtenmuseum) and the Tropenmuseum.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, it's quite similar to Denmark.
socializing_tips: Nope, I met some Dutch students in my courses, but mostly socialized with other internationals. There are a lot of international students doing their full degrees in Amsterdam though.

crucial_aspects: I chose to go to The Netherlands during my semester abroad because I wanted to go somewhere where the population spoke English at a high level of proficiency (without being native speakers). I chose to go to Amsterdam specifically because of its vibrant art scene and the many rich cultural influences from the consistent influx of people from all over the world. I chose the University of Amsterdam because they offer a lot of courses in English and are renowned for their academic standards.
overall_comments: The overall rating of my semester abroad is affected by the fact that the academic level at the University of Amsterdam was lower than I had expected, and by the fact that the housing provided by the University of Amsterdam through the company Lieven de Key was really poor.
info_ease: The international office at University of Amsterdam was really good at sending out updates detailing what to expect upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance from the international office at the University of Amsterdam in terms of filling out the forms in Mobility Online, and then there was a general introduction to the university approximately one week after my arrival. In the week before, there was the introductory week hosted by Erasmus Student Network (ESN Amsterdam), which consisted of a range of activities throughout the days and the evenings; some related to the university and others more related to living in Amsterdam.
arrival_comments: It might have been nice to have the general introduction to the university a bit earlier on, and also perhaps to have been more properly introduced to the many different campuses around the city before having to make one's way to classes.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The overall rating of my semester abroad is affected by the fact that the academic level at the University of Amsterdam was lower than I had expected, and by the fact that the housing provided by the University of Amsterdam through the company Lieven de Key was really poor.
registration_process: After being nominated by UCPH, I applied to the University of Amsterdam through their internal portal SiS. After I was accepted, I applied for courses through the same page.
registration_help: I did not really require help during the registration process, but I am sure that I could have reached out to the international office at the University of Amsterdam had I had any questions or concerns.
registration_success: I had some trouble registering for courses at the University of Amsterdam. First of all, the course options available for MA level elective courses were quite limited. Second of all, many of the courses I was interested in had been placed in the same time slot, which meant that I ended up having to register for courses that I did not have an immediate interest in.
registration_advice: I would urge future exchange students at the University of Amsterdam to be aware of the fact that the university schedules courses before the registration period begins, and that it is your responsibility as a student to ensure that the courses you have chosen do not overlap. You should also be aware of the fact that courses at UvA tend to have a smaller ECTS-load, which means that you have to register for more courses to meet the 30 ECTS per semester requirement than you do at UCPH during a single semester.
academics_comments: The overall rating of my semester abroad is affected by the fact that the academic level at the University of Amsterdam was lower than I had expected, and by the fact that the housing provided by the University of Amsterdam through the company Lieven de Key was really poor.
course_level: As a master's degree student at UCPH, I would say that the MA elective courses offered at the University of Amsterdam correspond to first/second year bachelor's degree courses at universities in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: Because I was doing MA elective courses that were part of different study programs, I find it difficult to speak of a specific style of teaching. In some courses, we mostly had lectures, even though they were described as seminars. In other courses, we did a lot of assignments and presentations, which made it feel more like an independent study course than a “regular" university course. In the best one of the courses, I participated in, the teacher invoked the pedagogical principle of “old school is real school," which meant that we were discouraged from bringing our computers or other devices to class, but were instead asked to bring a notebook and a pen, to keep us from being distracted and make us more actively engaged in the subject matter. It seemed like an extraordinary measure, but it worked really well. Everyone participated much more freely, and the classes were much more interesting. It was also a bit of a challenge sometimes not being able to hide behind a screen, but having to look everyone in the eye. In the courses I participated in that revolved around museums / art / design, we went on a few excursions which added a practical dimension to the courses that is sometimes lacking at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: During my semester abroad I was enrolled in the following courses: 1) Democracy and Distrust: An American Case History (6 ECTS), 2) Museums, Heritage and Digital Curation (12 ECTS), 3) Re-reading the Graphic Design Archive / Re-framing the Graphic Design Collection (6 ECTS), and 4) “Losing Earth"?: Activism and Diplomacy on the Environment and Climate since 1968 (6 ECTS).
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend that future exchange students at the University of Amsterdam enrol in the MA elective course “Losing Earth"?: Activism and Diplomacy on the Environment and Climate since 1968, which is taught by PhD Ruud van Dijk as part of the MA in History of International Relations. Ruud has taught the course independently or with a co-teacher from the MA in History of International Relations five times in total. It was really interesting to learn more about various (political) approaches to climate change during the twentieth century (and sometimes going back to the late nineteenth century). It was especially interesting to participate in the course because everyone had different academic backgrounds and different ways of understanding diplomacy/activism and the nature of climate change.
unexpected_costs: When we would go on excursions during courses at the University of Amsterdam, students were expected to pay for transportation and entrance fees on their own. In general, the cost of public transportation in The Netherlands was a bit of a surprise.
cost_comparison: Rent and transportation was definitely more expensive than I had anticipated, but groceries were less expensive than I had initially thought (compared to inflation-level prices in Denmark). Museum tickets are quite expensive even if one purchases a Museumkaart, which provides free or discounted museum tickets all over The Netherlands (only in state-funded museums!).
activities_available: All kinds of cultural, athletic, and social activities were available for students at the University of Amsterdam. At CREA near the Roeterseiland Campus, it was possible to sign up for crafts courses, language courses, music courses, and all kinds of athletic activities for a monthly fee (similar to Danish "aftenskole"). Unfortunately, many of the courses had already started when I arrived in Amsterdam, and the next ones on offer would go beyond the duration of my semester abroad. Still, it was possible to participate in any number of activities, if one did not mind that the courses had already started.
activities_recommended: I would definitely encourage future exchange students to visit some of the many museums in Amsterdam and in other Dutch cities. I would also recommend visiting some of the many parks in the city (especially during the summer!). I would recommend that you walk or ride a bicycle around the city, seeing as it really is the best way to get to know it. Riding a bicycle in Amsterdam does take a bit of courage - even if you are used to riding a bicycle in Copenhagen.
weekend_recommendations: I would similarly encourage future exchange students to visit some of the many museums in Amsterdam and in other Dutch cities during the weekends or holidays. Specifically, I would recommend a visit to designer Piet Hein Eek's studio in Eindhoven, which features a large collection of his furniture and also his factory. It is free of charge and most interesting if you have an interest in art / design. I would also recommend a visit to the beach Bloemendaal aan Zee whenever you need a break from the city (whether for a walk in the winter or a swim in the summer). Personally, I am a bit of a culinary enthusiast, so I would also recommend that you try some of the many wonderful cafés and restaurants for lunch or dinner.
culture_adjustment: During the introductory week, the university staff spoke a lot about the experience of culture chock. I must admit that I did not immediately see the relevance of talking about culture chock, as I consider the Dutch culture and the Danish culture to be quite similar. However, I have to admit that I did struggle a bit during the second- and third month of my semester abroad. Because of the block system at the University of Amsterdam (the fact that you have several small courses of a short duration during the semester), I found it really difficult to connect with my fellow students, and I felt a little lonely from time to time. A bit out of sync with everyone else.
cultural_challenges: The Dutch are quite direct and very forward, which can come across as rudeness/impertinence.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the cultural diversity of Amsterdam, even though I did find it a bit disheartening that cultural minorities tend to live in specific parts of the city.
top3_advice: 1) The academic level at the University of Amsterdam is not what you are used to at UCPH (to say nothing of the weird Dutch grading system), but do try to make the most of it anyhow. If nothing else, do enjoy that you have the time to cultivate academic- and non-academic interests on the side. Use your time wisely - in a way that is meaningful to YOU. 2) Choose courses whose subject matter go beyond your primary academic interests. 3) Do NOT accept housing from the University of Amsterdam in Zuiderzeeweg through the company Lieven de Key (!!), even if it means that you have to struggle to procure housing yourself.
other_useful_info: The Dutch grading system is very different from the Danish. In The Netherlands you are given a grade between 1-10 (with up to one decimal point), and what constitutes a passing grade differs from one course to the other (usually 5.5 or higher depending on the teacher). Your final grade is usually made up of four components, including active participation/attendance, an interim essay, one or more presentations during the course, and a final essay at the end of the course. Also, your teacher is the only one to review your performance (there is no “censor" to ensure fair treatment, so you have to keep in your teacher's good graces).
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was getting to know the city of Amsterdam. I find that it is always really rewarding and empowering in a sense to experience the sensation of being able to put a life together in a context different from the one you are used to.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was having to settle for courses that were outright dissatisfactory, and housing that was also extremely disappointing.

crucial_aspects: Amsterdam has one of the largest social science departments in all of europe. It is also a very charming city which I absolutely fell in love with. I also chose Amsterdam because of the short distance from Denmark, and because of the Erasmus grant
overall_comments: Amsterdam is a diverse city and as an expat you feel welcome there. It was easy for me to feel at home fast.
info_ease: It wasn't difficult. The University of Amsterdam has an International office which was very good at communicating important information once I arrived in Amsterdam. It was a bit chaotic during the summer holiday but they are generally happy to help at the international student desk.
arrival_assistance: The Erasmus Student Network threw a very well organized introduction week where I met so many nice people from around the globe whom I stayed in contact with during the exchange. Once I was enrolled as a student at the UvA, I got registered automatically in the information page for exchange students in Canvas where I received important messages from the International office, for instance an invitation to a welcoming lecture
arrival_comments: No complaints
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Amsterdam is a diverse city and as an expat you feel welcome there. It was easy for me to feel at home fast.
registration_process: Much of the registration process was handled by mobility online. But then there was some confusion about a language test a few weeks before I was leaving and the course registration process was especially pulling teeth because there was two different systems with different rules (one of them was a raffle of the registered and the other one worked with a first come first served principle) which was very confusing, but the international student service desk was always happy to help and it turned out just fine
registration_help: The international office answered all my questions. There was also good information in the introduction week about what other resources was available for students, for instance the UvA offered student counselling or psychological help for those who need it, and there was also an awareness about how Amsterdam is liberal with drugs and which consequences there can be of that, so exchange students were informed about a rehabilitation center for students too. There is a rich student life among exchange students and lots of activities to join in case you feel lonely or bored.
registration_success: I was lucky enough to get all the courses I registered for but that wasn't the case for everyone I knew.
registration_advice: Keep an eye out for the deadline/ registration dates and be ready by the computer once it opens if you have a course you really want to follow
academics_comments: Amsterdam is a diverse city and as an expat you feel welcome there. It was easy for me to feel at home fast.
course_level: The work load is about the same as in Denmark but there is different rules about absence and more written assignments than I was used to. Also the grading system is different and the passing grade is much higher than in the Danish system.
teaching_comparison: You can really feel there are more resources available. Teachers are more personally related to the students and put a large effort in giving constructive feedback on the work I handed in during the semester.
courses_enrolled: Secrets of Identity: Knowing others in practice Bodies in Public The Eternal pursuit of happiness: Philosophy, science and technology of well-being
recommended_courses: Secrets of Identity: Knowing others in practice was my favourite course during the stay The teacher Annerienke Fioole is super competent and kind, and she made a big deal out of learning everyone's names and overall she facilitated a good learning space. It was a small class / seminar group where I got to know a lot of Dutch people since many of the programmes in the UvA has been made all-English speaking. In the course I was able to do some fieldwork on a topic of choice which was fun.
unexpected_costs: Event tickets, concert tickets and festivals. If you want to go out you need to pay an entrance fee for a lot of places. Not that the price is high but there is a big event-culture in Amsterdam which means you also kind of need to know what is happening and when, which is kind of difficult if you don't have a network in the city beforehand
cost_comparison: Food in grocery stores is cheaper than in DK, especially in the discount supermarkets called Jumbo or Dirk van den Broek. It is also cheaper to go out for drinks at a bar than it is in Copenhagen. The ferry going from central station to Amsterdam Noord is free of charge. Entrance for cultural activities are generally expensive but if you plan to visit a lot of museums you can save some money by buying a museum card (450 DKK)
activities_available: Erasmus student network had a number of social clubs and activities during the semester for anyone interested. There was also the creative space and student café called CREA which offered courses in dance, drawing, singing, acting etc. for student friendly prices. And the USC is the university sports association where you can join most any type of sports discipline you desire
activities_recommended: I joined an applied ceramics course in CREA and enjoyed doing something non-academic in my spare time. I also joined the USC fitness membership which was super cheap and accessible and I was happy with their group classes
weekend_recommendations: Go to the museums: Van Gogh, Rembrandt huis, Eye film museum, Anne Frank Museum and many more. There is a lot of cute markets around the city where you can buy food, vintage clothing, jewelry and lots of other things: Waterlooplein, Noordermarkt, Albert Cuyp market. During summer definitely go on a canal tour or hang out in the parks with a book. Don't miss the American Book Centre. Enjoy the many cute cafés and bars, take a stroll through the 9 streets and de Jordaan.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy, Dutch culture is similar to Danish culture in a lot of ways.
cultural_challenges: Nothing in particular, but it seems it is not really socially accepted to wear a helmet when you bike which is confusing because the biking paths are busy
culture_appreciated: That so many different cultures are represented in the city which made me feel welcome as an expat.
top3_advice: Don't let the application procedure stop you from going abroad! Biking is by far the easiest and cheapest way to get around the city Join the ESN introduction week in the beginning of the semester
other_useful_info: I brought my own bike on the Flixbus from Denmark and used it every day. I also knew people who bought a cheap bike when they arrived and sold it when they went back. Be careful not to park your bike illegally though. During the first week I unintentionally parked my bike somewhere it was not allowed. My bike was removed by the municipality and put in a site called the 'fietsdepot' around 10 km west of the city centre. I had to go there and pay a fine of 22,5 euros to get it back.
most_rewarding: I got to know so many nice people from all around the world and became familiar with the city. I practiced my english skills and tried out other academic disciplines.
greatest_challenge: To go home :,)

UvA let me choose econometrics courses (that I was even academically pre-approved by UvA, based on documentation they had me spend time on collecting), but then later informed me that I couldn't enroll in them after all - so I had to choose courses that had nothing to do with my academic profile. As a student from UCPH (where economics is not seperate from econometrics) it is impossible to get into the econometrics programme at UvA - so if you're an econometrics student at UCPH they have very few relevant courses for you at UvA, at least at the master's.

course_level: Very low quality: Many of the classes consisted of student presentations of very poor quality; and they were mandatory, so I spent several hours a week listening to people who had no idea of what they were doing. This was made way worse by the clear lack of english speaking skills in many of the foreign students. Courses were also incredibly chaotic: you have 10.000 different pieces of information lying around in different places on Canvas and an online schedule that regularly gave you wrong information! How hard is it to make a schedule? I have never experienced anything so poorly administrated and executed in my education before UvA.
teaching_comparison: Mandatory classes consisting of student presentations. Woorks very poorly as described above. Almost all courses focused on remembering points from a handful of academic papers for the 2-3-hour exam. People just got ChatGPT to summarise the main points from these, learned nothing, and passed the exam. Courses and exams were overall without any independent thought or practical usefulnees. I acquired no tools. This was very different from most courses at UCPH, where papers are usually only a (small) part of the exam.

crucial_aspects: One of the most important aspects was they offer interesting and challenging courses, and that the university has a good reputation within my field of study. It was also important to me that the exams were held no later than end of January. I also chose UvA because Amsterdam is known to be a very multi-cultural city, and the Netherlands are considered a safe country.
overall_comments: The workload was higher than I anticipated based on the experiences that friends of mine had in other universities and countries. That is the main reason why I did not rate the experience 10/10.
info_ease: Very easy. Before and upon arrival UvA send out several newsletters containing relevant information about my stay.
arrival_assistance: There was an introduction day for exchange students at the Economics and Business department the week before classes strated, where we received a lot of information and went on a campus tour.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The workload was higher than I anticipated based on the experiences that friends of mine had in other universities and countries. That is the main reason why I did not rate the experience 10/10.
registration_process: As a master's students the registration process was different from the bachelor's students'. We received an email with a link to a registration form containing all the courses that the host university allowed us to apply for. It was easy to fill in, but you do not receive any e-mail confirmation after the form is filled in. Also, you have to log on to sis.uva.nl to find out if you were accepted into the courses that you applied for, as they will not send you an e-mail or anything when your course registration is accepted.
registration_help: You can write an email or call the Economics and Business Exchange office. They usually answer to emails within 3 days.
registration_success: I was accepted into all 6 classes that I applied for. However, before I knew which courses UvA would allow me to take, I had planned on applying for some different courses. I was able to apply for 4 out of 6 courses that I had planned to apply for, and I had to choose 2 new courses from the list of courses available to me.
registration_advice: Send them an email before course registration, to find out exactly which courses you are eligible to apply for according to the host university.
academics_comments: The workload was higher than I anticipated based on the experiences that friends of mine had in other universities and countries. That is the main reason why I did not rate the experience 10/10.
course_level: I took 1 BA course and 5 MA courses. The BA course was easy enough (as expected). One of the MA courses (Microeconomics and Game Theory) was way harder than I had expected, as it sounded easy according to the course discription, but the work load was very high and the way they grade the exams is different from back home (minor calculus mistakes can severely pull down your grade). For me, the rest of the MA courses were not too hard.
teaching_comparison: They expected you to study more independently than at KU. At KU we would have tutorial classes were the TA goes through all problem sets, but at UvA the tutorials were mostly like Q&A sessions.
courses_enrolled: Management Accounting 1 for Business (BA couse) Managerial Economics (MA course) Microeconomics and Game Theory (MA course) Behavioural Economics (MA course) Advanced Industrial Organisations (MA course) Advanced Game Theory (MA course)
recommended_courses: Managerial Economics: easy course, the professor is very nice. Behavioural Economics: it was fun, a lot to read, and the tutorial classes consisted of the students presenting a paper, so it was nice to do something different for once. Advanced Industrial Organisations: same professor as Managerial Economics. The professor said it was one of the most difficult courses in their Master's program (because of the "difficult" math), but I do not think it was that difficult - there are way harder courses back home. Advanced Game Theory: fun if you like game theory, the professor is a bit absent-minded, the work load is not too bad, and the exam is fair.
unexpected_costs: The only thing I can think of is that we had to buy all the equipment for the kitchen, as the dorm building throws everything out after you move out. This includes pots, pans, electric kettle, plates, cutlery, glasses. This ended up costing around 250 EUR (I shared this cost with my roommate)
cost_comparison: Dairy products and coffee in cafes were a bit cheaper. I feel like meat was more expensive, but not a lot. Restaurants and other groceries were more or less the same as in Copenhagen.
activities_available: USC (the university sports college) offers almost any sport you can think of (including a cheap fitness membership), but some sports are very popular so you have to be quick if you want a spot. CREA offers different dance and music classes and almost all thinkable creative courses (ceramics, painting, etc.). Also these classes are quickly filled up, so you have to be quick to get a spot. ESN Amsterdam host several parties, movie nights, trips abroad and trips to other Dutch cities, and other social events - some are free and some have a fee.
activities_recommended: Anything at CREA. Dutch Movie Night hosted by ESN Amsterdam. And I highly recommend participating in the ESN Introduction Program in the end of August - it is intense, but also a great way of meeting other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: Visit Belgium, or visit other Dutch cities like Rotterdam, Haarlem, Utrecht, Den Haag or Zandvoort (Den Haag and Zandvoort have nice beaches!). If the weather is good, you can even bike to some nearby towns. Get yourself a Museumcard! It is 65 EUR, but lasts one year, and you can visit many of the biggest and most famous museums "for free" with this card (400+ museums in the Netherlands, and around 50 museums in Amsterdam)
culture_adjustment: Easy enough as a Dane. The culture is not that different. They are straightforward people, it feels safe, and the way you interact with the professors is very informal, just like at home.
socializing_tips: In the break you should just talk to the person sitting next to you in class. If you are single, go on dates. Join a sport or creative class at CREA.
cultural_challenges: Especially in the service sector (restaurants, cafes, etc.) the staff can seem rude, but that is just because they are VERY straightforward and have this no-bullshit attitude.
culture_appreciated: How multi-cultural the city is, and how chill and informal people are.
top3_advice: Be open to new people and cultures, and try to meet new people that are not only Danes! Get yourself a bicycle as soon as you arrive! (Swapfiets is very easy to use) Be spontaneous and say yes to plans and invitations, and remember to have fun, and don't worry too much about the studies!
other_useful_info: Can't think of anything atm.
most_rewarding: Making new friends from all over the world (from Australia to Canada, and Botswana to Finland). And just being able to be more spontaneous than I usually would be back home.
greatest_challenge: Balancing studies with all the things I wanted to see and do while I was there. It is like you want to be a tourist and do all the fun stuff, but you are also a local and have to study and pass your classes.

crucial_aspects: In selecting my study destination, I prioritized two crucial aspects. Firstly, I sought a university environment where I could be intellectually challenged. This meant looking for institutions renowned for academic rigor and offering programs that would push me to excel academically. Secondly, I was keen on experiencing a different approach to studying. This encompassed a desire to explore alternative teaching methodologies, curriculum structures, and cultural perspectives on learning. By seeking both intellectual challenge and diversity in learning, I aimed to foster personal and academic growth in an enriching educational environment.
info_ease: Upon arrival, navigating the necessary information was a bit challenging due to the multitude of sources available. While I ultimately found the information I needed, the process was occasionally confusing. The abundance of sources made it difficult to discern the most reliable and relevant information. Streamlining the information dissemination process could improve the experience for incoming students, reducing confusion and ensuring quick access to essential information
arrival_assistance: When I arrived at my study destination, I received some assistance primarily through an introduction week. However, the focus of this orientation was more on familiarizing students with the university as a whole rather than specifically addressing the social and behavioral science department. While the introduction week provided valuable general information about the university, a more tailored orientation program specifically geared towards my field of study could have been beneficial in facilitating a smoother transition and integration into my academic program
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Preparation and Planning: Before the registration period begins, students are encouraged to review the course catalog or schedule to identify the courses they wish to take. This involves considering program requirements, course availability, prerequisites, and scheduling conflicts. Registration Period: The university announces specific dates for course registration, typically occurring before the start of each semester or academic term. During this period, students log in to the university's online registration system using their student credentials. Course Selection: Within the registration system, students browse available courses and select the ones they wish to enroll in for the upcoming term. They may need to input course codes or search by keywords to find the desired courses. Enrollment: After selecting their desired courses, students proceed to enroll in them through the registration system. This involves confirming their selections and officially securing a spot in each course. Confirmation and Adjustment: Once enrollment is complete, students receive confirmation of their course selections. They may have a window of time during which they can make adjustments to their schedule, such as adding or dropping courses, before the registration period closes. Waitlisting (if applicable): In some cases, popular courses may fill up quickly, leading to waitlists. Students who are unable to initially enroll in a desired course may have the option to join a waitlist. If a spot becomes available due to a dropout or additional capacity, students on the waitlist may be automatically enrolled. Finalization: At the close of the registration period, students' course schedules are finalized. They can view their complete schedule through the registration system or student portal. The course registration process at the University of Amsterdam aims to be efficient and accessible, allowing students to select and enroll in courses that align with their academic goals and program requirements.
registration_help: The exchange office
registration_success: In registering for classes, I encountered some challenges in securing all the courses I initially wanted. However, due to the variety of courses available, I was able to find suitable alternatives. It's worth noting that during the third block, options were limited, requiring me to select a course outside of my usual preferences. While I didn't get all my first-choice courses, I was ultimately able to construct a schedule that met my academic requirements and allowed for continued progress in my studies.
registration_advice: For future exchange students registering at my host institution, I would advise against loading up on courses solely in the first and second blocks due to the potentially overwhelming workload. It's beneficial to spread out your course load across all available blocks. Even if the options in the third block may not align perfectly with your preferences, consider selecting a course during that period to balance your workload and ensure a manageable schedule. Prioritizing a balanced course distribution can contribute to a more successful and manageable academic experience during your exchange program.
course_level: When considering the level of courses at the University of Amsterdam, it's important to note that the workload is notably higher compared to the University of Copenhagen. As such, I wouldn't recommend the University of Amsterdam to individuals who aren't organized or who prefer a less intensive study pace. However, for those who enjoy academic challenges and are willing to dedicate significant time to studying, the university offers valuable learning opportunities. The professors are deeply invested in their courses, providing a rich academic experience that can greatly enhance one's knowledge and skills in their chosen field
teaching_comparison: In comparing the style of teaching at my host institution with that of UCPH, there are notable differences. At the University of Amsterdam, classes tend to have fewer students, fostering a more intimate learning environment conducive to extensive discussions among both students and professors. Additionally, all classes are mandatory, and it's expected that students come prepared having completed the assigned readings. Unlike at UCPH, where there's more emphasis on individual responsibility for readings and attendance, failing to do the readings at the University of Amsterdam can significantly impact one's ability to participate effectively in class discussions and activities
courses_enrolled: - Imagining Technological Futures - Belief to Practice: Interpreting Religious Behaviour - Migration Lab
recommended_courses: When recommending specific courses to future exchange students, Imagining Technological Futures stands out as a top recommendation. This course offers a unique opportunity to explore innovative concepts and perspectives surrounding technology, providing valuable insights and fostering a new way of thinking about the subject matter. Beyond the content itself, the professor's approachability, kindness, and commitment to creating a supportive learning environment make the course particularly enriching. The inclusive atmosphere encourages growth, diverse perspectives, and alternative modes of learning, enhancing the overall educational experience for students
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: It was as expected.
activities_available: At my host institution, there were a variety of cultural, athletic, and social activities available for students, albeit with some shortcomings in orientation. While there were opportunities for athletic and social engagement, the orientation process regarding these activities was lacking. Despite this, students still had access to a range of events and initiatives designed to promote cultural exchange, physical activity, and social interaction. With improved orientation and guidance, these activities could play an even more significant role in enhancing the overall student experience at the institution.
activities_recommended: I did not really participate in any that was offered by the university.
weekend_recommendations: For visiting students looking to make the most of their weekends or holidays, I highly recommend purchasing a museums card and exploring other cities in the Netherlands. This card provides access to a wide range of cultural attractions, allowing students to immerse themselves in the rich history and heritage of the country. Additionally, venturing beyond the host city to explore different regions offers valuable insights into Dutch culture, architecture, and landscapes. Whether it's a day trip or a weekend getaway, exploring other cities is a fantastic way to enrich the exchange experience and create lasting memories.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture of my exchange site was remarkably easy, as the Netherlands shares many similarities with Denmark. The familiarity of cultural norms, values, and social customs facilitated a seamless transition and made me feel right at home. Whether it was navigating daily life or interacting with locals, the parallels between the two countries contributed to a smooth and enjoyable adjustment process
cultural_challenges: While adjusting to the local culture of my exchange site was generally smooth, I found one particular cultural difference challenging: the Dutch tendency to be more direct in communication compared to Danes. Getting accustomed to this straightforward communication style required some adjustment, as it contrasted with the more indirect approach common in Denmark. However, with time, I was able to adapt and appreciate the honesty and clarity that direct communication often brings to interactions.
culture_appreciated: One aspect of the culture that I most appreciated was the widespread proficiency in English and the highly international environment. The fact that nearly everyone was fluent in English made communication easy and accessible, eliminating language barriers and fostering a sense of inclusivity. Additionally, the diverse backgrounds and perspectives represented in the international community enriched the cultural experience, offering opportunities for cross-cultural exchange and collaboration
top3_advice: Be ready for a rigorous academic workload. - Expect to dedicate a significant amount of time to studying and coursework. - Prepare for challenging exams. Passing exams at my host institution may require substantial effort and preparation. - Consider bringing a coffee cup to school and utilizing your professor's ID card to access free coffee. This small tip can help you stay energized and save money while navigating the demands of academic life abroad.
other_useful_info: I do not think so
most_rewarding: The most rewarding aspect of my exchange experience was undoubtedly the vibrant international student environment. The presence of a diverse community of students from around the globe brought a wealth of perspectives and cultural insights to every interaction. Engaging with peers from different backgrounds enriched my academic and personal growth, fostering a deeper understanding of global issues and expanding my worldview.
greatest_challenge: The study load and exams.

crucial_aspects: I really found the courses at UvA interesting. And also that I haven't been in Amsterdam or the Netherlands before.
overall_comments: Of course it has been hard sometimes and I was surprised how much time I ended up using at the university, but I also found it really interesting and I feel that I have learned a lot! Being on exchange is a busy time with uni, friends and exploring and overall I feel that it ended up being much better than expected (even though I don't really know what I expected).
info_ease: I think UvA was really good at providing information and you always knew who to contact or ask if needed. So I think it was quite easy!
arrival_assistance: A got a lot of e-mails from the university - both before arrival and after arrival. The mails contained a lot of information about what steps should be done etc. They also hosted intro-meetings after arrival.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Of course it has been hard sometimes and I was surprised how much time I ended up using at the university, but I also found it really interesting and I feel that I have learned a lot! Being on exchange is a busy time with uni, friends and exploring and overall I feel that it ended up being much better than expected (even though I don't really know what I expected).
registration_process: You add the courses you want to a list divided on the different blocks (three blocks). You can choose courses that total 42 ECTS points - this is a good idea even though you only need 30 ECTS points since uni can't guarantee that you get all the courses you want/wished for. I ended up getting all courses so I deregistered the two courses I wanted the least and ended on 30 ECTS points:)
registration_help: Uni hosts an online info-meeting before course registration and you can also find information on their website.
registration_success: I ended up getting all courses I wanted - I even had to deregister a few. I found it pretty easy and it ended being a success.
registration_advice: Add a few more courses than you need to the list to make sure you will get enough courses - you can always deregister again.
academics_comments: Of course it has been hard sometimes and I was surprised how much time I ended up using at the university, but I also found it really interesting and I feel that I have learned a lot! Being on exchange is a busy time with uni, friends and exploring and overall I feel that it ended up being much better than expected (even though I don't really know what I expected).
course_level: I think the level was fine. I think we learn a bit more classical theory and methodology at UCPH. On the other hand I think they are a bit better to discuss and to be more 'modern' and address modern crises in the courses at UvA.
teaching_comparison: I found it quite different from UCPH. Of course we had lectures which were similar - however participation is more common and also more a part of the lectures than what I was used to. I had tutorials to every course (I was not used to that) and the teaching style was more discussing, 'playing' etc. The final grade also consists of different grades you got through different presentations or assignments throughout the course - so a bit more performance I would say.
courses_enrolled: Rethinking Sustainable Societies: New Perspectives (Course catalogue number 5512SSPB6Y), 6 ETCS points Love-Politics: Relationality, Futurity and Affect (Course catalogue number 7303S4004Y), 12 ECTS points Circular Economy (Course catalogue number 5512CIEC6Y), 6 ECTS points Degrowth (Course catalogue number 5512DEGR6Y), 6 ECTS points
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Circular Economy! Also Degrowth and Rethinking Sustainable Societies: New Perspectives. They were all interdisciplinary which was really interesting and fun to try!
unexpected_costs: Maybe I thought that grocery shopping would be a bit more cheap (as in Germany) - still cheaper than Denmark. Maybe I also experienced that I went out to drink coffee (and wine) more than I do at home (since it is cheaper). And also just a nice way to meet up with new friends:)
cost_comparison: Coffee and wine is extremely cheap compared to Denmark!
activities_available: Both creative activities and student athletics are available. At campus they also have some cafes. Some museums, cinemas etc. also have a students discount.
activities_recommended: Visit some of the many museums, go to the cinema and explore the nice and cheap cafes and bars in Amsterdam.
weekend_recommendations: In addition to go exploring Amsterdam I really enjoyed going on day- or weekend trips to other cities (Utrecht and Rotterdam) and also Belgium. It is very easy with the train and the FlixBus and not very far.
culture_adjustment: Amsterdam and Dutch culture in general are maybe not that different from Copenhagen and Danish culture. However, the Dutch people is maybe a bit more direct and less service minded. I also think there is some more competition and performance culture among students - even though they also do a lot of group work at uni. In addition, Amsterdam is very international and a lot of international students go to UvA. It makes it easy to adjust in a way.
socializing_tips: If you feel a good vibe with someone just ask if they want to grab coffee - or if you should do group work together. I feel like other students are curios about your home country as well and find it interesting to hear about exchange etc.
cultural_challenges: I missed rye bread a lot!! It rains A LOT. Sometimes the directness is a bit much. Bike helmets are NOT a thing at all - not even for children.
culture_appreciated: The cheap coffee and wine:) The directness and openness were also nice (sometimes the directness was a bit much). I also appreciate the biking culture (even though I think we are better at biking more safely in Denmark).
top3_advice: 1. There will be more assignments during the semester and you will maybe use a bit more time at uni than expected - but you will also be reading interesting stuff! (of course it also depends on who you are) I used the reading room at the library at campus a lot. 2. Go to the intro-week (even though the program is a bit weird) - it is a nice way to meet people! 3. There is a lot of things to do all the time - use the city. Also remember it is totally fair to feel the need to be alone and 'stand down' sometimes.
other_useful_info: The staff at uni is very helpful - use them if you have questions.
most_rewarding: I think I have learned a lot - both at uni-level but also personally. Also very exciting to meet people from all over the world!
greatest_challenge: To overcome linguistic insecurities - in the beginning I really tried to think every sentence I wanted to say in English through in my head. After a month I feel like this changed at I felt more relaxed and just talked.

crucial_aspects: Whether the university had interesting courses and researchers (that would teach the courses) in the field I was interested in (media). It was also important for me to go to a country that I could see myself have a future in both work-wise but also personally, if I would be interested in living and working in another country in the future.
info_ease: I think the UvA were really good at giving us the right information, and taking care of us exchange students when we arrived at the university. It was clear that they are used to students coming from abroad, which made it a very nice experience.

housing_how: I found housing on my own

I ended up having to register for random courses, since I didn't get the amount of courses that I needed in the first round, and by then most of the courses was filled up.
registration_help: UvA were very nice in helping me find available courses, so it was only information about the registration process that I needed more of.
registration_success: Not very as explained. I got 3 out of 5 courses I was interested in.
registration_advice: To register for all the courses you are interested in, and then see which of them you get, and then choose which of them you'll take.
course_level: I think the level was very suiting for the courses.
teaching_comparison: It was much less personal, there were different teachers each module in some of the courses, which I liked, since they were experts in that certain topic.
courses_enrolled: Global Digital Culture Privacy in Public Encountering the Americas: Latin America in the 21st century All-time bestsellers from Amsterdam The meaning of having children
recommended_courses: Definitely: Global Digital Culture Privacy in Public I think they were very interesting with super competent teachers. But generally I had very good experiences in each course.
unexpected_costs: There wasn't any unexpected costs, but it cost more to live there than I expected.
cost_comparison: Everything was generally more expensive. Grocery shopping, public transportation, and social life. So if you want to live in Amsterdam, you should prepare yourself that it will cost you a lot of money, that is not covered by Erasmus and SU (if you're from Denmark).
activities_available: I'm not quite sure, because I didn't really look into what the university offered. But my impression from others is that there were a lot of opportunities for different activities.
activities_recommended: Definitely doing the Erasmus intro week, I found a lot of great friends in that week.
weekend_recommendations: Go to other parts of the country as well – I enjoyed visiting Utrect. Otherwise, to use the city a lot, go for walks, check out what's new and happening. I followed a newsmagazine called AaMagazine, they posted a lot of great thing about what was happening in the city.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, Amsterdam was pretty similar to Copenhagen. But it's always difficult to adjust to a new city and country.
socializing_tips: Go to locations that are typically dutch, if you live in Amsterdam. Like local bars and restaurants outside of centrum.
cultural_challenges: Dutch people can be quite direct, which can seem a bit rude. But otherwise it was very similar to home.
culture_appreciated: Dutch people say things as they are. And they are very good at 'using' the city, so being in the city, going out for dinner and drinks and so on. So everywhere you go, there is a lot of people, which gives a really nice and warm feeling to the city.
top3_advice: Make sure to apply for enough courses. Make sure to save up enough money, it costs a lot to live in Amsterdam. Go to the Erasmus intro week, it gives you a really nice start to your stay. And arrive in the city in good time, so you can get settled before the intro-week begins, because it takes a lot of energy to socialize all the time.
other_useful_info: I don't think so, I think I've mentioned it all.
most_rewarding: Getting to know a new culture, meeting people from all over the world, and getting a break from your home-university, so I was filled with renewed motivation for my study field.
greatest_challenge: Being alone in a new country, without your friends and family, and the loneliness that comes with that experience.

weekend_recommendations: The museums of Amsterdam, the nightlife (Clubs, bars, etc.), Amsterdam also have really lovely parks and streets, so just walking around the city is very nice.
culture_adjustment: Danish and dutch culture seems quite similar, so it wasn't that much of a problem. The language is difficult to understand however, but even for this the university offers language courses.
socializing_tips: I had a hard time socializing with local students, and most of the people I met were also exchange students. But the ones I did meet were really easy to talk to.
cultural_challenges: The language, but other than that not much.
culture_appreciated: The people here are really friendly, and you always feel welcome wherever you go to.

most_rewarding: Getting to know people from all over the world, hearing their perspectives and experiences, and getting to know them.
greatest_challenge: Course registration was difficult, and I wrote a lot of e-mails back and forth with many different employees, but again, I received a lot of help.
other_comments: Enjoy your time, it is such a nice city and you will for sure have a great time!:))

crucial_aspects: When deciding on Amsterdam as my study destination, it was crucial for me that I went somewhere foreign but not too far removed geographically, I really liked the international profile of Amsterdam along with the dutch mentality. It was also important to me that I went somewhere I had never been before, such that I got exposed to somewhere entirely new. When going on exchange, this was my first time setting foot in Netherlands.
info_ease: Most things were provided for us. The exchange department has been very helpful in all requests and quick aswell.
arrival_assistance: Initially I did not have the need for much as most places and classes where easy to find. But I had some issues during the stay with selection of courses, I had not realized that their masters is 1 year, while ours is 2 years, this resulted in me not picking bachelor courses for the second of the 3 blocks. Thus only having 15 ects at first. But the exchange department here assisted me with picking courses that still had availability and our home exchange office were very good at guiding me. This being said, the information about the masters differing in course availability would have been great if communicated at first.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We had an information meeting in the first days and also Erasmus introduction. We went and picked up our student cards and explored the campus.
registration_help: The exchange office here was the biggest life saver. They were so helpful and quick in their responses.
registration_success: For the first part it went well. But I did not know i had to mix with bachelor courses. At first I registered only for first block masters courses, I though more courses would be available on the second round of applications, but due to the structure non where supplied. I had some issues with this that resulted in me having to pick the courses that were left. But it was all fine.
registration_advice: Check up on the rules and structure of the programs, especially if you are early in your masters. It can vastly differ, also inquire both home and host university for details on the structure. Our program was quite rushed as we had 6 exams, which ended early june
course_level: The level of the courses vastly differed. The masters' courses were occasionally quite advanced with new optimization methods being introduced. While some of the courses on the second part from the BA were very manageable. But due to the rushed time schedule I think they helped offset the stress a bit, making it a better experience.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. There were more of a expectation of participation here, with facilitated debates and case briefs being part of the curriculum. Also there were less assignments. This I very much enjoyed. However minimum bar is much higher here and the chances of flunking a courses if not well prepared are high. This should be a consideration, when taking into account that the schedule is very rushed and you commit to 30 ECTS passed. I've met other students from Europe that were only expected to pass 12-18 ECTS, so there is a stark difference, that will make a difference in how social you can be at times.
courses_enrolled: First block: - Economic Growth - Natural Resource Economics - Human Development Second block: - Investment and Portfolio Theory 2 - International Management - Industrial Organization
recommended_courses: Personally I really enjoyed, Economic Growth, Human Development and Industrial Organization. Economic growth was macro orientated and featured many different growth theories that were very interesting. We did not focus too much in on calculations and methods but were able to get a good overview of theories presented in a very good way. The professor was really good. Industrial Organization was a classic micro course, but all of the lecturers were so engaging and talented, this made it very enjoyable. Human Development was exciting, we had no assignments, only bi-weekly debates and one presentation. We explored a wide range of articles on different kinds of indicators of development and explored what kind of policies and actions through RCTS (also some of the lecturers research). This was very different from any class I've had at home and I thoughroughly enjoyed it, I can strongly recommend th

crucial_aspects: The Law Faculty at UvA is among the best in Europe which was important to me. Also, Amsterdam is just such a nice city to live in which was equally important.
info_ease: Very easy. Months before arrival UvA sets up a student e-mail where all the relevant information is provided.
arrival_assistance: All necessary information was provided on the e-mail and the dedicated staff were also super helpful during the entire stay.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Everything needed to register for courses is provided in due time. The registration process was intuitive and convenient and I did not face any problems during the process.
registration_help: The staff at UvA are always super helpful. Also, the UvA web-page is also helpful to get information on all relevant questions.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I signed up for. If you do not get all the courses that you registered for, there is an "eftertilmeldingsperiode" where you can perhaps get the course anyways. Many of the other students got the courses they wanted that way.
registration_advice: Nothing particular - as I said, it was fairly easy and straight-forward. The list of courses for exchange students can be found here: https://coursecatalogue.uva.nl/xmlpages/page/2023-2024-en/search-programme/programme/7324
course_level: In general, the courses were very theoretical and harder than at UCPH. Be aware that there are a lot of mandatory course materials and the work load was a lot higher than at the UCPH. The level of the exams appeared to be a bit easier than at UCPH. In almost all my courses, there were weekly hand-ins which was often a bit stressful.
teaching_comparison: The teaching at UvA is very interactive and encourages students to participate actively throughout the course. Generally, the courses are more "academic" and not as practical as what I am used to from UCPH. It took some time to adapt and get used to it, but it was a nice change and provided interesting insights.
courses_enrolled: Comparative Law, Advance Private Law in Context, Consumer Rights in the Digital Single Market, International Commercial Arbitration and European Contract Law.
recommended_courses: It depends on preferences. The first three mentioned courses were very theoretical and academic, whereas the last two were more practically minded. However, personally I enjoyed and would recommend both International Commercial Arbitration and Advanced Private Law in Context.
unexpected_costs: I signed up for a sports association through the University which was a bit expensive. Also, it is a good idea to rent a bike upon arrival. Course materials are often uploaded in Canvas, and it is thus not necessary to buy all the books which was nice.
cost_comparison: Amsterdam is an expensive city to live in. Rent on the private market was way more expensive than expected. Groceries and stuff like that is around the same price as in Denmark.
activities_available: Students were encouraged to sign up for different clubs. Some of my fellow students signed up for creative classes through the university. Personally, I signed up for a tennis class through the University which was very fun!
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining a club or signing up for an activity. As previously mentioned, the work load is very high at UvA, and I found it important to get a break from studying every once in a while. Also, Amsterdam is super rich in culture and has some amazing museums.
weekend_recommendations: One of my favourite activities was just walking around the city. The city is so beautiful - especially during the week where there are less turists (the amount of turists can be a bit overwhelming in the weekends). I would recommend to visit the Van Gogh museum, but tickets are often sold out and needs to be booked in advance.
culture_adjustment: Very easy - the Dutch people are very outgoing and friendly. Amsterdam is a very international city with many different cultures. Almost everyone speaks fluent English making it easy to communicate. All in all, I did not experience any issues adjusting to the culture.
socializing_tips: I mainly followed the MA programme "European Private Law" and the programme consisted of many different nationalities, and therefore I did not really get to meet many local students. However, the few I got to meet were very friendly. Always a good conversation starter to mention the bad weather (which is often even worse than in Denmark!).
cultural_challenges: Since the class-rooms were often very international with many different nationalities, there were many different cultures. However, I did not really experience any problems with cultural difficulties. All of the students were super friendly and nice regardless of nationality or culture.
culture_appreciated: The Dutch people are in many ways very much like the Danes, and it was therefore easy to get along with the locals. I really liked the biking culture.
top3_advice: 1. Be aware that the work load is a lot higher than at the UCPH which surprised me. It is important to be up-to-date on the readings as it will be difficult to catch up later. There is no time off for exam preparations. Also, it is common that you will have to do weekly assignments in all courses that need to be handed in. 2. If you are not offered student housing through the university, start looking for a room as soon as possible. Many students have to give up coming to Amsterdam because they simply did not start searching in due time. 3. If you have the option, I would advice to mix the courses between BA and MA courses, as MA courses appear to be much harder than the BA courses.
other_useful_info: UvA has really strict language requirements for being enrolled and you have to take a language test. However, if you take the 0 ECTS course "Legal English" at UCPH and has gotten 10 or higher in English A in High School, you can be exempt from the language requirements.
most_rewarding: My English skills have improved both written and orally which is really nice. But more important, it is super rewarding getting to work with people from other cultures that you would otherwise not be able to. It is also a great (and difficult) personal challenge moving to a new city and having to leave friends and family for a while.
greatest_challenge: Before the exchange, the biggest challenge was without a doubt finding housing which almost felt like a full-time job. During the exchange, it was challenging to adapt to another way of teaching than what I am used to. Since there were no time off before the exams, it was very difficult and stressfull to prioritize the time.
other_comments: I think it is important to flag, that an exchange in Amsterdam is not a "vacation". The courses are intense and the work loads are very high. However, if you like facing new academic challenges, I would highly recommend going to Amsterdam.

crucial_aspects: I picked my exchange destination based on my personal excitement about the Dutch culture, especially the lively Dutch way of life. The Dutch are known for their rich history and cool attitudes, while also not being fundamentally different from my Copenhagen lifestyle. The canals, the beautiful architecture and the location as a European hotspot inspired my final pick. On top of that, the chance to take advanced private law courses on UVA was a dream of mine. The many talented lecturers within the Master European Private Law (LLM) programme caught my intention already before choosing UVA, and I was eager to dig into the details of private law within this setting. Having international classmates and learning within a multinational academic community was a fantastic opportunity in my opinion.
overall_comments: My exchange trip to Amsterdam has been an overwhelmingly positive experience, filled with enriching moments that have left an mark on my personal and academic journey. One of the highlights has undoubtedly been the friendships formed along the way and developing friendships with people from all countries. However, the journey has not been without its challenges, particularly on the academic front. UvA's rigorous school curriculum and high expectations definitely tested my abilities and pushed me beyond my comfort zone. It was very challenging having to choose between friendships, experiences among others versus my studies. In conclusion, my exchange trip has been an overwhelmingly positive experience, marked by the formation of lasting friendships and a deep immersion into the Dutch culture. The academic challenges, while demanding, also contributed to my personal development.

One striking difference was UvA's emphasis on attendance and active participation; UvA placed greater expectations on regular attendance and active engagement in class discussions. This shift requires a recalibration of study habits and participation levels. The heightened expectations compelled me to be more disciplined in attending classes regularly and actively contributing to discussions.

I did find that the work load at school was very demanding and consequently, I didn't find the time to participate in such activities.
weekend_recommendations: To my fellow students, I wholeheartedly recommend Amsterdam as a must-visit destination. Firstly, I would recommend exploring the city by boat; strolling through neighborhoods like Jordaan, and discovering hidden gems in De Pijp. Secondly, the city is full of historical (and newer) museums. Most notably, the Rijksmuseum and the Anne Frank House, which are almost obligatory to visit. Overall, Amsterdam has a welcoming and open-minded atmosphere, which is evident when you visit the many cafes and night clubs. Amsterdam has a perfect balance of excitement and relaxation. It's a city that not only broadens your cultural horizons but also houses many night clubs and cool bars, if you're an outgoing and very social person.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture in Amsterdam was hard in the beginning due to the fact that Dutch people tend to keep to themselves. Initially, integration required effort. However, as I actively immersed myself in local activities, eg. joining cycle classes and yoga classes and visited local cafes with a book, the adjustment process became a bit smoother. In the beginning, I also found Amsterdam to be a great city to explore by yourself. Attending local markets, cultural festivals, and community gatherings with fellow exchange students also provided insight into the local way of life. I quickly established a weekend routine that included these activities, which overall helped me foster a sense of belonging. My number one tip would be to team up with fellow exchange students!
cultural_challenges: I found the Dutch people's mix of openness (or straightforwardness) and their tendency to keep them to themselves to be particularly challenging. While generally open and approachable, the Dutch also tend to maintain a degree of personal space and reserve, which initially posed a challenge in forming immediate connections with local people.
culture_appreciated: I most appreciated the unique aspects of Dutch culture and the everyday life. I cherished the local markets, which quickly became a weekend ritual. Overall, Amsterdam has a great ambiance with beautiful canals and historic architecture, which provided some "beauty" to the everyday life. Moreover, discovering local hotspots, such as hidden cafes and trendy neighborhoods like De Pjip or Oost added excitement to my stay. Clubbing and the social scene in Amsterdam were also highlights of my experience, and I really appreciated trying out the Dutch nightlife with fellow exchange students. The city boasts a diverse and inclusive club culture with a lot of techno scenes and aspiring DJs, which is different from the Copenhagen club culture, where the clubs can be quite similar.
top3_advice: 1) Prepare for Academic Rigor: Be ready for a higher level of academic intensity. The coursework might demand extensive reading and a deeper engagement with the subject matter. Ensure you're well-organized and manage your time effectively to meet the academic expectations. 2) Engage in Intro Activities: Attend the introductory activities offered by the host institution. I regret I didn't as this is an excellent way to establish a solid network of acquaintances early on. 3) Embrace Everyday Life in Amsterdam and UvA's Environment: Don't just focus on academics; immerse yourself in the vibrant everyday life of Amsterdam. Explore the local markets, cycle along the canals, and savor the unique atmosphere. Additionally, make the most of the environment at UvA; engage in extracurricular activities, join clubs, and participate in events to enrich your overall experience beyond the classroom.
other_useful_info: Opt for courses that align with your interests as you'll be dedicating a significant amount of time to studying.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding aspect of my exchange experience was probably - although it is a stereotypical answer - my personal growth. Immersing myself in a new culture, navigating different academic approaches, and forming connections with people from all over the world contributed significantly to my personal development. It was very rewarding to learn that you can establish a different life in a new city while meeting a lot of kind people. Enhancing my English skills was another rewarding aspect. Engaging in academic discussions, social interactions, and day-to-day communication in English not only refined my language proficiency but also boosted my confidence in English. Lastly, being in Amsterdam itself was a source of continuous reward. Exploring the city; strolling down the canals, biking to school, indulging in local cuisine (especially surinamese cuisine) and reading at cafes by myself, added value to my overall experience.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge I faced during the exchange was the academic rigor, with courses proving to be more challenging than anticipated. The workload, particularly the extensive reading and demanding assignments in International Investment Law and International Trade Law surpassed my initial expectations. The academic environment at my host institution demanded a higher level of engagement and dedication, requiring me to adapt quickly to the intensity of the coursework. It bears mention that I did choose Master courses only, which probably added to the work load. Balancing academic commitments with the desire to explore Amsterdam with other exchange students became quite a challenge as it required meticulous time management and prioritization. Despite the difficulty, overcoming these challenges added a layer of accomplishment to my exchange journey, contributing significantly to my academic development.

info_ease: I though it was a bit hard to navigate in all the mails with information from my home uni, the uni abroad and Erasmus. I though i got so many mails (some more relevant than others) and it was hard to know when the information was crusial or just good to know. And also a bit hard to remember, when wanting to look up the information, who the information was provied by.
arrival_assistance: The abroad uni was very good to send out news letters, where they had an event at uni called introduction to uni, that was very helpfull.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My university abroad was very structured and easy to adapt to, and the courses was very interesting. A little downside was that the uni required much more readings that i am used to.
registration_process: I could apply for 56 etcs point and then they made lottery and assigned me to courses of 30 etcs. I only got 24 etcs in first round and then i had to apply again in second round.
registration_help: They had a zoom meeting explaining how to do it which was very helpful. And it was possible to send mails and get quick replies!
registration_success: In the first round i only got 24 etcs of wanted courses, so for second round i had to apply again for a course of 6, and then i had to pick a course of the ones with free spots, and it was courses which did not really fit my field of study, so that was a bit unfortunate.
registration_advice: Be in contact with the exchange office at the abroad uni, they are very helpful, and can help make exceptions also.
academics_comments: My university abroad was very structured and easy to adapt to, and the courses was very interesting. A little downside was that the uni required much more readings that i am used to.
course_level: I found the level similar to the ones at KU, but they all required much more readings of scientific articles that i am used to.
teaching_comparison: I only had lectures, where as at KU im used to a mix of lectures and tutourials and classes.
courses_enrolled: Topic; Organisations in the media Education and work Topic; Political communication, campaigns and voters Topic; Always connected, youth, media and technology Topic; The language of strategic communication
recommended_courses: I would really recommend all of the topic courses: The language of strategic communication, Always connected, youth, media and technology, Organisations in the media, Political communication, campaigns and voters. They were all very relevant for the wants of working as a communication professional in the future. They used very recent examples and the lecturers were very competent and empathic and kind. They all had much readings but it was all mostly recent studies which made it very interesting readings.
unexpected_costs: Garbage tax being 140 euros payed once. Living far out i had to take public transportation more than i usually do.
cost_comparison: Expensive to use public transportation (more than in dk) Supermarked was probably the same, but maybe a bit less than dk, and then some specific things were more expensive Less expensive to go out for drinks and food (less than in dk)
activities_available: They had a whole day in the intro week telling about the all sports and opportunities at uni.
activities_recommended: I joined my local yoga studio, it was nice to have a routine when moving to another city.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going to the citys in the netherlands not far from Amsterdam; Utrecht, Rotterdam, Haag and Gent (in belgium).
culture_adjustment: Very easy, the culture in Amsterdam seems very similar to the danish culture.
socializing_tips: I did not really get any dutch friends at all. But it was super easy to get in contact with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: It is not a difference, but dutch people are a bit closed like danish people, and the studens spoke dutch to each other even though it was english lectures. This made it hard to get any dutch friends at lectures. But in generel Amsterdam is a very english speaking country, and it was super easy to get in contact with new people and getting new friends.
culture_appreciated: Making new friends, and experiencing how it is to create a new everyday in a new city.
top3_advice: Go to the introweek, it was there i made contact to the persons who became my friends at the stay. Rent a bike so you can get around. Use the provided study halls at uni they are very nice.
other_useful_info: That the exchange office and service helpdisk at uni are very helpful and quick to reply. And also that the lecturers are very kind and helpful too.
most_rewarding: The academic gain from my courses have been crucial to the direction i want to go further in my studies and carreer. Getting new friends. Being forced to practice my english, being more comfortable speaking english even though i still do gramma mistakes and have a danish accent.
greatest_challenge: Getting new friends while speaking english.
