crucial_aspects: A city where I knew a lot would be happening so I wouldn't be lonely and would still be fun even if the classes didn't live up to my expectations.
info_ease: UVA did well in informing you beforehand about what you needed to know in terms of practical things with moving to Amsterdam and are somewhat quick to respond to e-mails.
arrival_comments: Their examination system is way less streamlined than at UCPH - it took some effort to figure out the demands to pass from class to class.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: For your own sake, listen to their recommendation of doing 2-2-1 in the three blocks. I did 3-2-0, and my study pressure in the first block was really intense (it's 18 ECTS in two months including exams). I managed and passed, but if you're able to take a class in block 3, I'd probably say that's a good idea.
registration_help: Just e-mail them if you have any doubts - I didn't understand what courses were available to me at first but got help from someone who could explain it quite well.
registration_success: Very - except from the scheduling overlap.
registration_advice: What I said above - if possible: follow their guidelines in terms of study pressure.
course_level: Some of them were way above my level - even though I was allowed to sign up for them. My advice would be to keep in mind that if you're an MA-student and sign up for MA-courses outside of your own field (which you'll probably have to do at UVA since their MA course catalogue is limited), do keep in mind that you'll be thrown right into a course where everyone might've already been studying that field on their MA for a year or a half, and you're expected to keep up. UVA does so many assignments and midterms apart from just the final exams, so you constantly have to hand things in (or do presentations) which means that not understanding the material from week to week isn't reaaally an option. You have to both be constantly on track + do your final paper/exam. With that being said, in my experience the profs were also really nice, understanding and helpful in terms of guiding for final paper topics when you let them know that you were a bit out of your comfort zone. And at the end of the day I did pass all of my courses, some of them just took quite some effort.
teaching_comparison: Very different - at UCPH I'm used to a more personal teaching style where the prof for example knows your name and you have more seminars. At UVA my experience was, in some classes at least, that you felt more anonymous + I had more lectures.
unexpected_costs: The only thing was a water bill, but that's manageable. However, not a cost but unexpected: you might be eligible to apply for Dutch housing support for your stay!! Definitely look into that cause that's a great financial help.
cost_comparison: Going out + cafes were in general less expensive than at home, but then on the other hand I usually met up with my friends out which becomes quite expensive. My advice would be to save up beforehand and apply for scholarships if you have the time, cause in my experience, once you're in Amsterdam you want to be out in the city - and there are also tons of cultural events such as concerts, plays and so on to experience which also cost money. There are good youth/student discounts for cultural events though.
activities_recommended: Participate in the ESN introduction days to meet people! Even though the activities aren't that great and it's 80 euros or something - but you don't want to miss out on meeting your first friends there.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy - I think the most difficult part was to adjust to the academic culture with the block system and all the assignments and different examination system.
socializing_tips: It's definitely easier to socialize with other exchange students, but with the locals you should just make sure to exchange contact information before the class is over if you meet someone nice and then you can ask if they wanna study together one day and take it from there. It surely is more difficult because they already have their lives and friend groups established, but it is possible, and it's really fun because they know the city better.
top3_advice: Sign up for the housing lottery. Save up money before you go. Adjust your academic expectations - you're gonna have a lot of work to hand in on your MA at UVA, and you're not gonna have time to do well in everything if you also want to enjoy the wonderful city that Amsterdam is with the lovely friends you're gonna make.
most_rewarding: The friends I made and the experience in general of being able to move to a place where you don't know anyone or anything and establishing a really nice every day life there.
greatest_challenge: Dealing with the exams, assignments and the block system - veryyy different from UCPH with few classes and big projects for exams.
other_comments: Make sure in the beginning to take any opportunity to meet people!! I went to the ESN intro days, and even though they were 82 euros and the activities were not fun, it was very important that I went cause I met my very first (and some of my best) friends there. Just power through the awkwardness of it all cause you'll meet people that's for sure.

crucial_aspects: Many universities have a limited supply of courses taught in English. In Amsterdam, I was sure that they were good at speaking English, making it a safe choice with regards to the courses at the university.
info_ease: Very easy. You receive emails about every action you have to do. There is a very helpful exchange office at UvA that you can ask anything if you need help.
arrival_assistance: Again, the exchange office was very helpful. They could either provide the help themself or guide you to the correct place for help.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You received emails with good descriptions on what to do next. The deadlines were clearly indicated.
registration_help: The exchange office at UvA was very helpful.
registration_success: It was very easy. UvA sent a list that I had to fill within a week. I chose to change one course during my exchange, but that wasn't a problem at all.
registration_advice: Just make sure to check your email and follow the deadlines, then everything is quite easy.
course_level: The master at UvA is only one year, so it was quite intense being there for the first half year of their entire master. There's a lot of group work, and many presentations (compared to University of Copenhagen) which are there to make sure you work during the semester and not just before the exam. This can be a little stressful as an exchange student, as I didn't care about getting good grades, but just wanted to pass the courses. But it is a policy of the university so there's not a lot to do about it. With that being said, I think the teachers at UvA were really good and the quality of the courses was quite high (about the same as at UCPH).
teaching_comparison: A lot of group work and presentations at UvA.
courses_enrolled: Macroeconomics, Microeconomics and Game Theory, International Economic Cooperation, Behavioral Economics, Public Economics, Climate Change Economics.
recommended_courses: In general, the teachers at UvA are really good and motivated. I especially enjoyed the courses: Behavioral Economics, Public Economics, and Climate Change Economics. These are some topics that I find very interesting.
unexpected_costs: Not really any. But you have to be aware that you have to pay quite a large deposit in advance of getting your student housing (around 10,000 DKK + 1,5 months of rent).
cost_comparison: The supermarket and restaurants are a bit cheaper than Denmark. The public transport is based on how many km you travel. Since I lived a little outside the city, I think it was a little expensive to travel with public transport to the city. Most of the time, I used my bike that I rented at Swapfiets.
activities_available: A lot, but I didn't participate in much.
activities_recommended: Try to join one of the sports courses that they have. It's quite cheap, a fun way to try a new sport and meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: Enjoy the city, but also try to take daytrips to other parts of the country.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The Dutch are quite similar to the Danish.
cultural_challenges: Not really any.
culture_appreciated: They are very open compared to Danes. It's easy to start a conversation with a stranger (also because everyone is really good at English).
top3_advice: Don't know
other_useful_info: Not really.
most_rewarding: Experiencing being "all alone" in a different country. It is not as hard as one could fear. It is a fun challenge and you realize that everything will be alright in the end.
greatest_challenge: Same as above.

crucial_aspects: I've been in Amsterdam quite a lot because of familyy loving there, and have always felt a big connection to the city. So going there on exchange was the perfect opportunity for me to try and live there.

arrival_assistance: There was a science introduction day at campus that really helped in getting an overview of everything. I also met some great people that day
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

cost_comparison: Everything is cheeper in Amsterdam compared to Copenhagen
activities_available: All sorts
activities_recommended: CREA is a great place to do all sorts of creative stuff from dancing to painting
weekend_recommendations: There are sooo many things to do in Amsterdam, just get a bike and explore
culture_adjustment: very easy, I felt at home already a few hours after arrival
socializing_tips: Do a minor
cultural_challenges: The language is silly and I never learned it
culture_appreciated: The art scene, concerts, theaters, clubs, bars, community kitchens, squads, jazz. Its amazing
top3_advice: Do some easy courses so you have time to have fun. Go to the introduction week, it's a great way to meet people. Be open to everything.
other_useful_info: Just have patience in the beginning. It takes time to adapt and to meet the right people. But you'll get there and then its gonna most amazing months
most_rewarding: Amsterdam is very multicultural, and Ive met so many different people from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: You really have to get out of your conform zone and talk to people if you wanna make friends.. But its great and you learn so much from it!
other_comments: Just go!!!!

crucial_aspects: A crucial aspect in choosing my study destination was finding a university that offered a good study program closely aligned with my academic interests and career goals. I wanted a program that combined strong theoretical foundations with practical applications, providing both academic depth and relevant skills for the job market
info_ease: The process was a bit confusing and felt somewhat unstructured. It took some time to figure out where to find the necessary information, as there wasn’t a clear overview or central source for new arrivals.
arrival_assistance: Nothing really. There wasn’t much direct assistance offered upon arrival, so I had to manage most things on my own and figure them out gradually.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process was quite straightforward. I mainly had to get a document signed and approved by the university, which confirmed my course selections. Overall, the process was simple but not very detailed in terms of guidance.
registration_help: There was a career center where I think you could ask questions or get some assistance with academic or administrative matters. However, I didn’t make much use of it myself.
registration_success: I was able to register for all the classes I wanted without any major issues. The process went smoothly once the registration opened.
registration_advice: Make sure to pick the classes you’re genuinely interested in and confirm that they fit your schedule early on. It’s a good idea to double-check course requirements and get everything signed as soon as possible to avoid last-minute issues.
course_level: I took a mix of courses, including three at the master’s level and three at the bachelor’s level. The master’s courses were more research-oriented and required deeper analytical work, while the bachelor’s courses focused more on foundational theory and practical applications. Overall, the workload was balanced but slightly more demanding than expected.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was more interactive, with a stronger focus on class engagement and student participation. There were also more presentations and group discussions compared to UCPH, which made the classes feel more dynamic and collaborative.
courses_enrolled: Economic Growth Neuroeconomics Industrial Organisation International Business International Management
recommended_courses: I would recommend taking International Business and International Management. Both courses were taught by very knowledgeable professors who encouraged active participation and critical thinking. There were also plenty of class debates and discussions, which made the learning experience more engaging and helped develop a global perspective on business-related topics.
unexpected_costs: Traveling around turned out to be more expensive than I expected. While local transportation was affordable, longer trips and weekend getaways added up quickly, especially when factoring in accommodation and activities.
cost_comparison: Food and public transport were both less expensive than I expected. Groceries and meals at local places were quite affordable, and public transportation was reliable and reasonably priced compared to what I’m used to.
activities_available: Pretty much same selection as UCPH
activities_recommended: I played tennis during my exchange, which was a great way to stay active and meet new people. However, I’d recommend that future students choose activities that match their own interests — whether it’s sports, student clubs, or local events — since it’s one of the best ways to connect with others and experience the local culture.
weekend_recommendations: I’d definitely recommend traveling around the Netherlands. The country is easy to explore by train, and there are so many charming cities and cultural spots to visit. Places like Utrecht, Rotterdam, and The Hague are all worth seeing, and weekend trips give a great sense of the local culture.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy to adjust. People were friendly, open-minded, and spoke excellent English, which made daily life and communication very smooth. I felt welcome from the beginning.
socializing_tips: Just be yourself and stay open to meeting new people. I found everyone I met to be kind, polite, and easy to talk to. Joining group activities or student events is also a great way to connect with local students naturally.
cultural_challenges: The Dutch can be quite reserved at first, which sometimes made it a bit challenging to get to know people right away. However, once you start talking to them, they are friendly and direct, which I came to really appreciate.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the food and the overall lifestyle. People seemed to value balance and enjoy a relaxed pace of life, with time for socializing, outdoor activities, and good meals.
top3_advice: 1. Have fun and make the most of your time abroad. 2. Don’t be afraid to reach out and talk to new people — everyone is open and welcoming once you start a conversation. 3. Take time to travel around and experience different parts of the Netherlands; it’s an easy and rewarding way to explore the country.
other_useful_info: Rent a bike on the very first day. It makes getting around so much easier and helps you feel like part of the local culture right away. Biking is the main mode of transportation, and it’s both convenient and fun.
most_rewarding: The friendships I made were definitely the most rewarding part. Meeting people from different backgrounds and cultures gave me new perspectives and made the whole experience much more meaningful.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge was participating in debates and public speaking in a foreign language. It took some time to build confidence, but it was also a valuable learning experience that helped improve my communication skills.

crucial_aspects: For my choice of destination, it was crucial that I could combine a good study environment with a high level of academic quality.
info_ease: I remember it as quite easy. But I believe that it is always a bit difficult finding information at University websites other than the one you are used to.
arrival_assistance: The exchange coordinators were ready to welcome us at the University on the first day.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I was quite easy. The university sent us emails every time we needed to take action or register somewhere, which made the whole process easier. The entire course registration portal was also easy to use, and we were guided through it. However, it was a bit difficult to understand the university’s block system. It was divided into three blocks, but there were only courses available for exchange students in two of them. This caused confusion during the registration process and was also not ideal in terms of course planning in the block where we had to overload in order to reach our required ECTS.
registration_help: The exchange coordinators were very helpfull to answer questions through mail.
registration_success: The registration process was very easy. I had one course i wanted but didn't get due to limited seats.
registration_advice: Take the time to familiarize yourself with it, and if possible, discuss it with other exchange students from your home university. It can be a bit confusing to navigate on your own when it’s not something you’re used to.
course_level: The courses were quite a bit more difficult than expected, and there wasn’t really any consideration given to whether you were an exchange student or not. This put a lot of pressure on the exams, as it took quite a lot just to pass. It was a bit of an unfortunate ending that the majority of the exchange group had to resit at least one exam. If you choose UvA, you should definitely be prepared for some challenging courses.
teaching_comparison: They were pretty similar. Seminars and lectures. Some course were only lectures, but otherwise it was quite the same.
courses_enrolled: European Company Law Foundations of European Competition Law Private International law European Human Rights Law International Refugee Law
recommended_courses: Private International Law definitely. It was a pretty rough course but definitely the course I got the most out of.
unexpected_costs: Different taxes i.e. wastetax, watertax etc.
cost_comparison: Transportation were definitely more expensive than expected.
activities_available: i don't know - non that I know of
activities_recommended: Can't recommend anything unfortunately
weekend_recommendations: Arrange small trips around the country or countries nearby
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Amsterdam is very similar to Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: Unfortunately not, I only socialized with my exchange group
cultural_challenges: Non
culture_appreciated: The beautiful canals
top3_advice: Be open minded, don't go to easy on the courses, explore the city.
other_useful_info: The level of the courses. Don't choose UvA if you want it 'easy'.
most_rewarding: The people you meet!
greatest_challenge: Getting trough the courses. It was though, but I got through the challenge.

The only thing that was a bit difficult was how many exams there are at University of Amsterdam (UvA), because you have a lot of small courses of 6 ECTS, and many of those have midterm exams too.

arrival_assistance: I attended the welcome introduction lecture, but did not use any assistance.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was a really nice experience overall. It was such a good way to meet people from many different countries, and try to live in a different country. The only thing that was a bit difficult was how many exams there are at University of Amsterdam (UvA), because you have a lot of small courses of 6 ECTS, and many of those have midterm exams too.
registration_process: It is very easy to register for classes at UvA. You use the platform Glass, which is very simple, and it even show you how many spots are still available for the specific courses.
registration_help: In the online introduction for UvA they explained how to register for courses.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I registered for.
registration_advice: Look into which courses you can take in good time, so you are ready when the course registration starts.
academics_comments: It was a really nice experience overall. It was such a good way to meet people from many different countries, and try to live in a different country. The only thing that was a bit difficult was how many exams there are at University of Amsterdam (UvA), because you have a lot of small courses of 6 ECTS, and many of those have midterm exams too.
course_level: The level of education at UvA was in general very good, though it did vary quite a bit between courses. Some of them were fairly easy while others could be quite demanding with a lot of mandatory tutorials, assignments and both midterm and final exams. The professors were really good at lecturing in general. They seemed passionate about their field of study
teaching_comparison: It was similar, but I think it is a bit more focused on tutorials at UvA. And they expect the students to participate actively a lot in those classes, which can both be fun but also demanding at times. There was also more mandatory classes and quite a few assignments in some of the courses.
courses_enrolled: To get transferred as Work and Organizational Psychology: - Lifelong Learning: personal, organizational and societal perspectives - Current Topics: Equity, Diversity and Inclusion in the Workplace - Education & Work To get transferred as Advanced Research Design: - Social Research Methodology Elective course: - Intersectionalities: Race, Gender, and Sexuality
recommended_courses: My elective course "Intersectionalities: Race, Gender, and Sexuality" was such an interesting course, that I enjoyed thoroughly. The professor was very good, and we touched on discourses, social constructivism, colour-blindness, racialization, gender performativity (Judith Butler) and much more. The course "Current Topics: Equity, Diversity and Inclusion in the Workplace" was also pretty interesting. (I cannot recommend the course "Social Research Methodology". It had a big workload and they are very strict with grading).
unexpected_costs: Even though my phone should have the same data in thes rest of EU as in Denmark, it stopped working after 2 months, because more than half of the time within 4 months cannot be outside of Denmark, so that was an unexpected expense that I then had to get a dutch SIM and mobile subscription.
cost_comparison: Coffee was really expensive at most cafés. Eating out can also be very expensive.
activities_available: There is the USC sports club that is cheap for students, and they have a lot of different sports. I really enjoyed doing pilates classes there. And at Roeterseiland campus (the biggest UvA campus), there is the CREA café where some creative social events also take place.
activities_recommended: This place called Mezrab hosts open-mic story telling events on Wednesday’s which is a really fun experience. Besides that I also really enjoyed going to museums. With the museums pass that cost €75, you can get access to most museums across the Netherlands. There’s a lot of good ones in Amsterdam, but it is also nice when visiting other cities.
weekend_recommendations: Travelling. There is a lot of nice cities in the Netherlands besides Amsterdam (e.g. Utrecht, Haarlem, Leiden, Maastricht). Besides that it also only takes a few hours to get to Belgium, Northern France or West Germany. There is so much to see, and it is very easy to find people to travel with. And solo travelling can also be a nice experience.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The culture is pretty similar to the Danish culture with biking, partying, people keeping to themselves, not being that formal with professors etc.
cultural_challenges: I do not think anything was challenging in regards to cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: The biking
top3_advice: 1. There will be a lot of exams. It can be nice to look into what kind of exams (including midterms) your courses will have and prepare for the workload accordingly 2. There is no academic quarter at UvA 3. The resit exams for courses that end in December or January are not until in the Spring, so make sure to pass those.
other_useful_info: There are several campuses and depending on which courses you take you might have classes at two different ones in a row. So it can be difficult to make it in time. Biking is the fastest way to get from one to another.
most_rewarding: Meeting other exchange students from all over the world. It is so interesting and fun to learn about each others cultures.
greatest_challenge: Finding a balance between exploring Amsterdam, travelling and studying

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne et sted hen, der ikke var for langt væk fra Danmark, men samtidig føltes nyt og spændende. Derudover ville jeg gerne gå på et universitet, der udbød nogle interessante fag.
info_ease: Det var helt fint nemt, der var ikke nogle nødvendige informationer, jeg manglede. Dog skal man selvfølgelig være proaktiv og selv sørge for, at være opdateret.
arrival_assistance: Jeg fik ikke nogen officiel assistance, men det var heller ikke så nødvendigt. Alle de informationer, jeg skulle bruge, modtog jeg på mail. Jeg talte meget med andre, jeg mødte, der skulle gå på samme universitet som mig, og fik derved hjælp.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Man skal først orientere sig i universitetets kursuskatalog. Derefter melder man sig på de fag, man finder interessante og som udbydes på det rette tidspunkt, og så er det en lodtrækning, der bestemmer om man kan tage det. Det er et koorderingsarbejde, så man skal holde tungen lige i munden, når man skal finde ud af, hvornår kurserne udbydes, og om man kan tage dem.
registration_help: Kursuskataloget er nemt at orientere sig i, og derudover sidder der nogle søde mennesker hos universitetet og besvarer mails med alle de spørgsmål, man end måtte have.
registration_success: Jeg fik alle de fag, jeg havde ønsket.
registration_advice: Vær grundig! Det kan betale sig. Tjek at der ikke er nogle af dine fag, der overlapper - undervisningen er obligatorisk at deltage i for at bestå.
course_level: Jeg tog mit 5. semester af min bachelor på udveksling, derfor tog jeg kun BA fag. Fagenes niveau var meget BA-passende.
teaching_comparison: Der var to væsentlige forskelle. Først og fremmest var der blokstruktur på UvA, hvilket jeg ikke er vant til herhjemme. Det skal man lige vænne sig til! Derudover er de meget bange for AI, og ens viden bliver derfor hele tiden testet - gennem sit in-eksaminer og opgaver i løbet af undervisningen. Jeg oplevede ikke nogle skriftlige eksaminer, som mindede om dem, jeg er vant til i DK, men to mundtlige eksaminer og tre sit in / multiple choice eksaminer.
courses_enrolled: Love is a Bitch: Romance, Sexuality, and Desire in Popular Culture Cities and Change Amsterdam: Sensing the City Mindfulness across the lifespan Capstone: Interdisciplinary Literature Review
recommended_courses: Love is a Bitch-kurset var super fedt! Derudover synes jeg også, at mindfulness-kurset var spændende.
unexpected_costs: Jeg oplevede ikke nogle uforudsete udgifter.
cost_comparison: Det er dyrt at handle ind - meget samme prisniveau som i DK. Dog (lille tip): det er super billigt at gå i biografen, jeg vil særligt anbefale et CineVille medlemskab.
activities_available: Der var alverdens mulige aktiviteter, men jeg deltog ikke i dem, så jeg var ikke så godt orienteret omkring disse.
activities_recommended: Min veninde gik til basketball gennem universitetet og var meget glad for dette!
weekend_recommendations: Helt sikkert en tur til Utrecht - totalt hyggelig lille by. Derudover er mit bedste tip faktisk ikke at lave noget særligt - gå ture, sid på en café og kig på mennesker, gå på museum. Sådan oplever man ifølge mig byen bedst.
culture_adjustment: Meget nemt. Mindede utrolig meget om København.
cultural_challenges: Jeg synes i det hele taget, at både Holland og hollænderne minder meget om os selv. Der er ikke de helt store forskelle at tage højde for - udover at de cykler endnu mere crazy, end vi gør herhjemme, så man skal være obs, når man begiver sig ud i trafikken!
culture_appreciated: Hvor gode folk er til at mødes i det offentlige rum - de har en helt anden cafékultur end herhjemme, og det er super hyggeligt. Og deres markedskultur! Der er altid gode markeder i nærheden, særligt lørdag, søndag og mandag.
top3_advice: 1. Niveauet er højt på UvA, så det er ikke et "afslappende" udvekslingsophold, man skal se frem til. 2. Hollænderne er fantastiske til engelsk, så du får trænet dette - og lad vær med at stresse over at lære hollandsk, med mindre du synes, det er sjovt. 3. Udnyt de aktiviteter (såsom eksempelvis CREA), som universitetet udbyder, og kom til introdagene!
other_useful_info: Nej.
most_rewarding: Den selvstændighed, man tilegner sig på udveksling - man kan mere, end man tror, alene. Derudover selvfølgelig vennerne!
greatest_challenge: Helt sikkert at være væk hjemmefra. Det er noget, man skal vænne sig til.

crucial_aspects: Amsterdam is a very international city and known for being welcoming for international students. At the same time, the anthropology department ranks number 13 in Europe, which makes it one of the best places to study anthropology. The Netherlands is only 12 hours away with flixbus, which made it easy for people to visit me. Moreover, the city reminds me a lot of Copenhagen, but just in a slightly bigger version, so it was easy to feel at home.
overall_comments: Amsterdam and UvA is worth it! Go there!
info_ease: Very easy. The first week is an introduction week where the university provides a lot of information, and the same goes for the ESN introduction week, where you meet other Erasmus students, that are as confused as you are.
arrival_assistance: I was in contact via mail with the outgoing students' office, and they respond really fast. Apart from that UvA had sent 5-6 welcome mails beforehand, which provided a lot of information. In the introduction week we got a full tour of campus, and in the introduction days we also got a tour through the city, as well as some of the other campuses.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Amsterdam and UvA is worth it! Go there!
registration_process: It's some time ago now, but I think it was quite easy. As far as I remember, you have to register in SIS, and also get a UvAID. They messed up my birthday so I couldn't get access in the beginning, but after some calls it got fixed. KU takes weeks to respond, the UvA only takes days...
registration_help: Mails, their website, you can call the office.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. There was one course that I didn't get into in the first round, but after applying in the second round, I got it. So I was 10/10 successful.
registration_advice: Choose 12 credits in the first block, 12 in the second, 6 in the last- otherwise the workload will be too big.
academics_comments: Amsterdam and UvA is worth it! Go there!
course_level: I had not seen that I had applied for the bachelor thesis writing course, so I ended up having to write a form of bachelor thesis. The "theme courses" in anthropology are the third year anthropology student's bachelor thesis courses. They have two of these and together they make up their bachelor thesis. So the level was really intense, but so so interesting to be a part of. And well, now I have done a trial run of writing a bachelor thesis before actually having to writing it at KU. I took a first year musicology course, and the level here was quite easy, but since it was a whole other subject, it was also challenging at times. All courses are engaging the students the whole time.
teaching_comparison: The teaching is a lot more engaging. You really have to engage with and read all the texts for the classes. In one of my courses I was asked to write a weekly reading response where I summed up all the readings from the week and made my own argument based on this (a form of mini essay). I had to hand that in every Friday at 5pm. In my other course, I had to upload extensive discussion questions for the texts every Monday before the lecture, also providing an answer to your own question, with an argument. In my two other courses, we were asked to do weekly presentations, and in the other I had to do weekly group work. So you were kept engaged through the whole course. Expect a lot of time spent on uni. People actually sit there and reads until 9pm in the evening, which also means that the campus is generally more alive. There are a lot of good study spaces (not like CSS). In my course "Worlds in transition" we never went over what the texts were about, but had to directly use them. Since we were only 12 people in the class, you had to had read the texts and truly discuss and use them.
courses_enrolled: Worlds in transition: Rethinking Life in Times of Ecological Crisis Social Transformations in China Introduction to Cultural Musicology Environment & International Sustainable Development
recommended_courses: Worlds in Transition! Or any other course with Cristobal Bonelli. If you are interested in thinking abstract and getting your whole worldview changed, this would be a good match. It was like taking part in the Death Poets Society. Social transformations in China was also really interesting, and since I didn't really know anything about China, I learned a lot from it. And you also get to use your qualitative skills, by interviewing a person related to China for your essay in the end. Environment and International Development is a really intense four week course in January, and I really liked it.
unexpected_costs: I had bought a bike when I arrived, but it did not work, so I sold it again and had to rent a swapfiets, but I can recommend renting a bike from swapfiets. It is worth.
cost_comparison: Groceries are the same as in DK. Housing is really expensive, but that was what I expected. The technoclubs can be expensive sometimes.
activities_available: All kinds of stuff. Go look at CREA, they have all types of courses. Also take a look at USC, you can do all kinds of sports there. I took house dancing classes and met some of my best friends in Amsterdam. I also went bouldering and can really recommend that (they have three saunas at USC that you also get access to when bouldering. You are welcome;)).
activities_recommended: All the courses at CREA. You meet people who are based in Amsterdam, and in this way get a bit out of your erasmus bubble. Also go to the technoclubs or to some house events. Amsterdam is known for its house and techno scene. Go to ADE events. Check out Volkshotel, all kinds of stuff happens here. Every month the biggest flea market in Europe happens in IJ Hallen. Remember cash. Go take the free ferry to North. Go to the Ceuvel, a place where they have a lot of events and also a cute coffee that have implemented Degrowth-theory in praxis.
weekend_recommendations: Go see the other cities: Rotterdam, Utrecht, Den Haag. Go to all the cute Amsterdam cafes. Buy the Museumskaart! I often went to Huis Marseille and also FOAM- if you are into photography these are nice places. Go to the technoclubs: Tillatec, LOFI. And keep away from Rembrandtplein and Leidseplein. Except for Cafe de Alto, and Soceitit de Kring at Leidseplein- they are cool jazz places. There are also Bimhuis who has free jam sessions on Tuesdays. Go to Mezrab, a culture house where there is free storytelling nights on Wednesdays and Fridays. Ice skating at Jaap Eden in the Winter. Or ice skating in Museumsplein. I could keep going, but I will miss it too much if I keep writing. Just go to Amsterdam. It is really really worth it.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. It is like Copenhagen in many ways. Just more canals. And less serviceminded people in the cafes. Same weather (maybe even a bit better). No rye bread but the best bake-off section in Jumbo and Albert Heijn. If you know some German and English you are good to go; Dutch is a weird blend of this, and everyone speaks English.
socializing_tips: Ask if they want to drink a beer or cup of coffee with you. 1-2-3 you have met a potential friend.
cultural_challenges: Sometimes they can be a bit direct. They use their ring bell loud and clear. If you bike in the wrong place you will get a curse thrown after you- oftentimes something about your grandparents and cancer in Dutch.
culture_appreciated: The imaginative spaces that seem to emerge everywhere in Amsterdam. It seems like everything could be possible in this city.
top3_advice: Rent a bike from Swapfiets. Take a Crea course. Go out in the city and emerge yourself in it as much as possible- you can sleep when you get back to Cph.
other_useful_info: It can be really hard to leave again.
most_rewarding: Gaining academic motivation as well as getting really good friends. I thought this time would feel like a parenthesis, but I have rarely felt more alive.
greatest_challenge: Registration with the muncipality. My contract was a mess so it took me three times before I could register.

crucial_aspects: For me, the most important thing when choosing a study destination was academic relevance. I knew quite early on that I wanted to move in the direction of social data science / computational social science, both because I’m interested in the field itself and because I plan to apply for the Master’s in Social Data Science at KU. So I really wanted an exchange where the courses would actually matter for that path, and not just be “nice to have”. I spent quite a lot of time researching different universities and destinations, both in Europe and outside Europe, to see where you could study something close to social data science at bachelor level. I quickly realised that there are surprisingly few full bachelor programmes in this field. That’s why the University of Amsterdam stood out to me: it offers one of the first bachelor programmes in Europe fully focused on Computational Social Science. Even though the programme is still quite new, it felt like a unique chance to really explore the field and see how it works in practice. Besides the academic side, the city itself mattered a lot. Amsterdam felt like a place where I would genuinely enjoy living for a semester. In many ways it reminded me of Copenhagen. That made it feel like a safe but still exciting choice, and it turned out to be a very nice place to live and spend everyday life. I also considered options outside Europe, especially in the US, where there are strong academic environments in related fields. In the end, though, I’m very happy that I stayed in Europe and chose Amsterdam. Even if parts of the academic experience didn’t fully live up to my expectations, the overall experience – especially socially and personally – made it a really worthwhile exchange.
overall_comments: Overall, my exchange was an absolute blast, and I genuinely loved it. Coming home afterwards was surprisingly emotional, which I think says a lot about how meaningful the experience was for me. What really made the exchange special was the social and experiential side of it — meeting people, building friendships, living in a new city, and just being part of something different for a few months. The reason I wouldn’t give the exchange a full 10 out of 10 is mainly because of the academic experience, which for me was more disappointing than expected. That said, I also realised quite quickly that an exchange is not primarily about academics. It’s about everything around it. The courses are part of the experience, but not the main reason you go — and once I accepted that, I enjoyed the exchange much more. Academically, the programme I followed was very demanding in terms of time, with frequent small assignments, a lot of compulsory group work, and a very tight weekly structure. Personally, I found this quite frustrating at times, especially compared to what I was used to at KU. However, this didn’t take away from the overall experience in the end. If I had to give one piece of advice, it would be: go on exchange for the people, the city, and the experience. If you do that, the exchange can be incredibly rewarding — and for me, it definitely was.
info_ease: Overall, it was very easy. The University of Amsterdam is extremely well organised when it comes to welcoming exchange students. If anything, there was almost too much information at times — but that’s definitely a good thing. I received a lot of emails and practical information before arrival, which meant that even if I felt a bit stressed beforehand, I always had what I needed. Once I arrived, everything became much clearer. There were plenty of introductions and welcome activities, especially organised by ESN Amsterdam, which did a great job bringing exchange and international students together. There were social events, introductions, and even a big exchange party early on, which made it very easy to settle in and meet people. I also got my housing through the University of Amsterdam, which made the arrival process much smoother. Overall, it really felt like a university that is very used to hosting exchange students and has strong structures in place to support them. Personally, I didn’t need much help once I arrived, but it was very reassuring to know that support was always there. There are study advisers, international offices, student support services, psychologists, and even university doctors you can reach out to if needed. So even if things feel a bit overwhelming before the exchange starts, once you’re there you’re definitely not on your own.
arrival_assistance: I actually received quite a lot of support when I arrived, especially in the very beginning. The first thing was a two-day introduction organised by ESN (Erasmus Student Network), which focused mainly on social activities, getting to know other exchange and international students, and just having fun together. That was a really nice way to arrive, because it immediately gave a sense of community and made the first days feel much less overwhelming. The week after, there was a more academic introduction day organised by the university, combined with additional social activities on the surrounding days. There was also a big welcome party, which was honestly a lot of fun and a great way to meet even more people early on. In addition to the physical introductions, the university provided a lot of written information online — practical guides, emails, and resources you could read through at your own pace. I didn’t use everything, but it was reassuring to know that all the information was there if you needed it. Housing was also a huge part of feeling supported. I was lucky enough to get housing through the university, which made arrival much easier and removed a lot of stress. I ended up living very centrally, right by the canals, and that honestly had a big positive impact on my exchange experience overall. Looking back, I felt well taken care of when I arrived — both socially and practically — and it made settling into life in Amsterdam very smooth.

registration_process: For me, the course registration process was very easy and straightforward. Once I understood how it worked, I didn’t really have any issues at all. I personally knew very clearly which course I wanted to take in advance: the 30 ECTS first-semester course (“Foundations”) in Computational Social Science. Since it’s a full-semester package, registration was especially simple in my case. More generally, though, the University of Amsterdam has a well-structured system where you can easily look up all available courses before registering. Course registration happens during a specific, relatively short time window, so the main thing is just to pay attention to the emails and make sure you register within those days. One nice thing is that you’re allowed to register for more ECTS than you actually plan to take. If you end up getting all the courses you registered for, you can simply deregister from the ones you don’t want afterwards. That gives you some flexibility and makes the process less stressful. UvA also has a very good online timetable system (“Rooster”), where you can see all lectures, classes, and even exam dates in advance and build a visual schedule. Compared to KU, I found this system much clearer and easier to use, especially when trying to avoid clashes. Overall, my experience was that as long as you read the information you receive and keep an eye on deadlines, course registration at UvA is smooth and well organised.
registration_help: There was actually a lot of help available, both before and during the exchange. First of all, you receive plenty of emails with practical information, and the University of Amsterdam’s website is very thorough. Almost everything you might need — from course registration to practical matters — can be found online if you take the time to look. If there’s something you can’t figure out yourself, it’s very easy to get help. The International Office and study advisers are extremely approachable and helpful. I personally had quite a few questions for the International Office, and every time I contacted them, they were quick, kind, and very reassuring. It really felt like you were in safe hands. Even once you’re there, you never feel left alone. I didn’t have any major issues myself, but I knew other exchange students who changed courses or adjusted their study plans during the semester, and they received plenty of support with that. I also know people who met with study advisers just to talk through their semester or plans, and they all had very positive experiences. Overall, I never felt insecure or worried about not knowing what to do. There is always someone you can reach out to, and the university is genuinely good at helping exchange students — whether it’s about courses, planning, or practical issues.
registration_success: I was completely successful. I knew very clearly which course I wanted to take — a single 30 ECTS course — so the registration process was very straightforward for me. I only registered for that course, even though it would have been possible to register for more, and I got in right away. Everything went smoothly from the start, and I didn’t run into any issues at all. In my case, it was basically a 100% hit rate.
registration_advice: My main advice would simply be to read the information you receive and follow the steps carefully. If I had to give one piece of advice, it would be: go on exchange for the people, the city, and the experience. If you do that, the exchange can be incredibly rewarding — and for me, it definitely was.
course_level: For the specific programme I followed, I personally found the academic level to be quite low, especially compared to my background and expectations. Since it was a first-semester bachelor programme, a large part of the curriculum focused on introductory social science methods that I was already very familiar with. As a result, much of the content felt repetitive to me, particularly in relation to qualitative research methods. In practice, I found the coursework relatively easy, and I generally performed very well in the assignments. While that was of course nice, it also meant that I often felt under-challenged academically. I would have appreciated more depth, more reading, and more advanced discussions, especially given UvA’s strong academic reputation. That said, I think it’s important to stress that this experience is highly programme-specific. Because exchange students can only join the first semester of this particular programme, the level was naturally adapted to students who had just started university. In that sense, the level makes sense — it just didn’t align very well with my own academic background and expectations. From talking to other exchange students, I know that the academic level varies a lot across courses and programmes at UvA. Some exchange students found their courses very challenging, others found them manageable, and some found them easy. So my experience should not be taken as representative of UvA in general, but rather as something to keep in mind when choosing courses — especially if academic depth is a priority for you.
teaching_comparison: This comparison is again very dependent on the specific programme and courses, so I can mainly speak from my own experience and what I learned from other exchange students. In the Computational Social Science programme I followed, the teaching style was very workshop-based and attendance-heavy. There were many scheduled hours each week where you were expected to be physically present and actively working on tasks, often in groups. The semester was structured around two large projects, which was nice in principle, but it also meant continuous progress checks, weekly deliverables, and a lot of in-class work. Compared to UCPH, there was much less reading and much more focus on doing things during class time. More generally, from talking to other exchange students at UvA, I got the impression that teaching there is often more structured and guided than at UCPH. There tends to be more compulsory activities, more continuous assessment, and in some courses sit-in exams or tests that focus on knowing specific content or details. This is quite different from sociology at UCPH, where we don’t have sit-in exams and where there is typically more emphasis on independent reading, essay writing, and broader analytical reflection. Overall, I would say that the teaching style at UvA can feel a bit more school-like compared to UCPH — more attendance, more structure, and more continuous evaluation. That said, this varies a lot by course, and you can usually see the teaching and exam format in advance when choosing courses. Some students may really appreciate this structure, while others — especially those used to the UCPH style — might find it quite different.
courses_enrolled: "FOUNDATION: Appreciating the complexity of social challenges” (course catalogue number 738100001Y)
recommended_courses: I’ll be honest and say that I would only recommend the “Foundations” course (the first-semester Computational Social Science programme) if it really matches your preferences. This course can be a good fit if you: • enjoy having many scheduled classes and workshops • like working actively during class time • are comfortable with a lot of group work • enjoy hands-on social science methods • don’t mind relatively little reading, but a lot of compulsory in-class activities and continuous assignments If that sounds appealing, then the course can work well. Personally, I would have preferred a more advanced academic level, more reading, and more theoretical depth, so it wasn’t the right fit for me academically — but that’s very subjective. One thing I really want to highlight positively is the social and personal atmosphere of the programme. The learning teams are small, and I felt genuinely seen and appreciated as a student. I built very personal relationships with several lecturers and the programme study adviser, who were incredibly kind and supportive. There was a strong sense of community — including informal moments like coffee with lecturers, social gatherings, and even a shared end-of-semester dinner with staff and students. In that sense, the programme felt very warm and welcoming. So overall, I wouldn’t recommend this course by default — but I would recommend it to students who actively want this specific teaching style and structure. If your priority is academic depth and independent study, I would suggest looking at other courses. If you value structure, community, and hands-on learning, this course might suit you well.
unexpected_costs: I honestly didn’t encounter many unexpected costs. I biked everywhere, which made daily life very cheap and easy. I rarely used public transport, and I never really needed the metro. Of course, if you want to travel around the Netherlands — for example to cities like Utrecht, Rotterdam, or Nijmegen — you’ll need to buy train tickets, but that’s easy to plan for and not really a surprise. Many students rent a Swapfiets, which is very convenient, but I personally bought a second-hand bike for about €180, which worked perfectly for the whole semester (and I even brought it back to Denmark). Housing was by far the biggest expense, and aside from that, daily costs were quite manageable. Overall, there were no major unexpected expenses, and living costs were pretty predictable once housing was sorted.
cost_comparison: Overall, I found prices in Amsterdam to be quite similar to Copenhagen. Some things were slightly more expensive, others slightly cheaper, but on the whole the cost level felt familiar. One thing that surprised me a bit was takeaway food. I rarely bought takeaway, but when I did, I found it relatively expensive — in some cases even more expensive than in Copenhagen. That might partly be because I lived very centrally, where there are many tourists, but things like pizza and other standard takeaway options were not particularly cheap. For groceries, I mostly shopped at Albert Heijn and Jumbo. Albert Heijn can be quite pricey, but I would strongly recommend getting an Albert Heijn Bonus Card. The discounts make a huge difference, and they often have very good weekly or flash deals (sometimes 50% off on specific product categories). If you don’t mind the data tracking behind it, the Bonus Card really helps keep food costs down. Another good tip is to buy items that are close to their expiration date. Albert Heijn uses dynamic discounts that can go up to 70% off, especially later in the day. If you’re flexible with what you cook, you can eat very cheaply this way. Jumbo is generally a bit cheaper than Albert Heijn, and Lidl is also a good option if you live close to one. Personally, I found that with discounts and some flexibility, grocery shopping in Amsterdam was very manageable. All in all, I didn’t experience any big price shocks — especially if you’re coming from Copenhagen, the price level feels quite comparable.
activities_available: There were lots of options available if you wanted to get involved. The University of Amsterdam offers a wide range of sports and athletic activities through the university sports centre (USC), where you can join classes, gyms, and different sports clubs. I personally didn’t use this much, simply because I was already very busy socially and spent most of my time with friends. Socially, there’s a lot going on. There are student cafés (for example on campus), where students often hang out after classes, grab a beer, and socialize. On top of that, ESN (Erasmus Student Network) is very active and organizes many events for exchange students, such as introductions, parties, bar crawls, trips, and other social activities. There are also smaller social events connected to specific programmes or student networks. Overall, I’d say there are plenty of opportunities to be social, and it’s quite easy to meet people — especially as an exchange student. One difference compared to UCPH is the party culture. UvA doesn’t really have the same kind of student-organised parties that we’re used to in Copenhagen. Most parties happen out in the city, at bars or venues, rather than being organised directly by students themselves. That said, Amsterdam has a huge nightlife, so depending on what you enjoy, there’s still a lot to do. In short, there’s no lack of activities — it’s more about choosing what fits your interests and how social you want to be during your exchange.
activities_recommended: My biggest recommendation is to really prioritise the social side of the exchange. Explore the city, be curious, say yes to things, and focus on making friends. For me, the social life and experiences outside the university were by far the most important part of the exchange and what made it so memorable. Amsterdam is an amazing city to live in as a student. Just biking around, discovering neighbourhoods, cafés, parks, museums, and different parts of the city is already a big part of the experience. I would really encourage future exchange students to spend time getting to know the city and not just sticking to their immediate area. If you enjoy going out and dancing, I can very warmly recommend Skatecafé in Amsterdam Noord. It became our absolute go-to place during the exchange. It’s a very open-minded and welcoming venue with a great atmosphere and usually multiple dance floors with different types of music, depending on the night. The crowd is friendly, the vibe is relaxed, and it feels very unpretentious. Even though it’s a bit outside the city centre, it’s definitely worth the trip — just go a bit earlier in the evening to really enjoy it. Beyond nightlife, there are also plenty of informal social activities organised through ESN and other student networks, which are great for meeting people, especially at the beginning of the exchange. Overall, my advice would be: don’t overthink it. Be social, explore, and enjoy the freedom of being on exchange — those experiences are what you’ll remember long after the semester ends.
weekend_recommendations: My main recommendation is to take it weekend by weekend and be social. A lot of the best plans happen spontaneously, so I’d say follow the people around you, say yes to invitations, and just hang out together. That’s often how the most memorable weekends happen. The Netherlands is very easy to explore. You can take the train almost anywhere, which makes day trips or short weekend trips very simple. I did a small road trip with friends where we visited smaller towns and villages around Amsterdam, including old canal towns, farming villages, and fishing towns — which was a really nice contrast to city life. We also travelled to places like Flevoland (reclaimed land) and Friesland, which gave a very different impression of the country. Amsterdam itself also has amazing museums, neighbourhoods to explore, parks, cafés, and markets, so there’s always something to do even if you stay in the city. You’ll quickly get lots of recommendations from other students once you’re there. Overall, I’d say: don’t overplan. Be open, travel a bit, explore locally, and enjoy spending time with the people you meet — that’s what makes weekends and holidays during exchange really special.

socializing_tips: I personally spent most of my time socialising with other exchange students, especially the people in my student dorm, simply because we were in the same situation and very like-minded. That said, there were plenty of opportunities to socialise with local (Dutch) students as well, especially within my programme. My main tip would simply be: approach people and talk to them. Dutch students are generally very kind, open, and welcoming. They can sometimes come across as quite direct in the way they communicate, but that’s just part of the culture and usually meant in a friendly and honest way. If you actively want to meet more local students, it helps to take part in programme-related activities, group work, or student events. ESN events, bar crawls, cafés, and other social gatherings are also good places to meet both local and international students. Even though I didn’t personally feel the need to seek this out much — since I already had a very active social life — the opportunities were definitely there. Overall, I don’t think socialising with local students is difficult if you’re open, curious, and willing to take the first step.
cultural_challenges: I didn’t find any cultural differences particularly challenging overall. The environment was very international, especially within my programme, and people came from many different cultural backgrounds. Because of that, you naturally encounter different ways of communicating, behaving, and working together. At times, you could notice that people were used to different academic or social norms, which is completely normal in an international setting. I don’t think this ever led to any real clashes — it just requires being open-minded, patient, and aware that not everyone shares the same cultural references or expectations. One small thing to be aware of is that Danish humour and sarcasm don’t always translate well, so it can be useful to be a bit more mindful of how things might be interpreted. But overall, I experienced the cultural diversity as a positive thing rather than a challenge. In general, as long as you approach differences with curiosity and kindness, it’s very easy to adapt and enjoy the international atmosphere.
culture_appreciated: One of the things I appreciated most was how direct and honest Dutch people are in the way they communicate. In many ways, it felt quite similar to Danish culture, which made it very easy for me to adapt and feel at home quickly. I also really loved the biking culture. Being able to bike everywhere — to university, to friends, to cafés, and around the city in general — made everyday life both easy and enjoyable. It felt very natural and familiar, especially coming from Copenhagen. Overall, I found Dutch culture very easy to connect with, and I didn’t experience any major culture shock. The similarities to Danish culture made the whole exchange feel comfortable from the beginning, while still being exciting and new.
top3_advice: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? 1. Prioritise the social experience. Be social, say yes to things, and don’t stress too much about the academics. Of course, you can and should try to learn something — but if you feel demotivated academically or find the level different from what you’re used to, that’s completely okay. When the exchange is over, it’s the people you met, the experiences you had, and the memories you made that will matter the most. 2. Go all in on the university housing lottery. Do everything you can to participate in the University of Amsterdam’s housing lottery and be patient with the process. If you get the chance, I would strongly recommend choosing category 3 and, if offered, Prinsengracht. Also: check your email constantly during the booking period — housing offers are first come, first served, and timing really matters. 3. Be present and enjoy the time — it goes by fast. The semester passes incredibly quickly. Take time to reflect, enjoy everyday moments, and remember to take photos and appreciate where you are. Don’t rush through it — just be present, make memories, and enjoy the experience while it lasts.
other_useful_info: If there’s one thing I would really emphasise, it’s student housing. I’ve already written about this earlier, but it’s worth repeating: go for the University of Amsterdam student housing lottery. Don’t panic too early and don’t try to secure private housing before you know the outcome of the lottery. Follow the instructions carefully, be patient, and see if you get lucky. Only after you know the result should you start looking for other housing options if necessary. Beyond housing, my general advice would be to remember that there are a lot of people at the university who are there to help you. Whether it’s the International Office, study advisers, or other support services, don’t hesitate to reach out if you have questions or uncertainties. From my experience, they are very responsive, kind, and helpful — and you’re never expected to figure everything out on your own. Overall, if you stay on top of emails, follow instructions, and ask for help when needed, the practical side of going on exchange to UvA is very manageable.
most_rewarding: Without a doubt, the most rewarding part was the social experience — making friends, sharing everyday life, and creating memories together. Looking back now, that’s what really matters to me. While the academic part didn’t fully meet my expectations, that honestly doesn’t matter in hindsight. What stays with me are the friendships I made, the moments we shared, and the experiences we had together in Amsterdam. Those memories mean a lot to me, and they’re something I’ll carry with me for a long time. I wouldn’t change my exchange for anything. It was an incredibly special time, and I’m very grateful for it.
greatest_challenge: I didn’t experience any major personal challenges or difficult situations during the exchange. Overall, things went very smoothly. The main challenge for me was academic frustration, which I’ve mentioned earlier. I spent quite a lot of time on coursework that didn’t always feel very motivating or rewarding, and that could be demotivating at times. What helped was accepting that this feeling was okay and reminding myself that exchange is about much more than academics. Once I shifted my focus and allowed myself to prioritise the social experience and everyday life, things became much easier and more enjoyable. Interestingly, something very positive also came out of this challenge. Because the programme had close interaction with lecturers, I was able to get a short-term research assistant position with a professor during the semester. Through that, I worked on advanced quantitative and econometric modelling and learned a lot academically — much more than I had expected from the programme itself. It ended up being a really valuable and motivating experience, and it showed me that even when parts of the exchange are frustrating, unexpected opportunities can arise. Looking back, the challenge was real, but it also helped me grow and led to experiences I wouldn’t otherwise have had.
other_comments: Nothing more to add, apart from repeating how important housing is. If you take anything from this report, let it be the advice about the University of Amsterdam housing lottery, which I’ve described in detail above. That’s where my experience can hopefully be most useful for future exchange students. Other than that, enjoy it — exchange is something very special.

course_level: I would say on average the level is pretty similar to UCPH. But just like UCPH the difference in the level and workload of the courses can be very different. The biggest difference for me was that all exams i had where either completely without notes or only with very few. So you have to adjust to that, because i was used to being allowed notes, book, computer etc. at most of my previous exams.
teaching_comparison: Most courses were pretty similar with lectures and then problem classes. As mentioned, one of the biggest differences for me were the exams. Also i feel like i did more group work than at UCPH, though not all was mandatory. If you don't like the block structure, you should rethink studing at UvA. Instead of 2 blocks it's 3. Block 1 and 2 are 7 weeks each with 2 courses, and block 3 is only 4 (!) weeks with one course. The biggest difference compared to UCPH is that there is no week for preparation for the exams and also no free week after exams. So essentially you go directly from block 1 to block 2, then you have Christmas break without worrying about exams, which is nice. And then block 3 is in January. Because it's so short, its normally a more project oriented course. Also, i think there are more assignments, but i feel like they try to help you keep up with the course. Midterms are used much more than at UCPH, i had midterms in 2 courses, and it seemed like most other people i knew also had at least one midterm in both block 1 and 2
courses_enrolled: Advanced Quantum Physics History and Philosophy of Science Introduction Quantum Computing Introduction Computational Science Workshop Physics and Astronomy
recommended_courses: Advanced Quantum Physics was pretty hard for me, but it was the first time that the lecturer had that course, which might explain why he set the bar a bit too high. The lectures were a bit boring, i would say it was a very standard course. History and Philosophy of Science was surprisingly good. Kind of a humanities course, but the focus is on science. There is an essay each week, which i wasnt a big fan of. I feel like the course is pretty easy to pass, but not that easy to get a really good grade in. The exam was totally fine. So you need to be alright with some philosophy yap and writing essays, but then you get some fun facts about Einstein on the way. Introduction Quantum Computing was the best course i had. The lecturer was soooo structured it was amazing. He recorded every lecture and put up the notes. It wasnt too hard, but i still feel like i learned a lot. Good mix of classic problem classes and coding exercises. Would definitely recommend! Introduction Computational Science was pretty nice as well. The material isnt that hard to understand, but the assignments take a while to do. But if you are all right with coding a lot, i would recommend it. And it was nice to have an interdisciplinary course. I think it is most useful for bio-physics, but it was very good coding practice. Workshop Physics and Astronomy is a bit of a hit or miss. There wasnt really any other physics course in block 3. It is like a preparation course for the bachelor thesis, so if you want to take the course, make sure to write the course coordinator already sometime in september, so you are sure to get all the information about the course. You choose a workshop, theres astro, hospital physics etc. And then you make some kind of mini project/presentation/report. I did API workshop, which was astrophysics. It was sooo chill and that was great because then i could enjoy my last month in the city ;) Other workshops seemed like much more work, especially the Nikhef one.
unexpected_costs: Nothing unexpected really. I choose to rent a bike with Swapfiets, which was totally worth it. Around 20 euros a month, but if anything breaks, the repair is free. And you dont have to worry about getting rid of it once the exchange is over.
cost_comparison: Groceries and cafés were less expensive than i expected. I thought it would be the same as in Denmark, because the housing prices seemed to be very similar. But i would say it was more somewhere in between Germany and Denmark depending on which supermarket you went to. Public transport was as expensive as Denmark though, but just bike everywhere :) Memberships for sports other than a normal gym membership were also pretty expensive like in Denmark.
activities_available: A decent amount, but i didnt do that much myself. Science Park has really nice sports facilities: big gym, climbing wall, saunas, squash, tennis etc. So there were lots of opportunities to do something. For social activities i was just lucky, because i kind of had that with my student housing.
activities_recommended: Do some kind of sport, because many of the facilities are on the campuses so it's a good way to meet other students. And if you are not staying at some kind of student housing, befriend someone who does and go to their parties and stuff.
weekend_recommendations: It's a small country, so do some daytrips. Go see Utrecht, Leiden, Delft, Haarlem, Haag, Maastricht, all very cute cities. For longer trips Paris, London and many cities in Germany are just a train ride away. Belgium as well. But there is also a lot to do in Amsterdam!
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it's similar to Denmark.
socializing_tips: Just talk to people and ask them questions, because as an exchange student, you will definitely have some. I found most locals to be very friendly and open.
cultural_challenges: None really.
culture_appreciated: Biking, but i am kind of used to that. Everything was very efficient and digitalized, which was nice.
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy the city, it's beautiful and fun. Especially walk along the canals and hang out in Jordaan and De Pijp. Nightlife is good as well. Try stroopwafels (from the food markets), indonesian food and other Amsterdam specialties ;) 2. Make sure you are all right with the block structure at uni, but also, remember that everything is pass/fail, so allow yourself to experience the city and country instead studying all of the time. 3. Hope that you win in the housing lottery, and have a plan B if you don't or consider not going. As mentioned, the housing situation is crazy.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: The people i met (most were from my housing), and getting to enjoy such an amazing city with them.
greatest_challenge: Trying to balance studying and wanting to explore
other_comments: No

culture_adjustment: Very easy! Don't worry.
socializing_tips: Be brave and approach them. You are automatically interesting as an exchange student.

culture_appreciated: Brutal honestly, direct communication
top3_advice: Do it! Do it! Do it!
most_rewarding: love <3
greatest_challenge: Missing cool nature.
