registration_advice: To look carefully at the teaching languages for the courses and if choosing courses from different faculties, to check when the individual faculties start their classes because it might differ from faculty to faculty.
course_level: I had two courses for first year BA students and three courses for third or fourth year BA students (as the BA in Spain is 4 years).
teaching_comparison: The teaching was much more one-sided at UB compared to UPCH, meaning that the leactures mostly consisted of the professors talking and not a lot of discussions and class participation. We were mostly fed information and not encouraged to come to our own conclusions and reflect on the new knowledge.
courses_enrolled: Introducción a la historia de la lengua española (6 ECTS) Introducción a la literatura hispanoamericana (6 ECTS) Traducció desde l´Alemany (6 ECTS) Literatura i Holocaust (6 ECTS) Enseñanza del Inglés como Lengua Extranjera I (6 ECTS)
recommended_courses: To students who a very proficient in Spanish I would recommend Introducción a la historia de la lengua española, although it it also a very intense course. For German speaking students or simply students interested in German history or just literature, I will recommend Literatura i Holocaust, which was my favourite subject this semester and is taught by a wonderful professor. The downside is that it involves a lot of reading (three novels plus other texts), but the way the class is taught resembles UCPH more than most other classes.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: The public transportation was very good and much cheaper than anticipated. The T-Jove card valid for 90 days for ca. 300DKK including all 6 zones of Barcelona.
activities_available: I participated in the CATclub (Catalan Club) who organise weekly activities for students who want to learn Catalan and about Catalan culture and history. There is also a UB sports organisation, which I initially wanted to sign up for to play volleyball, but it was extremely intransparent and in the end I didn´t join the sports club.
activities_recommended: I will definitely recommend joing the CATclub. It was a great way to learn Catalan and an amazing opportunity to learn about Catalan customs with both Catalans and internationals and you get to do things and visit places that you probably would´nt have the opportunity to as a "normal" exchange student.
weekend_recommendations: I can highly recommend playing volleyball at the beach in Barcelona and also to make use of the transportation card and visit nearby beaches and towns. Barcelona also has great museums and cultural sites and there are many ways to enjoy them for free om certain days.
culture_adjustment: I felt that because the situation with tourists in Barcelona is very complicated right now, I wasn´t always welcome , even though I was an exchange student and not a tourist. But I often felt (with neighbours, people at the beach, etc.) that this difference didn´t matter and even though I speak Spanish and now also Catalan, that I was judged very quickly and constantly felt the need to prove that I wasn´t like "those other tourists".
socializing_tips: Definitely try to at least learn a little bit of Catalan. The Catalan identity is very strong, and combined with the growing resentment towards tourists in Barcelona, many local people are not too happy to hear English or sometimes even Spanish/Castellano spoken to them. Speaking Catalan to local people has been a gamechanger for me, as people are instantly more friendly and open and can see that you are making an effort.
cultural_challenges: The perception of time and what is considered being late, as I have often had to wait for people I had agreed to meet with and still struggle to get used to people not showing up on time (what I consider to be on time).
culture_appreciated: The spontaneity. I also really like how protective Catalan people can be of their language and the effort they make to maintain it.
top3_advice: 1. Don´t underestimate the role the Catalan language plays here. Don´t come there and expect everyone to speak Spanish with you or that most things will be in Spanish (let alone English). 2. In most cases, for example when you are unsure about exams, grades etc., you can ask your professors - don´t be shy! 3. Join the CATclub activites! It was really one of my highlights.
other_useful_info: The historical building of the UB is very beautiful and definitely worth a visit - and the library there is amaying and much nicer for studzing than the ones at other UB campuses.
most_rewarding: The people that I met and the friendships I made.
greatest_challenge: Paper work, problems with our landlord and apartment.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to explore Spanish culture, and it was the destination in Europe that I wanted to live in the most. I was also interested in learning more Spanish and wanted to improve my skills. It is a city that many people enjoy because it combines the beach and the city, which I also loved.
info_ease: I actually thought it was okay to find information. They were okay quick to answer emails, but it can be a bit tricky to figure out the websites and such.
arrival_assistance: They had like a welcome session for all of the exchange students, but I didn't learn that much there, and it wasn't like a mingle, but more of a sit and listen. They talked about the Catalan culture, which was nice. Nevertheless is was okay that they had that and you got introduced to Erasmus and such.
arrival_comments: They make could have introduced the school more, like the basics. Things like sports, the classroom systems, canteens and so on.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There was a day where the registration opened, and we had to sit ready to register because it was first-come, first- served basis. They had technical difficulties when we had to do it haha, so it was 40 minutes of sitting and not knowing. You had to make sure yourself that the courses and exams didn't overlap
registration_help: They send e-mails with instructions.
registration_success: We got alle the courses that we applied for and wanted. It didn't seem that difficult to get. There were only 1 English class per course.
registration_advice: It isn't that important that the classes is aligning perfectly after each other, because it is quite easy to catch up if you skip sometimes to go on trips and so on - and you are probably going to skip sometimes.
course_level: I would say that the academic level were as expected, but we underestimated it in the beginning, so we didn't show up that much, and then when midterms came, we were a bit surprised that it was more difficult than expected; but that is because we didn't read a lot, so I wouldn't say it is hard, but you have to keep up and stay updated, maybe that is obvious haha.
teaching_comparison: It is quite different from Denmark, as the classes very smaller - around 20-30 people, but they didn't take attendance or partipication. I personally liked it with the smaller classes, but in the end we missed UCPH level and teaching a lot. Each course had different exams and ways of teaching. In Game Theory, we had two exams (midterm and final) and three assignments that counted toward the grade. But in Industrial Organization, for example, we had two continuous evaluation tests and a final exam. It can be a bit confusing that they are different. In the beginning, we had to choose for almost every course whether to have continuous evaluation (exams throughout the course plus a final) or just one final exam. We chose continuous for all of them, but in the end, we realized we could have just chosen the single final exam, because we had to pass that no matter what.
courses_enrolled: Macroeconomics III (366726), Game Theory for Business (363712), World Economic History (366714), Industrial Organization (363669), Public Sector Economics (363652)
recommended_courses: I would recommend Macroeconomics III (366726) and Game Theory for Business (363712). These were my favorite courses with great lecturers. World Economic History (366714) was also very interesting, but we didn't go to a lot of classes. I think we were a bit surprised that Industrial Organization and Public Sector Economics were a bit more demanding that we thought (not crazy). I would probably have chosen some courses I found a bit more interesting than these if I could chose over again. It was basically a repetition of Micro I and Micro II back home, but without a lot of calculations, so I must say that I have learned more about the mechanisms and theory of Micro now instead of just the calculations from the courses, so that is nice to bring back haha.
unexpected_costs: You eat a lot in restaurant because the food is so good there, which were where I spend a lot of money. You also go on a lot of trips.
cost_comparison: The supermarket was pretty much the same as in Copenhagen, but restaurants, shopping and other things were cheaper. We got 3 months for 336 kr in total (T-Joven card), and then you can use all the transport you want unlimited for the time period. That was the best thing. I visited a lot of cities with just a T-joven card, because it stretched that far outside of Barcelona like Sitges, Montserrat, Vilanova I la Geltrú.
activities_available: Non existing I would say haha. One of my friends tried signing up for soccer, but were unsuccessful.
activities_recommended: I dont know.
weekend_recommendations: Go outside of Barcelona!! I rented a car and went on a Costa Brava roadtrip. Go to Montserrat and hike. Take a one-day trip to the cities around Barcelona. There are so many nice places in Spain. Some of my friend also went to Andorra and hiked, which was beautiful, but go there while it is sunny unless you have warm clothing. Take the train to Badalona if you want a more chill beach. Some also visited Madrid, Lissabon.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. People are so sweet, and had no unpleasant encounters. They are good at English, but they start with speaking spanish to you, so if you learn some basic saying, you can get by in spanish in the supermarkets, coffee shops and so on. I never felt unsafe, but maybe because we lived in the center with a. lot of people.
socializing_tips: No sorry. We mostly talked to other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: I dont think I found anything challenging about the culture, but some things are maybe a bit more outdated than in Denmark. I think everyone was so nice and welcoming.
culture_appreciated: I dont have any new comments.
top3_advice: Get a T-joven card. Go on a lot of trips outside of the city. Explore different areas in the city.
other_useful_info: I thought I needed more warm clothes for like November-december, but it was only cold cold for like a week. Much warmer than I thought. I still went out In the day in just a sweater in December.
most_rewarding: I really enjoyed spain. The weather was amazing. Good cheap coffee (the best were at uni), great food, so many cutes places.
greatest_challenge: I thought that I would meet more people from other contries.

I did not get any projects/subjects too choose from for my bachelor, so I ended up with a little weird subject that did not really fell into my interest. Apart from that the instruments in the laboratory were really old and did not always work properly and therefore I felt like I did a lot of the same work 3-4 times instead of just 1 time and even then, the results seemed a bit untrustworthy and I did not really feel I got as much out of it as I could since I did a lot of the same work in the laboratory.

culture_appreciated: The British students are really friendly and nice when you get to talk to them.

most_rewarding: All the new friends and new people and cultures I got to meet.
greatest_challenge: To prioritise between doing school work and doing fun things with my friends.

Furthermore I was contacted by the Pharmacy Tutor for an induction meeting and contacted by my academic advisor, who was a professor from the Pharmacology Department and who lectured a lot of the lectures from the courses I had chosen. She also offered having meetings throughout the semester with other students, talking about our wellbeings or if anything concerned us.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I did not have that many expectations for the exchange, but it turned out to be such a great experience that I would recommend to everyone!

I didn't have to apply for a visa because of the length of stay in the UK was under 6 months, therefore I only had to send a copy of my flight ticket as proof of the date I entered the UK.
registration_help: International Mobility before arriving to the UK and academic advisor after arriving to the UK. Both were very helpful and also helpful to know who to ask for help if they didn't know the answer themselves

Advanced topics and trends in pharmacology had a much higer workload and required good memorisation. weekend_recommendations: Explore the city of Bath and go on trips to surrounding areas in the UK

cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the Brits being so friendly, kind and welcoming

study_field: East and Southeastern European Studies (Balkan Studies)
crucial_aspects: Relevant to my field of study. Interested in the history of the country
info_ease: I received a general information package upon arrival with different brochures with information about tourism and activities as well as information on practicalities such as bus cards or student restaurants but crucial information on courses and registration procedures at the different faculties was harder to obtain. Some faculties (Philology) are used to receiving foreign students and there everything went pretty smooth. In some other cases no one was able to tell me what I had to do in order to get started or who I had to talk to. Information regarding classes on the university's webpage was sometimes inaccurate or not up to date. Some professors I had contacted prior to my arrival never replied and remained unreachable either physically (because of corona restrictions) or by email. Some information I received from different contacts was also incomplete, conflicting or outright misleading. All in all obtaining clear replies on simple things such as schedules or links to online classes was sometimes challenging.
arrival_assistance: All the staff was helpful but did not necessarily have the relevant information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I was warmly welcomed at the international office and given information about administrative practicalities such as visa, bus card or student restaurants. For the rest, I was first redirected to staff in each of the different faculties where I was supposed to have courses. Faculties are very independent and each has its own registrations procedures so the staff at the international office could not provide more information and the staff at one faculty cannot say if the registration procedure is similar in another. There is no common system between them. Administrative and teaching staff sometimes seemed surprised to see groups of foreign students coming to their faculty and seemed unaware of any specific registration procedures. For each of the faculties, I was told to go through standard registration procedures that required each time to provide passport copies, ID pictures and several forms only to understand later that no one knew whether this was necessary. One faculty had an IT-system for registration which was useful. For example I had to provide in total around 8-10 ID pictures, mostly in order to make booklets (indeks) that seem useless to foreign students. In the end the administrative part of the registration won't help you with the academic part even if you complete everything. Just contact teachers directly.
registration_help: Staff at the international office was helpful with regards to Erasmus documents
registration_success: Not so successful. Several of the courses I had chosen did not work out for different reasons. Corona restrictions made it difficult to get ahold of anyone at their office. I ended up choosing classes mostly based on how easy it was to communicate directly by email with teachers.
registration_advice: My advice would be to contact staff and especially teachers by email directly as soon as your first learning agreement gets validated and double and triple check the details directly with them. If a particular teacher is slow or difficult to communicate with via email and cannot provide clear information, just consider switching to another class. Generally, everyone is very sweet and helpful, but under constant pressure. So it is better to be proactive and ask everyone if they have information. Most teachers are nice and will send information about practicalities for the coming semester. The situation varies a lot from faculty to faculty. Some are used to receiving foreign students and have standard procedures and IT systems etc, others not. Also things might have gotten better after corona. Many courses will not be taught in English, even though they have a description in English on the webpage. It can be a good idea to clarify that with the teacher as well. In any case, be prepared to receive information last minute, including readings, syllabus, locations

registration_comments: Svalbard is a very special place and people who go here tend to fall in love with the place.
registration_process: There's is only a limited amount of courses and they come in course packages. So if you sign up for one of them you also must sign up for the other one. But it was very easy. When you apply to UNIS you apply to the courses, not the university itself. That means that if you're accepted you're automatically enrolled in your courses and don't need to do more.
registration_help: There is a student advisor at UNIS for each department (geology, biology, geophysics and technology).
registration_success: I got the classes i wanted.
registration_advice: None really. It's quite simple.
academics_comments: Svalbard is a very special place and people who go here tend to fall in love with the place.
course_level: It was a good level, not too hard. You can do more or less depending on how much time you are willing to invest, so it sort of depends on yourself how hard and detailed you want to make it (especially in your individual project).
teaching_comparison: UNIS has a lot more field work. It is not the classical university experience with lectures and following exercises, but instead we have more integrated classes. In general there is a lot of practical work which I personally really like.
courses_enrolled: Marine geology The quaternary and glacial geology of Svalbard
recommended_courses: I particularly liked the marine geology course, because I'm really interested in marine science. We went on a week-long cruise to the north of Svalbard and had a lot of lab work, which was really cool. The other courses are also very good. It just depends on your interests!
unexpected_costs: Food is ridiculously expensive! Be prepared to at least double your food budget compared to Denmark. Also, you'll probably find yourself buying a lot of outdoor equipment during your time up here :) especially if you're here in spring where you can rent or buy a snowscooter.
cost_comparison: FOOD!
activities_available: none by the host institution, but there's plenty of things going on around in the city. Seems like there is always some kind of festival going on.
activities_recommended: Get out and go hiking! Go to the cabins for the students.
weekend_recommendations: hike :) Look at the adorable reindeers :) there is surprisingly many things you can spend time on here. Most of them involve nature.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Everyone are exchange students and are keen on getting friends, so everyone are very open.
socializing_tips: You're living in the same building so just go to the kitchen and talk. Also, UNIS organises a friday gathering every week where all of UNIS staff and students are invited which is a good way to socialize across departments.
cultural_challenges: none.
culture_appreciated: like mentioned, there is not really a norwegian culture here because of all the exchange students.
top3_advice: Rest before you get here, because you won't have much time for it up here with all the hikes and things that are going on :) Save up money so you have enough to buy food and don't starve. Don't worry too much about making friends. It is no problem because people are so kind and open.
other_useful_info: I can't think of any at the moment.
most_rewarding: Being able to go outside into the nature was so rewarding and amazing. The academics was also very rewarding and it made me realise that I want to pursue a degree within marine science.
greatest_challenge: Managing academics vs sparetime. Often you just want to go outside, but you need to work once in a while.
other_comments: enjoy! It's amazing.

crucial_aspects: At der var et universitet, hvor jeg kunne finde gode kurser, som kunne erstatte de kurser, jeg skulle have på KU. Derudover var det vigtigt for mig, at det var en by, der havde god adgang til naturmuligheder og ikke var større, end at jeg kunne gå rundt fra sted til sted uden behov for offentligt transport. Jeg ville også gerne finde et sted i Norden for at kunne udforske de nordiske sprog og nuancer.
overall_comments: Jeg har virkelig været glad for at være på Bergen Universitet og i Bergen by. Det har været en rigtig god oplevelse at bo med lokale og indgå på lokale norske kurser.
info_ease: Det har været let tilgængeligt med information, som er blevet sendt til én både før og under opstarten på opholdet. Den internationale studievejleder på Bergens psykologiske fakultet har også været en stor hjælp ift. at få godkendt ens mulighed for at deltage på diverse kurser.
arrival_assistance: Jeg mødte og fik det sidste hjælp til kursusoptagelse hos den internationale studievejleder på Bergens psykologiske fakultet.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Jeg har virkelig været glad for at være på Bergen Universitet og i Bergen by. Det har været en rigtig god oplevelse at bo med lokale og indgå på lokale norske kurser.
registration_process: Der var gode instruktioner til at ansøge på Bergen Universitet, hvor der kom mails med vigtige datoer, diverse koder osv. Så det var ret ligetil at følge ansøgningsproceduren på UiB.
registration_help: Universitetets hjemmeside med gode instruktioner, mails med vigtige informationer samt mailkorrespondance med den internationale studievejleder på Bergens psykologiske fakultet
registration_success: Det var et puslespil at få obligatoriske bachelorkurser til at gå op med kurser på værtsuniversitetet - at det matcher i ECTS, sværhedsgrad, pensum, forhåndsgodkendelser osv. Men der var et godt samarbejde med universitetets internationale studievejleder, hvor hun kontaktede de fagansvarlige på ønskede kurser og fik afklaring på, om de ville have en udvekslingsstuderende med på deres kurser. Derfor var hun en kæmpe ressource i den store proces dét er at finde matchende kurser. Derfor kunne jeg søge de fire kurser på StudentWeb i juni måned, som vejlederende allerede havde undersøgt, at jeg gerne måtte følge.
registration_advice: At meget ender med at lade sig gøre, og at det oftest går op i sidste ende - selvom det kan føles som mange blindgyder og uløselige puslespil undervejs i processen.
academics_comments: Jeg har virkelig været glad for at være på Bergen Universitet og i Bergen by. Det har været en rigtig god oplevelse at bo med lokale og indgå på lokale norske kurser.
course_level: Jeg tog kurser på det 6-årige professionsstudie i psykologi på deres 4. og 5. år. Jeg tænker, at niveauet på de valgte kurser passede godt overens med niveauet på KU.
teaching_comparison: Da der optages færre på deres professionsstudie i psykologi, var vi kun 30-40 mennesker til alle timer. Derfor var undervisningen meget inkluderende og nærværende, hvilket jeg satte stor pris på. Underviserne var meget interesserede i at høre de studerendes pointer, hvilket gav en god dynamik i undervisningen.
courses_enrolled: Psykologisk Behandling (14 ECTS), Psykologisk Kartlegging (6 ECTS), Vitenskapsteoretisk perspektiv og Etikk i Klinisk Praksis (5 ECTS) på professionsstudieet i psykologi samt Innføring i Metode (5 ECTS)
recommended_courses: Psykologisk Kartlegging og Psykologisk Behandling var favoritterne. Der var virkelig mange undervisningstimer i disse kurser, hvilket var en god og hyggelig måde at blive godt kendt med alle sine studiekammerater. Ligeledes engagerede og engagerende undervisere.
unexpected_costs: Måske at man generelt bare bruger flere penge, når man er på udveksling (diverse ture osv.), men at man sagtens kan gøre det uden at blive ruineret :-)
cost_comparison: Jeg havde på forhånd indstillet mig på, at Norges priser ville være højere, men alligevel blev jeg overrasket over det i dagligvarebutikkerne. Grøntsager etc. er bare dyre. Mens andre ting, såsom kaffe på en café eller lokal bustransport, ikke var forskellig fra danske priser.
activities_available: Sammen (studentorganisationen i Bergen) har mange sociale og sportslige aktiviteter, man kan deltage i. Både bålture på fjeldet, abonnement til deres fitness-centre osv.
activities_recommended: Tage på hytteture i DNT-hytterne - det er noget helt særligt.
weekend_recommendations: Fjeldture (både i byfjeldene omkring Bergen og i fjeldene med bus-/togture fra Bergen) og hytteture. Generelt at komme på tur rundt om og i Bergen.
culture_adjustment: At bo og studere med norske studerende gjorde det nemt at komme ind i den "lokale kultur".
socializing_tips: Jeg var glad for at bo og studere med norske studerende, så det vil jeg gerne give videre som en anbefaling.
cultural_challenges: Der er selvfølgelig en lille sproglig barriere, men hvis man taler langsomt og tydeligt, så går det helt fint :-)
culture_appreciated: At folk generelt var hjælpsomme og venlige.
top3_advice: Bergen er skøn og har en størrelse, der gør, at du føler dig hjemme meget hurtig. Naturen er helt fantastisk omkring Bergen, så jeg vil anbefale at komme en masse ud på tur. Og jeg vil anbefale at blive medlem af DNT og bruge DNT-hytterne.
other_useful_info: At meget kan lade sig gøre med kurser osv., når man først er kommet afsted :-)
most_rewarding: At man på 4-5 måneder virkelig nåede at føle sig hjemme i Bergen

crucial_aspects: For me it was important that the host university offered courses that were relevant for my study and were interesting. Furthermore, I chose Norway as my study destination because of its beautiful nature. In addition, I wanted to study in Europe and a place where I could feel safe during a time with the pandemic.
overall_comments: For me it has been the best decision in my life to go on an exchange. I have learned so much, both academically, but also about other cultures and about myself.
info_ease: It was fairly easy. I got all the information I needed via email.
arrival_assistance: I had to pick up my keys at a service center located very close to my student accommodation. The personnel at the service center was very informative and willing to help.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: For me it has been the best decision in my life to go on an exchange. I have learned so much, both academically, but also about other cultures and about myself.
registration_process: The registration process was a bit of a hassle, because it wasn't entirely clear what courses I was able to take or not. It was first clear after I moved to my study destination in the beginning of the semester, which was too late in my opinion. I think this was due to lack of communication between UCPH and the host university, and I hope for future students that this will be improved.
registration_help: Email and information on the University's website.
registration_success: I were very lucky and were able to register for all the classes I wanted to take.
registration_advice: Start in good time to find out which courses you think might be interesting and be sure that you have the right prerequisites for taking the courses. Don't be afraid to contact the host institution and ask questions about any doubts you might have.
academics_comments: For me it has been the best decision in my life to go on an exchange. I have learned so much, both academically, but also about other cultures and about myself.
course_level: I took mainly master courses even though I'm a bachelor student, and I actually find the level quit easy. I think it was way easier to get good grades compared to at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: I think there was more focus on memorization compared to problem solving at UCPH. The exams question were mainly multiply choices, which are very different from my exams at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Immunology Animal science Lipid Biochemistry from chemistry to disease Developmental genetics
recommended_courses: Immunology is a very intense, but interessting course, which gives an introduction to the immune system and its general functions and perspectives to autoimmune diseases and cancer. I was really happy about the course lipid biochemistry, because it gives you a deeper understanding of the functions and structures of different lipids, and how these lipids play an important role in many disease like Alzheimers. In this course I also wrote a paper about a specific lipid, which was really interesting.
unexpected_costs: I went on many trips, which costed a lot of money, but definitely were worth it.
cost_comparison: I already knew that groceries are very expensive in Norway, but vegetables are insanely expensive. In addition, the prices for alcohol are very high (three times Danish prices). The prices for fish, especially salmon are fairly cheap.
activities_available: There is an organization called Sammen, which really takes care of students and which offers cheap training facilities, cafeterias and various social activities and events and much more. Especially in the beginning they organize a lot of events to let people meet each other and make friends.
activities_recommended: All outdoor activities. Hiking in Norway is absolutely amazing and is the perfect break for studying. I also climbed a lot, which was so much fun.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the old part of the city and the harbor, it is very cozy. Experience the beautiful nature is a must.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. Norwegians are very similar to Danes, and are very friendly.
socializing_tips: I socialized mostly with other international exchange students, but if you want to socialize more with locals you can for example become a volunteer in different student organisations or debate clubs. In one of the first week of the semester, we had a tutor-week arranged by the University, where we met up with older Norwegian students from our Faculty and did a lot of games together. We had a lot of fun.
culture_appreciated: The Norwegians relation to the nature and healthy mentality.
top3_advice: Be openminded and curious, pack some good hiking shoes, and be aware that you are gonna spend a lot of money (it is worth it).
most_rewarding: My friendships with people from all over Europe and the amazing memories we have together.
greatest_challenge: To speak English in the beginning, but you get use to it fast. The mountain Lyderhorn :-)

crucial_aspects: I knew I wanted to stay in Europe because of the covid situation. I decided on Norway because I like the language, the nature and would like to explore more of the country. I was also important to me that the university I chose offered relevant courses for my study.
overall_comments: I has been an amazing experience, and I would recommend every student to go abroad.
info_ease: It took some time to orientate myself in the many different universities course catalogs. But other than that it was fine.
arrival_comments: It was a bit difficult to know which faculty I belonged to and also who I should contact to get the signature for the learning agreement. But in the end, it all worked out.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I has been an amazing experience, and I would recommend every student to go abroad.
registration_process: Find the courses for you in the course catalog, apply for it on time and wait for an answer.
registration_success: I allayed for two and i got them. So I am very pleased.
registration_advice: Make sure to check and know all deadlines. There are a lot of deadlines when appling for exchange. So be sure to write them down and not miss them.
academics_comments: I has been an amazing experience, and I would recommend every student to go abroad.
course_level: The level in Norway has been the same as in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: One of my courses (Web design) at UIB has really surprised me in the best way. It has been very interesting and a more interactive and hands-on way of learning than I am used to, which I really enjoyed.
courses_enrolled: DIKULT105 WEB DESIGN I DIKULT203 ELECTRONIC LITERATURE
recommended_courses: If you are a beginner and you are interested in learning to code websites, I would really recommend the WEB DESIGN I course.
unexpected_costs: Not so unexpected but if you want to also explore the country and do some trips, you might want to save some money for that.
cost_comparison: Food and alcohol are very expensive in Norway, so take that into account.
activities_available: I join the sammen gym membership and some of the social things they planned like ice skating.
activities_recommended: Go hike the seven mountains. It is a must while being in Bergen.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking, exploring the city of Bergen, exploring the nightlife (Ricks, Heidis beer bar), go on trips. I went on a glacier tour at Folge fonna glacier. Was so amazing.
culture_adjustment: Norway and Denmark are pretty close in culture, so very easy.
socializing_tips: I lived at Fantoft student housing where you will meet a lot of exchange students, so i did not get to meet so many norwegians. For me that wa okay because it was nice to spent this experience with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Nothing :)
culture_appreciated: The hikinh culture they have here in Norway, and that there fell snow in December!
top3_advice: - Live at Fantoft where you will meet so many exchange students - Say yes to everything! ¨ - Explore more of the country than just Bergen while you are here.
other_useful_info: It is a very good university.
most_rewarding: The amazing people I have met.
greatest_challenge: Learning how to code hahah. I studied web design. It was challenging but so rewarding in the end.
other_comments: If you have the possibility to go on exchange! Go for it!

crucial_aspects: Because of COVID, it was very important for me, that it was close and that it was a country where I knew that if anything happened in regards to COVID, that I would be okay. Other then that I wanted it to be somewhere cold and where the nature would be a huge aspect of my stay - which it did.
overall_comments: I LOVED being on exchange. It has been the best half year of my life and I would recommend it to everyone. I honestly cannot come up with on bad aspect of it that would make it a 9/10 instead of a 10/10.
info_ease: I found it very easy, but I'm also the type of person who just seek information right away and I normally do not wait for people to contact me. When in doubt about something just ask the universities or who ever it is that you need to get into contact with - they are there to help.
arrival_assistance: The Sammen organisation in Bergen are super good at guiding you and making your arrival as well as stay easy and smooth, so that was really nice.
arrival_comments: I was VERY pleased with it, but again, that is because I seek the information when in doubt. I do know that some of my exchange did not have the same experience as me, but 9/10 times that was because they missed an email or did not seek the information themselves. Sammen is really good at letting you know what, when and how, if it is important. Example; they provided us with covid information every time there had been a press conference in Norway - that was SUPER helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I LOVED being on exchange. It has been the best half year of my life and I would recommend it to everyone. I honestly cannot come up with on bad aspect of it that would make it a 9/10 instead of a 10/10.
registration_process: I got told when and how to register and that was what I did.
registration_help: There was a very great guide that told you how to do everything.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted, and I even registered for four more courses than I should, which was great since I then could figure out what courses was interesting while being there and trying them out.
registration_advice: Stay calm, everything will be perfectly find. The people in Bergen are super helpful so don't panic.
academics_comments: I LOVED being on exchange. It has been the best half year of my life and I would recommend it to everyone. I honestly cannot come up with on bad aspect of it that would make it a 9/10 instead of a 10/10.
course_level: I think the level was pretty much the same as inn Copenhagen. I just had an advantage of the courses being offered to non-social science students as well, so I luckily knew a lot of the stuff.
teaching_comparison: Very much the same.
courses_enrolled: SANT290-1 and SOS119
recommended_courses: I don't really have any to be honest. Maybe I would recommend, if you have the opportunity to also look at other faculties and what courses they offer. Also, it's a good idea to look at how they are placed so your courses doesn't over lap, or that you at least know if they do over lap.
unexpected_costs: It wasn't really unexpected, but I went on a lot of trips with friend and in general it didn't go on exchange with the intention to save money. Trips are great and you make a lot of great memories from them, but they are also super expensive, which is something to keep in mind
cost_comparison: Fresh salat in general and beer are super expensive compared to Denmark. But local transport on the other hand is quite okay compared to other prices in Norway.
activities_available: There are SO many which are organised by the organisation Sammen.
activities_recommended: Hiking, skiing or snowboarding in Voss, swimming in Gammel Haugen, meeting other exchange students, KODE-museums - there are SO many. And also, you don't have to go very far to see other places and a lot of beautiful nature.
weekend_recommendations: Please go to Lofoten And also sign up on DNT so you go on great and cosy hiking trips different places in Norway - it is the most koselig/hygge experiences ever.
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: As a Dane, it is definitely easier and norwegians are very open to speaking with Danish people. If you follow Sammenbergen on Instagram, they have a lot of activities. You can also stay in contact with your group from Fadderuken if you are going in the Autumn semester.
cultural_challenges: Non
culture_appreciated: The openness to talk to other people
top3_advice: Say 'yes' to as much as possible Enjoy the nature Live in the moment
other_useful_info: You can rent free hiking and skiing equitment at BUA. Use the days you have with sunshine: there are plenty of days to stay inside (cause it's raining a lot haha), so please get out when the sun is shinning.
most_rewarding: My friends - I love them to death. And discovering my love for nature.
greatest_challenge: Accepting FOMO and finding a good balance between studies and free time.
other_comments: Please go on exchange to Bergen. It is the best place, if you ask me. It doesn't matter that it's close to Denmark - it is still a very great experience. And it is only an advantage to speak a language so close to the Norwegian language.

crucial_aspects: I was supposed to go to California but that fell through partly due to COVID, so my focus became solely on a place not too far away with a good academic reputation. Bergen fit that mold.
overall_comments: It was a good experience overall
info_ease: There is a big student center where you can easily get help. Writing over e-mail was a bit frustrating since the response was slow but upon arrival, it was pretty smooth to just seek help in person.
arrival_assistance: I got help with transport card for students, gym and overall mental wellbeing.
arrival_comments: Pretty good. Again, everything was available at the student center.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was a good experience overall
registration_process: I found the courses I wanted on the website and wrote to Toril since the courses were masters level and im undergraduate student.
registration_help: Toril was able to get me the courses I wanted.
registration_success: I got everything I wanted.
registration_advice: Go after the courses you want! Even if they arent on your level, you might get lucky like I was.
academics_comments: It was a good experience overall
course_level: Mostly masters and one undergraduate.
teaching_comparison: We had more classes but the level seemed about the same. More social since we had to interact more and do group work at almost all classes.
courses_enrolled: Pedagogiske perspektiv på læring Psykologisk Kartlegging Psykologisk Behandling
recommended_courses: All of them were great.
unexpected_costs: Everything was MUCH more expensive than back home. Norway is very expensive so bring more money than you expect to use!
cost_comparison: Everything was more expensive. Going out to eat or have a drink was crazy expensive.
activities_available: Concerts, events, talks, group hiking, movie clubs etc
activities_recommended: Bergen is a very beautiful city so I would recommend exploring by foot. Also all the cultural events.
weekend_recommendations: Take the fløyen, ulrikke, KODA museum
culture_adjustment: Very. Norway and Denmark is quite similar in culture.
socializing_tips: Norwegians are much more open than Danes in my experience, especially if they know you arent a local, so I would just say be open and speak to people! They will probably come to you too.
cultural_challenges: None really.
culture_appreciated: How open people were. I also appreciate that the language was similar to Danish so I could take classes in Norwegian!
top3_advice: 1) Bring more money than you expect! 2) Take advantage of all the beautiful sites not just in Bergen but other cities! 3) People are really friendly, so if you show interest in them, you can really get to know lots of people
other_useful_info: Not really.
most_rewarding: The people I met and also getting insight into how they view psychology in Norway.
greatest_challenge: I did feel lonely at times, but that was my own fault.
other_comments: GO! Being on exchange has been great overall. Learning to be more independent and gaining insight into a different culture is always a good thing.

crucial_aspects: I was doing clinical rotation at Haukeland sjykehus, where I went to the orthopedic department and the emergency room. When choosing destination it was important to me that I would be able to communicate with the patients so that I would get the most learning out of my experience at the hospital. Therefore I chose Norway as my destination. I love nature and Bergen is a city surrounded by mountains where nature is no more than 30 minutes away by foot. This too, was a crucial aspect choosing the study destination.
overall_comments: I loved Bergen! I would definitely do it again and I'm definitely going back to visit soon! The nature at Vestlandet is amazing and I enjoyed many weekend trips on foot, skis and climbing. At the hospital I loved my time at the orthopedic department, but it would have been nice with a schedule. at the orthopedic department I had a very nice tutor who showed med around the first day and told me where to go each day. I didn't get a schedule at the ER either, which made it hard to know where I should be and when I should be there. On the other hand I got to see many very interesting cases and a lot of different cases. The docters all in all were super nice, both at the ER and the Orthopedic department, but I wouldn't recommend choosing the ER as a part of a clinical rotation. Sometimes it was so hectic it was hard to know what I was supposed to do, and where I was supposed to be. So if I went again I wouldn't choose the ER and I would definitely be more insisting on getting a schedule (on paper) for my time at each department.

culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Seek private housing with one or more local roomies instead of staying in one of the student housings.
cultural_challenges: None - the Norwegians are very friendly people, can keep a bit to themselves, maybe even more than us Danes, but I think we understand them very well.
culture_appreciated: The way they made use of their amazing nature! Everyone - from young kids to the elderly went on hikes and stayed in shape.
top3_advice: - Bergen is a quite small city. If you are looking for a bustling metropol, go another place. I definitely missed some of the city life I'm used to in CPH. - Don't be fooled by the relatively low academic requirements at the lectures. The exams are not easy. - Bring your outdoor equipment - in my opinion your stay will become much better if you enjoy the nature like the Norwegians.
other_useful_info: Covered above
most_rewarding: Being in the nature - I miss the mountains.

crucial_aspects: I went to Svalbard due to the unique nature and geology. The courses sounded exciting - and it has lived up to my expectations! I Wanted to go to the arctic and learn more about this, since I'm interested in climate and the poles are really affected by changing climate - and Svalbard must be one of the best places to learn about this!
info_ease: I think it was easy, but I was very happy that we were serval students arriving the same day, so we could figure things out together!
arrival_assistance: In the reception in UNIS the receptionist gave us a lot of information. Also, we had a 3 days "course" were information about courses, UNIS and living in Svalbard and studying in the arctic were given.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I went to the receptionist and she helped me. It was super easy.
registration_help: The receptionist at UNIS
registration_success: I got into the courses I applied for...
registration_advice: Apply for courses that you have the background for
course_level: I think the level was good. In one of the courses I took I had heard of many of the processes before, since I had a course covering approximately the same in my program in Copenhagen. But it was more focusing on Svalbard and that was very interesting. I came to Svalbard because I wanted to do a lot o field work and I have learned a lot about that!! There is a lot of written reports and bigger projects and much work is done independently - and I have learned a lot from this, since I had no real experience in writing before!
teaching_comparison: In Copenhagen we get a lot of help always and we have lectures and exercises every week (so a lecture about something and then an exercise about the same thing). In UNIS this is different because you need to do field work when the sun is still up! Therefore we had a lot of lectures in the first course where almost all knowledge were told - then we did field work and wrote reports, and had only a few lectures after the field work. In the course that started later we had topics like in copenhagen and often an exercise in the end of the week, but also here the written part were a bigger part than at home. Also, the field work in this course were the end of many lectures, and after this there were 1 month of writing report and working independently in the lab.
courses_enrolled: AG-210: The Quarternary and Glacial Geology of Svalbard (15 ECTS) AG-211: Arctic Marine Geology (15 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I would recommend these courses for geology! But I know they will be changed in 2-3 years...
unexpected_costs: I did some tourist things, for example a trip to Pyramiden (1400 DKK) Also, the fee for rifle permit (250 DKK)
cost_comparison: I was expecting everything to be expensive.. and it was.
activities_available: Nothing from UNIS. But there is a gym, swimming pool, football and hockey... And it does not cost that much and there is often student rabat.
activities_recommended: Be part of the gym and/or the sport activities!
weekend_recommendations: Go for hikes!! Must go to the student cabin and I will also recommend Nordenskiold cabin. Visit Longyearbreen and/or Larsbreen and the ice caves when its cold! Visit Pyramiden!
culture_adjustment: Longyearbyen is a strange place with only 2600 people - many are norwegian, but in general there is a very international community here! But take part in local events is nice! (Ps. you need facebook to go to Svalbard since they have a group for everything fx Northern lights in Longyearbyen, Sysselmesteren, info in Longyearbyen... etc)
socializing_tips: There is no local students. Everyone is exchange students and I think that is really nice since every one want to get new friends!
cultural_challenges: I have met many different cultures and it is fun to learn from so many different people!
culture_appreciated: The international culture :)
top3_advice: Be open to meet new people! Go on a lot of hikes! Don't be afraid to try something new!
other_useful_info: We are in the arctic and there is a lot of outdoor activity and you can get cold - don't be scared of being cold and dirty - but enjoy your stay!!
most_rewarding: I have no idea... I have developed my social skills and my english and learned a lot in geology and learned to be much more independent in my work! I have hiked a lot and just enjoyed being here...
greatest_challenge: Writing the bigger project, doing research on my own and working in the lab and get to understand the samples and the processes!

registration_success: Really successful, i got all the classes i really wanted. One course I heard there were a long waiting list for, but I got a spot, and it was such a nice course.
registration_advice: It is really easy, and everyone are so sweet. So do it! It is an amazing experience to study at University of Bergen
course_level: The level of the courses were pretty easy compared to my home university. I had a master course, which i did not found that difficult. With that being said, I learned a lot of new stuff. And some of the stuff was repetition from courses in Denmark, but it was nice to learn it one more time.
teaching_comparison: It was really similar. Lectures and seminars. But we had a lot more of oral presentations than in Denmark. I think i have had 2 presentations in Denmark in 2 years, and here i had 2 presentations in 1 semester.

It was really nice to try out all the different types of learning, and i enjoyed that course a lot!

housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: Marte the university coordinator was very helpful.
registration_success: N/A
registration_advice: Just write them an email if you're unsure of what to do.
academics_comments: Everything but the academic aspect was a 10!

Walk around the city. I went to Hardness skogen to pick mushrooms but found out later that the forest beneath Ulriken was overflowing with funnel chantarelles.
weekend_recommendations: Went on a boat trip to Flåm, 5,5 hours, can recommend as well. Then took the train from Flåm-Myrdal, Myrdal-Voss, Voss-Bergen.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, Norway is very much like Denmark.
socializing_tips: I didn't, so no, sorry.
cultural_challenges: Not really, we are very alike.
culture_appreciated: I had a lot of help from one nurse and a doctor at the hospital with planning my trip home from Norway. I drove with my friend in a car all the way home through Sweden. They helped me plan the trip and one of them even had a discount for a hotel that she shared with me.
top3_advice: Bring an umbrella. Do it. It rains all the time. And waterproof everything. You can buy it there, but if you have it, bring it. Be open, enjoy your free time, don't spend it at the hospital, go see the city you live in. Don't be afraid to experience things alone if you don't have anyone to go with.
other_useful_info: If you like collecting mushrooms they have an app as well as physical "mushroom control groups" called "Soppkontroll". Mushrooms experts go through your basket and make sure you don't have any toxic ones.
most_rewarding: Experiencing another climate, another city and another healthcare system.
greatest_challenge: Feeling like I wasn't welcome or wanted at the hospital, and like I was really just a burden...
other_comments: Go go go. As I wrote, everything about my stay except the hospital department was 10/10!

crucial_aspects: The nature and the ability to apply for relevant courses.
info_ease: Very easy. UiB has a very nice website and it is easy to find information. But you have to be aware of deadlines and different things, but my impression is that it is easy to talk with the staff if you need help after you have arrived.
arrival_assistance: We had an intro-week and a day with presentations from our campus "responsible". And there are an office at all campuses if you need help.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You get an email with the procedure. I remember it being very simple. You get an account at Studentweb and then apply for courses. It is a very good idea to know what courses you can get in advance, and have the prior approval from your university.
registration_help: You can email the faculty you are applying and they will help you. I remember the employes at UiB being very kind and helpfull when I had some questions about the courses.
registration_success: I thought it was possible to get some courses that are obligatory at my home university, but I found out they didn't offer the courses at the autumn semester. So there wasn't a lot of courses to choose from, maybe only 4, and I needed 3.
registration_advice: Make sure that you know what courses you can apply to.
course_level: ECON116 Natur og ressursøkonomi was very easy and focusing on old litterature as Adam Smith and Ronald Coase with essay-assignments. ECON115 Development Economics was also kind of easy since I already have had courses that uses the basic terms, but also with a lot of new theory that I found very interesting. We had one essay assignment. ECON260 was the most challenging course with new mathematic methods and theory. We had one groups assignment and one indiviual assignment.
teaching_comparison: ECON260 was very similar to the courses we have at UCPH. It was similar to the microeconomics courses I already have had, but with new theory as Bertrand and Cournot, and a lot more. ECON116 was very different from what I know from Copenhagen, with focus on theory from former economist and with essay assignments which I have never tries before at the university. I was disappointed with the academic level.
courses_enrolled: ECON115 Development Economics ECON116 Natur og ressursøkonomi ECON260 Industrial organization and competition policy
recommended_courses: I would recommend ECON115 Development economics and ECON260 Industrial organization and competition policy. ECON116 was in norwegian.
unexpected_costs: Things I needed as new clothes and shoes, but also buying stuff for your room in the beginning and maybe for traveling or smaller trips during the semester.
cost_comparison: Alcohol is extremely expensive. Food is expensive as well, but I thought it would be worse. But it was probably because of the NOK being very cheap.
activities_available: They have a lot of different sport activities. Also many different choirs.
activities_recommended: I would recommend the 7 mountains in 7 weeks, which is a thing Sammen has started. Every Wednesday in the beginning of the semester they meet at 17:00 and hike on one of the seven mountains in Bergen.
weekend_recommendations: Go for a hike or take the train or bus to different places around Bergen. We went for a day-trip to Voss and a weekend trip to Tromsø. Bergen has a lot of pretty places to visit as Nordnes, Gammelhaugen and all the seven mountains.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. There is not a huge different between Denmark and Norway.
socializing_tips: Participate in the intro week "Fadder uken", where you meet other Norwegians who have also just moved to Bergen and are starting their first semester.
cultural_challenges: Nothing.
culture_appreciated: The nature.
top3_advice: 1. Participate in the intro week.
other_useful_info: Buy some nice hiking shoes and an umbrella or rain-clothes. There is a very nice sport outlet in Bergen as well.
most_rewarding: The nature. It is very different from what we have in Denmark.
greatest_challenge: I don't know.

crucial_aspects: That I could speak and understand the language. I really wanted to explore other Nordic countries and feel closer to Scandinavia. And then the nature in Norway of course.
info_ease: Pretty easy. There was a lot of introduction and events and so on. And everyone from UiB were really nice to answer all our question via email.
arrival_assistance: I needed help with courses and I changed courses at one point, so that was my primary concern. And then I needed help finding psychologist and Sammen at UiB also helped with that.
arrival_comments: The only thing was that the student organized welcome was centered a lot on drinking and a bit messy. Messy in like organization and planning... so I didn't have the best experience there and didn't go to all the events. But I heard a lot of other people on other faculties had a good experience
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You have to apply for acceptance of your courses and that decides whether you can get your courses or not. My institute are very sweet and open so they say yes to almost everything, so that really nice when you go on exchange and want to try something else. And then regarding choosing university I just looked in Mobility One. And then I have a coordinator here in Denmark who answered all my questions. I also went to a zoom meeting twice about exchange.
registration_help: I had a zoom meeting, a physical meeting and then a coordinator. And also a Facebook group for all KU students going to the Nordic countries
registration_success: Very. 10 out of 10. I also changed courses doing my stay.
registration_advice: I didn't have any problems so I don't know if I have any advice. Maybe talk to your coordinator and ask questions if you are afraid that you can't get your courses. Check and see how open your university is with you taking different courses
course_level: It felt easier than was I was used to at Copenhagen. But I think that might be because I had more time and didn't have a job either. I had peace to focus on my studies and that gave me a chance to be really well prepared.
teaching_comparison: Pretty much the same, but in a smaller class which I enjoyed a lot. That gives more room for conversation.
courses_enrolled: Electronic Literature Current Anthropological Research: New Technologies and the Future of the Human The Frontier of Anthropological Research: Times of War. Cultural and Symbolic Landscapes in Contemporary Eastern Europe
recommended_courses: All of the above. I study anthropology and tried courses on Digital Culture which was really nice. If your university allows it try something else. Maybe more practical or a different subject that you are used to. It's fun for you and it's really nice for your brain to try and think differently. I came back to Copenhagen with more energy to study again and a new way of seeing different dilemmas
unexpected_costs: I had to go to the doctor a lot, so that. And then also trips and climbing. I didn't count on going on that many trips but then I ended up renting a car and so on. But personal experience and costs but still unexpected.
cost_comparison: Public transportation! So cheap compared to DK
activities_available: All sorts. BSI is so great at offering different stuff. There is literally anything. And if you don't find anything Bergen is a city of culture, so I'm pretty sure you can find something.
activities_recommended: Volunteer, join a sport or a student club. Go to local events
weekend_recommendations: Take the train an hour away and hike. Take a car to Sotra (lovely!!!). Go to Kanadaskogen and look for mushrooms. Swim in the fjord. Go to søbadet. Go to the club Rommet or Landmark or Kulturhuset. Go fishing. Take the boat. Go for a walk in Sandviken
culture_adjustment: I took about a month but it felt easy in retrospect. But I also joined a student club and the helped tremendously.
socializing_tips: It was easy because I speak danish, but... Maybe try and find activities where there is a mix of international and norwegian students
cultural_challenges: None. Maybe the age gap a little bit. I was 25 and a lot of bachelor students in Norway are way younger. But I didn't bother. And I met plenty of peers
culture_appreciated: Nature:) People, so kind:)
top3_advice: Join something. Be a volunteer or join a sport anything. It helps a lot when you are new. Say yes a lot. If you want a more local experience then try to find housing on your own with other norwegian students.
other_useful_info: I didn't live at Fantoft, but I heard that a lot of international students enjoyed it and it creates friends and some social ties pretty quick. So if you fear loneliness I would recommend going there. But I would still recommend trying to find housing with Norwegian students and get a more local experience.
most_rewarding: The people, the break from my everyday, the nature
greatest_challenge: Settling in. The first month I cried a lot haha. I felt introduction week (fadderuken) was horrible, but then I found my people and then everything turned around. And classes began and I love learning new things

crucial_aspects: I would like to go somewhere with a different nature than what I was used to, and preferably a place where i could speak the mother language. That i why Bergen became my destination.
overall_comments: Do it if you would like to study in a different environment than you are used to, and would like to try out new things and routines outside of what you are used to from home.
info_ease: Things went quite easy. However, the mobility online website is a bit confusing. It is also frustrating that it seems like Copenhagen University and the host university (in this case Bergen) didn't seem to "speak together". I had some trouble with my courses, and i had to have several separate mail correspondences with each of the universities, because no one seemed to have the responsibility..
arrival_assistance: Many of the information, you get on your mail from the host university. However, there were some confusion about the intro days. You had to seek out a lot of information by yourself. But the Studentcenter (studentsenteret) is very helpful if you have any questions!
arrival_comments: The "freshers week" programme is not working. It is badly coordinated (at least at the faculty of humanities) and there is a great lack of activities without the main purpose being drinking alcohol. I managed to participate in the activities i felt like doing, but for people who find new social situations hard, I think the intro programme needs some rethinking.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Do it if you would like to study in a different environment than you are used to, and would like to try out new things and routines outside of what you are used to from home.
registration_process: I wished to register for courses taught in norwegian. They are not in the course list for exchange students in the "studentweb" website, so I had to email the faculties in which my courses were taught. That was a bit of a mess, and a lot of back and fourth emailing, but in the end, it all worked out, you just need a bit of patience.
registration_help: UIB are very polite and helpfull. You just need a bit of patience, as the responding time can be a bit long, especially during summer- and christmas vacation.
registration_success: It all worked out in the end and i got the courses i wished for.
registration_advice: If you're in doubt, send an email to UIB. They are very helpful.
academics_comments: Do it if you would like to study in a different environment than you are used to, and would like to try out new things and routines outside of what you are used to from home.
course_level: One of my courses, I felt like was below my level. The other one was similar to what I am used to.
teaching_comparison: I had much fewer teaching hours than at UCPH. In one of my courses, seminars where student driven and not obligatory.
courses_enrolled: KVIK201 and KVIK102.
recommended_courses: KVIK201!
unexpected_costs: Various trips.
cost_comparison: Vegetables are quite expensive! And beer if you like that :)
activities_available: You can do almost everything!
activities_recommended: "Spire" is a very nice and welcoming group of students that are the Bergen part of a Norwegian environmental and development organization. I would also recommend the wednesday hiking ( 7 fjell på 7 uker) organized by Sammen. If you like fishing, the BSI fishing club is also very very nice people!
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes! and sleep in a DNT hut! For hiking, i would recommend Gullfjellet and Hananipa. Fpr trips to DNT huts, I went to BT-hytta and Høgabu! So amazing, and a true norwegian experience.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Bergen is a very welcoming city and people are very nice. My experience is, that is is easiest to get in touch with other norwegians by joining one of the student clubs/activities.
socializing_tips: Join one of the student clubs/activities!
cultural_challenges: Norwegian people seem to have a friends group and sticks to it. But it's the same thing about danes I think. My best advice would be to attend to or engage in one of the student clubs or student activities. And there is plenty!!
culture_appreciated: Norwegian people really like to "hygge". Maybe even more than danes does!
top3_advice: Be open! Try out new things. This is a chance to try out something new for a couple of months. It is okay if it gets hard sometimes. You are away from home and maybe on your own. But most people are nice, and there is always something to do in Bergen! look out for the posters on the streets with activities, koncerts and so on. Be a volunteer in something, try out a new sport, check out "Sammen", they have A LOT of things going on. Meet new people and enjoy the nature. Go on trips! DNT is a fantastic opportunity.
other_useful_info: When in doubt, go to the student center.
most_rewarding: The nature. I really really enjoyed it and miss it a lot now.
greatest_challenge: Being away from home and people I love. But when i felt lonely, I searched for something to do outside the apartment, and I almost always got in a better mood. Meeting people, attending activities and being in the nature always helped.

registration_process: It was not too complicated. I had to sign up for courses that were pre-approved, and upon arrival, get a student card. recommended_courses: I would recommend especially the geohazard and structural geology course; it's a great opportunity to learn about the local geology and circumstances that are not thought as much at least in my own university. weekend_recommendations: The nature and mountains surrounding Bergen.
culture_adjustment: Really easy, as it's similar to my own.
socializing_tips: Join the clubs and activities, it can be hard to make friends without doing something together, as people aren't very outgoing.
cultural_challenges: Maybe that people are more reserved.
culture_appreciated: People were kind, helpful and easy to be around.
top3_advice: Consider your pre-approval courses as your final choices, explore the nature around the city and join some of the university activities to make friends.
other_useful_info: Buy the monthly plan for the bybane transport.
most_rewarding: The nature and the teaching at university.
greatest_challenge: Breaking through and making friends.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a university with a high level of teaching, and the University of Bergen has a good reputation especially for its high quality courses in Nordic literature. Furthermore, I wanted to broaden my knowledge and academic skills, so I took the opportunity to take a course in ethnomusicology, because I have always been interested in the topic. Lastly, it was important for me to go somewhere with beautiful nature, because there is not much of that in Denmark and the mountains in the Bergen area are gorgeous!
overall_comments: It was a fantastic experience to study abroad, but it was also tough at times. It takes time to get used to the new place and the courses you will be taking.
info_ease: It was quite easy if you keep attention to the information you get before your arrival, and the information you get through UiB's own e-mails and digital systems.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation day for international students and an orientation day at the faculty I attended to. Besides that, the study guide was very helpful with information. However, it sometimes took them a bit long time to respond over e-mail.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was a fantastic experience to study abroad, but it was also tough at times. It takes time to get used to the new place and the courses you will be taking.
registration_process: I first checked the course list provided by the University in Bergen for international students. I chose a course in Nordic literary analysis and theory as that is what I am studying at my home university and it sounded very interesting and relevant to my own studies. I took the opportunity to take a course that is not available at my home university, which was a course in ethnomusicology. Then I got a pre-approval for these courses from the exchange department at UCPH. When the semester started I realized that there existed multiple course codes for my Nordic literature course. I decided to switch the course code and got a new pre-approval from UCPH, because the form of examination would be different than what I originally had accepted. By changing the course code I still attended the exact same course but instead of doing both a written and and oral exam, I only had to do a written exam. Because I only attended one semester at UiB it does not affect my future studies. Lastly, because I am Scandinavian it was possible to do the exam in Danish instead of Norwegian even though the course was taught in Norwegian. When I applied for this, my examination code changed to ZNORD-2 which was used on the original course code. This meant that I was an international student who passed a Nordic course in Norwegian. Besides writing in Danish, the examination was exactly the same as for everyone else.
registration_help: The study guide.
registration_success: After some time changing course codes, I was very successful.
registration_advice: Be sure to get all the information on the courses you can get, and check for deadlines and requirements for the individual courses. Being on exchange in a different university, you have the unique opportunity to try new courses that is not available to you at your home university, so you should consider trying something different and widen your perspectives.
academics_comments: It was a fantastic experience to study abroad, but it was also tough at times. It takes time to get used to the new place and the courses you will be taking.
course_level: Because I was a BA student at my home university, I was only able to take BA-leveled courses at UiB.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching consisted primarily of lecture based teaching and did not involve the students so much during the courses. This suited my nicely as I am very used to that from my home university and I am very interested in learning from the professors. However, I only had two lectures each week and because the students was not involved as much in the dialogue, it was a bit difficult to socialize with the other students because we did not speak much during the courses and we would only be gathered a few times a month. During the final lectures of my ethnomusicological course each student presented their field work project that we have worked on individually throughout the semester. This was a very nice ending to the semester, as it provided some variation, and it was interesting to learn about the other students' projects.
courses_enrolled: MUG105 Music in World Cultures and NOLI216 Nordic Literature: Literary Analysis and Theory
recommended_courses: I can recommend both of these courses. If you are interested in music from different cultures than what we are typically being exposed to in the Western world, Music in World Cultures is really interesting. You get to learn about how music is being used differently in other parts of the world and do your own ethnomusicological field work project in Bergen, where you get to explore a music community of your own choice. The Nordic Literature course is very interesting for anyone who deals with Nordic literature and want to be challenged on the topic. You will be exposed to new perspectives, as you will learn about a wide range of theories and why and how to use them.
unexpected_costs: The books were really expensive.
cost_comparison: Fresh vegetables are really expensive and going out to cafés, restaurants, bars etc. is also very expensive.
activities_available: Because I attended a music course, I had music practice spaces available to play either alone or with other people. Besides there was a pool available, various sport courts and the student cultural center Det Akademiske Kvarteret hosted many parties, quizzes and concerts for students. Furthermore, Bergen has a rich associational life and as a student you can become a volunteer in sports teams, photography associations, choirs and environmental associations to name a few.
activities_recommended: Go to concerts, quizzes and parties at Hulen and Det Akademiske Kvarteret. They both have student discounts and you can meet Norwegian students where they are a bit more open minded and meet new people in a more casual atmosphere. You should also go on hikes in the mountains as there are plenty of them in the Bergen area, if you are an outdoor person. Most of the museums have student discounts as well and have lots of great exhibitions. Litteraturhuset located in the city center hosts lots of events such as folk music concerts, poetry nights, talks etc. I play music as well, and I went to many jam nights at a bare called Stereo bare on Sundays, which is a great place to socialize and you can also invite your friends to jam with or just hang out.
weekend_recommendations: Going on hikes as well and see Edvard Griegs house Troldhaugen which is very beautiful. You should also check out the amazing wooden buildings at Bryggen. However, it is a big tourist attraction so be careful not to fall in a tourist trap.
culture_adjustment: Denmark and Norway is very similar culturally in a lot of ways, so it was not too difficult. However, nearly every grocery shops, supermarkets and other shops are closed on Sundays and on holidays, so make sure to do your shopping beforehand.
socializing_tips: As I mentioned before, you should meet them outside of a university setting. Norwegians as well as Danish people have a reputation of being very reserved so meeting them at concerts, parties or places with a more relaxed atmosphere helps getting the conversation going more easily. Most Norwegians grow up hiking in the mountains and will probably accept an invitation to do so.
cultural_challenges: Going out to cafés, restaurants, bars and so on is very expensive, so I did not go out as much as I am used to. The fact that almost every shop closes on Sundays and holidays was really irritating at times.
culture_appreciated: I come from Denmark so I am primarily used to flat fields everywhere outside of the cities, so having a beautiful view over the mountains everywhere was really amazing.
top3_advice: Bring hiking boots and gear to go on hiking trips in the mountains. It is a great way to socialize as you make wonderful memories together. The University in Bergen provides a lot of libraries. You will probably spend a lot of time in these, and most of them have a very nice atmosphere, so be sure to check the different ones out, so you know which ones works best for you. If you want to prioritize socializing, you should apply for a living space in a dorm. You will meet a lot of international students there, and if you become friends with them, you live close to each other so it is easy to hang out.
other_useful_info: Remember to check the semester dates, as these were different than what I was used to from my home university. The student guide is very helpful so do not hesitate to ask them anything if you have any questions, and remember to check your e-mail and UiB's digital sources for important information.
most_rewarding: Knowing that I am capable of doing well academically in other kinds of courses at a different university than what I am used to, gave me a lot of confidence. Furthermore, it gave me a huge confidence boost knowing that I can do well and thrive both socially and academically in a different country and become good friends with people from different parts of the world.
greatest_challenge: To balance being social while also doing my best in the courses. I am a very ambitious student, but a huge part of why I chose to study abroad was to make friends from different countries. Besides that I felt pretty homesick at times, but luckily I had good friends to keep my mind occupied during those periods.

socializing_tips: Live with them. And learn some norwegian. It really pays off.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The Norwegians' appreciation for nature and getting out. Ut på tur, aldrig sur.
top3_advice: Get out in the mountains around bergen - bring your outdoor gear. Go to some of the cute saunas around town - for instance Laugaren. If you're into climbing then you NEED to check out Vestveggen . It's a huge rope climbing gym right outside town and of course outdoor climbing in the area.
other_useful_info: Don't let the rain scare you. I was concerned before coming here but it was truly not that bad. And when the weather is nice there are a million things to do in this city and the mountains around it. The most amazing DNT hut I've ever been to called Stovegolvet is also definitely worth a mention and a visit.
most_rewarding: Nature!

other_comments: Bergen is a super cute place to go if you're into mountains, skiing, hiking, climbing - all that jazz. Stay curious of new places during your entire stay and you'll get some amazing experiences.

Don't do things to tick something off in a box. Quality over Quantity: what matters is the people you are experiencing things with and how you are feeling yourself. Not how many hikes or cities you get to see. 3. Be open and flexible: many things is happening during an exchange. But also remember "you-time" I recommend "tid for yoga": yogaplace in the city.
