crucial_aspects: Bologna is the ultimate student city. With the University of Bologna, the city is packed with young people from all over the world. It has this lively, welcoming vibe where it’s super easy to meet new people, whether it's at a café, a piazza, or during one of the many student events. You’ll never feel alone here, everyone is in the same boat, looking for new experiences and friendships. Food is a major part of any exchange experience. And in Bologna, it’s next-level. This city is the heart of Italian cuisine, known for tagliatelle al ragù, tortellini, and mortadella. Eating out is affordable for students, and there are tons of cozy osterias where you can get authentic, home style Italian food without breaking the bank. One of the best things about Bologna is its size. It’s big enough to have everything you need, bars, clubs, concerts, markets, parks, but small enough that you don’t feel lost in a massive city. You can walk or bike everywhere, which makes life super convenient. Plus, the city is full of stunning medieval architecture, and you’ll find yourself strolling under its endless porticoes no matter the weather. Bologna is right in the middle of Italy, which means you can easily take a train and be in Florence, Venice, Milan, or even Rome in just a few hours. The airport also has cheap flights all over Europe, making weekend trips super easy. If you want a city full of students, great food, a buzzing nightlife, and a deep history, Bologna should be at the top of your list. It’s the perfect balance between study and fun, tradition and modern life. By the time your exchange is over, you won’t want to leave.
info_ease: Finding the necessary information upon arrival in Bologna wasn't the easiest, as a lot of it had to be actively searched for rather than being readily available. There wasn’t a single clear guide for everything, so I had to ask around, check university websites, and rely on other students' experiences to figure things out. That being said, the information is there, you just have to look for it. While response times from some offices could be slow, especially for administrative matters, most things could be sorted out with some patience and persistence. Connecting with other exchange students and asking in Facebook groups or WhatsApp chats was often the fastest way to get answers. Overall, it requires some effort, but you’ll find what you need if you take the initiative.
arrival_assistance: When I arrived in Bologna, there was an online help desk available for new students, which was really useful. However, because so many students were logging in at the start of the semester, there were some delays in the process. It’s important to be patient, as it might take a few days to get fully checked in, even after starting your courses. That said, once you’re through the initial wait, the staff are very friendly and helpful, and the system works well. They made sure all my questions were answered and helped with any issues I had. It just requires a bit of patience at the beginning.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process at the University of Bologna is mainly done online, and getting through it can be challenging due to high demand at the beginning of the semester. The check-in system requires patience, as it can take several days before everything is finalized, even after classes have started. There isn’t really a physical office where you can go for direct help. If you try, you’ll likely be sent from one faculty to another without getting clear answers. However, once you do get through the online process, the staff are helpful and responsive, making sure everything is sorted out properly.
registration_help: Online help desk
registration_success: Registering for classes at the University of Bologna was very easy. The system allowed me to add and drop courses without much hassle, which was great in case a class didn’t turn out as expected. This flexibility made it simple to adjust my schedule and find the courses that best suited my interests. The university staff were helpful and understanding when it came to switching courses, so overall, the process was smooth and student friendly.
registration_advice: Be patient. The registration process can take time, especially with the online check-in system. It might take a few days before everything is finalized, so don’t stress if things aren’t immediately sorted. Stay persistent, check for updates regularly, and reach out for help if needed. Once you get through it, everything runs smoothly
course_level: The difficulty level of courses at the University of Bologna was quite varied. Some courses were relatively easy, while others were more challenging, depending on the subject and professor. The structure and expectations were different from what I was used to in Denmark, making the experience both interesting and sometimes unpredictable. There was also a big difference in exam formats. Unlike in Denmark, where exams tend to follow a more standardized structure, exams in Bologna could be multiple-choice, oral exams, handwritten written exams, or take-home assignments. This variety required adaptability, but it also provided a unique learning experience.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at the University of Bologna was quite similar to that at UCPH in terms of academic approach. However, one key difference was the class size here, the groups were much smaller, creating a more classroom-like atmosphere. Professors were very interactive, frequently asking questions and expecting students to engage actively in discussions. This made the lessons more dynamic but also meant that participation was expected, rather than just listening passively.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Italian Culture Visualizing The Italian Society Education Systems and Policies Social Studies of Science and Technology (LM) Applied Political Sociology
recommended_courses: Visualizing The Italian Society – The professor is truly passionate about Italian culture and does a great job of bringing it to life through film analysis. The course is engaging and offers a unique perspective on how Italian society is represented in cinema. Education Systems and Policies – This course is great for understanding higher education systems across different countries, especially since many exchange students share insights from their home universities. It provides a broad, comparative perspective that makes discussions both interesting and relevant.
unexpected_costs: One of the biggest unexpected costs was rent, especially if you want to live within the city walls. Housing prices can be quite high compared to other Italian cities. Another thing to be aware of is that imported groceries (anything not from Italy) are often more expensive than in Denmark. If you prefer certain international brands or ingredients, you might end up paying more than expected. Finally, there are a lot of small expenses that add up things like social activities, transportation, and everyday essentials. It’s just part of the exchange experience, but it’s good to budget for these extra costs.
cost_comparison: Rent can be quite high, especially within the city walls. Imported groceries, such as non-Italian brands or specific international products, are also noticeably more expensive than in Denmark. Eating out frequently can add up, even though many student friendly options exist. Everyday essentials and small purchases, like coffee or transport, can also accumulate into a larger expense than anticipated. Local Italian groceries, especially fresh produce, pasta, and cheese, are very affordable compared to Denmark. Eating at traditional osterias or student canteens can be relatively cheap if you choose wisely. Public transport is also reasonably priced, though Bologna is very walkable, reducing the need for it.
activities_available: The University Sports Centre (CUSB) provides numerous opportunities for students to engage in various sports at subsidized rates. Available activities include football, swimming, tennis, and more. CUSB also organizes tournaments and university championships, fostering a vibrant athletic community. Students can immerse themselves in a rich cultural scene through exhibitions, concerts, lectures, and other events organized by the university. The Collegium Musicum offers students the chance to join choirs or the orchestra, providing a platform to share their passion for music in a dynamic and international environment. Numerous student associations are active within the university, covering a broad spectrum of interests and providing ample opportunities for social engagement. These associations organize events, workshops, and gatherings, enhancing the social experience on campus. Additionally, the university offers incentives for students to spend their free time at theaters, cinemas, or participating in various leisure activities, further enriching the student experience.
activities_recommended: Bologna is perfectly located for traveling. You can easily take a train to Florence, Venice, Milan, or Rome for a weekend. It is a great way to explore more of Italy while on exchange
weekend_recommendations: In Bologna Climb the Asinelli Tower – Get the best panoramic view of the city from the top of this medieval tower. Explore the Quadrilatero Market – A historic market area full of great food, local delicacies, and a true Italian atmosphere. Visit San Luca Sanctuary – Walk the world's longest portico (covered walkway) up to this beautiful hilltop basilica. Enjoy Bologna’s Nightlife – Areas like Via del Pratello and Piazza Verdi are full of student-friendly bars and a great atmosphere. Discover the Hidden Canals – Bologna has a secret system of canals; check out the "Finestrella di Via Piella" for a unique view. Easy Weekend Trips from Bologna Florence (40 min by train) – Home to incredible art, museums, and beautiful streets. A must-see. Venice (1.5 hours by train) – The canals, gondolas, and historic charm make it a perfect weekend getaway. Milan (1 hour by train) – Visit the Duomo, go shopping, and experience the fashion capital of Italy. Verona (1.5 hours by train) – See Juliet’s balcony and the beautiful historic city center. Rimini (1 hour by train) – If you want a beach day, this is the best place to relax by the Adriatic Sea.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture in Bologna was quite easy, especially because it is such a student-friendly city. The atmosphere is welcoming, and since there are so many international students, you never feel out of place. One of the biggest cultural differences is the Italian pace of life. Things move a bit slower, especially with bureaucracy, so patience is key. Meals are also a big social event, with dinner often starting late in the evening. The locals are friendly and open, but it helps to know a few basic Italian phrases, as not everyone speaks English fluently. Learning simple greetings and ordering food in Italian makes a big difference in daily interactions. Overall, the combination of a vibrant student community, great food, and a relaxed lifestyle made it easy to settle in and feel at home in Bologna.
socializing_tips: The best way to connect with local students is simple. Just talk to them. Italians are incredibly friendly and love to chat, so do not be afraid to start a conversation. Even if some of them are not completely confident in English, they are usually eager to talk and will often help you learn some Italian along the way. Many students enjoy discussing food, culture, and everyday life, so even small talk can lead to new friendships. Whether it is during class, at a café, or in a bar, just be open, ask questions, and show interest. You will quickly find that most Italians are happy to engage and include you in their social circles.
cultural_challenges: One of the biggest challenges was adjusting to the slow pace of bureaucracy. Things like university registration, administrative processes, and even simple tasks such as getting official documents processed could take much longer than expected. Patience is essential when dealing with these situations. Another noticeable difference was the daily schedule. Italians eat much later than in Denmark, with dinner often starting around 8 or 9 in the evening. At first, it took some time to adjust, but eventually, it became a fun part of the experience. The concept of time is also more relaxed. Being slightly late is normal, and schedules are often more flexible. While this creates a laid-back atmosphere, it can sometimes be frustrating when you are used to a more punctual culture. Finally, although many Italians are very friendly and talkative, not everyone speaks fluent English. This could make communication difficult at times, especially in smaller shops or with older locals. However, learning a few basic Italian phrases helped a lot in these situations.
culture_appreciated: One of the things I appreciated most was how social and welcoming Italians are. People love to talk, whether it is in class, at a café, or even in the supermarket. It makes the city feel warm and inviting, especially for exchange students. I also really enjoyed the food culture. Meals are not just about eating but about spending time together. Whether it is a long dinner with friends or a casual aperitivo, food is an important part of daily life, and it creates a great sense of community. Another thing I loved was the relaxed lifestyle. While it takes time to get used to the flexible concept of time, it also creates a more enjoyable and less stressful environment. People take their time to enjoy life rather than rushing through it. Finally, Bologna’s history and architecture added so much to the experience. Walking through the beautiful old streets, surrounded by porticoes and historic buildings, made everyday life feel special. The city has a unique charm that is hard to find anywhere else.
top3_advice: Be patient with bureaucracy Things like university registration and administrative processes take time. The online check-in can be slow, and response times can be long. Do not stress if things are not sorted right away. Just stay persistent, check for updates regularly, and ask other students for help if needed. Enjoy the food culture Bologna is known as the food capital of Italy, and eating here is more than just a necessity. It is a social and cultural experience. Try traditional dishes like tagliatelle al ragù, tortellini, and mortadella. Go to local osterias, enjoy aperitivo in the evening, and embrace the slower, more relaxed way of dining. Take advantage of Bologna’s location Bologna is one of the best cities in Italy for travel. With fast train connections to Florence, Venice, Milan, and Rome, you can easily explore Italy during weekends and holidays. The airport also has cheap flights to other European destinations, so make sure to plan some trips while you are there.
other_useful_info: Do not get a bike. It will most likely be stolen, and the only affordable options are in poor condition.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was living in Bologna, a city that is truly special in every way. The atmosphere is incredible, filled with friendly and passionate people who make you feel welcome from day one. Whether it is chatting with locals at a café, meeting students from all over the world, or simply walking through the historic streets, Bologna has a unique energy that makes everyday life exciting. The food culture was another highlight. Bologna is the heart of Italian cuisine, and every meal feels like an experience. From the best tagliatelle al ragù to late-night aperitivos with friends, food is a central part of life here, and you can truly taste the love and tradition in every dish. The city’s dedication to football also adds to its charm. Whether you are watching Bologna FC play at the stadium or just experiencing the passion for football in bars and cafés, the love for the sport is everywhere. The locals live and breathe football, and it brings people together in a way that is amazing to witness.
greatest_challenge: One of the biggest challenges during my exchange was navigating the Italian way of doing things, especially when it came to bureaucracy and university administration. From the very start, the online check-in process tested my patience, with long waiting times and slow responses. Getting simple things like course registrations or official documents sorted out often felt like an endless cycle of being sent from one office to another. Another challenge was adapting to the unpredictability of daily life. In Denmark, things run on schedule, and information is usually clear. In Bologna, plans can change last minute, whether it is a professor moving an exam date or a shop randomly closing in the middle of the day for pausa pranzo. At first, this was frustrating, but over time, I learned to embrace the more relaxed Italian mindset and go with the flow. Language was also an obstacle at times. While many young Italians speak English, a lot of day-to-day interactions, buying groceries, dealing with landlords, or asking for directions—happened in Italian. Not knowing the language fluently made some situations tricky, but the locals were always friendly and eager to help, even if it meant a mix of broken Italian, hand gestures, and Google Translate. Despite these challenges, every difficulty came with a lesson. I learned to be patient, adapt quickly, and not stress over small things. Looking back, overcoming these obstacles made my exchange even more rewarding and helped me grow both personally and academically.

activities_recommended: I mostly enjoyed spending time with friends at restaurants, cafes, and going out for drinks.
weekend_recommendations: Visit Rome and the Dolomites and travel a bit around the country. Also just eat at the great restaurants in Bologna - it is much cheaper than eating out in Copenhagen.
culture_adjustment: I found it easy to adjust - I recommend arriving a week or two before school starts to explore the city.
socializing_tips: I didn't make any local friends and mostly socialized with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: There weren't really any.
culture_appreciated: The laid back attitude - my everyday life was a lot more laid back.
top3_advice: I would recommend going as soon as possible, such that you also have the opportunity to go abroad again. Treat the time as part holiday from university as the exams are generally much easier to pass. Enjoy your time.
other_useful_info: Start early finding an apartment and if possible find some people at your university you can talk to about the administrative stuff.
most_rewarding: The people I met along the way.
greatest_challenge: I can't answer this question.

crucial_aspects: Nice host city with interesting culture! Also warm weather was a bonus.
info_ease: It was not easy. Was difficult to see which courses were possible to take for the semester, not really possible to see before July/August. And then, the dates for exams are not published, you pretty much just have to wait until first class to find out. Also the fact that you have to hand in the online learning agreement much earlier at KU makes it more annoying. But everything will work out :)
arrival_assistance: Not really that much, as the uni staff were on holiday
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There is an option for early check-in around July, where you can check-in by video call. This was quite wasy, and then you just have to send them proof of your transport when you arrive.
registration_help: You can e-mail the international help desk. They were somewhat quick at responding, but not always very thoroughly or in fluent English. This you just have to get used to if you want to stay in Italy
registration_success: I succeeded eventually. But you can't know before hand, you just have to show up on the first day of class to see if you can take the course.
registration_advice: Deep breaths... take the anxiety and frustration as part of the experience haha. It will work out in the end!
course_level: Lower than that of KU. Perhaps the master courses were more at the same level of the bachelor courses at home. Less reading needed, so you can spend more time enjoying the city and travel!
teaching_comparison: Less structured, varies a lot from teacher to teacher. In that sense not as streamlined as at KU. But the professors are also often more flexible and willing to bend rules for you :)
courses_enrolled: Politics and Policies of the EU Political Behavior and Institutions Visualizing the Italian Society Urban Studies and Climate Change
recommended_courses: The first two you have to take if you're away on fifth semester. The last two were chilll, not demanding at all. Visualizing is cool if you like watching movies
unexpected_costs: I guess it depends a lot how you want to live, and how much you go out. Also depends on how much you want to travel, but if you can afford it there are so many nice places around Italy, so easy to get around by train
cost_comparison: Going out less expensive: 1,5 euro for coffee, 4 for spritz, around 10-12 for a pasta dish Getting groceries a bit more expensive than expected, but the Ecu supermarkets are cheap. Also Conad are somewhat cheap. You can get discount cards in both stores for students!
activities_available: Pretty much nothing. There is a bit through the Erasmus Student Network (ESN), they host some parties and trips. Otherwise you are very much let alone to take initiative
activities_recommended: Idk, become part of the WhatsApp group chat thorugh ESN. There people may arrange stuff, there was a football tournament and dinner shares regularly e.g.
weekend_recommendations: Hang out around the city! So many nice places like Giardini Margherita, Parco Montagnola, Basilica San Francesco. Cheap coffee and drinks. And go to Cassero for dancing! There is an instagram ('Bologna Parvenza') where you can see events thorugh the week. And travel around Italy!
culture_adjustment: I found Northern Italian culture to be quite similar to Danish. Besides, Bologna is a very international hub with so many exchange students
socializing_tips: Become part of the aforementioned whats app group. And perhaps just try to talk to people at cafes, bars, on campus and so on. View it as a learning experience!
cultural_challenges: Relations with professors are a lot less formal, so they might show up late, change dates on short notice etc. But also means they are more flexible with your needs.
culture_appreciated: Everrything about Italian cuisine is amazing. Also the slower pace of life I will miss, especially when the courses are pretty chill. In Bologna there is also a large student movement and a really interesting culture around social mobilization.
top3_advice: Enjoy
most_rewarding: Getting to know an amazing city, not just as a tourist rather as a local. Getting a greater insight into Italian culture, which is very different in different regions of the country. Getting new friends, whether Danish or international.
greatest_challenge: I think once you find housing you will have overcome the greatest challenge honestly.

crucial_aspects: I love Italy and I had heard a lot about studying in Bologna since it is a very well-recognized study city.
overall_comments: 9.5-10. The overall experience was sooo good, but of course some things could have been better.
info_ease: It was fine. I can't remember it that well. I think the best advice is to not stress too much about all the stuff beforehand, cause it is really chaotic and everything will work out in the end.
arrival_assistance: I am not sure. The university did send out a lot of information beforehand and they were actually very quick to reply on e-mail about questions (a lot faster than KU).
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: 9.5-10. The overall experience was sooo good, but of course some things could have been better.
registration_process: I can't really remember, but I am sure that it was very easy.
registration_help: Online meetings and e-mail. If you are in doubt of anything then book an online meeting, it really helps.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted (that was created). It is a bit stupid, cause when you apply for your learning agreement, you will probably have chosen classes that end up not get created, and then you will have to pick new ones from the list of classes that actually did get created. This is very chaotic and confusing, but it is not necessary to stress about, cause the law classes are really big and the learning agreement will get in place eventually.
registration_advice: Ask about pre-approval for A LOT of courses, cause you don't know which courses will be created, be overlapping or have a very late exam or bad exam form, so it's nice to be able to choose between a lot of courses (otherwise you will have more waiting time with your learning agremeent, if you need to wait for another pre-approval as well).
academics_comments: 9.5-10. The overall experience was sooo good, but of course some things could have been better.
course_level: It was low compared to Denmark.
teaching_comparison: It was SO bad in Bologna. A professor would just be talking about random stuff for two hours straight with no break and no powerpoint or other supporting material, so it was very difficult to actually follow what was going on in class. I think people from other countries are more used to this, cause they were really engaging in class and took notes to everything (literally everything) the professors said.
courses_enrolled: Comparative constitutionalism, Gender and the law, Fundamental Rights and EU law.
recommended_courses: The texts in comparative constitutionalism were very interesting.
unexpected_costs: Agency fee when booking an apartment.
cost_comparison: Grocceries in the big supermarket, eating out and drinks were less expensive than expected.
activities_available: I don't really know, but I think a lot.
activities_recommended: Get the ESN card (gives you discount on beer and ryanair tickets) and follow ESN Bologna on Instagram and attend some of their activities. It is a nice way to do some things that you normally don't do in Denmark. The free walking-tour was very nice, and every tuesday is pub night at the Irish Pub on via Zamboni, so the street is completely full (when the weather is ok).
weekend_recommendations: More of Italy! Modena, Ferrara (very cute), Parma, Firenze, Rome, more of South Italy (especially Naples and Matera!!)
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Attend as much stuff as possible (this means irish every tuesday). The city is full of students and people really want to chat, so it should be easy. Have aperol at Freuds, it is always full of students as well.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: The food and the nice people
top3_advice: Do it! Studying in Bologna is sooo amazing. You won't regret it (even though the teaching is very bad, but all the good things will out weight this!) And book a room in an international apartment and not just with other Danes.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: To live in Italy in such a beautiful city and to meet so many new amazing people.
greatest_challenge: Not that many

crucial_aspects: I have often visited Italy but always wanted to learn the language and get to know the lifestyle and culture more than what is possible on vacation.
info_ease: Not easy. In Italy l'informazione non informa. It is almost impossible to know what to do, the good thing is in Italy there are no hard (or soft) deadlines. Everything works out in the end
arrival_assistance: Not a lot. I had access to a virtual hub where a woman could answer questions. Unfortunately she gave me wrong information about some of my courses.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to make a zoom call to register my presence in the city.
registration_help: Again, not a lot of help. I had access to some zoom calls, but they didn't know a lot about basic questions.
registration_success: In the end it worked out, but it was a nightmare. Courses was approved, then cancelled with no communication. OLA process unnecessarily complicated. In Bologna, classes are not fixed until you have it in your OLA and you have taken the exam.
registration_advice: Ask local students about courses, because the workers don't know what they are talking about a lot of the time.
course_level: The level varied enormously between courses. Risk management was ridiculously easy, while Decisions and Investments was incredibly difficult, for example.
teaching_comparison: A lot of classes are 3 hours long with no breaks and no powerpoint (or maybe 5 slides). These type of classes are ineffective and uninteresting.
courses_enrolled: Riske management; Decisions and investments; Business models in creative industries; International economics and trade; machine learning for economists
recommended_courses: None of the courses I took.
unexpected_costs: I got a bike stolen, and I went to the hospital with a leg injury where I was charged 1200 DKK for an x-ray and a scan of my leg.
cost_comparison: Food was way more expensive that I had imagined. I would say a lot of groceries are roughly as expensive here as in Denmark.
activities_available: Don't know.
activities_recommended: Don't know.
weekend_recommendations: Bologna is in my opinion not a great city, so get out of the city as often as possible. Lots of fast trains to other cities, but buy tickets like at least a month in advance, because then it is pretty cheap, and otherwise it is fairly pricy.
culture_adjustment: Medium I would say, but I think it is a very subjective experience.
socializing_tips: Just do it. Italians are very friendly, and in my experience the students are perfectly fine with speaking English and help translating for you.
cultural_challenges: There are no systems. They make up complicated systems ad hoc for each individual situation. No two exams are alike. No one makes plans more than an hour in advance.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and openness of Italians
top3_advice: 1) Bologna is an extremely liberal city, if that is you that's great, but if you are the type of person who likes to wear a white shirt, reconsider your choice. 2) Be part of a club (like a dance class for example). It is a great way to meet locals. 3) Don't stay at the social hub or anywhere else in Bolognina. Try to get a place with the city walls in the southern part.
other_useful_info: I think I have covered most things already.
most_rewarding: The italian friends I made.
greatest_challenge: I really did not like the city, so coming to terms with that, I guess.

crucial_aspects: The university has some really niche and interesting courses that matches well with studying sociology.
info_ease: It was quite confusing for the first weeks to figure out the system and how to get the courses we wanted. But we heard from previously attending students that you just had to show up for the classes you wanted and then enroll later.
arrival_assistance: There was a personal check in, we did it online and received some information through there. Other than that i don't recall us getting any information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Same as above.
registration_help: emailing the professors is the best way to get help i would say.
registration_success: I got all the courses i applied for.
registration_advice: Be strategic with you courses and plan ahead a time schedule and ects points. It thought it was very stressful trying to match up the courses and make a schedule that fit with 30 ects and was manageable both with exams and time schedules.
course_level: A lot of the courses that fit my interests were MA courses. it was completely fine to follow even though they were above my level.
teaching_comparison: Very different from UCPH and way more relaxed and personal.
courses_enrolled: Political Ecology of Work, Atlantic and Global History of Modern Political Concepts, Geography and Cognition of European Territories, Introduction to Italian Culture
recommended_courses: Geography and Cognition of European Territories. Very cool teacher and a completely new way of thinking space and geography!
unexpected_costs: We had to put down a large deposit for our appartment.
cost_comparison: Train to other cities could sometimes be very expensive. so if you want to take the train around italy book tickets in good time in advance!
activities_available: I don't know.
activities_recommended: Going hiking in the mountains! join the outdoor whatsapp groups and find people to hike with through there.
weekend_recommendations: Going to Rome, Venice, Modena - Cities reachable by train.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Northern italy is very easy to adjust to.
socializing_tips: Speak with the students in class:)
cultural_challenges: Cant really think of anything.
culture_appreciated: bolognas very potent political and activist scene. Both the students and teachers were very engaged in activistic activities and frequently demonstrated or made school lockdowns in solidarity with Palestine. It was a very inspiring energy to be around.
top3_advice: Everything is very relaxed so don't stress:)
other_useful_info: The exam grading system is very generous, so don't worry about failing.
most_rewarding: Having a semester only with courses i had choosen for myself and the nice and slow tempo of italy.
greatest_challenge: Can't really think of anything.
other_comments: No i dont think so.

crucial_aspects: Ville gerne et sted indenfor EU, for at kunne modtage Erasmus. Italien har altid tiltalt mig, da min morfar plejede at bo der.
info_ease: Lidt forvirrende, især med valg af fag. Men universitetet har en hjemmeside med information til udvekslingsstuderende og man kan nemt komme i kontakt med dem hvis man har spørgsmål.
arrival_assistance: Online help desk, hvor man har et zoom-møde med en ansat på universitetet som kan hjælpe en.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Man skulle checke in online via et zoom opkald.
registration_help: Online help desk, hvor man kan snakke med uni-personale.
registration_success: Kunne få de fag jeg ville, der var ikke begrænsninger på antal. Det eneste problem var at finde fag uden overlap.
registration_advice: Tag det roligt, det skal nok løse sig. Det virker som et meget uoverskueligt puslespil i starten, men det kan godt lade sig gøre. På humaniora og sikkert mange andre steder er der ikke begrænsninger på antal, så du kan få de fag du vil have. Og man behøver ikke vælge i starten, så brug den første uges tid på at tage til de fag du synes lyder spændende og se hvad der er fedest.
course_level: Niveauet er under KU, i hvert fald humaniora. Tog kandidatfag og det var samme niveau eller under de bachelorfag jeg har haft på KU.
teaching_comparison: Meget forskelligt. Meget op til den enkelte underviser. Nogle fag mindede meget om hvad jeg er vant til og andre var noget helt andet.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Italian Culture Theories and Methods in Semiotics Semiotics of Psychopathologies Geographies of Language Cognition, Brain and Behavior: Multisensory Integration.
recommended_courses: Var meget glad for Semiotics, især introduktionskurset. Introduction to Italian Culture er de nemmeste ECTS jeg nogensinde har fået, men har ikke lært vildt meget.
unexpected_costs: Der er så mange gode restauranter, så spiste meget oftere ude end jeg havde regnet med.
cost_comparison: Det er ret billigt at spise ude.
activities_available: Forskellige sportsgrupper. Ellers mest Erasmus events, i hvert fald hvad jeg opdagede og som var på engelsk. Det meste er på italiensk.
activities_recommended: University Street Party, techno DJ midt på campus, virkelig sjovt og fedt!
weekend_recommendations: Rejs rundt i Italien, vandre i Dolomitterne og se de andre smukke byerne i nærheden.
culture_adjustment: Hang meget ud med andre udvekslingstuderende ikke så meget med italienere.
socializing_tips: Det er svært, de tager ofte ikke de engelske fag. Men prøv at opsøg de få der gør. Og ellers tag ud i bylivet og mød dem der.
cultural_challenges: Den manglende struktur og sammenhæng i undervisningen. Virkelig meget op til den enkelte underviser, hvilket betyder at stilen, niveauet og forventningerne var meget forskellige fra fag til fag.
culture_appreciated: Maden og deres mere rolige tilgang til hverdagen. De har ikke ligeså travlt.
top3_advice: 1. Det virker uoverskueligt med fagvalg og svært at finde hoved og hale i, men tag det roligt, det løser sig! 2. Start tidligt med boligsøgning. 3. Tag til Erasmus events hvis du vil møde andre!
other_useful_info: Hvis du skal rejse rundt i Italien er det ekstremt billigt med bus. Hurtigtog er markant hurtigere men også dyrere.
most_rewarding: Det sociale helt klart. At blive venner med folk fra andre lande.
greatest_challenge: At vælge fag, og at være i en by hvor man ikke kender nogen.

crucial_aspects: At det var inden for Europa, så jeg kunne få Erasmus; at byen var lille nok til at få et lokalt kendskab til den.
overall_comments: Jeg var VIRKELIG glad for mit ophold og jeg kan virkelig anbefale det pga byen, det lokale studieliv, madkulturen, det livlige gadebilledet. Min grund til 9/10 og ikke 10/10 skyldes nok primært den lidt flyvske struktur på fagene dernede.
info_ease: Det var ikke så svært som frygtet, men det handler om at få styr på sin Unibo-mail ret hurtigt og generelt bruge Unibo's hjemmeside, hvor man kan læse sig til helt vildt meget nyttigt.
arrival_assistance: Jeg mindes, at jeg fik en mail om, hvordan jeg skulle checke ind på universitetet.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Jeg var VIRKELIG glad for mit ophold og jeg kan virkelig anbefale det pga byen, det lokale studieliv, madkulturen, det livlige gadebilledet. Min grund til 9/10 og ikke 10/10 skyldes nok primært den lidt flyvske struktur på fagene dernede.
registration_process: Jeg husker processen sådan, at efter forhåndsgodkendelsen fra KU, skulle jeg udfylde min OLA (Online Learning Agreement) som så skulle underskrives at både KU og Unibo. Da jeg ankom til Bologna, skulle jeg checke ind, som jeg gjorde via et zoom-opkald, hvor jeg bare skulle vise mit pas og min billet for ankomst til byen. Dernæst skulle jeg bare melde fagene ind på min "study plan" på studenti online (via Unibo's hjemmeside) og ellers bare møde op (tror tilmeldelsen svarer til at være tilmeldt eksamenen herhjemme).
registration_help: De har både en mail man altid kan skrive til og tilbød også online Zoom-kontortider, som var behjælpelige, da vi skulle checke ind.
registration_success: Det var meget let og intuitivt at tilføje fagene inde på Studenti Online, hvor man skulle tilføje dem på sin "study plan". Derudover kan man tilgå fagene på Virtuale (svarer til deres Absalon) via et link dertil på fagets hjemmeside på Unibo.
registration_advice: Spørg andre, der har været afsted eller skal afsted. Vær ikke bange for at skrive mails om ting du er i tvivl om og gør det bare i god tid.
academics_comments: Jeg var VIRKELIG glad for mit ophold og jeg kan virkelig anbefale det pga byen, det lokale studieliv, madkulturen, det livlige gadebilledet. Min grund til 9/10 og ikke 10/10 skyldes nok primært den lidt flyvske struktur på fagene dernede.
course_level: Jeg havde 3/4 fag på kandidatniveau og 1/4 fag på bachelorniveau, og ingen af fagene var for svære.
teaching_comparison: Mundtlige forelæsninger, meget lig på KU. I ét af fagene (Consumer culture) overgik undervisningen halvvejs inde til elevpræsentationer, hvilket ikke fungerede optimalt, men indtil da, var det spændende. Og i et andet fag (Introduction to Italian Culture) var forelæsninger primært gæsteforelæsninger, hvor det formidlende niveau ikke var særligt godt desværre.
courses_enrolled: Aesthetics (12 ECTS) Theories and Methods in Semiotics (6 ECTS) Consumer Culture (6 ECTS) Introduction to Italian Culture (6 ECTS)
recommended_courses: Jeg vil helt sikkert anbefale både Aesthetics og Theories and Methods in Semiotics, især fordi begge forelæsere var meget dygtige og havde et højt ambitionsniveau og var meget struktureret i deres tilgang! Særligt vil jeg anbefale Aesthetics, fordi hele det emne bare var ekstremt inspirerende og spændende at lære om.
unexpected_costs: Vi skulle lægge et administrationsgebyr til dem, vi lejede lejligheden igennem, på cirka 2800 kr, som selvfølgelig var lidt dyrt, men det værd, fordi det muliggjorde lejligheden og gav også en del tryghed at vi havde kontaktpersoner dernede.
cost_comparison: Leveomkostningerne i byen er meget billigere end i København - fx at spise og drikke ude, kulturbilletter med studierabat (fx teater og biograf) og togbilletter. Det kom lidt bag på mig, at priserne i supermarkederne lignede dem i København ret meget - måske en anelse mindre, men overraskende dyrt ift., hvad jeg havde forventet af Italien.
activities_available: Vi fik ikke så meget info om det, men jeg ved fra egen søgning på Unibo's hjemmeside at der både er kor og andre ting, man kan melde sig ind i, så det er klart værd af undersøge.
activities_recommended: Billige biograf-og teaterture, fx var vi inde og se operaen La Boheme af Puccini til 10€ stykket. At tage ud og spise den gode mad på de mange trattoria! Maden er ekstremt lækker og billig og det fungerede bare som social lim at mødes om en spritz eller ragu. At gå eller lægge sig i giardini di margherita eller oppe i villa Ghigi ved Casa del Custode. At gå rundt i byen, den er lille nok til at man ikke behøver at bruge bussen. Ellers har de masser af nemme låne-cykler rundt omkring. Tage på bunkemarkedet oppe nord på, hvor du kan finde meget billigt tøj - hvis du har mod på at rode rundt i bunker:) Kigge ind i kirkerne. En af mine venner dernede startede vist til Spikeball og jeg meldte mig ind i et fitness med en veninde, hvilket var rigtigt fedt.
weekend_recommendations: De samme som ovenstående:)
culture_adjustment: Meget nemt. Man skal selvfølgelig overveje sprogbarrieren, som selvfølgelig stod lidt i vejen for den lokale forbindelse, men ellers synes jeg, at jeg hurtigt fik et trygt tilhørsforhold til byen.
socializing_tips: Snak med dem i pauserne til undervisning, eller opsøg dem på nogle af lokale, populære barer, hvor de også befinder sig.
cultural_challenges: Primært kun sprogbarrieren.
culture_appreciated: Den lidt tilbagelænede afstressede tilgang til livet. Den smittede af, og jeg tænkte undervejs, at jeg har aldrig haft de så godt som der. Jeg beundrede især den måde de tog ud i byen i hverdagen - ikke for at drikke sig fulde men for at være sammen og socialisere over en enkelt drink.
top3_advice: Overvej at lære noget basalt italiensk hjemmefra og tag det aktivt til dig, når du er dernede. Drop din kalender - jeg brugte den ikke dernede og det var en befrielse. Brug byen! Gå ud, spis ude, drik en kaffe ude, køb en is, gå i biografen.
other_useful_info: Det er (surprise) virkelig anbefalelsesværdigt at have en opsparing. Selvom det er relativt billigt i Italien sammenlignet med København, er det bare stadig dyrt at være på udveksling. Når det så er sagt, kan man også sagtens komme langt dernede uden den helt store opsparing - jeg tror jeg havde cirka 7000 kr's opsparing og fik derudover Erasmus-legatet.
most_rewarding: Mødet med andre søde og åbne udvekslingsstuderende. At få lov at leve en hverdag uden tidspres og alt for mange forpligtelser og ting at tage stilling til, som normalt følger med studielivet som ung herhjemme.
greatest_challenge: Klart det økonomiske aspekt - jeg havde ingen stor opsparing inden, og det begrænsede mig selvfølgelig også lidt - mest fra at tage nogle flere og/eller længere ture rundt i Italien. Og ellers sprogbarrieren, som lidt minder én om, at man "kun" er udvekslingsstuderende og ikke rigtig lokal.
other_comments: Glæd dig, hvis du skal afsted! Lav en opsparing, hvis du kan. Nyd at du kan spise og drikke ude uden at blive økonomisk ruineret:)

crucial_aspects: Course catalogue, exciting destination, possibility of receiving the Erasmus Grant to finance my stay
info_ease: I found mobility-online as well as the OLA platform difficult to navigate and sign correctly. The University of Bologna has pretty alright information online. All bureaucratic parts of the exhange that depended on mail-correspondences went frustratingly slow (OLA, Erasmus Grant, Course selection).
arrival_assistance: Not much. The University of Bologna (UNIBO) offers a online introductory presentation - but awfully late in the proces. A lot of information would have been reassuring to receive earlier in the proces.
arrival_comments: There's an online helpdesk at UNIBO where you can receive bureaucratic help through video-calls. If you get impatient with waiting on emails, the online helpdesk might prove helpful
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You check in online upon arrival. You enrol in courses through an online platform (studenti-online). You furthermore do the exchange paperwork of forhåndsgodkendelse at KU and OLA between host and sending institution.
registration_help: Online helpdesk, email guidance
registration_success: I experienced the course selection process as a nightmare, yet I at last ended up getting access to all the courses I wanted to. Be patient, be aware that the process is slow, make sure to register your choice of class in Studenti-Online (also before receiving OLA). There will be - especially as a student of Humanities - overlapping courses. Getting an overview of your timetable and avoiding course-overlaps can be difficult.
registration_advice: Take advantage of the "shopping"-possibility. I was first enrolled in a few courses that I ended up swapping from (bc they were not what I thought they would be/ I didn't enjoy the teaching method/ prioritising between overlapping classes) because it was so fairly easy. I went to a few classes just to check them out and was super excited by the professors or course contents. Wonderful experience that it was possible to change to these courses (as it is not the case at UCPH).
course_level: I choose a lot of courses outside of my field of study (mostly took courses in sociology, while I study philosophy at UCPH). The level was appropriate. The one MA-class in philosophy I did attend was similar to UCPH in difficulty.
teaching_comparison: I found some professor liked to "rant" without citing their sources, arguing their case by research or similar. Other professors were immensely knowledgeable and inspiring.
courses_enrolled: APPLIED POLITICAL SOCIOLOGY EPISTEMOLOGY (1) (LM) POLITICAL ECOLOGY OF WORK WOMAN AND SOCIAL SCIENCES - DONNE E SCIENZE SOCIALI WOMEN AND LAW - DONNE E GIURISPRUDENZA

cultural_challenges: The French culture of denial In France, denial is an art form, from the classroom to the parliament. It is not a denial of truth but of responsibility—a quiet refusal to acknowledge when something has gone wrong. Nowhere is this more evident than in the country’s proud tradition of public administration. Competition for entry into elite schools begins early. Years of hard work allow some of France’s brightest to study public administration - a degree that for many has led to ministry posts and, for a select few men, even the presidency. This obsession with public administration could lead one to think that the French might excel at it. Yet behind the polished façade lies a deeply rooted culture of denial—a habit of evading responsibility that seeps into everyday life. I encountered this culture firsthand as an exchange student. After missing out on a spot at the acclaimed Université de Sorbonne, I enrolled at the Université de Bordeaux, a choice I hadn’t given much thought to, but one that probably meant speaking more French than in cosmopolitan Paris. My main goal was to revive the language I’d left behind a decade earlier, when I studied for a year in Nantes as a 15-year-old. Participating in an exchange program through Erasmus can be a daunting task. Those who have tried it know the scale of bureaucracy that students need to conquer to participate in what can be an enlightening cultural exchange. But as I told the French Minister of Higher Education and Research, M. Philippe Baptiste, when I met him at the Erasmus headquarters in Bordeaux, the amount of exchange-related administrative work for the student “vaut le coût” - is worthwhile. In hindsight, I regret that well-intended white lie. I have now “studied” for more than two months at the Université de Bordeaux. I am still not officially enrolled in any of my courses. Two or three times a week I show up in an empty classroom, not having been informed of changes to the timetable. This involves choosing a 30-ECTS course load that must be approved by one party at the University of Copenhagen, signed by another, and finally signed by the Université de Bordeaux. After following a series of interesting economics courses at the Faculty of Economics for five weeks, I was told by the French university’s administration that I would not receive credits for the courses. I had to leave the courses and find new ones, to my professors’ regret and to my own, in order to honor the 30-ECTS requirement. The Faculty of Science, where I was registered, and the Faculty of Economics were apparently unable to transfer credits between each other, despite each faculty offering courses at the other. This meant my Erasmus grant would not be transferred any time soon, since I had to fill out a completely new learning agreement - a process that would take weeks. Had I not been lucky enough to secure Danish grants, I would soon be joining the queues of less fortunate people receiving food handouts from local charities. I spent my days emailing administrative personnel and showing up at the international mobility office, which was closed more often than not. A reply could be weeks in the making, if I was lucky enough to even get one. Most frequently, I was met by a version of “this is not our fault” spoken with the insouciance only the French muster. I was being kicked around and I was frankly appalled. As a 25-year-old master’s student from Denmark, this carelessness with respect to my time was a new and utterly stunning experience. To be fair, my French professors shared my frustrations and yet were not at all surprised by the ineffectiveness of the system. Of course, bureaucracy frustrates outsiders everywhere, but in France the pattern seems particularly entrenched, not merely procedural but cultural. That instinct - to deflect responsibility – runs deep. In France, I think of it as a culture of denial: not denial of truth, but of responsibility. It extends from university offices to the highest levels of politics, shaping much of French administration. The same impulse to deny responsibility appears in other domains. One striking example is the French refusal to acknowledge race - and therefore racial inequality. In my “Éthique et management” course, a discussion about bias in job interviews passed without a single mention of race. A hijab-wearing Black student, visibly dumbfounded, finally asked: “What about race?” The elderly white madame replied that in France, there is no such thing as race – everyone is simply French. Ah bon? I understand the historical roots of that reflex, but today it often serves to paper over the cracks of structural racial inequality. Again, a problem denied rather than confronted. This culture of denial poses endless difficulties for international students like me, but its cost to French citizens is far greater. They are governed by people who refuse to compromise in order to move forward. France’s administrative paralysis isn’t merely procedural - it’s cultural. Until the reflex of denial is replaced with a sense of shared responsibility, the country will remain caught between its administrative ideals and its bureaucratic reality. Bonne chance!

crucial_aspects: I have always had a dream of going to Canada, so being able to combine both academic and experiencing a new culture was a perfect. One of the reason for choosing Canada was its nature and the active lifestyle surrounding the campus and the city that I lived in.
info_ease: As I was traveling during covid-19 there were a lot of extra restrictions and regulations that I had to pay attention to, this made it way more difficult to find the necessary information as they basically changed every week. Other than that I thought it was quite easy to find the relevant information and our contact person in Canada was really great at helping out.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any due to covid. We were supposed to have a meet and greet during the first week, but weren't allowed to gather that many people cause of covid. This could have been really helpful as I had a few questions regarding daily life on campus and such.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I would fill out online form with my top 10 courses at my host university and then my contact person would sign me up for those courses that had free spaces. Don't worry if you don't get the courses you want. During the first 2 weeks of the semester you can drop in and out of courses and a lot of courses will be available by then and then you can just register for them yourself during those 2 weeks.
registration_help: Your contact person can help you out with all the questions that you have.
registration_success: 100%. I got in to all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Apply for everything even though you don't have pre-req needed for the class. The professors are really excited to have exchange students, so just apply for everything. GO ask your contact person, she can "hack" you into all courses that you want, and if there's room for it, she/he will do it, at least they did with me.
course_level: In general the level of the courses wasn't super high. I followed two second year classes, 1 third and 1 fourth year. All of them was doable and the workload per class isn't as high as at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: In all of my classes I did not have a textbook and all teaching was done via powerpoints. I really missed having a textbook as I personally like to read about the subjects rather than just listening.
courses_enrolled: HES 201 - Exercise Prescription HES 203 - Lifespan Physical and Motor Development HES 380 - Exercise Metabolism HES 488 - Cortical Control of Movement
recommended_courses: If you find metabolism interesting I would definitely recommend taking HES 380. The prof Jonathan is really great at explaining the stuff and puts all his time and effort into you getting as big as outcome as possible.
unexpected_costs: I wouldn't call the unexpected but I had to buy a lot of outdoor/hiking clothing as I wanted to do a lot of hiking.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping is a bit more expensive than Denmark, but on the other hand going out is a bit cheaper (Restaurant, cinema, bar etc.)
activities_available: There were a ton of options, some were shut down due to covid but most were up and running.
activities_recommended: Join one of the intramural leagues if you're into sport, this can be (Football, volleyball, dodgeball etc.) or join VOCO which is the outdoor club and through that you can borrow all outdoor equipment you need for going on a trip on your own.
weekend_recommendations: Banff and Jasper. Rent a car if you can and just go for a long ride to either of those 2 cities. The icefield parkway road going from Banff to Jasper is spectacular.
culture_adjustment: Easy. Canada is not that different from Denmark tbh. Get used to saying "how are you" and "i'm fine" whenever you step into a shop, meet people or whatever. They say it everywhere as a greeting.
socializing_tips: Attend classes, live in shared accommodations and join clubs.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Small talking. Canadians are really great at small talking.
top3_advice: Ask for help. There are a lot of ressources for you to use, you just gotta use them. If you want a course, apply for it even though you do not meet the pre-requisites. You only need 3 courses to be a fulltime student (At least I did). I found it hard to accept this fact, because most other student have either 4 to 6 classes per semester. But that just gives you more time for social events.
other_useful_info: Find a friend with a car. It can be hard to get around if you're not just going downtown but want to go out for hikes and other stuff.
most_rewarding: Getting to meet a lot of new people and improving my english.
greatest_challenge: Covid-19.

crucial_aspects: I visited Canada a couple of years back and fell head over heels in love with the country - The nature, the people, the multiculturalism - It simply had everything I could possibly want. Furthermore, I had been told that specifically British Columbia (BC), a province, in Canada was a really stunning place, so I searched for universities in BC. I knew that I also wanted to go to a place that could contribute academically to my studies, and therefore the choice fell naturally to the University of British Columbia (UBC) in Vancouver. UBC has an excellent reputation both academically, socially, and culturally. It is almost twice the size of KU and has an enormous percentage of international students, so I knew that it would be possible to connect with people from all over the world, which was a big wish for me. UBC is also a giant campus, which means that you can really get that "famous" campus experience, where you study and live on campus, which was a fantastic experience for me. It really is just like you see in the movies ;)
overall_comments: My overall experience was absolutely incredible! The only reason that it only gets an 8/10 is due to the infamous, annoying COVID, which affected my experience both before and a bit during my stay. Before going, COVID added a lot of problems and insecurities to the planning, and during the first month of my stay, everything was still online. We were also required to wear face masks during the entire stay there etc. But that is really the only bad thing I have to say about my experience.
info_ease: It was very easy - UBC has a really helpful team at their exchange office Go Global, who are always ready to help you with whatever you need, whether it is about academic questions, housing, or any other issues you may encounter.
arrival_assistance: I didn't really receive any assistance because I didn't need it - But UBC had made sure that I knew exactly where to seek help if it had been needed. My roommates at my dorm also helped me a lot with learning to find my way around campus, helpful tips, etc., so I got all the support I needed there :)
arrival_comments: Before arrival, the Go Global team held several orientation sessions, so I think we were all very prepared when we actually arrived at UBC. Furthermore, when I moved into my housing, I also got a lot of information from them, and then my roommates helped me with the rest - So really, I have no complaints.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My overall experience was absolutely incredible! The only reason that it only gets an 8/10 is due to the infamous, annoying COVID, which affected my experience both before and a bit during my stay. Before going, COVID added a lot of problems and insecurities to the planning, and during the first month of my stay, everything was still online. We were also required to wear face masks during the entire stay there etc. But that is really the only bad thing I have to say about my experience.
registration_process: As I remember it, there were two steps to it. First, you had to send UBC a list with 10 courses that you were thinking of taking while at UBC - It is basically just to make sure that you have had some thoughts about it. You don't have to actually take any of those. Later in the process, you had to send them a list of courses you actually wanted, and then the Go Global office actually did the registration for you. Then sometime later before your stay you could log in to the UBC portal and see which courses you had been registered for - I had gotten registered for 4 courses, which is the amount I wanted. Some of the ones I had wanted were full, but then they had just registered me for some of the other ones that I listed, so it worked out fine :)
registration_help: You could always write to the Go Global office, and you were also welcome to write to the professors if you had any academic questions about course content, exams, etc. They always replied really quickly and were very nice. The only problems I experienced were back at KU with the KU offices, but never with UBC.
registration_success: I got the amount and the courses that I had listed as wanted options :)
registration_advice: Don't be afraid to contact your professors about the courses - Sometimes the information about the course is not very specific on the UBC website, so it can be really helpful to get a better explanation from the profs themselves.
academics_comments: My overall experience was absolutely incredible! The only reason that it only gets an 8/10 is due to the infamous, annoying COVID, which affected my experience both before and a bit during my stay. Before going, COVID added a lot of problems and insecurities to the planning, and during the first month of my stay, everything was still online. We were also required to wear face masks during the entire stay there etc. But that is really the only bad thing I have to say about my experience.
course_level: I experienced the academic level of the courses at UBC to be lower than at KU. I'm used to doing a lot of work at KU in classes with relatively big papers to write all the time, and there is an expectation that you are capable of analyzing, discussing, and critically reflecting on complicated theories, methods, etc. At UBC, you were basically just expected to memorize everything that was said during lectures and in your textbook.
teaching_comparison: The teaching only took place as lectures - There was no classroom-style teaching at all in the courses I took, although the professors were very open to questions so that sometimes helped facilitate a bit of discussion in the lectures. You did not have to actively participate in lectures, but if you wanted a good grade, it was definitely necessary to take thorough notes since a lot of the exam questions were based on solely lecture material.
courses_enrolled: I took the following courses: - PSYC 102: Introduction to Social Psychology, Personality Psychology, Developmental Psychology, and Clinical Psychology - PSYC 300a: Abnormal Psychology - PSYC 314: Health Psychology - PSYC 350a: Psychological aspects of human sexuality
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend PSYC 314 and PSYC 350a. Both courses are not really something you can take at KU, and they were both extremely interesting and taught by some very talented researchers, Dr. King, and Dr. Goldsmith. - Health psychology changed a lot about my way of thinking about the connection between the mind, brain, and body, and has opened my eyes to an entirely new field in psychology. - Psychological aspects of human sexuality can be seen as an extremely elaborate form of sexual education from a psychological point of view. I have learned a lot from that course that I did not know - It treats sexuality as a very broad term, so expect to learn everything from the development of fetuses to critical discussions of gender to the male anatomy. Everything having to do with sex, sexuality etc is covered in that course.
unexpected_costs: I was surprised at how expensive phone plans are in Canada - Definitely calculate into your budget to spend at least 300 kr a month on it - And that is probably only if you can get a good deal. Besides that, be prepared for the fact that you might need to buy a lot of kitchen equipment. I was lucky enough to have roommates that were willing to share their plates, pots and pans etc, but I know a lot of people who had to buy all that stuff, which quickly adds up to a lot.
cost_comparison: More expensive: Phone plans and groceries - Canada, especially Vancouver, is not a cheap place to live. Specifically fruit, vegetables, and meat were really expensive, so calculate that into your budget I don't think that there was anything that was less expensive - Again, Vancouver is not a cheap place to live.
activities_available: There are plenty of activities to do - See my comment above. Besides that, UBC for instance has several gyms where membership is really cheap, so you can stay in shape while eating all those Tim Hortons donuts. The activities I participated in were primarily arranged by exchange students (including myself), so we really made it work on our own.
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend checking out the sports events - UBC is very proud of their Thunderbird teams, and has teams in Hockey, baseball, basketball, volley, and many other types of sports. Going to watch those games are always fun! Here you can really get that famous North American University movie vibe! Besides that I would definitely just go into everything with a yes-mentality - Of course not so much that you end up getting stressed out, but go out and meet people, go to the events, and get the maximum out of your stay!
weekend_recommendations: Vancouver is famous for easy access to skiing, hiking, watersports, etc - You can seriously ski in the morning, and jump into the water in the afternoon! So this place is perfect for all outdoor lovers, no matter what you enjoy! Personally, I love hiking, so all my weekends were spent in the mountains. Other than that, Vancouver Island is also a must-do - It's the most amazing nature place, the island is the size of Jutland, so there is plenty to do! I ended my stay with an American westcoast adventure because Vancouver is also so close to the border. So definitely calculate on spending a lot of money on trips - There are so many beautiful places to visit, both in British Columbia, bot also in some of the nearby provinces, for instance Alberta that is home to the famous Banff and Jasper nationalpark, which i would definitely recommend seeing!
culture_adjustment: Canada is in many ways similar to Denmark, except just nicer. They are very open to everyone, so expect to have a lot of conversations with random strangers ;) Canada really lives up to all the stereotypes that everyone is nice - But remember, that when people ask you “How are you?”, they don't necessarily want to hear everything about your day ;)
socializing_tips: Just be open and friendly, then everything will be just fine! And if you don't know what else to say, just start talking about hockey.
cultural_challenges: I didn't really find anything particularly challenging - Maybe just that Canada took COVID a lot more seriously than Denmark did at that time, so I found that my opinions about COVID policies were way more relaxed than a lot of the people i met i Canada.
culture_appreciated: The openness and friendliness - Denmark could really learn something from Canada about welcoming foreigners, and just in general taking more notice of the people you meet in your everyday life.
top3_advice: 1. In the beginning it can be hard to find a balance between your FOMO and then also having a bit of time to yourself - Be mindful of your own needs, but remember that this experience also only lasts a couple of months, so make sure to make the most of it. 2. Vancouver is very expensive - Make sure to have plenty of savings, apply for scholarships/grants or borrow money. It is so annoying to miss out on experiences just because your bank account says no 3. UBC is VERY pedagogic - Don't get offended if they treat you a bit like you're a child, they mean well. Remember that their students are typically a lot younger and en in general more inexperienced than Danish university students, so that is why they really try to take care of their students
other_useful_info: UBC has exchange students from all over the world, which is amazing. Remember to be respectful of other people's cultures, traditions, and so on - You may have heard a lot about other people's countries, and think that you know a lot, but you probably don't. Be curious - I found it extraordinary how my views of different countries have expanded and become more nuanced after having met so many different people.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding parts of the experience have been getting the chance to live in another country as great and beautiful as Canada and to feel all the personal growth that I have gone through. It would be too cliche to say that I have come home as a new person, but I see the world and myself differently now. I have definitely learned that my fate is probably not to stay in Denmark.
greatest_challenge: I will say that the greatest challenge was 100 % COVID's influence on the exchange - It made the move to another country very difficult and added a lot of insecurities during the planning. I actually moved my exchange from the autumn to the spring semester because of COVID, and I was honestly not sure that the exchange would be possible until my first day at UBC.
other_comments: Exchange is the greatest experience of my life, and I recommend everyone to go no matter where you're interested in going - But you should 100 % consider going to Canada, and specifically UBC. It was everything I ever dreamed of and more. Go go go.
