crucial_aspects: Good academic performance and opportunities, surrounding nature, great communities for exchange students.
info_ease: Relatively easy, the university provided a lot of good advice. The only thing was housing - a bit difficult to find when you're in another country. I didn't get housing on campus, so had to go search myself. Would have been nice to have had a contact overhere that might have been able to check out places (that they weren't scams) before paying a deposit/rent from overseas.
arrival_assistance: Welcome day on UBC, buddy group/student on campus that I could contact.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Easy to take and drop courses at UBC. I had good communication with them, and they responded to all of my questions.
registration_help: Office hours with professors or GoGlobal. Buddy program (student advice) Online ressources and communication
registration_success: Very - i got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Try out as many courses as you like - use the two weeks of free add/drop period when you get here. Dont stress too much, changes can be made conteniously.
course_level: I only took 300-coruses (year 3 courses). They varied a lot in structure and difficulty.
teaching_comparison: Very different from course to course. Generally, I had less hours at UBC on campus than I normally have at UCPH. The classes over here where bigger, and some of them only lectures (as opposed to a lot of group work, which I am used to having at UCPH). One of my classes had a lot of group work, which was nice. Then it is also easier to meet and get to know your fellow students.
courses_enrolled: Fertility, Families and Migration International Agricultural Development Introduction to Wine Science
recommended_courses: Fertility, Families and Migration - very interesting subjects and nice structure. No final exam but based on weekly tests and assignments. International Agricultural Development - much focus on group work, which is great for meeting other fellow students. Very engaged and flexible professor.
unexpected_costs: Food and housing was a bit more expensive than I thought. And then the madatory Upass (which is actually great and not very expensive when you consider it covers all public transportation while you're here) and the UBC health insurance.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than anticipated. But go to Sunrise market if downtown, produce is a bit cheaper there. Otherwice, look into "Sprouts" on campus - they provide community dinners/Fridges if your food budget is struggling.
activities_available: UBC has more than 100 clubs, and other activities as well. Lots of sports but also e.g. exchange club and other social initiatives. No excuse not to get involved.
activities_recommended: I joined a number of activites, but would generally just recommend to get involved in the campus clubs! A good way to meet people and also provides a lot of opportunity to see the area, city and explore different opportunities!
weekend_recommendations: I went swimming once a week with the triathlon club, which I found great! Even if you don't join a swimming team, go to the aquatic centre - it is free for students and very well equipped! Also, Join the VOC outdoor club. There you can rent gear and meet like-minded people to go on trips in the weekends and such. We used that club a lot, as do a lot of other exchange students. I joined the campus "Agronomy Garden" as I have an interest in making things grow. Further I joined a weekly fitness class in Muay Thai, to challenge myself and learn a new skill.
culture_adjustment: Very easy - The Canadians are very openminded and friendly, so I had no truble on that front.
socializing_tips: Get involved in the clubs and social life on campus! Some courses only have 1-hour lecrures, where you don't necessarily get to talk to a lot of people. Finding other channels to socialize it a good idea.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: The Canadians' friendliness and spirit for the outdoors! They don't mind that you're only here for half a year, they'll still want to make friends, and they're easy to talk to.
top3_advice: Go on trips and explore the outdoors in your free time - don't worry too much about missing school time or being a bit behind in your classes. Take advantage that you only need to pass. I learned a lot of new skills and improved some existing ones - e.g. long hikes, skiing, snowshoeing, rock climbing and more. Also, I lived with 4 other fantastic roommates and really enjoyed the social part of the exchange.
other_useful_info: It is easy to book cars through companies like Turo or Evo, especially if you find a few people to with. Then Gas is not too expensive, and you can go a lot of places in the mountains and do hikes, etc. Don't panic too much if you dont get housing on campus - it can be difficult, but everyone I went with and met had been able to find something they liked and somewhere affordable. I ended up enjoying staying off-campus a lot and wouldn't switch now.
most_rewarding: The community and friends that I've made - a lot of them I'll be able to see back home as well. Going on trips and seeing the amazing nature here is defininately also the thing to do here. Some of it is more expensive than others, but make sure you save up a little bit so your budget is not limiting you to do these opportunities!
greatest_challenge: Finding housing on my own - again it was difficult but not impossible, and ended up really appreciating it!
other_comments: Go to UBC, it's really the best exchange I can imagine!

crucial_aspects: I chose Vancouver in Canada due to the nature here. I wanted to go somewhere where i knew i could go on plenty of adventures and experience new things. But going to UBC also made it possible to go to a good school with exciting courses, which definitely was a motivation for going here too. Furthermore Canada is an english speaking country which made it easy to integrate with the culture.
info_ease: It was a bit difficult to figure out how the whole applying for courses worked and how you could change them, but i figured out that you can do that as well when you arrive. Otherwise it was easy to find information and you had people at go global you could write to if doubt of anything. We didn't have a lot of preparation from University of Copenhagen i would say, so some things you have to figure out yourself, and be sure to keep track of all deadlines.
arrival_assistance: I feel like i got the help i needed. There is a go global office you can go to if you have any questions, but also you talk to people who knows how everything works. So i didn't find it very difficult once i got here. Sometimes the mails they sent out could be a little confusing.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had to make a list of 10 courses in prioritized from 1-10.
registration_help: Not that much - you have to do most yourself. Even if you want other courses, but if you don't get the courses you want you can change it when you get there.
registration_success: At first i didn't get exactly what i wanted. But i changed 2 out of 3 when i got here to courses i would rather have and it turned out great.
registration_advice: Try out different courses in the beginning of the semester and see what you like. Professors are everything.
course_level: The BA courses here goes from 100-400. I had two 300 level courses and one 200 level courses. The level really depends on whether you've had the material before. You would normally go for 300 and 400 courses in your third year of BA, but if you would like to try something new, go after 100-200 courses.
teaching_comparison: I only had lectures with a lot of people, and in contrast to Denmark no one knows each other in the classes. Everyone is new, so don't be scared to reach out. You can also have smaller classes called tutorials or lab classes. Depends on the courses you take.
courses_enrolled: 200 Cognitive Systems (COGS) 306 Principles of Animal Behavior (PSYC) 301 Brain Dysfunction and Recovery (PSYC)
recommended_courses: I loved 306 Principles of Animal behavior because it's very different and the teacher is great. 301 was also good, a beginner courses for neuroscience. I didn't like Cognitive Systems that much - too abstract for my taste.
unexpected_costs: Expect to use more money than you thought you would. Everything cost money. And you don't want to miss out on experiences which also cost some money, but are definitely all worth it.
cost_comparison: Food is expensive (vegetables at least). Housing more expensive (i gave 6000kr per month but expect to give more if you live off campus)
activities_available: UBC has A LOT of clubs you can join. If you have an interest there's is 99% a club for it at UBC. So plenty of opportunity to sign up for clubs (anything from sports to knitting to equestrian).
activities_recommended: I recommend going out in the nature and hike hike hike! So many beautiful trips you can take over here. Also join clubs if you want friends other that danish people and other exchange students!
weekend_recommendations: Hike:) Go to banff and Jasper. And don't be afraid to skip a couple of days of school.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy. Canadian people are very nice and it's not that different a culture from Denmark. So it came very naturally to me.
socializing_tips: Talk to people in class! Everybody is eager to talk to people in the beginning of the semester because no one knows each other in the classes. And it's not weird to say hello to random people over here, it's just us Danish people that are a bit reserved.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: The kindness of the Canadians
top3_advice: Buy a student skipass if you want to go ski Definitely invest your time on adventures not on school - you will for sure pass your exams. Don't be scared to join new things, it's never as scary as you think
other_useful_info: Brings nips if you want your room to feel homey and cozy
most_rewarding: I learned to be more independent and proactive. Learning that school isn't everything and you should go out more and take initiative to do stuff. And i would never have been without all my experiences i got over here.
greatest_challenge: It can fell lonely sometimes, but it will pass.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: I have family living close to Vancouver and wanted to live close to them.
info_ease: It was a bit frustrating at times since the information came out pretty late so at times I would look for information without finding anything because the information was not out yet. But when the information did come out it was easy to find often found in email send directly to me.
arrival_assistance: Information sessions. You could also contact go global for further help.
arrival_comments: There were a few information sessions I attended and they gave us resources to who we could contact if we needed more help. I never needed this help so I can not say if it is good or not.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You first send in a document of courses you would consider taking (this is not a registration but just to get into the university) around may you will then be sent a course registration survey which you fill out. You will need to request more courses than you will be registered in. The email with the survey will explain the details. Go Global will then look at the survey and register you for some of the courses you have requested. After arriving you can change the courses you are registered in.
registration_help: You can always contact Go Global, they usually answer fairly quickly and are helpful.
registration_success: I got four courses I had wished for, they were 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th priorities. If I had wanted to I could have tried to get into my first priority after arriving but was pretty happy with the courses I had so didn't do that.
registration_advice: Don't panic, it's a bit overwhelming because there are so many courses with very little information about each and quite a few rules for what you can apply for. If in doubt contact Go Global at UBC they know all the details. If you don't get the courses you want definitely try contacting Go Global after you have arrived to hear if there is anything that can be done.
course_level: I had three 3rd year courses.
teaching_comparison: The overall structure was similar to UCPH. All my courses had big lectures and two of them also had smaller classes that focused mostly on problem-solving. The grading however is quite a bit different. Rather than having one big final exam, you have lots of smaller assignments, quizzes, mid-terms, etc. on top of the final, these all count towards your final grade.
courses_enrolled: MICB 302 Immunology MICB 306 Molecular Virology SCIE 300 Communicating Science
recommended_courses: All three that I had. Immunology and molecular virology worked very well together as the topics overlap. They were also both interesting and built upon what I had previously learned in courses at UCPH but go into much more detail. They are definitely relevant to Molecular biomedicine students. I also really enjoyed communicating science. It is a bit different from the others as it focuses more on group work than lectures. I think it is a good course as it gives you an introduction to writing both to a scientific audience (in the form of a scientific paper) as well as to a general audience (blog post, podcast, and video). The course also does not have any exams but instead assignments which I enjoyed.
unexpected_costs: I expected groceries to be about the same as in Denmark I was surprised to find it was more expensive. (A note to the numbers above, you could definitely live cheaper than I did, I went on quite a few trips, and in general, prioritized having a good time over saving money. The other fees are things like kitchen stuff, pillow, etc. which you need to get when you arrive)
cost_comparison: Pretty much everything was more expensive. Groceries are a bit more expensive and definitely makes sense to go to a low-cost grocery store (I like No Frills). Public transport is cheaper since you have to get a U-pass through UBC, this coast 950 DKK for the whole semester. It allows you to with all public transport in metro Vancouver.
activities_available: There is a club for just about everything. I would definitely recommend that you find one that fits your interests. There are options for lots of different sports, clubs for different religious believes, and various other hobbies.
activities_recommended: The varsity outdoor club, VOC. It is one of the more expensive clubs but it gives you access to some awesome trips. If you like climbing I would also suggest the aviary, it's a climbing wall on UBC. You can learn to do climbing either through the VOC or the aviary if you don't know how already.
weekend_recommendations: Try to get out of Vancouver too. Some recommendations I enjoyed: Bowen Island (a small island you can get to with the ferry great for a one-day hike), Vancouver Island (A big island, definitely recommend spending a couple of days here), Washington (Vancouver is really close to the US so a great opportunity to visit there as well I went to Seattle and the North Cascades National Park).
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, honestly not much different from Denmark.
socializing_tips: Getting to know local students is definitely harder than getting to know other exchange students. I would recommend joining clubs or putting effort into talking to the other students in your classes. Since there are so many exchange students who are all looking to meet new people it is easy to never really speak to anyone local if you don't make an effort to do so.
cultural_challenges: As I said there really aren't too many differences but one thing I did find different was that casual hang-outs didn't seem to be as common, often you would have a concrete plan on what to do when meeting other people (This might however just be because all the people were new to each other).
culture_appreciated: In general, people were very kind and helpful.
top3_advice: Take time to enjoy non-academic opportunities, depending on which courses you choose, students are very motivated to do well (this seems to especially be the case if they want to go to medical school) and while studying is important, remember to take time to enjoy being in a whole new country.
other_useful_info: There are about a million different things for you to do, and you won't be able to do them all so choose the things you think you'll enjoy the most and take some time to relax as well.
most_rewarding: Getting to know so many wonderful people and experiencing another culture.
greatest_challenge: Being away from all the people you know best and trying to make new friends while getting used to a new country and new courses can be very hard.
other_comments: Overall I loved going to UBC and living in Vancouver and would definitely recommend to other students.

crucial_aspects: First of all, I wanted to explore a destination with both different culture and nature compared to Copenhagen. I was very much dragged to the outdoor opportunities such as skiing, climbing, and hiking and wanted to explore what it's like attending a university with a large campus and a vibrant campus life. Furthermore, I was under the impression that the academic level was quite good and expected having some very interesting classes.
info_ease: In terms of classes getting the information was quite difficult. It was not possible choosing any courses beforehand and I had to show up and ask professors in person if I could attend the classes. Luckily, I ended up getting all the courses I was hoping for. Regarding practicalities it was quite easy since UBC has a lot of experience with both exchange students and new students in general that need a lot of information since many students travel to UBC from abroad.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance from the professors at the political science department and the department for public policy and global affairs regarding how to enroll in the courses. Regarding housing, I received a lot of information.
arrival_comments: I could really have used additional assistance on how to enroll in political science and public policy and global affairs courses because I felt like I was a lot on my own in terms of seeking the required information - especially since I needed my credits transferred to 30 ECTS points which created a lot of uncertainty before and the first weeks after my arrival.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I had to register for undergraduate courses beforehand, but I knew I wouldn't attend any of those since I got the impression that these could not get transferred to ECTS credits in my master study at UCPH. This meant I had to show up and address the graduate professors in person and ask for permission to attend their classes. After their permission, there was no problem with attending the graduate courses. However, it was possible for graduate students at UBC to register in the courses beforehand which meant that certain courses had extensive waiting lists, so I was lucky that the professors understood my special situation and allowed me to skip the waiting list.
registration_help: I couldn't find any general help regarding figuring out my possibilities of enrolling in the graduate courses. I had to see the graduate professors in person to enroll.
registration_success: I was successful and registered in all classes I wanted.
registration_advice: In political science and public policy and global affairs, I would enroll in undergraduate courses because this is what is needed in UBC's system. I would look into graduate courses and write professors of interest beforehand, explaining your special situation. Then I would show up to all potential classes the first week of classes and talk to the professors about the possibility of enrolling in their course. I would enroll in enough courses to make sure that you can get the credits transferred to 30 ECTS points and then I would drop some excess courses before the deadline.
course_level: I found that the level was varying at the courses, but all of the classes were interesting. However, all of the classes had fewer students attending that I'm used to and in all courses it was expected to participate actively at classes and to hand in assignments during the term. It was possible for me to participate with my academic and English level but I had to get used to the expectation of active participation which varies a lot from UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The classes had fewer students and it was expected to participate actively at classes and hand in assignments throughout the term which is not expected at UCPH. I also found that the relationship between the professors and students was closer and that the professors were very interested in the student's papers which was very nice.
courses_enrolled: Gender, Peace and Security (Public Policy and Global Affairs) Topics in Political Theory: Contested Territory (Political Science) Human Rights and the Environment (Public Policy and Global Affairs)
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend Topics in Political Theory: Contested Territory (Political Science) and Human Rights and the Environment (Public Policy and Global Affairs). Contested Territory was political theory which included a lot of knowledge on indigenous people in general and in Canada and the US specifically which is not something I have found on syllabuses in UCPH and the professor, Anna Jurkevics, was very engaged in the topic. Human Rights and the Environment is also highly recommendable, since it had a multidisciplinary approach to human rights from an environmental point of view and the professor, David Boyd, is the UN special rapporteur on human rights and the environment and had extensive knowledge within the field and is very inspiring.
unexpected_costs: I had to pay for all of my rent beforehand, some time during January.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping in Vancouver was more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: There were multiple social activities available through my housing offer such as hiking trips, crafts, and parties. Furthermore there are all kinds of athletic activities, including a free aquatic center at campus.
activities_recommended: I would highly recommend joining the climbing club, the Aviary, since it is cheep and people are very friendly and its very conveniently located at campus. Furthermore the outdoor club, VOC, arranges different outdoor trips which is a good way to explore the nature as a newcomer. Also I enjoyed joining the dancing club where I attended a hip hop team and performed at a show at the end of the term and furthermore had the opportunity to join other dancing classes throughout the term.
weekend_recommendations: I would highly recommend buying a season pass for Whistler skiing resort with student discount. I skied the whole term for around 3000 DKK and rented gear for the season and there are busses driving back and forth from Vancouver to Whistler and a lot of people also shared rented cars for day or weekend trips. This is my number one recommendation. Apart from that there are multiple hiking opportunities around Vancouver that are exceptional experiences.
culture_adjustment: I think it was quite alright. UBC and Vancouver is highly multicultural compared to UCPH and Copenhagen which was a big experience. This meant that most people were quite different from myself and gave me many new experiences.
socializing_tips: I would join clubs and different events for students in general or exchange students specifically.
cultural_challenges: Mostly that people in general were quite different from myself and you have to prepare to meet and socialize in different circumstances than you're probably used to.
culture_appreciated: Mostly that people came from many different cultural backgrounds and brought new perspectives and things to do together.
top3_advice: Make sure to attend a lot of events and join a lot of clubs. Make sure to take advantage of the outdoors such as skiing or hiking. And I would highly recommend staying in a shared unit in campus to have an everyday with people you probably wouldn't meet if you didn't.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Staying in a shared flat with other students and learning about their lives and culture which was very different from my own.
greatest_challenge: I think the greatest challenge was socializing with people quite different from myself who have other ways of life.

crucial_aspects: The Canadian nature in British Columbia because Canada was open after the pandemic.
info_ease: It was very easy. UBC provided us with very detailed emails with guides to find all neccessary information.
arrival_assistance: I was a law student so I was not allowed to participate in the GoGlobal orientation week provided by the university. However, Allard Law sent us with written information both before and at arrival.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: My registration process was different then the other exchange students' because I was a law student. I can therefore only provide information regarding the registration process for law students. It is a very stressful registration system before arrival because you register for courses 2 times. The first round is in June, where you are only allowed to register for 2 courses. In the next round you can register for the remaining courses you need to get full credits. Please remember that it is first come, first serve so you need to be ready at the exact time and even there I did not get the courses I wanted. It is your own responsibility that the courses you take not overlap both regarding the exam date and the weekly schedule. As a difference from University of Copenhagen, classes are mandatory to attend, and you often get graded for your attentance, so it is quite important that your classes do not overlap. Don't stress if you do not get the courses you wanted! The first couple of weeks of classes you are allowed to switch courses and normally people have registered for more courses then they need, so you can continue to check if the courses you want get available spots.
registration_help: We had a exchange counselor at Allard Law, who helped us if we had any questions in the registration process.
registration_success: It was not very succesful. The local students can choose courses prior to exchange students and the registration process is very stressful which means that I ended up with only 1 of the courses I initially wanted.
registration_advice: If you want very specific courses you need to me very fast in the first registration. Otherwise check several times a day when classes begin if people should drop the course. In general my best advice is to be flexible about the courses you want and pay attention to the exam form. The exam period is only 2 weeks and begins immediately after classes end. I had only one course with final exam, where the others were final papers you could write during the term. That made the exam period a lot less stressful and I could enjoy December more.
course_level: I was master student at UCPH but were only allowed to attend BA courses at UBC, again because I was law student. Futhermore, I could only choose Level 300 and Level 400 courses.
teaching_comparison: The courses I had were seminars (fewer students and more attentance required). Compared to style of teaching at UCPH the professors demand more attentance in class.
courses_enrolled: International environmental law Introduction to Asian Legal Systems Japanese Business Law
recommended_courses: I would recommend courses with a final paper as exam form. I really liked International Environmental law.
unexpected_costs: Canada has the most expensive phone bills in the world where the cheapest start around 400 DKK for 10 GB a month. Furthermore, food is crazy expensive! You would pay 3-4 times more for especially fresh fruit and vegetables compared to Denmark. Living is also really expensive. Even on campus for a shared room with 5 others they paid around 5,500 DKK.
cost_comparison: Living, phone bills, and food in general were much more expensive than expected. Going out for dinner (especially sushi) was cheaper.
activities_available: Everything! UBC has over 600 clubs.
activities_recommended: I joined the exchange club and the UBC triathlon club which I really enjoyed. I would recommend the exchange club no matter what your hobbies because they arrange multiple activities each month only for exchange students. I know other exchange students really liked the VOC club.
weekend_recommendations: We did a lot of travelling both in BC and in North America in general. I arrived two 3 weeks prior to school start and had 2,5 weeks vacation in the Rockies first and then in Whistler, which I can really recommend. Also if you are into hiking, the app "Alltrails" is very helpful so we went on hikes almost every weekend. I also visited Toronto, Vancouver Island, Hawaii and San Franscisco during the term because I only had classes Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy because Vancouver is very multi cultural.
socializing_tips: It is in general hard socializing with local students because you are only there for 4 month. I joined to triathlon club which almost only consisted of local students and that was a great way to socialize with the locals. My best tip would therefore be to join some of the clubs on campus.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The multi cultural society.
top3_advice: Enjoy the nature and arrive 2-4 weeks before so you have time to travel around in the beautiful country. Be open to new cultures, because Vancouver is a very multi cultural city where no culture is a majority culture. Socialize a lot in the beginning and prioritize the social activities so you quickly can make friends.
other_useful_info: Remember rain clothes!
most_rewarding: How much I learned about other cultures being abroad.
greatest_challenge: I did not have any great challenges.

crucial_aspects: I was interested in trying out a Northern American campus culture in an international community. Vancouver seemed like an exciting and multicultural city, but the most important factor to me was the opportunity of exploring the beautiful nature in the western part of Canada.
info_ease: It wasn't a big issue. Some information came pretty late but I never felt stressed out about it.
arrival_assistance: I moved into a residence on campus which was supported by local students. On our first day at campus, we had a full-day introductory program together with a small buddy group of other exchange students. The Go Global department at UBC was in general helpful to answer potential questions.
arrival_comments: Information about housing on campus wasn't really sufficient but the orientation related to the study-part was pretty ok.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: As a graduate student in political science, you need to contact the professors directly to apply for a spot on their course. It was a messy process because I needed to hand in a course registration list to Go Global at UBC (because that is just how the procedure is for every exchange student) even though this was useless for them because they couldn't register you in any graduate courses. You can only apply for spots on the courses after the ordinary application process for the local student has ended but as soon as this period has ended you have to do it as quickly as possible (before the courses fill up). I was told that I couldn't apply for "restricted courses" as an exchange student, but almost every graduate course was restricted, and it wasn't a problem to get enrolled in them - so don't worry about applying for restricted courses.
registration_help: Go Global (the exchange student department at UBC) was quick to answer any questions and helped me to figure out how to contact the professors on the different courses.
registration_success: Partly successful. I did get some interesting courses but it was not among my top choices.
registration_advice: Just get in touch with the professors as soon as possible to get enrolled in the courses you find interesting. And remember that you can drop/add courses during the first weeks.
course_level: It varied quite a lot. I had one course with very high requirements. Almost half the students in the class were PhD-students and the professor expected a lot in terms of both reading and participation in the class. The other courses I had were more relaxed. Still, it was on a high academical level, but the workload was similar to what I know from KU.
teaching_comparison: It is quite different. Every class consists of 15-20 students and it is not run as a usual lecture but more interactive with a lot of student participation (participation is also a part of your final grade). The teacher expects you to participate, and during the semester I had several presentations. With that being said, you are not expected to come up with some very comprehensive arguments every time you take part in a discussion. I found most of the discussions more down to earth compared to most classes at KU.
courses_enrolled: Development Discourses and Practices Developing Policies to Improve Population Health Migration and Citizenship
recommended_courses: Developing Policies to Improve Population Health was a great course. It consisted of students from both political science and population health and it was very valuable to take a class together with people studying something different from myself. Also, Veena Sriram (the teacher in this course) is great! She has some other courses as well, and I'll highly recommend her.
unexpected_costs: I found it in general pretty expensive to live in Canada, but the biggest (unexpected) cost was all the weekend trips I did. There is so much to see and do in this area if you like exploring the nature, and it is not for free.
cost_comparison: Groceries (especially fresh and healthy food + alcohol) was more expensive than I expected. Gas and cars are cheap.
activities_available: Pretty much everything you could imagine. Not that many targeted exchange students but it's rather easy to join the "normal" clubs and activities as an exchange student.
activities_recommended: Join VOC and make use of some of their nice trips if you are into outdoor things. Join one of the Thunderbird Sports Clubs if you like sports and want to make some Canadian friends. Go and watch some Thunderbird matches - especially Icehockey is nice.
weekend_recommendations: Go explore the nature around Vancouver, it's amazing. - Whistler is amazing for skiing in the winter and mountain biking in the summer. Make sure to buy a student season pass for Whistler. It's 600$ and a day ticket is up to 240$. - Squamish is amazing for climbing. - You have a lot of great hiking trails in the area that you can spend months exploring. - Vancouver Island is amazing, but go by car (or van) so you can explore more than just Victoria. Tofino is amazing for surfing and Campbell River is known as the salmon fishing capital of the world. - The Rockies are fantastic but make sure to have more time than just a weekend.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. Canadians are so friendly and they are used to welcoming people with different backgrounds.
socializing_tips: Join clubs on campus
cultural_challenges: Not really any I can think of.
culture_appreciated: How polite and friendly Canadians are.
top3_advice: 1. Apply for housing on campus 2. Join some UBC clubs 3. Get out of the city and explore the nature
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of
most_rewarding: Living together with people from other nationalities on campus and joining a UBC sports club
greatest_challenge: I can think of a few even though none of them were huge. It was special to move to a place where you knew no one - especially in the beginning. Also, it took some time to get used to speaking academic English in class.
other_comments: UBC is a fantastic university and Vancouver and the nature surrounding it is absolutely amazing. I would highly recommend to almost everyone.

crucial_aspects: I was actually supposed to go to Russia but due to its war of aggression against Ukraine, that was not an option anymore. KU's international office called me back when the war started, and asked if I was open to other partner universities. Given that I had previously done some writing on the Arctic and was toying with the idea to deepen my knowledge of the region, I told KU I was willing to go to any Arctic country. ...et voilà, a few months later I found myself attending Vancouver's University of British Columbia.
info_ease: Very easy. UBC and KU seem to have been long-time partners and both univeristies' international offices were sharing important information timely and easily understandable. Everyone I spoke to was helpful and very kind.
arrival_assistance: UBC assigned us international buddies that would show us around campus as well as regularly organize social events.
arrival_comments: Overall, orientation assistance was well-organized. However, it was targeted at undergraduate students; being an older Master's student, I had to be more active in collecting relevant information about registering in graduate (aka '5th year' aka 'Master') courses.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: When I got to UBC, I attended the undergraduate courses I was originally registered for. They were on Bachelor level, and by emailing the professors of some master seminars, explaining my situation and academic background, I was able to get into very interesting and challenging seminars.
registration_help: The professors themselves and readings previous reports of exchange students.
registration_success: As explained above, it was a bit tedious but very doable.
registration_advice: Talk to professors and the department's secretary directly if you wish to enroll in graduate courses. Be patient, be kind and persistent. If you are planning on doing undergraduate courses, the process is very easy and a no-brainer, thanks to all the resources you'll receive from 'go-global' (UBC's charming name for its international office).
course_level: All level of classes require weekly work. The graduate classes were comparable to the level of my master's classes.
teaching_comparison: I had to really engage with all the readings and write weekly comments, as well as do a few written assignment, including a bigger one at the end. Participation is also graded, which gives the classes a more lively feel.
courses_enrolled: - Security Challenges for Asian States and People - Development and Institutions - Special Topics in Public Policy: Territorial Disputes and Cross-Border Conflicts
recommended_courses: "Security Challenges for Asian States and People" was great, as professor Ramana continuesly exposed us to very different readings. Really, any class Ramana teaches, I would highly recommend attending.
unexpected_costs: The university transcripts cost 11 dollars. In general, I often felt like a customer rather than a student. There is no subsidized student food on campus (cafeteria style) but rather restaurants and fast food chains, that were often more expensive on than off campus. However, there are plenty of microwaves on campus, so that you can bring your own food. Also, housing doesn't really come with appliances, so there were many costs adding up for equipping the kitchen.
cost_comparison: Rent, groceries, and renting outdoor equipment.
activities_available: Many self-organized clubs are run by students and only require a small membership fee. I was on the social triathlon team and it was great fun - highly recommend! Free activities include the swimming pool, and Thunderbird sport events (football, ice hockey and alike).
activities_recommended: Join a club! That way you also get to meet local people and regular students
weekend_recommendations: Vancouver is super outdoors-y, so there are plenty of hikes in the area. Clubbing is not as big (and quite pricey) but a trip downtown is always nice. Try Earnest ice cream!!
culture_adjustment: There is plenty of information out there how the academic life is different, and its workload and challenges were not surprising. 'Local culture' was very UBC-focussed; at times it felt like an isolating island since everything was pretty far away from campus. I struggled a bit with the 'exchange student lifestyle'. Many of the international exchange students come from wealthy backgrounds and I found myself having to say 'no' more often than I wanted to - plans and trips and hikes were getting a bit excessive and were pricey.
socializing_tips: The social clubs are great for that. And classmates were generally always up for coffee.
cultural_challenges: The local students are used to a high influx of exchange students. I found it a bit hard to connect, as everyone was very aware we would leave soon.
culture_appreciated: There is always something to do and to see. The university and the respective departments always organize plenty of events (go to every 'Open House' of your faculty, the food is normally amazing!).
top3_advice: Be aware of a) your financial situation b) your academic background and wishes and c) of limiting beliefs you are bringing with you. Just because the academic style is different or things do not seem to make much sense at first, be patient and flexible. Enjoy the otherness!
other_useful_info: Sign up for event information of your faculty and join all the facebook groups. Also, don't let FOMO get the best of you
most_rewarding: My lovely roomies. We became really good friends and shared many emotional moments. Also, the seminars were challenging and I found myself cussing the workload at times. However, I learnt so much in a short amount of time and really expanded my academic interests.
greatest_challenge: The financial challenges and saying no to some plans (FOMO is real).
other_comments: Going abroad is always fun! It was easy to tell that UBC and KU have been working together for a while and the administrative process was easily manageable. UBC is a comfortable place to do an exchange semester; I didn't perceive my time as particularly exciting (Raincouver and Vancouver are not too different after all) but it is a good place to go if it is your first itme abroad.

crucial_aspects: First of all, I highly appreciated the surrounding nature of Vancouver in choosing my study destination since I am a big fan of nature, hiking, and other outdoor activities. Second, I enjoyed the big variety of available courses on UBC. This gave me great opportunities of expanding my study field with completely new perspectives and insights. Also, I wanted to go to a prestigious university with a high academic level. Lastly, I chose Vancouver since I wanted to attend university in an english speaking country so I could improve my english proficiency.
info_ease: I found it quite easy. I think UBC provided good guidance and information trough their informative emails.
arrival_assistance: On our first day (Imagine Day) we were assigned to a group and had a student advisor who showed us around campus. Afterwards we had the opportunity to attend some presentations with information on both academic and social aspects of studying on UBC, e.g., how to add and drop courses, what clubs to join, etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: During the first two weeks of school you have the opportunity of adding and dropping courses, so you could try out different courses and thereafter decide on which courses you would like.
registration_help: Go Global was helpful in providing information, and the UBC website also contains a lot of helpful information - not only with regard to the course registration process but also all other aspects of UBC life.
registration_success: It went pretty smoothly for me. I only had to drop and add one course, and I was very lucky to get the last seat in the course which I added.
registration_advice: If you find yourself really wanting a course but it's full, my advice would be to contact the professor. Often you can get on a waiting list (during the first two weeks people will drop courses and seats will be available) or they are willing to open op an extra seat in the course.
course_level: I had two 100-courses and two 200-courses. I found the academic level of my courses quite easy but also challenging in some aspects since the way of 'doing school' in Canada is very different from how we do it in DK.
teaching_comparison: Overall, I liked the teaching style at UBC. My professors were very engaged. They often encouraged to discussion and reflection and wanted us to participate in the classes - sometimes a bit too much, though. In terms of the exams, I found it a lot more about memorizing than critically reflecting, discussing, and likewise, on relevant topics. This way, it was very different from what I am used to from UCPH. But it was refreshing and nice to experience!
courses_enrolled: SOCI 101 Social Interaction and Culture SOCI 260 Work and Society INFO 100 (De)coding Information and Why It Matters FMST 210 Family Context of Human Development
recommended_courses: I highly recommend SOCI 260 and INFO 100.
unexpected_costs: Only a few days before my departure to Canada, I was unaware that my roomies and I had to buy all stuff for the kitchen. This was certainly an unexpected cost.
cost_comparison: Most items was more expensive than expected. Canada is an expensive country to live in.
activities_available: All kinds of non-academic opportunities was available. There is a wide range of different clubs to join on UBC! Especially there is great sport opportunities on campus.
activities_recommended: I have nothing to recommend since I did not participate in any non-academic activities other than a few times of drop-in iceskating. Therefore, instead I recommend that you actually join some!
weekend_recommendations: If you like nature, I recommend that you use the nature around Vancouver and do some hike! There is so many spectacular hikes around Vancouver. Also, I highly recommend going to Banff and Whistler!
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy. Canadians are so friendly, nice, and polite! It makes it easy to adjust to.
socializing_tips: Talk to people in your classes! It is nice to have a friend in class and to get to know lots of different people from different countries.
cultural_challenges: To be honest, I did not really find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and thoughtfulness of the Canadian people.
top3_advice: 1) Socialize, make new friends (not only other Danish students even though it seems secure), 2) If you have the slightest interest, join a club, sport activities or other non-academic activities, 3) Make sure to have fun; explore the city and the amazing nature!
other_useful_info: Can't think of anything at the moment.
most_rewarding: Getting to know so many new people from all around the world - it makes me feel very lucky.
greatest_challenge: Missing those at home and finding a good balance between schoolwork and having fun.

crucial_aspects: Først og fremmest ønskede jeg at besøge et engelsktalende land, da det gav langt flere muligheder ift. at vælge fag. Derudover ønskede jeg at stifte bekendtskab med Common Law-systemet. Jeg har altid gerne villet besøge Canada, hvorfor dette var oplagt. I forhold til valg af universitet i Canada, var det vigtigt for mig, at omgivelserne og landskabet gav nogle anderledes muligheder for at være aktiv f.eks. skiløb og vandring. UBC var derfor oplagt. Endelig fik jeg UBC anbefalet af en række bekendte.
info_ease: UBC holder nogle online pre-arrival introduktionsmøder, hvor de kommer rigtig fint omkring alt det væsentligste. De har meget fokus på at hjælpe, også med praktiske ting, og jeg er sikker på, at de ville have kunnet hjælpe mig, hvis jeg havde haft brug for det.
arrival_assistance: De holder introduktionsmøder på UBC, både et generelt og på det juridiske fakultet. Her får man en række information og ansigt på de mennesker, som man skal henvende sig til for hjælp. Jeg havde ikke brug for assistance, men var enkelte gange i kontakt med en vejleder omkring mere tekniske spørgsmål vedrørende eksamen. Hér fik jeg i hvert fald hjælp.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Man skulle registrere fag af to omgange, og det var først til mølle. På grund af tidsforskellen måtte jeg sidde klar om aftenen ved computeren, så det skal man lige være opmærksom på. Jeg fik heldigvis de fag, jeg havde satset på, men jeg kan forestille mig situationen er kaotisk eller stressende, hvis et fag pludselig er fyldt, og man ikke har forberedt sig på den situation. Man kan på deres studieportal lave lister med de fag, som man gerne vil have, så man hurtigt kan tilmelde sig det hele på en gang, når registreringen åbner. Jeg vil anbefale at man laver flere lister, så man er klar, hvis et fag er fyldt. Derudover, er det godt at vide at registreringen ikke er endelig - man har to uger til at prøve de tilmeldte fag og vælge andre i stedet, efter man er startet op. Hvis man er i tvivl om, hvilke fag man kunne tænke sig, kan man derfor møde op til flere forskellige fag, få en fornemmelse af fag og underviser, og derefter vælge endeligt (hvis der er pladser)
registration_help: Der blev sendt en række e-mails, men jeg synes det var lidt vanskeligt at finde alle informationer via studieportalen. Jeg satte mig grundigt ind i det, men det tog også en del tid. Der er nogle fag, som man ikke kan tilmelde sig som udvekslingsstuderende, og det havde jeg misset i første omgang. Jeg vil anbefale, at man bruger noget tid på at undersøge det inden registreringen starter.
registration_success: Jeg fik heldigvis dem jeg havde planlagt.
registration_advice: Sæt jer ind i det, så I er sikre på, at I ikke ender med fag, der har undervisning/eksamen på samme tidspunkt. Lav evt. lister klar med de fag I vil have, så registreringen går lidt hurtigere. Vær opmærksom på, at nogle fag har eksamen, mens andre har opgaver (Course hhv. Seminar) - selv gik jeg efter at have begge dele, så arbejdsbyrden blev fordelt mere jævnt over semesteret. Vær også opmærksom på undervisningstidspunktet. Jeg havde fx to aftenfag. Det var i princippet fint, men jeg arbejder selv bedre om morgenen, og jeg havde derfor svært ved at koncentrere mig i aftentimerne. Derudover risikerer man at gå glip af nogle sociale arrangementer, hvis man har meget undervisning om aftenen.
course_level: Det er svært at sammenligne direkte, da deres law school er struktureret anderledes. I princippet har man jo undervisning sammen med folk på 2. og 3. år, så på den måde kan det føles lidt lettere. Jeg oplevede dog, at der blev stillet nogle andre krav end hvad man er vant til og skolet i på KU. Der er eksempelvis meget fokus på deltagelse, og i alle mine fag udgjorde en præsentation en del af karakteren, ligesom deltagelse (og dermed også fremmøde) gør. Deres undervisning er ikke lige så stringent, som man er vant til, men til gengæld er der plads til større og mere kreative tanker. Det kan godt være lidt svært at vænne sig til, når man er vant til en meget speciel og systematisk tilgang til juraen. Overordnet set brugte jeg dog væsentligt mindre tid på forberedelse i løbet af semesteret. På mine fag var læsebyrden meget lav, og jeg brugte kun 3-4 dage på at forberede mig på eksamen (canadierne selv brugte max et par dage pr. eksamen). Jeg synes ikke det akademiske niveau var svært, og der bliver giver nogle ret fine karakterer i gennemsnittet (særligt, hvis man sammenligner med karaktererne herhjemme). Til gengæld er det vist ret svært at få de helt gode karakterer.
teaching_comparison: Undervisningen var meget anderledes, da deltagelse og præsentation udgjorde en del af karakteren. Det var tydeligt at mærke på engagementet fra de studerende. I mine fag, blev man ikke undervist slavisk i reglerne, men mere generelt i hensyn, udviklinger, samfundet osv. Det var ret fint at prøve noget andet, også selvom det ikke føles så 'juridisk'.
courses_enrolled: Topics in Tort Law - Mass Torts and Class Actions, Media and Entertainment Law, Topics in Corporate Law - Financial Accounting in Legal Practice
recommended_courses: Det kommer nok meget an på interesse. Jeg synes Class Actions var fedt, fordi det gav et virkelig godt indblik i Common Law systemet, og hvilken rolle deres domstole spiller i samfundet. Jeg forestiller mig, at andre processuelle fag kan gøre det samme. Financial Accounting er et fag, som kræver man er interesseret i regnskab og M&A - ellers vil jeg ikke anbefale det. Jeg var ret glad for det, men nogle elementer var svære, da det krævede man havde en baggrundsviden om canadisk corporate law og securities law. Media and Entertainment Law er et udpræget diskussionsfag, så hvis man er interesseret i at diskutere AI mv., er det et fint fag. Der var ikke rigtig et pensum, da jeg havde faget, og derfor var det en smule ustruktureret. Til gengæld kunne de studerende præge, hvad der skulle tages op i undervisningen.
unexpected_costs: Jeg havde måske ikke lige tænkt over, hvor meget det koster at anskaffe dyne, sengetøj, tørrestativ, tøjbøjler og andre lignende ting. Jeg havde taget meget få ting med, men man kan jo overveje, om det er værd at tage nogle håndklæder med selv.
cost_comparison: Fødevarer var meget dyrere end jeg havde regnet med, og det var noget jeg gentagne gange talte med de andre udvekslingsstuderende om. Almindelige dagligvarer, især frugt og grøntsager var meget dyrere end herhjemme.
activities_available: Der var rigtig mange sportsklubber og andet. Der var fx også en filmklub og en strikkeklub. Mange af klubberne holdt nogle gratis arrangementer i løbet af semesteret, som man frit kunne deltage i.
activities_recommended: Jeg vil anbefale at man tager til varsity games og ser UBC's sportshold konkurrere mod andre skoler, fx ishockey, basket og baseball. Hvis man kan lide at stå på ski/snowboard er der en ski-klub som arrangerede skiture og byture. Der er også en særlig klub for udvekslingsstuderende, som bl.a. holdt filmaften, vandreture og skøjtearrangementer. Jeg var desværre ikke selv så involveret i det, men jeg tror det er en god måde at møde nye mennesker.
weekend_recommendations: Jeg vil anbefale at man kommer ud og nyder omgivelserne, når vejret er godt nok til det. Hvis man får mulighed for at rejse, kan jeg varmt anbefale nationalparken Banff, som er noget af det flotteste jeg nogensinde har set. Hvis man ønsker at komme på mindre ture i løbet af semesteret, vil jeg anbefale at man prøver at lægge sine fag på få ugedage - jeg havde fx kun undervisning tirsdag og onsdag.
culture_adjustment: Selvfølgelig skal man vænne sig til, at alle taler engelsk, men folk er generelt virkelig søde og derfor føler man sig ret hurtigt hjemme i Canada. Der er en meget åben kultur, og folk er super hjælpsomme.
socializing_tips: Jeg synes selv det var svært, da vi kun havde én meget kort pause i løbet af undervisningen, hvilket jo ellers er et godt tidspunkt at tale med de andre. Det er en god mulighed at prøve at finde en gruppe til fremlæggelserne, da man på den måde kommer i snak med de lokale studerende også.
cultural_challenges: Jeg ved ikke om det er en kulturel forskel som sådan, men de studerende er generelt langt yngre, når de starter på uni i Canada, og det samme gælder mange udvekslingsstuderende. Mange er derfor kun 19-20 år, og det kan man selvfølgelig godt mærke. På jura er der dog krav om, at man har en undergraduate før man starter, så her er folk generelt ældre end på resten af universitetet.
culture_appreciated: At folk er meget åbne, søde og hjælpsomme.
top3_advice: 1) Man skal forsøge at se noget af naturen, hvis vejret og tiden er til det. Der er utroligt smukt omkring campus og Vancouver 2) Man skal få mest muligt ud af campuslivet, dvs. se games, deltage i fester der bliver holdt, og generelt opholde sig omkring campus centrum (bookstore, the nest, student building), hvor der sker rigtig mange ting. 3) Man skal ikke stresse så meget over at skulle afsted, da man sagtens kan få hjælp til diverse udfordringer, når man er kommet derover og i løbet af semesteret. De er generelt rigtig gode til at hjælpe og give informationer.
other_useful_info: Jeg var måske ikke klar over, hvor stor en betydning vejret ville have. Det regner altså rigtig meget, og der er virkelig stor forskel på UBC og Vancouver, når det regner og når solen skinner. Hvis man har et stort ønske om at vandre, skal man også være opmærksom på, at der er sne på mange af ruterne helt ind i april/maj. Det kan derfor give mening at overveje, om man hellere skal tage et efterårssemester. Er det omvendt vigtigere at kunne stå på ski er forårssemesteret ideelt, da sæsonen i Whistler vist ikke slutter før april. Det er godt at vide, at man kan købe billigere sæsonkort, hvis man er i god tid. Jeg mener vi sparede en del ved at købe før d. 19. november eller noget i den stil.
most_rewarding: Man lærer virkelig meget om sig selv, når man skal møde nye mennesker og ikke har nogle tætte relationer i nærheden. Man står alene med rigtig mange ting, og det er så fedt at vide, at man selv har kunnet klaret de udfordringer, der er opstået undervejs. Det har virkelig styrket min selvtillid. Det er også spændende at møde så mange forskellige mennesker - det lærer man også virkelig meget af. Endeligt er det bare fedt at have boet i et andet land og opleve kulturen på den måde.
greatest_challenge: Der har været et par perioder med meget savn, og hvor man har følt sig alene. Det tror jeg er svært at undgå, men det er selvfølgelig hårdt, når det står på. Det kan man jo tackle på mange måder, men jeg tror det er vigtigt at vide, at det er 'normalt' at få den følelse indimellem.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a place that had both cultural and academic opportunities. It was important to expand my english and therefore it should also be a country where they were speaking english etc. I think this was a great place to go, because it had a good university but besides that all the opportunities outside of the university, and not school-wise, were big and great too. And in the end I really wanted to go somewhere far away that could expand my horizon and let me explore new cultures, nature, activities, people etc.
info_ease: It was pretty easy
arrival_assistance: I did not really receive any assistance but quickly sought it out myself and then got help
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You got a login (a profile) to a special web page where you among others could find possible courses and register for/switch them etc.
registration_help: On the web page different options of help was possible and you could also contact someone if necessary
registration_success: I was pretty successful - in the beginning a lot of the courses were already full but during the first weeks it was possible for students to shop around, and that gave room for registering and trying out the classes I found interesting. In the end I had a good idea of most of them and could pick from that.
registration_advice: Give yourself the opportunity to shop around and get an idea about the different classes, because you cannot be sure about them before you join them/try them out. And be quick to register if you have your eyes on something special - check the courses regarding how full they are.
course_level: It varied - some of them were challenging while others were more easygoing and not that challenging. However studying in another language and in thise case another law system, and just country in general, is already a more challenging factor.
teaching_comparison: In all classes there were more than one teacher. It was a whole other way of teaching and building up a class than back at UCPH, but of course the different law system also played a role there.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Asian Legal Systems Topics in Comparative Law Conflicts of Law
recommended_courses: I don't have any recommendations - I think it depends on your own preferences and interests etc.
unexpected_costs: A higher rent when moving away from campus.
cost_comparison: Some of the groceries and food were more expensive. The rent in general.
activities_available: Different kinds of sports, clubs and sororities/fraternities. And also a museum close by etc.
activities_recommended: Perhaps joining a club because it opens up for you socially and is a fun way to try something new and staying stimulated while being away.
weekend_recommendations: So much!! It is a wonderful place with a lot of great trips/activities close by or within reach - go hiking, camping, explore the city, take a trip etc. Look up all the stuff you can do and go.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy
socializing_tips: Be open
cultural_challenges: Not that many
culture_appreciated: All of it - I like expanding my horizon.
top3_advice: 1) Be openminded and prepared for it to be different than back home 2) You can always get help but are also somewhat on your own so take up the challenge 3) Be aware of the housing situation
other_useful_info: People are sweet and helpful so don't be afraid to ask for help - and be open socially in general.
most_rewarding: All of it - it was a fantastic experience!
greatest_challenge: Being in another country so far away and studying in another language and in my case law system, however it was an experience.
other_comments: I will absolutely recommend going on exchange - and UBC (and BC/Canada) is a great place also, so I can recommend!!!

crucial_aspects: Det var vigtigt for mig, at det universitet jeg valgte udbød kurser som jeg fandt relevante for min faglige profil da jeg skulle udskifte grundfag og ikke tilvalg. Derudover var det vigtigt for mig, at universitetet helt generelt havde en forholdsvis god rangering og at jeg kunne læse mig til (ud fra andre evalueringer), at det var et godt studiemiljø for udvekslingsstuderende. Det var dog også ligeså vigtigt for mig at selve destinationen var spændende og havde meget at tilbyde i forhold til en masse smuk natur, sådan at jeg kunne opleve en masse uden for studiet også.
overall_comments: Jeg er så glad for mit ophold og især de nye venskaber jeg har fået. UBC har så mange muligheder for at opleve ting med sine medstuderende i form af events og andet arrangeret af universitetet eller organistationer forbundet med universitetet. Jeg var heldig at få værelse på campus, hvilket bestemt ikke gjaldt alle. Medvidere var jeg så også rigtig heldig med nogle virkelig gode roommates som jeg lavede mange ting med. Det faglige niveau på UBC er ret højt, skal man vide - måske mest af alt på den måde at der er mange opgaver og den endelige karakter bliver opgjort af flere forskellige ting i løbet af semesteret, bl.a. også hvor meget man deltager i undervisningen. Det er jo godt på den måde at man så virkelig er tvunget til at følge godt med i alle sine fag, men det betød også for mig, at jeg ikke havde helt så meget fritid til at opleve så meget uden for studiet som jeg gerne ville. Ens tid er på en måde mere strukteret for en end herhjemme (i hvert fald som humaniorastuderende) fordi man ikke kan vælge at bare arbejde intenst i to uger, og så slappe af i to uger, fordi der hele tiden er opgaver som skal laves og afleveres.
info_ease: Det var ok nemt. UBC sender mange emails ud, men man skal også selv holde godt styr på det og være vågen og huske at tilmelde sig diverse ting. Men der er meget reklame for events i starten af semesteret og så lange man husker at komme til introevents og læse sine emails, så går det ret nemt.
arrival_assistance: Jeg fik som beskrevet en masse emails med information. Den første dag var undervisningen erstattet med en "imagine day", som kort sagt bare var en introduktion til campus og hvad det tilbyder. Derudover har Go Global, som er dem der holder styr på internationale studerende, et kontor som er nemt at finde og hvor alle er meget behjælpelige med hvad end man har brug for. Jeg havde f.eks. ret mange problemer med at finde de rette kurser i forhold til credits og ECTS fordi jeg er kandidatstuderende, men blev optaget på UBC som bachelorstuderende (undergrad) og kun to undergrad-kurser. Man skal nemlig være opmærksom på, at det ikke er helt ligeså nemt at blive tilmeldt kandidat-kurser fordi man ofte skal have tilladelse af underviseren og fordi det er mere begrænset med hvor mange kurser der er og hvor mange studerende der er på holdene.

registration_process: Du skal selv gå ind på hjemmesiden og finde ud af hvilke kurser du vil have og være opmærksom på om de er åbne for udvekslingsstuderende og om at overholder pre-requisites. Alt den slags for man information om til det møde, men det er en rigtig god idé at have dannet sig et overblik over hvilke fag man eventuelt gerne vil tilmelde sig før mødet, for på den måde kan man stille spørgsmål osv omhandlende dem til mødet. Du skal tilmelde dig fag via en elektronisk tilmeldelsesblanket (nærmest som en survey på nettet) du får på mail og det er vigtigt at skrive både titel og kode og hvad der ellers er af formelle detaljer. Du skal vælge ti fag i prioriteret rækkefølge, selvom du nok max skal have fem (jeg havde fire), så det er en god idé at kigge i god tid og finde en masse forskellige. Efter en måneds tid kan man så tjekke på universitetets intranet/portal (Student Service Center) hvilke man er blevet tilmeldt og så skrive til Go Global (det internationale kontor som står for at tilmelde udvekslingsstuderende fag) hvis man vil forsøge at ændre det. Det er dog meget nemmere at få det ændret i add/drop perioden i de første to uger af semesteret, hvor du enten kan gøre det selv på hjemmesiden eller besøge Go Global kontoret og få dem til at hjælpe med det.
registration_help: Go Global er meget hjælpsomme og kan ofte finde ud af noget for dig. Jeg havde mange problemer med hvilke fag jeg skulle tilmelde mig, men jeg fandt en god løsning sammen med kontoret.
registration_success: Det var ikke super nemt. Jeg fik ingen af de kandidatfag jeg havde ønsket og et af mine fag jeg blev tilmeldt blev aflyst, så jeg måtte finde et andet. Jeg endte med at have et fag som stod nederest på min liste, så det var lidt ærgerligt. Men det har også noget at gøre med at jeg er kandidatstuderende og skulle udskifte mine grundfag, så derfor SKULLE de bachelor-fag jeg tog selvfølgelig være på et højt niveau og der var en masse frem-og-tilbage med KU og forhåndsgodkendelse osv. Jeg tror det er noget nemmere hvis man er BA-studerende og afsted med tilvalg.
registration_advice: At kigge på det hele et godt stykke tid i forvejen og ikke panikke for meget hjemmefra. De skal nok hjælpe når man kommer derover. Men hold øje med add-drop deadlines, for det er meget besværligt at droppe og/eller registrere sig i et fag efter deadline. Og hold KU i ørene hvis du skal have lavet din forhåndsgodkendelse om. Det var ret besværligt for mig fordi ingen svarede mig på mail, og jeg til sidst blev nødt til at ringe og få en kæmpe telefonregning pga det, og selv der var det svært at komme igennem.

teaching_comparison: Ret anderledes, mest fordi der er mange opgaver sammenlignet med HUM på KU. Jeg havde tre til fem afleveringer henover semesteret i hver fag plus ugentlige mindre opgaver i form af "discussion posts" online. Dog er eksamensopgaverne i slutningen af semesteret så en del kortere end herhjemme. Jeg havde ikke en eneste som skulle være over 10 sider (times new roman, størrelse 12, dobbelt linjeafstand). Jeg synes den akademiske standard er ligeså høj som på KU, den er bare fordelt lidt anderledes hvis man kan sige sådan og på en måde gør den store mængde opgaver at man bliver taget mere i hånden og der er lidt mindre selvstudie end på KU/HUM.
courses_enrolled: ENGL 365 Modernist Literature ENGL 368 U.S. Literature from 1890: War and American Modernism ENGL 370A Literatures and Cultures of Africa and/or the Middle East ENGL 375 Global South Connections
recommended_courses: "ENGL 375 Global South Connections" var et fag som jeg kom sent ind i fordi jeg blev nødt til at droppe et andet fag og så tage det i stedet. Men ej hvor er jeg glad for at det endte sådan. Det var kompliceret og svært og krævende, men virkelig spændende of lærerigt. Professor Kavita Philip er fantastisk vidende og jeg vil varmt anbefale faget. Det samme med "ENGL 370A Literatures and Cultures of Africa and/or the Middle East" fordi min underviser i det, Professor Suzanne James også bare er en virkelig god og sød underviser og materialet var rigtig spændende.
unexpected_costs: Jeg skulle købe mange bøger fordi jeg udelukkende havde litteratur-fag og jeg havde ikke styr på hvor jeg kunne købe dem brugt. Så måske det.
cost_comparison: Dagligvarer er dyre i Canada, især ost og grøntsager (jeg ved ikke med kød, da jeg ikke rigtig spiser det). Til gengæld er det ok billigt at købe mad/takeout på campus hvis man bare finder de rigtige steder (jeg vil foreslå The Delly in The Nest, hvor man kan få rigtig gode curries for ca 40-50 kr).
activities_available: Det er varsity sport på uni, altså universitets semi-professionelle sportshold. Som studerende er det gratis at tage til kampe, og jeg nød især at tage til hockey kampe. Der er også rig mulighed for at tilmelde sig eller starte nogle mindre sportshold (en af mine roommates startede fx et volleyball hold) eller til at gå til gratis fitnesshold hvis man bor på campus eller gå i fitnesscenter på campus (det koster dog lidt, men det er ikke dyrt. Tror det var 40 dollars for hele semesteret). Mit housing tilbød også en masse hyggelige events, som fx at male urtepotter, fælles morgenmad, bordtennis turnering og andet og der bliver organiseret fester og er endda en lille "natklub" på campus.
activities_recommended: Tag ind og se noget hockey. Og gør brug af de events der bliver tilbudt. Man kan altid smutte igen hvis det er kedeligt. Men ellers så bare tag ud og oplev Vancouver og naturen i British Columbia.
weekend_recommendations: Hvis man kan lide at stå på ski er der god mulighed for det når sæsonen starter i slut-november i Whistler eller på Cypress Mountain. Tag en færge til Vancouver Island og tjek All Trails ud for at finde en masse fede vandreturer. Hvis man har lidt ekstra tid og penge, så tag en tur til Banff eller Jasper nationalparker. For noget tæt på og gratis, så går en tur i Stanley Park og ned til strandene rundt om campus. Især Tower Beach er fin.
culture_adjustment: Ok nemt. Canadiere er virkelig søde, høflige, hjælpsomme og åbne. Kulturen minder på mange måder om USA, bare mere åben og hjertevarm, men amerikansk på den måde at alt er automatiseret og gjort nemt. Det gør det selvfølgelig også nemmere at vænne sig til kulturen når man taler sproget. Jeg var glad for at have så mange venner som også var internationale studerende, fordi vi så kunne undre og over ting sammen, men også tilvænne os ting sammen. Canada er et nemt land at begå sig i og Vancouver er en ret sikker by ligesom København.

cultural_challenges: Ikke rigtig nogle for at være ærlig.
culture_appreciated: Den oprigtige høflighed.
top3_advice: Søg om on-campus housing - det er en nem måde at møde folk. Tag til så mange events som muligt - det er også en god måde at møde folk. Vær opmærksom på også at indregne en masse tid til rent faktisk at studere og læse og brug campus og dine venner til at sætte jer og studere sammen.
other_useful_info: At Canada er et dyrt land, på nogle områder dyrere end Danmark.
