greatest_challenge: Tidsforskellen gør det svært at kommunikere med fx KU om vigtige ting og sager.

crucial_aspects: A good university in a beautiful location. The language taught and the reputation of the university.
overall_comments: I can really recommend doing an exchange on UBC. The only downside was that we were 40+ Danish students, which has its pros and cons, but something you have to consider if you chose to take an exchange at UBC in a fall semester.
info_ease: It was difficult to find the right information about the courses on the host universitys homepage. KU was helpful when I needed information before going there. After arrival they responded really fast when I needed it (something about my course registration), which was very important for my stay there (because I ended up with the courses I wanted).
arrival_assistance: I went to UBC's study abroad office a couple of time for help and information. And as mentioned above, I got help with the preapprovals after arriving, because I changed some courses during the first two weeks of the term.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I can really recommend doing an exchange on UBC. The only downside was that we were 40+ Danish students, which has its pros and cons, but something you have to consider if you chose to take an exchange at UBC in a fall semester.
registration_process: Most of it is done through KU, but finding the courses was the most difficult part because you have to look through the old course list and figure out which courses you are allowed to take, be aware of not taking courses that have lectures at the same time, etc. It was divided in several steps - back in DK, I had to make a list of ten prioritised courses, which felt like a waste of time, because I wasn't sure that I would get them and ten courses is a lot, when you only have to take three (as a postgrad.pol.sci.-student), and then in August I had write to the professors to get a signature that I could take their course, and that has to be done quite early in August (or mid August) because the courses get full, and then you are not sure to get a spot. But again the professors were quite fast at responding, whenever you contact them.
registration_help: We could write to UBC's Global Contact, and then they would respond within a couple of days.
registration_success: It took some time, but I ended up getting the courses, I hoped for.
registration_advice: UBC has a lot of great courses, so even though it feels frustrating to find the right courses and choose which ones you want, it is worth it, because if you find courses that are offered at your semester and writ
academics_comments: I can really recommend doing an exchange on UBC. The only downside was that we were 40+ Danish students, which has its pros and cons, but something you have to consider if you chose to take an exchange at UBC in a fall semester.
course_level: The courses were overall more demanding throughout the semester than I'm used to from KU. But once I got into the habit of it, I really enjoyed that way of teaching, because the courses I took were quite small and the professors actually knew our names and was interested in getting to know us and our academic interest, which I ended up enjoying a lot.
teaching_comparison: As mentioned above it is way more active way of taking classes, you have to participate in the courses (your participation is graded), you have to hand in assignments weekly or monthly, and I also had to host a full three hour class with one of my co-students. It can feel a bit stressfull in the beginning because it is quite different from UCPH, but I ended up enjoying it a lot because I learned way more about the subjects and became more confident in the subjects.
courses_enrolled: Policy Responses to Global Climate Change (with Milind Kandlikar) Topics in Canadian Politics: Urban Governance and Policy in Canada (with Carey Doberstein) Survey Design in Environmental Social Sciences (with Terre Satterfield)
recommended_courses: I believe that any courses with Carey Doberstein and Terre Satterfield would be great. They were really good professors and the courses I took with them was good. Milind Kandlikar is great as well but a bit more unstructured. His course was great because it is a cross-disciplinary course so the students had all different kind of academic backgrounds, which made the class really interesting.
unexpected_costs: Canada is really expensive, so make sure to have savings when you go there, because there is a lot of great opportunities to participate in, but it is expensive.
cost_comparison: I went on trips almost every weekend, and that was expensive, but worth all the money.
activities_available: A lot. UBC has a broad range of opportunities and they are all great, so make sure to enroll in something when you get there. There is so many opportunities so it is a help to have an idea of what you want to enroll in, when you get there.
activities_recommended: The Varsity Outdoor Club (VOC), they arrange great trips and you can rent outdoor gear from them.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the mountains as much as possible. Sign up for the VOC trips. Make an account on EVO, which is a car sharing opportunity that is great if you don't want to buy your own car.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, UBC are very inclusive and used to hosting international students, so you won't feel as the only non-Canadian. I mostly connected with other exchange students but made a couple of Canadian friends as well.
socializing_tips: Use the opportunities on campus to drink coffee, take a walk, do a quiz or something like that with the other students.
cultural_challenges: Being nuanced in expressing myself. It can be frustrating but also one of the good challenges of being on exchange.
culture_appreciated: The very easily accessible outdoor opportunities.
top3_advice: Apply for housing on campus (it is difficult to find housing off campus since there is a housing crisis in Vancouver), make sure to enjoy all the great non-academic opportunities that UBC offers, and enjoy the nature around Vancouver/British Columbia.
other_useful_info: Things will sort out, and you will meet a lot of nice exchange students who are struggling with the same things as you, and who are also up for making the most of your time abroad.
most_rewarding: Taking part in an international community
greatest_challenge: Keeping in touch with friends and family back home because of the time difference (9 hours)

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go a place where I could learn and get better at english as well as a different culture from the danish. I also looked into how the campus and teaching would differ to the way back home and which experiences besides uni the place offered.
info_ease: It was easy. I used the forms online from KU, was a part of their meeting online as well as used to website of the university I was approved for.
arrival_assistance: I needed some assistance regarding courses. I wrote GoGlobal an email and also had the opportunity to drop by their office on campus.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I recieved a file from UBC and had to prioritize my top 10 courses - they wanted 10 to be sure you got accepted into some. They registered me in 4 courses and I did not have to do more in the beginning.
registration_help: E-mail and in person help if needed - before and after arriving.
registration_success: I got into my top 4 classes, and had to drop one during the first 2 weeks.
registration_advice: The registration is pretty slow, and different faculties register at different times. Do not worry if you do not get into a course you want in the beginning, you also got the chance during the first weeks to add and drop courses.
course_level: I think the level of my courses were fine. They were all level 300 and gave me a lot of new knowledge.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. A lot of my courses were lectures (with 100-200 students) and then online quizzes, cases, assignments and discussion posts. The grade you get can be based on participation and the other things you have to do during the semester and not just a final exam. You have the possibility of a lot of hours with TA's and the profs to ask questions if needed.
courses_enrolled: FNH 313 - Food Microbiology MICB 302 - Immunology MICB 306 - Molecular Virology
recommended_courses: I really liked the Molecular Virology with Dr. Jean and prof. Graves. Really interesting to learn more about viruses. Great combination of general knowledge and applying that to specific well known viruses in the second half of the course.
unexpected_costs: Mostly having to buy myself stuff to be able to go e.g. camping, skiing, etc.
cost_comparison: The food were way more expensive than expected.
activities_available: the AMS UBC have more than +250 different clubs - sports, cultural groups, creative groups and way more - almost all you can think of. They are also good at promoting them in the beginning of the term. It can be a bit complicated and overwhelming to find out what to join because of the many opportunitues - but most clubs are open for late joining too. AMS also planned a lot of other fun things to join - quizzes, painting, yoga etc.
activities_recommended: I would look out for the exchange club! Good opportunities to do fun stuff with your fellow exchange students. I joined the badminton and also tried the knitting and sewing club. I was a part of the VOC - varsity outdoor club - were you can join different trips and rent gear.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the nature around Vancouver! In the summer you can hike and in the winter you can ski. I absolutely loved the nature and it is easy to plan and go places - look into setting up accounts for Turo or Evo to be able to get a car.
culture_adjustment: I did not find it hard to adjust. Vancouver is very multi cultural and everybody is very nice and helpful.
socializing_tips: Everyone are very friendly, do not be scared to talk to people in your classes or join clubs and get to know people that way.
cultural_challenges: NA
culture_appreciated: The friendliness among almost everyone.
top3_advice: You can find a lot of used stuff in different thrift stores around kits and downtown - but I was surprised how much I was using my sleeping bag and hiking boots, so if you got them at home bring them with you! The weather changes a lot, we had the hottest summer and then a lot of snow. It rains a lot too, apparently more than in Denmark. Be prepared for a busy schedule, there is a lot of things going on all the time and a lot of trips to go on!
other_useful_info: Prepare yourself for the biggest adventure. UBC is big and there is a lot of opportunities and things you can do almost everyday. I used instagram a lot and found the different accounts and they proved helpful with a lot of information. Be openminded and join trips with fellow students - we used whatsapp to arrange stuff. It is really nice to have a car for trips, a lot of other fellow students bought cars and sold them before going home,.
most_rewarding: The friends I made
greatest_challenge: To stay up to date with studies. I studied a lot alone because everyone seems to have different schedules. I missed a study group.
other_comments: This was the best and most amazing experience! GO GO GO.

crucial_aspects: That the university offered som courses that I found interesting (and enough different ones for me to have something to choose between) and that the location of the university was close to nature and outdoor experiences.
info_ease: UBC as a campus is well organized with many signs helping students find their way around, so I found it rather easy to navigate from the start. Moreover, I participated in an introductory activity organized by the university, which included a tour around campus and general information, which was both helpful and a good way to get introduced to other new students.
arrival_assistance: I found accommodation on campus through a Facebook group, which meant that my new roommates (who were on their 3rd year at the school) functioned as great helpers in navigating the new setting I had landed in. I could ask them any questions I had upon arrival and they'd explain and assist me in settling in. Other than that, Canadians are in general friendly and helpful, so whenever I'd be in doubt about something, I'd reach out to a stranger and ask them for guidance :)
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I registered myself through the university portal, which works a lot like the one at UCPH. In my case I got all the courses that I wanted, but actually ended up changing a couple of my courses after attending the first classes of the semester either because I didn't like the course or found other courses more interesting.
registration_help: I learned that even though a course is full, it is often possible to get a spot by writing and asking the professor directly. So even though you might not get granted a spot at first, try your luck by contacting the professor with a brief explanation on why you find their course interesting.
registration_success: I managed to get a spot on all the courses I wanted, which I think is realistic when studying sociology, since many of the relevant courses accept a large amount of students.
registration_advice: Register for more courses than you might consider taking to ensure yourself a spot. You can always drop courses after a couple of lectures when you've gotten a better feeling of what you'd like to study. UBC has an add and drop period, which is exactly meant for changing around. However, some courses are really popular, so those might be smart to have signed up for before hand, since there might not be any spots left by the start of the semester.
course_level: I found the level different from the equivalent level in Denmark in two ways: Academically the level was generally a little lower than at UCPH, but since the requirements and expectations are very different, I'd say that studying at UBC was more demanding. Strangely enough I found 100 level courses more demanding not academically but practically than 200 and 300 level courses, since the teachers of the first year courses demanded a lot more participance in the classroom and weekly assignments were more common as well.
teaching_comparison: Some teachers require in class attendance and grade on behalf of your engagement in class. Moreover, quizzes and weekly tasks were a part of many of my courses, which meant that teachers expect you to have read your stuff and be able to participate in class discussions. I found that a lot more motivating than the teaching strategy at UCPH (at least for sociology students), since it makes everyone engaged in the classroom and gives you a better sense of whether you're understanding the material ongoingly instead of just testing your abilities at the end of the semester with no possibility of improving if you've misunderstood something.
courses_enrolled: Sociology - Social Statistics 1 (SOCI 328) Social Work - Introduction to Social Welfare (SOWK 200) Latin American Studies - Introduction to Latin American Studies (LAST 100) Spanish - Beginner's Spanish 1 (SPAN 101)
recommended_courses: I'd recommend taking the opportunity to try out courses outside of your main field, since it really (at least in my case) gives you some renewed energy school wise and a new perspective on a lot of the courses you've already taken in your own field.
unexpected_costs: The mandatory health insurance purchased through UBC at $325 and the U-Pass (for public transport in Vancouver) at $180.
cost_comparison: I found myself going on many trips and some that were more expensive than I had planned for (surf trip, climbing trips, skiing trips), so these definitely made my exchange more expensive than expected (but were definitely worth it!). Furthermore, Vancouver is a really expensive city to be living in: Expect grocery shopping to be more expensive than is the case here at home (and more expensive than buying ready made foods), phone bills can easily cost you around 50 bucks a month and going out to bars you'll find your beers costing you quite a bit more than in Denmark as well. However, many facilities on campus are either free for students to use (aquatic centre, ice rink etc.) or fairly cheap to buy memberships for (gym, climbing wall etc.). So found myself being able to participate in activities around campus for a lot less of a cost than what I had expected :)
activities_available: UBC has a giant club universe, which I really enjoyed and took full advantage of! For every possible activity there is a corresponding club that anyone can join and in the first couple of weeks of every semester, the clubs arrange a big event with introductions to the different clubs and in many cases the possibility to do try outs in the different clubs around campus.
activities_recommended: Personally I joined (and can highly recommend) the outdoor club (VOC), the salsa club and a couple of the activities arranged by the bike club (The Bike Kitchen). These clubs are a great way to meet new people and get activated from the moment you start at UBC. Moreover, many of the clubs worked as an introduction to Vancouver as a city and especially the outdoor club arranged many trips out of town as well and to fabulous spots around Vancouver, which was a perfect way to get a break from university life and get to explore some more of Canadas amazing scenery.
weekend_recommendations: Go on trips! Vancouver is an interesting city in many ways, but if you're into nature then take advantage of the many amazing places that are within reach just outside of the city. Whether it's just a day trip, a weekend or maybe a reading break, there are spots that are so worth visiting and so so close! Rent an evo with a bunch of fellow students or join the VOC (outdoor club) and tag along on trips already arranged by other adventurous students :)
culture_adjustment: I found that rather easy compared to other places in the world, where the culture is more different from the Danish.
socializing_tips: Talk to your classmates :) From my experience many of the local students didn't necessarily have the time to engage in a lot of activities outside of school or in the clubs at uni, but the class room is a good mix of both local and international students, so that'd be the place to meet 'em :))
cultural_challenges: The degree to which I would encounter homeless people in the streets of Vancouver. Canada has a huge problem when it comes to dealing with homelessness, food insecurity, and addiction, which was clear in particular parts of the city centre. Being a privileged young university student, I found that rather challenging to get "used to" or live with.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness of Canadians! Although most of the Canadians I met were on my trips outside of Vancouver, these people inspired me a lot by engaging in conversations so naturally and with such interest! So many times I found myself talking to complete strangers who'd tell me about their culture, their life or even their family history, which made me feel very welcome and safe throughout my exchange.
top3_advice: First of all, be sure to save up a lot more money than you expect to use (Vancouver and British Columbia is expensive and wanting to see and experience everything while you're here doesn't make it any cheaper). Secondly, consider beginning you're search for housing well in advance - if you get housing through the university no worries, but in case you don't, start by becoming a member of the many different Facebook groups for housing in Vancouver and start looking at your options. Finally, know that you've chosen to study in a nature paradise, so if you're into any kind of outdoor activities, this is definitely the place to be! And be sure to bring any outdoor equipment you might have lying around at home, cus you'll definitely get a chance to use it while you're here :))
other_useful_info: Don't be too nervous about going so far away from home - UBC as a university takes good care of their exchange students and you'll get the chance to meet new people right from your first day of school :) And if you're looking for adventure, sign up for the outdoor club (VOC) cus they definitely are the easiest way to access amazing trip options and get to hang with lots of amazing people! And be prepared, time flies by oh so quickly! Even though you may have so many plans and ambitions about what to experience and get done before leaving again, sit back and relax once in a while and enjoy wherever the weekends end up taking you and whatever the people you randomly meet and end up hanging out with have to offer :)
most_rewarding: Volunteering at the Downtown Eastside Neighbourhood House on East Hastings once a week. If you want to get a closer feel of what the city is like from the perspective of less well of citizens and meet engaged and inspiring volunteers on a weekly basis, consider finding an organisation and joining them on some of their projects. This definitely gave me a completely different insight into what kind of city Vancouver was and what kind of initiative and lovely people that call it their home.
greatest_challenge: Slowing down. Dealing with fomo. To tell myself that I was doing all that I could to make my exchange as fun as possible and simultaneously letting myself slow down once in a while and enjoy doing nothing. So a piece of good advice: Whoever you end up spending your time with and whatever you guys end up doing, it won't compare with anyone else's experience of being on exchange cus it was your personal experience and what ended up being your adventurous four months away from home.

crucial_aspects: The two most important aspects to me were the that the study destination should have relevant courses to my study programme such that I could further my skills, and.. nature and mountains! The University of British Columbia fulfilled both those criteria as they offer a good selection of environmental / climate related courses taught at an equivalent level to that of KU, and the nature that surrounds Vancouver is astonishing.
info_ease: Practically all the required information was e-mailed prior to arrival or during the introduction week. I did not find that I was missing information regarding my studies or living conditions, etc.
arrival_assistance: There was no particular assistance provided upon arrival. From the airport you can make your own way to the university / accommodation, where check-in occurs by going to the common block / reception of your assigned residence. There you would get a folder with informative papers and your key. That aside, the introduction week contained a lot of informative and social events to kick things off, while most of the important/mandatory information regarding classes was delivered by e-mail and through Canvas (Absalon).
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process is rather lengthy and begins with your application. For pre-approval you may only need 30 ECTS, but for the UBC application you are required to list at least 10 courses you could potentially register for. The actual registration for courses happens over summer and is done by filling out an online form sent by UBC. In the form you fill out information about the courses you want, and rank them by most to least wanted courses. It is not certain that you get all your most wanted courses. For Masters students the process is a bit more complicated as it involves contacting the course instructors to receive permission to join their courses.
registration_help: Information about course registration was both e-mailed and we also had a zoom presentation / meeting in which UBC went over the process and the important deadlines. That aside one is free to contact UBC for more help during the process if needed.
registration_success: All the courses I ended up taking were ones I wanted, but not all my top-ranked ones. One of my courses were also cancelled upon arrival.
registration_advice: I think it is important to note that when looking at courses for pre-approval, be aware of what term (1 or 2) the course is offered, what timeslot it is assigned, whether exchange students are eligible for it, and what level (100-500) it is, and of course what campus it is offered at (Okanagan or Vancouver). Register for more courses than you need ECTS. It is easy to drop out of a course once you arrive (within first two weeks) through an online form, and some courses may be cancelled (especially higher level courses that have fewer students).
course_level: The academic level of the courses felt equivalent to that offered at KU.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching depends heavily on the lecturer and the course that you are taking. Common for all of the courses, however, is that they require a lot more weekly interaction than those at KU. There will typically be weekly readings, quizzes, case studies/small tasks, etc., that are mandatory and count toward your final grade (roughly 20% of grades are made up of "participation" type activities such as those listed). If you are used to hanging back and cramming for a final exam that counts 100%, then this will feel quite different and perhaps a bit more "high-school" like. There are also midterms (either one or two) that count for some 20% each. The upside is that the final exam typically only accounts for 30 percent of your grade and therefore feels pretty relaxed. Style of teaching will also depend on what type of class it is. In the course descriptions it will be denoted whether it is a "lecture", "lab", "hybrid", etc., style class. Some are interactive and require a lot of group work while others are mostly traditional lectures.
courses_enrolled: Environmental Impact Assessment Global Climate Change Environmental Philosophy
recommended_courses: I think that all three courses were interesting in their own way. Environmental Impact Assessment was a great course with an enthusiastic professor and involved a lot of group work and hands-on assignments with EIA. It is focused on the Canadian law / process, and there are a lot of interesting developments to follow, especially within climate change and indigenous rights. If you want a course that provides tangible (work-related) skills, this is a good one. Global Climate Change provides a basic overview of the Earth System and deals with a lot of radiation balance calculations. If you've taken Climate Change Mechanisms and Tipping Points I would not necessarily recommend this course, unless you want a more math-heavy approach to understanding the mechanisms. Environmental Philosophy followed an entire course book on different philosophical approaches / stances on environmental issues. It is a great course for learning how to rationally argue for certain environmental stances, and to ground them in logical reasoning.
unexpected_costs: I did not really encounter any unexpected costs. There are spontaneous trips that you may go on with other exchange students, and those costs can be difficult to plan for precisely.
cost_comparison: Overall the price level in Vancouver is very similar to Copenhagen. Groceries are perhaps a bit more expensive in Vancouver, especially if you are vegetarian.
activities_available: UBC has a huge selection of clubs to join. During the introduction week there is a club-day where all the clubs set up a booth and you can walk around and hear a little bit about what they have to offer. There are sports clubs (sailing, weightlifting, swimming, dragon-boating, martial arts, running, hiking, climbing, surfing, etc.) and more cultural/social clubs (movies, boardgames, environmental activism, chess, majong, science, etc.). It is highly likely you'll find a fun club to join if you're keen! I was part of the Varsity Outdoor Club and highly recommend it to anyone who is interested in all outdoors activities (hiking, skiing, biking, climbing). It is student run and volunteer based, so all events are hosted by fellow students. It is a great way to meet locals and other exchange students, and explore the beautiful British Columbia!
activities_recommended: Definitely go out in nature, in whichever way you prefer. British Columbia offers some of the most incredible nature you'll experience, and Vancouver is a hotspot for outdoorsy folks, so there will be no lack of opportunities to come by. There are loads of great hiking trails, some of them very challenging, that offer incredible views. It is also possible to mountain bike, climb, kayak, cave, surf, ski, etc. Whale watching is also a great experience - you are very likely to spot some humpbacks, and if lucky, some orcas as well!
weekend_recommendations: Visit the Museum of Anthropology on UBC. Go on a micro-brewery bar crawl. Hike up to Garibaldi Lake or Panorama Ridge.
culture_adjustment: There is barely any adjustment needed. Given that everyone speaks English, there is no language barrier present, and culturally there are not any significant differences that should make it difficult to adjust to.
socializing_tips: Chat with the people you sit next to in class - be open and take initiative to do things post class if you vibe with someone. Joining a club, or several, is probably the easiest way to meet likeminded locals that are likely interested in social activities.
cultural_challenges: There weren't really any cultural differences that I found challenging. If anything, tipping culture is the thing that stands out the most, but you get used to that pretty quickly.
culture_appreciated: For Vancouver particularly I really appreciated the love for the outdoors. It was super easy to meet people that were enthusiastic about outdoor adventuring.
top3_advice: 1. Bring all your outdoor equipment if you are into hiking / camping - you are going to need it, and buying it in Van isn't necessarily cheaper! Go explore all that BC has to offer. 2. If you want the most out of the social life, be a social butterfly! UBC is a massive campus and there are a lot of people. You can easily drown in the masses if you don't take initiative and engage in the clubs / social groups / residence activities. Exchange moves fast, stay on top of your academics so that you can say yes to all the fun activities! 3. Make friends with someone who has a car, haha. You're going to need it. EVO car share is a good alternative to owning a car, but if you want to truly venture out into the wilderness, you'll need a car or know someone with one!
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Exploring British Columbia with a bunch of good people. The ease with which one can be out in complete wilderness during the weekend is incredible and makes all the academic work during the week all the more rewarding.
greatest_challenge: I think that the academic system is sufficiently different from the Danish one that it can be a challenge to adjust to it. The week-to-week workload will feel more significant because there are a lot of small assignments that are graded. It isn't that the academic content is more difficult, it is just that all these small tasks and deadlines will shape your time more so than at KU. Stay up to date with the academics and it won't be an issue, but it can feel more difficult to recover from a setback.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study in a narrative English speaking country in order to not only be forced to study in English but also in my everyday surroundings. In addition, I wanted to go on an exchange far away from Denmark. I believe this desire was due to the fact, that I wanted to challenge myself and shake things up drastically.
overall_comments: I loved every bit of it.
info_ease: I was a little difficult. I was a bit confused about the fact, that UBC, KU, and GoGlobal didn't communicate with each other. And I had difficulties figuringer out the rules. I think I would have benefited from participating in a meeting at KU prior to my exchange, but no such meeting existed.
arrival_assistance: None. Except from big meeting arranged by GoGlobal at UBC for all the exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I loved every bit of it.
registration_process: I can't really remember. I guess I filled our an application form online.
registration_help: Not much. I got a contact person, but she wasn't really available. I felt like I was left to myself and a lot of emails back and fourth with the exchange departement at KU.
registration_success: I ended up being registered to all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Apply for what you think you want and then arrive and try it out. You can always change it up when you arrive.
academics_comments: I loved every bit of it.
course_level: I was very satisfied with the level. My professors expectations were quite high and we had a lot of readings and weekly assignments.
teaching_comparison: It felt a bit more like high school. My professors gave us weekly assignments to make sure that we did our readings every week. The attendance was mandatory as well. In general I felt like they were more strict at UBC that at KU.
courses_enrolled: ENGL 309 Rhetoric of Science, Technology, and Medicine SOCI 414 Feminist Theory SOCI 465 Sociology of the Arts
recommended_courses: ENGL 309 Rhetoric of Science, Technology, and Medicine SOCI 414 Feminist Theory
unexpected_costs: I didn't know that UBC demanded us to pay for a health insurance. I had already paid for one prior to my exchange, so I had to pay double.
cost_comparison: Food was very expensive. And phone plans was very expensive too, but I figured out a way to get my danish phone plan to work in Canada.
activities_available: A million different activities.
activities_recommended: I can recommend the Out Door Club and the race "Storm The Wall"
weekend_recommendations: Go hiking!
culture_adjustment: Easy:)
socializing_tips: Get housing and get involved in the clubs, I would say.
culture_appreciated: Canadians are very lovely and friendly people.
top3_advice: Go, enjoy, life.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: The friendships I built in Vancouver. And the fact that I improved my English skills.
greatest_challenge: British Columbia is very low on doctors which I why going to the doctor can be quite challenging. This was a struggle for me coming from a very well functioning medical care system in Denmark.

crucial_aspects: I always wanted to experience Canada, and Vancouver seemed like an interesting city close to nature. Furthermore, as a MSc student it was a lot easier to go to UBC than many of the other North American universities.
info_ease: I had already gotten most of the information I needed from the UBC Go Global website and from previous online orientations, so I didn't need much more information upon arrival. However, it seemed very clear who to ask for assistance if needed.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation on the first day (Imagine Day). It was pretty boring, as I had already heard most of the information beforehand. There was a small tour of the campus and some social acitivities, which was nice enough.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: First, I had to fill out the top 10 courses that I wanted (although I only needed to register for 3 as a MSc student). It was quite difficult because they were supposed to overlap as little as possible, and I could only fill in undergraduate courses (i.e. 100-400 level courses) and courses with no restrictions, as graduate courses are applied for through a different (and much more tedious) process. I got registered in some of the top courses, but in one instance the tutorial section was missing, and I had to register for it manually although I was supposedly not allowed to. For the 500-level course I took, I had to fill out a form and send it to the instructors, then to the section head and then to the department of graduate studies. The process was very slow, so I was still not registered at the beginning of the semester, but thankfully you are allowed to switch courses during the first few weeks of the semester. I also tried to enroll in another grad course, but it turned out that it was not really a course but more of a weekly discussion meeting, so that didn't work out.
registration_help: I got some help from Go Global, but they could not do much except telling me to be patient and advising me to attend the course I was not registered in until the registration came through.
registration_success: In the end, I was happy about my courses, although it took a bit of time and worries. One course was registrated through the form (but not the tutorial section, which I had to do myself), one course I registered for via the grad-course form, and one restricted course I registered for by writing to the course responsible. I had hoped to get more grad-level courses, but it was okay.
registration_advice: Make sure to find lots of courses that you are interested in attending, so that you have alternatives if you don't get your top priorities. Don't be afraid to try and register in restricted courses, just try and reach out to the course responsible. Ask Go Global for advice if in doubt.
course_level: Two of my courses were 400-level (but one of them was mostly attended by grad students) and one of them was 500-level. If you are a MSc student, be aware that many 400-level courses are attended by both undergrad and graduate students and can usually be approved as MSc-level courses. On the other hand, be aware that UBC has both thesis and non-thesis graduate programmes, and in some cases the courses aimed at on-thesis students may not be as academic as you are used to from UCPH (e.g. less focus on primary literature).
teaching_comparison: It was quite similar, but more focused on tests and assignments.
courses_enrolled: FOOD 521 Advances in food biotechnology FRST 475 Indigenous ecologies MICB 405 Bioinformatics
recommended_courses: MICB 405 was a very nice bioinformatics course, the teachers are great, and you get a good overview of different methods, applications etc. There is also a team project. I also thought that FRST 475 was extremely interesting and very different from other courses I have attended. However, the workload was surprisingly high. FOOD 521 was nice enough and had some labs and seminars, but the students came from many different backgrounds, and a lot of the lectures were repetition of basic molecular biology.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Greens and veggies are much more expensive than in Denmark. However, you can get cheaper meals at restaurants, and things like beer and coffee are generally cheap, too.
activities_available: There are a ton of clubs, which are introduced on the very first day of the semester. There are also great options for sports and exercise.
activities_recommended: I mostly made use of the free access to the aquatic centre. If you like swimming, it is a great option!
weekend_recommendations: Explore the neighbourhoods of Vancouver - especially East Vancouver (e.g. Commercial Drive, Main Street), West End and Stanley Park. Taste the local craft beer varieties and explore the vintage shops etc. Go hiking and skiing in the local mountains and Whistler. Visit Vancouver Island (especially Tofino), but make sure you have enough time to get around - it is not a huge island, but it takes a long time to get there and to drive around.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
cultural_challenges: Vancouverites are not very outgoing, so I found it a little challenging to get close to the local students. Also, many of the students I met were from India and China, and some of them did not speak very good English, which made communication a bit difficult.
culture_appreciated: I liked how polite everybody are - e.g. saying 'thank you' when leaving the bus. I really like that Vancouver is such a multicultural place, it is great to see people from all over the world living happily together.
top3_advice: 1) Know your priorities - if you want 'campus life', you need to live there or at least quite close. UBC is far from downtown, and the buses make getting around very slow. You can bike, but campus is uphill from downtown... 2) Be aware that you will probably have to hand in a lot more assignments, quizzes etc. than you may be used to. Plan any extended weekend trips accordingly. 3) Canada is huge, so don't expect to see a lot of it during your exchange. If you have the time and money, consider travelling around before or after your stay to see a bit more than just Vancouver and its surroundings.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Experiencing a different culture, getting some new perspective on Danish culture and my own place in the world.
greatest_challenge: Socializing with the local students, especially because I was a grad student and living far from campus (however, I knew beforehand that this would probably make it more difficult to be part of campus life - pros and cons)
other_comments: If you are keen on going skiing, consider going in the spring - there is no guarantee of cold weather in December.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go on exchange to explore topics within my field that weren't available to me at UCPH (mostly de- and postcolonial theory as well as just basic gender studies). But I got a lot more than academic insight from the exchange in terms of personal development, friendships, and nature experiences.
overall_comments: The only cons were a roomie who smoked indoors and the amount of assessment in the Canadian educational system.
info_ease: Very easy. UBC's Go Global office is very informative. You receive emails throughout the months before arrival with all sorts of information preparing you for the upcoming exchange. You can also always reach out to both Go Global and the instructors by email and they'll be happy to answer all your questions.
arrival_assistance: I don't remember receiving anything in particular because I didn't need anything. But there were a lot of offers and opportunities to seek help fx through course and career counseling, mindfulness and stress management, and conflict resolution if you were having difficulties with your roomies.
arrival_comments: Canadian students are generally younger than in the Danish higher educational system and therefore there's a lot of help to get just in general. The students are "treated" as young people who might not have that much experience with adult life. It can feel a bit condescending at times but it helped me to just think of the constant checking in as a gift you can accept but don't have to.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The only cons were a roomie who smoked indoors and the amount of assessment in the Canadian educational system.
registration_process: You're emailed all the necessary information from Go Global! The deadlines are different from what's written on the website but don't stress. You have to choose 10 prioritized courses that don't overlap (as far as it's possible) and you'll get appointed five of those. But due to the drop period in September, you have almost a whole month where you can still browse courses and go to lectures even if you have not registered.
registration_help: Again, Go Global is your friend.
registration_success: Completely successful. I got four out of four wished courses. But my field is also kind of niche, so I'm lucky that way.
registration_advice: If there's a course that's restricted or full or whatever - don't despair. Try to engage in conversation with the professors, send emails, or show up at the lectures. The system is way more flexible than they (UCPH and UBC) tell us. Also, when it comes to specific fields of research that we're told we can't study. I think the whole anthropology section is noted down as inaccessible for exchange students which ended up being not entirely true. Talk to people and stay curious. There are a lot of possibilities if you're creative.
academics_comments: The only cons were a roomie who smoked indoors and the amount of assessment in the Canadian educational system.
course_level: There are courses on levels between 100 and 500 (100-level courses being suitable for first-year students, 200 for the second year, and so forth). I took four 400-level courses. Initially, I wanted to take 500-level courses but you can't apply for those before you arrive, and by that time I was way too occupied with just finding my way through exchange and didn't want the fuss of changing schedules. And I was also happy with my choices.
teaching_comparison: It's quite different. Self-study is not a thing in the anglo-saxon education system. There might be mandatory attendance and the workload during the semester is quite heavy compared to UCPH. Depending on your courses more or less is expected of you, but I was required weekly to turn in assignments, complete quizzes, do presentations, and bring forth discussion questions. And then of course there are midterm exams, midterm essays, peer assessments, and exams. But it's important to stress that failing is fairly difficult and you can actually not turn stuff in or not show up for a test and still get a well-about average grade. I wish I'd known that.
courses_enrolled: 1) Colonialism and After 2) Religious Feminisms 3) Sociology of the Environment 4) Gender and Nation: Women's State in Modern Central, Eastern and Northern European Literatures and Cultures
recommended_courses: Colonialism and After might be one of the most important courses I've ever taken. Dr. Pierre is an expert in her field, and even though the lecturers were very hard-core in terms of difficult, violent, and sensitive subject matter it really turned my worldview around. Dr. Meadows who taught Sociology of the Environment is without a doubt the most engaging professor I've ever encountered in academia. I highly recommend everyone to take that course as well.
unexpected_costs: Housing before moving into permanent residence cost me an additional 5000DKK. And even though public transportation is free when you're a student I did spend quite a lot on busses (16DKK pr. trip) before being officially enrolled. And I spent a looot more money on weekend trips and vacations than planed, but no regrets there.
cost_comparison: Groceries are crazy expensive in Vancouver!!! And the taxes are high. So everyday shopping is expensive. And there's a liquor tax as well which will hit you hard if you like drinks...
activities_available: All of them... Painting, baking, yoga, political discussion groups, sports, varsity outdoor club, climbing, skiing and snowboarding, surfing. You won't miss anything.
activities_recommended: Hiking... Just go hiking. What UBC and Vancouver has going on for them is the sorrundings. And they're near perfect. Find someone to enjoy the nature with.
weekend_recommendations: Go hiking in Garibaldi Provincial Park (as well as just the Squamish area in general), go skiing or snowboarding in Whistler, and visit Vancouver Island for surfing and/or swimming and just enjoying the coastline. If you have more time I highly recommend the Canadian Rockies and North Cascades in Washington State.
culture_adjustment: Yes in general. Canada is a Western country and the people are very much like Danish. They're just more polite and open and extroverted. They will for sure approach you and try to engage in conversation even if you haven't initiated contact.
socializing_tips: Be as open-minded and polite as the people you meet and you will have no problem finding a lot of friends. And try not only talking with the other Danes. It can be a challenge because it's much easier to just stay within your comfort zone, but the international friends I got really taught me a lot and I wouldn't have had the same amazing time without getting to know them.
cultural_challenges: Only the fact that when the cashier greets you with a "Hi, how are you" they do not expect you to elaborate on your feelings.... Just answer "Good thanks, how are you"....
culture_appreciated: The kindness and the openness.
top3_advice: 1) Don't worry too much about passing your courses - you will. Prioritize a multitude of experiences in addition to the academic ones 2) Say yes to all the outdoor experiences you can get. If someone invites you kayakking - you go. 3) Even though it's easier to joust make friends with the other Danes, stay curious and get to know as many internationals as possible
other_useful_info: Don't worry too much about the grading. It can seem overwhelming to get marks on every single assignment quiz or presentation, but in the end, that won't be what you remember.
most_rewarding: The international friends that I made and the nature experiences.
greatest_challenge: One of my roomies smoking inside for sure, but we handled it. And I was always in a position to ask for help if needed. Otherwise, the stressing out about exams and midterms and assignments and what not - which is why I'm trying to stress that you shouldn't!
other_comments: Go! You won't regret it.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to visit an English speaking to improve both my professional and casual English skills.
info_ease: UBC Go Global made it easy to find and get help - something KU could learn from. They actually had a walk-in office with actual people you could talk to, not just a phone to call. WILD!
arrival_assistance: Help to find a new course, when my first course was meant for other students than me.
arrival_comments: "Imagine Day" - the first day on campus was a bit tame, and they did not have enough food even though they told us not to bring lunch
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Tedious, and very little information about each course. As a master's student, it was super laborious to actually getting permission to do gradiuate (500) level courses, requiring you to mail professors for permission, none of which replied to my mails. Additionally, the courses only have 1-2 sentences about the content available prior to enrollment, so you have no idea what you're signing up to. I had to change courses twice because the courses i got accepted to were either way too easy or aimed at other study-programmes
registration_help: If you knew which course you wanted to change, you could talk to GoGlobal, which were very helpful, and available throughout the entire schoolday in the first few weeks. Zoom presentation about course registration prior to departure.
registration_success: 5/10, i didn't get permission to attend any of the graduate(500) level courses i wanted to attend.
registration_advice: Just pick something, and change later, it's a lottery which courses you get, and which ones actually make sense for you to take, and most courses open up for switching around in the first two weeks anyway. unless you're computer science, then good luck.
course_level: I had courses that were more demanding then in DK, and some that were much less demanding, both of them 400 level. The focus is very different than in Denmark, so if you like memorizing useless information that you forget a week after your exam, then studying in Canada is for you. On a serious note, the course level was very appropriate, but many courses had a very large course load in terms of home-assignments.
teaching_comparison: I had both lectures and class teaching. Lectures were very concise but had great content. Class teaching felt a bit like danish high-school, with many questions, many of them a bit superfluous. Overall a much larger focus on memorization, something i found very annoying and not very useful. Less focus on translating what you learn into a project setting like we focus on in Denmark, more just memorizing what's on the slides or in the text.
courses_enrolled: BIOC402 Protein structure and function BIOL440 Plant genomics BINF548 Directed studies (similar to projekt udenfor kursusregi)
recommended_courses: BIOC402 (Protein structure and function) was a great but tough course, but gives you ALL information you will need to work with or study proteins. Dives deep into protein folding, interactions, structure determination and functional studies at a high level, but they are good at building your knowledge up from not knowing a lot. Probably in the top 3 uni-course i've taken in my 5 years of study.
unexpected_costs: Club memberships, accidentally spent 200 kroner calling a US number because i didn't understand their phone# system.
cost_comparison: Food shopping is very expensive, like considerably more expensive than in DK, if you shop in supermarkets. I did the majority of my shopping in a local Korean shop (Kim's Mart on Broadway), which was considerably LESS expensive than supermarkets in DK. Shop in non-chain supermarkets and save! Beer/alcohol is less expensive in restaurants/fancy bars, but more expensive in Liquor stores. Coffee is also less expensive than in Copenhagen
activities_available: Pretty much everything you could imagine. Every club from rowing, hockey, football, American football, swimming (all of these free), to skiing, hiking, horse riding, engineering (boats, rockets, robots), gaming, smoking cannabis and speaking mandarin. SO MANY
activities_recommended: Hiking-club offered free rentals of different equipment. Many were in the ski/surf club, though they were very poorly organized, and the organizers were very self-absorbed and just liked attention. An example was making people wanting a CHANCE to get tickets to a ski-trip run into the water at the beach in their clothes, most of them not ending up getting one. They seemed like jerks.
weekend_recommendations: Hike, hike some more, then do a hike, and after that you can hike. Vancouver Island is my new favorite place on earth. Go to the rockies as well.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Say thank you when leaving the bus, and expect to have strangers striking conversation with you at every conceivable moment. Vancouverites are very friendly!
socializing_tips: Do a project, or talk to people in class, though i didn't manage to talk to many.
cultural_challenges: The amount of homeless people in Vancouver was quite a shock, and tipping. Tipping is the root to all evil, just pay your employees a fair salary.
culture_appreciated: The openness and kindness from strangers was heartwarming.
top3_advice: Go on hikes Go to Vancouver Island Don't cry if you don't see a bear, though you probably will, they are friendly, but carry a spray in your group.
other_useful_info: Stay on campus if you're offered.
most_rewarding: Hiking
greatest_challenge: Finding friends, but stay on campus and it'll be no problem.
other_comments: Go hiking

crucial_aspects: I chose to study abroad mainly to better my chances of being granted acces to a specific master's degree. However, I also studied abroad to explore new cultures, meet new people, and to hike - a lot.
info_ease: Everything was made super easy for the exchange people in general. On the day of move-in, we were pretty much guided through the whole thing. Don't expect to hear a lot from the university till a week or two before move-in. They were awefully quite till right before school start, which is fine, if you know not to expect hearing anything from them.
arrival_assistance: Busses took students straight to their housing accomidations, after which several meetings were held about living in residence.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The course registration can be quite daunting. I ended up having to apply for merit multiple times because the courses available changed or because i didn't get a specific pre-requisite waived. I think the biggest issue is how long UCPH sometimes take to answer. Appart from that, things went smooth enough.
registration_help: I personally don't really know. I never felt the coordinator was very helpful. However, course instructors at UBCO really wanted to help me get into the courses i prioritised, so I had a lot of help from them.
registration_success: I decided to utilise my selectiveness studying a mix of biology and health and exercise science at UBCO. This deffinitely complicated things a lot. UCPH was completely fine with me doing this, however, UBCO were very confused with why a sport science student would apply for biology courses. I applied for "molecular genetics" but didnt get in, so I ended up studying "priciples in genetics" which was a fantastic and challening course. Appart from that, I got into all the courses I wanted to attend. Also, if you plan on applying for courses only within your specific education, I dont think you will have any issues with registration.
registration_advice: Apply for 10 courses, even though you only need 4 courses to be a full-time student. This gives you a back-up in case you wont be granted access to a specific course. Also, really make sure you take time and control your timetable. A lot of students didn't spend the time planning their timetable, resulting in them not being able to attend the courses they had planned to attend.
course_level: The courses I attended in HES were not as difficult as I was used to at UCPH. The courses I attended in BIOL were quite challening, but i expected this, attending biology courses without a background in biology. If you work hard, you can still do really well.
teaching_comparison: Very hard to say. The style of teaching varied greatly between the instructors. Some wants you to engage actively will have you do presentations, others read of powerpoint slides the whole lecture.
courses_enrolled: HES383 - Physical Dimensions of Ageing HES 380 - Exercise metabolism BIOL 300 - Advanced Cell Biology BIOL 265 - Principles in Genetics
recommended_courses: HES 380 - Exercise metabolism The course instructor, Jonathan Little, was an increadible teacher. I deffinitely recommend taking this course, if you are interrested in metabolism. BIOL 265 - Principles in Genetics Extremely challening and busy course, however, if you are interested in genetics and are willing to work hard, you will learn a great deal from Dr. D'Souza.
unexpected_costs: None. I would however recommend bringing an appropriate amount of money for all the recreational stuff you want to do. It is not cheap to go to the rockies every other weekend, haha.
cost_comparison: Going out for dinner is cheap. Groceries are a little more expensive than in Denmark.
activities_available: There are clubs for everything at UBCO. Me and my flatmates didn't join them though, since we wanted to do other stuff thn what the clubs offered.
activities_recommended: Go to Vancouver Island, Bannf, Jasper, Kootenay Mountain Range. My greatest memories of BC were made in those places.
weekend_recommendations: We rented a cabin in the Kootenay Mountains for 5 days. Unreal cozyness with a view. Do that.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. To be fair, I didn't spend too much time with canadians as my flatmates were from the UK and Australia and out culture were very similar. I did of course meet canadians, and it wasn't a challenge to adjust, because I didn't have to adjust much to engage in those conversations.
socializing_tips: Go and talk to people. Everyone thinks it's cool your from abroad and even more how well me danes speak english. If your nervous about it, remember how far away from home are and how cool it is that you put yourself on this journey. Now is the time to find that new you ;)
cultural_challenges: I prefer fewer and really close friendships and I dont care much for superficial relations. Throughout all my time at the UBCO, game nights and movie nights were held for people to mingle. I really dont care much for those types of events, and I always find those things hard. Luckily my flatmates became my best friends in Canada, so we stopped going quite early.
culture_appreciated: The general feeling of hospitality and that everyone greets each other. I really like that.
top3_advice: As mentioned earlier, my number one motivation to go was academic, however, remember to prioritise doing all the stuff you cant do at home. Go see nature. Make those new international friendships that will last you forever. Dont worry too much about your grades as they wont count on your danish transcript ( at least the didn't for me)
other_useful_info: Not really, no.
most_rewarding: Seeing incredible nature and meeting people that I now consider my friend. It is a special feeling looking at a world map, knowing a have friends in Spain, Norway, England, Scotland, Netherland, Australia, Canada, US, etc. I did not have that before my exchange.
greatest_challenge: Getting to the rockies as often as we wanted to. If you have the money, consider buying a car. It will make everything so much easier.
other_comments: You won't regret going!

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne være på et godt universitet der tilbød spændende kurser. Derudover var min store drøm at bo tæt på bjerge, så jeg kunne køre mountainbike, hike og stå på ski.
info_ease: Nemt.
arrival_assistance: Jeg blev tjekket ind i min lejlighed, fik en nøgle og blev vist hen til den. På første skoledag blev vi (udvekslingsstuderende) vist rundt på campus og der var et par forelæsninger med information om vores semester.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Man skal ikke lave nogen sprogtest (man skal bare have et skrift fra en underviser på KU der fortæller at du godt kan engelsk), og selve ansøgelsesprocessen er super nem da man ikke skal skrive en egentlig ansøgning.
registration_help: Det ved jeg ikke, men følgende side er rigtig god vejledning til udvekslingsstuderende der skal til UBC: https://global.ubc.ca/go-global/coming-ubc/coming-ubc-exchange.
registration_success: Jeg fik alle de kurser jeg gerne vil have. Men man skal generelt vide at kurserne på Computer Science er meget eftertragtede, så derfor bliver kurserne typisk fyldt op og du kommer nok på ventelisten. Derfor er det ikke sikkert at du kommer ind på de kurser du har søgt, men typisk lykkes det at komme ind efter at have været på ventelisten en uges tid efter semesterstart.
registration_advice: Man kan søge op til 10 kurser når man søger kurser. Mit råd er at søge alle ti. Så vil du nok komme på ventelisten på et par stykker af dem og så kan du efterfølgende afmelde dig nogle kurser hvis du kommer ind på flere end nødvendigt. Man kan nemlig godt afmelde sig kurser efter semesterstart på UBC. Jeg fuglte fx med i fem kurser til at starte med mens jeg var på ventelisten, og da jeg kom ind på de fire af dem som jeg gerne ville have afmeldte jeg mig det femte.
course_level: Der er seks niveauer af kurser på UBC som er indikeret af deres kursus-koder som varierer fra 100-600. 100-400 er undergraduate kurser og 500-600 er graduate kurser. Dvs. hvis du er på dit sidste år af din bachelor, vil det nok være 300-400 kurser som er relevante for dig.
teaching_comparison: Selve undervisningen lignede meget den herhjemme. Der var dog lidt færre øvelsestimer end hvad jeg er vant til. Måden de giver feedback på i afleveringer, synes jeg dog er dårligere end herhjemme. Typisk fik man bare nogle point og fik ikke så meget feedback på hvad man havde gjort forkert. Du kunne dog se hvilke opgaver der var forkerte og anmode om yderligere feedback. En ting der var lidt overvældende var at der var meget indhold i kurserne, mange aflevering og mange eksamener. Det er derfor en rimelig tungt bebyrdet studiehverdag hvis du gerne vil bruge weekenderne på andre sjove ting. Man skal tænke på at semesteret kun varer fra september til start december, så det er 30 ECTS point, presset ind på ca. tre måneder.
courses_enrolled: Computer Vision CPSC425 Machine Learning and Data Mining CPSC340 Applied Machine Learning CPSC330 Introduction to Artificial Intelligence CPSC322
recommended_courses: Applied Machine Learning og Machine Learning and Data Mining var to rigtig gode kurser. De to kurser går rigtig godt hånd i hånd hvis man har dem på samme tid da det ene kursus fokuserer på teorien og implementationen af machine learning algoritmer, mens det andet fokuserer mere på det praktiske aspekt - altså hvordan du bruger eksisterende biblioteker og implementationer af machine learning modeller til at lave rigtige projekter.
unexpected_costs: Køkkenudstyr mm. til lejligheden. Derudover så er Vancouver en meget dyr by, så det er meget dyrt at handle ind i supermarkederne. Det blev jeg overrasket over.
cost_comparison: Dagligvarer var dyrere end forventet. Dog var det ikke meget dyrere end i København at spise ude. Jeg brugte ikke nogle penge på bøger da jeg fint kunne følge med i kurserne uden, og da der i nogle kurser ikke engang var obligatoriske lærebøger. Derfor var det også billigere end forventet.
activities_available: Alt hvad du kan forestille dig er der nærmest en klub for på UBC: skiklub, forskellige sportsklubber inden for alle mulige sportsgrene (selv Quiddicth), akademiske klubber (fx klubber der fremstiller og programmerer robotter), festklubber og meget mere. Der er også en klub for udvekslingsstuderende.
activities_recommended: Skiklubben er god at være en del af hvis du skal ud og stå på ski. De tilbyder billige ture til kendte skiområder, og som noget nyt kan du leje ski af dem ret billigt. Jeg mener at man kunne leje ski gratis for 4 dage og 125,- for en uge.
weekend_recommendations: Tag ud og se og vandre i bjergene, stå på ski og oplev byen. Det er nemt at leje biler i Canada. Vi lejede tit biler og tog på længere weekendsture med overnatninger på fx hostels. Kan anbefale at leje EVO biler som står rundt omkring i byen og på Campus, eller at leje fra Turo. Jeg kan særligt anbefale at tage en weekend til Vancouver Island (særligt Tofino hvor der er godt at surfe er et besøg eller to værd) og skiløb i Whistler. Hvis man er til mountainbiking, så er der rigtig gode muligheder i Whistler eller i de lokale bjerge omkring Vancouver. Jeg lejede selv cykel i Endless Biking i North Vancouver og tog op til Mt. Fromme og Seymour hvor der er lokale gratis spor. Kan varmt anbefales, men det er ikke billigt.
culture_adjustment: Jeg synes det var meget nemt da det jo er et engelsksproget land og det derfor er nemt at snakke med alle. Derudover er Canadierne ekstremt flinke og kulturen er ikke langt fra vores egen. Man skal dog vende sig til storbyen hvor der godt kan være mange hjemløse osv.
socializing_tips: Snak med folk til forelæsningerne. Canadierne er generelt flinke og nysgerrige på sådan en udvekslingsstuderende som dig.
cultural_challenges: Der var ikke noget der var særligt svært.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to experience the amazing nature that British Columbia has to offer. The beautiful mountain views, the giant trees, and mirror lakes among others. I was also intrigued by the relatively new conversation about reconciliation regarding the colonial powers and their history with the original peoples of the land. UBC is placed on the traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Mosqueam People, which is both important and interesting to acknowledge and learn about. This played a central role in my choosing since I wanted to do my electives in Anthropology. UBC is known for having a great Anthropology programme.
info_ease: It was relatively easy. Imagine Day gave a great introduction and Go Global was helpful and accessible.
arrival_assistance: When I arrived I was still waiting for a positive response from a professor regarding enrolment into his course, since it was already full. I was lucky to enrol during my first day, since someone dropped the course, however it turned out to be an online course, which they rarely allow exchange student into. Go Global were, however, very helpful and let me take the course.
arrival_comments: The reason since I rate it 4 instead of 5 is that there was quite the line and I had to wait for a while to get help.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I didn't quite follow the official registration process, because I wanted to make sure, that I got the courses I wanted. Also, when at first, I did follow the registration process which included making a priority list of 10 courses, but I only got one of them - only one out of the three I had gotten pre-approved. Also, one of the courses I needed was a graduate course, but I could apply or register for grad courses online, but had to wait until end August to apply. Instead I contacted the professor directly and he helped me register.
registration_help: I didn't really find a lot of help available during the Summer Vacation. But I just decided to contact different people via e-mail, e.g. professors and student administrations.
registration_success: As I have already explained, I ended up registering for all the courses I wanted. So very successful.
registration_advice: 12. Be proactive and reach out to professors, student administrations and Go Global if you don't get the courses you want. Also, even if you don't get the course at first, show up to class and let the professor know that you're interested in registering. Also, in case a spot becomes available you won't have missed classes already.
course_level: I had two 400 point courses - one called PSYC413 in Social and Personality Development, which was online and didn't seem that difficult, but I enjoyed the learning method, that consisted in reading a few research articles and then answer questions on their subjects, research results etc. My other course ANTH400 History of Anthropology was definitely the best course of them all. It was pretty advanced in regards to the theories tought, but it was incredibly giving and I learned so much about the dark history of the Anthropological discipline and especially the history of Canada. I also had a 500 point course in Qualitative Methods in Anthropology. This course was difficult because it was pretty poorly structured and there wasn't a lot of guidance, since most participants were PHD-students doing their own research separately and having their own counsellor outside of the course.
teaching_comparison: At UBC there are no formal rules or restrictions on how to teach or structure a course. Therefore it is difficult comparing it to UCPH. But generally at UBC your final grade is made up of different components such as attendance, participation, smaller assignments, and class presentations, and a final assignment instead of only having a final exam.
courses_enrolled: PSYC413 Social and Personality Development ANTH400 History of Anthropology ANTH516 Qualitative Research Methods of Anthropology
recommended_courses: I would really recommend History of Anthropology to anyone interested in learning about anthropology. I have already learned a little about the main theories introduced but here I really learned it in context. My professor Sara Shneiderman was very inspirational and a great teacher. She initially said that this course was advanced for anthropology majors but she allowed me to stay and I ended up getting an A.
unexpected_costs: It was surprisingly expensive to buy fresh groceries. Compared to Denmark it cost quite a bit more. Also, the housing prices are pretty high in Vancouver, but this is a problem for almost everyone living there. There is a big housing problem resulting in a lot of homelessness.
cost_comparison: As said, groceries were more expensive which surprised me because we're always told that Denmark is so expensive. However, going out eating or getting drinks was less expensive compared to Copenhagen. And also books were free for my courses.
activities_available: There was a lot of options, but of course less when you're only there for one semester. I joined the surf-club and the film society. A lot of my friends were also part of the outdoor club, but I didn't find it necessary. I often went to the Gallery with my friends for karaoke nights, which was a really fun event and a good way to hang out.
activities_recommended: Definitely the surf club! We went to Tofino to surf and it was so fun and a great way to meet new friends - also Canadians!
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend driving to Banff! It's so beautiful and even though it's a 10 hour drive it was so worth it! Also, of course, go for hikes in Garibaldi and ski in Whistler. I also went to North Cascades in Washington state for a weekend and hiked around Mt. Baker. I spend my midterm break in Maui, Hawaii, which was so amazing.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The city's culture is pretty similar to Copenhagen. But the city wasn't that interesting in terms of culture and social events. I loved having the nature so close by.
socializing_tips: At first I thought that they were very unsociable, but then I realised that because of their school system, they don't necessarily know a lot of other students and are actually pretty happy to engage with other students. So talk to then, go to social events and be open to them. I met some local students and they were friendly and fun, but also pretty young and immature compared to the other exchange students that became my close friends.
cultural_challenges: Not a lot really. Mostly that other students were younger than me.
culture_appreciated: Their relationship and appreciation of nature. They are so aware of the nature around them and the fact, that nature is 'bear territory' etc. I just really appreciate how they spend a lot of time in and with nature and have a lot of respect for the animals.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared for the different ways of teaching and learning as it requires more active participation and attendance. But also reflect on your goals for the exchange - do you want to learn a lot and get good grades or do you just want to do the minimal to pass? 2. Try to create a schedule where you only go to class twice a week. This is very possible as many courses are either on Mondays and Wednesday or on Tuesday and Thursdays. This way you have a lot of time to go on adventure. 3. This is the most important one for me, but go on adventure! Really prioritise going on trips, hiking, surfing, skiing. British Columbia has some of the most beautiful nature you'll ever find, so really try to go and experience the most. Especially while the weather is still nice. In my experience going on hikes together is really a great way to make friends and get to know one another.
other_useful_info: If you find housing on campus really prioritise to go out and experience the city. There's a lot of cute and cool areas around the city. Especially in Mount Pleasant.
most_rewarding: If I should chose only one part, I would probably say that I realised how much I love being active in nature. But also realising that I don't have to go all the way around the world to experience this kind of nature. I have really come to appreciate living in Europe, having so much culture and history and amazing nature around me.
greatest_challenge: Definitely the social aspect. The other people from University of Copenhagen were pretty aggressive at first wanting to make friends and that resulted in a lot of social drama and people feeling excluded. Because of this I was pretty shocked and didn't really want to be part of a friend group that acted badly towards others. Instead I met other exchange students from other parts of Europa, whom I became super close with.
