culture_adjustment: Vancouver er en kæmpe by og der findes så mange forskellige kulturer, derfor er det også nemt at falde til. Folk er venlige og siger tak når de går ud af bussen.
socializing_tips: Snak med dem på dine kurser!!
cultural_challenges: Ikke rigtig nogen. Skulle vænne mig til at give drikkepenge, men det var sådan set også det. Derudover er det selvfølgelig også en del hjemløshed og alt hvad der hører med, men så længe man holder sig fra East Hastings, er det ikke noget der påvirker ens hverdag. Jeg er også vokset op på Istedgade, hvilket nok har gjort mig lidt hårdfør overfor den virkelighed.
culture_appreciated: Hvor søde de fleste mennesker er. Hvor billigt det er at spise ude.
top3_advice: Vær spontan og kom afsted på alle de ture du kan overskue! Midterm- og eksamensperiode kan være rimelig overvældende, så kom afsted før det tager over. Brug tid på at finde nogle steder du godt kan lide at være. Find en cafe du gider at sidde og studere på og gå nogle lange ture. Jeg studerede meget på 49th Parallel i Kitsilano og på Novella på Main st. Husk at find en balance i studie og fritid. Man er ikke kun afsted for at dygtiggøre sig fagligt, men også for at få nogle kæmpe oplevelser.
other_useful_info: Hvis du er glad for genbrugstøj, behøver du nærmest ikke at pakke noget!! Der er så mange fede genbrugsbutikker (Value Village, Salvation Army osv.)
most_rewarding: At få nye venner gennem mine kurser, at opleve naturen omkring Vancouver, at opleve Rocky Mountains.
greatest_challenge: At finde nye rutiner og danne en ny hverdag. Jeg gik næsten 25 km hver dag den første måned og fandt mig til rette og fandt steder jeg nød at være.

crucial_aspects: One aspect that was crucial for my decision of destination was that the country had a lot of beautiful nature to explore. Also, I wanted to be an exchange student in an English-speaking country
info_ease: Some information was more difficult to find than other. However, most of the time the information was easy to find!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process was okay but also a little confusing. There were a lot of different courses to choose between but not all courses were available for exchange students. This was a little confusing. However, it was very easy to register for a course but also to change courses during the semester.
registration_help: If I had any problems or questions with the registration process I could write an e-mail to the administration. They helped me a lot and answered very fast.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted
registration_advice: Research the courses thoroughly and write to the lecturers if you need any information about the course.
course_level: The workload was greater but the level of the courses was a little lower than UCPH
teaching_comparison: At UBC there are a lot of tests, quizzes and midterms, which are very different from the style of teaching to UCPH
courses_enrolled: Sociology of Family Crime and Society Shopping, Society, and Sustainability The anthropology of the Supernatural
recommended_courses: It was very difficult to find courses that suited my field of education and therefore I ended up with Sociology and Anthropology courses. This was not what I expected. However, 'Shopping, Society, and Sustainability' was a very interesting course!
unexpected_costs: Weekend trips with overnight stays
cost_comparison: Food in grocery stores is expensive but eating out at restaurants is very cheap.
activities_available: They had a lot of different opportunities such as surf clubs, ski clubs, gym, different sports clubs, pilates, dance class and much more. It was very easy to join these clubs.
activities_recommended: The surf club had a very fun surf trip to Tofino on Vancouver island. It was a weekend trip with a lot of different students from UBC. I great way to meet new people and learn how to surf. The pilates club was also a good way to both work out and meet new people. I would highly recommend these clubs.
weekend_recommendations: I can really recommend to go out and hike. Vancouver has so much beautiful nature, which is a big recommendation to explore! Also, we took some weekends trips to Whistler, Banff, Jasper and North Cascades in USA which was so nice. We went out hiking a lot but also experienced new cities and met a lot of other exchange students. I can also highly recommend that!
culture_adjustment: That was very easy. People from the local culture was so sweet and polite and I quickly felt at home in the city.
top3_advice: - Register courses that suit your field of education - Search for off campus housing as soon as possible - Go out and explore all the beautiful nature that Vancouver has to offer
other_useful_info: Join some of the clubs that UBC provides - it's a very good way to meet other exchange students from other countries!
most_rewarding: To create so many new friendships from all over the world and experience many aspects of Canada together with them!

crucial_aspects: Academic level, opportunities not available in Denmark
info_ease: It was fine
arrival_assistance: I cannot remember but remember the overall experience as smooth
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You send a list of 10 courses before going but you cant really find any course descriptions. Upon arrival you will gradually be registered on some courses and maybe on waitlist. You dont know if you will get in of the wait list and in the beginning you might have to follow along many classes due to this uncertainty.
registration_help: Not really any help.
registration_success: I got accepted to all the classes I was waitlisted on so overall very succesfull.
registration_advice: Look at the schedules and try and see if anything have been written about the course online on sites like reddit or similar. Some courses have a bad rep.
course_level: I took 4 300 level courses. I would say cpsc340 was really time consuming but als really rewarding. cpsc330 was a lot easier but still time consuming at times. cpsc322 was interesting. cpsc314 was overall easy. Overall spent more time on homework than anticipated but most of it was worth it due to the level of education.
teaching_comparison: Very similar. I had lectures and mandatory assignments. The assignments counts toward your final grade which is nice. Did not really use the lab sessions as it was just dedicated time to do assignments. My exams/midterms were all either with a cheatsheet or with no help (cpsc314)
courses_enrolled: cpsc340 cpsc330 cpsc322 cpsc312
recommended_courses: If you want to learn ML from the ground then definitely 340. By far the most time consuming course but the proff Jeff is fantastic and you have so many aha-moments. If you combine it with cpsc330 which is applied ML then 330 becomes a lot easier. In 330 you learn specifically how to go from dataset to ML-model whereas 340 is more theory based. If you want to have more freetime then skip 340.
unexpected_costs: Hmm nothing really unexpected.
cost_comparison: Shopping for everyday food is quite expensive. Phone plans are also expensive I was able to just keep my danish number due to an old sweet deal with my carrier.
activities_available: Really anything you like. They had a quidditch club for example.
activities_recommended: If you live on or close to campus then start a morning swimming "club" at wreck beach. Really nice way to start the day. Look out on the various clubs instagram pages for events - they sometimes plan parties and trips and you might want to join a club for one particular trip only which is totally fine.
weekend_recommendations: Go explore the mountains. Hike in the summer and ski in the winter. Buy the student ski pass. Get to Vancouver Island. Get to Seattle and watch an nfl game. Watch a hockey game. But mostly the mountain stuff
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: No it is pretty easy just be open minded and if you want to make friends then show up for social activities and take initiative to plan get togethers.
cultural_challenges: It can be a bit difficult to adjust to the amount of small talking but nothing major.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness
top3_advice: - You have a the time and money. You think you cant join the weekend trip because it is a bit too expensive or you have an assignment due. You will find the time somehow. Just go and figure it out afterwards. - Get out and explore the city/nature - Pray you get in to on campus housing
other_useful_info: If you are looking for great study spots: I found that the upper floor of the pharma building had some really nice spots to sit a few together. Otherwise if you are alone and just want to grind go to the basement of koerners library. The busses/trains are great and you can pay directly with apple pay until you get your upass. Sign up for evo and turo for car renting.
most_rewarding: Getting out into some crazy nature.
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to living off campus alone while a lot of my friends lived on campus with others

crucial_aspects: The selection of courses at the University and the nature in Canada
overall_comments: It is hard to be completely objective on the overall experience, because I had to end my exchange earlier than planned because of illness.
info_ease: fairly easy, although there is a lot of information, and it was sometimes hard to know who to ask for help.
arrival_assistance: We had some information meetings, and got some assistance regarding our living situation - but a kind of contact person would have been helpful
arrival_comments: I missed a little bit of understanding regarding how overwhelming it can be to travel to a new country and start at a new university.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It is hard to be completely objective on the overall experience, because I had to end my exchange earlier than planned because of illness.
registration_process: I think the hard part was the mix of having to register at the host university and also having to be in contact with KU about the registration, and 'forhåndsgodkendelse' and stuff like that. And also having to find out which classes were available to you - some classes you could only take on term 1 and I was there on term 2.
registration_help: I don't know - I don't think I got any help, but there was probably an email somewhere you could write to for help
registration_success: I think I had to change it once, because I had applied for some classes I couldn't get.
registration_advice: Don't stress too much about it, it was still a possibility to change classes after arrival - although you might have to be in contact with KU about that.
academics_comments: It is hard to be completely objective on the overall experience, because I had to end my exchange earlier than planned because of illness.
course_level: I took three 200 level courses and one 100 level course - which is 2nd and 1st year level - It was actually a bit hard to go 'down' in levels, as I was a third year student - I felt like they demanded more than they actually did. I could only take 100 and 200 level courses because I took classes from different academic fields.
teaching_comparison: A lot more interaction with the prof. - they demanded more of you, but a lot more help and private interaction was also available.
courses_enrolled: ANTH 206 - Witches, Vampires and Zombies: Anthropology of the Supernatural ANTH 213 - Sex, Gender, and Culture CRWR 206 - Introduction to Writing for the Screen GRSJ 101 - Introduction to Social Justice
recommended_courses: I would recommend Witches, Vampires and Zombies, to anyone who thinks anthropology sounds interesting, and who would find it fun or interesting to learn about the supernatural - I learned a lot about anthropology from this course, and the prof. was amazing. I also enjoyed writing for the screen - so if you have any desire to explore writing scripts, I recommend this class
unexpected_costs: There was a fee I had to pay on maybe 2000 Dkk - I'm not completely sure what it was for - but some of it was for a public transfer card, that was mandatory for some reason. maybe also some health insurance was covered in the fee?
cost_comparison: Groceries was expensive - but slowly you find out where to buy different things. Denmark is also expensive, so I don't think it was that big of a chok, that it might have been for people from other places in the world.
activities_available: I didn't look into it that much - but I heard from other exchange students that there were many outdoors trips and clubs to join. I'm more interested in art, films and music, and that was definitely not something that was easy to get access to.
activities_recommended: I heard good things about the outdoorsclubs. And also just in general to explore the nature in Canada.
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes, go skiing or maybe visit Seattle in USA.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy, the area is a University district, and Canadians are friendly. Although downtown can be a bit overwhelming, because of some pretty rough areas.
socializing_tips: Join clubs.
cultural_challenges: As a bit of an introvert, it could be challenging that people are very chatty.
culture_appreciated: Most people will help you if you ask.
top3_advice: Get to know the grading system - I got pretty stressed out because I thought I had to do more than was actually needed. Ask for help - your prof. are really interested in helping you out. Don't stress too much in the beginning, there's a lot to take in, and if you don't feel like going skiing or hiking in the first couple of weekends, there is plenty of time.
other_useful_info: More activity is required than at KU, so try not to be too perfectionistic about assignments and midterms etc.
most_rewarding: Living in a different country and trying a different university
greatest_challenge: Adapting to a different learning style and different expectations.

crucial_aspects: - Possibilities outside of uni; hiking, mountains, skiing, etc. - A university with a great international environment.
info_ease: Easy. UBC's website is well managed and pretty straight forward for exchange and international students.
arrival_assistance: GoGlobal had an introduction event for exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: After receiving my exchange spot at UBC and my UBC student number I was sent all the relevant information via my KU e-mail. I had to browse through the courses offered on UBC's database. They had short descriptions.
registration_help: I could always e-mail the university but it was not necessary for me.
registration_success: I got the four classes that I wanted. I ended up registering for five and then I just dropped one of them.
registration_advice: Don't worry. You have some time to change your mind when you arrive at the host institution.
course_level: My experience was that the level was a little bit lower than UCPH, more experience based than theoretical - but I did choose introduction courses and more creative courses.
teaching_comparison: I had a mix of big lectures with no student participation and smaller classes with a lot of class discussions.
courses_enrolled: ANTH 206: Witches, Vampires, and Zombies: Anthropology of the Supernatural GRSJ 307 - Gender, Race, Sexuality, and Popular Culture CRWR 205 - Introduction to writing creative nonfiction CRWR 206 - Introduction to writing for the screen
recommended_courses: I was really happy with all of my courses but if you're interested in films I would recommend Introduction to writing for the screen. It was interesting to try to write my own stuff and get a more practical insight in to how a film/series comes about.
unexpected_costs: Kitchen gear.
cost_comparison: Groceries and food in generel is quite expensive. That was definitely my biggest expense.
activities_available: All kinds! So many different clubs and associations you could join.
activities_recommended: A lot of my friends joined the VOC (Varsity Outdoors Club). They arranged a lot of outdoor activities and overnight trips.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the mountains! Hike, ski, whatever. It's beautiful.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Canadian people are super nice and open.
cultural_challenges: Probably that most uni students are quite young.
culture_appreciated: I loved that when you get on the bus, you actually greet the bus driver and when you get off again, everyone thanks them!
top3_advice: The work load can be quite extensive. Use the activities and associations available. Enjoy your weekends and go on a lot of trips!
other_useful_info: A lot of courses take attendance.
most_rewarding: Being surround by a completely different nature and environment.
greatest_challenge: The pressure of having to enjoy it all. Just relax, you can't do stuff all the time and you don't have to enjoy every single minute of it.

crucial_aspects: That the university surrounded by nature, and that there are many options to do outdoor activities like hiking, skiing and surfing. I also liked that the main language was english.
info_ease: I would say it was relatively easy to find information, and people were very helpful.
arrival_assistance: I would have preferred they there were more introduction days in the beginning of the exchange to be able to meet people. There was only one day (imagine day), which was a bit stressful, and its a bit harder to get to know people in classes.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was a bit confusing to register for classes, and understand the different faculties at the university. Furthermore, as an exchange student you have to rank 10 classes that you would like, and understanding the timetable and choosing the classes is a bit difficult.
registration_help: I don't know, because I didn't need help during the application process.
registration_success: I wanted some more creative classes, and those where a bit difficult to get, since students in those faculties have priority in those classes. The creative writing faculty is easier to get classes in.
registration_advice: If you dont get the classes you wanted in the first place, there is an option to change classes during the first two weeks of school. You can also talk to professors if there isn't space in their classes, since there might still be options to join the class.
course_level: I had 200 and 300 courses. I am on my third year of studying, so these courses fit relatively well. I would say 200 courses are easier than the courses I would have had in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at UBC is very different to UCPH. At UCPH you are more independant and you are only graded for the final exam. At UBC the assignments, quizzes and your attendance during the term are a part of your grade, and you have to do these to pass the courses. This was a bit stressful for me to get used to.
courses_enrolled: CRWR 203 Introduction to Writing for Children and Young Adults GEOG 210 Vancouver and Its Region GEOG 312 Climate Change: Science and Society GEOS 207 Introduction to Biogeography
recommended_courses: I liked the creative writing course I had, because it was different to any course I had before, and the teacher was very nice.
unexpected_costs: There is an obligatory health insurance from UBC which is around 1800 DKK in total. There is also an obligatory travel pass which is around 850 DKK for four months.
cost_comparison: Going out to eat is less expensive then in Denmark, but grocery shopping is very expensive in Canada (more than in Denmark). In general Canada is pretty expensive to stay in, especially if you take part in many outdoor activities. If you like skiing it is possible to buy a student season pass for Whistler for around 3500 DKK, but they get sold out.
activities_available: There are many available. There is a buddy program for exchange students where you can meet people. There is also an outdoor club, surf club, ski club, running club and so on. There are club days where it is possible to learn about the clubs. The clubs also arrange trips.
activities_recommended: Hiking, surfing (in tofino), skiing, rock climbing. The mountains are very close and it is possible to rent cars from turo or evo to go to the different places.
weekend_recommendations: If you like hiking there are many cute huts on top of mountains you can overnight in. For example by elfin lakes. If you go in september/october there might be bears (i saw seven on this hike), so remember to bring bear spray. There is also brew hut, which is a hut owned by the outdoor club. There is a rock climbing trip with the outdoor club in one of the weekends in september. Another weekend there is a surftrip with the surfclub. For the opening weekend of whistler there is a ski trip.
culture_adjustment: It is not that different to Denmark, and everyone was very friendly and spoke english, so relatively easy.
socializing_tips: Go on some of the trips with the clubs, and get put in a random car. You will most likely be placed with locals since they have cars. I met some nice local people on the surf trip by doing this. Otherwise having classes with group activities or field trips.
cultural_challenges: Not really any, they are just a lot more friendly in public than danish people. They drink less alcohol, and all bars close at 2pm.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and openness to doing outdoor activities.
top3_advice: - Save up a lot of money, because it is expensive. - Think about bringing a sleeping bag and sleeping mat if you like outdoor activities (you can also buy it there, but if you already have everything). - It is a beautiful place, with so many options to do things, so go to the mountains and hike and swim in a glacial lake <33
other_useful_info: It is a very big school, with a lot of exchange students. We were about 25 people from UCPH, and in total around 45 danish people (from other universities like CBS and DTU).
most_rewarding: The people and the insane nature being so close. Being able to go somewhere completly on my own, and having a great time.
greatest_challenge: It feels lonely sometimes, especially in the beginning, because none of your saftey people are there, but everyone feels this way.

crucial_aspects: An english speaking university with more English courses available. The right courses (for me it was psychology courses relevant for a sociology student). And a beautiful area, with much to explore beyond university.
info_ease: Mostly very easy. The few times I was in doubt, it was easy to get in touch with someone who could and would help.
arrival_assistance: Before arrival there was an online presentation for exchange students, which provided most of the help. I personally did not receive assistance, but only because I declined - there were many opportunities for assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I don't remember too much of it - maybe because they made it very easy. There was a lot of information long before arrival, so the only thing to do when I landed was to pick up my student ID
registration_help: Again, I sadly don't remember too much of it. But of what I do remember, any help that wasn't immediately available, was easy to find elsewhere.
registration_success: Almost completely. One course was full, but they quickly helped me register for another, and made sure to fit me in.
registration_advice: Simply follow the guidelines you are sent. Everything is far less complicated that it might appear. Also, it's easy enough to change classes if you are unhappy with the original ones after the first few weeks
course_level: All 3rd year courses
teaching_comparison: In many ways the same: lectures and reading with focus on critical discussions and in-depth understanding of the material. However, there is less group work seeing as exams at UBC are mostly individual multiple choice exams, and for the same reason, classes tend to lead up to the next midterm, so it feels like you are doing several sub-semesters.
courses_enrolled: Social psychology Evolutionary psychology Personality Psychology Cultural psychology Behavioral cognition
recommended_courses: All of them, no doubt. Each one had an incredible professor with so much knowledge and passion and a will to teach. But I think that the two courses that gave me most "fresh perspective" from my courses in UCPH, was evolutionary and cultural psychology. In each their way they tought "hard" topics with very "soft" measures and open perspectives.
unexpected_costs: My husband forgot to get insured, so a simple trip to the doctor cost us 8000kr. And housing was (as described earlier).
cost_comparison: As described before, housing is very expensive. The same goes for short term housing like hotels, hostels and the like. Books cost me nothing because the we're either offered as free PDF's, or easy to find for free.
activities_available: I did not apply to any myself, so I am not sure. But they have a big event on the first day with open stands hosted by students where you can sign up or simply inquire.
activities_recommended: As I didn't do any, I can't say. But if hiking and visiting greater British Columbia counts, I absolutely recommend that!
weekend_recommendations: See British Columbia! Be it big adventures a weekend in Squamish, or simply a day to Horseshoe Bay, the nature is simply stunning and more than worth your attention and time. Vancouver city also has heaps to offer, from markets to cafees, museums, parks, and of course the great (and plentiful) Asian cuisine.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Vancouver is very multicultural already.
socializing_tips: Be kind and respectful as always, and understand that students come from all over the world, and therefore have different social behaviors.
cultural_challenges: None that were significant or challenging. Be aware of tipping culture?
culture_appreciated: The diversity. Vancouver is not like the rest of Canada - it is a pot of Canadians, Americans, Chinese, Korean, Japanese and so much more.
top3_advice: You are not visiting a Canadian university - you are visiting a multicultural university! The exams are multiple choice midterms, so manage your time well to not drown in exams! It's not like doing 1 every end-of-term like we are used to. Don't worry about the beucracy. There is plenty of help to find both online and in person!
other_useful_info: Be ready for a different kind of exams and different grading policy. Multiple choice midterms are easy enough, but count towards your final grades, and it can be very challenging if you are not prepared for it.
most_rewarding: Either my courses (I have been so inspired by my professors!) or visiting the nature.
greatest_challenge: The exams. If you're not keeping up, it is easy to have a lot of pressure around the midterms - and there ARE a lot of them.

crucial_aspects: Recreational activites in the area such as skiing, surfing, climbing, hiking etc. + academic opportunities in the form of subjects not available at UPCH
info_ease: Very easy, UBC had held an information session before arrival and had sent all necessary information via email. The GoGlobal Office was very informative and helpful
arrival_assistance: Information meeting and tour around campus
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: To be enrolled in graduate courses, you have to ask each professor individually for permission to take their course and sign a document provided by GoGlobal. You do this either by email before you arrive (HIGHLY recommended) or in-person once you arrive. If permitted, you need to get the administration of the faculty to enroll you (fairly easy, just sent them an email). Although UBC does not officially allow exchange students in their graduate programme, I found that it was possible to get graduate courses anyway. However, I greatly recommend taking courses at the School of Public Policy and Global Affairs (PPGA) as well.
registration_help: The GoGlobal office was available, both via email and in-person, but they could not really help since you kind of had to do the process yourself and through a different way than the official process. I found that the best help was to ask former KU students for help.
registration_success: I got 2 courses that were my first priority and 1 that was my second priority
registration_advice: Graduate courses are difficult to register for but worth it in my opinion. However, you have to register in a very unstructured, non-official way (see above). Ask former KU students for help and begin in good time by emailing the professors whose courses you want to take. Also: it will all work out in the end, even though it is a chaotic process.
course_level: I found the level to be a bit lower at UBC than UPCH, meaning that getting good grades requires a lower - or at least different kind of - effort than at home. For graduate courses, you have to put in more effort on a week-to-week basis than back home because you are expected (required in some courses) to participate orally every week. You also have to hand in several assignments during the term and/or do presentations that account for part of your grade. On the one hand, this means that you have to put in (more) effort each week. However, this also means that your final exam or assignment does not decide everything. The amount of reading is generally lower than at UPCH but the amount of required assignments and written hands-in are definetely higher. If you are the type of student that does your readings and work every week, then the required effort is probably lower than at UPCH, but if you are the type that does all the readings in the final week of the semester, then the required effort might feel higher at UBC as you are forced to do at least a bit every week.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching varies greatly from professor to professor. At the School of Public Policy and Global Affairs (PPGA), seminars were 3 hours once a week and resembled a mixture of lectures, discussion and exercises, fairly similar to UPCH but with much smaller classes (5-15) and higher expectations for student participation. At my Political Science course, the seminar was also 3 hours once a week but teaching was entirely student-based discussion with no lecture or introduction from the professor. However, I think that was quite unique for the course and not representative of all political science courses.
courses_enrolled: Policy Dimensions of Energy Systems Global environmental politics Global governance
recommended_courses: Courses at the School of Public Policy and Global Affairs (PPGA) are really great if you want more policy and practically oriented courses. They are less "academic" and more "practical" in the sense that you learn less theory and frameworks and read less academic articles. Instead, you read texts from policy institutes, think tanks, and governments, engage more in actual empirical cases and practice skills such as international negotation, writing policy briefs, and oral debates.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: The cost of living in Vancouver is fairly high, so going grocery shopping for food items such as vegetables and dairy products are more expensive than in DK. Going out for dinner/movies/activites are generally a bit cheaper than Copenhagen but not a lot
activities_available: UBC has a club for EVERYTHING, so no matter what your interests are, you can find like-minded people to hang out with. However, since the campus is so huge, it is rare that the univeristy as such hosts anything in itself. Instead, events are hosted by individual communities, faculties, and clubs. Apart from clubs, UBC has its own farm, forest, beaches and several museums on campus.
activities_recommended: Join the Varsity Outdoor Club (VOC) if you like outdoor activities such as hiking, ski touring, climbing, and kayaking. The club plans tours almost every weekend which are open to join and only costs transportation and evt. gear rental. If you are a member, you can also rent all gear for free + it is a great place to meet really cool people.
weekend_recommendations: Get outside Vancouver and explore the amazing nature that British Columbia has to offer. Within only a couple of hours of driving, you can do almost anything outdoorsy. Go climbing in Squamish, ski in Whistler, hike in Garabaldi, kayak around the Gulf Islands, surf on Vancouver Island, and bike along the Sunshine Coast. You can almost always find a tour to join with the VOC (see above)
culture_adjustment: Super easy! People in Vancouver are extremely friendly, open and easy to talk to
socializing_tips: Join some of the clubs and sports teams and talk to the people in your courses. It is super easy to get caught in the exchange "bubble" where you only talk to other exchange students who are also looking for friends, but getting to know some local students is really great! Canadians are super friendly so just ask someone to have a cup of coffee or watch a hockey game on campus.
cultural_challenges: You have to adjust to the fact that people actually talk to strangers in Canada (as opposed to Copenhagen), but that is a great thing once you learn that you don't have to tell your entire life story every time someone asks "How are you?".
culture_appreciated: Everyone is really open, friendly, polite and hospitable! In addition, the city of Vancouver is very ethnically diverse meaning that you can meet people from literally all over the world.
top3_advice: Join as many clubs as possible, especially the VOC Go enjoy the nature outside the city every time you can Get housing on campus or at least nearby, unless you are willing to commute for a long time every day
other_useful_info: The semester is pretty short at UBC so if you can, plan to stay for some time after you are done. That will allow you to explore more of B.C. and hang out with some of the cool people you have met

crucial_aspects: There were several aspects: 1. I wanted to go to a place with beautiful nature nearby so that I could hike, ski and explore the city in the free time. 2. I wanted to try the real american campus experience, where you get to live on campus and experience the small city that the campus is. 3. I wanted to go to a place with many exchange students, danish as well as others.
overall_comments: Exchange was the best thing, if you are ever considering it, do it! The only reason why I gave it 9/10 instead of 10/10 was the academic level - The subjects was quite easy, but then again, you are on exchange, so what does it matter.
info_ease: Quite difficult. It was hard to find out which requirements KU had as well as the host university. Often we found out we had to do things upon arrival by talking to former exchange students in Denmark and by hearing from others and so on.
arrival_assistance: Not much. We received the key for our housing and were told there was an introduction day for exchange students, but other than that we pretty much had to figure out most of it ourselves. But I'll say, the introduction day ("Imagine Day") was quite good, and we were told all the necessary things.
arrival_comments: The assistance before arrival was not good. I reckon it would be quite easy to make a "to-do" list or a document where you wrote all the things exchange students would have to do before arriving. But upon arrival the assistance was decent.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Exchange was the best thing, if you are ever considering it, do it! The only reason why I gave it 9/10 instead of 10/10 was the academic level - The subjects was quite easy, but then again, you are on exchange, so what does it matter.
registration_process: The registration proces was quite easy. The most difficult thing was to have them approved at KU. As soon as KU approved the courses you add register yourself on the courses on UBC's site and hope there is spots available for them.
registration_help: Again, there wasn't any help from UBC but it wasn't necessary either.
registration_success: Of all the courses KU approved there was only 1 course that I wasn't able to get - But I just choose another one.
registration_advice: Just don't be late for two reasons: First of all, the pre-approval process from KU is pretty long, so it's stressful if you don't have time. Second of all, if you are not in good time most of the courses might be full and you will end up with some random ones.
academics_comments: Exchange was the best thing, if you are ever considering it, do it! The only reason why I gave it 9/10 instead of 10/10 was the academic level - The subjects was quite easy, but then again, you are on exchange, so what does it matter.
course_level: The level was quite easy, so if you want to get challenged do not hesitate to take som courses a little higher than usual. As a bachelor student on my fifth semester I had 3 300-level courses and 1 400-level course. The 400 level was quite hard, while the other ones was pretty easy. But don't worry, as an exchange student they will probably pass you if you give an effort and just talk to them. Also, I would recommend taking something that interests you. Although it might sounds nice that it's easy, you will loose interest quickly if it's both easy and not in your interest.
teaching_comparison: In all the courses you had midterms (1 or 2) and a final. So in all our courses the final only weighted 30% or 40% which is very different compared to UCPH where you only have a final weighting 100%. Also, on UCPH you often have a mix between lectures and teaching in classes. In all of my courses at UBC there were only lectures. There was also so called "Office-hours" which is a little similar to teaching hours at UCPH but they mostly just focus on your questions instead of doing Problem Sets or discussions. Normally, in many courses, there is also participation, which constitutes a share of your overall grade in the subject.
courses_enrolled: ECON 355: Introcution to International Trade ECON 333: Economic History of Modern Europe from the Paleolithic to the Industrial Revolution ECON 371: Economics of the Environment ECON 421: Introduction to Game Theory and Applications
recommended_courses: ECON 333 was quite nice. The lecturer, Mauricio Delichmann, is such a good man with a lot of passion and interest in the subject. Plus, it can get approved as Economic History back on UCPH if you are studying economics.
unexpected_costs: Almost nothing. Only thing was, I knew it was expensive being on exchange, but I had no idea it would be that expensive.
cost_comparison: Food was way more expensive than I thought. Just basic grocery shopping was pretty expensive.
activities_available: There is so many clubs to join. On the introduction day ("Imagine day") you get to meet all the clubs and join them. There is more than 350 clubs, but I would highly recommend joining the Outdoor Club which gives you access to cheap rental on hiking and ski stuff. Also, join the surf flub and go on their surf trip to Tofino!! Besides the club, there is Frat partys. Although you might seem a little older as a BA or MA student from UCPH you should go, at least a couple of times. Just seeing that the frat-culture actually exists outside of the movies is awesome.
activities_recommended: See my comment above! Also, play sports. It's such an easy way to get to know other people on campus. And just attend to the events in the beginning of the term such as Homecoming football game and exchange-betting parties.
weekend_recommendations: Go hike in the fall/ spring depending on when you visit, and then go ski in the winter. Use the weekends wisely, you will quickly realise how fast the time goes and how few weekends you suddenly have to do all the nice things. Here is a few recommendations: - The most important recommendation is a multiple-day trip to North Cascades National Park in Washington, USA (Do the "Cascade Pass and Sahale Arm Trail", best and most beautiful hiking route we did during the four months) - Panorama Ridge - Joffre Lakes - Vancouver Island - Banff National Park - Grouse Mountain - Cypress Ski Resort (Both for hiking when it's warm and skiing when it's winter) - Whistler Ski Resort (Both for hiking and skiing, although skiing is coolest. Consider buying the student pass if you are going more than 6 or 7 ski days) - Tofino (Surfing) Also, all exchange students have reading break in November. Here, we gathered a group and flew to California while others went to Yukon in northern Canada, but you can get creative!
culture_adjustment: Very ease. The Canadians were very polite. But to be fair, exchange students connect with exchange students, and a lot mostly end up with other exchange students.
socializing_tips: Join clubs! It's all about prioritising, and you have enough time to do it. Also, play sports. It's such an easy way to get to know other people on campus.
cultural_challenges: None.
top3_advice: 1. Do something in the weekends like hiking or seeing stuff! It's what you are going to remember when you get back. 2. To keep just a little motivation throughout the term choose courses that awakes just a little interest in you. 3. Socialize. The term is going to be so much more fun if you have someone to share it with. So seek clubs, sports, other exchange students and make new friends :))
most_rewarding: Getting new friends, experiencing a real american campus and experiencing Canada and Vancouver in the weekends.
greatest_challenge: Definitely all the things you had to do before arriving at the university. It was hard to figure out and hard to seek help.

crucial_aspects: I was drawn to Canada primarily for its beautiful and unique nature, which I had always wanted to explore, and the fact that it is an English-speaking country. UBC also has a strong reputation globally, especially in law. I was interested in experiencing a different legal system and academic environment.
overall_comments: My semester at UBC was incredibly enriching. I made international friends, gained insight into Canadian law, and had the opportunity to explore breathtaking nature - from coastal hikes to snowy mountains.
info_ease: UBC provided comprehensive online resources beforehand and detailed orientation sessions upon arrival. The Go Global office was responsive and helpful.
arrival_assistance: I received an orientation package, attended welcome events, and participated in guided tours. Student volunteers and the Go Global office were available for questions.
arrival_comments: The orientation made it very easy to settle in and meet other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My semester at UBC was incredibly enriching. I made international friends, gained insight into Canadian law, and had the opportunity to explore breathtaking nature - from coastal hikes to snowy mountains.
registration_process: Course registration was done online through the UBC Student Service Centre. Exchange students were given specific registration dates. It required some planning, as law courses were in high demand. It was easy to self-register online, and I even switched courses in the initial 2-week period without any problems.
registration_help: Academic advisors and the Go Global office offered assistance via email and drop-in sessions.
registration_success: I got most of the courses I aimed for, but had to be flexible with one or two options.
registration_advice: Have several backup courses ready and register as early as possible. Sign up for the waitlist if you are really interested in a course that has filled up, as people drop courses within the first 2 weeks.
academics_comments: My semester at UBC was incredibly enriching. I made international friends, gained insight into Canadian law, and had the opportunity to explore breathtaking nature - from coastal hikes to snowy mountains.
course_level: MA courses were more intensive, with higher expectations for independent work. The courses (naturally) focused a lot on Canadian law, but since the Canadian justice system is built different than was we have in Denmark, it was at times difficult to follow the lectures/syllabus.
teaching_comparison: UBC had smaller classes and more frequent assessments like quizzes, midterms, and group work. There was more emphasis on in-class participation and practical examples.
courses_enrolled: LAW_V 322 (3.0) International Law Problems LAW_V 393D (3.0) Green Rights and Warrior Lawyers LAW_V 410 (3.0) International Taxation LAW_V 461 (3.0) Corporate Transactions
recommended_courses: Focus on courses with an international perspective, as chances are this will be most relevant for your future studies. I learned a lot in LAW_V 461 Corporate Transactions and LOVED our professor in LAW_V 410 International Taxation even though the class was very difficult academically.
unexpected_costs: Some course materials weren’t available online and had to be purchased. Outdoor gear (e.g., hiking boots, rain jacket) also added up.
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive than expected, especially in Vancouver. Public transport was cheaper with the U-Pass.
activities_available: There was a wide range of clubs, from hiking groups to debate societies. UBC Recreation offered great gym and class options.
activities_recommended: Join the UBC Outdoor Club
weekend_recommendations: Visit Whistler, explore Vancouver Island, hike Grouse Grind, take weekend trips to the Rockies or Banff. Vancouver is a perfect base for travel and adventure.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. People were friendly and welcoming, and the culture felt both familiar and distinct from Europe.
socializing_tips: Join clubs early, participate in class, and attend campus events. Canadians are open but you need to take initiative.
cultural_challenges: The academic competitiveness and focus on participation was a shift from my experience at UCPH. Also, tipping culture took some getting used to.
culture_appreciated: The multiculturalism, respect for Indigenous communities, and the outdoor lifestyle were inspiring and refreshing
top3_advice: 1. Apply early for courses and housing – spots fill up fast. 2. Join at least one student club to meet people. 3. Take advantage of the stunning natural surroundings – pack for rain and outdoor activities!
other_useful_info: Plan your travel around reading week and holidays. Buy a rain jacket – it rains a lot in Vancouver!
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all over the world and learning about Indigenous legal systems in a hands-on academic setting. Also getting to ski and hike the BEAUTIFUL nature surronding campus.
greatest_challenge: Navigating the registration process and adjusting to the North American academic structure with its frequent assessments.
other_comments: This exchange was one of the most enriching parts of my education. I highly recommend UBC and Vancouver to anyone who enjoys nature and is curious about different legal perspectives.

info_ease: The information was easy to find, as the university made everything very clear for exchange students. A whole team only advising exchange students was fairly easy to get in contact with
arrival_assistance: The GoGlobal office was only dedicated to help with every part of the exchange experience of exchange students, thus they helped with issues regarding housing, health care and acedemic issues.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The university of British Columbia is a high performance university, were your skills are being challenged. However, very motivating and the courses are flexible in the grading system depending on the professor.
registration_process: Due to the changes in the system, the new platform that we had to register for courses and have a overview of the expenses and finances was 'workday'. This was easy to manage, as on the portal we were able to register for course way in advance and were able to see whether we are accepted to the courses or currently in the waiting list. registration_help: Again, the GoGlobal office was there to help about registration issues either thorugh e-mail or in person appointments.

academics_comments: The university of British Columbia is a high performance university, were your skills are being challenged. However, very motivating and the courses are flexible in the grading system depending on the professor.
course_level: I was taking 4x 400-level courses, which is very comparable to MA courses. The level is quite high and can not be compared with introductory courses
teaching_comparison: The biggest differences were the type of learning and examination. Almost all of my exams were hand written and professors did not use any digital devices to teach, and did not allow devices during the lecture and seminar. This is very different to UCPH teaching
courses_enrolled: Philosophy of Mind Philosophy of Perception Conceptions of the Self Sociology of the Environment

unexpected_costs: Washing card and topping up money for the washing

weekend_recommendations: A lot of hiking trips in the mountains either through bus and seabus, or with a rented car. Going to ski in the winter semester and to visit the cinemas and parks in the city

socializing_tips: Go to the events, and make sure to be in a group with other exchange students to experience the term together. Also do not miss on the events posted by the sports clubs and acedemic talks on campus
cultural_challenges: The tipping was a bit confusing as it is normally expected to tip 15% to 20%, however as this is quite a bit for a student it was not always sure if this must be done or not.
culture_appreciated: The politness of the candians. Even if people would exist the bus in the back, everyone would thank the bus driver for driving them. People were looking out for eachother, and were not shy to
top3_advice: Be sure to be ready for a possible tough semester depending on the courses you take! Be sure to sign up early for housing to have a higher chance to be living on campus. Think beforehand how much money you want or can spend, as it might be a bit more expensive. Be sure to make the best out of the nature around the area
other_useful_info: Be sure to have all neccesary travel documents when arriving in Canada and a physical credit card for the washing machines on campus
most_rewarding: The courses as they were challenging but also very intersting and being able to live on your own and with international students so far away from home in a new culture.
greatest_challenge: The management of courses and free time, and handling expenses
other_comments: I highly recommend anyone to go to UBC! What a wonderful experience for the self and the career!

crucial_aspects: UBC has a very good geography programme + Canada has some beautiful nature. Furthermore, I wanted to experience the "campus-life" at a big university in North America, and I wanted to improve my English.
overall_comments: UBC was a good university, and I had many great experiences (academic and in my free time). But it was also challenging to study in a different way than in Denmark. University in Canada includes more mandatory elements than in Denmark.
info_ease: Very easy.
arrival_assistance: Before arrival I got e-mails from UBC regarding moving in and starting at the university. Then we had a "welcome day" and we got a tour around campus + additional information about studying in Canada.
arrival_comments: Good level of information. Once in Canada, I could go to the GoGlobal office if I needed any help, and they were very nice.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: UBC was a good university, and I had many great experiences (academic and in my free time). But it was also challenging to study in a different way than in Denmark. University in Canada includes more mandatory elements than in Denmark.
registration_process: I registered through the University of Copenhagen, and then again through UBC. The application process has several rounds. First you just register, and then you have to choose courses later. You submit a list of 10 courses you want, and then get assigned four. It is possible to drop out/change courses the first two weeks of classes, so you can try a class and see if it is something for you if you are unsure.
registration_help: E-mailing with GoGlobal before arriving. After arrival it was also very easy to just go to their office.
registration_success: I didn't got the classes I wanted the most, but I was able to switch during the two first weeks of class. But I got assigned to courses on my list of 10 possible courses.
registration_advice: Try different classes during the first two weeks, and don't be afraid to change class. It's very nice that you can try a class and just drop it again if you don't like it.
academics_comments: UBC was a good university, and I had many great experiences (academic and in my free time). But it was also challenging to study in a different way than in Denmark. University in Canada includes more mandatory elements than in Denmark.
course_level: I took one first-year course, two second-year courses and a fourth-year course. The fourth-year course wasn't as difficult as I expected, and one of the second-year course was way more difficult than expected. So just read the course description to find out if it is too hard, and don't bother too much about the level.
teaching_comparison: Very different. The final grade is made up of one or more midterms, participation marks, small quizzes and a final. It was more like danish high school style.
courses_enrolled: EOSC 114: The catastrophic earth - Natural disasters. ATSC 201: Meteorology of storms. NRES: 241: Introduction to Geomatics for Natural Resource Management GEOG 497: The Arctic.
recommended_courses: NRES: 241: Introduction to Geomatics for Natural Resource Management. There is no final + it is nice to do computer lab. GEOG 497: The Arctic. Interesting and good course. Very nice professor. EOSC 114: The catastrophic earth - Natural disasters. Quite easy first-year course.
unexpected_costs: Expenses for apartment stuff when we moved in.
cost_comparison: Food is expensive (during groceries in the supermarket). To go coffee and food is cheaper or same level as in Denmark.
activities_available: All kinds of sports, crafting clubs, hiking clubs, book clubs, religious fellowships.
activities_recommended: The Outdoor Club hosts a lot of nice hikes/trips. I would recommend Rock Party with the outdoor club, which is a climbing trip to Squamish were you can learn to climb.
weekend_recommendations: See Vancouver, Stanley Park, Gastown. Take a trip to Whistler and Bowen Island.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy.
socializing_tips: Join a club on campus.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Canadians are very kind and nice.
top3_advice: 1. School can seem very overwhelming, but you will do fine even if you skip some classes. 2. Be prepared for public transportation in Vancouver. It is not as efficient as in Denmark. 3. Don't be afraid to talk to the professors.
other_useful_info: Save up money before you go. Canada is expensive.
most_rewarding: Trying to live in another country and meet local people. I also really enjoyed the beautiful view to the mountains.
greatest_challenge: Not feeling stressed about all the things I would like to experience. I had a bucket list of things I would like to see, but it was also overwhelming just to get my everyday life going.
other_comments: Don't stress about all the things you would like to see and do, it is also okay to do nothing in your weekends.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study at a good university where there were good opportunities for traveling and seeing beautiful nature.
overall_comments: Going on exchange was absolutely amazing. Though be aware that the term seems a bit short. Classes from September until early December and then exams in December and everything is done before Christmas. The academic level seemed pretty easy compared to KU.
info_ease: It was manageable but there were times where I had to reach out and spend a lot of time searching their whole homepage trying to find some info I felt I was missing.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival we basically got a key to the room and a one-pages with a bit of basic info. We had an introduction day to see the school which was okay but it was a mix of students from all majors so I never saw any of them again afterwards.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Going on exchange was absolutely amazing. Though be aware that the term seems a bit short. Classes from September until early December and then exams in December and everything is done before Christmas. The academic level seemed pretty easy compared to KU.
registration_process: We had to fill out something similar to a google form and then the exchange team would try to add you to classes. I was only added to 3 classes as it was full time so had to reach out and be allowed to be added to a 4th class. As exchange students don't fulfill any prerequisites it was not possible to add any classes on my own initially. After taking to them a few times they removed the prerequisites from 3 classes so I would be able to add myself to one of them if a spot became available.
registration_help: The exchange team (GoGlobal) were happy to help but the initial setup where you have to reach out and hope they can add you to a class before it's full was not a very efficient process. The course descriptions is nearly non existing for the classes (just 3 lines) so you have to reach out to each professor and ask for a course syllabus. All professors were very quick at replying.
registration_success: Somewhat succesfull. I got my 2nd, 5th, 8th and 10th priority. I was not possible to get classes from other faculties.
registration_advice: Start with the pre-approval of courses as early as possible. If they remove pre-requisites for some classes so you can add yourself then check frequently and be fast as it's first come, first serve.
academics_comments: Going on exchange was absolutely amazing. Though be aware that the term seems a bit short. Classes from September until early December and then exams in December and everything is done before Christmas. The academic level seemed pretty easy compared to KU.
course_level: The level was easy compared to KU. Basically it's impossible to fail a course even with mediocre effort.
teaching_comparison: Each lecture was 1 hour and 20 minutes with no breaks. Only one class had exercise/lab but it was 1 hour of going through the first 3 questions out of the roughly 12 questions for the assignment for the following week. I had already finished the assignment before the exercise class so I only attended the first one. They have office hours where you can talk to prof or TA every week if you have questions. You will have 1 or 2 midterm exams during the term and then 1 final exam. Many classes have assignments that counts for some of the grade and you will also get a few points for participation.
courses_enrolled: Econ 221 - introduction to strategic thinking with Hao Li (pre-approved as Micro 3). The class was very easy in terms of the math. Econ 333 - Economic History of Europe from the Paleolithic to the Industrial Revolution with Mauricio Drelichman (pre-approves as Økonomish Historie). Absolutely amazing class. Mauricio is a fantastic story-teller and makes the classes super interesting. One of the best professors and best classes I have ever had. Econ 356 - Introduction to International Finance with Emrul Hasan (økonomisk valfag). The class is similar to Economics of Exchange rates from KU. He added a bit of portfolio theory in the end. crucial_aspects: I wanted to take courses that were of personal interest to me, and were not offered at KU. Also, most of my family lives in Canada, and I have gone there a lot, but have never experienced living there before now!
overall_comments: Of course there were ups and downs, but overall, it was a fantastic time.
info_ease: We had an orientation event on the second day of term, which had a lot of helpful information regarding health facilities, clubs, stuff like that.
arrival_assistance: I got an information packet when I arrived at my residence on campus with a map of campus, emergency numbers etc.

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Of course there were ups and downs, but overall, it was a fantastic time.
registration_process: I was to fill in a preliminary course list as part of my application to UBC. When it was time to actually register classes, a lot of the courses I had wanted to take were either not available, or were simply not taking place. I don't think I knew which courses I was registered for until sometime in July. Whether that was because UBC had switched to a new database (Workday) and things were chaotic because of that, I don't know, but it was quite frustrating. When I decided to defer, the course registration was really easy, I just emailed Go Global the new courses I would like to take and they registered them for me right away.
registration_help: Go Global responded very kindly, and quite quickly, though admittedly during the first registration round for September it took a while to get an answer (I gather because everyone is registering and they get a lot of emails)
registration_success: For September, I got two out of four classes I had wanted, but for January, I actually got all the classes I wanted!
registration_advice: Have some backup options in mind in case the course you wanted is full/not taking place after all. Don't hesitate to email profs to see if there is any space left in their class - and remember there is a drop and switch survey a few weeks after term starts, so you are not stuck in the classes you chose in case you change your mind!
academics_comments: Of course there were ups and downs, but overall, it was a fantastic time.
course_level: I took two 400 level classes, as they are counted as graduate level at KU. UBC's grad level classes are 500, and those are a bit more complicated to get into, so I just went with the 400s instead. Otherwise I took two intro classes!
teaching_comparison: It was quite similar, but I think mostly because three out of four classes I took were quite small in size, and therefore largely practical and based on discussions. There was definitely a lot less group work. One of my classes was a lecture, so you don't really interact with the teacher at all besides listening which was new!
courses_enrolled: Audio Storytelling (400 level) - a mix of science communication and podcasting, so you learn also how to edit audio. Sociology of the Environment (400 level) - different sociological perspectives on how environmental change affects different people Intro to Creative Writing (200 level) - intro to different genres, such as fiction, poetry, memoir etc. Intro to Japanese (100 level) - intro to the hiragana, katakana and some kanji, and basic grammar points
recommended_courses: I really loved Audio Storytelling! I have never taken a class like it before, and really enjoyed being able to present scientific topics not as an academic essay, but in a podcast form. The teachers were incredibly kind, overall an awesome class. Also the teacher for the Sociology of the Environment class was incredibly nice and explained things really well, so even for me who had not really had much background in Sociology it was interesting and easy to follow along!
unexpected_costs: If you register for clubs, there is a small fee (5-20 CAD).
cost_comparison: Things are expensive, but I found it was comparable to Denmark
activities_available: All sorts - if you have an interest in anything, I would say pretty confidently that there is a club for it. You can watch hockey games, join painting or knitting clubs, there is language exchange stuff happening, all sorts!
activities_recommended: I took part in a Japanese language table as part of my Japanese course, where you talked to native Japanese speakers once a week, that was really fun. Otherwise, I was part of the photo society, which was also great - but again, it depends on what you're interested in!
weekend_recommendations: Explore Vancouver! There are tons of parks around (Stanley Park, pretty famous, or Van Dusen, Queen Elizabeth, or even Nitobe which is right on campus and free with your UBC card), cool cafés, and beaches (e.g., Wreck Beach, Jericho Beach, Acadia Beach...) You can go skiing on Grouse Mountain or in Whistler. I also know lots of people went to Banff, Seattle - all over! It's easy to stay on campus cause it's so beautiful, but try to explore the city as much as you can, too!
culture_adjustment: Very easy, I just missed good bread. Otherwise it was no problem at all haha!
socializing_tips: Just go up and say hi! It's scary, but you've got nothing to lose in the end. Also joining clubs is a great way to meet local students! Just be a kind human and be curious about the people you are meeting!
cultural_challenges: Tipping culture! It's quite high and expected in many places, which I found a bit stressful sometimes
culture_appreciated: People are so kind! Lots of people yell thank you at the bus driver as they are getting off, which I get a kick out off every time it happens. Also lots more small talk, like at the cash - really nice!
top3_advice: 1) In case you don't get into on campus housing, don't stress - but start looking early for housing off campus! Winter Term 2 goes from Jan to end of April, so housing options for September start going up as early as then. Just be aware of the different timelines, starting to look in July is going to be quite difficult! 2) Try to balance school and fun! I was quite focused on my classes because I was really enjoying them, but I do wish I had explored a little bit more! 3) Push yourself to get out of your comfort zone, and try all the things you are curious about! It is really easy to say "I'll do it some other time", but the exchange goes by super quickly (classes are only like three months in the end, exams take up most of the last month) so do all you want to do!
other_useful_info: The workload is different compared to Copenhagen, because there are lots of assignments during the semester, instead of only one big exam at the end. It took me a while to adjust to staying on top of everything, but it worked out fine - but just so you are aware of that, you might have to manage your time a bit differently! Also attendance counts towards your grade in some classes, so look carefully at the syllabus! And explore campus, it's awesome and huge and has so much to offer:)
most_rewarding: Meeting so many nice people from all over, and having so much fun together. For me, the classes I took were in things I was really interested in, and it made me think about where I want to go in the future, both academically and personally, and whether I might switch directions. I felt like I got to overcome a lot of anxieties, and explore the things I loved, which made me a lot happier and open as a person. And taught me that going out of your comfort zone does bring good things!
greatest_challenge: I think keeping up with all the course work during the semester was a learning curve for me. And finding friends was hard in the beginning, just due to the lack of events offered to meet people. Staying positive things would work out was a challenge, but it did all work out in the end!
other_comments: UBC is really big on supporting students, so if you are ever overwhelmed, don't hesitate to talk to the profs, they usually will give you an extension if you need one! Otherwise, going on exchange was an awesome time, and I think a great opportunity to grow as a person if you let yourself do so. There is an ice cream shop called Rain or Shine on campus - my favourite flavour was London Fog, but try anything there, it's delightful! I hope you have a great exchange if you decide to go with UBC: It is one of my favourites of the things I have done so far:)

activities_available: Plenty of athletic activities. I don't know about social, as I found most of my friends on my own.
activities_recommended: Whatever you want. There are plenty.
weekend_recommendations: Spend time with your friends!
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Talk the them in class!
cultural_challenges: Tipping at restaurants haha.
culture_appreciated: The welcoming attitude.
top3_advice: Do it! Utilize your time there. Make as many friends as possible.
other_useful_info: Know that Vancouver is an expensive city.
most_rewarding: The people I met and friends I made.

crucial_aspects: The language, the culture and the nature
info_ease: Pretty easy. Personally i think i was guided through the whole proces. Though i heard others think is was more difficult.
arrival_assistance: Very much assistance, they had an office for just us exchange students, and many information meetings in the beginning.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: you register before going, but after you start you have a add/drop period on 14 days. I found this easy, since it just online, and you can try different courses before finally choosing in the add/drop period. Something we should do in DK since you don't necessary know if a course is for you beforehand.
registration_help: just some student guiding, but not much, so you had to research yourself.
registration_success: Very, i got the ones i wanted. But i also did the work and information finding.
registration_advice: To educate yourself and look stuff up. I can't rely on getting the information, so you need to look for it.
course_level: Pretty low since I was in MA. But the type of educational system was different which made it harder.
teaching_comparison: They have a lot of mandetory part of the education. For example they count participation every class, and you have 2-3 assignment per week. This is different from the danish educational system, where the most weight are being laid on the exam.
courses_enrolled: The Politics of Terror International Political Economy Intersectional approaches to thinking gender Comparative Politics of Immigration
recommended_courses: The Politics of Terror - Very demanding course, but the instructor is one of the best i've had ever. So interesting topic.
unexpected_costs: In Canada you will need a car, and you wanna go skiing. Two very expensive things but also so worth it.
cost_comparison: Less: Public transport and coffee More: grossery shopping.
activities_available: Almost everything.
activities_recommended: Go to parties at The Koerners Pub on campus. Go to the gallery on wednesday for karaoke
weekend_recommendations: go out of the city skiing in Whistler or hiking somewhere. There are loads of trails, so just begin some place. You have to take a road trip to Banff, and you have to visit Vancouver Island.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. They are so sweet and very european like.
cultural_challenges: Nothing challenging.
culture_appreciated: The welcoming, and how nice they are to everyone, even strangers.
top3_advice: Keep yourself updated, make list, apply fro scholarships (vancouver are expensive), if possible, stay off campus (In kitsilano), go skiing, book loads of trips with you friends in the weekends.
other_useful_info: remenber that the courses you select from home are not set in stone. You can try different courses and choose in the add/drop period.
most_rewarding: the nature and the friends i've made.
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to the more active and mandetory school system.

crucial_aspects: Combination of opportunities related to outdoor activities, Vancouver city, academic level of UBC and teaching in English.
info_ease: very easy
arrival_assistance: guided by volunteers on arrival dy.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You have to preselect courses. But don't expect to get many/any of them. Then there is a add/drop deadline 2 weeks into the semester, this means people will drop a lot of extra courses that they have taken even though they are planning on taking them, which then leaves space for you to join. This however also means you will have to follow some courses you are not yet assigned to for the first 2 weeks.
registration_help: Only guides. A lot of contact with go global, who answered relatively fast. They were flexible. Professors also answered mails and did what they could to help out in general.
registration_success: Ended up getting 5/5 I wanted.
registration_advice: it all works out in the end.
course_level: I had 2x 400 level courses and 3x 300 level courses. 300 level where similar to what I did 1. year at KU. 400 courses were however sort of like a natural extension of 3rd year stuff back home, similar to what I would have done on 6th semester in ECON.
teaching_comparison: More lecture based. More intuition less math. Not as in-depth.
courses_enrolled: ECON 441: The Process of Economic Development ECON 421: Introduction to Game Theory and Appliances ECON 335: Demography, Human migration and Families. ECON 305: Honours Intermediate Macroeconomic Analysis II ECON 371: Economics of the environment
recommended_courses: ECON 441: The process of economic development. Amazing approach, great prof, great subject. Important state-of-the-art papers on culture, institutions and how they shape economies. ECON 421: Game Theory. Good and fun
unexpected_costs: I ended up going a lot to the US. 4 times in total to visit Yellowstone, LA, San Francisco and Seattle. Those trips were obv. very expensive. Skiing is also super expensive here.
cost_comparison: Eating out and food. Vancouver (Canada) is super cheap. A lot to do with current exchange rate though
activities_available: All sorts! Literally anything. I was a part of the Surf club, Outdoors club and Ski club. First and last also great for hosting house parties. And first two have great trips. Especially try to go to Rock party - a 3 night weekend in Squamish with rock climbing (with instructors) with 300 people, sleeping in tents and partying with DJ's and barbecues and such.
activities_recommended: Go hiking all the time! rent a car. Get out there fist and every weekend. skip class. Make every weekend extended and sleep in your rented car on parking lots. Get cheap flights to the US if you don't mind flying a bit since you're here - especially when Vancouver weather starts getting bad.
weekend_recommendations: Whistler and Squamish are just the best for outdoor activities. Try to go to Banff early as well (or when it's warm)! Also great in winter for skiing though. Vancouver Island is super cool. Explore it and see whales and bears and such.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Also helps its convenient and that people are open and easygoing.
socializing_tips: They are quite young and many are very boring tbh.
cultural_challenges: Boring campus life outside of specific clubs.
culture_appreciated: Asian food in Vancouver is best outside of Asia by far.
top3_advice: Consider bringing tent and such from back home. You will probably use it all. Otherwise join Varsity Outdoor Club, then you can rent gear for free. Plan weekends well in advance if you consider doing big trips. Don't but groceries on campus, go to No Frills (like netto)
other_useful_info: consider not living on campus if you can afford it.
most_rewarding: Nature is wild here! doing outdoorsy stuff all the time will be missed so bad
greatest_challenge: Cultural differences with roomies on cleaning. Missing people from back home - It is VERY far from Denmark. Not easy to get visitors.

crucial_aspects: The language spoken and the geographical location
overall_comments: It was fun, but the courses were very easy. 300 courses at UBC are basically fake, I mean they are equivalent to first year classes back home. Which means they are great if you want to do as little as possible but it get's boring fast. 400 classes is a massive jump in difficulty, it isn't more difficult than back home it's the exact same level, but because of midterms and the like you end up having a lot of work all the time, I wouldn't recommend taking more than 2 of those if you want any free time. The social life really doesn't exist if you don't get on campus housing. I was lucky to be going with a friend and met some people there. But I would almost advise people not to go if they don't get on campus housing, which is funny since you don't know if you get it until like 2 months before. All in all the experience is what you make of it, people are very young and the social aspect isn't all that great outside of the housing you get, something to keep in mind.

arrival_assistance: There was an introduction day in which everything you needed to know was explained
housing_how: I found housing on my own
