crucial_aspects: I wanted to go see the Rocky Mountains because I like mountains, skiing and hiking. I also wanted to go somewhere far away where I could still speak the language and understand the culture. I chose Calgary specifically because I had received recommendations from people who had been there and because I could live on campus.
overall_comments: I had a great experience and going on exchange was definitely one of the best choices of my life.
info_ease: Most of the information was available online or in e-mails they sent you. There was some practical information, but they did not tell you everything unless you asked them (write an e-mail or ask in person in the International House or International Student Services)
arrival_assistance: I checked in at the International House the day I arrived. They were helpful with answering questions, but otherwise, they expected you to figure stuff out on your own. In general, they only help you if you ask.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had a great experience and going on exchange was definitely one of the best choices of my life.
registration_process: You enrol in courses on the MyUCalgary portal website. But before you can enrol in a course, you need to get an approval from the host university by sending an e-mail to the relevant department where you document your prerequisites. A lot of the courses were not available to me because I didn't meet the right prerequisites or because they were full, so the actual number of courses I could enrol in was limited. The number was even more limited by the fact that UCPH also didn't approve some of the courses I wanted because they thought the courses were too easy for master students. If you're a bachelor's student, this might not be a problem. In my case, UCPH was much stricter than UofC when approving courses. I didn't meet all the official prerequisites for the courses I took, but UofC approved them anyway because I persuaded them. Beware, however, that UofC sometimes takes long to reply. I would recommend starting getting approvals from UofC before asking UCPH for pre-approval, as you can always choose not to enrol in a course if you don't get your approval from UCPH.
registration_help: UofC sends you an e-mail with all the necessary information about the registration process. You can also send e-mails to the departments or the professors if you have questions.
registration_success: I only got two of the courses I wanted originally, ECON 403: Public Sector Economics: Taxation and ECON 541: Monetary Theory. My two other courses were STAT 533: Survival Models and ECON 571: Competition Policy.
registration_advice: Start early. Don't let the prerequisites from UofC hold you back (unless you think you actually might not be able to complete the course). Check the library before you buy any textbooks.
academics_comments: I had a great experience and going on exchange was definitely one of the best choices of my life.
course_level: The academic level was in general comparable to UCPH but it depended on the course. My favourite courses were "ECON 403: Taxation" and "ECON 571: Competition Policy" where the professors (McKenzie and Church) were really good and I learned a lot. "ECON 541: Monetary Theory" was very easy and had a very little workload but was also boring. "STAT 533: Survival Models" was quite difficult, as I was unfamiliar with a lot of the content, and the workload was very heavy.
teaching_comparison: Professors took teaching more seriously and were very engaged; that was especially the case in ECON 403 and ECON 571 where the professors were Canadian and very experienced. Each professor had different styles, but compared to UCPH the styles were more like in high school where you sit in smaller classrooms. Most courses also had a lot of assignments that were graded. There were also midterm exams that counted toward the final grade. This made it more intense at the beginning of the semester compared to UCPH where only the final exam matters.
courses_enrolled: ECON 403: Public Sector Economics: Taxation ECON 541: Monetary Theory STAT 533: Survival Models ECON 571: Competition Policy
recommended_courses: If you're interested in industrial organization and competition policy, I would definitely recommend ECON 571: Competition Policy. If you like public finance and microeconomics, I would recommend ECON 403: Taxation. I originally didn't want ECON 571, but then I started finding it interesting and I'm glad I took the course. The workload was quite heavy though because I had to write a 25-page paper. In ECON 403, the workload was not that bad, you only had to do three short assignments.
unexpected_costs: I spent a lot of money on travelling, skiing and going out (this was mostly planned but not all of it). Including everything, I spent around 80,000 DKK on my stay. Almost 50,000 of this was related to necessities such as housing, flights, meal plan, insurance and fees.
cost_comparison: Most things are slightly cheaper than in Denmark, but groceries and cell phone plans are more expensive - especially cell phone plans! I got a plan from Bell where I paid $46 monthly for 4.5 GB which I would not recommend. You could find better options at Virgin or Koodoo Mobile. If you don't have a SIC, which I didn't, you also aren't eligible for the normal plans, so you need to buy a prepaid plan which is worse. Restaurants and petrol are considerably cheaper than in Denmark. In restaurants, however, and also in many other places like hairdressers, taxi drivers etc., you're expected to tip at least 15%. Sales taxes are also not included in the menu prices, so things aren't as cheap as they look!
activities_available: They have all sorts of clubs involving different sports, interests, religions etc. There's also a mentorship programme that international students can join. I joined it and got a Canadian mentor, but we didn't talk much, and after I became friends with the other exchange students, I didn't really need the mentor. I went to the Fitness Centre a lot which was free (you pay a mandatory fee).
activities_recommended: In the first weeks, definitely join the social events for international students and meet new friends. They don't notify you about all the events, so I would recommend going to the International Student Services after you arrive and asking about what events are coming up.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the Rockies and visit Banff and Jasper and Canmore! It can be difficult going alone when you don't have a car. But many other exchange students probably wanna go as well, so if you team up with them, you can rent a car (on Turo for example) and go together. I also went to Vancouver and British Columbia. I also joined the ski trip hosted by the Ski Club. At first, I couldn't get a spot, but then I signed up on the wait list (there was a link on their Instagram page). I also arranged my own ski trips with some other exchange students to Sunshine Village where we stayed in Banff.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. People are open and easy to talk to. Most of my friends, however, were other exchange students and not Canadians. The Canadian students might be friendly, but most of them are not interested in making friends with international students.
socializing_tips: Go to the frat parties. If you join the mentorship programme, you might also get a good mentor that will introduce you to other local students. Join the clubs and the ski club trip.
cultural_challenges: The urban landscape is different from Europe. Cities are made mostly for cars and not people. Sometimes, we had trouble renting AirBNBs because they didn't trust international students. You can only buy alcohol in designated liquor stores and you're not allowed to drink in public.
culture_appreciated: I forgot to tip sometimes which maybe made some think I was rude, but usually you can get away with it if you don't tip. I usually tipped 10-15%.
top3_advice: Start making friends as soon as possible. Go to the Rockies. Enjoy the moment and don't worry about school. Going on exchange feels lonely in the beginning, but everything will be okay. You'll find friends and you'll get used to your new life. Suddenly, it's all over, and you will miss it!
other_useful_info: Bring clothes for all sorts of weather, especially cold weather.
most_rewarding: Going to the Rocky Mountains and meeting new people from all around the world.
greatest_challenge: Arriving and leaving. It's a long flight, and in both cases, you have to readapt to a new lifestyle and a new country which is hard. But it's worth it!
other_comments: Go on exchange! You won't regret it.

recommended_courses: I liked Gender and Development. You learn many new perspectives and the teacher is nice.
unexpected_costs: I spent most my money on renting cars to drive to the mountains for hikes. I also spent money on a season pass for Lake Louise ski resort and gear (if you dont bring it from home). I brought all my skiing gear except skis, which i bought and sold again before going home.
cost_comparison: food is more expensive. The supermarket is 1 km away so a good saving tip is to only go once a week so you aren't tempted.
activities_available: The gym and aquatic center are free. You can also rent squash courts which is really fun.
activities_recommended: I loved all the active stuff
weekend_recommendations: go to the mountains as much as possible! It's absolutely beautiful. You can rent a car easily through the app Turo (like danish Gomore).
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: I choose a Canadian roommate which helped.
cultural_challenges: None, other than people are quite young. You just have to get used to it :)
culture_appreciated: Canadians are very friendly and it's easy to talk to new people.
top3_advice: Make the most of every weekend. It takes som planning but its definitely worth it.
other_useful_info: no.
most_rewarding: Living in a different place. UofC has many international students and they are ready to help.
greatest_challenge: I didn't find it too challenging. I mostly had tons of fun.
other_comments: Don't take school too seriously. I got A's in all my courses and didn't work too hard, although I attended all my classes and studied a day or two before a test.

crucial_aspects: That it was an English speaking country and that it was located near beautiful nature and mountains
info_ease: It was not so easy and it took a lot of effort
arrival_assistance: I was assisted to my room and they arranged social events in the beginning. I did not get a lot of help but I new where to seek help if I needed it.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Difficult to figure out a new system in the beginning but you get used to it
registration_help: You could always ask for help
registration_success: It took a lot of time to find suitable courses because some of them had restrictions regarding exchange students and all the courses had to fit together. It was a puzzle. I ended up changing a lot of the courses when I arrived at the university.
registration_advice: You can always change courses in the first few weeks of the semester, so if you don't like the courses you chose beforehand or if it is inconvenient for you, you can change courses when you arrive.
course_level: The level of the courses were very different. Some of them were difficult others were easy. The 200 level courses were very easy and not a huge workload whereas courses at a 400 level requires more work.
teaching_comparison: Very different. I had a bigger workload during the semester with more assignments and presentations than on UCPH which also counted in the final grade. I also had midterms in Canada, so overall more preparation during the semester at my host institution than on UCPH .
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Geology, Global Food Politics and Sustainability and Political Ecology
recommended_courses: Global Food Politics. Very nice teacher and the course has a good structure
unexpected_costs: transportation. Public transportation is not good in Canada so I used a lot of money on renting cars to get around.
cost_comparison: groceries were more expensive than expected. I think more or less everything was more expensive than expected.
activities_available: Almost everything. The university had all sorts of clubs that you could engage in. Both cultural, social, athletic and academic clubs. This was very good!
activities_recommended: Sport because it is always fun to do together and the university had a lot of 'free' facilities.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Rocky Mountains. I used many weekends in the mountains and it is very beautiful. I never got tired of it and you can hike in the summer and ski in the winter :D
culture_adjustment: People were very nice and welcoming so that made it easier but it is a challenge in the beginning
socializing_tips: the local students are open to socializing with international and exchange students but if you are living with locals it is easier
cultural_challenges: not anything specific but adjusting to a different school system and speaking another language
culture_appreciated: the very friendly approach they had to foreigners which is very different from Denmark
top3_advice: Find out what works for you <3
other_useful_info: no
most_rewarding: Living in another country so far away for a longer period and being in the nature with good friends
greatest_challenge: the school system
other_comments: no

crucial_aspects: I første omgang ville jeg afsted fordi det er en rigtig god mulighed for at være et sted længe, og prøve at have en hverdag i et andet land.
overall_comments: Eneste grund til at det ikke er 10, er nogle udfordringer boligmæssigt som ikke er gældende for alle. Jeg var bare uheldig.
info_ease: Svært. Hjemmesiden er ret dårligt, og det er svært at gennemskue hvilke fag der udbydes hvornår. Brug evt. dette link eller find den tilsvarende side til din studieretning, til at se om de fag du vil have, udbydes når du skal afsted (de ændrer ikke så meget fra år til år, så de fleste fra fall 23 vil gå igen i fall 24 fx) : https://geog.ucalgary.ca/manageprofile/courses
arrival_assistance: Vi blev taget rigtig godt hånd om. Der er en afdeling til internationale studerende hvor man kan komme hen i løbet af de første 14 dage og få svar på nærmest alt og hjælp hvis du endnu ikke har fundet noget fast at bo i. Jeg blev endda veninder med hende der hjalp mig dengang. Der er desuden en masse intovideoer man kan se inden ankomst ift hvad man skal huske at have styr på, hvilke transportmuligheder der er osv. Overall meget mere info end mange andre steder.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Eneste grund til at det ikke er 10, er nogle udfordringer boligmæssigt som ikke er gældende for alle. Jeg var bare uheldig.
registration_process: Det gik ret smooth. De forventer som et af de få Amerikansk/Canadiske universiteter ikke at du tager en language proficiency test som hurtigt koster et par tusind kroner. Du skal bare have en underviser hjemmefra til at skrive under på at dit engelsk niveau er højt nok.
registration_help: Der er et kontor der kun beskæftiger sig med internationale og alle deres papirer + man har en kontaktperson derfra som man kan skrive til eller få møder med og de gør altid hvad de kan for at hjælpe.
registration_success: Jeg tror jeg fik alle dem jeg gerne ville have. Man havde 14 dage inde i semesteret til frit at ændre sine fag, så man kunne prøve dem af.
registration_advice: Nogle klasser bliver fyldt ret hurtigt, så lad vær med at vente med at kigge, til ugen før du tager afsted. Kig når der åbnes for tilmelding.
academics_comments: Eneste grund til at det ikke er 10, er nogle udfordringer boligmæssigt som ikke er gældende for alle. Jeg var bare uheldig.
course_level: 200 er 1. års kurser og er meget introducerende til det at gå på uni. Jeg fandt ud af, at det typisk er 300 level kurser hvor der er den største arbejdsbyrde. 500 passede bedst i niveau for mig som er deres sidste år på BA. (jeg var afsted på 5. semester)
teaching_comparison: USA og Canada arbejder enormt meget med udenadslære generelt for mange studieretninger. De bruger næsten kun multiple choice eller true/false som eksamensform. Der er for mange, særligt business studieretninger, hvor gruppearbejde fylder meget.
courses_enrolled: Wind Science Arctic Systems Science Government and Politics of Africa Introduction to social and cultural Anthopology
recommended_courses: Arctic Systems Science og Wind Science vil jeg anbefale. Indholdet var spændende og underviserne er dygtige. Der var ikke fokus på en final exam som i de andre fag, men derimod opgaver i løbet af semesteret + meget nemme point i Arctic. Det gjorde at man ikke var nervøs for om man kunne bestå eller ej.
unexpected_costs: et recreation fee som man skal betale til skolen fordi man har adgang til til fx fitness, klatrevæg og svømmehal. Canada er et af de dyreste lande i verden at have telefon i. Men kan kan komme rimlig godt udenom ved at have World data hos CBB mobil eller købe et E-sim kun med data. En almindelig aftale i Canada koster hurtigt 330 kr /mdr for 20 GB pr måned.
cost_comparison: Telefonabonnement, offentlig transport er virkelig billigt - også Uber. Biler kan lejes billigt på appen Turo.
activities_available: Allervigtigst - Outdoor centre som har ALT hvad hjertet begærer til udendørs sport og ekstremsport + der udbydes skiture, vandreture, snowshoeing, paragliding og alt muligt andet som virkelig er fedt og relativt billigt. Der er 300 klubber som jeg ikke kan nævne på stående fod. For udvekslingseleverne var særligt Squash banerne, svømmehallen, fitness, skøjtehallen og ski-klubben populært.
activities_recommended: Vær i bjergene så meget som overhovedet muligt! Brug de faciliteter som skolen udbyder til at prøve noget nyt.
weekend_recommendations: Tag på flerdagsture til bjergene. Kør op til Jasper Nationalpark med en gruppe venner i en stor bil, stop på vejen og se bjørne, elge og vanvittig natur. Lej en Airbnb og tag på vandreture. Om vinteren er ski resorts kun 1-2 timer væk. Og oplev Stampede hvis du er her om sommeren / tag til et rodeoshow
culture_adjustment: Man lærte noget nyt om dem hele vejen igennem, men den første uge er en stor omvæltning. Bare det at se TV med tømmermænd giver indtryk.
socializing_tips: Sportshold eller klubber. Oplev et fratparty hvis du er til den slags Tag med til orientation day Snak med dem du sidder ved siden af i timerne - det er helt helt normalt for dem
cultural_challenges: Det skal opleves på egen krop
culture_appreciated: Det skal opleves på egen krop
top3_advice: Prioriter en masse tid til venner og oplevelser Calgary ligger i Alberta som er den mest konservative provis i Canada og dermed den med størst kulturel forskel. Desuden er det den billigste at leve i af landets storbyer og det regner aldrig.
other_useful_info: Nej
most_rewarding: Jeg var bare vild med det. Jeg kan ikke vælge hvad der var bedst.
greatest_challenge: At bo meget meget tæt med nogen man ikke kender på forhånd
other_comments: DO IT! Alle steder har pros and cons. Hvis du vil have vanvittige naturoplevelser og opleve de meget amerikanske Canada til nogenlunde pris, så er det her virkelig stedet

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go a place where there was amazing nature, and a high academic standard. These criteria was why I choose University of Calgary for my destination.
overall_comments: I had a great experience with the university and they were very helpful in the process of applying and arriving. Through my exhange they also helped a lot with figuring out the way of courses and so on. It was a great help, especially when you come as a new person to a foreign country.
info_ease: In general the university was very helpful and accommodating in the proces of arriving and so on. It was a bit difficult to figure information about courses, and in which semesters they are offered. But it was easy when we arrived, although it was a bit hard to figure out from home. The good thing was that the first two weeks are used to shop around and try out courses. For me that was a very nice way to do it, because i also found out that i didnt want some of the courses i applied for anyway.
arrival_assistance: They had different orientation events for the new students. Among others, they had a tour around campus that new students could join.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had a great experience with the university and they were very helpful in the process of applying and arriving. Through my exhange they also helped a lot with figuring out the way of courses and so on. It was a great help, especially when you come as a new person to a foreign country.
registration_process: I applied for 5 different places, both in Canada and Europe. I found the registration proces pretty easy, and i would say that university of copenhagen provided the needed information to make the proces easier. When i applied, i afterwards got a letter from UofC, saying that i was accpeted and i had the choisce to decline or accept the spot for the fall semester.
registration_help: I think the previous travel reports helped me to decide where i wanted to go. Furthermore, UofC also send different mails to help in the proces of registration in courses.
registration_success: I got all the classes i wanted.
registration_advice: I would recommend to register for more courses than you have to take. They have the first two weeks, where you are able to try out all the courses. And if you are registered for more than you need to have, you get the flexibility to choose which ones you want and still get the chance to try them out.
academics_comments: I had a great experience with the university and they were very helpful in the process of applying and arriving. Through my exhange they also helped a lot with figuring out the way of courses and so on. It was a great help, especially when you come as a new person to a foreign country.
course_level: The arctic system science was a undergraduate/graduate course. The level was good, and not too difficult but a really exciting course overall. The course i had at film studies was mostly for fun, but it turned out to be a really nice course.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at UofC is more like the danish high school, and in general very different than UCPH. It involves a lot of learning by remembering, because there is midterms and finals which often contains multiple choice/true false questions where your notes are not alllowed. Futhermore, some courses are graded on participations among other things, and it is therefore required to show up for lab and so on.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to film studies (FILM 201) Government and politics of Africa (POLI 371) Arctic system science (GEOG 502) Wind science (GEOG 506)
recommended_courses: I would definitly recommend the arctic system science and wind science, they were great! both the instructors/professors where great at teaching and were very motivating in the learning proces.
unexpected_costs: I spend a lot of the money i had on hiking in the weekends in banff nationalpark. For me going out, was not a big part of the experience, but it was the nature and the mountains. I did not have unexpected cost in that sense, but i was surpriced how expensive shopping for food was.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping is in general more expensive than in copenhagen. Especially vegetables. My best advice is to go to either real canadian superstore or wallmarts! ;) Eating out is not as expensive as in copenhagen.
activities_available: There is a lot of sport games at the university, that students can join for free. That is really fun to go and see! I did not explore the cultural activities at UofC, but there is probably some. They had some social activities in start for new students, and i would highly recommend to join thoose. It is a good way to get to know people.
activities_recommended: Icehockey, rodeo and the mountains. Rodeo was for sure a big experience, because it was so Alberta and very Canada. It was a lot of fun, because when i went we were a group of exchange students, and we were definetly the only ones who werent locals. It was a lot of fun to see and also a big cultural experince.
weekend_recommendations: If you are only in clagary for a short visit, my biggest recommendation is to go to the mountains. It is stunning and overwhelming, bit so amazing to see!
culture_adjustment: I think it was pretty easy. People are in general very welcoming and open. You can always ask locals and they will for sure help the best they can.
socializing_tips: I found local canadian friends in my courses, that is probably the best tip i can give. Just talk with all the people, and you will meet some great people both exchange and locals.
cultural_challenges: I did not find the cultural differences challenging, i found the culture very welcoming and open minded.
culture_appreciated: Again, the welcoming and open culture.
top3_advice: Look for housing in good time, if you are gonna live off campus. Use the oppertunity for great nature close by. Enjoy the stay, and take the chances for experiences that you wouldnt get back home fx rodeo, hiking and so on!
other_useful_info: No, i dont think so
most_rewarding: The mix of great university experince and nature!
greatest_challenge: Being in another country with a new culture. It is a great challenge, and also being so far from home and all the things you know. You learn a lot about how you work when trying to integrate into a new culture.

crucial_aspects: Wanted to study in an english speaking country was the most important aspect. Another aspect was that wanted to study at a west coast university, preferably in Canada.
overall_comments: University of Calgary was amazing
info_ease: Very easy. The international service coordinator did a very good job at providing information upon arrival and was also very easy to get in contact with
arrival_assistance: There was a welcome center at the university which all international students could show up at, at any time. Here we were provided with information regarding getting around on campus and upcoming events.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: University of Calgary was amazing
registration_process: To register for most courses you have to get a prerequisite approval which is described relatively thoroughly on the university website
registration_help: International student center, both physical and via email. They responded at least within 24 hours.
registration_success: Mildly successful, since not all courses that I intended to take was offered that semester.
registration_advice: Look up previously offered courses for that type of semester (fx "Fall")
academics_comments: University of Calgary was amazing
course_level: I only had 300- and 400-level courses, and the 400 level courses where clearly more difficult. The courses were still relatively easier than at KU.
teaching_comparison: Depends on the size of the course. The 300-level courses were larger lectures, while 400-level courses were smaller classrooms.
courses_enrolled: Industrial Organization Energy economics and policy Electricity markets Science and Philisophy
recommended_courses: Industrial Organization was the most demanding and a high level course, but also very interesting and rewarding.
unexpected_costs: None really
cost_comparison: Food is relatively the same as Denmark, take-a-way is cheaper though.
activities_available: Great fitness (gym) and sport facilities (squashm, badminton, basketball, football, hockey ect.)
activities_recommended: Sign up for a club or participate in sports with other canadians or international students
weekend_recommendations: Go to Banff national park (Skiing, Hiking).
culture_adjustment: Easy, people are VERY friendly
cultural_challenges: None really
culture_appreciated: People are very and open and friendly in general
top3_advice: 1. Just go, amazing place, with so much nature 2. Show up a all social events in the beginning 3. Enjoy your time there, you will mostly have more spare time than at KU
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Social connections, skiing and nature
greatest_challenge: dont know

crucial_aspects: Jeg har familie i Calgary hvilket var den primære årsag til at jeg søgte mod Canada. Udover min familiære relation så Calgary et mega fedt sted at studere hvis man elsker at bruge tid udenfor. I weekenderne tog alle udvekslingsstuderende ud for at hike, sport, byen og meget mere. Calgary er et godt mix af byliv og country living. Calagry er også en af de billigere byer at bo i i Canada - dog stadig ikke super billig.
info_ease: Meget nemmere end hjemmefra. Universitet hjælper mega meget med alt fra bolig til økonomi og transport. De bedste råd jeg fik var fra lokale og skolen var de bedste. Følte generelt at vejlederen fra KU var mega nederen og ikke hjælpsom hvorimod at de ansatte i Calgary gjorde alt for at hjælpe en.
arrival_assistance: Jeg fik meget hjælp ift. transportruter og hvordan man skulle betale skolen. Jeg fik ikke en boplads på skolen så derfor bookede jeg AirBNB og fandt ud af transportsystemet. Skolen hjalp mig med at få mit månedskort til at fungere og det kort gjorde at jeg sparede seriøse penge. I perioden hvor man skulle vælge fag, fik jeg meget hjælp, da jeg hoppede rundt mellem 5-7 fag og vidste ikke hvilke jeg ville have, men de rådgav mig godt og jeg fik styr på de 4 fag jeg ville have.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Var nemt nok, da stedet ikke kræver de højeste karakter og engelsk mundtlig test. Generelt er det noget biks baks med at søge udveksling, men tror Calgary var en af de nemmere steder at søge. Man skal bare være opmærksom på de givne datoer!
registration_help: Hvis jeg var i tvivl om noget skrev jeg til universitet og fik relativt hurtigt svar, men det afhang meget af hvilke mennesker jeg skrev til.
registration_success: Jeg kæmpede meget hjemmefra, da kursus kataloget for mit semester(efterår/fall) kom ret sent. Jeg valgte en masse kurser som ikke eksisterede og når jeg ville vælge kurser så havde jeg ikke de rigtige fag forudsætninger eller nok point til at kunne søge det fag. Men når du ankommer er der en prøve periode med kurser, som er omkring 2 uger. Tip, vælge alle de fag du vil have, selvom det kan være mange, jeg havde 7 i den periode og så kan du sortere ned til 4. Hvis du ikke kan lide nogle af dine fag så kan man nemt finde andre, bare tjek om fagene ligger oveni hinanden, for så kan du ikke vælge dem.
registration_advice: Bare følg guidelines som KU stiller til rådighed og så lige så snart du bliver accepteret skal du søge bolig på universitetet. Det koster 50$ at søge, men hvis du gør det tidligt så er det ikke dårlige penge at bruge. Jeg søgte sent (marts/april) og derfor var det spild af penge
course_level: Relativt nemme kurser jeg valgte, som ikke krævede det største af mig. Jeg havde et kursus hvor det var mutiple choice test hver tirsdag, men det var chill nok, da alle testene kun gjaldt for 2%. Generelt så vælg kurser som er nemmere, da det er mega nederen at skulle sidde med lektier til halsen i et andet land...
teaching_comparison: Det er meget nemmere i Canada, da alle studerende typisk er 18-20 og bliver babyet meget af lærerne og institutionen
courses_enrolled: Natural Disaster and Critical Earth Phenomena Global Environmental Change Thinking Spatially Digital World Warriors & Love: Greek Literature in Translation
recommended_courses: Thinking Spatially er et ArcGIS kursus, som er fedt og relevant for geografi og geologi studerende. Vi havde en ung lærer som var mega nice. Græsk var ikke hvad man forventer geologistuderende ville vælge, men jeg ville gerne lære noget andet og vi fik læst mange værker og analyserede dem i klassen, så det var mega fedt faktisk.
unexpected_costs: Man Uber meget når man skal hjem fra byen, så jeg brugte mange penge på den app.
cost_comparison: Mad var generelt billigt, men ikke så meget billigere end herhjemme.
activities_available: Skolen tilbyder virkelig mange aktivitet, som svømning, skøjte, volley, fodbold. Der er også foreninger til enhver etnicitet, religion, køn og hobby, mega fedt.
activities_recommended: Meld dig ind i nogle grupper og lær nogle af de lokale at kende. Typisk bruger man meget tid med andre udvekslingsstuderende, så at være i en gruppe kan være en fed måde at finde andre mennesker.
weekend_recommendations: tag ud og hike og river rafte! river rafte skal man gøre tidligt, da sæsonen slutter omkring slut september. I læseferien så tag ud og rejs, fx. Vancouver, som kun er en time væk. Hvis du vil rejse, så book billetterne tidligt, da det er billigst. Jeg tog til Montreal og det kan i den grad også anbefales, jeg var der i en uge og prøvede mange fede byting. Montreal minder meget om Europa, Frankrig specifikt.
culture_adjustment: Relativt nemt, da de lokale snakker engelsk.
socializing_tips: Hmm de alle er mega imødekommende, så bare vær åben og snaksaglig, ligesom de er.
cultural_challenges: De small talker meget, så det skal man lige vænne sig til, men det går hurtigt så får man alle de hurtige sætninger - great, how are you? etc.
culture_appreciated: Jeg elskede deres country ting, fx. linedance, der er begynder dage om torsdagene ved 21-tiden på Ranchmann's, det blev tradition at tage dertil og danse for os udvekslingsstuderende.
top3_advice: Det er en af de billigere steder i Canada, men det er ikke billigt, så spar penge op, søg legater, bare vær sikker på at du har nok penge, siden pengene hurtigt kan blive brugt på oplevelser og booking af biler.
other_useful_info: Hvis du har brug for hjælp, så kan universitetet være en kæmpe hjælp.
most_rewarding: Du bliver mega selvstændig. Du finder dine egne kurser, bolig, få styr på økonomi etc. samtidig med at finde venner og socialisere, så du bliver helt klart tvunget til at få styr på dit sh#t.
greatest_challenge: At få styr på alle sine ting, men ligeså snart der er gået en måned, så har du styr på næsten alt og fået forhåbentlig venner.

arrival_assistance: Full written guide, drop in hours and orientation program.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

activities_available: Basically everything sports related I joined the squash programme.
activities_recommended: Squash and rowing had great faciliteis and teams.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the mountains as much as possible.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, Canadians are nice and friendly.
socializing_tips: GO to some of the social events in the building you get into.
cultural_challenges: None really
culture_appreciated: Opennes

arrival_assistance: mostly from the emails the university had sent out before.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_help: The school, was quick to reply when i needed help which was nice.

recommended_courses: Cost-benefit was interesting, and i really enjoyed Risk management.

crucial_aspects: Berkeley is one of the most well known and highly renowned universities throughout the world and is top tier on almost every ranking out there. Combined with the unique placement close to San Francisco and a variety of interesting cities, nature, the ocean and national parks it offers everything you could imagine and dream of. The prestige itself was the major reason for choosing the university as it looks amazing on your CV, however the course selection, professors and in general the opportunities that UC Berkeley presents are just amazing
overall_comments: UC Berkeley is in general a great place. The academics are as you would expect (don't be scared - it isn't as intimidating and scary as it seems). The people are welcoming, the weather is great and the opportunities to go on weekend trips are fantastic. The only thing that draws me down to a 9/10 score is the number of homeless people and the crime rates. This is in no way unique to UC Berkeley however it does dampen the excitement a bit, and you should be prepared to take a Uber home from parties - the US has a different security level than EU no matter where you go. When that is said I hardly ever experienced anything unusual/uncomfortable that you wouldn't in Copenhagen. A highlight is definitely the people, the weekend trips and the overall experience of being at one of the most beautiful campus' on the planet with world famous scientists wondering the same paths as yourself.
info_ease: Very easy - UC Berkeley sends a lot(!) of informational e-mails, updates, recommendations and random links before you even set foot on the plane. This can be a bit overwhelming at times however a common sense for which e-mails are relevant and which are not will pull you through just fine. The UCEAP website offers a lot of guiding in when to apply for courses, where to get information and how to proceed. Be prepared for the high amount of bureaucracy that is a part of the US culture - fear not, if you by accident contact the "wrong" person they will happily assist you and try to help you towards the right places.
arrival_assistance: Obviously someone won't greet you at San Francisco airport with a sign saying "Welcome XX". When you arrive (especially if you arrive some time before the semester starts) it might even feel like a vacation. I would recommend arriving some time before start to let yourself fall into place, get to know your neighborhood, find out where you like to shop for groceries, meet some of the other people attending the university and get a normal life going. This might even be a good time to bond with a few of the Danes which might help you build relations to other international and American people later on as they probably don't attend the same courses as you.
arrival_comments: I was pretty satisfied, however the "Golden Bear Orientation" (GBO) feels a bit long and unnecessary at times. You will be grouped with random transfer students which means that a low of information might not be relevant as an exchange student. When that is said you should definitely attend the first coupe of days and see if you like it - give everyone and everything a chance, but be prepared to also plan something yourself. A lot of the students are under 21 which means they can't get into bars/pubs. As expected UC Berkeley also does not condone drinking during orientation which is great but might also put a damper on the social activities (Us Danes are just better as socializing with a beer or 2). When that is said I did attend during the pandemic so it was a mix of online and in-person activities which might have affected the program. You WILL be "forced" to do a number of online programs about alcohol, drugs, sex, mental health, relationships (you name it - they have it). This might feel comical and ridiculous at times - and it probably is. This is targeted new American students who might only be 17-18 years old and be moving out and living on their own for the first time. Therefore, it is not always relevant as an international student - but once again, it is an experience and certainly brings out some laughs and smiles along the way.

registration_process: They have a portal called "Calnet" where you signup for classes using the prefixes and number e.g. "MCB153". You can basically add the courses and try and tailor your schedule before the sign-up begins by adding them to your basket - so when the actual sign-up starts you just press a button to add the courses from your basket and you are signed up. Do yourself a favor and go on Youtube and search for UC Berkeley course signup or something like that. There are so many 5-10 minute videos showing the system and it is honestly a better sign-up system than UCPH.
registration_help: Multiple advisors on Campus are available - as mentioned Youtube is a great option as well. Just click around the site before the whole sign-up stress starts and do your "Homework" before hand. You can also e-mail some professors for special registration keys, however not all courses allow for this but it certainly does not harm you.
registration_success: Very successful. I got 4/4 classes that I wanted and then I later without problems changes 2 of my courses to some other courses. A quick tip is that a few weeks before semester start different "DeCals" will be published. They are basically student run courses with guest lectures that normally account for 1-2 credits. These are great if you just need that final 1 credit to reach the minimum required for a semester.
registration_advice: Don't panic if you are not enrolled in all the courses you want. The drop period is used by almost all students to switch classes and Berkeley is very flexible with switching classes. You can even go to the first lecture even if you are on the waiting list and talk to the professor after class about the possibility to enroll. Mention that you are very interested in the class, that you are an international student and they might even bump you up in the queue - they might even directly add you and expand the class with a few people extra depending on the demand.

course_level: Once again - don't be scared about the reputation of UC Berkeley, you will probably perform at the same level as in Copenhagen as long as you attend lectures and put in a normal amount of work.
teaching_comparison: They have a lot more guest lectures that present on their own research - this might at times be very high level as it is the world leading research that might even be nominated for a Nobel prize in years to come. Fear not, the professors and GSI's know when the material is "over" the expected level of competencies for Undergraduates and they will accommodate this in the midterms, quizzes, exams etc.
courses_enrolled: BIOE115 - Tissue Engineering IB118 - Organismal Microbiomes and Host-Pathogen Interactions MCB153 - Molecular Therapeutics MCB198 - CRISPR: Basic Principles and Applications
recommended_courses: MCB153 and IB118. MCB153 is a new course from UC Berkeley and is focused on a variety of different diseases and general issues with the human body and how to tackle, target and drug them. The course is very focused around research and how to bridge the gap between academia and a finished "product" i.e. a drug/medicine to treat the disease that basic research tries to understand. The professors Andrew Dillin and Sarah Stanley are both experts within their fields of work and through their long career has a broad knowledge of other researchers. These are often invited to guest lecture including a number of Nobel Prize winners. The course encourages discussion between students and researchers and is a pleasant learning environment. IB118 has many characteristics of a Microbiology/Immunology course from Copenhagen but also goes beyond standard text-book knowledge and presents cutting edge research.
unexpected_costs: Insurance is expensive! Also weekend trips might be an unexpected cost - however it is totally worth it because you get to see California and bond with the other people on the trip so definitely worth it.
cost_comparison: Again housing and insurance is just expensive in California. Alcohol on clubs and bars are the same price as Copenhagen.
activities_available: Every single one you can imagine. Go to the sporting activities (UC Berkeley American football, water polo, basketball, volleyball, tennis). The facilities are amazing considering that you are watching college sports and the atmosphere and collectiveness is wonderful to experience.
activities_recommended: Sports - see above.
weekend_recommendations: Yosemite, Las Vegas, Monterey Bay, San Francisco (Golden gate, Alcatraz etc.), Grand Canyon, Go to the Football game VS Stanford.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easily - the US culture is not much different from that in EU and Denmark in general. Be open minded and talk to people - try and engage in conversation and don't be passive.
socializing_tips: Be mindful and respective of other cultures, have an open mind and heart. In the start of the exchange try not to say no to anything or anyone. People will be making social arrangements a lot in the beginning and it is important to participate to find the right group of friends. With that said, later on it is okay to be picky and reject some "offers" to hang out.
cultural_challenges: Not really anything in particular
culture_appreciated: The social activities even when these include going to bars and restaurants where you might go above your budget. U really enjoyed the weekend trips even though they are expensive.
top3_advice: Everything is listed above
other_useful_info: Everything is listed above
most_rewarding: The academics, the social life and the weekend trips.
greatest_challenge: Adapting to the time difference and the fact you are on the other side of the world while your family, friends and loved ones are at home.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: I applied to study abroad particularly for the opportunity to attend UC Berkeley. It is not only one of the best public universities in the US, but also well-known for being progressive both academically and non-academically.
info_ease: I found the orientation information very easily accessible, and everything one needed to know was clearly communicated via email. So remember to check it!
arrival_assistance: If I'm not wrong, there was an option to be met by a ''mentor'' of sorts at the airport - I did not choose to do this. The orientation for international exchange student - called something along the lines of ''Golden Bear Orientation'' - was not the best. It is required (and expensive!), and while there were many activities offered to get to know other students and transfers, not everyone showed up. The food options that were included in the price were also subpar.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You register through CalCentral (Berkeley's own student website), where you receive a ''registration window''. This is essentially a period of time - usually a couple of days - in which you can register for your classes. More than often these classes are first-come-first-served. In some cases, you need a teacher's permission to enroll in their course, so for that you have to email them and ask beforehand. There is an adjustment period a few weeks into the semester, where it is possible to switch out classes if you did not find a right fit.
registration_help: The enrollment process was well-described on their website, and there was also the opportunity to contact advisors or anyone else in a suitable position for help.
registration_success: I had no problems enrolling in any of my classes, although it did take some time for me to figure out the system with ''reserved seats'' (which are seats in a course reserved for a special group of students - so while there might be 5 seats free in the course it could still be full if you do not fall into that special category).
registration_advice: Remember to check requirements, and how many seats are available for your student status. Email any professors for courses where you need their professors beforehand. Also, make a list (with backup-choices too!) of the courses you are planning to take before the registration window opens.
course_level: I took mostly undergraduate upper-division level courses at Berkeley, since I experienced they fit me best. Within my program, this usually meant that they consisted of smaller groups and were seminar-based, aka filled with discussions. I also took a graduate seminar which was challenging but very fun! As a senior student I also took (and dropped) a freshman class the first semester, since I found it a bit too easy, and the general crowd was very young.
teaching_comparison: Most of my courses were discussion-based and not lectures. We were all expected to have done the readings before class and everyone is encouraged to speak (indeed, your grade is often dependent on it). There were also weekly presentations by students which were the ground material for student discussions.
courses_enrolled: ART 26 - Moving Image: Foundations COMLIT 98BC - Berkeley Connect COMLIT 190 - Senior Seminar in Comparative Literature SCANDIN 250 - Seminar in Scandinavian Literature
recommended_courses: For anyone in the literature-field, I would recommend taking one of the senior seminars in the Comparative Literature-department. You are also allowed to take one graduate course per semester, which can be an interesting (and very rewarding) experience. However, not all professors admit undergraduates into their graduate courses. It is also nice to embrace the ability to ''shop around'' for courses, and try something new in a field outside of one's own. I took both a practical art class and a language course here, which was a lot of fun.
unexpected_costs: None that weren't expected, it was just all very expensive.
cost_comparison: I knew housing was expensive, but wasn't prepared for the equally high living expenses, like food.
activities_available: There are so many, and really everything imaginably possible. Most clubs and societies set up tables on the road before Sather Gate, so one can usually find something interesting there.
activities_recommended: Although I myself did not participate, I have had friends engaged in both choirs, dance clubs and sports. It is easy to join these things and they are also looking for new members. If one is more culturally inclined, there is also the BAMPFA student committee, which is connected to the local art gallery.
weekend_recommendations: Get around the Bay if you can! Make friends that have a car, or rent one (or use public transport). Both Oakland and San Francisco are great to explore by foot, but it is a bit trickier if you want to get across the bridge into Marin County. However, you are greatly rewarded with incredible nature and beaches. Enjoy the landscape of California and go on hikes, try surfing or other water-activities.
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy, since Berkeley in its values is a bit more similar to Denmark than the rest of the US. People are very talkative, and you fall into the ''small talk'' with the cashier or bartender quickly.
socializing_tips: This I found quite difficult, and the ones I met were through my classes. Since everyone has their individual schedules, it can be tricky to catch people before or after classes, so make use of the small breaks (if you get any).
cultural_challenges: People are usually down to chat, but less good at making concrete plans. Try reaching out if you find someone interesting and ask them to hang out with an actual date and time set in mind.
culture_appreciated: I really enjoyed the easiness with which people communicate with each other, and how open people are.
top3_advice: 1. Be open to other people and don't be afraid to make small-talk. 2. Use the academic opportunities available to you, and try something new both academically and non-academically. 3. Get out and get around! Berkeley is beautiful, but there is so much more to experience and see around the Bay Area and in California (and the US as a whole).
other_useful_info: It can be a bit unsafe, so don't go out alone at night, especially not if under the influence of alcohol.
most_rewarding: Meeting some really special people and getting to learn from some fantastic professors and students. And the weather!
greatest_challenge: My greatest challenge was trying to balance academic work with social life, and finding people with whom I share interests on such a big and busy campus.

crucial_aspects: In the process of choosing a destination, I was looking for a university with a good research profile that fits my academic interest. At the same time, I wanted to improve my English and be in a region that also interests me culturally. The Bay Area seemed like the perfect place for that.
info_ease: It was very easy. KU and Berkeley had many resouces available and were easy to reach in case I had questions. The Berkeley International Office kind of spams you with information, so it's hard to miss the important things. All communtication was quick and uncomplicated. The COVID regulations were a bit confusing as it was not sure if and how the States would let students in, but that's due to the unpredicable nature of the pandemic. The international office tried their best to give all the support I needed.
arrival_assistance: I used the resources available on the Berkeley International Office website. The mandatory Golden Bear Orientation week is supposed to provide new students with all information they need. I didn't attend because I got COVID, but also felt that at that time I already knew everything I needed for the start of the semester.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Classes are selected in Cal Central, the univerity's course system. A course catalog is available on the Berkeley website too, including all necessary information.
registration_help: Everythin should be covered in GBO and in the mails sent out by BIO and the university.
registration_success: Many classes I wanted to take were full when it was my turn to select. I had to be flexible, but in the end I ended up with classes I was interested in.
registration_advice: Select you classes as early as possible. It's a good idea to have a list of classes prepared beforehand, which gives you some flexibility in case courses are full. Don't waste your time on long waitlists.
course_level: The level of classes is similar to the ones in CPH but the workload is very high. I recommend taking as few classes as possible to not be burried in assignments for the entire stay. Many Berkeley students are stressed-out by the high workload and put a lot of pressure on themselves to perform well in the classes.
teaching_comparison: The lecures themselves are less personal than in CPH, but the contact to the professors is very casual. Many of them offer office hours which are great to talk about the materials, homework, or their research, and many of them offer to talk about personal issues too. The classes I had were structured into lecture, tutorial, and office hours and included weekly or bi-weekly assignments. Classes go for one semester with mid-terms and finals. Together with the scores on the assignments they determine the final grades.
courses_enrolled: Carbon Cycle Dynamics Geo-Information Systems Individual Research on Remote Sensing Chamber Chorus
recommended_courses: Carbon Cycle Dynamics was a great choice. It's taught by Inez Fung, who is one of the leading scientists in that field and one of Joe Biden's scientific advisors. Listening to her personal stories gave me a great insight in how the climate science community works and how it's connected to politics and economy. In her office hours we had great discussions about many climate change related topics.
unexpected_costs: The University tries to force students into their SHIP health insurance program. This is complete non-sense, as it offers the same as other insurances at an exorbitant price. SHIP can be waived with an insurance that complies with the university's standards. I waived it with the cheapest insurance I could find on https://www.isoa.org/ and just in case got a european international insurance on top (which is not accepted for the waiver, but covers more than ISO). Through that I could save a lot of money even though I technically was covered by 2 insurances.
cost_comparison: The prices are kind of similar, if not a little higher than in Europe. Housing is extremely expensive. The local transit (in the east-bay region) is free for Berkeley students. Also, the basic needs center hands out free food supplies once a week, which is another way to reduces costs if needed.
activities_available: Literally everyting you can think of. Some societies are very sought after at it can be that you have to pass several rounds of interviews to be accepted (mostly for business clubs).
activities_recommended: Getting involved in one of the many clubs at Berkeley is a good way to meet people and get involved in the unique campus culture in Berkeley. I joined the chamber chorus and took some DeCal classes in Swing dance.
weekend_recommendations: Get to know the Bay Area and everything that's around it, such as Yosemite NP, Kings Canyon NP, Sequoia NP, Lassen NP, Point Reyes, Santa Cruz, Big Sur, ... There's a lot to see! Californians are very outdoorsy, so its never a probem to get good recommendations and travel buddies. And as I said, the outdoor club might do the trick...
culture_adjustment: Very easy. I feel in many ways the american culture is not so different from the European (at least it's still a "western" society).
socializing_tips: I found friends in the co-ops, GBO, courses, and in the societies I joined on campus. Many students are open-minded and it is easy to make first contact. Despite the cliche that many americans seem superficial at first, I found people I'm sure I'm gonna stay in contact with beyond my stay abroad.
cultural_challenges: Berkeley and the Bay Area in general is in a severe housing crisis, which results in many people living on the streets. For someone coming from a country with a working social system and healthcare, it is shocking to see how big the gap between poor and rich is in the US and especially here in the Bay. Going to Berkeley sometimes seemed like being in the proverbial Ivory Tower, as the university provides good oportunities for their students, but massively contributes to the housing shortage in the city.
culture_appreciated: Berkeley probably is the most tolerant and diverse place i've seen so far. It's great to see how the university and the student body tries to fight discrimination as much as possible. This stands very much in contrast to many other regions in the US.
top3_advice: 1) Be fast and do things ASAP (housing, visa, tickets, etc) 2) Join clubs and societies to find people you like (and get out of the international bubble) 3) Don't let yourself be dragged into the stressed-out Berkeley mentality
other_useful_info: Bring warm clothes. Berkeley and especially SF is colder then you think!
most_rewarding: Being part of this amazing campus culture with all the traditions that I thought would only exist in the movies, and at the same time getting to know so many people with such a positive spirit who want to do something about the world's problems.
greatest_challenge: I had some trouble finding the right people in the beginning, as I had covid during the onboarding week and could not take part in the social activities. That, however, improved shortly after the beginning of the semester.

crucial_aspects: I chose UC Berkeley as my exchange destination for one because my brother lived an hour away. Another crucial point was the level of education that I expected from the institution I visited. UC in general is known for being a group of universities with a higher academic level than usual, and Berkeley, which I visited, has a very great academic reputation.
overall_comments: While the academic level of UC Berkeley was very high, that was mostly felt in the research department. The research department received most of the funding available, which left the education part rather underfunded and as a result made the courses resource strained. This was evident in the fact that the courses, while requiring much more work as a result of a very high workload, did not necessarily explore much more material than covered in the respective courses at KU. However, and I cannot stress this enough, what made my exchange experience the most worthwhile was the relationship I got with my professors. Your education at Berkeley and the rest of the UC locations will be greatly improved if you go to office hours with the professors and the TAs. This made for many interesting discussions and learning much more outside the curriculum.
info_ease: It depends on how much you've prepared beforehand. The US isn't known for its fantastic public infrastructure and it shows. The university is great at giving information about the university itself, the campus and its surroundings, and the local amenities, but outside that sphere you're on your own. I highly recommend preparing beforehand, such as reading about the public transport available and downloading Uber of Lyft beforehand just in case, and having a way of using data in the US before you take off.
arrival_assistance: I received help from the university most parts in relation to the covid situation in Berkeley. Omicron was raging at that time and given I had just landed I knew nothing about the situation or how I should go about dealing with it. I recommend getting in touch with the university if you have questions!

I had a course going for 15 weeks with 12 homework, 6 quizzes, a programming assignment, a midterm, and a final exam. All this for what amounted to 9 ects. In other studies the workload will be higher but not to the same degree, as science was known to have a hard workload.
teaching_comparison: There was a larger focus on interaction with the professors. We had professors constantly tell us to approach them if we had issues, and one professor sent mails to each of the students that did not pass the midterm to ask them what they struggled with and if they wanted to come to office hours. It also takes a lot more work to learn the same material, as evident in the example earlier, for which the material was the same as the material in the KU equivalent course.
