crucial_aspects: I have always wanted to come to the Bay Area to experience the pulsing start-up scene and better understand why this area in particular is so good at it.
info_ease: Really easy UC Berkeley treated UCEAP students much better than other international students from universities without an exchange agreement.
arrival_assistance: We where part of the orientation together with students transferring from other colleges and thus got the all needed information. If I could give some feedback it would be to taylor it slightly more to internationals as we got a bit to much irrelevant information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registration at UC Berkeley was very easy. I recommend doing it ASAP as you will need the papers for your visa application, which is a longer process
registration_help: If in doubt you can write the Berkeley International Office
registration_success: Very – UCEAP students get to register at the same time as transfer students (around 2 months before) and most of the courses I considered was not filled at that point. Additionally there is a add-and-drop period the first month where people change courses
registration_advice: One can sign up to at most 20 units at UC Berkeley, this is equivalent to around ~ 50 ECTS (I needed just 12 UC Berkeley units to get my 30 ETCS). I recommend using all of those 20 units and then drop courses later as some will get filled.
course_level: I took 1 graduate level course, ECON 230B Public Economics. It was the continuation of 230A which I had not taken but felt like I could still follow the course without any problems and the level was on par with a master's course at UCPH. I also took 3 upper-division undergrad courses (as a undergrad UCEAP student you are allow to take just 1 grad-course) though upper-division I would say the level is below what I had in the final year of my bachelor's degree. I believe the reason for this is the fact that people can choose courses much more freely than at UCPH and thus they have to start at a lower level to ensure people without a background in e.g. economics can follow an upper-division econ course.
teaching_comparison: The style itself is similar to that of UCPH, however the grading is not done anonymously as at UCPH. In some courses showing up to class is counted towards the grade and even in the case where it is not as grading is not done anonymously having some sort of relationship with the professor could help sway your grade. This I am personally not a fan of but just part of the system unfortunately.
courses_enrolled: ECON 230B Public Economics, ECON 148 Data Science for Economists, ECON 136 Financial Economics, UGBA 128 Strategic Cost Management
recommended_courses: ECON 230B is a great course for all economics masters students I would say and further it is currently taught by Emanuel Saez. ECON 148 is a great Data Science course with a focus on applications to economists but easily generalized to other social sciences and only basic economics is needed to understand the course. As DATA (their data science major) is quiet popular it might be easier to get ECON 148 than a DATA course.
unexpected_costs: To be honest not really that many unexpected costs I had foreseen most. The only thing is just that California, and the Bay in particular is crazy expensive.
cost_comparison: All prices are similar to what you would pay in Denmark except clothing where you can get some good deals.
activities_available: There are casual sports clubs e.g., running, hiking, dancing, etc. However, as UC Berkeley is a university with, lets be honest, many over achievers a lot of the clubs are centered around something more serious. I counted at least 10 different investment clubs and 20+ consulting clubs – I personally did not participate in this as I was not here for that reason.
activities_recommended: Go watch basket games and if in here during fall also football games, it is an experience especially when facing the UC Berkeley rivals from Standford.
weekend_recommendations: San Francisco is obvious but for something more go to the national parks e.g. Yosemite or Sequoia or take a plane somewhere. It is relatively cheap to fly to San Diego/Los Angeles/Las Vegas etc.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: It is difficult, I only have a few people I would consider friends from the US, most are very young.
cultural_challenges: Not really.
culture_appreciated: Very specific to the Bay Area, but the entrepreneurial spirit was nice to experience
top3_advice: Time is limited, make the most of it while you can. It is not as difficult as one might believe (some classes I considered easy for most last year bachelor's student or a master's student as long as they are within your field). Seize the day, just by talking to people I have ended up at networking events at investment banks and A.I. conferences in Palo Alto.
other_useful_info: Not really.
most_rewarding: Friendships
greatest_challenge: Balancing traveling and studies

crucial_aspects: Having always wanted to experience the american college culture first-hand, I felt compelled to go to a school in the US. Having a whole town of only college students around the university really helped the case for choosing UCSB in specific; while I did want the quintessential college experience, I still wanted to be in California, where I could (somewhat) easily go to SF or LA for shows or friends.
info_ease: People, both at my home university, and the university i was an exchange student at were incredibly helpful. Every time I had a problem that I needed additional information for, I would write a short message or email, and I would get accurate help very fast.
arrival_assistance: Since I was lucky enough to live in student housing, the whole process of picking up keys and move-in times was a bit confusing to me at first. After a short email correspondence, I was all set.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You would have certain pass times. When it was your pass time, you would simply log onto the website that was used for course registration (GOLD), and there you would select your class and the section time you wanted to attend (given that there were more available spaces)
registration_help: In the case you couldn't register for courses, you could email or book consultations with different people in the respective departments.
registration_success: I got all courses besides one. I had a problem with prerequisites not aligning perfectly, but after discussing it with 3-4 different people, it went to the chair of the department and then i was approved by my professor in the course.
registration_advice: Email, email, email. Book consulting, do it early and be consistent (to the point where you might be a little annoying)
course_level: I did a couple of upper-division courses, but I did not delve into MA courses.
teaching_comparison: The lectures were much shorter, and there was a bigger focus on sections.
courses_enrolled: Music Appreciation, Introduction to Astronomy, Machine Learning. Emerging Adulthood, Introduction to Human Sexuality, Programming Languages.
recommended_courses: Introduction to Human Sexuality. It was such a fun class. It was taught by an old couple that had a lot of knowledge to share. Despite the topic being a little odd, it was super insightful, and you learn a lot of things that you would never learn in standard sex-ed (even for european standards)
unexpected_costs: This was not really an unexpected cost, but the structure was unexpected. When you live in student housing, you pay rent for 3 months instead of doing it monthly.
cost_comparison: Beer and meat was a bit expensive. Costco Rotisserie Chicken was cheap, and so was their hotdog.
activities_available: Pretty much every sport you can think of. However, there was no american football. There was also a bunch of different clubs - meditation club, korean christian societies, and of course greek life.
activities_recommended: Join a sports club, and perhaps a club with a focus on work. By doing that you develop a strong network in the US
weekend_recommendations: Red Rocks (Nevada), Santa Cruz, San Luis Obispo, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Yosemite were some really fun trips. Hawaii is also great during thanksgiving - if you have no one to spend it with, you might as well enjoy an incredibly beautiful state.
culture_adjustment: It took me 1 months to adjust to everything. This is rather slow, but I found small unexplainable differences in culture that i was unable to ignore for some reason. After the first month it was a bunch of fun.
socializing_tips: Talk to people. Everyone is super open, and really interested in your "exoticness"
cultural_challenges: People being very friendly off the get-go.
culture_appreciated: People being very friendly off the get-go.
top3_advice: 1. Have fun, 2. Befriend the locals, 3. Look for unusual opportunities that are available in the US but not back home. In my case, an unusual opportunity was djing at local college bars.
other_useful_info: Not everyone will accept a danish drivers license as a valid ID
most_rewarding: Building relations all over the state. Of course, there has been a bunch of atomized experiences that I really enjoy, but I believe I will look back on my exchange with much fondness of all the people I met and befriended.
greatest_challenge: Learning to be more honest with everyone.

crucial_aspects: I wanted somewhere with good academic opportunities combined with a vibrant social life, which I very much found to be the case.
overall_comments: Highly recommend
info_ease: Overall okay, make sure to research a bit about the places where you can find the relevant information, but both the people at UCPH and UC Berkeley were happy to help. I would also highly suggest seeking advice among the other people how either have gone or are going to the same destination.
arrival_assistance: Mostly emails about the relevant events from the central office, although I gennerally found information for exchange students to be lacking. Often we were being lumped together with American transfer students who did not always face the same questions and problems.
arrival_comments: Be prepared to not know everything in the beginning, everyone is trying their best to have everyone informed but sometimes it will take some time before you know all the relevant information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Highly recommend
registration_process: After creating your login you can access the regestration site. Here you can browse through the available courses and build your class schedule which while a little complicated is actually super nice once you learn how to use it. Once you have build your schedule you can save that. You will then have a specific date where registration opens and you can get your preferred classes. I did not find it hard to get in to my classes as I applied early but spots fill up relatively quickly. Also REMEMBER TO CHECK YOUR EXAMS as they are all crammed into one week they may overlap, so be prepared with alternatives.
registration_help: A few emails were sent out, but you can find people explaining it on YouTube as well.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted but found out two of them had overlapping exams, so I later had to switch one of them out, which was not a problem.
registration_advice: Try to sign up as early as possible if you have a class that is very important to you.
academics_comments: Highly recommend
course_level: All the courses were upper division undergraduate courses the level was very similar to UCPH courses.
teaching_comparison: Gennerally it's similar. You do, though, have significantly less time spent in small classes/sections - often only one hour for every 3 hours of lecture meaning that the instructor/GSI has way less time to cover the material that the lecturer has covered in lecturer. This means more studying by yourself, so be prepared for that.
courses_enrolled: Game Theory in the Social Sciences Industrial Organization and Public Policy Public Economics The Chinese Economy
recommended_courses: All of the courses were good, I was particularly happy with Industrial Organization as the professor was really engaged in the material and had good sense of humor - although it was also the hardest course.
unexpected_costs: Food is expensive, so while I had food included in my housing I easily spend a lot on that especially because you have to tip everywhere.
cost_comparison: Buses are free (in the Berkeley area) which was amazing but food was expensive and also renting a car if you plan on day tripping.
activities_available: They have a club for almost everything, chess, soccer, quidditch, political groups, ball room dancing, music, journalism, entrepreneurship, basket ball and so much more. They have a dedicated day where all the clubs assemble on one of the plazas and you can hear more about them.
activities_recommended: As mentioned clubs are a great way to meet people, I also suggest attending some of the many activities hosted for both exchange students as well as all students in general. While some may be more interesting than others they are a great way to meet people especially in the first weeks.
weekend_recommendations: Remember to set money aside to go on weekend road trips. California is full of amazing nature e.g. Highway 1/Big Sur, Yosemite, Lake Tahoe, Sierra Nevada and so on. It's also relatively cheap to fly to amazing places such as San Diego, Mexico, Hawaii and Las Vegas.
culture_adjustment: I found Americans to be very open and talkative. The cultural differences aren't huge and people are generally happy to engage with you.
socializing_tips: As I said, joining clubs, attending university organized events, Taco Tuesdays are a big thing, even starting conversations with people in your classes can lead to unexpected socializing.
cultural_challenges: A lot of people at Berkeley are really ambitious and have busy schedules meaning that organizing hangouts can sometimes be a hassle.
culture_appreciated: How easy going and talkative Americans are. They are very easy to make friends with if you make the effort.
top3_advice: Be open to new experiences and people, you're almost guaranteed to have a fun time. Be prepared to be a bit confused/overwhelmed in the beginning as information is lacking. Go on several weekend/holiday trips, California is amazing.
other_useful_info: Remember that it's way easier to change classes after registration at Berkeley compared to UCPH so if your schedule is causing trouble or the class is not working for some reason research other cases you can swap it for (off course while checking that it works with your studies back home)
most_rewarding: The friendships I got and the trips I went on.
greatest_challenge: All the midterms/exams are in hand. If you're not used to handwriting be prepared for that.

crucial_aspects: I've always been fascinated with the country to which i travelled. Also, the weather is much better and I had an opportunity to combine sunshine culture with academic learning which is very different from Denmark.
overall_comments: California is extremely expensive which limits your opportunities. Furthermore, UCSD seemed extremely indifferent about the international students, we didn't get an introduction to anything, basically landed on Jan 4th and started school on jan 7th without introductions to classes, systems or enrollment. San Diego is a great city though, and the overall quality of life is high there.
info_ease: Really difficult. Felt like there was a big gap between UC and KU.
arrival_assistance: There was no help what so ever. I had an online 45 min course with 3 students talking about their lives. Non-school related mostly. That was it.
arrival_comments: Please do some sort of introduction to the system. People land 3 days before school starts due to quarter structure which means you can't even get into it once you're there before you start classes.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: California is extremely expensive which limits your opportunities. Furthermore, UCSD seemed extremely indifferent about the international students, we didn't get an introduction to anything, basically landed on Jan 4th and started school on jan 7th without introductions to classes, systems or enrollment. San Diego is a great city though, and the overall quality of life is high there.
registration_process: You use WebReg to sign up and EASy to get pre-reqs approved so you can take non-introduction courses. Be aware that the first 2 weeks are trial weeks so you can shuffle around courses there which I highly recommend.
registration_help: none.
registration_success: It went okay. I was lucky during my first quarter that what I ended up taking was open in week 2.
registration_advice: Register early! The good courses go quickly. Furthermore, try to time your classes, so you only have to be on campus twice a week. Use the free movement in the first two weeks to find what you like.
academics_comments: California is extremely expensive which limits your opportunities. Furthermore, UCSD seemed extremely indifferent about the international students, we didn't get an introduction to anything, basically landed on Jan 4th and started school on jan 7th without introductions to classes, systems or enrollment. San Diego is a great city though, and the overall quality of life is high there.
course_level: Undergrad courses from year 2-4. Most courses are pretty easy and geared towards memorization of specific syllabus stuff.
teaching_comparison: Very different and geared towards memorization. All tests are by hand and mostly without notes. Finals are buzzword bingo where they are just looking for specific words and concepts. You are not really encouraged to think by yourself a lot. I had 1 course which was a project exam over the entire 10 weeks, and that worked really well.
courses_enrolled: POLI 142A - United States Foreign Policy POLI 175 - Machine Learning/Social Sciences POLI 176 - Text as Data POLI 124A - Pol Conseq/Electoral Systems POLI 140D - It'l Human Rights Law Migrants POLI 145C - Interntnl Reltations After Cold War
recommended_courses: POLI 176 and POLI 175. They are taught with learning in mind and taught interactively via use of assignments and code alongs. Profs are experienced and competent. Be aware that softer poli sci courses are taught by lecture style only with very little interactive learning and little else than just reading.
unexpected_costs: Food is very expensive even when you live off of basic groceries. Regarding housing, bills for water, electrical and heating are not included in the base rent.
cost_comparison: Food is very expensive. Going out is fairly priced. Recreation such as the Zoo or museums are very expensive too.
activities_available: There are a few different clubs at school, but you are not introduced to them by the school, you have to find them for yourself. I found activities away from school instead.
activities_recommended: Surf! Go to surf school somewhere and find friends through sports such as volleyball, soccer, basketball or (like me) beach handball. Hiking is also very big and there are a lot of beautiful nature around!
weekend_recommendations: Surfing, hiking, exploring, sleeping in the desert. Trying Mexican food. Go watch baseball, watch basketball. Find small neighborhoods.
culture_adjustment: No difficulties at all. The American culture is well known, so I knew what to expect.
socializing_tips: It is very hard to get to know people at UCSD. Most people wake up, go to class, and then go back home. Find other international students, it can give you a nice base!
cultural_challenges: Americans talk A LOT and often they'll say things they don't mean: "We should totally go surfing next week" and then you don't hear from them in 5 months. You have to contact people and drive the social interactions, if you do not, no one will notice you and help you out of loneliness. Also, Americans are VERY loud in public, which takes some getting used to. They do not do it to be rude, that's just how they are.
culture_appreciated: The food, the sun, the chill vibe around the beach and surf culture.
top3_advice: Be aware of the quarter structure - I did 40 ECTS points because of it, and we had very little breaks. Bring money - California is awesome, but only if you can afford to do things like renting a car or seeing atractions. Be prepared for sketchy people - a lot of homeless and not-well people live there, and things such as public transportation can be scary.
other_useful_info: Please, be prepared for going to school from start Jan to mid June with few breaks. If you wanna take trips and explore, you can do it during the quarters without dying, but do it in the start of a quarter or after the midterms, they are not as intense there. Be aware of how important attendence is in your course.
most_rewarding: Getting to live on the beach and learn a new culture and skill!
greatest_challenge: Homesickness, loneliness and expenses
other_comments: Look for an American university with semesters - quarter structure means that you have to take 40 ECTS, go to school often and have to be there for app. 6 months which is a long time.

crucial_aspects: I’ve previously been on a language course in California as well as studying one year at Santa Barbara City College after high school. I always wanted to move back to California, and UCLA has been a dream school of mine every since I visited the campus for the first time as a 16 yo.
info_ease: It was rather easy, as long as you follow up on your emails etc. The International Office hosted an orientation day for International students. It was also held a welcome meeting for all study abroad students one evening as well. There is additionaly an online orientation you have to complete digitally. Remember to check you email for invites to all of these things. In general, the American people are super friendly and helpful - so please don’t hesitate to ask anyone about anything, and you will receive so much help!
arrival_assistance: There were tents outside my housing building with people who gave me the room card and showed me where I was located. My roommates helped me find the location to get a Bruin card (school id) and showed me around campus and the city.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I received an email from the Political Science deparment that they could guarantee only one course for students like me (in the UCLA system I counted as a third-year transfer student and pre-Political Science major (even though I’m in fact a graduate student). So I received a pte number for the class I most wanted. When you receive a pte number, it let’s you enroll in the class regardless if it says the class is full. Every student get’s a registration date and time, and my experience was that every quarter I received a few days earlier registration day than all of my other 7 roommates. But regardless I was prohibited from enrolling in a lot of popular Political Science classes I wanted because I was only pre-Political Science major, so I had to wait until the second enrollment appointment that comes up a bit later whereas many classes could have filled up. However, I found out that reaching out politely to Professors, they would almost always assign me a pte-number because they think a background as an international graduate student is so interesting they want to have you in their class. This is also the only way to enroll in graduate classes if you want to do that, since your major at UCLA is technically on underhraduate level the registration system won’t let you enroll automatically. In the first week or two of classes you can drop classes if you don’t like them after all, and enroll in any other class where a seat opens up.
registration_help: My first quarter the department helped me enroll in that one class I wanted, but the two other quarters I was on my own and the councelor literally didn’t reply until my enrollment appointment was over, so you have to be «on the ball» yourself a lot in the enrollment period.
registration_success: Very succesful.
registration_advice: Reaching out to the Professors directly. And please do not miss your enrollment appointment, be on time for registering before the classes fill up.
course_level: The level is approx like at home except you have a lot more school work to do than at KU.
teaching_comparison: At KU we are used to only having one exam at the end of the semester, but at UCLA you usually have at least one midterm, a final, and papers and quizzes throughout the quarter. The quarter is only 10/11 weeks and you have at least 3 classes, so you can make the math that there is almost always a test to study for or a paper to write. In my experience the graduate classes were a lot less work in, usually just a term paper. However, you cannot skip the readings! The classes are very discussion based. And for all your subjects, it’s quite impossible to read up just before your exam like is more common at KU. I really liked this aspect of the academics, you quite literally can’t be lazy over there haha.
courses_enrolled: International Law. International Development: culture, power and development. International Relations Seminar with Arthur Stein about the decline of the liberal world order.
recommended_courses: My favorite professors were Prof Chun and Prof Zipperstein - any class with them <3
unexpected_costs: That it was impossible to waive the UCSHIP insurance even though I had just payed for a super good insurance from home. Sl after many tries to waive it I had to pay for that which is like over 1000 dollar each quarter :/
cost_comparison: Daily coffees.. haha
activities_available: So many different kinds, I wish I got even more information about the clubs because the opportunities are unlimited.
activities_recommended: Take use of the facilites at school. B-fitness and Wooden Center, Sunset Rec etc.
weekend_recommendations: I went a lot to the beach at Santa Monica to tan when I had the time. I also went a lot to the Westfield mall at Century City. Hanging out in Westwood, to get a night-time snack at Diddy Riese cookies or going to in-n-out after parties. I also recommend to travel up to and see San Francisco, and down to San Diego. As well as Palm Springs for the Coachella Festival.
culture_adjustment: Easy because I’ve always felt very at home in America with the more friendly culture. Everyone is super interested in you as a foreigner and very helpful.
socializing_tips: When people say «let’s grab coffee sometime» actually hold them up to it and arrange for it by asking later when they are free for it. That’s how I got to know my best friend whi I met in class, and also many other friends.
cultural_challenges: Obviously seeing homeless and obvious psychotic people on the streets takes a while to get used to and not freaked out by them every time. I had some not-pleasant experiences in this regard. Also that the smell of weed is everywhere, it is so common since it is legalized.
culture_appreciated: Their friendliness, openness, and warm culture. The daily small talk. The gentlemen culture.
top3_advice: Be aware of the cost of UCSHIP at UCLA campus since you won’t be allowed to waive it here. Be open to people, experiences and many great opportunities will come your way. Say yes to everything (except drugs, hehe). Enjoy it, it passes way too quick and it is the most amazing time :)
other_useful_info: Funfacts: To know about the famous undierun at UCLA and the midnight screams during final weeks. Also the library is open 24/7 before midterms and finals - I’ve spent many whole nights at Powell Library haha.
most_rewarding: The friends I’ve made - many who I know will be my lifelong best friends.
greatest_challenge: I didn’t find anything particularily challenging.

overall_comments: Berkeley is a great place with very nice people! I had some great lectures there, who I connected with on a personal level. I can recommend

crucial_aspects: UC Berkely is a renowned university with high academic standards and some of the best professors in the world.
info_ease: There was a lot information to gather but I think the meetings (and particularly the slideshow from the meetings) were very helpful and informative. However, it would be convenient with one document in which all information you need for the specific UC campus is gathered because it is still very widespread where to find some specific information.
arrival_assistance: I was welcomed to the university by some guides for new students and exchange students.
arrival_comments: The UCEAP reciprocity website is very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Before you attend the university, you get a time slot from which you can make an early registration for courses. It is a good idea to enroll in the courses in the early registration phase, as some of the popular courses are quickly full. After that, when you arrive at Berkeley the first couple of weeks are a so-called "add and drop period" where you can attend different classes and are able to switch courses.
registration_help: A detailed description of the course registration schedule can be found at the university's website.
registration_success: I was somewhat succesful. I got most of the course that I wanted to, however, there was one course that I didn't get, which is because full-time students get earlier access for the early registration phase than exchange students, thus the cornerstone courses can be hard to register for.
registration_advice: Exploit the add and drop period and attend a lot of different classes in the beginning of the semester.
course_level: I both took undergraduate and graduate courses. I was at my first semester of my master's when I attended Berkeley, and I would say that the graduate courses were at a very high level (and extremely insightful) and can probably be compared to PhD courses at the UCPH, while the level of the undergraduate are in general quite low (even though you can find courses that are still at an advanced level on the undergrad).
teaching_comparison: There were a much larger focus on recent findings in research and explaining the economic trends, while the style of teaching at UCPH is much more textbook based.
courses_enrolled: Graduate Public Economics, Global Inequality and Growth, Topics in Economic Research, Econometrics: Advanced Methods and Applications.
recommended_courses: Public Economics at the graduate level with Emmanuel Saez and Mathilde Munoz is probably the most exciting and inspiring course I have through my entire time of studying. You learned very much and directly from the research frontier. I can highly recommend that course.
unexpected_costs: No unexpected fees
cost_comparison: Housing was very expensive. I knew before that it was expensive but considering what you get for the amount of moeny you pay then it was crazy.
activities_available: Almost all the types of sports you can imagine are available for students for free or for a very low expense.
activities_recommended: I was a part of a soccer club where we participated in a tournament against other teams of Berkeley students. I can very much recommend doing that sort of social activities.
weekend_recommendations: I very much enjoyed just spending time on campus and maybe going to San Francisco once in a while. For me the purpose of the exchange stay was not to explore the entire California, but on the other hand to try to get the sense of what it means to be a UC Berkeley student and to live like a local. Therefore, I didn't travel that much around but enjoyed my weekends in Berkeley/SF.
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Join a sports club or live at residence halls or co-ops.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The pride and identity associated with being a student of a top university.
top3_advice: 1. Be well-prepared before you go such that you can get the most out of your time while you are there. 2. Try not to live at an apartment or anything similar because living with many other people is a great part of the experience and you potentially get a huge international network and learn many things about other countries and cultures. If you want to save money look at co-ops instead of apartments. 3. Enjoy your time and try to be engaged in the UC Berkeley community by joining sports clubs, going to social events, and being active in your courses (e.g., it is a great opportunity that you are able to go office hours)
other_useful_info: I don't think so.
most_rewarding: The academic experience.
greatest_challenge: Balancing social life and academics.

info_ease: Blandet oplevelse. Gode råd: lav et dokument med alle dine emails og koder til de forskellige portaler, fordi der er mange ting at huske. Og lav en gruppechat med alle dem, som skal samme sted hen - det kan være uvurderligt at have flere øjne på tingene.
arrival_assistance: Man skulle melde sig til mindst et welcome event, så jeg var på en campus tour - dette var fedt, fordi her mødte jeg mange af de andre udvekslingsstuderende fra andre lande, som man kommer til at rende ind i resten af sit ophold.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Man får en individuel pass time, hvorfra man må melde sig på X antal point. Amerikanerne sidder klar præcist når deres pass time åbner, så nogle af fagene fyldes ret hurtigt. OBS: Husk selv at tjekke dette i god tid! Jeg missede min første pass time, fordi det var 3 måneder før afrejse, og ingen havde forklaret os systemet på det tidspunkt. Derudover husk at tjek før tid hvilke fag du vil have og om du har adgang til dette fag i UCSB's system - ellers vil jeg anbefale at skrive til en academic advisor eller en professor før din pass time, så de kan give dig en kode til registrere dig på faget.
registration_help: Jeg havde en academic advisor (han var indenfor psykologi, ved ikke om andre studier har dette) - men han clearede mig til alle de psykologi-fag jeg ville tage, så det var en stor hjælp. Så jeg kunne nøjes med at sende ham mine karakter-beviser fra KU en enkelt gang, og derfra "kendte" han mig, således jeg ikke skulle udfylde et skema hver gang jeg ville tage et nyt fag.
registration_success: Ret succesfuld. De fleste er meget hjælpsomme hvis du forklarer, at du er udvekslingsstuderende.
registration_advice: Vær ude i god tid og få en god ide om hvilke fag du vil have - du må også gerne tage fag i andre departments end din egen major.
course_level: Jeg tog upper division undergraduate classes, fordi UC aftalen kun er en undergraduate aftale. Dog var jeg i dialog med en professor på UCSB, som tilbød mig en plads på et lille graduate-fag, så det er muligt nogle gange at finde graudate fag, selvom det er lidt sværere.
teaching_comparison: Det er ikke dårlig undervisning, men det er lidt anderledes - de kører en del med tests og points, specielt multiple choice tests. De forholder sig ikke så kritisk til viden, men de er til gengæld gode til at huske den.
courses_enrolled: Laboratory in Advanced Research Methods Psychology of Gender Close Relationships
recommended_courses: Har ikke noget specifikt - de ændrer sig hele tiden, vær nysgerrig og undersøg noget der lyder sjovt, hvis du har plads til det.
unexpected_costs: Ikke uforventet men sæt lidt penge af til nogle ture (leje af bil, hotel osv.)
cost_comparison: Californien er ret dyrt, så husleje og mad er generelt dyrt
activities_available: Recreation Center (gratis) på campus har et vildt bredt udvalg af ting at lave Man kan melde sig på sportshold eller bare gå i fitness selv. Der er også svømmebaner og jacuzzi og tennisbaner til fri afbenyttelse
activities_recommended: Excursion Club er en studenter-drevet organisation, som tager på en masse ture og laver en masse små og store aktiviteter hver eneste uge. Koster 30 dollars at være med pr. semester
weekend_recommendations: LA, San Diego, Solvang, Yosemite, Lake Tahoe, Big Sur Hikes i lokalområdet
culture_adjustment: Både let og svært - amerikanere er meget snaksaglige, så det er nemt at møde folk, men alle udvekslingsstuderende jeg har mødt er generelt enige om at amerikanere er generelt sagt ret overfladiske og ret unge / umodne. Generelt fik jeg dybere relationer til andre udvekslingsstuderende end amerikanere, men det er stadig godt at få gode lokale tips fra amerikanere
socializing_tips: Sig ja hvis nogen inviterer med til noget som helst (hvis du har lyst self), men vær åben overfor nye ting.
cultural_challenges: Amerikanere er meget unge (de starter oftest på uni når de er 17-18) så man er ofte 4-5 år ældre end folk man møder. Dette kan godt lidt mærkes, fx når det handler om at bo sammen osv.
culture_appreciated: Meget åbenhed og meget umiddelbarhed. Der sker masser af spontane ting og det virker til at folk på UCSB sætter så meget pris på deres omgivelser og den smukke natur omkring campus, hvilket smitter meget af
top3_advice: UCSB er et dejligt lokalt sted - det føles meget trygt og man kan nemt komme til og fra det hele med cykel og bus. UCSB ligger ikke i midtbyen Santa Barbara - det ligger ca. 15 km væk fra byen, så det skal man bare være klar over. Man kan nemt og gratis tage bussen ind til byen dog (tager 20-30 minutter). Husk at nyd det hele, også regnvejrs-dagene. Tiden flyver afsted
other_useful_info: USCB har tænkt sig at prøve at give dig deres health insurance men den er altså virkelig dyr og der er mange penge at spare, hvis du waiver med en privat forsikring. ISO virker til dette og det er meget billigere.
most_rewarding: De relationer jeg har fået derfra og følelsen af at have stablet alt det på benene og det hele lykkedes i sidste ende. Det er det hele værd <3
greatest_challenge: Der er utroligt mange praktiske ting, der skal falde i hak samtidig - forsikring, fagregistrering, forhåndsgodkendelse, visum, bolig osv. Det bliver hurtigt overvældende, men det glemmer man når man først har løst det.

crucial_aspects: I am torn between choosing acedemic opportunities or explore new cultures, because they were equally influential in my choiec to go abroad for a semester. I wanted new imput, and I wanted to experience how it is to attend university in another country. As much as I love UCPH I also craved different perspectives and ways to approach learning about my major.
overall_comments: This exchange came at the perfect time for me, I gained so many awesome experiences, and I return with a renewed energy for mu studies and new eyes for my home city :')
info_ease: That was pretty easy. We all received an email with all the information. It was a little delayed but it came and everything was fine.
arrival_assistance: The UCEAP office (education abroad program) was very helpful - I recommend contacting them if you have any questions.
arrival_comments: I also called the UCEAP office with questions about my UCEAP application and got a hold of Paulette. She was so so helpful and she asisted me in bettering my application besides solving the technical issue I initially called her about.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: This exchange came at the perfect time for me, I gained so many awesome experiences, and I return with a renewed energy for mu studies and new eyes for my home city :')
registration_process: After applying for a minimum of three of the UC campus locations (where you submit a study plan for each location) you receive your placement and get your host university. Then you have to enroll in your courses during your pass time. This happens after a first come firs serve principle, and I recommend you enlist as soon as possible. Many of the courses require an add code to enroll (especially if you choose outside your enlisted major) - you can get the add code by writing the professor teaching the course. It's a good idea to know which courses you want and to have collected the add codes for them before yur pass time opens.
registration_help: I found emailing the professors directly very helpful.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted, but this can be more difficult to achieve with other majors. I study psychology, and the prerequisites for this major overlaps with the prereqs for many other social sciences.
registration_advice: As I wrote above: email the professors and enroll asap :)
academics_comments: This exchange came at the perfect time for me, I gained so many awesome experiences, and I return with a renewed energy for mu studies and new eyes for my home city :')
course_level: I found the level of my courses somewhat alike to the level we have at home at UCPH. This was not the case for some of my friends in other majors, who found them way easier. I don't think I have heard about someone experiencing them as more difficult at UCSB than UCPH, but the UCSB certainly offered different perspectives that were fresh and interesting to me.
teaching_comparison: There are more test, assignments, and midterm exams throughout the quarter than we have at UCPH - this takes some of the weight off of the final exams, it seems more spread out. This can be a bit much, as you have to keep track of a lot of deadlines - but the assignments are usually small and I liked doing a bit all the time instead of a lot during finals week. Also, the quarters are super short (10 weeks) and there are no weeks without classes where you can revise material - this was new to me and a bit annoying, but we all managed, and it was not so bad.
courses_enrolled: Metaphilosophy (4 units, PHIL), Developmental Psychology (4 units, PSYCH), Cognitive Development (4 units, PSYCH), Health and Well Being (4 units, EDU), Organizing Difference (4 units, COMM), Corporate Social Responsibility (4 units, COMM), Global Ideologies and World Order (4 units, GLOBL)
recommended_courses: Health and Well Being. I learned a lot and Professor Shism's teaching style was so engaging that we all got to know each other reall well.
unexpected_costs: The cost of groceries was higher than I expected. But we had a food bank on campus where you could pick up food for free, and that helped a lot. I recommend using that if you want to save money on groceries.
cost_comparison: Look above
activities_available: So so many. I personnaly, joined a soccer team, attended free pilates classes every wednesday morning, went on trips with the excursion club - and I also recommend you go to some of the events in Campbell Hall - they have an Arts & Lectures programme, and students arrange a screening of The Rocky Horror Picture Show (must see).
activities_recommended: Look above :)
weekend_recommendations: I recommend you get together a group of frinds and borrow or rent a car and go places. California has so much to offer and road trips are awesome - these have been my favourite part of the exchange.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. People are very open and easy to talk to, and they are going to be curious about you and your home country, so the icebreaker is easy. And the chill vibe of a surfy campus by the beach is hard not to love.
socializing_tips: The excursion club!! This is a perfect place to meet friends. I paid only 60 bucks for being a member for the time I was there. Otherwise attend shoreline activities and try to talk to people. Also: Isla Vista occasionally offers band parties where local bands (often consisting of UCSB students) perform - and they are really really good. You can follow the instagram @soundsofiv where they post about when and where the concerts will take place. Once or twice a year they move the band party to a location in the mountains, and that is a magical experience.
cultural_challenges: This is really not a thing I struggled with a lot.
culture_appreciated: Their openness. Californians are not shy, and you can easily have a full blown conversation with a complete stranger.
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy your time there before it runs out 2. Join Excursion Club and go camping 3. Go watch the sunset at Sands Beach
other_useful_info: They have awesome thrift stores in Goleta. Old Town Coffee in Goleta is a nice café. Apna in Santa Barbara Downtown is a nice Indian place. You must go check out The Funk Zone in Santa Barbara Downtown if you like a chill and cozy night life more than clubbing (there is also super nice here during the day).
most_rewarding: The people I met and the places I saw <3
greatest_challenge: The time difference and missing my family friend, and boyfriend at home. But it is manageable if you plan your calls :)

crucial_aspects: Best university world wide for my major. Interesting culture of city. I wanted to connect with my dads family who I knew quite poorly that lived nearby.
overall_comments: Big difference between studying at a Danish vs. American university. This change was at times frustrating.
info_ease: The most difficult thing was becoming a citizen of a new country. A lot of paperwork and moving takes up the most of your time. Integrating into the school was easy. Therefor the assistance I needed was more geared towards being a citizen in a new country, which I felt very alone in. I was not really exposed to information regarding these aspects, so I'd say it was not easy to find.
arrival_assistance: I didn't get any assistance.
arrival_comments: Orientation grouping was poorly designed. I was grouped with first year college students of the ages 17-18 from other countries. I had a tough time relating to them. Also the orientation week was very weirdly planned, as there were not very many activities. We just walked around with our group. Then suddenly there were new groups and again we basically just walked around campus.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Big difference between studying at a Danish vs. American university. This change was at times frustrating.
registration_process: I had to fill in some stuff online and then when I got there I could pick up my student card the first day of orientation.
registration_help: Phone, internet, in person help on campus.
registration_success: I got all the stuff I wanted.
registration_advice: Be quick to register for classes so they don't fill up. Often many spots are reserved for students doing a major, so there are only few spots that are open to all. When studying at Berkeley, you are often, depending of your major, required to take 13 units. This exceeds the 12 units that translate to 30 acts points. Look for fun and easy classes with no exams that give 1 unit to get to the 13 in total.
academics_comments: Big difference between studying at a Danish vs. American university. This change was at times frustrating.
course_level: Often very good lectures, and interesting topics. There could be more fun, abstract and challenging papers or exams.
teaching_comparison: Very different. I have come to appreciate the freedom, focus on critical thinking and cooperative learning of UCPH more.
courses_enrolled: Social Psychology Sociology of Policing Development and Globalization Cult Cinema
recommended_courses: Development and Globalization was great. More political economy heavy, even though it is listed as a sociology course but it is very informative and interesting and the professor is GREAT. Very case specific.
unexpected_costs: Phone deals feel like scams Weekend trips and other stuff just adds up... Insurance is crazy expensive. DEFINETELY wave the school insurance and get your own for 1/4 of the price.
cost_comparison: Food was part of the rent at my cooperative housing
activities_available: Everything.
activities_recommended: Great sport facilities. Again, there is everything you could even think of.
weekend_recommendations: National parks in the states are amazing. Renting a car and driving is a must. My university had a deal with enterprise car rental which made it very affordable and waved the young driver fee.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. Annoying bureaucratic interactions.
socializing_tips: Live in a coop (cooperative housing). Do sports or other activities.
cultural_challenges: People are more overtly proud. Can seem like bragging to a Dane.
culture_appreciated: People are very open and friendly.
top3_advice: 1 Live in a coop! unless you are very freaked out about bad hygiene. 2 Wave SHIP insurance, get your own. 3 Be super disciplined about school. So many papers, if you falls behind once, you might never catch up again.
other_useful_info: USA west coast is built for cars. If you don't have a drivers licence get some friends that do. Driving around and seeing the nature of California should be high priority.
most_rewarding: Hanging out with people at the coop and a roadtrip after school was over (and seeing all of my family).
greatest_challenge: School was often unmotivating.

crucial_aspects: Not only is University of Berkeley a well-known university, it is also located near San Fransisco. I always wanted to experience living in the US and experience their culture. Further more the Bay Area is a hot-spot for innovation within the field of Biotechnology which is what I study at University of Copenhagen.
info_ease: Not that is easy to be honest. I have felt quite alone in the whole process.
arrival_assistance: None? but there was a introduction week on campus.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was not that difficult. It was more the application for the student VISA that was quite a tedious process.
registration_help: Online platforms.

courses_enrolled: Cell Engineering Inorganic Chemistry in Living Systems Synthetic Biology Basic Principles of Drug Delivery
recommended_courses: I recommend BIOE148 and BIOE124. Fantastic Professors and exciting course material.
unexpected_costs: Food is more expensive than in Denmark.
cost_comparison: You get free local transport with your Berkeley student ID!!!
activities_available: I joined the Berkeley Cheese Club! Good vibes and opportunity to meet new people.
activities_recommended: I recommend the Cheese Club :)
weekend_recommendations: Go to Yosemite it is stunning!
culture_adjustment: I found it a bit difficult in the beginning to adjust the the large population of homeless compared to Denmark. It can also be quite difficult to make friends during lectures.
socializing_tips: Meet other exchange students. Join clubs and societies that is how local students socialize, only few Berkeley students socialize during lecture.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: Americans are very kind and easy to talk to. It is not unusual that someone will come up to you and compliments your outfit :). Berkeley students (within the Bioengineering department at least) are highly motivated and get shit done. Every time I had to do a group presentation, every single person in the group was very dedicated and finished stuff on time. I really appreciated that.
top3_advice: - Take a fun course like a dcal course - Ask for help from fellow exchange students! - join a club or sports team etc.! - Remember that maybe it can be lonely in the beginning but you will make friends. - start scholarship (legat) applications early
other_useful_info: It is not as difficult to pass courses compared to Copenhagen University.. so remember to enjoy your time in the US. Furthermore remember that your grade is actually up for debate. You can contact the professor and ask them what you can do to get a better grade (which I am really not used to). So if you are about to pass a course, go talk to the professor.
most_rewarding: Living in the US and the friends that I made <3
greatest_challenge: making friends while also balancing school. It was difficult for me to go out and socialize when I have had a full day of school and assignments.

crucial_aspects: I chose Califorina to try what the American college experience is like. I also wanted to explore national parks and have great nature experiences and California is great for this.
overall_comments: It is fun but it is also tough. six months was enough for me i wouldn't want to stay for a full year.

registration_process: You log into the website called UCSB GOLD. Here you can find courses for next quarter and add them to your basket if you find them interesting you can also start to plan you schedule here. You get three pass times. In the first pass time you can select up to 8 units which is approx. two courses within your major. For each passtime more courses opens up from other faculties and you can fill in more units. You can add or drop courses on the first week of class without penalty and if a course is full you can "crash" in the first week and talk to the instructor who can ive out add codes. It is a good strategy to add more classes than you expect to take and try it out.
registration_help: The advisors at the different faculties. On email
registration_success: I got most of them. Soemtimes they took place at the same time and that is just unfortunate.
registration_advice: Write emails if you want soemthing. it is almost always possible to get in somehow. and crash courses in the beginning but make up your mind fast, because the instructors chooses the people thay have seen participate.

unexpected_costs: Food is way more expensive than expected. People in student housing needed to buy a lot of kitchen supplies. Uber is also very expensive but useful.
cost_comparison: Food was way more. Beer was a little more. ialmost didn't buy books because the taches didn't follow/use them and published nice notes or I could get them at the library.
activities_available: there were a lot of clubs and nice facilities for physical activity.
activities_recommended: Join the Excursion club they do fun trips and it is a nice way to meet people.
weekend_recommendations: Roadtrip is a classic. You can get far. Go to channel islands. Surf at devs.

socializing_tips: Tag along with housemates when they go out and do something and host some parties.
cultural_challenges: I mostly found the food and eating habits different and at times challenging. I just expected it to be more like home.
culture_appreciated: Being invited to something by complete strangers. They are very open to new people.
top3_advice: No need to do more than 12 units even thouh it is possible. Buy a wetsuit and borrow surfboards from excursion club (their wetsuits are very old) Find a group of international friends that also wanna go around Califrnia in the weekends and split the cost of renting a car.
other_useful_info: Don't buy the UC health insurance search up ISO and get the same for half the price.
most_rewarding: The American friends i now know who will come visit me here and i can visit in the future. An understanding of how americans think and live.
greatest_challenge: Being away from my partner at home.

registration_advice: Plan out way ahead of time which courses you are interested in. Read up on UCI's reddit page how to enrol in impacted courses. Message administrative employees regarding how to enrol in impacted courses. Message professors politely and display your interest in their course to be admitted ahead of other students.
course_level: The academic level in the US is a joke and is akin to high school in Denmark. Some courses, e.g., professor Novaco's "Violence in Society" was quite challenging, however. Sociology classes at UCPH are MUCH more challenging and rigorous. I will say, however, that the structure of the courses at UCI is very easy to understand. I have experienced more often than not that the complexity of the courses at UCPH's Sociology department makes it difficult for professors to convey the intentions and learning goals of their courses, making the courses unnecessarily difficult.
teaching_comparison: Much more memorization instead of critical thinking and practical application. At UCI, it is a lot of multiple choice tests, and the critical engagement is limited to reflection papers without data collection or actual research practice.
courses_enrolled: FIRST QUARTER: Theories of Punishment The Social Animal Crime Measurement SECOND QUARTER: Violence in Society Crime, Violence and Social Conflict in the Global South
recommended_courses: The Social Animal Violence in Society The lecturers were much more skilled in these courses, and the courses were much more challenging. It seemed like the lecturers cared about our learning here, and that the lecturers enjoyed teaching.
unexpected_costs: The insurance was higher than expected since you pay it individually for both quarters I attended. Southern California is made for cars, and if you don't have a car or friends with cars, you will be spending exorbitant amounts of money on Uber. The public transport system is a literal joke. I cannot stress this enough that you should either buy a car in the beginning of your exchange to sell it once you leave, or set aside a significant portion of money for Uber. Also try to ride Ubers together in groups, since it is a lot cheaper. When renting at ACC, the lease period is 12 months, and I was only there for 6 months. The rent is paid 2 months in advance, meaning I had to pay 2 additional installments of rent for months I wasn't going to live there. This money is returned to me in USD in a physical letter to Denmark, which is absolutely ridiculous. This is back to ACC being owned by Blackrock - a thoroughly terrible corporation - and the fact that the US in some regards is not as digitalized as Denmark.
cost_comparison: Groceries were extraordinarily expensive, since rent costs in Irvine are artificially high, being owned by the private Irvine Company, and since many college students cannot get away from Irvine to shop. Tipping is a huge expense if you don't want your waiters hating on you. You can avoid tipping if you're never coming back to the restaurant/business, but if you plan on coming back, leaving a tip is smart.
activities_available: Much more than in Denmark. Most clubs were ethnically segregated though, which seemed kind of racist. Asians with Asians, Whites with Whites, etc.
activities_recommended: Hiking club, binge drinking in Newport and LA, going to the ARC Gym
weekend_recommendations: San Francisco, Yosemite, Grand Canyon, Tijuana, Los Angeles, Las Vegas.

cultural_challenges: None, really. One annoying thing is that Americans in the service industry tend to ask "How are you?" instead of just saying "Hi" which is kind of annoying, as it prompts a conversation you don't necessarily want. Probably another great reason to abolish tipping culture.
culture_appreciated: Outgoing-ness of Americans is great.
top3_advice: Don't be worried about making friends and finding people you connect with. It is inevitable. Watch out for stingy people. Identify them early on and steer clear of them, as lack of generosity is a huge red flag. I suppose stinginess is more prevalent on exchange, since everyone will be leaving soon anyways and don't need to keep up appearances and maintain social ties. Remember to focus on academics. Even though the difficulty of the courses is a joke, you can still learn a lot more by putting in effort.
other_useful_info: Don't miss the deadlines of ACC registration and payment. It is much earlier than you think.
most_rewarding: The people I met.
greatest_challenge: Transportation.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience the US education system, and the UC system had one of the best academic reputations among my options.
overall_comments: My study abroad program was at UC San Diego. Going there for the academics was a mistake - the upper division economics elective courses I took there were not very challenging. Had I known then, what I know now, I think I would have either avoided North America, or I would have taken the chance to do more courses outside of economics, as the breadth of your options far outweighs the depth.

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My study abroad program was at UC San Diego. Going there for the academics was a mistake - the upper division economics elective courses I took there were not very challenging. Had I known then, what I know now, I think I would have either avoided North America, or I would have taken the chance to do more courses outside of economics, as the breadth of your options far outweighs the depth.
registration_process: Received a 2-day timeslot where I was able to register for one or two courses. The option to sign up for the full allowed courseload was available later. Had to upload a photo for my student ID and fill out a form, then had to show up at the place where I would be living, where I received the key to my appartement. Roommates had move-in times on different days, so we didn't all arrive at the same time.
registration_help: Not sure - I found out what I needed for registration from information available online or in the registration portal.
registration_success: Got every class I wanted.
registration_advice: Register for courses early, and register for more than you intend to take. Dropping courses is easy in the first weeks of the semester/quarter, so you can keep the ones you like the best.
academics_comments: My study abroad program was at UC San Diego. Going there for the academics was a mistake - the upper division economics elective courses I took there were not very challenging. Had I known then, what I know now, I think I would have either avoided North America, or I would have taken the chance to do more courses outside of economics, as the breadth of your options far outweighs the depth.
course_level: Course level seemed lower than at UCPH, and most of the other exchange students I met doing social science or management thought the courses were too easy. Friends doing science seemed to have a much harder time with the courses.
teaching_comparison: We had lectures similar to the ones at KU, and then TA office hours, where a PhD student would go through homework problems with us. I especially liked the professors office hours, where you could come by with problems with the material, and get great help. Courses often had loads of assignments, which heavily influenced your final grade, meaning you had a fair bit of work, even though it wasn't very challenging.

recommended_courses: I would highly recommend: ECON 121 with Tom Vogl - reasonable course load, great office hours. I would have taken another course with him if I could. registration_advice: Nothing
course_level: During my exchange at UCLA, I took mostly undergraduate courses, which were generally easier than I expected. These courses often involved typical assignments, exams, and lectures, and the workload varied depending on the course. While some were quite manageable and didn’t challenge me too much, others required more time and effort, especially if they involved projects or group work. Overall, if you already have a strong foundation in the subject, the undergraduate courses are relatively accessible. However, UCLA also offers the opportunity to take graduate courses, which would have raised the difficulty level significantly. Graduate courses are designed for more advanced students and often require a deeper understanding of the material. These courses are more challenging, with a greater emphasis on independent thinking, research, and analysis. You’re expected to engage in more critical discussions, tackle complex problems, and produce high-quality, in-depth work. Additionally, if you were involved in research, that would also increase the level of difficulty. Research projects at UCLA are often cutting-edge and demand a lot of initiative, problem-solving, and critical thinking. While being involved in research would push you academically, it’s also an incredibly valuable learning experience. Whether you were contributing to an ongoing project or conducting your own, research at UCLA can be quite challenging but also rewarding for those interested in further academic pursuits or careers in research.
teaching_comparison: It is very similar but the classrooms are quite different and there is usually a lot of weekly homework that counts towards your final grade

crucial_aspects: It had to be outside of Europe and have a good amount of offered courses within my field of interest.
info_ease: A bit difficult. The websites are not that easy to navigate, and info regarding e.g. vaccines were hard to come by.
arrival_assistance: A lot of emails. You do receive most reminders of deadlines, updates etc. on email. There's also a mandatory online meeting with info.
arrival_comments: A lot of the info from the online meeting wasn't that useful to me, a lot of it was about finding a job.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It's more confusing than at UCPH. You get an alloted timeslot, and have to work out the schedule yourself. Most courses above course code 99 have prerequisites, so you need to make en EASy request and can't apply for the course until it's been approved. Once you're approved, you can enroll during your timeslot - but it's first come first serve, so have backup courses ready.
registration_help: I don't know, I didn't use any help.
registration_success: I mostly got what I wanted with a few exceptions because they were so popular. But UCSD has so many courses so you'll always be able to find something else. I had physics and chemistry of the ocean, marine microbiology, coastal ecology, ocean acidification, chemistry of the atmosphere and ocean, and satellite remote sensing. Any lab course is very competitive, so have backups for those.
registration_advice: Send out a lot of EASy requests, because not all professors are fast at approving you. For the most part I just wrote that I had the required courses during high school, and it worked.
course_level: All my courses were bachelor level and between course code 100-199, except for one course (satellite remote sensing) which was a mixed class of BA and MA.
teaching_comparison: It's much more like being back in high school. Mandatory attendance and multiple quizzes and assignments each week. The grade was also a split between these things, so e.g. 20% from your final, 20% from the midtmerm, 5% from attendance, and 55% quizzes and assignments. The lectures were much shorter, either 50 minutes or 1 hour and 20 minutes. Discussion sessions were extremely easy and didn't add anything at all.
courses_enrolled: SIO119 Physics and Chemistry of the Ocean SIO126 Marine Microbiology ENVR120 Coastal Ecology SIO174 Chemistry of the Atmosphere and Ocean SIO143 Ocean Acidification SIO135 Satellite Remote Sensing
recommended_courses: SIO119 and SIO143 are very interesting if you like the ocean! Also great professors. ENVR120 is amazing because you go on a field trip every week, and the homework is minimal.
unexpected_costs: They have fees for everything, so you have to pay a lot of weird fees for your semester. Also not unexpected, but tax is not included in the prices shown in stores.
cost_comparison: Food and rent is more expensive than in Denmark. Coffee is less expensive haha. A lot of everyday items are also cheaper. It's really just food and rent that's crazy.
activities_available: They have a club for absolutely everything; hiking, surfing, DJ'ing, dancing, furries, religion, bookclubs, keyboards, cooking etc. I was in the administration of a student run magazine.
activities_recommended: Sign up for a club or two, doesn't even matter which ones. Attend some of the events hosted by the university.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the area and the surrounding towns. Hike. Surf. Chill. If you're up for a longer trip (an 8 hour drive), Yosemite National Park is amazing.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Everyone is very sweet and welcoming, so it's not that difficult to strike up conversation.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really.
culture_appreciated: How open and welcoming they are.
top3_advice: 1) Start preparing as soon as you can - vaccines, visa etc. There are so many deadlines before arrival. 2) Find people to hang out with and work with in class, it makes it so much more enjoyable. 3) Chill! There are a lot of courses to choose from and a lot of people to meet! It'll be fine.
other_useful_info: Download the Pronto app for taking public transit! It's just like Rejseplanen. Get an American bank account so you can get either Zelle or Venmo, as it's what everyone uses.
most_rewarding: All the friends I made. Honestly unrivaled.
greatest_challenge: Traveling. I don't have a drivers license, and since I lived with Americans from the area, they weren't that interested in exploring. You can get around pretty easily by bus and trolley in the university area, but if you wanna go to another city, you need a drivers license. Find someone who wants to explore. That's my only regret.

crucial_aspects: A key factor in choosing my study destination was finding a university with strong expertise in persuasive technologies and behavioural design. I was also drawn to the opportunity for interdisciplinary collaboration between cognition and communication—an essential foundation for my academic and professional goals. Additionally, I valued a location that offered good weather, access to outdoor activities, and strong sports and fitness opportunities to support a balanced lifestyle during my exchange.
overall_comments: I truly valued the academic experience I had; however, my first quarter was extremely challenging due to bureaucratic obstacles that initially prevented me from living with other graduate students and enrolling in graduate-level courses. As an older student (33), I unfortunately faced discrimination and hostility from the undergraduate students I was housed with. Their priorities were centered around partying and socializing, which starkly contrasted with my academic responsibilities and lifestyle. This conflict escalated when they knowingly acquired a cat despite my documented allergy and began publicly targeting me with bullying on platforms like Reddit. They also repeatedly accused me of things I hadn’t done, leading to multiple five-hour mediation meetings with our RA that unfortunately only resulted in further gaslighting and emotional distress. These circumstances severely impacted both my physical and mental health and had a significant negative effect on my academic performance and overall well-being during the first quarter. After many exhausting hours spent navigating various departments—from the Ombuds Office and social workers to multiple housing offices—I was eventually approved to relocate to graduate housing. This transition dramatically improved my living situation and had a profoundly positive impact on the rest of my exchange experience. Additionally, the overall communication and coordination between UCSB and the University of Copenhagen (KU) could have been improved. Although KU informed me that, despite the exchange agreement being at the undergraduate level, it was common practice to allow students to enroll in at least one graduate-level course, UCSB expressed confusion and told me I was the first student they had to support in this regard. Fortunately, I received excellent support from the administrative staff in both the Communication and Psychology departments. That said, I experienced ongoing challenges navigating UCSB’s complex and highly bureaucratic structure. It was often unclear who to contact for specific issues, which led to confusion and delays in resolving problems. Communication with the EAP office was particularly difficult, as my assigned contact person was only available on certain days and often had long response times—making it harder to receive timely support when needed. Socially, I also found the experience quite isolating. As a graduate student, it was difficult to connect with peers. Most UCSB graduate students work in established lab groups or co-ops, which left little room for informal networking or new social connections. Without structured opportunities to meet others in a similar situation, I often felt quite alone during the initial stages of my exchange. Furthermore, the lack of a proper introduction or orientation to UCSB’s academic support systems made it difficult to access important resources early on. I was unaware of crucial tools such as the Disabled Students Program (DSP) (I have post concussion syndrome and ADHD) and was only able to apply for accommodations at the very last minute before my exams. Similarly, I didn’t discover helpful services like CLAS tutoring or exam preparation sessions until late in the first quarter—support that could have made a meaningful difference if accessed earlier. That said, I was also extremely grateful for individual professors who went above and beyond to support my academic journey. Their flexibility, understanding, and genuine encouragement played a crucial role in helping me succeed despite the obstacles. Despite the early challenges, I’m grateful for the resilience I developed and the academic and personal growth I experienced throughout the exchange.

Without a structured introduction or orientation tailored to exchange or graduate students, I struggled to navigate essential systems such as housing, class registration, and academic support services. Much of the information I eventually found was through trial and error or after receiving help from individual staff members or departments later in the quarter.
arrival_assistance: There was an introductory gathering organized by EAP, where we received a folder with some of the most essential information. While this was helpful as a starting point, I found that a lot of important details were missing—particularly regarding academic procedures, available support services, and how to navigate the university as a graduate-level exchange student. As a DSP student, I especially would have benefited from earlier guidance on how to access accommodations and support, as this information was not clearly communicated.

registration_process: The registration process itself—through the GOLD system—is fairly straightforward. However, I would have appreciated more guidance early on about how to navigate course waitlists and the process for sitting in on classes. My main advice to future exchange students is to be very aware of your assigned registration time, as it may occur during the night if you're in Europe, and popular classes fill up quickly. Sign up for as many courses as possible initially—you can always drop them later—and plan to sit in on several during the first week. Since course descriptions online are often very limited, attending the first class is often the only way to get a sense of the content, expectations, and teaching style. Be prepared for a chaotic first week, where you may need to juggle your schedule, arrive late, or leave early to sit in on multiple overlapping classes. Also, if you're on a waitlist, it’s crucial to attend the class from day one. Many instructors will automatically drop students who are waitlisted but don’t show up, so don’t assume you're safe unless you've been officially added to the roster.

registration_advice: Remember that in the U.S., professors typically hold a great deal of autonomy over their courses and are the ones who decide whether exceptions or modifications can be made. If you encounter any issues, reach out to them directly—and early. Clear, respectful communication often goes a long way. It’s also a good idea to schedule a meeting with the administrative staff in your department early on; they can be incredibly helpful when it comes to navigating course enrollment, waitlists, and academic procedures.
