Socially, I also found the experience quite isolating. As a graduate student, it was difficult to connect with peers. Most UCSB graduate students work in established lab groups or co-ops, which left little room for informal networking or new social connections. Without structured opportunities to meet others in a similar situation, I often felt quite alone during the initial stages of my exchange. Furthermore, the lack of a proper introduction or orientation to UCSB’s academic support systems made it difficult to access important resources early on. I was unaware of crucial tools such as the Disabled Students Program (DSP) (I have post concussion syndrome and ADHD) and was only able to apply for accommodations at the very last minute before my exams. Similarly, I didn’t discover helpful services like CLAS tutoring or exam preparation sessions until late in the first quarter—support that could have made a meaningful difference if accessed earlier. That said, I was also extremely grateful for individual professors who went above and beyond to support my academic journey. Their flexibility, understanding, and genuine encouragement played a crucial role in helping me succeed despite the obstacles. Despite the early challenges, I’m grateful for the resilience I developed and the academic and personal growth I experienced throughout the exchange.
course_level: The academic level at UCSB varies significantly depending on the professor, department, and class size. Class formats range from small seminars with 5 students to large lectures with over 500, each offering very different learning experiences. Smaller, seminar-style classes tend to promote intellectual engagement, discussion, and critical thinking, while larger undergraduate courses often rely on multiple-choice exams and emphasize factual recall over deeper understanding. In my experience, many undergraduate classes focused more on how much information you could memorize rather than how well you could analyze or apply it. This approach felt quite similar to high school, especially when compared to my Danish BA and MA education, which is typically more discussion-driven and encourages independent thinking and critical analysis. To make the most of the academic experience at UCSB, I strongly recommend reviewing course syllabi carefully, speaking directly with professors about their learning objectives, and, when possible, prioritizing upper-division or smaller classes. Not only will this help clarify expectations, but direct communication also increases the chance of building a supportive relationship with your instructor, which can be very beneficial
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at UCSB differed quite significantly from what I’m used to at the University of Copenhagen. In Denmark, courses tend to be more discussion-based, with a strong emphasis on critical thinking, independent analysis, and active student participation. Assessments often involve written essays and oral exams that require you to develop and defend your perspective. At UCSB—particularly in larger undergraduate courses—the teaching style was more lecture-driven, with a focus on memorization and multiple-choice exams. While some classes encouraged engagement, the overall structure felt more passive and content-heavy. That said, I found smaller seminars and independent study options more aligned with the academic environment I’m used to in Copenhagen. I also appreciated the flexibility some professors offered in adapting assignments to better match graduate-level expectations. One important thing to be aware of is that professors at UCSB are often leading experts in their specific research fields. While this is a great opportunity to learn from top scholars, their deep specialization can sometimes introduce bias in how content is taught and assessed—particularly in classes where multiple-choice exams reflect the professor’s particular interpretation of the material. Understanding their academic lens and expectations early on is key to succeeding and making the most of the course

Academically, I learned the most from PSY 163BG – The Active Brain. These classes pushed my personal boundaries, encouraged emotional growth, and gave me a much-needed ‘off-screen’ playground for self-expression and development.

top3_advice: 1. Be proactive and flexible about both course registration and social groups. Courses fill up quickly, and the system can be confusing at first—especially if you're in a different time zone. Sign up for as many classes as you can initially (you can always drop them later), sit in on multiple classes the first week, and don’t hesitate to contact professors directly—especially if you're waitlisted. The same goes for social life: finding your community takes initiative, especially as a graduate student. Explore clubs, dance classes, or fitness groups early, and don’t be afraid to show up alone—you often have to make the first move. 2. Prepare for a different academic culture and structure. The quarter system moves very fast and can feel very intense. Do not fall behind early on—you simply won’t have time to catch up later. Many undergraduate courses rely heavily on memorization and multiple-choice exams rather than critical thinking and discussion. Try to choose smaller or upper-division classes, and if you're a graduate student, speak with professors about adapting assignments to a more advanced level. Independent studies can also be a great way to tailor your learning experience. 3. Don’t underestimate the housing challenge. Housing in Isla Vista is expensive, competitive, and often shared with undergrads in a party-heavy environment. If you're a grad student, push early for graduate housing or explore UCSB-affiliated landlords. Be prepared to move—possibly more than once—and expect little control over who you live with. If you don’t get housing through UCSB, expect to pay between 7,000 and 15,000 DKK per month to share a room with up to four people in Isla Vista. The experience can vary a lot depending on your living situation, so advocate for your needs early.
other_useful_info: get a car if you can or at least a bike public transportation is pretty bad. Often the busses are full during primetime and they only goes a couple of times an hour.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the personal and academic growth that came from navigating a completely new system and environment. While there were many challenges—especially in the beginning—they pushed me to become more proactive, adaptable, and resilient. Academically, I was especially grateful for the opportunity to tailor some of my coursework to fit my research interests and to collaborate with inspiring professors. For me, it was a unique opportunity to combine classes from psychology, communication, and acting (theater)—a combination that allowed me to explore human behavior from both scientific and expressive perspectives. Personally, I also really enjoyed exploring California. I’m more of a city girl, so I found it quite difficult to adjust to life in Isla Vista, which felt isolated and very student-party oriented. But traveling around the state was an incredible highlight—I absolutely loved San Francisco, Napa Valley, Lake Tahoe, San Diego, and especially my dream spot, Venice Beach. The mix of academic stimulation and personal adventure made the exchange a truly transformative experience.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was the living situation in the first quarter. As a graduate student, I was placed in housing with undergraduate students whose priorities and lifestyles were very different from mine. This created ongoing conflicts, including severe allergic reactions when they knowingly brought a cat into the shared space, as well as social tension and even public bullying online. Navigating the housing bureaucracy to find a solution was extremely time-consuming and emotionally draining. It affected both my mental health and academic performance during that quarter. However, once I was finally relocated to graduate housing, my experience improved dramatically. This situation taught me a lot about advocating for myself, setting boundaries, and navigating complex systems—skills I know I’ll carry with me moving forward.

crucial_aspects: I mainly chose UC Berkeley because of its great reputation and academic opportunities, especially within my field of study. The weather in the Bay Area is also super nice, and SF is only a 25-minute train ride away :)
info_ease: Very easy, Berkeley is very good at providing resources for almost everything, you just have to know where to find it. Just be sure to check your Berkeley email frequently and attend the orientation meetings before your stay :)
arrival_assistance: I attended Golden Bear Orientation (GBO), which gives you an introduction to the Berkeley campus, traditions and values, and gives you the opportunity to meet other students (mostly transfer students) across many different majors. I highly recommend signing up for GBO! Apart from that, it is always possible to receive assistance with anything else from the Berkeley International Office.
arrival_comments: Make sure to keep an eye out in your email for a sign up link to GBO so you don't miss out :) They send you a lot (!) of emails, but it is worth at least skimming through them so you don't miss anything important (a lot of people missed GBO because they missed the email)
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It is just a website where you can "shop around" and add courses to your basket :) They also have a schedule planner so you can see your schedule with the courses you have chosen. You are assigned a specific date and time where your courses registration starts. This assigned date and time is not the same for all Berkeley students, so some of the courses might already be partly or fully filled by the time you can register for them. But don't worry, in most cases you should be fine; otherwise, just sign up for the course anyways, as a lot of people on the waitlist get in later on in the add & drop period in the beginning of the semester.
registration_help: I'm sure you can find lots of resources on the Berkeley website or CalNet :)
registration_success: I successfully signed up for all my classes. I was on the waitlist on one of them in the beginning, but got in a few days after I registered.
registration_advice: Apart from what I have mentioned above: Be sure to become familiar with what the add & drop period is and when it starts and ends. Again, don't be afraid to register for more courses than you need, as it gives you more flexibility, and you can just drop them later on. I think 20.5 units is the maximum though. You can also just get all the courses your registered for pre-approved by KU, and then just change your pre-approval once you finally have decided on which courses you are taking.
course_level: I can only talk about economics courses, as this is what I study. The undergraduate courses are generally not that difficult compared to KU, especially with regards to the math. However, the workload is quite high, as assignments, attendance, midterms etc. also count towards your grade, so you can't be going on too long trips if you want a good grade :) If you really want to be challenged academically, then choose as many graduate courses as you can.
teaching_comparison: It was honestly very similar, with big lectures followed by smaller discussions (taught by a PhD student) every week. You have to be way more formal in how you address your professors, but they are generally very willing to help and have lots of office hours.
courses_enrolled: Environmental Economics (ECON C125) Public Economics (ECON 131) Financial Economics (ECON 136) Foundations of Data Science (DATA C8)
recommended_courses: I can recommend all the courses I took. Public Economics is good, but it is also mainly about the US (whereas other economics courses are about more general theories), so if you don't care at all about the US public sector, I would probably avoid it. I heard that the course is better when it is run by Emmanuel Saez as opposed to Daniel Wilson (Wilson's exams are much more difficult, and he is not a very good lecturer). Financial Economics is a good course that provides a broad introduction to corporate finance, and it is not too easy or difficult. Environmental Economics is very interesting, but maybe a bit too easy. Foundations of Data Science is a really good course if you are completely new to Python. Within computer science and similar majors, it is a very famous course (both at Berkeley and in the US in general), and it is also the biggest course at Berkeley, so it is run extremely well. It is also not too difficult, but the workload is quite high. Apart from the courses I took, I have heard good things about Money and Banking (ECON 165). It is a very popular course, so be sure to register for it as early as possible.
unexpected_costs: Nothing really. You can find help with your budget on both the UCEAP and Berkeley website.
cost_comparison: You can save a lot of money by buying something other than SHIP insurance, but be aware that there is a slight risk that UC Berkeley won't accept your third-party insurance and then force you to pay for SHIP anyways. I used something called ISO International Student Health Insurance, which worked for me and the other Danish people who went to Berkeley that semester.
activities_available: They basically have everything you can think of, just check the website.
activities_recommended: Going on hikes in the fire trails is really nice, and they offer some great views over Berkeley and the Bay Area. Be sure to watch the sunset from up there one day :) For going out in Berkeley: Raleigh's hosts Taco Tuesdays every Tuesday Tap Haus is pretty nice and has lots of pool tables Go to Kip's if you want to dance Be sure to attend a few frat parties too! It is easiest to do it during rush week in the beginning of the semester. For going out elsewhere: I mainly went to SF, where I can recommend Monroe SF (really cheap drinks if you come really early (around 5pm) on Fridays), Audio SF if you like EDM, and generally the Cow Hollow/Pacific Heights area for bar hopping.
weekend_recommendations: Around the Bay Area: Sausalito, Muir Woods, Silicon Valley, Stanford, SF of course. Further away: Santa Cruz, Lake Tahoe, Yosemite, LA, Las Vegas, Grand Canyon.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, their culture is fairly similar.
socializing_tips: Attend Golden Bear Orientation and attend parties and events, especially in the beginning. International House has many cool events, and you can often attend even if you are not a resident (sometimes you just have to know a resident who can let you in). You can also join student organizations, but some of them can be pretty difficult joining because you won't be at Berkeley for a very long time.
cultural_challenges: None really, but maybe be prepared that random strangers will start talking to you quite a lot. There are also a lot of homeless people in Berkeley and around campus.
culture_appreciated: Americans are usually very nice and welcoming, so it is super easy to talk to new people and get to know them :)
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy 2. Your 3. Stay
other_useful_info: Remember that you can ask any questions you have in the Facebook group for KU students going on exchange to UC. Use the Berkeley Academic Guide when exploring courses.
most_rewarding: The people I met there and the many great experiences that we had together :)
greatest_challenge: Going home :(
other_comments: Remember to start your VISA application pretty early, as it can be a pretty long process, and you don't want it to hinder any other summer vacation plans that you might have. Also be sure to look into the health requirements in advance. I think you can also fullfill some of them after you have arrived, but I honestly wouldn't waste time on that.

crucial_aspects: I'd always felt drawn to California, so the exchange program was a great opportunity to combine exploration of that crazy place with academics. I chose UCLA as my first priority because of its great reputation and faculty in political science in combination with the high quality of life you only get in SoCal (it truly is always sunny!).
overall_comments: I had a fantastic stay in every way and could not recommend it highly enough.
info_ease: The UC system sends you massive amounts of information ahead of arrival, so as long as you read your email, you'll be fine. The only thing I found confusing was whether I was supposed to participate in an orientation program or not (I didn't), and I'm honestly still not sure. Either way you'll be just fine without, but it may be a way to get to know some people.
arrival_assistance: No personal assistance, but the Dashew Center (international student office) organized some events with useful information. Just check your email and reach out to them if you have questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had a fantastic stay in every way and could not recommend it highly enough.
registration_process: They release the course catalog (class planner) at MyUCLA, and then you have some time before your enrollment timeslot. Courses vary a lot in difficulty, exam format, and workload, so do your research ahead of your timeslot.
registration_help: They send you some guides, but what's more helpful is checking out the courses on your own to make an informed decision.
registration_success: Mostly successful. As a first-year master student, I was interested in taking at least some graduate courses, which the system doesn't let you by default (the exchange program is an undergraduate program, so you are registered as such in the UC system). You can email professors and ask for permission to enroll anyway, which they will sometimes grant. I ended up with two out of six courses on graduate level, which was OK. The undergrad classes varied a LOT - some were very good, and some less so. One class was a complete mess.
registration_advice: Check out Bruinwalk. Email professors for the course syllabus. If you like a course that's for graduate students, or one that has prerequisites, email the professor and ask for permission to enroll anyway.
academics_comments: I had a fantastic stay in every way and could not recommend it highly enough.
course_level: The two graduate courses I took were on a high level, even for UCPH. The undergraduate courses I took were generally easier analytically than at UCPH, but not all of them. I guess the general takeaway is that they don't expect you to conduct much independent research work on a high level, but they do encourage you to. You will usually get A's or B's for assignments that would've landed you a 7 at UCPH, but if you want to challenge yourself and submit something solid, you absolutely can.
teaching_comparison: Courses generally have lectures and discussion sections just like at UCPH. In some courses, attendance is mandatory. They generally require much more work during the quarter than at UCPH, but for the most part they're easier. Be prepared for pen and paper exams!!! Midterms AND finals! I'm a slow handwriter and this genuinely screwed me over in two classes that I otherwise would've received A's in but ended up with B's.
courses_enrolled: I was away for 1,5 semesters (two quarters). First quarter (fall): POL SCI 140B: National Institutions: The Presidency; POL SCI 260A: Survey Course in American Politics: Political Parties and Electoral Process; POL SCI 125A: Arms Control and International Security. Second quarter (winter): GLB HLT 100: Introduction to Global Health; POL SCI 163B: Colonialism, Discourse, and Democracy; PUB PLC C275: Advanced Technology: Public Policy, Regulation, and Law.
recommended_courses: POL SCI 260A with Lynn Vavreck was amazing, perhaps the best course I've had at uni ever. It was approx 10 PhD students and me in a small classroom for three hours every Monday, discussing a ton of great readings on a high level. But don't be shy, you can definitely keep up even though they're PhD (in most cases, they had studied as many years as I had - the university systems are different and in the US PhDs usually don't take a master's degree first). I liked PUB PLC C275 with professor Zipperstein who is just a darling - very lovable and knowledgeable guy. POL SCI 140B was super interesting but pretty demanding too. I really learned a lot from this class that I would never learn at UCPH. Highly recommended, just be aware that you have pen and paper midterm and final as well as a 15 page research paper, and that some of the material is pretty complicated. The other three courses (GLB HLT 100, POL SCI 163B and POL SCI 125A) were not the best. Global Health was interesting but pretty basic yet demanding in terms of workload. Arms Control was a complete mess. Colonialism, Discourse and Democracy was mostly quite boring but in the end I actually turned and learned to enjoy the class. It certainly isn't for everyone, though.
unexpected_costs: Nothing I can think of.
cost_comparison: Prices are generally high in California and LA in particular. Groceries can be very expensive (think 75 DKK for 12 eggs). This is another reason why the coop is such a crazy good offer, you get three meals per day included with your rent. The only food I've bought is while traveling and the occassional night out/hangover treat. You can even pack lunches and take them to uni. Insurance is expensive obviously, but you should have that covered before leaving. Uber is very expensive. Domestic plane tickets are pretty cheap.
activities_available: Every kind you can imagine... just go to the huge student fare in week 0 and see what you like!
activities_recommended: Use the amazing facilities! UCLA has 7 swimming pools on campus, a bunch of professional sports stadiums and tennis courts and free or cheap learning opportunities.
weekend_recommendations: This is VERY important! GO SEE CALIFORNIA! The national parks are amazing: Sequoia, Yosemite, Death Valley, Joshua Tree, ... Also make sure to take a trip eastward to Utah and Arizona, their parks are even better. I LOVED Zion national park (get the permit for the Angels Landing trail <33), and Monument Valley, Arches, Bryce, Grand Canyon are all super cool. And don't forget the iconic Pacific Coast Highway for a sublime road trip up toward San Francisco - Big Sur which you'll see on the way is magical. Last but not least, go to Hawaii!!! Check Google Flights for cheap tickets (I got a two-island return ticket for less than 300 USD). It's a unique experience that I wish I could do every year. Stay at the hostels and go on their daily tours (on Maui they're free). Overall, traveling was one of the main things I did because so many incredible places with so much variation are super accessible from LA. Just make sure you have some money saved up for it... (take that SU lån -- stay at the coop -- apply for a bunch of grants -- don't save on travel!!)
culture_adjustment: Very easy! Americans are famously open, and if you stay at the coop, which you should, you'll get a bunch of friends in no time. The only thing is sharing a room, that took some time for me but I ended up becoming really close with my roommates and kind of enjoying that way of living. Also, you'll definitely struggle getting around if you don't have a car, that's just how it is. UCLA gives you free public transport in the whole city, but it's extremely poorly connected. I bought a car and used it alllll the time. It was cheap! But it does require a lot of work in terms of insurance, parking, maintenance, etc. If you have the dream of driving through Beverly Hills in a convertible, you absolutely can -- I got a 2006 Toyota Solara for 2700 USD that worked close to flawlessly and that I sold for the same price at the end of my stay. Worth all the trouble and much more. Having to beg for spots in other people's cars just gets tiring very fast, and honestly driving is so much more enjoyable in the US.
socializing_tips: Stay at the coop :=)
cultural_challenges: I missed walking around to explore. I felt pretty constrained in my choices before I got my car, and even then, I still missed walking. LA is not a European city, you cannot walk between neighborhoods. For that reason getting to know LA is super difficult. Some neighborhoods are fine for walking (Santa Monica, Venice, West Hollywood, Westwood and of course the tourist spots), but getting to them is tough without a car.
culture_appreciated: The openness!
top3_advice: 1. Stay at the coop. 2. Buy a car. 3. Travel!
other_useful_info: DON'T buy the super expensive UC SHIP insurance. Get the much cheaper ISO Care student health insurance and get a waiver for UC SHIP. I also bought a travel insurance on top from Gouda.
most_rewarding: Traveling with all the friends I made at the coop.
greatest_challenge: Going back home.

crucial_aspects: It was important to find a place with great academic opportunities in my academic field and and with a vibrant and multidisciplinary environment. It was also important for me to live in a larger English speaking city where I could learn from the culture and gain new connections, both on a personal but also professional level.
info_ease: It was pretty difficult at the beginning. I arrived 3 weeks before the program started and it was difficult to gain information before the program started. I visited the UCEAP office at UCLA 3 times at my first visit at UCLA, but they didn't know they were representing the UCEAP program and kept sending me different places, until I called the UCEAP program and was insured it was that office. I had great difficulties finding a place to live and didn't get much help to find a solution.
arrival_assistance: Exchange student orientation
arrival_comments: There was a lot of confusion about which orientations I should attend, the one I had signed up for, wasn't registered at the right place, so I had to attend to different ones plus the one for exchange students, even though I still don't know if I had to attend all three. We didn't get basic knowledge such as what platform is used by the professors for homework, etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You go to bruin learn -> course registrations and then you can plan your schedule and sign up for the courses you want to attend.
registration_help: not really
registration_success: pretty succesful. In the first quarter I had a harder time getting the courses I wanted and that was accepted by my program at home, but at my second quarter I had better luck.
registration_advice: Be persistent and email the professors teaching the courses you want, sometimes more than once. Attend faculty events and talk with the professors there, that help me getting some of the courses I wanted
course_level: The BA level courses had more weekly coursework and TA discussion groups every week. I felt like they were a little lower level than my BA classes back home. The exams are way shorter than at UCPH. Each class has a clear description of what's expected of the student and how the class is graded. The KA classes level was very theoretical and high level.
teaching_comparison: I like that there was a structured plan for each course and that you know what's expected of you and what the grade you on.
courses_enrolled: First Quarter: Music Industry 115A Gender studies M114 Ethnomusicology: African american music ensemble 161P LGBTQD+ perspectives in pop music M137
recommended_courses: Ethnomusicology: African american music ensemble 161P is a gospel choir for all levels. It's a great way to meet other people and gain insights in the gospel music culture.
unexpected_costs: University fees, extra bank fees, extra doctors fees.
cost_comparison: Public transportation is very inexpensive.
activities_available: Everything you can imagine. there so many clubs and events!
activities_recommended: I would recommend any club or sports activity you find interesting. Stay posted on the MYUCLA website and calendar and sign up for all the newsletters. The international office host a lot of great events for international student where you can meet other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: Go out and explore L.A. Westwood is not the greatest representation of Los Angeles. Visit some of the national forests and drive up the coast.
culture_adjustment: I think It was easy.
socializing_tips: Talk to strangers and the people in you class. Go to event and talk to the people that are there. L.A. is a great city full of free events you can go to each week, I met a lot of amazing people by just talking to strangers and trying new stuff.
cultural_challenges: It's a more outgoing culture.
culture_appreciated: That itt's a more outgoing culture.
top3_advice: Be open minded. Ucla is big and there is a lot of systems/ bureaucracy, but once you figure it out it's not that difficult. Take advantages of all the opportunities and great organisations and clubs.
other_useful_info: It will be more expensive then you think. You can find most information on bruinlearn - Learn how to navigate it! Wise is a great bank alternative. UCHA COOP is a great housing opportunity. Mint mobile is the cheapest option. If you need to use cashapps you have to open an American bank account.
most_rewarding: The people I met and the new perspectives and knowledge I gained.
greatest_challenge: Finding a place to live of campus.

crucial_aspects: My decision to study at UCSD was driven by three key factors: the desire for an authentic American collegiate experience, a long-standing interest in California’s culture, and the university’s reputation for academic excellence. Specifically, San Diego’s consistent climate offered a welcome contrast to the Danish winter, providing an ideal environment for both study and personal growth.
overall_comments: Amazing once in a lifetime opertunity and experience
info_ease: Very easy, check your UCSD email frequently for information on events during welcome week.
arrival_assistance: To be honest, I didn't get much formal assistance from the uni when I first landed, but I found my feet through the off-campus housing portal. That’s actually where I met most of my international friends! Since I didn't know any others going from Denmark. I leaned on that international group early on. We ended up going to university events together, like the International Coffee Hour, which was a total game-changer for meeting even more people. My advice? Don't wait for a formal welcome—just start connecting with other internationals during the housing search.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Amazing once in a lifetime opertunity and experience
registration_process: Once you get into one of the UC's you get access to their website where you can enrool in cources make sure you do that on time if there are some specific courses you want.
registration_help: The international student service have events to help you socialize and adapt to the culture and campus one week before the beginning of the quarter.
registration_success: Very successful
registration_advice: People eventually drop out of courses during the first two weeks and you might be able to get the course even though you are waitlisted
academics_comments: Amazing once in a lifetime opertunity and experience
course_level: The level is easier than UCPH, enjoy your time there without any academic pressure. I put in 30-40% of the effort I normally put in at UCPH and managed to get a 3.85 GPA.
teaching_comparison: The courses have fewer students, and professors expect you to engage during lectures. Additionally, I had to do a presentation in 4/8 of my courses, which is unusual compared to ECON at UCPH, but don't fear, they are relatively gracious with the presentation grading.
courses_enrolled: I was there for 2 quarters 1 Q: Game theory (p), Labor Economics, Business Finance (from the MGT major) and public policy 2 Q: Machine learning in business and econ, Leadership and organization (MGT 162), Industrial organization (p) and Economics of development (p)
recommended_courses: Make sure you enrool in minimum 3 priority courses, which UCPH requires
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs other than traveling a lot. Be prepared to embark on travels and book your rentals like cars and housing in advance to save some money.
cost_comparison: Beers are much more expensive compared to DK, but other groceries are about the same price.
activities_available: The uni has clubs for any activity that you might be interested in, and they will do tableing during the first week.
activities_recommended: Go to the beach, go to all the national parks (grand canyon and Zion were one of my faves), go to vegas 5-6 hrs drive and party a lot in PB go to Hideaway on thursdays and Moonshine on Fridays and saturdays.
weekend_recommendations: Go on the Hike close to campus, like the "Ho chi min trial" La Jolla Shores Beach is the prettiest but there are other beaches close to campus that are nice to visit. Go taco hunting- SD has some of the best mexican food places (Get the cali burito (most value for money))
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy
socializing_tips: Put yourself out there and every new international is on the same boat seeking new friendships
cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: The friendly locals at la jolla and the laid back vibe of California
top3_advice: Get the insurance through ISO (international student health insurance) instead of UC-ship, and waive the UC-ship, this will save you around 3000 dkk. Get housing at costa verde (anatolia housing) if you don't get a spot a Ihouse, as the spots are limited, here you will meet other internationals. Get a car with your flatmates or by yourself for convenience, but keep in mind that parking spots on campus are limited and relatively expensive pr hour.
other_useful_info: Get memberships at the stores like vons or ralphs to save on gorceries Make sure you know which courses are offered in each quarter, as all the courses listed on the websites are not offered each quarter
most_rewarding: Getting to build new relationships across nations and getting to travel and experience a new culture with these amazing people
greatest_challenge: Although I didn't face many challenges, I did get a bit homesick early on. Once I adapted, it became one of the best experiences of my life

crucial_aspects: The University of California, Los Angeles is world renowned for its world-class mathematics department. I was drawn to the prospect of receiving education from some of the greatest mathematicians in the world.
overall_comments: Los Angeles is an expensive city to reside in, and our exchange agreement with UCLA is strictly for a six-month stay. Staying 6 months in a city where rent is typically $1500 a month was difficult for me financially. However, overall, I had a great experience abroad.
info_ease: I received most needed information through the host university’s email system. However, I missed a few events at the very beginning of my stay, as my UCEAP Reciprocity account did not link with my UCLA email at first. Instead, a lot of relevant mail got sent to my UCPH mail, which I did think to check regularly at the time. Luckily, this was quite easy to correct manually.
arrival_assistance: I needed assistance from the UCPH study guidance to confirm my arrival, as Mobility Online was broken at the time. I also received mandatory vaccinations from the Arthur Ashe Student Health and Wellness Center a few days after my arrival.
arrival_comments: The "iSTART orientation" and "SHAPE training" at UCLA felt like a huge waste of time. Moreover, it would have been nice to know that the mandatory vaccinations at UCLA were all covered by my (mandatory) US health insurance. I ended up paying 1100 kr. for vaccinations in Denmark that I could have gotten for free in the US.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Los Angeles is an expensive city to reside in, and our exchange agreement with UCLA is strictly for a six-month stay. Staying 6 months in a city where rent is typically $1500 a month was difficult for me financially. However, overall, I had a great experience abroad.
registration_process: We were forced to complete the "iSTART orientation" program. It was alright, but a lot of it felt redundant and mundane. I felt like time would have been better spent with study-focused mixer events, like the voluntary ones offered by the Dashew Center.
registration_help: The Dashew Center for International Students & Scholars is an on-campus building/institution designed for helping and guiding exchange students. They were incredibly helpful throughout (for instance, when I needed a TIN-number for my Danish bank), and I am thankful they were around.
registration_success: Very successful. I was told that I would probably not be able to enroll in more than two graduate courses for the duration of my stay. This was luckily not the case, as the mathematics department let me enroll in more or less all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: For anyone going on exchange to a UC campus during their master’s studies (like myself), my advice would be that one can typically enroll in as many graduate courses as they’d like, despite what UC might tell you at first. This can be an unnecessary deal-breaker for some, and I think it is unfortunate that the communication is not more clear.
academics_comments: Los Angeles is an expensive city to reside in, and our exchange agreement with UCLA is strictly for a six-month stay. Staying 6 months in a city where rent is typically $1500 a month was difficult for me financially. However, overall, I had a great experience abroad.
course_level: I took the following undergraduate courses (BA level): “Math 135 - Ordinary Differential Equations” and “Math 155 - Mathematical Imaging”. In addition, I took the following graduate courses (MA level): “Math 273A - Optimization and Calculus of Variations: Basic Optimization Theory”, “Math 246B - Complex Analysis”, “Math 247A - Classical Fourier Analysis” and “Math 254B - Topics in Real Analysis”.
teaching_comparison: It was mostly the same. Due to the federal funding cuts happening in the US at the time of my exchange program, there were no exercise classes in any of my courses. This felt a bit hollow, as I have had exercise classes at UCPH in all the courses I have taken thus far. Other than that, the courses at UCLA felt quite similar in structure to what I am used to.
courses_enrolled: In my first semester (that is, in my first quarter), I was enrolled in the following courses: “Math 135 - Ordinary Differential Equations”, “Math 155 - Mathematical Imaging” and “Math 273A - Optimization and Calculus of Variations: Basic Optimization Theory”.
recommended_courses: It is difficult for me to say, as I did not experience the courses in full due to the lack of exercise classes. However, I quite enjoyed “Math 155 - Mathematical Imaging”. As a pure mathematician, it was a nice (and rigorous) introduction to an interesting area of applied mathematics. Moreover, I also quite enjoyed “Math 247A - Classical Fourier Analysis”, but this course is probably more tailored to a dedicated pure math crowd.
unexpected_costs: There were quite a few unexpected expenses at the onset of the exchange program. There were fees associated with obtaining a US visa, like the SEVIS fee, the booking fee at the embassy and the price of being photographed by a licensed photographer. In addition, there were some mandatory fees that needed to be paid to UCLA before they would allow me to enroll in their courses. I am still not entirely sure what these fees were, but I was forced to pay them via the university’s billing service “BruinBill”. In general, I was quite surprised by the number of unexpected expenses that kept appearing in the beginning. Luckily, this evened out a bit toward the end of my stay.
cost_comparison: I had no expenses for textbooks and school supplies whatsoever. All of the courses I took either used freely accessible textbooks or free notes as class material. Conversely, I was a bit surprised about the high cost of living in LA. I was prepared to pay a higher rent than usual, but I did not expect the price of groceries to be about 20% higher than at home.
activities_available: By the nature of sports and athletics at US universities, it was not possible for me to participate in any sporting activity associated with UCLA, as these programs are strictly reserved for “student athletes” (meaning athletes who pretend to be students in order to play for the university’s sports teams). This was a bit disappointing to me, but I understand that it is a biproduct of a cultural convention. Luckily, there were many other social events organized by the university that I enjoyed attending. Specifically, I really liked the “Bruin Mixer” events organized by the Dashew Center. These events gave me a chance to meet other exchange students, who were also new in town, and were the basis of some of the best friendships I made throughout my stay.
activities_recommended: Personally, I did not do a lot of non-academic activities during my stay. I went to the beach once, which I would recommend. Moreover, I went out partying a few times in Westwood, Venice Beach and West Hollywood, which were all good experiences. However, by personal choice/preference, I spent a lot of time studying throughout my stay and I did not do much off-campus activity.
weekend_recommendations: Beside visiting the well-known tourist destinations around LA, I would very much encourage future exchange students to attend a few university sports games. The spectacle surrounding university sports in the US makes this quite intriguing (and typically also quite cheap if you are a student). In addition, I also found it quite entertaining to watch non-university sports games in the downtown area. Personally, I watched the LA Kings play in the NHL twice during my stay, but I also heard good things from friends who watched the LA Lakers and LA Rams play on other occasions.
culture_adjustment: Incredibly easy. Despite what you will hear in a lot of media nowadays, it is my honest impression that Americans are an overwhelmingly friendly, open and welcoming people. LA in particular seems to be a very inclusive place, and I had no trouble coexisting with the many people I met throughout.
socializing_tips: I would strongly encourage all exchange students at UCLA to participate in the “Bruin Mixer” events. These helped me immensely with socializing and finding friends when I first arrived.
cultural_challenges: It is hard to pin down exactly, but many things at UCLA (and in the US in general) insisted on encouraging a type of behavior that I would best describe as “play to the gallery”. For instance, many of the courses I took at UCLA had a system of “extra credit”, where one could obtain a better grade for a course by doing something mundane like attending a one-hour seminar. This seemed quite odd to me, as I ended up having a feeling that certain course grades were not representative of one’s academic performance, but instead a measure of how well one was at jumping though some arbitrary hoops that the lecturer had come up with. In my experience, this sentiment was echoed throughout many aspects of American culture, which I found quite different from what I was used to.
culture_appreciated: The hospitality and openness of the American people. The people I met were typically very accepting and inclusive and seemed to have little to no bias towards my cultural background. I found this inspiring.
top3_advice: My list of the three most important things to know before embarking on an exchange program at UCLA would probably rank as follows: 1) Save up a lot of money. Apply for as many scholarships as possible and save all the money you can whenever you can (i.e., by buying the cheapest possible plane tickets). LA is an expensive city, and you will have to make a living there for 6 months without a student job. 2) It is very common for both native UCLA students and exchange students to leave town for Christmas. If you are therefore staying for both fall and winter quarter, you should not plan on celebrating Christmas with fellow UCLA students. 3) The time zone difference of nine hours to Denmark makes communication with friends and family difficult. If you have important matters to tend to with people back home, do so before departing for LA.
other_useful_info: I would encourage all future exchange students at UCLA to make diligent preparations for housing in LA. Specifically, I would recommend people to make living arrangements with other exchange students from UCPH ahead of time. Having a roommate from UCPH would have helped me immensely throughout my stay, but, sadly, I had none. Worse yet, I later met other exchange students from UCPH in LA, who told me they were in the same predicament and that they would have been happy to share a room with me.
most_rewarding: I was (strongly) encouraged by a UCLA professor to apply for a PhD position at a university that she will be moving to shortly. The professor in question is a renowned mathematics professor, and obtaining this kind of acknowledgement from her means the world to me. I will be applying for the PhD position this fall. If anything comes of it, it will, in and of itself, be worth every penny and hour I spend throughout my stay.
greatest_challenge: The nine-hour time difference between LA and Denmark was at times difficult for me to deal with. I was never homesick, nor did I feel a strong need to stay in constant contact with people back home. However, it became increasingly frustrating that I could not reach family and friends about practical matters at normal times of the day. This was especially noticeable toward the end of my stay, when I had to sign up for courses and TA positions at UCPH and make plans for the Easter holidays with friends and family - all while the people I needed to contact were asleep.
other_comments: As mentioned earlier, I regret not having found a roommate from UCPH before departing for LA. I think this could, in part, have been helped by UCPH, if they had provided us with a list of other students, who were embarking on the same exchange agreement as us. It might be against certain GDPR laws to do so without permission, but from what I have heard, everyone from UCPH would happily have given permission for such a list to be sent out. Many exchange students from other universities received a list like this, and they were all very happy about it. I think it is a shame that we were not provided with one.

crucial_aspects: Academic excellence and school reputation, beautiful and large campus, proximity to family.
overall_comments: An absolutely fantastic experience that I would recommend to everyone!
info_ease: Quite easy to find lots of information. The hard thing to navigate was more the overload of information (see next box).
arrival_assistance: We were presented with emails, webpages, webinars, physical orientation etc. – all packed with information about how to navigate all aspects of Berkeley, special offers at Berkeley, advice on being at Berkeley, tips and tricks for doing well and Berkeley etc. I talked to other visiting students to figure out what information was essential and what information could be ignored. This definitely made it more manageable.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: An absolutely fantastic experience that I would recommend to everyone!
registration_process: Berkeley has an add/drop system with course enrollment opening up asynchronously for different groups at different times. Depending on what year you are, what you are studying and what program you are on, your enrollment will be different. It is not hard to find your time slot though, as it is pretty clear on their website. However, the process is still quite stressful as one has to "snatch" a spot as if it was a festival ticket (if one is applying to popular courses). And many people will choose way too many courses in this period and then drop them within 2 weeks after school starts in which case spots slowly open up in some courses, meaning you might still get a spot. So in reality there might be a 2 month delay between initial course enrollment and when ones final course schedule is decided.
registration_help: However, I still gave the process a 2/5 (and not a 1/5) on above scale as there is great "Academic advising" at Berkeley which you can contact easily and get assistance from.
registration_success: I was very satisfied with the courses I ended up taking, and so I would say that I was successful. However, I had my initial enrollment on July 15th and only ended up getting a spot in the graduate course I really wanted around September.
registration_advice: Don't despair if you don't get all your intended courses immediately. Just keep showing up to the classes and get on the waitlist as soon as possible! Then if a spot opens up and you get it, you won't be 2 weeks behind on classes. And if it all seems a bit overwhelming don't hesitate to ask fellow students once you arrive or contact academic advising within your department at Berkeley.
academics_comments: An absolutely fantastic experience that I would recommend to everyone!
course_level: I took three "Upper Division" BA courses, and one MA course. The "College of Letters & Science" only allows for exchange students to take one MA course, although I wanted to take more MA courses initially. However, the course combination I had was quite challenging for me, so I am glad I ended with only a single MA course. Although I will say that I heard at Berkeley that the Upper Division courses famously often have a higher workload (in terms of assignments and quizzes) than certain MA courses. Hence it might be very doable to do multiple MA courses. In this case, a tip is to apply through the Statistics Department (if possible), since I believe they don't limit MA courses – and regardless of department, one can enroll in basically any courses at Berkeley (I recommend "fact-checking" this by emailing the department and/or UCPH to clarify what is possible and what is not).
teaching_comparison: It was actually pretty comparable. Lectures were a bit shorter (50 or 80 minutes of actual lecture time), but then there were more sessions per week). Great teachers and courses at high levels. A big difference was the concept of "Office Hours" instead of TA sessions. "Office Hours" are designated time slots set aside by the professors for students to show up and ask questions in more intimate settings. I am used to TA sessions and I know that we are always allowed to show up at our professors' offices at UCHP, but at Berkeley it was very systematic and expected to show up at their offices, which I found pretty cool!
courses_enrolled: Upper Division BA courses: Introduction to Complex Analysis, Introduction to Partial Differential Equations and Introduction to Quantum Field Theory MA course: Differential Topology DeCal / Seminars (only 2 ECTS per course; these were "for fun"): Introduction to Go and Berkeley Connect.
recommended_courses: I wholeheartedly recommend the courses I took in the Math department: Introduction to Complex Analysis, Introduction to Partial Differential Equations and Differential Topology. I found my Introduction to Quantum Field Theory course hard to follow along with simultaneously and so I did not get as good an impression of this course. Looking back at it now though, I am very glad that I took it. I learned more than I thought at the time, and am glad to have seen the material. I also recommend taking a DeCal ("Democratic Education at Cal") which are these small "for fun" courses for 1 or 2 units, taught by other Berkeley Students. The Berkeley Connect course was also pretty cool, as we got to meet a Nobel Prize winner for a Q and A session and go on lab tours!
unexpected_costs: I hadn't done a big enough travel budget. Make sure to allocate money for fun experiences!
cost_comparison: Groceries were very expensive. So was the rent!
activities_available: Free gym with swimming pool, weight room, dance room, basketball courts, badminton courts, ping pong courts, climbing walls, squash courts etc.! Best part: You can borrow rackets and balls. There were also often different types of events or club meet-ups at the campus.
activities_recommended: Make sure to sign up for "Intramural Sports" (IM sports). Make sure to go to American Football games as often as you can (good vibes!). Also, be sure to try and attend other big sports events: Basketball games, baseball games, volleyball games, swim meets etc. It's a big part of college culture, and very fun to meet all the nice people that attend. Make sure to go to "Taco Tuesday" at Raleigh's Pub with friends. Even if you are not the big party-go'er, it's a lovely atmosphere and a cheap dinner. Just go at around 7 or 8 pm and enjoy the vibes! If you then like dancing, you can join the other's and go to "Tap House" when Rayleigh's close their outdoor area. Make sure to attend "The Big Game" if possible (student tickets are way cheaper than regular seating – and more fun!) Check out the "Rose Gardens" and the botanic garden. See if you can get to spend Thanksgiving with an American family (they have to invite you of course). This was an awesome experience!
weekend_recommendations: Go to Yosemite, Lake Tahoe and a proper trip to San Francisco if it's clear so one can see the bridge. Maybe visit Carmel-by-the-Sea or do a wine tasting in Sonoma county / Napa valley. Or check out guides yourself on the internet – California has amazing nature!
culture_adjustment: Very easy. People are extremely open and friendly.
socializing_tips: As long as you have the courage to say hi and not worry about looking like a fool, then you will have the best time ever. People are so nice if you meet them with a smile! Americans will be quite enthusiastic and optimistic – lean into it, and join them! There are lots of things to be excited about at Berkeley. Go to cafés with people from your classes after they end and talk about the material (or at least act like that's the plan, until you end up chatting about life instead ;) )
cultural_challenges: No important differences. However, I don't recommend talking politics with your friends. I avoided this on purpose for the most part, because I know that in America you will often vote on the same party and politicians as your family or childhood friends. So it was really hard for me to connect the person with the politics they supported often, because they honestly was just voting on a specific politician because they had learned to do so. Hence I don't think there's any good to come out of spending time on politics.
culture_appreciated: The openness, friendliness and level of excitement and energy I met every day. People did tons of stuff and were very larger-than-life characters, all very happy to share and ready to cheer you on!
top3_advice: - Be courageous and approach people you don't know. Don't be afraid to look or sound awkward, but instead turn it around and make it your goal to make a little bit of a fool out of yourself every day. Then you will meet tons of great people and have fantastic laughs. - Take classes you think sound interesting, not the ones you think will be easy. You will find way more people to connect with. - Say YES to experiences. Plan trips. Enjoy the campus (don't forget to go up the Campanile often – it's free for students!!)
other_useful_info: Don't be afraid to ask your fellow students and friends for help, tips and tricks. You'll figure most of it out once you get there. And once again, it is a big recommendation to stay at the I-house.
most_rewarding: That I learned to believe more in myself and embrace the fun of it.
greatest_challenge: Taking multiple hard courses at once, forcing me to abandon perfectionism.
other_comments: DO IT! Go on exchange! You will learn way more than you think – both academically and personally.

crucial_aspects: I had always wanted to study in the U.S at some point throughout my education, so I thought taking a semester on exchange in the U.S as part of my masters would be a great opportunity to do so. Moreover, I had never been to California before, and I have quite a few contacts there too. UC Davis also has a high academic level, which I also took into account.
info_ease: When I arrived, I had already received alot of information from the University of Copenhagen and UC Davis, which made my arrival easy. However, there were certain e-mails and info that I couldn't find on my own, but that both faculties were open to help with either way.
arrival_assistance: We had an orientation day where we met faculty staff and the dean of the law school. Our first week of class was with the 1L J.D students (1-years), so we were on fairly equal level and got a nice introduction to the legal landscape of the U.S.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration itself was quite straight forward. However, the courses that I first applied to after thorough research were all full, even though I did it within the deadline. I ended up having a meeting with a faculty member in order to find new courses. I ended up being able to shape my preferred schedule, but the courses themselves were not ones that I would have dreamt of having in the first place. However, I ended up enjoying the courses I took. The faculty staff also lets you know about waitlists, how to get on them and the likelyhood of getting the course. You also have the opportunity to take more classes than you need, and then drop them if you dont like them.
registration_help: As mentioned, the faculty staff was helpful in terms of any problems associated with course registration. E.g. they were helpful in terms of making sure that the amount of credits needed to fulfill the exchange ECTS requirements were met.
registration_success: I was not successful in registering for any of the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: I dont have any really, as I couldn't help that the courses were full, and I did it before the deadline. However, I would recommend having alternatives in case you don't get your 1st or even 2nd priorities.
course_level: Well, the level of education in the U.S isn't divided into BA and MA, but undergraduate and graduate. Since Law is exclusively a graduate course, I would say mainly MA courses are taken at UC Davis. However, there is a difference between "bar courses" (used for the bar exam) and non bar courses. Of the four courses that I had, only one was a bar course.
teaching_comparison: Very different. The socratic method (cold calling) is very common at the UC universities and in Law school in the U.S in general. At UCPH this is against the rules, so it took some getting used to. Also, many professors have zero laptop policies and some dont even use powerpoint slides. Moreover, at UCPH one's grade is based entirely on the outcome of an exam. At UC Davis it is a combination of class participation, assignments and the final exam. Moreover, there isn't an actual "exam period" as we are used to. Classes end only about a week before finals start. This was a source of stress for some, but the professors do take it into account when correcting finals.
courses_enrolled: Environmental Law, Constitutional Law II (equal protection and first amendment), Alternative Dispute Resolution & Election Law: Voting Rights Seminar.
recommended_courses: I found Environmental Law quite relevant, even though I was sceptical at first. It is a very specific subject, so probably not a good way to get a basic understanding of the legal system in the U.S. I really liked Alternative Dispute Resolution, and would highly recommend this. Constitutional Law II was good to get a broader understanding of the U.S legal system, and the professor is a well renowned scholar within the topic in the US. However, he did not use powerpoints and had no laptop policy.
unexpected_costs: The faculty at UC Davis had some strange one time fee payments that we had to pay, where a few cost over 1,000DKK. Books were more expensive than they had said the estimate prices are. I was also scammed for two months rent, and had to pay this double.
cost_comparison: Books (more expensive), Cellular data (less expensive), Food and groceries (more expensive).
activities_available: The ARC (Schools Recreational centre) had climbing, basketball, badminton, squash, gym, table tennis, crossfit, volleyball and boxing available. This was free through the school.
activities_recommended: Playing football for King Hall FC, as it is so much fun and a great way to meet new people, also across years of Law.
weekend_recommendations: San Francisco, Napa Valley, Lake Tahoe, LA, Yosemite, Las Vegas, Santa Barbara, Santa Cruz, Hearst Castle, Solvang, Sacramento, G-Street Wunderbar and Parkside. College football is also cool.
culture_adjustment: I found it pretty easy, and enjoyed being a real californian for 4 months!
socializing_tips: Join clubs, either sport or academic, go out in the weekends and travel when you can. In general take every experience you are offered!
cultural_challenges: Cold calling, no laptop policy, legal english vocabulary, the fact that sales tax and tipping is calculated after the price and that people at law school (in some instances) would not really speak to exchange students, because we are there for a short period only. (But you can help that by being social).
culture_appreciated: The fact that people are open and welcoming, the weather (until late October), all the beautiful sights to see in California, the cars, the restaurants, the food.
top3_advice: Know that Davis is quite a small university town, so there is only a limited amount of things to do. There are nice bars, cafes, stores, restaurants and sports faciliteis, but sometimes it is needed to take a trip to San Francisco or another location that has more going on. This does, however, make it a great town to concentrate for studying in.
other_useful_info: I think I covered it :)
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and getting the chance to live in a foreign country for a longer period of time. Being in California for 4 months, though not being too long, you are there long enough to gain alot of knowledge about the state, the people, the cities and the life in general. Also, being able to attend courses that are in English with people who have had English courses all their lives, and still being able to follow their level.
greatest_challenge: Finding housing!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a place that offered courses in English but where the native language wasn't English so I would have an opportunity to learn a new language. Additionally, I wanted to go to a place with a foreign and exciting culture different from Denmark as well as a smaller or town where culture is more well-preserved compared to big cities.
overall_comments: I was generally happy with my experience though it did prove to be more challenging than anticipated.
info_ease: It was slightly difficult due to the fact that some of the online information regarding schedules and classes were still being updated and adjusted. However, people (staff and professors) were very friendly and ready to help, either via email or in person.
arrival_assistance: Online student help desks were hosted once in a while for all international students, not just Erasmus students though I never attended one. Apart from this, I did not receive any assistance when I arrived. Professors and staff in the physics department hadn't been informed that I had arrived during the first day of classes and therefore weren't expecting me in class. Additionally, in one of the courses the professor hadn't been informed that I would attend her class at all though I was still able to follow her class. Disappointingly, there were no introductory events in order to meet other exchange students.

registration_success: I was able to register for all of the classes that I wanted that were available that semester.
registration_advice: Ask your program coordinator at the host university whether any course you might be interested in has been cancelled or moved to a different semester. This happened to a couple of courses I was interested in where that change hadn't been updated on the course website.
academics_comments: I was generally happy with my experience though it did prove to be more challenging than anticipated.
course_level: I took four MA courses and one BA course that was supposed to be a MA course but got combined with the equivalent BA course as it was an introductory course. The level and workload was generally easier than at UCPH though still interesting and rewarding.
teaching_comparison: More one dimensional and primarily lectures, not as much variety. One exception include a lot of potential for personalized and interesting lab work as there are few students in the program in general with a high professors to students ratio. The university boasts a big and varied research facility covering a lot of different fields and experimental setups.
courses_enrolled: Physics of Archaeology and Cultural Heritage Applied Biophotonics Ecological Climatology Astrophysics Machine Learning and AI (Part 1)
recommended_courses: 1. Physics of Archaeology and Cultural Heritage Such a unique and fascinating course but still with a big emphasis on physics where you learn about phenomena and methodologies that are also used in other fields. 2. Applied Biophotonics Very interesting and thorough course with a good mix of theory and experimental understanding.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Items were as I expected, generally very cheap though some public transportation slightly more expensive.
activities_available: Academic talks and musical performances were put on but that's about it. Some parties and bar nights for students were arranged but outside of university and on the initiative of volunteering students.
activities_recommended: Karaoke nights or bar nights every other Friday at two different bars in town, a place to meet fellow students.
weekend_recommendations: Explore Naples and the surrounding area (Campania). Hike a long the Amalfi coast and go for a swim, visit the old towns and villages, churches and museums, visit Pompei and climb Vesuvius, watch a football match either at Naples stadium or at a square/bar, visit the islands, plenty of stuff to do in the area; both cultural, outdoor, and city activities.
culture_adjustment: It was a little difficult to get used to the lack of structure and relaxed time management, both on campus but also regarding public transportation, traffic, etc. However, that was part of the fun and truly a culture chock (even though it was an anticipated one).
socializing_tips: Learn a little bit of Italian though on an MA level, most can speak good English.
cultural_challenges: Lack of structure regarding most aspects of life. Relaxed attitude to time, meeting hours, and deadlines.
culture_appreciated: Super friendly and open people! Delicious food and rich, cheap cafe and restaurant culture, super affordable and easy to go out.
top3_advice: 1. The chaos is frustrating but also part of the fun and the cultural experience. 2. The university is lacking both academically and socially but professors are very engaged and accommodating and social connections can be made through other channels like international group meetups in Naples. 3. The surrounding area is gorgeous and have a lot of opportunity for exploration and adventure. The south of Italy is truly a unique, fun, and exciting. ALSO, EAT AS MANY PIZZAS AS POSSIBLE!
other_useful_info: Go there for the cultural exchange rather than the academic exchange though the place do offer some unique academic opportunities.
most_rewarding: Getting a bigger culture shock in Europe (the south of Italy) than when I went to Bozeman, Montana in the US (during my BA).
greatest_challenge: The chaos and lack of structure as well as non-existing social events for Erasmus students to meet each other.

In addition, the country’s unique natural environment offered a valuable opportunity to experience learning in direct connection with diverse landscapes and ecosystems. Finally, the cultural dimension, including the chance to gain insights into Māori perspectives and ways of relating to nature, was an important factor that made New Zealand a particularly meaningful destination for me.
