crucial_aspects: I knew I wanted to take the opportunity of going outside if Europe, since studying is a relatively easy way of going somewhere without having to apply for jobs, long term visas etc. I love the ocean and warm weather and Cape Town didn't only have that, but also nature, city, culture (and wine). I speak several languages from before but this time I wanted to focus on experiencing the place and getting to know people, therefore I chose an English-speaking country. I didn't know much about University of Cape Town but when I listened to the principal's beginning of semester speech online while still being in Denmark, I felt it was something different than I was used to in the Nordics. There's another level of authenticity and humanity highly influenced by the very recent history of apartheid.
overall_comments: I was going to take courses within the anthropology department but ended up not actually being able to take any of them because they were cancelled last minute. Now I'm very happy about that because instead I got to connect with people from different departments and fields. My courses were in medicine&art, gender development and conflict in SA, and linguistics.
info_ease: The studies were half in person and half online so it was quite messy. Mainly to manage to register to courses and understanding the system since no one answered any emails. In the end a "deadline for enrollment" wasn't as set in stone as I thought and I could have avoided stressing about it if I knew that.
arrival_assistance: To be honest not much. The international team did organize some online sessions but to get answers to your questions was quite difficult.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I was going to take courses within the anthropology department but ended up not actually being able to take any of them because they were cancelled last minute. Now I'm very happy about that because instead I got to connect with people from different departments and fields. My courses were in medicine&art, gender development and conflict in SA, and linguistics.
registration_process: We did it online. But to be registered for courses you need to have signatures from course convenors and then submit that form to apply to the course in the student portal online.
registration_help: IAPO. But as mentioned it wasn't easy to get answers.
registration_success: I got the ones I wanted that were offered but many were cancelled last minute or only offered during the second semester.
registration_advice: Don't panic! Things will work out, many are in the same situation as you :)
academics_comments: I was going to take courses within the anthropology department but ended up not actually being able to take any of them because they were cancelled last minute. Now I'm very happy about that because instead I got to connect with people from different departments and fields. My courses were in medicine&art, gender development and conflict in SA, and linguistics.
course_level: A lot of written reports, and quite long ones. The courses had completely different requirements though.
teaching_comparison: The teachers and students were much closer in Cape Town. They were more personal and met their students at eye level. People were also sharing about profound suffering in their lives in class, and the teacher met it with kindness.
courses_enrolled: LANGUAGE CONTACT & GLOBALISATION ASL5310F AXL5103FS DEVELOPMENT, CONFLICT AND POLITICAL CHANGE AXL5412F CRITICAL MEDICAL HUMANITIES IN AFRICA
cost_comparison: Groceries were more expensive, I mostly ate out.
activities_available: A lot. Everything from scuba diving and hiking, to volunteering.
activities_recommended: Volunteering! Just to move out of the campus bubble, to see other sides of Cape Town and understand the socio-economic situation in society.
weekend_recommendations: Wine tastings, beaches, road trips, eating out, yogs etc etc
culture_adjustment: Surprisingly easy. I felt very at home, probably because it's so western-like.
socializing_tips: Talk to them in your classes. Ask questions when not understanding something instead of just assuming
cultural_challenges: That I felt I came from a very privileged context and didn't always feel entitled to express my opinion or view in certain situations. Not because they said so but because I thought it.
culture_appreciated: The incredible kindness. People are insanely kind. You will notice.
top3_advice: 1) In Cape Town you really get everything, ocean, mountain, nature, beach,city - use it and don't bury yourself in studies and books. 2) No matter how used or not used you are to travel there's always a level of loneliness in the beginning. Embrace that it will pass, engage in activities around you. 3) if you care a lot about grades you should know it's difficult to get good grades from UCT. They have a scale going to 100% but no one receives more than maximum around 80. When the grades then are transferred back to UCPH it might not look as good as you want them to.
other_useful_info: You don't have to pay administration fees (you pay nothing) to UCT. This was unclear to me, I payed and fortunately I should get it refunded.
most_rewarding: The environment, the people, the history.
greatest_challenge: Quite a lot of administrative struggles that took a lot of energy. If you live far from campus that can be a struggle to go there a lot but since I was doing combined online and in person teaching it was fine (lived in Sea point and studied at Upper Campus).
other_comments: Go!!!

crucial_aspects: Først og fremmest valgte jeg Cape Town pga. mit studie (forhistorisk arkæologi), men aspekter som kulturforskel og naturen fyldte mindst lige så meget.
info_ease: Jeg vil sige at universitetet var meget hjælpende, men til tider var der en del forvirring. Da jeg kom frem i lufthavnen havde de sat to studerende til at tage imod de internationale studerende, hjælpe os med at finde frem til vores accomendation og generelt var de gode til svare på spørgsmål om universitetet, byen osv.
arrival_assistance: Jeg havde noget rod med min bolig til starte med og min uvkekslingstutor var rigtig god til at give mig tips og tricks og hjalp mig med at bestille en uber.
arrival_comments: Universitetet var ikke særlig god til at besvare mine mails eller opkald. Til gengæld var de meget behjælpelige, da jeg var landet i Cape Town. De er meget pragmatiske anlagt, men de kunne godt være lidt hurtigere i "før ankomst- processen".
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Det her var en meget spædende og samtidig meget fustrendede proces. Jeg vil anbefale ikke at knytte sig for meget til de udbudte kursuser, som er beskrevet i kursushåndbogen, da de i sidste ende kan blive aflyst af forskellige årsager. Jeg tog selv kursuser fordelt over det humanistiske fakultet i både arkæologi, litteraturvidenskab og religion. Det skal lige siges, at jeg i sidste ende var meget tilfreds med mine kursuser, men at vejen dertil ikke var uproblematisk. Du starter med at søge to, tre eller fire kurser hjemmefra. Dem skal du så bruge til at få din forhåndsgodkendelse igennem KU (jeg fik først min et halvt år senere, så du skal ikke stresse over, hvis den ikke kommer ind af døren med det samme). Derefter skal du vente og se om værtsuniversitetet godkender dit kursusvalg i forhold til din egen uddannelse. Hvis de ikke godkender et eller flere af dine kursuser skal du ændre dem i de første uger af dit ophold. Dette er standard procedure og kan være enormt irreterende, men du kan tage det helt roligt fordi personalet på UCT er enormt hjælpsomme. Alt i alt vil jeg sige, at man skal have en mere pragmatisk tilgang til sit studieophold i Cape Town da ting ændrer sig og tit til DET BEDRE!.
registration_help: Det internationale kontor var super hjælpsomt og generelt var de forskellige studievejledinger meget opmærksomme på de internationale studerende og vores tusinde spørgsmål.
registration_success: Jeg fik 1/3 af de kursuser jeg gerne ville have, men jeg endte med at have tre kurser, som jeg ikke ville have byttet for noget andet.
registration_advice: Vælg de kurser som du syntes er spændende og givende ! husk at karakterende ikke påvirker dit nuværende gennemsnit, så vælg med hjertet. Vær tålmodig og optimistisk du skal nok finde en kursus-sammensætning, som er fed!
course_level: Højt niveau og der er mange afleveringer (flere end jeg var vandt til på KU). Dine karaktere komme til at være lavere, men som nævnt højere oppe, så tag det helt roligt og nyd processen i stedet. Du skal også have tid til at se andet end en skolebog. Cape Town er et magisk sted med så meget at se og gøre.
teaching_comparison: Hvis du ligesom mig ikke møder op til alle forelæsninger, så skal du være klar på at gøre dette. Det bliver forventet at du møder op og deltager i diskussionerne. Du SKAL møde op til en procentdel af kurset for at bestå. Derudover har de også en masse praktiske lektioner, hvor du prøver kræfter med den lærte teori.
courses_enrolled: The First People Resisstance and Postcoloniality Religion and Society
recommended_courses: Vælg kursuser som du syntes er interessante og jeg kan kun anbefale at tage kurser som beskæftiger sig med afrikansk historie eller kultur - Det er en god mulighed at få det ind under huden på!
unexpected_costs: Under mit ophold oplevede jeg ikke nogle uforventede omkostninger som sådan. Jeg brugte Uber lidt for meget da det var nemt og billigt og dette var klart min største udgift, da prisen varierer alt efter myldretid og distance. Man kan leve meget billigt i Cape Town og valutaens værdi er meget lav i forhold til den danske krone. Køb lokalt, så sparrer du også en masse penge.
cost_comparison: Forsikring var det dyreste og jeg endte både med en dansk rejseforsikring og sydafrikansk forsikring.
activities_available: Igennem klubberne bliver der arrangeret alle mulige former for fede aktiviteter. Ellers er der massere af NGO og shelters, som man hjælpe til i hvis man har mod på friviligt arbejde. De fleste aktiviteter jeg foretog mig var sammen med venner fra mit hus eller dem jeg mødte på UNI.
activities_recommended: Vandring (table mountain har så mange fede vandreture man kan tage på!), klatring, surfing, dykning, de mange markeder, secondhand stores, festivaller, tage til gudtjeneste (selvom man ikke er kristen), tage på nogle weekendture ud af Capetown til Stellenbosch, Franschhoek.
weekend_recommendations: I de længere ferie kan man både tage øst på til Garden Route, Se ørkenerne i Northern Cape (Karoo og grænsen til Namibia) og Western Cape (Cederberg, West Coast Nationalpark, Namaqua).
culture_adjustment: Både og. Der er meget energi og larm i Cape Town. Sydafrikanere er generelt med afslappede, men også meget energifulde, humoristiske og interesserede. Da hvide er en minoritet kommer de fleste danskere til at stikke ud og jeg skulle i starten lige finde ud af ikke at skamme mig over det. Det vigtigeste er at være åben! - resten kommer af sig selv.
socializing_tips: Lav en aftale og lav nogle aktiviteter sammen: kaffeaftale, vandretur, koncert eller andet.
cultural_challenges: Afrikansk tid haha. I Sydafrika har man et meget afslappet forhold til tid og mange kommer for sent til aftaler. Det skal lige siges at man vender sig til det.
culture_appreciated: Deres ærlighed, humor, energi og ligefremhed om apartheid og Sydafrikas komplekse historie. De er meget åbne og ikke fordømmende.
top3_advice: Vær åben, vis dine egne værdiger frem og lær fra alt det der er omkring dig på godt og ondt. Cape Town er magisk, tragisk, energifuldt og alt på en gang! TAG AF STED
other_useful_info: Spørg, spørg, spørg!
most_rewarding: Gode venner! et nyt syn på vores eget land, hvor meget vi tager foregivet og hvordan vi altid kan ændre os og vores syn på andre mennesker.
greatest_challenge: Visumprocessen og bolig! Start i god tid og vær grundig i processen, så du ikke skal gøre det om igen senere!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere with warmer weather then in DK. I also wanted to go to a place where I could get a new perspective on my academic learnings so fat. Cape Town was therefore an obvious first choice.
info_ease: It was very easy to find the information I needed. The most difficult thing was the courses they offered that semester, I figured it out ones I was there, but it was really stressful. The application process was easy but started later than I expected to. However, you do need to apply for a visa in quite good time and start preparing for the papers before you know if you have been accepted.
arrival_assistance: I was greeted by two local students that the University of Cape Town International office had arranged to meet the internationals in the airport. I got help to figure out how to read the course list and who to seek out to find if the course was still available. Furthermore, the week before classes started there was an orientation week, where we got a lot of information about UCT, Cape Town, and got to know our classmates.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You have to registrar online before you come to campus, but if you get declined on some of your classes you have to write to the professors and then they will tell if you can join the class. Then you can apply for that class online.
registration_help: Not a lot. A little from the international office, but you have to physically go to the different departments to check what classes they offer.
registration_success: two of the classes I original wanted was not available, but I was satisfied
registration_advice: You will figure it out and most courses are good with highly skilled professors
course_level: Some was high, others not so much. It was all fine.
teaching_comparison: It was different in terms of that people used them selves in the classes much more than in DK. In terms off speaking about their own experiences. I kept having a focus on relating it to the readings, and that was very helpful. In most of my courses the level was really high and the professors good. I had one course with mixing level, but I guess that is what you can expect.
courses_enrolled: ANS4405S: Visual Anthropology/Multi-Modal Anthropology AXL4402S: Thinking Anthropologically SOC5056S: Political Sociology
recommended_courses: AXL4402S: Thinking Anthropologically - To learn anthropology from a new perspective and get introduced to other types of readings/theoretics. - to go beyond the western world view and learn from a South African perspective SOC5056S: Political Sociology - One of the best courses I have ever had. Very high level. Difficult but so interesting
unexpected_costs: I would recommend to rent a car, it gives so much freedom! You can also Uber around, which is a bit cheaper, but its not to bad.
cost_comparison: Supermarkets have higher prices than you would expect. It is a lot cheaper to go out, but not so much to make you own (still cheaper than to go out/order all the time)
activities_available: Supermarkets have higher prices than you would expect. It is a lot cheaper to go out, but not so much to make you own (still cheaper than to go out/order all the time)
activities_recommended: Definitly join the rowing club, and join as early as possible. Join the mountain and ski club for nice hikes and a good way to get to know some locals.
weekend_recommendations: I would definitely do the Garden Route in the week holiday. I would also visit the Cederberg Mountains and some of the city up north-west.
culture_adjustment: It was easy. Cape Town is very westernized
socializing_tips: Join clubs, and say yes to stuff! annnd go on a festival! and join housing with locals
cultural_challenges: The poverty, which is not culture but it was just hard to see and know you could not do much about it
culture_appreciated: Peoples kindness
top3_advice: 1. You get a unique possibility to do so many outdoor activities, use it! 2. Cape Town is not a safe safe place, but do not let that scare you. Everything is going to be fine as long as you take your precautions like not going outside when it is dark (take an uber) 3. Take advantage of the semester and travel a bit after, but remember cape town is sooo fun in December aswell.
other_useful_info: Check out the different cafeterias at campus
most_rewarding: Doing a lot of outdoor activities, most of the time it was between 20-29 degrees which meant that it was possible to do so much, like hiking, going to the beach, running, walking in the forest ect.
greatest_challenge: The poverty are in some areas very low, which mean that the crime can be very high. The worst thing that happened though was that a lot of my friends got their phone stolen in clubs. But it is the same as in any big city. And cape town is one of the most safe bigger cities in South Africa. I found it very exhorting in the end that you constantly had to be fully attentive of your surroundings
other_comments: Cape Town and UCT are amazing! Cape Town will forever be in my heart and I will definitly come back

crucial_aspects: The avaibility to explore Paris and learn the French culture and language.
info_ease: It was okay. I received e-mails with info from KU and the host university via E-mail. But there was also a lot of information and things you need to find out yourself after arrival. I had some questions regarding the documents we needed to fill out, but the host university replied after some time so I could fill all the documents correct.
arrival_assistance: There was some welcome days where the Erasmus students received information and saw the university. We all got a french student as a "buddy". So you could always ask that person questions. The school employees was sweet to say where and who you can ask about stuff, but it is not always efficient so you need to have patience regarding information and student cards etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Very old system. It was easy enough to write to the person in charge of the legal department about your wished course registrations. But after that you need to register in person in different offices to know when and at what time your classes will be.
registration_help: You could always ask for help at the offices but not everyone was good at french.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted and they were kind to help with making sure you got classes that did not collide timewise.
registration_advice: Again, be patience with the informations and their system in France. It is not efficient but everything will work out.
course_level: I had both Bachelor (they call it Licence), Masters and LLM courses. The level was most easy on the licence and then moving up.
teaching_comparison: The courses in the different programs have very different teaching style from Copenhagen. Some courses they call TD´s which are like seminars in Denmark in a classroom. In most of those couses part of your grade will reflect on participation in class (like 10-20%). But don´t be afraid of that. It´s not that difficult to pass the courses compared to in Copenhagen. Some other courses are CM´s which are like lectures in Denmark. These courses will end with a final examination. I never had to prepare for any classes since there was no books. So everything the teacher say or the powerpoints is what you focus on.
courses_enrolled: Torts (TD) - 3 ECTS Corporate Law (TD) - 3 ECTS Writing contracts (TD) - 3 ECTS Business Law (CM) - 6 ECTS Intellectual Property (LLM) - 8 ECTS Company Law (LLM) - 8 ECTS
recommended_courses: I liked all my courses. My least favorite was Business Law because the professor spoke with a big french accent. In many of my other courses the teachers spoke very good english. Some of them were from english speaking countries.
unexpected_costs: Telefon abonnement - pga nye EU-regler skulle jeg de sidste to måneder købe fransk abonnement
cost_comparison: Nothing
activities_available: The ELSA organization organize different days and afternoons with activities for the Erasmus students doing Law. I didnt but I thought about joining the sports club. I registered for the French course to learn some French.
activities_recommended: Not sure. But hang out with the other erasmus students to do non-academic activities.
weekend_recommendations: Explore Paris and other cities nearby. Together with the other Erasmus students I went to Normandie and Bordeaux including wine tasting. I thought about going to Champagne area and other cities as well.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy.
socializing_tips: You can contact your "buddy" to socialize with french local students and the Elsa Organization which also host some different acti. You can also socialize with the french students from your classes.
cultural_challenges: The slow and inefficient systems in France.
culture_appreciated: The fact that it is so easy to find a cute café to sit and drink coffee and have a croissant. And just the whole vibe in Paris is amazing. The city is so beautiful everywhere.
top3_advice: 1. Live in Paris and get a monthly Navigo travel pass so you can get around easily in Paris and back and forth from University 2. Be patient with the French way of organizing and structuring courses, classes and more. 3. Socialize with the other Erasmus students in the introduction days. We became a big group of friends from the first days that hang out a lot.
other_useful_info: I had never had French lessons before but I got around fine. But it will be a advantage and much easier to speak with natives if you know some more French.
most_rewarding: The whole experience of exploring Paris streets, culture, food and wine. I got a lot of friends from all over Europe too.
greatest_challenge: To be more independent by seeking information and exploring.

arrival_assistance: I got help from my buddy through the ELSA buddy program. I was also able to ask the administration for documents and so on if I needed them. The day to day things I had to find a solution on myself.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was amazing. I got to know so many people and had a wonderful half year.
registration_process: I had to write a motivational letter and send additional material. I had to choose some courses. When I wrote the host university to get more insight on what the courses contained it was pretty easy from there. As stated before it just took a lot of time to get the approval after I sent the documents.
registration_help: I could write the contact provided by the host university. She was not always available in the application period but in the end, I figured it out on my own.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Ask for all the information you can get about the courses from the beginning. Start the process early on.
academics_comments: It was amazing. I got to know so many people and had a wonderful half year.
course_level: I had master-level, LL-M and license courses, which I needed to do to get 30 points.
teaching_comparison: I didn't have any courses where books were needed so I just had to write down what the teachers said and learn it by heart.
courses_enrolled: Business Law (GB) – 6 ECTS Intellectual property – 8 ECTS English equity and trust law – 6 ECTS Company law – 8 ECTS Torts – 3 ECTS
recommended_courses: English equity and trust law was the most interesting course that I had because the teacher was amazing and he really interacted. The torts course was the class I got the most out of.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: I didn't realize it would be so expensive to travel if it was not in the heart of Paris. I recommend buying a metrocard ("NAVIGO"). Eating out was way cheaper than expected.
activities_available: Everything from football to poetry clubs. There were many things you could join in on.
activities_recommended: Join the ELSA program - They have a tour day where they show you around Paris. There are also Erasmus Facebook groups that offer trips in France where you can get to know other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: All museums are free for students under 25 so go to different museums. Go on trips in France - the rapid train is super fast so you can get around easily.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. It's very similar to Denmark. Just remember to watch out for your things because there is a lot of thieves.
socializing_tips: Join in on the intro days and be open-minded. And join in on the different activities that are offered.
cultural_challenges: The language could be a barrier sometimes.
culture_appreciated: The food, the wine and the social vibe.
top3_advice: Look out for your phone because it is your most important tool and phone thieves are pretty common in Paris. Bring a folder with all the important information you will need including a printed version of insurance papers, so you know who to call if/when something gets stolen. Remember to study a little along the way so you are able to enjoy the last month as well although it is the examperiode.
other_useful_info: Try to socialize. It's the people around you that makes the trip worth it. And bring pens and paper for the exams and note-taking.
most_rewarding: The relationships, the food experience and so on.
greatest_challenge: The waiting time. You need to bring your patience as well.
other_comments: Enjoy it!

info_ease: It was a bit slow communication - but overall I figured it all out.

housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: We had a specific person in the Law faculty to help us.
registration_success: 100% succesful. Everything was fulfilled.

course_level: I got the opportunity to take LLM courses, which was a great experience. The level was higher that in the other courses. Furthermore the courses I had at masterlevel was some really good teachers, which also had quite a good level of advance.
teaching_comparison: Very different. Everything is in hand, and some of the teachers don't use PP or anything.

unexpected_costs: The transportation pass was more expensive that expected

activities_available: A lot. Both sports and activities. But I feel like there are more in the spring semster.
activities_recommended: I didn't try any. But some of the sports. But It was difficult to sign up for them.
weekend_recommendations: Museums, and other cities in France. Really easy to do by train
culture_adjustment: I feel it was actually okay. Eventhough they are really bad in English
socializing_tips: I feel the introduction days are really good for that

top3_advice: Try to learn a bit French before going. plan som weekendstrips and adventures. Sign up for some everyday actity (I did some yoga)
other_useful_info: dont know

crucial_aspects: I wanted to improve my French. I also love France and wanted to explore Paris.
info_ease: It was quite easy
arrival_assistance: They had many introduction meetings for exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Ms. Gomert deals with everything regarding to exchange students. In the first weeks you were allowed to try several courses and after you had to inform Ms. Gomert of which courses you actually wanted to attend.
registration_help: They were responding quite fast on e-mail.
registration_success: Some LLM classes were only for british or american students, which I found a bit sad, since I wanted to attend some of those classes. Some were despite from the syllabus, not available.
registration_advice: Get as many courses as possible pre-approved, because it is not certain that you'll be able to attend the ones you actually want to.
course_level: They don't teach you how to apply the law, but only what the law is. In many cases you could just read the law yourself.
teaching_comparison: It is very different from UCPH. At UCPH the students are much more involved during classes and lectures. The level at UCPH are much higher than at Cergy-Paris Université. You didn't have any books so the things you could be examined in, was what the professor said at a lecture or during class. The credits don't match the work burden. The most demanding courses are only 3 etcs, while courses where you are almost not involved are 6 ects.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to british law Torts Tort law (LLM) Corporate law Intellectual property Business law
recommended_courses: Corporate law, intellectual property and tort law (LLM). The professors are more motivated in these courses and don't just read the law for you.
unexpected_costs: Bolt and Ubers, since the metros close at 01
cost_comparison: Doing groceries are much more expensive in Paris than in Denmark
activities_available: they had many sports activities
activities_recommended: I didn't attend any
weekend_recommendations: Paris
culture_adjustment: Very easy - people are very friendly
socializing_tips: I mostly socialized with other exchange students
cultural_challenges: The language. The French students are not that good in English, and they prefer being with their own friend group.
culture_appreciated: People were good at helping you with your French if someone only spoke French.
top3_advice: 1) Don't live in Cergy 2) By a monthly navigo card with all zones 3) Don't live alone
other_useful_info: Don't go to the train station at Cergy Prefecture at night. It is very scary both in daytime and even more in the evening.
most_rewarding: To explore Paris
greatest_challenge: The language

arrival_assistance: My landlord took me to the apartment. At the UNi we had a welcome meeting
arrival_comments: Could have been better signs and waypoints
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_advice: French administration is not the most helpful in the world

courses_enrolled: Business Law IP Law Criminal Law Intro to British Law Rules of Evidence
recommended_courses: IP law was rather okay despite it needing some more hours to dive into the subjects. Rules of evidence was relevant but the exam was a "remember irrelevant stuff"-thing and should have been made to fit 2024
unexpected_costs: Drinks are quite expensive and you spend a lot of money on food etc.
cost_comparison: Possible to eat out at restaurants for less than in Copenhagen but bars etc were the same prices

top3_advice: 1) Do not do it for the academic purpose - the uni is not at high level academically 2) Do not live in Cergy, it is not a nice city - I lived in Pairs and took the train (RER A) 3) Find friends and be openminded
other_useful_info: All the english exams are kind of on top of eachother - I had five exams within a week and 3 within 24 hours - it was awful!!

crucial_aspects: I choose to study in Paris because I have a big love for the city and have always dreamed of living there.
info_ease: It was very easy. My home university was very helpful and available to answer questions and solving any issues.
arrival_assistance: I did not have any personal assistance, however, there were a group of students from my host university who made a WhatsApp group for all the Erasmus students to use when in need for help.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was very easy for me because I chose to follow the same courses that I had chosen before arrival
registration_help: There was always an LLM coordinator and a Erasmus Law coordinator available at the university to answer any questions. Additionally, there was also a group of local students who made a WhatsApp group to all the Erasmus students which we also could use for any questions.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: My experience was that a lot of local students were really helpful so my advice is to be in contact with some students from the host university as well.
course_level: Overall the level was quite low. My experience was that the courses were not difficult in a legal way. Instead, most of the exams were really about memorizing definitions of different terms, and not solving legal cases like I personally was used to do in UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The level of teaching was also very low compared to UCPH. Many professors in the law courses did not have a law degree - instead most teachers had a background in political science or international relations. Therefore, the courses often had a political angle and not legally heavy. Furthermore, some teaches were very unenthusiastic. For example, in some courses the teachers just read out loud some power point slides, did not really answer questions and always finished one hour early which was quite annoying when I personally had a 3 hour travel time back and forth to the university. Furthermore, some teachers were very traditional in their way of teaching. I had a teacher who did not use nor a whiteboard or power points, and instead just talked about the different subjects without any structure. This made it really hard to follow his teaching especially because the pensum for the exams was the teachers words - there were no pensum books at all.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to European Union Law (LLM course), Contract Law (LLM course), Argumentation and Negotiation, Business Law and Criminal Law and Procedure.
recommended_courses: I would recommend both the Criminal Law and the Introduction to the European Union Law because of the teacher. He was very structural and it was easy to follow his teaching. I would recommend Argumentation and Negotiation to students who would like a break from the legal courses as it was very easy and was mostly about creating and analyzing speeches.
unexpected_costs: Paris is an expensive city to live in so generally going out to eat, shop etc. can cost a lot.
cost_comparison: Most museums are free for EU citizens under 26. Transportation was also less expensive than I expected.
activities_available: There is a lot of different social activities - both sports and cultural activities. However, I did not join any of the activities because I lived far away from the university.
activities_recommended: There is a lot of things to do in Paris. I therefore recommend going to museums, different restaurants, flea markets etc. The students at the host university were really helpful with arranging trips to different museums, the Eiffel Tower etc.
weekend_recommendations: I spent two weekends travelling to other places in France - Normandy and Marseille - which I would really recommend. It is very easy to take the train from Paris to a lot of different cities in France. Since they have high-speed trains (TGV) it only took me 3 hours to travel from Paris to Marseille - and it takes around 9 hours by car.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. I found many people to be very helpful.
socializing_tips: There was a big Erasmus group at my university so I did not really get to socialize a lot with the local students. However, they were really helpful.
cultural_challenges: I found some teachers to be very traditional in their way of teaching. Furthermore, all the exams were written by hand and it is very normal to have multiple exams in one day. I personally had 3 exams in one day.
culture_appreciated: The cultural opportunities, the food and that I found the French people very openminded and helpful.
top3_advice: 1) Don't expect any legal-heavy subjects, 2) all exams are written by hand and expect to have multiple exams in one day, and 3) a 40 min - 1 hour train ride to the university from Paris. As the academic level is low, you can expect to have a lot of time to enjoy Paris, which I personally was very happy about.
other_useful_info: Sometimes I found the administration at the university quite confused so have patience if you need help with administrative issues.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was meeting other exchange students from all over the world!
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was having 3 exams in one day.

crucial_aspects: I found the connection between Denmark and France interesting and got the opertunity to experience Paris. The CY Cergy Paris university promoted themselves as a University with professors and educators with experience from a Paris private law aspect. Furthermore was i able to take all courses in english, which was the biggest factor in my choice.
overall_comments: It is fun but demanding.
info_ease: It was descent. I got emails informing me on when and where to meet.
arrival_assistance: We received at powerpoint with information, that i found very helpful during the semester.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It is fun but demanding.
registration_process: Easy. Most of the work was done from home in good time.
registration_help: Powerpoint slides from intro day had alot of info with phonenumbers, who had which responsibility (who to call if you needed to change courses), difference between CM and TD courses.
registration_success: One of my classes overlapped with another why i had to change, but otherwise i got the classes i wanted.
registration_advice: Arm yourself with patience. They are unable to speak english in person, but are happy to help when you send email. It just takes time. Furthermore be well prepared from home.
academics_comments: It is fun but demanding.
course_level: BA courses were way below the level in Denmark. This can be because of the english level in France. However the LL.M. classes were fine, why i think CY Cergy Paris University should consider offering more than just 2 LL.M classes to Danish students and 3 to UK/US students.
teaching_comparison: Little to nothing to read for every class but intense teaching while students take notes. Some classes were literally hours of the teacher reading up from a screen and students taking notes. Very different from Denmark which has no participation grade and alot of reading done from home to prepare for class.
courses_enrolled: UK Business law I Argumentation and Negotiation I Moot court and litigation LL.M. Tort law LL.M. Intro to french and civil law
recommended_courses: Do the same courses as i did. Argumentation and Negotiation is chill, same with Business law where you are not obligated to show up for class and can read from home. LL.M. courses are on a level that actually can challenge you a little. Chose intro to french law and civil law, because it's interesting to learn about the system in the country you are on echange in. Same with tort law which has a good professor and interesting to compare tort law in Denmark and France.
unexpected_costs: Nothing. Good tip is to prepare that everything is expensive and nightlife in Paris costs alot.
cost_comparison: Foods, like eggs, milk and cheese was cheaper than in Denmark. Furthermore eating out was less expensive than i initially expected.
activities_available: Handball, combatsports, Moot court competition, etc.
activities_recommended: ELSA had many events
weekend_recommendations: Experience Paris and outside of Paris. Café, boulangerie, restaurants, events (Fashion week and european cultural heritage days). Furthermore experience champagne east of Paris and Normandy west of Paris.
culture_adjustment: Easy in some ways. People in Paris are kind of rude especially in public transport. However many other people are helpful. It's a large city and you can feel that, but it doesn't take long until you adjust.
socializing_tips: Do some sports or go do activities in Paris like seeing museums, nightlife, etc.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Food, art and experiences. The vibe of Paris is that it's a city filled with different types of people which makes it very diverse and accepting. Furthermore it's so picturesque.
top3_advice: 1. Do not go there for an academic challenge. Go there if you wish to experience Paris and for gods sake do not live in Cergy, but find a place in Paris. Paris is worth the commute. 2. Be prepared for all the typical things (Where to live, transport to study, courses, economy) before you go so you can enjoy Paris 3. Take the french courses (they are free offered by the university)
other_useful_info: Apply for a room at Fondation Danoise. Any house in the CIUP is nice since you get to live in a dorm and automaticly meet other students who also are on exchange.
most_rewarding: The friends and experiences like normandy trip with friends from study, and motorcycle trip east of Paris to champagne and Ardennes. It's also a good location to get visits from friends. i experienced that many friends wanted to come visit and see Paris.
greatest_challenge: Speaking french. I evolved from being a person with no experience in french to ordering at restaurants and having simple conversations in french. Studying in english is furthermore a challenge itself which was cool to master.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: It was a place to improve my spanish. I found the history of Chile and current political tensions interesting. There is a department of geography, that offers courses, which I find interesting and fit with the rest of my bachelor program.
info_ease: It was easy to find information about entering the country with visa, covid-stuff ect. Especially with the helo of the international student office at Universidad de Chile (PME).
arrival_assistance: We received a lot of assistance from the PME team. Where the assistance was lacking, was at my faculty.
arrival_comments: Orientation from my faculty was very lacking, especially since there is a lot of difference between faculties, which made it hard for the PME team to guide us on specific issues. We didn't have any official orientation at my faculty (FAU).
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registrering to the institution was something we did online with guidance from the university. Quite easy. Registrering to courses was done through an email to the PME team. What made it a bit complicated was that course descriptions from many faculties came out late, and they had to move deadlines. Then some 1 or 2 weeks after we could delete courses. This was also done via email through PME. What made everything a bit confusing was that our registration on the universities online platform (like absalon in copenhagen university) - u-cursos - was very slow, which meant the first week(s), we had very little information (international students), though students and teachers at the faculty were very helpfull.
registration_help: The PME team were very helpfull.
registration_success: I didn't get the classes I wanted most.
registration_advice: Don't get stressed about it - everything will happen with time.
course_level: I had one course with a very high (nice) level. 2 with which the level could have been higher, mainly due to teachers repeating themselves a lot.
teaching_comparison: What I missed the most was exercises, which we have quite a lot of at UCPH, but they were completly absent in my courses at Universidad de Chile. The teaching style is more like class-room-teaching and reminds me a bit of gymnasium. I felt quite some professors spend way too much time talking about "nothing" and well essentially because of this starting the classes very late. Though it could just be an overrepresentation among the professors I had. I noticed there is a stronger hierarchy between students and professors, than I'm used to.
courses_enrolled: Electivo de especialización: Lugar, territorio, identidad colectiva y movimientos sociales Análisis y evaluación ambiental Gestión integral de cuencas
recommended_courses: Well I really liked my elective about social movements. Then I also enjoyed my course on watersheet management. I would probably recommend getting into the electives it seems professors and students are more motivated there.
unexpected_costs: That I used more money arriving the first month, since I was going out more to get to know people and not knowing the cheapest way to do things. Also since Chile is not that cheap and especially travelling can easily get expensive.
cost_comparison: Food was way more expensive than expected. And travelling.
activities_available: Like officially arranged from our university for all students I don't remember much. I remember a talk about gender - which was very interesting. And a talk about the proposed new constitution, but this I believe was arranged by students. I believe some people are arranged in some football. Then there were a lot of social activities arranged by students for exchange students.
activities_recommended: Since I don't remember anything that was more established, I'm not quite sure. I would recommend to go to one of these social activities for exchange students to get to know some people who are also on exchange.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Cajon de Maipo. It is super close to Santiago and there are really good climbing opportunities. Also with a good bus connection from Santiago is Valparaíso, which is super charming. For longer holidays I can recommend from own experience: Chiloé, La Selva Valdiviana and San Pedro de Atacama (or more so the area around).
culture_adjustment: I would say quite easy.
socializing_tips: Just go with what comes up. And of course being open and friendly.
cultural_challenges: Could be cheak-kissing, but honestly I got used to that pretty quickly.
culture_appreciated: That it has so many different things and consists of so many different cultures.
top3_advice: - When choosing courses you can choose more than you need and eliminate later. Use this to see the teaching style of the professors, and then not only choose according to subject, but also professor, since there are quite some differences. - Coming from UCPH things usually work quite "according to the book" and everything is on time. This is not my experience at my faculty, FAU, at UdC. But that's okay. Just taking all of this more relaxed, people at the university are generally quite flexible. - Get to know your fellow students at university. This has been for me the easiest way to get to know chileans, and I believe it can be more interesting than staying in the environment of exchange students, even if that is also quite a lot of fun.
other_useful_info: Santiago is a huuuge city. There is plenty to explore.
most_rewarding: New friendships, cultural exchange and better spanish.
greatest_challenge: To begin with I thought it was hard to get to know people. But I believe it also teaches, that these things just take some time. And well people are easier to talk to, when the weather gets warmer.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to Latinamerica because of the rich cultures and the fact that they speak spanish. I chose Chile because of the higher level of educational opportunities. Safety considerations is also crucial.
info_ease: Yes
arrival_assistance: The assistance was not the best. The study abroad program in Chile was slow to answer and didn't answer all my questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We had a week to try courses and was able to change if we wanted. I had to go to the office every morning to ask which classroom I had to go to in the first week, cause they didn't send us exchange students the information.
registration_help: An office for students and a exchange student counciler.
registration_success: After a while I found a match.
course_level: It was a good level. It matched me.
teaching_comparison: It was more about learning it all and remembering it for the exams. For the exams we were not aloud to use our notes. The learning in the classrooms were pretty much the same
courses_enrolled: Violencia y discriminación Semántica y Pragmática Lingüística Cultural Género y sexualidad en el Modernismo Derechos humanos y género
recommended_courses: Semántica y Pragmática y Derechos humanos y género y Género y sexualidad en el Modernismo The teachers to these courses were really good and very structured.
unexpected_costs: Didnt have any.
cost_comparison: Chile is more expensiv than other latinamerican countries. Especially the supermarket was more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: In the campus you could chose a big amount of sports for free.
activities_recommended: I did Pilates and that was very nice.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Valparaíso or the south of Chile.
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Just talk to them. Chileans are the most shy of the latinamerican countries, they say. But when you talk to them they ar e super nice.
cultural_challenges: The eating schedule. Dinner at 21 when I like to eat at 18.
culture_appreciated: The kindness and the proudness. They are very political Chile and really fights when there is something to fight for.
top3_advice: Be open, be patient and learn chilean spanish.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: The friends I got there and the travel opportunities. Also the language skills I improved.
greatest_challenge: Probably understanding the teachers when they spoke very chilean.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to practice my spanish and South America is a melting pot of new experiences, cultures, nature and lots of other aspects that made it a natural choice. Santiago has always been a relatively safe city in SA, which i can now confirm, it really is safe enough that it does not feel any different than capital cities in southern europe.
overall_comments: As a principle, I cannot rate it 10, as that means perfection and nothing ever is. With that being said, Chile and Santiago in itself were amazing and offered so much culturally, academically and socially.
info_ease: There is a great office at the Universidad de Chile, PME, which handle all the exchange students. There were two zoom meetings before arrival with general information and I also had contact with them through email as i needed some course descriptions.
arrival_assistance: Universidad de Chile was extremely helpful with all the information I needed - that does not mean that they solved the problems though. One thing to remember is that you have arrived in South America and therefore deadlines is now something negotiable. The class sign up was only done two weeks into the semester and the first day of school, I therefore didn't have the formal sign-up. But as the office said - there is no problem, 99% of the exchange students get the classes that they want (and I also did) it is just because their systems take time and the administration is on vacation.
arrival_comments: Every faculty has a PME assistant - it goes way faster if you contact the PME assistant at your faculty than the general PME administration and often, they will also give you better, more detailed, answers.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: As a principle, I cannot rate it 10, as that means perfection and nothing ever is. With that being said, Chile and Santiago in itself were amazing and offered so much culturally, academically and socially.
registration_process: You send in a wish list of courses before semester start. When school then starts, the first two weeks are for trying out and seeing how you like the classes. Important info here is that there are no "forelæsninger" everything is class teaching. Depending on popularity of the class, each subject is split into 2-4 classes. That means that if you have a class like "Politica Latinoamerica" you will have Politica Latinoamerica.1, Politica Latinoamerica.2, Politica Latinoamerica.3 and Politica Latinoamerica.4. This means that every number has a different schedule and a different teacher. This is extremely good for us exchange students because this means we can take the class that fits the best into our schedule AND most importantly, try out the different teachers. For me, the most crucial was understanding the professor and i therefore went to the different classes and saw which teachers mumbled, who spoke super fast etc. so I could limit my spanish language issue the most possible. Therefore the two weeks were actually a really good idea from Universidad de Chile and super helpful. After the two weeks, you send in your final wishlist with the designated 'number' of your class and you're placed and become an offical part of the class.
registration_help: The PME assistant at Facultad de Gobierno was extremely helpful and I just went to campus and walked up to her office anytime I had questions, no reservation needed.
registration_success: I got all of the classes i wanted and also the desired 'number' for each class. 99% of all exchange students get this, so please, do not worry.
registration_advice: Be open to their systems and try out the different teachers for each class, i promise you dont have to stay with the 60yo mumbling man.
academics_comments: As a principle, I cannot rate it 10, as that means perfection and nothing ever is. With that being said, Chile and Santiago in itself were amazing and offered so much culturally, academically and socially.
course_level: I had classes with both first year students, third year students and electives with people of all ages. You are free to do whatever you want.
teaching_comparison: There is no "forelæsninger" only class teaching, which is different, but not necessarily bad. I felt the difficulty level was low compared to UCPH, because it is way more memorizing and being able to say a bit about the readings. They also don't have one final exam at the end but rather 3-4 tests throughout the semester and therefore, in a test situation, you have less material to focus on and it is fresh in your mind.
courses_enrolled: Fenómenos Macroeconómicos AP01306-1 Política Comparada I CP1203-2 Política Latinoamericana CP3202-1 Desafíos de la Diversidad Culturel desde Latinoamerica ELEGOB06-1
recommended_courses: I really liked having an elective course as it was with an "outside professor" who only came in because this was her field of study. The people enrolled in this class were also all super motivated because they had chosen it, not because they needed it. It was very fun. I also loved the course "Política Latinoamericana" which was super interesting.
unexpected_costs: Chile is by no means super cheap and it did suprise me that i felt like Madrid/Rome prices in that it was cheaper than Copenhagen, but also not dirt cheap. I made sure to be out a lot and try lots of things, so I spent more money than I thought i would, but it was definetly worth it.
cost_comparison: Almost all museums are free for students, so use them!!! Restaurants were more expensive than i thought they would be, but a good empanada is only about 14 kroner, so eat those instead!
activities_available: Lots of different sports, everything is shown in the course catalogue.
activities_recommended: Lots of bars and clubs in Santiago make "theme nights" and i met a ton of people by going to these. They are a bit kitsch, admitted, but you meet people there and then when you hang out again, you just do it at a bar of your choosing, so no need to go more than a few times - it's just networking! I also need to give a special shout out to MiercolesPO (find them on Instagram), which is an exchange student club - and yes, it is just as american frat-coded as you think, but literally every exchange student goes to these parties every wednesday and so you know everybody, the music is okay and it's a good way to meet up with people you dont see everyday at your faculties. Do it!
weekend_recommendations: Chile is an enormous country and with so much to offer. I will try to list as many places as possible: 1) Cajon del Maipo. This is 30 mins outside of Santiago and was my first trip, it is easy to get to with public transport and a wonderful place for hiking and small villages with markets. Very easy weekend destination. 2) La Serena + Valle del Elqui. My second destination, we rented a car and drove up there (btw renting a car is easy and with no fuss, big recommendation). Beautiful and with lots of history - try Pisco at one of the old distilleries! 3) Pichilemu. This is out on the coast and the unofficial surfing capital of the world apparently - there is a great vibe, other internationals and of course, the water is amazing (cold though!). 4) Santa Cruz. The fancy wine area of Chile, we went here as a part of a larger roadtrip and it was beautiful, we might as well have driven around France - not necessarily the most chilean place, but beautiful nonetheless. 5) Parque Nacional Altos del Lircay and the Laguna del Maule. This is probably one of the most beautiful places I have ever been and it is rarely mentioned in guide books so i 100% recommend going and reserving a little hut up in the mountain and do beautiful hiking and roadtrips! 6) Mendoza. A lot of students went here in the middle of the semester as a way of refreshing their tourist visa (the student visa is expensive and takes time and nobody checks if you have it - just stay on the tourist visa!). When you cross the border to Argentina you get 3 more months and it works perfectly and mendoza is a beautiful wine town, so win-win! 7) Valparaiso/Viña del Mar. For some reason every guide book talks about these destinations but wow, so overrated. Go visit of course if you want but there are a thousand places in Chile that are more worth your time! 8) Chiloe. The most beautiful island down in Northern Patagonia, it just has a special atmosphere. Go visit! 9) Torres del Paine. Not much to say, it should really be one of the worlds natural wonders - it is expensive, be warned, but 100% worth it. The amount of foreigners is scary though, definetly not a destination where you will find chileans, it is too expensive for them. 10) The rest of the coast next to Santiago - I really liked Isla Negra and Algarrobo 11) The region Norte Grande. I did an amazing road trip up north in Chile by the cities Iquique and Arica and visited the Parinacotta volcano in 5000 meters altitude and it was amazing. There were almost no people, they are all down in San Pedro de Atacama, and it was cheap - huge recommendation. 12) Rapa Nui. I ended my exchange with one week on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and it was absolutely amazing, what an experience. Chile has a very extensive network of busses and my main form of transport was nightbuses or renting a car between friends. Go see all this amazing country has to offer!
culture_adjustment: I had visited South America before and I knew a little bit of what to expect - you are in the salsa dancing, reggaeton listening part of the world and you should act accordingly! As danes, we can be a bit 'boring' in comparison, so the goal is to find a golden middle, where you enjoy what Chile has to offer BUT where you're also careful that you don't lose yourself in the process and only live in the night.
socializing_tips: I must be honest, I only had a couple chilean students. Chileans are super friendly and it will be easy to strike up a conversation with them. I had some issues with the obvious age difference - most of the students will be 19-21 years old and they will also be in another place mentally. That does not mean that everybody is horrible and my chilean friends showed me lots of cool corners of Santiago and gave me good tips, but it was definetly easier to connect with other internationals.
cultural_challenges: No toilet paper in the toilet - seriously, even after 6 months, it is just such a habit that I had to remind myself every day.
culture_appreciated: I was able to get out of my bubble and really enjoy public dancing on the streets, karaoke, just generally taking up more space in the public sphere. As a dane, it is refreshing to see that it is possible to live differently.
top3_advice: 1) Go to all the events (especially MiercolesPO!) and meet as many as possible. There are tons of different universities around Santiago and because i participated in these events, I knew people from different universities and different majors - a huge plus. 2) Please wait with booking your accomodation, you will get rewarded and end up with the coolest place. 3) Embrace the spanish! It is hard and they speak very fast, but with a little willpower, you will get far.
other_useful_info: Take longs walks aroudn Santiago and get to know your new city, there are so many cultural institutions that are just waiting to be discovered!
most_rewarding: Meeting so many people from all over the world and finding out how much we actually have in common!
greatest_challenge: All my courses were in Spanish and my level was definetly not high enough when i arrived. Do your best, talk to your teachers, they only want to help you. I ended up passing all my courses, so it is possible!
other_comments: ¡Viva Chile!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to learn spanish and Chile was one of the safer options to choose from in South America. Also the nature.
info_ease: More or less. UCHILE had a lot prepared with online orientations before arrival and so on. On the other hand, a lot of that information was wrong and didn't apply to the facultuy of architecture.
arrival_assistance: The PME faculty had some orientations and introduction for PME- students at the "international faculty". I was not connected to the architecture faculty, and i therefore missed a lot of important information that would be relevant for me as a landscape architecture student only taking classes at that specific faculty.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registration to UCHILE was simple, but registrations to courses was super complicated and confusing. Again because the faculties do things very differently. First of all, some of the course descriptions came out days before first day of class. You have to send an email to PME with the classes you want and then they will check with the FAU if its possible. Because pretty much every other architecture student is connected directly to FAU, they are first in the application process. For the first 1-2 weeks you just show up at the classes you're interested in and ask if it's possible to join, which sometimes it is and other times not.
registration_help: The PME office was easy to go to, also teachers and other students
registration_success: I didn't get all the classes i wanted. Some of them were restricted if you were connected to PME and not FAU
registration_advice: Everyone is a bit confused. So just be a bit confused together and then you will figure it out.
course_level: I think the level was fine for me as my spanish was not my best. If you actually speak good spanish I would say the courses lean to the easier side, but it also really varies from course to course. Taller/design courses take a lot of your time.
teaching_comparison: It's very much listen to the teacher talk and take notes. You don't have one final exam at the end, but several tests during the semester. For these tests it's just about repeating what was said in class.
courses_enrolled: Taller 7: Integración de variables de gestión, Geografía urbana, Electivo de especialización: Experimentos Urbanos: Estudios de Impacto del Entono Construido en el Comportamiento Humano, Español para Extranjeros
recommended_courses: I would reccomend Taller 7 and Geografia Urbana. Taller courses take up all of the students time tho, and you can feel the stress in other classrooms when delivery is near. Geografia Urbana was really interesting, and also had a lot of group work which was a plus for the exams. Español para Extranjeros, I would only reccomend if you get credits for it, as I didn't get anything out of it.
unexpected_costs: The supermarkets are really expensive, so would reccomend going to the weekend markets. I have also used a lot of money to eat out and travel.
cost_comparison: Supermarkets were more expensive.
activities_available: Different talks
activities_recommended: Didn't try any of them
weekend_recommendations: There are a lot of good hiking opportuinities in Santiago and just outside. My favorit My favorite places are Pucón, Laguna del Maule, Pichilemu and Northern Chile.
culture_adjustment: I would say easy.
socializing_tips: I would say that Chileans are maybe a bit more "reserved" than other South Americans, so sometimes you might be the one to start the conversation
cultural_challenges: The work life balance in uni is difficult. The Chileans work A LOT and it's sometimes difficult when you have to coordinate group work. Also the Chilean spanish is hard
culture_appreciated: The generousity of the people. It's also interesting to see how the culture chances from south to north
top3_advice: 1) Make friends with the chileans in your class. The courses with field trips are a good way to do that. 2) Don't rely too much on the original course schedule/plan. Something a teacher says one day might not count the next. 3) Choose the fun courses and look up exam forms.
other_useful_info: Not necessarily for UCHILE. But for traveling a creditcard is essential (especially for car rental) as you can't use your debit card all the time.
most_rewarding: The friends i made and the opportunity to travel as much as i have.
greatest_challenge: The winter was tough. There is no heating in most of the houses, so you never really get warm in those months. The hot water bottle saved me. Also that even after a whole semester here, the thick chilean dialect is stil impossible to understand.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to improve my Spanish! And I love outdoor activites like hiking, trekking and camping and have had a big wish for a long time to visit chile. Also safety wise it was one of the safer countries in LATAM.
overall_comments: I loved Chile! Beautiful country, the chileans are really nice and was generally happy about my exchange. Downside was quite a lot of time needed to be spend on school (mostly for architecture it sounds like, friends from economy, social science etc barely had any work)
info_ease: My coordinator at Uchile was really helpful, and answered fast on both email and it was possible to show up at his office. There was a lot of different (and lacking) information about my orientation at the faculty of architecture, but through talking to other architecture students i got the lacking information.
arrival_assistance: PME (my faculty) was a big help with questions etc. There was an orientation for exchange students which was a nice intro to the school and other students. It was confusing because I had classes at FAU, but didnt get the emails from them because my faculty was PME, so I missed quite a lot of important information I had to find out through the other architecture students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I loved Chile! Beautiful country, the chileans are really nice and was generally happy about my exchange. Downside was quite a lot of time needed to be spend on school (mostly for architecture it sounds like, friends from economy, social science etc barely had any work)
registration_process: A bit stressfull and confusing. At my faculty, FAU, we had to wish for courses before coming to chile, but when school started we had to attend all the classes we wanted to have, and ask the teacher if we could join the class. The teachers was often confused about whether we could join the class or not, and I feel like there was a lot of back and forth between the exchange office and the teachers. Some classes were also only allowed 3 exchange students per class, but the rules were bended in some cases and there were a lot more.
registration_help: Talk with the exchange coordinator at your faculty - they can sometimes help.
registration_success: I got almost all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Try not to stress, you will find courses even though the process is very confusing. And talk with the teachers and show interest for their course! I feel like a lot of them like excange students in general and wants to help.
academics_comments: I loved Chile! Beautiful country, the chileans are really nice and was generally happy about my exchange. Downside was quite a lot of time needed to be spend on school (mostly for architecture it sounds like, friends from economy, social science etc barely had any work)
course_level: The level itself wasn't too difficult. The big challenge for me was having all of my courses in spanish (ecspecially chilean spanish). I barely understood anything when I arrived.
teaching_comparison: a lot of tests with paper and pens, which is very different from UCPH.
courses_enrolled: I had Geografia Urbana, Taller 7, espanol para extranjeros and Experimentos Urbanos: Estudios de Impacto del Entono Construido en el Comportamiento Humano
recommended_courses: I loved geografia urbana! A lot of interesting knowledge about city development, also in santiago, and there was a 4 day field trip where i got my first chilean friends. In general try to pick the courses with field trips, Taller 7 was also nice because my professor (saveedra) was amazing. When choosing a taller ask the chilean students for which teachers are nice (and maybe understanding towards exchange students that are trying to learn spanish still or miss class sometimes because they travel etc.) There is also an instagram run by students at FAU called ayuditasfau where there are comments about the different teachers and courses. I dont recomment experimentos urbanos, too much statistics and a LOT of work outside class. Spanish was okay (if you get ECTS points for it), but didnt learn the most there because the classes were to big (17 students).
unexpected_costs: In general there wasn't any unexpected cost.
cost_comparison: Groceries are quite expensive in the supermarket, like danish prices. But you can get cheap vegetables if you go to the ferias (markets) like vega central. Sport is really cheap! I bouldered, played padel and squash for 1/4 to 1/2 of the price in denmark. Enjoy with new friends!
activities_available: In FAU there weren't that many clubs/sports (only football, basket, volley), but there was a really nice social student environment with boardgame club, friday bar each friday after class, and a lot of architecutre talks etc.
activities_recommended: There is salsa class for 15 DKK each tuesday, wednessday and thursday next to GAM at 8 pm. We loved it and went many times. Cinema is really cheap, sport is really cheap and there are a lot of free museums. Parts of the roads closes from sunday 9-14:00 so people can bike/run/etc and a nice way to run and see the city.
weekend_recommendations: I loved travelling and hiking around in chile! there are a lot of hikes just at the edge of the city, and also national parks easily accesible. Remember a credit card from back home so you can rent a car and drive around! we went on many roadtrips outside of chile, and drove around, and it felt safe enough.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. The chileans are generally really sweet and welcoming. The only difference I really felt ws in the work culture. Much of my group work we had meetings after 22:00/23:00/00:00 at night, and it wasn't unusual for my group members to work during the night often. Also when making plans to meet for example at campus to work, people was most often 1-2 hours late, or didnt show up. So pack away the danish puntualism and start being a bit late as well.
socializing_tips: Take the first step! The chileans are sweet and welcoming, but I often felt like I had to take a small first step to talk to them, or invite them to something, and then they almost immediately started inviting me to events, make plans afterwards etc. Made most of my chilean friends through field trips in classes.
cultural_challenges: The working hours. And also communicating in spanish. the young chileans use a lot of slang (but they will happily learn you some).
culture_appreciated: How funny chileans are. They are real joksters. Also how inviting they are, me and my friend got invited on trips, home to peoples familys houses without knowing people THAT well. It was really nice. And they love to show you their culture! Ask for where to learn Cueca for festias patrias or where to get the best completo.
top3_advice: 1. Try to get chilean friends. Some of my best culturally experiences and friendsships where because I got to know them . My spanish was too bad the first 2 months to properly get to know people in spanish, but I tried and practised and in the last past of my semester i felt more confident speaking in spanish with them. 2. Get out of Santiago! Santiago is amazing and has a lot of cultural offers, but Chile is so much more than santiago. Go north, go south and explore with friends and see the amazing nature. I have never seen so much pretty nature as here in chile. 3. Be open to people and opportunities, and invite people to the stuff you want to do! Often they want to join. Even though it was nice having chilean friends, it was also really nice having friends on exchange that wanted to do stuff with you, and also explore chile!
other_useful_info: Mentioned earlier. But in general talk with the office if in doubt about anything academic!
most_rewarding: Learning a new language, seeing beautiful nature and getting to know a lot of lovely people. I also love getting to know the chilean culture like learning to dance cueca for 18 sept, learning about chiles history etc.
greatest_challenge: Definitely having the classes and a life in spanish!! At times I was really frustrated when I didn't quite understand what was going on because of the language, I was short on time and had a test, and everything felt so difficult. But it all resolved everytime.
other_comments: Goooo! Chile was nice.

crucial_aspects: The language of the country and study opportunities.
info_ease: It was difficult at first not knowing the Uni and because the offices were closed a lot due to Covid but in the end it was rather easy.
arrival_assistance: The incomings office assisted with Uni card, library card, etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was a really simple online registration process
registration_help: The incomings office was really helpful
registration_success: Except for one class, l got into all the classes I wanted
registration_advice: Don't be shy to ask if you're unsure about something
course_level: I think it was about the same level of difficulty as it is at the university of Copenhagen
teaching_comparison: I felt like it was a bit more interactive but it depends on the Class
courses_enrolled: Comparing European democracies, international comparison of health care systems, who rules the economy, digital politics, institutional reform of the EU
recommended_courses: I thought Digital Politics and Institutional Reform of the EU were very interactive and fun.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Food is comparatively cheap.

activities_recommended: Definitely take part in the social activities by the incomings office to get to know the other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: Take a trip to Bonn, Frankfurt and the Vulkaneifel.
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy, especially if you have some basic knowledge of the language.
socializing_tips: Go to social activities and to bars and clubs.
cultural_challenges: There weren’t really any.
culture_appreciated: Everyone was welcoming and interested.
