crucial_aspects: To explore a European country, and experience a daily life in another culture.
info_ease: I think it was pretty easy. There was a lot of paper works and deadlines to remember. But I think that both University of Cologne and Erasmus team at KU were very helpful and sent all information, and answered questions fast.
arrival_assistance: The incomings team at the university arranged a lot of both practical and academic introduction events. And also, there were events of more social character to get to know the city and the other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The incomings team were very helpful in sending everything you need. However it does need a lot of time to both fulfill all the deadlines, and get everything done. Everything could be done online, which was very nice, and different from what I have heard about many other universities in Germany.
registration_help: You could always contact the incomings team, both online or in person.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Start in good time, have patience and pay attention to hard deadlines. They are not very flexible if you miss them.
course_level: I took more courses in sociology, than political science (which is what I study at home). Generally I think the level was okay, not too hard and not too easy. The assigned readings are however much less than what i'm used to at home, which I found super nice. It gives more space to actually dive into the assigned texts, and of course also more free time.
teaching_comparison: I took lectures and seminars. Both pretty similar to forelæsning and holdundervisning in UCPH. However the seminar courses were very small, which could be a bit intense.
courses_enrolled: - Democratic Theory and Practice - Diversity, Cohesion and Conflicts in Societies and Organisations - Social Inequality in Education - Contemporary Societies: Social Structure and Social Change - Analysis of Social Change - Capitalist societies and climate change
recommended_courses: All three courses except "Diversity, Cohesion and Conflicts in Societies and Organisations - Social Inequality in Education". The professor in this course seemed unprepared for the class sessions, and I personally did not like the format of teaching he provided. The three others were very interesting and different from each other - and courses I know from home. I would however recommend to take seminars, if you - like me - tend to get a bit unfocused during a lecture. Especially the course 'capitalist societies and climate change' with Philipp Golka was very nice, and he managed to create a very inclusive room in providing a good discussion.
unexpected_costs: You pay a pretty high semester contribution before going. However this covers 'free' transportation all over Germany (not ICE trains).
cost_comparison: Housing more expensive. Food/groceries not more expensive, but similar to danish prices I would say. Not much cheaper to go out to eat, but drinks are cheaper.
activities_available: There are a lot of activities such as sports offered by the University. Also Erasmus Cologne makes activities from city trips to nights out. I attended some of these in the beginning of my stay. It is a great way to get to know people. However I preferred to arrange things on my own with the people I got closer to. Also I had friends visiting from Denmark many of the weekends, which was a priority I had from the start. But definitely go to some of the events in the beginning, it is fun even though it can seem a bit wierd in the start.
activities_recommended: Explore the city, its many different areas, and just enjoy living in another city, without the many 'obligations' you maybe usually have at home.
weekend_recommendations: Go on day trips/weekend trips, Cologne connects so many places in europe by train, fx. Paris (4 hours aprox), Bruxelles, Amsterdam. If you are there during the winter, go to the christmas markets - also the ones in the center. Unlike the Danish ones, they are quite cute and very well-visited, so preferably weekdays are better than during the weekend.
culture_adjustment: Easy, very similar in many ways. However people are simply just very nice in this city, and I think that is really worth appreciating.
socializing_tips: I lived with a german girl, and I believe looking for housing with locals is the best way to get to know locals. I also did get to know some of the students from my courses, however more on a superficial level. Be open and go to events and stuff, if you want to socialize with the local students. However, I believe it is kind of similar to students at UCPH, that it is difficult for exchange students to actually 'get under the skin' of the locals.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find it very much different than Denmark. However there are of course some smaller differences such as paying cash, closed supermarkets on sundays an so on, but not particularly challenging ones, you just have to remember to bring cash and do your groceries on saturdays. What I found challenging was however the pretty high amount of homeless and very ill people in the streets. I found it hard to see people at the bottom of society receiving no help.
culture_appreciated: The openminded and friendly people. I think it maybe has to do with Cologne being a very multicultural and 'smaller' city, compared to fx. Berlin. I think people care less about being and lookin cool, and more on spending time with good friends and family. I really enjoyed the many Turkish restaurants and food experiences, and in general the more multicultural society, especially in Ehrenfeld, where I also found accomodation.
top3_advice: 1) Choose courses you find interesting, and wouldnt be able to choose at home. 2) If possible, find housing in a nice area. Do some research on areas you might find nice (I lived in Ehrenfeld, a very nice 'nørrebro-ish' area). It makes it much easier to do things close to your house. 3) Enjoy your time, be openminded to learn new things, even though Germany is similar to Denmark. I found it nice that it was not a huge culture chok, but rather, that I could enjoy the smaller and bigger differences between the cultures.
other_useful_info: Make sure to double check when your classes are taking place. Some might even be on saturdays.
most_rewarding: Experiences a different kind of daily life, enjoying time by myself more and get to know people from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Knowing how much you should study and memorize for a one hour written sit-in exam.

crucial_aspects: I speak a bit of german, and thought it would be fun to become semi fluent
overall_comments: It has been the most amazing time. I don't think you can understand how much we europeans truely have in common, untill you live and breath the community.
info_ease: It was a bit tricky, but the staff at the uni were very sweet and well-meaning.
arrival_assistance: Mostly guidance from the incommings team around the bureacracy of it all. A lecturers also helped secure me a spot on course which would otherwise be unavaliable to me due to my study background, which was nice of her. In that instance the usual pathways were less helpful.
arrival_comments: The buddy program didn't work that well for me, since the person assigned didn't have any time, but I think I was just unlucky.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It has been the most amazing time. I don't think you can understand how much we europeans truely have in common, untill you live and breath the community.
registration_process: I think it cut three years off my life expectancy.
registration_help: The incommings team is worth gold
registration_success: This is perhaps the biggest tension point. For political science, they have very limited classes. They also comfirm your space very late in the process of registration. If you have a lot of requirements regarding the classes to take in exchange, and you study politics on the bachelor level, I'd recommend another uni. I did not end up getting the classes I needed, and have had to extend my bachelors as a consequence of that. The limited and confusing selection combined with the fact that the allocation took place so late was a major hurdle at the start of my exchange. If you are en econ or business student, I don't think you will face the same challenges, since they have a wider selection in those areas.
registration_advice: Don't be afraid to ask for help.
academics_comments: It has been the most amazing time. I don't think you can understand how much we europeans truely have in common, untill you live and breath the community.
course_level: I took one MA course where the difficulty level was adjusted for me as a bachelor student. This will probably not be possiple under normal circumstances. Anyhow, if you are studying political science at KU, you will likely not ecounter anything you can't handle.
teaching_comparison: There was a bigger emphasis on presentations and generally smaller classes for political science. You had a close relationship with the lecturers, which was fun.
courses_enrolled: Authoritarian Politics Authoritarian Legality, Agency and Administrative Law in China Social and Welfare policy in the US Electoral Rights - Cleavages and Trajectories across Political Systems Digitalization & AI: Shaping the Future of European Politics and the Way We Study It
recommended_courses: Take what you can as a poltical science student. There's not much to choose from. Authoritarian Politics was fun though, since the lecturer is pretty eccentric. Authoritarian Legality, Agency and Administrative Law in China was also really fun, but write to the leacturer Hannah Klöber directly if you want to take it. Otherwise they probably won't let you.
unexpected_costs: They have a semester fee, that I put under "other", which covers amongs other things transportation. Beer is cheap though if you go to places like Soylent Green or Späti.
cost_comparison: Beer
activities_available: A lot of sports and some social events. Pics and Cems (I think they're called) made some fun events.
activities_recommended: Pic's and Cems club is good, and finding some fun people in the intro week, and build a social circle around that. Expect to spend a lot of time drinking.
weekend_recommendations: I mostly stayed in cologne, since I've travelled europe quite a bit. Go to Bonn at one point, and maybe use the fact a lot of cool places are only a train ride away.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. Germans and danes are not that different. Learn the language though.
socializing_tips: Learn german, and accept that you will struggle in the start. Also be insistend. The german is by nature anti social. It is our job to break open their shell. Talking to the people in your classes help, they are too polite to refuse.
cultural_challenges: the Germans take to easily on cancelling plans. Or the classic: "I am tired, I go home now".
culture_appreciated: Carneval is really fun.
top3_advice: Find housing early, force yourself to be social with new people (not too many visits and phone calls from friends) and become a regular the the metronom - wonderful jazz bar.
other_useful_info: Try to find housing south of the river, it's nicer.
most_rewarding: Deutsch sprechen
greatest_challenge: Learning to speak german. Also finding housing,
other_comments: Schrotty is a good club, Soylent Green is a great bar, and the germans are fun when you get to know them.

crucial_aspects: I had a strong desire to pursue an area of study, that I had become interested in during the previous semester. I then compared programs for the subject, security studies, between the Us partners that UCPH had. That compared with my general feeling of the different universities led me to pick CU Boulder.

crucial_aspects: The academic ranking of the university was important. It was crucial for me that I could take econ courses at the graduate level. This was one of the universities where this seemed feasible. I also wanted to go to a place I had never been before, and that I was unlikely to travel to otherwise.
overall_comments: The best half year of my life. I had a wonderful exchange!
info_ease: Quite easy. The international office (ISSS) was responsive and helpful if I needed anything.
arrival_assistance: My courses hadn't shown up in Canvas even though classes were just a day away, so I asked the international office about this. Turns out, this was standard practice at CU Boulder for many professors.
arrival_comments: There were student orientations that guided you through a lot of information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The best half year of my life. I had a wonderful exchange!
registration_process: I think it differs across apartments. For the economics department, I had to ask my professors for permission directly.
registration_help: I am not aware. I think the department of the course you want to enroll in can help you.
registration_success: I was very successful as I registered for all the courses I wanted. For one of the courses, I was waitlisted until the classes started. At this point, several students dropped the course, allowing me to enroll.
registration_advice: Start researching the courses and the enrollment process early, so you know if you have to ask for permission from professors, which you should do before the enrollment date.
academics_comments: The best half year of my life. I had a wonderful exchange!
course_level: I had one 1000-level course (General Psychology), which is the lowest level, and it was indeed quite easy and pedagogical. I also had ECON 4848 – Applied Econometrics, which was really simple if you've encountered regression analysis before. ECON 4626 – The Economics of Discrimination and Inequality is not that difficult, but it requires critical thinking and the exams and papers are graded harshly. ECON 8686 - Labor Economics II is a p.hd. course, but despite of this, the level isn't too difficult given that you have some prior knowledge of applied micro methods and papers.
teaching_comparison: The classes I had were smaller and more engaging. Student engagement was more encouraged than at UCPH. Also, there were many quizzes, assignments, and exams throughout the semester, which were all a part of the final grade.
courses_enrolled: PSYC 1001 - General Psychology ECON 4626 - The Economics of Inequality and Discrimination ECON 4848 - Applied Econometrics ECON 8686 - Labor EConomics II
recommended_courses: I would recommend ECON 4626 – The Economics of Discrimination and Inequality by Jeffrey Zax and ECON 8686 - Labor Economics II by Brian Cadena. Both encourage critical thinking, and they are both very useful as an economist. The professors are brilliant, and they encourage students to participate actively in the classrooms. Jeffrey Zax, especially, asks a lot of questions to students (he will only pick those who volunteer to answer the questions, however). Brian Cadena is really knowledgeable about labor economics and, in particular, immigration.
unexpected_costs: Nothing much really. I just didn't expect the prices to be that high.
cost_comparison: Most things were more expensive than I expected (e.g., food, housing). In general, I think food (both restaurants and groceries) and, in particular, housing is a fair bit more expensive in Boulder than in Copenhagen. As an exchange student, there are no student fees, but you still have free and unlimited access to many nice facilities, such as the recreation centers. The main recreation center is huge, and houses a gym, swimming pools (both indoor and outdoor), volleyball courts, badminton courts, basketball courts, indoor soccer court, etc. You also get a free bus card that you can use for both Boulder and Denver (as well as intercity transportation between them)
activities_available: A lot of free events were offered. For instance, free ice skating, free bowling, hiking, free live concerts, college sports games, and free meditation. In general, there were a lot more activities available to students than there are at UCPH!
activities_recommended: Hiking or biking is nice as the mountains are so close that you can walk to the trails from campus. The main street in Boulder (the Pearl Street Mall) is beautiful and has a lot of interesting shops and restaurants. It is also great for people watching. Enjoy the sun on one its many rooftops with a view of the mountains. For day trips, I recommend Rocky Mountains National Park, Red Rocks Amphitheater, Denver, and Colorado Springs (garden of the gods). Colorado is beautiful, and there are many places to explore! Neighboring states such as Utah, New Mexico, and Wyoming (Yellowstone is “just” 8 hours away from Boulder) are also worth a visit if you have access to a car.
weekend_recommendations: See my answer to the previous question. I did a road trip to Utah with my friends, which was very successful, so I can recommend that if you have a long holiday. Travelling, in general, is recommendable. Denver airport is a little over an hour away from Boulder by bus.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. People are very friendly. I had already done a previous exchange in the U.S., so maybe that is why it was easier for me.
socializing_tips: Be open to meeting new people and trying new things. There are quite a few welcome events for new students, which is an excellent way to meet locals. You can also talk to them in class or join the clubs. Most are open to playing sports with you in the recreation center if you ask them.
cultural_challenges: Not much. Some Americans talk a lot and can be a bit braggy.
culture_appreciated: People are open to talking and engaging with strangers. In general, the residents were also very open to meeting new people, which I much appreciated.
top3_advice: 1. Get out there and meet people. This is the quickest way to meet new friends. But even if you're not successful initially, you can try again because there are many opportunities for meeting new people throughout the semester.
other_useful_info: Show up on the first day of class, or the professors might drop you from the course! Also, look up semester bike rentals at the university. They have bikes of good quality that you can rent for around $40-$50 for a semester.
most_rewarding: Meeting some wonderful people and growing as a person. It was very fun to study there as well, and the classes were quite rewarding.
greatest_challenge: Moving into the place I was living, which had a lot of people. However, after attending a couple of dinners, I was quickly comfortable with staying there.
other_comments: If you have questions, feel free to reach out to me at cdm525@alumni.ku.dk

crucial_aspects: I've always been fascinated by the US in general and by the idea of studying in the US, so that was always my top priority in choosing destination. More specifically, I chose CU Boulder because it's in a great location right next to the mountains providing many opportunities to hike, climb, ski etc. Furthermore, I was very drawn to Boulder, since it's a university town, so a lot of the town is centred around the university. I also read a lot of student reports on Boulder that were very positive.
info_ease: It was extremely easy. There was an international student orientation the week I got there, where I received all of the important information and picked up my ID-cards.
arrival_assistance: As mentioned above, I simply showed up to the orientation, where I received all of the necessary information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registering for courses was fairly easy. I simply found courses at the appropriate level that all sounded interesting and then got my academic advisor to sign up for them by sending them an email, since you can't do it yourself as an exchange student. After picking courses, I just got them approved through KU, and then there were no other issues.
registration_help: You have an academic advisor who is very helpful, who can guide you through the whole thing and help you sign up for classes.
registration_success: I got all of the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: When picking courses I looked at two things: how interesting the course sounded, and how the teacher was rated. Don't think too much about the teacher's rating, if the class sounds interesting to you, but it can also make the class a lot less enjoyable, if you have a bad professor. My experience with professors were mostly good though.
course_level: I took three 4000-level classes, which is officially equivalent to the third year at KU, but they were much easier. I also took one 3000-level class, which was probably my most difficult class, since it was very different to what I do normally and was a class from a different faculty.
teaching_comparison: On the whole, it was a lot easier. Unlike at KU, where I had both lectures and classes with two different teachers, in Boulder I had just one professor doing both lectures and classes at the same time. It felt a lot more like high school than university in my opinion. For the most part, the classes were in the style of lectures, but were very discussion based, so it didn't necessarily feel like a lecture.
courses_enrolled: - Natural Resource Economics - Economics of Entrepreneurship - International Political Economy - Economic Growth
recommended_courses: I learned most from Natural Resource Economics and from International Political Economy. In Natural Resource Economics, the professor was incredibly engaged and interesting, and I learned a lot about natural resources in general and how they work in the US. International Political Economy was also a very interesting class and very different to what I normally do at KU. It was essay-based and every week we read articles about different political economy-oriented issues and then discussed them in class. It challenged me in a good way.
unexpected_costs: I went on a few trips that ended up being fairly expensive, but it was definitely worth it.
cost_comparison: I was shocked by how expensive housing is in Boulder. I payed $1000 a month, which is even in the low end of how much you could end up spending. Food is also very expensive compared to Denmark, both food from the supermarket and when you eat out.
activities_available: Anything you can think of. They seemingly have clubs for anything.
activities_recommended: I was part of the Alpine Club and went on a few trips with them, which I highly recommend if you're into climbing. I also frequently went to the climbing gym at the rec center, where I met some really great people too.
weekend_recommendations: There are many beautiful places to visit both in and around Colorado. Go up to the Rocky Mountains National Park if you're into hiking and beautiful views. I also went on a trip to Yellowstone National Park, which was amazing, but you need to have access to a car to get there. Through the Alpine Club I went to Utah to go climbing over the weekend, which was a lot of fun too. Lastly, for Thanksgiving break, I went with some of my roommates to Chicago. Basically, it's a lot easier to go to different places in the US once you're already there, so either try to tag along on a trip or arrange your own. There are an endless amount of opportunities. I would also recommend going clubbing or to concerts in Denver if you're into that kind of thing.
culture_adjustment: It was extremely easy, since my roommates were so incredibly welcoming. They immediately made it feel like home.
socializing_tips: Join clubs and engage in them. I didn't make too many friends from my classes, since I didn't spend that much time in classes, so seek out people with similar interests and I'm sure you will have no problem socialising. It's also a lot easier if you live with Americans that all have friends already you can meet.
cultural_challenges: Everything seemed very overwhelming at first, because it's such a big country and just going grocery shopping for the first time was a very intimidating experience, since there a million options for every single food item and the places are so huge. I also had to get used to how open and talkative Americans are, but I also love them for that.
culture_appreciated: Americans are all (mostly) really nice, generous and welcoming, and I felt extremely welcome as a non-American living in their country. I also love the culture that is unique to Boulder with how active and healthy everyone is, since I'm like that too.
top3_advice: 1. Live with Americans if you can. 2. Don't worry about school. It will be a lot easier, and you should spend most of your time experiencing life in Boulder, because it is unlike Denmark in almost every way. 3. Join clubs or try to engage in campus life in some other way. There are so many opportunities. You just have to grab them.
other_useful_info: One thing I forgot to mention is that you can switch classes during the first couple of weeks, if you don't find one or more of the classes interesting. I switched one of my classes, and it was definitely worth it.
most_rewarding: Gaining so many American friends and having had so many unique experiences that I wouldn't otherwise have had.
greatest_challenge: Leaving. Being away for one semester is strange, because I very quickly felt at home and fell in love with being there, and then all of a sudden it's over. All I can say is: Try to enjoy every day you have there, because even if each day isn't perfect in and of itself, you will look back on your time there fondly.

cost_comparison: Food and housing was quite a bit more expensive than I expected. I was extremely lucky to find housing at "only" 4300 DKK a month. Everybody else paid way more (up to twice as much). Food was also a bit more expensive than expected. Especially fruits and vegetables cost a lot.
activities_available: There were a ton of cool clubs. The university recreation center provided a lot of athletic activities for free such as a gym, clinbing wall, tennis courts, a pool, and many more sports.
activities_recommended: I would definitely check out the student societies and clubs. I can recommend the Alpine Club for anyone interested in climbing and the outdoors.
weekend_recommendations: Going on trips during the weekends were the highlight of my trip. Colorado has so much to offer in terms of nature, and the neighboring states, Utah and Wyoming, are also very beautiful.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. It is very much as you would expect from movies and television, but it is till very interesting.
socializing_tips: Join the student clubs!
cultural_challenges: The towns and cities are very car-centric. Not having a car or knowing anyone with a car makes it way more difficult to really enjoy what Colorado has to offer.
culture_appreciated: The openness and friendlyness of the americans.
top3_advice: Try to take MA courses, rent a bike through the university, and start looking for housing early on (try different groups on Facebook).
other_useful_info: No not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: Meeting local americans and experiencing the american culture.
greatest_challenge: I did not have any great challenges.

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne til USA, da jeg gerne ville opleve den amerikanske universitetskultur og kiggede derfor på de forskellige universiteter i USA. Her synes jeg bedst om Boulder grundet deres flotte natur og omgivelser.
info_ease: Der var rigtig mange forskelige informationer, som man skulle have styr på og huske og det blev dermed et ret forvirrende process.
arrival_assistance: Vi havde en vejleder på universitet og derudover var der en introdag.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Det var meget nemt. Der var en hjemmeside, hvor man kunne se alle de forskellige kurser og i hvilket tidsrum de lå og så kunne man bare vælge blandt dem. Hvis der var nogen forudsætninger for at tage kurset, så skulle man dog lige have godkendt, at man havde haft det i DK. Der stod ikke så meget om de forskellige kurser inden, så det var svært at vide så meget om dem inden man mødte op første dag.
registration_help: Havde ikke brug for hjælp med mine kurser, men der var en vejleder man kunne skrive til, hvis det var nødvendigt.
registration_success: Jeg fik alle de kurser jeg gerne ville have fra start af. Havde dog lige overset at en af dem ikke var "in person", og skulle dermed skifte lige inden studiestart. Dette var også nemt og kurset jeg gerne ville have var stadig ledigt.
registration_advice: Søge kurser når tilmeldingen åbner sig, da nogen af dem godt kan blive optaget, hvis man venter for længe. Sørg for de alle er "in person".
course_level: Jeg havde et rigtig svært kursus, men dette var også en blanding af BA/MA kursus. Derudover havde jeg 3 BA kurser, som var nemmere end dem vi har tilsvarende i DK
teaching_comparison: Vi havde normale forlæsninger ligesom på UCPH. Dog var der mange flere afleveringer og midterms, som endte med at tælle med i den samlede karakter, som er anderleds end herhjemme.
courses_enrolled: EBIO 1210-001 General Biology 1 DNCE 1301-010 Hip-Hop Dance Technique 1 MCDB 1150-001 Introduction to Cellular and Molecular Biology BCHM 4720-010 Metabolic Pathways and Human Disease
recommended_courses: DNCE 1301-010 Hip-Hop Dance Technique 1 var virkelig et godt kursus og en god pause. Dog var det også ret tidskrævende og underviseren forventede man tog det seriøst, men helt sikkert det sjoveste kursus.
unexpected_costs: Føler ikke der for noget uforventet.
cost_comparison: Mad for dyre end forventet i Boulder. Jeg fik dog mad i hverdagen der hvor jeg bode, så dermed betalte jeg kun i weekenden eller når vi spiste ude.
activities_available: Der var mange forskellige klubber man kunne melde sig til gennem skolen og derudover lavede de tit aktivtiter - det gjorde jeg meget brug af i starten og var en god måde at møde nye mennesker på.
activities_recommended: Jeg var i en kort stund en del af kajak-, hiking- og roklubben, hvilken jeg kan anbefale
weekend_recommendations: Jeg var på mange weekendsture rundt og se nabostaterne, hvilke var nogen vildt gode ture. I thangsgiving var jeg på den klassiske Utah/Arizona tur, som jeg helt klart vil anbefale alle som skal til Boulder. Ellers lavede vi mange små halvdags hikes i både weekender og efter uni.
culture_adjustment: Synes det var meget nemt, da jeg ikke synes der var den store forskel. Dog både jeg på et internationalt kollegie, hvor der var folk fra hele verden, så her oplevede man meget kulturforskel, hvilket var sjovt at opleve, men ikke noget der gav nogen problemer.
socializing_tips: Jeg hang mest ud med de andre danskere som var afsted eller med andre udvekslingsstuderede, men hvis man gerne vil have locale venner, så er en anbefaling at melde sig ind i nogen klubber gennem skolen.
cultural_challenges: Synes ikke der var nogen.
culture_appreciated: Folk i USA er super flinkt og vil gerne både hjælpe og snakke med en.
top3_advice: Vær åben fra start og lav så mange sociale ting som muligt, men lad vær med at få stress, hvis du ikke lige har fundet dine bedste venner fra dag et - det skal nok komme. Lad vær med at stress over skole og prøv at få så meget socialt ud af det som muligt.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Fik helt klart oplevet meget socialt og har fået meget ud af det på det personlige
greatest_challenge: Man kunne til tider godt stresse over om man havde fået venner nok og om man gik glip af noget, hvis man havde en dag man ikke skulle noget, men synes hurtigt man kom over det, da man så udnyttede de dage til at slappe af, da der ellers skete meget det meste af tiden.

crucial_aspects: For mig var et vigtigt element at modersmålet i landet var engelsk, og derudover at de havde skøn natur.
info_ease: Jeg føler at der var mange informationer der godt kunne have været gjort lettere tilgængelige eller informeret bedre om. Derudover føler jeg at det godt kunne være lidt svært at navigere i hvilke kurser man skulle tage, da de i USA, eller i hvert fald CU Boulder ikke rigtig skriver hvad kurserne indeholder. arrival_assistance: Der var en dag planlagt af universitetet til at informere os om kultur forskelle og andre relevante informationer. Føler dog de burde have gjort meget mere for at give os en bedre social start i gruppen af udveksling studerende. De holdt ikke andet end den ene dag specifikt for os.
arrival_comments: Jeg føler godt at der kunne have været meget mere specifikt for udvekslingsstuderende, men samtidig føler jeg at universitetet generelt har rigtig mange ressourcer hvis man rækker ud efter dem. De er gode til at hjælpe studerende (også udvekslingsstuderende) der kæmper lidt med pengene, de har mange sociale arrangementer generelt for alle studerende, og koordinations vejlederen var faktisk rigtig god til at svare på spørgsmål.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Selve tilmeldingsprocessen var meget lige til. Man skulle lige oversætte alle de kurser man havde haft, da der var prerequisites, men ellers var det meget let. Det svære var mere at vælge kurserne da de ikke er særlig velbeskrevet.
registration_help: koordinatoren i USA. Hun svare hurtigt og effektivt på mails.
registration_success: fik alle dem jeg ville have.
registration_advice: Tror ikke du får brug for råd, bare husk at meld dig til.
course_level: Jeg tog 2 introduktionskurser, som derfor var meeeget lette, og så tog jeg et kursus som var et tredjeårs kursus og et der var et fjerdeårs.
teaching_comparison: Føler det var meget det samme med forlæsninger og regnetimer i nogle af fagene, men samtidig gør de sig også rigtig meget i quizzer, i nogle fag flere gange om ugen som alle tæller med i din karakter.
courses_enrolled: Hip hop 1001 Sociology 1001 Modern inorganic chemistry Organic chemistry 2
recommended_courses: Enten Hip hop eller sociologi. Føler hip hop var meget underholdende og et godt sted at møde andre folk (dog var folk på kurset ret unge da det var et førsteårs kursus) og en god måde også at lære lidt om kulturen i USA. Sociologi derimod var virkelig lærerigt og lærte mig meget om USA og hvordan ting hænger sammen der. Det er dog et kursus der giver point for at møde op og synes forelæsningerne var virkelig kedelige. Føler mere at det var det man læste i bogen der var godt. Det er dog et kursus man skal sætte lidt tid af til da man også får point for at færdiggøre kapitler i bogen, så det er et kursus der er lidt svære at slacke i, da meget af karakteren baseres på participation.
unexpected_costs: Maden i Boulder er rimelig dyrt, men man kan dog udnytte buffpantry som giver en gratis mad, og det kan sænke ens omkostninger betydeligt. Det benyttede jeg mig dog desværre ikke så meget af før til sidst
cost_comparison: At klatre er rimelig dyrt i Boulder. Offentligt transport og at låne cykler var gratis. De har et fitnesscenter med pool på campus der er gratis. Husleje var dyre end jeg havde forventet.
activities_available: universitetet har en app hvor de lægger alle de events ud som der er løbende, hvilket var så smart, for de holder virkelig mange fede events, hvor man kan få gratis mad og ting, og møde en masse nye mennesker. Det var både kulturelle og sociale events. Derudover har universitetet en masse klubber hvor du kan være aktivt, og de har også idrætsfaciliteter .
activities_recommended: Jeg vil kæmpe meget anbefale hikingklubben, men man skal være god til at hoppe på nogen ture i starten hvis man får plads, da det bliver koldt før man ved af det.
weekend_recommendations: Hike i Chautaqua, og når du bliver træt af det, kan man hike mere nord for campus også. Hvis muligheden er der, tag ud og klatre udenddørs eller tag på nogen ture til rocky mountains national park, og camp evt. ved indian peaks
culture_adjustment: Let.
socializing_tips: De er meget snaksaglige, så bare vær åben for det, så er det meget overkommeligt.
cultural_challenges: ikke rigtig nogen
culture_appreciated: Hvor åbne, snaksaglige, imødekommende, og hjælpsomme folk er! Folk er virkelig gode til at få en til at føle sig inkluderet og synes bare det er mega spændende at du er der.
top3_advice: - Husk internationalt kørekort, du må kun køre i Colorado de tre første måneder du er der uden et. - Der er en mega god genbrug, så pak ikke for meget tøj haha - Brug Buff Pantry!!! Det er en guldgruppe, og du sparer mega mange penge ved at få gratis mad.
other_useful_info: nej
most_rewarding: Jeg tror for mig var det at være på udveksling sådan helt generelt. Det gav mig en lidt anden mentalitet til tingene. Jeg fik lavet og oplevet super meget, jeg måske ikke ville have været så god til at få motiveret mig til at få gjort herhjemme. Jeg mødte en masse nice mennesker, og man havde det bare mega sjovt i de specifikke omgivelser og med det gå på mod
greatest_challenge: At man bruger en masse tid og energi hele tiden, men også at skulle finde en balance med studiet og tid til bare at slappe af.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to the US with the typical American college experience with campus, sports and so on. I wanted to go somehwere that has a great outdoors life and where I could go skiing. I was looking to have the perfect end for my university time and this fulfilled that dream.
overall_comments: I was happy to hear that American universities were currently quite unpopular among Danish students, so my hopes were really high to get in and so I got my first priority as well.
info_ease: I was flooded with welcome newsletters and so on from the American international office. It was a bit chaotic but after looking through everything you need, you will get a sense of what and when you have to do. Both international offices were quick to assist so there was always an answer. Shoutout to Pernille at this point.
arrival_assistance: I arrived 2 weeks before the scheduled international welcome day where I also swung by the university to collect my student card, and you could also ask questions there on the spot.
arrival_comments: They got a new head of exchange students counsellor now (Jessie), and he made it his mission to overhaul the whole websites and checklists of what you need to do and he seems to love his job so my guess is that it will only get better.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I was happy to hear that American universities were currently quite unpopular among Danish students, so my hopes were really high to get in and so I got my first priority as well.
registration_process: At the mandatory international welcome day, registration occurs on campus with all the other international students, no matter if you're exchange or full time student. Before that, they tell you what to bring and what to expect and so on. It's all pretty smooth as long as you read every email and newsletter you get. At the end of the welcome event, you will be put in a room with all the other exchange students, this is where you have to look for people you think you will get along with. I was unlucky enough to sit at a table with people I had nothing in common with, so it was a challenge to get into other groups. You will find your people eventually, but these welcome events determine how soon you will find your people.
registration_help: Boulder's international office ISSS is always very happy to help as they have probably heard every question you ask them already before.
registration_success: I got everything I wanted. As a master's student you have the choice to do either two graduate courses or 1 graduate course and 2 undergraduate courses. For the graduate class you actually need to have pre-requisites from their earlier classes from that maior, but I was told to just contact the head of that study department and she registered me into the graduate class that I wanted. For the undergraduate courses you just have to sign up as long as there as seats available.
registration_advice: I recommend doing 3 courses as you spend more time on campus and meet more people. Most classes are twice a week for 1h 15 mins each. If your Copenhagen schedule allows it, choose classes you would never get in CPH or Europe actually, they have very fun or specific classes. Learn something new and not something you have seen already 3 times before.
academics_comments: I was happy to hear that American universities were currently quite unpopular among Danish students, so my hopes were really high to get in and so I got my first priority as well.
course_level: One graduate class which was mixed with senior undergraduates. Two undergraduate classes from the first or second year. Freshman classes start with 100 until 400 for the senior classes. Graduate classes start at 500 until upwards. The higher the number, the more intensive the class. Lower classes are quite easy, of course it depends on the professors but it is mostly common sense and mediocere time management and then there is no way you will fail that class. Graduate classes are more work intensive, depending on the class you have a lot of homework or assignments.
teaching_comparison: Much more mandatory homework than from my experience in CPH. Again, it also depends on the teaching style from the professors. Some want to engage with the class, others will show more videos in their lectures as it is hard to engage with a class of 200 people. Most classes have 2 midterms and then a final. Some teachers put more emphasis on homework and less on exams. All in all I had a mix of midterms, homework, weekly quizzes, Canvas discussion assignments and cumulative exams.
courses_enrolled: GEOG 2321: The Grography of Skiing and Snowboarding with Noah Molotch GEOG 4712: Political Geography with John O'Loughlin GEOG 5271: The Arctic Climate System with Mark Serreze
recommended_courses: All of them. I looked up all the professors from my shortlist that I made on ratemyprofessor.com and there you can see what the professors and the courses are like. Serreze is the highest rated professor in the geography department and he is really an absolute legend. I am convinced that John O'Loughlin knows everything as he is also 78 years old, this was material wise my favorite course as I really learned a lot. Noah's class was quite easy as it is a sophomore class and he is just super passionate about going skiing. The class is low effort but quite nice and you get to tell people that you are studying skiing academically. This was the second time the class was offered as well so it is still a bit new but there were 200 people in that class who were eager to go skiing. (No you don't go skiing with the prof but he likes getting pictures from us in the powder.)
unexpected_costs: Groceries are kind of the same price as DK depending on where you shop. I went out a lot, ate a lot, did a lot of trips. My most unexpected cost was probably a spontaenous trip to San Francisco as I unexpectely got tickets to Fred again. I was also very lucky and I could use a friend's car as she was not here for the semester so I also had to pay for driving around a bit. The most unexpected cost is the rent that I'm still paying as we couldn't find someone to take over my room.
cost_comparison: Phone can be cheap but I still went with an unlimited Tmobile subscription for 50$. Eating out is quite expensive as you always have to consider the tips. If you're careful you can get really cheap flights. We went on a 9 night trip for Thanksgiving to Chicago, Miami and New Orleans and all the flights cost less than 300$. If you wanna go skiing, go for the Ikon Pass, as day passes at the resorts are stupidly expensive. I also took a 25 meals mealplan which cost around 250$. One entry to the dining hall will then be around 10$ and then you can stay there for as long as you want and eat as much as you can and want.
activities_available: The student recreation center is the best thing that campus has to offer. You can play literally any sport you can think of, either by yourself, with friends or just random people. I played a lot of basketball, pickleball and squash. For 6$ you can rent ice hockey gear which I did with my roommates. In the beginning of the semester there is a 'Be involved fair' where literally every club from the university has a stand and you can sign up for. I went to one rowing training but I had to stop as training times interfered with my class schedule. There is also a club for basically any sport, hobby, religion, ethnic group, study department and so on.
activities_recommended: Make as much use of the recreation center as possible, it is a perfect example on where all their tuition money is flowing into. Go on hikes around Boulder, explore campus and the area. If you have American roommates, make them take you around and just tag along to anywhere. Accept every invitation you get no matter what it is for. Going out is super fun. As Boulder is not an enormous city, you will find your way around quite quickly and it will feel very homey.
weekend_recommendations: Go explore with people you meet or your roommates. I have done a roadtrip with my family before the exchange to Wyoming, Idaho and Utah with Yellowstone, the Grand Tetons and so on. I camped a night in the Great Sand Dunes with my roommate which was amazing. Roadtrips to Rocky Mountain National Park, visits to Denver. Rodeos are really fun! I have never seen so much sun continuously in my life, the weather is always good and we had high temperatures until November. We even saw the Northern Lights! Sadly this year was a late and warm ski season but as soon as it starts you can go skiing to Eldora, Arapahoe Basin, Copper Mountain etc. If you know you wanna go skiing, buy the pass as early as possible. Thanksgiving break we went to Chicago, Miami and New Orleans. I had one friend visit me where we went to New York as well. You will meet a ton of people and the spontaneous trips are always the most fun. And try to see many of their sports teams, the sports culture is amazing.
culture_adjustment: Easiest thing I've ever done. Everybody is so welcoming. There may be many stereotypes and they might be true from time to time. The food scene is of course maybe a bit different, but I realized at some point that I will be okay with not eating the same stuff that I eat at home, so I fully indulged and tried to taste as many American foods as possible.
socializing_tips: Don't sit in last row as there will be the students who don't wanna talk. Keep going back to the same spot for every class and boom you will have a buddy in class. Americans are the friendliest creatures and you will feel just like in a movie because it is exactly the same. However, a lot of them are scared to make friends with internationals as those will leave again pretty soon. The people who will be in the same shoes as you are all the other exchange students who are also looking for friends and it will be those that you will likely hang out with the most. As soon as you meet new international people, especially in the beginning, ask them to put you in any of their social media groups. In the beginning everybody just wants to be involved and not be alone. Everybody will always know someone else, so just tag along.
cultural_challenges: Travelling to the Southern states means they will have most likely a different political view. While I have had no bad experience with a Trump supporter, it is not difficult to identify them. Even though Colorado is quite advanced, recycling is basically inexistent. Car dependency is real, but your American friends are more than happy to drive you. Most Americans you meet are generally quite concerned about the current political situation and while I had no bad experience with it, it should not be forgotten. The Visa application was the most stressful part.
culture_appreciated: The genuine friendliness of the Americans. I appreciated the absence of annoying "Why are you going to the US" questions from back home, because the Americans are so happy you're there and every exchange student shares your enthusiasm. It is very easy to settle in when everybody speaks the same language. I most appreciated the sports culture, both as a fan and player.
top3_advice: 1. Say yes to every invitation. 2. Make the most of the recreation center and campus. 3. Don't invite too many friends from home, it will prevent you from having the full experience.
other_useful_info: Don't sign a year long lease and be friends with your roommates. Forget your European diet. Money will come back and kilos can be dropped. Boulder is btw the fittest city in the US.
most_rewarding: Living the dream and making friends from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Leaving and saying goodbye, which proves to me that it was worth it.
other_comments: Go live the dream, cowboys and cowgirls. I genuinely had fun writing this, I hope this helped and if this doesn't convince you, I don't know what will.

I did not receive and introduction to the system, the norms or the academic life on the university. I felt thrown into it without being able to find out what or where. Everthing I got to know about the system I found out myself or by asking other erasmus students. The only "introduction-invitation" I got was to an event that was at the same time as my classes, I there had to choose to get an introduction to my class(and exams) or an introduction that I didn't know was going to be academic related or personal-get-to-know-each-other-as -Erasmus-students related. It felt stupid to plan those two things at the same time and I went to the introduction to the class and exams. In hindsight I cannot tell which one had been best.

course_level: I had courses that were all in relation to each other regarding art, movies, literature or linguistics. It was a good combination because they supported each other in material and content.
teaching_comparison: It was confusing, different and felt like taking high school all over again. There was almost no text or material to support the classes. It was most of all ONLY the word of the professor or resumes of original text that we had as citation on powerpoints. It felt anti-academic and very high school like. I did not have a single book and in many classes I just had to write down what the professor was saying in contrast to actually support it with academic writings and books.

recommended_courses: Cine Español. The professor was amazing and it included the spanish history, culture and creative life.
unexpected_costs: only a broken phone, but otherwise nothing.
cost_comparison: The train in between Córdoba and Málaga with Renfe. The cost was between 20-40 euros with train.
activities_available: There was advertisement for sport and clubs, but I never figured out how and the informations for Erasmus students was very poorly done - there was never anything that told us about the social activities.
activities_recommended: The city is amazing, and during the spring there is a lot of festivals. I would recommend the wine festival, la feria, las cruces de mayo. But these were not in relation the my host university.
weekend_recommendations: the hikes close to Córdoba or to see Sevilla, Málaga, Granada and other places in Andalusia. Córdoba is a great city and the people living there is so amazing and welcoming.
culture_adjustment: Outside of the university it was easy because people was so sweet and I got some friends that were also on Erasmus.
socializing_tips: The local students didn't really wanted to spend a lot of time with us. It felt like they were very used to Erasmus students and perhaps also used to many Erasmus students only wanting to party. This was not my case, I wanted to know more, and to learn more.
cultural_challenges: That students and professors are often late and that it's more chill.
culture_appreciated: The openness, the food, the way that the people are sweet and welcoming outside of university, the way of looking at life.
top3_advice: The language will become better, the city is amazing and the Andalusian culture is so heartwarming and fun.
other_useful_info: I would tell them to try not to stress over the confusing and the difficulties, it will keep being confusing so no need to stress.
most_rewarding: Being close to my family and having the possibly to speak to them more often.
greatest_challenge: The entire proces.

crucial_aspects: The availability of a strong program in my desired field. A culture that I was interested in exploring.
info_ease: Very easy. The exchange program at UoC is very well run and quite organised, even if information sometimes would come slightly later than I was expecting, I was at no point forgotten.
arrival_assistance: E-mail introduction, offer to help set-up student ID. Offer to have an intro meeting at exchange office.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I received temporary papers automatically and was easily temporarily registered. Getting an actual student ID, turned out to be a little difficult and required a Greek SIM card and going to a Vodafone shop, eventually I gave up and used my temporary papers.
registration_help: Quick response from the exchange office, which was in general excellent.
registration_success: NA I was registered for my clinical rotations from home, and it could have been tweaked a little, but overall there were no issues.
registration_advice: Try to connect with people who have exchanged to UoC before, or even try to get in touch with local students. The departments are very different and it’s not obvious in what ways from reading about them.
course_level: Clinical rotations so not really courses. The theoretical level compared to KU is quite high. As an 11th semester student the level of independence and amount of practical work was lower compared to home. Generally speaking less independence and preparation for practicing alone and more focus on teaching skills and knowledge in the clinic under supervision.
teaching_comparison: As above, with the caveat that the difference from department to department was very large. Generally more 1 to 1 with the same doctor over extended periods of time.
courses_enrolled: Rotations in Internal medicine Anaesthesiology Rheumatology
recommended_courses: All rotations have my warm recommendation, but anaesthesiology would be absolutely amazing for anyone interested in doing it. Very hands on, a very good culture in the department, general culture not too dissimilar from home, but with options to do a lot of hands on work. Rheumatology was a specialised department with a high degree of research activity, and quite broad patient base. Internal medicine would be useful for practicing clinical skills and theory especially as an early clinical experience, but older patient population means Greek language knowledge would have been useful to work more independently.
unexpected_costs: Nothing major, booked return flight late, which made it very expensive.
cost_comparison: Housing more expensive. Social life, and seeing the surrounding areas less expensive
activities_available: Different social clubs: choir and chess to football. City has cheap gyms and football fields.
activities_recommended: Everyone enjoyed the hiking club, from party people to outdoors people.
weekend_recommendations: Going camping in the south and east of Crete away from the most touristic places. Renting a car and going Roadtripping on the island. Hiking and mountain climbing. Island hopping to the neighbour islands. Social life in the city is very easy and fun.
culture_adjustment: The culture is very very different, but people were friendly and used to having guests. Some things(like the shouting) never really settled. In general I was comfortable from day one though.
socializing_tips: Get a WhatsApp group going with the other exchange students, more people find more social events. Spend some time at the hospital, the greek students have rotations of a month in each department, so you see the same faces every day. Use the buddy programme it worked well for some.
cultural_challenges: Greek people are very loud and sometimes shouting at each other mostly. That people are very often late without any explanation.
culture_appreciated: The openness and happiness to share. The pride in the work that is being done, and in being good at a task or sharing some knowledge.
top3_advice: Expect it to feel a little chaotic. Be patient. Try to keep up with Greek lessons, it is not impossible to learn some.
other_useful_info: Don’t be afraid to ask the exchange office.
most_rewarding: The perspective it gave on what we do well and what we don’t do so well at home. And the appreciation of how good the system actually is at home, but how people can make things work in other ways, and that no place is perfect.
greatest_challenge: Language! I wish I had started studying harder and using it more early, because people will switch to their own language, and in the end of 14 weeks, even if you(as me) gave up early, at the end you will understand more than you think.
other_comments: I think the focus on basic skills make it a perfect 7th-8th semester exchange. It is very difficult to work independently, if you don’t speak Greek. However you will have more close supervision and more chances of practicing basic clinical skills and have at least as much theoretical teaching. You will get to test yourself in a different environment and you will get to present patients in a different way. The social life and free time will be awesome, and the people and the city is really nice. It will feel as a vacation even if you work as hard as at home. And it will be a more unique experience than going to a more “safe” Northern European university.

crucial_aspects: When I chose my destination, I was seeking a place that would provide me with fruitful knowledge at the hospital, but also a city that would provide me with plenty of things to do during the weekends. I was also looking for contrasts from what I am used to - both culturally, gastronomically, climate-wise and within the medical field.
info_ease: So and so, the majority of the information that I needed for the paperwork prior to my arrival was provided by my sending institution, which was a big help. However, I still needed to have an overview over, what I need to submit at which dates and who I needed to contact to get these documents and information. Sometimes it would be unclear exactly which type of documents and information that I needed to fill out in different schemes (for instance the OLA), but both my sending institution and my host university was very good at responding within reasonable time frames.
arrival_assistance: I got assigned an ESN buddy from the host university, got invited to the big ESN-group chat on WhatsApp and from the Erasmus office I got some information about where to show up and what to bring for my first day at the hospital.
arrival_comments: I was overall semi-satisfied with the orientation. During my stay, I could always write to Stella and she would get quite rapidly back with a response. However, I would have appreciated some more orientation about where to go for my surgical rotation - I just found a department myself and showed up there, which also worked nicely, but also a bit of a homemade solution.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After I got nominated by my sending university, I filled out an online application form in which I applied for courses and filled out some personal information about myself.
registration_help: The erasmus-coordinator Stella Melina was good at answering my mails, when questions appeared.
registration_success: I got all the clinical courses at the hospital that I applied for.
registration_advice: Have an overview over the deadlines and documents you need for the registration.
course_level: The level of the theoretical aspect of the clinical rotations was quite high, due to the cases being quite complicated - sometimes details would be lost due to language barrier. The opportunity to practice procedures, such as NG-tubes, arterial punctures and urinary catheters was also nice - but it does demand that you show initiative. I do recommend showing the log book as early on as possible.
teaching_comparison: The greek style of teaching at the hospital is pr default more observational and less interactive than what we know from UCPH. However, I did figure that showing initiative and interest opened a lot more doors for being involved with the patients and getting more responsibilities in the clinic.
courses_enrolled: Clinical clerkship in internal medicine Clinical clerkship in surgery
recommended_courses: I did 5 weeks in the vascular surgery department - I would highly recommend this for future students also. The doctors are passionate about teaching, translating and involving you.
unexpected_costs: I purchased my own scrubs for the hospital, since the hospital did not provide me with these.
cost_comparison: Food in general was cheaper than expected - specifically the food at the tavernas was cheaper; this enabled me to have weekly dinners out on restaurants and still sticking to my budget. Also many attractions were free entrance, which often meant that you just had to pay for the transportation to that given attraction. Furthermore more expensive items include cosmetics and dairy products such as milk and greek yoghurt
activities_available: Every month we would recieve a calendar with these kind of activies from ESN comittee. Amongst the cultural activities could be wine tasting, cooking classes, cretan festivals and trips to other cities. registration_comments: It has been a great experience and I am so grateful for the opportunity provided by KU. The language barrier was greater that I anticipated which made the learning experience challenging (therefor 9/10).
registration_process: II was a bit confused by the process, as the learning agreement had to be filled out before the application was due. However, it couldn't be signed by KU until I received the acceptance letter from UoC, which made the situation very unclear. The next student going to the same destination also encountered the same issue and reached out to me for help. I think this process should be better organized and clarified. Additionally, I spent a lot of time finding the right courses to fill out the learning agreement, as the UoC website was not very informative.
registration_help: KU signed the learning agreement before the acceptance letter.
registration_success: Succesful - I got all the departments I wanted.
registration_advice: Have trust that it will work out. Everybody also wants to help, but the response might be a bit delayed.
academics_comments: It has been a great experience and I am so grateful for the opportunity provided by KU. The language barrier was greater that I anticipated which made the learning experience challenging (therefor 9/10).
course_level: As I was on a clinical clerkship, I rotated through four different departments. In each department, I tried to integrate into their workflow by attending rounds, observing surgeries, participating in outpatient clinics, and engaging in other activities. The level of learning largely depended on how much I was included in these activities. Some departments provided more opportunities for hands-on learning and discussion, which greatly enhanced the experience, while others were more observational due to their workload and priorities.
teaching_comparison: In the bigger picture, the style of teaching at my host institution had many similarities to that of UCPH. However, there were some notable differences. In clinical clerkships in Denmark, it is usually made very clear who the students are assigned to and what the schedule for the day looks like. At my host institution, this aspect was less structured, leaving it up to the student to figure out who to follow and what to focus on. This lack of clarity sometimes made it exhausting to navigate, especially as not everyone had the time or energy to accommodate an international student in their busy schedules. Additionally, I would have appreciated more lectures. For example, having a weekly lecture for all Erasmus students, delivered by different departments, could have significantly increased the overall learning outcome and provided a more structured educational experience

recommended_courses: I would highly recommend the neurosurgery department. It was the best department I attended during my clinical clerkship. The learning outcome from this department was outstanding, and the experience was truly exceptional.
unexpected_costs: Laundry costs - it was more expensive than I expected.
cost_comparison: Eating out was less expensive than I expected and the supermarket was more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: The university had a library, a gym and a swimming pool. The ESN hosted so many great events.
activities_recommended: Join all the ESN events
weekend_recommendations: All the great beaches, all the great museums and also go for a trip to Athens (go by boat with student discount or flight). The other students visited Santorini by boat (student discount as well).
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture was very easy for the non-academic aspects. I absolutely loved the Greek culture and the warmth of the people, which made me feel welcome and comfortable. On the academic side, I had to adapt to a more flexible approach to scheduling and time management.
socializing_tips: The Greek students are very easy to talk to and very including. I would recommend getting a buddy as well through ESN.
cultural_challenges: As mentioned, the more flexible approach to scheduling and time management. That 8.00 might be 8.00 but it could also be 8.30 ish
culture_appreciated: The warm and including culture of the local people. And the food.
top3_advice: 1) Be Proactive and adaptable: unlike the structured system you might be used to, you will need to take the initiative to figure out your daily schedule and find someone to shadow in the departments. This might feel challenging at first, but it's an excellent opportunity to develop independence and adaptability. 2) Learn basic local language skills: the language barrier can be a challenge, so having some basic knowledge of Greek or being prepared to use translation tools can make a significant difference in your ability to follow the workflow. 3) Embrace the local culture: the warmth and hospitality of Greek culture are incredible, so take the time to enjoy it outside of academics. Engaging with the local lifestyle and building relationships will enrich your experience. AND participate in the ESN events - this is also where you find many of your new friends.
other_useful_info: If you are a medical student attending the hospital, you should know that the canteen offers free lunch for students. I wasn't aware of this until three weeks into my stay, so make sure to take advantage of it right from the start!
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was creating new international friendships and becoming part of a group of Erasmus students. Sharing the experience of exploring Greek culture together was truly amazing and made the exchange unforgettable.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during the exchange was feeling unwelcome in certain departments and struggling with the language barrier. It was difficult to communicate effectively and to find opportunities to learn, often requiring extra effort to advocate for myself and be included.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to live in a city which was not too big to be explored within the 4 months of my exchange. It was also important for me that the highlands of Scotland was so close, so I could go on weekend trips and hike in the beautiful nature. Furthermore, finding courses I could take at the university that would allow me to get pre-approval at KU was crucial for my choice of destination. This was of course easier in Scotland as an English speaking country, where I could follow all courses at the university.
overall_comments: I had a lovely exchange at University of Edinburgh (UoE). The student association at the university has a very strong presence and AMAZING facilities (honestly, they have a flipping castle in the middle of campus!). There are around 100 or more societies, with sports, music, theatre and academic related. Great place to meet lots of people :D And the Erasmus Student Network also has a good handful of activities, where it's possible to connect with other exchange students :) Edinburgh is a beautiful, easy and comfortable place to live and have a great exchange. But I must say, that the autumn semester in UoE is very short. It only lasts from 20th of September to mid December (my last exam was due 13th of Dec). Although it is nice to have the Holidays off, it was a very short time to learn the course material (13 weeks) where in the last two weeks, it was almost impossible to follow the lectures and read the course material, as the exam papers were already released an the hand in dates approaching (1st and 2nd of December for me). I thought this was a shame, as I believe I could have learned much more from the professors and curriculum at UoE if I had had more time. Might be that it is a longer semester in the spring, and therefore more time for diving into the course material and spend time with all the lovely people you will meet on your exchange.

arrival_assistance: The Vistiting Students Office were very helpful and respond very quickly to all my emails. And they give you checklists on what documents etc you will need on arrival at the UoE. Although I was a bit on my own in figuring out immigration rules with Brexit and covid. Ended up not being that difficult, but I brought all the documents anyway.
arrival_comments: They could have been clearer on helping with covid and brexit immigration issues. The information on their webpage focus mainly on the rules for non-EU citizens. But I also didn't ask them directly to help me with this. They would probably have helped if I had asked, but I figured it out on my own.

registration_process: UoE do not tell visiting students what 3rd and 4th year (last years of bachelor) courses are available for exchange students until mid July. And the learning agreement needs to be signed by KU and UoE with the courses you're expected to take by 1st of August. This is a prerequisite for the Erasmus grant application and hence has consequences for when the grant is dispersed. This was quite stressful for me, as I couldn't do anything until UoE had released the courses available for enrollment, and then had to apply for them in their online platform, which also don't work very efficiently. If a course is full you have to keep applying for it every day and hope that a space opens up. And you can only change your courses until 1st of September. But lots of students do change courses in the first couple of weeks, so it's often possible to get the course you want. And I also did get the courses I wanted and needed for KU. It was just a stressful process, as I also had to hastily get new reapprovals for other UoE courses from KU.
registration_help: The Visiting Student office tried their best to help and answer quickly and I could go for a meeting with them. But the system is not the smartest.
registration_success: I got the courses I wanted in the end.
registration_advice: Get a bucket full of preapprovals before you go on the exchange. I mean 3-5 different reapprovals for each KU course you want to take at UoE. This way you will have more freedom if the courses are full and you need to change.
