registration_help: You can place all the courses of your interest in a week calendar when you apply for the courses. That was quite helpful, I found. Still, you should be aware that the courses may take place at different locations.
registration_success: I got the three courses I had initially applied for. When I wanted to swap courses later on, I got my second priority, so all in all satisfactory.
registration_advice: Use the online device on MyEd that places the courses in a week calendar. Be aware that you can swap courses, so you might want to join some extra courses in the very first week. Thereby, you will be introduced to more courses and, hopefully, you'll discover the ones in your interest.
academics_comments: I have had a wonderful stay overall and would highly recommend anyone to study abroad in Edinburgh if they are given the change. That said, it is an expensive city (country) to live in and the heating bills were shockingly high which meant we couldn't afford having heat on during the cold periods. In terms of the actual studies, I had hoped for more teachings since I only had 6 hours a week for 10 weeks. In Copenhagen I am used to 8 hours for 14 weeks and, considering the money other students pay to study here, I believe you'd be in your good right to expect more. The quality of the teachings though, were all fine.
course_level: I enjoyed following MA courses and found the level very similar to the one back home. I have since my arrival been told by other students from UCPH that they could only apply for BA courses due to new rules. I hope renegotiations with University of Edinburgh will enable future UCPH students to follow MA courses to fulfill the potential of the exchange.
teaching_comparison: The teachings were good but in my opinion there were too few (2 hours a week for 10 weeks). That said, I do appreciate that you get a more nuanced final grade over here: the grades you get from presentations, essays, and final essays/exams all count and constitute one final grade per course.
courses_enrolled: The European Union in International Affairs, Climate Change, Justice, and Responsibility Environmental Risk: Politics, Ethics, and Communication
recommended_courses: I would recommend all three but I also believe there are many other interesting courses. E.g. I would have liked to also follow the course Anthropology and Environment. The teachers on each of my courses seemed very passionate about their research areas and, equally important, very interested in how the students felt about the topics we covered throughout the semester. The EU in International Affairs were very well structured; Climate Change, Justice and Responsibility provided a very interesting philosophical approach to climate change; and the course on Environmental Risks were funnily creative as we were given a lot of freedom in our essays.
unexpected_costs: Heating bills in the winter
cost_comparison: Most stuff were more expensive than I had expected it to be. Accommodation, food (quite similar to back home), trains etc. Only things that I found less expensive were hair cuts and pints due to student discounts.
activities_available: I know that there are plenty sports societies but I am not too aware of the cultural and non-sport ones that surely can be found here too.
activities_recommended: I would recommend any future student here to start their exchange by joining a community. Again, sadly, I was distracted by my UCPH exams at that time and then had to settle in.
weekend_recommendations: The city itself is amazing and includes a lot of places and things worth exploring. So first of all, I encourage other students to just walk around the city and enjoy its unique architecture and green areas. The trains are very expensive but if you book stuff early on, you might be lucky. Otherwise, if you've got a drivers licence (I didn't) rent a car and travel the country. I went up north to Inverness and Loch Ness and drove past the West coast on my way back. I would have loved to explore a lot more of the country but being able to drive seems quite helpful around here. Glencoe Valley is a MUST, but Loch Ness was great too. There is also a lot of Harry Potter stuff to explore if interested - both in Edinburgh and around the country. There are also several things nearby (St. Andrews, Glasgow, Melrose Abbey, Rosslyn Chapel, Alnwick Castle etc.).
culture_adjustment: The expensive student accommodation through the university turned out to do me a favour as I found a private flat instead. Here, I have been living with three English students who have introduced me to the culture, their friends, and all sorts of stuff around the city. In other words, that was surprisingly easy to me but primarily because I ended up where I did.
socializing_tips: Socialising with local students is a bit challenging if you are on exchange in the spring semester since most students seem to have settled and made a lot of friends already. That said, they seem more used to and welcoming towards exchange students than we are in Copenhagen, and they are usually impressed by our level of English (since most locals don't speak anything but English). So don't be afraid; both by flat mates, class mates, and pub mates have all been kind and welcoming towards me. It won't do any damage to join someone's table and have a drink with some strangers who might turn out to be your friends for the rest of the semester. (They might even be used to drive in the 'wrong' side of the road.) There are many other international students who, like you, will be looking for someone to share their Scottish adventure with, so don't hesitate to reach out though it feel slightly awkward at first considering the "reserved" Danish culture.
cultural_challenges: The culture is very similar to back home, but the Scottish Accent might be challenging at first. In Edinburgh it is less challenging though but as soon as you turn towards Glasgow or up north you'll experience a stronger accent.
culture_appreciated: The pub culture is amazing! My flat mates would take me out five times to grab a beer the very first week. And I do not say that because we went out clubbing every night. To the contrary, what I found great was that we'd just go for a pint of two - nothing wild - just to catch up, and then we'd turn back home. Of course football is a big thing over here as well which I appreciated as it pushed me to the pubs where I met some nice people.
top3_advice: Make sure to experience the city and the country while you are here. I would have loved to experience more. Prioritise joining a society or some sort of student community in the very first weeks as they seem to do a lot of events at the start of each semester (if possible, avoid UCPH exams that overlap with the introductory weeks at UoE) Enjoy your time here; the teachings at least are over before you know it.
other_useful_info: If you struggle finding accommodation try SpareRoom. Just like in Copenhagen, the competition is high, so write as many as possible and hopefully you'll succeed in finding a nice flat eventually. (I lived in Newington just next to the Meadows which is a great area and close to the campus for social sciences)
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of nice people from around the world and experiencing what it is like to live in a different country.
greatest_challenge: The cold temperatures during winter times. As stressed, do make sure to pack some warm clothes in case you don't have heating included in your monthly rent.
other_comments: Enjoy your stay! Edinburgh is a wonderful city and the nature of Scotland really is something special! :)

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience a new culture and I have always been interested in studying and living in the UK. It was crucial for me that my host university offered interesting courses within my field.
info_ease: It was quite easy to find the information I needed upon arrival if I just kept myself updated on all of the emails I received. I would say that if you are not reading all your emails leading up to your exchange it is easy to miss something important, so they are definitely worth reading!
arrival_assistance: I was assigned a student advisor which can be reached most days of the week and can help you with anything related to your studies, life at the study destination and personal matters. If they cannot help you, they will tell you about all the services that could then instead answer your question or help you. I was therefore never left stranded, as I had a lot of people to reach out to for help.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: To sign up for courses I had to send a prioritised list of the courses I was most interested in signing up for, along with my application for the university itself. I could choose up to five courses and then they try to assign you the courses you put at the top of your list, based on availability.
registration_help: You could email the Visiting Student Office if you had troubles with your course registration but I did not do that, so I don't have experience on that.
registration_success: I was very successful in registering for the classes I wanted. I got the courses I had placed second, third and fourth on my course registration form, but the reason I didn't get the first one was because they decided to only teach it during the spring semester, while I was there during the fall semester. I was very happy with my courses and now I am very grateful that those were the courses I received.
registration_advice: I would read the information provided about how to register for courses and look at a lot of courses, both within and outside of your study field. I found many interesting courses outside of my field. Only list the courses you would be happy to take on your prioritised list, as it could happen that you don't get the ones you most want.
course_level: The courses I took were third or fourth year courses for the undergraduate programs and I found them to be challenging but not too challenging.
teaching_comparison: I loved the teaching style. The use very interactive styles of teaching and the courses I had all had interactive seminar sessions and discussions which was very nice. What I loved most about the teaching style is that you get a lot of feedback from your teacher for your work during the semester compared to UCPH so when I submitted my final essays and exams I had a lot of constructive feedback to work with. I do not like how little feedback we get at UCPH and we often do not get even one sentence of feedback from our teachers during the entire semester, not even for our final exams. I feel like I learned a lot more during the semester at my host institution, and actually learned about ways I needed to improve on, something that I had never gotten a comment about at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled in Nations and Nationalism, Sociology of Emotions and Sociology of Medicine.
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of these courses to future exchange students, especially Sociology of Medicine and Sociology of Emotions. They had great teachers and I learned so much about these interesting topics.
unexpected_costs: I did not experience any negative unexpected costs during my exchange but I did travel more than I expected so I would expect to spend some money on traveling.
cost_comparison: Food was less expensive than I expected because I heard of the cost of living crisis and thought everything would be very expensive but it was still quite affordable compared to Denmark.
activities_available: There were so many clubs and activities offered by my host institution, it is actually quite impossible to not find something that interests you. They have a few hundred student societies so you can join anything you want. It is incredible.
activities_recommended: I joined the university gym, the Pole Dancing Society and the Scandinavian Society, which were all great. The gym is affordable compared to how much you get (it is huge and has everything). I started doing pole dancing at the Pole Dancing Society as I had been wanting to try it for quite a long time now and it was so much fun. The Scandinavian Society was also very fun to meet other people.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend visiting students to go on some ESN trips as they allow you to travel outside of the city and see more of the country, which is very beautiful. I went on ESN trips a lot of my weekends.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy, as the weather and culture is not too different from what I was used to. I also made it easier that I stayed in an English-speaking country so being a part of the culture was easier.
socializing_tips: Definitely go meet as many people as you can the first few weeks! You will be so tired and it will be quite a lot in the beginning but you will eventually find your friends and then it becomes much easier. I was mostly friends with other exchange students that I met through ESN meet-ups, so definitely show up to those.
cultural_challenges: I did not really find any cultural differences especially challenging.
culture_appreciated: I loved the city, it was so beautiful and the people are very nice.
top3_advice: I would tell them to try to meet as many people as they can in the first few weeks because eventually they will find their core friend group. Try as many activities as you can, the university has so much to offer and mostly quite cheap. Enjoy every single moment, the exchange goes by so fast and even though it can be hard to be away from family and home, you are only exchange once in your life so make the most of it!
other_useful_info: Most people are actually very open and want to get to know you, so put yourself out there.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was without a doubt the friends I made. We met during welcome week and stayed so close during the entire semester, they became my family. I will forever be grateful for Edinburgh for bringing us together.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was not having anyone I knew close to me in the unfamiliar circumstances. I have lived away from home for some years now, but it is hard to go to a new country and not have anyone there, where it is completely your responsibility to make close friends. But these challenges only make you grow so I would still recommend doing an exchange.

registration_process: We had to register twice, both at the visiting student office where you had to answer a few question, and then the formal one where you had to register your arrival with your passport and flight tickets. I found the informations about these a bit lacking. They had not informed us of the one at the visiting student office which made the process a bit stressful as we had to do it in a hurry to not face any consequences.
registration_help: you could always email the visiting student office, and they respond really quick
registration_success: I got almost all the classes i wanted. The only reason i did not get the third one I wanted was because overlapping courses, which you have to be aware of when applying for courses
registration_advice: do everything in good time, as the responding time might be a bit slow
academics_comments: Edinburgh in itself is a really chill and cozy town, i really loved it. The only thing that disappointed me a bit was the low level of critical thinking during lectures.
course_level: I took 2 third year courses and 1 fourth year course
teaching_comparison: I found that the teaching was a bit different. The teaching at UCPH is a bit more practical, at least in anthropology. I was a bit surprised that the had not tried to write ethnographically or done fieldwork during their BA, and only did it for their dissertation. The critical thinking was not as high either. It seemed like empirical data from the texts we read were more important than theory, which made it feel like there wasn´t a big knowledge to different theories
courses_enrolled: Anthropology and Africa, War and Peace, Culture and Power
recommended_courses: War and Peace: Its a very interesting course that touches upon war and peace and how anthropology can study these complex subjects. The lecture made the course very interesting and he was good at facilitating the class discussions as these subjects can be very sensitive to some people. I liked how war was focused on from another perspective than only destruction and death
unexpected_costs: The rooms we moved in to were completely empty, so we had to buy literally everything from duvets, to pots and pans
cost_comparison: Eating out is more expensive than i thought, otherwise its much like danish prices i would say
activities_available: There are more than 100 societies available for students, so you can almost do everything you want
activities_recommended: I didn´t really participate in any societies, as i felt like i made a lot of friends outside of them
weekend_recommendations: go to the highlands, explore the city and the nearby cities, go out and eat, go to the park meadows, go clubbing
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy i would say, the scotts are very kind and friendsly
socializing_tips: Just start a conversation when you´re doing class discussions, or after class
cultural_challenges: It wasn´t really challenging, but it doesn´t really matter what day of the week it is people still go to the clubs and pubs, so be prepared to party a lot if you´re into that
culture_appreciated: Probably the hospitality and how helpful people were
top3_advice: be prepared for a lot of exam stuff (especially anthropology) - midterms and finals have to be written while you also go to class, so it can be a bit stressful Talk to the professors, they are really sweet and want to make you feel comfortable with talking in class even though english might not be your first language Be open towards everyone, thats the easiest way to find friends
other_useful_info: Just have fun and enjoy the time there
most_rewarding: probably the people that i met
greatest_challenge: Understanding the scottish accent was a big challenge in the beginning i would say

crucial_aspects: English speaking country where you can still get the Erasmus Grant
info_ease: A whole welcome week was planned for new students and exchange students. Guided tours around campus, how to use the library etc.
arrival_assistance: Assistance from other students studying in the same field and exchange coordinators
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The process was very clear and easy understandable. You book a time through a mail they did send, then you arrive and they help you and it was very easy.
registration_help: Other students, people helping showing the way and the exchange coordinators.
registration_success: I was successful but it was hard to figure out which courses I could take.
registration_advice: It is very easy, just talk to other students or go to campus and ask for help and they will tell you what to do.
course_level: The level of the courses was higher than what I am used to.
teaching_comparison: Very similar. Really good teachers and professors, ready to help and answer questions.
courses_enrolled: Structure and Function of Proteins Immunology Molecular Genetics
recommended_courses: Immunology, a very good and interesting course Structure and Function of Proteins, small tests every week to make you keep following up and no final exam
unexpected_costs: Nothing unexpected, I was planning on spending a lot of money on tours around the country and to other countries around
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping is less expensive than back home, and the same by going out for food. Rent and housing is more expensive
activities_available: A lot! Almost too many societies you can be a part of including sport, cultural and other social things
activities_recommended: Societies. From Scandinavia, the Scandi Society. If you are knitting, another society for that. If you like sport or Taylor Swift, there are societies for that
weekend_recommendations: Go on the trip with the Erasmus Programs, they have tours all over the country. Go out, see museums, hiking.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, Scottish people are so nice and very helpful to let you know about the best spots in town.
socializing_tips: Become a part of all the whatsapp groups! Its a good way to meet people and see what events others are attending.
cultural_challenges: Only that you cant buy alcohol after 10pm and going out everything closes at 3am or 1am. Otherwise it was very similar
culture_appreciated: People being so welcoming, the nature and the city it self - it was like being a main character in a movie.
top3_advice: Become a part of the WhatsApp groups Use all the free opportunities for students through all the societies Join societies and use the library to study
other_useful_info: Take some interesting courses, use all the student discounts and societies to meet friends from all over the world
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of amazing people from all over the world, friends for life. Having some interesting courses - now I know what master I will take back home in Copenhagen
greatest_challenge: Learning in a new way. At this point I have gotten used to the lectures and how everything works in Copenhagen - in Edinburgh things were different but very good as well - but getting used to the differences was a challenge

crucial_aspects: The courses offered and the academic staff. Also learning other approaches and academic traditions. And traveling: meeting people, getting new experiences and living in a different place.
overall_comments: My stay was great, really did not want to back home at the end of it. And absolutely loved Uni of Edinburgh academically.
info_ease: Not that easy. There was a bit of red tape and a lack of information regarding registering and getting settled. That was on the part of the recipient uni, however. The Erasmus part of the process was seamless.
arrival_assistance: I received great assistance on several occations. Often information was lacking, but talking to one of the contact persons resolved it each time. I think personal assistance in adminstrative matters is more common in Scotland than in Denmark (that is, less automated), so that was a bit of a cultural lesson. My student advisor and others were extremely helpful and accommodating.
arrival_comments: It was really good. Also the students at my dorm were good at making us feel welcomed (I stayed at Riego Street in Edinburgh).
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My stay was great, really did not want to back home at the end of it. And absolutely loved Uni of Edinburgh academically.
registration_process: Do not remember entirely but think it was going to a certain meeting at a certain time and get a "yes you are here" stamp.
registration_help: There was the student advisor who was generally available for all sorts of questions. It was really nice to have such a general point of contact.
registration_success: Again, it did not work when I did it online--but then I went to the office where they did it and I was immediately registered at courses that I had wished for.
registration_advice: When in doubt, ask someone. Do not hesitate to reach out.
academics_comments: My stay was great, really did not want to back home at the end of it. And absolutely loved Uni of Edinburgh academically.
course_level: I did elective courses on level 10--which are third year courses--and there were both undergrads, grad students and PhD students.
teaching_comparison: Fewer people in class, more time for questions, more time with professors (I only took electives so it is really not comparable to regular classes).
courses_enrolled: Gender and environment Race and ethnicity Sociology of medicine
recommended_courses: Sociology of medicine was a revolutionary course to me, big recommendation. Very medically technical and so politically relevant as an approach to scientific aspects of modern politics.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Food was as expensive as in Denmark; housing was much more expensive.
activities_available: All of them. So much happening, especially uni-related.
activities_recommended: Depends on your interests. Go visit several societies to find out which seem nice.
weekend_recommendations: Go hiking! You cannot go in winter, so try and take a week or two during the summer break to go to the Cairngorms or the Trossachs or around Inverness.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. However, Scots (and Brits in general) are not comfortable with (even partial) nudity which is a common sight in Denmark.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The language (haha). Also Indian food. And pub culture.
top3_advice: It is not that different from Denmark culturally or academically. Do not despair if it is hard to meet locals; as a friend you are an ephemeral investment. People are younger than at Danish unis.
other_useful_info: There are so many places to study and so many campuses; check as many out as possible.
most_rewarding: The classes. Also the people that I made friends with.
greatest_challenge: Writing my final essays.

course_level: easy, but poorly structured

courses_enrolled: Global Connections since 1450 English Discovery of Russia, 1556-1664 Themes in Modern European History
recommended_courses: Not the ones I had!
unexpected_costs: The language requirement!
cost_comparison: The books, all were available online.
activities_available: All the kinds I imagine.
activities_recommended: Idk
weekend_recommendations: Sightseeing, it depends of the city of course!
culture_adjustment: A bit hard. I loathe the british food culture (ew), but the overall city was easy to get around. Luckily Edinburgh is as much digitalised as CPH! People were very kind:-)
socializing_tips: Join clubs, attend stuff, be open!
cultural_challenges: The food!
culture_appreciated: Their openness towards others, and kindness towards strangers.
top3_advice: Get out of the city some days (e.g. the highlands) Explore! walk around, also in the not-so-touristed places Get a alternative accommodation outside the city centre, (e.g. Portobello where I lived), to get a glimpse of the suburban areas and stuff tourists do not see.
other_useful_info: Nope

crucial_aspects: The city and country itself, I had long wanted to live in Edinburgh city since I last visited it. The university was also fairly well known as a good university which sealed the deal for me.
info_ease: Easy. The exchange student office at Edinburgh University is very helpful and answers questions quickly.
arrival_assistance: Edinburgh sent me check lists of what things I needed to do in order to confirm and check in at Edinburgh University. Furthermore, welcome week offered loads of events to meet new people both inside and outside your study.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: They send you an email welcoming you and tells you to show up for "international check-in", which is basicly where you show up with your passport and they confirm your attendance. Then, you also do a check-in at your particular study, and then your done.
registration_help: You could email the office for exchange students, which is how I asked for help.
registration_success: One of my classes I didnt get, but I was generally happy with the course that replaced it.
registration_advice: Get it over with fast, it doesnt take long.
course_level: MA courses were very focused on class discussions which made them engaging and challenging without being too difficult.
teaching_comparison: fairly similar, however the classes were smaller at Edinburgh, some classes we were only 10 people.
courses_enrolled: Gender, politics and representation The Middle East in International relations Survey in the Middle Eastern Politics
recommended_courses: I would recommend the two Middle Eastern classes, even though I had never taken a class of the middle east before they were still fairly introducory.
unexpected_costs: Housing was more exspensive than expected, however I found something fairly cheap compared to other places - in general be expected to pay between 6000-9000 kroner for a room.
cost_comparison: Cost of living in Edinburgh is less costly than Copenhagen, so eating out at restaurants and cafés, going for drinks and buying groceries were generally 20-25 pct cheaper than in Copenhagen.
activities_available: Again almost anything you can think off is a society at Edinburgh University, and they all create events - sometimes the events are open to non-members, other times you have to be a member of the society to join.
activities_recommended: The wine society was really fun and a great way to get to know new people. If your into sports, I also recommend joining one of their sports-societies, which is student-led but still very high-quality (and good for the price!).
weekend_recommendations: A lot of museums is free in Edinburgh, so I recommend that. Also going on a weekend-trip to the highlands is a must, I personally went to Isle of Skye, which was absolutely stunning. Scotland has some of the most beautiful nature.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, its quite similar to danish culture.
socializing_tips: Engage in welcome week and join a society, people are very eager to make new friends. Join the Erasmus students group chat, its very active during the first couple of week with people looking to meet new people. Welcome week can be quite overwhelming, there like 20 events everyday, but choose a couple each day and dont worry about missing some of them - you cant make them all!
cultural_challenges: I didnt really find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: Pub-culture is amazing in Edinburgh, generally the night-life is very lively and people are very nice.
top3_advice: Start early (but not too early) when finding housing. I started 2 months before, but my search really began around 1,5-1 month before my move-in date, because most rooms are only offered or rented out a month in advance. Apply for student housing at the university even if they tell you its not guaranteed - you might just be offered something anyway! Join a society - Its a great way to get to know new people, and there really is something for everyone. Be patient - Edinburgh University is generally really late in confirming your exchange. I got my final confirmation that I had been accepted as an exchange student from Edinburgh University in late July, and the semester starts september 11th! So if you haven't heard from UED, dont panic, they are generally late in confirming their students attendance.
other_useful_info: There are not many study-seats at the libraries, so remember to get up early during exam period if you want a seat at the library - or sit at a cafe.
most_rewarding: The social aspect of EUD, they have one of the most well-developed student-led social scene I have ever experienced.
greatest_challenge: Transportation to and from campus via bus- It wasn't a huge problem, but the buses are often 10-15 min late which can be a bit annoying.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial to pick an English-speaking destination where I could also see myself in the culture, which is why Edinburgh was perfect. It also has a clear connection to English literature so it made perfect sense for me to go there
info_ease: You get emails about everything so it is quite easy to figure out
arrival_assistance: Assistance is available if you need and you are told of your options
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was different in my case as I was on a special agreement
registration_help: You could email people at the university for help if you wanted but that was kind of it
registration_success: I ended up just applying for ten different courses and hoping I got just any of them, which was a bit sad as I also wanted some other courses that was outside of my special agreement
registration_advice: I'm not sure, hopefully it's a bit more clear in the future
course_level: The level was pretty much the same as at home, though we spent less time on individual material which made the work load a bit heavier and didn't seem to go as much in depth as I am used to
teaching_comparison: The classes were much smaller which was a bit intimidating and you were more expected to be prepared for seminars. Answers also seemed more standardised than at home
courses_enrolled: Working Class Representations, Horror and Mystery, Ideology and Literature
recommended_courses: Working Class Representations turned out to be my favourite course, I found it very interesting and the professor was very welcoming and open to discussion
unexpected_costs: I expected the accommodation to provide pillows, duvets and kitchen stuff but the apartment was completely empty when i got there, so expect to buy everything from a pillow to pans, pots and cutlery
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive though it is almost the same as Copenhagen
activities_available: Everything, you could join any society you wanted, from sports to cultural societies to book clubs
activities_recommended: Get out of your comfort zone a bit, try some Scottish dancing or something like that. Also, take your chance to explore the city and the country
weekend_recommendations: Go to the Highlands and experience the country, it is magnificent
culture_adjustment: Really easy as it is very similar to Denmark, the people are just more friendly
socializing_tips: Speaking with the Scottish students is really easy as they are typically very open, though a lot of the English students can be a bit harder to get close to
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and the fact that they really cater to their culture and are proud to show it with honesty and humour
top3_advice: Bring warm clothes if you are going for the autumn semester, try the local food, even if it is not great, socialise and meet people
other_useful_info: Enjoy your time and the city as there is really nothing like it
most_rewarding: Experiencing the culture and seeing the country which I have fallen a little bit in love with
greatest_challenge: Sharing a kitchen with four others

crucial_aspects: I had heard good stuff about the University of Edinburgh and thought it would be a great fit with my academic interests.
overall_comments: I had a really nice exchange. Liked the University, the courses, the lecturers, the city, and especially the nature in Scotland.
info_ease: Not the easiest I would say, but thankfully one of my friends was going on exchange at the same uni, so we could help each other out.
arrival_assistance: I received none. I had rented a townhouse from a private landlord with two other danes, so it had nothing to do with the uni.
arrival_comments: I felt a bit on my own at first, but it was partly my fault. I thought the post grad arrangements sounded more chill and fun.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had a really nice exchange. Liked the University, the courses, the lecturers, the city, and especially the nature in Scotland.
registration_process: I had to show up with my passport and my plane ticket. It took less than 10 minuttes.
registration_help: I was assigned a student administrator that I would reach out to if necessary. It wasn't.
registration_success: It took a few week to get my schedule to work out, but once it did it was fine. At first I was assigned two courses that overlapped.
registration_advice: Check the mails from your institution and reach out to fellow students if you're lost.
academics_comments: I had a really nice exchange. Liked the University, the courses, the lecturers, the city, and especially the nature in Scotland.
course_level: The level was nice. It suited my academic level nicely.
teaching_comparison: Quite similar. Shorter lecturers and seminars, but similar style and also similar readings.
courses_enrolled: Gender and Environment, The Anthropology of Energy in the Global South, and Digital Global Development
recommended_courses: The Gender and Environment courses was really really interesting. I had been introduced to some of the texts prior to the course, but I learned a lot of new stuff that I will be taking with me in my future studies.
unexpected_costs: None really. Edinburgh is similar to Copenhagen. A bit less expensive overall.
cost_comparison: Our housing was quite expensive, but food was less pricy than what I had expected.
activities_available: Many. I signed up to a gym close by the uni. It was very nice.
activities_recommended: Get out of the city! Go on hikes and explore the stunning land!
weekend_recommendations: Get out of the city! Go on hikes and explore the stunning land!
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Go to the social events even though the sometimes suck. Be bold on the courses or around the city and talk to strangers and ask to keep in touch.
cultural_challenges: I struggled a bit with my spoken english.
culture_appreciated: The nature.
top3_advice: Pick courses so you have lots of freetime to go on hikes outside of the city.
other_useful_info: Check out the Bothy Association.
most_rewarding: New academic insights and encounters with the nature.
greatest_challenge: My english.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial to me that by going on exchange at the University of Edinburgh I could perceive fields within Anthropology that were not possible at the University of Copenhagen to the same extend.
info_ease: It was quite easy. The University of Edinburgh and the University of Copenhagen both sent several emails with information as well as when action was needed to do apply for courses etc.
arrival_assistance: There were a couple of introduction meetings. And email to the student advisor was available at all times.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The course registration process was very different than what I have been used to in Denmark. The whole thing is online, but at first when you apply for classes before arriving you do not know how they are scheduled, which caused me and my fellow exchange students to have a lot of overlapping classes, when the schedules are finally ready in august/beginning of september. However you can change your course enrollments until the end of september which gives a lot of flexibility. However some of the courses I was hoping to get where full which resulted in that I where not able to get the combination of courses I was hoping for.
registration_help: The student advisory office could help with the applications for course enrollments and it was possible to do multiple enrollment applications to change courses. My experience was that the information needed to apply for course enrollments where all available online.
registration_success: I would say that 2 out of 3 classes where exactly what I hoped for.
registration_advice: But in work to find the best combination of courses possible with your schedule. I spent a lot of time trying to make the puzzle add up and I believe it paid off.
course_level: In my experience, the level of courses was much like in Copenhagen. However, the participation of students in discussions was not as high as I am used to in Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: It was quite similar. A mix of lectures and seminars.
courses_enrolled: Digital Global Development The Anthropology of Energy in the Global South Gender & Environment
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend the 'Gender & Environment' course because it engages with critical ecofeminism (and so much more), which is something I have not had the chance to work with at the University of Copenhagen.
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs beside transport which I were not planning on spending so much money on.
cost_comparison: Food in supermarkets was usually a bit less expensive than I had thought. Eating at restaurants was more expensive.
activities_available: A lot! I recommend participating in all the fairs (sports fair, club fair etc.) in the beginning of the semester. Both academic and non-academic possibilities.
activities_recommended: Participating in some sort of sports activity. Because it is a nice way of meeting people from the uni and engaging with them in a more relaxed setting.
weekend_recommendations: Going on hikes, sleeping in bothys (the Scottish equivalent to shelter in Denmark), going on trips to the highlands, Isle of Skye, and exploring if there are any concerts or anything you would like to do. A lot of bars play live jazz music in the afternoon/evening as well. And all museums are free.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy I think.
socializing_tips: People were really sweet in my courses and I primarily socialized with them about our courses, readings and so. Also I think it is important to remind oneself that it is not because there is anything wrong with you if you have a hard time socializing with the local students. You are only there for a couple of months so I had the experience that a lot of locals did not engage too much with exchange students. But there are plenty of other exchange students to do a lot of fun stuff with.
cultural_challenges: Not really any actually.
culture_appreciated: The nature and theater is as well a big thing in Edinburgh.
top3_advice: 1. Exiting courses and competent professors. 2. Great if you want to explore beautiful nature while studying. 3. Edinburgh is a University city and there are a lot of students, which is nice.
other_useful_info: I did however spent more time on my studies than I expected I would.
most_rewarding: That I went on exchange with 2 friends I already knew from Copenhagen. It was important for me that we had this experience together and could explore the country together.
greatest_challenge: Being away from friends and family for a long time. Not being able to take a break in the same way.

crucial_aspects: That my study destination was an English-speaking country, that the university scored highly in various academic rankings, that the university offered different societies and other social initiatives that made is easier for visiting students to meet students from other countries and cultures, and that the university was located in a beautiful city, full of things to experience.
info_ease: Relatively easy. The University of Edinburgh were great at communicating what to expect and where/how to find the information I needed.
arrival_assistance: Every visiting student were given a personal Visiting Student Advisor to communicate with and reach out to, if needed.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The process was through OLA, where the host institution had to approve the courses I wanted to enroll in. There was also a matriculation process, where I needed to upload various documents to prove my arrival, and that I had been successfully enrolled in three courses, equivalent to 30 ETCS.
registration_help: The visiting students office.
registration_success: When I registered for courses before coming to Edinburgh, I was only succesfull in enrolling in one of the three I wanted. But after the semester had begun it was a lot easier to register for other courses, and I ended up with the ones I wanted.
registration_advice: If you don't get the classes/courses you want before starting the semester, fear not :) It is very easy to apply for other options, once you are there, and the course registration is open two weeks into the semester. Almost everyone I met, ended up with at least one og two other courses than they originally registered for.
course_level: I was only able to take 1st of 2nd year courses, and not 3rd year courses, even though I was in my 3rd year. But is was okay, because the courses I had were still very interesting and I did not experience that the academic level was beneath what I was used to from UCPH.
teaching_comparison: I felt that the teaching style at Edinburgh Uni was a more captivating and involving.
courses_enrolled: Contemporary Cinema Visualising Scotland Music 1A: Psychology of Music
recommended_courses: Visualising Scotland. I registered to this course later than the others, but it ended up being the course I enjoyed the most. Our professor was very competent and captivating in his way of teaching, and the course offered an exciting insight into Scottish culture and history that I did not know beforehand. When you spend an entire semester in Scotland, it feels important to know about its culture, and this course provided that information in an instructive and captivating way.
unexpected_costs: Train tickets for day trips. But if you buy a Railcard you save a lot of money.
cost_comparison: Coffee was a lot less expensive than Copenhagen prices. Rent was more expensive.
activities_available: I joined different societies, e.g. The Film Society (FilmSoc), and the Scandinavian Society.
activities_recommended: The societies and the welcome events in week 1.
weekend_recommendations: Go on as many little trips as possible. Scotland is full of beautiful little cities that are easy to get to by train :) The Highlands, the grand and beautiful nature up north, is also a big and very recommendable experience.
culture_adjustment: Very easy I would say. People were very friendly and openminded.
cultural_challenges: That the cars drive in the opposite side of the road - watch out, when you cross the street!
culture_appreciated: That people were so friendly, openminded and hospitable. The lady in the bakery would call you "love", which was such a nice gesture :)
top3_advice: 1. Make use of all the different societies that Edi Uni has to offer 2. Go to your classes - the semester is quite short, and the assignments were a lot easier to write in those classes I had attended the most. 3. Choose a living situation, where you live with other young people. It's a great way to meet new friends.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: The lovely people that I met.
greatest_challenge: When I missed my family and friends from back home.

crucial_aspects: To get the Erasmus Grant and an English-speaking country.
info_ease: Easy
arrival_assistance: Intro week and help from the visiting Student Office
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The Visiting Student Office sends you a link, where you can see what courses are available. From that link, you also pick what courses you would like to take. It is recommended that you pick some extra courses, in case your first choice is not available. After you have submitted the formular, you get a confirmation email from the Visiting Student office, informing you whether your chosen courses have gone through or you have to choose other available courses.
registration_help: Visiting Student Office was helpful.
registration_success: I got 2 of the 3 courses I wanted. I submitted the formular just 2 days after I received the link - which was late if you want the popular courses.
registration_advice: Choose your courses as soon as you get the link. Or else, you can risk that you do not get all the courses that you want - especially if that course is a high-demand course.

crucial_aspects: - The possibility of receiving an Erasmus grant - An interesting course catalogue - It was an English-speaking country - The possibility of going on trips in the highlands - An interesting and beautiful city - The university's good academic reputation and ratings
info_ease: It was a bit confusing at times, because we received a lot of different emails with a lot of information from different senders. It was possible, however, to find most of the information needed, either by looking through the emails or by contacting the study abroad advisors.
arrival_assistance: I was assigned a study abroad advisor who I could turn to for help.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: When applying for the university (in May), you have to make a list of the courses you would like (but this is only to give the university an idea of which courses you would like, it's not a final choice). You can read about most of the available courses on the online 'course finder'. The official registration process begins in July where you apply for the courses that you want through an application form. When a decision has been made, you receive an email from the university. If you do not get enrolled in the courses that you applied for, you have to make a new course application. If you want to make changes, it can be done either through a new application form or by sending an email to the visiting students office, depending on which college you belong to. You can change courses until week 2 of the semester.
registration_help: The visiting students offices at the University of Edinburgh were available and quite helpful. Also, the university has a website which can help you create an overview of the courses that you are interested in, to make sure the course schedules do not overlap.
registration_success: I got most of the courses that I registered for. However, I was a bit disappointed that some of the courses that I had found through the course finder were not available to me (as an exchange student) in the actual registration process.
registration_advice: Checking out the course catalogue when choosing your exchange destination is important. You should make sure there are a lot of different courses that you would be interested in taking and keep an open mind throughout the process, because the course catalogue may change, even shortly before semester start. At the University of Edinburgh, it is possible to change courses within the first two weeks of the semester. Also make sure to check out the schedule (if possible) to make sure the lectures don't overlap.
course_level: I took both 1st and 4th year courses, so the level naturally differed quite a lot. However, I think the reading and the subjects that we explored were generally on a high level, and the lecturers seemed very competent. Sometimes I found the discussions between students a bit disappointing compared to what I am used to, but that might have something to do with the age difference (generally undergraduates from other countries are younger than the Danish students).
teaching_comparison: The ratio between lectures and self-study was different. At UCPH I am used to having 20-25 hours of lectures/tutorials, while in Edinburgh I only had 8 hours weekly (but a larger amount of reading). The in-class teaching style and the student-lecturer relationship was similar in many ways. However, I experienced a larger focus on the students' learning process/experience (e.g., by asking the students to write 'reflective course diaries' which were part of the final assessments/exams). Furthermore, the autumn semester at Edinburgh is very short (only 11 weeks), which made it quite intensive. Sometimes it felt like there was not enough time to process the things we learned about.
courses_enrolled: A) Conservation Science (ECSC10036) B) Environmentalism: Past and Present (STIS08010) C) Sustainable Development 1a: Introducing Sustainable Development (SCIL08008)
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the courses, but for different reasons. Course B (2nd year course) and C (1st year course) had a broader academic approach and welcomed students from many different fields of study, which made it easy to participate as an "outsider" at your host university. Course A (a 4th year course) was more narrow and there were higher/more specific requirements for the students' academic background (it required some fundamental knowledge of ecology). The workload and level was higher on course A and B. To me, it was nice to have courses with different levels of ambition, but I guess it depends on how much you wish to delve into your studies vs. prioritize other things (social events, trips, etc.) on your exchange stay.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Groceries were cheaper than expected (tip: If you live nearby one of the bigger Sainsbury's, make sure to get a Nectar card - it's free and gives you some good discounts!). Coffee and beer prices were also cheaper than in Denmark. I was also happy to find out that all teaching materials were freely available online, so we were not required to buy any books.
activities_available: There were a lot of clubs to join, especially sports clubs. The university also has a gym (called Pleasance) with great facilities, and the membership fee is not too pricey (around 650 DKK for the whole semester). There were also various social events for Erasmus and other visiting students, especially in the welcome week.
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend joining the gym - it's a great opportunity to get some physical activity into your everyday. Plus the gym has a sauna, which is really nice on the cold and wet autumn days. I would also definitely recommend going to a ceilidh (traditional Scottish folk dance) at Stramash, it's a lot of fun and a nice way to experience some local culture. Another nice thing to know is that most museums in Edinburgh have free entrance.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the different areas of the city, and go on trips to see some of the beautiful Scottish highlands. I really enjoyed going on trips, including: - Day trips to Pentland Hills south of Edinburgh - Hiking to and sleeping in a bothy (we went to Over Phawhope Bothy). - Hiking some of West Highland Way - Car trip to Isle of Skye - Day trip to Pitlochry, including a hike to Ben Vrackie - Visiting some smaller Scottish towns, including Stirling and Oban
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy, the Scottish culture is not that different from the Danish.
socializing_tips: It can be hard to get to know locals, but I believe talking to people in classes and maybe at pubs is the best way to do it.
cultural_challenges: Nothing in particular. I was sometimes surprised that the cafes in Edinburgh close quite early compared to Denmark, but that wasn't exactly a challenge.
culture_appreciated: The pub culture is great - it is a more informal way of going out compared to Denmark, which makes it easier to do on an everyday. The pub atmosphere is really nice and cosy and it is a great place to hang out, whether you want to go for a coffee, a pint of beer, or some food.
top3_advice: 1) Make sure to go on trips into the highlands (and maybe plan a bit ahead, the semester is so short). 2) Be prepared to spend a lot of time on your studies, especially in the last part of the semester. You often have to write your midterms and final exams while you still have classes/lectures, which can be stressful. But try not to let it take up all of your time and energy in your last weeks there. 3) If you have the opportunity, I would recommend arriving a week or at least some days before the welcome week. It's nice to have some days to get settled in your accommodation, get a little familiar with your new area, and to start exploring the city before the semester starts.
other_useful_info: Make sure to check you university emails daily before and upon arrival - there is a lot of important information and things you have to do in the beginning. And contact your student advisor if you have questions.
most_rewarding: One thing that I really enjoyed about being on exchange was how it offered me the chance to have a different everyday life, with less plans and commitments than what I was used to. Naturally, I still had to spend a lot of time studying, but it was a nice sort of "break" from a busy life at home. At the same time, it also makes you realize and appreciate the things you miss at home. Other than that, I have really enjoyed the opportunity to go on trips and explore the beautiful Scottish nature. The trips are definitely some of the greatest experiences from my exchange stay.
greatest_challenge: Language was a surprisingly big challenge for me. Speaking English in informal everyday contexts is one thing, but academic English is challenging on another level. It was often a barrier for my participation in class, which was frustrating. However, my language skills also improved during the semester, which was a positive experience.

activities_recommended: Jeg ville helt sikkert anbefale at tilmelde sig en society eller to. Som regel mødes man en gang om ugen og laver en eller anden form for aktivitet, så det er en super god mulighed for at komme ud og lære andre studerende at kende.
weekend_recommendations: Tag ud og se byen og landet! Jeg købte et togkort i den tid, jeg var her, så jeg kan få billigere togbilletter - at være på udveksling giver en helt fantastisk mulighed for at lære landet bedre at kende, så jeg ville helt sikkert anbefale at tage ud så meget som muligt.
culture_adjustment: Danskere og Skotter er heldigvis relativt ens i deres tilgang til verden, så det var ret nemt at falde til.
socializing_tips: Societies er helt klart en god måde at mingle med de lokale studerende! Ellers er undervisningen og gruppearbejde en god måde at lære folk at kende på.
cultural_challenges: Edinburgh har en kæmpe andel af udvekslingsstuderende, så her er studerende fra alle dele af verden. Til tider kan det godt give kulturelle udfordringer - men ellers har der ikke været nogle problemer.
culture_appreciated: Skotterne er utroligt venlige og åbne mennesker. Og så er maden ret god.
top3_advice: 1) Vær åben overfor at lære folk at kende - deltag i et par societies og sørg for at komme ud og møde andre mennesker. 2) Tag udenfor Edinburgh! Skotland har en helt fantastisk natur, og et togkort kan hurtigt betale sig selv hjem mange gange. 3) Spørg om hjælp, hvis der er noget, du er i tvivl om. Univeristeterne i Storbritannien har ry for at være en smule selvophøjede, men alle underviserne og de administrative medarbejdere er virkelig søde og vil så gerne hjælpe, der hvor de kan.
other_useful_info: Husk at følge med i vigtige deadlines, både fra Københavns Universitet og UoE, og især i den første tid - der er en del at holde styr på!
most_rewarding: Det har helt sikkert været at møde en masse søde mennesker og få nye perspektiver på mit fag. Det har været helt fantastisk at opleve undervisning på en helt anden måde og med helt andre indgangsvinkler, end jeg har været vant til derhjemmefra.
greatest_challenge: For mig har det helt sikkert været at skulle balancere en masse ting på samme tid. Udvekslingsdeadlines, nye fag, nye mennesker, et nyt land - men det har 100% været det hele værd i sidste ende.

crucial_aspects: My crucial aspects were mainly interests in terms of my degree.
info_ease: Fairly easy. The visiting students office always made sure to send out information, thereby giving us a great and secure start to our exchange.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance by the visiting students office and the student association upon arrival. Many arrangements for settling in, getting to know my fellow exchange students, etc. were made for us. That helped immensely.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process consisted of uploading personal information to your student record, and then waiting for that approval. Thereafter attending a drop-in session to get fully matriculated.
registration_help: Help was available online, by emailing the visiting students office or attending their drop-in sessions.
registration_success: Not very successful due to a limited amount of courses available to visiting students, prerequisites and interests. However, the courses I did end up taking worked out for the better in the end.
registration_advice: To either call the relevant office or go there in person to seek answers. They are busy, and by email it might take days to obtain an answer. So it makes the process much more smooth. Regarding courses, to accept that you might not be able to enroll in the ones you hoped for, but that it can turn out useful and exciting regardless.
course_level: The level was high and they were well-organised. To be able to pass 60 credits (1 semester), one had to take three courses of 20 credits each. This is equivalent to 10 ECTS per course at UCPH, and in order to pass a semester there it has to be 30 ECTS. Just something to keep in mind, because the workload might be higher than at home (depending on the faculty and style of teaching of course).
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was quite different from UCPH. It consisted of two parts: the lectures and then the tutorials. The lectures was around 50 minutes long and consisted of different teachers explaining and introducing themes, working methods, etc. on the subject of the course. The tutorials was also around 50 minutes, but the purpose was to explore said theme or method more in depth, creating discussions and developing the skill set for the specific course. Some tutorials also discussed the readings from the lectures.
courses_enrolled: I took three courses: - History of Art 1B - Art at the Crossroads of World Cultures, 500-1700 AD - Ethnography: Theory and Practice - Drawing and Design Thinking
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of them for different reasons. The history of art course taught me about art from all over the world and how the discipline is in the midst of a decolonisation process. It made me realise some of our biases, our assumptions and how most of them can easily be put to shame. It made me able to further develop my ability to analyse and derive information and ideas of an art piece by the impact "close looking" have on it. The ethnography course taught me how much the studies of us as human in different scenarios makes our outlook on life change. How storytelling can affect the way we see different sets of people on a far greater scale than anticipated. Hereby also the possible problems with representation. The drawing and design course gave me a change to be creative in my studies, while still learning and seeing the way in which design and creating narratives help us change things in life, and how it is communicated to people. They all share a sense of realising a current bias in the way we view the world, and how it has changed and changes. They also share methods of analysis, problem solving and applying theory to practice in different ways.
unexpected_costs: Nothing.
cost_comparison: In general it is less expensive in the UK than in Denmark
activities_available: Various types of activities: social evenings, dances, badminton tournaments, hikes, museum trips, etc.
activities_recommended: I would recommend the social ones the most, because it is a great opportunity to meet people, both visiting students and permanent students. Some are free, some are not. So that is also something to keep in mind.
weekend_recommendations: Edinburgh is a very walkable city, so it is a great city to explore on foot (even though their public transport is very efficient around the city center). It has many great parts of town, so it is fun to see the different sides of it. Otherwise to take a train ride into the countryside. Many of my friends have done it and absolutely loved it.
culture_adjustment: Super easy, because people here are very friendly and very warm. The only slightly difficult thing was keeping in mind that they ride and drive on the left side of the road.
socializing_tips: It is very likely that you'll end up having shared courses with local students. Since the tutorials are in smaller groups I met many local students that way and through group projects.
cultural_challenges: Probably getting accustomed to speaking in a foreign language (English) most of the time, both academically and in my life outside of university.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciate the general sense of friendliness that the local culture consists of. The people are incredibly nice and talkative in a manner that makes one feel more at ease.
top3_advice: First of all to enjoy it fully, to keep an open mind and to accept the challenges because they will make you grow.
other_useful_info: Nothing I can think of.
most_rewarding: The friends I've made and the people I have met during my stay has been one of the most rewarding experiences while on exchange. Apart from that how many challenges and unforeseen circumstances I can actually handle.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was settling in, getting used to the way courses are taught and finding a routine.
other_comments: Noone I can think of

crucial_aspects: That the destination had a english speaking majority in order to make the socialisation easier.
overall_comments: I learnt a lot both academically and personally and wouldn't have been without the experience
info_ease: It was very simple, there was good information and communication from the university, and you could easily get in touch with the office and lecturers if you had questions
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any assistance when I arrived as it was not necessary
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I learnt a lot both academically and personally and wouldn't have been without the experience
registration_process: Courses were enrolled through the school's application portal with easy to follow templates and guides
registration_help: If you had trouble finding courses, you could write to your assigned advisor at school
registration_success: I got 2 out of 3 of my first priorities because one of the courses was full, but I'm happy with the courses I ended up with
registration_advice: Apply early to maximise your chances of getting the courses you want. And maybe take advantage of the fact that you can get 1st and 2nd semester courses approved, even if you're on your master's programme
academics_comments: I learnt a lot both academically and personally and wouldn't have been without the experience
course_level: I took 3rd and 4th year undergraduate courses, but some of the people I spoke to also got 2nd year courses approved
teaching_comparison: Classes are divided into smaller groups, for most of my courses there were around 40-50 people per class, so the teaching is more interactive and you are assessed on your active participation in class. But it's possible to do well in terms of active participation simply by participating in group discussions, you don't necessarily have to participate in plenary
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled in 1) Social and Political Movements, 2) Populism: pathology or panacea?, and 3) Party politics and the welfare state
recommended_courses: I can recommend all the courses, but I found the populism course particularly educational and relevant and not a course I have had the opportunity to take at UCPH
unexpected_costs: You should be aware that when you move in to your accomodation, everything is completely empty, meaning you have to buy your own pots, pans, plates, duvet, pillow etc.
cost_comparison: The prices are almost the same as in Denmark, but you save a little on beer and coffee, especially as a student, simce there are often student deals on beer :)
activities_available: There were a lot of societies available, there is definitely something for everyone!
activities_recommended: I was in the scandi society and a knitting society, which are highly recommended for socialising
weekend_recommendations: I went on several trips on weekends to visit some nice towns nearby. I went to Stirling, Glasgow and Newcastle, among others. I was also in London twice as it's only 4 hours by train. I can also only recommend going on a highland tour.
culture_adjustment: It was easy! I found the locals to be very friendly and the culture is very similar to Denmark
socializing_tips: I mostly talked to other exchange students, but if you want to socialise with local students, there are plenty of opportunities to do so in the classes of the courses you are enrolled in
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: I really liked their pub culture, it made it easy to socialise on weekdays as you weren't necessarily too late for school the next day
top3_advice: 1) Be open to all new experiences, even if it can be overwhelming at first 2) say yes to as much as possible, you'll regret it if you don't experience a lot 3) Prioritise the social over the academic! Take advantage of your grades being transferred as pass/fail
other_useful_info: Bring some personalised items to your room, it means a lot to feel at home and have some memories from home
most_rewarding: definitely the socialising and the community you get with other fellow students. It's a very special experience and something you'll never experience again. It's hard to explain to others, but you get to live in a bubble where you only have to relate to the few people who are also away on exchange, all the things that take time at home don't take up your time when you're away, neither work, family, or other obligations
greatest_challenge: I think the hardest part was missing home at first, but as time goes by, other things take over and you have to remember that everything is exactly as it was when you left when you get home... which is actually a bit difficult when you come home and feel like you've experienced a lot, while those around you don't understand how the last 5 months have offered a lot of experiences
other_comments: Prioritise keeping in touch with the friendships you've made through exchange! They are the only ones who can understand your experiences, thoughts and frustrations after you return home

crucial_aspects: I chose my destination based on which university offered interesting subjects in sociology. In addition, I had heard good things about exchange to Edinburgh from a fellow student and I wanted to go to a place that was not too far from Denmark, so that I could easily get visits from friends and family.
info_ease: Very easy - UoE sends a lot of e-mails. A little too many in my opinion.
arrival_assistance: I got assistance via e-mail. However, the system at UoE is very user friendly, so it was easy to find information. In addition, me and my friends that was also on exchanged helped each other out.
arrival_comments: UoE is very helpful and provides you with a lot of information. However, at times the e-mail flow was very overwhelming with a lot of e-mails about the same things being send over and over again. This led to a feeling of information overload.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration proces is very user friendly, as they use a website where you fill in your information.
registration_help: My coordinator at KU and e-mail assistance from UoE.
registration_success: Not very successful. I ended up with only one of the classes i originally applied for. However, UoE have two weeks where you can make course change request, so ended up with some other interesting courses.
registration_advice: Apply as soon as possiple. I was in the last round of applying, and I think I would have had less stressful time and end up with the courses i wanted if I applied earlier on.
course_level: The level is good for an exchange student that have to adjust to a new system, language and uniwork. However, the courses are very topic specific which can make it hard to align the courses and essays with your field of interest. Compared to my studies at KU I feel like I learn more during a semester at home, as we have more group work, longer assignments and work with more complex theories.
teaching_comparison: It was pretty much the same. We had lectures and self studies. However the semester is shorter and there is more individual work than group based work.
courses_enrolled: Social and Political Movements The Social Life of Food Crime and Detection in Literature
recommended_courses: Social and Political Movements Crime and Detection in Literature
unexpected_costs: I didn't know that I had to buy my own duvet, pillow and kitchen stuff to my accomodation.
cost_comparison: Food was less expensive, but you still end up using a lot of money going out as you want to socialise with the other students.
activities_available: A lot - UoE has a lot of societies so you can pick and choose from a large amount of different activities.
activities_recommended: Film society. Very cosy and a chill way to meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the highlands of Scotland – beautiful nature. And explore nearby cities by train. I went to Stirling, Linlithgow, Glasgow and Newcastle. Very cosy cities for day trips.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. People small talk more and are more polite in Scotland, but that is just a plus when you are new in town.
socializing_tips: Participate in the societies.
cultural_challenges: I found it easy to tap into the scottish culture as scots are very nice and polite. The challenging part for me was to live with other exchange student from very different cultures. Here were some differences in relation to how one is social and treats common areas.
culture_appreciated: The cosy pubs where everyone is welcome (even pets and kids) and the very polite and warm scottish people.
top3_advice: Apply for grants so you can afford a nice accomodation and life in general, commit to uniwork as it gives your everyday life structure and have fun in the city with fellow exchange students.
other_useful_info: Be prepared to do indvidual uniwork and write essays.
most_rewarding: I have gained the courage to throw myself into the academic world abroad and have proven to myself that I do not give up even though the process is extensive. Furthermore, it has been rewarding to meet new people and get the opportunity to explore another university and city with people who have the same enthusiasm to learn and try new things. On a personal level, I have generally become an even more independent person.
greatest_challenge: It was challenging to be away from my friends, family and boyfriend. However, you learn that they are all there when you return home and that Scotland is not that far from Denmark if you want someone to visit/come home for a visit yourself.

teaching_comparison: The style was in some way better - more student involvement - and in some ways worse - a lot less hours of teaching.

top3_advice: Enjoy the societies Enjoy the feedback on exams And eat all the pastries that you can
