crucial_aspects: Being relevant to my degree (English-speaking country), having a culture, history, and nature that interested me and being easy to get to.
overall_comments: Lots of unique experiences and new opportunities to explore a new culture and country and experience a new university, teaching methods, and different way of assessing work.
info_ease: It was fairly easy to find the information, but there was a lot of information to stay take in, which made it overwhelming.
arrival_assistance: E-mails from the university with exchange student events and I got assigned a specific person at the university I could write to with any questions relating to my exchange.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Lots of unique experiences and new opportunities to explore a new culture and country and experience a new university, teaching methods, and different way of assessing work.
registration_process: I do not remember it in details, but I just had to follow instructions I got through e-mails and fill out some personal information about myself and my study and write by course wishes.
registration_help: There were e-mails I could write to, though I did not do this.
registration_success: I was very lucky and got all of my first choices, however I know this is far from the case for everyone.
registration_advice: Just follow the instructions you are given and do it as soon as it is possible, to hopefylly register for the classes you want.
academics_comments: Lots of unique experiences and new opportunities to explore a new culture and country and experience a new university, teaching methods, and different way of assessing work.
course_level: I took on 1st year course and two courses that could be taken either on 3rd or 4th year.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was pretty similar with lecture-like classes and sometimes group-work. The tutorials were quite different though, with quite small classes (12-ish people) and a more assignment-like structure where we went through one problem or question either on the class or in smaller groups.
courses_enrolled: Sociolinguistics Scots and Scottish English Linguistics and the English Language 1A
recommended_courses: Sociolinguistics and Scots and Scottish English I really enjoyed, but I think it could have been fun taking a course focusing more on the history of Scotland/Edinburgh or a culture-study or something like that they only offer to exchange student i.e. then you know that it will probably be interesting for exchange students and a great way to meet other exchange students.
unexpected_costs: Having to buy everything I needed for the kitchen and bedding.
cost_comparison: I think the prices are similar to Denmark, maybe a little cheaper.
activities_available: Lots of sport clubs, social clubs etc., weekly parties, dances etc. really anything you could think of.
activities_recommended: Joining the Erasmus-activities, and going to a lot of things in the intro week.
weekend_recommendations: Isle of Skye, Glasgow, the turisty things in Edinburgh. There are a lot of groups tours specially for exchange students that you can book.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, it is not that different from Danish culture.
socializing_tips: It was a lot easier for me since I lived in student accommodation with other local students, but if you are up for it just try to speak with people in your lectures and tutorials!
cultural_challenges: How different written exams and assessment is here. Other cultural differences were more fun than challenging.
culture_appreciated: How welcoming everyone is and the many things to experience.
top3_advice: It is expensive to go on exchange so save for it, search for housing in good time, research as much as you can before you go so there are less stressful things to figure out when you get there.
other_useful_info: That the written exams are handwritten and that there is nothing in the kitchen if you get student accomodation.
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of new people, challenging myself and getting to experience so much of Scotland.
greatest_challenge: Having to do a lot of things by myself and not have my support network from home close by in hard times.

crucial_aspects: That they spoke english. And then what i thought of the courses, and how the university sounded when i researched them.
overall_comments: It was way more stressfull then anticipated, and one of the courses was too time consuming compared to what I got out of it. But it wasn't all bad, so overall a 6/10
info_ease: Easy enough. They send us a lot of information, not all of it relevant to me, so I had a bit to sort through, but much of the information was there. The rest I could email them about
arrival_assistance: I was assigned a student advisor who I had to have a meeting with early on. Which was great, as I could email him about anything I was unsure of.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was way more stressfull then anticipated, and one of the courses was too time consuming compared to what I got out of it. But it wasn't all bad, so overall a 6/10
registration_process: I remember, when applying to the university, instead of a letter of recommendation (or something else that wasn't needed for me to send in) i had to attach a word document with courses i wished to have ranked from 1-10, with the top 1 pick with a high likelyhood of being approved. And it was. I think it was my 1st, 3rd and 4th pick I ended up getting. I could at most add 10 courses, but I only added 6ish. Then on the portal/website, it would show up which courses I got, wether each of the courses I had wished for had been approved. And when they did I was set. I emailed them early august, as I hadn't gotten courses, and they answered quickly with a course. And then I was all set
registration_help: An email address. their website, and their course catalog.
registration_success: Pretty successfull. Only one I didn't get.
registration_advice: Contact the host institution if you feel they need to do something soon to move the process along, but of course dont be annoying about it. Like email them if your missing just one course. I probably waited longer than necessary to email, as they updated my courses right away.
academics_comments: It was way more stressfull then anticipated, and one of the courses was too time consuming compared to what I got out of it. But it wasn't all bad, so overall a 6/10
course_level: third year courses
teaching_comparison: I think I work better with the structure we have in UCPH. But thats because I work best when there is more external structure, which I feel there is more of at UCPH than UoE. In addition, UoE had fewer of what they call tutorials, which are equivalent to our "class session" i.e. classes with 20-30 people. Most weeks were only lectures and Lab. They had no set coursebook only recommended reading, a few mandatory articles for assesments, and the lab manuals to read. So unlike UCPH I did not have to buy a specific book. I just showed up to lectures, and if I needed to know more, I could look at there recommended reading, which was often research articles, which were free to read, or google and find the info there.
courses_enrolled: Molecular genetics 3, molecular microbiology 3, Structures and functions of proteins 3
recommended_courses: Molecular microbiology 3. I did not know much about microbiology before, but I thought it was a good course. the hard part was that I had to write an essay that was 30% of my grade. We got a list of possible topics, and the one I picked, I knew nothing about but now I'm really glad I picked it as I learned a lot of interesting things. Molecular genetics 3 as well, but thats because the structure of that course was more similar to the structure back home. And the lab session we did was amazing, at least to me.
unexpected_costs: I had to visit the dentist. Which I included in "personal spending". Memberships for society. All societies I looked at ranged from 5 pounds to 40. The sports ones tended to be more expensive I spend way more on food than I had planned. But I did go out to eat or order takeout way more than I normally would, so that's why. I ended up spending twice as much on food than my planned budget, but that was a choice I made.
cost_comparison: groceries. I expected it to be cheaper, as I always hear about Denmark being more expensive to live in compared to other countries, but I feel like my money spend on groceries and food (eating out at a resturant or similar not included) was comparable to back home. I had set money aside in my budget for school books, but there was none for me, All we read were research articles, and those are free through the insititute, if not just online.
activities_available: 100+ different societies, sports included. Theres everything from baking to badminton. Some based on activities, like hill walking, and others based on culture, like scandisociety, and then even more just aimed at international students
activities_recommended: Join a society. Good way to try something new, and meet people
weekend_recommendations: Remember to relax and recharge. There is so much to do, its easy to do too much.
culture_adjustment: A bit hard. But there was a lot of similarities
socializing_tips: Not really. UoE has so many international students, I mostly ended up hanging out with other international students.
cultural_challenges: They drive on the wrong side of the road. Nothing in particular stands out, but the whole "being in a different country alone, without people I know" was challenging.
culture_appreciated: The Ceilidh, which is the scottish folkdance. The friendliness
top3_advice: 1) Be aware what you need personally to make it a good stay. While you are there, how does your everyday look? does it work or does it need to change? are you focusing too much or too little on something? In that regards dont overstuff your calender, as it takes a lot of energy being in a different country, so you might not have the energy for all the new things and the old things. 2) the budget never works. Everyone i talked with ended up spending more than they had planned, so have some back up. But you could be better at budgeting then me, I might have been optimistic. 3) The things I enjoyed the most were the parts I was not expecting, so try something new you have no idea about, it might surprise you.
other_useful_info: Remember to take breaks. If you can, get there before the introweek. I got there 4 days before introweek, and that was not enough time to be settled, I feel, as the intro week is packed. But only as packed as you want, as nothing is mandatory (beside that one session on campus, thats either mandatory or just highly recommended to attend, as it has vital information)
most_rewarding: Molecular microbiology 3, I learned most in that course, and might influence the master program I wanna do. The societies, I tried out different things, as many of them have free events in the first week.
greatest_challenge: Managing my time. I should have spend more time looking at my energy levels, and not just the things I wanted to do.

crucial_aspects: English-speaking country as I'm studying English, close to Copenhagen and of cultural interest to me.
info_ease: Pretty easy, got a lot of emails.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance from the study abroad-team at my host university, they were super helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to go down and sign in physically, but it was easy. I booked a time slot and went down and got registered.
registration_help: I think all kinds of help was available if you needed it.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: just take it easy even though the amount of information can feel overwhelming. Just show up to what you have to and everything will be fine. Reach out to your guide if you need help with anything.
course_level: I think the level was fine and matched the level I'm used to from UCPH.

I found out that all the other lit students were taking a course on reading theory, which I was not - so that would have been nice to know, as I often felt that the seminars were more about what we thought of the novels personally rather than us discussing them in relation to relevant theory/criticism.
courses_enrolled: Mystery and Horror, Body in Literature, Edinburgh in Fiction.
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of the above, but I especially enjoyed mystery and horror. The instructor was great and the content was super interesting.
unexpected_costs: None really.
cost_comparison: Food is a bit less expensive than in DK. The same for restaurants and bars, which was really nice. Housing is definitely more expensive than in Copenhagen.
activities_available: So many. Erasmus had multiple parties, there were endless clubs/student societies - basically anything you could imagine, it was great.
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining the Sexpression club.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the isles! I went to the Isle of Skye and wish I could have gone again. Arran is accessible as well.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. People are so friendly and I loved the pub.culture, it's very much like in DK just a bit more chill.
socializing_tips: Move into a flat outside of campus. I got friends for life this way, and they were truly such a big part of my exchange and daily life. It would not have been the same without them.
cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and openness of the people in Edinburgh.
top3_advice: 1. Be open to new people and new experiences. 2. Hang out with your flatmates and let them show you around. 3. Remember to do the things you think of doing - go out to the restaurants, go to the bars, go to the museums (many of them are free). Go to Arthur's seat, the seven hills of Edinburgh, go to the Pentlands, itøs so accessible!
other_useful_info: no
most_rewarding: My new friends. I got to meet so many amazing people because I kept an open mind. I connected with people from all over the world, and I'm super thankful for my new friends. It was not at all as scary as I thought it would be to be alone in a new place.
greatest_challenge: Having to go home again... I wish I could have stayed for 6 months at least.

crucial_aspects: The destination. I considered doing my master's degree at this university, and this was a way to try it out.
info_ease: It was actually relatively easy, but there are often waiting times for responses, especially from the host university's administration. Therefore, it's crucial to remain calm, as many things only fall into place towards the end of the process.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance, and I did not feel that I needed it.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to fill out a lot of forms, which took a long time. But it's actually quite simple—you just need to make sure you have enough time for it.
registration_help: The University of Edinburgh has a very detailed guide on how everything should be filled out. They also held some online meetings where you could ask questions if there was anything you were unsure about.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted. It’s only relatively late in the process that you make your final course selections. At the University of Edinburgh, you can also change your courses after you arrive.
registration_advice: Find peace in the fact that many things only fall into place towards the end of the process. I have only encountered kind administrative staff at the University of Edinburgh, so just stay calm, they will help you if anything goes wrong.
course_level: I took courses equivalent to first- and second-year levels, even though I was in the final semester of my bachelor's degree. I was really happy with my courses and would recommend others to take what are called "Level 8" courses. I found that my workload was much lighter compared to other exchange students who took higher-level courses
teaching_comparison: At the University of Edinburgh, the learning approach is very self-study oriented. You spend a lot more time reading compared to the University of Copenhagen. In all three of my courses, there was a mix of lectures, which included everyone taking the course, and tutorials with around 15 people. However, lectures made up the majority of the teaching.
courses_enrolled: Trauma in Society - CNST08002 Popular Religion, Women and Witchcraft in Early Modern Europe - DIVI08013 Scottish Studies 1A: Conceptualising Scotland - SCET08006
recommended_courses: I chose three courses from three different faculties, selecting them mainly based on subjects I knew I wouldn’t be able to study in Denmark. I would particularly recommend the course "Trauma in Society - CNST08002" at the University of Edinburgh if you're interested in psychology, neurobiology, and therapy.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Food costs are roughly the same as in Copenhagen. However, beer is really cheap—just remember to bring your student card when going out!
activities_available: There’s a club for everything! The University of Edinburgh has a very detailed program where you can visit all the clubs during the first week before classes start.
activities_recommended: Go to "Stramash" and take part in the Scottish dance ceilidh! It's a fun experience, and a great way to dive into Scottish culture!
weekend_recommendations: Take trips to the Highlands! I booked a guided tour to the Isle of Skye in the Highlands with other exchange students through the company "MacBackpackers". It was an amazing experience and a great way to explore the beautiful Scottish landscape
culture_adjustment: It's really easy. Scottish culture is similar to Danish culture in many ways. Plus, there's a large international community in Edinburgh, so there's a place for everyone.
socializing_tips: The Scots are easy to talk to, so don't be afraid to strike up a conversation
cultural_challenges: I did not find any differences challenging
culture_appreciated: I really appreciate the relaxed, easy-going, and helpful culture in Scotland.
top3_advice: 1: Don’t live further than 30 minutes from campus. I walked every day from campus to my accommodation, and I really appreciated how easy it was to get around Edinburgh on foot, especially on weekends. Having everything within a 30-minute radius is something I miss most about Edinburgh. 2. Ask a local student to grab a coffee after class. I never did this in Denmark, but in Scotland, I did it often and made some really great connections. As an exchange student, it’s easy to end up hanging out mostly with people from your home university, but connecting with locals can really enrich your experience. 3. Plan weekend trips to the Highlands or Glasgow. You’ll likely spend most of your time in Edinburgh, so make sure to plan a weekend or two to explore the Highlands or visit Glasgow! It’s a great way to see more of Scotland and make the most of your exchange.
other_useful_info: Create a Facebook Messenger group with the others who are also going. In our chat, we could keep track of deadlines and other practical information we had received. We also shared frustrations and gave each other good advice. We all met up once we arrived in the city, and I ended up getting a large part of my social life from that group.
most_rewarding: At first, it was difficult because everything was in English. Sometimes I felt like I couldn’t express myself as precisely as I wanted to. But you get used to speaking English on a daily basis, and eventually, you don’t even think about whether what you're saying sounds strange, like you might do in the beginning.
greatest_challenge: That everything was in English.
other_comments: Just do it. It is a life changing experience.

crucial_aspects: Culture and place. I didn’t want to be too far away from home but I did want to experience another culture.
info_ease: Not too difficult but also not that easy. A lot of us exchange students were extremely confused and the administration system at the University of Edinburgh is a bit of a mess
arrival_assistance: I got a lot of letters and was a part of a Facebook group for exchange students
arrival_comments: It’s very confusing and everything was kind of scattered across the different university buildings and it is easy to get lost in Edinburgh
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Oof. I can barely remember. There are a lot of link and pamphlets etc that you get once you’ve been accepted, so you just have to click on them and then that should lead you to what you need.
registration_help: Pamphlets, Facebook Groups and e-mails
registration_success: Very! I got the classes I wanted, though the archaeology class I got was not my first choice but I still enjoyed it very much and I can highly recommend Introduction to Gaelic language and culture as well as Celtic Civilisations 1A (both belong to the school of linguistics). You learn a lot about Scotland as well as its place in the world
registration_advice: Patience and deep breaths. A lot of coffee
course_level: I had two first year courses and one third year course. There was a clear difference between them but that weren’t that difficult. Though be prepared for the amount of assignments and quizzes etc. at the start it was really intense because of the speed in which the classes were going. You get a lot of knowledge in 1-2 hours and they are speaking very fast.
teaching_comparison: Hmm. It was a lot of seminars and lectures, every Friday we had workshops in smaller group were we discussed topics. A lot like KU.
courses_enrolled: Bronze Age Civilisations in the Near East and Greece Introduction to Gaelic Language and Culture Celtic Civilisations 1A
recommended_courses: Definitely the Celtic and Gaelic ones! They were amazing and so exciting especially because you learn a lot about Scotland’s culture, history and traditions.
unexpected_costs: I didn’t have any unexpected costs other than me being an impulsive buyer and had to buy an extra suitcase for my flight home.
cost_comparison: Food is surprisingly cheap, as well as Books and public transportation (which I only used a couple of times). A lot of the museums are free but the tourist attractions such as Mary King’s Close and Edinburgh castle are expensive.
activities_available: There were Pub Crawls, Karaoke Nights, Ceilidhs and a lot of trips for Exchange students
activities_recommended: I think I most enjoyed walking around Old Town as well as Edinburgh’s Christmas Market, they are both free (except for all the stuff you can buy in the stores) and it is the best way to experience the culture.
weekend_recommendations: Exploring the city! Hiking Arthur’s Seat, seeing Carlton Hill, and I would suggest joining a University Community such as The Occult Club (it’s a vibe). I’d also suggest getting a tattoo (I did!).
culture_adjustment: Easy. In the end it’s a European citadel it’s not that different except for the Pipers stationed in Old Town.
socializing_tips: The week before semester start is a golden opportunity otherwise don’t be afraid to talk to people in class, they tend to be really nice.
cultural_challenges: Nothing.
culture_appreciated: The Bagpiping and the Gaelic language it’s uniquely ‘Scottish’ and it’s amazing.
top3_advice: 1. Choose a course based on what you find interesting (does not necessarily have to do anything with you actual class/education) 2. Take the bus from the airport when you arrive, it’s not too expensive. 3. Just enjoy it! Do what you think sounds fun and interesting! Don’t worry too much about the grades (as long as you pass the class nothing else matter).
other_useful_info: It’s your trip, what is my experience does not have to be yours. Do what you feel is right.
most_rewarding: The trip itself was so rewarding and just knowing that you can do this on your own is such a rewarding accomplishment.
greatest_challenge: My anxiety can give me difficulties with social interaction, and the amount of people in Edinburgh can be a bit overwhelming.
other_comments: You, as a pedestrian, are allowed to cross the road even if the light is red.. people can actually get a bit annoyed if you don’t…

crucial_aspects: I had heard great things about UoE, both academically and Edinburgh as a city of both study opportunities and history. So, I wanted to be part of both the university and of the life of the city.
overall_comments: No additional comments.
info_ease: Quite easy. Once I got the hang of it, it was straight forward.
arrival_assistance: I didn't need anything, to my knowledge.
arrival_comments: No additional comments.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: No additional comments.
registration_process: I had to go to the arrival centre and check in with my passport. Then I had to check in again at uni. And then that was that. Pretty easy.
registration_help: There were signs all over campus, guiding me to the correct rooms.
registration_success: Very much so. I got my top three picks.
registration_advice: Make sure to book your accommodation in good time.
academics_comments: No additional comments.
course_level: I took all electives, so it was quite a nice semester - I got to study all the things I found interesting.
teaching_comparison: It was very similar, though the seminars were an hour shorter at UoE, so we didn't go as much into depth with the readings as be do at home. But the faculty, and their methods of teaching, were quite similar.
courses_enrolled: The Making of Modern Fantasy Reading Science Fiction Haunted Imaginations: Scotland and the Supernatural
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of them, they were absolutely amazing.
unexpected_costs: Not any, but the housing was definitely more expensive than I had thought it would be. I paid over double of what I pay at home.
cost_comparison: Housing, definitely was more expensive. Books, though, are much cheaper.
activities_available: There are many clubs available for students to join.
activities_recommended: I didn't enrol in any non-academic activities. But definitely go to the Highlands, the cafés, the book stores. Edinburgh, and Scotland as a whole, has a lot to offer.
weekend_recommendations: The Highlands! And the other cities, like Glasgow and St. Andrews.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Make friends in your classes.
cultural_challenges: None. Scotland and Denmark are quite similar.
culture_appreciated: The sound of bagpipes wherever you go. Seriously.
top3_advice: Beware of the cost of housing. The semester is way shorter than at UCPH. If you're doing literature, be prepared to read at least three books per week.
other_useful_info: I think I've said it.
most_rewarding: Getting to live in Edinburgh and experience the city as a local (kind of, anyway).
greatest_challenge: Having enough money to live after housing was paid.
other_comments: No additional comments.

crucial_aspects: The breadth of academic opportunities. I knew UoE would have a plethora of interesting English Lit courses and I was not dissapointed!
overall_comments: When prioritising courses, choose something you maybe wouldn't otherwise have tried! At UoE you do three courses (at least in my case) and getting to immerse yourself in something novel is so worth it.
info_ease: The information itself was accesible, the amount is just, unsurprisingly, overwhelming. Prepare and familiarise yourself with the different platforms and you'll be fine.
arrival_assistance: The Visiting Students Office at UoE helped me with some of the initial processes
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: When prioritising courses, choose something you maybe wouldn't otherwise have tried! At UoE you do three courses (at least in my case) and getting to immerse yourself in something novel is so worth it.
registration_process: The UoE course registration process was confusing at first, as the availability of courses on the registration page did not reflect the actual availibility. I got in contact with the Study Abroad office and was luckily assured of the availibility. There is plenty of detailed information on the courses themselves which helped a lot.
registration_help: The Study Abroad office
registration_success: I got two of my top five courses. The third was not a priority of mine, but I ended up loving it!
registration_advice: Try something you wouldn't have at your home institution!
academics_comments: When prioritising courses, choose something you maybe wouldn't otherwise have tried! At UoE you do three courses (at least in my case) and getting to immerse yourself in something novel is so worth it.
course_level: Due to the difference in BA programme lenghts in Denmark and the UK, I was only able to take 3rd year courses. Because of this, the expectatons in the 3rd year courses felt more like 2nd year courses to me personally.
teaching_comparison: Overall, the same level of congeniality and openness as I have come to appreciate at UCPH were present at UoE. The professors were invested in the students opinions and in many instances, the seminar's direction were led by the students.
courses_enrolled: Early Modern Comedy, Shakespeare: Modes and Genres, and The Making of Modern Fantasy.
recommended_courses: All of the above! The Shakespeare course demands a bit of prior interest, of course.
unexpected_costs: Not many unexpected costs, personally. The travel insurance, but I fixed that before leaving. It is worth to prepare yourself for the cost of food and grocery items.
cost_comparison: I personally couldn't take advantage of this, but many of my friends got the Young Scots card (available for under 21s) which gave them mostly free public transport!
activities_available: Too many to count. The UoE societies are truly astounding, and of these many are completely free!
activities_recommended: Dancing classes, walking groups, book societies!
weekend_recommendations: Go to the highlands! ESN does guided weekend trips all over the highlands, really worth it. Bus-travel (FlixBus etc) is the best travel method in my opinion, both due to cost and scenery on the way.
culture_adjustment: Incredibly easy. The scottish people are so wonderfully welcoming and I never felt alone or unwanted.
socializing_tips: Go to welcome events, make plans, go on trips together, study together, sign up for non-academic classes together!
cultural_challenges: Literally only understanding the Glaswegian accent.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and openness. The amount of celtic and gaelic cultural remnants and traditions still upheld by the locals.
top3_advice: Explore the city as much as you can Visit the highlands and hike if possible Make friends with both locals and other exchange students
other_useful_info: Pack less than you think you will need, really only the necessities. In my case, I acquired 45 books for a criminally low price and making room for that in my luggage will be interesting.
most_rewarding: Meeting my new group of friends from all over the world. I know that this group will last beyond this exchange and I am eternally grateful.
greatest_challenge: Making time for all the stuff I wanted to do.
other_comments: Prepare yourself for different kinds of examination/essay writing expectation (at least in the case of English lit). For instance, at UoE, being able to present close-readings of several texts within a narrow wordcount is the key, rather than a single (or comparative) close-reading.

crucial_aspects: The academic level at the University of Edinburgh. The student environment in Edinburgh. English-speaking country.
info_ease: Quite easy. Obviously a lot of new information at the beginning. But I think the guidance from my home institution and my host institution was great.
arrival_assistance: Not really any assistance. A few mails with basic information from the visiting student center.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You just simply had to list up the courses you would like to follow throughout the semester in a prioritized order.
registration_help: Not really any help. But it was quite easy to figure out yourself.
registration_success: Pretty successful.
registration_advice: Do the registration the minute you receive the registration link. The courses are filled up super fast.
course_level: First and second year courses were on a quite low level. However, the third and fourth year courses were quite complicated and on a high academic level. Lots of reading as well.
teaching_comparison: More lectures and less seminars.
courses_enrolled: Scottish Legal System International Law Courtroom Rhetoric and Legal Doctrine
recommended_courses: If you go to Edinburgh as an exchange student, I would definitely recommend Scottish Legal System, as the course gives you a basic understanding of how the legal system in Scotland and the UK works.
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: In general, living in Edinburgh is very expensive. Especially housing. But food and beers are not cheap either.
activities_available: So many different opportunities. Over 300 societies.
activities_recommended: The hill walking society.
weekend_recommendations: Go hiking in the Scottish Highlands.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. In many ways, Scotland is not too different from Denmark.
socializing_tips: Participate in all the social activities in the beginning of the semester. That is when friendships are made.
cultural_challenges: Nothing.
culture_appreciated: The UK pub culture.
top3_advice: Edinburgh is a very expensive city to live in, so remember to save up quite a bit of money before going. Go explore the Scottish Highlands at least 4-5 weekends throughout the semester. Sign up for courses the minute you receive the registration link.
other_useful_info: Have lunch at the mosque kitchen right next to Old College. Super delicious food.
most_rewarding: New friendships.
greatest_challenge: Finding a place to stay at the very beginning. Spent the first ten days in a hostel.

crucial_aspects: The country and environment was very important to me, and Scotland was the perfect fit in that regard.
info_ease: It was pretty easy, they are very helpful and experienced when helping exchange student as they have many visiting student at the University of Edinburgh.
arrival_assistance: I went to talk to the visiting student office, and I wrote emails back and forth with the office as well to get answers to my questions.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was a bit complicated with all the paperwork necessary, but that is to be expected.
registration_help: The visiting student office was very helpful and answered the questions I asked, and provided advice when needed.
registration_success: I was not very succesful with my classes, I had apparently given them the course list incorrectly, and I therefore did not get the classes I wanted, but I ended up enjoying my classes anyway.
registration_advice: Make sure to reach out and ask if they have received all the paperwork needed, to make sure that everything goes as plan.
course_level: I took two third year courses and a single second year course as was adviced my the visiting office. This helped a lot with settling in, but also later when writing the exam as it was somewhat easier.
teaching_comparison: It was very different, and I needed to adjust to the new style, and sometimes it worked well, but other times it was difficult to do everything required in the course. I still prefer the teaching at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Shakespeare: Modes and Genre Contemporary Cinema American Innocence
recommended_courses: I enjoyed all three of my courses, but especially American Innocence, it was the course I wanted the least, but the course I enjoyed the most.
unexpected_costs: I sometimes had to pay for films for my course, but other than that, everything was pretty much expected.
cost_comparison: The housing was insanely expensive, and it shocked me just how expensive it was.
activities_available: There were many different options, everything from salsa dancing to film club to swimming societies. There are plenty of opportunities.
activities_recommended: I did not join any societies, but I was interested in joining the film soc, and a gaming club.
weekend_recommendations: Go and see other parts of Scotland than Edinburgh, such as Glasgow, Aberdeen and the Highlands.
culture_adjustment: It was easy, I like the culture and the people, so it was not challenging to adjust.
socializing_tips: Find common interests.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Their kindness, it was refreshing coming from Copenhagen where people can be a bit cold.
top3_advice: Be open-minded. Face challenges head-on. Ask for help when you need it.
other_useful_info: Prepare to be challenged, but also relax, you are all in the same boat.
most_rewarding: Getting to attend my dream university.
greatest_challenge: The academic work, it was challenging trying to find the right rhythm.

crucial_aspects: Language spoken at institution, cultural richness of country, opportunities to explore nature, course selection
info_ease: It was okay; we were just spammed with tonnes of information from Edinburgh University, which did make things rather complicated at times; overall, however, information could be located and used in due time
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any specific assistance upon my arrival to Edinburgh; we received, again, multiple e-mails from the university, especially regarding immigration/ check-in, which was rather nice.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I just had to fill out an online form with my priorities and send it as quickly as possible, as courses are granted on a first come first serve basis. This was a bit stressful, however, it was very quick and easy to fill in.
registration_help: We were able to turn to our student advisors on the CAHSS faculty. They were really helpfull towards us exchange students who did not know anything about the procedures at Edinburgh. Furthermore, when I arrived, they also really helped me with changing some of my courses.
registration_success: I was really successful; I got enrolled in 2 out of my 3 top priorities.
registration_advice: Please just be really quick to register your course wishes, when you receive an email stating that you can now enroll in courses for the semester. This way, you will be very likely to receive your preferred courses.
course_level: The courses were rather okay; I did also choose some first-year courses, which of course were in some ways easier to follow; however, I still found some of the topics complicated and therefore really interesting to follow.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at Edinburgh is quite similar to UCPH; we had a lot of lectures combined with seminars/ tutorials. However, I was not used to being assigned to such small classes; tutorials are special classes with only 5-10 students per class and 1 tutor, which was very new to me. However, it gave a really relaxed and informal learning environment that I really appreciated.
courses_enrolled: 1) The Scottish Legal System 2) International law – ordinary 3) Innovations from Global South Actors
recommended_courses: I would recommend Scottish Legal System to all future law exchange students; It was a rather complicated and large course, however, you really get to explore and learn about a quite unique legal system and you learn to read cases from common law systems, which I found really interesting to learn.
unexpected_costs: I was not surprised by any specific costs
cost_comparison: Eating out/ going to pubs is not as cheap as other countries
activities_available: tonnes of student societies from everything to rugby, wine club, debate Harry Potter etc., tutoring, lots of international student events.
activities_recommended: join some societies; these are great ways to meet new people, and you will be able to find at least one you like in the ocean of opportunities :))
weekend_recommendations: Go explore Edinburgh city! Explore the highlands of Scotland! I want to go back next summer and explore even more of the highlands and Scottish isles; there is so much to see and do!
culture_adjustment: It was really easy! the culture is very alike that in Denmark, and I really did not find any massive culture shocks at all
socializing_tips: please just talk to students in your tutorial groups or societies; everyone is just trying to have fun and meet new people.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any particular challenging cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: I loved the pub culture! It was an amazing way to just chat and have fun with tonnes of different people.
top3_advice: 1) please start looking for housing early! 2) I would recommend arriving to Edinburgh 2 weeks before terms starts as a gateway for you to get familiar with the city and maybe start some exploring! 3) don't be afraid to ask questions; we were all very confused when we arrived, however, there are a lot of people both at ECPH and UoE who will do anything in their power to help you settle in on your exchange.
other_useful_info: no
most_rewarding: meeting new people and traveling in a different way!
greatest_challenge: trying to make a home of an entire new city in a country I had never visited before, where I did not know anybody. However, Edinburgh did become my home, and I really miss it already!

crucial_aspects: It was crucial to my choice of destination, that there would be a mixture of good social opportunities and academic opportunities, where I could at the same time explore new cultural aspects first hand. Edinburgh was the perfect balance, where I had heard of other peoples' good experiences both with the university's social life and the city and area surrounding it.
info_ease: It was relatively easy to find most information. The only thing to look out for is that there is a lot of information to check out beforehand.
arrival_assistance: After arriving at the destination the university was very helpful, as one could show up at their office and gain assistance in anything from questions about the studies to changing courses etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration was mostly straight forward, the only exception being that not all processes that we were asked to do was required for exchange students. This included English proficiency tests under certain circumstances.
registration_help: There was in general a lot of information available on both KU's and Edinburgh's university page, and you could probably also call the University of Edinburgh's offices during their opening hours to get further assistance.
registration_success: I was not very successful in getting the classes that I actually wanted, as it was given on a first-come-first-serve basis, and there was only 1-5 free spots per course by the time we as exchange students were offered any subjects. I therefore ended up with my 14th and 15th priority for example, but this turned out to be a positive surprise in the end.
registration_advice: I would recommend to not stress too much about which subjects you end up with initially. This is because you can change courses up to a month into the semester according to the guidelines when I was there. I could therefore change the subjects which I did not want. I also know many others who changed courses to have more 1st-year courses as they were seemingly easier than 3rd- and 4th-year courses.
course_level: The level of the courses vary a lot, as some courses can be viewed as easier, whereas others can seem very burdening in contrast. There is not any absolute rule to the difference of level of the courses, other than the general trend of 1st-year courses being easier than later courses most often.
teaching_comparison: You have to be prepared for the teaching style to be quite different, as the courses are often either exclusively seminar-based or a mix of lectures and tutorials, which are shorter meetings in small groups.
courses_enrolled: LAWS10252 - Street Law: public legal education in the community LAWS10262 - International Human Rights in the Digital Era LAWS08114 - International Law Ordinary (semester 1)
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the following courses that I was enrolled in: LAWS10252 - Street Law: public legal education in the community LAWS10262 - International Human Rights in the Digital Era LAWS08114 - International Law Ordinary (semester 1) I would recommend these cases as they were of differing work loads, and gave a broad insight into different fields of law, and offered very different teaching styles.
unexpected_costs: There was not really any unexpected costs experienced, however it should be noted that costs add up and many small visits can suddenly have quite a cost.
cost_comparison: Food was in general more expensive than expected, as you need to know the right places to eat at, as the base-cost of most places are very similar, and only few places offer similar experiences at much lower prices.
activities_available: There was a plethora of sports and various social groups, like film and hot chocolate groups, to participate in, which I know many students were happy with. It can be a bit more difficult to interact with these as exchange students given that less people want to interact much with people they know will be gone just three months later or so.
activities_recommended: I would recommend to participate in any that you find interresting. It is mostly just about going in with an open mind, and then you will meet nice people and have plenty of fun for sure.
weekend_recommendations: I would definately recommend to read through the long list of student societies, as there are so many that you can find social groups no matter what your interests or hobbies are.
culture_adjustment: It was relatively easy to adjust culturally to being in Edinburgh. The only thing that could be challenging to some, is that the food is very different to what we are used to in Denmark. However, this shouldn't be a big issue at all, and you may even find new habits in the city that you don't have at home.
socializing_tips: It can be recommended to be in a university-led accommodation, as you can meet many students this way even if you don't participate much in the student led societies.
cultural_challenges: The one I personally found most challenging was to adapt to the food available, however this was no major issue.
culture_appreciated: I most appreciated the social aspects of the culture as people were in general very friendly and helpful. There was furthermore also always opportunities for a good party with friends, where you could also meet new people.
top3_advice: The most important things I would say would be ahead of time with looking for accommodation, both private and university accommodation, as this will reduce stress ahead of your arrival, I would also recommend to do join as many social activities and societies as you can, so you can figure out which ones you like and in general meet many new people. Last I would recommend not to worry too much about which subjects to get initially as these can be changed later, as spots become available as other students change subjects and as you figure out what you actually like. And in general - be open minded!
other_useful_info: I would also recommend to have some extra savings when you go to Edinburgh, as there are many opportunities to travel around in Scotland and the broader UK. Having a good budget for travels to cities and nature can only be highly recommended.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of the experience was to go to somewhere completely new and meet many new people and face the challenges of studying abroad in a new state and culture.
greatest_challenge: There wasn't many big challenges, but the largest one was probably the balance between not falling behind on studies, whilst trying to keep up with as many social activities as possible, as lots were available.

crucial_aspects: I've always wanted to visit Edinburgh. The culture and the landscape of Scotland were my main reasons, as well as the fact that the language wouldn't be a problem.
info_ease: At arrival, easy enough - before going, very difficult!!
arrival_assistance: Not a lot, but I didn't need it.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: International check in with pre-booked time slots at campus. Very easy.
registration_help: Volunteers.
registration_success: Very successful, but that was only because of help from the contact person in Copenhagen - she basically did it for me after I hadn't received ANY information from the host information a month before arrival.
registration_advice: Be patient.
course_level: Postgraduate level courses.
teaching_comparison: Much more discussion and participation-based teaching.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to experience the univeristy culture in the UK, especially with the many student networks and societies they have.
info_ease: I think it has been quite easy to find the information that I needed, and I always knew who to get in touch with if I had questions related to either study or accomondation.
arrival_assistance: I haven't reveived any assitance at my arrival but I had a check in with my student advisor during the semester which was really helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I had to schedule an appointment for international check in and drop by the visiting student office to check in there as well. The registration was pretty easy, you just have to be aware that there are to separate check ins. With the courses I just applied for them online and it was really easy to make changes to your course list too.
registration_help: You can always ask your visiting student advisor and they usually get back to you very quickly.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Look at the description of the courses and the type of exam they have too. Personally, I had three courses that were all year 3 or 4, and while I was for the most part happy with my courses, it would have been nice to have a course with a bit lower expectations/work load. Maybe just consider the balance between study work load and activities you want to do in your free time.
course_level: I had two year 3 couses and one year 4 course.
teaching_comparison: I think the style of teaching was more enganging and based on discussions, epecially the tutorials. It was very rare that the teachers would run through an article but instead they would situate the theories within a broader context and use the articles to facilitate a discussion on a certain topic.
courses_enrolled: I took 'Culture and Power,' 'Spectacles and Crowds: anthropology through publics' and 'The Internet and Society.'
recommended_courses: I think spectacles and crowds was my favorite course because it was really engaging and very interesting theories. We had group presentations every week, which on one hand was a lot but on the other the amount of reading was less compared to my other courses which was really nice. I think culture and power was interesting too as it deals with extremely relevant political issues.
unexpected_costs: I didn't really encounter unexpected costs, but when I moved in I had to buy a few new things which added up in the end.
cost_comparison: Eating out and going to cafés is less expensive than in Denmark I would say, and housing was definetly more expensive than I thought it would be!
activities_available: A lot of different things. You can play a variety of sports through the uni's sports union, there are a lot of societies and networks to be a part of as well and they host almost weekly socials for everyone.
activities_recommended: I tried a few different societies' events and joined the mountaineering clubs' weekly bouldering session which was super fun and a good way of meeting new people. I also went on an erasmus week-end trip to Isle of Skye which I totally would recommend. The nature was so beautiful and I met some really sweet people on the trip.
weekend_recommendations: I would reccommend to go on a trip to the highlands or just explore the many cute areas of the city. I went a few places, but think the best were Glenfinnan (the Harry Potter bridge:)) and Isle of Skye were my favorite. In Edinburgh, I can recommend Stockbridge, Portobello beach, Leith and ofc Old Town!
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
cultural_challenges: I don't think the cultural differences were that challenging, but I find it really inspiring how Scotland has preserved a strong cultural identity.
culture_appreciated: People were always very open and kind which I love
top3_advice: Firstly, I think the university of Edinburgh has a lot of interesting courses and really good teachers who focus on engaging the students. Seconldy, the semester is quite short and the university's exam period is a bit more pressed than back home, so try to prioritize your studying and don't be afraid to reach out to your student advisor. Thirdly, the teaching style might be different from what you are used to, but I really enjoyed the opportunity of learing and studying in a another way.
other_useful_info: I think it is important to consider your courses and the level of them well. I chose a course outside my field and the course itself ended up being very confusing. If I were to do this again, I think I would choose maybe just one course that seemed a little 'easier' to give more room for fun activities and other things beside uni stuff.
most_rewarding: I would say meeting new people and other international students. Sharing such a big experience and making a lot of memories together just makes a really special bond which I am very grateful for.
greatest_challenge: Probably having time to do all of the things that I wanted to. I think uni can easily take up a lot of time but that it is also so important to connect with new people and try new things while being abroad!

cultural_challenges: They speak english very well and sometimes with a accent.
culture_appreciated: Pub culture, friendly in public spaces.

other_useful_info: If you want student accomondation you have to call them everyday in the last month, and the you might get some thing as close to one week before. If you want to find private housing SpareRoom was helpfull.

crucial_aspects: That they speak English so I could understand the locals. That the city seemed nice, and that there was a nice selection of courses.
info_ease: It was a bit difficult at times, but I think the people at KU-Abroad was very helpful!
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any really, I didn't need it:)
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The courses I applied for weren't available, and then when we had to like apply a second time after we've been accepted the full course list wasn't available either so I just signed up for something and then I was just appointed to some courses that were at the bottom of my list, but then I could just apply for them to be changed when the course list was updated, but that wasn't until maybe the middle of august. But really nice that you can change course during the first two weeks of classes, I changed one of my courses in the first week and that was also really easy.
registration_help: There was a website that explained how to do it, and other than that I just emailed the uni a few times, and they were always quick to respond.
registration_success: In the end I got them, but it took some patience in waiting for the course list to be updated. Even though there were some courses I really wanted that weren't available at my semester, which was really a bummer, there were some new courses that were cool.
registration_advice: Don't stress out about the courses that you apply with, they are probably a bit different when you have to sign up for them later, but there will probably still be some nice courses when the time comes.
course_level: I took one year 2 course, one year 3 course and one year 4 course.
teaching_comparison: The lectures were quite similar. The tutorials is not something I've tried before, but it was really nice. We were around 6-12 people each time in my tutorials and then we just talked with a TA about the week's readings and themes, they were quite intense sometimes, especially when we weren't that many and the TA expects you to talk, but they didn't say anything if you said you didn't have anything to add, at least in my tutorials.
courses_enrolled: Gender in the contemporary world, anthropology of displacement and migration, culture and power
recommended_courses: Anthropology of displacement and migration!!!! It was so good, and the professor Lucy Lowe is a great teacher!
unexpected_costs: Not really anything I can think of
cost_comparison: The food shops are quite similar in price as Denmark, the bus is way cheaper than I thought, like 1-2£ for where ever you wanted to go.
activities_available: There are so many clubs and societies it's crazy! There's a crochet and knit society, a winter swimming society, and a society that just go around testing chips in Edinburgh! And then a lot of sports, but they are a bit more clubs, at least some of them, where there's try outs and everything, not like KU-studenteridræt.
activities_recommended: Definitely all of the erasmus stuff and the international events that the uni throws, it's a great way to meet other international people.
weekend_recommendations: The highlands! It's sooo beautiful! In Edinburgh you should just explore the city and go out where there aren't that many tourists and students, like out in Leith and down Easter Road, or Bruntsfield also really nice! And try get the train to Glasgow, it's a really cool city and very different from Edinburgh, but the people are really nice!
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it felt very normal very quick. The fact that I can speak the same language as everyone is very nice, and it's just such a cosy city.
socializing_tips: No not really, I didn't really talk with a lot of local people, mostly international people. I think if I would have been more involved in some of the societies I probably would have talked more with some local students.
cultural_challenges: I can't really think of anything major. In the quiet areas of the library a lot of people still talk, a bit annoying, but that's it.
culture_appreciated: I really like how all of the professors use microphones and give out microphones to the students when they have a question, that's really nice! Uhh and at cafés they really like cake, like not just all of the fancy pastries from the copenhagen bakeries, this is caaake, and it's really good. Generally people are very different and you see a lot of different ways to dress and act, and think that's really cool, compared to how Copenhagen sometimes can be a bit pretentious and take itself very serious, Edinburgh doesn't really do that, in a very nice way.
top3_advice: The rent is really expensive! The city is really nice! The course list is really unreliable.
other_useful_info: Even if you think you're english is good, some of the accents of the professors and TA's can be a bit challenging, but even the native speakers think that so.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people:)
greatest_challenge: maybe the fact they you don't really get "læseferie" and they have midterms in the middle of the semester while you still have your courses to read for, so you don't have time to read in the middle of the semester and then a month later there's finals and because you haven't had time to read you have to read for your final while you also have courses.... But they have extensions where you can get 4-ish days extra to do your essays, so that's nice!

socializing_tips: Join societies - otherwise it's impossible.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find anything challenging,
culture_appreciated: That people always said hello on hikes and that the city was very chill and mellow.
top3_advice: 1. Try to find accomodation outside of the University. Use sparerooms.co.uk, Facebook or other platforms. 2. Join a club or a society. other_useful_info: Try a real scottish breakfeast!

crucial_aspects: I have visited the city several times before and really liked it. Therefore, I thought it would be interesting to attend a semester there. I had also heard great things about the university from others who had been there on exchange.
info_ease: Overall, I think it was quite easy to find the information that I needed to know upon arrival as there were several information meetings, guided tours, etc. The visiting students office was also very helpful with all my questions.
arrival_assistance: When I arrived at my study destination, there were information meetings for visiting students where they informed us of all the practical aspects of the exchange and where we could meet other exchange students. There was also a lunch for all visiting students at my faculty where we could meet each other and ask questions about our exchange.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I contacted the visiting students office by mail a month before the semester began as I had not heard anything about course registration. They informed me that I should contact the School, which I did. They then asked me to fill out a document with five priorities for courses and granted me my top three priorities.
registration_help: I did not receive any information about course registration, but both the visiting students office and the School were very helpful when I contacted them.
registration_success: Very successful. I got my three top priorities.
registration_advice: If you do not hear anything from them about course registration, contact them. They are very helpful.
course_level: I think the level of courses is comparable with the level of courses as UCPH. It was mostly academic articles like at UCPH. The amount of reading was the same, maybe a bit less.
teaching_comparison: I had three different kinds of classes: lectures, seminars and tutorials. Lectures are the same as at UCPH and the seminars are comparable to classes (holdtimer) at UCPH. In tutorials, you sit in a small class of around 10 people and discuss the readings and the questions of the week. The questions are provided in advance so you can prepare for the discussions in the tutorial. I found this very rewarding as it enabled you to really discuss the readings in depth. Seminars are 2x50 minutes whereas lectures and tutorials are 50 minutes each.
courses_enrolled: 1) Politics and Governance of Crisis 2) Russia in Global Politics 3) International Security
recommended_courses: I would recommend all three courses, but especially Russia in Global Politics. It was such a fascinating course with interesting readings and the teacher was really good at disseminating knowledge and structuring the course.
unexpected_costs: I did not really encounter any unexpected costs. I thought I might have to buy books, but there were no books on any of my courses' reading lists.
cost_comparison: The accommodation and costs for my phone were more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: There were many different activities available at the host institution. At the beginning of the semester, there is a kind of activities fair where you are introduced to all the societies at the university that you can join.
activities_recommended: I would recommend to engage in as many as possible as this is probably the best way to meet new people. I really enjoyed the yoga society as it was a nice break from the studies and the yoga instructors were very good. The yoga society also held social events.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend other visiting students to explore the city and travel to other cities such as Stirling, Glasgow and North Berwick which are all close to Edinburgh and easy to visit by train.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy to adjust to the local culture. Everyone was very kind and welcoming.
cultural_challenges: I did not really find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: How welcoming and kind all people were to me – and very polite on public transport.
top3_advice: 1) If you struggle with anything, academic or non-academic, please reach out to them. They are very kind and helpful. 2) Do not worry about writing essays. There are workshops and the teachers are very understanding and can help you with all your questions. 3) Do not stress about all the practical aspects. It may seem daunting at first, but there are so many people you can reach out to for help.
other_useful_info: There is a Facebook group for KU students in the UK. In there, you can reach out to hear if others are going to the same university as you. I found it really helpful to know others who were in the same position as me, who I could share the experience with and talk with about practical aspects.
most_rewarding: I really improved my English and, I think, became more confident both academically and non-academically.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was that it was quite difficult to meet people. There was not really any community in my accommodation and it could therefore be quite lonely at times.

crucial_aspects: Primarily a personal connection to the destination since part of my family is from that country. Therefore, I wanted to explore the culture further and also get to know new people - so the social aspects of exchange were also part of my motivation. Lastly, I had heard people talk positively about the university.
info_ease: Relatively easy. There was a lot of information to navigate in which could feel slightly overwhelming. But all the necessary information was there.
arrival_assistance: None.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I had to do an international check-in in the welcome week and confirm my attendance at the law faculty.
registration_help: I honestly cannot remember. I did not make use of it but I am sure that there was plenty of information on websites and phone numbers to call if one had questions.

registration_advice: Have not got any advice. It was very straightforward. Just get it done quickly I suppose so that you do not have to worry about it.
course_level: I thought the level was adequate. Had not had many courses in English at UCPH but still found it easy to follow in Edinburgh. However, I also grew up speaking both Danish and English so I had an advantage. But all in all, I found the level of the courses not to dissimilar to the level at UCPH - if anything, the level was slightly lower/easier than at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Very similar for the most part. Edinburgh University made use of lectures where the teacher taught and seminars where dialogue between teacher and students was encouraged - just like at the law faculty at UCPH. However, in one of my courses, we also had "tutorials" which were essentially small seminars where we were very few students (say 5-6 ish) that talked with the teacher about the reading for the specific tutorial.
courses_enrolled: Commercial Uses of Rural Land, Courtroom Rhetoric and Legal Doctrine, Introduction to Criminal Justice
recommended_courses: I personally enjoyed Commercial Uses of Rural Land. However, this is probably mainly due to my interest in renewable energy. The overall aim of the course was to tackle situations in which traditional use of rural land (agriculture) met more modern uses, such as renewable energy projects, agritourism, and so on. Admittedly, most of the course focused on agricultural law rather than renewable energy projects but I still very much enjoyed a course regarding rural land - probably partly because I very much associated land with Scotland. The other two courses were also quite interesting. Courtroom Rhetoric and Legal Doctrine dealt with rhetoric used by Cicero in Roman courts of law so the course was more focused on rhetoric and history opposed the "hardcore" law. Introduction to Criminal Justice focused on the criminal justice system (policing, prosecution, prisons and so on) so this is probably quite interesting if you like sociology - with a focus on criminal justice obviously.
unexpected_costs: Did not encouter any unexpected costs... Also, the costs above are incredibly rough estimates. I know how much I spent in total but not the specific amount on food etc. Housing, however, is quite accurate.
cost_comparison: I was quite lucky getting a relatively cheap uni accommodation compared to how expensive housing in Edinburgh can be. So housing was definitely more expensive than I had expected - I just got quite lucky. I think food was slightly less expensive than I had expected - both in supermarkets and eating out.
activities_available: Everything you can think of. There were incredibly many societies and sports clubs.
activities_recommended: Personally, I joined the university's hillwalking club which was one of the best things I did during exchange. It was a great way to meet likeminded people and a fantastic - and cheap - way to explore the Scottish highlands. So if you are interested in hiking/hillwalking, I cannot recommend it enough.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking with the university's hillwalking club (or the mountaineering club if you are more into rope-climbing), explore Edinburgh (there are so many things to do: museum, botanical garden, walks up Arthur's Seat, Salisbury Crags, along the Water of Leith), take the train to other cities in Scotland, such as Glasgow, Stirling and St. Andrews.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. But I am also half British which might have helped. Although, I got the sense that the other Danish exchange students found it quite easy as well.
socializing_tips: Definitely join a society or sports club.
cultural_challenges: Do not think I found any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: Hiking and pub culture.
top3_advice: 1. Join a society/sports club to meet new people 2. It is okay to hang out with other Danish exchange students as you will get new friends whom you can easily meet up with at home. But try to get to know locals as well - for instance through sports clubs. I did both and know have some new fantastic friends in Denmark but also great friends in Edinburgh who I can go back and visit. 3. Explore Edinburgh and Scotland while you have the chance. Try not to fly back home - unless you have to obviously.
other_useful_info: Sign up for courses quickly.
most_rewarding: Getting to know new people and, also, explore Scotland with the hillwalking club.
greatest_challenge: Finding time for everything. I had an amazing time but did not allow myself much rest as I always said yes to every offer. Which I am glad that I did cause it resulted in so many great experiences but I was also very knackered when I got home haha.

Take the difficult course! It has given me so much clarity about my upcoming bachelors project and even though it did take away from my free time, I am so happy I did it. The exchange isn't only about making friends around the world - don't underestimate the power of academic contacts at a university that ranks as good as University of Edinburgh does.

arrival_assistance: The university assisted me in securing student accommodation after I had arrived in the city, despite the fact that I had technically missed the application deadline. registration_process: They email you instructions on how to check in, and it’s easy to contact them if you have any questions about the process.
registration_help: See above. They also have lots of information on their homepage.
registration_success: They operate on a first-come, first-served basis, which is why I didn’t get the courses I initially wanted. Changing courses was a lengthy process once I had already started attending classes, but I managed to switch to two new courses. However, I know that others were not as fortunate as I was. There are limited spots in several of the more popular courses for exchange students, and this could be communicated more clearly in the course offerings.
registration_advice: Be quick to submit the courses you want when you receive the email from the university instructing you to do so. Make sure to familiarize yourself with the different courses and their requirements beforehand. I only chose courses that were assessed through coursework, so I didn’t have any written or oral exams. I was very happy with this choice, as it made my semester much easier.
academics_comments: The city is quite expensive to live in, and finding housing was challenging. Furthermore, I did not get the courses I had initially hoped for + the teaching was different from back home (more opinion-based than factual; very different from the law courses at KU)
course_level: I only took honours courses, which are attended only by third- and fourth-year students. As a result, the level was slightly higher. However, I wasn’t particularly challenged by the content itself—my main challenge was adapting to the different teaching style. See below.
teaching_comparison: There was a greater emphasis on critically engaging with the law and expressing our own opinions on topics such as EU law and various legislations. This differed from KU, where the focus is on being presented with facts and legal principles and then connecting them. At UoE, the approach was more discussion-based and encouraged innovation (at least in the courses I took). For instance, in Strategic Decision Making, I had to develop my own project, and in EU Law, I was required to pose a critical question about the EU and respond to it with my own perspective. In other words, there was a strong focus on formulating a clear "main argument."
courses_enrolled: 1) Strategic Decision Making: Game Theory and the Law 2) Human Rights Honours 3) EU Law Honours: Foundations
recommended_courses: The Human Rights Honours course was great; the topics covered were very interesting, and the exam consisted of a 4000-word essay on one of the topics studied.
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive than expected. However, books are online making it unnecessary to buy them. Food is cheaper; ate out a lot instead of making food at home (hence the value at personal spending).
activities_available: So many clubs and societies to join! Great way to meet other people as well.
activities_recommended: Sport-clubs. There was a Scandi-society where I attended some of their events as well; great way to be able to speak danish :)
weekend_recommendations: Go out to the Highlands! I can't recommend it enough.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Edinburgh is not that different from Denmark.
socializing_tips: Go to pubs or join the societies.
culture_appreciated: How relaxed and kind people were. It's a "slow" city; almost empty on Sundays as well :)
top3_advice: 1) Take time to find accommodation; consider teaming up with other Danes who are also going to the city (for example, through the Facebook group that is set up) 2) Be open to meet other people (not only other Danes !) 3) Remember to relax; you also bring your everyday life with you, so don’t try to have plans every single day.

most_rewarding: The people I met, and the memories we have together now.
greatest_challenge: The housing-situation! Don't underestimate it.
