other_useful_info: Always just go physically to the exchange student office to get help. Much easier than writing mails and they are very friendly and helpsome.
most_rewarding: Learning about Scotland and the Scottish people.
greatest_challenge: Finance, in some way. Otherwise not very challenging. I found the university and the people I met overall very helpful and friendly. I never found myself alone or so confused that I couldn't find the best solution to my problems.

crucial_aspects: The quality and reputation of University of Edinburgh was a significant factor for choosing that destination for my exchange. Moreover, I did consider the economic benefits of being able to receiving Erasmus scholarship while being abroad, as well as the fact that english was the main language being taught and spoken there. Finally, I really appreciated the culture and nature Scotland offered.
overall_comments: My study abroad experience did live of to most of my expectations. Scotland (and Edinburgh specifically) is an amazing destination for exchange students, since it is a very international hub for many travellers and nomads.
info_ease: Easy. I received a lot of information from my University. A bit overwhelming actually considering the amount of emails and links they sent me.
arrival_assistance: I got quick responses from my contact persons.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My study abroad experience did live of to most of my expectations. Scotland (and Edinburgh specifically) is an amazing destination for exchange students, since it is a very international hub for many travellers and nomads.
registration_process: I just followed the guidelines provided in the emails I received.
registration_help: Email correspondences with KU and EU
registration_success: I got all the classes I applied for. It was difficult - and a bit frustrating - to get classes outside my programme, because I was on a special exchange agreement (Psychology). They were pretty strict about me not taking classes outside of the agreement, and not very flexible even thought I had mandatory courses I needed to find.
registration_advice: Read your emails and act when they tell you to. Reach out to either KU or EU if you have any questions, they will help you.
academics_comments: My study abroad experience did live of to most of my expectations. Scotland (and Edinburgh specifically) is an amazing destination for exchange students, since it is a very international hub for many travellers and nomads.
course_level: I took 3d year courses (meaning people were in the end of their bachelor programme). This was great, since people were not totally new in Uni, which was nice because a lot of the first years are also very young and inexperienced.
teaching_comparison: I was surprised however of the amount of self-study and read-load compared to classes. This is personally not something I prefer over seminars and in class discussions.
courses_enrolled: Science of Close Relationships (PSYL101412025-6SV1), Natural Language Processing for Psychologists (PSYL101862025-6SV1) and Evidence and Enquiry: Research (NUST080262025-6SV1)
recommended_courses: Science of Close Relationships (PSYL101412025-6SV1) and Natural Language Processing for Psychologists (PSYL101862025-6SV1) were great.
unexpected_costs: Buss pass and also I had to buy ALL the things I needen in my dorms (from pillows, duvets, sheets and a bin to cutlery, pots, pans and knives). This cost my more than 1000dkk alone. Also, I spent a lot of money just exploring the city (going out for dinner, lunch and coffee) which is expensive.
cost_comparison: More.
activities_available: Everything - sports, book-clubs, soup-society, hot-chocolate society, politics, journalism, riding, sailing, hiking, art, debates, social voulenteering and many more.
activities_recommended: I was part of the hill walking, but never got to attend any of their trips. I do think however it would have been fun. Also the yoga society of you are in to that.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the highlands (Inverness is a good destination to base yourself)!. Isle of Skye was amazing. I went with Erasmus and met a lot of nice people there, though the trip itself was a bit rushed.
culture_adjustment: Easy. The scots look a lot like us danes.
socializing_tips: Join societies or take part in the student accommodation events - I met most of my friends through that (most international students though).
cultural_challenges: The university social scene was a lot different than in Copenhagen. A lot of the social groups people engage in are through societies, which if you come from a danish background where you get a class you enrole in through your bachelor programme can come across as a bit odd.
culture_appreciated: The oppeness of the Scottish when travelling around and the love they have for their country. Also, the pub culture - very unique and diverse way of socialising and drinking compared to Danish bar culture.
top3_advice: Prepare which courses you want to take in advance. This is a major help in order to not be surprised by the rigidity of the process. You may change courses within the first 2 weeks so there is space for testing out something if you'd like. Also, engage in the social events in the beginning of the semester. Most people meet their groups in the beginning.
other_useful_info: If you are younger than 22 you can apply for a young scots card which gives you discounts on busses. Also try the African wrap in front of Appleton Tower...
most_rewarding: The people I met, and the connection I now have to Scotland and now Edinburgh. Also the improved academic confidence I've gained since studying in another language on my own in a whole new academic system.
greatest_challenge: Understanding the guidelines and requirements in the assessments were a bit challenging since it was so different from the KU standards, and also not having anyone to consult with (a study group) on different tasks. Some of the final assessments were pretty challenging, others were easier than in Denmark.

crucial_aspects: Jeg havde hørt mange gode ting om universitet og googlet mig til at det var et godt læringsmiljø.
overall_comments: Jeg har virkelig nydt universitets måder at lære på, og dejligt at prøve noget anderledes end Københavns universitet.
info_ease: Tror altid det er lidt bøvlet ift udvekslings med synes Edinburgh university havde nogle gode guides.
arrival_assistance: Vi blev taget godt imod af studiekontoret, men introugen var lidt kompliceret og uoverskueligt planlagt.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Jeg har virkelig nydt universitets måder at lære på, og dejligt at prøve noget anderledes end Københavns universitet.
registration_process: Man mødte fysisk op på skolen og blev registreret diverse steder, både ift universitetet og erasmus.
registration_help: Men blev tilknyttet en studievejleder som man altid kunne kontakte.
registration_success: Jeg fik de kurser jeg søgte og var godt tilføj, blev kun nød til at skifte et fag da skema overlappede.
registration_advice: Spørg om hjælp hvis du er i tvivl om noget! de er søde til at hjælpe.

teaching_comparison: Meget mere interaktiv, men jeg nød at bruge noget nyt. til eksamen skulle vi aflevere to essays per fag og vi fik dybdegående feedback, som var mega fedt.

unexpected_costs: Offentlig transport er nødvendig hvis man ikke bor i centrum og det var lidt overraskende når man er vant til bare at bruge cyklen i kbh.
cost_comparison: Mad var lidt billigere og det var dejligt! Vi drak mange øl og nød pubkulturen men det er ikke en helt billig livsstil, trods populariteten.
activities_available: Virkelig alt, til en enhver smag.
activities_recommended: Prøv lidt forskelligt af.

cultural_challenges: Ingen tror jeg.
culture_appreciated: Hvor søde, venlige og snakkesalige de fleste var.
top3_advice: Tag til pubquiz, gå en masse ture og nyd byen skønhed, man vil komme til at savne den.
other_useful_info: nej.

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne på udveksling for at få muligheden for at bo i et andet land og opleve andre undervisningsformer. Jeg valgte specifikt Edinburgh, fordi jeg syntes at byen virkede fed, og desuden er den tæt på naturen, hvilket var noget der tiltalte mig. Universitety of Edinburgh har også et godt ry inden for mit fag (filosofi).
overall_comments: Jeg var rigtig glad for min tid på udveksling og det er generelt en oplevelse jeg vil anbefale. Dog trækker stressen ved al bureaukratiet (før, under og efter!) lidt ned. Man skal være klar på, at det op til man skal afsted lidt er minimum et deltidsarbejde, med alt der skal udfyldes, sendes og koordineres. Det kommer jeg virkelig ikke til at savne. Desuden synes jeg, at det housing jeg var i kunne have været bedre. Men overordnet har jeg fået nogle virkelig fede oplevelser, mødt en masse mennesker, og fået et nyt syn på både mit eget fag og hvad universitetsundervisning kan være, og ville ikke have været det foruden.
info_ease: Virkelig nemt. Modsat KU er University of Edinburgh virkelig gode til at holde én opdateret, måske endda for gode. Jeg fik utrolig mange mails og påmindelser om, hvad det næste skridt var i hele ankomstprocessen. Det var en smule overvældende, men det var meget nemt at det hele løbende blev sendt til én.
arrival_assistance: Man fik tildelt en student advisor gennem deres Visting Student Office, som man kunne skrive til eller dukke op hos i deres drop-in tid. Desuden kan man både ringe og skrive til Visiting Student Office som helhed, hvis man er i tvivl om noget, hvilket var rart. Desuden, som sagt, mange mails og information på deres hjemmeside og Learn (deres Absalon).
arrival_comments: Der var virkelig mange ting man skulle når man ankom, men man blev informeret om dem alle og det var nemt at finde information. Jeg følte mig lidt overvældet, men heldigvis ikke retningsløs i min ankomst. Desuden virkelig rart at det var så nemt at komme i kontakt med deres udvekslingskontor, jeg vil anbefale ikke at tøve med at ringe heller, da det var en stor hjælp for mig flere gange.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_process: Man skal både til en international student registration, registrere sig inde på selve Visiting Student Office, og hente sit studiekort på biblioteket.
registration_help: Masser af mails! Og desuden Visiting Student Office og kontaktperson, som har ekstra mange drop-in timer i den første uge.
registration_success: Jeg fik i første omgang de fag jeg havde søgt (dog var nogle af dem lavere prioriteter), og da jeg søgte om udskiftning af ét af fagene fik jeg også den godkendt.
registration_advice: Jeg fik selv kun fag jeg havde ansøgt, og havde ikke problemer med mine kursusvalg, men jeg ved at nogle af de andre fik mange afslag på fag og endte med at få nogle, de ikke have ansøgt i første omgang. Jeg vil anbefale at være åben. Du får nok ikke alle de fag du gerne vil have, eller nogle der nødvendigvis føles relevante til dit studie, men det kan ende med at være ret interessant alligevel. Også, husk at du kan skifte dine fag de først to (vistnok) uger af semestret. Desuden, tjek mails, selvom der er mange. Både fra KU og UofE.
academics_comments: Jeg var rigtig glad for min tid på udveksling og det er generelt en oplevelse jeg vil anbefale. Dog trækker stressen ved al bureaukratiet (før, under og efter!) lidt ned. Man skal være klar på, at det op til man skal afsted lidt er minimum et deltidsarbejde, med alt der skal udfyldes, sendes og koordineres. Det kommer jeg virkelig ikke til at savne. Desuden synes jeg, at det housing jeg var i kunne have været bedre. Men overordnet har jeg fået nogle virkelig fede oplevelser, mødt en masse mennesker, og fået et nyt syn på både mit eget fag og hvad universitetsundervisning kan være, og ville ikke have været det foruden.
course_level: Jeg endte med at have ét 4.-års fag, ét 1./2.-års fag, og ét 1.-årsfag. Bacheloren i Skotland er 4 år lang, og derfor svarer et sidsteårsfag til et 4.-årsfag, og der synes jeg niveauet var virkelig godt og tilpas ufordrende. De andre to fag synes jeg var på lavere niveau ift. undervisning på KU, og der bliver generelt forventet mindre af en.
teaching_comparison: Mit ene fag (The Philosophy of Fiction) bestod kun af et seminar én gang om ugen. Holdet var højst 20 mennesker stort, og seminarene bestod af at vi alle sad i rundkreds på stole og løst diskuterede ugens tekster. Det er en meget anden form for undervisning end den måde seminarer fungerer herhjemme, da den føltes meget mere involveret og der var lagt meget mere op til diskussion med underviseren. Desuden havde de andre fag også virkelig små tutorial hold ud over forelæsningerne, så der var lagt op til at alle skulle sige noget. Dog forventes der i det skriftlige generelt mindre af én. Jeg havde fag der kun bedømte på coursework, hvilket betød at jeg skulle skrive en midtvejs- og afsluttende opgave. Begge var under 5 sider.
courses_enrolled: The Philosophy of Fiction Understanding Gender in the Contemporary World Literary Studies 1A
recommended_courses: The Philosophy of Fiction! Underviseren Dr. Stacie Friend var virkelig dygtig, og faget var super godt niveau. Kan også anbefale Understanding Gender, det var ret basalt i de emner det dækkede synes jeg, men virkelig god introduktion til tværfagligt at arbejde med køn.
unexpected_costs: Det var ikke som sådan uforventet, da jeg havde læst i flere af de her skemaer, at det ville blive en udgift men: at skulle købe alt ved indflytning i student housing. Gryde, pande, skåle, bestik, dyne, pude - alt. Det blev rigtig dyrt tilsammen, og føltes desuden meget ubæredygtigt, da mit specifikke housing ikke havde et system, der tillod at donere/give tingene videre til nye studerende, når man flytter ud.
cost_comparison: Offentlig transport (bus) har en flat rate, så uanset hvor langt du tager dem koster det det samme. Nederen, hvis du skal kort, virkelig smart og fedt, hvis du skal langt. Jeg tog personligt sjældent bussen, men udnyt at du kan komme virkelig langt rundt i/uden for byen for ret få penge. Man skal desuden ikke rigtig købe bøger til fagene.
activities_available: De har en virkelig aktiv Student Association med over 200 societies, så man kan finde noget der passer til hver en interesse man kunne have. Jeg var med i få, men det er en virkelig fed mulighed at have og gjorde, at universitetsmiljøet føltes virkelig levende. Der var altid noget at lave.
activities_recommended: Vær med i en society! Det behøver ikke at være noget vildt, men man kan finde mange billige og fede ting at lave gennem dem. Min personlige anbefaling er yoga-society, som har meget billige yoga-timer og arrangementer.
weekend_recommendations: Udforsk byen, der er mange gode ture at gå. Tag til Stockbrigde og gå langs Water of Leith. Eller tag ud i naturen, en bus kan som sagt få dig ret langt.
culture_adjustment: Rimelig nemt, den skotske kultur er ikke meget anderledes end den danske, ud over at folk er en smule mere udadvendte.
socializing_tips: Societies - selvom der generelt på universitetet er en kæmpe overvægt (føles det som om) af internationale/udvekslingsstuderende.
cultural_challenges: Ikke rigtig nogle.
culture_appreciated: Folk er meget venlige og udadvendte generelt. Desuden pub-kultur, som handler om meget mere end at drikke, folk bruger dem lidt som mødesteder/kulturhuse, og der er ofte quiz, livemusik o.a., hvilket gør pubs hyggelige på en anden måde end danske barer.
top3_advice: 1. Ikke lad studiet overtage din al tid, nedprioter det lidt for at opleve så meget som muligt 2. Gå mange ture i byen, det i sig selv er virkelig en oplevelse 3. Prøv noget nyt, i societies eller på anden måde, selv hvis du kun gør den ting én gang
other_useful_info: Ikke stress over det faglige! Desuden er Edinburgh Universitet virkelig gode til håndholdning, meget bedre end KU, så hvis der er noget du er i tvivl om med kurser, indskrivning, accomm. - ring eller skriv til dem. Det gør det hele meget overskueligt. Nyd det, men ikke pres dig selv heller - det føles som om man skal nå alt muligt, men i sidste ende er det, der er fedt, bare at have været afsted.
most_rewarding: At komme ud af min komfortzone og opleve at bo og studere i et andet land.
greatest_challenge: At savne venner og familie derhjemme.
other_comments: Bureaukrati is temporary, udvekslingsminder is forever - seriøst, det er det værd.

crucial_aspects: English speaking and in Europe.
info_ease: There was a lot of information (more than I needed), it would have been nice to recive one sigle mail.
arrival_assistance: Not really any.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: When officially approved for the exchange, you applied for each course (and some extra) and send a separate document with priorities. After getting (some) of them it was possible to wish for change. But it was way easier just to change the courses the first two weeks after the semester started!
registration_help: You get an academic cohost who can help you once arrived :)
registration_success: Succsessful
registration_advice: I did not manage to change into the courses I wanted beforehand, but it was easier to change once arrived. I got some of the courses I applied for rejected, instead of trying to convince them that I had the prerequisites. In the first two weeks of the semester it is allowed to change your courses (ass long as there are still spots available, which there where in all the courses I wanted). Use these two weeks to hear what other students, who have taken the courses or know someone who has, say about them!
course_level: Level. One course a bit harder, but in general the courses easier, but exam harder (compared to the rest of the course).
teaching_comparison: For most of my courses there were one tutorial exercise with four lectures, so we have more tutorials in Copenhagen. (Some of) The lectures were more interactive in Edinburgh – two of them had the structure of students submitting questions beforehand and then the lecture was just about answering them.
courses_enrolled: Category Theory: A really nice course! Quite time-consuming and abstract, so you must like this, but the lecturer was really good and motivating. Combinatorics and Graph Theory: Cozy enough but not that advanced. Commutative Algebra: Some of the curriculum was already covered by Algebra 2 at home, except the coursenotes in Edinburgh was a bit confusing and unstructured (but the lecturer really sweet!). Fundamentals of Operational research: Nothing really happened in the lectures, but the topics were not too bad. Informatics 1 – Introduction to Computation: A first year programming course in Haskell. The tutorial exercises was quite cozy, the rest a bit waste of time (what you can expect of a first year course).
recommended_courses: Category theory! (The same lecturer are having Axomatic set theory every second year, and category theory the other). The rest OK, but you don’t miss out on a lot not having them :)
unexpected_costs: Not really any.
cost_comparison: A lot of the social stuff happened at a pub, so the money spend on pubs added up quicker than I had expected. Food and a lot of other stuff a bit cheaper than at home.
activities_available: I was a part of: Math-society – they had some academic activities and some different socials, it was nice (especially in the first couple of weeks) to have a place to meet some of the other math students that I saw around in the lectures. Canue club – we vent river kayaking, which was really cool! It was a lot of the same people, they where really nice, but most of them had known each other for a long time Moutainering club – this was a really big society, I felt like it was new people I met every time I showed up for something. Had activities almost every day of the week (and a camping trip every other weekend) (every Tuesday there was hill running and Wednesday wild swimming in the morning and bouldering in the evening, and Thursdays some social). Focused a lot on climbing. People showed often up in groups. ESN (Erasmus) – A joined their trip to the Isle of Skye. A really beautiful trip!! But I am not sure I would recommend it – it was a lot of time in a bus, and very touristy (having 20 minutes breaks to take a lot of pictures and then returning to the bus). Dirty weekenders - every sunday they vent doing some gardening (sometimes planting trees) in the area of Edinburgh. Some very sweet people.
activities_recommended: Join some societies! But I do think I focused a bit to much in the local students instead of exchange students – they have the same mentality as you about only being there for a short time, so it is easier to make a friendgroup from this, than people who already have a friendgroup.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the highlands.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, not that much of a difference except in English. And maybe some more smalltalk with people in general.
socializing_tips: Join a society
cultural_challenges: I found the welcome week a bit challenging. A lot of things happened during the week and I met a lot of people I only talked to once, and not really any I ended up becoming friends with. A lot of the social activities was focused around the societies, and not the studies.
culture_appreciated: A lot of really friendly people
top3_advice: Have a look at the welcome week schedule before start so it doesn’t seem as overwhelming Maybe reach out to someone from your own university before going just so you have someone you know from the beginning Its okay to feel lonely at times, you are in a completely new country without your network from home. Sometimes I felt there was some pressure about having the best semester of your life, but remember that it is also an everyday life you are going to have.
other_useful_info: I have written what I could think of in the previous questions :)
most_rewarding: To be taken out of the everyday life I know and rethink what I actually like to do and spend my time on, instead of just what I usually do.
greatest_challenge: For me it was to get to know some people good enough to feel relaxed around them, I am lucky to have some great friends from home that I missed a bit.
other_comments: Enjoy :)

crucial_aspects: language
info_ease: Most of it was easy - but the information from my home university was sometimes quite different than the one received by the visiting university, which made it difficult. Another difficult part was doing the online learning agreement and the pre-approval of courses, since courses get updated very late (1/7) and my home university is closed throughout July, so I didn't get my OLA approved before leaving.
arrival_assistance: not any specific assistance.
arrival_comments: everything was something you had to choose to attend yourself. It was also difficult understanding the difference between the international check in and the proof of attendance - many people mixed them up and only attended one of them.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: we had to go to one office to register that we had arrived and then also book an international check in. It was smooth whilst doing it, but difficult figuring out the practicality beforehand
registration_help: visiting student office by e-mail
registration_success: got all my courses
registration_advice: expect that courses you've put into your first pre-approval will be different ones you end up taking. they'll put in the updated courses in july in the course catalouge. Don't spent to much time finding good courses the first time.
course_level: same level as UCPH. 2/3 of my courses were third year undergraduate / first year postgraduate. These were the same levels as UCPH. Took one course made for second year undergraduate, but a different subject than my main one in UCPH, which made the level appropriate as well. I had two essays per course for the semester, which meant a total og 6 exams, which is more than i'm used to. The exams were "practical coursework" which means essays of 1000-3000 words, with a self-made question or you get handed one. The essays are like discussion papers, and not research papers which we mostly do at UCPH. it's not that difficult, just a different writing style. Most semester I spent on doing essays, since the semester is only 10 weeks, and the first three essays are in october and the second round of essays are in the beginning of december.
teaching_comparison: Lectures and tutorials are only one hour duration. I had one seminar which was 2 hours. I only had teachings 7 hours a week, which is a bit less than in UCPH. The tutorials and and seminars were mandatory and attendance was registered. However, if you could not attend, you could just write your professor and e-mail and it was fine. the tutorials are very few people (14 in one) and people are not as active during class as in UCPH. The professors are very good and open towards questions (not in lectures).
courses_enrolled: Religion and society Understanding Public Policy Social Demography
recommended_courses: Religion and society - Michael, the professor, is fun and its really an interesting course learning about a bunch of different religions, without it being overly theoretical. Social Demography - also good, especially the tutorials, leaning a lot of excel and understanding demographics.
unexpected_costs: transportation (bus) was quite expensive, and you cannot get around with a bike, so buscard is a must.
cost_comparison: Groceries are cheep. Going out, same as Copenhagen (coffee, beers, dining etc)
activities_available: everything you can think of. There's a "society" for everything
activities_recommended: I didn't join any, but I think the gym was good.
weekend_recommendations: Go around in scotland. The highlands (anywhere, but Ben y Vrackie is fun to climb), St andrews. Also go for a walk in the pentlands, arthurs seat or walk around in edinburgh - also leith.
culture_adjustment: Easy, they're so nice people.
socializing_tips: Go to a pub :)
cultural_challenges: Not with the scots - but there's a lot of chinese students, who keep very much to themselves. They're not easy to get to know.
culture_appreciated: Pubs.
top3_advice: Pack warm clothes, also for wearing at home. The apartments are very badly isolated. Bring enough money for going out. Best thing about Edinburgh is the pub-culture. Be prepared not getting a lot of local friends - you mostly get other exchange students as friends.
other_useful_info: It's a short semester, so get the most out of it. You're only there for 3,5 months ish. Don't stress about the exams, you'll pass no matter what!
most_rewarding: getting better at speaking english and living in another country
greatest_challenge: living with people I didn't know beforehand.
other_comments: Drink some guinness :D

crucial_aspects: The courses available where very important to me, as well as an exciting location.
info_ease: Fairly easy – I did sometimes struggle with the University's webpage, as you could be sent around through a million links before you find the necessary information, but you always find the information, you needed.
arrival_assistance: We got a few lectures and tours for visiting law students, which were quite helpful. We did not have a full week of introductory stuff though, you mostly had to seek out events and information yourself.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You would send a form with priorities for your courses and then a student advisor would try to get you those courses. You would hear back a few days after to see if you were able to get any of them.
registration_help: They were very good as sending emails and guides on how to do this.
registration_success: It was very hard to get the classes I wanted. I had a clear picture of what classes I wanted, but most of them were already full or they would have a policy, where they would only accept 2 visiting students or something like that. I was able (after a tough battle of sending many new course requests) to get 2/3 courses I wanted, so it turned out alright.
registration_advice: Be persistent and keep trying to change your courses! They will do their best to listen and help out.
course_level: I was mostly in 3/4th year classes but also had a class that was both BA and MA students.
teaching_comparison: Fairly different – I only had 3 two-hour seminars a week and the teaching style varied greatly. One teacher would do it more lecture-style, another focused on group discussions and another had more class-wide discussions. We did not really do any presentations or cases.
courses_enrolled: Human Rights Honours Business and Human Rights Global Legal History
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of them, as I quite enjoyed them. I was able to learn something new in all of them, but also felt I had the relevant background knowledge.
unexpected_costs: Not any really. I think I spent most money on social activities, such as going out with friends to a pub, which can become quite expensive, when you do it quite often.
cost_comparison: Groceries were mostly cheaper than at home. Other stuff such as coffee and food was quite expensive, just like home. Also, if you are over 22, you need to pay full bus prices, which always amounts to 2 pounds per trip.
activities_available: There were so many clubs and activities. They had a gym, sports classes, different societies (language societies, hobby societies, social societies) and also exchange student specific societies.
activities_recommended: I would recommend going on some of the Erasmus Student Network trips to see some of Scotland! I also think the gym was very good, and would also just recommend joining different societies of your interests. I joined the yoga society, knit and crochet society, dance society and Scandinavian society.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend exploring as much as Edinburgh as possible, but also trying to see more parts of Scotland. I went on hikes in the Highlands and small trips, such as to Glasgow.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, I don't think the culture was too different from the one at home.
socializing_tips: From my experience, you are mostly introduced to other visiting students or international students, both through social events and your classes. I think most local students I met were freshman in the first week (who were all 18) or a few people in my classes, hence I did not engage with them a lot.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any differences very challenging, the Scottish dialect could be hard to understand sometimes though.
culture_appreciated: I think the Scottish culture is so rich, full of so many traditions and so much history. I mostly loved the kindness of the Scotsmen – they were always very easy and nice to talk to! I also loved the pub-culture and the live music culture, as you could often find traditional Scottish music nights in the bars and clubs.
top3_advice: Go to all the events in the first week, make friends with as many people as possible and explore the beautiful surroundings.
other_useful_info: I think the University is very good at providing it, so be calm that you have it under control, they will always let you know about an upcoming deadline etc.
most_rewarding: The friends I made and the wonderful memories we had together.
greatest_challenge: Probably the last two weeks of writing final exams, that was tough.

crucial_aspects: I wanted the destination to have a good university with interesting courses. I wanted a city with history and culture. I wanted a destination where I would meet people from all over the world- not just other Danish students.
info_ease: I think it was quite easy. KU has most information on their website and everything else you get on mail. Uni of Edinburgh mostly communicate via mail.
arrival_assistance: When I first arrived to my accommodation, there were multiple people handing out keys and information. An introduction meeting for exchange students was held by my student advisor, which was very helpful. During the entire semester, there were staff and other students in my dorm that were available to me if I had any questions or concerns. Uni of Edinburgh was great at communicating about all events and stuff happening via mail. The University also has an app for all events happening during the welcome week and semester. My dorm also had a Facebook group. The welcoming lasts an entire week and consists off a lot of different events across the whole University or just your school. You can choose to attend the events, but you're not obligated to. There are many opportunities to meet new people.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I had to go register at "international arrivals" at the school, at the library to pick up my student card and at the exchange student office. The University was good at making it clear what I had to do.
registration_help: I had a student advisor and I also had staff at the accommodation I could ask.
registration_success: Most classes fill up very quickly, however when you arrive at the Uni most people change courses within the first 1-2 weeks, and you have an opportunity here to have the courses you want.
registration_advice: Read the emails from the Uni and attend the information events/meetings.
course_level: The topics of the courses were interesting. However, in my opinion the quality of the teaching is not as good as KU. My courses were graded on coursework I did throughout the semester and one course had a 10% participation mark as well.
teaching_comparison: There are more lectures than seminars. I did not have to buy or read any books, just online articles.
courses_enrolled: Global Legal Systems, Street Law: public legal education in the community and EU Law Honours: Foundations
recommended_courses: Global Legal Systems was interesting, but required a lot because it consisted of lectures twice a week, workshops once every second weak, 2 assignments throughout the semester and a moot court as the end of the semester. Street Law was not very legal. We did not really have classes or books. We just had to do one presentation on a legal topic at a charity center. EU Law was good, but still less "legal" than the courses at KU.
unexpected_costs: Cooking utensils, duvet and pillows. Remember that you do not get the entire Erasmus grant when on exchange. Some of it you receive after you get home.
cost_comparison: I thought I would have to spend money on books, which I did not. Also I think food is generally less expensive than in Copenhagen.
activities_available: The University has a lot of student societies.
activities_recommended: The gym has a lot of good classes. I also attended some of the events hosted by the Scandinavian society, which were good.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city. Stockbridge is cozy.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. The people are friendly.
cultural_challenges: Not really any.
culture_appreciated: The people are very open, polite and easy to talk to.
top3_advice: It is a very diverse city with students from all over the world. Do not get too caught up in the studies- enjoy the city and culture. Take the opportunities you are given to make friends.
most_rewarding: You grow from going outside of your comfort zone and meeting new people.
greatest_challenge: Being away from everyone you know and sharing kitchen and bathroom with so many people.

crucial_aspects: I chose University of Edinburgh because it is a well-respected university in a vibrant city with lots of opportunities to grow both personally and professionally, and I also liked that Edinburgh is well connected, making it easy to travel and explore other parts of the UK.

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

recommended_courses: Music 1A: Psychology of Music (MUSI08069) was very interesting, and the teacher was super engaging and fun to listen to. However, the academic level felt quite low compared to what I was used to at University of Copenhagen. Soundtracks for Screen (UG) (MUSI10112) was a course for both third-year BA and MA students. I really enjoyed the course overall, but I sometimes felt that the teacher expected too much from visiting students, since many of the other students had already taken his class the previous semester and were familiar with material I had not previously studied.
unexpected_costs: Apart from my personal spending on things like going out, clothes, and toiletries, I also spent quite a bit of money on travelling. I made many international friends during my exchange, and we often travelled together to different places, so a good amount of my budget went toward plane tickets and trips.
cost_comparison: In general, the city is much cheaper than Copenhagen, and it is definitely possible to budget well when it comes to food while still eating well. There are also many places around the city that offer student discounts and deals.
activities_available: There were lots and lots of clubs and societies for all kinds of interests, so it was very easy to find activities and meet people with similar hobbies.
activities_recommended: Definitely take the opportunity to explore Scotland, especially the Scottish Highlands, they are absolutely gorgeous! I would also recommend visiting Glasgow, or renting a car with friends and travelling down to England or Wales. There is so much to see and do, and travelling around the UK during exchange was one of the most fun parts of the experience.
weekend_recommendations: There were lots of opportunities for day trips and weekend travel. I went to Glasgow a couple of times, and once I travelled to Cardiff to watch a rugby match. Some of my friends also took the bus to London for weekend trips, so it was very easy to explore different parts of the UK.
culture_adjustment: I am from Irish heritage and have grown up around the culture, so I can’t fully speak for others, but from what I saw my international friends adjusted very quickly. The people here are very friendly and always willing to help, which makes settling in much easier.
cultural_challenges: I didn’t find any major cultural differences particularly challenging, and overall it was quite easy to adjust. If anything, there were only small differences in academic expectations and teaching style compared to what I was used to, but nothing that caused real difficulties in settling in or adapting.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated how friendly and welcoming people were, as well as the strong student culture in the city. There were always lots of events, societies and social opportunities.
top3_advice: First, make sure to apply for classes early, as many fill up quickly and options for exchange students can be limited. Second, take advantage of student life and societies, as there are lots of opportunities to meet people and get involved. Third, make sure to dress appropriately for the weather, as it can get quite cold and wet!
other_useful_info: One extra thing that might be useful is to be open-minded and proactive in the beginning, since it can take a little time to figure out course options, housing, and how everything works. Once you do, though, everything is well organised and support is easy to access. Also, getting involved in student societies early really helps you settle in and meet people quickly. I used the student website "learn" to write to other exchange students to meet up.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was making so many lifelong friendships!
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was feeling homesick at the beginning, which is quite normal when you first move abroad. However, once I settled in and got involved in student life, it quickly became much easier. You end up enjoying it so much that you won’t want to leave!

crucial_aspects: Wanted to experience uni in the UK, great city plus the highlands and Erasmus.
info_ease: Pretty easy. Almost an overload of information
arrival_assistance: My student advisor
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I remember it as pretty easy. You upload a prioritized list of ten courses with your application and finalize it in July, but there is still plenty of time to change if you regret after you arrive. Just talk to your student advisor.
registration_help: Student advisor after arrival and a CSE email that responded pretty quickly in the summer
registration_success: Got my 1st, 3rd and 4th priority.
registration_advice: Don't stress about it if you're a science student. I heard from friends who did humanities that it for them is more difficult.
course_level: I would say the level is around the same, but the workload was a little higher during the semester. This is also because one of my courses did not have a final exam and therefore had a larger amount of in course assessment.
teaching_comparison: Lectures were quite similar except in SFP3 where a lot of the lectures were flipped learning. There were more focus on general learning among the students and less on the final exam which was very nice. The tutorials with theoretical exercises were more class based like high school and less where you just get a bunch of assignments and then TA's walk around and help like at UCPH. There were also way more graded in course assessment hence the weight of the final exam was less. In one of my courses, I had already passed the course before my exam. And the lab sessions are significantly less independent! Sometimes it really felt like being a TV chef or something which made them quite easy and cosy, but not that educational.
courses_enrolled: Immunology 3, Structures and functions of proteins 3 and Pharmacology 3
recommended_courses: I liked all my courses. I probably learned the most from Structures and functions of proteins 3, but it was also pretty high demand with a lot of assessments. Just be aware of this and remember there is no grade pressure on you as an exchange student so focus on learning! Immunology 3 and pharmacology 3 were both very interesting and required less work. The course organizers in immunology were fantastic.
unexpected_costs: It's quite expensive to buy all the stuff needed when moving into a student accommodation.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping (lidl) was quite cheap. Book shops were everywhere and books were very cheap compared to DK. Museums were free. Beers at pubs could vary quite a lot but a lot of places give student discounts so remember your card. You also just live less frugally than at home, so even though everything except housing is cheaper then save up/apply for grants.
activities_available: Everything
activities_recommended: The hillwalking club is great and gives you the opportunity to go on pretty hardcore hikes at remote places with only a few other people. I definitely recommend if you wanna hike and you'll meet some very nice people. Also joining another sport you find interesting is a very nice way to meet and befriend locals. This was the main way for me at least.
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes with the hillwalking club, in general explore the highlands and other scottish cities. Also remember to socialize in the weekends and go to the pubs and party! Don't spend your weekends studying any more than necessary.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy.
socializing_tips: Join sports clubs or societies. This is definitely the easiest way. You can also ask people from your study groups as there is quite a lot of group work at the school of biology.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and inclusiveness of the locals. It is much more easy meeting people you don't know than in Copenhagen. Also just the pub culture.
top3_advice: Don't worry too much about all the practical stuff. It's gonna work out all fine. Be openminded and try out new things. Go a bit out of your comfort zone in the beginning, but also remember you'll be there for a long time and that friendships are not necessarily made in the first week. Become a regular at a place or 2. It gives a very nice sense of belonging. And explore the highlands!!!
other_useful_info: Apply for the grants which you can only apply for from September. A lot of other exchange students get excluded from this since their exchange begin in august. Also the weather was way better than expected.
most_rewarding: Establishing an everyday life in a new country and all the great people I met.
greatest_challenge: The intense socializing with a lot of new people in the beginning. This was pretty demanding
other_comments: Go go go!!!!!

crucial_aspects: I chose Edinburgh, because it is a good university and a beautifull city. It was also nice, that they speak english and that i got an Erasmus scholarship.
info_ease: It was pretty straightforward.
arrival_assistance: They do a comprehensive welcome week, when you arrive with events happening every hour of every day. They take you on walks around the city, introduces you to the universities societies, and there are pizza dinners with you student advisors and academic cohorts. I hav free pizza every day that week.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You look at the course list. Then you wish 10 courses or so. A month before the exchange they give you some of you courses. If they clash, you have time to change your courses upon arrival in edinburgh. It is very easy to make course changes. You just text your student advisor. You can switch courses until third week of the semester.
registration_help: My student advisor was very helpful and always replied fast.
registration_success: Very successfull. I got the courses, I wanted.
registration_advice: Don't worry too much. You can figure it out, when you get there.
course_level: The level was pretty similar to back home.
teaching_comparison: In the physics courses, they prefer to tech using slides rather than blackboards. I prefer slides. In general, they focus a lot on physical intuition and experimental results and often skips the long - if not all - mathematical derivations. Also, all the exams are two hours and without notes. You are only allowed to bring a calculator, so if you have one already, it is a good idea to bring it to Edinburgh.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Condensed Matter Physics Nuclear and Particle Physics Numerical Recipies Introduction to Computer Systems (Informatics course) Geometry (Math course)
recommended_courses: Introduction to Condensed Matter Physics: Well structured and interesting course. Lecturer is nice. Can recommend. Nuclear and Particle Physics: This course is horrible! Each part is only about 12 lectures, which means that everything is very rushed through and on the surface. There is not time to motivate or explain any of the results, which just have to be accepted. Both lecturers are bad at explaining and have no sense of connecting the course prerequisites to the content. The notes are useless. Numerical Recipies: Well structured course. You learn some nice numerical tools, but not anything groundbreaking compared to the mandatory computing courses in Copenhagen. Is a lot of work throughout the semester. It is worth focussing on the checkpoints rather than the workshops. Geometry: Very good and inspirering lecturer! Involves som cool math and explains some tools with great application in physics. Can highly recommend!
unexpected_costs: The accomodation was very expensive but manageable.
cost_comparison: Alchohol is pretty expensive.
activities_available: They have pretty much every society, you can imagine available to all students. Everyone are very nice, and they are easy to join.
activities_recommended: I joined the Canoe Club and MathSoc FC. I can highly recommend both!! It is a great way to meet some local students. The Canoe Club does kayak trips on "white" rivers around Scotland. You don't need any experience, and it is great fun. It is basically river rafting, which is insane, but very thrilling and an amazing experience. An exciting way to engage with the nature and see some of Scotland. Everyone are very nice, and they do a lot of socials. MatchSoc FC is the football team asociatioated with the Math Society. The have five-a-side practices and a game on the weekend every week. it is a great way to play some footy and play with some true, british football boys. Everyone are very nice and they do socials.
weekend_recommendations: I enjoyed going on hikes in the beautifull landscape. There a lot of nice spots close to Edinburgh. I went to the Pentland Hills and Pitlochry. Otherwise I played football and went on kayak trips.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Join the societies. THey are all run by local students.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find it challenging.
culture_appreciated: I attended a few Ceilidhs. It is a traditional scottish repetitive partner dance. They play some folk music and someone tells you the steps. It is a bit like Lancier, only more fun. A must do! I also enjoyed going to the pub to watch football games and attend pub guizzes.
top3_advice: I don't know. DO IT
other_useful_info: Most important: dont worry! Especially about accomodation and courses. They don't allocate university accomodation before two/three weeks before the semester starts, and everyone I know got something. I also know people, who went there without having a place to live, and the unviersity helped them get something instantly.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was the friends I made. Edinburgh is a very international city, so I met people from all over the world, and I had so much fun getting to know them and their culture.
greatest_challenge: I chose some pretty difficult courses, so at times I found it chanllenging to balance academics with enjoying my time abroad. It is maybe worth picking an easy course or two.
other_comments: No.

I also wanted to strengthen my English.
overall_comments: I had trouble with getting the classes I wanted. I ended up liking the classes I got in the end, but would still have preferred to be without the initial trouble and still also would have liked to partake in the classes they told me I couldn't register for.
info_ease: Fairly easy, I did not have too much trouble with that initially. What I would have liked to know prior to even applying was that some modules would not be available for me as an exchange student. That was sadly the majority that I wanted when I applied, and nobody made me aware of it before I was on campus for welcome week.
arrival_assistance: University staff drove me to my private accommodation with my luggage for free after arriving in Exeter by a (self paid) bus arranged by university to go from Heathrow Airport to campus. I also used the drop in sessions to figure out what was happening with my modules.
arrival_comments: The international welcome team was very accommodating with drop in sessions throughout the first few weeks.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had trouble with getting the classes I wanted. I ended up liking the classes I got in the end, but would still have preferred to be without the initial trouble and still also would have liked to partake in the classes they told me I couldn't register for.
registration_process: I sent a module "wish list" in June, I think. I think I had to apply for 6 or 8 classes. Then I got my final modules after arrival, and then you could also try to change modules within the first few weeks if you did not get what you wanted.
registration_help: I don't remember what was available when I applied at home, but on campus they had drop in sessions every day for the first few weeks of term for international students.
registration_success: Somewhat. I got some classes that were good in the end, but I had applied for UoE for some specific courses in curation that I ended up not being allowed to take. I was quite disappointed by that as it did not say it anywhere beforehand. Then UoE assigned me for another class, and then a few days later contacted me saying that I could not get that class even though they had already registered me in it and because it was a mandatory course for an MA. I ended up being in another mandatory MA module at another programme, so I don't know why that one wasn't a problem. I did get one module that was high on my priority list.
registration_advice: Make sure to check if the classes you want are actually eligible for exchange students. I don't know how though as they do not write it explicitly if a module is not.
academics_comments: I had trouble with getting the classes I wanted. I ended up liking the classes I got in the end, but would still have preferred to be without the initial trouble and still also would have liked to partake in the classes they told me I couldn't register for.
course_level: It was kind of similar to UCPH but in some ways a bit lower. During presentations people were allowed to read out loud from their papers/computers which would not be the case in DK. I had a lot of readings for my classes but around the same as . I think it also depends a lot on the modules/programme you study, as some of my business student friends in Exeter did not have much reading to do but instead many classes.
teaching_comparison: It felt very similar to what I have been used to at UCPH. The classes were small (typical for MA in humanities in Exeter), but so are mine at UCPH. In "Cultures of Creativity" we did some more experimental things, but that reminded me of my BA that I studied at The Danish School of Media and Journalism (DMJX). Examination is different at UoE than UCPH. I did not have any specific end of term exams. Instead, they comprised of different tasks throughout the term, and all the credits got put together for one grade per module. My final credit/grade was made of the following: Intercultural Communication: 50% essay, 25% group presentation, 25% video cast (video recording of a presentation) Cultures of Creativity: 50% digital portfolio, 50% essay
courses_enrolled: DRAM143 Cultures of Creativity (15 ECTS) SMLM087 Intercultural Communication: Key Concepts and Theories (15 ECTS)
recommended_courses: Both were good. In "Cultures of Creativity" I got to be creative and reflect on my own practice as a well as discussing the pros and cons of the creative industries. "Intercultural Communication" was interesting to do in an international setting.
unexpected_costs: Transfer fees from my bank when paying rent. I also spent a lot on "personal spending" but that includes all clothes, trips to Boots, trips around the UK, cultural and social activities.
cost_comparison: Books. I got access to all study materials through the university library.
activities_available: All kinds. They have +100 different societies ranging from hide and seek to sports to photography to Taylor Swift.
activities_recommended: They host "international cafes" where you can get a free pastry and hot beverage which is a nice way to meet other internationals too. Pub quizzes are a lot of fun. And join some societies if you feel like it.
weekend_recommendations: Do go on trips! I went on many train trips with friends. We used our reading week to take an 8 hour train to Edinburgh directly from Exeter which I would really recommend. Do look into getting a youth train pass (you can buy it in the Trainline app) as it's quickly gained if you plan to travel by train just a bit. I went to Edinburgh, Glasgow, Manchester, London, Bristol and Lynmouth for overnight stays. For one day trips I did Plymouth, Exmouth, St. Ives, Sidmouth, Bath – and my studies didn't suffer. I'd recommend them all. The national park Dartmoor is amazing too!
culture_adjustment: I did not have any troubles with that.
socializing_tips: I mainly spent time with other international students, as there was also more international than local students in my classes (which is pretty common for MA modules).
cultural_challenges: I did not find anything particularly challenging as I think Danes and the Brits have quite similar manners. The locals do drink a lot though. And the cashier might call you "love" or "darling", but that's just a sweet gesture.
culture_appreciated: Cream tea and the good chips with cheddar and vinegar. They are also more open/small talk more with strangers than Danes, I'd say.
top3_advice: 1: Participate in the welcome things that UoE has planned: They do a lot and you'll definitely meet some sweet people there. Just go, even if you're going alone - you'll find your people, even if you are a late 20's student like me and not an 18 year old fresher. 2: Make sure you are eligible for the classes you really want. Perhaps double check with UoE before you go if they are very important for you. 3: Do go on all the little trips your heart desires with the people you meet. It's great fun to see more of the UK that isn't London. And the train ride to Scotland was actually nice as you cross through so much of the UK on the way.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of right now.
most_rewarding: The people I've met, places I've seen and getting back a photography spark. I've also gotten ideas for my thesis through my courses.
greatest_challenge: The UK being expensive and wanting to do everything. Do try to apply for scholarships, I did get one from Augustinusfonden.

crucial_aspects: It was important that I was interested in the city I would be living in, and that the university has some courses that I found interesting.
info_ease: The university had the most important information collected for exchange students which made it easier. The information on the official websites is often in French, so that made it harder.
arrival_assistance: The university had a welcome day for all exchange students where there were different presentations about the practical things (courses, resident permits, safety) and introduce the different associations at the university. Some of the presentations were in French but the majority was in English. The university had made a welcome package with information about the semester, what we were required to do upon arrival. The exchange office has throughout the semester send emails with details and deadlines regarding taxes etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Each faculty have a meeting where they specify the process for registration, so there are some differences. There are two weeks of classes before you can register for courses so you can try different once. I received an email with a link for the registration and then I had two weeks to get it done.
registration_help: At the meeting there was a presentation with the information, and you could always email the different faculties. There was also some information in the welcome package and the presentation on the welcome day.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. At UNIGE you aren’t allowed to take master courses if you aren’t on your master, which limited some of the courses I wanted but the selection was fine without master courses.
registration_advice: When you select the courses, you can’t switch so make sure it is courses you like and try a few different courses.
course_level: The level was very different. I took two courses that were easy and seemed like high school level. The other three courses they had the same level and workload as UCPH.
teaching_comparison: It was mostly lectures but in most of the courses there were groupwork for reports and presentations.
courses_enrolled: The many faces of Philanthropy Business and society Environmental economic International Political Economy Labour Economics
recommended_courses: I found International Political Economy and Labour Economics very interesting. It was also the hardest courses with the biggest workload.
unexpected_costs: I didn't know you would have to pay taxes when on exchange. It was only 25CHF ( around 200 DKK) but it was unexpected. I also didn't know that you needed to open a deposit account for housing, which was around 100CHF (800 DKK)
cost_comparison: The prices are quite similar to prices in Denmark but a little more expensive. Buying groceries and eating out is more expensive.
activities_available: There were so many. Cultural: theater, photography, orchestra, dance etc. Athletic: soccer, ice hockey, yoga, volleyball, skiing (mostly in the spring semester), hiking etc. Social activities: groups for religion, volunteering, and for different academic interests etc.
activities_recommended: I feel like a sport is always a good way to get to know new people but something that is interesting for yourself. ESN Geneve also have a lot of activities that you can join.
weekend_recommendations: Go hiking and skiing. Visit the UN. Join the events ESN host - they have a lot of different ideas. Travel to other places of Switzerland.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. Geneva is a city with a large international community, so I think that made it easier.
socializing_tips: Team up with local students for groupwork and/or join associations and local events
cultural_challenges: In some of the group work it was very clear that we were used to different expectations but other than that there really weren’t any.
culture_appreciated: I think what I appreciate the most about the culture in Geneva is that it is a blend of a lot of cultures and there is room for everyone.
top3_advice: - Geneva is a really nice city, but stores and most restaurants are closed on Sundays, so it is very quiet on Sundays - Most exams are closed book, multiple choice, so often it is more about learning definitions and not about critical thinking. - There are a lot of events and activities that you can join both at the university but also ESN Geneve, which I found really helpful in the start to make friends.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was learning new people and having some great experience with them. Volunteering at the UN was also very interesting and fun.
greatest_challenge: I think the most challenging part was arriving and having a period where I didn’t live in the student accommodation but in an Airbnb, which made it harder to get into a routine.

overall_comments: As I am in law, this will be reflected throughout the evaluation.
info_ease: It was very easy to find the needed information upon my arrival. Université de Genève as well as UCPH was very organized when it came to providing the needed information.
arrival_assistance: We had a mandatory orientation meeting explaining all the necessary information. We were as well provided with a nice flyer with a step-by-step overview of all the things we needed to complete.
arrival_comments: I couldn’t have been more satisfied with the help and orientation provided by Université de Genève. It was super organized, and everyone was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: As I am in law, this will be reflected throughout the evaluation.
registration_process: The first week or so of classes, it is possible to try all the different classes that you might be interested in. I found this very nice, as it gives an opportunity to try the classes before choosing them. I didn’t buy the books/polycopié before after choosing. However, it was still possible to look through some of the material, as it is shared on Moodle too (corresponding to Absalon). The course registration process is a two-step process, first you register for the courses. Later, you register for the exams. Everything is done through the university’s ‘portail’. It is very important that the courses you want to take and do the exam in, is registered twice (both the course registration and later the exam registration as well). As mentioned, you will be well informed about this multiple times.
registration_help: The process of registering for courses at University de Genève is explained during the mandatory orientation meeting, in the flyer with the step-by-step overview and during the courses.
registration_success: It is my understanding that you can register with all the classes within the Faculty of Law. However, there are some ‘seminars’ where UNIGE students have priority as these are mandatory for their memoire (master thesis). It is possible to take courses at different faculties - and institutes (as a part of the CTL). I took all my classes at the Faculty of Law as to why I have no experience with this. It was, however, once again well explained by Université de Genève.
registration_advice: Make sure to register for the courses and exams respectively. If courses and exams are taken as a part of the CTL, they should be registered specifically for this. It is explained once you get to the university. Be aware, the CTL must be applied for separately. This can be done even before you arrive in Geneva.
academics_comments: As I am in law, this will be reflected throughout the evaluation.
course_level: Generally, I found the level of the courses to be easier than the once at UCPH, when considering the grading. However, the level of the courses differs depending on which of the courses you chose. To my understanding, the professors have a lot of autonomy to choose the type of exam etc. Some exams are multiple choice, for example. These are obviously easier. Others are open or closed books. I recommend that you double check with the professor how the examination is, it is usually explained during the first class, but it is not always clear.
teaching_comparison: Like at UCPH, you usually only have two hours of class per course per week. They estimate four hours of preparation for each class. I used more time than that. Most courses are six ECTS meaning that you will have to take five classes (30 ECTS). I found that to quite a lot in the beginning, but I got used to it some weeks in. I found it to be nice being able to do multiple courses. Most of the classes are lectures, not case work as it is at UCPH. Once again, it depends on the course. Most courses are recorded, and it is thereby possible to rewatch them after class.
courses_enrolled: Comparative Methodology: Contract Law WTO Law and Practice Practice of International Humanitarian Law European Competition Law Organisation internationale (in French) Twi French language courses (no credits)
recommended_courses: I can especially recommend WTO Law and Practice and Practice of International Humanitarian Law (IHL). I found the professors to be very knowledgeable within their field. For IHL, I signed up for the optional pleading. I pleaded with a German girl on a provided topic. The topic was the naval blockade imposed on Paletstine, by Israel. It was very interesting to work this practically with the conflict. It was a bit demanding, but when you did the pleading, you were only examined on International Armed Conflicts (part I of the course), and not Non-International Armed Conflicts (part II of the course). Furthermore, I can recommend Organisation Internatioanle. Challenge yourself by taking a course in French. Improving your French in Geneva is rather difficult, as a lot of people are international students, and/or speak English. I found it difficult in the beginning, I understood almost nothing, but this improved rather quickly. Most courses are recorded so that you can rewatch them on Mediaserver. Alternatively, you can choose a course you have already had before and thereby know. Like the Internal Market of the European Union (Droit du marché intérieur de l'Union européenne).
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: It is more expensive to buy groceries and to eat and drink out. In general, Geneva is a quite expensive city.
activities_available: There are a lot of different sports and cultural activities offered through the university. The student associations are very active and happy to welcome you.
activities_recommended: I volunteered at the Croix-Rouge genevoise with an elderly lady two hours a week as well as at retirement home once a month. I had a lovely time. It was furthermore a really good way of getting insight in the Swiss culture, meeting locals and improving my French.
weekend_recommendations: It is easy to get around Switzerland by train. Personally, I was interested in experiencing the four different languages spoken and how the culture differed in the different regions. I travelled with an interrail ticket, but you can also get some ‘supersaver tickets’ for a decent price. The nature is wonderful. I really enjoyed hiking.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy to adjust. Geneva is a wealthy and safe city. In many ways it reminds me of Copenhagen in that regard. Stores and restaurants close quite early and a lot of places are closed on Sundays. Applications etc. are mostly made by mail, not online.
socializing_tips: I joined Croix-Rouge and talked to students in the different classes that I had. Do not be scared to initiate the conversation. Join a team sport or the musical.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Swiss people are very polite. I was very curious about the society; direct democracy, the cantonal differences etc. Geneva is particular for its international environment.
top3_advice: Université de Genève is a very good university both academically and regarding its activities (cultural and sports as well as student associations). Make use of free French classes. The sooner you sign up for the language classes, the greater chance there is to get your preferred class. Go and explore Switzerland while you are there.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: Meeting wonderful people and finding my path academically and professionally. Experiencing Geneva’s international vibe. I found it to be very stimulating.
greatest_challenge: Prioritizing my money wisely ;)
other_comments: Go - you will not regret it! Bon courage!

crucial_aspects: The academic opportunity was crucial for my decision. Being able to study at two prestigious universities in the field of international law at Geneva Graduate Institute and University of Geneva through the highly motivated and demanding Certificate of Transnational Law (CTL) has indeed given me a special insight of international law.
info_ease: Upon arrival to Geneva, I received all the necessary administrative and academic information needed for my stay. During the first orientation week, both the IT department and the respective faculties had organized an orientation programme.
arrival_assistance: See the above mentioned comment.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Registration process consists of a two folded process. The first process starts two weeks after the beginning of the semester, where you have to sign op for the courses that you want to follow. The second step is similar, since you have to register for the exams in the afore mentioned courses that you have decided to sign up for.
registration_help: You can always receive additional help either through your exchange coordinator, your faculty or through the general office for incoming exchange students.
registration_success: I was able to register for all the classes I wanted to attend.
registration_advice: It is important to carefully read the received emails regarding the registration process, since it contains some important deadlines that you need to respect.
course_level: All my courses were at the master level at the faculty of law, since all courses at the bachelor level were all teached in french.
teaching_comparison: The teaching of style varied a lot. Some of the courses including a requirement for active participation while some courses did not even required physical presence.
courses_enrolled: - European competition law (6 ECTS), - Comparative law: contract law (6 ECTS) - International Humanitarian Law (6 ECTS) - Compliance with international law (6 ECTS) - Business and human rights: politics, law and policy (6 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend law students to apply for the Certificate in Transnational Law, which allows you to apply for two courses at the Graduate Institute.
unexpected_costs: I did not expect such a high cost for daily shopping, especially groceries and general living expenses.
cost_comparison: The general costs of living is higher than in Denmark.
activities_available: During the first orientation week, you will be presented to all the possible clubs and societies that you can become a member of during the semester.
activities_recommended: I would recommend signing up for a sport or gym.
weekend_recommendations: Due to the central location of Geneva, I would recommend to visit France and Italy during your stay.
culture_adjustment: Geneva is one of the most international cities in the world with a very high percentage of international citizens living there so it is very easy to live there.
cultural_challenges: Some of the locals do not speak English fluently and it can, therefore, be difficult to hold a conversation with them, as a large part of them primarily speak French or German.
culture_appreciated: The culture of Geneva is very international but on the other hand, it is also a very conservative town as regarding the night life and the fact that all supermarkets and shops are closed every Sunday.
top3_advice: First, you have to get an accommodation through the university agreement, since it is too expensive to rent an apartment or studio on the private market. Secondly, you should expect to put some effort and hours into your studies. Thirdly, you should participate and sign up for some of the clubs and societies that are being offered by the university in order to fully experience the exchange life as well as meeting new people.
other_useful_info: It is important to socialize a lot in the beginning in order to find some new friends during your exchange.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange was definitely to study together with so many international students from all over the world and hear there different perspectives on law and life in general.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my stay was to speak and improve my french.

recommended_courses: Competition Law was very interesting and a bit more challenging than the other subjects. Arbtitration Law was easy to follow if you were not in the mood for a challenge. Law of trust is interesting, also a bit challenging and a nice oral exam with a good Professor.
unexpected_costs: More expensive to live in Geneva than I expected. Grocery shopping is expensive.

socializing_tips: I was mostly with other danish students. Otherwise I would join the sport activities like dance or some vulenteer work to get to know the others.
cultural_challenges: There was not any cultural differences that was challenging.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated that the people were clean, polite and did not throw trash. I Appreciated that the city held a lot of co-students, elder people and families. It is a city good for working and studying.
top3_advice: Do not postpone your readings to the exam, do them during and then you might not have to study as hard in the exam period. Since the subjects have such little credits (6 ECTS) you will end up having to do 5 exams. Take as many small trips outside Geneve as you can. More Hikes in Switzerland or visit Italy. Grocery shop in Lidl or use Too good to go, then you can save some money.
other_useful_info: No, Law was not to demanding, and we had a lot of time for other things. Some of the other faculties, barely leaves any time for anything other than school.
most_rewarding: That I got so many new danish friends. And that I learned a lot about completely different cultures. In my residence there was everything from Mexican to Russian and Japanese. I heard all about their home cities, cultures and opinions. Very exciting.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was just being away from home or to manage some of the practical errands. Like residence permit or insurance. But it was not that challenging.

culture_appreciated: I mentioned that already

Through this process, you not only obtain knowledge about other (exciting) cultures, but you also learn to understand what characterises your own. Moreover, improving languages – in my case French and English – is pivotal if one seeks an international career, and on a personal level as one becomes better in navigating in the mighty world.
