crucial_aspects: Geneva is one of the best places in the world to study international law. Especially since the Certificate in Transnational Law program, which is offered at the faculty of law at the University of Geneva, allows you to take up to two courses at the Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies, one of the highest-ranked universities in the field of international law. Of course, the nature in and around Switzerland is incredibly appealing. You can do endless, astonishing hikes and skiing trips with the mountains and lakes all around the country, and it is really easy to go to the neighbouring countries, Italy and France, as well.
overall_comments: My stay has been amazing. Really nice people from all around the world, and Switzerland has so much to offer. The only downside is how expensive it is here.
info_ease: I think it's been fairly easy. The only thing is that a lot of the information available on the UNIGE website, as well as information that you get from old school letters, is in French. That makes it a bit more complicated, but with all the translation tools available, for example AI assistants, I've managed without knowing much French.
arrival_assistance: All the incoming exchange students had an intro session on the Friday before the start of the semester, where we got all the information we needed about things like application for residence permit, opening a bank account (necessary for receiving the SEMP grant), applying for courses and so on.
arrival_comments: It would've been nice if all of the relevant pages for exchange students on the university's website were translated into English
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My stay has been amazing. Really nice people from all around the world, and Switzerland has so much to offer. The only downside is how expensive it is here.
registration_process: There is a limited registration period, but the staff at uni are kind to inform you about it so that you don't miss it. You have the possibility to try out different courses before making the final registration. First you register for the courses, and then later, you register for the exams, which is binding.
registration_help: The staff, including some of the professors, helped explain the process. You help each other among the other exchange students.
registration_success: At UNIGE, I got all the courses that I wanted, but I didn't get the two courses at the Graduate Institute that I applied for, even though I had 5 priorities. I ended up only getting one course at the Graduate Institute, which was my last priority.
registration_advice: Keep the deadlines in mind!
academics_comments: My stay has been amazing. Really nice people from all around the world, and Switzerland has so much to offer. The only downside is how expensive it is here.
course_level: I haven't gotten my grades at the time of writing this, but overall, I think it's quite doable. It depends a lot on the individual course, though. In some courses, you have close to no readings to do prior to the classes, but in others, it's quite extensive. In my experience, the workload at the Graduate Institute is quite a lot bigger than that at the UNIGE, but I don't think the level is much different. I think the level is comparable to the level of the English courses taught at the UCPH.
teaching_comparison: It varies a lot from course to course. In some of the courses, the classes are recorded. Some of them require you to show up to the classes. Some of them use a participation bonus system. The course I had at the Graduate Institute, International Investment Law, had participation bonus, but also the other way around, so you would get deducted if you didn't show up or participate, when you were on the panel. You were assigned with two classes where you were expected to be extra well prepared as part of the "panel".
courses_enrolled: Comparative Methodology: Tort Law International Intellectual Property Law Internet and IT Law Economic Analysis of Law International Investment Law (at the Graduate Institute)
recommended_courses: While you're here, I think it's worth it to go for the Certificate in Transnational Law. This means that you have to take a Comparative Methodology course. Besides that, I really liked Internet and IT Law. Especially one of the two professors, prof. Alberini, was excellent. International Intellectual Property was nice, but quite demanding. I highly recommend going for one or two courses at the Graduate Institute as part of the Certificate in Transnational Law program.
unexpected_costs: In general, the prices in Switzerland are high. That wasn't too unexpected.
cost_comparison: I was pleasantly surprised that public transport in the entire canton of Geneva is free for students up to the age of 25. As a young student you can also get a group day pass (up to 4 people) valid for the entire country for only 80 chf, which is incredibly cheap compared to the normal price. Unfortunately, I've been too old to get the good deals, so it's been quite expensive for me. If you're too old for the benefits, I'd recommend getting the half-fare travel pass as soon as possible, if you see yourself going on trips around Switzerland.
activities_available: The ESN network hosted many different activities throughout the semester. There's so much going on, and the activities available vary from club nights to sports, to hikes, to skiing, to sightseeing.
activities_recommended: Hiking, skiing, visiting the smaller towns around Switzerland. The incredible nature in and around Switzerland is what makes Geneva stand out in my opinion.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking, skiing, visiting the smaller towns around Switzerland. The incredible nature in and around Switzerland is what makes Geneva stand out in my opinion. It's a no-brainer to go to France and maybe also, depending on what you like, Italy, Spain, Germany.
culture_adjustment: The overall vibe is a lot like Copenhagen, I think. And it's very international here, so I'd say it's quite easy.
socializing_tips: Make an effort during the first few weeks. That really helps you in the long run. I think the welcome week hosted by the ESN was a really great way of getting to know many people.
cultural_challenges: The fact that the supermarkets are only open till 19.00 and closed on Sundays is annoying. But you get somewhat used to it along the way.
culture_appreciated: If you want to try out your French, people are very kind and understanding. And almost everyone knows English, so if you get stuck in a sentence, you can (almost) always switch to English.
top3_advice: Put in the effort in the beginning. Not only socially, but also in terms of getting your bank account set up, getting your residence permit etc. It's way better to just get it out of the way compared to having it hanging over your head for several months. Show up to classes. For me, it was a good way to maintain a normal every day life, and it's nice to see your classmates on a regular basis without having to plan something every time. And you have plenty of time doing fun stuff in the weekends, since almost everyone has Fridays off and I also had Mondays off.
other_useful_info: As a Dane, who is also too old for the public transport benefits, it's been nice to have a bike here. I bought one on Facebook Marketplace and will sell it again, but you can also rent one for your entire stay. Kind of like Swapfiets.
most_rewarding: Getting to know all sorts of amazing people from all around the world.
greatest_challenge: The troubles of getting a bank account, residence permit, etc. The entire administrative system is based on physical letters back and forth.

crucial_aspects: Good international student environment, opportunity to improve my French.
overall_comments: Really recommend going to Geneva for exchange, because of its very social exchange student environment, there are both ESN (Erasmus Student Network) + UNIGE’s own welcome days and intro week events. Those are really good for making new friends. Also the city is a good size - small enough to get a grip of it but big enough to keep exploring new places. Plus the amount of new exchange students is good - approx. 300-400 people, so that you’ll get to know most of them, (or at least reckognize familiar faces), since you bump into each other at uni or go to the same events in the city.
info_ease: Pretty easy, good help from the connected Erasmus Student coordinators at UCPH + UNIGE. The course catalogue wasn’t fully updated before my arrival in Geneva, which made it a bit harder and more stressful putting together a course schedule/study plan + I noticed some of the courses were overlapping.
arrival_assistance: Welcome days/Introduction week for all exhange students + emails with important information.
arrival_comments: Look at the course catalogue thoroughly before going, because some courses might be overlapping or have “tutorat”/class teaching at the same time at the same time as other courses.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Really recommend going to Geneva for exchange, because of its very social exchange student environment, there are both ESN (Erasmus Student Network) + UNIGE’s own welcome days and intro week events. Those are really good for making new friends. Also the city is a good size - small enough to get a grip of it but big enough to keep exploring new places. Plus the amount of new exchange students is good - approx. 300-400 people, so that you’ll get to know most of them, (or at least reckognize familiar faces), since you bump into each other at uni or go to the same events in the city.
registration_process: You have the first weeks of the semester to trying out several different courses and then register later, it’s nice because you can try out some before signing up. I did find creating your own study plan/course plan yourself a bit stressful, and making it work without having (or at least not many) overlapping courses. It can be tricky since L'UNIGE mostly have 3 and 6 ECTS courses, and also it’s your task to do make an actually working study plan, I didn’t receive any help whatsoever.
registration_help: Not a lot, you’ll have to find the right courses that adds up to 30 ECTS yourself. I think this is pretty common and pretty much everyone going on exchange has to do this, I just wasen’t quite aware that it’s basically just our own problem, if you can’t make the study plan work out and get accepted on the right courses. I did get enrolled to all the classes I wanted (7 in total, because I took 4 x 3 ECTS courses plus some 6 ECTS courses). I’ve not heard of people not getting in to the courses, they wanted to take - I don’t think this i a problem for anyone at L’UNIGE luckily. I did write an e-mail to L’UNIGE about getting permission to take courses from more than 2 faculties (normally you’re only allowed to choose from 2), because I struggled with finding relevant courses only choosing from 2 (and them being mostly in English), but they were super nice and gave me permission, since the course I wanted from the third faculty was relevant for my study area.
registration_success: I managed to make a nice study plan, with courses from Social Science, Environmental Science, and Economy and Management. The geography department at L'UNIGE is located at Social Science, where I took the course in French 'Géographie et écologie urbaine’, which was super interesting (about the evolution of cities and future sustainable cities and ways of living, all with a very critical approach). The couses I took from environmental science were very very good as well - my overall favourite course of them all was "BES Assessing the Multiple Values of Nature", about human-nature relationships, NCP's and more modern and inclusive ways of valuing ecosystems and Ecosystem Services. We did some interesting GIS work (recreation map of nature using SoME posts) and talked about environmental ethics having philosphical discussions. The teacher Martin Schlaepfer is incredibly good. “FND Climatic Change" was an easy version of "globale geosystemer" and very introductory - can recommend if you’re studying geography at UCPH and want an easy and non-stresseful course (no assignments, only lectures, that I just went quickly through before the exam, still went good).
registration_advice: Look at which courses have an exam at the end and which ones don't!! Because I ended up having 7 courses in total but "only" 3 exams in January, because some of the courses had a presentation in December as the "final exam". Was very nice that I only had 3 exams. Some other students at the uni had a little more than me or none at all. If you are able to speak a bit of French and want to be better at it (I had done Fransk A in highschool, but not spoken until the summer before my exchange), I recommend taking at least one real uni-course in French. Even though it sounds crazy hard, it’s worth it and not so hard. After 1 or 2 months I got into it and ended up doing an oral exam in partly French (Frenglish). I really did a lot of progress with my French speaking skills. A lot of exchange students choose French courses at uni even though they are not fluent at all, so you're not alone being bad at it in the beginning. I only took one, but almost regret not doing more courses in French. It was hard in the beginning, but then suddenly clicked and got easy - honestly totally doable, and so happy I improved my French to a level where I can read and speak it kinda fluently now.
academics_comments: Really recommend going to Geneva for exchange, because of its very social exchange student environment, there are both ESN (Erasmus Student Network) + UNIGE’s own welcome days and intro week events. Those are really good for making new friends. Also the city is a good size - small enough to get a grip of it but big enough to keep exploring new places. Plus the amount of new exchange students is good - approx. 300-400 people, so that you’ll get to know most of them, (or at least reckognize familiar faces), since you bump into each other at uni or go to the same events in the city.
course_level: Lower than UCPH, but depends on courses + faculty. Social Science was known for being a bit lower than UCPH, Economy and Management is easier if you choose “management” courses, but the “economy” courses are haaard. Science is in a general pretty high level - but the environmental science department at the Science faculty is the same at UCPH, I’d say, maybe a little bit lower level… or at least I found it easier to get higher grades.
teaching_comparison: Pretty much the same.. maybe a bit more of lectures and less class teaching and discussions than UCPH….
courses_enrolled: “T206059 - Géographie et écologie urbaine”, “S240009 "The Many Faces of Philanthropy”, E4E187 "Assessing the Multiple Values of Nature”, “T207003 - Emotions, behaviors and collective action”, “14E150 - FND Climatic Change”, “SA24 - Grammaire B1 at MDL, “SA24 - Expression orale” at MDL.
recommended_courses: “BES Assessing the Multiple Values of Nature”!! It also included a city walk in Geneva, where we learned about the nature and biodiversity initiatives. And “Géographie et écologie urbaine”. L’UNIGE is a good university for urban geography (or human geography in general) - mostly their French courses though. Heard good things about “Histoire écologique du monde contemporain” (about cities, (urban) ecology etc.) + the course “Cities in transition” (they had a super interesting field trip/excursion) and “Cities and Social Change”. I was allowed to take some master-courses that were really interesting.
unexpected_costs: Fees for getting the residence permit (approx 500 DKK) + a fine in the bus of 800 DKK for not having a valid ticket:(
cost_comparison: You get the SEMP-scholarship as an exchange student from the EU at L’UNIGE. This is similar to the Erasmus scholarship (approx 4000 DKK per month). I didn’t end up spending that much more money than I came with on my exchange - I had the SU, SEMP-scholarship and got a private scholarship from Hedeselskabet of 12000 DKK. In general Geneva is known for being cheaper compared to other cities in Switzerland e.g. Zürich. When buying groceries in Lidl + having a La Farce membership (volunteer-driven organisation that gives out free food once a week) I ended up spending almost less money on groceries than i Cph. You can also go to France (10 mins away) and food is cheaper. Meat and fish is extremely expensive in all over Switzerland though, but as a vegetarian it’s fine. Free public transportation for students of 25 or younger. Doing trips to other places in Switzerland is expensive - that’s why I got a half-fare travel card (can recommend if going a lot on hikes/visits to other cities in Switzerland). Wine and beer at stores is pretty cheap. There are many free sport-activities at the university too.
activities_available: So so many associations/clubs, and they are super welcoming for new students + Exchange students. The EDD Association for “Students supporting sustainable development” is nice, they hosted an apéro (kind of student bar event) at their beautiful urban rooftop garden at Uni Dufour (view of the alps etc) in the beginning of the semester, that I joined and met people that became my friends. All the associations are good places to meet people and locals. You can also just join their events, like the apéro’s (what I did) and especially in the beginning of the semester. I was too busy to join an association fully, but if staying a year, I’d totally have done it. Very good university sport activities too - me and some friends signed up for funk dance class, and had a lot of fun. They have so many different types of sports classes.
activities_recommended: Volunteer at La Farce (volunteer-driven organisation that gives out free food once a week with a chili, alternative vibe), a lot of local + exchange students join it and you can get a subscription for free to collecting food once a week (fresh veggies, eggs, pasta etc.) and it’s a very vibrant and cute social spot with free events like hip hop classes, free guestlist to cool technoclub Le Zoo, free french classes, parties, free restaurant visits every monday and more. I met nice people while having a couple shifts as a volunteer there. I also spoke and improved my French + I saved so much money on groceries. There are lot of things happening in Geneva and many different types of people (more diversity than I’ve experienced in CPH), you just have to look for them (for example at events, uni and parties).
weekend_recommendations: - Hang out at Bains des Pâquis: Sun bathing, winter dipping, doing saunas og hammams. Also the very best place to eat cheese fondue in a relaxed atmosphere.
culture_adjustment: Easy, very much like Danish culture. Though I do think that local people and students are more open to chat and mingle with exchange students than in DK - but might also be due to the fact that Geneva is such an international city, everyone is from everywhere.
socializing_tips: Like mentioned before, classes (just be proactive, ask for their number and go for coffee), language tandem/buddy, La Farce or uni-associations
cultural_challenges: The strict dorm rules at La Cité Universitaire, where you have to be quiet after 22:30, otherwise if you’re being too loud talking to people in the kitchen, the guard will come and tell you to go to bed and be quiet…
culture_appreciated: That it’s such an international environment in Geneva, mostly all of the students at the University of Geneva come from other places than the city itself - either other parts of Switzerland or other countries. Many people are international and have studied abroad for a longer time. That means no one seems narrow-minded and most are interested in getting to know you and hearing about where you’re from and your culture etc. I also appreciate that you can go to so many different beautiful cities within a short distance of eachother, fx just within Switzerland you can go lovely cities Bern, Lausanne, Basel, Lugano, Zurich and some of the smaller mountain villages. AND you can go to Grenoble, Lyon, Turin, Paris (only 5 hours away by train) and many more cities that are in other countries but close to Geneva/Switzerland - perfect for exploring more of Europe. Good traditional food in Switzerland is a plus too.
top3_advice: 1. Learn French during your exchange at L'UNIGE, it's totally doable. If you know a little it's easier though (but also you can take complete beginner classes (and might get up to 6 ECTS for doing it) too). The main language is French and everything like signs, many e-mails etc. are in French (usually also translated to English). 2. People studying at L’UNIGE are down-to-earth and level-headed, imo. They are not only there to party. I mostly just went because I wanted to improve my French though:)) 3. It’s not crazy expensive like you hear people say (since you get both SU + SEMP scholarships, and student accomodation is same price level as in DK) - I heard that Zurich is way more expensive than Geneva 4. Extra: Do prioritize making sure you don’t miss the welcome week/welcome days the week before the semester starts - this is the social moment to meet people and future friends. Imo it’s best going a week before the welcome week, so you have time to both settle in & going to the welcome week events.
other_useful_info: institution? * DON’T SPEND TOO MUCH TIME ON UNI, SPEND LESS THAN YOU’RE USED TO AT HOME, YOU’D REGRET IT OTHERWISE. There are many exchange-spots for UCPH-students at University of Geneva, which also gives the opportunity to create a Danish-people network - we were around 15 Danish students at University of Geneva and hung out a lot + helped each other with necessary paper work like getting the residence permit and so on. The autumn semester goes from Sep-Feb, so people went home for Christmas and exams started in January. I thought this was nice, because then I came back for a more chill study vibe to saying goodbye go Geneva. Also I was lucky to only have 3 exams in the end of January, so didn’t feel that stresset about it. Extra adivce: MDL's language courses are also a good place to meet other exchange students. - Join the ESN events (Erasmus Student Network) - this is where you meet other exchange students in the beginning of the semester (my good friendgroup was made within the first weeks by meeting people there - specifically the ESN city tour during the welcome week). - Volunteer at La Farce - Join an association (or just their events, like apéro) at L'UNIGE - Use the apps Totem and The Fork for discounts at cafés, restaurants and stores
most_rewarding: Meeting extremely nice people, that will be my friends for life. Becoming fluent in French.
greatest_challenge: Not having friends and family close by whenever needing them, if feeling down.. but in our friendgroup we became each others family:) And it’s not far away from DK too. Exam season was a bit tougher, since it was more exams and a longer study break than I’m used to.. I felt the level in classes was way lower than at geography in UCPH though, (started studying for an exam 24 hours before and got a good grade even though)
other_comments: The more you integrate in the Swiss culture, the better the experience, you’ll get, I think. If you get a social network there, learn the language, learning about the culture and where the good and cute spots in the city are, you’ll end up feeling like you’ve got an attachment to the place and feeling more like it’s been a fullfilled exchange. I’ve got friends from Switzerland and all over the world now, that are coming to visit in CPH and I’m gonna visit in the future. But it definitely also took some effort and social energy to mingle with people (and spend a lot of money on coffee dates with friends, but worth it all:)).

overall_comments: Overall, my exchange experience in Geneva was very positive. The city itself is vibrant and well-organised, offering a high quality of life and a strong international atmosphere. However, Geneva is relatively small, which means that fully experiencing the region often requires travelling outside the city. While this is not a drawback in itself, it does make the experience more expensive, as transportation, accommodation, and daily expenses quickly add up. In general, Geneva is an exciting and culturally rich city, but it is also one of the most expensive places to live. Everyday costs such as food, housing, and leisure activities are noticeably higher than in many other European cities. As a result, careful budgeting is necessary, especially for students. Despite these challenges, the city’s unique location makes it easy to travel to nearby destinations in Switzerland and neighbouring countries, which greatly enriches the overall exchange experience.

The application process for courses and exams follows a completely different structure than what Danish students are used to, which can be confusing without clear guidance. As a result, it requires extra attention and independent effort to ensure that all deadlines and requirements are met correctly. While the necessary information is provided, a more structured and transparent overview of these processes would have made the transition smoother.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere, where there was a focus on the social life. I heard about the social offers that Uni of Glasgow had with sports clubs and societies. I also wanted to go somewhere, where I could explore the country and I speak the language.
info_ease: Quite easy
arrival_assistance: University of Glasgow was very helpful in answering all questions I had and also had a lot of offers in fresher's week for international students, i.e. a tour around the city and a mentor-program
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: 2 week drop period at beginning of term, where I would be assigned to the pre-applied courses but I could change if necessary
registration_help: The Uni is very helpful with answering questions. They are very fast during the drop period - I changed a course and it was super easy. They even reserved a spot on the course I wanted, without dropping me from the other one, while I was waiting for approval from Copenhagen
registration_success: very
registration_advice: Apply for courses because they interest you and don't worry if they are not approved immediately, they are usually given right before or in the first week of term .
course_level: level 2,3 and 4
teaching_comparison: different from course to course and level to level - it depends on the course convenor. However, prepare to be more active in class - some professors cold calls a lot
courses_enrolled: jurisprudence, level 2 Principles of Healthcare law, level 3 Criminal law: theory and doctrine, level 4
recommended_courses: I took Jurisprudence partly because I read in previous reports that it was easy - the course was fine, but the exam was difficult, maybe because of a new exam type. However, the course was still good and the curriculum was easy
unexpected_costs: The sportsmembership was more than expected. Also trips, and going out to eat a lot
cost_comparison: food - I didn't cook much
activities_available: Too much to count :) So many clubs and societies and most of them had a social every week or every other week. Definitely worth joining a club or two
activities_recommended: mountaineering club has different hiking trips every other week. Go to as many tasters as you can in the freshers week, so you can try the clubs
weekend_recommendations: Trips around the country! Rent a car (at Arnold clark) and drive to the islands! I saw northern lights on orkney.
culture_adjustment: Yes, people in Glasgow are super friendly - only the accent is a bit difficult
socializing_tips: Just go up and talk to strangers, they are very helpful and kind - especially at pubs :) go to the socials with the different uni clubs or just go out for a pint or two at the GUU beer bar (glasgow university union)
cultural_challenges: not much, they are more open than the Danes
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and that they befriend you at parties. If you meet people at a party, they will often text you afterwards to meet up for coffee or something else to make friends with you.
top3_advice: pack for a rainy day (or 20) :)) Go on trips early in the semester, so you won't stress about exams go to different club socials
most_rewarding: Everything! I loved Glasgow :)
greatest_challenge: The accent - but even other Scots struggle with the Glaswegian accent :))

crucial_aspects: A broad variation in offered English courses + less effected by COVID-19
info_ease: The University of Glasgow could have done better as I did not get a lot of information before the semester started unless I asked myself.
arrival_assistance: A lot of chaos in the beginning as I got my courses in the same week as they started. It was difficult to get assistance as all the teachers were busy answering everyone's mails as most people were very confused about their courses
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was easy enough to choose courses before arrival but a lot of people only got 1-2 of the courses they asked for
registration_help: Asking the erasmus-assistants
registration_success: I was lucky enough to get all of the classes I wanted
registration_advice: Choose a lot of different options when you choose your courses in case you do not get your first priorities. It is very difficult to change courses when you arrive.
course_level: Depending on the chosen courses, the level is often not the same as on KU. I would say it is easier

recommended_courses: My favorite course was competition law. The level is similar to the one at KU and the teacher was amazing!
unexpected_costs: Renting cars for trips
cost_comparison: Everything costs pretty much the same as in DK
activities_available: Any kind! Easy way to meet people
activities_recommended: Go to a lot of club-tasters in the beginning! All the clubs offer free classes during the first couple of weeks before you have to pay.
weekend_recommendations: Go on trips in the country, drink pints, eat chips, cheese and gravy while you're hungover
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Choose a club and go to their socials
cultural_challenges: Scotland is not that different from Denmark so I don't remember having any problems
culture_appreciated: The open and welcoming local people
top3_advice: Search for housing early, save a lot of money before and just enjoy it!
other_useful_info: Bring an umbrella
most_rewarding: Living in another country having fun all the time

arrival_assistance: I did not receive much, but had some fellow students who helped me.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We just had to file the Erasmus documents a we were already enrolled into moodle.
registration_help: E-mail service, very quick answers.
registration_success: Not succesfull, very disapointed but it ended out okay.

teaching_comparison: More discussion based.
courses_enrolled: Business law, Intellectual property law and Anti discrimination law in practice.
recommended_courses: The Ip law course I would highly recommend, however if you're only here for 1 semester you will only get half of the syllabus (e.g. copyright and trade mark, but not patents and design). I would also recommend Anti-discrimination law.
unexpected_costs: It's expensive to go on trips around the country, but also a must!
cost_comparison: I ate out a lot and the foodscene in Glasgow is great.
activities_available: I joined the whisky society and Ultimate.
activities_recommended: Definetely sign up for a sport society. It's the best way to meet new people and they have socials (nights out) every wednesday which is a must! You can join a society as a beginner, it does not matter and during/after freshers week they all have taster sessions.
weekend_recommendations: Go on trips to the islands or highland. Big recommendation for Isle of Mull (better than Skye, which is also beautiful). For a single day trip Loch Lomond (train to Balloch) is nice.
culture_adjustment: Easy, the nicest people i've met.
socializing_tips: Go to sports socials.
cultural_challenges: The accent can be tricky.
culture_appreciated: The going out culture and the chattyness.
top3_advice: You can drink the water, but it tastes horrible. Don't bother to buy the books, most are available online or you can borrow them in the UNI library. Go on as man trips as possible in the beginning of your stay, suddenly exams are around.
other_useful_info: Never order half a pint and the ciders taste great. Go to society socials!
most_rewarding: The general forthcomingness of the people.
greatest_challenge: Getting my courses.
other_comments: If you are going on trips the best way is by car. It's a bit weid to drive in the wrong side of the road, but you will manage. It's definetely the best and cheapest way. Can definetely recommend Arnold Clark for car rental, sometimes you get a free upgrade and we never had any trouble with them. Avoid easyrent and other cheap places.

crucial_aspects: I have travelled to Scotland before and loved the mix of beautiful nature and citylife which made me choose Glasgow. In addition to this, going to an English-speaking country seemed to make it easiest for me socially. I was also aware that this was my last chance to do an exchange to the UK through the Erasmus+ programme because of Brexit.
overall_comments: I would have loved to have met more Scottish people at the university. I'm not rating it a 10 because I also found that it was significant difficult for exchange students to find accommodation, something that impacted both mine and others experience negatively. The process of getting courses was very confusing as well, resulting in me not getting the courses that I hoped to.
info_ease: Not very easy. Mostly from my sending institution. The receiving institution didn't offer much information about process of application for courses.
arrival_assistance: The visiting team was a great help with any uncertainties I had. Overall, the communication with the institutions was fine, but not having ever been on exchange before it can be hard to know what exactly to ask when you yourself have to seek the information.
arrival_comments: Again, the visiting team was great in assisting me.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I would have loved to have met more Scottish people at the university. I'm not rating it a 10 because I also found that it was significant difficult for exchange students to find accommodation, something that impacted both mine and others experience negatively. The process of getting courses was very confusing as well, resulting in me not getting the courses that I hoped to.
registration_process: Overall it was fine. You had to seek the information independently and I also ended up paying for a language assessment test that wasn't needed as this wasn't clear. But if you seek information by e-mail they are happy to help.
registration_help: They had guides but mostly you had to email to get the information that applied specifically to you.
registration_success: Not succesful. I applied for 3 different courses, but as I was not informed that I didn't get 2 of those courses, I didn't know that I had to apply for two new courses and how. Instead I just wasn't registered. I quickly had to write and call just to get registered for any course.
registration_advice: Have the registration done as early as possible and just write the visiting team with anything you are uncertain of, because you are not going to get that information anywhere else.
academics_comments: I would have loved to have met more Scottish people at the university. I'm not rating it a 10 because I also found that it was significant difficult for exchange students to find accommodation, something that impacted both mine and others experience negatively. The process of getting courses was very confusing as well, resulting in me not getting the courses that I hoped to.
course_level: The level of the courses (in the assessment) at my host/receiving institution were lower than at UCPH. This could be a bit confusing to accommodate to.
teaching_comparison: They were very different. Not much theory was discussed in my classes at the host-institution. It seems that at my host institution, the teaching was very focused on active participation and discussion in smaller groups of people. At UCPH we mostly have lectures, but I know that they try to incorporate discussions although this can be difficult when you are more than 100 students. At UCPH we have classes of smaller groups of people to discuss the lectures, but it seems that these classes are removed to save money although they are very useful, especially to discuss theory.
courses_enrolled: 3 courses of 10 ECTS credits each. Migration, Settlement and Belonging. Ways of Living: Studying different worlds. Sociology of Cognition.
recommended_courses: Ways of Living as it was different from the courses at UCPH. The two others discussed themes I had already had mostly covered back home. I didn't get to choose the courses myself.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Food, both eating out and groceries, are a bit cheaper. Housing is veery expensive and difficult to find.
activities_available: Every kind you can think of! There are so many opportunities.
activities_recommended: I joined the community choir as it was very casual and I didn't have to commit for a whole year. It was great, also socially!
weekend_recommendations: I really liked the guided weekend trip I did to Isle of Skye. But go to the highlands! It is beautiful and you can go by train but I would stay for a night. There's also one-day hiking trails closer to the city which is great to do on a weekend, but go early as it gets dark early.
culture_adjustment: Very easy as their way of living is pretty close to what I am used to in Denmark. They are very polite and open.
socializing_tips: It was difficult, but talk to them in class and most importantly, join a club! Also, living with someone local could also be a great way to meet other locals.
cultural_challenges: None were challenging.
culture_appreciated: They are very down-to-earth and open to other people.
top3_advice: 1. Be aware of the possibilities of housing as soon as possible when applying for the exchange. 2. Don't get too attached to getting specific courses as you probably won't get the ones you want. They are all great and you are going to learn something useful anyway. 3. Say yes to everything social, especially in the beginning of your stay. You are probably going to have a nice time even though it can feel overwhelming. But also; respect your own boundaries - you don't have to be friends with everyone.
other_useful_info: You probably will mostly be with other exchange students, so try and meet people from other nationalities than you own! Also, a plus about going somewhere not too far from Denmark is, that you are able to easily go back and visit in years to come and see the city again! It also meant that my friends and family from Denmark could visit me during the weekends. It was great to share my new city with them.
most_rewarding: The friendship I got with my roommate. Also, the experiences in Scottish nature were amazing so make sure to get them even though you feel busy.
greatest_challenge: Definitely finding accommodation.

crucial_aspects: The university had a good reputation, there were student-friendly facilities, and the university was located in an English-speaking country.
overall_comments: It would have been a 10/10 experience if not for the pandemic and the industrial strike that took place during my stay.
info_ease: It was alright. There was a lot of information, which made it difficult to navigate.
arrival_assistance: I booked some appointments with the Visiting Students team. Also, I was connected with an Erasmus adviser in case I had any further queries.
arrival_comments: The staff was ready to help immediately after arrival. However, it took a while (and quite a lot of correspondence with different people) before I found my contact persons.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It would have been a 10/10 experience if not for the pandemic and the industrial strike that took place during my stay.
registration_process: I applied for courses before I went to Glasgow. In the introduction weeks, it was possible to change the courses (also after you have attended a few tutorials).
registration_help: I was connected with an Enrollment adviser. Furthermore, it was possible to message the course convenors.
registration_success: Fully successful. I also changed one of my courses during the stay.
registration_advice: I do not have any advice. The staff are so helpful.
academics_comments: It would have been a 10/10 experience if not for the pandemic and the industrial strike that took place during my stay.
course_level: The level of the courses was overall appropriate. I had three courses: one honours level and two undergraduate levels.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was very similar to the University of Copenhagen's style. The main difference was that all the tutorials were compulsive to attend, and they were more question-based and less group work-based. It was essential to prepare all the questions because the lectures could ask out of nowhere.
courses_enrolled: Roman Law Of Property & Obligations (LAW1007) Foundations of Evidence Law (LAW2052) Intellectual Property Law (Sem 2) (LAW3038)
recommended_courses: I would recommend IP-law due to Brexit. We took a post-Brexit view in the course, which was interesting since the UK still uses EU law, but at the same time, tries to be independent and develop its own case law. Furthermore, I would recommend Evidence Law if others want to try a course concerning common law.
unexpected_costs: Membership in the sports organization of the University (GUSA) and membership in the Handball team
cost_comparison: Housing and food were more expensive than expected. However, transport and beers were less expensive.
activities_available: Everything. Also, activities I did not even know existed.
activities_recommended: Anything. It is a great way to meet new people, think of something different and practise your English.
weekend_recommendations: Explore Scotland in general. Also, the Northern part of England is quite beautiful.
culture_adjustment: Easy, the Scottish culture is similar to the Danish.
socializing_tips: Join some of the activities at the University and chat with people in the classrooms (yes, we do not do that in Denmark, but it is pretty normal in Scotland).
cultural_challenges: The public transport system is way different. You cannot count on it, timewise.
culture_appreciated: The friendly people.
top3_advice: 1) Remember to enjoy every minute and try as much as possible! 2) It is always raining and windy. But sometimes it is in ridiculous circumstances that the funniest moments happen, so always remember a raincoat (so you do not get sick). Also, I would recommend hiking shoes if you are out of the city on an adventure. 3) Take to the fayres and chat with randoms
other_useful_info: There are good public transport deals in Scotland, so spend an afternoon researching the possibilities. Furthermore, it is prevalent to have student discounts (compared to Denmark), so remember to ask in the shops, bars etc.
most_rewarding: To be outside my comfort zone, improve my English and make friends for a lifetime.
greatest_challenge: The fact that you are on your own.
other_comments: Undoubtful the best decision I ever made.

crucial_aspects: I found it important that there was courses on the university within a field that I found interesting. However, I also went on exchange to explore new cultures and have a personal experience.

I had problems with the online platform for making the learning agreement - the text on the website was confusing and my receiving university did not receive it to sign, so I had to send it manually. Another irritation was that I had to make proof of arrival and departure for both receiving and sending university, instead of having a shared formular or something.

recommended_courses: Contemporarty Debates in Media Sociology and Understanding Empire were two good courses. The methods course was very beginner level.
unexpected_costs: Remember to set aside money for small trips to the countryside, and for other weekend-activities.

activities_recommended: I joined the Walking Society for going on hikes in the Scottish nature. I also recommend joining the Mature Students Association. A mature student in Glasgow is 23+, and for a small membership fee, you get access to a reading room, kitchen and other stuff in a small cool clubhouse at the university grounds.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the highlands! Especially Isle of Skye, Glencoe, Loch Lomond and the rest of the West Highlands.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Join a club or talk to people in your class.
cultural_challenges: There was not really any challenges. Scottish people are very friendly and easy-going.
culture_appreciated: Pub-culture. Go to a pub-quiz, small concert or just have a pint at the pub.
top3_advice: Start searching for accommodation as quickly as possible!!
other_useful_info: Be sure to go to some activities during Fresher's Week that is the intro-period at Glasgow Uni. That is where you might make new friends.
most_rewarding: Enjoying Scotland. Both the people and the Nature is some of the best in the world.
greatest_challenge: Finding accomodation.

crucial_aspects: The University of Glasgow is the the fourth- oldest university in the English speaking world. The university is also in top 100 rank of best universities in the world. Despite the beautiful architecture of the building, the university is also known for graduates as Adam Smith, Kelvin and many more. The Law School is very known in Scotland, which is one of the reasons why I chose the University. The campuslife is also very nice and the university is known for hosting a lot of different activies to students of all kind. The academic opportunites and the modern and including spirit of the university was the reason why I chose it,.
overall_comments: The administration before the abroad experience was not good. Two weeks before the application to "study abroad for Erasmus students" the University told us that Erasmus students are not guaranteed to be accepted unless they have an accommodation in Glasgow. You couldn´t reach the university during this whole period. It was also difficult to contact them in relation to choosing courses for the semester. Despite all the experience and the administration was good.
info_ease: It was easy. The University sent us a form with all the important information about the city and the university before our arrival.
arrival_assistance: Nothing
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The administration before the abroad experience was not good. Two weeks before the application to "study abroad for Erasmus students" the University told us that Erasmus students are not guaranteed to be accepted unless they have an accommodation in Glasgow. You couldn´t reach the university during this whole period. It was also difficult to contact them in relation to choosing courses for the semester. Despite all the experience and the administration was good.
registration_process: It was online, and easy. But very slow.
registration_help: Not much. The administration did not answer the questions because of the lack of capacity. It took forever to get responses back. I contacted previous students to get the relevant documents for my registration processes.
registration_success: I only got one course that I wanted due to the lack of capacity from the other courses.
registration_advice: Do it as soon as possible. And maybe contact other students for help. It may seem like a helpless procress, but when you are done then its worth it. The administration becomes very quick at responding and helping you as soon as you are accepted in the Uni. The University of Glasgow is a very good University and therefore would I recommend to trust the process.
academics_comments: The administration before the abroad experience was not good. Two weeks before the application to "study abroad for Erasmus students" the University told us that Erasmus students are not guaranteed to be accepted unless they have an accommodation in Glasgow. You couldn´t reach the university during this whole period. It was also difficult to contact them in relation to choosing courses for the semester. Despite all the experience and the administration was good.
course_level: The level of courses was a bit easier than I´m used to in my home university. There were a lot of reading in every lecture both essential and additional reading.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was not that different from my home institution. One course was online lectures with different videos from our professor. The two other courses worked as “Questions and Answers” in class. For each lecture, we got some questions to help us understand the lecture. We went through these in each class. The different thing was that I´m not used to having classes without any PowerPoint or other supplement to the class. The teaching style in one of my courses was a dialog with the teacher and the rest of the class without any PowerPoints and no breaks. I´m used to breaks in my home institution and we did not get any in Glasgow. This made the classes very long and it was different to concentrate the whole time.
courses_enrolled: Roman law of Property and obligations law, Criminal Justice and Contemporary issues in Healthcare law.
recommended_courses: Criminal Justice. If you are interested in criminal law then take this course. It gives you a good insight of the criminal justice system in UK and in Scotland.
unexpected_costs: A lot of ubers because the transportation system in Glasgow is not good when you are out late. From uni to the city center it costed around 12 pounds. It depends of course.
cost_comparison: Coffee, groceries and beer.
activities_available: There were a lot of different social activites available. Glasgow Union (GUU) had all kinds of different clubs you could be a part of. They also had a very good and cheap kitchen where me and my friends used a lot. Nice food. GUU also had their own night clubs only for students. Very good. Close to the union was the "students only gym". I did not attend my self but I heard from others that it was very good and cheap.
activities_recommended: Travel all over the country. It is a very beautiful country with nice people. The muserums are also free which is very nice.
weekend_recommendations: Do a highland trip and go to Isle of Sky and Glennfinnan (Harry potter bridge). It is unreal. There are also different kinds of islands you can go with your erasmus friends on the weekends. Also visit Edinburgh. It is an amazing city and only 1 hour by bus from Glasgow Burchanen Bus station.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. Scottish people are very friendly and polite. They are willing to help you in every situation which is very nice. Denmark and Scotland are very similar countries and cultures which made it a lot easier to adjust. Just go to a pub and order a Tennant (beer) or an irn bru and then you have already adjusted to their culture.
socializing_tips: Join a society or try to socialize with them in your class. Scottish people are very friendly and they are happy to show you around the city.
cultural_challenges: The food culture was a lot different from what I am used to. They also sell eggs outside of the fridge in the supermarket which also is weird.
culture_appreciated: Their politeness and friendliness and the focus on students' mental and physical health
top3_advice: 1. Try Irn bru (their national drink) 2. Live close to Campus 3. Explore Scotland (Highlands, other cities) in weekends
other_useful_info: no
most_rewarding: Meeting amazing new people from all over the world and exploring Scotland with them. I really love nature which also was one of the reasons why I chose the University. Scotland is known for their nature, so make sure to travel to the highlands and to Isle of Sky. Everything was just so nice about Scotland.
greatest_challenge: Understanding Scottish and the transportation system in Scotland.
other_comments: no

crucial_aspects: I've spent time abroad in England beforehand and loved the experience. So it was very natural for me to go to Scotland as an extension of that experience. I've always loved the idea of Scotland and wante to experience the culture and people myself.
info_ease: It was ok. Their systems can be quite tricky to work out - especially getting courses was a very tedious process. I'd encourage others to not put too much faith in getting their initially approved courses. I thought I'd be able to have courses outside of my faculty (Sociology) - but that was not allowed. Neither were Master-level courses which was a shame.
arrival_assistance: Assistance in picking courses - but only due to how convoluted the process was.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Had to fill out an arrival form - which was easy enough. Then I had to show up to an office where I was officially registrered and got my student ID - pretty easy overall
registration_help: Not much - they're very busy upon student arrival so communications are very hard to come by
registration_success: Getting classes is terrible. As an international student you are second in line to choose courses (Glasgow Uni's own students get to pick first) so many courses are already filled when they're available to Erasmus Students. The enrollment process is also way too tedious - you have to send a lot of emails and accept the fact that you will probably have to select at least 2 new courses. The course catalogue provided by the university is also not up to date - at least it does not properly show which courses are available on what semesters. So just have in mind that you will have to settle on some courses you might not have thought to take. You are also not allowed to do Master-level courses. While there are certainl interesting courses on their Bachelor's it is a shame not to have that possibility - especially because it narrows the amount of courses available to international students drastically.
registration_advice: Don't put too much faith in getting your pre-approved courses. Have patience - the enrollment is VERY slow and VERY tedious. You might not have any courses at all until October depending on your (un)luck. And don't choose Master courses - you won't get them.
course_level: Not Masters
teaching_comparison: A lot of it was very good - in smaller classes with about 30 people. Lecturers were very passionate and immensely knowledgeable which is great.
courses_enrolled: Understanding Empire Contemporary Debates in Media Sociology Quantitative Methods in Social Sciences
recommended_courses: Understanding Empire - It's an amazing course on Imperialism and it's consequences taking both a very historical and sociological view of mechanisms and causes of Imperialism and how consequences manifested from this. THe course lecturer, Andy Smith, is an absolute delight to have and is so passionate about teaching - I'd recommend any course he teaches. If you are interested in media sociology take Contemporary Debates in Media Sociology - it's a great course as well with a very good lecturer. DO NOT TAKE THE QUANTITATIVE METHODS COURSE - IT IS AWFUL
unexpected_costs: Generally - high housing costs and public transportation, as well as Ubers.
cost_comparison: Food is cheap compared to Denmark - even their vegan options (like meat replacements) can be found pretty cheap if you look in the discount shops (Iceland, Farmfoods). Pints are also cheaper!!!
activities_available: There are loads of clubs and associations to join on the uni - I'd recommend going to the sports clubs' taster sessions were you can try out the different sports. Don't feel bad if you don't have the time to properly join though - there's loads to do anyways Join the walking society if you're interested in smaller hikes
activities_recommended: Find a good pub with a good pub quiz! They're all over town and is a great way to spend an evening with your friends. Join the gym - it is decently priced for students - but it is absolutely huge - and comes with a swimming pool, sauna, steam room and free spinning classes!
weekend_recommendations: GO TO THE HIGHLANDS. There are student organized trips - like going to Isle og Skye See if you can climb some the higher mountains (called Munroes). Visit Edinburgh
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy if you enjoy drinking pints
socializing_tips: Everyone is friendly and striking up conversation is very easy. If you want to socialise more - join a sports club or an association there's also a Nordic Society if you feel homesick
cultural_challenges: They drive in the wrong side of the road,so biking is not recommended
culture_appreciated: Friendliness
top3_advice: Go to the highlands at least once - it is truly beautiful Go to the Old Toll Bar on the Southside (by Kinning Park station) - Seriously it's THE BEST BAR in Glasgow by far, and has something going on everyday (live music, dj's etc.) And their wednesday pub quiz is amazing. I am not kidding go there. at least once. There's always something to do in Glasgow - whether it be going to pubs, joining a sports club or a society - find something that interests you and stick to it. You will probably not get around to everything on your bucket list.
other_useful_info: Whisky tastings! Go on a tour of the Clydeside Distillery!
most_rewarding: Making new incredible friends
greatest_challenge: Housing - make sure you're looking out for rooms early

crucial_aspects: I wanted somewhere that was very gothic and that gave Hogwarts vibe with interesting subjects, and I got that from university of Glasgow
overall_comments: there were some administrative issues
info_ease: Somewhat easy. The univerisity of Glasgow was good at helping and they gave very useful information. there was also a welcoming team (online) and if one wanted to then you could book an introduction or something like that (I didn't do that)
arrival_assistance: We had to watch some videos about how it would be to study there and just an introduction in general to choosing courses etc. Really helped with any confusion
arrival_comments: There were however some issues with the administration. They took in 2000 people too many, and they mixed up my classes so I got 2 almost identical ones. it was hard getting in contact with them because there were so many people experiencing issues and the wait was up to 7 days. When I finally got in contact witht hem then i was given a choice of 3 subjects (all law) (none of which I wanted) and i had to pick one because I needed the ECTS points. I then had to write home to my home univerisyt to check if they could tranfers my points for the new classes because I had not gotten the other one pre approved. They said that it would probraly not be a problem, but I had to just take the class and hope that it got approved. luckely it got approved, but it was very stressfull. therefore I did not have all of my classes until it was the end of week 2/ start of week 3. I know many other exchange students also didn't get enrolled in the right courses (like me) and some couldn't see their schedule. There were therefore many issues with the administration, but once it got settled then it was fine. it was just a bit stressful and uncomfortable for 2 weeks, and honestly, I was never supposed to have had 2 identical classes (I was told it shouldn't even be an option), and since it took them so long then I couldn't get the ones I wanted because by then they were already booked up, so I kind of ended up having the classes that no one wanted All in all then everything else was fine, but there was a huge mess with the classes and schedules for the exchange students (most likely because of covid). When I finally got in contact with someone, then they were very kind and helpfull
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: there were some administrative issues
registration_process: You had to book a slot so they could check your visa, you meet up at the time and place, they check it and you are good to go.
registration_help: You could always ask people who where there to help or you could email the visiting students team
registration_success: I got 2 out of 3 classes that I wanted... i got to almost identical ones (one was scots law and the other were common law but in the same subject(criminal law)) and because of this mistake then when they had to move me then the other 4 classes that I had requested as backup (in case I didn't get the ones I really wanted) were already filled up, so I had to choose from the ones that were left... this really sucked because I couldn't do anything different, it was the University who had made a mistake... I know this happened to multiple people or other issues in the same genre, such as not being able to see your schedule, not being on the moodle page etc etc...
registration_advice: I would advice that you apply for 5-6 courses even though you might need less (I needed 3), just in case your class gets booked! I did this myself but because of the administrative mistake then I didn't matter in the end, but it is still a good idea, because if everything had worked as it should, then I would most likely get all the classes that I wanted.
academics_comments: there were some administrative issues
course_level: The level was somewhat the same if not easier. I would not pick classes where you are supposed to know something about the English constitution etc, since we don't know about that in Denmark (not a part of our legal education), but if it is learning something completely new (like healthcare law or criminal law or roman law), then the level seemed the same or easier in spite of it being in English/Scottish
teaching_comparison: We had lectures and tutorials. lecture= forelæsning, tutorial= seminarundervisning. healthcare; had only lectures where we were about 50 people ca. criminal law; had lectures where we where the entire year and tutorials where we were about 10-15 people on each team roman law; this was a year 4 class, so we were about 20 people ( reminds me very much of "seminar" as back home)
courses_enrolled: Principles of Healthcare Law Criminal Law of England and Wales introduction to Roman world
recommended_courses: Would recommend first year classes if you want to have time to experience other stuff, but I would recomend year.3 or 4 if you want to study-study
unexpected_costs: I used Uber a lot. I broke my foot so had to be transported around so that was a bit more expensive
cost_comparison: Drinks are only 4-6 pounds but a bottle of gin is 18 pounds in a supermarket
activities_available: there where book clubs, sports clubs, movie clubs, social clubs, fandom clubs, baking clubs etc etc! so many options
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining a club if you want to make friends easily! I met one of my closest friends at a mature student mixer and my other friend group I met at Taylor swift/ Shrek karaoke event that the 2 clubs held! if you are kind and open-minded then there are a lot of people who want to be friends! there are also many students in town; I met a girl at a coffee shop where we just chatted, so it is also possible to meet people off campus
weekend_recommendations: the highlands, Edinburgh is only a train ride away! I went on trips with international students ( I would not recommend viva tours) and it was so fun! I saw Scotland for a cheap price, and I made new friends! I went on maybe 6-7 tours like that and I always did it alone and at the end of the day, I always made at least one new friend!! it is possible to do it alone and still enjoy stuff, so I would say go for it! would also recommend Luss, it's not that far away and the nature is pretty if you pick a good hiking route
culture_adjustment: It was super easy! there is not much of a change except that the cars are driving on the other side of the road
socializing_tips: Just be kind and open! Join clubs and not just the erasmus club!! and speak to your fellow students
cultural_challenges: none really, only the car thing (which is minor)! and the clubs close a bit early
culture_appreciated: the kindness and it was fun hearing about the Scottish culture
top3_advice: found housing (early), be openminded and it can be a bit lonely at times (and that is okay)
other_useful_info: i really enjoyed naked soup, i went there every thursday with my friends for a cheap lunch and it is such a great vibe
most_rewarding: I really pushed my boundaries and learned so much about myself. I feel more independent since I have lived in another country and studied in it!
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was the academics and the making of friends. You have to put yourself out there in a different way and you are on 24/7 but I think it is worth it
other_comments: Enjoy the time, it really flies!!

crucial_aspects: Exploring Scotland and a different legal system.
info_ease: A bit difficult due to an excessive amount of information from the universities but manageable.
arrival_assistance: Almost none. Assistance in regard to register at the university and with courses wasvery difficult to get assistance with as they had not prepared for the number of students arriving.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to meet up at the University to register with my passport.
registration_help: Limited avaible help due to the high number of incoming international students - I had to figure everything out on my own by asking people around and the like.
registration_success: Again, due to the university's lack of preparation for the high number of students I was registered for two of my planned courses whereas the last one was decided for me by the faculty.
registration_advice: Make sure to be in contact with other students from your sending institution and contact the university/faculty before you leave for exchange in regard to the registration process since there are a lot of things to consider and do when you arrive.
course_level: Bachelor courses
teaching_comparison: Two out of three courses were primarily taught virtually and could be viewed at anytime which was very convenient as opposed to UCPH who shut down virtual teaching after COVID-19. Apart from that, the teaching style at UofG was similar to that of UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Criminal Law and Evidence Advanced International Law International Private Law
recommended_courses: I would recommend Criminal Law and Evidence as well a Advanced International Law as they were interesting and the knowledge I gained with these courses, I can use (to a smaller degree) in relation to my education at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: Housing prices.
cost_comparison: Transportation (more expensive that expected) and coffee (less expensive than expected).
activities_available: UofG have over 100 different societies which included focus on different sports, nationalities, gender, sexual orientation, several types of hobbies, legal societies etc.
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining one or more societies at the university, explore Glasgow and the highlands, the pubs etc.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely the Scottish highlands and Edinburgh. There is a Facebook group called 'International Student Tours (Scotland) Glasgow' which arranges trips to Loch Ness, Isle of Skye etc. and you see and learn a lot about Scottish culture and history - however, you only stop at beautiful view points between 10-30 min. so if you want to see these things in a a more relaxed setting you should arrange a trip yourself with some friends. You can visit the Isle of Arran by travelling with train from Glagow Central Station to Ardrossan Harbour and then with ferry to Brodick Station. You can visit the Devil's Pulpit (Finnich Glen). And lastly, explore Glasgow which is a hidden pearl behind the "touristy" Edinburgh.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, the locals were extremely friendly and open.
socializing_tips: Join some societies and clubs at the university and go to the pubs, nightclubs etc. The local students are a bit reluctant to talk to international students but many of them are also a bit younger than e.g. Danish students as some begin studying at the university at 17. However, the more mature and older local people are generally very friendly and a heart-warming people.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness, history/tradition and humour.
top3_advice: 1) Involve yourself with all the possibilities that UofG has to offer, incl. events, societies etc. 2) Do not underestimate the academic level - especially if the legal system is different to yours. 3) Make sure to meet people from all over the world and go on trips during the weekends.
other_useful_info: The academic level is high - like at UCPH - so make sure to not neglect or underestimate your studies.
most_rewarding: Meeting wonderful people and making friends which I'm still in contact with as well as having explored Scotland and the Highlands.
greatest_challenge: 1) International Private Law - Was a difficut subject when you did not receive any introduction to Scottish law beforehand and no consideration was given to international students. The teacher and staff strikes during the semester also did not help and the workload and exam did not match the knowledge achieved throughout the very short semester.

crucial_aspects: Scottish nature and outdoor opportunities.
info_ease: It was quite easy. I just paid attention to my email both at KU and at Glasgow. However, I found the enrollment process quite stressful, since Glasgow University where short on staff, which made the repsonse time quite long
arrival_assistance: I did not really receive any assistance. I had to seek out a lot of information myself.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: In the first week I went for my visa registration on campus. Afterwards I finallised my course-wish list. But I did not end up getting any of the courses I initially applied for.
registration_help: There was hardly any help available in person. I contacted the exchange supervisor a couple of times, but I had to wait almost 5 days between answers, which was very irritating
registration_success: As I mentioned, I did not get any of the courses I wanted. It was only when I actually arrived in Glasgow that I was able to see the University's final course catalogue.
registration_advice: Don't get too stressed about the long registration process, and long waiting time. Prepare yourself for the possibility that you will not get any of the courses you have planned for
course_level: I would say there is a bit more reading for the different sessions. I did not have any lectures but only seminars. I would say the academic level was a bit lower than at UK, but I did not really mind it.
teaching_comparison: No lectures, only seminars. More groupwork than at KU. Also there are midterms exams, and the semester is only 10 weeks. So all in all, more intense than a semester at KU
courses_enrolled: Sociology of Cognition - How Do We Know What We Know? Ways of Living - Studying Others Aftermath of Atrocity
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend the two last courses. The first was an introductory course to anthropology, but it was nice to dive into some classic texts and get presented with new terms and theories. Aftermath of Atrocity was very interesting course; it dealt with how societies and groups of people move on, find justice and reconciliation after atrocities such as mass genocide, ecocide, civil wars etc. The lecturer used a lot of anthropological documentaries, photos and so on the compliment the teaching
unexpected_costs: I had prepared to a lot of trips to the Scottish Highlands, which can be quite expensive due to trains, transport, accomodation. In that light, I did not really have any unexpected costs during my semester. But I will note, that groceries and eating out in Scotland is a lot cheaper than in Denmark
cost_comparison: Groceries and eating out was less expensive. Everything else was more or less the same as in Denmark
activities_available: A lot of sport activites were available. I did not join a whole lot, because I wanted to focus more on my trips to the Highlands and around Scotland
activities_recommended: Join the walking society. Make sure to get out the city, the highlands and Scotland is very beautiful. One trip is NOT enough
weekend_recommendations: Isle of Skye Moffat-region. Stay overnight in a bothy (the scottish version of a danish 'shelter') Oban - cute fishing village on the west coast Loch Lomond - beautiful plays for days trips out of Glasgow Inverness - capital of the Highlands Visit Edinburgh - a whole other vibe and city than Glasgow, so it is nice to see and experience the difference between these two cities
culture_adjustment: I think it was quite easy. Scots are very friendly and welcoming
socializing_tips: Do not worry about your english-level, you will get by just fine.
cultural_challenges: I did not really encounter and challenging cultural differences. Scottish youth culture seems to be fairly similar to the Danish
culture_appreciated: The warmness and friendly vibes of the scots.
