crucial_aspects: Interesting courses and academic opportunities, possibility for creating social network and the destination to be economical accessible.
overall_comments: I assume 10 being the best in the above question.
info_ease: Very easy: The host university had a great introductional 'webinar' before arrival with a lot of useful information on e.g. public transport, necessary apps for the university and city, cultural differences, etc. Furthermore, the host university had a monthly newsletter with additional information on special events in the area and important deadlines on the university. Upon arrival a very detailed information sheet was send by the host university. Overall, I found myself to be informed upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: When arrived at my study destination, a short welcome/introduction meeting was held at the university, where further information was given. Including how to find one's class room and making sure that our student ID was ready, etc. I have not sought any specific assistance out - just attended the scheduled meetings, where I found to find all the needed information.
arrival_comments: Very professional approach at my host institution and the contact persons were very helpfull and open-minded.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I assume 10 being the best in the above question.
registration_process: I received some information by email on how to navigate and how to apply for courses. Finding the specific courses relevant for me was a bit time-consuming as the semester is structured a bit differently compared to UCPH. So some courses, I would have liked to take, were not possible because of study pace and ECTS-points. Otherwise, the registration process itself was easy and not complicated: on arrival I went to the student information center and got my courses accepted through their system and got my student ID. And I was ready to attend my courses.
registration_help: The student information center at my host institution - super helpful, did most of the additional registration in their system at arrival.
registration_success: Once I got to know which courses I had gotten, everything went smoothly. It was the process of finding the right courses, which was a bit time consuming and troublesome. I did not get my first priorities in courses, but the courses I ended up in were very interesting.
registration_advice: Be open-minded towards the courses. Some subjects might have been covered in earlier courses at your home university, but the approach and was of teaching/discussing can be very different in different countries and/or universities. And take your time with the registration process; it might take a bit longer than expected.
academics_comments: I assume 10 being the best in the above question.
course_level: The two courses were based on a discussion-approach. We had lectures once a week and a discussion class once a week, which is less physical presence than what I have been used to at my home university. The reading amount was suitable for a 15ECTS-course and we were to write short reflection on the readings for each week. One presentation on our final paper was to be held and then the final paper was to be submitted as the exam.
teaching_comparison: Less teaching, more discussion among us students. We did go through some of the theories and approaches but far from everything on the reading list, which I am used to at UCPH. So overall, there was more flexibility and self-study which was great in order to meet up with other students at the library, etc.
courses_enrolled: GS2101 Critical Studies on Gender Equality Policy and Diversity GS2207 Body politics from feminist perspectives
recommended_courses: I would recommend the two courses I was enrolled in - if one is interested in the subject. The flexibility enables that one can schedule different activities and makes it easier to attend e.g. ESN events. But choose courses and subjects which you find interesting - there is a greater possibility of meeting people with the same interest.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: I did not pay for internet nor for laundry, all additional costs such as water, electricity, etc. was part of my housing rent. Many expenses were more or less the same as in CPH; I was keeping an eye on the development of the Swedish crown (SEK) - but overall it was low throughout my stay. Therefore, the expenses were lower than expected.
activities_available: Knitting events, informational speeches, networking with fika. The host institution itself did not arrange that many activities but made students aware of events arranged by others. The host institution arranged an event were all student unions and different student driven clubs were presented to the exchange students. The host institution offered a free swedish class.
activities_recommended: If possible, take part in the events hosted by ESN (Erasmus Student Network) as they plan cultural activities and fun nights - a great way to get to know other exchange students and makes it easier to settle in fast. I took a Swedish class as well, since the university offered it for free. Furthermore, make sure to do something fun - I attended a pottery class in swedish and went frequently to the gym, where I tried some new sports. Go to close-by cities and visit the archipelago. Sign up for the "Studentlistan"; you can buy very cheap last-minute-tickets to the teater and opera.
weekend_recommendations: Make a trip to close-by cities such as Allingsås or Marstrand and go to Stockholm (one can find some cheap train tickets from Gothenburg!) and a must is to go to the archipelago (Skærgården) - my favorits were the southern islands. Sweden has lots of beautiful nature, so I spend many weekends on hikes. There is something called "Fritidsbanken" were one can borrow outdoor-gear for free; perfect for students!
culture_adjustment: Very easy: Sweden and Denmark are very similar in culture. There are, however, differences which might be somewhat surprising as one tend to think that the countries are almost the same. My experience is that Sweden has a more laid-back culture; deadlines weren't taken too seriously in class or in swedish class and coming a bit late to social events was not considered rude.
socializing_tips: It requires a greater effort to make contact with the locals from your side. Many will probably have an approach a la "you're only here for one semester, why should I invest in you", why you yourself have to be more outgoing/outreaching. It is, however, easier to socialize with local students when coming from CPH/DK. If you attend courses with international students, as I did, do some things in your spare time which allows you to meet local students.
cultural_challenges: The cultural differences weren't that noticeable. I was surprise of the laid-back culture at the university.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and I got to appreciate the laid-back approach.
top3_advice: Make sure to attend as many events/activities as possible when arriving: this is how you get to meet people. You only get to stay one semester so make sure to integrate yourself quickly in order to get the most out of your exchange. Website: make sure to take a look at the host institution's homepage as they are announcing events and important deadlines. And don't hesitate to contact the institution if/when you have questions. Enjoy! Time goes by fast. Eventually make a list of things you would like to know, experience, see. Ask your professors for academic events if interested - such as study programme celebrations, inspirational speeches, etc. Professors often know what happens at the faculty.
other_useful_info: Instagram was a great source for inspiration on places to visit, flee markets, open air concerts, etc. So check it out! The host institution and the different faculties and studenterkår also have instagram profiles - make sure to follow them as well.
most_rewarding: Getting to know people, challenging myself in regard of having to create a network from scratch and attending events on my own, get to try new hobbies, getting to know different academical approaches and having to explain/argue in an understandable way so the audience understands your points clearly.
greatest_challenge: Attending events on my own in the beginning and very overwhelming getting to know so many people. And the darkness; I did not expect it to be so much more dark - and how long time it takes for spring to arrive.
other_comments: There will be ups and downs. Some days may not be very interesting, other days may be overwhelming.

Other internationals will be more open to connecting with you.
culture_appreciated: The Swedish efficiency and organisation. Fika.
top3_advice: Find housing fast, preferably through the University. Don't have too high expectations on making friends with Swedes, it is more likely you will be friends with other internationals. Prepare for an even darker winter.

greatest_challenge: The darkness in the Winter. Socialising with local students.

registration_process: It is a very different system as Sweden does "pace". This means that most often you will only have one course at a time if it has a pace on 100%. I had to 15 points courses both on 100% pace meaning a had one from september-november and then a course from november-january. So you do the exams during the semester. This also means a lot of courses can't be combined as they have to be in different periods of the semester or have the same pace fx both on 50% meaning in total 100%.
registration_help: You could always ask the administration and they had really good examples to help. But it was difficult to find combined courses as a lot where on the same time. So i had to compromise with my choices to make it work.
registration_success: In the end i got just what i wanted but i also only had 3 possible combinations of courses so i would be satisfied no matter the outcome.
registration_advice: Look at the paces and times of the semester! This makes it immediately clear which subjects you can combine so you don't fall in love with two courses in the same period.
academics_comments: Gothenburg is not necessarily a destination a lot of people choose. But that is really lovely because then you will meet many different people from many different countries and not just rely on danes. Also got several swedish friends!
course_level: It was very similar to the danish level. But because you only have one course at a time i only went to school 1-2 times at the most 3 times a week. I had a lot of readings and home written papers though which was more demanding during the semester but then less during the exam period. They also have mandatory seminars which also required more preparation.
teaching_comparison: It was very similar traditional lectures with the same breaks and meeting hours. Some of the teachers have also worked at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Global gender studies and Human rights in policy and practice
recommended_courses: Especially Human rights in policy and practice! Learned so much from that course especially in this time in the world. I already had gender studies before this course but a lot of topics were still new or elaborated so i would also recommend this.
unexpected_costs: Trips and fika (afternoon coffee and cake)!
cost_comparison: Alcohol and groceries.

You can also go to Oslo or Stockholm. And please visit all the lovely second hand stores.
weekend_recommendations: Islands, Oslo, Stockholm visit other friends in europe! Go on the ESn trips. Party, go to funny bars and FIKA!!
culture_adjustment: Very easy as a dane. You don't have to speak english at cafes or when shopping. The Culture is also basically the same.
socializing_tips: Often there are also swedes in your course. I gained swedish friends that way. Otherwise dare to engage with others when going on bars or cafes. But class is definitely easiest.
cultural_challenges: Not many, maybe that they don't really bicycle. Also that pretty much can't smoke anywhere but since i don't it was just nice. Also systembolaget where you buy alcohol is closed after 15 on saturdays so always have some beers or wine at home.
culture_appreciated: Fika again, just love how they always prioritise coziness. Also how polite they are was really lovely.
top3_advice: 1. Really go through the courses and see if they match in time and pace 2. They really want you to pass so don't feel to strongly about failing or missing assignments 3. Enjoy all the lovely cafes, libraries and school facilities
other_useful_info: Have an international bank account as Revolut as it allows free international payment. The app is exactly like mobilepay.

greatest_challenge: It is scary to study at another school you don't know the expectations and level. But you truly develop from a challenge. Even though everything was new in different in the beginning it ended up being the most relaxed and beautiful time through my whole university experience.
other_comments: Go to GU and have fun!

crucial_aspects: The specialisation "Forest and Nature Management in times of climate change" offered at the university of Göttingen resonated most with my interests and future career aspirations.
info_ease: We received most of the relevant information per email and from the international student coordinator. It was also quite useful to talk to other students who had done the exchange before or studied at the university of Göttingen already for longer. There was always someone to ask for help.
arrival_assistance: We received most of the relevant information per email and from the international student coordinator.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: We received help from our international student coordinator.
registration_success: I could register for all the classes I selected.
registration_advice: Remember to register for each semester!
course_level: Since I did not have a background in forestry, the level of courses was fine for me. However, for people with a background in forest and nature management, courses might have been perceived as repitition and a bit superficial.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was very different to the one at UCPH. First, there were less contact hours, i.e. only few hours of lectures each week and students were expected to study independently for the rest of the time. There was less group work, both in lectures and for assignments. Furthermore, the exams all took place at the end of the semester within 1-2 weeks, which increased the work load towards the semester much more. We also had only one oral exam, all the other exams were written. Generally, the atmosphere and relationship between students and teachers was much more anonymous than at UCPH.

recommended_courses: Monitoring of Forest Resources: very useful knoweldge about design of data collection and statistics Forest Management under Different Climatic Conditions: excursions and interesting insights into (German) forest management practices and climate change Bioclimatology and Global Change: very essential basic knowledge about our climate system and Biosphere Remote Sensing Image Processing with Open Source Software: very useful practical knowledge about the use of QGIS and Pyhthon

cost_comparison: None

culture_adjustment: It was quite easy for me, but I was also quite familiar with the local culture of the exchange site.
socializing_tips: I recommend to participate in the sports offers of the university or join other university groups.
culture_appreciated: Honesty and a very direct way to communicate

registration_comments: The fact that a lot of my classmates also chose to spend their second year in Göttingen made it really easy for me establish a healthy study/life balance. The size of the city was also very conducive for regular get togethers.
registration_process: For my program it is pretty straight forward, since we only had one restricted elective module, that we could choose out of a pool of 3 options. First you sign up for the courses at the beginning of the lecture period, sometimes there are deadlines, or passwords for course contents, so that you have to at least attend some of the lectures. The actual registration for the exams starts later, and then it is important to register. Usually it is being advertised regularly by the lecturers, and the process is also not very complicated.
registration_help: Asking classmates i guess, for me there was no help required, so i can not answer properly.
registration_success: 100% I got all the courses i wanted, and i registered all of them on time.
registration_advice: Just be aware of the registration deadlines for the exams, but they re usually pretty long, around after the christmas break.
academics_comments: The fact that a lot of my classmates also chose to spend their second year in Göttingen made it really easy for me establish a healthy study/life balance. The size of the city was also very conducive for regular get togethers.
course_level: There were some rather demanding courses like "monitoring of forest resources", or bioclimatology. I enjoyed attending the lectures and studying together with my classmates in the library. The other courses also had an appropriate level, except of the electives. The ECTS there felt a little easier earned then in the compulsory modules.
teaching_comparison: It was at times less intimate in Göttingen, i guess the style there is still a little more odl fashioned. I preferred the teaching style in Copenhagen, but i also got along really well with the lectures in Göttingen. We also had less assignments, since the entire semester is aimed towards the exams at the end, which are failry long and hard to study for. But all in all it was still a good experience, and i probably learned as much as i did in Copenhagen
courses_enrolled: 1. Monitoring of Forest Resources 2. Forest management under different climatic conditions 3. Bioclimatology and global change 4. Research planning 5. Ecological funtions of wildlife: implications for conservation and management
recommended_courses: Monitoring of forest resources: It really sharpens your mind and teaches you accuracy. You have to calculate and use logical thinking. It is by far the toughest, but for me the most rewarding subject even though the teaching style was a little strict, compared to what i was used from Copenhagen. It is one of the few subjects that teaches some kind of statistics and that is essential in this field in my opinion. Forest management under different climatic conditions: This was a nice balance to monitoring, it was about applied silviculture, it included a bunch of excursions, and it was very visual and interactive, i really enjoyed this module
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs in my case
cost_comparison: No items were more or less expensive than i expected. I think food is surprisingly cheap in Germany, also the cantines at the university.
activities_available: Through the university you can join many different sport clubs or get a membership for the gym or the swimming pools. The vaiety of available options was very big, and the fees very reasonable
activities_recommended: Going to bars, and doing sports via unisport. A trip to the Harz mountains is always worth a visit, and it is not too far too.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking, going to bars, the library and doing sports.
culture_adjustment: I am German, so there were no Problems
cultural_challenges: No challenges
culture_appreciated: I like the high level of conscientiousness and the general accuracy/scrutiny in Germany
top3_advice: Get ready to write long written exams at the end of the semester. Study throughout the semester, because the exams will be in very short intervals. And try to keep up your relaxed temperament, germany is not so bad afterall
other_useful_info: Nothing that i have not mentioned before.
most_rewarding: Spending my days at library with my study group before the exams. I never had such a yielding studying experience, and i never benefitted that much from my classmates before.
greatest_challenge: The greates challenge was the delay of my master thesis, other than that i was very focused on my studies and enjoeyed every bit of it

registration_comments: It has been the best time of my life! I have met my best friends from all over the world

course_level: It was a good level because they were easier than the ones I have in Copenhagen which was perfect considering they were in Spanish.

courses_enrolled: Introduccion a la psicologia (at anthropology) Español como lengua extranjera (at centro de lenguas modernas) Métodos y técnicas de investigacion de antropologia Developmental psychology (at the faculty of education) Historia del arte y patrimonio historico (anthropology)
recommended_courses: i liked the class Métodos y técnicas de investigacion de antropologia which was the most anthropological one where you get to make 2 interviews in spanish on a theme you choose to investigate. History of art was also interesting and the teacher Adrian was very good. I really recommen español como lengua extranjera as you take it with other exchange students and it's an easier class than the other courses and there is a nice environment in the class and very god teachers.
unexpected_costs: The laundry was 3€ and the dryer was 2,5€ at my residence.
cost_comparison: The taxis were cheap. But I travelled a lot to different cities and the busses can be a bit expensive. But I recommend you using blablacar or Amovens where you share a car with other people and it's faster than the bus.
activities_available: The university has a cultural centre called casa de porras, where there is all kinds of activities.
activities_recommended: I loved dancing and you can also go to the gym, play padel tennis, go swimming, go hiking, do ceramics, yoga, meditiation and many more activites.
weekend_recommendations: Go out eating tapas that you get for free with your drink. Go on the trips organized by Best life experience, Emycet and ESN, which is guided and transportation is included and it's cheaper than going on your own. Go to the beautiful viewpoints san miguel alto and san nicolas in Albaicin. Go to the live music places at eshavira club, planta baja, bohemia jazz cafe and there are many more.
culture_adjustment: Very easy! I felt more at home than in Denmark
socializing_tips: In your classes the spanish students don't always talk to you so approach them and say hi! You have nothing to lose! It's very easy making friends with other exchange students through the events of best life experience, emycet and esn
cultural_challenges: Everything is closed in sundays and also everyday around 14-17 o'clock
culture_appreciated: Everything!
top3_advice: Go there with an open mind where you will meet many new people from all over the world. Expect som long days at uni where they don't give you breaks, but it's worth it when you have the best freetime ever without much sleep.
other_useful_info: You should get a permission of residence called NIE at the oficina de extranjeria of the municipality (ayuntamiento). You can ask the international office of the information.
most_rewarding: The amazing people and I really loved going dancing bachata and salsa and they developed my spanish language skills a lot.
greatest_challenge: At the beginning it was difficult understanding the professors in spanish, because they also wore a mask. But you will get used to it quickly.

crucial_aspects: I wanted something different, and as I applied the "leftover" spots, there weren't many spots that I believed qualified as being very different from Denmark. Furthermore, I picked Spain because of the weather, culture and the people.
info_ease: Universidad de Granada was very good at making the transition smooth and the orientation was very thorough.
arrival_assistance: We had to orientation meetings, one for the whole university and one for the faculty of political science. We were offered mentors, and easy access to the Internalization Office
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I signed up for classes when i applied for the university, but you can also change your courses within the first month. I didn't do that, so I don't know how that works
registration_help: The internalization office was very helpful
registration_success: I got the classes I wanted
registration_advice: A groups are morning classes and B groups are evening classes (I had classes till 22, which was very unexpected)
course_level: I took 4 4th year courses and 1 3rd year courses, and they were not too difficult
teaching_comparison: It was very different. The classes were more "high school" like and not lecture based.
courses_enrolled: Political systems in the Maghreb, Sistema político y juridico en la UE, Política Comparada, Theory of democracy: Gender and interculturality, International organizations
recommended_courses: Many of my courses were very disappointing as some of the teachers were very unstructured and sometimes just didn't show up for class (Theory of democracy), and the teaching style was often very monotone and indifferent. I would recommend Political systems in the Magreb, the EU course and Política Comparada. The latter two ONLY if the future students speak spanish.
unexpected_costs: Granada is insanely cheap, and I did not have any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: In Granada you get free tapas when your order drinks, so you spend very little money on food - with that said groceries are not that much cheaper compared to DK
activities_available: There are Erasmus organizations that plan everything that your heart could ever desire including sports, social activities, cultural trips, etc. The school also offers sport activities
activities_recommended: Join some of the Erasmus groups as they are a great way to meet new people and experience Granada. There's also a Spanish school where you can learn Spanish, and I hear great things about that school (Center of Modern Languages)
weekend_recommendations: Visit other cities close to Granada, go hiking in Sierra Nevada or join events with the Erasmus groupss
culture_adjustment: For me the cultural shock was very intense and it took me at least 2 months to get used to it. But I think this goes for any place that isn't your home country.
socializing_tips: There is a pretty big language barrier, so it is best if you speak Spanish; if not there are not a lot of Spanish students who are proficient in English
cultural_challenges: Constant car honking; language barrier; more rudeness towards strangers compared to Denmark; often not very good service
culture_appreciated: The life of the city and the sense of community that was very apparent
top3_advice: - Speak or learn to speak Spanish - The classes are based a lot on active participation, so there are many presentations, papers and seminars that are mandatory - Some courses have different groups with different teachers. The individual teacher can decide on the exam, and whether or not there should be an exam. Research which group has the exam
other_useful_info: It's a very accommodating university, and if any questions should arise, the University is very helpful. I didn't personally take any sociology classes, but I know the "Sociology of Life" course wasn't very popular amongst my friends who took it.
most_rewarding: Learning Spanish, at least well enough to pass my Spanish exams
greatest_challenge: As mentioned, I had two Spanish courses and I only started learning Spanish in the Spring of 2023. This was very stressful, and even my friends who were way better at Spanish than me also struggled. So I would say only choose Spanish courses if you are actually comfortable speaking and listening to Spanish.

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The part that was most difficult was finding courses that could be equivalent to the courses I had back home, the application itself and the different types of documents to upload I actually found pretty easy to do in Mobility Online.
registration_help: You could ask questions at the welcome meetings, and could email and text the exchange office, I also found that the exchange students were good at helping one another
registration_success: I got all of the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: To keep all the documents you're asked to provide in one place so they can easily be found and also to ask if you're unsure.
course_level: The reports I read stressed that the level was a lot lower than the classes in Copenhagen, I would agree with this partially. Rather, I found that UGR uses a completely different type of learning then we're used to. Essentially, all of the classes are just about remembering information and being able to recite this information, there is very little discussion or debate if any, and you're rarely asked to analyze or compare which is what I'm used to.
teaching_comparison: It is clearly a more traditional learning environment, where what the teacher says, is what is correct and there is a lot less room for debate. Depending on the teacher I also experienced some getting slightly upset if I asked critical questions, however this isn't applicable to everyone and generally speaking I thought most of the teachers were nice enough.
courses_enrolled: International Organizations Theory of Democracy: Gender and Interculturality Sistemas Políticos de Países Emergentes (Political Systems of Emerging Countries) Politica Comparada (Comparative Politics) Sistemas Políticos y Jurídicos de la UE (Political and Judicial Systems of the EU) With these classes Comparative Politics + Political Systems of Emerging Countries = DAK3 Political and Judicial Systems of the EU + International Organizations = EP And Theory of Democracy was an elective course
recommended_courses: I'll be honest I don't have a specific class that I thought was very good. Instead, my recommendation would be to take some classes in Spanish if your goal is to learn Spanish. I had a lot of friends who only had classes in English, and then just didn't learn a lot of Spanish because it's hard to make friends with locals. While the Spanish classes are obviously harder, it also felt like a different way to get something out of the teaching, since the level is generally low.
unexpected_costs: None really, it's cheap to live in Spain and I didn't have to buy any books for my classes.
cost_comparison: Everything was less expensive than I expected, especially groceries you could get by really cheaply. Also if you go to the cafeteria at the University, you pay like 30DKK and get a very substantial meal, which I would often do and it saved me a lot of money.
activities_available: I know they had different sports activities and did movie showings etc. they go through them at the welcome meeting
activities_recommended: I wouldn't know.
weekend_recommendations: Granada is a very cozy town and I know a lot of exchange students also visit a lot of cities nearby like Cordoba, Sevilla, Malaga and also go to Sierra Nevada to hike or down to the beach. Generally, I found Granada to be a really nice place to live, even if it might be a bit boring to be a tourist in.
culture_adjustment: Obviously it's harder to adjust when you're also trying to learn a new language, but I think I found it pretty easy to adjust to the local culture
socializing_tips: Genuinely, just start a conversation, this is another reason I was happy to have classes in Spanish. The exchange students are usually pretty bad about only hanging out with other exchange students, but because I was in classes where I was one of very few international students, it made it a lot easier to talk to the spanish students. In my experience the local students were so welcoming and eager to invite you to things if you just said hi.
cultural_challenges: It was very weird to have classes in the evening, my classes from 8-10pm specifically was hard to get used to. I think the hardest thing was the language part, mainly just forcing yourself into situations where you'll be speaking Spanish.
culture_appreciated: I love how extroverted the Spanish people I became friends with were, and how easy they made it to be a part of their group even though my Spanish was terrible. So the people would absolutely have to be number 1, but the tapas culture if also amazing.
top3_advice: 1. That it is a very different type of learning which can feel very frustrating at times 2. If your goal is to learn Spanish, in my experience, you have to do more to achieve that then just be in Spain 3. Making local friends is not actually as difficult as it feels and really made my exchange
other_useful_info: Not really, but I remember that it can feel like such a chaotic experience to go through the process of registering and picking classes etc. So if you have any questions about what I've written in this evaluation or just questions in general you can text me on messenger, my name is Viktoria Ringsmose.
most_rewarding: To learn a new language and to make some great friends
greatest_challenge: To learn a new language and to get used to the different learning environment

crucial_aspects: For one, U of Guelph is the only university in Canada with an Animal Science program. Furthermore, the university in Guelph offered some very interesting courses. Other than that, I really wanted to try and live in Canada after being here on vacation several years ago.
info_ease: It was very easy! I can definitely recommend registering in the university's START International program (it's free!) because you get to arrive earlier than the rest of the students, which means that you can settle in and get more used to everything before classes commence. Also, they provide a lot of useful information AND free food. :))
arrival_assistance: The only assistance was the START International. You have to move all your luggage by yourself, and unless you know anyone in the country, you're pretty much on your own. People here are extremely friendly though, so you might be lucky to find someone to help you - or at least point you in the direction of help.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There wasn't much to it.. If you just check your different email accounts regularly, they pretty much guide you through the process. The exchange coordinators at the host institution replied quickly, and the only problem I had with the process, was that I didn't know until late Spring if I was actually going.. The host institution only needed a few documents from me and after submitting them, I just had to wait until I got my acceptance letter. From there, I filled out my information and preferences in the housing portal and I started browsing on the university's home page.
registration_help: Because I'm in Animal Science, I had a Science coordinator assigned to me and he helped me with all kinds of questions. If he didn't have the answer, he would help me figure out who to contact instead.
registration_success: I had made a list of 10 courses and I got 5. Thankfully, I got the one courses that replaced a mandatory one from U of Copenhagen! I really liked all of my courses, so I was lucky. It also won't hurt emailing the professor in charge of a specific course, if you didn't get registered for it the first time around. They are more often than not willing to let you into the course anyway; you just have to fill out a waiver. And if you then end up having too many courses, you can always drop one (or two). You just have to do it before the last day of classes.
registration_advice: See my comment above. Also, if you have the chance, go for courses that you can't find in Denmark! I really enjoyed my Indigenous course! I found that the level of education was generally lower than at home so don't sweat it if you end up with 5 courses. That being said, more 2nd and 3rd year courses tend to have midterms and exams so if you want to avoid that, try registering for 4th year courses. All in all, take the time to look through the different programs and the courses they offer; you might find an interesting course that you didn't know existed.
course_level: As I mentioned before, the academic level of education is generally lower than what we're used to in Europe, but most of my courses were still interesting.
teaching_comparison: 1. We weren't required to read anything before coming to the lectures. They had recommended readings but you didn't have to read it to be able to do well in the courses. 2. The lectures themselves were similar to those at UCPH, although we didn't really have guest speakers. Also, it seemed more like they were reading out loud from a script rather than making it engaging. 3. The assignments in most of my courses were graded by TA's (teacher's assistants) rather than the professors themselves. 4. I only had 3-ish hours of lectures per course per week. Except for the one distant-education course, I was enrolled in. It took me between 30 and 60 minutes per week to finish the readings and the quizzes. 5. Assignments are much more important at my host university. On one hand, I really liked the fact that the grades from the assignments had an impact on the final grade. On the other hand, we had so many assignments that we just went from one to the other.. It got quite stressful sometimes.
courses_enrolled: ANSC*4010 Animal Welfare Judging and Evaluation ANSC*4560 Pet Nutrition ENGL*1030 Effective writing IES*1010 Intro to Indigenous Environmental Science and Practice
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend registering for an Indigenous course if you have the chance. It's a great way of learning about the different ways of thinking and acting, and it also gave me a better understanding of how Indigenous Peoples have been and still are being treated in today's society. Also, these courses tend to be more down to Earth, and we even had our lectures at the Arboretum at the north end of campus. If you're in Animal Science and interested in nutrition, I would definitely choose Pet Nutrition as well. You'll get a better understanding of the different nutritional components of dog and cat food, and you'll even get to create your own recipe.
unexpected_costs: I ended up doing some traveling out west but other than that, I wasn't really surprised by any unexpected costs. IMPORTANT! the housing fee had to paid in full before arrival! It wasn't paid on a monthly basis which means that I paid ~23000 DKK in August.
cost_comparison: I think I was expecting things to be more expensive than at home but it turned out that groceries and books were around the same prices as in Denmark. Clothes etc. were a lot cheaper than at home!
activities_available: More than I could count! There were so many different things happening all the time that I didn't have time to go to even half of them.. There is definitely something for everyone - and I mean EVERYONE.
activities_recommended: I found out that I really like going to hockey games - both the games at the university but also the ones in downtown Guelph. In general, I will just recommend future exchange students to try as many different things as possible. Even if you don't find that one perfect club/activity, you will at least meet a lot of new, interesting people. It's a great way of making connections and maybe even friendships. TIP! Don't be afraid to go to an activity alone! People are more inclined to approach you if you're not surrounded by a bunch of people.
weekend_recommendations: Maybe rent a car and go hiking in the areas around Guelph. Or take a weekend trip to Toronto or Niagara Falls. On the weekend, the farmers' market in Guelph is open and it's just lovely! It's quite small but you can get some great things there. Their apple cider donuts are amazing! There is a huge farmer's market in the neighboring city called St. Jacobs Farmers' Market and it's incredible. You could easily spend a whole day - or maybe even a full weekend - there!
culture_adjustment: I found it very easy. Canadians are in general extremely friendly and helpful so if you just keep an open mind, you'll do just fine. One thing, that was tricky getting used to was mentally adding taxes to everything.. The price tags show the price without taxes so you have to mentally add the 13% yourself which takes some time getting used to. Especially at restaurants where you also have to tip the waiter.
socializing_tips: As mentioned before, don't be afraid to go to social gatherings alone and if you're just friendly and outgoing, it won't be difficult to socialize. Also, if you feel like you are bonding with someone, ask them to go out for a cup of coffee or to meet up for lunch on campus. I made some great friendships just by meeting up with a couple of people weekly.
cultural_challenges: The taxes.. ;))
culture_appreciated: I absolutely loved the friendliness and openness I was met with most places! Although it didn't always seem sincere (especially in grocery stores), I really liked that people greet each other with "How are you?". Even if people couldn't care less about you or your day, it's still ingrained in them to be friendly. And then most of the time, people would actually mean it and it could just make my day being met with a smile and that question.
top3_advice: 1. Don't forget to enjoy your time in a different country! This is a once in a lifetime experience so make sure to not spend too much time studying. 2. While enjoying the non-academic parts of the stay is essential, it's also important to keep up with your courses. It would be foolish to just make it go to waste by failing everything. Make an effort, please! 3. Make friends! Go to the different activities happening and see what happens. You are definitely going to become friends with some of the other exchange students but I can only recommend also getting to know some of the Canadian students.
other_useful_info: You will experience three seasons (Summer, Fall, Winter) while being there in the Fall semester so pack accordingly. Also, don't worry about packing Winter clothes; you can buy it when you get to Canada. This will also work out better for you since the clothes are more suited to the extreme weather changes compared to the things you get in DK. Especially boots and coats!
most_rewarding: Just being there and experiencing a new country with everything that comes with it.
greatest_challenge: Knowing that the people, I got to know, are living so far away from me.. Some of the people, I met, became like family to me and I don't know when I'll get to see them again. :/
other_comments: If you have a chance to go on exchange, GO! I cannot recommend it enough!

crucial_aspects: A place that I haven't been to before and a place that I found interesting
info_ease: It was fairly easy, it helped that I had a fellow student going to the same university
arrival_assistance: We had an exchanges team that we could e-mail and we had a start orientation where we got to meet the other exchange students. Unfortunately this orientation did not provide us with any practical information like where to get books, how to find our classes, where to get supplies for the kitchen etc. it mainly focused on the social aspects.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: First you have to find 8-10 courses that you would like/have to take, you have to get a pre-approval of the courses from your home university before you can apply to register. You also have to make sure that you have taken the right courses at your home university that would give you access to the courses you wish to take at your host university. On top of that you have to make sure non of the courses overlap in the schedule both with lectures and with the final exams. Some courses require an approval from the professor, so you would need to fill out the approval from with help form the exchange team or the professor. Sometimes if the exchange team says they can not help you get into a course, try to contact the professor directly. After you made sure of all of the above, you can apply to register, you will get assigned to 4-5 courses, and you can change and drop courses in the start of the semester.
registration_help: You can e-mail the exchange team or the professors. They also provide a PDF guide on how to register for courses.
registration_success: I was successful, I got into the courses I wanted to
registration_advice: Do not be afraid to contact the professors, they often want to help when you explain your situration.
course_level: The level of the courses was lower than expected, but I also took some 2nd and 3rd year courses where I probably could have taken 4th year courses. The final exams was a lot easier.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was similar, a lot of lectures, more and easier assignments at the host university than at UCPH, and less oral presentations at the host university. When grading assignments they would focus more on grammar and form than on the science, which I found very different.

unexpected_costs: All the kitchen supplies and bedroom supplies you have to buy when you first move in
cost_comparison: food was more expensive than I expected
activities_available: There were all sorts of clubs: k-pop, Caribbean community, indian community, muslim community, christian community, charity, innovation, international community, dance, soccer, swimming, rowing, book clubs, outdoors clubs, the list keeps going.
activities_recommended: I really liked going to the fitness center, and I enjoyed going to the events that the clubs put on.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going to Toronto, and to go to other provinces in the Canada, it is fairly cheap.
culture_adjustment: I found it really easy
socializing_tips: Do not be shy, maybe get involved in some clubs with a majority of local students or play sports.
cultural_challenges: People are very polite and will small talk to you in class, but often they will be hesitant to talk to you outside of class. And remember to tip service people and they add tax to everything even thought it is not on the price tag.
culture_appreciated: How nice and friendly people are, and how open and accepting they are.
top3_advice: Do not be shy, go outside of your comfort zone and remember to have fun.
other_useful_info: I don't think so
most_rewarding: All the friendships and memories I made
greatest_challenge: Finding time to do all the things I wanted to do, the times went by so fast.

crucial_aspects: I had the impression that the students were better in their practical skills than we were taught back home. And because it was another Nordic country did I aspect their English level to be around the same as my own. Other than that, I found it interesting to go to Finland because it is not a typical travel destination, and I would probably not have visited the country if it wasn't for an exchange.
overall_comments: The language was a big obstacle in my learning. And because either a student or a teacher didn't speak/ didn't want to speak English in the group most of the teaching would be in Finnish. Some teachers were better at staying in English, but a lot was really bad. Also, when there was a procedure that did not happened all the time, like a urine catheter, we would never get the opportunity to try (Other than in Saari) because the teacher would only ask in Finnish or the students would already have picked someone to do it without asking. Some departments were good, but it really depended on the students and the vet that was there. The Winter in Helsinki it though because people are very closed off and there are not a lot of social activities. But the spring is nicer, and people open more up, and it becomes easier to do outside activities I would recommend going here if you are interested in farm animals because you get to do a lot of practical work in Saari (the production animal hospital) and visit actual farms like in a normal practice. The problem here is that you must rely on the Finnish students to give you a ride because you can't go there with public transportation. And that some of the teachers here don't really speak English so you can't choose which teachers you would like to go on farm visits with, so sometimes you can end up looking at horses all day when you wanted to look at cattle.

registration_success: I only applied for the rotation and not for any courses so it was succesful
registration_advice: It was easy to change weeks in the hospital before arrival but afterwards when you had started it was almost impossible to change between the departments because there were too many students in the departments I wanted to be in as well
academics_comments: The language was a big obstacle in my learning. And because either a student or a teacher didn't speak/ didn't want to speak English in the group most of the teaching would be in Finnish. Some teachers were better at staying in English, but a lot was really bad. Also, when there was a procedure that did not happened all the time, like a urine catheter, we would never get the opportunity to try (Other than in Saari) because the teacher would only ask in Finnish or the students would already have picked someone to do it without asking. Some departments were good, but it really depended on the students and the vet that was there. The Winter in Helsinki it though because people are very closed off and there are not a lot of social activities. But the spring is nicer, and people open more up, and it becomes easier to do outside activities I would recommend going here if you are interested in farm animals because you get to do a lot of practical work in Saari (the production animal hospital) and visit actual farms like in a normal practice. The problem here is that you must rely on the Finnish students to give you a ride because you can't go there with public transportation. And that some of the teachers here don't really speak English so you can't choose which teachers you would like to go on farm visits with, so sometimes you can end up looking at horses all day when you wanted to look at cattle.
course_level: I only had practical learning in the small animal hospital and in the production animal hospital. There were no lectures and no exam but just practical day to day learning.
teaching_comparison: Hands on: Even though I didn't have as much hands on learning as the Finnish students I still got to do more then I would have back home. It is nice that the students gets to try a lot of stuff so it isn't the first time trying it in practice life. I improved skills like ultrasound, placing an iv-catheter and surgical skills. Time: The tempo in the hospital was very slow which could be frustrating but also gave you a lot of time to try technics and to be able to finish the paperwork and not be stressed which was nice.
courses_enrolled: I did the rotation where I was in these departments: small animal general polyclinics, diagnostic imaging, small animal internal medicine, on-call duty, small animal hospital special clinics; dermatology, cardiology and exotics and neurology, ophthalmology and dentistry, anesthesia small animal, surgery small animals and in the production animal hospital.
recommended_courses: I would recommend doing weeks in small animal internal medicine, small animal hospital special clinics; dermatology, cardiology and exotics and neurology, ophthalmology and dentistry, anesthesia small animal, surgery small animals and the production animal hospital. Anesthesia can be a little hard because there is a lot of people, and it can be a little stressful so they can quickly switch to Finnish. In diagnostic the teachers in ultrasound are really good at explaining in English but it is the nurses what takes the pictures in x-ray, and they don't really speak English, so it is hard to learn anything in there. They also have an MRI and CT machine, but the students are not really allowed in there.
unexpected_costs: Having to buy supplies for the apartment. Even though I brought as much as possible in reuse, I still spend 80 EUR.
cost_comparison: Groceries, alcohol and going out to eat was really expensive and so was going out to a bar. Public transportation was cheaper than I had expected and was easily accessible.
activities_available: We had our social tutor who introduced us to some events but often quite late. We had one international dinner with the tutors but other than that there was nothing planned for us. I followed ESNunihelsinki for information about international event and were told by other students which event I could come to
activities_recommended: Go to some of the events planned by ESN to meet other exchange students, make friends with the Finnish students so they can tell you about the events that are happening. But Vappu (the 1th of May) is a really big thing in Finland and you should definitely be in Helsinki for the parties in the streets surrounding that day.
weekend_recommendations: Experiences in Helsinki: All the touristy stuff you can easily do in the city: o Café Regatte: both in wintertime where you can walk on the ocean but also when the ice is melted, and you can just enjoy the beautiful view. Recommended at sunset o The Cathedrals: Both the white and the Russian. o The libraries: the national library of Finland and Oodi o Old market square o Temppeliaukio Rock Church o Helsinki Zoo o Esplanade Park with Havest Amanda o Suomenlinnia o National Museum of Helsinki o Löyly sauna o Sompa sauna – Free and a lot of locals here. Be prepared for a lot of nudity and a true Finnish experience. Outside Helsinki: o Turku: one- or two-day trip o Porvoo: half to one day trip o Tampere: one day trip o Tallin, Estonia: two day trip o Lapland: didn't manage to go myself but would definitely recommend it. 3 to 5 days - When the snow has melted/Hiking: o Kuusijärvi/ Sipoonkorpi National Park: Not that far from Viikki. Have a very nice sauna as well o Central Park o Roihuvuori Cherry Park – Kirsiklapuisto: for the cherry blossom o Lammassaari o Kaisaniemi Botanic Garden o Walk in the districts: Töölö (and around the lake), Torikorttelit, Kruununhaka, Katajanokka, Kallio and Eira o Nuuksio National Park: A bit of a journey from Helsinki but definitely wroth it. You can also sleep in the forest. Places to eat: - Fat Raman: the one in Kallio - Hills Dumplings - Teurastamo - Lie Mi - The market hall - Somewhere where you can get a good salmon soup ;)
culture_adjustment: I would recommend trying to learn some Finnish before going there. Even though I only spoke very little it helped me a bit in my day-to-day life because a lot of the people there only speaks Finnish. Otherwise, the culture is much like the Danish, but the Finnish people are more introvert and can be hard to get to know.
socializing_tips: I started talking with the students about other stuff than academical learning, so they would relax more in speaking English. A lot of them are introverts so they will often not start a conversation with you by them self. So don't be afraid to speak to them and I always wrote to the students I like and asked them if they wanted to do something outside the hospital and they always wanted to. Also just being honest and not speaking about superficial stuff helped getting true friends
cultural_challenges: Definitely the language barrier. The Finns are often not bad in English, but they are very unsure about speaking English and because a lot of them are not that outgoing, it can be hard to get friend.
culture_appreciated: Vappu and going to the market square after winning the world championship in ice hockey. Also just in general being outside in the nature. It is very easy to find a green area anywhere and I loved that.
top3_advice: Be prepared for the language barrier. Maybe it was worse for me because of covid but it was really hard getting people to speak English and staying in English. I would say you have to be pretty persistent and not shy to feel comfortable in this. I recommend you download google translate to you phone, so you can translate the journals in that way. Otherwise use the computers on campus and the translations app “Deepl” to understand the journals. You can also ask to get access to “provet” from home, so you have time to prepare from home. Find the tutor in the group. In almost every group of students there is a tutor, so that person can help you understand what is going on if there is something you don't understand or need help with. Don't be afraid to speak your mind. If there is a lot of Finnish or you don't feel included in the group start talking with the students about it. If this feels over your boundaries you can always talk with the exchange coordinator Eeva. I did this a lot and it really helped. Try to become friends with the Finnish students. They can be hard to get to know in the beginning but once you have them as friends everything becomes much easier.
other_useful_info: I think I got most of it down here but if you have any more questions, you are welcome to contact me.
most_rewarding: Getting to be part of true Finnish experiences and not just feeling like a tourist. It was easier for me to get invited to these events because I prioritized being with the Finnish students. Also improving my practical skills both in small animals and in large.
greatest_challenge: The language and feeling like I had to proof myself all the time.

crucial_aspects: Because of the uncertainty caused by covid-19, it felt easier to be in a Nordic country (more likely the exchange would actually take place). I also thought it was nice to be in a big city because of the cultural activities etc. (for instance also when you do not know so many people). Finland seemed more exotic than the Scandinavian countries and at the same time, the university offered many interesting courses and was ok ranked.
info_ease: It was provided on the website and send directly to me by e-mail. The echange coordinators were very helpful.
arrival_assistance: The first week was filled with introductions. Tutors (other students) were very helpful and even offered to go to immigration authorities etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You have to apply both there and at KU. You need to provide a learning agreement before the course plan is available and need special forms for each step. I highly recommend an excel-sheet with course codes and course names, both for first and second priority courses (in case the final course offer differs from previous years).
registration_help: The exchange coordinators at Helsinki University were very helpful to answer on e-mail.
registration_success: The IT system was brand new and there was some technical issues, but I e-mail study support and they then enrolled me manually
registration_advice: Do not stress. The professors and the support team will help (just write them by e-mail) and you can even be enrolled later. Another good thing to know is that you can register for more courses than you need, go to the first lecture, and then unenroll yourself. You can even just decide not to show up, because only courses you pass are registered.
course_level: Some master courses were recommended on first year of the master or last year of the BA. Those courses were generally too easy.
teaching_comparison: Less hours with exercises/calculations, mainly just lectures. Quite many courses contain homework/assignments. In some of my courses they contribute to the final grade and in others not. In some courses, there are no traditional exams, instead you have to fill in a learning diary.
courses_enrolled: Field crop quality, basic biotechnology applications in forestry, breeding of crops, plant biochemistry and cell biology, wood science, environmental technology in agriculture - theoretical bases, responsible business management in the global bioeconomy, BLUP and variance components
recommended_courses: Wood science was really good with hands on and it is something you cannot get in Denmark (perhaps not very relevant in a Danish context, but fun) Breeding of crops was nice, because they breed more crops (including apple and strawberry) for winter hardiness than we do in Denmark
unexpected_costs: I spent more on activities and trips than expected.
cost_comparison: Candy is cheap - and you can go to Tallinn and buy alcohol like the Finns
activities_available: There are lots of student unions with different themes. Most of them in Finnish, but some in English and in Swedish.
activities_recommended: I joined a Swedish speaking student group. It was a nice way to meet some Finnish people and not only international students. I will also recommend going to sitsits. It is an event, normally on a weekday, where the student unions eat dinner, sing lots of songs and drink snaps.
weekend_recommendations: It is nice to go to Porvoo, Soumenlinna, Sipoonkorpi and Nuuksio. If you have more days off, it is nice to rent a cottage (on air bnb eg) and a car with some friends. I went to the area around Savonlinna with some other Danes. You can go to national parks and at night in sauna - and most often there is a lake nearby.
culture_adjustment: It is quite similar to the Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Join some student groups and go to sitsits. There is a table plan and so many songs that you can go even if you do not know anybody.
cultural_challenges: The Finns do not nod or smile on the street - or even in national parks. They are friendly when they finally start speaking.
culture_appreciated: Sauna
top3_advice: Join student groups, know that you can drop courses if you find them boring and enjoy the nature
other_useful_info: Ask the student help - they answer fast and are willing to help
most_rewarding: To meet people from all over Europe and just to spent some time in new surroundings after a year in lockdown at home
greatest_challenge: To get to know Finnish people

overall_comments: Loved all of it!

arrival_assistance: I was receiving emails, and also invited to activities by an active social buddy.
arrival_comments: Course registration was a nightmare
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: I wrote the exchange student help desk which also gave me a few useful links, but it was a little tough.
registration_success: Pretty succesful. Just watch out for deadlines too.
registration_advice: Start early, but not too early (: Maybe just contact the student exchange help desk as soon as possible and ask them when and where you can do all the registration.
academics_comments: Loved all of it!
course_level: Very similar to KU, but beware that some courses are tougher than others. And for 30 ECTS, you need 6 courses, since they are all 5 ECTS. You will have 3 at a time. Try to get some easy ones, but I found I could generally guess which ones were easy.
teaching_comparison: Very similar to KU.
courses_enrolled: Full Stack Web Development Advanced Research Topics in Data Science Seminar on Neuroinformatics 7 Finnish beginners' course for exchange students Seminar on Computer Vision
recommended_courses: I liked the seminars a lot.
unexpected_costs: My accounting is a little inaccurate. But generally alcohol is more expensive, and everything else i marginally less expensive. I feel like it evened itself out.
cost_comparison: My accounting is a little inaccurate. But generally alcohol is more expensive, and everything else i marginally less expensive. I feel like it evened itself out.
activities_available: The Erasmus student network was very active, so check that out. The gyms were nice. Oh, and the student cafe's made some reasonable food for very low prices!
activities_recommended: The Erasmus student network was very active, so check that out. The gyms were nice. Oh, and the student cafe's made some reasonable food for very low prices!
weekend_recommendations: Nuoksio National Park, any of the national parks (!!), Lapland, 1-day boat trip to Talinn, try a nice sauna, eat and drink in downtown Helsinki (e.g. Punavuori).
culture_adjustment: Very similar culture. It is a Nordic country after all. People are generally less chit-chatty, and generally more modest. I really enjoyed my time in Helsinki!
socializing_tips: Check out the student unions. Ask your welcome buddy about them. They throw all the parties, and I think some are especially welcoming to exchange students.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: That they were slightly more modest. But expect Finns to be very similar to Danes (:
top3_advice: Enjoy it! I loved it so much. See my recommendations on what to do. Make sure to enjoy the nature! And have sauna trip with sauna drinks!
other_useful_info: See my comments on course registration
most_rewarding: Getting to know Finland, a little finnish, and learning about our Nordic cousins!
greatest_challenge: Alcohol was a little pricey.
other_comments: Loved it! Hyvää Suomi!

socializing_tips: Finns are easy to befriend when they are drunk.
cultural_challenges: None.

top3_advice: 1) Pack some warm clothes. Finland is the real north. 2) Definitely go to a smoke sauna in Löyly or Kuusijärvi 3) The Uni is great, but check out the courses beforehand if you really want to specialise in some specific subject.
other_useful_info: Definitely go to all introduction events and you'll be fine.
most_rewarding: Travelling around Finland.
greatest_challenge: Keeping up the motivation to study.

crucial_aspects: University of Helsinki has an excellent Aleksanteri Institute, which the center of advanced Russian studies
overall_comments: The reason why I put 9 instead of 10 is that even though I enjoyed my stay, Helsinki is a really expensive city, so I came with a minus on my bank account. Even the Erasmus Grant couldn't fully cover the expenses. So I would recommend Helsinki to people, but will warn them about the costs.
info_ease: Pretty easy. The University of Helsinki had sent several newsletters, which were very helpful.
arrival_assistance: Tutors and orientation week with all information needed for exchange students
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The reason why I put 9 instead of 10 is that even though I enjoyed my stay, Helsinki is a really expensive city, so I came with a minus on my bank account. Even the Erasmus Grant couldn't fully cover the expenses. So I would recommend Helsinki to people, but will warn them about the costs.
registration_process: It was quite challenging to figure out how their system SISU, is functioning. It doesn't have user-friendly software, and sometimes, even if you register in advance and fulfill the requirements for the course, you still have a risk to be kicked out of the course for no reason.
registration_help: Only guidance how to use SISU in the orientation week. Otherwise, if I had a problem, I had to contact the teacher of the course.
registration_success: 70% out of 100% Even when a course was in English, but was not open for exchange students, I had to fight for the right to being registered in the course by convincing the administration. Luckily, they were very quick to response and help me with the process. Otherwise I've been rejected an access to one course, but I didn't get a satisfactory information what I have to do in this situation.
registration_advice: Prepare yourself for not getting the courses you want, therefore ask the services what to do in the situation, when the course is not available.
academics_comments: The reason why I put 9 instead of 10 is that even though I enjoyed my stay, Helsinki is a really expensive city, so I came with a minus on my bank account. Even the Erasmus Grant couldn't fully cover the expenses. So I would recommend Helsinki to people, but will warn them about the costs.
course_level: All six courses were at the MA level, which required a lot of reading, projects, essays etc
teaching_comparison: It depends. I was surprised to experience that some of my teachers used creative methods to help us memorize stuff. I also appreciated that the teachers came up with the questions or detailed description on the task, which we could use for writing our essays. The University of Copenhagen is unfortunately way back in that matter. Teachers expect from us that we can figure out ourselves, but didn't even get guidance on how to make a good question for research. We had to figure ourselves out, which is a totally stressful process. If you are going to use this feedback for the improvement of our education system in Denmark, please convince the teachers to come up with meta questions, which could be a good start for finding your own question. Not only for BA-level, but for MA-level as well.
courses_enrolled: - Russian legal system and law - Interactions and responses - EU human rights - Land question and sustainable development - China and Russia in Central Asia - Qualitative Interview Method in Sociology
recommended_courses: - Russian legal system and law Because you get exclusive insight perspective on Russian legal system. The teacher, Marianna Muravyeva, is the best - EU human rights It gives a post-structural perspective on EU
unexpected_costs: Mandatory membership in the Student Union = 208 DKK
cost_comparison: Food and accomodation are more expensive here. It is cheaper to eat in canteens (22 DKK per meal) than buying in supermarkets.
activities_available: Evert kind: sport, political, study related, festivals, cultural events for students from humanities, cultural events for every student in Helsinki.
activities_recommended: First of all, there are a lot of opportunities, and sometimes you feel that it is overwhelming to catch up on all of them. So, therefore I would recommend to contact the student organisation, which is related to your study track. Fx Russian and Eastern European Studies have Sasha organisation, where they arrange movie nights, draw-along with Bob-Ross etc. There you can meet people, who share the same interest as you. It's good to join UniSport, a sport student organisation. Sport is good for the health and soul, and they have sauna. I didn't join the organisation though. I had already major expenses.
weekend_recommendations: Many cinemas in Helsinki have English subtitles, so foreigners can enjoy movies, too. A lot of museums have free entrance days.
culture_adjustment: A bit challenging. Finns are very social people at first glance
socializing_tips: Join a student organisation. Finns will be forced to speak to you, and you get friends out of it
cultural_challenges: Social awkwardness Cold and dry climate (buy thermo clothes and a lot of cream!) Dark humour Finnish students work way more than Danish students, they are quite stressed.
culture_appreciated: I really liked that the administration and teachers responded to me right away or the next day. Unfortunately, the University of Copenhagen is way back in that sense Saunas The universities in Finland take care of the students; canteens and student accommodations get subsidies from the government. Respect for one's personal space. Even if it's crowded, you feel that you have a space for yourself. I don't experience it here in CPH Beautiful language, actually
top3_advice: - Prepare for extra expenses - Join a student organisation and other student cultural events, like Independence Day or the 1st of May. This is where you can experience the real student life in Finland. - It's okay to feel alone
other_useful_info: Not what I can think of right now
most_rewarding: New acquittances Perspective on the Nordic country, which is quite ignored in Denmark, I think. New insights into Russian and Eastern European Studies
greatest_challenge: Keeping up with a lot of essays. It's hard, but you learn a lot by using the materials in written form
other_comments: Not what I can think of

crucial_aspects: The courses available mattered most. It was a plus if the institution was in a bigger city
info_ease: Really easy. The sending institution provided news letters via email and all the needed information was also easily available on their website.
arrival_assistance: As mentioned monthly newsletters were provided both before and during the exchange. The first week of exchange included an orientation week where I met other exchange students, local student tutors, I could get my documents signed, I received a card so I could use public transportation at a discounted rate. I could get my question about course registrations answered.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I received an email with a link and information about what I needed to do. I then registered through their website. I needed to register for an IT user account before having access to the online portals. I recommend that you register to everything as soon as you can as some of the processing has a bit of a wait time.
registration_help: There were plenty of online guides. I had information in the news letters from the University of Helsinki. I could also email any questions I had.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted-
registration_advice: You can't sign up for any classes before your study right begins. The rules for signing up for classes and dropping classes is also a lot more relaxed than that at University of Copenhagen. So don't stress about it. You can sign up for more classes than you need and the try them out for a week or two and then drop the classes you don't want. The prerequisites stated in the course unit are not so strict. If you are in doubt about whether or not you have the required knowledge to complete a course, contact the teacher of the course. The teachers are really relaxed and more often than not will let you take a course even if you don't have the necessary prerequisites.
course_level: I took one BA course and five MA courses. Overall I would say that the academic level was slightly lower compared to UCPH
teaching_comparison: Very similar though the exercise sessions were a little less frequent compared to UCPH. The workload and exam types varies a lot from course to course.
courses_enrolled: Basic Course in Hydrology, Polar oceans and ice, Stratospheric Dynamics and Chemistry, Arctic climate change, Numerical Meteorology I, Geophysics of Snow and Ice
recommended_courses: For student interested in geophysics, I would recommend Geophysics of Snow and Ice. We went on a 2 day field trip where we gained practical skills in measuring snow properties and drilling ice samples from lake ice.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: They were what I expected
activities_available: Discounted gym, different student organisations
activities_recommended: If you like singing there is an international choir called Overall just experience as many of the student events that you can. I really recommend Vappu, Shrove Tuesday sledding event and student organised trips to Lapland, Stockholm or the Baltics
weekend_recommendations: Go on holidays to Lapland during the winter. Go on daytrips to Porvoo, Tallinn, Turku, Nuuksio National Park. Visit Hanko and Åland if you have the time.
culture_adjustment: Easy, it's very similar to Denmark. Most signs, info on foods etc. is also written in Swedish so as a Danish speaking person it's easy to figure everything out.
socializing_tips: Talk to people in your classes. Like Danish people, Finns are very nice and friendly but most people will not be the ones to initiate the conversation.
cultural_challenges: There weren't any really.
culture_appreciated: The closeness with nature. How easy it is to just get out of the city and go for a hike.
top3_advice: Don't stress about signing up for the courses. The rules and deadlines around courses are a lot more relaxed than at UCPH. And you can drop courses easily so consider signing up for more courses than you actually need to take, try them out for a week or two and then drop the ones you don't want. Ask your teachers if you are ever in doubt about whether or not you can take a course. They are usually pretty easygoing and friendly. The prerequisites in the course descriptions seems more strict than they actually are. Also the teachers can move exams, teaching schedules and assignments as they want to. I was allowed to take the exam in one course another day because I had a field trip in another course. Enjoy Finland and take lots of trips around the country. I would especially recommend going on one of the student organised trips to Lapland.
other_useful_info: Unihome has one location for exchange students where as Hoas seems to have several locations. Unihome is more expensive and further away from the city center than most Hoas buildings. Unihome is close to the Viikki campus. Unless you are studying at Viikki campus, I would recommend you choose Hoas instead of Unihome. You are only offered one accommodation through your University of Helsinki application and it is not necessarily the provider (Hoas or Unihome) that you chose when you applied. There are some private student housing providers that you can find on your own. E.g. Antti Korppi Student House which had several empty places in the spring semester. They are cheaper than the Unihome private apartments.
most_rewarding: The friends I have met and the field trip I went on in the course Geophysics of Snow and Ice.
greatest_challenge: The periods (what corresponds to the blocks at the Faculty of Science at UCPH) are short (1-2 weeks shorter than at UCPH) so the academic period feels intense and stressfull as the exams are always nearby.
other_comments: Go on an exchange. It is worth it in every way.
