arrival_assistance: Eeva at University of Helsinki gave me all the information I needed my first day. Also she was the best person to contact before and during my stay. She answered every exchange student so fast and was very willing to help out.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The hardest part was the Finnish language.
registration_process: I applied for a long time ago and wanted to go to Norway but the University in Norway didnt offer a exchange period for students in 2025 which my university didnt know about (I was the one the contacted the universities). My university offered my other places to go to and I found that Finland have a production animal hospital there students can go with the vets for farm visits. I was confused for a long time if I should go since I couldnt go to Norway. Very late I decided to go and Eeva from University of Helsinki offered me a stay directly. I think my contact person from Copenhagen was not very happy with me that I was so late but as the Finnish mentality, they was very happy to have me and I felt very welcome even though I applied late.
registration_help: Eeva at University of Helsinki and contact person for exchange at my university through email. They also helped me through the process with learning agreement etc. Also got a lot of information through University of Helsinki website.
registration_success: Very successful, wanted to follow rotation A with focus at large animal which I also did.
registration_advice: Plan your exchange in time, because everything takes a lot more time than I expected. I did manage to do everything in one semester (with forhåndsmerit etc) but it was stressful. University of Copenhagen answer email much slower then University of Helsinki so the host institution was never a problem to get everything in place in time.
academics_comments: The hardest part was the Finnish language.
course_level: Clinical rotations at the University hospitals (small animal, equine and production animal) as the most important part of veterinary medicine program. I got work and practice right beside the vets and have real own patients/cases. All from small animal internal medicine patients to surgery on a cow at a farm.
teaching_comparison: All the teachers/vets in Finland are in general much nicer, no judging and also with the mentality of learning by doing. There was also more cases to practice and follow during my stay and more focus at the practical skills rather then journal writing. I should easily question anything without a feeling as a stupid student. The equine hospital staff was so nice and since I been there I can again consider to see myself as an equine vet. The equine hospital in Copenhagen I think has scared me more than developed my skills. I think I learned more of 3 months of stay in Finland then I have a whole year of clinical rotations in Copenhagen. The Finnish students have the whole 5th years just with clinical rotation at the hospitals and only practice things besides the vets (as a example they are 6 weeks in total at production animal hospital during the year). In Copenhagen we also have lectures/courses through the clinical year and I learn more of doing the practical things.
courses_enrolled: Clinical rotation/practice - Small animal general polyclinic - Small animal surgery, anesthesia - Small animal internal medicine ward - Small animal surgery operating theatre - Equine hospital x3 weeks - Production animal hospital x4 weeks
recommended_courses: Anesthesia week and surgery operating theatre at small animal hospital. You have to go to Production animal hospital, you will get a experience for life. One day I had cow reproduction at a farm and we examined about 80 cows. Learned a lot! Long day without lunch but in the late afternoon we got dinner inside the farmers house with the whole family and they were very sweet to us.
unexpected_costs: I lived by myself so my house rent was probably higher then if you chose to live with others. I also have my money in swedish crown so it was even more expensive for me then the numbers in Dannish crown. I think the food is expensive but probably suits well to the cost in Denmark. Wifi and electricity was included in the rent just payed for my phone. I had my own books with me that I already had bought during the beginning of my master. Books are also available in almost every ward at the hospitals.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping and also public transport fees.
activities_available: The tutors organized gatherings etc for the exchange students. We also had a international dinner night which was very nice. I think they have sports at Uni-sport, but I found out it was cheaper for me to train at the local gym in my area so I did that.
activities_recommended: Visit the city center and just stroll around. The cathedral is very beautiful and in the old market hall I tasted very nice reindeer delicacy. The city is much calmer then Copenhagen but still alive with a lot of things and culture to explore, like the museums.
weekend_recommendations: One weekend I went to ski in Vithi ski center together with the other exchange students. It was a very nice and sunny day, it was quiet expensive so count on minimun 80 euro for one day of skiing.
culture_adjustment: When I arrived in January it was very much as in Sweden, people are introverted and are mostly at home. I felt very lonely and had hard to connect with the other students since the didnt talked so much with me. Later in the semester I felt that people opened up more and didnt felt scared to talk english or swedish with me.
socializing_tips: Talk with the tutors, they are the best!
cultural_challenges: Were introverted persons as a start, also these students had know each other for more then 4 years so it wad a little bit hard to connect with them. I also think they had a lot in school and tried to survive the hardest year of vet school. Otherwise are Finnish people very nice and gently so when I just continued to talk to them it got easier and I felt that they probably are shy in the beginning.
culture_appreciated: The kindness of Finnish people, no judgement and also were willing to help out if you ask them for anything.
top3_advice: 1. Go there in the end of February or beginning of March instead, other exchange student arrive then and it was not so dark at that time. You can still get the winter experience in the beginning of your stay and be there when the spring arrive, and also attend Vappu at the 1st of May. I left before Vappu but the Finnish student talked so much about it and it felt it was something to look forward to. 2. Explore the Finnish nature! 3. Go to production animal hospital, the teachers are really nice there and the drive around at the Finnish country side was a experience. You can also get cheap housing through the university during you stay there.
other_useful_info: Email Eeva whenever you have a question. I would also say that you need to have a erasmus grant to help with the costs! Otherwise go with the flow and just enjoy the experience.
most_rewarding: Days I had alone with the farm vets. The Finnish people had exam some days so I went alone in the car with the vet. For example I treated a uterine prolapse and did teeth rasping at 10 horses.
greatest_challenge: The Finnish language, farmers didnt speak english or swedish and sometime vets talked a lot in Finnish with the other students. But it depends on the vet you are with, some of them only speak english (as in equine hospital).
other_comments: Go to Finland! You will learn a lot, explore beautiful nature and meet new friends!

crucial_aspects: Availability of subjects interesting to me. Destination not too similar to my own culture, and not a place I had been before.
info_ease: The university of Helsinki had assigned 3 tutors to my group of about 20 exchange students. Two of these students were themselves international students, and knew the challenges we could face as non-Finnish people. The University of Helsinki had arranged introductory presentations and excursions to get all the bureaucracy done. It felt like I was helped most of the way.
arrival_assistance: Tutors, help with signing up for subjects, help with discovering extra curricular activities, invitations to social events, excursions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Course registration is messy and confusing. Registering to subjects involves 2 websites, one for searching and one for signing up. On the other hand, the process is infinitely more flexible than UCPH, as you can apply for any number of subjects and then just drop out if you realise you don't want to finnish the course. The credits are only binding once you finnish the exam.
registration_help: Tutors, this is the only thing that was not described very well by the university in any official place that I found. But the tutors were very helpful, and a full afternoon was dedicated to choosing subjects for the whole semester
registration_success: Very succesful, and the flexibility of the system also allowed me to change subjects a few weeks in, as I was dissatisfied with certain courses. UCPH can learn from this.
registration_advice: Sign up to any and all course sthat sound interesting, and try out 1 or 2 lectures. If it seems to difficult, you don't have time, or it is not interesting to you, just drop the course. You end up with the ideal semester this way. Also consider the possibility of doing the MOOC courses which are fully remote and online. The university has great facilities for studying on campus (club rooms, IT rooms) so you can be social with other students doing the same thing, but decide on your own time and terms when to work on the courses and when to complete them. This way, you make time for social activities and excursions.
course_level: Tried some masters courses. If they were too hard I dropped them and did a bachelors course instead
teaching_comparison: Physical lectures are similar. emphasis on student participation in tutorials to a greater extent than mine at UCPH (i.e. students working on blackboard, discussing solutions). Helsinki and other Finnish universities make available very high quality online courses which can be worked on and finnished on your own time. These courses offer subjects that a re not taught physically. These are great and I am envious that Finnish students have this option.
courses_enrolled: networking technologies, combinatorial optimisations, functional programming I and II, Cyber security intro, topics and project, Finnish for exchange students
recommended_courses: If you want to engage with Finnish culture in any meaningful way, the Finnish course for exchange students is very good, because it teaches you spoken Helsinki Finnish. Finland has many local varieties, and no one actually speaks standard language which is what is taught in online courses such as duolingo. I had prepared with duolingo in advance, and I straight up had to unlearn what I had been taught, because it was not useful in everyday situations. Cyber security is a great online course, very relevant today, and very fun exercises such as snooping cookies, finding secret messages and a project of making an app with flaws from the OWASP top 10 that you then have to fix. Combinatorial optimisations is an interesting subject and is taught by a very engaging lecturer, Matti Järvisalo, highly recommend, if you like optimisation problems (Simplex, dual simplex gomory cuts etc)
unexpected_costs: winter clothes
cost_comparison: Food is very cheap because student canteens are subsidized by student unions. Denmark can learn from this. Other prices were generally comparable to Danish prices
activities_available: I had a subsidized gym membership. The gyms have saunas. I was member of the comp-sci student association which held parties and other activities. Many clubs for many fields of interest. There is a day "tori" where all the associations are ligned up in stalls outside the main university building in the city centre, and students can meet the associations.
activities_recommended: Try at least one "sitsit" which is a traditional Finnish student party. Go to sauna at least once. If in Helsinki, you can go to Sompa Sauna which is a free sauna run by volunteers.
weekend_recommendations: Bring camping and hiking gear and make use of Finlands beautiful nature, They have an abundance of national parks with lean to shelters and open wild huts where park service leaves firewood for visitors. Tampere is the next big town in the region, 2 hrs by train. Very beautiful but slightly smaller city. Home to the worlds oldest public wood fired sauna and a very good and fairly priced food market "kauppahalli". Don't go to turku, not worth the time. it's expensive and hideous. Try to go to Lapland while it is still warm enough to camp out. if you do you can make it a very affordable trip, as train tickets have student discounts, and you save the accommodation by camping out. lapland is great in winter as well. Skiing in Finland is OK, not amazing, but still fun. I enjoyed a day of skiing in Levi.
culture_adjustment: I didn't adjust before the last month.
socializing_tips: Join an association, and do activities. Finnish people don't smalltalk. And I don't mean like Danish people don't smalltalk, they do not talk AT ALL. You are WEIRD if you talk to someone you don't know. So lower your expectations and just try to get to know people by doing things together with them.
cultural_challenges: Finnish people don't like talking to strangers whatsoever, even lightheartedly. Finnish people are not comfortable speaking English, and they don't want to.
culture_appreciated: Sauna, sitsit, student associations
top3_advice: Enjoy nature while it's warm, learn some basic finnish, lower your expectations for interacting with Finns
other_useful_info: Look for student discounts, there are many. The only place where you can talk to Finns almost guaranteed is in the sauna. A safe icebreaker is just asking something about the sauna, they love talking about it.
most_rewarding: Associations, sauna culture
greatest_challenge: Finnish people

crucial_aspects: I didn’t want to go to a destination I already knew a lot about, and I knew very little about Finland and its traditions.
info_ease: Before arrival, a lot of information is sent by both the University of Helsinki and the home university. You are also added to a tutoring group with students from the same faculty. We had one tutor for Finland who helped us sign up for courses and complete the necessary paperwork. This tutoring group was a good foundation for meeting other Erasmus students.
arrival_assistance: We received assistance with signing up for courses and learning how to get around. There was one day dedicated to applying for a “citizenship” and obtaining the travel card.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was a lot of work with a short deadline, but everything was very well explained on the university website. The main part is to get pre-approval of courses so that you can have your OLA approved.
registration_help: The host university held some online QA sessions, and was also very good at answering emails.
registration_success: At arrivalt, it was at the end of the registration period, and almost all the interesting courses for me were already full. Some courses also suddenly changed their status from being available to exchange students to being only for degree students. It was a real challenge to get into courses, and in the end I only had 10 credits out of the 30 that would have made sense for me.
registration_advice: You can’t sign up earlier than your arrival, so it’s important to consider what to do if you don’t get into your courses. I would also really recommend looking into MOOC exams, as they are easy credits that you can complete from home whenever it suits you.
course_level: All master level, but I would say the courses were easy.
teaching_comparison: It was alot of online teaching, and short classes compared to UCPH
courses_enrolled: Food Additives, 5 ECTS
recommended_courses: Food additives and Chromatographic and Other Separation Techniques in Food Analysis were nice courses.
unexpected_costs: In the first week alot of things needs to be paid, student union, erasmus union, gym membership eg. Finland is expensive, especially when traveling around.
cost_comparison: Prices are similar to those in Denmark, but I would say it costs more to buy fresh food here. Student lunch at the UniCafe is €2.95, which is really affordable.
activities_available: During the first week, there is an introduction to different associations, and you can find an organization for almost every interest. I would recommend getting the UniSport membership. The classes are very nice, and the gym is well equipped.
activities_recommended: Hiking arround helsinki is really nice, also go to sauna (sompasauna and kuusijärvi is very nice)
weekend_recommendations: Go on a cabin trip with your friends, rent a car and a cabin. A week in Lapland is a must, whether with or without snow, Lapland is amazing.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. Finns are very welcoming and pleasant people to be around.
socializing_tips: Attend the Erasmus events and be open to meeting new people, even if you already have your tutoring group. Also, remember to do what you want, if the people in your group don’t share the same interests, you can always find someone who does.
cultural_challenges: Mainly the language.
culture_appreciated: Finns are very friendly and well-organized people.
top3_advice: Go! Helsinki is a really nice city, but don’t expect too much. The university is very helpful, if you need help it is just to reach out.
other_useful_info: The university has a lot of traditions, which are really nice. But if you’re looking for a big party destination, Helsinki is not the place to go. The Pizza in the unicafe EE is really good :)
most_rewarding: The cultural friendships with other Erasmus students, as well as with local Finns I met through sports classes.
greatest_challenge: Getting into courses, and later obtaining the new pre-approval.

crucial_aspects: Location — close to nature, easy to travel to my home country (Slovakia) by train.
info_ease: It was rather easy, I only had to search for the information about housing myself.
arrival_assistance: I had a buddy that waited for my on the train station and walked with me to the dorm, helped to move in (also translated from German to English).
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Necessary to fill out several documents, but it was very similar to filing up the documentation for UCPH. To register into platforms for teaching, it was fairly straightforward.
registration_help: Course coordinator, coordinator of exchange students.
registration_success: I got into all classes I wanted to.
registration_advice: Finding courses on the teaching platform to register for them can be tricky (Ilias). If you cannot find any course, try to text the responsible teacher or your course coordinator. Then you have to register for the exam, which is done on a separate platform (HohCampus).
course_level: Some courses were somewhat general, they could go more in depth. Others were of what I expected and I had a lot of freedom to choose my own projects.
teaching_comparison: Very similar, teachers share their presentations beforehand, which makes it easy to take notes. However, exams are written by hand on paper. I prefer UCPH style here.
courses_enrolled: Weather and climate physics, Project in Landscape Ecology, Climate change, Mitigation and Adaptation (offered by UPCH), Global change issues.
recommended_courses: Weather and climate physics — goes more into physics of climate, GHG, radiation, fundamental equations to understand movements of air, water and mass parcels.
unexpected_costs: There was a water pipe burst in our building not fixed for several days. I was traveling at the moment, but other students had to either move to a friend's place or to buy extra water (for drinking, basic hygiene, etc..) or to go to airbnb.
cost_comparison: Food was less expensive than what I expected. Housing was more — the area is notoriously known for high prices.
activities_available: Lots of sports available (dance, yoga, gymnastics, frisbee, football, martial arts...) were available on the campus for a small fee.
activities_recommended: Sports activities. They are cheap and tutors are usually very good.
weekend_recommendations: Explore nature nearby, Wilhelma ZOO, Swabian Alps, Esslingen Am Neckar.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy, but I had my own programme for the most of the time and met other international students.
socializing_tips: There are pubs and parties happening multiple times a week on the campus.
cultural_challenges: Not speaking the language naturally leads to being excluded from the locals that already formed their cliques — not dissimilar to anywhere else.
culture_appreciated: Equal rights to everybody.
top3_advice: Living on campus means everything is close by (lectures, sport activities, parties, dinning hall), but you will be somewhat excluded from the city. Some teachers do not respond immediately, and you need to send them a reminder, or even knock on their door. Sometimes just reach another person instead. This area is very close and well connected to other countries in Europe by trains and buses (France, Austria, Switzerland, other regions of Germany). I suggest to use this opportunity.
other_useful_info: Food is cheaper than in DK, even cheaper than in some other countries in EU. Eating outside is can be comparable or a bit cheaper.
most_rewarding: Seeing the country's nature and meeting some of my best friends there.
greatest_challenge: Not responding teachers. I still struggle to get my grades from 3 months ago.
other_comments: It was amazing to have the option to go and travel :) Thank you for the support.

crucial_aspects: There are several aspects that were crucial to my decision to choose Hong Kong and HKU as my study destination. First and foremost, I have always been attracted to the cultural diversity and vibrancy of Hong Kong. I know many people who either travelled to Hong Kong or lived and worked there. I've only ever heard great things which is one reason why I've wanted to visit Hong Kong for years. As a major international city, Hong Kong offers a unique blend of Western and Eastern cultures where most of the population speaks English. I was excited to immerse myself in this dynamic and vibrant environment and learn more about different cultures and perspectives. Another important factor for me personally was that HKU seemed to have a great supportive and inclusive community at HKU and offered a range of resources and services to help students thrive academically, socially, and personally. Furthermore I really appreciated that all classes (except some Chinese language classes) are taught in English and that the prime medium of communication at HKU is English. Finally, in a city such as Hong Kong where so many different cultures exists side by side and with a lot of people working in different time zones or work schedules, the city never really sleeps and one can always get ones favourite food at almost any time of day! Shout out to dim sum restaurants that open at 4am!
overall_comments: Though I loved my stay in Hong Kong and the city itself, I did have a few issues with the (local) residence hall I was assigned and personally I prefer the teaching style at University of Copenhagen.
info_ease: Very easy! Whenever some information were not to be found or were unclear, the department CEDARS at HKU would respond to emails really quickly.
arrival_assistance: Personally I don't think I got any assistance when I arrived in HK, but I don't feel like it would really be needed.
arrival_comments: HKU hosted a lost of diffrent kinds of orientation at arrival, which was really nice! I didn't need any assistance, but I know some people who did, and it worked really well according to them.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Though I loved my stay in Hong Kong and the city itself, I did have a few issues with the (local) residence hall I was assigned and personally I prefer the teaching style at University of Copenhagen.
registration_process: To be honest I don't really recall the registration process at your HKU, but that might be because of how easy I found it. I think you had to sign up for classes two weeks before the semester start or something like that. There was also a add-drop period for the first week (I think... we were affected by very bad weather aka typhoons and black rain which meant we had a two week add-drop period).
registration_help: One can always email CEDARS and they will answer quickly! Be aware of the 6/7 hour time difference to DK though.
registration_success: I was successful in registering for all the classes I wanted. Except one, but it turned out something went wrong with the system at the course weren't available for exchange students. However most courses I wanted were available to everyone, but it might differ from faculty to faculty (I was at the Faculty of Engineering).
registration_advice: Don't decide on all classes in advance! Go and use the one to two week add-drop period to figure out which courses you like (and where it might be easiest to make friends).
academics_comments: Though I loved my stay in Hong Kong and the city itself, I did have a few issues with the (local) residence hall I was assigned and personally I prefer the teaching style at University of Copenhagen.
course_level: In my opinion, the levels of the courses I took varied a lot. I had some very easy courses that took almost no work and then I had courses where no one seemed to know what was going on. As I study data/computer science I heavily depend on having exercise classes, which was not really a thing at HKU. Typically each course has one to two lectures (each between one and three hours) and then one to two hour tutorials (which is typically used a phd student lecturing) a week. Some courses had a lot of courses work and some had almost none.
teaching_comparison: See above answer.
courses_enrolled: CHIN 9511 - Cantonese as a foreign language COMP 3220 - Principles of operating systems COMP 3258 - Functional programming COMP 3314 - Machine learning LING 2067 - Natural language processing
recommended_courses: CHIN 9511 - Cantonese as a foreign language! If one has the opportunity to take classes outside the scope of ones bachelor/master I think Cantonese as a foreign language is a good option. It was quite demanding, as a lot of people spoke a little Canto, even though the course were supposed to be for absolute beginners. As a result of this our teacher expected everyone to be at that level. I also really enjoyed the machine learning class! The professor were really brilliant and the same can be said for the NLP course. Though the NLP course is mainly a lingustics course, I found it quite interesting to get another perspective, as I will likely take a "real" NLP course at UCPH. Functional programming was fun and I learned a lot, but the course was way too difficult and most people struggled to get through. Principles of operating systems was wayyy too much work. We had one to two assignments each week and the lectures where not very interesting...
unexpected_costs: I don't remember any unexpected costs. Also, personal spending does not include traveling, but rather snacks, coffee, HK milk tea, cinema, karaoke, etc.
cost_comparison: Hong Kong is a very expensive city especially if you want western products and want to eat at western restaurants and stuff. Often, things like coffee will actually be a bit more expensive than Copenhagen (and dairy products are very expensive - 250 kilogram butter was 62HKD!) but I still think eating out is generally cheaper than Denmark. Going out is also bit expensive even though alcohol bought directly in stores is cheaper than in DK... a lot of time people just meet up outside at a pier, hangout there and buys drinks from 7-eleven. Vegetable in supermarkets is less cheap that I expected so go to the wet markets to buy vegetables. And be aware that some instant noodles can be pricy as well! In general in Hong Kong, you can live really cheaply but you can also choose to spend a lot of money. It totally depends on your budget and preferences. Remember that most of the people you'll likely meet will be students who don't receive SU or has a job, so their spending will typically match that of a fairly poor student.
activities_available: Everything you can imagine! The cultural festival activities-things my friends did was something they just started this year and some were exchange students, so don't worry about not finding a club or other activities to join!
activities_recommended: Dragon boat! Smaller activities hosted by the uni (can typically be found in their daily information letter). Join college/hall activities if possible!
weekend_recommendations: Go eat! Take the star ferry, and the ferries to out lying islands and go on some hikes! Visit the markets like Wan Chai Market (day market - you can find many great things there actually) and Ladies Market (night market - quite touristy). Also go jam2 caa4 (yum cha - directly translated means to drink tea but it means to go eat dim sum). You should definitely try the small local places like Sun Hing in Kennedy Town but also the really large more modern style dim sum restaurants like Victoria Harbour Restaurants. Remember dim sum is meant to share, so bring lots of friends! There really is something to do for every mood, person and preferences! Don't forget to just walk around and soak in the city (and it's sounds and smells) even though it's really hot and humid...
culture_adjustment: I found it easy. My uncle lived in HK for quite a while when I was younger, so HK was quite what I expected. Some people might think that the culture is a bit rude and the manners at especially local restaurants can seem bad and gross to foreigners I think, but people are always really friendly and helpful<3 The tempo is a bit faster in Denmark, especially at the cashier's or at restaurants (it's not uncommon to queue for 30 mins before entering a bar/restaurant). The biggest culture shock for me was probably the heat and humidity combined... I know some people whos clothing got mouldy because of the humidity. And the amount of people almost everywhere!
socializing_tips: Hong Kong is in a lot of ways very westerns and a lot of local and international students are very used to foreigners so it's easy socialising with everyone. As everyone needs to speak English (as the medium of instruction is always English, except language courses ofc, it's easy to communicate with everyone. I also meet a lot of local students whos ethnicity was not HK or Chinese but everyone seems really well included!
cultural_challenges: The hall culture in the local hall were the most challenging for me I think, but it's really not something that you can't get over.
culture_appreciated: It's difficult to put into words, as I loved everything about Hong Kong! I actually liked HK so much I think I will (if in any way possible) move there at some point! Though maybe not forever... rip HK:(( Obviously, one of the things that makes Hong Kong so easy to be in and so enjoyeble is the perfect mixture between the east and the west - there will simply always be something for everyones taste!
top3_advice: Apply for the colleges in Kennedy Town! Prepare for really hot and humid weather. Just enjoy Hong Kong as much as possible!
most_rewarding: Getting to call HK my home and making friends and acquaintances in this new place and culture completely different, and yet not, from Copenhagen. Keeping in contact with the friends I made after leaving is also really rewarding to me.
greatest_challenge: The hall... to be fair, I could have applied to change halls, but I didn't realise because it was in the second week. And again, it was an experience I don't think I wouldn't be without today!
other_comments: Go to Hong Kong!!!

crucial_aspects: I was attracted to the multicultural aspect of Hong Kong, and I wanted to explore that. I had already known that I wanted to go there back when I was in high school, so it was merely about finding the right time to do so.
info_ease: HKU is quite helpful, although it is very easy to become overwhelmed with the constant updates about everything and the events. You need to have a good head on your shoulders to organize all of the information yourself too.
arrival_assistance: HKU provided us with some information for finding our way to the dorms, in the form of instructions on how to get a cab from the airport. They sent out a bunch of information about how our dorm rooms work, and step by step on formal procedures before settling in, plus rules.
arrival_comments: There were some events in the beginning for exchange students, but gradually, it sort of weaned and you had to quickly figure out what was tailored to locals and what was tailored to exchange students. I know some of my friends joined clubs they thought would be international since HKU is an English school, but the club activities were conducted in Cantonese. That was a bit of a wake-up call.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Relatively easy, the website is sort of outdated but it didn't really matter. We had a add-on drop-off period which i used to drop some courses i found out weren't really for me anyway. Everything works pretty efficiently.
registration_help: During the orientation week, we were supplied with various emails we could get in contact with for help.
registration_success: I got the majority i wished for, although i was denied some which i struggled to understand why because they didn't state a reason.
registration_advice: Make sure to check again and again whether a course you want is available. I wished to sign up for a criminology course that was full, but when i checked in later it was open again because someone dropped it. So make sure to check a second time.
course_level: The level was okay, it wasn't particularly harder than KU, nor was it easier. Some courses had very loose expectations. All of the courses I took had mandatory attendance, plus they expected us to complete all the assignments, presentations, in-class tests, reports, and portfolios. To say that it was overwhelming is an understatement. Even if it was easier, I feel like I did more in a semester at HKU than I've done in my entire time at HKU. I wanted to tell them, "Sheer output is not a good measure of talent. How am I supposed to write anything good if I have 10 other reports to complete at the exact same time?" enough said.
teaching_comparison: Most of my professors were well-educated and seemed very knowledgeable about their study of the field. I enjoyed the discussions we had, even though, at times, it felt like they delegated their work to their PhD students who weren't quite on their level yet.
courses_enrolled: GLAS 2114 China in northeast Asia GLAS 3102 The EU as a global actor HKGS 2017 Postcolonial Studies: the case POLI 3020 Hong Kong politics SOCI 2067 Crime and the media
recommended_courses: GLAS 3102 The EU as a global actor: Amazing and attentive professor, his classes were a joy to attend. We had great discussions in class, and I truly felt like I learned so much in a short span of time. The class is also smaller, so it's much easier to facilitate debates.
unexpected_costs: Student activities are not cheap! It costs a ton of money if you wish to attend student parties, go out to dinner with your new friends, or even join a sport. Hong Kong is the most expensive place in Asia to live for a reason.
cost_comparison: Public transport is super affordable! The phone bill was quite inexpensive, too. What was more expensive than expected was food. One would think eating out is expensive, but surely making your own food is less. Nope, both are just expensive. Everything is expensive. If you want to go to Hong Kong and eat Western food, buy pasta or bread from the supermarket, think again: unless you're a millionaire or something.
activities_available: There were a bunch of things. Hiking groups and sports to join, such as archery and tennis. There were also art clubs and language clubs. Of course, most of it is suited for locals since the vast majority is conducted in Cantonese. I wanted to sign up for archery but had no way to do so because they requested payment via an app that requires a Hong Kong credit card, which I couldn't get because I was only there for one semester.
activities_recommended: Go to the parties, even if they lowkey suck most of the time, you'll still get to hang out with your friends and also meet a bunch of other people along the way.
weekend_recommendations: Go and visit the smaller islands of Hong Kong, there are so many! and they differ a lot from the main island, so go and explore to your heart's content.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy for me since i had already been on exchange to a different asian country, so i sort of knew what to expect.
socializing_tips: Don't start out the conversation by discussing politics; it's a super sensitive topic. Just be open and follow their lead. Most locals are afraid of messing up in English when speaking with us exchange students, so just be nice and patient.
cultural_challenges: The public spitting, the constant crowding of people wherever you go. I swear, here back home, we have rush hour, right? Hong Kong rush hour is 24/7; don't panic when in tight crowds. Just move along with the wave of people, and please don't fall. Also, people will stare, they have no shame about it, especially older men, just stare back. Also, accept the fact that awareness of your surroundings is overrated; people will stop in the middle of the road to look at their phones, and they will also stand right behind you when you're getting money from an ATM.
culture_appreciated: Hong Kong people are open to sharing their culture with others, which is great. Everyone speaks English, too, to varying degrees, but it's still understandable and helpful. People are generally kind, and because Hong Kong has so many foreigners, you typically won't feel out of place. I felt at home.
top3_advice: 1. Save as much money as you can in advance, you will need it. 2. Choose a dorm, finding an apartment by yourself is nearly impossible and just not worth it (unless you're going on an exchange with your partner) 3. Explore Hong Kong, whether that be by yourself or with other exchange students. There are so many sights to catch.
other_useful_info: Nothing i haven't already mentioned yet.
most_rewarding: I genuinely feel as if I have grown and matured as a person. Now, whenever I get anxious about doing something trivial back home, I remind myself, "You've lived in Hong Kong, if you can do that, you can do this." It actually works!
greatest_challenge: People can be complicated. You're gonna meet folks whom you probably don't like very much, but that's just part of life. Someone might hurt your feelings, but it happens, and you have to move past it. I would remind myself that literally everyone is confused about everything and no one knows what they're doing when they're on exchange. It was my first time studying at HKU, and the same goes for all of my friends.

registration_process: The registration process at my host institution in Hong Kong was relatively straightforward, but it did involve several steps to ensure everything was in order for my exchange semester. Here’s how it generally went (as I remember): Pre-Arrival Preparation: Before arriving, I had to complete an online pre-registration form provided by the university. This form included my personal details, program information, and any course preferences I had. I was also required to submit my proof of enrollment and some supporting documents, like a copy of my passport and visa. Course Registration: After orientation, I logged into the university’s online course registration system. I had to select and enroll in my courses based on the availability and prerequisites. The system had a clear interface, but it was crucial to act fast since some classes filled up quickly! I also consulted the academic advisor regarding course loads and requirements, which provided clarity. Submitting Documents: Once I had my classes sorted out, I had to submit some additional documents, such as health insurance proof and a completed registration form detailing my chosen courses. This was done both online and in-person at the international office.
registration_help: There are advisors to reach out to from both your faculty and from student-support networks.

When I logged into the online course registration system, I found that there had been some discrepancies in the course catalog. Some of the classes I initially intended to enroll in weren't available, as the catalog had outdated information. This caused quite a bit of confusion and frustration. As a result, I ended up having to choose elective courses instead of my preferred options. While some of the electives turned out to be interesting, it wasn’t what I had set out to study. I reached out to the academic advisor to discuss my options, but by then, many of the popular courses were already full. Overall, I learned the importance of being flexible and adaptable in such situations, but it was disappointing not to get into the classes that aligned with my academic goals. I would recommend future students to double-check course availability ahead of time and have backup options ready, just in case any issues arise with the registration process.

course_level: A different grade system and it was refreasing. The grade wasnt just an oral/written exsam but spread on different assignment throughout the semester
teaching_comparison: Much the same - same level of respect but also friendlyness (less formal) between teacher and student :)
courses_enrolled: JAR257F Climate change: past, present and future JAR251F Application of Remote Sensing in Earth Sciences JAR256F Volcanic succession in Iceland and climate evolution in Iceland JAR622M Glaciology
recommended_courses: the ones with fieldtrip as part of the course
unexpected_costs: surprised by the expensive food,
cost_comparison: Vegetables and fruit was expensive, meat was very expensive
activities_available: Hiking and the gym and karaoke nights and trips with my mentorgroup
activities_recommended: Hiking and the gym - a form of exersice
weekend_recommendations: Go on trips - find inspiration from other students or the internet, rent a car and go!
culture_adjustment: Easy - meeting other peopl (mentor group) in the same situation helped us bond
socializing_tips: Talk to them in class, other it was a little hard to meet them
cultural_challenges: None - all was an experience
culture_appreciated: The friendliness
top3_advice: 1. Make a plan of all the deadlines - cause they keep coming and youll forget them 2. Join the mentor program 3. Go explore the country
other_useful_info: Look at my advises
most_rewarding: The friendships and memories
greatest_challenge: Finding the motivation to do schoolwork when every thing around you is new and exciting

crucial_aspects: The quality of the university and the experience of Iceland as a country to live in
info_ease: The incoming division from the host university was very good at providing the information needed
arrival_assistance: There were held several events from the international division at the host university. Tutor meetings were also arranged and helpful to get information
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was easy to choose courses and sign up for them, even though some courses required special documentation and were denied at first. Then I had to provide documentation for certain things related to either language skills or previous courses taken.
registration_help: The incoming division was very helpful whenever needed
registration_success: The timetable was not available until one week before semester start, and there were many overlaps - due to this I was forced to change some courses and couldn't get all the courses I wished to do
registration_advice: Make sure that you apply for a broad range of courses that you like. There will be overlap and you won't be able to follow all courses that you wish, so in this way you can choose better. Also make sure to get more courses pre-approved by the home university.
course_level: The quality of the courses was very good
teaching_comparison: It was overall very similar, however few things were different. There were more excursions in the course, which was very nice. Then, we had discussion sessions in smaller groups, were we had focus on different topics of the course, and had to present papers to our peers.
courses_enrolled: Soil Science Natural hazards Environmental Microbiology Cartography and Map Design
recommended_courses: Definitely Soil Science and Natural hazards, as they are very specific for Iceland and very interesting! There are field trips in both of the courses, and they were amazing.
unexpected_costs: When I moved in to the student housing, I had to buy my own router to get access to the internet.
cost_comparison: It was more or less the same level as Copenhagen, some things were cheaper, others were more expensive.
activities_available: The university has a gym on campus with really good prices for students. There is a bar on campus, which is the meeting point for all internationals, and has really good student prices as well.
activities_recommended: Definitely Studentakjallarinn, the bar on campus. I took a language course, which was really interesting, but quite costly, but I would still recommend it.
weekend_recommendations: Try to travel outside of Reykjavík as much as possible, there is so much to see and the weather usually is nicer outside of the capital :)
culture_adjustment: It is not very easy to fully integrate in the Icelandic society. Mostly I was hanging out with other international students
socializing_tips: Sign up for the buddy exchange, it is a great way of getting to know local students and other internationals
cultural_challenges: It is hard to get to know Icelandic people at first, but when you really try, they are super nice! It is in this way kind of similar to Denmark
culture_appreciated: I really enjoyed the abundance of outdoor activities and the spirit of it in the culture of Iceland
top3_advice: 1. Travel as much as you can 2. Apply for many courses, also pre-approval from KU 3. Enjoy the life outside of university
other_useful_info: Again, try to apply to many courses, so you have a backup in case they overlap and you have to change the course selection
most_rewarding: The experience of getting to know so many other international students in an easy way, the chance to get to know the culture and to see a lot of this beautiful country!
greatest_challenge: The weather (especially the constant strong wind) and the long nights in winter

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study in English, and they do offer English speaking courses at University of Iceland. I have dreamed of going to Iceland for long, so that was the main reason I chose this destination.
overall_comments: It was great, only would have wished I went on more trips and partied more!
info_ease: I would say fairly easy, and if I could not find the information myself I could always email either KU or the University of Iceland.
arrival_assistance: I got a mentor. I only met with my mentor one time, but I could always write her if I had a question. There is a help desk at the main building at university where they help students getting a student ID and so on. I could also write teachers to ask about courses.
arrival_comments: When I arrived, numbers of Covid cases rose so most of the orientation was canceled or made online, which of course was a disappointment, but also understandable. Students wanting to go abroad, no matter where they go, should be aware and accept that this might and probably will happen. I think the mentoring program could have been better. They talked about arranging trips around Iceland for exchange students, but there were no trips as far as I know. This was a bit disappointing. I think a lot of the socializing I had to do myself, it was not like they had a lot of events I could go to and thereby meet people. So this was a bit tough, but I found good friends myself. They have good student support of you reach out though - it is possible to attend mindfulness classes and they also have a therapist that you can book an appointment with if you need that.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was great, only would have wished I went on more trips and partied more!
registration_process: Very easy. If you only stay one semester you just have to go to the help desk and say you have arrived, and you apply for a student card. I got a kennintala, which is like a CPR number because I moved my address to Iceland. That is very easy too, you just go to Registers Iceland and they register you. The number you also use when you go to the doctor, if you get a job and so on.
registration_help: At the help desk they told me to go to Registers Iceland to get a Kennintala. I could also email the international devision to get answers to my questions.
registration_success: They have a good system where it is possible 15 days after classes have started that one can change courses. This is all done online. I had to do this since two classes overlapped. One thing that makes it slightly difficult is that they have a min. 60 % rule. It means that at least 60 % of your courses (so 20 ects) has to be in one school/faculty. So you can't just choose random courses. Therefore I ended up taking a course I did not really want, but the other courses I wanted were online, and I did not want any online courses. Courses within one faculty, for instance humanities, do mostly not overlap, but if you take courses within different faculties they might overlap, and then you have to re-elect courses.
registration_advice: Be aware of the min 60 % rule.
academics_comments: It was great, only would have wished I went on more trips and partied more!
course_level: There is more work during the semester than at KU. Less reading, but more tests that count towards your final grade. I had tests in all of my subjects, so I always had to do some kind of work. The texts I read was easier than at KU. I think my courses did not go so much in depht as the courses at KU. The exam was easier than exams at KU.
teaching_comparison: I had teaching in class and traditional lectures. This was a lot like how it is at KU, but perhaps a little less formal.
courses_enrolled: ENS 101G How Language Works I: Sound and Word (5 ects) ENS 102G The Talking Animal (5 ects) ÞJÓ 506G Performance Studies (10 ects) ÍSE 025G Icelandic - the Basics (10 ects)
recommended_courses: I would recommend Performance Studies and Icelandic - the Basics. The teacher in performance studies is one of the best one I have had. He cares so much for his students and for the course. Gives great feedback and is a fun and great teacher. Take it if you like theatre, dance, music and theories about how everything we do can be seen as a performance. You will go on small field work trips by yourself which is also cool. I would also recommend Icelandic - the Basics if you would like to learn Icelandic. It is fun and I am happy I learned some Icelandic because it made me feel more like home, and it is also cool to be able to go to stores and actually be able to communicate in Icelandic. The teaching is good too and I would say as a Danish speaker it will not be that difficult to learn Icelandic, even though they have cases in their grammar.
unexpected_costs: My hiking boots needed fixing which costed 1100 DKK
cost_comparison: Public transportation is cheap. Taking the bus anywhere for 1 hour and 15 minutes costs 25 DKK. Cheese is very expensive. Sodas and some candies are cheap.
activities_available: There is a gym and a sauna at university which only costs 250 DKK for half a year. They also had some dance classes I did not attend.
activities_recommended: Going to the pool Knit - I met knitting friends at Kex hostel, where they have different events, here also a knitting event. Become friends with other exchange students and hang out
weekend_recommendations: Go out and see the wonders of Icelandic nature. Rent a car or take the bus somewhere. Go to the pools, either the public once or Sky Lagoon that is a bit more luxiurious.
culture_adjustment: The culture is kind of like the Danish culture. I did not find it easy to get Icelandic friends, so I think you really need to work for this if you want Icelandic friends too. I would say that there is a good relationship between Denmark and Iceland, but remember that Iceland used to be a Danish colony, so you might get a comment or two about this when you tell people that you are Danish. People still learn Danish at school, but few can really speak it, and also many do not like having to learn Danish.
socializing_tips: If you have classes with Icelanders, talk with them instead of just chatting with exchange students.
cultural_challenges: It was difficult to get Icelandic friends. It is not easy to bicycle in Reykjavík, which I missed to do a lot.
culture_appreciated: That everyone goes to the pool to hang out - it is kind of like going to a park in Copenhagen to chat with friends.
top3_advice: - Bring warm clothes - It is useful to have a drivers license, but if you do not, just find some friends that have so you can go on road trips - Find a job so you can afford more trips and go more out. Also it is a great way to get to know more people
other_useful_info: Take lots of Vitamin D
most_rewarding: Getting to know a bunch of new people and experiencing the nature. Going on horse back riding trips.
greatest_challenge: Feeling lonely and being homesick in the beginning. It wears off, but it happened to me hard in the beginning
other_comments: Just go! You won't regret it. I felt pretty safe staying in Iceland considering Covid. Not many people live there so it felt safe, and it was easy to get quick tests if needed.

crucial_aspects: To me the study destination was not that important at first. I just wanted to go abroad to explore a new culture. Then I found out, that in Iceland, I could combine this with courses about Danish literature as well as the connection between Danmark and Iceland. In this sense, my courses became very much related to my studies at home.
overall_comments: It has been an amazing experience to study abroad. I have learned a lot about my self and how to deal with a new culture and school system although it is similar to the danish school system. Also I have met so many cool people as well as I have used my English language a lot more.
info_ease: It was very easy to find information. The university did help me a lot as I could both write them, if I didn't understand the information online, and they offered a great introduction online (due to COVID) in the beginning of the semester.
arrival_assistance: I arrived later than the official dates of the beginning of the semester, because I had an exam at home. Thereby I didn't have the chance to get assistance physically. When I arrived, everyone was very friendly and helped me creating a study card, get access to the portals etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It has been an amazing experience to study abroad. I have learned a lot about my self and how to deal with a new culture and school system although it is similar to the danish school system. Also I have met so many cool people as well as I have used my English language a lot more.
registration_process: I registrated my courses at home, and when I arrived, I had to confirm my choice of courses. It was possible to change courses if you wanted to, but I did not, so it was a very easy process.
registration_help: I could always write an email and they would answer very quickly.
registration_success: I was very successful. I got all the courses I applied for at home.
registration_advice: I got the courses I applied for at home. In the meantime I know a lot of students, who changed their courses after they arrived, and it was very easy. So don't be afraid to choose a course, because you can change it. Also, sometimes the courses applied for at home are not offered when you arrive, hence why you will need to re-registrate courses, but that is not a problem.
academics_comments: It has been an amazing experience to study abroad. I have learned a lot about my self and how to deal with a new culture and school system although it is similar to the danish school system. Also I have met so many cool people as well as I have used my English language a lot more.
course_level: The academic level was a little bit lower than at my home university. Two of my courses were taught in danish, hence why it was easy for me to follow these courses. We had a lot of reading to to in those courses, but not many tasks. My third course was taught in english, and it was thereby more challenging for me, and there were more tasks.
teaching_comparison: It was very similar. The big difference was the amount of people within the courses. Whereas we normally are about 25 students in a class at home, we were only 7 students in two of my courses here in Iceland. Therefor the teaching was even more dialogue based than at home.
courses_enrolled: 1) Bilingualism 2) Forholdet mellem Danmark og Island 3) Skandinavisk samtidslitteratur
recommended_courses: Both bilingualism and Skandinavisk samtidslitteratur
unexpected_costs: When you move to another place, there will always be uexpected costs such as specific things for your room (to me it was for example a blanket and decorative pillows) and basic elements for the kitchen. Also, you can never know how much money you will spend on trips around the country, social events etc.
cost_comparison: tofu was super cheap and I used it a lot for my cooking. Besides that, almost all items in supermarkets were a lot more expensive than at home. On the other hand, some cultural events were cheaper than expected, as some of the museumentries were even for free.
activities_available: I used the school gym very much, and there is a student cellar with a lot of cool events. Other than that I bought a card for the local swimm, and used this a lot during my stay.
activities_recommended: The gym and the pools! It is a nice way to get exercise and hang out with your friends at the same time.
weekend_recommendations: I would highly recommend renting a car in the weekends and go on roadtrips. It is not expensive if you can fill up a car, and there are so many magnificent places to see and experience around Iceland.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. Denmark and Iceland are very similar countries, and many groceries are from Denmark, as well as icelanders also know a lot of the danish language.
socializing_tips: I was so lucky, that some icelanders also had the courses taught in Danish, and because we very so few student, we got to know each other very well. I know it can be difficult to get to know the local students when you are an exchange student, so I think - if you want to get to know the locals, you should participate in social events at campus and don't be afraid of reaching out.
cultural_challenges: I did not find anything challenging
culture_appreciated: I appreciated how the icelanders are more 'loose' than in Denmark. Both within the school system and in the every day. The atmosphere is less busy and if you for example miss a deadline, you are now caught in the system, but instead they are understanding to human mistakes.
top3_advice: 1) The academic expectations are less high 2) It is a very small university - which I found pleasent - but it means that sometimes you are just a few students in a class 3) Everyone is so nice and helpful
other_useful_info: no
most_rewarding: to meet new people, to practice my english language and to experience how to live in a foreign country
greatest_challenge: It was challenging that everything was more expensive than at home

crucial_aspects: The size of the place mattered a lot to me as smaller places tend to have a better community. I also looked into the housing opportunities on beforehand. I also chose my destination because of its shared history with my home country and to know more about the culture. It was important that the place was in the EU or had similar agreements as another EU country to make it more available.
info_ease: Quite easy - we had some introduction days where we got to know campus and were told what we needed to do.
arrival_assistance: The days of introduction and the opportunity to write to the international office at the destination which was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: As far as I recall I only had to show up to the student desk at the university center and here i registered within a few minutes. I choose my classes when I applied for the university. I had some trouble in figuring out the online tools for accessing my classes but I figured it out in the end.
registration_help: I could e-mail the International office or ask for help at the student desk. We also had a big exchange student - WhatsApp group which helped a lot.
registration_success: I had to change one class as my destination university did not allow for me to take a master level course as I am a BA - student.
registration_advice: Do as much as you can from home so you don't have to struggle with OLA agreement, picking new courses and so on when you get started as there is a lot to do in terms of getting settled when you arrive.
course_level: The courses at times seemed very easy when they were directed toward exchange students. Not a lot to read and the expectations of our academic level were quite low. My more field-orientated course was way more stimulating.
teaching_comparison: It was quite similar. Classroom lectures, group work and some essays and presentations.
courses_enrolled: Icelandic Culture, Icelandic Nature and Cultural Legacy, and The Cognitive Turn: Form and Meaning in Language and Litterature.
recommended_courses: I would pick one course that was directed towards exchange students and then the others more specific towards my actual field as two "exchange student" courses were a bit too much and too similar.
unexpected_costs: Costs of buying a router for my room, cost of fixing my jacket, the overall cost of going on trips, and so on.
cost_comparison: More! I spend way more money than I thought I would.
activities_available: Dance class, some musicals I think, and some other opportunities as well, but they were not really being marketed.
activities_recommended: I would recommend arranging some on your own. My school did not do much to facilitate any social events so I would encourage that more - more parties or events in general. If that is not available, I would ask the international office or try to seek out opportunities myself.
weekend_recommendations: Drive out on road trips - it's all that really makes sense in Iceland. Renting a car and driving out.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy - it is very similar but I was supprised in terms of the more relaxed approach to everything.
socializing_tips: Stay at student housing!
cultural_challenges: The aspect of planning and being organized was challenging at times. For instance, when I picked up the key to my student housing I was not told that I needed to sign my lease agreement later at the school. I only figured that out weeks later from another exchange student.
culture_appreciated: Even though the planning and organizing was challenging it was also really lovely and I am defiantly going to try to be more like that when I go home. Not thinking too far ahead or making too specific plans helps with stress and makes you more present in the moment from a personal perspective.
top3_advice: Try to stay at student housing, be prepared to be very socially active in the first weeks, and save up money!
other_useful_info: I would encourage them to think of it as if they were going to live there. 5 months might not seem long but it makes you more relaxed and easier to consider it a more permanent thing. I did not get the Icelandic social security number because I thought I did not need it - and officially I didn't because I only stayed for 5 months. But looking back it makes a lot of things like going to the doctor, getting a library card and everything so much easier. And you save a lot of money from it.
most_rewarding: Getting to know a lot of international people has really been quite amazing. Also getting to live in another country has put an entirely new perspective on my home country and has made me think about doing my masters in another country. It has definitly opened up my perspective.
greatest_challenge: Getting settled and starting my everyday life in another place was quite challenging. Feeling like I was constantly forgetting something was also quite difficult - like have I done everything I should from home, am I getting the most out of my experience and so on. And also the first week was difficult because you really want to - and unfortunately need to - make friends fast.

crucial_aspects: Getting introduced to the language.
overall_comments: Amazing!
info_ease: Very easy.
arrival_assistance: Tutor network and orientation days helped a lot.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Amazing!
registration_process: Announcing my arrival at the relevant desk, that's about it.
registration_help: Coordinators
registration_success: Easy and streamlined through the website and app.
registration_advice: Be sure that all you remember all your documentation, when you go to fill out paperwork.
academics_comments: Amazing!
course_level: I took two courses on MA level, just because I could and the subjects interested me. This made the workload pretty intense though.
teaching_comparison: Pretty similar, except for one class where we -the students- essentially had to plan the class discussions ourselves.
courses_enrolled: SAG506M: The Uses of History in Putin's Russia/Pútín og misnotkun sögunnar í Rússlandi UAU018M: The Arctic Circle UAU107M: Climate Change SAG716M: The Medieval North

activities_recommended: Tuesday night karaoke at Gaukurinn.

socializing_tips: Strike up a conversation! Don't expect much enthusiasm right away, Icelanders are pretty withdrawn. Ask them how much they hate the Danish.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere where I could explore nature and have great nature experiences. It was also important that I was able to have courses in different subjects and themes. It was also important to me that the courses were taught in english, or another language that I already knew.
info_ease: I got send most of the information on my Ku mail, furthermore there was a welcome meeting that I attended. Most of the information was quite easy to acces, but I had to find some information myself.
arrival_assistance: There was an information meeting for new students which was quite informative as to where I could search for further information about almost amything.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We had to find courses online and apply to them. The registration process in itself was not very difficult, but it was a bit of a hassle to find the courses available that semester, as it was not all updated in the course catalog.
registration_help: There was a help desk at the university,
registration_success: I first registered for courses that overlapped, so I had to reregister. Once that was done it was quite easy. It was not difficult to deregister from a course, the most difficult part was to find exactly which courses were available at which times, the course information pages were not the same, as the teacher was responsible for their own page.
registration_advice: Do not be afraid to reregister for another course if the first ones do not fit, just be sure to deregister from the exams.
course_level: The level was not as high as in Copenhagen. It was not easy, but the amount of reading was not as high. I only had mixed levels courses, so they were very general, and that might have something to do with the levels.
teaching_comparison: On the other hand there was a lot of tests and assignments during the semester which is very different from my courses in Copenhagen,
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled in Anthropology of gender, environmental anthropology, Being Icelandic and Basic Icelandic 1.
recommended_courses: Depending on your interest I found Being Icelandic and Basic Icelandic quite informative. I got to have a deeper understanding of the culture and learned a small bit of the language which I appreciated. I also enjoyed both the other courses, and they both awakened a deeper interest, but as they were mixed level open courses they were very general, so it should rather be seen as introductory courses, which I did not know when I registered for them.
unexpected_costs: I was on quite a lot of trips and spend a lot more money on renting cars than I had expected. I also ended up doing a ring road road trip which was quite expensive. Other than this I used a bit of money on furniture and decorations for my room as it was very sparingly furnished.
cost_comparison: Coffee is quite inexpensive which was a really pleasant surprise. You can easily go to a cafe and only pay around 30-35 dkk for a coffee.
activities_available: In the beginning of the semester there were a few parties, I believe there might have been a soccer tournament and a beer pong tournament as well. All in all there was not that many activities available.
activities_recommended: The welcome days,
weekend_recommendations: I would really recommend exploring as much of the country as possible. Especially in the beginning (or end) when the highlands are still open.
culture_adjustment: It was quite similar to danish culture, but be aware that Icelanders are even more closed off that Danes in general.
socializing_tips: Try to become friends with the Icelanders in your dorm, even though it can be a bit difficult,
cultural_challenges: The closed off-ness.
culture_appreciated: The easy going way of living, even though it means that time management is not a great competence.
top3_advice: Utilize your free time to go on hiking and sight seeing trips, especially when the highlands are open. Don’t think to much about the money you are spending, it will be worth it. Be open and try the local cuisine, even though it might not look appealing it is fun to try,
other_useful_info: If you like hiking bring your gear with you as it is quite expensive to buy in iceland, if you do buy it there, be sure to get a tax free voucher, and get the money back in the airport,
most_rewarding: I loved all the nature, and I will definitely be coming back to Iceland sooner rather than later.
greatest_challenge: I expected to get a lot of local friends, which was quite difficult, as some are a bit stand off-ish to exchange students, but instead I got a lot of international (and danish) friends.

crucial_aspects: I was very inspired by the courses the University of Iceland offered. Especially the aspects of Ethics of Nature.
overall_comments: I definitely had an amazing stay in Iceland. I especially enjoyed the courses and the beautiful nature.
info_ease: It was pretty good.
arrival_assistance: We were given mentor groups, where we met some of the other students and had an Icelandic person as our mentor to tell us about Iceland and give us recommendations in general.
arrival_comments: I felt safe and knew who to contact if I had any questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I definitely had an amazing stay in Iceland. I especially enjoyed the courses and the beautiful nature.
registration_process: I found some courses at home that I applied for pre-approval for. When I first came to the university, I changed one of my courses and changed it on Ugla. Then I re-send a pre-approval to my home university.
registration_help: I just went to the international office at the University of Iceland on campus, and asked them what to do.
registration_success: Very succesfull.
registration_advice: Just ask the international office at the campus. They where really helpful.
academics_comments: I definitely had an amazing stay in Iceland. I especially enjoyed the courses and the beautiful nature.
course_level: Some of the courses I had were both for BA and MA.
teaching_comparison: Common for the style of teaching at UCPH and the University of Iceland was that the students were orally active. But in UCPH I am used to the exams at the end of the semester, whereas in Iceland it was distributed throughout the semester. We had a lot of smaller assignments and reports that we had to hand in, which could be stressful. My best advice is to make a calendar for yourself, where you put in all the deadlines. This helped me organize my studies.
courses_enrolled: Ethics of Nature Project in Ethics of Nature Icelandic Nature and Cultural Legacy Pronouncing and Listening Speech and Expression
recommended_courses: Ethics of Nature. This course was so inspiring to me, and I really liked the way of teaching. The course provided philosophical perspectives on nature and the current climate crisis.
unexpected_costs: I used most of my money on trips on the weekends. This was definitely worth it, but I was surprised at how much money it was to rent a car, etc.
cost_comparison: Alcohol in general was very very expensive. But actually coffee in cafes was not that expensive. In general, the groceries were also pretty expensive, but this did not surprise me that much. The bus and the fitness were also pretty cheap.
activities_available: Mostly it was fitness, but I also attended dance classes at Háskóladansinn, which was really nice and cheap.
activities_recommended: If you have the possibility just sign up for something. For me, it was really nice to attend both yoga and dance classes, because it was a nice way to meet other people, but also just to get some movement during some of the dark months.
weekend_recommendations: In general, I really enjoyed the trips during the weekends. It was so nice to see other parts of Iceland, but also just to hang out with some of the other students at the student cellar (the beer is also pretty cheap there). But also just to relax, and enjoy Reykjavik. I also enjoyed the sea behind the student housing a lot and just went on long walks.
culture_adjustment: For me, it was pretty easy. Icelandic culture is in most ways not that far from the culture I am from.
socializing_tips: I met some Icelandic people at student housing (I shared a kitchen with one), but also I met Icelandic students at the dance lessons. But to be honest, I mostly spent time with other exchange students, because this was more accessible.
cultural_challenges: Iceland is of course a pretty expensive country. This meant that I did not go out that often. But it helped that we had the student cellar because if was more affordable. Also, I had two experiences, where I was going on trips that got canceled due to the weather conditions. This was a bit disappointing, but the weather just controls the activities in Iceland in another way than I am used to.
culture_appreciated: I definitely loved the swimming pools in Reykjavik. I bought a half-year card, which I used maybe 2-3 times a week throughout the year. This was amazing, and I miss it a lot.
top3_advice: 1. The country is pretty expensive. Personally, this meant that I did not go out as much as I would do at home (go to restaurants, bars, etc.). But I actually enjoyed this. I used most of my money on trips on the weekends, which was a great priority looking back. Iceland is so unique in nature, and I had great hikes when traveling in the weekends. 2. Sign up for something! For me, it was really great to have some activities throughout the week that I had to go to. Thereby I met nice people, and also I was a nice way to get some everyday routine. 3. Go to the pools! This was such a nice way to spend time with the other exchange students and a very unique way of being outside in all kinds of weather.
other_useful_info: Go on trips during the summer period, before it gets too late because of the weather conditions.
most_rewarding: A good mix of inspiring courses, and Icelandic nature. This is both in regard to the trips on the weekends, and also in regard to the walks I did in Reykjavik near the coast. I enjoyed the mountains and the green moss so much.
greatest_challenge: I found the way of teaching (with the many assignments) a bit stressful and in some periods I had a lot to do in my courses. Sometimes it was difficult to find the balance between school work and being on exchange in a foreign country and all the experiences and emotions that follows,
other_comments: I would definitely recommend going to the University of Iceland as an exchange student. Iceland is such a unique country, and the level of teaching was definitely fulfilling in the humanistic field.
