crucial_aspects: I chose the University of Iceland because of the courses available and because I wanted to explore the naturel phenomena on the island.
overall_comments: I had hoped to do more courses in gender studies but unfortunately there was not that many in English.
info_ease: I was very easy to find the information. The course catalogue is very accessible and it was easy to understand what courses were available to me. The university's website offered a link to the student housing website, which meant that I could sign up for housing immodestly after receiving my nomination from my home university. If I had any questions the internation office at the University of Iceland was very helpfull and responded very quickly to my emails.
arrival_assistance: I asked them many questions about all sort of things and they replied within a few days.
arrival_comments: I changed courses after arriving and because of the different grade system they were not sure if I was allowed to do the courses. I think it would be nice if they for future reference knew what grade on the international scale they consider to be a "first grade". Maybe a B or C. I don't know. I was just a bit stressfull because I worried I would not get enough ECTS points.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had hoped to do more courses in gender studies but unfortunately there was not that many in English.
registration_process: So when you apply for the university (this was mainly formalities because I had already been given the spot by my home university), you send them the courses you wish to take: course name, number and amount of ECTS. If something is wrong they will email you so you can correct it. I had signed up for a course that ONLY master students could do, so I had to choose something else. The first two weeks you can unregister and register on new courses. I ended up doing non of the courses I had originally chosen. The proces is very easy, I would say. Except the whole thing with the grade average. I still don't know what 7.25 is on an international scale.
registration_help: Lots. The international department is really nice and helpfull and the faculties are helpfull as well.
registration_success: Very. I got the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: In Iceland they are more laid back when it comes to deadline and registrations than in Denmark, so if you run into trouble they will help you fix it. And you can visit their office and talk to them and everything. Reflecting back on it, they were very accessible.
academics_comments: I had hoped to do more courses in gender studies but unfortunately there was not that many in English.
course_level: I had some courses which were for both masters and bachelor students. The majority of my courses were for both. You just had to have finished a certain amount ECTS and have a certain average.
teaching_comparison: I had a research seminar where we discussed art theory for three hours. That was amazing and more of flat structure than what you experience at UCPH. Compared to my program at UCPH, there was more mandatory work which counted to your final grade. At my home program we usually do assignments doing the semester and they have to be approved for us to take the exam. But in Iceland these things counted a certain percentage. I thought that was nice, cause then when I did my final exam, I had already done 60% of the work.
courses_enrolled: Research Seminar A: Socially Engaged Art Hollywood: Place and Myth Icelandic Nature and Cultural Legacy Ethics of Nature
recommended_courses: I would actually reccoment them all. The Icelandic Nature and Cultural Legacy was a bit boring and we never really went into depth with anything. However, the reason I chose this course was because of the field trips and they were okay. I might choose a different course. Then again the courses did not demand that much for me and that was very nice. Then I had a lot of time to explore the city and the island. The final exam of the course is a sit down exam. And some of the questions were a bit hard cause we were not allowed notes. However, nobody failed. I don't think they bother failing anyone because everybody on this could are exchange students. The research seminar was SO cool. I was very much in love with this course. Bothe the professors and the students had very different backgrounds and we had such interesting dialogues about art theory and the colonial traditions in modern art theory. The Hollywood course was also great: Nikita is very inspiring and it is such an interesting perspective on Hollywood. It was about the history of the institution, censurship, the Hollywood dream, and how films from Hollywood portray Hollywood. Almost like a self-portrait. Highly recommend! Also! In this course I had to do one presentation and one paper which was about 8 pages. However, we could always chose our own topics which meant that you did not have to read everything to do well on the exams. Ethics of Nature: I LOVED THIS COURSE. It was so interesting and again a course where people had very different backgrounds. We read some great texts, which has stayed with me and one of the themes of this course inspired my bachelor project.
unexpected_costs: Not unexpected, but the trips around the island is expensive. We would rent cars, cottages, camper vans and go away for several days to hang out. The pools were not very expensive but an important part of the experience. I would not have been without any of my trips. I did both weekends, longer trips, and day trips. It was incredible.
cost_comparison: Some foods were much more expensive but some were the same. Some were even cheaper. The eggplant was ridiculous expensive. Alcohol was also very expensive.
activities_available: Film clubs, a student gym (very cheap: 300 dkk for the entire semester), dance lessons.
activities_recommended: The Japanese film club was very nice. And the gym: they had yoga and pilates courses there which were free.
weekend_recommendations: THE NATURE! Iceland is like a different planet and you can drive for thirty minutes and then it looks like you changed planets again. It is the most incredible nature I have ever seen.
culture_adjustment: I was pretty chill. There is many overalps with the Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Hmm. I met one local. The rest was other exchange students. We really enjoyed the course we had together and discussed the texts after class as well. A Dutch girl and I went to the locals art studio to do a writing exercise. That was really cool, especially because I got an introduction to the art facilities available to the Icelandic youth.
cultural_challenges: It can be challenging that they are more laissez-faire than other than in Denmark. Particularly, if it is about a course or a deadline or something. Then it is challenging. Some old men also wanted to make me responsible for the Danish colonial past; that was a bit challenging. The accessibility to medicine was very frustrating. The pharmacies closed early and on the weekends and then you can't get anything. Not even paracetamol. It was the same with alcohol. The alcohol shopped closed at 7, and then you had to buy it at a bar - which was very expensive. The public transport is VERY limited, if you are from Western Europe. There were electric scooters, bike, and pedestrians on the same areas. It is a very car-friendly city. The suburbs are very inaccessible if you do not have a car. And there is basically no busses going around the island. There is one to the harbour with the ferry for the Westmann Islands and one bus for Akureryi. That is it. No trains and no metros. So, remember your drivers licens or make friends that have theirs.
culture_appreciated: The pools were amazing and I miss them. Everyday. Culture was very accessible; there was a lot of free concerts and I saw Björk do a DJ set. And it was free. It is a very local culture, so you feel somewhat integrated very early.
top3_advice: It is expensive: so save up some money if you can. The nature is incredible and you have to experience it as well if you are going. It is a great way to get close to the other exchange students and make friends. I really enjoyed it! Sign up for student housing as early as possible. Make friends with other exchange students because they would LOVE to go on trips and explore the island. I visited many places that I did not know existed. Also: do easy courses. I loved my courses but I enjoyed that, I did not need to study that much for them. The majority of the time, I just went to the lectures and that worked out great.
other_useful_info: It is possible to apply for a grant at Den Dansk-Islandske Fond. This grant was not mentioned in Legathåndbogen, so check that out. I did not apply but I know several people who received it.
most_rewarding: The nature, the people, the inspiring courses that I did. The atmosphere of the city. It is incredible. I highly recommend it.
greatest_challenge: I think the greatest challenge is the economy. There is so much to do which is just incredibly expensive. I do think it is worth it, but I have spent so much more money than I usually do in Copenhagen.
other_comments: There is basically no crime, but the nature can kill you. Don't turn your back on the ocean if you visit the black beach on the south coast. And enjoy visiting one of the only capitals where the tourists wear hiking clothing in the city center.

crucial_aspects: The choice to study at the University of Iceland was driven by my deep passion for inclusion, diversity, and cultural exchange within education. Iceland's unique academic environment, characterized by its emphasis on innovative approaches to pedagogy and second-language acquisition, offered an ideal setting for me to advance my academic and personal goals. As someone born and raised in London to Danish and French parents, I have always navigated multiple cultural identities, giving me a strong understanding of the challenges and opportunities faced by international and third-culture children. This background inspired my desire to research and contribute to educational systems that support multilingual and multicultural students. Iceland's remarkable literacy rate, its commitment to equitable education, and its culturally rich environment made it an inspiring choice for my Erasmus exchange. The University of Iceland's curriculum offered a perfect fit for my academic interests, allowing me to study subjects such as second-language theories and pedagogy, crime and social deviance, and Icelandic for beginners. This focus not only aligned with my goal of becoming a pedagogy researcher specializing in multilingual education but also provided invaluable insights into the ways language shapes cultural identity and inclusion. Additionally, the opportunity to volunteer as a teaching assistant at the International School of Iceland strengthened my practical skills in teaching Danish and English to children from diverse backgrounds. I was also drawn to Iceland because of its dynamic and ever-changing landscapes, which reflect the sense of exploration and growth I seek in life. By immersing myself in Icelandic culture, learning the language, and exploring its breathtaking natural scenery on weekends through hikes, ice climbing, and sailing, I hoped to develop a deeper connection to the country and its people. For me, understanding a culture begins with its language, as it offers a window into the values, expressions, and worldview of its speakers. Ultimately, my decision to study in Iceland was fueled by a desire to challenge myself academically, culturally, and personally. I wanted to live in a country that fosters innovation, inclusion, and respect for diversity, and Iceland offered the perfect setting to further these aspirations.
info_ease: Here's a possible response to the question: Finding the information I needed upon arrival in Iceland was somewhat challenging, as much of it was not readily accessible or centralized. I often felt I was on my own when it came to navigating practicalities like settling into housing, understanding the university system, or even finding basic services in Reykjavík. However, this experience also highlighted the Icelandic mindset of helpfulness and openness. Whenever I reached out for assistance, whether it was from university staff, fellow students, or locals, I was met with genuine kindness and a willingness to help. This made the process of figuring things out much easier and less stressful. For example, when I struggled to find details about transportation or university facilities, a quick conversation with someone on campus or in the community often provided all the guidance I needed. Although the lack of upfront information presented initial hurdles, the approachable and supportive attitude of people in Iceland turned these challenges into opportunities for connection and learning. It also encouraged me to be resourceful and proactive, skills that I carried throughout my exchange semester.
arrival_assistance: Upon arriving at my study destination in Iceland, I did participate in an orientation program offered by the university. However, true to the Icelandic mindset, the program was somewhat late, slightly unorganized, and much of the crucial information was shared after I had already figured it out on my own. While the orientation was helpful in providing an overview of university life and connecting with other exchange students, the lack of structure meant that I had to take a proactive approach to learn key details, such as navigating campus facilities and managing practical matters like transportation or setting up essential services. That said, the Icelandic attitude of friendliness and helpfulness made it easy to get assistance when needed. Whether it was university staff or fellow students, people were always approachable and willing to answer questions or point me in the right direction. This combination of self-reliance and community support turned what could have been a challenge into a valuable learning experience.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process at my host institution was very straightforward. All the instructions were available on UGLA, the university's online portal. With just a few clicks, I could easily register for courses or make changes to my schedule. The process was user-friendly and efficient.
registration_help: There wasn't a lot of direct help available, but if you needed assistance, you could always go to student services. They were helpful and ready to support with any questions or issues you might have had.
registration_success: I initially faced some challenges with course registration, as there were frequent scheduling conflicts or courses that were not directly relevant to my degree. However, after reviewing the available options and making adjustments, I was able to successfully register for the courses that aligned with my academic goals.
registration_advice: My advice to future exchange students would be to carefully review the course offerings early, as there may be scheduling conflicts or limited options relevant to your degree. It's important to be flexible and proactive in making adjustments. If you're unsure, don't hesitate to reach out to student services for guidance. With some patience and planning, you'll be able to register for the courses that suit your needs.
course_level: In terms of teaching style, I do prefer the way courses are taught at UCPH. While it was interesting to experience the teaching methods in Iceland, I found that the way courses were evaluated varied greatly. At UCPH (for my Pedagogy course), I appreciated having one large assignment followed by an oral exam, which allowed for a deeper focus on the material. However, in Iceland, the assessment formats ranged from that structure to many smaller assignments spread throughout the semester. From an Erasmus perspective, this made it difficult to balance academic work with other crucial aspects of the exchange experience, such as traveling on weekends.
teaching_comparison: Additionally, the teaching approach felt different. In some courses, while the assigned readings were important, I felt that class discussions primarily focused on reviewing and talking about the content rather than critically analyzing it or comparing it to previous readings. This was something I missed, especially as all the modules I took were in subjects that I did not have a prior academic background in, such as language and culture or criminology. It would have been beneficial to have more opportunities to discuss the readings critically, compare them with earlier texts, and explore the broader theoretical context, as I have experienced at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Second Language Theories and Pedagogy, Crime and Social Deviance, Languages and Culture, Icelandic for Beginners
recommended_courses: I would recommend Icelandic for all exchange students, the teachers are fantastic and are brilliant in not only teaching the language but also informing you on current events and culture. Crime and Social Deviance was also a favourite, the professors are so engaging, the class is always keen to discuss relevant topics and it is really easy for anyone to follow along even if you do not have a background in criminology.
unexpected_costs: Extra was paid for regarding a doctors appointment and gym/ bouldering memberships.
cost_comparison: Whilst I was prepared for being in an expensive country, there is no denying that it is an expensive country to live in as a student. However, luckily regarding trips or food it was easy to split the cost between people, both benefiting a social life and economic means.
activities_available: In terms of cultural, athletic, and social activities available for students, there was a gym that provided a variety of classes, which were really fun to attend. My personal favorite was the kettlebell class. However, beyond the gym, there weren't many organized activities for students. There was a dance club organized by some students, but it was not officially run by the university. Other than that, the options for social or cultural activities felt quite limited. This lack of options was disappointing, especially for students who may not be interested in sports. It made it more challenging to find opportunities to meet people and socialize in structured ways, which would have enhanced the overall experience.
activities_recommended: For non-academic activities, I would highly recommend future exchange students to try bouldering. The community at the bouldering gym is incredibly warm and welcoming, making it a great way to meet people and feel included. It is also an ideal activity because it can be done year-round, regardless of the weather, which is particularly valuable in a country where outdoor conditions can be unpredictable. Bouldering offers a perfect balance of physical activity, social interaction, and fun, making it a fantastic way to enrich the Erasmus experience.
weekend_recommendations: When it comes to weekend or holiday activities, Iceland offers endless opportunities for exploration. I would recommend breaking up your trips to focus on specific regions, as this allows you to get the most out of your time. For example, you could spend one weekend exploring the Westfjords, another weekend discovering the South Coast, and another driving through the Diamond Circle. This way, you can truly appreciate the beauty and uniqueness of each area without feeling rushed. However, it is important to plan these trips carefully, particularly regarding the best time to visit each region. Many areas can be closed off during the winter months due to weather conditions, so researching accessibility and safety ahead of time is essential. Proper planning will ensure that you make the most of your weekends and holidays, while also staying safe in Iceland's ever-changing environment.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture in Iceland was both an exciting and rewarding experience, though it did come with its challenges. As a third-culture kid (TCK), I've had the privilege of experiencing various cultures, which made it easier to adapt to a new environment. However, moving to Iceland presented some unique aspects that required patience and openness. Iceland's culture is deeply rooted in its natural surroundings, which I found to be both beautiful and humbling. The country's rugged landscapes and outdoor lifestyle became a significant part of my adjustment. I made a conscious effort to immerse myself in Icelandic nature by hiking, ice climbing, and exploring glaciers, which allowed me to bond with the local environment and community. It was through these experiences that I truly felt connected to Iceland and its people. Language was one of the most important factors in understanding the culture. As I was keen on learning Icelandic, I attended beginner courses and practiced regularly, which not only helped me communicate better but also gave me deeper insights into the Icelandic way of thinking. I believe that to truly understand a culture, you must understand its language, and this was certainly the case in Iceland. The local people were warm and welcoming, though I did notice that their social norms and communication styles can be more reserved compared to the cultures I'm accustomed to. Nonetheless, my time as a teaching assistant at the International School of Iceland also gave me an opportunity to engage with Icelandic children and teachers, which helped me understand the local education system and cultural dynamics better. Overall, while there were challenges in adjusting, particularly with the language and some social nuances, my commitment to embracing Iceland's culture through language learning, outdoor activities, and engaging with locals made the adjustment process smooth and deeply enriching.
socializing_tips: Living in student accommodation and meeting local students in town were key to my social experience in Iceland. At the university, student housing is a hub of activity, and many locals live in the same dorms as exchange students. This made it easy to meet Icelandic students, especially since shared kitchens and common areas were great places to strike up conversations. I made an effort to speak Icelandic, even though I was still learning, which often led to friendly interactions. Locals appreciated the effort, and it gave me a genuine way to connect with them. Outside of campus, I spent a lot of time in Reykjavik's bars and cafés, where locals often gather to socialize. I found that these places were perfect for meeting people in a more relaxed setting. Most Icelanders are open to chatting, and since many speak English, it was easy to get conversations started. Still, I'd often try using the Icelandic phrases I had picked up, which made a big difference. Even if my language skills weren't perfect, they were happy to engage with me and appreciate the effort. What I loved most was how much locals valued personal connections, even in busy social settings. Icelandic students have a laid-back but genuine approach to socializing, so I never felt pressured. Whether in a student dorm or at a local bar, I found that simply being friendly, trying out Icelandic, and embracing the local atmosphere helped me form real connections with Icelandic students.
cultural_challenges: One of the cultural differences that I found particularly challenging was the reserved nature of Icelanders, especially in social situations. As someone who is used to a more outwardly expressive culture, like the British or even Danish, I initially found it a bit difficult to gauge the level of friendliness or interest in conversations. Icelanders can be quite reserved at first, especially in larger group settings, which might make it feel like it takes longer to build a connection. However, I soon learned that once you get to know them, Icelandic people are warm, friendly, and welcoming, but they just take a bit more time to open up. Another aspect I found challenging was the pace of socializing. While Icelandic students are very friendly, socializing often takes place in smaller, more intimate settings rather than large, loud group gatherings. It's a more subdued form of social interaction compared to what I was used to, where casual interactions in larger groups or public spaces are common. At first, this felt a bit isolating, but once I understood that the local social culture revolves around close-knit conversations and smaller groups, I was able to adapt. Additionally, the importance of personal space and silence was something I had to adjust to. Icelanders are comfortable with silence, and it doesn't always mean that someone is disinterested or uncomfortable. I'm used to filling silences with conversation, but in Iceland, I found that being quiet together can actually strengthen connections. It took me a little while to get comfortable with this quieter social dynamic. Lastly, the long, dark winters were a challenge to adjust to. Icelandic winters are harsh, with long periods of darkness, which can affect the social atmosphere. It took some time to adapt to this change in light and the impact it had on daily life and social energy, especially when everyone tends to stay indoors more during the colder months. Despite the darkness, I found that the cozy, intimate social gatherings that happen in cafes and bars during these months are a beautiful part of the culture, but it was still an adjustment. Overall, these cultural differences were not impossible to overcome but did require me to adjust my expectations and be more patient with the pace of socializing and building relationships in Iceland.
culture_appreciated: There were many aspects of Icelandic culture that I truly appreciated during my time there. One of the most striking was the deep connection to nature. Icelanders have a profound respect for their environment, and this is reflected in their daily lives and the way they interact with the landscape. The love for outdoor activities such as hiking, glacier hiking, and even ice climbing is not just a hobby but an integral part of their identity. I found that spending time in nature allowed me to connect with locals and experience the country in a meaningful way. Another aspect I appreciated was the sense of community. Iceland is a small country, and there's a strong sense of togetherness, especially in Reykjavík. Whether it was at the local cafés, pubs, or through university events, people were very welcoming and eager to engage with one another. This sense of familiarity and shared experience was something I really valued, and it made me feel at home, even though I was far from my own country. The Icelandic approach to education and inclusivity also stood out to me. The emphasis on equal opportunities for all students, regardless of background or ability, resonated with my own academic interests in pedagogy and educational psychology. Icelandic universities are known for being progressive and innovative in their teaching methods, and I felt fortunate to be part of that environment. This focus on inclusivity also extended beyond the classroom, as I saw it reflected in the welcoming attitude towards international students and diverse cultural backgrounds. Iceland's respect for tradition, yet willingness to embrace modernity, was another aspect I found fascinating. Icelanders are proud of their rich cultural heritage, from the ancient sagas to their folklore, yet they are also highly progressive and forward-thinking. The balance between honoring the past while being open to new ideas was something I admired and felt a strong connection to. Lastly, the Icelandic concept of hygge—the warmth and comfort that comes from being together in a cozy setting, often with a hot drink or by a fireplace—was something I found incredibly comforting. During the long, dark winter months, these small moments of coziness and togetherness became a cherished part of my experience. Overall, I deeply appreciated Iceland's strong sense of community, its harmonious relationship with nature, the inclusivity within its education system, and the warmth in everyday interactions. These elements made my time there memorable and allowed me to feel truly immersed in Icelandic culture.
top3_advice: If you're a UCPH student heading to the University of Iceland for an exchange, I would say the most important things to keep in mind are to fully embrace the outdoors, make an effort with the Icelandic language, and be patient with the social dynamics. First, Iceland's natural beauty is such a defining part of life there. The country is a paradise for outdoor enthusiasts, and you'll find that hiking, glacier exploring, and even ice climbing are integral parts of daily life. Locals take full advantage of the stunning landscapes, so don't miss the chance to get out and explore. It's a fantastic way to bond with Icelanders, as outdoor activities are a key part of their culture. In terms of language, I'd recommend learning some basic Icelandic, even if it's just a few phrases. While English is widely spoken, making an effort with the local language will be deeply appreciated by the Icelandic people. It's a great way to show respect for their culture and helps you connect with locals on a more personal level. Don't worry if you're not fluent right away—just trying to speak Icelandic will go a long way. Lastly, socializing in Iceland can be a bit different from what you might be used to. Icelanders tend to be more reserved at first, and socializing often happens in smaller, more intimate settings rather than large, loud gatherings. It can take a little time to break the ice, but once you do, you'll find that they are very welcoming and friendly. Patience is key here—friendships in Iceland tend to develop slowly but deeply. By embracing these aspects of Icelandic life, you'll find your exchange to be a truly enriching and unforgettable experience.
other_useful_info: One thing I would highly recommend for future exchange students heading to the University of Iceland is to take full advantage of the student services and resources available on campus. The university offers various support systems, from language courses to academic advice, and they are incredibly helpful in making your transition smoother. If you're struggling with anything, don't hesitate to reach out for guidance. Icelanders are generally very approachable, and the staff at the university are there to support international students. Also, be prepared for the weather! Iceland's weather can be quite unpredictable, with frequent changes throughout the day. Even during the autumn, it can be sunny one minute and rainy or snowy the next. Investing in good outdoor gear, especially waterproof jackets, sturdy shoes, and layers, will make your experience a lot more comfortable, particularly if you plan to explore the outdoors, which I strongly recommend. Another piece of advice is to embrace the slower pace of life in Iceland. While Reykjavik is vibrant and full of cultural events, life in Iceland overall tends to be more relaxed compared to big cities in other countries. Things close early, and there's a much greater emphasis on quality time with friends and family, so adjust your expectations accordingly. Don't rush—take time to enjoy the small things like a good cup of coffee in a cozy café or a walk around the city or nearby nature. Lastly, while Reykjavik is a great city, don't forget to explore other parts of the country. Iceland's small population means the country feels like a close-knit community, and many students take trips to places like the Golden Circle, Westfjords, or even remote villages. Traveling around the country is not only an amazing experience but also an excellent way to bond with both Icelandic and international students. Overall, just be open to new experiences, immerse yourself in the culture, and take time to appreciate the stunning surroundings—your exchange in Iceland will definitely be a unique and rewarding experience.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience at the University of Iceland was the opportunity to immerse myself in a completely new culture while simultaneously pursuing my academic interests. Being able to engage with Icelandic students, learn their language, and explore the local culture on a deeper level was incredibly enriching. It wasn't just about the academic courses or the travels, but about the way the experience shaped my understanding of education, cultural diversity, and human connection. I particularly valued the chance to volunteer as a teaching assistant at the International School of Iceland, where I worked with children from diverse backgrounds, helping teach Danish and English. It was not only a great way to improve my own language skills but also a deeply fulfilling experience to be part of an inclusive educational environment. The connection I formed with the students and staff there felt meaningful, and it strengthened my passion for working with international children and researching the challenges they face in different educational systems. Additionally, living in Iceland gave me the unique opportunity to experience a culture that is so deeply tied to its environment. The constant changes in the landscape, the vast wilderness, and the way Icelanders engage with nature left a lasting impact on me. Being able to regularly hike, ice climb, and even visit remote islands made me feel more connected to the land and gave me a renewed appreciation for the world around me. The combination of these personal and academic experiences made my exchange truly unforgettable.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange at the University of Iceland was adjusting to the long, dark winters. Coming from a place with more daylight and milder winters, I found the extended periods of darkness during the autumn and winter months particularly difficult. The lack of natural light can have a noticeable effect on mood and energy levels, and it took me some time to adjust. I had to be proactive in managing this challenge by staying active outdoors, making an effort to connect with friends, and participating in social activities to avoid feeling isolated. Additionally, there was the challenge of integrating into a culture where people tend to be more reserved, especially in social settings. Icelanders are warm and welcoming, but they don't always engage in the same type of spontaneous, casual socializing that I was used to in other places. It took time to learn how to approach social situations and understand the pace of building friendships, which required a bit more patience and effort on my part. However, while both of these challenges were tough at times, they also taught me valuable lessons in resilience and adaptability. Over time, I learned to embrace the slower pace of life, make the most of the daylight hours, and enjoy the quiet, intimate social interactions that are characteristic of Icelandic culture. These experiences, though challenging at first, ultimately added to the richness of my exchange and made the whole experience more rewarding.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial for me that there was opportunities to explore nature close to the exchange university.
info_ease: There was a lot of help to be found at uni, making it relatively easy to find information.
arrival_assistance: There was a whole week of arranged activities for exchange students - both social and more info-oriented. The International Office at my university has been very flexible and helpful both before exchange and throughout it all.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had to register at the Student Help Desk in one of the main buildings of the university and then log in to your mail and the intranet. Extremely easy, quick, and straight-forward.
registration_help: The student help center and the international office were both open every day. The uni website was helpful as well.
registration_success: Course registration could be done online in the university's own intranet/communication platform. Here I could change and add courses on my own up until deadline for registration and cancellation. At HÍ there's a rule that exchange students have to have a certain amount of credits (60 %) within their own major faculty despite being on exchange on an electives semester from your home university. No exceptions.
registration_advice: If you want more credits than 40 for a semester e.g. if you want a language class (10 ECTS) and a weekend course (at least 2 ECTS) on top of your semester credits (30 ECTS), this cannot be done online, but has to be registered at the international office. They are very helpful, and this will only take a few minutes. But the advice from me would be to not overwork yourself - you will have your hands full with everything else on top of uni. Also consider the examination type and the workload/weekly hours of the course. I was very pleased with not having only oral exams or teaching every day.
course_level: I had 6 ECTS on a shared BA and MA course; 10 ECTS MA course; 10 ECTS MA course (classes with the BA students); 4 ECTS in an individual research project on BA and MA level.
teaching_comparison: I experienced much more group-based work at Hí than at UCPH, and a lot more professors encouraged engaging academically with your own experiences and situatedness - something I do not experience at home.
courses_enrolled: HSP722M: Ethics of nature HSP725M: Project in Ethics of Nature LAN116F: Introduction to Cartography and Geovisualisation NLF108F: Nordic Modernism and Avant-Garde - From Edith Södergran to Anarchy on the Internet
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend Introduction to Cartography and Geovisualisation (or Cartography and map design for the BA students), if you're into this. I have a background in humanities but it was no problem for me to participate in this class; there will be something for both the cultural history, design/aesthetics oriented and software skilled students. Ethics of Nature is also highly recommended. Despite a bit loose structured teaching this class is an opportunity to meet people from other cultures and discuss current topics, as a lot of both Icelandic and foreign students take this class. Incredibly interesting and important syllabus.
unexpected_costs: 100 DKK for library card at The Nordic House. Registration fee for the University Choir. Fees at the doctor and the dentist (payed by my insurance).
cost_comparison: Going out and buying food in Reykajvík is just expensive - especially if you value organic groceries as I do. Buying a 10-trip card to your local pool (approxiamtely 300-400 DKK) gives you a cheaper and nice way to hangout with your friends that costs you less than visits to the café.
activities_available: Gym, choir, hiking trips, karaoke nights, sight-seeing bus trips.
activities_recommended: I was happy with the university choir - also as a good base for your social life at HÍ.
weekend_recommendations: Rent a car and go on a trip - get out to see the nature. Or, in the warmer seasons before the light is gone, go hitchhiking to cities or nature close by Reykavík. The hike of Esja is nice and easy to get to; Geysir and Snæfellsnes are close by as well. But the best tip would be to either come before uni start/stay longer to have some time to explore.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: This can be difficult. Easiest if you're both engaged in a social activity together or doing group work. But don't shy away from asking them, they're just not quite as up front as the exchange students.
cultural_challenges: More cars, less bikes. A lot more calm and laissez-faire than Copenhagen - both good and bad in the adjustment phase.
culture_appreciated: The outdoor and pool culture. And the laissez-faire attitude for sure grows on you.
top3_advice: Take your time to choose your classes - you can move them around after uni starts. Academically, you can consider this semester as more creative and free, so try out something new as you're only returning to UCPH with pass/not passed and not your usual grades. Seek out social activities and groups yourself while you're there. Often it isn't the speed-dating session first week that provides you with your new friend group but your courses, a random meeting, or the club/dance class/language workshop/choir/gym you've joined.
other_useful_info: Bring wool to wear in the colder seasons, and apply for grants to ease your financial situation. Definitely don't bring books, as the national library and The Nordic House can provide you with all you need in both Danish and English. Biking is terrible, so make sure to have a helmet and the courage to bike around Reykjavík. Though, if you're up for it, it makes everything so much easier - and you don't have to use the unreliable buses.
most_rewarding: Getting to know so many new friends, and living in such a wild environment and nature. To be surrounded by mountains everyday is a blessing.
greatest_challenge: The few sun hours is no joke. Take your vitamins, go to the pool, hang out with your friends a lot, eat real food. But all Icelanders feel this as well, so just embrace it.

culture_adjustment: Somewhat easy and you can go to the pools which is a very local culture. However Icelandic people can seem like they mind their own buissness they open up and are very friendly when you get to know them. Do activities with them and you make friends and thereby trying the local culture through icelandic people.
socializing_tips: Attend the orientation days in the beginning and go to ESN events as well as asking in the main exchange whatsapp group if people want to go on trips to see Iceland nature.
cultural_challenges: That icelandic people seemed a bit closed and was a bit hard to get into conversation with but once you actually speak with them they were really friendly.
culture_appreciated: The pool culture was really nice and they party quite a lot which is nice for making friends. Also just a general outdoor oriented mindset.
top3_advice: Have a saving as it is quite expensive to go to study in iceland eventhough you get a bit larger Erasmus+ grant. Attend all the events and activities to make friends as they are priceless to make your exchange amazing. Course grading and work is different from UCPH with a lot of graded presentations and groupwork as well as tests and quizzes.
other_useful_info: Have a driver licence or make friends with somebody that has one to make sure you can go on trips to see the whole island with trips in the weekends. Grocery shop in Bónus or Kronan as they are cheapest. Make food for multiple days to save money. Get a bus pass if you live off campus.
most_rewarding: The friends i made throughout the semester as well as the beatiful nature i got to experience here.
greatest_challenge: The different work from UCPH throughout the semester with a lot of ongoing grading and work. Timemanagement can be difficult with balancing socialising and keeping up with studies.
other_comments: Go to Iceland to study for one semester, i can only recommend it! A beautiful country and amazing experiences awaits with nice people and incredible nature.

crucial_aspects: I am very interested in the Icelandic language. I have previously been there to learn it, and I wanted to get better at it. I have also worked for a professor at the University of Iceland (remotely from Denmark). I could take a course in Old Norse literature which I found fascinating and relevant to my education, even though I mainly study historical linguistics.
overall_comments: I think the exchange itself was very good - it was not too difficult to get everyting in order and to move to Iceland. I learned so much from being there as well. My only complaint was that I wasn't allowed to choose language courses. I really wanted to learn more Icelandic and Old Norse, but I could only do that in my spare time, so I really didn't make that much progress with regards to that. I was however very lonely and I had a hard time making friends, and I lost contact with my friends back home. Because I am autistic, I really struggle with these things, and it was hard to make it through the semester while being so lonely, but that is my own problem, and it hopefully won't be a problem for most other exchange students.

arrival_assistance: They gave me useful information at the help desk, and there were many introductory meetings and social events for exchange students the first week. Nothing to complain about at all.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_process: I believe that originally had to select my courses back in April or May in some online portal for upcoming exchange students. When I showed up in August, I just had to talk to the people at the help desk and show them my passport. It was very easy really.
registration_help: The people at the help desk could answer questions, and we were given plenty of information the first week. I had some questions during the initial application back in April that I could get answered because they didn't reply to my emails, but it all worked out in the end.

I really wanted to learn more Icelandic and Old Norse, but I could only do that in my spare time, so I really didn't make that much progress with regards to that. I was however very lonely and I had a hard time making friends, and I lost contact with my friends back home. Because I am autistic, I really struggle with these things, and it was hard to make it through the semester while being so lonely, but that is my own problem, and it hopefully won't be a problem for most other exchange students.
course_level: I thought they were similar in difficulty to the ones at UCPH. There was one 'Languages and Culture' that was a good deal more on the easy side.
teaching_comparison: The main difference is that there are many more assignments throughout the semester and that the final exams are not quite as intense. I think this is a much, much nicer way of doing things!
courses_enrolled: Old Norse-Icelandic Literary Corpus - Overview and Main Questions: An introduction to Old Norse literature and its historical context. Vocabulary Acquisition - Research and Theory: An introduction to research into vocabulary acquistion in mainly English, but to a lesser extent also other languages. Languages and Culture I: A broad course covering the social aspects of many languages, with a few classes dedicated to each (Arabic, Latin, indigenous languages, English et cetera).
recommended_courses: The courses on Old Norse literature and vocabulary acquisition were really good, the teachers were serious, and I found the information that I learned useful. 'Languages and Culture I' was too unsfocused and covered too many different things, and I don't think it was that interesting or useful.
unexpected_costs: I was undergoing medical examinations in Denmark before I left for Iceland. This started half a year before I went to Iceland, but it dragged out, and I had to go to Denmark no less than three times. Those plane tickes cost quite a bit of money, and they are included in the 'other fees' (along with all the stuf I had to buy for my flat, since I couldn't bring everything with me on the plane). It was also very expensive to send all the stuff I had bought back to Denmark. I had to send several packages, and I had to pay toll and VAT for each of them.
cost_comparison: The prices were similar to those in Denmark. I wasn't really that surprised.
activities_available: There was a gym on campus, but apart from that I am not really sure.
activities_recommended: Again, I didn't participate in any, so I can't comment on it.
weekend_recommendations: It is definitely important to explore the countryside outside of Reykjavik. I don't have a drivers licence, so I had to go on bus trips. They university also organises bus trips to historical sites. The ones organised by the university are much better than those offered by tourist companies!
culture_adjustment: Danish and Icelandic culture are very similar to each other, so it was very easy.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find it difficult at all.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the Icelandic language, and I wish I had had more time to study it.
top3_advice: While the nature is very exotic in Iceland, the rest of Iceland feels very much like Denmark, so don't worry about cultural issues, it is easy to fit in in Iceland. It is easy to use English in Reykjavik, and many people even speak Danish or Swedish. The process of applying to go on exchange seems very confusing while you are going through it, but it will work out in the end. Once you show up at the university before the semester, it is very simple from there. It is only possible to bring so many things with you on the plane, so be prepared to spend a good deal of money when you arrive, especially if you get an empty flat like I did.
other_useful_info: Not really, I don't think so.
most_rewarding: I learned so much from being completely on my own in another country. I got a lot better at dealing with unforseen problems while also managing my studies. It is a very enriching experience that university students shouldn't miss out on!
greatest_challenge: My greatest challenge was the loneliness and isolation, because I had a hard time making friends and keeping in touch with my friends in Denmark. I think that many exhange students may face this problem, but is much worse for someone with autism. But I don't think it should deter you from going on exchange!

crucial_aspects: I had visited Iceland before, and loved the country. The nature is stunning, as well as friendly people and a safe environment. In terms of my studies, the country seemed to offer interesting aspects.
overall_comments: The university was a great place, did however feel lonely in the beginning.
info_ease: It was fine, I had to go to the University to gain access to the University intranet. After that it was quite simple.
arrival_assistance: When arriving at the university, I found the student service (was a little confused about the place), and they gave me my password for the intranet, as well as a little information. However, mostly received e-mails.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The university was a great place, did however feel lonely in the beginning.
registration_process: Logged into an UGLA portal, and then had to choose courses. I had quite some trouble logging into the portal, since you had to use your university email (with a special ending). I also had some difficulties choosing courses that fit 30 ECTS. But in the end, the courses that I had were very relevant.
registration_help: You could email to XX at host uni (Name removed) the responsible person for exchange students. However, I ended up getting help from another exchange student in Denmark.
registration_success: I got all the classes i wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure to start the process early, since it takes a while to figure it all out. Answering time from the University is also not very quick. And remember to get approval from your home university early as well.
academics_comments: The university was a great place, did however feel lonely in the beginning.
course_level: The level was quite similar to the one at Copenhagen University.
teaching_comparison: There were more hours mandatory at the University. The final grade in a course is based on many activities throughout the course, not only a final exam (quizzes, many submissions, reports etc.). The exams were also mostly closed-book.
courses_enrolled: Cartography and map design Global Climate Change Physical Geography The Arctic Circle Natural Hazards
recommended_courses: The Artic Circle is a course based on your attendance in the conference in October, and two papers afterwards. It is a really fun experience. I can also recommend the cartography course, if you want to learn QGIS. Global Climate Change had focus on both the physical processes and the societal/political/human aspects of climate change, which I also really enjoyed. Physical geography had some field- and labwork regarding soil science, which were interesting.
unexpected_costs: The busses out of Reykjavik are quite expensive, and generally "tourist acitivities". Eating out/coffee is expensive.
cost_comparison: It is quite affordable to rent a car, especially if you are sharing it 5 people (remember to get insurance, the weather is wild!) Chocolate and skyr is cheap (compared to DK), meat is really expensive.
activities_available: There is a choir, student associations and a gym, where there is some nice activities.
activities_recommended: Join the gym, it is cheap and nice. And join "dog day" on Wednesdays, where a cute dog comes to visit from Red Cross.
weekend_recommendations: Go on car trips to the Westfjords, Kerlingafjöll, Snæfellsness, Vestmannaeyar, the lava tunnel and see the glaciers. Go for horse riding or kayaking.
culture_adjustment: Easy, since it is very similar to Denmark.
socializing_tips: The local students were not always that keen to socialize with the exchange students. However, the other exchange students were very nice.
cultural_challenges: Less social activities than I am used to at home (I live in a social dorm, and my department at the University is also active).
culture_appreciated: Friendly people, generally talkative if you start a conversation. Very chill and safe place.
top3_advice: 1) Be ready to study a lot, for submissions, tests and closed book exam (however, very rewarding academically). Remember to study with friends, that makes it way more fun. 2) Try to participate in activities, go on some trips etc. with people from early on. It is important to make some friends. Generally, find activities outside of University to do. 3) Keep in contact with friends and family at home - and ask them to come visit you. It had multible visits, and it was amazing.
other_useful_info: There a lots of nice places to study at Campus, and also help to get from the student counselling, service etc. I had a little job as a "note taker", which can be recommended (remember to check your University e-mail).
most_rewarding: Experiencing beautiful nature, got some really lovely friends from all over the world, and progressed academically.
greatest_challenge: Feeling lonely, especially in the beginning.

crucial_aspects: Interesting nature and culture. University with good courses.
info_ease: It was easy, most of the needed work was done before arriving. The University has a student desk, that is very helpful and they mostly answered quickly per email.
arrival_assistance: I needed to go to the student desk to complete my arrival at the university, which gave me and the university the information needed. After this I got access to my timetable for my courses and the university's website for students, where the relevant information is found.
arrival_comments: It would be nice if you could get access to the information before arriving physically at the university.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The university has a helpful guide on their website. I had to apply in May, which was fairly easy, except for the fact that I had to choose courses at that time and the university hadn't published their available courses for the semester yet and it could not match my pre approval of courses from my home university, since I had to choose from a list.
registration_help: The university´s international division has an email that can write - but I had to remind them to answer a couple of times. Physically on campus they have a student desk.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Get pre-approval for more courses than you need just in case, since it takes a couple of weeks to get the approval.
course_level: The level was more or less the same as at my home university, considering the reading volume and level but the exams were a bit easier than at home.
teaching_comparison: I had to do research papers in all my courses, had group presentations and in-class-assignments which was different from at home.
courses_enrolled: Transnational climate law, Themes on International and European Environmental Law, International Human Rights, Basic Course in Public International Law, The United States Legal System and American Constitutional Law.
recommended_courses: The Basic Course in Public International Law was very interesting.
unexpected_costs: The student housing did not have any furniture or kitchen utensils, so I had to spend a lot of money on that.
cost_comparison: Housing and food was very expensive
activities_available: A lot of activities were available.
activities_recommended: The university gym was very cheap but also very small.
weekend_recommendations: Rent a car and go see the nature.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it is pretty close to the danish culture.
socializing_tips: A lot of people speak danish.
cultural_challenges: The language was harder to learn than I expected.
culture_appreciated: It was easy to adjust to since it is close to the danish. I really enjoyed seeing the nature.
top3_advice: Start planning early, sign up for student housing early, rent cars and go see the nature.
other_useful_info: Participate in the orientation days.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all parts of the world and experiencing the beautiful nature of Iceland.
greatest_challenge: The planning before I arrived.
other_comments: I totally recommend doing your exchange in Iceland!!

arrival_assistance: Our professors offered a lot of assistance, as well as the student office.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We were partially registrated online, and had to finish the process at the local student office. This was all very straightforward and well-organised. Mobility Online has so far been the hardest part to navigate of the exchange.
registration_help: The student coordinators were available through email, or you could go to the student office.
registration_success: I got into all my desired classes, as none of them were at the same time.
registration_advice: Keep an eye on your emails, and read them thoroughly as to not miss a deadline.
course_level: Some of my classes were tailored to international students, and therefore very easy to follow along with. As I took some classes outside my usual studies, I had to get used to some of the requirements within essays etc, but the professors have generally given clear instructions. I have been able to follow along all of them quite well.
teaching_comparison: Most of my classes had a similar teaching style, with the exception of an online class.
courses_enrolled: Jane Austen and her feminist Legacy Being Icelandic: Icelandic Folktales, Beliefs and Popular Culture Past and Present Introduction to the History of Iceland: From Settlement to Modern Times Conversation I (Spanish) British and European History
recommended_courses: I would strongly recommend the class "Introduction to the History of Iceland: From Settlement to Modern Times", as I have learned so much about Iceland and it gave me a good understanding for the country and its culture. The professor I had this semester was very talented, and she teaches a great class.
unexpected_costs: Furnishing the student apartment.
cost_comparison: Most things were even more expensive than expected.
activities_available: Through the university gym you could access different classes.
activities_recommended: The swimming pools around the city!
weekend_recommendations: Go on all the roadtrips you can and see the country, try also to go on some hikes!
culture_adjustment: Yes, it is quite similar to Denmark.
socializing_tips: It is hard to get in contact with them, I was lucky to find some friends through my classes.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The appreciation of nature.
top3_advice: Be prepared for the prices and the weather. Rent a car with friends and go on as many roadtrips as possible. Enjoy the northern lights, so they can make up for the many hours of darkness in the winter.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Finding friends and learning to knit with them, seeing the country and learning new things.
greatest_challenge: The initial loneliness.

crucial_aspects: The USA has a huge impact on the rest of the western world. Hence, I think it is important to have a fair impression of this nation, it's people and the American culture. Then I also know that the USA is very strong in physics, so that is a good bonus.
info_ease: Pretty easy, both the people in Illinois and in Copenhagen that had to help me where very help full.
arrival_assistance: There was a huge welcoming event for all incoming exchange students and my administrative college also hosted a lot of social events.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You are enrolled as an undergraduate student, so if enrolling in graduate courses, you have to proove that you are a graduate student at your home institution. This is easy. If you are not a physics student. In which case you will have to convince two people simultaneously that you are a graduate student. And they are not exchaging information. Very frustrating.
registration_help: The physics administration, but they were not super efficient. An easy fix was to simply show up at the grad-student administration office.
registration_success: Not very, but there where some good alternatives. The Physics department's administration at UIUC is super annoying though. It was very hard to convince them that I was a graduate student.
registration_advice: Be in good time, and send all information to everybody you have to contact. Also in the US, you can try out different class and change course concurrently. So give everything that seems interesting a shot.
course_level: The physics courses is on a comparable (maybe slightly lower) level compared to copenhagen. But they are still very challenging. The graduate statistics course I took was very easy though and I have heard similar stories from other students in order majors.
teaching_comparison: A lot more sitting in class rooms and following the flow of the lecturer. At UCPH you can study the way that suits you bet, but that is not an option at UIUC. You very much have to follow the structure of the classes.
courses_enrolled: Computational Statistics (STAT 525) Condensed Matter Physics 1 (PHYS 560) Introduction to Subatomic Physics (PHYS 470)
recommended_courses: All of the above are pretty good, especially the STAT 525.
unexpected_costs: Non, it is pretty up front expenses.
cost_comparison: Food is pretty expensive in the supermarket. So eating out is pretty compettetive compare to denmark.
activities_available: Whatever you desire.
activities_recommended: Whatever you desire.
weekend_recommendations: See the Amish that live in Arthur Illinois. It is a very interesting experience.
culture_adjustment: It takes some getting used to. I think I had a good group of friends after 3-4 weeks. And my neighbours were very nice.
socializing_tips: Do it! Americans a very approachable so go to them say hello. Talk and you will do well. Also find somebody to do something with. I found some gym-bros to go running and training with.
cultural_challenges: Americans are approachable but very hard to "really" get to know. Unlike danes who are unapproachable, but once you get them drunk they start talking.
culture_appreciated: It was very nice and "low-stakes" to hang out with americans in the Track and Field club. Partying with european exchange students was amazing :)
top3_advice: 1: Talk to people, they are friendly and approachable on average (and you will go crazy if you don't.) 2: Remember to party, I spent too much time studying. And exams are easier in the US than in Denmark :) 3: Make sure to get around the US while you are there. It is an amazing, beuatiful and shockingly large country.
other_useful_info: Take chances. Remember you are only there for 4-8 months. And it is pretty low stakes. So try to get to know yourself and make some friends and connections from all over the world. This is not the time for hiding away in your room.
most_rewarding: All the connection I know have both in Europe, The US and East Asia as a result of having gone on exchange.
greatest_challenge: The first few weeks where you do not yet have a network are pretty tough.

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne til Nordamerika, da jeg altid har fascineret mig meget for USA og Canada og godt kunne tænke mig at opleve hvordan det er at studere der.
info_ease: Det var meget nemt. Fik en velkomst mail med alle de informationer jeg skulle bruge.
arrival_assistance: Jeg fik ingen assistance
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Jeg skulle fremføre bevis på at mit engelsk var godt nok, jeg skulle uploade mine eksamensresultater, et udskrift af mit bankkonto, vaccinationer og underskrive en masse dokumenter. Det var lidt forvirrende, så jeg vil anbefale at gå i gang i god tid.
registration_help: Jeg kunne altid kontakte lederen på host university og få hjælp af ham/hende.
registration_success: Det gik ganske godt. Var lidt forvirrende at forstå systemet til at starte med, men føler jeg traf nogle gode valg.
registration_advice: Begynd i god tid, da kurserne hurtigt fyldes op, og man derfor ikke kan være sikker på at få det kursus man gerne vil have. Ikke vælg 18 credit points i alt, så vil du ikke have tid til at have det sjovt. Så sigt efter en 14-16 credit point.
course_level: Eksaminerne er meget sværere end i DK, men det der undervises i er på samme niveau. De går meget op i at man løser matematikken uden brug af computer, hvilket gør eksamernerne svære. Dog normalfordeler de karakterne, så man skal ikke være bange for at dumpe, så længe man bare ligger omkring gennemsnittet.
teaching_comparison: Man havde forelæsninger og regnetimer. Men helt klart langt flere forelæsninger end regnetimer, sammenlignet med UCPH.
courses_enrolled: General chemistry II, Fundamental organic chemistry I, Elementary organic chemistry II, Physical chemistry II
recommended_courses: Alle kurserne jeg tog var meget gode, så kommer an på hvad man er til. Physical chemistry II var et meget hårdt og tidskrævende kursus, men man lærer en masse. General kemi II er godt til at opfriske alle aspekter af kemien og der lærte jeg også en masse nye ting. Hvis man er til organisk kemi, så var de to kurser jeg tog også virkelig gode og fik en masse ud af dem også.
unexpected_costs: Vaccinationer, wifi router, dyne, pude, alle køkken redskaber (Troede det var inkluderet)
cost_comparison: Maden var ekstremt dyr. Både når man var ude og spise, men også bare at handle i supermarkedet. Alle priserne var prisen uden tax, så der blev også inkluderet 10% tax på alle de varer man købte, når man havde bippet dem ind.
activities_available: Alt! Det ville være for omfattende at nævne dem alle, men jeg tror at man kan finde noget, lige gyldigt hvor specielt det så end er.
activities_recommended: At tage ud at rejse rundt i landet i efterårsferien og/eller i weekenderne. Der er mange muligheder for at tage tog/bus rundt i landet og flyve hvis det er en længere tur og ikke super dyrt.
weekend_recommendations: Tage til Californien, New York, Chicago eller florida. Jeg var selv i Californien i efterårsferien og i New York og Chicago i nogle af weekenderne og det var super fedt.
culture_adjustment: Det var ganske nemt. Det eneste man lige skal vænne sig til er de meget strikse regler omkring alkohol. Man må ikke gå rundt udenfor og drikke en øl på samme måde som i Danmark
socializing_tips: Join en sports klub eller student organization. Det er her man virkelig får mulighed for at møde nogle amerikanske elever. Til forelæsningerne er man så mange i en forelæsnings sal at man typisk ikke lærer så mange at kende.
cultural_challenges: Jeg følte ikke at der var nogle kulturelle udfordringer.
culture_appreciated: Jeg elsker campus livet og hvordan hele byen bare er bygget op omkring campus og alle de muligheder der var på campus. Det var super fedt at opleve hvordan der bliver gjort så meget for eleverne på universitetet at det er en hel oplevelse at gå rundt på universitetet. Det kunne være noget man mangler i Europa.
top3_advice: 1) Start i god tid med at udvælge kurser, så I får det i gerne vil have. 2) Kom tol universitetet i god tid før studiestart og deltag i alle de intro arrangementer der er. Det er her man virkelig møder en masse mennesker og får dannet nogle forbindelser til resten af semesteret. Når først semesteret starter, bliver det sværere at møde nye føler jeg. 3) Join en sportsklub eller elev organisation. Det er en virkelig dejlig måde at møde nye folk på. 4) Forsøg at finde bolig lidt uden for campus. Her er boligpriserne langt billigere og boligerne langt bedre. Der kører busser rundt som er gratis for alle elever. Busserne kører hvert 5/10 minut og stopper alle steder, også uden for campus. Ligegyldigt hvor du bor vil du være max 5 min fra et busstoppested, hvorfra det tager max 10-20 min indtil campus.
other_useful_info: Nej, alt er angivet i boksen ovenfor.
most_rewarding: At møde så mange internationale elever og rejse rundt i USA med dem var en kæmpe oplevelse. At være på et så livligt og stort universitet hvor der foregår så meget var også en kæmpe oplevelse.
greatest_challenge: At få pengene til at løbe op. Alt i USA er ekstremt dyrt og jeg fik ingen legater. Så brugte min opsparing. Havde ikke lyst til at vende hjem og være helt bankerot, så måtte tænke over mit forbrug. Hvis jeg havde haft nogle flere penge, var jeg helt klart blevet en måned ekstra og rejst rundt i USA. Ens visa udløber nemlig først en måned efter at semesteret slutter, så hvis man har pengene og tiden til det vil jeg helt klart anbefale at gøre dette.

recommended_courses: Arabic for Non-Native Speakers (Level 5)

activities_recommended: I did not try any of the non-academic activities

registration_help: The people at the Erasmus office helped.
registration_success: We used the first weeks to go to different classes to see witch level was best for us, therefore I could stay at the level I was comfortable in. I did not have to registrer anything before.
registration_advice: Arrive around one week before your classes start so you have time to settle and registrer. It is also good to think about how much time you want to use for school work. For example if you choose a hard level, you will learn a lot of arabic but you need a lot of time to study. It's also possible to choose an easier level and use more time to get to know the country. It all depends on what you want to use your time on and if you learn arabic best form classes or from making local friends.
course_level: There are nine levels. One is beginner and nine is almost native speaker. The levels may be fluent because people choose the courses themselves, in my class some people spoke fluent while some spoke basics.
teaching_comparison: Both places has a close class where you get to know everyone, and the people are very friendly. A part from the beginner levels the teachers only speak arabic in class, which was different from UCPH, but I learn a lot from it.
courses_enrolled: I was in level 6 at the Language Center.
recommended_courses: Depends on their level. If they have studied arabic for 1,5 years like me, I would recoment level 4 or 5.
unexpected_costs: Taxi is around 20-30 DKK, but I got suprised that you have to take taxi all the time and then it's expensive in the end.
cost_comparison: The gym is very expensive (500-1000DKK) every month, alcohol is also more expensive than in Denmark. Sunscreen is also very expensive. In bigger supermarkets the food may be a bit expensive. If you go to the smaller supermarkets and local restaurants the food is very cheap.
activities_available: Dabke dance, football and calligraphy. I think there are more that I don't know about.
activities_recommended: All of them at the university. I also recommend to go the Jordan Trail that has a lot of hikes and there are also a lot of yoga classes.
weekend_recommendations: I recomment the trips with the university that goes almost every weekend to different parts of the country, it's cheaper than travelling by yourself. I recoment The Dead Sea, Wadi Rum, Petra, Wadi Mujib, Um Qais and Aqaba.
culture_adjustment: It is a very different culture and you should be prepared for that. It was not hard but you will get some surprises and questions you will never get in Denmark.
socializing_tips: Have a language partners. In generall people, are very open, especially at the university. It's easy to talk to people on the bus, on the street etc. In general people are very intrested in talking to foregniers. Note that it's not normal for all Jordanians to socialize between genders.
cultural_challenges: Gender equality is not the same as in Denmark. Talking to men, you sometimes have to be very clear of your own boundaries.
culture_appreciated: The hospitality. People are very welcoming and always care about you a lot.
top3_advice: 1: Don't compare everything to Denmark, or think that everything is better in Denmark. 2. The people at the language center are usally alone in a new country too. They are very nice and easy to be friends with. 3. If you have questions about the culture, don't be afraid to ask! People are very to happy to explain and tell you about their culture.
other_useful_info: In Jordanian culture time works very different than in Denmark. People are more spontaneous and might not follow a schedule. Try to see the value of that, it's very relaxing, even dough it might feel wierd in the beginning.
most_rewarding: Making friends from so many countries and cultures and learning a lot of arabic in a small amount of time.
greatest_challenge: Learning to understand the local dialect in the beginning. It felt a bit frustraiting in the beginning to not understand anything, after studying arabic before, but after some time I learnt a lot.
