courses_enrolled: ELU2010 Language Through Literature and Place: Reading Yorkshire (39798) ENGL2030 Writing Environments: Literature, Nature, Culture (39506) ENGL3046 Parts, Periodicals, Newspapers: Literature and the Nineteenth-Century Press (40346)
recommended_courses: I would recommend them all, but I found ELU2010 Language Through Literature and Place: Reading Yorkshire (39798) especially interesting because it centered around literature that was written or takes place in Yorkshire, and we went on field trips to explore Leeds, which was very informative and immersive.
unexpected_costs: I got a meningitis vaccine when I arrived that cost 900 DKK, because there was a little card on my desk in my dorm that said "Meningitis Kills" and strongly advised me to get one - that had not been clear from the university's email correspondence.
cost_comparison: Coffee and tea in cafe's are much cheaper over there.
activities_available: There were over 300 societies I could become a member of that had all kinds of activities and socials. I was part of the book club, the English society and the art society.
activities_recommended: Go to the society fair in the first week of the semester and see which society fits your interests.
weekend_recommendations: Visit Haworth where the Brontë-sisters lived. Visit London. Visit Edinburgh. Visit the Lake District.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The people in Leeds are very kind.
socializing_tips: Get involved in the societies - many local students are part of them.
cultural_challenges: It was very hard to find unscented products for personal hygiene.
culture_appreciated: The kindness of the people - everyone called each other "luv" and "darling".
top3_advice: Go to the society fair at the start of the semester. Try to get accommodation on campus - many activities take place in Leeds University Union which is on campus. Enjoy all the libraries.
other_useful_info: Beware of the fact that the University of Leeds only provide provisional grades - the final grades are set in June and might cause problems with graduation.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and going on an adventure alone.
greatest_challenge: The first day was hard, where everything is new, but as soon as that first day was over it was great.

crucial_aspects: I wanted a place with interesting classes and from where I could travel and see the rest of the country
info_ease: It was very easy- Leeds has a "before you arrive" guide and information sessions when you get there
arrival_assistance: There was a bit of mix up with the taxi company, but the university paid for a taxi to take to me to my student accommodation upon arrival and the student accommodation office were wonderful as well
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I just had to choose which ones I liked online and then I was signed up for it
registration_help: You get a contact person at the school you're attached to and you can write them - the student hub and international office also has lots of opportunities and they are happy to help
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted and I was allowed to change one of them 1 week in
registration_advice: Remember to check the 'isa' box when browsing for courses and ask questions if you're unsure about anything!
course_level: I'd say they are a bit easier than at UCPH
teaching_comparison: the classes are smaller and there are a lot more "chat with the person next to you work" which also meant that you had to prepare more than I do at home - but I liked that and I've brought it home with me. The seminar tutors are lovely and good at contextualising what you're saying
courses_enrolled: Drama text and performance One about Charles Dickens and Dickens adaptation Other voices: One about other voices in Victorian Literature
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed 'Drama: text and performance' - it is a first year course about theatre history and for assignments you had to do your own adaptation of plays discussed in classes
unexpected_costs: You have to buy all the "inventar" for your accommodation and that is a lot
cost_comparison: Cinema tickets and theatre tickets- they are wonderfully cheap!
activities_available: There are a lot of societies of all sorts. Lots of societies also arrange some sort of ball each semester so look out for those if you're interested
activities_recommended: I never really went but the film society had some awesome movie showings. Many socities also have a 'Give It A Go' (GIGO) in the beginning of the semester where you can try it out and see if you'd like to continue
weekend_recommendations: 10000% go see York, it's really nice. Go see the nature around Yorkshire. I'd recommend Ilkley moor, Skipton, Grassington and the cute towns around Yorkshire. Also take the train to Edinburgh
culture_adjustment: Easy. I'd say there are less europeans in the UK compared to a few years ago (damn u, Brexit!!!) but so many lovely people
socializing_tips: Join societies or talk to them in classes
cultural_challenges: The small talk aspect - we are so much more direct in Denmark, and there are a lot more polite chitter chatter there before you get to the "real deal"
culture_appreciated: I loved how people acknowledge each other - everyone says thanks, cheers, and sorry when you're holding the door or stuff like that
top3_advice: 1) Remember deadlines 2) Go see stuff outside Leeds too 3) Have lunch at Kirkgate market (and go check out the Corn Exchange)
other_useful_info: Don't be afraid to talk to your teachers. And if you're interested in literature and theatre go check out the Playhouse Lab
most_rewarding: I've been introduced to so many new topics I didn't knew existed and I learned a lot literature. I enjoyed the cultural and academic aspect
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was probably in the beginning of my stay, when the taxi was seriously delayed and I got to accommodation too late, but I called the security (they are on Campus 24/7) and they were extremely nice and helped me. I also had to get used to the architecture and the fact that there are a lot more trash on the street than back home- but that was culture shock and it passed rather quickly
other_comments: Go, enjoy the many accents, the bad weather, and the people!

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to go to the UK and it was important for me to be sure of housing opportunities. I also wanted to go to a student city.
info_ease: Very easy. The accommodation was very welcoming with information and they offered a bunch of options for new students such as a campus walking tour and other introduction activities.
arrival_assistance: The university offered a pick-up service from the airport, which made transport very easy. My school, the business school, hosted events for exchange students only which provided both information and opportunities to connect with other students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I applied for modules before the summer holiday and I remember the more difficult part was the danish system of what I was allowed to take.
registration_help: They were very responsive on their emails. I wrote with some questions for my pre-approval application and reagarding enrolment in post-graduate modules.
registration_success: I wanted to take some masters level modules which I wasn't allowed since I was enrolled in the bachelors programme.
registration_advice: Start looking in good time to relieve yourself of time pressure. Also the module codes are labelled with 1,2,3-thousands according to year of study.
course_level: The level was lower than at UPCH, which I had expected, since they are not renowned for their economics programmes. I found it pleasant to relax and be able to focus on social events and trips.
teaching_comparison: The style was quite different. The lectures were only 1 hour each and fewer than at UCPH. So less contact hours and the seminars had a different structure. It was much more discussion based and relevant to attend. The exams and assignments were more essay based and more focused on critical thinking and discussion rather than problem solving and mathematical methods.
courses_enrolled: Advanced Macroeconomics, Moderns theories of money and monetary policy, Applied econometrics, The international economic environment, Behavioural economics, and introduction to effective decision making.
recommended_courses: I found Moderns theories of money and monetary policy very interesting but also challenging. The module Behavioural economics was very interesting as well and easy to follow since it didn't have any direct pre-requisites.
unexpected_costs: I hadn't thought of needing to buy a duvet, plates, cutlery and pans on arrival. We ended up all sharing the kitchen supplies which made it less expensive and wasteful.
cost_comparison: Groceries and coffee out were less expensive than expected. I hadn't formed any expectations about budget and planned on spending accordingly but without restrictions. I spent about 1000DKK on travel and trips each month.
activities_available: There is something for everyone.
activities_recommended: I enjoyed some of the events from the music union library, the nordic society and get out get active trips.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend that you go out in nature on some hikes and see the beautiful landscapes around. Also just try some of the amazing restaurants and student discount options they have at many places. Definitely go on an Otley run ;)
culture_adjustment: not that difficult.
socializing_tips: Join a society or go to their events and chat.
culture_appreciated: The ability to socialise and how chatty many people are out and about.
top3_advice: Exchange is what you make it, don't be afraid to ask and talk to people and enjoy your time there.
other_useful_info: Put yourself out there and Leeds has so many wonderful things to offer.
most_rewarding: All the great friends and memories I've made.
greatest_challenge: Finding a new routine and different communication with your teachers

crucial_aspects: That it was a country where English was the first language, and that the country was within Europe.
info_ease: It was very easy, as the University kept us updated
arrival_assistance: I did not need any assistance.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The process was very long, and the University were very slow with getting back to us with a confirmation of acceptance, modules etc.
registration_help: You were able to contact the uni by email.
registration_success: I got 3 out of 4 classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Have patience. Make sure you do everything as soon as possible, because the sooner you complete the different steps the quicker you'll get through.
course_level: The level of the courses were for 3rd year students, but felt a bit complicated sometimes as an exchange student because of the language barrier.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was very good and professors would be available if you needed help. The lectures were shorter (1 hour) compared to the lectures at UCPH, and they would have seminars/tutorials with up to 10 students, where the curriculum would be discussed. The classes were devided into "units", so after each unit there would be a tutorial/seminar which would sum up that unit and discuss everything. All classes during the unit would be lectures only, but where there was a chance to ask the professor questions too.
courses_enrolled: LW3591 Criminal Justice: Policing, Sentencing and Rehabilitation 2021-22 SEM1 LW3351 Criminology (Study Abroad) 2021-22 SEM1 LW3271 Human Rights in the 21st century (Study Abroad) 2021-22 SEM1 LW3231 Employment Law (Study Abroad) 2021-22 SEM1
recommended_courses: I found Employment Law and Criminal Justice as the best courses. Employment law was so well structered, that the professors made sure you would be able to do the assessments without any struggle.
unexpected_costs: Covid-19 Day 2 test
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than expected.
activities_available: There were many options, compared to UCPH. There was a club available for every sport you can think of.
activities_recommended: I joined non-academic activities based on my own personal preference and my beliefs so I can only recommend to join the activities which you're interested in as it will help expand your social circle.
weekend_recommendations: The University offers a lot of activities during weekends and holidays, which you can join. If not, then going to other parts of the countries was how I spent most of my weekends and holidays.
culture_adjustment: The culture in UK is very similar to the one in Denmark, but I got adjusted easily also because of the accommodation I stayed at, as the girls would tell me how they do certain things. For instance, in England they have eggs in their cupboard and not in the fridge.
socializing_tips: My best advice will be to live somewhere with students.
cultural_challenges: I found it difficult that the busses were on the opposite side, as the driving in the UK is opposite to the driving direction in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: People are very humble and helpful and they apologise way more.
top3_advice: 1. Make sure to socialise and give yourself time to do so 2. The University is very close to accommodation so I would recommend to stay at the uni accommodation. 3. It is a very multi cultural University so you'll meet a lot of people with different backgrounds
other_useful_info: The university is placed 20 minutes away from the main town.
most_rewarding: Getting a chance to be a part of physical teaching again and mostly the new friends I made.
greatest_challenge: To not get behind in studies. You get behind easily as they don't give work in the first two weeks, and then all of a sudden they load you with a lot of pages to read so it's difficult to make a routine.

crucial_aspects: The language and country was essential when choosing my destination. Furthermore, the modules offered persuaded me to choose the University of Leicester, compared to other universities in England.
info_ease: The study abroad team had provided plenty of information before arrival and responded fast through email regarding any queries. I was also provided with a personal tutor who sent bi-weekly e-mails to check in and he could assist in finding answers to any questions I might have. The information regarding who to contact in certain situations was good, and if you did not know who to contact to get an answer, everyone was happy to help find the person who could answer.
arrival_assistance: I stayed in student accommodation so the reception provided assistance and information pamphlets. Furthermore, the university offered informational presentations regarding school facilities, COVID regulation and more.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The university sends out an email with a guide on how to register for modules and other relevant information. You choose four 1st, 2nd and 3rd priorities and will be informed on which modules you get before arrival.
registration_help: The guide provided all the necessary information. Otherwise, the study abroad team is quick to respond to e-mails with any questions you might have.
registration_success: I got all my first priorities.
registration_advice: Choose modules you have previously been interested in. Choose modules with an international perspective.
course_level: The level was pretty much the same as UCPH. There might be a little less reading required. The professors provided a lecture guide to each topic with a great overview of each topic. This was helpful in addition to the required reading and powerpoint.
teaching_comparison: There are more lectures than at UCPH, and there are no seminars in the same way. Usually each topic would contain a certain amount of lectures with 40-50 people and at the end of each topic we had tutorials. For the tutorials we would be 6-9 students in a room with our professor, where we had prepared a case and questions. The professor would present the case and ask questions and it was up to the students to answer. The tutorials were a great opportunity for discussions and going into depth with each topic. The material and books were online and free. You could also borrow the books from the library.
courses_enrolled: Family Law Intellectual Property Law Contract Law Human Rights in the 21st Century
recommended_courses: Human Rights was very relevant and involved with current issues. Intellectual property was a little more challenging, but the professor was very competent and good at teaching complex topics in tangible ways.
unexpected_costs: None. Spent more on personal spending than first anticipated.
cost_comparison: The train to and from the airport is quite expensive.
activities_available: There are so many different societies, clubs and sports. There is definitely something for everyone. Cannot recommend it enough.
activities_recommended: I played football and futsal. The girls are so nice and welcoming to any level of skills. Once every week they hosted socials with different themes. If you want to play matches you get to travel to different cities, e.g. Oxford, Nottingham, Loughborough and so on. The football club definitely made my time in Leicester amazing.
weekend_recommendations: It is quite easy to travel to London, Nottingham or Manchester or other cities using the train line. I went to Wembley stadium and King Power stadium to watch matches. I also recommend watching football in a pub, as it is something to experience in England. Rugby is also big in Leicester and is worth going to a game even if you do not know the rules due to the atmosphere.
culture_adjustment: The people are so including, it is almost difficult not to adjust to the local culture.
socializing_tips: Definitely join a society, club or sports! Participate in social events at university and the accommodation.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The people are very nice, including, helpful and friendly. The football culture was fun to be emerged into as well.
top3_advice: 1. Join a society or a club. 2. Participate in tutorials 3. Make time for the social aspect of your exchange, because there is room for both studying and having fun.
other_useful_info: Participate in the social events at the university and accommodation, as it is a great way to be emerged into the student life and making friends. Enjoy it because the time goes by so fast.
most_rewarding: The social aspect! The people are great and I have definitely made friends for life.
greatest_challenge: Putting myself in uncomfortable situations socially before I knew anyone.

crucial_aspects: The modules as well as the country
info_ease: Very easy
arrival_assistance: The receptionist provided me with assistance
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: They send you documents that you just fill out
registration_help: You can e-mail them or pop by their office
registration_success: Very successful
registration_advice: Choose modules from the same year
course_level: You can do either under graduate or post graduate modules
teaching_comparison: Smaller classes and more lectures
courses_enrolled: Commercial law, Criminal justice: Prosecutions and Trials, Dispute Resolution and Criminology
recommended_courses: Commercial law, the professor is very enthusiastic
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Food is less expensive, and so is dining out
activities_available: Everything imaginable, sports, knitting etc.
activities_recommended: Lacrosse, the students I talked to really enjoyed it.
weekend_recommendations: Visit other cities, Nottingham and York are very nice and not too far away
culture_adjustment: Very easy, except for the bread section at the supermarket
socializing_tips: Sign up for a society
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: That it is very similar to that of Denmark
top3_advice: Make sure to live at the city campus, try out a society, go to Sonrisa to eat
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Making so many new friends
greatest_challenge: Being away from my family
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: Because of COVID I wanted a place that was within the EU with an institution that had a good reputation and courses that were relevant to my interests. Belgium fulfilled all these requirements.
overall_comments: N/A
info_ease: Easy enough. I had to do some digging on the university pages, as well as sign up for orientation days, which were very helpful
arrival_assistance: Orientation Days with all information that Erasmus students needed to know, organised by the University.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: N/A
registration_process: When students arrive they are instructed to go and register in one of the KU Leuven buildings as students. Then, you register for your courses online in the Toledo portal.
registration_help: Instructions from Orientation Days and the academic supervisor in KU Leuven
registration_success: That was a bit tricky. Some courses I had chosen where not available for me and I had to switch. But overall all courses were interesting so I believe it worked out in the end
registration_advice: Keep in mind that to get 30 ECTS you need to register for 5 or 6 courses. It's a lot of coursework and exams will be difficult as a result. But if you're interested in the subjects you will have fun
academics_comments: N/A
course_level: All of them where MA level
teaching_comparison: In KU Leuven the atmosphere is a bit different than UCPH. Continuous discussions in class are encouraged and sometimes the professor spends a lot of time answering questions. Classes are also bigger with more participants. Most professors are quite friendly. In some courses, students are expected to give oral presentations and answer questions about them.
courses_enrolled: Media Ethics Husserl in Context Metaphysics Philosophy of Technology East and West perspectives Political Philosophy
recommended_courses: It depends on someone's interest! Political philosophy is highly recommended because the professor makes the topic very engaging. Husserl in context is a must for those interested in phenomelogy, but it requires a lot of intense studying of difficult texts. Philosophy of technology deals with relevant, modern subjects. Overall all the courses I attended were interesting.
unexpected_costs: If you can, avoid coming to Leuven from Charleroi Airport, its pricey and confusing. Also be aware that Leuven is filled with delicious food in restaurants so you will spent some time there. And it's well connected so expect to be doing quite a bit of travelling
cost_comparison: Fruit can be expensive, and for some reason meat is very pricey. Other than that, it was quite affordable
activities_available: The sports centre is free for students and there's many different training facilities and a pool. There's also a student cinema which offers discounts. Student clubs and societies organise trips, talks, parties etc.
activities_recommended: Take advantage of the sports centre, for certain. And the discounts at Cinema Zed. There's also ice rink place near the town for ice skating .
weekend_recommendations: , Do some travelling to Flanders, Brussels or Wallonia. Visit the restaurants and cafes in Leuven. Visit the churches and the park. There's so many things to do!
culture_adjustment: Very easy, Belgians are quite friendly and helpful. There were no problems.
socializing_tips: Don't miss Pangea events, particularly in the beginning. It's very easy to make friends because the town is quite small and there is a huge student population.
cultural_challenges: Language. It's useful to know that Belgium is divided in two regions based on language. In Wallonia people speak French, in Flanders, people speak Dutch. Therefore, French is quite useful (and largely unwelcome) in Leuven. But in Brussels, which is 20 minutes away by train, everyone speaks French. This is something a foreigner needs to adjust to. At least, people in Flanders speak good English.
culture_appreciated: The food is amazing. German portions with a French flair. Additionally the history of Belgium is very fascinating and people can see the WW1 sites and museums dedicated to WW1. Also, Belgium is famous for its comic book tradition. And the architecture in towns is very interesting.
top3_advice: E mail the dorms in advance about a room. Note that the coursework will be challenging because you have to select a lot of courses. Remember that you will have fun regardless.
other_useful_info: KU Leuven is demanding, so bare it in mind. I managed to balance socialising and studying quite well, but exams were difficult. Make sure to make friends to support you through the process. Still, it is a great experience.
most_rewarding: The friends I made, as well as all the topics of the courses and the professors' approach. It definitely expanded my perspective as a student and as a person. I learned a lot.
greatest_challenge: The exams. But they can be beaten.
other_comments: Go to KU Leuven, you won't regret it!

crucial_aspects: The fact that the universities reputation was well renowned. Furthermore was it important that the destination was a place that I hadn't visited before.
info_ease: It was easy upon arrival because it was a university that focused on their international students and you saw all the other students who had the exact same problems as you.
arrival_assistance: How to get internet, how to go around in the city, important dates for the academic year etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The thing that dissatisfied me was the process of courses, which first was accepted a month in to my time at the exchange university, which made me nervous. Luckily everything did go well in the end and I can be glad that the lectures were recorded.
registration_help: It was really just about time
registration_success: The exchange university didn't gave me any restrictions but i just had to manage with my host uni., because it was mandatory classes I had to take there.
registration_advice: Look at the list of what courses that has been accepted before.
course_level: The level was high and only lectures. It was nice but gave a lot of time for reading at libraries. I would say that the level was as in UCPH, but the perspective of psychology was different.
teaching_comparison: I really missed small classes, because I think that gives the best understanding of the texts. But else it was really good and most of the lecturers were really good
courses_enrolled: Psychology of Learning Cognitive Science Consumer Behaviour Laboratory Animal Science Quantitative Research Methods Philosophy of Education Migration & Culture in Educational Relationships
recommended_courses: Philosophy of Education Migration & Culture in Educational Relationships
unexpected_costs: Nothing rather unexpected
cost_comparison: The most things were more cheap in Belgium, but not much.
activities_available: KU Leuven gives a sports card for Erasmus students for free. This allows you to do more than 80 sports activities that is well coached by other students or coaches. They also offer an indoor beachvolley field which is a very nice opportunity.
activities_recommended: Do sports and see the other cities of Belgium everything is much more close.
weekend_recommendations: Enjoy being in the center of europe
culture_adjustment: It was rather easy for me as a fellow european.
socializing_tips: Join a residence where people from the local country lives as well. Seek the student associations and try to find someone willing to talk english.
cultural_challenges: That Belgian people often go home in weekends and therefore only is in the city from monday-thursday.
culture_appreciated: The beer, fries and their reasonability.
top3_advice: You need to follow your course rather attentively Enjoy the student activites such as (cantus, 24h run etc.) Explore the different cultural aspects you meet in an international milleu
other_useful_info: rent a bike
most_rewarding: The most rewarding thing was the friends you got
greatest_challenge: Being away from your own country and try to fit in to another culture

crucial_aspects: The academic tradition; the importance of continental philosophy in Leuven
info_ease: Quite easy
arrival_assistance: I don't think I received anything, but I did not miss it either.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You register whatever course you wish to take on uni-website. Very easy. And I found it very nice that I could choose whatever I wanted. There are no limits on the amount of students on the courses, so there is no stress about that. One can do whatever one wants, which is very nice.
registration_help: The institute is very open for helping. I mailed them when in struggle and they replied very quickly.
registration_success: Extremely successful - I got in to all the courses I wanted, and everyone else does as well (as far as I know)
registration_advice: No advice from me. Look up all courses one could be interested in and try to read the descriptions carefully.
course_level: Very high levels (on philosophy courses). The institute has a long and proud tradition for its philosophy and it is very ambitious. I am not used to the high expectations and high ambitions and this was both very inspiring and stressful.
teaching_comparison: The teaching itself is similar, I think.
courses_enrolled: Continental Philosophy (B-KUL-W0W10A) 6 ECTS Phenomenology and Contemporary Continental Philosophy (B-KUL-W0EB3A) 5 ECTS Social and Political Philosophy: Seminar (B-KUL-W0AN6A) 4 ECTS Phenomenology (Texts): Seminar (B-KUL-W0EE4A) 4 ECTS History of Education (B-KUL-P0T31A) 5 ECTS International Relations and European Integration since World War II (B-KUL-F0GA3A) 6 ECTS
recommended_courses: Contiental philosophy, Phenomenology and Contemporary Continental Philosophy, Phenomenology (Texts): Seminar
unexpected_costs: Housing first of all. I paid way more than what the usual student does.
cost_comparison: I thought that food was cheaper, but it is very similar to Danish prices.
activities_available: Sports centre, I did not use it. ESN (Erasmus student network) (arrange both sports, cultural and social events).
activities_recommended: Try to connect with people from your institute (Institute of Philosophy). People there helped me a lot and guided me through the local and cultural life, and gave me lots of recommendation. I also joined the introduction week, but did not really enjoy it. However, I got friends which I hung out with the first months. It was helpfull, but I ended spending more time with philosophy students.
weekend_recommendations: I did not travel around a lot, but simply just drank beers and danced during the weekends. I enjoyed this as it felt more like home, as I did not go out travelling every weekend in CPH. Try to hang out with people both in clubs/bars but also in friends' homes.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy.
socializing_tips: Just be yourself.
cultural_challenges: The study culture - very disciplined and stresfull. As the university expects more from the students than they do in CPH (for example way more learning by heart), one simply needs to study a lot. I find this a bit toxic. Too much pressure, though also inspiring at moments.
culture_appreciated: The culture of the institute, contiental philosophy.
top3_advice: Take care of yourself in the exam period. It is going to be extremely tough (6 exams) Be open to people that does not look like yourself. Be disciplined and choose courses you really like.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Continental philosophy (it is a thing in Leuven!). In CPH, it has becomes so penetrated by analytic philopshy that many professors simply ignore that there are others way of thinking. In Leuven, the understanding of what philosophy is way broader and more openminded that it is in CPH.
greatest_challenge: 6 exams (+ essays, presentation). Very stressful, full of panic attacks.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: The positive associations I had to Belgium. I have only heard good things about Belgien people and Belgium as a whole and for that reason I wanted to explore it more.
info_ease: The information is relatively easy to find. Though it can be a bit difficult to figure out exactly which information you need when, but I had few difficulties finding the relevant document/links when I knew which one I was looking for.
arrival_assistance: We participated in a lecture/information class on where to find relevant links/documents and where to ask for additional help.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You look for the classes you want and are available for you to take on a website. Then you enroll in them on the online student platform.
registration_help: The proces was covered in the introduction and information lecture in the first week. Additionally you have the option of going to a class before commmitting further to it.
registration_success: Some courses had different requirements than were stated on the website for example some courses were only for students with a specific degree in KU leuven. Other than this very succesful.
registration_advice: Try out a lecture with the professor before committing to the course.
course_level: I only took master courses. These were of similar or slightly lower difficulty than what I have been used to at Copenhagen University.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is rather similar to that of UCPH. KU Leuven similarly used group work, individual work and lectures.
courses_enrolled: Global politics and Diplomacy Public Affairs EU Trade Policy Human Computer Interaction China and Global Politics North Africa, the Middle East and Euro-Mediterranean Relations
recommended_courses: I would highly suggest taking the public affairs and global politics courses. The professors are both great and the courses provide highly relevant knowledge for our studies.
unexpected_costs: I ended up going out to eat a lot more than I expected.
cost_comparison: Most things are a bit cheaper than in Denmark.
activities_available: Sportwise they have a Gym with a special student discount and they have sports offers for pretty much anything you can imagine every week. The European student network (ESN) and other organizations create a lot of different events which you join. There is a huge variation in these events.
activities_recommended: I would recommend trying out a cantus and a bunch of the things organized by ESN Leuven.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going to Brussels, Brugge, Ghent and Namur on trips.
culture_adjustment: The culture is pretty similar to the Danish one so it is not much of an issue.

crucial_aspects: KUL is highly renowned academically, and I wanted to challenge myself and to try to study in a way that I wasn't accustomed to. Furthermore, I wanted to challenge myself by going to a place I'd never been before, where I had no network whatsover, and where I was forced to speak a lot of English if I had to establish one.
overall_comments: I was overall very pleased with the academic level of the institution, though some exams were tougher than others. I've also never had as stressful of an examination period before. In the end, the best part of the experience was getting to know a ton of people from a lot of different places, many of whom have become close friends of mine.
info_ease: Very easy. Leuven is a massive student city with plenty of internationals, and both the university and the city authorities are used to having a lot of foreigners arriving every semester. The KUL-website is quite easy to navigate and often updated, and you're sent loads of e-mails and papers that aim to help you get settled quickly. Both the university and the town authorities are also quick to answer any questions you may have.
arrival_assistance: Nothing in particular.
arrival_comments: See above. The university makes sure to keep in touch with you at a quite steady pace, and in the introduction week, there are several lectures intended to get you properly settled - both regarding your faculty, and your practicalities.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I was overall very pleased with the academic level of the institution, though some exams were tougher than others. I've also never had as stressful of an examination period before. In the end, the best part of the experience was getting to know a ton of people from a lot of different places, many of whom have become close friends of mine.
registration_process: I don't remember too much of it, but for university, you have to create your university user and file some practical information, and subsequently grab your student card. For the town hall, see above. After the process, a police officer would come by your home at an undisclosed time to ensure you're actually staying there.
registration_help: Plenty of brochures, webpages etc. Furthermore, both the university and city authorities were quick to answer any questions you may have.
registration_success: Almost wholly succesfull. As far as I know, there's no limit on how many students can attend a given class - classes are mostly lectures, in which the professor talks in an auditorium with limited individual participation from students. The difficulty stems firstly from getting a combination of courses to reach a total of 30 ECTS-points, while simultaneously not having the courses overlap. Many of the English-language courses are held on the same days, so there likely will be some overlap. Planning your courses will likely take a few hours.
registration_advice: Pick up your student card as quickly as possible, as you'll use it to enter certain facilities like university libraries, as well as to attend certain events.
academics_comments: I was overall very pleased with the academic level of the institution, though some exams were tougher than others. I've also never had as stressful of an examination period before. In the end, the best part of the experience was getting to know a ton of people from a lot of different places, many of whom have become close friends of mine.
course_level: The academic level is like in Denmark, but the main spike in difficulty consists of the number of courses required to be enrolled in. Courses award ECTS points at 3, 4 or 6 points, so you'll have to attend quite a few courses. Not all courses require preparation prior to classes, but it goes without saying that a collective curriculum of 6+ courses makes for a lot of required material to study in the examination periods.
teaching_comparison: The teaching is based on lectures, in which the professor talks aloud to students in an auditorium. Questions are welcome and usually encouraged, but generally no individiual participation is required. The curriculum is usually the slides that the professor brings as well as what the professor says during class. There's often no textbook. I rather missed the teaching method at UCPH, in which most classes are seminars with more interactivity and a more informal setting. When it comes to grades, it seems to me that for quite a few classes, the difficulty subsists first in passing, and then getting a good grade - this is not the case for all classes, but for some, you genuinely worry that you won't pass your exams, despite putting in a lot of time and effort.
courses_enrolled: Private International Law Judicial Protection in the European Union European Company Law European Contract Law EU Economic Law Restorative Justice
recommended_courses: Private International Law is very interesting, but the level of abstraction is very high in many parts of the course and the grades granted are notoriously low. Professor Van Calster told is in the first lecture that the rate of passing the course was about 65%, with pre-Covid levels being around 75%. The course focuses on jurisdiction and applicable law in international disputes with focus on the Brussels Ia-Regulation, Rome I and Rome II Regulation as well as case law of the CJEU, so while the subject is very good to be familiar with, the low average grade and possibility to fail makes it difficult for me to recommend it. If you do so, be aware that the exam requires a lot of preparation. Note that professor Van Calster is going on a one-year sabbatical as of Summer 2024, so your experience may be different. European Contract Law is very intense as it is placed over the course of two weeks entirely, despite being a 6-point ECTS course. You will have to take into account that some classes will have to be skipped, and depending on if courses are recorded, you will have to prioritise. Professor Kadner Graziano is very knowledgeable, incredibly friendly and encourages student participation and discussion, and the course itself gives very useful and fascinating insight into the contract law of not just European, but international jurisdictions. The exam requires a good amount of preparation, but if prepared correctly, is quite managable. I highly recommend the course. Judicial Protection in the European Union revolved around what actions can be brought to the CJEU, and how its inner workings are. The course included a voluntary excursion to the CJEU (with limited possible spaces - be quick to reserve when they're offered!), and was quite interesting. Do note that professor Wathelet had his last semester of teaching as of Spring of 2024, and I believe the course will change quite a bit from now. It's difficult to say how and what will change, so whereas I'd normally recommend it, I don't know what the course will look like in the Autumn semester of 2024. European Company Law was interesting, and mostly focused on the European directives attempting to harmonise company law throughout the EU. If you're already familiar with company law (which I recommend being, and which the course itself states as a prerequisite), this will be a good way to get insight on the background legislation of the articles in your national company law. The examination is oral, and while rather tough, you do get to use all PowerPoints and other notes in your preparation time. EU Economic Law is similar to European Company Law, but focuses on competition law, and secondly on the internal market and the free movement of goods, services and establishment. While I'd usually recommend the course, professor Devroe had his last semester of teaching as of Spring 2024, so I don't know what changes will be made to course. Restorative Justice is interesting enough, but I wasn't that big of a fan. It's a criminology course so the method was unfamiliar to me. The exam being given via a mix of class participation, a 10-page paper and a presentation is a good way to mix up the mostly handwritten, 3-hour exams, however. Recommended if you need to get rid of 6 ECTS-points and feel like trying something that isn't law.
unexpected_costs: Lunch and having an evening beer became very frequent social activities, and while neither were particularly costly in themselves, their frequency added quite a bit to costs. My rent was about 40-50% higher than what would've been paid if I got a room through KUL, but in exchange I got my own bathroom, kitchenette, a bigger bed etc., and therefore the costs were expected.
cost_comparison: Groceries are generally the same price as in Denmark. Meat might occassionally be more expensive. Beer is a lot cheaper, particularly when compared to the styles being offered. Whilst a regular lager might not be that much cheaper, some of the heavy trappist beers are both more widely available and significantly cheaper.
activities_available: All sorts. The sports card provides access to the entirety of the sporting facility, and the different student organisations host a wide variety of different events - excursions, sporting events, pub-crawls, social gatherings, language-learning events etc.
activities_recommended: Attend as many events during the introduction week as you can. You will likely meet a lot of your very good friends there, and since the Belgian and the international students mostly keep to their own groups, it's granted that you'll see some of the people you meet again and again during your exchange. Take advantage of the different events on offer throughout the semester as well, and do attend a cantus. If possible, try to go to a more private one.
weekend_recommendations: Belgium is very nicely connected by train, and via the national railway services, NSCB, you can get some very cheap tickets (6,50-7,50 €) going anywhere in the country. Brussels is just over 20 minutes away, but Ghent, Antwerp, Brügge, Dinant, Namur and similar are all very nice day trips. Other than that, enjoy the events on offer and time with your friends. Belgian students go home on the weekends, so the city is mostly locals and international students on Friday evenings through Sunday afternoons.
culture_adjustment: Rather easy. Belgium doesn't differ that much from Denmark, and even then, I rarely socialised with Belgians. It was a predominantly international environment, with no one culture needing to be adjusted to.
socializing_tips: No. Belgian students are a lot more prone to be open and speaking English while inebriated, so you might have a chat at a fakbar or similar. Otherwise, not really.
cultural_challenges: None in particular.
culture_appreciated: The beer culture for sure. Very easily available, affordable, and varied. I highly recommend stepping a bit out of your comfort zone and trying some things you haven't before - the variety is incredible.
top3_advice: If you decide to go to KUL, be prepared for an academically challenging exchange. You're not guaranteed to pass your exams, and you will have to put in a lot of effort to pass all 30 ECTS points. That being said, it's in no way impossible, and the amount of international friends you'll make who will be suffering through the same with you makes it and your relationship with them all the more special. Be proactive, both socially and academically. Everyone's on equal footing, and people are incredibly nice and helpful. Be sure to relax and enjoy your time there. An Erasmus is a fantastic opportunity to get to know a lot of great people, so while the studying might be challenging, always remember to take good breaks and unwind.
other_useful_info: Be certain that you want to also have a rather hectic exchange when choosing KUL. Read other travel reports and experience reports.
most_rewarding: While I aimed to go to KUL for the academic challenge, I found that the biggest benefit from having gone there was the many friends and experiences I made during my stay. It was incredibly rewarding to get a close relationship with people from many different places, particularly other citizens of the European Union, with which you share rights, political systems, legislation etc.
greatest_challenge: While it's incredibly daunting to go to a foreign country with an unfamiliar way of studying, entirely without a network, it all becomes surprisingly easy very quickly. Adjusting to everything is difficult at first, but before long, everything becomes familiar. There are lots of people around to support you as well.

weekend_recommendations: Go to Brussels if you live in Leuven at check out all the vintage shops, art nouveau houses (all Victor Horta houses are so special - book well in advance especially for Hotel Solvay), experience the jazz and techno music and eat a lot of good food. I would also go to Ghent, Brugge and Antwerpen. Also, take the train to Amsterdam, Paris, Lyon, Marseille - so easy when you are in the middle of western europe.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. In Brussels it is mostly french speaking which I love, and you feel like you are in a french city.
cultural_challenges: Not the most welcoming people, so the attitude can be somewhat rude if you are an outsider, but then again I also met the most welcoming and friendly Belgium people. Figure the trash system can be difficult and you would think that the city of EU would have developed a more clever system, where it was not out in the open, but in the ground or in big trash bins. They do not collect their dog poop, and many have a dog, so be careful where you step.
culture_appreciated: I love the jazz and techno mix, and bying a croissant in Brussels by French speaking people and then jump on the train to Leuven, where people speak Dutch and the architecture in this little city is so special and beautiful.
top3_advice: Only go if you are ready to use a lot of time on figuring out courses and ready to fail a few. There system is completely different from ours, so half of their grades are failing grades and you are being graded in a way where are not taught at in UCPH. I think I used too much time on school it self, and figuring out the school system, so I barely had time to also enjoy myself in the way I experienced, which I really regret. I think at other places you could go there will be a better balance between school and enjoying yourself. At least I am never this worried about exams and passing at my home university - I know if I study and follow the course, the chance that I would fail is very little, where here I am so scared to fail half of my courses, even though I really have studied throughout the semester and prepared weeks in advance for the exam.
other_useful_info: If you do not like to party during the day and study in the weekend, really think about living in Brussel instead.
most_rewarding: If I pass all my exams that would be the most rewarding part.
greatest_challenge: Figuring out the school system and to make it match with mine a home since courses here are rewarded 6 and 3 ECTS and at home it is 7,5 ECTS.

crucial_aspects: A destination which prioritizes the students social life
info_ease: Reletavely easy and manageable
arrival_assistance: Fellow students and coordinators
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_success: Perfectly succesful
registration_advice: Be aware that the classes time schedules don't collide with each other. Choose courses with as many ECTS's credits as possible (6-credit courses) - because the work load doesn't align with ECTS-credits (så a 3-credit course can be as demanding as a 6-credit course = therefore choosing 6-credits courses will releive a lot of stress in the examination periode)
course_level: The courses at KU Leuven is very demanding, which the professors don't hide. They require a lot of work just to get a passing grade, and since it's the professors who decide what comes to the exams it's very important to show up to every lecture. Though, even if you do, it is sometimes still expected that you know more than what is being taught in class in the exams
teaching_comparison: The classes at KU Leuven was much less interactive compared to how it's dione at UCPH. In the majoirty of the classes, the lectutres consist of the professor presenting a topic and the students listening and writing notes to whatever is being said. There are not much (if any) preparation before the classes at KU Leuven. It's the professors' words and not books that are the most important thing to pay attention to throughout the courses.
courses_enrolled: - International Taxation - International and European Human Rights Law - International and European Legal Theory - European Insurance Law - Global Law - European Criminal Law - Law of World Trade Orginization
recommended_courses: - Global Law: One week intensive course, with professors from all over the world. Interesting with different perspectives, and the exam is over with quickly - International and European Legal Theory: Has a very dedicated professor. The course gives you a different perspective on law school and the classes are much more interactive than other "traditional" law courses.
unexpected_costs: You have to buy specific trash bags for the different recycle systems
cost_comparison: The course mateiral was less ecpensive than expected. But since you can't bring any electronic devices to the exams, printing documents (your notes, powerpoints etc.) was more expensive than expected.
activities_available: You were able to join the sports centre and there were many different Fakbars open every day of the week, where you could meet other students.
activities_recommended: Join as many social events, like the Cantuses and orientation week activities (internatonal dinner, ice-breaker events etc). That is where you will meet new people and form connections and thus built your social life
weekend_recommendations: Take the train and visit other cities in Belgium (Ghent, Antwerpen, Brussels or Brugges). And if possible visit cities other countries that are easily accessible from Brussels (Amsterdam, Paris, Luxembourg or London)
culture_adjustment: It was hard in the beginning, but after 4-6 weeks in the city, I felt at home
cultural_challenges: It was hard to navigate the everyday things, like how to recycle your trash, what to do before registering at the city hall and all of the rules regarding your living situaiton
culture_appreciated: Everyone is very open and helpful
top3_advice: 1. Show up at ALL lectures and take good notes, so you're not as stressed in the exam period (which is a VERY stressfuld period at KU Leuven) 2. Be openminded and yes to as many social happenings as you possibly can - the friends and memories are what you will remember and appreciate when you leave, and it is also those that will carry you through the tough periods in the studies 3. Don't be afraid to make friends outside of your own faculty (and definitely friends from other institutions than your home institution)
other_useful_info: If you're only wanting to go on exchange to have a chill and not academically demanding semester, do NOY choose KU Leuven
most_rewarding: The friendships I made and all the memories we created together in our spare time
greatest_challenge: To settle in in the beginning - finding a friend group and figuring out "where you belong" in this new environment

crucial_aspects: A mix of different things. I wanted an english speaking country to improve my english skills and to explore the Irish culture and meet the Irish people which I heard a lot of good stories about before going.
overall_comments: My overall experience is actually a 11 out 10. Accepting the exchange spot in Limerick was truly the best decision made. First of all is the Irish culture absolutely amazing. People are so kind, open and welcoming, which gave me the feeling of being part of the culture very quickly. I made a lot of new friends - both other internationals and Irish - which was the best way to exchange cultural experiences. The University of Limerick (UL) offers a lot of interesting courses, the professors are competent and UL is very progressive and including in many ways. Campus holds a lot of different faculties so you get the chance to meet people who study different educations than yourself and you can join a lot of very nice sports and social clubs and societies on campus. A lot of young people live in Limerick and the Castletroy area, which gives you the feeling of living in a 'study city'. Ireland has A LOT of pubs, Guinness and truly amazing nature that calls for a lot of hikes. I really recommend everyone to go on exchange in Limerick. I was so happy that I did and I wished that I could attend an extra semester myself!
info_ease: It was very easy! University of Limerick provided me with all information needed. Students had the chance to attend two weeks online orientation before semester start. My academic coordinator at UL was very helpful and replied to emails very quickly, which was very helpful. The reason that I dont rate the assistance 5 out of 5 is due to accommodation issues. Unfortunately, I did not get a spot on the on-campus accommodation. Therefore I had to find accommodation on my own, which was very difficult (due to housing crisis in Ireland) and the assistance from the university was very little.. They tried to provide students without accommodations with websites etc. but it was still very difficult and I felt a bit 'left alone'.
arrival_assistance: All internationals got picked up in the airport in Dublin.
arrival_comments: UL staff are very friendly and helpful regarding all academic inquries!
housing_how: I found housing on my own

course_level: The academic level at UL is a bit lower than UCPH but for me that was not a problem. The lectures and readings were very interesting.
teaching_comparison: I attended two lectures and one tutorial each week. In the tutorials the weekly assignments were discussed, which was very helpful and interesting and a good way to participate in class-discussions with other students. The workload at UL compared to UCPH was a bit bigger each week. Students were to hand-in small assignments before attending lectures and tutorials. We also did a presentation in one of my courses. Both weekly assignments and presentations are a part of the final grade. The reading workload every week was smaller than at UCPH (and all the reading are free!!). I handed in a larger assignment in all of my 5 courses at mid-term and in the end of the term. I had no oral or sit-in exams. You have to hand-in all your assignments on your own. In my courses groups were not a choice, unfortunately.
courses_enrolled: I attended 5 different courses: Nationalism, Ethnicity and Conflict Policy-Making in the European Union Comparative European Politics Sociology of Gender and Popular Culture International Organizations and Global Governance
recommended_courses: I REALLY enjoyed Nationalism, Ethnicity and Conflict, Sociology of Gender and Popular Culture and Policy-Making in the European Union. But the professors in all courses were very engaged, competent and helpful. My two other courses were a bit of a repetition of courses that I already attended at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: Housing was more expensive than expected. I chose to spend a lot of money going on weekend trips with my friends. That was really worth it!
cost_comparison: Food is cheaper than in DK if you go to Aldi or Lidl. Spar, Tesco and Dunnes Store are a bit more expensive but still cheaper than DK. Lunch at UL are the same prices as at UCPH.
activities_available: UL offers so many different sports clubs and societies. I was so surprised but it is an amazing way to make new friends - especially local friends - with same interests as you! I joined the UL kayak club, which was so much fun and a VERY good way to get to know lots of Irish students. We went on a weekend-trip, a lot of river trips and pool sessions every week. I also joined the Outdoor Pursuit club, which offered climbing and hike-trips. Unfortunately, it was very difficult to get a spot on the hike-trips due to the big demand so I ended up going on hikes with my friends on our own. But the climbing sessions were very good. Other than that UL arrange day-trips around Ireland throughout the semester. I joined a trip in the beginning and that was a very good experience and a cheap way to get to see new places in Ireland. The university pub 'Stables' has an international night every friday which is a very nice way to end the week!
activities_recommended: If you wanna experience the real Irish craic then join the kayak club ;-). All international students are very friendly and open! Join the social events in the beginning of the semester to meet all the other Erasmus students. We had some big Whats-app groups where international students organized social meet ups and parties throughout the semester. That was very nice.
weekend_recommendations: I really recommend going on weekend trips. I arranged a trip with my other international friends almost every weekend. We used GoCar which is a cheap and easy solution. It is way easier to go by car and you get used to the traffic very quickly! Hostels are OK cheap as well. We did a lot of amazing hikes in Killarney National Park, Wicklow Mountains, Sligo, Dingle Penninsula, Waterford and Connemara National Park. The nature is SO stunning so bring some good hiking boots, download the hiking app "Alltrails" and go explore! You won't get disappointed. We also visited the big cities; Dublin, Cork, Galway and Belfast in Northern Ireland. These places are 'must see' as well! Most Irish people travel home to their parents in the weekends so most going outs, house parties and social events with irish people are during the week. If you are going to Limerick during the fall semester then remember to attend 'Christmas Day' in November - ask an Irish friend for more information. Promise me! you don't wanna miss out on that one!
culture_adjustment: Very easy - Irish people are the best people! For me Limerick felt like home very quickly.
socializing_tips: Again; JOIN A CLUB! All my Irish friends are people that I met in my clubs - especially the kayak club. We did a lot of parties together and a Christmas Dinner in December. For me that was the absolutely best way to get to know Irish people and the Irish culture.
cultural_challenges: The accent is lovely but can be difficult at times ;-) and then the Irish slang. Get some Irish friends who can teach you about 'craic', 'sound', 'class' and all the other words that they use all the time ;-).
culture_appreciated: Irish people are so friendly. I really appreciate that I got so many nice Irish friends while staying in Limerick.
top3_advice: - Really enjoy your time in Limerick! Time is running way too fast. - Join as much social events as possible! Go on trips around Ireland, join clubs and go to house parties. (Yes, the house parties in College Court are as good as they say - don't miss out ;) ) - Don't stress too much about the academics. The Professors are so helpful and they check-up on the students throughout the semester, you will get used to writing in english very quickly and assignments and exams are doable.
other_useful_info: Spend some time on finding accommodation if you don't get on-campus accommodation. Start as early as possible!!. It can be difficult but don't give up! Try to call a lot of landlords instead of emailing and do skype-calls before paying anything! Join the 'UL freshers' groups or 'rent in Limerick' on Facebook. In these groups other students are looking for roomies and landlords are looking for tenants. Airbnb is a solution as well, but unfortunately landlords charge very high rents at the moment.
most_rewarding: I am very thankful that I got to know the Irish culture and that I got so many good new friends - both Irish and other internationals. Limerick might seem as a very small city, but trust me! It has so much to offer. I REALLY enjoyed my stay and I will recommend everyone to go on exchange at UL. My exchange in Ireland was beating all my expectations. It was four very very happy months!
greatest_challenge: The only challenge was that the semester ended and I had to leave Ireland.
other_comments: Just do it! Limerick is the best second-home you could ever wish for.

crucial_aspects: The fact that it was in an English-speaking country and that I was able to get courses pre-approved.
overall_comments: I had the best study abroad experience at University of Limerick! I can only recommend UL as a host university as the university offers a broad selection of opportunities for you to try out during your stay. Furthermore, Irish people are the most open-minded and welcoming people, and they are very easy to become friends with.
info_ease: Very easy. Once I was accepted at UL, the university sent a lot of emails with information.
arrival_assistance: Firstly, the university offered a pick-up service from the airport directly to the university when the international students arrived, which was very convenient. In the first week, there was an introduction week where all the needed information about course registration, how to find your way around at the university, formal requirements, ect. was presented.
arrival_comments: The international coordinators at UL are very friendly and ready to help you, and they answer emails very quickly if you have any questions before or upon arrival.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had the best study abroad experience at University of Limerick! I can only recommend UL as a host university as the university offers a broad selection of opportunities for you to try out during your stay. Furthermore, Irish people are the most open-minded and welcoming people, and they are very easy to become friends with.
registration_process: When you get accepted at UL you register online for ten modules but it is not guarantied that the modules will run, so the registration is not binding. You can find a book of modules with descriptions of the modules online at the university's website. In the first two weeks of your stay, you can attend all the lectures of the modules you consider taking. This gives you a chance to chose the modules you find the most interesting. After the two weeks, you fill in a blanket with the modules you want to take, get it signed by the Erasmus coordinator, and then upload it at "Sulis" (the UL version of Absalon).
registration_help: The Erasmus coordinators are always ready to help you. You can also always talk to the lectures if you have any questions about their module.
registration_success: I got all the modules I wanted.
registration_advice: Attend a lot of different lectures in the first two weeks! Some of the modules that you initially was planning on taking might not fulfil your expectations while others might surprise you. As a psychology student you can take modules from other faculties as electives which is a good opportunity to learn something different from what you are used to at your home university.
academics_comments: I had the best study abroad experience at University of Limerick! I can only recommend UL as a host university as the university offers a broad selection of opportunities for you to try out during your stay. Furthermore, Irish people are the most open-minded and welcoming people, and they are very easy to become friends with.
course_level: The academic level is a bit lower than UCPH, but I did not find that this was a problem for my exchange experience.
teaching_comparison: The number of students at the lectures are way smaller which allows a lot more interaction both with the lecturer and with the other students. In general, the style of teaching is more personal and some of the lecturers even learn the names of the students in their module. However, the classes are not as critical as at UCPH, and some of the modules just go through the textbook material.
courses_enrolled: Advanced Research Methods, Developmetal Psychopathology, Abnormal and Clinical Psychology, Empirical Psychology and Sociology of Gender and Popular Culture.
recommended_courses: Sociology of Gender and Popular Culture! The lectures are very interesting with a high academic level, the assignments are challenging, and the lecturer is very passionate, communicative and entertaining.
unexpected_costs: I spent a lot of money on weekend trips around Ireland.
cost_comparison: Groceries were cheaper than in Denmark, but beer and food on restaurants were almost the same.
activities_available: All you could wish for! There is a club or society for almost every interest you might have. Furthermore, the university arranged different kind of social and cultural events during the semester.
activities_recommended: Make sure to join at least one club or society. I would highly recommend the Kayak Club (no previous kayak experience needed) or the Outdoor Pursuit Club, which offers both hiking, climbing, caving and orientering.
weekend_recommendations: Explore beautiful Ireland! Go to Killarney National Park, Connemara National Park and Wicklow Mountains for beautiful hikes, Go to Dingle, Northern Ireland and the west coast in general for stunning nature spots, and go to Dublin, Cork, and Galway to explore other irish cities. Ireland has a car sharing system called GoCar where you can rent cars at a fair price even when you are under 25 years. This makes travelling around Ireland very easy.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The Irish people are the most friendly, welcoming and warm people you will ever meet.
socializing_tips: Join a club or society. This is the easiest way to become friends with the local students. Otherwise, try to make it to a house party in College Court ;)
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The people! As mentioned previously, the Irish people are the best.
top3_advice: 1. Join a club or society as it is the best way to get to know some Irish students. The club members are very open to international students and the clubs offer a lot of social life. 2. Enjoy every day of your stay! You are only there for 4 months and time flies by so fast. 3. Make an effort to get Irish friends. They are very friendly, great fun and throw some wild parties.
other_useful_info: Try your best to get on campus accommodation as it will make the practicalities during your stay a lot easier.
most_rewarding: The social life with the other international students and the Irish students.
greatest_challenge: The day when I had to leave, but once I arrived everything worked out perfectly.
other_comments: Again, I would highly recommend the Kayak Club. The people are so nice and helpful and white water kayaking is so much fun!

crucial_aspects: That is was easy to access academically - or in other words compatible with my danish syllabus. Furthermore that I was intrigued by the culture, and the nature of the country.
info_ease: Somewhat easy. A lot of information goes unsaid, so when I left I was a bit unsure how it all would go, but upon my arrival, I got confirmed that everything indeed was under control.
arrival_assistance: A bus from The University of Limerick was waiting for me when I arrived. The reception to my village was also open so I could get the keys to my apartment - I arrived quite late, so this was really nice. I felt well taken care of upon my arrival.
arrival_comments: I was confused about certain things - like whether to bring bed-linen (I didn't need to so I made the right call luckily) and other small stuff like that, but all the essential parts were very clear.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was fine! A bit overwhelming but I guess that is the case with every Erasmus stay. Overall okay :)) I found it a bit confusing, but they will write to you if you forget anything, so it's all good.
registration_help: You could mail both the host and home instituaiton. If I remember correctly there was also a booklet of help if you needed it.
registration_success: They only make the official booklet of modules available to you (where you can see what courses to take) available last minute, so sometimes your pre-approval will not be applicable and you would have to start over with this - this happened to me which was a bit frustrating. But apart from that, there is a lot of nice people willing to help you to the best of their abilities, and they are used to dealing with international/Erasmus students. When you are an Erasmus student they will also have two weeks when you arrive before you choose which course you want to take - this is quite convenient as it gives you time to figure everything out before your settle on a module.
registration_advice: When it comes to modules keep your calm. It can be a bit frustrating but it will probably work out!
course_level: The courses at University of Limerick were good, but in general a bit lower than at the University of Copenhagen I would say. I also greatly missed a critical approach as a lot of it was taught as "this is how it is".
teaching_comparison: I liked the exams/assignments better here! it was very nice and also manageable for an Erasmus student! Apart from that quite the same, apart from the fact that there isn't as much student participation in the classes at UL.
courses_enrolled: PS4031 - PSYCHOLOGY AND EVERYDAY LIFE PS4097 - DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHOPATHOLOGY PS4107 - ABNORMAL AND CLINICAL PSYCHOLOGY SO4001 - INTRODUCTION TO SOCIOLOGY SO4118 - THE SOCIOLOGY OF GENDER AND POPULAR CULTURE
recommended_courses: SO4118 - THE SOCIOLOGY OF GENDER AND POPULAR CULTURE This was very good and opened my horizons to great topics - you are able to gain such a nuanced perspective on otherwise polarized debates - truly wonderful! Can be recommended even though I study psychology and not sociology.
unexpected_costs: Spend a lot more money on going out (beer - a lot of it) than I expected, but it was very much worth it!
cost_comparison: In general, Ireland was a bit more expensive than I expected - maybe the same or a little lower than in Denmark, but quite close.
activities_available: So many! it is hard to name them all! UL really has these things nailed down. There were numerous clubs with so many activities of all tastes and weekly trips to Irish attractions all over Ireland. I was also a part of the student ambassador program which was amazing. Really nice all of it. If you want to do something, there is always people down to join you - from knitting to sports!
activities_recommended: All of them! Especially the Student ambassador program if that is possible, and if not the weekly trips - they are very nice!
weekend_recommendations: In terms of nature: Killarney National park for hikes. The Slea Head Drive for some VERY beautiful nature by car. In terms of cities: Adare is nice. Galway is a must! I also heard that Belfast should be amazing. I personally didn't like Dublin that much.
culture_adjustment: Easy. I was a bit surprised by the 'lad culture' but apart from that, it was quite nice. People are very friendly - and not faced by the cold!
socializing_tips: Seek them out :)) I spend most of my time with international students, which I don't regret, but I know some people used online meeting sites such as Bumble to meet locals.
cultural_challenges: The 'lad culture' can be a bit intimidating and uncomfortable at times. Apart from that, it was really nice!
culture_appreciated: People are so kind and welcoming! I also enjoy the small talk a lot!
top3_advice: Rainwear of course - especially if you want to go for hikes! It rains so much here, that they do all planned activities irrespective of weather.
other_useful_info: Limerick has been known as a rough city, but not it is mostly fine. Although be aware of drugging and spiking at nightclubs (I've only heard about it in clubs, but never experienced it myself). And although Limerick is quite safe, it is better to walk home with a friend if it is night.
most_rewarding: The people. They are so great. It is indescribable. Also, the nature is breathtaking. Really something you have to experience for yourself.
greatest_challenge: Dealing with FOMO - there is so much great stuff to do all of the time which I really wanted to do.

crucial_aspects: Pga corona, følte jeg mig mere sikker ved at vælge en destination der ikke var for langt væk, samtidigt syntes jeg det ville være fedt at kunne forstå og snakke med de lokale.
info_ease: UL (University of Limerick) er super gode til at tage sig af "abroad"-studerende sammenlignet til hvad jeg har hørt om andre steder. Og deres personale er rimelig nemme og komme i kontakt enten via mail eller telefon eller reception (hvis man bor på campus)
arrival_assistance: Vi havde en uges "intro" men det var ikke det bedste eller mest tjekkede, (og det var online), men de gav nogle vigtige informationer og resten fandt jeg som regel vha de andre ERASMUS studerende. De ventede dog til aller sidst at snakke tilmeldelse af fag (meget unikt for UL, så kan man ikke få sine fag inden man kommer, men først når man er ankommet) hvilket var ret stressende især fordi jeg fandt ud af at der var nogle fag på hjemmesiden der alligevel ikke blev udbudt og skulle finde et nyt fag hurtigt og få godkendelse fra KU (som ikke er de hurtigste til at reagere).
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Jeg synes det var rigtig stressende ikke at få mine fag at vide og godkendt på forhånd da der "kun" er 3 uger til at finde sine fag, og selvom jeg ikke havde de største valgmuligheder så var det alligevel ret besværligt at få det til at gå op så både UL og KU var tilfreds og godkendte - så meget at jeg var nødt til at spørge om forlængelse til fagtilmeldelse (hvilket jeg fik) men det betød at jeg var bange for at mangle ECTS point og miste mit legat
registration_help: Jeg havde en kontaktperson på UL men han var rimelig clueless så det var mig der skulle have styr på det hele også ift KU
registration_success: Det hele lykkedes tilsidst og jeg fik godkendt mit sidste fag, men det betød at min førstemåned var mere stressende end det havde behøvet at være
registration_advice: Prøv evt at skriv eller ring til UL omkring fag for at være helt sikker på at de tilbydes i det semester og på UL da jeg oplevede at de ikke oplyste det på deres "booklet" af tilbudte fag
course_level: Det var måske lidt under KU-niveau ift læsemængde, men det er meget anderledes undervisning, hvor man skal være meget mere aktiv i timerne, hvilket jeg syntes var mega fedt.
teaching_comparison: Jeg syntes som sagt at jeg kunne meget bedre lide at fagene var mere "hands on" og brugte cases og eksempler fra virkeligheden, men det var ikke særlig teoretisk tungt eller så gennemgik de teori jeg allerede havde været igennem på bacheloren.
