crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a university which was not in a big city and which also had a good academic programme. It was definitely a plus that University of Limerick was in an English-speaking country, and that it was not very far from Copenhagen either.
info_ease: There was a lot of information given to us by the UL Erasmus team as well as from the UCPH coordinators, so I would say we had all the necessary information.
arrival_assistance: The UL Erasmus team had planned a whole orientation week just for international students when we arrived, so we could get to know each other, the university and a bit of Ireland as well, which was really thoughtful. They gave us social and academic support and overall were very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process was a bit confusing, because we had to registrate several times on different platforms. When our semester begun, we had a "trial period" of about 4 weeks, where we could try out different courses before deciding on which ones to follow. This was very nice, as you were able to meet the professor, check out the course plan and exam form before enrolling in the course, but it of course dragged out the process quite a lot.
registration_help: There was a lot of help available from the Erasmus team and all the professors were very helpful with answering questions both in class and via email.
registration_success: There was no limit on the amount of international students who could enroll in courses, so you were able to choose whichever course you wanted, which was really nice.
registration_advice: Do not stress about it before going, just show up at UL, see which courses are available and try out as many as possible before deciding.
course_level: The theoretical level was definitely lower than what I am used to at UCPH, and there was almost no required reading in my courses. Instead we had to write a lot of essays where we had to research literature and structure assignments ourselves, which we were not used to.
teaching_comparison: Almost all of my courses consisted of one or two weekly lectures and a weekly tutorial, all in smaller classes of about 20-40 students, so it was a lot more personal that the lectures I am used to.
courses_enrolled: 1) Comparative European Politics 2) Policy-making in the European Union 3) Russian Politics 4) Government and Politics in Ireland 5) Nationality, Ethnicity and Conflict
recommended_courses: I recommend them all except Government and Politics in Ireland - the course focuses a lot on Irish political history and Irish bureaucracy, and it is quite difficult to keep up with that level of detail when you are not Irish.
unexpected_costs: There were not any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Almost everything costs the same as in Denmark - grocery stores and restaurants are a bit cheaper, but not a lot.
activities_available: There were so many clubs and societies, almost anything you could imagine - there were clubs for kayaking, fencing, photography, soccer, climbing, running, sailing, dancing, yoga, reading and fashion, just to name a few.
activities_recommended: I would especially recommend kayaking and surfing. There are sessions every week so you are able to keep up with the club and really get to know the other members, and they plan a lot of weekend trips which are so much fun. But generally are all the clubs very nice, so I would recommend just trying a bunch of different ones.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely travel around Ireland and go on hiking trips. I would recommend Connomara, Galway, Dingle, Killarney and Wicklow. Dublin is also not far away and the bus goes all night, so definitely spend some Saturdays in Dublin once in a while - you can really do a lot in a day.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy - Irish culture is very open and not too different from Danish culture.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences really challenging.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the openness towards international students, as it is not that common in Denmark. Also the pub culture in Ireland is just really great and chill!
top3_advice: 1) Join clubs! Most courses you will take will mostly be with international students, so being in the clubs are a great way to meet and befriend Irish students 2) If you live on campus, remember to go into Limerick city and use its cafés to study and pubs to party. I would especially recommend Canteen and Nancy Blakes 3) Start your exams early. I mostly had to turn in essays which I had all semester to do, but I ended up having to do most of them in a hurry at the end of the semester, which was a shame - at the end of the semester you want to enjoy the place and your friends while you can, so you don't want to be stressing over exams by then.
other_useful_info: Get an Irish phone number quick so you can order groceries from Dunnes and Tesco.
most_rewarding: It was really rewarding getting a lot of new great friends, both Danish, Swedish, Australian, German and Irish (and more). All international students are away from home and their usual friends so everyone are very open to meet new people, so it was quite easy to get new friends and get close to them fast. It was also very rewarding just trying to live in another country, and Ireland really is a great place. I felt very lucky to experience their lovely culture and amazing nature, and I can't wait to come back to visit - it definitely already feels like a home away from home.
greatest_challenge: Moving to a different country is generally challenging, just because you need to learn many things from scratch - where to grocery shop, how to take the bus, etc. I had never been to Ireland before coming to Limerick, so it was a bit overwhelming in the beginning, but there are so many international students in the same situation, so you will figure it out together.

crucial_aspects: First of all it depended on whether or not I could find the courses that resembled my mandatory courses from KU. And I realized I didn't know much about Ireland besides that the people should be very warm and open so overall it seemed like a perfect destination.
info_ease: There is a lot of information about almost everything on the university's website, and if I couldn't find the necessary information the UL Erasmus team was very helpful and answered almost immediately.
arrival_assistance: In the weeks leading up to the start of the exchange we received weekly emails containing a lot of information about social and academic stuff that was nice to know about. housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Overall it is an easy process but there is multiple registrations because they operate with a trial period of 3 weeks where you get to try different courses before selecting your final choice of courses. registration_help: You can find much on the website and otherwise the Erasmus team was helpful with any question.
registration_success: Very succesfull! I also ended up registering for a course that wasn't officially offered to exchange students but I wrote to the course leader and she told me that I could join the course if I wanted to.
registration_advice: Try many different courses in the trial period to see what you think of the professor and the course. Sometimes you get surprised.
course_level: I found some of the courses quite easy - especially on the theoretical level. But others where perfectly challenging and I felt like I learned a lot.
teaching_comparison: Compared to political science at KU there were a lot less people attending the lectures which made it more like what I had in high school. courses_enrolled: - Policy-making in the European Union (replaced EP) - Comparative European Politics (replaced DAK3) Elective courses: - Nationalism, Ethnicity and Conflict - Russian Politics - Sociology of Race and Racism
recommended_courses: I really liked 'Nationalism, Ethnicity and Conflict' and 'Sociology of Race and Racism'. Both had very skilled professors and interesting topics which also touched upon Irish examples
unexpected_costs: none
cost_comparison: It is almost the same as in Denmark. Groceries and restaurants are a bit cheaper but not much.
activities_available: There are so many options available for students at UL. All the clubs and societies are listed here: https://ulwolves.ie
activities_recommended: This was some of the best! There are so many clubs and societies so I definitely recommend joining these to meet a lot of new people and try new things. Some of the clubs also do weekend trips which is great fun and you get to meet a lot of Irish students as well as other internationals. I enjoyed the kayak and surf club a lot and went on a weekend trip with both of the clubs which are some of my best memories from my time in Ireland.
weekend_recommendations: Ireland is not the biggest country which is great because then you get to see a lot of it! I went on a lot of weekend trips either through the clubs or self-planned with other exchange students and that is so nice! There are many busses going different places and otherwise you can rent a car and go on adventures. I also travelled around in Ireland for two weeks before the semester started and that was really nice. That way I got a taste of the country before everything really started. Also because there are so many things happening during the semester so there is not enough time to see everything. At least there wasn't for me. But go and hike, and surf and stroll around in the cute cities. I recommend Dingle, Killarney, Connemara, Galway, Achill, Slieve Liegh, Aran Islands, Wicklow, Westport.
culture_adjustment: Personally I think Ireland's culture is not so far away from Danish culture so I didn't find it difficult at all. And of course there are some differences but nothing I found difficult. Irish people are very open and chatty and I think that was a very positive cultural difference:D
socializing_tips: Join the clubs and societies! It is a great way to connect with other students. And also the orientation week seemed really nice.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any.
culture_appreciated: The Irish people's openness and that they were always so helpfull. I am definitely also gonna miss the pubs so much!! Their pub culture is like nowhere else with pints, live music, dance and great vibes. And then also their amazing nature
top3_advice: 1) Go and explore Ireland - they have much to offer from cozy small towns and pubs to beautiful mountains and hiking places 2) join clubs or societies - a great way of meeting people and enjoy the campus and Limerick 3) remember to enjoy yourself during a week of school - you can study in Limerick city to make it more cozy and celebrate in one of the many pubs of the city.
other_useful_info: Remember the advices on housing - otherwise have fun and enjoy your time. Time goes by so quickly
most_rewarding: The nature and experiences with that and the people you meet<3 I enjoyed every moment I had exploring Ireland but I enjoyed it even more because of the people I shared it with. It is really a unique experience to meet so many new people from different places of the world.
greatest_challenge: Of course moving away from home can always be a bit challenging in the beginning especially but you figure things out along the way and that is also nice to know. I felt more confident in myself which is something I take back home.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a country with beautiful nature, good courses, many university clubs and with good reviews regarding both the Erasmus+ program and housing. University of Limerick in Ireland had it all, so it became my first priority. I'm extremely happy that I got to go to this destination and I can't recommend it enough. :)
info_ease: It was very easy to find information and UL was really good at informing their incoming students in general.
arrival_assistance: I received a lot of assistance. We received a weekly email leading up to our start and we would get replies to our emails within hours almost. There was a lot of events in our first week at campus (and throughout our stay) and we could always ask for help if needed.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There was designated sites for modules and courses which can be found here: https://bookofmodules.ul.ie – all this made the progress very easy.
registration_help: If you had questions regarding courses you could always send an email and expect a reply shortly after. The professors I asked for previous syllabus were also quick to respond.
registration_success: I was successful and got the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Just ask questions and send emails.
course_level: Some courses were fairly easy, while others were perfectly challenging. I felt like I learned quite a lot during my exchange.
teaching_comparison: There was almost no group work, and assignments were individual. UL also used PowerPoint presentations, and their lectures were fairly similar to KU. It was less theoretical, which was a nice change from KU.
courses_enrolled: - Policy-making in the European Union (replaced EP) - Comparative European Politics (replaced DAK3) - Nationalism, Ethnicity and Conflict (elective) - Russian Politics (elective) - Sociology of Gender and Popular Culture (elective)
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of my three electives. I really learned a lot in Russian Politics and I really enjoyed Sociology of Gender and Popular Culture. Nationalism, Ethnicity and Conflict was also great, which taught me more about the Irish history too.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter anything unexpected. Personal spending differes quite a lot depended on how many trips we did. I only had to buy one book online, the rest was already provided.
cost_comparison: The cost of food is about the same as in Denmark if not cheaper.
activities_available: There is a lot available for students at UL through the UL Wolves clubs and societies: https://ulwolves.ie/
activities_recommended: I really enjoyed the Kayak Club. Went on a weekend trip and tried white water with them which was great. I also got to try a house party with them at Halloween. A great way to meet the locals since not many internationals joined this club. The Surf Club was a bit too popular unfortunately so I gave up on that in the end. The same was the case for Outdoor Pursuits. They took too many students in without being able to take them all on hiking trips. I applied almost every week but never got a spot. The Yoga Society was also great.
weekend_recommendations: We went on trips around the country almost every weekend. I really recommend going to the country side and enjoy a stew and a Guinness at the local pubs. You'll almost always find great live music there. I loved Connemara and Killarney National Park. Use All Trails for finding great hikes. You should also check out Belfast, interesting history. There is a lot to do in Ireland and I didn't get to try everything I wanted to.
culture_adjustment: Very easy both due to the language but also the people. The Irish people are very helpful and friendly. Everything seems to work fine most of the time.
socializing_tips: Join the clubs and societies! And go to pubs of course.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find anything challenging in particular. Their hostels might be less clean with mold being a bit more common than what is good.
culture_appreciated: I will miss the pub culture a lot and the events around campus. I will really miss the clubs and societies here, which are a lot more student controlled than at KU.
top3_advice: Ask questions (you'll get answers), join clubs and enjoy the beautiful country of Ireland!
other_useful_info: I think I've covered most of it.
most_rewarding: The people I met there. I will never forget this time because of them.
greatest_challenge: Having to leave all of this behind. It was the best semester I've had and probably will have.
other_comments: Remember to say yes! Go on that trip and don't focus too much on school only. I had a big assignment while I was away in Edinburgh and it turned out just fine writing it in a loud hostel :)

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an english speaking country, rich on culture and nature; Ireland seemed like a perfect fit.
info_ease: In the upcoming weeks you will receive a weekly mail with all the information you'll need from UL. If you had any questions, they were very helpful and quick to respond.
arrival_assistance: We had an orientation week for all erasmus students where we were introduced to Irish culture, UL in general and many new friends from all over the world through several events and workshops throughout the week. It was a very nice start and I met most of my friends during this week.
arrival_comments: Very friendly and helpful! Do not hesitate to ask for help.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: First week of school you are able to try all the courses you are interested in. By week three or so you have to apply for the courses you want to apply to. You have to make sure that all courses has been formally approved by the home university and registration will be on their platform "brightspace". You need to take a surplus of courses at from you own departing (For instance, I had to choose three psychology courses out of five)
registration_help: We had a lecture where they described the process during orientation week and they were available on mail and in office if you needed any further help.
registration_success: It had no issues with registering courses. Some of the classes had a limited amount of spaces for exchange students, but I didn't seem to be any problem getting a spot.
registration_advice: Attend as much as possible during the first weeks. It was a great help when choosing your final courses. They'll explain all the mandatory assessment to pass the course, which gave you a great indication of the workload for each course.
course_level: In my experience workload was higher than in KU as you have to take five courses, but at a bit easier level.
teaching_comparison: It differed a lot depending on the size of the course. In big courses you'll typically have two hours of lectures (either consecutively or spread out over two days) and then one mandatory tutorial. Smaller courses you have lectures and tutorials in one, where discussion and team work was a big part of the teaching style.
courses_enrolled: PM4035 - Psychology of Work (Arbejds- og organisationspsykologi) PM4013 - Principles of Human Resource Management (Arbejds- og organisationspsykologi) PS4031 - Psychology and Everyday Life (Valgfag) PS4045 - Advanced Research Methods (Avanceret forskningsdesign og videnskabsteori) PS4097 - Developmental Psychopathology (Valgfag)
recommended_courses: If you are interest in clinical psychology I will recommend you to take Developmental Psychology - it offered a lot of interesting debates and guest lectures.
unexpected_costs: I spend a lot of money on Uber home from town when busses wasn't running anymore.
cost_comparison: Hostels could be a bit expensive during prime time - but definitely worth the money if you want to explore beautiful Ireland.
activities_available: So many options! I was a part of the surf and kayak club. Fun, social and a good opportunity to meet irish students and to go on weekend trips around Ireland. Craft was very nice and cozy as well.
activities_recommended: I will recommend all of the listed clubs from before. Specifically kayak was fun as you get to go on the lake and not just the pool.
weekend_recommendations: Go around Ireland! It is easy to rent a car or go by bus. I had great time in Galway and Killarney, but I have so many other "must visit" places. I also went to Northern Ireland and Scotland - plane tickets are quite cheap from Ireland.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Everyone was so nice and welcoming.
socializing_tips: Go to pubs and mingle - that's the favorite irish thing to do. And join clubs! They'll throw social events and weekend trips, where you get to meet others. Participate in as many events as you can handle during the orientation week as you can handle - people are all seeking friends and are more approachable.
cultural_challenges: Can't really think of any. Maybe they way they dress for going out - shorts dresses throughout the whole year (rain was not holding them back).
culture_appreciated: How friendly the irish people were and the beautiful hikes!
top3_advice: Be prepared for a very difficult process in finding accommodation if you don't succeed with on campus accommodation. Apply for housing elsewhere before or as soon as you receive a rejection letter. If you need a bike, you by one at the UL market on in the beginning of the semester. It's a bit pricey, but very easy and he offers to take it back for half of the price at the end of the semester. Ireland is a very proud country with a lot of history - be careful when choosing religious and historical topics :-)
other_useful_info: Bring rainwear and hiking boots. If you want to use the pool facilities at UL you have to wear a swimming cap - so bring one from home if you already have one. Otherwise I visited Decathlon quite a few times. They have it all and to a quite decent price as well. Also it's very cheap to go the cinema there. It was a nice thing to do with friends, when you were a bit socially exhausted, but still wanted to do something. If you are lucky enough to have nice weather while you are there; take a swim in Shannon River. There is a "beach" on campus.
most_rewarding: All my friendships and hikes a achieved during my stay. I loved the cozy pub culture as well and all the live music.

crucial_aspects: I had a hard time finding study destinations, where I could get the modules I needed. Limerick ended up being one of the only options I found, and I thought it was a plus, that I would receive an Erasmus grant and that Ireland is rich in beautiful nature and interesting culture.
overall_comments: I really had a great time and met the best people.
info_ease: University of Limerick sent out emails with a lot of information prior to arrival. They were really helpful.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation week for exchange and erasmus students, that supplied us with a lot of helpful information, and social events to help you meet new people.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I really had a great time and met the best people.
registration_process: I don't remember exact process, but we just had to give them relevant information, make a preliminary list of 10 modules, apply for accommodation, etc.
registration_help: University of Limerick was really helpful, as they supplied step-by-step instructions on how to registrer.
registration_success: The final registration for classes is done in the second-third week of the semester - I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: I found University of Limerick to be very helpful - it was more the other processes, such as the learning agreement, that I found complicated.
academics_comments: I really had a great time and met the best people.
course_level: Easier than at KU in terms of the theories and the content we had to learn - but I found the workload pretty intense in the latter part of the semester.
teaching_comparison: Not as much student engagement in the modules I had - most of it was just lectures. The style of teaching at KU is focused on being able to use different theories and think critically - this I found to be a lot less prominent in the teachings at University of Limerick. Much of the content of the modules were taught as factual or "this is the way it is", which I found to be a bit simplistic.
courses_enrolled: Advanced research methods, The Psychology of Work, Principles of Human Resource Management, Developmental Psychopathology and Sociology of Race and Racisms.
recommended_courses: Sociology of Race and Racisms! Very, very interesting module. Gave really good insight into both historic and contemporary issues - and also gave insight in Irelands history.
unexpected_costs: Electricity was not included in my rent - and electricity is super expensive in Ireland!
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive - but the cost of living I would say was less expensive than expected.
activities_available: Stables, the on-campus bar, hosted international night every friday. There were so many different clubs and societies available - I tried yoga, outdoor pursuits club, dance and archery.
activities_recommended: I enjoyed the yoga society and Outdoor Pursuits Club - OPC organised hikes every weekend, and also a few weekend trips.
weekend_recommendations: Travel! I went on trips to Galway, Cork, Belfast and Derry. Getting around to the different cities were fairly easy. There is also a few companies that organises daytrips on the weekends to different locations in Ireland. Through them I went to Dingle, to Aran Islands and Cliffs of Moher. Many of these places can be quite difficult to reach unless you have access to a car - so if not, I would recommend going on some of these trips. I also did some hiking trips with my friends - we went to Moylussa, which was a really nice mountain, not too far by bus from Limerick.
culture_adjustment: I found it fairly easy. Irish people are really nice, and the orientation week made people settle in pretty quickly.
socializing_tips: Join clubs and societies, that would be your best opportunity to meet Irish people. But they are generally more talkative and outgoing than danish people, so you would also often socialise with locals, when you went out to different pubs. However, the Irish students are often a lot younger, than what I was used to from Denmark. They could be as young as 17 years old, and I sometimes found the age different to be pretty apparent. I spent my time with other exchange students, which I did not regret. The other exchange students were closer in age, and I really enjoyed that we were having the same experience - everyone is really open, and everyone wants to make the most of their time on exchange.
cultural_challenges: The nightlife is quite different - people go out quite early and they really dress up, in miniskirts etc.
culture_appreciated: I really liked how friendly the Irish people are. I also love the nature, and the pub culture with live traditional music.
top3_advice: Limerick is probably not going to be your favourite city. Coming from Copenhagen, it was a very different experience to stay in Limerick, as it is not the most beautiful city and not a lot of stuff is going on. However, I would just embrace it. You are only there for a short while - and I would say that it made my experience better in some ways. It is part of the experience to try something different, and it was a lot of fun, to build a life for yourself in a place, where you maybe couldn't picture yourself beforehand. Another thing is, just be open and say yes to things. An exchange semester passes by so quickly, so just try to be present and enjoy it. Don't get to stressed out about academic matters - it will probably work out.
most_rewarding: I really met some amazing people, that I built very close friendships with. We had a lot of fun. It was also very rewarding to have a semester away from my busy life at home. At home I have more obligations - uni, work, different friend groups, volunteering, family, etc. It was really nice to have a semester where I only had to focus on two things - my exchange friends and my schoolwork. I loved the spontaneity that followed from this, and having a friendgroup that I hung out with almost everyday - both at university and outside of it. An exchange semester is still very busy, but just in different ways. There is also going to be things you won't find the time to do, because you want to do it all, while you are there.
greatest_challenge: Saying goodbye to my friends when I had to go home. It is hard to say goodbye to people when you have been used to seeing them everyday, and then not knowing if and when you are going to see them again, when you all go home.
other_comments: Just go!! It is going to be such a nice experience!

arrival_assistance: A lot! University of Limerick is clearly very exchange-friendly, as they had a program for the students from the start of the exchange period. housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_help: Online help as well as in-person assistance.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Look for accommodation in good time. If you do not get on-campus accommodations, It can be difficult to find something. However, reach out to UL off-campus accommodation assistance - they are great help and very kind.
course_level: Some required prior courses others did not.
teaching_comparison: The teaching did not go as much into depth compared to UCPH. There was a less critical analytical approach at some of the courses and I did, to some degree, miss nuance and a more critical stance (however not all classes were pure psychology!!).
courses_enrolled: The psychology of work, Principles of Human Resource Management, Advanced Research Methods, Developmental Psychopathology and The Sociology of Race and Racism.
recommended_courses: Definitely the Sociology of Race and Racism - it was pretty mind-blowing. I loved the professors approach to sociology and the quality of teaching was very high. Very interesting papers as well!.
unexpected_costs: I went traveling a lot around the country. Even though I do not regret this at all, it will cost a lot, so it is a good Idea to make a budget and save up, if you want to go exploring. Food is also almost the same as in Denmark. Going out is cheaper though.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive
activities_available: Almost everything you can imagine. There's over 70 clubs! UL is known for its sports, so there is great facilities, even though I did not use them much. If you live on campus you also get free entrance to the gym.
activities_recommended: I tried out Outdoor pursuits, yoga, dance and archery. I was very fond of the yoga as well as archery and outdoor pursuits. In terms of other social activities I would generally recommend going to a lot of the events organized by the university.
weekend_recommendations: Go on as many trips as possible! Ireland is very beautiful.
culture_adjustment: quite easy - Ireland is not that different from Denmark in that sense.
socializing_tips: Joining clubs and events.
cultural_challenges: I mostly just found them interesting. Ireland has a long and complicated history of being oppressed which Is still very present in the countrys cultural identity and narrative. Despite of this, they are a proud and incredibly kind and welcoming people
culture_appreciated: How exceptionally warm, interested and welcoming everyone was. There's also a rich, musical history (irish music at most traditional pubs) which is a lot of fun! It is also one of the most politically activistic countries I have been to which I found very interesting and inspiring.
top3_advice: Pack for all sorts of weather Save up You are bound to have a good time.
other_useful_info: if you wan't do doing the outdoor pursuits, bring hiking boots! (they are required to go on trips).
most_rewarding: All the lovely people I got to meet, including almost every irish person. Also I really loved traveling around the country.
greatest_challenge: Money!

crucial_aspects: When choosing the destination it was important for me that the university was situated within a city where there were lots to do in weekends, school breaks etc. Also, I choose to study abroad in England as I have family living here and have always had a wish to stay in England for a longer period of time.
overall_comments: I really enjoyed my stay! Everything was well organised and I really don't have much negative to day about my study abroad experience.
info_ease: I found it easy to find information. If I couldn't find the information I needed, it was easy to find contact information.
arrival_assistance: There was an optional campus tour just after I arrived, which helped me getting to know the area and meet new people. Also, there was a welcome event for study abroad student after a couple of weeks were I met a lot of new people who became my best friends here.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I really enjoyed my stay! Everything was well organised and I really don't have much negative to day about my study abroad experience.
registration_process: I registered for my courses before I left my home country and go them accepted just before the start of the semester. I found the module guidance given by the university very helpful when choosing my courses.
registration_help: The module guidance showed an overview of the different courses/modules and I choose 50 % of my courses within my field of study and the other 50 % within other departments.
registration_success: I applied for 6 different modules and got 5 of them pre-approved by the University of Liverpool and finally got accepted to 4 of the modules. I really enjoyed the modules and there were no timetable clashes, so everything worked out really well for me.
registration_advice: I applied for modules spread over 3 different departments and one of my biggest concern was timetable clashes. For me this worked out really well and I ended up with two whole days with no teaching, which instead gave me plenty of time to prepare for classes. Therefore, my advice is to just go with whatever you find interesting and try something new within other departments if you wish to.
academics_comments: I really enjoyed my stay! Everything was well organised and I really don't have much negative to day about my study abroad experience.
course_level: I had two year 3 modules (level 3), one year 2 module (level 2) and one year 1 module (level 1).
teaching_comparison: I was surprised with how little teaching there were compared to what I was used to at UCPH. For each module I had 1 hour of lecture and 1 hour of seminar each week which resulted in 8 hours of teaching per week. This resulted in less group work and group assignment however I was very well-prepared for the classes as I had lots of time to prepare.
courses_enrolled: COMM301 - NEWS MEDIA AND SOCIETY. COMM312 - Introduction to Strategic Communication 202122-MKIB155 - CONSUMER BEHAVIOUR 202122-SOCI213 - Understanding Digital Culture & Society
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed SOCI213 - Understanding Digital Culture & Society. The teacher was really great and we had very interesting discussions of technologies' impact on society.
unexpected_costs: Nothing really.
cost_comparison: Food is a bit cheaper in the UK than in Denmark. Laundry was more expensive than expected.
activities_available: All different societies for whatever hobbies or interests the students might have. There a lovely gym that I have used a lot and it even has a swimming pool.
activities_recommended: Join a sports club or society, it is a good way to meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the cities close to Liverpool, there are really many places worth visiting. I went to Manchester, Leeds, Chester, York, Peak District and the Lake District. I can really recommend trips with wearedaytrippers as they plan day trips departing from Liverpool.
culture_adjustment: I found it easy to adjust. Local people were very welcoming and interested in international student.
socializing_tips: Go to as many of the planned events at the beginning of the semester as these were crucial for me to make friends. Also, be open to get to know new people throughout your stay as you will constantly meet people you haven't spoken with previously.
cultural_challenges: Not really anything except that I had to adjust to the Scouse accent that was a bit difficult to understand at first.
culture_appreciated: I think msot of the culture is similar to Danish culture.
top3_advice: Consider what is important for you when choosing accommodation on/off campus, studio apartment or shared housing. Be aware that you have a lot of teaching-free time during the week, as there are not a lot of hours of teaching. Really enjoy it and have an open mind towards all the new people you will meet, it has really been the most amazing experience for me to meet so many people from different countries.
other_useful_info: Many study abroad students have gone travelling during holiday breaks (we had a three week spring break) and at the end of the semester. It is a good idea to save up money to have the opportunity to go on travels with your new friends.
most_rewarding: I really enjoyed the campus aspect of the university especially that I only lived 5 minutes from where I had my classes. It was such a lovely atmosphere experiencing all the students living and studying in the same area. Also, I really developed my English language skills which is really rewarding.
greatest_challenge: At the end of the semester I had three really intense exam weeks where I had to write my assignments along with having teaching in my modules right until the end.

crucial_aspects: - The nature and environment in the country. - That it was a partner university so I was sure the educational standards were the same as my home country. - New culture I could experience - Good recommendations of the destination
overall_comments: Had the best experience in Ljubljana! I already miss it and will forever cherish this ERASMUS experience.

arrival_assistance: We were given a personal student tutor who could help with any questions and/or recommendations and you could always get help and information from the International Office at the faculty.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Had the best experience in Ljubljana! I already miss it and will forever cherish this ERASMUS experience.

registration_help: If I had any questions I could always contact the international office in Ljubljana and also get help from my own university (UCPH). They always responded very quickly and were very helpful.
registration_success: No problem. I had my clinical rotations and got signed up by the international office to the right departments and was sent a schedule with dates and departments very quickly.
registration_advice: If you have any questions, just ask for help. They respond very quickly.
academics_comments: Had the best experience in Ljubljana! I already miss it and will forever cherish this ERASMUS experience.

courses_enrolled: Clinical rotations in surgery: Throracic Surgery and Oncology Surgery Clinical rotations in internal medicine: Gastroenterology and Vascular medicine Clinical rotations in anesthesiology - Neuro surgery and more.
recommended_courses: All my rotations went very well! Thoracic Surgery was amazing and I truly had the best mentor. They let you do a lot and assist everyday and do surturing. Oncology Surgery was also great and they put you in the programme so you know when you are assisting at a surgery. Also, the rotation in anesthesiology was very special and my mentor taught me a lot of procedures. Definitely recommend.
unexpected_costs: You have to bring your own hospital clothes and wash it yourself! It is not available at the hospital for students. So I had to purchase white scrubs in the beginning. (approximately 25 euro for doctors coat and 30 euro for clinical pants and 5xwhite basic t-shirt 25 euro)
cost_comparison: Groceries are very similar to Denmark in prices, but going out for a beer or wine is very cheap! 2 euros for a glass of wine, same with beer most places.
activities_available: Many different sport activities! Also had a medicine party at the beginning of the semester.
activities_recommended: Join the Erasmus trips! They have so many great offers, such as wine tasting, cave trips and Christmas market tours to different cities and countries.
weekend_recommendations: You can rent a car very cheap when you are a student. So drive to the Triglav national Park and go for some amazing hikes! Kranjska Gora and the area around Ratece was one of my favorite places to go. During winter season, go skiing! Also the coastal city of Piran is beautiful.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. People were very welcoming and almost everyone speak English very well.
socializing_tips: You meet many new friends at the Erasmus Trips. It's also always great to grab a drink with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: The language was a little difficult, so communicating with the elderly (especially patients) could be difficult.
culture_appreciated: The positive spirit and their proudness of their country and language.
top3_advice: - Be active. Show your interest to the doctors and they will bring you along to everything - Bring your scrubs from home! - Enjoy every single day - time flies way too fast!
other_useful_info: Bring a small notebook that you can write your daily experiences into.
most_rewarding: The people I met and the friendships that were created.
greatest_challenge: The language. But the website slonline.si was a great help!
other_comments: Just go for it and apply for exchange! You will not regret it!

culture_adjustment: It was not a problem.
socializing_tips: The faculty have local students on the introduction day who you can get to know. You also meet local students on your clinical rotations, so I would say, that you just have to be open minded, ask them to meet for coffee or beer.
cultural_challenges: Not really.
culture_appreciated: The Slovenes are very helpful and great people.
top3_advice: Get to know the locals, since they are very nice and can show you their country (and nice wine and food). Get to know your tutor/supervisor at the hospital and be initiative so you can learn and do more. Explore the nature (mountains, waterfalls, and forests).

Lastly, find recommendations as soon as possible.

greatest_challenge: I was usually the only Erasmus student in the departments, which could feel a little lonely at times - but again, the doctors are very friendly.
other_comments: Always stay open-minded and curious :)

crucial_aspects: Choosing Lucerne, Switzerland as a study destination for law students hinges on several pivotal factors. First and foremost, the academic reputation and excellence of the law programs play a pivotal role. Lucerne's universities should offer a strong foundation in legal education, thereby fostering a promising legal career. Also, I thought it would be great to train my German language skills as well as English. Moreover, the local and cultural ambiance of Lucerne are crucial; its breathtaking landscapes and rich cultural heritage offer an environment that complements your academic journey. This picturesque setting provides opportunities for extracurricular engagement and networking, which can be invaluable in the legal field. I also thought it would be fantastic to meet new people and peers, and get to know other cultures as well, from countries all over the world. And the academic environment is great. Additionally, the presence of internship and job opportunities within or near Lucerne is a decisive factor. Gaining practical experience while studying is indispensable for law students, facilitating a smoother transition into the legal profession post-graduation. In summary, the choice of Lucerne as a study destination for law students is a multifaceted decision, encompassing academic quality, language proficiency, cultural appeal, and career prospects.
overall_comments: It was a great experience!
info_ease: Easy I would say. The international team at the University made it easy and they were great at communicating and making events for the new students.

course_level: The level was in the middle – not too easy, not too hard. But some of the courses are mandatory! The Swiss people are much more concerned about this than UPCH.
teaching_comparison: UPCH is harder.
courses_enrolled: Copyright in the Digital Age, Internet Law, Introduction to Swiss Law, Introduction to the Common Law System, Law and Economics and Negotiating and Drafting International Commercial Contracts.
recommended_courses: Introduction to Swiss Law as this course is both out of campus and at the campus. When out of campus, you go to monuments, and you get a little food and background info about Switzerland. But this is only in the beginning.
unexpected_costs: Transportation was really expensive, and food as well. I felt like food sometimes was almost double of the Danish prices. My food budget was way too low put and I needed to use almost all of my savings on just living okay. I never ate out as it was ridiculously expensive. There was an indian restaurant close to our University and it was 27 francs for a butter chicken. It is around 200 DKK.
cost_comparison: Food and transportation. Generally, the prices felt around 20-30 % higher and food sometimes 50 % higher than DKK. Do not go here if you do not like to spend money! I was kind of jealous of some of my peers that went to Italy and Spain as they ate out every night while all I got was homecooked rice and pasta. We ate out sometimes but mainly pizza and kebab.
activities_available: Different kinds within what you normally would expect. Football, volleyball, dance, etc.
activities_recommended: The dance lessons was pretty fun. I did not try more than those as I also had to study and do a lot of other things.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend them to travel the country. A travel pass for a month cost around 2500 DKK. It is very expensive but the transportation is good and it has beautiful views. Participate in the student environment such as the ESN and make many new friends. Go out and explore the night life as well and bring the big wallet as drinks are pretty costly ;-)
culture_adjustment: It was more or less easy. The Swiss are more conservative people who likes they "private space", but they are not too far away from Danes.
socializing_tips: Participate in the activities around you. Both through the University and the ESN-programme. If you live at the associated student organisation's campus, you will also make friends if you live with the other people in a shared flat. For the local students it is more hard, as they are not as willing to be with you as the international students. But you can always meet some at the campus or just talk to them at the University, even though that might be a little odd. Especially since they speak Swiss German.
cultural_challenges: The Swiss are more closed people and they do not socialize with foreign people that much. When going out, they stay a lot in their own groups, people say. Also, they are not so used to date a lot, they stick with one partner and are more loyal I would say. Danes are more free and like to speak with people, especially when drunk.
culture_appreciated: Hmmm. I think I appreciated the cultural aspects about the nature the most. A big part of Swiss culture is just being, wandering and skiing in the Alps. I liked that compared to flat Denmark.
top3_advice: 1) Be yourself but also be curious about other people. 2) Go out, have fun and enjoy your time. Do not worry too much about school and grades, this is the time of your life! 3) Bring a big wallet and do not look too much at the prices. Money comes and goes, memories stay forever.
other_useful_info: Prepare as much as you can in advance and read the e-mails you get from both Univeristy of Lucerne and University of Copenhagen. And also, bring warm clothes but do not expect you can pack everything because that is impossible.
most_rewarding: The memories to be honest. And the relationship with myself – I got to know myself much better and I realised how beautiful the world is. Coming from the pandemic into this was really rewarding.
greatest_challenge: The social aspects and the money-aspect. It was hard to socialize 24/7 almost. At the end, I spent much more time alone and it was really nice. I made some local friends and spent time with them also instead of ONLY being in the bubble of the exchange students. Also, the money-aspects was rough. I felt broke all the time. Also my friend from Denmark, who was also there on an exchange, thought the same. She was kind of sad at times about it. Because we could not go out and eat, spend too much on drinks etc. We really had to watch our money.
other_comments: Just enjoy it and have fun. Do not think too much about small details. Socialize but also spend time alone to experience and travel.

crucial_aspects: It was important to me that it was possible to take interesting courses in English and that the destination was located close to nature. I was also interested in the culture and way of living. I was looking for a smaller city, hoping for a more local and international experience with other exchange students, as I was the only Danish student during my semester.
info_ease: Very easy. All information was available on the University of Lucerne website or through Mobility Online
arrival_assistance: I had one question about what to fill in on Mobility Online, and I simply sent an email to the University of Lucerne exchange department
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration was done through Mobility Online, and registration for help with finding accommodation was also available
registration_help: If help was needed, you could always email the Office of International Relations.
registration_success: I was able to take all the classes I wanted and could even sign up for more than required. This allowed me to try the classes before deciding which ones I wanted to continue throughout the semester. I also believe it is possible to attend classes without taking the exam, as you only need to decide which exams you want to take around mid-November.
registration_advice: Be aware that you have to sign up for exams yourself.
course_level: I am used to a higher workload, with more required reading, at my home university, however the classes i have at home usually carry more ECTS points witch could explain this. I think it was manageable to follow the courses even though they were master’s level courses.
teaching_comparison: It was quite similar, with seminar-style classes and a high level of interaction. Due to the small class sizes, there were no large lectures. I liked that some classes were broadcast, so I could rewatch them when sick or while preparing for exams.
courses_enrolled: International Human Rights Law International Banking & Capital Market Regulation International Sports Law Introduction to Swiss Law Law and Society in a Global Context International Law of Contemporary Media
recommended_courses: I really liked the course Law of Contemporary Media, as it is very relevant since media plays an important role in globalization. You participate in a moot court as part of the course, which is an interesting way to engage more deeply with the topic. I would also recommend Introduction to Swiss Law, as you gain a lot of background knowledge about the Swiss legal system, and the course includes some interesting excursions I also would recommend Sports Law if you are into sports, is educational to learn about sport for a law perspective and is quite drifferent for the other classes i have taken.
unexpected_costs: Printing at the university is quite expensive, so it might be cheaper to buy legal texts from a bookshop.
cost_comparison: Food cost around 20% more, but it really depends if you eat out, cook with friends ect. Transportation was more expensive than expected, even tho you get the halbtax. Sports Classes was free through uni
activities_available: The university offers a wide range of different sports classes. They also invited us on a boat ride, dinners and a classical concert
activities_recommended: I really enjoyed going to yoga, and it was also a great way to meet new friends. I would definitely recommend going on hikes, as nature is very accessible from Lucerne.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend visiting Como, which is only a two-hour train ride away and gives you a real Italian vibe. I also really liked Lausanne and smaller cities during the summer. If you enjoy skiing, I would definitely recommend doing that, and even if you don’t, visiting mountain towns like Engelberg or Zermatt is still worth it.
culture_adjustment: We had a cultural class during the introduction week, where we became aware of cultural norms in Switzerland and potential misunderstandings. It is not very easy to become friends with local students, and most of your social life is with other exchange students. I also do not speak Swiss German. In everyday life, I did not experience many cultural differences.
socializing_tips: It can be challenging if you do not speak German, but I did interact with local students through classes and yoga.
cultural_challenges: I had to adjust to a new culture, but I did not find it particularly challenging. Living with different cultures was more educational than challenging overall.
culture_appreciated: The love and respect for nature, as well as the international perspective in Switzerland.
top3_advice: It is quite expensive, but you will learn a lot about cultures from all over the world and become very close to other exchange students, as you are not many studying abroad at the same time.
other_useful_info: I quite like being the only one form Denmark as you get to meet more for all around the world and make new internationalt connections. I also like it being a smaller uni, as you naturally get to know people you study with.
most_rewarding: Being able to travel around and experience Switzerland after a hard-working summer. It was also very rewarding once everything was settled with school and accommodation and you started making friends. It gave a feeling that the exchange would be a success.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge was setting up a new everyday life with a new culture, new friends, and a new university. However, this was also where I learned the most.

This meant that I had a lot of different courses to choose from, which was also nice. It was important to me that I found courses which were interesting to me, and UoM had pretty much anything an anthropology student could wish for.
overall_comments: The academic part of the stay was great. However, I had a terrible living situation which influenced the overall enjoyment of my stay.
info_ease: It was pretty easy, as soon as I had attached my email to a student account at Manchester I received a lot of e-mail with information regarding my start there. I was not informed that single-semester exchange students are not offered student housing through the UNI. I was not informed about this before I wrote their accommodation department, which was very disappointing.
arrival_assistance: We had an intro-meeting with an ERASMUS coordinator, and were pointed in different directions to receive campus tours, join communities and so on. Overall the student center and help you could get there was great. I almost never felt in need of more information, and when I did, it was usually. easy to find.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The academic part of the stay was great. However, I had a terrible living situation which influenced the overall enjoyment of my stay.
registration_process: This part was decently easy, I just had to write which classes I wanted to a coordinator who contacted me. When I did it wrong, she tried to help me.
registration_help: A coordinator was there to help.
registration_success: I was not registered for any classes upon arrival, but this was quickly fixed by people at the uni when I wrote them. Even though some of the classes I had asked to be in had been 'filled' due to the registration being open for local students, I was put in these classes. So do not fear, they were very accommodating in this regard.
registration_advice: Try to check through the host-institutions student-net service whether you have been enrolled in classes or not as soon as you have access.
academics_comments: The academic part of the stay was great. However, I had a terrible living situation which influenced the overall enjoyment of my stay.
course_level: The level was high, which was what I desired. The staff expects a lot of you, and there is a lot of reading, but if you are ready to put in the work, you will get so much great education in return.
teaching_comparison: It was pretty similar, although most classes did not have the portfolio-type of assessments as we do at UCPH. It depends a lot on the teacher as well, as the teaching staff is very diverse in gender and nationalities. The teachers did a lot of extra-curricular events which were nice.
courses_enrolled: Anthropology of Visions, Senses and Memories Anthropology of Displacement and Migration Screening Culture
recommended_courses: All of the above. They were all great. Visions was a course centered around phenomenological and sensual approaches in anthropology, both theoretically and methodically, as ways of generating knowledge with interlocutors. Andrew Irving teaches the course, and is a very inspiring and laid-back character with a lot of research on his resume. Displacement and Migration was a great course which centered around different themes of migration. Sebastien Bachelet was teaching the course at the time, and was a great educator. Screening Culture takes you through all of the main ideas, theories, themes and methods of filmmaking within the anthropological genre. A great course if you are interested in filmmaking as an anthropological tool.
unexpected_costs: Not any, really. I rented a bicycle for the months I was there which saved me a lot on bus-fares. Manchester is a very decent city to cycle around.
cost_comparison: Food is not cheap. Also, heating was included in my rent, but some of my fellow students got slapped with gas charges in the winter.
activities_available: All sorts of sports-stuff. The student-union ran a bar where you could meet others.
activities_recommended: Student union stuff-
weekend_recommendations: Visit Liverpool. Eat curries.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy, the English are like the Danes in a lot of ways.
socializing_tips: Go to the student bar, also in the daytime. People hang out there. Talk to the people in your classes, they are very talkative and used to exchange students.
cultural_challenges: The food culture. They don't cook too much, and so the kitchen where I lived was disgusting and not very well equipped. The alternative is take away, which is mostly really unhealthy food.
culture_appreciated: Curries. Pub-culture is a sight to behold.
top3_advice: Try to find housing from home. Prepare to study. A lot. It's great. Get a bicycle.
other_useful_info: Large campus, lots of people. If you want friends, you have to engage others.
most_rewarding: The academic outcome of my stay was fantastic.
greatest_challenge: My living conditions. Small expensive room, mildew in common areas, very cold and dirty.

Jeg er vandt til blok struktur og kun at have 2 fag ad gangen, og skulle pludselig have 6 fag (30 ECTS), hvilket har været en smule overvældende. Godt nok svarer et 10 credit fag i Manchester til 5 ECTS-point, men vil sige at workloaded for hvert 10-credit fag er meget mere end, hvad der forventes af et 5 ECTS point fag i dK, hvertfald for mit vedkommende med de fag, som jeg havde valgt. Jeg vil anbefale at kigge på de forskellige kurser, og vælge nogle af dem, hvor man skriver en opgave, der uddgør en hvis procentdel af den samlede karakter, så man kan sprede workloaded og ikke skal være så stresset under eksamensperioden.

Genes evolution and development er et godt kursus, hvor man lærer mange interessante ting og der bliver inddraget en masse eksempler fra virkeligheden. Molecules and cells in human disease havde meget fokus på en masse pathways, og er virkelig komplekts. Der er en masse man skalhuske, og det er cotent heavy Haematology er virkelig spændende Endocriology er også et fedt kursus, der er relativt lige til Introduction to virology er også et spændende kursus, hvor man for 30% af sin karakter skal skrive en opgave, hvor man designer sin egen virus
unexpected_costs: Mit telefon abonnement fra Danmark virkede her, så det skulle jeg ikke betale for. Hvis man mealprepper kan man sagtens handle ind for ca. 20 pund om ugen. Jeg brugte mest af alt penge på cafeer, mad og shopping, så det er virkelig idividuelt, og varrierer fra måned til måned

socializing_tips: Tag til alle møderne! Det er der, hvor jeg mødte mine vener. Den første tid er vital for at finde sine venner, da det er der, hvor semesteret endnu ikke er begyndt, og folk har massere af tid. Manchester udbyder så mange muligheder for at deltage i studentermiljøet og få venner, så gør brug af det!

culture_appreciated: Inde jeg kom var jeg ret nervøs for at skulle tale engelsk, da det ikke er noget jeg gør så ofte derhjemme. Dog var folk super imødekommende, og man følte aldrig, at man ikke var på lige fod med dem.

other_useful_info: Fedt uni
most_rewarding: Fik mødt en masse fantastiske mennesker fra hele verden, og Manchester var så god til at tage imod os alle.
greatest_challenge: Har heldigvis ikke haft nogle store udfordringer ved at være her.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to explore a new city and country, without compromising with the academic level. I specifically applied for Universität Mannheim because it is has a high ranking within social science and the location is really attractive. The city is 'only' around the size of Aarhus and the architecture is nothing to write home about. But it is beatifully located between the rivers Rhine and Neckar and has good transport opportunities to other large cities and great nature experiences. For me, it was very important to be somewhere that was different from Copenhagen and Mannheim was perfect for that.
overall_comments: I would rate my stay a 9, because I had an amazing experience, but I was affected a little bit by COVID restrictions. Nothing too severe though, and it was never really a problem.
info_ease: The university webpage can be messy, but with time I was able too look up everything I needed to know. The university's international office is very good at sending informing email. But be patient, things works slower in Germany.
arrival_assistance: The international office and the economics department held several Zoom meetings before semester start. This was very nice.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I would rate my stay a 9, because I had an amazing experience, but I was affected a little bit by COVID restrictions. Nothing too severe though, and it was never really a problem.
registration_process: The course catalog is released some time in during the summer holidays. It contain all information you need. You sign up for courses through the univerisyt platform Portal2. The exam registration comes later, some time in the middle of the semester. The university does not release the exam dates with the course catalog, these come later. However the university guarantees that no exams overlap as long as you stick with courses from the same department.
registration_help: The webside offers some guidance, but I would suggest to ask another student for help if you need it.
registration_success: I got all the courses that I wanted.
registration_advice: Take a breath when you get frustrated with how late the course information is released. You will manage everything in time, no problem.
academics_comments: I would rate my stay a 9, because I had an amazing experience, but I was affected a little bit by COVID restrictions. Nothing too severe though, and it was never really a problem.
course_level: I found the level very similar to what I am used to. At least it was not more difficult than at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: There is mostly only lectures and the few exercise classes I had were focused on student presentations. The grading is different, in most of my courses my final grade was made up of in-class presentations, assignment and a final exam. I really liked this, because it reduced my stress at the final examination, because at had already passed some of the class. I made more presentations than usually. I think I did 6 in total. But I only had one home assignment during the semester.
courses_enrolled: Banking and bank regulation (5 ECTS), Economic and financial market policy (5 ECTS), Chinese economy (5 ECTS), Poverty and inequality (7 ECTS), Health economics (7 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed 'economic and financial market policy'. The course had some theory, but was mainly focused on current issues. We also did a case presentation where we where asked to find information on and present our own solutions to issues. 'Chinese economy' was interesting because UCPH does not offer something like it. The professor was super motivated and was very open to question we had and giving advice on our exam-report. 'Poverty and inequalty' brought new perspectives on the subject, which was super interesting.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay an initial fee to the university. Also you also pay a broadcasting fee in Germany. This is approx. 18€ a month.
cost_comparison: Food, drinks and rent are much cheaper than Copenhagen. You can by lunch in the university cafeteria or around the city for 3-5 euros. Public transportation is as expensive as in Copenhagen. If you travel to larger cities with the ICE trains might even be more expensive. With the student card you can travel for free in the local area after 7pm and in the weekends. I used this a lot to explore the area around the Mannheim.
activities_available: There is a sports club through the university. The offer a wide range of different sports. I went to some of their yoga classes, which were really nice. There is also a crazy long list of different student organizations. Take a look and show up for the ones you find interesting. I participated in some events from AEGEE Mannheim, which was great.
activities_recommended: Take part in the exchange student events arranged by ESN VISUM Mannheim. This is great way to meet other internationals. Sign up for the buddy program. Your buddy is a local student, who knows the city and the university. I like to swim, so I went a lot to the pool Herschelbad.
weekend_recommendations: Visit cities like Heidelberg, Speyer, Frankfurt and Weinheim. Go hiking in the hills behind Heidelberg or Neustadt, the views are amazing. Do a wine-hike, the area is big on wine production, especially Riesling. If you go in fall, then definitely visit Christmas markets and drink glühwein. Watch a handball- or icehockey game. The two teams in Mannheim both play in the best german league.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Even more if you know some basic german. Most older germans and even some students are not very good in english.
socializing_tips: Go to all the erasmus events, do not be scared to show up alone, many others are in the same boat as you.
cultural_challenges: Remeber to always have cash on hand. You can pay with card in supermarkets and larger stores, but at restaurants and bars, cash is the way to go.
culture_appreciated: I only met super friendly and open people. Everywhere I went people were so nice and invited me along to the things they did.
top3_advice: Remeber to enjoy your stay. Exchange is so much more than just academia. Go hiking, get beer in Jungbusch and have a coffee at the rivers.
other_useful_info: Train is cheaper than flying. If you can overcome the long travel time, this is the easiest way to arrive.
most_rewarding: The amazing people I met. I am definitely going back to visit them.
greatest_challenge: The practical stuff with the university. But this was a small thing compared to the entire stay.
other_comments: Don't dicard Mannheim just because you do not know the city. It is a student city filled with great people who will make sure you get the best stay possible.

crucial_aspects: International focus, learning German and the prices
overall_comments: Highly recommended
info_ease: The University is helpful and you can contact them with problems, the city administration is difficult if you don't speak German, so I recommend getting a German-speaker if you don't
arrival_assistance: I got a buddy who could help me and I got the contact info of the person responsible for international law students - these two helped with everything I needed. There were introductionary lectures as well, but they proved somewhat redundant, as the info was easily available online
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Highly recommended
registration_process: You write an email asking for classes and then later you write an email asking for a student-ID. Very easy.
registration_help: Help was not necessary, however they did offer (badly) translated versions of the forms relevant when dealing with the city.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Get a German-speaker when dealing with non-university important stuff (such as getting a German number or dealing with the city at all).
academics_comments: Highly recommended
course_level: I got MA-programmes as well, and they were not too difficult. Don't be scared by the 1-hour exams, as they are pretty simple questions (a la RJM) and the oral exams are also easier. There is not the same solemnity in German exams as in Danish exams.
teaching_comparison: The material was exclusively covered by the professors, so (almost) no student presentations, but participation was encouraged and sometimes graded.
courses_enrolled: European Private Law Comparative Law I: European Legal Traditions German Constitutional Law International Arbitration EU Fundamental Rights
recommended_courses: Comparative Law, for the professor (prof. Brandt) who is really great. EU Fundamental Rights, if you don't mind a competent, but intense professor International Arbitration, as it gives you an understanding for basic arbitration and is a really good introduction into the arbitrational world.
unexpected_costs: Germany is, comparatively, cheap and thus I eat out and went out more than at home. You could easily live for less then I did. There aren't many "unexpected" costs beyond a semester fee of about 100 euros.
cost_comparison: Everything seemed cheap
activities_available: Sports had their own department and beyond that there were many clubs avaliable. They can be found on the website.
activities_recommended: I did not personally perticipate in many activities, but the gym membership is free.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Heidelberg - it's beautiful and historic and free with the semester ticket. Beyond that there are wine-fields, small towns and France nearby.
culture_adjustment: German culture is close to Danish, so adjusting is easy. As regards the other international students, I recommend taking what they say at face value, what you might think is sarcasm or a joke, might very well not be - and try to keep an open mind.
socializing_tips: I mostly socialized with other internationals
cultural_challenges: Smoking indoors is not prohibited - incredibly frustrating.
culture_appreciated: The food, as I love German food - especially at the Christmas Market
top3_advice: Do the summer academy if possible, it is kinda pricey, but you'll meet a lot of people and get a solid foundation in German which is really helpful. If you drink, then go to Jungbusch. Enjoy your time - five months are not that long.
other_useful_info: Remember the exchange rate - things might not be as cheap as they appear.
most_rewarding: Getting to know people from across the world and thus understanding the world a little bit better.
greatest_challenge: Germany is, unlike Denmark, a very analogue country, so if there is an option to do things online, it's usually incredibly bad.
other_comments: I can strongly recommend going - Mannheim is absolutely a great place to study abroad. Should you have any questions, please contact me on zmb695@alumni.ku.dk or +4524798715

crucial_aspects: It was crucial to me, that the university offered courses, that I found interesting. Furthermore, I wanted to go somewhere in Europe with a great school. Lastly, I wanted to improve my german, why Germany of course was the obvious choice.
overall_comments: I recommend all students to do it! It is an experience for life.
info_ease: It was very easy. The university of Mannheim was absolutely incredible during the whole process.
arrival_assistance: We got a lot of assistance. We could attend an introweek, where they held a lot of meetings both revolving physical stuff like where is the cafeteria, library and how to get books at the library, where to find school counselling and so on.
arrival_comments: Again, the University of Mannheim is incredible and very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I recommend all students to do it! It is an experience for life.
registration_process: We just forwarded and e-mail explaining first and second priority of courses, and then a few weeks later, we either got it confirmed or denied. I did not hear about anyone not getting their priority.
registration_help: You could always e-mail the team, both the general team of the University of Mannheim and also the departemental exchange coordinator.
registration_success: I got my first priority, so very successful.
registration_advice: Just make sure to check your e-mail, so you know when to do what.
academics_comments: I recommend all students to do it! It is an experience for life.
course_level: I think the level was equivalent to the level at UCPH. The only thing I was struggling a bit with in the beginning, was studying in english. We only have one mandatory english course on the bachelors of Law, why I wasn't really familiar with academic law in english. However, this came to me very fast, and everything went very well.
teaching_comparison: It compared fine, I would say. The only thing was that some of the professors used the "harpun-metod", where they just point out a student, and want them to answer. But for me this was fine in the end, even though I usually hate it. I still don't prefer it, but you get used to it. Furthermore, it is not all the professors, that do this. Also we are used to work in groups on the Bachelors of law at UCPH, but this was not something I really did during my semester at the University of Mannheim. I do not know if this was due to covid, or just because they do not use it in the courses I attended.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to German Constitutional Law An Introduction to the Law and Legal System of the United States International Arbitration EU Fundamental Rights
recommended_courses: All the courses I followed were really interesting and I would recommend all of them. I think that you really should choose the Constitutional Law course since it makes sense to study the Constitution of Germany now that you are there. It was also super interesting to get an introduction to how things work in the United States also since UCPH doesn't really provide with a similar course. The professor was a lawyer from the US, and she was just straight up cool. The professor in EU Fundamental Rights was one of the most competent people I have ever met. She works for the Commission, and so she has a lot of practical experience. This course also provides you with very different and new knowledge compared to what you get from the mandatory course EU-law at UCPH. I love the area of procedure so International Arbitration was an obvious choice for me. Again the professor was very talented. So, I would really recommend all of them!
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs. And I just want to add that the personal spending was on travling. Furthermore, I normal do not use this many money on food, but I just ate out all the time because it was so cheap!
cost_comparison: I was a little surprise with how cheap food was.
activities_available: The University of Mannheim provides with like 100 different things that you can do! Extremely many sports etc. You could even play quidditch! The gym was available for free, you could do yoga, soccer, running, dancing - like every sport I know (almost) you could do. There were also some different students club, that you could attend.
activities_recommended: I didn't really get to involve that much in student clubs or other sports than the gym, but I would totally recommend you to do that, since it sounded super cool!
weekend_recommendations: Mannheim has the perfect location! You can travel by an ICE train and be in Paris by 3 hours! Other than that there are so many beautiful small cities close to Mannheim like Heidelberg, Weinheim, Karlsruhe and Heppenheim. Also if you have the chance, I would recommend you to travel to Munich (and attend Oktoberfest if possible) and then from there travel to Berchtesgarden - it is close to the boarder of Austria and it is absolutely stunning!
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. Of course there are some differences but the Germans are very kind!
socializing_tips: I shared a flat with a local student, so for me that was kind of easy. But other than that just attend the student clubs or do stuff that the University provides for you. For me I was mostly together with incoming students, so I don't know if I specifically have any tips.
cultural_challenges: I actually did not find anything in relation to the German culture very challenging.
culture_appreciated: Well the Germans are very sweet and helpful!
top3_advice: 1. Make sure to check your e-mail - they provide you with all you need to know there! 2. If possible live in a student accommodation! It is a very easy and cool way to meet knew people! 3. Buy a semesterticket via the University - it is not expensive and you can travel very far with it! (kind of like ungdomskort)
other_useful_info: Not specifically the University, but do not be put off by Germany's slightly old-fashioned way of life. In many places you can only pay with cash, and you have to go down physically and register in the municipality. But it's easy enough once you get used to it.
most_rewarding: It is hard for me to choose. But I would say the academic outcome, the personal outcome and all of the people I met. I have learned so many things about other cultures and I have met the most amazing people. It is very hard to describe in words here, but trust me - it is amazing.
greatest_challenge: For me it was probably adjusting to talk and read in english, but again I think I adjusted kind of fast, so I wouldn't call it a challenge. I'm like an extroverted introvert so I really need my time alone to get some energy for more socializing. However, I also love being with people all the time. So for me it was a little hard to find the balance of really wanna go to hang out with people, but also to be able to make sure that I got the rest that I need.
other_comments: I cannot say how much I recommend going to Mannheim. It is fantastic University, they communicate well and also in english! You are in the heart of southern Germany so it is really easy to travel. Now I know that you also do exchange for the academic outcome, but remember to live and enjoy the fact that you easily and also kind of cheap can travel!
