culture_appreciated: The hospitality and humour.
top3_advice: Pack some warm clothes, lots of money and adjust your expectations to what subjects you are able to attend. Otherwise enjoy the amazing city of Melbourne and the wonderful country Australia.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Unfortunately not the academics, which I had high hopes about. However, I have had some amazing experiences hiking and camping in the beautiful national parks.
greatest_challenge: I didn’t find anything particularly challenging. Maybe communication with family and friends in DK due to the time difference, but this wasn’t even really a problem.
other_comments: Go! You won’t regret it.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a country where I was fluent in a language, so I could fully benefit from the experience. I have been to Australis before but I wanted to experience it as a resident and not just a tourist. Melbourne is very similar to Copenhagen culture with their huge coffee and food-scene, which ultimately drew me there
info_ease: KU is OK at providing the information needed, but you also need to stay alert to make sure there are not any deadlines you are missing. Going on exchange is a ton of ''paperwork''
arrival_assistance: University of Melbourne had an office or ''spot 1'' if you needed information or help, also during your stay, with anything related to the university. The system in regards to applying for different courses was also easy to figure out. However UniMelb is so big that it can get a bit overwhelming - the amount of exchange and international students made the first week of orientation almost disorganized, even though they had put a lot of work into it
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Described above
registration_help: A lot through UniMelb online, Orientation week and also Stop 1, the student office
registration_success: I got into all the classes I registrered for
registration_advice: There is a test period where you can go the different classes to see whether it is something for you. I ended up changing a few of them - so please take advantage of this opportunity!
course_level: I would say that the level at UniMelb was pretty high in general. I could tell the level 1(2) classes were easier than the level 3.
teaching_comparison: Way more active - barely any lectures, a lot of seminars and presentations. The students carried the lectures a lot of the time
courses_enrolled: Islam in the Modern World, Social Problems in Japan, Philosophical Issues: Race and Gender, Gender and Contemporary Culture
recommended_courses: Social Problems in Japan was by far my favorite course! The professor was so enthausiastic and I learned so much during that course (I have previously studied Japanese studies, which was definitely a pro but you can easily follow the course with no previous knowledge to Japan or Japan language/culture)
unexpected_costs: The public transporation in Melbourne is fairly expensive - 5 AUD for a ride, 2.5 AUD if you get the student discount card. Also, travelling around Australia during my stay was more expensive than I thought
cost_comparison: Flights around Australia, public transportation. Rent is also more expensive than in Copenhagen I would say Coffee and food is quite a lot cheaper than in Copenhagen.
activities_available: A lot of different sport-activities but also cultural clubs
activities_recommended: I did not partake in any
weekend_recommendations: Great Ocean Road weekend trip, Noosa, Byron etc Me and a couple of friends did a van trip around WA for 3 weeks, that was the most unique and unforgettable vacation I have ever done
culture_adjustment: Easy, Australian culture is basically just European culture
cultural_challenges: The slang was more difficult that I could have imagined, that took me quite a while to get used to as they use it a lot A LOT
culture_appreciated: The friendliness!! Unlike anything else, my favorite thing about Australia is for sure the people
top3_advice: It is a great campus with a lot of good fascilities, use them - also take advantage of stop 1 if you need help. UniMelb might be a top university, but do not let that scare you. Do the assignments and you will be fine
other_useful_info: GO, it was the best 7 months of my life. I loved UniMelb
most_rewarding: Meeting new friends (for life) and living abroad. Travelling around Australia.
greatest_challenge: The exam period was quite tough, but not unbearable. (I find KU exams tougher)

crucial_aspects: I found that the University I chose had the most interesting subjects of all the places I looked into. Furthermore, I really wanted to live in Australia, so that was a part of my decision as well.
overall_comments: I loved studying abroad, and can recommend it to anyone! I will say though, that it was expensive, and getting funding is not as easy as one might think. I applied for approximately 20 grants and got none of them (might be a me problem, who knows, but it's worth taking into account).
info_ease: It was okay, the University of Melbournes website is a bit confusing, and there's too many portals to navigate in. But once you know where to look, information is easily acquired.
arrival_assistance: The University provided free transportation from the airport upon arrival. You have to order it by email some time in advance, but they drive you all the way to your destination, and you get to meet some other students at the airport which is nice after a long journey.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I loved studying abroad, and can recommend it to anyone! I will say though, that it was expensive, and getting funding is not as easy as one might think. I applied for approximately 20 grants and got none of them (might be a me problem, who knows, but it's worth taking into account).
registration_process: Once you get the confirmation from your home institution, the University does provide you with some video guides on how to register. You register through a portal you probably will never use again. Watch the videos thoroughly, I found that it was a bit of a tedious process, but there is help, so don't wait with all the practicals, get started early on. This will also ease your mind when applying for your visa, as you will need the CoE from the university before you can do that :)
registration_help: You could email the exchange student supervisors, but the University of Melbourne has a huge chunk of exchange students, and the reply time could sometimes reflect that. They do have a ton of video material to guide you, so that is a bonus!
registration_success: I did register into all of the classes I wanted, but only because I took my time getting to know the system of time slots and what nots. It can be a bit confusing to figure out if the classes are at the same time or if you can change the timeslots - sometimes you can, but it depends on the size of the subjects. I found that there was a lot of lectures offered in the faculty of Economics, but not at the faculty of arts.
registration_advice: It is all worth the hassle.
academics_comments: I loved studying abroad, and can recommend it to anyone! I will say though, that it was expensive, and getting funding is not as easy as one might think. I applied for approximately 20 grants and got none of them (might be a me problem, who knows, but it's worth taking into account).
course_level: I took both level 1, 2 and 3 subjects* (they are not called courses, at UniMelb). As a third year student, the level 1 subject was too easy and the level 3 subject was good! The level 1 subject was in the faculty of arts and the level 3 subject was in the faculty of law. My level 2 subjects were both in Econ, and they were challenging.
teaching_comparison: There is mandatory tutorials each week for each study. The grading system is not only based on the exam but also on the tutorial attendance and assignments. There is many assignments, and the mandatory attendance was a stress factor, but the lectures were of such high quality!
courses_enrolled: 1. Introductory Macroeconomics 2. Globalization and the World economy 3. Global Environmental Politics 4. Sustainability: Hope for the Earth?
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Global Environmental Politics. The lecturer is so talented, and the big research essay we got to write (70% of the grade) taught me so much and was really fascinating. If you are interested in climate change and politics, I can't recommend this enough.
unexpected_costs: I had to go to the doctor a few times, and unfortunately also had to go with an ambulance once, and it is expensive. The insurance covers approximately half, but getting medical blood tests etc is very expensive.
cost_comparison: Cafés and restaurants are cheaper than at home, and its great (and so tempting to spend a lot of money all the time). I also bought a bike from Facebook Marketplace and that was super cheap too.
activities_available: They don't really host parties the same way as at KU, but the introduction week is really fun and they have a lot of shenanigans happening. It wasn't really clear if they offered any cultural events that wasn't students rallies (they have a lot of those) - it is a huge campus, and any event hosted by the institution can be a bit overwhelming.
activities_recommended: Again, I would recommend their gym. It's cheaper than the local gyms, and its easy to go directly from lecture to the gym.
weekend_recommendations: I went to Phillip Islands, Great Ocean Road, Tasmania and New Zealand. It was all so so amazing, and I cannot recommend going on trips enough! My roommate had a car I could borrow and did often go on hikes in national parks with my friends - there is a lot of great hiking opportunities in and around Melbourne if your budget is not for the bigger trips.
culture_adjustment: As I got an off campus housing situation, I got a lot of local friends which was really great for my feeling of belonging. There is a great culture for not gatekeeping your friend groups, so if you want to be a part of a friend group it is not impossible :)
socializing_tips: I only have 2 friends from campus, they were both exchange students and we met at an exchange party. It is hard to get friends from campus, but try to connect with someone you like at the tutorials.
cultural_challenges: There isn't many, but the biggest one is that they are way younger at the universities in Australia versus here. I'm 27 and most people I met was 18-20 ish. It's not bad, but it could be a little alienating to be that much older.
culture_appreciated: People are open and easy to talk to!
top3_advice: Buy a bike (and don't be scared to ride it on the left side!) Get an opportunity to buy/rent/borrow a car once in a while to get out of the city hustle. Trust me, you'll need it. Take your time deciding on the right subjects - they have so many but don't let that overwhelm you, if you do your research you will get an opportunity to study such interesting subjects!
other_useful_info: Can't think of any
most_rewarding: The trips I took to the nature sites. It was so amazing to be in such different environments, and go explore all the opportunities to see the Australian wild.
greatest_challenge: Loneliness and anxiety was a big one for me, but the institution provide free professional counseling if you ever feel overwhelmed or alone. I used 4 out of six sessions, and helped me a lot. I know some other students who did the same, and it is really helpful.
other_comments: This is a long survey :)

crucial_aspects: It was many-fold. First and foremost, I wanted to go on exchange in an English speaking country, which reduced the number of options. Secondly, I wanted to visit a country too far away to visit on a smaller vacation. After picking a country I looked for a large city with a good university.
info_ease: Pretty easy. Their student administration Stop 1 works very smoothly.
arrival_assistance: I needed to get a student ID and enroll in other courses than I had initially planned.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You enroll in courses online. It was a bit tiresome as a postgradute student because you have to contact various Lecturers and have them accept that you live up to the course prerequisites.
registration_help: The Unimelb course handbook and Stop 1.
registration_success: Somewhat succesful. I had a lot of overlaps. Luckily, you can change your courses until quite late in the semester.
registration_advice: Enroll in more subjects than 30 ECTS and then go to different courses and check them out.
course_level: The Bachelor's courses very comparable to or easier than Bachelor's courses on UCPH. The Master's/Honor's courses very comparable to or perhaps slightly tougher than similar courses on UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Very comparable. The only difference might be that assignments and mid-semester tests count towards your final grade on Unimelb.
courses_enrolled: Positive Political Economics (ECON40009 or ECON90037) Econometrics of Markets and Competition (ECOM90017) Experimental Economics (ECON30022) Elements of Data Processing (COMP20008)
recommended_courses: I would recommend all my courses except Experimental Economics. Unless you want a very easy, but quite dull course. Teaching was not great either. Positive Political Economics was a tough, but extremely rewarding, theoretical course, but Eik Swee (The lecturer) has a challenging way of teaching, where he forces students to think hard about the questions he put forth before answering them. As Aaron, the Lecturer in Econometrics of Markets and Competition said: you cannot find many courses like this where it is not a PhD course. It had a quite large workload in terms of assignments. But you learn Matlab from scratch and learn how to estimate advanced structurcal models with heterogenous agents. Elements of Data Processing was comparatively easier course if you have any experience using Python. Half of the course was in Machine Learning which was why I picked it.
unexpected_costs: I had to live in a hostel both in the start of and the end of my visit, which costs more per month than the other housing I found.
cost_comparison: Others payed way more for housing than me, but I had an hour of transportation each way to and from Uni.
activities_available: There is a very good fitness on campus, which is cheaper than working out in other gyms in the city.
activities_recommended: Sign up for Foodrelief. It is a program where you can receive free frozen meals once a week.
weekend_recommendations: Plan on spending a month or two before or after the semester where you go travelling. The West Coast, the East Coast, Grampians, Wilsons Prom, Phillip Island, Mornington Peninsula, Great Ocean Road, Uluru (Ayer's Rock)
culture_adjustment: Yes, I mostly spend time with Danish people.
socializing_tips: No. My best guess is that around 80 percent of the students in Economics and Business are Asian people so there is quite a big cultural barrier.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Australians are very relaxed and down to earth. If you have an open mind you can easily end up in a conversation on a bar, café etc.
top3_advice: 1. Save enough money and plan on going travelling before or after the semester. 2. Foodrelief and Fairy Floss Real Estate. 3. Socialise with other Danish people from UCPH after you know where you are going. If you do not link up with locals it provides another nice way of having a semester abroad.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Getting better at English, living in a country far from friends and family.
greatest_challenge: The exam period. Because I did not study that hard during the semester I had a lot of catching up to do.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to and English speaking country as well as a place I'd never been before. Furthermore, I chose University of Melbourne because of its interesting subjects and good reputation.
info_ease: It was pretty easy.
arrival_assistance: None... I accidentally booked the pickup from the airport to the wrong date and was denied access to the vehicle even though my friends that I was going to stay with got in and there were plenty of space.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: When I arrived I went to orientation where I got all of the instructions on how to register properly.
registration_help: Student support worked very well.
registration_success: I registered as soon as the system allowed me to, hence I got all the subjects I wanted with very few clashes.
registration_advice: Do it as soon as possible and plan from home. Also have a few back-ups approved from both University of Copenhagen and University of Melbourne. I ended of changing one of mine after classes started as I did not like the one I originally chose. It was very easy because I had gotten my back-up approved beforehand.
course_level: I did one first year as my "for fun" elective (Australia in the Wine World). Two second year subjects and one third year. The subjects were definitely not too hard - nor too easy.
teaching_comparison: At University of Melbourne they gave me a lot of tests and other assignments to complete during the semester. These accounted for part of my final grade. I really liked this style of teaching as it took part of the pressure away from the final exams.
courses_enrolled: Australia in the Wine World (AGRI10039) Pharmacology: How Drugs Work Stem Cells in Development and Regeneration Plant Biodiversity
recommended_courses: I would in particular recommend Stem Cells in Development and Regeneration if you are interested in Stem Cells. It is a very interesting and well structured subject that gives both a lot of information about the basics and the newer research within the stem cell field. I also really liked Plant Biodiversity as it gave a good insight in Australia's flora. Australia in the Wine World was also a lot of fun with weekly wine tastings and lectures.
unexpected_costs: I had to buy my own Pans, pots, duvet, pillow etc on my student accommodation.
cost_comparison: Food was a bit more expensive than expected. But I didn't have to buy any books for university.
activities_available: There a so many clubs and societies. Sports, languages, food, arts, and music just to name some.
activities_recommended: I joined the Sexpression and the Swifties societies. They were a lot of fun to be part of. I also joined the gym.
weekend_recommendations: Great Ocean Road, Dandenong Ranges, Phillip Island, Grampians, wine districts (all for a day- or weekend trip). Sydney, Brisbane, Tasmania, Gold Coast are for holidays.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. There are also a lot of other exchange students from all over the world.
socializing_tips: Go to unimelb's events for exchange student, attend orientation week, and if you live a Unilodge Lincoln House then go so some of their events too.
cultural_challenges: None in particular. The Australians are not that different from Danes and they are very nice and welcoming people.
culture_appreciated: People are very easy to talk to and will help you with anything if needed.
top3_advice: Make sure to travel around and see some of Australia's nature - also during the weekend. Plan which subjects you want to enroll in before you go. Go the the socializing events in the start of the semester.
other_useful_info: I can't think of anything.
most_rewarding: Making new friends and traveling Australia and New Zealand.
greatest_challenge: The exam period was pretty though as I had three exams in three days.

crucial_aspects: Choosing a destination where english was the main language spoken. Plus good options to travel and exploring while studying.
info_ease: Fairly easy. UniMelb has a pretty good step by step guide to prepare you and their website is quite straight forward/easy to navigate. The only thing I struggled a bit with was figuring out their time tabling system regarding classes.
arrival_assistance: Stop 1 is really good to help you with anything university related. They can be a bit slow to answer e-mails, but you can also just show up upon arrival and someone will be able to help you with whatever you need.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Just follow their step by step guide and everything should be good
registration_help: Stop 1
registration_success: As mentioned above, I did have a few technical issues but Stop 1 helped to sort it out. However, when applying for tutorial times don't get surprised it you don't get allocated to the the ones you wished for. All my tutorial timeslots ended up being changed anyways, and you can always change around - even after the semester has started.
registration_advice: Use the handbook when navigating subjects, and maybe try and avoid subjects with mandatory attendance. At least I found that a bit annoying.
course_level: The level was way below University of Copenhagen, both at BA and MA. I discovered that a lot of the business and economics related subjects had a very high percentage of students from Asia, who didn't really speak english that well. Unfortunately, this really affected the level of teaching as class discussions or group work was either impossible or very awkward.
teaching_comparison: Pretty much the same with a mix of lectures and tutorials. However, the exam style was quite different as you had to turn in assignments all throughout the semester which would then make up your final grade.
courses_enrolled: Public Relations and Communications, Politics and the Media, Campaigns and Elections + Public Policy Lobbying Strategies
recommended_courses: Public Policy Lobbying Strategies was a really interesting as it was a bit more hands on compared to courses at UCPH and the teaching staff were just amazing.
unexpected_costs: When moving in to 'The Lofts' the apartment was almost completely empty so we had to buy bedding and kitchen stuff. You could also buy a package in advance but it was a bit expensive (2000 DKK) and much cheaper to just go to Kmart upon arrival.
cost_comparison: It was a bit cheaper to dine out compared to Copenhagen. However, in the grocery stores fruits and vegetables were quite expensive as well as dairy products such as cheese and yoghurt. I great tip saving tip is using 'Union Mart' on campus where you can access free groceries, and they also host events multiple times a week with free food/meals on campus. You can check out their instagram on @umsu_welfare.
activities_available: There were a lot of clubs at uni, and you can meet them all during O-week.
activities_recommended: I personally didn't join any, but did go to the pub crawl hosted by the surf club which I highly recommend, it was so much fun. It definitely seemed like a very social club with lots of parties if you're into that.
weekend_recommendations: There is so much do, but some of my personal highlight were Tasmania and Great Ocean Road + Grampians. But remember to get an international drivers license so you can go on roadtrips!!!
culture_adjustment: Easy, Melbourne feels quite European
socializing_tips: Honestly, I didn't really make any local friends. But maybe through some of the clubs???
cultural_challenges: All the coffee shops close really early, like 2 or 3 pm. Maybe not the biggest thing, but I did find it quite annoying.
culture_appreciated: Aussies are quite outgoing
top3_advice: Just do it!!!
most_rewarding: Getting to experience living in another country
greatest_challenge: All the time and planning that goes into it beforehand. But it is all worth it in the end.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to Australia because I wanted to attend a university with an international environment and the semesters in Australia often started in February which meant I had good time after my exams in Denmark to go to Australia.
info_ease: There is a lot of information and it is not always easy to find - and sometimes you don't even know that you should look for it. However, I find that University of Melbourne was really helpful and responded quickly to any questions.
arrival_assistance: University of Melbourne held a pre-departure meeting where they told a lot of practical information. They also have a free airport pick-up which is nice to know about.
arrival_comments: OSHC was a bit confusing but ended up working out fine.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It is a bit confusing since you first apply for the classes you want to take and then a few weeks after you have to apply for the specific time you want to join the class. Most of my classes only had one option whereas others could decide between different times to have their classes. However, you can switch classes in the first 2 weeks of semester if you don't like the class (and there is an available spot in another class) which I thought was really nice.
registration_help: Their Study Abroad team was very helpful.
registration_success: I got all I wanted.
registration_advice: Know the dates for when to apply for classes and when to choose the specific time you want to attend class.
course_level: I took four MA courses. I mostly took classes in International Relations, and they were less theory-heavy than at UCPH. It is probably due to the fact that people studying a MA in IR doesn't need to hold a BA in IR.
teaching_comparison: Some classes were more discussion-based but otherwise it was a combination of a quick lecture in the beginning and then discussions afterwards.
courses_enrolled: SOCI90026: Social Policy and Urban Problems POLS90065: Cyberpolitics in International Relations POLS90051: Technology and Power in World Politics POLS90050: Terrorism and Insurgency
recommended_courses: I would recommend 'Technology and Power in World Politics' with Daniel McCarthy. Daniel is such a good teacher and I learned so much from the class.
unexpected_costs: To get your student visa, you have to pay for an OSHC which is a medical health insurance. However, I also payed to have a Danish travel insurance and therefore my expenses for insurance is quite high. However, I did have an accident where it was nice to have the Danish travel insurance to help with the process.
cost_comparison: Generally Australia is quite expensive so I ended up using a bit more than I expected.
activities_available: Anything from different sports to book club etc. There is also a surf society that hosts three surfing camps per semester.
activities_recommended: In orientation week there will be some days where you can meet the different sports clubs and organisations and I would recommend to just walk around and have a chat with them and try out what you like.
weekend_recommendations: Explore Melbourne and Victoria and also the rest of Australia - but remember that Australia is really big, so it might be a good idea to do some research on what you really want to see, because time and money flies. I really enjoyed exploring Tasmania and Western Australia.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Just start a conversation, they are very open.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and openness.
top3_advice: 1) Remember that Melbourne weather can get quite cold during autumn and winter. Bring warm clothes! 2) Check up on what happens in the city; there is always something going on. Night markets at Queen Victoria Market, exhibitions etc. 3) Enjoy it!
other_useful_info: Enjoy it and be openminded.
most_rewarding: Living in a new country.
greatest_challenge: The time difference to Denmark. It was hard sometimes to plan times to talk with friends and family back home.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an English speaking country to enhance my English skills as much as possible. I also wanted a renowned university and to be able to study subjects which interested me.
overall_comments: I really liked Australia and Melbourne Law School. Great School, great country.
info_ease: The University sent plenty of information regarding arrival, pick-up from airport and commencement of academic year.
arrival_assistance: I receive help in choosing my subjects and organising my timetable.
arrival_comments: The University of Melbourne 'Stop 1' service is incredible.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I really liked Australia and Melbourne Law School. Great School, great country.
registration_process: Uploading a lot of documentation. Filling out a lot of forms.
registration_help: Calling the uni. Watching online guides from the uni. Reading guides sent by the uni.
registration_success: Not very succesful. I ended up with some of the subjects that I really wanted and some subjects that I really didn't want. I applied early, but the approval of my subjects took a while and when I finally received the approval the class was full.
registration_advice: Calm down when at home in Dk. The help at Stop 1 is incredible and they will help you fix everything.
academics_comments: I really liked Australia and Melbourne Law School. Great School, great country.
course_level: Three undergrad subjects and one graduate subject. The Melbourne JD is very difficult so I would not recommend only taking grad-subjects.
teaching_comparison: Quite similar.
courses_enrolled: Principles of Business Law Intellectual Property Law Legal Language Family Law
recommended_courses: Family Law.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Mandatory BUPA insurance.
activities_available: Over a hundred clubs and sports clubs. I joined a few clubs and found it very easy and nice.
activities_recommended: Book-club. Feminist and queer collective.
weekend_recommendations: Go out. Melbourne has a great night life. See a footy-game. Go skydiving.
culture_adjustment: Easy. Australians are nice.
socializing_tips: Join clubs!!
cultural_challenges: none.
culture_appreciated: Humor is similar to the Danish.
top3_advice: Utilize the UMSU. Go out. Enjoy the campus.
other_useful_info: Not really
most_rewarding: Everything.
greatest_challenge: Exams in a very different way than what I am used to. Huge hall with 3000 people at once. Strict rules.

crucial_aspects: To experience and explore a place I normally wouldn't have the opportunity to
info_ease: Would make more sense to have this question asked earlier in the process since it's been so long since I applied now. I remember most of it to be easy, but there definitely also were some stuff that weren't as clear.
arrival_assistance: An orientation week, I guess.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Again, can't remember it that well anymore. But there were a specific time frame where you had to enroll and you had to make a prioritized list over the courses you would like to enroll in and which days you would like your tutorials to be.
registration_help: You could e-mail the university questions which I did at one point as I wasn't sure about something with the dates.
registration_success: I got all the classes I asked for. I was less lucky with the days I wanted but it was possible to change this in the start of the semester.
registration_advice: Just to do your research.
course_level: I think the academic level is higher back home or at least done very differently. There is a lot more focus on theory and it's more academic in Denmark than here. I did do some courses that are quite different to the ones I have at home, so those might have been a bit harder for me to navigate in but not necessarily because I think the level was high - just that it was different from what I am used to.
teaching_comparison: Again, less theory. For all of my classes I would have one tutorial and one lecture for each course. The lecture would just be us listening to the lecturer, whereas the tutorials would have less people and most of the times, you would have to work on some small tasks and talk. However, it differed a lot from each tutorial depending on the subject how much engagement you would have to participate in.
courses_enrolled: Text and Audio Journalism Visual Communication and Digital Media Crime and Culture Popular Culture: From K-Pop to Selfies
recommended_courses: I personally especially liked Text and Audio Journalism as it was very practical and the learning style was different in a good way. The assignments were creative and fun as well.
unexpected_costs: Maybe how empty the rooms are and how much you need to buy yourself for the kitchen etc.
cost_comparison: Groceries and housing are really expensive. I pay 1/3 at home for my own 1-bedroom student apartment and here I live with four other people as well.
activities_available: There are a lot of different clubs. Some have to do with where you're from - however, it was mostly clubs for different Asian countries. (none for Northern Europe). Different sports, both basics like football but also bush walking and diving.
activities_recommended: If you leave in one of the student accommodation, I would definitely recommend to do the free and social activities provided here. You pay a lot of money to live here, so you might as well and it's also a good way to meet people. Sometimes there will also be free food involved, so it might also be a good way to sometimes save a little money.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely to go and explore other parts of Australia. If you're in Melbourne/Victoria, then do the the great ocean road tour. There are also a lot of nice markets here as well.
culture_adjustment: Very easy - it's quite similar to our culture at home.
socializing_tips: I think it's hard to socialize with the locals as you're mostly around other exchange or international students. I personally would've loved to meet more locals, than what I did.
cultural_challenges: None, I think.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness of the Australian people. Also interesting to learn more about Australian history and the indigenous people, especially.
top3_advice: Be open and participate in the free activities. Use your time well, Australia is a very big country so you unfortunately won't be able to experience everything. Remember to enjoy yourself and your time here!
other_useful_info: Maybe be prepared that a lot of people might be younger than you, especially if you're a bit older yourself when doing the BA. I am 25 myself and were living with mainly 18-19 year olds, which sometimes can be a bit tough. They are all very lovely people - however, I find that I am in a different place in my life than most as they for instance have never tried to live by themselves before etc. I was expecting to be older than most, but I didn't expect people here to be that young.
most_rewarding: Getting to travel and explore Australia. Also, it's definitely a good life experience to be on your own so far away from everything and everyone you know. I have found myself doing a lot of things that I probably would've been to scared to do normally. You get more adventurous.
greatest_challenge: Maybe to plan your time here and navigate between travelling, socializing and your studies.

crucial_aspects: Australia is so far away from Denmark, so wanted to explore it and see all the stuff there.
info_ease: Would say it was easy enough.
arrival_assistance: Did not really require anything, but otherwise I could just have went by Stop1 at the campus.
arrival_comments: The orientation is a little bit lacking, so you have to do most of the work yourself regarding getting friends and such. You are basically just invited to show up to get a water bottle and a grilled sausage on white toast..
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Was quite easy, had to submit a study plan regarding which subjects I wanted to take and the academic requirements.
registration_help: Don't know - did not need it.
registration_success: Yes got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: You can switch subjects in the first two weeks of the semester, so if you discover some subjects are bad, then you can switch them.
course_level: 3 of my subjects were extremely easy and 1 of my subjects was quite hard.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was generally quite bad compared to UCPH, with exams just being pure memorization and lectures just being lecturers reading from slides for 3 hours..
courses_enrolled: Derivatives Securities Applied Risk Management Quantitative Analysis for Finance II Macroeconometrics
recommended_courses: Derivatives Securities: It was an extremely easy and boring version of Financial Decision Making; I can only recommend it if you want an easy subject during your exchange semester, as you do not need to study at all or follow the lectures to pass. You also need to buy a calculator. Applied Risk Management: Was close to being the most boring subject I have ever had, as the lecturers just consisted of the lecturer reading the slides for 2-3 hours. The exam was basically doing Excel calculations by hand with a calculator, so you need to buy a calculator. I cannot really recommend it. Quantitative Analysis for Finance II: The material itself should be quite interesting, but the lecturer was garbage, as he was using a previous lecturer's material and slides, but he did not understand anything about it, so any single time he was asked questions, he said it would get back to us, which he did not. It consists of three easy online tests on Canvas and then one final written research paper, so if you want to have one less exam, then go for it. Macroeconometrics: is an extremely interesting and hard subject covering Bayesian econometrics in macroeconometrics and is basically a combination of a seminar in macro, the advanced macroeconometrics subject at UCPH, and a subject in Bayesian Econometrics. I required a constant high workload and would easily say that 95% of my studies at Melbourne were spent on this subject. The lecturer, Tomasz Wozniak, is quite entertaining and good, but he also demands quite a lot. I can recommend this subject if you want to challenge yourself during your exchange, but otherwise, do not consider this subject at all. It is quite hard and takes so much time.
unexpected_costs: Not sure if I encountered any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Alcohol is so expensive, except from wine, so it is not that fun looking at your bank account day after a pub crawl.
activities_available: Basically anything you can imagine, there was a whole week of clubs expo at campus, where you can meet all the clubs.
activities_recommended: Surfing club: they are so fun and hold a bunch of events Mountaneering club: You get a discount in outdoor shops if you join. Social running club: Free coffee after a 3km run each friday. Soccer club: Playing soccer with other international and some locals every saturday.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking in Victoria, travelling around in Australia. Go to Tasmania, Northern Queensland and go scuba diving at the Great Barrier Reef. Go to Sydney. Also head out to the outback and see Uluru, but there is no reason to be more 1 day at Uluru. Go surfing down in Torquay, head to Wilsons Prom. Great Ocean Road
culture_adjustment: The student life is a bit weird as there is a clear divide between the domestic and international students, but the aussies are cool.
socializing_tips: It can be a bit hard to socialize with the local students, because you can easily have classes, where there are no australians and you are the only non-asian student. There are also not any student bars at campus, so you kinda have to show up to club events and such to find australians, but they are easy enough to become friends with if you manage to find them.
cultural_challenges: Australians are very friendly, but a lot of students at Uni Melb are not that social or outgoing, so can be a bit hard to get friends if you don't show up to everything.
culture_appreciated: The politeness and general niceness.
top3_advice: Live close to campus so you can attend events there. Travel a lot. Join clubs.
other_useful_info: Have a driver's license or prepare to find some friends, who will drive you around. :)
most_rewarding: Getting so many new friends and exploring and doing so much new stuff. Hiked so much on so many great trails. Took a Scuba diving certificate at the Great Barrier Reef, which was so worth it.
greatest_challenge: Being in a completely foreign country with no friends can be a bit hard when you just arrive.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go outside of Europe and preferably to an English-speaking country.
info_ease: University of Melbourne has an airport pickup service free of charge, but you must sign up for it around three days before you need it. Additionally, there is an orientation week which is quite nice, however it can be a bit hard to figure out which subjects to take in the beginning and which of them fit together in the timetable. housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_help: Stop1

teaching_comparison: The assessment happens a lot more throughout the semester as opposed to UCPH where the final exam accounts for the entire grade. There are more small assignments as well as midterms.
courses_enrolled: Australia in the Wine World Stem Cells in Development and Regeneration Microbes, Infections and Responses Performance, Potential and Development
recommended_courses: Australia in the Wine World was quite fun and with weekly wine tastings. Stem Cells in Development and Regeneration was very interesting and I really enjoyed it. Microbes, Infections and Responses was less of an immunology subject than I expected. It was mostly about different pathogens and their mechanisms. Performance, Potential and Development was quite easy going and only had two hours of teaching a week.
unexpected_costs: To study at UniMelB you need an overseas healthcover insurance.
cost_comparison: Housing was very expensive, but coffee is cheap ;)
activities_available: There were so many different societies.
weekend_recommendations: Rent a car and drive to Wilsons Promontory National Park, it is absolutely stunning. We had six days off at some point and flew to Tasmania, I really recommend doing that as well. You can also drive on Great Ocean Road and combine it with a trip to the Grampians or take a short trip to Sydney. The possibilities are almost endless. A day trip to Phillip Island is also great.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, the culture is not that different from our own.
socializing_tips: Talk to people in your classes and join a society.
top3_advice: Look forward to it, you are going to have an amazing time and the time will fly by way too fast. Get started early on with the weekend trips or you won’t be able to do all of them.
most_rewarding: It was all really great.
greatest_challenge: The time difference to the people back home was sometimes a challenge.

crucial_aspects: It was important that the destination was vastly different than Denmark, preferably both in culture and nature. It is a plus that the education is in english as it made learning and communication easier. That the destination had a good study culture, and a good university
info_ease: Fairly easy. As soon as you were on campus everything was much easier than online
arrival_assistance: Their help center (STOP 1) was always good at troubleshooting, and helped me with my health insurrance
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It is a bit overwhelming trying to find the right information on their website, and which subjects i could enroll in

registration_success: It is hard to expect which subjects are good. I ended up changing some after some time. When you get to the campus it is easier to get a feel for the subjects.

cultural_challenges: not any really

crucial_aspects: Det var vigtigt for mig at komme på udveksling i et engelsktalende land. Derudover valgte jeg efter at kunne opleve noget helt andet og kunne rejse rundt steder, som man ellers ikke lige kommer forbi.
overall_comments: At tage på udveksling er en ret unik mulighed, og jeg vil, ligesom de fleste andre, anbefale alle at tage af sted!! Når man er kommet over alt det administrative op til afrejse, som godt kan virke lidt overskueligt, så er det virkelig virkelig fedt.
info_ease: UniMleb bruger mange ressourcer på deres internationale studerende, og de har en service (Stop 1), som man kan skrive til om alt, hvad man er i tvivl om. Ansøgningsprocessen til UniMelb er lidt lang med mange informationer der skal udfyldes, men her er de en god hjælp.
arrival_assistance: Vi fik mails fra universitetet med alle de informationer vi skulle bruge frem mod studiestarten og orientation week. Der kunne godt have været mere info om de sociale arrangementer, da der er ret mange, og det er svært at gennemskue hvilke der er arrangeret af UniMelb, og hvilke der er arrangeret af forskellige foreninger på uni.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: At tage på udveksling er en ret unik mulighed, og jeg vil, ligesom de fleste andre, anbefale alle at tage af sted!! Når man er kommet over alt det administrative op til afrejse, som godt kan virke lidt overskueligt, så er det virkelig virkelig fedt.
registration_process: I første omgang skulle man lave en liste i excel med de fag man ønskede at tage. Derefter ansøgte man endeligt om 4 af dem.
registration_help: Hvis der var problemer, var Stop1 ret tilgængelige til at hjælpe.
registration_success: Vi oplevede, at nogle fag ikke blev oprettet på vores semester, men ud af de fag, som reelt blev oprettet, fik jeg de 4 fag, jeg havde søgt.
registration_advice: Vær ude i god tid med at ansøge om fag på UniMelb, hvis du søger postgraduate subjects. Postgraduate fagene har limits på antal studerende, så de fag bliver hurtigere optaget end undergrad fag.
academics_comments: At tage på udveksling er en ret unik mulighed, og jeg vil, ligesom de fleste andre, anbefale alle at tage af sted!! Når man er kommet over alt det administrative op til afrejse, som godt kan virke lidt overskueligt, så er det virkelig virkelig fedt.
course_level: Jeg havde udelukkende undergrad subjects, så niveauet svarede nok til begyndelsen af bacheloren i jura.
teaching_comparison: Jeg oplevede, at der blev brugt mere tid på diskussioner i tutorials (holdundervisning), og samtidig var underviserne meget tilgængelige til at svare på spørgsmål mv, hvis man skulle have brug for det. Det varierede selvfølgelig alt efter hvilket fag, men fx Legal Language var meget diskussionspræget.
courses_enrolled: Legal Language, Intellectual Property Law, Principles of Business Law, Corporate Law.
recommended_courses: Legal Language var et nemt fag, men ikke super interessant. Det omhandlede samspillet mellem jura og litteratur og havde intet med egentlig jura at gøre, som vi kender det derhjemme. Eksamen var et essay, hvor man skulle diskutere nogle af fagets emner, så det var meget abstrakt ift. hvad vi er vant til, men nemt at komme igennem. Intellectual Property Law mindede meget om informationsret på KU's bachelor, og her var det mere spændende at kunne sammenligne regler og lovgivning på tværs af retssystemer. Principles of Business Law var helt basic forståelse for aftaleret, kontraktsret, erstatningsret, forbrugerret mv. Hele faget foregår online, men eksamen er fysisk (!) i juni. Det meste er multiple choice, så ret nemt. Corporate Law er en overbygning af PBL, så der forventes en smule mere. Det var også et interessant fag ift., at sammenlignedansk selskabsret med det australske system. Jeg ville anbefale alle undtagen Legal Language.
unexpected_costs: Australien kræver at man køber en sundhedsforsikring (OSCH), som cirka koster 2300 kr. Derudover koster student visa cirka 3250 kr. Jeg købte ikke lærebøger, fordi man kunne klare sig med online versioner eller uden, så det var forventet udgift jeg ikke skulle afholde.
cost_comparison: At handle ind er ligesom i Danmark, men at spise ude er lidt billigere og kaffe er ret billigt (cirka 5 AUD for god kaffe). At rejse rundt er lidt dyrt (særligt hvis man er vant til Asien fx), men det hele værd.
activities_available: Der er alverdens klubber: surfclub (hvor man mest bare drikker goon og fester), mountaineering club, alle sportsklubber (kampsport, volley, fodbold, atletik mv), underwater club (SCUBA dykning, hvor man også kan tage certifikatet ret billigt), vinklub (der tager på vinturer og holder fester), skiklub mv.
activities_recommended: Join de klubber som du synes kunne være fede at få et fællesskab i. Følg GSA og UMSU på SoMe, da de afholder mange små arrangementer på uni i løbet af semestret.
weekend_recommendations: Tag på roadtrips ud fra Melbourne, fx hikes (Wilsons Prom og Dandenong Ranges), se strandene ved Mornington Peninsula, tag på vintur i Yarra Valley, se Great Ocean Road mv. Rejs rundt i Australien når vejret bliver koldt i Melbourne. Se og oplev Melbournes forstæder, der har så mange små cafeer, butikker mv.
culture_adjustment: Det var ret nemt, da der ikke er så mange forskelle. Jeg tror dog de fleste vil opleve lidt hjemve i starten, men når man først får opbygget en hverdag, så er det hele nemmere.
socializing_tips: Join foreninger på uni, da det ofte er lokale studerende, der står for dem.
cultural_challenges: Den eneste må være, at australiere er mere afslappede og fx går i et heelt andet tempo på gaden, som godt kan virke lidt stressende, når man er vant til tempoet i København, men sikkert er meget sundt at adapte til.
culture_appreciated: At australiere er mere åbne og snaksaglige end man er vant til i Danmark.
top3_advice: Deltag i så mange arrangementer som man orker i starten. Rejs så meget, som dit budget tillader.
other_useful_info: Husk trøjer og en jakke til om vinteren, det bliver koldere end man lige forventer. Og en adapter til stikkontakter og evt. en dansk forlængerledning, hvis du bruger mange strømstik normalt :)
most_rewarding: Jeg har mødt en masse nye mennesker, fået en masse oplevelser, rejst, fundet ud af at man godt kan bygge et liv op i en by på den anden side af jorden og få en hverdag der, og lært en masse om andre kulturer og om mig selv.
greatest_challenge: At omstille sig til en ny hverdag i en helt fremmed by uden venner, familie og arbejde. Men det er samtidig også noget af det fedeste ved udveksling at prøve at have en hverdag uden de forpligtelser man har derhjemme, og hvor man kan planlægge præcis det man har lyst til fra dag til dag.

crucial_aspects: The most important aspects in my choice of study destination were the quality of education, the relevance of the program to future career goals, campus facilities and location, and cultural and social opportunities.
info_ease: I feel it was quite easy to find the information I needed
arrival_assistance: I only got help with some small things through the university
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process at my host institution was straightforward. First, I had to fill out an online application form and submit the necessary documents, such as proof of previous education and passport details. After receiving an acceptance, I was given access to the institution's portal where I could register for courses. Upon arrival on campus, I attended an introduction day where we received further information and help with any remaining formalities.
registration_help: There were different kinds of help available. For example, IT support was available to ensure we could use the institution's online systems correctly. Help was also available to switch courses.
registration_success: I was very successful in registering for the classes I wanted. I got a seat in all the courses I wanted without any problems.
registration_advice: Start early
course_level: The level of the courses was very appropriate. There was a good balance between theoretical teaching and practical applications. The professors were competent and committed, and there were good opportunities to get extra help and guidance if needed.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was different as there was more participation from the students and a greater focus on discussion in class. There was also not a final exam, but instead several ongoing assignments that all counted towards the final assessment
courses_enrolled: Gender and Health Mental Health Sustainability and Healthcare Health Policy
recommended_courses: I can recommend all four courses
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs during my stay.
cost_comparison: During my exchange, I found that many groceries were more expensive than expected. On the other hand, it was often cheaper to go out and eat, both in restaurants and cafes. Public transportation was also significantly cheaper than I expected.
activities_available: My host institution offered a wide range of cultural, sporting and social activities for students. There were a lot of different clubs to join (diving club, surf club and many others)
activities_recommended: I would recommend future exchange students to participate in the social and cultural activities. It's a great way to integrate into the local study environment and get to know new people across cultures.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend other students to take advantage of the opportunity to explore the destination and other nearby places during weekends and vacations.
culture_adjustment: It was relatively easy to adapt to the local culture. I found that people were welcoming and open to international students, which made it easier to feel welcome. There were also a lot of other exchange students
cultural_challenges: Time differences can be a challenge at first, but it's something you get used to quickly.
culture_appreciated: I particularly appreciated the rich cultural history during my exchange. Learning about the history behind local traditions, indigenous people and historical sites was a great experience. It gave me a deeper understanding of the development of society
top3_advice: 1. Be open to new cultural norms, traditions and ways of interacting. 2. Get involved in social and academic activities on campus. It's a great way to meet new people and make friends 3. Take the opportunity to explore and learn more about the country and region where your host institution is located.
other_useful_info: Try to find out about accommodation options in advance. Sometimes it can be difficult and stressful to find accommodation when you arrive.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the personal growth and new perspectives I gained. Living and studying in a foreign culture broadened my horizons and strengthened my ability to adapt to different situations.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge during the exchange was adapting to a new culture and creating an everyday life in a foreign country

courses_enrolled: COMP90086 - Computer Vision ECON90080 - Macroeconomics PPMN90056 - Business and Government POLS90034 - International Policymaking in Practice
recommended_courses: Computer vision was quite interesting but covered a range of topics beyond machine learning. The class on advanced macroeconomics was taught based on a 1998 book. The content felt outdated and the enthusiasm of the professor felt a bit limited but it was still a relevant introduction to advanced macroeconomic modelling with microfoundations. Business and government was a highly disappointing class. The teacher, Valarie Sands, seemed not very knowledgeable of the topic and lacked the ability to convey knowledge in an interesting way. culture_adjustment: Quite easy. Aussies are friendly and open.
socializing_tips: Join a club
cultural_challenges: In many of my classes there were many students from overseas. I experienced that there was a language barrier and different cultural expectations around some groupwork in some of my classes.
culture_appreciated: Melbourne has a lot to offer. There are many cool little cafés and spots all around town to explore.
top3_advice: I'd recommend finding off-campus housing. It's cheaper to find a sharehouse and it's a great opportunity to stay with some locals in a sharehouse.
other_useful_info: Course enrollment is frustrating and you might not get into the courses you would like to - particularly as an interdisciplinary SDS student. other_comments: I have had a previous stay abroad in Canada at the University of Toronto and got the impression that the quality of teaching at North American universities is significantly higher than in Australia.

crucial_aspects: I considered several aspects of the destination including the culture in the country, the quality of my program at the university, my interest in the available subjects, and the size of the international and exchange community at the university/ in the city.
info_ease: The University of Melbourne has a lot of online resources for exchange students, which made it easy to access any information I needed before and upon my arrival. They also had an orientation scheduled for all new exchange students with all the information we needed. It's also possible to show up in person at Stop 1 for personal assistance.
arrival_assistance: I had to visit stop 1 for help regestering in one of my subjects. I had problems with assigning myself to the subject as it requires a prerequisite and my documentation for the prerequisite had to be approved by the course coordinator. I had uploaded it in my initial application to the university, and then the university was supposed to get the approval for me. However, they had not gotten it before I arrived, but made sure I got it after I contacted them at Stop 1. It took some time, but it got sorted out eventually.
arrival_comments: I would advice anyone going to University of Melbourne to not hesitate contacting stop 1 for help.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I was easy as the university made a guideline on how to register.
registration_help: You could make an online request for help or show up at stop 1.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. They often offer more than class within each subject, but I managed to get both classes on campus and at the times I wanted.
registration_advice: Don't hesitate to ask for help at Stop 1.
course_level: In my experience the classes are overall easier than I'm used to at home. It differs from subject to subject, but it is definitely easier to achieve a good grade with less effort. That said I definitely felt like I learned something in my classes.
teaching_comparison: Every professor have their own style of teaching just like at home, and some styles of teaching suits me better than others, just like at home. The biggest differences was the structure of the grading, as we are used to one final exam at the end of the year, whereas at UniMelb I had at least two assignments in each subject that counted towards my final grade. In some of my classes I also had group presentations that were graded. The experience of working in groups was very different from what I'm used to. It felt more like individual work that we collected into a group presentation, rather than a group effort. Furthermore, we were assigned groups and didn't have any say about who we wanted to work with. Even though it's more time consuming, I definitely prefer doing group work the way I'm used to from home, as I learn more that way and the result is better.
courses_enrolled: Bioethics in Practice Infectious Disease Epidemiology Gender & Health Nutrition Politics and Policy
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed both Bioethics in Practice and Infectious Disease Epidemiology. We only get a brief introduction to ethics in our program at home, and I think it's really interesting to learn how to apply ethics in practice. I really liked the professor and there was a nice dynamic in the classroom, with many great discussions throughout the semester. I enjoyed Infectious Disease Epidemiology as it was nice to dive into a specific branch of epidemiology. The professor was also really good, the class material was really interesting and this was definitely the subject where I learned the most.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: I spend a lot more on groceries than I'm used to at home, and I spend more money eating out than I usually do. Some items are more expensive than in Denmark, while some are less expensive.
activities_available: It seams like there is something for everyone. They have a list on their website.
activities_recommended: There are many free or low-cost activities and events around the city all year around, but especially in the summer, such as free concerts, free festivals, and night markets. Make sure to do some research and use the city as much as you can. I would also recomend to travel either on longer trips, weekend trips, or day trips. There are many beautiful places in Australia. For most of them I would recomend renting a car, so make sure to get an international drivers licence before leaving for Australia.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the national parks all around Australia, for a weekend trip 'the Grampians' or Phillip Island is very nice. Take the train to the beaches, go to museum (many are free), see the city from the Skydeck, go to Queen Victoria Market (or night market), explore Fitzroy, Carlton, or Brunswich. Go to Fitzroy market in weekends, and go for coffee often - it's good and cheap.
culture_adjustment: Melbourne is the most 'European' city in Australia and is full of international students. It always takes some time to adjust to a new place, but overall it was easy for me to adjust and I felt comfortable and at home in Melbourne.
cultural_challenges: NA.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness of the people in Australia and the laid back feeling.
top3_advice: - Remember to enjoy the city and travel as much as you can - Ask if you have any questions, there are plenty of resources at uni to help you - Get some friends who are also on exchange, as they are at the same situation as you
other_useful_info: All of the above.
most_rewarding: The people I met was the best part, as they contributed to makinng the experience even better.
greatest_challenge: Getting settled in a new routine in my new soroundings

crucial_aspects: First of all, I wanted to go an English-speaking country. I also wanted to go outside of Europe, and I have always wanted to go to Australia. I had heard really good things about Melbourne and UniMelb from previous students, which is why my choice ended on Melbourne.
info_ease: I don't really remember any big issues, so it was probably pretty straight forward to find most of the information needed.
arrival_assistance: UniMelb offered free transportation from the airport to your desired address in Melbourne. You just had to sign up (I think it was 48 hours) before the pick up.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Pretty straight forward. The registration website was running really slow so it took forever, but other than that, pretty easy.
registration_help: Not really sure, didn't really use any help.
registration_success: I ended up getting all the classes I wanted. If one of your classes is full, you can just keep an eye on it, since people back out/change their classes before the semester starts.
registration_advice: Do it at some point where you have plenty of time for it.
course_level: I took two level 1 courses and two level 3 courses. I found the level 3 classes to be a little bit easier the than level of KU courses. The level 1 courses was pretty easy too.
teaching_comparison: The courses consist of lectures, classes and practicals like they also do at KU. The exams are broken up into different assessments during the semester, which all count towards your grade, instead of having one final exam. Also UniMelb records all of the lectures, so you can either watch them live from home or watch them later. Really nice if you want to go on weekend trips or if you have overlapping courses.
courses_enrolled: Developmental Neurobiology (NEUR30005) Stem Cells in Development & Regeneration (CEDB30004) The History of Cool: Fashion & Attitude (DPSS10007) Australia in the Wine World (AGRI10039)
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed and would recommend all of my courses. Developmental Neurobiology was pretty straight forward and not so electrochemistry heavy, but more biology focused which was really nice. I found it very interesting and learned a lot from it. Stem cells was really cool, where we learned a lot about the current techniques and where we are in the field today. Some stuff also overlapped with what I had learned in developmental neurobiology, so the two courses went pretty good together. The history of cool is a really fun subject, and something completely different from what I'm used to. It is an online course, but it only has one lecture + one tutorial a week, so it was not an issue for me. Very easy course, and it does not have a final exam (you just hand in a final assignment). That was super nice, so I had more time to focus on studying for the exams for the other subjects. Australia in the Wine World was also super fun. You do have to put in a little bit of work, and show up for the lectures/pracs, but it was really fun to have a winetasting once a week, and I really learned a lot about wine which is such a nice skill to have.
unexpected_costs: Don't really think I had any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Groceries is pretty expensive. Eating out is a bit cheaper than in Copenhagen, and coffee especially is very cheap.
activities_available: UniMelb has a lot of different clubs and societies. I joined the athletics club which uses the track on campus. There is also a gym on campus which is super nice and convenient.
activities_recommended: Go on weekend trips to different parts of Australia. The country has so much to offer and so much to do.
weekend_recommendations: I went to Kangaroo Island, Tasmania, Sydney and also drove the Great Ocean Road. I also spend a little over a month on the West Coast after the semester ended, which I highly recommend!
culture_adjustment: Melbourne is pretty similar to Copenhagen, so it was pretty easy.
socializing_tips: Since the lectures at uni is being recorded, not so many people show up for them, so I found it a bit difficult to socialize with local students. However I met a lot through the track team, so I recommend signing up for clubs instead.
cultural_challenges: Can't remember any.
culture_appreciated: The open-minded and helpful attitude everyone has. People are much easier to approach here than in Copenhagen.
top3_advice: Enjoy it and be prepared to spend a lot of money.
other_useful_info: I bought a bike to get around the city. Much easier than the tram system.
most_rewarding: The friends I met down here. Since you really only have each other, you get really close in a short period of time.
greatest_challenge: To find time to do all I wanted to do here. Could easily have spend a year here!

crucial_aspects: As I'm dyslexic it was important for me to choose a university which would provide similar assistance to that of UCPH. I knew I wanted to study outside of Europe to experience a new culture and possibly travel during the semester. Choosing an english-speaking country was also important to me, to allow easier communication with local students.
info_ease: The university was great at providing the necessary information. An introduction lecture was given the first day and during orientation week a lot of information is provided, so try to come if possible.
arrival_assistance: The university provides a shuttle service from the airport to your accommodation. That was really helpfull after such a long journey. They also send out several emails with the schedule for the orientation week so browse through and see what you want to join.
arrival_comments: Stop 1 is really helpfull. It is located on campus and is open every day. You don't need to book an appointment, but it is the best place to have any question answered.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: First you register/apply for a number of courses. You normally will register for more than you need to be a full time student. After the university has approved your choices they will open for enrollment. Some courses might be full at first, but as students needs to create their own timetable spots may become available if others choice to drop the class. So keep an eye out during the enrollment days.
registration_help: The university sends out an email describing how to enroll in each subject, and how many you should apply for. They will assess each course you apply for in terms of you meeting any criteria, but also all of your subjects together. I got a course of pharmacology rejected because the institute though it was better for me to focus on another pharmacology course. They felt both courses might be too much to take on.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. As mentioned one class was rejected, but I has only chosen to register for this as a backup.
registration_advice: Pick from interest. Only take classes that you are interested in and maybe try something completely new. I chose to have 2 more easy courses in terms of assessment, and this was a nice balance.
course_level: I took a single first year class, two second year classes and one third year class. All of the classes were not too difficult, and reading was not required to understand the material.
teaching_comparison: Lectures are like UCPH, but can be streamed if preferred. During the semester be prepared for quizzes and tests that count in your final grade. The quizzes, midsemester test and final examination are all closed book, and in addition focuses on more smaller details like names of proteins or processes rather than the overall understanding like on UCPH
courses_enrolled: Our Planet, Our Health (UNIB10017) Australia in the Wine World (AGRI10039) Pharmacology: How Drugs Work (PHRM20001) Stem Cells in Development & Regeneration (CEDB30004)
recommended_courses: I would recommend them all except (UNIB10017). This was just really weird structured, not very interesting and very easy.
unexpected_costs: Due to where I lived I had to spend some money decorating the place. It was just not furnished for a longterm student to live there. I spend about 4000 DKK getting stuff for the kitchen and my room.
cost_comparison: Overall public transportation was a lot cheaper and easier to use than I had expected, so that was a nice surprise. It was very easy to take public transportation to different national parks in the area around Melbourne.
activities_available: Unimelb has a wide variety of societies and clubs. I joined Musex which is a society for exchange students. They host a few parties throughout the semester, and other events. I also joined Swifties society as well as Drawing and painting club. Signing up to clubs costs 5 dollars, and the events can cost an additional few dollars.
activities_recommended: I would recommend all the clubs that I joined, and just joining something in general. They host really nice events and it is a great place to meet other students.
weekend_recommendations: In Melbourne I would recommed simply getting to know the local area fast. There are plenty of places to see, and time goes by really fast. Go see an AFL game and visit many of the markets in the city. A short drive from Melbourne is Great Ocean Road, Philip Island and Wilsons Promonotory which is also worth seeing. Just travel as much as possible. We went to Tasmania on an extended weekend (6 days) and would highly recommed going.
culture_adjustment: It was really easy to adjust. People are very nice and helpfull in addition the city is very liveable.
socializing_tips: Go to events in the beginning and sign up for sports or societies.
cultural_challenges: No major differences. Be aware that a lot of the bars and clubs close at 1 am, so choice wisely when going out.
culture_appreciated: Overall the culture is much like in Denmark and other places in Europe. Australians are super friendly and talkative, so don't hesitate to ask anything.

crucial_aspects: When choosing my study destination, it was important to me that it was in an English speaking country as one of my primary purposes with studying a semester abroad was to improve my English skills. It was also important to me that the destination was in a country far from Denmark with a culture different from Danish culture, as I wanted to experience student life in a completely different setting in a country with a different approach to studying law at university level. Lastly, it was particularly important to me that the destination was in a common law country as I wanted to study and become familiar with common law (as opposed to civil law in Denmark).
info_ease: It was quite easy. The University of Melbourne is very exchange student-friendly and provides all the information you need upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive much assistance. All the information you need is made available online and the few questions I had were answered by the friendly staff at the "Stop 1" service desk. There was also a mandatory orientation event for exchange students when I arrived.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process was basically just to fil out certain information on a website and submit a few documents. The whole process, step-by-step, was laid out in an e-mail from the university. It was very simple.
registration_help: As mentioned above, the whole process, step-by-step, was laid out in an e-mail from the university and further information about each step was available online. If you have any problems or difficulties with the registration process, there is also a phone number you can call to get help.
registration_success: I was very succesful and got all the classes I registered for.
registration_advice: Everything will go smoothly if you just follow the instructions you receive from the university.
course_level: The level of the courses varied a lot, and the graduate level courses were quite difficult as they built on knowledge from prerequisite courses that you have not had as an exchange student. As an example, I had the course "Contracts", which was very difficult as it presupposed knowledge about legal concepts and principles in common law and equity that we are not familiar with in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was very similar to that of UCPH and included both lectures and seminars.
courses_enrolled: 1) Contracts 2) Global Human Rights Law 3) Free Speech and Media Law 4) AI, Ethics and the Law
recommended_courses: I would recommend the courses listed as nos. 2) - 4) above. These are all great courses that are taught at a level accessible to exchange students and give valuable insights into Australian law within the respective areas of law.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Accommodation was way more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: As I did not participate in such activities, I am not sure what kinds of activities were available.
activities_recommended: As I did not participate in non-academic activities, I, unfortunately, do not have any recommendations.
weekend_recommendations: There are many great things to see and do in Melbourne and Australia. I definitely would recommend other visiting students to travel as much as possible to the different parts of Australia and experience the incredible nature Australia has to offer.
culture_adjustment: It was extremely easy. Australians are such nice people and the culture is in many respects very similar to Danish culture. In Melbourne, the culture is very relaxed.
socializing_tips: I mostly socialized with students from other countries, i.e. visiting students, and therefore do not have much experience with socializing with local students.
cultural_challenges: The thing I found most challenging was the language as Australians use a lot of slang - which can make it difficult to understand what they are saying!
culture_appreciated: I really loved the very easy-going and relaxed vibe and their love for great coffee and good food.
top3_advice: First of all, only take courses that have prerequisites if you are up for a challenge - they are inherently difficult to exchange students. Secondly, do not stress about exams. They might seem difficult, but in my experience the exams turned out to be manageable and the examiners were reasonable. Lastly, enjoy your time at the university and make sure you take advantage of the opportunities you have to go explore this amazing country.
other_useful_info: I believe I have covered this in the sections above.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part, on a personal level, was definitely that I got meet so many interesting and nice people from many different countries and cultures and that I got to experience the incredible nature in Australia.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was studying at the university, but I believe this is how it is supposed to be. Although the teaching style is similar to that of UCPH, it is just a challenge to study at university level in another country, where things are just a bit different, everything is in English etc.
other_comments: N/A

top3_advice: If you are a University of Copenhagen (UCPH) student heading to the University of Melbourne for an exchange program, here are the three most important things to keep in mind: 1. Academic Rigor and Course Selection The University of Melbourne is renowned for its academic excellence and rigorous coursework. Make sure you: Select Courses Wisely: Choose courses that align with your academic goals and interests. Pay attention to prerequisites and the workload of each course. Engage with Faculty: Take advantage of the opportunity to engage with professors and faculty members. Their expertise can provide valuable insights and enhance your learning experience. Stay Organized: The academic system might differ from UCPH, so stay organized and keep track of assignment deadlines, exam dates, and course requirements to manage your workload effectively. 2. Embrace the Cultural Experience Australia offers a rich and diverse cultural experience that extends beyond the classroom. Make sure you: Explore Melbourne: Melbourne is known for its vibrant arts scene, diverse food culture, and numerous festivals. Take the time to explore the city and immerse yourself in local activities. Engage with Locals: Interact with Australian students and locals to gain a deeper understanding of the culture. Participate in university clubs, societies, and events to make new friends and build a network. Travel and Discover: Australia has stunning landscapes and unique wildlife. Use your free time to travel and experience the natural beauty and attractions, such as the Great Ocean Road, national parks, and local beaches. 3. Prepare for Practicalities Moving to a new country requires careful preparation to ensure a smooth transition. Make sure you: Arrange Accommodation Early: Student housing can be competitive. Secure your accommodation as early as possible, whether it's on-campus or off-campus. Understand Visa Requirements: Ensure you have the correct student visa and understand the conditions attached to it, including work rights and healthcare coverage. Budget and Finances: The cost of living in Melbourne can be high. Plan your budget carefully, taking into account accommodation, food, transportation, and leisure activities. Look for student discounts and consider part-time work if your visa allows. By focusing on these three key areas—academic preparation, cultural immersion, and practical arrangements—you'll be well-prepared to make the most of your exchange experience at the University of Melbourne
