crucial_aspects: Due to covid it wasn't possible for me to go to either Canada or Australia, to do what I love most: skiing and surfing. Therefore I chose the next best thing, which was to get as close as possible to the mountains within the borders of Europe, and hopefully get to ski a bit during my excahnge. At the same time I wanted to do my exchange in a country with a culture and climate very different from Denmark to expand my horizon and actually feel like being away from home. Therefore Milan in northern Italy seemed like the best choice for me. And it certainly was.
info_ease: It wasn't the easiest thing in the world to find my schedule, so I missed my first lecture, but it wasn't the end of the world. You just have to be patient and read the emails you receive, and there is most likely someone to write if you are missing some information, but everything is a bit slower in Italy - they rarely stress, so you shouldn't either.
arrival_assistance: All the assistance regarding the academics was via email, which worked fine, but you have to be patient. Might have been due to Covid, but I'm not sure. But there is a great student organisation called Erasmus students network (ESN), who plans an intro week with a lot of activities and you can always reach out to them as well for help, but mostly regarding non-academic stuff. There weren't any tour of the university or so, as it has many different campus in the city.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I was strongly recommended to follow a master programme, in order to avoid the overlap of classes. This I did but I chose to only take two out of three of the courses from this program, as the last one didn't fit my education. Therefore I had to find one more course which didn't overlap too much with the other program, and one that was taught in english and with the correct amount of credits.
registration_help: Not much help, other than the recommendation to follow the master program, but it is possible to email the professors and ask them questions about their course.
registration_success: I got what I wanted, but had to change my original choice of the third course, as it overlapped too much and all of sudden was taught in italian instead of english as the website said.
registration_advice: Take it easy and don't stress too much about it. You have plenty of time to change your courses if you aren't satisfied or run in to other complications.
course_level: I took master courses in order to have english lectures. The syllabus was big, but the level was fair even though I wasn't a master student yet.
teaching_comparison: We only had lectures, so I really missed some classes with task solving or journal club, because I don't learn very well from just listening. Therefore the exam preparation was heavier than expected, as it felt like I had to learn everything from scratch, but I guess it's different from person to person, how they learn best. Also, we didn't have any text books, so we didn't have to prepare anything for the lectures, so I didn't do any self studying before the exam preparations.
courses_enrolled: Pathogenetic basis of disease Applied pharmacology to biotechnology Communicable and non-communicable diseases
recommended_courses: Pathogenetic basis of disease is a very big course for 12 credits about a lot of different diseases from cancer to cardiovascular diseases, which was quite interesting. Our exam was multiple choice, but in Italy there is no guarantee that the exam form is the same from year to year. Applied pharmacology to biotechnology was more focused on methods of diagnosing and drug-treatment. Both traditional drug treatment like iboprofen and the problems regarding this, but also new methods like RNA interference and monoclonal antibodies. A big part concerned use of fluorescent tools as biosensors. The exam was oral. Communicable and non-communicable diseases was the third course outside the master program. Again concerning many different diseases, like diabetes and cardiovascular diseases, but also infectious diseases. Some of the syllabus overlapped with pathogenetic basis of disease, but that wasn't a problem - only nice with some repetition. The exam was an oral one with one professor, and a written multiple choice with the two other professors.
unexpected_costs: My wallet got stolen in the metro, with some cash. Later my phone got stolen as well but on the street, but my insurance covered it. Be aware of your bag always, and don't put anything in your pockets. Personal spending includes about six trips to other parts of Italy, like Sicily, the Dolomites, Cinque Terre and Venice.
cost_comparison: Going out to restaurants and bars is less expensive than Denmark. The same for alcohol in general. Supermarket prices are fairly the same. Taxis and public transportation is cheaper as well.
activities_available: The organisation that I mentioned earlier, ESN, is really big and active for my university (La Statale) in Milan. It is run by other students who volunteer to make the Erasmus students stay in Milan as good as possible. They planned all kinds of activities during the entire stay; beach volley, wine dinners, aperitivos, day trips to nearby cities, museum trips, city tours and many other things. If you buy the ESN card for 10 euros, you are allowed to participate in all of it.
activities_recommended: All of them, especially in the beginning. It is a great way to meet other people fast and make friends, who you can plan your own trips and activities with. And you can really feel how engaged the volunteers of ESN are in making this the best time of our lives.
weekend_recommendations: Visit nearby cities! It is easy to get around with train. I really liked Cinque Terre, which was extremely beautiful. ESN has a trip to Rome for alle Erasmus students in Italy, which was a lot of fun as well. If you don't get a spot you can also go there by train yourself. Venice was amazing as well, but we waited until January to visit this city to avoid the big crowds of tourists, which was definitely the right choice. And go on the Snow Week Erasmus skiing trip as well! It was amazing.
culture_adjustment: It was a bit difficult to adjust in the beginning, but Italians are very nice people. Some doesn't speak english, but it wasn't a big problem.
socializing_tips: Be prepared for the Italian lifestyle! Organizing, planning and deadline are not their best skills, to put it nicely. You have to be patient, and don't stress too much about deadlines, because they don't.
cultural_challenges: Their laid back life style which also includes authorities including the university and the police - I spent 4 hours at the police station in the waiting room only to fill out a paper and hand it in, which took less than 10 min. Also most police don't speak english. We also had to be very patient regarding our exam dates. In Italy the students communicate with the professors trying to find a suitable date for the exam. And then the professors talk about it and then get back to the students. So it is a long process, but the bright side is, that you can choose between a couple of dates and not just one. You get used to the laid backness eventually.
culture_appreciated: The eating and winery. I loved all the italian food and wine. It's a big part of being italian.
top3_advice: Be patient always. Don't stress too much, cause italians never do, and enjoy the country, explore as much as you can.
other_useful_info: No, everything has been said.
most_rewarding: Experiencing Italy, but not just from a vacation point of view but as a citizen. Also made me appreciate the danish culture a bit more and really expanded my horizon.
greatest_challenge: I found it difficult sometimes to be away from my family and home, and always feeling a bit like a stranger, because I didn't speak italian and doesn't look italian at all. But you get used to it as well, and eventually feel more familiar with the city and also the language if you take the language course. At the end an italian even asked me for directions, which felt like a little win :))
other_comments: Bring clothes for summer and winter and explore the city and country as much as possible. Don't stress about uni too much - the professors are quite flexible with Erasmus students, so take advantage of that.

crucial_aspects: I have always been drawn to Italy; the history, food, art, architecture and literature. I have always admired Umberto Eco who lived in Milan, and loved the stories of Italo Calvino that also have connections to Milan. Furthermore, the Italian academy has a rich tradition, different from the Danish - another reason for visiting.
info_ease: It was quite hard. University websites are notoriously difficult to navigate, and Unimi's is no different. There was perhaps a lack of communication from both UCPH and Unimi in the early days of the stay, where insecurity is high.
arrival_assistance: I recieved an e-mail maybe 10 days after arrival on where to collect my student card, but this e-mail conflicted with information on the uni-website.
arrival_comments: It was clear that there would be a lot of administrative work on my own hand, which I of course did not enjoy too much. However, when I sought help, everyone was generous with their assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: First I had to enroll in the uni erasmus portal. This was easy. Later on, once I had gotten my email-credentials, I had to register for courses, which was a bit more difficult, since there were troubles with the pre-approval (and also not always reading lists available for the Unimi-courses).
registration_help: Lots of help was available, just not very easily. There wasn't a desk where you could show up to get help. Emailing the professors and coordinators was probably the best way to get help.
registration_success: I took me maybe 10 attempts to get to the right courses, in part due to last-minute re-scheduling of one of my courses. Once I had found the four courses I needed though, everything was great.
registration_advice: Look through the course catalogue and send out mails VERY early. Be persistent (maybe even annoying), university-bureaucracy is stubborn and slow (this was my experience in both Copenhagen and Milan). If possible, try and make some calls, so that you can get immediate answers.
course_level: As mentioned above, there was a lack of readings in most courses - however there was also room for personal effort.
teaching_comparison: There is more of a historical and an oral tradition in Milan. 4/5 exams were oral - in Copenhagen I haven't had one yet, and wont have one for at least a year. It was very nice developing my on-the-spot-arguing-skills and rhetorics. I nice and welcome change.
courses_enrolled: History of Regional Integrations (6 ects) Journalism, Media and Politics (9 ects) Comparative Legal Traditions (6 ects) Comparative Politics and Development (9 ects)
recommended_courses: I would honestly recommend all the courses, they were fantastic. The professors were very kind and skilled, and the objectives of the courses aligned with all of my interests, and adressed challenges of crucial importance. With regards to the Journalism, Media and Politics course, be sure to ask for some readings - and try to lobby for a larger classroom.
unexpected_costs: The deposit for the apartment was expensive.
cost_comparison: Living was very expensive.
activities_available: I did not really look into this - except of course the Italian courses that were excellent.
activities_recommended: Definitely go for the language course and take in as much as you can. I think the world would be a better place if everyone spoke more different languages, instead of just arrogantly assuming english is spoken everywhere.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Bergamo Alta! And Mantova, Lecco and Verona! Vicenza is also beautiful. Visit museums everywhere, as well as palazzi, restaurants etc.
culture_adjustment: Very easy! The Milanese were very kind, welcoming and actually (quite unexpected for at metropol) patient with my Italian.
socializing_tips: Reach out early in the semester/trimester, dont be timid!
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Coffee, food, relaxed attitudes, beautiful language that I could listen to all day. Architecture, art.
top3_advice: 1. Start planning early! Reach out to local students as soon as classes begin. 2. Find a local café that serves good coffee, and start going there regularly, and experience true, local Italian coffee-culture. 3. Leave the city and go see some of the fantastic places around Milan. Do one-day trips from 08-20, try local specialties.
other_useful_info: I lived with two other students (Danish as well). That was great. We had an emergency situation, where I was very glad to be along friends. I can recommend looking for flatmates.
most_rewarding: Learning Italian. No doubt. And some fun exams.
greatest_challenge: Time management, and courage to reach out and arrange activities.

crucial_aspects: First and foremost, I wanted to try living in a different country and having my daily life there. Due to the Covid-19 situation, I had to choose a destination in Europe for this. I have always enjoyed traveling to Italy due to the culture, the people and the food, and on top of this the Covid situation there seemed to be rather stable. Secondly, I wanted to go on exchange to further challenge myself academically. Going to Italy made sense for me, since they too are a part of the EU and allow for the choice of EU-related courses. Thirdly, I wanted to go to a country in which I could travel around. Italy is great for this. There are many beautiful places to explore and traveling around is not that expensive.
overall_comments: Overall it was an enjoyable experience. While I will not rate it higher than 8, I still would not change my past decision of going on exchange to Italy. Going on exchange is definitely something I believe everyone should experience.
info_ease: Not easy. The university in Milan has a very poor website for orientation and their physical offices can be confusing to navigate. They respond and do in fact help you, if you contact them per mail, but generally I found it quite frustrating, that I could not easily find answers to my questions or worries. On the plus side, bureaucracy does not really exist in Italy, so even if you miss a deadline or forget something, they fix it for you either way.
arrival_assistance: None. I had to find it myself on their website and/or go physically to their offices to pick up my student card.
arrival_comments: Whilst I only rate it as a 1, there is not really that much to do upon arrival except for sending the university information about insurance and picking up your student card. A good trick is to getting in contact with other erasmus students and hoping they can explain or help you with it. That is how I figured out how to access the online student portal and my student mail.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall it was an enjoyable experience. While I will not rate it higher than 8, I still would not change my past decision of going on exchange to Italy. Going on exchange is definitely something I believe everyone should experience.
registration_process: As stated above, you log into the "Unimia" student portal and choose the courses you wish to register for and press accept. You have to write the course information in manually, but the process is quite simple.
registration_help: Whilst the registration proces is simple, it does not contain much useful information, meaning information about the various courses has to be found in different places on the university website. Some of this information is "public", and some of this information you cannot access without logging in to the student portal.
registration_success: Very successful, I got all the courses I had applied for.
registration_advice: Try and figure out whether or not the courses overlap with each other. It can be annoying to have classes during the same hours, since "attendance" matters for the final exam. Do not worry about the exam dates, you have the option of attending each exam in each course in December, January and february - choice is yours.
academics_comments: Overall it was an enjoyable experience. While I will not rate it higher than 8, I still would not change my past decision of going on exchange to Italy. Going on exchange is definitely something I believe everyone should experience.
course_level: The level of the courses was quite varying. In some courses the professors simply expected us to know stuff, which some had never heard about before, and in other courses they explained the contents and teachings as if it was middle school. While this is said, I do not believe the level was in any way hard, and passing is easy.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is very different, but this is also what makes it fun to try. Attendance is not at thing at UCPH, while it definitely is in Italy. You cannot simply skip too many classes. The style of teaching is also different and the professors expect you to participate and answer their questions. Most professors do not expect you to, but it matters for the overall grade.
courses_enrolled: M&A: The contract European Monetary Law Competition law and economics Smart cities, artificial intelligence and digital transformation law Negotiation, mediation and sustainable conflict resolution
recommended_courses: Competition law and economics M&A the contract
unexpected_costs: Not really any large ones as far as I remember. I did however spent unexpectedly a lot on traveling, going out and shopping.
cost_comparison: Drinks were more expensive compared to other italian cities. Transportation by train is also expensive if you plan on traveling a lot. Food is quite cheap and so is coffee.
activities_available: None except for a volleyball team which not many exchange students were a part of. The beginning of the semester included some social activities thanks to ESN (Erasmus Student Network), but compared to the many other universities in Milan, the social activities at UniMi were not great. Find your own group of friends and plan your own social stuff! This is not so hard
activities_recommended: Travel! Cities like Bologna, Parma and Venezia are not far from Milan. Flying to Sicily is also not that expensive. Go to other parts of Italy, visit museums and go out and have nice food and drinks. Lots of opportunities to watch sports such as Football. If you go in the Autumn semester you can go watch Formula1 in Monza.
weekend_recommendations: Spend time with the people you meet here. Go out town with them to have a good time, be cultural or to travel. Do not worry too much about the studies; passing is easy and you do not need to study too much for the individual classes. Have a good time while it lasts.
culture_adjustment: Not that hard. Especially if you arrive a week or two before the actual semester starts. I think its a subjective question, but I would not say it is hard.
socializing_tips: Sign up for various whatsapp groups and try and make friends in that way. You can ask if anyone wants to go out and have a drink or see X or Y place together. Participate in the ESN social events and be outgoing. You can also make good friends through the classes you attend.
cultural_challenges: Language. If you do not speak italian, it can be hard to communicate in some places. You will manage though. I do not speak any Italian, and I did not find it challenging.
culture_appreciated: The food and the drinks. And the beauty of the country in nature, history and architecture.
top3_advice: 1) Go some time before the semester starts to settle in your own tempo. It makes the start less stressful 2) Try and make friends through WhatsApp groups for exchange students. These can be found by asking around or through the big "erasmus milan" facebook group. 3) Use the time here to relax, enjoy yourself and generally just have a good time. Sure, there are exams to pass and stuff to study, but make the best of your time
other_useful_info: I think I have covered most of this in my previous answers.
most_rewarding: The friendships you make and the fact that you get to exit your "normal" routine back home to live a new, temporary life in a different country (with amazing food and drinks).
greatest_challenge: Deciding to do all my exams in the month of December. I do not regret this, but it was tough to have 3 exams in 3 days.
other_comments: No. I think my above answers cover the exchange period well :)

crucial_aspects: The country and city had to be interesting.
info_ease: Because of covid, I felt a little alone in the beginning. There was no welcome events and all communication with the Erasmus office was digitally, so you had to just wait patiently for them contacting you with what to do next.
arrival_assistance: I got information on what to do via email.
arrival_comments: I asked the other students at campus a lot. They were very sweet and helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You can do most online. Information aren't posted a long time in advance online. When registering for classes, I would recommend waiting untill classes have begun. You can register for classes until just before the exams.
registration_help: I asked the other students - they're familiar with the systems, and they speak Italian so they can ask for help if something isn't working properly.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted
registration_advice: Be patient and ask the other students for help and advice.
course_level: I took ma-level courses, because they were taught in English, and it wasn't a problem to keep up.
teaching_comparison: It's similar - lectures with some student participation. Exams were very different though.
courses_enrolled: Bristish Theatre Studies and Performances Social Media for Environmental Communication Representation and Image Theories Intellectual and Cultural History
recommended_courses: I liked all my courses. Intellectual and Cultural History is super interesting if you'd like to know more about Italian history and Italian politics and culture. British Theatre Studies and Performances is a very cosy and chilled course. The professor is super sweet and the other students were very open and nice as well. You don't have to do much to keep up with the course and if you're a little interested in the arts, cultural, or theatrical scene of Milan, you will mostly just sit and talk about that and go to see plays together (also in English).
unexpected_costs: I spend a lot of money on food, but mostly when traveling and going out to dinner at night.
cost_comparison: The cheapest air bnbs around Italy are 40 eur a night, and if you hope to go to Rome, book in advance.
activities_available: I didn't really engage much with these, so I'm not entirely sure on the options available. I know the ESN arranged a lot of stuff, but I didn't participate.
activities_recommended: I enjoyed traveling around Milan and exploring more of Italy. Especially going on one-day hiking trips.
weekend_recommendations: See more of Italy! Milano is far from the nicest place in Italy, but it's well connected. It's a nice place to start exploring from.
culture_adjustment: You have to be patient with a lot of things. Everything seems very unorganised from a Danish perspective and often things take longer or seem inefficient. Italians don't stress so try not to stress either.
socializing_tips: The local students are very nice and open but you might have to be the one who approach them and start the conversation.
cultural_challenges: Italian bureaucracy. Especially around exams. I found it helpful to just ask the locals and then do like them. And don't stress about it, often you can talk to the people in charge and work something out.
culture_appreciated: If you embrace it, it's super nice that many things are more relaxed. Trains and exams are difficult to figure out, but if you get it wrong or it takes you longer it's often not an issue. No one really has everything under control, so they don't expect you to have it either. Ask the locals for help.
top3_advice: Don't just stay in Milan, explore the country! It gets cold in winter and Milano is too hot in summer, so try to get out of the city. Be patient, and ask the students for help. The best, local restaurants and (coffee) bars are not the most fancy looking but often the sleezy ones.
other_useful_info: You will probably be asked for your "codice fiscale". Don't bother applying for one, the process takes forever. If you search for "codice fiscale generator" online you can generate a fake one which will work just fine for most purposes.
most_rewarding: Getting to travel around Italy and the food and coffee culture. I enjoyed the simple way of cooking with only a few ingredients, but ingredients of the highest, most tasty quality. I also really enjoyed eating late in evening, starting with a small pasta dish perhaps followed up by a pizza and dessert. I've also become slightly addicted to my after-lunch espresso.
greatest_challenge: I did my exchange in my last semester of my bachelors which ment I was very busy also writing applications and planning what to do next. My biggest regret is not having more time to just enjoy Italy and explore Milano, instead of sitting inside working.

crucial_aspects: Weather, courses in English, food and culture.
info_ease: You don't really get any information from the university before going. Once the semester starts they will send you some emails, you just need to figure out stuff when you get there.
arrival_assistance: Emails, you can contact the Erasmus coordinator Massimo Costa.
arrival_comments: Almost no information, but it worked out fine and they are generally very flexible with Erasmus students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You register online in Unimia, super easy. It was harder to find information about the courses and their schedules, some of which was only posted right before the semester began. You can change your registrations for a while so you can try out different courses.
registration_help: You could email the Erasmus coordinator.
registration_success: Everyone gets the courses they want is my experience. I got every course I wanted.
registration_advice: It's hard to figure out the schedule because the courses overlap and you need to take a lot of course to get 30 ECTS. So check all the schedules and make an excel sheet or something. Try out different courses - you can change your choices.
course_level: It was very different from course to course, some were super easy and some a bit harder, but the level was generally lower than UCPH.
teaching_comparison: There are not many required readings so it's more about listening to the teacher and taking notes. Some teachers require participation and do cold calls.
courses_enrolled: International Climate Change and Energy Law Legal Clinic on Arctic Studies Public Administration for Sustainable Development Sustainable Transport: Legal Issues Comparative Contract Law
recommended_courses: 'International Climate Change and Energy Law' was very interesting and a bit more challenging than other courses. Also 'Sustainable Transport: Legal Issues' was a very interesting topic and the teacher interacts a lot with the students.
unexpected_costs: It's expensive to get into clubs in Milan.
cost_comparison: The regional trains are super cheap, you can get to Lago di Como for 5 euros. And you don't need to buy any books for uni. Also drinks and food are pretty cheap when you eat out, but supermarkets are just as expensive as Copenhagen if not more.
activities_available: They have a sports union (CUS) where you can sign up to do a lot of different sports. CUS also have ski trips which I participated in and enjoyed very much! Otherwise, there does not seem to be many activities which are inclusive towards exchange students.
activities_recommended: The ski trips and maybe join a sport through CUS. Also, ESN (Erasmus Student Network) arranges a welcome night before the semester begins - go to that, it's where I met all my friends.
weekend_recommendations: Travel! Lago di Como is so close and has the most beautiful hikes (can recommend Mandello del Lario for hiking). I also really liked Turin which is also close by. There are so many beautiful places in Italy and Milan is very well connected by train.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy
socializing_tips: Try to take courses with Italian students (not just Erasmus students) and talk to them there.
cultural_challenges: Italians often don't like to speak English even though a lot of them are better at it than they say.
culture_appreciated: Aperitivo (going out to drinks before dinner)! And Italians are mostly really nice and helpful if you want to practice Italian.
top3_advice: You get almost no information, but don't stress - you will figure it out once you get there. Try to get a good course schedule so you have some days off to do one-day trips. And just relax and enjoy amazing Milan!
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Meeting new people from different countries and traveling around beautiful Italy.
greatest_challenge: It was a bit stressful to figure out everything with the courses in the beginning.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: To pick a country / city that is as different as possible to Denmark so I get to experience new culture, social life, learning and school system.
overall_comments: I had the time of my life. Amazing people, interesting course and fantastic city.
info_ease: I was missing some information, but the professors and university staff is very open to help. I just send out mails to the different professors and other relevant staff - they respond very fast and helped me out.
arrival_assistance: There was assistance from the Erasmus coordinator and from the volunteering Erasmus Network.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had the time of my life. Amazing people, interesting course and fantastic city.
registration_process: You fill out a formular about the course you want to take at the institution and that's basically it. Following you need to make sure you have access to all the relevant online platforms used (contact the professors directly).
registration_help: The Official Erasmus coordinator was able to help with any relevant problems.
registration_success: I got all the Classes I wanted without problem - even if all the classes was master and im still doing my bachelor.
registration_advice: Have patient and relax - even if the system seems to simple and a little outdated it will work out.
academics_comments: I had the time of my life. Amazing people, interesting course and fantastic city.
course_level: I found that the level was varying a bit. Some classes was more difficult and some a little easier - also depending on how much background knowledge I had that was relevant for the course.
teaching_comparison: Very different. Very long lectures and a lot of knowledge you just need to remember. Lab was nice since you actually got to do a lot of stuff on your own, but there was still assistance to help you if you felt lost.
courses_enrolled: ADVANCED MOLECULAR BIOLOGY MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY BIOINFORMATICS AND MOLECULAR MODELING PHARMACOGENOMICS, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY, ORPHAN DRUGS
recommended_courses: Advanced molecular biology was a great course - I loved the teaching and we also got to spend time in lab. The work burden is a little big since there is also presentations and homework, but I really learned a lot.
unexpected_costs: You go out a lot, so even if food and drinks are cheap you spend a lot.
cost_comparison: Food, living and drinks is less expensive than expected
activities_available: I didn't do so many activities with the university.
activities_recommended: The Erasmus network is great for arranging events and meeting people.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city and student environment with local people - and travel as much as possible. I wish that I had spend more time going to cities nearby and on weekend getaways.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy since the Italians are such openminded and social people.
socializing_tips: They are not all the best with English - if you can learn basic italian before going or have patience when speaking with them. And don't get offended if they don't want to speak to you - its probably just because they are shy and embarrassed about their English and not about you personally.
cultural_challenges: The dinner time was too late - they eat dinner at 22/23 and im used to eat 18/19.
culture_appreciated: I appreciate the social and open culture. I love the Aperitivo culture as well - they fact that you can go out for one drink / beer and it doesn't have to be more than this - and you get to socialize.
top3_advice: Learn a little italian if possible - there are still a lot of young people not speaking English, so this could help you socialize easier with the locals. Take advantage of all the possible social events you find interesting - They are so good at creating events (especially Erasmus) and this way you not only meet other exchange students, but also local italiens who volunteer in the network. Travel and experience as much as possible - there are so many great options.
other_useful_info: I don't know.
most_rewarding: The friendship both locals and internationals, the language improvement by being forced to du presentations and exams in English and the culture - I really like everything about Milan.
greatest_challenge: In the beginning I found it challenging to settle down and meet people - but it changes fast, as soon as you get in to a rhythm with lectures and social life.

crucial_aspects: I wanted a well performing school in a city with cultural relevance. I wanted a city were it was possible easily to travel around. Also, a city whit equality in the community and open minded people.
info_ease: It was kind of hard to figure out information about if I have gotten the classes that i replied for. I just showed up in class without any knowledge about that I was accepted.
arrival_assistance: I received information on were to get my erasmus studentcard.
arrival_comments: I general Erasmus students needs more information about the classes. I did not get information on which classes I was accepted in. I did not get information about were they would take place and when. I think that Erasmus people needs a guide to the University of Milans platforms such as Unima and Ariel. Both of the websites are quite hard to figure out.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The process was fine to register at the University. But it was kind of hard with the classes and no notice about confirmation/redjection.
registration_help: I could write the erasmus team on the school.
registration_success: I just showed up in the classes I replied for, without knowing that I was registred.
registration_advice: Write the Erasmus team from the University of Milan. That is the best help you can get.
course_level: I was a BA in Denmark, but did Master classes. I did that because I could not get any classes on english at BA level within my field.
teaching_comparison: Very different. In both of my classes we used the hours of the teaching classes to do exames - also in front of the whole class. In one of my classes we had 6 weeks of teaching program and 6 weeks of presentations (exams) from the students. I found that really odd. Furthermore, both classes both had written and oral exams, though it is written on the course description that there are only one exam in each. It seem like that the teachers choose themself how they wants to examines. In addition, there was no censors during the exams.
courses_enrolled: 'Datafied Society' and 'Social and Political Attitudes'
recommended_courses: I liked Datafied Society. It is really relevant class with the newest theories about data, algorithms, social media platforms and issues around these themes. It is really relevant for people who are interested in communication and marketing.
unexpected_costs: Non
cost_comparison: Fitness is really expensive in Milan. I paid 3000 DKK for 6 month (including student discount)
activities_available: Everything. They both has tennis and football competitions, City tours and parties.
activities_recommended: The first gathering of Erasmus people. Here you can meet new people which is in the same situation as you.
weekend_recommendations: Visit other cities. It is very easy to travel by train from Milan. You can go all over Italy. It gets really warm from May, and around 35 degrees in June. Here I would recommend to go to the seaside or to Lake Como which is only 40 minutes away by train and cost 5 euros.
culture_adjustment: It was really easy. Milan is a big city like Copenhagen, the culture is a bit different, but people are very welcoming and much more openminded compared to danish people.
socializing_tips: Just visit a lot of bars or go to the University parks. Dont worry, people will reach out to you.
cultural_challenges: They eat really late - be prepared for that. Restaurents opens around 7.30. They are still a bit traditional and the men has more power than women.
culture_appreciated: That Italians are really openminded and always reach out to strangers.
top3_advice: 1. The University system is very different from KU. But dont worry, there is nothing wrong about you not getting answers or information. You just show up and you will figure it out. They are not so structured. 2. The classes are not necessary the same as you expected at all. 3. Be prepared for the heat. It is really hot in June/July with no wind and no sea-side.
other_useful_info: Milan is huge, so just walk around the beautiful city and get lost in the nice and old historical buildings.
most_rewarding: The social life - to get to know italian people and the culture.
greatest_challenge: Understanding their structure - They are way more "loose" than danish people. Anything will be fine in their opinions, no stress is needed.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: It was important for me to go on exchange because I like to travel and I think that university-exchange is a unique possibility to try out how it is to have a daily life in another country. It was more or less incidientelly that Milan became my study destinationen since I had to choose between the remaining spots (restpladser). Nevertheless I chose Milan because I thought it could be nice to explore an European country and because I was curious about the Italian culture. Also the food and the weather was attractive.
overall_comments: I am grateful that I had the opportunity to study in Milan. The semester has been the most exciting and interesting semester. Milan as a study destination is highly recommended.
info_ease: I don't remember this process as a big thing, but I'm not a big planner either. We were also a group from Denmark, so we shared information and helped each other. There was a bit confusing about what courses you could choose on the specific semester. It is an advantage if you are a bit proactive - I had two 3-point courses which I only found out was available because I wrote to the professors.
arrival_assistance: Not much, so in the beginning it could be a little confusing to find the right classrooms. But I think the ones who arrived to Milan earlier than me had a tour at the University.
arrival_comments: If you are in doubt, reach out to the University or the other students and they will help you.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I am grateful that I had the opportunity to study in Milan. The semester has been the most exciting and interesting semester. Milan as a study destination is highly recommended.
registration_process: It's is very flexible - you can just keep on changing courses if you like.
registration_help: I wrote to Massimo Costa, if I was in doubt of anything.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. It doesn't seem like the professors reject anyone from taking a class, if you just ask them nicely.
registration_advice: It is not a problem to get the courses you like. The thing that can be difficult is to take courses which don't overlap and to make up a good daily schedule.
academics_comments: I am grateful that I had the opportunity to study in Milan. The semester has been the most exciting and interesting semester. Milan as a study destination is highly recommended.
course_level: Lower level than UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Some professors will include the students more in the lessons.
courses_enrolled: An introduction to italian private law in a comparative perspective. Comparative contract law. EU law on business and human rights. European labour law. Fundamental rights in the European Union. Constitutional challenges in the EU.
recommended_courses: Can recommend all of them. The professor in comparative contract law (Marchetti Carlo) was very good.
cost_comparison: Rent and the supermarket was more expensive than expected - it is not cheaper than copenhagen. Wine, coffee, eating out and train tickets were cheap.
activities_available: There were some e-rasmus events.
activities_recommended: Explore the citylife in Milan. Make some new friends. Try diffrent restaurants. Go for aperitivo. Jump on the train. Exercise. Read books. Learn the basic italian language.
weekend_recommendations: Varenna (Como-lake), Sirmione (Garda-lake), Bologna, Venice, Florence, Umbria, Cinque Terre.
culture_adjustment: The italian lifestyle is laid-back and they take their time. This also means that some things can be slowly and events sometimes changes in the last minute. For me it was easy to adjust to the local culture. I think it depends on how much you like to plan your time ahead.
socializing_tips: Choose some courses where they are. The courses I took was almost only exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Sometimes the communication can be a little aggressive.
culture_appreciated: The people, the food, the humor, the good vibes.
top3_advice: There is a lot of diffrent ways to go on an exchange - do what you like and enjoy. Milan is a great city.
other_useful_info: Not more than I already wrote and most of the things you will find out by yourself in time.
most_rewarding: To make new friends. To learn the italian culture. To stay in the center of Europe and be close to a lot of beautiful places. To improve my English skills.
greatest_challenge: Missing my friends and boyfriend at home.

crucial_aspects: That there appeared to be enough courses I could use as substitutes for the obligatory courses at home, as well as it being placed in an interesting location.
overall_comments: What brought it down from 10 is all the administrative problems I had regarding getting pre-approvals for courses. But it was definitely still worth going.
info_ease: It was fairly easy.
arrival_assistance: I got some emails with useful information from the international office at the host university, office hours of a person you could go to if you had issues, and an introduction event held by volunteer students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: What brought it down from 10 is all the administrative problems I had regarding getting pre-approvals for courses. But it was definitely still worth going.
registration_process: You did it through their online platform where you could choose the ones you wanted.
registration_help: You could write to the international office and they could help you
registration_success: Very
registration_advice: It is pretty simple, and you don't have to do it immediately - you can try out multiple classes and then decide which ones you like the most.
academics_comments: What brought it down from 10 is all the administrative problems I had regarding getting pre-approvals for courses. But it was definitely still worth going.
course_level: Mostly the level was fine. In one course 'Comparative Political Systems' however, it felt more like being taught the contents of the course book than actual comparative politics, which was really irritating.
teaching_comparison: All the classes were much smaller than the normal classes, and felt like a mix of a lecture and classroom discussion. There was a much bigger focus on learning facts by heart than getting the bigger understanding of the subject.
courses_enrolled: Comparative Political Systems European Economic and Monetary Law Multi-level Legal System Global Criminal Organizations Workshop: Human Rights and the Ombudsman
recommended_courses: One course I would recommend NOT taking is Global Criminal Organizations if the professor is Landolfi Francesco. He took an interesting course topic and made the class absolutely horrible by being both a really bad teacher and having a terrible attitude toward the students. European Economic and Monetary Law, Workshop: Human Rights and the Ombudsman, and Multi-level Legal System were all fine.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Getting coffee was super cheap, however getting a cup of tea was often ridiculously expensive. Mostly the prices were fairly close to the Danish ones, though a bit cheaper.
activities_available: The local Erasmus Student Network group held a lot of events throughout the semester. However, for most of them you had to pay to participate.
activities_recommended: Travel. Milan is a great base for day or weekend trips, and it is super easy to do!
weekend_recommendations: Do go up on the roof of the Duomo, the view is beautiful. There are a lot of beautiful cities close by, my favourites for a weekend trip are Cinque Terre and Venice!
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy, the biggest for me was what was considered normal 'eating times', but as you could cook yourself it wasn't really an issue.
socializing_tips: Living in a dorm helped, especially as I had an Italian roommate, but generally it is pretty hard to do as you are mainly in an exchange student bubble with other exchange students. My best suggestion would be going to a lot of the Erasmus activities as they were hosted by Italians. Especially those regularly playing beach volley sounded like they got pretty close.
cultural_challenges: There wasn't really any.
culture_appreciated: That everyone were a bit more easygoing instead of just always hurrying from A to B. This also includes going out way more often, both for just a coffee or for dinner.
top3_advice: Enjoy and have fun! Yes, you do need to study some, but it is important to prioritize going out, traveling and just having fun and exploring the new place you are at. Eat out a lot - it is Italy and the food *is* good. Be prepared for a lot of chaos and things that don't go the way you want them to, but in the end it is definitely worth going anyway.
other_useful_info: Not really
most_rewarding: As cliché as it sounds, the friendships I've made.
greatest_challenge: It was for sure getting pre-approvals for the obligatory courses at home that I had to find substitutes for. It was an issue even before I left, where I had to send course wishes back and forth many times in order to finally find some courses that would get approved as a substitute for 'Europæisk Politik'. Then, when I got to Milan, it turned out that those courses that were supposed to be held the semester I was there had been moved to the next semester. So then I had to frantically search for new courses that could be approved. In the end it was solved, but only after about three weeks after classes had already started. This was a giant stress factor.

other_useful_info: Not really. But again, try to sort the housing situation and make that work.
most_rewarding: The cultural experience, new friends and memories.
greatest_challenge: Mathematical Statistics was a challenge. Apart from that, some administrative stuff can be frightening in the beginning as it does not necessarily work out smoothly. crucial_aspects: The available courses and the culture of the country.
info_ease: It was made relatively easy as I stayed in a student accommodation with other international students in the same situation as myself and with other native students who were able to guide. If I had to find all the necessary information about living in Milan and going to UniMi im assuming it would have been a great deal more difficult to figure everything out. That said, the contact with the Erasmus coordinator was very effective, and I had that contact for great guidance as well.
arrival_assistance: I received information about practical matters for school through the professors at the university. For the rest of the practical information I relied on other international students and the Erasmus team.
arrival_comments: I always had the opportunity to ask the Erasmus counselor, which was a nice safety net, but it could have been communicated better, that they could help with a very wide range of practical questions.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Had to search for the classes in the student portal and assign yourself to them.
registration_help: A thorough guide.
registration_success: I didn't have problems registering for classes, and if I had difficulties, there was a guide.
registration_advice: Use the guides available on the website rather than waiting for an e-mail reply from the institution.
course_level: I had masters levels courses.
teaching_comparison: It is more interactive at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to R, Advertising communication, Economics of Communication and Behavioral Sociology.
recommended_courses: Behavioral Sociology. The professor is obviously interested in what he is teaching, which shows and makes him more interesting to listen to. Furthermore it is the most varied of the classes I took.
cost_comparison: Fitness/gym was double the amount of the average in Denmark. Long haul train tickets and public transportation in general was much cheaper, which made it very easy to explore the country via train.
activities_available: There was many social clubs, and the ones I encountered was mostly about politics/student rights.
weekend_recommendations: In the city I would recommend areas such as Brera or Porta Venezia for the atmosphere, both by day and night. For exchange students staying in Milan I would recommend taking the train to cities such as Bergamo, Verona and Genova for one day trips.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier, but it wasn't really that big of a problem.
culture_appreciated: The openness of the people I met. It was very easy getting to know new people and making friends.
top3_advice: - A lot of the practical stuff will not be completely done by the time of arrival, but can be done upon/after arrival. - Get to know natives from the courses, they can be very helpful with the practical understanding of the school system/exams etc.
most_rewarding: The social part was very rewarding.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was navigating a new school system, where the employees of the institution that I encountered mostly spoke Italian.

crucial_aspects: When choosing my study destination, I thought a lot about the country's culture. I wanted to go somewhere different from the Denmark, and then I landed in Italy. Their way of living is a bit different than from Denmark. They are not in a ‘rush' like we are in Denmark, they take their time to do things and they always have time to sit down and take a coffee or a cold drink after school.
overall_comments: My overall study abroad experience was great. I met a lot of new friends from different countries and cultures and I learned a lot about myself. It was refreshing to study at a new school with a different approach to teaching. Here you were not so much prepared to the classes, you were more listening to the professor and not asking a lot of questions. Furthermore, you got a new student group with new people there came with new perspectives and way of seeing things.
info_ease: All around it was ok to find the information I needed upon arrival. But the information afterwards towards the school in Milan was a bit more difficult as you didn't know where to look for the information, and when you don't know what to look for, then you don't know if you need any information. Furthermore, there was just a lot of new information to deal with
arrival_assistance: Well when I arrvied at my campus (place to stay during the semester) I was met by the campus's secretary, which didn't speak english, and after that I met with the campus's boss who provided me with more information - but again, he didn't really speak that good english.
arrival_comments: Well, I was satisfied, by I find it hard to arrive at new place where you can't really communicate with people.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

Here you were not so much prepared to the classes, you were more listening to the professor and not asking a lot of questions. registration_process: You went on the host university's intranet and then you clicked on register your courses online and you went on a portal, where you could write the name of your courses and how many credits they were.
registration_help: There was a guide where you could see how to do it.
registration_success: It went really well. I did it right the first time - as i followed the guide.
registration_advice: Just follow the guide, and everything will be alright.
academics_comments: My overall study abroad experience was great. I met a lot of new friends from different countries and cultures and I learned a lot about myself. It was refreshing to study at a new school with a different approach to teaching. Here you were not so much prepared to the classes, you were more listening to the professor and not asking a lot of questions. Furthermore, you got a new student group with new people there came with new perspectives and way of seeing things.
course_level: The level of my courses was ok. I took MA courses. The syllabus niveau and amount of pages to read was the same as in Denmark. But I found classes a bit different than from Denmark. I didn't have to engage in dicussions with the professor (I wasn't necessary) so i wasn't really challenged in the syllabus before the examines. But we had to do some presentations where we could discuss with the professor.
teaching_comparison: In Denmark, we dicuss a lot and we are prepared before the classes. At my host university, you don't know what to read before the examine and therefore you can't really dicuss the subjects.
courses_enrolled: Advertising Communication Digital Society Behavioural Sociology Introduction to R
recommended_courses: Digital Society. Here you could discuss a bit more with the teacher about the subjects and the course have a lot of new and interesting themes and subjects, which are up to date with the technology there are today. And I like how they connect technology with the society and we learn how it works together and affects each other.
unexpected_costs: I didn't really expect any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: I think that transport was cheaper than expected. For around 16 euros each month you can use all the busses and metros inside the city.

activities_recommended: Arrange trips yourself!
weekend_recommendations: Go to other cities and experience the food and churches! There is a lot to come after!
culture_adjustment: It took some weeks. But I was really tired in the beginning. The most difficult thing to adjust to, was that I had to sleep with a roommate. Because of that, I went later to bed which was hard for me. Furterhmore, I was also hard in the beginning to adjust to the food.

cultural_challenges: Sleeping later and eating later
culture_appreciated: That they taking things a lot easier. They are not in a rush. They always have time for a coffee or a drink during the week.

other_useful_info: You can't expect to know everything - as it's a new school and system you attend. But take it easy - everything will be okay.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people, cultures and that I learned a lot about myself, as I was in a new country where my frames of living was challenged - in a good way!

crucial_aspects: My destination very much depended on the courses the university would offer - the courses had to match those offered at home. Besides the courses, the geographic location and appeal of the location also played a significant part in my choice.
info_ease: Not very easy. Overall the whole process up to the travel day was complicated and not as straightforward as you could hope.
arrival_assistance: I met other students from back home that were able to help, including the International Mobility office in Milan and at home in Copenhagen.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process required our attendance to collect our Erasmus student card. There was not much to that.
registration_help: International Mobility office.
registration_success: Together with a couple others, we were able to find the appropriate courses, although we had to change one in the beginning. We managed to cover 27 ECTS, leaving us with 3 ECTS remaining. We will make up for those at home by writing an assignment of a specified length of our own interest and choice that will need approval.
registration_advice: Do your thorough research from home, and be open to change the course at your arrival if you can already tell a) either it's not in your interest or b) the duration is too long.
course_level: From my perspective, 2 out of the 4 courses I had, met similar standards as at home. These were Time Series Analysis and Game Theory. A significant difference from UCPH and Milan University, was the limited amount of home assignments. As we know from home, these take up a lot of time and require a lot of work. We barely had any of such during our stay.
teaching_comparison: Less digital than at home - exams were by hand. They combined lectures with classroom exercises, although classroom exercises were very limited.
courses_enrolled: All courses were trimester courses: - Times Series Analysis (6 ECTS) - Game Theory (6 ECTS) - Business History (6 ECTS) - New Business Startup (9 ECTS)
recommended_courses: Time Series Analysis and Game Theory
unexpected_costs: I had a bedbug incident in the beginning of my stay which led to some unexpected costs. Dovevivo (the agency) covered the majority, but I still had to pay for my living costs during my temporary stay outside my apartment.
cost_comparison: Food and drinks were relatively "cheap" considering it's Milan. Also, train tickets to go outside Milan were very cheap in comparison to e.g. Danish train rides.
activities_available: The usual sports. I tried to sign up for football, but the coach only spoke Italian and we were 200 participants trying out for the Uni team, and they were only letting in 12 players. The chances of getting in, were very slim.
activities_recommended: Non
weekend_recommendations: Go outside Milan for one-day visits to nearby towns/cities. We were also a group that rented a van for 3 days and went on a joyful trip across Italy (from Milan to Padova to Trieste and back). I can highly recommend doing that.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy.
socializing_tips: The Italians are very social and open to Erasmus students. We were often approached by the locals that we studied with. Just like any place, be open and ready to socialise.
cultural_challenges: Italians barely eat any breakfast and they eat late. I more or less continued my normal eating habits, yet I also tried to adjust a little to try it out.
culture_appreciated: Italian food, drinks, coffee and late-night evenings.
top3_advice: 1) Enjoy and don't stress out too much - although you may lack information here and there, it usually always works out 2) Go on weekend trips and explore Milan city 3) Go to San Siro stadium ;)
other_useful_info: Prior to your trip, ask around in your friend groups if they may know anyone that is doing a similar exchange as you to Milan - I managed to meet some of the first people (that I still socialize with today) when I arrived because of this.
most_rewarding: New friends, new stories to tell and very little Italian
greatest_challenge: Was when I first arrived and knew no one. You had to sightsee the city yourself, eat out by yourself, and entertain yourself. I worked out very well, but got a little challenging and frustrating after just a week.

crucial_aspects: When choosing a destination, I knew I wanted something within Europe (partly due to the Erasmus agreement among other things), however, I also wanted to experience a different culture from what I was used to in Copenhagen. I feel, I found this in Milan. The city is super nice and have so many things to offer, and the location invites for travels in the nearby regions. The culture is quite different from the Danish, which I find super interesting and there were plenty of things to learn about this new environment. Further, I of course also valued the academic level of the university, where I could find English subjects that interested me. Thought the semester, I was quite satisfied with the classes I attended, and it was a great bonus for me that I found courses which could substitute mandatory courses at Copenhagen University.
overall_comments: When all this is said, I do not think that the destination is the most important aspect of an exchange. As long as you arrive with an open mind and you are excited for the challenge to come, the destination will be secondary. I absolutely loved my exchange semester, but this was mainly due to all the people I met and the experiences we had together.
info_ease: In Milan, or Italy in general, they are much more chilled and relaxed than we tend to be here in Denmark, and therefore, the information came quite late. However, I was staying at a student residency where I was able to check in the day I arrived, which made the arrival super easy. Regarding university, courses and so on, the relevant information came a week or two before classes started.
arrival_assistance: At the student residency, I was meet by the receptionist. Although his English proficiency was limited, there was no problem getting my key and finding my room. Here I soon meet Italian and other international students, who could help if there was some kind of problem of difficulty. At the university, people were also kind to help getting around and understanding the new educational system.
arrival_comments: There was not a lot of orientation upon arrival, but I got all the necessary information, and enough for me to begin the semester. It is a process of learning by doing and not to be embarrassed to ask the questions that might arise.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: When all this is said, I do not think that the destination is the most important aspect of an exchange. As long as you arrive with an open mind and you are excited for the challenge to come, the destination will be secondary. I absolutely loved my exchange semester, but this was mainly due to all the people I met and the experiences we had together.
registration_process: Once you are accepted at the university, you get a login to a personalised student website where much of the information can be found. On the front page there was a link to the course registration. Once you register here, you will be admitted to the course and you do not have to wait for an approval mail. Then you can download an app, where you find the timetable and any news if, for example, the lecture is cancelled or moved to another room.
registration_help: There is an Erasmus coordination (Massimo) who helps the international students with anything university/course related. It was super easy to just send him an email if there was a question, but it was also possible to set a meeting with him, if something more in depth was needed. I took a course at a different faculty, which I at first did not have access to, but in that situation, I got all the help I needed.
registration_success: One of the courses I had gotten pre-approved, ended up not being registered as a course that semester. However, I had gotten a few additional courses pre-approved in advance in case anything like this would happen, and could therefore just choose one of the other courses. Thus, I ended up with the classes I wanted, three of which I have been able to get approved as mandatory courses at Copenhagen University.
registration_advice: It was very easy to register for courses, so I do not think this should be a big concern for future students. Many of my friends also decided to swap from one course to another later in the semester without a problem. As mentioned, they are much more chilled and relaxed concerning these formalities in Italy than what we are used to in Copenhagen.
academics_comments: When all this is said, I do not think that the destination is the most important aspect of an exchange. As long as you arrive with an open mind and you are excited for the challenge to come, the destination will be secondary. I absolutely loved my exchange semester, but this was mainly due to all the people I met and the experiences we had together.
course_level: In general, the courses were easier than what I have been used to in Copenhagen. I was challenged in especially one class, but the rest did not require as much work and effort as I expected even if it was masters courses.
teaching_comparison: For each of my five courses, we had two lectures a week for two hours (in total, four hours per course). We did not have any tutorial classes, but in some lectures there was time dedicated to solving problems and so on. For the most parts there were not any “take home assignments”, however, in one of the courses, there was a mandatory group presentation as part of the final grade. In some classes, we could also take a mid-term exam, which would make the final exam easier.
courses_enrolled: Game Theory - 6 ECTS (substituting microeconomics III) Business History - 6 ECTS (substituting economic history) Time Series Analysis - 6 ECTS (substituting econometrics II) Ethics Economics - 6 ECTS (elective) Sustainable Development in Global Trade (WTO) Law - 6 ECTS (an elective law course)
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend taking the three courses I got approved as mandatory courses in Copenhagen. Time Series Analysis was a bit challenging, but in the end I think it has been worth it. I found Game Theory very interesting, and the professor teaching was very motivating, dedicated and good at her job.
unexpected_costs: When I first arrived at the student residency, I spend a bit of money on different kitchen supplies. I was not expecting this, however, considering the monthly rent, I do not think I am entitled to complain.
cost_comparison: Going out for dinner was cheaper than I expected, but this also meant that I went to cafes and restaurants quite often.
activities_available: The ESN group arranged everything from city tours and sport nights to pub crawling and nights out at different clubs. Further, they also planned trips to different cities and places around Italy. I went to these kinds of events in the beginning, however, after some time and after developing a group of friends, we attended the events less and less. But it was nice and reassuring to know that there is always some kind of social event or gathering.
activities_recommended: I did not attend many planned activities in larger groups throughout the semester. However, I really enjoyed playing paddle tennis with my friends from time to time. It was super easy and convenient to rent the courts in the morning, on days classes started at 12 or later.
weekend_recommendations: Milan is very well connected to the rest of Italy both by train and bus routes (which you can find at very low prices). I would definitely recommend taking advantage of this on the weekends either just as a day trip or to stay a night. Some of my favourite places to visit was Bologna, Turin, Lake Como, Portofino and Lugano in Switzerland. The weekends I spend in Milan, I really liked going to different antique/vintage markets around the city and just explore different areas (Navigli, Porta Venezia, Brera, China town).
culture_adjustment: Of course it will take more than half a year to really adopt to a new culture, and for me there was definitely also a language barrier. However, I did not find it difficult to live with the culture and I have a much better understanding of the culture and way of life. I feel that I quickly got used to and adjusted to the way locals interact with each other and the daily lifestyle.
socializing_tips: My greatest tip for socialising with local students is to live at a student residency or an other type of shared housing. Here you see people everyday and it is super easy to start a conversation in the kitchen or common areas.
cultural_challenges: I did not find the cultural differences to be all that challenging, but if I have to mention one it would be with the lack of organisation and structure. At times, this could be a bit frustrating but I quickly got used to it, and sometimes even saw it as an advantage.
culture_appreciated: I absolutely love the Italian cuisine, and this alone has been a great appreciation of mine. All though I at times found the lack of organisation and structure challenging, I have really come to enjoy a more relaxed mindset without too many worries.
top3_advice: 1) do not stress too much about choosing the right courses and such, you will receive the needed information and there is always the possibility of making alternations later on 2) be open to meet new people anywhere and anytime 3) just go on trips, attend events and enjoy it as long as it lasts
other_useful_info: I think I have already mentioned the most important, but get the subscription to public transportation in the beginning, and do not worry about getting an official fiscal code, the one you can get online is enough.
most_rewarding: As cliche as it sounds, the most rewarding part of my exchange was all the amazing people I met and close friendships I developed. It was quite special living abroad for such a relatively short amount of time, and I feel I have developed so many close relationships in a very short amount of time.
greatest_challenge: To me, the greatest challenge was to make time for everything I wanted to experience while living there, and balancing studies and social life.
other_comments: Enjoy :))

crucial_aspects: It was important for me to choose a destination that really interested me. I chose Milan in Italy for my love for Italian culture, food, history and language.
info_ease: All study related information, and information about the socializing Erasmus Student Network, was all sent directly to me before my stay.
arrival_assistance: I was assigned a Buddy through the Erasmus Student Network that could help me answer questions about university and general questions about the city/country.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After having been granted, and accepted, the spot, I received an Email from the university with an online application formula, easy to fill out. This formula includes filling out the courses the student wishes to attend.
registration_help: All the technical details, about semester start dates, deadlines, academic coordinators and department, was all given in this Email.
registration_success: I was very successful. I found out relatively late that my preferred courses were overlapping a bit. So I continued my search for courses after lectures began, and could easily change a course. It would seem that very few courses had a limited number of spots.
registration_advice: Have multiple courses in mind when you search, in the case that you cannot / will not attend one of the courses in the end.
course_level: I was a Bachelor student when going to Milan. In Milan, Bachelor courses are taught Italian and Masters courses taught in English. Therefore I chose 3 Masters courses and 1 bachelor course (given that I knew some Italian and was able to follow the classes). This meant that the academic level was a bit higher that what I was used to, but in the end, the difference was not big.
teaching_comparison: Attending university in Milan, in my experience, was solely attending lectures. There was no books to read before lectures and no assignments to do before or after lectures. This of course meant a lot free time, but the end, I found exam studying quite difficult, given the limited number of resources (only lecture slides). Compared to in Copenhagen, where we have lectures, seminars (with assignments), and previous exams to use as exam training, the University in Milan lacks a lot of learning methods.
courses_enrolled: Molecular Analysis and Traceability of Biotechnological Products Biologia Molecolare (Molecular Biology) Molecular and Cellular Microbiology Molecular Pharmacology and Immunology.
recommended_courses: Molecular Pharmacology and Immunology was a very interesting two-part course, having one exam in Pharmacology and one exam in Immunology, Lectures were very interesting, and was the course I had the most fun with.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Public transport in the city was much less expensive than expected (22 euro pr. month + 10 euro for a travel card (one time purchase)). Additionally, food in supermarkets were quite cheap as well. Housing was very expensive.
activities_available: There are many announcements on campus for sports clubs, theater clubs etc.
activities_recommended: Sport.
weekend_recommendations: Organize trips to other cities in Italy as well. The train networks are really good, and it is so easy to arrange one-day trips to other cities. Milan has a lot to offer as well, so be a tourist in your own city as often as you can.
culture_adjustment: Mostly easy. The toughest part was adjusting to their not-so-strict relationship with time, with most Italians being late for appointments.
socializing_tips: Go to a lot of events in the beginning - you are sure to find someone you click with, and the locals really want to help you on your way as well.
cultural_challenges: The student-teacher relationship. The professors are addressed as Professor followed by last name, and if you speak in Italian to a Professor, they are addressed in the formal way of speaking. This was not challenging, but definitely a significant cultural difference.
culture_appreciated: The spontaneous meetings hosted so often, such as meeting for a coffee or a drink, or watching sport on the local bar in the evening.
top3_advice: Do it, even if you're scared. I was. Attend the social activities early on. Even though the study is important, and much time should be used on that, get to explore the country and culture as much as possible - it is an experience you'll never forget.
other_useful_info: Attend lessons and start to study early on as well.
most_rewarding: Improving my Italian language level as time went, understanding new words used often in the daily use.
greatest_challenge: The self discipline needed to study on your own - the habits you have for studying at home (such as your good study partners) are not all applicable in the way the study is taught on the host university.
other_comments: Buon viaggio :)

crucial_aspects: In general I just love Italy, so Erasmus was a great personal opportunity for living in Italy.
info_ease: The University of Milan webpage contains a lot of information, but I needed to search for it myself, because I did not receive a lot of information directly from University of Milan.
arrival_assistance: The assistance there was; was a visit at the international mobility office of University of Milan. I got stamped my proof of attendance, an opportunity to ask questions and a goodiebag. It should be mentioned, that it was not a lot of assistance.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I made a study plan on the platform Unimia belonging to the University of Milan.
registration_help: It is possible to send an email to the international mobility office of the University of Milan.
registration_success: I was very succesful and I got exactly the courses I wanted. It is possible to change courses while you are at the exchange and it is possible to attend to courses at another faculty.
registration_advice: Take it chill, everything is going to be fine, when you are in Milan.
course_level: The level was a little bit lower than the level at Copenhagen University. However still a high level. I took some master courses as well.
teaching_comparison: It is smaller lectures, where the students participate more and in some classes there are student presentations.
courses_enrolled: I had the courses; Public Economics, International Economics and Policy, Economic History and Empirical Methods for Inequality Analysis. It should be mentioned, that the University of Milan has a trimester system on the Social Science faculty.

crucial_aspects: Good location, not too far from Denmark, and has a good law program. I wanted to go somewhere I haven't been before.

arrival_assistance: I received a lot of information through e-mail.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

Not a lot of study material either.
unexpected_costs: Not really any. You have to buy a router for internet if you live on campus, but I didn't have to because I lived in the main building were it worked.

activities_available: Not really anything that I know of at my University. But ESN was a very good organization for exchange students!

weekend_recommendations: Go on trips! Visit all the Italian cities you can around Milan. I went to Switzerland and France as well by train, so easy!
culture_adjustment: It took a couple of weeks. It was not super easy but once you get used to it, it's very fun.
socializing_tips: Again, join ESN. You will meet so many exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Italians are very laid back, so even University and exams are quite informal. It was surprising how you could have an oral exam in a room with other people. It was also difficult to communicate sometimes, as most Italians aren't good at speaking English.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated how open and friendly Italians are. The food was amazing!
top3_advice: Travel as much as you can Don't focus too much on school, it is not hard to pass Try to learn Italian
other_useful_info: Try to attend the Italian language course that is offered.
most_rewarding: All the traveling and meeting new people.
greatest_challenge: Getting used to the culture and learning Italian.

registration_success: I registered for all the classes I wanted that were available for the semester.
