courses_enrolled: Gender Justice Negotiation, Mediation, and Sustainable Conflict Resolution Law, Culture, and Development in a Global World Smart Cities, Artificial Intelligence, and Digital Transformation Law International Commercial and Investment Arbitration
recommended_courses: I would recommend Gender Justice for the exams and curriculum as well as the professor who was very passionate about her topic and teaching. I would also recommend Negotiation as it was not a very legal course and also had a big element of psychology. Keep in mind that a part of the grade consists of doing a recorded negotiation simulation in groups. And Smart Cities had a very easy written exam. I would NOT recommend the arbitration course because of the professor who is very unserious and not mindful of the students, and is very harsh at the oral exam.
unexpected_costs: Electric bill.
cost_comparison: Less expensive to travel around than I had expected and possible to find cheap rooms if necessary.
activities_available: Those that the ESN offered.
activities_recommended: Traveling around since Milan is perfectly located for travels around the north of Italy and as well as neighboring countries.
weekend_recommendations: Weekend trips around the country, going out to restaurants, seeing the city (museums, cultural sites, the opera, going to the top of the Duomo)
culture_adjustment: For me very easy, but it requires an interest in immersing yourself in the culture and wanting to experience the local life and stay positive and keep and open mind about the people and the culture.
socializing_tips: Find a common interest or sit with other people in the class and not just other Danish or international students and just go for it. Italians are very open and welcoming.
cultural_challenges: There were no cultural differences I found challenging.
culture_appreciated: The language and the mentality of the people.
top3_advice: Keep an open mind, and chose courses both based on your interest and also the difficulty. other_useful_info: Nothing I can think of.
most_rewarding: Learning the language and living with the Italian mentality and culture.
greatest_challenge: Living in the moment.
other_comments: No comments.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to stay within Europe and go to a university, which UCPH already had an agreement with, to make the planning easier. It was also important to me that there was a wide range courses available in English, which seemed interesting and relevant to me. And I had already been to Italy several times before, so I knew I would like the place and culture.
overall_comments: The information before my stay was very lackluster, so the practical parts consisted more of guesswork than guidance. But after getting used to their way, the duration of the exchange itself was enjoyable enough. I liked the classes and professors I had, and got to experience something different from what I'm used to. Unfortunately, their rules for exams are not as suited for exchange students, as I had to take 8 exams over two months, while staying there for longer or permanently allows you to space them out over a year. I found this take up more of my time, than I would have wished for, and resulted in not getting to travel as much around the country as I had planned on.
info_ease: I had to find almost all information myself, looking through their website and different portals, sometimes with outdated information and dates. The exchange office was out of office for almost all of August, and when we started receiving the first information in September, we were asked not to contact them with any questions apart from cancellation of our exchange etc. This meant that it was hard to know when the classes and intro days started, and thus when to book flights and accommodation etc. I was also assigned to a different faculty than the one I wanted to take my courses at, which meant that (even after asking to be moved to the correct one without success) I couldn't get access to the pages with information on my courses, such as course material, or that the start of a certain class had been postponed a week.
arrival_assistance: An intro day was held by the Erasmus Student Network, which was nice, but was more regarding their offers (bars/restaurants, sports days, city tours etc.) than practical information. Mot much assistance was given by the university itself, apart from finally getting information on course registration and such after classes had begun.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The information before my stay was very lackluster, so the practical parts consisted more of guesswork than guidance. I found this take up more of my time, than I would have wished for, and resulted in not getting to travel as much around the country as I had planned on.
registration_process: You have to sign up for an intranet called Unimia, where you can sign up for the courses you want. You also don't pick the courses from a list like at UCPH, but simply by typing them out. This, combined with the fact that you don't get any confirmation that you actually have been registered, gave me a lot of doubts on whether that was the actual registration. But it turned out to be the right way.
registration_help: The email with the instructions arrived after the courses had begun. Searching through the website and hoping that I was doing the correct thing, was what got me through it.
registration_success: I was admitted to all of the courses I registered for, despite not getting any confirmation or declination, as mentioned.
registration_advice: Have a lot of patience with the information and trust that you are doing it right.
academics_comments: The information before my stay was very lackluster, so the practical parts consisted more of guesswork than guidance. But after getting used to their way, the duration of the exchange itself was enjoyable enough. I liked the classes and professors I had, and got to experience something different from what I'm used to. Unfortunately, their rules for exams are not as suited for exchange students, as I had to take 8 exams over two months, while staying there for longer or permanently allows you to space them out over a year. I found this take up more of my time, than I would have wished for, and resulted in not getting to travel as much around the country as I had planned on.
course_level: I only took master's courses, as they were available in English, but I found the difficulty to be very similar to what I'm used to. Some parts were more difficult and other easier, depending on how much I knew about the topics beforehand - but that is hard to avoid.
teaching_comparison: I had a few practical and theoretical/computational exercises in a few of my courses, but otherwise it was solely lectures. I definitely missed the problem solving, which I am used to have at UCPH. You were also not expected to buy/read books for the courses, but the professors often still had recommendations.
courses_enrolled: - Cell therapy and gene silencing - Molecular pharmacology and immunology - Communicable and non-communicable disease - Biomarkers: From identification to exploitation
recommended_courses: I specifically liked the course "Cell therapy and gene silencing". It had a practical laboratory exercise and a theoretical on CRISPR, which I found to be a very nice change of pace. The subjects discussed during the lectures were also interesting to me and tied well in together with my previous courses in Copenhagen.
unexpected_costs: Accommodation ended up being very expensive for me, but otherwise I don't think anything surprised me.
cost_comparison: Public transportation within Milano is very affordable in comparison to Copenhagen
activities_available: City tour, restaurants/bars/clubs, trips to other cities, sports day, museum trips etc.
activities_recommended: As mentioned, I only attended the city tour, and I would recommend it. It was a nice way to see the different areas and buildings and hear about the history behind them.
weekend_recommendations: Exploring the city or other cities, though be prepared for a lot of people in the central part of Milano - especially on days off. In my experience trips taking up your whole weekend are better placed within the first two months of your exchange, before the exams begins.
culture_adjustment: For me, it took a week or two to get used to the culture. When not in the area of the campus, most people don't speak English, so being prepared for that and picking up a few Italian words is very helpful.
socializing_tips: Some of my classes barely had any international students and already knew each other from past semesters, which made it harder to socialize, than in some of my classes, where nobody knew each other. But everyone I met was very friendly, and I was also invited to cafés/restaurants and parties, so I would recommend just being open meeting new people. And attending the Erasmus event's will obviously also help meeting new people.
cultural_challenges: In the beginning, it felt a little weird not being able to speak to people, when we didn't share a common language. But after a while I picked up some phrases and got more used to finding other ways to communicate.
culture_appreciated: A lot of people being very friendly and helpful.
top3_advice: - Don't expect the practical part of registration and getting information to be easy, but trust that it will work out. - Even though it might be overwhelming when still feeling like you are settling in, the beginning of your exchange might be the best time to go on trip to other cities (due to exams in Dec-Feb). - Be open-minded: A lot of things are done differently regarding course structure, exams etc.
other_useful_info: The campus is spread out across a big part of the city, so it can be a good idea to check where your different classes are located, when choosing them. But be prepared that the location given on their page is not always accurate, and it might take some time to find the first time.
most_rewarding: Challenging myself by living in a different country and getting used to a different educational system and culture.
greatest_challenge: Just being away from most of the things in your life, you are used to, in general. Finding new ways to make things work. And of course the various challenges with course registration and faculty assignment, as mentioned throughout my travel report.

crucial_aspects: I initially wanted to go to Bologna more than anywhere else because of the culture and tradition and student atmosphere in the city. I ended up in Milan which was my 3rd choice. I accepted it immediately because it was still in Italy which was what my country of preference.
overall_comments: The whole process of going on exchange is very long and tiring. It tones the motivation to go on exchange down a bit. I understand, though, that it is necessary. However when finding proper accommodation is so difficult and expensive as it is in Milan, it gets really annoying being on exchange, out of your comfort zone. Of course I am responsible for not having found proper accommodation before I arrived in Milan but it is extremely difficult! I feel that there should be some extraordinary warning when applying. The Erasmus Student Network in Milan was great, the university was not. - They have no social events for student, or at least exchange students are not made aware. - The university is scattered over a vast area of the city. - The student information services are very poor. The app is pretty important and it's only in italian. It is really difficult finding your way around the university buildings. - The structure of classes is in some courses non-existent. It's unclear what the requirements are during the course. In some instances the method of teaching even changed drastically. - I had a 6ects course with a curriculum of at least 400 pages which is around half of the curriculum of a normal 15ects course at UCPH. - Italians are terrible at systems and structure. I had an exam where no one in the class was given any information about the exam except for the location. The exam turned out to be pure chaos. - I was registered for an exam but was removed from the exam again, seemingly without a reason. I didn't even receive any information about the withdrawal of the registration so it was probably just a system failure. That was the last chance to attend that exam and it was not possible to attend exams online. All in all, I liked the idea of trying new things, being part of another culture but the conditions for a good educational exchange were simply terrible.

crucial_aspects: To be in Europe, to get to a warmer climate, to go to a culturally and historically rich country.
info_ease: Very difficult; The university administration is inefficient, slow, and often does not do what is required.
arrival_assistance: None.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registration was very difficult due to the poorly maintained online page courses. I had trouble getting a learning agreement up until only a few days before, even though I started 3 months prior. I have had to send manual e-mail reminders and complaints several times to even get any answers, responses, and actions in my exchange registrations. The largest problem has been the long waiting times from Milano and the insufficient information that had me applying for courses that were not viable for me anyways.
registration_help: The only real help was that of my home university - any attempt to contact Milano was met with long waiting times.
registration_success: The original courses that I had originally planned to attend at Milano was one of the main motivations for applying to the university. A few weeks before going, I was told that these courses were not available for me anyway - a fact that was not made clear from any received information. This was incredibly inconvenient since everything was planned and paid, and I wouldn't be able to stay home and register for classes at my home university instead. The only sensible option was to go; If possible, I would have stayed home, but was robbed of that choice by the incompetent staff in Milano
registration_advice: Make sure you really want to go no matter what courses you wish to attend; Any unforeseen circumstances will be relayed last minute.
course_level: While I attended master courses in Italy, the academic matched that of bachelor courses in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: It was very lecturer-heavy with little to no student involvement and no required reading, compared to my home university.
courses_enrolled: Cell Biophysics; Mathematical Modelling for Biology; Measurement of Nanoscale Interactions and Data Analysis; Nonlinear Dynamics in Quantitative Biology; Structural Bioinformatics;
recommended_courses: Structural Bioinformatics: This course offers a practical introduction to biological molecular dynamics in all shapes and sizes; The lecturers are very skilled and the learning outcomes are valuable for anyone in bioinformatics.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Rent in Milano can be very expensive if you choose to find your own accommodations without the help of the University.
activities_available: Milano has one of the best Erasmus environments in Europe due to its high member count; They are excellent at organising events where you can get to learn new friends.
activities_recommended: Go to the initial Erasmus events, and take advantage of the fast and cheap inter-city trains with which you can reach most Italian cities in a few hours. Try to see as many different cities as possible, and find a stable group of friends to travel with.
weekend_recommendations: Take advantage of the fact that Milano has a ton of cafés and bars; Espressos and drinks are pretty cheap. Otherwise I would recommend doing train trips to visit other cities; Milano can get very urban and expensive in the long run.
culture_adjustment: People in university are very kind to exchange students, and you'll often find that young people are eager to help you train your Italian.
socializing_tips: Work up your Italian beforehand.
cultural_challenges: People seem less motivated at university, which can be tough; A lot of people are late or outright skips class. Italians can be very cynical about other people.
culture_appreciated: The Laissez-faire approach to exams; Last minute registration, flexible dates, no strict rules, and trust from the teachers.
top3_advice: 1. Start early with your registrations; Write and remind them the moment you think something is taking too long. Italian administration is notoriously unreliable. 2. When you get there, find a group of people you enjoy travelling with and plan as many trips as possible to as many different destinations as possible; For a small-ish country, Italy is incredibly diverse. 3. Try to learn some Italian beforehand, and go there 1-2 weeks before your classes start - social events orchestrated by the Erasmus Student organisation (ESN) usually start mid September; Otherwise it will give you some time to visit some of the more faraway places like Roma or Napoli.
other_useful_info: Make sure to research whether your area of housing is safe or not before booking; Theft, harassment, and robbery are a lot more commonplace than in Copenhagen.
most_rewarding: Getting a network of friends all over Europe from the Erasmus organisation.
greatest_challenge: I struggled with a series of unfortunate experiences like getting pickpocketed, sexually harassed, threatened, and assaulted. While I was a bit more unlucky, most exchange students I knew encountered at least one of these incidents while in Milano. Be sure to know which areas of Milano are risky and be careful when alone at night.

crucial_aspects: First and foremost, I looked at the courses available at the study destination. It was very important to me that the destination provided some interesting and relevant courses. Furthermore, I also wanted to go somewhere with a rich cultural and literary history, where I would be able to got o a lot of museums and do other cultural activities.
overall_comments: Overall my exchange experience was amazing, however, there was some administrative issues which made the experience a bit stressful especially in the beginning, as I felt like I did not have enough information.
info_ease: I found it quite hard. There was an office for international students where I could go and get some guidance, but there was a lot of information which I would have preferred to have before my arrival. This, for example, includes knowing exactly what courses I was going to attend, and when they would begin.
arrival_assistance: I went to the office, and they did help somewhat.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall my exchange experience was amazing, however, there was some administrative issues which made the experience a bit stressful especially in the beginning, as I felt like I did not have enough information.
registration_process: The registration process was quite easy, but finding courses was hard because a lot of the course's information came late, and furthermore, there was a lot of courses that did not end up being created, so it was hard to tell which courses you could actually take in the given semester.
registration_help: Again you could go to the office for international students, however, it was very limited what they could help with in regard to choosing courses.
registration_success: I was very successful, as I ended up registering for all the classes that I wanted to attend.
registration_advice: To be patient, as the process of finding courses and making a schedule where they all fit together can be long, but in the end you will figure it out.
academics_comments: Overall my exchange experience was amazing, however, there was some administrative issues which made the experience a bit stressful especially in the beginning, as I felt like I did not have enough information.
course_level: The level depended on the specific course, but in general I would say that the level of the courses was average.
teaching_comparison: In Copenhagen I am used to a mixture of lectures, group-work and student participation, however, in Milan it was almost exclusively lecture. I found this quite strange, as I believe that group-work and student participation are greats ways to learn.
courses_enrolled: Globalization, Social Justice and Human Rights (6) Journalism, Media and Politics (6) Contemporary English Literature (9) Human Development and Mobility in a Changing World (9)
recommended_courses: I would recommend Contemporary English Literature and Human Development and Mobility in a Changing World, because I found both of these courses extremely interesting, and moreover, the professors were very dedicated to their subjects.
unexpected_costs: I had to buy some kitchen equipment, which was unexpected.
cost_comparison: The housing was a lot more expensive then what I expected. However, the transportation was cheaper than what i am used to in Copenhagen.
activities_available: ESN created a lot of different bot cultural, athletic and social activities which you could participate in and where you could meet a lot of other exchange students.
activities_recommended: I would recommend participating in some of the ESN events. Particularly, I liked a pasta-making course and to visit nearby cities.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend that they go on trips to the nearby cities such as Verona, Venice, Lake Como etc. These cities are all fairly easy to reach by train and bus, and they are all very beautiful and cultural interesting places.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy, as the difference between Italian culture and Danish culture isn't too shocking. Of course there are some major differences, but personally I think it's exciting to get to experience and learn about other cultures.
socializing_tips: I think the easiest way is to talk to the local students during classes. You can either before or after a class approach them and talk to them about the course.
cultural_challenges: It seems to me that Italy may have a more laid-back approach to academics then what I am used to in Denmark - for example in Milan I didn't really get a study plan for any of my courses, which for me was quite challenging as I like to have an overview of the reading material.
culture_appreciated: I love Italian art, so I very much enjoyed visiting a lot of museums and such. Also the food is very lovely and especially Aperitivo is a quite nice concept.
top3_advice: To be patient, keep your mind open, and maybe make sure to have some savings beforehand, as going on exchange can be quite expensive, especially if you want to go on a lot of weekend trips and such.
other_useful_info: I was unaware that the oral exams would be so different from what I am used to in Copenhagen. All my oral exams in Milan was in held in a big room where all the students arrive at the same time, and then you do the exam one by one in front of everyone. For me, this was quite strange and uncomfortable, so I think it's worth being aware of it beforehand.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from so many different cultures and countries and hearing about their lives etc. Furthermore, I got to visit a lot of beautiful cities in the weekends, which was also full of great experiences.
greatest_challenge: For me, finding housing was the greatest challenge.

recommended_courses: Following courses can be directly transferred to courses at UCPH and are very suitable for our study programme: - Game Theory => Mikro III - Business History => Økonomisk Historie - Causal Inference and Policy Evaluation => Applied Econometric Policy Evaluation (p) The teacher in Risk Managament was very ambitious, but also strict. Corporate Finance was OK, but not very inspiring teaching style...
unexpected_costs: I bought an e-Sim through Vodafone at the Duomo to get more wifi.
cost_comparison: The prices is a bit lower than Copenhagen, but I also went out more and travelled more, so in the end I spent more money than at home - but it was worth it!
activities_available: Erasmus offer different cultural and social activities, you can attend.
activities_recommended: Just enjoy being a part of the Italian life and explore Milan.
weekend_recommendations: Visit other cities in Italy! I liked Bergamo, Florence, Bologna and Como. Also try to get the cheap tickets for the Teatro alla Scala. You can also get very cheap youth tickets for museums!
culture_adjustment: The Italians are very hospitable and enjoy sharing their culture. However, the language barrier can be challenging, but you will get use to it.
socializing_tips: I liked living at a dorm to meet other Erasmus students. There are plenty of danes from Copenhagen, you will bump into, but it also nice and interesting to meet students from other countries.
cultural_challenges: Primarily the language barrier...

most_rewarding: The new friends I got while I was away and the academic motivation I came home with after a change in environment.
greatest_challenge: To be patient and to learn that everything will work out.

socializing_tips: Get some friends with which you can meet up and hang out. Uni classes is a good spot
cultural_challenges: With roomates, there were very diffrent ideas of how clean and how noise you could be.
culture_appreciated: The culture about food, drinks, hanging out, eating for a long time and enjoying it
top3_advice: Remember to enjoy - 6 months goes very quickly. Go out to aperativo whenever you can.
other_useful_info: The rest shoul be figured out.
most_rewarding: The friends, the academic achievements and in general living in a nother country for 6 months.
greatest_challenge: Housing in general. My first housing was very bad.

crucial_aspects: The food, the country, the easy accessibility, the opportunity to travel to nearby places.
info_ease: Fairly easy.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any particular assistance upon arrival.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We used an online portal called UNIMIA - you could easily change courses during your stay.
registration_help: I do not know what kind of help was available, as I mostly asked fellow Erasmus students if I needed help.
registration_success: I was successful in registering for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Don't worry about changing courses - it is easy and can be done several times!
course_level: The level of the courses was not particularly high in comparison to what I was used to at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was a bit more formal at UNIMI, as the professors did not have as much of a personal bond with the students.
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled in the following classes: - Smart Cities, Artificial Intelligence, and Digital Transformation Law - Gender Justice - Law and Policies for Social Rights Protection in Europe - Comparative Labour Law - Public and Private Partnership for Sustainable Development
recommended_courses: I would recommend Gender Justice as it teaches you a lot about Women's Rights in general, as well as Comparative Labour Law as the professor is very friendly and teaches the students well.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Food in supermarkets was less expensive, shopping was a bit more expensive.
activities_available: I did not participate in any activities through the host institution.
activities_recommended: I would recommend any of the activities provided by the Erasmus groups! A great way to meet other students.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend visiting lake Como, as it is easily accessible by train. I would also recommend visiting the neighboring cities such as Verona, Torino, Parma and Bologna.
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy - people are very friendly.
socializing_tips: Try approaching the local students during aperitivo - in my experience they are very open to talking to international students!
cultural_challenges: The only challenging part of the culture was the language barrier.
culture_appreciated: The food!!
top3_advice: If you want affordable housing go further north, don't worry about changing courses in the beginning as the process of switching courses is fairly easy, and enjoy the food!!
other_useful_info: Not off the top of my mind.
most_rewarding: Making new friends and experiencing living in a different country.
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to a different lifestyle.

crucial_aspects: Fo find a destination that had exciting oppotunities- culture, food, history. And to find a destination that was not too far away from Denmark.
info_ease: Somewhat easy. The OLA was a bit complicated. But all mails we recived with deadlines and so on was helpfull.
arrival_assistance: Not so much assistance. No kind of official introduction because the trimester at the political science faculty - university of Milan -started much earlier than other faculties. So the introduction was too late for us who have been here for more than one month.
arrival_comments: Massimo Costa, the erasmus coordinator at university of Milan was kind and answered quickly on emails.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to register for courses myself, and register for exams. We had a "guideline" how to do it, so it was easy.
registration_help: "how to" guides online.
registration_success: Very successful. I got the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: just follow the guides, its easy
course_level: Some courses were easier than in Denmark, some was the same level i would say. Very different structure and system.
teaching_comparison: Not many exercises during class, as I am just to on economics in Denmark. Whe exams were also very loose, many students did not take it serious a cheated. No exam-guards, and nothing about to put bags and phones away as we are used to in Copenhagen.
courses_enrolled: 1. trimester jan-mar Data-driven economic analysis Economics of Inequality
recommended_courses: I find all my courses for relevant. Economics of inequality was easy if you are used to using STATA.
unexpected_costs: none
cost_comparison: Food and drinks are less expencive, but that i also expected.
activities_available: There were several oppotunities to engage in activities on campus, BUT every email about such things was in Italian, so difficult to know which one is important.
activities_recommended: Use the app Dice. Here you can find a lot of different events in Milan.
weekend_recommendations: to on trips to other cities, eg. Verona, Bergamo, Como, Hiking tours near Lake Como I visited Rome for a weekend, went by train. Very easy.
culture_adjustment: Easy,
socializing_tips: I didn's got many local friends. But just be open and ask to go to apperitivo or coffee together
cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: the late dining, and culture with apperetivo
top3_advice: Be open in the beginning to find new friends. Even though it can be challanging, it is fun to hang out with others. The system is very loose, so if you are confused about anything, just ask, or send emails to the professors.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: The people I met and hang out with. The many coffees before and after school where we were studying together.
greatest_challenge: My living situation. We has problems in my apartment, and no one took responsibility for anything, and that caused some problems.

arrival_assistance: Not that much - most of the times I had to contact the mobility office and not the other way around.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: A great experience - always great to challenges yourself and try something new.
registration_process: Do the ground work your self - the amount of info isn't always enough.
registration_help: I don't know, I did not use it.
registration_success: Succesful, I got all the classes I applied for.
registration_advice: Do the sound work your self - the amount of info isn't always enough. Contact the uni, don't wait for them to contact you.
academics_comments: A great experience - always great to challenges yourself and try something new.
course_level: Not as high as at my home uni.
teaching_comparison: The teachings were quite old fashioned - teacher talking for 1,5 hour and little to none student interaction.
courses_enrolled: LAW AND HISTORY NEGOTIATION, MEDIATION AND SUSTAINABLE CONFLICT RESOLUTION HISTORY AND INSTITUTIONS OF EAST ASIA ITALIAN LANGUAGE
recommended_courses: Go to Italy for the experience, not the courses. If any, do the language courses, they're free and definitely worth your time - great teachers and great way to meet new people.
unexpected_costs: Gyms are expensive
cost_comparison: Public transport in Milan is cheap - 22 euro pr. month.
activities_available: Many, but again, didn't use them.
activities_recommended: Be social, try to meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: In Milan there's always something happening, go to a concert, football match or take a train somewhere.
culture_adjustment: Fine.
socializing_tips: They're not great at talking to anybody else than them selves.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The cuisine.
top3_advice: Enjoy, don't do it for the classes but the great experience it is to do an exchange.
other_useful_info: Try to make local friends - you'll see the city/country in a total other way.
most_rewarding: The new friends I made.
greatest_challenge: The old fashioned way of teaching - something one has to be prepared for when doing exchange.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to Milan because it is a beautiful city, and because I love Italy.
info_ease: I found it a bit hard to find out what should be done and when - I received a lot of emails, but it was hard to know when I needed to do something. The many emails were very confusing.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance
arrival_comments: We did not receive any information on how we could find the timetable, exam dates etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We had to go to the Erasmus office and they had to sign the proof of attendance. Then we had to register for the subjects we wanted. This was a bit difficult, as it was difficult to see when the individual subjects had classes, and as it was not possible to see when the exam was. It was therefore difficult to draw up a schedule. At last we had to register for the exam, which I also found difficult, because you could only register for oral exams, and it was not made clear how to register for written exams.
registration_help: As far as i know there was no help to be had anywhere. I think you could go to the Erasmus office, but in general I don't think there was much help to be had.
registration_success: Not very succesful. I did not get any of the classes that I wanted in the first place. Many of the subjects I had initially chosen, I suddenly couldn't choose, and the classes were on top of each other in the subjects I could choose.
registration_advice: Don't expect to get any of the classes you want in the first place, as they may not be available after all. Also, expect to spend quite some time, to choose the classes.
course_level: I think the level of the courses were very low. We did not have to read anything through the semester, and overall, the teachers did not expect much from us. Furthermore the exams were quite unorganized and loose.
teaching_comparison: Very loose! AT UCPH they are a lot more coordinated and structured.
courses_enrolled: Access to justice in a multilevel constitutional system Law and policies of social rights protection in Europe Competiton law and economics Comparative Labour law Smart cities, artificial intelligence and digital transformation law
recommended_courses: Smart cities, artificial intelligence and digital transformation law was a very nice course and had an easy written exam.
unexpected_costs: I did now expect to use that many money on food. Groceries were very expensive.
cost_comparison: Local transportation was less expensive than I thought. You can get an ATM card for 22 €
activities_available: Erasmus hosted a lot of events for other exchange students.
activities_recommended: Watch a football match at San Siro, walk up the Duomo, Go to the Prada Museom, Brera-museum and the botanical garden in Brera.
weekend_recommendations: Visit lake Como (including the beautiful city Bellagio). Also visit Bergamo, Crema, Verona, Rome and Genova. Watch a football match at San Siro
culture_adjustment: I think it was very easy
socializing_tips: Talk to the local students in class, as you may not see each other outside of school.
cultural_challenges: I did not find it challenging
culture_appreciated: I kind of liked how loose the Italians were, including their way of hosting an exam.
top3_advice: You can expect to spend a lot of time choosing and coordinating your classes. The exams can be held in different ways, and you can not know in advance when these will take place. You need to get an italian tax-code (codice fiscale) !!! it may be hard to get, but you will need it in many ways.
other_useful_info: You need a tax code!! (codice fiscale)
most_rewarding: I got a lot of new friends from my own country, as we were a lot of danish exchange students in Milan. I also learned (from having two or three exam per week) that I should not stress that much about an exam - I just need to trust that I have done my best, based on the time we had to prepare for the exams.
greatest_challenge: The planning and scheduling - we constantly had to plan and schedule everything (including exams as we did not know in advantage when these would take place) and it was a bit stressful.

crucial_aspects: I chose my destination according to the lifestyle I would be experiencing. I think Italy is a perfect place for exchange if you want to meet new people and become a part of the italian culture, since most italians are very open and hospitable.
overall_comments: It was amazing and I can only recommend it!
info_ease: Overall, La Statale was good at informing about the formal things like trimester dates and guides to the university website etc. It got more and more confusing with exam formalities and communication during the trimester, but I also realized that they are more easygoing with deadlines and general university formalia, so you should not stress about it, even though the systems are very different from Copenhagen.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It was amazing and I can only recommend it!
registration_process: We did not have to settle on any courses until a month or more from arrival, so plenty of time to go to different courses and see what you like. After you found out which courses to take, you went to Unimia (the university website) to register and then you got a confirmation.
registration_help: You could write to your contact person in Milano, if you needed any help. I also wrote to the professors in charge of the course if I had any questions.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted, and I think most people did.
registration_advice: Use the first month to go to different classes and get to know the themes and maybe the exam form, so you know what suits you best.
academics_comments: It was amazing and I can only recommend it!
course_level: I did not find it challenging to take MA courses while being on my BA. The courses were very interesting, but the exams were easier than at home, so I had more focus on just learning new things and less on the final results.
teaching_comparison: Very different from home, since the teachers rarely called for us to interact in class. Also much less focus on references and theories but more a general overview of the topics, we discussed. If you wanted to use theories and references, you could read about them in the books available for studying, but if was not a demand for the exams.
courses_enrolled: Geopolitics of Migration Globalization, Social Justice and Human Rights European and International Migration Law Narrating and Negotiating Identities
recommended_courses: I would recommend the European and International Migration Law to anyone interested in the EU laws and international law on this specific topic. It was very interesting to learn about even though I never had a law course before. Geopolitics of Migration and Globalization, Social Justice and Human Rights was also interesting to learn about, especially in a country like Italy, because migration is on another level there, and the associated dilemmas are different from what we know. All courses except from Globalization (etc.) were on a new masters, which was offered for the first time when I went there, so the education was still in a process, which you could feel sometimes, but overall very interesting topics to touch upon, especially when learning about migration in a country like Italy.
unexpected_costs: Apparently electricity in Italy is the most expensive in Europe, so everyone got a huge bill, if they lived in rented apartments.
cost_comparison: Cheaper to go out for food and drinks, and you get more value for money than at home. Also cheaper to get around with public transportation and train rides to other italian cities. But of course, since it is cheaper, you do it more than at home, so it still ends up being expensive to live like this :))
activities_available: You could play sports and be in different clubs, but I did not use any of the offers actually.
activities_recommended: I did not use the activities.
weekend_recommendations: Go out of town when you have time, since Milano is perfect for taking the train around Lombardia. It's beautiful to go to the towns around Como or Garda. Also Torino, Firenze, Bologna, Genova, Bergamo and Verona are amazing to visit on a short trip. If you like skiing you can easily get to the mountains also. Otherwise Milano has a lot to offer, and you can enjoy the museums or the parks, and always get an aperitivo.
culture_adjustment: It was easy enough, if you just have patience and try to see things from the local's perspective in stead of your own. If you want to, you can learn a lot from the locals.
socializing_tips: I had all courses with a very small group of people from Italy, so they approached me, and then you just have to be open and suggest to hang out outside of school.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier could be a challenge sometimes, since not all italians are very good at english. Otherwise the bureaucracy in general can be quite frustrating, when compared to danish standards, and you have to have patience. But it is charming.
culture_appreciated: The hospitality and friendliness of the locals. You quickly become known in your local bars and cafées by the employeed, which is very cute. And of course the food, drinks and coffees were amazing.
top3_advice: One hundred percent do it! Milano is perfect for travelling around Italy, experiencing the italian lifestyle and still be in a big city, which is more organised than most italian cities. It is also very international, so you will meet both locals and foreigners everywhere.
other_useful_info: Most BA courses are in Italian, so check the MA opportunities before going.
most_rewarding: Meeting local friends and being introduced to a completely different way of living - also way more different and rewarding than I thought. It was also amazing to experience how Italy works and the associated rewards and problems for the locals.
greatest_challenge: Going home :)

crucial_aspects: I have always wanted to try living in Italy. My family and I have been coming there my whole life and I have studied the Italian language for a long time. I wished to try living la dolce vita in Bella Italia. Apart from that, I saw it as a good opportunity to get the Erasmus grant as support, so I didn't suck dry my savings.
info_ease: That was difficult. You definitely need to seek out all information yourself and find out who you can email your questions to. It puts a lot of responsibility, time and work on yourself, when you go to Milan on exchange. But to some degree I think that concerns going on exchange in general.
arrival_assistance: There is an Erasmus office with a coordinator, Massimo Costa, who is good at responding fast to emails. But the academic assistance was almost non-existing. I found it really hard to make it all add up and I had to figure it all out myself.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I can't even remember it now. But it was quite a bit of work to make it all up and figure out how to take courses on different master programmes to make it add up and how I made sure that it didn't overlap too much.
registration_help: Not much.
registration_success: I ended up with some courses that covered topics that I was very interested in, so I guess it added up fine. But also a lot of complications and not a lot of options that could work out.
registration_advice: Explore the unimi website and look in the course catalogue and look at the class schedule to see if it overlaps. Ally yourself with someone else if you can and figure it out together.
course_level: Specifically my courses were pretty hard because of everything described so far. But students at other faculties said it was way easier than what they were used to at home.
teaching_comparison: No curriculum in books, only slides for studying. Very dry lectures, not much class interaction.
courses_enrolled: Communicable and non-communicable diseases Pathogenetic basis of disease Applied pharmacology to biotechnology Italian language course
recommended_courses: Pathogenetic basis of disease. I enjoyed this class. A lot of pathologic basis of different diseases. A big course with 12 ECTS but only a multiple choice exam. It was interesting. Communicable and non-communicable diseases had the most interesting topics, but this is a no-go recommendation, as it has two parts and two exams and the professor responsible for the first part is super intimidating and unhelpful and arrogant and failed everyone including me at the exam. Italian language course could have so much potential and I was looking forward to it but unfortunately in was online on microsoft teams and it is impossible to learn that way.
unexpected_costs: Cannot think of anything.
cost_comparison: Public transport is super cheap and their public transport system is amazing with perfect metro lines, the beautiful tram and busses. A travel card with a monthly subscription was only around 20 euros a month, so super cheap. I made sure to take advantage of cappucinos for the general price of 1,5 euros and cocktails and wine for 3-7 euros. Eating out is also cheap, so we did that a lot. Grocery shopping is not that much cheaper, but still some! Especially veggies and fruit.
activities_available: Huge Erasmus student network in Italy! I was sure that I was gonna take advantage of that and spend a lot of time on that but I ended up finding friends through school and also a lot of danish students from UCPH that I hung out with instead. But a lot of fun social events and opportunities to meet new friends through ESN.
weekend_recommendations: Bologna is beautiful and centro storico there is classic italy vibes, so cozy. I wish I could have taken a trip to the dolomites and done some hiking. But como and the other lakes are also beautiful when the weather is nice. The old town in Bergamo is also breathtaking at golden hour.
culture_adjustment: I felt at home pretty fast.
cultural_challenges: All the academic differences for sure.
culture_appreciated: Their way of enjoying life.
top3_advice: 1. Go down to Italy before school starts. It starts super late in late september/early october, so I wish I had enjoyed some summer time there and done some traveling before school started. Because time goes fast and then there are exams already in december. 2. You have to be patient and not stress about all the practical and academic stuff, because the italians don't stress. Things are confusing and takes time.
other_useful_info: Maybe learn a bit of Italian before? Not all italians speak english and they can be rude because they feel insecure when trying to speak english.
most_rewarding: Getting to feel at home in another country. When I came back to Milan after Christmas, I had a strong feeling of feeling at home when people spoke Italian around me. The weather, the going out culture.
greatest_challenge: The academics and the exams. I had a rough time getting through that in december and january.

crucial_aspects: I love Italy and would like to learn more about the culture and become a part of it.
overall_comments: Milan is great - huge recommendation from me:)
info_ease: The website of University of Milan is very confusing, so I was very confused before arrivel, but I was sent the most important things by email.
arrival_assistance: I did not really receive any assistance, but I had a contact person from Unimi, who I could write to and step by his office, but I could have used more information in the beginning.
arrival_comments: There where no introduction or any activities for new international students, which was very disappointing.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Milan is great - huge recommendation from me:)
registration_process: Cant even describe all of it, but I had to find courses and send to the host institution and they had to approve that they where available. But when I first has it all in place, it went quite easy.
registration_help: A contact person from university of Milan, who was nice to help, but didnt always answer all questions or understood the problem. But he was nice and it all worked out.
registration_success: Very succesfull when I first found the courses available.
registration_advice: Take a deep look into the course catalogue and make sure which tri- og semester the course is available at and which faculty your subject is placed under, it has a lot to say about when you have to start your trimester or semester.
academics_comments: Milan is great - huge recommendation from me:)
course_level: Everything was much lower level than at UCPH. Everything from reading, lectures, exams ect. was very easy. I would say the level of the MA at UNIMI was lower than the BA at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: More lecturing and less group work. But a lot of discussion in class, more that at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Marketing (Advanced) Human Resources Management Consumer Culture Digital Cultures and Communication Research
recommended_courses: I would recommend Digital Cultures and Communication Research because the teacher (Gandini) was very good and the course was interesting even though it was a low level.
unexpected_costs: Just that the rent is so much higher than expected and in generel Milan is a very expensive city
cost_comparison: The rent is so much higher than expected and in generel Milan is a very expensive city. Coffee is cheaper than expected - but that is about the only thing (also some types of food).
activities_available: There are some group chats with Erasmus students, which have a lot of activities, but not really anything from the university itself.
activities_recommended: Follow @daysofmilan on Instagram and check out her recommendation for Milan
weekend_recommendations: Aperitivo and a lot of it - Milan has the best aperitivo (when you go out for drinks after school/work and get free snacks). Visit Navigli for drinks and try all the delicious restaurants in Milan. Also go to Lake Como.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, great food and great wine - easy to adapt to. But italians take everything very slow and easy, they are never on time and transport is not to trust.
socializing_tips: Not really, they keep a lot to themselves. But if you ask anything they are very nice!
cultural_challenges: Them not being on time and generally they have low situational awareness, which can be annoying. Also they talk a lot in class when the teacher is speaking, very rude.
culture_appreciated: The part about never stressing and always being kind to new people. And of course the food, the best part of Italy.
top3_advice: 1. Save money before, rent is expensive and you will eat your money up in great food and drinks! 2. Be openminded to new people and say yes to new things 3. Enjoy - once in a lifetime to be able to life your best life in Italy
other_useful_info: Check in good time when the trimester or semester starts, it changes from faculty to faculty
most_rewarding: Making new friends for life <3
greatest_challenge: The economic part - more expensive than expected.
other_comments: Go to Milan - it's worth it :)))

crucial_aspects: Jeg har altid gerne ville prøve at på i en sydeuropæisk storby, og fandt Milano fuldstændig oplagt til at prøve dette, og samtidig fuldføre mine studier.
info_ease: Det var nemt at få den rette og nødvendige information. Udvekslingskoordinatoren i Milano var meget tilgængelig og hjælpsom, og hjalp mig med diverse spørgsmål.
arrival_assistance: Udvekslingskoordinatoren hjalp mig med at forstå, hvilke fag jeg kunne søge. Da jeg var afsted, var der stort set ingen fag udbudt på antropologi, hvorfor jeg måtte søge andre valgfag, og her var udvekslingskoordinatoren til stor hjælp.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Den første uge af semestret, kunne man prøve forskellige fag af, inden man kunne vælge dem endeligt. Det fungerede godt, da man her fik mulighed for at blive lidt klogere på, hvad de forskellige fag omhandlede, før man tog sin beslutning. Det var derudover nemt, at registrere sine fag, og der var ingen begrænsning på, hvor mange elever, der var på hvert fag.
registration_help: Udvekslingskoordinatoren var til rådighed ved eventuelle spørgssmål.
registration_success: Det gik strålende!
registration_advice: Prøv forskellige fag af, før du beslutter dig endeligt.
course_level: Niveauet til kurserne var meget svingende. De forventede ofte, at man vidste en del, og man kunne godt få indtryk af, at niveauet var højt, men dette afspejlede ikke det endelige niveau til eksaminerne.
teaching_comparison: Det er væsentligt anderledes. Der er stort set kun forelæsninger, og ingen holdundervisning, og som studerende er man ikke særligt aktiviteret og involveret, man lytter for det meste blot.
courses_enrolled: Geopolitics of Migration European and International Migration Law Narrating and Negotiating Identities Globalization, Social Justice and Human Rights
recommended_courses: Disse tre fag: Geopolitics of Migration, European and International Migration Law og Narrating and Negotiating Identities, var alle på en kandidat, der hedder 'Migration Studies and New Societies'. Hvis man interesserer sig for flygtninge- og migrationsområdet, er det nogle ok fede fag. Dog er der et par gentagelser på tværs af fagene, og kvaliteten af undervisningen er MEGET svingende. Niveuaet var klart højest i 'European and International Migration Law', men det var også her, hvor jeg selv fik det største udbytte.
unexpected_costs: Ikke nogen
cost_comparison: Mad og drikke er generelt en smule billigere end i Danmark
activities_available: Der var helt sikkert en række muligheder, men ikke noget jeg blev gjort særligt opmærksom på.
activities_recommended: Jeg vil klart anbefale at udnytte de gode togforbindelser i Italien, og tage på weekendture til både Comosøen og en masse af de andre omkringliggende byer og naturoplevelser.
weekend_recommendations: Se ovenstående.
culture_adjustment: Det er meget nemt at falde til i den italienske kultur.
socializing_tips: Snak med de lokale til og mellem undervisningen. De er oftest mega udadvendte og gæstfrie. Jeg oplevede f.eks. at blive inviteret med til en bachelorfejring i Torino, hvilket var en stor oplevelse.
cultural_challenges: Ikke nogle særlige udfordringer.
culture_appreciated: Deres mad- og drikke kultur.
top3_advice: - Vælg nogle fag, der afspejler din faglige profil herhjemme også. - Opsøg de lokale til undervisningen - Tag på weekendture i området
other_useful_info: Ikke lige umiddelbart
most_rewarding: At få lov til at bo og opleve en sydeuropæisk som Milano, og samtidig passe mine studier. Milano er den skønneste by, der har så meget at byde på.
greatest_challenge: At tilpasse mig det faglige niveau, hvilket var svært, da mine kurser spændte bredt og gik i mange forskellige faglige retninger.

crucial_aspects: Love for italian culture, cuisine and the location itself.
info_ease: Rather difficult at first, but thankfully I got good guidance from the Erasmus coordinators. Also, I had several friends also on exchange, which made it easier for all of us as we could share tips and tricks for getting into the rhythm of studying in Milan.

recommended_courses: Conflict Management and Negotiation was really interesting! It had a level of psychology, and the professor was really motivating and created an inspiring learning environment.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Italian foods are really inexpensive. Some foods common in Denmark were not as cheap or available. Eating out wasn't very expensive. Coffee is really cheap!
activities_available: I didn't participate in any organised activities by Erasmus og the university. Clubs, restaurants, and shopping were really good though.
activities_recommended: Eat out. A lot.
weekend_recommendations: Bologna, Como.
culture_adjustment: I didn't find it that hard. There is of course differences, but overall fine to adjust.
socializing_tips: Ask them about recommendations.
cultural_challenges: The hierarchy between students and professors was probably my biggest cultural challenge. Also their education system is quite different. The level and quality is not that high, and for exams you must memorise everything. This was really challenging.
culture_appreciated: The food and the weather.
top3_advice: The teachers levels of English may vary, you need to be proactive if you want information regarding exams, lectures etc., the exams are very different from the Danish exams.
other_useful_info: It was really helpful to have a network of other Danish students. And roomies, wouldn't have been without that.
most_rewarding: Getting international friends - it really is an amazing experience.
greatest_challenge: Handling the exam forms, as the exams are time pressuring and closed book.

crucial_aspects: Milan is rich in history, art, and culture, which made it a very attractive destination for me. Familiarizing yourself with Italian customs, etiquette, and cultural nuances can enhanced my overall experience and facilitate interactions.
overall_comments: Studying in Milan has been an incredible experience, marked by significant personal growth and a unique journey of self-discovery. The challenges I encountered while navigating a new academic and cultural environment were instrumental in pushing my boundaries and expanding my horizons.
info_ease: Upon arrival in Milan, it was easy to access the information needed. The city has a well-organized infrastructure and a wealth of resources designed to assist newcomers. Clear signage, readily available maps, and helpful information centers made navigating the city and understanding essential services straightforward.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival at my study destination in Milan, the support and assistance provided were quite helpful, although there were some instances where the process seemed less structured, particularly when it came to choosing courses. In Italy, there is often a more flexible and dynamic approach to certain administrative aspects, and this can be perceived as "last minute" compared to more structured systems.
arrival_comments: Over time, I learned to adapt to this aspect of the Italian academic system. While it might seem last minute initially, it became a part of the cultural experience, teaching me to be more flexible and open-minded in my approach. The informal and adaptable nature of certain administrative processes eventually became a characteristic that I not only accepted but also embraced as part of the unique experience of studying in Italy.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Studying in Milan has been an incredible experience, marked by significant personal growth and a unique journey of self-discovery. The challenges I encountered while navigating a new academic and cultural environment were instrumental in pushing my boundaries and expanding my horizons.
registration_process: Initially, it required pre-approval from my home institution, Copenhagen University. However, the actual selection of courses took place only after arriving at the host university in person. Upon physical presence at the university, I had the opportunity to choose my courses. Interestingly, the available courses sometimes differed from the ones I had initially selected back home. This variation added an element of adaptability, as I had to be flexible and open to exploring alternative subjects. Throughout the semester, there was an option to attend classes before making a final decision on whether to commit to those specific courses. This flexibility allowed for a more dynamic adjustment of the academic schedule, enabling students to tailor their coursework based on personal preferences and academic interests.
registration_help: There was a form of study office or academic support center available to assist students with various aspects of their academic journey.
registration_success: Registering for the classes I initially wanted turned out to be a bit of a challenge. The process required a higher level of self-discipline and adaptability. While the courses I had in mind were not always readily available, I learned that taking a flexible approach and being open to alternative options could lead to a rewarding academic experience. In navigating the registration process, I discovered that many courses required a degree of self-management. Creating a schedule that aligned with my academic goals and personal preferences became my responsibility. This level of autonomy meant that success in class registration was not only about getting the desired courses but also about shaping a schedule that suited my overall objectives.
registration_advice: Remember, many students go through the same experience, and institutions are generally well-equipped to support exchange students during the registration process. Trust the journey, stay positive, and enjoy the adventure of studying in a new and dynamic academic setting.
academics_comments: Studying in Milan has been an incredible experience, marked by significant personal growth and a unique journey of self-discovery. The challenges I encountered while navigating a new academic and cultural environment were instrumental in pushing my boundaries and expanding my horizons.
course_level: The level of courses at my home institution in Copenhagen was generally perceived as higher compared to those at the host institution in Milan. While the overall academic standards and the depth of subject matter were commendable in both places, there were notable distinctions in terms of teaching methods and communication styles.
teaching_comparison: In Denmark, the educational system places a strong emphasis on interactive learning, critical thinking, and student engagement. The courses are often designed to encourage independent research, class discussions, and a high level of student participation. The teaching methods are structured to foster a deep understanding of the subject matter and promote analytical thinking. On the other hand, in Milan, I observed that the teaching methods were somewhat different. The communication style tended to be more traditional, with a greater reliance on lectures and less emphasis on interactive discussions. While the teaching content remained at a high level, the approach to conveying the material differed, placing a slightly stronger emphasis on traditional lecture-style teaching.

activities_recommended: Museums: Milan is home to several museums, including Pinacoteca di Brera, Leonardo da Vinci Science and Technology Museum, and Museo del Novecento, where you can explore art, science, and modern art history. Theater and Opera: Enjoy a theater performance at La Scala or experience an opera show in one of the city's beautiful opera houses.
weekend_recommendations: Parco Sempione: Relax in this large city park surrounding Sforza Castle. Perfect for unwinding, strolling, or jogging. Navigli District: Explore the charming canals in the Navigli area, filled with trendy cafes, shops, and art galleries. Shopping: Milan is known as a fashion capital, so indulge in shopping at trendy stores and shopping streets like Via della Moscova and Corso Como.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture of my exchange site was surprisingly easy. The people were welcoming and friendly, making the transition smooth and enjoyable. Interacting with locals and fellow students provided valuable insights into the cultural norms, social customs, and daily life in the community.
socializing_tips: To be open, approachable, and proactive in seeking out opportunities to connect with local students. Building relationships takes time, so be patient and enjoy the process of cultural exchange.
cultural_challenges: One cultural difference that I found particularly challenging during my exchange was the language barrier, which, in turn, contributed to some cultural nuances. In Italy, particularly in more reserved or formal settings, language proficiency plays a crucial role in communication. While many Italians speak English, there were instances where my limited proficiency in Italian posed a challenge, especially in academic or administrative contexts.
culture_appreciated: The food and the osteria vibes with local people
top3_advice: Being present, immersing oneself in the local culture, and building connections—will contribute to a more fulfilling and enriching exchange experience at your host institution.
other_useful_info: Not really
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was gaining the opportunity to see my everyday life from a different perspective and having the time to engage in new activities and learning experiences. Stepping out of the familiar environment of my home institution allowed me to broaden my horizons, both personally and academically. Experiencing daily life in a new cultural context provided valuable insights into alternative ways of living, thinking, and approaching various aspects of life. It allowed me to challenge my preconceptions, question assumptions, and develop a more nuanced understanding of the world. Having the time and freedom to explore different aspects of life, whether through cultural activities, social interactions, or academic pursuits, was immensely rewarding. It provided space for personal growth, self-discovery, and the acquisition of new skills and knowledge.
greatest_challenge: Challenges in finding a balance between cherishing the newfound independence and navigating the emotional aspects of being away from the familiar support network. Over time, it became an opportunity for personal growth and resilience, teaching me to embrace change and cultivate connections in diverse settings.

culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Learn some Italian.
cultural_challenges: Regarding school, everything is very "unplanned" and us students are poorly informed. I never really knew what was expected of me at the exams, nor what the exams consisted of exactly.
culture_appreciated: Other than the food and Aperitivo - The easy-going and relaxed vibe (except when it comes to school).
top3_advice: 1) Save up some money so you can experience what Milan has to offer. 2) Don't worry too much about the lack of information - everything will work out in the end! 3) Don't stress about not doing something new every day. other_useful_info: Make sure to apply for the codice fiscale before you leave Denmark. It's much, much easier than having to obtain it once you have landed in Italy (I'm speaking from experience).
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and being able to spend my weekends traveling.
greatest_challenge: Getting my codice fiscale, making sure my courses didn't overlap, and not being properly informed about how/when my exams would take place.

overall_comments: Best decision I have made so far! 10/10
info_ease: Italians are very helpful if you ask. Therefore, you may not receive all the information upon arrival that you are used to in Denmark but the answer is always one email away. The Erasmus office at the uni was very helpful and quick to respond.
arrival_assistance: Again I received info from the Erasmus office at my uni.

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Best decision I have made so far! 10/10
registration_process: The registration itself is easy and you have plenty of opportunities to change courses within the first couple of weeks. You just have to find the course, ECTS, professor and then write it in the UNIMIA online platform, where you also register for exams and so on.
registration_help: You can write to the Erasmus office or directly to the faculty. But I think it was difficult to find where I should write to the faculty, because they use an online platform for communication.
registration_success: I was successful in registering. Although one course was cancelled because the professor had become sick, so it had to find another course.
registration_advice: Look at different courses that might interest you and then write them down. Thereafter, look them up in the uni's calendar, so you can see if the time schedules clash or not. Sometimes the professors allow you to attend their course even though you are not able to attend every class every week, because you maybe have a different course at that time. I would recommend that you try and have no classes on either monday or friday, if you want to be able to travel for longer/long weekends :) Also look out for what kind of exams the courses have, because some exams are considerably easier than others. If the courses say that attendance is 'mandatory', that does not mean that you have to write your name or check-in every time you go to class. For some courses you have to, for others the professors don't bother taking attendance even though it says that they do. So go to the classes and see what that professor does.
academics_comments: Best decision I have made so far! 10/10
course_level: Level was lover than in Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: The teaching is more focused on you attending and asking questions. I did not have to buy any books because the professors provided all the reading material on the online platform Ariel. The written exams are by hand and the oral exams are in front of the people in your class.
courses_enrolled: Gender Justice (6 ECTS) Comparative Labour Law (6 ECTS) Artificial Intelligence, law issue and sustainable development (6 ECTS) Public and Private Partnership for Sustainable Development (6 ECTS) Environmental and Food Law (6 ECTS)
recommended_courses: Courses I would recommend: I would really recommend taking the course ' Comparative labour Law' with Marco Biasi. The course gives you a general overview of labour laws around the world and the history behind labour. The professor is very sweet, funny and accommodating and tries to make everyone feel good. The exam is either oral or multiple-choice (you get to choose). I would also recommend taking Environmental and Food Law. It is a very interesting course built up by two different areas, with one professor teaching Food Law and one teaching Environmental law. The professor are good at involving the students and making it interesting with relevant reading material and you also learn a lot about the political side. Student who attend the classes get to write an assignment as their exam, while you can also choose to take a written exam. The courses Artificial Intelligence, law issue and sustainable development and Public and Private Partnership for Sustainable Development are interesting/practical enough for you to use some other the knowledge in the future. The exams are 'written exam with 3 questions' and for the other one it is a group powerpoint presentation. Courses I DO NO RECOMMEND!: Do not take 'Gender Justice' with Costanza Nardocci. The course itself is very interesting and deals with a lot of politics and sociology. But the professor is very intimidating and degrading. She does not create a healthy environment for learning and does not answer your questions or emails. The exam is oral + 2 written assignments, she will not explain what you can expect to encounter in the exam and she will judge your performance based on her mood that day.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs. The SU and Erasmus scholarship covered all my usual expense + the majority of my travel cost. But of course I used different amounts for travel, depending on where I went.
cost_comparison: The food in the supermarket is around the same cost as in Denmark. Eating out is a bit cheaper than in Copenhagen and travelling is cheap, if you buy the train tickets/flight tickets around 2-4 weeks before.
activities_available: The uni did not really have any non-academic opportunities.
activities_recommended: If you are interested in sports, join a WhatsApp groups chat through ESN, where people who have similar interests arrange training sessions. I would personally recommend going to the museums, going traveling through Italy and go to the ESN events. You will meet all of your friends through ESN and they also organise a lot of different non-academic activities.
weekend_recommendations: Go travelling! go out at night with your friends and eat some good italian pizza and pasta. I really recommend going for 1 day trips to Lake Como, Lake Garda, Torino, Bergamo, Venice. I went on a fantastic weekend trip to Firenze + Bologna and on another weekend trip to Palermo (Sicily) + Napoli. Would recommend!!! Loved Sicily <3
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. Italians are very polite but you have to be patient. They don't all speak English fluently, so be accommodating and try and learn some basic words/sentences, this will help you a lot.
socializing_tips: Go to the ESN events! you will meet the Italians that are volunteers/organizers there. That's how I got local friends. Otherwise, talk tot he Italians in your courses or rent a room in an apartment where other Italians live.
cultural_challenges: When the uni or dorm writes that something is not possible, it usually is perfectly possible, but you will have to write/call several times in order to get it sorted. They don't want to do extra paperwork.
culture_appreciated: The relaxed attitude to life, the passionate way they speak to you and greet you.
top3_advice: The Erasmus Office (Massimo) is your best friend. When in doubt write an email. Remember to take 1-2 days off from ESN events and social things every week. It is so much fun to be social but you will get burnt out if you don't also prioritize relaxing. Travel at any opportunity, don't be afraid ti write into the ESN chat and ask people if they want to go out or travel somewhere. There are always people in the same situation as you <3
other_useful_info: Get the ATM travel card, it's only 22 euros pr. month for students and get the CartaFreccia on the Trenitalia website, for student discounts on quick trains.
most_rewarding: The friends I gained from all over the world, the travelling/social events, and the new perspective on different countries in europe/world, which only underlines how privileged we are <3
greatest_challenge: The hardest part was the first couple of days where you realise that you are ON YOUR OWN. But as soon as you find some friends (go the the ESN events), then you will see that everyone is on their own, but it is not as scary, when you have others to share/support you on your journey :)
other_comments: Don't overthink it <3 everything will work out :)
