My classes overlapped, so I had to apply for entirely new classes to avoid scheduling conflicts. However, this cannot be verified when applying for credit transfer for the classes. It is important to note that you should not feel assured of obtaining all the credits applied for since they often overlap. Nevertheless, it is very easy to switch classes, and you can do this yourself midway through the semester, so there's no need to stress about it.
registration_advice: Register for the classes that you find most attracting and if they overlap, then ask other students about classes that they have registered for and if they are good. You can afterwards just change classes.
academics_comments: I am overall very positive and happy about my exchange stay in Milan and I would recommend everyone to go. Unfortunately, the University, however, had some deficiencies. First and foremost, there was not the same level of assistance regarding how to navigate, how exams were conducted, or a general understanding that not everyone was from Italy. Therefore, you had to find all informations by yourself down to the smallest detail and arm oneself with patience when it came to practical matters. The university is very beautiful and you really get the feeling of being in a Harry Potter movie, but unfortunately, the exterior doesn't quite live up to the interior. It's an old university where it's very hot in the summer and super cold in the winter time. Additionally, the professors were generally not very helpful or keen on answering questions.
course_level: The level during the semester is much easier than in Copenhagen, but I found the exams challenging because the professors don't provide information on how the exams will be conducted or what is expected. The difficulty level is much lower throughout the semester, as you don't receive textbooks nor the same amount of homework. However, you have 5 courses instead of 2 or 3, so there might be more work leading up to the exams.
teaching_comparison: It varies from professor to professor, but generally, they were a bit more distant and formal in their teaching approach. It was important to address them correctly and not be too personal in your interaction with them. Additionally, not all of them were proficient in teaching in English.
courses_enrolled: Access to Justice Comparative Labour Law Gender Justice Smart Cities, Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation Law Law and Policies of Social Rights Protection in Europe
recommended_courses: I would recommend the course: Law and Policies of Social Rights Protection in Europe The teacher is very nice and understanding. Moreover, I liked the form of the exam. You had to do a large assignment and then talk about the assignment in the end of the course. Moreover, I would recommend the course: Smart Cities, Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation Law The teacher is very nice and the exam is very easy. You just have to answer some easy questions in the end of the semester about your own thoughts about the main topics.
unexpected_costs: There are a lot of very nice cities close to Milan.Therefore, I spend a lot of money on adventures outside Milan by train. However, I will recommend this to everyone.
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive than I thought.
activities_available: I don't know.
activities_recommended: I dont know.
weekend_recommendations: Go outside Milan and visit other cities like Verona, Bergamo or Lake Como. It is easy and cheap by train.
culture_adjustment: I think it was quite easy and Italians are in general very sweet. However, many Italians dont speak English and sometimes it was hard to undertand each other.
socializing_tips: My experience was that the local students did not attend any of the English classes. Therefore, I mostly meet other exchange students from different counties, which was also very nice. However, I had very sweet Italian neighbors, who invited us for dinner and drinks and we became good friends. Therefore, my advice is to just approach people, be open, and friendly.
cultural_challenges: The professors are way more formal in how they approach people. Furthermore, they don't have the same culture regarding waiting times, so I often waited a very long time at places such as post offices, supermarkets, or general in public institutions. I experienced that there wasn't the same respect for other people's time.
culture_appreciated: Italians are very open and I liked how everyone just talked to each other on the streets and in bars and stuff.
top3_advice: 1. Have patience - Everything takes a long time in Milan, so don't stress about missing a deadline 2. Look forward to live in Milan - It is an amazing experience and I will never forget my time here. 3. Be openminded and experience as much as you can - Throughout the semester, you have a lot of time outside school hours, so just experience the city and all the beautiful places and go outside Milan for the weekend.
other_useful_info: I dont think so.
most_rewarding: Getting to know so many new people and be familiar with a new city, that I look forward to get back to.
greatest_challenge: Being away from my friends and family back home. Luckily, Milan is only 2 hours away fromDenmark, so I was happy to get a lot of visitors.

crucial_aspects: The weather and the food, and that it was the furthest destionation from Denmark possible during the bachelor's degree
overall_comments: It was amazing! Can only recommend it
info_ease: It was pretty straightforward. Just do as you're told in the mails you get sent and ask any and every question you may have to Massimo Costa (the erasmus coordinator)
arrival_assistance: Not really anything other than Massimo Costa and the mails
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was amazing! Can only recommend it
registration_process: You get a mail and they tell you exactly how to do it.
registration_help: You can always email Massimo Costa and he'll find every answer you need for you.
registration_success: Before going, I had a lot of classes I wanted to attend. Some of them I couldn't however, because they overlapped with each other. Especially the cool private law classes, most of them sadly overlap.
registration_advice: Take your time before choosing a course. There's not really any deadline for registering, so just go to each class you think is interesting and see if it is for you - i switched class a couple times during the semester.
academics_comments: It was amazing! Can only recommend it
course_level: A lot of the classes are way more theoretical than in Copenhagen. You learn theory, a bit of economics and a lot of social sciences, instead of the more classic hardcore law that we have in Copenhagen - atleast during the bachelor's courses. Aside from that, they also have really small courses all at 6 ECTS, which means it can sometimes feel like you learn a little about everything - which can feel like learning nothing! The classes are all interesting in their own way, but their exams were for the most part super easy, so no worries.
teaching_comparison: It really depends on the course. Overall, as mentioned, I would say it was a lot more theory, a lot more knowledge about society as a whole and the role in which law plays in it, and not so much the classic learning of how to apply the law.
courses_enrolled: M and A: The Contract Artificial Intelligence, Legal Issues and Sustainability European Monetary and Economic Law Theory and Practice of International Tax Law Comparative Labour Law
recommended_courses: I would honestly recommend all of them, they each had something good about them. My main recommendation - and the one which I felt was both the most difficult, time consuming, but also the most rewarding and the one I felt I learned the most from - was M and A: The Contract. In this course, you learn how to read M and A contracts and understand them as well as the M and A process. The professor uses the socratic method of teaching, which means he basically just asks the students a lot fo questions for the most part and tries to engage us as much as possible. He can be a bit scary and straightforward, but it forces you to read the contracts in advance and prepare for classes, which means you actually learned something! It felt like an advanced version of Obligationsret from back home with an international and practical twist. Monetary law has an easy exam, it's just a powerpoint presentation about a self-chosen subject that relates to monetary law. Tax law has a really cool professor, who is really engaged. The subjects were interesting, and it felt like you learned a lot about tax evasion, which is always cool. Artificial Intelligence had a slightly bad professor, but she knew her material. The course covered a variety of legal issues connected with AI, such as AI-weapons in warfare, AI-systems and tort liability etc. You got a good introduction into new legislation from EU and the UN on the way and I really enjoyed learning these things. Labour Law sounded really boring for me, but I was pleasantly surprised. The professor is amazing, he is really down to earth and cracks jokes and made learning interesting. The subjects themselves were also not the typical boring old labour law - it was very focused on the future of labour: workers rights in digial platforms such as Uber, workers rights in the metaverse, workers rights with regard to corporate law etc. The course was also comparative, so you got an insight into a variety of different jurisdictions and you got an excellent feel for the actual thoughts and "hensyn" behind the rules.
unexpected_costs: Not really any tbh
cost_comparison: Eating out is pretty much the same as in Denmark, as well as grocery shopping. Meat is a bit expensive in the shops. Buying drinks is cheaper most places.
activities_available: The university itself didn't really offer that much. But the ESN events were really cool and helpful for meeting new people, especially in the beginning! There was something for everyone, museum trips, trips to other cities, food tours etc. I met some cool people through the ESN events that I kept in contact with during my entire stay and did cool things with.
activities_recommended: Go to the ESN food tour, that was pretty cool. In general just go to the ESN things in the beginning and meet some exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: Travel to other cities! If the weather is good, go to Lake Como (especially Bellagio). Go to venice during the off-season, go to Florence, Veronna. Plane tickets are also pretty cheap, so you could go to Napoli (amazing food) or further south to Sicily
culture_adjustment: 90% of the time it was pretty easy. And then sometimes it was kind of difficult. Mostly, not knowing the language kind of really was annoying at times, because Italians hate speaking english and mostly don't know it. Also they don't really have the same strict following of rules that is in danish culture.
socializing_tips: Live in a student dorm where you're surrounded by them :) Or go to the ESN events and talk to the organizers, they are super nice! Tell Giulia I said hey.
cultural_challenges: Same answer as before.
culture_appreciated: The food of course. And the warmth of the people mostly, especially some of the professors surprised me - the prof in tax law bought aperol and snacks for the entire class!
top3_advice: 1. Don't forget to enjoy it, soak it in and really just relish in it. Time will fly and all of a sudden you'll be back in Denmark again, scrolling through your camera roll and living the good memories. 2. Write a diary, film some videos when you're out, take lots of pictures! Trust me, you're gonna be thankful you did when you're back home and want to relive the good old times. 3. Try to meet different people when you're down there. There are lots of danish students going to Milan, so it can be really easy to just surround yourself with danish people, go to danish parties etc. But trust me, meeting people from different cultures, meeting italians, partying with them and becoming genuine friends is so so rewarding.
other_useful_info: Buying someone a drink goes a long way for making many friends.
most_rewarding: The food, the trips and mostly the people. I made some really good friends down there and they truly made my experience amazing.
greatest_challenge: Not knowing the language, as well as the occasional loneliness or missing people from home.
other_comments: Nyd det for helvede!!!!

top3_advice: - Use time on checking the courses before comming there. But don't stress out if you get confused as this will be more understandable when coming here. - Try to find courses you are interested in, and come to lectures this is a great way to get included to activities after school with local students. - Dont choose to challenging courses, exchange is also about having the time to get to know a different culture/people and country.
other_useful_info: University of Milan has a lot of different faculties, so checking where the lectures of your courses is smart, so you don't have to run between different locations of the city to get to your lectures.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange was all the great people I met and got to know from all over the world. I learned a lot from getting out of my comfort zone as I didn't know anyone from before. I developed myself a lot both, academically and personally.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was the feeling of not having a huge net of people around me. This was mostly a challenge in the beginning, before I got to know people.

activities_available: There were several opportunities to join trips around the city/country together with other students
activities_recommended: I didn't go trough activities with the university but planned trips with other students trough the Erasmus WhatsApp group

culture_adjustment: It took a months time to get into a new routine but Milano is fairly easy to get used to if you are used to live in a bigger city.
socializing_tips: It can be kinda tough (at least on the master) because it seems like most local students have their groups of friends. I was lucky enough to have a class where we had group work and that was an easy way for me to start talking to some of the locals.
cultural_challenges: I dont know if challenging is the right word but they are less strict with administrative things. Deadlines are not as serious here which also means that it can sometimes feel a little chaotic, like there is no control over it. Its just very different for what I'm used to in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: The more relaxing atmosphere and that its cheap to go out and socialize with people
top3_advice: Say yes to day trips with new friends. don't stress about being late for class. Learn a little bit of italian beforehand - that will get you a long way.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Getting ou of my comfortzone and getting friends from around the world
greatest_challenge: The language barrier because not alot of people speak English well.

crucial_aspects: I knew I wanted to go to Italy first of all. I have lived there many years and have a strong connection to the country and I wanted to go back.
info_ease: It was easy! We were will informed
arrival_assistance: Just the e-mails from Mobilityonline which were super helpful
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was pretty confusing, a lot of deadlines and some miscommunications between the institutions which turned out to solve itself but it stressed me out a lot.
registration_help: Massimo was available on e-mail but sometimes takes a bit to reply
registration_success: It was easy since I have open electives. Only struggles was the time tables of different classes clashing sometimes.
registration_advice: Think about the exam when you register. Oral exams in Italy are in front of the whole class, written exams are by hand and usually graded quite hard. So maybe my advice would be to not be too over-confident when choosing subjets, you will have more fun if you choose something managable.
course_level: The level is generally quite 'low' compared to Denmark, but the exams questions and the way they percieve knowledge consumption is so different from ours in Denmark. Expect direct questions to small bits of the curriculum, no analysis or broad questions.
teaching_comparison: I replied to that above. Way more old-school and not as collaborative. Hours of talking and no breaks.
courses_enrolled: Globalization, Social Justice and Human Rights Geopolitics of Migrations Mythology and its Media British Theatre History
recommended_courses: British Theatre History was interesting and well-structured. The exam was oral and a bit scary but the teacher was good at preparing us.
unexpected_costs: No unexpected costs really but I was suprised by how expensive Milan was. It was very overwhelming.
cost_comparison: Rent was insane. But also general shopping and groceries can become very expensive if you're not good at budgeting. The metro card was super cheap and easy!
activities_available: Many Erasmus events but also academic clubs and sport facilites
activities_recommended: If you are looking for friends in the beginning, go to the Erasmus parties etc. Also eat in the cafeteria at the campus and talk to people in the classes.
weekend_recommendations: Milan gives you a great starting point to travel Italy! I went to Bergamo, Crema, Como, Firenze, Rome and Genova.
culture_adjustment: I have lived in Italy many years and speak Italian so for me it was like returning home. But Italy can be overwhelming if you are not accustomed to it, but that is part of the beauty of exchange to discover a new culture without too many inputs to influence you before.
cultural_challenges: I found Milanese people to be quite cold compared to the south where I have lived before. Also Milan is big and transportation (though organised) takes a long time. Especially during the night when the metro closes, it is impossible to get around which was also expensive because then you have to take a taxi.
culture_appreciated: I love Italy. So everything. Language, the people, the music, the bars, the coffee shop, the food. Go to Italy if you wanna emerge in this, otherwise it will probably be stressful.
top3_advice: 1. Save up a lot of money. 2. Stay in a place that is well connected with metro or tram. Busses can be a bit unreliable. 3. Remember how lucky you are to have the opportunity to go on exhange! So enjoy it.
other_useful_info: Don't be afraid to ask for help and even though uni is very different and sometime stressful, remember to go enjoy Italy during the time off. Travel!
most_rewarding: Getting to know Milan and meeting some of my new best friends. Socially it was way over my expectations and I had so much fun.
greatest_challenge: Probably money. It was very expensive. Also some areas are not extremely safe so be careful around certain zones especially at night.

crucial_aspects: The destination was pre-defined in my study program. I choose the program/track because of the academic area, but I was also excited about the location because I like the Italian language.
info_ease: Initially, the needed information was available, however, I faced a lot of bureaucratic/communication struggles when deciding to return to Denmark for the second semester.
arrival_assistance: We had a welcome day where we met our teachers and got a tour of the campus so it was easy to find our classrooms once classes began.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We needed to fill out a pdf study plan and send it to our head of studies.
registration_help: We could only really email our head of studies or the universities administration whenever we hit a blockade that prevented us to register properly.
registration_success: I enjoyed my classes, both the mandatory ones, which were most of them, but I was also happy that we could take electives in different faculties etc. I had a very nice elective in geology.
registration_advice: Don't hesitate to reach out to the professors if you have doubts about lecture scheduling etc before registering.
course_level: They were appropriate in my opinion. Some were repetitive compared to my courses on the bachelor, but others were more challenging because they were on a new topic.
teaching_comparison: At UCPH lectures are more interactive. In Milan it was mostly just the professor speaking for the entire lecture. It was really nice with lots of excursions in Milan though.
courses_enrolled: Laboratory in Sustainable Livestock Production Laboratory in Sustainable Water Management Laboratory in Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization Geological Environments and Structures Agricultural Systems and Soil Science Italian level A1 (SLAM)
recommended_courses: Laboratory in Sustainable Water Management was very appropriate within my programme and the exam project was a good way to use the knowledge in practice. Geological Environments and Structures was super interesting and challenging if you haven't had geology before. Agricultural Systems and Soil Science is good for repetition. but not a challenging course for natural science students who've had soil science before.
unexpected_costs: I didn't encounter additional unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Housing was super expensive. Eating at restaurants/cafées and public transport was considerably cheaper than in DK. Grocery shopping was similar to DK.
activities_available: We were not introduced to social activites at the university and din't really integrate with the other students there.
activities_recommended: I went to the gym, but not through the university.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking by Como/Lecco was super nice.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy. Italians are welcoming in my experience.
socializing_tips: Not really since I didn't manage to do it. I lived with an Italian, which is the only thing I can recommend to immerse in the culture and get a local network.
cultural_challenges: Bureaucratic stuff taking ages and not getting clear directions on course registration, exams etc early on. And Italian showing up later, classes sometimes starting on time and sometimes not depending on the professor.
culture_appreciated: Cheap coffee, hospitality, great food and beautiful language that is fairly easy to understand.
top3_advice: Look for housing early, have patience in terms of adminitrative parts and enjoy!
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of now.
most_rewarding: Challenging myself personally to push outside my comfort zone and explore a new culture, meet new people and have an open mind about new experiences.
greatest_challenge: Having a smaller social circle and not stressing out about the administrative stuff moving insanely slow so not being able to plan much in advance out of fear of not passing/getting my thesis approved etc.

Comparative Contract Law and International Criminal Law is also recommendable. cultural_challenges: N/A
culture_appreciated: Friendliness, happiness, the food and drinks, and the rich culture that evolves around these foods. activities_available: Social activities included welcome parties, movie nights, and group excursions to nearby cities or landmarks. There were also student clubs and organizations to join, covering everything from music and arts to outdoor activities and volunteering. It was a great way to meet people and experience local culture.
activities_recommended: Social activities to meet a lot of new people worldwide
weekend_recommendations: I highly recommend exploring both the local area and nearby cities during weekends or holidays. Take time to visit local landmarks, museums, and parks—it's a great way to experience the culture. If possible, go on day trips to nearby cities or scenic spots. In Italy, for example, places like Lake Como, Cinque Terre, or Florence are all beautiful and easily reachable. Also, try to attend local festivals, markets, or concerts for a more authentic experience. And don't forget to enjoy the local food scene—whether it’s a casual café or a fine dining experience!
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture at my exchange site was relatively easy, but it took some time to fully get comfortable. People were generally welcoming, and there were plenty of opportunities to learn about the local customs and traditions through social events and interactions with locals. The language barrier was a bit of a challenge at first, but many people spoke English, which made things easier. Immersing myself in local activities, trying the food, and getting involved in university events really helped me adapt. It was a gradual process, but overall, it was an enjoyable experience.
socializing_tips: Look out for university parties, local festivals, or casual meetups—these are often relaxed environments where people are open to chatting and making new friends.
cultural_challenges: One of the cultural differences I found challenging was the pace of life. In some places, things move much more slowly, especially when it comes to service in restaurants or waiting in line. It was a bit of an adjustment compared to the faster pace I was used to.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the strong sense of community and the importance placed on socializing in the culture. People often make time for meals with family or friends, which created a warm and welcoming atmosphere. I also loved the emphasis on food and tradition; every meal felt like an experience, and it was great to try so many local dishes. The relaxed attitude toward life, with a focus on enjoying the moment, was something I truly admired as well. Additionally, the deep appreciation for art, history, and local customs made exploring the area rich and fulfilling.
top3_advice: Start the registration process early, embrace the local culture and be flexible and patient
other_useful_info: Costs can add up quickly, especially in larger cities. Plan ahead and try to set a monthly budget for things like food, transportation, and leisure activities. Local markets and cooking your own meals can help save money.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the opportunity to immerse myself in a new culture and gain a deeper understanding of the world. I really enjoyed meeting people from diverse backgrounds, learning about their perspectives. Academically, it was rewarding to experience a different approach to teaching and learning, which broadened my academic horizons.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was adjusting to the differences in academic systems. The approach to assignments, exams, and even the overall structure of the courses was quite different from what I was used to.

arrival_comments: Just send the university an email if you have any doubts, they are always very helpful
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You receive an email with a link to which courses you can take. Then you just fill out a form with the info for the courses that you want. I got all the courses I wanted and my experience is that everyone did. I changed some of the courses after arrival which was also very easy. There wasn't really a deadline to change courses so you can try out different ones and then just change your course registration at UNIMi after a week or two.
registration_help: I just sent an email to Massimo with my questions and he answered very fast
registration_success: Succesful
registration_advice: Don't stress about course registration. Just follow the steps in the mails from UNIMI and ask Massimo questions if you have any.

courses_enrolled: 1) Comparative Labour Law, 2) International Refugee protection and sustainable development, 3) Law and policies of social rights protection in Europe, 4) European monetary and economic law and 5) International, European and comparative environmental law
recommended_courses: Comparative Labour Law was interesting and a good introduction to labour law. It focused on very relevant areas of labour law such as platform workers. Super nice and fun professor. The exam was either an oral exam or a written exam with 20 multiple choice questions and two open questions. I took the written exam which was easy, but take the oral exam!! It was even more chill, students were just asked a couple of basic questions. European monetary and economic law was interesting and had an oral exam where you presented about a topic you choose yourself. Law and policies was very easy and the professor was nice. The exam was a written paper on a topic that you choose yourself and there was a short oral exam where you just explained parts of your written paper to your professor (kind of like a synopsis eksamen).

activities_available: ECN arranged events that were alright in the beginning to meet people
activities_recommended: Go to some of the ECN events in the beginning to meet other exchange students
weekend_recommendations: Going to football games at San Siro! Lake Como and Bergamo are very nice and easy to get to from Milan. I also took the train to Venice, Rome and Firence which was fun!
culture_adjustment: Very easy. They are more relaxed.
socializing_tips: Just ask if they want to grab a coffee or an aperol after class
cultural_challenges: That teachers and students were sometimes very late
culture_appreciated: The food, the bars, the football matches at San Siro. People are very nice, fun and chatty
top3_advice: 1) Don't be afraid to ask people if they want to go out to dinner, bars or anything. I went on exchange on my own and found out that everyone was eager to get to know each other and have fun so just be open and reach reach out to people 2) Time goes by very fast so enjoy it 3) Do fun things such as travel in the weekends and be spontaneous
other_useful_info: Seats in some classrooms are limited so be early to class if you want a good seat
most_rewarding: Meeting new friends
greatest_challenge: Missing people from home. BUT don't have too many visits from home, because you also want to spend weekends and free time with your new friends
other_comments: Have fun

culture_appreciated: The food culture! And also the people is very passionate and positive! Beautiful architecture too
top3_advice: It is important to be dressed appropriately. The style is not as relaxed and free as in Copenhagen. He failed me in a subject and I didn't understand why and when I tried to have a dialogue with him he was quite unpleasant. You have to be prepared that there can be some hassle with the practicalities and university rules when you are on exchange because things are different than at home. But you also learn from it.

crucial_aspects: I chose Milan as my study destination because of its strong academic reputation in law, particularly its focus on international and European legal studies, which aligned perfectly with my educational goals. Additionally, I love the italian culture, offering an environment where I could grow personally and professionally. The opportunity to improve my italian language skills in an immersive setting was another important factor.
overall_comments: It was truly a once in a lifetime experience. Would absolutely recommend it for everyone considering a semester abroad.

registration_comments: It was truly a once in a lifetime experience. Would absolutely recommend it for everyone considering a semester abroad.
registration_process: The registration process at Statale in Milan was relatively straightforward but required careful attention to deadlines and documentation. Upon arrival, I had to complete the initial registration at the International Office, where they provided guidance on the necessary forms and procedures. This included submitting my learning agreement, proof of enrollment from my home university, a copy of my passport, and health insurance documentation. I also received access to the university’s online platform, where I could register for courses and track my academic progress.
registration_help: Assistance from the International Office was invaluable, and we also supported one another as students navigating the same process.
registration_success: Very successful - I had all the courses I wanted to have.
registration_advice: My advice to future exchange students registering at Statale in Milan is to start early and stay organized. Make sure to carefully read all the emails and instructions from the International Office, as the process involves multiple steps and specific deadlines. Additionally, be proactive in reaching out to the International Office or your program coordinator if you have any doubts—they are usually very responsive and willing to assist. Finally, don’t hesitate to ask for help from fellow students, as they can provide tips and share their own experiences navigating the process.
academics_comments: It was truly a once in a lifetime experience. Would absolutely recommend it for everyone considering a semester abroad.
course_level: The courses at Statale were generally well-structured and provided a solid foundation in international and European law. While the level of difficulty varied, most courses were accessible and offered a good mix of theoretical knowledge and practical application. Some courses were more introductory, which was great for broadening my understanding of specific areas, while others were a bit more advanced, involving detailed readings and case discussions. The professors were supportive and encouraged critical thinking, but the pace of some courses was manageable. While the academic program wasn't overly demanding, it still allowed me to gain valuable insights into the subjects I studied, and I felt that the learning experience was both informative and practical.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at Statale in Milan was quite different from that at UCPH. While there were lectures, there was little emphasis on self-study or homework. Most of the learning occurred during the lectures, and the focus was more on listening to the professor rather than engaging in group work or completing assignments outside of class. In contrast, at UCPH, there is a much stronger focus on active participation, group discussions, and independent study, with a higher expectation of homework and self-directed learning. At Statale, the workload was lighter, and I found the academic environment to be more relaxed with less pressure for ongoing assignments and more freedom during the semester.

These courses not only broaden knowledge in key areas of law but also provide a solid foundation for students who want to pursue careers in international or EU law. activities_recommended: To join every beer pong/wine bar event to socialize with other students. Also, to join on trips that are arranged, such as the trip to Germany and the ski trip!
weekend_recommendations: To go on day trips to other parts of Italy. I highly recommend visiting a mix of local and nearby destinations during weekends and holidays. In Milan, take time to explore the different districts. For a peaceful getaway, head to Lake Como for stunning views and charming towns, or visit Verona to see Juliet’s balcony and immerse yourself in the city’s rich history. Lake Garda, Venice, Florence, Turin and other cities are also beautiful. Lastly, be sure to check out student events and local markets, as they offer great opportunities to connect with others and experience Milanese life.
culture_adjustment: super easy. the italian people are so nice and easy to connect with.
socializing_tips: to go to wine bars, cafes and restaurants near the school to socialize with the locals. also, to join or try sports if that is of any interest.
cultural_challenges: One of the main differences was the pace of life. In Italy, especially in Milan, everything tends to be more relaxed and unhurried, which was a shift from the more efficient, time-conscious culture I was used to in Norway. This difference extended to daily life, such as dining habits—meals in Italy are often longer and more social, with a strong emphasis on enjoying the moment, while in Norway, meals tend to be quicker. Another cultural adjustment was communication style. Italians tend to be more expressive and spontaneous, with lively conversations and frequent use of gestures, whereas Norwegians are more reserved and tend to value quiet, direct communication. Lastly, while I appreciated the warmth of Italian hospitality, I had to adjust to the more informal and sometimes chaotic approach to organization, which is quite different from Norway’s more structured and orderly way of doing things.
culture_appreciated: There are so many aspects of Italian culture that I truly appreciated during my time in Milan. One of the highlights was the strong sense of community and family. Italians place a lot of value on spending time with loved ones, and it was inspiring to see how meals, celebrations, and even everyday moments are often shared with family and friends. I also really enjoyed the Italian approach to food The Italian sense of style, both in fashion and architecture, also stood out to me. Milan, being a fashion capital, is full of creative energy, and the city’s beautiful historical landmarks and design-oriented spaces reflect a deep appreciation for aesthetics. Finally, the Italian attitude toward life—embracing the present, enjoying the little things, and maintaining a strong connection to culture and history—was something I found truly inspiring and enriching.
top3_advice: Embrace the relaxed pace of life: The atmosphere in Milan is much more laid-back compared to the more time-structured environment at UCPH. Don’t be surprised if things move slower than you’re used to, especially when it comes to meals, socializing, and even certain administrative processes. Take this as an opportunity to slow down, enjoy the moment, and embrace the Italian way of life. Prepare for less structured academic life: Unlike UCPH, where there’s a strong emphasis on participation, homework, and group work, Statale’s academic approach is more lecture-focused with fewer assignments or interactive classes. You’ll have more flexibility with your time, but it’s important to stay disciplined and keep up with the reading and exams on your own. Explore Milan and Italy: Milan is a fantastic base for weekend trips, whether it’s to explore nearby cities like Verona or Lake Como or diving deeper into the cultural treasures within the city itself. Don’t just stay on campus—take the opportunity to immerse yourself in Italian culture, try new foods, visit museums, and travel as much as possible. The city has so much to offer, and it’s an experience you won’t want to miss.
other_useful_info: Save money!!
most_rewarding: the friendships I developed and the italian lifestyle.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange, it was adjusting to the differences in academic structure. The lack of regular assignments and less structured interaction with professors took some getting used to, especially since I was accustomed to a more interactive and assignment-driven academic environment at UCPH.

crucial_aspects: The country and city of destination were crucial when choosing. Within the scope of that; the culture. Most importantly, how the country, city and university was recommended by former exchange students from the sending university.
overall_comments: Great experience and it fulfilled all the ambitions for me. A life long memory.
info_ease: Quite easy. Didn't have too many problems to find the information. And also, fairly easy to get in touch with the administration. They were very helpful and answered almost immediately.
arrival_assistance: Several mails containing the essential information and guides. Especially by the receiving university and its administration.
arrival_comments: Again, the administration of the receiving university were providing the essential information upon arrival. Maybe a tiny bit late, but I received it in fair time.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Great experience and it fulfilled all the ambitions for me. A life long memory.
registration_process: We got mails with information and guides. We went down to the office that registred our arrival, and it all went very smooth. There was also arrows printed on walls etc. at the place to find the right room.
registration_help: Mailing the coordinators with a quick response. Very smooth process, and their was even an information-window by the entrance of the building.
registration_success: Very succesful. I registered to all the classes I wanted and it worked out nice on my personal schedule. Easy process, and the administration and/or teachers were willing to help with this matter.
registration_advice: Save the important mails. Ask other exchange students for help if needed. Try a lot of courses before choosing to register, because you may find some courses more interesting than others - even if they didn't sound interesting at first.
academics_comments: Great experience and it fulfilled all the ambitions for me. A life long memory.
course_level: Very engaged teachers. High level in the classes of the courses, but the exams are relatively easier. The teachers sets understandable ambitions for the course and helps the students to increase their learning time by time.
teaching_comparison: A bit different. You had to attend classes with a minimum of 70-80% - if you didn't make any deals with the respective professors. The classes focused primarily on theories, little to no focus on practice.
courses_enrolled: Comparative Industrial Relations Systems, Labour Law and Environmental Sustainability, Comparative Contract Law, International Human Rights Law and International Criminal Law.
recommended_courses: Contract Law. Great teachers that gives you exciting aspects of contract law - especially between the civil law system and common law system. This course was easier to perspective into our own legal system with international variations.
unexpected_costs: I don't know if it's unexpected, but you were going out eating or shopping more often than at home, because you're in a different country with different people. I probably went a bit over budget in this matter.
cost_comparison: Dining out was less expensive. A lot of italian people meets at restaurants or bars in stead of their respective homes.
activities_available: Some tournaments. Especially football (five-a-side), tennis and running.
activities_recommended: Maybe go to some of the football tournaments. They sounded quite funny and is probably a great way to get to know new people and cultures.
weekend_recommendations: Different cities. Napoli, Bergamo, Monza, Como etc. Plan some trips with fellow students - exchange students or not.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. Very international city with a lot of tourism. The locals get somewhat used to a lot of different cultures because of this.
socializing_tips: Just be upforward. Don't be hesitant to meet up with new people or talk with people from different cultures.
cultural_challenges: The temper and slow way of living.
culture_appreciated: The calmness. I liked that it was a bit more chill and not so stressful in the daily life of living in Milan.
top3_advice: Plan some nice trips, be outgoing and talk with the professors. Making deals with professors regarding lectures and schedules can be quite rewarding.
other_useful_info: Not at the moment. I think the other boxes sums up the most important aspects for me.
most_rewarding: Friendships and understanding of other cultures. I got to learn a bunch of new people that I still talk to after the exchange ended.
greatest_challenge: Missing home, my family and friends. But that was also one of the main parts for me going on exchange.
other_comments: No.

most_rewarding: To have so much freetime, and meeting a lot of new people as everyone is open to have fun and go out. It was nice to just be able to go for a run and having nothing else to do that day. I really enjoyed seeing so much of Italy!

crucial_aspects: I had visited UNIMI before and the university and city seemed to fit what I wanted to experience during my Erasmus. I knew they had a great faculty of philosophy, something I wanted to explore - an opportunity to have courses that interested me, and wasn't necessarily related to my studies in Rhetoric at Copenhagen Uni. Another aspect was my familiarity with italian culture - I have traveled there a lot, but I wanted to experience how an everyday life would look like. To have a structured stay while experiencing another culture was crucial.
info_ease: It was quite easy: the staff at UNIMI was ready to help with necessary questions. But I would say that to have a backbone, some kind of fundament, which I had with fellow students from UCPH, helped a lot. If the staff at Unimi couldn't help, we just tried out different stuff, which eventually helped. To be transparent with the knowledge you gain along the way. Otherwise I would say that Unimi was helpful with their mails. They sent a lot of helpful mails along the way, while reassuring that everything would be okay - that we just needed to be patient. They were professional while laid back - it was great.
arrival_assistance: The students helped each other a lot. To have a network between students was quite helpful. The staff at UNIMI was also helpful - sending us mails. Also we asked the professors if we had any questions regarding the semester, the structure etc. But to find out answers yourself in a new city was also character-building one might say.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration is done at their site Unimia. Unimi sent a mail that described how you register for both exams and courses - so this part went quite smooth. Where it gets messy is when trying to find out which courses you want, and to plan them so they don't overlap. This part can take some time, because not all classes and their time-schedule are released at the same time. Therefore you must be patioent and trust the process. It will take time; it can get chaotic and messy, changing courses throughout the stay. My recommendation therefore is to try to keep updated, and just attend a class that you found interesting, just one time to see if it's something for you. You can always restructure your courses, something Unimi was quite open about.
registration_help: Talking to other students, speak to the professors. This way you get a sense of what the courses are about, how they are structured, how they teach etc.
registration_success: Quite successful, everything worked out eventually. I wanted to focus on philosophy and intellectual history - and that's what I got.
registration_advice: Show up to different classes, speak to the professors and the other students. But also, don't think too much of it, sometimes it's okay to stick with your initial feeling, and not change courses too much: this way you don't fall behind, and also; which clarity comes freedom, freedom to explore the city, and a not so worried mind regarding the courses. It brings calmness to do it quick, and then stick with it. Sometimes the course you thought was interesting actually isn't all that, but then just stick with it - too much changing around can create chaos, so rather spend your energy drinking Apperol Spritz and eat great food than worrying about courses - trust your gut.
course_level: The level of the courses very generally speaking lower than at UCPH. The amount of reading was generally lower than at Cph, and the 'background' knowledge of humanities (theories, history etc.) was lower - sometimes I got quite surprised by the difference in basic-common-ground knowledge. And also the level of participation; at cph I'm used to a high level of debating and participation in class, but at unimi it wasn't the culture, it was more listening to the professor without questioning anything - the critical awareness was lower. But this is okay: then you'll experience both academia and the culture.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was generally constituted by lectures with presentations. The professor spoke, the class listened. In Cph you're invited to debate and discuss the text - this was not the case at Unimi. Some professors tried a bit, but the culture among the students was generally just listening without questioning.
courses_enrolled: GLOBAL INTELLECTUAL HISTORY LANGUAGE AND METAPHYSICS TEACHING WORKSHOP: PERFORMANCE AND PERFORMATIVITY INTELLECTUALS, POPULAR CULTURE, COLLECTIVE IDENTITIES: ITALY AND EUROPE IN THE 19TH AND 20TH CENTURIES
recommended_courses: Language and Metaphysics. The students were fun, and philosophy is a huge faculty in Milan. You'll get to make some presentations regarding the topic, and to debate and share examples is a huge part of this course. Which always a great thing. And the atmosphere is great among the students; you can disagree on certain things, but nothing gets personal, which is very important! So if you want to get stimulated by debating the students and the professor - this class is for you.
unexpected_costs: There were some costs regarding the housing - some Italian tax. But generally nothing was unexpected: I knew that a lot of my budget would go to eating out, going out in the evening etc.
cost_comparison: everything was generally speaking cheaper than in Copenhagen: but the supermarkets was extremely cheap compared to Cph: you could live really well for a small amount of money.
activities_available: quite many; didn't attend anything
activities_recommended: Go to the Cinema! The culture of cinema is huge in italy and milan. Small cinemas, big cinemas, outdoor cinemas. You'll get to meet the locals, have a chat over a beer. And it's really cheap! 6 euros for a ticket. At the Cinema was were i hanged out; and where I met a lot of locals.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the Cinema! Or take a train to Genova or Como, swim a little. The train system in italy is really good, and cheap. So take a look where you want to go, and just book a ticket; it can be great to 'reset' the city you live in, and return with an open set of eyes again.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy: the locals were all very friendly! But the italians like to run late. So just chill out, thats what the italians like to do.
socializing_tips: Just speak to them
cultural_challenges: Not much actually - thats just personal I think; I loved every bit of the culture, and it wasn't challenging to adjust.
culture_appreciated: The openness of italians. Very friendly everyone. Thats something I'll take with me; to have an open mindset, to just relax and chill out; grab a drink if necessary. Of course the weather helps with this, but I'll try to incorporate this lifestyle in Cph. We could all learn a little by this.
top3_advice: Trust the process. Everything will eventually work out. Don't stress.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: To have a personal connection to another city. To learn about the italian culture, and to incorporate this in your own life. It's not necessarily something you'll notice right away, but when you return you can definitely feel the difference. And also a lot of great and unique stories!
greatest_challenge: Honestly, I dont know: for me, everything was just as I dreamed of. Sometimes I missed talking my own language, but alora; then you'll recognize how crazy and lovely it is that you're actually living in another country. It's a great opportunity.

crucial_aspects: When choosing Milan as my study destination, the potential for cultural experience and personal growth played a pivotal role in my decision. Milan, as a global hub of art, fashion, and design, offered an unparalleled opportunity to immerse myself in a culture rich in history and creativity. From exploring iconic landmarks like the Duomo and The Last Supper to engaging with the vibrant local traditions, I knew that living in Milan would deepen my appreciation for Italian heritage. The city's dynamic blend of modernity and tradition provided countless opportunities to learn, connect, and experience life in a truly cosmopolitan environment. On a personal level, studying in Milan promised significant growth. Living in a bustling international city challenged me to adapt to new environments, embrace cultural differences, and build independence. Navigating daily life in a new country, whether learning Italian phrases or understanding local customs, helped me develop resilience, flexibility, and a more global perspective. Milan was not just a place to study - it was a transformative experience that enriched my worldview and shaped me both personally and culturally.

Many of my pre-approved courses were unavailable, so I had to go through the process of obtaining new pre-approvals and updating my Online Learning Agreement. However, registering courses on the UniMi website was straightforward since you simply enter the course details manually.
registration_advice: Finding available courses can be a challenging process. Even after selecting your courses, one or more may become unavailable once the term starts. Additionally, ensuring that your chosen courses fit into a schedule without overlaps can be difficult, often requiring further adjustments and changes. However, the option to register as either attending or non-attending can provide more flexibility, making it easier to manage overlaps and accommodate your schedule.
course_level: I was surprised to find that there were no mandatory readings for each class, only for the exam. Otherwise, attending the classes was easy, though at times the Italian accent made it a bit challenging to fully understand.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style varied across courses. Some classes were more interactive, encouraging participation and discussion, while others followed a more traditional, PowerPoint-style approach. Regarding group work, I had one course that included a group presentation as part of the exam. Some classes fostered more inclusive and engaging environments, while others were more focused on lectures and slides.
courses_enrolled: I attended the following courses on MA-levels: Journalism, Media and Politict (9 ects), Digital Society (9 ects), Corporate Communication (9 ects) and a Workshop in Iconology and Iconography (3 ects).
recommended_courses: I highly recommend the Workshop in Iconology and Iconography for exchange students interested in art history. The professor was exceptionally knowledgeable and an excellent teacher, and the course included fascinating excursions. Additionally, when in Italy, taking art courses is a must—it’s the heart of art history, offering unparalleled opportunities to study masterpieces in their cultural context.
unexpected_costs: I had to pay an administration fee for the housing, which was non-refundable. I noticed after paying that students get a discount booking on SpotaHome - which could have been nice to know beforehand.
cost_comparison: The food both in restaurant and in the supermarket were more expensive than expected, but the drinks were often less expensive.
activities_available: There were exchange activities organized for students at La Statale, which I thoroughly enjoyed. These events offered great opportunities to meet other international students, make new friends, and explore Milan together. The activities ranged from cultural tours to social events, and they helped me feel more connected to both the university and the city. I appreciated how these events allowed me to immerse myself in the local culture while also sharing experiences with fellow exchange students.
activities_recommended: I would recommend being part of the ESN Whats App groups and email system, so you get notifications whenever there's an erasmus event going on.
weekend_recommendations: Milan is a city full of exciting opportunities to explore, relax, and immerse yourself in Italian culture. Here’s a guide to help you make the most of your weekends and holidays: 1. Restaurants to Try Dongio: A quiet spot for reasonably priced Italian dishes paired with good wine. Osteria Serafina: Indulge in a luxurious experience—try their famous pasta prepared in a giant parmesan wheel. (Remember to book in advance!) Rovello 18 and Tram Tram: Both offer authentic Italian cuisine in cozy settings. Osteria di Fortunata: Located in the trendy Brera district, this chain serves delicious handmade pasta. Il Brutto: Perfect for weekday lunches with a menu that changes bi-weekly. 2. Cafés for a Relaxing Break Gelsomina: A charming café with Italian decor Breaddy Bakery: A budget-friendly spot for brunch, lunch, or a hearty lasagna. Loste Café: A Milanese take on Copenhagen-style cafés, featuring excellent pastries. Crazy Cat Café: A quirky spot where you can enjoy brunch or aperitivo while spending time with friendly cats. They also host fun events like drag bingo! Panificio Davide Longoni: Savor their focaccia or a ham sandwich with Dijon mustard. Signor Lievito: The place to go if you’re craving cardamom buns or cinnamon rolls. 3. Must-See Museums Palazzo Reale: Visit for rotating exhibitions on art and history. The Last Supper Museum: See Leonardo da Vinci’s masterpiece, but be sure to book tickets at least two months in advance. Pinacoteca di Brera: Milan’s answer to the Louvre, with an impressive collection of Renaissance art. Villa Necchi: Step into a 1930s Italian villa, a preserved time capsule of luxury living. 4. Other Landmarks and Activities Duomo Milano: Climb to the rooftop for breathtaking views of the city. Teatro La Scala: Attend an opera or simply tour this historic theater. Bagni Misterioso: If it’s summer, cool off at this outdoor pool, which also offers food and drinks. 5. Parks for Relaxation Parco Sempione: A large and beautiful park, perfect for picnics or leisurely walks. Giardini Indro Montanelli: A romantic park with fountains and a smaller castle—great for dog lovers! 6. Shopping Spots Calzedonia: Stock up on stylish tights and leggings. REHUB or Humana Vintage: Explore these vintage stores for unique finds. East Market Shop: A treasure trove of retro clothing. 7. Bars and Nightlife Rizla: Budget-friendly and potent drinks for just €3.50. De Amicis Uno: A must for aperitivo fans; enjoy an Aperol Spritz with a generous snack platter. Trattoir La Darsensa: Known as the "Danish Bar," this lively spot offers a mix of live music, dancing, and good vibes on weekends. Alcatraz: A massive dance club with performances that make for an unforgettable night out. Bar Basso: Allegedly the birthplace of the negroni sbagliato. They serve these iconic cocktails in generous portions. Tempio del Futuro Perduto: A techno club with an industrial vibe, perfect for fans of electronic music. It’s a go-to destination for late-night dancing on weekends. King’s Pub: A lively bar with an international crowd. Known for its fun and interactive vibe, it hosts beer pong nights every Thursday, making it a great place to meet new people and enjoy a laid-back evening. 8. Markets to Explore San Marco (Monday and Thursday) or Fauché (Saturday): Browse for fresh produce, snacks, or unique souvenirs. Porta Romana (Friday): Perfect for a relaxed morning of market shopping.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture in Milan was a smooth, albeit gradual, process. As a cosmopolitan city, Milan blends traditional Italian culture with international influences. The people were warm and welcoming, and I found that participating in daily activities—whether it was ordering coffee at a café or shopping at the local market—helped me get in tune with the city's pace. Since Italians generally prefer speaking Italian, learning some basic phrases proved to be incredibly useful for navigating everyday life.
cultural_challenges: One of the cultural differences I found particularly challenging was the slower pace of life compared to what I was used to. The slower response times in emails, the more relaxed attitude towards deadlines, and people strolling slowly on the streets were initially a bit frustrating. However, over time, I adjusted and learned to embrace the more laid-back rhythm of life.
culture_appreciated: I most appreciated the Italian emphasis on enjoying life and savoring the moment. The long, leisurely meals and coffee breaks were a highlight for me, as they encouraged not only relaxation but also meaningful social interactions. The Italian approach to food was another aspect I loved—the focus on fresh, high-quality ingredients and the joy of sharing meals with friends really resonated with me.
top3_advice: Be Patient and Adapt to the Pace: Milan has a more relaxed pace of life compared to what you might be used to at UCPH. Things like response times, deadlines, and even the general rhythm of daily life can be slower, so it’s important to be patient and flexible. Don’t rush—embrace the slower pace and enjoy the moments, whether it's a long meal or a coffee break. Explore Milan and Beyond: Milan is a dynamic city with a mix of modern and historical attractions. Take time to explore the neighborhoods, art, museums, and nearby cities. Milan's public transport makes it easy to travel, so don’t miss the chance to visit other parts of Italy or even nearby countries on weekends. Stay Open to New Experiences: There will be many opportunities to get involved in cultural activities, events, and social gatherings—whether organized by the university or local groups. Stay open to new experiences, even if they are outside your comfort zone. These events, from local festivals to student meetups, will help you integrate, meet new people, and enrich your time abroad.
other_useful_info: Yes, I think a useful tip would be to learn some useful italian phrases (either on Duolingo or join an Italian course). Simple greetings, ordering food, or asking for directions in Italian can help you feel more integrated and appreciated by locals.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was definitely the opportunity to be on my own and gain new confidence. Living in a new city, navigating daily life, and handling challenges independently helped me grow in ways I hadn't expected, even though at times it was rather stressfull. Beyond the cultural and academic experiences, the sense of self-assurance I gained from managing everything on my own was truly invaluable. This newfound confidence is something I’ll carry with me for years to come.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was adjusting to the slower pace of life in Milan. While it can be refreshing, the slower pace sometimes made everyday tasks, like dealing with bureaucratic processes or waiting for responses, feel frustratingly drawn out.

crucial_aspects: I wanted more practical experince in my academic work, since KU often offers courses that relies heavily on theoretical aspects. I, therefore, chose course such as conflict management and negotiation, that had a lot of practical work.
info_ease: Quite hard. Italy is not known for being very structural, and we didn't get any information until quite late in the proces (some information, you also have to ask for yourself before getting it). The only orientation event that did occur was regarding social events outside of academia.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any. We had to find courses, their locations and their starting date by ourselves. But everyone had the same problems, so it was a good conversation starter.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration is very flexible. You get a guide on how to do it and you can change your courses up until their exam dates. There also doesn't seem to be a cap on when the courses are full.
registration_help: We got a guide on how to do it from our Erasmus coordinator through email.
registration_success: Almost everyone I talked to had to change their courses because they were overlapping. As exchange students, you take classes from different masters, meaning that they will likely overlap. Have this in mind, when looking for courses: It is good to have several prefered options!
registration_advice: Don't get too attached to a course. It might be cancelled, be overlapping with other courses etc. Make sure to get pre-approval for a lot of different courses, that you are interested in.
course_level: The level is easier than at KU. I think it is because the Italians' English skills aren't as good, and they therefore have it easier in English-spoken classes than in Italian-spoken classes.
teaching_comparison: It was more practical, which was what I wanted. There was more class exercises, presentations, roleplays, oral participation etc.
courses_enrolled: Conflict Management and Negotiation; Corporate Communication; Journalism, Media and Journalism; Digital Society.
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of them. Conflict Management and Negotiation was particularly fun, because you learn a lot about your personal conflict patterns and get to do roleplays. Digital Society is also very nice, because the American professor is super good at teaching and you learn a lot of exciting things on the societal impact of technology. Highly recommend!
unexpected_costs: Some social events, you have to pay for. Otherwise, it is mostly if you need house appliances that are provided in your household.
cost_comparison: Food is as expensive as Copenhagen. However, drinks are way cheaper.
activities_available: There are a lot of universities in Milan, and therefore also a lot of different social clubs doing events. Most of them are only going to clubs however, be aware of this. The official event coordinators are ESN, but also clubs such International Week exists.
activities_recommended: I had a lot of fun going to Kings Pub every thursday with my friends, meeting other students and doing beerpong. It was with International Week, and in the beginning everyone was talking to everyone - a good place to make friends!
weekend_recommendations: Go to cities around Milan! Especially Cinque Terra was beautiful.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. I already have Italian friends from back home, so they introduced me to places, people etc.
socializing_tips: Go to the social events in the beginning of the semester! Everyone is meeting each other here.
cultural_challenges: The Italian way is quite laissez faire. Everything is up to negotiation and never set in stone, making everything very flexible.
culture_appreciated: The welcoming atmosphere. Everyone is welcome in the Italian families and at their dinners etc.
top3_advice: Don't stress, everything will work out just fine. Go to social events in the beginning and be open. Use your time to see the city and the people around you, school is less stressful than you think.
other_useful_info: Porta Romana and Porta Venezia are the closest and nicest areas to live in.
most_rewarding: Getting practical academic experiences. Also having Italian friends, getting their recommendations and going to Italian family dinners.
greatest_challenge: Having enough time to do everything you wish to do.

crucial_aspects: It was important to me that it was a place in Europe, and that the university offered some exciting courses that I could use in my future career. At the same time, I love Italy, and Milan is the perfect place to go if you want both a vibrant city life and the opportunity to travel around Italy.
info_ease: I found it relatively easy. Milan's university has a good website that's easy to navigate, where you can find useful information about the different courses and more.
arrival_assistance: None. I think there was a lack of an introductory week for all Erasmus students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The university has a portal called Unimia, which includes a specific section for Erasmus course registration. It's very easy to register for courses or make changes if you change your mind.
registration_help: There is an email you can contact for assistance, and there's also a how-to guide available in the portal.
registration_success: Very successful, as there was no issues and I got the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Just go into Unimia, and it's quite intuitive what you need to do
course_level: Overall, the level was fine, and it was easy to keep up.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was very similar to how a lecture would be conducted in Copenhagen. However, there isn't as much reading required to do at home.
courses_enrolled: Corporate communication Journalism, media and politics Data analysis Digital society
recommended_courses: I guess it depend on what you study field is, but I can recommend all the four courses I took, as the teachers are very good and dedicated, and the teaching is engaging.
unexpected_costs: Not really any.
cost_comparison: I guess the food in the supermarket was more expensive than I thought. t's a bit like the prices in Denmark, with some things, such as pasta, being cheaper.
activities_available: I dont know
activities_recommended: I dont know, as I did not attend in any.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend dining at the many great restaurants, having aperitivo, and visiting museums, such as the Prada Fondazione, which is worth a visit. There are also many great flea markets on weekends, including one every Saturday at Navigli. I would also recommend taking a day trip or weekend trip to the cities near Milan, such as Bergamo, the Como lake or Genoa.
culture_adjustment: I think it was fine and easy. It's not much different from Denmark.
cultural_challenges: Not really any.
culture_appreciated: The food culture, which is rich and diverse, reflecting both traditional Italian cuisine and international influence. I enjoyed especially the tradition for Aperitivo and their cheap coffee.
top3_advice: 1: Take your time to familiarize yourself with the different courses and decide which ones you'd like to take. You might risk having overlapping courses on the same days and times, so it's good to have alternative options in mind.
other_useful_info: Not really besides the tree things I already mentioned.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was that I had a really great teacher who taught me a lot and inspired me on what to write about in my bachelor project. In addition, I've made many new friends and truly had an unforgettable time.
greatest_challenge: I don't think I've experienced anything that was particularly challenging.

crucial_aspects: I've only been to Italy once in my life and that was a very long time ago. I've always admired the Italian culture from afar and have always wanted to spend more time in the country. Thus, being able to spend a semester in Milan was ideal for me, also considering the fact that I've heard so many great things about it from friends who've gone there previously. It was also important to me that I had heard that the academic level - at least as far as for Erasmus students are concerned - was quite limited compared to the level at my home university. As checked out above, the most important thing for me was in no way the academic outcome - it was the experience to live abroad and have a good time. It wasn't an absolute deal breaker for me, but the possibility to receive the Erasmus grant was also one of the pros by choosing a destination within Europa, and within Europe there was little doubt that Milan would be my preferred destination.

registration_success: It was very easy. I got all the courses I wanted and I was able to change them during the semester if needed.
registration_advice: Just follow the instruction sent to you by email, and if you are in any doubt, contact the person of contact at the host university.
course_level: The content of some of the classes could at times be challenging but the exams were easy.
teaching_comparison: It was a lot less student interactive and it was more in a lecture format-
