recommended_courses: Competition Law and Economics: very interesting course and the teacher is knowledgable European Monetary and Economic Law: interesting content and the exam is easy (15 minutes presentation, 2 people, topic of your own choosing) Law and Policies of Social Rights Protection in Europe: easy exam, just a written paper and a very short "defense" of the paper. Collective Redress and Sustainability: the teacher is a bit special, however, the exam is alright and you can make the assignment after you go home. Comparative Labour Law: very entertaining teacher.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: You can eat and drink quite cheap if you find the right places.
activities_available: No idea.
activities_recommended: - Going to the San Siro to watch football. - Exploring the culture of the city (the Duomo, the museums etc.) - Eating and drinking. - Finding local spots. - Going on trips around Italy (I would especially recommend going to Napoli).
weekend_recommendations: The same as the above.
culture_adjustment: It took a few weeks (mainly because I didn't have school for the first few weeks), but it came quite quickly after that.
socializing_tips: We were many Danes so I spend most time with them. Some of my friends went to activities (salsa dancing, cooking courses etc.) and had success with that.
cultural_challenges: In Milan they are very bad pedestrians.
culture_appreciated: The food and the wine and the fact that the locals actually wanted to speak Italian if you tried.
top3_advice: 1) really don't spend too much time at school - just enjoy. 2) when making a decision to do or not do something, remember that this is (probably) a once in a lifetime opportunity. 3) find a place to stay that you actually like being at.
other_useful_info: Not anything else than already mentioned.
most_rewarding: Having fun with lovely people and just being able to enjoy life without having to think about school or work.
greatest_challenge: The kitchen in our apartment wasn't the best.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to go to Italy due to the people and culture there.
info_ease: Pretty easy. The international mobility office were very helpful.
arrival_assistance: If I had any question Massimo was always fast at replying on emails.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Course registration opens quite late compared to the University of Copenhagen. So have patience. And you can register to courses after they have started. It can therefore be a good idea to go check out different classes in the first weeek or two to figure out what you like.
registration_help: You can read about the different courses online, write the professors if you have any questions, or write the international mobility office if you have any practical issues or questions.
registration_success: Very. I got all the classes I wanted. I don't think they have a limit on how many people can participate in the classes.
registration_advice: Go check out many different courses in the first week as they can be quite different from their online description.
course_level: All my courses were at MA level, and where not that difficult (easier than the University of Copenhagen).
teaching_comparison: It was smaller classes, attendance, and more active participation. I also had presentations in almost all of my classes. On the other hand the curriculum was a lot smaller.
courses_enrolled: I took two trimesters. At the first trimester I had: "Global Challenges to Democracy", "History and Politics of North Africa and the Middle East" & "Workshop: Human Trafficking/Smuggling". At the second trimester I had: "Contemporary Challenges: Migrations and Cultural Diversity", "Contemporary Challenges: Labor Market and Inequalities" & "Asylum from the Field: Borders, Struggles, and Integration Practices".
recommended_courses: My favourite class was "Workshop: Human Trafficking/Smuggling". It was really interesting, very different from what we learn at the University of Copenhagen, and the professor was really good. I also really liked the class "History and Politics of North Africa and the Middle East", however it is a lot of history. And the professor of the class "Contemporary Challenges: Labor Market and Inequalities" was also really good.
unexpected_costs: I decided to travel in Italy a lot, which I used a lot of money on.
cost_comparison: Coffee and eggs are very cheap. In general it is cheaper to go out than in Denmark, but more expensive than the rest of Italy, and not that cheap.
activities_available: I don't know, I didn't attend any.
activities_recommended: I didn't attend any.
weekend_recommendations: Go travel. There is a lot of places you can easily access from Milan. Go see the lakes, Liguria, etc.
culture_adjustment: Very easy as Milan is a more international/European city.
socializing_tips: Attend classes alone (without other Danish exchange students). That was how I met most of my international friends.
cultural_challenges: In the beginning I found it difficult to adjust to the different administrative system. However, over time it was fine. The exams are also a bit different, but again it was fine once you had tried it a first time.
culture_appreciated: The openness and more laid back attitude - being able to enjoy the everyday life more.
top3_advice: Don't panic if you get all of your information last minute, it is all going to be fine.
other_useful_info: The international mobility office are very kind and helpfull, so write them an email if you have any issues.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and cultures.
greatest_challenge: Probably some unexpected practical issues with our apartment, but it all worked out.
other_comments: Just enjoy it and don't be afraid to speak to new people :-)

crucial_aspects: I've been to Italy many times, but never Milan. I have heard a lot good things about University of Milan, so I thought that was ideal.
info_ease: It was a bit difficult to understand the university system at first, but people were very nice to help you.
arrival_assistance: I was invited to a Erasmus information event and I had close contact with my Erasmus coordinator at the university
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: At first I didn't understand how it worked, but after consulting some local students and my Erasmus coordinator, it made more sense, and I could apply for the courses I wanted more or less.
registration_help: Answer above.
registration_success: I got almost all the courses I wanted
registration_advice: Ask your Erasmus coordinator if you need help or write directly to the teachers who offers the course you want - maybe they can help you.
course_level: I didn't feel like there was a big difference beside the age-difference of the students.
teaching_comparison: It was more "loose". Not always well-prepared (teachers were often late) and there was a lot of classes where it was just the teacher during a presentation, but without any power-points or possibility to take notes.
courses_enrolled: Cultural History of the Modern Period British Theatre Wars of Images Classical Mythology and it's Media
recommended_courses: Cultural History of the Modern Period Wars of Images
unexpected_costs: Nothing
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive Transport was less expensive
activities_available: There were events for students and student bar. You could also join various sportevents
activities_recommended: The social ones where you get to meet your fellow students
weekend_recommendations: Get to know the city by walking around. Take small trips to Genova, Bologna etc. in the weekends by bus/train
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy
socializing_tips: All the other students were very friendly - they often come up to you just to talk for a little bit (same goes for the locals around the city). People are very welcoming.
cultural_challenges: The way the university system worked was very different from the danish system.
culture_appreciated: The friendly people, the food and the relaxation of the italians
top3_advice: Find housing in good time Ask for help at your university if you are in doubt of anything Enjoy it!
other_useful_info: It might seem confusing at first, but people are there to help
most_rewarding: The feeling of being a "local" and the connections to so many people
greatest_challenge: The last part of the second semester.

crucial_aspects: The crucial thing was that I could go with my friends and experience the Italian culture and youth life with them.
info_ease: Very easy
arrival_assistance: Just talking with fellow students
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was all done online, applying for the courses. It was a bit difficult to find the courses relevant to my field of study as there were so many different ones.
registration_help: I dont know, me and my roomies figured out by our self
registration_success: I got the courses i wanted
registration_advice: Spend some time reading and looking for the many different opportunities regarding courses
course_level: I found the level easier than in Denmark. The only thing that could be difficult was understanding some of the teachers' English accents. But the level of teaching was not difficult.
teaching_comparison: It was similar, it was classroom teaching where the teacher teaches and students can participate like in Denmark.
courses_enrolled: Corporate Communication Digital Society Languages of the media Coding for Computational social science
recommended_courses: I liked Digital Society. The teacher Christopher Anderson was very skilful and the subject matter was exciting and interesting
unexpected_costs: Nothing unexpected
cost_comparison: The housing was expensive, more than i thought
activities_available: There was erasmus parties and sport activities for the students
activities_recommended: I would recommend attending as much as possible, especially if you are travelling on your own.
weekend_recommendations: Travel around in Northern italy, flixbus or train is very cheap, so go to Como, Genoa, Torino, Modena or parma. These places was so nice and cheap to explore
culture_adjustment: I lived with 3 other danes, so it was very easy and safe to be in a different culture. The Italian culture is not that different, just drink some coffee/beers and watch AC Milan :)
cultural_challenges: I didnt find any differences challenging
culture_appreciated: That they eat late and that the cafes, restaurants and the city are never dead
top3_advice: Make sure you have saved money before your stay. Experiences are first priority, school is 2nd. Go to the San Siro
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: The solidarity with those you are travelling with
greatest_challenge: That everything is in English

crucial_aspects: availability and desire to live in specific country.
info_ease: it was straight-forward to find find the needed information.
arrival_assistance: I received good assistance from destination coordinator.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was overall doable, but there is a lot of things to keep track on.
registration_help: There was a coordinator to help, with many office hours.
registration_success: I was very succesful and it was easy doable.
registration_advice: Not all classes have in depth descriptions, so chose classes you know fit you you needs.
course_level: The level of the courses was not the same as UCPH. In my experience the academic level was lower than that of UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was very comparable with that of UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Digital society, Languages of the media, Corporate communication and coding for computational social sciences.
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend Digital Society, as it goes hand in hand with Communication and IT teachings, and the teacher Christopher Anderson is very competent.
unexpected_costs: Cant really recall any unexpected costs, as we were well prepared.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping was cheaper than expected. But overall cost of living is comparable to Copenhagen.
activities_available: You could sign up for a variety of sports clubs.
activities_recommended: The aperitivos are very much fun, and a good way to socialise.
weekend_recommendations: There a lot of things to do an many places to go. But a day trip to Lake Como, Bologna and other close destinations are very recommendable.
culture_adjustment: It was easy, and people were very nice.
cultural_challenges: There weren't any cultural differences that I found challenging.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated the way of socialising and spending time together in Italy.
top3_advice: Have savings ready, Make use of the socialising events and make sure to see and enjoy the city.
other_useful_info: Be prepared for exams like multiple choice and be prepared for smoking everywhere.
most_rewarding: To live in a new city and experience a new culture first hand.
greatest_challenge: To tell my self it was okay to not do anything some of the weekends.

crucial_aspects: Jeg ønskede at opleve landbrug og vinkultur i norditalien ved siden af mit studie
info_ease: Der var god hjælp at hente på mail fra udvekslings koordinator på Milanos Universitet.
arrival_assistance: Udlevering af studiekort, og hjælp til at skifte fag.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Kursus tilmelding skete ved online at udfylde hvilke fag man ønskede. Så kom man på en liste, så underviseren også vidste at man var en del af holdet.
registration_help: Mobility koordinator og medstuderende
registration_success: Successful.
registration_advice: Forsøg at forhøre dig hos nogen der tidligere har været på udveksling i samme by, både ved. husning og hvilke fag der er tilgængelige og interessante indenfor dit studieområde.
course_level: Jeg havde indtryk af at forventningerne var markant lavere end på KU, på trods af at pensum var stort.
teaching_comparison: Lidt mere 'gammeldags'. Studerende har ikke meget indflydelse på debatter i undervisningsrum. Professor holder forelæsning og der stilles ikke mange spørgsmål.
courses_enrolled: Philosophical Analysis Rules, Reasons and Norms The Politics of Mobility, Displacement and Asylum Workshop: Iconology and Iconography
recommended_courses: Især Philosophical Analysis var fedt og anderledes fra filosofi kurser på KU med en grundlæggende intro til metafysik vedr. eksistens og tid. Og desuden en meget empatisk og passioneret professor.
unexpected_costs: Jeg var nødt til at købe et lokalt telefon abonnement, fordi min egen roaming i udlandet åbenbart var begrænset.
cost_comparison: Indkøb var markant dyrere end forventet.
activities_available: Mange aktiviteter både planlagt af ansvarlige for udvekslingsstuderende, og på studerendes initiativ.
activities_recommended: Der ligger mange små landbrug lige udenfor Milano, som kun tager 15-20 min. på cykel at komme ud til. Desuden store parker kort udenfor byen med store badesøer.
weekend_recommendations: La Scala er meget smuk.
culture_adjustment: Meget nemt.
cultural_challenges: Intet
culture_appreciated: Stor kultur for udeliv alle ugens dage også om vinteren, og fantastisk mad. Restauranter er billigere end i Købehavn.
top3_advice: Hvis du ikke har fået noget at vide, så er det hele oftest fint nok. Men jeg missede en mail fra Milanos universitet lang tid inden mit ophold hvor jeg skulle have oprettet en profil på et link. Det løste sig heldigvis, men man skal huske grundigt at læse mails.
most_rewarding: En god læring at opleve hvordan andre tilgår nogen af de samme emner som bliver tilgået på egen uddannelse.

crucial_aspects: Ever since I was a child I have travelled a lot in Italy and my love for the country and the italian culture has grown bigger with time. Therefore I saw exchange as my chance to explore the italian culture more deeply. Also before exchange I started attending Italian language class which was also why I choose Italy to get a chance to improve my Italian.
info_ease: Coming from a different system it was a bit confusing and overwhelming at the beginning to find the information I needed, however Massimo (exchange contact at La Statale) was and has been super helpful thoughout my exchange in Milano. He was very easy to get in contact with and get things done.
arrival_assistance: When I arriving in Milano Massimo helped us with the practical things connected to the university.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It is a bit confusing with the information about which course you can take and which ones you can't. The information is not all at one place. I took me some time to figure the system out. Also getting the ECTS points to add up was a bit difficult but I think it is partly due to being used to another system.
registration_help: I tried surfing around on UNIMI's webpage and wrote to Massimo if I needed help.
registration_success: There was one course that I couldn't get because it wasn't held anyway and then it took sometime to find a new course that could replace the course. So almost totally succesful.
registration_advice: You must take your time to familiarize yourself with the website and how to find information. In addition, you should be aware that ECTS is different than at KU. In UNIMI the typical courses are 6 or 9 ECTS.
course_level: The bachelor courses at UNIMI are somewhat easier than those at KU, while the master courses at UNIMI are more comparable in difficulty to KU's bachelor courses.
teaching_comparison: There is not the same amount of group work as at KU. It's more like being at a lecture.
courses_enrolled: Language of the Media Journalism, Media and Politics Human development and mobility in a changing world How to use international survey data for social research World literatures in English
recommended_courses: All of them. The professors were super proficient and the things taught in class were very interesting. Specially I liked Language of the Media because the professor was skilled communicator and made teaching very exciting by making it relatable to the students' lives.
unexpected_costs: Something related to my apartment such as different types of bills
cost_comparison: Public transport was cheapier than expected and what I am used to in Denmark. Housing was more expensive than I tought. Food was more expensive than I tought.
activities_available: You can attend different types of team sports as the university and there are friday bars at some of the campus'.
activities_recommended: Try to go the the friday bars at the university. It is a nice way to meet local students and other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: The trains run frequently and are not particularly expensive. Plus flixbus is also big in Italy. Therefore, I would recommend traveling around the country as much as possible.
culture_adjustment: It was a bit difficult to start with, but I quickly learned that Italians take things at a different pace and their everyday life is put together differently than the Danes.
socializing_tips: Try to sit next to an Italian in class and talk to them during breaks. It is a chill way to get to know them.
cultural_challenges: Italians are more chill and less stressed than Danes. They do things at a slightly different pace, which is healthy for Danes who are used to being bus.
culture_appreciated: Italians are better so seize the day than Danes, which is something many of us could learn something from.
top3_advice: Take your time to familiarize yourself with their website. Get used to things happening at a different pace. Group teaching is more like a lectures.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: The people I meet and shared a lovely and exciting time with.
greatest_challenge: Figuring oout the educational system.

crucial_aspects: For me, it was important that the university I was going to was going to align with my current education, but it was also very important to choose a place that I could experience a lot in, and be able to try a different culture. I also saw the opportunity to pick a country, where I could easily travel to other cities on weekends, and get to see as much as possbile.
info_ease: It was relatively easy, our coordinator had before arrival sent a lot of emails with all the important information that we needed upon arrival, and we also met up with him where we could ask questions
arrival_assistance: Our coordinator was great at assisting us, and I also asked friends who also were on exchange in Milan
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We had received emails regarding our arrival, so when we came to Milan, we went down to our host university and got our proof of arrival, as well as the opportunity to ask questions, and masssimo was a great help. Afterwards we needed to change our courses, which could quite easily be done through the host university website.
registration_help: Our coordinator was more than happy to help, and using my own network was also very helpful.
registration_success: I would say I was quite succesful, I did end up changing most of my courses upon arrival, due to them overlapping a lot. Therefore I needed to change half of my courses, but ended up arranging it so I only had one overlap.
registration_advice: Just make sure to check every information you get before arrival, because it will make life a lot easier upon arrival. Also be prepared to change your courses once you arrive, to ensure there isn't any overlap, and still then be prepared to have a little overlap, but that is something that you can hardly avoid, but as long as you manage to minimize them and then make sure that your attendances still are registered, then you should be good.
course_level: I feel as if the academic level was a bit lower, compared to Denmark, both still good! It felt not quite as technical as it is at University of Copenhagen, which is fair, because I know we are quite far, but it could be felt, also with the classmates that were local. The exams were also very different.
teaching_comparison: It was quite similar, although I would say it was in general less coordinated then it is here at UCPH. But otherwise I feel it was the same style of teaching most of the time.
courses_enrolled: Digital Innovation and Management Languages of the Media Digital Society Coding for Computational science
recommended_courses: I loved Digital Society! The teacher Chris Anderson was great and I learned a lot!
unexpected_costs: We had to pay tourist taxes to our apartment upon arrival which was around 180 eur pr person.
cost_comparison: The food and drink at restaurants and bars were cheaper than expected which was very nice! The groceries were quite similar to Denmark I would say.
activities_available: The ESN-programme offered a lot of different events, but this was something I did not took part of, so im not sure what exactly they offered, I know they offered trips, picnics, parties and cultural activities, such as museum watching.
activities_recommended: Go see the near-by cities and experience more of Italy! It is very easy to take a train or a flix-bus to many of the cities for quite cheap which I would highly recommend. For example Como is only one hour away on the trip. also during the hot summer days, there are some pool areas within the city.
weekend_recommendations: On the weekends, go visit the markets! There are a lot of great ones, my favorites were the Navigli Canal market and the market in Brera. Also just go around the different parts of the city and explore, I loved china town and Brera. And also to go to other parts of italy on the weekends or days off.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, it has a lot of the same culture, so it wasn't all that different to Denmark.
cultural_challenges: I think maybe the forwardness of some Italians were a bit challenging, or at least something I had to get used to. The Italian men were not afraid to look at you or talk, which you had to get used to.
culture_appreciated: Just the like classic italian more cultural way to live. Where it is normal to go out to eat, or sit and enjoy a glass of wine after work, the slower paste of life, is something I really appreciated
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy your time as much as you can, and make sure to visit other parts of Italy, since it is so easy! 2. Go out to drink and eat, it is so cheap and there are so many good places and opportunities! 3. Always enjoy the sunny days as much as possible! It rains a lot of the days, so when the sun is out, you have to be outside as well
other_useful_info: remember to check the weather everyday, in case you need to bring an umbrella. Check out all the thrifting/vintage opportunities, both all humanas, but also the vintage stores, there is a great street with 'bivio' and like 7 other thrift stores in one small street.
most_rewarding: Just getting an experience of a life time, and get the opportunity live in another country for a semester. The experience as a whole is something I will remember for the rest of my life, and that I find very rewarding
greatest_challenge: I think it might be to have to put your life on pause for half a year, and really try yourself, It is quite a big change that you need to get used to, and you don't have your people from home around you. So I would say the most challenging is missing the people from back home.

crucial_aspects: The university of Milan offers a lot of different course for law students, which i thought sounded interesting.
overall_comments: The overall experience of exchange was good. It is fun to live in a different country with a different culture, and so is going to a different school with a quite different way of structuring the teachings. It was fun interacting with the other exchange students and there was plenty of arrangements made for exchange students, which made that seamless to do. I did however have many difficulties with my landlord, which was a thorn in the side. And i also found it a bit disappointing, that i had very limited interactions with Italiens in the same age range as me, this was among other things because the classes in english were almost only attended by exchange students.
info_ease: It was very easy. All the information was made available primarily through mails that was sent out at the appropriate times. Furthermore the erasmus office at the school are very friendly and helpful, so if you ever have any questions, they will happily help you out.
arrival_assistance: Upon arrival you go to the erasmus office, where i got my student card and my proof of attendance signed for the first time. Here you also got various information and answers to any questions you had. There is also a student organization called ESN, which had a welcome meeting, where they gave a lot of helpful information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The overall experience of exchange was good. It is fun to live in a different country with a different culture, and so is going to a different school with a quite different way of structuring the teachings. It was fun interacting with the other exchange students and there was plenty of arrangements made for exchange students, which made that seamless to do. I did however have many difficulties with my landlord, which was a thorn in the side. And i also found it a bit disappointing, that i had very limited interactions with Italiens in the same age range as me, this was among other things because the classes in english were almost only attended by exchange students.
registration_process: There is a big catalogue of courses from where you can choose which ones you want. In the specific course in the catalogue there is a link to a calendar, where you can see when the classes are. When you have picked some courses, then you go to the student portal (Unimia), where you just write which courses you picked.
registration_help: The process was described in an email. Besides that i am not sure, as i did not use any other help.
registration_success: As far as i know you can pick any class, without any rejection or the like. I do not think they make a cap on how many students can attend the different courses.
registration_advice: To make sure you find different courses that do not overlap, as the attendance is mandatory. And as the courses can be at different campus', also check which campus the courses are in, as you might not have time to go from one campus to another, if you pick to classes which are right after each other.
academics_comments: The overall experience of exchange was good. It is fun to live in a different country with a different culture, and so is going to a different school with a quite different way of structuring the teachings. It was fun interacting with the other exchange students and there was plenty of arrangements made for exchange students, which made that seamless to do. I did however have many difficulties with my landlord, which was a thorn in the side. And i also found it a bit disappointing, that i had very limited interactions with Italiens in the same age range as me, this was among other things because the classes in english were almost only attended by exchange students.
course_level: I found the level to be lower in Milan than it is in Copenhagen. However, there is also something to be said about how the teaching is structured differently. In Copenhagen classes are not mandatory and you are not evaluated on in class performances, however there is a difficult (mostly written) exam at the end. In Milan the classes are mandatory and you are evaluated on in class performance, however, the exams at the end are easier and often oral.
teaching_comparison: The teaching in Milan is mostly just the teacher presenting the material and asking questions to the students. In Copenhagen you have to prepare presentations and cases for the classes, which i barely had any of on exchange.
courses_enrolled: 1. INTERNATIONAL REFUGEE PROTECTION AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT 2. TRADE LIBERALIZATION AND LABOUR RIGHTS 3. EUROPEAN MONETARY AND ECONOMIC LAW 4. COMPETITION LAW AND ECONOMICS 5. LAW AND POLICIES FOR SOCIAL RIGHTS PROTECTION IN EUROPE
recommended_courses: COMPETITION LAW AND ECONOMICS is a very well made course with a good teacher, but it was also the hardest course i had on exchange. EUROPEAN MONETARY AND ECONOMIC LAW is a very interesting course if you are into european law. LAW AND POLICIES FOR SOCIAL RIGHTS PROTECTION IN EUROPE also has a good teacher and is a not only instructive but also thought-provoking course.
unexpected_costs: Lawyer fees for the problems with my landlord.
cost_comparison: Transportation is way cheaper than i expected. Housing is more expensive than i expected.
activities_available: I do not know if the university actually provided any, besides an italian course.
activities_recommended: Sightseeing.
weekend_recommendations: The horse racing course next to the san siro, and of course going to see football matches at the san siro. Also taking the trains to different italian cities, it is easy and fast to get there, and it is fun to experience different cities.
culture_adjustment: It probably takes a week or two, but it is not difficult in general.
socializing_tips: Not really. As i mentioned above there are almost only exchange students in the english courses, and as there are not many activities arranged by the university, then you probably have to seek them out elsewhere.
cultural_challenges: A lot of Italians do not speak english.
culture_appreciated: How laid back and unworried it is. It also seems that most problems can be fixed if you ask nice enough.
top3_advice: 1. Check when the classes are for the different courses, so you do not get overlapping classes. 2. Make a contract with your landlord. 3. Show up to the arrangements made by the student organizations (especially at the start of your exchange).
other_useful_info: It can be hard to find your classroom at first, so go to the campus before you actually start school, and find out where the different classrooms are.
most_rewarding: Making friends from all parts of the world.
greatest_challenge: My rental situation with my landlord.

crucial_aspects: I thought Milan was a dynamic international hub with strong career prospects in the legal field and international law.
info_ease: I thought it was very easy.
arrival_assistance: We got an email from Massimo about where to sign our Proof of Attendance. Very easy.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We already had access to the Milan University student platform before arrival, so we knew when and where we should be the first day.
registration_help: Student information.
registration_success: 100'% successful. No issues.
registration_advice: Try some different classes before you register. You can try different classes the first week (or two) - but notice that most professors notices when you are not attending.
course_level: Most of them are easy, if you are attending student.
teaching_comparison: It is more "old fashion" where they registrer your attendance and you get graded for what you say in class, etc.
courses_enrolled: Comparative Contract Law Scientific Innovation and Legal Challenges of Food regulation Space Law International Criminal Law Cultural Diversity and Human Rights Law
recommended_courses: International Criminal Law and Comparative Contract Law. Great professors and interesting subjects. I do not recommend Cultural Diversity and Human Rights Law since there where no informations about exams.
unexpected_costs: Lost my deposit. Stay away from double-sided tape.

crucial_aspects: My interest in the culture of the country, the weather, and the university's large offering of interesting courses in international law, EU law, etc.
info_ease: 95 % of the information was sent by University of Milan's contact person, so that was quite nice. However, I think it would have been nice to have received more of the information at an earlier time so that one would not have had to check one's E-mail more or less every day in order to stay up to date on the next step in the process leading up to the exchange. For me personally, not knowing and just awaiting further instructions also at times was rather stressful. The other 5 % takes some time to find when you have to navigate the website(s) of another university, but over time you get more and more familiar with their systems and websites.
arrival_assistance: All international students need to pick up their student ID card on location and also have their proof of attendance form signed, so I went to the international students' office and received assistance with this.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You need to enter the courses' names, codes, ECTS points, and professors into a dedicated site on the UNIMIA platform.
registration_help: You can always text the University of Milan international students' office or ask the course professor. However, in my case they were not always clear on whether or not I could actually attend their course. Therefore I strongly recommend asking all questions over E-mail so that everything is in writing if you run into any problems in connection to registering for the exams (which I find unlikely, but better safe than sorry).
registration_success: Very successful. I had no problems once I actually registered the courses. The only problems were the initial problems regarding whether or not I could attend certain courses.
registration_advice: Follow the guide which will be sent out by the University of Milan international students' office. If you are unsure if you can follow a certain course, ask the professor of the course.
course_level: To be candid, the academic level was shockingly low compared to the level at the University of Copenhagen. It took me 2 days per exam to prepare, which is extremely little time compared to the 7-10 days per exam I usually spend for courses at UCPH. Although to be fair, the law courses at the University of Milan are for the most part only 6 ECTS, whereas the ones at UCPH are usually 7,5, 10, or even 15 ECTS and thus requiring more time preparing for the exams.
teaching_comparison: There were only one class per course which was taught by the course professor(s). They were for the most part closer to classical lectures than seminars. I prefer the style of teaching at UCPH with the seminars which provides for more discussion of the readings and requires a greater degree of participation from the students of the class.
courses_enrolled: 1) Workshop on Human Rights and the Ombudsman 2) International Law and International Law on Sustainable Development 3) European Monetary and Economic Law 4) Competition Law and Economics 5) Sources of Law and Fundamental Rights in AI
recommended_courses: No. 3, 4, and 5. Also any courses taught by Filippo Croci and/or Luca Toffoletti.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Food, drinks, coffee, etc. and also public transport was less expensive than I expected.
activities_available: There are WhatsApp group chats where students get together for instance to play football, go to the theater, or go out to drink a beer on the weekends.
activities_recommended: Travel as much as possible on the weekends! It is worth all of the money. If you like football, I also recommend going to the Stadio San Siro.
weekend_recommendations: Travel as much as possible. I can recommend going to Verona, Venice, Naples, Sardinia, and Lugano. Prioritize meeting new people from other cultures and countries in the beginning of the exchange.
culture_adjustment: That is a complex matter, as there were definitely certain aspects of the Italian culture I did not enjoy and other aspects I absolutely loved. All in all, it was not that hard - but I found it to be very important to speak a basic level of Italian for doing everyday tasks such as grocery shopping or going for a coffee, as it is very likely that the Italian employee will not be able to speak English with you.
cultural_challenges: The Italians have no spatial awareness in the public space, so they will just be standing in the middle of a crowded room for no good reason instead of getting out of the way. It was also very common that the professors were late to the classes, not infrequently by 10+ minutes, which was shocking to me as we in the Nordic countries consider that completely unacceptable.
culture_appreciated: The general kindness of the Italians and their openness to socialize, their passion for their cuisine, the language, the caffetterie and their prices, the idea of "take it slow", and their huge passion for football.
top3_advice: (1) Remember to enjoy the exchange, as before you know it, it will be all over, (2) remember to register for the exams within the stated deadlines, and (3) go to Milan 1,5-2 weeks before classes start in order to get familiar with the city, meet new people, and get settled into your residence.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and establishing friendships across the European continent.
greatest_challenge: Getting used to a completely new everyday routine in a foreign country.

registration_process: Coming from UCPH, it can be quite confusing to register for courses. The concept is totally different that in Copenhagen, and not at all as formal and rigid. However, it takes some getting used to. Generally, you have to just try out the courses without registering it anywhere. When you have then settled for a course, you enter Unimi's students portal and register for the course there. You have to remember, to register for the exam at the end of the course also.
registration_help: Many of the professors were very willing to explain in detail how it is done, when you initially are trying out their courses.
registration_success: It was easy, and I got every course that I wanted.
registration_advice: Accept the lack of familities that you may be used to from a university back home, and ask the polite professors in order to get a grasp of the concept.

courses_enrolled: International Criminal Law Labour Law and Environmental Sustainability Scientific Innovation and Legal Challenges of Food Regulation Comparative Contract Law International Organizations and Sustainable Development
recommended_courses: Especially Comparative Contract Law, and Labour Law and Environmental Sustainability was a joy for me.
unexpected_costs: Not many.
cost_comparison: Food was less expensive than back home. However, we spent a lot of money on trips, tickets and eating out.
activities_available: There was an ERASMUS-organization that welcomed us.
activities_recommended: Take time and weekends off to go on trips around Milan - Florence, Como, Bologna etc.
weekend_recommendations: Go on a lot of trips around Italy!
culture_adjustment: It was very easy, and very joyful.
cultural_challenges: There was a certain language barrier. Furthermore, people did not seem as busy, as they may seem in Denmark, and that may be a little irritating when you yourself are in a hurry. But my best advice is to settle down, lower you shoulders and follow the rhythm.
culture_appreciated: I really came to appreciate the laissez faire-lifestyle in the end.
top3_advice: It is going to be more expensive, that you think. So save up, and boost the "unexpected expenses" part of your budget. Take it easy upon arrival, and feel your way around the university. Get a feel for how they do things compared to UCPH. Remember to enjoy the city, the surroundings and all the other exchange-students!

most_rewarding: Getting new friends, and getting all of those experiences that you would never get, if you just were to go to Italy on vacation!
greatest_challenge: Not many, really.

crucial_aspects: Chance to explore a new culture through various aspects of everyday life.
overall_comments: Overall, I find that the process from applying for an exchange to actually arriving at the university is extremely poor. There is an absolute lack of information on how to find details about everything from exams to courses and teaching, etc. In general, it seems as though there is very little communication between the host university and the home university regarding teaching practices in Milan.

The University of Milan had uploaded their new courses under the wrong academic year, so the selection was broader than my initial point of departure. It would have been helpful to know what to pay attention to in terms of how Italians “work” within an academic setting.
arrival_assistance: None really
housing_how: I found housing on my own

There is an absolute lack of information on how to find details about everything from exams to courses and teaching, etc. In general, it seems as though there is very little communication between the host university and the home university regarding teaching practices in Milan.
registration_process: It was fine, we just had to sign a document confirming the arrival date.
registration_help: I’m not entirely sure, as I didn’t really make use of it, but we could always write to Massimo.
registration_success: The University of Milan does not offer any psychology courses, so I had to take subjects that fall quite far outside my field of study. I was registered for all the courses I applied for, but I wish that the courses for the new academic year had been uploaded before the start of the semester, so I could have applied for different courses than the ones I ended up taking.
registration_advice: Be aware that you can apply for new courses during your studies, so if you realize that you do not want to take the course you have been approved for, you can always switch to a new one and apply for a new pre-approval.
academics_comments: Overall, I find that the process from applying for an exchange to actually arriving at the university is extremely poor. There is an absolute lack of information on how to find details about everything from exams to courses and teaching, etc. In general, it seems as though there is very little communication between the host university and the home university regarding teaching practices in Milan.
course_level: The academic level was easier than at home, but of course you need to get used to the fact that all concepts and terminology are in English.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style is very different from that in Denmark. It is much more unstructured and laissez-faire. Some lecturers take attendance in class, while others do not. Exam dates change frequently, and students have the option to choose between several dates for when they want to take an exam. There is very little required reading for classes; instead, students have more teaching hours than at home.
courses_enrolled: Globalization and Cultural Diversity, Global Social Dynamics, Research Design, Human Resources Management
recommended_courses: Depends on what you find interesting.
unexpected_costs: We had some miscommunication
cost_comparison: We had misunderstood some parts of our contract, which meant that we each had to pay 2,500 DKK for something, and I was surprised by how expensive gym memberships were.
activities_available: Something called ESN arranged many social activities.
activities_recommended: Not sure.
weekend_recommendations: Take a trip to Lake Como or Bologna.
culture_adjustment: It was okay overall, but Italians have a very different lifestyle compared to Danes, so I found it particularly challenging in an academic setting.
cultural_challenges: Answered above.
culture_appreciated: Italians are generally very hospitable and helpful if you ask for assistance, and their unhurried approach to life, without constantly rushing, is probably something we could learn from.
top3_advice: Check the course lists regularly, don’t hesitate to ask for help when something is unclear, and be prepared to be flexible, as things may change along the way
other_useful_info: Milan is quite expensive, so be prepared for it to cost a bit :)
most_rewarding: Meeting other exchange students and building a great social life. It has been amazing to experience how Italians just enjoy an aperitivo before dinner and take the time to socialize and relax.
greatest_challenge: The academic differences.

academics_comments: Great city, not that great a university. The Erasmus team at the University is doing a pretty good job at creating opportunities to meet new people.
course_level: Much lower academic level compared to UCPH, much of the content was introductory and the course contents were confusing and incoherent at times. They focus on learning things by heart, which is not really a very effective way to actually learn something instead of learning the students to analyse and use the theories themselves.
teaching_comparison: Pretty much the same, classroom teaching and some group projects. They check attendance sometimes, but not consistently and the academic level is lower.
courses_enrolled: Global Criminal Organizations, International Law, Multi-Level Legal Systems, Global Politics
recommended_courses: International Law because the professor is able to speak English properly and actually try to teach the students to analyse and use the course literature on real cases. Global politics is also okay, but if you're studying political science at UCPH, you will probably have read all the course literature before. I recommend choosing some courses at first and then changing afterwards, once you have assessed if the professor is able to teach in English.
unexpected_costs: My landlord tried to keep my deposit and ending up taking some of it.
cost_comparison: Housing is more expensive than expected. Transportation however is very cheap.
activities_available: Tuesday bars, pubcrawls, football and other sport activities arranged by the students themselves. And short day trips outside Milan.
activities_recommended: Go to some parties and Erasmus activities to find new friends.
weekend_recommendations: See other cities, the trains is cheap and it is easy to visit Rome, Florence, Turin, Venice, Bologna etc.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, Italy is still Europe so not that different from Denmark.
socializing_tips: Nope, I did not really socialize with the Italian students, only international students.
cultural_challenges: I did not really find anything that culturally challenging.
culture_appreciated: The food is amazing.
top3_advice: Be careful not to get scammed when finding an apartment, take advantage of the food and restaurant scene in Italy and go visit some other cities around Milan.
other_useful_info: Don't be afraid to go to some Erasmus events alone and make new friends, it pays off.
most_rewarding: Seeing Italy and enjoying the Italian cuisine.
greatest_challenge: Finding friends in the beginning, and the academic level at the university, which were disappointing to say the least.
other_comments: Nope.

crucial_aspects: Before going, I had heard many positive things about going on exchange to Milan. For me, it was a combination of the academic opportunities, the chance to meet new people, as well as the food and the culture that made me want to go there.
overall_comments: I really enjoyed my Erasmus exchange in Milan, where I met many great people from all over Europe and the world. During my stay, I had the opportunity to experience beautiful nature and cities, as well as taste a variety of delicious food and wines.
info_ease: Overall, I think the preparation process was satisfactory. I received many emails from the university in Milan informing me about the next steps, and I was also contacted regarding accommodation. However, efficiency is not a word Italians like, and it is necessary to be patient when waiting for replies, whether from the university or in relation to accommodation.
arrival_assistance: The Italian Erasmus coordinator, Massimo, was very helpful. He could easily be contacted by email and usually had a solution or an answer to any questions. He also has a office you can go to.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I really enjoyed my Erasmus exchange in Milan, where I met many great people from all over Europe and the world. During my stay, I had the opportunity to experience beautiful nature and cities, as well as taste a variety of delicious food and wines.
registration_process: Before arrival, you receive links by email where you can find information about the available courses. Course registration takes place after arrival, and it is therefore not necessary to register for courses in advance. This allows you to change courses if they do not meet your expectations or fit your schedule. Once you have decided which courses you wish to take, you simply register for them through the university’s online platform.
registration_help: Not a lot of help, i just figured it out my self
registration_success: I changed three out of my four initial courses, as they did not fit together at all. However, everything worked out well in the end. Patientce is the key word.
registration_advice: It is a good idea to try out several different courses before registering for them. Additionally, I would recommend choosing courses from the same degree programme, as all the first exam sessions are typically scheduled in January. I would also strongly recommend asking the professors in advance when they plan to hold the exams. I did not fully realize this until it was too late, which resulted in having five exams within a ten day period. This was a very stressful experience.
academics_comments: I really enjoyed my Erasmus exchange in Milan, where I met many great people from all over Europe and the world. During my stay, I had the opportunity to experience beautiful nature and cities, as well as taste a variety of delicious food and wines.
course_level: I only took master’s level courses, as there were no English taught courses available at the bachelor level. However, I found that the academic level of the master’s courses was generally comparable to, or in some cases slightly lower than, the level of bachelor’s courses in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: In Milan, teaching mainly consisted of two to three hour lectures where students primarily listened to the professor. There were no exercises, laboratory work, or group assignments. I found this teaching style monotone, and at times the quality of the teaching was limited, partly because some professors were not very proficient in English.
courses_enrolled: - Methods in Bioinformatics - Molecular and Cellular Microbiology - Genetics, Cellular and Molecular Biology - Biotechnological Products and Processes
recommended_courses: The course in Bioinformatics, as the exam consisted of a project that could be completed either individually or in groups.
unexpected_costs: I had to buy a new phone, since my old one got stolen. I also spend quite a lot of money on traveling around.
cost_comparison: Groceries were generally cheaper than in Denmark, and I also found that eating at restaurants was slightly more affordable. As a result, we ate out quite frequently. Beer prices were more or less the same as in Denmark, whereas wine was very cheap. Public transportation was also very affordable.
activities_available: The ESN (Erasmus student network), organize a lot of different activites, sports and parties. They also plan trips to rome or even germany.
activities_recommended: I would recommend travelling around with friends during the exchange. We visited Rome, which was a great experience, and we also spent a few days in Morocco, which was very exciting. Additionally, Milan itself offers many opportunities for social activities, whether it is going to a bar, a restaurant, or a club.
weekend_recommendations: - Go to some of the cities near milan - Grab a beer with some friends - Go on a hike
culture_adjustment: I think it was very easy. I quickly met some new people.
socializing_tips: Not really. Most of the people that i spoke with and befriended was also exchange students.
cultural_challenges: I experienced a relatively high level of bureaucracy, and administrative processes were sometimes inefficient, which required a lot of patience.
culture_appreciated: Italy has excellent food and wine, as well as many impressive monuments with a long history. I also loved that coffee is so cheap there.
top3_advice: - Meet new people from other countries and cultures. Don’t only socialize with other Danes, otherwise you won’t learn much. - Be very patient. - Save some money in advance. I ended up spending much more than I initially expected.
other_useful_info: It can be a bit stressfull going on exchange, but everything will work out, since there is a solution for almost everything.
most_rewarding: When i passed all my exams. I had five exams in ten days. I was sure that i could not do it. But it all, worked out in the end. It always does.
greatest_challenge: Finding courses that fit into my schedule was challenging. I also did not particularly enjoy the teaching style in Italy.

recommended_courses: Conflict Management and Negotiation. The professor (Francesco Tomasi) is great.

crucial_aspects: Academic relevance (Milan for MA in History of Art) and availability of English language courses.
info_ease: Easy and accessible, I did not have any problems in this regard.
arrival_assistance: I had to show up at the international student desk - there was nothing particularly complicated that I needed help with.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Online registration through the university website, I had to add the name of the course, the professor, and the amount of ECTS credits on a list, which could later be updated easily.
registration_help: I never needed it, but I assume that I could have contacted the international student desk.
registration_success: Mostly succesfull, but not fully - I had problems registering for one out of four classes. This was due to very limited spots in the class as well as a lack of transparency regarding the process of signing up for this one particular type of class on the programme website.
registration_advice: Avoid trying to sign up for any workshop-classes, as they have a different process of signing up and some only have 8 spots available. Spend some extra time trying to figure out which other classes in English are available. Some courses are available for different amounts of ECTS credits, so you might be able to mix and match a bit to make sure you have the required amount for Erasmus but not too many for your home university.
course_level: I found that half of my courses were very relevant and maintained a high standard, while the other half seemed less relevant and the teaching goals of those courses were a bit unclear.
teaching_comparison: I found that they were more focused on memorization than discussion (or analysis for that matter), which I did not expect from MA classes. The teaching style was very different, with little in-class engagement with the students, although this depended a lot on the individual professor.
courses_enrolled: Ancient Documents in Their Visual and Performative Context Computational Methods and Techniques for Historical and Cultural Studies Cultural History of the Modern Period The Politics of Mobility, Displacement and Asylum
recommended_courses: "Ancient Documents in Their Visual and Performative Context" and "The Politics of Mobility, Displacement and Asylum" I would absolutely recommend! Professor Lucia Cecchet ("Ancient documents...") and professor Luca Ciabarri ("The Politics...") were engaging, the structure of the courses was clear, and they maintained a high academic level in a welcoming learning environment.
unexpected_costs: It was sometimes difficult to find space in the libraries, so I ended up sitting more in cafés than I do at home.
cost_comparison: I think the high rent in the city meant that I expected other neccessities to be very expensive as well, which (by my home country's standards) they are not - although it is definitely more expensive than most other Italian cities.
activities_available: There were discounts for some cultural institutions - other than that I mostly encountered ESN Milano. The events ESN Milano organized seemed interesting, but sadly they usually filled up very quickly, and I only managed to go to their weekly meeting at a bar.
activities_recommended: I recommend going to some of the meet-ups early on - I met some of my closest friends there. Don't be afraid to ask your classmates to get coffee after class!
weekend_recommendations: Go on day-trips to near-by cities, I especially recommend Bergamo and Lecco. A lot of the museums have really good student discounts. Some of the art museums that I enjoyed the most were Novecento, Pinacoteca di Brera, Pinacoteca Ambrosiana, GAM, and Fondazione Prada.
culture_adjustment: I was fairly easy - Milan is also a very international city, so it might have made it easier. I think most of my friends found the city and culture welcoming, even if we came from completely different parts of the world.
socializing_tips: Go for a coffee or try to organize aperitivo with the people in your classes - this is easier if you mostly follow courses from one degree.
cultural_challenges: I think the cultural differences were mostly interesting, not particularly challenging. I think I was also fortunate to be surrounded by kind and open-minded people.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated how open and easy to talk to my fellow students were - and I really enjoyed how easy it was to grab a quick coffee or a quick drink. It didn't have to be a big, planned thing, which I really enjoyed. I also really liked going to the different markets and seeing the city that way.
top3_advice: Put yourself in situations without a lot of other UCPH students - there's a lot of us, but I think a big part of the experience is getting out of a Danish bubble. Don't expect the teaching styles to be similar to the ones in UCPH: it's a very different approach, but even if it's not to your preference, it teaches you something about how academia works. You can follow courses as an attending or non-attending student, but I would definitely recommend being an attending student, as it provides both structure and is a great way of meeting friends and experiencing academic culture.
other_useful_info: Some of the courses are available for different amounts of ECTS credits, so you might be able to take a 9 ECTS course as a 6 ECTS course, which can make it easier to get the correct amount of ECTS credits.
most_rewarding: The people I met! Spending time experiencing the city with new friends and just taking time to do so. Milan is really beautiful and full of culture and things to see, whether it's markets, museums, restaurants or architecture.
greatest_challenge: I think adjusting to some of the different teaching approaches, but also the exam season was quite intense (three exams in one week). I definitely spend more time studying for each exam than I needed to, as the grading system seemed more relaxed than it is in UCPH (in my experience, at least).

crucial_aspects: It was important for me to go on exchange to a place where I could feel at home, while still experiencing a different culture, without being too far away from home. I therefore felt that Italy was the perfect destination, as I have always felt a strong affection for the country, while at the same time it is not very far from Denmark. I believe that what particularly attracted me to Milan was the strong Danish community there. Although I find other Italian cities more attractive in some respects, it meant a great deal to me that many other Danish students were also going on exchange, especially since I was travelling alone. In addition, Milan is very centrally located, making it easy to travel around Italy. This was also a decisive factor in my choice of Milan, as it opened up many opportunities for travelling throughout the country.
info_ease: I found it really confusing in the beginning, especially because the course selection process was very unclear and, in practice, something that was only resolved once the classes had already started. I found this particularly frustrating. Otherwise, the process was manageable, as it was easy to contact staff members in Milan, and we also had an information meeting at home, which helped ensure that we were reasonably well informed.
arrival_assistance: We received several emails informing us that we had to report our arrival at the Erasmus office, and we also received emails regarding course selection. However, I feel that the information could have been communicated more clearly and in a more informative way.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The entire process of registering for courses was very confusing. There was very little information provided until just around the time of arrival. In addition, putting together a course schedule was extremely difficult, at least in my case, and it varied greatly from student to student. I had received pre-approval for around 15 courses, and there was not a single combination of these courses that did not involve timetable clashes.
registration_help: It was possible to communicate with some members of the university staff.
registration_success: As mentioned earlier, it was not really possible for me to put together a schedule without my courses overlapping. This was therefore very frustrating, as I had to figure out which courses I could take without being required to attend every session. Fortunately, this was possible for most courses, as there were options such as being registered as non-attending, or where attendance was not mandatory. In addition, it was possible during the first two weeks to try out different courses, which also made the process a bit easier. As a result, I did not have my final schedule until around the end of September.
registration_advice: Make sure to get as many courses pre-approved as possible, as it is reassuring not to have to apply for pre-approval while you are already abroad, but instead be able to choose freely among the courses you have already had approved.
course_level: I would say that the overall academic level is somewhat lower than at my home university. I took three master’s level courses and one bachelor’s level course, and I did not feel that the master’s courses were noticeably more advanced than my own academic level. That being said, it could at times be extremely difficult to understand what the lecturers were saying. Several of my lecturers had very strong Italian accents, and it was often almost impossible to understand them, which naturally made the classes more challenging. In addition, in one of my courses we were required to give a presentation where the lecturer expected us to demonstrate knowledge from our bachelor’s degree, as he assumed that we already held a bachelor’s degree in the subject of the course. This was somewhat challenging, as we were all actually completely new to the subject.
teaching_comparison: It was actually very similar, as we primarily have a lot of classroom-based teaching in rhetoric, which was also the main form of teaching in Milan. Courses often included both presentations and written assignments, which contributed to the final grade, and I actually found this quite beneficial. In addition, the exams were very different from those in Denmark. The written exams were handwritten and not very well organised. The oral exam I attended also took place in front of the entire class, which I found somewhat uncomfortable.
courses_enrolled: Corporate communication Journalism, media and politics Media theory and AI Introduction to italian literature
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend Journalism, Media and Politics. I was especially impressed by Christopher Anderson, who is an American lecturer.
unexpected_costs: It was slightly more expensive to live there than I had expected.Things like groceries were considerably more expensive than I had expected.
cost_comparison: groceries were more expensive than expected, and eating out in Milan is quite more expensive than in the rest of Italy.
activities_available: There were quite a few opportunities to join sports clubs, but it was not really something I engaged in. In addition, a number of parties were organised, but this was also not something many of us Danes participated in. We mostly spent time together with other Danish students and found our own activities to take part in.
activities_recommended: I would recommend participating in some of the parties, especially at the beginning. Otherwise, I would say that it might be better to try to find your own activities and experiences.
weekend_recommendations: I would definitely recommend travelling around Italy. Milan is a great city with excellent transport connections throughout the country, so I would recommend this one hundred percent.
culture_adjustment: It was fine, and I did not find it particularly difficult.
cultural_challenges: Not really anything.
culture_appreciated: The food :)))
top3_advice: 1. Make the most of your time and explore as much of the country as possible. 2. Dare to do things on your own, even if it feels uncomfortable at first. 3. Remember that everyday life will eventually set in, so try not to overwhelm yourself. It is also completely okay to take time for yourself, even though it can be easy to feel like you are missing out if you are not part of everything.
other_useful_info: Be patient with the Italian education system, as it is very different from the Danish one. They have a very laissez-faire approach to education. In addition, the examination formats are also quite different: written exams are handwritten, and oral exams often take place in front of the entire class.
most_rewarding: Definitely the opportunity to travel extensively around the country. In addition, I made many great Danish friends, but I also learned a lot about myself, as I went abroad on my own and lived alone for the first time.
greatest_challenge: Definitely having to live alone and manage on your own in a completely new country. It can be intimidating at first, but I believe it makes you much more independent and teaches you a great deal.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere with a lot of international students and I wanted to go to a country within the EU. Furthermore, I did not want to go somewhere where school would be very time demanding. Apart from that, I have always liked Italy.
info_ease: It was difficult. You need to find the information yourself on the website of the university regarding courses and so on. However, the most crucial thing are sent to you via e-mail, which helps.
arrival_assistance: There was the responsible person, Massimo, at the University of Milan. He was quite helpful and answered my questions quickly. However, there was not really any guidance on how to navigate the school or websites of the school.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: In the beginning, you can 'shop courses' and try different courses. It is easy to register them. You receive an email with the registration process. I tried one course that I did not end up taking. It is very chill and relax and everyone got the courses they wanted.
registration_help: There was a guide, which was sent to us via e-mail. You can always ask the teachers.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Try to make a good schedule. I was off on Mondays which was very nice, and if you have breaks between classes that is nice, because you can always grab a coffee with your classmates
course_level: All the courses were easier than at my home university. There was almost no preparation before class. However, some classes are harder and more demanding than others, but never as demanding as at Copenhagen University.
teaching_comparison: In some classes, your grades depended on your contribution during class. Furthermore, we did not do group work and a lot of classes were just listening. The classes I took were only seminars and not big lectures.
courses_enrolled: 1) Competition Law and economics 2) Theory and practice of international tax law 3) Smart cities, Artificial intelligence and digital transformation law 4) International, European environmental law 5) Roman law
recommended_courses: Competition law and economic and theory and practice of international law were the most useful ones and the ones were I learned the most. If you want a very easy exam and no homework, the smart cities class is a good choice. I would not recommend the environmental law class.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Rent can be quite expensive. Furthermore, the general cost of living (restaurant and so on) is cheaper than in Copenhagen, but Milan is probably the most expensive part of Italy.
activities_available: I did not really engage in the activities hosted by the host university and to be honest, I do not know whether they hosted any for international students. It was more via the ESN community.
activities_recommended: Engage in the ESN activities - especially in the beginning. People are very open.
weekend_recommendations: Do trips around Italy with Flixbus. You can see Verona, Florence, Venice or Bologna
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy. However, there was a language barrier and sometimes Milanese can be a bit rude if you do not speak Italian.
socializing_tips: I did not socialize that much with Italian students, but my experience is that once you talk to them, they are pretty open.
cultural_challenges: They are a bit more relaxed here and sometimes things are not that organized.
culture_appreciated: I loved their apperitivo concept and their sense of style.
top3_advice: 1) They tell you that exams are in January. That is not necessarily true - I had all mine in December before Christmas. Each course has four rounds of exam dates, one in December, two in January and one in February. You can choose which ever you prefer. So, you do not need accommodation until January (that was at least the case for law - regarding Medicine it was different) - Law courses first start around late September (mine started around 20th of September) - Don't stress regarding course registration and exam registration - you will receive intructions.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: I got to know Milan very well, which is very nice. Furthermore, I met so many amazing people and I think it made me more open and able to talk to a lot of different people.
greatest_challenge: In the beginning you have to get used to everything and the fact that all your routines are different, but as soon as school starts, everything feels normal.

crucial_aspects: It was one of the few universities in Europe where there was no language demands except for English. I also wanted to go with a friend, and this was the place where it was most certain that we would both get a spot.
info_ease: It was very difficult. There were noone to help us figure out how to log into the systems, noone to help show us the ways to the correct rooms (which were hard to find), there were noone to explain the italian university system to us and noone that tried to get us to be a part of their university culture. Very isolated experience in that sense.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance. We got one email that explained which office to get the stamp of approval that we had arrived, and that was all.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We did not register for courses until the semester had already started. That is just how it works in the Italian universities. The courses were easy to find and a lot of information was available, but it was a bit hard to find out where and how to actually register.
registration_help: None as far as I remember.
registration_success: Luckily I got all of the classes that I wanted. I think that is pretty normal in Milan.
registration_advice: Don't stress about it. You can change your courses until pretty late in the semester, so you can browse around a bit.
course_level: The academic level was not very high. It was easy to follow the masters courses even though I am a bachelors student.
teaching_comparison: I had lectures exclusively. No exercise classes, no laboratory work, no group work, no student presentations, no reports and nothing to do at all except just lectures with professors talking. Not very inspiring.
courses_enrolled: Ecology Genetics, Cellular and Molecular Biology Methods in Bioinformatics Cellular and Molecular Microbiology
recommended_courses: Ecology was a great course with a broad and inspiring curriculum. The professors were so nice and very accommodating of exchange students. The rest of the courses were just okay.
unexpected_costs: A lot of us, myself included, got our phones and personal belongings stolen/robbed. It is nice to calculate a buffer amount to be able to buy new things in emergencies.
cost_comparison: Groceries were less expensive than I expected, and also the coffee is very cheap. Everything to do with fitness and exercise is completely out of budget and very expensive.
activities_available: I do not know. I never saw or heard of any opportunities, so they were not very advertised for if there was any.
activities_recommended: Again, I don't know that there were any.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely go on day-trips to all of the surrounding cities and go on a lot of hiking trips in the beautiful italian nature. It is also possible to go to Switzerland to hike, and that is also wonderful. Furthermore you can easily take the train to Rome, Florence and Venice, and that is obviously worth the trip!
culture_adjustment: A lot of people do not speak English, so you have to wing it a bit, but other than that, the italian culture is pretty easy to understand and integrate into.
cultural_challenges: The difference in time management. Danish people are used to meeting at the exact time that was agreed upon - this is not the case in italy. People will constantly be late, and that is just part of the culture.
culture_appreciated: People were very open, kind and helpful. Everyone wanted to talk and socialize.
top3_advice: Expect to go there for the experience of different culture, but not for the academic level.
other_useful_info: The exam period is really stressful for exchange students, as we have to go home and cannot participate in the structure they have in italy. It is very normal for them to fail exams or just to retake them if they are not satisfied with their grade, but exchange students have to go home and therefore cannot afford to fail the exams. This is not what their system is built for as it is very normal to fail.
most_rewarding: The social life. It was amazing to get a friend group from all over Europe. I also really enjoyed all of the day and weekend trips.
greatest_challenge: The financial aspect was very stressful.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a country that was culturally different from Denmark, but not too far away, so friends and family could visit. Italy's culture, food, outgoing and chill approach and especially the beautiful country and cities were crucial for my choice of destination.
overall_comments: I really really recommend going to Italy. It is the most beautiful, charming and amazing country. There is much to see and experience in Milan, and the city has a great size - there is much to do in 5 months, but you still get the feeling that you know your way around the city after a while, and you can walk from one end of the city to the other in like an hour or so. Very charming even though it has a bad rep to a lot of people - there are so many charming areas that give you that authentic Italian experience, and also more modern areas, a very interesting combination. Sooo many good restaurants and bars, the university is beautiful, and it is a lively and fun city. I loved it.
info_ease: I would say that it is a stressful process figuring out everything, and it is very confusing as you do not always know who to contact with the different issues you face. But it is very much worth all the trouble.
arrival_assistance: We had to check in at the International mobility office where Massimo Costa helped us sign our proof of attendance paper. We also received some emails along the way to inform us about practical things from Massimo. He was quick to reply to emails and helpful. There was also a group of volunteer students part of ESN that arranged a bunch of activities throughout the semester for Erasmus students to participate in and get to know each other. I did not go to any of them, but I think other people did. They had a big meeting in the beginning where they introduced us to all kinds of practical things about Milan, the university etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
