Very charming even though it has a bad rep to a lot of people - there are so many charming areas that give you that authentic Italian experience, and also more modern areas, a very interesting combination. Sooo many good restaurants and bars, the university is beautiful, and it is a lively and fun city. I loved it.
registration_process: You make a pre-approval before coming to Milan to show UCPH that there are in fact relevant courses to take, and then you make a new one when you actually choose your courses in Milan and send that home again and then fill out your online learning agreement. So you also need to change your OLA once you have your actual courses figured out. When applying for the pre-approval they ask for a course code and that is just the combination of letters and numbers when you click on the course, e.g. Global Social Dynamics has the code SSD SPS/07. When you click on the course, there is a button at the right called Lessons timetable that you can click on and then you can combine different courses you want to take to see what your schedule would look like, that is very helpful when trying to figure out what courses to take and what schedule would work for you.
registration_help: Not really any help honestly
registration_success: Not all the classes I had looked at in the spring were actually available when I came to Milan in september, but I figured it out and chose other courses that were also relevant.
registration_advice: If "Value change and global societies" with professor Biolcati Rinaldi Ferruccio is available, I would really recommend it. He is an amazing professor, so good at explaining complex phenomena in an understandable way, and he is super nice and friendly. I would not take Global Social Dynamics with professor Triventi, it was like a crash course in sociology and just waaaayyyy to much information with 150 slides sometimes. He never had time to go through all of it, and it was just too much info about stuff that was so so so irrelevant. Do NOT recommend.
academics_comments: I really really recommend going to Italy. It is the most beautiful, charming and amazing country. There is much to see and experience in Milan, and the city has a great size - there is much to do in 5 months, but you still get the feeling that you know your way around the city after a while, and you can walk from one end of the city to the other in like an hour or so. course_level: Very easy as I explained. If you just show up to class and study for the exams, you will be fine.
teaching_comparison: The professors are definitely bright and knowledgable, but many courses are very low level and basically just rote learning. But I found most of them interesting.
courses_enrolled: Value change and global societies (recommend!) Global Social Dynamics (do not recommend) Globalization and cultural diversity (similar topics as in Sociologiske teoriudviklinger in Copenhagen, so it was an advantage for me that I had already had this course at home) Journalism, media and politics (it was okay but very common knowledge I feel like. We were examined only on the basis of a book we should read, the "open" questions were only based on this book)
recommended_courses: Value change and global societies had very interesting topics such as immigration and immigrants' attitudes towards other immigrants, how they gradually assimilated to the opinions of the natives etc. It was basically about values and why values change in societies and what mechanisms cause this change, and then we looked at different aspects of values so values and attitudes towards immigrants, climate, gender roles, homosexuality, religion and secularization. GREAT course!
unexpected_costs: Not really any unexpected costs
cost_comparison: Going out to eat is not so cheap as you would expect from Italy, but alcohol and coffee is much cheaper. And all the Italian groceries are cheap, but other groceries are like Danish. Public transportation is very cheap if you download the ATM app and buy a student pass for 4-5 months, it's like 88 euros which is like 165 kr. per month and then you can travel all you want with metro and tram.
activities_available: ESN arranged activities like tennis matches, football etc but I did not participate in any
activities_recommended: Running maybe, there are many good parks to run in
weekend_recommendations: Take the train to other cities outside Milan such as Parma (!!!), Lake como in the summer, Bergamo, Firenze, Bologna etc. There is a pretty good railway system from Milan to many cities, so it is pretty easy to travel around. Can be expensive sometimes but it is also possible to find cheaper tickets.
culture_adjustment: Easy, the Italians are very outgoing and when going out people love to talk to you when they notice you are not from Italy. They are very curious and proud of their country and love to talk about it and where they come from in Italy. The food is amazing, the attitude is laid back and easy going. This can also be a challenge though, because they never meet deadlines, they are often late and don't respond to messages and do not get things done which can be so very frustrating. The public transportation workers often strike because of bad conditions and salary, so I think we tried at least 10 times in the 5 months in Milan that the metro did not drive because of strikes. And then it is impossible to get around, because the busses often do not show up.
socializing_tips: I mostly talked to other exchange students
cultural_challenges: As I said before, the Italian way of doing things which is slow and the exact opposite of the Danish way. I really missed UCPH's way of doing and organizing things.
culture_appreciated: The food, the passionate people, who love their country, going to football matches in San Siro, the way they really know how to make even the most random places cozy - they are even better at "hygge" than we are in Denmark. They have the most amazing and beautiful restaurants, both modern and also old fashioned, traditional and authentic. They hang out in the streets all year long where they drink their wine standing on the side walk in front of the bars if there is not room inside the bars, even in december and january. The food culture is just amazing, they love their food, and the way they are so traditional and rigid about it is amazing. They are a nice people who really have certain norms, like not drinking cappuccino after 12 o clock, and they will laugh at you if you order it after 12... They dress to impress, and they always greet each other politely.
top3_advice: Have patience in Italy! Eat your way through the country. Relax, it will all work out, they don't stress so you don't have to either. They are helpful and they know that Erasmus students are also there to enjoy Italy, so they are less strict with us. They are accommodating to Erasmus students and want to help us through the process.
other_useful_info: ESN offers a student card that you can buy for 100 kr. and this gives you access to the activities that they arrange, but it also gives you discount to Ryan Air which flies to Bergamo airport where you can easily take a bus to Milano Centrale, the central station, so I bought that and that way got cheap flight tickets back and forth. Fly to either Bergamo or Linate. From Bergamo there is a bus right outside the airport that takes you straight to the central station for 12 euros, and you just buy they tickets at the bus, don't buy them in advance. They drive all the time and there are many of them. Ryan Air only flies to Bergamo. If you go to Linate you can fly with easyjet e.g. and take the metro directly to the city within like 15 minutes. crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to southern Europe, Italy, Spain or Portugal, and with my education it left me with Milan as the only option.
overall_comments: I really loved living in Italy, meeting new people, both other danish students (which there were many of) but also other international and italian students. The only reason why it's 9/10 and not 10/10 would be some of the educational aspects such as logistics, teachers and exam methods.
info_ease: I did my exchange with 3 friends from my study, so finding all information was easier, being 4 people searching for the correct information etc., but it was not the most easy as I remember. Especially doing the logistics with choosing courses was pretty difficult.
arrival_assistance: The Erasmus office in Milan had wrote us an email, etc. and we could also ask the administration at the Erasmus office there, when we went to register our date of arrival. But we had to ask many questions to figure everything out.
arrival_comments: There were some different Erasmus meeting days in the beginning, but you had to be acquainted with the Erasmus email or instagram in order to know this. The university itself had no such introduction day or campus tour or anything. It would have been nice to have a campus tour and knowledge of reading spots and libraries etc. around campus.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I really loved living in Italy, meeting new people, both other danish students (which there were many of) but also other international and italian students. The only reason why it's 9/10 and not 10/10 would be some of the educational aspects such as logistics, teachers and exam methods.
registration_process: We received a bunch of mails with our login and an italian e-mail address, and then we has to register online (to unimia.it) our selfs i believe.
registration_help: I don't recall any help, other than writing to the university Erasmus office for help.
registration_success: I got most classes I wanted without any overlapping courses, but it was a big puzzle.
registration_advice: Examine the different courses from the course list on the university website before arriving, but don't expect to get the courses you want, since the schedules are finished one week before the courses start, so you cannot plan the final classes from home. And I would personally recommend not taking too many classes with oral exams, since they are very much different from the exams in Denmark, and not very nice to attend.
academics_comments: I really loved living in Italy, meeting new people, both other danish students (which there were many of) but also other international and italian students. The only reason why it's 9/10 and not 10/10 would be some of the educational aspects such as logistics, teachers and exam methods.
course_level: The MA courses were the only once in english, and the level of the courses was generally lower than those at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was almost exclusively lectures, 2 hours long and often without breaks. We didn't have other teaching material than the powerpoints from our professors, but that was enough to study for the exams. However, I missed the different SAU and theoretical exercises from UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Cell Therapy and Gene Silencing (7 ETCS), Molecular Pharmacology and Immunology (6 ETCS), Molecular Bioinformatics (6 ETCS) and Genetics, cellular and Molecular Biology (12 ETCS). 31 ETCS in total.
recommended_courses: Cell Therapy and Gene Silencing (7 ETCS) was pretty interesting I think, and nice teachers, some laboratory classes as well. Molecular Pharmacology and Immunology (6 ETCS) would have been easier if we had had Immunology before, but it's manageable without. Molecular Bioinformatics (6 ETCS) was not the most interesting I must admit, but the exam was relatively easy. Genetics, Cellular and Molecular Biology (12 ETCS) was easier since the curriculum covered many courses that I have had before at UCPH, however the exam was oral, and the teachers (one of them in particular) was kind of rude. So I would't necessarily recommend this course.
unexpected_costs: The only thing I can think of is that we had to buy a lab coat that costs 38 euros (I forgot mine in DK)
cost_comparison: The transportation was very cheap, the ATM card for students were only 22 euros pr. month, also groceries in general are very delicious and cheap. Going to the gym however is very very expensive in Milan, which came as quite a shock.
activities_available: There were some different events, and also lots of different Erasmus events, so it was pretty easy to meet new people.
activities_recommended: I would recommend maybe attending some of the Erasmus meetings and/or events especially in the beginning, and then just talk to people if they seem nice, and ask them out for a coffee friend-date or dinner or something.
weekend_recommendations: I especially recommend taking some weekend trips to the surrounding cities in Italy via train or bus. In the summer I went to Genova and Sori. In the fall I went hiking at Como lake, I also visited Bologna, which is so beautiful and also full of students, and Bergamo for Christmas markets. In january went skiing in Aprica, which was very nice as well.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy, it's not exactly a culture shock living in Italy, but there are maybe some different étiquettes when addressing elder and professors, compared to Denmark.
socializing_tips: Just approach the students in your classes, they are very friendly and helpful in general! (They often go out for aperativo after classes in the afternoon)
cultural_challenges: Many places, they don't speak good english, so that can be a bit challenging.
culture_appreciated: The food, the social life and the more relaxed italian mentality.
top3_advice: Don't hesitate to approach someone you don't know. If you cannot figure something out at our host institution, write to the Erasmus coordinators and just know that the Italians are not very structured or well organized, so sometimes it can longer to figure everything out, but just remember that everything will be solved at the end, so don't stress too much about it (even though it can be a bit frustrating, coming from Denmark:)).
other_useful_info: Nothing other than their slower and less optimized organization and coordination skills.
most_rewarding: The cultural experience and meeting new people
greatest_challenge: It was not knowing everything in advance, and sometimes figuring things out in the last minute, but it worked out always, so it taught me that I can let go of control a bit more than I initially would.

I even changed courses halfway through the exchange, and this worked without any problems. Looking back, we stressed unnecessarily about the process, as it was quite flexible. From a Political Science perspective, there were also more courses that could be approved by my home university than initially expected, which meant we had real choices and were able to take the courses we wanted.

The registration process itself was straightforward and worked smoothly through the university’s website, without any major issues.
academics_comments: Overall, I had a good study abroad experience. The food was great and quite affordable, as were drinks, and Milan has a good nightlife. It’s a very beautiful city and easy to get around. Academically, the courses were easier than I expected, which had both upsides and downsides. It gave me more free time, but it was also less challenging than I had hoped. There were many Danish students, so I mostly spent time with them and didn’t make as many Italian friends as expected. Still, it was a positive and enjoyable experience overall.
course_level: The overall level of the courses was lower than I had expected. The academic workload was relatively light, and the requirements were generally manageable. This made it easier to balance studies with social life and exploring the city, but it also meant that the courses were less academically demanding than I am used to. Overall, the level was accessible and suitable for exchange students, though perhaps not very challenging.
teaching_comparison: Compared to UCPH, the teaching style was more similar to classroom-based teaching, with a stronger focus on lectures. In most courses, the lecturer did most of the talking, and student participation was limited and largely optional. This also seemed to vary somewhat between courses. One of the biggest differences was that many courses had mandatory attendance requirements, which we are not used to at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Multi-Level Legal System (This year the course changed from 6 to 9 ECTS. On its own, it could be credited as “European Politics”; otherwise, it had to be combined with “European Monetary Law”.) European Monetary Law (Credited as “European Politics”.) Political Order, Violence and Institutions (Credited as DAK3 at my home university.) Law and Policies of Social Rights Protection in Europe (Elective course.)
recommended_courses: I would recommend the courses I chose, as they turned out to be quite manageable. In particular, I would recommend Political Order, Violence and Institutions, which I found very interesting and well taught. For Political Science students from UCPH, the content aligns well with material we are already familiar with, which makes the course easier to follow. I know some students chose Comparative Political Systems for DAK3, but I personally found it to involve more continuous assignments and workload. Instead, Political Order, Violence and Institutions felt like a better and more balanced option. I would also strongly recommend Law and Policies of Social Rights Protection in Europe, which had an excellent lecturer and was both engaging and well structured. Multi-Level Legal System and European Monetary Law initially felt quite difficult, mainly because they are law courses, which we were not used to. However, the exams turned out to be quite relaxed, especially European Monetary Law, where the exam was essentially a PowerPoint presentation. I would recommend taking Multi-Level Legal System as a non-attending student, as the lectures were hopeless to follow due to language issues. Unfortunately, there were no real alternatives, as the course was needed to obtain credit for “European Politics” at my home university.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any major unexpected costs. Food, thrift shopping, and public transport were relatively affordable (I would recommend getting a monthly transport pass). There were no required book purchases. The most expensive costs were entrance fees to clubs.
cost_comparison: Drinks were cheaper than expected, especially Aperol spritz (for example around 3.5 EUR at Bar Picchio). Otherwise, prices were more or less as expected. Food at supermarkets was slightly cheaper than in Denmark, but not by much.
activities_available: Not much, felt like it was mostly for Italian students, but really didn't look it up either.
activities_recommended: Download the "DICE" app for information, and look at the infoboards on campus. Or better ask the local students!
weekend_recommendations: Go to Genova!!
culture_adjustment: Easy! People are friendly and wants to help!
cultural_challenges: I did not find any major cultural differences particularly challenging. Most differences were easy to adapt to and part of the experience. At times, administrative processes could feel a bit less structured than what I am used to, but nothing that caused real problems. Overall, the cultural differences were manageable and not a major challenge.
culture_appreciated: Food!
top3_advice: Relax, everything works out. The university in Milan is quite flexible and relaxed, and people are generally willing to help if you need it. There is no need to stress too much about the process. Be mindful of exams and transport. Oral exams are usually the easiest option, so it’s worth considering this when choosing courses. Getting a monthly metro pass is highly recommended, as public transport makes it easy to get around the city. Try to engage beyond the Danish bubble. Many courses have WhatsApp groups where both practical information and social activities are shared. Joining these early can help you meet more international and Italian students. It’s also worth exploring thrift shops like Mercatino, which are some of the best and often located slightly outside the city, as well as local markets beyond the well-known ones by the canals.
other_useful_info: Some courses may overlap in their schedules, but it is often possible to make it work. I would recommend speaking directly with the lecturers, as they were generally understanding if you missed slightly more classes than formally allowed.
most_rewarding: New friendships<33
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was the lack of clear information about exams and exam formats, which caused unnecessary stress. In addition, deadlines were sometimes handled quite flexibly by lecturers, which took some getting used to.

crucial_aspects: I love Italy, Italian food and wanted to be able to explore a country within Europe further. I also wanted somewhere not too far away, so that I will have a "second home" where I can easily come back.
info_ease: It was a little bit tricky to find information about when classes would actually start. Our classes for science started on october 1st, which was two weeks later than people who took social sciences. But this just wasn't stated very clearly anywhere.
arrival_assistance: The coordination office in Milan was helpful when we wrote emails about courses and information, but the answer was often that the information wasn’t available yet (the Italian way).
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The process was a bit difficult since there was almost no information in advance. I spent to much time choosing classes I wanted before going and then found up the schedules wouldn't work. At least it is very easy to go to some different classes the first couple of weeks and not choose anything definitely. They are very loose in that sense, you can go and experience the teacher, see the location and learn about the course before you have to decide on anything. Registering the courses on the Milan course registration could be done about one month into the semester.
registration_help: Not much, we found everything on the website.
registration_success: Not very successful since the schedule couldn’t work out. I wanted courses from some different master programs and the classes were just overlapping too much or had ECTS points that didn’t add up.
registration_advice: Don’t be too set on the classes you want and therefore also don’t stress about choosing classes on your application or anything beforehand. But maybe have a list of interesting classes that you want to check out when you arrive. And then you can find out what the schedule is like, exam type and the location once the information is available. Also maybe choose more classes form the same master program will be helpful
course_level: They were easy to follow.
teaching_comparison: It is boring. There were mostly lectures, and then one course had a three-day lab assignment but that was the only change from the classroom lectures. Classes were very small, about 10-40 people (maybe because the master programs were small). Most teachers were sitting down while teaching. Also there is no scheduled break in a two hour lecture, some teachers stop 15 minutes early but you never really know, and sometimes they just talk for 2 hours straight. Exams are also very different. It was difficult to get any information about the form of the exam and we had no previous exams/example questions to use for studying. For oral exams, they are typically done in front of the rest of the class, which sounds worse than it actually is, but be prepared that it is different.
courses_enrolled: Cell therapy and gene silencing (7 ECTS) Genetics, cellular and molecular biology (12 ECTS) Molecular bioinformatics (6 ECTS) Molecular pharmacology and immunology (6 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I would recommend Cell therapy and gene silencing because the topics covered were interesting and the teachers were better. It is also part of a master program that I would encourage to do more classes with, since it had more of a “class-feeling” compared to the other programs. This class also has a lab part which I thought was a nice activity (and not very difficult). Bring your own lab coat if you choose a lab course! I do NOT recommend "Genetics, cellular and molecular biology" if there is still a teacher named Luisa. She hated Erasmus students and was the worst teacher I have ever experienced. I also don’t recommend Molecular bioinformatics if you want to actually learn programming or anything practical, as it is very theoretical and didn’t give me the bioinformatics skills that I was hoping for (also for preparing for the Master). Molecular pharmacology and immunology was alright, some interesting topics and the professors were okay.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Gym membership was way more expensive than expected. Looked at many different places and it was like 100 euros per month + 100 in signup fee. Transportation is cheap, 165 DKK per month for unlimited travel in Milan.
activities_available: The Erasmus organization had a lot of social activities for exchange students to join.
activities_recommended: Maybe try and join Erasmus activities. I think it is a good place to meet different people, especially from lots of different places. Me and my friends bought the membership card at the beginning for €16 but never attended a single event, so just consider whether that is something you're interested in.
weekend_recommendations: Go see the Dolomites. I was sad that I didn't go in the fall when it was still warm enough to go, because once winter comes, the hiking routes close down. Everyone said it was really beautiful! And take the train/flixbus around the country, it is very easy and cheap. I arrived in September when it was still very warm and I would recommend going to the coast around Genoa to go to the beach. Also try to book a time slot to see The Last Supper painting that is in Milan. It is very cheap (2€ for students) but the slots fill up early, so try to book it long time in advance. Going to football games at San Siro stadium is also pretty cheap for most of the games, so you can go see Inter or AC Milan.
culture_adjustment: It was easy, except for accepting that the pace is just slower in Italy and there is less structure. Class schedules and course registration is done last minute and the classes might start on time or 15 minutes late, you never know. Most young italians speak English, and with time you will learn a few words that help you get by.
socializing_tips: Do it! I tried to do it a little too late. Just ask to go have an aperitivo after school, it’s very informal and everyone is welcome.
cultural_challenges: I thought the teaching methods for the most part were boring and unstructured, and I think the lack of structure is what was most challenging to me.
culture_appreciated: The food and they like going out and meetup. They go out for business lunch, go out for aperitivo after school/work and go out for dinner and drinks. It is also a lot cheaper than in Denmark, so enjoy!
top3_advice: Don’t go for academics, go for the food, living in a big city and the beautiful country.
other_useful_info: Don’t stress about course registration, you will figure it out once you get there. Classes might be in different locations so remember to look at that. One thing I would also recommend is to not spend too many weekends having visits from back home. I had my family and friends wanting to visit me, but remember to say no to some, so that you can spend your weekends going on trips and exploring the country more. I spent too many weekends as a tour guide.
most_rewarding: I thought it was really cute to make so many new friends and meet so many new people. There are many Danish students in Milan, and everyone is really open so you have many opportunities to hang out and talk to new people. Just remember that everyone is here for the same thing and do some friend-dating!
greatest_challenge: Not having enough money for travelling:)

crucial_aspects: I've always been in love with Italy, which was my main motivation - 2 of my priorities were in Italy (Bologna and Milano). I have since learned that Milano University is held in high esteem both nationally and internationally.
info_ease: For me it was quite easy, with emails sent by the international office guiding me in the right direction, and answers to my explanatory emails. Milano University's webpages are somewhat easy to navigate, so applying for new courses (the courses I had chosen had scheduling conflicts or weren't offered in the Autumn semester) was easy.
arrival_assistance: Emails to and from the International Office. YesMilano also have great guides. I don't quite remember who led me to them, maybe that was ESN Milano Statale.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After getting access to Unimia and MyAriel (the main webpages for students at Milano University), registering for courses is quite easy. The second box on the Unimia site is for Course Registration that also includes a guide. It is also quite easy to modify study plans. Finding details about courses is quite easy to find on MyAriel.
registration_help: Other than the guide on the site itself, the International Office also sent a guide (that was, as I recall, the same guide).
registration_success: Very successful. I did have to change some of my courses while in Milano, but it all worked out.
registration_advice: Follow the guide, don't be afraid to change courses if there are scheduling conflicts or other issues.
course_level: All my courses were Master level courses, with course literature etc. suitable for the level.
teaching_comparison: Not too different, lots of class lectures. More student presentations than I am used to at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Advanced Ontology Philosophical Analysis Language and Metaphysics Human Resource Management
recommended_courses: The best course I had was Advanced Ontology, so if future exchange students are interested in philosophy this course is recommendable.
unexpected_costs: Nothing that comes to mind really.
cost_comparison: Buying groceries is definitely cheaper than in Copenhagen, but other than that, prices are fairly similar.
activities_available: I didn't really search for such activities provided by my host institution, and instead searched for opportunities outside of my host institution.
activities_recommended: See above.
weekend_recommendations: For weekends and holidays, there are a wide arrange of museums, beautiful places in the city and a lot of churches so that is some things to do. Visiting other parts of Northern Italy (personally went to Cremona, and has a visit to Como and Bologna planned). Plenty of nice cafés and bars to hang around in, get a coffee or an aperitivo.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy, I somewhat feel at home in Italian milieus.
socializing_tips: ESN Milano Statale has a lot of social events. Also spontaneous invitations on their Whatsapp group can also appear. I would also recommend drinking a coffee or an aperitivo after class with your classmates.
cultural_challenges: The language.
culture_appreciated: The Italian café culture and their general openness and curiosity.
top3_advice: 1. Dress for the occasion - the weather in Milano goes from freezing/near freezing in the Winter, to 30+ degrees in summer and early autumn. So a wide arrange of clothing is recommendable. 2. Never be afraid to ask for help or directions, Italians - Milanese included - are very friendly. 3. Remember to enjoy yourself outside of academia. Milano has plenty to offer.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Within Academia it was all the new knowledge I learned - analytical philosophy (which my philosophical courses were) is completely new to me. Outside of Academia it was all the interesting people I met. From locals to other Erasmus students.
greatest_challenge: The course Advanced Ontology.

crucial_aspects: I had dreamed of going to Italy for a long time, since I am really interested in Italian culture and language. I had Italian as my third language in high school, and also really wanted to improve my skills in this language. So it was also a personal connection that drew me to the destination.
info_ease: Most of the information I needed was sent to my e-mail by the exchange office from UCPH or my host institution, or otherwise it was available on the Unimi-website. If I had any questions I e-mailed my sending or host institution, and they were always very helpful.
arrival_assistance: We received an e-mail telling us to go to the exchange office to get our proof of attendance document signed, and emails about how to register to courses, which was helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There were clear guidelines for how to register in the e-mails, and you could also try different classes before registering in order to be sure which classes you were interested in attending, so it was quite flexible.
registration_help: The guidelines from the host institution.
registration_success: Very, we got all the courses we wanted and were locky that their schedules didn't overlap.
registration_advice: Since many of our courses were mandatory, we didn't have as much freedom in choosing which ones we wanted to attend. So some of our mandatory courses found place at a really annoying time during the day (from 3-6 p.m., four times a week). If I could have chosen freely, I would have chosen classes that had a good schedule instead of the content of the courses, since being on exchange for me was more about exploring the city and making friends than the courses.
course_level: Even though the courses were MA, the level was much lower than the bachelors courses at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Not quite good; 1,5 hour long classes with no breaks, where the teacher talked and talked during the whole class with very few class discussions and group work. It was really hard for me to concentrate and to be sure of what I was expected to learn from the courses.
courses_enrolled: Research Methods in Social and Political Science Employment, Inequalities and Discrimination in the Global Labour Market Human Resources Management Conflict Management and Negotiation
recommended_courses: If you study psychology and are on exchange during the 5th semester of your bachelor's programme, I would recommend all of these courses together, since they were the only ones that didn't overlap in the schedule, and since the are approved as the mandatory courses you are supposed to have during the 5th semester at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: During the first month, there were a few unexpected costs in getting our apartment ready such as extension cords, storage for the bathroom and an extra chair.
cost_comparison: I used more money than I expected on traveling around the country and visiting many different cities, however this was very well-spent money that resulted in amazing experiences that I wouldn't have been without. Going out to dinner was less expensive than I expected; we found many places that served amazing food at really good prices.
activities_available: You could be a member of the Erasmus network (ESN), where there were different trips, walks around the city and sometimes parties you could participate in. I was a member, but very rarely used the offers.
activities_recommended: I would recommend traveling around the country, walking around the city and enjoy the parks, architecture, museums, restaurants and bars.
weekend_recommendations: I would really recommend traveling to different cities in Italy and seeing how they differ according to their geographical location. It can also just be a day trip, it doesn't have to be a long holiday. My biggest recommendations are Venice, Verona, Bologna, Rome and Naples, and if possible, go with some of your new friends.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, I didn't find Milan that different from Copenhagen. If you like Italian culture, then you will find it nice adjusting to the culture:)
socializing_tips: I found it quite hard to socialize with the students from my class, since there were very few class discussions and group work, and since the classes I attended were second year masters courses, so the other students seemed to be quite established in who they were friends with. We ended up going on a trip to Verona with some people from our class during the end of the semester, which was really fun. I really wanted to make a local friend, so I ended up downloading an app called Bumble and going on some friend-dates, which I would really recommend.
cultural_challenges: Sometimes understanding the Italian-English accent.
culture_appreciated: The vibe in the city, people really using the city; there were always kids playing in the park, many people sitting at bars and cafés. I really appreciated going to trattorias, enjoying the weather, drinking negronis.
top3_advice: Don't worry too much about the exams, don't have too many guests from home/don't go home too often while you are there; it will go by so fast, so enjoy it while it lasts and enjoy your free time, and go to as many bars and restaurants as you want (enjoy that it is much cheaper to do this than in Copenhagen).
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: The most rewarding feeling was meeting many new people, especially people from my own campus and study field at UCPH, which I would have never met if not on exchange. It was also really rewarding challenging myself to live in a new city, and quickly feeling like it was my home. And also the academic level being much lower than at UCPH; it was really rewarding having more free time and being able to go to so many different cities and feeling free to do this without worrying about school.
greatest_challenge: Not worrying too much about the exams and not being sure what I was expected to learn from the classes; looking back, I would have spent much less time on school, since the exams ended up being quite a lot easier than expected. And another great challenge was missing my friends and family back home.

crucial_aspects: The university itself was the most important factor in my decision. Università degli Studi di Milano (UNIMI) offered courses that were relevant to my academic interests, especially within social and political sciences and digital society. It was important to me that the courses aligned well with my degree at UCPH and that they would contribute meaningfully to my academic development. In addition, UNIMI has a good reputation, and Milan is an international city with many opportunities both academically and personally.
info_ease: It was relatively easy to find the necessary information upon arrival. UNIMI provided clear instructions through email before arrival, and as long as you followed those instructions carefully, the process was straightforward. Most of the essential steps were explained in advance, which made the transition smoother.
arrival_assistance: The university provided good assistance. There were offices dedicated to Erasmus students, and staff members were available to answer questions either in person, by phone, or via email. They were helpful when dealing with administrative tasks such as registration and documentation.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: - You had to go to an address for the office for Erasmus students and then Massimo helped you.
registration_help: You had to visit the Erasmus office physically, where Massimo and his team helped with registering for courses. They provided guidance and assistance, but it required preparation and patience.
registration_success: Not completely successful. Some of the classes I was interested in conflicted with each other in terms of schedule, which made it impossible to take all my preferred courses.
registration_advice: Prepare well in advance and carefully read all emails and instructions from the university. Course schedules may change, and flexibility is important. It is also helpful to have backup course options prepared.
course_level: The level of the courses matched my expectations and academic background. They were neither too easy nor too difficult.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at UNIMI was more traditional and “old school” compared to UCPH. There was more emphasis on lectures and less interactive discussion. At UCPH, teaching is generally more discussion-based and student-centered, whereas at UNIMI it was more lecture-focused.
courses_enrolled: Courses taken: Research Design Research Methods in Social and Political Sciences Lab: Advanced Digital Methods Digital Society
recommended_courses: I would especially recommend Digital Society because the exam format was manageable and interesting, and the content was highly relevant to modern social and digital developments.
unexpected_costs: I did not experience any significant unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Food were pretty expensive.
activities_available: I don't know.
activities_recommended: I recommend purchasing a transportation card, which makes it easy and affordable to travel around Milan and nearby areas.
weekend_recommendations: I highly recommend visiting Lake Como, especially during warmer months. It is beautiful, easy to reach from Milan, and offers a great opportunity to relax and explore nature.
culture_adjustment: It was easy to adjust to the local culture. Italians are generally friendly, open, and welcoming.
socializing_tips: The easiest way to meet people is through classes and university activities. Simply talking to classmates and participating in group work helps build connections.
cultural_challenges: There were no major cultural challenges, although the academic system was different.
culture_appreciated: Italian people have a very positive and relaxed attitude toward life. The social culture, food, and lifestyle were very enjoyable.
top3_advice: Three most important things future students should know: Search for scholarships and financial support early. Living abroad can be expensive, and financial planning is important. Be prepared to spend more money than expected, especially on food and daily living. Do not hesitate to go on exchange. It is a unique and valuable life experience.
other_useful_info: Be open-minded, flexible, and willing to step outside your comfort zone. An exchange semester is an incredible opportunity for both personal and academic development.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was living in another country and fully experiencing a new culture for an extended period. It helped me grow personally and broaden my perspective.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge was adapting to the academic system, which was different from UCPH. However, this was also a valuable learning experience.

crucial_aspects: The opportunity to go somewhere with my friends where we could experience another culture together and see what it’s like to attend school in Italy instead of Denmark.
info_ease: It was difficult at first. You have to create your own class schedule, and it took us several hours because many of the classes overlap. It’s also hard to understand the exam formats, and the meeting times are more or less decided by the teachers as they go. There’s a very ‘we’ll figure it out’ approach, whereas in Denmark you’re used to a much stricter structure.
arrival_assistance: I wrote a lot of emails back and forth to the teachers because I was missing information. During the first week here, you can also go to as many classes as you want to find the ones that fit you. The first week with the class schedule is very confusing.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: As mentioned earlier, it’s very confusing. It’s really a puzzle that has to fit together. We also ended up with more schoolwork than we’ve ever had in Denmark. You start by attending a lot of different classes to find the right ones, after first trying to see which courses are offered and how they are scheduled. Then you ‘shop around’ between classes during the first two weeks. Depending on your courses, you might already have your first exam early on, it depends on whether you are an attending or non-attending student. Throughout the semester, you have ongoing exams, and in some courses you also finish with a final exam. Registration for exams opens 2–3 weeks before the exam date, so you need to remember that as well.
registration_help: There’s no organizational support, but the teachers are very kind and helpful. It almost seems like they’re used to getting a lot of questions
registration_success: I didn’t end up with the courses I initially thought I would take. There was an overlap in the schedule, so I had to find some others.
registration_advice: If you’re in doubt, just send an email to the teacher listed for the course. They are very helpful
course_level: Going to school here is different from back home. The expectations are different, and my impression is that people have very mixed feelings about whether it’s harder or easier. For me personally, this has been the most demanding semester of my entire studies, because we had exams every other week, so there was constant reading, whereas I’m used to everything being concentrated at the end. I wouldn’t say the academic level is difficult, but I still haven’t figured out their grading system
teaching_comparison: I probably prefer the Danish system, but my impression was that there were also many Danish students who felt comfortable with the way schooling and exams work down here.
courses_enrolled: DIGITAL SOCIETY RESEARCH METHODS IN SOCIAL AND POLITICAL SCIENCE RESEARCH DESIGN LAB: ADVANCED DIGITAL METHODS
recommended_courses: LAB: ADVANCED DIGITAL METHODS - It was only 3 ECTS, but the teacher is good, the format is good, and the exam was straightforward
unexpected_costs: Having a wisdom teeth removed.
cost_comparison: Eating out was cheaper than expected, not a lot cheaper, but cheaper than in Copenhagen. Otherwise, everything was pretty much as expected for living in a big city. The coffee was, of course, cheap, about 2 euros for a cappuccino, so you can’t complain about tha
activities_available: There is this option where you can join ESN, which I think is organized by some students. You pay a one-time fee (around 15 euros, I think), and then you can take part in lots of activities that are posted continuously in a WhatsApp group. I didn’t use it myself, but I can see how it could be beneficial for students to meet this way.
activities_recommended: The ESN club as mentioned before.
weekend_recommendations: Go to COMO!!
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
cultural_challenges: One difference that many of us Danish students have talked about is that all the Italians just talk during class. It feels very disrespectful and was something we didn’t expect people to do.
culture_appreciated: The food, and sharing a bottle of wine in the evening with my friends in beautiful surroundings.
top3_advice: Check your alumni email Keep yourself updated on the Mobility Online portal Do good research on courses before you come here, it will help you when you need to register
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: Living with my closest friends and experiencing another culture.
greatest_challenge: It’s always good to be challenged when it comes to speaking English and presenting, so I’ve found it nerve-racking but beneficial in the long run.

crucial_aspects: I am studying psychology and wanted to go on exchange in Italy - Milan was the only option in Italy, otherwise I would have had to arrange the exchange by myself. Therefore I chose Milan.
info_ease: It was very easy. The University is very good at sending the information that you need. Information about courses was a bit more difficult. The information needed to find courses and apply and so on was very good, but it wasn't until a week or so before the semester started, that we got information on what courses was actually created and the schedule, but this was not a problem, just a bit of a wait.
arrival_assistance: Good information on email and good answers to any questions. Not at specific event or anything where you got to meet other exchange students, but this happened along the way either how.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registration went fairly easy, information on how to do it was sent to us. I don't remember it that much, but one or two months before the semester we had to do some registration; checking your email is enough, then you wont miss anything.
registration_help: Information from the University.
registration_success: I got almost all the classes I wanted. The only reason I didn't was because two of them were scheduled at the same time, but it all settled in the end and probably in a better way than I had originally planned.
registration_advice: Just read you email and all will be fine:-)
course_level: The level was not as it is at KU. The courses were easier and with a smaller workload. It was difficult in the way, that it was a different way of learning and not knowing what the level for the exams were, but in general it is easier than at KU. At the University of Milan, the one that KU has an agreement with, they do not have a psychology faculty, so the courses were a part of degrees oriented towards human ressources and social and political science, so in that way the courses are also a bit different than one might be used to, and not oriented that much towards psychology.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was quite different. It mostly consisted of teacher holding a lecture for one hour and half without a brake, and then that was that. No working in groups or answering question. Also not that many assignments if any.
courses_enrolled: Employment, inequalities and discrimination in the global labour market + Human ressources management; this was instead of Arbejds- og Organisationspsykologi. Research methods in social and political science; this was instead of Avanceret forskningsdesign. Conflict management and negotiation; this was an elective course.
recommended_courses: The courses that were instead of the mandatory courses were fine. I would recommend the elective course Conflict management and negotiation; the professor were a psychologist, and the course were the best one of the ones I had - more participatory lectures.
unexpected_costs: Not really any.
cost_comparison: It was much as expected.
activities_available: I didn't really use them, so I am not sure, but I know that ESN also hosted a lot of activities.
activities_recommended: Going out to experience the city:-)
weekend_recommendations: Going on trips to other parts of Italy. Trains are very good and also Flixbus is a good and cheap solution.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy.
socializing_tips: I think the best tip would be to try and talk to them in class. I didn't really get to talk to any. I think this was partly because the lectures wasn't very interactive and the local students already knew each other, so people mostly stuck to themselves and were quick in and out of class.
cultural_challenges: There were differences, but I didn't really find them challenging, just different :-)
culture_appreciated: The more slow tempo and spontaneity. Also the culture of going out more during the week, eating out and so on.
top3_advice: Try to do practical things in good time, go out and explore the city and other parts of the country, if you want to meet other nationalities - try to make an effort to speak to others in class or use the activities hosted by ESN. There are usually a lot of Danes on exchange in Milan, so trying to meet others takes some effort, but being with other Danes is also really nice and it can entail friendships that you can bring home.
other_useful_info: Not really.
most_rewarding: Seeing different parts of Italy and experiencing the culture and differences in this across the country. Meeting new people! Learning about a different education system and learning styles.
greatest_challenge: It wasn't as such a challenge, but the teaching was different.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go on exchange somewhere with lots of young people, plenty of opportunities in the city, and easy access to travel destinations nearby. It was also important for me to be able to complete my mandatory courses while on exchange.
info_ease: It was relatively easy to find the necessary information. However, the Italian university system is somewhat slow and bureaucratic, and most of the information was provided shortly before the start of the semester.
arrival_assistance: We received the relevant information via email
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was possible to register for a wide range of mandatory courses. Although many of the courses overlapped in the timetable, it was manageable, as attendance was not required every time.
registration_help: Most of the relevant information was available on the university’s website.
registration_success: We were able to register for most of our mandatory courses. It was also possible to change courses during the first two weeks of the semester.
registration_advice: Do not stress too much about course selection, as there is flexibility at the beginning of the semester and it is possible to switch courses during the first weeks.
course_level: The overall academic level was lower compared to UCPH. The exams were significantly easier, lasted a maximum of one hour, and consisted of only a few handwritten questions on paper.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was more traditional and old-fashioned. However, all lecture slides and course materials were available on the university’s website. There were no assignments, which resulted in a lower workload.
courses_enrolled: Game theory: Mikroøkonomi III Time series & forecast: økonomitri II Business History: økohis Global and climate change economics Coding
recommended_courses: Game theory: Mikroøkonomi III Time series & forecast: økonomitri II Business History: økohis they are easier than at UCPH
unexpected_costs: Our rental required weekly cleaning, which cost around €20 per time. Some students experienced higher costs. Gym was very expensive, around 700-1100 dkk
cost_comparison: Food and drinks were generally cheap. A cappuccino cost around €1–2, and a pasta was €12–15. Train tickets and flights were also relatively cheap.
activities_available: There were many Erasmus-organized events available, including social gatherings and trips. However, we did not participate much in these, as we had already met many Danish students early on and therefore spent most of our time with them. The city also offers a wide range of sports activities, gyms, and several public swimming pools located in the city center.
activities_recommended: Milan is centrally located in Europe, making it very easy to travel by train to several cities. The train system is easy to use and relatively cheap. I would therefore recommend traveling to nearby cities and regions, as well as exploring Milan itself. The many museums, bars, cafés, and restaurants.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend using weekends to travel to places such as Lake Como, the Dolomites, Portofino, Naples, and Rome. Milan also has great shopping and vintage markets, cultural events and partying
culture_adjustment: It was very easy to adjust. There were many exchange students, and the culture is not very different from the Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Participating in social activities, visiting cafes and bars, and interacting with students during classes.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier, as not everyone speaks English.
culture_appreciated: The cafe culture, affordable coffee, aperol and croissants, and the aperitivo tradition.
top3_advice: Do not stress too much about choosing courses. Remember to experience the city and not spend to much time on schoolwork the exams are easier. Find an apartment early
other_useful_info: Secure accommodation early and be aware that some exams are held in January.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many kind and sweet people.
greatest_challenge: Finding an apartment with a nice location

crucial_aspects: The University of Milan offered courses that aligned well with my studies in Communication and IT, particularly within communication, organisation, and technology. In addition, the opportunity to study in an international academic environment and to experience everyday life and culture in Italy was an important factor, as I wanted to challenge myself both academically and personally.

arrival_assistance: Upon arrival, I received assistance mainly through the host university’s orientation activities and information materials.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process at the host institution involved an in-person visit to the Erasmus office upon arrival
registration_help: Massimo, the erasmus responsible

course_level: the academic level was manageable and intellectually stimulating. But the MA courses were difficult, since I am on my bachelor.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at the host institution differed from that of UCPH in that it was generally more lecture-based and instructor-centred. At UCPH, there is typically a stronger emphasis on student participation, discussion and critical engagement.

activities_recommended: Traveling in Italy, exploring the city and surrounding regions, engaging in cultural activities such as visiting museums and exhibitions, and experiencing local food culture are also highly recommended.
weekend_recommendations: Lake Como and going to art museums.
culture_adjustment: Overall, it was relatively easy to adjust to the local culture. The environment was welcoming, and everyday interactions helped facilitate the adaptation process.
socializing_tips: I would recommend actively participating in classes, group work and student activities, as this provides natural opportunities to meet local students. Being open, showing interest in the local culture and making an effort to communicate in the local language can also help. Additionally, joining social events or informal gatherings organised by the university or student groups can make it easier to build connections.
cultural_challenges: One of the more challenging cultural differences was the more flexible approach to time and organisation compared to what I am used to at UCPH. Administrative processes and communication could sometimes take longer, and schedules were occasionally less predictable. However, adapting to this difference also encouraged greater flexibility and patience, and it became easier over time.
culture_appreciated: The appreciation of culture, history and food

Engaging with different perspectives, academic traditions and cultures broadened my understanding of my field of study. At the same time, living abroad strengthened my independence, adaptability and confidence, making the overall experience highly valuable.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during the exchange was adapting to the exam formats and assessment methods at the host institution. The structure, expectations and evaluation criteria differed from those at my home institution, which required adjustment and careful preparation.

arrival_assistance: We had a short chat with Massimo when we got our proof of attendance signed. Other than that it was mainly emails we got sent from the institution that guided us.
arrival_comments: The administration was really busy since so many students go on exchange in Milan. Everything was very confusing in the beginning and not the easiest to figure out but everything ended up being solved.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_process: You can an Email with a guide. This is okay to follow, but it was unclear if you actually was enrolled to the course. I remember that to some courses i wrote to the professors so they could enroll me if they were locked or something. It is easy to communicate with the professors, just write to them.
registration_help: Im not sure. Not a lot but maybe you could have written to unimi.in? But they were busy as written.
registration_success: I was 100% successful at the end
registration_advice: I would visit different courses in the introduction weeks before registration to specific courses. You can just show up and listen to the introduction of the courses, hear about exam forms and get a feeling of the professors. This is smart because you can just sign up for the course later in the semester when you know the schedule and exam forms. We had a very though out plan before we went to Milan, but didnt end up like that at all because of schedule overlaps, late exams and locations far away. So we changed the courses on our OLA some weeks in the exchange and that was fine.
academics_comments: I truly had an amazing experience during my exchange. I loved living in Milan and would recommend it to others who may prioritise academic opportunities less. While the exchange was challenging in several ways, including academically, it was everything beyond the studies that had the greatest impact on my exchange experience.
course_level: In general the level was fine for me to follow. I think they have less details in their materials and more concepts so fine if you miss something. Some courses i took were build ups of courses from their bachelor that i hadn't had in DK, so we did some self study to follow but it was fine.
teaching_comparison: They are some differences. They have more scheduled hours on uni and till very late. Every wednesday and thursday we had classes until 17:30. Also they almost only have lectures which are 2 hours long and have no breaks. Sometimes the professors begins later or stop earlier. You dont really know and that is confusing. I found i very hard to concentrate for so long. especially when you had 4 lectures a day so 8 hours. The professors tend to sit down instead of presenting out to the class. This was not so motivational. And also they dont have any problemsolving classes on the side of the lectures and no previous exam sets to practise on.
courses_enrolled: Cell therapy and gene silencing (7 ECTS), Molecular pharmacology and immunology (6 ECTS), Molecular bioinformatics (6 ECTS) and Genetics, cellular and molecular biology (12 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I would recommend Cell therapy and gene silencing. The professors were the best i had and the only course with some laboratory work so more variation than just lectures. Also a good level to follow but still new topics. Its a mix of cell therapy in laboratories, pharmacological aspects and virology. The exam was also good, a multiple choice and open questions. Molecular pharmacology and immunology had 2 open questions for each part, you had to pass both pharmacology and immunology (so actually 2 exams). One of the teachers spoke italian english so i didnt understand anything. Both parts were interesting though. Molecular bioinformatics was very boring to me. The exam was multiple choice and open questions for 1 hour. Genetics, cellular and molecular biology easy to follow since it reminds a lot of courses from out bachelor in DK. One of teachers were a little scary and the exam as well. It was verbal and in front of fellow students but this is very common in Italy
unexpected_costs: Skitrip 6000. Had to get an italian phonenumber and data. Labcoat 350.
cost_comparison: More expensive was fitness. Actually impossible to do. They only have yearly or half years memberships but you need medical check and so much. Less expensive was local transportation, groceries, busses to other cities, coffee.
activities_available: They could have had a students fitness of some sort but our campus didnt offer that. They have a tuesday bar - Tipsy. I went there once and cheap aperol.
activities_recommended: Visit a lot of restaurants since it is a lot cheaper and more fun than in DK. Visit museums and markets (Remira marked was a personal favorite). Travel to nearby cities, Genova and the coast was nice in the summer. Skitrip also. China town has good food.
weekend_recommendations: The same as above
culture_adjustment: It took me some time since i like structure and breaks throughout the day. They dont really care so much about that. You just have to relax and hope that everything ends up working out because it will even though there is a lot of uncertainty. The cheap coffee was easy to adjust to.
socializing_tips: Ask if they want to have apperitivo with you. They drink aperol all time at the day. We socialised the most in our laboratory class since we were put in random groups so maybe take courses that do that.
cultural_challenges: Some exams are very loose and some are kind of nerve-racking. Our professor just handed out the exam 10 minutes before the actual start and told us to begin. But people were still arriving and some even came 10 minutes late but got extra time. Those 20 minutes i couldnt concentrate at all. All the written exams are by hand. The verbal exams are often in front of your class mates. Everyone meets at the same time in the morning and then "først til mølle" princip. I ended up as on of the last student so i sat in the class room for 4 hours without lunch. Remember snacks.
culture_appreciated: Its a love hate relationship for me at least with their looseness and uncertainty. They are just more relaxed and dont stress so much about what should happen next which was a good practise for me to experience. In general they are just more out in the city enjoying every days of the week eating out, drinking wine, aperitiv ect. Doesnt matter if its monday or friday they drink wine and chat.
top3_advice: Be patient with the registration process and choosing courses. Try to shop a bit in the beginning before choosing your final courses. Take initiative to meet other people, even if it is just other danish people. It kind of feels like friend dating and is a bit challenging but worth all the effort. Eat out a lot, drink drinks, visit nearby cities, try new things. Find people who want to share same experiences as you. Their cinemas are so cheap (6 euros) but remember to find version original to get english and not italian. Apollo club was a fun night club.
other_useful_info: It is very different when the masters begin on different campuses. We had courses from 1st october and the laste exam 29th of january. Some other KU student began mid september and ended in december. So we had a whole extra month in Milan which was good and bad depending on your situation.
most_rewarding: The new friendships i got and all the memories we made together. There is something really special about sharing new experiences and living in a new city with people that makes you very close.
greatest_challenge: Trying to adapt to all the differences. Being "omstillingsparat" when things didn't go as planned or hoped. Also i went on my first skitrip which was challenging.
other_comments: No
