crucial_aspects: My erasmus exchange in Belgium was a unique opportunity because of the courses in translation and interpretation offered at UMONS that cannot be found in Denmark in the same context. It was also important for me that my study language french was spoken at the destination of my erasmus, and I was very interested in exploring another francophone culture than the one in France.
info_ease: I had trouble finding information about my courses and where I had to be at campus. However, my teachers and fellow students were very helpful, and everything worked out in the end.
arrival_assistance: The erasmus responsable teacher at my host university met with me before the semester started and showed me around the campus. She also helped me change my LA with recommended changes and schedule-coordination. There were several events for erasmus students where we got a lot of useful information about municipal registration, student activities, classes, etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process was quite confusing. My host university has a lot of small courses from 2 to 5 ECTS per course, and many of them overlap. You can't be sure that you will be able to follow all of your courses from your original LA. Apparently this is not only for erasmus students.
registration_help: The doors to the secretariat were always open and the secretaries could always help. I also had a lot of help from my teachers and fellow students.
registration_success: I could registrate for approx. 30% of the courses in my original LA, but the new courses that I was recommended to replace the last 70% were much better, I think.
registration_advice: Don't lock yourself onto the courses that you chose before going on your exchange. They will most likely have to be replaced because of schedule changes, a level too low or too high or that the course won't even be offered that semester. Keep an open mind and don't be afraid to ask for help, because you will definitely need it. Find out who is qualified to recommend courses for your particular academic profile.
course_level: All of my courses was in MA level, except for one course that was in BA and one course that was for erasmus students in general.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at UMONS is definitely more practical, whereas it's much more (if not exclusively) theoretical at UCPH. This makes sense because the courses at UMONS prepare you for a very practical job, namely translation and interpretation. Personally I much rather prefer the style of teaching at UMONS, especially because it's so speech-oriented, you spend a lot of time practicing the studied language. In UCPH we spend a lot of time studying french in danish, and reading a lot of fictional literature. In my erasmus exchange, my speech qualifications and vocabulary has developped more than it has in three years.
courses_enrolled: French as a Foreign Language, Introduction to translation, Translation DA-FR, Translation FR-DA, Consecutive Interpretation DA-FR, Consecutive Interpretation FR-DA, Simultaneous interpretation, Liaison-interpretation, Translation Workshop.
recommended_courses: All of the above. If you are interested in translation and interpretation in French-Danish, these give you a great introduction to the subject. However, the master-courses are a bit tough in the beginning for someone who has never tried interpretation before. The other students in the master already have some theory in the baggage from the bachelor. But the teachers are really good and they will help you as much as you need, so it's really doable.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay 5 euros to register your address in Mons at the local foreigners' office and they require passport photos which will cost an additional 8 euros in the supermarket, if you don't already have some. You also have to report to the foreigners' office when you want to cancel your address in Mons, but you can do that by mail so you avoid paying 5 euros again.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping in the city was a lot more expensive than I had imagined, even being aware of the inflation. Beer is cheaper than soda.
activities_available: There were traditional competitions such as; cart race, the mons cup (football), cheerleading, and more. There were also cultural activities like different concerts and La Journée Internationale where students from all departments at the EII-FTI faculty had prepared food and decorations from the country whose language they were studying. I know there were also several athletic activities but I never really looked into it.
activities_recommended: If you go in the spring semester, definitely go see the cheerleading competition. It means a lot to a lot of UMONS-students and they really make a big deal out of it! Besides, it's a great opportunity to get to know some belgians students over a few beers. Make sure to also join the Journée Internationale at EII-FTI, especially if you study at that faculty, and make sure to cook something from your home country - your department will be able to sell a lot more tickets if they can tell people that a real person from that country made this dish.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely visit other cities in Belgium, both in Wallonia and Flanders. It's an interesting country with a lot of ancient towns with beautiful architecture and a lot of cultural and lingual diversity. Belgium is also located in the heart of Europe, so you can travel to many interesting places around Central Europe, only 1 to 4 hours from Brussels.
culture_adjustment: It was not that complicated, as the belgian culture in Mons is quite similar to french culture because of the town's proximity to the french border, and I've already lived in France before so I am familiar with this culture. However, Belgians are very subtle and indirect, more than Danes. Therefore I had to tone down my excitement and energy level a bit to adapt to my surroundings (but maybe that's just me as a person).
socializing_tips: Don't be afraid to approach the local students, even if they don't approach you first. They may seem shy at first, but they will embrace you once you get to know them a bit. The best way to socialize with local students is if you both have a beer in your hand.
cultural_challenges: Belgians don't talk about they're feeling so much. From a Dane's point of view, I found them a bit cold and uninterested at first and it took me a while to figure out that they are not insensitive, they are just a bit less intimate with people who are not their partner.
culture_appreciated: Once you are friends with a belgian, you will always be. They are super friendly and open, and they will welcome you any time. They are also not pompous and they are very open to foreign cultures.
top3_advice: 1) Be prepared to change your LA 2) Your french level is going to improve A LOT 3) it is easy only to hang out with other erasmus students, but try to get to know belgian students as well. It is a great way to be more familiar with the university and the belgian culture.
other_useful_info: 99% of the streets in the city are made with paving stones, and they are rough to walk on. So bring practical everyday shoes, and leave the heels at home!
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange was my classes and the encouragement from my teachers. I found a new interest for interpretation and translation that I wouldn't have gotten if I had stayed at my home university. I got the chance to visit the interpreters and translators at the EU institutions (EU Court of Justice and EU-Commission) and I strongly consider pursuing interpretation as a profession.
greatest_challenge: I found that I was usually the oldest person in the company when socializing with other erasmus students or even local students (except the one other student in my master classes). It could be challenging at times, as I was occasionally missing the company of people my own age or older, but it was not a crucial problem at all.
other_comments: Erasmus exchange is one of the best decisions any university student could ever make. I highly recommend it, regardless if it's in Belgium or any other country.

crucial_aspects: It was a very unique opportunity to study translation between french (which I study) and danish (my first language) in a country with native french speakers.
overall_comments: It was a very good experience. I really enjoyed being abroad, it is so worth all the troubles and confusions in the beginning. People were so helpful and I felt so welcome at the university. Because it is a small city I quickly felt at home. The classes I took also didn't have many people in them so we quickly felt close and got to now each other and the professors.
info_ease: Very easy, I got a lot of emails upon arrival, that explained what I had to do
arrival_assistance: Some of the teachers were very helpful and helped me and my friend find our way, choose the right subjects and assist us in getting settled.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was a very good experience. I really enjoyed being abroad, it is so worth all the troubles and confusions in the beginning. People were so helpful and I felt so welcome at the university. Because it is a small city I quickly felt at home. The classes I took also didn't have many people in them so we quickly felt close and got to now each other and the professors.
registration_process: There was an online registration process where I could donwload my certificate, read about the rules and upload a picture to get my student badge. Then there was a welcome day with a lot of introducing information. I also had to make an appointment at the immigration office and get a permit, which was not complicated at all - but the proces is very analogue:)
registration_help: A lot of intro meetings were you could ask questions, and they were very helpfull if you called or e-mailed with general questions.
registration_success: Very successful. I had some help from the teachers that could recommend which classes to take.
registration_advice: Know that they are not super strict about deadlines, you dont have to stress about not knowing the entire proces beforehand. They are super helpful.
academics_comments: It was a very good experience. I really enjoyed being abroad, it is so worth all the troubles and confusions in the beginning. People were so helpful and I felt so welcome at the university. Because it is a small city I quickly felt at home. The classes I took also didn't have many people in them so we quickly felt close and got to now each other and the professors.
course_level: I had a translation class with a course on third year of BA and two translation classes with year 1 of MA and then a class of french as a second language only for exchange students.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. I studied part time, so I only had 15 ECTS. But I had approximately 10 hours of class, which is almost the same amount of hours as 30 ECTS in Copenhagen. On the other hand, there was not the same amount of preparation and homework. In the translation classes the style of teaching was very practical and not so theoretical. In the FLE (français langue étrangère/french as a second language) it was very mixed. But the teacher I had was often a bit confusing to follow. It was not very structured in general.
courses_enrolled: UT-BM-TRAINT-031-M: Scandinavian Languages Translation (part 1) – 3 ECTS UT-B3-TRAINT-105-M: Translation and Introduction to Interpretation: Danish – 4 ECTS UT-BM-TRAINT-045-M: Translation into French: Scandinavian Languages – 2 ECTS UT-BM-TRAINT-102-M: FLE (French as a second language) – 6 ECTS
recommended_courses: I would really recommend the translation courses I had. We were quite few students, so there was more time to go into depth with what we thought was interesting, and the teachers were so nice and very committed. On the other hand, I can really not recommend FLE (French as a second language) - it was weird and I didn't really get anything from it.
unexpected_costs: It is pretty much the same as in Denmark
cost_comparison: Soap and houshold articles were a bit more expensive, food maybe a bit less expensive. The beer was very cheap:)
activities_available: There was a lot of different sports. There was also "conversation tables" were you could practice speaking french. There is also a choir called la Chœur du Pôle hainuyer. I took part in this choir - and it was a highlight of my week
activities_recommended: I can really recommend the choir la Chœur du Pôle hainuyer. I joined it at the beginning of the semester. There wasn't an admission test, but the level of the singers were quite high, because a lot of them studied at the conservatory. But it is open for all who study or work in the Hainaut district. It is free and it was very fun, and an excellent way of meeting people and practicing pronouncing french words:)
weekend_recommendations: The other small towns nearby, Bruxelles or even a day trip to Paris. When I was in Mons from september to january, I got to see both the mobile "amusement park", the christmas market and the light festival - all in the big square in the city. There are also a lot of places to drink beer and hang out all over the town.
culture_adjustment: I was on exhange with a friend from Copenhagen, and it made it easier. Overall I did not find it that different from Denmark. In the beginning I was very preoccupied with getting settled and fixing all sorts of paperwork, that I didn't think too much about adjusting to the culture. I felt very much at home. It is a small town, where you quickly get a local feeling. I felt that the people are much more talkative and open than in Copenhagen, which I had to get used to, but ended up really enjoying.
socializing_tips: Studying together, eating lunch together. Participating in the erasmus activities or parties. Talk with the students/people you live with. If you live in a university accomodation, you could eat your dinner in the kitchen and then meet the people you live with. Go out in the city and hang out in the bars or cafés.
cultural_challenges: People seem more social than in Denmark, but this I learned to enjoy:)
culture_appreciated: Speaking the language. And also the more relaxed approach to paperwork and exams.
top3_advice: Dont stress too much about deadlines and the confusion at first - it gets easier. All of the trouble of getting everything in order to go on exchange is so worth it when you get there. Remember that there is no right way of going on exchange. You dont have to get perfect grades or even feel that you learn that much - living abroad, making new friends and meeting a new culture is also important parts of going.
most_rewarding: The feeling of speaking french more freely than when I first got there. And also feeling proud for having completed a semester abroad
greatest_challenge: The dirty kitchen were I lived. The FLE course. The way of teaching was not my cup of tea. And not spending all my money in the second hand shops:)

crucial_aspects: The opportunity to study translation between french and danish. And to speak more french in general.
info_ease: Very easy. There were meetings with the mobility-department and the university has a housing-department that was easy to find and where I could go and get my key for the housing.
arrival_assistance: The mobility department distributed a lot of information via e-mail and at information meetings. The teachers from my department helped me choose my courses.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It is quite simple to register for courses - the whole process of completing learning agreements and getting them signed takes some time, but I had a lot of help from the erasmus coordinator at Umons and from my teachers.
registration_help: The mobility-department hosted information meetings about the process of getting the learning agreement completed. This was very helpful. The teachers in my department looked at my LA and helped me choose the right courses.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Ask your teachers and coordinators for help. And ask your fellow students what courses they like.
course_level: I took courses in translation from french into danish on MA-level.
teaching_comparison: It is much more practical, with more physical class-time and less homework.
courses_enrolled: Translation from French into the Foreign Language (Scandinavian Languages) Translation into French : Scandinavian Languages Translation and Introduction to Interpretation : Danish Danish Translation (part 1) Introduction to Translation : Danish Français Langue Étrangère (FLE) Danish terminology Translation of Specialised Scandinavian Texts English translation (part 1)
recommended_courses: All of the translation courses. FLE was not very relevant and took up a lot of time. The terminologi course has interesting elements but is not very relevant to students from Copenhagen.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Regular groceries were slightly less expensive than I expected. Beer is very cheap.
activities_available: I know that there are very cheap athletic activities at uni. Each department/faculty has a student-organization that hosts parties/activities.
activities_recommended: Go to the parties hosted by the student organizations. I know that there is also a organisation for exchange-students that hosts activities, which seemed like a good opportunity to meet people.
weekend_recommendations: It is relatively easy and cheap to get to other belgian cities or Paris. Mons is also a lovely town, with lots of bars and thrift stores. There are also museums that are free to visit on the first sunday of each month.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy.
socializing_tips: Go to the parties hosted by the student-organizations. Maybe make an effort to find their instagram accounts or similar to know if something is happening.
cultural_challenges: The students in Mons typically leave to go home on the weekends - this means that they usually party/go out on thursdays, and that the town can seem a bit empty over the weekend, so it's nice to go on trips on saturdays or sundays.
culture_appreciated: The Belgians seem very open, talkative and helpful.
top3_advice: Don't stress too much about the whole registration process. Belgians tend to worry less about deadlines than danish people do, and the teachers and coordinators are hugely helpful if you ask them. If you take translation classes, speak all the french you can there! This of course goes for other situations as well, but the classes really are a great opportunity to practice and to discuss translations with your teachers and fellow students.
most_rewarding: Getting to speak french regularly.
greatest_challenge: The issues with the residence where I lives.

I also wanted to go to a destination, that would help me improve my language skills. So I choose Montpellier because I had French in high-school and I wanted to improve so that I would be able to have academic conversations. It was of course also crucial for me that the destination was safe and that it had some good opportunities to enjoy my freetime as well.

The only reason why I haven't given it 10/10, is because it's been a little messy with my supervisors and with the communication of the courses and what was obligatory to go to and what was expected of me because it is not the same as in Copenhagen.

arrival_assistance: I got help from the International Relations and I got help from a friend, who lives here.
arrival_comments: I arrived pretty late because I had exams in Copenhagen, while some of the introduction courses were going on, so I didn't receive all the information at first. I struggled a little in the beginning, but there was some introductions and a French students took a group of us (Erasmus students) on a tour of campus and explained some things to us and gave us his contact information, so we could always ask.

registration_comments: It's been an amazing experience! I've learned so much and I've had the best time here. The only reason why I haven't given it 10/10, is because it's been a little messy with my supervisors and with the communication of the courses and what was obligatory to go to and what was expected of me because it is not the same as in Copenhagen.

registration_help: The International Relations and the professor.
registration_success: Very succesfull. It all worked out in the end.
registration_advice: Begin early and keep sending them emails if they don't reply. They might not have seen your email.
academics_comments: It's been an amazing experience! I've learned so much and I've had the best time here. The only reason why I haven't given it 10/10, is because it's been a little messy with my supervisors and with the communication of the courses and what was obligatory to go to and what was expected of me because it is not the same as in Copenhagen.
course_level: I had one bachelor course, but it was in French, so the level was pretty fitting for me. I did two projects, which were both challenging academically and then I had a course in English, that was very different from what I was used to, so it also challenged me in that sense.
teaching_comparison: It was pretty similar other than the fact that the students talk during the lectures. If they think it's boring, they will just start small-talking and the professor doesn't really care.
courses_enrolled: International Entrepreneurship Nutrition Humaine Project: INFOGEST digestion Project: Consumer Research
recommended_courses: It's difficult to say because the projects were a really big part of my semester, but the Nutrition course was good. The Entrepreneurship course was a little messy, so maybe try to find something different if you need that kind of course.
unexpected_costs: It costs money to go to the doctor and I was surprised how expensive it is. It also costs a lot of money to get bloodtests etc.
cost_comparison: It's a little cheaper to buy food in the supermarket than in Denmark, but when you go out for dinner, the prices are pretty much the same as in Copenhagen (maybe a little cheaper).
activities_available: There were a lot of activities available. I didn't attend any of the ones at the university though because I was too late to get the approval from the doctor and then I couldn't sign up. I did sign up to a gym though and that was a really good quality gym.
activities_recommended: Be a part of the Erasmus Life Montpellier group and the ESN Montpellier. They have so many events, where you meet all the other Erasmus students.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Pic Saint-Loup, go to the beaches Carnon and La Grande-Motte. Travel around - go to Nîmes, Marseille, Lyon and all the other charming French cities.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy as soon as I got more comfortable with speaking French and as soon as I made some friends and got settled into my residence.
socializing_tips: Take initiative and be open and don't be afraid to speak French.
cultural_challenges: That the French are pretty laissez-faire. They are not very punctual and it can be difficult to make appointments with them.

most_rewarding: All the friends I made and all the experiences we had together.
greatest_challenge: To get comfortable with the French systems and the French way to do things.

other_useful_info: No

crucial_aspects: I chose Murcia because it is a less known city, and I wanted to visit a new place rather than a city I had already been to
info_ease: I found it challenging to get the information I needed. I was frustrated that my courses overlapped, which meant I had to choose new ones that needed approval from different places. Fortunately, they were quickly approved by my university in Denmark, but in Spain it took a bit longer. My university was also relocated to another place, and it was difficult to figure out where the different courses were held.
arrival_assistance: I contacted my advisor here in Murcia whenever I needed help. Unfortunately, she didn’t respond to my emails quickly, and there were times when she couldn’t provide answers to my questions either.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I don't remember, but remember to check your emails
registration_help: You can get help from your advisor, and there is also an Erasmus office where staff are available to assist Erasmus students.
registration_success: Apart from the 2–3 times where there were scheduling conflicts, I managed to get into some good courses
registration_advice: I would advise future exchange students to start the registration process as early as possible and carefully check for any course overlaps themselves, as these are not flagged automatically. Be prepared to make changes and stay in close contact with your advisor. Don’t hesitate to reach out to the Erasmus office for help – they can guide you through the process if it becomes complicated. I would also recommend choosing the course 'Español de América' it was interesting and educational, easy to follow, and very popular among Erasmus students.
course_level: Some courses were more difficult than others. The ones labeled “optativa” were easy, while the ones labeled “obligatoria” were more difficult.
teaching_comparison: The teacher talks a lot and the students talk less. Many of the teachers use PowerPoint, but I had one teacher who didn’t use any materials at all, so you had to be good at taking notes in his class (he teaches the course 'Perspectivas actuales de la lingüística'). Sometimes they give assignments, both group and individual. Some teachers require that assignments be handwritten on blank paper using a pen. Some classes are called 'práctica' – these are sessions you must attend to earn good points toward your final grade. A paper is handed out where you have to sign to confirm your attendance. Some teachers, not all, might also give small in-class tests from time to time.
courses_enrolled: - Español de America (Do yourself a favor and choose this course) - Perspectivas actuales de la lingüística - Literatura española. Narrativa - Teoría de la literatura y literatura comparada - América, sociedades de frontera: cultura e identidad (This course is from a different bachelor's program, not one under 'Lengua y Literatura Española'. I had to choose it because my other preferred courses overlapped, but I ended up loving it. However, the teacher sometimes gives a short test at the end of a topic, which counts for 1 point)
recommended_courses: Español de América!!!!
unexpected_costs: An unexpected expense was probably that, in addition to the €220 I had to pay for the apartment each month, the landlord asked me to pay an extra €100 for utilities that is, for water, electricity, and internet.
cost_comparison: non
activities_available: An organization called ESN organizes various activities in Murcia that you can take part in. They even organized a trip to Ibiza. You can follow them on Instagram their handle is @esnmurcia. Another website that also offers activities is murciawelcomesyou. In Spain, they use the app WhatsApp a lot, so make sure to have it downloaded.
activities_recommended: Go to parties that's where you meet people and other Erasmus students. Also, go to the festivals in Murcia there's always something happening out on the streets.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend that you also travel to other cities, such as Alicante, Cartagena, and Mazarrón, because it can get a bit boring to stay only in Murcia for five months
culture_adjustment: I have been on exchange before, so I wasn’t very surprised.
socializing_tips: Just jump into it, be talkative the other Erasmus students are on exchange just like you and are easy to talk to.
cultural_challenges: They eat late in Spain, which I found challenging, and the shops are closed on Sundays.
culture_appreciated: The streets stay lively late into the night, especially during festivals, when everyone comes out to watch, celebrate, and take part in the atmosphere.
top3_advice: 1. Practice writing by hand and memorizing, because during exams you write on paper by hand and without any aids. 2. There can be long breaks between your classes for example, you might have a class from 8-10, and then your next class doesn’t start until 15-17 3. There are usually classes in the evening
other_useful_info: - Buy water from the supermarkets, as the tap water isn’t clean (that’s what my roommates told me) - Always carry cash with you, you never know when something might happen, like a power outage, and you’re left without anything to eat (this happened to me during a blackout in Spain in 2025).
most_rewarding: What I found most rewarding was that my roommates didn’t speak English, so we only spoke Spanish it really helped improve my Spanish skills.
greatest_challenge: My biggest challenge was probably when there was a fire hazard in my apartment. I was living in an old apartment where not everything was in good condition, and the fire department told us we couldn’t sleep there that night. I had to find a hotel on the same night.

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)
crucial_aspects: I was looking for a water specialization with an engineering approach to have a good balance and combination with the scientific approach seen at KU.
info_ease: Very easy, the international team at BOKU distributed a checklist with all the information and links
arrival_assistance: We had an online introductory week to get information on libery access, campus classrooms, and others. It was very useful. Later, the international team at BOKU prepared a city tour for all internaitonal to assist.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: you first need to do the in-person registration at the host University and get your ID card, if not you are not able to register online for any course. So consider this and arrive at least 2 weeks before the courses start. Some courses have high demand, so if you can even get your BOKU ID before, the chances of getting to the courses you want are higher. If suddenly you see that a course is full, contact the professor and let him/her know that you are interested and what it can be done to increase the possibility of you getting in.
registration_help: Buddy program and Austrian students, in general, are happy to help as the BOKU system of courses is different than in other universities. So ask around. Courses at BOKU tend to overlap and depending on the type of course (lecture, exercise or combines) the requirements of assistance are different. All this is well explained by the international team at BOKU, but also do not be afraid of asking other students for insights.
registration_success: I registered to all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Be organised. As courses overlap and they start and end at different times, you need to be structured and understand the demanding of each course.
course_level: I took all master's courses.
teaching_comparison: You have different types of courses at BOKU, and depending on that the style also differs. Also, depending on the ECTS, which tends to be low hence you have to do a high number of courses to get to the 30 ECTS, whether you go in-depth on the topics or is more an overview. You can see all this on the course description on the BOKU online platform once you get your credentials (process that needs to be done in person unfortunately, so be aware of arriving before the classes start!)
courses_enrolled: Water Resources Planning and Management On Site solutions for Water Supply and Sanitation Master's thesis seminar Decision support systems Integrated flood risk management Irrigation design Ecological river landscape management Aquatic biomonitoring and -assessment Hydrological processes and modelling Water supply and wastewater treatment Case studies in sanitary engineering
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Case studies in sanitary engineering and On-Site solutions for Water Supply and Sanitation. On the latter, the professors had a lot of onfield experience so it was rewarding to learn from them. The Case Study one was very hands-on, I chose a topic and work with a supervisor on investigating and doing a report to present at the end of the semester, I even organised my time as I wanted since we just had a meeting at the beginning of the semester to divide topics, and then met at the end to present the report. So it was a great modality and I went in-depth on sanitation in emergency situations, which is a topic I like.
unexpected_costs: I had an unexpected cost but it was personal, I needed to go to see my family for a health emergency my father had.
cost_comparison: In general, everything was as I expected as the International team at BOKU also gave information on this. To consider: the transport expense is not exactly real, in the sense that I bought the annual pass (as the semester pass for public transport was only for students under the age of 26). So I bought the annual transport pass which costs around 320 euros, so on that item, I put an approximate of that amount divided on the course of 12 month.
activities_available: Picnic, salsa dancing, night outing, WhatsApp group to organise among ourselves, a city tour of the historic part of Vienna.
activities_recommended: The city tour was amazing!! You got the chance to know more about Austrian history.
weekend_recommendations: There are towns you can go to for a day or weekend, like Merk, Hallstatt, and Graz. You also don't have to miss the Danube National Park (only accessible by bike) Also, always check the internet as the Vienna Municipality organises a lot of events throughout the year (even in 2022 when COVID was an issue). We had Christmas Markets and an ice ring in winter. In summer music and film festivals outside :) It was lovely!
culture_adjustment: The challenge in Austria is the language. Outside BOKU hardly anyone speaks (or wants to speak) English. So this can bring difficulties in paperwork and communication with the government.
socializing_tips: Austrian are in general very open, so try to make groups for the courses with them so that you get the chance to know them more closely.
cultural_challenges: The language, as said before. The challenge in Austria is the language. Outside BOKU hardly anyone speaks (or wants to speak) English. So this can bring difficulties in paperwork and communication with the government.
culture_appreciated: The number of traditions they have, which are beautiful, the architecture, the local food, the music, dance and opera, and the history!
top3_advice: - You can easily get overwhelmed with the courses as they are a lot and the overlaps make you feel anxious all the time. If you are in general a self-demanding person, it will be hard not to only focus on the study part of the exchange. But try to give you time to also get to know Vienna and the city. So schedule daily work in the afternoon when you finish the courses, or something else. But make sure you make time for the cultural exchange as well as the academic one. - Go to all the Christmas markets, do a tour of all the options the city had, and do not miss the ice skating ring in January at the Rathaus. - In summer. google/ask for the schedule of activities, there are tons of free activities outdoors to do and do not miss going to the Danube canal for a swim! The local Vienna beach style :)
other_useful_info: If needed the international team at BOKU has weekly online consultation hours that you can find on the BOKU Website. So you can enter and have a quick chat with them for and they answer all questions!!
most_rewarding: Everything! I really loved Vienna and the knowledge I got and developed
greatest_challenge: The language barrier for the paperwork I needed to do.
other_comments: Follow the checklist that the international team at BOKU sends you before arriving, it is user friendly and very useful!!

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)
crucial_aspects: Firstly that it was a good university (rankings etc.) with some really interesting angles on/focus areas with regards to my areas of interest in my academic field. Secondly it also mattered to me that Vienna seemed like a super interesting city with lots to explore.
overall_comments: You have to be ready to spend quite some time on bureaucracy/paperwork. But apart from that, it was really really great (and definitely worth it)
info_ease: Very easy, BOKU is quite structured with providing checlists and information meetings about nearly everything (which is also crucial because their system is in some ways very different from that of UCPH)
arrival_assistance: In addition to all the information meetings, the international office as well as the coordinators for my specific programme were always very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: You have to be ready to spend quite some time on bureaucracy/paperwork. But apart from that, it was really really great (and definitely worth it)
registration_process: You first have to register preliminarily online some time before arriving (you get an e-mail about this), and later you have to book an appointment online for in-person registration at the study services at the main campus. Thereafter you get your student login and student card, and is able to register for classes etc.
registration_help: The International Office at BOKU is there to help, and the BOKU Study Services themselves are also very helpful
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted, not all in the first try but because the system at BOKU is quite different from UCPH: in most classes the deadline for deregistration (which is individual for each class) is a couple of weeks or more into the course, and even if you don't deregister you will not have to take the exam, then you just don't get the ECTS – and you can take all the classes you want, no matter ECTS, and also go to all the exams, then you just have to pick which ones you want on your transcript. Because of this, most students register for more classes in the beginning of semester than they intend on taking, and then they check them out in the first couple of lectures and decide which ones they're gonna keep. So even if you are still on waiting list for a course you really want at semester start you can just ask the professor if it its ok that you attend anyway, and then you'll probably end up getting a registered spot during the first week or so (unless the class is extremely popular and you're super far down the waiting list, but then the professor will tell you that).
registration_advice: You have a lot more freedom in choosing and trying out classes and experimenting with new topics at BOKU, which is super nice, but also quite chaotic at first. Especially because there's not really a strict system (like the schedule places A-D at UCPH) for which weekdays and for how long the courses are, you'll have to check that out for each class. And that means that there'll probably be a lot of overlap between your classes, also your compulsory ones. But as this is the system, the professors also know that this is how it is, and will probably state what is the minimum expected attendance for their class in the first lecture. It also depends on class type (see https://boku.ac.at/en/international/themen/international-students-coming-to-boku/a-good-start-plan-your-studies-at-boku/wie-plane-ich-mein-studium-an-der-boku-vor-der-ankunft/kurstypen), and of course how much overlap you can handle yourself. But it is almost impossible to get around having a bit of class overlap, I think – make sure that the overlapping classes are at the same campus then, when you have to run between them!
academics_comments: You have to be ready to spend quite some time on bureaucracy/paperwork. But apart from that, it was really really great (and definitely worth it)
course_level: I would say that it's pretty much the same as at UCPH. Most classes are fewer ECTS though, so in that way they're of course lighter and often more narrow/focused, but then there's more of them. The field excursion courses are often easier (not all of them though), but then you have to be ready for spending days in row away, and often also paying yourself for transport etc (but it's definitely worth it, you can get to see some amazing places).
teaching_comparison: That actually differed a lot to me. Some classes were a lot more traditional/conservative lecture style than at UCPH, but then at the other hand some were far more experimental and interactive. There's a really broad scope, maybe it also depends a bit on the department (although I don't really know) That is also definitely one of the things where it is so great that you can try the classes out, and if the teaching style doesn't work for you, you can just deregister.
courses_enrolled: 831312 Plant and environment 812342 Ecology of aquatic systems 912317 Air pollution effects on forest ecosystems 912317 Ecology and management of the rhizosphere in ecological engineering 911312 Rhizosphere processes and application to agriculture and soil protection 31304 Ecology and population biology of plants in agro-ecosystems 833317 Formulation of questions and experimental design in ecological research 912338 Current advances in ecology and soil science 790387 Microbial ecology and geomicrobiology
recommended_courses: I think most of my classes were really great but these 2 definitely stood out to me: 934002 Gender, food systems and natural resources: This is one of the best university classes I've ever had. It was 3 intense weeks in what is actually the university holiday between semesters, very interactive teaching style, about as the name says natural resources and food systems and the way these are accessible or not to people and cultures, and how we use them and how we see them, and the role of gender in it all, but also about different kinds of research. For me as a very clear natural science student it really put everything into new systems and perspective for me, and the lecturer Stephanie Lemke is amazing. And it doesn't matter if you know anything about this beforehand, people have all sorts of different academic fields and focuses at this course. You just have to be reasy for 2-3 really intense weeks, but it is so worth it. 833317 Formulation of questions and experimental design in ecological research: On paper a somewhat introductory statistics class. The curriculum is quite classic biology/natural science statistics I guess but the lecturer Marcela is amazing at her stuff, so even though I've had some statistics before I felt like a learned a lot of new things, and the things I'd had in other classes before, I actually really LEARNED here, if that makes sense. I think everybody should take this class it is such a good investment, especially for your thesis and stuff like that. And it is actually really fun and manageable!
unexpected_costs: There were a few smaller fees for registering Vienna, for the Student Union (compulsory) at BOKU, and for a few excursions (not compulsory, depending on classes). All of these were around 20 euro each, as I remember.
cost_comparison: Most prices are very similar to Danish prices, eating out is a bit cheaper. In contrast to at UCPH, I didn't spend any money on study books - everything was provided as PDFs (I don't know if this is a general thing, though).
activities_available: A lot of clubs and events and friday bars and volunteer opportunities in the environmental/agricultural area. Crucial to mention here is that I was on exchange during lockdown, so I did not get the full picture of this, but I definitely got the impression that the social part of university life is very important to BOKU and therefore very well supported - a lot of possibilities.
activities_recommended: I was a volunteer at the BOKU garden, which is a "wild" utility garden driven by BOKU students at the outskirts of Vienna. Super cosy, great people, and a really nice break from studying/city life. Apart from that, meet the locals by going to the friday bars, the concert, the "stammtisches" (cosy meetings at bars), everything. There's plenty to choose from! (Kinda academically, but still not directly part of "school") it is often possible to volunteer or just get student access at some of the many (!) interesting seminars hosted by BOKU and that way get to experience some really interesting talks and excursions.
weekend_recommendations: Do a Stadtwanderweg (local hiking routes) in the nearby mountains, visit the opera, or one of the many many museums, go for a swim in the Donau, or get cheap standing tickets for one of the operas. See if there's a funny/interesting festival going on. There's always SO much to do in Vienna. don't even know, there's so much to do in Vienna. Or
culture_adjustment: Coming from Denmark it was quite easy. Sometimes things were a bit more formal, especially at university, but apart from getting used to that it was very easy to adjust.
socializing_tips: Go to many social events at BOKU, maybe get a hobby like taking dance classes or join the Boku garden or something. Some say that Austrians are quite distanced/hard to befriend, but I didn't find it much different than Denmark (which has the same reputation, to be fair), so you need a bit of stubbornness in making new local friendships but it is definitely possible (and worth it)
cultural_challenges: The culture is a bit more formal generally, with more use of titles (such as Dr etc) and courteous expressions so coming from very direct/informal Denmark it might be a good idea to really be conscious about acting politely(not that the difference from Denmark is that big, but it is the only thing I would say sometimes could be a bit challenging or just different)
culture_appreciated: Vienna is just a sprawling, cultural city, with such a rich, culturally mixed (and also very tragic of course) history, that is in some ways very different from the rest of Austria, it seems - and also in some ways very Austrian of course. It is just a lot, in the very best sense.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared for some time-consuming bureaucracy, it is worth it. 2. You will definitely get some academic (and cultural) experiences that you can not get at UCPH. Enjoy that. Take advantage of the freedom in choosing and dropping courses to explore new fields and angles. 3. Don't get scared away by the rumoured "coldness" of Viennese people. It is really not that different from Denmark.
other_useful_info: Just again - everything I've written here has also been from a lockdown perspective, so maybe some things are quite different when not in lockdown, I don't know.
most_rewarding: Actually just studying natural/environmental science in a country with such a different hsitory, location, climate, geography etc. than Denmark was so rewarding, and really gave me a new perspective on many things.
greatest_challenge: Lockdown. Haha. Apart from that, it is of course tough at times to be away from everything you know, always dealing with new systems that you don't understand. I think it is for everybody, that should not be a secret. But you learn so much from it as well, and it is worth it.
other_comments: Go!

culture_adjustment: The relationship between students and professors are not so easy to adapt to, it feels a little less friendly here. The opening hours of the university is also quite restricted and there are not so many study places available.
socializing_tips: The Austrians are very friendly!
cultural_challenges: None, apart from the language of course.
culture_appreciated: People are politically active and there are many small demonstrations and organizations, that is quite cool. But at the same time there is the classical culture, like all the operas, museums etc.
top3_advice: 1. You have to plan your schedule real carefully, things are not ordered nicely in blocks and fits together in your schedule, YOU have to make everything fit, that you do not miss the mandatory activities in each course, and spend a lot of time organizing this. 2. Go to Tüwi and Stammtisch to meet people, enrol in an USI sports course. 3. Take many excursion and seminar courses and few lecture courses
other_useful_info: Go for it
most_rewarding: Vienna is a really nice city, especially in summer. Enjoy all the culture, events, openair cinemas, swimming in Donau.
greatest_challenge: Meeting new friends during lock-down and online teaching.
other_comments: I can warmly recommend taking the night train from Hamburg to Vienna and book the "liegewagen" for a good night's sleep and enjoy the landscape passing by outside the window :-)

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)
crucial_aspects: I have family connections in this city, and I am considering moving in here for the future, so having an exchange here was a wonderful opportunity for networking and getting to know the academic and working culture.
info_ease: There were information sessions during the info days, the website provided a lot of information and checklist about practical information as well.
arrival_assistance: I have participated in the info days, and I had a buddy as well to assist in specific questions
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process is comparable to total anarchy. The places are filling up very quick, but that doesn't matter, because the courses still might or might not be held at an uncertain time schedule. Personal connection to the lecturers is very essential, because even if not registered, it is possible to get a place in the course if asked nicely. It is impossible to avoid clash of courses at 30 credits, and the workload is always uneven, because the schedule is not known at the time of registration.
registration_help: The lecturers and the administration were always happy to help and they were responsive, even if they couldn't always answer questions, a solution could be found to every problem.
registration_success: At the end, I managed to register and finish all the courses in my learning agreement, but it was very stressful and uncertain (one course's timetable wasn't fixed until May, and it was held at the end of June, at the last week of the semester)
registration_advice: Register for more courses than it is stated in the learning agreement, to have back-up credits if some courses don't work out. Expect an uneven workload and a really long easter vacation (I had no courses or study activities for almost the entire April)
course_level: The courses in general were a bit of a lower level than I would prefer - I also missed a better literature list for each course (courses had 3 to 4 academic books as recommended reading with no chapter specified)
teaching_comparison: It was less practical, and some of the courses desperately needed context and structure for their content. A lot of detail information was given (for example about detailed molecular pathways), but there was no information about their practical application or was it even expected to be learned for the exams.
courses_enrolled: Advanced practical course in biochemistry; Antibodies and beyond - emerging fields in antibody engineering; Biology of aging; Cell factory - plants; Developmental genetics; Flow cytometry and cell sorting in biotechnology; From sequence to structure: prediction, modelling and molecular dynamics of protein structures; Patent law and strategic patent management; Proteomics; Practical course in environmental biotechnology; Seminar in biotechnology;
recommended_courses: Biology of aging - Exciting course about a relatively new and growing field of molecular biology Cell factory - plants - Interesting practical course with some really flashy experiments Practical course in environmental biotechnology - Cool supervisors and concept for an experiment, although a bit low-level The seminars - only for easy credits, because they are very little effort and time input for the credits that they are worth
unexpected_costs: The registration in Vienna city must be renewed after 4 months of stay, which cost a small amount of money, but mostly it was the time spent on it
cost_comparison: Food were more expensive than expected, but food prices are high in every country right now.
activities_available: The University Sports Institute Vienna offers amazing, very cheap sport opportunities.
activities_recommended: The University Sports Institute Vienna
weekend_recommendations: The city has an overwhelming variety of cultural events, food festivals, hiking and ski opportunities.
culture_adjustment: It was easy, since I am from Hungary (the neighbor country) so I have cultural ties with Austria
socializing_tips: Socializing definitely happens while eating, so prepare for a few additional kilos to be gained during the exchange.
cultural_challenges: The food - there's so much of it!
culture_appreciated: The food - it's so good!
top3_advice: Prepare for an uneven workload, register for more courses than you need, and don't take the exams too seriously, because the grading is very lenient.
other_useful_info: The rules are very flexible, and there is a laid back atmosphere in the institution, so there is a great opportunity for personalization.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding experiences were mostly personal - I really liked the city of Vienna for the cultural and the natural environment, and I have met my current romantic partner.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was to take the academic part seriously - I felt that the lecturers were too lenient, and the requirements were too low, therefore it was difficult to put a lot of effort in the studies.

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)

culture_appreciated: The language. the natue. the openness. the many possibilities in the city.
top3_advice: Be open to changes in your plan of courses during your mobility, and get inspired from other students courses. Attend one of the language courses before the semester starts that BOKU are giving. I met really nice people here, and it give you a lot to be able to talk with people in german. Find privat accommodation like a WG (Wohnung gemeinsam).
other_useful_info: I rented a bike from Swappfiets for the whole stay and also bought a semester-ticket for the public transportation.

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)
crucial_aspects: That they had courses within my academic interest
overall_comments: Only a 7 as I did not like the structure of the host university.
info_ease: Fairly easy
arrival_assistance: There were welcoming days with presentations on what and how to do things, opportunities to have a friends~buddy, and a lot of social events
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Only a 7 as I did not like the structure of the host university.
registration_process: Firstly before arriving we had to come up with a list of courses we wanted to take. Then after arrival when we recieved the login information and could actually acces the platform and sign up for courses and see additional information very little of what we had planned ahead and spent time on before leaving could be used as the time tables etc. did not work out. So a lot of time, at least 10-20 hours, was spent during the first weeks to search for courses and making them align so that attending the classes was possible. Sadly, many of us ending up taking courses out of practicalities and not academic interest. Furthermore, a lot of paperwork has been required of us throughout the stay and often it is the same documents that have to be sent to different people or uploaded on different platforms resulting in a lot of stress as you constantly felt like you had forgotten something which could be of importance.
registration_help: They had a lot of presentations in the beginning on how to navigate and then an email and office where you could go (however long responds time on email). For each degree a tutor/older students was hired to help out. This was very nice. They would arrange social events, remind us of deadlines, and answer questions.
registration_success: Once I had found courses that fitted each other time wise I was lucky to get in on all of them.
registration_advice: That one need to prepare for a lot of paperwork but that it is doable with a good cup of coffee and steady nerves.
academics_comments: Only a 7 as I did not like the structure of the host university.
course_level: For some courses the academic level was very high and for others low. But in general the small courses didn't offer you a lot of time to actually get to know the taught stuff so much information was lost unfortunately. The courses with a high level often expected you to have previous knowledge even though it wasn't necessarily stated on the course description.
teaching_comparison: It was very based on classical lectures. Very little interaction between students and professors. And also very little interaction between students. And when there was interaction one could clearly tell that they did not have a lot of experinece with it.

cost_comparison: Groceries were more or less the same, a bit cheaper. However, eating and drinking out is a lot cheaper.

socializing_tips: They are very friendly once meeting them. But you have to make an effort.
cultural_challenges: That people seem a bit grumpy but actually they are not (necessarily at least;) )

most_rewarding: To experience living in another country.

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)
crucial_aspects: My specialisation and the offered courses at the host univserity
info_ease: Sometimes a bit confusing as some webpages had other information than others, or documents were not up to date. Overall, I managed.
arrival_assistance: The head of studies for my programme was really, helpful and understanding.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There are some obligatory courses, some restricted electives and free electives. You chose the course in the catalogue and register. If the course is really small (20 people) you sometimes get on a waiting list, in case the course is already full (usually not the case for obligatory courses, as they are comparably large courses). In the end, some people deregister so that you might still get in. i felt some professors were quite flexible with registering you manually even after deadlines.
registration_help: There is an administrative coordinator and there are some webpages to gain information from.
registration_success: Registering for all the courses was easily possible. The problem is rather in managing overlaps.
registration_advice: register for everything your interested in. Go to the course the first week and see if you enjoy the teaching style and can handle the workload. if not, for most of the courses you can still deregister within the first two weeks of the semester. Watch out for the exam dates. It can happen that you have a super stretched exam phase, starting in december ending in March. or that you have all your exams in 1,2 weeks.
course_level: The level of the courses was ok with me as I have had already a lot of courses during my previous studies. Stillt was intense sometimes, as complicated things were mentioned only shortly and not explained as there is no time for this in 1.5 hours per week. And then it is hard to catch up because there are so many courses in one week.
teaching_comparison: As the courses only take part around 1.5h a week, time is missing to really get into detail or do anything yourself. Mainly its lectures. That I didn't like so much. I enjoyed it a lot in Copenhagen that you have phases were you work yourself and that you have enough hours and days per week to get into a topic. Additionally, in Copenhagen you could focus on your two courses, which is great. At BOKU you need to superficially deal with 7 topics, which is a bit unfulfilling for me.

unexpected_costs: Rent increase. Student ticket for public transport only under age of 25.
cost_comparison: Rent. Sport courses.
activities_available: Sport courses, weekly gatherings, ball, movie nights
activities_recommended: The ball is in the Wiener Rathhaus which is really beautiful. sport courses to meet people.

culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Attend the social activities, do sports courses.
cultural_challenges: Relaxed (slow) organisation at institutions. Missing digitalisation.
culture_appreciated: Enjoying every place, where you can sit outside. The city is so much concrete, but people sit and chill everywhere to share a drink etc. Even if the seats are directly at a big street.

Gather together in winter. If you don't organise a gathering yourself, you might end up doing nothing/feeling alone. Come here during summer.

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)
crucial_aspects: I originally thought I could study oenology there, since Vienna grows wine within city limits and there were several courses about it, but it turned out those courses were in german, which I missed when I signed up.
overall_comments: I had a really great experience, but every paperwork aspect of it was very chaotic and anything but easy.
info_ease: I had done a lot of research on the website in advance, so I knew pretty much everything beforehand. For me the challenging part was the application process before I arrived.
arrival_assistance: I took part in the introduction days, where everything was explained with regards to how to pick courses and what was expected of us.
arrival_comments: Be aware that a lot of things in Austria in general requires you to book appointments in advance, show up at offices, pay with cash and that not everyone speaks english.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had a really great experience, but every paperwork aspect of it was very chaotic and anything but easy.
registration_process: The process in itself was easy enough, you book an appointment and show up and pay.
registration_help: Read on the webpage for incoming students and call your coordinator if you need help.
registration_success: I managed to register for all of my classes because I was ridiculously early in Vienna (3 weeks prior to the start), but I think it would have been fine if I came later. Excursions and labwork books up fast.
registration_advice: It seems weird that you have to be there in person, but you get used to it.
academics_comments: I had a really great experience, but every paperwork aspect of it was very chaotic and anything but easy.
course_level: Overall, fairly easy level. But the system...most courses are 3 ECTS, so you end up taking 10 courses in a semester, some has multiple exams and there is no structure in schedule, so everything overlaps. A lot.
teaching_comparison: As mentioned, completely different system. Much freer, teachers were more easy-going (and answered emails really fast), but not structure. Overlaps everywhere, you are really on your own. Almost no reading in most of my classes, it was just about being there in person and take notes. Seminars are seminars YOU give (important to know). It feels like they have taken courses and split them into different parts: lectures, excursions, seminars, labwork.
courses_enrolled: Python for beginners, Gender, nutrition and right to food, biotechnology for sustainable innovation and environmental protection, Food biotechnology, German internsive course, German for beginners II,Molecular biology of fungi, genetic modified organisms in the environment, food packaging technology,
recommended_courses: The foodpackaging course was surprisingly good I would say. And gender, nutrition and right to food is very interesting because it is completely different from any other course I have had.
unexpected_costs: Get an austrian phone subscription, your danish one will stop working (google fair use policy)
cost_comparison: Public transport was very very cheap and so was going out (beer)
activities_available: Everything. A lot of different sports, music and different parties and trips.
activities_recommended: I recommend going out and trying things in the beginning, but don't try to do everything (like I did). You can't, there is just too much.
weekend_recommendations: If you like hiking, bring your hiking gear. I didn't and I regretted it.
culture_adjustment: Easy. The culture is a bit more old-fashioned (cash, paper, conservative), but still very european. The language barrier was real though, since I spoke zero german before I went there.
socializing_tips: Join USI classes and talk to people in class. It is very very easy to stay in the "Erasmus bubble" with all the other exchange students (but that is also fun). Oh, and Tinder. If you are single, that is a very very easy way to meet local people.
cultural_challenges: Their insistance on using paper, cash and physical, pre-booked appointments for everything.
culture_appreciated: That there was also something happening. If you want, you can find a new place to explore every night all days of the week. The raves were fun too. The dancing and the fact that people just know how to do that was also cool.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared for having to send the same information multiple times (but people are nice) 2. The courses will seem like a complete mess because the system is nothing like here, but it will work out, I promise. 3. Vienna is amazing and has a lot of opportunities.
other_useful_info: Book more courses than you need, always attend the first class (otherwise you get kicked out of the course) and then drop the ones you don't want afterwards. BOKU has sort of a "trying out" period, so you are not bound to the courses for the first times there.
most_rewarding: There were so many parts. Living in a bigger city, meeting new cultures and subcultures, new people from all over the world, gaining academic confidence by taking classes outside my own field.
greatest_challenge: The bureaucracy. If you are gone for longer than six months or sublet your place, please please please prepare yourself to be kicked out of the danish system. I had to deal with A LOT of stuff suddenly because I no longer had a permanent danish address. And I thought I was prepared. It works out in the end, it will be okay, but the experience was not fun.

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)
crucial_aspects: That the university had courses that were intersting and that I could see myself living in the chosen city.
overall_comments: The quality of the courses/acedemics is what makes me not give it a higher score.
info_ease: Really good. I think BOKU provided all the information I needed. And we had 5 intro days one week before the start of the studies where we got introduced to everything.
arrival_assistance: Presentations at the orientation week and emails with lists concerning how I should register for BOKU etc.
arrival_comments: I think BOKU was really good at welcoming us.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The quality of the courses/acedemics is what makes me not give it a higher score.
registration_process: You sign up to more courses than you want to take. You will need to take about 10 courses because of the low number of ECTS per course. Then you spend approx. the first two weeks trying out different courses, and dropping the ones you don't like. There is a lot of overlap so often you have to decide between several courses that you like because they are held at the same time. Most people have a pretty good idea of their schedule after 2-3 weeks. But I didn't have a clear idea until maybe November. I was very indecisive, and I found it stressfull and hard to decide what courses I wanted. There are so many courses you can choose from and you always have a chance to change your mind, even very late in the semester. In that sense I like the system at KU more, that ones you decide you can't go back. It suits me better.
registration_help: They tell you about the registration process during the welcome days. Some courses were not open for registration and then I think I contacted either the professor of the course or the secretary. And they answered all my questions.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: It is of course an advantage to sign up as early as possible if you want to be sure to get the courses you want. But I think I would have still gotten the most of the same courses if I signed up later. So also don't stress too much about it. A lot of courses did not have waiting list and everyone was accepted.
academics_comments: The quality of the courses/acedemics is what makes me not give it a higher score.
course_level: My impression was that courses at Muthgasse (biotech, food science, water management) was way more technical and hard and the courses at Türkenschanze (where I took most my courses) was a lot easier and the level of "science" was pretty low. But it might just be me. I found it difficult to find courses that were not too hard (I often didn't meet the prerequisite) or not too easy. I think I ended up with choosing a lot of easy courses which is also why I'm not super satisfied with the academic side of my exchange.
teaching_comparison: It differs a lot. I had both one-way communication courses and more discussion based courses. There is also seminars where there might be a small lecture and then the students have to present afterwards. If you want lab courses you have to choose courses that are strictly for the lab, as it is not integrated into the other courses like at KU. I did not like the small courses. I felt like I didn't learn much. I also didn't have a single book for any of my classes because there was none: there was no literature to read before the lectures. You just show up and listen. But this part I actually liked.
courses_enrolled: Environmental bioprocess engineering, Exploratory data analysis with R, Field camp I - introduction to mountain forestry and forest sciences, Formulation of questions and experimental design in ecological research, Gender, food systems and natural resources, Intensive german Course - Beginners, Physics of snow, Processes in enzyme technology, Soil ecology
recommended_courses: Field camp I which is in the second week of October. It was a really nice chill time with other Erasmus students. If you have been to the welcome week you don't need to go on the field camp for the social aspect, but it is still a good time. Formulation of questions and experimental design in ecological research: One of the few courses where I felt like I learned something. First half is pretty basic statistics that you might already know but I still think it was a good refresher. Soil ecology: good lecturer, very easy to follow, only con is that it is Wednesday at 8am. Physics of snow: By far my favorite subject. If you have the money (around 380 euros) and you like skiing you should really go. We had 4 lecturers that were pretty interesting and then a 4-day excursion to Leogang. It says online only the ones with the best test scores get to go on the excursion but everyone that wanted to got to go. Also you don't need the prerequisites. It was very easy to follow. Intensive german Course: I took this primarily to meet people but the welcome week was enough. I would recommend it if you would like to pass 3 ECTS before the semester starts.
unexpected_costs: If you are above 26 you can't get a student transportation card and you have to get a "jahres card" which is a lot more expensive. In the end I also ended up getting a really big fine because they could not withdraw money from my account. My friend had the same problem, so look out for that if you subscribe to anything while in Vienna.
cost_comparison: Drinking coffee and eating out is a bit cheaper than in Denmark. You can get cheap standing tickets to the Opera.
activities_available: Tüwi café was really nice to hang out in between lectures, and served nice lunch. Every Tuesday there is international stammtisch (which is like a Friday bar on a Tuesday). There is also sports that you can sign up for at uni Wien. They open for registration end of September I believe. It is very popular so you have to be fast. The BOKU ball (a formal dance).
activities_recommended: I would recommend going on trips to the mountains and the nearby european cities (e.g. Prague, Budapest and Bratislava) and the nearby cities (e.g. Graz and Salzburg). Buy a Vorteilscard through öbb, that way you can get 50% off your train tickets.
weekend_recommendations: I went to skiing resort just outside Vienna both for cross country skiing and downhill skiing called Stuhleck. I would also recommend getting a cabin in the mountains somewhere and go on hikes or ski. Bratislava is nice for a small day trip. If you have several days go to Prague or Budapest.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: I didn't socialize that much with local students, but I did live with a few in my flat share that I became friends with. So maybe live in a flat share with local students if it is important to you. Also the Physics of Snow course was almost entirely Austrian students and I felt I got a lot of Austrian culture through that.
cultural_challenges: None. The viennese are known to be rude, but I didn't experience that at all. The culture is pretty similar to Danish culture. It was very easy to get along.
culture_appreciated: Vienna has a ball season (ball as in a dance), and there is the BOKU ball that is very viennese and was fun to attend. Also a lot of people go to Operas and theaters.
top3_advice: 1) Go to the welcome week and talk to a lot of people and try and find at least one person you click with. Attend as many things as you can the first couple of weeks (without draining yourself too much). It is an investment. 2) If you meet someone you click with ask what courses they are taking, and try and see if you have common interests. Then you get to spend more time together. I talked with a lot of nice people during the intro days but I didn't keep in contact with them as we had seperat classes. 3) There are some courses that are very popular among Erasmus students. If you want you can take either a language course or a cultural course. That way you will meet a lot of Erasmus students.
other_useful_info: Not really
most_rewarding: Meeting new people. Adapting to a new city and setting up a life for yourself.
greatest_challenge: Deciding on courses. And also missing out on things. In the beginning something social was always happening. I found it hard to say no even if I was tired, which is not a usual problem for me.
