registration_success: When I registered, there were already a lot of the courses that were filled up, because too many students registered in the courses. I was on the waiting list for a lot of courses. I was not really satisfied with this process, because it was a bit stressful not to be sure which courses I would get, and to make the puzzle of a schedule so that the courses would not overlap too much.
registration_advice: If it is possible, I would maybe arrive 1-2 weeks before the semester starts, to have time to make the schedule. Then I would make a long list of courses, so there is both a plan A, B and C... Sometimes you can also ask the professor by mail or by entering the first class, if there should be a place free anyway, if you are on the waiting list for courses.
academics_comments: It has been a very nice experience, and I have met some fantastic people during my exchange! For the personal and social part, it has really been an 10/10 experience.
course_level: I think some of the master courses were a bit difficult, but also because it was a bit in another studyfield than I have. For example I had a master course in climate change that was really interesting, but also challenging.
teaching_comparison: It really depends on the course... Some of the lectures were a bit more monologue than at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: - Biocultural diversity in rural landscapes (eng.) - Biodiversity and conservation of mountain forests (eng.) - Climate change and global aspects in planning and spatial development (eng.) - Deutsch Konversation III (ger.) - Deutsche Fachsprache B (B2+) (ger.) - Einführung in den Möbel- und Innenausbau (ger.) - Exkursion Verkehrswesen (ger.) - Fish farming and aquaculture (eng.) - Freies Zeichnen (ger.) - Gehölzkunde (ger.) - Introduction to urbanism (eng.)
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend to choose some more easy courses if possible. It is really difficult so find enough courses to fill 30 ECTS, so I think it is important not to stress yourself too much with too many difficult courses! I would recommend the Freies Zeichnen course, if you like to draw. It is a very nice course that is only for one week, where you go to the city centre to draw architecture and plants. If you are interested in plants, then I would really recommend the Gehölzkunde course. Even though it is in German, is there a lot of the same words to describe plants as in danish. There is a lot of plants to learn though!
unexpected_costs: I had to buy climbing shoes for a climbing course I took. I also had a fine for not being registered in Vienna (remember to do that).
cost_comparison: I did not have to buy a lot of books for uni. Only a scriptum for one course, and some drawing materials for another course.
activities_available: BOKU has a lot of social events! There is a student driven cafe/bar/shop and they are also organizing events and parties. Keep an eye on the posters hanging around at BOKU with all sort of events.
activities_recommended: Really nice to do a sport, also a possibility to meet new people. There is also a WhatsApp-group for Erasmus and incoming students - here they will also write about events and parties:)
weekend_recommendations: There is a lot of nice museums in Vienna! Look out for free entrances, some days you can be lucky to get in for free. The music and theatre scene in Vienna is also very big. Vienna is also very close to beautiful nature: The Nationalpark Donau Auen, Donau Insel - where you can swim in the Donau river, The Wiener Wald and the nearby "hills" or mountains where you can easily access with some 1,5-2 hours of train. There is a lot of hiking routes from Vienna - called Stadtwanderwege. Last but not least is there a lot of neighbor countries to Vienna! It is quite cheap and easy to go to f.x. Bratislava, Budapest and Prague.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, the viennese people are very calm and mostly very nice.
socializing_tips: Take part in local events, play sports ect.
cultural_challenges: Some waiters can be a bit grumpy, but this is supposed to be the style as far as I know.. Remember to give tips!
culture_appreciated: That the Austrians do not stress so much and like to go out to eat and drink coffee.
top3_advice: - Take your time to do the registration and all the bureaucratic stuff... Even though it can feel stressful because of the deadlines, do not worry - it will be fine and work out! - Participate in the introduction week! It is such a good way to meet new people and make new friends:) - Ask as many questions as you want if you are in doubt of something. Ask BOKU, buddy, other Erasmus students, your roomies ect.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: The people I met at BOKU and the social life at campus.
greatest_challenge: The bureaucratic stuff was a big challenge, but I think I also learned something from it..
other_comments: It is really nice and rewarding to try and study in another country! Good luck :)

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)
crucial_aspects: It did my erasmus in the frame of a double-degree, so my choices of university were pretty limitied. Academic quality and course offer were my top priorities.
info_ease: It was pretty easy, the administration was very helplful when needed.
arrival_assistance: Local uni staff was here for any question, and organised some meeting to introduce the stay.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Courses get filled really quickly. To register to it, you need first to be registered at the uni, that can only be done in person. In other words, the earlier you arrive in Vienna, the more choices of class you have. In reality, you can always try to mail a professor if his class is full and you really want it.
registration_help: Contacting directly the professors can be game changing when a course is full. If you could not register for all classses, ask around you and for sure you'll hear feedback and get plenty of ideas for other courses you could take instead.
registration_success: I arrived beginning of September so I still had some choice. For someone arriving at the end of the September, it might get more complicated to get all their courses.
registration_advice: At BOKU, the timetable isn't organised in hours block like in KU. This means that a lot of classes partly overlap. When looking at the classes, check carefully at the class schedule, at which campus the course is (two main campus at ~30min from each other), what class type it is. Some classes can be easily missed (so overlap isn't much of a pb), but some are seminars cannot be missed (making overlap impossible). The course system is pretty chaotic compared to KU's. As a general rule, I'd recommend to be as flexible as possible there. Write to professors in case of overlap and trouble, they are used to students having these issues.
course_level: Level highly depends on the course. You can always drop out a course in the first weeks in the level is not adapted and take something else instead. Also the courses are always super small credits, so you never really get in any depth in a subject. The difficulty is not really the course itself, but having to deal with like 10 different subjects at the same time during the semester.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is pretty much the same, though maybe less "discussion-based" and more top-down than in Denmark.
courses_enrolled: Meteorological conditions and precipitation Climate change scenarios and regional impact Meteorological data analysis and visualization Weather, climate and society Seminar in global change and ecosystems Integrated flood risk management Remote sensing and GIS in natural resource management Decision support systems Geo-data management Exploratory data analysis with R
recommended_courses: There's a ton of classes offered at BOKU, prioritize what you like most. If you miss some credits and lack space in your timetable: "Exploratory data analysis with R" and "Integrated flood risk management" are two good examples of courses you can easily overlap with seminars. Both could be taken with nearly no attending. Good in case you have no space left in your timetable but still need credits (good quality of online material).
unexpected_costs: I did not have any unexpected costs. Be careful though, you'll need to pay by cash a lot of things, especially in bars or cheap restaurants. That's even more true when you go out of the city. So just be sure to always have a bit of cash when going out.
cost_comparison: Any item is cheaper than in Copenhagen: housing, groceries, going out for food, drinks, cinema, museum, .....
activities_available: Students could join some cultural and sport events offered by the student union ÖH or ESN. MUSI offers a lot sport opportunities for a cheap price. You'll be mixed with students and staff from all universities in Vienna, which is also nice to meet other people.
activities_recommended: I'd recommend to join some of the ESN events, especially in the first weeks. It's the best way to meet some internationals that are also new to the city and that are seeking to make new friends. I'd also suggest joining a MUSI sport activity, to meet more local people. Speaking a bit of German could help for the sport class + it's also a great way to learn it.
weekend_recommendations: - With about 1h train towards the west, you can reach a lot of moutains and really nice hikes. If you're under 26, I'd suggest to get the "Vorteilscard Jugend" from ÖBB, the national train company, to get cheaper trains for the year. - City-wise, Budapest and Prague are also a few hours of train from Vienna. Regiojet (a czech train company) offers attractive prices for both destination.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy. At university, you'll get to meet a lot of people ready to share about Vienna.
socializing_tips: As mentionned above, I'd recommend to join some sport course at MUSI, maybe one of the best way to meet new (local) people. At Uni or anywhere, you'll be able to meet a lot of locals. Speaking German is the biggest key to socialize with local students.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any challenging cultural difference. The hardest part was to get used to Austrian bureaucry.
culture_appreciated: Vienna is vibrant city, at the heart of Europe, meaning it has some kind of unique mix of germanic, latin and slavic worlds blended together. People here will like to know more about you and your country. The hiking/outdoor culture is also great here (that's even more a thing for Western Asutria people, like in Tyrol):
top3_advice: - Be ready for the administrative work at BOKU + with the mess of class registration. However, you can't do much about it, so just try to be flexible. - Go around and visit Austria. Time goes really fast in Erasmus. - Most importantly, have fun!
other_useful_info: Learning/speaking some German will make your life easier at any aspects (city administration, university administration, socialising, etc)
most_rewarding: Meeting so many amazing people and learning so many new things has been an incredible experience. Studying in another country is truly enriching, and I highly recommend it to everyone. It opens your mind to different perspectives, new ways of doing things, and unique approaches to problem-solving. While Austria and Denmark may not be worlds apart culturally, the differences are just enough to make the experience both eye-opening and rewarding.
greatest_challenge: My biggest challenge was adjusting to Austrian bureaucracy, understanding how the course system works here, and figuring out how to fulfill all my credit requirements. The first few weeks were especially stressful and frustrating, as I often had to make last-minute changes, for instance because the entire schedule for a class would be changed just the day before it was supposed to start.
other_comments: If you’re part of a double degree program and writing your thesis at BOKU, don’t expect to finish it in just one sharp semester. While it’s theoretically possible, it seems nearly impossible in practice. Local students often take up to a year to complete theirs. Of course, the timeline depends on you and your supervisor, but I’d recommend planning for at least 6 to 7 months just for the thesis. Also, keep in mind that even after you’ve finished writing, you’ll need an extra month before your defense due to administrative procedures.

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)
crucial_aspects: I liked the profile of the university and that it mainly focies on organic agriculture and sustainability. I also have a good friend who stayed in Vienna for year and really liked it.
info_ease: Very easy. We were well welcomed and information was easy to get.
arrival_assistance: I got assigned a budy who contacted me before arrival and was happy to answar questions. We had multiple welcome days with lot of information and we could always contact a erasmus responsible via email.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registering at campus is easy. You meet up on the office and get a card and so on. Registering for courses is a bit more difficult.
registration_help: You could write emails with questions and you got lot of information on the velcome days.
registration_success: Very succesfull. I registered for more courses than I need and then went to the first lecture to see how it was before deciding. This was very commen and a great way to find the right courses. In general I was happy with the corses i ended up with. However, I found some of the small courses a bit superficial.
registration_advice: Try the first lecture before you decide and dont get too stressed about the many courses and schedules. Some overlaps are okay. And do some excursions, they are great!
course_level: My general experience was that the course level was lower than at KU but some courses did take more time for for example reeding and assignments than I was used to. For me reeeding up for exams also took more time than at KU because you have so many different courses and maybe shorter lectures meaning you had to read up on more yourself.
teaching_comparison: The courses were more divided into either lectures, seminars or excursions where it is more a mix at UCPH. You could therefore choose courses that was only excursions and field work or couses that was only lectures and not interactive at all. Therefore its a good idea to make sure you have a mix.
courses_enrolled: - Soil fertility and soil ecology in organic agriculture - Agroecology - A science, a practice and a movement - Interdisciplinary excursion on organic agriculture - Organic horticulture (vegetables and ornamentals) - Stress physiology of plants - Methods of measuring stress resistance in plants - Agroforestry in mountain regions - Case studies in organic grassland management - European regulatory framework for organic production - Intensive German Refresher Course - moderate advanced - Multidisciplinary field trip in wildlife ecology - Soil protection
recommended_courses: Soil fertility and soil ecology in organic agriculture had a good teacher and was interesting also with some field work and had an early exam. Agroecology - A science, a practice and a movement was a very different structured course with a lot of interesting reading material, discussions and group work. Interdisciplinary excursion on organic agriculture a 2 day excursion were we saw a lot of interesting organic farms. It was really well structures, inspiring and a lot of fun. Case studies in organic grassland management was also a really nice excursion to a great institute in the mountains, but a lot of group work online for the exam. Stress physiology of plants was a nice lecture class and i learned alot, but maybe some more workload than other 2 ECTS courses.
unexpected_costs: I used the city a lot more than back home. Went to many cafees, bars and so on.
cost_comparison: Many things are similar to Denmark. Goung out for food and drinks/coffe is cheaper.
activities_available: There was yoga, salsa and drumming lessons every week, either for free or very cheap. There was a really nice festival at campus arranged by TUWI the student bar organisation.
activities_recommended: Go to the TUWI festival and try out the salsa.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the nature around Vienna and go to the Heuriger (small wine cafees in the wine fields around the city). You can find cheap sport courses at the sport univerisity USI. Its nice to bike around in the city, but be carefull not to fall in the tram lanes. Go to donau insel in the summer and in winter try some of the small very cute cinemas all around the city. As a student you can see all the movies you like for 22€ a month in the small cinemas if you get the non-stop kino abo.
culture_adjustment: Really easy i would say
socializing_tips: Do the excursions that are multible days and the seminars where there is group work-
cultural_challenges: Nothing really? Just adjusting to being a new place and find new friends at first.
culture_appreciated: Theres a more layed back culture than in DK, and a big culture for going our for a drink in summer or a coffee in winter. And its really easy to find vegan and vegetarian and organic food.
top3_advice: Campus and the people at campus arre really nice and layed back - theres a bit of a hippie vibe in the best way. Its nice with the many small courses eventhough it seems a bit confusing. Try and see if you can find housing outside campus, it gives a lot to the exchange experience.
other_useful_info: I would reccoment getting a bike
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of new friends and being more on your own in a new city.
greatest_challenge: The first month as difficult because because i didnt know people very well and the winter is really cold and windy in Vienna, so it was a bit difficult exploring the city and finding things to do.

institution: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)
crucial_aspects: I first of all wanted to go somewhere, I could take some interested courses, and BOKU has an extensive and very interesting course catalogue. Besides that I was very keen on going to a destination that wasn't too bleak and sad during autumn and winter. I love the Austrian Christmas markets, and there's a great "wine hiking" season in Vienna as well, so I think it's a great destination for the A/W semester, also good opportunities for hiking and skiing of course. I also really wanted to go traveling while on exchange, and I got to discover a lot of neighbouring cities and countries from Vienna. Lastly I was happy to improve my German as well
overall_comments: I had a fantastic exchange semester, I definitely recommend Austria, Vienna and BOKU as an amazing exchange destination! The academic level of the courses is somewhat lower than at KU and it was a kinda stressful having to take so many small courses at the same time.
info_ease: In my experience the information was good. There was a zoom meeting for all incoming exchange students in May, we received a lot of e-mails with check lists and we had 5 intro days before the semester start, which was really great (also for the social aspect). I had the feeling that both the BOKU administration and the Buddy students were very available to help. The only thing that was difficult in terms of information is that you can't plan your courses and schedule before you physically register at BOKU.
arrival_assistance: E-mails, presentation at intro week, briefing when I registered at the university, I also had a Buddy assigned who I could ask questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had a fantastic exchange semester, I definitely recommend Austria, Vienna and BOKU as an amazing exchange destination! The academic level of the courses is somewhat lower than at KU and it was a kinda stressful having to take so many small courses at the same time.
registration_process: You make an appointment to go to the Türkenschanz campus to register, you get your BOKU card with your Matrikelnummer and then you can make a profile on the website BOKUonline. On BOKUonline you register for courses and can see your schedule, exam dates, grades etc..
registration_help: There was good help both from the administration like from the Internation Relations office and also from other students and the "buddies". The Studo app is really useful, where you can see previous students' review of the courses, the Erasmus WhatsApp groups are great, and genereally if you e-mail the IR-office or the professors, they are all very helpful and nice, in my experience.
registration_success: I was pretty succesful! Think there was 1-2 courses I wanted that I didn't get, but it wasn't really a problem, since the course catalogue at BOKU is so extensive that you have loads to choose from. It also helped me that I arrived already a month before the semester start, so I could get the spots before others. I signed up to maybe 30 courses to try them out and then scaled down and ended up with 10 courses of 30 ECTS total I quite liked after a month or so of deciding.
registration_advice: If you can arrive early to do you registration etc, I would say do it. Generally it's also advised to sign up to all the courses you find interesting at the start, so you make sure you get a spot, and then you can start seeing how they all fit together in your schedule. The first two weeks of the semester a lot of students try out many different courses and thereafter make their decision. If you don't get into a course, sign up to the waitlist anyways, and also maybe email the professor and you can even show up to the first lecture to ask for a spot. This worked for me. Also use the Studo app to see the reviews of the different courses by other students, it's super super useful!
academics_comments: I had a fantastic exchange semester, I definitely recommend Austria, Vienna and BOKU as an amazing exchange destination! The academic level of the courses is somewhat lower than at KU and it was a kinda stressful having to take so many small courses at the same time.
course_level: I would say the level is generally lower than at KU. I was doing my 5. semester on my bachelor and had mainly masters courses, and I didn't find them very challenging. From my own experiences and what I've heard, the courses at campus Muthgasse (biotech, water technology, green chemistry, food science etc.) are more difficult than the ones taught at main campus Türkenschanz (natural resources, biology, nature management etc.). Also the final exams are often just paper and pen, so not with any notes or books available like a lot of exams at KU are. Sometimes you get the possible exam questions before to prepare, or you can find old ones on Studo, so it's more just about memorising the curriculum.
teaching_comparison: At KU the courses are generally bigger like 7.5 ECTS and therefore also contain more styles of teaching within one course; a course can have both lecture, exercises, excursion, project and/or lab work all in one. The style of teaching at BOKU depends a lot on the course, where the teaching style is defined by codes such as VO, VS, VU, VX, EX etc., where V means lecture, S means seminar, U means exercises, X means excursions and so on. So that means unless you choose a specific course for it, you might not have any lab or group work at all in the whole semester. Also, there are no books, so you save that money and generally don't have to read for the classes, unless you have a course where it is part of the student assesment and clearly defined before. This is very different from KU, where you have to read loads, so it was a pretty nice break, but it also means you need to go to the lectures to learn stuff.
courses_enrolled: Aquaculture in practice - lectures and field trips. Biobased and biodegradable plastics. Conservation biology. Development research and practice. Ecology of aquatic systems. Environmental toxicology (in German: Umwelttoxikologie). Field camp I - introduction to mountain forestry and forest sciences. German for Science (BOKU specific topics) - Course A (B2+). Intensive German Refresher Course - moderate advanced. Organisational behaviour.
recommended_courses: My top recommendation is the Field camp I! It's six days excursion in a cabin in the lower alps with a group of 20 ish mountain forestry students - really cosy, super interesting and not a difficult course to follow. I also very much recommend the German courses, especially the intensive German before the semester starts, which is a chance to make friends early and check off 3 ECTS before the semester even begins. Aquaculture in practice was about fish production in lakes and consisted of four field trips and only two lectures, so it was super easy. Conservation biology (the master course, not the bachelor!!) was relaxed and pretty interesting. Develppment research and practice and Organisational behaviour were both interesting, had 10 minute tests at the start of each lecture and no final exam - they were the only courses I had with mandatory classes and reading material.
unexpected_costs: My Danish phone bill got really expensive after 4 months abroad, so then I chose/had to get extra data with an Austrian sim card through Airalo. I also wasn't aware of the fee when you register your address at the municipality/"Magistrat" - apparently if you use another ID than your passport it is a lot cheaper.
cost_comparison: I think I expected the general prices to close to as cheap as they are in Germany, but a lot of the time it was similar prices to Denmark. Groceries are pretty much as expensive as in Denmark. Fun things like going out to eat or to the cinema and stuff like that are generally cheaper though. Wine and beer is quite cheap, shots and cocktails not cheap. The food at the uni canteen is not cheap, but the döner shop at uni is a very good alternative.
activities_available: There were lots of social activities; such as the whole intro week, the weekly international table, the "Stammtisch", creative Tuesday and lots of other events organised by BOKU, the student bar "Tüwi" and by the ESN. The BOKU Ball was the biggest highlight! You can join different well-priced sports through the USI (like the KSI at KU), and BOKU has an american football team and basket ball team, the BOKU Beez, that play against other university teams.
activities_recommended: The BOKU Ball! It was so much fun and a cool experience being at a traditional ball at the Rathaus. Participate in the Stammtisch and the events and trips planned by the ESN. Check out the 7., 8. and 9. district for great coffee shops, bars and thrift stores! Go traveling and experience more of Austria and the neighbouring countries.
weekend_recommendations: Go traveling! If you get the Jugend Vorteilskarte (25 years or younger) you can get 50% discount on all train tickets within Austria. I think the card costs around 20 euros, so it's definitely worth it if you do a couple trips. Within Austria I went to Salzburg and on a cabin trip somewhere two hours from Vienna and also on a few hiking trips. I also did a daytrip to Bratislava and weekendtrips to Prague, Brno and Budapest.
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy for me personally, since the Austrian and Danish culture isn't too dissimilar. I also have lived in Copenhagen for a few years and in Berlin for two years, and I would say Vienna is kind of like a good mix between those two cities.
socializing_tips: Attend courses with excursions or group work, or sign up to sports classes through USI or attend some of the other events at BOKU like creative Tuesdays, salsa dancing etc.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find the cultural differences too challenging, it's not so dissimilar from the Danish culture. I think I just sometimes felt Vienna was a bit crowded with people and traffic compared to Copenhagen, but it's still quite clean and safe and nothing compared to other big cities, so not something big to complain about haha. I missed being able to cycle on my bike everywhere easily and the ocean.
culture_appreciated: I thought it was really cool to experience a country with a culture that has been shaped by both western, eastern and southern European influence. The Austrian history and society has many layers and I didn't know as much about it before I came as I do now. It was fun to experience the fancier Viennese culture like the balls, the opera and the coffee houses. The mountains, the wine hills and all the nature around also really influence the culture, I really enjoyed hiking and especially the "wine hikes" in the 19. district.
top3_advice: 1) Get to Vienna 2-4 weeks early to register on site so you can start registering for courses and maybe even do an intensive German course, which is well worth it. My first month before semester start I also already made a lot of friends through different Erasmus WhatsApp groups and got to know the city better! 2) Try to find accomodation in the sweet spot between BOKU and the city or somewhere with good public transport. Some cool districts are 7., 8. and 9., I lived in the 17. district by Alser Straße station on the U6, and that was great for both getting to campus quick and out in town. 3) Try to take courses that don't all have a final exam in the last semester week, it will make it a lot less stressful - some have exams earlier, some have mandatory attendance at lectures and then no final exam and some have a paper or a presentation instead. Also look into doing courses with field trips/excursions included or courses that don't run for the full semester. If you prioritise a bit of time to work out your courses and your schedule, you can make your life a lot easier and the semester much more enjoyable!
other_useful_info: Download the Studo app to see your schedule easy and to check other students' reviews of the courses and get their old exam papers. Download the Wienmobil app for transport tickets within Vienna and the ÖBB app for tickets in the rest of Austria and to the airport. Get the ESN card to go to their parties and on their trips, it also gives you good discounts on Flixbus and Ryanair and other stuff.
most_rewarding: Meeting all the amazing people I did, traveling around that part of Europe and having a semester where I had to figure everything out for myself. I had time to reflect a lot on what I like to do with my free time, what kind of people I like to surround myself with and what actually interests me academically. I was also happy with how much my German improved in the time I was there and now I know a bunch of Austrian slang that I may never use again in my life, but it's cool!
greatest_challenge: Even though I had a roommate and spent time with people nearly every day, I did feel quite lonely sometimes. It can be difficult to not have your go-to people around you if you want to do something, but also don't have the social energy to meet with people you don't know very well yet. It could also be really hard to prioritise your time and energy sometimes, since there always seems to be plans you can partake in, but you also need to rest and study once in a while. The Erasmus FOMO is real, and you need to learn to listen to yourself and your own needs
other_comments: It might seem like a lot right now, but I promise all the work is worth it once you are on your exchange! I had a lot going on in my life when I applied and I also doubted at times if it was the right thing to go, but I am so happy I did it in the end. Remember to listen to yourself and take time to figure out what makes you happy and prioritise doing those things. Your exchange might not go exactly how you pictured in your head, or you might not find "your people" in the first week (my best friends from exchange was people I only started talking more to in my last two months there), and you might not get the courses you want, but it's still all gonna work itself out! Viel Erfolg, bussi baba!

crucial_aspects: The academic opportunities offered at the university, along with the nature and sports opportunities that exists in the country. The university is highly ranked in Australia and it was interestereting to experience my degree in english and in another country. Furthermore, the country has amazing nature, and opportunities for activities that we don't have in Denmark, such as surfing. The fact that the country is difficult to visit due to its placement, was also something that made me want to got her for exchange. Lastly, I wanted to challenge myself by living in a whole new country alone.
overall_comments: Due to covid-19 almost all of my classes were online. This made the social aspects of the exchange more difficult, as I didn't meet many people in the university. It required a lot of extra effort to meet people outside of the university. Furthermore, I couldn't find any study groups in my classes, and thus I couldn't share ideas or study together with other students in the classes. As I was completely new to the university and the way of teaching, this made the beginning of the exchange stay challenging.
info_ease: The university had introduction days which provided a lot of necessary information. These included basic information on the campus and on the university's social clubs for students. Though the introduction was good, I still had trouble to know where to seek help if if I had questions regarding my courses later on in the stay. This meant that I wrote emails directly to the professors of my classes, which might have resulted in extra unnecessary work for them.
arrival_assistance: The introduction days mentioned above. There was no extra assistance upon arrival. I believe that it would have been beneficial to provide exchange students with a "buddy-student" from the university, who could help the exchange students to start up the courses. It was difficult to navigate physically on campus, and even more difficult to navigate on the teaching platforms used for online classes and assignments. I would have appreciated to have a contact person, who was an existing student on the university, that I could ask practical questions in relation to studying.
arrival_comments: Though I found the navigating physically on campus and online on the teaching platorms difficult, I still found the orientation in the introduction days beneficial and succesfull. Going on exchange it is expected that you have to spend some time and effort in order to get familiar with the teaching methods and the areas, so I think it would be difficult to completely avoid that. However, I think that future exchange students would benefit a lot from a "buddy-student" from the university.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Due to covid-19 almost all of my classes were online. This made the social aspects of the exchange more difficult, as I didn't meet many people in the university. It required a lot of extra effort to meet people outside of the university. Furthermore, I couldn't find any study groups in my classes, and thus I couldn't share ideas or study together with other students in the classes. As I was completely new to the university and the way of teaching, this made the beginning of the exchange stay challenging.
registration_process: Finding courses in my degree was difficult, due to the university's semester structure. The university has a three semester-structure, which means that exchange students need to take an intense three-week course before the actual semester begin, in order to obtain enough ECTS-points. Furthermore, the point-system obtained from the courses was not the same in for the University of Copenhagen, and the points had to be converted. I spent a lot of time and effort on finding new and relevant courses, that did not overlap with courses I had previously received at the University of Copenhagen, by thoroughly reading the course information of the different courses offered.
registration_help: The university had an email address that you could write to. However, due to the time difference and the fact that they got a lot of emails from students, the response-time was very long. This made the process stressfull, as registration had to be done within certain deadlines. I would suggest the university to offer "buddy-students" from the university to all future exchange students. This would have been an extremely helpful thing, that would have made the experience way less stressfull. In my own case I contacted all the students from the University of Copenhagen who were going to the same university as myself during the application process, so that we could socialize and help each other with practical questions.
registration_success: I succeeded in my registration of classes. The was however due to the fact that I could consult with my brother and boyfriend, who had both been on exchange in Australia previously. Furthermore, I began well ahead of time, which I would recommend all future exchange students to do.
registration_advice: To ask previous students that's been on exchange on the university for help, and to begin the process well ahead of time. Furthermore, it's important to set aside plenty of time for the process, as it is more time consuming than one might might think initially.
academics_comments: Due to covid-19 almost all of my classes were online. This made the social aspects of the exchange more difficult, as I didn't meet many people in the university. It required a lot of extra effort to meet people outside of the university. Furthermore, I couldn't find any study groups in my classes, and thus I couldn't share ideas or study together with other students in the classes. As I was completely new to the university and the way of teaching, this made the beginning of the exchange stay challenging.
course_level: They were high level, and required much effort. Due to the exam structure of the university, where each course is divided into two or three exams taken throughout the semester, it was important to attend all lectures and tutorials. There was not time to study for the fina exam, as I'm used to at the University of Copenhagen. I would say that I used more time studying during my exchange, than I do at my home university. This I think can also be explained by a general lack of working in study groups, which I find very beneficial at my home university.
teaching_comparison: The style was similar to the teaching style at the University of Copenhagen. However, there were more lectures and less tutorials. This meant that I had to do more studying on my own than I'm used to.
courses_enrolled: PHCM9012 Health Promotion & Social Perspectives of Health, PHCM9050 Immunisation Policy and Practice, PHCM9786 Global approaches to Cardiovascular Disease, Diabetes & Cancer Prevention, BEES6601 An Introduction to the Sydney Environment
recommended_courses: BEES6601 An Introduction to the Sydney Environment. Though this was an introduction course, that only lasted three weeks, it was the only course where I met other students as it was fully physical. The course was meant as an introduction for all exchange students, and it gave me a crucial introduction to studying at the university overall. It was a perfect introduction, and I really recommend all exchange students to take this course. The content of the course was not as interesting for my degree, as my other courses. However, it introduced me to the social, physical and historical context to Sydney, which made the exchange a lot more interesting for me. The professors were extremely helpful, and the course was a great experience.
unexpected_costs: I didn't encounter many costs that I hadn't expected. However, several of the costs were way higher than I had anticipated. The only unexpected cost was the one of the student visa, which was very high. Future students should be aware of this cost.
cost_comparison: The costs of flight tickets from Denmark to Sydney and return, was a lot more expensive than I expected. I bought the tickets well ahead of time, and it was still very expensive. Furthermore, the costs of phone and internet, as well as public transportation were high. I bought a used bicycle upon my arrival, which significantly lowered the costs of public transportation. However, many buses and trams didn't operate at night, resulting in quite expensive taxi and Uber costs. Biking at night is not recommended, as there are no bicycle lanes, and people drive very close and fast to cyclists.
activities_available: The university offered more than 200 different clubs. This included sports, academic and other kinds of clubs, such as cooking cubs and clubs where you could learn new languages. I was impressed y the amount of different clubs offered at the university.
activities_recommended: I would recommend students to join sports clubs, such as the outdoor basketball or surfing club. This allows you to meet other students, as well as take advantage of the beautiful and unique nature, that Sydney has. The people I know, who participated in these clubs met a lot of friends in this way - both from the university, and other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend future students to travel around the area. There's a lot of national parks and beaches close to Sydney that are very beautiful and easy to reach by train, bus or car. Plan and structure your studies, so that you have time to travel and explore the area. In the longer holidays, most students leave Sydney, and this is a great opportunity to go on a longer trip, eg. travelling the coast or other parts of Australia. I recommend taking advantage of the fact that you are a place in the world, that is difficult to reach, and that most people don't get to see.
culture_adjustment: The culture is very similar to the culture in Denmark. The only significant difference is the alcohol culture, as beers etc. are way more expensive in Australia compared to Denmark. However, there's still plenty of social gatherings and parties, so this is not a problem for the overall experience.
socializing_tips: Attend the first days of school (introduction). This offers a lot of social events and important information. It's nice to know other exchange students, as you probably face some of the same challenges, and in this way you can help each other. Furthermore, I recommend joining some of the social clubs to meet local students, as local students use the clubs a lot. Lastly, it's important not to live alone. The easiest way to meet new friends is to live at campus.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find adapting to the culture challenging at all. People in Australia are in general very ope and helpfull, so this was not a problem at all.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the opportunities for surfing, and the nature surrounding Sydney. This is very unique, and I highly recommend future students to take advantage of this.
top3_advice: 1. Set aside plenty of time to find good and social housing. This might mean that you have to reach out to previous exchange students for help, or spend a lot of time on social platforms such as Facebook or Flatmate.com. However, a good housing is fundamental to the experience. 2. It's also important to attend classes, as there are examinations throughout the whole semester. If you want to have time to explore the area and travel, you have to plan and structure your studies from the beginning. 3. Make sure that you have money saved up. The cost of they stay is very high, and you have to be prepared to pay a lot for housing, insurance, visa and flight tickets.
other_useful_info: One of the most important things is to reach out to a previous exchange student at the university. Make sure you have someone from the University of Copenhagen, who has been on exchange on the same university, that you can contact regarding practical questions.
most_rewarding: For me, the most rewarding part was to experience the nature and surfing opportunities, as well as getting new friends. However, I also found it very exciting to experience my degree in another country, and to be able to compare the similarities and differences in the public health degree, when delivered in Sydney compared to Denmark. The academic content was extremely rewarding and unique.
greatest_challenge: The most challenging part was navigating on campus and the university's course structure, as well as getting familiar with the platforms for online lectures, tutorials and exams. I hope future students will have physical attendance in their courses, as I believe this would have made both the academic and social aspects of the exchange easier.
other_comments: Exchange is a wonderful experience, that I will remember for the rest of my life. It has been extremely rewarding both socially, personally and academically. I would recommend it to everyone.

crucial_aspects: English speaking country, a destination I havn't visited before, university close to the city and nature, university with welcoming atmosphere and culture for exchange students.
info_ease: KU and UNSW (University in Sydney) were helpful to provide information in the process of applying to the university, applying for visa etc.
arrival_assistance: I arrived the day before orientation and received the information I needed study-wise at orientation day.
arrival_comments: The university in Sydney (UNSW) were sometimes pretty slow at replying to emails. To set up the student account and chose courses was time demanding (long waiting time for answers). So best tip is to be patient and know that they're also able to help you sort it all out when you are there in person.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: They send a lot of emails and the process was pretty easy to follow. Some of them ended up in spam which ended up causing me some trouble, however it worked out in the end. At first you apply to the host uni, get accepted and apply for visa.
registration_help: It was possible to email and call the university. However, as the exchange got closer the university support also got more busy and answer time got pretty long.
registration_success: Two of my initial chosen courses were full so I had to change. However, I ended up being happy about the courses I got.
registration_advice: Be aware of emails ending up in spam, and once registration for courses start and activation of student profile at the host institution be careful to it all before deadlines.
course_level: I chose two courses in my study and two courses outside my study. I would say that the level fitted me well, sometimes I felt that some of it was repetition of stuff I had already learned and other times it was knew approach (other methods, instruments in lab, computer programs). The two courses outside of my study were at a level so I could keep up, courses where it wasn't necessary with any prerequisites.
teaching_comparison: The style was a bit different and it was very obvious that the university had been shut down and doing online teaching during covid. Many of the Australian students hadn't been in lab in a while and in-person exercise classes were also just reestablished. The connection between students and with the professor was therefore a bit different from KU, where everybody knows each other and are used to work with one another in person.
courses_enrolled: Chemistry courses: Quantum Nature of Molecules, Environmental toxicology Others: Marine environment, Risks and Impacts of Changing Climate
recommended_courses: Environmental Toxicology was a good course and a course that is not offered in the BA at KU. Also intersting with the Risks and Impacts of Changing Climate
unexpected_costs: Traveling around in the weekends and holidays will also be quite expensive.
cost_comparison: Groceries and eating out was expensive.
activities_available: Almost everything you can think of.
activities_recommended: Exchange in Sydney calls for surfing and outdoor activities at the beach. I also heard the climbing club was a lot of fun.
weekend_recommendations: Diving course, go surf, surf camp, spend days at the beach, go party with your friends, go on hikes around Sydney, go to the Blue Mountains, go see a concert in the Opera house, go to sport events, BBQ at the beach, Longer time off (spring break i.e.): Travel the East coast (Cairns to Brisbane), Melbourne (and Great Ocean Road), Byron Bay,
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy, the lifestyle in Coogee (Sydney) fitted me very well. It's a beach suburb of Sydney and the vibe is very laid back, people are very active and friendly. I lived with many danes and dutch people so the culture wasn't that different in the house.
socializing_tips: Talk to them in class and get coffee together after class, help each other out. If it's somebody who's interesting, plan to do something after class. A good ice-breaker is also to ask for advice or good ideas of what to do in the area (food places, places to go out etc.).
cultural_challenges: I can't think of any differences I found challenging.
culture_appreciated: Australians are very friendly and easy to talk to. The laid back, sun-is-always-shining vibe also suited me very well. The opportunity to do activities in the everyday life that you don't normally do in Copenhagen.
top3_advice: Choose classes so you are flexible to plan your week, be open and attend everything social etc in the beginning, don't hesitate to ask and reach out to other students/professors for help, advice or just to chat.
other_useful_info: There is a lot of things you can commit to (social wise) so it's just about choosing.
most_rewarding: The people I met and the memories we created together.
greatest_challenge: To balance study and socializing/exploring. Make sure to attend study but also prioritize social cultural experiences.

Moreover, the level of law schools in Sydney are generally really good, which of course played a part in my choice of study destination.

arrival_comments: Not much orientation, decent information available.

crucial_aspects: It was crucial for me to go to a destination far away from home, but still in a culture that would be easy for me to live in. Personally, I wanted to see something entirely different from Denmark, but still be in a place where people spoke English, so it would be easy to get to know people where I went. I also enjoyed the weather a lot compared to home... And the beautiful nature of course. Academically, it was important to me to go to an English-speaking country, as my guess was I would learn more there than in a non-English-speaking country. Furthermore, I wanted to go to a uni with high academic standards and interesting courses.
info_ease: There was an orientation meeting for all exchange students at the beginning of the semester, which was helpful to go to. Other than that, my host uni was hard to get into contact with, I feel like. They were slow at responding to e-mails, and their websites and systems were hard to figure out. I got some help from my fellow Danish exchange students, but it was clear that the exchange team at the host uni was very busy.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation meeting for all exchange students at the beginning of the semester, which was helpful to go to. I also received some e-mails from the host uni, but the amount of information was so overwhelming that it had the opposite effect. It was very hard to know which information was nice to know, and which was need to know.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process was long and infuriating. First, you have to apply for courses in a system called Endeavour. UNSW will then approve or decline your courses there. You need to apply for as many courses as you can, as it is better to have a lot of "pre-approved" courses. Afterwards, you have to apply again for the courses in their student system called myUNSW. It was a long, hard process, as UNSW had very limited spaces for students in their law classes. I got rejected for many courses before finally getting some of the ones I wanted, so you have to be very patient in the process and accept the fact that you might not get all the courses you want.
registration_help: There is an exchange team at UNSW who helped me. They were helpful ones you finally got a hold of them, but bad at replying for the most part.
registration_success: In the end, I actually got some nice courses that didn't collide with each other. But it was a long way coming and took some time after I got there.
registration_advice: Have patience. Don't stress that you don't have all of it figured out before you go. Course registration can be done even after you've started classes, even though it's of course nice to have figured out before. I think I had my final registration done about a week before I started classes.
course_level: The level of courses was a bit easier than at home, but harder to follow because of the language barrier. Both the BA and MA courses were, in my opinion, easier to pass than at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching in Australia is very different from Denmark. First of all, you don't just get graded on a final exam. Your participation in classes gets grated, and you often have quizzes and research papers during the semester which also get graded. Classes are compulsory to be at. You have to state your own opinion - both in class and in your written assignments. That's a whole other way to learn than at UCPH. It has its ups and downs - depending on who you are. I thought it was nice with a change, but also a bit harder during the semester to keep up with your assignments and the quizzes and also concentrate on participating in class.
courses_enrolled: LAWS3623 - The Criminal Trial LAWS8058 - Managing Workplace Change and Conflict LAWS8168 - The Australian Legal System in Comparative Perspective CRIM1011 - Introduction to Criminal Justice
recommended_courses: All of my courses were nice, and very different from one another. The Criminal Trial was nice, the teacher was very sweet and interested in the Danish legal system. She also arranged for me to see an Australian criminal trial, which was very interesting. The Australian Legal System in Comparative Perspective is made for law exchange students and was a nice way to get an introduction to how their legal system and laws work. It's a very intensive course with a lot of studying though.
unexpected_costs: I was not expecting to travel around Australia as much as I did. I took lots more trips outside Sydney as I did expect. So did everyone else. Save up to go travel as well while you're there. You want to experience the city as well, so it's nice to have money to have drinks and go out to eat from time to time.
cost_comparison: The cost of living is expensive. Food was expensive, alcohol was expensive, and housing was very expensive. Our gas and water bill was also very much more expensive than I'd thought. Flights to and from DK are very expensive as well Avocados and coffee is cheap and good :)
activities_available: I did not look into it that much, but there were a lot of activities to participate in. There is also a gym and a pool at campus.
activities_recommended: I did not participate in any, as I did not feel like I had the time.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely go to Byron Bay and Melbourne for long weekends. Drive the great ocean road in Melbourne. Surf on Bondi Beach on your weekends. Go for at least two weeks to Western Australia in a camper van - most amazing vacation of my life. I stopped for two weeks in Bali on my way home. I would also recommend doing that.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy, I feel like. Australia has a very western culture like Denmark.
socializing_tips: Australians are very open. Talk to them in class :)
cultural_challenges: I didn't find the big cultural differences with Australians, other than they're all really fascinated by the fact that you've traveled a lot. There are a lot of Chinese students in Australia, and I felt the social distance to them was big. They're not unfriendly, but they keep a lot to themselves, and it can be hard to socialise. There is also just a big cultural difference and language barrier, which is hard to overcome.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated the nature a lot. Although Sydney is a big city, their nature is still unbelievably beautiful.
top3_advice: 1) Studying there is not a piece of cake. Although it is easier to pass courses, they read twice as much as we do at UCPH. It is more busy during the semester, but I chose courses without final exams, so I didn't have an "exam-period" per se, which was nice. 2) Be patient in your communication with the uni. 3) Be open-minded in your choice of courses. You're not guaranteed all the courses you want.
other_useful_info: I had a friend who had been at the same uni the year before me. It was really nice to have a person to ask questions.
most_rewarding: Getting to know a lot of new people, learning about an entirely different legal system, and seeing places I would never had imagined seeing in my lifetime.
greatest_challenge: I didn't expect it to be that hard to study in English - but it was. Although I'm pretty good at English, academically it is challenging to keep up. Everything takes twice as long to read, and twice as long to write.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an english speaking country, so that I would be going to class with domestic students rather than only exchange students. Furthermore, I wanted to go somewhere relatively far from Denmark to increase my chance at meeting different cultures. The specific university was chosen because of their very informative website and of course the many great courses they had to offer within my field.
info_ease: It was very easy, as the university has a student hub where you can get all the information and guidance you need face to face, rather than having to search for it online. However, the university is not good at answering e-mails. I would recommend to write to the individual professors rather than the general mail.
arrival_assistance: The O-week offers students, new or continuing, a great overview of campus and its possibilities. Furthermore, at the start of enrolment, you get some obligatory courses on Moodle that you have to complete, which is all about different procedures of the university. This really made me feel that the institution is well organised.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The process is not necessarily difficult but does have a lot of steps. First, you need to find courses in the course handbook. Then you get access to a portal where you have to apply to get accepted to each course. It is recommended that you apply for acceptance for more courses than you need, because the acceptance is not the same as secured enrolment. Some courses gets accepted right away while some take a while. Then you get access to the actual enrolment application, where you can sign up for courses. However, this is a "first come, first served" kind of deal, so you have to be fast, depending on how popular your courses are. The other issue is that the system prohibits you from applying to courses that have overlapping schedules. This can be tricky and might mean that you have to go back to the first portal and apply for another course. Once you are enrolled however, it is easy.
registration_help: The website and portals are pretty intuitive and informative on their own. You also receive an email with instructions.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted except for one. The one I did not get offered a waiting list, which I did not dare to join, so I opted for quickly finding another course. However, my friend joined the waiting list and was enrolled the next day. So overall, it was not too difficult to get the courses you initially wanted.
registration_advice: Use the course handbook and make a list of courses you might be interested in. Choose more than you need. In that way, you have a lot of possibilities to get what you want and not having to go back and reapply. Make sure you keep an eye on your email, so you can be ready to apply the moment the portal opens. If you are doing the summer term or another short term, be aware that there are less courses offered on these.
course_level: I took mostly first semester courses even though I was studying on my sixth semester. This was mainly due to the "prerequisites" which are the requirements you need to full fill to be able to get accepted for the course. A lot of courses from the higher levels requires you to have studied another course at UNSW. However, you can successfully (as I did for one course) argue that a course from your home university makes you eligible. The academic level in general is quite low/easy though. The reading is way lighter than at KU and the exams are also significantly easier. It is also very apparent that the students are much younger, as it is not unusual to start university at 17.
teaching_comparison: The professors are very personal and extremely open for student contact. It is much less academic, in the sense that it is much less formal. You as a student are often asked for your opinion rather than sticking to theory. This does take some getting used to. All my courses consisted of both lectures for the entire class, maybe 100 students, and tutorials (seminars) in smaller groups with a lot of group work.

recommended_courses: I would recommend all of them! All of them were extremely engaging and taught me a lot of new things. My favourite was Media, Race, Politics though, as the professors were amazing and the course work was truly eye opening.
unexpected_costs: The student visa is extremely expensive, maybe 7000 kr. Furthermore, the cost of living meaning buying everday food and supplies is also very expensive. However, the university offers an assortment of free groceries once a week which was a life saver.
cost_comparison: Generally groceries was super expensive, but asian food and asian groceries were very cheap. It was a very big hack to go to asian markets, which can be found everywhere, and buy in bulk. Coffee is cheap also.
activities_available: The university has a million clubs and societies you can join which is all presented in the orientation week. You can do anything from surf-club to chess-society, to activism. There is ALWAYS something happening at campus. Furthermore, there is a regular gym, a climbing gym and a swimming pool on campus.
activities_recommended: If you attend the Paddington Campus (or not) you can take small introductions to some of their amazing art facilities and then you are free to use them in your spare time. There are photo labs, camera equipment, ceramics studio, 3D-printers and much more.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely go to the Blue Mountains for hikes. Visit all the beautiful beaches. Go on a surf camp. Go to Feathersdale Zoo where you can pet wallabies and kangaroos. Go to Newtown and Marrickville.
culture_adjustment: The Australians are very friendly and very generous. It is generally a very easy society to fit into, as the people are very laid back - sometimes even too much.
socializing_tips: It is a bit of a challenge, because almost half of all my classes were exchange students. Another difficulty is that, as stated previously, the students are much younger than the average Danish student going on exchange. I did not find many friends in my classes, but on campus in general you can find likeminded people. Take it easy - you will find your people.
cultural_challenges: The age difference was probably the biggest if we are talking university. Other than that it is a very easy going culture. Sydney is super multi cultural so there are a lot of different places to go and every suburb is completely different. Take some time to try out different neighbourhoods to see where you feel like spending your time.
culture_appreciated: The diversity of the cultures you can experience. You can see the high class business people in the CBD, visit the Chinese food marked in Chinatown, be a beach babe on Bondi or go to underground techno raves in Marrickville. Sydney definitely has something for everyone.
top3_advice: - the university has so many opportunties outside of classes - try them out! UNSW has so many recourses compared to KU - put what you have learned from KU a bit on standby, as they do things a bit differently. However, they are very helpful. Use your professors and don't be afraid to write them an email if you have questions - choose some fun and exciting new courses - the university has so many to offer
other_useful_info: The university is beautiful and has a lot of outside areas for studying and lounging.
most_rewarding: I think the most rewarding part was to start somewhere where you don't know anyone or anywhere and then in the end feeling a very strong connection to the place and the people.
greatest_challenge: It was a big challenge to find real friends and not just acquaintances. However, it was worthwhile.
