crucial_aspects: A friend of mine is studying at the same university and he highly recommended it and it was always a dream for me to go to Australia to explore the culture and nature and I wanted to go to an English speaking country.
overall_comments: I really enjoyed my exchange semester, it was cool to explore a new university and a new academic culture, and meeting international students which allowed me to learn a lot. It was fun to explore new courses, which gave me the opportunity to widen my academic horizon. And this country is truly amazing, the culture, the weather, the nature, the food. And it was also nice to escape the danish winter and change it to summer.
info_ease: I feel like I always was able to get the information I needed, wither by asking my host university, or reading the fact sheets from my host university. I also had a student guidance counselling at KU to get all the information I needed. For the visa and flights I did my own research.
arrival_assistance: I was always able to email my host university ( the response was super fast like within a day) or at KU ( which took a little longer, about a week).
arrival_comments: It was very well organised, I could tell that they put a lot of effort into it. I got all the information I needed. It was nice to meet the other international students, they did games, a campus tour and a lot of uni clubs introduced themselves ( like over 80 ) so it was nice to meet like-minded people.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I really enjoyed my exchange semester, it was cool to explore a new university and a new academic culture, and meeting international students which allowed me to learn a lot. It was fun to explore new courses, which gave me the opportunity to widen my academic horizon. And this country is truly amazing, the culture, the weather, the nature, the food. And it was also nice to escape the danish winter and change it to summer.
registration_process: When I remember correctly ( it has been a while ) I first applied at KU to be chosen for exchange and my two priorities were UNSW and USYD, in early December I got the notification that I was granted a spot from KU, I think in April I got an email from UNSW that I was chosen, and that I can login to Endeavour, their exchange program, which had a step by step guide and status with deadlines. I had to apply for pre-approval for possible courses at the faculties and I then send it for pre-approval for KU. I got my official Certificate of Enrolment in early June, with allowed me to apply for my student visa, my visa got approved a week later and then I booked my flights. All in all I am very happy with the process, there were some up and downs, especially when I had to chose the courses, because some were canceled, but if you are the fact sheet its pretty easy.
registration_help: With any question I just emailed UNSW and someone from the Europe exchange team helped me pretty fast.
registration_success: One course in the winter term was cancelled which was about the Sydney Opera house, which was sad because I know its danish design. For the winter term there were only 3 or 4 courses available for master level, and one was Australian las which is not really my area, but I ended up in Future Leader lab, which was hoarsely such a fun and informative course, one of the best courses I had! I was able to get into all the other courses I wanted, the only thing was time-management, because the courses were located at different campuses, so I had to choose based on the times. I can recommend looking easy because the seminar time are booked very fast and then you are only left with time slots in the evening.
registration_advice: Like it is very straightforward forward. I think I got the CoE quite late, so I could only apple for my visa vera late and the flights were pretty expansive. For the courses, the ones in the winter/ summer term are pretty limited, but its actual just exchange students or students who need extra ETCS take those courses, some students at UNSW did not even knew about the winter term. I would recommend being flexible with the courses, maybe choose 4 or 5 because of possible overlays with other courses, but I was bale to get in all the courses I wanted.
academics_comments: I really enjoyed my exchange semester, it was cool to explore a new university and a new academic culture, and meeting international students which allowed me to learn a lot. It was fun to explore new courses, which gave me the opportunity to widen my academic horizon. And this country is truly amazing, the culture, the weather, the nature, the food. And it was also nice to escape the danish winter and change it to summer.
course_level: I think the level was okay, 3 courses were a good load for the semester. The assignments are quite a lot, so you are never bored thats for sure. My grades were pretty good and I defiantly learnt something new, especially during the course Future Leader Lab and Graphic Design and Society.
teaching_comparison: I would say it was quite similar. The teaching language was English, it was a mix of lectures and seminars and group work as well as individuals projects. I like that the courses Future Leader Lab and Graphic Design and Society were quite practical with excursions and photo projects compared to the rather research based and theoretical courses I had at KU.
courses_enrolled: Winter term: Future Leader Lab T3: Graphic Design & Society, Social Media Campaigning, Digital Cultures
recommended_courses: I highly recommend the Future leader Lab Course. I was so much fun, the instructors put a lot of effort into it and there were a lot of excursions to firms like KPMG were we talked to sustainability officers and also to entrepreneurs focussing on sustainable leadership which was super inspiring. It was also nice because the course mainly consisted of international exchange students who all were new to Sydney so it was also nice to meet new people.
unexpected_costs: Public transport is quite expansive, since you cannot book a monthly plan. Alcohol and going out was also quite expansive.
cost_comparison: I would say in general life is less expansive than in Copenhagen. It is still a big international city so rent is quite high. I would say going out was more expansive than I thought. Travelling was expensive but worth it. The domestic flights in AUS are pretty cheap which was nice.I like to read and thereare multiple libraries so books were free.
activities_available: There were some events for it and also clubs.
activities_recommended: I would recommend joining a club if it is convenient for you , its a good way to meet like-minded people.
weekend_recommendations: I did a lot of research on instagram, like must see things in Sydney. I also asked some locals about their favourite places. I would say of course the basics like the harbour bridge, the opera, Bondi beach. I further really liked the Bondi to Coogee walk, Watsons bay ( and hotel), all the parks, the botanical garden, Taronga Zoo, Darling Harbour Fireworks, try all the food its amazing, hidden and rooftop bars, try surfing, seeing the sunset, go running at the coast. In the surrounding area the blue mountainy, Manly, Palm beach, Cronulla and the Hunter Valley.
culture_adjustment: I would say fairly easy, it took me a while to realise that I am not on vacation because I never lives in such a warm climate with a beach. It is harder than I thought to befriend Australians because they like to stay in their own bubble. Once I found a job I was also nice to have colleagues and ask them for places to see and it also gave me more of a routine and it was also nice to earn money and save for travelling
socializing_tips: Join clubs and go to the events ARC ( the student association) offers. I am not the biggest party/ club going person but they had some events. Join running clubs or other sports. I also see my colleagues as friends as we are internationals so finding a job is also a good idea.
cultural_challenges: The biggest difference was that they are driving on the other side of the road, I was kind of dangerous as a pedestrian. Also everything kind of closes early, the coffee shops, and clothing stores, and bars. The Australians defiantly like waking up early, at 6 everyone was out for a run, also depends on the suburb. Also, all the people are so nice.
culture_appreciated: I really like the active culture, and the wake-up early culture and everyone is so chilled here.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared that there are a lot of international students and cultural differences. 2. There a lot of assignments. 3. Join some clubs to meet new people.
other_useful_info: The courses are not easy, you have to work quite a bit. I was surprised that there were hardly any Australians in my class and 90 % were from China and there was quite a big language barrier.
most_rewarding: Australia is an amazing country and seeing the sun everyday defiantly contributed to my well-being. It was nice being on campus and meet your friends at the beach. It was also nice to get a job and experience the work culture. Life is pretty chilled down here, it seems like everyone is active and doing good. And traveling around was also amazing.
greatest_challenge: I would say meeting new people. I am an introvert and quite sensitive to lot music so going in clubs is not my favourite. The first two weeks where you meet like 100 people and everyone is going out was a lot for me. But I also met amazing people in my courses, at running clubs, through Instagram, at work and through friends.
other_comments: Just do it! I am so thankful that I got the opportunity to come here for exchange. It is so cool to actual live here as a student, go to work and find a routine to really settle in and find your people. Sydney is an amazing city there is so much to do, to see and to explore. Travelling is insane, it looks like a dream. And it is a great way to broaden your academic horizon with some new courses you are interested in. And make sure you go on the winter semester so that you have summer here.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to get far away from Denmark, get acquainted with a different legal system than the Danish one, wanted to go somewhere warm, wanted to go somewhere with many Danes and wanted to live in a big city.
info_ease: I found it easy to find the information I needed - both the information I needed from KU and the information I needed from my host university.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any assistance, but I had received regular emails from my host university with information on how and when to register for courses, what events were organised on campus for exchange students, etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I had to write a lot of information for them, upload many documents etc., but the process was relatively easy as I was guided through everything and they clearly and easily stated what information they needed from me.
registration_help: During the process, I got help from both UCPH and UNSW. I received help via email, where both parties were quick to respond to my questions.
registration_success: I had to wish for about ten courses for the host university. Unfortunately, I couldn't rank which ones I wanted the most. I didn't get the ones I wanted most - but I did get the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Set aside a lot of time for it and familiarise yourself with the process.
course_level: The level was appropriate and comparable to UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Attendance at classes was compulsory, there were regular mandatory assignments, mandatory presentations and more focus on student involvement.
courses_enrolled: Worlds Religion Conflict of Laws Criminal Law Criminology: An Introduction
recommended_courses: I would recommend them all. All the courses had exams at home, which I thought was nice as several UNSW courses have physical exams that have to be written by hand. Worlds Religion, Criminal Law and Criminology: An Introduction were all easy courses at a relatively manageable academic level. The reading load was not very high and the courses were all introductory courses. Conflict of Laws was really exciting (the most exciting course of them all), but also really difficult. There was an insane amount of syllabus and you had to know a lot of rules, including a lot of common law concepts, which can be difficult when you are not used to the legal system from home.
unexpected_costs: I don't think there were any unexpected expenses.
cost_comparison: Prices were much the same as in Denmark. However, it was cheaper to go out to eat and buy a cup of coffee, while it was a bit more expensive to buy groceries.
activities_available: UNSW is a really big university, so all the societies, clubs, activities etc. that you can imagine were possible. There were all kinds of sports clubs and there were film clubs, creative clubs, party clubs, religious clubs, loneliness clubs, exchange student clubs etc.
activities_recommended: I wasn't a member of any clubs, as I met a lot of other people through my courses, knew people from home in Denmark etc., so I didn't need it.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend going to a surf camp, travelling around a lot of Australian cities, experiencing nature, going to the Blue Mountains, going to Slip'n (a bar where all Danes in Sydney meet on the first Thursday of the month), experiencing all of Sydney's many tourist attractions, going for a run and enjoying the beaches.
culture_adjustment: Very easy - the culture is similar to Denmark in many ways. However, Australians are much more welcoming than Danes, so that's just positive.
socializing_tips: Talk to other students when you have classes, join associations and attend events at university.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any challenging.
culture_appreciated: That the locals were so nice, helpful and welcoming.
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy it - time goes by quickly 2. Don't spend too much time studying for the courses - have fun. 3. Be approachable, talk to people at university, come to classes and be social
other_useful_info: No, there isn't.
most_rewarding: Get to know a different school system, be challenged personally and academically, develop my professional English, meet a lot of people, get the opportunity to get to know another culture, be on my own (away from busy Denmark) and get the opportunity to live in another country for free (I applied for and received a lot of grants that could pay for all my expenses while I was away).
greatest_challenge: Being so far away from friends and family. Even though there is FaceTime and you can easily text with them, it can be a challenge to find time to do so due to the time difference.

crucial_aspects: I had friends in Sydney, and a martial arts club I knew that I was going to join before applying, but UNSW's academic and career opportunities definitely cemented my choice.
overall_comments: UNSW is extremely welcoming towards international and exchange students, and organizes a ton of onboarding experiences to ensure students are well integrated into campus life. I quickly made new friends, got comfortable exploring campus, and joined a student club. The courses are well structured, ensuring an organized learning environment, and I got to apply theory in practice, equipping me for a future career setting.
info_ease: Fairly easy. The UNSW Abroad & Exchange Team is quick to reply, given that you have been polite and very specific in your enquiries. Additional important information will be provided via email and the UNSW website, including tutorials and valuable information.
arrival_assistance: Airport pickup, email reminders regarding student ID, UNSW student introduction, campus tour, faculty welcome, and O-week.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: UNSW is extremely welcoming towards international and exchange students, and organizes a ton of onboarding experiences to ensure students are well integrated into campus life. I quickly made new friends, got comfortable exploring campus, and joined a student club. The courses are well structured, ensuring an organized learning environment, and I got to apply theory in practice, equipping me for a future career setting.
registration_process: During your exchange application, you will apply for courses through Endeavor. You can read about the specific courses and their requirements via the UNSW Handbook, which will be emailed to you by the UNSW Abroad & Exchange Team. Once your courses have been approved, you can watch a YouTube tutorial on how to register for the courses through myUNSW.
registration_help: Emails detailing the necessary steps, including links to tutorials, and online assistance with the UNSW Abroad & Exchange Team.
registration_success: I registered for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Browse through the courses and make a backup list, as you will have to apply for extra courses in case the class is fully registered. My favorite course was the one I took to improve my CV rather than for pleasure. I personally did not enjoy the online course I took purely because of it being online, so if you can do all your classes in person, I high recommend doing so.
academics_comments: UNSW is extremely welcoming towards international and exchange students, and organizes a ton of onboarding experiences to ensure students are well integrated into campus life. I quickly made new friends, got comfortable exploring campus, and joined a student club. The courses are well structured, ensuring an organized learning environment, and I got to apply theory in practice, equipping me for a future career setting.
course_level: As an MA student, you cannot enroll in BA-level courses. The level of courses is high and includes a lot of reading, weekly tests, group work, tutorials, monthly assignments, and exams throughout the trimester.
teaching_comparison: The lectures are structured in a similar format. The tutorials are a mixture of seminars and group work.
courses_enrolled: BEES6601-Sydney Environment (T2 25), LING5003-Language Technology (T3 25), MODL5106-Text Analysis for Translation (T3 25), and LING5015-Discourse Analysis (T3 25).
recommended_courses: BEES6601-Sydney Environment (T2 25), if you are interested in Sydney wildlife and want to go on hikes, or have general concerns about spiders, snakes, and sharks. LING5003-Language Technology (T3 25), if you are interested in the current and emerging technologies that will influence the future, e.g., AI, Python, corpus linguistics, translation tools, etc., and how to work with them. MODL5106-Text Analysis for Translation (T3 25), if you plan on working with interpreting or in translations. The course gives you a good foundation of how the industry works, what to think about when translating in practice, and how to apply theory in practice. LING5015-Discourse Analysis (T3 25), if you are interested in linguistics and discourse, and want to develop your transcription abilities.
unexpected_costs: Visa
cost_comparison: Public transportation is not too bad.
activities_available: Go to https://www.arc.unsw.edu.au/ to read all about the social activities available for students.
activities_recommended: A sportsclub! It provides a community and makes sure you get in some weekly exercise. I personally recommend Taido.
weekend_recommendations: Do a weekend trip to the Blue Mountains, Byron Bay, Jarvis Bay, and Melbourne. For holidays, go to Perth, Tasmania, or Uluru.
culture_adjustment: Australians are very cheerful and will welcome you with open arms. If you look lost, they will offer you help without having to ask. Within a couple of weeks, you've pretty much gotten the hang of things around here in terms of local grocery stores, coffee shops, bars, etc.
socializing_tips: Join a club or society, and talk to your classmates during class breaks. Join the events on campus, and go on the guided tours.
cultural_challenges: Not a lot to be fair.
culture_appreciated: How multicultural Sydney and Australia are.
top3_advice: Don't underestimate the winter and rainy weather. It takes a little while to find your social group, and that is ok, you will find your people here. Get out of your comfort zone, explore the city, and meet new people.
other_useful_info: https://www.unsw.edu.au/student
most_rewarding: Improving my overall English proficiency while honing my academic skills.
greatest_challenge: The time crunch of a trimester. Your schedule will be pretty packed with studying as an MA student, but it will be extremely rewarding in terms of acquired skills and knowledge.

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne længere væk fra Danmark, for at udnytte at jeg havde et halvt år til at udforske landet, og så var det et plus at det er engelsk-talende.
info_ease: Nogenlunde, UNSW har en mail som sender bolig-mails ud, men de begyndte først for alvor 2 uger før afrejse, og der ville jeg helst geren være sikret en bolig. De har en masse klubber som man først får info om i starten af et "rigtigt term". Winther term er altså uden social clubs og events.
arrival_assistance: Der var en informations dag ugen før term begyndte. Derudover er de gode til at sende mails om info. Jeg ville også råde til at kontakte andre fra DK eller KU, der skal til samme universitet. Det hjalp en del.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Det ligner meget ansøgelses processen til udvekslingsophold. Det er en ekstern server, så det tager lidt tid at komme ind på den, men så virker den fint. Man skal bare være obs. på deadlines.
registration_help: Jeg tror man kan både ringe og skrive til universitet, men selve registreringen var meget lige ud og beskrevet godt.
registration_success: Jeg fik alle mine fag. Der var dog en jeg blev frameldt igen, fordi jeg glemte at betale for et class-trip. Jeg blev dog hjulpet til at vælge et andet fag og det var ret nemt at skifte.
registration_advice: Husk at tjekke jeres Uni-mails. Vær forberedt på at fag kan clash, hvilket man først finder ud af tæt på term start, men der kan man også få hjælp af studievejledere.
course_level: Jeg ville sige, at det faglige niveau generelt er lavere end på KU.
teaching_comparison: De har ingen bøger man skal købe, så pensum er kun i forelæsningerne, turtorials, lab eller materiale de sender ud. Det er meget varierende undervisning, men nemt at forstå både undevisere og slides. Og så blev næsten alle mine forelæsninger optaget så man kan gense dem. Eksamen tæller kun for en del af din endelige karakter. Du får point for opgaver og tests gennem semesteret. Jeg bestod alle mine fag før eksamen.
courses_enrolled: Jeg tog: MSCI0501 The Marine Environment, 7.5 ECTS (Winther term) BINF2010 Introduction to Bioinformatics, 7.5 ECTS (Term 3) MATH1031 Mathematics for Life Sciences, 7.5 ECTS (Term 3) MUSC2706 MUSIC ENSEMBLE, 7.5 ECTS (Term 3)
recommended_courses: Heeelt klart musik faget. Faldt over det ved et tilfælde, da jeg havde tilmeldt mig kor for sjov i min fritid og fandt derefter ud af, at jeg kunne få credit for det, hvis jeg også tilmeldte mig et Handbell ensemble, hvilket også var mega sjovt og en kæmpe oplevelse. Intet af det kræver særlig musikkunnen, men man skal gerne kunne læse noder.
unexpected_costs: Kun at bolig var så dyrt også koster australsk student visa næsten 7k.
cost_comparison: UNSW har foodhub, hvor man kan få gratis madvarer, hvilket gjorde at jeg kunne spare en del på madbudget. Der er også mange events med gratis frokost osv. Generelt var mad billigere end i DK.

crucial_aspects: I chose Australia because it had long been a place I genuinely wanted to experience. I was excited to explore the unique nature and landscapes and to live in and discover major cities such as Sydney and Melbourne. Academically, Australia was also an excellent fit, as UNSW Sydney is a globally recognised university, particularly strong in law, which made it a highly attractive destination for my exchange.
overall_comments: I could not have wished for a better destination than Australia. Especially Sydney.
info_ease: There was a joint orientation upon arrival, and I personally didn’t have many questions. However, it seemed easy for students to access the support they needed, and others appeared to get help quickly – for example with course changes and administrative questions.
arrival_assistance: There was a joint orientation as mentioned.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I could not have wished for a better destination than Australia. Especially Sydney.
registration_process: You are given a list of available courses and then have to submit requests for the courses you want. However, even if a course appears on the list, you can still be rejected from it after applying.
registration_help: Support was primarily available via email – you could contact the relevant office directly with questions and receive guidance that way.
registration_success: In the end, I was able to register for the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Be patient. The process can feel chaotic, but it usually works out in the end. Also, keep in mind that you can change courses at the beginning of the semester if you realise a class is not the right fit, but you need to do it early within the add/drop period.
academics_comments: I could not have wished for a better destination than Australia. Especially Sydney.
course_level: I took one undergraduate (BA-level) course and the rest were postgraduate (Master’s-level) courses. As an exchange student, we were only allowed to enrol in one undergraduate course, so the majority of my classes were at Master’s level.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was quite different from UCPH. Attendance was expected, and class participation counted towards the final grade. In that sense, it was a bit more “high school-like” compared with the more independent format I am used to at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM IN COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS AND SPORT LEGAL PROJECT MANAGEMENT: BUSINESS STRATEGY, PRACTICE SYSTEMS, INNOVATION AND CHANGE INTRO TO CHINESE REGULATION OF INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of the courses I took. They were relevant, well taught, and overall a very good experience. The Chinese-related course, however, was noticeably more demanding in terms of workload and difficulty, so I would recommend it especially for students who are prepared for a heavier course load and a steeper learning curve.
unexpected_costs: One unexpected cost was the extra surcharges added when dining out - many restaurants charge a weekend surcharge and/or a public holiday surcharge. In my experience, these were typically around 5–20%, which can add up over time.
cost_comparison: Having a beer or eating out in very touristy areas (e.g., around the Opera House or at Bondi Beach) was cheaper than I expected. Prices were generally similar to other parts of the city, rather than being significantly higher just because it was a tourist hotspot.
activities_available: There was a very wide range of cultural, athletic, and social activities available - honestly something for every interest and preference.
activities_recommended: As mentioned earlier, I didn’t personally make use of the non-academic activities, so I can’t recommend specific ones based on my own experience.
weekend_recommendations: I travelled a lot within Australia during weekends and holidays, which I can highly recommend—it’s a great opportunity to see more of the country. At the same time, I would also suggest making sure to explore the city you live in. I was away so often that I didn’t get to see as much of Sydney as I would have liked.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy to adjust to the local culture, as it is quite similar to Europe and feels generally Western in everyday life and social norms.
socializing_tips: I mainly spent time with other Danish exchange students, so I did not socialise extensively with local students. In several of my classes there were many Chinese students who did not speak English, so while they were very kind, communication was limited. If I were to give a tip, it would be to actively seek out settings where locals are more likely to engag rather than relying on the classroom environment alone.
cultural_challenges: I did not experience any particular cultural differences that I found challenging.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated how laid-back Australians are and how relaxed the everyday pace feels. It was a noticeable contrast to a busy routine at home where things often move quickly, and it was genuinely refreshing—it helped me slow down and really unwind.
top3_advice: Make the most of it while you’re there—travel, explore, and say yes to experiences. Try to stay calm even if practical things (course registration, housing, admin) feel frustrating at times; it usually works out in the end. Enjoy it and be present—the time goes by incredibly fast.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was all the experiences I had and the friendships I made. Going on exchange has been the best decision I made during my studies.
greatest_challenge: Apart from the course registration process, I didn’t experience any major challenges during the exchange. Overall, the transition was smooth and I felt well settled.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: English-taught classes, and distance from home - Australia is very far away, so it felt like a good place to spend 6 months as it offered a basis from which to travel around that part of the world.
overall_comments: Please see questions 15 and 44
info_ease: The information sent by UNSW ahead of my arrival was very comprehensive so I felt very prepared.
arrival_assistance: They hosted a welcome event for all of the exchange students which went over the basics. There is also an exchange society which we were told could help us if we needed - I did not use it but it is apparently quite helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Please see questions 15 and 44
registration_process: 1. You apply for approval to join the courses that you want. This is additional to the KU pre-approval. You can apply for approval of 3x as many classes as you can take (e.g. I could take 3 courses in Term 3, so I could apply for approval for 9). Some of my applications were rejected as I did not meet the required criteria (e.g. some courses were reserved for people doing specific degrees). 2. Once you have been approved, you log into the portal (called Moodle) and can enrol in courses. If the course is full, you can join the waitlist. Once you have enrolled, you can change your mind up until 2 weeks into term. 3. A few weeks after the course enrolment, you can register for lectures and classes (either online or in-person) depending on what times work for you.
registration_help: UNSW has the Nucleus in the library, which is open from 10am-5pm every weekday. They could help you with pretty much anything relating to university, including registration for classes.
registration_success: I got into every class I wanted. However, some of my friends were not as lucky, especially those taking papers with the law school as the classes were smaller. I was very proactive in checking when course/class registration opens (at least twice a day).
registration_advice: You will not get a notification when registering for classes opens, so check the portal regularly, as classes fill up quickly.
academics_comments: Please see questions 15 and 44
course_level: I did four courses, all at MA level (see below). However, one class (LAWS8168) was combined with the BA version of that class (LAWS3368), so we learnt the same content. But the MA students had to write a longer essay.
teaching_comparison: My programme at UCPH did not involve any lectures - instead we had 2 classes a week. However at UNSW, each class would have one lecture and one class. The classwork would be based on the lecture, so attending the lecture was vital.
courses_enrolled: 1. The Australian Legal System in Comparative Perspective (LAWS3368) 2. The International Political Economy (POLS5122) 3. The Politics of International Law (POLS5125) 4. Development, Human Rights, and Global Health (COMD5002)
recommended_courses: The International Political Economy (POLS5122) was excellent. Very current, up-to-date, and interesting readings. It examined the development of the existing global order and US hegemony after WWII, and how this impacts today’s politics, including Trump’s second term, the rise of China, tech billionaires, and global warming.
unexpected_costs: While you have to pay 7,000 DKK for health insurance, the insurers will only usually pay out 50% of the total cost. E.g. I had a routine medical exam for 900DKK, and only received 450DKK from the insurers. I expected 100% of the fee to be paid, but apparently 50% is the usual policy.
cost_comparison: Fresh produce (e.g. fruit/vegetables) and meat is much cheaper than Denmark, so food shopping was cheaper. Healthcare is more expensive (see above).
activities_available: UNSW has very good sports clubs which train on campus. They have different levels, so you can play at a high level or more casually. UNSW hosted some aboriginal cultural events (such as Welcome to Country) which were very interesting and very . There were societies (e.g. exchange societies) which hosted events such as hikes, drinks, socials. There are over 300 societies at UNSW covering pretty much everything.
activities_recommended: I found that all of the societies/activities were geared towards undergraduates, so I did not participate much. But, I did do Arc Sport, which is a casual practice/friendly games on Wednesdays in various sports.
weekend_recommendations: The Great Barrier Reef, Kakadu National Park, Uluru National Park, New Zealand
culture_adjustment: I found it very easy as I am from the UK, which is a very similar culture to Australia.
socializing_tips: I did not socialise with local students often, as no one in my class was Australian (see question 15 above and 44 below). For general socialisation, join Facebook groups and go to events hosted by them, even if you do not know anyone. Australians are very friendly so it is easy to join these sort of events.
cultural_challenges: Early morning culture (starting the day at 5am) took some getting used to.
culture_appreciated: Relaxed culture, friendly people, easy access to the beach, very stress-free culture.
top3_advice: 1. Please see question 44 below about the biggest challenge. 2. The workload is a lot higher than UCPH 3. The marking is much harder than UCPH
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and seeing new parts of the world.
greatest_challenge: The vast majority of postgraduate students enrolled at UNSW are from China. My class had 375 students enrolled, and 374 of them were from China. This is obviously not an issue in itself, but barely any of them spoke passable English and so did not participate in class; if they were asked a direct question by the teacher, they would rely on Google Translate or ChatGPT to answer. While in some ways this benefitted my learning, as I essentially had a one-to-one tutorial (as no one else was participating), it was particularly limiting in terms of social life as I was unable to speak to my classmates without resorting to Google Translate. It also limited employment opportunities, as I was told you cannot get a job on campus without knowledge of Mandarin. Further, I think a very valuable part of a Masters’ Programme is learning from your peers, as well as the teacher, so being unable to communicate with my peers limited my experience both academically and socially.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study in an English-speaking country. Australia not only offers well-respected universities but is also a travel destination that can be difficult to visit independently, given the significant distance and costs involved in traveling from Europe.
overall_comments: I had a fantastic time overall
info_ease: it was easy.
arrival_assistance: I did not need any assistance upon arrival, as everything was completed prior to arrival.
arrival_comments: I did not need any assitance upon arrival, so I cant answer this. However, it was my perception that the orientation and assistance available at UNSW was good.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had a fantastic time overall
registration_process: Apart from course registration, the registration process was easy.
registration_help: E-mail correspondance from people at UNSW, who were not very helpful.
registration_success: In the end, we got a 'final list' of courses available to exchange students. From this list, I got everything that i registered for, but there were not too many courses to choose from.
registration_advice: Do not spent too much time on it. Await communication from UNSW on e-mail follow the steps there. It will also be possible to swap courses in the beginning of the semester, so no need to worry too much about courses. Wait for the final list of courses that exchange students can register for. Dont waste your precious time, like I and others did!
academics_comments: I had a fantastic time overall
course_level: Pretty easy to be honest.
teaching_comparison: There is more group work and a higher level of interaction between teachers and students at UNSW compared to UCPH. Additionally, grades are not determined by a single final exam; instead, they are weighted across various assignments that must be completed throughout the semester.
courses_enrolled: The Australian Legal System in a Comparative Perspective, International Relations and Sport, Legal Project Management, Introduction to Chinese Regulation of International Business.
recommended_courses: Overall, the courses were quite interesting. I particularly enjoyed my first three subjects and would highly recommend Legal Project Management. While most of the courses were relatively easy to pass, the Chinese Regulation course was not the best course, additionally, it required a 6,000-word individual assignment worth 60% of the final grade, which felt disproportionate for a 6 UoC/7,5 ECTS course.
unexpected_costs: Visa 7000 DKK, plane tickets for 11.000 DKK, Australian health insurance (mandatory) - 1.500 DKK. I don't recall the amount I spent per month on food, personal expenses and other fees, so the figures provided above are a bit inaccurate. I also spent heavily on travel, social experiences, eating out etc., so my numbers shouldn't be taken as a standard baseline. I finished the semester at the end of November, but keep in mind that I stayed for an additional two months having fun in Sydney and travelling a lot. In total, expect to pay around 90.000 +/- DKK in total for 5 months in Sydney with costs being higher depending on the ammount of travel, social experiences, duration of your stay etc.
cost_comparison: Food was cheaper than Denmark, housing was more expensive.
activities_available: All types of sports activities, parties etc.
activities_recommended: Surfing or other sports you are interested in picking up.
weekend_recommendations: Going to the beaches and enjoying happy hours at different pubs and bars. Travel to other places in Australia, such as the East and West Coast. Also, I highly recommend going on a surf camp, it was a great experience! Watch out for events in Sydney, there is a lot happening all the time, especially in Spring and Summer time.
culture_adjustment: Easy, Australians are very nice and fun people.
socializing_tips: Just be friendly.
cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: Australians are very calm and down to earth.
top3_advice: Just enjoy your time! It will be an unforgetable experience.
other_useful_info: Dont worry, things will work out, especially everything regarding course registration.
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of great people and travelling around in Australia.
greatest_challenge: Being far away from friends and family.
other_comments: Make the most of your exchange semester. Say yes to new experiences, stay open-minded, and embrace the chance to meet people from all over the world. Your exchange is what you make of it!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an English-speaking country, outside Europe, and to a place where it is warm
info_ease: It was very easy to find the informations
arrival_assistance: The university offered free airport transportation when I arrived. We also had an introduction day with a barbecue and social events, where there was an opportunity to get to know other exchange students
arrival_comments: The introduction day could have been better organized, but it was nice to meet other exchange students that day
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: First, you had to apply for approval to take certain courses. Later, you had to enroll in the courses through another portal. There, you needed to adjust your schedule and secure your spot before all places were taken.
registration_help: I didn’t use any assistance, so I’m not sure. However, from my experience, they respond to emails quite quickly
registration_success: I got a spot in all the courses I applied for. However, due to some scheduling conflicts, I couldn’t get all of my first-choice courses. I decided to switch a course at the last minute and still got a place, so in the end, I got everything I wanted.
registration_advice: It’s smart to apply for approval for all the courses you are considering, as it makes it easier later when you need to apply for a final spot in the course. You can only apply for a course once you have received approval to do so. It took some effort to figure out and get the schedule to work, especially if you want flexibility and fewer school days.
course_level: I took mostly beginner to intermediate courses, combining practical skills and foundational theory in humanities, design, and economics. The level was easier than UCPH. Much easier to get higher grades
teaching_comparison: I took a mix of design and economics courses. The economics courses were similar to UCPH, with lectures and tutorials. The design courses were more like high school classes, where you sit in a classroom, are taught something, and then work on it practically
courses_enrolled: HUMS1010, DDES1043, DDES1150, ECON1202
recommended_courses: I really liked all my courses. They were very different from each other, and I enjoyed trying something other than the typical economics and computer science courses. I liked DDES1043, as it taught me skills in publication design that I will always be able to use. But I also liked ECON1202, where we went a bit more in-depth into basic mathematics within economics
unexpected_costs: The student-visa was expensive. They also require you to have health insurance in Australia, which also costs around 1,700 DKK. The university helps you with this
cost_comparison: Travel around was expensive. The prices are around the same as in Denmark. Groceries were on the expensive side. Tak-away a little less expensive as expected
activities_available: Everything you could possibly dream of. There were so many clubs, covering everything from sports to matcha
activities_recommended: Join a club. I never did, but I wish I had. It helps you build a bigger network
weekend_recommendations: Travel around Australia. It’s a huge country with so much to offer, featuring very diverse cultures and landscapes. I loved every place I visited
culture_adjustment: It was very easy, and the culture is very Western and somewhat similar to Denmark
socializing_tips: It wasn’t easy to start conversations with the locals, as there are many international students. I found it easier in courses where I didn’t know anyone, as that encouraged me to talk with local students, both international and domestic
cultural_challenges: Not really any. The biggest difference is that Australians live a very active lifestyle in the mornings, with activities already in full swing from 6 am
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the work-life balance, as many Australians prioritize free time and social life, which is inspiring compared to more stressful environments
top3_advice: - Live in Coogee (close to the Beach) - Find a good balance between freedom and school, you’ll manage to get through your studies - Take courses that seem manageable and interesting to you
other_useful_info: The university is easy to get in touch with and provides good information from start to finish. You don’t need to worry too much about the university. Lecturers are friendly, and help is always available
most_rewarding: I think the most rewarding part was creating my own everyday life in a completely new country. It was fun to experience a different university and see how it operated
greatest_challenge: I found it an easy country to be in, and it was easy to communicate with people because they spoke English. I don’t think I faced any major challenges in that regard

crucial_aspects: It was quite important for me to be in an English speaking country, where I had an idea of a somewhat similar culture and open, inviting people. I felt it would make it easier to hang around locals and truly get to know the place. Additionally, I wanted to go somewhere I didn't know too much about already, where I could immerse myself in a different culture and heritage than that of Europe.
info_ease: UNSW made it very easy to find the required information, and if it wasn't readily available they were quick to answer questions or good at hosting meetings beforehand. Also, most information you need will be sent to you multiple times via e-mail, which is very convenient.
arrival_assistance: UNSW helps with free airport pickup if you let them know when and where you're going.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registration is a bit of a hassle. You have to enroll in double the amount of courses you are able to take, to make sure you can get the amount of courses you need. Then at registration you need to select courses that don't conflict in the schedule. It's just a way more complicated system, than that of KU.
registration_help: Dates and procedure was available and you could write the administration if you had questions, but they are generally not able to help you get on courses or have them approved.
registration_success: I luckily got the classes I wanted, but only after being on the waitlist for a long time, as courses fill up fast.
registration_advice: Follow the dates for enrollment and registration. Courses fill up fast.
course_level: Levels of the courses somewhat match the level at KU.
teaching_comparison: In terms of assessments, I was surprised at how many parts of the course counted towards my grade. Typically, 4 elements (Quizzes, Assignments, Labs, Reports, Exam, etc.) count towards the final grade. Other than that, it was somewhat similar with most time spent on lectures and tutorials. I was however surprised that tutorials require attendance.
courses_enrolled: BEES6601 An Introduction to the Sydney Environment, CEIC8102 Advanced Process Control, FOOD8110 Advanced Food Chemistry, CHEM2041 Analytical Chemistry
recommended_courses: Winter term courses are a great way to have a soft landing into a different university. They are typically angled towards local culture, nature, etc. It's good way to get to know the place you are in. I really liked how BEES6601 gave me a crash course in everything that makes Sydney what it is. The nature, culture, environment, people. It's a very reflective course that makes you compare Sydney to home.
unexpected_costs: I broke my wrist here, and while the Overseas Student Health Coverage did cover most of the hospital expenses, I had about 4000 DKK in out of pocket costs, since I was first at a private GP (Which was however recommended by the OSHC) and sent to a private clinic for scans, which were very expensive.
cost_comparison: I was surprised at how expensive the visa and visa requirements were. The visa set me back 7000 DKK, with 1900 DKK on mandatory health insurance, and 2200 DKK for an English proficiency test. Other than that, housing is incredibly expensive here, as well as groceries and going out. Eating out was however cheap compared to Copenhagen.
activities_available: Pretty much everything you can think about. ARC which is the Student Association have more clubs than I can count.
activities_recommended: I personally did not take part in many of the activities, but have heard great things of the outdoors club. They do camping, hiking, canyoning trips around Sydney which are very cheap. It's a great way to see the amazing nature while meeting both locals and other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: Rent a car. Go on trips up or down the coast. Fly to some of the other parts of Australia and do a road trip to experience nature. I went to Fiji for 9 days which was equally amazing. See all the national parks surrounding Sydney. Blue Mountains, Royal National Park and Kuring-Gai Chase National Park are all within an hour drive from Sydney.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The culture in Sydney is very international and somewhat european, so it's not so difficult to adjust. UNSW however is very asian. Lots of asian societies, restaurants, cafes.
socializing_tips: I had a very difficult time finding the local students, as most people in my courses were Chinese international students. Also, most local students still live at home, so they are not really in the areas where most international students live.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really. I was surprised at how many Chinese international students were at the uni, and I had a bit of a tough time interacting with people in class. However, I lived in a big house with many international students that were great to hang out with.
culture_appreciated: The laidback beach lifestyle.
top3_advice: 1. Cost of living is very high, even compared to Copenhagen. Make a realistic budget. 2. Register for classes in due time. They fill up fast. 3. Consider what the purpose of your exchange is before you go, to plan what level of effort you want to put into your courses, to plan where you want to live, or how you want to spend your time while you're here.
other_useful_info: Make sure to read up on course outlines before registering for classes. Think about how you want to spend time here. I ended up having way too complicated classes here, so I had to put a lot of time and effort into understanding core concepts of the courses.
most_rewarding: Meeting a bunch of great people from all over the world, and sharing the experience of exploring Sydney and Australia with them. It's truly an amazing place, and there are so many people eager to make friends and have a great time here.
greatest_challenge: I personally had an idea that I wanted to have some challenging courses to learn a bunch, but in reality I was nowhere strictly for academic purposes. So a lot of my time went into studying rather than enjoying this amazing place with all the people I had met. A lot of my friends here had way easier courses to maximise the time for trips and enjoyment. My courses were very hard, and I had a tough time navigating the different assessment system to plan how much time and effort to put into each part of the assessment.

weekend_recommendations: Fokuser på Australien. Der er så mange fede steder. Så man behøver ikke rejse til andre lande.

crucial_aspects: I've always wanted to travel to Australia, so I thought it was a great opportunity to be able to study whilst traveling the country. Also a big part of my decision was that the weather is nice and sunny.
overall_comments: It's the best decision. School load is typically less than at home (at least for me and the other exchange students I've talked to). And it is such a great opportunity to be able to experience another culture whilst going to school.
info_ease: Pretty confusing to be honest. But luckily there is other people who have done it before, and it always works out. It can be a bit frustrating in the beginning though. Mostly the info on school and classes were hard to find.
arrival_assistance: Not anything in particular that I remember. UNSW had a intro meeting and barbecue for exchange students but that was about it. They don't do much to be honest.
arrival_comments: They could have made more events so that the exchange students could get to know each other. But it is also a bit hard because I think there's more than 300 exchange students at UNSW - so it is a big group.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: It's the best decision. School load is typically less than at home (at least for me and the other exchange students I've talked to). And it is such a great opportunity to be able to experience another culture whilst going to school.
registration_process: So when you get the welcome letter, you have to look into courses. They have three different platforms regarding courses, which makes it very confusing. You have to apply to be approved by UNSW to enroll into courses. It is hard to figure out what courses are available and being offered in my term. When you get approved it doesn't mean that you have been enrolled, it just means that you have met the prerequisites. This is quite annoying because I also had to get approval from Copenhagen University and I didn't know if I'd end up being able to take the course. To make things even more confusing, because I am a law student, I didn't get to pick from my approved courses. UNSW sentt out a list to law exchange students of the courses that were available for us to take - so none of the ones I had looked into beforehand ended up being the courses I got. From the list that were sent to me I had to prioritse between courses, and then they'd enroll us accordingly.
registration_help: They have an E-mail, and I think they are alright at replying. Sometimes it can be a couple of days. They don't have a phone number.
registration_success: not at all. But I ended up being happy with 3/4 of my courses, so it worked out okay.
registration_advice: Know that it is frustrating, confusing and that there's so many unnecessary steps - but everything will work out. I know of many that wasn't enrolled in enough courses when they got here. It is easy to make an appointment with school counseling when you're here. Also the first week of the semester is always drop in/drop out week.
academics_comments: It's the best decision. School load is typically less than at home (at least for me and the other exchange students I've talked to). And it is such a great opportunity to be able to experience another culture whilst going to school.
course_level: I took easier classes on purpose and made sure to take courses that didn't have any sit-in exams, so that I had more time to travel. So the classes weren't too challenging. Generally, I think the level is pretty low.
teaching_comparison: It depends on the course. Some courses are very much class room teaching, and then other courses are more lectures.
courses_enrolled: Winter Term (WT): Australian Legal System In A Comparative Perspective. Third Term (T3): 1) International Relations and Sport, 2) Legal Project Management, 3) Introduction to Chinese Regulation of International Business.
recommended_courses: Australian Legal System In A Comparative Perspective - Talks about the Australian legal system throughout time and the professor is very interested in other countries' systems. Class full of exchange students. International Relations and Sport - it has nothing to do with law. It is a run-through of historical events where sports have been used as a diplomatic/political arena.. Legal Project Management - VERY enthusiastic professor and very practical oriented class. I found it very interesting.
unexpected_costs: It is more expensive to buy groceries (but certain groceries). I've spent way more money on travelling than I thought I would. But there's so much to see and visit when you're here so it is very much worth it.
cost_comparison: more expensive: groceries. Less exenspise: eating out and coffee (!!)
activities_available: A lot, but I didn't look into it.
activities_recommended: Didn't try any.
weekend_recommendations: Around Sydney: Blue Mountains, Coastal walks (Coogee-Bondi, Spit-Manly, Coogee-Maroubra), ferry to Manly, explore surry hills, paddington and newtown (vintage shopping is great here). Outside of Sydney: Vantrip on the West coast is amazing. So crazy landscape and wild life (important to time it with weather though!). Noosa, Byron Bay and Whitsundays on the East Coast are also magical places.
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: no - maybe go to some social run clubs. From my experience they keep to themselves and they don't really see much point on socialising with exchane students who will leave soon.
cultural_challenges: Can't think of any.
culture_appreciated: Social, active life style.
top3_advice: To remember that it is a Trimester Uni (at least until 2028, where I think they go back to two Semesters). UNSW start date is much later than all of the other Sydney Uni's. This is quite annoying since many of the exchange students in Sydney had been here for a month when I arrived. This made it a bit harder to find people I connected with, because many had already found their friend groups by the time I arrived. So I recommend coming earlier.

crucial_aspects: For det første, var Nizwa langt fra min første prioritet da jeg havde prioriteret både Egypten og Jordan over. Det blev tilbudt som min tredje prioritet som jeg på ingen måde havde regnet med, hvis jeg skal være komplet ærlig. Derfor kan det være svært at svare korrekt og oprigtigt på dette spørgsmål.
overall_comments: Jeg har sat den til 5 da jeg mener at der var mange komplikationer med instituttet på universitetet i Nizwa, og må erkende, at det havde en stor effekt på mit indtryk af opholdet i Nizwa. Generelt set var der ikke særligt godt styr på ting dernede, og de virkede dybt uprofessionelle i deres håndtering af deres arbejde. Tit gik det ud over os elever når det kom til alt hvad der handlede om organisering. Herunder pressede de på med at få os til at deltage i interviews, at få taget billeder, og få taget video som de kunne bruge til at promovere deres institut og dermed få flere elever. Det var sjældent at de tog et nej for et nej, selvom det var det der blev givet udtryk for, og skuffelsen og ærgrelsen var klar at se i deres ansigt hver gang man ikke havde lyst til at deltage. Det skabte en mærkelig dynamik mellem os der generelt set var ret anspændt og negativ. Det var i realiteten ret ubehageligt. Derfor havde vi heller ikke mere at gøre med selve instituttet end højst nødvendigt. Vores lærer har til gengæld været fantastisk, og han har for mig været store dele af redningen af opholdet. Undervisningsmæssigt var han dygtig, og socialt skabte han en ramme som gjorde at vi kunne føle os tilpas i et fremmed land. Hvor at kulturforskellene nogle gange kunne ramme os med instituttet var han god til at prøve at forklare, og var stort set altid på vores side når det kom til problemerne med instituttet.
info_ease: Helt abnormt svært. Vi fik en generel gennemgang af hvordan semestret ville foregå, og hvordan vi kunne finde ud af ting. I realiteten var det dog reelt set svært at få hjælp til tiden hvis det var at man havde problemer dernede. Det blev typisk skubbet til at det blev ligegyldigt.
arrival_assistance: jeg fik ret meget hjælp af en mand ved navn Walid Riyami, som vi var blevet sat i kontakt med før at vi var ankommet til Nizwa. Han var en kæmpe hjælp til både at finde bolig, finde lidt relationer i Nizwa, og at blive introduceret lidt til universitetet og campus.

overall_comments: I truly loved my exchange experience overall, but I faced significant challenges with the university’s administrative system. My teacher was without a doubt the best teacher I’ve ever had — incredibly dedicated and supportive. However, the institute itself was very disorganized. They issued us the wrong certificates, with incorrect nationalities and misspelled names. The administration had no understanding of Erasmus procedures, including the required number of teaching hours and the rules for attendance. At one point, they even threatened to reduce our hours due to misunderstandings about these rules. (<we consulted the teacher - (name removed) and fixed the misunderstanding) but this shouldnt be problems that the students should have to worry about The teacher was not given any proper syllabus or plan from the institute, which caused a lack of clarity about what the University of Copenhagen required. Still, he managed to give us the best learning experience. this we consulted the teacher about (ulla) and also fixed the way through The textbook we were given was also problematic. It was full of errors, and the texts were either too difficult or too easy — in both cases, completely mismatched with our actual level. As for student life, it was also quite difficult. Especially for women, finding an apartment outside the university to avoid the 10 PM curfew was nearly impossible — if it hadn't been for Walid, a contact we got through our teacher Ulla, we wouldn’t have managed at all. Walid helped us with absolutely everything — things that were essential but that we had received no information about from the university. He spoke to the police to help us obtain our resident cards, arranged transportation, and made sure we understood how things worked both practically and academically. He also helped us understand the local culture and guided us into it — he even invited us to celebrate Eid with his family. When we had issues with our apartment, he came himself to help us. Without him, I honestly don’t know what I would have done. And yet, he isn’t even employed by the university. I strongly believe that the University of Copenhagen should consider the possibility of officially hiring him to support incoming students — without him, this experience would not have been possible. Lastly, the location of the university is quite impractical unless you have a car and a driver’s license. Without that, I honestly wouldn't recommend going.
info_ease: It was not very easy to find the information I needed upon arrival. There was little planning in advance, and it felt more like we had to show up and figure things out ourselves. Luckily, everything worked out in the end because we received a lot of help from Walid.
arrival_assistance: I didn’t receive any real assistance from the institute, nor did I get the necessary information before or upon arrival. There was an initial meeting that explained what was supposed to happen at the university, but in reality, things turned out quite differently. Fortunately, our teacher helped us a lot in understanding how the university system worked and supported us in getting properly settled into it.
arrival_comments: We didn’t receive any help with the process of getting our ID cards until 2–3 weeks after arrival, by which time Walid had already guided us through it. The card was needed much earlier, for example to get permission to drive a car in Oman and other essential things, so the lack of timely support was a real issue.

institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
crucial_aspects: Studying abroad in USA was an opportunity that I couldn't say no to. I was hoping for an adventure, and to study at a high-profile university at the same time.
overall_comments: All in all it is really something I would recommend to everyone.
info_ease: Easy to find information. It's hard to remember everything though - write things down in your notes app.
arrival_assistance: My roommate (who was on his third year) helped me a lot, I don't know what I would have done in the beginning without him. He showed me around, and took me to a lot of places, games, etc. Check your emails! Both from your home institution and from your institution abroad.
arrival_comments: A small percentage of all the information was either hard to understand or only explained briefly. But everything is going to work out fine!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: All in all it is really something I would recommend to everyone.
registration_process: Everyone gets the chance to enroll in the courses that they want. That's a lot of students registering for the same courses at the same time. If you succeeded, good for you. But if the classes are already full you need to be quick with the alternatives. You get two chances(waves) to enroll, so don't stress too much if weren't too successful the first time. The teachers respond really quickly, so send them an email if you have any questions. Find their @ on the university website.
registration_help: Instructional emails and attached PDF's. Be sure to read and understand the attached files.
registration_success: It worked out in the end. I emailed two professors and they were both really nice and let me on their courses. Just be polite, tell them who you are, why you want to enroll in their course. 99% of the time they'll let you on their course.
registration_advice: Enroll on an LFIT (Lifetime Fitness) course. It's just 1 credit, but you get to play sports, run, or whatever you choose to do. Check the university course catalogue.
academics_comments: All in all it is really something I would recommend to everyone.
course_level: I had one course on 100-level and three courses on 200-level. That might have been too easy academically. A friend of mine from back home had some courses on 300-level and that was challenging, she told me.
teaching_comparison: The class sessions don't differ too much. More homework compared to back home though. In some courses a part of your grade is based on proof that you read/made your homework.
courses_enrolled: 181 Sports Psychology 206 Analysis of Sport Skills II 273 Research in Exercise and Sport Science 276 Human Physiology
recommended_courses: 276 Human Physiology was by far the best course I had all semester. I learned a lot. Tough course, but Dr. Ondrak was a really good teacher. I really liked her style of teaching. 273 Research in Exercise and Sport Science was disappointing though. The professor was 77 y/o and taught via zoom. Difficult to stay focused for 1,5 hours when someone is talking about statistics on Zoom.
unexpected_costs: There were more fees that I had to pay than I thought there would be. As an example I just paid 9 usd to get my transcript (a PDF file) from the host institution.
cost_comparison: Restaurants and take-out is cheaper compared to Copenhagen. Get yourself a VIC-card and save 5-10 dollars when you grocery shop. The card is free, just tell them you're a student.
activities_available: Intramural sports are nice. Besides that I played a round of disc golf five days a week. Their course is really nice - both if you're new or not to the sport. I've gotten to know a handful of very nice people on the course.
activities_recommended: I would recommend meeting people through sports. I did it through disc golf and soccer, but you can basically sign up for anything and you're gonna meet some nice people there.
weekend_recommendations: Charlotte is a very nice "small" city. Raleigh is boring I would say. Me and the boys went road tripping through Savannah, Georgia down to Saint Augustine, Florida. That was a really good trip. Rent a car or go with someone with a car - most Americans have their own car.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Once they detect an accent and that you're from abroad they curious.
socializing_tips: Smile, choose a chair next to some nice-looking people, and hope for the best. If you're lucky you end up sitting next to a friend, and if you're not - change your seat next class! Intramural sports is also something I would definitely recommend.
cultural_challenges: Quick tip: Don't discuss politics or anything similar to that with Americans. I tried to avoid it all through the semester and I am pretty sure I managed to avoid some sticky situations. Be nice and they will be nice to you. That goes everywhere I guess.
culture_appreciated: They're extremely friendly and welcoming. "Do you want to come with me to the game tomorrow? I can pick you up if you need a ride..." They're also more talkative and curious than most Danes. They WILL ask questions :))
top3_advice: 1. I upgraded my phone/data deal in order to be able to data roam in the US. Although they stated they would cancel it after a few weeks (the deal was only for roaming on vacations), they never did. I ended up not paying very much the entire semester. That also meant I didn't need to acquire an American phone number or eSIM. 2. Americans are mostly really nice, but I found it a lot easier to socialize with fellow Europeans. Trust me, you're not the only European, Scandinavian, or Dane. I was lucky to become very good friends with two Germans, one Swede, one Dutch, and one Dane with whom I met at an introduction meeting for students from abroad. For me at least, it was easier to relax when I was chilling with my European friends compared to Americans. I don't know why. 3. Have fun, find people whose company you enjoy, and don't waste your time. The time goes by fast.
other_useful_info: Michael Jordan (Google him if you don't know him lol) went to UNC - they're gonna ask you if you know who he is. If you want to go to the States, I would definitely recommend UNC.
most_rewarding: The friends I got and the memories we now share.
greatest_challenge: To get enough sleep lol.
other_comments: I might have been lucky, but I truly feel like that if you follow your guts, you're gonna end up having a good time.
