institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
crucial_aspects: I was especially motivated by the prospect of visitng a part of the United States, where I don't think I would have gone otherwise. It also appealed to me that UNC Chapel Hill is such an old and charming campus, heightening the feel of an "authentic" college experience.
overall_comments: Only drawback being the administrative and logstical part of it - some of it having to do with the school's protocol, but mostly just unforeseen matters that took up just a little more energy than I wash they had.
info_ease: Since you already have your UNC e-mail set up before leaving for your stay, you can feel pretty confident that you will receive all necessary information there, or at least have someone to ask. Nicole, who is in charge of the exchange programme is the absolute best, and went above and beyond to make sure we felt prepared for our exchange.
arrival_assistance: As mentioned before, Nicole offered a lot of assistance. We were also made aware of a What'sApp group that we could join beforehand, where current exchange students were also available for answering questions that we might have.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Only drawback being the administrative and logstical part of it - some of it having to do with the school's protocol, but mostly just unforeseen matters that took up just a little more energy than I wash they had.
registration_process: You register on the school's general portal, ConnectCarolina, which is also where you'll pay for on campus housing, meal plans, and any other fees that go directly to the school. It's also where your transcript will be uploaded, where you can see your class schedules once you are registered, and more or less everything that has to do with your semester at UNC. As exchange students, we are in the last "wave" of enrollment, which means that the American students have first pick of all the classes offered. The first thing you are advised to do, is look through the course cataloque, and add courses to your "shopping cart" this can be done before your enrollment slot opens up, and I would definitely recommend doing this at the first chance you get. You will then receive a designated slot for enrollment, which is time specific, and it is likewise recommended that you are ready at that time, because courses get filled up quickly. What is very, very important to remember is, that this process is super chaotic, and everyone (teachers included) are very well aware of that. For the sake of the exchange you are required to be enrolled in the number of credits that have been specified, but just know, that most likely, these are not the courses you will end up taking. The first week of classes is "shopping week", where class registration is still open, and you can switch around according to availability. You will be urged to contact the proffessors of courses that are full, but that you might need as a specific requirement from your home institution, or that you just have a certain interest in, and in most cases, it will be possible to work around logistics. My best advice is just to trust the process and know, that one way or another, you will end up with the right amount of credits, and courses that fit your needs.
registration_help: There were several guides available through the exchange portal and UNCs website in general, but it was hard figuring out, which courses were offered when. I also experienced some classes having one description in the registration portal, but then being introduced to have completely different contents when I showed up for the first day of classes.
registration_success: I found out, that a lot of the film related classes that had first caught my attention in the course catalogue, weren't offered in the spring semester, where I had my exchange. Make sure to check up on this as soon as you are able to - I am pretty sure it can be done through ConnectCarolina. As there weren't any specific requirements for the courses I had to take, I had a little fun with registering for a course such as "Chinese Science Fiction", which I ended up really enjoying! Of course, you have to have your courses approved from KU. Apart from the fact that many of the courses I had had my eye on weren't offered in the term I was there for, I found it relatively easy to register for the classes I wanted. Obiously, some classes will just be so popular, or restricted in some way, that it is almost impossible, and I had a couple of those experiences, but ended up just accepting that I wouldn't get in to those.
registration_advice: Start researching courses as soon as you are able to. Also, do yourself a favour and check out the proffessors of the courses on ratemyprofessor.com. Don't hesitate to get a little pushy if professors don't reply to your e-mails, and honestly just trust the process, bacuse 99.9% of the time, things will work out in the end. Once again, Nicole is also a great asset during this process - ask her!
academics_comments: Only drawback being the administrative and logstical part of it - some of it having to do with the school's protocol, but mostly just unforeseen matters that took up just a little more energy than I wash they had.
course_level: The courses were not necessarily more difficult than at KU, but they were definitely structured differently, and have higher expectations regarding participation. The courses all have numbers, and they state the level, so the higher the number, the higher the level - the degree to which this acutally held true was differing.
teaching_comparison: As mentioned before, the expectations regarding participation are quite different. For each course, the teacher will share how they make up your final grade, and oftentimes class participation and attendance make up a certain percentage of your final grade. Then, most of the classes I had also had small, weekly assignments that all counted towards the final grade. In my experience, it did feel like the expectations were higher, as well as the overall workload, but it also meant that everything didn't just depend on your final exam. Additionally, the written exams at the end of the semester were often less lenghty and comprehensive than what we are used to at KU.
courses_enrolled: History of American Sreenwriting (COMM 430) Chinese Science Fiction (CMPL 545) Literature and Cinema (ENGL 381) Introduction to Gender Communication (WGST 224)
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend History of American screenwriting to scholars of film and media - or others interested in the course. It is a little like Film History, but the angle is a little different, as are the movies highlighted. I also really enjoyed Chinese Science Fiction, just because it was so completely different than the courses I usually take.
unexpected_costs: It's hard to say specifically, but I was generally surprised at the cost of living - most of the time it's at least as expensive as Copenhagen, if not more. Buses are free, which is quite great, but many times we would end up Ubering, which is obviously an extra expense
cost_comparison: Books are pretty expensive. It is almost always possible to rent books, and this is really great option, since you probably won't be bringing them back with you anyways. Generally I would say, the estimated costs that the school present, at set very low. I spent quite a bit more than I though I would, but it all depends on how much you spend on trips, going out, groceries etc.
activities_available: There were many different clubs to attend, and as exchange students we were automatically able to take advantage of the recreation centers, and could also sign up for all the different sports and workout classes that were offered. I did a variety of yoga, pilates and barre classes, and they were really relly great. The instructors are mostly students, but very very capable and it was just an amazing thing to be able to do, without having to pay for a gym membership. The pool is also open outside of the swim club's training hours, and I highly recommend taking advantage of that as well.
activities_recommended: There were som many different activities available and I would recommend attending as many of them as possible! Sports is a huge thing at UNC - fall is football season, and spring is basketball season. I would definitely recommend going to some of the games!
weekend_recommendations: Definitely walk out to Carrboro on the weekends or whenever you have the time - it's a little bigger than Chapel Hill, there's a farmer's market on the weekends and the vibe is just A+. If you get the chance, visit Asheville - it's a bit of a drive, but it's really beautiful, and the town itself is great. I took a hiking trip out to Stone Mountain, which was organized by the school activity center, but I know that North Carolina is generally known for having really great hiking spots, so I would definitely check that out too! Wilmington is also a great place to visit, if you want to go to the beach, and the town itself is also quite charming. We drove to Miami during spring break, and stopped in Charleston and Savannah on the way, and especially Savannah really exceeded my expectations - both cities are absolutely beautiful, and rich with culture and history.
culture_adjustment: I found it surprisingly easy. Obviously, there will be some cultural differences, but I found it easy to kind of pick anc choose which aspects I wanted to adopt, and on which occasions I chose to hold on to more "european" values and customs ;)
socializing_tips: In my personal experience, living with local students really made a big difference. Similarly, making friends with exchanges students who also lived with local students, allowed me to create a substantial network of local friends.
cultural_challenges: It can at times, be challenging not to have a car. Biking is possible, but the infrastructure is just not really made for it, and people don't take care to look out for cyclists. I was lucky to have two roommates who had cars, so longer shopping trips for example were made easier when driving with them. It is possible to rent cars, but it isn't really that cheap - otherwise Uber is obviously an easy alternative. Also I think, especially living in Copenhagen, you have to get used to the fact that can't, or shouldn't, walk everywhere. This is both due to the long distances and infrstructre, but also as a safety precaution. I ended up buying a pepper spray (which is legal, and can be bought at Target) - not necessarily because I ever felt personally unsafe, but beacuse things did happen occasionally, and you might as well take the safety precautions available.
culture_appreciated: There is definitely a different vibe at American colleges, because it is such an integral part of the students' life - as opposed to here, where most people have so many things going on outside of school. I really liked the feeling of belonging that that instilled in you as a student, whether it be hanging out on the quad during breaks, or at big sporting events. Specifically I really enjoyed the hospitality and friendliness, that I experienced in North Carolina and the surrounding states.
top3_advice: Don't be afraid to take time for yourself while you're away. You will probably experience an intense need to be social all the time (especially at the beginning), and that's perfectly fine and also important, but you're also gone for such a long time that you start establishing an everyday, and during that time it is perfectly fine - if not necessary - to take some time for yourself to read good books, talk to your friends/family at home or do something by yourself like a workout class or walking to Carrboro. Definitely take advantage of all the (free!) options for recreation - workout classes, clubs etc. You will definitely spend more than the estimated amount on your exchange in general, and also just while you're there. It's just more fun if you have financial wiggle room.
other_useful_info: Even though it's a huge cliché, make sure you enjoy your time there and make the most of it! There's probably something else, but you'll figure it out in due time.
most_rewarding: I really enjoyed making friends with the other exchange students, and generally just the feeling of making an everyday life for yourself in a new place and a foreign country. You have a different freedom, because there are a lot of obligations that you can leave behind at home, and that is quite unique.
greatest_challenge: I think there were two things that I found most challenging. First thing was being away from my boyfriend and my family. No matter how independent you might be, I don't think this is ever something you can work your way around. But you can of course make plans to talk/facetime and stuff like that, and that makes things a little easier. Second, I found the logistical aspects a little challenging. I had to open an American bank account in order to pay my rent, and that just proved incredibly challenging (partly because I hadn't gotten an American phone number at the time). In my experience, there were a lot of these practical/logistical things that I struggled with in the first month, but they all worked out, it just took a little time.
other_comments: I can almost guarantee, that you will not regret going on exchange - whether it be at UNC or anywhere else!

academics_comments: Ville ønske jeg havde udfordret mig endnu mere
course_level: Jeg synes niveauet var lavere end i Danmark. Professorerne virker mere dovne og min oplevelse var at de ikke rigtigt benyttet bøgerne. Der var tit hvor der ikke var noget pensum uploadet til forelæsningen og jeg spurgte min professor om jeg skulle læse i bøgerne eller hans powerpoints som eksamensforberdelsem, dertil svarede han, at han synes jeg skulle kigge i powerpoints. Så generelt gennemgår de alt hvad man skal vide til forelæsningerne, hvilket endte ud i jeg slet ikke købte nogle bøger til mine fag, men bare brugte powerpoints til at forberede til eksamen. Som alle mine Amerikanske klassekammerater også gjorde. Derudover er eksamenerne hovedsageligt skriftlige og 50-70% multiple choise. Det er alt andet end lige nemmere. Man skal dog være forberedt på at de alle sammen foregår i hånden, hvilket overrasket mig lidt i starten. Men jeg endte op med at klare mig rigtig godt.
teaching_comparison: Jeg synes det var rigtig godt. I nogle af mine fag var det var mere som at være tilbage på gymnasiebænken. Der var rigtig meget tovejskommunikation hvilket jeg virkelig fandt fedt. Det gjorde man ikke sad og faldt i søvn. Derudover er underviserne meget engagerede og meget hjælpsomme, da de rigtig gerne vil have deres elever klarer sig godt. En ting jeg synes var meget kontroversielt var, at man kunne optjene point - dvs, du kunne forbedre din karakter, ved at række hånden op i timerne. Der var nogle gange hvor professoren sagde "You can earn an ekstra point for answering this!" som regel var det ret svært, men jeg bed da på nogle gange og fik mit point. Men jeg synes det er noget pjat, men det undrede mig egentlig ikke - Typisk Amerikansk ;)
courses_enrolled: Human Metabolism. Exercise Testing and Perscription. Exercise physiology. Outdoor sport activities.
recommended_courses: På mit universitet UNC Chapel Hill. Kan man tage LFIT (lifetime fitness) for 1 credit. Hvilket svarer til 2,5 ECTS ish. Det er virkelig sjovt og en rigtig god måde at møde folk på. Der er mange forskellige at vælge imellem alt lige fra. Outdoor sports, som jeg havde, til jogging, beach volley, indoor sports, soccer og resistance training. Det er i den grad værd at vælge. Det er dog obligatorisk for UNC students, at tage i løbet af deres bachelor, så nogle af dem er ikke særlig engageret. Men overordnet er det rigtig sjovt og en god måde lige at få en pause fra skolearbejdet på. og de forventer ikke at man har nogle færdigheder indenfor det man vælger.
unexpected_costs: Der er nogle gebyrer de opkræver. Der var noget der hed "Admin fee" som kostede 300 dollars. Det kom lidt bag på mig, men tror alle skal betale det. Det er vigtigt at være opmærksom på hvad de opkræver af bøder, gebyrer osv. For nogle gange prøver de bare at få penge ud af dig, de ikke er berettiget til
cost_comparison: Synes deres Meal plan og deres housing var MEGET dyrt. Især i forhold til hvad man får. Man skal jo stort set købe alt selv til sit værelse - noget så simpelt som en lampe var der ikke. Meal planen var dog rigtig god! Kan kun anbefale det, hvis man lever på campus. tror 99% af de studerende der lever på campus har den. Den har åbent fra 08:00 til 24:00 og madden er super fin. Plus der er en rigtig god mulighed for at mødes med medstuderende og venner og socialiserer sig.
activities_available: Jeg benyttede det rigtig meget til at møde folk. Der er stort set uanede mængder af sportsklubber og de er super søde og inkluderende. jeg spillede selv Volleyball, Squash og spikeball
activities_recommended: Jeg spillede rigtig meget volleyball og squash og mødte mange søde Amerikanere igennem den klub. Folk jeg brugte det meste af min tid sammen med faktisk. Vi endte med at tage i byen i og på ture osv.
weekend_recommendations: Jeg var ikke selv særlig meget på tur. Jeg havde ikke rigtig råd. Men de to nærliggende byer Durham og Raleigh er super skønne og der er mange fede natklubber og barer, det var primært der jeg brugte det meste af mine weekender ;)
culture_adjustment: For mig var det egentlig rigtig nemt. Man kan komme rigtig langt ved at smile og være åben. Det kræver ikke flydende engelsk skills overhoved at komme ind på folk. Amerikanere er meget åbne og inkluderende og synes det er spændene med folk fra Europa. Mange af dem har jo aldrig prøvet at være udenfor USA Før. Derudover er de ikke så meget anderledes end i Danmark, man skal ikke forvente et kæmpe kulturchok.
socializing_tips: Meld dig ind i klubber. Der er så mange forskellige klubber, så der er med garanti noget man kan finde ud af og synes er sjovt. Der er et vanvittigt godt sammenhold i de forskellige klubber og folk er meget inkluderende. Hvis man er åben og bare prøver at snakke med folk, så skal man nok finde nogle venner som inviterer en til forskellige ting ret hurtigt. Dog er der meget mindre "Jantelovsadfærd" I USA så folk er ikke bange for at juble og fortælle at de er gode.
cultural_challenges: Det kan være svært at læse folk til tider. Jeg tror primært det er pga. sprogbarrieren, at det kan være svært at aflæse folk. Derudover er Amerikanere meget overfladiske til tider, hvor man nærmest kan få opfattelsen af at man er bedste venner, men så bliver man ignoreret næste gang man mødes. Så hvis jeg skulle give et råd, så skal man passe på med at forvente for meget af de "venner" man får og så tage det lidt med et gran salt.
culture_appreciated: Jeg synes Amerikanere snakker meget mere til hinanden generelt og mindre sky end danskere, hvilket er super fedt. Så kan jeg også godt lide, at det er okay at sige man er god til noget og rose sig selv.
top3_advice: Meld dig ind i klubber (det er ofte gratis) Køb meal plan (hvis du bor på campus, husk det kun er første- og andens års studerende der bor på campus) Hvis du godt kan lide at feste, så vælg et andet universitet end UNC
other_useful_info: Fitnesscentrene er meget dårlige. udstyret er gammelt, ofte går det i stykker, der er for lidt af det og de er oftest proppet til randen med mennesker. Vent med at køb bøger til du har været til de første par forelæsninger, det er ikke sikkert du behøver dem. Folk er meget seriøse med deres uddannelse på UNC, da det er et af de bedste offentlige Universiteter i landet og derfor meget annerkendt. Forvent at brug mange penge på diverse ting til dit værelse.
most_rewarding: Fået nogle gode Amerikanske venner og oplevelser. Jeg har fået meget mere gå på mod i livet, jeg tør kaste mig ud i nye ting. Bekymrer mig meget mindre om hvad andre folk tænker om mig.
greatest_challenge: Jeg blev hurtigt venner med en gruppe andre internationale studerende inklusiv min roomie som også var international studerende . Men så skete der nogle ting som gjorde, at de begyndte at lukke mig ude og lave ting uden mig. Jeg opfangede ret hurtigt, at jeg blev holdt lidt udenfor og de medførte at jeg følte mig ret alene i en uges tid. Men så besluttede jeg mig for at flytte til et andet dorm, begynde at melde mig ind i alle mulige klubber for at møde nogle nye mennesker og få nye venner. Det var mentalt meget hårdt, men jeg fik hurtigt nogle nye Amerikanske venner igennem sportklubberne og fik en ny Amerikansk roomie som var super skøn, vi endte med at blive bedste venner, og han havde en bil som jeg fik lov at låne lige så tosset jeg ville. Så jeg er faktisk glad for at det endte som det gjorde og at jeg valgte at droppe den gruppe som jeg ellers hang ud med de første 14 dage.
other_comments: Det er meget nemt at finde sammen med andre exchange students, men prøv at få nogle amerikanske venner også, da det gør oplevelsen meget mere interessant, da man virkelig kommer ind og mærker den amerikanske kultur på en helt anden måde ved at hænge ud med lokalbefolkningen.

arrival_assistance: I received a lot of assistance from the UNC ISSS. They host a lot of events and you can always schedule a meeting if you need help.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Look at the deadlines for course enrolment, and if you need to join a course where you need prerequisites, write an email to the professor a month or two (at least) before enrolment opens, so that you can register for the course in time. Communication with professors is key, and you're gonna spend a lot of time doing this, but it is necessary of you want the good courses.
registration_help: Again, the ISSS office will help you, schedule a meeting once in a while if you have any questions.
registration_success: Mostly succesful, I got my mandatory classes because I reached out to the professors a few months ahead of time, and I secured a spot before the classes got full. If I had not done this, my entire exchange program could not have been possible. The courses fill up QUICK, and exchange students are last in line for registration so reach out to professors and make a private agreement before it opens.
registration_advice: Spend a day or two looking at the courses available for your exchange semester and write down which ones you want to take. When the registration opens be quick to secure a spot. And if its a mandatory course for your degree, write an email to the professor.
course_level: Took courses from 100-400s (BSc level), I took an extra course such that my workload was 37.5 ECTS instead of 30. Courses are easier, but as you get to 300s and 400s it will get harder, I took two 400s and one 300s and two 100s. It is very hard to fail a class, but also hard to get a good grade. I spent 20-25 hours a week on homework, but its a part of the experience and if you keep up midterms and finals wont be that hard.
teaching_comparison: Much more engaging.

recommended_courses: Check out the professor on ratemyprofessor.com before enrolling in a course. If the professor in that course has bad reviews, pick another course.
unexpected_costs: UNC Admin fee is $300, mandatory and DO NOT BUY their insurance! Get your insurance from Tryg (its ~4000DKK) and use it to waiver UNC's insurance (which is more than double the price of Trygs).

socializing_tips: Just be yourself and talk to people.
cultural_challenges: The tipping culture.
culture_appreciated: Americans love dressing up all the time and decorating if there is a football game or halloween etc. There is always something to celebrate so go out and enjoy the festives.
top3_advice: 1) Do not live on campus. 2) Reach out to professors before enrolment opens to secure your spot in a course. 3) Give it 110% socially!
other_useful_info: Arrive a week before school starts and get to know the area before it all begins!
most_rewarding: The great people I met on my exchange.
greatest_challenge: All the paperwork and emails, you will get there in the end but its a lot work.

socializing_tips: Be prepared and opens for differences in culture and how they build connections. Americans for example are very open.
cultural_challenges: The openess, as a Dane, could sometimes be difficult to tackle as we pride ourselves on personal space and not being rude, intrusive etc. whereas Americans do not have that concern at all.
culture_appreciated: Somehow also the Americans openess, it felt different and nice to meet so many people who were so friendly and talkative.

Then you have to wait till you get there and ask the professors if they have room for you in their class. During the first week of class, you can try them out and drop them if you don't like them.
registration_advice: Register for classes as early as possible and try them out when you are there, u can always change classes after the first week. You have to keep in mind that they don't tell you if the classes are overlapping, so you have to check that yourself in terms of making your schedule.
academics_comments: I had a wonderful semester there! The pros of living in a "small" city like Greensboro in the US are you form close bonds with people there, and you have to go on trips to see the US on the weekends and holidays. The campus is really nice, they always have so many events, and nice facilities u can use for free. The Food is alright there (the caf'), but compared to other campuses they have a good reputation. Because it's a small city you quickly develop traditions (fx going to Corner Bar every Tuesday to get 1 dollar beer) and that brings the internationals close together. The cons are that is a small city with less to do compared to staying in a big city, and that the academic levels are mixed depending on the professor.
course_level: Very different course levels depending on the course, mostly easy. The multiple-choice exams were somewhat easy.
teaching_comparison: It was very similar to UCPH with PowerPoint lectures - just listening and taking notes. In one of the courses, we had to do a presentation for the class.
courses_enrolled: - History and Theory of Design I. - History of Fashion - Film Appreciation - Global Perspectives on Body, Culture, and Dress.
recommended_courses: I liked Global Perspectives on Body, Culture, and Dress, because it's in my interest area. In general, courses/classes with Dr. Trisha Kemerly are good. She is a really talented professor.
unexpected_costs: A lot of Uber's because public transport is bad.
cost_comparison: Everything was more expensive than I thought, but it was bad timing because the dollar was so high.
activities_available: They have a very good gym and sports facilities. They have a free museum close to campus. A lot of social events on campus every week. The bus is free for students so it's easy to go downtown.
activities_recommended: Go to Corner Bar every Tuesday to get a one-dollar beer, go to Limelight on Thursdays, and go to Arizona Petes on Fridays to watch line dance. Go on road trips to hike around North Carolina and you can get a cheap bus ride (Flixbus or greyhound) to the bigger cities.
weekend_recommendations: Visit the bigger cities and go on road trips to hike.
culture_adjustment: It was somewhat easy. Americans are usually really nice. But the area is a bit rough so you have to take precautions.
socializing_tips: Take part in the activities and be open.
cultural_challenges: I missed my freedom in terms of transport and feeling safe - I can't just walk everywhere alone.
culture_appreciated: The Americans are very nice, open, and talkative.
top3_advice: Enjoy the multiple-choice exams while you can Practice small talk and being open like the Americans Go on trips with friends!
other_useful_info: It's a social thing to have the full meal plan from the caf. You see people there all the time so it's a nice place to socialize and meet new people - it is kinda like in the movies.
most_rewarding: Being able to experience the US with very nice people from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Taking some time to relax.
other_comments: Just do it!

institution: University of North Carolina at Greensboro
crucial_aspects: The culture relating to my major. As I'm majoring in English, I wanted to surround myself with the English language in order to improve my spoken English. However, I also wanted to experience a culture that was very different from the Danish culture, and as I've been to England multiple times and find the culture quite similar to Danish culture, I opted to go to America instead.
info_ease: It was fairly easy and there were people there to help and guide you in the first couple of days.
arrival_assistance: There was a guide on where and how to pick up the room key, and when I arrived to the building there was a student representative to greet me and help me get the key and student card.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I had misunderstood the level of courses that I was required to take, so I registered a bit late. This also meant that I ended up with two courses that weren't necessarily that interesting to me, but the two other courses were at the top of my priorities. I also ended up really enjoying one of the courses that weren't my first pick at the beginning.
registration_help: As said, the professors were generally pretty good at answering e-mails, and you also have your DSO (Dee) who can guide you a bit.
registration_success: 50/50, I got two out of four that I wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure that you are 100% certain that the courses you want are at the level you need. So for example, I was required to ONLY take level 400 courses as I was a major in Denmark, but an undergraduate in USA, so all my courses would have the numbers 400-499. This is what I didn't understand in the beginning, and I chose courses from 300-499, which meant that I was "rejected" and had to choose new ones.
course_level: As said, I was on my second semester of the MA at UCPH, but because my grades weren't good enough to get nominated as a graduate student at UNCG, I had to take undergraduate courses. This is why I only had the options between 400-499 courses, which is kind of unusual as far as I could understand. Generally you'll have more room to choose different courses, my situation just limited my options.
teaching_comparison: It was much more based on how you could apply what you learned in real life. I generally feel that UCPH teaching is based very much on academia, books, theories, etc. Although UNCG of course also applied theories to the learning, the assignments and final exams were focused more on personal experiences and how you could use those theories to explain some things that might go on in your own real life.
courses_enrolled: Family Communication (COMM), Communication and Friendship (COMM), African History and Cultures through Film (LLC), Environmental Justice (SWK)
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the communication courses, the teachers were relatable, understandable, and prioritised including their students in the classroom. They used examples from their own personal lives which made it easy to relate to them and understand what they were trying to teach us.
unexpected_costs: PayPal fees when transferring money to UNCG. Also, taxes in everything you buy, and tips for everyone.
cost_comparison: Housing was definitely very pricey given the state of the apartments.
activities_available: Basketball, soccer, tennis, softball, baseball, fitness, social gatherings in Tower Village, and much more.
activities_recommended: Definitely the sports games and just explore campus and downtown Greensboro. Take day trips to Charlotte, Wilmington, Charleston, etc.
weekend_recommendations: I went to Puerto Rico with a group of girls during Spring break and it was lovely. Go to bars and clubs downtown during the weekends; Limelight on Thursdays, Arizona Pete's on Fridays, Grey's Tavern on Saturdays, One Thirteen roof top whenever, Corner Bar and Jake's (close to campus). Go to all the states/cities that you want to see when you're there; it's not every day you get to go to the states. I recommend New York and Miami, but heard great things about Chicago and Tennessee as well. Go to Texas; if you go to Austin, make sure to live downtown as I went there and lived just in the outskirts which wasn't that nice.
culture_adjustment: It took some time, but fortunately I had some really great roommates and friends who were there for me if I needed it. Definitely had to get used to the food as well.
socializing_tips: Just talk to them whenever you can; during classes, in the cafeteria, at parties, etc. Unfortunately, I did notice that many students were kind of closed off during classes and sometimes difficult to approach.
cultural_challenges: The fact that you basically had to have a car in order to go to shopping centers or Target/Walmart. Although there were busses, it wasn't always the easiest solution, and so I sometimes spent quite some money on Ubers.
culture_appreciated: People didn't really seem to care about what other people thought about them. Coming from Denmark where people tend to be a little snobby and self-conceived, it was really freeing to be around people who didn't seem to care about what you're wearing or how you look in general.
top3_advice: Research your options for meal plans and housing; I do recommend Tower Village as most international students are there, but I could have saved quite a lot of money by cooking at home. Make sure that you are certain about what level of courses you need, so you don't end up having to do a late submission like I did. Socialize wherever you can; the connections I made with a lot of different people made my experience 100 times better. It also helps when you get homesick!
other_useful_info: If you get the meal plan "Unlimited 110", remember that you have 110 "Spartan Meals" that you can get around campus; EUC and Spartan Markets. Also make sure to use your flex money around campus; Bojangles, Chick-Fil-A, Panda Express, etc.
most_rewarding: The development in my language and the friends I made there.
greatest_challenge: Feeling out of place at times, missing the people who know me 100%.
other_comments: Enjoy it, time flies when you're there.

crucial_aspects: The language and level of education
info_ease: I think the pre-arrival process was quite tricky and I felt very much alone in the process.
arrival_assistance: I both received help from my accommodation in those matters and from Fiona Hayes and Christopher Sargeant regarding academic issues
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Basically, I just had to show up and register close to the Portland building during the first few weeks. I had to bring my passport and a lady asked me a couple of questions.
registration_help: Fiona and Christopher were both at service whenever we needed help during the first few weeks. Also, I received a lot of information on my Nottingham email, which was a great help.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: I would advise you to not panic about not knowing things. My schedule was announced a couple of days before the semester started, which I found very stressful - but everything worked out.
course_level: All of my courses were on level 3.
teaching_comparison: It is much more engaging, and it is expected of the students that they participate in the discussions. I guess that is the difference between the Danish and English law systems; English law is more dynamic.
courses_enrolled: Advanced Tort, Foundations of Criminal Evidence, Classical Legal Theory
recommended_courses: Classical Legal Theory. This course gives you a great understanding of what law is from a philosophical perspective and furthermore prepares you for your next semester (retsfilosofi etc.). It strengthens your analytical skills and gives you a great understanding of different jurisdictions around the world.
unexpected_costs: Expenses for kitchen equipment, bedding, etc.
cost_comparison: The abovementioned
activities_available: All kinds! Please join a society and buy a one-semester membership in David Ross Sports Village if you are in to sports (you can buy that in their reception, it is not available to buy online for only one semester).
activities_recommended: I would highly recommend the climbing society. They do loads of socials, and every Wednesday they go climbing and then go to the pub. This was the best way of getting to know English students, as it can be quite hard in other ways to meet with them. I have so many really good friends from Climbing soc! Also - join the Travel Society! This is a great way to see the UK, and you cannot plan it cheaper yourself.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend you to go travel with the Travel Society. They do both day trips and weekend trips. Furthermore, take a trip to London during the weekend or go watch a football game in Manchester. Nottingham is in the middle of England, which is quite an advantage.
culture_adjustment: Very easy indeed. English culture is not very distant from Danish culture.
socializing_tips: As beforementioned, go join a society! This is the easiest way to interact with English students.
cultural_challenges: I struggled the most with the language actually. Even though I speak English fluently, my head could get really exhausted, and I couldn't express myself as deliberately and freely as I am able to in Danish.
culture_appreciated: English people are some of the kindest people. I will indeed miss being approached as "my love" and "darling" by the staff in the supermarkets or by the bus driver.
top3_advice: 1. Please ask a student who has been to Nottingham before regarding all the pre-departure stuff; I really struggled with all the planning and could have needed some help in that area. 2. Join a Society. 3. Go explore the country and use your time abroad as a break from home. Do not stress too much about school; if you study everything, you could choose to do nothing but school. Allow yourself to focus on other things as well.
other_useful_info: Use the library for studying! I practically lived at Hallward, and that was amazing. All students use the library and then we had lunch together. That was fantastic!
most_rewarding: My English has improved A LOT. I have gotten so many amazing international friends. Furthermore, it has opened my eyes regarding working abroad. I feel much more confident and ready to meet new people.
greatest_challenge: Time management. There are so many things I wanted to do.
other_comments: Remember to enjoy it while it lasts. 3 to 4 months is NOT a long time.

crucial_aspects: I found the opportunity to travel to a prestigious university important for my career progression as it would allow me practice my english and gain exposure to a completely new cultural environment.
info_ease: Very easy.
arrival_assistance: We were given a 'buddy' who was a student at the University of Nottingham who had previously student abroad at University of Copenhagen, who was there to help and introduce us to the university. Besides that there were many introduction meetings etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I registered befor arrival. We simply had to send an email to our Erasmus Coordinator at the host institution on which modules we would like to study.
registration_help: You could ask staff members for help.
registration_success: I was able to register for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Register for the courses you are most interested in.
course_level: Was ok.
teaching_comparison: At UCPH we mainly have seminars and a few lectures. At UoN we mainly had tutorials and lecturers.
courses_enrolled: Employment Law Foundations of Criminal Evidence UK Human Rights Law
recommended_courses: I would recommend employment law as it is a very interesting and useful course.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Food is less expensive.
activities_available: There were many social activities arranged by the host institution and by the accommodation.
activities_recommended: Join the different societies.
weekend_recommendations: Explore England - see Oxford, York, Cambridge etc.
culture_adjustment: Was easy as the culture is similar to the Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Participate in all events.
cultural_challenges: None really.
culture_appreciated: The English people are very open and friendly.
top3_advice: 1. Attend to as many of the activities/events in the beginning of the semester as possible. 2. Join some of the student societies. 3. Participate in the lectures and tutorials.
other_useful_info: Don't forget to explore England!
most_rewarding: Personal development and development of language skills
greatest_challenge: Being alone in a different country.

crucial_aspects: When I was choosing between destinations, the most important aspect for me was that I could be a place where I felt I would love the environment and the University was well known. When choosing I was between either the US and the UK, but ultimately decided the UK as both have common law, and also being a bit closer to the European legal market. University of Nottingham has an amazing campus and sports facilities, and there are green spaces everywhere. It was also "easy" to find accommodation through the University although a bit expensive and troublesome if you become a graduate student.
overall_comments: My overall experience in Nottingham was great. I made some great friends, had some exciting courses, and Nottingham was close to a bunch of really nice cities in the UK. I however have had quite a bit of trouble with the accommodation team of University of Nottingham, and would recommend any other student to not find housing through the University if they are 1) Upgraded to graduate student or 2) Plan to leave before the end-date of the semester.
info_ease: When I arrived it was somewhat easy to find the information I needed to know upon arrival. I quickly figured out I had to get my student card from the Students Union (and not the security office).
arrival_assistance: I did not receive and assistance.
arrival_comments: I had been promised someone would be ready to welcome me even though my flight and bus to University of Nottingham (UoN) was to arrive quite late. However, when I arrived there were no-one there to help me, and I instead was lucky to find some staff that was walking around so I could get my room. When you arrive in the Spring semester there is not really a orientation week, rather you meet some of the other students when the tutor (the official you speak to from Nottingham) hosts some gatherings for the exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My overall experience in Nottingham was great. I made some great friends, had some exciting courses, and Nottingham was close to a bunch of really nice cities in the UK. I however have had quite a bit of trouble with the accommodation team of University of Nottingham, and would recommend any other student to not find housing through the University if they are 1) Upgraded to graduate student or 2) Plan to leave before the end-date of the semester.
registration_process: The first weeks you are able to participate and try the classes you can sign up for. I would recommend going to those you are interested in, and then later decide. UCPH was also great and amazing when it came to approval of courses. If I remember correctly you just sign into your Nottingham account and then sign up for the classes (or you can write and get help from academic affairs which I got).
registration_help: As stated above, you could get help from academic affairs if you had trouble signing up for a class. I suppose you could also ask the professor running the class about what the class is about.
registration_success: Very successful, as I did not experience any problems (except the class where I did not have the proper prerequisites).
registration_advice: It is rather easy, and do not worry about it.
academics_comments: My overall experience in Nottingham was great. I made some great friends, had some exciting courses, and Nottingham was close to a bunch of really nice cities in the UK. I however have had quite a bit of trouble with the accommodation team of University of Nottingham, and would recommend any other student to not find housing through the University if they are 1) Upgraded to graduate student or 2) Plan to leave before the end-date of the semester.
course_level: The level of courses I had were graduate level courses (as I got approval). I would say they are quite a bit easier than those of Danish Law Master Courses.
teaching_comparison: Some of the teaching was quite different while some was the same. I.e. Criminal Justice was very much only focused on discussion and you would sit in a horse shoe-formation, and there would not really be a plan for the class other than the theme and some readings. IP Law classes were however more like just the professor speaking and not seeking that much input.
courses_enrolled: 1. International and Comparative Patent Law, 2. International and Comparative Trade Mark Law, 3. Fair Trials, Human Rights and Criminal Justice, and 4. Global Competition Law and International Business
recommended_courses: I would recommend the criminal justice class if you are interested in criminal law. I really liked the teaching where you discussed a lot, and I was also a huge fan of the topics. It gave me quite a bit of insights even though the professor is rather special and takes some time to adjust to. IP law classes were also good, however the professor I would say was very experienced and noted IP-law professor, but maybe did not prepare that much for class (instead relying on memory). Competition law was an amazing professor, but I was not that interested in the topic after having it some times.
unexpected_costs: It is a little difficult for me to write what unexpected costs were; I tried living rather cheap while being in the UK. Unexpected costs were more those were you decide to travel around the UK or decide to go to concerts and such. I feel Nottingham can be quite cheap if you get accommodation that is cheap (possible self-catered) and do not do that much. It all depends on how much you want to do.
cost_comparison: Flying was less expensive that I imagined when travelling around the UK, Uber was not that expensive when travelling. While I did know the price of my housing, it was most definitely still very expensive. Alcohol was around the same price as in Denmark.
activities_available: There were some social activities, but I would say you should go find them yourself.
activities_recommended: Go see some concerts as there are a lot fo well-known artists. I went to Sam Smith and Eden, but know Maroon 5 was there too. I would also recommend going to Ye Olde Jerusalem (supposedly the oldest pub in England). It is built inside a cave and looks cool. Also go see the Nottingham Castle and the Criminal Justice Museum.
weekend_recommendations: Except travelling all over the UK, I would recommend further students to go to the city right by "Beeston". It seems very chill and, while some say it can be a bit unsafe at night, I never had any bad experiences there. They are a Tesco Express, some nice places to eat, and some cool rurals.
culture_adjustment: English culture is very much like Danish culture. I would however say to bring your physical ID / Passport when going out and getting alcohol, as they do not accept the digital ones like they do in Denmark and they HAVE to check if they think you are under 25 (you still only need to be 18 to drink however(.
socializing_tips: When there is a zoom meeting at the start of the semester for incoming exchange students, go and see if you can find them on instagram or somewhere else and then meet up. Try and socialise as much as possible. You will als get a student tutor who will and can introduce you England / Campus life (but these vary on how active they are).
cultural_challenges: There were not really any. When you go and party people are a bit more rude (and drunk) than they are in Denmark. In the UK they also party every Wednesday instead of the weekends usually (you can still find large parties on Fridays though - not so much on Saturdays from my experience).
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the way you get to learn a lot more English, especially law English. The culture is again very much like Denmark, but being able to go to pubs and drink for quite cheap is rather nice. I did not appreciate the bad coffee though...
top3_advice: 1. Know if you want to go for graduate courses before going and make your accommodation decision based on that. If you get them, do you want to stay the whole trip, or (usually) end a month before and not do anything while having a room? 2. Do not live catered. I remember previous exchange students from DK that went to UoN all recommended me to live off-campus / self-catered, but I did not listen as I thought it would be interesting to have the "UK experience". It is however very difficult and annoying to live with fire alarms going off every day. 3. Remember to see all that the UK has to offer. The nature is quite beautiful; go and see Manchester and try and take the train ride there. You will see some amazing hills on that trip. Also go see Ireland if you can or Scotland; I went to Dublin which was okay, but Northern Ireland, Belfast, (part of UK) was such a pretty city.
other_useful_info: The exchange is usually 5 months so you will not have difficulties with visa. You can however not work AT ALL while being there which is not so nice if you would want that. You also do have quite a bit of time off during the semester, as you have 3/4 weeks off during Easter Break, and then only one week of classes after.
most_rewarding: Learning that I am able to live in a foreign country by myself. I have considering doing an LLM in a foreign country, so now I know I am able to live away from family.
greatest_challenge: It is of course very hard not seeing your family and friends, but from my experience it becomes completely okay as you make some new and really good friends. Exchange friends are just like you, and they also are looking for other people to talk with.

crucial_aspects: No aspects, I just chose the place that looked like could be fun.
info_ease: It was fairly easy. Some of the information I had to seek and find out myself, but other than that, emails were sent with information regularly.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance. There were information meetings in the beginning and of course emails, but not really anything other than that. We were assigned a buddy from the study destination, that was from that University in the beginning, which I found helpful in terms of meeting new people.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I arrived, and told them my name at the informative meeting for exchange students, they crossed me off, and that was it.
registration_help: We had a contact person for exchange students.
registration_success: I was a bit confused about classes. I ended up registering for 4 classes (because of the credits I needed for my home university), which I found overwhelming, as we normally do 3 at most at my home university. I would have liked more information about classes as an exchange student.
registration_advice: I do not know, registation was not that hard. However, if you are a postgradstudent, and can do undergrad courses, I would recommend that, because I found out too late, that I could do all undergrad courses as a postgrad exchange student. If I would have known before going, I would have done all my courses undergrad, as I could have done 3 instead of 4, and gotten the credits I needed, without feeling overwhelmed.
course_level: If I had known I could have done all BA classes, I would have done that. I felt there was too much material for the MA classes, when thinking about the amount of credits you got for the one class. I also did not think they took into consideration, that a student could have up to 3 other classes, than that one class. I liked the one BA class I had better, because the readings were proportionate. In terms of level, I would say my MA readings were generally harder to understand and longer, than my readings for my BA class.
teaching_comparison: The readings were very different and all online. At UCPH we normally have a book for the course that we can turn to and reference, which I prefer much more. Having different readings that say different things became confusing for me in the assessment period in terms of choosing and including the 'right' thing. Also, I would have difficulties multiple times when it came to access the readings that were listed.
courses_enrolled: 1. International Humanitarian Law 2. Equality and Discrimination in the Criminal Justice System 3. Economic and Social Rights 4. Philosophical Foundations of Criminal Justice
recommended_courses: I would recommend BA classes generally, as I found my one BA class more understandable than the MA ones. However, I enjoyed having Economic and Social Rights as well, because the teacher was very talented and made the course very interesting in terms of explaining and teaching us the material.
unexpected_costs: I would not say I encountered costs that were unexpected.
cost_comparison: The gym
activities_available: All kinds, very impressed. Just a shame because I thought it was too expensive for me
activities_recommended: I tried out for the basketball team in the beginning, that was very fun.
weekend_recommendations: Go see other parts of the UK as well! It is beautiful! Brighton, London, Manchester, Peak District.
culture_adjustment: It was not very hard.
socializing_tips: Just be yourself and be open to meeting new people.
cultural_challenges: Nothing challenging, just that british people tend to be much more talkative in the day-to-day life.
culture_appreciated: The kindness and openness
top3_advice: Enjoy it, it goes by very fast! I would recommend the BA classes Be open to meeting new people
other_useful_info: Not particularly.
most_rewarding: the friends I made and all the new things I learned about myself.
greatest_challenge: Being far from my family and home, especially during the assessment period, where stress and anxiety tends to be high for me.

crucial_aspects: English speaking country
info_ease: Very easy they had like into sessions for exchange students
arrival_assistance: A buddy, she was on exchange to the University of Copenhagen a year prior.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: From what I remember there is one day sometime in the first week, where all the international and exchange student gather outside of Trent building to register WITH their passport and proof of flight ticket.
registration_help: every kind, the staff was very accommodating.
registration_success: I got all 3 classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Honestly go for international law classes offered they are objectively so much easier, because it's something entirely different to study regional law.
course_level: I took level 3 courses
teaching_comparison: it depends on the module, but they offered tutoring, which was a more intimate class with maybe 8-10 students where they exclusively covered exam content. classes are only 1 hour long. all their lectures are recorded and that was really helpful during the exam period.
courses_enrolled: Issues in Company Law International Humanitarian Law Foundations of Public International Law
recommended_courses: the international law courses, and if possible the ones with an assignment as the final exam. I knew an exchange student who was done with all exams in early January. if you do choose to take Issues in Company Law, Colin is genuinely one of the best teachers I have ever had.
unexpected_costs: Laundry, it's no joke. the costs add up quick.
cost_comparison: Uber is very cheap in Nottingham.
activities_available: genuinely every kind, and you didn't even have to be from that ethnicity or whatever to join their events. Everyone was very open.
activities_recommended: I quite enjoyed going to the gym at David Ross, I met some very nice people there. go hiking if can, we don't have that back home in Denmark. go on day or weekend trips to neighboring cities.
weekend_recommendations: again, travel to neighboring cities. go to a ice hockey game. attend a variety game between UoN and Trent. picnic in the Downs with all your friends is a must. try all the different food places, Nottingham has Pepes, Wingstop, Nando's and so much more in city center. try boating on Highfields Lake. nottingham host events in city center like the Christmas market
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Nottingham has a very diverse community.
socializing_tips: Talk to anyone and everyone. I cannot stress this enough everyone is so welcoming and everyone wants to make friends. have breakfast and dinner with new people as often as you can. speak to people in your halls.
cultural_challenges: none.
culture_appreciated: the diversity and openness.
top3_advice: enjoy it, because time on exchange flies by. take photos and videos of everything anf everyone. say yes to plans, the most spontaneous plans ended up being the most memorable and enjoyable.
other_useful_info: George Green > Hallward library Portland is a great place to meet new people
most_rewarding: you meet a different version of yourself on exchange, these new experiences, the exposure, it all shape you into something new.
greatest_challenge: I stayed over Christmas and when you become so accustomed to people around you at every hour of everyday. it was very hard to stay in a place that felt like a ghost town when everyone left for break. Because being on campus means mostly only student or faculty member are browsing around on the grounds. when everyone is gone, it is SO lonely.

crucial_aspects: The most crucial thing for me was to visit an English speaking country so that I could better my legal English skills. Furthermore, I wanted to choose a university that valued diversity and social well being for the students, which UoN definitely provided.
info_ease: For UoN, they really do take you by the hand and help you each step of the way. At no point of my arrival did I feel lost or uncertain. I knew where I had to be and when. They also send mails out frequently that explained where we could find the information needed to keep up with our schedule and etc.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any additional assistance.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: UoN has its own portal and they send you a thorough description of how you register into both the institution and also the modules that you want to take. On their website, they also have a step by step guide of how to fill out everything and what documents you should have ready for registration.
registration_help: You could always contact IT or the exchange students center.
registration_success: Very succesful, I got all the classes that I wanted. But you have to be fast when it comes to registering for the modules because they work with the first come first serve principle.
registration_advice: Just read all the emails and the guides that they give you. Then breathe and take it a step at a time.
course_level: I took all level 4 courses and my contact person/adviser from UoN did warn me that the classes may be a bit hard. I did not feel that way. The classes were easy enough to follow, even with a background in Danish law. It really did help that I have gotten my LL.B. already because now I know how law works and which methods to use when studying. There is still some adjusting to do but nothing that is too bad.
teaching_comparison: Because I am an LL.M. student I only had seminars, which differs from my experience that I had at UCPH in my undergraduate. I did though like how the professor engage with the students and don't give us too many readings for the class but rather explain the topic of the day and lets us use the knowledge that we have gained on an issue that the professor has written on our study page the week or day before.
courses_enrolled: Fundamental Principles of Business and Commercial Law, Private International Law of Intellectual Property and International Investment Law.
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of them.
unexpected_costs: Cost for trips that I took with the uni - Trips to local cities around England
cost_comparison: Everything is less expensive than here in Denmark. Groceries and just personal goods especially.
activities_available: I took dance, ice skating and also did some travelling with the travel society
activities_recommended: Do some type of sport!! I cannot stress this enough. It is the best way to meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: If you can visit the different cities around England, then do it. A lot of my friends also went to Scotland or Belfast, because it is easily accessible.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy.
socializing_tips: Be open, smile and say "Hi, where are you from? What do you study?" This always starts a good conversation.
cultural_challenges: Mostly the very specific saying that they have in Nottinghamshire county. Things like "tea" being dinner or "ey, up!" meaning hello.
culture_appreciated: How open and non-judgemental everyone is.
top3_advice: Be open, be kind and say yes to all opportunities
other_useful_info: Arrive a couple of days before school starts because it gives you time to explore the city you live in now. Also, walk around one day with google maps to help you and see if you can memorise some things. I did this and after a week and a half I could find my way around the city without any form of help and also knew what busses would take me where.
most_rewarding: Meeting the most amazing friend group and experiencing life with them.
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to everyday life in another country alone - But it also made me grow personally and academically.

arrival_assistance: A good amount of e-mails and contacts persons to reach out to. Also a contact buddy, which was a student who, in my case, had been on exchange in Copenhagen and was ready to answer any questions.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_help: Contact persons we could reach out to if need be.

teaching_comparison: The teachers/professors are very good (at least on the courses I took). Very open for questions and stopping by their office if you would need that.
courses_enrolled: I had Issues in Company Law, Intellectual Property and Maritime Law
recommended_courses: IP and Issues in Company Law was very good courses with good teachers. Maritime law is interesting but the professor, even though he is very good at what he does, is strict and the course is tough(er) to get good grades in.

activities_recommended: Go to pubs and travel with your friends.
weekend_recommendations: Dublin, Glasgow and Edinburgh are all very nice cities.

cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Going to pubs and playing pool with the guys you meet. Very easy and nice to do every week.
top3_advice: Maybe join a society if you're interested in a sport or activity. There are A LOT of options. Go the extra mile to talk to people. Makes the exchange way more fun. Travel in the UK. It's very cheap and there are a lot of nice places.
other_useful_info: Not really.
most_rewarding: Going to pubs with the other exchange students. Easy and fun way to socialize with the friends.
greatest_challenge: Didn't really experience big challenges. Maybe saving money would probably be the most generic one, but I had the opportunity to work during my stay, so not the greatest problem for me.

culture_appreciated: Their openess to foreigners and their focus on cleanliness in Ningbo.

most_rewarding: The friendships I made along the way. I made friends from all over the world by trying new things and being open.

crucial_aspects: It was important for me that the destination was somewhere I have never been before, as well as the location of the university in the given country.

arrival_assistance: I didn't really recieve any assistance, except for emailing questions to my home- and host university.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

weekend_recommendations: i would strongly encourage people to explore the rest of china in the weekends and holidays. I went to Shanghai multiple times, beijing, shenzhen and much more during my weekends.
culture_adjustment: it wasnt that difficult, because UNNC is an international university.
socializing_tips: i found it the easiest to find local friends during my classes.
cultural_challenges: learning to use all the apps, that are essential to living in china.
culture_appreciated: i loved how accesible everything was

other_useful_info: use your tutors! they know everything.
most_rewarding: making new friends and exploring China.
greatest_challenge: juggling exams with the want to adventure. I, and all the other exchange students i talked to, experienced a kinda stressful feeling, because we didn't want to waste our time i China, but also wanted to do well in school.

crucial_aspects: Since I have earlier had problems with home sickness it was important for me to choose a country with a similar culture to mine. However I still wanted to explore something new, so I chose a destination where I knew that was possible. Since I am from Denmark, Norway was the perfect destination for that. The culture (and language) is similar, but the nature is so different and beautiful.
info_ease: I went on exchange at the University of Oslo. They have a great website with all the information about what you need to do before you enter Norway and when you arrive in Norway. They have guides on how to apply and so on, and they even have a packing list and a video showing how to dress like a real norwegian. I went there during the autumn semester and got to experience three very different seasons with weather from 25 celcius degrees to -10 celcius degrees. However, it was more tricky to find information about the COVID-19 situation, since they announce the new restrictions and so on with very short warning. So a good advice is to stay updated everyday.
arrival_assistance: The university arranges a buddy week (introduction/orientation week) in the week before the semester starts. In this week we did a lot of social stuff like barbequeing, trips and games. This created a good foundation for new friendships and it was an easy way to meet new people. During this week we also got a tour around the campus, information about the university and activities you can do besides your studies. We also had a small sightseeing in Oslo.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You have to register for courses in a program called Studentweb. Here you also find your dates of exams, grades and so on later in the semester. You choose courses of 30 credits in total and wait and hope to get the ones you have registered for. If you do not get accepted to the course you wanted you will have another opportunity to apply for the courses that are still available.
registration_help: At the website of the University of Oslo it is possible to find guides that explains how to register.
registration_success: The courses are not present in studentweb all at once (some are shown later than others). This meant that when I wanted to register for courses I could not find all the courses I wanted. The University of Oslo recommended me to apply as soon as possible for courses to be sure to get the ones I wanted. So to be sure to get the two courses I found a third course that was not my first priority, but ok, and registered for all at ones.
registration_advice: The registration period is long which makes it possible to wait for all your wanted courses to show, but it will decrease your chances of getting in. Therefore I would advice to do what I did and apply as soon as possible so that you are sure to get at least some of the courses you want. I ended up finding the last course very fun and interesting, even though it was not what I wanted to begin with. Also, use the website of the University of Oslo! A lot of help is to be found there!
course_level: Two out of three courses were a mix of bachelor and master students. However I did not find it hard to follow the classes. The difference between thoses courses and the course with only bachelor students is that the two mixed courses were more specified on a subject as fx Henrik Ibsen or time in audiovisual media. I found the level very similar to the courses at the University of Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was very similar compared to UCPH. In one of my courses we had lectures once a week where we learned about a topic and a seminar the day after where we talk more about a specific text or film related to that topic. The other courses consisted only of seminars, which I have not yet experienced at the UCPH, however I do believe that this kind of structure exists as well. However one thing differs. Eventhough all of my three course were 10 credits, two of them only lasted half a semester. This reminds a bit of a block structure.
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled the three following courses: MEVIT1110 - Audiovisual Aesthetics MEVIT3529 - Audiovisual Media Temporalities: Temporality in Films, Series, Games and Social Media IBS2105 - Ibsen Between Cultures
recommended_courses: I was in generel happy with all three courses, but I would mostly recommend the course MEVIT1110 - Audiovisual Aesthetics. It is perfect if you are interested in film or media in generel. At each lecture we started out learning about a specific term like mise-en-scene, different forms of editing and so on. After an hour we would watch a movie and then end with a small lecture about that specific movie. The day after we would have a seminar where we practised using what we learned about the day before. A very well structured and relaxing course, but also the course where I learned the most.
unexpected_costs: Your new friends probably want to travel around all of Norway with you, so make sure to save up some money for this! I spent around 3000 DKK but depending on how many places you want to visit the expenses can go up or down.
cost_comparison: Food in Norway is in generel a bit more expensive than in Denmark. However it you go to the right stores (Kiwi and Rema 1000) it is possible to find good deals and cheap brands. The alcohol is way more expensive. In supermarkets it is possible to find beers for a good price but if you go to a bar the cheapest beer can easily be three times as expensive as a cheap beer in Denmark. A good advice is therefore to use the student bars. Museums and similar activities often have a great student discount, which makes it possible to experience cultural things while you are away. A good advice is just to expect everything to be a bit more expensive, look for the discounts and make use of SIO free events.
activities_available: SIO have fitness centers around in Oslo, one located on campus. Not far from campus is another fitness center with swimming pool and tennis and badminton courts that you can book. In the beginning of the semester the university will arrange association days where you can learn about all the different associations. A few examples of associations are choir, outdoor, knitting, d&d and way more! There is definitely something for everyone. At campus they have lots of cafes and places to eat (with vegan options as well). Not far from campus is a place called Chau de Neuf which is a bar for students. Here they throw parties, concerts and make other events. On campus they also have a lot of student driven bars and if you want to get cheaper drinks you can become a volunteer here. In the beginning of the semester SIO arrange a weekend where you can get free tickets to different activities around the city. This semester it included trips to a theme park, SUP boarding, a guided tour in the opera house and way more.
activities_recommended: If you like sports and outdoor I would recommend to go hiking in the mountains around Sognsvann, or other places outside of Oslo. If you do not like outdoor but does like sport I would recommend joining the gym (Athletica). They have lots of centers around the city and a very student friendly price of only 205 NOK pr month. This give you acces to group sessions, the swimming pool, the badminton and tennis court and all the centers. I would also recommend keeping an eye of the events that SIO arrange (perhaps on their facebook or instagram). It is cheap and you meet a lot of other students. A good way to meet other students is to join an association - especially because you here meet people with the same interests as you.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend them to go hiking! The nature is so beautiful and looks different everytime you go out. If possible take a trip to another city in Norway like Bergen, Trondheim or Stavanger. I was in Tromsø and it was the greatest and most beautiful experience of my life. Also, I recommend to go to a student bar and get a feeling of the student life in Oslo. And of course, go on a sightseeing in Oslo cause they have some beautiful attractions like the opera house, the new munch museum and the royal palace.
culture_adjustment: My feeling is that the people in Norway are very similar to the people in Denmark. Besides that the culture is also very similar, and this made it easy to adjust. I have a few norwegian friends in Oslo from earlier so for me it was easy to understand norwegian. My experience however is that even though you do not feel comfortable with the norwegian language before, you will learn it very quick.
socializing_tips: Since I already knew some students in Oslo it was easy for me to meet more local students. If you do not know anyone beforehand I will recommend to join associations, try to socialize during seminars (there will always be norwegian students in your class) or volunteer at the student bars.
cultural_challenges: I did not find anything challenging regarding cultural differences, since the differences are very small
culture_appreciated: I appreciated how the norwegian students reminds me a lot about the danish students.
top3_advice: Explore the nature, take part in SIOs events and be open to new experiences
other_useful_info: Enjoy your stay, time will go fast!
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience is my new friendships. It is so interesting to meet and be a part of all these different cultures!
greatest_challenge: At the University of Copenhagen all my courses are in danish, so the biggest challenge for me was to suddenly have lectures and seminars in english - and especially exams!

I wanted to improve my Norwegian language, but alsio to understand the development of the Norwegian language better. In many ways, I think that the Danish language could learn a lot from Norwegian Bokmål. In addition to the choosing the destination, exploring the nature in Norway was also one of the main reason to choose Oslo Universitet. The mountains, the fjords and the natural phenomenas that Norway can offer was definitely also a main factor for choosing Oslo. Furthermore, it is easily to explore the nature such as the mountains, the fjords in Oslo. It only takes 30-40 min. with the tramp to go to the mountains. You can in the Summer or in the Autumn visit the many islands that are in Oslo Fjords and in the Winther you can easily go skiing in the mountains.
