crucial_aspects: I chose my destination based on my personal interest in Arctic Science, and UNIS is the best university offering hands-on insight into the physical geography of a High-Arctic setting as well as specialised Arctic geographic field methods.
overall_comments: It has been the best educational and social experience I have ever partaken in. UNIS is a highly professional university with dedicated and competent staff, and the remote setting means that everyone get to experince the true Arctic and partake in the local community.
info_ease: Before arrival all necessary information was sent to me via email, from how to arrive from the airport to the first day at UNIS. From there information was communicated by teachers on a regular basis.
arrival_assistance: When arriving at the university you enter the reception where you state your name and are handed a letter with all information you need as well as an access card to the university, library, printing etc. and you are directed to your first location, where you receive further information. Simple and easy.
arrival_comments: As always, when at a new institution it can be hard to find your way around, so further information about where rooms are located could have been helpful. But you can easily yourself take a walk around the halls and locate the rooms, that are all named, in advance.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It has been the best educational and social experience I have ever partaken in. UNIS is a highly professional university with dedicated and competent staff, and the remote setting means that everyone get to experince the true Arctic and partake in the local community.
registration_process: You apply for the courses through the UNIS website. UNIS sends you a link with an offer in case of admission, and you confirm if you wish to attend. And that is it.
registration_help: KU contacted UiO that sent me a link to register in (a formality). You register yourself at UNIS directly through their website and can always contact them via email or phone if help is needed. They respond immediately (so does UiO).
registration_success: I applied for the classes I wanted, and was lucky to get a place at all of them.
registration_advice: Look through the course catalogue on their website (under studies) and apply for anything you find interesting. UNIS will admit you to all the courses you want if there is space. And then you can choose and accept the courses you want to attend.
academics_comments: It has been the best educational and social experience I have ever partaken in. UNIS is a highly professional university with dedicated and competent staff, and the remote setting means that everyone get to experince the true Arctic and partake in the local community.
course_level: The level of the courses are very high and hands-on as the university is located in the setting you are studying. I have learned more about physical geography in the six months I was there, than I have the last three years at a theoretical education at KU.
teaching_comparison: KU is solely based on theory minus 1-2 courses. UNIS is solely based on field work minus 1-2 courses. It provides you with skills that are highly usefull and sought out in the field of Arctic Science.
courses_enrolled: AG-204 The Physical Geography of Svalbard AG-221 Arctic Physical Geographical Field Techniques
recommended_courses: These two courses are intertwined and are highly recommended to take together. I would highly recommend these two courses (if they still exist) as they provide a profound insight into the entire field of Arctic geographical science. Besides these, there are plenty of very good master courses with the same type of focus, such as glaciaology and hydrology.
unexpected_costs: I had a hospital bill of about 400.00
cost_comparison: Food is very expensive as everything is shipped there. Alcohol is slightly cheaper than mainland Norway as Svalbard is taxfree. There are a lot of nice sportshops where items are also slightly cheaper than mainland and UNIS students can get discounts there too (10-15%).
activities_available: The student counsil organised parties, dinners, bonfires, bingo, and other social events. They also arranged a regular night at Svalbard Bryggeri for students with 20% discount every other Saturday. There are a kayak club, and a local gym where you can exercise, play volleyball, floorball, swim etc.
activities_recommended: Hiking in the area is the best way to see Svalbard. There are endless beautiful hikes to do around town (grab a bunch of people and a riffle and head out into the wilderness) to the mountain plateaus or to Nordenskiöldtoppen (1050 m a.s.l.). Join all the local events: Dark Season Blues Festival (blues festival), Arctic Chamber music festival (classical music), talks in Kulturhuset, the cinema, visit the local bars, waffle and game nights at the church, and visit the dogyards. UNIS also has a student cabin in Bjørndalen that you can borrow which is a really nice valley to visit and where you and your fellow students can have a bonfire and cook dinner together.
weekend_recommendations: Same as above. There are also boat trips to Pyramiden and Barentsburg that are definitely worth a trip.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The town and community are very small and everyone are very nice. Be polite and greet everyone, and your stay will be very pleasent.
socializing_tips: All students are there for a limited time, there are no local students. This also means that everyone partakes in all the social acitivities, so you will get to know everyone. You will have a kitchen where you meet people, and as all students live in the same building, you will eventually meet everyone, maybe at the kitchen-to-kitchen party?
cultural_challenges: I found no such challenges, as everyone you socialise with are new to the area, and therefore act very nice and inclusive to all. The town is small and quite, so treat it that way.
culture_appreciated: I appreciate the small town and community, and the closeness to wilderness and wildlife, how people live under nature's conditions and not the other way around.
top3_advice: The environment is cold and teaching is based on field work, so bring warm and practical clothes (hiking pants, wind and waterproof jacket and good hiking boots). Remember that you also have to go to class and attend parties, so also bring nice clothes (i forgot this). Take advantage of you time there, and go on as many hikes as you can while there is still daylight.
other_useful_info: Don't worry too much about the application process through another university, as that will sort out, just make sure that you have an application in with UNIS with the courses you want to apply for. You can find all you need to know about the town, proper clothing, safety etc. at the UNIS website. Your first week at the university is a safety course, where you learn everything you need to know about safety: hiking in the field, travelling by ocean, and polar bear safety, so you need not worry about any of this.
most_rewarding: Everything! The courses were absolutely brilliant, the field work was amazing, the weekend hikes were breathtaking, and the occasional, daily reindeer encounter is just adorable.
greatest_challenge: Your limitations are moved when you work your way through the wilderness of Svalbard, whether it is crossing a wild river, fearing to fall in, or hiking to the plateaus, and have a fear of heights. Afterwards you feel like you can do anything.

arrival_assistance: Information per mail.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_help: Erasmus coordinator and coordinator at different departments helped me through the process of finding courses that suited me since my initial choices were not all available in the end.
registration_success: One of the courses I wanted to take was not available in that semester as it turned out. They updated the course list very late I would say, so when time came for me to register, most of the courses I had set my eyes on were not even available.
registration_advice: Be aware that the courses shown in the course lists online might not all be available when the time comes for registering. If you are Scandinavian speaking, do ask if there is the possibility to take courses given in Norwegian, if you don't find suiting courses among those offered to exchange students in English.

recommended_courses: The futures of work - in the field of human geography, very interesting, and makes you reflect on your own future of work. Inspiring professor teaching the course.

activities_recommended: Nature is amazing around Oslo. Go for hikes, skiing, go out to the islands. There is a lot to explore if you are an active person.

culture_adjustment: Easy. Since I am Swedish it is not much of a difference. I would say its like a mix of Sweden and America in a weird way. crucial_aspects: I am studying public health and Norway is a country where health care has a high priority. Norway is to some extend similar to Denmark in the way they organize health care, but there are also some differences. I thought it would be interesting to go to Oslo University, because they offer some very interesting courses, that I am not able to take in Denmark. Furthermore I thought it was interesting to get another perspective on the subject of public health that I could take with me back to Denmark in my further studies and career. I believe that my stay in Oslo has provided me with that. Additionally I really like to be in the nature, thus the norwegian nature and the opportunity to experience that was also a crucial reason for choosing Oslo as my study destination.
overall_comments: I thought the courses were very relevant and interesting. Furthermore I got some new friends and I generally really enjoyed being here.
info_ease: I thought it was quite easy to find the information that I needed to know upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: I attended an online introduction to Norway, but that was more to the culture and what to expect. I also attended a meeting with the international coordinator at UIO when I arrived.
arrival_comments: I would have liked to have a more thorough introduction where I would also meet more (exchange)students from the university
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I thought the courses were very relevant and interesting. Furthermore I got some new friends and I generally really enjoyed being here.
registration_process: I was in contact with an international coordinator at UIO, who also signed my online learning agreement. When he saw on the learning agreement which courses I wanted to register for he made sure that I was signed up for those. There was one course which was outside the faculty and for that course I needed to contact the course leader and the other faculty in order to sign up, but that was also rather straight forward.
registration_help: See the above description.
registration_success: There was just one course that wasn't available afterall. But other than that I could register for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Take contact to the international coordinator/person in charge of the online learning agreement, they are happy to help.
academics_comments: I thought the courses were very relevant and interesting. Furthermore I got some new friends and I generally really enjoyed being here.
course_level: All the courses I took were on a masters level, but I experienced that some of the courses had a somewhat lower level than what I am used to at University of Copenhagen. Thus, that was a bit disappointing.
teaching_comparison: In some courses the teaching style was quite similar. I had three courses that lasteded to two weeks each. This is very different from what I have experienced before. I got used to these short courses, but I think I learn more from having the course spread out over a longer period. Further I had a few courses where the academic level was lower compared to UCPH.
courses_enrolled: HELSEF4405 - Kjønn, kropp og medikalisering PSY4116 - Sentrale temaer i anvendt helsepsykologi HMAN4210 - Leadership, Management and Organization Development INTHE4113 - Introduction to Medical Anthropology: Key Concepts and Perspectives HELSEF4511 - Digitalisering, samhandling og innovasjon
recommended_courses: HELSEF4405 - Kjønn, kropp og medikalisering. I really liked this course. But I would also recommend introduction to medical anthropology
unexpected_costs: I don't think I encountered any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Almost everything was more expensive than I expected. Norway is just a very expensive country to live in.
activities_available: There was e.g. a weekend course in cross-country skiing that I participated in. Further it was possible to students to be a member of a sportsclub at a reasonable price. There were not too many social activities which was a shame.
activities_recommended: I thought it was a lot of fun to attend the cross country skiing course. I really wanted to learn it and it was also a fun way to meet some new people. I know that they make more sports activities like that and I really like that.
weekend_recommendations: I spend a lot of weekends in the winter going cross country skiing. It's possible to do it just outside of Oslo which is really nice and so much fun. When the weather became better I really enjoyed going on shorter as well as longer trips to the nature to hike and experience the nature. Furthermore Oslo is a nice city with lots of museums and nice neighborhoods to explore.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy. I think there are a lot of similarities between Denmark and Norway.
socializing_tips: I got a few local friends because I had courses in Norwegian. I would say that this is a good way to meet some local people.
cultural_challenges: I didn't experience any very challenging differences
culture_appreciated: I really appreciate that Norway offer so many opportunities to be outdoors. And it's great to experience how so many Norwegians also use the outdoors.
top3_advice: Be prepared that everything is very expensive. If it wasn't for the grands that I was lucky to receive I would have had a hard time to make it work economically. Know that it takes some time to adjust both to "normal life", but also to the new university and new courses, even if the culture and university is quite similar to your own. And I would very much recommend going to Norway if you enjoy being outdoors - they have a lot of things to offer here.
other_useful_info: If it's possible try and see if you can attend an introduction week even if it isn't offered at your specific study. I know people who could then attend an introduction week of another study/faculty. Just contact the international coordinator and see if they can help you find a solution.
most_rewarding: I really enjoyed getting to know the small differences between the norwegian and the danish culture. Those are things that I wouldn't have noticed if I was just here on a short visit. Furthermore I really enjoyed most of the courses that I was able to take here. That provided me with new knowledge and new perspectives, that I don't think I could've gotten in Denmark. I also really enjoyed being able to experience the beautiful nature of Norway!
greatest_challenge: I think it was a challenge to get local friends. I had hoped to get more local friends, but I mainly became friends with other international students.
other_comments: No :)

unexpected_costs: Not much - Pretty much the same costs as denmark
cost_comparison: Alcohol and food is very expensive, but clothes, especially outdoor clothes, are cheaper then in Denmark
activities_available: The UiO SiO provides a platform for students to create and share their own student association, where you can search and apply to those, that peak your interest.
activities_recommended: Anything that requires you to be a group,or do something together - Sports, boardgames, politics. This is the best way to meet other students outside of school.
weekend_recommendations: Make use of the beautiful nature of Norway - Visit the mountains or spend time in the parks. During winter, use some of the winter sport oppertunities, which aren't possible in Denmark
culture_adjustment: Very easy - Danish and Norwegian culture is very similar.
socializing_tips: Talk to people - Like in Denmark, we are very closed off untill we actually talk to people, and then people are quick to open up slightly. And just be honest about trying to find new friends.
cultural_challenges: Crosswalks are less regulated by lights and more by trust in the other person - Many crosswalks don't have light regulation outside the center of Oslo, and there's not a sophisticated bike lane system like in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: the norwegian connections with nature, and their philosophy of "life to work", instead of the other way around.
top3_advice: 1. Enjoy the ride - There will be up and downs, but ultimately make the short amount of time you're aboard be as enjoyable as possible. 2. Carpe diem/Seize the day - You're experiencing a new country, and things will be different. Embrace the differences, and use them to learn about your own culture and yourself. 3. Take your time - Adjusting to a new daily life an take a while, and it differs for each person. Allow yourself to be frustrated with the changes, without blaming yourself because "You should be adjusted by now". You're your own bets ally in the exchange, so don't become your own worst enemy.
other_useful_info: Learn to prepare lunches from home - Food is expensive, and therefore cafeteria food will also be expensive from what you're used to.
most_rewarding: Learning and experiencing a new culture, and broaden your horizon, both in terms of language, people and culture.
greatest_challenge: Missing the usual everyday life, you had gotten used to before leaving. You will experiene homesickness and missing your friends and family, which can be tough. However, getting through that and learning to appreciate what you are returning home to, is a great personal growth as well.

crucial_aspects: Having the opportunity to take part in an internship with practical fieldwork and hands-on experience with great resources and facilities in a great and interesting location was the main reason in choosing Svalbard. Additionally, I wanted to get to know the location in which I will be staying for 5 months next year as part of my masters thesis work.

Really enjoyed Svalbard, it has great resources at the university and the accommodation, and they are always helpful when you need something. The location is very remote and the only reason the experience isn't a 9 or 10 is that the recreational side of Svalbard is limited with requiring a rifle and flare gun to go outside the town for hikes as well as no real social or recreational groups available.

Additionally, it is easy to acquire information from other students in addition to the reception at UNIS who are always happy to help.

arrival_comments: My orientation was sufficient however that was due to my supervisor taking care of me and explaining everything in this aspect. For students that are going to study there, I believe it is a bit more difficult and you need to seek information from reception at UNIS.

unexpected_costs: If you come prepared with all the necessary gear, no costs are unexpected.
cost_comparison: Not more than I expected but food and especially fresh fruit and vegetables are really expensive due to the isolated nature of the town. I would recommend buying the frozen vegetables for this as they are much cheaper. However due to the lack of paying taxes, the outdoor gear as well as alcohol is relatively cheap compared to mainland Norway.
activities_available: While there is a gym in the town, there are no cultural, athletic and social activity groups for students available. You have to really make your own group with people, the most popular activity in the summer is hiking while in the spring I know skiing and snow mobile trips are very popular. There is a big Facebook messenger group chat with all the students in Svalbard in which you can try and meet people outside your classes. Additionally, most people party on Friday nights, so that is also a good place to meet people to make a group of friends.
activities_recommended: Definitely find a group and go hiking around Longyearbyen and beyond if you are there in the summer as it is amazing views and a great way to explore the island.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking, go on a ferry around the island and go in the sauna.
culture_adjustment: Very easy as you are constantly around internationals in the accommodation and the culture is very much like Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: There are no real local students, they are all internationals. Just go out and meet people, you will find everyone in the same accommodation so its easy.
cultural_challenges: None, it is the same as an international student at KU
culture_appreciated: That everyone is an international student and in the same boat. Everyone is very open.
top3_advice: Be ready for cold weather and make sure to bring appropriate clothes although you can buy outdoor and warm clothes there. Food is very expensive, be aware of this. The expenses can stack up without you even noticing. Lastly, you NEED a rifle to go out of town and it is highly recommended and required in some instances that you need another person to go with you. Don't go past the polar bear warning signs without being prepared.
other_useful_info: Don't hesitate to contact UNIS reception and the student services as they are really helpful.
most_rewarding: The beautiful landscapes and amazing wildlife.
greatest_challenge: The weather.

crucial_aspects: The location (high Arctic) and fieldwork included in the courses (since little fieldwork is conducted at my home university).

The courses were chaotic, and some did not live up to their own course descriptions. We were overburdened with too much compulsary work but the academic level was not high enough. Thus, we were stressed, but our professors did not go in depth with the material, and we did not have enough time to study on our own to compensate for this. recommended_courses: These three courses are the ones to take for environmental science students in the spring at UNIS.
unexpected_costs: It is very cold in March (coldest month) and I had to buy some extra layers for field work. Going on guided trips in your free time in Svalbard is very expensive, so it's a good idea to put some money aside for just that.
cost_comparison: Vegetables were very expensive. The canteen is also very expensive, so it is better to prepare your own lunch.
activities_available: The housing provided some activities, such as knitting, painting, waffle night. Some student groups volunteered to plan hikes, and there is a cabin that you can be lucky to book (through a lottery). There is also student equipment, that you can apply for for your own private trips. There was one dinner in the beginning for people doing the safety course, and some friday gatherings where you could by some canned beers during the semester. Also, there were some extracurriculum lectures at UNIS which was interesting. But no parties at UNIS and the friday "bar" closed very early.
activities_recommended: Go on a lot of hikes, because the nature is beautiful and the landscape and weather changes so quickly (24h darkness to 24 sunlight in just a few months). Fruene is a cosy café where you can get cheaper yarn for knitting every thursday.
weekend_recommendations: Again, go on hikes.
culture_adjustment: The culture is not difficult adjusting to, other than the fact that there isn't a lot of high cultural offers. It is my perception that most locals are families or people living there for natural experiences, so if you like art museums, quality music, cinema, etc., you will miss it here. It is the nature that is interesting here.
socializing_tips: Every student there is international.
cultural_challenges: none comes to mind.
culture_appreciated: the culture for hiking, and enjoying nature.
top3_advice: 1. Prepare for the courses to be unorganised. 2. Become a member of Longyearbyen Travel Club - then you can go on boat trips for example for a reduced price. 3. Be aware that the Arctic is a challenging place to live which can be overwhelming at times. With no sunlight in the winter, snowstorms, and a lot of energy spent on keeping warm, you should make sure to get your vitamins and tend to yourself. With polar bears in the wild, extreme weather and avalanche risks, a lot of preparation goes into a hike.
other_useful_info: Bruktikken is a "store" where you get second hand clothes for free.
most_rewarding: The experiences in nature and the social life.
greatest_challenge: Dealing with the Arctic winter.

registration_process: First I applied at Oslo University. Then I applied for courses at UNIS in October (the course registration deadline at UNIS was before getting an reply from Oslo University). For the course registration you could only apply for courses within the same department by prioritizing the courses in order. But since the courses were in different blocks and I wanted to register for several courses and from mixed departments, this was super confusing. So I had to e-mail UNIS and explain them my wishes in order to make it clear (it was just not possible through the course registration system). I applied for 5 courses and after some weeks I got answers from most of them. Most of them I was told I was disqualified while I got a waiting list spot on one course. So not enough to do the exchange at all. I e-mailed UNIS because I did not agree that I was disqualified and then they changed this so I got a spot in another course. But at this point I still only had 1 course of 10 ECTS, so I still needed two more. In my desperation I saw that the registration deadline was extended for a few courses, so I registered from one there and got a spot. Now I only needed 1 more course, and the only thing i could do was to hope I would get a spot in the course I had a waiting list spot. On December 8 2023 I got the message that I was offered a spot through the waiting list and I accepted the offer. So only then I had enough courses to go on the ERASMUS exchange. So this was exactly 1 month before the semester started, so I had to fix equipment for high arctic, housing and flight tickets with very short time and this was super stressful.
registration_help: I could call and email UNIS.
registration_success: Not super successful at first, but apparently, if you argument against the decline, you can change the decision. So in the end, I was pretty succesful with registering for the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: If you do master exchange, good luck. It is super messy and stressful. My advice is to send motivation letter and maybe even a recommendation from your professor to succesfully register for the classes you want. UNIS say they dont want that, but apparently, people do this.
academics_comments: I went on exchange due to academic interests, but it ended up being the outdoor and social experiences that made it a great stay rather than the courses
course_level: Not high, most people both BA and MA could have followed the courses
teaching_comparison: Much more practical and much more fieldwork. Not a lot of reading and theory, but a lot of presentations, posters and discussions
courses_enrolled: AB-329 Arctic Winter Ecology, AG-330 Permafrost and Periglacial Environments and AG-342 The Marine Cryosphere and its Cenozoic History
recommended_courses: I would recommend Arctic Winter Ecology, the topics are super interesting and the professors are super motivated. I also partly recommend Permafrost and Periglacial Environments, since it is a super interesting topic, but our professors got sick so someone else took over the course with very short notice. Therefore, it was lacking some content and structure. The Marine Cryosphere and its Cenozoic History is also a super cool topic, but this was a very low intensity course with very little class activities, so I was a bit bored.
unexpected_costs: I was on Svalbard in the spring semester, so snowscootering and skiing are super central activities. This is some serious expenses if you want to take part in this. But if you do exchange in Svalbard in the fall semester, this is none of your concern.
cost_comparison: Food is more expensive. Equipment is less expensive because there is a great second hand community in Longyearbyen and also the sports stores are tax free.
activities_available: There are a few bars in town, and there is also a friday bar at UNIS.
activities_recommended: I really enjoying doing outdoor activities, such as skiing, scootering and hiking. I highly recommend this since Svalbard has stunning nature.
weekend_recommendations: Outdoor activities with friends.
culture_adjustment: Super easy since the norwegian culture is close to danish culture
socializing_tips: No students are really local in UNIS
cultural_challenges: Norwegians are sometimes speaking norwegian even with internationals around. Also, they tend to socialize more with internationals when they drink alcohol and tend to be less extroverted e.g. in class
culture_appreciated: Norwegians are very happy with outdoor activities
top3_advice: Dont take a decline on course registration too serious, just explain why you think you are qualified and their decision might change Think about what you like to do in your free time when deciding if you go to svalbard in spring or summer season. If you like the extreme, scootering and skiing, you need more money but you will also have an amazing time. Be ready for fomo though! On the other hand, if these are not things you appreciate, choose the fall season, but be prepared that you are stuck in Longyearbyen with 2500 inhabitants and that you can more or less only get as far away from town as you can walk.

crucial_aspects: Going on exchange in Norway allowed me to get visits from home, but also to be closer with family living in Norway. Moreover, I was motivated to go there because of the nature and I found the courses that UIO supplied more interesting than in other universities.
info_ease: It was very easy, since UiO is very good at informing and sending relevant information in advance.
arrival_assistance: The department of social sciences at UiO sent a lot of relevant emails, which helped me a lot.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You can registrer for courses at Studentweb. However, the registration proces for master students can vary a bit. I experienced some troubles with it, but UiO was fast to respond at help me out.

course_level: I followed three master level courses that all had some kind of orientation toward master thesis. In one of them I learned to do a literature review since the exam had this form, and in the others I had to choose a methodology that had relevance for my master thesis. I found this very useful and I felt that the courses had a clear purpose on preparing the students for their master thesis.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was more intimate, personal and also more practical oriented in terms of writing af master thesis but also in terms of labor market skills. Hence, the style was a bit less focused on research and theoretical knowledge, and more on providing the students with actual skills to use in the future. This is different from UCPH in my opinion.
courses_enrolled: Course: STV4031 - Field Research for Political Science Course: STV4445B - EU and the Nation State - Institutional dynamics and political processes Course: STV4447 - Education policies in theory and practice - Policymaking in Norway and around the world
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of the three above listed courses, since they all contributed with valuable and new insights, and they were all very well structured. I felt that teachers in all three courses managed to create a safe space and good learning environments.
unexpected_costs: Norway is a big country, and if you want to explore it you have to either pay a lot for flight tickets to get to the northern parts or train tickets that can be expensive as well. Furthermore, going skiing is also expensive. Especially if you have to rent all the equipment yourself. However, I highly recommend doing so anyways!! But all in all, Norway is just very expensive to live in as a student, but they have many good offers for students that is worth looking into.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping is just very expensive. Especially vegetables, cheese and bread can be very expensive in supermarkets. Alcohol is expensive too - especially at cafés or restaurants. Also if you plan on being outdoors a lot, the right gear can also be quite expensive, but also worth it (Skiijackets, hiking boots, hiking pants etc.).

socializing_tips: Try to learn or speak norwegian - it makes you bond better. Also sports activities can be good.
cultural_challenges: I did not experience any.
culture_appreciated: Norwegians are very kind and helpful, and I enjoyed how much being outdoors is such a big part of many Norwegians everyday life.
top3_advice: 1. Choose courses that you find interesting so that you are more motivated to engage in the class discussions as the classes are more intimate 2. Use the campus! It is filled with very nice reading spots and cafés. 3. The level of the courses are pretty similar to those in UCPH, but be prepared that the attendance to a lot of the lectures and seminars are mandatory
other_useful_info: UiO is very helpful and you can most of the times get the help you need
most_rewarding: Becoming so well known with the norwegian nature, culture and language, and also having great experiences with new friends both in Oslo and on trips to other parts of the country.
greatest_challenge: My economy was definitely a challenge during my exchange. It is my experience that it is more difficult as a student going to Norway to get student grants since we get the highest Erasmus grant. Således kunne jeg opleve forskelle og ligheder blandt disse forskellige sundhedsvæsner. Ydermere ville jeg gerne erfare hvordan karriere mulighederne er her i Norge, da jeg har et ønske om at vende tilbage til Norge i mit fremtidige virke, som læge. Slutteligt var det vigtigt for mig, at vælge en destination hvor uddannelse og supervision er i højsædet, hvilket jeg ved at Oslo Universitets hospital er kendt for, sådan så jeg kunne lære mest muligt.

registration_comments: Generelt en rigtig god oplevelse, med fine arrangerede ophold.

Hvad der kan optimere denne proces er vanskeligt at sige, da man selvfølgelig skal have fat i en masse ansvarlige på de respektive afdelinger for, at sikre at jeg kan komme på klinisk ophold.

courses_enrolled: Kliniske rotaioner i 3 mdr. på hospitaler.

weekend_recommendations: Det er svært at have kliniske rotationer og rejse, da man kun har weekenderne fri. Men der er meget at lave i Oslo by og hvis man er til natur, er der også mange gode ture, at gå i og omkring Oslo.
culture_adjustment: Det var nemt. Kulturen minder meget om den danske. Det har kun været udfordrende med helligedage og søndage, da alle supermarkederne er lukkede, hvilket man lige skal være opmærksom på.
socializing_tips: Det har jeg desværre ikke har stor mulighed for, da jeg ikke har været eksponeret for dette. Men jeg ved at der for medicinstuderende er en større fest i foråret, hvor der er god mulighed for at lære norske medicinstuderende at kende.
cultural_challenges: Blot at supermarkederne var lukke om søndagen, men det var ikke en reel udfordring, men blot en tilvænningssag.
culture_appreciated: Alle er meget flinke og imødekommende samt inkluderende.
top3_advice: - Prøv at komme med til into uge for andre medicinstuderende i starten af dit ophold - Tag til ESN aktiviteter - Har et ophold henover maj-måned, da der sker mange ting i byen bl.a. nationaldagen
other_useful_info: Norge er et stort land, og man vil gerne opleve meget, når man er her, men der er virkelig mange ting i og omkring Oslo, som er værd at dykke ned i.
most_rewarding: Jeg har lært mange dygtige og søde læger at kende under mit ophold. Alle har, det meste af tiden, været imødekommende og villige til at lære fra sig. Det er spændende og udfordrende at opleve og leve i et helt nyt land, men ikke mindst meget værdifuldt og inspirerende.
greatest_challenge: Man er meget på hele tiden, og når man også har forskellige kliniske ophold kan man godt blive drænet for energi, men samtidig er det også spændende at se noget forskelligt.
other_comments: Ved ophold med kliniske rotationer på 3 mdr. vil jeg klart anbefale 4 rotationer. Det er netop nok til, at man får set noget forskelligt. Så ideelt 3 uger på hver afdeling.

crucial_aspects: As I was born in Denmark, but have spent 7 years as a child living in Sweden, the opportunity to be able to live in Norway and to therefore have lived in all three Scandinavian countries, are something I will enjoy looking back at in the future.
info_ease: Very easy, Oslo did a great job of providing great information that was easy to find. I found it easier than finding information at University of Copenhagen.
arrival_assistance: There was in the orientation week several lectures on how to find information and where all the important information were to be found.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I found it very easy, there were always a clear guide as to what I was supposed to do and how, they have a great and easy system, making it approachable for all.
registration_help: Lectures in the orientation week, both English and Norwegian sites, and a manageable webpage for students.
registration_success: Very, one of my classes was cancelled shortly upon arrival. But I quickly found another course suitable for my likings, and were able to switch to the new course quite easily.
registration_advice: Not much, just take it easy, it will all work out in the end. Oslo is a very modernised and easily managed university, and they make it easy for students and exchange students to discover how everything works.
course_level: They were great, easier for me as an English student, but they fit great with my degree and subject of study. But they were great, and the teachers were great. The Norwegian Life and Society course was made for international students and it was a very great and enlightening course, with a great introduction and run-through of Norway and its society, culture, and history.
teaching_comparison: It was in several ways similar. But it was also dissimilar. The teachers at Oslo were more close to the students and spoke of everything and also of more personal matters and how that might have affected them min their lives compared to what the teaching were about. Whereas Copenhagen is more straightforward and the teachers does not engage with the student's in the same way.
courses_enrolled: NORINT0500 – Norwegian Life and Society ENG2324 – Homotextuality: Queer Literature in English ENG2307 – Late 20th Century Literature in English
recommended_courses: Anything Nils Nissen (who taught Homotextuality: Queer Literature in English) teaches is worth everyones attention. He is a great teacher, and I really enjoyed his class. Audrey Camp was also a great teacher (Late 20th Century Literature in English) her class was informative and very exciting.
unexpected_costs: Many things in Oslo are free, but museums and other attractions have to be paid for (however Oslo offers a great deal of student discount)
cost_comparison: Norway is often considered to be an expensive city, and it is. But because the currency has been so low during my stay (100 DKK has been ca. 68-63 NOK) it was a great experience and things became less expensive for me because of the currency.
activities_available: There are a great deal of activities, UIO Blindern has both a sports club, and several places for social activities. Oslo is likewise hosting several outings and different social arrangements for the students, both for international and for Norwegian students.
activities_recommended: Museums, there are a great deal of different exciting museums to see and explore. Skiing in the winter. It only takes about 45 minutes from the city centre to get to the closest and bigger ski hill in Oslo Hiking, Sognsvann and other places in and around Oslo are beautiful places to walk and hike, both in the winter and in the summer. Sailing, there are several boats sailing from Aker Brygge to different islands around the Oslo fjord. And traveling, Norway is a big and great country with MANY different sceneries and a majestic landscape worth all the money. If you are here in the spring/summer semester. 17th of May was a great experience and so beautiful to watch.
weekend_recommendations: Museums, there are a great deal of different exciting museums to see and explore. Skiing in the winter. It only takes about 45 minutes from the city centre to get to the closest and bigger ski hill in Oslo Hiking, Sognsvann and other places in and around Oslo are beautiful places to walk and hike, both in the winter and in the summer. Sailing, there are several boats sailing from Aker Brygge to different islands around the Oslo fjord. And traveling, Norway is a big and great country with MANY different sceneries and a majestic landscape worth all the money.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, Norwegian and Danish people are quite similar.
socializing_tips: Talk to them! both international and Norwegians. Norwegians understand Danish! And if you try, you should be able to understand Norwegian quite well too. And speak with other exchange students from your home university. There might be someone you will get along with rather great.
cultural_challenges: There wasn't really any.
culture_appreciated: That it is so similar to Denmark. That is great.
top3_advice: Explore the city! It is smaller than you might think. Don't be afraid to take risks and explore new things Enjoy the winter, even though it might seem long, dark, and cold, it is also beautiful to experience a white winter, unlike in Denmark. The summer here is great. And the midnight sun is so enchanting each time you are awake when it is late.
other_useful_info: Blindern might seem dull. But there are many many fine things to find at the campus.
most_rewarding: To be able to live in Oslo and experience a place, city, and culture that is not Danish, has been great and so rewarding.
greatest_challenge: Personally, I had a difficulty finding many friends. However, I was content with those I found. And it was great to have family visit and show them the city and its beauty.

crucial_aspects: I decided to go on exchange in Oslo because it's within Europe, and I find it exciting to connect with other young people from across the Nordic region and Europe. Oslo is home to a highly regarded university with a renowned anthropology faculty, which was a major draw for me. On top of that, Norway's stunning landscapes offer a unique natural beauty that we simply don't have in Denmark.
info_ease: I found it very easy to access the information I needed, both before and after arriving in Oslo. The university's administration was highly approachable and responsive, and my accommodation was managed directly from the same campus where I studied. Everything was well-organized and intuitive, making the whole process seamless.
arrival_assistance: I received great support with arranging my accommodation, obtaining a student card, and discovering the introductory activities for exchange students on my campus. Additionally, I was guided on how to navigate the teaching portals and access course materials, which made settling in much easier.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I received emails with helpful links and guidance for course registration, and the platforms and portals I needed to use were straightforward and easy to navigate. Additionally, there was plenty of detailed information about the courses available beforehand, including exam formats and schedules, which was really convenient and made the process much smoother.
registration_help: I had the option to reach out to the office at the University of Oslo whenever I had questions or needed clarification about anything.
registration_success: I was able to enroll in all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure to check the exam dates and the class schedule to ensure that the courses you choose align well and don't conflict with each other.
course_level: I was satisfied with the overall level of my courses. I did take one course outside of anthropology, which was an introductory class on gender equality in the Nordic region. While I found it a bit basic, given its introductory nature, it was still engaging and interesting overall.
teaching_comparison: Compared to the teaching style I'm used to at the University of Copenhagen, I was very pleased with my experience. I enjoyed both my courses and my instructors, and I felt that, unlike at KU, there was less pressure and fewer unrealistic expectations placed on students regarding how much they could accomplish. It created a more balanced and less stressful learning environment.

recommended_courses: SOSANT2510 SOSANT2110
unexpected_costs: no one
cost_comparison: Food
activities_available: https://www.uio.no/english/student-life/associations/alphabetical/
activities_recommended: Make sure to take part in the orientation week!
weekend_recommendations: I highly recommend exploring places like Frognerseteren and Vettakollen for breathtaking views and hikes. Check out the Deichman Library for its modern architecture, and don't miss the Opera House, where you can walk on the roof for stunning cityscapes. Spend time in St. Hanshaugen and Grünerløkka for cozy cafés, vibrant streets, and a great atmosphere. A walk along the Akerselva river is also a must, as well as visiting the Munch Museum to dive into Norwegian art and culture. And there's so much more to discover—Oslo has something for everyone!
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture was very easy. The atmosphere was welcoming, and since there are many similarities between Nordic cultures, it felt natural to settle in. People were friendly, and the city has a relaxed vibe that made the transition smooth and enjoyable.
socializing_tips: If you're going on exchange to Oslo, I've got a few tips for you when it comes to meeting local students! First of all, make sure to join some student organizations or clubs. The university has tons of options, and it's a really easy way to meet people who share your interests. Also, don't skip the social events like parties, cultural evenings, or any activities organized by the university – they're great for breaking the ice. One thing I found really helpful was joining study groups for my courses. It's a natural way to get to know people, and it helps with coursework too! Also, spend time in the campus cafeteria or common areas – locals hang out there a lot, and it's a good place to strike up a casual conversation. Even though most people understand danish, learning a few Norwegian phrases is a great way to make the conversation flow.. Don't forget to check out some of the local student hotspots in Oslo, like Grünerløkka or St. Hanshaugen. These are super popular areas for students to hang out and relax. The most important thing is just to be open and proactive. Don't wait for others to approach you – introduce yourself, ask questions, and show curiosity about their culture.
cultural_challenges: nothing
culture_appreciated: What I appreciated most about the culture in Oslo was how people embrace the outdoors and prioritize enjoying life. I loved the tradition of going on hikes in the mountains or forests on Sundays – it's such a refreshing and grounding way to spend the weekend. I also really enjoyed the café culture; people seemed to take their time at bakeries, strolling around the city, and simply relaxing with friends or family. There's a lovely balance between being active and taking the time to unwind, which I found both inspiring and comforting.
top3_advice: 1. Be Prepared for Housing Arrangements: Most exchange students use SiO, which manages student housing in Oslo. It's a great option because it's reliable, the accommodations are well-maintained, and they're usually close to the university and city center. Apply as early as possible, and if you want to meet other students, consider choosing housing where you can share a kitchen. 2. Embrace the Outdoor Lifestyle: Norwegians love spending time in nature, and you'll have incredible opportunities to explore it too. Whether it's hiking to places like Vettakollen or Frognerseteren, or taking a stroll along Akerselva, make sure to take advantage of Oslo's amazing outdoor spaces. Pack some good walking or hiking shoes – you'll need them! 3. Plan Your Courses and Schedule Carefull: Check the course catalog and schedules thoroughly to make sure your courses don't overlap, especially with exams. The university provides detailed information about each course, including exam formats and timetables, so use it to your advantage. The system is straightforward, and you can usually get all the courses you want if you plan ahead. Bonus tip: Take part in the introduction week! It's a fantastic way to meet both local and international students and get settled into life in Oslo. Also, don't hesitate to reach out to the university administration if you have any questions – they're super helpful!

crucial_aspects: I've been to Norway before on vacation and loved it. I also have friends and connections in Norway which I knew prior to my arrival on exchange. I wanted to live and study in a country that is similar to Denmark i.e. not too much of a culture shock. Norway is a beautiful country with opportunities for hiking, skiing and other experiences in nature which are not possible in Denmark in the same way.
info_ease: Quite easy. In the beginning the University of Oslo had an orientation week which covered all the basics. This is ranged from navigating the course registration to extracurricular activities and life in Oslo itself. The university website also provides a lot of useful information but it can be a bit information dense.
arrival_assistance: I did not need assistance.
arrival_comments: I was pleasantly surprised at how much the host university cared about our arrival and wellbeing. On the first day of the orientation week, everyone was asked individually if they had arrived safe and sound and had found housing. In case someone hadn't found housing, the host university would help them find housing as soon as possible.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It is a chaotic system. There are limited spots for each course and the deadlines are very late. As a result you don't know if you received a spot on a course until after the semester has already begun. I did not get into 2 out of my 3 applied courses and had to hastily apply for new courses. Luckily the student help/information office moves quickly during the course registration time. I learned that a lot of the Norwegian students apply for 10+ courses at a time for each semester and then drop out of the ones they are unable/unwilling to attend. This is one possible workaround for the current system so you can ensure you have enough courses to cover all 30 necessary credits for the exchange semester. But naturally this further exacerbates the problem. As an exchange student, you must be extra careful to select courses that do not have conflicting time schedules. There is no handy way/system to do this; you must go to every course web page and manually check that their time tables do not conflict. This is because most students at the university follow set study tracks (that do not have conflicting courses), but as an exchange student you are wholly responsible for figuring this out yourself.
registration_help: The Student Information office was incredibly helpful. They have office/telephone hours and usually reply to e-mails quickly. They helped me quickly select and apply for new courses with empty slots.
registration_success: Initially I only got into 1 out of 3 courses I applied for. But I ended up being quite happy with my final set of courses.
registration_advice: Be aware that you might not get into the courses you initially wanted. Make sure that the time tables of the courses do not conflict.
course_level: Compared to UCPH, the level of the courses is not as high. The courses take less of your time and a lot of material is a bit easier to understand. This meant that I had more free time to do other things besides studying. There are not as many mandatory assignments or weekly exercises and there is less reading material in general.
teaching_comparison: The overall structure and style is very similar to UCPH. Some reading material, some lectures and mandatory assignments which must be passed to qualify for the exam. However, some courses do not have exercise classes at all. I was not used to this, since almost all classes at my institute at UCPH have had weekly exercise classes.
courses_enrolled: Natural Language Processing Artificial Intelligence in Energy Informatics Advanced Database Systems for Big Data
recommended_courses: All courses were pretty good, but I thoroughly enjoyed and learned a lot from Natural Language Processing in particular. Besides computers, I have always had an interest in language, so to see computer science and linguistics combined in this way was very interesting.
unexpected_costs: I had to furnish my room myself. Even though I bought everything second hand, this was still relatively expensive.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive. Groceries cost more in general, especially meat and fresh produce. Going out for dinner and drinks in town is incredibly expensive. Especially the drinks part. Public transport is much cheaper than in Copenhagen if you're a student. A monthly fee of around 284 DKK a month and you can get in and around every part of Oslo. I did not need to spend money on books. All course materials were published in the course pages of my courses. Depending on what you're studying, you might be just as fortunate, otherwise expect more spending in this category.
activities_available: There is a large number of student organizations and activities to join, including student-run bars, sports/outdoors clubs (river rafting, hiking) or social gaming/quiz nights.
activities_recommended: Definitely join the first couple of quiz nights for international students during and after the orientation week. It is a great way to get to know other international students!
weekend_recommendations: If possible go on hiking trips or visit other cities/towns in Norway. I and some other exchange students went to visit Bergen by train, which was a really fun trip.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, since Denmark and Norway are quite similar culturally. I had no trouble reading and understanding Norwegian as a Dane, but your mileage may vary depending on the languages you speak.
socializing_tips: This part can be a bit tricky, since Norwegians can take a bit to warm up to you (as a generalization). Just try to join activities and clubs and you will probably find people you click with, but it will take some time. Classes and group work can also be good ways to meet people.
cultural_challenges: There were no particularly challenging cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: In general, Norwegians are kind and honest people. Also their Taco Friday tradition is great!
top3_advice: Be open-minded. Going on exchange was a different sort of experience than I thought it would be, but that isn't a bad thing. Your expectations might be different from reality, so just try to keep an open mind. Don't be afraid to reach out to people or ask for help! If you ever need help or someone to talk to, there is always someone to talk to. Whether it be the study information office or your fellow students. Prioritize fun things and new experiences. Time is short. Your exchange stay will fly by. Use the time to do things you want to do!
other_useful_info: Bring warm clothes and ski clothes if that is your thing. It might get cold and snowy in late fall/early winter!
most_rewarding: Going on exchange really helped me get out of my comfort zone and grow as a person. At times it can feel demanding or scary, but I also learned how to deal with a new life situation. I now know that wherever I decide to go, I'll figure something out. It has also been very rewarding to meet all kinds of new people that I wouldn't have met otherwise and I've had experiences that I otherwise wouldn't have had.
greatest_challenge: Probably arriving all alone in an empty room and not knowing a single person in the city on the very first day. It is an incredibly humbling experience. My first thought upon arrival was: "What did I just do?!" Luckily, this feeling is only temporary. Once the semester starts and you begin meeting people, the feeling goes away.

crucial_aspects: That there was relevant courses I could attend.
info_ease: It was relatively easy to find information, besides that starting date of our studies which was very vague. It seemed like the date changed all the time, and there was a lot of confusion about which week was "buddy week" and when courses started.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive assistance, besides information on studies and buddy programme.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Very easy, you receive several informative emails, which has links to follow. You first have to be accepted by sending institution to a spot, and when this is done, you have to apply directly to UiO. When this is accepted, you receive emails with information on making a account in student web, where you can also apply for courses.
registration_help: Their study guidance was very helpfull.
registration_success: I got all the courses I registered for in the first place. Although it should be said that they made us believe that we probably weren't going to get a spot because other students were prioritised. This was stressing and confusing, and made many of us register for too many courses than we needed, just to be sure. The process of registering is challenging though, as you have to get the course accepted to your programme, which requires a few phone calls and emails. This is because you are not accepted for the courses as a default.
registration_advice: Register for a couple too many courses as a backup. You can also "drop" courses as you go, if you find it uninteresting or irrelevant. There is a couple of weeks from course start to deadline for registration, so you can change courses even if you started them. Also, be prepared to make som calls to get the courses in you programme at Studentweb.
course_level: Similar levels as at UCPH. However, in all courses the exam form was a closed book, which requires a lot of cramming. This was unusual for me, as I have not had these for a couple of years, and they are not necessarily the best exam forms for my kind of study. The one BA course I had required a lot more than MA, which I found unusual.
teaching_comparison: We had lectures (ca. 3-4 hours per week/per course) and in two of the courses there was 2-3 hours of colloquia, where we could work with assignments and group work. I found that these were very beneficial.
courses_enrolled: BIOS5710 Advanced Cancer Biology BIOS5610 Eukaryotic genes and genomes BIOS3920 Forskningslitteratur i kreftbiologi
recommended_courses: BIOS5710. This was a really interesting course, with lots of variation in the lectures, and an amazing teacher.
unexpected_costs: I dont thing there was something unexpected.
cost_comparison: Food and alcohol was expensive, even with the NOK being weak. Concerts and clothes were surprisingly cheap, maybe because of the currency.
activities_available: There was an organisation called SiO, who arranged all sort of activities, both running club and flea markets for everyone, not only international students. ESN was an organisation for Erasmus students and international students, that also arranges cultural trips and events. SiO (studerende i Oslo) also has gyms around the city, where you could get a membership for around 250 NOK/month.
activities_recommended: Being a part of a sportsteam is an easy way to get to know Norwegians.
weekend_recommendations: Go on hikes, and enjoy the nature. Notice when there is flea markets (e.g. Sundays at Grünerløkka). If you can, travel away from Oslo to see some other parts of Norway.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy.
socializing_tips: Join a sports team or club. Or during classes.
cultural_challenges: The Norwegians can be very introvert and not very interested in talking to strangers and make new friends. This is challenging when you dont know anyone.
culture_appreciated: Their national holiday 17th of may. And their joy of nature.
top3_advice: Remember to ask for student discount (clothes, beer, food, tickets) Remember that all shops close on Sundays, and the few that are open are very very expensive, and very small. Know your own limits, and put value in close friends instead of many. You will need it. Exchange is hard, so know when enough is enough, because you will always miss out on something, and that is okay.
other_useful_info: Remember that alcohol is only sold in limited time slots. Only beer is sold in regular stores, and if you want wine etc. you should go to vinmonopolet.
most_rewarding: Getting a small family of friends from across the world. When you are there for a limited amount of time, and dont know other people, close friends are the most comfortable and important thing.
greatest_challenge: Keeping calm in having fomo, and being comfortable about it.

crucial_aspects: UiO, unlike UCPH, offers maritime law courses and a maritime law LLM and I want to work with maritime law
info_ease: It was quite easy. The website is not ideal, but a lot of information can be found with some patience. Information on course registration was not straight forward, but if you read the e-mails etc. and have patience and faith, you'll get there. Additionally, the semester starts off with a buddy/intro week, where you can ask questions. I had to “argue” with the helpdesk to get the correct dates on my Erasmus, so be aware of that. Also be aware of the fact that the contact person at the law faculty is practically impossible to reach. You have to CC the faculty itself on your e-mails, when you try to get in touch with her.
arrival_assistance: None really
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You receive an e-mail about what courses you can apply to. Remember that you can actually apply to more courses than they tell you – just look at the full course list on the website, for instance you can take classes in Norwegian as a Dane. When you apply for these courses, you just have to send an e-mail to the law faculty, and they will sign you up for that course. For the rest of the courses, you have to use the login that you receive via sms some time before registration opens and use it to login to Studentweb. Then you just apply for the courses that you want. You should definitely apply for more courses than you need – I applied for 50 ECTS and got them all – later you can withdraw from the courses. I recommend applying as quickly as possible. I heard rumours that the courses a allocated on a “first come first served” basis, but I honestly don’t know if it’s true. Anyways, I applied pretty much the day registration opened and I got all my courses immediately. The Norwegian students don’t apply until after the first week or two have passed. There were quite some frustrations with the registration the first couple of weeks in my kitchen and in general, but I think that the problems sort of fixed themselves over time. I know that not everyone got the courses they were hoping for, but just keep in touch with your faculty and you’ll find a solution.
registration_help: Every faculty has its own helpdesk that you can contact over the phone, via e-mail or just in person. It is quite easy to find a contact person on the website.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted without any problems.
registration_advice: Apply for more ECTS than you need and do it when registration opens. No reason to wait.
course_level: Varied a lot. Some things were very easy, other things matched my expectations
teaching_comparison: They don’t use reading lists. They tell you what the curriculum is, and each lecture has a name/heading, but they expect you to guess what part of the curriculum is relevant for each lecture. I prefer the structure of UCPH. I had no seminars, only lectures. It was fine. The classes were rather small. No groupwork. Nothing to hand in. We didn’t practice the exam, so the first time we really saw an exam paper was at the exam. I know that some of the other courses were more structured, especially those in Norwegian, but it was a general experience that UiO lacked structure compared to the Danish way. I just want to emphasize that I really liked my courses, despite preferring the UCPH structure. Many of the lecturers were specialists within their fields and it’s a huge bonus.
courses_enrolled: Maritime Law Marine Insurance Maritime Law: Safety, Competition and EU
recommended_courses: Maritime Law: Safety, Competition and EU Even if you haven’t thought about maritime law yet, it’s a very interesting course. It mainly focuses on current issues within shipping and it’s a chance for you to explore some new topics without reading 1.000 pages on the legal aspects of shipping. Highly recommended. A great opportunity to become a shipping nerd.
unexpected_costs: My Danish phone provider only allowed me to use data outside of Denmark for four months. It was not unexpected as I knew it before I left, but I guess it could be unexpected for some. I just got an eSim in Norway to cover my data use in addition to my Danish subscription.
cost_comparison: The Norwegian prices are very much like the Danish. Yes, groceries are a bit more expensive, but if you live in Copenhagen, you won’t be surprised by the prices in Oslo. Note that beer/alcohol is quite expensive and that the rules about alcohol are different from Denmark. Public transport for a month as a student is however cheap. 466 NOK to travel with all public transport in the city.
activities_available: SIO is a great option for students in Oslo. They offer both housing and cheap gyms all around town in addition to hosting social activities. I recommend becoming a member of SIO Sports. They have six gyms that offer a wide range of activities, e.g. yoga, swimming, bouldering etc.
activities_recommended: Many of the clubs/associations offers free introduction lessons/hikes etc. Just go have fun and try a lot of stuff. I went on a hike with OSI Friluft and that was great
weekend_recommendations: I went to Tromsø and Trondheim during my exchange. I didn't go to Lofoten simply because I had no time left. I flew to Tromsø with some friends from my kitchen and I took the train (Dovrebanen) to Trondheim alone. Both trips were great, but I especially liked the train ride to Trondheim, very beautiful and a nice little getaway. Oslo also has a lot to offer, e.g. the islands in the fiord, Ekebergparken, the forest etc.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The Norwegians are basically Danes with ski.
socializing_tips: Take Norwegian courses or join a club
cultural_challenges: The lack of rye bread and decent cheese. I ended up having rye bread delivered by my parents to Oslo like the other Danes.
culture_appreciated: Being outdoor is a big part of the Norwegian culture and it's great
top3_advice: 1. Have patience. Everything will be alright despite your initial frustrations over UiO. 2. Travel. Exchange is fun and as a student you can get some pretty great prices on trains/flights in Norway, so go explore! 3. Enjoy your stay. Grades are not everything, so spend some time on your hobbies and go on some hikes with new friends.
other_useful_info: Norway is a lot like Denmark, so don't worry too much. Remember Copenhagen is only 1 hour away by flight, so you can always go home for a weekend if you feel like it.
most_rewarding: Making a second home with good friends abroad
greatest_challenge: Understanding how UiO works

But if you have previous experience with cold weather and proper layering, you probably have most of this stuff already.
cost_comparison: Groceries were really expensive, but it was expected. On the other hand there was no transport cost, because the city is literally only 2 km wide. If you're staying in the spring semester, there might be an extra cost when it comes to renting/buying a snowscooter.
activities_available: There is a very nice sports opportunities in Longyearbyen with a sports hall, climbing wall, swimmingpool, football field, ice-skating, dancing, run-club, shooting club and I could go on. And then of course so much hiking!
activities_recommended: Go hiking. See the ice-caves and the sunset from the mountain tops. Eat lunch with the reindeer. Just get out of the house:)
weekend_recommendations: Get some sports going, hike, get to know some locals and you might find yourself on a free sled-dog ride:)
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Norwegian is themain language, but everyone speaks english.
socializing_tips: No local students.
cultural_challenges: It was just very intercultural, so occasionally things got lost in translation, but nothing severe.
culture_appreciated: The small-town feeling, where everyone came to the northern-most Blues Festival, and where everyone shows up in support for the big-band.
top3_advice: 1. Many layers when it comes to clothing 2. Facillitate connections both among people from you course and your kitchen, as well as students who've been here for a long time. Then you get all the tips and tricks, and might be able to buy their old flare gun. 3. Vitamin D pills, or the polar night will strangle you in the darkness.
other_useful_info: Show up early to friday gathering. It's not as fun if everyone shows up late.
most_rewarding: The people and the nature. Everyone is kind, and I can honestly say I've never been to a more beautiful place.
greatest_challenge: The polar night. 24h darkness is not that fun after a while.

crucial_aspects: I chose Oslo because I wanted to stay in the Nordic region, study in beautiful nature similar to Bornholm, and take courses in genetics that fit my academic interests. The combination of strong academics, nature, and being close to my family was crucial for my choice.
info_ease: It was easy to find most of the information I needed upon arrival. The only part that was difficult was getting details about my courses, since the final confirmation came quite late.
arrival_assistance: I received clear guidance from the university through their welcome materials, and I could always call the student help service if I had questions. They were very helpful and made the arrival process easier.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process at the University of Oslo was straightforward. I activated my student account online, completed the required forms in the student portal, and attended the welcome day where everything was explained. The only challenging part was that course confirmations came quite late.
registration_help: There was good support available. I could call the student help service whenever I had questions, and they guided me through practical steps and general information.
registration_success: I was fully successful in registering for the classes I wanted, and I got all the courses I applied for.
registration_advice: My advice is to stay patient and check the student portal regularly, because course confirmations can come late. If anything is unclear, contact the student help service — they respond quickly and are very helpful.
course_level: The level of the courses was as expected. They were academically challenging but manageable, and the teachers explained the material clearly. The workload was reasonable and fit well with my background in molecular biomedicine.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at the University of Oslo was similar to UCPH, with a mix of lectures and independent study. The structure was a bit more relaxed, and the teachers were very approachable. There was also a strong focus on student participation.
courses_enrolled: I was enrolled in the following courses during my first semester: • General Toxicology • Human Physiology • Bioinformatics for Molecular Biology
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the courses I took, because they complemented each other well, and the exam schedule and teaching plan were very well aligned. This made the semester both manageable and enjoyable.
unexpected_costs: I had an unexpected one-time cost of DKK 1,500 to have the furniture removed from the apartment.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than I expected, while public transport was cheaper and very cost-effective.
activities_available: There were many activities available, including cultural events, student clubs, sports facilities at SiO Athletica, and social gatherings organized by student associations. It was easy to join both athletic and social activities.
activities_recommended: I would recommend travelling around Norway, especially going to places like Stavanger, and doing lots of hikes. The nature is amazing, and hiking is a great way to experience the country and spend time with other students.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend exploring Norway’s nature on weekends — hiking, visiting fjords, or taking short trips to cities like Stavanger. It’s a great way to relax and experience the country beyond campus.
culture_adjustment: It was easy to adjust to the local culture, as Norwegians are friendly and the lifestyle is very similar to Denmark. This made the transition smooth and comfortable.
socializing_tips: I don’t have specific tips for socializing with local students, as I went on exchange with my partner and spent most of my free time with him.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: I especially appreciated the calm atmosphere, the closeness to nature, and the strong focus on work–life balance.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared for higher food prices, but enjoy that public transport is cheap and reliable. 2. Stay patient with course registration, as confirmations can come late. 3. Use your weekends to explore nature — hiking is one of the best parts of living in Norway.
other_useful_info: It’s helpful to plan a budget before arriving, as small daily expenses can add up. Also, make use of the university’s support services — they are very responsive and make the whole experience smoother. And don’t miss the chance to travel and hike; it’s one of the biggest advantages of studying in Norway.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the hikes. Exploring Norway’s nature made the whole stay unforgettable.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during the exchange was the high food prices, which made budgeting more difficult than expected.
