crucial_aspects: I've always wanted to travel NZ, and especially to go there and stay for a longer period of time. So I thought exchange was the perfect opportunity to visit this beautiful country, get to know nice people doing the same thing, and to experience a different university and academic style etc. I chose Dunedin specifically because I'm from a big city, Copenhagen (and I study here as well), so I wanted to try a smaller, student city - which Dunedin is. Dunedin is close to wildlife and nature, is on the South Island (which I personally really wanted to travel), and has a great university campus and resources for students. This checked all my boxes: nature, good campus vibes, South Island. Christchurch, Wellington and Auckland just seemed like too large cities to go study abroad in, because I chose NZ for the nature - but if you want a big city experience in NZ, I bet they are great.
overall_comments: What a wonderful experience. This study abroad felt like a break from the usual routine at home, still studying but in a completely different setting, you're on your own and can do exactly what you please. Dunedin was a great place to come and just feel at home, kiwis are so friendly and welcoming, the University of Otago is great. I met really cool and friendly people (even friends for life), travelled a whoooole lot, and learned a lot about myself. NZ is just a stunning country.
info_ease: Easy. The orientation week was very informative and had lots of events as well, so there is no lack of information upon arrival. They are really sweet as well.
arrival_assistance: I got my keys at the UniFlats office and the Campus Watch even drovev me home (I arrived at midnight).
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: What a wonderful experience. This study abroad felt like a break from the usual routine at home, still studying but in a completely different setting, you're on your own and can do exactly what you please. Dunedin was a great place to come and just feel at home, kiwis are so friendly and welcoming, the University of Otago is great. I met really cool and friendly people (even friends for life), travelled a whoooole lot, and learned a lot about myself. NZ is just a stunning country.
registration_process: You browse the courses, register them of their student portal eVision, and wait for approval. Then you accept their offer. (I think, it's a long time since I applied).
registration_help: Lots, there are emails to write to and they are super helpful.
registration_success: Very succesful. I even changed courses which was easy enough, just had to get a new pre-approval from UCPH.
registration_advice: Try something different, you have the chance with basically no risk cause it's just pass/fail for UCPH (at least is was for me). Browse the courses, find something you like and go for it!
academics_comments: What a wonderful experience. This study abroad felt like a break from the usual routine at home, still studying but in a completely different setting, you're on your own and can do exactly what you please. Dunedin was a great place to come and just feel at home, kiwis are so friendly and welcoming, the University of Otago is great. I met really cool and friendly people (even friends for life), travelled a whoooole lot, and learned a lot about myself. NZ is just a stunning country.
course_level: COMP161 was pretty high level for a first semester course - but I'm also a humanities student, so I probably found it more difficult than others would. MAOR102 was a nice level, pretty easy and interesting. ENGL220 was also not so overwhelming in the course load, also because English is my major so a lot of the material was repetition of my third semester anyways.
teaching_comparison: Really different in the way they assess your work. You do work throughout the semester which counts for x amount of your total grade - so this was really nice compared to the 100% of your grade being assessed at one exam, end of semester. The teaching style was pretty similar with lectures and classes, but you're mixed with people from all sorts of majors, not just your own major, so that was different.
courses_enrolled: MAOR102 - Maori Society ENGL220 - Creative Writing: Reading for Writers COMP161 - Computer Programming
recommended_courses: MAOR102 is great for exchange students, a loooot of people I knew took it. The Maori are New Zealand's indegenious peoples, and MAOR102 is a great first semester course introduction to Maori society, culture, history, colonization, and present social issues. It's a great way to learn and understand contemporary NZ political issues, its culture and history, etc. The course was easy to follow, 2 lectures a week and a weekly 1 hr tutorial. The workload wasn't too bad at all, but the exam was a bit specific with some of the details from the course, but it was fine. COMP161 was challenging for me because I study English and have no computer programming experience. They teach Java, and it is a lot of work. But I did learn a lot, and I passed the course - I expect it to be a bit easier if you have some programming experience or interest, just know you do need to put in some work to pass, but it's doable - I did it and I'm in the humanities.
unexpected_costs: I don't know how much I spent on food, I often went out to eat (which isn't that cheap) but groceries are also expensive. Also don't know how much personal spending I did, A LOT is the answer. I traveled a lot and did a bunch of activities that were not cheap - but worth it! Communication (phone number and data) is more expensive than in DK. A good tip is to buy a package duty free in the airport when you land, I got Spark for 2x3 months with unlimited data and that was great. it was around 1000 kr. for 6 months use (ish) and that's apparently really good price.
cost_comparison: Some things in the supermarket are really expensive (like 25 kr. for 1 avocado) because they have to be imported I guess - it really is island life. Coffee 'only' cost like 30 ish kr. for a large latte, so that was less expensive than I expected.
activities_available: UniPol is a free gym with lots of facilities, it's huge and offers classes as well (but you have to pay for these). The OUSA (Otago University Student Association) has a building which offers so many clubs, really cheap lunches, free weekly breakfasts, they have facilities you can rent for free (a workout room, a sauna), they offer condoms, tampons, pads, safe drug use advice etc. It's a great place to go as a student.
activities_recommended: Go on weekend trips. You should just get into nature and tramp, hike, drive around and see all the beautiful places NZ has to offer.
weekend_recommendations: Mt. Aoraki was probably the most beautiful national park I've ever seen, close to it is Lake Tekapo and Lake Pukaki. Lake Tekapo is in a dark sky reserve, meaning the stars are stuuuunning. Fiordland and Milford Sound is a must as well, just stunning. Te Anau is a great hub for going hiking the great walk called the Kepler Track, and where you can stay when visiting Fiordland (if you aren't camping in a tent). The Catlins have georgous waterfalls and is only an hour or two south of Dunedin. Queenstown is a blast, has partying all year round, adrenaline activities like skydive and bungee jump, and is also a great place for winter sports like skiing and snowboarding. Really fun for a weekend trip w your mates, we did a wine tasting tour of the region. Wanaka is close by Queenstown and is a more chill place for ski sports and beautiful mountain hikes (Roy's Peak fx.) Further north is Kaikoura, a little beach town with wonderful water wildlife spotting oppurtunities. You can go whale watching and swimming with dolphins, see a giant seal colony and albatross as well. That place is absolutely glorious and almost spiritual. Abel Tasman national park is also really stunning, especially in summer: bays, tropical feel, coastal.
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy! My main culture chok when arriving in NZ is that kiwis will greet you with a "how are you?" to which you answer "good, how about you?" before you can start conversation with shop assistants basically. It's nice when you get used to it. Kiwis easily strike up conversations with strangers, which is very foreign to us Danes, but it was actually so nice and freeing to speak to a bunch of people without it being a big deal and just being straight up nice.
socializing_tips: I mostly socialized with other exchange students, so can't really help here. But I guess join the clubs, they have so many to choose from!
cultural_challenges: Probably the extroverted-ness of kiwis is what struck me most. But it was actually really nice to experience.
culture_appreciated: Kiwis love for and connection to nature. People just go out into nature all the time. And their open-ness to strangers/foreigners, that was so refreshing compared to DK.
top3_advice: 1. TRAVEL NZ!!!!!!! As much as you can, it is absolutely amazing. Do it with someone, do it alone, just do it! You'll meet amazing people at hostels, at the uni, etc. 2. Join clubs and attend the O-week, that's a good way to get to know some people and find some friends / get experiences you wouldn't have on your own. 3. Enjoy it.
other_useful_info: (probably shouldn't say this, but the academic level is not as high as at UCPH, at least that wasnt my experience - so dont spend all your time studying haha, just enjoy your time and experiences!)
most_rewarding: Learning to travel alone, I felt incredibly independant because now I know I can travel alone, and even move to the other side of the world and meet amazing people and make friends. That's a huge validation for myself about myself, and I'm really proud of it. And obviously, the most reqarding part was seeing beautiful NZ, the mountains are just magical. Everywhere you look is georguos, literally.
greatest_challenge: Probably missing home, being a bit lonely. And also being stressed about not using my time in NZ to the fullest - which I did, but I felt a little guilty almost sometimes. But that's exactly why I came on exchange, so I could be in NZ for longer and not feel stressed. JS
other_comments: JUST GO TO DUNEDIN, YOU WON'T REGRET IT.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a place where I could experience some beautiful nature and live in a city smaller than Copenhagen, to feel more connected to the nature and the places around me. I also read about the UniFlats that University of Otago offer, and thought it was really nice to have housing secured before I moved here, as that made it very easy to find a place to live, and gave me less worries. I also wanted a country that spoke english as I am more confident in that language.
overall_comments: I can highly recommend living in UniFlats through the University of Otago as they made a great match with me and my flatmates, you are sure that you have a place to live, when you arrive in Dunedin, and they are always quick to fix stuff in the flat, if there is anything broken. They are also great at hosting events for international students.
info_ease: Pretty easy, there is a lot of information on the university's website, and they also sent me a lot of information and hosted webinars when I was signed up to study there.
arrival_assistance: In UniFlats there is a KiwiHost, who is a person from New Zealand that live with you and can help you to figure out where to get the right resources for any problem that might occur. UniFlats also have an office and the university have a team called "Campus Watch" that will be quick to help you if you ask.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I can highly recommend living in UniFlats through the University of Otago as they made a great match with me and my flatmates, you are sure that you have a place to live, when you arrive in Dunedin, and they are always quick to fix stuff in the flat, if there is anything broken. They are also great at hosting events for international students.
registration_process: I had to apply for acceptance at the university, but if KU already gave you permission to go on exchange at that university, the host university will almost always accept you. Remember to apply for a visa in good time. Have a look at all the papers and make sure you have documentation to show which relevant papers you have taken at home, if you want a paper at the host university with prerequisites.
registration_help: Webinars, online folders, information on websites, I could e-mail international student guides
registration_success: Very succesful, I got the three classes that I wanted in the end. Remember, that semester 1 in Denmark is semester 2 in New Zealand and vice versa.
registration_advice: Watch the webinars, and ask questions if you have any. Don't leave it all to last minute, remember to stay updated every time the university sends out an email.
academics_comments: I can highly recommend living in UniFlats through the University of Otago as they made a great match with me and my flatmates, you are sure that you have a place to live, when you arrive in Dunedin, and they are always quick to fix stuff in the flat, if there is anything broken. They are also great at hosting events for international students.
course_level: In New Zealand the courses/papers are grouped in different levels according to how hard they are, how much knowledge you need before taking them, and what year you are in preferably. First year courses are level 100, second year courses are level 200 and third year courses are level 300. I had one course of each level, and I thought they were all at a reasonable level. The courses that I had the least background knowledge on were the hardest, but I also think that my level 300 course was a bit harder and more time consuming than the other courses.
teaching_comparison: In University of Otago they have a lot of practical sessions in each class, which I really liked, as you get to talk about the material from that week in smaller classes. You also have to turn in assignments regularly and the grades for the assignments count towards your final grade for the course. This means that all of my exams are only worth 50% of the total grade of each course. The lectures are also way shorter, and I felt like I had more free time (and time for homework of course).
courses_enrolled: MAOR102, Māori Society ECOL211, Ecology of communities and ecosystems MARI302, Biology and behaviour of marine vertebrates
recommended_courses: I would recommend taking a class on Māori culture, as it is an important part of New Zealands history and culture. Either "Māori performing arts" where you learn traditional Māori songs and dances, I really regret not taking this course, it seems like a lot of fun, and an easy course. I can also recommend Māori society if you prefer learning about the culture in a classroom. Also try to find some courses that have field trips to get out and see the local area too.
unexpected_costs: When I went travelling with my friends we had to rent cars becuase the public transport doesn't go a lot of places, so that was a bit more expensive. The food is also way more expensive than I thought it would have been. A cucumber can be up to 40 DKK for example.
cost_comparison: Food in the supermarket was way more expensive, but going out to a restaurant or cafe was cheaper than Denmark.
activities_available: The University hosted quiz nights, inter-college competitions, sport-competitions, there is a free gym and group sports at unipolar, there is a free music room at OUSA, where you can play music. Every wednesday there is free breakfast at OUSA, and 4 dollar lunch every day (except weekends) also at OUSA.
activities_recommended: I would recommend using the free gym at Unipol, and going to all the social events both through the university, UniFlats, and the clubs. I can recommend exploring Dunedin, go to the peninsula, St. Clair beach, Mount Cargill, see glowworms for free at Nichols Creek, get a BeeCard for the bus, it is really cheap to take the bus around Dunedin. Go for adventures and rent or buy a car to se the rest of the county!
weekend_recommendations: Go for hikes either in the local area or in the rest of the country. Go to the local Farmers market every saturday in Dunedin. Spend time with your friends and flatmates.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy to adjust to the culture. For me, I just had to adjust to speak and write english all the time, which was a bit hard at first, because almost all of my flatmates were native english speakers, so I felt very insecure about my accent and my vocabulary. But donøt worry! It comes to you easily after some training, and everybody loves a cute danish accent. Otherwise, I love that Dunedin is a student city, so there's a lot of students around all the time and a lot of stuff going on always.
socializing_tips: The kiwi's can be a bit hard to befreind, but I can really recommend joining the social clubs and going to their events and volunteering, that helped me get to talk to some kiwi's. Otherwise I of course met them in my classes, but it is a bit hard to talk inbetween lectures, as everyone is rushing to get to their next class. But I made some friends in the practical lessons and if you are braver than me, you can also try and sit next to some of your classmates in the lectures.
cultural_challenges: I don't think I was really very challenged, except that I didn't know anyone in my classes at first, so I had to think more about socialising in my classes.
culture_appreciated: Sausage sizzles, friendly kiwi's, student life, partying, going for hikes, enjoying nature, social gatherings through the uni or social clubs.
top3_advice: Get as much money saved up as you can, try and get some scholarships, apply early for scholarships and grants and remember to get a recommendation from a teacher. Just apply for all the scholarships you see, it really worked out nice for me! Apply to live in UniFlats! They are great. Buy some nice tramping boots! If you like nature you will need them.
other_useful_info: People often ask "how are you", and the usual answer is just "Good, how are you", no matter how you feel, don't be thrown off by this funny interaction
most_rewarding: Meeting my wonderful flatmates, learning to be independent in another country, overcoming the troubles that I had with help from my flatmates, learning how strong I am, and how much I can overcome on my own.
greatest_challenge: Speaking and writing and learning in english. All. The. Time. But I had good periods and worse periods, it is important to know though, that it will always get better again, even if you are feeling a bit challenged at any moment.
other_comments: Go on exchange no matter what!! It's amazing and you grow so much from the experience.

crucial_aspects: For me it was important to try and travel a bit further away than I usually would, somewhere where I had no safety blanket and was forced to stand on my own two feet. I also really wanted to go to a place I had never been before.
overall_comments: It was just absolutely amazing. I didn't really let myself have any expectations, so I wouldn't end up disappointed. Instead I ended up having the best time of my life. The people were so friendly and welcoming, the nature and culture is out of this world and uni was also a really good experience.
info_ease: They bombard you with welcome letters and information, so everything was fairly easy to figure out from the get-go. And both Uniflats (where I lived) and the people working at the uni-offices were helpful and eager to assist whereever you may need it.
arrival_assistance: A lot of mails and letters from the university and from Uniflats. They had meetings in the beginning to give us all the information. You could also always contact somebody if you needed help.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was just absolutely amazing. I didn't really let myself have any expectations, so I wouldn't end up disappointed. Instead I ended up having the best time of my life. The people were so friendly and welcoming, the nature and culture is out of this world and uni was also a really good experience.
registration_process: You apply for courses on something called Evision before you arrive. After arriving you still have a few weeks to change courses if you want to. It is fairly easy and self-explanatory as soon as you get access to Evision.
registration_help: There are always people you can write an email to, or they have help desks and info-days where you can talk to people about the different courses
registration_success: I was lucky and got all the classes I applied for, though some of the ones I had looked at before I arrived were no longer available. I did end up changing some courses just before the deadline, which was perfectly fine.
registration_advice: Look outside of your degree. You are free to take intro to astronomy, even if you study history, or programming, even if you study medicine. It is the perfect time to experiment. I ended up taking a music class, even though a study film and media, and it was really cool and I ended up loving it.
academics_comments: It was just absolutely amazing. I didn't really let myself have any expectations, so I wouldn't end up disappointed. Instead I ended up having the best time of my life. The people were so friendly and welcoming, the nature and culture is out of this world and uni was also a really good experience.
course_level: Their systeme if built up so that 100-level classes are mostly first-year classes, 200-level is second year, and so on. So just be aware of that when you look at courses.
teaching_comparison: They are fairly similar, though you have a lot of smaller test and exams during the semester, something that I am personally not used to. I found it a bit stressful, but it also meant that the final exams did not count as much, which ended up being nice, as you would rather spend the last few weeks with your friends.
courses_enrolled: Film Music, New Zealand Cinema, and Media and Intercultural Communication
recommended_courses: New Zealand Cinema is really cool, as you also learn alot of New Zealand history and about Maori culture in film and real life. So it is a window into the history and culture, but without only being about that.
unexpected_costs: As it often happens, you find some friends, and you end up wanting to do a lot of fun stuff together, and everything unfortunately costs money. but it is worth it!
cost_comparison: Groceries are a bit more expensive then back home. Especially vegetables, the closer that you get to winter. Coffee at cafés is really cheap, but be aware, most of them already close at 14-15, which is sometimes a bit annoying. Because NZ is a very multicultural country, you can find a wide variety of ingredients in the average supermarket, and that is often cheaper than back home.
activities_available: There are a looooot of clubs and societies that you can join. The most popular one is the tramping club, which has a lot of trips to different beautiful places around New Zealand during the semester. But there is almost anything you could dream of. and it is an amazing way to meet new people.
activities_recommended: Go on hikes! See as much as you can. Rent a car and drive somewhere beautiful. Don't waste the fact that you are in one of the most extraordinary places in the world, because it truly is.
weekend_recommendations: GO ON TRIPS! Especially in nature! You can always see a town or a city, but the mountains, lakes, beaches, glaciers, fiords and so on are what makes New Zealand so unique, so don't miss it!
culture_adjustment: Easy, they are friendly, welcoming, and the culture is not much different than ours. Just be respectful of the Maori people, their language and their culture, it is very important.
socializing_tips: I became close to my neighbour, who happens to be from Wellington, but I know that many people didn't talk a lot to kiwi students. But the best place would probably be one of the clubs or societies.
cultural_challenges: I didn't really find anything difficult. They are overly friendly in shops, which can be a bit draining sometimes.
culture_appreciated: Their friendliness and welcoming personalities and openness towards other cultures and religions.
top3_advice: 1: Get out of your comfort zone, try new things. 2: Travel around New Zealand. 3: Make the most of your time there, but don't stress too much about what you haven't done, just enjoy what you are doing, you can't see it all in just one semester.
other_useful_info: Be open minded, try not having too many or too high expectations, just let it happen.
most_rewarding: Getting out of my comfort zone and meeting new people and challenging myself academically and socially
greatest_challenge: I was really afraid of being lonely, so far away from everything and everyone I know. But what I quickly realised is that just about everyone will feel like that when they arrive. So do not worry, you will meet tons of amazing people, and you will have the time of your life!

registration_success: You get contacted by an employer from the host university who gives you a list and a guide on how to do it. crucial_aspects: There were ... main factors. info_ease: Both the "International Office" and "UniFlats" (the ones that organises the housing) were really quick to reply to correspondence before my departure. They had an online introduction meeting with helpful information.
arrival_assistance: At the online introduction meeting we had received information about how we could get to our housing, pick up our keys, etc. During the first week before classes started the "International Office" and "UniFlats" had arranged different information meetings and social events upon arrival, which was a good way to meet knew people, and get the necessary information.

registration_process: Once you have officially been accepted you get acces to sign up for courses. registration_help: I mainly wrote with the International Office
registration_success: I got all the classes that I applied for.
registration_advice: If possible within the courses that you would like to take, try and see if you can keep either your friday (potentially monday) open. Quite a lot of exchange students do this, as it makes it easier to go on weekend trips.
course_level: I took one 100, one 200, and one 300 level course. I mainly found the 300 level course to be a lower level compared to 3rd year courses in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: I had more laboratory hours compared to my usual courses at UCPH, but on the other had we didn't have any "practice classes", where we would go over the material
courses_enrolled: MAOR102 Māori Society MICR223 Infection and Immunity GENE314 Developmental Genetics
recommended_courses: I would recommend taking MAOR102 Māori Society. For me personally it was nice to learn something about the Māori culture, how they got to New Zealand, and "their role" in society today. It is a relatively easy course with a multiple choice exam.
unexpected_costs: It wasn't really an unexpected cost, but i ended up spending quite a lot on different weekend trips.
cost_comparison: Vegetables were more expensive than I had imagined. Especially during their winter season. Eating out and going out for coffee cheaper than in Denmark
activities_available: There are quite a lot of different clubs that you can sign up for. It seemed that the most popular ones amongst exchange students where the tramping (hiking) club and the skiing club.
activities_recommended: There is quite a nice gym at the university (UniPol) where you get free access, and it is relatively cheap to sign up if you wan't to join the group fitness classes.
weekend_recommendations: During the mid-semester break I did a tour on the South Island which I can highly recommend. Dunedin is a great spot for going on weekend trips throughout the semester, and I would recommend going to Milford Sound and Queenstown.
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy. The culture in New Zealand is a lot like the Danish culture. I would say that the main difference is that people in New Zealand tend to be more "welcoming"
socializing_tips: If you arrange your housing through UniFlats you will be living with someone from New Zealand, and are likely to meet their friends. Otherwise I found it the easiest to meet people from New Zealand in the classes where we had group projects. If you start a conversation with the locals, they're usually really nice.
cultural_challenges: I don't think that there was anything i found particularly challenging, but I found it a bit odd that people are barefoot on the streets and in the grocery stores.
culture_appreciated: The appreciation for the nature. The nature in New Zealand is really beautiful, and for most people in New Zealand protecting the nature is an important part of their culture.
top3_advice: Make sure to attend the different social events in the beginning (especially the week before classes start, where you have an international orientation), as this is where it is the "easiest" to meet new people. Try and see if you can plan some weekend trips, and explore New Zealand during the mid-semester break. If there is a rugby game with with New Zealand's "All Blacks" I would highly recommend trying to get tickets (even if you don't know any of the rules)
other_useful_info: At the Otago Polytechnic's Beauty School you can get different student led services, such as a 1 hour massage for 40 DKK.
most_rewarding: Getting to travel around and make memories with new friends.
greatest_challenge: At the beginning you can feel like you're very far away from everyone you know. Both due to the distance and the time difference

crucial_aspects: I've always wanted to go to New Zealand and thought going on exchange there would be a great way of experiencing the country. I was drawn to University of Otago specifically because it's on the South Islands and close to a lot of beautiful nature and experiences.
overall_comments: I had a really good time at Otago! I got to see a lot of New Zealand and experience kiwi culture.
info_ease: Very easy, you receive a lot of information by email prior to your arrival. During orientation week, there's also a few different information sessions that'll provide you with all the information you need.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had a really good time at Otago! I got to see a lot of New Zealand and experience kiwi culture.
registration_process: You get a notification in the student portal once course selection is open. You then go through a few different steps to select your courses. Once you've selected your courses you send them in for approval. It's possible to change courses after the semester has started, so don't stress too much about it.
registration_help: There's a guide on their website, but you can also contact the university by email if more assistance is needed.
registration_success: I got all of the courses I applied for. Most of the courses have unlimited capacity, so you're almost guaranteed a spot as long as you meet the prerequisites.
registration_advice: Read the guides on their website thoroughly before choosing courses. Also, check out the schedule of the courses before choosing them. You can plan your week so that you don't have courses on Fridays for example, if you want to be able to go on long weekend trips.
academics_comments: I had a really good time at Otago! I got to see a lot of New Zealand and experience kiwi culture.
course_level: I was pleasantly surprised with the level of the courses. I took only master's courses, and they were all both interesting and challenging.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching of the public health classes were pretty similar to what we have at home. I mostly had 3-hour lectures with discussion throughout the sessions. The most different thing was the assessment. Instead of exams, I had assignments which all counted towards my final grade. (Other study fields have exams, but they usually only count for some of the grade)
courses_enrolled: PUBH712: Foundations of Hauora Māori PUBH733: Environment and Health PUBH741: Hauora Māori- Policy Practice and Research PUBH743: Health Promotion Programme Planning and Evaluation
recommended_courses: I enjoyed all of my classes and can recommend all of them to public health students. I would recommend taking some sort of class on Māori culture. A lot of my friends took the Māori performance class, which looked like a lot of fun!
unexpected_costs: I didn't have any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Food was a bit more expensive than expected, and is pretty comparable to Danish prices. Coffee was really cheap, and would usually cost around 25 kr. Local public transportation was also pretty cheap
activities_available: The University has lots of different clubs and societies, and there's also a gym that's free to use. The student association (OUSA) offer a range of different recreational activities you can sign up for in the beginning of the year.
activities_recommended: I didn't join any clubs, but I did sign up for a pottery class through OUSA. I can highly recommend the pottery class, as it was lots of fun and a great way to unwind a bit during the week. The teacher and the other students were all super nice, and it was a really good experience. You also get to take home whatever you make, which is a great little souvenir from your exchange!
weekend_recommendations: I recommend going on trips and hike. New Zealand has a lot of beautiful nature, so you should definitely take advantage of it! There's a lot of beautiful places near Dunedin, but I also really enjoyed the West coast of the South Island, mt Cook and Abel Tasman. It's also pretty fun to go to a rugby game - and Thursday night karaoke is a MUST! If you have the time and money, I would definitely recommend going to one of the pacific islands! I went to Cook Islands during the easter break, and I had the best time! It was such a unique experience and one of my favourite parts of my exchange trip
culture_adjustment: Very easy, I don't recall any major cultural differences
socializing_tips: I only had classes with local students, which made it pretty easy to make local friends. Another great way of meeting local people is to join a club or recreational activity.
cultural_challenges: I didn't experience any major cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness of the kiwis! I also really enjoyed learning about Māori culture
top3_advice: 1) Explore New Zealand's beautiful nature. 2) Plan your studies so you have time to go on weekend trips. 3) Go to the social events in the beginning of the semester. It's a good way to meet new people and where most people make friends
other_useful_info: Not anything that comes to mind!
most_rewarding: Exploring New Zealand, making new friends, learning about different cultures
greatest_challenge: At times, I felt really stressed about not having enough time to see all the things I wanted in New Zealand. It took some time to accept that New Zealand is too big to fully explore during the semester while also having school to attend to
other_comments: I think Otago is a really good place to go for exchange, as the University does a lot to accommodate for their international students. Everyone lives close to campus, and there is a pretty good student life! New Zealand is also such a beautiful (and safe) country to explore.

overall_comments: It was definitely an up and down. The beginning was quite harsh (hadn't found my people yet, stressful, bad weather), while the end was amazing (good friends, better weather, not as stressful).
info_ease: Very easy.
arrival_assistance: Students services helped with the registration and settling in. There is also something called Ask Otago, where you can always go to or call for help with basically everything.

course_level: I took one 400-level and two 700-level courses which are all considered postgraduate.
teaching_comparison: My courses at the Department of Public Health were very similar to the ones at KU. It was lecture-style, but we could always ask questions and there were small group works every now and then. We also had to read book chapters and listen to podcasts etc. before the class. My course at the Department of Anthropology was a lot more interactive and intimate, building on weekly forum posts and intense discussions, so quite different to KU.
courses_enrolled: Anth431 People, Culture and Development; Pubh732 Using Epidemiology in Public Health Practice; Pubh736 Economic Evaluation.
recommended_courses: Honestly, all of them but keep in mind your previous knowledge and skills. Pubh732 was a little boring since I already knew a lot of the course content from my previous courses during my BA and MA. Pubh736 was the most hands-on and perhaps the most valuable for me in terms of skills and knowledge acquired. Anth431 was amazing because of the teacher and my fellow students, and really helped in gaining a new perspective on international development (aid).
unexpected_costs: Maybe medical expenses. I had to visit the urgent doctors once which cost me 90$ (as an exchange student you qualify for the local rate). I could have reclaimed that with my insurance but I didn't find the time to do so and didn't have the motivation to familiarise myself with that process.
cost_comparison: Groceries were extremely expensive, especially fresh produce. But prices also varied greatly, when I first arrived, a cucumber would cost 9$, while it was sitting at 3$ by the end of my stay. The bus was fairly cheap with 2.50$ per ride. Eating out is cheaper than in Denmark.
activities_available: Basically everything, from ski club to jiu jitsu, to tennis and arts and crafts. The gym is free for every student and it also rents out outdoor equipment like surfboards, bikes or tents. There were some events for students (mostly rganised by uniflats) to visit places or socialise. There was also the opportunity to volunteer.
activities_recommended: Volunteer and get your Global Impact Scholar Programme certificate. I can highly recommend the Good Deed and Feed as well as the Reading Oasis. I also had a good time at the Tennis Association (we played each Friday). i also joined the Women in Health Network Otago which was really nice for networking.
weekend_recommendations: Surf at St. Clairs, go for hikes (e.g. Highcliff Track), visit the Botanical Gardens and Baldwin Street, go for trips (e.g. Queenstown, Christchurch, Mount Cook, Lake Tekapo, Wanaka, Invercargill etc.). There is so much to see, but you do need a car for most things. The buses only go as far and often only drive once an hour. Also, definitely visit a rugby match.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, not too different from Northern/Western Europe and previous places I've been to.
socializing_tips: It is honestly very difficult to make local friends. Most exchange students only really connected with other exchange students. Try to go to house parties and try to befriend people in your class. Other than that, the only option is to join clubs and societies with locals in it or just be super open and talk to everyone.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really.
culture_appreciated: The wonderful singing and dancing culture of the Maori. Also, everyone is a lot more open, friendly and laid-back here which can be very nice.
top3_advice: 1. Don't have too many expectations since it will be different than what you're imagining it to be. 2. Be open-minded and try to use every opportunity you can to go out and meet up with people. 3. Enjoy your time and don't be afraid to tell people when things are rough and you need some support.
other_useful_info: Dunedin is a small and run-down town with an intense party culture. You might feel a little out of place when you're over the age of 20 and not into constantly drinking and partying.
most_rewarding: The connections and memories I made along the way.
greatest_challenge: Probably my flatmates and the housing situation. I'm used to being abroad for months so that was fine for me but I did miss my partner, friends and family back home. The time-zone difference was also rough.
other_comments: I was very disappointed that I, as an international student at KU, had absolutely no opportunity to connect with the Danish KU students, so I had to come here completely alone, while all the Danish students connected beforehand. That just didn't seem fair and while I understand that I'm not Danish, I still live in Cph and go to the same University as the other students.

info_ease: Pretty easy. The University of Otago pretty much holds your hand throughout everything, I almost felt smothered by their involvement.
arrival_assistance: Lots of seminars at the start. Loads of emails throughout the stay, as well as AskOtago at campus and a department just for international students
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: They'll send emails with everything you need to know
registration_help: They are very fast to respond to emails
registration_success: You are garanteed a spot in the papers you want
registration_advice: None
course_level: I found the courses quite easy, don't be scared to apply for a course over your "level"
teaching_comparison: I had less readings to do and my classes where very discussion-based compared to back home. A lot of small assignments throughout the semester
courses_enrolled: Conservation biology, Maori Society and Ecology og invasive and introduced species
recommended_courses: They were all very insightfull and unique to NZ
unexpected_costs: You need a car to travel the country, I would think about buying one at the start otherwise the rental fees can get quite expensive

activities_available: Loads of clubs to choose from, free fitness center and UniFlats does a lot of events too
activities_recommended: Join the tramping club, if you like hiking
weekend_recommendations: Travel around! The uni is 3-5 hours away from amazing places like the southern alps etc
culture_adjustment: Very easy, they are a mix of american/british/australian - not really any culture shocks
socializing_tips: Join clubs, talk to class mates - find your own housing with locals
cultural_challenges: Very car centric compared to dk
culture_appreciated: Very relaxed culture

greatest_challenge: The time difference to home

crucial_aspects: A place that was a fit with my academic interests. And I really wanted to go somewhere, I had never been before and expierence a completly new culture and country.
info_ease: Fairly easy, both University of Copenhagen and Otage University was easy to communicate with and help with the stuff that i was uncertain about.
arrival_assistance: The university provided a service where you could apply for uniflats (flats that were meant for exchange students), which made the whole living situation very easy. And you could go to them for all sorts of questions, and they kept their office open for long periods in the beginning of the semester. They also organised different information meeting you could go to, for different sorts of information and as a way to meet other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The application process was fairly simpel, it was through a website called Evision, which you will recieve login. It was very intuitive once you are in the website, and they will send notifications so you know, what need to do, and if they need any extra information.
registration_help: There was a link to a page with frequently asked questions, and they had a mail adress you could also send questions to
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Do it as soon as possible, and dont be too nervouse about the pre-requirements for subjects neede to take the class, as long as you have had some similar subjects earlier in your study.
course_level: I took two 100 level classes, which did not require a heavy workload, and was mainly aimed for either first years and other students who hadn't taking classes in that field before. I also had a 200 level class, which definetly was a bigger challenge, but I thought it was a very fitting level, where i was able to learn new stuff and was challenged in a good way.
teaching_comparison: The duration of my classes were shorter at Otago university, lectures only lasted 50 minutes. All the exams were written in hand at Otago University.
courses_enrolled: Pacific societies, Rivers and runoff, Geographies of sustainble futures
recommended_courses: I really liked the course: Pacific societies as i learned a lot. It felt very authentic since a lot of the lectures were from the pacifics themselves, and therefore could speak about their cultures and expierences.
unexpected_costs: If you want to travel then you either need to rent a car or pay for public transport which is not great
cost_comparison: groceries were more expensive than expected. Since I live a 2 minute walk from university I luckily didn't have to pay much in transpiration.
activities_available: All sorts, they have so many differents activities. They hosted a day in the beginning of the semester were you could sign up and just learn more about the different clubs at the univeristy.
activities_recommended: Join a club, because it is a great way to learn some new people. Make sure you attend the activites provided by uniflatts as this was a god way to learn other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: Rent a car and explore all the great nature New Zealand has to offer
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: Joining clubs is a good way to learn some of the local students, and just be brave and open and talk with people in your class.
cultural_challenges: I don't really think there was anything
culture_appreciated: I really liked how maori culture was incorporated in normal day life.
top3_advice: Be open, try new things and explore the country
other_useful_info: no
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all over the world
greatest_challenge: Being so far away from home

crucial_aspects: I prioritized convenient and social housing opportunities highly. I didn't want to live in a very big city, and I wanted to a place where you could also get a lot of experiences outside of university life.
overall_comments: I enjoyed my stay very much. The social, cultural and personal aspects of my trip was great. The only downside was the very limited selection of courses relating to my study (physics), and the academic side of my trip suffered a little from this fact.
info_ease: Quite easy. The entire university is located at one central campus, and there are a multiple 'help hubs' where you can ask all sorts of questions and get help with all the administration. The university also hosts a lot of events during the introductory week for new international students, so you feel both welcomed and pretty well informed.
arrival_assistance: Introductory events hosted by the university, and the entire housing was organized by university's housing organ (called UniFlats)
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I enjoyed my stay very much. The social, cultural and personal aspects of my trip was great. The only downside was the very limited selection of courses relating to my study (physics), and the academic side of my trip suffered a little from this fact.
registration_process: You get an account on their administration platform (eVision) and apply through there.
registration_help: There was one online seminar that talked about the registration process. For specific course advice, I believe you would have to email the relevant faculty. I got some advice for choosing one of my courses through email.
registration_success: I got the classes I wanted, and it was my impression that that was the case for everyone I spoke to.
registration_advice: Don't worry if everything is not completely in place before you leave. You still have time to change your courses once you are at the uni, and it might be easier to get advice once you are there. I ended up swapping one of my courses for another one into the first week of classes, and it worked out fine.
academics_comments: I enjoyed my stay very much. The social, cultural and personal aspects of my trip was great. The only downside was the very limited selection of courses relating to my study (physics), and the academic side of my trip suffered a little from this fact.
course_level: I had one 100, one 200 and one 300-level paper – corresponding to first, second and third year papers, respectively. You could tell that the courses was meant for someone early in their university life.
teaching_comparison: Too many powerpoint shows that were just shot off without intention. The lectures were generally shorter (only 50 minutes) and usually felt quite rushed.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Marine Biology (MARI112), Electronics for the Sciences (PHSI245), Experimental Physics II (PHSI381)
recommended_courses: The content of Electronics for the Sciences was interesting. It was a quite small class (only 5 people), though, and that dragged it down a bit. The Marine Science paper was interesting for someone with no biology background – very much overview level, though, nothing in depth or heavy substance, but it was interesting and there was a few field trips which meant that I got out the classroom a bit, which was nice.
unexpected_costs: Nothing too bad. You often want to go on weekend trips (Dunedin not being a very big city) and that does come with some costs.
cost_comparison: Food is quite expensive in the grocery stores. Drinking coffee out on cafés were quite cheap.
activities_available: Many different student hosted clubs for all kinds of stuff – check it out clubs on the otago OUSA website.
activities_recommended: I was a part of the tramping club (OUTC), which hosted some weekend trips and a weekly morning swim, which I became quite fond of. The sauna at OUSA is top notch and a nice place to a small chat to some locals.
weekend_recommendations: All the lovely nature on the south island (and north island), which is very accessible from Dunedin with a car. There are lots of amazing hikes nearby. Go roadtrip around New Zealand. Take your bike for a ride down Signal Hill. You will find lots of things to do, even though the city is quite small
culture_adjustment: Very easy. People are more friendly and outgoing in public than what we are used to in Denmark, but they have very much the same down-to-earth atmosphere, and maybe even a bit of Jantelov engrained in them.
socializing_tips: Maybe joining the clubs is one of the better ways to do it. I met some friendly local students, but the people I became good friends with were all internationals.
cultural_challenges: None really. Maybe that there is a person hired in the supermarked only to pack your groceries, so where you are used to stressing around in REMA 1000 trying to pack up everything, you just end up standing and staring awkwardly while you wait. But for real, people are friendly and easy to strike up conversations with, and since you also speak their language, you feel somewhat at home pretty quickly.
culture_appreciated: Learning about the Maori culture (original people of New Zealand) was really cool!
top3_advice: (1) Live with UniFlats (2) Go to the OUSA sauna at least once (preferably thrice a week) (3) Have fun and make use of the opportunities that present themselves along the way
most_rewarding: The personal experiences and friendships. Academically, it was probably just improving my oral english
greatest_challenge: I did feel a bit of home sickness every now then,

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

crucial_aspects: Different climate, relative proximity to home country and a good educational system
overall_comments: Very nice stay
info_ease: It was very easy, a Kuumi student were there to help with the apartment and was very good at answering questions
arrival_assistance: There was a kuumi student from the host university who welcomed me, and helped me get settled
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Very nice stay
registration_process: It all happened digitally, but a student coordinator was there to help
registration_help: Student coordinator
registration_success: I got in to all the classes, most of them turned out to be online, which for me was a downside, as I went abroad to experience another study culture on campus, which I feel like I missed when having to study from my apartment most of the time

activities_recommended: I really enjoyed trying out a lot of different sports activities, like the Futsal, volleyball, fitness boxing and Ultimate frisbee.

culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy and similar to the danish one.

cultural_challenges: Not really any
culture_appreciated: The general friendliness and openness
top3_advice: Be prepared for a lack of sunlight, sign up for different events and activities in the beginning, and then figure out what you wanna do more of and what not. Make sure to call a student advisor, and discover if all the classes in your study field are online
other_useful_info: not particularly
most_rewarding: For me, the most rewarding thing, was probably the development of my everyday English, which I could feel get a lot better during my stay, but overall it was just all a great experience
greatest_challenge: I think the lack of sunlight took me by surprise, this comined with the fact that most of my study hours were spent online was a bit hard. Luckily there were all these sports classes and events that helped out a lot.

academics_comments: The academic was not good, but the place was beautiful.

activities_recommended: Non, maybe sauna

crucial_aspects: I wanted to stay in the Nordic countries, so that the health care system would correspond somewhat to the danish one
overall_comments: Language barrier was bigger than expected.
info_ease: It was fine.
arrival_assistance: I was showed to the hospital by the university exchange coordinator, They helped me get an ID card, showed me to the uniforms and the lockers and dropped me off with the doctor responsible at my first internship.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Language barrier was bigger than expected.
registration_process: There was a lot of problems with UCPH wanting you to do a study exchange and Oulu University only accepting traineeships. It was a lot of back and forth and didn't seem like anyone knew anything. I felt very lost during the process, but it all ended well.
registration_help: Emailing with the UCPH exchange coordinator and the Oulu exchange coordinator.
registration_success: Not applicable
registration_advice: Be patient and see if you can get help from a former exchange student.
academics_comments: Language barrier was bigger than expected.
course_level: 12 weeks of clinical internship.
teaching_comparison: Varied a lot between the departments. Some were very similar, some not. Advice would be to be very proactive and keep asking questions and be specific about practical skills you want to learn.
courses_enrolled: 5 weeks of internal medicine, 5 weeks of surgery, 2 weeks of anesthesiology.
recommended_courses: Cardiology, Emergency medicine, Traumatology, Urology and Anesthesiology
unexpected_costs: Not really much. If you want to travel, that can be quite expensive.
cost_comparison: Cafeteria at the hospital was 3 euro for students - very cheap. You can rent sports equipment for free at LIKKE in the city. Travelling expenses were a bit more expensive than expected.
activities_available: They have a sportsprogramme called UNI-move. I didn't use it.
activities_recommended: Learn to do cross country skiing, very accessible in Oulu. Winter swimming and sauna.
weekend_recommendations: Lapland. Hiking, cross country skiing, snow mobile, ice fishing.

socializing_tips: It is difficult as you'll mostly likely live in pure exchange dorms. Try to talk with the younger doctors in your internship.
cultural_challenges: Main issue was language barrier. A lot of people (including some doctors) don't feel that comfortable speaking English.
culture_appreciated: They enjoy if you are straight forward, so don't be afraid to ask to learn stuff. They only interpret it as interest and it will make your internships a lot better.
top3_advice: Be more proactive than you expect. If someone invites you to an activity, say yes. Enjoy the nature.
other_useful_info: You need a signature for attendance every day. If there are national holidays (like easter) you will have the days off.
most_rewarding: Going skiing in lapland.
greatest_challenge: Language barrier.

crucial_aspects: Relevant courses, big international community at the university and an active student culture with events.
info_ease: Fairly easy.
arrival_assistance: There was a local student who helped us with introducing us to the university and city. He showed us where to find relevant information and showed us around.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_help: The study coordinator was very helpful.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: It's simple, but if the registration period has passed, then write to your study coordinator at the host university.

culture_appreciated: The sauna culture was great.
top3_advice: You have a lot of free time in your studies so use it to explore and experience things. crucial_aspects: When I started my studies I always knew I wanted to go abroad for a semester. Choosing Spain was a combination of wanting to see life at an European Hospital different from Denmark (differences and similarities), explore a different culture, learning spanish and the thing that convinced my most of all to go to Spain was the previous students great recommendations.
info_ease: I think the emails I received from both universities would be a little confusing at some point and I had a bit of difficulties knowing exactly what to do when, but then I just wrote to the universities for help and they were both very helpful, so I wish I had just done that sooner.
arrival_assistance: Only communication through e-mail. The receiving at the hospital was very poor and when I finally found the person in charge of my stay at the hospital he only spoke spanish, so it was a bit difficult to understand everything for me.
arrival_comments: I could have wished for more information regarding my stay upon arrival and maybe someone welcoming me and showing me around at the hospital the first day and getting me in contact with the other medical Erasmus students in Hospital de Cabueñes. That would have been very nice.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I was a little confused at first and found it difficult finding the hospital departments, but ended up finding it on wikipedia. Hospital de Cabueñes has a lot of different departments, so it was a good opportunity to try out fields that you are thinking about specializing in and maybe have not been able to try at your host university. I chose 4 different departments and was able to be at them all. And again if in doubt it is easiest to just write and ask.
registration_help: It was difficult to find the information, but I usually got all of my questions answered if I just wrote an email and asked.
registration_success: I got all the four specialities I wanted to try.
registration_advice: Find the departments in wikipedia and just ask if you can go to the departments you found interesting. I did four different specialities, which meant one for three weeks, and I found that suitable.
course_level: Final semester
teaching_comparison: I did not have any classes, but I thought the doctors overall did a great job explaining and including me. The only time this didn't happen was when they were too busy or my spanish was just not good enough and their english also not good enough
courses_enrolled: 12 weeks clinical rotation - 3 weeks in internal medicine - 3 weeks in hematology - 3 weeks in pediatrics - 3 weeks in neurology
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend hematology, they were the nicest doctors to be with and I felt more included than anywhere else in the hospital. Pediatrics was very hard for me to stay in because my spanish wasn't good enough for them and I didn't feel included at all, but maybe it would have been different if my spanish was better
unexpected_costs: No
cost_comparison: Especially drinks were far less expensive than in Denmark. The apartment was a bit more expensive, than I could have hoped for, but overall everything was less expensive than in Denmark
activities_available: The Erasmus Team planned a tapas party each thursday night, which I can highly recommend. At first I thought people were a bit young and very crazy party people, but after giving it a second chance I met amazing people, which I wished I had gotten to know sooner. Also they planned hiking trips, volleyball tournaments and a trip to Ibiza.
activities_recommended: Go surfing! You can rent a board and/or take classes. "Skool Surf" even has a danish-speaking instructor
weekend_recommendations: Rent a car (around 66 euro for a day) and drive out to explore beautiful Asturias, like the small town Cudillero (!) and Lastres, and the amazing mountains Picos de Europa.
culture_adjustment: The opening hours in the shops and restaurants are very different, because they close down doing the siesta, which was a bit hard to get used to, but once I did, I really enjoyed taking naps. Also people don't go out to eat until 21-22, but it wasn't a problem as soon as you got used to it.
socializing_tips: Go to "Jueves de Tapas", the tapas party on thursdays in Gijón. The event is on the Erasmus Gijón-Facebook page. It can be a little intimidating at first, but it was a great way to meet people. Also I would recommend to write to the person in charge of your hospital stay and ask him to get you in touch with the other medical Erasmus students at the hospital. I didn't do that, but I wish that I had, because I met some great friends far too late in my internship.
cultural_challenges: The language! Very few people speak english, and since my spanish wasn't that good it was challenging and sometimes quite lonely, but still I always managed in the end.
culture_appreciated: The lifestyle is very chill and people are very nice. Gijón is an amazing town, with great seafood, sidewalk cafés and a big beach with many dogs!
top3_advice: If in doubt don't waste your time trying to figure things out yourself, just ask. Try the specialities you find interesting and try to ask if you can go with the same doctor most of the time. I really enjoyed the opportunity of getting to know people better that way and not just being another random student every day. If you want to try a procedure or to do the medical examination, you usually can, so don't be afraid to ask
other_useful_info: I bought a used bike for 150 euro and sold it again for 75 euros when I left. I can really recommend it! It seemed like a lot of money at first, but I really loved my route to the hospital each day and having the opportunity to go for trips in the weekend. I think that it actually saved me money in the end, since I didn't take the bus at any time.
most_rewarding: Experiencing another culture and learning that even though your danish guidelines tells you treat one way, it is not the only right way to treat a patient - that was a very interesting perspective for me. Also I got the opportunity to examine things I haven't done before like a neck-back-stiffnes, a large abdominal tumor, splenomegaly and listening to many hearts and lungs with my stethoscope
greatest_challenge: The language again. Most doctors were very kind, spoke great english and really tried to explain, but I also met some doctors who didn't even wanted to try to explain to me in english, and I lost a lot of important information this way. Also I wasn't really able to speak to patients, but when I was with the kind doctors it wasn't really a problem, and sometimes I was with a local medical student or a resident, who would explain things to me.
other_comments: I began learning Spanish a year before my trip, so if you want to go, but don't speak spanish yet, don't let it stop you! Even though it was challenging for me sometimes, both taking evening classes before and not being able to understand everything, I had an amazing trip and would really recommend it. Gijón is also an amazing place so it is a win-win!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to live in a city that was not too small nor too big. Also I wanted to live in a Spanish city to learn more about the Spanish health care system and improve my Spanish. A big plus was that Gijon is located in between the mountains and the sea, so there are lots of great outdoor options!
overall_comments: Overall my erasmus exchange in Gijon was amazing! The only reason for it not being a 10 was the little information from the hospital before arriving.
info_ease: To find the information about my clinical rotations and clinical tutors, I needed to send a lot of e-mails. Some weeks before arrivel I managed to get in conctact with Monica who works at the Faculty of Medicine in Oviedo. She organized my learning agreement and my clinical rotations. Also I got an e-mail from the Hospital of Cabueñes with information about the departments at the hospital.
arrival_assistance: My first day at the Hospital I went to the secretaría to meet SIlvia (the responsible person for erasmus students). She helped me to get an ID card, uniform etc. At the University we had a welcome lecture for all international students about how to get a student card, bus card etc.
arrival_comments: I was satisfied with the orientation from the Faculty of Medicine, but from the Hospital I did not get so much orientation before arriving. I did not know what time or where to show up the first day, for example. Luckily everything was sorted out my first day at the hospital :)
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall my erasmus exchange in Gijon was amazing! The only reason for it not being a 10 was the little information from the hospital before arriving.
registration_process: See previous comment.
registration_help: There was an office you could go to at the Faculty of Medicine in Oviedo to get help. I got all the help I needed from Monica though e-mails.
registration_success: I did not have classes, only clinical rotations. I could choose where I wanted to do my clnical rotations, and Silvia at the hospital was very helpful to make sure I was placed at the departments that I wanted.
registration_advice: All the details about your clinical rotations will be sorted out when you arrive at the hospital, so no need to freak out (like I did) :)
academics_comments: Overall my erasmus exchange in Gijon was amazing! The only reason for it not being a 10 was the little information from the hospital before arriving.
course_level: I did clinical rotations at Urgencias, Anestesia and Pediatria (12 weeks in total)
teaching_comparison: In Spain there was more time for one-to-one supervision. Normally I was assigned a young doctor as my supvervisor the whole day and we did most of the examinations together.
courses_enrolled: I did clinical rotations at Urgencias, Anestesia and Pediatria.
recommended_courses: Anestesia was really good!! Not that many other students (so you get a lot of hands on and supervision) and super nice doctors!!
unexpected_costs: I chose to buy a surf board and a wet suit, which was quite expensive, but totally worth it!!
cost_comparison: Buses from the cities in the north of Spain were a bit more expensive than expected. Transportation in Gijon, food and housing was cheaper than expected.
activities_available: The erasmus group in Gijon organized tapas nights, city sightseeing, trips to Bilbao and Portugal and much more :)
activities_recommended: Join the hiking group to see some of the beautiful national parks in Asturias, join the social tapas nights and some of the trips!
weekend_recommendations: Go hiking!! Picos de Europa is a must, also los acantilados del infierno and Parque de Somiedo. Go travel and see the surrounding small cities in Asturias: Ribadesella, Llanes and Lastres.
culture_adjustment: I have lived in Spain before and I lived with Spanish students, so for me it was quite easy to adjust to the local culture. Be open minded, ask a lot of questions and you will feel more and more Spanish :)
socializing_tips: Join a sports acitivity, surfing class, hiking or the tapas nights!
cultural_challenges: The meals! In Spain they have lunch at 15 and dinner at 22. Make sure to fill your scrub with lots of snacks, because there is no lunch break at the hospital before 15.
culture_appreciated: The people!! They are so open and welcoming, and it's very easy to make new friends.
top3_advice: Come prepared to the hospital (bring your books and practice some Spanish vocabulary used at the hospital), bring hiking equipments and enjoy the beautiful Asturias!
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: To be able to attend patients individually in another language and to meet so many other students from other countries.
greatest_challenge: To be "alone" in a new city. The first week where everything was new: the hospital, the poeple, the city was definitely the most challenging one.
other_comments: I will recommend everyone to go on erasmus exchange. It has been a memory for life!!

crucial_aspects: I wanted a destination where I could combine clinical training with language immersion. Gijón offered the opportunity to gain hands-on experience in a hospital setting while improving my Spanish skills. Additionally, the chance to experience a different healthcare system and live in a culturally rich and naturally beautiful region like Asturias made Universidad de Oviedo an ideal choice. Furthermore, since I did not have more SU, the Erasmus grant was crucial.
info_ease: Very little information was provided in advance by the international office or faculty coordinator. Fortunately, the local Erasmus Student Network (ESN) offered support. Practical details—such as hospital schedules, a hospital map, and course expectations—only became clear on my first day at the hospital. I also had to change the order of my rotations due to coordination issues between departments. However, once I found the right administrative office, things started falling into place. What I learned most from my stay in Spain was this: everything will eventually work out—it just requires more patience, flexibility, and acceptance of limited upfront information.
arrival_assistance: See answer above
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process was somewhat unclear at first. I was told I had to wait until December to register for February rotations, which made obtaining pre-approval and completing my grant applications difficult. However, with persistence and many phone calls, I managed to outline a plan for the rotations I wanted. Although the schedule was later adjusted, I ultimately secured all my preferred placements. I did not receive much information in advance, so I had to be proactive upon arrival. I visited the international office at Hospital de Cabueñes and met the coordinator in person to arrange my clinical rotations. Some departments were not well coordinated, requiring me to adjust the order of my rotations initially. Once I identified the correct contacts, the process became much smoother. Flexibility and patience were essential throughout.

course_level: All of my time was spent on rotations rather than traditional lectures, so the “course level” was like clinical rotations in Denmark. Because all instruction and patient interactions were in Spanish, I not only practiced terminology and patient–doctor communication but also had to think and respond quickly in a second language, which added an extra layer of challenge and learning. Compared to Denmark, I found that specialists in each department had more time to teach and mentor students. In some rotations, I could spend a full hour discussing a complex case with a consultant or observing a procedure step-by-step—opportunities that are rarer back home due to faster patient turnover. The work culture was different, too: doctors often worked longer hours overall but took regular, relaxed breaks. It wasn’t unusual for a consultant to pause mid‐morning for a coffee and a chat about teaching points, research interests, or cultural differences in patient care. That unhurried atmosphere made it easier to ask questions, refine clinical skills, and absorb new practices, all while refining my Spanish in a supportive environment.

activities_recommended: Additionally, the local Erasmus Student Network (ESN) organized cultural events, weekend trips, and social gatherings, such as tapas nights and hiking tours. These activities were a great way to meet other students and explore the region. But since I stayed with my boyfriend and he was not allowed to join, I did not participate. If you're older join Crossing Gijón.
weekend_recommendations: Visit Barcelona, Madrid, Playa de Nora, Oviedo,
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture in Gijón was relatively easy, especially with an open mind and a bit of patience. People were warm, welcoming, and curious about international students. The pace of life was slower than in Denmark, and I had to get used to the later meal times and more flexible approach to time and organization. Once I embraced that, I really enjoyed the relaxed atmosphere, social coffee breaks, and strong sense of community.
cultural_challenges: One of the most challenging cultural differences was the lack of structure and punctuality compared to what I’m used to in Denmark. Information was often provided at the last minute, and schedules could change without much notice. It required flexibility and sometimes a bit of persistence to get things organized. Also, the late meal times and long lunch breaks took some getting used to, but over time I adapted and came to appreciate the more relaxed rhythm of daily life.
culture_appreciated: I especially appreciated the warmth and openness of the people in Gijón. There was a strong sense of community, and I often experienced genuine interest and kindness from both hospital staff and locals. I also enjoyed the relaxed pace of life, the daily social rituals like coffee breaks, and the emphasis on enjoying good food and conversation. The natural beauty of Asturias—with its beaches, mountains, and green landscapes—added to the overall experience and made everyday life feel rich and balanced.
top3_advice: Be flexible and proactive – The organization can be less structured than at UCPH. You might not get all the information you need in advance, so be ready to ask questions, show up in person, and follow up multiple times if necessary. Things usually work out—but not always on the first try. Learn as much Spanish as you can beforehand – Most communication at the hospital (and in daily life) is in Spanish. Having a solid foundation in the language will make both your clinical learning and social experience much smoother and more rewarding. Enjoy the local culture – Embrace the slower pace, take part in social rituals like coffee breaks, and explore Asturias’ stunning nature. Living in Gijón offers a great balance between professional growth and personal enjoyment—make the most of both!
other_useful_info: Yes—here’s a final tip that could be useful for future exchange students: Bring more patience than you think you’ll need. The administrative processes can feel unstructured, and communication is often last-minute. Don’t panic—ask around, visit offices in person, and talk to other students or hospital staff. Things will eventually fall into place. Also, consider arriving a bit early to settle in, get to know the city, and practice your Spanish. And if possible, live close to the city center—walking along the beach is a luxury that makes every day better!
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was gaining the confidence to communicate effectively in Spanish in a clinical setting. Being able to take patient histories, discuss treatment plans with doctors, and truly connect across language and cultural barriers was incredibly fulfilling. It also gave me a new perspective on healthcare and deepened my understanding of what it means to be a good, empathetic doctor—no matter where in the world you are.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during the exchange was the lack of structure and clear communication, especially in the beginning. Information about rotations, schedules, and expectations was limited or provided at the last minute, which made planning difficult. I had to be very proactive, flexible, and persistent to get the information I needed and ensure that everything worked out. While it was frustrating at times, it also taught me valuable lessons in adaptability and problem-solving.
