crucial_aspects: I chose Australia as I was curious about cultural life as well as exploring nature. In addition, Australia has top ranking universities.
info_ease: Most information was relatively easy to obtain.
arrival_assistance: At the University of Queensland, there is a pretty extensive orientation week, which focuses on social wellbeing as well as academic support.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There are some pretty helpful tools available to see which courses clash etc. You can check the enrolment criteria as well as other course information in a so-called "course profile" online. Even when the semester has started, it is possible to change your courses for some time.
registration_help: E.g. the tool "UQ Planner" where you can insert courses and design your own schedule.
registration_success: Somewhat successful. However, I experienced that even as a master student in Denmark, I was still only allowed to take undergraduate courses. Some exceptions can perhaps be made if you contact the professors of the course.
registration_advice: Make sure you meet the enrolment criteria for courses or have some backup courses in mind in case you are not eligible for your first priorities. On the university's website, you can also use a filter that only shows courses that are eligible for exchange students.
course_level: Some of my courses were at a challenging level, while most of them were fairly easy to keep up with.
teaching_comparison: I experienced that I was not reading as much as I do at my home university. Instead, I had to engage more actively in classes and prepare something for each week. Exams are different as assessment activities are distributed throughout the semester, e.g. one assignment is 30% of your grade etc.
courses_enrolled: PSYC2040 Social and Organisational Psychology MGTS2603 Leading and Managing People SOCY3329 Qualitative Social Research
recommended_courses: MGTS2603 Leading and Managing People I found that all students in this class enjoyed attending class. It was always very engaging and active. However, you have to want to participate in group work.
unexpected_costs: Not unexpected, but you have to apply for OSHC as an overseas exchange student and of course you also have to pay for a student visa.
cost_comparison: You can get a 50% discount on public transport in Brisbane as a student.
activities_available: All kinds of clubs you can even imagine. In the beginning of the semester, you can check them all out in the great court.
activities_recommended: Explore the nature and beaches in Queensland.
weekend_recommendations: Gold Coast, Stradbroke island, Moreton island - these can be explored on a day trip. I also went to New Zealand, Sydney, K'gari/Fraser island and Cairns. Lastly, I went to Uluru in the northern territory, which I can strongly recommend as this was a very special place.
culture_adjustment: It was easy. Australians are mostly open and also really helpful.
cultural_challenges: Not really any.
culture_appreciated: The openness to meet other people.
top3_advice: 1. Join QUEST. 2. Remember to keep up with school work during the semester and not just at the end. 3. There is a broad selection of courses, so choose something that you find interesting even though it might differ somewhat from your field of study.
other_useful_info: You can follow UQ clubs etc. on social media. Oftentimes, there will be different events at campus (e.g. puppy cuddling, painting etc.)
most_rewarding: Getting to meet other exchange students from around the world.
greatest_challenge: Coordinating group work that had to be completed every week (only goes for some courses)

crucial_aspects: It was crucial to me that the university would have a lot of social opportunities. And the University of Queensland (UQ) has a broad variety of student clubs, so I think that anyone would be able to find at least one, they would like to join. Besides that, it was very important to me that I was able to find courses that I found interesting.
overall_comments: I found that the courses were much easier compared to studying at the University of Copenhagen. At times I felt a bit disappointed by this, but it really allowed me to go on trips and explore the country.
info_ease: UQ has a orientation (O-)week, which provides a lot of information and opportunities to meet other exchange students. They had so many events, that it felt like you had to prioritize between them. However, I chose a 3-weeks course which took place before O-week. Therefore, I had to figure out things before, but UQ has a Student Central where you can go with all your questions, which made it very easy to obtain information.
arrival_assistance: I had the e-mail address for the one, who was responsible for UQ's exchange students, so I could also directly ask her. But besides that I really found that the Student Central was very useful during my entire stay.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I found that the courses were much easier compared to studying at the University of Copenhagen. At times I felt a bit disappointed by this, but it really allowed me to go on trips and explore the country.
registration_process: It is now awhile ago, but I don't remember it as very difficult.
registration_help: It was possible to write to Søren, who is the one from UCPH that is responsible for exchange students going to Australia and New Zealand.
registration_success: Getting the permission from UCPH was very slow, but applying at UQ was very easy. You can easily change courses at UQ, also in the beginning at the semester. It was my impression, that exchange students from other European countries had chosen more courses that they needed, so that they could try them out.
registration_advice: Don't stress too much about it.
academics_comments: I found that the courses were much easier compared to studying at the University of Copenhagen. At times I felt a bit disappointed by this, but it really allowed me to go on trips and explore the country.
course_level: I found that the courses were easier than studying at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: UQ has multiple assignments through out the semester, which could be between 5%-45% of your final grade. So I found that I had to pay more attention to deadlines through out the semester. Only one of the courses, I had, had a final exam whereas the others just had final assignments. The final assignments allows for greater flexibility.
courses_enrolled: Food for a Healthy Planet Cost Benefit Analysis & Project Evaluation R and Python for the Life Sciences Academic English & Thesis Writing for International Students
recommended_courses: R and Python for the Life Sciences was the best course, I had. We were very few students in the classroom, and I had the experience that the content of the course was at the level, I expected. I gained a lot of useful knowledge by the completion of this course.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay for Overseas Student Health Care (OSHC).
cost_comparison: Housing was very expensive. And I did use a lot of money for traveling, but that was my own choice.
activities_available: I think there are more than 200 clubs, so I can't list all of them. I joined the mountain club, running club, skiing club, exchange club and the association for public health students.
activities_recommended: I would definitely recommend QEUST, which is the exchange students club. It is a great way to meet other exchange students, and they offer trips to places near Brisbane. I also met some friends through this club, and we planned trips on our own. Besides that I'd recommend UQ SRC (the running club) and UQ MC (the mountain club). Both clubs are very social and a great opportunity to meet Australians.
weekend_recommendations: There are so many places to go! Just nearby is the Gold Coast, Sunshine Coast, Glass House Mountains, Noosa, and Byron Bay. I'd definitely also recommend traveling further away to places like Melbourne, Sydney, and Tasmania.
culture_adjustment: I found that Australia is not that different from Denmark.
socializing_tips: You should join some of the clubs. In my experience socializing during classes is not that common.
cultural_challenges: I found it a bit challenging that everything closes earlier than I'm used to in Copenhagen.
culture_appreciated: People are very kind and easy to talk to. It's a very welcoming place to arrive.
top3_advice: 1) You should not stress about finding accommodation. It's very common that people make arrangements to see different flats before arriving without having anything in particular. 2) Be prepared to spend some money on traveling. Would be shame not to explore this great country. 3) UQ has a lot thing happening through the semester (e.g. mental health week). Follow the student union on Instagram to see what's going on during the different weeks.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of right now.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many people, mostly from around Europe.
greatest_challenge: Adjusting to the high temperatures and the humidity. Also the sun sets very early.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere far away and preferably english speaking. I wanted to challenge myself by going somewhere far away from my safetynet.
info_ease: The UQ website is very well organised so it's easy to find the information you need. I also got emails with reminders and additional info
arrival_assistance: All exchange and study abroad students were encouraged to attend a welcoming session the week before classes commenced where all necessary information was given. Further sessions were also held for specific areas e.g. choosing courses.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There is a course catalogue with all the courses available. You can search on key words, faculties etc. It's a lot to go through, but that just means there's a lot to choose from which is good. There is also a list of courses pre-approved for exchange students, but you can always ask to get other courses approved as well. For some courses there are recommended or required prerequisites. You have to piece your own timetable together. Lectures are recorded and uploaded so they are allowed to clash. Other activites (lab, class work etc.) are for most courses offered at different times for different groups, so you just have to choose the right groups to make your timetable work.
registration_help: The exchange coordinators are very helpful at getting the courses approved. Contact via email
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted
registration_advice: Take your time to look at courses. Normal study load is usually four courses of 2 units (7,5 ects) each, but choose 5 or 6 to get approved since some might be rejected. Don't worry about the time table. Clashing lectures are no issue since all lectures are recoreded and uploaded.
course_level: The academic level in Australia is generally not as high as I'm used to in Copenhagen. This is alright since it gave me more time to explore the country while still keeping up with my studies.
teaching_comparison: I had lectures plus lab work and normal classes in some courses. For all of my courses there was no receommended readings for the lectures. Some courses had one or two recommended books, but is was never used in class. The material needed to pass the courses was in the lectures and the lecture notes. There were more assignments than I'm used to, but that also meant that none of my exams accounted fro more than 50% of my final grade.
courses_enrolled: MARS1001 - Living Oceans BIOL3006 - Molecular Cell Biology II DEVB2000 - Stem Cells, Development & Developmental Disorders DEVB3001 - Developmental Neurobiology
recommended_courses: DEVB3001 - Developmental Neurobiology was my faverite course. However, it was also the most chanllenging course. The lecture material is mainly based on academic papers and new reseach which is very interesting. You get a lot of fun fact from thsi course. DEVB2000 - Great introductory course to developmental biology. I mainly chose it for tehe lab work as you get to do IVF on mice, which was pretty cool
unexpected_costs: Australia is generally just as expensive is Copenhagen.
cost_comparison: Coffee is cheaper in Brisbane than in Copenhagen. Especially on campus. Public transport is quite cheap as a student.
activities_available: All clubs you can possibly imagine are availible at UQ. Sports, creative, social, religious, cultural etc.
activities_recommended: QUEST and UQ Surfers make a lot of great trips and parties. Great place to meet ither people especially international students.
weekend_recommendations: There is a lot of places to go from Brisbane on weekend trips. This includes SUnshine Coast, Rainbow Beach, Gold Coast, Byron Bay and the many national parks in the area.
culture_adjustment: Australian culture is very western, so it's not hard to adjust
socializing_tips: Join some clubs
cultural_challenges: Many (white) older Australians are very openly racist, especially towards the indegenous people (aboriginal) and asians. This took me by suprise. The younger generaltion are much beter though. Partying in Australia is a bit different than in Copenhagen. Most bars and clubs close a 2 at the latest. This also means that Australians tend to go out earlier (around 8 o'clock)
culture_appreciated: There are free public BBQs everywhere
top3_advice: Don't live on campus Use your weekends to go explore the area around Brisbane Use the first few weeks to meet a lot of people
other_useful_info: Relax a bit study wise. The level is lower than at UCPH and I feet that not as much is expected to get a good result.
most_rewarding: Getting to live in Australia and explore the country
greatest_challenge: Going to teh other side of teh world all alone is a bit daunting at first. But everything will sort itself out. You will get friends and you will have a wonderfull time. Don't worry!

crucial_aspects: Culture and opportunity to do outdoor experiences in nature
info_ease: To be fair, there is a lot of practicalities and it is an overload of information in the beginning, and the most important things might get lost in the information such as finding cheap accomodation if you're not able to pay a huge amount to stay at a student accommodation (there are other opportunities), creating a bank account and starting to study at a new place. It is a big deal to go on exchange - a lot of practicalities, but you grow from that as well.

arrival_comments: Could have told us more about how the assessment summary works and that it is only a percentage of the full grade and what it takes to pass a course, since it is very different from Denmark and other countries
housing_how: I found housing on my own

course_level: BA

other_useful_info: There're free breakfast and dinner, a shop with cheap grocery stuff for students and so many social arrangements all the time. The Redroom is the uni's own bar!

crucial_aspects: I have always wanted to study abroad. And I wanted it to be somewhere far away so that I could truly experience feeling independent. Australia specifically has alway fascinated me in that it is a western culture that is isolated so far away from anywhere else. Their nature and wildlife were truly some of the most amazing I have ever seen as it is so different from anything else I have ever experienced. Furthermore the academic level of the universities in Australia is very high, so I feel it allowed me to develop myself intelectually. Lastly, it was bonus that Australia is an English-speaking country, so that I really got a chance to develop my academical English - both spoken and written - which I believe will help me in my future studies and career.
info_ease: It was somewhat easy, but it definitely takes some effort to get used to an entirely different education system.
arrival_assistance: University of Queensland specifically had a department for exchange students and study abroad that was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: UQ's system is fairly easy and intuitive compared to other universities I imagine.
registration_help: E-mail support and FAQ's

Beware, in Australia the difference between second and third year courses can be very significant in terms of assesments and hours spent each weak, so I do not recommend getting third year courses only.
teaching_comparison: It was similar however, you feel more independent at UCPH. More of the classes at UQ were compulsory.

crucial_aspects: When choosing my study destination, several factors made the University of Queensland (UQ) and Australia the ideal choice for me. UQ's strong reputation for academic excellence, particularly in psychology and cultural studies, was a key factor. The university offers a diverse range of courses that align with my interests in clinical and cultural psychology, providing me with the opportunity to explore these fields from a global perspective. I was particularly drawn to UQ’s emphasis on innovative research and its commitment to addressing societal challenges, such as mental health and social inclusion, which resonate deeply with my academic and professional aspirations. Beyond academics, the cultural richness of Australia played a significant role in my decision. As a multicultural country with a history of both colonial and Indigenous influences, Australia offers unique insights into the intersections of culture, identity, and psychology. I was eager to learn about the experiences of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, particularly in relation to mental health and well-being. This perspective was not only academically enriching but also highly relevant to understanding diversity and inclusion in a globalized world. The welcoming and laid-back Australian culture also appealed to me. I valued the opportunity to engage with people from diverse backgrounds and to immerse myself in a society that emphasizes community, resilience, and a balance between work and leisure. Brisbane’s vibrant city life combined with its proximity to stunning natural landscapes, such as beaches and rainforests, made it an inspiring environment for both personal and academic growth. In summary, UQ’s academic excellence, coupled with the cultural richness and inclusivity of Australia, made it the perfect destination to broaden my knowledge and develop my skills as a future psychologist.

crucial_aspects: I chose this study destination because I have close family and personal connections in the Brisbane area, and because the University of Queensland offers a strong academic environment that aligns with my interests.
info_ease: It was generally very easy to find the information I needed. Both KU and UQ provided clear and helpful information channels. UQ has many different platforms and webpages, which took a bit of time to navigate in the beginning, but overall the information was easy to access.
arrival_assistance: I participated in O-Week, where I received a lot of practical information and support that helped me settle in quickly.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process at UQ was straightforward. I had to apply to UQ quite early, and course enrolment opened a couple of months before arrival. About a month before the semester started, I was able to select my timetable. Overall, the steps were clearly communicated and easy to follow.
registration_help: There was plenty of help available. UQ provided lots of guides and step-by-step instructions through their online portals, and it was easy to contact staff if I had any questions.
registration_success: Very successful. I was able to register for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: My main advice is to make full use of the UQ portals, where all the guides and step-by-step instructions for registration are available. They explain the process very clearly and make enrolment much easier.
course_level: The course structure was a bit different from what I am used to, as a larger share of the assessment consisted of presentations, weekly quizzes and continuous assignments. Overall, however, I found the courses to be slightly easier than at my home university.
teaching_comparison: The overall teaching style was quite similar to UCPH, with a structure based on lectures and tutorials. The format felt familiar and easy to adapt to.
courses_enrolled: ECON7200 Economics of Financial Markets, ECON7333 Big Data and Machine Learning, ECON7460 Health Economics, ECON7760 Economics of Climate Change
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend ECON7333 Big Data and Machine Learning, as it uses R throughout the course, and I was very happy to be introduced to practical coding and machine-learning tools in a structured way. I would also recommend ECON7200 Economics of Financial Markets, which covers concepts introduced during the bachelor’s programme at UCPH and builds on them in a very applied and engaging way.
unexpected_costs: The main unexpected cost was the visa. It was very expensive, and since I also needed an extension to stay over Christmas, the additional fee made it even more costly than I had anticipated.
cost_comparison: Public transport was much cheaper than I expected, it costs only around AUD 0.50 per fare, regardless of distance within Queensland. Groceries were roughly in the same price range as in Denmark, although some items were noticeably more expensive and others cheaper. Eating out was generally a bit cheaper than in Denmark, and coffee was significantly cheaper, often around half the price of a to-go coffee in Copenhagen.
activities_available: There were plenty of cultural, athletic and social activities available. UQ offers a wide range of student clubs, including surfing, climbing, hiking, diving and volleyball, as well as many non-sport clubs for students looking for social or cultural activities.
activities_recommended: I would especially recommend joining the UQ Mountain Club. I was very happy with it, they offered rock climbing twice a week and organised several hiking trips. You don’t need any prior climbing experience to join, which makes it a great way to try something new, meet people and explore Queensland.
weekend_recommendations: I would definitely recommend prioritising the inland mountains — they are absolutely stunning and often overlooked by visiting students. Of course, exploring the beaches on the Sunshine Coast and Gold Coast is also essential. I also travelled to New Zealand and was completely blown away. There are plenty of great destinations with relatively cheap fares within Australia as well, such as Cairns, the Whitsundays and the Blue Mountains.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. UQ has a highly international and student-focused environment, which made adjusting to the local culture straightforward.
socializing_tips: A great tip is to join non-academic clubs or student groups. It’s one of the easiest ways to meet local students and build a social network outside the classroom.
cultural_challenges: I didn’t encounter any major cultural differences that were challenging. Australians and Danes are quite similar in terms of communication style and everyday culture, so the adjustment felt very smooth.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the early-morning culture and the generally high level of outdoor activity. People are very active and spend a lot of time outside, which creates a really positive atmosphere.
top3_advice: Join non-academic clubs: it’s one of the best ways to meet people and become part of the social environment. Start your housing search early: the rental market moves quickly, and being prepared makes the whole process easier. Embrace the outdoor culture: Australians are very active, and taking part in the outdoor lifestyle really enhances the exchange experience.
other_useful_info: t’s useful to know that UQ has many different online platforms, which can feel overwhelming at first. But once you get used to them, everything becomes very easy to navigate. UQ has an enormous number of clubs, so going to Market Day in the first week is a great way to discover communities and activities you wouldn’t have expected
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part was exploring Australia’s nature, from the mountains to the beaches, and experiencing a completely different outdoor culture.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge was the planning beforehand. Even though the information channels were very good and made the process manageable, there was still a constant stream of practical things to organise before arriving.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to Brisbane, Australia, as I wanted to be somewhere with amazing nature, weather, people and with a lot of things to experience.
overall_comments: My experience was amazing! I would recommend it to everybody. You get amazing friends for life that you're able to go on trips around Australia with every weekend, and experience so many things with all the time. UQ was a really good uni, which was an added bonus.
info_ease: UQ had sent a lot of emails beforehand with a lot of information, and a lot was available on their website as well. The first week of uni there is called Orientation Week, which is a week dedicated to introducing new students and exchange students to the uni.
arrival_assistance: During Orientation Week there are a lot of different lectures and stuff you can go to to get information on things, get guided tours around the uni, and meet other students. Here you can ask any questions you may have as well
arrival_comments: I had no trouble
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: My experience was amazing! I would recommend it to everybody. You get amazing friends for life that you're able to go on trips around Australia with every weekend, and experience so many things with all the time. UQ was a really good uni, which was an added bonus.

registration_help: Both UQ and UCPH were easy to get in contact with over mail if you had any questions! I had no troubles.

The only thing was that the courses you take have to be approved for exchange students. So if it doesn't specify on the course description that its approved for exchange students, you have to write the UQ exchange student coordinator to hear if the course can get approved. UQ also has a list on their webpage with courses that are pre-approved for exchange students, you can browse through
registration_advice: In the beginning of June UQ opened up a timetable feature on their webpage, where you could see what time of the week lectures for the different courses were. I recommend choosing courses where you get Fridays off, so you can go on weekend trips!
academics_comments: My experience was amazing! I would recommend it to everybody. You get amazing friends for life that you're able to go on trips around Australia with every weekend, and experience so many things with all the time. UQ was a really good uni, which was an added bonus.
course_level: The level of the 3rd year courses here were about the same as 3rd year courses in Denmark. The teachers were really good, sweet and helpful.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is different from UCPH in the sense that they have multiple assessments throughout the semester here that count towards your grade and not only a final exam. There were things like assignments, quizzes, presentations, and midterms. All the lectures here were also recorded, which meant that very few people showed up to the lectures. Lab (practical classes) were however mandatory, so this is were I met most of my friends in my courses. Also, all exams in science courses here are closed book.
courses_enrolled: Molecular Cell Biology II (BIOL3006), Microbial Genomics (MICR3004), Evolution (BIOL2201), and Living Ocean (MARS1001)

In Evolution and Living Oceans I learnt about Australian nature and marine life, which I thought was really cool.
unexpected_costs: Some unexpected costs were the mandatory Australian Health Insurance (OSHC) which cost 1700 kr, and the Australian student visa which was 6650 kr. I can also add to this budget that I spend about 2200 kr per month on travelling.
cost_comparison: Public transport in Queensland is only 50 cents! Alcohol was pretty expensive though. Overall, you have to be prepared for things to be expensive in Australia.

Every exchange student (even some from QUT) are in this club, and they do pub nights every Thursday, weekend trips to Noosa, Byron Bay and Moreton Island, and pub crawl parties. I would also recommend the UniDive club - I got my diving certificate here with some other exchange students, and it was amazing. The surf club was also good. Be prepared to sign up early for club events, as the tickets sell out fast!
weekend_recommendations: In Brisbane: Felons, West End Market, BBQ at Kangaroo Point Weekend trips: North Stradbroke Island, Moreton Island, Gold Coast, Springbrooke, Byron Bay, Noosa, Sunshine Coast, Rainbow Coast, K'agri, and much more! During the mid-semester break I recommend going on a roadtrip in Northern Queensland

socializing_tips: Join club! And talk to them in classes

culture_appreciated: Australians are very social, open and kind. Talk to the locals, they love giving recommendations.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study in an English-speaking country outside of Europe and chose my university based on its course offerings.
info_ease: Very easy. UQ prepared online modules and webinars that you can complete before your arrival, which help you find all relevant information.
arrival_assistance: Before the first week of classes, UQ has an orientation week with intro-sessions specifically for exchange students as well as optional sessions for all new students to UQ, such as campus and library tours, speed-friending, wifi setup and tech-sessions, etc. They also have a market day where you are introduced to all the social clubs at uni, which really helps you settle in and make new friends.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: UQ has a broad course catalogue, which can be a bit overwhelming, but you can filter though the options and search for course codes with certain themes such as DEVB for developmental biology courses. The registration process was quite easy. You had to choose four courses when applying at UQ, but these can easily be changed afterwards.
registration_help: Student central and the study abroad office is always ready to help.
registration_success: I had no issues getting the courses I wanted and it seemed that UQ adjusts the courses to accept as many students as possible. One of the courses had 3x as many students as the previous semester, so the course was adjusted with more workshop and lab time slots. In my understanding, you therefore don't really compete for a spot on the course but rather on your preferred timetable, which you put together yourself. Lectures are always recorded, so they are allowed to clash, and workshops and lab-work are offered at different timeslots, so you can piece together a timetable that works for you.
registration_advice: I was a bit stressed about the registration process being quite "late", because I did not want to apply for my visa or buy plane tickets before I was officially enrolled, but everything worked out fine. I would also recommend finding some back-up courses in case you get rejected or want to switch out your courses. In the first two weeks of classes you can add and drop courses, and you can even drop courses until later in the semester. Some people enrolled in five courses to begin with and then dropped one course later on, so you can try out your courses before committing, if you are in doubt.
course_level: Generally, the level was easier compared to KU, though there were many assignments throughout the semester which I was not used to. As long as you attended the classes the assignments were not so difficult, however, they often require you to be a bit more creative or work with you scientific communication skills which I found refreshing.
teaching_comparison: The assignments count towards the overall grade in the course, so my final exams only counted 40-50% of the overall grade. The rest was either assignments, quizzes or lab work. Only some parts of the assessment are "hurdles" required to pass the course, and exams are not always hurdles. We also had more group assignments than I am used to from KU. So compared to KU, the assessments are more spread out throughout the semester instead of focusing on one final exam.
courses_enrolled: Stem Cells, Development and Developmental Disorders (DEVB2000) Analysis of Scientific Data (STAT1201) Microbiology & Immunology (MICR2000)  Entrepreneurial Mindset and Ideation (TIMS1301)
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Stem Cells, Development and Developmental Disorders (DEVB2000), we got to do IVF on mice which was really cool and I found the course really interesting. I also highly recommend Microbiology & Immunology (MICR2000), the course had really good teachers and was well organized. The assignments were quite interesting and focused a lot on scientific communication. It gave a good and thorough introduction to microbiology, however, it did not go into much depth with immunology.
unexpected_costs: The Australian government recently made the visa application for students more expensive with a price of 6.814 DKK just for applying for the visa. In addition to this, you will need a mandatory health insurance, which you can add through UQ for 1.747 DKK for the entire stay.
cost_comparison: Groceries are generally just as expensive as in Denmark, with meat being a lot cheaper and alcohol being much more expensive. Public transport in Queensland is only 50 cents per ride, so you can travel all the way to the gold coast or to Noosa/ Sunshine Coast for only 50 cents! UQ also has many discounts on campus. You can get coffee for 3 AUD at certain time slots, and you can buy cheap left over groceries such as pasta or chickpeas for less than a dollar.
activities_available: UQ has over 200 social clubs ranging from sports, hobbies and all kinds of interests.
activities_recommended: I was part of QUEST (a club for exchange students) and UQ surfers, both of which plan pub crawls, weekend trips and parties. I also joined the Marine Society, who planned snorkel trips, and fun day tours and movie nights. Marine Biology students might be the nicest people you will ever meet.
weekend_recommendations: Brisbane is located perfectly for weekend or day trips. Gold Coast, Noosa and Sunshine Coast can all be visited by train, and Moreton Island or Stradbroke Island (Straddie) can be visited on a day trip or on a nice weekend trip. You are guaranteed to spot a wild kangaroo on Straddie - they are everywhere.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it was not very different from home and Australians (especially in Brisbane/ Queensland) are very friendly and open.
socializing_tips: Clubs are easy ways to get to know local students. You can also just start conversations with your classmates. People are used to having classes with different people all the time, so people are really open and easy to talk to.
cultural_challenges: Restaurants, cafes and bars close much earlier than what we are used to. Many cafes close by 2pm, restaurants by 9-10pm and bars by 12 and some by 2 at the latest.
culture_appreciated: Australians are very friendly and easy to talk to. People thank the bus driver after their ride, and sometimes you randomly start talking with the people sitting next to you at a restaurant. You greet your neighbors and talk with strangers in elevators. You say thank you to everyone for everything all the time, and I really enjoyed the generally positive energy towards complete strangers.
top3_advice: 1) See as much as you can of Australia. It is such a beautiful country 2) Join clubs, go to social events, even if you going alone and don't know anyone. 3) Meet people in O-week and come to club try-outs. Even of you don't join the club you will meet so many new people.
other_useful_info: Most exams are written by hand, so you might want to freshen up your handwriting ;)
most_rewarding: Exploring Australia and meeting so many amazing people
greatest_challenge: It is very far from home and the first weeks might be a bit challenging, but everything will work out. UQ also has so many good ressources, so if you feel stressed, lonely or homesick you can have (I think up to 10) free counseling sessions at student central.

crucial_aspects: I decided to go on exchange because I was really attracted to the idea of studying abroad. I wanted to gain a broader, more international perspective on law, which I think is essential for today’s lawyers. Additionally, having traveled solo in the past, I’ve experienced firsthand how much personal growth comes from stepping outside your comfort zone. I knew this exchange would be an opportunity for both professional and personal development.
overall_comments: I am really excited and grateful for my exchange in San Diego. Overall I have no complaints, but of course, there is always some things that could have been improved.
info_ease: It was very straightforward. The university provided a lot of helpful information and was great at explaining every aspect of the exchange, whether it was about visas, insurance, or course selection. They were always quick to respond and remained very supportive even after our arrival.
arrival_assistance: received thorough assistance with our visa, including clear guidance on what we were allowed to do and what we weren’t. Additionally, they provided us with important information about insurance and practical details for living in San Diego, which helped us settle in smoothly.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I am really excited and grateful for my exchange in San Diego. Overall I have no complaints, but of course, there is always some things that could have been improved.
registration_process: Getting accepted to USD involves meeting several requirements. First, you need to pass the TOEFL test with a minimum score of 93, which can be challenging. Second, you must provide at least one recommendation letter from an academic who is familiar with your legal skills and qualifications. Third, you’ll need to secure health insurance that meets USD’s strict requirements. This can be difficult, but after trying several options, we eventually found suitable coverage through Gouda. Finally, you must demonstrate sufficient financial resources, which requires proof of at least 120,000 DKK.
registration_help: It was possible to ask questions to USD regarding what the different requirements included.
registration_success: It was very successful—I managed to get almost all the courses I wanted. Once you’re accepted at USD, they invite you to an individual orientation session that explains how to search for and apply for courses. During this meeting, they also provide guidance on the number of credits you need and recommend courses that are well-suited for international exchange students.
registration_advice: Start good time in advance on preparing your documents for the application. Talk with other students who are in the same situation as you. Speak with former students if you know any.
academics_comments: I am really excited and grateful for my exchange in San Diego. Overall I have no complaints, but of course, there is always some things that could have been improved.
course_level: The courses i
teaching_comparison: No in the states they use the socratic method, where dialogue and active participation is bearing elements in the teaching. This is very different from UCPH, where there is no expectation, that you participate in the classes. It's therefor important to be prepared for classes.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to US Law Corporate Innovation Contract Drafting Legal Writing and Research Negotiation
recommended_courses: I highly recommend all of these courses. Intro to US Law is mandatory, but I thoroughly enjoyed the other four courses as well. My schedule only required me to attend classes two days a week, and many of the courses didn’t have a traditional final exam. Instead, grades were based on assignments and submissions throughout the semester. Negotiation was a fantastic and enjoyable class. The professor was incredibly kind, approachable, and showed a genuine interest in the international students. Each class involved preparing for roleplays, where you were paired with a random classmate. This was a great way to connect with American students and improve your English skills in a fun, interactive setting. Corporate Innovation had a higher academic and legal level compared to the other courses, with higher expectations for students. However, it was incredibly engaging and focused on how AI is impacting the legal profession and innovation. The exam consisted of writing a paper and presenting it to the class. Although the assignment was challenging, I learned a great deal from this course and highly recommend it for those interested in the intersection of law and technology.
unexpected_costs: I did not expect it to cost so much just to live in San Diego. Even though I knew it was expensive before, I thought I had made a realistic budget beforehand. However it costed so much more than I intended even though I did a lot of grocery shopping and tried to spend less money on going out.
cost_comparison: In general everything was super expensive, but especially grocery shopping and going out to eat/drink etc. was more expensive than I expected. Also food in the cafeteria at school was super expensive. Gasoline was less expensive, that I expected.
activities_available: They held all kind of activities all the time. You could engage in social clubs or
activities_recommended: I enjoyed surfing. San Diego is a hot spot for surfing, so if you’re even slightly interested, it’s definitely worth giving it a try. The city also offers many social clubs, often centered around sports or outdoor activities. Joining one of these clubs is a great way to meet locals and connect with others who share your interests. You can easily find these social clubs on Instagram.
weekend_recommendations: Spend days in the beach. Go to La Jolla and watch the sealions. Visit Downtown San Diego, Old Town and Little Italy. Visit Navy Seals Museum. Spend a day surfing. Walk around in Pacific Beach area.
culture_adjustment: I found it very easy. Americans are incredibly open-minded, making it feel natural and effortless to strike up a conversation with a stranger.
socializing_tips: Go up and talk to people on the beach or at bars. Participate in the social clubs mentioned above.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The beautiful nature and the americans openminded attitude. It really spreads positive energy.
top3_advice: 1) prepare your administrative documents good time in advance. Make deadlines for your self, so you don't loose track of important deadlines. 2) Go on roadtrip and explore as much of california as possible. 3) Get out of your comfortzoen and try to engage with Americans (and not only Danes or other scandinavian exchange students). By embracing their culture of being open minded and non-judging, you can make so many good relations and have interesting conversations.
other_useful_info: Take the time to thoroughly review all the specific requirements for applying to USD. Create a detailed timeline with deadlines, and schedule important appointments with your teacher, bank, U.S. embassy, TOEFL test center, and any other necessary institutions. Acting early is crucial, as the process is lengthy and involves significant administrative work. Being proactive will help you stay on track and reduce stress as you navigate the application process.
most_rewarding: Living in San Diego and being part of it's laid-back, sunny, surfing culture. People are so happy, active and genuine.
greatest_challenge: Being on my own, far from everyone and everything familiar, was a challenge. Stepping out of your comfort zone will inevitably feel strange and uncomfortable at times, but that’s only because we do it so rarely. Try to embrace the experience—being on your own can be incredibly rewarding. Once you’ve done it a few times, you’ll realize it’s not as intimidating as it seems. In fact, it can be an opportunity for growth and self-discovery.

However, upon arrival and after a lot of research I found that this required first obtaining a Californian driver's license. I ended up long-term-renting a car instead from the rental company recommended by the university. This ended up being a good experience. However, because I had not ordered a rental car in advance, I only got a rental car after several weeks. The limited availability of public transportation in San Diego meant that the first two weeks was a bit boring and troublesome, and felt a bit wasted.
arrival_assistance: The exchange staff at USD were friendly and offered their help when necessary.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Course registration went smoothly and the guidance on courses were helpful.
registration_help: I talked to a supervisor while registrating for courses.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: I would prioritize registrating for courses with classes on the same days so that you have a long weekend to travel. I had all my courses on Monday and Wednesday. This meant that I could leave on a roadtrip for San Fransisco or Utah on a Wednesday evening a only get back Sunday without missing any classes.
course_level: I found the level of the courses and the examination quite easy. To me the UCPH requirement that you must be a Master's student with a GPA of at least 7 on the Danish scale in order to even apply for the University of San Diego seems very unnecessary. The classes were easy to follow as a person with good command of English, and a lot of exchange students from other countries displayed a level in English and in law that was way below a typical danish level.
teaching_comparison: The teachers were generally very kind and knowledgeable and I learned a lot. We were told that the socratic method would be used a lot. However, this wasn't the case. Thus, it resembled the teaching style at UCPH a lot. However, the teachers generally spend more time talking about irrelevant subjects such as their academic accolades or telling stories with no or little legal educational content. Slashing these irrelevant subjects, the classes could probably have been generally 30-minutes shorter while still providing the same education.
courses_enrolled: Negotiation Intro to U.S. law International Energy Law Corp Innovation and Legal Policy Legal Writing and Research (GRAD)
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of the courses. Negotiation, Intro to U.S. law, and Legal Writing and Research (GRAD) all had very easy forms of examination which was particularly nice as an exchange student. For International Energy Law, and Corp Innovation and Legal Policy I had to hand in a paper of about 15-20 pages including footnotes. I had written several papers in English on my Bachelor's and Master's in UCPH already to this turned out to be easy as well. But you should consider whether you want to write to papers during your semester or not. All of the classes concerned subjects that are useful in a Danish context as well.
unexpected_costs: Several fees in relation to applying for a passport, the TOEFL-test.
cost_comparison: Housing, food, cell phone subscription.
activities_available: Different team sports. Watching sports such as basketball and football.
activities_recommended: I would recommend roadtripping in the weekend, trying surfing, watching basketball games at USD.
weekend_recommendations: Nature such as Yosemite, Sequoia and Kings Canyon, Zion, Bryce Canyon (all before winter sets in around November). Antelope canyon, Grand Canyon, Death Valley. San Fransisco, Big Sur, Los Angeles, Hawaii. Attend an NBA game in LA.
culture_adjustment: Minor differences but overall it was easy.
socializing_tips: Prepare for U.S. citizens being very open and use this openness to make some friends. I have played some basketball and beach volleyball in Denmark and used these hobbies to connect with people.
cultural_challenges: All our friends would go to bed very early, so we often didn't hang out that long. I don't know if this was a general cultural difference.
culture_appreciated: The openness and that people seem to be chilling a lot in San Diego on the beach.
top3_advice: You're in driving distance (in U.S. terms at least) to some of the most diverse and incredible nature in the world, and gas is so cheap compared to Denmark. Take advantage of this during your (hopefully) long weekends. Make some american friends on or off campus - it's easy and it makes the stay so much more fun and authentic. Sometimes you will feel lonely and miss your friends back home, sometimes it will be an administrative mess, but when you look back you will most likely look back at some of the best and most rewarding experiences in your life so far.
other_useful_info: You definitely need a rental car for your whole stay. Dirt Cheap Car Rental which USD recommends are great and transparent.
most_rewarding: Roadtripping in the incredible nature, and making real friends in the U.S. who e.g. took me to an american military base to play basketball, hosted an american "friendsgiving" and a halloween party, and surfing and playing beachvolleyball at the beach.
greatest_challenge: The first few weeks craving friends while being stuck in a boring neighborhood far from the sea without a car to get around.

crucial_aspects: The crucial aspects in choosing my study destination were the academic profile of the University of San Diego School of Law, the opportunity to strengthen my international and comparative legal skills, and the overall study environment in San Diego.
info_ease: Very easy
arrival_assistance: I got all the assistance I needed in regard to my visa
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The process is very easy. You have a call beforehand with the person in charge of the exchange program. On this call the person assign you to your desired courses. You then show up, buy/rent the books and you are good to go.
registration_help: Help in regard to basically everything except for housing.
registration_success: I got all the courses that I wanted
registration_advice: Choose wisely. Research the courses thoroughly beforehand in regard to the exam type, day of classes etc. Some courses are definitely more difficult than others. So choose according to your ambition.
course_level: At some courses the level is high, on others the level is low. It really depends on the subject and professor.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style is very different. In the U.S. the professor use the Socratic Method (cold calling), so be prepared for class assignments. The professor's structure their courses completely by themselves - they are very enthusiastic.
courses_enrolled: Intro to U.S. Law Legal Writing & Research Finance & Accounting for Lawyers Securities Regulation International Business Transactions
recommended_courses: Intro to U.S. Law is mandatory. Legal Writing & Research is very assignment based (there is no exam). It is a pass/fail class. Finance & Accounting for Lawyers is based upon calculations in connection to accounting and finance (preferably for students who likes to use a calculator). Securities Regulation is a difficult course. Lots of reading (approximately over 1.500 pages) and tough exam. The professor is though really good and inspiring. International Business Transactions is a good class for UCPH students as the course revolves around concepts that are somewhat similar to the ones covered at UCPH. So a MA student from UCPH definitely has an advantage when taking this course. This is though based on what classes the student participated in at UCPH.
unexpected_costs: VAT on all sorts of products. Prices do not include VAT, so be aware of that. It is not like in Denmark where the price includes VAT.
cost_comparison: Renting a flat is definitely more expensive than in Denmark. If you want to live comfortably expect to spend +- 10.000 DKK. This will though give you a place in a safe area where you can have your own room.
activities_available: Everything you can imagine. All sport activities is available. There is not a lot of social activities of the kind we know them in Denmark.
activities_recommended: Use the gym - the facilities is great! Also a great soccer field.
weekend_recommendations: Visit Grand Canyon, Sion National Park, go to Mexico for 1 day, travel around San Diego (PB, MB, La Jolla, Del Mar and North Park).
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. I experienced San Diegans as very polite and open minded. They are very extroverted and open for conversation.
socializing_tips: Be open and proactive. Do not hesitate to propose social activities. People will not reject you in a bad manner.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: The fact that the culture is very social.
top3_advice: Be openminded. Reach out - be proactive. Ask former exchange students that went to USD where to go so you don't waste time.
other_useful_info: The professors are very helpful and like to engage with the students. Use this opportunity to discuss ideas, get perspectives etc.
most_rewarding: Experiencing a society that is filled with decency and politeness.
greatest_challenge: Can't think of one.

crucial_aspects: São Paulo is the economic center of Latin America. Furthermore, USP is ranked the best university in Latin America.
info_ease: USP is difficult to arrive to. Luckily, the international coordinator was helpfull in guiding me when choosing which faculties to study at. Be aware that USP has various campus and they are spread all over the state.
arrival_assistance: My faculty (FFLCH) hosted a welcome week. I recieved valuable information and met many other exchange students. Be aware that the welcome week orientation is in Portuguese. However, one can attend classes taught in English at USP.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Once you get accepted you need to apply for courses. The courses that USP has online are old courses and the new courses will not be posted until very last minute. Therefore, you must apply to courses that won´t be offered. However, the faculty you apply to will still be your host faculty and will facilitate everything on your behalf (even if you end up not taking courses there afterall). I recommend to apply for courses from only one faculty and to choose a faculty you are most interested in. Be aware that as an exchange student you can attend all faculties and attend very different classes, so enjoy this opportunity.
registration_help: There is an international coordinatior from USP that can help you. Once you have applied to a specific faculty, their international department will be your point of contact.
registration_success: It is very confusing to get an overview of the classes available. You will need to spend a long time to crosscheck different faculties´ courses and to see the level of the course. When you wish to register you can email the professor directly or the international department of the faculty of the course. They are very flecxible to exchange students and I was allowed to do my exam in English even though the class was in Portuguese.
registration_advice: See above
course_level: The courses have the same level as in Denmark. Be aware that attendance is mandatory. Most master classes are 4 hours long and the teacher expects discussions among the students.
teaching_comparison: UCPH is more flexible. Studying at USP is more like attending high school in Denmark, where the participation in class can affect your final grade and attendance is mandatory.
courses_enrolled: EAD5933 - Geopolitics and Corporate Strategy FLS6195 - Cities, government and public policies
recommended_courses: If you do not speak Portuguese, I would recommend you to look at the courses offered by FEA. They have many courses in English.
unexpected_costs: I didn´t have unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Food at USP is very cheap.
activities_available: There is great amount of sport activities that you can do for free. There is a free cinema showing movies every day and there are many museums which are free.
activities_recommended: Participate in sports.
weekend_recommendations: Try the parties in USP, enjoy the city and its museums, visit the neighbourhood of Liberdade, go to the beaches.
culture_adjustment: The Brazilian people is very warm and kind. Even though I don´t speak Portuguese I did not have any problems getting by with Spanish and English. At USP many speak English and in São Paulo you will also find many people who speak English. However, the majority do not speak English.
socializing_tips: Join the parties at USP. There are parties every weekend.
cultural_challenges: I didn´t find anything challenging.
culture_appreciated: Warm people.
top3_advice: 1: Only apply to courses from one faculty when seeking your acceptance at USP (to avoid bureaucratic chaos). 2: Join the parties. 3: Eat in the local restaurant. Food is only 2,5 DKK.
other_useful_info: Make your appointment to the federal police already when you arrive. Later they have a long waiting time and you will need the document from the police to apply for the cheaper buscard.
most_rewarding: Good parties and great friends.
greatest_challenge: The language barrier.

overall_comments: I had an amazing time in my time abroad. Met so many nice people, the courses were interesting and challenging and I still felt like I had time to really see the most of the country while staying there.
info_ease: Not everything was easy to locate. The website for the University is very big and certain things were just difficult to find. I did get mails to help me through the beginning but there were still some unanswered questions that I had difficulties finding. Also, I was dissappointed to learn only a few days before, that they had a week of orientation for exchange students before the semester started. Because I had not heard or read anything about this, I was not able to attend any of these events unfortunately.
arrival_assistance: Not much to be honest. It could have been a bit better. In my first week I was really confused about my schedule, how the university webportal worked and even where to go for help about these things. People were friendly though, and when I finally got hold of the right person I got help. But administratively things went a bit slow, which made me miss out on some things in the first week.
arrival_comments: A lot of information had to be given obviously, and I did receive a great deal of such, but there were still lack of information that I would have wanted and needed when arriving. Especially considering my schedule.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had an amazing time in my time abroad. Met so many nice people, the courses were interesting and challenging and I still felt like I had time to really see the most of the country while staying there.

registration_help: People.

registration_advice: Book a time slot in advance.
academics_comments: I had an amazing time in my time abroad. Met so many nice people, the courses were interesting and challenging and I still felt like I had time to really see the most of the country while staying there.
course_level: As I was a MA student, I had MA level courses.
teaching_comparison: More seminar structure with the professor, as I am used to more lectures and then class teaching with more of a teaching instructor. Because the seminars ran with fewer students in the room, I really enjoyed the way that you get to talk a lot about the subject matter and get the hints and clarifications from the professor as well. The level of education was however pretty much the same and both types of teaching do encourage to discussion and making up ones own oppinion (which is important in my field of study)
courses_enrolled: Freedom POL6619. About the concept of freedom in political theory (leaning towards political philosophy) Feminist and Decolonizing Approaches to International Relations- bodies, coloniality, knowledge POL6611. Title is selfexplanatory for the course.
recommended_courses: Both courses were quite nice, but I guess it depends what ones interests are. I personally really enjoyed the Freedom course, as I liked the political philosophy aspect of it. However if one is interested in feminism/decolonisation and International Relations that course was quite interesting as well.

cost_comparison: I had expected food prices to be a bit less actually, but in reality they were quite similar to danish prices.
activities_available: Societies. And a bunch load of them. There are societies for all kinds and all types of interests. Different sports societies, walking society (for hiking), dancing societies, music societies, baking society, even tea society and duck society were a thing! Also, the students union is great and one if not the best in the country. University parties take place in the union multiple times a week. Furthermore there are also small activities done by global campus and the residence life team (some better than others though). Another quite nice thing is the "Give it a go" - concept, where one can find tours and trips to different cities and activities often in the weekend. It's a nice and easy way to get to do some sightseeing while there.
activities_recommended: Join a society! There are so many, so should be possible to find something to like, it is great fun and just a perfect way to meet new people. I also found socities a good way to interact more with the brits and local students, whereas it otherwise is quite common for exchange students to hang out with other exvhange students (also nice, but to get to meet local people are a nice way to get a better sense of the culture your in)
weekend_recommendations: There is the Give it a go, that often has trips to different cities on the weekends. I travelled a lot (with my flatmates and other people I had met) to different cities or towns around England, which was a nice way of experiencing the country. Also, the Peaks district! A national park just next to Sheffield, where so many go on hikes and enjoy nature, so beautiful - and a must! Otherwise Sheffield has a lot of nice cafés and parks to visit and enjoy.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy I would say. The first couple of weeks can be quite overwhelming though, and it's okay to need some time to settle in. However if one is comfortable with english things settle themselves quite easily to be honest. Just give it a little time and remember to talk with people. Also, try to go on trips or excursions to see different parts of the country.
socializing_tips: I think the best way is to get involved with societies. Depending on the courses one takes, it is also possible to get to know people through group work and such.
cultural_challenges: The way the brits don't know how to insulate their housing. So cold... Also, the food is not the best, but if you can settle for a pint and a pie, all will be fine. oh and also, Sheffield is really hilly. As in REALLY hilly, one's legs will be strong:)
culture_appreciated: The university culture, students union and societies were just so nice. Sheffield definitely feels like a student city which I quite enjoyed. I also actually enjoyed that most people just walked everywhere. Definitely got my average stepcount up!
top3_advice: Try to join as many activities, excursions and societies as is possible with your time. Get to know people, and if you are in doubt about anything ask - Brits wanna help but won't always reach out by themselves, needs to be asked. The studies are important, but try to make the most of your stay! It is once in a life time, sometimes I would chose an excursion over the weekly reading (oops!)
other_useful_info: It is nice to have a students accomodation. Be patient with the administration things and ask for help in the students union if any worries of any kind comes up.
most_rewarding: Friends, people, new culture. Actually quite nice to get to speak so much english for a longer period of time. Traveling a lot while there was also quite nice. Also, I stayed for about a month after the semester had ended because I continues to have my accomodation available. In that time I really tried to make the most of my stay, travelled a lot, and tried to go to many different places in Sheffield to exerience the city.
greatest_challenge: The first two weeks. Just seemed very overwhelming, and I struggled with not having my schedule and such. Hang in there:)

recommended_courses: The first one is definitely a must, I would recommend that class for sure. And the second one, the two others wasn't that exciting in my opinion, becuase as I wrote above the classes was little to semiliar to each other
unexpected_costs: I travel more than I thought I would. It was a must to travel around UK, and the School makes some of the trips really cheap, but You need to be fast cause they will be sold out fast. So we made some trips me and my flatmates on our own. So we went to Liverpool, Manchester, Leeds, Birmingham, York, Oxford, London, Glasgow, Edinburg, Dublin etc, And I also travel to France and Spain. Sheffield is cheap, and I could have lower expenses, but it is a life experiences, so don't wanted to holdd back. But we cocked a lot home also.
cost_comparison: Food in general. if you go to stores such as Aldi and Lidl, it is so mcuh cheaper than Denmark. Veggies where cheaper. But also candy and ben&jerry.
activities_available: There where many language/cultur societies, and also a lot of sports.
activities_recommended: In general I had an amazing flat, so we did a lot of things together, in our own, but diffenately travel around, it was such an amazing way of seeing different cities, hearing different accents. People are so nice and try to make friends outside your own comfort. In our flat there where 3 sweds and 1 norwegian, and they talked the scandinavian language to each other, and I told them that I would appriciate if we talked english, cause I wanted to improve my English. And they respected that, but they still talked in their own language among each other, which made some of the others be little frustrated cause they wanted to be part of the conversations. So be carefull with finding people that speaks the same language, cause it is ofcourse more convient to speak your own language, but you also wanna learn. We made a group for our class, and I meet a lot of my classmates outside the school that way, and got a bigger networking that way. And in general be more curious about other peoples languages/cultures. It has been the most amazing thing to try being on exchange. And remember to be open about other peoples culture/opinions because and try to understand and engage in conversation about others. I have learned so much about so many other different cultures than the English one. So in general be curious, and try to get out of your comfort zone.
weekend_recommendations: Like a said above, travel, try new things, ask people out i git invited to one of my classmates Chinese New Year, although he didn't invite the whole class, it was stilll an experience. And try to do somethings you haven't done, be openminded.
culture_adjustment: It wa quite easy. In the beginning it was bit difficult to understand central-Northern british accent, but a long a you just ask polite if they can speak slower mot people will try to speak so you understand. And please ask as many times as you can if you don't understand cause otherwise you wouldn't learn. The teachers are also aware of the amount of exchange students, so just remind them some times of they speak fast or you don't understand them.
socializing_tips: I found it bit difficult socialising with the local students. But we made a whatsapp group (get used to it, they use WhatsApp a lot), and we went out 3 times, and from there it was easier to socializ. But it is bit difficult because they have their own friends and families around. So it is more typical to socialise with exchange students.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any cultural differences particularly challenging, they are really polite, and I really liked that. But there are strikes all the time, and that was bit of a challenge, because some our classes got canceled. Trains got canceled often. So it could be expensive sometimes to take the uber
culture_appreciated: I loved they are so polite, everyone is up for a chat. They are in general interested to hear about your and your culture. But they also don't mind explaining about their own culture.
top3_advice: 1. Remember to be openminded, and ask as much as you can about anything, the teachers are really kind, and wants to help you if they can. 2. if you are dislexes the papers that you submit shows that you have dyslexia, so that is not a problem at all. We could diffenitelly learn from that in UCPH. 3. Enjoy the possibilities that is offered. Go in trips, try new things, and speak english as much as you can.
other_useful_info: Don't be afraid of the exchange. The times flies away so fast. Speak english as much as you can, eventhough you're unsure about the accent/pronounce, because there is so many other students that also don't speak english as their first language. I didn't get good grades in english in high school, but I learned so much in these almost 5 months.
most_rewarding: I have friends and network around the world, I have improved my english skills, I have learned to experience things in a different way. I'm so independent now, much more than I was before going, and I have had a lot of self-growth.
greatest_challenge: The beginning of the exchange where everything was new, and I didn't know how the exchange would be. But you get used to talking english everyday all day really fast, and you will settle down really fast also. Remeber that 5 months goes fast!
other_comments: I would recommend everyone that has the possibility to do it! Go on exchange! it has been the best. Don't be afraid, but be curious! you will learn so much

crucial_aspects: The courses that the university offered was one of the deciding factors for me choosing Sheffield.
info_ease: It was very easy, the university sent a lot of emails regarding arrival and registration at the university as well as student support.
arrival_assistance: I received emails with information on the arrival and getting to the university.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I received an email on how to register with the university, what to bring and then I could book a time slot that suited me in the introduction week.
registration_help: There was staff at the registration itself.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I initially applied for when I applied with the university.
registration_advice: It is an easy process when you read the emails they sent with information and look on their website where there is also information for incoming students.
course_level: The level of the courses was similar to KU and it was as I expected. I had two year 2 courses and one year 3.
teaching_comparison: The lectures were really good and very interesting, held by professors who are specialists in their areas. We had two 50 minutes lectures for each class every week and then we had some tutorial every other week in each class (these are similar to seminars at KU, but with smaller groups around 8 people). The tutorials were really good as it was a safe space where we could discuss the content of the class.
courses_enrolled: I took three courses: Race, Gender and Crime, Advanced EU Law, and Children and the Law.
recommended_courses: I would really recommend Race, Gender and Crime. It was a criminological course drawing on events and cases from society, which was really interesting and very different to anything offered at KU.
unexpected_costs: The cost of trip I would take while being there.
cost_comparison: Grocery shopping is less expensive than in DK.
activities_available: The Students' Union has a lot of different clubs and societies for both sports, academic things, culture etc.
activities_recommended: I would recommend to join a society and do social things with others who have the same interests as yourself. I did ice skating and also some creative workshops.
weekend_recommendations: I would really recommend going for a walk/hike in the Peak District which is really beautiful and close to Sheffield. Otherwise, I would recommend visiting some of the other cities close to Sheffield, such as York, or to go on the day trips that the Students' Union arrange.
culture_adjustment: Very easy as I have lived in England before.
socializing_tips: I would just say to be open and say yes to social activities.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: I like that it is very multi-cultural.
top3_advice: To be open and social and to enjoy it because time goes by so fast.
other_useful_info: It is always good to be up to date with information and deadlines.
most_rewarding: All the good experiences, the day trips, and making friends for life.
greatest_challenge: There was a lot of train strikes during my exchange which sometimes made planning trips a bit difficult.

crucial_aspects: I've always been fascinated about USA and I wanted to experience it in person. The US college is quite different than European ones, I'm really glad I got to study there for semester abroad.
info_ease: It was very easy, USF offered exchange meetings where all the exchange participants got all the necessary information. Contact with exchange coordinator Lauren Strange was also supreme.
arrival_assistance: With the help of Lauren Strange we manage to fulfill my exchange courses requirement and found best study path for me.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: After arrival we had less than a week to fulfill visa requirements and pick our classes, not all classes were offered and some needed prerequisite courses, which might lead to the need to change our initial preapproval for courses.
registration_help: Exchange coordinator Lauren Strange made sure we all fulfill the visa requirements on time and took great care of this process, providing assistance and guidance in case of any doubt or troubles while registering.
registration_success: I didn't meet all the requirements for all the courses I wanted and some of them were not offered. My course IT&Cognition had quite specific main subject which was little hard to replace but at the end Lauran and I found a solution that was accepted.
registration_advice: Prepare some backup courses and prepare for the need to pick a new one if the course wont be offered, but there's nothing to stress about the process it quite simple and USF exchange coordinators provide all the necessary help needed.
course_level: I found my courses relevant to the courses I take at UCPH. Hopefully I can use the gathered knowledge during writing my masters thesis.
teaching_comparison: US academic approach differs from the one offered at UCPH, which means UCPH approach is more interpersonal, while USF provides more guidance and weekly assignments and various methods to check if the student actually prepares for the class. It was really exciting to experience how it looks like to study in America and I think it definitely broadens my horizons and keep me prepared in my academic field.
courses_enrolled: Global Cyber Ethics, Business Intelligence, Python for business analytics and Intro to psychological science
recommended_courses: I found Intro to psychological science the most exciting and relevant to my course cognitive science. It let me have a look on broader perspective of the psychology aspect.
unexpected_costs: It's hard to move around Tampa without own transportation, the public transport doesn't really exist if we want to go to city center or to the beach, uber and lyft were the transportation we had to use, or carpool with our american friends
cost_comparison: books are quite expensive depending on subject it can cost up to 1050 dkk for a single coursebook
activities_available: Swimming, basketball, football, soccer, bike club, martial arts and many more, USF really have a lot of sport clubs
activities_recommended: Bike club was really fun, they make long trips and weekly training sessions.
weekend_recommendations: For someone who never visited USA I definitely recommend seeing NY its worth it, and Miami as well. During fall exchange it is interesting to experience Thanksgiving. Americans are very welcoming, so after you make some friends there is a high chance they will invite you to celebrate with them since they know we don't celebrate it or have anyone to celebrate with since our families are bk home.
culture_adjustment: I adjusted quite fast, some Americans had a tough accent, but I got used to it pretty fast.
socializing_tips: Join some sport clubs it's really worth it.
cultural_challenges: The way of contacting your professors must stay very formal.
culture_appreciated: The attitude fo Americans towards exchnage students, families were very welcoming and invited use to see how they celebrate American holidays such as thanksgiving.
top3_advice: Don't stress and have fun, it's a lifetime opportunity to study at US campus. Take your time to really explore it and take the most of your time there.
other_useful_info: Plan your trip wisely USA is huge and it can be too expensive to see everything.
most_rewarding: Being able to experience. the way of American lifestyle as college student
greatest_challenge: Meet the deadlines of the assignments, especially if you go for weekend escapes to travel around the country.
