crucial_aspects: Heritage, language practice, academic opportunities
info_ease: Not very easy. I had severe communication issues with the recieving institution in the weeks leading up to the exchange as well as the first couple of weeks, leading to me missing the first weeks of courses as well as having to stay at a hotel, since my acommodation was blocked due to recieving institution forgetting to forward my information.
arrival_assistance: There was a welcome day on the 6th of september, which was very informative. Sadly, any information before this date was very sparse, and it led me to miss courses.
arrival_comments: In more detail: The recieving institution explicitly asked not to recieve any e-mails in july and august, as any issues would be solved in late august/early september due to vacation scheduling. I was granted a CROUS accomodation, that was organized through the university. For this I am very grateful. However, in the weeks leading up to my travels and move-in date, I recieved no information about my room. I tried reaching out to recieving institution to solve this, but getting no responses, I decided to show up at my logement, and found out that the university had forgotten to forward my information, almost resulting in me losing my room. In the end I had to stay five days in a hotel, as I could not access my room before the university forwarded my information, and it was impossible to reach anyone from the university. I tried showing up on september 1st at the faculty to actually speak with someone, but to my surprise, the office was exeptionally closed on this date. Moreover, I had many issues recieving my academic schedule resulting in me missing the first couple of weeks of courses. This made the time leading up to my exchange very stressful, the first weeks very frustrating, and the following weeks quite stressed as I had to catch up on a lot academically from the very start. I have spoken with several exchange students, who faced the same or similar issues as me.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You would send your learning agreement to the administrative office, who would then inscribe you. Once you did this, you had to make your own timetable, and just assume that inscription was possible. Sometimes courses were not visible on the timetable, so you would have to contact the admin office to fix this problem.
registration_help: There was a dedicated person working with all the exchange students. He was extremely helpful but also very busy.
registration_success: I had to change one course as it was not available in the period I had chosen.
registration_advice: Assume that you are getting the courses you choose, don't wait for a confirmation.
course_level: I had one first year BA course, four third year BA courses and one 2nd year master course.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style varied from course to course but in general it reminded me more of high school in Denmark in the sense that the teacher does role call and you are expected to show up unless you have a doctor's note that your are ill.
courses_enrolled: Économie Industrièlle Jeux et Stratégies Advanced Programming and Data Visualization Histoire des concepts économiques 1 Economics and Business Management Theory of Knowledge
recommended_courses: If you haven't had Videnskabsteori yet, I recommend taking Theory of Knowledge. Économie Industrièlle and Jeux et Stratégies were both very micro-oriented and in a similar style to UCPH with a lot of exercises.
unexpected_costs: Because I lived in a CROUS, I had to buy pillows, towels, bedding, plates, cups, pot, pan etc. There was nothing when I arrived.
cost_comparison: Don't buy insurance from home! You can buy way cheaper insurance for students in France! I did this mistake, and since my insurance policy was in danish, my logement did not accept it, so I had to buy another insurance. Also, I did extra french classes which cost me 250 euros + an exam that cost 40 euros.
activities_available: So many I can't list them. Look into ESN and AESES for a start.
activities_recommended: ESN had many great activities for meeting new people. Unisport was also great for the same reason.
weekend_recommendations: Travel around. Get a carte fluo, take the train to the villages in alsace, go hiking.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: I was surprised at how social everyone were. In the first conversation it is normal to ask for someones contact info and also to go to activities together.
cultural_challenges: Everything is closed on sundays. Even supermarkets. During lunch a lot of things are closed as well.
culture_appreciated: Politeness and acknowledging even strangers' presence. Everyone holds the door for everyone.
top3_advice: If you don't get an answer to an important e-mail within a couple of days, write again, insist, show up at their offices.
other_useful_info: If you are a BA student in economics, you need to know french. At least B1, B2 preferrably. Exams are all written in hand.
most_rewarding: The social connections with both locals and other international students.
greatest_challenge: Logistics. Before and during the exchange.

crucial_aspects: It was important for me that there was different classes to choose from, and that there were classes that I had a genuine interest in. It was also important to me that the host university took into account that everyone might not be on the same high level, especially in regards to language skills.
info_ease: There was a lot of emails being sent out with the information that you needed, however it also meant that there were a lot of email to go through if you needed to find the right information.
arrival_assistance: I had some help regarding registration for classes.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You register on their version of mobility online, and when you've followed all the steps you're classes become visible for you in their system
registration_help: I didn't really use a lot of the help offered, but it seemed that help was offered in all aspects; mental health, IT, proof reading of assignments, help for exchange students etc.
registration_success: I had applied for an extra class than what I needed to, just to be sure I got what I wanted, and then they wrote back to me and told which classes where at the same time and what they recommended to do and which class to remove, so I ended up with the 3 classes that I wanted from the start.
registration_advice: Make sure you are thorough, because you can (apparently) overlook steps, but the people at the university are good to help when needed.
course_level: I took classes that were for year 3 students, but it was also possible for exchange students to do classes for year 1 and 2, so it was mostly yourself that chose the level of course that you wished for
teaching_comparison: It didn't really. The only similarity was that a professor was teaching the class. There wasn't a lot of preparation for class, and it was more voluntary than obligatory to do - you didn't need or weren't expected to buy the books for the classes, and could get them at the library if you wanted to. Even if there was material to be read, the teachers didn't really write out which chapters to read, so I suppose you found a chapter that correlates with the theme of the class
courses_enrolled: Housing Law, Sports Law & Law, Film and Popular Culture
recommended_courses: If possible I would recommend to choose classes that aren't to bound to the country you're in. If there are classes that are more universal, that makes it easier to understand and apply, and to take with you after you go home.
unexpected_costs: There wasn't really any
cost_comparison: Food was less expensive than I expected. Also going out didn't need to be expensive - you could just choose a place that was less expensive, which most of them were
activities_available: There was a gym on campus plus a lot of other athletic clubs. There were also different scottish events through the semester
activities_recommended: The university has a student union that's really cozy - you can just chill, eat some food, watch sport, play games and it is also possible to get some drinks if you like that.
weekend_recommendations: The highlands and really most of the things Scotland is known for - just search for trips online and there are so many different ones to go on.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy since Scotland isn't that different from Denmark when you are not local or moving their permanently.
socializing_tips: It seemed like a lot of students were really just doing their own thing, but finding someone to talk to indoor classes might be the easiest way to socialize.
cultural_challenges: The accents :-)
culture_appreciated: That it wasn't the same as Denmark, but still not to far off so that it was all new and scary
top3_advice: Be careful when looking for housing. There is another kind of group work going on, but that doesn't have to be a bad thing. The exams are hand-written on campus
other_useful_info: The local transportation is way different that in Denmark, and you might need to be patient and open for different kinds of transportation at different times of the day.
most_rewarding: Trying to live in another country
greatest_challenge: Not losing hope after getting scammed.

crucial_aspects: When choosing my study destination I focused on multiple factors; if there were any courses available which I was interested in, the legal system (common law), the quality of the education provided (USYD is a high ranking university in law) and my interest in the country and culture. As I have always wanted to travel Australia it seemed a natural starting point for my research, and luckily USYD had many courses available that I found very interesting, as well as a high level of education and social engagement amongst students. I especially loved that the university facilitates 200+ social clubs between students and has a very active student union that often arranges social events.
info_ease: You get a lot of information from the university prior to arrival and before the beginning of the semester, which makes it a lot easier to ease into studying at USYD. Highly recommend attending the introductory seminars/intro week, as a lot of useful information is given there (as well as in the emails received before the start of the semester).
arrival_assistance: I received a lot of emails with useful information from my study abroad advisor from USYD, as well as an introductory seminar and the opportunity of 1:1 meetings or video calls for personal assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Once nominated by UCPH you eventually get an email from USYD with a link to their platform with the information you need to fill out. Very easy to navigate and fill out by yourself; just remember to do it before the deadline.
registration_help: Study abroad advisor was available to help with any questions.
registration_success: I was very lucky and got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure to get your courses pre-approved by UCPH ASAP after having received the list of available courses from USYD as your application must be submitted with pre-approved courses 2 weeks after you receive the enrolment email. I had to call the administration at UCPH and have them push my pre-approval application through quicker. Also aim to get 8-10 classes pre-approved even if you will only be studying four classes at USYD; that way you'll get a pre-approved class no matter whether you get your first priority or not.
course_level: The academic level of the courses was very appropriate and at the same level as the courses at UCPH. However, as they are taught in english, certain legal terms and references to case law unknown to non-Australians makes the classes a bit harder/makes them require a bit more research.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is very different to the one at UCPH, although classes at both universities consist of a subject being taught by the lecturer with student engagement. At USYD it is mandatory to attend at least 70% of classes in person in order to pass the class. Moreover, there can be/most likely is mid-semester assignments, on-call, presentations and final assignments which must be passed, which requires a lot more work throughout the semester, as they all count towards your grade.
courses_enrolled: LAWS5179: IP: Patents & Trademarks LAWS5152: Medical Law LAWS5163: Sports Law LAWS5128: Media Law: Defamation and Privacy
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed almost all of my courses, Media Law being the exception, but this was only due to the lecturer - the material itself was interesting and could be fairly easily understood. Medical Law is a very interesting course but harder than the others as there is no book and the curriculum consists of PDF's (approx 1000 pages) with a collection of case law, articles and sections from various regulations. You really have to stay focused in class in order to gather the key points and importance of the various material.
unexpected_costs: Rent doesn't cover gas/electricity/internet, so this had to be paid separately. You are also obligated to get an Australian insurance on top of any travel insurance you might have. This, along with the visa fees, adds up.
cost_comparison: Rent is expensive (as expected) so definitely try to budget more than you might end up needing. Definitely recommend batch cooking as well as groceries are not cheap (slightly more expensive than in DK).
activities_available: 200+ social clubs as well as a fitness center with a special member price for USYD students. Loads of social activities throughout the semester as well.
activities_recommended: If you like to keep active definitely sign up for the USYD gym - great facilities with a pool, tennis, squash and basketball/volleyball courts as well.
weekend_recommendations: The Blue Mountains are a must! It's just a 2hr train ride from Sydney and has many great hikes. I also did a weekend trip down to Jervis Bay, a weekend trip up to Hunters Valley and longer trips to both WA (Perth-Coral Bay) and up the East Coast (Brisbane-Cairns) and I highly recommend seeing as much of Australia as you can as it is a beautiful country with many different sights to see.
culture_adjustment: The culture is very close to the Danish culture, so very easy to adapt to.
socializing_tips: Just make the effort and attend social events/talk to people; most people in Australia are very nice and welcoming.
cultural_challenges: Cafés close at around 14, so afternoon coffee is not an option.
culture_appreciated: The diversity, openminded-ness and welcoming attitude of most people.
top3_advice: 1. Join some social clubs/events/etc. 2. Most books are available online/at the library so save your money 3. Download the app "Lost on campus" as classrooms can be tricky to find
other_useful_info: Remember to apply a student card before the beginning of the semester - you need it for a bunch of stuff (discounts etc.) so it just makes it easier to have it collected before all the fun begins.
most_rewarding: Getting to see many different parts of Australia and meeting new people along the way.
greatest_challenge: Keeping on top of all deadlines for assignments while still remembering to enjoy exchange and being social.
other_comments: Don't bring sunscreen from home (it doesn't work) but definitely buy some. Also it gets a lot colder than expected so bring a jacket/hoodie.

crucial_aspects: An English speaking destination that offered different culture/nature etc than Copenhagen.
info_ease: It was easy, all info is provided.
arrival_assistance: There was a few intro days to help you get settled in.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I dont remember it as difficult.
registration_help: I did not need help.
registration_success: There was only one class I didn't get offered.
registration_advice: Apply for many classes.
course_level: Similar to Denmark.
teaching_comparison: It was more like a class than a lecture, more group work, more homework, more was expected from students.
courses_enrolled: Leadership, Digital Business Innovation, Responsible design for innovation and Introduction to Interface Design.
recommended_courses: Leadership and Introduction to Interface Design were really good.
unexpected_costs: Food is quite expensive, so is traveling around in Australia. Also health care was a jungle for me to figure out and I did not get all costs covered even though I had both danish and australian insurance.
cost_comparison: Rent was really expensive.
activities_available: There was a lot of clubs and sports, but I did not participate.
activities_recommended: Did not participate in any.
weekend_recommendations: Blue Mountains, Byron Bay, Melbourne etc.
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: No, it was quite hard to meet locals, at least at your own age at uni
cultural_challenges: They go to university earlier than danes, meaning people are quite young at uni
culture_appreciated: The openness, friendliness, easy going lifestyle
top3_advice: Have some sort of temporary housing figured out when you arrive, then find more long term accomodation when you arrive. Live close to the water if possible, it is worth the travel back and forth to live next to such beautiful nature. Enjoy every minute and try to be as open as the Australians are, it goes by so quickly.
other_useful_info: I think I have stated everything above.
most_rewarding: Living in a country that is so friendly and open, healthy and active, it is a very inspiring way of living that I will take with me home. Further, amazing new friends and better English skills.
greatest_challenge: Meeting local friends, I mostly gained more danish friends or exchange students from other countries.

crucial_aspects: The location, and the great reputation of the univrsity of sydney.
info_ease: Very easyly acceptable.
arrival_assistance: none
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Very easy. just write to your exchange counccelor
registration_help: Many different. A very good advicer from USYD.
registration_success: Very easy, and casual registration style. You can change units up until the first week of studying. Very unlike UCPH.
registration_advice: Dont only take hard units. Try some fun ones aswell.
course_level: 4 units of study. Very good level
teaching_comparison: Not good. To much online studying
courses_enrolled: Aplied genomics Aplied Microbiology in a changeging world What is this thing called sience Introduction to programming
recommended_courses: Microbiology in a changing world. really good practical experience
unexpected_costs: Cleaning fees at the ocomedation
cost_comparison: Beer and cigarrettes where really expensive avodoes and mangoes nice and cheap
activities_available: A lot of different. More the UCPH for sure
activities_recommended: Rock climbing trough the BWS
weekend_recommendations: Magnetic island Cairns Basically the hole east coast
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: Go to all univesity plant events in the begining
cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: The friendlyness of the Australians in general
top3_advice: Bring lots of money for trips Get a job in sydney, it helps a lot. Dont stick to danish people all the time
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Seeing the australian nature
greatest_challenge: Making ends meet sometime, qua, get a job.

crucial_aspects: When I choose to go on exchange, I wanted to go to Australia because my parents have lived in Australia. I then looked into the different schools, and wanted a good school with interesting classes in a fun town with many opportunities. And then I found University of Sydney which matched all my criteria.
overall_comments: Exchange was the best experience, and I am so glad I took the chance and went on exchange.
info_ease: I think University of Sydney was really good at giving information before and upon arrival. They had introduction days and an introduction meeting where they informed us of all the practical information but also all the good to know or fun to know.
arrival_assistance: We had a counselor that send us e-mails guiding us through the first couple of weeks. My counselor was really helpfull, I has to switch classes so I had to meet up with her. She was good at guiding me through my different choices and helped me with my timetabel/schedule.
arrival_comments: The only problem, was that they send too many mails - but that is better than too few.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Exchange was the best experience, and I am so glad I took the chance and went on exchange.
registration_process: We choose 10 courses and then my host institution got approval from the teachers to all the courses I was able to take. Then I online choose the 4 courses I wanted to be enrolled in. I later switched a class before arrival, and to do so I just had to write and email to my counselor and she was able to change my enrollment.
registration_help: Our counselor was able to help us with any questions we had. Also the homepage of University of Sydney was helpful with details of the different courses.
registration_success: I think the whole process was stressfull, a lot of things to take into account and think about all the time.
registration_advice: Take good time to choose the right classes for you. Don't choose 4 classes that seem very hard, find a good mix. If you regret or doubt a class don't hesitate to ask your counselor for advice. Also don't stress too hard over the classes, most students drop and switch class within the first two weeks of school.
academics_comments: Exchange was the best experience, and I am so glad I took the chance and went on exchange.
course_level: I mostly had courses for students on their 3rd year of their bachelors.
teaching_comparison: Pretty much the same, we had lectures, practical classes and workshops. So very much like my classes at University of Sydney
courses_enrolled: Biochemistry of Human disease Human neuroscience in Health and disease Learning in outdoor education Infectious diseases
recommended_courses: You have to take learning in outdoor education. It is a class only for exchange students, where you explore the Australian nature while you get to know people from all over the world. My other classes I also really enjoyed, they were hard so took a lot of my time. I would probably recommend not taking that hard classes together. I should have switched one of them out with an easier course,
unexpected_costs: Visa cost 3500, which is a lot. Then alcohol is expensive in Australia, going out in general is very expensive. Traveling in Australia is also expensive.
cost_comparison: I was lucky all my books were online, but books are expensive.
activities_available: They have different clubs like different language clubs, cultural food clubs and adventure clubs.
activities_recommended: I would recommend using hostels when traveling and going on the trips arranged by the school for exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: I think Melbourne is really cool to visit. Western Australia is a must in my mind. It was really cool, you have the red sand and the beautiful blue ocean. Just very pretty and so different. In my mind the east cost is overrated. I would do a weekend trip to Byron bay, magnetic island and whitsundays. The rest of the east coast I would skip. Also great ocean road is very beautiful, and if you like nature and hikes this is the perfect place.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, Sydney is very much like Copenhagen. The atmosphere is very casual.
socializing_tips: Be open and not afraid to just ask them a question. Australians are very kind, helpfull people, so honestly should not be a problem if you just talk to them.
cultural_challenges: Their school system is very different from ours. That was a little hard figuring out in the beginning. Usually they don't take a master, since they are done after the 4th year of their bachelors - this makes the courses in science at least a little bit more carrer orientated. Also they can take majors and minors.
culture_appreciated: The chilled atmosphere. You have a large city and then the beach right next to it - which is really amazing.
top3_advice: 1. Come with an open mind 2. Throw yourself out there and try things you normally would not. 3. Enjoy it, it is over before you know it
other_useful_info: Buy your sim-card at the airport that is less expensive.
most_rewarding: All the friendships and traveling. Australia is beautiful and has so much to offer.
greatest_challenge: Being away from your support system at home. All people went through some kind of home-sickness, and it is so normal. Talk to your new friends they probably know the feeling and want to help you the best they can.
other_comments: Enjoy ! I wish it was me going on exchange again.

crucial_aspects: First of all, it was important for me, that the country i was going to stay in, was an english speaking country. Secondly, i knew that australia was an amazing place, due to prior travelling.
info_ease: It was decently easy - the exchange student advisor at USYD was great at responding to emails quickly, and overall she provided all the necessary information regarding the important dates and other important reminders.
arrival_assistance: The student advisor at USYD.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had to send multiple emails to the student advisor in order for you to get your student ID, but once you had that it was smooth sailing.
registration_help: Again, the student advisor assigned to exchange students was great.
registration_success: I got all the classes i wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure to get there in time for the introduction week, very helpful for teaching you how to find you way around the campus and they tell you all that needs to be done for the registration.
course_level: I took three third year courses relevant to my degree, and they were all great. The lecturers and the lectures themselves were interesting. There was a fair bit of overlap with courses i had previously taken at UCPH. Expect to spend a significant amount of time on assignments and other school related tasks.
teaching_comparison: Teaching is very similar, except for the fact that multiple assignments needed to be completed as part of the courses.
courses_enrolled: BCMB3003, Biochemistry of Human Disease, BCMB3004, Beyond the Genome CHEM3121, Chemical Biology EDUH4052, Learning in Outdoor Education
recommended_courses: If you have an interest in chemistry and biology CHEM3121 is a great course. Dont take this course unless you have done second year chemistry already though. BCMB3004 was also great - Stuart, the lecturer, was incredibly passionate and intelligent, making the class very interesting. Also the stuff we were taught was very cutting-edge, making it even more interesting. Lab in this course is a bit subpar though. For learning about Australia itself i recommend EDUH4052. This course will teach you about the Australian environment and nature, and take you on two gorgeous trips to the Blue Mountains and the Royal National Park, which was a great way to explore and meet other exchange students.
unexpected_costs: Some courses require you to pay an extra amount (EDUH4052 requires a fee in order to participate in the field trips) Drinking a lot with other exchange students quickly becomes expensive:)
cost_comparison: Prices in Sydney are generally speaking similar to Copenhagen, so nothing too out of the ordinary. Smoking is incredibly expensive.
activities_available: Millions upon millions of different clubs, that all seemed fun.
activities_recommended: SURFING!! Renting a car and driving around the coast. Eating well. Parachuting.
weekend_recommendations: Again, drive up and down the coast. Its a great way to explore the country. Sydney is also massive, so make sure to explore most of it.
culture_adjustment: Easy, very western culture in Australia.
socializing_tips: Say hi and dont be a prick.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The focus on being outdoors all the time was very refreshing. In Bondi, where i lived, everyone was fit, ate well and spent all their time in the sun, which was something i quite enjoyed being a part of.
top3_advice: Dont focus too much on school, and enjoy that you are on exchange. Dont enroll yourself into multiple challenging courses - instead i recommend doing random courses that you think might be fun or interesting. There is no shame in doing a first year course in something new, just because you think it sounds fun (unless you truly are there for studying and not for the experience) Make sure to start socializing early, as having a group of friends greatly enhances the experience and reduces stress.
other_useful_info: Cant think of any
most_rewarding: Spending time getting to know new people and exploring the vast nature.
greatest_challenge: The start of the exchange was by far the hardest - You're alone, with no place to live, no friends or family. You're on your own, which can be intimidating and stressfull. However, it was also incredibly rewarding to overcome this, and i definitely dont think that this is something that should withhold you from doing an exchange.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere outside of Europe where I had never been before and I have always wanted to go to Australia.
info_ease: Very easy
arrival_assistance: There were several orientation days and we always had the opportunity to contact our study abroad advisor at USYD if we had any questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You have to choose courses when sending your application to USYD but you can change your courses all the way up to the end of the first week of classes. You can even have a say in what your timetable will look like as you can request certain time slots for each class.
registration_help: We could always contact our study abroad advisor and we could even book a meeting if necessary.
registration_success: On USYD's website it says that OLET courses are available for exchange students. However, that turned out to be untrue. Apart from the OLET courses that I wanted, I was successful in registering for the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: As long as you keep an eye out for emails about deadlines you will have no problems with registration.
course_level: I chose courses on many different levels. All of them were at a good level - not too easy and not too difficult.
teaching_comparison: There were a lot more students enrolled in all of my courses than what is usually the case at UCPH. The teaching was therefore less personal than what I am used to. The teaching style is also more like in Danish high schools than Danish universities with compulsory attendance in classes and more assignments that also count towards the final grade.
courses_enrolled: Computational Chemistry Learning in Outdoor Education Australian Wildlife Biology Introduction to Indigenous History
recommended_courses: If you are interested in learning about Australia I would definitely recommend Learning in Outdoor Education and Australian Wildlife Biology. In Learning in Outdoor Education you learn about bush walking and being in nature and you get to go on a one day trip to Royal National Park and a three day trip to the Blue Mountains. In Australian Wildlife Biology you learn about lots of different Australian animals and I found this very interesting and useful, especially when I travelled around Australia after the end of the semester.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Transportation was cheaper than expected. Housing was a lot more expensive than expected.
activities_available: Lots of different clubs and societies so there is something for everyone. The student union also offers lots of activities, events and trips.
activities_recommended: I would recommend taking part in some of the free activities and trips that are arranged by the student union (USU) and they also have some events you can attend for a small fee. Sign up for some clubs as well - they may have some interesting events and even if they don't chances are that they will have free food.
weekend_recommendations: Travel as much as you can! There are so many incredible places all around Australia. The Blue Mountains (just outside of Sydney) is a great place to spend a weekend hiking in the mountains. The botanical garden is great as well.
culture_adjustment: Very easy since Australia is quite ‘European'. Of course there were differences but not anything that was hard to adjust to.
socializing_tips: Choose courses that are not only meant for international students and sign up for the Mates Abroad program.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Australians are very polite and easy to talk to. I found the Aboriginal culture very interesting and fascinating.
top3_advice: It might seem like a huge step to move to another country (and it is!) but it is not as scary and difficult when you get here as you may think. I arrived in Sydney almost two weeks before the main orientation day and almost three weeks before classes began and I think that it was a great decision. It gave me time to figure out everything and explore the city before I had to focus on university. If you have the opportunity try to choose some units of study that are different from what you would choose at home. Being on exchange is a great chance to try something new and learn about the place where you will be living for some months.
other_useful_info: Make sure you get a Concession Opal Card for public transportation in and around Sydney so that all of your journeys will be half price.
most_rewarding: Living in another country for a quite long period of time, meeting new people and experiencing many parts of the country after the semester ended.
greatest_challenge: To be honest I did not really encounter any challenges but if I have to mention one it would probably be figuring out the right balance between doing good at the university while still taking enough time to explore and enjoy the city and Australia in general.

crucial_aspects: It was important to me that the people were speaking English, that I could get far away and that the university had interesting units.
info_ease: Very easy, there were many introduction events.
arrival_assistance: We had a person we always could email, plenty of information at the introduction events, and actually had the option of getting to know an Australian through the “Mates abroad” program.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I just looked up the units that I wanted and applied for them through an email to our contact person. If it was then accepted, it appeared on a website where I then could choose my schedule if the same unit had multiple available hours.
registration_help: I could write to our contact person about everything and she would answer within 1-2 days.
registration_success: 100%. I got everything I wanted.
registration_advice: Take your time choosing units, as there are so many.
course_level: I did two master units and two “honors” units, which is on a level that is technically above bachelor level, but not advanced enough for them to call master.
teaching_comparison: There was greater variation between the units. One unit gave us a ton of videos and an online quiz before we then later in the week met up to do exercises regarding the same subject as the videos and the quiz. Another had no preparation but just worked through four papers and then taught us the theory relevant for the papers along the way. It varied a lot.
courses_enrolled: PHYS4016, PHYS4126, CSYS5010, CSYS5040
recommended_courses: I would recommend PHYS4016 and CSYS5040. PHYS4016 gives a great perspective on how to treat data correctly and has a very intuitive way of teaching. CSYS5040 offers great freedom and primarily is about bombarding the student with methods that could then be used in the final project of this unit.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Dining out was a bit more expensive than expected, but public transport was much cheaper.
activities_available: You could join multiple sports clubs and clubs related to everything from board games to physics and country of origin.
activities_recommended: You should definitely join the academic club related to your study, as they have many social events where you can meet likeminded people.
weekend_recommendations: Blue Mountains is supposed to be beautiful. The Royal Botanical Garden is amazing as well.
culture_adjustment: Very much, as the culture is very similar to the “northern European culture” I am used to.
socializing_tips: Join as many clubs as possible! You don't have to show up if you end up not liking it, and most of them are free.
cultural_challenges: It was a bit confusing in the beginning how all the social and sports clubs went through the university.
culture_appreciated: How open they were! People I barely knew invited me over for Christmas!
top3_advice: - Join as many clubs as possible - Live in student dorms – this will also give you a lot of friends! - Remember to “be a tourist” as much as possible!
other_useful_info: Be sure to get an Opal Concession card as soon as possible, as this will cut the public transport expenses in half.
most_rewarding: The kindness I was met with and the amazing nature.
greatest_challenge: Probably to find the balance between school and fun – it is easy to prioritize school a little too much.

crucial_aspects: Engelsktalende land.
info_ease: University of Sydney var meget hjælpsomme med til at besvare spørgsmål.
arrival_assistance: Jeg fik en masse information både fra studevejlederen tilknyttet udvekslingsstuderende og fra universitetet i Sydney.
arrival_comments: Masser af sociale arrangementer.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: På University of Sydney starter med at søge om forhåndsgodkendelse på for op til 8 fag, hvorefter man tilmelder sig de fire fag (ved fuldtidsstudie), som man gerne vil læse. Det var okay nemt og studievejlederen man var tilknyttet i Sydney var rigtig sød til at svare på spørgsmål og hjælpe på mail inden man tog afsted.
registration_help: Man er tilknyttet en studievejleder på University of Sydney, der kun hjælper udvekslingsstuderende, så de har styr på tingene og er gode til at hjælpe og svare på spørgsmål.
registration_success: Jeg fik alle de kurser, jeg gerne ville. Der var dog et kursus, der efter forhåndgodkendelsen blev omdannet til et lynkursus, så det kun tog 1 måned i stedet for et helt semester. Efter anbefaling fra studievejlederen tog jeg ikke dette kursus, da det ville betyde, at jeg ikke ville have meget tid til andre ting og ville gå glip af sociale ting og oplevelser. En ting der er lidt anderledes fra KU er, at man selv tilmelder sig i prioriteret rækkefølge, hvilke holdundervisning (og nogle gange forelæsninger), man gerne ville have. På den måde kan man selv sammensætte ens skema ved f.eks. ikke at tilmelde sig undervisning på en fredag eller mandag, så man kan tage på forlængede weekendture. De fleste kurser havde undervisning på flere dage af ugen, så man kunne sammensætte ens eget skema meget fleksibelt.
registration_advice: Når man søger forhåndgodkendelse og tilmelder sig fag kan man på University of Sydney's hjemmeside se kursusplanen, bl.a. hvor mange afleveringer, der er i løbet af semesteret, og om der er eksaminer. Her kan man vælge lidt strategisk, hvis man vil undgå eksamen eller ikke have for mange afleveringer.
course_level: Selvom jeg var afsted på kandidaten tog jeg kun bachelorkurser, da det er svært at få kandidatfag på udveksling. Niveauet var ikke super højt, så det var okay nemt at følge med. Jeg kunne godt have valgt fag, der udfordrede mig mere akademisk, men jeg valgte at prioritere det sociale og oplevelser.
teaching_comparison: I de fleste kurser var det den klassiske forelæsninger og holdundervisning.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Project Management, Introduction to Health and Healthcare, Health Promotion og Mental Health Rehabilitation
recommended_courses: Jeg vil IKKE anbefale Introduction to Health and Healthcare, hvor engagementen fra både holdunderviser og andre elever var ikke-eksisterende. Det kan selvfølgelig ændre sig fra semester til semester, men undervisningen var også meget basal og nogle gange lidt for pædagogisk og gymnasie-agtig. Mental Health Rehabilitation var rigtig spændende, men desværre kun online, så man havde ikke samme interaktion med andre studerende eller underviser, hvilket man mangler lidt. Health Promotion var meget fedt, da man lærte om sundhedskampagner i Australien og dermed fik et godt og spændende indblik i det australske sundhedssystem og -tilstand. Project Management var også meget praktisk orienteret og selvom det ikke var sundheds-specifikt, var det stadig spændende og meget FSV-relevant.
unexpected_costs: Jeg endte med at bruge langt flere penge på at spise ude og på aktiviteter og oplevelser, men jeg havde også meget indstillingen om, at jeg ikke ville sige nej til noget og er rigtig glad for at have fået alle de gode stunder med ens nye, men hurtigt tætte, venner med.
cost_comparison: Det koster sjældent mere end 5-10kr at tage bussen selvom man tager den 1 time til stranden, hvis man får et concession (student) Opal kort, som er Sydneys svar på rejsekortet. Som udvekslingsstuderende kan man bestille et concession Opal card, så det kan kun anbefales. Derudover kan man købe alt (gryder og diverse køkkenting, sengetøj sov) i Target og Kmart og det er meget billigt.
activities_available: Jeg var med i Yoga society, hvor der var tre yogahold om ugen hele semesteret. Man betalte 20kr for at være med hele semesteret og derefter kunne man blot deltage i alle de yogahold, man havde lyst til og især Chi's hold var rigtig godt. Derudover var jeg medlem af Social Dancing Society, som havde salsa, jive og bacchata undervisning hver uge. Da det er social dancing skulle man ikke komme med en partner, og det var en rigtig god måde at lære nogle flere mennesker at kende. Man betaler omkring 30kr per undervisningsgang, men til gengæld er det også en professionel underviser, som sørger for et trygt og enormt sjovt miljø. Begge klubber kan kun anbefales! Generelt kan det kun anbefales at melde sig ind i nogle af de enormt mange klubber der er, da det er en god social mulighed og mange fede muligheder. Man har mulighed for at snakke med og høre om alle klubberne under welcome fest, som er en uge med klubbernes info-telte, gratis mad og en masse underholdning og aktiviteter.
activities_recommended: Bare sørg for at meld jer til nogle af alle de fede muligheder. Jeg kan personligt anbefale yoga society og social dancing society.
weekend_recommendations: En weekend til Blue Mountain er et must. Derudover var jeg både på dagstur til Hunter Valley på vinsmagning og dagsture til hhv. Central Coast og Jervis Bay, som begge var skønne ture og især Jervis Bay er et rigtig smukt område. Man kan også nemt tage en weekendtur til Melbourne og Byron Bay med enten fly eller nattog/-bus.
culture_adjustment: Australien er ret vestlig og ikke så anderledes fra Danmark, så det var ikke så svært at vænne sig til. Australierne er til gengæld enormt venlige og imødekommende. Det var spændende og chokerende at høre om Australiens historie og om aboriginals manglende rettigheder, så det kan anbefales at sætte sig lidt ind i det, når man er afsted.
socializing_tips: Meld sig ind i klubber og snak med studerende i undervisningen. Det er dog nemmere at socialisere med andre udvekslingstuderende, da de har samme mentalitet med at få mest muligt ud af det halve år og de også er nye til byen, mens lokale studerende har deres almindelige hverdag og for dem er det bare endnu et semester ligesom man selv kender fra derhjemme.
cultural_challenges: Der var ikke rigtig nogle kulturelle forskelle, der var svært at vænne sig til.
culture_appreciated: Jeg værdsatte virkelig, hvor venlige og hjælpsomme australierne er.
top3_advice: Meld dig ind i klubber. Sig ikke nej til oplevelser. Nyd det maks for det går så hurtigt
other_useful_info: Selvom det kun bliver 16-17 grader i vinteren, så føles det koldere end vi kender det fra Danmark, så vær forberedt på måske og gå i Kmart og køb en billig vinterjakke og husk ikke kun at pakke shorts og tshirts.
most_rewarding: At få en international, tæt vennekreds med venner fra hele verden og dele en masse ture og oplevelser med dem.
greatest_challenge: At tage afsted på udveksling helt alene og skubbe sig selv ind i sociale situationer uden at kende nogle, hvilket har givet nogle rigtig tætte venner.

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte Sydney for jeg gerne ville læse i et engelsktalende land, hvor der var gode muligheder for at surfe og opleve natur.
info_ease: Det var relativt nemt. Jeg havde en god vejleder som skrev mails om vigtige ting.
arrival_assistance: Min studievejleder
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

crucial_aspects: A good selection of relevant courses at a recognized university, and of course the Australian lifestyle
info_ease: Be aware that University of Sydney emails you a lot of information up front (and its very repetitive so the relevant points often drown). It's helpful if you read all of it. This information can only be found in the emails received so keep them! They don't have a website or anything you can go look at.
arrival_assistance: Emails with information and an introductory meeting for all exchange studies.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process was very messy because they kept changing the availability of courses so I had to re-register several times and I didn't end up with the courses I wanted to. You register online but you have to read the instructions carefully because its not obvious how to use the system.
registration_help: You could also send you advisor an email or show up at certain locations on campus where they offered pop-up assistance
registration_success: Not very successful. They changed a lot of classes from being offered both in-person and online to only online. A lot of classes were also cancelled last minute. I ended up having some online-only courses because I didn't know what to do. Initially, they offered a wide variety of courses that seemed very interesting, but in the end, the options were disappointingly limited.
registration_advice: I think my experience was coloured by this being the first 'in-person' exchange semester after COVID. Hopefully it's not going to be like this in the future, as people return to campus.
course_level: The level of the courses was very basic. Don't expect anything to ground-breaking, but you could be lucky of course. However, the workload is high because you are expected to hand in a lot of assignments and engage during the tutorials. I ended up studying a lot more than I am used to.
teaching_comparison: USYD operated with mandatory tutorials in most classes. The called your name to make sure you were there and you were expected to actively participate and contribute to group discussions. Lectures were much of the same, even though I also had classes that mixed the lecture and tutorial to a large, interactive session.
courses_enrolled: US-China Relations Globalisation and Governance International Security Strategy and Security in the Indo-Pacific
recommended_courses: US-China relations is the only course I would recommend. The lecturer was exceptional and it was very interesting, attempting to look at US-China relations from the perspective of both sides. Workload was very high!
unexpected_costs: Temporary housing until I found a place to stay ended up being a lot more than I hoped. In general, everything is expensive in Sydney.
cost_comparison: Vegetables are very expensive..... Housing and other things like internet subscription and SIM cards are very expensive compared to what you get. Gyms are very expensive too!
activities_available: everything! Sports clubs, religious and cultural clubs, everything in-between (e,g, the chocolate society) on-campus bars and concert arenas, lot's of free introductory events
activities_recommended: Sign up for all events in the introductory period and meet a lot of people! Events often had free drinks, snacks, food and merchandise
weekend_recommendations: The city has so much to offer and I enjoyed the nice coastal walks such as Rose Bay - Hornby Lighthouse, Bondi - Cogee and Spit - Manly. Get out of the city and see the Blue Mountains too
culture_adjustment: Easy to adjust to Australia, but I was surprised by the amount of Asians at the university. There was actually a bit of cultural adjustment to do because the university was tailored more towards its Asian students than Australians. I went to an 'afternoon tea' at my faculty that turned out to be dumplings, spring rolls and sodas which was quite funny. The level of English was also not what I expected, you are apparently allowed to study in English at an English university without knowing English (sometimes they provided Chinese translations or auto-translate the lectures to Chinese). It was very hard to connect with my fellow students because it was difficult to communicate.
socializing_tips: Good luck finding them!
cultural_challenges: Australia is not that different
culture_appreciated: I got my share of Australian culture off-campus, not on campus. I like how Australians in general are very active people, early risers and enjoy their time outside
top3_advice: Be vigilant when it comes to housing, it's important for whether you get a good stay. Location is important, public transport is fine but Sydney is really huge! Don't put too much effort into your assignments, have fun instead!
other_useful_info: Time goes fast, plan your travels in advance
most_rewarding: I have met a lot of amazing international students that I am looking forward to staying in touch with! Sydney is also such a fun city to stay in
greatest_challenge: Finding housing in the beginning!

cultural_challenges: I think Australia is a lot like Denmark, so it is easy to get around and talk to people.
culture_appreciated: I think people were very friendly and nice, and I think it was nice to see how much they talked about and respected the aboriginals and the culture from the indigenous people.
top3_advice: Take some courses that are interesting but also fun and different. Be outgoing and go to the social events. Enjoy your time there, the time passes by so fast.
other_useful_info: It is a good idea to walk around campus before your first class, it is a big campus so you can easily get lost.
most_rewarding: Getting to know a lot of new people, learn about the country and its culture and the new friendships I got.

crucial_aspects: I have always wanted to experience Australia because of its beautiful, grand and very different nature, because of the possibility of surfing and because of the friendly reputation the people there has. It was also important for me to go to an English speaking country because I think I would feel more isolated if I was not able to speak the native tongue. I wanted to choose a bigger city because I wanted to be a part of a larger exchange-student community. All of those factors made me choose the University of Sydney.
overall_comments: Even though I have rated my experience quite high, I would like to add that it is not always smooth sailing. I felt that the application, visa, and preparation phase was difficult with the amount of help available which was frustrating at times. A tip is that it is very nice to be in contact with people who have gone through the same process before you. Being on exchange far from home also comes with its practical and mental challenges. And one thing I think is important to remember is that whatever you might struggle with back home will not disappear when you go on exchange. It might even become more clear to you which I actually think is a good thing but also a thing worth knowing. All that being said, I am very glad that I went and I would gladly do the entire thing again.

I often felt like I got the most help from students who had gone to Sydney on exchange before me.
arrival_assistance: Other than e-mails I had an opportunity to get an in-person drop-in session with my advisor which I took, and that was really helpful (much more so than the e-mails).
arrival_comments: I came a little late, so I missed some of the social introductory events. I felt like there should have been more of those but since I could not attend the ones two weeks prior to the semester start it is hard for me to comment on the overall orientation. I would advise people to get to Sydney at least two weeks before semester start, so they can settle in socially before classes start, however it is not paramount.

course_level: Level 1000 is first year, 2000 is second year and so on. However we got recommended to do 2000 units even when it was our 3. semester because apparently they are a bit ahead, but I think you can also do 3000 units. I would advise to do a mixture between 2000 and 3000 so you don't get too much work because it is extra heavy when you also have to adjust to living in a different country.
teaching_comparison: It was more supportive I think. There were more in-semester assignments and quizzes that counted towards the final grade. I personally quite enjoyed that because it made it easier to follow along and made the final exam less nerve-racking. In my units there were some quite cheap points to get as well which was nice. You do not have to be as controling of your own learning as you do in UCPH. This might have been because of covid, but all lectures and classes were not only streamed online but also recorded and put up on canvas, which I found really helpful. I think they are going to do that even after covid, because we did have classes where you could meet up in person, where they also streamed and recorded most activities.
courses_enrolled: MIMI2002: Microbes, Infection and Immunity BIOS2171: Human Neuroscience in Health and Disease BCMB3003: Biochemistry of Human Disease EDUH4052: Learning in Outdoor Education
recommended_courses: Definitely EDUH4052 because it is a good way of getting to know other exchange students and you get to go on two very cool field trips were you explore some of the beautiful nature around Sydney. It is not a very difficult course so it also frees up time to explore Sydney and work more on your other courses. Hugh recommendation for this course. MIMI2002 had a great structure and great professors. They both stopped this semester but hopefully their replacements are going to run the course in a similar way. I think it was a fine introduction to the immune system but there is a lot of focus on bacteria, vira and specific diseases which the name also indicates. One of the reasons why I picked it, was because I heard that it was nice to have had some immunology before Humanfysiologi. BIOS2171 was a good introduction to the nervous system even though I wasn't too thrilled by the professors. However they were really sweat, which was nice. BCMB3003 was not greatly structured and the in-semester exam (a half-way point exam that counts for a smaller fraction of the final mark than the final exam) was very difficult because the professor responsible for the course didn't seem to have the best idea of what his students knew. It was stressful at times with lab-reports requiring more work than the marks awarded for them suggested, but I thought the topics in the lectures were quite interesting. Overall I was happy with my courses, however you might be able to find better once and it obviously also depends on interests.
unexpected_costs: The visa application is quite expensive. I think it was 3000 and something DKK. I haven't included cost of traveling but that is obviously one of the most expensive things. Well worth it though. I used 10.000 DKK on a group tour to the East coast on spring break and I do not know I much I used after the semester ended but it wasn't cheap.
cost_comparison: The prices in Sydney are generally a little higher than in Copenhagen. I found that a few items were cheaper. For example milk.
activities_available: Too many to mention. They had a chocolate society. I never did, but I should have joined the bush-walking society.
activities_recommended: Bush-walking society even though I wasn't a part of it. I met a lot of people that I really liked late in the semester who had all been a part of that, and I think bushwalking is a good way of exploring Australian nature.
weekend_recommendations: Make sure to go on weekend trips to different places in and around Sydney. I liked the beach walk from Bondi beach to Coogee beach. You can take surf lessons on Bondi or Manly beach however I would recommend going on a surfcamp. They will probably get advertised to you. Blue Mountains National Park and Royal National Park are really worth a visit (also more than one). You are going to those two with EDUH4052 if you take that class. 8-figure pools and mermaid pools are some places to visit in Royal national park. I never went there but palm beach in north Sydney should also be cool. Some of the popular clubs in Sydney are Scary Canary, Ivy and Club 77. On longer holidays I would recommend visiting the East coast of Australia. I personally went from Brisbane to Cairns. Also Uluru in the red center of Australia, Tasmania, Melbourne and the great ocean road, and Byron Bay are all very cool places. I heard a lot of good things about the nature of the west coast too, but I never went there.
culture_adjustment: The culture is very western so it was relatively easy. There is a couple of things that you have to get used to still, but it is only nice that it is a little bit different. I felt as if it was more open and friendly than back home.
socializing_tips: Just be open and friendly. They most likely will be. And if you find someone you click with invite them for a trip to the beach or for a drink. Remember you only have 4-6 months and you have nothing to lose.
cultural_challenges: Almost everyone (also other exchange students) will ask "How are you doing" or "How is it going" whenever they see you just as a formality. Sometimes I would start telling them how I was actually doing while all they were looking for was a simple "Good. You?"
culture_appreciated: Probably the friendliness.
top3_advice: Treasure your time there and remember that it goes by quicker than you think. When you meet nice people be sure to use time with them. See Australia. It is not every day that you are on the other side of the globe.
other_useful_info: There probably is, but I can't come to think of anything right now, but therefore I will suggest to get in contact with someone who has been there before, so that you have someone you can ask all the questions you might have.
most_rewarding: The people I got to know well and travel with after the semester had ended.
greatest_challenge: It can feel lonely at times when you are that far from home and most people you know. Fortunately, University of Sydney is such a big university that other students from your course most likely will also be there, and that can be very helpfull in that regard.
other_comments: Sometimes you will hear only good things about people's experiences with exchange and I feel like it is important to tell that it is also challenging and at times tedious (applications and practical stuff) or difficult (mentally) but the rewarding side is so much greater than the efforts made. I would do it again in a heartbeat, and I am very happy that I went.

crucial_aspects: I primarily chose Sydney University due to the location, not the university itself. I have been to Sydney before, and I had friends and family there I really wanted to see again. The last time I was in Sydney I never got to really experience the city due to Covid, so I thought exchange would be a perfect opportunity to go back to see more of the city and the rest of Australia. USyd also has a good academic reputation and the weather is generally good in Sydney which were both bonuses.
info_ease: Very easy. Already in the week before orientation week the uni held introduction meetings where they gave a bit of information about the layout of the campus, the events during the orientation week and what to expect from the rest of the semester. They also gave tips on which apps to get to make settling into Sydney and uni life easier.
arrival_assistance: We were all assigned a student adviser who could help us find answer to any questions we had about the university campus and orientation events, or more academic related question such as about lectures and signing up to different units. My adviser changed a couple of times which made it a bit confusing or hard to get a hold of them sometimes, and they generally took a while to answer due to them receiving many messages, but overall they were very helpfull.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After getting accepted to the exchange program we were sent a list of available units/classes during the semester we would be there. Initially we could chose as many units we wanted and the different faculties then had to evaluate whether or not we could take the units. From the list of approved units we had to choose 4 units to start out with but during the first two weeks of lessons you were able to drop/change units as long as it was approved by USyd and Copenhagen uni.
registration_help: We only had our student adviser who told us about the process and had to process all our requests to drop/change units but she could not guarantee our requests would be approved or advise us on how relevant the different units were for our studies.
registration_success: In the first round of unit requests many on my list were rejected due to 'lack of required prerequisites', but when I explained how I did have equivalent prerequisites most of them were approved. However, one of the units I wanted the most was never approved and another was cancelled a week before lectures started so I had to chose another one.
course_level: Two of the units I ended up taking were 3rd year level so it was meant to be an extension on material we had learned about before in units back home, but it ended up just being a repetition of the same material we had already heard about in previous courses and didn't add much extra. So overall these were not that high academic level even though they were supposed to be the highest level I took there. The other unit was lower level (2nd year unit) but was on a completely different area than the courses i've had back home, so it was a lot more challenging. Overall, the academical level felt a bit lower but I had to spend a lot more time on uni work due to assignments throughout the semester, rather than just having a final exam.
teaching_comparison: To some extent I really enjoyed having the assignments throughout the semester as it took some pressure off the final exam and allowed you to test your understanding during the course. However, often they were also really time consuming considering the amount of marks you could actually get from the assignments, so I recommend getting started on them early. I really didn't enjoy the style of the lectures as many of them were still only offered on zoom or both zoom and in person, but only 15% of the student showed up in person which made it hard to meet people in the classes and was clearly frustrating for the lecturers. The lab sessions were also a bit of a joke a lot of the time. They had really good facilities but the experiments weren't planned that well and a lot of time were wasted during the the lab sessions.
courses_enrolled: Learning in outdoor education EDUH4052 Microbes, infection and immunity MIMI2002 Beyond the genome BCMB3004 Biochemistry of human disease BCMB3003
recommended_courses: I highly recommend doing the Learning in outdoor education. It is a really good way to meet other exchange students as it's not even offered to local students and Wayne who runs the course was amazing. It was quite an easy course to do as there was no final exam, the course finished right after mid-term and most of the lecture time was used on two hiking trips to the Royal national park and the Blue mountains. MIMI2002 was also really interesting as it was mostly new material we learned about and the two women in charge of the course were very organised and had a great relationship with each other and their students. They were clearly interested in us learning as much as possible and always put in a lot of effort to explain extra stuff to us or share extra material for us to look at if we wanted. The only downsides were that all lectures were online and that there at times were a bit too much material to get through it all. Unfortunately this course will not be taught by either of them anymore, so the structure might change for future semesters. BCMB3004 was a lot of repetition from previous courses i've taken but Stuart who taught the course was really good. It was clear he was an expert in the field of proteomics and he went above and beyond to ensure everyone could keep up and were enjoying the course.
cost_comparison: Groceries were quite expensive, especially if you don't shop at Aldi, Coles or Woolworths and buy the store's own brand. Renting cars/campervans is also very expensive in general but if you're under 25 years old there's also an extra cost added due to insurance for young drivers.
activities_available: The uni has a lot of clubs and societies that you can join such as yoga, bushwalking, cheerleading, rugby, debate, and many many more. Most of them are introduced at the societies fair in orientation week but others you have to hear about from other students. Some of the societies are free to join and others you have to pay a fee which is usually not that high.
activities_recommended: The yoga society was really good and only cost 5$ for the whole semester.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely go to Melbourne, it's close and you can usually get flights at an okay price if you go on a weekend trip. In my opinion Melbourne had a much better cultural scene and nightlife than Sydney so it was nice to experience. I also really enjoyed going to Byron bay further up the east coast and travelling around the South-west loop in Western Australia (this is a lot further away though and tickets are more expensive). If you don't do the learning in outdoor education course then going to the blue mountains is a must, the Figure 8 pools in the Royal national park is also supposed to be cool but hard to plan due to the tides, and I never got to see Jervis bay but really wished I had time to.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it's very similar to danish culture (very western) but has more beach culture and fancy coffee.
socializing_tips: I didn't meet many local students at the uni as most of them didn't show up to the lectures, so mostly I met locals through my housemates, at the QMB parties or through other friends that had met locals. Sign up to different societies where it's not only for exchange students and just start conversations with them. The local students don't seem as interested in making new friends as the other exchange students and aren't as inclusive so you have to put more effort into socialising with them.
cultural_challenges: there aren't really any that I found challenging
culture_appreciated: The coffee, if you're not already a coffee addict there's a real risk you will become one. I also really enjoyed Australia's appreciation of nature and outdoor activities, I definitely think I'll try to go hiking a lot more in Denmark after doing it so often in Sydney.
top3_advice: 1. Stay up to date with the assignments throughout the semester and get as many marks as possible from these as it takes a lot of pressure of the final exam (if you even have one). 2. Sydney doesn't only have great weather. We had sooooo much rain most of the semester there due to the weather phenomenon called La Niña, so don't only bring summer clothes and don't expect everyday to be a beach day. 3. Shop at Aldi, not Foodworks
other_useful_info: .Don't stress too much about picking units you want to take before arriving. During the first 1-2 weeks you have the option to switch units if you find out your chosen ones aren't for you, if they're too difficult, too easy, etc.
most_rewarding: All the people I met! There were so many lovely people I shared my time and experience there with, that I know I'll continue to talk to and see even after leaving.
greatest_challenge: Staying motivated during the zoom lectures

I wanted to go to an English speaking country, and I also wanted to explore a new place and have lots of amazing travelling/nature experiences, which Australia has. I also wished to go to a good university which would be relevant on my resumé, but this was not my first priority.

But I figured out that KU helped me a lot when it came to the important stuff, so everything worked out in the end. But it is a good idea to talk to someone who has been abroad already to help the process.
arrival_assistance: I received help on getting the right courses (I had not finalized this from home, which I was upset about). My student coordinator in Sydney helped me A LOT, and KU helped me as well.
arrival_comments: They were very helpful with my courses
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had a really good experience. Academically, it has not been my most interesting semester. My sense is that Australia is not as good at receiving international students and creating social places for them to meet as many other places, so I had to take a more active approach in making friends, and I knew a lot of people from back home, which was also nice in the beginning.
registration_process: It was easy to find courses at University of Sydney, the hardest part was just knowing what would be accepted by KU
registration_help: I had a student coordinator at the University
registration_success: I got the classes I wanted
registration_advice: It was easiest for me to get the courses when I arrived in Sydney (I had problems before, but I set up an in-person meeting when I arrived in Sydney). You can change your subjects up to two weeks after arriving in Sydney.
academics_comments: I had a really good experience. Academically, it has not been my most interesting semester. My sense is that Australia is not as good at receiving international students and creating social places for them to meet as many other places, so I had to take a more active approach in making friends, and I knew a lot of people from back home, which was also nice in the beginning.
course_level: I took three 3rd-year economic courses: Public Finance, Strategic Behaviour (Mikro III), and Development Economics, and they were not on a higher level than at KU. It was very straightforward. I also had a first-year course, History and Philosophy of Science.
teaching_comparison: There was participation requirements in Philosophy of science, and mid-term exams that counted towards the final grade, which was different. But I liked this, as we had less pressure on the final exam.
courses_enrolled: Public Finance, Development Economics, Strategic Behaviour (Mikro III) and What's This Thing Called Science? (Videnskabsteori).
recommended_courses: I liked that I got 4 mandatory courses - but I cannot recommend development economics, it was not very interesting and I would have preferred taking a more interesting elective course instead.
unexpected_costs: There is a mandatory health ensurance, which was a little expensive. The visa was also a little expensive. There were a bunch of fees of my campus housing.
cost_comparison: Basically the same level as in Denmark, some things are more expensive and some things are cheaper
activities_available: I did not find any suitable for me, but there are definitely some
activities_recommended: I heard that the Skiing club should be fun to be a part of (they don't go skiing, but it is a fun society)
weekend_recommendations: Uluru was the biggest experience. Furthermore, you should go to Blue Mountains and maybe Byron Bay
culture_adjustment: Easy. I mostly hung out with other Danish people and Scandinavian people.
socializing_tips: I did not really socialize with local students
cultural_challenges: Nothing particular
culture_appreciated: Outgoing, down-to-earth people
top3_advice: That everything will be fine! I had a million questions about how everything practical would work out, but it was all fine in the end.
other_useful_info: Nothing particular
most_rewarding: Travelling around and the people I met
greatest_challenge: Meeting new people during the first couple of weeks! But after this, everything was fine.
other_comments: No comments

crucial_aspects: Preceding all else, a bit of catharsis: Do not(!!!) attend USYD on exchange if you are a MSc Statistics, or a MSc Mathematics student wanting to take masters-level (‘post graduate in USYD-lingo) statistics, data science, biostatistics or mathematics courses, because you will not be able to.
overall_comments: The low rating above should primarily be taken as a reflection on the toil and anguish with which I had to acquire courses. A rating of approximately 9 might otherwise have been given as the courses for which I toiled ended up being decent and I otherwise had a thoroughly pleasant time. Having made mates from around the world that I've met on multiple occasions since, and will continue to do so thrice more before the end of 2023. The city is awesome with great opportunities for exploration “til lands, til vand og i luften” with the mountains to the north (90 min), west (120 min) and south (70 min) away, the sea 30 min to the east, and the harbour going through the city. Sydney is massive, and different neighbourhoods have different plannings and different concentrations of expat populations such that you get new types of restaurants, bars, decorations and atmospheres in different areas giving you many things to explore. The nightlife is a bit dry, with most places closing very early and everything, especially alcohol, being very expensive. The city has decent S-Bahn - style public transport, though this is limited during later hours, inhibiting nightlife possibilities further. Cycling is possible, but rarely are dedicated or protected bike lanes available. You should thus be careful especially for the first month when you're getting used to the paradigm of driving on the left side of the road, and in particular all the unexpected ways cars, trams or other bikes could hit you when they don't travel in the way you expect them to. Australia has endless possibilities for travel and exploration, near and far, whether you want cold, hot, low or high, cities or vast empty landscapes. I managed to travel thrice during my exchange: 1. I spent the month previous to the start of the semester travelling via Istanbul (half day transfer), Singapore (6 days), Darwin (5 days), Cairns (9 days) and Sydney (14 days). 2. I did an eight day road trip during spring vacation with three of my mates to Hervey Bay and back. (Travelling the east coast is very popular) 3. Travelled for six weeks after my exchange semester, in which I took two SCUBA diving certificates in Sydney (5 days), road tripped (four days) to Melbourne via Canberra and Kościuszko NP in a relocation campervan (awesome, basically free way to rent a car/van in Oz), explored Melbourne (6 days), walked the OLT in Tasmania and saw Hobart (7+3 days), took another relocation vehicle from Melbourne to Adelaide via the Great Ocean Road and the Grampians (3 days), spent Christmas in Adelaide (5 days) before I flew home via Perth after (10 days of) exploring the nearby areas, taking Quokka selfies, going on tours, base jumping, as well as kayaking and snorkelling in perfect turquoise waters. My mates mostly chose to travel northwards to QLD or to travel to “nearby” destinations such as Fiji, New Zealand, Bali, Jakarta, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, Hawaii and Taiwan. Travelling to and from Australia is a far way and may involve many stops and airlines. Be sure to check visa and baggage-size and weight -requirements for each hop. When travelling Australia, note that the vastness of the country, even near the largest cities and for the closest attractions, require access to a car (!), a willingness to spend >600 DKK / day going on guided tours, or great enthusiasm and ability to cycle. There's some online debate as to whether an international or English-languaged-driver's-permit is necessary for EU-permits. To rid yourself of having to worry about possibly finding out the hard way, consider getting an international driver's permit while you are still in Denmark. They cost very little here, but take a couple of weeks to be made, if you think you might want to drive. Alternatively you can get official translations (50 AUD at the Danish Consulate General in Sydney) of any non-English-languaged driver's licence at most consulates (there's Danish representation in the larger Australian cities though you'd have to look up whether they are seasonal) If you are going to have mates or your family visit you doing your exchange, have them get an international licence as well, if they plan on travelling in Australia. Also have them apply for their tourist visa months (!!!) before their travels, as the tourism visa occasionally takes a long time to process. Consider that weather in Oz can be intense, and that seasons (which are not uniform across the country) should be more heavily considered when planning travel - especially if you are similarly inflicted with a predisposition against high temperatures as is the typical Dane.
info_ease: Main difficulty for me was getting courses sorted. An official USYD international study abroad adviser will be designated, and they will send you info leading up to and during the intro week of your exchange. There's a couple of opportunities to ask academic questions when you arrive, but the answer to any academic question will have its conclusion long been foretold. Non-academic questions can be asked before and after your arrival at the regular USYD student services. Most attempts to enquire with them about academic matters will lead to a deferral to your international study adviser for academic questions. Your international study abroad adviser will be very overworked, only answers by mail, and may at times take over three weeks to respond.
arrival_assistance: There is an intro week. They show you around campus and arrange some games as well as a couple of tours of, and activities in -the city. You should have all your courses cleared with USYD before you arrive, and preferably way before you arrive.
arrival_comments: If you go, call USYD student services before arrival to Australia (for example via Skype) to get your USYD email and access to Canvas set up.
