There's some online debate as to whether an international or English-languaged-driver's-permit is necessary for EU-permits. To rid yourself of having to worry about possibly finding out the hard way, consider getting an international driver's permit while you are still in Denmark. They cost very little here, but take a couple of weeks to be made, if you think you might want to drive. Alternatively you can get official translations (50 AUD at the Danish Consulate General in Sydney) of any non-English-languaged driver's licence at most consulates (there's Danish representation in the larger Australian cities though you'd have to look up whether they are seasonal) If you are going to have mates or your family visit you doing your exchange, have them get an international licence as well, if they plan on travelling in Australia. Also have them apply for their tourist visa months (!!!) before their travels, as the tourism visa occasionally takes a long time to process. Consider that weather in Oz can be intense, and that seasons (which are not uniform across the country) should be more heavily considered when planning travel - especially if you are similarly inflicted with a predisposition against high temperatures as is the typical Dane.
course_level: See above. Note you cannot take post-graduate units as a BSc student. To this day I still haven't received an answer regarding whether fourth-years could take postgraduate units.
teaching_comparison: Attending during semester 2 of 2022, we had hybrid education due to continued covid fears. There is an increased focus on continued assessment via quizzes, weekly or multiple assignments, or projects. As such, you should expect a decent amount of work during the semester as well. As compensation, my final exams in each course only accounted for 40%, 60%, 0% and 33% of the final grade.
courses_enrolled: COMP5048: Visual Analytics, COMP5318: Machine Learning and Data Mining, DATA5441: Networks and High-Dimensional Inference, STAT5003: Computational Statistical Methods.
recommended_courses: Don't go to USYD if you are MSc Mathematics and especially MSc Statistics if you cannot see yourself studying a combination of four of the units present in the lists linked to above. The above lists of units are updated for the academic year 2024, and I see no sign that you'd be able to attend the STAT or DATA units I did, lest you desire to endure a months-long, attritional battle of calls and mails. You could choose to do QBUS (Quantitative BUSiness) units, but these are sort of the ‘wrong way around' being targeted at business students that want to do quantitative stuff, instead of quantitative students that want to do business. You might be able to sign up for the COMP units above. Maybe especially if you have a Computer Science background or significant number of units therein. I was able to appeal my failed applications to attend *any, including introductory first year* COMP units by circumventing the official registration process and mailing the course-coordinators, lecturers and computer science institute, getting their approval, and then forwarding this to my USYD international study adviser via the ‘regular' USYD student services to exert maximal pressure and get the slightest consideration for my case beyond declaring that computer science units are off-limits to anyone not studying computer science, no matter the level or content of the course, or abilities of the exchange student. Had I done the exchange again, I'd have changed COMP5048 for COMP5328: Advanced Machine Learning, as STAT5003 and COMP5318 shared a decent bit of their curriculum (though taught so as to be implemented in R and python respectively) and COMP5048, while teaching some ideas of how to work with graphics and interactive graphics in particular, was not really material you couldn't learn elsewhere as well.
unexpected_costs: Airfares cost approximately 8000 DKK each way. I left my rental contract ten days prior to the agreed upon date, and the rental company charged me a week's rent of 275 AUD for ending the contract early, no matter that they had someone in the next day. A mate of mine got a 130 AUD = ~ 650 DKK ticket during their spring road trip for going 68 kph in a 60 kph zone. For insurance, I paid 2860 DKK for IDA's travel insurance made for exchange stays, and 348 AUD = ~ 1750 DKK for the USYD-obligatory Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) which I bought from CBHS. I got covid in Singapore on my way to Australia resulting in 5k DKK extra cost that was taken care of upon my return by the above travel insurance. JetStar temporarily mislocated my checked baggage when travelling between Cairns and Sydney, resulting in be having to buy 700 DKK worth of basics. This was covered almost immediately by my travel insurance. The high personal spending above is an estimate, but mainly reflects the fact that I went travelling for a total of 12 weeks during my exchange. I spent very little on public transport as I lived within walking distance to uni. I paid 10 AUD / month for basic phone services.
cost_comparison: You'd think Copenhagen to be more expensive than Sydney. As with all things in Australia, it was the other way around. The price of food when I went in July 2022 - January 2023 could be considered comparable to if you in Denmark were to always go shopping for organics in Irma or Meny in Hellerup. I only found coconut-milk, pre-made curries from ALDI, haircuts, and domestic biscuits on discount to be less expensive. Price of accommodation was comparable to private market rates for rooms in shared flats in Copenhagen when I arrived, but became massively more expensive when I left. Alcohol is massively more expensive than in DK at all but a few pubs, and in all supermarkets. Public transport in Sydney is comparable to that of Copenhagen, (but basically free on Sundays). Renting automobiles is rather expensive as compared to classical European vacation destinations at 120 AUD / day, which makes the option to do relocation drives a lot more desirable if it fits. There's no true Australian equivalent to European budget airlines, which makes air travel within Australia rather expensive.
activities_available: Some events are organised for exchange students by the university study abroad team. For those you'll have to sign up quickly. Lots of opportunities via the clubs, see USU website and above.
activities_recommended: As above, there are lots of clubs that you can engage with, and lots of things to go explore in the city and nearby.
weekend_recommendations: See above. You could easily make a weekend out of going to Canberra or Newcastle, or an extended weekend out of visiting Melbourne. Alternatives closer to Sydney include the Blue Mountains, Royal, Ku-ring-gai-Chase and Sydney Harbour National parks, Manly and shelly beach, go to palm beach, Bondi beach, Bondi to Coogee walk, explore the CBD, go explore West Sydney's neighbourhoods and food (for example on the T2 or T3 to Cabramatta, Parramatta or Liverpool), try Sydney's secret bars or the many gaybars on Oxford Street, go to Kings Cross or the posh east and north east Sydney neighbourhoods such as Rose Bay, Vaucluse and Mosman. Note that ferry transport is excellent and can take you to many different places within the harbour.
culture_adjustment: No problems at all. There is a lot of internationals.
socializing_tips: Australians are a difficult breed to socialise with at uni lest you engage in clubs, as there is no natural or canonical social activity on campus. Most exchange students group together with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Nothing of note. A decent portion of the international students have lower confidence in their English than what I've typically perceived at UCPH.
culture_appreciated: The Australians subscribe to the British pub-concept, which I appreciated a lot as opposed to the more thunderous bar-concept that we typically go with in Denmark.
top3_advice: 1. Go to alternative universities than USYD if you are MSc Statistics or similar (check the lists). Make sure whichever uni you exchange to, that the approval for courses at your host institution is solid and settled before you arrive. Make sure that you know what the content, programming languages, degree of abstraction of each course is, prior to your arrival, and that these are satisfactory to you in terms of prerequisites and interest. 2. If you go on exchange, arrive at your destination at least two weeks early, to get to meet people. For example by staying at a hostel. Exchange students typically group together, and the groups typically solidify very quickly. Once the semester starts, they will suddenly be blocking off 30, 40, 50 hours a week on studying that was free to explore the city and socialise previous to the start of the semester. 3. Exchange is often romanticised. Consider that most stays, even the ones that do not go as wrong as mine, will involve a non-insignificant amount of multi level planning and coordination, and is often a significant undertaking both prior to and during the stay.
other_useful_info: It is possible to attend USYD as a Math Econ student if you are willing and allowed to take ECON units, of which there are plenty (see above link), or if you are going during your BSc
most_rewarding: 1. Getting to meet new people 2. Getting to live and travel new places 3. Getting to contrast your regular life with an alternative one in a very natural and safe environment
greatest_challenge: Getting approval for units commensurate to my academic maturity as a fifth year statistics student.
other_comments: Nah.

crucial_aspects: I preferred an English-speaking country, and I have always wanted to visit Australia
info_ease: It was a bit difficult to manage everything, especially since we were the first group from our university on that exchange agreement, so there was no one to ask for advice. It all ended up working out really well, but I left before everything was finalized for my bachelor's project, which I have been writing during the exchange
arrival_assistance: I attended a meeting at the school where I received help organizing my schedule (bachelor's project)
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It can be a bit challenging to get everything sorted when registering from home.
registration_help: You're assigned a coordinator who can assist, but it takes some time to get a response.
registration_success: I got the classes I wanted, but it was troublesome, and initially I was assigned a schedule with clashes (overlapping hours).
registration_advice: Try to familiarize yourself with it from home, but don't stress if you leave without having everything completely under control. It's a very different school system, and schedules are typically sorted out during the first few weeks. (It's a very common issue for both international and domestic students.)
course_level: My impression is that the classes are 'easier' than back home. But it's also a different system, and it takes a bit of time to figure out how they set up assignments, etc. However, the level allows you to travel and enjoy your exchange country while still keeping up with the coursework
teaching_comparison: It reminded me a lot of what I know from UCPH - I've had lectures, practicals (labs), tutorials, workshops, etc
courses_enrolled: CHEM3120: Environmental and Analytical Chemistry PCOL3012: Drug Design and Development And in addition, I was involved with a research group where I worked on my bachelor's project.
recommended_courses: I have spoken with a coordinator here about the possibility of opening up the option to take pharmacy courses for future exchange students. The courses I took while studying at USYD were not directly relevant, especially drug design and development, which were quite basic compared to the classes I usually take at home.
unexpected_costs: The kitchen was without utensils, etc., so I had to go out and buy plates, pots, etc. Similarly, I had to buy a duvet, etc.
cost_comparison: Public transport is really cheap. Groceries are slightly more expensive, but eating out is cheaper.
activities_available: There are a lot of clubs and societies. In the first week, there is a welcome festival where all clubs and societies have a booth where you can come and learn about all the opportunities available. There is a club for everything.
activities_recommended: I have played squash and been part of a yoga society. I have also signed up for a surf camp. I can really recommend it.
weekend_recommendations: I have visited Tasmania during the mid-semester break (rented a car), explored Melbourne and Newcastle. There's also plenty to see around Sydney. I would also recommend visiting the Blue Mountains National Park (2 hours by train from Sydney). After the semester ends, I've booked a trip to Uluru and Cairns.
culture_adjustment: I don't think I've experienced any major cultural differences. Most of the cultural differences I've noticed have been due to meeting other exchange students from all over the world. However, I would say that Australian culture is quite similar to Western culture.
socializing_tips: I have primarily met local students in my classes. For example, suggesting to grab a coffee together or meet up to work on assignments has been common. (I have mainly socialized with other exchange students outside of school). However, I have often been the only exchange student in my classes.
cultural_challenges: The biggest difference might be that the city is more lively in the morning (rush hour at coffee shops is before work), and then it becomes quieter later in the day.
culture_appreciated: I don't think I've experienced any major cultural differences.
top3_advice: Join a club or society and remember, Australia also gets cool during winter, so bring a jacket and a raincoat. I would recommend opening a bank account—it's free for students. This way, you can avoid large fees, especially on your rent. Order your Opal card quickly (half-price for students) (opal card = travel card) It's much easier if you have an Australian phone number (you can easily buy a SIM card at Aldi)
other_useful_info: USYD is really good at hosting a lot of welcome events at the beginning, so you quickly meet a lot of friends.
most_rewarding: It has been rewarding to experience that I can move to the other side of the world and build a daily life for myself. Additionally, I have practiced my English and am now more comfortable with it. It has also been rewarding to meet a lot of nice people.
greatest_challenge: The hardest part was getting everything sorted with school and accommodation before I arrived
other_comments: I am so glad I took this opportunity to go on exchange, and I would really recommend it.

A lot of the info was given several times, and you could have skipped the introduction week as much (if not all) of the information given here was repeated at the information events in th actual starting week.
arrival_assistance: I did not need assistance, as my units had been confirmed by USYD before arrival.
arrival_comments: Only complaint would be information overload. This was most likely because the university engages in so many aspects of the student's life, meaning you received information not only about things related directly to studying at the university, but also about water safety, housing, scamming (housing, telephone, e-mail), food services, social clubs and events, police, medical service and more.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I was a bit disappointed in some of my units, but positively surprised on others.
registration_process: You sign up through an online portal and then you later receive notice whether you have been assigned to the unit. You should list more units than desired, as you might not be assigned and/or approved to all. I was not approved for two units, as I did not meet the requirements (I had not send anything forward, which is a possibility), but I was allowed to do one of them anyway (I don't know why).
registration_help: You can mail with the international student coordinator. She was super busy, and would take a week or so to reply.
registration_success: I wanted classes that were advertised to be open for exchange students in their online catalogue, but this was apparently a mistake. In the end I got four units I wanted, where two of them were units I choose because I could not get any other units within my main field of interest.
registration_advice: Do not choose this university because of the units before you have looked at the actual list of units available for you. For this, you have to mail the student coordinator and ask for the list.
academics_comments: I was a bit disappointed in some of my units, but positively surprised on others.
course_level: In genereal, the level of the units seemed lower than at UCPH. The students seem to have less experience with academic writing. I was pretty challenged in one class, but this class was also outside of my faculty (I am political science student and the class was as their computer science faculty).
teaching_comparison: I find the instructors/teachers teaching the discussion classes better at UCPH. In some units, the classes were pretty much an extra mini lecture (in a bad way).
courses_enrolled: Chinese Politics Issues in Public Policy Principles of Data Science Visual Data Analytics
recommended_courses: If you already have some experience with machine learning, then you might be disappointed with Principles of Data Science. In the beginning it was way to easy (I believe to introduce people with no former experience to quantitative methods to the subject), and then later you will work a new algorithm or approach every week. This was fine, but because the unit is pretty demanding in terms of assignments during the unit, I found myself not focusing enough of on the weekly material (where I would have gained more relevant knowledge) and too much on the group assignments. If you are looking for a very easy low demanding unit, Visual Data Analytics is a good choice. Chinese Politics was interesting and the teacher good, and you do not need to know much of this area beforehand. Issues in Public Policy was difficult when you do not know a lot about Australian politics and history, but nonetheless an interesting look into this and also cases broader than just Australia. This unit was very much case driven.
unexpected_costs: Food (grocery shopping) and gym was super expensive.
cost_comparison: Eating out and public transport was a bit cheaper than expected.
activities_available: Everything you can think of... Many sports you could do on campus: climbing/bouldering, football, swimming, archery, volleyball, fitness, fitness classes, self defense. Many social, academic, religious clubs as well.
activities_recommended: For free you can attend a spors tournament between faculties, each week a new sport. You sign up though you faculty's facebook page.
weekend_recommendations: Many things going on the city you can do like concerts, sport events and such. Also enjoy the nature and beaches.
culture_adjustment: Easy. Most students on master level are international students. In general, it is easy to find friends and people to talk to. More difficult to find deeper connections, which I found more difficult to establish with non-scandinavians. I think this is a cultural difference.
socializing_tips: Attend social events or even just chat up someone around campus. People are very openminded like that. I found made a friend just by sitting next to him in the library.
cultural_challenges: The greeting of "how are you" lol. You are not supposed to actually answer, I ended up just trying to say it before the other person.
culture_appreciated: Openness and outdoor.
top3_advice: 1. Get your hands on the (secret) list of actual availlable units before deciding on this uni. 2. Prepare yourself for debt (SU-loan, maybe) unless you have a good savings account 3. Research areas to live in and the whole housing situation
other_useful_info: One heads up might be group work. Almost all exchange students I knew endured som bad experiences, where group members would slack and not contribute. I believe this is due to the workload in terms of assignments during the semester and the pressure some students feel for obtaining good grades. I had two groups, one which was great (apart from a non-trivial language barrier (they were Chinese), and another with was the worst group experience I ever had. Therefore, be aware of this issue early in a project, so you can address the situation accordingly. Also, if you take classes at the Business School and Computer Science, you might experience to be the only non-Chinese student in your class. This is because very few Australians get a master and Australia receives many Asian and specifically Chinese international students.
most_rewarding: Living a new place and gaining new friends and experiences. Not having all the commitments as back home gave a lot freedom.
greatest_challenge: Striking the right balance between studying and having a good time.

registration_advice: Play around with your schedule and move tutorials! I was able to create a schedule without to many holes and days that were fully off because I spent quite a lot of time moving stuff around.
course_level: Mostly took first year courses as I wanted to do something different from my degree. Would recommend, definitely also helped with the workload not being as intense later in the semester.
teaching_comparison: Shorter lectures accompanied by tutorials. Was definitely challenged by the workload, as I am used to one big final exam at the end, but at USYD the workload is spread across the semester in smaller assignments and presentations. Just something to get used to, and quite nice that your final assignment at the end of the semester won't determine your whole grade.
courses_enrolled: ARHT1001: Style and Substance: Introducing Art History FILM2002: Film Genre, Genre Film GCST1601: Culture, Power, Identity INDG1001: Introduction to Indigenous Cultures
recommended_courses: "INDG1001: Introduction to Indigenous Cultures" is very uniquely Australian and teaches you a lot about important Aboriginal history and culture. Very vital in my understanding of Australian society. Art history was also very fun and educational, great lecturers.
unexpected_costs: Hostel stay for the first few weeks before finding accomodation.
cost_comparison: Get a concession card for Opal (public transport)!!! Will cut down public transport costs in half. Food and groceries are generally slightly cheaper. Also almost all museums are free, take advantage of that. Housing is generally pretty expensive.
activities_available: Clubs. A few events the first couple of weeks, good way to meet especially other international students.
activities_recommended: Film society! Very much recommended, on every week and everyone is chatty. Made many friends there. Also go on the free USU day trips, good way to meet people and cool trips (for free).
weekend_recommendations: Go on many foreshore walks! Close to Sydney is Blue Mountains, very cool nature. Take the train to Kiama + Wollongong to see something out of Sydney. For longer breaks, go to Tasmania! Very different vibe and cool nature.
culture_adjustment: Easy. Slang is weird, but aussies are more than happy to explain.
socializing_tips: Talk to people in class! Other students are also just trying to make friends, and it's really nice to have a buddy in class. Join societies and clubs! Even if it's not fully your thing, just go for the first few weeks to meet people.
cultural_challenges: Students are generally quite young when starting uni in Australia, so if you're older than 20, you might be the oldest in your class. Nothing to do about it, so just be prepared to hang out with some teenagers.
culture_appreciated: General friendliness and openness.
top3_advice: Use the paid version of flatmates to get more responses. Go on hikes and appreciate the cool nature and beaches. Talk to people! Aussies are generally very friendly and curious on people from other countries, so don't be afraid to just go up to someone and chat. You're on a different continent, so who cares if it's a little embarrassing!
other_useful_info: WEAR SUNSCREEN! No ozone layer in Australia, so get SPF 50, and don't bother bringing anything from home.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and getting a routine on the other side of the world. Travelling to new places in Australia and seeing incredible nature.
greatest_challenge: Going home and leaving your new friends behind :( Also getting used to a different academic system, but you'll manage!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to improve my english, and I wanted to go far away. Furthermore I didn't know too much about Australia, so I thought it'd be a great opportunity to learn and see a lot of new things. I choose Sydney, because I wanted to live in a big city.
info_ease: Easy. There's lots of numbers to call, but I didn't remember needing them.
arrival_assistance: University of Sydney provided a free pickup from the airport to my accomodation, and that was great.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Easy enough. However, sometimes quite a long waiting time to get a reply over mail from my Study Abroad Adviser, but the answers were always very detailed and helpful.
registration_help: There was numbers to call, sometimes I called someone wrong, but then I was referred. Also mailing my Study Abroad Adviser from USYD.
registration_success: I got registered in the classes that I wanted to take - except for one class because of a prerequisite that I didn't fulfill, but then I just applied for another unit, which was easy enough.
registration_advice: Read the mails carefully and get your stuff done before the deadlines.
course_level: I was doing my 5th semester abroad, where I did three 2nd year units and one 1st year unit.
teaching_comparison: Less self studying abroad, they are very thorough with explaining concepts and you get a lot of practice by doing the tutorials.
courses_enrolled: AREC2005, MATH2023, FINC2011, QBUS1040
recommended_courses: AREC2005 was interesting (and easy to pass). You learn some Python in QBUS1040, and they hold your hand all the way.
unexpected_costs: Experiences are more expensive than what I first imagined, and alcohol is super expensive (200DKK for the cheapest bottle of vodka 70cl)
cost_comparison: Alcohol and parties were more expensive, transportation was less expensive. I didnt have to buy books, which was also a pleasant surprise.
activities_available: So so many, like more than 200 clubs.
activities_recommended: Anything tbh, just try some new stuff out that'll challenge you (but dont beat yourself up if you end up going less than expected)
weekend_recommendations: Blue mountains, beaches. Just nature stuff in general. Do trips with friends or solo and enjoy.
culture_adjustment: Easy enough, like 8/10 easiness.
socializing_tips: Just go and talk to them, sit next to someone you think looks local in class.
cultural_challenges: Australians wake up super early and party early and cafe's arent open in the afternoon.
culture_appreciated: The beach life, the chill vibe. The shortenings are also funny.
top3_advice: Try to join a club. Don't be afraid to sit next to someone in class. Don't be afraid to ask for help.
other_useful_info: Hmm, ABS cafeteria has lunch for 6 bucks if you have the USYD app (hopefully also when you get there, but at least when I was there). Lectures are almost always recorded and most units doesn't take attendance, but check for every single unit.
most_rewarding: Meeting the people I met and the trips I went on (e.g. in midsem break)
greatest_challenge: Accepting that there's things in Denmark I'll miss out on. And finding the sweet spot to how much I should study vs free time.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an english speaking country with similar cultural values as to Denmark.
info_ease: It was pretty easy. There was a lot of information, maybe a little to much (i gor a bit overwelmed by the amount).
arrival_assistance: There was a meeting with our study abroad adviser at USYD.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There were not certain time lots given for course (on their course website) so it was a bit confusing when I had to choose them. There are alot of time lots for the course so there is a possibility of overlapping classes.
registration_help: Whenever I had any questions I could write to my study abroad adviser.
registration_success: I got the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Chose the classes that you find interesting, both relevant to your degree or not.
course_level: The course were at a similar level as in Denmark or easier.
teaching_comparison: At UCPH I have fewer lectures, more laboratory and more theoratical exercises than I had at USYD.
courses_enrolled: Computational chemistry. Proteins in cells. Chemistry of biology chemistry. Molecular self assembly.
recommended_courses: I would recommend all my course (maybe not Proteins in cells - it was pretty boring and the lecturer was pretty bad at explaining). The computational chemistry course was the biggest surprise to me - I expected it to be the hardest (as an organic chemist), but it turned out to be my favorite course.
unexpected_costs: Allthough you have health insurance - you will still have to pay to see a doctor (it is cheap though and you may get reimbursed by your insurance.)
cost_comparison: The expenses in Australia is pretty similar to the expenses in Denmark. The public transportation is way CHEAP compared to in Denmark. Mealplan was included with my accomodation.
activities_available: USYD have several gyms, cultural clubs and sport clubs. You could sign up for the chocolate club or play quidditch.
activities_recommended: Go to the beach, swim/surf and go for a pint.
weekend_recommendations: Go explore as much of Australia as you can. It is a very big country with lovely diverse nature. Go to the beach, for a pint or to a concert. I spent Christmas and New years in Australia - it was very different, but lovely.
culture_adjustment: The australian culture is very similar to danish culture. Australians are very freindly, warm and welcoming. We have similar humor and drinking culture, so it is easy to get along with and make australian friends. They find danes exotic.
socializing_tips: Go for a beer, to the student bar or for a consert.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find big cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: They are openminded, warm and friendly.
top3_advice: Enjoy your stay - it is going to be over in no time. It will be challenging live so far from Denmark, but it is easier than you might think. It is a bit nerve wrecking meeting new people so far from home, but you will make friends.
other_useful_info: Talk to the local students - they will have great recomendations on what to see and do. They will no the best place to go for a beer.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and making new friends.
greatest_challenge: The time difference of 10 hours was the biggest challenge, when I wanted to talk to friends and family at home.

crucial_aspects: It was important to me that the host university had a high academic ranking. Furthermore, it was crucial that the destination was a country that I hadn't visited before.
info_ease: It was quite easy to find the needed information about the university and the courses. However, it was quite difficult to obtain information about finding
arrival_assistance: In relation to information about courses, timetables, exams and other information regarding the semester, USYD provided a lot of guidance and held several orientation events during the first weeks.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process took a lot of time but it was fairly easy as USYD's exchange counselor provided a lot of guidance and sent several reminders regarding deadlines etc.
registration_help: USYD's exchange counselor, Jane Andrews, was able to answer all questions regarding registration.
registration_success: I applied for eight different classes. I was eventually offered five of them.
registration_advice: Begin the registration proces as soon as possible as it takes a lot of time.
course_level: My four courses were exciting but quite difficult. The coursework was quite heavy and it took a lot of effort to understand the basics of Common Law. Furthermore, two of my courses (Corporations Law and Evidence Law) were mandatory for domestic postgraduate students and, therefore, the courses built upon the knowledge that the domestic students had obtained in previous courses.
teaching_comparison: It was more or less the same. USYD had, however, introduced a 70 % attendance requirement.
courses_enrolled: International Commercial Arbitration. IP: Copyright and Designs. Corporations Law. Evidence Law.
recommended_courses: International Commercial Arbitration. Professor Chester Brown is a top-level lecturer and he has a lot of practical experience with arbitration. Furthermore, the relevance of the course is not limited to Australia.
unexpected_costs: The cost of the Student Visa is around 3.000 DKK
cost_comparison: Housing in Sydney is more expensive than in Copenhagen
activities_available: USU (University of Sydney Union) hosts a lot of events during the semester. Everything from concerts to food markets.
activities_recommended: Attend as many social events on campus as possible as it is a great opportunity to get to know your peers.
weekend_recommendations: Explore Sydney. For longer trips, go to The Blue Mountains and Royal National Park.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. Despite the location on the other side of the planet, Sydney seems very European.
socializing_tips: Reach out to the local students during class.
cultural_challenges: Be prepared for a lot of small talk due to the common "How are you doing?" every time you meet someone.
culture_appreciated: People in Sydney are very friendly and open-minded.
top3_advice: Explore Australia as much as possible both before, during and after the semester. Save up a lot of money - you will undoubtedly spend a lot of money. Be completely sure before accepting the courses that you're offered - it will be close to impossible to change them after the semester has started.
other_useful_info: Avoid courses that are mandatory for domestic students. You will lack a lot of the prerequisites needed (especially the understanding of Common Law).
most_rewarding: Living in Sydney for almost five months is one of the greatest experiences I've ever had.
greatest_challenge: The coursework

crucial_aspects: It was crucial for me to choose a destination where english was the native language in order to improve my English. Other than that I wanted to experience a university which ranked higher than UCPH. However, the main reason that I prioritized USYD over for example Singapore were the opportunities to experience the unique nature in Australia during my exchange.
info_ease: It was pretty easy to find information that I needed upon arrival. USYD sent out a lot of e-mails in the months preceding my arrival containing basically everything I needed to know for the first few weeks of being there. It was almost bordering on too much since it also covered basic stuff like remember to have your boarding passes printed for boarding the plane etc. There were also study abroad advisers from USYD that were available to answer any possible questions.
arrival_assistance: There were several introductory "lectures" that could be attended even before the official orientation week started to learn about life in Sydney/Australia with information concerning shopping, banking, public transport use etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You receive a list of courses available for selection, you select the ones you want and after that you receive a list of which courses you were approved for/had space and then from that list you select four courses that you wish to attend.
registration_help: There is a study abroad adviser that you can email with questions regarding the process.
registration_success: There was only one class that I didn't get even though I selected it as there weren't any more slots in the class. Apart from that I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Remember to look at the exams. Some classes have 80 minute pen and paper exams which makes it difficult if you have terrible handwriting (like me).
course_level: The level was about the same as at UCPH, however, it is made more difficult as you (presumably) arrive without a common law background and no knowledge of the Australian legal system and how their federal and state legislation interact with each other.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was pretty similar to UCPH with a mix between lectures and classes wherein student participation was expected. However, there is more work spread out through the entire semester.
courses_enrolled: LAWS5143 Interpretation LAWS5151 Media Law: Contempt and Open Justice LAWS5180 IP: Copyright and Designs LAWS5183 War Law: Use of Force and Humanitarian Law
recommended_courses: I would recommend War Law. The subject matter is really interesting and the lecturer is incredibly knowledgeable and passionate about the field. The context in which law is used is also very different from any other course I've ever had.
unexpected_costs: I didn't really run into any unexpected costs, however, I did spend more money on travelling around Australia than I was expecting. Completely worth it though!
cost_comparison: Groceries were actually more expensive than I expected. Coffee was less expensive (thankfully).
activities_available: There were a lot of activities available to students. At the beginning of the semester there is a big welcome fest in which all the clubs at the univeristy set up a booth to promote their club. These clubs basically cover every interest imaginable from bible study to anime to Taylor Swift to food. There are also two gyms on campus that it is possible to sign up for which includes access to a climbing center, swimming pool etc. There are also a lot of political rallies on campus that it is possible to attend.
activities_recommended: Personally I didn't join any of the clubs but I travelled as often as possible. I would definitely recommend travelling around Australia whenever possible. It is an amazing country!
weekend_recommendations: If it is just a day trip then going to the Blue Mountains two hours away from Sydney is amazing. There is a hike called the Grand Canyon walk which is beautiful. During the springbreak I did a roadtrip on the east coast which was amazing. I'd definitely recommend doing a roadtrip like that to see the Daintree Rainforest, the Great Barrier Reef, Magnetic Island and more. The sights and nature there is simply amazing. I'd also reommend visiting Tasmania if you get the time. The people down there are very welcoming and has some of the most beautiful hikes.
culture_adjustment: Incredibly easy. I didn't really run into any problems.
cultural_challenges: I didn't really run into any cultural differences that I found challenging.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated the openness of Australians. People very very nice and welcoming.
top3_advice: 1. Find housing through USYD 2. Remember to look at what kind of exams the different classes have 3. Remember to enjoy your time. Time passes by quickly
other_useful_info: The workload is spread out over the entire semester instead of being focused on a few weeks of exams. Also be aware that certain clashes can occur with exams as you may have two short term exams on top of each other. I ended up with a three-day and a weeklong written exam that both had the same due date.
most_rewarding: Meeting fellow exchange students and the entire experience of living in a new country and city.
greatest_challenge: Finding housing in the beginning.

cultural_challenges: Maybe that stores close quite early compared to at home. Australia also have many strange rules and regulations that can be quite difficult to understand sometimes.
culture_appreciated: The relaxed lifestyle.

greatest_challenge: Being far away from friends and family.
other_comments: If anyone is wondering whether they should go on exchange - just do it! It is the most amazing, rewarding, and challenging thing that a student can do, and it will change your life. :-)

crucial_aspects: As a highly ambitious student with a strong interest in small animal emergency and intensive care, I wanted an exchange destination that would provide advanced clinical experience in a high-standard teaching hospital. The University of Sydney was ideal because of its well-structured clinical rotations, access to specialized services, and exposure to unique aspects of veterinary medicine, such as Australian wildlife. Additionally, its reputation for hands-on learning and student involvement in patient care made it a perfect fit for my career goals.
info_ease: It was not easy. Information was scattered across different platforms, and I had to reach out to various contacts to get clarity on administrative procedures, schedules, and logistics. A more centralized and comprehensive guide for incoming exchange students would have been helpful.
arrival_assistance: I received great assistance from the staff at Camden campus, especially from Debbie Sheehan, who was incredibly helpful in guiding me through the process. However, I received less assistance from staff at Camperdown campus, and I had to figure out many things on my own.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Everything was ready for me upon arrival, so no additional registration at the university was needed. I received my name badge at the student support office at the Camperdown campus and my access card during orientation day at the small animal hospital.
registration_help: The student support office had staff available to assist with administrative questions, and I could also get help over email with fast response times.
registration_success: The process went very smoothly, and I got into the courses I wanted. However, I did not get them in my preferred order. Instead, I was placed in a single study group for the duration of my rotations rather than changing groups every two weeks. This turned out to be beneficial, as it allowed me to build stronger connections with my group and settle into a routine.
registration_advice: Make sure to inform the university of your arrival date well in advance so they can prepare your name badge and access card ahead of time. This will help streamline your first few days on campus.
course_level: The courses were at the master’s level and consisted of clinical rotations at the university teaching hospital under the guidance of senior veterinarians. The training was intensive and hands-on, providing valuable experience in real patient cases.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was more interactive, and students were given more responsibility, which significantly boosted our confidence. We were trusted to make clinical decisions under supervision and had a more active role in patient care. Additionally, spending two weeks on each service (instead of shorter rotations) gave us enough time to become comfortable with the workflow and fully absorb what we were learning.
courses_enrolled: - Wildlife Medicine - Surgery - Anaesthesia - Referral Medicine - Emergency and Critical Care - Primary Care
recommended_courses: I highly recommend: Wildlife Medicine – This is a unique opportunity to work with Australian wildlife, something we don’t get much exposure to in Denmark. It is incredibly rewarding and a rare experience for European veterinary students. Referral Medicine – The senior veterinarians in this rotation are outstanding teachers, and the cases are complex and challenging, requiring critical thinking and research.
unexpected_costs: - My computer broke and I had to get it repaired for 2500 DKK - Vaccination against Q-fever is mandatory for every veterinary student in Australia. That was another 1500 DKK expense
cost_comparison: Accommodation was slightly more expensive. Otherwise fairly similar to Denmark
activities_available: Unfortunately, there were no organized cultural, athletic, or social activities specifically for exchange students in veterinary medicine.
weekend_recommendations: I highly recommend traveling along the east coast of Australia before or after the exchange. I personally visited Noosa and Fraser Island and had an amazing experience. Since Australia is so far away, it’s worth taking the time to explore the country while you're there.
culture_adjustment: Very easy! My Australian classmates were incredibly warm and welcoming, making the transition smooth.
socializing_tips: The students have been studying together for over six years, so their friend groups are well-established. However, they are very friendly and welcoming if you take the initiative. Be outgoing—don’t hesitate to ask if you can join them for lunch, drinks, or dinner after school. They will always say yes!
cultural_challenges: I noticed a significant difference in the approach to treating animals with severe diseases. In Australia, there is a stronger inclination to pursue advanced diagnostics and treatments, even in cases where euthanasia might be a more common decision in Denmark. This was interesting to observe and made me reflect on different perspectives in veterinary medicine.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated the active lifestyle in Australia. People make the most of nature, spending time at the beach, in the forest, or doing outdoor activities whenever they get the chance. The culture of waking up early and starting the day with exercise or time outdoors was something I really enjoyed.
top3_advice: Start planning early! I started planning my exchange almost two years in advance, and it really helped me secure funding, housing, and my preferred courses. Find accommodation close to the university. The hours at the hospital are long, and Sydney is a massive city—commuting for hours every day can be exhausting. Living nearby will save you valuable time and energy. Make time to enjoy Australia! The veterinary courses at USYD are demanding, both mentally and physically. It’s easy to get completely absorbed in school, but don’t forget to take breaks. Plan your weekends and explore—you’re in one of the most beautiful countries in the world!
other_useful_info: Be aware that you need to buy all your own clinical scrubs. Each rotation has different clothing requirements, so instead of buying everything new, I recommend buying second-hand from older students. There’s a Facebook group where students sell their used scrubs, which is a great way to save money and avoid unnecessary purchases.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding aspects were: The friendships I made—I met incredible people and built lifelong friendships. Expanding my professional network—I had the opportunity to work with highly skilled senior veterinarians and gained valuable contacts for my future career. The immense learning experience—both theoretically and practically, I have grown so much as a future veterinarian.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge was the long and exhausting hours at the hospital. Some days were 10–12 hours long, with a constant high patient flow and no real breaks. It was an adjustment to work at that intensity, but in the end, it helped me develop resilience and time management skills.

info_ease: The exchange university was extremely helpful, so I was able to e-mail them when I had any question.
arrival_assistance: I hadn't recieved a welcome email from the university hopsital upon my arrival, but shortly after emailing the medical school I heard from them right away.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

registration_success: I didn't attend classes, but were at a clinical elective at three different departments of my own choosing.

teaching_comparison: A bit less independent work at the hospital compared to when you attend a clinical elective in Denmark, but is was mainly due to them having a totally different IT-system and way of rounding the patients.
courses_enrolled: Clinical elective at three different departments, 1 month at each department.
recommended_courses: Not relevant.
unexpected_costs: Some unexpected costs in relation to my student visa application.
cost_comparison: Groceries were a bit more expensive than in Denmark, but eating out were cheaper than excected.
activities_available: Not relevant.
activities_recommended: Not relevant, since I didn't spent time at the university itself, only the hospital.
weekend_recommendations: Spent as much time as possible exploring both Sydney but also north and south of Sydney. There are many beautiful national parks only a short car- or train-ride away. Also do take longer trips around Australia, you might as well when you've travelled that far. My biggest recommendation is going for a trip to the Northern Territory to visit the Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, the Australian people is very open and friendly.
cultural_challenges: There's nothing that challenging coming to mind.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness, the humor and slight sarcasm, and the melting of many different cultures into one.
top3_advice: Use the helpful student counselors at USYD, make sure to engage socially, and throw yourself into speaking English - I promise you that your English academic vocabulary will enhance greatly.

most_rewarding: The independence and assertiveness I gained along during my stay.
greatest_challenge: The first days where you were completely alone in a new big city.

housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_process: They need a lot of information as your transcript of records, photo of yourself, your intended units (not binding and you have about 1-2 weeks to change your mind). If your grades are a bit lower you need a roof of English proficiency
registration_help: Yes, you could contact the uni if you had any questions.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Look into if there are exams (not all courses have that) and look at the schedule (when they are released) as you are not allowed to have clashing classes.
academics_comments: It was very good, the begninning was very confusing because they are not used to accepting pharmacy students from Copenhagen University, so you got a lot of different information.
course_level: The BA level of pharmacy classes were quite easy. A lot of the syllabus were things that we had already covered in the classes at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Yeah, a mix of lecures, labs and classes were you solved tasks.
courses_enrolled: 1. Bachelor Thesis (Pharmacy Honours) 2. Outdoor Education 3. Drug Design and Development
recommended_courses: Outdoor Education. It is a class that a lot of exchange students do. It is chill and you meet a lot of cool people from around the world.
unexpected_costs: Visa, Non-refundable acceptance fee (accomondation) and student services and amenities fee.
cost_comparison: Transport and food (was cheaper than my offical budget which I listed here).
activities_available: Almost everything you can imagine. They had over 200 student clubs.
activities_recommended: Hiking, surfing, wakeboarding, food society and if you wanna learn about another culture then you can also join their society.
weekend_recommendations: Go around and travel as much as you can. See as much of Australia as you can cause it is truly a beautiful country. Everything from Western Australia, Uluru, Tasmania, East Coast and much more. Also a lot of things to do around Sydney (and many beaches)
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Start talking to them from the first class. People here are very welcoming and are happy to include you.
cultural_challenges: A lot of small talk and you have to get used to the dialect haha.
culture_appreciated: The diversity from the Aboriginals to the Australians.
top3_advice: Bring sunscreen (UV here is dangerous). Be open to meet people from other cultures. Remember to take time for yourself to recharge.
other_useful_info: Sydney is an expensive city, escpecially things like alcohol cost a lot. But honestly a great experience, and the city is wonderful. You will quickly meet other students who shares your passions.
most_rewarding: Meeting so many people from so many different cultures. Really got a good friend group who showed me different perspectives.
greatest_challenge: That people will challenge your beliefs and your viewpoints. Sometimes it can feel annoying but just embace it.

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne til et engelsktalende land, hvor der var mulighed for at møde mange forskellige typer mennesker, samt mulighed for at rejse og gå på opdagelse. Samtidig findes der rigtig mange utroligt gode universiteter i Australien.
info_ease: Mit værtsuniversitet var gode til at sende (meget) lange e-mails med alt information, jeg skulle bruge. Dog synes jeg mails mv. kom meget sent ift. deadlines (ofte fik man ikke mere end et par dage til at reagere) og én enkelte gang kom e-mailen efter deadline...
arrival_assistance: University of Sydney var gode til at have en hel uge af introarragementer mv. Der var også mulighed for at få gratis transport fra lufthavnen ved ankomst - bare vid at det tager ca. 2 timer, hvor du bare venter :')
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Man kan ønske op til 8-10 kurser. Det er ikke alt man kan deltage i som udvekslingsstudent og universitets egne studerende har første valg desværre.
registration_help: Intet: Man skal undersøge på USyds hjemmeside - søg på units og find hvert kursus' Outline. De tilsender et excelark med de kurser som vi kan tage.
registration_success: Jeg fik dem jeg ville have, men desværre lå undervisning i to af mine fag oveni hinanden, så jeg blev nødt til at skifte. (Man skal komme til 70% af alt undervisning, så det er umuligt at have to fag på samme tid)
registration_advice: Ønsk så mange fag som muligt så du har bedre muligheder for at skifte. Vær fleksibel.
course_level: Mine kurser var 5000-level (de blev dog også udbudt som hhv. 2000-level og 3000-level (BA-niveau))
teaching_comparison: Undervisningen minder utroligt meget om vores forelæsninger.
courses_enrolled: Conflicts of Law Criminology War Law The Rule of Law and its Value
recommended_courses: Criminology War Law Conflicts of Law forudsætter et rimeligt godt kendskab til Australsk lovgivning og kan derfor være vanskeligt til tider The Rule of Law and its Value (med Michael Sevel) var utroligt kedeligt. Vi nåede aldrig pensum igennem, fordi han altid kom ud på sidespor, han havde ingen powerpoint og snakkede bare løst i 2 timer eller viste YT-videoer.
unexpected_costs: Visum til Australien er virkelig dyrt (1.600 AUD). Jeg rejste desuden en del undervejs/efter hvilket var dyrt og ikke medregnet her.
cost_comparison: Internet/telefoni er billigt (selv med adgang til at ringe til DK). Offentlig transport og taxi er også billigere end Danmark. Jeg brugte ingen penge på at købe bøger, da universitet gav gratis online adgang.
activities_available: Alt næsten. Der var klubber for alle interesser - både faglige, kulturelle og sportslige. Det var rimelig dyrt at melde sig ind i det egentlige universitets sportscenter, men klubber var ikke dyre i sig selv (ca. $5 for et semester)
activities_recommended: Kom til alle introarrangementer som universitetet tilbyder. USU (den største forening) har rigtig mange gode tilbud og event.
weekend_recommendations: Jeg brugte meget tid på at rejse (inkl. weekend ture) Jeg kan anbefale: Længere ture - Tasmanien - Western Australien (særligt Exmouth og Broome) - Uluru og Darwin - At køre fra Cairns til Brisbane - Fiji Weekendture: - Jervis Bay - Newcastle - Hunter Valley - Blue Mountains
culture_adjustment: Utroligt let. Australierne er imødekommende men meget svære at blive venner med (de er meget overfladiske i deres interraktioner - tænk ligesom amerikanere) Kulturen er ikke ulig den danske. Jeg tror bedst den kan beskrives som en blanding af britisk og amerikansk kultur.
socializing_tips: Mød op i de forskellige klubber og foreninger. Hvis du virkelig mener det, så skal du selv være meget proaktiv. Ellers prøv en datingapp ;)
cultural_challenges: Det kan være hårdt at være væk fra sine venner og familie. Mange fik hjemve undervejs. Det er helt normalt. Det er desuden utrolig trættende de først ca. 2-3 uger ift. at tilpasse sig kulturen og sproget. Du kommer til at være meget træt konstant.
culture_appreciated: Som sagt - de er virkelig imødekommende, venlige og snakkesaglige (især uden for byerne) Australierne er altid klar til at hjælpe. De er desuden (mere end i danmark) klar til at folk er mangfoldige. De er vandt til internationale studerende, immigranter og minoriteter.
top3_advice: Spar op: Det er et dyrt land. Vær klar til at presse dig selv lidt ud af din komfortzone. Man bliver nødt til at være proaktiv for at få venner Glem skolen: Det er ikke lige så vigtigt at studeret. Prioritet at tage på udflugt fremfor at skrive et essay. Eller kommer du til at fortryde det.
other_useful_info: *Vær komfortabel i dit eget selskab!* - Det bedste råd jeg fik. Man kan hurtigt få FOMO, men nogle gange går kalenderen bare ikke op, og så må man være klar på selv at lave noget.
most_rewarding: De venskaber jeg fik. Jeg er blevet et mere tolerant og tålmodigt menneske. Jeg er blevet mere selvstændig og selvsikker.
greatest_challenge: Det kan føles som om man skal nå det hele og man bliver virkelig hurtigt stresset. Accepter at man ikke kan nå det hele og sæt realistiske forventninger til dig selv og dit ophold.

greatest_challenge: only the first day, when I didn't know what to do.

crucial_aspects: I studied at the University of Sydney (USYD) during my final semester of Bachelor's degree in Pharmacy. My previous travels to Australia during my gap year between High School and University left an immense impact on me and made me safe assured in choosing USYD as my top priority over the other options: Dublin University, Bath University, and Zürich University. Career opportunities were also an important factor in my decision.
overall_comments: Overall a great study experience
info_ease: The international study coordinators at USYD were extremely helpful - big thanks to them! However, the digital platforms, particularly the timetable system, could be more improved by making it more user-friendly and compliant.
arrival_assistance: I recived help with setting up my time table to include my preferred units of study as well as finding the most suitable timeslots.
arrival_comments: Very good!
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Overall a great study experience
registration_process: 1) Students receive a USYD student ID number, which is required to create their University of Sydney application account online. 2) The application must include personal details such as full name, address, academic background, and other relevant information. 3) Applicants must apply for an approved visa—specifically, the Student Visa (subclass 500)—through the Australian Government’s Department of Home Affairs. 4) Proof of sufficient English proficiency is required, such as a high school diploma (if applicable) or results from an approved English test like the TOEFL iBT. 5) Applicants must also obtain Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC), a mandatory health insurance for international students in Australia.
registration_help: Suppor during the application process was limited, so I relied on advice from students who had previously gone through it to help guide me.
registration_success: My application was very successful, and I was able to enroll in all the classes I had hoped for
registration_advice: Do your best to complete the application on your own, and don’t hesitate to seek help if anything is unclear
academics_comments: Overall a great study experience
course_level: The courses were generally on the same academic level as UCPH. However, the workload, measured in hours spent on studying, were noticable lighter at USYD.
teaching_comparison: Significantly less time was spent on laboratory work and report writing at USYD compared to UCPH. Aside from that, most aspects of the coursework were quite similar.
courses_enrolled: EDUH4052 Learning in Outdoor Education, PCOL3012 Drug Design and Development, and PHAR4815 Research Methods
recommended_courses: EDUH4052 Learning in Outdoor Education: This unit offers a unique opportunity to explore the diverse Australian landscapes in New South Wales alongside other international students. Designed specifically for exchange students, the course provides a great chance to connect with fellow participants while engaging in outdoor learning experiences.
unexpected_costs: Student Visa 500: 7,264 DKK OSCH health cover: 1,812 DKK English ToEfl iBT: 2,000 DKK
cost_comparison: Student Visa (2x the expected)
activities_available: There’s a wide range of societies and social clubs - too many to count! No matter your interests, there’s something for everyone.
activities_recommended: Surf Society: A fun and energetic group known for great vibes both in the water and at their legendary parties. They are known for their yearly surfcamp/party! Bouldering Society: A lively and active club that explores a variety of climbing gyms and bouldering centers across Sydney. Unofficial Run Club x Fishbowl Sydney: One of Sydney’s best run clubs, offering scenic runs and a strong community vibe—conveniently based near Bondi Junction.
weekend_recommendations: Go travelling! Australia is a great country to travel in. It's almost to big. I would personally reccomend the following: Sydney: - ALL the beaches (Manly, Shelly, Coogee, Bronte, Bondi, etc.) - Blue Mountains - Glebe or Paddington markets (Saturday) - Taronga Zoo - Watching Aussie Footy (Australian Football) Melbourne: - Great Ocean Road and The 12 Apostels - Philip Island and Pingvin parade - Shopping and café tours Other places to go... - Byron Bay - Fraiser Island - Magnetic Island - Whitsundays Islands - Great Barrier Reef (Cairns)
culture_adjustment: Expect to spend about a month settling in and adjusting to the new environment.
socializing_tips: Try to join as many events as possible at the beginning of the semester - there is many to choose from, and it’s a great way to meet new people. With so many students at USYD, it can feel overwhelming, so focus on finding a smaller group of friends you really connect with. Spend time together doing simple things like cooking, going on trips, or watching sports and movies. It makes the experience much more enjoyable and grounded.
cultural_challenges: Studying at USYD requires a high level of independence. You need to manage your time effectively to stay on top of your coursework and fully participate in classes.
culture_appreciated: The fun and laid-back Australian lifestyle is something special:)
top3_advice: 1) Make an effort to meet as many new people as you can 2) Stay open-minded and embrace the diversity of different cultural backgrounds 3) Be inclusive and kind - everyone deserves to feel welcome when being on exchange far from home
other_useful_info: Share your knowledge across borders and support both international and domestic students with academically challenging tasks. At UCPH, we have a strong foundation in pharmaceutical sciences and it's worth sharing!
most_rewarding: Learning more about my field of study (Pharmacy), while learning other culturally different backgrounds
greatest_challenge: Being independent and establish a network of new friends far from Denmark.
other_comments: Enjoy your stay at USYD!

crucial_aspects: That the main language was english and that it was a city i wanted to live in and explore.
info_ease: Very easy, the contact person was very good at providing thorough information and guides.
arrival_assistance: Once I arrived we still recieved some emails from the contact person, and on the first day there were orientation were a lot of information was given as well as ressources to use for help during our stay.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You get a login to a website where you list the units you wish to undertake (list 10, but you will only enrol in 4) and these are then approved or denied by the department depending on if you have the prerequisites. Then you choose the 4 you wish to take and a few weeks before school starts you can state preferences for your timetable. It is possible to change the chosen units before school starts and during the first few weeks.
registration_help: The contact person sent emails with guides on how to do everything and was available for questions, so it was not difficult to do.
registration_success: I was approved for 8/10 of the ones I listed so I could easily choose 4 and also managed to change a unit during the orientation week with no issue.
registration_advice: Take your time and follow the guide. Spend time early to make a list of the subjects that you might be interested in so this can be narrowed down as opposed to only having 4 and then scrambling to finde others if it doesn't work out.
course_level: I took two 2000 level courses (2nd year), and two 3000 level courses (3rd year).
teaching_comparison: The exam is only worth around 50% of the grade and the rest comes from assignments, reports and quizzes during the semester so you have work to do, and this is often group work. Some units have no exam and so the grade is based entirely on what you do during the semester. I had no books and very little assigned reading compared to KU.
courses_enrolled: Australian Wildlife Biology Biology Experimental Design and Analysis Beyond the Genome International Health
recommended_courses: I enjoyed Australian Wildlife Biology as it was very informative and we got to go to the zoo 5 times as part of the teachings. Many other exchange students took it and so it was not expected that you had any previous knowledge on animals or biology.
unexpected_costs: There were some fees for the accommodation as well as a deposit of around a months rent which I had not budgeted with
cost_comparison: The visa was more expensive that i thought it was around 3500 DKK but transportation was very cheap and a trip with bus usually only costed around 5 DKK
activities_available: There were SO many different clubs - pretty much everything you could think of.
activities_recommended: The yoga club was very good and cheaper than studios.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely do a surf camp! Blue mountains is also very nice to visit and spend a weekend in.
culture_adjustment: quite easy
cultural_challenges: Nothing was challenging, maybe the Australian accent and slang could be a bit difficult sometimes.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and helpfulness
top3_advice: Enjoy it, try and find a balance between taking some rewarding units but also some that are a bit easier so you can have more free time.
most_rewarding: The people I met during my stay and the friendships we build as well as the experiences we shared.
greatest_challenge: With the time difference you could sometimes feel a bit lonely and cut off from everyone back home, as they usually woke up when you day was almost finished.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere that had academic courses which interested me and were not offered at KU, and also somewhere with a lifestyle I thought I would enjoy
info_ease: Yes
arrival_assistance: None
arrival_comments: There was a coordinator who emailed all the international students and told us how to register for classes, dates of orientation week, how to get health insurance etc., but most things I did on my own
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Exchange students are only able to take certain courses, meaning that not every class listed online is open to exchange students. The academic coordinator sends you a big excel spreadsheet of courses and you select 6-8 which you are interested in on the registration portal and then find out whether or not you are accepted
registration_help: The academic coordinator was available when you had questions and she always responded quickly
registration_success: I got into every class I wanted
registration_advice: Just make sure that you do everything as soon as you can to make sure you have the highest chance of getting into the classes that you want because they can fill up if you wait until the last minute. Otherwise it is an easy process
course_level: All of my classes were at the MA level across different faculties
teaching_comparison: I much preferred the teaching style at University of Sydney. Classes were much more engaging and their was more out of class responsibility. We had several different assignments throughout the semester which contributed to your overall grade instead of a single grade like at KU. I found the teaching style in Sydney to be more interactive and representative.
courses_enrolled: International Relations Food and Water Security Dynamics of Human Rights Violations Population Health and Development
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the International Relations course because it was new and interesting to me and gave me a much better idea of how complex global systems are in relation to my degree (Global Health). The Human Rights course was also really interesting and we had good assignments which allowed us to be autonomous and pick a topic we were interested in while also being critical through course material
unexpected_costs: Nothing unexpected
cost_comparison: Nothing unexpected
activities_available: Probably a lot but I did not do any
activities_recommended: Finding a job definitely allows you to meet more people especially as a masters student. Helps to have some income as well
weekend_recommendations: There lots of cool road trips to do up an down the coast and just explore Australia in general
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: If you are a masters student I feel like everyone is fairly established in their life so don't expect to make a ton of friends through university. It is fairly international I just found it easier to meet people outside of university
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: Pretty laid back but still has a good city energy
top3_advice: 1. Definitely find a part time job at a bar or coffee shop etc. Important to earn some money because Sydney is not cheap but also a really good way to meet people who live in your area 2. Look for your own housing. The university options are not great but they are guaranteed and that is also an easy way to make friends. However a lot of them are bachelors students so if you are getting your masters it is a much younger crowd 3. Apply for the student Opal (transport) card as soon as possible, it will make your public transport costs way cheaper. Also do not expect to bike anywhere, it is not like Copenhagen in that way
other_useful_info: It is a different environment than Copenhagen but super easy to adjust to. I would just recommend trying to make your own life outside of the university. Live close to the beach if you can, find a cool job, and get out and explore when you're free
most_rewarding: I enjoyed my classes but I loved the job I had and the people I met through that. That is certainly the thing that made me feel the most settled
greatest_challenge: None, it was super easy
other_comments: None

cost_comparison: Eggs and beers are way more expensive than in denmark
activities_available: i joyned the bushwalkers society who go on several hiked in sydney region. Also teh yoga society

It is nothing special and far away from the beach, but it is the easiest way to meet new people!

most_rewarding: All the people I have met from all over the world.
