course_level: Jeg synes det var nogenlunde det samme som derhjemme. De fag jeg tog havde ikke meget amerikansk ret i sig så det gjorde det hele meget nemmere. Hvis jeg havde haft fag, der var med amerikansk ret havde det nok været lidt sværere at vende sig til. Mit indtryk hos de venner jeg havde, der var internationale studerende og havde fag med amerikansk ret, var at det tog dem lidt længere tid at forberede sig, men at det var til at overkomme.
teaching_comparison: Det beror meget på hvilken professor du har. Generelt bruger de cold calling i USA, hvilket flere af mine venners professorer gjorde brug af. Ingen af mine professorer gjorde dog brug af denne metode, hvilket gjorde undervisning meget lig den vi har på KU.
courses_enrolled: International Environmental Law Mediation Negotiating Disputes Into Deals Workplace Investigations LLM Legal Research, Writing, and Analysis Legal English
recommended_courses: LLM Legal Research, Writing, and Analysis og Legal English er obligatoriske. Alle de andre fag jeg tog vil jeg dog klart anbefale. Jeg må indrømme at jeg ramte plet med hver og en af dem. Jeg havde Stephen McCaffrey i International Environmental Law og han var en virkelig god professor. Undervisningen var spændende uden nogen nævneværdig workload og så var han ganske enkelt en virkelig rar person. Derfor tog jeg også til flere af hans office hours. Han er en virkelig stor og anerkendt juridisk aktør i international environmental law så han har mange spændende historier om sager, hvor han f.eks. har repræsenteret lande. Vi afsluttede faget med at tage til hans gård for at spise frokost og drikke nogle øl og vin med ham. I mediation havde jeg Fhanysha Gaddis som var super sød og venlig mod de studerende. Mediation var rimelig nemt at forstå grundet der gælder stort set samme spilleregler som i Danmark og det ikke er juridisk tungt. Undervisningen var meget interaktiv, da vi lavede mediation i små grupper i hvert seminar. Grundet vi havde professor Gaddis som underviser fik jeg også et certificat for at jeg havde bestået et mediationskursus i Californien. Det er en lille sjov gimmick at kunne sige man har gjort. I Negotiating Disputes Into Deals havde jeg Jeff Proske som professor. Det var et online kursus, hvilket gjorde det rimelig afslappet og ligetil. Det var heller ikke juridisk tungt og var derfor som international studerende et oplagt fag at tage grundet forhandlingsteknikkerne jeg lærte er universelle. Vi skulle lave virtuelle forhandlinger undervejs, hvilket var ret sjovt. Professor Proske var også helt fantastisk. Han var en virkelig rar person, så ethvert fag du kan tage med ham vil jeg mene kan anbefales. Det at have en rar professor gør rigtig meget for faget. Jeg tog til mange af hans office hours, hvor jeg også fik en del rejseråd med på vejen. Workplace Investigations var nok det fag, som jeg brugte mest forberedelsestid på. Pensum var kun ca. 110 sider, så det siger alt om hvor meget tid jeg brugte på at forberede mig generelt under mit semester. Der var flere forskellige professorer undervejs, da de er flere fra samme kontor, der deler undervisningen i faget. Alle var super søde. Faget var spændende, interaktivt og ret ligetil at tilgå som international studerende. På ingen måde juridisk tungt.
unexpected_costs: Da jeg var afsted opstod der en mulighed for mig at stå på ski i Californien. Det kostede dog en del penge at tilkøbe forsikring til det, at købe skipas og at leje udstyr. Det var dog det hele værd, skal det lige siges.
cost_comparison: At bo på hotel rundt omkring i USA følte jeg var dyrere end i Europa sammenlignet med den kvalitet man fik. Bøger var også virkelig dyre. Den eneste grund til mit budget til pensumbøger er "lavt" var pga. jeg var heldig at låne bøger fra andre.
activities_available: Der er en okay mængde foreninger på universitet som afholder arrangementer. Jeg deltog i nogle og de var ganske fine. Der er Bar Review hver torsdag, men jeg deltog kun i én, så det er begrænset hvad jeg kan sige om dette. Den ene jeg deltog i var dog ganske sjov. Mit indtryk var dog, at din deltagelse i Bar review beroede meget på hvilken vennegruppe du ender i. Der var også en lille gruppe, som spillede fodbold i løbet af semesteret og en større gruppe, der organiserede basketball kampe. Jeg begyndte at spille en del basketball i løbet af mit ophold, hvilket var ret sjovt. Derudover tog jeg også en del i fitness, som var lille og gammelt, men havde sin charme. Der er også et pool bord, som var et godt sted at møde nye mennesker og have det sjovt. I kontoret lige ved siden af var der gratis snacks og drikkelse. På hvert semester udbyder SBA også nogle rigtig gode pladser for nedsat pris til byens NBA holds, Sacramento Kings, kampe.
activities_recommended: Deltag i Bar Review som minimum i starten, idet det hjælper på at få opbygget noget socialt. Tag i fitness, da jeg mødte flere medstuderende fra mine fag der og endte med at blive gode venner med dem grundet denne fællesnævner. Køb helt sikkert en billet udbudt af SBA til en Sacramento Kings kamp, da det er alle pengene værd.
weekend_recommendations: I weekenden kan du tage til bl.a. San Francisco, Lake Tahoe, Yosemite National Park, Napa Valley, Redwood National Park. Der er virkelig mange smukke områder i nærheden og mange gode vandrestier, så du kan næsten ikke gå forkert. I dine ferie kan jeg anbefale at tage til San Diego, Hawaii, New York, New Orleans før eller under Mardi Gras, Seattle og Las Vegas.
culture_adjustment: Jeg følte det var ganske okay. Dog skal man lige vænne sig til 1) måden amerikanerne snakker på, 2) at du mere eller mindre altid starter en samtale med "how's it going"/"how are you doing" og 3) kulturen omkring drikkepenge, som jeg egentlig aldrig helt fik ind under huden.
socializing_tips: Det er dig, som skal lære folk at kende, og ikke folk der skal lære dig at kende. Amerikanere er lettere at interagere med/få en samtale op at køre med end danskere. De snakker meget gerne til fremmede uanset om det er i køen til supermarkedet eller når du er i fitness. Derfor kan jeg kun anbefale selv at være en samtalestarter og hilse på alle på din vej. Det efterlader et positivt indtryk og folk vil hurtigt huske dig, hvilket afføder venskaber og et stærkt socialt netværk.
cultural_challenges: Kulturen omkring drikkepenge - hvornår bør jeg give og hvornår bør jeg ikke - var lidt svær at finde rundt i. Derudover så har amerikanerne også et lidt andet forhold til at drikke end os, idet de i min optik - og efter min erfaring - begynder at opføre sig umodne sammenlignet med når vi danskere drikker.
culture_appreciated: At folk var gode til at hilse på hinanden, når de gik forbi hinanden, samt at amerikanerne var virkelig gode samtalestartere samt gode til at holde samtalen kørende.
top3_advice: 1) Hvis du kan, så køb en bil. Du kan altid sælge den, når semesteret er slut. Du får svært ved at komme rundt i Californien uden en bil - her taler jeg rigtig meget af egen erfaring. Plus du bliver træt af at være afhængig af andre.
other_useful_info: Jeg vil anbefale at tage til McGeorge, hvis du 1) vil opleve Californien, 2) vil opleve kulturen i USA helt generelt og 3) vil have pulsen lidt ned.
most_rewarding: At jeg lærte mig selv og USA bedre at kende samt fik opbygget venskaber på kryds og tværs i verden.
greatest_challenge: At prøve at få arrangeret ture i weekenderne. Jeg ville have været denne udfordring foruden, hvis jeg blot havde haft en bil selv.

crucial_aspects: Kultur og relevante fag.
info_ease: Meget af den information der er på deres hjemmeside kan bruges, men er nogle gange lidt svært at forstå hvordan det skal bruges. Men lige før man starter bliver der holdt nogle forskellige oplæg, hvor man får meget information.
arrival_assistance: Lige før man starter får man en masse information. Der er både en studenterforening der hjælper, og kontoret der er tilknyttet. Skriv til kontoret på UTokyo hvis man har nogle spørgsmål.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Meget lang og ret kompliceret. Man skal udfylde helt vild mange dokumenter fordi Japan ikke er særlig digitaliseret og moderniseret. Dermed overfører de ikke basal data til hinanden, og du skal dermed udfylde informationer for alle forskellige servicer og institutioner.
registration_help: Du kan læse om noget af det på hjemmesiden, men er ikke så godt. Skriv heller til UTokyo kontoret, de er meget behjælpelige og svare hurtigt.
registration_success: Jeg fik alle de fag jeg gerne ville have.
registration_advice: Det er lidt en kamp, men bliv ved og så skal det nok lykkes. Husk at være opmærksom på at du udfylder de rigtige informationer, da Japanerne ikke er så fleksible hvis du skriver noget forkert.
course_level: Københavns niveau er bedre end her, selv om de bolstre sig med at de er et af de bedste i Asien. Så bare rolig.
teaching_comparison: Der er flere oplæg og aktiv deltagelse, men det er som oftes også en del af karakteren. Man kan også godt finde fag der er mere forelæsnings orienterede.
courses_enrolled: Public Policy and Energi Policy Process and Negotiations Public Policy and Politics Energy Security International Energy Security
recommended_courses: Hvis man er interesseret i mere policy level klima og energi så tag de fag jeg tog. Ellers syntes jeg også Policy Process and Negotiations var ret godt da man lærte ret mange ting. Overordnet har jeg ikke arbejdet så meget med policy så syntes jeg havde en ret stejl læringskurve.
unexpected_costs: Hvis man gerne vil rejse rundt i Japan, og her gerne bruge Shinkansen, så regn med at bruge mange penge da det er ret så dyrt.
cost_comparison: Mad og øl. Man spiser ret meget ude da der er så mange gode steder at spise til billige penge.
activities_available: Der er rigtig mange klubber, men de er alle sammen japansk talene. Så hvis man vil være en del af dem så skal du kunne japansk.
activities_recommended: Jeg klatre ret meget, så jeg blev gode venner med nogle nede i min lokale klatreklub.
weekend_recommendations: Der er rigtig mange steder, både dagsture og weekendturer. Næsten alle steder er nice. Men tag nok op i bjergene, da det er meget rart at komme ud af byen en gang imellem.
culture_adjustment: Det er nemt nok. Du får flere passes når du ikke er japaner, men altså der er mange ting man lige skal vende sig til.
socializing_tips: Det kan godt blive lidt svært, da selv universitetet studerende japanere er meget dårlige til engelsk. Dog på min skole er der også en god sjat fra EU og andre engelsk talende lande.
cultural_challenges: At Japanerne er dårlige til engelsk.
culture_appreciated: Mad, venlighed, renlighed, æstetik og mærkelighed.
top3_advice: Vær parat på at hvis du gerne vil blive gode venner med Japaner skal du Japansk. Underviserne er mere engegeret i dig, og vil gerne hjælpe dig med din fremtidige karrierer. Husk ikke at blive taget af den japanske arbejdsetik.
other_useful_info: Det er et fantastisk land, tag ud og spis en masse mærkelig mad, drik nogle øl med venner.
most_rewarding: Nye venskaber og nye måder at se verden på
greatest_challenge: Japansk undervisning - det er pisse svært

crucial_aspects: My primary motivation in choosing Tokyo as my destination was a personal interest in the destination. I wanted to improve my Japanese, to spend time with friends in Japan, and to get to know the country better. Additionally, University of Tokyo is a very famous and well regarded university in Japan. I was curious to experience what studying there would be like.
overall_comments: I had a great semester in Japan, and for anyone who is considering I would say: Go! You won't regret it. No matter what your experience is, I'm certain you will learn a lot and have many fun and memorable experiences.
info_ease: I found the arrival procedure quite confusing (as well as the visa application process prior to arriving). UTokyo however were great at helping and my contacts there answered all my (many) questions and helped me out when needed.
arrival_assistance: I had a tutor assigned who went to the ward office with me and helped me register for classes etc. I could also ask the international student advisor at my graduate school any questions that my tutor couldn't help with. Because I stayed in a university dorm, I also had support from the dorm in the form of various guides on how to do things, e.g. go to the ward office to register my address and pay my first rent.
arrival_comments: I was satisfied, no additional comments.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had a great semester in Japan, and for anyone who is considering I would say: Go! You won't regret it. No matter what your experience is, I'm certain you will learn a lot and have many fun and memorable experiences.
registration_process: We had an orientation for international students at my graduate school where we received practical information, student ID, and we also were each assigned a desk in a private reading room.
registration_help: I was assigned a tutor to help with course registration etc. The international student advisor also answered any questions my tutor couldn't. Additionally, my supervisor, a professor in my graduate school, was great. He showed me around campus and seemed to really take an interest in helping me make the most of my time at UTokyo. Generally, I had a lot of support at Utokyo.
registration_success: I registered for all the classes I wanted, and I was happy with my choices. However there were some courses marked with both Japanese and English, and it was my understanding that I couldn't take those classes with my limited Japanese abilities, but several other students did – so something to watch out for when you choose classes, although it says both Japanese and English you may be able to take the class with only English abilities. If you're unsure, ask the professor.
registration_advice: Look through the course catalogue and don't be afraid to take classes which may not initially sound like they're for you (one of my courses, Anglo-American Law (Special Study), had a description entirely in Japanese which made me think it was mostly aimed at Japanese students, but actually all classes were held in English, and the professors were American). Use the initial period to try out different classes and get an impression of the professors and the workload. Ask the professor if you have any questions.
academics_comments: I had a great semester in Japan, and for anyone who is considering I would say: Go! You won't regret it. No matter what your experience is, I'm certain you will learn a lot and have many fun and memorable experiences.
course_level: Because the examination form is quite different from what I'm used to at UCPH, I don't think it really makes sense to compare the level. For most classes I was evaluated based on a final paper or several papers turned in during the course of the semester. It wasn't particularly difficult, but because it was so different from what I'm used to at home I ended up probably spending more time and energy than needed on my assignments.
teaching_comparison: All my classes at UTokyo were seminar based, and the classes were generally small compared to what I'm used to from home. The professors seemed to have quite a bit of freedom in how to arrange their classes and evaluate students, so for example the length, form etc. of papers would differ depending on the professor/class. My impression was that the Japanese classes were more lecture based and had written examinations more like those I'm used to at home, so perhaps the differences in teaching style were also related to my taking classes in English.
courses_enrolled: Anglo-American Law (Special Study) Sociology of Law (Special Study) / Japanese Law as Viewed from Abroad Comparative Law (Special Study) / Law and the Formation of Transnational East Asia Oriental Legal History (Special Study) / Law and Society in East Asia Japanese Intermediate-2 Speaking Japanese Intermediate-2 Integral
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Japanese Law as Viewed from Abroad with Professor Foote. The class provided a great introduction to various areas of Japanese law, to comparative studies more generally, and as most students in class were domestic students in the professional law school program, I also had an opportunity to learn more about them and the legal profession in Japan which was really interesting. Law and the Formation of Transnational East Asia proved to be another (surprising) favorite class. Two professors teach this class together which made the dynamic more interesting than if it had just been one person talking. The subject matter is unlike anything I've learned before but really interesting. Lastly, in Anglo-American Law (Special Study) I thought Professor Sarah Cleveland was brilliant, although I think the visiting professors in this course change from semester to semester, so you should check the course catalogue to see who is teaching.
unexpected_costs: I didn't encounter any unexpected costs. I was however surprised how inconvenient it was to pay my bills. At first I thought I would have to get a Japanese credit card. I ended up paying my rent by taking out cash each month and then transferring it at the bank. The dorm gave us a guide for this, so it's not that it was very difficult to figure out, I just found it odd that there wasn't an easier way to do it.
cost_comparison: Living in Japan generally proved to be quite inexpensive. Food and drink is cheap, transportation can add up but I had a commuter pass so that helped. My biggest expense ended up being travelling which I did a lot of (I've put this in the category "Personal spending"). There are definitely opportunities to travel cheaply, e.g. using highway busses and chain hotels, but I ended up often opting for the comfort and speed of flying or taking the shinkansen which of course was then more expensive.
activities_available: I took Japanese language classes through JLCSE. They also held some cultural events. I participated in a calligraphy class, and there was also e.g. a kimono wearing event. I think there's probably more activities at Komaba campus where all the undergraduate students have their classes than there are at Hongo. Of course if you join a club or circle they'll have more offers. There was a student festival at Hongo campus in May. There's also a gym in Hongo, I didn't use it but heard good things about it from those who did.
activities_recommended: If you have an interest in any sports or crafts, and if you want to make friends with local students, clubs or circles seem to be a great way to do so. If not, there are also plenty of other ways to meet people. Living at the dorm, someone was always going on some trip or doing something, so there were plenty of opportunities to participate in things.
weekend_recommendations: Tokyo is a great city to live in. There's always something going on and you'll never be bored. However, it can also be crowded and tiring, so on weekends and holidays I would recommend travelling around Japan and especially seeing more of the countryside. There were so many places I enjoyed seeing on day- or longer trips. Just some highlights: the Izu peninsula is great and not so far from Tokyo, Karuizawa I really liked as well, if you enjoy hiking there's many hiking opportunities close to Tokyo, e.g. Mt Mitake, Mt Tsukuba, Mt Nokogiri, the Jogasaki coast, as well as longer hikes further from Tokyo such as the Kiso Road, Mt Fuji etc. I also travelled to further away places such as Hokkaido, Shikoku and Kyushu. Flight tickets are pretty cheap, and being in Japan for a longer time is a great opportunity to see those places you wouldn't necessarily on vacation. If you're here during the summer don't miss the festivals and fireworks. And if you want to see cherry blossoms, make sure to arrive in March as they bloom earlier and earlier every year – some students who arrived in the beginning of April almost missed the blossoms entirely which was a shame. In general, enjoy the seasons as they come and go – if you're here during the spring, you'll have the rainy season and the hot and humid summer, but you'll also have cherry blossoms, azaleas, and my favorite, the hydrangeas which you can see blooming all over Tokyo in June.
culture_adjustment: Some things were easier to adjust to than others. Generally though, I didn't find anything particularly difficult. Everything is different but that's part of the experience.
socializing_tips: Not really, just be friendly and talk to people. If you take classes in English, usually the Japanese people in those classes will be those who are already comfortable speaking English, so it shouldn't be impossible to talk to them. Generally though, I think the consensus is that while everyone is really friendly it can be hard to make deeper connections with local students. But don't let that scare you. Talk to people and enjoy the opportunity to be surprised and delighted at how different but also similar we all are.
cultural_challenges: I guess the language barrier was the biggest challenge. Even though I can understand a lot, I often found it difficult to participate in conversations in a natural way.
culture_appreciated: The convenience and the friendliness. And the food!
top3_advice: 1. Before you leave, there will be lots of paperwork and practical tasks of e.g. applying for your visa and subletting your apartment. These things may make you question why you're bothering to go on exchange at all, but don't worry, it's worth all the trouble. 2. Everyone else is as confused as you in the beginning. Don't be afraid to ask questions. Japanese people are incredibly friendly and helpful, and even if you make mistakes, don't worry as you can always find a solution. 3. If your classes are at Hongo, enjoy the campus – Sanshiro pond, the library, the gingko trees, the arched hallways. I miss it already.
other_useful_info: There's probably a lot, but I don't remember everything now. You will have a lot of questions and maybe sometimes things will seem difficult, but everything will work out.
most_rewarding: Any time I spoke Japanese, was understood, and made connections with people. Any time I felt that I understood the culture and fit in. Just the general joy of making a life for yourself across the world, of eating and travelling and experiencing, and of reflecting on my life at home and understanding it better - both the good and the bad - because of the added outside perspective.
greatest_challenge: I found being away from family and friends at home difficult. The time difference means that when you wake up, everyone at home is asleep, and when they wake up, you're probably in class or otherwise too busy to talk, then when you get home in the evening they're at work. Dealing with a loss in the family at home while I was abroad was the hardest time during my exchange.
other_comments: None.

crucial_aspects: I had already been to Japan before, so I knew what the country was like. But the aspects were probably affordability, great food, interesting culture and a big city to explore.
overall_comments: UTokyo gets 9/10 for me, with one point reducted due to problems with course selection and lack of social aspects at orientation. I studied at the graduate school of economics, so if someone reads this, everything related to the school will be different for other graduate schools / undergraduate.
info_ease: I would say that overall, the information is quite easy to find, but there is a lot of information to keep track of. Most of the difficult stuff is pre-arrival. Once you arrive its relatively simple, and you get an entire book with information that you can look through.
arrival_assistance: Before I arrived, I was assigned a tutor. My tutor helped me signing up for several things at the local municipal office like health insirance and other stuff. I think this proccess would be quite overwhelming without someone speaking Japanese, so that was nice. Second, we had an orientation. Here we got needed information, and I wasnt really unsure of anything. 40% of it was in Japanese because some people were not comfortable speaking English, but that was also a little fun to experience so not really a problem. The only thing that could have been done much better was some sort of social activity, or just a chance to meet people. I naturally met the only 3 other non-asian people out of 50 attendees, because we knew we could speak English, but there wasnt really any chance to meet the other economics students which I thought was a shame. 2 of them became my closest friends, but without the orientation I would probably have had less of a social experience
arrival_comments: One point reduced because of no social activities. I know that the under-grad program had some meet and greet stuff. I have also studied in the US where there were several events extending the orientation.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: UTokyo gets 9/10 for me, with one point reducted due to problems with course selection and lack of social aspects at orientation. I studied at the graduate school of economics, so if someone reads this, everything related to the school will be different for other graduate schools / undergraduate.
registration_process: From home there is a course catalog you can browse, which is quite easy to use. If you are a graduate(master), remember to use the graduate catalog. When you arrive, they will also explain at the orientation. Then, you have two weeks to 'shop' courses, where you can show up to any course. Next, you will have to finally choose the courses you want. The first week is normally not important, so skipping this is fine, if two courses are at the same time. The second week they start to go through important material, so it would be good not skipping this. You need 6 courses at economics. So you can maybe go to 8-10 the first week, then go to 7-8 second week if you are still unsure.
registration_help: You can always go to the economics office. They are very helpfull, responds emails within one day, and there are people speaking English.
registration_success: I had mixed experiences. You can get any course you want, its not like in some US uni where they fill up. The course registration itself is good, and easy to understand. You dont have to get permission from professors and other stuff like that, therefore 5/5. But I had two problems. First, I tried to registrer for two seminars, where you just had to listen to researchers present their papers. It was a little bit to ensure low workload for myself, but it was actually also good for me in relation to my thesis. Then in the middle of week two, I was told I could not register for them. So then I basically had to register two courses without the 'shopping' opportunity. It said nowhere I couldnt go to them, so I had no way of knowing. Second, when I had to register for the new courses with short notice, I chose one course that was a quarter course (half semester, but still 2 credits). Therefore I completed that course after 2 months, and had 5 courses to still complete. However, you need to have 6 credits in each quarter(term). I basically had 7 in the first, then 5 in the second. Then I was told (also at the end of the shopping week, in 2nd term) I had to register for a 7th course. It did say this in one sentence in the prerequisite paper I read 3-5 months prior, but I just understood it as I needed 12 credits total. It also doent make any logical sense, but the Japanese really stick to the rules. Since I also had problems with the two seminars, and someone confirming my courses were fine, I dont get why I wasnt told this.
registration_advice: If you are in doubt about your courses, or maybe just in general, ask the office about your registration and get it confirmed. They have a person who will look through all your courses and tell you (late) if something is wrong. I think the registration itself is 5/5 and very easy, I guess I was just unfortunate. If I had to do it again, I would ask the office to confirm all my courses, and confirm I didnt have to register more for the whole exchange.
academics_comments: UTokyo gets 9/10 for me, with one point reducted due to problems with course selection and lack of social aspects at orientation. I studied at the graduate school of economics, so if someone reads this, everything related to the school will be different for other graduate schools / undergraduate.
course_level: Level depends. You can also registrer 2/6 courses at other departments. I did 3 (because of the extra one) at public policy (statskundskab), which was much easier than economics. Some economics courses were easy, but you still had to do some assignments. Some were quite hard. I did a data science course where I coulndt (and didnt really want to waste my time) hand in two huge assignments cause they were so difficult. Workload per cource is also less than KU, but you have more courses. I had a lot of assignments the last month/2 weeks. This was quite intense, but rest of semester was overall chill. Workload public policy - 2*10 pages paper or 10 page paper and 5 min presentation. Workload economics - read 3 papers and write a summary/discussion + 3 econometric assignments with 5-10 questions (little long, quite easy though)+ 10 page research proposal or 8x15 min quiz + 3 home assignmens with 10 questions and read 2 papers.
teaching_comparison: Not similar at all. Most courses are around 10 ppl, so there is room for discussion. Its almost like a TA session at KU. Grading is also very different between courses. Some will be +50% class participation. Some will be presentation based, some test and some assignments. I mostly had assignment based grading, by choice, because I didnt want to read a ton of material and discuss. It is very easy to pass courses, and also relatively easy getting a good grade. I got several A's without much effort.
courses_enrolled: - International Trade I (pretty good course) - Data Science for Practical Economic Research (Very difficult. Should be called "Computational theoretical econometrics modelling". There is NO data in this course) - Institutional Analysis of Japanese Economy I (More of a history class in Japanese economy in samurai times) - Policy and Governance in Contemporary China (Public policy. Quite good, would recommend) - Science and Technology in International Relations (Public policy. Very easy, didnt learn much) - Labor Economics I (Good refresher for econometrics, quite easy) - Energy Systems (Engineering/public policy. Fun/different and easy if you had physics A in highschool)
recommended_courses: International Trade, P&G in China, Labor economics. All relatively fair workload, and interesting topics Some people did a Japanese class, didnt hear good things about it, but thats what the shopping week is for
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Everything is not as expensive as people think. I would say overall its around 2/3 Danish prices, maybe less. housing 3k, eating out is around 50-75DKK. Often drinks 40 DKK at a bar/club. You can probably be completely fine on your SU, if you can live on a budget. If you can get grants you should be covered.
activities_available: In Japan they ahve a lot of clubs. They have them for almost anything to my understanding. There are both clubs and 'circles'. I think cirles are the less serious one. Normally exchange students cant join the real clubs.
activities_recommended: Some of my friends joined the less serious football club, which they liked and its a good place to meet new people. Just try to find them on the internet or instragram(just send them a DM). I think there were 4+ not serious football clubs. The serious ones train 5 times a week or something.
weekend_recommendations: Probably visit Okinawa, Osaka, Kyoto or other places in Japan, many people went there. Often you can join a group of exchange students. It also takes more than 4 months to explore all of Tokyo, so you can also just stay in the city.
culture_adjustment: I think it was fine, but some people might get a bit of a culture shock. Japan is very different from Denmark, but it is clean, safe and organised. So you will feel that its different, but probably not in a bad way.
socializing_tips: Join a sport club is probably the easiest. There was not that many Japanese ppl in the English courses, and I don't see how someone would casually get to know them in that setting. As all other people, Japanese are more open to talk over a beer/at bars, so thats maybe also an option. There also was some language exchange events, didnt go to them though
cultural_challenges: Language is the biggest one. Get google translate downloaded, and use the camera function for text. Don't speak extremely loud in the train, noone talks there.
culture_appreciated: Probably politeness and how clean and nice. And the food. Overall Japan is a very nice country to live in
top3_advice: 1. Get your paperwork done early and keep a good overview 2. If you go alone, try to make some friends at the dorm/orientation early on, and be a bit proactive to meet people. I think maybe could be a bit difficult to meet new people a month into the exchange. 3. Pro tip: in the iPhone wallet, you can create a suica/passmo card. Do it once you arrive. You can transfer money directly on your phone. The card works as a credit card in 90% of Japanese stores. Normally you have to get the card in a machine, ant add money with cash. 10x easier to get it in the wallet.
other_useful_info: Maybe be strategic with your course selection in relation to what you want to get out of your exchange. I think its pretty easy to see if a course will be hard or easy. If you want to travel and explore, try to get some courses on the same days, with lower workload, then yoy can have a lot of freetime. If you want to go for the academics, I think many interesting academic courses with high worload was also offered. If you want, you can have courses where you get to discuss directly with the professor every class.
most_rewarding: I think just the overall day to day lifestyle. I was living in Shibuya, I could go out to eat good food every day, I had some good friends to explore with and Tokyo is just very cool overall
greatest_challenge: (1) Language in combination with food. If you want to explore japanese restaurants, you will end up in a situation where noone speaks english, and the menu is hand written so goole cant translate it. Plus, many restaurants serve some weird stuff like intestines. If you are picky with your food, you probably want to make sure they have a translatable menu. But often these restaurants are very very good. (2) Yakitori is not like in 7-11 in Denmark. If you order a mixed platter, half of them will be with stuff like chicken liver, - skin, or some meat you cant chew. So be aware

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience a culture vastly different from Denmark, and had wanted to revisit Japan for a longer period of time after my first holiday there.
info_ease: UTokyo sends a lot of emails with necessary information, and although there is a lot to look through, I found that it answered all of my questions to satisfaction.
arrival_assistance: I mostly received assistance in form of email, though I was made aware of the globalisation center on campus in case I had any questions I needed answered in person.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The first few weeks of classes you're able to sign up for as many courses as you like and swap between them. After the deadline, you're locked into your courses.
registration_help: We were able to ask questions to the professors in charge of the global program at the start of the term, and the office for global students was open throughout the registration period.
registration_success: I registered for all of the courses I wanted, and switched one of my courses at the end of the registration period with no issue.
registration_advice: Try out some different courses before you settle, and take into account which campus the courses are located on, what form of exam (if any) and other relevant info on the syllabus.
course_level: I found the courses fairly easy in terms of level.
teaching_comparison: The flow between lecture and class discussion was much less strict at UTokyo, though the form was pretty set with few variations.
courses_enrolled: Comparative Analysis on Regional Organizations as Security Actors Art and Feminisms in Japan since the 1960s East Asian Thought Multiculturalism in Japanese Society Southeast Asia in Global Context Earth System Governance Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Human Security-Southeast Asia and Japan in Global Society
recommended_courses: I think the Multiculturalism in Japanese Society and Southeast Asia in Global Context courses are both very interesting and give a good look into the region if you're interested in leaning more about Japan and of Southeast Asia
unexpected_costs: You need to pay for national health insurance (about 300 dkk/month) once arrived in Japan, no matter if you already have health insurance and/or other insurance
cost_comparison: Food at restaurants and convenience stores is way cheaper than in Denmark. Vegetables and fruit however are very expensive.
activities_available: There are clubs (serious endeavors with practice several times a week) and circles (more relaxed with 1-2 meetings a week) for a range of different sports and other activities such as book clubs, tea clubs etc. Note that most of these activities happen in Japanese.
activities_recommended: There is a group that sets up social events such as monthly lunches, parties and the like. A great opportunity to meet other students, local and international alike.
weekend_recommendations: Going to Kyoto and Hiroshima are a must, as is seeing Mount Fuji up close.
culture_adjustment: I think it was a bit difficult to adjust to, as there are a lot of unwritten social rules that you need to figure out on your own

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study at a top-university in a non-native English speaking country.
overall_comments: Overall a good experience but nothing out of the extraordinary.
info_ease: There was a lot of information from University of Tokyo. They sent email after email with loads of info. However, this made it a bit difficult to navigate in all the rules as there was almost too much information to read through it all.
arrival_assistance: I had a long email-correspondance with one of the administratives from the University of Tokyo exchange programme (USTEP). They respond quickly and can provide further info. I was in doubt with how many courses to choose, which courses I was eligible for etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall a good experience but nothing out of the extraordinary.
registration_process: You sign up for courses in a pre-registration period. The first two weeks you attend all possible courses that you are interested in. At the end of the two weeks you cancel the registration for the courses you don't want and you end up with your desired courses. There is a course page for UTokyo courses. However, many of the English courses are not available for USTEP students. Be aware of this and select only available courses for USTEP. The course page is only updated with full course description and possibly curriculum 1-2 weeks prior to semester start.
registration_help: The UTokyo USTEP office was quick at replying and answered my questions about signing up for courses.
registration_success: I got the courses I wanted from the course list with available courses. I was a first year graduate student during my exchange, but the system is different in Japan so I was a 4th year undergraduate student at UTokyo. This meant I was not eligible for graduate courses which was a pity. There were a lot of interesting econ graduate courses which I could not sign up for and instead I had to choose among a few graduate econ courses available for undergraduates and courses in other departments. I tried asking if I could sign up for a graduate course with help from USTEP, but I was not allowed even though I had done the pre-requisites. I suppose Japanese rules are a bit strict and bureaucratic so do not expect to be allowed to sign up for courses you are not eligible for.
registration_advice: Look up all available courses - there are many. I found econ courses at other departments such as Environmental Economics at Department of Agriculture. Be aware of the requirements from UTokyo as they are different than the requirements from KU. According to KU, you have to do 7 courses as an undergraduate student and 4 (graduate) courses as a graduate student to bring back 30 ECTS. However, these requirements are different when at UTokyo. Here the only requirement is the amount of hours per week: Undergraduate students have to do 12 hours a week (one course is typically 2 hours). That means you have to do 6 courses per week to fulfil the requirements. Some courses are in the first term, some in the second term and some in both terms. Other courses are intensive courses and last only a weekend or a few days at the end of the semester. The intensive courses do not count towards the 12 hours a week goal but you can still get ECTS-points from KU for these courses. So you need to have 6 classes per week during both terms in order to fulfil the requirements and then you might need more classes to fulfil KUs ECTS-requirements. It is quite tricky, but somewhere in all the info given the rules are stated.
academics_comments: Overall a good experience but nothing out of the extraordinary.
course_level: I had expected very high academic level, but I was not very impressed with the level. The courses were more superficial than back home at KU. There was a bit of math but the students were not supposed to know any of it. Some courses had a high level but most of them were very easy and did not require any readings and some of the were like advanced high school subjects. I expect some of the graduate courses to be high level like at KU, but it is not the case for all of them.
teaching_comparison: My courses were fairly small classes with 20-30 students and one professor. The professor did a presentation and depending on the course and the professor, there could be group discussions or standard lectures as at KU. Some courses also had student presentations, I only had to do a presentation in one course. Most courses had many components leading to the final grade whereas I am used to the final exam counting 100% of the grading. In most courses participation (i.e. attending the class) gave points towards final grade.
courses_enrolled: I had 7 courses (listed from best to worst): "Seminar in International Politics" (= "Contemporary Chinese Diplomacy"), "Japanese Economy II", "Environmental Economics", "Contemporary Capitalism, Financial Crisis, Poverty and Class Struggle", "Development Economics", "Institutional Analysis of Japanese Economy II" and "Start-up and Venture Capital".
recommended_courses: I would recommend "Contemporary Chinese Diplomacy" with professor Akio Takahara and "Japanese Economy II" with professor Takeo Hoshi. These courses were very good, probably also because the professors were very good. I would take any course with these professors. "Contemporary Chinese Diplomacy" might be one of the most interesting courses I have ever taken even though it has almost nothing to do with economics - it is a public policy course. I thought I knew a fair bit about China and Chinese politics but I learned so much and had very interesting discussions with other students. The professor had immense knowledge about China and their historic political development and strategic politics. Since it was a seminar, we had 45 min. to discuss with other students in every class about some suggested questions or whatever else we wanted to discuss regarding China. It was unique to be able to discuss relations to China with students from China, India, France etc. and the other students were very well informed about China. "Japanese Economy II" was exactly what was needed as an econ-student in Japan since we were presented with many different topics on the development of the Japanese Economy (labour market, industrial policy, monetary policy etc.). Takeo Hoshi is maybe the leading professor at the econ-programme and had written the book on the syllabus, so he gave good insights to all the possible struggles the Japanese Economy is facing. All other courses had no requirements for reading. "Environmental Economics" was an interesting topic, but unfortunately it was presented in a quite boring way. The professor of "Contemporary Capitalism" (Manuel Yang) was the most interesting speaker I have had. He was so good at speaking and telling stories and we watched movies and discussed topics regarding capitalism in very laid-back manner. I learned almost nothing, but it was quite fun. "Development Economics" had a very interesting syllabus but we did not touch upon any of it nor were given the texts. There were no exercises and no slides provided. It was a cozy setting, but the level was very low and I did not learn what I expected from the course. "Instutional ..." was a graduate course, but I did not understand the professor's English, so I did not attend any of the lectures. The exam was 100% final grade and the material was the professor's own papers on samurai-economics 400 years ago. I found it very boring and a frustrating course to have chosen. "Start-up .." consisted of a superficial touch on finance, and then we just made up our own fictive firm and did a pitch (in groups of 10). I learned almost nothing.
cost_comparison: I expected Japan to be a bit more expensive, but due to weak Yen the exchange rate was very good. This made everything cheaper than expected. Housing was very expensive, but eating out was quite cheap and convenient. Taking the Shinkansen with visitors (who had JR Pass) was very expensive for me, but it is a great experience nevertheless.
activities_available: There are many clubs and circles at UTokyo in all kinds of hobbies. Clubs are more serious and meet up maybe 5 times a week. Circles are more relaxed and might be easier to join as an exchange student. I wanted to play badminton, since I knew the sport is popular in Japan. I managed to find some circles, but some of them did not allow foreigners. However, I joined a circle called Hikousen. It was very fun and interesting to meet locals and speak with them (even though most did not speak English). They were very friendly and I highly recommend trying to join a circle.
activities_recommended: Tokyo has just about anything one could imagine. You could play the sport/hobby you usually practice back home, but you could also try something completely new. There are endless opportunities in caligraphy, table tennis, video games, tea clubs etc. I would recommend trying to join some kind of club/circle/thing you want to practice/do. It is a great way of actually meeting locals in a non-academic environment and a big insight to Japanese culture. Also, go for walks seeing the neatly done Japanese gardens, go into one of the endless small temple sites in the city, go out of the city and to an onsen bath (or sento).
weekend_recommendations: You could easily spend 5 months only in Tokyo and not have seen it all. Go out to explore new neighborhoods and try to do some trips outside the city. I recommend at least once going to a more rural place in Japan to experience the tranquility and often more run-down places and stay at a Ryokan or Minshuku. Japan and Tokyo are almost two different and separate countries.
culture_adjustment: The Japanese culture is very different, and I feel like there are a lot of unwritten rules. However, since Japanese are typically shy, you will probably not be told if you do anything wrong as a foreigner. But do your best to accommodate yourself in the culture, it is very appreciated when foreigners are polite, know a few words of Japanese, don't talk on the trains, line up like the locals etc. I found it quite easy to adjust to the culture since it is like a more extreme version of the Danish culture: People mind their own business even more, are more shy talking to strangers and are even more aware of not being in the way of others.
socializing_tips: Join a club/circle.
cultural_challenges: Probably all the unwritten rules about ones behaviour. The most challenging might be the rules I did not get to know and thus being unpolite without knowing. Try to do your best and they will appreciate you trying to blend in.
culture_appreciated: How everyone is so polite and helpful. Very friendly place to be.
top3_advice: 1. Check up on the UTokyo rules beforehand. 2. Try to immerse yourself just a bit in the culture and Japanese rules. I suppose it is very appreciated and shows some respect for their unique culture. After a few months you will notice the tourists in the trains taking up all the space and talking loudly, please do your best not to be like the tourists. 3. Don't be sad if you do not get to do everything you wanted in Japan/Tokyo - there are simply too many things to see/do and you will for sure miss out on something.
most_rewarding: Trying to live in Tokyo. It is one of the craziest, largest and most unique cities in its own way.
greatest_challenge: Being away from friends and my girlfriend. No matter how much you are prepared for this, you just can't find equal friends as the ones back home.
