crucial_aspects: During my bachelor's I had taken a 2-year minor (sidefagspakke) in Japanese studies, but had been prevented from doing my exchange trip then, due to Covid. So Japan was a natural choice for my semester abroad now. I applied to University of Tokyo partly because of its academic reputation, but mostly because of its cultural history, which stretches back to the late 19th century, and the modernization of Japan during the Meiji period. At this time, the great author Natsume Sōseki, in whose oeuvre I am interested academically, taught here for a while.
info_ease: Relatively easy. The only real hurdle was the registration at the city ward office, and the issuance of my national health insurance card – very few people in the administration speak english. But all went well, only patience is required, really.
arrival_assistance: At the dormitory there was a very helpful help desk, and I went through an informative orientation at the university.
arrival_comments: It would have been nice to have a student tutor to show around and give information about the facilities, extracurricular activities etc., but apart from that everything was good!
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You only finalised the registration a couple of weeks into the semester – until then you could "shop around" and try dfferent things. A bit confusing, with having to find info through the various IT systems, but great that you can wait and see how the class feels before committing.
registration_help: I got the help I needed from the support team at my graduate school, as well as from my academic advisor/host.
registration_success: I got the classes I wanted, with no problems.
registration_advice: Shop around and try different courses in the first week – keep an open mind, and you'll definitely end up having fun and learning a lot.
course_level: There was a lot of reading, and more (but smaller) exams than I'm used to – partly because I took two extra courses, because of some rule that said I had to have 10 hours of weekly classes. All of my courses were dicussion-based MA courses, so you really had to read for every week, but the material was pretty interesting, and the discussions were not too difficult to participate in.
teaching_comparison: Again, all of my classes were discussion-based, and had you do multiple student presentations etc. as well – I didn't find a single lecture class for MA level. But the kinds of critical discussions of texts were similar to what I am used to from seminars at the faculty of humanities at home, so there were no great difficulties.
courses_enrolled: "Explaining" japanese religion: a critical approach Gender and sexuality in japanese arts and culture Historical perceptions in Asia – exploring various memories of world war 2 Visual culture, technology, and the everyday life Law and the formation of transnational East Asia The future of writing
recommended_courses: All of the above. The courses at my graduate school – Interdisciplinary Information Studies – can all be recommended, I feel like. And see if you can find a class on some kind of East Asian history taught by Matsubara at the faculty of Law, he's great!
unexpected_costs: Bank transfer fees, but they are not THAT overwhelming.
cost_comparison: You can eat pretty well for not a lot of money. Most things are less expensive than at home. And the national health insurance is a pretty good investment (and also mandatory...).
activities_available: They were a bit difficult to find – especially as an MA student, I think. Many clubs were closed to exchange students who were only there for a semester. But the school festival was great, and the sports facilities at campus were pretty exceptional as well, and pretty cheap. Also, a language exchange program was offered, but I didn't have time to participate.
activities_recommended: Go exploring in Tokyo, it is an amazing city! So many good, cheap places to eat (and drink!), nice museums, whole district of antiquarian bookshops, festivals (matsuri – you should definitely go to some, not least the fireworks ones!), very good thrift shops, etc. And take some trips to the mountains, as well – there are great places to go hiking.
weekend_recommendations: Again, go to the mountains. For example to Hakone, which really isn't too far away. Also, you can take the bullet train (or the cheaper night bus) and get to pretty much anywhere on the main island pretty fast – at least a weekend's stay in Osaka or Kyoto is definitely recommended, or go during Golden week!
culture_adjustment: Some people were a bit difficult to approach – there are definitely cultural differences in how we communicate and form relations. And many japanese are not very good at spoken english, which they are very shy about speaking. But most people are kind and really want to help etc. Though my experience was that I quickly formed a bubble of other european exchange students...
socializing_tips: If you live in a dorm, really do try to speak to people coming and going, cooking in th kitchen etc. – some of them really want to communicate, but most are very shy. And feel free to e.g. organize a night out – your co-habitants will most likely be impressed by your initiative.
cultural_challenges: There is definitely a language barrier, and even though I speak a bit of japanese, communication with some was difficult.
culture_appreciated: Kind people, good food, amazing cultural sites (museums, temples and shrines(!!!), theatres), beautiful nature, etc.., and most everywhere feels very safe.
top3_advice: You'll need to go through a lot of paperwork – but don't stress about it, everything always goes fine in the end, in my experience. And have patience with the IT systems as well. But do try to be on time when handing in papers, paperwork, coming to class, etc.. The japanese are punctual and appreciate that in other people. Show up to a lot of courses during the first week, and try to feel out the vibe there, before committing. And try to find time to go on a couple of trips. Skip a class or two, if need be, but remember: most classes have mandatory presence, so use your skips wisely, not just on sleeping in! And don't use too many saturdays at the library.. Get out and go to a festival – there's bound to be one going on somewhere in Tokyo! Enjoy your trip. <3
other_useful_info: You will receive your transcript (required for the credit transfer etc.) veeery late. But it will arrive eventually, though you might need to stall the SU people... And remember: the trains in Japan only run until midnight!
most_rewarding: I can't choose, but just being there, and having to figure out what to do on a sunday – and then going to some temple with friends I only just made – was amazing.
greatest_challenge: Being very far from home, and in a +8 hour time zone sometimes made me feel very disconnected from everyone at home.

crucial_aspects: I chose to study at the University of Tokyo because it was far from Denmark. I wanted something completely new, and it definitely was. I also chose it because of its emphasis on discussion-based teaching, its reputation as the best university in Japan, and one of the best in the world—so I assumed the academic level would be very high. That assumption was somewhat mistaken.
overall_comments: It was an incredible experience. I wouldn’t give it a 10/10 because some of the courses I took were purely lecture-based, without practical exercises or much opportunity to process the information in depth.
info_ease: The university was great at guiding students through the necessary steps for a smooth transition. There are many small deadlines to keep track of, which can be a bit tedious, but overall, you just need to remember that they want you to succeed and will help you reach your goals. The staff is there to support you, even if it’s easy to forget that sometimes.
arrival_assistance: There’s an orientation meeting a week before classes start, late september, but it didn’t provide much new information. They showed this website, which I found useful:
arrival_comments: Just keep track of the deadlines!
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was an incredible experience. I wouldn’t give it a 10/10 because some of the courses I took were purely lecture-based, without practical exercises or much opportunity to process the information in depth.
registration_process: Students have one week to try out different courses, but you should attend the ones you plan to take from the very first class. It’s a decent system. If you’re studying in the fall, I recommend scheduling most of your classes early in the week since there are many extended weekends where Mondays are off.
registration_help: There’s an office with staff who are very helpful whenever you need assistance. It's called the Global office and is located in the middle of Komaba Campus.
registration_success: I got into all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: I’m unsure whether I’d recommend Japanese language courses. They’re structured very much like elementary school classes, and the timing isn’t ideal if you want to finish your main classes early in the week.
academics_comments: It was an incredible experience. I wouldn’t give it a 10/10 because some of the courses I took were purely lecture-based, without practical exercises or much opportunity to process the information in depth.
course_level: I was unsure about which master’s program to pursue, so I took a broad selection of courses pointing in different directions. That wouldn’t have been possible in Copenhagen, at least not with the number of courses I took and the flexibility of just needing to pass as an exchange student. The teaching quality wasn’t particularly strong, but it worked fine for a "gap semester." However, if I were staying for a full year, I think I would have found it frustrating.
teaching_comparison: Overall, the academic level was fairly easy, likely because the university accommodates students from very different educational backgrounds and has to find a common denominator, which is the lowest. There were very few academic resources available when I struggled with something. Often, I had to Google my way through problems, which is difficult for technical topics. At KU, there are many places to seek guidance if you’re unsure about something, which I missed. On the other hand, not having to buy textbooks was nice—but at times, I simply didn’t know where to look for information when I got stuck. That’s not something I’ve experienced at KU.
courses_enrolled: Neuroscience & Symbols + Mind & Mindfulness → Okay courses. Sustainable Architecture + History of Architecture in Tokyo → Decent. Climate Repair → Great professor, lots of discussion. Material Dynamics 1 & 4 → About large climate systems, a bit boring but informative.
recommended_courses: Climate Repair—the professor was fantastic, and the discussions were engaging.
unexpected_costs: I traveled a lot, which was unexpected but highly recommended! I walked a lot and campus is right next to the dorm so didn't take to much public transport for chores, only for travelling.
cost_comparison: If you shop at a proper supermarket like OK Everyday Low Price, not My basket or conbini, you can live quite cheaply by cooking at home. Some people claimed eating out is so cheap that cooking isn’t necessary, but I disagree. It’s like eating out in Italy—it might be affordable for a week or two, but over six months, it adds up significantly.
activities_available: The university occasionally offers discounted tickets for events via email. The student card from UTokyo also provides excellent museum discounts around Tokyo.
activities_recommended: Go to Okinawa or Ōshima—amazing island vibes!
weekend_recommendations: Winters in Tokyo are dry and sunny. It feels like an April/May day in Denmark—slightly chilly, but if you find a sunny bench, you can sit in a t-shirt. That really surprised me. So just use some weekends in Tokyo and go to local markets.
culture_adjustment: English is widely spoken in Tokyo. In rural areas, not so much—but with smiles and gestures, you’ll manage. People are generally very kind. So you won't feel to lost and can somewhat adjust fast. It feels very Danish somehow.
socializing_tips: There’s a bit of a højskole atmosphere—many people are eager to meet new friends, so it’s easy to find a group.
cultural_challenges: Just be respectful and mindful, and you’ll navigate things just fine.
culture_appreciated: I enjoyed the shrines but the one in Nikko is the greatest. After seeing that you will have seen them all!
top3_advice: 1. If you want to specialize deeply in one field, stay in Copenhagen. But if you want to explore a variety of subjects, UTokyo is the place to be. That’s its biggest strength. 2. Enjoy it, go hiking, and take solo day trips just to wander and explore. 3. Go to Ni-chōme in Shinjuku and party! Many clubs are free and incredibly fun.
other_useful_info: If you live in Komaba, try to take all your classes there. Just avoid Hongo Campus (purely science courses) and International Village.
most_rewarding: It’s a transformative experience—you’ll gain so much confidence and a go-getter mindset.
greatest_challenge: The only downside? You’ll always want to be outside, experiencing new things—you just can’t relax!

crucial_aspects: My main motivation for choosing Tokyo, and Japan in general was the opportunity to gain international academic experience in a country with a culture very different from my own. I felt that living in Japan would give me valuable new perspectives, as I had never been to East Asia before.
info_ease: It was not very easy, as only a limited number of people spoke English, which made practical tasks such as registering my address and arranging insurance quite challenging. However, everything related to the university itself—such as the admission procedure and course registration—was more straightforward. The staff at the International Students Office were very helpful and always willing to answer questions, which made the process much smoother once I knew where to turn for assistance.
arrival_assistance: I was assigned a tutor who helped me with many of the practical matters, such as registration procedures, and who was available to answer various questions during my first weeks. The International Students Office was also very supportive and always ready to clarify the things my tutor could not assist with. In addition, the dormitory where I stayed (Mejirodai) had very kind and helpful staff who provided guidance on everyday matters.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The registration process was a bit confusing at first, as the Academic Affairs System (UTAS – similar to KUnet) is not very intuitive and takes some time to get used to. Fortunately, I had a tutor who guided me through the steps and answered my questions regarding both the initial admission procedure and the course registration. In addition, there were several orientation sessions for international students where we received detailed information about the registration procedure, course options, and other practical matters. The orientation for my specific graduate school, however, was conducted in Japanese with a translator present, which made it a bit difficult to follow everything in detail.
registration_help: Both my assigned tutor and the International Student Office were of great help throughout the semester.
registration_success: I was able to register for all the courses I wanted without any major problems. The process is done directly through UTAS as soon as the course registration period opens. During the first week of the semester, you also have the opportunity to “trial” classes, which you can later drop if you did not like them during the first week. One important thing to be aware of, however, is the language requirement. If you are not comfortable speaking Japanese, it is best to choose courses labeled only as “English” rather than those listed as “English/Japanese.”
registration_advice: Consider the workload of every course you take, as it can vary significantly depending on the professor and the type of class. During the course registration week, take advantage of the opportunity to try out as many classes as possible. This will give you a better sense of the teaching style, workload, and content before you decide which ones to keep. I would also recommend trying to keep Fridays free if possible. Having a three-day weekend made it much easier for me to go on longer trips around Japan and abroad.
course_level: The courses were not especially difficult in terms of content, but they required a different academic approach than I was used to. Most of the classes I took were based on jurisprudence and legal research rather than traditional legal dogmatics, which meant that I had to adjust my way of thinking and studying. It took some time to get used to analyzing broader theoretical, comparative and sociological perspectives instead of focusing primarily on the application of legal rules. The evaluation methods were also quite different from what I had experienced at home. Instead of written exams, assessment was usually based on a final paper or a series of smaller papers submitted throughout the semester. In addition, class participation was an important factor in the overall grade. While this system was not necessarily more difficult, it required more continuous engagement and preparation during the semester.
teaching_comparison: All of my classes at UTokyo were seminar-based. The class sizes were noticeably smaller, which created a more interactive atmosphere. Each class also had its own particular style, especially when it came to evaluation methods—some relied on a single final paper, while others required several smaller assignments combined with active participation.
courses_enrolled: Anglo-American Law (with p. Masayuki Tamaruya), Sociology of Law (with p. Dimitri Vanoverbeke), Comparative Law (with p. Carol Lawson), International Commercial Law and Negotiation Strategy (with p. Masayuki Tamaruya). 8 credits in total. Very competent and friendly professors. Highly recommend these courses.
recommended_courses: I would honestly recommend all of the courses I took, as each of them offered valuable insights and perspectives that I would not have encountered at home. Taken together, however, the workload was heavier than I initially expected—across my classes I ended up writing roughly 13,000 words in papers.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: In general, Japan turned out to be noticeably less expensive than Denmark, but this really depends on the category of spending. Everyday items such as food and drinks were often cheaper. Public transportation can add up, but with a commuter pass (that you can get since you are a student) it becomes more manageable and quite affordable compared to Danish standards. On the other hand, certain things were more expensive than I expected. Travelling around Japan can quickly become costly and many imported goods that you are used to (like fruit and vegetables) were also surprisingly expensive. Overall, though, the cost of living felt lower than in Denmark, provided you adapt to the local way of doing things.
activities_available: There were certainly many cultural, athletic, and social activities available, but in my experience most of them required a fairly good command of Japanese in order to fully participate. That said, my dormitory organized informal social activities, which made it easier to meet both international and Japanese students.
activities_recommended: I would strongly recommend travelling and eating out as often as you can.
weekend_recommendations: In Tokyo itself, you could spend months exploring different neighborhoods. For short trips, I would highly recommend places like Karuizawa, Nikko, Kamakura, Kawagoe, and various nearby mountains such as Mt. Mitake, Mt. Takao or Mt. Fuji. If you have more time, it is worth exploring Hokkaido and the Kansai region. Travelling abroad is also easy, for example Seoul, Hong Kong or Shanghai.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy overall. Of course, there were many differences compared to what I was used to at home, but most of them were positive and simply part of the adventure of living in Japan. Everyday life in Tokyo is very convenient, people are generally extremely polite and helpful, and public transportation makes it easy to get around. While some things—like the language barrier or certain bureaucratic processes—took a bit of getting used to, I never felt that it was overwhelming.
socializing_tips: Living in a dorm is definitely the best option, as it places you right at the center of social life and makes it much easier to meet both international and Japanese students. Beyond that, the most important advice is to be open-minded and willing to start conversations with as many people as you can. Joining shared meals, study groups, events, trips and so on is also a good way to build connections.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier was by far the biggest challenge. Many (in my experience most) Japanese people do not speaking English very well.
culture_appreciated: What I appreciated most was the incredible convenience of everyday life in Japan.I was also impressed by the overall cleanliness of the cities and public spaces. Finally, the friendliness and politeness of people stood out.
top3_advice: 1. Don’t let the initial paperwork and practical taskss care you off. It may feel overwhelming at first, but it is absolutely worth the effort once you arrive. 2. Be social and make the most of your time. Say yes to invitations, join group dinners, and spend time with the people around you. 3. Take the initiative. Be the one arranging trips, dinners, gatherings. 4. Use the course registration trial week wisely. Try out as many classes as possible, have strategic days off so you have time for longer travels. 5. Take time to explore Japan beyond Tokyo and explore the rest of Asia as much as possible. 6. Keep in touch with the friends you make at UTokyo.
other_useful_info: Nothing in particular that I haven’t already mentioned above.
most_rewarding: For me, the most rewarding aspects were the combination of academic, personal, and cultural experiences. On the academic side, it was a privilege to study at such a highly respected university and to learn from competent professors. On a personal level, I really valued the chance to use English on a daily basis and to interact with people from many different backgrounds. Finally, exploring a culture so different from my own was incredibly enriching.
greatest_challenge: The biggest challenge for me was finding the right balance between academic responsibilities and social life. In the end it was not overwhelming, and I feel that I managed to find a good rhythm.

crucial_aspects: First and foremost it had to be at an ambitious university, since I wanted to try studying at one of these world renowned institutions. Secondly it had to be someplace far away, so that I could experience a culture very different from my own.
overall_comments: I had a very nice and enriching experience, but the academic aspects did now quite live up to expectations.
info_ease: It was pretty easy. The university had made a really nice guide website, which had all the info you needed. A highlight included a timeline with loads of important deadlines! If anything it was almost a bit too much info, since the website seemed a bit daunting to begin with. However, it really was a great assistance.
arrival_assistance: I did not need any assistance, since the information was quite clearly laid out for me.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had a very nice and enriching experience, but the academic aspects did now quite live up to expectations.
registration_process: Very straight forward. There was a website with available courses for exchange students. Find the courses you want, go to the UTAS site and search for them, and press "Register" before the first week. For all my courses that was it, but for some more competitive courses there was a selection process. You could also drop any courses you wanted for the first few weeks, or even enroll in different ones, in case you changed your mind.
registration_help: Very swift help by mail, and some open offices where you could go and ask.
registration_success: Not very, since a lot of them were changed between applying for the university and actually enrolling. Although, after figuring out Japanese/English courses were in fact okay, I got some nice replacement courses anyway.
registration_advice: Be creative and make sure to try to apply for any course you like. Don't ask for permission, ask for forgivness.
academics_comments: I had a very nice and enriching experience, but the academic aspects did now quite live up to expectations.
course_level: The level of the courses was extremely varied. Some where trivial first and second year stuff, while others where more geared towards graduate students. Since they have four year undergrad programs in Japan, many courses are open for both fourth year undergrad students as well as graduates, so the level can vary a lot.
teaching_comparison: UCPH had way better teaching in almost all aspects, at least for my faculty. The lectures here were all 105 minutes long with no break, and only rarely any interaction between or with students. The assignments were confusing and sometimes poorly made, often with a distinct lack of connection to the stuff from the lectures. You are expected to take a lot of courses at once, so there is not enough time to read up on any one course, without getting behind in another. The exception is the language courses for learning Japanese, they were very nice.
courses_enrolled: Modern Physics and Machine Learning, Particle Physics, Quantum Field Theory II, Nuclear Physics, Data Chemistry, Non-equilibrium Physics, Quantum Chemistry III, Universal Biology, Japanese Beginning 4
recommended_courses: Of the courses I had: Nuclear Physics, Particle Physics, Japanese Language courses and maybe data chemistry. They also had a lot of courses called "Global Liberal Arts", which sounded quite fun, but just not for my field of study. I heard the Women in Science course was quite nice.
unexpected_costs: Not many unexpected, but a lot of things were just slightly more expensive than I had first assumed. Especially travel is expensive, if you want to go anywhere far.
cost_comparison: Food and rent first and foremost. The cheapest option at my dormitory was rent at 2500 dkk, but then they tack on utilities and maintenance, so in reality the minimum is over 4000 dkk. Eating out is about half the cost of Denmark, but cooking at home on a budget is actually a bit challenging, and can quickly add up to more than expected.
activities_available: There were loads of potential "circles" which you could join, but in order to get much out of them you kind of had to speak Japanese. They did have a few nice events aimed at international students throughout the semester, such as the International Lounge and various cultural events.
activities_recommended: The International Lounge (Friday lunch at Hongo campus) was a great opportunity to meet other students, both local and international. Cultural events such as tea ceremonies and workshops were also fun as well.
weekend_recommendations: There is too much to list here. Japan is full of stuff to do, Tokyo especially, and there is something for everyone, so it boils down to personal preference. One thing of note is that flights to neighbouring countries are super cheap, so it is also a great opportunity for a trip to South Korea or Taiwan.
culture_adjustment: No problem, Japan is a nice and safe country, so it feels very comfortable.
socializing_tips: It is unfortunatly quite difficult to socialize with local students. The absolute best way to do so would be to speak Japanese, and then to join a circle and make friends there. If you don't speak Japanese, which most of course don't, then the International Lounge is a nice place as well.
cultural_challenges: I spoke with some other international students, and there are almost three distinct barriers with the Japanese students. First and foremost there is a language barrier, since most of them don't speak much English. Secondly there is a cultural barrier, since our background and life is so different from theirs. Third is a personal barrier. There is a tendency in Japan, to stay within somewhat professional relations, which does make it difficult to build lasting friendships.
culture_appreciated: The politeness and respect for other people. The general level of safety and consideration of others' comfort.
top3_advice: I would say try to learn at least some of the language, it is very fun and rewarding. And the earlier you start, the more you'll get out of it furing your stay. Also take a language course, since they are super fun. Try not to stress about passing the courses. As far as I can understand, it is not supposed to be difficult at all to get at least a passing grade. Make sure to travel and experience the country as much as possible.
other_useful_info: There is a lot of specifics.
most_rewarding: Experiencing the country and learning the language.
greatest_challenge: Maintaining motivation for my courses and making friends.

crucial_aspects: That it was far away geographically and culturally. I wanted to live a daily life in a setting I was not used to back home.
overall_comments: It was hard in the start to find a good rhythm in the daily life, but once I figured that out, it opened the door to many new experiences and things to do. There are of course so many things to do, and I only did a handful of them. It would probably take take a whole life to all the things you want to do, and that probably would not be enough either. I am happy with the things I managed to do, but I also want to go back for more experiences some day.
info_ease: Fairly easy. We got all the necessary information by mail, and although there were lots of mails to read through, it was pretty straight forward to know all the essential things to do. There was also a good website from the university which guided one through the whole procedure from start to finish.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any special assistance.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was hard in the start to find a good rhythm in the daily life, but once I figured that out, it opened the door to many new experiences and things to do. There are of course so many things to do, and I only did a handful of them. It would probably take take a whole life to all the things you want to do, and that probably would not be enough either. I am happy with the things I managed to do, but I also want to go back for more experiences some day.
registration_process: We had sort of 2 catalogues that showed the same courses. I used the public catalogue to find the courses I wanted to take and then found them again in the registration website. It was important to make sure that you picked the same courses, as some of them was called the same but had different course codes depending on whether you were undergrad or master's student. One of the courses I took I found on a flyer we got handed at the introduction, this was for courses specifically designed for exchange student. These courses also showed up in the public catalogue, but I would not have been made aware of them, if not for the flyer.
registration_help: I think we could always write them an email, but I didn't need help so I'm not exactly sure.
registration_success: Successful. There were room for anyone who wanted to join the classes I wanted. There was one course I wanted to take that I couldn't because it wasn't allowed for exchange students to take that course.
registration_advice: Do a proper search of which courses are available and what level they are on. I sometimes had to search other faculties than my main faculty, because some courses that was about something within my field was distributed by another faculty.
academics_comments: It was hard in the start to find a good rhythm in the daily life, but once I figured that out, it opened the door to many new experiences and things to do. There are of course so many things to do, and I only did a handful of them. It would probably take take a whole life to all the things you want to do, and that probably would not be enough either. I am happy with the things I managed to do, but I also want to go back for more experiences some day.
course_level: Technically I didn't take any Master level courses. But some of the courses I took had one course code for undergrad, and one course code for masters, and I was connected to the undergrad course code. So the level of the course could be argued to be on master level, even though it technically was a bachelor course for me.
teaching_comparison: I think that it's very hard to top the quality of the teaching at UCPH. Some of the lecturers were very good at teaching the subject matter in a cohesive and clear way, but there were also some whose explanations were hard to follow.
courses_enrolled: Modern Physics and Machine Learning Nuclear Physics Particle Physics Quantum Chemistry III Quantum Field Theory II Topics In Information Science II Universal Biology Women In Science
recommended_courses: Nuclear Physics, Particle Physics and Women In Science were definitely the courses that fit my level and abilities as a new 3rd year bachelor student the best. And they also fit my interests the best. I think Universal Biology, Topics In Information Science and Modern Physics and Machine Learning are also good courses if you are very interested in those subjects, but they were a bit harder I feel like.
unexpected_costs: Nothing
cost_comparison: Food in restaurant were pretty cheap compared to Denmark but vegetables and other groceries were more expensive.
activities_available: Football, baseball, Japanese kanji writing etc. I don't know how many or what they could be as I didn't partake in any, but there were definitely a bunch.
activities_recommended: Taking the trains, it is a joy. The public transport system is so good, especially in Tokyo, and local transportation is really cheap.
weekend_recommendations: Chiba prefecture, Nikko, Hiroshima, various sightseeing places in Tokyo, for example: Tokyo Tower, Ueno Park, Eastern Gardens and so on.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, I like the local culture a lot, people were very friendly.
socializing_tips: They are pretty shy towards foreign student a lot of the time if they can't speak English well. Some who can speak English are pretty out going and are looking for people to speak to, so those opportunities are definitely there.
cultural_challenges: Well, with the toilets you just have to press the button to spray water in your butt and get it over with as soon as you can, because it opens up new worlds of sitting at the toilet. It is definitely not something to be scared of. I didn't really think the differences were challenging as those differences was something I wanted to explore and seek out, so I was very open minded from the start. I think maybe the most challenging part was their very binary gender world view.
culture_appreciated: The people are kind and generous and helpful. People don't push each other on the metro and people were thoughtful of each other. It was like living in a giant bee hive where everybody did their part but still saw themselves, but importantly also each other, as individuals. Whereas in western society we only see ourselves as individuals, and always put our priorities before others.
top3_advice: Housing: There are two main choices when it comes to the housing provided by UTokyo: Mejirodai International Village (MIV) and Komaba Lodge (KL). The commute to Hongo campus is only 10 min faster by living at MIV, but the commute to Komaba campus is much faster by living at KL, as KL is right next to this campus. So it depends on which campus you are mostly going to be at, which means that you need to take a look at courses beforehand. Another thing is that MIV is clean, new and has good facilities and a good common area but it feels a bit like a prison sometimes, there are cameras everywhere, you are not allowed guests inside your room or on your floor, it is split up into binary genders and you have to have your keys with you to go to the toilet. Whereas KL is a bit dirty and old, but people are allowed to visit each other and I get the feeling that it's more open, it is also close to Shibuya if one like to party. I lived at MIV and I was happy living there, but I would also have been happy living at KL for other reasons. There are pros and cons of both places, so it's up to you to weigh them according to your needs. Lunch: You can become a member of Coop for a fee. Then you can get lunch for 20% off. The thing is, you get the fee back at the end if you remember to go to the office, so it's basicly free 20% off in the cafeterias and Coop shop if you have the membership. Local transportation: Depending on how many days of the week you are going to a campus, you can maybe make it cheaper for yourself if you get a transportation pass thing. I didn't get it because it was not worth it for me. Also: Get a PASMO card in the airport as you arrive, you need at least 2000 yen to get it, and it will be much easier in the long run to have it rather than buying tickets, so you might as well get it as the first thing when you arrive.
other_useful_info: There are 2 main cafeterias at Hongo campus: one is just in front and underground of the Yasuta auditorium, this is the largest cafeteria and has a bit more dishes than the second one, but you are underground. The other one is located right next to the bus stop and science buildings, in the same building as the Coop office thing. This cafeteria has windows and is less crowded at lunch time, so this was my favourite place to eat lunch. If you have classes both at Hongo and at Komaba I would recommend living at Komaba Lodge instead of MIV. But if you live at MIV, Ikebukuro and Iidabashi are pretty close by, only 2 metro stops in either direction on the Yurakucho line, and here there are a lot of places to get food and other things. If you want used books, CD's, LP's or Pokemon cards, go to BookOff, it is a really nice store with a lot of locations around Tokyo. I got a fairly rare CD from one of them for pretty cheap. There are also some pretty cool train lines at the harbour area that I can recommend to take. Also, if you arrive at Haneda Airport, I would highly recommend to take the Tokyo Monorail instead of the other train.
most_rewarding: Living a daily life in Tokyo.
greatest_challenge: Overcoming home sickness the first month, but it gets a lot better when starting courses and meeting a bunch of people.

crucial_aspects: I have a personal connection to Japan with friends in the north of the country. Therefore, Japan was an attractive destination to me. I had been there on multiple occasions and the possibility to live a few months in Tokyo was an exciting prospect.
info_ease: The Graduate School of Frontier sciences was very forthcoming with administrative help, yet finding relevant information was a bit like pulling teeth. Finding out how and when to register for classes was difficult and some of the info i received was misleading and led me to not be able to attend a course that I was excited about. That was frustrating.
arrival_assistance: Supervision, help with housing (did not take up this offer), administrative assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was messy. For a long time I was not sure what courses would actually be offered. The curriculum is only finalized rather late after I had applied for pre-approval. Luckily the curriculum of the previous year (the one found online) is quite accurate, but it added an unnecessary level of stress at the time not knowing if I would actually be able to take the courses. The registration is also overly complicated. As an exchange student I needed to hand in a physical course registration sheet with along with a physical approval of my supervisor. Then I was unable to take one of the courses I was officially registered for since there was a separate selection procedure internal to the course. This was frustrating, since the administrative office in my graduate school had told me I had to do nothing else if I was registered. I had to once again get a physical approval from my supervisor for a different course etc. etc. Moreover, there is a lack of understanding at many levels when it comes to exchange students, especially when you take courses at multiple graduate schools. Everyone seems to think that different rules and procedures apply.
registration_help: Administrative help and help from the supervisor.
registration_success: Mostly successful but the situation explained above was annoying.
registration_advice: Get in touch with the professors or teaching assistants of courses you want to take and inform them of your interest in the class and ask them whether there are any special requirements or procedures you should be aware of.
course_level: It varied very widely; some were extremely easy and basically free credits, others were quite tough and yet others again were easy but required far too much boring work.
teaching_comparison: Varies on the graduate school and the teachers. The better ones are extremely interactive and practical, and that in the political sciences. The more basic courses are about the same as in CPH, with one very important difference. The hours per class are a lot less, only 1:45 per week per class or so, so courses cannot go into depth on one subject. This is silly.
courses_enrolled: Graduate School of Public Policy / 5130076 International Organizations for Sustainable Development Graduate School of Public Policy / 5123485 Environmental Economics Graduate School of Frontier Sciences / 47220-98 Sustainability Science: Japanese Perspectives Graduate School of Frontier Sciences / 47221-37 Field Exercise on Sustainability Science Graduate School of Frontier Sciences / 47220-29 Fundamentals of Sustainability Science
recommended_courses: Graduate School of Public Policy / 5130076 International Organizations for Sustainable Development Great course. Every week you get speakers from different IOs, so you get real insights into the work in these organizations. The speakers change from year to year. This is followed by student discussions and then a Q&A. From a Climate Change standpoint maybe not always super relevant, but extremely interesting and engaging. Graduate School of Public Policy / 5123485 Environmental Economics Very tough course that could be taught better, but interesting and engaging. I do not agree with many of the concepts that were being taught, but it is good an important to understand how environmental economics functions. Don't come here for a critical approach to EE.
unexpected_costs: Taking a cab when the trains stop at midnight. Not recommended.
cost_comparison: Food and drinks. Also, public transport. I just had to commute a lot on one of the more "expensive trains" which added up. But per trip that expensive train was only 30 dkk.
activities_available: Not sure
activities_recommended: Travel
weekend_recommendations: Explore Tokyo and surroundings. Travel the country.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Only through classes.
cultural_challenges: Sometimes the politeness but not often.
culture_appreciated: Architecure, history, nightlife.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared for an administrative mess and be proactive in getting in touch with profs whose classes you want to take. 2. Reach out to internationals via available forums (we had a Whatsapp group) and make sure to join events. You will find your people quickly. 3. Take a few interesting classes but try to take most with little coursework if possible. You want to be able to enjoy your time and not be stuck summarizing academic papers each week just for the purpose of summarizing academic papers.
other_useful_info: Not as of now.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people. Living in an amazing city. Winter in the north.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to expand my academic knowledge on Japanese Film and society, and get a better understanding of intercultural communication.

arrival_assistance: Upon arrival we had a guide from the USTEP or Global office, which provided us with insights and knowledge on everyday life in Japan and the steps we needed to take in order to move in to accommodation and such.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: A link was provided to a webpage were you will out a registration. This was fairly easy, but make sure to collect all the needed data in prior, so that there will be no issues with your application.
registration_help: Serval emails were provided if you had any questions regarding the registration.
registration_success: I was successful in getting into all the classes I wanted, but please note that the globe program courses only have few studens - often below 20, so sign up as early as possible to make sure you get the courses you really want.
registration_advice: Read through the course catalog easily to get some inspiration for which courses you would like.
course_level: The levels were easier but, I also had a lot of courses compared to KU. Here I usually have two that are fairly heavy and in Japan I had ate, which varied in level.
teaching_comparison: The overall teaching style was very different depending on the course and the expectations the individual professor had. This is all bought to the attention of the students pretty early on - so make sure you don't load up on all the heavy courses but take various different level ons, so it doesn't tak up all you time.

unexpected_costs: The Kitchen supply that I had to go out and purchase - even though I thought it would be provided.
cost_comparison: The far traveling - if by train is pretty expensive I would suggest to use the bus.
activities_available: So there would be bon-bon parties and onigiri cooking classes - and other gatherings to get to know each other and befriend the local students.
activities_recommended: I would suggest for a trip to Hiroshima to learn about the history that Japan suffered after WWII
weekend_recommendations: Don't go to the super touristy parts, since they will be filled - but go on little hicks in the areas around them - and you can really find some hidden gems.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty thought not knowing the language, so that you can communicate with the locals - so I would suggest to take the courses and practice. Overall it all worked out in the end.
socializing_tips: I would suggest you ask them for their advice on what to see in Tokyo or Japan - and ask them to join your day trips. - and attend the Go Tutors events to meet the local students who are interested in International students.
cultural_challenges: Maybe the overall approachability, the Japanese seems a little closed off in the beginning, but give them time and get to know them, and there will be true and great friendships there.
culture_appreciated: The fact that everything runs so smoothly - the trains on time and that everyone is super polite towards each other.
top3_advice: Apply for more courses then you need and drop the additional ones, once you know which ones you get. Don't be afraid to ask a local student if they would like to hang out or do something together - for the most part they will say yes. Be open towards the Japanese culture and the people there - and share your own culture with them - so bring some snacks so they can learn about Denmark - they really are just as interested in you as you are in them :)
other_useful_info: Don't hesitate to reach out to the institution and ask them anything - they are quite good at replying quickly.
most_rewarding: The friendships that I made and the overall new cultural appreciation I have for other people - who might experience the world differently, but still have a lot in common with me.
greatest_challenge: Getting back into a more heavily course load, where you have serval different courses which may be about very different things - so it requires a lot of studying - but you also learn a lot.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to a country Ive never been to and also go to a good university.
overall_comments: Really great overall. One of the best experiences of my life.
info_ease: Very easy. UTokyo sends a lot (maybe even too much) information in advance and everything is organised really well.
arrival_assistance: We had a welcome event and everything related to the university and courses was explained there. We also got divided into smaller groups with UTokyo students (buddies) that were also always there to answer questions. There is also an office for exchange students on both campuses where you can talk to someone in person if there are any questions.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Really great overall. One of the best experiences of my life.
registration_process: You can look at the course catalogue beforehand but it is only finalised right before classes start. You get a two week trial period to sit in all the courses and then you register by the end of the two weeks. This is also recommended because many classes expect you to be there from the very beginning.
registration_help: The registration process was explained on orientation day and you could also reach out to your UTokyo buddies or the student office at all times.
registration_success: I got into all of the classes I wanted and also heard that the spots are overall not that competitive, so you should be able to get the courses you want.
registration_advice: Take the time to check out all the classes you are considering. Some are very different from the course description, so its good to get a feel for the course and lecturer before choosing it.
academics_comments: Really great overall. One of the best experiences of my life.
course_level: The level is overall quite low in the courses for exchange students aka the english speaking courses. Japanese students typically take a lot more courses than the exchange students so the individual level of each course is quite low and most of them only consist of a 1.5-2 hour lecture a week. Most classes take attendance, which is a bit annoying, but the requirements to get an A in a course are pretty low and the final exam is often just a short report or project.
teaching_comparison: Its similar I guess. You have a lecturer that gives a lecture. Perhaps there is a bit more participation expected from the students at UTokyo because some count participation as part of the grade.
courses_enrolled: I took Gender Data Gap, Environmental Economics, Development Economics, Chinese Diplomacy, Japanese Foreign Policy, and Start Up and Venture Capital.
recommended_courses: I liked Gender Data Gap, we talked about gender issues in data and it was a very interactive course, but no prior experience with data work was expected. The final grade consisted of a presentation and final report. Environmental and Development were okay, the level was quite low, and you just had to write a final report. Chinese Diplomacy and Japanese Foreign Policy were interesting if you are generally interested in the subjects. In both the final grade consists of the presentation of a paper and a final report. Start Up and Venture Capital was very fun. The lecturer used to be a VC head in Japan and has a lot of practical experience. We had to develop our own start up in groups which was super fun.
unexpected_costs: Nothing really unexpected. You do have to enrol in Japanese health insurance, even if you are already insured back home, but it is pretty cheap.
cost_comparison: It was pretty much how I expected. I went to eat out every meal (also a lot of Kombini and Canteen), but it is of course a bit more expensive than only cooking at home. Although it does not make that big of a difference in Japan and the food is so great. I also travelled quite a bit around Japan and China, which can get quite expensive as Shinkansen and flights are not that cheap. But if you can its so worth it! Japan is such a beautiful country and travelling around East Asia is also great.
activities_available: There are a lot of activities at UTokyo. They are divided into clubs and circles. Clubs are very competitive and train 4-6 times a week, so I would only join if you are up for this and already an expert at the sport/ activity. Circles are pretty chill and you can join at pretty much any level. I joined the Taekwando circle as a beginner, which was very fun. The only difficulty might be finding a club/ circle that accepts English speaking students, as a lot of them are in Japanese. But you can get a feel for this from the way they are presented on the website. There is also an info event for a lot of English speaking clubs and circles at the beginning of the semester, which I would really recommend going to!
activities_recommended: Join any circle you are interested in to learn something new and meet Japanese students!
weekend_recommendations: Go around Tokyo and Japan as much as you can there is so, so much to see! I went to Kyoto, Osaka, Nikko, Nagano (Shiga Kogen to ski), Hakone, and Okinawa in Japan. All were really great. I also went to Shanghai and Beijing in China which was also super fun. I would also recommend to stay in Japan a bit longer after the semester ends to travel more. We can live in the dorm until the end of March in the winter semester, which is really convenient.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Everything in Japan is so convenient and easy to understand. Japanese people are very polite and helpful so if you have any questions there is always someone to help.
socializing_tips: I became friends with my UTokyo buddies and met other local students through joining circles.
cultural_challenges: Most Japanese people do not speak English very well. Its not a big problem in daily life but it makes it a bit harder to immerse yourself in Japanese culture, because its harder to fully participate if you dont know the language.
culture_appreciated: The. food. is. amazing. !!
top3_advice: Go to the canteen a lot (and get a COOP membership early on for cheaper meals). Go around Tokyo and Japan as much as you can. Max out your stay in Japan by staying until the end of the semester (if possible)!
other_useful_info: Do not expect a crazy academic challenge and go more for the experience and culture! Its such an amazing opportunity we get to have by going on exchange.
most_rewarding: Meeting amazing people. There were other exchange students from all over the world and I made really great new friends. Also meeting Japanese people and hearing about their experiences and world views was very interesting.
greatest_challenge: Leaving and saying goodbye :(
other_comments: I would 100% go again (also to UTokyo over other Japanese universities), so I think you will have the best time as well!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to study in an Asian country since I have never been in Asia before.
overall_comments: Best time of my life so far.
info_ease: The University of Tokyo provides a comprehensive program timeline and to-do list that covers everything important for the exchange. This includes everything university related and also mandatory administrative procedures (residence registration, health care etc.). It's an easy to find and easy to understand google site that is continuously updated with relevant information.
arrival_assistance: There was a mandatory orientation day where the most important information was covered. We were then grouped with other people from the exchange program (ca. 8 people) and UTokyo students (1-2 people). The UTokyo students showed us the campus and we could ask them questions about campus life, life in Japan or whatever interested us. They would also organize social events with the group like day-trips to places around Tokyo, watching fireworks, dinners, visiting temples etc. throughout the whole duration of the semester.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Best time of my life so far.
registration_process: If you are a USTEP student, you search for courses you are eligible to take in the online course catalogue. Make sure you meet the language requirements if you want to take a course that is taught in Japanese. You must enroll in a minimum of 6 periods per week, which is very manageable. This means, even if KU requires you to only do 4 courses, for example, you still need to do 2 extra courses as required by UTokyo. You register your classes in the first weeks of the semester on UTAS and afterwards you use UTOL for class instructions etc.
registration_help: The University of Tokyo provides very clear instructions on how to register courses. You will find them in the aforementioned program timeline and to-do list.
registration_success: I was able to register every class that was pre-approved without any issues. I also tried to take a Japanese-language course but my level was too low to attend the Japanese-language beginners course. That confused me a bit. However, I could still do a non-credit Japanese-language course. Additionally, there are some popular classes with limited capacity (mostly film or photography related courses). You don't necessarily have to register them as fast as possible but it's very likely that they will be overfilled. The instructor will then either raffle or filter out by conducting a survey which you have to fill out in time.
registration_advice: If possible, try out new scientific fields you were always curious about. Also, the seemingly non-challenging courses about film etc. can be way more time-consuming and demanding than anticipated.
academics_comments: Best time of my life so far.
course_level: In my view, the courses were not as demanding as courses at KU. It shouldn't be an issue to achieve a passing grade. However, some classes bind grades to attendance, so sometimes you have to be careful not to miss any classes without a valid reason.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was quite similar. However, my courses consisted mostly of seminars, instead of larger lectures. For some classes we only had about 4-10 students which made it way more personal and interactive.
courses_enrolled: Venture Capital Food Safety and Risk Analysis Data Chemistry Research Methods and Japanese Foreign Policy Women in Science Chemistry Engineering Japanese (non-credit)
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the Venture Capital class and Data Chemistry. These courses had very intriguing topics and good instructors. I can also recommend doing a non-credit Japanese language course if you want to learn basic Japanese.
unexpected_costs: Nothing really unexpected but if you plan to travel around Tokyo and Japan, you will obviously face higher monthly transportation costs.
cost_comparison: Groceries, especially fresh fruit and vegetables were more expensive than I expected. On the other side, you can get meals in the canteen for very cheap if you get a COOP member card. Also a lot of places (museums, tourist attractions, parks etc.) have a student discount, so it never hurts to ask :)
activities_available: UTokyo has clubs and circles for nearly everything. Clubs are intensive and competitive while circles are more recreational – just keep that in mind. You can do all kinds of sports (e.g., football, volleyball, baseball, karate, archery etc.), cultural activities (e.g., japanese traditional music, tea ceremonies, art) and countless more social activities (e.g., poker, debating, model trains, beyblades, shooting or airplane flying). Just check out UT-Base online or look out for the wooden signs that are prominently displayed around campus to find your favorite clubs and circles.
activities_recommended: I can recommend joining at least one circle in order to have the full campus-life experience. Whatever you want to do, there will definitely be a club or circle for it. It is a good way to connect with local students. But it might be hard to join some circles if you don't speak Japanese.
weekend_recommendations: If you have the financial resources, you should definitely travel around Japan or even neighboring countries (China, Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam). Public transportation allows you to travel long distances cheaply and swiftly. There are a lot of beautiful places close by such as Nikko, Yokohama, Kamakura or Fuji. Tokyo is also such a vast city, so if you have time you should explore it as much as you can. You will always find something new and exciting. But of course, you shouldn't miss other bigger cities like Osaka, Kyoto or Hiroshima as well.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy, although it may take some time. You can always look up the do's and don'ts online or ask a person from Japan about proper social etiquettes. The rest is just exposure therapy.
socializing_tips: Socializing with local UTokyo students might be easiest if you can conversate in Japanese. Unfortunately, most Japanese students do not speak English on a level that is comparable to Danish or European standards. Nevertheless, you can still make friends with UTokyo students as I believe most people are good-willing and kind. Sometimes, you may find yourself be approached by curious students on campus, other times it doesn't hurt to make the first step yourself. A great way to organically meet local students is through clubs and circles.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier was stronger than I anticipated. Many people do not really speak English (fluently), so you might get into situations where you have to completely rely on a translation tool. Yet, people seem to appreciate it when you at least try to speak Japanese. I can recommend learning some essential Japanese phrases as preparation.
culture_appreciated: The food culture. You can find affordable restaurants with delicious meals everywhere, around the clock. I loved going out every day to eat and drink together with friends. It was something I could not afford doing as a student in Europe, especially Denmark.
top3_advice: Join a circle or club. Get the COOP member card for cheaper canteen meals. Travel around Japan as much as you can.
other_useful_info: If you want to impress random Japanese people, you can just tell them that you study at "Todai".
most_rewarding: Attending courses in academic fields I could not take previously as part of my studies and making new friends from many parts of the world.
greatest_challenge: Saying goodbye.
other_comments: I would go on exchange in Tokyo again if I could.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to choose a country that I found interesting, and I wanted to study in a bigger city. Besides, I wanted to study at a good university that had interesting courses that I could take. I also chose an English speaking country to improve my English and to ensure that my courses were internationally relevant.
overall_comments: Very good on a personal and social level. A bit of trouble with housing and other logistic aspects e.g., help/ with/information on credit transfer and such. Overall, very good experience.
info_ease: I found that it was not very readily available online, both with housing (independent from the university) and with the university as well, for instance about how many credits I would need to be a full time student, and whether I was accepted to my classes or not. The UofT websites are quite confusing, even with a login. Before the arrival, I had issues with applying for on-campus residence, which I originally wanted to do. A lot of information was restricted for me, and the one e-mail contact did not reply before the deadline.
arrival_assistance: The exchange student coordinator Andrew is very kind, and was helpful when I e-mailed him with questions. Besides this, there was not a lot of assistance.
arrival_comments: I could have needed a bit more information and guidance from both my home and destination university, e.g., an overview of deadlines and links etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Very good on a personal and social level. A bit of trouble with housing and other logistic aspects e.g., help/ with/information on credit transfer and such. Overall, very good experience.
registration_process: I don't quite remember the specifics, but my login came in an email, and I made an online appointment to get my student ID, which was easy to do. I registered for classes online as well, which I remember was a bit more tricky, but also fine.
registration_help: We had an e-mail to our coordinator Andrew.
registration_success: Not that succesful. Two of my top three choices were not created - I got in to two of my five choices. I had to find additional classes, which took a while to get accepted, even after the classes had started.
registration_advice: Make a document with all the information in the many e-mails/other contact information you have received beforehand, and don't be afraid to e-mail all of them, if you're not sure which one is the right for you to contact. This way, you will find a contact you can ask questions to if you have problems with registration. Don't be afraid to reach out to other exchange students in real life or online, or even regular students who might know where the physical office is located.
academics_comments: Very good on a personal and social level. A bit of trouble with housing and other logistic aspects e.g., help/ with/information on credit transfer and such. Overall, very good experience.
course_level: I had two third year courses which was my major (economics), and one course at 1 year level at another, closely related major (political science).
teaching_comparison: Mostly similar, but some differences. There is more contact between the professor and students, which might be because the classes were smaller. There is more debate at UofT than UCPH, which I appreciated. The curriculums felt a bit scattered. Grading at UofT also differs a lot, which I did not necessarily appreciate. I did not like the teaching style of the tutorials as much, and it is strange that our tutorial tutor is not the TA - the ones who teach us are not the ones who grade us, which makes it complicated when getting and understanding feedback on essays.
courses_enrolled: ECO302H5 ECO335H5 POL115H5
recommended_courses: I will recommend ECO335H5. It is a small class which allows for more questions. Very interesting and relevant course with materials that updated every week.
unexpected_costs: Very expensive to have a phone number and data (300DKK). Taxes on every purchase as well as culturally mandatory tips. A lot of processing fees when paying with an international card, both in person and online. High living costs. It is important to be aware of changing exchange rates as well.
cost_comparison: More expensive: housing, phone bill, transportation, groceries. Nothing was less expensive than expected except maybe Starbucks.
activities_available: I believe there were many, but I am not sure as I didn't attend any.
activities_recommended: I have no recommendations specifically, but I would recommend joining one to meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend Montreal and Banff. Traveling is a bit expensive, but worth it with friends, since you get to experience more of the country. Taking one-day hikes is also great for bonding and getting a break from the city. I personally believe that it is more worth it to spend more on a vacation some weekends, and then doing less expensive activities (like a dinner party) other weekends rather than many restaurants etc.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. The culture is not very different. The hardest part was getting used to the amount of homelessness.
socializing_tips: Talk to the people in your class. However, I mostly socialized with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: The social culture at the university is different, and it is harder to get into as an exchange student.
culture_appreciated: The outgoing, friendly attitudes of the Canadians. The culturally inclusivity as well.
top3_advice: Consider whether you want to live downtown, even if your campus is Scarborough or Mississauga - there are more opportunity/life there, but there is also travel time. Attend the first couple of events for exchange students, and don't be afraid to reach out during and after - other exchange students also don't know anybody and are looking for friends. Ask the local students what they do for fun/what is worth to do. In Canada the night life is quite different, but it is fun wherever the students are - they know the best places and are very open to include you.
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of.
most_rewarding: I did experience a lot of personal development and have made life-long friends. Having to figure out everything on my own and succeeding is also a very rewarding feeling.
greatest_challenge: The logistical aspects, before, during and after the exchange.

arrival_assistance: They showed me where my housing were when i arrived and there were a service desk I could ask for help if needed

teaching_comparison: The lecture are similar. The tutorials are more about you getting help with the assignments than about the readings.

recommended_courses: ENV201H5 - Enviromental Management GGR361H - City planning and development Both really interesting and the structure where really good
unexpected_costs: That the natur parks had fees often

activities_recommended: I joined a lot of the yoga classes
weekend_recommendations: Montreal is a nice city 6 hour away which were nice.
