crucial_aspects: I was looking for a city and university that could provide a wide range of cinema courses and additional courses, which I would not have the opportunity to find at the University of Copenhagen. I ended up choosing Toronto because of the way the city centers cinematic events, and because of UofT's cinema program. Furthermore, Toronto is a diverse and multicultural city, which I wished to find as well during my exchange program. Toronto has a big city life, where different cultures meet, but is also surrounded by much beautiful nature. So it is easy to get all the good aspects of Canada.
info_ease: UofT was good at providing information upon arrival. The professors were good at handing out maps to find the classrooms, and if there were ever any questions, I could easily call someone and ask for help.
arrival_assistance: I was provided with a mentor, who was either an exchange student who had been here since August/September or a Torontonian citizen- and UofT student. The mentor was connected to 5-6 exchange students and helped out with finding our way around the campus and how to access university facilities such as fitness and creativities.
arrival_comments: The whole orientation was good, but often updates were needed due to Covid.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You have to fill in a Google Sheets document and apply for the courses you have an interest in. There will be three different rounds, where you can apply for courses and drop them.
registration_help: It is easy to contact the university for help. They usually answer within a couple of days. Also, check the 'timetable' for available courses.
registration_success: I did not get the courses I wished for at first, but the courses I ended up with were great! Many courses have a wide title and therefore, the professor chooses an overall theme for the course. I had a course called Special Topics in Cinema as a Social and Cultural Practice, which ended up being a course in Film Festivals. It was so great, and not a course you would find in DK. In the end, I could not picture having other courses than the ones I had, and I would not have changed anything if I could. What to take from this is that you might have to compromise with courses, but in the end, they are all really good and it is good to try out something you may not have picked as your first priority. For me, however, three out of four of my courses would have been my first priority of I knew of them to begin with.
registration_advice: Register for something that is not a part of your program, but still has a connection to your program! I chose a course in gender studies called 'queer and transgender studies,' which easily may be applied to cinema courses and the representation of queer and transgender people on the global screen.
course_level: The course levels are a little easier than those at the University of Copenhagen. The readings are the same level and difficulty, but more free creativity is included in assignments and finals. However, if you choose a course you have not had before, then maybe not choose a third-year course as that will be slightly difficult to follow.
teaching_comparison: You have to engage in classes for grades, which is very different!
courses_enrolled: CIN340H1 - Special Topics in Cinema as a Social and Cultural Practice (overall topic: Film festivals) CIN260H1 - Selected Topics in Cinema Studies (overall topic: The Global Romantic Comedy) CIN380H1 - Global Screen Worlds WGS376H1 - Studies in Queer and Trans
recommended_courses: ALL OF THEM! If you can find a course where Carrie Reese teaches, you should not question it. I had two courses with her, and she is a great and fun professor. Global Screen Worlds is always taught each semester, and it is very knowledgeable. I had fun with all my cinema courses and attended a lot of screenings as well. The course I had in Queer and Trans was as well very very giving and fun to engage in. You learn how to be critical of what you read and express your own opinion, which is very refreshing to include in academics.
unexpected_costs: Toronto is a very expensive city and grocery shopping is expensive unless you do it in the right places! Phone bills are expensive as well.
cost_comparison: Groceries and phone bills.
activities_available: Fitness, music lessons, choir, group workout, film classes, running clubs, hockey, basketball, planting, yoga, etc. You can do everything you think of.
activities_recommended: Go to Barre! It is a group workout with an instructor that happens every Monday to Thursday morning/evening. It is 45 minutes of full-body workout sessions and so much fun (and tough).
weekend_recommendations: Go to Montréal and Vancouver, or rent a cabin out of the city and do some hiking! Explore the city because it has so much to offer! I always find myself wanting to try something new and I never feel like running out of stuff to do. Toronto has different neighborhoods such as Chinatown, Koreatown, Little Italy, Greektown, etc. There is a lot of nature in the area as well, which is easy to access.
culture_adjustment: Very easy! Everyone is so friendly.
socializing_tips: Never be afraid to reach out or start talking to someone! Canadians are very friendly people and if you just walk up to someone and say hello, then you probably already made a friend.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The diversity. You find every culture in Toronto.
top3_advice: 1) Don't expect that you can choose any course on the registration list! The only courses available can be found in the timetable. 2) Make sure to attend clubs and sports linked to the university, and also attend the university sports matches! 3) Choose one course that is not a part of your program at home. Something fun and different!
other_useful_info: Libraries are free for students and cozy to study at.
most_rewarding: Making friends from all over the world and finding a new home on the other side of the planet.
greatest_challenge: Balancing social life and school. I cared about my courses because I liked them so much. But at the same time, I wanted to spend most of my time exploring the city - especially during exam periods.
other_comments: Go to Toronto if you consider it!!

crucial_aspects: Destination: Toronto, Canada. The cross-cultural atmosphere that fills everyday life in Toronto is one of the main reasons why I chose an exchange stay at University of Toronto (UofT) really appealing. In addition, UofT has the reputation of being among the best in the world and has a highly recognized faculty of economics, which is essential for me studying economics.
overall_comments: I had an amazing experience. The only thing was that the first month in Toronto was in lockdown, and the University was online for the first two months.
info_ease: It was ok despite the fact that I arrived in a lockdown. The online system is quite similar to the one at University of Copenhagen.
arrival_assistance: I only had contact with the exchange office if I had questions, they never contacted me. However, when you contacted the exchange office they were always sweet and helpful.
arrival_comments: We had one online orientation, but due to Covid we did not have any get together events through UofT. It would have been nice with more social gatherings for exchange students through the University.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had an amazing experience. The only thing was that the first month in Toronto was in lockdown, and the University was online for the first two months.
registration_process: You had to sent a document for each course you wanted to be listed in. As an exchange student you are not able to click through the system the same way as normal registered students. So, it was a lot of work! Also with getting new pre-approvals from University of Copenhagen.
registration_help: The office. They were busy, but quick and very helpful.
registration_success: I got most of the courses I wanted to.
registration_advice: It takes a lot of work if you are a graduate student (in Denmark) applying for undergraduate courses at UofT, because getting pre-approvals from UCPH and also be approved to take the course at UofT can be very complicated. However, it all works out, and the office is very helpful. Just be patient.
academics_comments: I had an amazing experience. The only thing was that the first month in Toronto was in lockdown, and the University was online for the first two months.
course_level: 300 and 400 level courses, which is considered 3rd and 4th year courses. The level was definitely ok.
teaching_comparison: Very similar, lectures each week and in some courses additional TA-hours. However, one of the big differences is that you are judged by hand-ins, midterms and final exams. So, your grade is depended on work during the entire semester and not only exam. I really liked this structure.
courses_enrolled: - Market Design (400-level) - Health Economics (300-level) - Markets, Competetion, and Strategy (300-level) - Energy and Environment, Economics, Politics, and Sustainability (400-level)
recommended_courses: I was a big fan of 'Market Design' and 'Energy and Environment, Economics, Politics, and Sustainability'. Both of these courses had one big final paper. For the market design course I had to develop a mechanism, that solved a market problem, and for the Energy-course, I had the chance to write about the current gas-crisis in Europe. This was really interesting to me. I like when I can use my knowledge in a real situation.
unexpected_costs: Groceries were much more expensive than expected.
cost_comparison: Groceries are very expensive! Canada is importing many food products, so vegetables and fruits are more expensive compared to Danish prices. However, going out to eat was not that expensive compared to making food at home. So, you have an incentive to explore the many great restaurants in Toronto :)
activities_available: I was a part of a choir and used the athletic center a lot with friends.
activities_recommended: Especially to use the many difference athletic options that UofT offers.
weekend_recommendations: Go out and enjoy the many good food spots in Toronto. It's affordable and very good.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Canada is not that different from Denmark as I would expect other places to be.
socializing_tips: Make sure to be a part of the exchange WhatsApp groups, and maybe also some of the discord groups.
cultural_challenges: There are quite a lot of homeless people, and that was hard for me to accept.
culture_appreciated: The diversity in Toronto is amazing, and that is also reflected at the University.
top3_advice: -> Save money before traveling and apply for scholarships, so you can explore and travel while being there - Canada is AMAZING -> Explore Toronto and its diversity -> Join WhatsApp and Discord chats. It's where (exchange) students connect.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: I have learned and experienced so many things during the last 5 months. However, the most rewarding part must be the many new friends I have made through these months. I have made friends for a life time.
greatest_challenge: Being apart from family and friends back home. I'm very close to my family and friends in Denmark, so being apart from them for so long definitely was a challenge. However, it was worth it, and you meet so many new interesting people, that the 5 months goes by so fast. Before you know it, you are back home again.
other_comments: You should definitely study abroad. It is an amazing opportunity and a life time experience.

crucial_aspects: Most important was academic opportunities. However, practicality also played a role, where I at University of Toronto (UofT) was able to find two courses replacing mandatory courses for my degree.
overall_comments: University of Toronto and the city of Toronto was overall a good place for studying abroad. I was able to find very interesting courses, there was many exchange students at UofT hence many opportunities to socialize and Toronto was a nice city to live in. My overall rating of the stay is influenced negatively by the limitations because of Covid-19 during the stay and the different educational system.
info_ease: The only information, which was difficult to find (changing a lot) was information regarding Covid-19 travel restrictions to Canada.
arrival_assistance: The inbound exchange office provided us with the necessary information regarding the academics and to some extent Covid-19 restrictions. Unfortunately, because of Covid-19 was orientation online.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: University of Toronto and the city of Toronto was overall a good place for studying abroad. I was able to find very interesting courses, there was many exchange students at UofT hence many opportunities to socialize and Toronto was a nice city to live in. My overall rating of the stay is influenced negatively by the limitations because of Covid-19 during the stay and the different educational system.
registration_process: From what I remember, the inbound exchange office email us google forms we used to apply for the courses. I think there was in total 3 applications rounds, since it is not certain that you will receive all the courses you applied for in a given round.
registration_help: All the relevant information was provided by the inbound exchange office, and I didn't needed additional information/ help.
registration_success: I was quite lucky and was able to get 4 out of 5 courses I applied for in the first round. The only course I didn't get was cancelled. However, two of the courses had waitlists with +200 students and therefore very sought after, which is the reason I feel quite lucky with the registration process. In the second round I applied for my final course and was placed on the waiting list. I got into the course before the start of the semester.
registration_advice: Apply as soon as you get the google forms from the inbound exchange office. Additionally, I prepared documents with course descriptions from KU translated to justify having the necessary prerequisites. From what I remember they were quite strict in relation to prerequisites. Finally apply for as many courses in the first round as possible. You can always drop courses afterwards.
academics_comments: University of Toronto and the city of Toronto was overall a good place for studying abroad. I was able to find very interesting courses, there was many exchange students at UofT hence many opportunities to socialize and Toronto was a nice city to live in. My overall rating of the stay is influenced negatively by the limitations because of Covid-19 during the stay and the different educational system.
course_level: I feel the courses in general had a lower theoretical level compared to UCPH but then covered more topics.
teaching_comparison: It was very different and quite difficult going from normally focusing on two courses to have five courses simultaneously. Furthermore, the courses in general had many elements contributing to the final grade in forms of discussions, assignments, midterms, final exam, group projects or quizzes. In one of the courses, I had in total 28 elements contributing to the final grade. The intensity of the semester and overall workload was therefore higher at UofT. I feel the teaching style reminded me more of the teaching style in gymnasium rather than at UCPH. My feeling from group projects, lectures, and discussions with other students in the courses was that they were a lot more focused on grades rather than learning the topics/theory covered. Likewise, I sometimes had the feeling that the lectures were too focused on the final exam/ assignments.
courses_enrolled: APM236: Application of Linear Programming ECO326: Advanced Economic Theory, Game Theory STA302: Method of Data Analysis 1 STA314: Statistical Methods for Machine Learning 1 ECO372: Data Analysis and Applied Econometrics in Practice
recommended_courses: I was able to have APM236 replace OR1 and ECO326 replace MikØk2. However, the courses I enjoyed the most was the three other courses. In general, for all 5 courses the professor was very good at teaching and communicating their knowledge. STA314 covered both supervised and unsupervised machine learning. The pace of the course was very intense, and the course covered a lot of algorithms: K-NN, decision trees, linear regression, logistic regression, ensembles, SVMs, PCA, K-means and probabilistic models. And general methods: maximum likelihood, entropy, optimization with gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent, and Bayesian inference. The implementing part of the course is doable, but I spend quite some time on the assignments with python programming. STA302 is in the beginning covering theory of linear regression, which I had before in previous courses but in the end introduce topics like Box-Cox transformation of variables, Akaike Information Criterion, Bayesian Information Criterion, backwards selection, forwards selection and stepwise selection within linear regression. Finally, is the focus more practical and I wrote a final report using the IMRAD structure, which I think is a good exercise before a bachelor thesis. ECO372 focussed on when you can conclude causality from observational data in an economic setting. The course introduced first the Rubin causal model, which is a framework using potential outcomes to estimate causal effects. In the end of the course, the lectures also covered some of the methods developed by Angrist and Imbens for which they received a Nobel price in Economics in 2021. The course was interesting because it focused on many recent research papers.
unexpected_costs: I had to travel to Stockholm to get the student visa, which was unexpected. No other major unexpected costs related to the exchange but the cost of travelling round Canada was a bit higher than expected.
cost_comparison: Food in groceries stores was more expensive than expected but eating out was a bit less expensive than expected. Getting a Canadian phone plan was also expensive, and I ended using my Danish phone plan with international coverage.
activities_available: Explained in the previous comment.
activities_recommended: I would recommend socializing with the other exchange students. There was many other exchange students and I enjoyed socializing with many interesting people from all over the world.
weekend_recommendations: I enjoyed exploring Toronto, which have many things to offer. I went to a couple of NBA games and really liked the atmosphere. Toronto is also very diverse, and you can therefore find many interesting places to eat or grab a drink. I can also recommend attending Toronto International Film Festival. Finally, going out on road trips was also very nice and Canada/Ontario has a lot of nice places. I can recommend Algonquin Park, Bruce Peninsula National Park and Killarney Provincial Park.
culture_adjustment: I didn't have any difficulties at all.
socializing_tips: I socialized mostly with other exchange students. I feel like Covid-19 limited socializing with many of the local students e.g. part of the lectures was online and restrictions on campus.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any cultural differences challenging.
culture_appreciated: The diversity in Toronto!
top3_advice: Be good at prioritizing, since it was difficult to balance both socializing with exchange students and following the interesting courses. Go out on road trips away from Toronto and experience some of the local culture and amazing nature.
other_useful_info: Not additional to what I have already wrote.
most_rewarding: Interesting courses and the relationships with some of the other exchange students.
greatest_challenge: Covid-19.

crucial_aspects: There were a lot of different aspects that I found important when choosing my destination. First of all I chose Canada since I have been very fascinated by the country and would like to go there and experience their culture and learn about the country. I have also heard that University of Toronto (UofT) is a very good university and I therefore hope that it can have a small effect on future carrier options that I went there for a semester. However, for most part it was important that I chose a destination that I found very attractive and where the culture and values reminded me slightly of back home, so I wouldn't feel too foreign in a place I had to live in for four months.
overall_comments: My overall study abroad experience was amazing, but UofT was absolutely horrible at facilitating meet-ups for exchange students... I, and all the others were extremely lucky that we figured it out ourselves, but UofT made no effort what so ever in contributing to our social lives.
info_ease: It was really easy... It's been a while since then, but I don't recall I had any problems with finding the necessary information
arrival_assistance: I was a member of a Facebook group for all exchange students that helped a lot and provided some information, but otherwise we were a lot left on our own. UofT's systems however was quite easy to navigate in after everything had been set up (Student card etc.)
arrival_comments: I don't know if all this is a lot due to covid... All orientation was online which might have impacted my experience a lot. I have no clue on who to write if I had any problems, but there wasn't any major problems I couldn't solve myself, and they had some clear how-too's on their website on how to set up all the UofT-platforms etc., that was really helpful. A good thing to remember is that you can always write to the student-exchange mail, and then they will help you. That's what they are for.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My overall study abroad experience was amazing, but UofT was absolutely horrible at facilitating meet-ups for exchange students... I, and all the others were extremely lucky that we figured it out ourselves, but UofT made no effort what so ever in contributing to our social lives.
registration_process: As an exchange student you just receive a mail on how to register for courses. The registration process itself was really easy, but finding out what kind of courses I was allowed to take was reallt difficult. However, they also had a guide in the top of their registration process, which made it so much easier. Overall, if you just take your time to understand the system, then it really isn't difficult, but actually quite intuitive.
registration_help: I don't remember needing help for registration so I actually don't know... But there is always the exchange mail you can write to and get some help if needed.
registration_success: Very succesful. I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Take your time to understand their system, then it's quite easy... And registre as quick as possible for the courses you are sure you want. Some courses fill up quite fast, so the faster you are the more sure you'll be you get the courses you want.
academics_comments: My overall study abroad experience was amazing, but UofT was absolutely horrible at facilitating meet-ups for exchange students... I, and all the others were extremely lucky that we figured it out ourselves, but UofT made no effort what so ever in contributing to our social lives.
course_level: I found the courses difficulty at UofT very fitting for me. I primarily chose 200level courses, which is second year courses on the BA and therefore were supposed to be lower level than what I am (I went on fifth semester, meaning third year), but I think it's important to remember that your classes aren't taught in your native language. It wasn't hard to follow, but I found the level I chose very fitting.
teaching_comparison: I feel like I was thrown back to High-school some days (Gymnasiet). We had to do some assignments in each course during the semester as well as tests or discussion posts. I felt like we were kept an eye on all the time, which I am not sure I liked... But at the same time it was a way of ensuring that we kept up with the class and readings. Then our final grade is a mix of how well we did in these different aspects during the semester. It was definetly a lot different than the style of teaching at UCPH where everyone just have to perform at the exams... There are pros and cons on both teaching styles I think, but it was difficult getting used to in the beginning.
courses_enrolled: Sociology of Crime and Deviance (SOC212H1 F), Urban Sociology (SOC205H1 F), Introduction to Environmental Studies (ENV100H1 F).
recommended_courses: Urban Sociology was a nice course. It was really interesting and I feel I gained a lot of new knowledge. - The same for Sociology of Crime and Deviance, however I didn't really like the professor and also found the course really stressful because the tests we had to do was terrible.
unexpected_costs: I don't think I had any unexpected costs actually... A small thing could be that you always forget that the prices listed (on everything!!) is without tax (around 13%) and you ALWAYS have to tip... So things in general were always a different price than at first anticipated.
cost_comparison: Groceries were a lot more expensive for some reason in Canada... Especially vegetables. Their phone services (Canadian SIM-card) is also way too expensive in my opinion. Coffee was on the otherhand a lot cheaper and dining out in general slightly cheaper than in Denmark.
activities_available: They have a lot of different options for sports and working out. But that's it. I think they might have a lot of cultural and social options as well, but because of Covid I think the different offers weren't too visible.
activities_recommended: Do some sports! Go with some other exchange students and try some different things out.
weekend_recommendations: Niagara Falls is of course a must, and I think it is quite easy to go Algonquin National Park or Montreal for a weekend, but actually I would suggest just to explore Toronto. Go to Toronto Islands, visit clubs and bars and restaurants, the distillery district, and the CN tower with some of your new exchange-friends from other countries. Don't look at exchange as you have to see the entire country you are visiting, because that's not possible. Instead, just try to get the experience of living and feeling at home in another city. That experience is quite remarkable as well.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy since Canada is also largely a part of the Western culture. However, the locals always start a sentence with "Hi, how are you doing", and you should just answer "I'm fine, how are you doing", but don't expect anymore than that. They are just being polite.
socializing_tips: I didn't do that a lot, I primarily hung out with other exchange students from other countries, so unfortunately, no.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find any cultural differences challenging, I think.
culture_appreciated: I don't really know... Maybe I appreciated that it reminded me largely of Denmark so I could focus on getting to know the people and the country instead of thinking of how to fit in.
top3_advice: 1. Don't use too much time on studying... A big part of going on exchange is also experiencing the culture and getting to know a lot of exchange students from other countries. - Networking! 2. You are left a lot to yourself, and even though there are mails you can write to for help you should be prepared to figure a lot of things out yourself. It can be challenging but also very valuable in the end to know that you did it. 3. Choose to study at St. George campus if possible! UofT has three campuses, but the other two (Scarborough and Missisauga) are a bit fare out of Toronto. St. George is in the middle of Toronto and close to downtown, which is where you want to be.
other_useful_info: A lot of people say that you should go on exchange alone/by yourself, but I went with two other girls from my study at UCPH... It was a coincidence, but for me it was the best decision to go with someone I slightly knew... It helped me a lot. So do what's best for you and don't let other tell you that it is wrong to go with someone you know in advance. As long as you are still open-minded and willing to get to know new people and hang out with them as well.
most_rewarding: Might be a bit of a cliche, but I had some personal problems before going so that I got through my exchange and still see it as an amazing experience is a huge victory for me.
greatest_challenge: Being fare away from my best friends and family for four months and feeling really alone sometimes.

arrival_assistance: Der var guides på universitetets hjemmeside, og man fik tilsendt en masse mails - de var dog ikke særligt gode til at svare på nogen spørgsmål.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Man søger kurser i flere runder. Der var en detaljeret guide til hvordan det foregik.
registration_help: Udover information på hjemmesiden, skal man ikke regne med meget hjælp.
registration_success: I første ansøgningsrunde, fik jeg kun tildelt halvdelen af de kurser jeg søgte, men det lykkedes mig at få nogle andre i næste runde.
registration_advice: Søg i første runde, og sørg for at have læst kravene grundigt igennem.
course_level: Alle mine kurser var på 300-niveau, hvilket passede meget godt med hvad jeg var vant til hjemmefra.
teaching_comparison: Der er betydelig flere tests og opgaver end på KU. Tit tæller den endelige eksamen kun for 20-35 pct., mens resten af karakteren kommer fra opgaver og quizzer i løbet af semesteret.
courses_enrolled: Jeg tog tre kurser - normalt skal man have fem for at have full course load, men KU angav at jeg ikke behøvede at tage flere. Det skal man være glad for - hvis man tager fem kurser, skal man være indstillet på rigtig meget arbejde! - Canadian Arctic & Subarctic Environments: 8/10 - Resource & Environmental Theory: 5/10 - Water Resource Management: 1/10
recommended_courses: Undgå for guds skyld Water Resource Management! Hvis man er interesseret i naturgeografi, var udvalget ikke særlig godt på St. George - jeg tror man skulle have været ude på Mississauga.
unexpected_costs: Mobiltelefoni er virkelig dyrt i Canada. Jeg fik efter omstændighederne en fin deal, men betalte stadig ca. 250 kr. om måneden for 10 Gb data.
cost_comparison: Normalt kan som dansker rejse næsten hele verden rundt, med undtagelse af Norge og tildels Schweiz, og regne med at betale mindre for tingene end man gør derhjemme - ikke i Toronto. At handle ind i Toronto er rigtig dyrt, og der er et temmelig begrænset udvalg. At gå på bar i Toronto er lige så dyrt som herhjemme, men øllene smager elendigt. Offentlig transport er ineffektivt, men til gengæld prissat som i Danmark. Man skal ikke tro man er taget til USA. For det første kommer der 13 pct. vat oven i næsten alle priser, og hvis man spiser/drikker ude, skal man også betale tips (min. 15 pct., men helst omkring 18-20 pct.). Oven i det kan man så lægge diverse bankgebyrer, så man ved aldrig helt hvad man har betalt før det dukker op på kontoen. Det eneste positive (prismæssigt) er, at det er forholdsvist billigt at tage ud og spise på restaurant, og der er et stort udvalg af spisesteder.
activities_available: Det var svært at få et overblik, og jeg tror corona gjorde det sværere. Når det er sagt, så der var mange gode sportsfaciliteter, og man kunne dyrke de fleste sportsgrene.
activities_recommended: Jeg ville klart anbefale (hvis man kan lide at dyrke sport), at melde sig ind i Intramurals. Kort sagt dyster de forskellige colleges på universitetet i en masse sportsgrene, og alle er velkomne. Jeg spillede fodbold for mit college (som jeg fik tildelt tilfældigt da jeg startede), og spillede en masse kampe. Det er en god måde at møde canadiere på!
weekend_recommendations: Toronto er en stor by, og der er da også meget at se og lave, men man skal ikke forvente New York. Udover den relativt lille kerne, er meget af byen forholdsvis tom og hovedsageligt residential. Man skal gå rundt og udforske byen, for der en masse fede "etniske kvarterer" (Koreatown, Little Portugal, mv.), som man klart ikke finder i København. Udover det fungerer byen lidt som et fængsel - den er alt for stor til at man kan tage offentlig transport ud af den, så med mindre man lejer en bil, er det begrænset hvor meget af nærområdet man får set. Hvis man ikke har været i Canada før, ville jeg anbefale en dagstur til Niagara Falls (tager ca. 2 i tog - gør det imens der er varmt), og ellers at leje en bil og køre østpå mod Quebec. Montreal og Quebec City er begge fine byer (drop Ottawa, det er udelukkende en administrationsby), og der ligger en masse flotte nationalparker. Faktisk ville jeg klart anbefale at tage til Montreal på udveksling i stedet (hvis man ikke er bange for fransk), det virkede som en betydeligt mere spændende by. Generelt er det vestlige Canada noget mere storslået naturmæssigt, og det er klart et visit værd hvis man ikke har været der før. Igen ville jeg klart anbefale at tage til Vancouver i stedet for T.O., med mindre man kun vil have byoplevelsen. Ps. Tag ind og se noget sport, de har både baseball, fodbold, basketball og ishockey (men det er rimelig pebret).
culture_adjustment: Udover de canadiske flag og cannabisbutikkerne, er Toronto som en hvilken som helst anden anonym, grim, amerikansk storby. Hvis man har været i USA før bliver man næppe overrasket. En positiv ting er dog, at byen føles meget tryg - jeg følte mig aldrig utilpas, til trods for at byen er så stor som den er.
socializing_tips: Det bliver ikke helt nemt. Det var meget svært at få kontakt til dem i undervisningstimerne, da der ikke var nogen social interaktion, og professorerne ofte droppede pauserne. Jeg mødte nogen til sport, og det er formentlig den nemmeste måde at gøre det på. Generelt hang de udvekslingsstuderende meget ud med hinanden - ikke at det nødvendigvis er et problem, da der er rigtig mange udvekslingsstuderende.
cultural_challenges: Der er en masse småting der kan hobe sig op, men det er altid tilfældet når man flytter til et nyt land.
culture_appreciated: Svært at sige...
top3_advice: 1. Overvej om Toronto er det rigtige sted i Canada. 2. Find bolig i god tid, så du ikke skal stresse over det. 3. Engager dig i det sociale - du får formentlig ikke noget ud af det akademiske alligevel, så mor dig i stedet.
other_useful_info: Hvis man gerne vil have storbyoplevelsen, så tag til New York eller Asien. Toronto er en kæmpe stor landsby. Hvis man gerne vil opleve noget natur, eller noget ægte canadisk kultur, er Toronto ikke den rigtige by at gøre det i.
most_rewarding: Det var sgu rart at lande i Kastrup.
greatest_challenge: Jeg var afsted i fire måneder, og de sneglede sig virkelig afsted. De første uger var sjove - byen var ny, og der var en masse begivenheder med de andre udvekslingsstuderende. Men da studiet rigtig gik i gang, havde alle folk travlt, og lige pludselig havde man mange timer man skulle få til at gå. Det føltes lidt som en meget lang ferie, men ikke på den gode måde.
other_comments: Hvis du ikke har læst noget andet, så læs dette: med mindre du selv har betalt for at tage på et Ivy League college, så kommer undervisningen til at være ca. den samme som på KU, så fuck om universitetet er mere eller mindre prestigiøst, tag hen til det sted hvor du kan bedste tur ud af det, og se så meget som muligt. Jeg ville ønske jeg var taget til et varmt, eksotisk sted, hvor jeg kunne have haft det skide skægt.

crucial_aspects: It had to be a good university in an english speaking country, preferrably in the US or Canada. The main criterea was global university rankings of the university as well as the ranking of the economics department (as that is what I would be taking courses in). It was preferred if the university was located in or near a major city.
info_ease: UofT did provide me with basic information, for instance where I could pick up my ID card and what locations my courses took place in. However, I was given a digital tour of campus, which made little sense, as all the courses I took were in-person. I was not provided any help with housing (i applied for all colleges, and did not recieve any offers), so I had to find my own. We were provided with a facebook group, but overall the help from the University was quite minimal, I don't know if this was due to covid restrictions at the time I arrived.
arrival_assistance: Again, the digital tour of campus. But that was it.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After sending in your application, UofT will send all the digital information you need periodically leading up to the semester start.
registration_help: Regular E-Mail updates.
registration_success: Medium, it was reasonably easy to get into courses in Economics (my major), but getting into courses outside of Economics was impossible for me (I tried to enroll in some math courses). The application process required A LOT of paperwork. You had to fill out a 3-page form individually for every single course you applied for.
registration_advice: Apply early on, so you have plenty of time to find courses in case you are denied some in the first round.
course_level: I mainly took 3rd and 4rth year bachelors courses, as when I was applying to UofT i was still writing my bachelor's thesis, which was required to apply for MA courses.
teaching_comparison: A LOT more group work at UofT, of the five courses I took, three of them predominantly were group work. Secondly, in Denmark we usually have one big exam at the end of the course. At UofT, this is very different, as most courses have a midterm, a final, which each count about 30% and a bunch of small assignments spread out throughout the semester to cover the last 40%. The work load is a lot higher at UofT because of this, where a lot of the time is spent writing essays and making powerpoint slides rather than going through the material (in my opinion). However, you are not at risk of failing at the final exam in the same way at UofT because you are required to do a lot of course work during the semester, which is quite nice.
courses_enrolled: ECO339 - Labour Economics ECO349 - Money, Banking and Financial Markets ECO365 - International monetary economics ECO428 - Classical Economic Thought ECO466 - Empirical Macro and Policy
recommended_courses: ECO339 was really enjoyable, the professor gave absolutely amazing lectures with lots of interaction with the students. ECO428 Was also great if you are interested in the history of economics, it is not exactly a standard economics course but I really enjoyed it
unexpected_costs: SIM card service is EXTREMELY expensive in Canada. Also, the books were more expensive than I was used to.
cost_comparison: Food was surprisingly expensive in Toronto, eating out in restaurants cost almost the same as buying food from your local grocery store (also due to eating in restaurants being quite cheap, about 75-85 DKK for a good sit-down meal). Rent is expensive, but not much worse than Copenhagen.
activities_available: Very little, maybe I didn't hear about them, or else they didnt happen because of Covid.
activities_recommended: The gym was good.
weekend_recommendations: Definately try to get out of the city into some of Ontarios nature. It is really amazing! Also take a trip to Quebec to see a completely different side of Canada.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, Canadians are very welcoming.
socializing_tips: Yes, students were quite easy to talk to when you finally get the opportunity.
cultural_challenges: Nothing super different really.
culture_appreciated: Canadians are very polite and welcoming, I had the great opportunity to be invited to some cottages up north, which were absolutely spectacular experiences for me.
top3_advice: 1 - The workload at UofT is very high, you should know this before going 2 - Definately try to socialize as much as possible in the very beginning of your semester so you get to meet people 3 - Get used to studying and working way before the final exams, as a lot of the grade is determined through smaller projects
other_useful_info: Nothing more than the above.
most_rewarding: Meeting the locals and other exchange students. I met some really great people.
greatest_challenge: Getting settled in. There are a lot of small things that need to be done when you arrive. Whether it is VISA stuff, finding housing, opening a bank account or figuring out the local shops/transportation. There are a lot of small things that end up taking a lot more time than you would think.
other_comments: Be very careful when transferring money to canada, I made the mistake of using a bank transfer and was ripped off by the exchange fee, use a transfer service like transferwise or just use your visa card from Denmark whilst you are there.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere, where the main language was English but I also wanted to go somewhere that was very different from what I am used to. Canada was the perfect place for me as it seemed familiar but also quite different from Europe and Denmark.
overall_comments: I really liked being abroad and getting to explore a new setting.
info_ease: Because of the Covid-19 pandemic I needed to get a study permit, which is not usually needed when going for just one semester. To get the study permit I needed to get my biometric taken and this is only possible to do in either Berlin or Stockholm, which ment that I had to do a trip during my exams in June in order to get my application processed. I found that it was generally hard to find the information needed as the guidelines kept changing.
arrival_assistance: University of Toronto did not really provide any assistance apart from a few mails. We had an online orientation which was pretty much the only information we got. But I think the lack of assistance was due to the covid-19 pandemic as the university was not able to do events as a welcome to the students from abroad.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I really liked being abroad and getting to explore a new setting.
registration_process: We had to fill out a google analysis for each course that we wanted to take.
registration_help: There were some websites to guide us but it was really hard to figure out what was possible.
registration_success: I got all the classes I registered for so in the end it worked out.
registration_advice: I would recommend being mindfull of what is required to be a full-time student and not register for too many courses.
academics_comments: I really liked being abroad and getting to explore a new setting.
course_level: I chose 200 level courses mainly
teaching_comparison: The way of teaching was quite different than at UCPH and there were a lot of work during the semester instead of in the end, which is what I was used to.
courses_enrolled: Urban Sociology Sociology of Crime and Deviance Introduction to Environmental Studies
recommended_courses: I really liked Urban Sociology
unexpected_costs: I had to get a mandatory ensurance provided by the university which was quite expensive and I was not told that I was supposed to print out something or register again in order for it to work so I am not even sure I would have been able to use it.
cost_comparison: I was quite surprised that the groceries where generally quite expensive. Especially dairy and bread.
activities_available: There were a lot of sports opportunities as well as cultural but these where mainly shut down due to covid-19.
activities_recommended: I did not do a lot of university provided activities as they were not available at my stay but I recommend using the sports facilities.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend going to the Toronto Islands especially in the summer where you can swim in the lake.
culture_adjustment: It was quite easy.
socializing_tips: I mostly met Europeans
cultural_challenges: I was surprised how much smalltalk is expected of you in Canada.
culture_appreciated: I really liked how the city had a lot of different neighborhoods and how they were very different from each other.
top3_advice: 1. Give yourself the opportunity to explore the city and walk around and not be buried in schoolwork all the time. 2. Visit the Toronto Islands 3. Go see either a hockey or basketball game in Scotia Bank Arena
other_useful_info: Walk or bike around the city instead of using the public transportation (which is generally really bad and always late). When you walk around you really get to know the city and being away from home you have the time to walk everywhere.
most_rewarding: I found it very rewarding to be able to just walk around and not have the usual responsibilities that I have at home.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge was being away from my friends and family as well as my room at home. It took some time for me to adjust to living somewhere else.
other_comments: I would recommend doing something to make your living space nice. I bought some small decorative things to make it feel more like home and I really think it helped with getting myself comfortable so I was able to explore and enjoy the experience. The room you have is very much your relaxation base and this is an important place to feel good.

crucial_aspects: I liked that they speak English in Canada, and i really wanted to experience the North American culture. Furthermore it seemed they had some good sociology programs.
info_ease: Not very easy as KU were'nt very informative in their guiding sessions. But I figured everything out eventually.
arrival_assistance: Not very much. I pretty much had to figure everything out myself. But it was fairly easy to contact the counselors for studying abroad they had at the university.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We had to get a student card, which was kinda a proces but it wasnt difficult it just took some time to get it.
registration_help: You could ask their department for foreign students, and they were often helpful.
registration_success: I got all the courses i wanted.
registration_advice: Go for undergraduate courses if you're going on your bachelor. They are way easier. I had 100 and 200-level courses and they were good and not too easy of difficult.
course_level: I took 100 and 200 level courses.
teaching_comparison: There was a lot more active participation in the form of weekly quizzes and assignements or writings that you had to do sp be prepared for that. But when you get the hang of it, it was actually very good.
courses_enrolled: Urban Sociology Sociology of Crime and Deviance Introduction to Environmental studies.
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the courses I had. THe teachers were good and the course material was good.
unexpected_costs: None really
cost_comparison: Groceries were pretty expensive.
activities_available: There was fitness and you could go swimming in their gym, but not that many social activities. ot that I knew of at least.
activities_recommended: Use the gyms and fitness opportunities at Hart House and the athletic department.
weekend_recommendations: Try to see as many of the neighborhoods as you can. And walk instead of taking the subway s you get to see the city.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
cultural_challenges: It was legal to smoke weed, and that was pretty different. Toronto is very multicultural which was interesting but nice. There are a lot more homeless or otherwise challenged people in the streets compared to Copenhagen but it was never scary.
culture_appreciated: The multiculturality and the culture in general.
top3_advice: Just enjoy the city and pick courses that are not too hard so you have time to explore the city.
other_useful_info: I only had to have three courses to be considered a full-time student. But try to talk to the administration at KU to see if you can do the same, and don't pick too hard courses.
most_rewarding: Meeting other people and getting to know the city.
greatest_challenge: Avoiding spending too much money. :)

crucial_aspects: Canada was a country I've found particularly compelling since I was a teenager, and eventually, that interest narrowed down some more into Toronto, specifically -- I read that the University of Toronto, specifically, was an exceptional university, so I couldn't help but narrow my focus a little more, and so that's where I chose to study. Another crucial aspect was the immense interest in the country itself, particularly the province of Ontario, and I wanted to study in a very central and urban place in order to get the most in-your-face cultural experience that I could. Furthermore, I also very much wanted to better understand what it would be like to be a long-term resident in Ontario, as I plan to move there at some point in my early 30s. Lastly, I was searching for a place where I might experience some more unconventional ways of learning and of being instructed, and I figured there was a higher likelihood that I might find those unconventional methods at a university in North America--and at the University of Toronto, I certainly did, and it truly was a blast!
overall_comments: Overall, this my time as an exchange student at the U of T has influenced me for the better, and by "for the better", I mean to an extent that I expect will affect my future in a very, very beautiful way.
info_ease: Quite easy. I had no pressing questions or uncertainties upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: There was a virtual "Inbound Exchange Orientation". The information I was given at this orientation was very helpful and even relieving throughout the term over there.
arrival_comments: None.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall, this my time as an exchange student at the U of T has influenced me for the better, and by "for the better", I mean to an extent that I expect will affect my future in a very, very beautiful way.
registration_process: It was fairly straightforward. At the U of T, what I had to do was send in individual applications for each of the four courses I wanted to take. Then, if you later wanted to switch one course with another, you had to send a course application form AND a course drop form--this was something I had to do, which was fine, really. I got a bit nervous later on because I was on the waiting list for half of the courses I had applied for, but I was high up on those lists and eventually, I got into every course I wanted to get into.
registration_help: When it came to course registration, there was a sort of PowerPoint / PDF with a step-by-step process, which was fairly helpful. There was likely other forms of assistance readily available, though I didn't really end up needing them.
registration_success: I knew what to do, and I did those things, and I got what I wanted, so I was quite successful.
registration_advice: My main advice would be this: Talk to the right people, pay close attention to advice and instructions--basically, just make sure to know about *everything* you need to do, how to register for the courses you truly feel that you want that are available to you, and to be aware of any and all deadlines. Otherwise, it can be very, very stressful, and something you weren't otherwise expecting could pop up seemingly out of nowhere, making for a much more awkward process. And, of course, I would suggest to take courses you think you would enjoy a lot, because traveling and living in a social environment that's very different from the one you're used to can already be quite exhausting at times, but that's just me I guess.
academics_comments: Overall, this my time as an exchange student at the U of T has influenced me for the better, and by "for the better", I mean to an extent that I expect will affect my future in a very, very beautiful way.
course_level: The four courses were on varying 300-levels: Medieval Literature - 311 Contemporary Poetry - 349 Contemporary American Fiction - 365 Environmental Imagination - 377
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at the University of Toronto was, from my experience, much more free in the sense that there was a lot of space for creative approaches to complex problems and academic projects. I felt like I was given more chances to apply aspects of my own individual personality (not just my intellectual abilities) to projects I was tasked with.
courses_enrolled: Medieval Literature (ENG311 H1 S) Contemporary Poetry (ENG349 H1 S) Contemporary American Fiction (ENG365 H1 S) The Environmental Imagination (ENG377 H1 S)
recommended_courses: Well, I can really only speak for the courses that I was enrolled in during this semester. And, really, I recommend all of four of them. However, I didn't enjoy Contemporary Poetry as much as the others, but that's mainly because I don't like poetry -- though, with that said, if an exchange student is especially interested in improving their close-reading skills significantly, I would very highly recommend taking Contemporary Poetry, as it often deals with some very cryptic texts with extremely compressed meaning. Out of all four of them, Contemporary American Fiction is the one I would recommend the very most! We had to go through soooo much material, but it was so wild and fascinating, and the professor that in that course was a total blast, and he was exceptionally encouraging. Contemporary American Fiction was most certainly my favorite course at the U of T during my semester there.
unexpected_costs: I went to get a quick check-up at the dentist for some gum/tooth aches I was experiencing pretty much non-stop -- since the health insurance plan doesn't cover dental, I had to pay about 800kr for that check-up ... and it wasn't even a full check-up, just one that was concentrated on area in pain.
cost_comparison: I honestly didn't expect that cheese would be so expensive in Toronto. On the other hand, juice was almost weirdly cheap. Chips were also slightly cheaper, though I was sort of expecting that for some reason.
activities_available: There would have been far more of such activities available if it weren't for the pandemic. However, the city of Toronto itself is extremely culturally diverse, so cultural activities at the U of T are probably rich and plentiful. As far as athletic and social activities go, I'm not even a hundred percent sure. The classes and their projects can be very social. I do believe I saw a group of students carrying out some lacrosse practice.
activities_recommended: Example: I can recommend checking out novelty restaurants, such as "Stormcrow Manor", which is like a big geeky restaurant, and they make pretty awesome science fiction and fantasy themed food. Basically, there are several "weird" restaurants worth checking out in Toronto.
weekend_recommendations: I would certainly recommend the Royal Ontario Museum, the Art Gallery of Ontario, and Ripley's Aquarium. There are also many interesting restaurants to visit, such as Stormcrow Manor (a geeky restaurant with themed meals and drinks--they make an amazing French onion soup, too). There are also a lot of interesting stores, such as The Monkey's Paw, a rare book store known for having some pretty weird and weirdly specific books (went there several times). The parks in Toronto are also just amazing--I went to High Park to go birdwatching, and there is so much beautiful life in that city, it's truly astounding. Also, just walking around the city of Toronto with no particular goal in mind can be very interesting, as there really is a lot to do, and it can be fun to just "figure it out" as you go along, and perhaps find something that really resonates with you. It's all pretty cool.
culture_adjustment: It wasn't easy, but it wasn't excruciatingly hard either. Of course, my mother tongue is English, which is what most people speak in Toronto, so that certainly made it easier for me to adapt.
socializing_tips: All I would say is to socialize with other students in whatever way you're comfortable with (though it always helps to be aware of certain social formalities if there are any that are especially different from the ones you're used to--just to make you feel like you're on more solid ground).
cultural_challenges: Some formalities were a bit surprising. For example, total strangers would say "how are you?" as part of a greeting--for example, "Hi there, how are you?" "Hi, I'm good, how are you?" "I'm good, thanks" ... it was a bit awkward to get used to, and I don't think I stayed long enough for it to completely stop feeling weird to me. However, I adapted, and it was fine, though very occasionally I got a bit of a stare for not reciprocating the "how are you?" bit. Tipping culture was also a bit challenging, as I'm really just not used to that, and sometimes if I felt I didn't tip "enough", I would feel a bit guilty. I would certainly recommend looking up Canadian tipping conventions.
culture_appreciated: Something I noticed was that a lot of people in Toronto were very, very good with small-talk, and because of that, social environments can be quite inviting, which I very much enjoyed, particularly since I'm not always very keen on initiating conversations. I can often be quite nervous and awkward around strangers, but in Toronto, that wasn't too much of a burden because it was just surprisingly easier to communicate with people (as long as they were friendly). Of course, you can never generalize, but this is what I experienced when it came to interacting with strangers. It was very nice, and it was interesting.
top3_advice: 1: If you're not already well used to a consistently heavy workload (and by heavy, I mean *heavy*), be prepared, and make sure to organize leisure-time and study-time in a way that reduces stress without sacrificing efficiency/productivity while you study at the U of T. 2: Don't forget to have a good time--I'm aware this may be a given, but there are so many fun, interesting things to do and experience in Toronto (and at the university as well), and between the periods of hours-long work, you're definitely going to want to find good ways to unwind. 3: The campus I was attending is totally beautiful and full of smart, interesting students--so, I would highly recommend interacting with fellow students and being proactive during group projects, as there's so very much that can be learned even from the other students there.
other_useful_info: Besides what I've said in preceding comments, not that I can think of at this exact moment.
most_rewarding: Paying attention during class, studying sufficiently--making it through the heavy, heavy workload was extremely rewarding, as I had no idea I was capable of doing that as successfully as I did. That was probably the most rewarding part of it all, and it has certainly improved my work ethic considerably. It's tough as hell, but in the end, having really applied myself, I feel quite proud. I feel like I'm capable of more than I was before. I'm very happy about this.
greatest_challenge: Again, the workload. Since several exams are dispersed throughout the semester, I had to almost constantly study one or several exams all while getting through near unending heaps of homework.
other_comments: Not that I can think of.

crucial_aspects: There were multiple aspects that were crucial for choosing my study destination. I wanted to study at a university with a high academic level and also a university with a big campus to experience that kind of study environment. I also wanted to live in a city with diverse cultures, and Toronto was a perfect choice. Lastly, I wanted to study at a university that offered courses that suited my academic profile and would help me in my future studies.
overall_comments: The reason for not choosing a higher is due to the fact that Covid-19 was still affecting social life and also the accessibility at the campus during the first two months of my study abroad.
info_ease: It was very easy to find all the important information from the University of Copenhagen. The websites for studying abroad are very good. The websites from the University of Toronto were a bit harder to navigate, but it was also fairly easy.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any assistance from the University of Toronto other than some e-mails with information about the study and social groups. We had to figure almost everything out by ourselves, which was done by asking other exchange students. They could have made an exchange group with some introduction for those who want to join.
arrival_comments: Maybe the little assistance was due to Covid-19, which did not allow exchange students to meet at the campus during the first months.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The reason for not choosing a higher is due to the fact that Covid-19 was still affecting social life and also the accessibility at the campus during the first two months of my study abroad.
registration_process: I received the necessary e-mails for registration, which were very intuitive and made the process easy. I would recommend doing it as soon as possible as you have to do an online to obtain your student card, and the number of these meetings is limited. For registration for courses we received multiple e-mails with the different rounds of registration, which helped a lot.
registration_help: E-mails with the necessary information.
registration_success: I was very successful. I got all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Find the courses you want very early in the process as the first round of registration is very early.
academics_comments: The reason for not choosing a higher is due to the fact that Covid-19 was still affecting social life and also the accessibility at the campus during the first two months of my study abroad.
course_level: I found the level very high. I had to study a lot, but it was also what I wanted to challenge myself.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. At the University of Toronto, they focused a lot on midterm exams. So even 2 weeks into the course we had midterm exams that affected our final grades. At UCPH the grading of courses is based on the final exam at the end of the semester. So, if you want a good grade at the University of Toronto you have to work and study throughout the whole semester where it at UCPH was based on the final exam.

recommended_courses: PHC401H1 Drug Transport Across Biological Membranes and PHC421H1 Biomolecular Interactions and Thermodynamics I. These two courses focused very much on specific topics and I would very much recommend these if you are interested in these topics.
unexpected_costs: Covid tests.
cost_comparison: The housing was much more expensive than expected and also the food.
activities_available: You could join every kind of sport team and also join for tournaments even if your exchange eas only one semester.
activities_recommended: Join the intramurals (sport tournament).
weekend_recommendations: Go to games (basketball, ice hockey etc.) and eat out (very good and diverse).
