However, I started classes on January 7th, and was finished with exams and everything April 15th which means I only had school for three months and a week which, to me, was timeframe I would have wished was longer, as I hadn't properly settled in and made friends until around the two month mark (leaving not that long to fully enjoy that studying abroad life). I'm a bit introverted though, so might not be a problem if you're more extroverted / quicker at making friends :) The upside of this short term is that I had an amazing long summer break to go explore the remaining parts of Toronto and Canada :)
course_level: I had two 200 level courses and two 300 level courses (two rhetoric courses, two literature). I don't think the work level / expectations to students differed from 200 level courses and 300 level courses, but was more up to the professor of the course. Like my 200 level 'Introduction to Canadian Literature' was probably the one with the lowest expectations in regards to how well thought out your essays had to be, whereas my rhetoric course on that level had bigger requirements :) But seriously, try to put some 'easy' courses in there! If all the courses are going to be challenging for you, your workload could be A LOT if you want to do well.
teaching_comparison: Varied from class to class. From KU I'm used to classes with 30-60 people in them with part lecture/part group work and discussion (always a practical element). At UofT I had classes like that, but also classes that were only discussions or only lectures.
courses_enrolled: ENG252H1-S (Introduction to Canadian Literature) WGS380H1-S (Feminist Graphic Novels) WRR201H1-S (Theories of Rhetoric: A History of Persuasion) WRR3081H-S (Selected Topics in Writing and Rhetoric: Visual Rhetoric)
recommended_courses: My favorite courses were (surprisingly?) the ones that weren't rhetoric! Feminist Graphic Novels was an AMAZING course, and ended up being my favorite despite having chosen it as my "lol course". The class is super intersectional, and covers a wide range of topics, the text selection is phenomenal, and there's a fine line between 'academic observations' and personal experiences in the class discussions. Highly recommend! Intro. to Canadian Lit. is a great class for learning a bit about Canadian culture and history from a different angle! Each week was basically a different period in literature with a text from that time period, and the lecture would offer lots of cultural and historical context for help unpacking, starting from First Nations voices and settlement narratives to modern day criticisms on Canada's multiculturalism policy from minorities :) I was pretty nervous as I didn't know anything about Canada, but if you just turn up to the lectures and listen (and read), it will be pretty easy to pass :)
unexpected_costs: Groceries were definitely a lot more expensive than expected...vegetables were a lot more expensive than in Denmark :) I did a lot of personal spending because I wanted to be able to go out and experience the things I wanted to do.
cost_comparison: Groceries were more than expected. Going out is same prices as in Denmark when you add 13% tax + 15-20% tip to the price :)
activities_available: Honestly a lot! Workout classes, fitness center, great student theatre productions, clubs and so on. The harthouse website has them on there, you just need to know it exists!
activities_recommended: I went to the theatre productions / festival (very high level student productions) and a few of the exchange student events.
weekend_recommendations: Kensington Market is so cute -- also has a very fun (and professional) open mic night on tuesdays at Supermarket Bar. Toronto Islands is great and cute if the weather is nice! And ofc. you need to watch Ice Hockey! In general, just go and explore the city :) And spend money on all the amazing food you can't get at home like soup dumplings, Caribien, actually authentic Mexican (Taco Gus at Kensington) and much more. For every country's cuisine there's a restaurant. But like obvious stuff like ice skating and Niagara Falls. Taking the train to Montreal or Quebec is also a great way to spent reading week.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, no big culture shock. (I have lived in the US before though, so you might have a different experience). The biggest difference is definitely that Toronto is extremely multicultural compared to Copenhagen (which I loved), and VERY queer friendly (yes, way more than Copenhagen).
socializing_tips: Just talk! They're pretty nice so just go ahead! And like get their Instagrams and/or phone numbers and stuff. But yeah, sit down and chat with the person next to you in class.
cultural_challenges: Mostly just figuring out what the expectations / genre conventions of "the undergraduate academic essay" were and like what was expected academically. Night life is also a bit different, as the clubs close at 2 (yes), and are pretty dead if it isn't Friday or Saturday, and you aren't allowed (in Ontario) to walk around with alcohol in public, but weed is legal and very much allowed (and smelt) everywhere...but nothing actually challenging :)
culture_appreciated: The stereotype of Canadians being very nice and helpful IS true, and it feels much more authentic than in the US. Over 51% of people living in Toronto are born outside Canada, so Toronto is incredibly multicultural which is very fun to experience (and makes for great food experiences), but it's definitely also a 'hustle city'. Toronto is also the most queerfriendly place I've ever visited/been which is awesome! Church Street has some great queer clubs and events to go to, and queer PDA is frequently seen everywhere in the city.
top3_advice: 1. Don't get too caught up in UofT's hustle culture...you don't need to do all the readings or write the most amazing essay, you just need to pass. Explore the city.
other_useful_info: Be aware that you might have to sign up for courses more than six months in advance!! check your email!!!
most_rewarding: Leaning into the 'big city lifestyle'. It sounds dumb but walking around Toronto with iced coffee from Tim Hortons made me feel like 'that girl', and I really recommend leaning into all the unique experiences that living in a city of that size can bring (like there being great concerts, a drag scene, amazing restaurants and so on). And making connections and friends of course.
greatest_challenge: Making friends, hahah. Not that it was that hard, but I definitely felt lonely and overwhelmed for the first month and a half, but I also turned in my bachelor assignment three minutes before the deadline a day before my flight to Canada, so I just hadn't had a lot of time to process / had had a few stressful months before my stay which did impact my first time in Toronto.
other_comments: Toronto is an amazing city! The neighborhoods vary so much, which means that the city has a lot of different vibes to offer depending in where you're walking around. And please, if you end up at UofT EXPLORE the libraries and don't just go to Robarts - there are so many cute small and Harry Potter-esque libraries if you explore a bit (Emmanual College is a good place to start).

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience what it was like to go to a north american university. University of Toronto had an interesting selection of courses, which weren't available at my home institution or at many other universities. A good Anthropology Department.
info_ease: Fairly easy. The process was quite simple as it is quite easy to study in Canada for a Dane.
arrival_assistance: There were various presentations held via zoom that introduced international students to important aspects of studying and living in Canada. Introduction to both housing and health care in Canada, with options for more information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The university course list was available online, though quite late comparative to the pre-acceptance process at the home university, which caused some minor problems. When released however the registration was fairly easy there was several different registration periods, were you had to fill out a google doc with your desired courses. You could change courses and drop them even after the beginning of the term.
registration_help: There was an online presentation with all the necessary information, if needed you could also e-mail the office who were very responsive and helpful.
registration_success: I got all the courses that i wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure to register for courses in the first round as that is when it is easiest to get them. Don't be nervous about registering for quite a few as it is easy to drop them if you change your mind, though ideally before the courses begin.
course_level: I took some 2nd and 3rd year courses, the 2nd years being outside of my main field. I found the general level quite good if a little lower then what i am used to at my home institution. The courses in general were quite forgiving with botht the amount and the level of the readings being a bit lower. The courses i took were quite general and thus there was some overlap with things i had learned about prior. The courses outside of my main field were quite easy to follow and i definitely recommend them.
teaching_comparison: There were quite classic 2-hour lectures and some group instructions. There was a greater emphasis on interaction between students and professor in the lectures, but less talk with the person sitting next to you. Also note that you are graded on participation much like in Gymnasiet. The instruction were a bit strange they were more like an extension of the lecture with relatively little option for working with other students, they were also quite short only 1 hour. There is a much greater focus on home work, with at least four different papers written in each class which alongside the exam make up the bulk of your final grade. I found the papers a bit strange to write, it was difficult to reach the level of abstraction usually expected in exams in Denmark and at times they felt like busywork, which took up a lot of time for very little return.
courses_enrolled: ANT344H1 F: Political Anthropology ANT384H1 F: Special Topics in Society, Culture and Language HIS264H1 F: Critical Issues in Canadian History PHL269H1 F: Philosophy of Race
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the courses, but in particular Philosophy of Race and Special Topic in Society, Culture and Language. These were really interesting and gave a perspective very different from one you usually get in Denmark. The two other courses were good as well but the was quite a bit of overlap between the Political Anthropology and thing things i had already learned about on the Anthropology Bachelor in Denmark. The Canadian history course was interesting if you want to learn more about Canada and it's history but really is designed towards Canadian students.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay health care insurance to study at the University, they offer a plan. Transportation is a must, the inner city is navigateable by foot or bike, but outside of the center most things are designed around cars and if you don't have one busses of subway.
cost_comparison: Celluar service and data are incredibly expensive in Canada, try and get a plan from Denmark. In general prices are quite simmilar to Denmark, drinks, snacks and going out to eat is cheaper, whilst groceries are more expensive. Transportation system is fairly cheap.
activities_available: Everything honestly, there is a great culture around student driven clubs and activities, so you can find pretty much anything and everything that interests you.
activities_recommended: I took part in some board game and some movie clubs which were really nice. There also is a camping and outdoors club which is nice for exploring a bit outside the city.
weekend_recommendations: There are some nice museums and like in Toronto. Toronto in general is massive and has lots to offer. Try to watch some university sports teams it's free and a pretty fun experience even if you're not into sports. Also explore a bit outside the city or visit Montreal, Niagara Falls or even the US. Things are a bit further away but Toronto is fairly well-connected to the sorroundings.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. Canadians are in general quite friendly and polite, there is a lot more small talk and conversation everywhere which can be scary for introverted danes, but it's ok. Everyone speaks english and many people do it with accents so don't be nervous about how you speak it is easy to understand one another. There are lots of cars and Canada in general is built around having them so it's a little trickier to get around if you don't have one especially outside the city.
cultural_challenges: I don't know if i did. Maybe the time difference but you get used to it quickly.
culture_appreciated: People are generally nice and friendly and open-minded. It's a very multicultural society that's open to people. Canadian culture seems to be the culture of many different peoples and that was nice to experience.
top3_advice: Don't be too nervous it's a nice place with a high quality of education and friendly people Try and find a place to stay early on, it helps. Do things outside of education as well, it is supposed to be an experience.
other_useful_info: Not really. Have fun!
most_rewarding: Experiencing a completly different place and culture.
greatest_challenge: Finding a place to stay two weeks before going.

crucial_aspects: The ranking of the university and the city itself.
info_ease: There was not really any information for exchange students in the beginning of the semester, so you mostly had to figure things out yourself.
arrival_assistance: I didn't receive any assistance upon arrival
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process comes in multiple rounds, where you fill out your course requests in a Google Analytics formula each time.
registration_help: The description of the registration process in the email is very thorough and easy to follow.
registration_success: I got the requested classes during the first round, so it was quite easy to choose courses.
registration_advice: Make sure to look out for the course request deadline as it is only a window of about one week.
course_level: The level is probably quite high by North American standards and a lot of people are very ambitious, but the style of teaching is very different from what we are used to.
teaching_comparison: Very different. The courses are much more about calculations and doing things without aids, and much less about intuition and actual understanding of the course material, which we are used to at UCPH. However, this is probably just the way things are in North America.
courses_enrolled: International Monetary Economics Advanced Microeconomics - Game Theory Introductory Philosophy of Science Markets, Competition and Strategy
recommended_courses: International Monetary Economics is a very good course to take, and the professor is really good at teaching and explaining.
unexpected_costs: Phone service is expensive in Canada (around 300 kr per month for a basic subscription).
cost_comparison: Food and drinks are pretty much the same price as in Denmark, so a bit more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: They have different athletic clubs and social clubs, but there are so many that it is difficult to find out what the best things are.
activities_recommended: I don't know
weekend_recommendations: The nature outside the city is really cool - I can definitely recommend seeing Niagara Falls and going to Algonquin National Park, which is about three hours by car from Toronto.
culture_adjustment: It is quite easy given the English language and the similarities to Danish culture
socializing_tips: U of T is not a very social university, so I think the best way is to participate in some of the social clubs and activities around campus.
cultural_challenges: Not anything in particular
culture_appreciated: Not anything in particular
top3_advice: Look for housing as early as possible Read travel reports about courses before deciding as they differ a lot in quality Look for public transportation options before deciding on housing
other_useful_info: Not anything I haven't mentioned
most_rewarding: It is a great experience to live in another country and to live in a city that is so much bigger than Copenhagen
greatest_challenge: Since people speak English and most things are pretty similar to things in Denmark, I wouldn't say that there are a lot of challenges

overall_comments: Had a very good academic neuroscience program

arrival_assistance: Facebook groups, email, mostly online.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution

registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted. Both on 300 and 400 level.
registration_advice: Some courses are very popular so make sure to registrer for those in the first round. You can easily register for courses you are not sure to take cause you can easily drop them into the semester.
academics_comments: Had a very good academic neuroscience program

courses_enrolled: Neurogenomics HMB360 Laboratory in Neuroscience HMB310 Neuroscience: Cellular & Molecular PSL445 Neurobiology of Behaviour HMB300 Advanced Topics in Neurophysiology CSB432
recommended_courses: Neurogenomics HMB360 - very good teacher, teamwork, friendly environment, great syllabus Neuroscience: Cellular & Molecular PSL445 - high tempo, higher level, new professor at every lecture Neurobiology of Behaviour HMB300 - very interesting content, nice creative assignments Advanced Topics in Neurophysiology CSB432 - very good teacher, you learn about the most novel research and techniques in the field, very exciting and great assignments and presentations, you learn relevant skills for a future in science and research such as presenting correctly and writing grant proposals.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Books were none Housing was less expensive Food was more expensive

cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: The kindness, openness, and the huge amount of international students.
top3_advice: If you wanna learn a lot and something that is exciting to you, you have all the freedom to do so. You will figure everything out when you get there - but it was nice to arrive 1 week or so before classes begun. Reach out and talk to other students. They want to make friends with you - they find exchange students especially cool hah.
other_useful_info: Thoroughly go through the syllabus and the marking scheme. Make a scheme over all your assignments, quizzes, attendance, exams, etc. because there is a lot and you can easily loose track and miss deadlines if not.
most_rewarding: Get to study with other students at UofT. Making friends with people living there. Get to learn from great professors.
greatest_challenge: Keeping track of all the different courses' syllabus and deadlines. Finding out the marking scheme.

crucial_aspects: I chose Canada because I wanted safe place, that was different enough to be interesting but similar enough to Denmark as to not be to overwhelming. And I chose Toronto because they had the best university for math in Canada.
overall_comments: The university and the city was great, but a combination of a way to difficult course and a suppar housing situation made it less fund then I had hoped.
info_ease: Very easy, no problem at all.
arrival_assistance: The university hosted a guided tour and an information meeting.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The university and the city was great, but a combination of a way to difficult course and a suppar housing situation made it less fund then I had hoped.
registration_process: They send an email with a questionaire that you had to complete before a certain deadline. Actually there was multiple emails, as you could register in later rounds if you didn’t get what you wanted initially or if you changed your mind.
registration_help: Nice email service.
registration_success: Very. I got the ones I wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure you meet the course prerequisites, and alternatively compare the prereqs to similar courses at KU.
academics_comments: The university and the city was great, but a combination of a way to difficult course and a suppar housing situation made it less fund then I had hoped.
course_level: I took 3rd and 4th level courses, but both of my 4th level courses were joint grad and undergrad courses.
teaching_comparison: VERY similar.
courses_enrolled: Combinatorics, Introduction to logic, set theory and Riemannian Geometry
recommended_courses: Introduction to logic and Set Theory as these two courses goes very well hand in hand, and are very interesting, and you can’t really get the same at KU. unexpected_costs: Homadorma took some fees for reserving my accomadation that were quite high (4000 kr in total)
cost_comparison: Flight tickets were expensive (8000 kr)
activities_available: Every club imaginable, and lot’s of sports teams and fitness rooms/opportunities.
activities_recommended: Go to the museums in Toronto. They are great!
weekend_recommendations: Go to Algonquin national park if you are able, and a must see is of course Naigra Falls.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. It is a lot like the US.
socializing_tips: Canadians are very nice, so if you tell them you are an exchange students, then they become really friendly and chatty.

crucial_aspects: A country were people spoke English, and an academically strong university
overall_comments: Overall it was a positive experience looking back.
info_ease: It was pretty easy to find the needed information.
arrival_assistance: They are very good at answering their email regarding any questions you have. However, the response time can be a couple of days. You have to figure out a lot yourself, a big one being housing, however they do have "good tips", that I did not use.
arrival_comments: Pretty mediocre. They look at you only academically. There wasn't that many events for socializing hosted by the university, and you have to be the one taking the initiative.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall it was a positive experience looking back.
registration_process: You get the course list and a timetable builder. Then you have to fill out a google forms with the courses you'd like. Also note, that you can search for as many courses as you would like, and they will give you at most 5. So I would recommend searching a ton of courses in round 1, making sure that they are interchangeable, and then drop one course if needed later on.
registration_help: Timetable builder and course list. The course descriptions are quite short, which is a shame.
registration_success: 6/10. As computer science was very oversubscribed I wasn't able to get all the course I wanted.
registration_advice: If you want to study something in Computer Science, I would highly recommend Operating Systems and Kuei (Jack) Sun as a professor. He is brilliant, and the course is very interesting. However, it is also a very tough course, and you should be prepared to spend a lot of time on the course.
academics_comments: Overall it was a positive experience looking back.
course_level: The course material is similar if not easier than what is offered at the University of Copenhagen for the same year. However, their emphasis is placed more on you doing a bunch of work, rather than you knowing the course material. The grading also reflects this, as a minor mistake with the correct methodology usually ranks lower than the correct result with incorrect methodology.
teaching_comparison: I preferred UCPH
courses_enrolled: CSC236, CSC207, APM236, CSC369
recommended_courses: CSC369 - a tough course, but very interesting
unexpected_costs: Housing is very expensive.
cost_comparison: I bought the bikeshare Tangerine annual membership. This costs 120cad for the version I bought. However, I used this as my primary way of getting around, which saved me a lot, as I feel the public transport is quite bad in Toronto. Mainly due to the trams using the same lanes as cars, and there is a lot of traffic in Toronto. So unless you live next to one of the two subway lines I would recommend just using the bike.
activities_available: Athletic mainly. Unlike Danish universities, there is not a lot of emphasis on the students socializing.
activities_recommended: If you enjoy some specific sport, there is most likely a team that you can sign up for.
weekend_recommendations: As I was pretty swarmed with studies I didn't get to travel as much as I would've liked. However, I would have loved to visit some of the nature there is in Canada. My main regret is not going to see Banf national park.
culture_adjustment: Pretty seamless. However, there is a lot more homelessness and drugs, which is quite unusual.
socializing_tips: People talk to randomly a lot more than in Denmark. Most people won't second guess it, if you just start talking to them, so do that! However, my best tip is to just create a post in the UofT inbound exchange facebook group explaining your interest, and you might find a group of friends to hangout with with that.
cultural_challenges: Homelessness and drug use. It is quite common to see people on some hard drugs walking down the streets. After having visited both New York and Toronto, I would say Toronto is even worse, even though it has been quite a few years since I was in New York.
culture_appreciated: People being open to talking. If you overhear some conversation during class, most people are open to you just joining in.
top3_advice: Find housing early, my tip Airbnb. Search a bunch of courses in the first round, such that if you don't get in, you have something to fallback on. Figure out if you are going to prioritize the academics or social beforehand, and choose courses after that choice. There is a lot of variation in how much work a course takes.
other_useful_info: If you can, try to find a place to live near campus. It is not quite downtown, but it will most likely be where you spend the most amount of time.
most_rewarding: Trying something different. I was getting quite comfortable in my own shoes here in Denmark, and enjoyed trying something different.
greatest_challenge: The personal relations you leave back home, and trying to keep in contact.

crucial_aspects: - Reputation of host university - Subjective attractiveness of host country - Number of available places
info_ease: - Easy to navigate, as a lot of information was provided (often multiple times)

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Manually in the graduate office
registration_help: Personal help from the employee at the office
registration_success: Not successful, as other full-time students could register earlier.

course_level: Pretty comparable in terms of difficulty. More research-based project work with your own chosen project. Smaller courses, more school-like feel.

courses_enrolled: Computational Imaging Topics in Storage Systems Algorithms for Private Data Analysis
recommended_courses: Computational Imaging is a great introductory course with a lot to learn. Also, there is a project in which you can choose the topic on your own.
cost_comparison: Groceries are more expensive. In general, the cost of living is slightly higher than in Denmark.
activities_available: Sports clubs, introduction events, student committee organised parties
activities_recommended: All the introductory events, also organised via Facebook. Great way to meet people at the beginning of the semester.
weekend_recommendations: Drive to Algonquin National Park Fly to Banff National Park Go to Toronto Islands See sports games (University ones are for free)
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Sports clubs. Otherwise, in the courses it was not as easy to socialize with others.
cultural_challenges: Competitive culture in class.
culture_appreciated: Diversity and positive attitude.
top3_advice: - Apply early for housing, as it can be expensive and far-off if you apply too late. - Try to see as much as possible in the city, go to games of sports you have never seen before, join clubs to socialize with Canadians. - Studying is even more self-responsible than UCPH, try to allocate your time accordingly.
most_rewarding: - Meeting a lot of new people, some of which have become good friends - Experiencing the life in a really big city and the differences to Copenhagen
greatest_challenge: - Organise and manage in the beginning, settling in, furnishing the student room

crucial_aspects: I guess the main aspects and motivating of me choosing Toronto was that I wanted to get outside of Europe and experiencing a different study culture than teh European one. Another motivating was me wanting to visit Canada and I had heard a lot good things about Toronto as a city and UofT in general.
info_ease: It wasn't really all that easy in terms of courses, registration and administrative stuff. You can prep as much as you want, but must of the stuff you kind of had to figure it out on your own, when you got there. That was kind of tough when KU was very strict with the pre-approval on courses.
arrival_assistance: I feel like the assistance was all-right. Courses were quite easy for me to get enrolled, but there weren't really any information before I arrived though.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was all right. They were very flexible with dropping courses and enrolling for new ones compared to KU. But it was a bit of a jungle before you arrived.
registration_help: The inbound exchange office provided some help, but not a lot. Though they helped me get enrolled to one course, which was quite nice. I just showed up at their office at UofT.
registration_success: I think I was able to get about 3 out of 4 of the courses I requested.
registration_advice: Get as many courses pre-approved as possible and then select the courses when you get to UofT. It is very easy to enrol and drop courses.
course_level: The level of courses vary from KU in two ways. I guess the workload throughout the semester can be more as there are more assignments and mandatory participation and your grade depend on these things. Quite often the exam is between 20-50 % of the grade.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was a lot more involving with the students in class I would say. We didn't really have big classes with hundreds of people, which I am used to back home.
courses_enrolled: Microeconomics for policy analysis Politics in Europe East European Politics - Topics in comparative politics Economics of Global Trade
recommended_courses: I would say I liked the Eastern European politics course the most as it was probably the most challenging and interesting course I had.
unexpected_costs: You do a lot of stuff while you are on exchange, so just a lot of stuff, but it definetely worth it.
cost_comparison: Coffee is pretty cheap compared to DK :). Grocery stores tend to be expensive when it comes to like vegetables, but then all types of meat are very cheap. But most prices are just like Copenhagen all in all.
activities_available: Oh I did a lot of stuff. I joined the outdoor club, where we were on a trip to Blue Mountains. Then I joined the tri-campus team in soccer, where we won the championship, so that was very nice and a good experience. Besides that I played basketball and joined in as many activities as I could. I reccomend doing the same.
activities_recommended: Go travel around Canada. Go to Banff as it is beautiful. I went skiing aswell in november. Go to various sports games in Toronto either Uni games or pro sports such as baseball, hockey and basketball. Go to concerts! Chances are your favorite artist plays in Toronto.
weekend_recommendations: Banff, sports, ice-skating, concerts and so on. Even go to New York and of course Niagara Falls.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy. Canada is probably a good mix between American and European culture.
socializing_tips: Just talk to them in classes. People are so open-minded as people come from places all over the world.
cultural_challenges: Hmmm. People study mostly late-night, which I find very weird. If you go to the study library at like 8-9 pm it is packed in contrast to 9 am, where there are no-one.
culture_appreciated: Just talking to so many different people from all over the world.
top3_advice: Say yes to everything especially the first month. You are bound to make friends and experience so many incredible things.
other_useful_info: Be positive. Try to do everything even though it is expensive. It is definetely worth it in the end. Like go to Montreal aswell.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and just having a different day-to-day life than what you are used to.
greatest_challenge: Hmmmm maybe just being so far away from home from time to time. Not being really close to your family, girlfriend etc. Besides that the exchange stay was a blast.

crucial_aspects: Finding a place where I could pursue my academic interests, whilst being somewhere interesting.
info_ease: It was ok, sometimes a bit difficult
arrival_assistance: I got emails from the office of international experiences about how to do different things, but that's all.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There were three rounds of course registration. You then have opportunity to drop or get new courses up till a week after the course start, which is nice.
registration_help: The office at the international experiences in Toronto were very helpful. I went to them several times to talk about problems with course registration, and they helped out.
registration_success: I am a computer science student, and these courses were very popular. Which resulted in me being waitlisted in 3 out of 4 computer science courses. I thus didn't get the courses I wanted, so I needed to take some other courses, which I didn't find as interesting.
registration_advice: Make sure you have alternatives for courses that you would like. Register as soon as the registration is available.
course_level: I did 300 and 200 level courses, which relates to 2 and 3 year bachelor courses.
teaching_comparison: It was more collaborative or more of a discussions. My classes were smaller, and thus the lectures were more interactive.
courses_enrolled: The design of interactive computational media. Technology in the modern world. Data, computation, and the mind. Introduction to work and organizations.
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the courses Technology in the modern world and Data, computation, and the mind.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Food, and going out for dinner.
activities_available: A lot of clubs and sports. There where a club fair in the first week.
activities_recommended: Sport clubs, they have a lot of fun activities.
weekend_recommendations: Go to montreal, Banff, or rent a cabin near algonquin with friends.
culture_adjustment: It was ok, not too different from home. Just a very big city.
cultural_challenges: Not that many.
culture_appreciated: Very talkative, outgoing and nice.
top3_advice: Make sure you find courses in time. Reach out to other people and find housing with them. Sign up for clubs or other social things.
other_useful_info: There isn't much intro done by the university, so try to do some yourself.
most_rewarding: The courses ending up being very interesting. And all of the friends I found and made memories with.
greatest_challenge: Living alone, and having to meet people.

crucial_aspects: A course on minds and machines (ended up not being offered)
overall_comments: Great university and a great city to study in.
info_ease: Very easy.
arrival_assistance: There was an orientation that covered the most important things.
arrival_comments: The orientation did not leave anything left to be desired.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Great university and a great city to study in.
registration_process: You show up to orientation to be registred and there is a pretty simple formula online to register for courses.
registration_help: Email and office hours.
registration_success: Very.
registration_advice: You might not be able to get all the courses that you see in the course catalogue so be sure that you have back up courses you are fine with taking. It is very normal for students in Toronto to go outside there field to meet breadth requirements and as such there are a lot of courses that are beginner friendly.
academics_comments: Great university and a great city to study in.
course_level: I had a single introductory course and the rest were either second or third year courses.
teaching_comparison: A lot bigger classes with less engagement from students. People meet minimal requirements for the courses and don't seem to know the material. At home it is more streamlined and more prerequisites are required.
courses_enrolled: Ethics: Death and Dying, Social and Cultural Theory, Introduction to Chinese Philosophy, Freedom, Responsibility, and Human Action.
recommended_courses: Freedom, Responsibility, and Human Action. A very concise and great course on free will. Martin Pickavé is an excellent professor and the syllabus is very carefully selected. It will give you exactly what you need to get into the subject with out being to much of a work load.
unexpected_costs: If you don't have a Canadian credit card the fees will add up to a lot.
cost_comparison: Generally, groceries are more expensive than expected and street food is less expensive.
activities_available: Most sports, board games, martial arts, video games etc. Different locally driven bars. Different department-specific events like book sales.
activities_recommended: Escape rooms are abundant and cheap – they are a good way to bond with people you don't know too well. Go up the CN tower at least once, go watch ice hockey, football and baseball.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the distillery district on weekends, or Maddison's. In reading week, Banff is a beautiful place to go. It is also a lovely town.
culture_adjustment: Took a couple of days to orient myself but after that very easy.
socializing_tips: Download WhatsApp.
cultural_challenges: The classes are all very divided, it seems more individualized.
culture_appreciated: There is so much diversity and with it so many things to do and try and taste.
top3_advice: Download WhatsApp, Get your T-card early, Get a bike plan.
other_useful_info: Kennsington Market and Spadina has some great food. Record stores have a lot bigger selection than here in Copenhagen. Explore!
most_rewarding: Doing things with new friends and exploring on my own/learning how to study in a new place.
greatest_challenge: Being willing to take some risks and do stuff you wouldn't normally do at home. Getting out your comfort zone.
other_comments: Toronto is so huge so start exploring early, once you are done with your exam you'll wish you had more time to do stuff in the city.

crucial_aspects: A school with a good reputation and a nice mix between Canadian culture and the more American culture. Many sports teams as well (hockey, basketball, baseball etc.)
info_ease: Easy enough.
arrival_assistance: No assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You receive an email with a google form you need to fill out with the courses you wish to take. They do multiple rounds of these, so you can decide pretty late what courses to take, though they need to be approved of course. Also, you can drop and take new courses a few weeks into the semester.
registration_help: There is a page where you can look at what course combinations are feasible and how your schedule looks.
registration_success: I got into all four of mine.
registration_advice: Accept that you do not know for sure what the courses are about and the important dates. Other than that, just find some courses which you think resemble courses you could take back home.
course_level: The level is definitely lower, but you can feel that they previously have been focusing on other things, because at some points you felt slightly behind and at other points you felt way ahead. The professors were mostly very good, but the teaching assistants were not the best at helping with the types of problems you would be required to solve.
teaching_comparison: It is quite similar, although the weekly exercises at UCPH are way more rewarding.
courses_enrolled: ECO310 - Empirical Industrial Organization ECO313 - Environmental Economics and Policies ECO314 - Energy and the Environment ECO324 - Economic Development
recommended_courses: I would recommend ECO314, if you're interested in the environment and how it is related to economics and geopolitics. If you like some light STATA work, then ECO310 is a good choice.
unexpected_costs: Things as mandatory health insurance at the university, which made no sense. And also getting used to tips and taxes at restaurants etc.
cost_comparison: Prices on different groceries are very different. But generally food is quite expensive.
activities_available: You can join an endless amount of clubs - there's something for everyone. Gym access and tickets for the university team sports games are free for students
activities_recommended: Go to a Raptors, Maple Leafs or Blue Jays game, a very different experience compared to sports games back home. Also, go to Niagara Falls.
weekend_recommendations: Take a trip to Algonquin, Montreal, or Banff.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. But get used to the fact that people attending university in Toronto are very young.
socializing_tips: I would recommend going to one of the club activities. If you like running, then the run club (UTRC) is a good place to socialize.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really, but get used to big cars and limited biking options.
culture_appreciated: I really like some of the sports culture (primarily the fact that the level of the hockey and basketball are so much higher than back home), and the people in Toronto (and Canada in general) are mostly very friendly.
top3_advice: 1. Apply early for housing. The people I spoke to that stayed at Tartu enjoyed that, and it's not too expensive. 2. Go to some of the activities that people suggest (you can get added to a big whatsapp group chat with every exchange student at UofT). That's how I met almost all the people I was with. 3. Focus on doing well at your midterm tests. You only need 50% to pass the course, and the exam schedule in December (for fall semester) can be very tight, so if you prioritize some of the early opportunities to score points you can enjoy the last weeks of your stay way more.
other_useful_info: Not really. But I would say that you shouldn't focus too much on school and enjoy the city. You generally receive pretty high grades, so even though you fear that you are gonna fail, it will be alright if you put in just some effort.
most_rewarding: Seeing what studying at a completely different university feels like, and meeting some very nice people.
greatest_challenge: At some points, it was a little tough that you weren't able to see friends and family from home, but luckily I found some nice people to hang out with over there and a semester is not that long.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere I had never been before and also where I knew I would be able to see a lot of nature without having to travel too far. Toronto is a nice and diverse city, but if I had to choose again I might have chosen a destination that was even closer to nature if possible.
overall_comments: I had a nice time in general and everything went well, but the study system is very different from what I am used to, so I found it quite hard to find a proper 'flow' in how things worked study-wise over there.
info_ease: I felt like I had to seek out information myself upon arrival instead of having someone helping you. We didn't get that much information about the system or how classes worked and all that stuff, so I had to ask around myself to learn that stuff.
arrival_assistance: I got some assistance with switching my courses around when I first arrived, because I had some trouble with some of the courses.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I had a nice time in general and everything went well, but the study system is very different from what I am used to, so I found it quite hard to find a proper 'flow' in how things worked study-wise over there.
registration_process: I had to see available courses at one website and then get them pre-approved. After this there were rounds for applying for the courses where you have to be precise when writing your prerequisites because you otherwise could be rejected from having the course.
registration_help: I found help on campus after I had arrived, so they helped me in-person.
registration_success: I was successful but some courses were listed as in-person when they were actually online, which I did not think was okay at all.
registration_advice: Dont take any online classes when you're on exchange.
academics_comments: I had a nice time in general and everything went well, but the study system is very different from what I am used to, so I found it quite hard to find a proper 'flow' in how things worked study-wise over there.
course_level: I had two second-year courses and two fourth-year courses. I felt like the workload was big, but also because they had another style of teaching.
teaching_comparison: In Amy second-year courses I felt like they had to make sure that we did everything properly and attended the classes etc. We weren't as 'free' to take responsibility for our own learning which I found quite annoying seeing that it sometimes felt like being treated like a kid.
courses_enrolled: EEB268, Plant and Microbial Diversity PSL280, Introduction to Physiological Adaptions of Marine Mammals PSL480, Diving Physiology of Marine Mammals FOR413, Wildlife Ecology & Conservation
recommended_courses: FOR413, Wildlife Ecology & Conservation was my favorite course! Jennifer the professor is the best and sweetest teacher I've had in a long time and besides this she was very good at including present cases in her lectures, so it felt like there was a point to discussing the stuff we did in class.
unexpected_costs: Nothing big, but I was glad that I had my big winter boots and so on with me there.
cost_comparison: Housing is very expensive and groceries are too.
activities_available: Almost everything was available. I joined a running club.
activities_recommended: Running club was really nice - It was two days during the week and people were very sweet and you weren't obligated to show up.
weekend_recommendations: Niagara Falls - take a day out of the calendar to go there by train. its very nice. I also went to Calgary, Banff and I wish I had more time there! It was incredible!
culture_adjustment: Very easy, everybody is very sweet and its all in English so its not that hard.
socializing_tips: Be open and say hi to people. If you have any questions then don't be afraid to ask them also to the local student. They often know things the best and they are most often very happy to help.
cultural_challenges: I didn't find anything that difficult with cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: It is very diverse compared to Denmark and that was very nice to experience.
top3_advice: Be open and ask the locals (maybe your classmates) what to see and do around the city. They often have good recommendations. Expect to be a bid stressed during the first month seeing that you need to settle in and find your way around. Exploit the time you have and say yes to as many experiences as possible. It worth the tiredness in the end.
other_useful_info: If you live close to campus it might be nice for you to buy a used bike instead of taking public transport.
most_rewarding: All the friend you get out of it and everything that you see and experience.
greatest_challenge: Joggeling your time between having to do some school and wanting to see your friends and do social stuff most of the time can be a struggle.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere that was in a big city, that was different from what I know and an english speaking country. Furthermore, I mostly chose Toronto because of the academic opportunities
overall_comments: Overall I had a good and fun experience, but I lived a bit far from campus and I had an insane amount of work for university, which ended up taking up a lot of time, even though I learned a lot
info_ease: It was fairly easy to know what to do in a practical sense, and it was a smooth start to all my courses.
arrival_assistance: We had an introductory meeting at the university with other international students, showings around campus and a lot of emails.
arrival_comments: Even though it was easy to navigate, it would ahve been nice to see more organized events for us to meet people when we arrive.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall I had a good and fun experience, but I lived a bit far from campus and I had an insane amount of work for university, which ended up taking up a lot of time, even though I learned a lot
registration_process: You get approved by KU, then you have to send a formal application to the university, get courses approved and follow the steps on mobility online.
registration_help: There was a coordinator for Canada who was available to answer questions, and a facebook group was set up for students going to Canada to communicate with each other.
registration_success: I got preapproved for 15 courses, and only four of them ended up being available for the semester, so there was not much of a choice to be made in my case.
registration_advice: When you apply for courses, KU approves as many as 15 courses, and since when you are doing this the academic timetable for the term when youre going on exchange (fall 2023 in my case) is not availbale yet, so you have to choose based on the calendar of the current year. I recommend applying for as many courses as you can, since anything can happen and that way you have more to choose from.
academics_comments: Overall I had a good and fun experience, but I lived a bit far from campus and I had an insane amount of work for university, which ended up taking up a lot of time, even though I learned a lot
course_level: I took one level 4 course, one level 2 course and one level 3 course. I found that the level for my level 3 courses was adequate, the level 4 course was very complicated and had a lot more workload, while the level 2 course was much easier. These two balanced each other out, but I definitely 100% recommend considering level 4 courses thoroughly before choosing them, if you are a year 3 student, because the difference in level was quite clear, and most canadian students do not tak emore than 2 level 4 courses at the same time.
teaching_comparison: As i mentioned, I feel that we were not treated with as much independence and had more homework .
courses_enrolled: Confronting global change, Ecosystem ecology, Principles of ecological agroforestry, Topics in applied conservation.
recommended_courses: Ecosystem ecology was a great course, it included a field trip and a lot of fun lab excercises. The teacher, Shelby Riskin, remembers all her students names and creates a very intimate atmosphere in the classroom. The workload was not too bad, it was mostly done in groups, and we had no final exam which was nice.
unexpected_costs: The transport is really expensive, and having a social life as well.
cost_comparison: Eating out is less expensive than copenhagen, but groceries are more expensive.
activities_available: There are a toon of activities on campus, both non-competitive sports teams (intramurals), drop-in fitness classes of all sorts in the 3 gyms on campus, and countless clubs.
activities_recommended: I recommend the uTOC club, an outdoor club that organizes activities in nature off campus. I went kayaking with them and on a weekend cabin trip by the blue mountains, which was a great experience. If you enjoy running then the running club is also a nice way to see the city.
weekend_recommendations: Go for brunch, visit the parks and islands before it gets too cold, and honestly just walk around and explore neighborhoods.
culture_adjustment: It was not that hard, I had to get used to people not having their main friends in their classes and the campus life.
socializing_tips: Its easy to talk to people if youre not shy, but making friends with locals is always mroe difficult than with other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: The student life is very different from back home, it is way more challenging and people spend a lot more time studying.
culture_appreciated: I appreciated how international it was, you meet people and cultures from all over the world, which is safe to say we are missing in Copenhagen.
top3_advice: - Try to find housing in the city, I regretted living so far from campus. - Use the campus and all the non-academic opportunities - Have fun and dont worry too much about doing too much all the time, it is going to be very intense and fun so taking days for yourself is a good investment.
other_useful_info: Choose things you think might be fun because you might end up spending a lot of time on them:)
most_rewarding: What I learned on my courses and the people I met.
greatest_challenge: Balancing studying with work life.

crucial_aspects: It was about experiencing living in an English-speaking country and encountering new academic challenges.
info_ease: You also had to be proactive, but the UofT inbound office was good at disseminating information and responding to inquiries quite fast
arrival_assistance: I didn't really receive any assistance when I arrived, expect for an information meeting
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: First, you could see all the possible courses in their catalouge and create a possible schedule for your courses to make sure there wasn't any conflicts with the courses. Then they send out a formula for you to fill out with the relevant course requests.
registration_help: They sent out guides on how to apply
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted
registration_advice: Use some time to make a schedule for your courses and apply for them all in the first round. There's plenty of options to change and drop courses later on - so if I was in-between two courses I would apply for both of them and have the option to drop one of them later on.
course_level: I primarily had 3rd year courses.
teaching_comparison: Most of the courses I had were only lectures whereas I at UCPH also have instruction classes.
courses_enrolled: ECO365H1 - International Monetary Economics ECO316H1 - Applied Game Theory ECO342H1 - Twentieth Century Economic History: Institutions, Growth and inequality CSC108H1 - Introduction to Computer Programming
recommended_courses: I would recommend ECO316 and ECO342 if they're studying economics, because it can be transferred as Micro III and Economic History. And CSC108 was a great introduction course to Python.
unexpected_costs: Not unexpected costs, but I would make room in my budget for experiences and travels.
cost_comparison: I was surprised, that I didn't have to buy any books for my courses. There were some recommended books, but not any required ones.
activities_available: All sorts!
activities_recommended: I didn't really join any clubs. But I would recommend following all the different Instagram profiles, to see which activities there's going on.
weekend_recommendations: I would explore the city, go to hockey games or travel around (I would recommend paying Banff National Park a visit).
culture_adjustment: I found it quite easy actually. There's a lot of international students as well.
socializing_tips: To be honest, there were mostly international students in my classes, so I found it hard to socialize with local students. I mostly hung out with the other exchange students.
cultural_challenges: The only thing that comes to my mind is the tax and tipping system - it's very different from Denmark.
culture_appreciated: I think it's hard to say as Toronto is very multicultural. But generally the friendliness.
top3_advice: I would recommend finding other exchange students as well. Use the facilities at school - there are many great places to study, work out and such. Don't be afraid to reach out to the offices, they're very helpsome and answers quite fast.
other_useful_info: It is a university in the middle of the city - so you don't get the same 'college'/campus experience as you might get other places in Canada.
most_rewarding: The ability to live in another country and get to know a lot of other exchange students.
greatest_challenge: My greatest challenge was to attend courses all alone and navigate through that.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to find a university that was ranking wise at least as good or better than KU. UofT was perfect as I had challenging graduate courses while also being able to travel a lot!
info_ease: Most things need to be figured out on your own, but it is definitely doable. Go to one of the introductions (there are only a few). But most can be found on their website if you click around.
arrival_assistance: Barely any. Most things you'll need to figure out on your own. There is a club fair in the start and some introductory events which are nice, but other than that not much.
arrival_comments: There just isn't much in intro in grad school anywhere I think.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I couldn't register courses via acorn, but I emailed someone (details in next box) and after that everything went pretty smooth.
registration_help: I emailed an administrator from the department of statistical sciences (graduate). I had a zoom meeting with the administrator and a professor and got all the courses I wanted! NOTE: You cannot register on acorn (like you're supposed to) so contact someone depending on your area of study. Multiple people had this issue.
registration_success: I got every class I wanted.
registration_advice: Especially if you are a graduate student: Reach out to someone at your department to ensure they know what courses you want. Some people had trouble getting courses.
course_level: I took Advanced Time Series, Advanced Computational Statistics and Time Series. I really enjoyed the courses, however the two advanced courses were tough and we did not have many exercises to prepare for the exam. (and passing as a graduate student is 70% or above btw, they do curve the grade if the course is really hard in stats)
teaching_comparison: More applied. I was used to having lecture notes written by my professors, but there most classes are done with slides (A north American thing).
courses_enrolled: Advanced Time Series; Advanced Computational Statistics; Time Series
recommended_courses: I liked all of my courses, but MCMC (monte carlo markov chain) which we had about in Advanced Computational Statistics.
unexpected_costs: (btw I biked in toronto that's why transport was low) Traveling costs are not included.
cost_comparison: Food. Most foods are simply more expensive in grocery stores. Eating out is cheaper in Toronto than in Copenhagen, but still expensive in the long run.
activities_available: 3 free gyms at st. george campus, plenty of sports, really nice sports facilities. (Plenty to do in toronto)
activities_recommended: Joining a club is fun. And join or create an instagram group with other exchange students. (We had a big one with 250 exchange students!)
weekend_recommendations: Algonquin provincial park super nice in fall! probably also summer or spring. (Autumn colors are beautiful) We had a reading week and vancouver/ whistler is super nice if you like nature and hiking!
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, Toronto is super international friendly. A lot of people are international!
socializing_tips: Go to clubs and engage whenever possible.
cultural_challenges: The food. Finding a new rythm for that.
culture_appreciated: The international environment. (not much canadian culture though)
top3_advice: 1. Find housing early 2. Find groups of exchange students (in big insta groups a lot of people suggest events or happenings in the start!) 3.Travel
other_useful_info: Be open and try new stuff.
most_rewarding: Meeting other exchange students and traveling with them.
greatest_challenge: Finding housing, figuring out all information and food habits.

crucial_aspects: I chose U of T as it was an English speaking university and because it seemed to provide a unique academic opportunity for me.
info_ease: The biggest challenge was sifting through every mail to make sure that you did not miss an important link or piece of information. It could be helpful to simplify the entire process and reduce the number of emails.
arrival_assistance: We had a 1 hour introduction talk which was quite good, everything considered. A nice woman helped me with an issue, I was having.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We were asked to fill out Google Forms-formulas with the course in question and the prove of eligibility given the required prerequisites.
registration_help: We were giving an information sheet.
registration_success: Almost entirely unsuccesful.
registration_advice: Have a good look at the prerequisites and be prepared to apply for a "backup" course.
course_level: I did two 300-level courses, one 200-level course and one 400-level course.
teaching_comparison: I must admit, I prefer the Danish style of teaching. There is a very large use of PowerPoint (or similar) at U of T and it seemed that normal practice for students is to write notes directly on the slides using an iPad. I prefer that my professors use blackboard.
courses_enrolled: CSC263 - Data Structure and Analysis PHY407 - Computational Physics PHY331 - Biological Physics PHY392 - Climate Physics
recommended_courses: None of the above.
unexpected_costs: UHIP - the mandatory University Healthcare plan, however it allowed me to save on buying one from my insurance company.
