Learning things by heart is important, there's less discussion in class than in Denmark. It's not always easy to follow a class if the teacher is talking for two hours straight in French without any kind of powerpoint or writing on the blackboard. Also, class attendance is mandatory and may have an impact on your grade
courses_enrolled: Introduction à la sociologie Théories sociologiques De la cité à l'urbain Creative writing Key concepts of the Anglophone world Expression écrite et orale en français La littérature, la société et les arts aujourd'hui : l'image et la littérature Langue écrite universitaire C1 Culture et société B2/C1
recommended_courses: Creative writing Introduction à la sociologie
unexpected_costs: I had to buy a housing insurance (one time payment for a year) which is mandatory in France Transportation fee is low because I bought a second hand bike when I got there
cost_comparison: Food is a little bit cheaper than in Denmark, especially if you go to the market. Train tickets are quite expensive if you want to take trips to other places in France. Books are much cheaper than in Denmark
activities_available: A LOT of different activities: bouldering, dance classes, tennis, swimming with SUAPS and it costs almost nothing compared to Denmark. I know that the university offers different kinds of workshops and extracurricular activities as well
activities_recommended: Definitely sports classes, but also festivals, film clubs, theatre etc.
weekend_recommendations: Mont St Michel, Nantes, Paris, kayaking on the Loire, seeing the castles in the area. In the longer breaks there's a bit more time to travel, so maybe Toulouse or Bordeaux there
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. It helps a lot if you speak some French though
socializing_tips: Do Tandem language exchanges for meeting French people. Involve yourself in sports or other activities, talk to people in class and don't be afraid to talk to strangers. Try to become friends with other people's French friends if you can
cultural_challenges: It took a little while to get used to the school system + remembering saying 'vous' instead of 'tu' + French bureaucracy
culture_appreciated: The food, the language, the books, the people ... it's been great almost all of it
top3_advice: Be prepared for paperwork Enjoy that you're in France and that you're doing an exchange - uni is important, but it's just as important to meet the other exchange students and discover the city Try to speak French even though you think that you make a lot of mistakes, most people are nice and patient
other_useful_info: It's all a bit confusing and stressful in the beginning, but it will be fine after a few weeks
most_rewarding: How much my French has improved + all the great people I met and the things we did together
greatest_challenge: Fitting in the school system and navigating covid, wearing masks all the time etc.

crucial_aspects: That the city was very student friendly, that costs of living weren't too high (rent, utilities, food, going out, etc.), that it would serve as a good learning environment for getting a good grasp on the language and the culture, so as to help me assimilate and better comprehend the country and its people (France, in my case).
overall_comments: I went to Tours, in the central region, and had a great time. People were very nice and accomodating. I struggled with being shy and lacking confidence in the French that I spoke upon arrival, but most people were kind and understanding, and I improved a whole lot over the 3 and a half months that I spent in the city. You also not only learn to appreciate the culture and people living there, but also the cultures of all the other exchange students, and even your own. The world is put into perspective, and you learn that we are not so different after all.
info_ease: It was fairly easy. A few months before departure, the international office at the university provided us with a booklet containing a lot of very useful information regarding accomodation, emergency services, healthcare, student life, general life in France, cultural tips, tips for dealing with homesickness, tips for making friends, etc.
arrival_assistance: We were all welcomed at the international office upon arrival, where we had to finalise our inscription. Many questions were answered here, and we were provided with the contact info of the international coordinator, who would answer further questions, should they arise. They also organised events for the exchange students the first two weeks of our stay, where a lot of information was presented.
arrival_comments: There were very few things that they could not help us with, and those things were usually solved through a Google search or asking a friend.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I went to Tours, in the central region, and had a great time. People were very nice and accomodating. I struggled with being shy and lacking confidence in the French that I spoke upon arrival, but most people were kind and understanding, and I improved a whole lot over the 3 and a half months that I spent in the city. You also not only learn to appreciate the culture and people living there, but also the cultures of all the other exchange students, and even your own. The world is put into perspective, and you learn that we are not so different after all.
registration_process: It was only a matter of making an appointment with the international office, an appointment that took around 30 minutes, and then later speaking with the coordinator assigned to you (usually a teacher), who would help you get an overview of your classes and your schedule.
registration_help: There was an international coordinator, who helped us with general questions, and then our own coordinator, who helped us with university related matters.
registration_success: I was able to take all the classes I wanted, but I think I got lucky. I think I spoke with others who had a bit more trouble with it.
registration_advice: There is not much advice to give, the process is fairly intuitive.
academics_comments: I went to Tours, in the central region, and had a great time. People were very nice and accomodating. I struggled with being shy and lacking confidence in the French that I spoke upon arrival, but most people were kind and understanding, and I improved a whole lot over the 3 and a half months that I spent in the city. You also not only learn to appreciate the culture and people living there, but also the cultures of all the other exchange students, and even your own. The world is put into perspective, and you learn that we are not so different after all.
course_level: As mentioned above, it varied quite a bit.
teaching_comparison: It was more square and old fashioned, and not as engaging as the teaching done at UCPH, but that is likely due to the more authoritarian school system they still have in France. At UCPH I appreciate that teachers and students see more eye to eye.
courses_enrolled: Oral French - a class for exchange students to help them improve their spoken French. Culture and Society - a class for exhange students to help them learn about and understand French culture and society while doing various linguistic exercises. French oral and written expression - a class on French grammar (so the name of the class is a bit misleading) English language and history - a class on the history and evolution of the English language. American civilisation - a class on American history, culture and society Translation from French to English Translation from English to French Introduction to the history of music - a class on classical music from around 1200 to around 1700
recommended_courses: The class on the history of music was quite interesting and the teacher was very charismatic.
unexpected_costs: Nothing in particular.
cost_comparison: Groceries were a bit more expensive than back home. Bakeries, on the other hand, were so, so cheap, it was lovely to go and get fresh crossaints and bread for around 1 euro a piece.
activities_available: For the humble fee of 25€, you could join up to 3 sports classes for the entire semester. I took rock climbing and lindy hop dance classes, both of which were great fun. Apart from that there is a rich student life with clubs and societies. I didn't take part in that however. There is also the ESN, which hosted a slew of gatherings for the exchange students.
activities_recommended: The sport offer is such a good deal, and a great way of meeting people. The ESN gatherings were a good way to get to know other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: The Loire valley, where Tours is situated, is chock full of castles and beautiful landscapes. The international office often organise trips to these castles on Saturdays. Otherwise, there are great opportunities to go visit the neighboring cities as well as Paris, for that matter.
culture_adjustment: Not too difficult, the biggest issue was the above mentioned issues with language (confidence in my own level, difficulties in terms of comprehension). The authoritarian school system was a bit tedious as well, but it was managable.
socializing_tips: Just don't be afraid of speaking to them initially. I made the mistake of letting my lack of confidence get too much in the way initially, but it's the best way to learn. The university offers "tandem sessions" where you can go speak with French students for an hour, half an hour in French, the other half an hour in another language (mostly English).
cultural_challenges: Getting adjusted to differentiating between "tu" and "vous" instinctively. Since it's "tu" when speaking to everyone back home, it was a bit weird to have to remember to speak differently to people.
culture_appreciated: The general openness of the French. It's easy to feel a difference as a Dane, but it was a breath of fresh air that people weren't hesitant at all to strike up conversation with complete strangers. I also appreciated that it is much more common to greet people in general, particularly in shops.
top3_advice: 1. Avoid the CROUS accomodation if you can! It's cheap, sure, but the quality reflects that. I lived there for a week before I found private accomodation. The kitchens are small and really ill equipped; four hot plates and a microwave is all they offer 12-14 people per kitchen. Being almost 2 meters tall, I was also very uncomfortable in the small bed. I was unable to lie down at full length and had to curl up my legs. 2. Don't be afraid to engage with your classmates despite language difficulties. Most of them are happy to help. 3. Be sure to sample some of the excellent restaurants in the city. My recommendations are "Au Chien Jaune" and "Dagobert." For a lovely bar experience check out "Le Serpent Volant."
other_useful_info: If one of your goals is to improve your French, be prepared to encounter a lot of everyday expressions and words you will never have heard of during your formal French studies. It is fun, however, so keep an open mind!
most_rewarding: 1. The friends I made from all over Europe. Now I'll have somewhere to crash in almost all of the continent's four corners. 2. The improvements I have made in terms of my French. I have gained much more confidence in my abilities to speak the language and engage with French people.
greatest_challenge: The initial difficulties I faced due to the language barrier. It contributed a bit to a feeling of loneliness and homesickness.
other_comments: I was luckily not too affected by the pandemic during my stay, but that might not be true for your exchange. Either way, do not hesitate to do an exchange semester, it is such a great experience.

crucial_aspects: A place with courses in English + a place with relevant courses + a nice country
info_ease: From University of Trento there is a nice guide for exchange students. I had more problems before arrival with KU and trying to work out deadlines with slow email responses, not a correct sign-up and unclear information about the learning agreement.
arrival_assistance: The University of Trento has a good ESN-organisation with information about living in Italy. Plus we had an orientation session at the university with practical information.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You just put the courses in your Online learning agreement. You don't sign up any other way. And you have two weeks to make your decision, so it's also possible to attend some courses and then change your mind.
registration_help: E-mail correspondence with the international office.
registration_success: I could go to all the classes I wanted
registration_advice: Try out a lot of courses in the beginning, so you know better what you want. Read online about the exams for every courses (There's a difference between attending and non-attending students)
course_level: The courses were not that difficult compared to the level at KU.
teaching_comparison: In Trento, you had to do a lot of presentations before being able to write the final essay for the exam. At KU, you only need to write the exam (usually).
courses_enrolled: Civil Societies and Contentious Politics, Corso di italiano A1a - II periodo (intensivo), International Economics (Basic), Labour Rights in the Global Economy, Party Politics and Democracy in Europe, Sociology of collective action
recommended_courses: The italian course is nice to get knowledge about Italy and a basic understanding of the language. I liked Party Politics and Democracy in Europe as well because the subject was very political-science. The Civil Societies and Contentious Politics-course had a nice, engaged teacher, I can recommend that as well.
unexpected_costs: The phone bill was a bit higher than expected, but I stayed with my Danish company. Would have been cheaper to buy an Italian simcard.
cost_comparison: Eating/drinking out is very cheap compared to Denmark. Groceries are not that different from Denmark
activities_available: UniTrentoSport, Erasmus Student Network, other free open events.
activities_recommended: Events organised by Erasmus Student Network (ESN) in order to get to know a lot of people. If you want to get to know more italian students, go to Bruno.
weekend_recommendations: Hiking! Go to the mountains all around the area A lot of small, nice museums to discover as well Trento is an easy link to take the train to other Italian regions.
culture_adjustment: The food culture is different (eating later for example), but not that hard to adjust to.
socializing_tips: Play a sports. You can go for free to beach volley courts and play with italians.
cultural_challenges: Eating later. Living slow (slower walking, slow in the supermarket, trains/busses are almost always late). But it's okay to work with.
culture_appreciated: Italians being very friendly and open to speak. The delicious food.
top3_advice: Go to the events with other Erasmus-students to make friends. Go on hikes in the mountains. Find housing in the city center.
other_useful_info: Exam sessions are usually in June, July and September. You can choose yourself which of the dates to attend. And if you don't like your grade from the first exam, you can reject the grade and try again the next date of exam.
most_rewarding: Living on my own in a new country, creating "a life" from scratch - and then finding out it's not so bad to be by yourself, because it forces you to try new activities and talk to new people. My new friends are what is most rewarding.
greatest_challenge: To leave home for the unknown.
other_comments: I can only recommend others to go on exchange. Especially in Trento. Here you have the perfect combination of doing outdoor sports like hiking, climbing, biking, swimming and skiing; while still enjoying the lakes during the summer, going for drinks at bars and eating pizza with your friends. The city is small, so meeting friends around the corner is the best. And also that everyone lives close, so "meet me at the duomo" is the classic starting point.

In terms of public transport, we blitz the circulation pass for 70€, enabling a 1 year subscription on “free” transport in the whole Trentino region. This has been very usefull and worth it for us. It can for example be used for taking a direct bus til Lake Garda (1,5 hours)
cost_comparison: Wine is cheaper. And eating out is a bit cheaper Maybe. Its difficult to give an estimate of what everything costs (above) because it varies a lot from every week.

Participate in a lot of ESN (Erasmus student network) events, and their trips (for example, I went with Them to october fest in munic) Visit a lot of cities in Italy with other Erasmus students, and make friends. I visited Florence, Rome, Venice, Bologna, Milan and verona, which are all nearby. Use the ESN discounts on Ryanair, Spotahome (apartment rents for travels during the semester) and FlixBus. You can use theese from when you get your ESN card after arrival. Visit countries around Italy, Austria, Slovenia, Hungary… Go on ski trips. You can also buy a whole-season dolomites ski pass for 900€ ish. Go to Decathlon and buy/rent sport equipment. Go to Scarletta (the bar everyone goes to) and go to kareoke on baccus on tuesdays. socializing_tips: Be open and talk to people in class, on bars or when meeting Them in the bus or whatever.
cultural_challenges: They don’t have the same relationship to, that its respectfull to be silent in public spaces, eg the bus. They just listen to loud things in their phones, without headphones. culture_appreciated: People are very chill, and mostly happy. The food culture is good
top3_advice: Trento is a relatively small city. The small city means, that the nightlife is for example not the biggest. However, we’re 300 Erasmus students in a small city, and we meet each others on the street and at the bar evwryone goes to. This is super cozy. Consider if this would suit you. Be open, prioritize experiences and adventures over School, and have fun. Enjoy your Erasmus!!
other_useful_info: Buy the circulation pass and use it to explore the whole trentino region Use the free gym, Palestra rossa, using the app “opera4you”

info_ease: It wasn't that easy. I had to write my professors on certain occasions. The italian university system is a lot different than the danish system. That being said, there wasn't a need for a lot of information. You just had to show up in class and listen carefully, and most things would be explained.
arrival_assistance: I had a "contact person" who helped me and the other Erasmus students. And I could always ask at the Infopoint, if I had any doubts.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Well I guess everything went smoothly. I chose my courses when I was still studying in Denmark. I had to change one course in my learning agreement, but that was fairly easy. Upon arrival I headed to the Infopoint and they registered my arrival. After that I was enrolled in my courses.
registration_help: The Infopoint, my Erasmus "buddy" and I could also contact the coordinator from UNITO if needed.
registration_success: Very successful
registration_advice: I don't know, it seemed quite easy, but you don't get a lot of info if you don't ask for it.
course_level: The courses varied. If was difficult to know what to expect at the exam. I didn't know what to read either. Everyone else in class were writing almost everything the teacher said down. In some philosophy classes so many philosophers were introduced to us students, that remebering all of them seemed a bit unrealistic. Quality-wise, the level of teaching was rather low on most courses. The students just had to take notes and remember them by heart. But in the end the exams were quite easy.
teaching_comparison: We didn't work in groups, which I was getting used to in Copenhagen. We had to take a lot of notes, which I never felt was necessary before. At UNITO, the students rarely ask questions to the teacher. The communication is rather one-way, whereas at UCPH we have conversations with the teacher and our classmates. I prefer the classes at UCPH.

unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Food is more expensive than expected in Italy, especially if you like good quality cheese.
activities_available: I think there were some sport acitivities available, but I never went. Flyers were handed out in front of the university with theater workshops and things like that.
activities_recommended: I got some fine experiences from rowing on the river Po.
weekend_recommendations: I enjoyed going out of the city, especially to the mountains.
culture_adjustment: I study italian culture in Denmark, so I wasn't that difficult to adjust.
socializing_tips: Not really, they are quite young the students in Turin, much younger than me.

Particularly on the language front, given that I can now confidently say I speak Spanish fluently both colloquial but also academic.
course_level: 5 Courses, each 6 ETCS points.
teaching_comparison: It certainly felt like I was back in high school. For me, I was very sad about the teaching style simply because they were obviously competent and smart educators, however, their teaching style was simply to provide us with information. You had to simply memorise everything and you didn't use the information in a critical manner, nor were you given reason for why it was important to know or remember what you were told. For example, I took a class in art history, where our teacher had a module on islamic art in Spain and how some churches are old mosques and how you can tell - we could have talked about the political part of it, the reconquistas and so on or even the interesting differences between islamic art not portraying persons versus christian art which does. But not, we were simply told that islamic art doesn't portray persons without our educator going into detail about why this is, given that there are obvious religious/cultural reasons for it.
courses_enrolled: Historia del arte, lecturas contemporáneas hispanoamericanas, Español de América, Español coloquial, El español y las lenguas del mundo hispánico
recommended_courses: Español de América is very interesting and la profesora Milagros Aleza Izquierdo is a really lovely woman. The subject itself isn't very difficult, especially if you have had phonetics prior to the class, but it's very interesting to hear and learn about both the phonetic, but also the lexical differences in language between different Spanish speaking nations. I would also recommend Español coloquial, I took this class in the international class so the educators are aware of our limits as students. Here our educators were Marta Pilar Montañez Mesas and Antonio Briz Gomez. Marta is a delight and a really engaging educator. Antonio is the expert of the subject in all of Spain and it's great to have him as educator. Here the focus is on sociolinguistics, colloquial language, and transcriptions. I personally prefer studying history and literature, normally as those subjects interest me - but I would not recommend to do that here, as they do not engage the students in a meaningful way, making it simply boring.

arrival_assistance: I didn't receive much assistance other than at a very simple "welcome-meeting" for the Erasmus students. Apart from that we were pretty much left to figure things out ourselves. Whenever I emailed the study guidance office of my faculty in Valencia, it would take them weeks to answer, and the few times I went to the office, they would ask me to leave and not come back, because they couldn't do anything to help me with my questions. Questions concerning my schedule, subjects and other practical university things. The lack of assistance or help resulted in a lot of confusion, not just for me, but for a lot of the Erasmus students. I missed the first 1,5 months of lessons in one of my subjects, because the administration at the university was so slow, and they didn't assign me to the classes, before much later. My home university (University of Copenhagen) wasn't of much help either. It also took them a long time to respond to on emails, so I truly felt that I was on my own with all my doubts and questions, and that was quite frustrating and demotivating.

crucial_aspects: That I have heard good about the university of Valencia and the city in overall
overall_comments: The beginning was a bit confusing with the matriculación
info_ease: It was easy. I got everything important send on email and it was easy to follow all the steps
arrival_assistance: I had a local student as a "buddy" that offered help if needed. I didn't need to use it though, but it was nice to know that someone at my own age was available
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The beginning was a bit confusing with the matriculación
registration_process: We had a 2 week period of matriculación where we could change courses as we wanted. Afterwards, it was binding. I found it a bit confusing because I had to make sure that any of my classes overlapped. At the same time it was a good, because I had scheduled a course from home that I no-way was interested in attending. So it was good that I was able to change but at the same time it was a confusing process, because the courses also got full quickly and I had to choose some that I semi-wanted
registration_help: Not much help. The secretary just informed about the procedure but we had to handle it ourselves
registration_success: In the end I made 3 out of 5 of those I expected to do from home
registration_advice: Knowing that there's a big chance of changing some of the courses you plan from home - either because the course doesn't turn out as expected, the level is too high or you simply find another one more interesting. academics_comments: The beginning was a bit confusing with the matriculación
course_level: It was really different from course to course. I had one course that was super easy that didn't took much effort to pass. On the other hand, I had 3 other courses that was really difficult to pass. All the teachers demanded a lot. So despite they represented the same credits, the level and work load was really different
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is really different. In UCPH it's way more self-studying and the responsibility to succeed is on your own. Here, the system is more like highschool in Denmark with tasks during the course that you have to hand in or tests. In some of my classes, the teacher also took notes of the absence / presence that had an influence in the final evaluation
courses_enrolled: Spanish and languages of the Hispanic world (35518) American Spanish (35517) Norms and correct usage of Spanish (35660) Lecturas contemporáneas hispanoamericanas (35530) Expresión oral y escrita en el español académico y profesional (35538)
recommended_courses: I really liked "American Spanish". The teacher was really good and I learned a lot from there. "Lecturas contemporáneas hispanoamericanas" was also really interesting but way more demanding. We had to read 3 books during the semester + hand in 2 comments about a short story and do tests.
unexpected_costs: I subscriped to a bike-company that has bikes all over the city. I didn't use the public transport too much but the bike was really useful. Besides that I subscriped to a gym also. I did not spend anything on books for uni, since everything was available online
cost_comparison: The rent but I was also out in last minute and I prioritized to live as central as possible
activities_available: There was a lot of sports-offerings that you could subscripe to for a little amount
activities_recommended: The sports offerings. I did not attend to any myself, but I heard from a lot down here that it was great (fx the surf school that the uni had a collab with)
weekend_recommendations: Travel to the other cities around. I went a lot to the coastline between Valencia and Alicante and there are so many small, cute villages on the coastline. It is easy going there with either train or bus and it's nice to come out of the city to a smaller more local environment
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy knowing some stuff from home. Fx that you write formally to your teacher on mail, but that the oral communication is pretty much like in Denmark. I expected a more formal environment in the class room but it was really casual
socializing_tips: Speak spanish and be open
cultural_challenges: I found the local students a bit reserved and not that interested in interacting with erasmus-students. Maybe because there's so many in Valencia, I don't know. But for me, the university could do a bit more effort
culture_appreciated: That the spanish people are really open and sweet. They are not reserved as some people in Denmark can appear. They like to talk and have an interest in you
top3_advice: 1. There's a lot of exchange students in Valencia. It takes an effort to get to know the locals 2. Have patience in the beginning with the matriculation. It will be solved in the end 3. Enjoy and try to go outside Valencia as well. There's so many beautiful places around
other_useful_info: Since the faculties are far apart, maybe it's the best to just choose courses from 1 faculty. I was supposed to take from different ones, but found it too confusing in the beginning so changed to only my own
most_rewarding: To try to live in Spain and experience the culture for more than just 2 weeks vacation. Get friendships from different european countries
greatest_challenge: To approach people I don't know and speak to a lot of new people. To adjust to a different uni-system and the work-load in the courses.

crucial_aspects: Since I started planning my exchange during the pandemic and did not know when all the restrictions would end I wanted to optimize my chances of the exchange actually taking place, which is the reason why I chose a destination in Europe and one of KU's partner universities. I also wanted to go somewhere where I would at the very least have a passing knowledge of the language so I would have a chance of understanding what has going on around me when I was not the one directly spoken to. Lastly I liked that at TiHo you could choose to which clinics you were going to spend your time in, so that you could focus on your area of interest.
info_ease: Easy in terms of enrollment, but fairly difficult in terms of schedule/ program for my stay.
arrival_assistance: I had a meeting with my contact person who helped me get enrolled and handed me som papers with a map of the campuses, information on how to access the e-mail etc. Then I was given a tour of the clinic by the veterinarian in charge of international students there and shown to the service where I was to spend my first week. I did not get the full introduction until the end of the week when the next of the clinical cycles were starting up. This was when the new students and I was presented with the schedule, got another tour of the clinic and got an introduction to the different services we would be cycling through and how the cycle worked.
arrival_comments: I would have really liked to have received a schedule or program before arriving so that I knew what to expect going in.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After receiving a spot through the KU application I was put in contact with my contact person who sent me an application form I need to fill out to be provisionally accepted. Later I was asked what clinics I was interested in staying at during my exchange. I was officially enrolled after arriving at TiHo.
registration_help: I had a contact person at the international office who I could ask questions and who would remind me of deadline etc. which was great.
registration_success: I expressed interest in spending time at the small animal clinic and the exotics clinic and was awarded a spot in the clinical cycle in the small animal clinic.
registration_advice: Nothing, it was really easy and I felt like I was well guided through the process.
course_level: I felt like I was well equipped to take on the course and that the level of the course was good.
teaching_comparison: Since TiHo is a referral hospital they do not really do the first consultations/ general practitioner stuff such as vaccinations, chipping etc. Since the consultations were generally more specialized the students did not really have any patient responsibility, which lead it to be somewhat limited how much we got to do during a consultation (generally we got to take an anamnesis here and there and do a general examination, but it was a lot of standing around and listening). Whenever blood samples were taken one of the students would generally get to do it, and the same was the case with placing venous catheters. Since we did not have patient responsibility we also did not have to write the medical records or going home letters etc. Since we did not have to do any paperwork we unfortunately sometimes ended up with days with quite a lot of time of us just sitting around waiting for something to happen/ a patient to show up, especially when there was not all that many patients booked in. They also have quite a few interns and phd students who I sometimes felt was prioritized over the PJ students*, since they where usually the ones who got to be 1st assistant in surgeries, did the anamnesis, had to write the medical records and so on. At TiHo they hospitalize way more patients than at KU which also meant that we had to spend far more time looking after these patients (around 3 out of 10 weeks spread out over day-, night-, and weekend shifts) which I did not feel like I I gained all that much from since I rarely knew the patients and why they were receiving the treatment that they received and usually did not have the time to go look them up to gain insight into their medical history. *PJ students = Practical year students
courses_enrolled: I did a practical year cycle at the small animal clinic
recommended_courses: Since I only took one course I will just list the services I liked the best. I really liked neurology, dermatology, ophthalmology and ultrasound as well as reproduction despite there unfortunately being too many people and too few cases for the week I was there.
unexpected_costs: An administrational fee of €352
cost_comparison: Food and rent was generally more inexpensive than back home.
activities_available: Hochschule Sport which offers different sports for free/ low fees to enrolled students ESN (Erasmus student network) - I was not made aware of this organization by TiHo, but by one of my flatmates who had done an exchange herself. They arrange trips and events for international students and whatever germans who want to join in as well in the city and surrounding area.
activities_recommended: If you are there during the spring/summer I would recommend going canoeing/kayaking/SUPing on the Leine/Ihme rivers, since it gets pretty hot in the city and is a nice way to spend a hot day. The city is pretty flat and has a lot of bike lanes so if you have a pair of rollerblades I would recommend bringing them since it seems like a fun way to explore the city. The zoo and Herrenhäuser Garten are also worth a visit.
weekend_recommendations: When you get enrolled and pay the administrational fee you also get a semester ticket which allows you to travel on public transportation throughout all of Lower Saxony for free. You can therefore go to cities such as Bremen or Hamburg for a day trip at no extra cost, which is a fun way to spend a day.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy since the cultures are rather similar.
socializing_tips: Speak German since a lot of the students are very insecure about their English or speak it poorly. I did not really follow this advise myself if I am being honest, but it worked out and my understanding was generally good enough that I understood it when they spoke German to me and could help supply English words if they spoke English to me and were struggling finding the right words.
cultural_challenges: They are way less digitalized than we are in Denmark and pretty much everything gets printed out and there are way less computers just standing around where you can look up the patients. The germans were also generally rather bad at taking breaks to make sure that they get to eat lunch. You could also feel that there was somewhat more of a hierarchy compared to what I am used to.
culture_appreciated: How much they care for animals. I was continually surprised how far a lot of owners were willing to go in terms of treatment of their animals and how dog friendly of a place Germany is.
top3_advice: 1) Brush up on your German, it will make life way easier for you 2) Do not bring any clothes for the clinic, you get some at the clinic. The only thing you need to bring is a stethoscope and maybe a belt since it can be a challenge to find pants that fit 3) Bring/ rent a bike, it is a great way to get around the city - especially to get home when you have nightshifts
other_useful_info: During a cycle you rotate through the different services or a combination of services spending a week in each service or pair of services eg derma and ultrasound or ophthalmology and oncology. You rotate in pairs or a 3 person group as was the case for me since the cycle was already filled so I was a bit of an extra. On Mondays we would have a 2 hour seminar in the afternoon and on Thursday we would have a 1 hour x-ray case based seminar, so on these days we got to leave the clinic early otherwise days were generally from 8 till 17. The cycle include one week of nightshifts, one weekend of dayshifts, and one weekend of nightshifts. If you have a dog and you want to bring it you can. The students have a room where we ate lunch etc. and you can keep your dog there in a crate while you are at the clinic, which quite a few of the students did.
most_rewarding: Gaining a really good understanding of the language, so that by the end of my stay I could more or less understand everything being said to me even if I could not respond as well in German.
greatest_challenge: The language since it did lead me to sometimes not participating as much as I probably could because I was not always sure I understood a question correctly.
other_comments: My German proficiency was me taking German back in folkeskolen and gymnasiet and then not really using it since, so if that is the same for you do not let that scare you off of going to Germany on exchange. The people there were generally really nice about letting me answer in English or switching to English around me if I was the only one there.

crucial_aspects: Jeg ville gerne til et engelsktalende land, og pga. corona virkede Canada som det land hvor der var størst sandsynlighed for at jeg kunne komme ind i landet. Jeg fokuserede meget på de udbudte kurser på de forskellige universiteter. Jeg valgte UVIC fordi jeg kunne tage keramik og forskellige fag indenfor arkæologi og biologisk antropologi.
info_ease: Det var ikke specielt let. Det hele blev ekstra kompliceret af coronaepidemien, hvilket gjorde at jeg skulle have lavet en study permit. Den kunne kun laves i Stockholm. Jeg synes ikke informationen fra KU var særlig fyldestgørende desværre. UVIC var tilgengæld rigtig gode til at hjælpe og afholdt flere zoom-møder for udenlandske studerende, så vi kunne få hjælp til study permit, vacciner mm. Der blev også afholdt zoom-møder (fra UVIC) så vi kunne få hjælp til at tilmelde os kurser osv. Dem anbefaler jeg at man deltager i, så er det meget lettere at undgå at misse deadlines. UVIC svarede også hurtigt og kompetent på emails. KU svarer ikke særlig hurtigt.
arrival_assistance: UVIC er rigtig gode til at hjælpe, og de afholdt en masse arrangementer på universitet for udenlandske studerende. Man får hjælp til at tilmelde sig kurser og kan få rundvisninger på universitet. Der er også flere sociale begivenheder man kan deltage i. Man får ikke hjælp til housing desværre, da UVIC slet ikke har nok on-campus housing til alle de studerende der gerne vil have det.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Man får et log-in til en side, hvor man skal tilmelde sig kurser. Der er et bestemt tidspunkt hvor tilmeldingen åbner, og det anbefales at man sidder klar, så man hurtigt kommer på. Hvis man ikke får en plads direkte kommer man på venteliste. Mange på ventelisten får en plads på et tidspunkt, da en masse hopper fra lige op til studiestart.
registration_help: Zoom-møder og man kunne sende emails til UVIC.
registration_success: Jeg fik kurser jeg gerne ville have. Ikke alle de kurser jeg havde kigget på hjemmefra kunne jeg få. Nogle blev ikke udbudt i det semester jeg var afsted og andre karambolerede med andre kurser jeg hellere ville have.
registration_advice: Bed om hjælp hvis du mangler den. De er super søde til at hjælpe!
course_level: Jeg havde kurser til første, andet og tredje år. Jeg var afsted på mit tredje år af min bachelor. Kurserne var lettere end i Danmark synes jeg. Grunden til at nogle af mine kurser var førsteårskurser var fordi jeg ikke kunne tage de efterfølgende kurser uden at have introduktionskurset først. Men selv mit tredjeårskursus var relativt let.
teaching_comparison: Meget forskelligt. Universitetet i Canada minder mere om gymnasiet end uni i Danmark. Man har masser af afleveringer og deadlines og små opgaver hele tiden. Alle ting man laver bliver graded og alt tæller med i ens samlede karakter. Det var lidt irriterende at man ikke selv kan planlægge og styre sin tid, fordi der hver uge var flere nye deadlines man skulle bruge tid på. Det er dog ikke super svære opgaver, men de tager lidt tid. Det er meget designet til at man skal "lære" at gå på universitetet og man bliver holdt meget i hånden. Helt anderledes end universitetet i Danmark.
courses_enrolled: ANTH240 Archaeology ANTH250 Biological Anthropology ANTH347 The Pleistocene Archaeology of Africa AE303A Introduction to Ceramics Wheel and Hand Techniques
recommended_courses: Keramikkurset var mega sjovt! The Pleistocene Archaeology of Africa var også virkelig spændende. Biologisk antropologi var spændende, men ikke særlig højt niveau. Arkæologi var meget en introduktion og lidt "tørt".
unexpected_costs: Ikke noget.
cost_comparison: At spise ude er billigt, men råvarer var ok dyre. Huslejen var dyrere end jeg håbede.
activities_available: Virkelig mange, men jeg deltog ikke.
activities_recommended: Jeg deltog ikke.
weekend_recommendations: Tag ud på ture i naturen. Man kan hike, og der er virkelig smukt. Jeg var på flere hike-ture og det var ret fedt! Man kan også bade på stranden (om sommeren). Det er også skønt at tage færgen til Vancouver.
culture_adjustment: Relativt let. De fleste af mine venner var dog også selv udenlandske studerende, eller canadiere der kom fra andre dele af Canada.
socializing_tips: Deltag i arrangementer på universitetet.
cultural_challenges: Det ved jeg ikke helt.
culture_appreciated: Folk er meget venlige!
top3_advice: Begynd at søge efter bolig i god tid og brug meget tid på det.
other_useful_info: Brug UVIC og skriv mails hvis du har spørgsmål. De er søde til at hjælpe.
most_rewarding: Kurserne var mega fede og jeg mødte en masse søde mennesker fra hele verden.
greatest_challenge: Corona gjorde det besværligt at komme afsted.

crucial_aspects: That the university offered courses on documentation of endagered languages. The choice of Victoria also came about because I had friends there.
overall_comments: My stay was super great, but at times the workload from UVic was too much and I got stressed. Sometimes, this meant that I would spend my weekends working instead of going out and exploring the area.
info_ease: Very easy. The exchange coordinators sent out plenty of e-mails to prepare us for our stay, also informing us where we could find additional information.
arrival_assistance: UVic's exchange coordinators hosted many meetings upon arrival to introduce us to many aspects of UVic life. The instructors and students were also very helpful in answering my questions on studying in Canada.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: My stay was super great, but at times the workload from UVic was too much and I got stressed. Sometimes, this meant that I would spend my weekends working instead of going out and exploring the area.
registration_process: You get a list with courses that are recommended for exchange students, and you can also look on the website for additional courses if you wish. Before registration opens, you may have to submit information on prior courses if the course you want to take has prerequisites. The coordinators are quick to let you know whether or not you can get into the course, and if the course is open at all. Then you get a time slot allotted for some time around May, and at that time, you can begin registering for courses. You go into the university's website (where you have to make an account), and then you search for the courses. Then you see if there are any vacant spots on the course, and then you register. If it is full, you can stand in line and wait for someone to deselect the course.
registration_help: The exchange coordinators sent e-mails with thorough instructions on how to register for courses and information on what courses were suggested. They were also quick to answer questions.
registration_success: I got into all the courses I selected from the list of suggested courses. However, many of the courses I had seen in the university's course catalogue were not offered that term, unfortunately.
registration_advice: Do it early! And try to find information in the course catalogue on whether or not the course will be offered in your term.
academics_comments: My stay was super great, but at times the workload from UVic was too much and I got stressed. Sometimes, this meant that I would spend my weekends working instead of going out and exploring the area.
course_level: They were not as challenging as what I have been used to at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: In general, there was more lecturing, with instructors just repeating the content of the assigned readings, and less room for questions and discussions. When there were discussions, they were also more about personal opinion and social/political issues, whereas at UCPH I remember it being more academic. One course, however, (LING 387: Task-based language teaching) had it very opposite, where students presented and experimented with planned lessons most of the time. This course also had extreme enthusiasm and activity based learning. Furthermore, tests were more about remembering facts than applying methodologies than what I remember from UCPH.
courses_enrolled: IS 101 - Indigenous Studies Foundations LING/PSYC 370 B - Child Language Acquisition LING 387 - Task-based language teaching LING 431 - Community-based language revitalization
recommended_courses: IS 101 was super fascinating, since I learned about a side of Canada that I would probably not have heard about otherwise. Also, it helped me develop a new outlook on life, realizing how cultures can be different and how people relate to each other and the world. The instructor in LING 387 was extremely enthusiastic, and her methods of teaching helped me learn a lot. She provides food every lesson and creates a very friendly atmosphere, so it is a good time. There is a lot of work, but the rewards are definitely tangible.
unexpected_costs: The study permit did cost more than I expected, especially because I needed my fingerprints scanned, which I had to go to Stockholm to do - the other closest option was in Germany.
cost_comparison: I thought groceries would be cheaper than in Denmark, but they were just as expensive - Walmart was pretty much the only affordable supermarket. UVic, however, did have a food bank where you could get free food once a week, which helped a lot. Phone data plans were quite expensive. Transportation with bus and ferry was cheaper than I had expected.
activities_available: Sports clubs, a caving club, dance classes, color run (combined with Holi), karaoke nights, pub quiz, etc.
activities_recommended: Karaoke night, pub quiz, color run, the caving club
weekend_recommendations: Go to nature, there are many great spots to visit all around. In the city, I would recommend the game arcade, board game cafes, the Beacon Hill park, the Royal B.C. museum, the harbour, Mount Douglas.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy, it was not too different from the Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Just talk to them, they are usually quite willing to get to know you. Ask them about Canada, or tell them about Europe, I had good succes with that.
cultural_challenges: Sometimes, I found it hard to give constructive criticism. It seems that Canadians prefer positivity and avoid anything resembling negativity, so they will add a lot of positives when giving feedback. Also, sometimes I found this focus on positivity and being upbeat annoying if the situation didn't call for it. Furthermore, personal opinions were shared quite intensely, which I wasn't used to.
culture_appreciated: The willingness to talk to strangers and the thankfulness the Canadians showed (they would say 'thank you' after lessons and when going off the bus). I also appreciate how much people in Victoria go on hikes in nature. Also, the population here is very diverse, so you get to see many cultures co-exist.
top3_advice: 1) Use the UVSS food hamper, it will save you a lot of money. 2) Bring your hiking boots, and don't forget your rain jacket. 3) Especially if you live on-campus, remember to get out and see the city of Victoria!
other_useful_info: Be prepared to do a lot of work. Get started soon so it doesn't all pile up and become unbearable.
most_rewarding: Meeting many different people with interesting stories to tell. Experiencing breath-taking nature. Changing my outlook on life and gaining confidence by being self-sufficient.
greatest_challenge: The workload for sure.
other_comments: No =)

arrival_assistance: The university hosted some great orientation events, both for international students and for "normal" students, which was really helpful and a great way to get familiar with campus while at the same time meeting new friends.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I got everything out of the exchange that I wanted: I met some great people, explored Canada and its beautiful nature, and got the "campus-experience" at the university.
registration_process: As an undergraduate student you have to fill out some papers that prove you meet the prerequisites for the courses you want to take. A bit of a bother. As a graduate student, I found it a bit difficult to figure out, if they would approve me for the courses I wanted to take, but generally I got the sense that if it is in your area of expertice, they are very happe to let you register for graduate courses as well.
registration_help: The international advisors were very helpful with this proces. And extremely fast at answering emails, which was really nice!
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: I found it to be a bit of a long proces, so be prepared for that and allocate the necessary time for it.
academics_comments: I got everything out of the exchange that I wanted: I met some great people, explored Canada and its beautiful nature, and got the "campus-experience" at the university.
course_level: I took masters courses, and I found the level to be equivalent, if not a bit more advanced, than KU. Most graduate students at uvic do research, which I found to be a bit daunting - but so much to learn from them!

However the small class size and discussion-based type of courses also means that there is expected much more of you, you have to read and come prepared for class, and actively engage in discussion. Different that KU, but I think I learned more this way.

cultural_challenges: no particular thing

greatest_challenge: Missing my boyfriend.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go where there were beautiful nature close by the university, interesting courses taught in English, not too many other students from KU and not too big a city.
overall_comments: Just go! You wont regret it :)
info_ease: Pretty easy. They had good emails with information and an online orientation program before arrival.
arrival_assistance: There were a lot of orientation events for international students on campus arrranged by volunteering students. It was very helpful, informative and fun events and you got to meet other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Just go! You wont regret it :)
registration_process: First you have to make sure you live up to all prerequisites and fill out and send in the aplications for courses with prerequisites. Then you get a time slot, which is the same for every exchange student, to register for classes. Beforehand it is a good idea to have made a list with all the classes you want (and no overlapping classes), because then you can just click on one button and register for all the classes on that list at the same time.
registration_help: You get a mail you can write to if you have problems with getting into one class or something.
registration_success: I got all classes I wanted. No classes were full when I had to register, so dont stress too much about that.
registration_advice: Send in prerequisite applications for too many courses, and register for too many courses because then you can try them out in the first weeks and just drop the boring courses. You are probably gonna find at least one class very boring in the first week so its a good idea to have back ups, and therefore have already applied to fulfill prerequisites so you easily can register for the course or already have registered for it so it hasnt filled up.
academics_comments: Just go! You wont regret it :)
course_level: I took one second year course and 3 third year courses.
teaching_comparison: It is kinda the same with some courses with only big lectures for hundreds of students, others with smaller class lectures (30 students), and some with class lectures and then class labs or class tutorials (15 students). There is more work during the term, which counts towards the final grade, and some courses have mandatory attendance and weekly hand-ins of notes or weekly quizzes on the curriculum (i managed to avoid that in my courses though).
courses_enrolled: AE303A Introduction to ceramics wheel and hand techniques EOS 350 Understanding the oceans GEOG 252 Introduction to coastal geography GEOG 376 Process Geomorphology
recommended_courses: The ceramics course was really fun and a nice way to have less academic. It takes a lot of work though, but I would say it is worth it anyways. The Process Geomorphology was the best course I have had ever. It was so interesting and a nice mix of lectures and interesting labs. I had to fight to get it because I didnt fully live up to the prerequisites, but I talked to the professor when I got to UVIC and after sending in a lot of documents it worked out. Understanding the oceans starts out as a lot of repetition for a geographer student having had GGS, but then it changes and is actually a really nice course about specific problems in the ocean and sometimes a more thorough explanation of stuff than GGS. The coastal geography is not really recommendable. The teacher was very boring, but at the whole grade was only made from easy assignments, so it meant that I had one less exam in december which gave me more time to travel.
unexpected_costs: A mandatory health insurance and bus pass from UVIC, but then you could go to the Uni doctors and you could travel as much on the bus as you want to (you can get out of the bus pass if maybe you have a bike and are not planning on using the bus too much but the health insurance is mandatory).
cost_comparison: The phone plans are very expensive in Canada. Fresh fruits and vegetables are more expensive than in DK. It is possible to find cheaper housing, but I wanted to live close to campus and didnt want to spend to much time searching for other options.
activities_available: They have sooo many different clubs and organisations you can join. Sport clubs with all kind of sport you can imagine, organisations for every subject you can study, and other clubs with all kind of stuff you cant even imagine (a caving club, a fencing club, a pickles club...)
activities_recommended: The caving club, it was such a fun and different activity I would never have done in DK. The people in the club are really nice and the caving trips were really fun. The climbing club, you can very cheap go to the climbing gym once a week and get all equipment and climb! The outdoor clubs, the surfing club, the whitewater rafting sometimes make trips in the weekends, where you can go with other students and get to see a part of the island, try a fun activity and meet some fellow students (or bring your own friends).
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend you to, other than joining a club and going on a trip with them, to go on as many trips you can with your own friends in the weekends and holidays. See Tofino, Strathcona, Soothe, Vancouver, Whistler, Seattle, Banff, and so on. It makes the whole exchange experience so much more worth it, when you get to experience so much!
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Canada is not that different from Denmark, just a bit more americanized.
socializing_tips: Try to talk to local students in your class or in clubs. Or if you live with canadians.
cultural_challenges: It is not that easy to really become friends with canadians. They have their own friends, you are only there for half a year. It is easier to become friends with other exchange students.
culture_appreciated: They are so nice. Everybody says thank you to the busdriver when they get off, the hold the door for you, they want to help you all the time.
top3_advice: Go to as many orientation events as you can the first week, that is where you meet other exchange students and make friends. Go on trips and explore the island (and the main land) as often as you can! Try to talk to canadian students in your class and in clubs, it is nice to come home and actually have gotten to know some canadians as well (and not only other europeans) :)
other_useful_info: Dont hesitate to write to somebody from uvic if you have any questions, they are very helpful
most_rewarding: All my friends I got and all the trips we went on!
greatest_challenge: It is hard to actually become real friends with canadians and not just become acquaintanced. It is hard to start over and make new friends, and to become really close to people in only four months. But just give all you've got, give it time and enjoy it anyways.

crucial_aspects: Det betød meget for mig om at det var et engelsktalende sted og et sted hvor jeg kunne se mig selv bo og have base i et halvt år. Jeg var også meget bevidst om at det var et land/område som jeg var nysgerrig på i forvejen og eks. at jeg havde et ønske om at udforske og være rejsende i netop det land/område. Så jeg gik efter et sted hvor der også var masser af oplevelser (eks. kyst, vand, bjerge, skov, mulighed for vandring og exploring). Det specifikke uni betød ikke det store. Herefter søgte jeg om forhåndsgodkendelse på KU og udfylde informationer til Uvic som beviste at jeg også opfyldte deres krav. Jeg fik afvist et par enkelte og måtte søge om ny forhåndsgodkendelse på KU. Herefter fik jeg et timeslot hvor jeg skulle logge ind på Uvics hjemmeside og tilmelde mig de kurser som jeg var forhåndsgodkendt til. Det var lidt stressende da nogle kurser godt kunne være fyldt op.- Det er en god ide at have 2 kurser i baghånden som du kan bruge hvis dine andre muligheder ikke bliver til noget.
registration_help: Jeg brugte Uvics kursus værktøjer til at sammensætte mit skema så jeg ikke anmodede om kurser som lå på samme tidspunkt. Det er dit eget ansvar at sammensætte skema uden at timer overlapper. Jeg fik desuden hjælp til at anmode om nye kurser af 1 af mine kurser blev afvist. Administrationen er meget gode til at hjælpe for at få det til at gå op.
registration_success: Jeg havde et kursus jeg ikke kunne få, men endte med at finde et godt alternativ. Jeg var meget godt tilfreds til sidst og synes jeg havde en god fordeling af nye/sjove kurser og noget som var meget relevant for min uddannelse.
registration_advice: SLAP AF! Sæt dig ind i deres kursusprogram og hjemmeside. Det kan være ne jungle at finde rundt i, så invester tid og energi så du også får nogle fag du gerne vil have. Kig på kruser fra andre fakulteter! Det er en virkelig god mulighed for at lære noget nyt!
academics_comments: Jeg er SÅ glad for at jeg endte i Victoria, Canada! Byen har en perfekt størrelse til et semester udveksling. Ikke for stor og ikke for lille! Det er først noget jeg er blevet bevidst om på bagkant.
course_level: Jeg havde både 200 og 300 niveau kurser.

recommended_courses: AE303A Introduction to Ceramics Wheel and Hand Techniques var virkelig sjovt og anderledes! Underviseren Mary var SÅ sød og imødekommende. Det var sjovt at have et kreativt kursus (som man kan få MERIT for!!) og det var fedt at komme ned i værkstedet efter en lang og tung akademisk dag!
unexpected_costs: Jeg brugte langt flere penge på mad og at spise ude/gå på cafe og hygge. Jeg bruget også MANGE lommepenge på at tage på ture, oplevelser, fritidsaktiviteter/klubber, leje af bil og airbnbs når vi var på tur. Det var dog forventet.
cost_comparison: Mad var dyrere, men offentlig transport var billigere. Vancouver Island er ikke et billigt sted, og er lidt dyrere end KBH ift. mad
activities_available: Jeg var med i cavingklubben, klatreklubben, SUPklubben, En alt-mulig-sports-klub, En journaling/dagbogs/skrive klub, Antropologiklubben for studerende Der var klubber for alle og alt! både faglige og sociale.
activities_recommended: Jeg vil anbefale cavingklubben, dvs. en klub hvor man kravler i/explore grotter. Vancouver Island har mange grotter og den her klub har sygt gode medlemmer som bare har styr på sikkerhed, planlægning og det praktiske. Jeg ville ønske jeg selv meldte mig i Whitewater Surfing klubben, men jeg hørte om den for sent!
weekend_recommendations: Downtown, Fishermans Warf, Mt. douglas, goldstream provinsial park, Sooke provinsial park, Strathcona Provinsial park, Mount Douglas, The Rockies, Whistler, Vancouver. Snak med folk og lokale studerende, de har sikkert gode anbefalinger!
culture_adjustment: Ok nemt. Lokale studerende er meget imødekommende, men det var klart mest internationale studerende jeg hang ud med. Jeg vil anbefale ikke at bo med studerende fra dit eget land/uni, for det bliver for ´nemt´ kun at hænge ud med dem
socializing_tips: Meld dig in i klubber! Snak med folk til dine timer i pauserne. Folk er ofte interesserede!
cultural_challenges: Ingen udtalte udfordringer
culture_appreciated: Canadierne er meget easygoing og ikke så uptight. Nyd det og smid din dansker mentalitet om at være reserverede
top3_advice: 1. GLÆD DIG! Uvic er et virkelig dejligt sted, du får campus oplevelsen, men bliver ikke total overvældet. Det er et hyggeligt campus og en endnu hyggeligere by! Jeg var i Vancouver flere gange, men Victoria vinder på alle parametre som den dejliste by! 2. Skaf en cykel. Det er rart at kunne bestemme selv om man vil gå, cykle eller tage bussen 3. Hold din fredag fri i dit skema. Du planlægger selv dit skema, så du kan sørge for at have en ekstra fridag i ugen hvor du har tid til at tage på tur/explore. Næsten alle mine venner gjorde det samme og vi NØD virkelig at have ture med en ekstra dags fri i mens andre var nød til at tage til 1 times undervisning før de kunne stikke af sted.
other_useful_info: Uvic er et meget inkluderende Uni, det er en tryg campus hvor der er plads til ALLE mennesker og typer <33 nyd det og bidrag til diversiteten
most_rewarding: Nye venner, nye oplevelser og en pause i mine studier herhjemme
greatest_challenge: At have undervisning på engelsk, at have råd til alle de ting jeg gerne ville nå (spar godt op så du har en buffer og ikke føler dig begrænset). Jeg havde et arbjede hvor jeg arbjede online for en dansk virksomhed imens jeg var af sted. Set i bakspejlet var det kun en stressfaktor og ikke de få ekstra penge værd. Få besøg af venner og familie hjemmefra, men ikke for meget, du kommer til at være travlt optaget af dine egne nye venner og alle de ting der konstant sker på campus og i området. Jeg havde besøg over 3 omgange i op til 2 uger af gangen og det var lidt for meget.

crucial_aspects: Smaller city, close to nature, far away from Denmark, English speaking country, "The American University Experience"
overall_comments: My overall study abroad experience was severely (negatively) affected by personal matters at home.
info_ease: Fairly easy and my host university also provided very quick email responses to my questions. The first week was quiet as most of the students who were going to live in residence has not yet arrived.
arrival_assistance: The International Centre for Students provided tons of introduction and social activities the first week before school started. Residence Service provided the information and help neccesary for move-in etc. After the first week community leaders in residence also provided help and information.
arrival_comments: However it was also a bit overwhelming and I had to choose between acties as attending all would have been too much.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My overall study abroad experience was severely (negatively) affected by personal matters at home.
registration_process: - I spend MANY hours reading about the different courses in the course calender - I made a list of 10-15 possible courses - I applied for prerequisites - I prioritized and made a time scheduele in their registration platform - I registrered at my designated time and got all of my course wishes
registration_help: A thourough email guide, video tutorial, material on the webpage, Zoom meeting and help through phone or email.
registration_success: Very succesful.
registration_advice: Be ready to spend a lot of time choosing your courses and preparing for the actual registration.
academics_comments: My overall study abroad experience was severely (negatively) affected by personal matters at home.
course_level: I had 100, 200 and 300 level courses corresponding to the first 3 years of a bachelor/undergraduate (in Canada a bachelor degree is 4 years). I found the courses to be a step below the level of my Danish courses. However based on the University system's differences you will not only meet first year students in 100-level classes, it is a lot more mixed and it is normal to take some courses quite different from you primary study area.
teaching_comparison: Classes and lectures were similar but some were expecting a bit more interaction and participation from student (this was in some courses also part of your final grade). Your grade does not only rely on the final exam as in Denmark which I both liked and disliked. It took a lot of pressure of the final exam but gave you no chance to fall a little behind on reading etc. As mentioned above they also put a lot of more focus on assignments, quizzes etc.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Anthropology Primate Behavioural Ecology The Search for Life in the Universe Introduction to Ceramics - Wheel and Hand Building Techniques
recommended_courses: All of them! But I was a little overwhelmed by the report and assignment workload in The Search for Life in the Universe even though it was a really interesting astronomy course including observatory experience and labs. Introduction to Anthropology was a great and broad introductory course with a really nice and modern professor and fun and interesting preparation material. Primate Behavioural Ecology was my favorite course. Such a great teacher and it had no final exam but instead a poster project that taught me a lot. I also made a Canadian friend in this course. I also enjoyed Ceramics and recommed it to anyone who likes being creative. However be prepared of a teacher grading hard and to spend a lot of time in the studio outside of class.
unexpected_costs: Laundry, change of flight tickets, taxi a few times, medication
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than expected (especially grocery shopping)! The rest was about what I expected and about the same level as in Denmark.
activities_available: First-Nation cultural experiences, lots of sports (including fitness and swimming pool), clubs (I encourage future students to look into this), international student events, residence events, Student Wellness Centre, Multifaith, Vikes etc.
activities_recommended: I encourage future students to look into the clubs because there are so many opportunities and interests covered in them.
weekend_recommendations: Nature and animals (I saw several bears, eagles, seals, otters, orcas, humpback whales etc)! Plan trips around Vancouver Island, take the ferry to Vancouver, Port Angelses (Washington State, USA) or Seattle. Go on lots of hikes and spend some time in downtown Victoria as well. Go to the beach (very close to UVic) and take a bunch of beautiful photos. I also did a road trip in Alberta (Banff and Jasper) before my exchange stay.
culture_adjustment: Fairly easy. The Canadian people are super friendly and polite. They put a lot of focus on equality for minorities such as indigeneous people or people with handicap. The Canadian accent is not difficult to understand and you will not be the only one who have a foreign accent.
socializing_tips: Try to engage with the Canadian students in your classes or at clubs/events. Don't be afraid to take initiative, you will most likely be met with a possitive experience but you also have to put yourself out there. People probably won't come to you first but will include you when you have opened up.
cultural_challenges: None. It was a perfect balance of something similar and something new. The only cultural thing I missed was probably Danish food.
culture_appreciated: The friendlyness and willingness to help. That you were always asked if you are okay with this and that. I also really appreciated their views on climate and nature and equal rights for everyone.
top3_advice: - Bring your outdoor gear! - Be prepared to study in a different way than in Denmark (and don't be afraid of the courses being too hard). - Take advantage of all of the opportunities that UVic provides - from social activities, to counceling, to a diverse array of courses and nature and opportunities for experiences all around. Don't be afraid to try new things and put yourself out there, but also remember that you can't do it all and it is important to take personal breaks as well.
other_useful_info: Be aware of the housing situation and know that Canada is NOT a cheap country to live in. Ask for all the help you need (also maybe more than you need) - they are very willing to help. UVic is located on an island and it is not possible to enter or exit the island by other means than ferry or plane. Remember to apply for eTa (Canada) and ESTA (USA) so it will be easy to go on trips and cross the boader. Know that it is definetly most easy to get around (outside of the greater Victoria area) by car. Remember that your grades go back on your Danish transcript as pass/no pass, so invest some of your time outside of the academics.
most_rewarding: My travel experiences. Canada is an amazingly beautiful country! My English language skills improved as well as my ability to produce reports and assigments in writing. Trying to be completely on my own with my family being so far away was rewarding in a developing manner.
greatest_challenge: Personal circumstances back home which made me isolate and miss out on a lot of social relationships and opportunities for activities. I felt very alone and far away from everything and everyone in having to deal with personal matters happening at home during my stay. I considered going home several times but decided to stay. I ended up being 5 reports behind in one of my courses that I then had to write in the final week. It was probably one of the hardest thing I have ever had to do in such a short time. I had already gotten extensions but I tried reasoning with the professor (without succes) that my personal circumstances should allow me to miss some of them.
other_comments: Go for it! Choose UVic for it's unique location, for it's size (both the city and student body) and for it's many opportunities.
