recommended_courses: I liked the taskes we had to do in 220033-1 UE GESKO B: UE JOUR Journalism - it was very practical and we had good discussions about our work. Also 480045-1 VO Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian Regional and Cultural was very nice! I liked the professor a lot.
unexpected_costs: I went home to Denmark a couple of times, that costed extra...
cost_comparison: Most things a similar to DK in terms of pricing. Alcohol and going out is a bit cheaper, shopping is kind of the same.
activities_available: Theres always a lot going on in Vienna. Some at the university but besides uni sprot and ESN i didn't use the university offers much.
activities_recommended: There are always many options in and around Vienna - go to one of the museums, outdoor raves, bouldering gyms, wine hikes, old cafés, hang out in the parks, at Donauinsel, fleamarkets - 1000things is a good SoMe account to follow.
weekend_recommendations: The same as above - and take advantage of the fact that you are in Austia! Go hiking, climbing, swimming or whatever fits you.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. It's similar to DK.
socializing_tips: No. I hung out with international students mostly. Maybe speak german? Try Bumble Friends? Idk. Uni is not very social and it was not a priority of mine to make local friends rather than other friends. A WG might also be a good place to make local friends.
cultural_challenges: Non.
culture_appreciated: To me it's not very different but I did appreciate how proud of their culture they were. Also stupid sometimes, but mostly nice.
top3_advice: 1. Vienna is an amazing city! Use it and all it has to offer! 2. Go for seminar classes - then you don't have as many exams in the end (also because the courses are small in terms of ects) and it is more social and have more discussions. 3. The professors are happy to help! Ask questions, for help with projects and so on.
other_useful_info: I think it's important to be aware of what type of courses you take. Don't go for too many lectures with multiple choise exams in the end... NOT fun.
most_rewarding: I really really had a good time, especially the last two month where I found my base and friend group. I think everyone should go. Even though it's also hard sometimes.
greatest_challenge: The homesickness that comes and goes. It's hard to be far away from home when something is going on, that you would like to be part of. Not all days are good. They also aren't at home, that's maybe worth remembering... But then just rely on your new friends! They feel the same way sometimes - eveyone do!
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: I was supposed to go to Asia in the previous spring, but had to cancel due to Coronavirus. Choosing a destination closer to home seemed to increase the likelihood of a successful exchange. Also, University of Vienna was one of the few universities that had mathematics courses at a level that i thought would be beneficial.
info_ease: Possible but not trivial. It would have been nice to know that the statistics department was at another faculty and thus had a different deadline for course registration.
arrival_assistance: I recieved an e-mail at before i arrived with information about what to do.
arrival_comments: A physical welcoming event at the local department would have been nice. I had to figure out the location of all the classrooms on my own. It would also have been beneficial to have an introduction to the various student activities/networks in the math department. I kinda felt like I was being left out to dry.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I hardly remember it.
registration_help: I recall getting help from UCPH exchange office and they were quite helpful and flexible.
registration_success: I got in all the classes i wanted - mathematics privilege.
registration_advice: If you want to take applied math courses, both statistics, operations research and finance are on the faculty of economics, so be sure to check their course catalogue and registration deadlines.
course_level: Appropriate level for master degree.
teaching_comparison: The seminars were very good. UCPH has a severe issue with participation in seminars/exercise classes. In Vienna all students participated, and the seminars were much more instructive. In Vienna, the seminars/exercises were taught by faculty, where on UCPH they were taught by other students.
courses_enrolled: Seminar in statistics Dynamical Systems and Nonlinear Differential Equations (VO and SE) Biomath seminar Kinetic Theory Applied to Biology
recommended_courses: Biomath Seminar and Seminar in Statistics as well as Dynamical Systems.
unexpected_costs: Nothing that i can recall.
cost_comparison: Transport was cheap.
activities_available: Either there were no non-academic activities, or i did not encounter them.
activities_recommended: Many small theaters with indie movies.
weekend_recommendations: Many other European cities that are just a couple of hours away by bus.
culture_adjustment: Most young people speak english just fine. Tipping and paying in cash is a hassle.
socializing_tips: I only managed to connect with other internationals. I never had anything more than casual conversation with locals.
cultural_challenges: Lack of collective activities made it difficult to make friends. Having something like student revues or throwing parties to work on something common would have made it much easier to make friends. At least the danish model of creating engaging student envieronments is based on having the students engage in common activities. Also, the lack of common areas on campus diminished the opportunity to make friends by working on homework together.
culture_appreciated: I found that Austrians were good at giving space to each other in a social setting, such that no particular individual would fill the entire room.
top3_advice: Go to the ESN events. Enjoy the parks. Asian food places are generally the best option if you are vegetarian.
other_useful_info: The administration is quite loose, in stark contrast to UCPH. The professor of a course can sign you up at will, even after the registration deadline, so writing emails solves most issues. On the other hand, examination formats and dates are not finalized until the semester is almost over, so it's incredibly difficult to plan your return, unless you can accept planning to wait all summer potentially for nothing. While riding public transport multiple times a day for an entire semester, I did not encounter a ticket control once. If you wish, you can easily ride without a ticket.
most_rewarding: The experience of having to make it more or less on your own in a new envieronment.
greatest_challenge: Figuring out if a course was challenging because of a different approach to the subject or because it is poorly taught. Making friends.
other_comments: If you are in doubt about whether to go, think about if you really want to go on exchange or you just want to do it because it sounds cool.

crucial_aspects: To find the place interesting, to have never been there before.
info_ease: Quite easy as you are given mobility coordinators and such. The hard part was coordinating my home and receiving institution regarding deadlines and dates and such. For instance, I had to "pretend" to choose courses in advance so I could fill out the forms for my home university, even though the course catalogue for the receiving institution was only released a few weeks before the start of the semester. It is possible but it is a little messy.
arrival_assistance: In the abovementioned case, my mobility coordinator was able to work with me and submitted my forms even with the incorrect courses listed so that I could get my Erasmus grant in time and so on. We worked out that I could submit things again with the correct courses when it was possible.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You choose from a course catalogue and get spaces according to how many spots are available. There is also a dropping period which made it easier to figure out how to do the points that were needed for the home uni as well as host uni (at least half of your ECTS has to be in your home department).
registration_help: Not much but I and others from my home university coordinated with each other which helped a lot.
registration_success: Fine, although we ended up with a bigger course load than we are used to.
registration_advice: Coordinate with other people if possible - it makes it less stressful. Also please note that Vienna differentiates between "VO" (lectures) and "SE" (seminars). Seminars expect you to participate actively and hand in assignments during the semester, etc.
course_level: MA
teaching_comparison: Quite different - much more "class teaching" with active participation and assignments during the semester. The classes varied a lot though, as the teachers had a lot of impact on how it was run. One teacher liked to sit in a circle of chairs and one preferred to talk at the white boards, etc.
courses_enrolled: Political Sociology (VO), Urban Sociology (VO), Imagining Mobility (SE), Borders and Mobility (SE), What is Power (SE), Digital Visuality and Popular Culture (SE), Writing and Representing in Science and Technology Studies (SE)
recommended_courses: I would recommend any STS courses for specifically sociology students as we do not really go into that at ucph - in Vienna they are really into it and I found it very interesting and opened my eyes for some cool topics and theories I think I will bring with me home as well. The STS courses I took were Borders and Mobility and Writing and Representing in STS. Borders and Mobility was particularly interesting and I really liked my lecturer, Fredy Gamez.
unexpected_costs: The registration forms sometimes cost mony. I had to pay 30 euro for a form for registrating for living in Vienna.
cost_comparison: Groceries were less expensive than I thought. Also the public transport for a trip here and there was very inexpensive - I rented a swapfiets bike however instead and only opted for the public transport every once in a while.
activities_available: There were student bars at my department but it was not very easy to be there if you didn't speak german I found. I think there are clubs for different things, but to be honest, I didn't really investigate these opportunities.
activities_recommended: Join a club if possible? :D
weekend_recommendations: Go see every museum possible and go on small trips to picturesque spots! Kahlenberg and Schönbrunn are good examples - they are close by the city but offer something the downtown areas don't :D
culture_adjustment: Quite easy.
socializing_tips: Talk to other exchange students in your classes or where you live. And go to "travel bars", a lot of exchange students/travellers hang out here.
cultural_challenges: There are SO many registration processes and a lot of it includes showing up at some office in person and receiving a piece of PAPER with a physical signature/stamp. I and others from the same home uni found this very confusing to navigate. For instance, you have to register yourself as a citizen living in Vienna upon three days of arrival and show up at office 1 and fill out a form which will be stamped and signed, then you take this piece of paper and call office 2 (in a different part of town) and get a time slot a month in advance to register there. Then you are registered in Vienna. Then you have to DEregister when leaving, also with a time slot and so on. I know of some who just skipped this process, but I also heard you get a fine if you do.
culture_appreciated: Very beautiful city with so much going on. There are small festivals for art/music/etc., exhibitions and Wiener-concerts all the time. Lots of orchestra concerts, and much of the time there are free ones!
top3_advice: Apply for grants if eligible, they are a lifesaver. I applied to maybe 4 but only got one, so do research on that before travelling and make sure you exhaust your possiblities in this area. Don't get overwhelmed by all the processes of registration and paperwork - it seems impossible at times but it works out. See as many cultural things as possible, there are plenty of options! Make time for it.
other_useful_info: I recommend getting a bike if you are comfortable biking. The lanes are NOT like in Copenhagen - traffic is much more chaotic and cars are not at all as aware of you, but it is a great way to get to know the city and how it connects and to move around more freely! I rented at Swapfiets which was very easy and that way you know it is in good condition.
most_rewarding: Getting to know a foreign city that I will be able to return to and know in a different way than a tourist ever could!
greatest_challenge: Figuring out all the paperwork and deadlines and matching it with my home university.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to explore the city of Vienna.
overall_comments: I generally really liked the experience and thrived in Vienna. The only downside was figuring out a different system.
info_ease: It was a little bit difficult to figure out the system and how to registrer as a resident in the city.
arrival_assistance: There was an introduction by the Erasmus team at the university but some of the information was given a little late in relation to the deadlines of the municipality.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I generally really liked the experience and thrived in Vienna. The only downside was figuring out a different system.
registration_process: The registration of arrival at the university was pretty easy as we were given the needed information via e-mail in due time.
registration_help: We had a specifically appointed coordinator who was concerned with our field of study and I found that she was able to answer most questions and help.
registration_success: I found the system a little difficult as there was a lot of prioritizing and practicalities to take into account. Further I had some difficulty as a non-German speaker as there was a limited amount of English courses.
registration_advice: Be open to not getting the courses you want and be open to trying the available English courses.
academics_comments: I generally really liked the experience and thrived in Vienna. The only downside was figuring out a different system.
course_level: The level was all right but it was clear that a lot of the other students were not doing 30 ects points at the same time and that the lecturers expected a little more work due to this.
teaching_comparison: Similar but a lot more participation from the students than what I was used to.
courses_enrolled: VO Introduction to Urban Sociology VO Political Sociology SE Digital Visuality and Popular Culture (P4) SE Writing and representing in Science and Technology Studies SE STS, Borders and Mobility Imagining mobility Reading Seminar: What is Power? Approaches in Social Theory
recommended_courses: I liked the courses in the STS department as it introduced me to a whole new way of doing social science.
unexpected_costs: There were quite a few fees related to registration at the municipality.
cost_comparison: Drinks and living was generally okay however I was surprised of the prices of food being similar to Danish. Further I was surprised at how expensive the museums and cultural experiences were. However there were also a lot of free options available and organized by the city.
activities_available: There was a gym but I did not use it.
activities_recommended: Definetely take the time to research the free cultural opportunities in the city as there are many and the museums are very expensive. There are a lot of open air concerts and movie theatres. Further I would recommend checking out all the cafes and nice flee markets in the different areas.
weekend_recommendations: Go to flee markets and try swimming in the Donau Kanal in the sommertime.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Going to bars and be open.
cultural_challenges: There were not many differences really. Maybe the use of cash and the fact that a lot is closed on sundays.
culture_appreciated: The cafe culture and the free cultural opportunities organized different places in the city.
top3_advice: 1. Be aware of the bureaucracy and that it takes time. 2. Experience the cafe culture in the different neighborhoods. 3. Be sure to visit the old campus at Uni Wien
other_useful_info: It is nice to rent a bike and then be able to ride around the city and get around very easily.
most_rewarding: Getting to experience the city.
greatest_challenge: The different registrations and bureaucracy in general.
other_comments: Vienna is a very great city! I would totally recommend going there!!! And make sure to experience the Wiener Symphoniker at some of their free concerts.

crucial_aspects: That I could go with my two friends, that is seemed like a nice city and that it was in Europe.
info_ease: Not too easy, but I had two friends with me, so we could help each other.
arrival_assistance: We received help from the mobility coordinator from Vienna University.
arrival_comments: I think it was a good orientation, but there was still a lot to figure out yourself.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: We had to show up to and orientation, which was short and sweet. I found it very difficult to find courses in English within my own field of study (sociology), but ended up finding some courses in STS and Anthropology. But it was very difficult making it match the 30 ECTS that was required from UCPH in English and Master levels, but I managed in collaboration with my two friends who took the same courses. This also made making the Online Learning Agreement quite complicated, as the deadlines for this and the deadlines for when we knew if we were admitted to the courses we wanted didn't match.
registration_help: We asked our mobility coordinator and she was helpful to a certain degree.
registration_success: I took all the course I thought I could get, and got into enough to reach 30 ECTS.
registration_advice: Maybe start out in good time, and trust that it will be alright.
course_level: I thought the level of the courses were fine. It was clear that it was masters level though, and as I had to have 7 courses to reach 30 ECTS it was quite a big workload. I had many courses outside of my own field of study, so some of it was quite. confusing to me, but still very manageable.
teaching_comparison: There wasn't as many lecture were you only had to listen, but much more participation and you also got points for participation, which I found very different from Copenhagen. In my courses you pretty much just had to show up to get the participation points though, and do a bit of presentations, so it was fine. A lot more group work and talking to the people in the class, but it differed quite a lot from course to course. The have different types of courses, so you can choose what type of teaching you like. I had one reading seminar, where we discussed texts, and there was little lecturing from the teacher, and I (surprisingly) really liked that course.
courses_enrolled: Imagining Mobility, Popular culture and digital visyality, Writing and representing in STS, What is Power? (reading seminar), Political Sociology, Urban Sociology, STS Borders and Mobility,
recommended_courses: Really depends on what your interested in. Can't recommend Urban Sociology, as I didn't like the lectures at all. Can recommend: What is Power, STS Borders and Mobility, Political Sociology.
unexpected_costs: Registration fees for the municipality.
cost_comparison: drinks were cheap, and i didn't have to buy any books.
activities_available: I don't really think there were any, but I didn't look into it either.
activities_recommended: Can't say.
weekend_recommendations: Go out and eat cake and drink cofeee. And drink Spritzers. There are A LOT of things going on in the city, also for free, so look into that. Go to Kahleenberg for a good view over the city, or drink spritzers or go to the open air cinema on top of the stairs of the public library. Otherwise just enjoy the city, it is soooo beautiful.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Didn't manage, other than the people who lived in the same dorm as me, but they were also mostly not from Vienna. Met some people going out, that we hung out with.
cultural_challenges: There was a lot of paperwork and bureaucracy in regards to registration, but otherwise nothing.
culture_appreciated: The coffee culture.
top3_advice: Be sure to enjoy the city while you are there, and remember to not use all your time studying. Find some people to share your experiences with.
other_useful_info: It can seem like there is a lot of registration things that you have to do, but as long as you stay on top of it, you will be fine. Also I got a Swapfiets bike, which was very nice and pretty cheap, but the public transportation was also pretty good if your not much of a biker.
most_rewarding: Living in such a beautiful city with some of my best friends.
greatest_challenge: All of the registrations both at uni and at the municipality office.

crucial_aspects: First the fact that Austria was not a long way from my home country. Second that german is spoken (I would like to improve my german skills). Third that UNI Wien offered a lot of English law courses.
info_ease: I think it was quite easy. The UNI Wien website is user-friendly.
arrival_assistance: I attended an orientation session.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: U basically just register through u:space (it is very easy), and you can look up all the courses at Ufind.
registration_help: You have the possibility to call the UNI (which I also did, and they were very helpful).
registration_success: I got all the classes that I wanted. I registered for 60 ECTS to be sure to get 30 ECTS, but that wasnt necessary at all ! But it is always possible to deregister.
registration_advice: I only registered for classes with Continuous assessment of course work, those courses have mandatory attending but then you dont have big exams in the middle of July. In some of my courses, I only had to deliver in two assignments. And in most of my classes we would just have an exam in the last class.
course_level: It was lots easier than in Denmark ! The level is still fine, but it is easier. I also think it has to do with, that the English courses at UNI Wien are 3-4 ECTS only. And then most courses dont have heavy reading.
teaching_comparison: At UNI Wien we didn't have lectures. But only classes, which was nice. So the students were very engaged in the classes.
courses_enrolled: - International Investment Law - International Economic Law - International Protection of Cultural Heritage - International Legal English - Women in Law part 2 - Drafting and Negotiating Cross-border M & A and Joint Venture Contracts - Introduction to US Law - Protection of Intellectual Properties in the Fashion Industry.
recommended_courses: I believe that the International Legal English course is great, since it is extremely relevant for all exchange students. I also found International Protection of Cultural Heritage interesting and also Protection of Intellectual Properties in the Fashion Industry, since it is not possible to do such courses at my home university. In general I really enjoyed all my courses.
unexpected_costs: Not really any.
cost_comparison: I was surprised that we didnt have to buy any books. So a great advice, even though the courses are provided with a reading list, you dont have to buy them, since the will provide pdf or online book. And also you can buy a semester ticket at WienMobil for the public transport, which covers free transport within Wien for only 75 EUR for the whole semester.
activities_available: UNI Wien has USI which is a sports institution, which really offers ALL you can think of. The have a really nice Welcoming reception at the begining of each semester for exchange students.
activities_recommended: Lots are avaliable - ESN and also EBN organises events all the time. Check their websites out. For example both organisations are doing a ski trip, hikes, parties, board game nights, pubcrawls, museum visits, BBQ etc.
weekend_recommendations: - See a museum (Wien has a lot to offer example SISI museum, National Museum of Art, Upper Belevedere) - Go for a walk in the Schönbrunen Castle Park and even see the museum inside. - Go for a walk in the inner city and enjoy all the pretty buildings - hofburg palace, the opera, Stephansdom etc.) - Go to Gerstner in the inner city (next to the Opera) and eat cake while enjoying the outstanding interior. - Do a picnic in Volksgarten or Burggarten. - Go swim at the Donau Island - Go for a Hike through Vienna and up to the Wine marks (example Mayer am Nussberg) - Take a trip for skiing (maybe Zell am see) or hiking - or just to see some big Austrian mountains. - Take a trip to Budapest (only 2,5 hours in train) - Take a trip to Bratislava (less than 1 hour in train)
culture_adjustment: It was very easy, Austria is not that different from Denmark.
socializing_tips: Really just use ESN and EBN !! Then you will meet other people. And then make sure to become a member of the whatsapp group of ESN UNI Wien, people write all the time, and there are so many people, who would like to do stuff.
cultural_challenges: None
culture_appreciated: People were very polite.
top3_advice: (1) Dont be nervous to spend some time alone in the beginning. It is normal to feel overwhelmed, and there will come plenty of social activities that you can attend to. (2) Think of that you are all in the same spot. Every Erasmus student has an interest in getting to know new people. (3) Believe in yourself, it will all be great ! And it is going to be one of your biggest experiences in life.
other_useful_info: I think it has been written in this report.
most_rewarding: That I realized that I am capable of so much more, than I thought. Sometimes I was very out of comfort zone.
greatest_challenge: To try and live alone and just stand on one's own feet.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to stay within Europe (more convenient, Erasmus Grant, language, and cultural reasons). Vienna is central in Europe so many travel opportunities to surrounding areas. I had never visited but heard great things about the city (all true!!). Affordable housing/living prices (compared to other destinations or major capitals in Europe).
overall_comments: I was very pleased with my choice of destination - it is an ideal exchange city in my opinion.
info_ease: No major issues allthough the process can seem a bit extensive/long/complicated from home. Lots of formulas and administrative processes. But when arriving it seemed fine and easy enough. Wien Universität was also easy enough to communicate with (communicated with my coordinator at my department which was easy!). Great orientation sessions by the international office and ESN network in the beginning also with all info we needed to register adress, arrival date, course selection etc.
arrival_assistance: The international office had several info meets/events that you could attend upon arrival with lots of info and you got your certificate of arrival. The ESN network held some events (more social than assistance, but still fine!). And my own department (anthropology) held a small welcome event for exchange students (nothing crazy or very informative - we weren't many people but still good to attend). There was also a formal welcome event by the uni itself! So all in all we were taken good care off i think.
arrival_comments: I'd give it 4 or 5. I had found most info already online so didn't need that much assistance and i think the uni/ESN/department did a good job at giving assistance. Only negative part is just that it all seems very complicated sometimes - so much paperwork, and lots of things to take care of when leaving/arriving. But it all worked out and all students are in the same situation :)
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I was very pleased with my choice of destination - it is an ideal exchange city in my opinion.
registration_process: Course lists are available quite late before the start of the semester. Then you just register for lots of courses generally (more ects than you need) and then test the courses in the first weeks before the deregistration deadline (a few weeks after semester start). A bit weird process when you don't know it but also cool to test the courses. Sometimes you'll be on the waiting list but many people will deregister and then you'll get the spot. You find course lists in the site u:find and register in u:space where you also then deregister the ones you don't want to do anyway.
registration_help: Info about this was giving at the orientation session/welcome event by the international office. Theres different types of courses (lectures, seminars) but i think it was simple enough once we got started and i got all the info about their system. I also got questions answered by my mobility coordinator of my department via mail so it was fine.
registration_success: I got all the classes i wanted and also the extra ones i had registered for and then deregistered later. I also took 2 MA courses to try it and also because it was so hard to find enough (30 ects) BA courses in english that wasn't on the same days/times....
registration_advice: Spend some time on it in the beginning. When the course list becomes available look at all the ones you want and see if its possible, make a schedule, check they don't overlap too much. Register for too many courses, try them out, and then deregister some. I made my Learning Agreement after the deregistration period was done and i knew the exact courses i was taking. Also remember after arriving in Vienna to go register your address at the municipal district office (the uni/international office gives info on it also). Must be done in person with a signed document. And you also have to deregister once you leave.
academics_comments: I was very pleased with my choice of destination - it is an ideal exchange city in my opinion.
course_level: Some courses were good and some were not good at all. Even one of my MA courses wasn't the best so i think in general the department of anthropology at CPH is just a bit better. More progressive, modern, better professors etc. So i didn't have the best academic experience but i also wasn't expecting it to be better than UCPH. I also didn't prioritize the academic aspect of my experience massively but i still did very good in most of my courses. The workload around exams though was huuge. Writing exams in 6 courses is so much work. I know most local students never take 30 ects because the workload with 6 courses becomes too much. This is very annoying since its the end of the exchange.
teaching_comparison: Lectures (VO, means Vorlesung) are just lectures with a written exam of some sort at the end which is 100 percent of the grade. Seminars (SE or PS) is with continous assesment so you get assesed for work in class, participation, presentations etc. plus a final paper. I had a mix of the two kinds which i recommend. All seminars would be too much work but all lectures would be too boring i think.
courses_enrolled: PS BM2 New Critical Perspectives SE BM7 Selected Topics in Political Anthropology SE MM3 Sexual identities and/or orientations SE MM3: Thinking with Things: Anthropological approaches to material culture VO Introduction to Circumpolar North VO New critical perspectives in social and cultural anthropology
recommended_courses: I really liked the seminar in political anthropology. I did not like the lecture in New critical perspectives in social and cultural anthropology. There was maybe 100 people in it, it was unstructured, not a great professor, not a lot of substance or valuable content. The seminar of the same name was fine though. I think the course list changes very often, maybe every year/half year, so not sure these classes will be available for next fall semester
unexpected_costs: None really. Theres a small fee for the ESN network (like 25 euros maybe). I ate out more than in CPH so more cost in personal spending + trips, events etc. I booked trips with the ESN network like a ski trip which cost a bit but its worth it to get some experiences and meet some people.
cost_comparison: Housing was cheaper than in CPH. Going out for food and drinks is way cheaper so its very nice to go out for drinks and food and many people, also students, do it more often. Transportation is cheap! 75 euros for a semesterticket that lasts all semester and then you take all transport in Vienna.
activities_available: The USI sports institute is cool for joining cheap sports of very different kinds! Check it out, the list of sports is avaible just before semester start and sells out quickly. I joined a runningclub (ca 45 euros) and a pilates course (ca 50 euros) and they were both once a week all semester and i was very pleased with it.
activities_recommended: The USI sports courses. ESN events, also they host trips like ski weekend og sightseeing trips to other areas like Salzburg etc. I recommend: All the museums all over Vienna, walking around looking at the architecture, sitting in traditional viennese cafes drinking coffee and eating cake, going to bars (beer is okay cheap, like 4-5 euros), going to Naschmarkt (flea market every Saturday but many bars/restaurants/food stalls all days a week), go hiking in the mountains and go to Heuriger (wine taverns, only in warmer months), if it's a winter semester then attend a Wiener ball (january/february) (i went to TU ball), visit all the christmas markets (in December), go to Donau, go to Prater... the list goes on and on.
weekend_recommendations: I went on a skitrip with ESN, a self organized ski trip to Kitzbühel, a day trip to Bratislava. I went hiking in the mountains/hills around Vienna (look up the Stadtwanderwegs, they are great hiking routes in the areas around Vienna and often easy to reach with public transport. My favorite area to hike in/visit was Nussberg/Kahlenberg in the late summer for good hikes, good views, fresh wine in the great outdoor wine taverns.) Many went on weekend trips to Prague, Budapest, Salzburg, Graz or other sourrounding cities! Really recommend,
culture_adjustment: Very easy. It's a lot like Danish people/Copenhageners. The stereotype is that Viennese people are rude - i did not find it to be true, or i just didn't find them any different than Copenhageners. A lot like Scandinavians they are a bit more introverted, don't talk to strangers etc., but i think that suits me well being Danish. Everybody was kind if you got to talking.
socializing_tips: You generally meet more erasmus people than local people. I met some in classes but mostly i met local people through my thursday running club - but if you want to make friends in these scenarios you have to be a little out there and talk to the locals yourself, say hi, chat, ask for contact info etc.
cultural_challenges: I didn't speak fluent german so maybe that was sometimes more foreign for me but i quickly caught on and it was fine. It's not hard to lean the basics. No big cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: I like that Vienna has a great cafe-culture - people sit in cafes/bars and drink coffee, beers, chat, and just hang out or read. It's cheaper so more accesible and affordable to students and creates a great atmosphere and lively vibe with all the outdoor cafes. I also appreciated the very cultural vibe of the city with a lot of history, museums, architecture, lots of great thinkers, music artists/composers, just lots of art/history/academic culture...
top3_advice: 1. It's a great choice of host destination!! The summer/late-summer/spring is wonderful but the winter is also great actually (christmas markets made it great ;)) so both semesters are great choices. 2. Try to see a bit of the country and nature. Go skiing in the alps, hiking in the Wienerwald, go to Prater, Donau, all the great nature of Austria. 3. Austria is a little bit traditional still and a bit bureaucratic. Lots of paperwork still when it could be digital. They also use cash still!
other_useful_info: Attend ESN events to meet exchange students. There are options both at the Universität Wien and the TU (technical uni), you can attend at both of them! I also made friends from TU.
most_rewarding: I met a lot of great people and eventually made a very good small regular friend group. People are very outgoing and friendly because everybody is looking to meet new people so make sure to attend som events in the beginning and make an effort to make friends, and then you'll get a great group to share the experience with. It was also a rewarding experience for me to spent a lot of time in my own company (going on hikes alone, eating out alone, going to a bar/cafe alone, going to museums alone) - it was a healthy and good experience for me.
greatest_challenge: As i think everybody might experience, i did deal with some homesickness in the middle of the stay. It's hard to avoid i would say, so just accept it and let i pass slowly, let your friends know how you feel (they might feel the same!!), and i even booked a weekend trip back to CPH to see some friends (its cheap and a 1,5 h flight). It lasted on and off a few weeks for me, and overall i loved being there and my new friends, but it was also hard to get into a routine and you do spend more time alone while on exchange than i've been used to. All of it is healthy/normal and i learned a lot from this experience.

cultural_challenges: The formal way of approaching people is a thing that differs from Denmark. At uni you have to approach you teacher more formal and especially when you write emails etc.
culture_appreciated: Vienna is a very special city as it has so much history and culture, which was one of the reasons I chose to do an exchange programme there.
top3_advice: I chose to attend a German course in September that was organised by sprachenzentraum, which is part of the University of Vienna. As the semester doesn't start until October, it was a great opportunity to get to know the city, improve your German and meet some new people before starting your courses. other_useful_info: Familiarise yourself with all the practicalities in advance
most_rewarding: For me it was also particularly special to go on exchange all by myself, to build a life in a foreign city without knowing anyone, but in the end having built up a large network, it was very rewarding.
greatest_challenge: Creating a balance between studying and making new friends and exploring a new city and country.

registration_process: Everything worked through the online ufind portal, finding courses and their description. I had a lot of problems with accidently signing up for MA courses, which i was not allowed to follow, and then i didnt find out it was a MA course until the first day of class. It was a difficult portal to navigate in, but with attention and time it is doable.
registration_help: The Erasmus students admin was available several times per week for in person help or on the phone.
registration_success: It worked out, but i had some trouble with filling out half my ECTS points with English language courses in my nominated field - so i ended up having to take a German course, which i failed.
registration_advice: In terms of relations, and getting to know people, you really have to say yes to everything that is offered in the beginning, because it stops very quickly. Bureaucratically, you have to go to the municipality office in the district you are staying and register your residency within 3 days, or you can be fined! After that you have to go to the central office within a month, and register that you have sufficient funds via the Erasmus grant. Academically, i would say try to take fewer seminars, and more lectures. The seminars often have bigger exams, like essays, and can in some cases involve data collection etc. Lectures are written exams, either multiple choice, written questions, or essay questions. However, lecture exams are often written in hand!
course_level: Because i wanted to take my classes in English, i had to take classes from across semesters, so i also had some first semester introduction to sociological classics.
teaching_comparison: The seminars are more independent, its often PHD students doing classes they themselves have formulated. So they are often are lot more interesting. Also i has one teacher who was a declared Marxist, which i doubt would be welcomed in Copenhagen.

recommended_courses: Introduction to Urban Conflict, with Ajin Tas was a very eye-opening course, introducing me to new and more global perspective's. New Critical Perspectives in Social and Cultural Anthropology, with Mafe was also academically extremely awarding. and Guided Reading: Classics of Sociological Texts with Pavel Pospech was just a joy - Pavel is a very good teacher.
unexpected_costs: i didnt have any unexpected costs

activities_available: almost none, just a few introductions in the beginning.
activities_recommended: none

cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: The food culture, and the love of nice quality things! There are a lot of affordable really nice food and amazing restaurant options. In the supermarket the quality is really good, unlike Denmark where the main selling point has become discount. The Austrians expect quality, and i love them for that.
top3_advice: Remember to register your residency at the municipality office! Remember to register to more courses than you need, because you wont get into all of them, and be sure that the courses dont overlap - and remember to deregister for seminars you wont be following anyway before the deregistration period is over. And finally, you can register to take exams in lectures even if you didnt follow the course, and you can register to courses at any time during the semester - this means you can change if something is too boring or too difficult.

crucial_aspects: Vienna seemed both perfectly close to and perfectly far away from Copenhagen both in terms of distance and culture. Additionally, it is very easy to travel to neighboring countries from Vienna which I planned to from the start. I also thought learning some German would be fun.
info_ease: It was quite easy. The university gave the necessary information about semester start in advance and in simple terms. Anything I was unsure about I could find out on the university's website. Access to information about registration of residence with the authorities was also sufficient.
arrival_assistance: The university had sent a mail about choosing an orientation session. At the orientation session the important things were discussed and you could ask any questions you might have had.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: If I remember correctly, the registration process was simply attending your orientation session and validating the u:card they give you there. Registering for courses was done through u:space. Here, it's notable that you could sign up for as many courses as you wanted. It was a simple process.
registration_help: The university was always available to answer questions.
registration_success: I got everything I wanted, although these courses differed a bit from my originally intended choices because of scheduling conflicts.
registration_advice: Sign up for more courses than you need. I signed up for twice as many. It's a bit of a puzzle to figure out which courses conflict with each other and to what degree. This is important to look at before making your final choices as many courses require regular attendance to pass. Also keep in mind that you may have a lot of exams during the last week depending on your courses. I made sure to spread mine out so I essentially had half my "exams" before Christmas break. The form of examination varies a lot, too.
course_level: Like I said, the level of the courses was generally lower than for (mandatory courses) at the University of Copenhagen. It felt a little superficial sometimes, but that might be because the courses are smaller (2-4 ECTS). However, among the courses I had, a few were probably closer to what I'm used to in Copenhagen.
teaching_comparison: It was more lecture based. The teachers were open to questions, and in some courses the grade depends on participation, but it was still less interactive than I was used to. In a few of my courses, the lessons would start with going through the homework which I found to be unusual. Some courses will have you do a presentation with a partner, but the law campus doesn't have good study spaces for that.

other_comments: Vienna is a beautiful city, and I'm glad I chose to go there. It's warm in the summer and cold in the winter, but I had a great time the whole stay.

arrival_assistance: There was an intro-meeting one of my first days, but with pretty scarce information to be honest.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I first of all had to find courses that correlated with my mandatory courses at KU, which was very very hard. Especially cause the courses of the coming semester weren't out yet, so i just had to kinda guess based of last years courses, and a lot of them ended up not being there in the end, so it was pretty much a waste of time. Besides that there was not a lot of course information, so i had to email most of my professors. Uni Wien also has a system where you don't know whether you will get a spot on a course up until the last minute (actually not until the start of the semester). This really stressed me out, but i would recommend writing your teachers and explaining them your situation if you're stressed about it, a good handful of my teachers made exceptions for me because of my exchange situation.
registration_help: I could write my mobility coordinator, but to be honest she was not to much help. I had to spend a lot of hours figuring it out myself by writing emails to teachers, looking at the uni website, asking the administration etc.
registration_success: I ended up actually getting all the classes that i needed. It just took a lot of work and time.
registration_advice: Start researching classes before you even apply for the exchange. Don't be afraid to be very annoying and just email or call all the people you need answers from - it will help.
course_level: I took one BA course, the rest was MA. It was mainly because there wasn't any english BA courses that correlated with the mandatory courses i had to take. The MA courses was not too difficult for a UCPH BA student, some of the courses the academic level was perhaps even lower, but that probably depends on the person and the course.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was different from course to course. Generally it seemed like at Uni Wien there wasn't a lot of overall "rules" or universal structure for the courses, as the demands, style etc. varied a lot. There was a lot more mandatory participation and assignments, but the readings were easier.

registration_help: The Erasmus coordinators on-site offered office hours to help with the registration and Louise Diamant at UCPH was also very helpful!
registration_success: It was a hassle and took 3-4 months of sending new courses to get them pre-approved at UCPH and figuring out which courses you can attend at UniWien. In the end it worked out with getting the courses I needed.

housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: While the city and the department and everything was great, I do feel that the classes in Denmark are better structured.
registration_process: You can find all the courses on u:find where you can also sort by language. Personally I didn't really find the website very user friendly, but it gets the job done. Often they don't put the courses until a month before the classes start, so it's hard to plan ahead. You can however register for more classes than you need, try them out, and then deregister within a week or two. Something to be aware of though: they have mandatory attendance for seminars (SE), but not for lectures (VO). So while seminars might be easier to make friends, you would have to show up for almost every single one, and have to do make-up work for classes that you miss.
registration_help: The department was very kind to help if anything was unclear. The teachers are generally very helpful and are willing to answer all questions over e-mail! Even before you arrive at the uni.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted, they prioritise exchange students in registration.
registration_advice: Remember to check whether it's a seminar (SE) or a lecture (VO), since I almost only signed up for seminars and had to show up for all classes. Seminars also have continuous assesment, meaning there's mandatory participation and often smaller assignments throughout the semester - I often had to hand in my notes for each text every week, to prove I had done the reading. Lectures usually only have a final exam with no assignments throughout.
academics_comments: While the city and the department and everything was great, I do feel that the classes in Denmark are better structured.
course_level: The courses are smaller than at CPH (usually 5 ECTS), so you need to have many more courses than usual. Of course since they are pretty small courses, they are not as difficult either.
teaching_comparison: I really liked many of the teachers! However the seminars are way more focused on student participation, which sometimes was great and sometimes not so great.

other_useful_info: Only that you DON'T NEED TO SPEAK GERMAN.

greatest_challenge: You constantly meet new people, which is great, but it's also hard to get real deep friendships in such a short amount of time. I kinda regret not staying for a whole year, since that's pretty common for other countries.

crucial_aspects: For me, the rich culture of Vienna was highly tempting, making it a destination I would choose. Furthermore, I think the city fits my interests very well, and I was eager to quickly build a "normal" daily life while I was abroad, which I could see happening in Vienna. I speak fluent German, which helped me find my way around and connect with the locals. Nevertheless, everybody speaks English very well, so I think that would not have been an issue anyway.
info_ease: The Uni Wien was very helpful in giving information about the study start and what to organize before and upon arrival. The information about the courses and the course schedules was missing until the beginning of the semester for some courses, so for figuring out which courses to register for, some information was missing.
arrival_assistance: There was a mandatory orientation meeting where things such as registering in the city of Vienna, course registration, and the ESN network were introduced.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The Uni Wien contacted me by email with highly detailed step-by-step instructions which were easy to follow.
registration_help: The Uni Wien has some information available on their website. If needed, it was always a possibility to contact the Erasmus board, and they usually answered quickly.
registration_success: Very successful. The University of Vienna has VO classes (Vorlesungen), usually with no limit on participants. Then they also have SE (seminars) and UE (Übungen), where you apply, but you are not guaranteed a spot. For these, it is necessary to prioritise registrations. Sometimes people end up on the waiting list, but here it is very important to still show up for the first session, as some registered people might not show up, which leaves a free spot. I succeeded in getting all the classes I wanted, even though I was on the waiting list for some classes to begin with.
registration_advice: Even though the registration seems a little chaotic compared to KUs, it ends up falling into place upon your arrival, and the classes that you register for at the beginning do not necessarily need to be the ones that you also finish.
course_level: The level of the classes is similar to the level at KU. From my experience, some of the exams were a little easier than KU's, but it depends on the courses. Some classes (the seminars) do not have final exams.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style depends on the type of class. Some are more interactive (the semiars) while the VOs were plain lectures with almost no interaction.
courses_enrolled: Methods in Molecular Biology Science in Society Laboratories Biology and Evolution of Archaea Applied Machine Learning for Biological Problems Seminar in Genetics - Molecular Biology of RNA Genome Structure and Evolution Epigenetics - From basic mechanisms to medical applications
recommended_courses: Seminar in Genetics Epigenetics Evolution and Biology of Archaea
unexpected_costs: none
cost_comparison: Public transport is much cheaper than in Copenhagen. I got a semester ticket for 75 euros, which covered the four months that I was staying in Vienna. Groceries and going out was more or less the same as in Denmark.
activities_available: The University of Vienna has a lot of different sports classes that are pretty affordable. Be aware that the registration opens ~a month before the semester, and the classes are very popular, so you have to register for them in time. I went to a lot of free museum days/nights while I was in Vienna, and you can also get some cheap tickets for the theaters and operas as a student.
activities_recommended: Visit the museum on free days, as they are a little expensive usually. Visit a Spritzer Stand, which is the Austrian Fredagsbar. Some of my friends went to a traditional Austrian Ball, which is also a great experience.
weekend_recommendations: Go on a Skitrip if you are in Vienna in the winter semester. You can do a Daytrip to Semmering or a weekend tour to one of the many skiing areas in Austria. Budapest is only 2 hours away so that is also a great weekend destination.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Vienna is not that different from Copenhagen
socializing_tips: The local students are a little reserved as everybody has their own everyday life. The Uni Sport is a good opportunity to get to know the local students, and also attending the seminars is a good opportunity as the classes are smaller and you will occasionally do some group work.
cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: I loved the Kaffeehaus culture in Vienna
top3_advice: You do not need to speak German There are a lot of great things to do in Vienna and the surroundings The weather is better than in Denmark
other_useful_info: It is worth attending seminars
most_rewarding: The friendships that I made
greatest_challenge: Balancing studies and other activities. It is definitely worth prioritizing friends and activities.

registration_process: I applied for courses in the beginning/middle of September. About a week later, it was possible to see my assigned courses on u:space. Exercise classes have continous assessment, and lectures end with an exam (which you also need to sign up for at the end of the semester. )
registration_help: The incoming mobility coordinator for my field of study was very helpful when I didn’t get a spot in one of my courses. He encouraged me to contact the StudienServiceCenter who secured me a spot.

registration_advice: My impression is, that a lot of local students sign of for more courses than needed and deregister after a couple of weeks. Hence; if you do not get a spot in a course, you can show up in class the first couple of times, and ask the teacher if there is a free spot. At least three (out of 25) people in my class got a spot this way.
course_level: The courses were similar to danish courses in respect to difficulty. Most of the BA courses are held in german, and hence you should be able to understand german. I did though get the option to present in english in some of my courses, as I felt more comfortable this way. I took one course in english (Mathematical Logic), and my impression was, that most students in this class was exchange students. This was also by far the most difficult course and I was told, that it was structured differently that most other courses at the mathematics department.
teaching_comparison: The courses from the BEd was interesting and difficult in a different way than I am used to. The courses from BSc was very similar to those in Denmark. For the exercise classes you are asked to note which exercises you have succesfully solved each week, and may be asked to present those in class. The grade you recieve in based on the amount of exercises you have completed during the semester. You are not allowed to bring notes for the exams in Austria.

recommended_courses: The language course in September was amazing. First of all, I got the apportunity to improve (and refresh) my German skills before the semester began, but the course also included a social programme. I went on a hike to Kahlenberg, attended two choir sessions, joined a walk in the city centre and participated in a picnic and a party. There was also an option to watch different Austrian movies and take extra German lessons in the evening. It was a very nice introduction to the city and culture of Austria.
unexpected_costs: Wifi at my dorm. But it was only 5 euros per month.
cost_comparison: It was cheaper to go to a café than in Copenhagen. A cup of coffee cost about 5 euros.

weekend_recommendations: ESN club, museums and the opera/theaters. They often have discounts for people aged under 27 or 30, or student discounts. Remember to bring your student ID. Hallstatt and Bratislava should be nice to visit. I sadly didn't go to any of them. Christmas markets!! (Go in the end of November, not in December).

socializing_tips: Talk to people in class and at your dorm.
cultural_challenges: Oppening hours. Always bring cash! There are still places (resturants, cafés and especially churches) that does not take card.
culture_appreciated: Christmas markets, museums and concert halls. The many incredible dishes, that my friends made me taste.
top3_advice: Be aware of the registration system of courses. Go to the ESN events. Sign up for a language course.
other_useful_info: Be aware to type the exact adress of University buildings into Google Maps. Google Maps can not always differ between them, and the University has buildings all over the city. (I once went to the wrong building in another part of the city, 30 minutes away from the correct one....)
most_rewarding: The people I met. The many cultural experiences i have gotten. Not only Austrian once. Fx. I was invited to thanks giving by a friend a met at my language course.
greatest_challenge: I missed my family and friends at home. I found my courses very challenging.
other_comments: Be aware that not every day will feel like an adventure. Most days will actually be quite boring and similar to your everyday life at home. But that’s okay — that is also part of the experience. Don’t stress about having to experience something all the time. You probably need some breaks and Netflix time. I did.

crucial_aspects: I chose Vienna as my destination primarily for two reasons: that the University of Vienna is high-quality university, and that I have previously really enjoyed the city of Vienna.
info_ease: It was very easy to find all necessary information. The Erasmus-Incoming team at the University of Vienna is very communicative, and they send all the information you need by email and refer to pages on their websites. The available information was very detailed.
arrival_assistance: There were frequent orientations, making it easy to attend one shortly after arrival. Other than this orientation I did not need any assistance.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Course registration is very simple. At PolSci, you can apply for as many courses as you want and prioritize them based on your preference. You then get assigned all courses where you get a spot. The only challenging part was that the registration process takes place close to semester start which meant that I needed to ask UCPH if they could speed up the pre-approval process (which they were able to do).
registration_help: You can reach out to the Erasmus-Incoming team as well as coordinators and professors, but I did not find it necessary to do so.
registration_success: I applied for twice as many courses as I needed just in case and got into all but one. You can deregister from courses until 2-3 weeks into the semester, meaning that you get to try out different courses if you're uncertain about which you want to take. This was a really nice option.
registration_advice: Ask UCPH if they can give you a quicker pre-approval if it usually takes a long time, so you can have peace of mind about the pre-approval. And if you get waitlisted for a course you really want, stay on the waitlist - many students deregister for courses in the first couple of weeks, so you may get a spot.
course_level: I chose more demanding courses (according to the permanent Uni Vie students) due to interest and found the coursed to be a bit easier than UCPH.
teaching_comparison: It was more portfolio-style with several deliverables during the semester (you can also choose courses that only have one final sit-in exam, but these give less ECTS-points). The classes are also more classroom discussion than teaching.

weekend_recommendations: Take advantage of the opportunity to travel by train to nearby cities. There are many nice places in Austria, e.g. Melk, Hallstatt, Salzburg. Outside of Vienna it is super easy to take weekendtrips to Prague and Budapest - I really recommend that.
culture_adjustment: Very easy
socializing_tips: Take some courses that include group work
cultural_challenges: None

crucial_aspects: I had never visited, but heard a lot of great things about Vienna.
info_ease: There was a general introduction seminar, which was okay. There was also an international office, with limited opening hours, but very helpful and kind people. Lastly there was also an introduction seminar at juridicum which was far to late.
arrival_assistance: As I said you could go to the international office yourself, and the mandatory introduction seminars.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Very DIY. You have to put together your own schedule, which is quite complicated, as you have to attend a lot of classes (each only being worth between 2 and 4 ECTS points), and most if not all classes have mandatory attendance, meaning that you have to spend quite some time electing classes.
registration_help: As I said a seminar at juridicum, but which took place after the deadline. There also was some help to find online.
registration_success: It took some time, but I was somewhat satisfied.
registration_advice: Registrer for as much as possible, then you can always deregister later. Also if you are put on the waitlist for a class you want, you will basically always get the spot, if you just show up for the first class.
course_level: A bit lower in general then in Copenhagen, it was however very dependent on the teacher.
teaching_comparison: Almost no group work, mostly lectures, with involvement of student. But again very dependent on the teacher, with some having far more student interaction, and some classes being totally different.

unexpected_costs: Fees from registration at the municipality.
cost_comparison: Most things were cheaper than in Denmark, but don't expect, as cheap prices as other places especially in southern or eastern europe.
activities_available: Non that was very suitable for Erasmus students in my opinion, but one or two of my friends from Erasmus did join some sport activities.
activities_recommended: Non really, especially if your German isn't that good.
weekend_recommendations: Travel to other european cities, visit museums and see an opera. Definitely go and do a heuringer when possible. culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, it's not very diffrent, or though a bit more religious.
cultural_challenges: Not really, Austrians aren't the friendlies people in the world, but that isn't exactly what the Danes are famous for either. There is some cultural differences with the other Erasmus students as well, so be open minded.
culture_appreciated: The wine, and the use of nature.
top3_advice: Go to as many Erasmus events as possible at the beginig of the stay, so that you make other Erasmus friends. Make sure to experience some of the history and culture by going to stuff like the museums and the opera. Vienna is also a great hub for traveling, so do that.
other_useful_info: Be aware that juridicum is quite a horrible building with no windows in the classroms and way too few spaces for studying.
most_rewarding: The Erasmus friends from all over Europe I made.
greatest_challenge: Having so many classes at the same time.
other_comments: Your system is terrible, I filled this thing out for the third time now, as it keeps login me off, without saving the things I wrote. If you make this kind of thing mandatory, at least have some systems that actually work.

crucial_aspects: Courses and country
overall_comments: I give it not 10, because I had a not so good studying experience at my faculty. But the social and cultural experience made it all worth it. I will also write a disclaimer here, saying that most of my critiques below concerns the Faculty of Mathematics, Information and Mechanics, and other Erasmus students I got to know from other faculties had a better experience.
info_ease: General information about the university was fairly easy to find, but there was given absolutely no information about or introduction to specifically my study or faculty. This was pretty bad, I had to find out everything myself through websites and teachers and other students. I strongly recommend asking the international coordinator related to your faculty for help and guidance.
arrival_assistance: I was offered a mentor (a student from the university to help settle in the city), which I declined, but in hindsight it would have been helpful to have someone tell relevant information about the faculty.
arrival_comments: Again, I got no information or orientation specifically about my study, you really have to write and ask coordinators yourself about everything. But this is maybe different for the bigger larger faculties, I think they got more information and an introduction.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I give it not 10, because I had a not so good studying experience at my faculty. But the social and cultural experience made it all worth it. I will also write a disclaimer here, saying that most of my critiques below concerns the Faculty of Mathematics, Information and Mechanics, and other Erasmus students I got to know from other faculties had a better experience.
registration_process: It depends on the courses you wish to take. The course registration periods are different for different faculties. When it comes to registration, some courses you can register yourself on USOSweb, which is the student platform like KUnet. Other courses the faculty coordinator has to register for you.
registration_help: You could write the faculty coordinators for help on e-mail.
registration_success: I got registered for all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: I lost a lot of time trying to figure out registration to courses at different faculties on my own. It is very confusing and there was different information on different sites. Just find the courses that you wish to take, and then write the faculty coordinators and ask how to register. My faculty coordinator was very helpful in registering and un-registering me to courses. I also found that the registration period was different for Erasmus students than regular students. I think it is also a good idea to ask for a meeting with the faculty coordinator just to find out how everything works on this particular faculty. USOSweb has a course catalogue, use this for finding courses. Also write to the course coordinator or professor associated to each course about prerequisites, level, course participation and examination method even though there are some information on USOSweb. I experienced that the courses I took had prerequisites not stated on the course page, so I had to cancel them, find new courses and restructure my whole schedule, which was tedious. So find som backup courses! Furthermore, the professors were very flexible in regards to examination method, which was both good and bad. Examination dates were rescheduled, suddenly I had to do assignments not stated on the course page, and an oral part of the examination was also possible even though on USOSweb it said only written. So talk to them before the course and talk about expectations to the course. This can of course be different on different faculties and studies!
academics_comments: I give it not 10, because I had a not so good studying experience at my faculty. But the social and cultural experience made it all worth it. I will also write a disclaimer here, saying that most of my critiques below concerns the Faculty of Mathematics, Information and Mechanics, and other Erasmus students I got to know from other faculties had a better experience.
course_level: The academic level for me seemed high, and I think this is because the teaching style was very different in the courses I took at UW, than what I am used to on MATH at UCPH. The teaching style together with the smaller classes results in a more loose and intuition-based teaching rather than technical and thorough as I experience it at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: There was not may people attending the courses that I chose, and it was my impression that there was not as many people enrolled in Mathematics as at UCPH. The smaller classes together with the fact that often course participation counts into the examination assessment, means that the teaching is often very discussion-based. At UCPH I am used to separate lectures by the professor and then exercise sessions with a TA, but at UW the two things sometimes was mixed together and the professor conducted all of the 2x90 minutes of teaching each week. The structure of the courses was often very loose. In most of my classes no curriculum was stated and almost no information given about classes on an online platform. Everything happened at the classes, so ask the professor if you want to know curriculum for next class beforehand.
courses_enrolled: I took the following math courses: Differential Geometry, Algebraic Topology and Number Theory. I then also took two courses outside of math: Geography of the World, and Educational Walking Tours in Warsaw.
recommended_courses: I would recommend Number Theory, as the teacher is very good and the theory is nice. I would also recommend Educational Walking Tours in Warsaw, it is a fun way to get to know the city and meet other international students!
unexpected_costs: Nothing I remember.
cost_comparison: In general, Warsaw is much cheaper than in Copenhagen, and a nice coffee is only about 20 kr. But watch out, because everything is so cheap you want to go out all the time, and adapt a new lifestyle, and probably you end up spending more money than you would in Copenhagen.
activities_available: There was language exchanging events, city game events, trips to other cities, sports tournament weekend in the south of Poland, and Erasmus parties at some clubs.
activities_recommended: I would recommend the city trips and language exchanging events, they were chill ways to get to know other people.
weekend_recommendations: I really enjoyed the techno clubs and jazz clubs. In general the area Srodmiescie Poludniowe is super nice. I recommend cafes at Plac Zbawiciela; going to free Chopin concerts on Sundays in the summer at the Chopin monument in Lazienki park; use the university library BUW and its garden; drinking at night by the Vistula river (the only place it is allowed to drink in public); go to Bazar na Kole in the weekend; the museum of modern art Zacheta; the Jewish cemetery; try milk bars (cheap good polish food); and in general explore by bike all the weird, different districts.
culture_adjustment: The polish seem very closed and not very accommodating. I found it difficult arriving in winter and the city seeming dead and cold and people unhappy. For example strangers often think you are weird if you smile to them in supermarkets, and the service at restaurants/cafes are often not super kind and bad. But this is just how it is, and a reason for this is also that people can get uncomfortable by speaking english. But you get used to it quickly, and as soon as the summer arrived and the weather got better, the city totally blossomed and there are many green areas and people seem happier!
socializing_tips: Just talk to them even if they seem reserved and not interested. My experience was that they would not say hello or start an interaction, but as soon as I took initiative they actually wanted to talk.
cultural_challenges: That the polish people are very closed and reserved people.
culture_appreciated: The food! And the city is actually very international. I also appreciated that they valued being quiet and behave properly, and I also felt very safe in the city (probably due to the fact that it is forbidden to drink in public).
top3_advice: Be prepared for very unstructured and/or flexible teaching, and consider the benefits of this. Ask for help - do not try to figure things out by yourself. Warsaw is so great and interesting, it seems at first like a strange disrupted place, but use time on understanding the history of the city and talking to local people. You will learn to love the contrasts in the city and the culture!
other_useful_info: My main advice: Unless you want to go on exchange exclusively for studying, you will regret having to use a lot on time on studying, if you also interested in actually getting to know the city and making friends. So choose courses you think you can overcome easily, while also using a lot on time on socialising!
most_rewarding: Meeting some like-minded people from other countries, that I consider friends for life, and experiencing a country with such a different history than Denmark.
greatest_challenge: Trying to figure out a balance between studying and having a life outside the university.
other_comments: Warsaw is really an interesting city, and worth getting to know! I really fell in love with it. I think I would have a very different, perhaps worse experience if I went there on winter semester. Go for summer semester!
