crucial_aspects: Within Europe and the Erasmus program I found Warsaw to be one of the most different and interesting places in terms of culture.
overall_comments: My great experience does not relate to my academic outcome at all. The courses were often chaotic, unorganised and on a lower level than I expected.
info_ease: Fairly easy, even though I often struggled when it came to University of Warsaw. For a handfull of courses they didn't have descriptions on the course or the syllabus etc., which University of Copenhagen demanded in order to accept the courses as replacements for my obligatory courses.
arrival_assistance: I recieved a lot of assistance and information about study life, the city, housing etc. Both from the university and the local Erasmus network. Still I missed assistance with the courses and having them accepted. It was pretty stressfull as my OLA was only completed very late and therefore late before I recieved the Erasmus grant.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: My great experience does not relate to my academic outcome at all. The courses were often chaotic, unorganised and on a lower level than I expected.
registration_process: It was a first-come-first-served system of the Erasmus courses. This part worked well, but since I needed regular courses I had to email all the professors from the courses I wanted to get personal permission to join the courses. After this permission I then had to email my faculty coordinator with screenshots of the emails from the professors before they officially could register me. To top it off this also could only happen after the application proces of both Erasmus and regular students was concluded. This meant that I was put back in line in both cases. I had to wait to register for the few Erasmus courses I had room for, because I had to wait to know my schedule with regular courses. This left me with only the Erasmus courses that still had room.
registration_help: I emailed my faculty and my Erasmus coordinator a lot, but often felt like my problems fell between two chairs.
registration_success: In the end the success criteria was to cover all my obligatory courses. In this regard it ended in a successful way, but I would have like to be able to choose some elective courses that interested me more and not just some I had to take to fill up my schedule after I was put back in line by the system.
registration_advice: Be patient and don't hesitate to write emails to people if you are in doubt.
academics_comments: My great experience does not relate to my academic outcome at all. The courses were often chaotic, unorganised and on a lower level than I expected.
course_level: A part from a few exceptions very low. Even from some of the MA courses I learned about thing I had learned about before going to university. For a lot of the courses you passed by giving a presentation to the rest of the class and not having too much absence. In these cases the teacher often didn't seem to care too much and around 80% would get the best grade without much effort.
teaching_comparison: Not at all. I had 10 different courses at the same time. All with a professor in small classes. The idea is good but the professors lacked basic teaching skills.
courses_enrolled: Economics of the European Integration, Political Institutions in the EU countries, Decision-Making Procedures in the EU, Who runs the World? Girls? Gender & World Politics, Comparative Politics, European Primary and Secondary Law, European Institutions, Comparative Political Systems I, Religion and Politics in Orthodox World, Ukraine: Culture and Identity.
recommended_courses: "European Primary and Secondary Law": the professor was extremely good, structured and engaged. Made the courses very interesting. "Religion and Politics in Orthodox World" and "Ukraine: Culture and Identity": the two courses were similar and had the same professor, who was very engaged and nerdy about her field. Also two themes that you wouldn't often have the possibility to dig into to.
unexpected_costs: It turned out to be very expensive to travel 'green'. At all times it would have been cheaper to take a plane than the bus/train, but since I wanted to travel green I ended up spending a lot of money on transportation. Especially around Christmas and New Years where I went home to my family. Here the cheapest tickets ended up costing me more than 2000kr. to get back and fourth.
cost_comparison: In general the pricelevel of groceries etc. Of course it was still cheaper than Denmark, but it was higher than expected from Warsaw and "Eastern Europe" beacuse of the heavy inflation and housing crisis the last two years. Cultural stuff was supprisingly cheap. Theathers, cinemas, concerts, museums and art all had huge student discounts which gave a lot of opportunities.
activities_available: A lot of different things. Some hosted by the institutions, but in general just huge student discounts on cultural activities, let alone a catalogue of sports activities at the university you could sign up for.
activities_recommended: The cultural ones. Warsaw is rich on theathers, museums, concerts and art at a very high level and available at low prices.
weekend_recommendations: I was at a handfull of weekend trips to other places in Poland. In all cases the places we visited was very different from Warsaw, so I highly recommend exploring the country. The regional trains are also very cheap with student discount. I can recommend Lublin in the East, Bielsko-Biala and Krakow to the South and Gdansk to the North. Especially I recommend Zakopane: a city/area in the mountains close to the Slovakian border. You can ski in the winter and hike for the rest of the year in beautiful nature.
culture_adjustment: Not too hard, but it also helped a lot to have a lot of other Erasmus students in the same situation as you to share your experiences with.
socializing_tips: To join regular courses so you meet non-Erasmus students. If you live in a dorm you automatically also get to talk to other people. The Erasmus Student Network volunteers are often local as well and are always happy to talk.
cultural_challenges: The amount of hierarchy and respect for authorities. You didn't get a personal bond with your professors or the personel in the dorm because there was a very defined hierarchy. Also the amount of patriotism/nationalism among the Polish people. It was hard to get used to that these thing might mean different things in this context than my own back in Denmark. The lack of trust in authorities (the police for example) from normal people.
culture_appreciated: The co-excisting of Soviet culture (architecture, state-funded cafeterias to secure cheap food) and a more Western culture with diversity, political awareness etc. Both contains things that is specific for Warsaw and not the rest of Poland.
top3_advice: - Even if you don't get a huge academic outcome you still get to experience Polish culture and have a pretty good idea about Polish culture and the Polish people, which might confront some stereotypes about Eastern Europe and Post-Soviet states. - Warsaw is an amazing and interesting city with a lot of possibilities. Take your time to explore concerts, museums, art etc. You will experience some things that you are not able to elsewhere. Also, the areas of the city is very different. I encourage you to spend days to visit other parts of the city. - Exchange can be tough socially. A million things is happening all the time with hundreds of new people. Try to avoid FOMO as much as possible. Take your breaks and find time to do things on your own. Try to find 'your people' instead of just a big group drinking beer every night. It is nice and fun to party, but remember that this is not where actual friendships are made. It isnice if you make friends for life, but even if you want stay in touch it's also valuable that you shared experiences, fun and conversations in an exchange bubble for 4-5 months.
other_useful_info: Mostly the information I gave about registration for regular courses and housing at the dormitory.
most_rewarding: To be very upfront in terms of making friendships. Everyone is in the same situation, so it's perfectly normal to ask someone out on a friend-date. It can be a very rewarding situation to be in. I also allowed myself to make friends I usually wouldn't have made at home. Because I knew the friendships didn't have to last forever, but it was enough that it was an interesting relation. This is meant as a good thing, even though it might not sound like it.
greatest_challenge: To have privacy and relax because I lived in the dorm in a small room with a guy who was always there. I struggled to recharged my batteries.

teaching_comparison: he academic style in general was noticeably different between the two universities. Classes at UCPH were typically structured around active discussion, encouraging students to participate, share their perspectives, and critically engage with the material during each session. In contrast, at UW the teaching format tended to be more traditional and centered on lectures, where the professor delivered the content and students listened and took notes, with fewer opportunities for spontaneous group debate. Another significant difference concerned preparation for classes. At UCPH, it was expected that students would read several academic articles or chapters before most sessions, meaning that the discussion in class could build on previous independent study. This approach required students to stay consistently up to date with the reading material. At UW, however, such preparation was not required for the majority of courses, and readings—if assigned—were often supplementary rather than essential for participation in class. Despite these differences in teaching style and expectations, the grading systems at both institutions were relatively similar. In both cases, assessment commonly took the form of written essays, oral examinations, presentations, or project reports. As a result, although the learning environment and classroom dynamic varied, the methods used to evaluate students’ knowledge and understanding were largely comparable across the two universities.

recommended_courses: I would recommend the course “Geopolitical Tuesdays,” which I took during the first semester of my exchange program. It turned out to be one of the most engaging and intellectually stimulating courses I attended. Throughout the classes, a wide range of current and relevant global topics were explored in depth, allowing students to gain a better understanding of the rapidly changing geopolitical landscape. What made the course particularly interesting was the diversity of guest lecturers. Many sessions were conducted by researchers and experts from different academic backgrounds, frequently representing foreign universities. This provided a unique opportunity to hear multiple perspectives, often shaped by the political and social environments of the lecturers’ home countries. The primary focus of the course was on analyzing contemporary international issues, including global power dynamics, regional conflicts, and emerging political trends. Thanks to its practical approach and exposure to experts from abroad, “Geopolitical Tuesdays” offered a valuable and enriching academic experience that went far beyond standard classroom learning.
unexpected_costs: There were no unexpected costs that I encountered.
cost_comparison: The groceries turned out to be more expensive than I had originally expected. Before arriving, I assumed that everyday food shopping would be significantly cheaper compared to Denmark, but in reality the difference was not as noticeable. Many basic items, such as fresh produce, dairy products, and pantry staples, were priced only slightly lower, and in some cases almost the same as in Danish supermarkets.
activities_available: There were lots of activities available, mainly related to sports, languages and different cultures.
activities_recommended: I would like to recommend participation in the events during orientation as they allow you the make a lot of friends from different courses and participate in fun activities such as pub crawls and sightiseeing of the city center.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend to go to Krakow and Gdansk, visit museums in Warsaw such as the Jewish history museum.
culture_adjustment: I was easy as I am Polish.
socializing_tips: Try to learn some basic phrases in Polish, as it can make a noticeable difference in everyday interactions and help local people become more open to socializing. Even simple expressions like greeting someone, thanking them, or ordering something politely can show appreciation for the local culture and effort on your part.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences between Poland and Denmark. In Poland people seem a bit more open to helping and talking to strangers.
culture_appreciated: I appreciate the local cuisine the most.
top3_advice: I would recommend to learn a few basic phrases in Polish, try the local cuisine, take some extra language classes and participate in the free sports classes available at the university - they are really good and the sports facilities are great.
other_useful_info: Try to take advantage of the language and sports courses offered at the host institution, as these opportunities are often unique and not easily available elsewhere. At many universities, such courses either do not exist or require additional fees, whereas during an exchange they are frequently included as part of the student experience.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of the experience was successfully defending my Master’s thesis, which I had spent the entire summer semester writing. After months of research, planning, drafting, revising, and refining my arguments, standing in front of the committee and presenting my findings felt like a true culmination of the effort I had put in.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge I faced was finding a supervisor for my thesis, primarily because I had no prior experience or established connections with lecturers at the host institution. Unlike at my home university, where I already knew the teaching staff and had a sense of their research interests, academic styles, and personalities, at the new university I had to make this decision without any previous interaction or insight. This made the selection process more difficult, as choosing a supervisor is not only about matching research topics but also about finding someone with whom you can communicate effectively and feel supported during the writing process. Since I lacked personal familiarity with the faculty, I had to rely on course descriptions, staff profiles, and recommendations from other students to make an informed choice. Overall, it was a challenging situation that required careful consideration and a degree of trust in making such an important academic decision without the benefit of existing relationships.

So he just sent out a google forms questionnaire with all the subjects in English at the faculty of psychology. However, I wanted to take courses in Polish, so I had to email him afterwards to add me to the polish courses. This was a few days before the semester was to begin, so I was scared that I would not get in. I was the only one who has 12 exams and who had to lock myself in the library. At psychology, the other students also had some things to do, but it could not be compared to the amount of work I had. If so, consider taking a few courses at other faculties - then you can get the "typical" Erasmus courses that are less demanding. Coming from Denmark, where everything is so expensive that you barely enjoy going out to a restaurant or a bar, being in Poland felt like a blessing.

crucial_aspects: The cost of living in Poland is relatively affordable compared to other European countries. Poland's rich history and vibrant culture were significant draws. I have heard that traveling in Poland is incredibly convenient and enjoyable. Poland was relatively undiscovered for me, and I was eager to learn about its unique culture and history. The vibrant Erasmus community provided a strong support network and enriched my experience.
info_ease: It's very easy. The University of Warsaw (UW) hosts a Zoom meeting to provide all the necessary information. They also send detailed information via email, making it easy to find everything you need.
arrival_assistance: A tutor from the European Student Network (ESN) and an orientation by both ESN and the school provide all the necessary information, including how to sign up for classes. They offer excellent assistance upon your arrival, making it easy to settle down.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: UW opens the registration for all students, then its first come, first serve, however they also give you guide you can follow, which is great, however their website is not user friendly.
registration_help: UW provides detailed online information, including specific timeslots for various services. You can find out when and where to meet up on campus to get help with registration problems.
registration_success: Overall, my experience was quite successful. There was one class I didn't get, but I managed to secure all the others.
registration_advice: Be patient, it will solve it self, and their are help from the school or students.
course_level: I took Erasmus courses at the BA level, and they were quite manageable. Generally, you don't need to study beforehand unless specifically asked to. However, it's important to follow the lectures and participate in class activities, as your participation will be assessed. I also took one MA course, which was similar in structure and difficulty to the Erasmus courses.
teaching_comparison: It's a mix of self study and team work, just like UCPH.

unexpected_costs: Visa and Residency Fees: There were some unexpected fees related to visa applications and residency permits. Social Activities: Participating in social events and exploring the city with friends sometimes led to higher expenses than anticipated.
cost_comparison: Food and eating out

activities_recommended: ESN activies!!
weekend_recommendations: Zakopane: Perfect for outdoor enthusiasts with great skiing in winter and hiking in summer. Gdańsk: A beautiful coastal city with rich maritime history and stunning architecture. Kraków: Known for its medieval core, vibrant culture, and historic sites and auschwitz: A somber, important historical site near Kraków, offering a powerful experience. During the weekends in Warsaw please visit the museums. They are really good.
culture_adjustment: It was easy to settle in. People were very open-minded, kind, and welcoming.
socializing_tips: Attend most of the events organized by ESN; that's where you'll meet your friends.
cultural_challenges: One cultural difference I found challenging in Poland was the direct communication style. People are very straightforward, which can sometimes feel blunt if you're not used to it.
culture_appreciated: I loved Polish cuisine, especially pierogi and bigos. The strong family values and hospitality made me feel welcome, and the vibrant arts scene was inspiring. The warmth and generosity of the Polish people left a lasting impression on me.
top3_advice: The University of Warsaw has a vibrant student community. Join clubs, attend events, and make connections with both local and international students. This will enhance your experience and help you build lasting friendships. While many people in Warsaw speak English, learning some basic Polish phrases can go a long way in making your stay more enjoyable. It shows respect for the local culture and can help you navigate daily life more easily.
other_useful_info: Picking up a few basic Polish phrases can significantly enhance your stay. It demonstrates respect for the local culture and makes navigating daily life much easier.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was definitely the friendships I formed. Meeting new people from different backgrounds and cultures enriched my time abroad and created lasting memories.
greatest_challenge: Language barriers, and being away from home. However, overcoming these challenges made the experience even more rewarding and helped me grow personally and academically.

registration_help: The correspondence with the exchange coordinator was really helpful in this regard. The speed of getting an answer was really comforting in this confusion.
registration_success: Many of the classes I wanted to take were either not on offer for the winter semester, or were at the same time as my mandatory courses. The courses I were able to register to, were however very good.
registration_advice: Don't stress about figuring everything out before you arrive in Warsaw. There is time to change courses, and drop out during the first month. Also try to register to non-Erasmus courses, they are a lot more interesting. Just send the professor of the course you want to take an email. They are usually very friendly and appreciative if exchange students want to take their courses, and answer very quickly.
course_level: It was a lot less structured and easier than what I have at UCPH. Many subjects were without a very concrete curriculum, and was instead just the professor talking. The exams were in many cases, especially in the Erasmus courses, just a 10 min presentation.
teaching_comparison: There was a lot more focus on "class-participation" and we were graded based on this participation. This made for a weird forcefulness and stress for the students around trying to say as much as possible during class. This method, while well-intentioned, was more to the detriment of learning and participation than contributive.
courses_enrolled: European Primary and Secondary Law, Decision-Making Procedures in European Union, European Institutions, Comparative Politics, Comparative Political Systems (I), Foreign Policy of Central and Eastern European Countries, Continuity and Change in American Society, Security Arrangements in Peace Processes: Theory and Practice, Evolution of the Welfare State: a Global perspective.
recommended_courses: I recommend taking European Primary and Secondary Law, Decision-Making Procedures in European Union, European Institutions, Comparative Politics, Comparative Political Systems (I) as they together cover the mandatory subjects for the Political Science exchange semester (DAK3 and EP). I also really recommend Foreign Policy of Central and Eastern European Countries and Evolution of the Welfare State: a Global perspective, as these courser are really interesting, with very knowledgeable and passionate professors which were really inspiring. Take Continuity and Change in American Society if you want to have the funniest subject you will ever have.
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Food, its really easy to get it cheap at Milk Bars - Very recommended.
activities_available: ESN at university of Warszaw had events three days a week, every week. A lot of different activities were on offer; from axe throwing, to polish practice to squirrel watching.
activities_recommended: Climbing at Crux is really cheap and nice. You can get into most museums by paying only 2 zloty as a student, and there are a lot of good ones: Zacheta, Polin etc. Cinema is also cheap and really good, i went once a week. Recommend going to Cinema Amondo.
weekend_recommendations: Trains are pretty cheap for students and there are many really nice cities around Poland. I really recommend seeing Krakow and Gdansk for a weekend trip. It can also be really nice with a day trip to Lodz.
culture_adjustment: Polish people are very nice and friendly, as long as you act nice around them you'll be fine.
socializing_tips: Take non-Erasmus subjects.
cultural_challenges: There is a lot more hierarchical relations, especially with professors.
culture_appreciated: Slavic hospitality.
top3_advice: Enjoy yourself. Don't take it too seriously, and enjoy all the cultural opportunities.
other_useful_info: Take advantage of how much cheaper it is to eat out, do various activities, museums etc.
most_rewarding: Getting to know how amazing of a country Poland is.
greatest_challenge: Not eating out all of the time, it was nice and cheap.

crucial_aspects: chose my study destination to combine strong expertise in ecology and biodiversity research with unique field opportunities in the Białowieża Forest. The Double Degree between the University of Copenhagen and the University of Warsaw offered both molecular and ecological perspectives, as well as valuable international experience.
overall_comments: It was a fantastic stay where I learned to work much more independently and take responsibility for projects. The field courses were excellent and very educational. The only reason I cannot give a top score is the enormous amount of administrative work it required. The University of Warsaw handled administration very well, but there was almost no support from KU, and we were often misinformed or instructed to do things incorrectly through the official administrative channels. We still haven’t received answers to some questions we asked KU more than four months ago.

arrival_assistance: Both guided tours, welcome meetings, social events and booklets

activities_available: The University of Warsaw offered a wide range of cultural and social activities for students, including language courses, museum visits, and international student events organized by ESN. There were also hiking trips and nature excursions.
activities_recommended: Join ESN events, its a great way to meet Polish students that want to engage with foreigners
weekend_recommendations: I highly recommend visiting the Białowieża Forest, one of Europe’s last primeval forests and an unforgettable destination for anyone interested in nature and biodiversity. The Hel Peninsula and Gdańsk are perfect for coastal trips, with beautiful beaches and rich maritime history. Kraków offers stunning architecture and cultural heritage, and for hiking or skiing, the Tatra Mountains in southern Poland are absolutely worth a visit.
culture_adjustment: t was okay, but quite different from Denmark, so it took some time to adjust. Once I got used to the pace and communication style, it became much easier and very rewarding.
socializing_tips: Yes, talk to people in your classes and ask them for advice for what to do.
cultural_challenges: The lack of smiling in public was hard at first, but the main challenge was that many people, even at the university, spoke only Polish, which made everyday communication more difficult at first. Combined with a more formal communication style, it took some time to adjust, but it became easier over time.
culture_appreciated: People were very welcoming once you got to know them, and there was a genuine interest in nature, local traditions, and food. I also enjoyed how much outdoor life are part of the culture. Its just very diffrent to Denmark in a refreshing way.
top3_advice: Find someone at UCPH who is familiar with the administrative side of the Double Degree or Erasmus process otherwise, you may spend countless hours trying to solve issues on your own and risk delaying/losing SU payments. Be proactive in communicating with both universities and keep written records of all correspondence. Take advantage of the field courses and research opportunities they are incredibly rewarding and a great way to connect with both students and professors.
other_useful_info: Join a lab group if possible and participate in conferences and fieldwork
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange was the opportunity to work independently on real research projects and field courses, especially in the Białowieża Forest. It was incredibly valuable to conduct fieldwork for my master’s thesis in one of Europe’s last primeval forests, while gaining hands-on experience and building strong collaborations with researchers and students. Joining FUNDIVE was an amazing decision.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was the lack of clear administrative support from the University of Copenhagen. Communication with the Outgoing Students office was often confusing, and I was repeatedly told that taking 45 ECTS was not possible within Erasmus, even though these 45 ECTS are part of my officially approved Double Degree programme with the University of Warsaw. Several requests were delayed for weeks because staff were on vacation or unsure who had the authority to answer. Even now, my Online Learning Agreement still contains errors that have not been corrected despite multiple attempts to resolve them. The University of Warsaw, in contrast, handled all administrative matters efficiently and provided excellent support.

crucial_aspects: My boyfriend is from Poland, and I went to Poland with him the summer before my Erasmus. I really like the polish culture, and thought it was interesting to stay in a Central European country. It learned me new perspectives, and expanded my horizon. I think it helped me get a bigger understand of the importance of EU and the different conflicts in Europe.
info_ease: Warsaw University was really helpful providing information about my stay, and we had several online meetings before. Both my mobility coordinators in Denmark and Poland was quick to answer and a big help. If I had any questions I quickly got an answer and help, so I found it easy finding the information I needed before arrival. The only difficulties was the Erasmus proces with OLA etc. which took a long time and was difficult.
arrival_assistance: I had a wonderful mobility coordinator who was available 24 hours always responding and helping us. I also had a "Buddy/mentor", who is a polish friend we can apply for to help us doing our stay. My mentor ended up being one of best friends at my stay and biggest supporters, she helped me if I had any questions and was a big help. I felt like we had a lot of assistance, and Warsaw university has a 2 week long intro week, and many WhatsApp groups that can help.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registration is pretty late, and near semester start. But it was okay since you can be pretty sure to get all of the courses you want, and they inform well about the registration process. We register at their website for Erasmus courses, and write to the professors by mail if we want to take regular courses. I got all of the courses I wanted, even though half of mine was regular courses
registration_help: The mobility coordinator was good at helping, and we also had online meetings before about how to register
registration_success: 100% succesfull
registration_advice: Be sure about the schedule and that the classes is not at the same time. It is a long process, especially with OLA, but it work out in the end. There is good options to cancel classes if regretted, and the professors almost never says no to take extra students, if there is not enough spaces on the website.
course_level: Very different, some of my classes had good professors that made the course interesting, others seemed a bit unprepared. So very mixed.
teaching_comparison: It´s more similar to high school in Denmark since the classes is mandatory, include activity and presentations in your grade. Students is very involved in the teaching, and there is a lot of the exams that is multiple choice. Most of the exams is written by hand.

cost_comparison: Prices in average half price of Denmark (groceries etc). But housing was pretty expensive if not staying in a dormitory. Prices as expected since I visited Poland before, but if you don't know Poland is more expensive that expected (still not expensive compared to Denmark).
activities_available: All kind of activities: museum trips, parties, social events, language courses, events for seeing the city etc. I think everything imaginable is available, really good offers
activities_recommended: Go to movie nights (didn't do myself but seemed nice), heard good about international dinner, taking polish intensive course, just meet with people especially in the beginning, many went to multipub every wednesday. My biggest recommendation is to get a polish mentor
weekend_recommendations: My favourite places (in ranked priority) in Poland: - Zakopane for hiking - Gdańsk (see the city, Second World War museum) - Wroclaw - Kraków (see the saltmine, castle and Auschwitz) - Malbork (to see the castle, near Gdansk so trip can be combined but I did it in a one-day trip) - Poznan - Lublin - Bialystok (national park) - Lodz In Warsaw: - Wilanow palace - POLIN museum - Uprising museum - Royal castle - Botanical garden Restaurants: - Nabank (brunch) - No. 34 coffee and breakfast - Bar Rascal - Tikhari modern Georgia - Same Krafty (beer) - Księgarnia Wrzenie Świata (Café to study - silent żonę) - and many other places, so many good food places!!! -
culture_adjustment: I think it was pretty easy to adjust to the local culture, but as a dane you need to get used to having a really formal reaction to the professors.
socializing_tips: Get a polish friend, not be shy to ask people If there want to hang out (everyone just want to get to know other people and get friends)
cultural_challenges: Not many, only the things with the professors described before
culture_appreciated: The history and the polish people is very proud
top3_advice: - Explore Poland - Be open and don't be afraid to ask people if they want to do anything with you - Dont stress about studying but enjoy the experience and value your time there
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of
most_rewarding: All of the people I met and getting to know more about Poland and its history and people
greatest_challenge: When my Erasmus ended and saying goodbye to all of the people I met
other_comments: Really recommend to go, the best months of my life

courses_enrolled: Media pluralism and diversity, Media and democracy, The Dilemmas of Criminal Policy, Anthropology of Photography, European Union in a New Global Order og Academic Visions: Lectures and Discussions (1).
recommended_courses: Jeg var fin tilfreds med mine fag! De to mediefag var spændende, hvor vi bl.a. kiggede på pressefrihed i de forskellige lande, som var præsenteret i undervisningen, skulle lave en fremlæggelse - omkring enten demokrati (vi fremlage om satire) og et diverst sted (vi fremlage om Den Røde Plads) - og derefter diskutere/snakke om det. Samtidig var underviseren vildt sød! Kriminalitetsfaget var meget specielt, hvor vi diskuterede dilemmaer omkring kriminalitet, men blev stillet nogen vanvittige spørgsmål, som kræver meget mere viden end vi har. Det blev lidt underligt at man skulle forholde sig til rigtig store spørgsmål omhandlende kriminalitet, når man ikke blev præsenteret for noget viden eller teori. Anthropology of Photography var enormt ustruktureret og kedeligt, men et rimeligt nemt fag. Dog en sød underviser. European Union in a New Global var nok det fag, hvor vi lærte mest. Det er en gammel diplomat, som underviste os, der nok ikke har sit pædagogikum i orden. Han var rimelig streng og stod bare og snakkede uafbrudt i halvanden time, hvor det så blev forventet af os, at vi skulle opfange det hele og i forvejen ligge inde med en del viden. Eksamen var en skriftlig eksamen på skolen, som vi var ret nervøse for, men som i sidste ende ikke krævede så meget for at bestå, som han ellers havde præsenteret det. Nok det fag, hvor vi lærte mest, men også krævede mest af os. Timen lå desuden om aftenen. Det sidste fag: Academic Visions: Lectures and Discussions (1) var blot halvanden time hver anden uge (også kun 1 ECTS), hvor forskere kom og præsenterede deres projekter, hvilket var ret spændende. Man bestod ved at stille et spørgsmål. Underviseren var også enorm sød. Overordnet for alle fag er, at præsentationer, aktiv deltagelse og fremmøde er det vigtigste.
unexpected_costs: Offentlig transport er billigt. Man kan få et et 'rejsekort' for 180 zloty i 90 dage med ubegrænset i hele Warszawa, hvis man er på sin bachelor. Det er en smule dyrere på kandidaten - eller hvis man er over 26 år - men, stadig til en god pris. Man kan derudover tage tog med 50% rabat, som bachelor studerende under 26 år.
cost_comparison: Det var ikke nær så billigt at handle i supermarker, som forventet, men stadig billigere. Ellers ikke andet. Alt var billigt og gode priser, som gjorde alt lidt sjovere!
activities_available: Ved ikke.
activities_recommended: Udforsk byen og byerne omkring Warszawa.
weekend_recommendations: Tag til Zakopane! Uden tvivl yndlingsstedet i hele Polen, så så så dejligt. Vi var der både om sommeren og efteråret. En skjult perle. Ellers er Lublin og Lödz en anbefaling, som en endagstur. Krakow er flot, og tag til Auscwitcz, men husk at bestil en guidet tour i flere måneder forinden. Vild oplevelse. Vi besøgte også urskov i Bialowieza, for at se bisonokser, hvilket ikke er en anbefaling. Kaotisk at komme derhen, og ikke værd at se. Ellers er byen, Wroclaw, også enorm hyggelig. Gdansk var også flot, men meget turistet. Byer som: Poznan og Torun ville vi også gerne have nået, hvis vi havde mere tid. Generelt en stor anbefaling at besøge flere byer rundt i Polen. Det er en kæmpe overraskelse, hvor hyggelige deres byer er.
culture_adjustment: Helt fint. Udover polakker ikke er det mest smilende og imødekommene folk, og godt kan være en smule uhøflige, hvis man ikke taler polsk. Ellers nemt nok.
socializing_tips: Det kommer nok an på om det er ens formål, hvilket det ikke var for os. Det nemmeste er nok at bo på skolens dorms, hvor der foregår en masse socialt. Ellers snak til undervisningen. Man får også en del at snakke om, når man har fag med præsentationer, der giver anledning for at være nysgerrige på hinandens kulturer, historier og hverdagsliv og spørge yderligere ind.
cultural_challenges: Polakker kan være svære at danse med, og ikke altid så søde og hjælpsomme. Der er også mange, som ikke snakker engelsk, hvilket godt kan være en udfordring. Der er bestemt også mange enormt rare og søde mennesker i Polen!
culture_appreciated: Polens spændende historie. Det har været virkelig interessant at være del af, når man kommer fra et land som Danmark, hvor historien ikke definerer vores hverdag på samme måde. Polens historie spiller stadig en kæmpe rolle i dagens Polen, som både mærkes hos menneskerne og i det generelle gadebillede.
top3_advice: 1. Hav tålmodighed med systemet. Det kan være virkelig udfordrende og langtrukkent. 2. Tag dig tid til at planlægge dine fag, så du ikke sidder tilbage med en masse krævende eksamener, men kan bruge tid på at være social og opleve byen og vælg fag, så du har mulighed for en forlænget weekend. 3. Udforsk Polen, så meget du kan! Det er et så spændende land med en hel masse skjulte perler. Jeg er blevet helt vild med det efter mit udvekslingsophold!
other_useful_info: Ikke rigtig.
most_rewarding: At opleve en hel masse i et land, som jeg ikke har haft kendskab til. Samtidig med at jeg fik lov til at gøre det med en dejlig veninde. Det kan helt sikkert noget at tage alene afsted og bo på kollegie, men det kan virkelig også noget, at dele oplevelsen med en anden, så energien bliver lagt i oplevelser. Hvilket har været hovedprioriteren for os, og fungeret helt vildt godt.
greatest_challenge: At skulle finde tryghed og opbygge en hverdag man trives i, hvilket viste sig at være markant nemmere end forventet.
other_comments: Tag afsted! Alle glemmer Polen, men det land har så meget potentiale. Mange spændende steder, billigere priser, lækre restauranter og en markant anden kultur end den danske.
