People in the dorms are younger, but being a couple of years older doesn't matter. Go live in dorms. Go to one American football game early on, realise it sucks and then never attend another.
other_useful_info: Dick's bugers is just okay... Don't get fooled by the hype.
most_rewarding: My roommates
greatest_challenge: My roommates

crucial_aspects: I wanted to find professors and researchers doing work in my areas of interest.
info_ease: Everything was fairly easy in that regard. Main issue was signing up for Master's level courses from a university-wide exchange spot, as that is an extremely involved and non-obvious process at University of Washington side
arrival_assistance: I received a welcome tour around the campus from the US side of the exchange. It was also fairly easy to contact the study abroad department on the US side.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It's relatively easy to sign up for bachelors-level (undergrad) courses, as long as you write to the teacher explaining how you fulfill the prerequisites from the courses you already took elsewhere. Registering for anything Masters (400 and 500 level) is borderline impossible. Professors unfortunately have very little say in who gets admited - you are the last in the administrative priority list and any UW student will get in before you every time. You have to fill out special forms for every single one - sending emails to professors is not enough.
registration_help: We could book or pop into a course advisor's office. They are very helpful about figuring out the signup process in general, but dont expect them to make any exceptions in terms of where and when you can signup for courses (thats part of the behind the scenes process)
registration_success: I was lucky enough to find a good research opportunity that I managed to sign up for. If not for that, I would mostly be forced into Bachelor level courses. I managed to get into one strictly Masters level course through the form application I mentioned earlier.
registration_advice: Start filling out forms early. Dont bother writing emails to professors until you get some sort of a response from the form. If you manage to find a professor looking for researchers, sign up - you can get credits for that. The research work is on an exceptionally high level in terms of what you can learn and contribute to.
course_level: As explained in the student advice above - I took one Masters level class in Compilers which was extremely pragmatic, well-explained and useful, although the workload was quite high. I took one Leadership class from Bachelor's level. Rest of my time I did research with PhD students.
teaching_comparison: There is way more workload expected per credit (even if you translate into ECTS). Its much less flexible - at UCPH I was mostly doing projects and learning through those, whilst at UW you will have more traditional homework.
courses_enrolled: Leadership in Theory and Practice; Introduction to Compiler Construction; Data Science for Social Good Seminar; Research and Reading;
recommended_courses: Research at UW is extremely good. My lab mates were very competent PhD students, always on top of the latest publications. Introduction to Compiler Construction was a very informative course. All theory was explained in terms of the homeworks we were doing (which were all part of a single larger project). All necessary knowledge was explained as needed (e.x. you dont have to be a master at Assembly, as all the necessary parts were re-introduced for the project).
unexpected_costs: Nothing out of ordinary
cost_comparison: Dorm "deposit" is non-refundable
activities_available: There were social events happening nearly every day. There is a gym-membership included in Housing Foundation Card (the meal plan). All the sports facilities are exceptional. There are all sorts of sports available (e.x. kayaking, archery, soccer, basketball, swimming)
activities_recommended: Gym is very good. Sign up for archery class (good as a social event), or any other class you are interested in - you will definitely find your favorites.
weekend_recommendations: Try flying around the West Coast if you can afford it. Las Vegas, Vancouver, Texas are all great destinations. There is also a hiking club and student clubs available for socializing.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy, had to wrap my mind around undisclosed sales taxes and tipping culture.
socializing_tips: Sign up for your favorite spot and just pick one of the many widely advertised events that happen constantly.
cultural_challenges: Mostly around the crime rate. There is a lot of crime and drug addicts on the streets. You have to be very careful where you go, especially at night (but unfortunately violent crime also happens in broad daylight). Police will not come, the ambulance most likely neither.
culture_appreciated: People are extremely chatty and open. You can strike up a conversation with anybody on the street at any time - thats the norm, expect others to do the same :) You will easily find people to hang out with at bars and other social gatherings.
top3_advice: Get involved in some organized activities to make friends. Find researchers and professors that are looking for more people - you are no cost to them and will profit immensely from the opportunity. Go out and explore the country - just be careful around the drug addicts in cities.
other_useful_info: Get Amazon Prime - you will get everything you need for day-to-day living there.
most_rewarding: Meeting bright like-minded people who mentored me academically and exploring the beautiful nature of the US.
greatest_challenge: Registering for classes at an appropriate level.

crucial_aspects: Level of education.
info_ease: Things were mostly available through the communication of the university.
arrival_assistance: Online communication and one introduction meeting.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Took place online. Often required contacting professors directly about specifics.
registration_help: The guide given to all students on the registration platform.
registration_success: Very. Only obstacles were overlapping courses.
registration_advice: Invest time in planning. Take the opportunity to explore the catalogue.
course_level: The university I attended (UW) had a numeral structure (100-400) that determined the level of courses. Everything below 300 compared to Danish high school levels and were quite unsatisfying. Everything above 300 compared to Danish university courses, although with more essays and weekly written assignments.
teaching_comparison: Less readings; more writings (essays etc.); in-class discussions; professors often reflected upon material in relation to contemporary politics, which often gave the impression of a partiality and lacking objective, critical approach.
courses_enrolled: Jewish Philosophy. Jewish poetry. MENA Illustrated. Popular Film and The Holocaust. A Tale of Two Cities: Tel Aviv and Jerusalem. Supervised Study with Translation.
recommended_courses: Philosophy courses.
unexpected_costs: Price of certain goods.
cost_comparison: Was given free public transport as included in the program. Social events like concerts were often free or at a very low price.
activities_available: A few events took place for international students the first few weeks. During the semester there was an active program of talks, concerts, exhibitions etc. available for all students.
activities_recommended: Exploring the city. Finding a social group and integrate into their daily lives with everything included (partying, hiking, playing sports etc.)
weekend_recommendations: Night life. Hiking. Sports. Cultural events.
culture_adjustment: Rather easy; American students find foreigners exciting and very interested in showing you their way of life.
socializing_tips: Really just approach someone that seems interesting (e.g. in class) and there is a high chance they will welcome you into their friend group.
cultural_challenges: Age difference.
culture_appreciated: Hospitality.
top3_advice: Make sure to enjoy both the urban sites and the sorrounding natural areas as these are easily available. Cross your social boundaries and make an effort to establish a social circle. Enjoy the on-campus facilities (IMA, concert halls etc.)
other_useful_info: Try and socialize among American students rather than other exchange students if possible.
most_rewarding: Got to experience American university life with everything included.
greatest_challenge: Crossing social boundaries and creating a social network. The first couple of weeks/month can be very lonely.

crucial_aspects: High academic standards, language I was somewhat comfortable with and the opportunity to experience something new
overall_comments: I have nothing but good things to say about the University and Washington State at large, but it was an insane time to live in the US, both politically, and financially. course_level: Most of my courses were BA level, but I took one class at MA level as it looked fun

courses_enrolled: Archeology 101: feeding the world Dynamical systems and chaos Distance and time Mathematical methods in Classical Mechanics Chinese Imperial History 1287-1846 Public Outreach in Astronomy
recommended_courses: Any class with Prof Chris Laws is fantastic, he's a great guy. unexpected_costs: Giving up the meal plan to cook myself and buying kitchen supplies
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive, basic living tools like comforters, blankets and the like was dirt cheap
activities_available: A really great massive gym complex, a lovely bundle of clubs and a blossoming social life.
activities_recommended: Hiking is fantastic in the region, otherwise you can pick and choose based on interest
weekend_recommendations: Go to Canada (I went to British Colombia myself) it is really pretty up there. There is also plenty of things to explore in downtown Seattle and Washington State at large, once again based on interest.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, though I struggled a bit with the current political climate in the US (the university was more aligned with my views, so it is more the country at large that made me feel unsafe)
socializing_tips: Talk to them whenever you get the chance! The only fun you have is the one you make for yourself, and the same goes with social opportunities, you should just dive in head first!!
cultural_challenges: Gun laws
culture_appreciated: Øhm it was a really accepting culture at the university, accepting you regardless of race, culture, sexuality and non-violent worldviews
top3_advice: Be prepared to put on a few kilos unless you cook yourself, grab the chances that arise early on to socialize with the other exchange students as well as the local student, and lastly have fun, even though your surroundings are not always optimal!
other_useful_info: Not at the moment no
most_rewarding: The people I met.
greatest_challenge: The constant feel of unease, caused by a mixed bag of the lax weapon laws in the US, the obvious difference in wealth plain to see on the streets and the political climate that amongst other things targeted scientific research (local student within my field of physics were leaving off scientific terms such as "cis" and "trans" because funding was getting cut based on buzzwords like these

crucial_aspects: University of waterloo is well known for its strong Computer Science department, being the best in Canada and I also wanted to live in Canada.
info_ease: Getting from Toronto airport to waterloo can be done by bus, and then in waterloo you can get a uber or a bus to your accommodation on the day of your arrival.
arrival_assistance: There were some tours showing the university and the different buildings.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There is a website called quest.uwaterloo where you can select the classes.
registration_help: Not much really, on the course website you can find classes you are eligible for.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: If you are a Master student for example I chose 2 computer science classes (my major) and then I chose a non-CS class. I recommend that you try a new class on something that interests you and has a bit lower workload as your exchange is not only about academia. A language class can be fun for example.
course_level: It's a very fast paced environment where you will have many assignments and a research project in most classes. You need to do some reading and definitely spend a lot of time on the assignments as they are supposed to be rather difficult.
teaching_comparison: The teaching was similar, you have a good relationship to the teachers but most of the tutorials were online which could still be because of covid.
courses_enrolled: - Data-Intensive Distributed Computing - Introduction to AI - Italian language class
recommended_courses: I recommend my three classes, I enjoyed the combination of AI, Big data and a complete different class on a language a lot.
unexpected_costs: Mobile phone bills are expensive in Canada. The food is also expensive because of high Tax and Tip
cost_comparison: Transportation was free for students which is great
activities_available: Amazing sports facilities (Many basket ball courts, Badminton, martial arts, full ice ring for hockey, full indoor soccer field, 2 gyms). In addition, you can watch the university teams play against other unis on weekends. There were also many events on campus to take part. You have many food options on campus such as kebab, subway, starbucks inside the buildings.
activities_recommended: I recommend joining an intramural, which is a sports league where you compete against other students on a weekly basis. I did it with squash and met many people and had lots of good games.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend visiting Toronto (2h bus), Montreal (6h train or 1.5h flight), New York (1.5h Flight) and Mexico (4h flight to Cancun).
culture_adjustment: Very easy, the culture is not different from europe
socializing_tips: Engage in sports, go to events in the first weeks and sit next to other students in class to meet new people.
cultural_challenges: There are not as many partys as for example in Denmark. Alcohol can only be bought in liquor stores. But there are no student bars from the uni and generally on campus there is never alcohol. This is not a problem but it was interesting to see the difference.
culture_appreciated: Canadians are generally very friendly and helpful, it was always easy to ask for help when needed.
top3_advice: 1) The sports facility is amazing, make sure to pick some new sports to learn. I started squash and muay thai for example 2) You need to work to pass the classes, this is a rather competitive uni and I had a similar workload to my masters in ucph. 3) Travel around! The grade conversion is Pass / Fail which means you should not aim for 100 and spend all day studying
other_useful_info: I highly recommend to book a trip over reading week, and also to score high points on the first assignments so that you can have less to study in december and travel around.
most_rewarding: Visiting new places and making friends with locals.
greatest_challenge: Balancing traveling and keeping up with classes.

crucial_aspects: Jeg vil bare gerne til et engelsk talende land uden for Europa, og jeg vidste at Canada havde meget smuk natur og var meget multikulturel – derfor endte jeg med Canada

Uddannelsessystemet var også helt anderledes end herhjemme, der er konstant deadlines til midterms, test og opgaver – så det skal man lige lære at junglere Waterloo er ikke den fedeste by, så man skal ret langt væk for at se smuk natur og der er man ret afhængig af at have bil.
info_ease: Ret nemt, der kom mails ud om det ting man skulle vide og der var gratis shuttlebus fra lufthavnen.
arrival_assistance: Der var introdage de første par dage hvor man fik de informationer man skulle bruge – de har også ret mange internationale studerende på Waterloo, så det er nemt at få hjælp.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

unexpected_costs: Da der ikke var så meget at se i Waterloo rejste vi meget rundt i Canada og USA, hvilket betød at vi brugte mange penge på at leje biler og købe flybilletter.
cost_comparison: Det var cirka det samme som i DK måske lidt dyre. Du kunne rejse gratis rundt i Waterloo og Kitchener med dit UWcard
activities_available: De kunne tilbyde en masse forskellige klubber indenfor næsten alle sportsgrene
activities_recommended: Jeg deltog i "learn to skate", hvor man lærte at stå på skøjter, det kostede 60$. Det vil jeg helt klart anbefale, udover at man både skal skaffe skøjter og hjelm selv.
weekend_recommendations: Tag ud og rejs i weekenderne, der sker ikke det store i Waterloo udover fester i "bunkeren" (kælderen i WCRI)...
culture_adjustment: Ret nemt, kulturen minder meget om herhjemme, og Canada er et meget multikulturelt sted.
socializing_tips: Deltag i forskellige klubber!
cultural_challenges: At det er helt normalt at snakke med fremmede
culture_appreciated: FOlk er så søde og hjælpsomme
top3_advice: 1. sommertøj, vi havde 30 grader i flere uger efter vi ankom 2. god vinterjakke og støvler 3. en mini vægt til at veje din kuffert når du engang skal hjem og har købt alverdens ting
other_useful_info: Spring ud i det, og husk at der er en masse udvekslingstuderende i præcis samme situation som dig, og lad vær med at brug al tiden på at studere!
most_rewarding: Alle de internationale kontakter man fik.
greatest_challenge: At balancere skole og venner

crucial_aspects: It was crucial that my destination was English speaking, and had a broad variety of courses within my field of interest.
info_ease: Before leaving for Australia there was a zoom meeting with the study abroad/exchange programme at UWA where a lot of information was explained and you could ask questions. These people were also very good at responding to emails throughout the process. Upon arrival, there was an info meeting in orientation week with a further introduction to Australia, Perth, UWA and the people who we could contact in case of problems with anything.
arrival_assistance: See above
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: First you apply for the units you are interested in - apply for more than 4 just in case some are not approved. After arriving in Australia I got access to an online timetable application. In the application you add the 4 units you would like and then the app shows you what your timetable would look like. You can add/remove/change units to figure out what timetable works best for you. After you are done you apply for that timetable. In some units there is flexibility to choose alternative days for labs/tutorials or an online options for lectures in case you have some timetable clashes.
registration_help: The student central and the different faculties on campus were very helpful.
registration_success: I was approved for 7 units and then I choose the 4 that fit best together in my timetable.
registration_advice: If you are in doubt, just message them, they are very kind and quick to respond.
course_level: I had two third-year units and one second-year unit that were of similar difficulty to UCPH, and I had one first-year unit (Active leadership) which was very chill and fun.
teaching_comparison: Lectures and labs were very similar, but one thing that was quite different was the continual assessments - every lab and assignment counts 2-15% of your final grade. There are also mid-semester test which count 20-30% of the grade.
courses_enrolled: GENE3340 - Molecular Genetics II MICR2209 - Intro to Infect Diseases & Immunology NEUR3301 - Advanced Neuroscience 1 SSEH1104 - Active Leadership 1: Dev. Leader. Skills
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed all of my courses, especially GENE3340. Mark and Belinda who run the unit are super nice and helpful and every other week they held an extra lecture for those interested where they discussed articles within the field of molecular genetics.
unexpected_costs: Eating out and drinks are very expensive in Australia, but in a residental college all meals are included.
cost_comparison: Food and drinks are very expensive.
activities_available: Trinity residential college offer activities every week - including themed dinners, gallas, fund-raiser, inter-college sports, and trips to local attractions. Especially during orientation week, there were several activities every day. At uni there were also heaps of free opportunities for exchange students like free gym memberships (for 1 month), new sports opportunities (beginners squash, tennis, swimming, and others) 6 weeks for free), trips to the zoo and aquarium for all exchange students during orientation week.
activities_recommended: All of the above
weekend_recommendations: Buy a second-hand car (2000-3000$) or befriend someone with a car and do heaps of weekend trips! there are so many beautiful places around Perth but the public transport is not great. I bought a car with two friends and sold it again after the semester we sold for 300$ that what we bought it for. Kalbarri, Karijini, Exmouth, Margret River, Esperance, Denmark, Albany, and the Pinnacles - just some of the beautiful places within reach of Perth!
culture_adjustment: The people were super nice an friendly, which made it very easy to adjust.
socializing_tips: Go to as many events and free trips during orientation week as possible. You will meet many people which makes the exchange experience a lot better.
cultural_challenges: It takes a week or two to adjust to speaking English 24/7 and the jetlag does not help;) but after that you quickly adjust.
culture_appreciated: The beautiful nature of Australia and the great effort the Australians make to honour the aboriginal land and culture. For example - every lecture at UWA starts with an acknowledgement of country (just a 30 second thing)
top3_advice: 1) The semester is shorter (only 12 weeks) and therefore more intense than at UCPH 2) The campus is quite big, so I would recommend getting a bike (there are free bikes at Trinity) 3) All exams and tests are on paper, even essays
other_useful_info: There is a lot of help to get at UWA, so don't be afraid to ask. As a student, you can get a lot of help for free like a uni mentor, a chat with a counsellor, a therapy dog visit every Wednesday, and a great study environment. There are several libraries and big grass areas and cafes to study on campus.
most_rewarding: Completing a full semester in a second language, while still having a great time and exploring the beautiful state of WA on the weekends.
greatest_challenge: Finding a good balance between during well in my units and also enjoying my time and exploring Western Australia. It takes a while to settle into a new routine, but once I figured out what worked for me I could really enjoy the experience.

crucial_aspects: I chose to go to UWA in Perth, Australia because they offer a lot of relevant environmental units. The units offers some perspectives on environmental issues that can't be found in the unit handbook at Copenhagen University. Additionally, the weather is nice in Australia and it is nice that they speak English (it makes both social and academic life a lot easier).
info_ease: Quite easy. They have a welcoming week at UWA when you arrive - where they are good at giving information. It is also possible to communicate with UWA's global learning office through email and facebook before arriving in AUS.
arrival_assistance: They helped me find accommodation through email before arriving. Also, they gave a good introduction to everything throughout the welcome week (first week in AUS).
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: They have a system that works fine. So just look through their unit handbook and register through the portal (that they'll help you access). In general, the global learning office guides you through everything.
registration_help: Whatever help is needed :)
registration_success: I registered for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: You might need to have a backup plan with extra units if the timetables clash - but the GLO can help.
course_level: The workload is bigger but I found the level a bit lower.
teaching_comparison: The workload is bigger because you're assessed throughout the semester (how depends on the units). I found the level a bit lower but I had to prepare for classes a lot more because I was assessed on participation in some of my units. Also, I had fewer classes a week than at UCPH - so more time was spent on making assignments and preparing for class.
courses_enrolled: Environmental History Environmental Policy and Planning Understanding Global Politics Culture, Ecologies, Extinction: Environment and Society in a Time of Crisis
recommended_courses: Environmental History was very interesting and the teacher Joseph was very good. Also, the unit style was like a workshop with discussions - it was therefore a good opportunity to talk to other students. Description from the unit: "What factors have shaped human dealings with the natural world? How have people changed the environment? And how have different societies responded to environmental change over time? These are the questions at the heart of this unit, which offers an introduction to the flourishing field of environmental history."
unexpected_costs: None unexpected really. I ended up purchasing a car with two other girls which has been amazing. It is quite expensive to rent one and very cheap to buy one (we just sold it for more than we bought it for).
cost_comparison: Food is very expensive and alcohol is crazy expensive. Also, my housing was quite expensive (but that can be done cheaper).
activities_available: There were some trips at the beginning for international students. They had a lot of sports that were possible to join (also, some for free for international students).
activities_recommended: Join as much as you can comprehend. Have a look at the active lifestyle program it offers multiple sports for free for international students.
weekend_recommendations: Western Australia is amazing. Go to Exmouth or Margaret River if you get the chance.
culture_adjustment: Australian culture is not that different to Danish - so that wasn't difficult. Also, Australians are more outgoing and easy to talk to.
socializing_tips: Australians don't seem to go to uni to make friends, to be honest... So It is not like an "American-College-Experience". If you wanna socialize with local students I'd recommend you to live at a residential college.I got a job at a bakery and socialized with people from work - which was a really great experience for me. I'd definitely recommend that as well - you're allowed to work 40 hours every second week with a student visa.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really.
culture_appreciated: Australians are very chill and outgoing.
top3_advice: - Bring more clothes than you think - the winter is longer than you think - Go to the beach as much as possible and enjoy that the sun always sets over the ocean - Double R at campus has really good coffee :)) (Australia in general has great (cheap) coffee and nice bakeries - so take advantage of that
other_useful_info: Pica bar in CBD is great. Also, Miller and Baker (the place I worked) has rye bread!!
most_rewarding: Being on your own in a country so far away is very rewarding. I think I've learned a lot from being independent. Also, the units I've taken were very rewarding because they gave me some interesting new perspectives on human-environment relationships. I think they've helped me come up with an idea for my bachelor's thesis.
greatest_challenge: Going home again and leaving Perth.

crucial_aspects: The units UWA offered and the possibility of living on my own. (No college dorms)
info_ease: Very easy. The orientation team at my uni sent out a lot of information (emails) before arrival, so I knew what to expect. I also got a uni-mentor, which is a student who will help you with any questions you might have throughout the semester.
arrival_assistance: We had orientation week (the first week) and they had scheduled a lot of activities so felt like I got to meet people and see campus right away. However, you did not have to participate in everything, so it was totally fine to stay home or by yourself if that felt right. There was no pressure at all to participate.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Orientation week gave you information about units, deadlines, schedules and other free services offered at campus.
registration_help: SESA and Exchange and Study Abroad advisers were there to help with any questions throughout the semester.
registration_success: I got all the units that I wanted from the beginning. My impression was, that everyone studying abroad got their preferred units.
registration_advice: Ask questions if there is anything you are unsure about. There is always someone available to help you.
course_level: I took level 1 units (BA 1. year) even though I was a 3. year student. The level were quite easy and there was a lot of introductory classes such as essay writing, referencing and such. But it was all right since UWA use a different reference style than UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Everything is different in terms of grades. They use marks in Australia and you are given marks throughout the semester that eventually will make up your final mark (your grade). You are given participation marks in most units which will be 10% of your final mark. The teaching is therefore very different since they take attendance and expect you to be prepared for every tutorial (class). Lectures are quite similar to UCPH but do not expect a lot of students to attend the lectures since that is the only time they do not take attendance. There was a lot of assignments throughout the semester which was not something I expected. But teachers are so nice and will help you with just about anything if you ask.
courses_enrolled: MGMT1135 Organisational Behaviour MKTG1203 Introduction to Marketing MGMT1136 Management and Organisations COMM1002 Cultures, New Media and Communications
recommended_courses: It really depends on what you are interested in and currently studying. I really enjoyed COMM1002 because it had a creative aspect where we got to work in Photoshop.
unexpected_costs: Fees when using my Danish creditcard. Be aware of this when you use your Danish creditcard. I opened an Australian bank account to avoid the fees, which is free and you can very easily transfer money from your Danish account to your Australian.
cost_comparison: Uber rides are very cheap. And so is public transport. On your first day on Orientation week you can go to The Guild Village on campus and buy a Smartrider (Rejsekort). You will automatically get a student discount and cheaper fares in general throughout your stay.
activities_available: All different clubs and social events. Music, sports, hobbies, specific interests such as Harry Potter, photography, religion, law, political clubs etc.
activities_recommended: UWA has a theme every week throughout the semster. One week is pride week, another week is sustainability week. There are tons of events on and off campus which is mostly free events and lots of opportunities to help out or join. Lots of talks, concerts and other events too.
weekend_recommendations: Fremantle is located 30 min with train from Perth and has the best market on weekends. Also the beaches in Fremantle are amazing.
culture_adjustment: Very similar to the Danish culture. So very easy.
socializing_tips: If you live with Australian students then you will know them and their friends. Australians are very laidback people and will take you anywhere (like their friends' parties). In my experience people will host parties or get togethers all the time. Also connecting with other international students are a great way to meet people.
cultural_challenges: Don't think too much about who is buying what. Australians are likely to buy you a drink/beer/food without expecting you to pay them back. This is in my opinion very different to the Danish culture. Also get used to strange haircuts, people walking barefoot in the street and using Australian slang that you are not quite sure what means. Everyone is so friendly and happy, so just don't think too much.
culture_appreciated: The casual, laidback culture and everyone is asking you how you are doing ALL THE TIME :-)
top3_advice: 1. Don' spend too much time overthinking what you say and do (and not do). 2. Use your studentcard for discounts at cafes, restaurants and stores 3. Wear sunscreen everyday
other_useful_info: There are a lot of events and social things going on at campus everyday. Don't stress yourself about attending everything. That is impossible. Remember to listen to yourself.
most_rewarding: Completing a semester abroad. This has always been a dream of mine, and I feel very good about my decision.
greatest_challenge: Living by myself in a new place. You spend a lot of time by yourself and that can be daunting at times.
other_comments: Enjoy your stay and remember to make it your own. Do what feels right and don't feel like you have to attend every party or social event if you are not up for it.

crucial_aspects: I wanted an English-speaking country and I have always wanted to go to Australia
info_ease: Pretty easy. I had a few issues but I emailed UWA and they were very helpful! KU was not the best but that is just typical KU
arrival_assistance: I swapped a few units and they helped with that. That was no problem.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You just choose the units you want. This is done on their website. However, because I accidentally saved before actually choosing any units, the page was locked. I had to email UWA to let them know what units I wanted. It was easy but still a bit annoying.
registration_help: Email
registration_success: I got all the units I wanted
registration_advice: Find units that sound interesting. You can always change once you are at uni. This must be done during the first week but they tell you that. Many other internationals recommended one of my units, so it is worth talking to other people about your choices.
course_level: I only chose first-year courses and electives. They were all easy except for my phycology unit. But that was due to the fact that I have never done a lab report. I struggled a bit with the scientific aspect of that unit.
teaching_comparison: They value participation more and you are marked on the basis of that. "Introduction to Indigenous Heritage and Knowledge" was different from the other units because they wanted the seminars to be like a conversation. But that was interesting to try. The last half of "Cultures, New Media, and Communications" was online. I did not particularly like that aspect because it meant that we had to write on a discussion board inline several times a week.
courses_enrolled: Active Leadership (SSEH1104) Boodjar Moort Katitjin: Introduction to Indigenous Heritage and Knowledge (INDG1160) Cultures, New Media, and Communications (COMM 1002) Psychology: Behaviour in Context (PSYC1102)
recommended_courses: Active Leadership and Boodjar Moort Katitjin: Introduction to Indigenous Heritage and Knowledge were good. They did not require much work which is perfect when you are on exchange. And they were interesting. In active leadership, you have to choose between kayaking, stand-up paddling and mountain biking. You then learn about leadership in relation to the chosen activity.
unexpected_costs: Not really any
cost_comparison: Food is expensive. Fruit, vegetables, and meat from the supermarket are expensive. And alcohol is so expensive. I drank a lot of beer and you can easily pay 80-100 for a six-pack. Public transportation is cheap.
activities_available: I joined the gym which was nice.
activities_recommended: Go on the trips that uni arranges. You can meet many people through that.
weekend_recommendations: Go on small trips with your new friends. I did not do that much but I enjoyed my weekends in Perth hanging out with my roommates. There is a study break in September where many people went north to Exmouth or Karijini National Park. I went with a group to Exmouth which was fun. However, I mostly did it because I had fomo. I was not really in the mood for a trip so maybe consider that. After the semester, me and a friend from uni went on a road trip down South all the way to Esperance and spent 6 weeks doing that. I preferred to go on a big road trip in the end and then spent most of my time in Perth and close around, but everyone is different.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Everyone is so friendly and inclusive
socializing_tips: Do what you want to do. If you find yourself in a group of people that feels off, go find some other people. There are many internationals and you can easily find your kind of people.
cultural_challenges: They drink a lot! And they go hard when they party.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness. And the inclusiveness.
top3_advice: Do what you want to do. Do not feel pressured to do what other people do. Do it at your own pace. Other than that, just enjoy your time and see this as an opportunity to experience a different life and meet new people.
other_useful_info: Housing is expensive and a challenge. Beer is ridiculously expensive.
most_rewarding: Meeting my roommates and the group of international students that I ended up becoming friends with.
greatest_challenge: Not really any challenges. When I arrived, I was a bit stressed and anxious about the housing situation but it worked out well. And if you have a partner at home, it can be hard, if you are not in a good and healthy relationship.
other_comments: Enjoy your time. And make it your own. And it is pretty cold in Perth. Even at the end of October and November. Colder than you think. Bring jeans, long-sleeved shirts and jackets. The houses are not good in the winter and it can be pretty cold inside.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience new culture and nature and get a different setting from what I am used to back home in Denmark. So, it was not only for the academic aspect I chose to go to Perth, but also for the personal experience and testing my own boundaries.
overall_comments: I loved it!! At first you had to get into it and get to know the others. And the weather was really terrible in the beginning. But after 1-2 months everything fell into place and I have met the nicest people and experienced what Western Australia has to offer - which is a lot.
info_ease: I was quite easy and they were very helpful when you wrote to the university (UWA) regarding any questions.
arrival_assistance: There is a intro week for all the exchange students, so you get to meet all the others who are in the same boat as you - thus it becomes easier to adjust and know what to do.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I loved it!! At first you had to get into it and get to know the others. And the weather was really terrible in the beginning. But after 1-2 months everything fell into place and I have met the nicest people and experienced what Western Australia has to offer - which is a lot.
registration_process: They send you all the info and everything you need to do - so that is quite easy.
registration_help: You can write to either the University in Copenhagen or the one you are going on exchange to - both are very helpful.
registration_success: I had a bit of trouble getting the right conversion from the class in UWA to UCPH, because I took some classes which were the same as Micro and Macro 3 in Denmark. But when I wrote UCPH again, they changed it so I could get merit for it. But I got every class I wanted at UWA.
registration_advice: Read the unit outlines of the classes as it helps a lot with choosing which ones to choose.
academics_comments: I loved it!! At first you had to get into it and get to know the others. And the weather was really terrible in the beginning. But after 1-2 months everything fell into place and I have met the nicest people and experienced what Western Australia has to offer - which is a lot.
course_level: Felt a bit lower than in Copenhagen, but it was good.
teaching_comparison: It was more like high school, which was a bit annoying as I enjoy the self study method in Denmark. And at UWA everything you do during the semester is going to reflect in your grade, as the assignments also count in the final grade - not just the actual exam.
courses_enrolled: Applied Macroeconomic Money, Banking and Financial Markets Game Theory and Strategic Thinking Environmental Economics
recommended_courses: I really liked them all actually - except the environmental economics, but I think that is just because it isn't my cup of tea.
unexpected_costs: Australia is very expensive in general, so just the cost of groceries and other necessities were quite a chok.. just as pricey if not more pricey than Copenhagen.
cost_comparison: everything, but coffee and public transport is cheap - and cars are cheap
activities_available: many clubs and sports are available
activities_recommended: joining some beginners sports which they offer exchange students is fun
weekend_recommendations: buy a car and go on weekend trips and to the beach every time you can! It really pays of and you can sell it again afterwards.
culture_adjustment: quite easy. Australians are so nice
socializing_tips: get a job
cultural_challenges: there are a lot of crazy people approaching you on the streets ://
culture_appreciated: the nature and the nice people
top3_advice: Get a job so you get to know Australians as you mostly get to know other exchange students at uni, buy a car so you can go on many roadtrips and bring warm clothes as it is colder than you expect in july/august/september
other_useful_info: what I mentioned above is the most important
most_rewarding: the friends I have made and the experiences we have created together in Perth and on our trips
greatest_challenge: sometimes you have slumps and miss people at home, but it will go up and down - and mostly up!
other_comments: enjoy and have fun - school is important but the experiences made outside of school are the ones I will remember! And say yes to everything

crucial_aspects: I love to travel and have always wanted to go to Australia so what better opportunity than exchange? I actually thought I would prefer being on the east coast but I am so happy that I got to go to Western Australia even though it was not my first priority. I really think that this part of Australia is so underrated and has so much to offer and explore which for me was very important.
info_ease: UWA was really good at passing on information and it was easy to navigate the website to find what you needed. If by chance you could not find it every member of the study abroad team was super helpful and fast at replying.
arrival_assistance: There were an orientation week for all the exchange students before uni strat. Here we got a ton of important information like how to navigate campus, use lms (the same as canvas), where to find information and got to ask questions if we had any. There were arranged some "team building"-"get to know each other"- activities during the day time which were nice but not really anything to expand our social life after school-hours (unless you were a collage resident).
arrival_comments: Overall orientation was good but I would have loved if they had arranged some evening/night activities as well.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: I can't really remember it in detail to be honest but it was just to follow the steps online and fill in the appropriate information. And if you had any questions it was easy to contact the study abroad team and get help.
registration_help: The study abroad team <3 I send them a ton of mails with every little problem/question and they never failed to help me or fix the problems for me.
registration_success: I was very successful with registering for classes. I got all of my first priorities except the ones that I was not eligible for. As a bachelor student, you are not allowed to enrol in any master unit and as an exchange student from KU, you are not allowed to take any units at the school of medicine which is nice to know when looking at units.
registration_advice: Look at the timetable for the units when choosing what you want to choose. This can help you avoid too many schedule clashes and is also a great way to choose units that will give you a desirable schedule so you can avoid mandatory classes Friday afternoon if you are planning a weekend trip somewhere (just nice to have in mind).
course_level: I choose 3 first-year units and only 1 third-year unit so as a third-year student the level was lower than back home.
teaching_comparison: All the lectures were recorded and uploaded so you do not really have to show up in person at any point if you do not want to. However, most of the units have tutorials which are either mandatory or your participation will be a part of your assessment and count in your final grade. Throughout the semester you will have tests, assignments etc. which are a part of your assessment too so it is a bit important to be aware of this. For most units, you will have been through around 50% of your assessment before the final exam which means that the exam only counts 50% of your final score. So if you do well during the semester you can be lucky to pass the units before the exam or only have to score a small amount of points on the exam which is nice when you have multiple to study for.
courses_enrolled: Neuroscience in society (NEUR1001), Advanced Neuroscience 1 (NEUR3301), Drugs that changed the world (PHAR1101), Active leadership 1: Developing leadership skills (SSEH1104)
recommended_courses: I would recommend Active leadership 1: Developing leadership skills. This is not a unit where you get academically challenged (at all) but this is a great unit to actually get some friends in school and have fun with other exchange students as well as the locals. It is more like a "sports science unit" based on teamwork and leadership techniques challenged in group dynamics during task solving on a mountain bike, a paddleboard or in a kayak.
unexpected_costs: I bought a car which of course give some unexpected costs like insurance, registration, mechanic bills and gas,
cost_comparison: The price of vegetables is really depending on the season. A cucumber costed 20dkk the first months but ended up being more like 5-10dkk at the end of the semester. Everything organic was crazy expensive as well and some of the fruits like grapes were just expensive all the time (75-100 dkk/pr kg).
activities_available: At UWA sport it was possible to play tennis, squash, and volleyball, do stand-up paddleball or join the gym. At the gym you could also do yoga-, zumba-, cross-fit- and other classes. There was also an outdoor pool at the university which you could be a member card to and use in the opening hours. One time the school's Electronic Music Appreciation Club arranged a festival/concert/party-thing called eclipse which was pretty fun. We found the event on Facebook so maybe there would have been more things like that if we knew where to look but I am not sure.
activities_recommended: Find a friend and take them to some of the UWA sports activities. It is kind of nice to have something to do together with some of the other exchange students as well even though it is not so, thing crazy. You can also join some of the gym classes or just rent out a squash court every now and then. I also met a girl who signed up for a ceramic class every Wednesday (not anything connected to UWA tho) which sounded really fun.
weekend_recommendations: Buy a car/rent a car and drive as far up and down as you can. I really enjoyed the coastal way and towns up til Exmouth (north) and down south around Albany and Denmark. The nature is so beautiful and diverse in Western Australia, it is amazing! I have been told that Karijini National Park should be incredible but I did not have the time to go there as it is far from Perth.
culture_adjustment: All the Australians are so nice so it was pretty easy.
socializing_tips: From my experience, most of the local students don't really go to school to find friends. A lot of them have friends from high school, work etc. and when you don't follow all the same units it can be hard to really connect. They are all very friendly but it is easier to connect with the other exchange students. If you want some local friends I would recommend finding a job or renting a room in a shared house where you can have Australian roomies.
cultural_challenges: Nothing I can think of.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated how nice the Australians are. Everyone is super helpful and I especially member when I was travelling in the mid-semester break when two guys offered to help us get some air out of our tiers so we could go to this really nice snorkel spot and also showed us the way there.
top3_advice: 1. Bring some warm clothes and a rain jacket! Even though it is Australia and Perth you arrive in winter which means a lot of rain and cold weather. 2. It is really great to have a car in Western Australia so check out Facebook marketplace and find a good deal. 3. If you think you are gonna struggle financially it is pretty fun to get a job (depending on what of course). You will get to meet some fun local people who can show you the best places in Perth AND the service jobs plays pretty well so it is a win/win. (The others were a lot of practical things so I will add one more: 4. Say yes! This is a time when you get the opportunity to experience so many incredible things and sometimes it is important to get out of your comfort zone and go on a road trip with some of your new friends or join a fun club. Even if it seems a bit hard and scary it will be worth it in the end.)
other_useful_info: No, I think I covered most of it
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of this experience was the friendships and memories I made. I have had so many incredible moments that I will never forget and it was really rewarding to get out of my comfort zone and just take the experience a day at a time.
greatest_challenge: I think the greatest challenge was that it was nothing like I thought. It is important to acknowledge that the exchange-experience is really hard to imagine before you are living it. It might not be as you expected but for me, it ended up being even more and giving me a greater outcome than the semester I had expected.

crucial_aspects: One of my best friends went on exchange to Australia when she was 15 and has felt ever since that it's been her second home. It's been a motivation for me since then to visit the place that means so much to one of my closest. Additionally, I've spoken to several friends and family friends who've visited the west and east coast of Australia, telling me how the west coast is much less touristy, un-spoiled, and has so much beautiful nature. I come from a small town in Denmark and have always appreciated nature, water, open spaces, chill vibes and people. And I'm not much of a big city person so Perth and the authentic west coast was very appealing to me. I looked up universities on the west coast and found that UWA had several units I found very interesting, so everything worked out.
info_ease: Very easy. Everything was available online but if anything was unclear or difficult to find I found that everyone I asked was very eager to help.
arrival_assistance: A well-organized orientation week with plenty of opportunities to ask for any help you might need. Guides to online access to everything you needed to know, unit enrollment, schedule management etc. was provided throughout the week, and you were familiarized with several orientation week organizers whom you could ask anything.
arrival_comments: Some of the content during the orientation week was a bit unnecessary but overall it was a great way to meet other international students and definitely worth attending.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had to enroll in units online which was super easy. Afterwards you had to make your own schedule which was quite nice since you can just plan your week like you want to.
registration_help: Online guides, staff from the orientation week and at the office on campus, and you could also just send an e-mail.
registration_success: Completely. I originally wanted two units which I was denied but when I talked to one of the coordinators from the orientation week I was accepted into the units anyways. Super easy!
registration_advice: Just ask around if you have any questions, everyone's eager to help!
course_level: Generally a bit easier than units at UCPH, I'd say. But the workload during the semester was definitely heavier since there were continuous assessment, quizzes, mid-semester exams etc. which made it a lot more stressful compared to UCPH. But this also forced you to keep up with the curriculum which was quite nice and made the study break for final exams lighter.
teaching_comparison: It was quite different due to the continuous assessments, and in general it was much more high school-like since students are also graded on class participation which really removes the 'self-study' component that most students from UCPH are used to. I didn't really like it but some people do. However, this also made the teachers more engaged and 'personal' than back home which was really nice.
courses_enrolled: PATH5151 Molecular Pathology, PATH5131 Anatomical Pathology, APHB5503 Neuroendocrinology, SSEH1104 Active Leadership (SUP)
recommended_courses: If you're interested in diagnostics, both molecular pathology and anatomical pathology are quite nice. I especially enjoyed the lab work in anatomical pathology where we made our own slide sections and histology stainings. These are only offered to master's students though. The content of neuroendocrinology was super interesting but the teaching was a bit unstructured, unfortunately. The final essay was a nice wrap up for the unit contents but this unit is also only offered to master's students. Active leadership is an undergrad unit which was super easy and a great way to meet new people. The workload was super light and it was super fun to do stand up paddleboarding (you could chose kayaking or mountainbiking as well) and all you had to do was to solve some challenges within your team. Highly recommend this unit to also be able to focus more on other units and to give yourself a break during the week.
unexpected_costs: I bought a car with three other Danish girls. We got one really cheap ($2000) on Facebook Marketplace but a car comes with quite a lot of expenses, e.g. just the gas! However, this was the best buy I made while I was in Perth.
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive than expected. Coffee was super cheap compared to Copenhagen so I ended up spending much more money on coffee than back home but it was a really nice luxury!
activities_available: Free introduction courses for different sports were offered to international students, as well as 1 month for free at the gym on campus. However, the introduction sessions were during the 'school day' so I always had classes. We heard a lot about different clubs but it didn't really seem like it was something that people actually made use of which was a shame. And it was quite difficult to join a sports team, nobody could tell me how to join a volleyball team even though I asked several different people.
activities_recommended: Don't really know.
weekend_recommendations: Buy a car (if you're staying the entire semester, otherwise rent one for a weekend) and go on heaps of roadtrips and explore WA, that's what makes the whole thing worth it!
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Australians are super friendly and welcoming in general.
socializing_tips: Staying at the colleges is probably the best way, or maybe being very consistent in making an effort to speak to local students at uni. It's not very common for students in Australia to make friends at uni since most people hang out with their friends from middle/high school!
cultural_challenges: Maybe the fact that Australians don't make friends at uni very often. However, the international students were very eager to make friends and if you're open to it you can definitely make some friends for life at uni, most likely just not the locals.
culture_appreciated: The people. I love the people. And I love how multicultural Perth is and how there's room for everyone everywhere. The Australian way of everyone just being kind, open-minded, welcoming, thoughtful, and super polite. I felt that it motivated me to act in the same way and always just lifted my mood. Meeting so many different people have definitely been the best part of my exchange stay.
top3_advice: Be mindful of the continuous assessments for better and for worse - it's gonna help you out in the end even though it might be stressful during the semester. Be openminded - ask around for which ever questions you might have, be open to meeting new people. Buy a car!
other_useful_info: The weather in Perth was not as I (or any other exchange students) expected. It was very rainy for almost the entire semester, especially the first months. Two pairs of long pants was not enough. They told us that the weather wasn't usually like that but I don't know if I believe them! I'd say to not count on the weather to be summer-like until the end of the semester. Bring a raincoat and an umbrella, it'll come in handy. Of course there are sunny days as well but I was definitely expecting there to be many more sunny days from the beginning.
most_rewarding: Being overwhelmed by so many new impressions but still finding a balance between uni, figuring out who was my people and who were just nice acquaintances, keeping up with the continuous assessments but also wanting to go on roadtrips every chance that I got, adjusting to a new city and always trying to get the most of every experience, but also needing to take a breather at times. And having said this, traveling along the entire west coast in our car, especially down south, with everything this included has definitely been what made my exchange stay so fantastic. Spending so much time with these people in the car, exploring the beautiful nature, meeting so many interesting people.
greatest_challenge: Finding a balance. I found that I had to be very aware of when I was challenged in a good way and when I was too overwhelmed by everything, especially during the first month with new impressions and during periods at uni with many deadlines. But this was also part of what made it all worth it. Talk to people about what you're experiencing, most of them will feel the same way or at least be able to relate and understand!
other_comments: Go-go-go on exchange, it's the best decision I've ever made. And if you appreciate beautiful nature and quiet spaces, Perth and WA is the place to be. It's the most beautiful place I've ever visited. Sunsets in Perth just hits differently (and you can't watch the sunset on the east coast:))!

crucial_aspects: Der var andre gode kitesurfere, så jeg kunne træne samtidig med at jeg fortsatte min uddannelse.
overall_comments: Perth er et fantastisk sted.
info_ease: Nemt. Der er god service på UWA. De har ansatte der udelukkende tager sig af study abroad studerende. De svarer på mails samme dag man har sendt dem.
arrival_assistance: Fik hjælp til hvordan jeg skulle indskrive mig på mine valgte fag.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Perth er et fantastisk sted.
registration_process: Totalt nemt, fleksibelt og god service. Man kan ombestemme sig op til en uge efter at semesteret er startet.
registration_help: Drop in and mail.
registration_success: Fik alle units jeg ville have.
registration_advice: Don't worry
academics_comments: Perth er et fantastisk sted.
course_level: Havde ét 1. års fag, ét 2. års fag og to 3. års fag.
teaching_comparison: Der var ikke plads til lige så meget fordybning som på KU. Vi lærte meget om mange emner, men det var overfladisk. Mere kontakt med professoren. Færre timer på uni, men også mindre arbejde helt generelt.
courses_enrolled: Environmental Economics, Game Theory and Strategic Thinking, Applied Macroeconomics og Derivative Products and Markets
recommended_courses: Hvis du er polit-studerende skal du helt klart have "Game Theory and Strategic Thinking" og "Applied Macroeconomics". De giver merit for mikro 3 og makro 3. Environmental Economics giver merit for prioriteret valgfag. Til sidst vil jeg anbefale faget "Active Leadership". Mange af de andre udvekslingsstuderende havde det, og det er det nemmeste i verden. Man kan vælge mellem at cykle, ro i kajak eller stå på stand up paddle.
unexpected_costs: Fik kun visa til slut December, men ville gerne blive her til Januar, så skal købe nyt visa til 2000kr.
cost_comparison: Priserne er sikkert også steget i DK, men alt er dyrt hernede. Den billigste kasse øl koster 200 kr. og mad er også dyrt. Benzin er billigt (7,5kr/literen), og det selvom vi er midt i en energikrise. Det er også billigt at spise ude.
activities_available: Alt tænkeligt. Festerne på uni er til gengæld elendige. Nattelivet i Perth er heller ikke imponerende. Jeg havde de sjoveste aftener i Fremantle.
activities_recommended: Tennis fordi de har gode faciliteter.

other_comments: I can definetely recommend UWA to students who study natural science!

crucial_aspects: I have always wanted to go to Australia. Of the available possible partner universities I found UWA to be the most intriguing one due to its location in Perth. I was intrigued by the remoteness of Perth (it is the world's most isolated metropole) and the city's access to beautiful beaches as well as the close by Rottnest Island ("Rotto").
overall_comments: It has been one of the most transforming experience of my life. I have learned so much about the world and thereby also about myself.
info_ease: UWA was very good at informing and guiding exchange students.
arrival_assistance: Courses, guided walks, emailed information etc.
arrival_comments: It was good.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It has been one of the most transforming experience of my life. I have learned so much about the world and thereby also about myself.
registration_process: To be honest, I do not remember it all that well. I remember that I had to supply information on courses passed at my home university. Then based on this information it was assessed whether or not I was allowed to study a given course at my host university. I remember the assessment being quite strict with several of my requested courses being denied.
registration_help: The information in the application portal.
registration_success: As said, somewhat unsuccessful. But I did expect rejection on some of them though.
registration_advice: You're allowed to apply for a total of 8 courses. I will recommend that you apply for all 8 courses in case some of your requests are denied.
academics_comments: It has been one of the most transforming experience of my life. I have learned so much about the world and thereby also about myself.
course_level: I study comparative literature at UCPH and hence did English courses at UWA. The overall academic level was lower at UWA with discussions being less theoretical than what I was used to. I did not mind this at all, however.
teaching_comparison: I much preferred the teaching style of UWA. Lectures were 1 hour, tutorials were 1,5 hours compared to 2 and 3 hours respectively at UCPH. Furthermore student assessment was based partially on classroom participation which made sure that most of the class was engaged compared to UCPH where assessment is not based on classroom participation wherefore there will often only be a couple of students actively participating at the seminar.
courses_enrolled: Great Moments in Art (HART1000) Netflicks: Cinema and Long-Form Television (ENGL2401) Romanticism and Revolution (ENGL2604) Shakespeare: Page, Stage, Screen (ENGL3602)
recommended_courses: All of the above.
unexpected_costs: Alcohol is really expensive in Australia and Western Australia in particular.
cost_comparison: Alcohol.
activities_available: They had everything and all sports.
activities_recommended: Whatever you're into.
weekend_recommendations: Explore as much of Perth and Western Australia and the Rest of Australia as possible. It is a magnificent place!!
culture_adjustment: Easy. Australians, and people from Perth in particular, are easygoing, pragmatic, and have a good sense of humor.
socializing_tips: Talk to them about sports. They love their sports in Australia. In Western Australia they prefer footy (AFL) to rugby (NRL).
cultural_challenges: I know its a controversial thing to say but sometimes I did not feel comfortable around the indigenous (aboriginal) population. I had some bad encounters with people trying to pick a fight. But I did also meet some really nice, funny, and passionate aboriginal people, so I don't want to generalize.
culture_appreciated: The beach-culture. Australians is a coastal people like the Danes. They love their beaches, their surfing, their swimming, their boating, their sunrises and sunsets. It's very endearing.
top3_advice: 1. In Perth, they are very strict with alcohol 2. If you want to see the South Western Australia (Margaret River, Albany, Esperance etc.) make sure to go during the Australian summer, when the weather is good (October - March), cause you can always see the Northern parts of Australia during the Australian winter. 3. Check out Rottnest Island.
other_useful_info: Get a "Transperth" Card as soon as possible - it's basically a rejsekort for Perth. Get the Uber app.
most_rewarding: Seeing the country and forming friendships with people from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: Nothing really...
other_comments: Go for it, you're gonna love it!

crucial_aspects: I wanted something with new environments and nature to see, great opportunities for travel, a majority of English speakers and relatively good academic status for the university itself.
info_ease: Quite easy. Easier than my home university if I am being honest. They do a pretty good job of letting you know the basics in the intro week, so make sure to make it to a few of the events there, also to meet new people. They also have an extensive academic support network that is usually always accessible, right on campus, if you have any questions.
arrival_assistance: Intro week, emails of good info, as well as a welcome package in the airport with a prepaid sim which was very helpful!
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Relatively straightforward, but the visa is quite daunting and expensive (about 1000 euros), which may be intended for longer academic stays. Don't get too scared by all the questions in the visa (like I did) as they usually approve them immediately and just set aside a good amount of time to complete it and get familiar with the required documents, so you can obtain them before the deadline of submission.
registration_help: UWA has a website and email for enquiries which they usually answer quite quick. Aside from that, the welcome letter contained a good bit of info and you can also register for a pre-departure zoom session where they take you through most of what you need to do, which I recommend. Most of the info is on the exchange part of the UWA site, so have a good read through that.
registration_success: I got all 4 of the ones i wanted.
registration_advice: Prepare a good few months in advance to avoid too much stress. Moving to a new country will be daunting, but take it one step at a time and you'll make it through the process. Once you're there you sort of forget the application process and it's minor perils.
course_level: I took one first year course, one second year course and two third year courses, but you can definitely make it easier or harder for yourself by selecting other courses. I found that this level was just about what I could fit in and I would have loved less work to do at times:
teaching_comparison: A bit more memorizing to do and a less intuitive and rhetorical approach than what one may be used to in danish education, closer to an "American" way of teaching. This does differ between courses though.
courses_enrolled: I took Plants in action, Neuroscience in society, Clean, green & ethical animal production and Ecological processes.
recommended_courses: Neuroscience in society and ecological processes were my favourites. Lecturers were passionate and the courses well structured and expectations reasonable. Especially ecological processes taught me a lot.
unexpected_costs: Opening a bank account, although this was not necessary. Visa was also very expensive.
cost_comparison: General amenities and food were quite expensive as there weren't really any equivalents to budget stores like Rema 1000 or Netto. Coles was the cheapest option for groceries and for bigger items and accessories go to kmart.
activities_available: Sport and lots of clubs! They do an orientation day early in the semester with a booth for every club and sport opportunity, so go there if you want an overview of the options. Most of these are also basically free to participate in. I personally joined the rollerblading club and bought my own pair of blades which was great fun. Rolling to class in the mornings definitely made the semester that much better and the campus is quite clean of debris and full of little spots to jump.
activities_recommended: Join a club or a sport.
weekend_recommendations: Use the bigger study breaks and the time after exams to do roadtrips, north and south! North is best to do in the australian winter/spring as it is still very warm at that time and will likely be too hot during summer, where the south is more appealing. Exmouth and Karijini national park were highlights, offering great snorkeling and captivating desert respectively. The desert is highly recommended as it is just so exotic and peaceful. Me and a friend managed to get a van incredibly cheap through a relocation company, so look into that if you want to save money, although it does come with certain restrictions, so read the fine print. Other than that Perth has great bush parks and beaches and quite a few snorkel/diving spots. If you have an advanced divers license, the UWA underwater club offers pretty cheap dives throughout the semester, so check that out.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. Australians are very welcoming and easygoing, although there may be some slang to get used to. A lot of Australian also get up quite early in the morning and go to bed earlier than in europe, which makes for shorter nights out on the town if that's your thing. I personally found this quite nice and that I got more sleep than back home, also helped by the close proximity to campus of course.
socializing_tips: Do the intro events at the start of the semester, even you feel a little tired or stressed. Talk to people at uni after class if you get the chance and if you live at a college, don't be afraid to join new people at their meals in the dining hall. Talking to the locals will get you great tips for things to do and see and you'll get to know a bit more about the culture, making your stay much better.
cultural_challenges: Uni students are generally a bit younger than in Denmark and at a college you might live with people who are as young as 18, so be prepared for some occasional gaps in maturity when talking to other students. This mostly affects the vibe of social functions where people tend to drink a lot more unrestrained. I found that most Australians I met at uni were between 19-21 of age.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness and lack of formalities. They take some getting used to, but after a while you might find that your shoulders drop a bit.
top3_advice: Explore the nature as much as you can, spend time with locals and go to the beach, even when you assignments due.
other_useful_info: Consider getting a car with friends and get a smartrider card to save money on public transport.
most_rewarding: The nature and the experience of self-reliance while living in another country. Hiking the cape to cape track and doing roadtrips were great experiences and I can highly recommend.
greatest_challenge: Finding enough time for everything and battling the inevitable FOMO.
