crucial_aspects: I am very fond of the mountains both in regards to skiing and hiking and therefore thought it would be ideal to go to Switzerland to be able to spend my free time in the mountains. I also wanted to go to a German speaking country to improve my German. I heard that UZH is a very good Uni with a high academic level.
info_ease: There is always a lot of information upon arrival. Everything always work out, so dont stress too much. I received a very adequate information sheet from UZH about everything I needed to know before and upon arrival which was very helpfull. Furthermore I got the needed information from the student housing before my arrival also. So you are provided with the information you need by email! Not much need to search for it yourself.
arrival_assistance: I attended a welcome event where you receive information about registering in the country, helath insurance exemption and the SEMP scholarship (if granted one). There is an student service office in the main building where it was easy to get your questions answeared. Otherwise they student service was very quick at replying to emails!
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Registering for the courses was very easy! Also you can register/deregister until some time in October, which gives you the opportunity to try out different courses before you finally decide which ones you will be taking.
registration_help: Maybe a guide at UZH website. But it was very easy.
registration_success: Very succesfull. I even registered for some courses I didnt want to take at the end, and also then was it very easy to deregister.
registration_advice: Just go to studenter service website, search the course you want and register. Very easy.
course_level: The level is high! So you do need to study a lot of you go to UZH. But very interesting courses!
teaching_comparison: I took only economics courses. Like at UCPH there were lectures and exercise classes in each course. The lectures were very similar to what I was used to but in the exercise classes I was used to from UCPH to do the given assignments myself with help from at TA. At UZH it was however the TA who went over all the exercises and you were just taking notes. Also all the exams are handwritten.
courses_enrolled: Behavioral Finance Labor Economics Public Debt Management Global Poverty & Development Economics Advanced Microeconomics I Advanced Macroeconomics
recommended_courses: If you are and BA economics students take Advanced Microeconomics I Advanced Macroeconomics Because they can probably get approved as Macro III and Micro III. Behavioral Finance was very interesting as well but a though course with assignments every week.
unexpected_costs: Not really any. You do travel a lot by train, maybe more than I expected, and therefore do use some money on train tickets.
cost_comparison: I had heard that public transport was very expensive but was surprised to learn that it was cheaper than expected because i could get student discount. Eating out was very expensive.
activities_available: There is a free gym located at many different locations around Zurich. Very nice! They offer so many different classes.
activities_recommended: Sign up for ASVZ (the gym) and try out different classes. Also sign up for events with ESN Zurich. They do a lot of nice events for exchange students and you get to meet a lot of nice people!
weekend_recommendations: Explore the rest of Switzerland on the weekends! If you are traveling in a group of 4 below 25 you can travel all over Switzerland for one day for inly 20CHF. Very cheap
culture_adjustment: Quite easy I would say. Switzerland reminded me a bit of DK.
socializing_tips: Go to ESN events or just other event in general.
cultural_challenges: The Swiss where a bit closed and reserved. I mostly spoke with other exchange students.
culture_appreciated: The mountains and the active lifestyle the Swiss have. They also enjoy hiking and usually spend their weekends in the mountains.
top3_advice: Go to welcome events and meet people. Explore the whole of Switzerland - so beautiful.
other_useful_info: Dont worry if you get an accommodation a bit far from the city center. Most students live a bit far away and commuting time up to 50 min is normal. Its difficult and expensive to find a place to live in the center.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people from all over the world, getting new friends and having the experience of living in a different country.
greatest_challenge: In the beginning when you dont know anyone it is hard and a bit scary to socialize. So to just put yourself out there and try to talk with strangers were a great challenge for me!

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience life in another european city as well as wanting to feel close to home in order to have friends and family visit during my stay. As I am also a student studying with a chronic illness it was important to me that I knew the country I would study in had somewhat a similar lifestyle allowing me to stay in my routine that helps me navigate my illness. It was furthermore crucial to me to choose a university with high ranking of academic skills as well as choosing a city and country allowing me to experience different aspects of the culture within the country. I was i Zürich and really appreciated being able to experience Switzerland's mountains.
overall_comments: The dorm that was offered to us as exchange students was not the best and affected my social experience. Furthermore the kitchen was extremely difficult and in bad condition making it close to impossible to actually cook food and I ended up spending double my budget on food.
info_ease: . I found that the office for incoming students at UZH was extremely helpful and prepared me well, sending relevant documents and links in time letting me know how I should manage. I was surprised by the extra administrative work when arriving in Switzerland, with having to register at the Kreisbüro/Stadthouse, health insurance and rental agreement, as I was not prepared for it to be part of the administrative preparation and how much time and effort that had to be put into it and also the cost of it, came as a bit of a surprise for me, but the office for incoming students at UZH was extremely helpful with the guides they sent out with mail, and furthermore living with other exchange students to ask for advice. The preparation was a bit of a hazzle and cause of frustration due to separate deadlines and processing time at my home university that didn’t match up with UZH, but the student counselling was very helpful at both universities to make it work, and it worked out in the end. Furthermore, I am an exchange student studying with disabilities, studying part time with exemption due to chronic illness. This of course gave me some more preparation due to having to receive exemption from both my home university and host university, but I found that it was absolutely no problem with UZH. It can be a bit overwhelming with all the administrative work, so I would recommend keeping it organized, seeking help, asking friends and start early.
arrival_assistance: I found that the instructors at UZH were really engaged, dedicated and ambitious with their academic research and my classes were very inspiring and has been very profound for furthering my academic competences. I have enjoyed and appreciated the study environment and academic level of UZH. Something I very much appreciated was the teaching style as well, encouraging students to be active learners, participating in discussion, giving suggestions for the reading lists, and also the instructors inviting different speakers to be the expert on research themes, arranging excursions within Zürich (this was a great bonus as an exchange student to further understand the culture of Switzerland) and also bringing in relevant, interesting and current casework. UZH is also very well prepared and a great environment for exchange students providing an international community, making it approachable to study as a non-Swiss student. And the Incoming office guides you all the way and have already prepared answers to all your questions, not one time did I feel like I didn't know what to do or how to handle as they had already prepared me.
arrival_comments: I attended the mandatory introduction at Zürich University but really missed a more comprehensive introductory week of activities to meet other exchange students in an environment focusing on social relations.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The dorm that was offered to us as exchange students was not the best and affected my social experience. Furthermore the kitchen was extremely difficult and in bad condition making it close to impossible to actually cook food and I ended up spending double my budget on food.
registration_process: The process of booking courses was a bit different, than what I am used to. You have to make sure yourself that every course go together and dont intersect. I struggled a bit with having to organize my own classes across day/time/location and found it to be a bit of an issue, also when I had chosen different classes that fit with time/day/location, that some of them still would intercross on certain times with exams. But the teachers were very helpful and solutions oriented in making it work. Furthermore you could sign up for the courses and try them out and then cancel them by October, making it possible to try out which ones you prefer. I did not take part in that option as I needed the pre-approval of courses beforehand. Some of the courses had limited participants to it was a good option to book more courses than needed to be sure to get a spot and then cancel afterwards. Also you needed to be aware if the course was at the level for your studies as well as taught in english.
registration_help: You could call or email the incoming student office and they answered within very short time.
registration_success: I registered for all the courses I had hoped
registration_advice: Try to find courses in academic fields you know before hand, this gives an advantage when studying at a different university as you already have so beforehand knowledge and therefore can more quickly understand the theme presented from a different point of view. Also be aware your course is taught in english if thats important to you, this also gives you the opportunity to engage with other exchange students. And something I found I had been really smart about was to choose courses with exams that you feel confident in as well as exams that was done before Christmas. Being strategic about this allowed me to nit be stressed about exams, receiving good grades as well as being able to enjoy the end of my semester without exams to focus on traveling to places I had missed as well as saying goodbye to friends I made and organize my moving-out/de-register/arriving home process in a much more relaxed way.
academics_comments: The dorm that was offered to us as exchange students was not the best and affected my social experience. Furthermore the kitchen was extremely difficult and in bad condition making it close to impossible to actually cook food and I ended up spending double my budget on food.
course_level: I am really going to miss studying at UZH, it has been an absolute pleasure and privilege to attend a semester of my master’s at the University of Zürich. I found that both the instructors and the students were really engaged, dedicated and ambitious with their academic research and my classes were very inspiring and has been very profound for furthering my academic competences. I have enjoyed and appreciated the study environment and academic level of UZH.
teaching_comparison: Something I very much appreciated was the teaching style as well, encouraging students to be active learners, participating in discussion, giving suggestions for the reading lists, and also the instructors inviting different speakers to be the expert on research themes, arranging excursions within Zürich (this was a great bonus as an exchange student to further understand the culture of Switzerland) and also bringing in relevant, interesting and current casework.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to postcolonial studies Rethinking sexualities, intimacies and normativities Gender, work and space
recommended_courses: All of my courses: Introduction to postcolonial studies, Rethinking sexualities, intimacies and normativities and Gender, work and space. I think all of the courses were interesting and relevant and presented me with the newest research, all of the teachers were extremely dedicated and extremely good teachers. Each course gave me something different and each course was of my personal academic interest and furthered my academic skills. The courses also enlightened me on some of the same themes but from different perspectives.
unexpected_costs: For registering and de-registering living in Zürich I had to pay each time.
cost_comparison: The transportation and food options in Switzerland were much more expensive that participated, as well as having to spend more money on food due to the kitchen facilities.
activities_available: Free sports facilities at university Free cultural walk in the city at the beginning of the semester One introduction at uni
activities_recommended: To participate in introductions as its where you will get relevant information and meet other exchange students.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the swiss mountains - they are magnificent and extraordinary and is such a wonderful way to spend your weekends and getting a study break.
culture_adjustment: I think it was extremely easy as Switzerland is not that much different to Denmark and as I have travelled to similar countries before. Especially in Zürich there is also a great international environment making it really easy to adapt. I have found it easy to integrate into the local culture and navigate the life of being a student at UZH. It has given me a great personal understanding of what it takes to work internationally as well as establishing a new life and everyday habits in a different country.
socializing_tips: Be open, say yes, ask, stay curious and dont be afraid to invite yourself. And its also okay to not want to socialize all the time.
cultural_challenges: Switzerland is very conservative, there are a lot of strict rules and normative hierarchical behaviour that I had to get used to, but it was not at to any extent that I found challenged my stay. Everything was extremely expensive, and it also sometimes felt like they would make money wherever they could.
culture_appreciated: Following the conservative culture and strict rules also comes a very well organized society making different processes run smoothly and effectively and therefore easy to navigate in. For example their trains alway run one time :) I have felt extremely comfortable and safe in Zürich. And also coming from the expensive lifestyle is a high living standard which is really nice.
top3_advice: - Appreciate the high academic level of the teachers and choose courses you are knowledgable in beforehand. - Apply for a lot of scholarships, Switzerland is expensive and even more expensive than you might realize. - GO TO THE MOUNTAINS!!! They are breathtaking and the swiss nature is just amazing, check in for the season to make sure its open and not dangerous, its a great way also to socialize with new friends as you usually go in groups with other exchange students. And gives you so much more energy and motivation to do academic work in between. Sunday is the day everyone goes as the stores are closed.
other_useful_info: Academically, UZH have provided an exceptional environment that have strengthened my academic competences and enriched my educational experience and challenged my perspective to research. The international community at UZH facilitated a smooth transition for exchange students and the office for incoming students have been of great guidance and help. I have been very pleasantly surprised, as it has been positively more ambitious than what I am used to. The University of Zürich and the education provided to me during my exchange semester, is one of the things I will miss the most. I feel extremely privileged to have been able to receive such high level of educational improvement.
most_rewarding: Life in Switzerland has been an absolute pleasure, of traditional and modern cultural experiences, personal growth, and the joys of Zürich living standards. The city's cultural offerings and the opportunities for nature experiences, with hikes in the weekend has contributed significantly to my overall experience. Ultimately, my time in Zürich has been marked by comfort, safety, and easy integration into local culture, led by the incoming team at UZH. The experience offered not just academic growth but also valuable insights into working internationally and establishing a life in a foreign country. Personally, it has made me a more solutions-oriented, culturally aware, and globally conscious individual and has provided me with a great personal experience that has contributed to my worth of self and a new perspective on the life I live and the culture I come from. I am really going to miss studying at UZH, it has been an absolute pleasure and privilege to attend a semester of my master’s at the University of Zürich. I found that both the instructors and the students were really engaged, dedicated and ambitious with their academic research and my classes were very inspiring and has been very profound for furthering my academic competences. Overall, it has been an extremely enriching experience both personally and academically and I would recommend everyone who can to study at UZH.
greatest_challenge: Something that has been a challenge has been to keep up with my physical health, especially when suffering from a chronic illness, I am forced to take great care of my health, but it has been difficult to eat as healthy as I usually do, due to the conditions of the kitchen. It has also been difficult to exercise, even though UZH offers free exercise at campus (which I think is great), I have usually found the classes to be an overwhelmingly large number of participants as well as the classes and the app descriptions to being only in Swiss and having to take public transport for at least 30-40 min to go. I have looked up the options to become a member at a fitness-center, but the expenses for that have been way above my budget. I have tried to exercise in my room and outside as much as possible, but it has felt isolated and not as giving as doing it in a proper space. I would have wished there had been more focus on social events for exchange students to get to know each other, that was not necessarily something that had to be arranged by ourselves. I found that especially at my dorm with 170 people with one kitchen was overwhelming and caused me to isolate in my room more than I had wished to.
other_comments: I chose my exchange to be close to my home country to have friends and family visit as well as going home for Christmas, an opportunity I have appreciated very much and have been a bonus to my exchange to be able to share it with people I care about from home.

crucial_aspects: I chose my destination due to the large amount of course choice within my field and the many researchers and project associated with my specific academic interest. I went to my destination because I wanted to learn new things relevant to my studies and later career, meet and network with new people within my field, and experience new research environments.
info_ease: It was very easy. The Incoming office university held an introductory seminar with all necessary administrative information, and the administrative and academic staff at my institute were very helpful whenever I had additional questions.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance from the Incoming office at my university, as well as the administrative and academic staff at my institute.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Very simple - the registration was done simultaneously with the information meeting at the start of the exchange stay.
registration_help: General and personalized help from the Incoming office.
registration_success: I was very successful, and even took the opportunity to switch one of my classes out for one that was more relevant to me after the first two weeks of the semester.
registration_advice: Follow the instructions sent out in emails before the stay very closely - if you do, most things will probably go very smoothly.
course_level: The level of courses varied quite a bit, however, in general, I though it was appropriate with the background I came from.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style was mostly the same, seminar-based style I've experienced at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Diversity of Indo-European Languages, Methods in Evolutionary Language Science, Conditions of Language Dynamics, Written Paper in Language Diachrony and Typologies of Linguistic Structures.
recommended_courses: I would recommend Conditions of Language Dynamics, since it was very well structured and taught, and since it covers a topic (the mechanisms and nature of language change) which I've not seen courses focusing on elsewhere. I would also recommend Methods in Evolutionary Language Science to anyone who has a little bit of experience with statistical analysis beforehand (I found the level to be slightly too high, since I only had experience with qualitative methods from before), and Typologies of Linguistic Structures to anyone who would like a basic overview of linguistic typology.
unexpected_costs: Having to get extra travel tickets to get to my host country due to massive train delays.
cost_comparison: Certain medicines were more expensive than expected. Some food, e.g. vegetables, were less expensive than expected.
activities_available: See above for sports. There was a city-tour organized by the Incoming office, and other than that, social events organized by student clubs at my institution as well as academic talks for both students and staff.
activities_recommended: I would recommend to try out the sports if you're interested (probably a great place to meet people), as well as to attend both academic and social events put on by your institute or within your field of study.
weekend_recommendations: Travel around the country (especially for hiking and skiining) with the train is nice if you have the money for it (trains are very expensive). Other than that, making plans with fellow students in courses or from your housing to do things together in the city is nice.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: Go to events put on by your institution or by the student clubs associated with your specific field of study. Be friendly and chat to people in your courses.
cultural_challenges: The biggest difference was the use of polite pronouns to university staff - this was slightly tricky, as this is not necessarily a tradition when communicating in English, but part of the German-speaking culture in the host city.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness - in general, people were more open and chatty than is normal in Denmark.
top3_advice: 1. The cost of living is high, but honestly, Copenhagen is not that much cheaper. 2. Try to do any medical errands and go to the doctor in Denmark before you leave, as I've heard this can be very expensive. 3. If you know you want to see the Alps and travel around, plan ahead - the half-fare travel card might be very worth it. Another cheaper way to travel is to join ESN's trips, which is also a great way to make friends.
other_useful_info: Some courses at the university are so-called "two-semester"-courses, where all of the teaching takes place in the first semester and the examination usually in the second semester. If you chose courses like this, double check with both universities (host and UCPH) that this is compatible with your one-semester exchange.
most_rewarding: Meeting students and academics within my field of study and hearing their different perspectives.
greatest_challenge: The reason I went on exchange was essentially only academic, so I sometimes felt demotivated to engage socially and develop friendships, as I would rather have worked on longer-term relationships in at home Copenhagen.

crucial_aspects: That i could travel and visit some beautiful nature.
info_ease: Very easy.
arrival_assistance: My department arranged a meet & greet.
arrival_comments: Went extremely smooth.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: I could pre-book my courses which made it really easy.
registration_help: UZH were helpful through email.
registration_success: I got all the courses that i wanted.
registration_advice: Don't stress about it. It will work out. They are extremely helpful at UZH.
course_level: Equal to UCPH I would say.
teaching_comparison: Equal to UCPH, but less group work.
courses_enrolled: Privacy in a Digital Society Youth and Digital Technologies Quantitative Methods Data Analysis Introduction to Machine Learning for Social Sciences
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the data analysis course.
unexpected_costs: Everything is expensive so prepare yourself.
cost_comparison: Take away is really expensive.
activities_available: ASVZ.
activities_recommended: ASVZ
weekend_recommendations: Hop on the train and visit mountains, cities or go on a hike!
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy.
socializing_tips: Say yes to student accommodation and socialize through there. By far the easiest.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really.
culture_appreciated: I really enjoyed the football culture. Go to Letzigrund and watch Grasshoppers or FC Zurich.
top3_advice: Download Swype and get a cheap e-sim card. Sign up through ASVZ. Travel!!
other_useful_info: Be open minded and say yes to hikes or other activities with fellow students!
most_rewarding: All the traveling, hiking and skiing.
greatest_challenge: The kitchen situation at my dorm. 170 people and only one kitchen. That was horrible.

crucial_aspects: The aspects of my choice that was most important was to live in a city with a lot of possibilities for things to do besides your studies. Here I chose University of Zurich because it also enabled me to during the weekends to go on hikes and ski trips. For my destination it was also important that I lived in a place where I could feel comfortable but still experience a lot of different cultures and new experiences, and therefore Zurich suited this really well because it is a very international city with a lot of exchange students.
overall_comments: I have never regretted making the choice of going abroad, it has been one of the best decisions for my own personal well-being and for the experience of going somewhere else while still learning and progressing in your career.
info_ease: Sometimes it was quite difficult, especially with regards to when you had to upload wishes/proposals for which courses you were gonna take at the host university because it was really difficult to find the correct courses that I could apply for as an international student. Apart from that it was a nice experience with UCPH providing us with the necessary information and the same thing with UZH providing us with information, e.g. with regards to applying for student accommodation
arrival_assistance: We had both a mandatory introduction that applied to all international students where they told us about e.g. how to apply for a residence permit, insurances, how to use public transport and different social and study-related activities. As law students we also had a specific mandatory introduction where they told us more about the teachings at the faculty of law, and how you applied for courses with the different deadlines and how the exams functioned.
arrival_comments: I think it was great that they made these introductions mandatory because I could imagine that people otherwise would skip them.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I have never regretted making the choice of going abroad, it has been one of the best decisions for my own personal well-being and for the experience of going somewhere else while still learning and progressing in your career.
registration_process: You just had to upload your personal data and had to provide them with different documents. I then afterwards checked which courses were available for me and got these pre approved at my home institution in order for me to able to apply for these at the host institution.
registration_help: I actually don't really know since I didn't make use of any help offered
registration_success: This went really well, but the good thing about going on exchange in Zurich is that you are not bound initially by your choice of courses since the deadline of which courses you want to have is first 3-4 weeks in to the semester. This means that in the first couple of weeks you can go around to different classes and test out different courses to see which one you prefer and find the most interesting. That way you can also coordinate a little more with other people if you want to have the same courses, and you also find out a little bit more about what kind of exam the different courses have. UZH offers mobility exams which are exams that can be taken remotely and are oral, and I primarily took courses where this was an option since I prefer oral exams over written ones.
registration_advice: Get pre approved all the courses you find interesting by your home university so that you are able to have them in your learning agreement that you have to make while you are on exchange so that your credits can be transferred. Go a little around and try out different classes - I think I tried out 8-9 classes before I decided on which 5 classes I wanted to have.
academics_comments: I have never regretted making the choice of going abroad, it has been one of the best decisions for my own personal well-being and for the experience of going somewhere else while still learning and progressing in your career.
course_level: Some courses were a little more easy than others. I had some courses where there was a lot of reading material bearing in mind that it was only a 6 ECTS course, but then I also had courses where the only material for the exam was the powerpoints and what the professor had said at the lectures. The good thing is that the majority of the courses are being recorded and you can therefore watch them back. All of my courses there were no attendance requirements which meant that your participation in class didn't count in your grade, some classes count participation in their grading.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was only lectures and very one-sided in the sense that it was the professor explaining the stuff and us taking notes to what they said. There was not that much interaction, only a few times where the professor would ask small questions to the audience. In many of the classes the professor also did not provide with any reading material or only gave us additional/recommended material if we wanted to add on to the things they told at the lectures.
courses_enrolled: Internet Law (6 ECTS), European Economic Law (6 ECTS), International Financial Law (6 ECTS), Introduction to U.S. Business Law (6 ECTS) and Introduction to Sports Law (6 ECTS)
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend the ones in English because from personal experience the ones taught in German can be very hard to follow along in, and you cannot be sure that they will speak a little Swiss-German in them which is very different to the standard High-German that you learn in school. I would also recommend taking some of the courses that focus on the international or EU aspects of law, or explaining the fundamental principles of a certain law area because that would be more relevant for you in your future rather than learning about some niche Swiss legislation.
unexpected_costs: When you arrive you have to pay around 60 CHF for a residence permit. You also need to pay for specific trash bags that cost 16 CHF for 10 bags because you cannot just use normal trash bags.
cost_comparison: It is very expensive to go to restaurants, and therefore I have not really been out to eat while being here. Everything that involves a service is quite expensive because the minimum wage in Switzerland is quite high. The groceries are not that much more expensive than Denmark, maybe on average 10% if you just go to Lidl or Aldi.
activities_available: The university through something called ASVZ offers a lot of sporting activities, e.g. badminton, spinning, yoga, paddle and much more. There is also a lot of different sporting associations that do a lot of different things, but I have not attended any of this. ESN Zurich also offers a lot of fun stuff where I for instance went on a skiing trip, paragliding, and bar crawl, and they do a lot of different things.
activities_recommended: Go on skiing trips around the country or Austria, there is a lot of options that are only 1-2 hours away (Engelberg, Pizol, Arosa, Andermatt, Lax, Davos, St. Anton), so you can easily do it in a day-trip if you want to. When the weather is a bit more nice do hiking trips (Grindelwald, Brienz, Lauterbrunnen, Mürren, Thun, Stoos, Grosser Mythen, Seealpsee, Mount Pilatus). Otherwise visit some of the nice cities around in Switzerland (Luzern, Thun, Basel, Chur, Lausanne, Geneve). If you are in Zurich go and take a swim in Limmat, or if you want to go out go to Langstrasse.
weekend_recommendations: I also went on a trip to Italy in Milano, Como and Lugano for my easter break, which is a big recommendation. You can also easily go to other countries if you want to, e.g. France, Austria, Spain, Netherlands, but I just did not have that as my priority.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it is very similar to the lifestyle of Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: I actually do not really know since I do not know any Swiss students and have not really got to learn any, but I would imagine attending some events of the student associations for instance.
cultural_challenges: There was not really any cultural differences I found challenging.
culture_appreciated: People can be a little reserved but if you just first start talking to them they are very nice and talkative.
top3_advice: Apply for a student accommodation (WOKO) - it will make it so much easier for you to get to know people and attend social events. Apply for the mobility exam courses - they are a little easier to pass and you will both be with Swiss and exchange students in these classes Do not expect the semester to just be a piece of cake, I would say it is definitely easier than in Copenhagen, also because the grades do not matter, but the exams are not just you presenting a powerpoint that you made the night before
other_useful_info: There is a very big exchange student community since the two universities (UZH and ETH) are located right next to each other, and both of them accept a lot of foreign students
most_rewarding: Even though it has been great attending UZH, the best part has no doubt been to get to know a lot of people from around the world. That is also what I loved about my exchange is that it is not the most popular destination for Danish law students at least, and therefore I got to know so many people from around the world, even though in the end I ended up hanging out the most with people from Sweden and Norway
greatest_challenge: I have not been away for such a long period before in my life from my family and friends, but even though I sometimes missed them there was also so much going on at your exchange that you at some points would "forget" it a bit because the days just went by so fast.

crucial_aspects: Both exploring a new destination with great opportunities of outdoor adventures but also a good university to challenge myself academically.
info_ease: It was fairly easy finding information as i used KU, UZH webpage and contacts and earlier students who went on exchange here. UZH was especially very helpful upon arrival with different deadlines, questions etc.
arrival_assistance: Not any.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It is quite easy to sign up for courses. You have a website where you can read about the course content, the requirements and the time of the lectures. Then you just sign up on that portal. Note that some courses requires an application. Some courses are block courses (sign up early) and others are for the full semester. As an UZH student i also took a course at ETH which was super cool. Be aware that the courses' ECTS points are way lower, i had 7 courses (3 courses with 6 ECTS and 4 courses with 3 ECTS). You can change courses after the semester starts, so you can try out the ones your are curious about. But note that if you want to change the course can bee full before the deadline. I would recommend signing up to several, maybe more than 30 ECTS, try them out and then deregister the ones you do not want to take.
registration_help: I did mostly talk to other students or texted the TA's.
registration_success: Alright. I figured out late that I could take ETH courses as well, so some of them were already full. In general I would have preferred to sign up as early as possible to get the courses that get full fast and have more options available.
registration_advice: Get an overview of the courses you like, sign up early, try them out and then deregister if you do not like them.
course_level: The level of the courses was alright, like at home.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was quite similar to the style at home. But the seminar classes are different, they are smaller and you discuss a lot more.
courses_enrolled: Operations Management Introduction to Strategic Thinking Ethics, Sustainability and Financial Markets Sustainable Investing Real Estate Finance Gender Economics Energy Economics and Policy
recommended_courses: Energy Economics and Policy at ETH and Sustainable Investing at UZH was very interesting courses and a cool professors.
unexpected_costs: None specific.
cost_comparison: I was expecting it to be quite expensive so I was not surprised. But you can do groceries fairly cheap and the cheap supermarkets are not far from danish prices.
activities_available: The host institution have ASVZ as the sports club where you can go on trips and just do many sports. ESN also do a lot of trips and events which are cool.
activities_recommended: I went skiing a lot which was amazing and later in the season it was more hiking. Both are really great and a good way to go on weekend trips with other students.
weekend_recommendations: The beautiful nature, it is amazing and easy accessible by public transport. The Jungfrau region and Appenzell region is beautiful.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it is not far from the danish culture.
socializing_tips: Just try to mingle with people that you have courses with. I only lived with exchange students so meeting locals was mostly through courses.
cultural_challenges: There is a bit more hierarchy, so the way you approach and write the professors are way more formal.
culture_appreciated: The very structured way of handling things like residency, practicalities through uni etc.
top3_advice: Weekend trips are a great way to explore the nature, both winter and summer. You are going to study some also, uni is relatively demanding. Do uni housing of possible.
other_useful_info: no
most_rewarding: The housing experience as that was fundamental for meeting people, doing small things in our everyday life here.
greatest_challenge: The academics.

crucial_aspects: The nature in Switzerland and the possibility of improving my german. And to experience a different health care system than the danish one.
info_ease: The exchange office in Zurich sent out most of the documents (and other practical information) you needed upon arrival. That was very helpful. They also have orientation-nights where they tell you a lot of good, practical information regarding your stay.
arrival_assistance: The exchange office in Zurich were extremely kind and fast at replying if you had a question, so they are a fantastic help.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It can be a little tricky to keep track of all the things you need to do when registrating. But again, the exchange office is very helpful in that proces and are there to answer all questions you may have. They also tell you, what you need to be aware of, and what type of information they need from you. That makes it a lot easier to navigate in.
registration_help: The exchange-coordinator has an e-mail, which they respond very quickly to. And if you really have a problem, they may call you or offer, that you can call them.
registration_success: Very succesfull. I had to send my wishes to the exchange-coordinator, and then she booked the classes for me. That's how it works with medical exchange but from what I've heard not other study-areas.
registration_advice: Be aware of deadlines and start the process in advance, so you don't end up in a last-minute-situation!
course_level: The level was the same as the level af UCPH.
teaching_comparison: It was the same but they do have more lectures, than what I'm used to at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Clinical courses: Pediatrics, radiology, nuclear medicine, pathology Elective module: Public Health Lectures: dermatology, forensic medicine, pediatrics, general medicine, hematology, kidney diseases, anaesthesiology, emergency medicine
recommended_courses: I really liked the clinical course in Pediatrics.
unexpected_costs: You have to pay for some mandatory things for instance your residence permit.
cost_comparison: It was actually pretty much how I expected it. The prices are a little higher than the danish prices but not as high or different as I thought they would be.
activities_available: They have free gym at the different campuses, with a lot of different options, both gym-classes and "normal" gyms. Furthermore, they have numerous cafeterias and different student bars.
activities_recommended: I would recommend the gym! They are very nice!
weekend_recommendations: Experience the nature!! It's absolutely amazing. If you're under 25 (and four people travelling together) they offer a "Friends-pass" with the train, which makes even longer trips very cheap. I can for sure recommend that!
culture_adjustment: That was very easy. The culture in Switzerland is pretty similar to the danish culture.
socializing_tips: The local students are very nice, but you often have to be the one taking the first step. But when you do, you'll experience that they are quite friendly!
cultural_challenges: I didn't experience challenging cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: That being active (skiing, hiking etc.) is a big part of the swiss culture. I really loved that.
top3_advice: -Keep track of the things (beside registration at the university) that you have to do (like getting a residence permit etc.). Especially in the beginning there are different practical things, you have to do. -They offer german courses in the beginning of the semester. I would sign up for one. It gives you a chance to adapt to hearing german on a daily basis, and you get the chance to meet other students, that signed up as well. -Be openminded and smile - then you'll have an amazing time!
other_useful_info: Say yes if they offer you student housing. It may not be luxury, but it takes away some stress regarding finding a home and also gives you an opportunity to meet other students.
most_rewarding: The people I met during my exchange. The experience would not have been the same without them.
greatest_challenge: They teach in german, so in the beginning you'll need some time to adapt to that. But after a short period of time you don't pay attention to it anymore - and you really end up improving your german skills!

crucial_aspects: The mountains and beautiful nature - and how safe Switzerland is
info_ease: Very easy - UZH sends out mails regularly and with clearly stated deadlines. They also answer emails quickly and are very helpful
arrival_assistance: There was an intro meeting for exchange students with info about arriving in Switzerland and how UZH works
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The website is pretty complicated but they have videos on how to navigate it which helped greatly.
registration_help: Apart from videoes they also answer emails quickly - the professors usually do as well
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted since there were no restrictions on number of students - very easy process!
registration_advice: I recommend signing up for more classes than just 30 ECTS and then trying them all out until registration closes so you are sure the professor is good and the course material is interesting. Many course descriptions were a bit lacking so really the only way to really know a course is to experience it. But remember to deregister of course!
course_level: It reeeeeeeeally depends. I took 5 courses since almost all courses at UZH Law are maximum 6 ECTS. I recommend you do not exceed 5 courses! Some of the courses were very complicated and others were extremely easy. It really depends. But in general the level is very high and there are a lot of expectations of the students. If you are looking to have a chill semester where you can slack off do NOT go to UZH. But if you are looking to learn a lot at a great institution then I would greatly recommend it.
teaching_comparison: It was mostly seminar style teaching with the professor teaching from slides. All my classes were recorded which was a great help. There was also in many of my courses the oppourtunity to get extra credit by either doing student presentations or moot court or the like. I did not do any of this but I'm sure this could be enjoyable. Overall the professors were very nice and smart - but don't call them by their first name still.
courses_enrolled: Corruption and organized crime. Fintech, Blockchain and the Future of International Finance. Principles of corporate law. International trade regulation. Law and economics.
recommended_courses: Corruption and organized crime is a very easy course with a nice professor - guaranteed pass. Principles of corporate law had two great and skilled professors but requires a lot of work. I, however, learned a lot and had a great time. International trade regulation was also a great course - the professor was really great and smart and classes were interesting and very relevant to todays climate.
unexpected_costs: It costs 55-70 CHF to register in Zürich, which is mandatory. If you move you have to pay this again.
cost_comparison: Everything was more expensive - perhaps except croissants, they're the only cheap thing i Switzerland.
activities_available: Free gym and gym classes and the like through the uni sports facility called ASVZ - download the app and register. It's great and everything is free.
activities_recommended: Go to BQM on Polyterasse after classes. Introduce yourself to Swiss people in your courses. They're reserved but very nice! avoid paying for clubs or going to clubs on Saturday as it is more expensive than Friday (and Thursday is usually free).
weekend_recommendations: Go hiking every Sunday. Everything is closed anyway so Sunday is the perfect day - seriously! And try to go skiing as well!
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The Swiss-Germans are very similar to Danish people - reserved but nice once you get to know them. But they are more polite in all ways.
socializing_tips: Just introduce yourself - I found getting to know Swiss students very easy. They're all great at English and very nice!
cultural_challenges: None to be honest. I felt very at home quickly. Maybe the fact that when Swiss people blow their nose, they do it veeery loudly, which is very annoying.
culture_appreciated: How outdoorsy and inviting the people were. They also really love their country so they give great tips on what to see and what not to see. Everything is also very safe and proper - trains run on time and you don't feel unsafe walking alone at night as a girl. And trains and busses run all night on weekends which is very nice!
top3_advice: 1. Make sure you have enough money!!!!! If you go to Zürich on a tight budget, you will not have much fun. It is absolutely one of the most expensive cities in the world, so don't go if you want to save money! 2. Try many different courses at UZH before choosing your final ones 3. When UZH sends out an e-mail with all incoming students, contact all the Danish ones and make a group! We did this during our semester and we ended up going hiking together every Sunday and doing many other fun activites. You make great friends you can bring home and it ensures that you will not be lonely even for a second in a new country. Seriously!! This is a major hack!
other_useful_info: Be aware that pretty much all written exams are written by hand on paper with pen and you have to print everything. Very old-school and your hand gets very tired from writing so much. But the main campus is so beautiful and everything was great!
most_rewarding: Everything to be honest. But the hikes were next level.
greatest_challenge: Money. Switzerland is just crazy expensive - especially eating out.

crucial_aspects: That it was a German speaking area, and that the relevant faculty of the university was comparable or higher than that of my home university. Additionally, that the opportunity was available to take language courses if I found it necessary. Lastly, that the city but also the country as a whole was safe and accessible.
info_ease: Pretty easy, since the exchange university provided many details and links to help me prepare my self as much as possible to the challenges that could face me when I arrived. Furthermore, they informed me of the duties I had when I arrived in regards to providing information to the city office and so on.
arrival_assistance: I did not receive any direct assistance, but I'm sure it could have been provided if I found it necessary.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had to fill out informations on mobility online, and attach relevant documents, but otherwise it was pretty simple. At one point a Learning Agreement had to be provided, but here one should just use the template provided by the host university.
registration_help: I'm sure the relevant help was available if I found it necessary.
registration_success: I was successful in registering for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Have your documents in order, since some of them will be provided to you in a physical format. Otherwise, just be diligent and double check everything has been done.
course_level: The difficulty of the courses may seem higher than that of the home institution due to a more old school way of teaching. This is evident when it comes to the examination, where in most cases no previous exams are provided to practice on. Sometimes the solutions to the problem sets will also not be provided, which means that it is vital that one show up for the TA-sessions.
teaching_comparison: As mentioned above, at points the teaching style could come across as more old fashioned, but that said, everyone was always very kind and helpfull if I had any questions. It is just on the student to ask the questions to achieve the highest learning outcome.
courses_enrolled: Normative Economics, Financial Crises, Advanced Corporate Finance, Econometrics for Development Economists, Stress Testing of Banks, Bank Treasury Management
recommended_courses: Normative Economics, Financial Crises, Advanced Corporate Finance, Econometrics for Development Economists, Stress Testing of Banks
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Eating out was a bit more expensive than I had imagined, which is to say that it is very expensive.

There are plenty of cultural events around the city, where many of them are for free as a student. For social activities, the ESN organises several events.
activities_recommended: Even though I did not myself participate in them, I have heard many good things about the ESN events, which many exchange students participate in during the first weeks of the exchange.
weekend_recommendations: There is an endless array of hiking opportunities, many of which I used myself. Otherwise the city is full of music events, many of which are classical and free for students. Visiting the other large cities is also really fun, alongside skiing, and lastly going to see an ice hockey match is a great experience.
culture_adjustment: It was easy enough, since the differences are relatively minor.
socializing_tips: Swiss people are very kind and open, so don't be afraid to talk to them, especially those who you have courses with. That way you will build a connection when you talk with the week after week.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any cultural differences challenging apart from the language.
culture_appreciated: The orderliness, punctuality and calmness.
top3_advice: Even if you want academically challenging courses, remember that you are on exchange and that you most likely also want to experience other things too, and thus it can be difficult to excel academically while taking time off to enjoy other sides of the country. Say yes to every opportunity you get offered for activities. Enjoy it, since the time flies.
other_useful_info: For public transport, but the Half Fare Card, since that will cut fares by 50%. Think about whether it makes sense to open a bank account to save money. Read as many things as you can to be as prepared as possible to when you first get there.
most_rewarding: To meet and socialise with swiss people.
greatest_challenge: Speaking the language.

crucial_aspects: When choosing my study destination, it was crucial for me to go to a country that felt safe and stable, so I could focus fully on both my studies and daily life. At the same time, I wanted a university with a high academic level, where I would be challenged and gain real academic value from the exchange. Finally, the course offering mattered a lot: I specifically looked for a place where I could take advanced courses like Advanced Microeconomics (Mikro 3) and Advanced Macroeconomics (Makro 3) since they are mandatory at economics.
overall_comments: Overall, my study experience in Zurich has been amazing. I’ve made some really good new friends, explored the local culture, and I can genuinely recommend Zurich as an exchange destination. At the same time, the academic level is very high, so it’s important to be prepared for a demanding workload and high expectations—but that is also a big part of what made the experience so valuable.
info_ease: Upon arrival, there was a lot of information to take in, but much of it was provided in advance. The University of Zurich (UZH) sent many formal documents beforehand, which helped make the practical and administrative side clearer. I didn’t get much information from KU, mostly the approval of courses.
arrival_assistance: When I arrived in Zurich, I received helpful support through a general information session where we were given everything we needed to get started, including the student card and practical guidance on topics like insurance and migration/registration requirements. In addition, there was a separate information session specifically for the Faculty of Business, Economics and Informatics, which I would strongly recommend attending as well, since it provides more targeted and relevant information for students in those programs. They held these faculty specific information meetings for every faculty.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall, my study experience in Zurich has been amazing. I’ve made some really good new friends, explored the local culture, and I can genuinely recommend Zurich as an exchange destination. At the same time, the academic level is very high, so it’s important to be prepared for a demanding workload and high expectations—but that is also a big part of what made the experience so valuable.
registration_process: The registration process at UZH is quite simple at first: you sign up for your courses online and you can adjust your choices during the first month. However, from the beginning of October you can no longer change courses, so your final selection has to be settled by then. After finalizing your courses, you must complete a Learning Agreement listing the courses you are taking. This document has to be signed in order by me, KU, and then UZH. In my case, the process took a long time because KU could not sign before my final course approvals were uploaded in Mobility Online, and afterwards UZH was relatively slow with their part. Even though the first month is flexible, I would therefore recommend being well prepared and having a clear idea of which courses you want to take before arriving.
registration_help: The kind of help available was mainly administrative support from KU. In particular, the studievejleder at KU has been amazing throughout the process. Since the course approval office at KU was sometimes slow, the studievejleder was especially helpful when I needed answers quickly, as they were able to follow up and speed up the process.
registration_success: I was very successful in registering for the classes I wanted, as the course registration process at UZH is easy and straightforward.
registration_advice: My advice to future exchange students is to go in with a clear idea of which courses you would like to take, and to start the course approval process as early as possible. Even though you can adjust your course choices during the first month at UZH, the formal approvals and paperwork can take time, so being prepared early makes the whole registration process much smoother.
academics_comments: Overall, my study experience in Zurich has been amazing. I’ve made some really good new friends, explored the local culture, and I can genuinely recommend Zurich as an exchange destination. At the same time, the academic level is very high, so it’s important to be prepared for a demanding workload and high expectations—but that is also a big part of what made the experience so valuable.
course_level: The level of the courses was generally very high. During my exchange I took a mix of courses – three at Master’s level and two at Bachelor’s level – and the workload reflected that. Since most courses are 6 ECTS, you typically need to take five courses in total, which makes for a full schedule.
teaching_comparison: The teaching style at UZH was quite similar to UCPH in structure, since most courses had both a weekly lecture and an exercise session. However, the exercise sessions worked a bit differently: you are expected to complete the problem sets in advance, because the Teaching Assistant mainly goes through the solutions in class. In that sense, the exercise class often feels more like an additional lecture where the TA presents the full solution methods rather than a session where you work through tasks during class. A very positive difference was that some courses were recorded, which was really helpful, since it gave me the option to rewatch lectures (and exercise sessions) and clarify things afterwards if I was uncertain about parts of the material.
courses_enrolled: Advanced Macroeconomics (L+E) (Master course at UZH) Advanced Microeconomics I (L+E) (Master course at UZH) Behavioral Finance (L +E) (Bachelor course) Markets, People, Politics (L&E) (Bachelor course) Advanced Corporate Finance I (L+E) (Master course)
recommended_courses: I would recommend Advanced Macroeconomics (L+E) and Advanced Microeconomics I (L+E), since they are core/mandatory courses within economics and fit well into an economics study plan. I would also recommend Behavioral Finance (L+E) because I found it genuinely interesting, and the teaching quality was high – the professor was very good, which made the course both engaging and rewarding. If you are studying economics, they will get two Nobel Prize winners in development economics from Summer 2026. Try their courses.
unexpected_costs: I did not really encounter any major unexpected costs. Most expenses were predictable, but one cost to be aware of is the registration/administrative fee when you register yourself after arrival, which was 55 CHF.
cost_comparison: Overall, everyday life in Zurich is simply expensive — it’s widely regarded as one of the most expensive cities in the world to visit and live in, which you notice quickly in day-to-day costs. This was especially noticeable when it came to food: meals at the university are pricey, and groceries can add up quickly. In particular, some vegetables in supermarkets can be surprisingly expensive, so it’s worth keeping an eye on prices and planning your shopping accordingly.
activities_available: A lot of cultural, athletic, and social activities were available for students, especially through ASVZ. Through ASVZ you can join almost any kind of sport; some activities are free, while others require a small fee. This is a really nice opportunity because it’s not only a great way to stay active, but also an easy way to meet other exchange students - and even Swiss students as well. Personally, I used ASVZ for tennis, where you sign up based on your level, which made it accessible and well organized.
activities_recommended: Attend the Polyball, which takes place at the end of November. Go to ASVZ sports activities and, if possible, taking language courses. Both are great ways to meet other exchange students in a natural setting, build a social network quickly, and feel more integrated in everyday life in Zurich beyond just the academic environment.
weekend_recommendations: On weekends or holidays, I would recommend spending time exploring Zurich itself. A boat trip on Lake Zurich is a really nice way to see the city from a different angle, and if you are there around Christmas, the Christmas markets are definitely worth visiting. I would also suggest walking around the old town (Altstadt), visiting the university areas (Law library), and seeing some of the city’s highlights like the Opera House. If the weather is good, take the Polybahn to the Polyterrasse (ETH) and enjoy a beer there.
culture_adjustment: Adjusting to the local culture was quite easy for me. In many ways, Swiss people are a bit similar to Danes – friendly and polite, but also fairly reserved, so I wouldn’t expect people to automatically reach out first. Once you take the initiative yourself, it becomes much easier to connect and feel comfortable in the local environment.
socializing_tips: Local students can be fairly reserved, so my main tip is to be proactive and not take it personally if people don’t reach out first. I would also strongly recommend signing up for a buddy program if it’s available – some buddies are really kind and can help you integrate by introducing you to their friends and inviting you into their social circles, which makes it much easier to meet locals. Otherwise through sports.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any major cultural differences particularly challenging. Swiss culture felt quite similar to Danish culture, and it was easy to adapt overall.
culture_appreciated: What I appreciated most about Swiss culture was the combination of amazing nature and a society that is extremely well organized. The outdoor opportunities are incredible. You can go hiking or even go skiing simply by taking the train, which makes it very easy to be active on weekends. At the same time, the infrastructure works really well: the train and tram system is efficient and reliable, and it feels like you can get everywhere quickly and smoothly.
top3_advice: 1. Start housing early and be prepared not to get a dorm. Many students don’t get a room through UZH (e.g., Meierwiesenstrasse), so begin looking well in advance and be careful with scams in Facebook WG groups. 2. Be prepared for a high academic level and a different exam format. The courses are demanding, and many exams are handwritten, sit-in exams (often around 1.5 hours), so you need to study consistently and not rely on last-minute preparation. 3. Plan your courses and approvals early, but use the first month wisely. Course registration is easy and you can change courses during the first month, but the Learning Agreement and approvals can take time—so come with a clear idea of what you want to take and start the approval process early to avoid stress.
other_useful_info: Be aware that Zurich is expensive, so budgeting matters – especially for food – and having a plan for housing and course approvals early can save a lot of stress.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was meeting Swiss people and getting to know locals beyond the exchange community. Building those connections made the stay feel much more authentic and helped me understand Swiss culture and everyday life in a way you don’t get as a tourist.
greatest_challenge: The greatest challenge during my exchange was studying for the exams. The academic level at UZH is very high, and preparing for the exam period was the toughest part of the entire exchange experience.
other_comments: I think that’s it - overall I’ve been really happy with the exchange and would definitely recommend Zurich

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere, where I could build on something language-culture-wise, so improving German was a big consideration. I considered Germany, but found this difficult as the semester periods were not well aligned with the Danish system. Furthermore, I wanted to go somewhere with access to hiking opportunities/nature.
info_ease: Rather easy, UZH has a good website and if I could'nt find the answer there, the professors and exchange coordinators were really quick at answering my emails. However, there is a lot of things to consider when going to Switzerland (outside of the EU), regarding mandatory health insurance, tax obligations, SEMP grant etc. But everyone was helpful, if I reached out.
arrival_assistance: There was info-sessions I could sign up for in the week before the semester started. Here I attended a mandatory info-meeting, a cultural workshop, a city tour and a library introduction. Only the info-meeting was mandatory, and here I also picked up my student ID. In addition to that I subscribed to the buddy-program, so I got teamed up with a Swiss political science student from Zurich and a German exchange student, with whom I really got a nice support. I can for sure recommend signing up for this. It of course always depends who you get paired with, but my experience was really positive, and I ended up being really good friends with them and having lunch together every Wednesday.
arrival_comments: UZH is really organized, but Switzerland is also quite old fashioned. I received my grant in cash, and a lot of communication with authorities when I arrived was by physical mail or at the city hall.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: They have an offer for exchange students, where you can be pre-placed at the courses, because they know it can be a puzzle. So I was well-informed by email and just had to sent my wishes to the exchange-coordinator and I got all the courses I asked for. Also, it is possible to change courses a month into the semester, if you are not satisfyed with a course. I did not do this, as I did not want to re-do the proccess with KU, but I know many who did this, and it was quite simple.
registration_help: The coordinators were very informative, so this part was not to difficult.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wished for.
registration_advice: Just calm down regarding this, they are super helpful, and it is my impression that they really prioritize exchange students. And you can even change within a month after the semester has begun.
course_level: It varied a lot from course to course. Generally the workload was spread out over the semester, which I found was nice. So I had to hand in different essays, questions, do presentations etc. during the semester. I would say the level and the syllabus on the courses I attended was lower than bachelor level at KU.
teaching_comparison: I only had seminars, and this can be compared with class-teaching (holdundervisning) at KU, just without a corresponding lecture. I would recommend to have a mix of lectures and seminars, also as the seminars demand a lot of participation and preparation which could be stress-full in some weeks with five seminars + a German course I took on the side. However, as I only had seminars, I have no exams in January, but exclusively term papers to hand in end December/start January. The work-load is quite a lot, but I like the flexibility of not having sit-in exams. I asked my professors about this already before I arrived in Zurich, and therefore planned my exchange to end at Christmas all along. From what I have heard, the lectures are pretty similar to KU.
courses_enrolled: Citizen representation in the EU (6 ECTS) China's Governance (6 ECTS) Switzerland in the modern world - More than cheese and chocolate (6 ECTS) Climate targets in Europe (6 ECTS) The political economy of culture (6 ECTS)
recommended_courses: Citizen representation in the EU (6 ECTS) - This was my favorite!! Really good discussions and I learned a lot about the EU institutions at the same time. The professor is such a good teacher and moderator, but I think he is going to Strassbourg, so maybe they won't offer this again :-(( China's Governance (6 ECTS) - This is a great course if your prior knowledge about China is small, the professor is really nice and encouraging, however it was a bit repetitive, as we did the same almost every week. Switzerland in the modern world - More than cheese and chocolate (6 ECTS) - This course is not super academic, but I really learned a lot about the Swiss history and political system. Also, excursions to voting ballots and a colonialism walk through Zurich was a part of the course. We too had some external presenters talking about migration in one session and gender equiality in another. Climate targets in Europe (6 ECTS) - I can NOT recommed this course. It was super unstructured and I was generally confused with the ends and evaluation criteria on the work we did. The political economy of culture (6 ECTS) - The readings in this course is super interesting and I used the term paper a bit as preperation for my bachelor thesis in the coming semester, as he focused a lot on methodology also. The professor is nice and considerate, but talks a lot. I enjoyed that it was a rather small class, we were eight students in total. Can be a bit much to have four hours in a row, but at the same time, there is only six meetings.
unexpected_costs: I got scammed with housing, so there I lost 6000DKK, and as a result my rent was a lot higher than I had expected it would be. I had to pay around 450 DKK, when I registered at the city hall.
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive, and I also think groceries are quite so. Regarding trasport, bars, restaurants etc. I find the price levels similar to Copenhagen - So not cheap, but I expected Zurich to be expensive.
activities_available: The Erasmus Student Network arranges a lot of things, I did not really go, but know a lot who went to cultural dinners, hikes, bar-meet-ups etc. At political science there is the association 'Polito', with whom I went on a trip to Geneva and visited the UN.
activities_recommended: I would STRONGLY recommend the sports-association ASVZ, which is free for exchange students. I did sports 3-4 times a week at center all around the city. It is super flexible and convinient, I just loved it. To mention some of the things I tried: Yoga, pilates, aerial yoga, jazz dance, t-bow balance, combat training, muscle pump, cycling (spinning), body forming, step arobic etc. This is the best, just try out as much as you can!!
weekend_recommendations: Explore the Alps!! I went on several hikes on sundays, as everything is closed on sundays. I also went skiing one weekend in Zermatt. You can save money on train tickets by booking in advance (or being under 25 years old) Go visit the other parts of Switzerland, and explore the linguistic and cultural differences in the small country. I went both to Geneva in the French-speaking part and Lugano in the Italian-speaking part. I also visited Luzern and Bern, which are both in the German part and wort a visit!
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, the Swiss are very closed in the public sphere, like in Scandinavia, perhaps even more reserved.
socializing_tips: Many students are super closed and quiet in the beginning, but I had luck making some Swiss friends by being super direct and suggest to have a coffee or study together. But they did not come to me, except for my buddy. The Swiss are very warm and kind, it just takes some time to warm them up.
cultural_challenges: Swiss German is really difficult to understand, but everyone speaks 'Hochdeutsch' and mostly also English. But you can get far by greeting people with 'Grüezi'! I found it a bit strange that everything was so old-fashioned regarding registration in the city, but it is an exiperience to go to the postal-office or go to the immigration office.
culture_appreciated: Their punctuality and that everything was so organized.
top3_advice: Bring a lot of money, attend a lot of free sports and register for a mix of seminars and lectures.
other_useful_info: If you study political science, don't expect the historical main campus as center for your classes. Our campus is right next to Oerlikon station.
most_rewarding: Meeting new friends, learning a lot about Switzerland and improving my German.
greatest_challenge: Finding housing

crucial_aspects: The courses, the language in the country and the nature.
overall_comments: Amazing student city and talented teachers.
