I felt that the university and teachers were very helpful if I had any issues. I had a few issues with the place I was staying at, but it got solved.
registration_process: I don't remember it to be a difficult process. I spend some time looking at possible subjects (you are only allowed to choose between subjects in the "exchange" subject catalog). You then have to apply for a max of 8-10 courses at VU in the beginning. They did not approve all of the classes that I applied for so it ended up taking some time for me to find classes that both VU and KU could approve. The way I understood it, you aren't allowed to take classes that are part of a research master, which limited the psychology courses that I could take. But I managed and both universities were of great help in the process. If I had any questions I could write to the "exchange officers", who were very sweet and helpful. They were also very quick at responding to my emails. VU would send out long e-mails with a lot of information about important deadlines and what to thing about before arriving.
registration_help: See comment above
registration_success: I wasn't allowed to take some classes, but I got all the classes that I (at the end) chose to take.
registration_advice: It might seem overwhelming and you'll need some logistical skills to put together your own plan for the semester. But it's more the pre-approval of subjects which can be an annoying process. You can sign up for a maximum of 6 subjects (you usually have 5 in total pr semester) and the different periods (there are 3) have different deadlines for registering. When a period starts you have 1 week to de-register. So in the first period, I signed up for three courses and tried out all three of them in the first week before choosing my final two classes for that period. You can do the same with periods 2 and 3, as long as you only signed up for a total of 6 classes at the same time. How it worked was, that VU would add the courses that I had sent to them (and that they had approved) to my plan. Then I could choose which classes to sign-up for.
academics_comments: In general, I had a really good experience with my exchange. I liked my classes, the level of teaching and workload was similar to KU. I felt that the university and teachers were very helpful if I had any issues. I had a few issues with the place I was staying at, but it got solved.
course_level: I think I only had master-level courses. Some were of a higher level, but I'm not sure I felt the difference as the courses, in general, were different.
teaching_comparison: They were similar. I had lectures, but also some classes with group work, which differed from each other. I also had one class where we did fieldwork on a goat farm, which I really enjoyed. It really depends on what classes you choose to have. Most classes have a good description, some more detailed than others.
courses_enrolled: Essentials of Media Psychology (instead of an elective) Sensemaking in Organization (instead of Work and Organizational Psychology) Changing Organizational Culture (instead of Work and Organizational Psychology) Disability and Development (instead of an elective) Advanced Organizational Research Skills (instead of advanced method)
recommended_courses: I found all of them very interesting. It was nice to have very different courses.
unexpected_costs: 10 euros for membership at the FAM association
cost_comparison: Public transport is similar to at home (so expensive). Some groceries were (either a bit or a lot) cheaper than in DK, incl. alcohol, soft drinks, coffee, etc. Activities and dining out were similar in price.
activities_available: There were a lot of different sports teams/activities that you could join. They also had drama, dance, and other types of creative classes on campus. There were different student associations that you could sign up for (some with a small members fee), some of which were connected to a specific faculty or study line.
activities_recommended: I signed up to become a member of the FAM association, where everyone is welcome. I paid a members fee of 10 euros for a year. They had a lot of different events throughout the semester and it was a nice way of meeting other internationals as well as Dutch people. If you would like to, the association will assign you a "family" (of 4-6 people) based on your interest. You'll then get a budget lasting a semester that you can spend on activities that you would like to do together as a family. I highly recommend doing this and becoming a member of FAM.
weekend_recommendations: Explore the city of Amsterdam and go to some of the museums as well as the city hall. Visit some of the cities nearby! There are so many pretty cities around Amsterdam (ex. Haarlem, Utrecht, den Haag, etc.). There are also castles and fortresses around Amsterdam. The public transport is good so it's easy to travel around.
culture_adjustment: The local culture doesn't differ that much from Danish culture. I just thought that it was funny to experience the differences, but I didn't experience a "cultural shock". However, the city (and the country in general) is very international, so there are people from all over the world – only those that are born in the Netherlands can have a nother cultural background.
socializing_tips: Sign up for a student association and the buddy program. That was how I got Dutch friends! And attend all different kinds of social events.
cultural_challenges: I found the traffic to be more chaotic than in DK. People are not following the "rules" as much so pay extra attention to that! Giving tips is kind of similar to ad home, but I felt like people were doing it more in the Netherlands than in DK. When arriving, I was told that a lot of Dutch people love their agenda/calender and that they like to plan stuff in advance. I didn't find it to be that extreme (similar to at home), but maybe still a good idea to keep that in mind.
culture_appreciated: The biking culture. I love to bike so it was great that i could continue to do that! The similarities in culture also made it easier to adapt and plan activities with others. I also liked that it isn't as formal (ex. the relationship between teacher and student) like it is in DK.
top3_advice: Have an open mind and be ready to experience and explore new things! Almost everyone speaks (at least some) English, but try to learn the most basic phrases in dutch. You only have to pass your subjects, because the grading systems are different and KU doesn't want to "translate" and transfer the grades. So all your subjects will just be a pass at KU (unless you don't pass a subjects ofc)
other_useful_info: Get a bike! Either buy a used one or sign up for Swapfiets. Get yourself an OV-card (dutch version of Rejsekort) and if you get a Dutch bank account you can sign up for a subscription that can give you some discount on public transport.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people from all over the world, as well as experiencing a new culture (as well as learning about other cultures from my friends), and exploring new cities!
greatest_challenge: I don't know. I didn't think that there were any great challenges during my stay.

unexpected_costs: Moving expenses.
cost_comparison: Housing and transportation
activities_available: There was a movie theater on campus, a sport center, many restaurants and bars.
activities_recommended: I did not participate in many activities on campus, as many of my friends did not live on campus but lived in the city. Therefore, most of the acitivities I would recommend are there. I would recommend getting a Museumkaart. You pay 60 euros and then you have access to all museums in the Netherlands for a year. I used that a lot as Amsterdam has many museums. I would also recommend visiting Bimhuis on Tuesday evenings. Here the students at the conservatory give free jazz concerts. This is a very fun event with a lot of other students and a cheap bar. It normally lasts till 1 am. I would also recommend going to the OBA libraries to study. They normally have a lot of good study-spots with nice views and good (cheap) coffee. In the fall they also have an event called Museumnacht, which is similar to the Danish Kulturnat. Here all the museums are open during the night and some of them almost turn into night clubs. About once a month there is also a fleamarket in IJhallen in Noord. This is the biggest fleamarket in Europe and is a very fun activity to due. I would definitely recommend going to Noord and experience that part of the town. It is a lesser known part of the city, but very fun and diverse.
weekend_recommendations: The same as above. I would also recommend visiting some of the other cities close to Amsterdam such as Leiden, Rotterdam, Utrecht, Haag and Haarlem. These cities are all very accessible and fun to see. I also rented a car for a day with some friends and drove through some of the country-side North of Amsterdam. I would definitely recommend that.

socializing_tips: Participate in the introduction week.
cultural_challenges: There were very little, but I did find another work-ethic with the people I met on exchange, and the Dutch people tend to be a bit more direct in my opinion.
culture_appreciated: The welcomming of internationals and the willingness to speak English and include other cultures. I think the Netherlands was very including and as an international it was easy to adjust.

other_useful_info: It is important to note that you need to be registered with the municipality. This is very important when finding a place to live, because of the big housing crisis there are many places where you can live but where the landlord do not let you register. This is illegal and can cause you a lot of problems. Therefore it is important to check beforehand if you can register at the address.
most_rewarding: The people I met.
greatest_challenge: Creating a new home that feels like home, knowing that you will leave it soon.

crucial_aspects: I visited Amsterdam before my exchange and I really liked the city and I could imagine myself living there. Additionally, I have heard a lot of good things about Dutch universities.
info_ease: It was a long and a bit complicated process to figure everything out before my exchange but it was really worth in the end. When I had any questions about the exchange I emailed either my home or host university and they always tried to help.
arrival_assistance: My university in Amsterdam had organized two days of practical introduction days where you could find many answers to questions about e.g. registration, insurance, language courses. Vrije Universiteit has a big and quite organized exchange programme, which is very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: My host uni sent me emails about all the steps I had to follow.
registration_help: You can always email the exchange office at the VU.
registration_success: I chose to register for a minor, which the host university suggested. I chose the minor Social and Organizational Psychology because I wanted to take some classes that were similar to A&O at KU, which I would have followed back home in the 5th semester.
registration_advice: By choosing a minor you won't have any subjects or exams that overlap and you will also see some of the same people in the different classes which can be quite nice and familiar.
course_level: I had a lot of multiple choice exams and I think the educational level at KU is a bit higher. I enjoyed that the courses, assignments and exam preparations did not take up so much.
teaching_comparison: It has a similar structure - I had both lectures and classes for most of the courses.
courses_enrolled: Evolutionary psychology M&D: Individual and Organizational Diagnosis Professional Skills Human Resource Management Group Dynamics
recommended_courses: I liked the course Professional Skills because it was so different from the courses that I have had at KU. It was very intimate and helpful because it was more practical (e.g. working on your networking and presentation skills) and entailed a lot of self-reflection.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Supermarket items are less expensive but going out for dinner or drinks is quite similar to DK. I can recommend to bike a lot as public transport is quite expensive over time.
activities_available: You can register for the gym and sports classes at uni.
activities_recommended: The university in Amsterdam has a great focus on sustainability. They have some great events and activities that revolve around that.
weekend_recommendations: I stayed a lot in Amsterdam over the weekends because there was so much to explore and so many great events I wanted to attend. It is also nice to go on a small trip to the beach which is really close or to Belgium.
culture_adjustment: It was easy to adjust because the Dutch culture is quite similar to the Danish culture.
socializing_tips: If you get a job in the city or do some group work with local students.
cultural_challenges: Biking in Amsterdam is more chaotic than in Copenhagen but you get used to it pretty quickly.
culture_appreciated: I think in general that the Dutch culture is very lively and laid back, which is nice to experience. Additionally, Amsterdam is very international which creates a great diverse atmosphere.
top3_advice: Try to explore many different areas in Amsterdam, as they all have something different to offer. Having a bike in Amsterdam is really helpful. It is nice to have some money saved up for your semester abroad so you can enjoy it fully and don't have to worry about money.
other_useful_info: Getting a Revolut bank account makes it easier to transfer money internationally.
most_rewarding: I got to know so many great people from all around the world and Amsterdam is just such a great city to live in. I would really recommend doing your exchange in Amsterdam!
greatest_challenge: I don't think there were any great challenges during my exchange. The registration process before your exchange can be difficult but it is worth it in the end.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to study in Amsterdam, so that was my main criterion. But I also wanted to be able to sign up for interesting courses, which VU indeed offered!
info_ease: The exchange committee did a great job sending out e-mails before I arrived in Amsterdam, which was very nice, and I thus knew where and how to seek out the information I needed in regard to housing and university. The webpage of VU is, however, a bit confusing and it was difficult to orientate in there when needing certain information and it took some time to get used to it.
arrival_assistance: We had an introduction day at VU where we had an introduction lecture with the head of the exchange team about the university and the Netherlands in general, as well as a guided tour around campus, and time to get to know the other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Registration through OnlineMobility, online learning agreement and pre-approval of courses, and then registration on VU's own webpage for registration and course which was quite easy and accessible.
registration_help: The exchange committee sent us e-mails continuously throughout the registration period and before arrival in Amsterdam, which was a nice help for the whole registration process.
registration_success: I was able to have most of the classes I wanted and had pre-approved from UCPH. However, the university did not have that many classes (taught in English) in their psychology department (my study area), why I had to sign up for a lot of classes outside my own field. This furthermore also meant that I could not find courses in Period 6, and thus had to take more courses in the two previous periods which was a bit tight and stressful.
registration_advice: VU offers a lot of very interesting courses and I was so happy myself with the courses I ended up with, but I would advice you to consider more courses than you might end up having as you might not ending up with your first choice.
course_level: Master's level
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching at VU was overall very similar to the teaching at UCPH but differed in the amount of presentations and assignments you had to make, and I did end up having to do presentations in all my classes as well as 1-2 assignments and finals (I had 5 courses). The structure of the semester was also very different from UCPH, which made the style of teaching different as you had to go through the curriculum in only 6 weeks before you then had exams and then starting a new period with new classes.
courses_enrolled: Philosophy of Mind, Brain and Behaviour Neurophilosophy and Psychiatry Diversity in Organizations Neuroethics and Society Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses of Psychological Interventions
recommended_courses: I would recommend Neurophilosophy & Psychiatry as well as Neuroethics & Society, which were both really interesting and I learned a lot of perspectives on questions regarding mental illness, neuropsychological perspectives, ethics in treatment and enhancement and much more. Furthermore, the course Diversity in Organizations was really great and had so much interesting readings and lectures, and I learned a lot about diversity, inclusion, equity, biases and more.
unexpected_costs: The costs of public transportation was way higher than it is in Denmark which took me a bit by surprise. I, however, ended up renting a bike (which I can really recommend) and thus only used public transport when needing it or not being able to bike to my destination.
cost_comparison: More expensive: - Public transportation - Food Less expensive: - Housing - Bike rent - Sports membership
activities_available: Cultural and social activities available through ESN (Erasmus Student Network) and the Buddy Program through which events were arranged and you could go on trips internally or outside the Netherlands as well. Athletic activities were available through the Sports Centrum which was located at campus and at the housing campus, where you got a lot of discount on a membership if you were a student at VU.
activities_recommended: If you want to experience Amsterdam and Europe, I would recommend ESN as a good way to do so.
weekend_recommendations: Visiting the local spots in Amsterdam, including museums (Stedelijk, Rijks, Moco, Van Gogh), markets (Noordermarkt, Leichengrach, Albert Cuijpt) as well as experiencing the canals and the inner city with the nine streets and old beautiful houses.
culture_adjustment: Amsterdam and the Netherlands in general is very similar to Denmark and Copenhagen, so I found it quite easy to adjust to life abroad. The biggest challenge was to adjust to the academic life and challenges as they differed a lot from UCPH.
socializing_tips: Sign up for student housing (living in a dorm really helped with a lot of socializing on daily basis) and join the activities offered by ESN and the Buddy Program.
cultural_challenges: I did not find the cultural differences that challenging. Mostly, it was the academic challenges that was most difficult to adjust to.
culture_appreciated: I really liked Amsterdam a lot and the city is so beautiful. I really appreciated spending 6 months there and adjusting to their lifestyle.
top3_advice: - Expect a lot of work to do at the university (especially if you are taking MA courses) - Use your weekends and holidays to explore the city as well as the surrounding areas and other cities, as the Netherlands really has a lot to offer. - Sign up for university housing - living in a dorm was a really nice way to have daily contact with other exchange students and have a community throughout your stay abroad.
other_useful_info: NO
most_rewarding: I really liked to experience of living abroad and getting to know a new city, culture, new people, a new university, and way to study, as well as getting to know people from all over the world. I would really recommend going on exchange if you are thinking about it.
greatest_challenge: Definitely the academic pressure. I loved the university and the courses I took throughout the semester, but the deadlines including many presentations and assignments was quite challenging for me to keep up with, which I was not prepared for.

The Anne Frank house is really nice and Museumsplein is a great place if you like museums) Go to Jordaan a really nice area with canals, nice shops and cozy cafés Go to the Albert Cuyp market. You can get some really good both dutch and non-dutch food and you should definetly get a freshly made stroop wafel Take a walk in the Pijp. Many nice restaurants, bars and cafées For partying Amsterdam has a great night-life as well. So if you enjoy partying take a night out and experience Amsterdam party life. If the weather is nice, then rent or borrow a bike and take a bikeride around the city. You get to see a lot of Amsterdam and experience it like a local on the bike.
culture_adjustment: Easy
socializing_tips: Join for everything possible in the beginning. That's how you met new people. However the dutch students are not that interested in socializing with internationals, so expect to make a lot of international friends and not that many dutch friends...
cultural_challenges: none
culture_appreciated: It's very similar to my home country, so that made it easy and nice to adapt.
top3_advice: 1. Try to find student accomodation where you meet other people. Dorms with shared kitchen is a good opportunity to meet new people when you're alone in a foreign country. 2. other_useful_info: It might feel a bit overwhelming at times especially in the beginning, but talk to the other exchange students (they definetly feel the same). And try to join as many activities as possible in the beggining, cause this is the time to socialize and meet people that you can hopefully enjoy the next 5-6 months with. most_rewarding: All the experiences and friendships I got from it
greatest_challenge: The way exams are done at VU and trying to balance new friends, new country and new university all at once

crucial_aspects: Social aspects and academic opportunities
info_ease: It was a difficult process, but Vrije University did a lot of webinars helping the process
arrival_assistance: We had a whole introduction day with a lot of information, which was good - but not a lot of follow up, and some of the information we got did not appear on Canvas, so when we needed the information we could not find it
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We had to apply for courses for the first period from November to mid January. It was first come, first served, which would have worked out fine for me if I was allowed to apply with a letter from my home university indicating I would finish my bachelor degree in January instead of my bachelor diploma (as I had to do master courses, and I was not done with my bachelor degree at the time of registration). The information of the courses were easy to find, but not always fully representable as I had a course where the professor messaged me after I was registered telling me that I was not able to take the course, as it was not my study area, but reading the course description I would be able to do it.
registration_help: The assistance regarding courses I received was bad. I was going on my exchange on my first semester on my master, which means that I had to do master courses. Unfortunately, I had not received my bachelor diploma before after the deadline of course registration, which meant that Vrije University would not accept my registration for my master courses. I had sent a letter from Copenhagen University indicating that I would finish my bachelor degree, but Vrije did not accept this. I had to figure out a solution myself, and I did not receive a lot of help in this chaotic proces. This resulted in me not being able to take one of the courses I needed to take from Copenhagen University, and therefore I could finish all 30 ECTS, but had to take 24 ECTS. I was very frustrated that they did not do a conditioned registration (that I could register for master courses on the condition that I passed my bachelor), as this means that I have to take extra courses in Copenhagen.
registration_success: Not very, as I described above - I had to find 2 bachelor courses in the first period instead of the master courses I planned to do, which made my process very difficult and unfortunately prevented me to do the courses I had to do
registration_advice: Have a lot of back up courses since the ones you plan to do might not be accepted
course_level: I had to do a mix of master and bachelor courses as I was not allowed to do master courses in the first period as I described above
teaching_comparison: At Vrije I think they are more generalizing (since they have periods, so you need to go through a lot of curriculum on a short time) while UCPH is more in depth (because of the semester structure)
courses_enrolled: Stress and health, Leading organizational change, Cross cultural management and Thought leadership in business (and field methods and linguistic analysis)
recommended_courses: Cross cultural management was very interesting, and it was a plus to have a different background as an exchange student as it made the course more relevant
unexpected_costs: I had to go to the doctor a couple of times, and the first time they did not accept my European Health card - therefore, I had to pay myself. This was unexpected
cost_comparison: The living expenses were close to the ones I am used to in Copenhagen, so most of it was just as I expected
activities_available: They had an Erasmus student network that organized a lot of social things for us as well as trips. Besides that, there was a sports center with a lot of classes and a fitness center
activities_recommended: The Erasmus student network was amazing in the beginning before you get your friends, so you can get to meet all the other exchange students
weekend_recommendations: Bike around the city and explore the less touristy areas - and find a lot of the cute bars, there are many
culture_adjustment: It was harder than expected as I thought my home culture was more similar than it actually was
socializing_tips: The Dutch people are happy to talk in class, so that is a good place to talk with locals
cultural_challenges: The straight forwardness and lack of patience in the culture
culture_appreciated: The openness towards others
top3_advice: 1) You learn many cultures as there are many exchange students coming to Amsterdam - so it is a multicultural environment, where you can learn a lot, so this is an amazing opportunity 2) The period system can be stressful as the periods are shorter than usual 3) The student dorms are a little out of the city, but it is a very nice place with green areas and nice people
other_useful_info: not that I can think off no
most_rewarding: Meeting other exchange students and learning a lot about myself and different cultures
greatest_challenge: To adapt to the culture, because I did not expect it to be so challenging

crucial_aspects: A good university, a place within the EU, a place to meet new people from different cultures
overall_comments: I have made many new connections with people, which has really been an enriching experience. However, the courses and school has been very demanding and difficult.
info_ease: Easy enough.
arrival_assistance: There were help to get both at university campus and dorm campus. However, I did not use it.
arrival_comments: They did not have enough spaces at orientation, tour, etc. for all exchange students, which I found very weird. You had to sign up way in advance to get a spot.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I have made many new connections with people, which has really been an enriching experience. However, the courses and school has been very demanding and difficult.
registration_process: You can register online.
registration_help: I do not know, help was not necessary. However, there was a pretty thorough description of the process on VU's website.
registration_success: I succesfully got enrolled into all my chosen courses. I did not have any issues. If I wanted to change workgroup, this was sometimes also possible, even after the course had started.
registration_advice: Do it in advance! I was a little late with officially registering for courses, which did end up becoming a bit of a stress factor.
academics_comments: I have made many new connections with people, which has really been an enriching experience. However, the courses and school has been very demanding and difficult.
course_level: They were more difficult than expected.
teaching_comparison: The style is quite similar, lectures and workgroups/tutorials (øvelsestimer). However, there were much more to prepare, and I had more assignments during the semester here. Also, the exam was not the only thing that counted for the final grade, assignments, attendance, etc. were also included. Additonally, all exams were closed-book exams, meaning you do not have any aid at all during the exam.
courses_enrolled: I took a minor called "Sustainability: Management and Innovation". It consisted of the five following courses: • Grand Challenges for Sustainability, 6 ECTS-points • Shared Value Creation, 6 ECTS-points • Organizing Sustainable Innovation, 6 ECTS-points • Sustainable Business Processes, 6 ECTS-points • Marketing Sustainable Innovations, 6 ECTS-points
recommended_courses: I can personally recommend Grand Challenges of Sustainability and Marketing Sustainable Innovations. I found these the most interesting, and the others I did not necessariliy care about.
unexpected_costs: My computer broke, so I had to pay for the reparation. Insurance covered most, but I had to pay the self-risk.
cost_comparison: Alcohol is cheaper than expected (especially wine at the grocery store). Public transport is more expensive than expected.
activities_available: They have a sport and cultural center. They also have student organizations you could join.
activities_recommended: The sport centre is a good place to attend classes or go to fitness, and it was on my dorm's campus which made it very easy to go.
weekend_recommendations: The museums here are great (personally I recommend Straat, Fabrique des Lumieres, Stedelijk, and van Gogh), and they have some cute cafés! Also, the canals and Vondelpark are a great place to go for a walk. And I personally fell in love with the area called Jordaan. Haarlemmerstraat (close to the central station) has some very nice secondhand shops that I often frequented.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. The Dutch culture is pretty similar to Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Not really, it was very hard actually meeting Dutch people here. I did make a few Dutch friends, but that was because we took some of the same courses.
cultural_challenges: I am used to a biking culture, however, people here bike without much discipline. They do not stop for pedestrians at cross walks, signal when taking a turn or similar. They bie as if they own the city, so be aware of that.
culture_appreciated: People here are in general much more open. They greet you and smile if you make eye contact, which is really nice.
top3_advice: 1. Go to as many social event in the beginning as possible! It really helps you network and get a social circle! 2. Of course you have to spend time studying, but also prioritize exploring Amsterdam and other cities close by! Enjoy that you are not in Denmark! However, please attend the lectures, they sometimes will provide information that's in the curriculum but you may not find online (in Canvas) otherwise!! 3. Remember to prioritize yourself! You will have a lot of new experiences here, which can be very enriching but also overwhelming. So taking time for yourself every once in a while is necessary.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: The people and connections that I have met here. I know that I have made friends for life because of this experience.
greatest_challenge: To manage the study load with the social life.

crucial_aspects: I chose Amsterdam due partly to academic opportunities, since they have some nice urban planning courses available, and party due to Amsterdam being a very international city with a lot of international students, meaning that i could get by fine with English.
info_ease: Very easy! I didn't have any problems.
arrival_assistance: During the introduction week, the university hosted a practical matters day, where international students could get everything they needed done, or get information on how to get it done. The exchange office was also pretty helpful if you contacted them.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Before registering for courses, you have to apply for approval for the courses you'd like, after which you can register for the courses you were approved for. You can both choose a minor or individual courses.
registration_help: There was a catalog of all the courses available to exchange students in the different faculties. Other than that, the exchange team were pretty easy to contact if you had any questions or problems.
registration_success: At first, i only got approved for 2 of the 8 courses i applied for. However, after some back and forth with the exchange team, i got approved for all but one course.
registration_advice: If you think you are eligible for the courses, make sure to ask again if you at first don't get approval! They overlooked some things in the first approval, but were pretty helpful once i asked again.
course_level: The level and workload of some of the courses was pretty low. In some ways this was pretty nice, since it meant i had time to do a lot of other stuff than just study, but for some of the courses the level was so low, that the courses were kind of unmotivating/uninteresting.
teaching_comparison: Pretty similar, especially for the courses from the social science faculty. There was a lot less group work though, and all the exams were individual except for one group presentation, which only made out a small percentage of our grade. Also, there were more multiple choice/essay based exams instead of the papers/projects i'm used to from UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Development and Globalization: Anthropological Perspectives; Urbanism and Landscape Architecture; Identity, Diversity and Inclusion; Urban Culture and Public Space; Designing Solutions for Global Sustainability
recommended_courses: I really loved Development and Globalization! The professor was really passionate and engaging, and the course material was really interesting. I also loved Urban Culture and Public Space. The professor was very engaging, and the course material was really interesting. For this course we had to write a paper based on fieldwork on a public space, which was really fun! I also really liked Urbanism and Landscape Architecture. The course material was very interesting, although the lectures were kind of boring, because they pretty much just went through the chapters assigned for each week. For this course we had to write a paper on the development of a city, which was also really fun!
unexpected_costs: Not much. Going out was pretty expensive both due to drinks being expensive and due to public transport stopping pretty early outside of the weekends, so we had to take ubers home quite often.
cost_comparison: Overall i think it was pretty similar to Copenhagen. I spent more on food, but i think that might have just been because i treated myself a bit haha
activities_available: There were some clubs available at the university, however i didn't really participate in them. There was a really nice gym though which had a lot of classes such as spinning, kickboxing, yoga, poledancing etc. There is also a buddy program, which i did actually sign up for. I think it was a pretty nice way of getting to know people, although i met a lot of people at the dorms, so after a while i didn't really participate in the activities through the program.
activities_recommended: Get a museum card! Amsterdam has a lot of really nice museums, and they can get quite expensive, so even though the museum card seems expensive at first, it pays for itself pretty quickly. Also, i really enjoyed the gym and the classes you could take through it.
weekend_recommendations: Amsterdam has a lot to see and do! I spent most of my weekends either going out, going to museums or going to some of the many markets (can recommend IJ Hallen). Otherwise, the Netherlands has a lot of really nice cities that are worth a visit! I only went to a few, but wish i went to more.
culture_adjustment: Very easy! Culturally, Denmark and the Netherlands are very similar.
socializing_tips: Good luck haha. I don't know, it can be pretty difficult unless you make a lot of effort. They are pretty nice though! There are so many exchange students though, so i mostly hung out with other internationals.
culture_appreciated: For the international students, i really liked how open everyone was to meeting new people and making new experiences.
top3_advice: Be open! There are so many people from a lot of different backgrounds that you can learn a lot from. Make the most of your time. It is pretty easy to get caught up in schoolwork, but make sure to take time to see and experience the city! There were a lot of things that i wanted to do, but never got around to. It can be a good idea to make lists of what you want to see and do, and don't be afraid of asking people if they want to join! Enjoy it! Exchange is an amazing and unique opportunity. Before you know, it's over :'(
other_useful_info: Probably obvious, but get a bike! Public transport is really expensive and biking around is a nice way to experience the city. You can find really cheap used ones online, although they can be pretty sketchy. Otherwise, Swapfiets is a good option.
most_rewarding: Getting to know people from all over the world. You make a lot of friends from different places, and visiting is a good excuse if you ever want to travel:)
greatest_challenge: Not having your usual support system and saying goodbye once it's all over.

crucial_aspects: I wanted a city which would feel like home. I had applied for a few different destinations in Europe and I'm happy I ended up in Amsterdam.
overall_comments: It was more difficult being away from home than I had anticipated.
info_ease: Very easy - VU is very structured and much easier and faster to get in contact with than KU.
arrival_assistance: There was a whole canvas page with all the information you needed. You could also go to the international office or write them an email. They usually respond within one day.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was more difficult being away from home than I had anticipated.
registration_process: You receive emails about all the steps you have to go through.
registration_help: You could call or email the international office.
registration_success: I successfully registered for all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Be aware that the uni has periods instead of semesters. This makes finding courses that don't overlap a bit more tricky, but as long as you keep it in mind, it will be fine.
academics_comments: It was more difficult being away from home than I had anticipated.
course_level: Some courses I took were first year level making them really easy because it was a lot of repetition from stuff I already learned at home, which was nice because there wasn't as much pressure. Other courses were very interesting because they were completely new to me, but then that of cause I had to spend more time studying for them. In general I would say that the level is not higher than at KU.
teaching_comparison: Nearly only lectures for all my classes, whereas we have more seminars as KU. The style is more interactive which is something you have to get used to. The seminars I did have were way less structured and not very helpful compared to KU. Also be aware that in some courses, attendance is mandatory.
courses_enrolled: P1: Comparative Politics: Democracies and Other Regimes (DAK) + Philosophy and the Ethics of Political Violence: Peace, War and Terrorism (valgfag) P2: EU Governance in an International Context (EP) + The Governance and Politics of Social Problems (DAK+EP) P3: Philosophy CIS L&S-MKDA (valgfag)
recommended_courses: All of them. Obviously you have to take the courses which substitute DAK and EP, but two of them were also really easy so that was great. I also liked both of my electives - the one in P1 because it is kind of like PT but with a twist and focus on conflicts and the one in P3 because it was focused on African philosophy which I thought was an interesting point of view.
unexpected_costs: Nothing.
cost_comparison: In general it is a little less expensive than in Denmark to get coffee or go out to eat at restaurants. Supermarkets are generally the same level of cost as in Denmark.
activities_available: There is a sportscenter at campus Uilenstede which has a lot of fun classes - I really recommend the zumba class, the pump class and the step class.
activities_recommended: I recommend going to classes at the sportscenter because you get to meet new people and it is also a fun way to hang out with your friends.
weekend_recommendations: Utrecht is a lovely city if you're looking for a trip out of Amsterdam. I spent most of my time in Amsterdam getting familiar with the city and going to cafes and restaurants with my friends, it is such a great city to wander around in! I recommend the areas De Pijp and Jordaan. Also I really enjoyed going to markets - there are tons of them all around the city on different days even during the winter.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, it is very similar to Denmark but you have to get used to the more aggressive way of biking.
socializing_tips: I didn't really do that.
cultural_challenges: That you cannot park your bike anywhere you want - there are specific places where you are allowed and the municipality will remove your bike if it's not in a certified place.
culture_appreciated: The markets, being able to bike everywhere, the quality of food.
top3_advice: 1. Try to get accommodation at Uilenstede, that's where you will find your friends 2. Be open and talk to people, everyone is there for the same purpose 3. Be excited that you're going to an amazing city that is easy to feel at home in
other_useful_info: I don't think so.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all over the world and getting to know everyone's cultures.
greatest_challenge: Homesickness
other_comments: Enjoy it!!

crucial_aspects: Academic and cultural aspects. The academic level af Vrije Universiteit is very good. And Amsterdam is a beautiful and interesting city to live in.
info_ease: The VU exchange team is very helpful and you receive plenty of information upon arrival. They are also extremely quick at responding to emails.
arrival_assistance: I received several emails concerning practical matters and student housing beforehand. I also attended a webinar on course selection for exchange students. The exchange team organizes an introduction week, where you also will be informed on many important matters.
arrival_comments: Going on exchange will always involve a great amount of dealing with bureaucracy and administrative work. But if you actively search for the information available, it is a lot easier.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: After accepting your mobility from KU, you register at your host institution before a certain date.
registration_help: Informational emails. I also wrote several emails to the exchange team at Vrije Universiteit and they were helpful and quick to respond.
registration_success: I was able to successfully register for all my classes.
registration_advice: Just be on time and look out for the dealines.
course_level: The Netherlands is overall recognized for a high academic level. My courses varied a lot in difficulty, some were easy and some were quite challenging. Look out for the course manual, which describes a certain amount of points for each course (100, 200 or 300). Courses with 300 are higher level. Passing a course with minimal effort is not always certain at Vrije Universiteit. But if you keep up with your lectures and readings, you will be fine.
teaching_comparison: In some of my smaller classes, the style of teaching was very engaging. It included group work, oral presentations, class debates etc. and i honestly found the style of teaching a lot more inspiring and motivating than at UCPH. However, most of my exams were multiple choice, which is very different from UCPH. So studying is mostly centered on just memorizing concepts
courses_enrolled: Comparative Politics: Democracies and Other Regimes EU Governance in an International Context The Governance and Politics of Social Problems Philosophy and the Ethics of Political Violence: Peace, War and Terrorism Philosophy CIS-L&SMKDA
recommended_courses: I can highly recommend the course Philosophy and the Ethics of Political Violence: Peace, War and Terrorism, taught by Prof. Dr. Fernando Enns and Dr. Andrés Pacheco Lozano. I genuinely enjoyed this course and i learned a lot. The two professors are very inspiring and engaging teachers.
unexpected_costs: Signing up for housing via DUWO. Paying for a bike subscription each month (but both costs are worth it)
cost_comparison: Housing was less expensive, as i signed up for a cheaper student housing option via DUWO.
activities_available: Many i think.
activities_recommended: I did not get involved.
weekend_recommendations: Enjoy the city's many parks, cafes, museums and markets. Visit the other famous Dutch cities nearby.
culture_adjustment: Very easy, Amsterdam is very similar to Copenhagen.
socializing_tips: Maybe not local students, but living in student housing makes it easy to socialize with other international exchange students.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really.
culture_appreciated: Very nice food markets and flee markets every weekend.
top3_advice: 1) enjoy what Amsterdam has to offer 2) live in the student dorms if you want to meet new people and socialize with people from different cultures 3) do not stress too much about school and enjoy your time
other_useful_info: It can seem overwhelming having many courses (5 in one semester) and having exams and mid-terms quite often. But in reality i never felt stressed a single time and everything worked out fine.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from many different cultures, making new friends and gaining new perspectives.
greatest_challenge: Bureaucracy and administration work from my sending institution.
other_comments: I highly recommend going on exchange to everyone!

crucial_aspects: The courses available, how good at english they were in host country, how organised they seemed both online and via e-mail.
info_ease: Very easy, Vrije Universiteit did a lot to make everything easy to figure out, and they very quick to respond over e-mail - super helpful!
arrival_assistance: They helped a lot with practical matters in the the intro week; registering with the municipality, signing Erasmus papers, housing, where to find help etc.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: So many steps, so many things to fill out and upload. It felt like a part-time job. But in the end I think that its just the exchange experience, and what everyone probably goes through.
registration_help: I could e-mail my host and sending universities (which I did a lot), and also some information was available online.
registration_success: Very successful, I got all of the courses I needed and wanted. And I found out immediately when i registered for them, which was super nice - no waiting time at VU.
registration_advice: Even though they open course registration quite late, in my experience, everyone got the courses they wanted, so be patient and know that it will all sort itself out. Also send e-mails to the incoming team, research yourself online on their website. They had quite a lot of information there aswell. They also had a webinar on the course registration which was super helpful.
course_level: I found the courses to be super hard. Prepare yourself for a lot of work. There is a lot more homework, assignments, group work and weekly tests, that I am not used to at my home university. I spent a lot more time on uni during my exchange than I have done at my home university.
teaching_comparison: much more group work, more "homework", more assignments, less lectures and more class. But I did have fewer lectures/classes overall compared to my home university, meaning that I had to be at uni less than I am used to.
courses_enrolled: Current Topics in Cognition, Evolutionary Psychology, Research Toolbox, Identity, Diversity and Inclusion & Group Dynamics.
recommended_courses: Evolutionary Psychology and Research Toolbox were the least work out of all of the courses I had, and Current Topics in Cognition and Identity, Diversity and inclusion were the most work out of all of the courses I had. Groups Dynamics was in between. I mostly enjoyed the course Identity, Diversity and Inclusion even though it was a bit more work. It was super interesting and the lecturer was really good.
unexpected_costs: There is a mandatory garbage and water bill, which are a bit expensive. I think the garbage bill (for the 6 months) was around 1000 DKK and the water bill was around 650 DKK.
cost_comparison: Going out is a bit cheaper than in Denmark, eating at restaurants and going to bars costs less money. Groceries are more expensive than in Denmark.
activities_available: So many! Both clubs, sports, support groups etc.
activities_recommended: Get a bike and bike around, its so easy and really nice to bike near the water. Also theres a really nice study cafe called NIO, that i wish I had found earlier than I did.
weekend_recommendations: Do a boat tour, do the Heineken Experience, bike through Vondelpark, see the Highland Cows in Amsterdamse Bos, go to Papeneiland for the famous apple tart. There are also so many nice cafes, restaurants bars. Especially in the areas Joordan and Bilderdijkstraat. Do day trips - my favorites were: Utrecht, Haag, Leiden, Zaandam.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. Amsterdam is very similar to Copenhagen. The Dutch people are great at english and super nice. The exchange students are all looking to make friends, so they are also super friendly and open.
socializing_tips: Go to the ESN events. There are so many espescially in the beginning. They do bar crawls, kaaroke night, city tour etc. and its very cheap to participate. Also the intro week hosted by the university is where I met all of my friends, so I would really recommend that you participate in that. Its one full week with a lot of different opportunities to meet people.
cultural_challenges: Nothing really.
culture_appreciated: The biking
top3_advice: You will find housing. Everyone I know on exchange in Amsterdam got housing through the university. Dont worry. You will get the courses that you need, even if it is last minute. Amsterdam is such a lovely city, get a bike and drive around. Its the easiest way to get around.
other_useful_info: I really recommend living in the Cornelis Lelylaan building near Lelylaan station. It was a perfect location.
most_rewarding: Finding friends from all over the world. Learning many new things about different countries and cultures. Living and becoming familiar with Amsterdam.
greatest_challenge: The courses and the amount of work I spend on uni. I had not expected that.

crucial_aspects: Minor in Geo-information Science. The opportunity to have a more GIS related profile.
info_ease: Very easy.
arrival_assistance: I participated in the introduction days, which was very helpful.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There was a great fact sheet available after acceptance, this described the necesary details. The process was really intuitive. The courses were easily registered together with introduction days etc. It's clear to see that WUR is very fond of having international students.
registration_help: The Erasmus coordinator at Wageningen University and Research.
registration_success: I had all the courses I wished for.
registration_advice: If you are going for the GIS minor, but don't have ArcGIS Pro skills (even if you have Qgis skills), take the introduction course in combination with Python for beginners for example. It's very specific, yet I did struggle a bit in the beginning, because I only knew Qgis. Python is also VERY useful in the other courses in the minor. I would have wished I had taken that combo.
course_level: The level of the courses is good for getting a proper introduction to Geoinformation science, when you are not a student of geography which was the case for me.
teaching_comparison: A little more tutorial based and less focus on showing before doing. Personally, I prefer the way at the courses I have had I GIS at my home university, that might be due to being used to that. To me it gives a better flow when the lecturer is explaining what and why he or she does what is done. That also leave more time to learn more because there is less 'self-study'. It's a tradeoff, because figuring thing out yourself from a tutorial also is a good way to learn. To compare I must say I feel like the GIS course I've taken on CPH university has covered more topics. Also, in comparison to the difference on only 1,5 ECTS point from a typical WUR course.

activities_recommended: Join a sports club.
weekend_recommendations: Due to Covid the opportunities has been limited. However the Netherlands has old big charming cities, like Utrecht, Nijmegen, Arnhem, Amsterdam etc. The vibe in these are very nice. Go explore!

socializing_tips: Join a sports association and CERES the study association.
cultural_challenges: None. However the density is quite high in the Netherlands in comparison to Denmark, so don't expect to be much alone, not even on a walk in the forest. That was a little challenging.
culture_appreciated: The openness. It was very easy to make friends and feel included.
top3_advice: Be early with finding accomodation. Get the access pass to the sports centre de Bongerd. Find a way to meditate other than taking a lonely walk in the forest. You might not be lonely!

It's very impressive (also the indoor garden at Lumen).

crucial_aspects: I originally wanted to go to Australia but because of corona this was not possible. I researched my opportunities for exchange in Europe and found Wageningen University and Research in the Netherlands. I was very impressed of the pictures of the campus with a lot of modern buildings and plants. Furthermore, it was described as a very international university with one of the best ratings among life sciences.
info_ease: It was very easy. Mails were sent and I was immediately assigned to a buddy program which is part of the AID where I got to learn to know people from abroad and from the Netherlands. We were assigned to two mentors who showed us campus, the city and who were open for questions. We went to do activities together both planned from the university and planned from the mentors.
arrival_assistance: I got help from my buddy mentors and I could always write to the exchange coordinator from the university.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Course registration is done through a platform called osiris.nl where you can read a small course description, a description of the exam and what is expected of you as a student. This is also where you sign up for courses. It was quite straight forward.
registration_help: The exchange coordinator could always be contacted if there were problems.
registration_success: Very successful. I got all the courses I wanted. I signed up from the beginning for the whole exchange period and was put on waiting lists for several of them. When the next period came closer I was accepted to the course. Some courses are mandatory for people of specific studies so these may be difficult to join, but if you sing up early it should be possible.
registration_advice: I can reccomend the Genomics couse. I cannot recommend the Plant biotechnology course.
course_level: The level of the exam matched what was tought in the course. Also all the courses start off by explaining very trivial material as it is supposed to be possible to follow courses from all types of studies. However, the exam for the course Plant biotechnology did not match what was tought in the lectures and during the practicals. The level of the exam was much too high and covered subjects not covered in the lectures. More than half of the students failed this course. I do not recommend it.
teaching_comparison: The days are much longer than at KU and sometimes I had classes from 8 in the morning til 18. However, there is almost always a 2h break in the middle of the day to meet up with friends or do sports. The long days also meant that the weekends were mostly free to be used for parties, meeting with friends or traveling.
courses_enrolled: Genetic Analysis Trends and Concepts Introduction to bioinformatics Plant biotechnology Genomics Plants and Health 1
recommended_courses: Genetic Analysis Trends and Concepts - it was really interesting with a lot of lab work regarding genetic traits and enthusiastic teachers. Genomics - it was a nice introduction to bioinformatics and the teacher was really nice.
unexpected_costs: Router had to be bought
cost_comparison: The food was much less expensive than in Denmark. Also all the stores and supermarkets were much cheaper. Public transport was very expensive. If you have a personal OV card it gets cheaper though. Then you have to have a dutch bank account.
activities_available: There were a lot of different associations which I could join, who organized a lot of social events.
activities_recommended: Especially the international organisations ESN and ISOW are good to join as an exchange student to get to know other people. Also, really nice sports facilities were available for a cheap fee.
weekend_recommendations: Visit the market and the Rijn. Go traveling. Go to parties at the international club and house parties.
culture_adjustment: It was very easy as dutch culture is very similar to danish culture. Dutch people are much more open than danish people which makes it easier to socialize with them.
socializing_tips: Socialising with the dutchies is possible at group work or at house parties.
cultural_challenges: There were not really cultural differences.
culture_appreciated: Dutch people are very open to meeting new people.
top3_advice: Say yes to all the opportunities especially at the beginning. It can be really overwhelming but I think you get used to being social and you learn a lot from it.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of new people and traveling a lot. The Netherlands is a very nice country with beautiful nature and it is located very central in Europe so it is easy to visit all the neighboring contries.
greatest_challenge: Failing a course.
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: A nice place to live and interesting courses at the university.
info_ease: Easy. The university in the Netherlands was very good at informing me about anything I needed to know, and there were also Whatsapp groups where you could ask any questions you had.
arrival_assistance: None as I just did everything myself, but they offered to meet you at the train station. A week or two later, there were also meetings at the university where they informed you about practical things like finding a doctor, using the university's intranet etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You find the courses you would like to take in the course catalogue, and then you choose them in Osiris, and you get a message/mail saying whether you have been accepted or not. Pretty similar to how it works at ku.
registration_help: You could ask questions in the Whatsapp group, and they also told a little bit about it in an email. You could probably also ask at the student service desk.
registration_success: I got all the courses I wanted to take, but I also did not apply to any courses with a limited number of seats where students from particular programmes had priority.
registration_advice: If you want to sign up for courses with a limited number of seats, make sure you sign up early, and also just keep the deadlines in mind in general.
course_level: I primarily took masters courses, but it was easy enough to keep up. I think the level is quite similar to ku. Some of the courses were meant for multiple different study programmes, which meant that they sometimes spent time explaining things that would be quite basic to some people to make sure that everyone understood what was going on. The practicals in the lab and the tutorials where we used Excel or different softwares were very good.
teaching_comparison: Lectures and tutorials were similar. The lab practicals were also similar, although some of them were more "free" as you just got a research problem/question and then had to plan the experiments yourself (with help/assistance from a teacher). Generally, we had more classes that I am used to (around 5 hours every day), but then we had less reading/preparation to do.
courses_enrolled: Life history of aquatic organisms, Microbial ecology, Molecular aspects of bio-interactions, Seed science and technology, and Wildlife ecology and conservation.
recommended_courses: I would recommend all the courses as they were all interesting, although Microbial ecology had quite a lot of overlap with the course Almen mikrobiologi at ku, and Life history of aquatic organisms also used a lot of time to explain concepts that most biology students already know (like natural selection).
unexpected_costs: I got an unfurnished room, so I had to buy furniture, curtains, etc.
cost_comparison: Conventional food was quite cheap, but some organic groceries were expensive. I also only had to buy one book in total while being there, so it was nice not having to spend much money on that.
activities_available: Many different types of sport at the university sports centre, the different student associations also hosted parties every week, and there were also some other events for students besides that from time to time like story telling evenings, talks, dinners, and farm visits.
activities_recommended: Join classes or teams at the sports centre (membership is extremely cheap). I also took an intensive one-week beginners Dutch class shortly after I arrived which was fun as you learned a little bit about the language and also got to meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: Visit some of the different cities/towns in the Netherlands as it is quick to get around with the train, and also see some of the nature around Wageningen.
culture_adjustment: Easy, it is very similar to Danish culture.
socializing_tips: Same as in Denmark.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Easy to talk with, helpful.
top3_advice: 1: Wageningen is a pretty small town, so not much happens there besides student activities, but it is easy/quick to get to other cities with more things to do. 2: Start looking for housing early as it can be very difficult, in my opinion using Idealis is best. But also do not worry if you only find something shortly before your arrival as that is the case for many people. You can get priority on Idealis' website a month or so before your arrival, and after I got that, I quickly found a room. 3: Do not worry too much about the exams as it is easy enough to pass.
other_useful_info: The train company NS has a weekend offer where you get unlimited travel during the weekends for only around 31 euros pr month.
most_rewarding: Trying to study at a different university in a different environment, and also meeting people from different cultures.
greatest_challenge: I was always worrying about the exams, but I ended up doing fine after all.

crucial_aspects: Wageningen University & Research has a great reputation in sustainability and life sciences, which fits my studies really well. I also liked the very international student community and the fact that the Netherlands is a safe, well-organized country with easy travel around Europe. Overall, Wageningen felt like a welcoming, student-friendly place to live and study.
info_ease: I would say it was fairly easy, there was a lot of emails with information. But you get the information really last minute.
arrival_assistance: When I arrived, I received mostly general information and practical advice from Wageningen University & Research, like guidance on housing, registration, transport, and daily life in the Netherlands. It wasn’t very detailed, but it was helpful for settling in and understanding how things work here.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration process at Wageningen University & Research was pretty easy and straightforward through the online system. The website guides you step by step, and exchange students are often recommended to follow a minor, which is kind of pre-planned and makes course selection easier. You do need to check yourself that classes don’t overlap.
registration_help: There was good support available if needed. You can email the exchange coordinators, and they are helpful with questions about courses, registration, or issues with learning agreements. The website itself also explains most things clearly.
registration_success: Overall, I was successful in registering for the courses I wanted. Not all courses are open to exchange students, but there are still many options, and almost all courses are taught in English.
registration_advice: My advice would be to double-check course codes and schedules after registering, especially for your online learning agreement. Make sure your courses don’t overlap, and honestly pick courses you’re interested in. If you’re unsure about anything, don’t hesitate to contact the exchange coordinators for help.
course_level: I took a mix of Bachelor- and Master-level courses at WUR. Overall, the level varied quite a lot. Some first-year Bachelor courses felt much easier than what I was used to, mainly because students start specializing earlier here. At the same time, higher-level courses were more demanding and required continuous work. The workload was generally high, even when the academic level felt lower, because of many assignments and group projects.
teaching_comparison: Compared to UCPH, teaching at Wageningen is much more focused on case studies, group work, and practical projects rather than lectures and final exams. There are fewer traditional exams and more continuous assessment, which means more weekly work but less exam pressure. It felt more applied and hands-on than at UCPH.
courses_enrolled: Introduction to Marine Sciences Adaptation and Mitigation Services for Society Introduction to Enviromental Analysis Sustainability Transistions: Past, Present and Future Adaptation to Climate Change
recommended_courses: I would recommend choosing a minor (course package) within a subject you’re genuinely interested in, as it gives structure and coherence to your semester. In general, courses with case studies and group projects are very engaging and help you apply theory to real-world problems. I’d also recommend avoiding very basic first-year courses unless you need them, as they may feel too easy compared to higher-level options.
unexpected_costs: One unexpected cost was how expensive public transport in the Netherlands is. I ended up spending more than expected on buses and trains, especially at the beginning before settling in. I suggest buying a used bike, saves you a lot of money.
cost_comparison: Overall, daily expenses were higher than I expected, especially groceries and transport. Public transport in particular was surprisingly expensive, so I would strongly recommend getting a bike as soon as possible, it’s much cheaper and also the most common way students get around. Groceries are kinda the same price as in denmark.
activities_available: At WUR there are a lot of cultural, sports, and social activities, honestly almost anything you can think of. There are many student sports clubs, cultural associations, parties, and events, and most of them are also open to exchange students, which makes it easy to get involved.
activities_recommended: I’d really recommend joining ESN Wageningen. It’s a great space for exchange students to meet each other, and they organize lots of events, parties, and social activities. They also sometimes arrange trips to other cities or even other countries, which is a fun and easy way to travel while meeting people.
weekend_recommendations: I’d recommend traveling around the Netherlands and nearby countries—cities like Amsterdam, Utrecht, or Rotterdam are easy to reach. Because the Netherlands is so well connected, it’s also perfect for weekend trips to places like Belgium or Germany. Even staying local is nice too, biking around Wageningen and enjoying nature is very underrated.
culture_adjustment: It was pretty easy overall to adjust at WUR. The environment is very international, so you don’t really feel out of place as an exchange student. Day-to-day life felt comfortable quite quickly.
socializing_tips: Honestly, I ended up making mostly international and exchange student friends, mainly because everyone is actively looking to meet new people. Dutch students can be friendly but tend to already have their social circles and keep a bit to themselves. Joining student associations, group projects, or social events helps, but it’s totally normal if most of your friends end up being international.
cultural_challenges: One thing I noticed was that Dutch students start university earlier than in Denmark, so many of them are quite young, which is sometimes noticeable in group work or social settings. I also never really learned Dutch, since almost everything was in English and I mostly spoke English with other internationals.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated how open, direct, and international the environment is. Almost everyone speaks English, which makes life very easy as an exchange student. I also liked the relaxed student lifestyle and the strong biking culture—it makes everyday life simple and enjoyable.
top3_advice: Remember you’re not only there to study—make time to explore the Netherlands and travel around Europe. Don’t stress too much about making friends; it happens naturally, especially with other exchange and international students. Be prepared to be independent, there is help available, but you’ll also have to figure out many things on your own.
other_useful_info: Even though WUR is very organized, daily life still requires initiative. Join activities, talk to people, and use the connections you make, other students are often your best source of help and advice.
most_rewarding: Meeting people from all over the world and building friendships through shared experiences. Living in such an international environment really broadens your perspective, both academically and personally.
greatest_challenge: Probably finding the right balance between studying and enjoying the exchange. I sometimes focused a bit too much on academics and had to remind myself to slow down and enjoy the experience outside university as well.

crucial_aspects: Prior to studying abroad, I had always been interested in Japanese culture and had visited the country before. I saw it as great opportunity to broaden my worldview, explore an interesting culture and also gain new academic knowledge. Additionally, it will enhance career opportunities.
overall_comments: I had a wonderful time overall. I gained a lot of new friendships, broadened my understanding of the world and traveled a lot around Japan. If you're interested in traveling to other Asian countries, that's also possible. The only major negative thing affecting my rating would be the amount of subjects relevant to my major, but I then had the opportunity to try other interesting courses.
info_ease: They provided a student handbook with a lot of information and had an office one could go for help, however I was still confused about some aspects.
arrival_assistance: There was a ceremony and Zoom meeting, however I was confused about some aspects of the course registrations because it was so different. They did not disclose how many courses I needed, and neither could KU, which created a lot of trouble getting my courses accepted for credits. So for almost 4 months I did not know whether my courses would count for credits or not.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had a wonderful time overall. I gained a lot of new friendships, broadened my understanding of the world and traveled a lot around Japan. If you're interested in traveling to other Asian countries, that's also possible. The only major negative thing affecting my rating would be the amount of subjects relevant to my major, but I then had the opportunity to try other interesting courses.
registration_process: It's an online lottery system which is very confusing. You don't know whether you will get the courses you applied for or not, so the right strategy is to apply to as many as possible so you can drop courses after gaining a spot (there are several rounds). I did not know this strategy, which resulted in not getting some courses I really wanted.
registration_help: Not a lot. I had to ask fellow students for help.
registration_success: I got most of what I wanted (although it was very limited for my major), but I did not receive one specific course I really wanted, sadly.
registration_advice: Apply for as many courses as possible and then drop the ones you don't need/want after.
academics_comments: I had a wonderful time overall. I gained a lot of new friendships, broadened my understanding of the world and traveled a lot around Japan. If you're interested in traveling to other Asian countries, that's also possible. The only major negative thing affecting my rating would be the amount of subjects relevant to my major, but I then had the opportunity to try other interesting courses.
course_level: My graduate school is an English program, so 9/10 were international students. This means a lot of different English levels, which can affect the quality of discussions. I would say the overall course level is a bit lower, and the grading is a lot easier than in Denmark.
teaching_comparison: Very different. At KU, I'm used to 1 presentations per course per semester, but at Waseda I had a lot more, but it depends on the courses, of course. I'm also used to not having a lot of assignments, but since you have more courses at Waseda, the workload is spread out and you have more homework per week. I had 17 assignments in total, 8 presentations and 4 final term papers.
courses_enrolled: Language and Mind, Cultural Critical Theories 2, International Cooperation and Peacebuilding and Race and Ethnicity.
recommended_courses: International Cooperation and Peacebuilding was nice because you gained a wider perspective of the world.
unexpected_costs: The high cost of housing is mainly due to the entrance fees, management fees, cleaning fees etc. For the boarding itself, it was only around 5300 kr. a month. I also had to pay for a VPN in order to bypass some censorship from the Japanese government.
cost_comparison: Fruit and vegetables are expensive. Eating out is affordable (25-75 kr). Domestic traveling can be very expensive, but it depends on the transportation chosen. Getting to Japan can be very expensive due to the distance. Phone plan is expensive and data is very slow in urban places.
activities_available: Plenty of sports circles.
activities_recommended: Sports clubs, the language and culture exchange buddy program in order to gain more friendships since it can be a little difficult with Japanese people (just like it is in Denmark!)
weekend_recommendations: Go to an izakaya with friends, explore cafés and museums. See some of the 80.000 shrines and travel around the country, even for day trips outside Tokyo. Each city is known for something else.
culture_adjustment: I was pretty familiar with Japanese culture but I still had to get used to the way of communicating (despite reading about it) and the usage of cash, slow bureaucracy and print-based systems. The social rules are very strong and you are expected to follow them, or else there will be consequences.
socializing_tips: Put yourself out there. Befriend someone they know to have a common link or join a club you can bond through. Join a buddy program.
cultural_challenges: Indirect communication, strict rules about what is considered rude (don't eat/drink while walking, certain way of eating, greetings, etc.). Not helping strangers in need.
culture_appreciated: Order and punctuality.
top3_advice: (1) Prioritize your time right or you will run out of time to explore Japan. (2) Make local friends, they will enhance your experience of the country a lot. The possible friendships are truly wonderful. (3) Learn at least some basic Japanese or you will struggle.
other_useful_info: Get a credit or debit card capable of using Yen. I used WISE to convert DKK to Yen. It will save you a lot of transaction fees.
most_rewarding: New relationships and wonderful memories. You also become a lot more open-minded and independent.
greatest_challenge: Not seeing loved-ones at home and doing everything by yourself in a different language.
other_comments: Remember that you represent a country and am a guest. Respect the local culture.
