In one course, I just had to do 4 30-minute quizzes during the semester, and that was it. In general, I spent probably 15-18 hours a week studying, which is a A LOT less than at UCPH.
teaching_comparison: The in-person classes were very small, maybe 8-10 people max. This made room for a lot of interaction with the teachers, which was great. There are no exercise classes, but the lectures feel like a mix of the two because of the high level of interaction. However, half my courses were on zoom. Anyone who has done classes on Zoom probably knows how boring it is, so I would not recommend taking these classes if you can avoid it.
courses_enrolled: Population Economics Statistical Finance Experimental Economics Applied Microeconometrics Market Design
recommended_courses: Experimental Economics was very interesting, and the teacher is fantastic. I would definitely recommend this course. Statistical Finance was interesting, and the quizzes mean you actually learn a lot. Even though it was on Zoom I did feel like the teacher made a good effort and I learned quite a bit. I would definitely recommend on taking the Japanese zero course (japanese language learning for people on level 0). I did not take it, and that is a big regret of mine.
unexpected_costs: You have to enroll in Japanese health insurance. This is not very expensive, maybe 200 kr. per month, but I did not expect it.
cost_comparison: Transport was less expensive than I thought. One thing to note is that all my transport fees were not actually university-related, since I could walk to uni in 5 minutes.
activities_available: Many different ones. Some I looked at were a temple-outing club, a formula 1 club, and a karate club.
activities_recommended: I did not really participate in any university-related non-academic activities.
weekend_recommendations: I would definitely recommend taking day-trips out of Tokyo to the various mountains and hills that you can hike on, such as Mount Takao and Mount Mitake. It is also quite easy to take longer trips to other cities, such as Hiroshima, Kyoto, Nikko, and Kanazawa due to the bullet train. In general, Japan is a great place to explore and I would recommend you do this :)
culture_adjustment: Easy, as I had been to Japan before. The most difficult thing is the language barrier. Not many speak good English, so you will have to get used to communicating with facial expressions, your hands and simple words. In the end, it wasn't that difficult and I quickly got used to it.
socializing_tips: I imagine joining a club is the easiest way.
cultural_challenges: Again, the language barrier. I would definitely recommend getting a translator app (such as google translate). You will sometimes experience people that speak no English, or menu cards that are only in Japanese. In these situations, my translator app was crucial. Google maps was also very handy for transport (like rejseplanen).
culture_appreciated: The politeness and service-level of the Japanese are incredible. I loved the food and I loved the temples and religious sites.
top3_advice: -Take time to travel around. -Live in a dorm -Accept that you will not always know what is going on, that people will speak to you in a language you do not understand, but just go with the flow and everything will be fine :)
other_useful_info: Bring deodorant, it is impossible to find.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and making friends all over the world. I would definitely recommend staying in an international dorm, for this reason. Other than that, I loved traveling around Japan, experiencing the amazing food, nature and cultural sites.
greatest_challenge: Language.
other_comments: I loved it, best 5 months ever.

crucial_aspects: As my major is Japan studies, going abroad to Japan is the obvious choice. I specifically wanted to go to improve my spoken abilities, so I wanted to be submerged in the language.
info_ease: Once I arrived everything was easy to figure out.
arrival_assistance: I got access to the last needed information, but I'm not sure if that counts?
arrival_comments: I was expecting more in-person orientation. I felt a little overlooked, especially before arriving, as the number of short term exchange students seemed pretty low and most international students seemed to last the entire semester. Covid was probably a factor, as it was very hard to get a visa for Japan, so most people didn't expect to be able to go.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There are three rounds of registration. In the first two rounds you can apply to classes and drop them, while in the third round you can only drop classes at my department. (I was not aware of the detail about the third round until very late). (For Japanese classes you could thankfully still add in the last round.) If you know how to play the system, you apply to every single interesting class in the first round instead of only taking the required number. This is especially true for Japanese classes that fill up quickly. It very quickly becomes a very stressful gamble if you only try to cover your holes and don't overcommit initially.
registration_help: There was a list of number of spots left (that I only found prior to the third round), but even though I came to them in tears, the administrators were unable or unwilling to promise me a spot (or promise to only give me one spot even if I applied to plenty in the last round). All they did was help me find classes that seemed unlikely to fill up.
registration_success: Despite all that stress, I'm pretty satisfied with the classes I ended up with. The main problem initially was that three of the four most interesting classes were at the same time, so I had to find some back ups.
registration_advice: Apply to every single interesting class in the first round instead of only taking the required number. Then you can whittle it down in the next two rounds. If you don't get your most desired class in the first round, you can non-stressfully apply again in the second (others may have dropped it), if you know you have enough credits to cover your requirements already.
course_level: It was comparable.
teaching_comparison: It was a lot more student led presentations. I really, really enjoyed that we could work on our grades during the semester as it made exam period way less stressful.
courses_enrolled: Language and Society, Language and Mind, Structure of Language, Discuss Documentary and News Programs in Japanese, Analyzing Japan through Public Advertisement
recommended_courses: They were all great! You can't transfer the Japanese classes if you're a MA student, though. As the Japanese department isn't at MA level, it doesn't count, even if you take the advanced classes.
unexpected_costs: I had to go to a doctor and that actually costs money there.
cost_comparison: I was expecting to find more places with cheap, fun clothing, but all of the cool stuff was really expensive.
activities_available: Lots of clubs were available! Especially if you speak Japanese.
activities_recommended: Absolutely see if you can join a club.
weekend_recommendations: Everywhere
culture_adjustment: I had been on exchange in Japan before, so I knew what I was getting into.
socializing_tips: Put yourself out there. Clubs are great, because then you can force yourself to go, even if it's hard.
cultural_challenges: My main cultural challenge was wondering if I was unknowingly being offensive. I didn't think too much about differences on a cultural level, rather on a personal one.
culture_appreciated: There's a lot of order and enough people that things have to be done right. There's also enough people that a lot of weird and amazing types of experiences are financially sound.
top3_advice: 1. Figure out the strategy for applying for classes before you go into it. 2. You can get far with katakana, even if you don't speak any Japanese 3. Enjoy living in Tokyo!!!
other_useful_info: I got the official acceptance letter from my department and dorm what felt pretty shortly before I left because of the difference in semester timing.
most_rewarding: I have many friendships completely in Japanese now
greatest_challenge: Time difference and distance to my friends. It's easy to feel alone when you're on the other side of the world and that's completely okay.
other_comments: I look forwards to going back

crucial_aspects: I love Japan and I have been studying the language for a year and a half. That's why I sought the opportunity to live and study here. I wanted to come to Tokyo because it's the biggest city in Japan, and I thought it would have the most experiences to offer.
overall_comments: I am very grateful to have come here. Because of my exchange, I have made friends with some local and international people. I have also improved my Japanese a lot, and I hope to use the language in my career going forwards together with my masters degree.
info_ease: There were many different online systems that I had to check for information leading up to and during my exchange, which was a little tedious and confusing at times. But all the information I needed was provided.
arrival_assistance: I received information online, and email and telephone support was made available to me by Waseda University.
arrival_comments: All the information I needed was provided online. However, it would have been nice to have received an in-person orientation at the campus to show us around as it would have felt more welcoming.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I am very grateful to have come here. Because of my exchange, I have made friends with some local and international people. I have also improved my Japanese a lot, and I hope to use the language in my career going forwards together with my masters degree.
registration_process: There was an online course selection system where you could read about and select the classes. The system was not that user-friendly but It worked.
registration_help: Email and telephone support were made available. Otherwise, the support office would likely have helped as well.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Taking Japanese classes as an added extra course was stressful for many. I just self-studied on the side whenever I had time which worked great for me.
academics_comments: I am very grateful to have come here. Because of my exchange, I have made friends with some local and international people. I have also improved my Japanese a lot, and I hope to use the language in my career going forwards together with my masters degree.
course_level: Some of the courses in English were offered to both bachelors, masters, and even Ph.D. students, so perhaps they were not as deep as I was used to on the masters, but still very interesting courses.
teaching_comparison: Felt a lot like the same style to me.
courses_enrolled: Contemporary Journalism NPO/NGO and the future Sustainable Development and International Development Cooperation Regulation and Trade Japanese Politics and Diplomacy
recommended_courses: Contemporary Journalism was very interesting. Its hosted by Hans Greimel, a real journalist that teaches evening classes at Waseda. He often has guest lecturers from people in the industry.
unexpected_costs: Did not encounter unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Fruits and vegetables are expensive here.
activities_available: There were university clubs for just about anything you can imagine. And if students want to start their own clubs they can register them with the university. However, a lot of clubs were unavailable to foreigners who don't speak Japanese.
activities_recommended: Go to the Intercultural Communication Center (ICC) at Waseda in building 3. They will arrange events, and also help you find a circle/club to join.
weekend_recommendations: It's Tokyo so there are hundreds of opportunities. Perhaps go see Asakusa in Tokyo, a famous temple. Or go to the famous Shibuya crosswalk and see that lively area.
culture_adjustment: Living here is very different from what I'm used to, but to me, it was all very interesting and refreshing.
socializing_tips: Japanese people can be rather shy, but it does not mean they don't want to interact. There are often people at the dorm to make friends with. Also, joining a circle is also a good way to make friends.
cultural_challenges: Japanese people have a particular culture of being polite and not bothering others. For example, this means not talking loudly on the trains. Foreigners often don't realize they're bothering the locals because the locals are often too shy or polite to tell them off, so be considerate.
culture_appreciated: Anywhere you go you feel safe here, and every place is clean and well-maintained. People are very polite and orderly. Also the food here is great and its relatively affordable to eat at restaurants here.
top3_advice: 1. Japan is a very considerate society, so be considerate in return. 2. learn some basic Japanese beforehand, the locals will appreciate your effort and a little goes a long way. 3. Make sure to experience all the sightseeing opportunities, travel destinations, and foods you can while you're there.
other_useful_info: Look on YouTube for videos about living in Japan and what to experience.
most_rewarding: Getting to experience all the things I had heard of before coming here. Going to karaoke, Japanese arcades, eating the food here, going mountain hiking, etc.
greatest_challenge: Exam season, when many assignments were due at the same time.

crucial_aspects: The university culture in Japan, but also just the culture in general.
info_ease: Not that easy always. The Japanese keep some information to themselves.
arrival_assistance: Nothing, apart from other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Too long to get into. But via their student net.
registration_help: an online meeting
registration_success: successful in registering for all of them
courses_enrolled: Islam in East Asia and Beyond Applied Scaling and Text Analysis Japanese Economy: Structural Issues Contemporary Journalism
cost_comparison: Going out for food is less expensive, but you generally go out more for lunch and dinner so food is in the end more expensive.
activities_available: Many circles - gokart circle, tea circle, farming circle, karate circle and other different kind of sports
activities_recommended: Enjoy the food.
weekend_recommendations: Go on a hiking trip to the mountains.
culture_adjustment: Many Japanese are shy of speaking English and many can´t speak anything at all. That makes it hard. But people are very helpful. You need an open mind.
socializing_tips: Join a circle or some of the university events.
top3_advice: It takes a lot of effort with procedures getting into the university. It is worth it all. Japan is cracking.
other_useful_info: You need to be ready for the bureaucracy and loads of paperwork.
most_rewarding: Enjoying a completely different way of living.

crucial_aspects: I am interested in a future career involving Japanese relations and GSAPS at Waseda had a reputation for good academic quality as well as academically active professors in fields I found interesting. Additionally, it was possible to participate in Japanese language classes outside of my major. As such, it seemed like a good match.
info_ease: There was a lot of information distributed through e-mail to us. I almost had a hard time because there was too much information coming out way. But I guess that is just part of going on exchange, especially outside of EU.
arrival_assistance: There were some orientation videos and materials as well as an online meeting. However, there was no offline meeting to help and introduce exchange students to each other. This might be a post-corona thing, but I thought it was strange that there was not physical orientation specifically for exchange students. So, lots of help for practical stuff, but very little social support. It was fine for me as I had contacts and friends in Tokyo already. But might be hard for others who come over to Tokyo for the first time.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: There are multiple rounds, so you can add and drop. So if a course was over-enrolled and you did not get it, you could pick something else. You can even try some of the classes and then decide. However, at the grad school, I got all my selected courses.
registration_help: I am not sure, I did not need more than the available material.
registration_success: I got all my courses at the grad school. It was harder to get a place in Japanese classes.
registration_advice: Be sure to check the schedule for each course and make a study plan with no overlaps. Also, some courses are intense courses, where you study double for half the semester. Don't do too many of those, but one (maybe two) might be good since your exams will then be distributed throughout the semester.
course_level: It depended on the Professor. So I would check out each professor's profile before and then choose. Most courses were easier than UCPH but some were just as challenging.
teaching_comparison: Much smaller classes, and a lot of classroom discussions with more interaction with the professor.
courses_enrolled: CJL Academic Debate: Learning Logical Thinking and Improving Presentation Skills 3-4 GSAPS Modern Japanese Society I: Japan Social Structure and the Life Course (E) GSAPS EU-Japan relations (E) GSAPS Global Sociology (E) GSAPS NGO/NPO - Theory and Practice (E)
recommended_courses: EU-Japan relations w. Professor Bacon. The professor is very knowledgeable and well-connected in the field. Expects participation from students.
unexpected_costs: A visit to the hospital!
cost_comparison: I ended up having to go to the hospital and feared I had to pay a huge bill even if my Danish insurance later covered it. However, it was much less expensive than expected!
activities_available: There are many hobby clubs but mostly used by undergrads
activities_recommended: I did not participate.
weekend_recommendations: There are many good day trips from Tokyo to get out of the city such as Enoshima.
culture_adjustment: I had experience with living in Japan before but Tokyo was the first. I never got used to the crowds, but preferred more quiet neighborhoods like Koenji or Kichijoji.
socializing_tips: There are language exchange programs at the university, which seemed like a good way to make friends interested in an international outlook. Especially since many do not speak English.
cultural_challenges: Japanese are very hesitant and a bit hard to get close to at first. However, many are curious once you break the ice.
culture_appreciated: There is usually great service and hospitality here, which makes it a good experience when you are exploring places and the city.
top3_advice: Look through the professors and choose courses based on their profiles. The academic level is manageable. As such, remember to explore the city, culture, and people instead of being too nervous about the academic stuff.
other_useful_info: The trains stop running around 00:00, beware!
most_rewarding: It was networking with other academics with similar interests as mine and building a new network here.
greatest_challenge: Choosing where to go for trips!
other_comments: No

crucial_aspects: I wanted to experience living outside of Europe and the US. and I wanted to get new perspectives on social science. Another import aspect for choosing Japan, is that the country is known for its technological innovations. As a Social Data Scientist, it was interesting to dive into this area and explore how digital designs are interwoven in Japanese society like for example digital art, games, transportation, contactless dining via robot waiters and autonomous security robots patrolling in the airport. Another thing that made me chose Japan is that the country is culturally rich and has beautiful nature for hiking in my spare time.
info_ease: Because of COVID the university was very late in giving me the information I needed and the Japanese Embassy was late as well because many was applying for a VISA now that the country had reopened. However, in the end everything worked fine.
arrival_assistance: I got assistance from the University which send me mails about things I needed to have in mind before entering the country and practical things I needed to do in the beginning of living in Japan, like for example getting a citizen card and enrolling in their health system. The dormitory – run by the university – was also very helpful if I had any questions about living in Japan.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You parents have to sign a lot of documents, you have to make a document explaining why you want to study at Waseda University and find a personal supervisor (this takes some time). Moreover, you have to prove that you financially can live in Tokyo (the SU-office will create a document for you). There is a lot of other documents, but I can't remember them all. Everything about the registration process is explained on the university's webpage.
registration_help: There is an office at Waseda University for international students where you can ask questions by email or phone.
registration_success: The course registration is very easy. It is very similar to the one on KU-net. I got all the courses I applied for.
registration_advice: If you register for courses outside of your faculty on Waseda University, you cannot cancel them. I took four courses (8 credits=30 ECTS) and I think this was the perfect number of courses where I felt academically involved but also had time to explore Tokyo and go travel.
course_level: The academic level is relatively easy. If I had to go on exchange again, I would find a University where the academic level is more challenging. On the other hand, it was very interesting to learn about International Politics and Immigration Politics through the lenses of Japanese lecturers. The university is also famous for its journalism courses, so it was interesting to learn about the differences in Japanese and western story telling and newsflow.
teaching_comparison: The format of the lectures is like high school/gymnasiet where you are between 25-10 students per course and the teacher knows your name. That way I became more engaged in the lectures and readings compared to the more the more anonymous lecture format in Denmark.
courses_enrolled: - Causal Inference in Social Science A (Basic) - Theory of International Politics (E) - Refugee and Migration Studies and Contemporary Issues - Contemporary Journalism
recommended_courses: Theory of ‘International Politics' and ‘Refugee and Migration Studies and Contemporary Issues' is mainly based on western theory, however the empirical cases we discussed was related to Japan which was interesting. Contemporary Journalism was also interesting because you learned about how news are created and you also learned about cultural differences in news making.
unexpected_costs: Buying things for your room like pillows and towels.
cost_comparison: Food in the supermarket is very expensive, but eating out is very cheap. You can get a super great meal at a very cozy restaurant for 60-100 DKK. Because the dormitory kitchen was very minimalistic and the food is amazing in Japan I decided to eat out a lot. That part you have to look forward to!
activities_available: The University provides many opportunities to engage in social activities: There are traveling clubs, different sport clubs you can join and there is also different cultural thing like a tea ceremony club or painting club.
activities_recommended: Karate is a lot of fun and you dont need to have any experience beforehand.
weekend_recommendations: It is very easy to travel because the public transportation system is so good. Lots of museums, beautiful Japanese gardens and hiking trips. You feel very safe when traveling and there is often someone who would like to help you.
culture_adjustment: In general people at Waseda University are very nice, however, some students are very conservative at the university and I found that very challenging. My dorm neighbor for example said things like “poor people are lazy people” or “women who give birth should not get any social support from the government because giving birth is like being on vacation” and another dorm neighbor used words like 'nazi-feminists' and showed me a blackface joke on YouTube. I also had one lecturer saying some racist things so I dropped the course.
socializing_tips: Engage in a club or some of the activities made on whatsapp groups for exchange students.
cultural_challenges: That some students and professors had very different political believes than I and said some very conservative things. I found that very overwhelming.
culture_appreciated: People are very polite and helpful in general. Japan has a very rich culture regarding art, handcraft, tea culture and architecture which I found very inspiring. I also find the approach towards nature inspiring too. Trash on the streets and in the nature is little, the tap-water in Tokyo taste good, they have a lot of parks and green areas, good public transportation, and it in general feel like many cares a lot about nature and environmental issues in Japan.
top3_advice: Look forward to all the amazing things you didn't know that you needed in life, like public bath/onzen, izakaya and jazz cafes.
other_useful_info: Most of the exchange students are around 18-24 years old.
most_rewarding: Experiencing a new way of living. Being on exchange feels like living in a bobble where you constantly experience new things and get new experiences. I definitely recommend going on exchange and Tokyo is a beautiful city to live in.
greatest_challenge: That some students have very different political beliefs from what I have experienced in Denmark.

crucial_aspects: Since I am studying Japanese Studies I have seen it as crucial to my studies to be able to go to Japan and immerse myself in the language and culture there.
overall_comments: Being able to go abroad has been a wonderful experience. However, I do find that the shift in academic level between Denmark and Japan a bit odd. I have taken seen that as mostly a part of a cultural exchange. What have been frustrating is overall the bureaucratic aspect of this exchange. The needed credits or ECTS has not lines up completely, and there has been very little understanding from either university. I would have loved to have had that as a pre-note before I went on exchange, that my chosen faculty did not offer up as many credits as KU wanted me to take.
info_ease: That was quite easy. Waseda sent out a thorough welcome package as well as an orientation meeting.
arrival_assistance: - see above -
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Being able to go abroad has been a wonderful experience. However, I do find that the shift in academic level between Denmark and Japan a bit odd. I have taken seen that as mostly a part of a cultural exchange. What have been frustrating is overall the bureaucratic aspect of this exchange. The needed credits or ECTS has not lines up completely, and there has been very little understanding from either university. I would have loved to have had that as a pre-note before I went on exchange, that my chosen faculty did not offer up as many credits as KU wanted me to take.
registration_process: Most of it was through an online form, no need for an TOEFL test - which is nice. I think it was fairly easy as far as I remember.
registration_help: Their webpage is a bit of a jungle, but I stuck with one faculty (SILS) and read about that one. They are quite sweet to answer emails if needed.
registration_success: The registration for course system at Waseda is a complete lottery. Which is super stressful, and continues into semester start. There are three rounds of lottery, and you are not guaranteed any courses. I would NOT recommend it to anyone who has to have a very specific course - because they can't help you. If you get in you get in, and they don't take any requirements from home universities into consideration.
registration_advice: Do not fall in love with any specific courses, but have at least 10 different you can see yourself apply to. Don't stress necessarily beforehand - you can't do anything about it anyway. If you don't get in within the first three rounds of application, they have what they call "relief course registration". Then you will get placed at a course where they have space left - which is either A) less popular courses or B) courses somebody has dropped since they got something else in the second or third registration round.
academics_comments: Being able to go abroad has been a wonderful experience. However, I do find that the shift in academic level between Denmark and Japan a bit odd. I have taken seen that as mostly a part of a cultural exchange. What have been frustrating is overall the bureaucratic aspect of this exchange. The needed credits or ECTS has not lines up completely, and there has been very little understanding from either university. I would have loved to have had that as a pre-note before I went on exchange, that my chosen faculty did not offer up as many credits as KU wanted me to take.
course_level: It wasn't any problem. Nothing too complicated of what I took. When on exchange at SILS you are not allowed to take introiuctinary courses, so be aware of that.
teaching_comparison: Lecture based, no discussions in barely any classes I took. Each class is a 100 minutes without break.
courses_enrolled: Anthropology of Religion, Japanese Art History, Jazz History, Comprehensive Japanese 4, Picture books in Japanese 3-5.
recommended_courses: The Jazz course was the best course that I had. But, I fear it was the last time it was provided as the teacher went on to be retired. The Anthropology of Religion has interesting reading and ethnographic films but the workload (even if the quality of it doesn't matter) became a bit troublesome. The picture books in Japanese was fun! We read picture books together and discussed them in Japanese. Then we had to write weekly reviews in Japanese, and in the end make a picture book each that we had to present! It was a great way of expanding vocabulary.
unexpected_costs: Buying stuff for my apartment. It was furnished but I still needed personal items as well as cleaning supplies and cloths racks.
cost_comparison: The national health insurance was way less expensive than I had thought!
activities_available: If you want to, you can join a club at the university. There are ALL kind of clubs. They take up a lot of time though. There were also a good bit of introduction parties and such when the semester started.
activities_recommended: I would recommend trying to attend some sort of festival! There are plenty, for all seasons, in Japan. It's great fun!
weekend_recommendations: Travel, travel, travel. Even if it's just day trips from Tokyo, do it! The public transport system in Japan is easy to follow and can take you far and near. I would really recommend looking around not only the inner city but also outside of it.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy. I have also traveled many times to Japan, and studies Japanese for quite a while.
socializing_tips: Not really.. The faculty I studied at had international students, and Japanese students with an international focus. I must admit I ended up with being friends with mostly international students.
cultural_challenges: The academic culture was probably my biggest challenge.. I am used to analysing and trying to form my own meaning about everything. It was quite a challenge to just take in lectures and then do no discussion.
culture_appreciated: The food!
top3_advice: Don't take more than the minimum amount of credits. It's busy enough as it is. Make use of the library and group rooms/study rooms - Waseda has really good facilities.
other_useful_info: Have fun OUTSIDE of the university. You will have many classes on the BA level, and so much homework.. But remember: the level is not as all as high as on KU. Quantity over quality!
most_rewarding: Meeting other exchange students, and being able to live in Japan!
greatest_challenge: Finding meaning in doing school on this level again.. It put a lid on the academic passion I admit. Also that everybody used chatGPT.

crucial_aspects: Japan's rich culture and respect for tradition has always intrigued me. The cultural influence that Japan has in the west is also very pronounced, so I wanted an opportunity to experience all of this first-hand.
info_ease: My dorm and school were extremely well-organized and helpful. I had no issues upon arrival.
arrival_assistance: I was provided with clear instructions on how to reach my dorm, how to apply for courses, and all other necessary pre-requisites.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Registration was pretty straight-forward, with a second registration round available if you wished to change courses.
registration_help: Student counselors.
registration_success: I got into all the classes that I registered for.
registration_advice: Be well-prepared and set aside a good amount of time to look into what courses you want.
course_level: University in Japan has a lot of mandatory participation, so be prepared to spend a lot of hours at school. The content is not too demanding but there are lot required tasks to be completed for every course.
teaching_comparison: Less 'læring på eget ansvar' and more 'fremmøde og deltagelse'.
courses_enrolled: Nihongo 1(1)D Nihongo 1(2)C Problem / Conflict Analysis and Resolution Social Business Trans-Pacific Perspectives on Work, Culture, and Society Cross-Cultural Organizational Behavior Academic Writing and Discussion in English Alpha (Essentials for Beginners) Academic Writing and Discussion in English Beta (Academic skills for Intermediate learners)
recommended_courses: Cross-Cultural Organizational Behavior was a very interesting course with broad perspectives on workplace culture and environment.
unexpected_costs: Nothing unexpected :)
cost_comparison: Eating out is a lot more affordable than in Copenhagen.
activities_available: A broad range of extracurricular activites were available: Music, Dance, Sport...
activities_recommended: I didn't participate in any of the activites arranged by my uni.
weekend_recommendations: Travel, travel, travel! See the countryside - so beautiful.
culture_adjustment: Very smooth transition for me – in Japanese people are very mindful of others, similar to Danish socialistic values.
socializing_tips: Don't be shy! Most Japanese students won't approach you - but they are very happy to engage when approached.
cultural_challenges: Don't recall.
culture_appreciated: The respectful coexsitence.
top3_advice: - Do some research on culture beforehand. - The hard part is getting all the paperwork done. - Enjoy
other_useful_info: Get your English Language Certificate in order as soon as possible in the application process.
most_rewarding: Time for reflection, meeting inspiring people and experiencing this rich culture.
greatest_challenge: Sleep issues :(

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to Asia and have always dreamed of going to Japan. I picked because of the country and city, not the university and academics. Waseda University was the only university in Japan that had courses relevant for my studies at home.
overall_comments: It was amazing, I loved being on exchange in Tokyo. The culture, food and city in general exceeded my expectations.
info_ease: Not easy. Waseda University's website can be quite a jungle. Moreover, many documents were needed to go on exchange to Japan and except spending a lot of time preparing these.
arrival_assistance: I didn't get much help. I did however live with other exchange students that went to the same university as me, so we were able to help each other a lot. The school also sent out a list of things we had to do upon arrival.
arrival_comments: It is an experience going to the Japanese city office, which is mandatory upon arrival as many don't speak english.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It was amazing, I loved being on exchange in Tokyo. The culture, food and city in general exceeded my expectations.
registration_process: The registration was easy to figure out and is over three rounds. Pick more courses than you need the first time as it is not sure that you get all your picks. You can drop courses in the second and third round. I got all the courses i wanted.
registration_help: Waseda University sent out multiple emails regarding course registration. They had all information needed.
registration_success: Very succesful as i got all the courses i wanted.
registration_advice: Apply for more courses than you need in the first round. Take the course "Japanese for zero beginners".
academics_comments: It was amazing, I loved being on exchange in Tokyo. The culture, food and city in general exceeded my expectations.
course_level: The academic level is easier than in Denmark and going to Waseda University is a bit like going to high school. You have multiple (4-5) weekly assignments. The exams are easy and in some courses I didn't have any exams.
teaching_comparison: Many assingments, a few presentations, more home work than in Copenhagen. I read way less and didn't prepare for exams much.
courses_enrolled: Immunology, 1 credit=2 ECTS-points Introduction to Computational Physics, 2 credits=4 ECTS-points Current Topics in Biosciences, 2 credits=4 ECTS-points Molecular Cell Biology A, 2 credits=4 ECTS-points Research Design and Analysis, 2 credits=4 ECTS-points Japanese for 'Zero' Beginners, 2 credits=4 ECTS-points Budo, 1 credit = 2 ECTS-points History of pre-Modern Japan, 2 credits = 4 ECTS-points History of Modern Japan, 2 credits = 4 ECTS-points
recommended_courses: Japanese for 'Zero' Beginners is a great course if you want to learn a bit Japanese and is a course for only exchange students. Except a big workload and weekly quizzes. History of pre-Modern Japan and History of Modern Japan are great courses where you go to museums and other trips every week. Afterwards, there is a weekly assignment. I really enjoyed these courses. Budo is a super fun course and nothing like going to university. Everyone pass the class and the teachers are super nice. Don't take research and design, nor Introduction to Computational Physics.
unexpected_costs: There is a mandatory national insurance in Japan for about 1700 yen (75 kr). every month.
cost_comparison: Eating put is super cheap and really good. I ate out around once a day. Fruit is super expensive in the supermarket and every fruit is huge.
activities_available: Waseda University have many many clubs but it is very hard to get accepted into. I wrote to four different and didn't hear back from any of them. You cannot join a sportsteam either.
activities_recommended: Join a club if you can.
weekend_recommendations: I went on trips almost every weekend with the friends i made at my dorm. You have to go to the Mount Fuji area (lake Kawaguchi). Other recommendations outside Tokyo is Nikko, Kansai-area (Osaka, Kyoto, Nara) and mountains as Mount Takao and Mount Otake. Tokyo is amazing and there is so much to see. Go explore all the big areas as Shinjuku, Shibuya, Ikebukuro, Akihabara, Ginza and Ueno.
culture_adjustment: I didn't find it hard even though there are big cultural differences. You quickly get used to the differences and learn how to act. The Japanese people are super polite, respectful and nice. They also queue up.
socializing_tips: Take courses that are not exclusive for exchange students.
cultural_challenges: The language barrier. Nonetheless, Google Image translate is a lifesaver and help you a lot.
culture_appreciated: The Japanese people are so respectful, helpful and nice. I love how quite the they are in public transport.
top3_advice: It a lot of work to go to Tokyo as you have to take a language test, take physical pictures that have to be sent to Japan, prepare 15+ documents and go to the embassy multiple times prior. It is however totally worth it! The food and culture is amazing. Live in a dorm. I got almost all my friends from the dorm i stayed at.
other_useful_info: N/A
most_rewarding: Experiencing Tokyo and Japan and meeting friends from all around the world.
greatest_challenge: The beginning, where you are far from everything, don't know anyone and can't speak the language.
other_comments: Learning to speak and read a bit Japanese is very helpful.

crucial_aspects: I have always wanted to experience Japan, so a semester abroad was the perfect opportunity!
overall_comments: Amazing experience! Although I would perhaps have preferred a more focused learning experience on Data Science topics (1-2 courses instead of the 5 that I enrolled in), I am very happy I could take university courses to learn about the Japanese culture and language (due to my study programme's "valgfrie valgfag" on the 5th semester).
info_ease: Relatively easy, but doing your preparation from home is a must. Luckily the application process from partnering Waseda University will guide you quite far and have plenty of online resources to access regarding coming to Japan.
arrival_assistance: I was lucky to get a dorm room (Hoshien Building 3, definitely recommend!), where I got assistance on getting settled and could contact a representative regarding any questions. But most information will be sent to you by e-mail/available online.
arrival_comments: There are several orientation events you can attend, where some are more socially oriented than others.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: Amazing experience! Although I would perhaps have preferred a more focused learning experience on Data Science topics (1-2 courses instead of the 5 that I enrolled in), I am very happy I could take university courses to learn about the Japanese culture and language (due to my study programme's "valgfrie valgfag" on the 5th semester).
registration_process: All information is available on their website. However, note that the course registration happens over three times.
registration_help: Waseda official website.
registration_success: Very lucky! Got all the courses I applied for.
registration_advice: Better to enroll in 1-2 extra courses that you find interesting, so if you don't get a spot on an important course, you have a back-up. Sometimes spaces free up in the second round, so you might get an extra shot at an over-enrolled course, but I wouldn't count on it.
academics_comments: Amazing experience! Although I would perhaps have preferred a more focused learning experience on Data Science topics (1-2 courses instead of the 5 that I enrolled in), I am very happy I could take university courses to learn about the Japanese culture and language (due to my study programme's "valgfrie valgfag" on the 5th semester).
course_level: The overall teaching quality is lower than University of Copenhagen, but luckily the course load is also lower and less difficult. Each course is worth 1-2 credits, which means you will have min. 8 simultaneous courses during a semester, which also limits the depth of each course (compared to DIKU's 2 courses at a time).
teaching_comparison: Not all professors speak English very well. They prefer lecturing or online assignments. Only the Japanese beginner language courses and a single Group Psychology course felt interactive.
courses_enrolled: Budo 01; Japanese for 'Zero' BeginnersG (Japanese course for International Student); Group Psychology; Advanced Intelligent Software; Introduction to Data Science gamma 03; Introduction to Data Science delta 04; Data Science in Practice 03; History of Modern Japan (1); Artificial Intelligence; Nihongo 1(1)J (Japanese course for International Student)
recommended_courses: Data Science in Practice 03: Nice practical application of data science, which is often very theoretic at universities. ; History of Modern Japan: Weekly museum visits for the first quarter. A good book to learn about Japan as curriculum. ; Japanese for 'Zero' BeginnersG (Japanese course for International Student): Good Japanese Language Course (in person, very basic) ; Nihongo 1(1)J (Japanese course for International Student): Good Japanese Language Course (online, learnt more here)
unexpected_costs: I took many opportunities to travel extended weekend trips by train and plane, e.g. Hakone (near Fuji), Okinawa, Hokkaido, Hong Kong, South Korea and Philippines. These expenses are not included in the above budget, but when you are in East Asia and meet nice friends to have nice experiences and travel with, you will want to seize those opportunities!
cost_comparison: Food was less expensive than I had expected, and way more delicious! I can walk to uni, so that is free. But travel expenses by train around town add up, even if it is still cheaper/around the price for the CPH metro. Some long-term residents get a bike, but I wouldn't recommend it for a semester, because you will be traveling alone and there are no bike lanes, so you have to bike on the sidewalk.
activities_available: Check the Waseda Circle guide online, they have almost everything.
activities_recommended: Experience the city, wander around, find a random small ramen shop. It will give you some of the best interactions and experiences!
weekend_recommendations: Day trip to Hakone in the summer/fall is a must. Winter/Christmas trip to Hokkaido was epic. You MUST visit Kyoto and stay for a day or two while you are here, you can travel by train.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy, but I am also used to traveling from having been on exchange before and I speak a bit of Japanese, which goes a long way for communication.
socializing_tips: Hang out in the common room if you aren't busy, sign up for introduction events, join a circle, find others who also enjoy your hobbies, find new hobbies, go out and have fun!
cultural_challenges: The Japanese will often follow rules to a fault, so bending the rules is unlikely to work and will be frowned upon. Do yourself a favour and stick to the rules of queuing and public transportation, i.e. extend common courtesy. However, don't stress too much. As a foreigner, Japanese people will be more accepting and they would rather mind their own business anyways.
culture_appreciated: People are really nice! Everyone is neat and orderly, and because everyone (including you) brings their trash home, the city is one of the cleanest and nicest smelling in the world, which is incredible when you realize it's the largest city in the world.
top3_advice: If you're interested, get a head start and learn some basic Japanese over the summer vacation. It will get you a long way! Duolingo isn't great, but it will get you further than doing nothing! Get an overview of your academic courses before you arrive, and make sure they don't conflict planning wise. Embrace the experience, go with other students on day trips and to karaoke spots in town, have fun.
other_useful_info: Enjoy the food. Actually, the canteen is incredible! And you can get a semester-long 10% discount by joining the university COOP organization. It will cost you a small fee and you hand in a 1.500 kr. deposit, but it is well worth it if you eat there regularly. You can collect the deposit back at the end of your semester. Also, travel card! Get a free Suica metro travel card in your Apple wallet and put like 4000 yen on it before you arrive. Then you can just tap your phone at the subway gates and on busses to travel around. Bullet trains require separate tickets and are kind of expensive.
most_rewarding: To get to experience Japanese culture, cheap and delicious food everywhere, cheap rent 20 minutes from downtown Tokyo (!!), and to meet a lot of nice and outgoing exchange students from around the world.
greatest_challenge: To keep an overview of weekly hand-ins and deadlines for 8-10 different courses at once, when you are used to focus on 2 courses :') Their version of Absalon website has a dashboard that will show you upcoming deadlines though. Pretty convenient.

crucial_aspects: I was interested in Japanese culture, nature and have a little bit of Japanese heritage. I wanted to live somewhere very different from Denmark but still a very safe place where I would be able to do solo traveling as a woman.
info_ease: Very easy. Waseda sent a lot of information that was quite overwhelming at first but there were also info meeting and these were also very helpful.
arrival_assistance: I received assistance from Waseda University about how to apply for courses and they answered some questions I had about the application process and system.
arrival_comments: Wasedas communication was very good and I received help quickly whenever I had questions. My uncertainty was more because of KU, who were much harder to communicate with regarding the exchange.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The course registration happens in 3 periods, so you first choose your top priorities, and then you can apply for new courses in the second and third registration. This process was quite confusing and it was hard for me to get the schedule I wanted because I couldn't apply for two courses in the same time period in case I didn't get one - then in the second period my plan b was full, so I had to choose something completely different.
registration_help: The SILS office was very helpful, but the system is very rigid and there is not much to do about it.
registration_success: In the end I got 6/7 courses that I wanted,
registration_advice: In the first registration, apply for as many of the courses you want as possible, because I didn't get quite a few of mine.
course_level: Generally, the courses were easier in terms of what was needed to pass.
teaching_comparison: There is more focus on attendance, participation and multiple courses with presentations.
courses_enrolled: State and Society in the Middle East, Thinking Power, The Politics and International Relations of the European Union, Nihongo 1 and Zero Japanese
recommended_courses: State and Society in the Middle East was my favorite course because the teacher was an expert and made the class very lively. It was also very easy with almost no readings, and I appreciated the time to explore Japan. Zero Japanese is a bit hardcore but in combination with Nihongo 1, it worked very well for me for learning basic Japanese. They are both for beginners though I would heavily recommend knowing hiragana at least before starting (I did with duolingo).
unexpected_costs: I was a bit surprised at how many housing fees there are. This makes it hard to calculate your monthly rent, as the fees could be as high as almost 2 months rent (for my 5 month stay).
cost_comparison: Eating out is very cheap but vegetables and fruits in grocery stores are not. It is very difficult/expensive to be vegetarian.
activities_available: There are hundreds of circles to join for sports, arts and gatherings.
activities_recommended: I enjoyed sports, because it was fun and easy to make friends with people.
weekend_recommendations: There are lots of great trips (day trips also) from Tokyo such as Nikko, Kamakura, Enoshima, Yokohama. I loved traveling and going to flea markets
culture_adjustment: Quite easy - I am quiet and polite as a person so the Japanese culture didn't feel too different.
socializing_tips: Almost all my Japanese friends are people I met in my dorm (at dinner). Otherwise I would say to be open and to initiate conversations, because many Japanese people can seem very shy, but a lot of the time they will enjoy speaking to you.
cultural_challenges: The language/cultural barrier with my Japanese friends made it hard for me to know whether we were friends in the beginning, because they don't share as much about their personal lives.
culture_appreciated: The politeness and respect for other people.
top3_advice: Hmmmmm... 1. To think carefully about which living situation to apply for: Do you want to make friends there? Do you want it to be cheap? How convenient do you want it to be? 2. Talk to your friends/peers at Waseda, cause they can in most cases point you in the right direction and make you feel like you're not alone with any issues you may be having 3. ?
other_useful_info: Be prepared for an annoying course registration system...
most_rewarding: My friends made it very memorable.
greatest_challenge: Communication with KU
other_comments: No

arrival_assistance: The manager was really helpfull with finding City Office. Waseda e-mailed me information as well.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: There are three different periods for registration - four if you count the one only for Advanced seminars. You can't drop Advanced Seminars once you've registered for them.
registration_help: They provide a guide - it is very long and slightly confusing.
registration_success: Not very. registration_advice: Wait till after the introduction day to register for anything.
course_level: Some were quite easy. Most of them don't have much reading material, and the material they do have are very easy. We only read academic articles for one course. But they were interesting - they just didn't require that much.
teaching_comparison: Mandatory participation was new for me - but that was quite easy to get used to. Also, I was writing a lot of very short essays/class reports. At university of Copenhagen I usually write 2-4 longer essays per semester.
courses_enrolled: Intensive Studies 9 (Survey of Japanese Literature 1) Intensive Studies 12 (Introduction to Japanese Culture and Civilization 1) Storytelling and Media (TCS quarter seminar) Intensive Studies 10 (Survey of Japanese Literature 2) Global Genre Fiction (TCS Advanced seminar) Adaptations of Classical Japanese Literature (TCS quarter seminar) Intensive Studies 15 (Introduction to Japanese Thought and Religion 1) Intensive Studies 24 (European Thought 2)
recommended_courses: Any course by Takai Shiho. I also really enjoyed Intensive Studies 15 (Introduction to Japanese Thought and Religion 1) .
unexpected_costs: Public transportation is expensive is you move around a lot.
cost_comparison: Food. And generally living.
activities_available: Clubs / circles, festivals
activities_recommended: I didn't really go to any so I wouldn't know.
weekend_recommendations: Traveling out of Tokyo. I really enjoyed Kanazawa.
culture_adjustment: The language barrier is always going to be a problem - but it becomes way easier over time. And people are so nice. Just do what everybody else is doing and you'll be fine.
socializing_tips: Classes.
cultural_challenges: Mostly just the language thing - but again, that is a me-problem.
culture_appreciated: People are very, very, very nice.
top3_advice: Don't stress too much about not hearing anything from Waseda - they send out information quite late, but they will send it. If you can't get a room in Waseda's own dorms, find a dorm yourself. Be prepared to spend some time at City Office (and if you don't speak Japanese, have google translate ready), and remember to tell them that you are a student when you're setting up insurance.
other_useful_info: Other exchange students probably have the same problems as you - so just ask them. It's easier to figure stuff out as a group.
most_rewarding: Friends.
greatest_challenge: Language barrier. The dorm.

crucial_aspects: I already knew quite a bit of japanese and wanted to take it further and living in Japan made that possible.
overall_comments: Best thing i've done.
info_ease: Not that easy to find if you havent prepared beforehand.
arrival_assistance: I received an orientation package but that was quite a bit after I arrived so I didnt really receive much help. I had to figure obligatory insurance, residence etc. out myself.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Best thing i've done.
registration_process: Waseda has a gambling esque roulette system where you have multiple sign up round and you're not guaranteed to get your course so you might find yourself in the last round of registration not having what you need and scrambling to get something that can give you credit at KU.
registration_help: Not really anything I went to them and asked if they could do something they just said to sign up for as much as possible that might give me credit but they couldnt guarantee anything.
registration_success: I was lucky and got what I wanted, but I know many that didnt get what they needed and thus couldnt fulfill requirements from their home unis.
registration_advice: In the first registration round sign up for anything and everything that might be able to give credits you can always drop later.
academics_comments: Best thing i've done.
course_level: A lot of the courses (even advanced ones) felt like entry level.
teaching_comparison: A lot more showing up to classes and taking attendance - show up and do your work it mostly doesnt matter how well you do it.
courses_enrolled: Japanese & Northeast Asian Security 51 Public Choice Theory and Japense Politics Financial Management 51 Comprehensive Japanese 3 Kanji 3
recommended_courses: i dont really have anything I recommend. If you like international relations take the security course very good professor and interesting perspective into how they view security policies in the east. If you like political science and also enjoy discrete math/logic public choice theory is fantastic and a very fun professor. I dont recommend any of japanese (CJL) courses their teaching style is quite bad and especially the kanji courses have insane levels of homework compared to the credits you get from the class so avoid that if you can. Comprehensive 3 also has a lot more homework than the other levels.
unexpected_costs: drinking and eating out every night also taxis.
cost_comparison: Drinking, food and taxis are very cheap, but beware if you do it every night you will spend a lot.
activities_available: Many types of sport and leisure activities like talking, painting etc theres basically a club for every hobby.
activities_recommended: I recommend the Paddy Fielders club (shortly called Paddy) a club where international students and japanese students meet up twice a week for 2ish hours and talk about anything they want. Great way to meet new people and theres also some language practive some times, but you can refrain if you do not want to. They also hold dinners and other events monthly which are really fun.
weekend_recommendations: I recommend taking a trip out to the middle of nowhere and talk to locals and just take it in. Hokkaido and Aomori are also great.
culture_adjustment: Very easy since I knew a lot about it beforehand - but I find the danish and japanese mindset is quite similar so its not too bad.
socializing_tips: They're reserved in the beginning but quickly open up.
cultural_challenges: Japanese people are very indirect they wont say what they think and will be a bit two faced at times its not malicious they're just not well used to being direct so the danish of communicating is hard for them and vice versa.
culture_appreciated: Hospitality and cleanliness.
top3_advice: Join a club or activity to make friends both local and other exchange students Go out as much as possible! your time is short make the most of it, it'll be over before you know it. Focus less on studying and more on the experience itself.
other_useful_info: I think ive said it all.
most_rewarding: Getting to know so many great people who ill hopefully know for life.
greatest_challenge: I got a 43 degree fever and had to go the hospital, but the japanese emergency operators were horrible and i had to call 8 hospitals in my delirious state for help and they all said no, it took around 1h on the phone before they sent and ambulance. After a few hours they threw me out on the street again in bad clothes barely any phone charge still sick having to find my way home. If you get sick dont wait until the last moment or the weekend - their healthcare basically stops on the weekends so its hard to get help.

crucial_aspects: I had always wanted to visit Japan, as I have always had an interest in their culture. And I have never lived in another country before. Therefore a semester abroad in Japan seemed like a match made in heaven.
info_ease: Well, all the information is there, but it can be a bit tricky to find, as Waseda sends a whole lot of documents (some of them important, a lot of them less so) around the beginning of the stay and navigating their website is no cakewalk either, as it is filled with a whole lot of pages. So not exactly easy, but not too bad.
arrival_assistance: Waseda University sends most of the information you need before you even arrive. And they host some in-person information events prior to the start of classes, that were pretty helpful as well.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: As has already been described by many others, the course registration is one big lottery consisting of three rounds of registration - do not expect to get the courses you set out to get. And the digital system in which you apply is very old school, not in a good way.
registration_help: Very limited to be frank - I spoke to the SILS office once or twice to help me sort out some issues I had.
registration_success: In the end I got most of what I wanted, but I also had to give up one/two courses I really wanted.
registration_advice: Be open to do some courses you might not would have thought to do initially - the one I enjoyed the most was a more or less random choice for me.
course_level: Very much like highschool - not the academic level I was used to from my BA at UCPH, and way too much homework. The reason I am giving it a relatively low satisfaction score has some to do with this, but also has very much to do with some very lackluster teaching I got from a couple of the professors.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching was not all that different, it was just way more homework, and a lot of it was not properly integrated in the face-to-face lectures.
courses_enrolled: - History of English Literature　01 - Music and Musicology - Python Programming for Digital Humanities　01 - Video Game Studies　01 - Nihongo 1 (1) - Japanese for 'zero' beginners
recommended_courses: I would highly recommend History of English Literature (or any other courses taught by Professor Tsukada). It was a very insightful an engaging, and the professor is very passionate and entertaining. I really enjoyed this course!
unexpected_costs: The National Healthcare; it wasn't unexpected but it was a bit more cumbersome than I thought to sign up for and to pay for. Very bureaucratic process.
cost_comparison: Most things were very cheap, compared to Copenhagen at least, as the yen is quite weak at the moment.
activities_available: Not too sure - a lot of them didn't seem suitable for international students, as you needed to be somewhat fluent in Japanese to attend. There is one I heard of, which was designed for international students, that was kind of a cultural exchange type of thing. Waseda Paddy it's called.
activities_recommended: - Get out of the city every once in a while - Tokyo is a very busy and crowded place, so it is very nice to do daytrips outside the city, seeing some more quiet parts of Japan. - Explore some of the many wonderful (and cheap!) food-places in around.
weekend_recommendations: Ok, just going to continue the list above here, hehe. - Go to a public bath (sento), preferrably one on the outskirts of the city, as they can be quite busy in the city. If you get the chance, please try onsen as well! - Read a book, and have a cold drink in a nearby park (watch out for crows though, I actually was attacked by one one time, haha). Or tag a friend along and throw a frisbee and eat ice cream :)) - Hike a mountain. - Go visit an arcade with a friend. - Travel the country; I went to Hokkaido (Sapporo and Hakodate) which was an absolute blast. - Visit Meguro Cinema: they have English movies every now and then, and it's a pretty cool spot. - Visit Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building in Shinjuku: tall building with an amazing view over city, and it's doesn't cost anything to go there.
culture_adjustment: Not easy, that's for sure. Culture shock was more significant for me than I had expected: language barrier and a plethora of unwritten rules can make be very overwhelming in the beginning.
socializing_tips: Not really, I didn't really make any local friends ...
cultural_challenges: The language for sure - lots of people do not speak English.
culture_appreciated: I really appreciated how everything just sort of works here; trains are on time, people respect each other when standing in line, public spaces are clean etc. People are very conscious that they are part of a bigger whole, and have to behave appropriately, which is what makes it all possible <33
top3_advice: - Be prepared that going on exchange is going to be challenging: personally I had way more culture shock than expected, felt way lonelier than expected and missed my friends and family each and every day. Bummer message, I know, but I don't think the general idea of what a semester abroad looks like is representative of the challenges. - Be curious and open-minded and make sure to not stall in your stay --> visit all places you might find interesting, eat something new. 9 times out of 10 these excursions, however tiny, will be worth it :)) - Make absolutely sure the school you're enrolling in can secure all the ECTS credits you need. As previously stated, SILS is not for students that are not already studying Japanese.
other_useful_info: If you're looking for something liberal artsy, and you don't already study Japanese, don't go to Waseda University, go for Tokyo University instead. And think carefully about whether Tokyo is the right place for you - I was very overwhelmed by the big-city-living, and think I would have actually prefered to go for a quieter town in Japan, if I had to change anything.
most_rewarding: As much as I was overwhelmed by culture chock, the challenges have made me learn a lot of things about myself. Ultimately, I think it's pretty healthy to get out of your comfort zone every now and then.
greatest_challenge: Keeping my spirits up - sometimes when the academic challenges and my homesickness got to me, I had a hard time seeing the point in studying abroad in the first place.
other_comments: DO NOT ENROLL IN SILS IF YOU ARE NOT STUDYING JAPANESE: Waseda and UCPH will not help you if you cannot get enough credits secured through English-taught courses. I had to spent way more time than I should have just figuring out a solution, and the solution was a very far from ideal.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to challenge myself to live and study in a completely new environment.
overall_comments: I did enjoy Japan as a destination but was wholly dissatisfied by the academic workload and challenge. For anyone going to Japan to study, beware that their standards are considerably lower and if your goal is to go there for an academic opportunity, you might be disappointed.
info_ease: The orientation for international students and material provided beforehand was great and will help anyone who is anxious about the bureaucratic processes, as well as registration procedures. However, every graduate school at Waseda does things individually, so I cannot speak for the others.
arrival_assistance: Orientation meetings, e-mails, etc.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

For anyone going to Japan to study, beware that their standards are considerably lower and if your goal is to go there for an academic opportunity, you might be disappointed.
registration_process: Course registration was available only a few weeks before the start of the semester - rather late. I was anxious about getting all the courses I had pre-approved, but this was not an issue in the end.

registration_success: I was able to successfully register for all classes I wanted/had pre-approved.
registration_advice: See my comments above about the registration process starting rather late.
academics_comments: I did enjoy Japan as a destination but was wholly dissatisfied by the academic workload and challenge. For anyone going to Japan to study, beware that their standards are considerably lower and if your goal is to go there for an academic opportunity, you might be disappointed.
course_level: I would say that the academic level/standard in Japan is shockingly low. I confirmed this with other exchange students who were not in the social sciences and they agreed with this assessment. Be aware of this when considering Japan as a destination for a scholarly challenge.
teaching_comparison: There are student-led discussions, but not to the level of KU. It largely depends on the professors, and I have found that Japanese professors prefer a lecture-type class.
courses_enrolled: Europe and Asia; Comparative Regionalism; Citizenship, Culture, and Community; Political Economy of Development;
recommended_courses: There are too many courses at Waseda compared to the few I took to be able to recommend a specific one.
unexpected_costs: Transportation in Tokyo is significantly more expensive than I had anticipated, due to the many different rail operators within the city and the greater region.
cost_comparison: See my comments above.
activities_available: There would have been regular events for international students at the University, but I did not partake in them.
activities_recommended: I did not partake in any non-academic activities at the school.
weekend_recommendations: Japan has an incredible rail network and there is a lot to do in the greater Tokyo region, such as hiking, cultural activities, exploring other cities, etc.
culture_adjustment: Be aware that the level of English really low and oftentimes non-existent, even in a metropolis such as Tokyo. Communication is often difficult and Japanese is a rather difficult language to master even at a basic level. However, Japanese people are very understanding of this and will do their best to accommodate you.
cultural_challenges: See my comments above about the Japanese language. I practiced Japanese for more than half a year and still found it very difficult to communicate, even at a basic level. However, it was rewarding to at least be able to read some of the signage, and this should not be a discouragement if you want to go to Japan.
culture_appreciated: The Japanese culture is widely known for its high levels of politeness. Even if you can never really be sure if someone is polite to you because it is a social convention or because they are actually a nice person, it nevertheless makes things like the communicative barrier a bit easier.
top3_advice: Be aware that the studying abroad can oftentimes be difficult, whether this be the distance from home, the academic challenge, cultural barriers, or other issues. However, I would strongly urge everyone to think about going on exchange, since this is an opportunity you will most likely never get again this easily in your life.
other_useful_info: Don't think about it too much. If Tokyo - or Japan - is a destination of interest to you, then do it. Even if you are a bit disappointed in the end, it is a valuable experience in your life that no-one will be able to take from you.
most_rewarding: I was able to travel a lot around Japan and appreciate the different facets of its nature, culture, cuisine, etc.
greatest_challenge: The fact that academically, it was a major letdown.
