crucial_aspects: 1. Common law jurisdiction. 2. English-speaking country. 3. Small university. 4. Outside Europe.
overall_comments: I enjoyed it, but it was hard work! You should only choose this law school if you go on exchange for academic reasons because you have to study a lot, also during the weekends.
info_ease: Very easy! W&L was helpful. I emailed with them about everything, and they also sent a packet from the U.S. to my address in Denmark with relevant information (primarily for the VISA).
arrival_assistance: Just before I arrived, I got an email with information about the orientation week. During the first day of that week, I talked with Dean Mason, and I got an information packet with all relevant information. She was helpful and told me that I could always reach out to her. The same thing did Hunter Swanson who is the international coordinator (for law school and undergrad). He also held a meeting for the international law students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: I enjoyed it, but it was hard work! You should only choose this law school if you go on exchange for academic reasons because you have to study a lot, also during the weekends.
registration_process: I just e-mailed with the law registar, and he sent a list of available courses that I could choose. I e-mailed back with my preferences, and then he fixed the registration. During the summer, I got my W&L e-mail, and then I was able to see my registrations on Workday (the app they use for course registration). Normally, the students register themselves, but the school does it for the exchange students which was very nice. But be aware that the American students register before the exchange students, so I could only choose between the less popular courses which was very annoying.
registration_help: See answer above.
registration_success: At first, I was not successful. Many of the courses I wanted were not available because they were already full. I only got 2 out of 4 courses. I was, however, lucky when I got there. One course got a free spot the day before we started, and I was able to get it. Thus I got 3 courses I wanted and ended up taking 1 that I did not prefer.
registration_advice: There is a drop/add policy the first two weeks. Check Workday just before start and then regularly afterwards to see if any new spots are offered because students drop the courses frequently in this period.
academics_comments: I enjoyed it, but it was hard work! You should only choose this law school if you go on exchange for academic reasons because you have to study a lot, also during the weekends.
course_level: Law school is grad level in the U.S which is equivalent to MA.
teaching_comparison: More readings. Your participation in class is part of your final grade. The professors check in the beginning of every class who is there and who is not. No fictive study cases which we have all the time in Copenhagen. The professors cold call, and if you are not prepared for class, they will ask you to leave. If you do not like speaking in class, this is not a place for you.
courses_enrolled: 1. Poverty Law (3 credits = 7,5 ECTS). 2. Business Associations (4 credits = 10 ECTS). 3. National Security Law (2 credits = 5 ECTS). 4. Alternative Dispute Resolution (3 credits = 7,5 ECTS).
recommended_courses: I would recommend all of them. They were different in many ways, but they were all amazing. It was a great way to try different subjects and teaching methods. 1. BA was heavy, as it is a bar exam course. You had to make case briefs for every case (usually 5-8 cases per class), and it was a lot of work. However, I really ended up enjoying it. The professor was so good! It was a wonderful experience having her. 2. ADR was amazing. The professor had been living in France for many years, so the amount of readings were on European level = less than the other classes. We had role plays in almost every class, and I improved my speaking a lot in these classes. We did different mediations and negotiations as well as one big international arbitration mock case. 3. National Security Law was my favourite. It was due to the different subjects in class, as I have specialized in human rights law which was the core of the class because American national security law usually conflicts with human rights. I also got a really close relationship with the professor. He was very helpful, also outside class. His teaching method was primarily him speaking and then open discussions in class. We also had different guest lecturers such as a FBI agent and attorneys working with international espionage and counter-terrorism. It was incredible. The exam was tough because it was a research paper (25-30 pages) which was a lot of work for only 5 ECTS. 4. I also enjoyed Poverty Law. The professor was a legend at W&L, and it was her last class before retiring after almost 40 years of teaching at the school. The class was about welfare law and social security law in the U.S. It was amazing to learn about because it is in such contrast to the Danish welfare society. Nothing less than a good experience. I felt really proud of being Danish, and it was shocking to learn about the American society.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: The utilities were higher than expected because of the energy prices and inflation. Buying groceries was also more expensive than expected.
activities_available: Everything! I enjoyed the athlectic center with the gym, squash courts and different classes (yoga, spinning, HIT etc.). I also loved the Outing Club, and I went on more than 10 trips with them (hiking, biking etc.). I was also part of different social clubs at the law school, and they did things such as potlocks, quizzes, trips to other towns, parties etc.
activities_recommended: Join the Outing Club! It is great to do things outside Lexington.
weekend_recommendations: Visit D.C, Charlottesville and Staunton. Take on trips with the Outing Club. Go to the parties. They begin early and end around midnight because everyone has to get up and study the day after.
culture_adjustment: It was easy, but I was also very open-minded.
socializing_tips: Talk with everyone if they seem interested! Be open and ask questions. Americans are open-minded and out-going, so they make you feel welcome in no time. However, the law students can be quite busy, so I enjoyed getting to know the undergrad students as well (on the trips with the Outing Club). They were less stressful.
cultural_challenges: Americans are loud in public. They almost yell when they are talking with each other. It was a bit difficult at first.
culture_appreciated: Americans and their openness. I felt so welcome.
top3_advice: 1. Be open and social. 2. Join different clubs and embrace all the options that the campus culture offers you. 3. Do the readings and participate in class. It will benefit you so much!
other_useful_info: As I already said, it is a lot of hard work! It is not an exchange stay with vacation vibes.
most_rewarding: The academics, the campus culture and the people I met during my stay. I got some really good friends and I will miss them dearly.
greatest_challenge: The academics (It will be stressful, but you will get used to it. It was amazing to learn so much) and being in a small town.

crucial_aspects: I wanted a break from my busy life in Copenhagen, where I studied full time while working a student job I felt truly miserable at. I had picked a lot of easy but boring electives during my 5th semester, which drained my energy and motivation to continue studying law in the first place. Exchange was therefore a convenient out from my job, in addition to being a much needed change of scenery. I heard a lot of good about the academics, and W&L is a small school with a low percentage of international students, so I really had to chance to get to meet and befriend some Americans. Fall 2024 was also an election year, so I hoped there would be a lot of interesting election-themed events going on.
info_ease: The university will send you all the information you need. Getting my VISA was a breeze, thanks to Hunter.
arrival_assistance: The Virginia Breeze Bus will drop you off on the other side of a highway with no sidewalk, so getting into town can be a bit scary. I was picked up by my mentor, but Hunter Swanson also offered to drive me to my place on the day I arrived.
arrival_comments: I had issues with signing up for the student-ID because I didn't have an American phone number, but I got it done in-person at the undergrad main building in a few minutes.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You send an email to the registrar, who signs you up manually. When a spot open up, you're sent an e-mail which brings you to a page where you can choose to accept the course.
registration_help: I arranged a zoom-meeting with Dean Drumbl to get a feel for the classes I was considering, which was very helpful. She went through each class with far greater detail than the course description, and talked about what was expected of students.
registration_success: I got all the classes I signed up and was wait-listed for.
registration_advice: Don't get scared by the wait-list.
course_level: Your workload will easily be 2-3 times as hard as UCPH.
teaching_comparison: Some teachers will cold-call, so be prepared to have the reading done for every class. Some professors don't permit laptops in their class, so I would recommend that you always print out your notes and bring them to class on paper. It also projects an image of professionalism that the professors like. Law is studied very differently in America, and relies almost entirely on reading case law. Quimbee is so, so helpful in concisely understanding the legal reasoning and outcome of a case. Use it often. Class sizes are a lot smaller, typically around 12-20 students. There's not the same level of anonymity, and teachers will learn your name before you learn theirs.
courses_enrolled: LAW 683 Mass Atrocities Seminar LAW 722 Mass Media Law LAW 733 Criminal Procedure: Investigation LAW 770 Employment Practices LAW 771 National Security Law and Practice
recommended_courses: Employment Practices was a waste of time, and the professor was not good at making the class interesting. National Security Law and Practice focused on how the constitution of the U.S. limits the presidents ability to invoke national security as a justification for his exercise of power. It really highlighted how the U.S. constitution is a living document, which has been tested and forced to adapt with the passage of time. Very interesting for anyone interested in American history. Mass Atrocities is an international law class. The final is a 17 page paper on a topic of your choice, so be prepared for that when you sign up. You won't be reading a textbook, but instead articles from all kinds of legal scholars, which can be quite different from the other classes. Professor Fyfe is great though. It's a class where you're strongly expected to participate. Mass Media Law does not have that much reading compared to other classes, but you'll have to make a moot-court presentation before your class at least once during the semester with a partner. It's a great way to meet people actually.
unexpected_costs: The U.S dollar gained value relative to the DKK during my time there, so I declined around 10% in purchasing power from the first to my last day.
cost_comparison: Books are criminally expensive. Taking the bus to D.C. is quite expensive, and ends up at 90$ for a round trip. Consider renting a car for a day if you can, it's often cheaper. I didn't spend a lot on food because I made a deal with two of my friends who were forced to buy more meal swipes than they needed, that they would swipe for me and once they ran out for the week, I'd take them out to eat at one of the many restaurants in Lexington. I will strongly recommend going to Napa Thai.
activities_available: Once a month the University would host some kind of party for all law students. W&L's version of a "Friday bar" is the flag-football tournament held each Friday afternoon right outside the university building. Afterwards, people go home and shower and then go party.
activities_recommended: Go to flag football! People are always eager to invite people to their teams, and you don't have to play if you don't want to get dirty of injure yourself.
weekend_recommendations: Thanksgiving is a big thing in America, and campus shuts down the whole week anyways. You might even get to see a whole different part of the U.S.
culture_adjustment: Very easy. People are friendly, and everyone speaks English.
socializing_tips: Be open-minded and outgoing. American Law students have already completed 4 years of undergrad college, and most have had some kind of job as well before starting. People are therefore more mature compared to UCPH, but they also have so much on their mind. Ask a lot of questions, and be sure to remind them of what you really like and appreciate about the U.S. Join a flag-football team. Parties start early, and end around midnight. It's very dissimilar to the binge-drinking parties you'll be used to in Denmark, and you'll do a lot of talking.
cultural_challenges: Getting used to saying "How are you" as a greeting, and greeting people as you pass by them in the hallways.
culture_appreciated: How people came up to talk to you, and how inclusive the social atmosphere were. If something was going on, people would make sure to invite you. I felt so welcome.
top3_advice: 1. Be prepared to do 2-3 times as much reading as you're used to. You will not be relaxing during your stay. 2. Be outgoing, open-minded, and join a flag football team. 3. Participate in class, get to know your professors and take office hours with them. It'll give you some much needed confidence, since getting dropped by parachute into a new legal system can be quite overwhelming.
other_useful_info: If you need help with anything, ask. I always received an answer to my mails within a few hours, if not minutes. Lexington is a very safe small town. I never locked the door to my apartment.
most_rewarding: Making some amazing friends.
greatest_challenge: The workload is no joke. It is incredibly rewarding, but you will be exhausted by the time you're getting home.

cost_comparison: Food

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere where English was the spoken language and then I also included thoughts about the covid-19 situation in my decision process. Additionally, I had heard from older students that Canada was a great country for an exchange stay.
overall_comments: I had a good exchange stay in Canada, but it wasn't without its challenges. In the beginning it was difficult as it was online, and campus was closed etc. - measures that had to be taken because of covid-19. Later when the restrictions lifted it was really fun and interesting. Western is a very social place, but this was limited during my stay, unfortunately.
info_ease: Upon my arrival campus was closed and everything had to be done via email or going through websites. In my opinion UWO has a lot of different websites pertaining all the different university-related things which can be very confusing. Within the first week where classes also start you have to figure out so many things and that is not easy to do when everything has to be online, so during my stay I didn't find it that easy to find the needed information.
arrival_assistance: After a few days the international office had a "zoom-party" with some information, but it was mainly for exchange/international students to "get together" and "meet" each other. It didn't seem like this was the normal procedure and if you're going on exchange in non-pandemic times, I suspect you could expect something different.
arrival_comments: I think the university did what they could when these restrictions were in place. They were available on email and had a day-to-day reply. The orientation about going to Western I thought were missing or not adequate.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I had a good exchange stay in Canada, but it wasn't without its challenges. In the beginning it was difficult as it was online, and campus was closed etc. - measures that had to be taken because of covid-19. Later when the restrictions lifted it was really fun and interesting. Western is a very social place, but this was limited during my stay, unfortunately.
registration_process: You get an email with a link to the registration page and a description of how to do. As an exchange student we have to do it a little different than the Canadians, so after choosing the courses in the system you have to write the office an email letting them know that you have locked in your choices. They will then put it in the system and let you know if you got a spot or if you would have to find another course.
registration_help: Besides the description staff are available on email. I found a course that I wanted to register for, but I was unsure if I had the prerequisites. I sent them an email asking whether I would be able to sign up for the course and they replied quick with a useful answer.
registration_success: Unfortunately, I had some problems with signing up for courses. I began looking at courses I wanted to take shortly after I received their email. When I had decided within the normal registration period, I wrote them an email and they confirmed. Then a month later I received another email asking if I still wanted to come to Western as I hadn't signed up for courses. Apparently, they hadn't locked in my registration properly and I had to choose among the courses that were available in the after registration where the options are more limited. Out of the first four courses I got one and among the three I then chose the second time I got all of them.
registration_advice: Be sure that they have your registration for courses locked in. If you want to read more about each course, you can find the course description on the faculty's website - it might be the one from last year, but I don't think they change a lot from year to year. UWO doesn't have a public health program, but they have medical science and health science and the combination of the courses these two programs have is very close to what we have at public health. Both programs don't have many courses that are available for exchange students, unfortunately, but there are some. In addition, you can look at other faculties as there are a lot of relevant courses for a PHS student outside of these two programs.
academics_comments: I had a good exchange stay in Canada, but it wasn't without its challenges. In the beginning it was difficult as it was online, and campus was closed etc. - measures that had to be taken because of covid-19. Later when the restrictions lifted it was really fun and interesting. Western is a very social place, but this was limited during my stay, unfortunately.
course_level: I had four undergraduate courses, three 4th year and one 3rd year. In my opinion they all had a fair academic level considering everything was in English as well. I did gain some new knowledge, but I also got the chance to use some of the knowledge that I had from UCPH and what I got at UWO in practice as my courses involved doing projects. I would like to add that some 4th year Canadians told me that having three module courses (which my 4th year courses apparently were) was a lot of work and that they didn't know anyone doing three module courses at the same time - so be aware of this. I managed well anyway but I do think I had a lot of work and readings throughout the term when comparing with some of the other exchange students.
teaching_comparison: In my courses with group work we had some lectures and then also time scheduled to work on the projects. My sociology course was a discussion-based course, so students talked as much - if not even more - than the professor. My economics course was a classic lecture style course where I did miss time put off for trying out the stuff we learned as we had a specific program to work in. Your grades are a collection of how you did on tests, quizzes, assignments, participation, and the final exam which is a lot different from how we do at PHS. And remember, some courses have mid-terms! I only had one, but it is some to take into consideration and look for when registering for courses.
courses_enrolled: EPID 3330G - Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis EPID 4615B - Health Economic Evaluation HEALTHSCI 4200G - Advanced Health Promotion SOCIOLOG 4422G - LGBTQ2S+ Populations
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed the LGBTQ2S+ course as I've learned a lot about those populations as well as Canadian indigenous culture (2S refers to two-spirited which is a thing among the indigenous populations). If you're interested to increase your knowledge about the populations, the living circumstances, and how to do research on them it is a great course. Additionally, this is the discussion-based course, so you really have a great chance to improve your spoken English. As you also get marks on contribution you would have to participate each week, but it is really rewarding. Further, Professor Waite is a really great teacher. I did not take the course but Canadians from my systematic reviews course told me that 'Major Diseases' is a really great course if you like epidemiology.
unexpected_costs: I didn't have any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: When paying for housing and meal plan you pay it all at once and I thought the payment was for a full year and you would get a refund by the end of the term. I only got a refund for the flex money I didn't spend on food (meal plan payment included flex money, I'm not really sure what it meant). This meant that I in total spend 38,000DKK on housing and meal plan which was a lot more expensive than I thought.
activities_available: During my stay we could use the pool and the gym. They also have a peer guide program you can sign up for where you get a Canadian student assigned. They are supposed to help you with whatever questions and queries you have, and they are also a great opportunity if you want to hang out with Canadians.
activities_recommended: I enjoyed going to hockey games, both at the university and at the local team (not NHL). The university games are free for students and tickets for the local team are not too expensive. Apparently, Western University is known for being a party school so the nightlife in London, ON, is busy. It's fun to try out a couple of times. My favorite place was Molly Blooms, which is an Irish pub with karaoke night on Sundays and Mondays. The karaoke culture here is fun as people will get up and dance to people's singing and just support the people up there. Also, I've heard homecoming (hoco) should be fun as well as foco (fake homecoming). These events take place during the fall. During the winter term there's St. Patrick's Day which is a big thing. People dress up in green and then have house/garden parties and you can just walk in and start talking with people.
weekend_recommendations: I spent reading week visiting Vancouver and Vancouver Island and it was really fun seeing the west coast as it is different to the east. Some of my friends rented a car and drove to Niagara Falls, Toronto, and Montreal, during reading week. If you have a car available during weekends going to the Falls is easy and I would also recommend going to the lakes. Compared to how big the country is, it is a short drive, and you get to see something else, as London, ON, can be quite boring. I also had the opportunity to go to New York during my stay and after the term I visited Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal, Halifax, and Cape Breton Island (this is a really nice place for hiking). I also went backpacking in Cuba after which takes some preparation, but you can go to the beaches (Varadero) in Cuba for quite cheap without that much preparation.
culture_adjustment: Quite easy. It looks somewhat similar to Danish culture and as the Canadians are so nice and friendly getting adjusted to the culture is very easy.
socializing_tips: If you take upper year courses (3rd and 4th) the classes are smaller - in my experience between 8 and 30 - which makes it easier to approach local students. Other than that, they are very open and polite, so if you just start a conversation they will respond and participate. I did it in some of my courses as I had some questions and after talking about schoolwork the conversation shifted into a more informal conversation.
cultural_challenges: It can be a bit challenging that they're younger. Some of them are really mature but they are in completely different place in life than we are. They are a maximum of 22 years old and only live away from home during the terms. They are not as independent as I think we are in Denmark and sometimes I would take this as a given.
culture_appreciated: The Canadian friendliness. I always had a feeling of being welcome and appreciated.
top3_advice: 1) Bring long underwear - it is great when the temperature drops to negative 10-20 degrees and you still have to walk to campus. 2) Don't expect too much of the city. London, ON, is not a great city per se. In my opinion it's a university city that comes to life when the students come back for the term. You basically go downtown for the hockey games, and bars. Other than that, you're mainly just hanging out around campus. 3) Be open to the variety of people you meet. They might seem young and immature, but they can still make great friends and you will learn from each other. This goes both for Canadian students and other exchange students. If you're inclusive in your behavior and are willing to broaden your horizon these people will really add to your exchange experience.
other_useful_info: Don't stress too much about deadlines. I experienced that the Canadian students would ask for extension of deadlines all the time, and these were often granted. The professors really want to help and are very accommodating of students' busy schedules. Also, use office hours. I didn't and I regret that. As were not used to office hours in the same way at PHS I didn't know how to use them, but if you're doing projects, they can really help you along the way and make sure the project is headed in the right direction.
most_rewarding: The people I've met. Canadians are not necessarily looking for new friends and don't initiate the first conversation - I think this applies for 3rd and 4th year students - but if you do, they will engage, and you would have expanded your network.
greatest_challenge: The first weeks were rough, and I think it was worsened because of the pandemic and the related restrictions. It was difficult to meet people and the first month had to be spent in our rooms (almost), so it was lonely. Also, because the Canadians stayed at home with their parents to save rent in January. But me and my roomie made some other friends at Alumni which introduced us to some of their friends and so on, so by the end of February my social circle had expanded a lot.
other_comments: Finding the balance between social life and academic work can be a bit tricky but ask around. Maybe there is some local knowledge on how to do a course or get help from your class mates or TA.

crucial_aspects: I really wanted to go to Canada, because I have heard so many great things about the country. I also saw Canada as a less extreme version of the US. I only chose Western University because it was one of the few universities that did not require an english test (I wanted to avoid the test, because it costs money to take it)
info_ease: It took some effort, but it was manageable
arrival_assistance: There was an 'introduction week' for international- and exchange students. The first day was dedicated to getting help with general questions about the university, housing, working abroad - really just any questions you might have.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You went to a website where you could browse through the courses available. As an exchange student, you are only allowed courses on the main campus. You had to select your chosen courses on another website, and then you had to wait for them to be approved. Once they were approved, the employees at the abroad department would enroll you in the approved courses.
registration_help: You could always email the abroad department with any questions. They are very friendly and quick to reply.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure that there are several courses that you might want to have, just in case you don't get the courses you first apply for. I have friends who didn't get the courses they wanted and then had to take other courses that they were completely uninterested in.
course_level: I think the courses and the academic level is lower at Western than at UCPH. Even the second-year course I took felt like Danish gymnasium. One of our assignments in my American Nightmare course (Introduction to American studies - a second year course) was "prepare a presentation to a ninth grade class and talk to them about wealth inequality in the US" (and then we just wrote the transcripts to the presentation).
teaching_comparison: Generally similar teaching style, but then there were often quizzes you had to do (once every other week for some courses). We were also graded for participation in two of the courses I took, so you had to be active in class.
courses_enrolled: American Nightmare; Advertising and Society; Technology and Society; Equity, Diversity, and Human Rights.
recommended_courses: I would recommend the Advertising and Society course. It was really interesting and thought provoking.
unexpected_costs: What I reported under 'insurance' is the total I paid for both the mandatory insurance from the university AND my own personal insurance. I only had one course book. All other courses had exclusively online material. So I only spent 150 DKK on books in total that semester. Regarding transport, I had to pay a one-time fee for a card that would allow me to use public transportation as much as I wanted (this was done through Western, and I just used my student card as my bus card). The card was actually valid for an entire year. It was not possible to buy public transport for just one semester.
cost_comparison: When you get a new sim card, you can expect really high prices on data compared to Denmark
activities_available: There are several clubs to join that focus on all kinds of things. There was also a street festival in the first month where everyone wore purple Western merch. For international- and exchange students, there was also a thing called "Global Café" that was held every Thursday where we would play board games, eat snacks, and get to know each other.
activities_recommended: Be very active in the intro week, because this is where you will meet new people and make friends. Most of the people I talked to during the semester were those I met during intro week. Also, join Global Café - it is a lot of fun.
weekend_recommendations: If you have a chance, you should definitely go to Banff National Park during reading week. I went there with my friend group, and it is just such a beautiful place! You should especially go see Lake Louise.
culture_adjustment: People are generally really nice and friendly, so it was easy to adjust.
socializing_tips: Like I said, I didn't really talk to many local students, so I'm not the best person to ask. It is probably a good idea to join a club. I did join a club myself, but I joined it with the friends I had already made during the introduction week. Exchange students and international students had their own introduction week separate from the introduction week for the Canadian students, so I didn't really meet that many local students.
cultural_challenges: There was nothing about the culture that I found particularly challenging.
culture_appreciated: This is a really small thing, but I really liked how most people said "thank you" when they got off the bus.
top3_advice: 1) Stock up on any Danish snacks/food that you can't get in Canada. 2) Bring warm clothes (or buy them in Canada) - especially if you are planning to travel somewhere colder during reading week 3) Be very active in getting to know new people during that first introduction week and just generally during the first two weeks of the exchange. It gets harder to find new friends after that.
other_useful_info: I can't think of anything.
most_rewarding: Getting to know other exhange students. I had a friend group of about 8 people and we were from all across the globe, which lead to some really interesting conversations.
greatest_challenge: Living off campus - it was just annoying to take the bus every day (especially because the busses were so unreliable). It was also a little sad to miss out on the social aspect of living with many other students.
other_comments: No other comments.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to North America, this was a great opportunity. It was important that the university tought some interesting courses, since I'm gonna spend 30 ects there.
info_ease: Reception was generally very friendly and useful. Sophomores are also very helpful and committed. You can always write emails to the different offices at uwo, they usually respond within a day.
arrival_assistance: When you check in they give you a map over campus and some advise to where the parties are and where the different offices are located. You can ask them anything.
arrival_comments: I had to figure out how to get tested for covid on my own, since i was randomly selected for mandatory test in the airport. I spend the entire first day on this, and all the receptionist could do was give me a quicktest kit, which is not considered a legitimate test in this case.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You go to some online platform and select the courses you want to get approved. Then when they get approved you have to write to the international office that it is approved, and they will enroll you on your behalf. When choosing which courses you want to be enrolled in, you have to make sure the classes don't overlap. They give you a online tool for this but this can be challenging and make it even more difficult to take all the courses you want.
registration_help: Didn't get much help until i got on campus.
registration_success: Unsuccessful.
registration_advice: Write to them and send them a list of the courses you have taken. This might shorten the time it takes to get stuff approved etc. but most importantly, i think that UCPH only shares your course transcript from when you sign up for studying abroad (which was november in my case i think) so if you take any courses in the next semester and even the last half of the first, they might not be on your transcript and therefore it can be difficult to get courses approved at UWO. Also if you are studying physics, try and apply for mathematics, computerscience and/or astronomy courses also, since pure physics apparently isnt that popular/available at UWO.
course_level: Since i had never taken any astronomy courses, i was struggling a bit in 3303A. The rest was fine. 2801A has a research project which make up almost half of the course. 30% of the grade on the project report was how good and fluent your English was.
teaching_comparison: It depends on your professor. Most of our professors was good at teaching. They all had very different styles.
courses_enrolled: ASTRONOM 3303A Galaxies ASTRONOM 2801A Observing the Stars PHYSICS 2110A Oscillations and Waves PHYSICS 4662A Magnetic Resonance Imaging
recommended_courses: I only liked 4662A in MRI since i can use the part about nuclear magnetic resonance NRM. This was a course on my level. As was 3303A. 2110A was very easy since i knew most of it already and 2801A was almost high school level.
unexpected_costs: Tipping is a big thing and the bartender reminded us in the first week we were there. We travelled a lot so thats why my personal spending is high. Also i bought winter clothing but that was expected. Renting cars can be difficult to do cheap, especially if you are under 25.
cost_comparison: Tipping, phone plans are notorious for being expensive in Canada. I am still not sure about whether the meal plan is worth it.
activities_available: A lot. There is a lot of clubs at the university. You better sign up for those you like in the beginning of the semester since some of them get filled up quickly. Ask around or check online.
activities_recommended: I would not recommend the outdoor club unless you want to sign up as a driver (class 2 drivers license required??). I didn't get to go on a single trip outside London.
weekend_recommendations: Rent cars and go somewhere. We drove to Chicago and back over a weekend (~6 hours drive). In reading week we went to Vancouver for like 9 days which was great. Sign up for some clubs on campus or go out in London. The nightlife is pretty good.
culture_adjustment: Not that difficult. Tipping was the hardest part to get used to. Grocery shopping is not as easy, but no problem.
socializing_tips: Go to bars and sign up for clubs.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Nightlife and openness to travellers from inside and outside of Canada.
top3_advice: Course registration is a mess so start early and dont be afraid to write to them. Sign up for a club or find someone to go out with or both. This is the best way to socialize. Once you have friends you can start traveling with them.
other_useful_info: Summer lasts for a long time and when winter hits it get very cold fast.
most_rewarding: Travelling and experiencing Canada.
greatest_challenge: Staying motivated to study. Saving money.
other_comments: If you want to save money you should plan ahead and buy tickets etc. early. Especially VIA rail and car rental.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an English speaking country and because I have already lived in the U.S I wanted to try and experience Canada.
info_ease: It was pretty easy, I got an e-mail with all the information and I was able to sign up for orientation.
arrival_assistance: We had an orientation week where we got information and mingled with other exchange students.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was okay. The university emailed us a month before with the information, however, the classes you could take was extremely limited as an exchange student which made it really hard. I had to register for classes around 4 times because there were something wrong each time even though I had elective courses.
registration_help: It was possible to email the administration but it was a little frustrating as they had a few days of response time.
registration_success: I did not get any of the classes I wanted and therefore had to pick what was available.
registration_advice: You can only take classes at Main Campus and classes with no prerequisites and you can only do essay courses and half year courses.
course_level: The level was okay but there is so much more work than on KU. You have to take around 4-5 classes for a semester and each class requires you to do work every week besides reading like a weekly quiz, essay, discussion posts and tests.
teaching_comparison: It was very different, you are less independent in your studies as there is always something you have to do, like a quiz in one course every sunday evening which makes it hard to plan your own time as it has been planned for you already. You kinda just have to do everything when the professors want you to whereas at KU you can kinda plan your own time as long as you get it done.
courses_enrolled: Gender and Fashion American Nightmare/Politics Power, Oppression and Privilege/Philosophy Mystery and Detective Fiction/English
recommended_courses: I would recommend American Nightmare, we had a really nice professor and it was an interesting course.
unexpected_costs: Phone plans are very expensive in Canada as well as groceries. You also have to tip, so that is an extra cost always when eating out, going to the hair dresser and stuff like that.
cost_comparison: Phone plans Groceries
activities_available: There were a lot of clubs you could sign up for. I signed up for the outdoors club but they release their trips on random times so if you don't notice within an hour it will be filled up. I missed out on a trip because I was taking a nap.
activities_recommended: I've heard really good things about the Outdoors club. They usually have a lot more to offer than when I was there, but unfortunately they have been suffering under the pandemic too. They have some cool trips so make sure to keep an eye out.
weekend_recommendations: Go to Toronto or Niagara Falls
culture_adjustment: If you are used to Canada or the United States you will already know the differences and then it is pretty easy to adjust.
socializing_tips: Make sure to go to the orientation and participate in the events they offer, it'll make it easier to make friends as everyone is kinda in the same situation looking for friends.
cultural_challenges: I don't really find it challenging but people are a lot more offended by things here than in Denmark, so try and be respectful of that.
culture_appreciated: People are very open and friendly and you can always find a friendly stranger.
top3_advice: 1. Don't think too much about school, you will learn just as much by exploring a new culture and being on your own, so as long as you do what is required you need to try and experience the rest after. 2. Go travel as much as you can. 3. Make a lot of friends from different places.
most_rewarding: I think being on your own in a foreign country is a good challenge for yourself and you get to learn a lot about yourself and grow from it.
greatest_challenge: I think the greatest challenge is being away from everyone you know on big days, but try and distract yourself by going out with your friends or traveling, because then you won't really notice.

crucial_aspects: The aspects that were crucial to choosing my study destination were that it was English-speaking, that previous students' experiences had been great, and that the course catalogue had a lot of classes that I thought looked super interesting.
overall_comments: Absolutely a 10. Honestly, the reason why I haven't gotten around to writing this review before now is because I simply don't know how to describe how fantastic my experience was! I hadn't even been in Toronto Union Station for 2 full minutes the day I first arrived looking for a train to take to the university, when I had already made two new friends from Israel. They were also going to be exchange students at Western, and even living in the same building as me! I enjoyed every minute I had with all the amazing people I met from ALL around the world! I remember when I first arrived in the suite late at night the 31st of August, I was unlocking the door to my room when all of a sudden two of my suitemates stuck their heads out from each of their doors, and it was at that exact moment, that I just knew that it was going to be the best. semester. ever. Since that day, we've been pretty much inseparable. I knew it all along, but especially the very last morning when everyone woke up at 5 AM to wave goodbye to me and I got on the bus, it hit me that I had truly made these friends for life. And guess what?! Not one day has gone by since I left Canada that I haven't talked to them in some way or another, whether that's by audio on the phone, sending pictures or funny jokes, snaps, or whatever it is!
info_ease: Super easy! Western was really good about emailing us updates of what we needed to keep an eye out for, so I just booked a ticket to Toronto and figured that I would figure it out along the way, which I did! Everything is in English and most of the time French too, so it wasn't hard at all.
arrival_assistance: Once I arrived at Western and “checked in” there was a free taxi that took the friends that I had just made and I to Alumni House where we were going to be living, and a goodie bag with snacks and all the information we needed for the orientation events the next day. The university was also really good at hosting a plethora of activities that really allowed you to get to know the others who were there. In addition, everyone is assigned a soph, both relating to an individuals' housing and also for their faculty, which act as an older brother or sister and give tours, showed us around, and really helped us feel welcome and at home.
arrival_comments: I highly recommend participating in O Week. It might be an expensive wristband, but it was so worth it in the way that it really allowed me the opportunity to bond and make a ton of new friends already in the first week of being there. Other than that, the counselors and advisors at the (IGAB) international and graduate affairs building were super helpful in answering any questions one might have.

If you don't meet the prerequisites, and are denied a course, don't worry, you can just request another! Don't hesitate to contact the student center and ask for help, I did that, and was even able to sign up for a second-year French course (even though I study molecular biomedicine) by showing them documentation of having studied sufficient French in high school and taking a quick placement test.

registration_advice: Just remember to check that courses that you are interested in are being offered on the main Western campus, not King's, Huron, or Brescia.

course_level: If you are going on exchange in the first half year of your third year studying in Copenhagen, I would recommend taking courses in the 2000-4000 level. The level of courses that I took when I was there were a French translation course and an Immunology (only lecture) course at the 2000 level, a Genetics course at the 3000 level, and a Neuroscience (essay) course at the 4000 level.
teaching_comparison: It was very different. In Copenhagen, other than a few mandatory labs, the only thing that counts for your grade is the final exam. At Western, it was much more like the American/Canadian system where you have a lot of homework due and have a lot of projects to turn in and quizzes/tests to take throughout the semester which make up about 70% of your final grade, whereas the final exam only makes up the remaining 30% or so. Personally, I prefer that much better, since it helps me stay on track and I also have a better idea of what I am expected to know for the final exam. Not only that, but you work hard for your grade the whole term and know that with the final exam, depending on how much you prepare, you can pretty much only drop one letter grade or increase it by one letter grade. Note that Western's grading scale might be different than you expect: A+ = 90-100 A = 80-90 B = 70-80 C = 60-70 D = 50-60 F = 50 or below
courses_enrolled: Anatomy and Cell Biology 4451 F/G Integrative Neuroscience French 2305 A/B Translation: Comparative Stylistics Microbiology and Immunology 2500 A/B Biology of Infection and Immunity Biology 3592 A/B Principles of Human Genetics
recommended_courses: I would recommend taking ANY of the courses that I took (listed above). Each was super interesting in its own unique way and had a different learning structure/strategy for how the class was run. In French class we would get a few exercises from a little book from the 1960's assigned to have done by the next class. In the Genetics course, we had a big case study project where we had to pretend to be genetic counselors and “teach” various concepts to the patient and their family, we also had a forum where we would read papers and post questions open-ended questions/respond to others' questions, a bioethics team-debate and reading logs. In Neuroscience we had weekly written assignments and one really big presentation, and finally, the Immunology course was just lectures and grading based on the midterms. It was refreshing that they were all set up differently!
unexpected_costs: I didn't really have any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: All of the items were about the same price that I had expected.
activities_available: There was homecoming, intramural sports, house-related craft events like door-decorating, movie nights, and cultural events like global cafe each Thursday that focused on cuisine and traditions from a different country around the world each week.
activities_recommended: Some of my friends/roomies and I would go to the recreation center in the morning, either to use the bike machines or go to the pool. It's so well-equipped and the pool is huge. You can also go for a walk in one of the nearby local parks. I was there during autumn and it was SO BEAUTIFUL when the leaves started to turn red orange and yellow and fell from the trees. In late October, one day we went to Ross Park (only a five minutes walk away from Western) and we took the most INCREDIBLE photos in heaps of bright orange leaves!!! You might also want to go to an Apple farm or a Pumpkin patch, the nature is wonderful! Lastly, in December, my roommate found out Mariah Carey was having a Christmas concert in the Scotiabank Arena in Toronto, so we went and it was THE. BEST. EXPERIENCE. EVER! If you can find things to do like that, you'll make some great memories! Towards the end, the World cup in soccer was also playing on screen at the Spoke (the student restaurant/bar), so it was really exciting for me to go see it with my French friends when France was playing.
weekend_recommendations: I highly recommend visiting Toronto and Niagara Falls on a weekend or holiday. For Toronto, you can book a bus on Megabus that departs at 6 AM right outside Elgin Hall and drives directly to Toronto in a little over 2 hours, and you can take the same bus back in the evening for only about $25 dollars each way. When I came I took the train, which is also do-able, it's just more expensive and takes a long time, so if you can, you should go by bus. You can also travel by plane during reading week, that way you have more time to explore another place in Canada and have more than just a three day weekend/thanksgiving off and can go somewhere farther.
culture_adjustment: For me, I found it super easy to “assimilate” when I came to London and also in adjusting to the school system, as that was what I had once been used to having grown up in the US. Of course, I can't say for sure that this wasn't special in my case, because London is in fact apparently very similar to the American model, but it really seems as if the other exchange students that I lived with (and some of whom are still there), are having a blast! Everyone that I have talked to who went to Western all said that they had a fantastic experience there, so I really think that Western just has a really good exchange program and is very open and welcoming. I know for my part at least, I was really lucky in that everyone I met was super nice and friendly, and that it wasn't hard to adjust to at all!
socializing_tips: Don't be afraid to introduce yourself and talk to people in your classes, everyone is super nice! It's also a good idea to form/join a study group with Canadian students from your classes even if it is just with one other person and meeting at the library or something. Everyone is super down-to-earth.
cultural_challenges: Luckily I didn't find any cultural differences there challenging!
culture_appreciated: This might not fall under the culture aspect, but I really like how, by living on campus, especially with the “old fashioned” buildings it really felt like a boarding school setting, which I thought was really nice when everyone was so kind there, so you were living with your best friends! Also the fact that strangers aren't afraid to talk to you was very refreshing! Once, my suitemate and I took the bus to go to the farmer's market and a elderly Canadian woman in the bus started talking to us and asking us how we liked Western and gave us recommendations about what to try from the farmer's market. I remember her mentioning “the cherry fritters.” Then, by coincidence the next Friday morning the following week, the same woman happened to be on the bus and we could recognize her and again we talked on the way there. A real Canadian local! How fun!
top3_advice: I would tell a fellow student who is coming to Western to 1. Keep an open mind; I really had no idea what to expect when I came, but I had an open-minded mindset and was ready to try living in a new place, thrive with learning, and meet a bunch of amazing people! 2. Don't overpack, you will thank me later. Especially books, they are so heavy and a hassle! 3. If you have the chance, write someone a card, maybe to someone in your family or an old friend, it's so nice to have a homemade postcard with an envelope with your Canadian address on it, a Canadian stamp, and it'll bring back so many good memories! Plus, they might even send one back to you! ;) 4. If you are going in the fall, collect some orange leaves right after they have fallen from the trees and press them in a book for about a week or so and they'll be perfect, you can even make a garland out of them! I still have mine in a box as a souvenir and I love it!
other_useful_info: Nothing that I can think of!
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the friends I made. I still talk to my friends I met in Canada every single day. In January I even went to Lyon to visit one of the friends I made after she had returned to France from London. How cool is that!
greatest_challenge: It might sound hard to believe but I really believe my exchange was the most perfect exchange that I could ever wish for! I really didn't find anything challenging while there. The only thing, which is not even a big deal or anything, was that the vacuum never really worked, and it didn't matter which one you tried; but honestly, I'm happy it didn't because you should know how many laughs we've had lugging that thing around and “complaining” to the front desk time after time and them promising a new one by the end of the semester, and people returning each “new” one (even though they weren't new at all) after accidentally cutting over the wire and returning it, bahaha! It's kind of one of those, “if you know, you know” moments! So even that, I wouldn't change!
other_comments: If you come to Western I hope you have as much of a blast as I did!!!! :)

crucial_aspects: I chose Western University in Canada as my study destination because I searched and found that they offered some interesting courses. In addition, one of my main motivations for going on an exchange was to improve my academic English and meet people from all around the world. Western University is very multicultural, and I thought that this would also expand my personal understanding and connections with people from other cultures.
overall_comments: It has been an amazing experience to meet so many new people from around the world, live on campus, and study in a new environment. However, it is not very convenient to get out and explore other cities around London, ON, if you don't have a car.
info_ease: I found it easy to find the information I needed for arrival. However, there might be a lot of emails sent with different information, so I would recommend flagging the important emails or printing them out.
arrival_assistance: I received assistant from the International and Exchange student facilitators and volunteers the day after I arrived. There was a meeting section for Winter Exchange and international student, which was a good opportunity to ask all the question I had and also meet new people. In the beginning I had a lot of question regarding the courses, which was quickly answered both though E-mail and in person on their International and Exchange student office. Additionally, because I chose to stay on Campus, I also received assistance with my accommodation and quick overview of the campus.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: It has been an amazing experience to meet so many new people from around the world, live on campus, and study in a new environment. However, it is not very convenient to get out and explore other cities around London, ON, if you don't have a car.
registration_process: I found the course registration process to be manageable, but some courses required specific requests and were not available for exchange students. If there was a course I was interested in but couldn't enroll in before arriving, I recommend reaching out to the professor with a motivation letter to see if enrollment is still possible after course start.
registration_help: The International and Exchange office was helpful in answering any questions or providing assistance with course registration. The university also has a more user-friendly website for course registration and opportunities.
registration_success: On Western University, course grades are not solely based on one exam, but can be determined by several factors, such as midterm exams, attendance, blog posts, and presentations. This was different from what I was used to, as it involved many deadlines.
registration_advice: I recommend registering for a full course load before the exchange start, but if it feels like too much and you have space in your program, don't be afraid to drop one of the courses. The way they study is very different from what I was used to at my previous courses at KU. It's also a good idea to have a backup plan in case you don't get enrolled in one of the courses you wanted or if it turns out to be different from what you expected. If you need help with courses, reach out to the International and Exchange Student office, as they have a good overview of what's possible. Even if you don't meet all the requirements, try to explain why you might be a good fit for the course and why you're interested in it.
academics_comments: It has been an amazing experience to meet so many new people from around the world, live on campus, and study in a new environment. However, it is not very convenient to get out and explore other cities around London, ON, if you don't have a car.
course_level: I feel that the course levels are nearly the same as at home, although it might depend on which course level you take. I found that I already knew some of the content in my courses, but a large part of it was new. I took courses at the 3rd and 4th-year levels and found the level comparable to UCPH. They don't often provide previous exam sets for exam preparation.
teaching_comparison: I had two courses that only consisted of lectures, which was very similar to the teaching style at UCPH. The third course was a lab course, which I found to be very different as it consisted of a lot of lab report assignments and attendance. Attendance and professionalism in class were also marked in addition to knowledge. Overall, I really liked the lab course as it focused a lot on the overall understanding and details of the experiments.
courses_enrolled: BIOCHEM 3386B—Clinical Biochemistry 3620G: Immunology Laboratory Physiology 4520b: Stem Cells and Regenerative Medicine
recommended_courses: 3620G: Immunology Laboratory - I liked the laboratory part of the course and it's a good way to improve your writing skills. Physiology 4520b: Stem Cells and Regenerative Medicine The teachers are really good and interesting topics. The course also includes blog discussions.
unexpected_costs: 13% TAX
cost_comparison: There are a few items that can be more expensive. Firstly, drinks at the clubs tend to be pricier. Secondly, vegetables can also be relatively costly. Lastly, if you don't have a study permit, purchasing a SIM card can be an additional expense.
activities_available: A wide variety of activities was available, including social activities for international/exchange students and athletic options due to easy access to the Western Student Recreation Centre.
activities_recommended: I highly recommend signing up for the Adventure Club. I enjoyed it because it allowed me to go on several trips such as the Maple Festival, snow tubing, and hiking trips. Attending different trips was easy since you signed up for each one individually, making it convenient to fit into your schedule. Additionally, I suggest attending the Global Café, an event primarily attended by international and exchange students. It's a great opportunity to meet new people from around the world.
weekend_recommendations: During spring or fall, consider going on a trip to a Maple syrup farm. You can also explore downtown where you'll find a board game café, market, and other fun activities like escape rooms. If you prefer not to spend too much money, venture outside and explore the nature surrounding the campus. Additionally, keep an eye out for free or affordable events organized by the university. Moreover, I highly recommend participating in different events or activities during the weekdays as they serve as a refreshing study break.
culture_adjustment: The first month was challenging because the study system at the University of Copenhagen is very different. However, after one month, I found it easier to navigate around campus and the city.
socializing_tips: I recommend attending the different events at the beginning and signing up for a peer guide. A peer guide is someone who knows the campus and can also be a hangout buddy.
cultural_challenges: One aspect I found challenging was that people don't hug as much as I'm used to in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: People were very friendly, easy to talk to, and extremely helpful if you had any questions.
top3_advice: 1. Western is a multicultural university, providing an excellent opportunity to learn about Canadian culture as well as other cultures. 2. I appreciate the fact that it's a connected campus, making it convenient to meet up with friends during study breaks, even if they're studying in a different field. The campus offers pleasant outdoor areas and study spaces. 3. I recommend choosing to live on campus. I really enjoyed the atmosphere in Alumni Hall, and it's easier to hang out in your room or your friends' rooms during the evenings. The meal plan can be expensive, but it's not always mandatory for exchange students. I suggest not signing up for it or canceling it to save money while still being able to eat well.
other_useful_info: Bring warm clothes as it gets really cold during the winter.
most_rewarding: I made a lot of new friends from different places around the world. I improved my English-speaking skills.
greatest_challenge: I had to adapt to a new study system and I proved to myself that I was capable of passing my courses in another country and a different study environment.

crucial_aspects: As a psychology student, a crucial consideration in selecting my study destination was the availability of English-taught programs. Canada had always been at the of my list of preferred study destinations, so it made sense for me to pursue my studies there.
info_ease: It was quite easy. Prior to my arrival, the university communicated via multiple emails, providing detailed guidance on where to seek information or assistance if required any. They also had an international office where they offered support and guidance.
arrival_assistance: I had some trouble with the courses that required approval by KU, so I received assistance from their international office to navigate through the process. The university also organised an international orientation week tailored for international and exchange students, featuring various gathering and networking opportunities to connect with fellow international peers.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Before my arrival, I received an email from the International office as Western containing a link to the courses offered for that term. I then had to inform them of the courses I wished to take, and the international office handled registration process on my behalf. As an exchange student, I wasn't able to register the courses independently - but it worked out fine.
registration_help: The International office was available to help.
registration_success: Navigating the course requirements was a bit challenging since Western really put focus on prerequisites and antirequisites, and KU has specific course requirements too. Nevertheless, it worked out in the end.
registration_advice: Make sure registrations and approvals are completed before your arrival. While it's technically possible to register after you arrive, it's honestly best to avoid that because the approval process at KU can take some time. Additionally, it's important to note that desirable courses at the host university can fill up quickly.
course_level: It was fine - I didn't find it overly challenging, and they offered very interesting and engaging courses.
teaching_comparison: The course structure leans more towards lectures, with relatively less emphasis on group work or discussions, which suited my preferences. The final grade is typically a combination of assignments, participation in discussion forums (in some courses), midterms (multiple-choice), final exams (multiple-choice), and semester projects (some courses). Personally, I find this grading style preferable as it encourages and motivates continuous study and engagement throughout the semester. Additionally, they schedule lectures and classes at significantly different times compared to KU. For instance, in some courses, I had lectures scheduled from 7 pm to 10 pm - I personally didn't mind.
courses_enrolled: Clinical psychology, Maladjusted mind, Forensic psychology, and Research methods
recommended_courses: Forensic psychology was honestly so interesting. We worked with real-world police cases and investigations, delved into criminology, and explored the complexities of psychopaths and the criminal mind. Personally, I found it incredibly fascinating.
unexpected_costs: N/A
cost_comparison: Phone bill was a little higher than in Denmark, but it was fine. And grocery shopping is a bit more expensive than in Denmark - but you get used to it.
activities_available: There were so many different activities you can participate in, ranging from different music genres, dance styles, and sports to ethnic and religious clubs. During the first few weeks of the semester, they host a clubs week where you can learn about all the clubs available!
activities_recommended: Honestly, there's something for everyone based on their interests. For instance, I'm a fan of K-pop, so I joined the K-pop club. I really felt like there was a club for every interest. But you're not limited to just one club - I was a part of multiple clubs simultaneously.
weekend_recommendations: If you have the opportunity, I highly recommend exploring other parts of Canada. If not, at least consider visiting Toronto and Niagara Falls; but if you're there during the fall semester, I'd suggest visiting Niagara Falls in the fall rather than winter - it can be a bit grey in the winter. London is a great town, but it is mainly a university town, so a lot is revolved around the university - which is great, but if you wish to see more of Canada then definitely go to other regions. You can easily travel to Toronto with the Flixbus for only 20 CAD! Also, I would definitely recommend to go skiing at Boler Mountain in the winter. Above all, just enjoy your time and try to step out of your comfort zone - you'll find that there are a lot of great people out there.
culture_adjustment: It was actually not as difficult as I expected. As I mentioned earlier, London is a university town so you'll be spending a lot of time on campus. However, Western University really prioritizes diversity, which made it easier for me to feel like I belonged.
socializing_tips: Again, there are plenty of clubs you can join to meet people - so I would definitely recommend giving those a try. But most importantly, just have fun and don't be afraid to step out of your comfort zone.
cultural_challenges: I can't think of anything particularly challenging.
culture_appreciated: I was pleasantly surprised by how open and friendly everyone was. In Denmark, people can sometimes be a bit reserved, but I didn't encounter that in London at all.
top3_advice: 1) Step out of your comfort zone! Western University offers a diverse community, so take advantage of this by participating in various clubs, events, and activities to meet people from different backgrounds and cultures. 2) Different learning style - Western's course structure may differ from what we know at KU. They put emphasis on lectures, assessments, midterms (multiple choice), projects etc. The midterms and exams are multiple choice so it's a lot about memorising the material compared to how it works at KU. 3) Explore Canada - go to different regions! Canada is renowned for its natural beauty and pretty landscapes!
other_useful_info: Make sure you have saved up some money - London is quite expensive compared to Denmark (in some aspects). And don't hesitate to ask for help - whether it's for academic guidance or otherwise! Secure housing well in advance (but don't commit to anything before seeing the place!), and make sure all your courses are approved before you go. But remember to have fun while you're there and don't focus solely on your studies!
most_rewarding: The people I med during my time there, the friendships I formed (I still speak to a lot of them), and the memories I created are truly unforgettable.
greatest_challenge: Dealing with all the red tape - getting courses approved and finding suitable accommodation was quite a hassle. But thankfully, I didn't encounter any major challenges while I was there.

crucial_aspects: A university in an English-speaking country. A bigger variety of interesting classes. Somewhere far away and vastly different from Denmark. A university with special flair for my field of studies, anthropology.
info_ease: It was fairly easy, but improvements could be made.I recieved a lot of emails, it did feel like I was drowning in emails for a while. Fewer emails with more informations and HIGHLIGHTED deadlines would be perfect.
arrival_assistance: I think I could have sought out assistance, but I didn't need any. I did recieve help from their Housing services to find a dorm, but this I did before I arrived in Canada.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: We had to go to a specific building on the other side of campus to registrer and get our house keys. However, they did provide free taxis for us to get to our dorm after. It was a slow process.
registration_help: Don't know.
registration_success: I was very successful, I got the classes I wanted. I applied for pre-approval for 7 classes, I was approved for 6. I then applied for 4 classes at the university (equivalent to 30 ects), and I got all 4. I had no scheduling issues.
registration_advice: Just follow the deadlines. In my expereince you'll get the classes you want, if you apply within the deadline ( social science faculty).
course_level: It was fairly easy to follow the classes. I found my classes to be more interesting than the ones, I have had at KU. The grade is given based on multiple assignments, quizzes, mid-terms and final exams. This means the workload through the year is a little higher than at KU, however, the final exam season is way less stressful, because you secure marks through the year.
teaching_comparison: It was pretty similar, I had less tutorials. I only had one weekly tutorial, and it was very easy to follow. My lectures were between 2 and 3 hours long, so same as KU or a bit longer. Some of the teachers spoke pretty fast, but the English is very easy to understand. I would say the style of teaching is quite similar to KU.
courses_enrolled: Language, Gender and Sexuality (anthro and linquistics) Cultures of the Middle East (anthro) Advertising and society (sociology) Women and Third World Development (sociology)
recommended_courses: Women and Third World Development was a very interesting class focused on inequality and gender in many different countries. The amount of reading for the class was fitting. The professor was pretty good. The grade depended on a mid-term, one 10-page assignment and a final exam. Language, gender and sexuality was also a very interesting course. It focused on gender and sexuality, whilst taking an anthropological perspective on the way we use language. A good fit, if you're interested in both anthropology and linquistics.
unexpected_costs: None.
cost_comparison: Food and activities were more expensive than I had expected. You can spend less or more than this. In Canada, they don't add tax to the price listed in stores. In Ontario you pay 13% tax. Some of the other provinces, you pay 5% instead. I didn't get a phone plan while there, I could use my Danish one still. But I heard from people, that it was quite expensive, the cheapest phone plans were around 30 cad (165kr. per month), but many were like 50 cad (275) for 20 GB. Nothing was less expected than I thought.
activities_available: Outdoors club, global cafe, different sport clubs etc. Many clubs. Also a nice cafe on campus, where you could study or hang out. It transformed to a bar at night.
activities_recommended: Just participate in a bunch.
weekend_recommendations: I went to Banff during a break, which was amazing. Also Vancouver is really nice. Niagara falls is close by. Canada has a lot of natural parks, see as many as possible while the weather is still warm, seasons change fast.
culture_adjustment: Easy.
socializing_tips: Be friendly. I met nice people in the classes I took and also at the dorm, where I lived. I also met people through people. The locals are pretty open and talkative.
cultural_challenges: Tips (15% is considered pretty low) is expected. Weed is legal, so you're not necessarily in a bad part of town, if it smells like weed. Bars close at 2, and you're not allowed to drink on the streets.
culture_appreciated: People are nice, it is common to say 'thank you', when you exit a bus. The nature is amazing.
top3_advice: Live on campus, it is close to downtown and to uni. You can get an app for some stores to collect points and get discounts. Make sure to plan weekend trips as soon as you can, time goes by fast, and public transportation isn't great, so trips require some planning and possibly renting a car.
other_useful_info: There are Facebook-groups for people attending universities, I texted with a couple of other Danes going to the same place as me. It was nice knowing someone already before arriving.
most_rewarding: Getting to live in and experience a different culture while taking classes I found genuinly interesting. Meeting new people from all over the world.
greatest_challenge: I don't know.
other_comments: No.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go to an English speaking country and the Canadian nature is beautiful.
info_ease: There are a lot of different websites and it was a bit difficult navigating in the beginning but I managed. There is a very good and helpful student counselor for international students, who returned emails within a day. That helped a lot.
arrival_assistance: I only arrived a couple of days before school started so most of the help I received was from friends. I did go to a couple of orientation events, but those were useless for international students, so if I could do it over, I would not spend money on the O week.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You look through the course catalogue and find courses that look interesting. They have an online course builder that makes it easy for you to see if you have overlapping courses. On this website you can see the number of available spots and the hours of lecture and tutorial. When you have chosen the courses you want to apply for, you go to another website where you make the request. It takes some time before you see whether you got the courses or not (depending on the time you make the application). If you don't get the courses you want, you apply again for different courses. Courses have different letters depending on what kind of course it is and what time of year it is offered, so make sure to check the course letter before applying.
registration_help: The international student counselor was very helpful.
registration_success: It was pretty simple once I cracked the code and I got three courses the first time I applied. The second time I applied I got my last course. I wanted to drop one course and add another one within the first week of school and that was easy as well.
registration_advice: Check the course codes before applying for forhåndsgodkendelse. I applied for a lot of courses that is offered during the spring semester and I was there in the fall.
course_level: I had 1 first year course, 1 second year course, 1 third year course, and 1 fourth year course. None of the courses were too difficult and some of them could have been more challenging, but that suited me fine and gave me more spare time.
teaching_comparison: Only one of my courses used a book so everything we had to know for the exam was presented during lectures. Two of my courses were only lectures and had no tutorials. All courses had midterms and some also had marks for participation and assignments, so the exam did not count 100%.
courses_enrolled: Biology 4355F, the biology of aging Biology 3592A, human genetics Microimm 2500A, biology of infection and immunology Psychol 1002A, psychology as a natural science
recommended_courses: Biology 4355F is the best course I have taken during my bachelors so far. The professor was great and the topics he covered was so interesting and has opened my eyes to how interesting aging processes are.
unexpected_costs: Groceries are a lot more expensive than expected. Cell phone service is also expensive.
cost_comparison: Groceries are a lot more expensive than expected. Cell phone service is also expensive.
activities_available: A lot of clubs, both sports and others.
activities_recommended: I did not attend any.
weekend_recommendations: Travel as much as possible! Prioritize to see nature in the early fall and cities later on because of the weather.
culture_adjustment: Very easy.
socializing_tips: I met a lot of locals when going out at night.
cultural_challenges: None.
culture_appreciated: Everyone is very friendly and talkative and they want to help you in any way they can.
top3_advice: 1. Live on campus or close by. 2. Try to place your classes on the same days so you can go away on a long weekend. I was off thursday and friday and that made it much easier to travel. 3. Choose interesting courses and not just easy ones. It makes it so much more fun to attend class.
other_useful_info: Don't spend money on O week, it is mostly for first year students and not exchange. If you need cooking supplies, plates, cutlery etc. go to a thrift shop instead of buying it in stores. It is much cheaper.
most_rewarding: Academics was great and especially the aging course.
greatest_challenge: Everything has been pretty easy.

registration_advice: Keep an eye on the deadlines and use the international team assigned to help if you are in doubt about anything.
