crucial_aspects: I wanted to travel further than Europe and explore new cultures and universities.
info_ease: It was difficult to find all the information through Westerns website. But when you get accepted to the university you will start getting emails upon arrival that helps with practical stuff like how to get housing, what should you pack and how do you register for courses.
arrival_assistance: The only assistance i got was through email and i was mostly about UNI stuff.
arrival_comments: The first week was intro-week for International and Exchange students it was great but mostly information, the socializing part was mostly up to yourself. They don't have games and stuff for students to get to know each other. The second week was O-week an intro-week for the first year students. This is also something you can attend, but you have to pay for it. It has more events like shows and a concert, but still you have to kind of just talk to people you meet on the go.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: It was very difficult to figure out exactly how to apply for courses. First you had to visit student.uwo.ca where you had to apply for courses. Remember to also use another application called Draft A Shedule and chech if you're different courses can be taken together. Courses called a number and B (like 4355B) is in the spring while courses in ending on A is in autumn semester. There are also other codes like C, D, E and F but i dont remember exactly what they were.
registration_help: You could write to goabroad@uwo.ca which was very helpfull and wrote back within some minutes usually.
registration_success: I got 3 out of 4 courses i applied for and ended up changing one course in the beginning of my semester.
registration_advice: Try to apply as soon as you get accepted to the university, and browse a bit around the website student.uwo.ca and check your email frequently.
course_level: I took courses in level 1000, level 2000, level 3000 and level 4000. I would definitely recommend taking courses 2000 or above. Level 1000 courses are very basic and usually has a lot of reading and boring mandatory extra stuff because it is for first year students that has to learn how to attend university.
teaching_comparison: Pretty similar
courses_enrolled: PSYCHOL 1002A - Psychology as a Natural Science (do not recommend, it is a methodical course with lots of basic reading and a lot of mandatory attending) MICROIMM 2500A - Microbiology and Immunology (basic course in immune system, bacteriology, virology and other infectious agents - only thing is that it has 2 midterms and one exam) BIOLOGY 3592A - Principles of Human Genetics (good course) BIOLOGY 4355F - The Biology of Aging (best course i ever had!)
recommended_courses: BIOLOGY 4355F - The Biology of Aging (best course i ever had!) The professor Dr. Robert Cumming is a really great teacher and it has some very interesting lectures with lots of papers. Theres no reading in the course, only in one small asignment.
unexpected_costs: UHIP is a mandatory health insurance which costs around 1500.
cost_comparison: Food is very expensive in Canada also buying groceries in the supermarked, so if you can try to make big meals or make food with others and share the cost.
activities_available: The recreation center (træningscentret) is free for students and very nice! Also all games on campus are free :) Other activities: - Homecoming (HOCO) here you should wear purple ;) - Global cafe on every thursday
activities_recommended: Watch some of the games on campus like the first football match in O-week and attend HOCO. Explore London city and do different activities like escape rooms, iceskating, hockeygames, christmas markets, dinning and concerts.
weekend_recommendations: - Banff National Park - Montreal - Vancouver - Niagara falls - New York - Apple farms in London Ontario - Watch an ishockey game with London Knights - Toronto
culture_adjustment: In general it was easy to adapt to the culture. But be aware of taxes (13%) and tips (around 10-20%) each time you buy something. Also if you live off campus groceries shopping can be difficult because you have to either walk far (compared to copenhagen) or have a car.
socializing_tips: Go out partying in downtown and do events. Living on-campus makes it a bit easier to socialize with local students.
cultural_challenges: Remembering to calculate taxes and tips when trying to figure out what things would cost
culture_appreciated: People are asy to talk to and the older people are nice in Canada. Our neighbours an elderly couple were the best you could ever wish for and invited us over for christmas dinner.
top3_advice: - try to make plans ahead if you wanna travel - get use to checking your different courses for mandatory quizzes and tests - getting Canadians friends is very difficult, while exchange students are usually more open to meeting new people
other_useful_info: - it is nice to live close to a supermarked, if not you should consider having a car - Ubers are lifesavers when getting home drunk...
most_rewarding: Getting to experience a different culture. I though Canada would be somewhat similar to Denmark, but actually i ended up being very suprissed about how different it felt. It was a great experience and i had a lot of fun traveling and living with friends and meeting other exchange students. A great tip is to go traveling somewhere else like South America after your courses are done in the end of december!
greatest_challenge: Having to figure out another university system and getting use to having more free time.
other_comments: Have a great stay and remember to take some photos because you will forget a lot of the things you experience if you dont have pictures or other kinds of reminders.

crucial_aspects: I preferred an English speaking country overseas with beautiful nature.
info_ease: Finding the deadlines was at times difficult, and searching for courses was also a bit complicated.
arrival_assistance: The international/exchange team were very helpful in answering questions and there was an orientation week for international students where a lot of questions were answered.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: First you had to go to a webpage and apply for confirmation from the faculty that you are eligible to take the course, and after that you have to send a mail to the International Learning Team and ask them to enroll you in the course, if you were accepted to take it.
registration_help: The International Learning Team – they were quick and helpful, when you contacted them.
registration_success: Quite succesful, but I also applied for big and broad courses.
registration_advice: Ask the uni if you need help. It is not worth it trying to figure things out yourself. The mail is goabroad@uwo.ca.
course_level: Easier or similar to Danish levels depending on the year of the class (i.e. 1000 courses were easy, 3000 were somewhat similar to Danish levels).
teaching_comparison: Lecture slides contained a lot more information than back home and there were not any required books in any of my classes – meaning no preparation necessary for class. Exams and midterms were multiple choice or short answers, so you have to know a lot of specific things rather than being able to use an overall knowledge to answer essay questions. Lastly, our course grades consisted of several components, i.e., quizzes, attendance to tutorial hours (typically a low percentage of the total grade), midterms, and assignments.
courses_enrolled: 2500A Microbiology and Immunology 3592 Biology – Principles of Human Genetics 1111A Health Sciences – Achieving Balance and Meaning 2020A Psychology – Drugs and Behavior
recommended_courses: 2500A had an interesting immunology unit (about a third of the total course), the parasitology/virology unit was quite interesting, but the exam on this unit was too specific and hard and the same goes for the bacteriology unit. 3592A was interesting but similar to a course back home in Denmark. The professor Patrick McDonald was very good and invested though, so I didn't mind learning it all again:-) 1111A was very easy and quite interesting, but you were only allowed to miss two tutorial hours without a valid explanation, which sucks a bit since they were not very useful. 2020A was very interesting, but you could only have written or printed notes for the exam and there was a weekly quiz, meaning that you had to watch the 3 hours of lectures (posted online, but 6 hours with comprehensive note taking...) within a week, so not so flexible, but also not possible to fall behind:-) Hated the exam (VERY specific with only hand written notes, so time was wasted flipping through notes to find answers), but thought most content was very interesting. Not too much psychology, mostly facts about different drug classes.
unexpected_costs: The university health plan (~1500 kr.), which was mandatory although I had an extended travel insurance from home with high coverage
cost_comparison: Almost all food (especially cheese, but also vegetables) and data was way more expensive than expected. Access to the recreation center (gym, pools for swimming, and many other sports) was however included in the price paid to the university (~2500 kr.) which we only thought covered mandatory bus card and health insurance, so that was a pleasant surprise.
activities_available: Weekly 'Global Café' for exchange students, free home games for all sports teams (we watched American football and ice hockey), the recreation center as mentioned before was free, homecoming weekend, and a bunch of small initiatives such as therapy dogs you could pet in the exam week etc. which you do however have to look out for on the uni's social medias to find out are there. There is also a café called The Spoke and one called The Grad Club which frequently host events such as trivia night. Lastly you can also attend free student concerts, which is actually a fun opportunity even if you are not typically interested in music at all.
activities_recommended: Anything you have the energy for honestly – don't hesitate to do something you would like to try! And go to some of the uni sports games, it is very extravagant and a very different (but fun!) experience than you would ever have back in Denmark. On instagram follow @londonblo.g as they post both news from London and information about upcoming events in town such as Christmas Markets:-) And go watch a hockey game at Budweiser Gardens in London or a baseball game in Roger's Centre in Toronto – but figure out the overall rules beforehand, otherwise it might not be too fun:-)
weekend_recommendations: Save up money for a loooot of trips! London in itself is not too interesting (but give it a chance hehe), but Canada has so many gorgeous national and provincial parks to visit. Be sure to plan when you want to go where early on, as different times of fall is good for different places. I went to the Thousand Islands area, Banff, Algonquin, and Bruce Peninsula all within a month (late September to late October), but there are many recommendations online as to when you should go where for optimal experiences:-) I also highly recommend traveling in an RV or a camping van if you go to the provincial/national parks (and remember to book camp sites)!
culture_adjustment: You have to consider taxes and tips all the time, which is annoying and confusing, and also everything is very big –stores, distances, roads etc., so it's not as charming and cozy as in Denmark.
socializing_tips: Local students will typically be younger than you as they start uni, when they're 18 or 19, and many of them just moved away from home, meaning that the majority (at least in my experience) were quite young and immature, so I would actually recommend socializing with other exchange students instead. If you want to meet local students you should just go to one of the many bars/clubs just about any day of the week...:-)
cultural_challenges: The taxes and tips, the not so charming mega centres located just about anywhere in Canada, and the fairly high amount of homeless people, who don't seem to receive any help. Also Canadians drive anywhere meaning that supermarkets might be placed out of walking distance from your home making it difficult to do grocery shopping.
culture_appreciated: Many (especially older) Canadians are very kind and open, and they seem to genuinely care about having a good conversation with you. Also (in London, Ontario at least) almost all people say thank you to the bus driver, when they get off the bus, and I think that is very cute.
top3_advice: 1. Campus is beautiful, and London town might seem a bit rough, but do yourself a favor and look for hiking spots in and around the city, cute cafes or other fun experiences instead of discarding the town too quickly! 2. Maybe I was lucky with my courses, but most aren't TOO hard to pass (and remember your grades won't get transferred), so please don't forget to allow yourself to go on extended weekend trips and skipping a few lectures to get the most out of the unique travel opportunities Canada offers. 3. Follow a lot of the uni's social media accounts to know, what is happening and when, as they have many events that you won't necessarily know about, if you don't check, what they post.
other_useful_info: As mentioned before, if you have any questions (mainly about academics or your exchange spot), write to goabroad@uwo.ca – they're super helpful and sweet!
most_rewarding: All the experiences I got to have with my friends both small everyday things and big trips and getting to meet and talk to people from all over the world – even if I might never see them again.
greatest_challenge: The time difference – it was sometimes hard planning calls home. And also spending more money than I'm used to without earning any:'-) (but the money spent is worth it!)
other_comments: Don't forget that a lot of days are spent doing everyday things such as cleaning, studying, cooking etc. just in another country than Denmark, meaning that not every day is an adventure, and that is totally okay! You can't have non-stop perfect exchange days for four months straight.

crucial_aspects: Ever since meeting my current roommate (who's Canadian) here in Copenhagen, I was SO inspired to explore the country. Have always been a believer that if you're so lucky and privileged to get the chance to go abroad, go as far away as possible if you can! Of course Europe is lovely and has a LOT to offer, but personally I'm so, so happy I chose to visit a country further away and less generally accessible. When do I ever get the chance to randomly go to Canada again for 5 months?
info_ease: Western will send you so many mails with information, it's almost overwhelming. Especially if you're also in residence on campus (then double the amount of mails). Make sure to read the emails regularly to keep up with them! They are super good at providing information though, and Nicky Cottee is so sweet.
arrival_assistance: There was a ton of help to get, especially in the beginning. You always have someone to reach out to, and there's different orientation events for only exchange students in the beginning. They're really taking care of you.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: It was quite different than the registration process at KU. Here, it's a bidding system, so you'll get a certain amount of points you can spread out as you wish over X amount of courses you want. You will also get access to statistics on how many points you needed to offer for this course last year - it's kind of a supply and demand system: If the course has few spots and lots of students are interested, it'll cost more points in order to increase your chances to get into the course.
registration_help: You could always reach out to Nicky Cottee, she replies fast!
registration_success: Got all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: I can really recommend taking a look at the stats to get a feeling of how to distribute your points. There might be a course you expect to be super popular, but then you'll see that almost everybody gets into the course + the opposite! Also, you'll only get access to the actual course catalogue a month or so before the semester starts, and you'll realize that half the courses you wanted is in the spring semester / fall semester! But there were still lots of cool courses.
course_level: To my knowledge, everybody in law school at Western (maybe this applies to Ontario or even Canada), has a bachelors degree (undergrad) in *something*, could literally be whatever. Met a girl who did her undergrad in biology, and another one in literature or something. So law school at Western is really only 3 years TOTAL, where our in Denmark i 3 + 2 years. The level of courses was not the same in all courses, and this highly depended on the professor. One of my courses was almost too easy and another one was really challenging for me.
teaching_comparison: It *really* depends on your prof. I had a total of four courses, and in one of them, the prof would randomly call out students to answer questions, in the second one the prof was just monologuing for 90 minutes straight, in the third one every student participated so much it made you feel bad to not say anything in class. Also, attendance is mandatory, which honestly is great (and something I think KU should do more), because it creates a great sense of community in the classroom - you know that you'll see your classmates. I'd say participation is expected on paper, but not all professors cares about it equally. EXAMS: In neither of my courses, I had to attend a physical sit-down-for-5-hours-exam or oral exam - all of my courses would end with a written paper at around 12-25 pages per course.
courses_enrolled: Environmental Law Food Law Outer Space Law Intellectual Property Law
recommended_courses: I was happy with all of my courses. The prof in Environmental Law was super down to earth (easiest course of the four). Food Law was quite challenging, because the prof really expected a lot of the students individually. We did two simulations / negotiations during the semester, and this was being taken very seriously, and generally there was a huge focus on discussions in the classroom. Outer Space Law was super cool too, and the prof is super sweet and helpful. Intellectual Property Law is also a great course, the classes are more like lectures, where there's less student participation (than say, Food Law).
unexpected_costs: Since the transit system in London Ontario is so bad and unpredictable (at least it was included in your Western One Card!), I ended up Uber'ing a LOT. This was not always absolutely necessary, but sometimes the busses were so inconvenient, that I saw Uber'ing places as an investment in utilising my limited time in Canada, lol! It can also be rather cheap sometimes.
cost_comparison: VIA RAIL... The only (basically) train system in Canada is ridiculously expensive - it can be cheaper flying. I can recommend renting a car, it's much cheaper than you'd expect (book a giant pick up truck just because you can).
activities_available: There was a club for pretty much anything you can imagine, and the students really cares about it! It's SOOO great, and I really wish it was like that at KU. Western will host some sort of club-day in september where you can walk around to all the clubs (i think there's more than 150) and chat with them.
activities_recommended: Travel! Join clubs! And if you go to bars and social events arranged by the university, chat with the locals!
weekend_recommendations: Go travel as much as you can! London can be quite boring. It's so easy to catch a flixbus to Toronto or even go to The States. Montreal is cool (Quebec is very different from the rest of Canada) and Calgary / Banff was a blast!
culture_adjustment: Quite easy! Took me some time to understand the tipping culture though! Ask a local about this.
socializing_tips: Go to all the social events arranged by the university, get to know your roommates, and enjoy the openness and friendliness of Canadian people!
cultural_challenges: The tipping and in general dining / service culture! If you're at a bar and you sit by the table, you have a server, and you're not supposed to go up to the bar and order. Also, it's mandatory for bars / pubs to serve food (at least in Ontario), and the food is usually totally allright!
culture_appreciated: The friendliness of Canadians. They are really including you in whatever. I was invited over for Thanksgiving by three different people / families and spent Christmas there as well!
top3_advice: 1) Your performance in class and grade is not everything - you're on exchange! View it as one big learning experience in so many other ways than just academically. 2) You will be invited to stuff. Say YES to everything (if you're comfortable), even if someone is just inviting you to go grocery shopping. 3) I went to Canada in the end of July 2025 and got home at the end of January 2026 - best decision ever. Added two whole months to the exchange semester! Do the same if you can!
other_useful_info: Bring your physical driver's licence, because you WILL be ID'd, even at restaurants.
most_rewarding: Canadian people are truly amazing. They will make you feel at home SO quickly. They love small talk - enjoy it!
greatest_challenge: 1) Whenever the time came to write the final papers, it was tough at times. But a great alternative to the classic 5 hour exam in law school in DK. 2) Returning home.
other_comments: Go! Go! Go!

crucial_aspects: The academic resources they have at Yale was one of the main reasons for me to choose to go on exchange.
info_ease: In relation to Yale University it was great, and if there was something I couldn't find, they responded to my e-mails within a few hours. In relation to visa to the US it was horrible.
arrival_assistance: Nothing really. I met with my advisor at Yale, but that was something I arranged myself. There were nothing social either - but maybe because of covid.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: At Yale you just register a week or two in advance. You register through "SIS" (sis.yale.edu) when course registration opens. You can see all courses at courses.yale.edu.
registration_help: I contacted some different people at Yale. They were a great help.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure to check out courses at other departments as well.
course_level: I only took graduate courses at Yale. I think it was quite challenging. The other students were all Ph.D.-students at Yale, and many of them had already read most of the books we had on syllabus. Furthermore, they were used to talking and discussing a lot.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching differed a lot at Yale from that of UCPH. At Yale we were in general around six-ten people in each class which means that you have to participate a lot. It was more like a discussion group/reading group where we read a book for each class and then we discussed the book in class. We didn't discuss main arguments or something similar. Instead it was very dependent on what we as students found interesting in the book, what we would criticize etc.
courses_enrolled: 1. Inequality, Race, and the City 2. Feminist and Queer Theories 3. Methods in Gender and Sexuality 4. Stratification and Inequality Workshop
recommended_courses: I would really recommend to participate in on of the workshops at the Sociology Department. First of all, it's a great way to get to know the other Ph.D.-students at the Sociology Department. Second, it's a really great format where it is mainly guest lectures or the other Ph.D.-students that present their research. We had guest lectures from professors at some of the other Ivy League Universities, Google etc. I can recommend Inequality, Race, and the City as well since Elijah Anderson is the professor and he is a very huge thing in the Chicago School and in Race-theory in general.
unexpected_costs: Nothing
cost_comparison: Food and drinks are so expensive - especially vegetables, fruit etc. Furthermore, heating etc. is very expensive.
activities_available: I played tennis and went to the gym. Otherwise, I just participated in some different events.
activities_recommended: Go to the Yale theatre, cabaret, concerts etc. There are a lot of great and cheap opportunities. Go to the graduate student bar.
weekend_recommendations: Go to New York. I went there every second weekend. Go hiking in New Haven - Sleeping Giant is a great place for hiking.
culture_adjustment: Fine. Most people are very sweet and much more open than people in Denmark.
socializing_tips: There is a community for people from the EU. Otherwise, go to some of the events - often you will get to talk to someone. Otherwise, you have to be very outgoing to get to know people.
cultural_challenges: The students work ethic is very high. They read a looooooot!
culture_appreciated: That everyone is so open and easy to get to know.
top3_advice: 1. It's tough, so be prepared to read a lot. 2. It can be challenging to get to know people, but try to go to a lot of events in the beginning. 3. Enjoy the facilities and resources at Yale, but don't spend all your time on reading, going to classes etc.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: Gaining confidence, speaking a lot of English, getting to know people from all over the world, and it's great to have Yale at the CV.
greatest_challenge: Covid, -25 degrees, online classes, and no social events in the beginning was very tough.

registration_help: You could reach out to people at Yale for help.
registration_success: I registered for all the classes I wanted.

crucial_aspects: I was interested in universities with rich social environments and found that Yale-NUS College is a residential college which I was very excited about.
info_ease: Very easy. The website for Yale-NUS College is easily accessible and easy to navigate compared to many other universities.
arrival_assistance: I had a contact person who kept in touch and was beyond helpful. Because of Covid they could not pick me up at the airport but otherwise that is custom as well. I tested positive for Covid upon arrival and had to isolate for 10 days at my hotel, and Yale-NUS also assisted me through this process and even sent me care packages throughout my isolation.
arrival_comments: Because of my covid isolation I did not participate in their orientation program, but they set up Zoom for the informational parts of orientation. However, even after orientation when I arrived after isolation everyone I met was beyond helpful and someone waited for me when I finally arrived on campus to introduce me and show me around.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Registration is very easy and you are guided through every step by Yale-NUS College. They will contact you anytime you need to fill out anything and help you through the process. Going on sem abroad can be overwhelming because of all the paper work, but for me it was very simple because of the help provided by Yale-NUS.
registration_help: As stated above I was guided by a contact from Yale-NUS through the process and I could also contact them if I had any questions or doubts.
registration_success: I was unsuccessful. Yale-NUS reserve spots in all classes for exchange students so you don't have to worry about classes filling up as much. However, exchange students sign up for classes only a few days before classes start which can be stressful and if you want to take classes in another field of study than from that which you study at home, you have to personally email the professor of the class and ask for permission to join. I thought this process of asking permission to join the class was automated and therefore, I didn't get the classes I wanted and only had time to sign up for anthropology classes. Overall the registration process is very different and much more complicated than at KU so be prepared for that.
registration_advice: Registration was confusing for me because it all had to be done very fast and I was still in isolation. I imagine that if I had been on campus I could have just popped by an office and instantly receive the help I needed so don't worry about it.
course_level: The workload is big as they have multiple assignments for each class and you have to be participating in class with questions and discussions. Thus, it can be difficult to skip readings and focus on assignments. However, the professors I had were very lenient towards exchange students and encouraged us to enjoy our time in Singapore and not stress.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching is much more hands on. Studying anthropology I had to conduct several field researches on my own guided by my professors. It was an amazing experience since teaching back home has become much more distanced and about listening to lectures from professors. I have learned so much from my anthropology professors at Yale-NUS.
courses_enrolled: Ethnic Diversity of Japan Marriage and Kinship Multispecies Ethnography Religion, Ritual, and Magic
recommended_courses: Multispecies Ethnography Marriage and Kinship Ethnic Diversity of Japan
unexpected_costs: My plane ended up being very expensive because of Covid fees. I also did not expect all the costs from just legal documents. Singapore's bureaucracy is very complicated and a lot of miscellaneous fees popped up from this.
cost_comparison: Alcohol is also VERY expensive. However, if you eat food at hawker centers instead of restaurants, food is very cheap. Also the rent is excellent considering it INCLUDES meals from the dining hall. Basically if you're on a budget (as I was) you can survive your whole stay in Singapore on only the 4000,- each month. If you go you have to remember to either bring sheets and a cover for sleeping or buy something cheap at e.g., IKEA as the room you get only has the furniture and mattress and not the duvet or pillow or sheets. I have put 5,000 in "other fees" as Singapore is centrally placed in South East Asia and you definitely should travel a bit if you go.
activities_available: There were SO MANY clubs! Also they had an infinity pool, a swimming pool for athletic swimming, several dance studios, two fitness centers. They also had different clubs that can bring you around Singapore and so many activities throughout the semester. You will never be bored!
activities_recommended: You should join their adventure club. I was a part of it and we went hiking, kayaking, and biking. At the end of sem they planned a hiking trip to the Malaysian Highlands.
weekend_recommendations: There are many places to go in Singapore and also islands around it which I mostly did since borders weren't open yet because of Covid. However, if borders had been open I would definitely have taken a bus to Malaysia and travelled around South East Asia on the weekends. Singapore is very small after all.
culture_adjustment: Very easy for me at least. I did not feel any big differences from back home.
socializing_tips: Just talk to them. They are open and curious to talk to other people and love to show exchange students around Singapore. I made friends for life there.
cultural_challenges: I did not find any challenging cultural differences on campus or with the Singaporean people, but I did find the amount of surveillance by the government challenging. Singapore is a very authoritarian state and I sometimes had a bit of anxiety by how controlling the government is and how much they keep and eye on everyone. Classes at Yale-NUS are not surveilled but classrooms at NUS which is right next by and where Yale-NUS sometimes borrow rooms are surveilled and even bugged.
culture_appreciated: Yale-NUS has 40% international students and I appreciated the diversity and the openness to talk about the world and each others cultures so so much.
top3_advice: Bring a sweater because the air condition is real. Bring sunscreen because sunscreen in Singapore is expensive. Don't eat pizza in Singapore - actually, don't eat any Italian or similar Western food because it is SO overpriced and it tastes crappy. Singaporean food tastes much, much better and is cheap at Hawker Centers.
other_useful_info: Even though a lot of students take their studies very serious and can be found at the library 24 hours please don't let that freak you out. I was very chill with my studies and my professors was completely okay with that and I got good grades. So don't let the academic vibes scare you.
most_rewarding: All the friends I made. The students at YNC are so amazing, considerate, and inspiring.
greatest_challenge: My whole experience with testing positive for Covid was very stressful because the health department lost my results and I had to go through the whole bureaucratic machine. But YNC was so helpful in the process.

crucial_aspects: I was interested in Armenia's long history as a cultural meeting pot, but the most compelling aspect was definitely its strong Persian department at Yerevan State University, and the country's closeness to Iran.
overall_comments: It was a very good experience, despite some trouble at the start because of a mismatch between how the courses were described and how I came to experience them. However, after the first month, I loved it there.
info_ease: It was very difficult. The country was a new participant to Erasmus+ and the information was disorganized and scattered all about, despite the best and most helpful efforts of my professors and the university officials.
arrival_assistance: Not much, unfortunately. My own home university of Copenhagen was not very helpful at all, but after I got to know them, the International Cooperation Office at Yerevan State University really did their best to be helpful.
arrival_comments: I think that as a new student, they were not very helpful, but after I learned about the Foreign Students Office and International Students Office, and got used to asking my professors, I felt really well taken care of.

registration_comments: It was a very good experience, despite some trouble at the start because of a mismatch between how the courses were described and how I came to experience them. However, after the first month, I loved it there.
registration_process: First off, I contacted Professor Lia Evoyan at the International Cooperation Office and requested a course list. Then I applied for courses through pre-approval at Copenhagen University, and once I had the pre-approval I sent her my Curriculum Vitae, an Online Learning Agreement, a picture of my passport, a written application with my motivations and my academic transcript and waited until I received a confirmation. To select my courses, I messaged the individual professors listed under those courses in the Foreign Students section of the YSU webpage.
registration_help: Mainly asking questions of the professors at the host university and the International Cooperation Office.
registration_success: Very successful.
registration_advice: Talk and question your professors at YSU as much as possible! Be polite, but they're all really nice and patient about helping you.
academics_comments: It was a very good experience, despite some trouble at the start because of a mismatch between how the courses were described and how I came to experience them. However, after the first month, I loved it there.
course_level: I felt the courses to be adequate to my academic level, though I should add that the courses I took with professor Liana Petrosyan were, initially, quite below my level, and it was only after we had gotten a good sense of each other that they reached a good level. This was not a flaw with her as a professor, though, just a lack of familiarity.
teaching_comparison: I think that it was broadly quite similar, though it is difficult to evaluate given most of them were taught one-on-one.
courses_enrolled: Persian Language, Caucasian (Tati) Persian, Modern Iranian History, Iranian Culture, Iranian Media Domain, Iranian Literature, IRI State Order and Management Systems
recommended_courses: If you are linguistically inclined like me, do not miss out on taking a class with Professor Artyom Tonoyan. He is great, so passionate, fantastic to talk to, academically very skilled and great at challenging you. All around some of the best classes I've had. I also recommend taking classes with Professor Noonik Darbinian. She is both academically very good and also among the kindest souls I have ever met. Taking a class with her is a delight.
unexpected_costs: None that I remember.
cost_comparison: Food was really cheap! Buying clothes was about the same, however.
activities_available: I am not aware of any dedicated specifically to students of YSU. However, there is a local Erasmus+ group for foreign students which does regular activities like going to Gyumri or seeing Khor Virap or similar.
activities_recommended: I definitely recommend watching a performance by the National Armenian Ballet!
weekend_recommendations: The National Ballet, Khor Virap, Gyumri, Lake Van... there are so many places to see in Armenia.
culture_adjustment: It was a little difficult, because most Armenians do not speak English.
socializing_tips: I definitely recommend learning some basic Russian phrases, and how to read Cyrillic. This will make it a lot easier.
cultural_challenges: Armenians are very conservative, so as an LGBT+ student, this was a little scary sometimes.
culture_appreciated: Armenians are SO RELAXED. Coming from Denmark, which is very formalistic and bureaucratic, where everything has to be scheduled and done by email, it was so refreshing you could just walk up and talk to someone in the flesh, as well as how loose and informal people would be with things.
top3_advice: You are coming from a country that is very strictly rules-based, formalistic, scheduling-based etc. Armenia is not like that. If you are attached to those things, like having clear schedules and a clear framework, then you need to keep that in mind.
other_useful_info: You can use Yandex for basically everything. It's crazy.
most_rewarding: Definitely, the most rewarding part was getting to know my professors and the slow feeling of getting better and improving, where I had originally feared I would not be able to.
greatest_challenge: Working on my bachelor's thesis at the same time as I was there.

crucial_aspects: To be honest I was looking at many different countries, but for some reason South Korea and Yonsei University just seemed to be the most interesting option for me.
overall_comments: Overall I loved my time as an exchange student, and I completely fell in love with Korea in my months there, but because I got unlucky with both my housing situation (at first) and got covid, then I can't rate the experience as 10. I would still definetely recommend anyone to go to Korea and attend Yonsei University, which both have a beautiful campus and an amazing location in Sinchon and near Hongdae, but just make better housing decisions than me.
info_ease: Because of corona everything was online, but we did get some pretty detailed emails with loads of information and The office of international affairs was quick to answer my emails throughout the exchange. But having said that, then there was still things that I didn't know far into my stay, because we never got to have the off-line orientation.
arrival_assistance: They sent us an email with loads of pdf's and then there was some kind of online game where you could log in an "meet" each other, but because I only received the email the night before, then I didn't get to attend, since the meeting was over before I knew it existed.
arrival_comments: Because of corona nothing really worked properly, but that will hopefully change.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Overall I loved my time as an exchange student, and I completely fell in love with Korea in my months there, but because I got unlucky with both my housing situation (at first) and got covid, then I can't rate the experience as 10. I would still definetely recommend anyone to go to Korea and attend Yonsei University, which both have a beautiful campus and an amazing location in Sinchon and near Hongdae, but just make better housing decisions than me.
registration_process: They will give you an extensive manual as to how to apply, and if you follow that it is easy enough. Long story short, at first there is a bidding round where you get 72 points and then you can bid on the different courses you want (here it doesn't matter when in the period you apply). If you don't get the courses you want in the first round, then there is a second round where you can apply for remaining spots (here it is the first to register that gets the spot). It is the same principle in the add/drop period.
registration_help: I think you could probably write to the office of international affairs, but it wasn't necessary for me. If you don't get into a class, or want to register for a class that isn't normally allowed for exchange students, then it is possible that the professors teaching the course can help you.
registration_success: I ended up with all the classes I wanted. I got Virus and Host and Immunology in the first bidding round, and Cancer biology in the add/drop period (since it isn't normally available for exchange students, I had to write an email to be registered). I always wanted a course about Korean culture, but I ended up not getting the one I first applied for. I was still allowed to participate in the first class, where I ended up not liking the professor. I then applied for another Korean culture class in the second round of registration, which I then got.
registration_advice: Be sure to know which classes you want to apply for, and check what mileage (points) people in the previous years bid - this will give you some kind of idea as to how many points you should bid. If you don't get the courses you want in the first round, then be sure to be ready for exactly when the next round opens - the spots could be gone in a couple of minutes.
academics_comments: Overall I loved my time as an exchange student, and I completely fell in love with Korea in my months there, but because I got unlucky with both my housing situation (at first) and got covid, then I can't rate the experience as 10. I would still definetely recommend anyone to go to Korea and attend Yonsei University, which both have a beautiful campus and an amazing location in Sinchon and near Hongdae, but just make better housing decisions than me.
course_level: I took biomedicine courses on level 3000 and 4000, both of which were appropriate in level. The lectures and books were on the same level as at KU (in Immunology we used the same book as is used here in DK), but to me it seemed as if even though the exams were on that same level, then they were more lenient on the grading than here in DK.
teaching_comparison: At Yonsei each 3 credit course has 3 hours of lectures each week. There isn't any problem solving/SAU classes, but it is a bit different from professor to professor how the lectures go. Some will talk the entire time (Virus and Host), some will have questions and involve the students in the lectures (Immunology to some extend but mostly Cancer biology) and in some there are lectures and then discussion between the students (Korean Food and Culture).
courses_enrolled: I took 4 courses, where 3 were related to my studies and then 1 about Korea: Cancer biology (LST4002) Immunology (BTE3403) Virus and Host (BTE4610) Korean Food and Culture (IEE2084) For other students I would recommend taking either 3 or 4 courses, since I was quite busy at times and there is so much to explore in Korea outside of university
recommended_courses: I liked all my courses. While Korean food and culture didn't have anything to do with molecular biomedicine, I still found it really interesting and fun (although I did end up spending more time on it than I expected). Cancer biology was probably my favourite course, and even though it isn't normally available for exchange students then if it isn't filled up, you can write the professor and ask for permission (and he's really nice). Virus and host was also really interesting. Immunology was the course I had the hardest time with, since the professor isn't very good. If you want to have an Immunology course I would recommend reading in advance, otherwise it is pretty hard to follow along with his lectures.
unexpected_costs: In my first apartment I had to pay for everything in advance, and then when I wanted to move, he wouldn't give me the remaining months back. I therefore ended up spending about 10,000 DKK more on housing than I expected (but this isn't a part of the 4000 DKK I wrote for housing).
cost_comparison: As everybody else will tell you, fruit and vegetables are very expensive in Korea (I would recommend finding street vendors that sell them - then the price is reasonable). Going out eating in restaurants is really cheap compared to DK, but since I ended up going out for both lunch and dinner, it still cost a lot of money overall. If you want to spend less on food then I recommend to eat lunch from the cafeteria at Yonsei, from convenience stores or finding other cheap places (Boxsquare close to Yonsei have many cheap options) and to not going to as many cafes as I did .
activities_available: Because of corona, Yonsei didn't have anything available when I was on exchange. The only thing I know was possible was the buddy programme, but I didn't receive any information about it before it was too late to apply, but I would have applied if possible.
activities_recommended: I think Yonsei outside of corona have some interesting programmes, so check that out, but otherwise just go out and explore the city and country.
weekend_recommendations: See as much of South Korea as possible. Seoul is a wonderful city with so many different things to see, so go out and eat amazing food from restaurants and cafes (their cafe culture is amazing), go to museums, palaces, temples and parks or just go around and explore a certain area (or mountain) and I assure you every day will be filled. Trips outside of Seoul is also a must. I visited Busan (Songdo marine cable car, Gamcheon village, Haeddong Yonggungsa temple and Gwangalli and Haeundae beach), Jeju (Udo Island, Hallasan mountain, O'sulloc tea museum, Seogwipo city, etc.), Incheon (Chinatown and Wolmido), DMZ and Sokcho/Seoraksan National park (visit when the leaves change colour. The trip to Ulsan bawi is the most popular, but Geumganggul cave is the most beautiful trek).
culture_adjustment: Although I haven't been to Korea before, I have been to other places in Asia in my gap year, which might have been a factor in not experiencing any culture shocks. You have to get used to it being difficult to interact with many locals, since their English isn't the best, but it still always worked out.
socializing_tips: Because we weren't allowed in-class lectures, then I didn't socialize very much with local students. The few I got to meet were other exchange students' buddies, so I guess the buddy programme is a good way to start.
cultural_challenges: Other than the language barrier then there wasn't really anything that was challenging
culture_appreciated: All of it - from how many old traditions are still kept alive to how new and modern so much of the country is. Everything from the busy cities to the peaceful nature was amazing.
top3_advice: 1. Don't be afraid to find accommodation after you have arrived, just arrive early 2. If possible, plan your classes so you can have a long weekend and go on trips (I personally only had classes monday-wednesday) 3. Everyone is there to get new friends, so be open minded
other_useful_info: No - just enjoy your stay!
most_rewarding: Getting to know and live in another country
greatest_challenge: My housing situation and getting covid and spending a week in a government quarantine facility on the other side of the country

registration_process: Had to log in at night when registration opened, using a point system to choose courses I wanted. Got told that we had to use Internet Explorer to enter the website which was difficult, because I had a Mac, but it worked in the end with Google Chrome.
registration_help: The exchange student helpdesk, answers e-mails quickly and were helpful.
registration_success: At first I only got half the courses I wanted, but after staying on the waitlist I got all the courses I wanted.
registration_advice: Make sure you have a few courses you want, in case you dont get the ones you want the most. Also, the website is very slow when the application opens, but you just have to be patient and wait.
academics_comments: Had a great experience, though corona restrictions made it harder to enjoy the city fully.
course_level: The level was pretty much the same in terms of academic level and workload.
teaching_comparison: Much more formal and less room for class discussion. Had a couple of exams that was more based on memorizing class material, but other than that it was quite similar.
courses_enrolled: Analysis of international financial markets Economics of energy and science Regional economics International money and finance
recommended_courses: Would recommend the course in analysis of international financial markets and economics of energy and science. They both had great professors, and exciting course material.
cost_comparison: Groceries are a bit expensive, especially fruits and vegetables, but it is very cheap to eat out, so I did that a lot.
activities_available: I joined a buddy club, and went out with them one night. Very nice way of meeting people, and there were more activities with the buddy club available. activities_recommended: I would recommend joining a buddy club at the university.
weekend_recommendations: I would recommend going to Busan and Jeju, both very nice places with lots of stuff to do. In the weekends I would recommend going hiking in Seoul, there many good hikes around the city and is a great way of exploring Korea and getting out of the busy city.
culture_adjustment: It was not very hard to adjust to the local culture, even though some things took some time to get used to. Seoul is also a very modern city, so Koreans are used to western culture.
socializing_tips: I had online class, but the local students did not seem interested in socializing during class hours. I would recommend joining some social activities on campus.
cultural_challenges: Could be challenging engaging socially with Koreans sometimes, because of the language barrier.
culture_appreciated: Very beautiful country, with interesting culture and good food. Also loved Seoul, with endless possibilities to explore and a fun nightlife.
top3_advice: Make sure to have some money so you can explore other places in Korea. Pack some warm clothes, it gets pretty cold there in the winter. Sign up for the buddy program, to meet other exchange students.
other_useful_info: Figure out the conversion from Korean credits to ECTS with UCPH. A couple of other students I met from UCPH got a different conversion than I did, and had to take more courses than I did for the same amount of ECTS.
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of new people from around the world, see a lot of beautiful places and experience a new culture,
greatest_challenge: Corona restrictions limited the possibility to meet new people, but there still ways to go out and have fun anyways.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to choose a destination on another kontinent to try to have the biggest culture shock as possible. Further I wanted to choose a destination that I found interesting in cultural and historical matters.
overall_comments: Without covid it would probably be 10/10 but the restrictions dragged down a bit.
info_ease: Quite difficult. I took a long time of research to find alle the neccesary information.
arrival_assistance: I experienced a lot of guidance from the students who had a stand in the airport for helping exchange students with transport and delivery services to use during the mandatory quarantine.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: Without covid it would probably be 10/10 but the restrictions dragged down a bit.
registration_process: It is a bidding system where you have a total amount of points of which you can bid a certain amount of each course you wish to have. After this there is an add drop period where students can cancel their registration which will open up more seats.
registration_help: We received emails with guidance from the university. Further they were fast to reply when emailing.
registration_success: I only got 3 out of 5 courses. But I secured a spot on the last two courses by writing directly to the professors who was teaching the courses.
registration_advice: Make a plan beforehand for what you will do and make sure to familiarize yourself with the system.
academics_comments: Without covid it would probably be 10/10 but the restrictions dragged down a bit.
course_level: It was easier
teaching_comparison: A lot more of student participation was required a large part of the final grade was decided by your participation in class. The professors will also cold call you if you do not participate. This actually creates a dynamic style of teaching where it is possible to have class discussions even though the classes was online.
courses_enrolled: 1. Comparative corporate law and governance 2. Mergers and Acqusitions 3. International Business law 4. International Human Rights 5. Korean Law and Politics
recommended_courses: Comparative corporate law and governance. The professor was great and was mostly just functioning as a moderator of the class discussion with only a small amount of an actual lecture. We were only 7 students in class all from different countries which made it possible to have very good class discussions.
unexpected_costs: I did not have an actual kitchen so I was eating out a lot.
cost_comparison: Food was more expensive than expected
activities_available: There were a few student clubs
activities_recommended: I did not participate in any non-academic activities through the university
weekend_recommendations: Travel around Korea. Visit other big cities such as Busan or visit the DMZ. Further you should spend a lot of time in Seoul. It is one of the worlds biggest cities and there will always be new areas for you to discover. Personally I enjoyd hiking in the mountain areas within Seoul and visiting museums or just visiting different neighborhoods.
culture_adjustment: It was easy. There are a lot of exchange students who are in the same position as you are and therefore it is very easy to make new friends.
socializing_tips: Be open minded and go out a lot! Do not be afraid to talk to strangers. Further make sure to get contact informations on the people you meet - Seoul is a big city and chances of you running into them again randomly is small.
cultural_challenges: A lot of Koreans are not good in English which made it difficult to socialize with the locals. However those who are comfortable speaking English are very kind and helpfull.
culture_appreciated: The hospitality from the Koreans! They are all very helpfull and wishes for you to enjoy your stay in their country which made it a very nice environment to be in.
top3_advice: 1. Make sure to do a lot of research before going. It will give you a big advantage when choosing courses and finding housing. 2. Be outgoing and do not be afraid to talk to new people. There is a lot of exchange students who also just arrived and is in the exact same situation as you are in so it is in everybody's interest. 3. If you have to go to quarantine due to covid, give priority to find a good apartment to do the quarantine in. 14 days is a lot in the same room, and if you pick a cheap place you can easily end up with a small room with only a mattress and no windows. Do not use the quarantine services but instead book a nice apartment and make sure to do your research on how to order food and groceries before going. Further make sure to buy some bottles of water and some food in the airport to get you through the first days if something doesn't work out for you in the beginning.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: The privilege of being able to live in another part of the world and all the new friends from countries all over the world
greatest_challenge: When arriving in the airport not knowing anything and going straight to a quarantine apartment where I had to figure out how to order food and water.

crucial_aspects: South Korea was the obvious choice for me since I study Korean studies and had a mandatory semester abroad. But even if I wasn't a Korean studies major, I would still have chosen South Korea, because the culture and university structure is different from Denmark, and I thought it would be really interesting to explore something completely different than Denmark.
overall_comments: Covid-19 sadly affected my semester abroad a lot.
info_ease: It was both easy and hard - I had to be really careful and make sure I had everything under control related to covid-19 restrictions and such. But all other information - how to apply directly to the University, how to apply for a visa, how to find recommendation was simple.
arrival_assistance: Yonsei University's study abroad department was really helpful throughout everything and so was the study abroad department at KU. I received assistance from KU with forhåndsgodkendelse and what to do if I couldn't get the courses that I needed. From Yonsei I received assistance with course registration, how and where to pick up my student ID, how to apply for Korean registration card, sim card registration and how to navigate the covid-19 restrictions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own

It's a good idea to check out how many point were needed to get into the course the previous years - that what I did. For KLI (the language program) they have unlimited spots, so you can bid 1 point and get in.
registration_help: You could contact the administration and they would try to help the best they could. The professors were also helpful.
registration_success: I got every class that I wanted.
registration_advice: Check the amount of points were needed the previous years and try to aim above that when bidding points. if you don't get your class, try and contact the professor. Most of them are really helpful and will register you for the class.

course_level: The language program was really really good. i learned a lot. But the other classes were kinda easy compared to the classes in Denmark, so I wasn't challenged academically.
teaching_comparison: For the regular classes, there wasn't any student involvement. We just listened to the professor throughout the entire class and that was it. For the language program, it was very much like how it is at Copenhagen which was nice.
courses_enrolled: Intensive Korean Language program level 3 (KLI) Contemporary Korean Cinema and Society Korea-US relations
recommended_courses: I would recommend KLI as it was really challenging and I learned a lot. We were forced to speak a lot which helped.
unexpected_costs: I don't remember any unexpected costs
cost_comparison: Housing was more expensive than I thought. it's definitely possible to find something cheaper. Also, the books-section was a one time payment, so I paid 500kr once for my books.
activities_available: Nothing because of the covid-19 situation
activities_recommended: If you can, join the buddy program.
weekend_recommendations: All of the historical sights are really beautiful. I also really liked Lotte World and enjoyed my time there. Explore the restaurants behind the busy streets and in the basements. The more it's hidden the better the food is.
culture_adjustment: Both easy and hard. I knew what to expect but it was also difficult to navigate.
socializing_tips: Just be nice and you'll be fine.
cultural_challenges: The not talking on public transportation rule. I still find it odd.
culture_appreciated: How nice most people were and helpful.
top3_advice: Try to hang out with other exchange students, explore outside of the city and try to hang out with the locals.
other_useful_info: No
most_rewarding: The language program and talking to locals
greatest_challenge: Living alone in a foreign country where most people don't speak English.

crucial_aspects: The courses that were available were very important. Not all countries or universities have elaborate theologian studies or courses. But due to the nature of most universities in Korea, they all offer great and progressive programs in my field of study.
overall_comments: The amount of work I had to do here, while also writing my final thesis was way too intense. I can not recommend that for anyone, instead I would go during a regular semester.
info_ease: It was alright. The school would send my emails about it, and there were different online forums that would keeo you updated on activities and so forth.
arrival_assistance: A big meeting were held within the first couple of days and there we were provided with all the information we needed. A handbook was also given to everyone.
arrival_comments: Every question was answered, and it was very clear that they a used to exchange students and the process of helping them in the beginning.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: The amount of work I had to do here, while also writing my final thesis was way too intense. I can not recommend that for anyone, instead I would go during a regular semester.
registration_process: You get a certain amount of points and then you divide those points between the courses you want. The more points, the higher your chance of getting it. That's the first round. Then you will either have gotten the courses you want or not. The second round you can then either drop the courses you don't want, or look for new courses that are available if you didn't get the courses you wanted.
registration_help: They offered to help you register many times and also sent out a whole guidance powerpoint about the courses and how to register.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Don't stress too much about the course registration. The teachers are easy to talk to, so you can always try to get your desired course by talking directly to the teacher.
academics_comments: The amount of work I had to do here, while also writing my final thesis was way too intense. I can not recommend that for anyone, instead I would go during a regular semester.
course_level: Like I said before, two of the courses were great, the last one was just unacademic and unprofessional.
teaching_comparison: The style is very similar, the teacher gives a lecture and based on the lecture you discuss different viewpoints.
courses_enrolled: Intro to Psychology Society and Human Behavior Wisdom and the Art of Life
recommended_courses: Intro to Psychology and Society and Human Behavior was great. A good introduction in the basics of both psychology and sociology. The teachers are really nice and engaging.
unexpected_costs: Although I had a travel insurance from home, it was mandatory to pay the local health insurance as well, which was 71000 KRW every month. I did not expect that at all.
cost_comparison: Food is inexpensive, clothes is inexpensive, coffee is cheap. Fresh fruit and vegetables is expensive and so is everything branded.
activities_available: None. Exchange students were excluded from most activities.
activities_recommended: Go outside the campus, become friends with other exchange students, but also don't stay inside your exchange bubble. Try to explore Korea locally.

socializing_tips: Socializing with local students is difficult because they take different courses than exchange students. So no, but learn as much Korean as you can from home.

Not wearing a bra is considered sexual and wearing low cut necklines or showing your shoulders is also extremely sexualized. culture_appreciated: The eating culture is great, also the silence is public transportation is amazing.
top3_advice: Get out as much as possible, feeling alone is normal, it's expensive to be away from home.

greatest_challenge: Not having my friends, family and partner with me.
