crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere much different to where I had been before
overall_comments: I really liked Korea, but going on exchange is a lengthy, and sometimes stressful, process, especially when it comes to certain required documents, and this process isn't done just because you've arrived in the country.
info_ease: Pretty easy. I had researched general stuff like transport beforehand, and I learned most of the school related stuff quickly
arrival_assistance: We had an orientation for foreign students, detailing everything about campus life, rules, clubs, and such. here we also received a guide book and a map of campus, which was very useful for getting around at first.
arrival_comments: They went over most things at the orientation, and the rest could be found in the extra guide.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I really liked Korea, but going on exchange is a lengthy, and sometimes stressful, process, especially when it comes to certain required documents, and this process isn't done just because you've arrived in the country.
registration_process: there are like three stages. in the first you bid some points on the courses you want, and after not getting them you move on the the next stage. stage two is first come first serve on the remaining courses, but actually you don't really know if the courses will be cancelled until the registration process is over. sometimes they also increase the number of seats, if classes have many applicants. you just don't know which is the case until the registration process is over. I think there's a third stage, but I got the courses I wanted after the first two. as a last resort, you can write specific teachers for courses you didn't get, and maybe you can still get in.
registration_help: you get an email with information about the process. read it carefully, because it's hard to understand. you can of course write the university for help.
registration_success: By some crazy stroke of luck I managed to get all of them.
registration_advice: If you're on exchange for the experience rather than the academics, you may consider tailoring your schedule to that. I took four courses, and they were all on Mondays and Wednesdays, meaning I had more time to travel or look around seoul. Exams are usually held instead of classes, so doing this means, you'll probably have to take several exams in one day.
academics_comments: I really liked Korea, but going on exchange is a lengthy, and sometimes stressful, process, especially when it comes to certain required documents, and this process isn't done just because you've arrived in the country.
course_level: I think the level was okay. each course is smaller than the ones in Denmark, so expect them to have a slightly smaller syllabus as well.
teaching_comparison: some courses were just listening-lectures, while others had more class participation. at UCPH we have smaller classes to supplement lectures, but that doesn't exist here. this gives you more free time, but it also means you'll have to study a bit more yourself if you want to do well. I found that the subjects in the international student category were a bit easier than the regular courses, use that information how you will. like at UCPH, buying books is optional, it really depends on the subject and exam structure, which vary widely.
courses_enrolled: Real Estate Finance and Economics Principles of Marketing Money, Banking and Finance Cosmopolitanism and Critics
recommended_courses: I would recommend Priciples of marketing for anyone even slightly interested in the topic. it's an introductory course, so it should be easy to follow for most people, and I personally found it pretty interesting. Also, only take Real Estate Finance and Economics if you are really interested in the topic. I thought it sounded kind of interesting. I was Wrong.
unexpected_costs: ARC-fee, I didn't know you had to pay for that
cost_comparison: restaurants are very cheap and the food is very good
activities_available: Mentors Club: Korean students arrange meetups with bigger groups of foreign students. all foreigners join this club. these groups will go eating, clubbing, or whatever activities they may decide on. in my experience it dies out after the first couple of months, but it's a good way to meet other foreign students. International Club: host a few group activities. I think you can participate in up to two. Each activity usually happens three times in a semester, they include: movie night, game night, seoul exploration, dance class, and a couple others. Buddy Programme: A foreigner is assigned a Korean "Buddy", they can do activities and exchange languages with. this is poorly advertised, and apparently it starts pretty late on in the semester.
activities_recommended: Any of the above mentioned. Just building some relationships from the get-go is really helpful. if you get a Korean friend or too that is also extremely helpful to experience the culture from the Korean perspective, whic is very interesting.
weekend_recommendations: Visit Busan or Jeju. the east coast is nice if you like the ocean. Suwon is pretty close to Seoul. Gapyeong is a bit further away, but is close to Nami Island, which is a tourist hotspot, and the area also has some great dakgalbi. Of course there are plenty of things to see in Seoul as well.
culture_adjustment: Pretty easy, being nice and respectful until you understand the gist of the culture is helpful
socializing_tips: join clubs, that's usually where Korean students wanting foreign friends go. there are also apps, which can get you in contact with locals, but you probably know those already. many Koreans are interested in talking to foreigners because they want to improve their english.
cultural_challenges: The drivers can be pretty crazy. I don't usually get car sick, but riding Korean busses and Taxis have made me reevaluate that part of my identity. bicycles don't always have their designated lanes and will use the walkway instead, and being aware of this was something I had to get used to.
culture_appreciated: It's very clean. people don't just throw their trash in the street, and will instead carry it around until they find a trash can, which are very rare in Korea.
top3_advice: Prepare beforehand when it comes to transport, courses, and things you want to see. Try new things. there are plenty of entertainment options which you may see as niche and weird, but which turn out to be really fun when you actually try it. clubs and such can help introduce you to that. also, there is so much good food, and going out eating with a Korean will show so many more options. At some point you have to apply for the ARC. this can be done through the school, which should be simpler, but I'm not sure it is. Reading up on that before going would be a good idea, to make sure you have, or can get, all the required documents easily.
other_useful_info: Get apps like Naver/Kakao maps, Kakao T(for Taxi service), Kakao Talk (messaging app, used by all Koreans, register account as soon as possible, you'll need it right at the beginning), Papago (translating text and images), Y-attend (used at Yonsei to check attendance status.
most_rewarding: Being on my own in an unknown culture helped me grow a lot, and it gave me many experiences I wouldn't want to be without. Going on exchange has been one of the best decisions of my life, so I do recommend it to anyone interested.
greatest_challenge: I got lonely from time to time, since I didn't have my family or friends with me, but getting out and exploring the country really helped me get through that and made the experience much better.
other_comments: Korea is a great destination for exchange. It's clean, safe, and has plenty to offer.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to visit a country that was culturally different from Denmark. An important aspect in choosing the university was how much focus was put on their international program and the opportunities given to exchange students.
overall_comments: The overall experience was great and I would definitely recommend Yonsei to anyone who dreams of studying in Seoul. My only 'complaint' is how little information students were given about the academic expectations and their performance, which lead me to stressing unnecessarily over tests and thinking I would fail classes I ended up doing great in. So even though East Asian universities may seem academically daunting, and Yonsei being a part of SKY, one should not be discouraged from studying abroad.
info_ease: Yonsei did a fine job of informing international students of the necessary deadlines etc. via email. We were always informed in due time, though that was sometimes only a few days in advance - I would have liked to receive the information a bit earlier (but that might just be my personal need to plan far in advance).
arrival_assistance: The international help disk in the Global Lounge was of great help IF you personally reached out to them. With that said, my biggest complaint about being an international student at Yonsei was how many things we were left to deal with on our own or was poorly managed by the school. For one, the school did not inform us properly about exemption from NHIS (which you for sure will be able to get!), which I had to find out about through other exchange students. It wasn't a difficult process but it was quite difficult to find the correct documents and information about how to apply. In addition, my best advice would be to apply for the ARC on you own and NOT through the school (since this took aaaages and was really inconvenient) by either arriving in Seoul before the semester starts or booking an appointment at the immigration office near Yonsei BEFORE arrival, since the waiting list is extremely long in September/October. My last gold nugget would be to not bother with opening a bank account (unless you get your ARC really early) and simply get a pre-paid Korean credit card. It is really easy and was simply a life saver!
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_comments: The overall experience was great and I would definitely recommend Yonsei to anyone who dreams of studying in Seoul. My only 'complaint' is how little information students were given about the academic expectations and their performance, which lead me to stressing unnecessarily over tests and thinking I would fail classes I ended up doing great in. So even though East Asian universities may seem academically daunting, and Yonsei being a part of SKY, one should not be discouraged from studying abroad.
registration_process: There are three rounds of course registration. In the first round you are given a number of points to wage on the courses you want, BUT even if you place the maximum number of points on a course exchange students will always be prioritized last, so you are not guaranteed to get it. In the second round you can try your luck on other courses, if you didn't get the ones you liked in the first round, and in the third and final round you can drop courses or add ones that now have open spots.
registration_help: The whole process was described in an email, but I would HIGHLY recommend to watch some youtube videos on the process!
registration_success: I got none of the courses I initially wanted when choosing Yonsei (so don't apply for the Underwood majors!), but I ended up with 3 okay-ish courses.
registration_advice: Do some research into which courses are even available before applying to Yonsei, and once the process starts be prepared to settle for your plan B, C or even D.
academics_comments: The overall experience was great and I would definitely recommend Yonsei to anyone who dreams of studying in Seoul. My only 'complaint' is how little information students were given about the academic expectations and their performance, which lead me to stressing unnecessarily over tests and thinking I would fail classes I ended up doing great in. So even though East Asian universities may seem academically daunting, and Yonsei being a part of SKY, one should not be discouraged from studying abroad.
course_level: I had to do two 2nd year courses and a 3rd year course. I was technically considered a senior (4th year) at Yonsei, so the courses were definitely below my level.
teaching_comparison: There was zero to no interaction with the students and we were not informed very well about the expectations and how we would be graded. It was actually quite frustrating that professors did not follow their own syllabi and the tests were not discussed at all in advance. It is also a complete mystery to me how we were graded, since in one of my courses I got a 64% on the midterm and a 32% on the final but ended up with a B+.
courses_enrolled: Design of polymeric materials Organic chemistry 2 Linear algebra and it's applications
recommended_courses: Design of polymers was by far the most interesting of my three courses, so I'd say it was worth it. The professor was quite good. I would not recommend organic chemistry 2 if you have already done anything similar at KU - it doesn't cover much new compared to the mandatory organic chemistry course on first year chemistry/nanoscience. At last, linear algebra was honestly quite boring BUT since it's such a useful topic, I would recommend it if you haven't already done a course on the subject.
unexpected_costs: I went on a trip to Japan which wasn't part of the budget... Plus all the concert tickets I hadn't expected to buy.
cost_comparison: Finding a cheap prepaid SIM card turned out to be more difficult that I'd thought. I recommend https://www.chingumobile.com/, which most people seemed pretty happy with
activities_available: The Global club arranged dance lessons, museum meet-ups, MTs, sports etc... It was quite competitive to be a part of some the clubs, but there were also a lot of one-time fun activities
activities_recommended: I heard a lot of good things about 'English society' which I sadly wasn't a part of... That i definitely regret! I'd also highly recommend to watch the Yonko games and take part in the Akaraka night.
weekend_recommendations: Definitely visit Busan and/or Jeju if you get the chance. It was nice to get out of the huge city of Seoul and experience more of nature. I'd also recommend hiking in Bukhansan for the same reason. And if you like music be sure to go to at least one concert! It quite easy to get tickets through Interpark, Yes24 global, and Melon.
culture_adjustment: I didn't struggle to much with the cultural differences.
socializing_tips: Take part in the mentor program! I got a very nice Korean mentor, Yuna, whom I became great friends with.
cultural_challenges: Being Caucasian I felt alienated at times. People don't assume you speak Korean, so people might talk about you, give you weird stares, and just generally make you feel different and out of place. That was one feeling I never really got used to.
culture_appreciated: How many things there were to do in Seoul - alone and with friends. You'll never feel bored, and I really miss all the fun cafés, weird shops, and exciting foods
top3_advice: Don't stress about academics! It's really difficult to plan your trip ahead, so you'll constantly have to make changes and you'll be more busy than you expect. So don't feel pressured to spend hours at the library. Take part in at least one club or mentor program - this was how I found the friends that carried me all the way through the semester. And lastly, the boring tips: find a SIM card online in advance (you'll save a lot of money!), do some research on the public transportation (buy a Tmoney card at the airport and take the subway from Incheon to Seoul - don't bother with the bus, it's a waste of money), begin the ARC process as soon as possible, and remember that you can get out of paying NHIS.
other_useful_info: Things will not go as expected - get used to that thought ;)
most_rewarding: The thoughts and reflections about my life and my priorities. Getting away definitely gave me a new perspective on the things I've been dealing with back at home.
greatest_challenge: More than once I felt overwhelmed and stressed. The loneliness got to me at times and I felt my exchange had to live up to unreasonably high expectations.

crucial_aspects: A high quality university, that was placed somewhat centrally in my desired city. I also had a personal interest in the culture in Korea, which also affected my search in destination.
info_ease: Fairly easy. The university International office would send out emails with necessary information, however they were sometimes send out at the last minute. I would suggest joining the big Exchange Student group chat on Kakao to find more information. As to the arrival in the airport I made sure to double check that I had all the necessary documents, through the korean embassy and through YouTube guides (the Corona rules were updated regularly and many travel youtubers would make updated videos on these procedures).
arrival_assistance: I did not need any assistance.
arrival_comments: The orientation was good, and you got a pamphlet with most of the information you could need. After the orientation there was a Buddies Night Intro party with a dinner before. I would suggest going to this, especially the dinner, if you want to meet other exchange students, especially if you live off campus and don't get to meet others at the dorms.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: You had a certain amount of points (miles) to allot between then classes that you wanted to take. You could prioritise the certain classes by adding more points to these, giving you a greater chance to get the class. I found this to be a good system as it wasn't based on first come first served, but on prioritising you classes with points. That way you didn't have to compete with the regular students who have a greater knowledge of the system, in order to get your classes.
registration_help: There was an information pamphlet that explained the system and how to allot points. I would suggest to read this through thoroughly. Other than that I'm not sure, as I didn't need further help.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: I would suggest knowing what classes you want to take, in what time slots, and what their codes are beforehand. Write them down, so that you can easily just copy paste them into the system. Also check out how many points students in the previous year allotted to the specific classes to give you a guideline as to how many you should give them in order to get the class.
course_level: I took 3rd and 4th year classes, both of which was on a level comparable to the final year of the the KU bachelor.
teaching_comparison: Some classes were taught with lectures as we know them from KU, however, there were no exercise based classes to assist the lectures, which was something I personally missed. Other classes were taught as a lecture and exercise class combined which was not the best way of teaching in my opinion.
courses_enrolled: Virus and Host Immunology Korean 1
recommended_courses: I would recommend all exchange students to take the basic language course (korean 1). It will make you much more confident in getting around and speaking korean to the local community.
unexpected_costs: Hospital visit that was covered by insurance, but I had to pay up front myself. Fees for ARC application, and for NHIS if you don't get excempt.
cost_comparison: Transport is super cheap, a trip around Seoul using the buses and the metro normally costs around 7 DKK.
activities_available: There is the Buddies program, which is where you get a mentor, and get to meet other exchange students. There are many different clubs you can join, just beware that some do not accept international students or don't accept exchange students staying for only one semester. You can ask them at the club fair. There were also a Global program where you could join cooking classes, dance classes, day trips etc. This is explained at the orientation.
activities_recommended: I would recommend the Buddies program (good to meet other exchange students), the Yonsei English Society (good to meet korean and international students), and some of the global classes (good to immerse yourself in korean culture). Also there are many different group chats on Kakao you can join, such as hiking or getting dinner together.
weekend_recommendations: Go on day trips or weekend trips around the country. I would suggest finding time to go to Busan and Jeju Island. I also went to Ulsan and Gyeongju both beautiful places. I would also suggest to try to see as much in Seoul as possible, such as Namsan tower, Bukhansan, and Lotte World. The weekends are also a good time to go eat Kbbq and go partying in Hongdae and Itaewon, or go to cute cafes and stores.
culture_adjustment: I found it fairly easy, my only issue was finding out what to eat for breakfast..
socializing_tips: Join clubs with both international and korean students.
cultural_challenges: That it is somewhat unusual to eat dinner alone, and many places you need to be 2 or more people to eat.
culture_appreciated: That people could respect your private space and that everything was open quite late. It made it seem like Seoul was always alive and it made me feel very safe that there were always people around on the streets.
top3_advice: Apply for your ARC as early as possible (you can apply through yonsei but it takes longer to arrive), make sure your student id works in the library (it is the best place for serious studying, but sometimes the id doesn't work and you need to get a new one issued), and join as many activities provided at the University as possible!!
other_useful_info: Not host institution but important nonetheless: If your credit or debit cards for some reason doesn't work, it is possible to get a prepaid debit card from a vending machine called Namane. It really saved me many times, as my card kept on getting declined in stores. The vending machines are located at major stations and there is one in Hongdae in a book store.
most_rewarding: Meeting new people and experiencing the Yonsei culture. The students have a lot of pride in their university and they have an ongoing rivalry with Korea University, which results in the Yonko games (I would suggest going to the baseball game it was really great also if you don't usually watch sports games).
greatest_challenge: The language barrier and always seeming like the odd one out. You do however get used to it fast.

crucial_aspects: A place where I could gain a lot of new experiences
info_ease: The information is readily available, yet it is very self-reliant. Normally at UCPH, if you ask for further information or guidance, they will help out quite a lot in my experience. At Yonsei University, and South Korea in general, my experience was that this wasn't the case to the same extent. Nonetheless, everything worked out without too many problems.
arrival_assistance: The university regularly sends out emails with all the relevant information you need. This makes it easier to know what you need to do. There was also scheduled an introduction day, where we were informed of all we needed to know. Furthermore, one of the universities biggest clubs provides mentors to a group of students. You get your mentor and group early on. This is a great way to mingle with students from all around the world, as well as you being able to consult your mentor regarding any questions.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: Registration is very different from UCPH and a bit more difficult. Basically, it is a 3-level system based partly on bidding. At the first level, you get a certain amount of points and bid for courses. Whether you get the course depends on certain factors such as: is it related to your major? Are you a foreign student (national students get spots first)? How much did you bid on the course? At the second level and third level it's a first come first served basis reg. the courses that still have spots left after the first level. The system is therefore quite competitive. One should also notice, that there arent' that many courses for exchange student. Yet this also depends on what one's major is.
registration_help: Not much help. You have to follow the academic guideline provided. When I tried to reach out for help, they were not optimal at providing the information I needed.
registration_success: I did not get all my first priority classes, but was very happy with the ones I ended up with.
registration_advice: Watch a youtube guide and make sure to read the academic guideline properly before starting registration. Perhaps download past year's guidelines in advance. You might not get all the courses you want, yet ultimately, everything should work out.
course_level: The level depends on which course it is, yet generally, it is more or less the same level as UCPH. The format is very different, as one is graded not only on exams but on different factors as well, such as attendance, class participation, presentations, etc.
teaching_comparison: Depends on which course it is. The different professors had very different teaching styles. Some classes had more lecturing, others had more group discussion,s and so on.
courses_enrolled: Theories of International Relations The Rhetoric of Dreams Anthropology of North & South Korea
recommended_courses: Theories of International Relations - if you want to get a better understanding of contemporary theories of international relations, as well as getting better at making and presenting your material. The Rhetoric of Dreams - if you want something that is very creative and unconventional Anthropology of North & South Korea - If you want to learn more about North Korea
unexpected_costs: None
cost_comparison: Seoul is generally a tad bit cheaper than Denmark. You can easily get a good meal for 50 kr. A large Big Mac meal is currently 38 kr. Nothing was really more expensive than expected, except certain types of food, like pizza.
activities_available: There are tons of clubs that one can join. Almost all exchange students join the mentors club, which is good for socializing, especially if you get a very social mentor.
activities_recommended: I only joined the mentors club
weekend_recommendations: Go to the other cities of the country and experience different places outside Seoul. Japan is close by too, so you can visit at a fairly cheap price.
culture_adjustment: The language barrier is the main problem and you can also tell that foreigners typically make their own groups. So there is a kind of parallel society within the country.
socializing_tips: Join clubs, speak with the Korean students in your classes (if there are any), make friends with other foreign students who have been here for longer. Go out to establishments where local students frequently visit.
cultural_challenges: Nothing too major, yet there are some minor differences.
culture_appreciated: I appreciate how social people are here. They love to go out and eat and drink together. The city is lively every day, with people going out and having fun together.
top3_advice: Make sure to find some friends and to socialize early on Make sure not to focus excessively on your studies Don't be nervous about anything, you'll have a great experience
other_useful_info: A lot of foreigners have problems with their credit cards sometimes not working here
most_rewarding: All of it. Difficult to pinpoint.
greatest_challenge: Course registration. Besides that, everything was quite easy.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to go somewhere far away and have somewhat of a culture shock while still being in a place where I could imagine myself living for several months. I'd heard great things about Seoul from friends that have stayed for a longer period of time, and I was not disappointed!
info_ease: I think the people at Yonsei were really good at sending emails with the necessary information when I first arrived. You do however have to keep up with the many emails they send, but as long as you stay organized it's really easy to find information about almost everything.
arrival_assistance: I asked for some help regarding the different course registration periods from the International Office of Affairs, and they were pretty fast to answer.
arrival_comments: I wish they were better at informing us about the social events in the beginning. I learned about the social gatherings at the on-campus orientation, and since it was a first-come, first-served registration, I missed out on the opportunity to sign up. I also only heard fromt the buddy/mentor program in November, towards the end of my stay, which is a bad unfortunate.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: As I remember, there were several rounds. The first round is like a bidding system, where you have x points, and you give out the points according to which courses you want the most. Then you have a course add and drop period, where you can drop courses if you didn't like them and add new ones from the courses that still have spots open. Lastly there's a last round where you can only drop courses.
registration_help: I wrote a lot to the professors on the different courses with questions about the syllabus, workload etc., but you can also contact the International Office of Affairs or Yonsei Global on campus, where the have volunteers who can help answer questions.
registration_success: In the first round I got all the courses I wanted. Unfortunately one of the courses wasn't at all what I thought it would be, and I tried signing up for Korean language, but failed. If you want to take a Korean class remember that you can only apply in the first bidding round because they have an assessment test in the first class. After that it's impossible to join, so I had to join another class which I ended up loving.
registration_advice: Be prepared that some of the courses on the course list might not exist anymore. It's a good idea to have backups, if you don't get into the course you want. If you want to take Korean classes, don't be like me, and remember to apply in the first round!
course_level: I took 4 BA courses and one MA course accidentally, but the professor lightened up the syllabus for me, so I didn't have to read as many articles as the MA students.
teaching_comparison: A looot of lecture style classes, and not a lot of group discussions like at UCPH. I had to do quite a few in-class presentations, but other than that I spent most days in class just listening to the professor speak.
courses_enrolled: Intro to Korean Studies, Understanding K-pop, Korean Popular Culture and Korean Wave, Ecological Anthropology and The Two Koreas in Film and Literature
recommended_courses: Honestly I would recommend all of them except Understanding K-pop, unless you are very into K-pop. Ecological Anthropology and The Two Koreas in Film and Literature were my favorite courses, and I've gotten the most out of them academically compared to the others.
unexpected_costs: Nothing that I can think of.
cost_comparison: Food is less expensive than in Denmark, but still around 50-60 dkk. Even though it's generally more expensive to buy food at the grocery store, it is still possible to save some money and cook at home from time to time. Alcohol is crazy cheap as well as public transportation. Rent for an apartment is around the same price as Copenhagen, depending on the area you live in. Busses to visit other cities in Korea are quite cheap and easy to find, and I definitely recommend going on a few trips out of Seoul.
activities_available: Sports, dance, cooking, journalism, lgtbq+, photography etc. There were so many!
activities_recommended: I didn't join any, so unfortunately I don't have any recommendations.
weekend_recommendations: Go to the palaces, temples and museums in Seoul. Visit the parks! And definitely go on trips out of the city, especially if you enjoy spending time in nature. I can recommend Gyeongju, Jeonju and Sokcho! I also went on a Templestay, which is a fun, unique experience!
culture_adjustment: I had to get used to the fact that people bumped into me on the streets, and that nobody speaks on public transport. Other than that I thought it was pretty easy to adjust.
socializing_tips: Honestly I feel like the campus at Yonsei was very divided between the Korean students and the exchange students. Despite the clubs and mentor/buddy program, I dont really know how you could socialize.
cultural_challenges: Heavy drinking is pretty normal, especially during moments of socializing or bonding. I've definitely gotten drunk more and gone out way more compared to what I do in Denmark (although drinking is also a thing here lol). That being said no one is forcing you to drink, but I will say there is a lot of social pressure on the fact that everybody should get drunk together. Also, when you go to small local restaurants, they don't want people to spend a long time on their meal or by talking afterwards. Me and my friends have been rushed out of restaurants as soon as we finished eating a number of times.
culture_appreciated: I loved the food, the nightlife, the art and culture scene, the stark contrast between the traditional and the modern as well as the crazy, beautiful, never-sleeping chaos that is Seoul.
top3_advice: 1. It is a big university, so it's easy to feel a bit small and anonymous. Make an effort in the beginning to find some friends to make everything seem a bit less overwhelming. 2. Don't spend crazy amounts of time and energy on the assignments. I found that the level of requirement was a lot lower than what I'm used to. 3. Even though the campus is nice, there's not a lot of spots outside of the library where you can study. There is however a lot of nice cafe's in Sinchon, where you can study in peace. My favorite was 'you want some', where you can sit in the window and look at the trees. Their insta handle is @cafe_youwantsome
other_useful_info: Don't drown in the many deadlines. I found it useful to write everything down in one document, so I never lost track of when I had to submit different things
most_rewarding: I learned so many things, not only through my classes at Yonsei but also through enjoying my time as a tourist there. It was amazing that every day I would go to class for some hours, and then have the option to spend the rest of the day exploring Seoul.
greatest_challenge: For me it was a little bit hard finding the balance between school and leisure time in the beginning. There were so many things I wanted to do and see during my stay, but I also felt a bit of pressure to keep up with the readings and assignments. I will say that even though the professors make it seem like they expect you to do everything and do it thoroughly, they still know that you are there on exchange and probably studying isn't your first priority. So enjoy your time exploring! Even though I accepted that I wouldn't be able to keep up with everything at uni, I still got fine grades in the end.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to live and study in a very different culture from what I am used to. And as I had previously visited South Korea during a vacation I chose this destination.
info_ease: Yonsei was very good at explaining everything and we got a lot of mails from the Office of International Affairs with all the information needed.
arrival_assistance: I arrived quite far in advance before the semester started, so I did not receive any assistance. I do not know whether this is available from Yonsei.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: The registration proces is divided into multiple rounds. In the first round you get 72 points to "bid" on the courses you want. You can see the average of points for the previous years on the course website to get a feeling for how popular the course is. In the second round it is first come, first serve where you can register for courses that are not filled up.
registration_help: You get a lot of information from the university explaining the whole progress. If you need any information about a specific course you can write to the professors.
registration_success: I got all the classes I wanted.
registration_advice: Have multiple plans for what courses you want to take as you a not guaranteed any place. Make sure the classes do not overlap, as attendance is part of the grade - so you have to show up to the classes.
course_level: The level of the different courses varied a lot. Some of my courses were of the same difficulty as I would expect at Copenhagen and some were easier.
teaching_comparison: It is very different. There are only lectures and no class hours where you go though the material. Also as you are taking 5 different courses at the same time, the courses were more superficial than the courses in Copenhagen.
courses_enrolled: Genetic analysis Virus and host Biotechnology in Diagnostics Cancer biology Basic Korean III
recommended_courses: Cancer biology was really good. It is not officially open for exchange students, but the professor let me take the course anyway. I would also recommend taking a Korean course, just to be able to know the basics in Korean.
unexpected_costs: I had to pay for the national health insurance (you can try to get an exemption). You also have to pay a one time fee for the ARC application.
cost_comparison: Restaurants are very cheap to eat at. Transportation is very cheap also. But fruit is very expensive.
activities_available: There is a really nice buddy programme, where you are paired with a local student and a group of international students. This is a really nice way to meet new people. They also plan activities for all the buddies to do together. I also started doing Taekwondo for international students, which was really fun! I also participated in some language exchange programmes. But a lot of the social clubs are not open for international students, unless you are fluent in Korean.
activities_recommended: I would recommend the buddy programme, as it is a really good way to meet new people.
weekend_recommendations: Seoul is so big that there is always something to do in the city! But doing weekend or day trips is really nice as well. I would definitely suggest going to Busan and Jeju. Nami Island is also really beautiful.
culture_adjustment: I would say it is quite easy. Everyone is very welcoming and willing to answer questions if you have any.
cultural_challenges: Sometimes the large language barrier is a bit challenging to navigate.
culture_appreciated: Seoul is such a vibrant city and there is always something to do. In addition the country is very safe, so you never feel uneasy walking anywhere.
top3_advice: Start with all the practical things as soon as you can, this especially includes applying for the ARC. I arrived and applied very early, but still only received my card in October as there is a massive rush in the applications at the start of the semester. Just experience everything you can while you are away!
other_useful_info: Not that I can think of right now.
most_rewarding: Meeting a lot of new people and experiencing such a different culture together. The university culture in Korea is also very different from the Danish, with games between the universities (that of course are very important to win;))
greatest_challenge: The language barrier is always difficult to navigate, but it always works out anyways.

crucial_aspects: Jeg valgte Yonsei University, fordi det var det universitet med de mest relevante fag for mig.
info_ease: Lige da jeg ankom, var der ikke rigtig nogen information at hente om hvor man var, og hvordan man kom rundt. Men dagen efter blev der holdt orienteringsmøde.
arrival_assistance: Efter den første nat var der orienteringsmøde om kollegierne og et par dage efter var der generel orienteringsmøde for de nye udvekslingsstuderende, hvor vi bl.a. fik kort over campus, vigtige datoer og aktiviteter m.m.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: Du får x antal point alt efter om du er BA- eller KA-studerende, og så kan du byde på de kurser, du gerne vil have. Jo flere point du byder, jo mere vil du gerne have faget. Så i første runde er der ingen først-til-mølle.
registration_help: Man kunne skrive til de forskellige ansvarlige for kurserne. Jeg fik dog ikke svar på mine spørgsmål.
registration_success: Jeg fik i første omgang kun ét af fire ønskede fag. Men jeg fandt efterfølgende tre meget gode alternativer, jeg ikke fortryder.
registration_advice: Find ud af, hvor populære de kurser, du gerne vil følge, er, så du ikke "spilder" point på kurser, du næsten 100% kommer ind på.
course_level: Havde fag med andre KA-studerende. Det var ikke specielt svært at følge med.
teaching_comparison: Det var meget anderledes. På Yonsei bliver man ikke kun bedømt på den endelige eksamen, men også på ens deltagelse i undervisningen (som egentlig bare betyder, at du skal vise at du lytter og prøver at forstå, man behøver ikke at sige noget nyt og banebrydende), på afleveringer og fremlæggelser gennem semesteret samt måske enkelte tests (og terminsprøverne, hvis du er BA-studerende)
courses_enrolled: Intensive Korean Language 1 Globalization and Human Rights in Literature Culture and Globalization Families in East Asia: Representations, Norms, and Realities
recommended_courses: Globalization and Human Rights in Literature Virkelig god og venlig underviser, som var god til at engagere de studerende. Vi havde en masse gode samtaler og diskussioner. Og så var vi vidt omkring i litteraturen set gennem menneskerettighedsbrillerne. Vi snakkede om racisme i USA, undertrykkelse i Nordkorea, Holocaust, immigrantfamilier i Australien, sort arbejde, migrantarbejdere i Kina og meget mere. Virkelig spændende. Så vil klart anbefale kurset, hvis man er interesseret i både litteratur og menneskerettigheder.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any
cost_comparison: Fruit is very expensive
activities_available: Der blev afholdt YonKo-games mens jeg var der. En årlig begivenhed, hvor Yonsei University og Korea University kæmper mod hinanden i forskellige sportsgrene. Det var stort. Ellers var der nogle ture, man kunne melde sig til for et vis beløb.
activities_recommended: Find en klub at være med i. Ikke alle klubber tager imod udvekslingsstuderende, der kun er på udveksling i et semester. Andre gør. F.eks. Yonsei STEP, hvor man mødes to gange ugentligt og lærer latin- og standarddans. Kan varmt anbefales.
weekend_recommendations: Husk at slappe lidt af. Prøv en ny cafe, eller tag hen på en, du har været på før. Syng hjertet ud i et coin-karaokerum eller tag til et større med flere af dine venner. Besøg forskellige attraktioner, tag på internetcafé, kattecafé, fulgecafé.
culture_adjustment: Syntes ikke, det var et problem. Jeg faldt hurtigt godt til.
socializing_tips: Meld dig ind i en klub og vær opsøgende. Mange koreanske studerende (har de fortalt mig, efter jeg har lært dem at kende) er ret generte og har ikke den helt store tro på deres egne engelskkundskaber. Men ræk ud, brug oversættelsesprogrammer om nødvendigt, og så vil du nok få et par venner for livet
cultural_challenges: Man skal lige vænne sig til, at det er et meget hierarkisk land, især sammenlignet med Danmark. Havde selv lidt svært ved ikke at kalde mine undervisere deres fornavn
culture_appreciated: Høfligheden, hjælpsomheden og ærligheden. Og den store tiltro, folk har til, at man ikke tager hvad der ikke er ens eget. Det er meget normalt at se computere efterladt på et cafébord, mens ejeren er på toilettet eller noget andet.
top3_advice: Vær åben for nye oplevelser og mennesker. Tag dine studier seriøst, men husk også at nyde opholdet og at slappe af. Vær i nogenlunde form - campus er rigtig stort og der er rigtig mange bakker.
most_rewarding: At bo på kollegie og være med i en klub. Jeg har fået så mange gode venner og bekendtskaber og en hel masse gode minder.
greatest_challenge: Sprogbarrieren

crucial_aspects: The courses available for exchange students at host university as well as economic possibilities to live there.
info_ease: It was overall quite easy. My host university provided lengthy emails with all information needed to know where to go and what to do the first couple of days.
arrival_assistance: Offline introduction event. Visa and residence and mandatory healthcare insurance being handled through a third party company for a relatively small fee.
arrival_comments: South Korea had a complicated bureaucratic Visa system leading to a lot of time spent on completing their tasks.
housing_how: I found housing on my own
registration_process: After succesfull application, you would receive your account to their internal platform where registration happend in 3 rounds. First round is by milage/points "bidding" on which courses you would want. The more points you bid on one course the higher the chances you would get that course. This could be very hard to know which courses is popular and thus hard to get into, as you cannot easily find the bidding results from last year. If you did not get the courses you bidded for then in the second round you could register for remaining spaces in other courses by a first come first serve basis. Last round were the last possible opportunity to get into a course and would only happend by contacting the respective professor and getting a signature on a special application.
registration_help: Not that much if you do not know anyone who has attended the university before. There is a discord server for Yonsei University with alumnis that can answer your questions.
registration_success: In the first round i actually got 4 out of the 5 courses i wanted. However, later i found out one of my courses was unavailable for exchange students leading to me needing to find two whole new courses in the second round.
registration_advice: Check the courses you want how much available space there is and allocate your points accordingly. I.e. if there is only 20 spaces use more points. Korean Language courses are extremely competitive so allocate a lot of points Have some backup courses so you dont need to find new courses between the first and second phase of registration.
course_level: I had 3 courses where the level was harder and/or more extensive than what i had tried before at UCPH (which was the local level 4 courses). I had one course (local level 3) that was similar to and a bit easier compared to UCPH. My last course (local level 2) was much easier compared to UCPH.
teaching_comparison: There is a lot more focus on rote learning compared to UCPH and the detail level was a bit less however there was a lot more topics to cover. Syllabus was much more extensive than UCPH courses of the same ETCS level, but as said level of detail a bit less.
courses_enrolled: Cancer Biology Functional Genomics Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain Virus and Host Introduction to AI and its application
recommended_courses: Cancer Biology - An amazing professor with good english and teaching skills. Overall a very well planned course. Giant recommendation!! Molecular biology or signal transduction or similar courses is needed as a requisite otherwise it will be a hard course. Functional Genomics - It is a very very hard course with a LOT of material on the syllabus, however if you are interested in 'Omics you get a really good foundation of all the different methods for 'Omics work. Microbiology/biology/general chemistry or similar is required as a requisite. Virus and Host - a overall good course focusing on virology and virus-related immunology. A good introduction to both topics if you have not had a lot of experience in these topics. However some biology / medicinal requisite is needed.
unexpected_costs: Mandatory healthcare insurance and a subscription to a company helping you with your visa application (residence card issue) after arriving A lot of housing fees Furniture not provided at most rental. For me it was luckily only a duvet/pillow and all kitchen items
cost_comparison: Food in supermarkeds are more expensive then i expected however eating at resturants is much less expensive. Public transport is 7.5 DKK pr trip no matter the distance/time
activities_available: Multiple sports days both for viewing and participating Social Clubs Introduction and farewell parties Mentor/mentee partnerships both 1-1 and in a group Paid social/langauge courses and events
activities_recommended: The group mentor programs allows you to meet a 20-25 other exchange students leading to easy friendsships. Introduction party is practically just a night out in a bar, however it allows you to maybe meet some new friends. Sports days and other paid events are high quality and allows you to have some fun
weekend_recommendations: Take on trips arranged by local temples or foreign tour arrangers. The tours made by Simple Spaces is really a recommendation, however you need to know someone that lives at their facilities to participate or ask them at their bar in HBC.
culture_adjustment: Relatively easy in some situations and hard in others. There are a lot of cultural and social norms when in public and when greeting Koreans. Please remember to study this to really increase your chance of good interactions
socializing_tips: At the university a lot of local students keep to themselves as it is a place of study. Here they do not really want to talk to you. However at events,, clubs, bars, mentor groups, social clubs they are as easy to talk to as everyone. I would recommend meeting them here
cultural_challenges: There are a lot of really weird legal complicated rules with apartment rental. Please find an english-speaking agent to help you. The trash sorting system is complicated and sometimes requires a bit of Korean to buy the correct trash bags as they are not displayed in any stores, you can either ask your landlord or the internet how to ask for them in stores. A lot of places only take local credit cards so cash is a must. Your public transport card is only available to purchase with cash
culture_appreciated: The vibes of the city of Seoul at all times is great, safe and foreigner accessible. You would really get to experience the Korean Culture especially if you can say a few Korean words as they instantly like you just by you saying Hi and thank you in Korean. It has amazing hiking and nature possibilities closeby which is a recommendation.
top3_advice: Extensive research in course selection Try all the different local restaurants in your area Be organised in your insurance and visa application. Keep all important documents on paper and digital for it to be much smoother.
other_useful_info: Most danish insurance is good enough to qualify for exemption of the mandatory health insurance of Korea leading to a good amount of money saved. Convenience stores are the place to go for garbage bags, transportation cards and a cheap meal.
most_rewarding: Meeting local students and receiving their help to study as a korean. Experience the many different parts of Seoul as each district is different and can provide you with new experiences The many beautiful hiking places
greatest_challenge: Getting my deposit back from my landlord as he was not that great at english and could only transfer it to a korean bank account which i did not own. Therefore my earlier comments on housing.

crucial_aspects: I wanted to try to live in a completely different country far away, which didn't have the main language English. For me I had never been to Korea, and knew very little about the country, but I had heard good things, so that's why I chose it.
overall_comments: I really enjoyed my stay in this amazing country. There was always more to see and the food was great. People were sweet. I can only recommend choosing Korea for exchange.
info_ease: It was very easy, because I had gotten an email on which bus to take through my dorm - International House - also download navermap (instead of google maps). It will show the way and offer all the public transportation possibilities. I took out some cash at the airport and bought a simcard, all of which one could have probably done cheaper from home. Then I bought the bus ticket and found it outside the airport.
arrival_assistance: I got to live at the university dorms. There were two - International House (only common rooms and for girls) and SK Global House. I lived in International House, and when I arrived there was a reception where I got a key-card and could ask questions.
arrival_comments: I had gotten a lot of emails with information and I was overall well-informed.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: I really enjoyed my stay in this amazing country. There was always more to see and the food was great. People were sweet. I can only recommend choosing Korea for exchange.
registration_process: You got some points that you could bid on courses with, and some courses can be a bit competitive. You have to look at the older years bidding averages to get a feel for how much to bid.
registration_help: We got information through mails. It is a bit complicated, so you have to read up on it.
registration_success: I did bid too many points on the wrong courses, so there was one course I didn't get. Another course they didn't have my semester, that I thought they would have. I only took specific study abroad classes, so they were pretty easy to get into though. Also I was on exchange on my masters, but since I hadn't completed a full year I was called a 'senior', which meant I could only take one graduate course and the rest was undergraduate. This will also be written in the information you get.
registration_advice: Read up on the proces. Also have in mind that you can also take tennis, taekwondo, dance or Korean classes if you have enough points for it, and Copenhagen University will allow it. It just won't be on your final exam paper. The physical activities only counted as 1 point.
academics_comments: I really enjoyed my stay in this amazing country. There was always more to see and the food was great. People were sweet. I can only recommend choosing Korea for exchange.
course_level: I was a master student but since I hadn't passed a full year, I could only become a 'senior student', which meant I had to take undergraduate courses and could only take one master course.
teaching_comparison: It was more high school style where you had to be there to get points for either participation or to avoid getting absence. Also you had to be more active in class and do presentations and assignments during the semester.
courses_enrolled: Law and justice, Ecology of human development, Traditional korean society and modernization, Korea-US relations, Bio-security, (+tennis).
recommended_courses: I really enjoyed Bio-security, which was my graduate courses. We were a small class with a passionate teacher.
unexpected_costs: I did eat out a lot. If you eat at restaurants it's going to be 50-80 kr each time and if you eat at e-marts (like 7-eleven) it's going to be cheaper, but also just mostly instant ramen or gimbaps/onigiri. Also there is really good and cheap food at the cafeterias at uni which will be approximately 30 kr.
cost_comparison: Eating out got expensive because I did it a lot.
activities_available: There were soccer, fencing, board games, climbing, dancing, language, band, tennis club, table tennis, lacrosse etc. There were a whole fair with clubs, that you could sign up to, but I don't remember all of them.
activities_recommended: I would have tried climbing if I had gotten in. I didn't engage a lot in these activities, but they looked fun.
weekend_recommendations: You can go on small trips - I did Busan, Suwon and then I also went to Taiwan. There is also a lot of small markets around in Seoul and tourist spots that are good to visit. I also went to Hongdae and Itaewon to dance and drink a few drinks.
culture_adjustment: I found it easy. People are very sweet and polite, and also very used to foreigners since there is still a lot of american soldiers stationed in Korea + there it tourists.
socializing_tips: Sign up for the student clubs, because they most often also have social events with food and beers.
cultural_challenges: I think for me I mostly had to get used to living at a dorm with a roomie. Other than that I don't really know.
culture_appreciated: The food, the kind people, all the things you could go see.
top3_advice: Read up on the courses available and the bidding system. Remember to get a TOEFL-test, if they still require it. Also I had to get a Tuberculosis test and certification to live at my dorm. I don't know if these are the most important things though. Maybe just remember to have fun. Many people travelled a lot, but I found it a bit stressful, because I also just wanted to enjoy the exchange experience. So don't stress about it and do what you feel like.
other_useful_info: Eat at the good cafeterias at uni.
most_rewarding: Experiencing a new culture and getting a little break and distance from your own life. Using this opportunity to try random hobbies and just do what I feel like.
greatest_challenge: It felt a bit strange and lonely at first, because it was so far away from everything. Just let it pass and try to enjoy, it will be fine.

crucial_aspects: Several aspects of my motivation were rather crucial. Academical opportunities to explore the subjects chosen and being able to combine them with my background at UCPH as a Geography student is especially important to me. However, there is also the fact that biogeography is different everywhere you go, and as such, getting a taste for more of it in a different continent and place from what I've seen so far in my life is something I will not just go by. Besides these things, however, I also have a taste for traveling the world and exploring new cultures and their people. As I was feeling somewhat at an impasse in my life, it also came to be something that has helped me overcome the depression I fell into during autumn last year, and knowing myself, I knew that if I got to be thrown into a new place and life to be for a while, I would (and have) feel much better.
info_ease: It wasn't easy at all to be frank. As I only had the final confirmation of my stay abroad in late December (and left on January 5th), I had to arrange everything both here and there in a very short time frame, and thus also found myself very much overwhelmed with figuring out sometimes even basic things that if given the proper time and such to arrange it would've been a breeze. Luckily, I very quickly got in contact with several key personnel from York University there who could help me in all aspects - especially that of ensuring I was properly admitted to my classes and what not.
arrival_assistance: Like mentioned in the above question, I received a lot of help especially from the study leaders of both Environmental Science and Geography, Ann and Anne, without whom I would not have made it far in navigating everything. But also my fellow students and classmates would ensure I got fit well in nicely with all technicalities and overall just a good welcome.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: The process was very complicated due to several factors - for one, the host institute changed the time of the stay from the fall to the spring semester. Secondly, I received my final "acceptance" for this change very late in December, and thus I had already in fact prepared my life around not going at all in the spring semester, which led to a whole array of complications not only in regards to the stay and what not, but also because of my life, my apartment and what not back home. So I had a very stressful Christmas to say the least.
registration_help: Not a whole lot. Luckily, my friend and I were both going to the same host university, so we could help one another with everything from ensuring each other's to-do lists, and also just figuring things out. The contact that was assigned to us from UCPH was, unfortunately, answering neither their emails, phone calls or anything else in regards to helping out in the unique circumstances that I was in.
registration_success: As the time of the semester changed from fall to winter, I was, unfortunately, unable to get the exact classes I originally applied for that had a heavy emphasis on field studies and related things. So naturally due to Canada's local climate, there are no field trip courses in the winter semester. But besides that, after a direct conversation with my study leader at York University, I was able to enroll in exactly the courses I wanted to do, which helped me immensely.
registration_advice: Get in direct contact with the advisors and such over there personally as soon as you can, it will help you a lot more compared to simply wreaking through the things on your own.
course_level: I picked four courses that all had a very high workload, and as such when I got corona over there and fell sick, I knew immediately I had to cut one down despite having already completed some 40% of said course. Overall, my courses were focused around biodiversity and biology, but still with biogeography as its core. But for someone who did not even have biology in high school, it was a lot of hard work to get into courses that were specifically for fourth year biologists, which in turn for me personally led to me learning a lot academically as I was being challenged constantly, but could also for some mean major setbacks.
teaching_comparison: The style was incredibly different. At home, we are used to studying at our own pace fully until the exams, then we show up and 100% of the grade is dependent on the exam, which can be both a lot, but also means less stress during the semester overall. At York, however, there are constant deadlines that all have a minor influence in your grade, and this can add up to your workload a lot if you're also just trying to learn the basics of things as well besides it. It took a lot to get used to this type of learning, but I am also grateful at my resolve in going through it properly.
courses_enrolled: Biogeography. Biodiversity. Ecology & conservation Science.
recommended_courses: The above courses are specifically catered to someone like me who has an interest in both biology and geography. But there are a multitude of courses that I feel the future exchange student is better suited to figuring out what works for them specifically.
unexpected_costs: Corona testing at the time I needed it was very expensive over there.
cost_comparison: Food. Although I knew there was a meal plan that I needed to have, I did not think food would be as expensive as it was. Although it could have been worse than what I spent. I would have been capable of preparing much better, and more nutritious foods at a much lower cost on my own compared to the canteen foods.
activities_available: There's a multitude of sports, club activities and more you can be involved in. I found myself in a lot of different activities with my fellow students.
activities_recommended: I doubt I can cater to all interests in that regard.
weekend_recommendations: Get a bit out of Toronto as well. But also ensure that you get to see what the city has to offer overall that you can be part of.
culture_adjustment: It was quite alright, although there are some differences, it was easier to find similarities with people, and I found myself quite liking the culture and work ethic that the Canadians possess.
socializing_tips: Smile and greet the world!
cultural_challenges: I mostly found a lot of them peculiar or funny, to be honest. One of my good friends there has a knack for apologizing at things that is no one's, and least of all their fault, which I found very entertaining as it was something that pertains to a lot of Canadians. But overall, it's really just about finding that common ground and recognizing that all people are different no matter the cultures they're from.
culture_appreciated: I personally found the welcoming attitude of the Canadians to be the greatest thing about it all. No matter when or where, they will find the time to stop and talk with you on a personal level, even if you're only meeting them by chance for the very first time!
top3_advice: Firstly, it is important to recognize that to do things, in general, is a little expensive over there. So it is important to ensure your financial stability, but also that it's okay to use the money for things that add value. Academically, you will most likely be working individually for most of your courses and items, which can be a challenge to some. Although there is group work as well, all important things rely on your ability to personally structure and prepare all your own things and to see ahead. Go see some Ice Hockey! And various other sports! These kinds of things are a craze over there, and it is awesome! I very much regret the fact that I'm such a klutz on the ice myself compared to what I could have been, and seeing them definitely did not make that better, but that's alright!
other_useful_info: Not a lot beyond what is already described. Keep an open mind and get out of your comfort :)
most_rewarding: To me, I would highlight the fact that you get to expand your network all around, which is also a big part of my life as a university student and part of what I believe it is to work at this level of education and type of education I possess so far and continue to study - my networking is not purely contained within Copenhagen or Denmark as a whole, but rather the whole world, which I believe adds a lot to my perspectives.
greatest_challenge: The short deadline with which I had to prepare properly was by far the biggest obstacle to me alongside getting corona shortly before the exam period.

crucial_aspects: Personally, it was important to me that the study destination I chose could provide me another aspect to the law and the legal system than what I had been taught at the University of Copenhagen about the Danish/EU legal system. Canada was perfect in this regard, as most of the country follows the common law system. By choosing Toronto, it not gave me another aspect on how the law works in the province of Ontario and Canada, but also how the legal system works in other common law countries. I believe this is a crucial aspect (and also a huge benefit) when considering making a career in an international environment, which is my goal. Moreover, I specifically chose Toronto, Canada (as opposed to other Common law jurisdictions), because I have personal connection to the destination.
info_ease: It was fairly easy to find the information that you needed to know. The office for exchange students and international students are very helpful, making sure that any and every question you have before and right on arrival are answered.
arrival_assistance: The student counsellor for exchange and international students at Osgoode invited exchange students over before semester start, so we could say hi, and I even got a quick tour of the Law School by one of the counsellors, as I was a winter exchange student and the introduction week for international students are held during the fall semester.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_process: You will get an e-mail in July/August from Osgoode, which guides you through the course registration process, regardless of whether you are enrolled for the fall or winter term. You have to prioritize the courses you would like to take, and the courses are randomly assigned (no first-come first-serve basis). It is all done online and then you will get your courses by august. If you don't get the course you wanted, you can put yourself on a waitlist. In the first two weeks of every semester, you have the chance to change courses and drop out, and if you are waitlisted you might get accepted into a course you wanted in this time period. However, after the period is over you are locked with the courses you have chosen. Keep in mind that the classes proceed normally in this period, so if you change courses is up to you to catch up and eventually hand in assignments that have been due in this period of time.
registration_help: The Student Services and their counsellors are always there to help and guide you, including the exchange student coordinator, who works in the same place. They can all answer your questions. Moreover, there is an academic orientation for all new exchange students too, where any questions about courses and exams, student activities etc. were answered and explained.
registration_success: I was fairly successful. Out of my initial five courses that I wanted I got registered to my top three courses.
registration_advice: Do not take more than one seminar course, unless you like to write a research paper at the same length as a bachelor thesis. I did not know this and took two seminar courses, and I had to write 2 x 30 pages papers.
course_level: The courses available to you as a masters student are upper year JD courses, meaning second and third year courses.
teaching_comparison: The style of teaching depends on the course. In some classes, you will get participation mark and have to sign a sheet stating that you were in class. Therefore, the teaching and grading reminds me of the method used in Danish high school. To these classes it is important that you show up and participate actively. In seminar courses, it is usually the teachers talking, but you will have to do a little presentation in these courses as the grading is 80% your paper and 20% the presentation and/or participation. I also had hybrid classes, where some of it is online (zoom or audio lecture) and some in-person. It is common to show up and actively participate in class. Unlike UCPH, the grade is not based on one final exam (only in few courses - and even in these courses you can ask the professor, if you can write an optional paper, which weighs some of your marks). In most courses, the professors give you the option or require that you write an optional paper/do some assignments, so the exam is not 100 % of your mark. As opposed to UCPH, there are no oral examination - all in person examinations are usually between 2-3 hrs, otherwise you can get take-home examination, where the exam spans from 4 to 48 hrs depending on the course. In seminar courses, you will have to write research papers and submit before a specific date and time. Unlike UCPH, in most courses you are not required to buy books, as the professor hands you the material. In the few courses where a textbook was required, the professors claimed that not having the books will not make you fail, if you just studied the case law and the powerpoint slides.
courses_enrolled: Advanced Torts Taxation of Corporate Transactions Trademarks Legal Drafting Commercializing Intellectual Property
recommended_courses: I would definitely recommend Legal Drafting, as it is such a practical course. You learn how to read and draft different types of contracts and the practical pitfalls, very interesting and definitely the best course, as it gives you so many tools on how to handle Canadian and American contracts. If you are interested in IP law, I would specifically recommend the Commercializing IP course. This course focus not only on the law, but also on the business and strategical aspects of IP, i.e., how businesses earn money by through IP, very interesting and also super practical. It is a seminar course, meaning you will have to write a paper or case study on a business using a IP strategy or a IP problem.
unexpected_costs: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.
cost_comparison: Groceries are more expensive than I expected.
activities_available: The primary student government is called "Legal&Lit", and it is responsible for coordinating and funding numerous professional, athletic, social and extracurricular activities at Osgoode Hall Law School. Make sure, you will get their weekly emails to your Osgoode email, so you don't miss out on all the fun activities they host. I can almost guarantee that there is something for anyone, as they really have branched out and have so many different clubs.
activities_recommended: Legal&Lit hosts plenty of pub nights and social activities. It can be every thing from trivia nights, to panel debates, to ski trips and galas. I strongly recommend other exchange students to participate, as it will help you create a better network, and the other students are so nice and welcoming, so there is nothing to be afraid off. Some of the activities takes place at the JCR room (a hang out place at Law School) and others take place in downtown Toronto.
weekend_recommendations: The city of Toronto, Niagara Falls, if they have time and money, then definitely some of the other provinces in Canada or even the US.
culture_adjustment: It was fairly easy. People are so nice and welcoming, and they love small talk here.
socializing_tips: Just keep an open mind and attend classes, and you will make friends in no time. Canadian students are really friendly and super helpful. They naturally make sure that you are included in group work etc., if you tell them you are an exchange student and you instantly feel as if you have always known the local students. In most cases, regarding schoolwork, exams and even social activities, the best advice came from my peers. They are for sure better at giving you the ins and outs of how Law School works and how to have a good time. So, spend some time making friends in every class - as it can really be beneficial for you in the end.
cultural_challenges: None that I can think of. If you don't like small talk, then that can be a little challenging. Oh, and also remember to tip, when going to bars and restaurants! And, VAT is not included in the price, when you are shopping.
culture_appreciated: The friendliness of the people here and how multicultural this place is. You really meet a lot of interesting people.
top3_advice: 1. Keep a positive attitude and an open mind - sometimes it can be daunting and hard to move to a whole new place on your own, but it will all work out for you with the right mindset. 2. Try to make friends with other students - it can be really helpful, not only academically but also socially (which is just as important in order to thrive, because it can be hard to adjust and at times lonely moving to a new country. 3. If you feel overwhelmed with the amount of courses and the work load, it is actually really normal. Even the local students feel the same pressure as you. In Denmark, we are used to 2-3 courses per semester, whereas it is quite normal to have 4-5 courses in Canada. But, do not get discouraged, just make sure you do everything in good time and then it is not so hard to juggle that many courses at once.
other_useful_info: You don't have that much time before semester ends and exams start (sometimes the last class and the first exam can be within one week), therefore do not wait until last minute to study for the exams or do your assignments. PLAN PLAN PLAN, make sure you have a solid plan in regard to where you will stay, your courses, what you want to see etc.
most_rewarding: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience is the fact that I now know that I can live alone and study in a foreign country. I have learned so many things not only academically but also on a personal level. There are so many things that I have gained from this trip, which I can use in order to enhance both my career and personal life.
greatest_challenge: Being so far away from everything and anything you know, it takes some time to adjust and in the beginning it can feel a little lonely - no one really talks about this, but it is actually quite normal for exchange students. However, the feeling passes away quickly, provided you keep a positive attitude and an open mind :-).

greatest_challenge: To adapt and find a rutine. In the end it felt like home, which made it weird to just leave. Rutine takes time but once you get that it is amazing how well you can feel in a foreign country.
