crucial_aspects: The language and the culture - I wanted to be able to speak the language so I only had to juggle the culture differences and the studies. Plus I had only heard fantastistic things about Canada. I initially wanted to go to the US, but ended up not putting the US on my list because of politics and elections.
overall_comments: There is always a bit of administrative work, which can be quite a hurdle when you get there.
info_ease: We had an orientation made by students which was nice, along with a short orientation by the administrative staff which was nice. It was a little tricky because the campus/uni had barely opened after vacation when I got there.
arrival_assistance: We had several orientations that you could choose to go to.
arrival_comments: A little confusing since the uni wasn't quite upon.
housing_how: I found housing through my host institution
registration_comments: There is always a bit of administrative work, which can be quite a hurdle when you get there.
registration_process: We had to make sure that there was no overlap between what we choose and they changed professor when we had to start our courses. You register through a website similar to the CPH website.
registration_help: You could contact the school and advisors, and they were very helpful.
registration_success: I got all the classes that I wanted, but they have a great concept where they make it possible for the students to change their courses the first 2 weeks in case you figure out that they classes really isn't for you.
registration_advice: Take the courses that are different and that seem exciting to you. It is all a new experience and you might as well take what you want. I also choose some classes that were comparable to the danish courses. Make sure to check where your exams lie and don't make a schedule that is overly exhausting for yourself. I had classes from 2:30-8:30pm each Tuesday and thursday and a class on Wednesday from 6:30-8:30 pm and I had 4 exams in 8-9 days, and while it worked out - I could definitely have planned it better.
academics_comments: There is always a bit of administrative work, which can be quite a hurdle when you get there.
course_level: I could only take BA courses.
teaching_comparison: It is very much a kind of lecture for some professors and some where late and left an hour early. Others were very engaging and recounted how they use their knowledge in real lift, which made it super interesting and exciting. One course that was different was about AI and that was very much a course based on discussion because there is almost no regulation, which was a nice break from "normal" law studies.
courses_enrolled: Patents, Evidence, Forensic Science, Emerging Tech: Law, policy & governance.
recommended_courses: Evidence with Goddard and walker - even though it was late at night they were incredible engaging and they made they subject very understandable and made overviews for the students with the general rules and the exceptions - They made the course known for being notoriously tricky into a very interesting course. Forensic science - they invited all kind of experts like the ones you see on television i.e. Ballistics, fingerprints, DNA, handwriting and forensic scientist.
unexpected_costs: The food was quite expensive because it was mandatory for me to have a meal plan.
cost_comparison: Books weren't as expensive as I only had to get one book. However I spent a lot on personal spending because it is cheaper to shop there for some stuff.
activities_available: They had a lot of clubs, from film to crochet, gaming, dancing and training - there was a lot for everyone. Be aware that this can clash with course schedule, which mine did so I unfortunately couldn't try the clubs except the gym.
activities_recommended: Maybe try the gaming if you want new friends or crochet if you're creative.
weekend_recommendations: Downtown and all the different culture"towns" - Chinatown, Koreatown, litte Greece and Italy We travelled to Montreal which I also recommend, as well as a maple syrup farm.
culture_adjustment: The culture was easy and people are extremely friendly and helpful, but you might get more international friends than Canadian friends. Also the time difference and having to act in a diffenrent language 24/7 is hard, so there might be a need for some time to adjust.
socializing_tips: Be open to the people and try to reach out first.
cultural_challenges: Their politeness is on a different level, so there is a lot of small talk, which isn't challenging, but you have to get used to it, when you come from a culture where people don't say hi or talk to strangers on the street. Also the way you address profs etc. is more formal than in Denmark.
culture_appreciated: I loved the small talk and the curiousity, friendliness and helpfullness of the Canadians.
top3_advice: Consider if you wanna live on campus i.e. because of meal plan. For public transport, depending on where you live, consider their Presto card. Engage in the orientations and the activities made by the students, They are very sweet and helpful.
other_useful_info: No.
most_rewarding: All of my new friends. You have a special connection because it is a very different experience, that is hard to explain to people who have not been on exchange, and you are very intensely together for 4-5 months. And new knowledge of a different legal system to which I can compare and discuss the danish system.
greatest_challenge: The first couple of weeks because of the time difference, the new environment and having to figure out a lot of different stuff in another language.
